Valuation of undertakings or assets of the company, wherever it is necessary. Evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems. And monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers and related matters. Section 177(5) then gives the committee the means to do it: it may call for the comments of the auditors about internal control systems, the scope of audit including the observations of the auditors, and review of the financial statement before their submission to the Board, and it may discuss any related issues with the internal and statutory auditors and the management of the company. Two consequences run off that list and both are examined. Because the committee recommends the auditor's appointment and reviews his independence and performance, the auditor's relationship with the company on those matters runs through the committee and not through the management whose figures he is auditing — which is what makes the committee, and not the finance function, the right addressee for a difficulty encountered during the audit. And because the committee approves related party transactions, a transaction entered into without its approval is an identified non-compliance with law, which the auditor treats as one under SA 250, communicates to those charged with governance, and considers for its effect on the financial statements and on his risk assessment.

citation.ref: Section 177(4) — the terms of reference of the audit committee specified by the Board, including the recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of the auditors, review and monitoring of the auditor's independence and performance, examination of the financial statement and the auditors' report, approval of related party transactions, scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments, valuation of undertakings or assets, evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems, and monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers — and Section 177(5), read with Section 177(7)

concepts.subsection: Section 148 — cost records and cost audit
concepts.statement: Section 148(1) empowers the Central Government, by order, to direct that particulars relating to the utilisation of material or labour or to other items of cost be included in the books of account kept by such class of companies engaged in the production of such goods or providing such services as may be prescribed. Section 148(2) empowers it, where it is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so, to direct by order that the cost records of such class of companies as may be prescribed, and which have a net worth or a turnover of such amount as may be prescribed, be audited. That audit is conducted by a cost accountant, appointed by the Board, and it is in addition to and not in place of the audit under section 143 — the two look at different books and answer different questions, and neither report is evidence that the other was not needed. Three limits are examined and all three are frequently missed. The cost auditor is not the statutory auditor: the proviso to section 148(3) provides that the auditor appointed under section 139 shall not be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records. Students look for that bar in section 144's list of prohibited services and do not find it there, because it is not there — section 148(3) contains it in terms. The cost audit report goes to the Board of Directors of the company, and the company furnishes it to the Central Government together with full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification contained in it, within the period the section allows. And the reservations in a cost audit report are not the statutory auditor's to disregard as a cost matter: they are audit evidence about the entity's costing, its inventory valuation, its capitalisation and its margins, and where they indicate a misstatement in the financial statements the statutory auditor deals with it in his own report. The company and every officer in default, and the cost auditor in default, are liable under the section's penal provisions.

citation.ref: Section 148(1) on the inclusion of cost particulars in the books of account, Section 148(2) on the direction that cost records be audited, the proviso to Section 148(3) that the auditor appointed under Section 139 shall not be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records, and Section 148(6) on furnishing the cost audit report to the Central Government with full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification in it, read with Section 144

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — the elements of a system of quality control
concepts.statement: SQC 1 applies to a firm in respect of all its audits and reviews of historical financial information and its other assurance and related services engagements, and it requires the firm to establish a system of quality control designed to provide it with reasonable assurance that the firm and its personnel comply with professional standards and regulatory and legal requirements, and that the reports issued by the firm or by engagement partners are appropriate in the circumstances. The system is built out of six elements and the list is examinable as a list. Leadership responsibilities for quality within the firm — the chief executive officer or the managing partners take ultimate responsibility for the system, and the firm's business strategy is never allowed to let commercial considerations override the quality of the work performed. Ethical requirements, including independence, with written confirmation of compliance with the firm's independence policies obtained at least annually from all personnel required to be independent. Acceptance and continuance of client relationships and specific engagements — the firm takes on and retains only what it is competent to perform, where it can comply with relevant ethical requirements, and where it has considered the integrity of the client. Human resources — recruitment, capabilities and competence, career development, and the assignment of engagement teams and of an engagement partner whose identity and role are communicated to the client's key management and to those charged with governance. Engagement performance, which carries direction, supervision and review, consultation on difficult or contentious matters, the resolution of differences of opinion before the report is released, and the engagement quality control review. And monitoring — an ongoing consideration and evaluation of the firm's system, including the periodic inspection of a selection of completed engagements. The policies and procedures are documented and communicated to the firm's personnel, because a policy nobody has been told about is not a policy. SQC 1 is the standard in force for Indian firms: the quality management standards that would have replaced it were deferred by the Council in March 2026 and have not taken effect.

citation.ref: the scope of SQC 1 over all audits and reviews of historical financial information and other assurance and related services engagements, the objective of the system of quality control, and the six elements — leadership responsibilities for quality within the firm, ethical requirements including independence, acceptance and continuance of client relationships and specific engagements, human resources, engagement performance, and monitoring — read with the retention period at para 83

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: ESG — the three pillars and the Sustainable Development Goals
concepts.statement: Two ideas sit underneath everything else in this chapter and students routinely blur them. Sustainable development, as the Brundtland report defined it, is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Applied to a business, it rests on three pillars, and those three pillars are what the letters ESG stand for. Environment covers the entity's climate policies, its energy use, its waste and pollution, its conservation of natural resources and its treatment of animals — the resources it draws in and the carbon emissions, water discharges and electronic waste it leaves behind. Social covers the relationships the entity has and the reputation it builds with people and institutions in the communities where it does business and along its value chain, including labour relations, health and safety, product safety and privacy, diversity and inclusion. Governance is the internal system of practices, controls and procedures the entity adopts to govern itself, make effective investment decisions, comply with the law and meet the needs of all its stakeholders, and it carries board diversity, executive pay, business ethics, anti-competitive practices, corruption and tax transparency. The second idea is separate and belongs to the United Nations rather than to any company. In 2015 the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted by all United Nations member states as a blueprint and a call for action by developed and developing countries alike, and there are seventeen of them — from no poverty and zero hunger through climate action and life below water to partnership for the goals. They are addressed to countries; a company contributes to them, and its ESG reporting is where that contribution becomes visible. ESG reporting itself may be qualitative, describing strategy and policy, or quantitative, carrying metrics and key performance indicators against goals, and a mixed approach adds the most to the quality of the disclosure.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — sustainable development as defined in the Brundtland report, the three pillars of Environment, Social and Governance and what each covers, and the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals adopted in 2015 by all United Nations member states

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: Integrated Reporting — the six capitals
concepts.statement: Integrated Reporting asks how an organisation creates value over the short, the medium and the long term, and it answers by tracking six stores of value rather than one. They are known as the six capitals, and the list is examinable as a list. Financial capital is the pool of funds available to the organisation for producing goods or providing services, obtained through debt, equity or grants or generated by its own operations and investments. Manufactured capital is the human-created, production-oriented equipment and tools available to it — buildings, plant, infrastructure such as roads, ports, bridges and water treatment plants. Natural capital is an input to production which the organisation's activities also affect for better or worse, and it includes water, land, minerals, forests, biodiversity and ecosystem health. Human capital is people's skills and experience, their capacity and motivation to innovate, their alignment with the organisation's governance framework and ethical values including its recognition of human rights, and their ability to understand and implement its strategy. Social capital is the institutions and relationships established within and between communities, stakeholder groups and other networks — common values and behaviour, the trust and loyalty built with customers, suppliers and business partners, and the organisation's social licence to operate. Intellectual capital is the key element in future earning potential, tied to investment in research and development, innovation, human resources and external relationships, and it is what determines competitive advantage. The reason the framework matters to an auditor is that an integrated report says something about resources no balance sheet carries, so it is a report about value creation and not a restatement of the financial statements — and a company already reporting on this basis may cross-reference those disclosures to the ones the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report asks for rather than writing them twice.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — Integrated Reporting and its six capitals: financial, manufactured, natural, human, social and intellectual capital, and the cross-referencing of integrated reporting disclosures to those sought under the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: BRSR — the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct
concepts.statement: Section C of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report asks for principle-wise performance disclosures, and the principles are the nine of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct. Two of the nine sit in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance, and although they are stated separately they interlock — environmental protection is bound up with stakeholder engagement and inclusive growth. Principle 1 is ethics, transparency and accountability: business decisions are open to disclosure and accessible to interested parties, policies and procedures keep ethics uncompromised, adverse effects are disclosed with more care rather than less, the value chain is encouraged to adopt the same principles, and the entity responds proactively to those who violate them. This is the principle under which an anti-bribery policy, the internal control mechanism behind it and the machinery for dealing with bribery and corruption complaints are disclosed. Principle 2 is safe and sustainable goods and services — design, production methods and technologies that minimise resource use, consumer education, and reduce, reuse and recycle. Principle 3 is the well-being of all employees including those in the value chain: no child, bonded or involuntary labour, freedom of association, living wages paid on time, a safe and harassment- free workplace, and skill development. Principle 4 is respect for stakeholders' interests and responsiveness. Principle 5 is respect for and promotion of human rights, read against the Constitution of India, national law and the International Bill of Human Rights. Principle 6 is protection and restoration of the environment across the whole life cycle of the product, with measurement of pollution, waste, energy and land use and a contribution to climate resilience in line with India's commitments including the Paris Agreement. Principle 7 is influence on public and regulatory policy, conducted so as to encourage fair competition and prevent human rights abuses. Principle 8 is inclusive growth and equitable development, including the impacts of land acquisition and of business-induced displacement. Principle 9 is providing value to consumers responsibly — reducing negative impacts, not restricting freedom of choice, disclosing adverse impacts accurately, and respecting the customer's right to privacy when handling customer data.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct against which Section C of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report seeks principle-wise performance disclosures, two of them in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: Global sustainability reporting frameworks
concepts.statement: Sustainability reporting has no single global standard yet, and the examinable skill is telling the bodies apart by what each one publishes and who it is addressed to. The Global Reporting Initiative is the most widely used framework in the world — an independent international organisation based in Amsterdam, used in over a hundred countries, with ninety-three per cent of the world's largest two hundred and fifty corporations reporting through it. It helps organisations report their economic, environmental and social impacts, and its report is addressed to all the stakeholders of the entity. The Carbon Disclosure Project captures environmental performance data — greenhouse gas emissions, water, forests and the supply chain — and reports on climate change, forests and water security to investors, buyers and other stakeholders. The International Integrated Reporting Council's framework sets guiding principles and content elements for an integrated report covering organisational overview, governance structure, business model, risks and opportunities, strategy, performance and outlook. The Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures was created in 2015 by the Financial Stability Board to help companies produce consistent climate-related disclosures, and unlike the Global Reporting Initiative, which serves a wide range of organisations, it is targeted at companies that predominantly handle financial-related interests, such as banks and insurance firms. The Climate Disclosure Standards Board framework was formed to help organisations disclose climate-related risks and opportunities. Then came consolidation: the Value Reporting Foundation was the result of the merger of the SASB Foundation and the International Integrated Reporting Council, and on 3 November 2021 the IFRS Foundation Trustees announced the creation of the International Sustainability Standards Board to deliver a comprehensive global baseline of sustainability-related disclosure standards for investors and other capital market participants. In March 2022 the International Sustainability Standards Board launched a consultation on its first two proposed standards, one on general sustainability-related disclosures and one on climate-related disclosures, the climate one building on the Task Force's recommendations and incorporating industry-based requirements derived from the SASB standards.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — global trends in sustainability reporting: the Global Reporting Initiative, the Carbon Disclosure Project, the International Integrated Reporting Council framework, the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures created in 2015 by the Financial Stability Board, the Climate Disclosure Standards Board, the Value Reporting Foundation and the International Sustainability Standards Board announced by the IFRS Foundation Trustees on 3 November 2021

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: Social Audit Standards — SAS 100 to SAS 1600
concepts.statement: Beyond the assurance standards on sustainability information, the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has issued a separate series called the Social Audit Standards, numbered SAS 100 to SAS 1600. They are not a form of financial audit and they are not a review of a report. Each one guides the Social Auditor in an independent impact assessment engagement of a Social Enterprise working in a particular field, and each sets out the audit steps and procedures to be applied in conducting the social impact assessment. Each Standard states the minimum requirements to be followed, and where a law or a regulation establishes additional requirements those are followed as well, so the Standard is a floor and not a ceiling. The series follows the fields the enterprises work in: SAS 100 on eradicating hunger, poverty, malnutrition and inequality; SAS 200 on health care including mental health care, sanitation and safe drinking water; SAS 300 on education, employability and livelihoods; SAS 400 on gender equality and the empowerment of women and LGBTQIA+ communities; SAS 500 on environmental sustainability and climate change including mitigation and adaptation and forest and wildlife conservation; SAS 600 on national heritage, art and culture; SAS 700 on training for rural, nationally recognised, Paralympic and Olympic sports; SAS 800 on supporting incubators of social enterprises; SAS 900 on other platforms strengthening the non-profit ecosystem; SAS 1000 on livelihoods for the rural and urban poor including small and marginal farmers; SAS 1100 on slum area development and affordable housing; SAS 1200 on disaster management including relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction; SAS 1300 on financial inclusion; SAS 1400 on access to land and property assets for disadvantaged communities; SAS 1500 on bridging the digital divide and addressing misinformation and data protection; and SAS 1600 on the welfare of migrants and displaced persons. The board that issued them is the same one that carries the Institute's sustainability work generally, which is why the series sits in this chapter and not in the chapter on related services.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the Social Audit Standards SAS 100 to SAS 1600 issued by the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, guiding the Social Auditor in independent impact assessment engagements of Social Enterprises and setting the minimum requirements for a social impact assessment

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3400 — accepting the engagement and setting the examination procedures
concepts.statement: Before he accepts an engagement to examine prospective financial information the auditor considers five things, and each of them changes the work rather than merely the fee. The intended use of the information. Whether it will be for general or limited distribution. The nature of the assumptions — whether they are best-estimate assumptions or hypothetical ones. The elements to be included in the information. And the period covered by it. He also considers the extent to which reliance on the entity's historical financial information is justified, and, as in any engagement, he agrees the terms in an engagement letter. Two refusals follow: he should not accept, and should withdraw from, an engagement when the assumptions are clearly unrealistic, or when he believes the prospective financial information will be inappropriate for its intended use. Once accepted, the nature, timing and extent of the examination procedures are set by seven considerations: the knowledge obtained during any previous engagements; management's competence to prepare prospective financial information; the likelihood of material misstatement; the extent to which the information is affected by management's judgement; the sources of information management used, their adequacy and the reliability of the underlying data, including data derived from third parties such as industry statistics; the stability of the entity's business; and the engagement team's experience with the business, with the industry and with reporting on prospective financial information. In performing the procedures the auditor assesses the source and reliability of the evidence supporting management's best-estimate assumptions, which may come from budgets, debt agreements or industry publications. Where hypothetical assumptions are used, every significant implication of them must have been carried through the information: if sales are assumed to grow beyond current plant capacity, the prospective financial information has to include the investment in the additional capacity, or the cost of an alternative such as subcontracting. He also verifies that the hypothetical assumptions are consistent with the purpose of the information and that there is no reason to believe them clearly unrealistic.

citation.ref: the matters considered before accepting an engagement to examine prospective financial information — the intended use, general or limited distribution, whether the assumptions are best-estimate or hypothetical, the elements to be included and the period covered — the obligation not to accept or to withdraw where the assumptions are clearly unrealistic or the information would be inappropriate for its intended use, and the matters determining the nature, timing and extent of the examination procedures

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3400 — presentation and disclosure of prospective financial information
concepts.statement: A forecast is only as honest as the notes around it, so SAE 3400 gives the auditor a checklist for assessing the presentation and disclosure of prospective financial information and of the assumptions underneath it, over and above whatever a statute, a regulation or a professional pronouncement separately requires. The presentation must be informative and not misleading. The accounting policies must be clearly disclosed in the notes to the prospective financial information. The assumptions must be adequately disclosed in those notes, and it must be clear whether each one is a best-estimate assumption or a hypothetical one; where assumptions are made in areas that are material and subject to a high degree of uncertainty, that uncertainty and the resulting sensitivity of the results must be adequately disclosed, because a reader shown a single number cannot see how far it moves. The date as of which the prospective financial information was prepared must be disclosed, and management must confirm that the assumptions are appropriate as of that date even though the underlying information may have been accumulated over a period of time. Where the results are expressed as a range, the basis of establishing the points in the range must be clearly indicated and the range must not be selected in a biased or misleading manner — a range whose ends were chosen to flatter is worse than a single figure, because it wears the appearance of candour. And where the entity's accounting policy has changed from that disclosed in the most recent historical financial statements, the reason for the change and its effect on the prospective financial information must be adequately disclosed. The consequence of failing these tests is not a note in the file: where the auditor believes the presentation and disclosure are not adequate — for example where the information fails to disclose adequately the consequences of highly sensitive assumptions — he expresses a qualified or an adverse opinion, or withdraws from the engagement.

citation.ref: the assessment of presentation and disclosure — informative and not misleading presentation, accounting policies and assumptions disclosed in the notes with best-estimate assumptions distinguished from hypothetical ones, disclosure of uncertainty and the resulting sensitivity of results, disclosure of the date as of which the information was prepared, the basis of establishing points in a range and the bar on a biased or misleading range, and disclosure of any change in accounting policy from the most recent historical financial statements

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3400 — modifying the report on prospective financial information
concepts.statement: An examination of prospective financial information carries two conclusions in one report — a negative assurance statement on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis, and an opinion on whether the information is properly prepared on the basis of those assumptions and presented in accordance with the relevant financial reporting framework — so the ways it can go wrong are more than one and SAE 3400 pairs each fault with its own answer. Where the auditor believes the presentation and disclosure of the prospective financial information are not adequate, he expresses a qualified or an adverse opinion, or withdraws from the engagement; the example the standard gives is information that fails to disclose adequately the consequences of assumptions which are highly sensitive. Where he believes that one or more significant assumptions do not provide a reasonable basis for the prospective financial information — whether it was prepared on best-estimate assumptions, or on hypothetical assumptions given the purpose for which it was prepared — the answer is not a qualification: he expresses an adverse opinion setting out the reasons in the report, or he withdraws from the engagement. The logic is that the assumptions are the whole foundation, and information built on a foundation that does not hold cannot be partly relied on. And where the examination is affected by conditions that preclude the application of one or more procedures he considers necessary in the circumstances, he considers either withdrawing from the engagement or disclaiming the opinion and describing the scope limitation in the report. Two boundaries are worth holding on to. The auditor never expresses an opinion that the results shown will be achieved, so no modification is ever a statement about achievability; and the refusal at the acceptance stage — no engagement where the assumptions are clearly unrealistic or where the information will be inappropriate for its intended use — is a different rule from these, because it operates before any report exists.

citation.ref: the modification of the report on an examination of prospective financial information — a qualified or adverse opinion or withdrawal where the presentation and disclosure are not adequate, an adverse opinion setting out the reasons or withdrawal where one or more significant assumptions do not provide a reasonable basis, and withdrawal or a disclaimer describing the scope limitation where conditions preclude a necessary procedure

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3402 — the description of tests of controls and the reporting of deviations
concepts.statement: What separates a type 2 report from a type 1 report in practice is not the opinion sentence but the attachment. In a type 2 report the service auditor's assurance report must include a separate section after the opinion, or an attachment, describing the tests of controls that were performed and the results of those tests. In describing them he must state clearly which controls were tested, identify whether the items tested represent all the items in the population or only a selection of them, and indicate the nature of the tests in sufficient detail to enable user auditors to determine the effect of those tests on their own risk assessments — which is the point of the whole document, since a user auditor who cannot see what was tested cannot use the report as evidence. Where deviations have been identified, the service auditor must include the extent of the testing performed that led to identifying them, including the sample size where sampling was used, and the number and the nature of the deviations noted. And the rule that decides most questions on this ground: the service auditor shall report deviations even if, on the basis of the tests performed, he has concluded that the related control objective was achieved. A deviation is not suppressed because it was survivable — the user auditor is entitled to know the population it came from and to reach his own conclusion about what it means for his entity. Alongside this the report carries a use restriction, stating that the report and, in a type 2 report, the description of tests of controls are intended only for user entities and their auditors, who have sufficient understanding to consider it together with other information including information about controls the user entities operate themselves. Modification is separate again: the opinion is modified where the description does not fairly present the system as designed and implemented, where the controls were not suitably designed, where in a type 2 report the controls tested did not operate effectively, or where the service auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence, and the report then contains a clear description of all the reasons for the modification.

citation.ref: the separate section or attachment to a type 2 report describing the tests of controls and their results, the requirement to state which controls were tested and whether the items tested were all or a selection of the population, the disclosure of the extent of testing including the sample size and the number and nature of deviations, the rule that deviations are reported even where the service auditor concluded the related control objective was achieved, the restriction of the report to user entities and their auditors, and the grounds on which the service auditor's opinion is modified

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3420 — engagement acceptance and a modified opinion
concepts.statement: Before agreeing to report on whether pro forma financial information included in a prospectus has been compiled on the basis of the applicable criteria, the practitioner works through a defined list. He determines that he has the capabilities and the competence to perform the engagement. On a preliminary knowledge of the circumstances and discussion with the responsible party, he determines that the applicable criteria are suitable and that it is unlikely the pro forma financial information will be misleading for the purpose for which it is intended. He evaluates the wording of any opinion prescribed by law or regulation, to satisfy himself that he will likely be able to express that prescribed opinion on the basis of the procedures this standard specifies. Where the sources from which the unadjusted financial information or any acquiree or divestee information were extracted carry a modified audit opinion, a modified review conclusion or an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, he considers whether the relevant law or regulation permits their use, or a reference to them in his report. Where the entity's historical financial information — or an acquiree's, in an acquisition — has never been audited or reviewed, he considers whether he can obtain a sufficient understanding of the entity or the acquiree and of its accounting and financial reporting practices to perform the engagement at all. And he obtains the responsible party's agreement acknowledging its own responsibility for adequately disclosing and describing the applicable criteria to the intended users where these are not publicly available, for compiling the pro forma financial information on the basis of those criteria, and for giving him access to all relevant information, to any additional information he requests, and to the people within the entity, its advisers and the acquiree from whom he determines it necessary to obtain evidence. The examined trap sits at the other end. Where the relevant law or regulation precludes the publication of a prospectus containing a modified opinion and the practitioner nonetheless concludes that a modified opinion is appropriate, he discusses the matter with the responsible party; and if the responsible party does not agree to make the necessary changes, he withdraws from the engagement or considers seeking legal advice. He does not soften the opinion to fit the prospectus. Separately, an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is available where a matter presented or disclosed in the pro forma information or its explanatory notes is fundamental to the user's understanding, but only where he has obtained sufficient appropriate evidence that the matter does not affect whether the information has been compiled in accordance with the criteria — and it refers only to information presented or disclosed in the pro forma financial information or its accompanying notes.

citation.ref: the matters considered before accepting an engagement to report on the compilation of pro forma financial information included in a prospectus, including the responsible party's acknowledgement of its responsibilities, and the course where law or regulation precludes publication of a prospectus containing a modified opinion — discussion with the responsible party and, failing agreement to make the necessary changes, withdrawal from the engagement or seeking legal advice — together with the conditions on an Emphasis of Matter paragraph

concepts.subsection: Sections 129(3) and 129(4) — when consolidated financial statements must be prepared
concepts.statement: Section 129(3) provides that where a company has one or more subsidiaries, including an associate company and a joint venture, it shall, in addition to its own financial statements, prepare a consolidated financial statement of the company and of all the subsidiaries in the same form and manner as that of its own. Section 129(4) then provides that the provisions of the Act applicable to the preparation, adoption and audit of the financial statements of a holding company shall, mutatis mutandis, also apply to its consolidated financial statements — which is why the consolidated statements are approved by the Board before being signed on its behalf and are laid before the annual general meeting alongside the standalone statements, and why the audit of them is an audit under the Act and not a courtesy. The company also attaches a separate statement containing the salient features of the financial statement of each subsidiary in Form AOC-1. The consolidation is made in accordance with Schedule III and the applicable accounting standards, and where a company is not required to prepare consolidated financial statements under the accounting standards it is sufficient that it complies with the consolidation provisions in Schedule III. The exemption is narrow and cumulative. A company need not prepare consolidated financial statements only if all three of the following hold together: it is a wholly-owned subsidiary, or a partially-owned subsidiary of another company whose other members, including those not otherwise entitled to vote, have been intimated in writing with proof of delivery available with the company and do not object; its securities are not listed and are not in the process of being listed on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India; and its ultimate or any intermediate holding company files consolidated financial statements with the Registrar which comply with the applicable accounting standards. Section 129(6) separately lets the Central Government exempt a class of companies by notification in the public interest. What does not exist is an exemption for temporary control or for operation under severe long-term restrictions on the transfer of funds: consolidation begins from the date the investor obtains control and ceases when it loses control, so a subsidiary acquired during the year and sold in the next is consolidated for both years it was controlled.

citation.ref: Section 129(3) on the preparation of consolidated financial statements where a company has one or more subsidiaries including an associate company and a joint venture, Section 129(4) applying the provisions on preparation, adoption and audit mutatis mutandis, the attachment of Form AOC-1, the three cumulative conditions in the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 on which a company need not prepare consolidated financial statements, and Section 129(6), read with Ind AS 110 on the absence of any exemption for temporary control

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xxi)
concepts.statement: CARO 2020 does not attach clause by clause to a report on consolidated financial statements. The Order applies to the auditor's report on the standalone financial statements of the companies it covers, and on consolidated financial statements only one clause operates: clause 3(xxi). Under it the auditor of the consolidated financial statements reports whether there have been any qualifications or adverse remarks by the respective auditors in the CARO reports of the companies included in the consolidated financial statements, and where there have been, he indicates the details of those companies together with the paragraph numbers of the CARO reports containing the qualifications or adverse remarks. That is the whole of it, and the shape of the duty is the examinable part. He is not answering the twenty other clauses again for the group. He is not preparing a separate clause-by-clause CARO report covering the parent and every Indian subsidiary, nor annexing one, nor supplementing the standalone CARO report with additional information about the subsidiaries. He is pointing the reader of the consolidated statements at the places where a component's own CARO report already carries a qualification or an adverse remark, so that something reported at the component does not disappear inside the consolidation. Two consequences follow. Only companies included in the consolidated financial statements that are themselves covered by CARO produce anything to report, so a component to which the Order does not apply contributes nothing to this clause. And the clause is a signpost rather than an opinion: it is not a modification of the opinion on the consolidated financial statements, and a qualification in a component's CARO report is evaluated separately for whether it says anything material about the consolidated financial statements as a whole.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xxi) — whether there have been any qualifications or adverse remarks by the respective auditors in the CARO reports of the companies included in the consolidated financial statements, and the indication of the details of those companies and the paragraph numbers of the CARO reports containing them, this being the only clause of the Order applying to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements

concepts.subsection: Audit of consolidated financial statements — written representations
concepts.statement: SA 580 requires written representations from management and, where appropriate, from those charged with governance, and in an audit of consolidated financial statements they are obtained from the management of the parent. Two of them are the general ones every audit takes, adapted: that the parent's management acknowledges its responsibility for a true and fair presentation of the consolidated financial statements in accordance with the financial reporting framework applicable to the parent, and that it has approved those consolidated financial statements. Beyond that the auditor obtains written representations on the matters material to the consolidated financial statements, and four are the standard examples. The completeness of the components included in the consolidated financial statements — the representation that answers the question the auditor can least easily answer alone, because a component left out of the consolidation leaves no trace inside it. The identification of reportable segments for segmental reporting. The identification of related parties and of related party transactions for reporting. And the appropriateness and completeness of the permanent and the current period consolidation adjustments, including the elimination of intra-group transactions. These representations do not change what a representation is worth. They are audit evidence, they are not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters they deal with, and they do not relieve the auditor of the procedures on completeness of components, on the consolidation adjustments or on related parties that he would otherwise perform. Their value is that they fix management's position in writing on matters where management holds information the auditor cannot independently generate, and that a refusal to give one is itself a finding.

citation.ref: Ch. Group Audits — written representations obtained from the parent's management in an audit of consolidated financial statements: the acknowledgement of responsibility for a true and fair presentation and the approval of the consolidated financial statements, and representations on the completeness of components, the identification of reportable segments, the identification of related parties and related party transactions, and the appropriateness and completeness of the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments including the elimination of intra-group transactions, read with SA 580

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — the constitutional position of the Comptroller and Auditor General
concepts.statement: Government audit in India is performed by an independent constitutional authority, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, through the Indian Audit and Accounts Department, and the Constitution itself carries the provisions that protect that independence. Article 148 provides for the appointment of the Comptroller and Auditor General by the President, and for a special procedure for his removal, only on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity; his salary and other conditions of service are determined by Parliament. Article 149 provides that he shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and the States, and of any other authority or body, as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament — and the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 is that law, defining his functions and powers in detail and providing that he shall hold office for a term of six years or up to the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, and may resign at any time by a letter addressed to the President. Article 150 provides that the accounts of the Union and the States shall be kept in such form as the President prescribes on his advice. Article 151 provides that his audit reports relating to the accounts of the Central or a State Government are submitted to the President or to the Governor, who causes them to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislative Assembly. The bodies within his audit purview are wide: all Union and State Government departments and offices including the Railways and Posts and Telecommunications; public commercial enterprises controlled by the Union and the State Governments, meaning government companies and corporations; non-commercial autonomous bodies and authorities owned or controlled by the Union or the States; and authorities and bodies substantially financed from Union or State revenues. For the commercial audit of companies in which Government equity participation is fifty-one per cent or more, the auditors are firms of chartered accountants appointed by him, to whom he gives directions on the manner in which the audit is to be conducted, and he may comment upon their reports, conduct a supplementary audit and order a test audit. A unique feature of that work is the constitution of Audit Boards, which associate experts in the relevant disciplines, discuss their findings with the enterprise's management and the controlling ministry before finalisation, have no separate legal entity, and work under his supervision and control.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — Articles 148 to 151 of the Constitution on the appointment and removal of the Comptroller and Auditor General, his duties and powers, the form of the accounts and the laying of his reports; the term of six years or up to the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, under the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971; and the Audit Boards constituted for comprehensive appraisals in commercial audit

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — the Parliamentary financial committees
concepts.statement: Parliament cannot itself scrutinise every annual account and every audit report, so it and the State Legislatures have constituted specialised committees to which those reports and accounts automatically stand referred, and telling the three apart is a standing question. The Public Accounts Committee satisfies itself that the moneys were disbursed legally on the service or purpose to which they were applied, that the expenditure incurred was authorised, and that re-appropriation was made in accordance with the provisions made; it also examines the statements of accounts of autonomous and semi-autonomous bodies audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General either under the directions of the President or by a statute of Parliament. The Estimates Committee examines the estimates in order to report what economies, improvements in organisation, efficiency or administrative reform may be effected consistently with the policy underlying them, to suggest alternative policies, to examine whether the money is well laid out within the limit, and to suggest the form in which the estimates shall be presented to Parliament; it does not comment upon a policy approved by Parliament, but where there is evidence that a policy is not leading to the desired results or is leading to waste, it is its duty to bring that to the notice of the House. The Committee on Public Undertakings exercises over the public sector undertakings the same financial control the Public Accounts Committee exercises over the functioning of Government departments: it examines the reports and accounts of public undertakings, examines the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General on public undertakings, and examines their autonomy and efficiency and whether they are being managed in accordance with sound business principles and prudent commercial practices. Its examination takes the form of a comprehensive appraisal or evaluation of the performance of the undertaking, including its policies, its programmes and its financial working. The Comptroller and Auditor General is described as the friend, philosopher and guide of these committees: his reports generally form the basis of their working, though they are not precluded from examining issues he did not raise; he scrutinises the notes ministries submit and helps the committees check the correctness of the facts and figures in their draft reports. The committees report to the legislature with observations and recommendations, the ministries are required to inform them of the action taken, and Action Taken Reports are presented in turn. The object throughout is to focus not only on the individual irregularity but on the defect in the system that produced it.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the Public Accounts Committee, the Estimates Committee and the Committee on Public Undertakings, their respective functions, the Comptroller and Auditor General's role as friend, philosopher and guide to the financial committees, and the Action Taken Reports presented to the legislature

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: PSU audits — the elements, and attestation against direct reporting engagements
concepts.statement: Every public sector audit is built out of the same three components, and the third is where financial, compliance and performance audit actually separate. First, three parties. The auditor — the role is filled by the Supreme Audit Institution of India, which is the Comptroller and Auditor General together with the Indian Audit and Accounts Department functioning under him, his senior functionaries in the States being the Accountants General. The responsible party, whose responsibilities are determined by constitutional or legislative arrangement, generally the auditable entity and those charged with its governance; the responsible party may be responsible for the subject matter information, for managing the subject matter, or for addressing recommendations. And the intended users, the individuals or organisations for whom the auditor prepares the report. Second, the subject matter, the criteria and the subject matter information: the subject matter is the information, condition or activity measured or evaluated against criteria; the criteria are the benchmarks used to evaluate it; and the subject matter information is the outcome of measuring the subject matter against those criteria. Third, the type of engagement, of which there are two. In an attestation engagement the responsible party measures the subject matter against the criteria and presents the subject matter information, and the auditor then gathers sufficient appropriate evidence to provide a reasonable basis for expressing a conclusion on it. In a direct reporting engagement it is the auditor himself who measures or evaluates the subject matter against the criteria. Financial audits are always attestation engagements, because they are based on financial information presented by the responsible party; performance audits and compliance audits are generally direct reporting engagements, because there is usually no statement by the entity of its own economy, efficiency and effectiveness for the auditor to attest to. That is why a performance audit report reads as findings, reasons and recommendations rather than as an opinion on something management prepared.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the basic elements of a public sector audit: the three parties of auditor, responsible party and intended users; the subject matter, the criteria and the subject matter information; and the two types of engagement, with financial audits always attestation engagements and performance and compliance audits generally direct reporting engagements

concepts.subsection: Section 138 with Rule 13 — which companies must appoint an internal auditor
concepts.statement: Section 138 requires such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed to appoint an internal auditor, and Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 is where the prescription lives. The appointee may be an individual, a partnership firm or a body corporate. Every listed company must appoint one, with no threshold at all. Every unlisted public company must appoint one if, during or at any point in the preceding financial year, it had a paid-up share capital of fifty crore rupees or more, or a turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding one hundred crore rupees, or outstanding deposits of twenty-five crore rupees or more. Every private company must appoint one if it had a turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more during the preceding financial year, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding one hundred crore rupees at any point of time during the preceding financial year. Three details decide most questions on this rule. The tests are alternatives joined by "or", so meeting any one of them brings the company in, and a company that fails the capital test on a small paid-up capital is still caught by its turnover. A private company has only two tests — turnover and borrowings — so the paid-up capital and deposits limits that apply to an unlisted public company are not read into it. And where an existing company gets covered by any of these criteria, it must comply with the requirement within six months of the commencement of such applicability, rather than waiting for the next financial year. What Rule 13 settles is only whether the company must have an internal auditor. Who may be appointed is section 138 itself, and whether the statutory auditor may use the function's work is SA 610 (Revised) and nothing else.

citation.ref: Section 138 read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 — every listed company; every unlisted public company with paid-up share capital of fifty crore rupees or more, turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more, outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding one hundred crore rupees, or outstanding deposits of twenty-five crore rupees or more; every private company with turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more or such borrowings exceeding one hundred crore rupees; and compliance within six months of the commencement of applicability

concepts.subsection: SIA 370 — reporting the results of an internal audit
concepts.statement: Reporting the results of internal audit is done in two stages and SIA 370 governs only the first of them. At the end of a particular audit assignment an Internal Audit Report covering that specific area, function or part of the entity is prepared by the internal auditor, setting out the manner in which the assignment was conducted and the key findings, and it is issued to the auditee with copies shared with local and executive management as agreed during the planning phase. Separately, on a periodic basis at the close of a plan period — normally quarterly — a comprehensive report of all the internal audit activities covering the whole entity and the plan period is prepared by the Chief Internal Auditor, or by the engagement partner where the function is outsourced, and submitted to the highest governing authority responsible for internal audits, generally the audit committee. SIA 370 deals with the internal auditor's responsibility to issue the first type of report and not the periodic one. The report itself must be clear and well documented and includes an overview of the objectives, scope and approach of the assignment; the fact that the internal audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Internal Audit, stated as such where the auditor can substantiate it with supporting evidence and documentation; an executive summary of key observations specific to the scope; a summary of the corrective actions required or agreed by management for each observation; and the nature of the assurance, if any, which can be derived from the observations. The Standard mandates no particular format or list of contents, because how and what to report is a matter of the internal auditor's professional judgement exercised in consultation with the auditee. Two rules are absolute. No internal audit report shall be issued in final form unless a written draft of the report has previously been shared with the auditee. And the report shall be issued within a reasonable time frame from the completion of the internal audit work. Conclusions are based on all the findings rather than on a few deviations, and controls found to be operating effectively are acknowledged rather than passed over, because a report that lists only failures misdescribes the entity. Where the internal auditor comes across any actual or suspected fraud or other misappropriation of assets, he does not wait for the report at all — he brings it to management's attention immediately.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 370, Reporting Results
citation.ref: the two stages of reporting internal audit results — the assignment-level Internal Audit Report issued to the auditee and the periodic comprehensive report prepared by the Chief Internal Auditor for the audit committee — the key elements of the Internal Audit Report, the absence of any mandated format, the rule that no report is issued in final form unless a written draft has previously been shared with the auditee, and the immediate reporting of an actual or suspected fraud to management

concepts.subsection: SIA 390 — monitoring and reporting of prior audit issues
concepts.statement: An internal audit finding that nobody closes is a finding repeated in next year's report, so SIA 390 makes the tracking of prior issues a duty with a named owner. The Chief Internal Auditor is responsible for continuously monitoring the closure of prior audit issues through the timely implementation of the action plans included in past audits, and he does it through a formal monitoring process whose elements are pre-agreed with management and with those charged with governance rather than invented after the fact. Monitoring and reporting here means the periodic tracking of issues raised during prior audits, the evaluation of the corrective actions the auditee has undertaken to resolve them, and the reporting of any open and pending matters to management and to those charged with governance, generally the audit committee. In practice the internal auditor's responsibility takes the form of an Action Taken Report on previous audits. The line that decides most questions is the one about ownership: the responsibility to implement the action plans remains with management. The internal auditor monitors, evaluates and reports; he does not implement, because implementing a control and then reviewing it are the two things one person cannot do. The rest follows from that. He reviews whether follow-up action has been taken on the basis of his report, and if no action is taken within a reasonable time he draws management's attention to it. Where management has not acted on his suggestions or not implemented his recommendations, he ascertains the reasons rather than simply recording non-compliance. And where management has accepted his recommendations and initiated action, he periodically reviews the manner and the extent of implementation and reports back, highlighting the recommendations that have not been implemented fully or in part.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 390, Monitoring and Reporting of Prior Audit Issues
citation.ref: the Chief Internal Auditor's responsibility for continuously monitoring the closure of prior audit issues through a formal monitoring process pre-agreed with management and those charged with governance, the Action Taken Report on previous audits, the rule that the responsibility to implement the action plans remains with management, and the review of the manner and extent of implementation with the recommendations not implemented fully or partly highlighted

concepts.subsection: Internal audit — performing the engagement
concepts.statement: A typical internal audit engagement runs in five steps and they are performed in that sequence. Step one, obtain knowledge of the business and its environment: meetings with key stakeholders, the Board and key managerial personnel to understand the business environment, the operations, the organisation's vision and mission and what top management expects of the audit function, together with an understanding of the standard operating procedures and financial statements, of the information technology landscape, the applications, the enterprise resource planning system and the management information system, and of the regulatory landscape and the laws applicable to the organisation. Step two, perform audit planning, under SIA 310, Planning the Internal Audit Assignment — and the gate that sits here is that the audit scope must be approved by the audit committee and the Board, not by the management whose processes are to be examined. Only once approved does the internal auditor share the detailed audit plan with key managerial personnel, schedule the work in advance, hold an opening meeting with key stakeholders and state the information and system access he needs. The detailed work plan is prepared by the audit managers and approved with the Head of Internal Audit or Chief Internal Auditor, and it is prepared after evaluating the major risks in the process under review and deciding the audit checks that will assess whether the control environment mitigates them. Step three, gather the required information, obtained so far as possible directly from the source, with checks on its correctness and integrity and advance intimation for anything needed at an interim stage. Step four, perform the audit checks: collate the data and run analytical procedures to identify key trends and outliers under SIA 6, select samples where needed under SIA 5, collect and store evidence under SIA 320, document the work papers under SIA 330, and issue any interim report only after review under SIA 350. Step five, report the internal audit issues — a draft report covering the process reviewed against the scope, the coverage and any exclusions, the audit period, and the gaps found with their business implication and the recommendation to close each one. A management action plan is agreed with a named owner and a timeline, the status of actions agreed in previous audits is reviewed and reported, and the final report is circulated and the findings presented to the audit committee, under SIA 360 on communication with management and SIA 370 on reporting results.

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — the five steps of an internal audit engagement performed in sequence: obtaining knowledge of the business and its environment, audit planning under SIA 310 with the scope approved by the audit committee and the Board, gathering the required information, performing the audit checks under SIA 6, SIA 5, SIA 320, SIA 330 and SIA 350, and reporting the internal audit issues with an agreed management action plan under SIA 360 and SIA 370

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Income recognition and asset classification
concepts.statement: A term loan turns non-performing when interest or principal stays overdue for more than ninety days; a cash credit when the account stays out of order. Once non-performing, the asset walks a ladder — substandard for its first twelve months as an NPA, doubtful once it stays substandard beyond twelve months, loss when identified as such — and income on it is recognised only on realisation, not accrual.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Long form audit report
concepts.statement: The LFAR is the RBI-prescribed questionnaire the bank auditor answers alongside the main report — advances, credit appraisal, NPA identification, internal controls, frauds — branch LFARs feeding the central auditor's consolidated one. It supplements the statutory report and does not dilute it: a matter grave enough to affect the true and fair view belongs in the main report, qualified, not parked in the LFAR.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 141 — Auditor disqualifications
concepts.statement: Section 141(3)(d) with Rule 10 draws money lines around the auditor's independence: a relative may hold securities of the company up to one lakh rupees face value; indebtedness to the company beyond five lakh rupees disqualifies; a guarantee for a third party's debt to the company beyond one lakh rupees disqualifies. The disqualification reaches the member, the firm and its partners, and one incurred during the term vacates the office.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(d) read with Rule 10

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xi)
concepts.statement: CARO's fraud clause asks three things: whether any fraud by the company or on the company was noticed or reported during the year, with nature and amount; whether any section 143(12) report was filed in Form ADT-4; and whether the auditor considered whistle-blower complaints received by the company. The clause covers fraud on the company by anyone, not only by its officers and employees.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xi)

concepts.subsection: SQC 1 — Engagement quality control review
concepts.statement: SQC 1 requires an engagement quality control review — an objective evaluation of the significant judgments and the conclusions reached — for audits of financial statements of listed entities, completed before the report is dated. The reviewer stands outside the engagement team, and the report cannot be signed past an unresolved difference with the reviewer.

citation.ref: Engagement quality control review requirements

concepts.section: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
concepts.subsection: Due diligence, investigation and audit
concepts.statement: An audit expresses an opinion on financial statements against a framework; due diligence is a purchaser-side examination of a target's whole position — financial, legal, operational — to price a deal and surface hidden liabilities; an investigation is a deep, targeted probe into a suspected specific matter, going wherever the suspicion leads. Scope, purpose and the reporting audience differ across all three; assurance levels are not interchangeable.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — propriety
concepts.statement: Propriety audit asks questions regularity audit cannot: not only was the expenditure sanctioned and lawful, but was it wise, economical, and free of personal advantage — would a person of ordinary prudence have spent his own money so? The C&AG's audit of public undertakings runs on both rails, and a transaction can pass every rule yet fail propriety.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

concepts.subsection: Peer review
concepts.statement: Peer review examines a practice unit's systems — whether its quality controls, documentation and compliance with technical standards for attestation services are adequate and were followed — through sample engagements. The reviewer evaluates the unit, not the clients: a review is not a second audit of any auditee, and its report speaks to the unit's systems, leading to a peer review certificate.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 139(6) — First auditor
concepts.statement: A company's first auditor (other than a government company) is appointed by the board within thirty days of registration; if the board fails, the members appoint within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting. The first auditor holds office until the conclusion of the first annual general meeting — and needs no ratification meanwhile.

citation.ref: Section 139(6)

concepts.section: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
concepts.subsection: Forensic accounting and investigation
concepts.statement: Forensic engagements run under ICAI's Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards and differ from audit at the root: the mindset presumes the possibility of fraud rather than neutrality, procedures chase evidence that will stand in legal proceedings — chain of custody, corroboration, documentation to litigation grade — and the outcome states findings of fact, not an opinion or an assurance conclusion. Materiality thresholds do not excuse small frauds from a forensic scope.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — scale-based regulation
concepts.statement: RBI regulates NBFCs in layers by size and risk — base, middle, upper and a normally empty top layer — with regulatory intensity rising through the stack: the upper layer carries bank-like requirements. The auditor's concerns scale accordingly: income recognition and asset classification norms, the layer's specific prudential requirements, and the statutory auditor's own direct reporting duties to RBI on matters such as non-compliance with the RBI Act.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies

concepts.subsection: Section 143(3) — The auditor's report
concepts.statement: Section 143(3) prescribes what every company audit report states: whether information and explanations sought were obtained, whether proper books were kept, whether the accounts agree with the books, whether the statements comply with the accounting standards, the section 164(2) director disqualification status, internal financial controls where applicable, and the rule-prescribed matters. Each is answered — a negative or qualified answer comes with reasons under 143(4).

citation.ref: Section 143(3)

concepts.subsection: Audit in an IT environment
concepts.statement: General IT controls govern the environment — access, change management, operations, backup — while application controls live inside each system, checking individual transactions: input validations, exception reports, interface reconciliations. Weak general controls undermine every application control running on that system, so the auditor tests the foundation before relying on what stands on it; automated controls tested once can be relied on across the period only if change management held.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 144 — Services an auditor may not render
concepts.statement: A company's auditor may not render, directly or indirectly, to the company, its holding or its subsidiary: accounting and book keeping, internal audit, design and implementation of financial information systems, actuarial services, investment advisory and investment banking, outsourced financial services, and management services. "Directly or indirectly" reaches the auditor's relatives, connected persons and entities using the firm's brand or network. Permitted other services need audit committee or board approval.

citation.ref: Section 144

concepts.subsection: Review engagements and agreed-upon procedures
concepts.statement: A review gives limited assurance in negative form — "nothing has come to our attention" — built mainly on inquiry and analytical procedures; an agreed-upon procedures engagement gives no assurance at all, reporting factual findings of the exact procedures the parties specified, for those parties alone to judge. An audit's reasonable assurance sits above both. Naming the engagement wrongly misleads every reader about what stands behind the numbers.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services (SRS 4400), read with Ch. Review of Financial Information (SRE 2400)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part II — Members in service
concepts.statement: A member in employment commits professional misconduct by paying any person a share of the emoluments of his employment, or by accepting any part of the fees, profits or gains of a lawyer, chartered accountant, broker or agent engaged by his employer. The profession's fee-sharing discipline follows the member into service — kickbacks on either side of an employer's engagements are the mischief.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part II

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Tax audit — Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD
concepts.statement: Every tax audit report carries Form 3CD, the statement of particulars; what varies is its cover. Form 3CA is used where the accounts are already audited under any other law — a company under the Companies Act — and it references that statutory audit; Form 3CB is used where no other audit exists, and there the tax auditor himself expresses the true and fair opinion on the accounts. Picking 3CB for a company duplicates an opinion someone else owns.

citation.ref: Section 44AB with Rule 6G

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(ii)
concepts.statement: CARO's second clause covers inventory and borrowings against it: whether physical verification of inventory was conducted at reasonable intervals with material discrepancies dealt with in the books — and, where working capital limits above five crore rupees are sanctioned against current assets, whether the quarterly returns filed with the banks agree with the books of account, with disagreements detailed. Statements to bankers and statements to shareholders must be the same statements.

citation.ref: Clause 3(ii)

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Government audit — performance audit
concepts.statement: Performance audit examines the three Es — economy (spending less for the same inputs), efficiency (getting more output per input), and effectiveness (achieving the intended outcome) — of a programme or entity, against criteria agreed or derived, reporting findings and recommendations rather than an opinion. It differs from propriety audit's transaction-level prudence test: performance audit judges the scheme, not the voucher.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

concepts.subsection: Interim reviews — SRE 2410
concepts.statement: The statutory auditor's review of a listed company's quarterly results runs under SRE 2410: inquiry of finance personnel and analytical procedures, sized for limited assurance, concluding in negative form. It is not a small audit — no control testing, no third-party confirmations by default — but the auditor who becomes aware of a possible material misstatement must extend procedures until the doubt resolves; the lighter vehicle carries no licence to drive past red flags.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information (SRE 2410)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — Responding to NOCLAR
concepts.statement: On becoming aware of non-compliance or suspected non-compliance with laws and regulations at a client, the member's response runs in sequence: understand the matter, raise it with the appropriate level of management and those charged with governance, urge rectification and disclosure, then judge whether further action — up to withdrawal or disclosure to an authority — is needed in the public interest. Confidentiality does not bar a disclosure the framework calls for; walking away silently is the response the framework rejects.

citation.ref: Responding to Non-Compliance with Laws and Regulations

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(iii)
concepts.statement: Where a company has made investments in, given guarantees or security for, or granted loans or advances in the nature of loans to any parties, CARO asks: the amounts involved (with related-party loans separately shown), whether the terms are prejudicial to the company's interests, whether repayment schedules exist and repayments are regular, overdue amounts beyond ninety days and the steps taken, whether loans were renewed or fresh loans settled old ones, and loans repayable on demand or without terms — again with the related-party share disclosed.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii)

concepts.subsection: Surcharge on individuals, HUFs, AOPs, BOIs and artificial juridical persons — the tiers, the 15% cap, and marginal relief
concepts.statement: For an individual, HUF, AOP, BOI or artificial juridical person paying tax under the default regime of section 115BAC, the income-tax computed under that section and under sections 111A, 112, 112A, 115BBE and 115BBJ is increased by surcharge at 10% where total income exceeds ₹50 lakh but does not exceed ₹1 crore, 15% where it exceeds ₹1 crore but does not exceed ₹2 crore, and 25% where it exceeds ₹2 crore. The 25% tier applies to the income-tax on the portion of income other than dividend income and capital gains chargeable under sections 111A, 112 and 112A; the surcharge on the income-tax attributable to that dividend and capital gains portion is capped at 15%. Outside the default regime a fourth tier survives: 37% where total income, excluding that dividend and capital gains portion, exceeds ₹5 crore, again with the 15% cap on the portion.
