Marginal relief accompanies every threshold: the increase in tax and surcharge caused by the income exceeding ₹50 lakh, ₹1 crore or ₹2 crore cannot exceed the amount by which the income exceeds that threshold, worked as the lower of the tax-plus-surcharge on total income and the tax on the threshold plus the excess income. Health and education cess at 4% is added after the surcharge and after marginal relief.

citation.source: Finance Act, 2025 — Part I of the First Schedule with section 115BAC
citation.ref: Surcharge at 10%, 15% and 25% on the default regime; 37% above ₹5 crore outside it; the 15% cap on dividend and section 111A, 112 and 112A gains; marginal relief at each threshold

concepts.subsection: Domestic company — 25% or 30% by the ₹400 crore test, the concessional regimes, surcharge at 7% and 12%, marginal relief
concepts.statement: A domestic company is taxed at 25% of total income where its total turnover or gross receipts in the previous year 2023-24 did not exceed ₹400 crore, and at 30% in any other case, with the special rates of sections 111A, 112 and 112A applying to its capital gains. A domestic company that has exercised the option under section 115BAA is taxed at 22% of total income, computed without the deductions the section lists and without set-off of losses attributable to them; a domestic manufacturing company set up and registered on or after 1 October 2019 that commenced manufacture before 31 March 2024 and opted for section 115BAB pays 15% on income derived from or incidental to manufacturing. For a company outside those two sections, surcharge is 7% of income-tax where total income exceeds ₹1 crore but does not exceed ₹10 crore, and 12% where it exceeds ₹10 crore, each with marginal relief: the tax with surcharge cannot exceed the tax on ₹1 crore (or the tax with surcharge on ₹10 crore) plus the income in excess of that threshold. The module's own worked case: on a total income of ₹1,01,00,000 at 30% plus 7% surcharge the tax would be ₹32,42,100, but is limited to ₹30,00,000 plus ₹1,00,000 = ₹31,00,000, a marginal relief of ₹1,42,100, before cess at 4%.

citation.source: Finance Act, 2025 — Part I of the First Schedule with sections 115BAA and 115BAB
citation.ref: 25% or 30% by the ₹400 crore turnover test for the previous year 2023-24; 22% and 15% concessional rates; surcharge at 7% and 12% with marginal relief at ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore

concepts.subsection: Section 91 — unilateral relief where India has no agreement, at the lower of the two rates
concepts.statement: Where income arises to an assessee in a country with which India has no double taxation agreement, section 91 grants relief if six conditions are all met: the assessee is resident in India in the previous year in which the income is taxable; the income accrues or arises outside India; it is not deemed to accrue or arise in India; it has been subjected to income-tax in the foreign country in the assessee's hands; the assessee has paid tax on it there; and there is no agreement for relief between India and that country. The relief is a deduction from the Indian income-tax payable of a sum calculated on the doubly taxed income at the Indian rate of tax or the rate of tax of the foreign country, whichever is lower, or at the Indian rate where the two are equal. The Indian rate of tax is the Indian income-tax, after any relief due under the Act but before double taxation relief, divided by total income; the rate of tax of the foreign country is the income-tax and super-tax actually paid there after all relief due but before double taxation relief, divided by the whole income assessed there. Income-tax in relation to a foreign country includes any excess profits tax or business profits tax charged by its government, any part of it, or a local authority.

citation.ref: Section 91(1) with its Explanation — the six conditions, the deduction at the lower of the Indian rate and the foreign rate on doubly taxed income, and the definitions of both rates

concepts.subsection: Section 90(1) — the four purposes of an agreement; section 90(2A) — GAAR applies even where not beneficial
concepts.statement: Section 90(1) empowers the Central Government to enter into an agreement with the government of any country or specified territory for four purposes: granting relief in respect of income on which tax has been paid both in India and there, or of income-tax chargeable under both laws to promote mutual economic relations, trade and investment; avoiding double taxation under the two laws without creating opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through evasion or avoidance, including treaty-shopping arrangements aimed at the indirect benefit of residents of a third country; exchanging information for the prevention of evasion or avoidance of income-tax under either law or the investigation of such cases; and recovering income-tax under both laws. Section 90A gives the same power to a specified association for a specified territory. Where such an agreement applies, the provisions of the Act apply to the extent they are more beneficial to the assessee under section 90(2), but section 90(2A) makes Chapter X-A, the general anti-avoidance rule, apply to the assessee even where its provisions are not beneficial to him.

citation.ref: Section 90(1)(a) to (d) — relief, avoidance without non-taxation, exchange of information, recovery; section 90(2A) — the general anti-avoidance rule applies regardless of benefit

concepts.subsection: Section 245RR — once a resident applies for a ruling, no income-tax authority or Tribunal decides the issue
concepts.statement: Section 245RR provides that where a resident applicant has made an application to the Board for Advance Rulings in respect of an issue for its decision, no income-tax authority or the Appellate Tribunal shall take any decision in respect of that issue. The effect is that a resident assessee cannot pursue both remedies at once — an appeal or revision before an income-tax authority or appellate authority, and an application for an advance ruling — in respect of the same issue; the application to the Board freezes the issue everywhere else. This sits beside section 245R(2), under which the Board shall not allow an application where the question is already pending before an income-tax authority, the Tribunal or a court, except for a notified resident applicant: the two provisions together stop the same question from being argued on two roads. Section 245P adds that a proceeding before, or a ruling by, the Board is not invalid merely because of a vacancy or defect in its constitution.

citation.ref: Section 245RR — restriction on appellate authority once a resident's application is made; section 245R(2) — no ruling on a question already pending; section 245P — vacancies do not invalidate proceedings

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties — Articles 26 to 31, and India's position as a non-party
concepts.statement: Tax treaties are interpreted on the principles of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969, in force from 1980, which codifies customary international law. India is not a party to it, but the Supreme Court in Ram Jethmalani v. Union of India held that its principles of interpretation, in particular Article 31, give a broad guideline for interpreting a treaty in the Indian context, and the Delhi High Court in AWAS Ireland read Articles 26, 27 and 31 with Article 51(c) of the Constitution as obliging a state to honour a treaty and not to cite internal law as a justification for failing to perform it. Article 26, pacta sunt servanda: every treaty in force is binding upon the parties and must be performed in good faith. Article 27: a party may not invoke the provisions of its internal law as justification for its failure to perform a treaty — so a contracting state should not dishonour its commitment by retrospectively amending its domestic tax law. Article 28, non-retroactivity: unless a different intention appears, treaty provisions do not bind a party as to any act, fact or situation before the treaty entered into force for it. Article 29: a treaty binds each party in respect of its entire territory unless otherwise intended. Article 31, the general rule: a treaty shall be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to its terms in their context and in the light of its object and purpose — ordinary meaning first, purpose only where that meaning is ambiguous or leads to illogical results — with the context comprising the text, preamble and annexes and any agreement made between all the parties in connection with its conclusion.

citation.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969
citation.ref: Articles 26 (pacta sunt servanda), 27 (internal law no justification), 28 (non-retroactivity), 29 (territorial scope) and 31 (general rule of interpretation); Ram Jethmalani v. Union of India; AWAS Ireland v. DGCA

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: Article 32 and the extrinsic aids — protocols, subsequent agreement and conduct, parallel treaties, commentaries
concepts.statement: Article 32 of the Vienna Convention admits supplementary means of interpretation, including the preparatory work of the treaty and the circumstances of its conclusion. The module, following Starke, lists the extrinsic aids to which one may resort provided clear words are not thereby contradicted: interpretative protocols, resolutions and committee reports setting out agreed interpretations; a subsequent agreement between the parties regarding the interpretation or application of the treaty, which Article 31(3) brings into the context; the subsequent conduct of the state parties as evidence of their intention and their conception of the treaty; and other treaties in pari materia, relating to the same subject matter, in case of doubt. A parallel treaty of the same country whose language is the same but clearer may be referred to for the intention of the parties, though its interpretation is not binding, and the Indian courts are not consistent on the point. Commentaries — Kanga and Palkhivala and Sampath Iyengar in domestic cases, Philip Baker and Klaus Vogel on treaties — and international articles and reports are treated as extrinsic aids, as in CIT v. Visakhapatnam Port Trust. A protocol is a supplement to the treaty that puts certain matters beyond doubt and forms part of it, so it is read with the treaty and not as an afterthought.

citation.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 with ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
citation.ref: Article 32 — supplementary means; Article 31(3) — subsequent agreement; Starke's four extrinsic aids; protocols, parallel treaties and commentaries; CIT v. Visakhapatnam Port Trust

concepts.section: Incomes which do not form part of Total Income
concepts.subsection: Sections 10(2) and 10(2A) — a member's receipt from the HUF, a partner's share of the firm, and Circular 8/2014
concepts.statement: A Hindu undivided family is a person and pays tax on its own income, so section 10(2) keeps the same income from being taxed twice: any sum a member receives from the family is exempt in his hands, but only where it is paid out of the income of the family or out of the income of an impartible estate belonging to the family. Section 10(2A) does the same for a partner: his share in the total income of a firm which is separately assessed as such is not included in computing his total income. The CBDT settled in Circular No. 8/2014 what the share is where the firm's own taxable income is nil because of an exemption under Chapter III or a deduction under Chapter VI-A — the income of a firm is taxed in the hands of the firm only and can under no circumstances be taxed in the hands of its partners, so the entire profit credited to the partners' accounts is exempt even though the firm paid nothing. The exemption also switches off clubbing: where a spouse's capital in a firm came from the other spouse's gift, section 64(1)(iv) clubs the proportionate interest on capital, but the share of profit is exempt under section 10(2A) and section 64 does not apply to income from a transferred asset which is itself exempt.

citation.ref: Sections 10(2) and 10(2A); CBDT Circular No. 8/2014 dated 31 March 2014

concepts.section: Incomes which do not form part of Total Income
concepts.subsection: Section 10(23C) — the 50% government-financing test, the ₹5 crore receipts ceiling, and the approved sub-clauses
concepts.statement: Section 10(23C) exempts income received on behalf of named funds — the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund and PM CARES, the Swachh Bharat Kosh, the Clean Ganga Fund, a Chief Minister's or Lieutenant Governor's Relief Fund — and of three tiers of universities, educational institutions and hospitals that exist solely for their purpose and not for profit. Sub-clauses (iiiab) and (iiiac) cover those wholly or substantially financed by the Government: an institution is substantially financed for a previous year if the government grant in that year exceeds 50% of its total receipts including voluntary contributions. Sub-clauses (iiiad) and (iiiae) cover those whose aggregate annual receipts do not exceed ₹5 crore, and the ceiling is applied to the person, not the institution — where one person runs universities and hospitals both, the aggregate of all their receipts must stay within ₹5 crore or neither sub-clause applies. Sub-clauses (iv), (v), (vi) and (via) cover funds and institutions for charitable purposes, trusts wholly for public religious or religious and charitable purposes, and the larger universities and hospitals, each on approval by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Income-tax.

citation.ref: Section 10(23C) sub-clauses (iiiab), (iiiac), (iiiad), (iiiae), (iv), (v), (vi) and (via) with the Explanation on substantial financing

concepts.section: Incomes which do not form part of Total Income
concepts.subsection: Sections 10(26) and 10(26AAA) — a scheduled tribe member in a specified area, and a Sikkimese individual
concepts.statement: Section 10(26) exempts a member of a Scheduled Tribe residing in an area specified in the Constitution — the North Cachar Hills, Karbi Anglong, Bodoland Territorial Areas, Khasi Hills, Jaintia Hills and Garo Hills districts — or in the States of Manipur, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram and Nagaland, or in Ladakh, on two kinds of income: income arising or accruing from any source in those areas or States, and income by way of dividend or interest on securities from anywhere. Section 10(26AAA) gives a Sikkimese individual the same two limbs — income from any source in the State of Sikkim, and income by way of dividend or interest on securities. The second limb has no geographic test, so interest on bonds of another State's government is exempt to a Sikkimese individual, while a business he runs outside Sikkim is not.

citation.ref: Sections 10(26) and 10(26AAA) — the specified areas and States, and the two limbs of each exemption

concepts.section: Incomes which do not form part of Total Income
concepts.subsection: Sections 10(30) and 10(31) — replantation subsidies from the Tea Board and the other commodity boards
concepts.statement: Section 10(30) exempts wholly the amount of any subsidy received by an assessee engaged in the business of growing and manufacturing tea in India through or from the Tea Board, on two conditions: the subsidy must be under a scheme for replantation or replacement of tea bushes or for rejuvenation or consolidation of areas used for cultivation of tea notified by the Central Government, and the assessee must furnish to the Assessing Officer a certificate from the Tea Board as to the amount received in the previous year. Section 10(31) extends the same exemption, on the same two conditions, to an assessee growing and manufacturing rubber, coffee, cardamom or another notified commodity, for a subsidy received from or through the Rubber Board, Coffee Board, Spices Board or the Board for that commodity. The subsidy sits apart from the Rule 8 split of tea income: the 40% business share of tea profits is taxable, but a Tea Board replantation subsidy is outside total income altogether.

citation.ref: Sections 10(30) and 10(31) — the scheme condition and the certificate condition

concepts.section: Income of Other Persons included in Assessee's Total Income
concepts.subsection: Section 64(1)(ii) — a spouse's salary from a concern in which the individual has a substantial interest, and the professional-qualification exception
concepts.statement: Section 64(1)(ii) includes in an individual's total income any salary, commission, fees or other remuneration, in cash or in kind, arising to his or her spouse from a concern in which the individual has a substantial interest. For a company, substantial interest means equity shares carrying 20% or more of the voting power beneficially owned by the individual alone or with one or more relatives at any time during the previous year; for any other concern, an entitlement of the individual alone or with relatives to 20% or more of its profits at any time during the year. A relative under section 2(41) is the husband, wife, brother, sister or any lineal ascendant or descendant. The clubbing does not apply where the spouse possesses technical or professional qualifications and the income is solely attributable to the application of that knowledge or experience; the Madras High Court in CIT v. Smt. R. Bharati read "qualification" widely, as the qualities the work needs so long as the work is technical or professional, so a model with skill and experience in her line is professionally qualified. Where both spouses have a substantial interest and both draw remuneration, the income is clubbed with the spouse whose total income excluding that remuneration is higher, and once included in one spouse's income it stays there in later years unless the Assessing Officer, after hearing that spouse, is satisfied a change is necessary.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(ii) with Explanations 1 and 2 and the proviso; section 2(41); CIT v. Smt. R. Bharati (1999) 240 ITR 697 (Mad)

concepts.section: Income of Other Persons included in Assessee's Total Income
concepts.subsection: Sections 64(1)(vi), (vii) and (viii) with Explanation 3 — son's wife, transfers for a spouse's or son's wife's benefit, and the first-day proportion
concepts.statement: Section 64(1)(vi) includes in an individual's total income the income arising to his or her son's wife from an asset transferred to her, directly or indirectly, without adequate consideration. Sections 64(1)(vii) and (viii) reach transfers to any other person or association of persons without adequate consideration, to the extent the income from the asset is used for the immediate or deferred benefit of the transferor's spouse or son's wife — so an owner who settles property on a company subject to ₹42,000 a year going to her son's wife is taxed on that ₹42,000. Where the transferred asset is invested by the spouse or son's wife in a business, or contributed as capital to a firm, Explanation 3 clubs only the proportionate income or interest on capital, the proportion being the transferred asset's value to the total investment on the first day of the previous year. The module's cases: a ₹7,00,000 gift from a wife into a husband's business whose own capital stood at ₹3,00,000 on 1 April splits the year's ₹5,00,000 profit 3:7, so ₹3,50,000 is clubbed with her, and if the same sum had been a bona fide loan nothing would be; a wife whose ₹5 lakh capital in a firm held ₹2 lakh of her husband's gift on 1 April has ₹32,000 of ₹80,000 interest on capital clubbed with him, while her ₹60,000 share of profit is exempt under section 10(2A) and is not clubbed at all. A gift between relatives attracts nothing under section 56(2)(x).

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(vi), (vii) and (viii); Explanation 3 to section 64(1) — proportion by the value of the investment on the first day of the previous year

concepts.section: Income of Other Persons included in Assessee's Total Income
concepts.subsection: Cross transfers — the deemed transferor, and clubbing only to the extent of the mutual consideration
concepts.statement: Where two people each transfer an asset to the other's spouse or minor child so that neither transfer is to his own relative, the income from the assets is nonetheless assessed in the hands of the deemed transferor if the transfers are so intimately connected that they form part of a single transaction and each constitutes consideration for the other. The Supreme Court in CIT v. Keshavji Morarji held that where two transactions are inter-connected parts of the same transaction so that the circuitous method was adopted as a device to evade tax, the clubbing provisions are attracted — each person is the indirect transferor to his own spouse or child. The clubbing runs only as far as the mutual consideration: where one brother gifts ₹6.5 lakh to the other's wife and receives ₹5.2 lakh for his own wife in return, the interest on ₹5.2 lakh is clubbed with each brother and the interest on the remaining ₹1.3 lakh stays with the recipient, because the cross transfer extends only to ₹5.2 lakh.

citation.ref: Section 64(1) as applied to cross transfers; CIT v. Keshavji Morarji (1967) 66 ITR 142 (SC)

concepts.section: Income of Other Persons included in Assessee's Total Income
concepts.subsection: Section 64(2) conversion of self-acquired property, Explanation 2 income includes loss, and section 65 recovery from the transferee
concepts.statement: Section 64(2) applies where a member of a Hindu undivided family converts his self-acquired property into property of the family after 31 December 1969, throws it into the common stock, or otherwise transfers it to the family without adequate consideration: the income from the converted property continues to be included in his total income, and on a total or partial partition the income from the share received by his spouse is deemed to arise from an indirect transfer to the spouse and is included in his income too. What is included in his income is excluded from the family's or the spouse's. Explanation 2 to section 64 says income includes loss, for both section 64(1) and 64(2), so a clubbed loss is set off in the individual's computation. Section 61 applies only to a revocable transfer by any person, while section 64 applies to revocable and irrevocable transfers by individuals alone. Section 65 lets the Assessing Officer serve the notice of demand for the tax on clubbed income on the transferee, who is then liable for the portion of the transferor's tax attributable to that income; the same applies to a house property whose transferor is the deemed owner under section 27. A demand on the transferor for the whole income of a house gifted partly to a wife and partly to a married daughter is invalid as to the daughter's share, which is taxed in her own hands because she is neither a spouse nor a minor child.

citation.ref: Section 64(2); Explanation 2 to section 64; section 65; section 27(i)

concepts.section: Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
concepts.subsection: Sections 88 and 89 — liquidation, the 30-day and 3-month clocks, and when a private company's directors pay
concepts.statement: When a company is being wound up, every person appointed as receiver of any of its assets — the liquidator — must within 30 days of appointment give intimation of it to the Commissioner under section 88(1). The Commissioner, after such inquiry as he thinks fit, must within 3 months of receiving that intimation notify the liquidator of the amount which in his opinion would be sufficient to provide for any tax, interest or penalty then or thereafter payable by the company. Section 88(3) then reaches past the company: where a private company is wound up and tax, interest or penalty determined on it for any period, whether before, during or after liquidation, cannot be recovered, every person who was a director at any time during the period for which the tax was due is jointly and severally liable, unless he proves to the Commissioner's satisfaction that the non-recovery cannot be attributed to any gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part in relation to the company's affairs. Section 89(1) makes the same rule for a private company that is not in liquidation, notwithstanding the Companies Act, 2013. Section 89(2) is the escape: where a private company is converted into a public company and the dues for the private period could not be recovered before conversion, the directors of the former private company are not liable for them — but a personal penalty imposed on a director stays his own.

concepts.section: Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
concepts.subsection: Sections 90 and 94 — partners jointly and severally, the retiring partner's one month, and a change in constitution
concepts.statement: Section 90 makes a firm and each of its partners jointly and severally liable for any tax, interest or penalty of the firm, notwithstanding any contract to the contrary and any other law — so a partnership deed that shifts the tax to one partner binds the partners and not the department. A retiring partner is liable for the dues up to the date of his retirement, whether determined on that date or not, and either he or the firm must intimate the date of retirement to the Commissioner by notice in writing; if no intimation is given within 1 month of retirement, his liability continues until the date the Commissioner receives it. Section 94 carries the same rule through three other events. On discontinuance of business by a firm, association of persons or Hindu undivided family, the dues up to that date are determined as if there had been no discontinuance and every person who was a partner or member at that time is jointly and severally liable, before or after. On a change in the constitution of a firm or association, the partners as they stood before and after the reconstitution are jointly and severally liable for any period before it, without prejudice to section 90. Dissolution of a firm or association and partition of a family's business are read as discontinuance. For the whole Chapter, a limited liability partnership is a firm, and "court" means the District Court, High Court or Supreme Court.

citation.ref: Section 90 with its proviso; section 94(1), (2) and (3); the Explanation to Chapter XVI

concepts.section: Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
concepts.subsection: Section 87 — a retrospective amalgamation; section 93 — death, partition of an HUF and the end of a trust
concepts.statement: Section 87 deals with an amalgamation or merger ordered to take effect from a date earlier than the order. Where any two of the companies supplied or received goods or services to or from each other between the effective date and the date of the order, those transactions are included in the turnover of supply or receipt of the respective companies and tax is payable on them; the companies are treated as distinct companies up to the date of the order, and their registration certificates are cancelled with effect from that date, not from the earlier effective date. Section 93 settles who pays when the taxable person is gone, save as otherwise provided in the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. On death, where the business is continued by the legal representative or any other person, that person is liable for the dues; where the business is discontinued, before or after the death, the legal representative pays out of the estate of the deceased to the extent the estate is capable of meeting the charge, whether the dues were determined before the death and unpaid or determined afterwards. Circular 96/15/2019 treats transfer of business on the death of a sole proprietor as a transfer under section 85, the transferee liable for the transferor's dues. On partition of a Hindu undivided family or association of persons, each member or group of members is jointly and severally liable for the dues up to the partition. Where a guardian's or trustee's guardianship or trust is terminated, the ward or beneficiary is liable for the dues up to the termination.

citation.ref: Section 87(1) and (2); section 93(1), (2), (3) and (4); Circular No. 96/15/2019-GST dated 28 March 2019

concepts.subsection: Sections 95 to 98 with Rule 103 — who may apply, the seven questions, why place of supply is not one, the ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 fees, and the two grounds of non-admission
concepts.statement: An applicant under section 95(c) is any person registered or desirous of obtaining registration, so a person who has not yet registered may apply, and a ruling may be sought on a supply being undertaken or proposed to be undertaken. Section 97(2) lists the seven questions: classification of goods or services; applicability of a notification; time and value of supply; admissibility of input tax credit; the liability to pay tax; whether the applicant is required to be registered; and whether a particular thing done amounts to a supply. Place of supply is not among them, and the module gives the reason: the Authority and the Appellate Authority are constituted under the State or Union Territory Act, with members not below the rank of Joint Commissioner under Rule 103, and are deemed the Authority under the CGST Act for that State, so a ruling runs only within that State and a question that spans States cannot be put to them. The application carries a fee of ₹5,000 under the CGST Act and ₹5,000 under the SGST Act; an appeal by the applicant to the Appellate Authority carries ₹10,000 under each, and an appeal by the concerned or jurisdictional officer carries no fee. Section 98(2) bars admission where the question is already pending or already decided in any proceedings in the applicant's own case, and rejection must be by a speaking order after an opportunity of hearing. Where the two members of the Authority differ, they refer the point to the Appellate Authority; if its members also differ, it is deemed that no ruling can be given on that point.

concepts.subsection: Sections 102, 104, 105 and 106 — six months to rectify, void ab initio for fraud, and the powers of a civil court
concepts.statement: Section 102 lets the Authority or the Appellate Authority amend its order to rectify any mistake apparent from the record within 6 months from the date of the order, whether the mistake is noticed by the authority itself or brought to its notice by the applicant, the concerned officer or the jurisdictional officer; where the rectification would enhance the tax liability or reduce the input tax credit, the applicant must be heard first. Section 104 makes a ruling void ab initio where the authority finds it was obtained by fraud, suppression of material facts or misrepresentation of facts, by an order passed after hearing the applicant; every provision of the Act then applies as if the ruling had never been made, but the period from the ruling to the order declaring it void is excluded in counting limitation. Under sections 105 and 106 both authorities have the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for discovery and inspection, enforcing attendance and examining on oath, issuing commissions and compelling production of books; they are deemed a civil court for section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 but not for Chapter XXVI of it; proceedings before them are judicial proceedings under sections 193 and 228 and for section 196 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860; and each regulates its own procedure.

citation.ref: Sections 102, 104, 105 and 106

concepts.section: Classification of Imported and Export Goods
concepts.subsection: The Customs Tariff — headings, sub-headings and tariff items, the three general explanatory notes, and the force of section and chapter notes
concepts.statement: The Customs Tariff Act, 1975 carries two Schedules: the First lists goods liable to import duty and the Second goods liable to export duty. The First Schedule follows the Harmonized System of Nomenclature of the World Customs Organization, with 21 sections grouping 98 chapters — the HSN itself has 97, and Chapter 98 for project imports is an Indian addition. Goods are classified to eight digits: a four-digit heading, a six-digit sub-heading and an eight-digit tariff item, and the rate of duty is shown against the tariff item, never against a heading or sub-heading. Six General Rules of Interpretation and three General Explanatory Notes are an integral part of the Schedule and have statutory force. The three notes: a single dash before a description marks a sub-classification of the heading, two dashes a sub-classification of the preceding single-dash article, and three or four dashes a sub-classification of the preceding one- or two-dash description; the abbreviation "%" against a rate means duty computed at that percentage on the value of the goods under section 14 of the Customs Act; and where no preferential rate is notified against an entry, the standard rate applies. Section notes and chapter notes are part of the statute and, as the Tribunal held in Saurashtra Chemicals, sometimes restrict and sometimes expand a heading and override it; the titles of sections, chapters and sub-chapters have no legal force. A note of one chapter cannot be used to read the entries of another. The module's example: a letter closing and sealing machine reads on both 8422 30 00 and 8472 30 00, and chapter note 2 to Chapter 84, which says heading 8422 does not cover office machinery of heading 8472, settles it under 8472 30 00.

citation.source: Customs Tariff Act, 1975 — First Schedule, General Explanatory Notes and Additional Notes
citation.ref: The three General Explanatory Notes; Additional Notes 1 to 3; Rule 1; Saurashtra Chemicals v. CC 1986 (23) ELT 283 (Tri-LB)

concepts.section: Classification of Imported and Export Goods
concepts.subsection: Rules 2(a), 5 and 6 with the cases — essential character, cases and packing, comparable sub-headings, Maestro Motors, Hewlett Packard and almond milk
concepts.statement: Rule 2(a) takes a reference to an article to include the article incomplete or unfinished if, as presented, it has the essential character of the complete article, and the article presented unassembled; railway coaches without seats are still coaches. Only goods needing minor adjustments have that character — goods still requiring turning, grinding, broaching, heat or surface treatment do not. Rule 5(a) classifies camera, instrument, gun and necklace cases and similar containers with the article they hold when they are specially shaped or fitted for it, suitable for long-term use and presented with it, unless the container gives the whole its essential character; Rule 5(b) classifies packing materials and containers with the goods when of a kind normally used for them, but not when clearly suitable for repetitive use — gas cylinders are classified apart from the gas. Rule 6 says only sub-headings at the same level are comparable. Parts suitable solely for a machine follow the machine unless a separate heading exists for parts, and parts of general use go to their own headings. Three cases carry the rest: in Maestro Motors the Supreme Court held that the interpretative rules apply to an exemption notification only where it names a tariff heading, and an item named without a heading gets the exemption whatever its classification; in Hewlett Packard a laptop imported with its operating system preloaded is classified and valued as one unit, because without the software it cannot work; and almond milk is classified under the residual tariff item 2202 99 90 at 18%, not as a fruit-juice drink under 2202 99 20, because Chapter 8 treats almonds as nuts and not fruit, and not as a beverage containing milk under 2202 99 30, because it contains none — Circular 113/32/2019 confirms it.

citation.source: Customs Tariff Act, 1975 — General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule
citation.ref: Rules 2(a), 5(a), 5(b) and 6; CC v. Maestro Motors Ltd 2004 (174) ELT 289 (SC); CC v. Hewlett Packard India Sales (P) Ltd 2007 (215) ELT 484 (SC); CBIC Circular No. 113/32/2019-GST dated 11 October 2019

concepts.subsection: Section 143 beyond the clock — who is a principal, supply straight from the job worker's premises, whose turnover it is, the job worker's registration and waste and scrap
concepts.statement: Job work under section 2(68) is any treatment or process undertaken by a person on goods belonging to another registered person; ownership stays with the principal, and the job worker may use his own goods besides the principal's. Section 143 is available only to a registered principal and is optional — outside it, sending inputs for processing is a supply on both sides. The principal may supply the processed goods to a third party straight from the job worker's premises, on payment of tax in India or without payment for export, after declaring those premises as his additional place of business, unless the job worker is registered under section 25 or the principal supplies notified goods. Such a supply is the principal's, not the job worker's: time, value and place of supply are determined in the principal's hands wherever the job worker sits, the principal issues the invoice, the principal executes the letter of undertaking or bond for an export, and the value counts in the principal's aggregate turnover under Explanation (ii) to section 22 and not the job worker's. The job worker, as a supplier of services, registers only when his aggregate turnover on an all-India basis exceeds ₹20 lakh, or ₹10 lakh in Mizoram, Tripura, Manipur and Nagaland, whether the principal is in the same State or another — inter-State supply of services below that threshold is exempted from compulsory registration by Notification 10/2017-IT. The Commissioner may extend the one-year and three-year windows by a further period not exceeding one year and two years respectively. Under section 143(5) waste and scrap generated during job work may be supplied by the job worker directly from his premises on payment of tax if he is registered, and by the principal if he is not. The value of moulds, dies, jigs, fixtures or tools the principal supplies need not be added to the value of the job work service under section 15(2)(b) where it has been factored into the price.

citation.ref: Sections 2(68), 143(1) to (5), 22 Explanation (ii), 24(i) and 15(2)(b); Circular No. 38/12/2018-GST dated 26 March 2018; Notification No. 10/2017-Integrated Tax dated 13 October 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 45 with Rule 55 — the delivery challan and its endorsements, ITC-04 as the intimation with its ₹5 crore split, and the e-way bill regardless of value
concepts.statement: Under Rule 45 inputs, semi-finished goods and capital goods go to a job worker under a delivery challan issued by the principal, prepared in triplicate with the Rule 55 particulars — number and date, names, addresses and GSTINs, HSN and description, quantity, taxable value, tax rate and amount, place of supply and signature — and two copies travel with the goods, one of which the job worker returns with them. Where goods move from one job worker to another, either the principal or the sending job worker may issue a challan, or the principal's challan may be endorsed with the quantity and description, and endorsed again for a further move; goods returned piecemeal need a fresh challan from the job worker, because the original cannot be endorsed for part. Goods sent straight from the principal's supplier travel on the supplier's invoice naming the principal as buyer and the job worker as consignee, with the principal's challan sent to the job worker directly; imported goods move from the customs station on a copy of the bill of entry with the principal's challan. Form GST ITC-04, listing every challan for goods sent, moved between job workers and received back, is the intimation section 143 requires: a principal whose aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year exceeded ₹5 crore files it half-yearly by 25 October and 25 April, and any other principal annually by 25 April. Where a principal in one State sends goods to a job worker in another, an e-way bill is generated by the principal or the registered job worker irrespective of the value of the consignment, and by the principal wherever the job worker is unregistered.

citation.ref: Rule 45(1) to (4) with Rule 55; Rule 138; Circular No. 38/12/2018-GST dated 26 March 2018

concepts.subsection: Section 245MA with Rule 44DAD(ii) — the five orders a Dispute Resolution Committee may be asked about
concepts.statement: A Dispute Resolution Committee may be approached only about a specified order, and the Explanation to section 245MA read with Rule 44DAD(ii) lists exactly five. First, a draft order referred to in section 144C(1), but only where the variation arises as a consequence of an order of the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA(3) or where the person is a non-corporate non-resident. Second, an intimation under section 143(1) after a return is processed, or under section 200A(1) after a statement of tax deducted at source is processed, or under section 206CB(1) after a statement of tax collected at source is processed, where the assessee, the deductor or the collector objects to the adjustments made. Third, an order of assessment or reassessment — with one exclusion that is the whole point of the limb, an order passed in pursuance of the directions of the Dispute Resolution Panel, which can never be taken to the committee. Fourth, a rectification order under section 154, and only one that has the effect of enhancing the assessment or reducing the loss; a rectification in the assessee's favour is not a specified order because there is nothing in it to dispute. Fifth, an order under section 201 or under section 206C(6A) deeming a person to be an assessee-in-default for failing to deduct or collect tax at source or to remit what he deducted or collected. For that fifth kind the section says what the variation is measured on, and it is not the tax: the variation refers to the amount on which tax has not been deducted or collected in accordance with the Act. Three conditions then have to hold on any of the five — the aggregate of the variations proposed or made does not exceed ₹10 lakh, the return has been furnished and the total income shown in it does not exceed ₹50 lakh, and the order is not based on a search under section 132, a requisition under section 132A, a survey under section 133A, or information received under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A.

citation.ref: Explanation (b) to section 245MA read with Rule 44DAD(ii) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — the five categories of specified order, the exclusion of an assessment passed in pursuance of the directions of the Dispute Resolution Panel, the confinement of a section 154 order to one enhancing the assessment or reducing the loss, and the variation in a tax deduction default measured on the amount on which tax was not deducted

concepts.subsection: Section 245MA with Rule 44DAD(iii) — who is shut out of the committee, and who only looks as though he is
concepts.statement: The order has to qualify and so does the person. The Explanation to section 245MA defines the specified conditions negatively, by listing four kinds of person who may not come. One, a person against whom an order of detention has been made under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, where that order has not been revoked on the report of the Advisory Board or on review within the times the proviso sets out, and has not been set aside by a court of competent jurisdiction. Two, a person against whom prosecution has been instituted for an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, the Prohibition of Benami Transactions Act, 1988, the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 or the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002, and who has been convicted under one of them. Both halves are needed: an institution of prosecution that has not ended in a conviction does not shut this door. Three, a person against whom an income-tax authority has initiated prosecution for an offence under this Act or under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or for the enforcement of a civil liability, or who has been convicted following such a prosecution. Four, a person notified under section 3 of the Special Court (Trial of Offences Relating to Transactions in Securities) Act, 1992. Rule 44DAD(iii) adds a fifth of its own — proceedings under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 must not have been initiated for the assessment year for which resolution is sought — and Rule 44DAD(iv) calls a person who satisfies all of this a specified person. What is not in the list is what the exam asks. A penalty levied under the Income-tax Act itself is nowhere among the specified conditions, so a person carrying a penalty under section 271D for a breach of section 269SS is not disqualified by it at all.

citation.ref: Explanation (a) to section 245MA read with Rules 44DAD(iii) and 44DAD(iv) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — detention under COFEPOSA, conviction after prosecution under the six named Acts, prosecution initiated by an income-tax authority, notification under section 3 of the Special Court Act, 1992, and proceedings under the Black Money Act, 2015 for the same assessment year

concepts.subsection: Rule 44DAB — how the committee decides whether to take the application at all
concepts.statement: Admission is a stage of its own and it has its own consequences. The committee first examines the application against the specified conditions and the criteria for a specified order. Where it considers that the application should be rejected it does not simply reject it: it serves a notice calling on the assessee to show cause why it should not be rejected, specifying a date and time for a response. A hearing is available but it is not automatic — the assessee has to request one, and where he does the committee must provide it through video telephony or video conferencing to the extent technologically feasible. The assessee furnishes his response by the specified date or within such extended time as the committee allows on an application made for the purpose. The committee may then reject the application or proceed to decide it on the merits, and where no response is furnished at all it may reject the application on that footing alone. Its decision either way is communicated to the assessee at his registered electronic mail address. Two things follow that students miss. A rejection does not close the assessee's ordinary route: he may still appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals), and the period the committee took in deciding on admission is excluded from the time available to file that appeal, so applying to the committee cannot cost him his appeal. And within 30 days of receiving the communication that the application has been admitted, the assessee must submit proof that he has withdrawn any appeal filed under section 246A or any application before the Dispute Resolution Panel, or state that no such proceeding is pending, failing which the committee may reject the application.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — the show-cause notice before rejection, a hearing on request through video telephony or video conferencing, rejection where no response is furnished, communication to the registered electronic mail address, and the exclusion of the period taken in deciding admission from the time available to appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals)

concepts.subsection: Section 245MA(2A) with Rule 44DAB — the three orders the committee may pass, and the two clocks that follow
concepts.statement: Once the application is admitted the committee may call for records from the income-tax authority, seek a report from the Assessing Officer, and call for further information from the assessee or anybody else by electronic mail. It then does one of three things. It may modify the variations in the specified order in a way not prejudicial to the assessee, decide on waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution under Rule 44DAC, and pass an order of resolution. It may decline to modify the variations but still waive penalty and grant immunity, and that order too is treated as an order not prejudicial to the assessee. Or it may make no modification at all and simply dispose of the application, and even that is treated as an order not prejudicial to the assessee. All three have to be passed within six months from the end of the month in which the application was admitted, which is not six months from admission. The committee serves a copy on the assessee and on the Assessing Officer for giving effect to it, and the second clock then starts: under section 245MA(2A) the Assessing Officer passes the order of assessment, reassessment or recomputation where the specified order was a draft order under section 144C(1), or otherwise modifies his order, in conformity with the committee's directions, within one month from the end of the month in which he receives that order. He serves the modified order with a notice of demand specifying a date for payment. Against the modified order no appeal and no revision lies at all, and where the specified order was that of an eligible assessee under section 144C(1) he cannot make a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel or appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) either — an eligible assessee chooses between the Panel and the Committee and does not get both.

citation.ref: Section 245MA(2A) read with Rule 44DAB — the three decisions open to the committee, all treated as not prejudicial to the assessee, an order within six months from the end of the month of admission, the Assessing Officer's conforming order within one month from the end of the month of receipt, and no appeal or revision against the modified order

concepts.subsection: Section 245MA(2) with Rule 44DAC — the relief no appellate authority can give, and what it costs to keep it
concepts.statement: The power to reduce or waive a penalty imposable under the Income-tax Act and to grant immunity from prosecution for an offence punishable under it is what separates this route from an appeal, and section 245MA(2) makes that power subject to prescribed conditions. Rule 44DAC supplies them. The committee acts on receipt of confirmation from the assessee that the demand has been paid, and grants waiver of the penalty imposable or immunity from prosecution or both in respect of the order that was the subject matter of the resolution, if it is satisfied that the person has paid the tax due on the returned income in full where such tax is available to be paid, and has co-operated with the committee in the proceedings before it. The order of waiver or immunity is in writing, the reasons are recorded in writing, and the committee may attach whatever conditions it thinks fit. There is one situation in which it cannot grant immunity at all: where proceedings for the prosecution of an offence had already been initiated before the date on which the committee received the application. And an immunity once granted is not unconditional — if the person fails to comply with any condition subject to which it was granted, the immunity stands withdrawn, and the provisions of the Income-tax Act then apply as if the immunity or waiver had never been granted at all.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAC read with section 245MA(2) — waiver or immunity on confirmation of payment of the demand where the tax on the returned income has been paid in full and the assessee has co-operated, no immunity where prosecution was initiated before the application was received, and withdrawal of immunity on breach of a condition as if it had never been granted

concepts.subsection: Rule 44DAB — the four things that end a dispute resolution proceeding part way through
concepts.statement: Termination is different from rejection. Rejection happens at the admission stage, on the material in the application; termination happens at any stage after that, and only on one of four grounds. The assessee fails to co-operate during the course of the proceedings. The assessee fails to respond to a notice issued to him, or to submit information called for by one. The committee is satisfied that the assessee has concealed a particular material to the proceedings or has given false evidence. Or the assessee fails to pay the demand required by the notice of demand. Nothing else will do, and in particular an assessee who simply disagrees with what the committee proposes has not given it a ground. Two safeguards run with the power: the committee must record its reasons in writing and must give the assessee an opportunity of being heard before it terminates. Where the proceedings are terminated the committee intimates the income-tax authority so that it may take the action the Act provides for.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — termination of dispute resolution proceedings at any stage for failure to co-operate, failure to respond or furnish information, concealment of a material particular or false evidence, or failure to pay the demand, for reasons recorded in writing and after an opportunity of being heard, with intimation to the income-tax authority

concepts.subsection: Why Chapter XIX-AA exists — the Settlement Commission closed, the Interim Boards, and what replaced neither
concepts.statement: The Income-tax Settlement Commission constituted by the Central Government for the settlement of cases ceased to operate with effect from 1 February 2021, and no application under section 245C for the settlement of a case can be made on or after that date. The applications already pending as on 31 January 2021 still had to go somewhere, so the Central Government constituted seven Interim Boards for Settlement by Notification No. 91 of 2021 dated 10 August 2021 to dispose of them. That deals with the past. For the future the Act took a different route altogether: with effect from 1 April 2021 a new scheme of dispute resolution was formulated, under which one or more Dispute Resolution Committees are constituted, in order to give early tax certainty to small and medium taxpayers and to settle an issue at the initial stage rather than after it has hardened into an appeal. The distinction matters because the two are easily confused. The Interim Boards are a winding-up mechanism handling a closed set of old settlement applications; the Dispute Resolution Committee is a forward-looking route open only on a specified order within the ₹10 lakh and ₹50 lakh limits, and it is not the Settlement Commission's successor in scope, in subject matter or in who may reach it.

citation.ref: Chapter XIX-AA read with section 245C — the Settlement Commission ceasing to operate from 1 February 2021, seven Interim Boards for Settlement constituted by Notification No. 91 of 2021 dated 10 August 2021 for applications pending as on 31 January 2021, and the Dispute Resolution Committee scheme with effect from 1 April 2021

concepts.section: Tax Planning, Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion
concepts.subsection: The four labels — planning, management, avoidance and evasion, and where the line actually falls
concepts.statement: The module opens the chapter on the distinction rather than on the rules, because everything after it depends on the distinction. Tax planning is arranging one's financial affairs so that, without violating any legal provision, full advantage is taken of the exemptions, deductions, concessions, rebates, allowances and reliefs the Act permits. Tax management is a different thing again and is not about reducing anything: it is compliance — keeping a register of the payments on which tax must be deducted so that each deposit is timely, obtaining declarations in Form 15G or 15H from depositors and forwarding them, remitting provident fund contributions before the due date. Tax evasion is the Direct Taxes Enquiry Committee's category, described by the Wanchoo Committee as a manoeuvre involving an element of deceit, misrepresentation of facts, falsification of accounting calculations or downright fraud — an attempt to avoid paying tax by illegal means. Tax avoidance sits between planning and evasion: a vast domain of methods which technically satisfy the requirements of the law and in fact circumvent it, with a view to eliminating or reducing the tax burden. The module then names the common forms of evasion, and the list is the useful part: misrepresentation or suppression of facts; failure to record investments in the books of account; a claim of expenditure not substantiated by any evidence; recording a false entry in the books; failure to record a receipt bearing on total income; and failure to report an international transaction, a deemed international transaction or a specified domestic transaction under Chapter X. All six constitute misreporting of income, which attracts penalty at 200 per cent under section 270A.

citation.ref: Section 270A read with the Direct Taxes Enquiry Committee (Wanchoo Committee) distinction between evasion and avoidance — the six common forms of tax evasion, each of which is misreporting of income carrying penalty at 200 per cent

concepts.section: Tax Planning, Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion
concepts.subsection: The doctrine of form and substance, from Duke of Westminster to Mc Dowell
concepts.statement: The English starting point is Inland Revenue Commissioner v. Duke of Westminster, that every man is entitled to order his affairs so that the tax attaching is less than it otherwise would be, and that his ingenuity cannot be punished with a higher tax. The departure came in Ramsay v. Inland Revenue Commissioners, where the court held that although a genuine document or transaction must be accepted as genuine, it need not be looked at in blinkers isolated from the series it belongs to — the fiscal consequences of a pre-ordained series of transactions intended to operate as such are ascertained by considering the result of the series as a whole rather than by dissecting it. Burmah Shell and Furniss v. Dawson went further: where avoidance is pursued through a series of transactions with no commercial or substantial value and the only aim of avoiding tax, the courts ignore the transactions and determine the liability as if they had never taken place. India followed Westminster in CIT v. A. Raman and Co. and in CIT v. B.M. Kharwar, the latter holding that the taxing authority is bound to determine the true legal relation resulting from a transaction and may unravel a device to find it, but that the legal effect of a transaction cannot be displaced by probing into its substance. The Supreme Court in Mc Dowell and Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer expressly disassociated itself from that last proposition, listed the evil consequences of avoidance, and held that tax planning may be legitimate provided it is within the framework of law and that colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning. Associated Rubber Industries applied the same thinking outside tax altogether, to a wholly owned subsidiary created with no assets of its own except investments transferred to it by the holding company and no income except the dividend on them: it was a device to reduce the holding company's gross profits and so its bonus liability, and the duty of the court was to get behind the smoke screen. What survives is a two-part rule. Where a transaction is genuine, its form governs and not its substance, and a transaction lawfully put through in one form is taxed accordingly even though another equally lawful form would have been taxed differently. Where it is colourable or a mere device, the question is not one between form and substance at all but between appearance and truth, and the authorities may pierce the corporate veil and look behind the legal facade.

citation.ref: Mc Dowell and Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1985) 154 ITR 148 (SC) read with Inland Revenue Commissioner v. Duke of Westminster 1936 AC 1, Ramsay v. Inland Revenue Commissioners (1982) AC 300, CIT v. B.M. Kharwar (1969) 72 ITR 603 (SC), CIT v. Motor and General Stores (P) Ltd. (1967) 66 ITR 692 (SC) and Associated Rubber Industries (1986) 157 ITR 77 (SC)

concepts.section: Tax Planning, Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion
concepts.subsection: Sections 95 and 102 — what an arrangement is, what a step is, and how wide a tax benefit is
concepts.statement: Section 95 is the applicability provision of Chapter X-A and it does three things. It allows an arrangement entered into by an assessee to be declared an impermissible avoidance arrangement and the tax consequence flowing from it to be determined. It says in terms that the Chapter may be applied to any step in, or a part of, an arrangement exactly as it applies to the arrangement as a whole, so a single step may be struck while the rest of the transaction stands, and Rule 10UA confirms that where a part is declared impermissible the tax consequences are determined with reference to that part only. And it opens with a non-obstante clause, so where it conflicts with another section of the Act it prevails. The definitions in section 102 are as wide as the section is. An arrangement under section 102(1) means any step in, or a part or the whole of, any transaction, operation, scheme, agreement or understanding, whether enforceable or not, and includes the alienation of property in it. A step under section 102(9) includes a measure or an action, particularly one of a series taken to achieve a particular object in the arrangement. A tax benefit under section 102(10) is far wider than a saving of tax, and covers six things: a reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax or another amount payable under the Act; an increase in a refund of tax or another amount under the Act; a reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax or another amount that would be payable as a result of a tax treaty; an increase in a refund as a result of a tax treaty; a reduction in total income; and an increase in a loss — in the relevant previous year or in any other previous year. So a deferral with no permanent saving, and an increased loss that has not yet been used, are each a tax benefit for the purpose of the purpose test.

citation.ref: Sections 95, 102(1), 102(9) and 102(10) read with Rule 10UA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — the non-obstante applicability of Chapter X-A to any step in or part of an arrangement, the definitions of arrangement and step, and the six limbs of a tax benefit including deferral, a reduction in total income and an increase in a loss

concepts.section: Tax Planning, Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion
concepts.subsection: Section 97 — the tainted element that is deemed rather than proved
concepts.statement: An impermissible avoidance arrangement needs the purpose test and one tainted element, and the third tainted element is that the arrangement lacks commercial substance or is deemed to lack it, in whole or in part. Section 97 supplies the deeming, in four limbs. Clause (a) is the codification of substance over form: the substance or effect of the arrangement as a whole is inconsistent with, or differs significantly from, the form of its individual steps or a part of them. Clause (b) catches four devices — round trip financing; an accommodating party; elements that have the effect of offsetting or cancelling each other; and a transaction conducted through one or more persons that disguises the value, location, source, ownership or control of the funds it deals with. Clause (c) catches the location of an asset, of a transaction or of the residence of a party where that location has no substantial commercial purpose other than obtaining a tax benefit. Clause (d) catches an arrangement that has no significant effect on the business risks or the net cash flows of any party apart from the effect of the tax benefit itself. Two of those terms are defined further, and both are defined broadly. Round trip financing includes any arrangement in which funds are transferred among the parties through a series of transactions that have no substantial commercial purpose other than the tax benefit, and it is judged without any regard to whether the funds can be traced to funds transferred to or received by any party, to the time or sequence in which they moved, or to the means or mode by which they moved. An accommodating party is a party whose main purpose in participating, directly or indirectly and in whole or in part, is to obtain a tax benefit for the assessee, and it does not matter whether or not that party is a connected person. Section 97(4) then names three matters that are relevant but not sufficient for deciding whether commercial substance is lacking: the period of time for which the arrangement has existed, the fact that taxes were paid under it, and the fact that it provides an exit route. Circular No. 7 of 2017 was asked to turn the first of those into a five to ten year safe period and refused, because a relevant factor is not a sufficient one.

citation.ref: Section 97 with sub-sections 97(2), 97(3) and 97(4) read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — the four deeming limbs, round trip financing judged without regard to tracing, timing or mode, an accommodating party whether connected or not, and the period of existence, payment of taxes and an exit route as relevant but not sufficient factors

concepts.section: Tax Planning, Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion
concepts.subsection: Sections 98 and 99 — what may be done to an arrangement once it has been declared impermissible
concepts.statement: Once an arrangement is declared an impermissible avoidance arrangement the consequence may include denial of a tax benefit under the Act or under a tax treaty, and it may be determined in whatever manner is deemed appropriate in the circumstances. Section 98 then gives illustrations, and they are much wider than a denial of a deduction. Any step in, or a part or the whole of, the arrangement may be disregarded, combined or re-characterised. The arrangement may be treated as if it had never been entered into. An accommodating party may be disregarded altogether, or the accommodating party and another party may be treated as one and the same person. Persons who are connected persons in relation to each other may be deemed to be one and the same person for determining the tax treatment of an amount. Any accrual or receipt of a capital or revenue nature, and any expenditure, deduction, relief or rebate, may be reallocated among the parties. The place of residence of a party, or the situs of an asset or of a transaction, may be treated as being somewhere other than where the arrangement puts it. And the arrangement may be looked through by disregarding any corporate structure. Section 98 adds three re-characterisations expressly: equity may be treated as debt or debt as equity, a capital accrual or receipt may be treated as of a revenue nature or the reverse, and any expenditure, deduction, relief or rebate may be re-characterised. Section 99 gives the same four powers for the narrower purpose of deciding whether a tax benefit exists at all — connected persons may be treated as one person, an accommodating party may be disregarded or merged with another party, and the corporate structure may be looked through. What the machinery does not do is balance the books across taxpayers: the Board's own clarification is that where a consequence is applied in the hands of one participant, a corresponding adjustment will not be made in the hands of another, because Chapter X-A is a deterrent provision and a matching adjustment elsewhere would blunt the deterrence.

citation.ref: Sections 98 and 99 read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — the illustrations of consequence including re-characterisation of equity as debt, reallocation among parties, relocation of residence or situs and looking through a corporate structure, and the refusal of a corresponding adjustment in another participant's hands

concepts.section: Tax Planning, Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion
concepts.subsection: Rule 10U with Circular No. 7 of 2017 — who Chapter X-A never reaches, and what 1 April 2017 actually protects
concepts.statement: Rule 10U keeps four things outside the General Anti-Avoidance Rules. An arrangement where the tax benefit arising in the relevant assessment year, in aggregate to all the parties to the arrangement, does not exceed ₹3 crore. A Foreign Institutional Investor who is an assessee under the Act, who has not taken the benefit of an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A, and who has invested in listed securities or, with the prior permission of the competent authority, in unlisted securities in accordance with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Foreign Institutional Investor) Regulations, 1995. A non-resident, in relation to an investment he makes directly or indirectly in a Foreign Institutional Investor by way of offshore derivative instruments or otherwise. And any income arising or deemed to arise, or received or deemed to be received, from the transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017. That last exclusion is the grandfathering, and it is about INVESTMENTS, not about arrangements: the rule then says expressly that Chapter X-A applies to any other arrangement irrespective of the date on which it was entered into, in respect of a tax benefit obtained from it on or after 1 April 2017. So an arrangement made in 2014 is squarely within the Chapter for a benefit obtained in a later year. Circular No. 7 of 2017 draws the boundary of the grandfathering itself. Shares brought into existence by a split or a consolidation of a grandfathered holding, and bonus shares issued on shares acquired before 1 April 2017 in the hands of the same investor, are grandfathered, as are instruments compulsorily convertible from one form to another on terms fixed at the time of issue. Lease contracts and loan arrangements are not: on accounting principles an investment is an asset held for income by way of dividend, interest or rental and for capital appreciation, and a lease or a loan is by itself not one. The same Circular settles that the ₹3 crore figure is tested on the arrangement or the part of it, in the Indian jurisdiction, for a particular assessment year, and cannot be read as a limit available to a single taxpayer.

citation.ref: Rule 10U with Rules 10UA and 10UB(1) read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — the ₹3 crore aggregate tax benefit floor, the Foreign Institutional Investor and offshore derivative instrument exclusions, grandfathering confined to income from transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017 with splits, consolidations, bonus shares and compulsorily convertible instruments inside it and lease and loan arrangements outside

concepts.subsection: Section 2(47A) — what a virtual digital asset is, and the four things the Government has taken out of it
concepts.statement: Section 2(47A) defines a virtual digital asset in four limbs. The first is any information, code, number or token which is not Indian or foreign currency, generated through cryptographic means or otherwise and by whatever name called, which provides a digital representation of value exchanged with or without consideration, carries the promise or representation of having inherent value or functions as a store of value or a unit of account including in a financial transaction or investment, and can be transferred, stored or traded electronically. The second is a non-fungible token or any other token of similar nature, which the Central Government has to notify; by Notification No. 75/2022 dated 30 June 2022 it specified a token which qualifies to be a virtual digital asset as a non-fungible token, but expressly not one whose transfer results in the transfer of ownership of an underlying tangible asset where that transfer of ownership is legally enforceable. So a token that carries a real, enforceable title to a physical thing is outside the definition, and one that does not is inside it. The third limb is any other digital asset the Central Government notifies. The fourth, added later, is any crypto-asset being a digital representation of value that relies on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or similar technology to validate and secure transactions, whether or not it already falls within the first three limbs. Against that width the Government may exclude assets by notification, and by Notification No. 74/2022 dated 30 June 2022 it excluded three: gift cards and vouchers, being a record usable to obtain goods or services or a discount on them; mileage points, reward points and loyalty cards, being a record given without direct monetary consideration under an award, reward, benefit, loyalty, incentive, rebate or promotional programme and redeemable only for goods, services or a discount; and a subscription to a website, platform or application.

citation.ref: Section 2(47A) read with CBDT Notification No. 75/2022 and Notification No. 74/2022, both dated 30 June 2022 — the four limbs of the definition including the crypto-asset limb, the non-fungible token carve-out for a legally enforceable transfer of an underlying tangible asset, and the exclusion of gift cards and vouchers, reward and loyalty points and subscriptions

concepts.subsection: Section 115BBH — thirty per cent, cost of acquisition and nothing else, and a loss that goes nowhere
concepts.statement: Where the total income of an assessee includes income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset, that income is taxed at 30 per cent under section 115BBH, and four restrictions travel with the rate. In computing the income no deduction is allowed under any provision of the Act for any expenditure or allowance except the cost of acquisition, so the brokerage, the exchange charge and every other cost of transfer is simply lost. No set-off of any loss is allowed against that income, so a business loss, a capital loss and a loss on another virtual digital asset are all equally unavailable against a gain on one. A loss arising from the transfer of a virtual digital asset is not allowed to be set off against income computed under any provision of the Act at all, and is not allowed to be carried forward to a succeeding assessment year, so it dies in the year it arises. And the asset need not be a capital asset: the definition of transfer in section 2(47) applies to a virtual digital asset whether it is a capital asset or not, which is what stops a dealer arguing that section 115BBH cannot reach his stock. Separately the receipt of a virtual digital asset without consideration or for inadequate consideration is taxed in the recipient's hands, because section 56(2)(x) now includes a virtual digital asset within the meaning of property: the aggregate fair market value on the date of receipt is income if it exceeds ₹50,000 where nothing was paid, and the difference is income if the difference exceeds ₹50,000 where something was paid — with the ordinary exclusions from section 56(2)(x), including a gift from a relative, applying as they do to any other property.

citation.ref: Section 115BBH read with sections 2(47) and 56(2)(x) — tax at 30 per cent, no deduction other than the cost of acquisition, no set-off of any loss against the income, a loss on a virtual digital asset neither set off nor carried forward, the asset need not be a capital asset, and the ₹50,000 limit for a receipt without or for inadequate consideration

concepts.subsection: Section 194S — one per cent, two thresholds, and the four sections it displaces
concepts.statement: Any person responsible for paying a resident a sum by way of consideration for the transfer of a virtual digital asset deducts tax at 1 per cent of that sum, at the time of credit to the resident's account or at the time of payment by any mode, whichever is earlier, and a credit to a suspense account or an account by any other name counts as a credit to the payee. Where the consideration is wholly in kind, or is in exchange for another virtual digital asset, or is partly in cash where the cash part is not enough to meet the deduction on the whole transfer, the payer must satisfy himself before releasing the consideration that the tax required to be deducted has been paid. The threshold has two figures rather than one. For a specified person it is ₹50,000 of aggregate consideration in the financial year, and a specified person is an individual or a Hindu undivided family whose total sales, gross receipts or turnover did not exceed ₹1 crore in business or ₹50 lakh in a profession in the financial year immediately preceding the one in which the asset is transferred, or who has no income under the head profits and gains of business or profession at all. For everybody else the threshold is ₹10,000. A specified person is also relieved of section 203A, so he needs no tax deduction account number, and he reports in Form 26QE within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction with a certificate in Form 16E, while an exchange files Form 26QF and any other person Form 26Q quarterly. Where two deduction sections meet, section 194S wins: where tax is deductible under section 194-O as well as under section 194S the deduction is made under section 194S, and once tax has been deducted under section 194S no deduction is required under section 194Q. The Board's guidelines settle three more overlaps — the deduction is on the net consideration after excluding goods and services tax and the charges the deductor levies for his service; a payment gateway need not deduct where the person actually required to deduct has done so; and on an exchange the tax is deducted by the exchange crediting the seller, or by the broker alone where a written agreement says so.

citation.ref: Section 194S with Rules 30, 31 and 31A read with CBDT Circular No. 13/2022 dated 22 June 2022 and Circular No. 14/2022 dated 28 June 2022 — deduction at 1 per cent, thresholds of ₹50,000 for a specified person and ₹10,000 for any other person, section 203A disapplied for a specified person, section 194S in preference to section 194-O, section 194Q displaced once section 194S is applied, and deduction on the consideration net of goods and services tax and the deductor's charges

concepts.subsection: Rule 6G — which form the report goes in, what opinion each carries, and when a tax audit report may be revised
concepts.statement: Rule 6G prescribes three forms and the choice between the first two turns on one fact only. Form 3CA is used where the accounts of the business or profession have already been audited under another law, such as the Companies Act, 2013 or the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008; the tax auditor then does not give an opinion on whether the accounts show a true and fair view, because somebody else already has. He annexes a copy of the audited accounts and of the statutory auditor's report to his own, and the only opinion he gives is whether the particulars in Form 3CD are true and correct, subject to his observations and qualifications.
