Clause (iii) is the narrow special case — salary payable by the Government to a citizen of India for service outside India is deemed to accrue here, though section 10(7) then exempts the allowances and perquisites paid outside India for rendering that service. Clause (v) sources interest by looking at who pays and what the money was used for. Interest payable by the Government is Indian-source. Interest payable by a resident is Indian-source unless the money was borrowed and used for a business or profession carried on outside India or for earning any income from a source outside India, and interest payable by a non-resident is Indian-source only where the money was borrowed and used for a business or profession carried on in India. The payer's residence therefore decides which limb applies, and the use of the money decides the answer inside it.

citation.ref: Section 9(1)(ii) with its Explanation, Section 9(1)(iii) and Section 9(1)(v)(a) to (c), read with Section 10(7)

concepts.subsection: Section 2(47) — What counts as a transfer
concepts.statement: Capital gains are charged on a transfer, and section 2(47) defines transfer inclusively so that it reaches a good deal more than a sale. It takes in sale, exchange and relinquishment of the asset, the extinguishment of any rights in it, its compulsory acquisition under any law, and its conversion into stock-in-trade. Clause (v) is the one that decides most questions — any transaction involving the allowing of the possession of immovable property to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Once the contract is in writing and registered, the price is paid or the buyer is willing to perform, and possession has passed, the transfer has happened for tax, whatever the conveyance deed says or when it is executed. Clause (vi) adds the other route people use to avoid a deed — a transaction which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of immovable property, including becoming a member of a co-operative society or entering into an arrangement of any other manner whatsoever. Legal ownership is simply not the test.

citation.ref: Section 2(47)(i) to (vi) read with Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882

concepts.subsection: Section 49(1) — Cost where the asset came without a purchase
concepts.statement: Where a capital asset came to the assessee on a total or partial partition of a Hindu undivided family, under a gift or will, by succession, inheritance or devolution, or on a distribution on the liquidation or dissolution of a company, firm or other body, section 49(1) deems the cost of acquisition to be the cost to the previous owner who last acquired it by a mode other than those listed, increased by the cost of any improvement. The section does not stop there. Explanation 1(i)(b) to section 2(42A) makes the period for which the previous owner held the asset part of the assessee's holding period, and section 55(2)(b)(ii) lets the assessee substitute the fair market value as on 1 April 2001 where the previous owner acquired the asset before that date, capped by the stamp duty value on that date for land or a building. The value at which the asset came to the assessee — a probate valuation, a gift deed figure, an accounting entry — has no place in the computation at all.

citation.ref: Section 49(1) with Explanation, read with Section 55(2)(b)(ii) and Explanation 1(i)(b) to Section 2(42A)

concepts.subsection: Section 50 — Capital gain on a block of depreciable assets
concepts.statement: Section 50 opens with the words "notwithstanding anything contained in clause (42A) of section 2", and that opening decides the whole section. Where a capital asset forms part of a block on which depreciation has been allowed, the gain is deemed to arise from the transfer of a short-term capital asset however long the asset was held, so no long-term rate and no section 54 style exemption keyed to a long-term gain is available. The computation under section 50(1) is a subtraction, not a matching of individual assets. Take the whole of the consideration for every asset of the block transferred during the year, and deduct three things — expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer, the written down value of the block at the beginning of the previous year, and the actual cost of any asset falling within the block acquired during the previous year. Any excess is the deemed short-term capital gain. Section 50(2) reaches the other case, where the block ceases to exist because every asset in it has gone. In either year no depreciation is allowed on that block, because there is nothing left on which to compute it.

citation.ref: Sections 50(1) and 50(2), read with Section 2(11) and Section 32(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 45(5) — Compensation on compulsory acquisition and the enhancement
concepts.statement: Compulsory acquisition breaks the ordinary rule that a capital gain is charged in the year of transfer, because the money often arrives years after the land goes. Section 45(5)(a) charges the gain on the compensation awarded in the first instance in the previous year in which that compensation, or any part of it, is first received — the year of the award and the year of the transfer are both irrelevant. Section 45(5)(b) then charges any amount by which a court, Tribunal or other authority enhances the compensation as a capital gain of the previous year in which that enhanced amount is received, so an enhancement decreed but unpaid is charged to nothing until it arrives. The Explanation to section 45(5) makes the cost of acquisition and the cost of improvement nil for the enhancement, since both were already used against the original award; expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with getting the enhancement remains deductible under section 48(i). Interest on compensation is a different animal altogether — section 56(2)(viii) puts it under income from other sources in the year of receipt, with a flat fifty per cent deduction under section 57(iv), and it never joins the capital gain.

citation.ref: Sections 45(5)(a) and 45(5)(b) with the Explanation, read with Section 48(i), Section 56(2)(viii) and Section 57(iv)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 28 — What the charge of business income actually covers
concepts.statement: Section 28 is the charging section, and most of its work is done by the clauses that follow the obvious first one. Clause (i) charges the profits of any business or profession carried on during the previous year. Clause (ii) charges compensation on the termination or modification of a managing agency or of any contract relating to the business. Clauses (iiia) to (iiie) charge export incentives — cash assistance against exports, duty drawback, the sale of an import licence and profit on the transfer of a duty entitlement — none of which are trading receipts in any commercial sense and all of which Parliament had to name. Clause (va) charges any sum received under an agreement for not carrying on any business or profession or for not sharing know-how, patent, copyright, trade mark or a similar commercial right, which reversed the older law that a non-compete receipt was a capital receipt. Its own proviso keeps out a sum received for the transfer of a right to manufacture or a sum chargeable under the head capital gains. Clause (vi) charges a sum received under a keyman insurance policy including the bonus, which is exactly what section 10(10D) carves out of its exemption.

citation.ref: Section 28(i), (ii), (iiia) to (iiie), (va) with its proviso and (vi), read with Section 10(10D) and Section 55(2)(a)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 37(1) — The residuary deduction and the four gates
concepts.statement: Section 37(1) allows an expenditure only after it has passed four gates. It must not be described in sections 30 to 36, so a claim that belongs to one of those sections is judged there and cannot be rescued here. It must not be capital expenditure. It must not be personal expenditure of the assessee. And it must be laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business or profession. Three Explanations then close the obvious escapes. Explanation 1 denies any expenditure incurred for a purpose which is an offence or which is prohibited by law, which is why a penalty for breaking a statute is not deductible while a contractual damages payment for a commercial default is. Explanation 2 denies expenditure on corporate social responsibility referred to in section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013. Explanation 3 spells Explanation 1 out to include a benefit or perquisite given to any person where that person's acceptance of it violates a law, rule, regulation or guideline governing him. Section 37(2B) sits beside them and bars advertisement in a souvenir, brochure, tract or pamphlet published by a political party outright.

citation.ref: Section 37(1) with Explanations 1, 2 and 3, and Section 37(2B)

concepts.subsection: Sections 57 and 58 — What other sources allows and what it refuses
concepts.statement: Income from other sources is a real head with a real deduction section, not a bucket taxed gross. Section 57 names some deductions specifically — a collection commission on interest on securities or dividend under clause (i), the repairs, insurance and depreciation on plant or a building let out under clauses (ii) and (iii) where the letting is taxed here, and fifty per cent of interest on compensation under clause (iv) — and then clause (iii) adds the general one, any other expenditure, not being capital expenditure, laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of making or earning such income. That general clause is what allows interest on money borrowed to buy an investment whose income is taxed under this head. Section 58 is the matching list of refusals. Clause (1)(a)(i) bars personal expenses, clause (1)(a)(ii) bars interest paid outside India without deduction of tax, clause (1)(a)(iii) picks up section 40(a) style disallowances, and clause (2) applies section 40A here as well. Sub-section (4) is the hardest of them — no deduction of any expenditure or allowance at all against winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, races, card games and other games of any sort or from gambling or betting, so the cost of winning is simply not recognised.

citation.ref: Sections 57(i) to (iv), Section 58(1)(a), Section 58(2) and Section 58(4), read with the Explanation to Section 2(24)(ix)

concepts.section: Aggregation of Income, Set Off or Carry Forward of Losses
concepts.subsection: Sections 70, 71 and 74 — Setting off and carrying a capital loss
concepts.statement: A capital loss travels along one road and it is a narrow one. Section 70(2) lets a short-term capital loss be set off against income under the head capital gains in respect of any capital asset, so it may go against a long-term gain as freely as against a short-term one. Section 70(3) is the restriction, and it runs the other way — a long-term capital loss may be set off only against a long-term capital gain. Section 71(3) then closes the head off entirely: a loss under capital gains cannot be set against income under any other head, whatever is left of it, which is why a capital loss can never reduce salary, house property or business income. Whatever survives is carried forward under section 74 for eight assessment years immediately succeeding, and the same asymmetry follows it — a carried short-term loss may be set against any capital gain, a carried long-term loss only against a long-term gain. Section 80 puts one condition on the carry forward, that the loss be determined in a return furnished within the time allowed under section 139(1), and section 74 requires the same business or asset in no sense at all, which is where it differs from section 72.

citation.ref: Sections 70(2), 70(3), 71(3) and 74(1) and 74(2), read with Section 80 and Section 139(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 143(1) — Intimation and the adjustments it may make
concepts.statement: Processing under section 143(1) is not a scrutiny and it is not a rubber stamp either. The return is taken, the total income or loss is computed after a closed list of adjustments in section 143(1)(a), tax, interest and fee are worked out, and an intimation follows which is deemed to be a notice of demand under section 156 where any sum is payable. The list is what must be known. Clause (i) an arithmetical error in the return; clause (ii) an incorrect claim apparent from any information in the return itself; clause (iii) disallowance of a loss claimed where the return of the year in which the loss arose was furnished beyond the due date under section 139(1); clause (iv) disallowance of expenditure or increase in income indicated in the audit report but not taken into account in the return; and clause (v) disallowance of a deduction claimed under section 10AA or under the deductions-in-respect-of-certain-incomes heading of Chapter VI-A where the return is furnished beyond the due date. Nothing outside that list may be done, so no question of fact and no view about whether an expense was excessive belongs here. The first proviso bars any adjustment unless an intimation of it is given to the assessee in writing or electronically, and the second requires the response to be considered, the adjustment being made if none comes within thirty days. The intimation itself must go within nine months from the end of the financial year in which the return is furnished.

citation.ref: Section 143(1)(a) clauses (i) to (v) with its first and second provisos, read with Section 156

concepts.subsection: Section 142 — Inquiry before assessment and the special audit
concepts.statement: Section 142(1) gives the Assessing Officer three powers before he assesses. Clause (i) is a notice requiring a person who has not made a return within the time allowed under section 139(1) to furnish one — no escapement need be alleged and section 148 is not involved. Clause (ii) is a notice to produce such accounts or documents as he may require. Clause (iii) is a notice to furnish information in writing, including a statement of assets and liabilities. Two provisos fence them. A statement of assets and liabilities not included in the accounts may be required only with the previous approval of the Joint Commissioner, and no accounts may be required relating to a period more than three years prior to the previous year. Section 142(2A) is the heavier power. Having regard to the nature and complexity of the accounts, the volume of the accounts, doubts about their correctness, the multiplicity of transactions or the specialised nature of the business, and the interests of the revenue, the Assessing Officer may direct the assessee to get the accounts audited by an accountant nominated by the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner or Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. It needs that authority's previous approval, and the proviso requires a reasonable opportunity of being heard for the assessee — his consent is nowhere in the section. Since 1 June 2007 the expenses of the audit are determined by that authority and paid by the Central Government under section 142(2D).

citation.ref: Section 142(1) clauses (i) to (iii) with provisos (a) and (b), and Sections 142(2A), 142(2C) and 142(2D)

concepts.subsection: Section 144 — Best judgement assessment
concepts.statement: Section 144(1) is triggered by any one of four failures — failure to make the return required under section 139(1) and no return under section 139(4) or 139(5) either, failure to comply with all the terms of a notice under section 142(1), failure to comply with a direction for a special audit under section 142(2A), or, having made a return, failure to comply with all the terms of a notice under section 143(2). On any of them the Assessing Officer shall, after taking into account all relevant material he has gathered, make the assessment to the best of his judgement. Best judgement means an honest estimate resting on some material, not a guess and not a punishment, and the assessment is appealable like any other. Two provisos govern the hearing. The first says no such assessment shall be made without giving the assessee an opportunity of being heard by serving a notice calling on him to show cause why the assessment should not be completed to the best of the officer's judgement. The second removes that requirement altogether where a notice under section 142(1) has already been issued before the assessment is made, on the footing that the assessee has already been asked and has already not answered. No approval of any superior officer is required — that belongs to section 153D, which governs a search assessment.

citation.ref: Section 144(1) with its first and second provisos, read with Sections 142(1), 143(2) and 153D

concepts.subsection: Sections 148 and 148A — The stage that comes before a reassessment notice
concepts.statement: Reassessment stopped being a matter of the officer's private reasons in 2021. Section 148 now permits a notice only where there is information which suggests that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment, only after the procedure in section 148A has been followed, and only with the prior approval of the specified authority under section 151. Section 148A is the pre-notice stage. The Assessing Officer serves a show cause notice on the assessee setting out the information relied on and giving a period specified in the notice to explain why a notice under section 148 should not be issued; the assessee replies; and the Assessing Officer then passes an order under section 148A(3), on the material on record and that reply, deciding whether it is a fit case. This replaced the practice built on GKN Driveshafts, under which the assessee filed a return, asked for the reasons recorded and objected afterwards — the objection is now heard before the notice rather than after it. Cases where a search is initiated or books are requisitioned are outside section 148A and go down the block assessment route in section 158BA instead.

citation.ref: Section 148 with its provisos and Section 148A as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 September 2024, read with Sections 151 and 158BA

concepts.subsection: Section 154 — Rectification of a mistake apparent from the record
concepts.statement: Section 154 lets an income-tax authority amend any order it has passed, any intimation under section 143(1) and any intimation under section 200A(1) or 206CB(1), to rectify a mistake apparent from the record. Four things fix its shape. The mistake must be apparent — an error of fact or of law that stares from the record and needs no long argument; a point on which two views are reasonably possible is outside the section, which is what T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers decided. The power runs both ways, and section 154(2)(b) expressly allows an amendment on an application made by the assessee, so it is not confined to the authority's own motion. Section 154(3) requires notice and a hearing before any amendment that has the effect of enhancing an assessment or reducing a refund. And section 154(7) sets the outer limit — no amendment after the expiry of four years from the end of the financial year in which the order sought to be amended was passed, a period measured from the order and not from the assessment year. Where the assessee applies, section 154(8) requires the authority to pass an order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is received.

citation.ref: Sections 154(1), 154(2)(b), 154(3), 154(7) and 154(8), read with T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers (1971) 82 ITR 50 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Section 264 — Revision at the assessee's instance
concepts.statement: Section 264 is the assessee's revision and section 263 is the revenue's, and almost every difference between them follows from that. The Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may act either on his own motion or on an application by the assessee, may call for the record of any proceeding under the Act, and may pass such order thereon, not being an order prejudicial to the assessee, as he thinks fit — so the worst outcome of a section 264 application is that it is refused. There is no requirement that the order be erroneous or that it be prejudicial to the revenue; those words belong to section 263. The power is wide enough to grant relief on a claim that was never made in the return, the restriction in Goetze (India) being a restriction on the Assessing Officer and not on the revisional authority. Section 264(3) gives the assessee one year from the date on which the order was communicated to him or he otherwise came to know of it, with power to condone delay, and section 264(5) requires a fee of five hundred rupees. Section 264(4) is the bar — no revision while the time for an appeal has not expired and the right of appeal has not been waived, and none where the order has been made the subject of an appeal; once the appeal time has run out unused, the bar lifts. Section 264(6) requires the order within one year from the end of the financial year in which the application is made.

citation.ref: Sections 264(1) to 264(6), read with Section 263(1) and Goetze (India) Ltd v. Commissioner of Income Tax (2006) 284 ITR 323 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Sections 260A and 261 — Appeal to the High Court and to the Supreme Court
concepts.statement: The Appellate Tribunal is the final fact-finding authority, and everything above it is about law only. Section 260A(1) gives an appeal to the High Court from every order passed in appeal by the Tribunal, but only if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law. Section 260A(2)(a) allows one hundred and twenty days from the date the order is received, section 260A(3) requires the High Court itself to formulate the question where it is satisfied one exists, and section 260A(4) confines the hearing to that question, with a proviso letting the court hear the appeal on any other substantial question of law for reasons recorded. Section 260B requires a bench of not less than two judges. A disagreement about how the Tribunal weighed the evidence is not a substantial question of law, and a finding of fact stands unless it is perverse in the sense of resting on no evidence or on irrelevant material. Section 261 then allows an appeal to the Supreme Court from a judgment of the High Court delivered on an appeal under section 260A, and only where the High Court certifies the case to be a fit one — it is not a route that bypasses the High Court. Beside all this sits section 254(2), which lets the Tribunal rectify a mistake apparent from the record and is not a rehearing.

citation.ref: Sections 260A(1) to 260A(4), Section 260B and Section 261, read with Section 254(2)

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 199 and Rule 37BA — Who gets credit for tax deducted, and in which year
concepts.statement: Deducting tax and getting credit for it are two different questions, and section 199 answers the second. Sub-section (1) treats the tax deducted and paid as a payment of tax on behalf of the person from whose income the deduction was made. Sub-section (3) leaves the details to rules, and Rule 37BA does the real work in two sub-rules. Rule 37BA(2) deals with the wrong person — where the whole or a part of the income on which tax has been deducted is assessable in the hands of somebody other than the deductee, credit goes to that other person, provided the deductee files a declaration with the deductor naming him and the deductor reports it in the statement. That is how a clubbed income, a joint holding or an income assessed in a successor's hands is dealt with. Rule 37BA(3) deals with the wrong year — credit is given for the assessment year for which the income is assessable, and where the income is assessable over more than one year, credit is allowed across those years in the same proportion in which the income is assessable. Credit therefore follows the income, never the deduction, which is why an advance taxed over two years splits its credit over the same two years.

citation.ref: Sections 199(1) and 199(3), read with Rule 37BA(2) and Rule 37BA(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 206AA — Deduction at a higher rate where the PAN is not furnished
concepts.statement: Section 206AA begins with a non obstante clause and lays the duty on the deductor, not on the payee. Where the deductee fails to furnish his permanent account number to the person responsible for deducting, tax shall be deducted at the highest of three figures — the rate specified in the relevant provision of the Act, the rate or rates in force, and twenty per cent. Sub-section (6) treats a permanent account number that is invalid or does not belong to the deductee as one that was never furnished, so a wrong number is no better than none. Sub-section (2) makes a declaration under section 197A invalid unless it carries the number, and sub-section (4) forbids the grant of a certificate under section 197 unless the application carries it, which closes both escape routes at once. The consequence of getting this wrong falls on the payer — a short deduction leaves him an assessee in default under section 201(1), with interest under section 201(1A) and disallowance under section 40(a)(ia). Sub-section (7) is the only relief, taking certain payments to a non-resident or a foreign company out of the section where the conditions in Rule 37BC are met.

citation.ref: Sections 206AA(1), 206AA(2), 206AA(4), 206AA(6) and 206AA(7), read with Rule 37BC and Sections 201(1) and 201(1A)

concepts.section: Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
concepts.subsection: Article 5 of a treaty — Permanent establishment and its three routes
concepts.statement: A treaty lets India tax a foreign enterprise's business profits only through a permanent establishment, so Article 5 decides whether Article 7 ever opens. The general definition in Article 5(1) is a fixed place of business through which the business of the enterprise is wholly or partly carried on, and Article 5(2) gives the familiar illustrative list — a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory, a workshop, a mine or a quarry. Article 5(3) is the construction clause, which makes a building site, construction, assembly or installation project a permanent establishment once it lasts longer than the period the particular treaty names, and that period differs from treaty to treaty. Article 5(4) is the exclusion, taking out a place maintained solely for storage, display or delivery of goods, solely for processing by another enterprise, solely for purchasing goods or collecting information, or solely for any other activity of a preparatory or auxiliary character. Article 5(5) is the agency route, which needs no premises at all — a person acting on behalf of the enterprise who habitually concludes contracts, or habitually plays the principal role leading to their conclusion, is a permanent establishment. Article 5(6) takes back out an agent of independent status acting in the ordinary course of his own business, such as a broker or a general commission agent.

citation.ref: Article 5(1) to 5(6) of India's double taxation avoidance agreements on the OECD and UN Model pattern, read with Article 7 and Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Rule 10CA — The arm's length range and the use of multiple year data
concepts.statement: Comparables almost never give one number, and Rule 10CA is the machinery that turns a spread of them into an answer. It applies only where the most appropriate method is the comparable uncontrolled price method, the resale price method, the cost plus method or the transactional net margin method, and only where the dataset holds six or more entries. Where both are true, the arm's length range is the set of data points lying from the thirty-fifth percentile to the sixty-fifth percentile of the dataset arranged in ascending order. Rule 10CA(4) then gives the test — if the price at which the international transaction has actually been undertaken is within that range, it shall be deemed to be the arm's length price and no adjustment is made. Rule 10CA(5) gives the consequence of failing it, and it is not the nearest edge of the range — where the transaction price is outside the range, the arm's length price is the median of the dataset. Rule 10CA(7) fixes how a percentile is read: multiply the number of data points by the percentile, and where the product is not a whole number take the data point at the next higher whole number, while where it is a whole number take the average of that data point and the one after it. Rule 10CA(2) and 10CA(3) allow the weighted average of up to three years of the comparable's data where the enterprise's own data for the current year is not available at the time the return is furnished. Where the dataset holds fewer than six entries the range has no application at all, and the arithmetic mean under section 92C(2) with the tolerance band in its second proviso is what governs instead.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(2) to Rule 10CA(7) read with Section 92C(1) and Section 92C(2) with its second proviso

concepts.subsection: Section 92CE — The secondary adjustment and the money that stayed abroad
concepts.statement: A primary adjustment fixes the profit figure on paper; the money is still sitting with the associated enterprise abroad. Section 92CE exists to reach that money. Sub-section (1) names five triggers, and only the first is voluntary — an adjustment made suo motu by the assessee in his return, an adjustment made by the Assessing Officer and accepted by the assessee, an adjustment determined by an advance pricing agreement under section 92CC, an adjustment made as per the safe harbour rules under section 92CB, and an adjustment arising from a resolution under a mutual agreement procedure under a treaty. Sub-section (2) is the machinery. Where the primary adjustment increases the total income or reduces the loss, the excess money or part of it which is available with the associated enterprise, if not repatriated to India within the time prescribed by Rule 10CB, shall be deemed to be an advance made by the assessee to that enterprise, and interest on that deemed advance is computed in the manner prescribed and charged year after year until the money comes home. India's design is a deemed advance bearing imputed interest, not the deemed dividend some other countries use, and it never taxes the primary adjustment a second time. Sub-section (2A) offers the way out — instead of repatriating, the assessee may pay a one-time additional tax on the excess money at the rate specified there, after which no further interest is imputed, no credit for that tax is available to him or to anybody else, and no deduction of it is allowed.

citation.ref: Sections 92CE(1), 92CE(2), 92CE(2A) and 92CE(2B), read with Rule 10CB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and Sections 92CB and 92CC

concepts.subsection: Section 92CB — Safe harbour, and how it differs from an advance pricing agreement
concepts.statement: Section 92CB(1) says the determination of the arm's length price under section 92C or section 92CA shall be subject to safe harbour rules, and the Explanation defines safe harbour as circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee. Two words in that Explanation carry the section — accept, and declared. It is not a margin the officer imposes and it is not a cap on an adjustment he is otherwise making; where the option is validly exercised the declared price is simply taken, and no determination of the arm's length price is made for that transaction at all. The rules are in Rule 10TA to Rule 10TG. The assessee exercises the option in Form 3CEFA for the eligible international transactions and the eligible assessees the rules describe, and the Assessing Officer or Transfer Pricing Officer may hold the option invalid, with an appeal against that to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner whose decision is final. Safe harbour and an advance pricing agreement are not two sizes of the same thing. An agreement under section 92CC is negotiated between the Board and one taxpayer for a stated set of transactions, binds both sides for the years specified and may be rolled back under section 92CD; safe harbour is a set of margins already notified in the Rules, open to anybody who fits the description and negotiated with nobody. A price fixed under the safe harbour rules is still a primary adjustment for the purposes of section 92CE(1)(d).

citation.ref: Section 92CB(1) with its Explanation, read with Rules 10TA to 10TG of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, and Sections 92CC, 92CD and 92CE(1)(d)

concepts.subsection: Section 9A — Fund management from India without a business connection
concepts.statement: Before section 9A, a global fund that let its manager sit in India risked two things at once — the manager's activity being read as a business connection under section 9(1)(i), and the fund itself being called resident in India. Section 9A removes both, and removes nothing else. Sub-section (1) says that notwithstanding section 9(1)(i), the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager acting on behalf of an eligible investment fund shall not constitute a business connection in India of that fund. Sub-section (2) says the fund shall not be said to be resident in India merely because the manager undertaking that activity on its behalf is situated in India. Neither sub-section is an exemption. Income of the fund that has an independent Indian source is charged as it always was, and section 9A(3) and 9A(4) hedge the relief with conditions on both sides. The fund must be a non-resident, resident of a country with which India has an agreement or a notified country, must not carry on or control a business in India, must be broad based in the way the sub-section describes, and must satisfy the corpus, membership and participation tests. The manager must not be an employee of the fund or a connected person, must be registered as a fund manager or portfolio manager or investment adviser under the relevant regulations, and must be paid at arm's length for the fund management activity. That last condition is the point most often missed — the manager's own remuneration is Indian income and is taxed here in full.

citation.ref: Sections 9A(1), 9A(2), 9A(3) and 9A(4), read with Section 9(1)(i) and Section 6(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 115JH — The year a foreign company first becomes resident in India
concepts.statement: A foreign company can become resident in India under section 6(3) because its place of effective management is here, and the moment it does, the whole Act begins to apply to a company that has never kept its records for the Act. It has no written down value computed under section 32, no brought forward loss determined under this Act, no unabsorbed depreciation carried under section 32(2), and no history of collection and recovery here. Section 115JH is the transition provision written for exactly that year. Where a foreign company is said to be resident in India in any previous year and it was not resident in India in any of the previous years preceding that year, then notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Act, the provisions relating to the computation of total income, treatment of unabsorbed depreciation, set off or carry forward and set off of losses, collection and recovery and special provisions relating to avoidance of tax shall apply with such exceptions, modifications and adaptations as may be notified by the Central Government. Sub-section (2) requires that notification to be laid before each House of Parliament. Sub-section (3) is the sanction — where in any previous year any of the conditions specified in the notification is not complied with, the benefit of the exceptions, modifications and adaptations is denied, and the Act applies to that company without them as if the notification had never been made. The section eases the mechanics of a transition; it exempts nothing and it charges nothing.

citation.ref: Sections 115JH(1), 115JH(2) and 115JH(3), read with Section 6(3) and Section 32(2)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Sections 44BBA and 44BBB — Aircraft operations and turnkey power projects
concepts.statement: Both sections deem a percentage of a stated aggregate to be the profits of a non-resident, and the work in an exam is always in the aggregate rather than the percentage. Section 44BBA covers a non-resident engaged in the business of operation of aircraft, and its aggregate has two limbs that are deliberately not symmetrical. The first limb takes the amount paid or payable, whether in or out of India, to the assessee or to any person on his behalf, on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods from any place in India — where the money was paid does not matter, because the carriage started here. The second limb takes the amount received or deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the assessee on account of the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods from any place outside India — here the carriage did not start in India, so the only connecting factor left is receipt in India. A sum for an inbound carriage that is also received abroad answers neither limb and stays out of the aggregate altogether. Section 44BB for mineral oil services and section 44B for shipping are built on the same two-limb pattern with their own connecting factors. Section 44BBB is different in shape — it covers a foreign company engaged in the business of civil construction or the erection, testing or commissioning of plant or machinery in connection with a turnkey power project approved by the Central Government and financed under an international aid programme, and takes a percentage of the amount paid or payable to it for that work.

citation.ref: Sections 44BBA(1) and 44BBA(2)(a) and (b), and Section 44BBB(1), read with Sections 44B and 44BB(2)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 44BB — Services and plant for prospecting for or extraction of mineral oils
concepts.statement: Section 44BB(1) covers a non-resident engaged in the business of providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used or to be used in, the prospecting for or extraction or production of mineral oils, and deems a percentage of the aggregate in sub-section (2) to be his profits chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession. Sub-section (2) has the same two-limb shape as sections 44B and 44BBA and the same asymmetry. Clause (a) takes the amount paid or payable, whether in or out of India, to the assessee or to any person on his behalf on account of the provision of such services or facilities or the supply of such plant and machinery used or to be used in the prospecting for or extraction or production of mineral oils in India. Clause (b) takes the amount received or deemed to be received in India by or on behalf of the assessee on account of the provision of such services or facilities or supply of such plant and machinery used or to be used in the prospecting for or extraction or production of mineral oils outside India. Work outside India paid for outside India therefore falls in neither clause. Sub-section (3) is the escape from the presumption — the assessee may claim lower profits, but only if he keeps and maintains the books and other documents required by section 44AA, gets his accounts audited and furnishes the report under section 44AB, in which case the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment under section 143(3). The proviso to sub-section (1) shuts the section out altogether where the profits are computed under section 42, section 44DA, section 115A or section 293A.

citation.ref: Section 44BB(1) with its proviso, Section 44BB(2)(a) and (b), and Section 44BB(3), read with Sections 44AA, 44AB and 143(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 9(1)(vi) — Royalty as Explanation 2 defines it
concepts.statement: Royalty is not defined by what it feels like; it is defined by a list. Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi) means consideration for six things — the transfer of all or any rights, including the granting of a licence, in respect of a patent, invention, model, design, secret formula or process or trade mark or similar property; the imparting of any information concerning the working of or the use of such property; the use of such property; the imparting of any information concerning technical, industrial, commercial or scientific knowledge, experience or skill; the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, but not including the amounts referred to in section 44BB; and the transfer of all or any rights in respect of any copyright, literary, artistic or scientific work including films or video tapes for use in connection with television or tapes for use in connection with radio broadcasting. That last clause carries the one exclusion worth memorising — it does not include consideration for the sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films. Three later Explanations shut escape routes. Explanation 4 says the transfer of all or any rights includes and has always included the transfer of a right for the use of or the right to use computer software, including the granting of a licence, irrespective of the medium. Explanation 5 says it does not matter whether the payer has possession or control of the right, property or information, whether he uses it directly, or where it is located. Explanation 6 says process includes transmission by satellite, cable, optic fibre or any similar technology, whether or not it is secret. What none of them can do is change a treaty: section 90(2) lets the assessee take the treaty definition where it is more beneficial, which is the ground on which Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence held that payment for a copyrighted article rather than the copyright is not royalty.

citation.ref: Explanation 2 clauses (i) to (v), Explanation 4, Explanation 5 and Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(vi), read with Section 90(2) and Engineering Analysis Centre of Excellence P Ltd v. CIT (2021) 432 ITR 471 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Sections 115AC and 115ACA — Bonds and global depository receipts
concepts.statement: The two sections look alike and are written for opposite people. Section 115AC applies to a non-resident, and covers three kinds of income — interest on bonds of an Indian company issued in accordance with a scheme notified by the Central Government or on bonds of a public sector company sold by the Government, dividends on global depository receipts of an Indian company or of a public sector company issued under such a scheme and purchased in foreign currency, and long-term capital gains on the transfer of those bonds or receipts. Section 115ACA applies to a resident, and not to every resident — the assessee must be an individual who is resident in India and who is or was an employee of an Indian company engaged in a specified knowledge based industry or service, or of its subsidiary engaged in such an industry, and the receipts must have been issued under an employees' stock option scheme and purchased in foreign currency. Below that difference the machinery is the same. No deduction under any of sections 28 to 44C or under clause (i) or clause (iii) of section 57 is allowed in computing the income, no deduction under Chapter VI-A is allowed from it, and the first and second provisos to section 48 — the foreign currency conversion rule and indexation — do not apply in computing the long-term capital gain. Section 115AC(4) then relieves a non-resident of filing a return under section 139(1) where his total income consisted only of income of the kinds that section covers and tax has been deducted from it.

citation.ref: Sections 115AC(1) to 115AC(4) and Sections 115ACA(1) to 115ACA(3) with its Explanation, read with the first and second provisos to Section 48

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Sections 196A to 196D — The collection sections written for particular non-residents
concepts.statement: Section 195 is the general provision for a payment to a non-resident, and sections 196A to 196D are four special ones that take particular payments out of it. Section 196A covers income in respect of units of a Mutual Fund specified under section 10(23D) or of the Specified Undertaking of the Unit Trust of India paid to a non-resident who is not a company or to a foreign company, with deduction at the time of credit or of payment, whichever is earlier, and a proviso allowing the treaty rate where a tax residency certificate is furnished. Section 196B covers income from units referred to in section 115AB and the long-term capital gain on their transfer paid to an offshore fund. Section 196C covers income by way of interest or dividends on bonds or global depository receipts referred to in section 115AC and the long-term capital gain on their transfer, paid to a non-resident. Section 196D covers income in respect of securities referred to in section 115AD(1)(a) paid to a Foreign Institutional Investor, again with a proviso for the treaty rate on a tax residency certificate. The distinction that decides questions is inside section 196D itself. Sub-section (1) requires deduction from the income in respect of the securities, and sub-section (2) says in terms that no deduction shall be made from any income by way of capital gains arising from the transfer of those securities. The investor is not outside the chapter; one stream is deducted from and the other is not, and the gain is charged in the assessment instead.

citation.ref: Sections 196A, 196B, 196C, 196D(1) and 196D(2), read with Sections 115AB, 115AC, 115AD(1)(a) and 195

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: The Multilateral Instrument and the principal purpose test
concepts.statement: The Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting does not sit beside India's treaties; it modifies them. Where both parties have listed a treaty as a covered tax agreement and their positions match, the Convention's terms are read into that treaty and applied as part of it. Two of its articles do most of the work. Article 6 rewrites the preamble to say the parties intend to eliminate double taxation without creating opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through tax evasion or avoidance, including through treaty-shopping arrangements. Article 7(1) is the principal purpose test, and its words are the exam — notwithstanding any provisions of a covered tax agreement, a benefit under that agreement shall not be granted in respect of an item of income or capital if it is reasonable to conclude, having regard to all relevant facts and circumstances, that obtaining that benefit was one of the principal purposes of any arrangement or transaction that resulted directly or indirectly in that benefit, unless it is established that granting it in these circumstances would be in accordance with the object and purpose of the relevant provisions of that agreement. One of the principal purposes is a far lower bar than the sole or the dominant purpose, and the burden then shifts to the taxpayer on the object-and-purpose limb. The test is a treaty rule and works without Chapter X-A being invoked at all, which matters because section 90(2A) makes Chapter X-A apply to an assessee even where it is not beneficial to him, and because section 90(4) makes a tax residency certificate a condition of claiming treaty relief rather than proof of entitlement to it.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Article 6(1) and Article 7(1) of the Convention, read with Sections 90(1), 90(2A) and 90(4) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.section: Incomes which do not form part of Total Income
concepts.subsection: Section 10 — An exclusion from total income is not a deduction from it
concepts.statement: Section 10 opens with the words "in computing the total income of a previous year of any person, any income falling within any of the following clauses shall not be included", and everything that puzzles students about it follows from those words. The income never enters total income at all, so it is not something taken out later. A Chapter VI-A deduction works the other way — under section 80A(1) it is allowed from the gross total income, and under section 80A(2) the aggregate of such deductions can never exceed the gross total income, which is only a sensible rule because the income was in the total in the first place. Three consequences follow from the difference and they are what an examiner tests. Expenditure incurred in relation to income which does not form part of total income is disallowed by section 14A, because it is being spent to earn something the Act is not charging. An amount excluded by section 10 is not part of gross total income, so it neither creates room for a Chapter VI-A deduction nor is reduced by one. And a partner's position illustrates all of it: section 10(2A) excludes his share in the total income of a firm separately assessed as such, with the Explanation fixing that share as the same proportion of the firm's total income as his share of profits under the deed bears to those profits, while section 28(v) charges the interest, salary, bonus, commission or remuneration he receives from the firm as his business income to the extent it was allowed to the firm under section 40(b). One stream is outside his total income and the other is squarely inside it.

citation.ref: Opening words of Section 10 and Section 10(2A) with its Explanation, read with Section 28(v), Section 14A(1) and Sections 80A(1) and 80A(2)

concepts.section: Assessment of Trusts and Institutions, Political Parties and Other Special Entities
concepts.subsection: Section 13 — Specified persons and the dealings that are deemed to benefit them
concepts.statement: Section 13(1)(c) withdraws the exemption where any income or property of a trust is used or applied, directly or indirectly, for the benefit of a person referred to in section 13(3), and section 13(2) saves the Assessing Officer from having to prove a benefit by deeming eight dealings to be one. Money lent to such a person without either adequate security or adequate interest or both. Land, building or other property made available for his use without charging adequate rent or other compensation. An amount paid to him by way of salary, allowance or otherwise for services rendered to the trust which is in excess of what may reasonably be paid for those services — the excess is what is caught, so a market-rate salary for real work is not hit at all. Services of the trust made available to him without adequate remuneration. Property purchased from him for more than adequate consideration, or sold to him for less. Income or property diverted to him in excess of one thousand rupees. And funds invested for any period in a concern in which he has a substantial interest. Section 13(3) is the list of who those persons are — the author of the trust or founder of the institution, a person whose total contribution up to the end of the relevant previous year exceeds fifty thousand rupees, a member of a Hindu undivided family which is such an author or contributor, a trustee or manager, a relative of any of them, and a concern in which any of them has a substantial interest, being not less than twenty per cent of the voting power in the case of a company. Section 13(1)(d) sits alongside and withdraws the exemption for funds invested otherwise than in the modes specified in section 11(5).

citation.ref: Sections 13(1)(c), 13(1)(d), 13(2)(a) to (h) and 13(3)(a) to (e), read with Section 11(5) and the Explanation to Section 13

concepts.section: Assessment of Trusts and Institutions, Political Parties and Other Special Entities
concepts.subsection: Section 13A — What a political party is exempt on, and on what conditions
concepts.statement: Section 13A exempts a political party registered under section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 on four things and no more — income which is chargeable under the head income from house property, income which is chargeable under the head income from other sources, income by way of capital gains, and income by way of voluntary contributions received from any person. Business income is not on that list, so a party that runs a trade is taxed on it like anybody else. The exemption is conditional, and the conditions are cumulative. The party must keep and maintain such books of account and other documents as would enable the Assessing Officer to properly deduce its income. It must keep a record of each voluntary contribution above the amount specified in the clause, with the name and address of the person who made it, other than a contribution by way of an electoral bond. Its accounts must be audited by an accountant as defined in the Explanation to section 288(2). And it must not receive a donation exceeding two thousand rupees otherwise than by an account payee cheque or draft, through a bank account or through an electoral bond. Two further conditions sit in the provisos — the treasurer or an authorised person must submit the report under section 29C(3) of that Act for the financial year, and the return of income must be furnished under section 139(4B) on or before the due date under section 139(1). Missing the return deadline costs the exemption outright.

citation.ref: Section 13A clauses (a) to (d) with its first, second and third provisos, read with Section 139(4B) and Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951

concepts.subsection: Section 44C — Head office expenditure of a non-resident and the adjusted total income
concepts.statement: A non-resident running a branch in India inevitably carries a share of the head office abroad, and section 44C caps what that share may cost the Indian exchequer. Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in sections 28 to 43A, no allowance is made in computing the income chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession in respect of so much of the expenditure in the nature of head office expenditure as is in excess of the amount computed under the section. The amount allowed is the lower of two figures — a fixed percentage of the adjusted total income, and the amount of head office expenditure attributable to the business or profession in India. The definition of adjusted total income in the Explanation is where the marks are. It means the total income computed in accordance with the provisions of the Act without giving effect to the allowance referred to in the section itself, and without giving effect to the unabsorbed depreciation allowance carried forward under section 32(2), the unabsorbed capital expenditure on scientific research, and the brought forward losses under section 72(1), section 73(3), section 74(1) and 74(3) and section 74A(3). Every one of those is added back, so a branch sitting on a large brought forward loss does not thereby shrink its head office allowance. The Explanation also defines head office expenditure as executive and general administration expenditure incurred outside India, including rent, rates, taxes, repairs or insurance of premises used for the business, salary and allowances of an employee or officer employed in head office management, travelling of any such employee, and such other matters connected with executive and general administration as may be prescribed.

citation.ref: Section 44C with clauses (a) and (b) and the Explanation defining adjusted total income and head office expenditure, read with Sections 32(2), 72(1) and 73(3)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 35AD and Section 73A — Specified businesses and the loss they throw off
concepts.statement: Section 35AD(1) allows a deduction of the whole of any expenditure of a capital nature incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of a specified business carried on by the assessee, in the previous year in which the expenditure is incurred, and the specified businesses are the ones listed in section 35AD(8) with their own commencement dates — a cold chain facility, a warehousing facility for agricultural produce, a cross-country natural gas or crude or petroleum oil pipeline network, a hospital with the prescribed number of beds, a hotel of the prescribed category, developing and building a housing project under a notified scheme, and the others named there. Section 35AD(2) requires the business not to be set up by splitting up or the reconstruction of an existing business and not to be set up by the transfer of previously used plant and machinery beyond the permitted proportion. Section 35AD(4) bars any deduction under the deductions-in-respect-of-certain-incomes heading of Chapter VI-A in relation to that same specified business, for that or any other year, once a deduction under this section has been claimed and allowed. Section 35AD(7A) then ties the asset down for eight years beginning with the year of its acquisition or construction, and section 35AD(7B) makes the deduction already allowed, reduced by the depreciation that would have been allowable under section 32 had no deduction under this section been given, the business income of the year in which the asset is put to any other use. A hundred per cent write-off of capital cost usually produces a loss, and section 73A is the provision for it — a loss of a specified business may be set off only against the profits of another specified business, and section 73A(2) carries whatever is left forward with no limit on the number of assessment years.

citation.ref: Sections 35AD(1), 35AD(2), 35AD(4), 35AD(7A) and 35AD(7B), read with Sections 73A(1) and 73A(2) and Section 80A(1)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 43(1) — Actual cost and the Explanations that cut it down
concepts.statement: Section 43(1) defines actual cost as the actual cost of the asset to the assessee, reduced by that portion of the cost, if any, as has been met directly or indirectly by any other person or authority. Everything else in depreciation flows from that one number, and five riders decide what it is. The proviso, inserted with effect from assessment year 2018-19, keeps out of actual cost any expenditure for the acquisition of an asset in respect of which a payment or the aggregate of payments made to a person in a day, otherwise than by an account payee cheque or an account payee bank draft or through a bank account or a prescribed electronic mode, exceeds ten thousand rupees. Explanation 1 deals with an asset used for scientific research and afterwards brought into the business — actual cost is the actual cost as reduced by the deduction already allowed under section 35. Explanation 3 lets the Assessing Officer, with the previous approval of the Joint Commissioner, substitute the amount he determines as the actual cost where an asset previously used by another person is acquired and he is satisfied the main purpose was the reduction of tax by claiming depreciation on an enhanced cost. Explanation 8 settles a question that used to be litigated — interest paid or payable in connection with the acquisition of an asset, for any period after the asset is first put to use, shall not be included and shall never be deemed to have been included in the actual cost, so it is a revenue deduction under section 36(1)(iii) instead. Explanation 10 says that where a portion of the cost has been met directly or indirectly by the Central Government, a State Government, any authority or any other person in the form of a subsidy, grant or reimbursement, so much of the cost as is relatable to it shall not be included in the actual cost.

citation.ref: Section 43(1) with its proviso and Explanations 1, 3, 8 and 10, read with Section 36(1)(iii) and its proviso and Section 32(1)

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Sections 179 and 167C — When the tax follows the directors and the partners
concepts.statement: Limited liability protects a shareholder from the company's debts, and sections 179 and 167C are the two places where the Act sets that aside for its own dues. Section 179(1) applies where any tax due from a private company in respect of any income of any previous year cannot be recovered from the company itself. Every person who was a director of that private company at any time during the relevant previous year is then jointly and severally liable for the payment of that tax — the test is directorship during the year the income arose, not directorship on the day the demand was raised or the day recovery failed. The escape is in the same sub-section and the burden of it sits on the director: unless he proves that the non-recovery cannot be attributed to any gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part in relation to the affairs of the company. It is not enough to say he was not involved; he must show the failure to recover was not his doing. The Explanation makes clear that the expression tax due includes penalty, interest, fees or any other sum payable under the Act. Section 179 reaches a private company only, and there is no counterpart for a public company. Section 167C is the parallel provision for a limited liability partnership in liquidation, putting the same joint and several liability, with the same defence in the same words, on every person who was a partner at any time during the relevant previous year. Section 178 is the different case again, and puts a duty to set aside funds on the liquidator of a company.

citation.ref: Section 179(1) with its Explanation and Section 167C with its Explanation, read with Section 178

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 281 — Certain transfers to be void against the revenue
concepts.statement: Section 281(1) covers the assessee who sees a demand coming and moves his property. Where, during the pendency of any proceeding under the Act or after the completion of it but before the service of a notice under Rule 2 of the Second Schedule, an assessee creates a charge on or parts with the possession, by way of sale, mortgage, gift, exchange or any other mode of transfer whatsoever, of any of his assets in favour of any other person, that charge or transfer shall be void as against any claim in respect of any tax or any other sum payable by the assessee as a result of the completion of the proceeding or otherwise. The window therefore opens with the proceeding and does not close when the assessment order is passed; it closes only on the recovery notice. The proviso gives two ways out and only two. The transfer is not void if it is made for adequate consideration and without notice of the pendency of the proceeding or of the tax or other sum payable, which protects a genuine buyer who paid a real price and knew nothing; or if it is made with the previous permission of the Assessing Officer, which is the safe route for a transfer the assessee knows about. Sub-section (2) confines the section to cases where the tax or other sum payable exceeds five thousand rupees and the assets charged or transferred exceed ten thousand rupees in value. The Explanation defines assets narrowly — land, building, machinery, plant, shares, securities and fixed deposits in banks, to the extent to which any of them does not form part of the stock-in-trade of the business of the assessee — so a trader selling his stock in the ordinary way is outside the section altogether.

citation.ref: Section 281(1) with its proviso, Section 281(2) and the Explanation to Section 281, read with Rule 2 of the Second Schedule

concepts.subsection: Section 94A — Transactions with a notified jurisdictional area
concepts.statement: Section 94A is what India does when a country will not exchange information. Sub-section (1) lets the Central Government, having regard to the lack of effective exchange of information with any country or territory outside India, specify it by notification as a notified jurisdictional area, and four consequences then follow for anybody dealing with a person located there. Sub-section (2) is a double deeming — where an assessee enters into a transaction and one of the parties to it is a person located in such an area, all the parties to that transaction shall be deemed to be associated enterprises and the transaction shall be deemed to be an international transaction, so the whole of the transfer pricing machinery in sections 92 to 92F applies whether or not anybody holds a share in anybody. Its second proviso denies the benefit of the tolerance band in the second proviso to section 92C(2). Sub-section (3) is a conditional disallowance rather than a flat one — no deduction is allowed for a payment made to a financial institution located in that area unless the assessee furnishes an authorisation in the prescribed form allowing the tax authorities to seek relevant information from that institution on his behalf, and no deduction is allowed for any other expenditure or allowance, including depreciation, arising from a transaction with a person located there unless the assessee maintains and furnishes the prescribed documents and information. Sub-section (4) deems any sum received from a person located in that area to be the income of the assessee where he offers no satisfactory explanation about the source of that money in the hands of the payer or the beneficial owner. Sub-section (5) sets its own floor for deduction at source — the highest of the rate specified in the relevant provision of the Act, the rates in force, and thirty per cent.

citation.ref: Sections 94A(1) to 94A(6), read with Sections 92 to 92F, the second proviso to Section 92C(2) and Section 206AA

concepts.subsection: The OECD, UN and US Models — where each came from, and whose taxing right each favours
concepts.statement: A Model Convention is a starting point for negotiation and is not legally binding on anybody; countries have adopted its articles verbatim, with minor changes, or not at all. Three Models matter. The OECD Model traces to 1927, when the Fiscal Committee of the League of Nations prepared the first draft of a Model Form for all countries; a convention was published at Geneva in 1946 by the Fiscal Committee of the United Nations Social and Economic Council and later by the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation in 1963; the OECD was established in 1961, with developed countries as its members, to succeed the OEEC, and approved the draft presented to the OEEC; the final draft in its present form came in 1977 and has been revised several times, most recently in 2017. It is essentially a model treaty between two developed nations and it advocates residence-based taxation. The UN Model began with an Ad hoc Group of Experts from developed and developing countries set up in 1968; the Group finalised the Model in its present form in 1980, and it has been updated in 2001, 2011, 2017 and most recently 2021. It is a compromise between the source principle and the residence principle which gives more weight to source, designed to encourage the flow of investment from developed countries to developing ones and to take account of sharing tax revenue with the country providing the capital. Its articles rest on the source country recognising three things — that income from foreign capital should be taxed on a net basis after expenses allocable to earning it, that the tax should not be so high as to discourage investment, and that revenue should appropriately be shared with the country providing the capital. The US Model is the one the United States uses in its own treaties and was last revised in 2016. Both the OECD and the UN Models are arranged in seven chapters; the OECD Model comprises 32 articles and the UN Model 31. The titles and preambles are almost identical, and the only difference is the order of two words — the UN title says the prevention of tax avoidance and evasion where the OECD says tax evasion and avoidance — with both preambles saying the parties do not intend to create opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through avoidance or evasion, including through treaty-shopping arrangements aimed at obtaining reliefs for the indirect benefit of residents of third States.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: The introduction and comparative overview in ICAI's Overview of Model Tax Conventions — the 1927 League of Nations draft through the OECD's 1977 form and 2017 revision, the UN Ad hoc Group of 1968 and the Model finalised in 1980 and last updated in 2021, the US Model of 2016, seven chapters with 32 OECD articles against 31 UN articles, and the residence principle set against the source principle

concepts.subsection: Article 4 — what makes a person a resident, and how the two Models break a tie
concepts.statement: Article 4 decides who may reach a treaty at all, and it does three jobs — it fixes the convention's scope of application, it settles double taxation arising from double residence, and it settles double taxation arising from taxation in both the residence and the source state. Under paragraph 1 of the UN Model a resident of a Contracting State is any person who, under the laws of that State, is liable to tax there by reason of domicile, residence, place of incorporation, place of management or any other criterion of a similar nature, and the term also takes in the State itself, its political subdivisions and local authorities, and a recognised pension fund of that State. The OECD Model's paragraph 1 is worded on the same lines with two things missing: it makes no reference to place of incorporation and it does not bring in a recognised pension fund. Neither Model treats as a resident a person liable to tax in a State only on income sourced there or capital situated there. Where an individual is a resident of both States under paragraph 1, paragraph 2 breaks the tie in a fixed sequence which is abandoned the moment one test decides — the State in which he has a permanent home available to him; if he has one in both, the State with which his personal and economic relations are closer, the centre of vital interests; if that cannot be determined, or he has a permanent home in neither, the State of his habitual abode; if he has an habitual abode in both or in neither, the State of which he is a national; and if he is a national of both or of neither, the competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement. For a person other than an individual paragraph 3 no longer uses a tie-breaker at all. Dual residence for a company arises where one State attaches importance to place of incorporation and the other to place of effective management, and place of effective management was traditionally the tie-breaker, used by India in some of its treaties. In the latest OECD and UN updates that has been replaced by a case-by-case approach, because of the number of tax avoidance cases involving dual resident companies: the competent authorities endeavour to determine the State of residence by mutual agreement, having regard to place of effective management, place of incorporation or constitution and any other relevant factor, on a determination the taxpayer requests through Article 25. Where they do not agree, the person gets no relief or exemption under the Convention except so far as they agree, though it remains a resident of each State for every purpose other than treaty relief.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 4(1), 4(2) and 4(3) of both Models — place of incorporation and a recognised pension fund in the UN definition and absent from the OECD's, the four-step tie-breaker for an individual, and the case-by-case competent-authority approach that has displaced place of effective management for companies

concepts.subsection: Article 5 — the four places the UN Model reaches a permanent establishment and the OECD Model does not
concepts.statement: A permanent establishment is what gives the source State the right to tax business profits under Article 7, so the article matters most to developing countries and it is where the UN Model departs from the OECD Model furthest. The comparable term in Indian domestic law is business connection in section 9(1)(i); business connection is the wider concept, so one may exist without a permanent establishment, though the absence of a business connection indicates the absence of a permanent establishment. The basic rule in Article 5(1) is the same in both Models and is cumulative — there must be an enterprise, it must be carrying on a business, there must be a place of business, that place must be at the disposal of the enterprise in the sense that it has the effective power to use it whether owned or rented, the place must be fixed in that it is established at a distinct place with a certain degree of permanence, and the business must be carried on wholly or partly through it. The definition carries no qualifying words such as unless the context otherwise requires, so it governs in all cases unless something specifically excludes it. Article 5(2) illustrates the term with a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory, a workshop, and a mine, oil or gas well, quarry or other place of extraction of natural resources. Four divergences then follow. Under Article 5(3)(a) of the OECD Model a building site or construction or installation project is a permanent establishment only if it lasts more than twelve months; the UN Model is wider, since it also covers an assembly or installation project and supervisory activities connected with one, and it requires only six months. Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model creates a Service PE where an enterprise furnishes services, including consultancy services, through employees or other personnel for periods aggregating more than 183 days in any twelve-month period commencing or ending in the fiscal year concerned; the OECD Model has no such provision and the presence must be tested under Article 5(1) instead. On agency, both Models reach a dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts or habitually plays the principal role leading to the conclusion of contracts routinely concluded without material modification by the enterprise; the UN Model goes further and constitutes a permanent establishment where the person does neither of those things but habitually maintains a stock of goods or merchandise in that State from which he regularly delivers goods on behalf of the enterprise. Finally the UN Model carries an additional Article 5(6) under which an insurance enterprise of one State is deemed to have a permanent establishment in the other if it collects premiums in that other State's territory or insures risks situated there through a person, except in regard to re-insurance; with no such article in the OECD Model, an insurer's permanent establishment falls to be decided under Article 5(1) or 5(2).

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 5(1), 5(2), 5(3)(a), 5(3)(b), 5(5) and 5(6) of the two Models, read with Section 9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 — twelve months against six for a construction site, the 183-day Service PE the OECD Model does not have, the delivery-of-stock limb of agency PE, and the UN Model's insurance article

concepts.subsection: Article 7 and Article 21 — the limited force of attraction, and where the UN Model lets the source State back in
concepts.statement: Both Models start from the same place on business profits: they may be taxed only by the residence State, and the source State gets a right to tax them only if a permanent establishment exists in its jurisdiction. What differs is how much the source State may then take. Under the OECD Model, once a permanent establishment is proven the source State may tax only such profits as are attributable to that permanent establishment, and nothing else. The UN Model amplifies that attribution principle with a limited force of attraction rule. The rule means that when a foreign enterprise sets up a permanent establishment in the source State it brings itself within that State's fiscal jurisdiction to such a degree that profits the enterprise derives from that State, whether through the permanent establishment or not, can be taxed there. So under Article 7 of the UN Model the profits taxable in the other State are those attributable to three things and not one — that permanent establishment; sales in that other State of goods or merchandise of the same or similar kind as those sold through the permanent establishment; and other business activities carried on in that other State of the same or similar kind as those effected through the permanent establishment. It is called limited because the second and third limbs reach only goods and activities of the same or similar kind, not everything the enterprise does in that State. Article 21, other income, shows the same asymmetry on the ground that is left over after every specific article. Both Models say that income effectively connected with a permanent establishment maintained in a Contracting State by a resident of the other is governed by Article 7; the UN Model adds that income effectively connected with a fixed base is governed by Article 14 instead. But the OECD approach gives the residence State the exclusive right to tax other income, whereas the UN Model contains an additional paragraph, Article 21(3), under which the source State may also tax it.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 7 of the two Models and Article 21(2) and 21(3) — attribution to the permanent establishment alone under the OECD Model against the UN Model's three limbs of permanent establishment, same or similar sales and same or similar business activities, and the extra paragraph letting the source State tax other income

concepts.subsection: Articles 11 and 12 — the one rate the OECD Model actually names, and the royalty the two Models define differently
concepts.statement: On interest the two Models agree on the structure and differ on one number.
