Paragraph 1 of Article 11 gives the residence State the right to tax interest and paragraph 2 confers a right on the source State as well, interest generally being taxed in the source State at a given rate on a gross basis. Where the beneficial owner of the interest is a resident of the other Contracting State, the tax so charged cannot exceed a specified percentage of the gross amount of the interest. The OECD Model specifies that percentage as 10 per cent. The UN Model specifies no figure at all and leaves the percentage to be established through bilateral negotiation. The definition of interest is the same in both — income from debt claims of every kind, whether or not secured by mortgage and whether or not carrying a right to participate in the debtor's profits, and in particular income from government securities and income from bonds or debentures including premiums and prizes attaching to them — and in both, penalty charges for late payment are not interest. On royalties the difference is larger and runs both ways. Under the OECD Model royalties arising in the source State and beneficially owned by a resident of the residence State are taxable only in the residence State, an exclusive right. The UN Model departs from that: royalties may be taxed in the residence State, and the source State may tax them too, subject to a ceiling on the gross amount where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other State, and that ceiling is again left to bilateral negotiation. The definitions differ as well. Under the UN Model royalties means payments of any kind received as consideration for the use of, or the right to use, any copyright of literary, artistic or scientific work including cinematograph films, or films or tapes used for radio or television broadcasting, any patent, trademark, design or model, plan, secret formula or process, or for the use of, or the right to use, industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, or for information concerning industrial, commercial or scientific experience. The OECD Model's definition leaves out two of those: rentals for films or tapes used for radio or television broadcasting, and equipment rentals such as rentals for industrial, commercial or scientific equipment.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 11(1) and 11(2) and Article 12 of the two Models — the OECD's 10 per cent ceiling on interest against a UN percentage left to bilateral negotiation, the residence State's exclusive right to royalties under the OECD Model against shared taxation under the UN Model, and the two categories of rental the OECD definition of royalties excludes

concepts.subsection: Articles 12A and 12B — two articles the UN Model has and the OECD Model does not
concepts.statement: Two whole articles exist in the UN Model with no counterpart in the OECD Model, and both give the source State a right the OECD Model withholds. Article 12A covers fees for technical services. India is the pioneer of the concept, which entered the Income-tax Act, 1961 in 1976, and several Indian treaties carry a specific provision for it. Paragraph 1 of Article 12A provides that fees for technical services may be taxed in the residence State but does not make them exclusively taxable there; paragraph 2 establishes the right of the country in which the fees arise to tax them in accordance with its own domestic law, subject to a limit on the maximum rate of tax on the gross amount where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other Contracting State, that maximum being established through bilateral negotiation. Fees for technical services means payments for managerial, technical or consultancy services, and it excludes three things — a payment to an employee, a payment for teaching in an educational institution or for teaching by one, and a payment by an individual for services for his personal use. Managerial involves applying knowledge, skill or expertise to the control or administration of a commercial enterprise; technical involves applying specialised knowledge, skill or expertise to a particular art, science, profession or occupation, so fees of regulated professions such as law, accounting, architecture, medicine and engineering qualify; and consultancy involves advice or services of a specialised nature. A financial institution's research, analysis or advice for a specific client is fees for technical services, while its payment and transmission services and its card services are not, because they apply no specialised knowledge on behalf of a particular client. Article 12B covers income from automated digital services and was added to the UN Model in its 2021 update, to preserve domestic-law taxing rights for States from which payments for such services are made. Its paragraphs 1 and 2 follow the same pattern as Article 12A — the residence State may tax but not exclusively, and the source State may tax under its own law subject to a percentage of the gross payments to be established through bilateral negotiation. Automated digital services is defined in paragraph 5 as any service provided on the Internet or another electronic network, in either case requiring minimal human involvement from the service provider, and the test in practice is whether the business can scale up to new users with minimal human involvement, where a non-automated digital business would see a proportionate rise in cost per unit. Paragraph 6 lists nine examples, including online advertising, supply of user data, online search engines, online intermediation platforms, social media platforms, digital content services, online gaming, cloud computing and standardised online teaching, but the list is only an indication and the paragraph 5 requirement must still be met. Paragraph 7 settles priority: Article 12B does not apply at all if the underlying payments qualify as royalties or as fees for technical services under Article 12 or Article 12A.

citation.source: United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 12A and Article 12B of the UN Model, neither of which appears in the OECD Model — the definition and three exclusions of fees for technical services, the 2021 introduction of Article 12B, the minimal-human-involvement definition of automated digital services in paragraph 5, and the paragraph 7 rule that royalties and fees for technical services take priority

concepts.subsection: Articles 13 and 14 — the share test the Models share, and the article the OECD deleted
concepts.statement: Article 13 is the most commonly used article and it taxes gains from the transfer of a capital asset, including a transfer of shares. The right may be exclusively the residence State's or shared with the source State. The article says nothing about what a capital gain is or how it is computed, both of which are left to domestic law, and it lays down rules for gains from alienating immovable property, immovable property forming part of a permanent establishment, ships and aircraft and so on. On shares the two Models are identical: the source State gets the right where more than 50 per cent of the value of the shares during the preceding 365 days is derived directly or indirectly from immovable property situated in that source State, and otherwise the residence State has the exclusive right. The UN Model adds one thing the OECD Model does not have — it lets a State tax gains from alienating rights granted under its own law where those rights allow the use of resources naturally present in that State and under its jurisdiction, which covers a fishing quota, a right to fell timber, a right to extract water, a right to explore part of the territory for oil, gas or minerals, a right to install wind or tidal turbines and a right to use the radiofrequency spectrum. It does not cover rights granted contractually between private parties even if the law protects them, so the alienation of an exclusive right to use know-how is outside it. On gains from alienating any property not covered by the other paragraphs, both Models give the residence State the exclusive right. Article 14, independent personal services, exists only in the UN Model. It was deleted from the OECD Model on 29 April 2000, on the basis of the OECD's 2000 report on issues related to Article 14, and the effect of the deletion is that income from professional services is dealt with as business profits under Article 7 of the OECD Model. Under the UN Model, income derived by a resident of a Contracting State from professional services or other activities of an independent character is taxable only in that State, except in two cases where the other State may tax as well. If he has a fixed base regularly available to him in the other State for performing his activities, only so much of the income as is attributable to that fixed base may be taxed there. If his stay in the other State amounts to or exceeds 183 days in the aggregate in any twelve-month period commencing or ending in the fiscal year concerned, only so much of the income as is derived from activities performed in that State may be taxed there. Professional services includes especially independent scientific, literary, artistic, educational or teaching activities and the independent activities of physicians, lawyers, engineers, architects, dentists and accountants; the list is explanatory and not exhaustive. It excludes industrial and commercial activities, which are business profits; professional services rendered in employment, such as a physician serving as a medical officer in a factory, which are dependent personal services; the income of artistes and sportspersons; and fees for technical services.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 13 of the two Models and Article 14 of the UN Model — the more-than-50-per-cent test over the preceding 365 days for shares deriving value from immovable property, the UN Model's natural-resource rights, and the deletion of Article 14 from the OECD Model on 29 April 2000 with its fixed base and 183-day alternatives

concepts.subsection: Article 25 — the mutual agreement procedure, and the four things arbitration turns on
concepts.statement: Where a taxpayer believes the treatment given by either or both Contracting States is not in accordance with the treaty, Article 25 is the route, and it requires the competent authorities of both countries to endeavour to resolve the conflict by bilateral negotiation. The UN Model offers two alternatives for the whole article, Alternative A and Alternative B, introduced in 2011. Under the OECD Model the taxpayer may make his request to either Contracting State; under Alternative A of the UN Model he must go to the residence State or the country of his nationality. Alternative B of the UN Model adds a reference to an arbitration process as part of the mutual agreement procedure, and the decision reached through it is binding unless a person directly affected does not accept it. Four differences separate the OECD Model's Article 25 from Alternative B of the UN Model and each is examinable on its own. First, the trigger: under Article 25B(5) of the UN Model arbitration may be initiated if the competent authorities are unable to reach agreement on a case within three years from the presentation of that case, whereas Article 25(5) of the OECD Model uses two years running from the date on which all the information required by the competent authorities to address the case has been provided to both of them. Second, who asks: under the UN Model arbitration must be requested by the competent authority of one of the Contracting States, and once the request is made the taxpayer is notified, whereas under the OECD Model it must be requested in writing by the person who initiated the case. Third, whether the decision can be departed from: Article 25B(5) of the UN Model allows the competent authorities to depart from the arbitration decision if they agree to do so within six months after it has been communicated to them, where the OECD Model has no such provision. Fourth, the article that supplies the relief once the case is settled is not Article 25 at all but Articles 23A and 23B, exemption and credit, and those articles address only juridical double taxation, where the same income is taxable in the hands of the same person by more than one State. Economic double taxation, where two different persons are taxable on the same income, is not addressed by them and must be solved by the two States in bilateral negotiation.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 25 of the OECD Model and Article 25 Alternatives A and B of the UN Model, read with Articles 23A and 23B — three years from presentation of the case against two years from the information being complete, the competent authority against the taxpayer as the party who requests arbitration, the six-month window to depart from the decision, and juridical rather than economic double taxation as what the relief articles address

concepts.subsection: The Inclusive Framework and the Two-Pillar Solution — what BEPS 2.0 actually is
concepts.statement: The fifteen Action Plans delivered in 2015 were the first BEPS package. What followed is called BEPS 2.0 and it is a different thing: not a further set of anti-avoidance measures but a reallocation of taxing rights and a floor under the rate. Two steps got there. First, an institution. Globalisation needed a dialogue wider than the OECD and G20 countries, so drawing on the experience of the Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes, the OECD and G20 countries decided in early 2016 to design a more inclusive framework in which countries and jurisdictions would participate on an equal footing; in June 2016, at the G20's request, the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS was established at Kyoto in Japan with an initial membership of 89 countries and jurisdictions, and as at 28 May 2024 it has 147 members. Its members commit to implementing the minimum standards and to taking part in the peer reviews. Second, an agreement. In July 2021, 134 members of the Inclusive Framework, representing more than 90 per cent of worldwide GDP, reached agreement on a two-pillar solution to address the tax challenges of digitalisation and to introduce a global minimum tax on the profits of large multinational enterprises; 139 countries and jurisdictions joined the agreement reached on 8 October 2021, the Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution to Address the Tax Challenges Arising from the Digitalisation of the Economy. It is the outcome of the work under Action 1, which had found in its 2015 report that the whole economy was digitalising and that it would therefore be difficult if not impossible to ring-fence the digital economy; that report gave options rather than recommendations and left countries to act in their own domestic law, which is what unilateral measures such as an equalisation levy were. Each Pillar has two parts. Pillar One is Amount A, the international framework for reallocating taxing rights over the profits of large and highly profitable multinationals, and Amount B, a simplified transfer pricing approach for baseline distribution activity. Pillar Two is the Global Anti-Base Erosion or GloBE Rules, which establish a minimum tax framework in each jurisdiction where a large multinational operates, and the Subject to Tax Rule, which lets a source jurisdiction tax back where it has ceded taxing rights under a treaty and the payment bears only a low nominal rate in the residence jurisdiction.

citation.ref: The Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution to Address the Tax Challenges Arising from the Digitalisation of the Economy of 8 October 2021, read with the establishment of the Inclusive Framework at Kyoto in June 2016 — 89 initial members against 147 as at 28 May 2024, 134 members representing more than 90 per cent of worldwide GDP in July 2021, and 139 countries joining the October 2021 Statement

concepts.subsection: Pillar One Amount A — who is in scope, how much moves, and which market gets it
concepts.statement: Amount A modifies both the nexus rule and the profit allocation rule, and it redistributes what the OECD calls super-profits to the market jurisdictions of a group, treating the multinational as a consolidated entity and allocating by formula rather than by attribution to an establishment. Three separate tests do the work and an examiner can build a question on any of them. Scope first. An in-scope company is a multinational with global turnover above 20 billion euros and profitability above 10 per cent, profitability being profit before tax divided by revenue; extractives and regulated financial services are out of scope whatever their size. Quantum second. Amount A is 25 per cent of the residual profit, and residual profit is defined as profit in excess of 10 per cent of revenue. So the same 10 per cent figure does two jobs — it is the profitability threshold that decides whether the group is in scope at all, and it is the routine return above which profit counts as residual. The residual is then allocated to market jurisdictions with nexus, using revenue-based allocation keys. Nexus third. There is a new special-purpose nexus rule which applies solely to decide whether a jurisdiction qualifies for reallocation under Amount A and which alters nexus for no other tax or non-tax purpose; Amount A is allocated to a market jurisdiction only if that nexus exists, and it exists on a market revenue threshold that depends on the size of the market itself — revenue of at least 1 million for a jurisdiction with annual GDP of 40 billion or more, and at least 250,000 for a jurisdiction with annual GDP below 40 billion. The smaller the economy, the lower the bar. To apply that test the group must first source its revenue, and revenue is sourced to the end market jurisdictions where the goods or services are used or consumed, with detailed rules by category of revenue, revenue falling in more than one category sourced by its predominant character, and revenue from supplementary transactions sourced with the revenue it supplements. For online advertising the sourcing principle follows the eyeballs of the viewer rather than the location of the advertiser, identified from an IP address, geolocation or other reliable commercial information. Where the end user genuinely cannot be located — cloud computing, where the group may not know where its customer's employees use the service — the group may use targeted proxies or allocation keys such as aggregated headcount data or macroeconomic proxies. The whole point of Amount A is that it transfers taxing rights over residual profits to jurisdictions where there is business activity regardless of physical presence.

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount A of the Two-Pillar Solution — global turnover above 20 billion euros and profitability above 10 per cent for scope, extractives and regulated financial services excluded, 25 per cent of the profit in excess of 10 per cent of revenue as the reallocated amount, and market revenue of 1 million or 250,000 depending on whether the jurisdiction's annual GDP reaches 40 billion

concepts.subsection: Pillar One Amount B — a simplified arm's length return for baseline distribution
concepts.statement: Amount B is the half of Pillar One that has nothing to do with reallocating super-profits. Where Amount A updates the international framework for large and very profitable groups, Amount B simplifies existing transfer pricing rules for all taxpayers, and it is aimed at one fact pattern — baseline marketing and distribution activities carried on in a country, which is the most frequent arrangement multinationals meet in the jurisdictions where they operate. Its purpose is to increase tax certainty, cut compliance and administrative cost, and particularly to assist low-capacity jurisdictions that often have no local market comparables to benchmark against. The Inclusive Framework released its report on Amount B on 19 February 2024 and published the pending design aspects on 17 June 2024. The framework runs in two steps. Step 1 is scoping: a tested party's activities are in scope where it is involved in a qualifying transaction and that transaction meets the scoping criteria. Step 2 is pricing, and it applies only if the transaction is in scope and only unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price is available — a reliable internal CUP displaces the whole simplified approach. Pricing itself has three sub-steps. Step 2-1 applies the pricing matrix to determine a return on sales percentage, the matrix being built from a global dataset of comparable companies engaged in baseline marketing and distribution whose financial information has been filtered by benchmarking criteria and the scoping conditions to approximate arm's length returns expressed as return on sales; the matrix is read across three pre-defined industry groupings and down bands of operating asset intensity and operating expense intensity. Step 2-2 applies the operating expense cross-check, a corroborative check that tests the matrix return against the tested party's own operating expense level and adjusts its profitability where the return on sales falls outside a pre-defined cap-and-collar range. Step 2-3 applies the data availability mechanism, which adjusts the matrix return upwards where the global dataset holds no or insufficient data for a particular tested party jurisdiction and there is evidence that the jurisdiction could reasonably be considered higher risk. To keep the compliance burden down the analysis behind the pricing matrix and the cap-and-collar rates is updated every five years unless a significant change in market conditions warrants an interim update, while the financial data and other datapoints are reviewed annually and updated where necessary. The approach as published is elective, and the Inclusive Framework continues to work on a framework that goes beyond the elective approach and is linked with Amount A.

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount B of the Two-Pillar Solution, reported on 19 February 2024 with the pending design aspects published on 17 June 2024 — scoping, then pricing by the matrix, the operating expense cross-check and the data availability mechanism, a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price displacing the approach, and the matrix updated every five years with the data reviewed annually

concepts.subsection: The GloBE Rules — who they catch, and how the effective tax rate that triggers them is worked out
concepts.statement: The GloBE Model Rules for the minimum tax were released in December 2021 and are designed to be implemented into the domestic law of each jurisdiction as an interlocking and coordinated system. Jurisdictions are not required to adopt them; this is a common approach, meaning that a jurisdiction which chooses to adopt them agrees to implement them consistently with the agreed outcomes. They introduce a 15 per cent global minimum tax. On scope, the rules apply to Constituent Entities that are members of a multinational group whose annual revenue in the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Ultimate Parent Entity is 750 million euros or more in at least two of the four fiscal years immediately preceding the tested fiscal year, so a single year over the line does not bring a group in and a single year under it does not take a group out. A multinational group means a group that includes at least one entity or permanent establishment not located in the jurisdiction of the Ultimate Parent Entity. Certain Excluded Entities are not subject to the rules — government entities, international organisations, non-profit organisations, and pension funds or investment funds that are Ultimate Parent Entities, together with holding vehicles used by them — but their revenue still counts towards the consolidated revenue test, and the exclusion does not take the group they control out of scope. The trigger is the effective tax rate and it is computed for each fiscal year on a jurisdictional basis, not entity by entity: the Effective Tax Rate is the total of the Adjusted Covered Taxes of each Constituent Entity located in the jurisdiction divided by the Net GloBE Income of that jurisdiction. Adjusted Covered Taxes are the taxes attributable to a Constituent Entity's income, taken as its current taxes for the year adjusted for certain timing differences, with allocation between entities in certain cases and with later additions or reductions identified and allocated to a jurisdiction and period. Net GloBE Income is the GloBE Income of all Constituent Entities in the jurisdiction less the GloBE Losses of all of them, and it is a positive amount if any — where there is a net GloBE loss the effective tax rate need not be computed at all and in most cases no top-up tax is due. That subtraction is jurisdictional blending, and it is the reason a profitable subsidiary and a loss-making one in the same country are looked at together. Note the asymmetry the examiner is likely to build on: whether the rules apply at all is decided on global revenue, while the effective tax rate that decides whether top-up tax is payable is computed jurisdiction by jurisdiction. If the jurisdictional effective tax rate is below the 15 per cent minimum, the jurisdiction is a low-tax jurisdiction and its entities are low-taxed constituent entities.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules released in December 2021 — annual revenue of 750 million euros or more in the Ultimate Parent Entity's consolidated financial statements in at least two of the four preceding fiscal years, the Excluded Entities whose revenue still counts, and the Effective Tax Rate as Adjusted Covered Taxes over Net GloBE Income computed on a jurisdictional blending basis against a 15 per cent minimum

concepts.subsection: QDMTT, IIR and UTPR — who collects the top-up tax, and how much it is
concepts.statement: Pillar Two answers two separate questions and they must be kept apart: how much top-up tax there is, and which country gets to collect it. On how much, the Jurisdictional Top-up Tax for a fiscal year is the positive amount, if any, of the Top-up Tax Percentage multiplied by the Excess Profit, plus any Additional Current Top-up Tax, less any Domestic Top-up Tax. The Top-up Tax Percentage is the positive percentage point difference between the minimum rate and the effective tax rate. The Excess Profit is the Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion. Notice which base each factor uses: the percentage is worked out on the aggregate profits, the Net GloBE Income, but it is applied to the excess profit after the substance carve-out, and that is deliberate so that groups keep the benefit of incentives on substantive activity. The Substance-based Income Exclusion is the sum of a payroll carve-out and a tangible asset carve-out for each Constituent Entity in the jurisdiction, equal to 5 per cent of the carrying value of tangible assets located there plus 5 per cent of the payroll costs of employees performing activities there; there is a ten-year transition in recognition of the impact on existing incentives and investment, during which the figures start at 8 per cent of eligible tangible assets and 10 per cent of eligible payroll costs and phase down to 5 per cent over the ten years. A de-minimis exclusion is available at the election of the Filing Constituent Entity for the low-taxed constituent entities of a jurisdiction where the Average GloBE Revenue of that jurisdiction is less than 10 million euros and its Average GloBE Income or Loss is a loss or is less than 1 million euros; the policy is to avoid a full effective tax rate computation where the top-up tax would not justify the compliance and administrative cost. On who collects, the model rules set a priority order of three rules. First is the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax, which lets the low-tax jurisdiction itself collect the jurisdictional top-up tax computed under the GloBE rules by introducing the charge in its own domestic law, preserving its primary right of taxation over its own income. Second, where the low-tax jurisdiction has no such charge, is the Income Inclusion Rule, under which a Constituent Entity that is the Ultimate Parent Entity located in an implementing jurisdiction and owning an ownership interest in a low-taxed constituent entity at any time in the year pays tax equal to its allocable share of that entity's top-up tax. Third, where neither the low-tax jurisdiction imposes the domestic charge nor the parent's jurisdiction has an Income Inclusion Rule, is the Undertaxed Payment Rule, which denies deductions or requires an equivalent adjustment in the other jurisdictions that have implemented the GloBE rules; it is a backstop to the Income Inclusion Rule and it transfers the levy to the group's other constituent entities.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax, then the Income Inclusion Rule, then the Undertaxed Payment Rule as backstop; Jurisdictional Top-up Tax as the Top-up Tax Percentage on Excess Profit plus additional current top-up tax less domestic top-up tax; the substance-based income exclusion at 5 per cent of tangible assets and 5 per cent of payroll with a ten-year phase down from 8 and 10 per cent; and the de-minimis exclusion at average revenue below 10 million euros and average income below 1 million euros

concepts.subsection: The Subject to Tax Rule — the treaty half of Pillar Two, and the 9 per cent that drives it
concepts.statement: The Subject to Tax Rule is the second component of Pillar Two and it is not a domestic-law rule at all; it is a treaty-based rule, and it works in priority to the GloBE Rules rather than after them. Its purpose is to let developing countries, as source jurisdictions, tax certain intra-group payments at source where those payments bear only a nominal corporate income tax rate in the hands of the payee. The understanding behind it is that where a source State has ceded taxing rights on outbound intragroup payments under a treaty, it should be able to recover some of them where the income is taxed, if at all, in the residence State at a rate below 9 per cent. It was developed for the priorities of developing countries, and Inclusive Framework members can adopt it by signing the Multilateral Instrument or by amending their treaties bilaterally when a developing member asks. Four limits define it. First, who: it applies only to covered payments made by an entity in a developing country to a group entity in another country, that is to connected persons, and developing country is defined by reference to gross national income per capita calculated on the World Bank Atlas method of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019, a figure to be updated regularly. Connected persons are defined by legal control, direct or indirect ownership of more than 50 per cent of the interests, or by a de facto control relationship. Second, how much: it applies only if the total sum of covered income arising in the source country exceeds a threshold of 250,000 or 1 million a year, depending on whether the source country's GDP is above or below 40 billion. Third, what: covered payments are interest, royalties, payments for distribution rights for a product or service, insurance or reinsurance premiums, guarantee or financing fees, rentals for industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, and payments for services. Fourth, at what rate: the specified rate is the difference between 9 per cent and the nominal rate applied in the residence State, further reduced by any source taxation already allocated to the source jurisdiction under other articles of the treaty. The module's own worked example is the shape to hold: a source State entitled under the treaty to withhold 5 per cent on a royalty, and a residence State taxing that royalty at a nominal 1 per cent, keeps its 5 per cent withholding and may impose an additional tax of 3 per cent, being 9 less 5 less 1.

citation.ref: The Subject to Tax Rule of Pillar Two, which works in priority to the GloBE Rules — a nominal corporate income tax rate below 9 per cent in the residence State, developing country defined as gross national income per capita of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019 on the World Bank Atlas method, connected persons at more than 50 per cent of the interests, a covered income threshold of 250,000 or 1 million by reference to a source-country GDP of 40 billion, and a specified rate of 9 per cent less the nominal rate less source taxation already allocated

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: The fifteen Action Plans — the three pillars they are grouped under, and the four that bind
concepts.statement: Base erosion and profit shifting means tax planning strategies that exploit gaps and mismatches in tax rules to make profits disappear for tax purposes or to shift them to locations where there is little or no real activity but the taxes are low, so that little or no overall corporate tax is paid. Following the 2009 financial crisis the G20 mandated the OECD to address tax avoidance; the OECD published its report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting in February 2013, the draft Action Plan in July 2013, and the final package in October 2015 with fifteen Actions. The Actions are structured round three fundamental pillars — introducing coherence in the domestic rules that affect cross-border activities, reinforcing substance requirements in existing international standards so that taxation aligns with where value is created, and improving transparency and tax certainty. Coherence holds Actions 2, 3 and 4; substance holds the preferential-regimes half of Action 5 and Actions 6, 7 and 8 to 10; transparency holds the ruling-exchange half of Action 5 and Actions 11, 12, 13 and 14; and Actions 1 and 15 sit across all three as horizontal. What separates the Actions from one another is not their subject but the level of commitment attached to them, and the OECD uses three words for it. A new minimum standard is a new rule to be implemented by all States, because non-implementation would spill over onto other countries, including on competitiveness; there are four, and they are Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14. Each is subject to peer review so that implementation is timely and accurate and the playing field stays level, and every member of the Inclusive Framework commits both to implementing them and to taking part in the review. A revision of an existing standard means an existing standard has been updated and will be implemented, with the caveat that not all BEPS participants have endorsed the underlying standards on tax treaties or transfer pricing. A best practice is not a standard at all but an optional recommendation, and it is what supports countries acting on mandatory disclosure initiatives or controlled foreign company legislation — which is why Action 3 on CFC rules and Action 12 on disclosure of aggressive tax planning are best practice and not minimum standards. On Action 3 the OECD's final report expressly declines to propose a minimum standard, because there was fundamental disagreement over the policy of CFC regimes, in particular whether a State should use its regime to protect other States' tax bases from earnings stripping.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The 2015 BEPS package of fifteen Action Plans, structured on coherence, substance and transparency — Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14 as the four minimum standards subject to peer review, against a revision of an existing standard and a best practice, with the controlled foreign company rules of Action 3 and the mandatory disclosure rules of Action 12 left as best practice

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 1 — the three options the OECD offered for the digital economy, and which one India kept
concepts.statement: Action 1 addresses the tax challenges of the digital economy, where business is conducted without regard to national boundaries and the link between an income-producing activity and a specific location dissolves. Before it, the physical location of a digital business's servers was used to fix the jurisdiction that could tax its profits, with the predictable result that servers were placed in tax-efficient jurisdictions while the income and the customers came from elsewhere. The typical taxation issues it names are two: the difficulty of characterising the nature of a payment and establishing a nexus between a taxable transaction or activity and a taxing jurisdiction, and the difficulty of locating the transaction or activity and identifying the taxpayer for income-tax purposes. The report offered three options for the direct tax challenges and recommended none of them, leaving countries to act in their own domestic law. The first was modifying the existing permanent establishment rule so that an enterprise engaged in fully de-materialised digital activities would constitute a permanent establishment if it maintained a significant digital presence in another country's economy. The second was a virtual fixed place of business permanent establishment, created where an enterprise maintains a website on a server of another enterprise located in a jurisdiction and carries on business through that website. The third was a final withholding tax on certain payments for digital goods or services provided by a foreign e-commerce provider, or an equalisation levy on the consideration for certain digital transactions received by a non-resident from a resident, or from a non-resident having a permanent establishment in the other contracting State. India acted on all three and now stands on two of them. The concept of significant economic presence, which resembles the virtual fixed place of business permanent establishment, was introduced by Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i): a non-resident's significant economic presence in India is itself a business connection, and it means either that the aggregate of payments arising from transactions in goods, services or property with any person in India, including the provision of download of data or software in India, exceeds 2 crore rupees during the previous year, or that systematic and continuous soliciting of business activities or interaction with users in India reaches at least 3 lakh users. Either limb applies whether or not the agreement is entered into in India, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business in India, and whether or not he renders services in India; and where the business connection is established this way, only so much of the income as is attributable to those transactions or activities is deemed to accrue or arise in India. The withholding option is section 194-O, under which an e-commerce operator that facilitates the sale of goods or provision of services of an e-commerce participant through its digital or electronic facility or platform deducts tax at source at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount of such sales or services or both. The equalisation levy option is the one India has now abandoned in both its forms.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) and Section 194-O, read against the three options offered by the OECD under BEPS Action Plan 1 — payments exceeding 2 crore rupees or interaction with at least 3 lakh users as the two limbs of significant economic presence, income deemed to accrue only to the extent attributable to them, and tax deducted at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount by an e-commerce operator

concepts.section: Fundamentals of BEPS (Base Erosion and Profit Shifting)
concepts.subsection: Action 15 and the Multilateral Instrument — what makes a treaty a Covered Tax Agreement, and when the Convention bites
concepts.statement: Action 15 is the machinery Action: it exists to put the anti-avoidance solutions proposed in the other Actions into the treaty network. The problem it solves is arithmetic. There are more than 3,000 active bilateral tax treaties, India alone having entered into treaties with more than 90 countries, and amending each one separately is slow and legally cumbersome, while putting the solutions only into domestic law would leave the treaties themselves available to tax evaders. A mandate to form an ad hoc Group to develop a multilateral instrument was approved by the OECD Committee on Fiscal Affairs and endorsed by the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors in February 2015; the Group, of more than 100 countries and jurisdictions including India, began work in May 2015 and adopted the text of the Convention and its Explanatory Statement on 24 November 2016. It was signed at Paris on 7 June 2017 by more than 65 countries. The United States and Brazil have not signed it, so an India-USA or India-Brazil treaty is governed by the treaty alone. The Convention has 7 parts and 39 articles, of which Articles 3 to 17 are the substantive provisions: Part I scope and interpretation in Articles 1 and 2, Part II hybrid mismatches in Articles 3 to 5, Part III treaty abuse in Articles 6 to 11, Part IV avoidance of permanent establishment status in Articles 12 to 15, Part V improving dispute resolution in Articles 16 and 17, Part VI arbitration in Articles 18 to 26, and Part VII final provisions in Articles 27 to 39. The Instrument does not amend the text of a treaty; it applies alongside it and modifies the application of some of its clauses on the later-in-time principle, so the treaty is not superseded. Everything turns on the Covered Tax Agreement. Article 2 defines one as an agreement for the avoidance of double taxation with respect to taxes on income that is in force between parties and which each party has notified to the Depositary as a listed agreement, so the matching principle governs: both sides must notify each other's treaty. India notified 93 jurisdictions when it ratified. India-Australia is a Covered Tax Agreement because both notified; India-Mauritius is not, because Mauritius did not notify India, its treaty having been amended in 2016 to carry BEPS provisions already. Flexibility comes from compatibility clauses, which resolve conflict between the Instrument and the treaty and come in four kinds — in place of, in the absence of, applies to or modifies, and in place of or in the absence of, the last being the most commonly used and the only one that can apply where only one party notifies — and from reservations, which are the opt-out. A reservation is defined by the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties as a unilateral statement by which a State purports to exclude or modify the legal effect of certain provisions, and a party may reserve for all of its covered treaties or a subset; reservations generally apply symmetrically and, exceptionally, asymmetrically. Reservations against a minimum standard are possible only in limited situations and on conditions, and of the four BEPS minimum standards only Actions 6 and 14 are minimum standards inside the Instrument, Actions 5 and 13 being implemented in domestic law instead. Timing is the last piece and it has two clocks. The Convention enters into force for a party on the first day of the month following the expiry of 3 calendar months beginning on the date it deposits its instrument of ratification. Once it is in force for both Contracting States, its provisions have effect for withholding taxes from the first day of the next calendar year beginning on or after the later of the two entry-into- force dates, and for all other taxes for a taxable period beginning on or after the expiry of 6 calendar months from that later date. India signed on 7 June 2017, deposited its instrument on 25 June 2019, and the Convention entered into force for India on 1 October 2019, with effect from 1 April 2020 at the earliest, notified under section 90(1) by Notification No. 57/2019 dated 9 August 2019. Where the other State has notified but has not ratified — Italy is the module's example — the Instrument does not apply to that treaty at all.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Articles 2, 34 and 35 of the Convention, read with Section 90(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Notification No. 57/2019 dated 9 August 2019 — 7 parts and 39 articles with Articles 3 to 17 substantive, the matching principle on a Covered Tax Agreement notified by both parties, the four compatibility clauses and the reservation mechanism, entry into force on the first day of the month after 3 calendar months from deposit, and effect from the next calendar year for withholding taxes and after 6 calendar months for other taxes

concepts.subsection: Sections 131(1), 131(1A) and 131(3) — Civil court powers, and how long books may be impounded
concepts.statement: Section 131 gives named income-tax authorities the powers a Civil Court has under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 in four matters and four only — discovery and inspection, enforcing the attendance of any person including an officer of a banking company and examining him on oath, compelling the production of books of account and documents, and issuing commissions. The authorities holding them are the Assessing Officer, the Joint Commissioner, the Joint Commissioner (Appeals), the Commissioner (Appeals), the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner, the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and the Dispute Resolution Panel referred to in section 144C. They act in a quasi-judicial capacity when they use them. Section 131(1A) lets the investigation wing — the Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director, Director, Joint Director, Assistant Director or Deputy Director, and the authorised officer referred to in section 132(1) before he acts — exercise those same powers where he has reason to suspect that income has been concealed or is likely to be concealed, even though no proceeding is pending against anybody. What section 131 never gives is a power to seize, and that is the distinction the section is asked on. Section 131(3) allows the authority to impound books of account or other documents produced before it and retain them for such period as it thinks fit, and the power is unrestricted for every authority except the Assessing Officer and an Assistant Director or Deputy Director, who must record reasons for impounding and must obtain the prior approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director before retaining them for more than 15 days, holidays excluded.

citation.ref: Sections 131(1), 131(1A), 131(2) and 131(3) — the four Civil Court powers, their exercise by the investigation wing where no proceeding is pending, and the 15-day limit on retention by an Assessing Officer or an Assistant or Deputy Director without prior approval

concepts.subsection: Section 132 — who may authorise a search, what may be seized, and what may only be restrained
concepts.statement: A search is authorised by a Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director, Director, Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner; an Additional Director, Additional Commissioner, Joint Director or Joint Commissioner may also authorise one, but only if empowered by the Board, and the officer he may then name is confined to an Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner or Income-tax Officer. The authorising officer must have reason to believe, on information in his possession, one of three things — that a person served with a summons under section 131(1) or a notice under section 142(1) has failed to produce the books called for, that a person who has been or might be served will not produce them, or that a person holds money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable articles representing income not disclosed. That reason to believe is not disclosed to any person, any authority or the Appellate Tribunal. What the authorised officer may then do divides into three. He may seize money, bullion, jewellery and other valuable articles found, except that bullion, jewellery or another valuable article which is the stock-in-trade of the business is never seized and only a note or inventory of it is made. Where the thing cannot physically be moved because of its volume, weight, other physical characteristics or dangerous nature, he serves an order under the second proviso to section 132(1) forbidding its removal, and that order is deemed to be a seizure — though even this deeming does not reach stock-in-trade. Where the reason for not seizing is anything else, the order he serves is under section 132(3), it is not a seizure at all, and it lapses after 60 days under section 132(8A); contravening it is punishable under section 275A with imprisonment for up to two years and a fine. Everything found in a person's possession during a search carries the rebuttable presumption in section 132(4A) — that it belongs to him, that the contents of the books are true, and that the handwriting, signature, stamping, execution and attestation are what they appear to be — and section 292C extends that presumption to anything found in a survey under section 133A and to anything delivered to a requisitioning officer under section 132A.

citation.ref: Section 132(1) with its first and second provisos and section 132(1A), read with sections 132(3), 132(4A) and 132(8A), section 275A and section 292C — the authorising ladder, the three limbs of reason to believe, stock-in-trade excluded from seizure, deemed seizure against a 60-day restraint order, and the rebuttable presumption extended to survey and requisition

concepts.subsection: Sections 132(8), 132(9A), 132(9B), 132(9C) and 132(9D) — the clocks that start when a search ends
concepts.statement: Four separate periods run from the end of a search, and the exam tests them against each other. For all of them the last of the authorisations for search is deemed executed on the conclusion of the search as recorded in the last panchnama, or, for a requisition under section 132A, on the actual receipt of the books or assets. Within 60 days of that date the authorised officer must hand seized material to the Assessing Officer having jurisdiction where he has none himself, and from then on that officer exercises the retention powers [section 132(9A)]. Within the same 60 days, or during the search itself, he may provisionally attach any property of the assessee to protect the revenue, for reasons recorded in writing and with the prior approval of the Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director [section 132(9B)]; that attachment dies on its own after six months from the date of the order [section 132(9C)]. Within the same 60 days, or during the search, he may also refer the property to a Valuation Officer under section 142A or to an approved valuer, who must report the fair market value within 60 days from the date he receives the reference [section 132(9D)]. Seized books of account and other documents run on a different clock altogether — they are returned within one month from the end of the quarter in which the assessment, reassessment or recomputation order is made, unless reasons for retaining them are recorded in writing and approved by a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director; and even with that approval they cannot be kept for more than 30 days after the assessment proceedings for the years to which they are relevant are completed [section 132(8)]. A person legally entitled to the books who objects to that approval may apply to the Board, which decides after hearing him [section 132(10)].

citation.ref: Sections 132(8), 132(9A), 132(9B), 132(9C), 132(9D) and 132(10) with Explanation 1 to section 132 — 60 days for handover, provisional attachment and a valuation reference, six months for the life of the attachment, 60 days for the valuer's report, and one month from the end of the quarter for the return of seized books with a 30-day outer limit after the proceedings are completed

concepts.subsection: Section 132B — what happens to the money and the assets taken in a search
concepts.statement: Assets seized under section 132 or requisitioned under section 132A may be applied against any existing liability under the Income-tax Act, 1961, the Black Money Act, 2015 and the other named enactments, and against the liability determined on completion of the assessment, reassessment, recomputation or block assessment that follows the search, including the penalty and interest connected with it, where the assessee is in default or deemed to be in default. Existing liability does not include advance tax. Where the seized assets are money, or partly money, the Assessing Officer applies the money and the assessee is discharged to that extent; other assets are deemed to be under distraint and may be sold in the manner laid down in the Third Schedule, and whatever is left after the liabilities are met is handed back at once to the person from whose custody it was taken. There is a route out for money the assessee can explain. He must apply to the Assessing Officer within 30 days from the end of the month in which the asset was seized and explain the nature and source of its acquisition to that officer's satisfaction, and the asset is then released, after meeting existing liabilities and with the prior approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, within 120 days from the date the last of the authorisations was executed. Where the assets seized turn out to exceed the liabilities, the assessee is entitled to simple interest at one half per cent for every month or part of a month, running from the expiry of those 120 days to the date the assessment, reassessment or recomputation is completed. In Hemant Kumar Sindhi the Allahabad High Court held that an existing liability means one crystallised by adjudication and a liability is determined only on completion of the assessment, so an assessee cannot have seized gold sold and the proceeds set against tax on income he surrendered during the search before any assessment is made.

citation.ref: Section 132B with the proviso to section 132B(1)(i) and section 132B(4), read with Hemant Kumar Sindhi and Another v. CIT (2014) 364 ITR 555 (All) — the 30-day application, the 120-day release, interest at one half per cent a month thereafter, and advance tax excluded from existing liability

concepts.subsection: Section 133A — the power of survey, when it may be exercised and what it stops short of
concepts.statement: A survey is not a small search, and every limit on it is examinable. An income-tax authority may enter a place within the area assigned to him, or occupied by a person over whom he has jurisdiction, or one he is authorised for, at which a business, a profession or an activity for a charitable purpose is carried on, whether or not it is the principal place, and any other place at which the person says his books or valuable articles are kept. He may require the proprietor, trustee, employee or anyone helping in the work to let him inspect the books and documents, to let him check or verify the cash, stock or other valuable articles, and to furnish information. On timing the section draws a line between two kinds of place — a place of business or profession may be entered only during the hours at which it is open for business, and any other place only after sunrise and before sunset. The hour of entry is fixed and the hour of leaving is not, so a survey lawfully begun at ten at night in a shop trading until eleven may carry on past closing. He may place marks of identification on the books, take extracts and copies, make an inventory of the cash, stock or valuable articles checked, and record the statement of any person; he may impound books after recording his reasons, but may not retain them beyond 15 days excluding holidays without the approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director. Under section 133A(4) he may not remove any cash, stock or other valuable article from the place at all — there is no seizure in a survey. Where a person refuses or evades, section 133A(6) gives him all the powers under section 131(1) to compel compliance. Section 133A(5) lets him collect information and record statements about a function, ceremony or event after it is over and before assessment proceedings for the relevant year begin. Every survey needs the approval of a Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner. A survey under section 133A(2A) is a narrower thing done for one purpose only, verifying that tax has been deducted or collected under Chapter XVII-B or XVII-BB: it may be entered only after sunrise and before sunset even at a place of business, and in it the authority may neither impound books nor make an inventory of cash, stock or valuable articles.

citation.ref: Sections 133A(1) to 133A(6) with the Explanation to section 133A — business hours against sunrise to sunset, the 15-day limit on impounding excluding holidays, the bar in section 133A(4) on removing cash, stock or valuable articles, and the narrower powers in a section 133A(2A) survey for verifying deduction or collection at source

concepts.subsection: Sections 133, 133B and 133C — calling for information, collecting it, and the faceless scheme
concepts.statement: Section 133 lets the Assessing Officer, the Joint Commissioner, the Joint Commissioner (Appeals) and the Commissioner (Appeals) call for named information — the partners of a firm and their shares, the manager and members of a Hindu undivided family, the beneficiaries of a trustee, guardian or agent, a statement of everyone to whom the assessee paid rent, interest, commission, royalty, brokerage or a non-salary annuity of more than ₹1,000 in a previous year, the payments and receipts of a dealer, broker or agent connected with a stock or commodity exchange, and under section 133(6) any information at all from any person including a banking company that will be useful for or relevant to an enquiry or proceeding. Section 133(6) is also exercisable by the Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director, Director, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Joint Director, Deputy Director and Assistant Director. Where no proceeding is pending, no authority below the rank of Principal Director, Director, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may exercise it without their prior approval — but a Joint Director, Deputy Director or Assistant Director may, and the Supreme Court settled the point in Kathiroor Service Co-operative Bank. Section 133B is a smaller power still: an income-tax authority, meaning a Joint Commissioner, Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assessing Officer or an authorised Inspector, may enter a place of business only during business hours and only to collect prescribed information, may on no account remove any books of account or valuable articles, and a failure to furnish what he asks for attracts a penalty of up to ₹1,000 under section 272AA. Section 133C lets a prescribed authority, not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner and authorised by the Board, issue a notice requiring information or documents to verify what it already holds, and process what comes back under the scheme made under section 135A for the faceless collection of information — the e-Verification Scheme, 2021.

citation.ref: Sections 133, 133B, 133C and 135A read with Kathiroor Service Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. CIT (CIB) (2014) 360 ITR 243 (SC) — the ₹1,000 reporting threshold in section 133(4), prior approval for section 133(6) where no proceeding is pending and the exemption for a Joint, Deputy or Assistant Director, the ₹1,000 penalty under section 272AA, and the e-Verification Scheme, 2021

concepts.subsection: Sections 119 and 119(2)(b) — what the Board may direct, and who condones a delay
concepts.statement: Section 119 lets the Central Board of Direct Taxes issue orders, instructions and directions to income-tax authorities, and section 119(2)(b) lets it authorise an authority to admit an application or claim for an exemption, deduction, refund or any other relief after the period allowed by the Act has expired, to avoid genuine hardship. A claim to carry forward a loss in a return filed late is a claim for other relief within that clause, which is what the Delhi High Court held in Lodhi Property Company Ltd. when a return carrying a loss was one day late. Circular No. 11/2024 dated 1 October 2024 puts the power in the hands of different officers by the size of the claim — a claim up to ₹1 crore for any one assessment year goes to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, a claim above ₹1 crore and up to ₹3 crore to the Chief Commissioner, and a claim above ₹3 crore to the Principal Chief Commissioner. What the Board cannot do is legislate: in CIT v. S.V. Gopala the Supreme Court held that it has no power to amend a legislative provision by issuing a circular. Circulars issued under section 119 bind the officers and persons employed in executing the Act and do not bind the appellate authorities, the Tribunal, the courts or the taxpayer, though a taxpayer may take the benefit of a circular that favours him.

citation.ref: Section 119 and section 119(2)(b) read with CBDT Circular No. 11/2024 dated 1 October 2024 and with CIT and Anr v. S.V. Gopala and Others (2017) 396 ITR 694 (SC) and Lodhi Property Company Ltd. v. Under Secretary (ITA-II) (2010) 323 ITR 441 — the ₹1 crore and ₹3 crore ladder for condoning delay, and the limits of a circular

concepts.subsection: Sections 269SU and 271DB — the duty to offer an electronic payment facility
concepts.statement: Section 269SU requires every person carrying on business whose total sales, turnover or gross receipts in business exceeded ₹50 crore during the immediately preceding previous year to provide a facility for accepting payment through prescribed electronic modes, in addition to whatever electronic facilities he already offers. Rule 119AA prescribes three and only three modes — a debit card powered by RuPay, the Unified Payments Interface, and the Unified Payments Interface Quick Response Code. The duty is to offer them, not to be paid through them. Failure attracts a penalty under section 271DB of ₹5,000 for every day during which the failure continues, imposed by the Assessing Officer, and no penalty is imposed if the person proves there were good and sufficient reasons for the failure. Two things narrow it. Circular No. 12/2020 dated 20 May 2020 says the section does not apply to a person having only business-to-business transactions, with no transaction with a retail customer or consumer, where at least 95 per cent of all amounts received during the previous year, including receipts for sales, turnover or gross receipts, come by a mode other than cash. And the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 was amended so that no bank or system provider may charge anyone, directly or indirectly, for using these modes, with Circular No. 16/2020 telling banks to refund charges collected on or after 1 January 2020.

citation.ref: Section 269SU with Rule 119AA and section 271DB, read with CBDT Circular No. 12/2020 dated 20 May 2020 — the ₹50 crore turnover trigger, the three prescribed electronic modes, the ₹5,000 a day penalty and the 95 per cent business-to-business relief

concepts.subsection: Section 281B — provisional attachment during a proceeding, and the bank guarantee that lifts it
concepts.statement: Section 281B lets the Assessing Officer provisionally attach any property of the assessee by an order in writing, in the manner provided in the Second Schedule, where he thinks it necessary to protect the interests of the revenue. It is available during the pendency of an assessment or a reassessment of income that has escaped assessment, and also for the imposition of a penalty under section 271AAD for a false entry in the books where the penalty likely to be imposed exceeds ₹2 crore, and it needs the prior approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director. The attachment is valid for six months from the date of the order. It may be extended for reasons recorded in writing by the same authorities, but the total period of extension cannot exceed two years, or 60 days after the date of the assessment or reassessment, whichever is later. The assessee can buy his property back out of it: where he furnishes a guarantee from a scheduled bank for not less than the fair market value of the attached property, or for an amount sufficient to protect the revenue, the Assessing Officer must revoke the attachment — within 45 days of receiving the guarantee where he has referred the property to a Valuation Officer, who must report within 30 days of the reference, and within 15 days in any other case. The guarantee is then live security. If a notice of demand is served and the sum is not paid in time the Assessing Officer may invoke it wholly or partly; if the assessee fails to renew it or furnish a new one for an equal amount fifteen days before it expires the Assessing Officer must invoke it; what is realised goes first against the existing demand and any balance to the Personal Deposit Account of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner; and where the guarantee is no longer needed to protect the revenue it is released forthwith.

citation.ref: Sections 281B(1) to 281B(9) — six months' validity with the extension capped at two years or 60 days after the assessment whichever is later, the ₹2 crore section 271AAD trigger, and the 45-day and 15-day windows for revoking an attachment against a scheduled bank guarantee with the Valuation Officer reporting within 30 days

concepts.subsection: Section 285BA with Rule 114E — the statement of financial transactions and what a default costs
concepts.statement: Section 285BA obliges the persons it names — an assessee, a prescribed person in a Government office, a local authority, a Registrar or Sub-Registrar, a motor vehicle registering authority, the Post Master General, a Collector under the land acquisition law, a recognised stock exchange, an officer of the Reserve Bank, a depository, a prescribed reporting financial institution and any other prescribed person — to furnish a statement of specified financial transactions or reportable accounts they register, record or maintain. Rule 114E sets the values and the reporting person for each. A banking company or co-operative bank reports cash purchases of drafts, pay orders or banker's cheques and of Reserve Bank pre-paid instruments aggregating ₹10 lakh or more in a financial year, and cash deposits or withdrawals aggregating ₹50 lakh or more in one or more current accounts; cash deposits of ₹10 lakh or more in accounts that are neither current accounts nor time deposits, and time deposits of ₹10 lakh or more, are also reported. Credit card bills are reported at ₹1 lakh or more in cash or ₹10 lakh or more by any other mode. Bonds or debentures, shares including share application money, a listed company's buy-back, mutual fund units and the sale of foreign currency are each reported at ₹10 lakh or more in a financial year. A Registrar or Sub-Registrar reports the purchase or sale of immovable property for ₹30 lakh or more, or valued by the stamp valuation authority at ₹30 lakh or more. And a person liable to audit under section 44AB reports the receipt of cash exceeding ₹2 lakh for the sale of any goods or services not already covered. The statement goes in Form No. 61A on or before 31 May immediately following the financial year in which the transaction is recorded. A defective statement may be rectified within 30 days of the intimation of the defect, or such further time as is allowed, and if it is not the Act applies as though inaccurate information had been furnished. Where nothing is filed the prescribed authority may serve a notice allowing not more than 30 days. Where the filer later discovers an inaccuracy he must inform the authority and furnish the correct information within ten days.

citation.ref: Section 285BA with Rule 114E and Form No. 61A — the ₹10 lakh, ₹30 lakh and ₹50 lakh reporting values, the ₹2 lakh cash receipt reported by a person liable to audit under section 44AB, the 31 May due date, and the 30-day and ten-day windows in sections 285BA(4) to 285BA(6)

concepts.subsection: Sections 285BB and 285BAA — the annual information statement, and the new crypto-asset statement
concepts.statement: Section 285BB puts the flow of information the other way round. The prescribed income-tax authority, or a person authorised by it, uploads into the assessee's own registered account an annual information statement containing the prescribed information in its possession. Rule 114-I names the officer as the Principal Director General of Income-tax (Systems) or the Director General of Income-tax (Systems) or a person authorised by him, names the form as Form No. 26AS, and fixes the timing — within three months from the end of the month in which the information is received. Six categories go into it: tax deducted or collected at source, specified financial transactions, payment of taxes, demand and refund, pending proceedings and completed proceedings. The Board may authorise the same officer to add information received from any officer, authority or body performing a function under any law, information received under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A, and information from any other person, to the extent it thinks fit in the interest of the revenue. Section 285BAA is the newest of these obligations and runs on the same machinery as section 285BA: a prescribed reporting entity furnishes a statement of transactions in crypto-assets for the prescribed period, in the prescribed form and to the prescribed authority; a defect may be rectified within 30 days of the intimation or such further period as is allowed, failing which the Act applies as though inaccurate information had been furnished; a person who has filed nothing may be given a notice of not more than 30 days; and a filer who discovers an inaccuracy must correct it within ten days. A crypto-asset for this purpose is the digital representation of value defined in section 2(47A)(d), which relies on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or a similar technology to validate and secure transactions.

citation.ref: Section 285BB with Rule 114-I and Form No. 26AS, and section 285BAA read with section 2(47A)(d) — the six categories of information, the three-month upload window, and the 30-day and ten-day windows on the crypto-asset statement

concepts.subsection: Section 288 — who may appear for an assessee, and who is shut out
concepts.statement: An assessee entitled or required to attend before an income-tax authority or the Appellate Tribunal may attend by an authorised representative, meaning a person authorised by him in writing to appear on his behalf — except where section 131 requires him to attend personally for examination on oath or affirmation, which nobody may do for him. The people who may be authorised are a relative or a person regularly employed by the assessee, an officer of a scheduled bank with which he keeps a current account or has other regular dealings, a legal practitioner entitled to practise in any Civil Court in India, an accountant, and a person who has passed an accountancy examination recognised by the Board under Rule 50. Accountant means a chartered accountant holding a valid certificate of practice, and it is here that the section does its work, because it excludes exactly the people who are too close to the assessee to audit him. For a company the excluded list is the section 141(3) list of the Companies Act, 2013 — a body corporate other than a limited liability partnership, an officer or employee, a partner or employee of an officer or employee, a person whose relative or partner is indebted to the company or its group in excess of ₹5 lakh or has given a guarantee or security for a third person's debt to it in excess of ₹1 lakh, a person or firm with a prescribed business relationship, a person whose relative is a director or key managerial personnel, a person already auditing more than 20 companies, and a person convicted of an offence involving fraud where ten years have not elapsed; a relative may hold security or interest in the company of a face value not exceeding ₹1,000. For an individual, firm, association of persons or Hindu undivided family it is the assessee himself or a member or partner and their relatives; for a trust or institution it is the author or founder, anyone whose total contribution up to the end of the relevant previous year exceeds ₹50,000, a member of a Hindu undivided family that is one of them, any trustee or manager, and their relatives. A relative of the assessee may hold security or interest in him of a face value not exceeding ₹1 lakh, be indebted to him for not more than ₹1 lakh and guarantee a third person's debt to him up to ₹1 lakh. And there is a rider that decides cases: being ineligible to audit an assessee or to furnish a report or certificate for him does not make an accountant ineligible to appear for him as an authorised representative. Where the matter is the valuation of an asset, section 287A lets the taxpayer attend by a registered valuer instead.

citation.ref: Section 288 with section 288(2) and the Explanation defining accountant, read with section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 and section 287A — the ₹5 lakh indebtedness and ₹1 lakh guarantee limits, the ₹1,000 and ₹1 lakh security limits for a relative, the ₹50,000 substantial contribution to a trust, and the rider that audit ineligibility does not bar appearance

concepts.subsection: Sections 245N, 245-OB, 245P and 245U — what an advance ruling is, who may ask for one, and who gives it
concepts.statement: An advance ruling settles a question before the issue arises, so that the litigation never happens. Section 245N(a) gives it five limbs, and each has its own applicant. A non-resident may ask about a transaction he has undertaken or proposes to undertake. A resident may ask about the tax liability of a non-resident arising out of a transaction he has undertaken or proposes to undertake with that non-resident. A resident of a class notified by the Central Government may ask about his own tax liability arising out of his own transaction, and the notification of 28 November 2014 makes that a resident whose one or more transactions total ₹100 crore or more. A resident of a notified class may ask about an issue relating to the computation of total income that is already pending before an income-tax authority or the Appellate Tribunal, and the notified class there is a public sector company. And any person, resident or non-resident, may ask whether an arrangement he proposes to undertake is an impermissible avoidance arrangement under Chapter X-A. Section 245RR stops a resident applicant running both remedies at once — where he has applied to the Board for a decision on an issue, no income-tax authority or Tribunal may decide that issue. Three Boards for Advance Rulings have given rulings since 1 September 2021, two with their headquarters in Delhi and one in Mumbai, constituted under section 245-OB; each consists of two members, each an officer not below the rank of Chief Commissioner nominated by the Board, and what it pronounces is appealable to the High Court. Under section 245P a vacancy or a defect in the constitution of a Board does not make its proceedings or its ruling open to question. Under section 245U a Board has all the powers of a Civil Court in respect of discovery and inspection, enforcing the attendance of any person including an officer of a banking company and examining him on oath, issuing commissions and compelling the production of books of account; it is deemed a Civil Court for section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and every proceeding before it is a judicial proceeding, but it is not a Civil Court for Chapter XXVI of that Code.

citation.ref: Sections 245N(a) and 245N(b), 245-OB, 245P, 245RR and 245U with Notification No. 73/2014 dated 28 November 2014 and Notification No. 725(E) dated 3 August 2000 — the five limbs of advance ruling, the ₹100 crore notified resident and the public sector company, three Boards of two members each not below the rank of Chief Commissioner from 1 September 2021, and the Civil Court powers

concepts.subsection: Sections 245Q, 245R, 245T and 245W — the fee, the grounds of rejection, the six months and the appeal
concepts.statement: An application for an advance ruling is made under section 245Q(1) stating the question, in quadruplicate, accompanied under section 245Q(2) by a fee of ₹10,000 or such fee as may be prescribed, whichever is higher. Rule 44E prescribes the higher fees by the size of the transaction for an applicant falling in sub-clause (i), (ii) or (iia) of section 245N(b) — ₹2 lakh where the transactions in respect of which the ruling is sought do not exceed ₹100 crore, ₹5 lakh where they exceed ₹100 crore but do not exceed ₹300 crore, and ₹10 lakh where they exceed ₹300 crore — while any other applicant pays ₹10,000 in all cases. The applicant may withdraw within 30 days from the date of the application. On receiving it the Board sends a copy to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner and may call for the records, and then allows or rejects. It shall not allow an application where the question is already pending before any income-tax authority, the Appellate Tribunal or any court, though a notified resident may ask even then; where it involves the determination of the fair market value of any property; or where it relates to a transaction or issue designed prima facie for the avoidance of income-tax, except for a notified resident applicant and except where the question is whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement. No application is rejected without an opportunity of being heard and the order must give the reason. Where the application is allowed the Board pronounces its ruling within six months from the receipt of the application, giving a hearing in person or by an authorised representative if one is asked for.
