Under section 245T, where the Board finds on a representation by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or otherwise that a ruling was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts, it may declare it void ab initio, and the Act then applies to the applicant as if the ruling had never been made, after excluding the period from the date of the ruling to the date of that order. Under section 245W(1) an applicant aggrieved by a ruling or order of the Board or of the Assessing Officer on the directions of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may appeal to the High Court within 60 days from the communication of the ruling or order, and where the High Court is satisfied that sufficient cause prevented him it may grant a further period of 30 days.

citation.ref: Sections 245Q, 245R, 245T and 245W with Rule 44E — the ₹10,000 minimum fee and the ₹2 lakh, ₹5 lakh and ₹10 lakh slabs against ₹100 crore and ₹300 crore, withdrawal within 30 days, the three grounds on which an application shall not be allowed, the six-month time limit for pronouncing a ruling, a ruling declared void ab initio for fraud with the intervening period excluded, and an appeal to the High Court within 60 days extendable by 30 days

concepts.section: Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
concepts.subsection: Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Black Money Act, 2015 — the charge, the year, and what may be deducted
concepts.statement: Under section 3(1) of the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 every assessee is liable to tax at 30 per cent on his undisclosed foreign income and asset of the previous year. The proviso moves the year for an asset: an undisclosed asset located outside India is charged on its value in the previous year in which the asset comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer, however long ago it was acquired. An undisclosed asset located outside India is one held by the assessee in his own name or of which he is the beneficial owner, and about the source of investment in which he has no explanation or gives one the Assessing Officer finds unsatisfactory; its value under section 3(2) is the fair market value determined under Rule 3. Total undisclosed foreign income and asset under section 4 is foreign-source income not disclosed in a return filed under section 139(1), 139(4) or 139(5), foreign-source income for which no return was filed at all, and the value of any undisclosed foreign asset — and income charged under this Act does not form part of total income under the Income-tax Act, 1961. Section 5 computes it harshly on one side and fairly on the other. No deduction is allowed for any expenditure or allowance, and no loss may be set off, whether or not the Income-tax Act would have allowed it. But from the value of an undisclosed asset abroad the assessee may reduce any income that has already been assessed to tax under the Income-tax Act for an assessment year before this Act applied, and any income assessable or assessed under this Act, provided he furnishes evidence satisfying the Assessing Officer that the asset was acquired out of it. Where the asset is immovable property that deduction is proportionate: it bears to the value of the asset on the first day of the financial year in which it comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer the same proportion as the assessed or assessable foreign income bears to the total cost of the asset.

citation.source: Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015
citation.ref: Sections 3(1) and 3(2) with the proviso, section 4 and section 5(1) and (2) — tax at 30 per cent, an undisclosed foreign asset charged in the previous year in which it comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer, no expenditure or set-off allowed, and the proportionate deduction for immovable property measured on the value at the first day of that financial year

concepts.section: Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
concepts.subsection: Sections 41 to 56 of the Black Money Act, 2015 — the penalties, the ₹20 lakh let-off and the prison terms
concepts.statement: The penalties under the Black Money Act are deliberately out of scale with the Income-tax Act. Where tax has been computed on undisclosed foreign income and asset, section 41 lets the Assessing Officer direct the assessee to pay, in addition to the tax, a sum equal to three times that tax. Section 42 charges ₹10 lakh on a resident other than a not ordinarily resident who holds a foreign asset as beneficial owner or otherwise, or is the beneficiary of one, or has foreign-source income, and fails to furnish the return required by section 139(1) before the end of the relevant assessment year. Section 43 charges another ₹10 lakh where he files but fails to furnish the information about such an asset in the return or furnishes inaccurate particulars of it. The proviso to both is the practical relief and the thing to remember: neither penalty applies in respect of an asset or assets, other than immovable property, whose aggregate value does not exceed ₹20 lakh. Where the balance is in a foreign currency account the rupee value is taken at the State Bank of India telegraphic transfer buying rate on the relevant date. Section 44 charges a penalty equal to the tax arrears on an assessee in default, and paying the tax before the penalty is levied does not save him. Section 45 charges not less than ₹50,000 and up to ₹2 lakh for failing without reasonable cause to answer a question, sign a statement, or attend or produce books in response to a summons under section 8. Under section 46(4) an order imposing a penalty needs the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner or Joint Director where it exceeds ₹1 lakh and is levied by an Income-tax Officer, or exceeds ₹5 lakh and is levied by an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner or an Assistant or Deputy Director. On the criminal side, wilful failure to furnish the return under section 49 is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for not less than six months and up to seven years and a fine, but prosecution is not attracted if the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year. Wilful failure to furnish information about a foreign asset under section 50, a false statement in a verification under section 52 and abetment under section 53 carry the same six months to seven years. A wilful attempt to evade tax, penalty or interest under section 51 carries rigorous imprisonment of not less than three years and up to ten years; a wilful attempt to evade payment of it carries three months to three years. Under section 54 the court presumes a culpable mental state and the accused must prove he had none, and under section 55 no prosecution under sections 49 to 53 is begun except with the sanction of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or the Commissioner (Appeals).

citation.source: Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015
citation.ref: Sections 41, 42, 43 with their proviso, 44, 45, 46(4), 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54 and 55 — three times the tax, ₹10 lakh each under sections 42 and 43 with no penalty where assets other than immovable property do not exceed ₹20 lakh in aggregate, ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh under section 45, the ₹1 lakh and ₹5 lakh approval limits, and rigorous imprisonment of six months to seven years under section 49 with three to ten years under section 51

concepts.subsection: Section 54 — Capital gains on residential property
concepts.statement: Section 54 exempts long-term capital gains on the transfer of a residential house only when the gain is reinvested in a residential house in India — purchased within one year before or two years after the transfer, or constructed within three years. Reinvestment in commercial property earns no exemption.

citation.ref: Section 54

concepts.subsection: Section 44AB — Tax audit
concepts.statement: Tax audit applies to a business at turnover above ₹1 crore, but the limit rises to ₹10 crore where cash receipts and cash payments each stay within 5 per cent of the respective totals. For a profession the limit is gross receipts above ₹50 lakh.

citation.ref: Section 44AB

concepts.subsection: Section 115BAA — Concessional company rate
concepts.statement: A domestic company that opts for section 115BAA pays tax at the concessional rate, must give up the specified deductions and incentives, and is outside MAT entirely — book profit tax does not apply to it at all.

citation.ref: Section 115BAA read with Section 115JB(5A)

concepts.subsection: Section 139 — Return filing
concepts.statement: A company files its return by 31 October of the assessment year. Where it must furnish a transfer pricing report under section 92E, the due date extends to 30 November. The 31 July date belongs to persons with no audit requirement.

citation.ref: Section 139(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 112A — Listed equity gains
concepts.statement: Long-term capital gains on listed equity shares where STT is paid are taxed under section 112A above an annual exemption threshold, without indexation. The rate and threshold are Finance Act figures and move; the structure — exemption slab, no indexation, STT condition — is the stable part.

citation.ref: Section 112A

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 44AD — Presumptive business taxation
concepts.statement: An eligible resident individual, HUF or firm with business turnover within the limit may declare profit at 8 per cent of turnover — 6 per cent for amounts received through banking channels — and skip books and tax audit. Companies and LLPs are outside the scheme, as are commission, agency and section 44AE transport businesses.

citation.ref: Section 44AD

concepts.section: Aggregation of Income, Set Off or Carry Forward of Losses
concepts.subsection: Sections 72 and 80 — Carry forward of losses
concepts.statement: A business loss carries forward for eight assessment years, but only if the return of the loss year was filed by its due date — section 80 makes the timely return the price of the carry forward. Unabsorbed depreciation lives under section 32(2) instead, needs no timely return, and has no eight-year limit.

citation.ref: Section 72 read with Section 80

concepts.subsection: Section 56(2)(x) — Taxation of gifts
concepts.statement: Money received without consideration is taxable as other-sources income if the aggregate from all persons in the year exceeds fifty thousand rupees — and then the whole amount is taxed, not the excess. Gifts from relatives as defined, and on the occasion of the individual's marriage, stay outside regardless of size.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 44ADA — Presumptive taxation for professionals
concepts.statement: A resident individual or firm in a specified profession with gross receipts within the limit may declare 50 per cent of receipts as income. The enhanced limit applies where cash receipts stay within 5 per cent. Declaring less than 50 per cent while over the basic exemption brings books and audit.

citation.ref: Section 44ADA

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 194-IA — TDS on purchase of property
concepts.statement: A buyer of immovable property, other than rural agricultural land, deducts tax at 1 per cent of the consideration where consideration or stamp duty value is fifty lakh rupees or more — and then on the whole amount, not the excess. The buyer needs no TAN; the deduction rides on the buyer's PAN.

citation.ref: Section 194-IA

concepts.subsection: Section 6 — Residence
concepts.statement: An individual is resident if present in India for 182 days in the year, or 60 days in the year plus 365 across the four preceding years. The 60-day limb stretches to 182 for a citizen leaving for employment or as crew, and to 120 for a visiting citizen or person of Indian origin whose Indian income exceeds fifteen lakh rupees.

citation.ref: Section 6(1)

concepts.section: Income of Other Persons included in Assessee's Total Income
concepts.subsection: Section 64(1A) — Clubbing of minor's income
concepts.statement: A minor child's income is clubbed with the income of the parent whose total income is higher, with an exemption of fifteen hundred rupees per child. Income from the minor's own manual work or from activity involving the minor's skill and talent stays with the minor.

citation.ref: Section 64(1A) read with Section 10(32)

concepts.section: Aggregation of Income, Set Off or Carry Forward of Losses
concepts.subsection: Section 71(3A) — House property loss set-off
concepts.statement: Loss under house property can be set off against other heads only up to two lakh rupees in a year; the balance carries forward for eight years, and then only against house property income. The interest deduction itself may be larger — the cap bites at set-off, not at computation.

citation.ref: Section 71(3A)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 43B(h) — Payments to micro and small enterprises
concepts.statement: Sums payable to micro and small enterprises are deductible only in the year of actual payment when paid beyond the time section 15 of the MSMED Act allows — and the usual escape of paying before the return's due date does not apply to this clause. Medium enterprises are outside it.

citation.ref: Section 43B(h)

concepts.subsection: Section 50C — Stamp duty value on transfer of land or building
concepts.statement: Where land or a building sells below its stamp duty value, the stamp value is deemed the consideration for capital gains — but only when it exceeds one hundred and ten per cent of the actual consideration; within that tolerance the actual price stands. The seller can also ask for a valuation officer's reference where the stamp value is contested.

citation.ref: Section 50C

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 40(a)(ia) — Disallowance for TDS default
concepts.statement: Where tax deductible on a payment to a resident is not deducted, or not deposited by the return's due date, thirty per cent of the expense is disallowed — not the whole of it — and the thirty per cent comes back as a deduction in the year the tax is finally paid.

citation.ref: Section 40(a)(ia)

concepts.subsection: Section 54EC — Capital gains bonds
concepts.statement: The 54EC exemption is only for long-term capital gains from land or a building or both, only up to fifty lakh rupees in a financial year, and only where the specified bonds are bought within six months of transfer. The bonds lock in for five years, and taking a loan against them counts as cashing out.

citation.ref: Section 54EC

concepts.section: Aggregation of Income, Set Off or Carry Forward of Losses
concepts.subsection: Section 79 — Carry forward on change in shareholding
concepts.statement: A closely held company loses its carried-forward losses if, on the last day of the year the loss is set off, shares carrying at least fifty-one per cent of voting power are not held by the persons who held them on the last day of the loss year. Eligible start-ups get a softer test — continuity of all original shareholders, or the seven-year window. Unabsorbed depreciation is outside section 79 entirely.

citation.ref: Section 79

concepts.subsection: Section 90(4) — Treaty relief and the TRC
concepts.statement: A non-resident claiming treaty benefit must hold a tax residency certificate from its home government; without it the treaty door does not open. The Act also lets the taxpayer choose whichever is more beneficial — treaty or domestic law — provision by provision, and a treaty can never be used to make the position worse than the Act.

citation.ref: Section 90(2) and (4)

concepts.subsection: Section 68 — Cash credits
concepts.statement: An unexplained credit in the books is taxed as income unless the taxpayer explains its nature and source to the officer's satisfaction; for share capital in a closely held company, the source of the source — the resident investor's own funds — must be explained too. Income taxed this way falls under section 115BBE: a sixty per cent rate plus surcharge, with no deductions, allowances, or set-off of losses against it.

citation.ref: Section 68 read with 115BBE

concepts.section: Income of Other Persons included in Assessee's Total Income
concepts.subsection: Section 64(1)(iv) — Income from assets transferred to spouse
concepts.statement: Income from an asset transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration is clubbed with the transferor's income. The clubbing follows the transferred asset's income, not income earned on that income — reinvested earnings belong to the spouse. A transfer before the marriage, or for adequate consideration, or under an agreement to live apart, escapes.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(iv)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 44AE — Presumptive income for transporters
concepts.statement: An assessee owning not more than ten goods carriages at any time in the year may declare presumptive income: for a heavy goods vehicle (over 12MT gross weight), one thousand rupees per ton of gross vehicle weight per month or part; for others, seven thousand five hundred per vehicle per month or part. Ownership months count, idle or running; declaring lower than the presumption invites books and audit.

citation.ref: Section 44AE

concepts.section: Tax Planning, Tax Avoidance and Tax Evasion
concepts.subsection: GAAR — Impermissible avoidance arrangement
concepts.statement: GAAR strikes an arrangement whose main purpose is a tax benefit and which carries a tainted element — non-arm's-length dealings, misuse of the Act, lack of commercial substance, or means not ordinarily employed for bona fide purposes. Both limbs must be satisfied; a tax benefit alone is legitimate planning. The rules spare arrangements whose aggregate tax benefit is within three crore rupees.

citation.ref: Sections 95-96, Rule 10U

concepts.subsection: Transfer pricing — Arm's length price methods
concepts.statement: The arm's length price of an international transaction between associated enterprises is determined by the most appropriate of the prescribed methods — comparable uncontrolled price, resale price, cost plus, profit split, transactional net margin, or other prescribed method. No hierarchy ranks them; suitability to the transaction, functions and available data picks the method, and CUP prevails only when true comparables exist.

citation.ref: Section 92C read with Rule 10B

concepts.subsection: Section 115JB — Minimum alternate tax
concepts.statement: A company not under the concessional regimes pays the higher of tax on total income and fifteen per cent of book profit — the audited profit adjusted by the section's own list of additions and deletions. Excess MAT paid becomes credit, carried forward to set against regular tax for up to fifteen years. Companies opting into section 115BAA leave MAT, and MAT credit, behind.

citation.ref: Section 115JB

concepts.section: Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
concepts.subsection: Section 270A — Under-reporting and misreporting
concepts.statement: Under-reported income draws a penalty of fifty per cent of the tax on it; where the under-reporting flows from misreporting — misrepresentation of facts, false entries, unrecorded investments, claims without evidence — the penalty is two hundred per cent. A bona fide explanation with disclosed material facts takes an addition out of under-reporting altogether; immunity under section 270AA needs tax and interest paid and no appeal, and never covers misreporting.

citation.ref: Sections 270A and 270AA

concepts.subsection: Section 263 — Revision of orders prejudicial to revenue
concepts.statement: The Commissioner may revise an assessment only where it is both erroneous and prejudicial to the revenue's interests — two conditions, cumulative. An officer's view that is a possible view after real enquiry is not erroneous merely because the Commissioner prefers another; no enquiry where enquiry was called for is the classic error. The window is two years from the end of the financial year of the order.

citation.ref: Section 263

concepts.subsection: Section 94B — Limitation on interest deduction
concepts.statement: Interest paid to a non-resident associated enterprise beyond one crore rupees is deductible only up to thirty per cent of EBITDA; the excess carries forward up to eight years. The section reaches loans guaranteed by the associated enterprise too, and spares banks and insurers. It caps deduction, not the interest's character — TDS and the lender's taxation run unaffected.

citation.ref: Section 94B

concepts.subsection: Section 9 — Business connection and significant economic presence
concepts.statement: A non-resident's income is deemed to accrue in India through a business connection — which since 2018 includes an agent habitually playing the principal role in concluding contracts, and since the SEP amendment, a significant economic presence built on transactions or user engagement in India without any physical presence. Treaty definitions of permanent establishment still override for treaty residents, which keeps SEP's bite mainly on non-treaty cases.

citation.ref: Section 9(1)(i) with Explanation 2A

concepts.section: Assessment of Trusts and Institutions, Political Parties and Other Special Entities
concepts.subsection: Sections 11-12 — Charitable trusts
concepts.statement: A registered trust's income is exempt to the extent applied to charitable purposes in India, with at least eighty-five per cent to be applied in the year — fifteen per cent may be accumulated freely. Falling short, the trust may accumulate for up to five years for a specific purpose by filing the prescribed statement, or treat income received late as applied when actually spent. Application now counts on payment, not accrual.

citation.ref: Section 11(1) and 11(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 50B — Slump sale
concepts.statement: A slump sale transfers an undertaking as a going concern for a lump sum without itemised values; capital gain is the deemed consideration — the fair market value computed under the rules — less the undertaking's net worth as cost of acquisition, with net worth computed on the prescribed basis, ignoring revaluations. An undertaking held over thirty-six months yields long-term gain even though depreciable assets ride inside it.

citation.ref: Section 50B

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 194R — TDS on business perquisites
concepts.statement: A person providing any benefit or perquisite arising from business or profession — foreign trips for dealers, gifted cars, sponsored gadgets, waived debts — deducts ten per cent of its value, where the aggregate to a recipient exceeds twenty thousand rupees in the year. The deduction applies whether the benefit is in cash or kind or partly both, and for benefits wholly in kind the provider must ensure tax is paid before releasing them.

citation.ref: Section 194R

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 35 — Scientific research expenditure
concepts.statement: In-house scientific research related to the business earns deduction of both revenue and capital expenditure — land excluded — in the year incurred; pre-commencement research expenditure of the three prior years is deductible in the year business begins. The weighted deductions of the past have sunset to one hundred per cent, and contributions to approved institutions ride their own approval-dependent limbs.

citation.ref: Section 35(1) and (2)

concepts.subsection: Corporate residence — place of effective management
concepts.statement: A foreign company is resident in India if its place of effective management — where key management and commercial decisions necessary for the business as a whole are in substance made — is in India that year. Board meetings held abroad do not settle it when the board merely ratifies decisions taken in India; conversely, active regional headquarters abroad making the decisions keep POEM outside. The test is substance over minutes.

citation.ref: Section 6(3)

concepts.subsection: Appeals — Commissioner (Appeals) powers
concepts.statement: The Commissioner (Appeals) may confirm, reduce, enhance or annul an assessment — the power to enhance makes the first appeal a two-edged forum, exercisable only after a reasonable opportunity to show cause. What the first appellate authority lacks is the power to set aside and remand the assessment for a fresh run; the appeal must be decided, point by point.

citation.ref: Sections 250-251

concepts.subsection: Buy-back proceeds as dividend — section 2(22)(f)
concepts.statement: For buy-backs on or after 1 October 2024, the company-level buy-back tax is gone: the entire consideration a shareholder receives is deemed a dividend under section 2(22)(f), taxable at slab rates with no deduction for cost, and subject to dividend TDS. The shares' cost is not lost — the transfer is computed with consideration deemed nil, manufacturing a capital loss that sets off and carries forward against capital gains only.

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(f) (Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024)

concepts.subsection: Deemed dividend — section 2(22)(e)
concepts.statement: A loan or advance by a closely held company to a shareholder holding ten per cent or more of voting power — or to a concern in which such a shareholder is substantially interested — is deemed a dividend to the extent of the company's accumulated profits. Repayment later does not undo the deeming; loans in the ordinary course of a money-lending business and certain set-offs escape it.

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e)

concepts.section: Aggregation of Income, Set Off or Carry Forward of Losses
concepts.subsection: Section 73 — Speculation losses
concepts.statement: Speculation loss sets off only against speculation profit, and carries forward just four years. A speculative transaction settles otherwise than by actual delivery — but eligible exchange-traded derivatives are excluded from the definition, while the Explanation to section 73 deems a company's share-trading business speculative unless the company falls in the carved-out categories. Delivery-based investing and F&O thus sit outside; a company churning shares as a business sits inside.

citation.ref: Section 73 with section 43(5)

concepts.subsection: Agricultural income — partial integration
concepts.statement: Agricultural income is exempt, but for individuals with net agricultural income above five thousand rupees and other income above the basic exemption, it enters the rate machinery: tax is computed on the aggregate, then reduced by tax on agricultural income plus the exemption limit. The farm income is never taxed itself — it pushes the other income into higher slabs. Companies and firms, taxed at flat rates, are outside the scheme.

citation.ref: Section 10(1) with Finance Act rate schedule

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 43B — Deduction on actual payment
concepts.statement: Certain sums deduct only when actually paid, whatever the books accrue: taxes, duties and cesses, employer contributions to funds, bonus and commission to employees, interest to banks and financial institutions, and leave encashment among them. Payment by the return's due date saves the year's deduction; converting unpaid interest into a fresh loan is expressly not payment, and the deduction waits for the converted loan's actual repayment.

citation.ref: Section 43B

concepts.section: Deduction, Collection and Recovery of Tax
concepts.subsection: Section 194Q — TDS on purchase of goods
concepts.statement: A buyer whose turnover exceeded ten crore rupees in the preceding year deducts tax at 0.1 per cent on purchases from a resident seller beyond fifty lakh rupees in the year, deducting on the excess. The mirror-image seller-side TCS on goods stood omitted from 1 April 2025, ending the old overlap where the buyer's TDS took precedence — the buyer's obligation now stands alone. Failure invites the thirty per cent disallowance for TDS defaults.

citation.ref: Section 194Q (TCS on goods omitted w.e.f. 1 April 2025)

concepts.subsection: Section 54F — Investment of any LTCG in a house
concepts.statement: Long-term gain on any capital asset other than a residential house is exempt where the net consideration — not merely the gain — is invested in one residential house in India, proportionately where investment falls short, capped at ten crore rupees of investment. The gates: not owning more than one other residential house on the transfer date, and no second house purchase within the lock-in windows. Section 54, by contrast, covers house-to-house and asks only the gain to be reinvested.

citation.ref: Section 54F

concepts.subsection: Section 139(8A) — Updated returns
concepts.statement: An updated return may be filed within forty-eight months of the assessment year's end — the window doubled by the Finance Act 2025 — on payment of additional tax that climbs with delay: twenty-five per cent of tax and interest in the first twelve months, fifty in the next, sixty in the third year, seventy in the fourth. It can only add to the tax take: no updated return may declare a loss, shrink the liability, or enlarge a refund.

citation.ref: Section 139(8A) with 140B (Finance Act 2025)

concepts.subsection: Section 40(b) — Partner remuneration limits
concepts.statement: A firm deducts working partners' remuneration only if the deed authorises it, and within the ceiling: on the first six lakh rupees of book profit (or a loss), the higher of three lakh rupees or ninety per cent of that slice; on the balance, sixty per cent — limits doubled by the Finance Act 2024 from assessment year 2025-26. Interest to partners caps at twelve per cent simple. From April 2025, section 194T adds ten per cent TDS on partner payments above twenty thousand rupees a year.

citation.ref: Section 40(b) (Finance Act 2024) with 194T

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 36(1)(vii) — Bad debts
concepts.statement: A bad debt deducts in the year it is written off in the books — since 1989 the write-off itself is enough, and the assessee need not prove the debt actually became irrecoverable that year. The debt must have been counted in income earlier (or be money lent in a lending business). Recovery of an allowed bad debt is taxed when received, and a successor cannot claim the predecessor's debtor.

citation.ref: Section 36(1)(vii) with 41(4)

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: ICDS — Income computation and disclosure standards
concepts.statement: The ten notified ICDS govern computation of business income and other sources for taxpayers following mercantile accounting — they change the tax computation, never the books. Where ICDS diverges from accounting standards, ICDS wins for tax; where ICDS conflicts with the Act itself, the Act prevails. Familiar divergences: expected losses on construction contracts are not anticipated, marked-to-market losses are generally ignored, and retention money follows the ICDS timing.

citation.ref: Section 145(2) with ICDS I-X

concepts.section: Assessment of Trusts and Institutions, Political Parties and Other Special Entities
concepts.subsection: Section 115BBC — Anonymous donations
concepts.statement: Donations for which a charitable trust maintains no record of the donor's name and address are taxed at thirty per cent — after a cushion of the higher of one lakh rupees or five per cent of total donations. Wholly religious institutions are outside the section entirely; mixed religious-charitable ones are caught only for donations directed to their educational or medical wings. The hundi at a temple and the box at a hospital answer to different rules.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC

concepts.section: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
concepts.subsection: Section 35D — Preliminary expenses
concepts.statement: Specified preliminary expenses — feasibility and project reports, engineering services, legal charges for agreements, and for companies the incorporation and issue expenses — amortise in five equal annual instalments from commencement or extension. The pool is capped at five per cent of the cost of the project (companies may take five per cent of capital employed instead); spending beyond the cap earns no deduction at all under the section.

citation.ref: Section 35D

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 1
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he allows any person to practise in his name as a chartered accountant unless such person is also a chartered accountant in practice and is in partnership with or employed by him. Two conditions have to hold together, and the second is not a substitute for the first. A semi-qualified assistant, however experienced, is not a chartered accountant in practice, so no employment contract lets him work in the member's name. A chartered accountant who holds no certificate of practice is a member but is not in practice, so he fails the first condition as well. A chartered accountant in practice who is neither a partner nor an employee fails the second — two independent practices cannot lend each other a name. What the clause protects is the public's ability to know whose judgement stands behind the work: the name on the door has to belong to somebody the Institute can call to account for what was done under it.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 1

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 5
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he secures, either through the services of a person who is not an employee of such chartered accountant or who is not his partner, or by means which are not open to a chartered accountant, any professional business. The clause has two limbs and either one is enough. The first limb is about who brought the work in — a tout, a broker, a business development consultant on a retainer, a relative who canvasses; anyone outside the firm's own employees and partners. The second limb is about how it was brought in, and it catches means that would be improper whatever hands performed them. The clause's own proviso saves the arrangements already permitted by items (2), (3) and (4) of Part I, so a lawful partnership or a permitted profit-sharing arrangement is not turned into misconduct by this clause. Clause 5 and Clause 2 are different questions about the same transaction: Clause 5 asks how the work was secured, Clause 2 asks where the fee went afterwards, and a commission paid to an outside agent for procuring work usually breaches both.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 5, with its proviso

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 9
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he accepts an appointment as auditor of a company without first ascertaining from it whether the requirements of the company law governing such appointment have been duly complied with — read today against sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act, 2013. This is not the same duty as Clause 8. Clause 8 makes him write to the outgoing auditor; Clause 9 makes him look at the company's own paperwork before he says yes. What he is ascertaining is that the appointment itself is lawfully made — that the notice the section requires was given, that any removal before the expiry of the term went through the special resolution and the previous approval of the Central Government that section 140(1) demands, that a resignation was filed as section 140(2) requires, and that the resolution was passed at a properly convened meeting. Both duties run on the same appointment, each is a separate misconduct, and satisfying one says nothing about the other. The incoming auditor who writes a faultless letter and never asks whether the outgoing auditor was lawfully removed is guilty under Clause 9 alone.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 9, read against sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 12
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he allows a person not being a member of the Institute in practice, or a member not being his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm, any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements. Read the second limb slowly, because it is the one candidates lose. A chartered accountant employed by the firm — a manager, a paid assistant, however senior — is a member, but he is not a partner, so he may not sign. Only a partner may sign on the firm's behalf. The documents named are the ones that carry an opinion or a set of numbers outward: a balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements. Authority does not travel by power of attorney, by a board resolution of the client, or by the absent partner's written instruction, because what the clause protects is the correspondence between the signature and the person answerable for it.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 12

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part III — Members generally
concepts.statement: Part III of the First Schedule binds every member of the Institute, whether in practice or not, and it holds three clauses. Clause 1 — not being a fellow of the Institute, acts as a fellow of the Institute; an associate who prints FCA, or lets a client believe he is a fellow, is caught here and not by the designation clause in Part I. Clause 2 — does not supply the information called for, or does not comply with the requirements asked for, by the Institute, the Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board or the Appellate Authority; silence towards the Institute's own machinery is itself professional misconduct, and no explanation about the merits of the underlying case answers it. Clause 3 — while inviting professional work from another chartered accountant, or while responding to tenders or enquiries, or while advertising through a write-up or anything provided for in items (6) and (7) of Part I, gives information knowing it to be false; the routes the profession opened up are the routes this clause polices. All three sit in the First Schedule, so a case under any of them goes before the Board of Discipline.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part III, Clauses 1, 2 and 3

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part IV and Second Schedule Part III — Other misconduct
concepts.statement: Other misconduct is a head of charge in its own right, and it does not need the member to have been doing professional work at all. First Schedule Part IV deems a member of the Institute, whether in practice or not, guilty of other misconduct if he is held guilty by any civil or criminal court of an offence which is punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or if, in the opinion of the Council, he brings disrepute to the profession or the Institute as a result of his action, whether or not related to his professional work. Second Schedule Part III deems him guilty of other misconduct if he is held guilty by any civil or criminal court of an offence which is punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months. The dividing line is the term of imprisonment the offence carries, not the sentence actually awarded and not the seriousness anyone feels about it. That line then decides the forum in the ordinary way, because the routing follows the Schedule: a First Schedule matter goes before the Board of Discipline, a Second Schedule matter before the Disciplinary Committee. The disrepute limb has no conviction in it at all — it turns on the opinion of the Council about the member's action.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part IV, Clauses 1 and 2, and Second Schedule, Part III

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 2
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he certifies or submits in his name, or in the name of his firm, a report of an examination of financial statements unless the examination of such statements and the related records has been made by him or by a partner or an employee in his firm or by another chartered accountant in practice. Four pairs of hands are permitted and no others — himself, a partner, an employee in his firm, or another chartered accountant in practice. Work done by anybody else will not hold the report up, however competent that person was and however carefully the member read the output: the client's own accounts staff, an outside consultancy of commerce graduates, a data analytics vendor, a retired banker engaged on contract. This is a stricter rule than the one about relying on the work of an expert, because a report of an examination of financial statements is not an area of specialised knowledge outside accountancy — it is the very thing the member holds himself out as doing.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 2

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 3
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he permits his name or the name of his firm to be used in connection with an estimate of earnings contingent upon future transactions in a manner which may lead to the belief that he vouches for the accuracy of the forecast. The clause does not forbid working on projections. What it forbids is lending the name in a way that reads to an ordinary reader as a warranty of the future. So the test is not whether the member did careful work, and not whether the assumptions were in fact reasonable — it is what the document, as it stands, invites the reader to believe. The safe form of words reports on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis for the projection, states that the projection is properly prepared on the basis of those assumptions, and says plainly that actual results are likely to be different because anticipated events frequently do not occur as expected. Words such as certified, verified or vouched attached to a forecast breach the clause even where every underlying computation is right.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 3

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part II — Clause 1
concepts.statement: A member of the Institute, whether in practice or not, is guilty of professional misconduct if he contravenes any of the provisions of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 or the regulations made thereunder or any guidelines issued by the Council. This is the clause that gives the Council's guidelines their teeth, and it is the answer to the student who asks whether a guideline is merely advisory. It is not: breaching one is professional misconduct under the Second Schedule, which means the case goes before the Disciplinary Committee and permanent removal from the Register of Members is on the table. The guidelines it carries include the ceiling on the number of tax audit assignments a member may accept under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961; the bar on accepting an appointment as auditor of an entity where the undisputed audit fee of the previous auditor for carrying out a statutory audit remains unpaid, sick units apart; the bar on accepting an appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it beyond the limit the guidelines prescribe; and the requirement that a member in practice maintain proper books of account for his own practice, including a cash book and a ledger. This bank does not recite the numbers in those ceilings — the requirement is named instead, and no question here turns on the figure.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 1, read with the Council General Guidelines issued under the Act

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part II — Clause 2
concepts.statement: A member of the Institute is guilty of professional misconduct if, being an employee of any company, firm or person, he discloses confidential information acquired in the course of his employment except as and when required by any law for the time being in force or except as permitted by the employer. This is the employment twin of the confidentiality clause that binds a member in practice, and the two are easy to swap in an examination. The practice clause sits in Part I of the Second Schedule and turns on the client's consent; this one sits in Part II, binds every member whether in practice or not, and turns on the employer's permission. The person who can release him is the employer, not the client, not the new employer and not his own conscience. Two doors lead out and no third — a law for the time being in force that requires the disclosure, and the employer's permission. The duty does not end when the employment does: information acquired at a previous employer stays confidential after he has moved on, which is exactly the situation a new employer will press him about.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 2

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part II — Clauses 3 and 4
concepts.statement: Two clauses of Part II of the Second Schedule punish dishonesty by any member, in practice or not. Clause 3 — includes in any information, statement, return or form to be submitted to the Institute, the Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board or the Appellate Authority any particulars knowing them to be false. Clause 4 — defalcates or embezzles moneys received in his professional capacity. Each has a lighter neighbour that a candidate must not confuse it with. Against Clause 3 stands Clause 2 of Part III of the First Schedule, which punishes not supplying the information at all: staying silent is a First Schedule matter, telling the Institute something the member knows to be false is a Second Schedule matter, and knowledge is what moves it across. Against Clause 4 stands Clause 10 of Part I of the Second Schedule, which punishes failing to keep a client's moneys in a separate banking account: that is a custody failure and it survives repayment, whereas defalcation is taking the money for himself. Both clauses here route the case to the Disciplinary Committee.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clauses 3 and 4

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 27 — Maintenance of branch offices
concepts.statement: Where a chartered accountant in practice or a firm of such chartered accountants has more than one office in India, section 27 requires that each one of such offices shall be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute, and failure to do so renders the member liable to disciplinary action. The member in separate charge must be a member of the Institute and, where the office belongs to a firm, must ordinarily be either a partner of the firm or a member in whole-time employment with it; he is expected to be actually in charge, attending the office, not merely named on a letter. The Council's general exemptions relieve the requirement of a second member where the second office is located in the same premises in which the first office is situated, or in the same city as the first office, or within the distance from the municipal limits of a city that the Council's guidelines prescribe — this bank does not recite that distance. In those cases both offices may be under the same charge. What counts as an office is decided by how the place is held out, not by how often it is used: a room at a member's residence carrying the firm's name board, or a place described to clients as an office where the member attends on appointed days, is a second office and section 27 applies to it.

citation.ref: Section 27, read with the Council's general exemptions from separate charge of a second office

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Sections 22A and 22G — the Appellate Authority
concepts.statement: Section 22A requires the Central Government to constitute an Appellate Authority consisting of a person who is or has been a judge of a High Court as Chairperson, two members nominated by the Council from among its own members, and two members nominated by the Central Government from among persons of ability, integrity and standing having special knowledge of law, economics, business, commerce or accountancy. Under section 22G a member aggrieved by an order of the Board of Discipline or of the Disciplinary Committee imposing a penalty may prefer an appeal to the Authority within the period the section allows from the date on which the order is communicated to him — this bank does not recite that period — and the Director (Discipline) may also appeal where the Council so authorises him. The Authority's powers on the appeal are wide: it may confirm, modify or set aside the order; it may impose any penalty, or set aside, reduce or enhance the penalty imposed; it may remit the case to the Board of Discipline or the Disciplinary Committee for such further enquiry as it considers proper; or it may pass such other order as it thinks fit. A proviso requires that the parties concerned be given an opportunity of being heard before any such order is passed. So an appeal is not a one-way door — the penalty can come back heavier — and the Authority sits above both disciplinary forums rather than beside them.

citation.ref: Sections 22A and 22G, with the proviso to section 22G

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — management responsibilities and non-assurance services
concepts.statement: A firm shall not assume a management responsibility for an audit client. This is one of the few places where the Code stops applying its usual machinery and simply says no: the threats created by taking the client's decisions cannot be reduced to an acceptable level, so there is no safeguard, and the only answer is not to do it. A management responsibility involves controlling, leading and directing an entity, including making decisions about the acquisition, deployment and control of human, financial, technological, physical and intangible resources. Setting policies and strategic direction, hiring or dismissing employees, directing and taking responsibility for the actions of employees, authorising transactions, controlling or managing bank accounts or investments, deciding which recommendations of the firm to implement, reporting to those charged with governance on behalf of management, and taking responsibility for the design, implementation, monitoring or maintenance of internal control are all management responsibilities. Providing advice and recommendations to assist management is not, provided management makes the decision. To stay on the right side the firm must be satisfied that client management makes all judgements and decisions that are the proper responsibility of management, and the client should assign an individual who possesses suitable skill, knowledge and experience to be responsible for the client's decisions and to oversee the services. Section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013 lays a statutory list of forbidden services on top of this for a company auditor, and the two have to be answered separately.

citation.ref: the prohibition on a firm assuming a management responsibility for an audit client, with the requirement that client management make all judgements and decisions and assign an individual with suitable skill, knowledge and experience to oversee the services, read with section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — long association and cooling-off
concepts.statement: Long association of an individual with an audit client creates a familiarity threat and a self-interest threat, because the individual becomes too sympathetic to the client's interests or too accepting of its work. The firm must evaluate the threat, weighing the nature and length of the individual's relationship with the client, his role on the engagement, how far the client's management has changed, and the nature and complexity of the client's accounting and reporting issues. It then addresses what it finds — by rotating the individual off the engagement team, by changing his role, by having an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team review his work, or by an independent internal or external quality review of the engagement. For an audit client that is a public interest entity the Code stops evaluating and starts prescribing: an individual shall not act as the engagement partner, as the engagement quality control reviewer, or in any other key audit partner role for more than the number of consecutive years the Code specifies, and must then serve a cooling-off period of the length the Code specifies for that role — this bank does not recite either number. During the cooling-off period he shall not be a member of the engagement team, provide quality control for the engagement, consult with the team on technical or industry-specific issues, or otherwise directly influence the outcome of the engagement. This rotation of the individual sits beside, and does not replace, the statutory rotation of the audit firm and of the individual auditor under section 139(2) of the Companies Act, 2013.

citation.ref: the long association provisions — evaluation of the familiarity and self-interest threats created by long association, and the mandatory rotation and cooling-off of key audit partners on a public interest entity — read with section 139(2) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — fee dependency and overdue fees
concepts.statement: Fees create threats in three directions and the Code deals with each separately. Where the total fees from an audit client represent a large proportion of the total fees of the firm, the firm's dependence on that client and its concern about losing it create a self-interest threat and an intimidation threat; the firm evaluates the threat and addresses it, for example by reducing the dependency, by increasing the client base, by having an appropriate reviewer who is not a member of the engagement team review the work, or by an independent internal or external quality review of the engagement. Where the client is a public interest entity and the total fees from it and its related entities exceed the proportion of the firm's total fees that the Code specifies for two consecutive years, the firm must disclose that fact to those charged with governance and discuss which action it will take — this bank does not recite that proportion. Fees remaining unpaid from an audit client for a long time, and especially where a significant part is still unpaid before the current year's audit report is issued, create a self-interest threat: the firm must determine whether the overdue fees are equivalent to a loan to the client, and whether it is appropriate to be re-appointed or to continue. Nothing here is cured by telling the reader of the audit report about it — disclosure to those charged with governance is a step in managing the threat, not a substitute for managing it.

citation.ref: the fees provisions — the self-interest and intimidation threats created by fee dependency, the disclosure to those charged with governance for a public interest entity, and the treatment of overdue fees as possibly equivalent to a loan

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — gifts, hospitality and inducements
concepts.statement: An inducement is an object, situation or action used as a means to influence another individual's behaviour — gifts, hospitality, entertainment, political or charitable donations, appeals to friendship or loyalty, employment or other commercial opportunities, and preferential treatment or rights. The Code splits the question in two. Where the inducement is offered or accepted with the intent to improperly influence the behaviour of the recipient or of another individual, it is prohibited outright, whatever its value; the accountant shall neither offer nor accept it, and shall not allow another to offer or accept it for him. Where there is no such intent, the accountant applies the conceptual framework, considering the nature, frequency, value and cumulative effect of the inducement, the timing of it relative to any decision or work being performed, whether it is customary in the circumstances, and the roles of the persons involved. On top of that sits a bright line for audit work: a firm, a network firm, or a member of the audit team shall not accept gifts and hospitality from an audit client unless the value is trivial and inconsequential. Intent is judged by what a reasonable and informed third party would conclude from the circumstances, not by what the giver or the receiver says he meant, and a gift timed to arrive while a disputed accounting question is open will not read innocently however small it is.

citation.ref: the inducements provisions — the outright prohibition where there is intent to improperly influence behaviour, and the rule that gifts and hospitality from an audit client may be accepted only where the value is trivial and inconsequential

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — network firms and what makes a network
concepts.statement: A network is a larger structure that is aimed at co-operation between firms and that is clearly aimed at profit or cost sharing, or shares common ownership, control or management, or shares common quality control policies and procedures, or shares a common business strategy, or uses a common brand name, or shares a significant part of professional resources. A firm belonging to such a structure is a network firm. Each of those tests stands on its own — a common brand name alone makes a network, and separate partnership deeds, separate profits and separate client lists do not undo it. What does not make a network is co-operation with nothing more behind it: an arrangement to refer work to one another, sharing an immaterial cost, or an association formed for a single joint engagement. The consequence is the whole point of the definition. Where a firm is a network firm, the independence requirements that apply to an audit client of the firm apply to the network firm too, so a financial interest, a business relationship, an employment relationship or a prohibited non-assurance service on the part of a sister firm is treated as though the auditor had it himself. The question in the examination is therefore never whether the sister firm is independent; it is whether the two firms are a network.

citation.ref: the definition of a network and a network firm, and the application of the independence requirements for an audit client to a network firm

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 141(3)(g) — the ceiling on company audits
concepts.statement: Section 141(3)(g) disqualifies from appointment as auditor of a company a person who is in full-time employment elsewhere, and a person or a partner of a firm holding appointment as its auditor who, at the date of such appointment or re-appointment, is holding appointment as auditor of more than the specified number of companies. This bank does not recite the specified number, and no question here turns on it — what is examinable is the shape of the count. Companies excluded from the count are one person companies, dormant companies, small companies, and private companies having paid-up share capital below the amount the section prescribes. The ceiling belongs to the individual, not to the firm: where a firm is appointed, the count is applied to each partner separately, so a firm cannot multiply its own headroom by putting a different partner's name on each report, and a person who is a partner in more than one firm adds together every appointment he holds anywhere. A partner in full-time employment elsewhere, and a partner who has already reached the ceiling, are simply not available to be counted. Before appointing, the company obtains from the auditor written consent and a certificate that the appointment, if made, will be in accordance with the conditions prescribed, which is where section 139(1) makes the auditor put his own compliance with section 141 in writing.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(g) with its proviso, read with section 139(1)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — service with and employment by an audit client
concepts.statement: People move between an audit firm and its client in both directions, and the Code answers each direction differently. A partner or employee of the firm shall not serve as a director or officer of an audit client, and shall not act as company secretary for one unless the role is purely administrative and law permits it; this is an outright bar, not a threat to be weighed. Coming in: where an individual who was a director or officer of the audit client, or an employee in a position to exert significant influence over the preparation of the accounting records or the financial statements, joins the firm, he shall not be assigned to the audit team if that service or employment occurred during the period covered by the audit report; where it was before that period, the firm evaluates the self-interest, self-review and familiarity threats and addresses them, for example by having an appropriate reviewer review the work he does. Going out: where a former member of the audit team or a former partner joins the audit client as a director or officer, or as an employee in a position to exert significant influence, the familiarity or intimidation threat is at an unacceptable level unless he has no significant connection remaining with the firm — no payments due to him except fixed pre-determined amounts, and nothing owing that is material to the firm — and he does not participate, or appear to participate, in the firm's business or professional activities. For a public interest entity a cooling-off period applies before a key audit partner may take such a position with the client.

citation.ref: the provisions on serving as a director or officer of an audit client, on recent service with an audit client, and on employment with an audit client, including the requirement that no significant connection remain between a departing partner and the firm

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 8
concepts.statement: Accepting an audit previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him in writing is professional misconduct. The duty is to communicate — the outgoing auditor's permission or no-objection is not required, and the purpose is to learn whether the change hides something the incoming auditor should weigh.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 8

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 1
concepts.statement: Disclosing information acquired in the course of a professional engagement to anyone other than the client, without the client's consent, is professional misconduct — unless law requires the disclosure. Legal compulsion and client consent are the only two doors out of the duty.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 1

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 4
concepts.statement: Expressing an opinion on the financial statements of any business in which the member, his firm, or a partner in his firm has a substantial interest is professional misconduct. The clause reaches the firm and the partners, not only the signing member, and no disclosure cures it — the opinion itself is barred.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 4

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 7
concepts.statement: Failing to exercise due diligence, or being grossly negligent in the conduct of professional duties, is professional misconduct. The clause needs no dishonesty and no client loss — signing what was never examined is the classic case.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 7

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 11
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice may not engage in any business or occupation other than the profession unless the Council permits it. The clause's own proviso allows a directorship simpliciter — an ordinary board seat without managing or whole-time office — unless the member or a partner is interested in the company as its auditor. General and specific permissions of the Council carve the remaining space.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 11

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 10
concepts.statement: Failing to keep a client's moneys — other than fees or money meant to be spent — in a separate banking account, or failing to use such moneys for their intended purpose within a reasonable time, is professional misconduct. The office account is for the firm's money; the client account is for the client's, and mixing them is the offence regardless of eventual repayment.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 10

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 7
concepts.statement: Advertising professional attainments or services, or using any designation other than chartered accountant on professional documents, cards or sign boards, is misconduct — a recognised university degree or a title indicating membership of an institute may be used. The Council's guidelines carve narrow permissions — write-ups within prescribed norms, websites on a pull basis — but self-praise pushed at the public stays barred.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 7

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 2
concepts.statement: Paying or allowing any share, commission or brokerage out of professional fees to anyone other than a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner, a deceased partner's legal representative, or a member of a permitted other professional body is misconduct. The clause polices the outflow of fees; referral commissions to clients, agents or relatives all fall on the wrong side.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 2

concepts.section: Ind AS 115 Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Costs to obtain and fulfil a contract
concepts.statement: The incremental costs of obtaining a contract are recognised as an asset if the entity expects to recover them, with a practical expedient to expense them if the amortisation period is one year or less. Costs to fulfil a contract that are not within another Standard's scope are capitalised only if they relate directly to an identified contract, generate or enhance resources used to satisfy performance obligations, and are expected to be recovered.

citation.ref: para 91 to 98

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Hedge accounting
concepts.statement: Hedge accounting is available only where the hedging relationship consists solely of eligible hedging instruments and eligible hedged items, there is formal designation and documentation at inception of the risk management objective and strategy, and the relationship meets the effectiveness requirements — an economic relationship between the hedged item and the hedging instrument, credit risk not dominating the value changes, and a hedge ratio consistent with actual risk management.

citation.ref: para 6.4.1

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Derecognition of financial assets
concepts.statement: A financial asset is derecognised when the contractual rights to its cash flows expire, or when it is transferred and that transfer qualifies for derecognition — which turns on evaluating the extent to which the risks and rewards of ownership are retained. Substantially transferring risks and rewards derecognises the asset; substantially retaining them keeps it recognised in full, with a financial liability for the consideration received; only when neither is clear does the entity move on to a control test.

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — Deferred tax in a business combination
concepts.statement: Fair value adjustments to identifiable assets and liabilities recognised on a business combination create temporary differences whenever the tax base does not move to match, and the resulting deferred tax asset or liability is recognised as part of the acquisition accounting — increasing or decreasing goodwill or the bargain purchase gain. The one carve-out is goodwill itself — no deferred tax liability is recognised on its initial recognition, because that would only inflate goodwill further.

citation.ref: para 15 and 19

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — Net investment in a foreign operation
concepts.statement: Exchange differences on a monetary item that in substance forms part of an entity's net investment in a foreign operation are recognised in profit or loss in the separate or individual financial statements of the entity concerned, but in the financial statements that include the foreign operation — such as the group's consolidated statements — those exchange differences go to other comprehensive income and are reclassified to profit or loss only on disposal of the net investment.

citation.ref: para 32 and 48

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — Sale and leaseback
concepts.statement: In a sale and leaseback, the seller-lessee applies the Ind AS 115 requirements for identifying when a performance obligation is satisfied to judge whether the transfer is a sale. If it is, the seller-lessee measures the right-of-use asset retained at the proportion of the previous carrying amount relating to the rights retained, and recognises only the gain or loss relating to the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor — not the full gain on the asset. If the transfer fails the sale test, both parties account for it as a financing.

citation.ref: para 99 and 100

concepts.section: Ind AS on Assets of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 36 — Timing of the goodwill impairment test
concepts.statement: A cash-generating unit to which goodwill has been allocated is tested for impairment at least annually, and the test may be performed at any time during the annual period provided it is performed at the same time every year; different units may be tested at different times. If some or all of the goodwill allocated to a unit was acquired in a business combination during the current period, that unit is tested before the end of the current annual period — the entity cannot wait for next year's cycle.

citation.ref: para 96

concepts.section: Ind AS on Disclosures in the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 33 — Diluted EPS and antidilution
concepts.statement: Diluted EPS adjusts profit and the weighted average number of shares for the effect of all dilutive potential equity shares, but a potential equity share that would increase EPS (or reduce a loss per share) is antidilutive and is excluded from the diluted EPS computation. Each issue or series of potential equity shares is tested for dilutive or antidilutive effect separately, not in aggregate.

citation.ref: para 41

concepts.section: Ind AS on Liabilities of the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — Contingent assets
concepts.statement: A contingent asset is never recognised, because that could bring in income that may never be realised — but it is disclosed when an inflow of economic benefits is probable. Once realisation becomes virtually certain, the asset is no longer contingent and is recognised, together with the related income, in the period the change occurs.

citation.ref: para 33 to 35

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 102 — Cash-settled share-based payment
concepts.statement: For a cash-settled share-based payment, the entity measures the goods or services received and the liability incurred at the fair value of the liability, and remeasures that fair value at the end of every reporting period and at settlement, with all changes recognised in profit or loss. Unlike an equity-settled award, the amount charged is never frozen at grant date — it moves with the liability's fair value until the award is paid.

citation.ref: para 30 to 33

concepts.section: Ind AS on Presentation of General Purpose Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 1 — Going concern disclosure
concepts.statement: Management assesses the entity's ability to continue as a going concern, looking at least twelve months from the reporting date, and prepares the financial statements on that basis unless it intends to liquidate or cease trading or has no realistic alternative. Where management identifies material uncertainties that cast significant doubt on that ability, those uncertainties are disclosed — disclosure, not abandonment of the going concern basis, is the standard's response short of an actual intention to liquidate.

citation.ref: para 25 and 26

concepts.section: Ind AS on Measurement based on Accounting Policies
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 8 — Correction of prior period errors
concepts.statement: A material prior period error is corrected retrospectively in the first financial statements approved after its discovery, by restating the comparative amounts for the period the error occurred, or restating opening balances if the error predates the earliest period presented. The correction bypasses profit or loss for the period of discovery — it adjusts the periods actually affected, not the current period's result.

citation.ref: para 42 and 46

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 103 Appendix C — Combinations under common control
concepts.statement: IFRS 3 pushes combinations of entities under common control out of its scope; Ind AS 103 pulls them back in through Appendix C and answers them with the pooling of interests method. Assets and liabilities come across at their existing carrying amounts, no fair values are recognised and no new goodwill arises, the only adjustments permitted are to harmonise accounting policies, prior period figures are restated as if the combination had happened from the beginning of the preceding period, the transferor's reserves keep their identity, and the difference between the consideration and the transferor's share capital is put to capital reserve.

citation.ref: Appendix C, paragraph 8 and paragraph 9; the reserve identity and capital reserve rules follow in the same Appendix, reproduced in order at para 13.3 of the ICAI Study Material chapter on Ind AS 103

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 103 — Contingent consideration after the acquisition
concepts.statement: How contingent consideration moves after the acquisition date is decided by how it was classified on that date. Classified as equity, it is never remeasured and its settlement is accounted for within equity. Classified as an asset or a liability within the scope of Ind AS 109, it is remeasured to fair value at every reporting date with the change in profit or loss. Only a change that reflects new information about facts existing at the acquisition date is a measurement period adjustment that touches goodwill; a change caused by the acquiree's later performance never does.

citation.ref: para 58, read with para 45

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — Ownership change without loss of control
concepts.statement: Once control exists, buying more of a subsidiary or selling part of it without losing control is a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners, not an acquisition or a disposal. The carrying amounts of the controlling and non-controlling interests are adjusted to their new relative shares, and any difference between that adjustment and the fair value of the consideration paid or received is recognised directly in equity and attributed to the owners of the parent. No goodwill is created or released, and nothing reaches profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 23 and B96

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Reclassifying financial assets
concepts.statement: Financial assets are reclassified when, and only when, the entity changes the business model for managing them. Financial liabilities are never reclassified. The change bites on the reclassification date, which the Standard defines as the first day of the first reporting period following the change of business model, so measurement carries on unchanged until the period ends. From that date the new classification applies prospectively, and previously recognised interest, gains and losses are not restated.

citation.ref: para 4.4.1 and 5.6.1, with the Appendix A definition of reclassification date

concepts.section: Accounting and Reporting of Financial Instruments
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Modifying a financial liability
concepts.statement: Renegotiating a borrowing is tested before it is accounted for. Terms are substantially different if the present value of the cash flows under the new terms, including fees paid net of fees received and discounted at the original effective interest rate, differs by at least 10 per cent from the present value of the remaining cash flows of the old liability.
