The authorisation is valid for IMPORT for twenty-four months from the date of its issue, and revalidation of an EPCG authorisation is not permitted at all, so capital goods not brought in inside that window cannot be brought in under it later. The export obligation runs for six years from the same date, which is a longer and quite separate clock. And the actual user condition on the imported capital goods runs until the export obligation is completed AND the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate is granted, so discharging the obligation in fact does not release the machine; the certificate does. How the obligation is measured also depends on where the goods came from: on a direct import it is reckoned on the duties, taxes and cess actually saved, while on domestic sourcing it is reckoned on the NOTIONAL customs duty, taxes and cess on the free-on-rail value shown in the Advance Release Order or invalidation letter. Where integrated tax and compensation cess are paid in cash on an import, that incidence is left out of the net duty saved provided input tax credit is not availed.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 5.01(d), 5.01(e), 5.03 and 5.08 of Chapter 5

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — tax base, the temporary difference, and the balance it produces
concepts.statement: Deferred tax is arithmetic before it is judgement, and the arithmetic has four steps. Take the carrying amount of the asset or liability in the balance sheet. Take its tax base — for an asset, the amount deductible against taxable economic benefits in future periods; for a liability, its carrying amount less any amount that will be deductible in future periods. Subtract one from the other to get the temporary difference, and classify it — where an asset's carrying amount exceeds its tax base the difference is taxable and produces a deferred tax liability, and where it falls short the difference is deductible and produces a deferred tax asset, with the signs the other way round for a liability. Then multiply by the rate expected to apply when the difference reverses. Three things go wrong at this step more often than the rest put together. The balance sheet figure is the deferred tax balance at the year end, not the year's deferred tax expense, which is the movement between the opening and closing balances. The temporary difference is not itself the deferred tax — the rate still has to be applied. And deferred tax assets and liabilities are never discounted, however far away the reversal is.

citation.ref: the definitions of the tax base of an asset and of a liability, and the requirements that taxable temporary differences multiplied by the rate give deferred tax liabilities, that deductible temporary differences give deferred tax assets, and that deferred tax liabilities and assets are not discounted

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — deferred tax on profit still sitting inside group inventory
concepts.statement: When one group company sells to another at a profit and the buyer still holds the goods at the year end, consolidation strips the profit out of inventory but the tax authorities do not. The seller has already paid tax on the sale, and the buyer's own tax return carries the goods at what it paid. So in the consolidated balance sheet the inventory's carrying amount is the original cost to the group while its tax base is the intra-group transfer price, and the tax base being the higher of the two makes the difference deductible — a deferred tax asset, not a liability. The measure of it is the profit still unrealised, which is the whole intra-group profit reduced in proportion to the goods sold on outside the group before the year end, not the whole profit and not the whole margin on the original sale. The asset is recognised where the buying company is expected to generate taxable profits to use it against, and it unwinds as the goods are sold outside the group, so the year's deferred tax movement is the change in the balance rather than the balance itself.

citation.ref: the example of a deductible temporary difference arising where unrealised profits on intragroup transactions are eliminated from the carrying amount of inventory with no equivalent adjustment for tax, read with the requirement that the tax base is determined by reference to the tax returns of each entity in the group while the carrying amount is taken from the consolidated financial statements

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — the deferred tax on a fair value exercise, and what it does to goodwill
concepts.statement: A fair value exercise on an acquisition writes the acquiree's identifiable assets up to fair value in the consolidated financial statements while the tax authorities go on using the figures in the acquiree's own books. Every uplift with no equivalent tax adjustment is therefore a taxable temporary difference, and the deferred tax liability on it is recognised as one of the identifiable liabilities assumed at the acquisition date. That matters to the arithmetic in a way that is easy to miss — the liability reduces the identifiable net assets, so it increases goodwill or shrinks a bargain purchase gain by exactly the same amount. The order of work is fixed. Book net assets, plus the uplifts, less deferred tax at the rate expected to apply on the uplifts alone, gives net assets at fair value; consideration plus the non-controlling interest measured on whichever of the two permitted bases the group has chosen, less those net assets, gives goodwill. The one thing the standard will not let the arithmetic do is recognise a deferred tax liability on the initial recognition of the goodwill itself, which would only inflate the goodwill it was computed on.

citation.ref: the requirement that deferred tax assets and liabilities arising in a business combination are recognised as identifiable assets and liabilities at the acquisition date and so affect goodwill or the bargain purchase gain, together with the exception for the initial recognition of goodwill; read with Ind AS 103 paragraph 19 on the measurement of the non-controlling interest

concepts.section: Ind AS on Items impacting the Financial Statements
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — which rate, and where the effect of a change in it goes
concepts.statement: Deferred tax is measured at the rates expected to apply to the period when the asset is realised or the liability is settled, using rates and laws enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period. Both halves bite. A rate change announced in a way that is treated as having the substantive effect of enactment counts even though the legislature has not finished with it, and a change enacted after the reporting date does not count at all, however certain it now looks — it is disclosed instead. And because the test is the period of reversal, a single rate rarely does the whole job when a rate change takes effect part way through the reversals — the differences reversing before the change go at the old rate and the rest at the new one. When a rate change moves a balance that is already there, the resulting deferred tax goes to profit or loss, except to the extent it relates to something previously recognised outside profit or loss, in which case it follows that item into other comprehensive income or directly into equity. And no discounting anywhere, however long the reversals run.

citation.ref: the requirement to measure deferred tax at the rates expected to apply to the period when the asset is realised or the liability settled, based on rates and laws enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period; the requirement that a change in rates is recognised in profit or loss except to the extent it relates to items previously recognised outside profit or loss; and the prohibition on discounting

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — carrying the non-controlling interest forward from acquisition to the year end
concepts.statement: The non-controlling interest is measured once at the acquisition date and then rolled forward, and both halves are arithmetic. At acquisition it is either its fair value or its proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets, whichever the group elected for that combination, and whichever figure is used goes into the goodwill computation alongside the consideration. After that the balance moves with the subsidiary — plus the non-controlling share of profit or loss, plus its share of other comprehensive income, less its share of dividends the subsidiary declares, and the balance sits inside equity, presented separately from the equity of the owners of the parent. Two things decide most of the marks. The subsidiary's results are consolidated only from the date control is obtained, so an acquisition part way through a year brings in only the months after it. And a dividend paid by the subsidiary takes money out of the non-controlling interest as surely as a profit puts it in, even though the group's own profit is unaffected because the parent's share of the same dividend is eliminated.

citation.ref: the requirement that consolidation of an investee begins from the date the investor obtains control and ceases when it loses control, together with the measurement of the non-controlling interest at the acquisition date and the attribution of profit or loss and other comprehensive income to the non-controlling interests thereafter

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 28 — rolling the carrying amount of an associate through a year
concepts.statement: The equity method is a single running balance, and every year adds the same four movements to it. Start at cost, which already contains the goodwill on acquisition — the excess of the cost over the investor's share of the net fair value of the associate's identifiable assets and liabilities — and that goodwill is never amortised and is never shown separately. Add the investor's share of the associate's profit, taken to profit or loss. Add its share of the associate's other comprehensive income, taken to other comprehensive income. Deduct distributions received, which reduce the investment rather than producing income, because the profit they came out of has already been picked up. The step candidates lose most often sits inside the share of profit — where the fair value of a depreciable asset at the acquisition date exceeded its carrying amount in the associate's books, the associate's own depreciation is too low for the investor's purposes, and the investor's share of the extra depreciation on the uplift is deducted before the share of profit is recognised. The other trap runs the other way, when the investor's share of net fair value exceeds the cost — that excess is a capital reserve recorded directly in equity, not income and not negative goodwill sitting inside the investment.

citation.ref: the equity method — the investment recognised initially at cost and adjusted thereafter for the post-acquisition change in the investor's share of the investee's net assets, with the share of profit or loss in profit or loss, the share of other comprehensive income in other comprehensive income, distributions received reducing the carrying amount, and the share of profit adjusted for depreciation of depreciable assets based on their fair values at the acquisition date; goodwill included in the carrying amount and not amortised, and any excess of the investor's share of net fair value over cost treated as a capital reserve recorded directly in equity

concepts.section: Consolidated and Separate Financial Statements of Group Entities
concepts.subsection: Ind AS 111 — what a joint operator actually puts in its own statements
concepts.statement: A joint operator does not carry an investment and does not equity account. It recognises its assets, including its share of any assets held jointly; its liabilities, including its share of any liabilities incurred jointly; its revenue from the sale of its share of the output; its share of the revenue from any sale of the output by the operation itself; and its expenses, including its share of any expenses incurred jointly. Each of those is then accounted for under the Ind AS that governs that kind of asset, liability, revenue or expense. Two features of the arithmetic separate a good answer from a plausible one. The share is not automatically the capital ratio — where the contract gives one operator the rights to the whole of a particular asset, or the obligation for the whole of a particular liability, that operator takes all of it and the others take none, and only the assets and liabilities the contract leaves unallocated are split. And an operator's own selling and other costs are its own in full, not shared, because they were never incurred jointly.

citation.ref: the requirement that a joint operator recognises in its separate and consolidated financial statements its assets including its share of any held jointly, its liabilities including its share of any incurred jointly, its revenue from the sale of its share of the output, its share of the revenue from sale of the output by the joint operation, and its expenses including its share of any incurred jointly

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — clean price, accrued interest and the dirty price
concepts.statement: A bond bought between two coupon dates carries interest the seller has earned and not yet been paid, and the market handles that by quoting two prices. The clean price is the quoted figure and it excludes accrued interest. The dirty price is what actually changes hands — the clean price plus interest accrued from the last coupon date to settlement, computed on the face value at the coupon rate for the days elapsed. Every settlement amount is built on the dirty price, never on the quoted one, and a repurchase agreement makes that visible in two steps. The first leg is the nominal value taken at the dirty price and then reduced by the initial margin the lender of money holds back as a haircut. The second leg is that first-leg amount carried forward at the repo rate for the exact days of the deal. The two mistakes that show up in the answer are settling on the clean price, which underpays the seller by the accrued interest, and adding the margin instead of deducting it, which lends more against the collateral than the collateral is worth.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — the duration of a portfolio of bonds
concepts.statement: A portfolio's duration is the weighted average of the durations of the bonds in it, weighted by the market value each bond represents, not by the number of bonds and not by a simple average across the holdings. Once that figure exists it does the same job it does for a single bond. Divide it by one plus the yield to get the modified duration, which the study material also calls volatility, and multiply that by the change in yield to get the predicted percentage change in the portfolio's value, with the sign reversed because price moves against yield. Applied to the portfolio's rupee value it gives the rupee gain or loss for a stated move in rates, which is what a fund manager is actually asked for. Three errors move the answer far enough to be visible in an option set — averaging the two durations without weighting them, using the Macaulay figure where the modified one belongs, and multiplying by one plus the yield instead of dividing by it.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — approximating the yield to maturity from a price
concepts.statement: Yield to maturity is properly the discount rate at which the present value of a bond's cash flows equals its market price, which means solving for a rate rather than computing one. The approximation the study material uses instead takes the annual coupon, adds the discount or subtracts the premium spread evenly over the remaining years, and divides by the average of the redemption value and the market price. Three things about it decide the marks. The numerator uses the redemption value rather than the face value where the two differ, so a bond redeemable at a premium is amortising towards the redemption figure. The denominator is an average, so dividing by the market price alone or by the face value alone gives a different and wrong answer. And the sign of the second term follows the price — a bond bought below its redemption value gains, so the term is added, and a bond bought above it loses, so the term is deducted, which is why a premium bond's yield to maturity is below its current yield and its current yield is below its coupon rate.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.subsection: Security Valuation — treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit
concepts.statement: A treasury bill, a commercial paper and a certificate of deposit pay no coupon. They are issued below face value and redeemed at it, and the whole return is that gap. The yield is the gap divided by what the investor actually paid, not by the face value, and then annualised by the days or months in a year over the days or months the instrument runs. Dividing by the face value understates the yield, because the investor never had the face value to invest, and this is exactly why an instrument discounted at a stated rate always yields more than that rate to the buyer. Two conventions matter and they are not the same convention. The study material annualises these money market yields on a 365-day year, or on twelve months where the period is given in months. It uses a 360-day year for accrued interest and for repo interest, which is a different calculation on a different instrument. And a front-ended discount is deducted from the face value to give the issue price before any yield is computed, so a hundred rupees discounted at nine per cent for six months is issued at ninety-five rupees and fifty paise, not at ninety-one.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the heads of the balance sheet under the Third Schedule
concepts.statement: Every banking company prepares its balance sheet in the form set out in Form A of the Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and its profit and loss account in Form B, or as near thereto as the circumstances admit. The form is not a presentational nicety: because the heads are fixed, a great deal of the auditor's work on a bank is deciding which head a balance belongs under, and several of the answers are counter-intuitive. Interest accrued but not due on deposits is not included under Deposits; it is shown under Other Liabilities and Provisions, which comprises bills payable, inter-office adjustments (net), interest accrued, and others including provisions — and the auditor specifically examines that interest accrued has not been clubbed with the figures of deposits and borrowings. Debit balances in current accounts are not netted out on the liabilities side; they are included under Advances. The balance in the inter-office adjustments account is shown under Other Liabilities and Provisions if it is in credit, and inter-office transactions are not borrowings and are not presented as such. Borrowings are shown as borrowings in India, split between the Reserve Bank of India, other banks and other institutions and agencies, and borrowings outside India, with the total amount of secured borrowings shown by way of a note to the relevant schedule; a clear distinction is made between rediscount and refinance, because rediscount does not figure under that head. Call loans made by a bank cannot be netted off against call loans received. And the figures of advances and investments in the balance sheet exclude the provisions made in respect of them to the satisfaction of the auditors.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — Form A of the Third Schedule to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the items disclosed under Other Liabilities and Provisions, and the rules that interest accrued is not clubbed with deposits and borrowings, that debit balances in current accounts are included under advances rather than netted on the liabilities side, that inter-office transactions are not borrowings, that rediscount does not figure under borrowings, and that call loans made cannot be netted against call loans received

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the items grouped under Other Assets
concepts.statement: Other Assets on a bank's balance sheet is a residual head that carries four things an auditor has to look at separately. Inter-office adjustments, where inter-branch accounts are normally reconciled centrally: the auditor reports on the year-end status of inter-branch accounts, indicating the dates up to which all or any segments of the accounts have been reconciled, and the number and amount of outstanding entries, giving debit and credit entries separately, and he takes the information primarily from branch audit reports. Interest accrued, which is examined to see that interest has been accrued on the entire loans and advances portfolio, with special consideration to overdue bills purchased or discounted, and that only such interest as can be realised in the ordinary course of business is shown under the head, on the principle recognised in AS 9 that revenue cannot be recognised where there is significant uncertainty about its collectability. Stationery and stamps, which includes only exceptional items of expenditure such as a bulk purchase of security paper to be written off over a period, valued at cost, normal stationery expenditure being charged to the profit and loss account; security stationery is physically verified at the year end and any shortage inquired into, because it can expose the bank to loss from misuse. And non-banking assets acquired in satisfaction of claims — immovable properties or tangible assets the bank has acquired in satisfaction of debts due or its other claims, held with the intention of being disposed of, verified against the terms of settlement, the court's order or the arbitration award, with ownership legally vested in the bank, recorded at the date of acquisition at the lower of the net book value of the advance and the net realisable value of the asset acquired, and subject to section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which prohibits a banking company from holding any immovable property, howsoever acquired, for a period exceeding seven years from the date of acquisition, except such as is required for its own use.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the audit procedures for the items under Other Assets, including the reporting on the year-end status of inter-branch accounts, the recognition of only such interest accrued as can be realised in the ordinary course of business on the AS 9 principle, the confinement of Stationery and Stamps to exceptional items valued at cost, and the recording of non-banking assets acquired in satisfaction of claims at the lower of the net book value of the advance and the net realisable value, read with section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 on the seven year holding period for immovable property

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — contingent liabilities and bills for collection
concepts.statement: A great deal of a bank's exposure never reaches its balance sheet, and the Third Schedule requires it to be disclosed all the same. The contingent liabilities heads are claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts; liability for partly paid investments; liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts; guarantees given on behalf of constituents, split between those within India and those outside India; acceptances, endorsements and other obligations; and other items for which the bank is contingently liable. Bills for collection are shown separately from all of them, because the bank holds those bills as an agent and they are not its own liability at all. The auditor's concern is that every contingent liability is identified and properly valued, and he obtains a management representation covering, among other things, that all off-balance sheet transactions have been accounted for as and when entered into, after following the due procedure laid down and supported by the underlying documents; that all year-end contingent liabilities have been disclosed; that the disclosed contingent liabilities do not include any crystallised liabilities of the nature of a loss or expense, which require a provision or adjustment in the financial statements instead; that the estimated financial effects are based on best estimates in terms of AS 29, including consideration of any reimbursement; that where guarantees have been issued on behalf of the bank's directors, adequate and effective arrangements exist for the commitment to be met out of the party's own resources so that the bank will not be called upon to grant a loan or advance on invocation and no violation of section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 has arisen; and that where a contingent liability has not been disclosed because the possibility of its outcome is remote, management's justification for that view is given.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the contingent liabilities disclosed under the Third Schedule and the separate disclosure of bills for collection, with the management representations the auditor obtains, including that crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense are not shown as contingent, that estimated financial effects follow AS 29, that guarantees issued on behalf of directors do not violate section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and that a justification is given for liabilities not disclosed as remote

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — the principal business test and registration
concepts.statement: Whether a company is a non-banking financial company is a question of fact answered by a quantitative test, not by what the company calls itself. Section 45-I(f) of the Reserve Bank of India Act defines a non-banking financial company as a financial institution which is a company; a non-banking institution which is a company and which has as its principal business the receiving of deposits, under any scheme or arrangement or in any other manner, or lending in any manner; and such other non-banking institution or class of institutions as the Bank may, with the previous approval of the Central Government and by notification in the Official Gazette, specify. To identify the principal business, both the asset pattern and the income pattern are taken as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet of the company. The company is treated as a non-banking financial company where its financial assets constitute more than 50 per cent of its total assets, netted off by intangible assets, and its income from financial assets constitutes more than 50 per cent of its gross income. Both limbs must be satisfied; a company meeting one and not the other does not qualify. A company that does qualify must register, because under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 no non-banking financial company may commence or carry on the business of a non-banking financial institution without obtaining a certificate of registration issued by the Reserve Bank and having the net owned fund of twenty-five lakh rupees or such other amount, not exceeding one hundred crore rupees, as the Bank may by notification specify, and the Bank may notify different amounts for different categories. The Reserve Bank has notified higher amounts for particular categories, with a phased timeline for existing companies in those categories. The auditor meets the same test from the other direction under clause 3(xvi)(a) of CARO 2020, which asks whether the company is required to be registered under section 45-IA and, if so, whether the registration has been obtained.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the definition of a non-banking financial company in section 45-I(f) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, the principal business test taking both the asset pattern and the income pattern from the last audited balance sheet with financial assets above 50 per cent of total assets netted off by intangible assets and income from financial assets above 50 per cent of gross income, and section 45-IA on the certificate of registration and net owned fund, read with clause 3(xvi)(a) of CARO 2020

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xvii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xvii) of paragraph 3 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 requires the auditor to state whether the company has incurred cash losses in the financial year and in the immediately preceding financial year, and if so, to state the amount of the cash losses. Four things follow from those words. The clause asks about a cash loss, which is not the same figure as the loss shown in the statement of profit and loss and not the same figure as an operating loss, so a company can show one without the other in either direction. The clause reaches back a year: the immediately preceding financial year is inside it whether or not the present auditor audited that year. The answer is not a yes or a no — where there are cash losses the amount goes in, and where there are none the clause is still answered, because paragraph 3 says the report shall include a statement on the matters specified rather than a statement only where something is wrong. And the clause reports a fact; it is not an opinion on the company's future and does not by itself modify the audit opinion. Two further provisions of the Order govern how the answer is given. Under paragraph 4, where the answer to any of the paragraph 3 questions is unfavourable or qualified, the auditor's report shall also state the basis for that answer; and where the auditor is unable to express any opinion on a specified matter, his report shall indicate that fact together with the reasons why he cannot. Under paragraph 2 the Order does not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi), so a subsidiary's cash losses are reported in the subsidiary's own CARO report and not under this clause in the consolidated one.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xvii), read with paragraph 2 on the matters every report under section 143 shall contain and on the Order's application to a report on consolidated financial statements, and with paragraph 4(a) and paragraph 4(b) on stating the basis for an unfavourable or qualified answer and on indicating an inability to express an opinion together with the reasons

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Sections 6, 8 and 20 with Regulations 10 and 11 — the certificate of practice, suspension, and the disabilities
concepts.statement: Section 6 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 says that no member of the Institute shall be entitled to practise, whether in India or elsewhere, unless he has obtained from the Council a certificate of practice; the annual fee for it is payable on or before the 1st day of April each year, and the certificate may be cancelled by the Council in the prescribed circumstances. A member who is not in practice is precluded from accepting any engagement to render services of the types normally rendered by a chartered accountant, even where the service needs no special qualification. The Council's settled view is that a member has no other capacity, separable from his capacity as a member, in which he can take up such practice: once he is a member he is bound by the Act and the Regulations, so a member suspended from practice, or whose name has been removed for misconduct, cannot during that period appear before the tax authorities or any other body as an income-tax representative and cannot argue that he does so in some other capacity. Regulation 10 makes the certificate liable to cancellation where the holder's name is removed from the Register, where the Council is satisfied after a hearing that it was issued on incorrect, misleading or false information or by mistake, where the member has ceased to practise, or where the annual fee has not been paid by the 30th day of September of the relevant year; a cancelled certificate is surrendered to the Secretary. Regulation 11 lets the Council restore a certificate cancelled for non-payment of the fee, with effect from the date of cancellation, on an application in the approved form with the fee, received by the Secretary before the expiry of the relevant year. Behind the certificate stand the disabilities of section 8, which debar a person from having his name entered in or borne on the Register: not having attained the age of 21 years when applying; being of unsound mind and so adjudged by a competent court; being an undischarged insolvent; being a discharged insolvent who has not obtained from the court a certificate that the insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part; having been convicted by a competent court, in or outside India, of an offence involving moral turpitude and punishable with imprisonment, or of an offence not of a technical nature committed in his professional capacity, unless pardoned or unless the Central Government has by written order removed the disability; and having been removed from membership on being found on inquiry guilty of professional or other misconduct, a person removed for a specified period being ineligible until that period expires. Failing to disclose that one suffers from any of these disabilities is itself professional misconduct. Section 20 lets the Council remove from the Register the name of a member who is dead, who asks for it, who has not paid a prescribed fee, or who is found to have been subject to a section 8 disability when his name was entered or to have become subject to one since, and requires it to remove the name of a member against whom an order removing him from membership has been passed; a name removed for non-payment of fee may be entered again on application and payment of the arrears.

citation.ref: Sections 6(1), 6(2) and 6(3), section 8 clauses (i) to (vi), and section 20, read with Regulations 10 and 11 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988, and the Council's view on a suspended member appearing before the income-tax authorities as set out in ICAI's Study Material, chapter 19, paragraph 4.1 and its Illustration 1

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: The Council's Know Your Client norms for members in practice
concepts.statement: The financial services industry worldwide is required to obtain information about its clients under Know Your Client norms, and the Council of ICAI, keeping in mind the standards of the profession in India, approved KYC norms of its own to be observed by members in practice. The norms are mandatory in nature and shall apply in all assignments pertaining to attestation functions, and the module's own illustration holds a member who gave consultancy, a compilation engagement and advisory services to a company that turned out to be part of a money-laundering group to have been bound to keep the information — his contention that he was not supposed to keep any information about the company is not valid. What must be kept depends on who the client is. For an individual or proprietor: the name, the PAN or Aadhaar number, a business description and a copy of the last audited financial statement, together with the type of engagement. For a corporate entity: the name and address, a business description, the name of the parent company where the client is a subsidiary, and a copy of the last audited financial statement; the type of engagement; and regulatory information — the company's PAN, its Company Identification Number, and the directors' names, addresses and Director Identification Numbers. For a non-corporate entity: the name and address, a copy of the PAN, a business description, the partners' names and addresses with their PAN, Aadhaar or DIN, and a copy of the last audited financial statement, together with the type of engagement. The three lists differ by design: the regulatory block belongs to the corporate client alone, the parent company is asked for only where there is one, and the individual is identified by PAN or Aadhaar where the entity is identified by its registration.

citation.source: Council of ICAI — KYC Norms for members in practice
citation.ref: Know Your Client norms approved by the Council of ICAI, mandatory in nature and applicable to all assignments pertaining to attestation functions, as set out in ICAI's Study Material, chapter 19, paragraph 4.7, with the three client types — individual or proprietor, corporate entity, non-corporate entity — and the general, engagement and regulatory information required for each

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: Audit risk in a not-for-profit body
concepts.statement: A not-for-profit body is audited under the same standards as anything else, and what changes is where the risk sits. Taking the three components in turn. Inherent risk rises with the field the body works in: an organisation operating where political and social questions meet can have its activities made risky by that alone, and where accusations and counter-accusations are being traded the auditor is not looking at an ordinary set of records. Receipt of foreign funds makes transactions inherently risky. Crowdfunded donations have to be seen in relation to the constitution of the body itself, which may make them risky — money raised for a purpose the objects do not authorise is a problem before it is ever spent. The credibility and integrity of the persons behind the body matter, because bodies of this kind can be used for money laundering and for misutilising funds given by donors. And where the previous year's accounts were not audited at all, inherent risk rises again through the probable effect of any misstatement in them. Control risk rises where a body whose activities were small has suddenly received substantial donations: formal controls may simply not be in place, and the absence of them can lead to non-compliance with laws whose consequences are severe — non-compliance with the foreign contribution law can lead to the cancellation of the body's certificate. Detection risk rises because the engagement is a first one: there may be a lack of understanding of what the body actually does, and that leads to inappropriate sampling or to a faulty application of the procedures chosen. Where deviations from established controls are found during the audit, the control risk assessment is revised, the revision flows into the assessment of the risks of material misstatement, and it may result in a modification of the nature, timing and extent of the planned substantive procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — audit risk in the audit of a not-for-profit body: the political and social field, foreign funds and crowdfunded donations seen against the constitution of the body as sources of inherent risk, the credibility and integrity of the persons behind it, the prior year's accounts being unaudited, the absence of formal controls after a sudden increase in donations and the consequences of non-compliance with the foreign contribution law as sources of control risk, the first-year engagement as a source of detection risk, and the revision of control risk and of the risks of material misstatement where established controls are found not to be operating

concepts.subsection: Foreign contributions and the audit plan
concepts.statement: Where a society or other not-for-profit body is registered under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 for the receipt of foreign contributions, the verification of those receipts is ordinarily where the audit goes deepest — the purpose being to rule out round-tripping, money that leaves and returns wearing a different name. The examinable point is not the procedure but what happens to the plan when the procedure changes. The audit plan must describe the nature, timing and extent of the procedures to be performed, and the extent includes deciding the sample sizes to be tested: leaving sample size to be settled later, at the moment each procedure is performed, is not a proper plan. The plan and the related programme are then reconsidered as the audit progresses, on the auditor's review and preliminary evaluation of internal control and on the results of the compliance and substantive procedures. And the auditor documents the audit plan and every significant change made to it during the engagement, together with the reasons for the change. The documentation of the plan is a record of the planned nature, timing and extent of risk assessment procedures and of further audit procedures at the assertion level in response to the assessed risks, and a record that the procedures were properly planned so that they could be reviewed and approved before they were performed. So an auditor who embarks on far more extensive work on foreign contributions than she first envisaged, and documents the procedures performed and the findings but not how the work was planned or why it changed, has left the gap the standard exists to close: the risk of not having conducted the audit according to professional standards in a qualitative manner, with nothing on the file able to show otherwise.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — the requirement that the audit plan include the nature, timing and extent of procedures with the extent covering sample sizes, the reconsideration of the plan and programme as the audit progresses, and the requirement to document the audit plan and the significant changes made to it during the engagement together with the reasons, illustrated by the audit of a society registered under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 whose procedures on the receipt of foreign contributions were extended to rule out round-tripping

concepts.subsection: A first-year not-for-profit engagement and receipts that cannot be vouched at source
concepts.statement: Two evidence problems recur in a first audit of a charitable body and they pull in opposite directions. The first is the opening balances. An initial audit engagement is one where the prior period financial statements were not audited or were audited by a predecessor, and a body whose accounts have never been audited is squarely inside it. The auditor reads the most recent financial statements and the predecessor's report where there is one, determines whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward, determines whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies, and performs procedures on the opening balances themselves. Two reporting consequences follow. If he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances, the opinion is qualified or disclaimed. If he concludes that the opening balances contain a misstatement that materially affects the current period, or that policies are not consistently applied or a change is not properly accounted for, presented and disclosed, the opinion is qualified or adverse. The second problem is a receipt nobody can trace to its source — cash dropped into a collection box, a donation given at an event without a name, money handed to a volunteer and brought in later. There is no external document behind it, so the completeness of the receipt can only be supported by the controls the body operates over the collection itself, and where those controls are absent the auditor should not expect to close the gap by asking for a certificate: written representations provide necessary audit evidence but do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own, and the fact that management has given reliable representations does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains. Nor does the expense of the work excuse it: the matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for the auditor to omit a procedure for which there is no alternative, or to be satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive. Where sufficient appropriate audit evidence cannot be obtained at all, what is left is a limitation on scope and the opinion is determined accordingly.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 510 on initial audit engagements where the prior period was not audited: the four procedures on opening balances and the consequences of being unable to obtain evidence about them or of finding them misstated; read with SA 200 as reproduced in the same chapter, that difficulty, time or cost is not in itself a valid basis to omit a procedure for which there is no alternative or to be satisfied with less than persuasive evidence, and with SA 580, that written representations do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: A material misstatement is not always a wrong number, and SA 705 (Revised) gives the Basis for Opinion section three different jobs depending on what is wrong. Where the misstatement relates to specific amounts in the financial statements, including quantitative disclosures in the notes, the auditor includes in that section a description and quantification of the financial effects of the misstatement, unless it is impracticable to quantify them, in which case he states in the section that it is not practicable to do so. Where the misstatement relates to narrative disclosures, he includes an explanation of how the disclosures are misstated. Where the misstatement is the non-disclosure of information required to be disclosed, he does three things: he discusses the non-disclosure with those charged with governance, he describes in the Basis for Opinion section the nature of the omitted information, and, unless prohibited by law or regulation, he includes the omitted disclosures themselves, provided it is practicable to do so and he has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the omitted information. Where the modification instead results from an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, the section carries the reasons for that inability. Pervasiveness is tested the same way whatever the misstatement looks like, and its third limb exists for exactly these facts — effects that, in relation to disclosures, are fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements are pervasive even though no figure in the primary statements moves.

citation.ref: para 21 on including in the Basis for Opinion section a description and quantification of the financial effects of a misstatement of specific amounts unless impracticable, with the requirements that follow it for a misstatement of narrative disclosures and for a non-disclosure of information required to be disclosed — discussion with those charged with governance, description of the nature of the omitted information, and inclusion of the omitted disclosures where not prohibited and practicable — read with para 5 on pervasiveness in relation to disclosures

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: There are two roads to a disclaimer of opinion, and only the first one is about missing evidence. On the first, the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on which to base the opinion and concludes that the possible effects on the financial statements of undetected misstatements, if any, could be both material and pervasive. On the second, the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding each of the individual uncertainties, and disclaims anyway: in extremely rare circumstances involving multiple uncertainties, he concludes that, notwithstanding that evidence, it is not possible to form an opinion on the financial statements because of the potential interaction of the uncertainties and their possible cumulative effect. Nothing is missing from the file. What is missing is the ability to say what the combination comes to. The word extremely is the standard's own, and it marks the road as rare rather than as an alternative to doing the work: a single uncertainty, however large, is dealt with under going concern reporting, under an emphasis of matter paragraph or under a modification for misstatement, and several uncertainties that can each be evaluated and added up are not this case either.

citation.ref: the requirement to disclaim an opinion when, in extremely rare circumstances involving multiple uncertainties, the auditor concludes that notwithstanding having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding each of the individual uncertainties it is not possible to form an opinion because of their potential interaction and possible cumulative effect, read with para 5 on pervasiveness and para 8 on the adverse opinion

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: Management would usually rather explain a disagreement in a note than have it in the auditor's report, and the note is management's stand on the matter while the qualification is the auditor's. The two are not interchangeable. Full disclosure by management does not by itself discharge the auditor; he exercises his own judgement on whether disclosure alone suffices or whether he must also modify the opinion, and an emphasis of matter paragraph is not a substitute for a modification. An emphasis of matter is available only for something appropriately presented and for which the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Once he concludes that a modification is warranted he may refer to management's note and then go on to give the facts, his own assessment, and the quantification and impact on the various captions of the financial statements so far as he can. The qualification is expressed in a clear and unambiguous manner as "except for" the effects of the matter; phrases such as "subject to" or "with the foregoing explanation" are not sufficiently clear or forceful and are not appropriate in the opinion paragraph. Where notes of a qualificatory nature appear in the accounts, the auditor states all his qualifications independently in his report so that a reader can weigh them, and a bare cross-reference to a note in the report does not automatically become a qualification — the report must state the matter from the auditor's standpoint and not from management's. Where he answers any statutory affirmation in the negative or with a qualification, his report states the reasons, and all qualifications are contained in the auditor's report itself.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — the distinction between notes on accounts and qualifications, the requirement that a qualification be expressed in a clear and unambiguous manner as "except for" rather than "subject to" or "with the foregoing explanation", the independent statement of all qualifications in the report, and the rule that a reference to a note does not automatically become a qualification

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: SA 705 (Revised) has its own communication requirement, and it is narrower and harder than the general one. When the auditor expects to modify the opinion in the auditor's report, he shall communicate with those charged with governance the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification. Two things follow. The trigger is the expectation, not the signature, so the communication happens while the matter can still be discussed and the misstatement still corrected — the auditor is required to discuss and deliberate the audit findings and the type of misstatements with those charged with governance. And the wording itself goes across, not merely the fact that there will be a modification; a board that is told "there will be a qualification" and first sees the sentence in the signed report has not been given what the standard asks for. This sits alongside, and does not replace, the SA 260 (Revised) requirement to communicate circumstances that affect the form and content of the auditor's report, and the separate SA 706 (Revised) requirement to communicate an expected emphasis of matter or other matter paragraph and its wording. Communicating a matter never makes a modification unnecessary, and agreement from those charged with governance is not one of the conditions for modifying.

citation.ref: the requirement that where the auditor expects to modify the opinion he shall communicate with those charged with governance the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification, read with SA 260 (Revised) para 16 on circumstances that affect the form and content of the auditor's report

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: Knowing the gates is not the same as recognising the facts, and SA 706 (Revised) gives a short list of circumstances in which the auditor may consider it necessary to include an emphasis of matter paragraph. An uncertainty relating to the future outcome of exceptional litigation or regulatory action. A significant subsequent event that occurs between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report. Early application, where permitted, of a new accounting standard that has a material effect on the financial statements. And a major catastrophe that has had, or continues to have, a significant effect on the entity's financial position. Two things run through all four. Each is a matter the financial statements themselves present or disclose, which is what makes an emphasis of matter rather than an other matter paragraph the right vehicle. And in each the auditor is content with the accounting — the paragraph draws attention to something correctly done, and states that the opinion is not modified in respect of it. The list is illustrative and not a checklist: a matter on it still has to pass both gates, so it must be one that requires no modification under SA 705 (Revised) and, where SA 701 applies, must not have been determined to be a key audit matter. A widespread use of these paragraphs diminishes the effectiveness of the auditor's communication.

citation.ref: the circumstances in which the auditor may consider it necessary to include an Emphasis of Matter paragraph — an uncertainty relating to the future outcome of exceptional litigation or regulatory action, a significant subsequent event occurring between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report, early application where permitted of a new accounting standard having a material effect, and a major catastrophe having a significant effect on the entity's financial position — read with para 8(a) and para 8(b) on the two provisos and para 9 on content and placement

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An other matter paragraph is the report's way of telling the reader something about the audit rather than about the accounts. Where the auditor considers it necessary to communicate a matter other than those presented or disclosed in the financial statements that, in his judgement, is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the auditor's report, he includes an other matter paragraph, provided two things: that this is not prohibited by law or regulation, and that, when SA 701 applies, the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter to be communicated in the auditor's report. The first proviso has no counterpart on the emphasis of matter side and is the one that is forgotten. When he includes the paragraph he puts it in a separate section of the report under the heading "Other Matter" or another appropriate heading. The recurring use in Indian practice is the division of responsibility: where the financial statements of branches or components included in the statements have been audited by other auditors, the paragraph states which branches, the total assets and the revenue they account for, that their financial statements were audited by those auditors whose reports have been furnished to the principal auditor, and that his opinion so far as it relates to the amounts and disclosures included in respect of them is based solely on those reports; ICAI's illustration of that paragraph also states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter. The test is always the subject matter, not the importance: a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements can never take an other matter paragraph however relevant it is, and a matter outside them can never take an emphasis of matter paragraph, because that paragraph shall refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements.

citation.ref: para 10 on the two provisos for an Other Matter paragraph — that it is not prohibited by law or regulation, and that when SA 701 applies the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter — with the requirement to include the paragraph within a separate section under the heading "Other Matter" or other appropriate heading, read with para 9 and with the illustration of an Other Matter paragraph on branch financial statements audited by branch auditors in Ch. Reporting

concepts.subsection: SA 706 (Revised) — Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter Paragraphs
concepts.statement: An emphasis of matter paragraph and a key audit matter answer two different questions, and the difference is where the importance sits. A key audit matter is one that, in the auditor's professional judgement, was of most significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period, selected from matters communicated with those charged with governance — the importance is to the AUDIT, and it is what required significant auditor attention. An emphasis of matter refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed that, in the auditor's judgement, is of such importance that it is fundamental to USERS' understanding of the financial statements. The two tests can pull apart in both directions. A matter may be fundamental to users' understanding — a subsequent event is the standard example — and yet not have required significant auditor attention, so it is not a key audit matter and goes in an emphasis of matter paragraph. A matter determined to be a key audit matter may also, in the auditor's judgement, be fundamental to users' understanding; it does not then get both, because an emphasis of matter is barred where SA 701 applies and the matter has been determined to be a key audit matter, and the auditor may instead highlight its relative importance by presenting it more prominently than the other matters in the Key Audit Matters section, for instance as the first matter, or by including additional information in the description of it. Where SA 701 applies, the use of emphasis of matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of the individual key audit matters.

citation.ref: the relationship between Emphasis of Matter paragraphs and key audit matters — that a matter not determined to be a key audit matter because it did not require significant auditor attention may nonetheless be fundamental to users' understanding and be included in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, that where a key audit matter is also fundamental the auditor may present it more prominently in the Key Audit Matters section or add information to its description, and that the use of Emphasis of Matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of individual key audit matters where SA 701 applies — read with para 8(b)

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 6
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he solicits clients or professional work either directly or indirectly by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview or by any other means. The words that decide most questions are "indirectly" and "by any other means": work canvassed through a solicitor, a banker, an employee or a partner is the member's own solicitation, and a member may not do through another hand what he may not do with his own. Two provisos sit inside the clause itself. A chartered accountant may apply for, request, invite or secure professional work from another chartered accountant in practice — approaching the profession is not approaching the public. And a member may respond to tenders or enquiries issued from time to time by users of professional services or by organisations, and may secure work as a consequence. The second proviso is then narrowed by the Council's own guideline: a member in practice shall not respond to a tender issued by an organisation or user of professional services in areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, such as audit and attestation services, unless the minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document itself, or the area is open to other professionals along with chartered accountants. The minimum fee must commensurate with the size, value, volume, manpower requirement and nature of the work. Paying a reasonable earnest money deposit or security deposit where the area is not exclusive is not interfered with, though an exorbitant one may be looked into by the Ethical Standards Board case by case, and a member responding to a tender maintains a cost sheet showing the persons involved and the hours to be spent, which the Institute may call for. The restraint exists so that a member keeps his independence of judgement and commands the respect of prospective clients; the satisfaction of existing clients is the advertisement the profession allows.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — soliciting clients or professional work directly or indirectly by circular, advertisement, personal communication or interview or by any other means, with the proviso permitting a chartered accountant to seek work from another chartered accountant in practice and the proviso permitting a member to respond to tenders and enquiries, read with Council Guidelines No. 1-CA(7)/03/2016 dated 7th April 2016 on responding to tenders in areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants and on earnest money deposits and the cost sheet

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 6: the Council's website guidelines
concepts.statement: The Council approved the posting of particulars on a website by members and firms in practice under Clause (6), and every stipulation in those guidelines is an answer to the same question: does this reach out to people who did not ask? No format is prescribed and there is no restriction on the colours used. The website must run on a pull model and not a push model, so that a person who wishes to locate the member gets the information only on a specific pull request, and nothing on the site may be circulated by the firm on its own, by email or by any other technique except on such a request. A member may not issue any circular, advertisement or material of any kind soliciting people to visit the site, though the website address may be mentioned on professional stationery and email. The permitted content is a list: name, year of establishment, addresses of the head office and branches with telephone, fax and email, the partners and employees with their qualifications and particulars, job vacancies including articleship, and — displayable only on a specific pull request — the nature of the services rendered, the areas of experience, the number of articled assistants and the nature of the assignments handled. Names of clients and the fees charged may not be given at all, except where a regulator in India or outside requires it, only to the extent of that requirement, only while it is in force, and with a statement in italics below the disclosure naming the regulator, its jurisdiction and the rule or directive requiring it. A passport style photograph is permitted. Articles, professional information, bulletin boards, professional updates and educational videos on topics of professional relevance are permitted. Chat rooms between members and between a firm and its clients are permitted with the confidentiality protocol observed, and a document management facility with distinct log-in and password may be provided. A firm may link to its page on a social networking site but may not solicit people to visit or like it. No advertisement in the nature of a banner or of any other nature is permitted. The address should be as near as possible to the name of the member or the firm, the site should ensure secrecy of client matters, it may link to the sites of ICAI, its Regional Councils and Branches and of Government, regulators and other professional bodies, and the information on it must not be at material variance from ICAI's own records.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the Council's guidelines for posting particulars on the website of a member or firm in practice, included under the Guidelines for Advertisement pursuant to the decision of the Council at its 388th meeting held on 6th and 7th February 2020: the pull and not push model, the bar on circulating the content or soliciting visits, the permitted particulars and those displayable only on a specific pull request, the bar on naming clients or fees except where a regulator requires it with the italicised statement below the disclosure, the passport style photograph, the social networking link without soliciting likes, and the bar on banner advertisements

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 6: the forms of soliciting the Council has ruled on
concepts.statement: Under Clause (6) the Council has ruled on particular forms of seeking work, and the pattern across them is that a bare statement of fact sent to people who already know the member is allowed while anything that reaches strangers or praises the member is not. In the press a member may not advertise for work or in a manner that could be read as offering to undertake work, and circulating letters to a small field of possible clients is equally barred; the exceptions are a request to another chartered accountant in practice, an announcement of a change in partnership, a dissolution, a change of address or of telephone number limited to a bare statement of facts with thought given to the area of circulation and the number of insertions, and a classified advertisement in the Institute's own journal or newsletter for sharing work, partnership or salaried employment carrying only the name, address, telephone, fax, email and social networking addresses with the factual position of experience and area of specialisation. Where a Government department, company, court, co-operative society or bank maintains a panel and the member knows of it, he may write asking to be placed on that panel and may quote fees on an enquiry received from it, but roving enquiries to any organisation that may have a panel are improper. A member may not mention his own or his firm's professional attainments in a book, an article or a presentation, though he may use the designation Chartered Accountant and the name of the firm. Greeting cards and invitations carrying the designation and the firm name are permitted only to clients, relatives and friends. Advertising an event organised by a firm is not permitted, but an advertisement for the firm's silver, golden, diamond, platinum or centenary celebrations may be published in a newspaper or newsletter. A member or firm may not sponsor an event unless it is conducted by a Programme Organising Unit of ICAI with the prior approval of the CPE Directorate, and a member sponsoring a corporate social responsibility activity may use his own name with the prefix CA but not the firm name or the CA logo. A firm profile may be shared with a prospective client only in response to that client's specific query. In a public interview or to the press, details must not highlight professional attainments and must be given only in answer to a specific question and only as fact. Advertisements under box numbers are barred, educational videos may be uploaded without naming the firm or giving contact details or the website address, and letters, emails or circulars addressed specifically to persons likely to need a chartered accountant amount to advertisement. A member may not accept original professional work from a client introduced to him by another member and should ask the client to come through that member. And the representation an auditor may make on removal is not a right to the audit: it must set out in a dignified manner how he acted independently and conscientiously and may state his willingness to continue if reappointed, without directly or indirectly canvassing for his continuance.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the forms of soliciting work on which the Council has ruled: press advertisements and their three exceptions, empanelment and the bar on roving enquiries, books, articles and presentations, greeting cards and invitations, celebration and sponsorship advertisements, sharing a firm profile only against a specific query, public interviews, box numbers, educational videos, work emanating from a client introduced by another member, and the scope of the representation an auditor may make under section 140(4) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Board meeting quorum — section 174
concepts.statement: Quorum for a board meeting is the higher of one-third of the total strength of directors (any fraction rounded up) or two directors. A director interested in an item under section 184(2) is left out of the count for that item, and telephonic assent from a director not participating by the prescribed video-conferencing means does not count as presence. Absent quorum, the meeting stands automatically adjourned to the same day the following week, same time and place, unless the articles say otherwise.

citation.ref: Section 174

concepts.subsection: Frequency of board meetings — section 173
concepts.statement: Every company holds at least four board meetings a year, with the gap between two consecutive meetings never exceeding one hundred and twenty days, and the first meeting within thirty days of incorporation. A one person company, small company, dormant company or private start-up needs only one meeting in each half of the calendar year, with a minimum gap of ninety days between the two — a relaxation, not the general rule.

citation.ref: Section 173

concepts.subsection: Board powers needing shareholder approval — section 180
concepts.statement: The board cannot, by its own resolution, sell, lease or otherwise dispose of the whole or substantially the whole of an undertaking, or borrow beyond the aggregate of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium (ordinary-course temporary bank loans excepted) — both need a special resolution of the shareholders first, obtained before the act, not disclosed to them after it.

citation.ref: Section 180

concepts.subsection: Retirement by rotation — section 152
concepts.statement: Independent directors are never liable to retire by rotation. Of the remaining directors of a public company, at least two-thirds must be liable to rotation, of which one-third (or the number nearest to one-third) retires at every annual general meeting, the director longest in office retiring first and being eligible for reappointment. Articles cannot exempt directors from rotation below this statutory floor.

citation.ref: Section 152(6)

concepts.subsection: Disclosure of directors' interest — section 184
concepts.statement: Every director discloses his concern or interest in any company, body corporate, firm or association of individuals at the first board meeting he attends in a financial year, and again on any change — a duty owed regardless of the size of the interest. Separately, an interested director discloses that interest in a specific contract or arrangement and does not participate in the board's discussion or vote on it; a contract entered in breach is voidable at the company's option.

citation.ref: Section 184

concepts.subsection: Contract of employment with managing or whole-time director — section 190
concepts.statement: A company keeps at its registered office a copy of its managing or whole-time director's contract of service, or a written memorandum of its terms where the contract is not in writing, open for inspection by members without charge during business hours — a members' right the board or the company secretary cannot narrow to itself or to the auditor.

citation.ref: Section 190

concepts.subsection: Consolidated financial statements — section 129(3)
concepts.statement: A company with one or more subsidiaries, including associate companies and joint ventures, prepares a consolidated financial statement in addition to its standalone statements, in the same form and manner, following the applicable accounting standards, and lays it before the annual general meeting alongside the standalone statements. Consolidation covers every subsidiary; it is not a management choice of which ones to fold in.

citation.ref: Section 129(3)

concepts.subsection: Board's report contents — section 134
concepts.statement: The board's report states, among other prescribed particulars, a director's responsibility statement under section 134(5), particulars of loans, guarantees and investments under section 186, particulars of related-party contracts in the prescribed form, the CSR policy and initiatives, and — for listed and other prescribed companies — a statement on the formal annual evaluation of the board, its committees and individual directors. These are matters the report must itself state, not particulars merely available on request.

citation.ref: Section 134(3)

concepts.subsection: Annual return and its certification — section 92
concepts.statement: Every company files its annual return with the Registrar within sixty days of the annual general meeting, or of the date by which the AGM should have been held where none took place, in which case a statement of the reasons for the default goes with it. Section 92(2) leaves the size line to the rules, and Rule 11(2) draws it at a listed company, or a company with paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more, or turnover of ₹50 crore or more: such a return must additionally be certified by a company secretary in practice in Form MGT-8. The two size tests are alternatives — crossing either is enough — and listing is a third, independent route in.

citation.ref: Sections 92(2) and 92(4), read with Rule 11(2) of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014 (Form MGT-8)

concepts.subsection: Rights issue procedure — section 62
concepts.statement: A rights issue offer goes to existing equity shareholders in proportion to their holding, stays open for not less than fifteen days and not more than thirty days, and carries a right of renunciation in favour of another person unless the articles exclude it. The board cannot allot before the offer period lapses or ahead of renunciation choices being exercised or declined.

citation.ref: Section 62(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Debentures — trustee and redemption reserve, section 71
concepts.statement: Section 71(5) stops a company from issuing a prospectus, or making an offer or invitation to the public or to more than five hundred of its members, for subscription of its debentures unless it has appointed one or more debenture trustees before that issue or offer. What pulls the trustee in is the kind of offer, not the size of the borrowing — the section names no rupee figure at all. Rule 18(1)(c) adds that the trustee comes before the prospectus or letter of offer goes out, and the debenture trust deed is executed within sixty days of allotment, so an independent party holds the security and enforces the debenture-holders' rights; the issuer's own guarantee is not a substitute for that office. Section 71(4) separately requires a debenture redemption reserve out of profits available for dividend, but Rule 18(7) as it now stands excuses listed companies, NBFCs registered under section 45-IA of the RBI Act and housing finance companies registered with the National Housing Bank; other unlisted companies keep a reserve of ten per cent of the outstanding value of the debentures.

citation.ref: Sections 71(4) and 71(5), read with Rules 18(1)(c) and 18(7) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014

concepts.subsection: Moratorium under the IBC — section 14
concepts.statement: On admission of a corporate insolvency resolution application, the adjudicating authority declares a moratorium barring institution or continuation of suits against the corporate debtor, transfer or disposal of its assets, enforcement of any security interest, and recovery of property by an owner or lessor in the debtor's possession; supply of essential goods and services to the debtor cannot be terminated during this period. The moratorium does not extend to a surety in a contract of guarantee for the corporate debtor.

citation.ref: Section 14

concepts.subsection: CIRP time limit — section 12 of the IBC
concepts.statement: A corporate insolvency resolution process must be completed within one hundred and eighty days of the insolvency commencement date. The committee of creditors may resolve, by a vote of sixty-six per cent of voting share under section 12(2), to instruct the resolution professional to seek one extension of up to ninety days — one only, never a second. The proviso to section 12(3) then caps the whole process at three hundred and thirty days from the insolvency commencement date, and that outer figure expressly swallows the time taken in legal proceedings relating to the process. The Supreme Court in Essar Steel read down the word "mandatorily" so a tribunal may go past three hundred and thirty days in an exceptional case where the delay is the tribunal's own, but that is a rescue, not the rule.

citation.ref: Sections 12(1), 12(2) and the proviso to section 12(3), as inserted by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2019

concepts.subsection: Committee of creditors — related parties and voting thresholds
