Where an All Industry Rate does exist but recovers less than eighty per cent of the duties actually paid on his materials, he applies under rule 7 for a special brand rate. Both applications run to three months from the relevant date, extendable on payment of the prescribed fee, and rule 9 caps any amount or rate at one third of the market price of the export product.

citation.ref: Section 75, with Rules 3, 6, 7 and 9 of the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Circular 254/11/2025 — Monetary limits for a section 74A notice and order
concepts.statement: Section 74A says what may be demanded; it does not say who may demand it. Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST dated 27 October 2025 does, extending to section 74A the scheme Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST had set for sections 73 and 74. Taking central tax alone: a Superintendent of Central Tax issues the show cause notice and passes the order up to ₹10 lakh, a Deputy or Assistant Commissioner above that and up to ₹1 crore, and an Additional or Joint Commissioner above ₹1 crore with no ceiling. For integrated tax both steps double, to ₹20 lakh and ₹2 crore. Where one notice covers central tax, integrated tax and cess together, the officer is fixed on the combined amount tested against the doubled steps, never on any single tax read on its own. The same three-tier structure governs a penalty-only notice under section 122, and where the demand grows past an officer's limit during adjudication the case moves up by corrigendum.

citation.ref: Section 74A, read with Tables II and III of Circular No. 254/11/2025-GST dated 27 October 2025, which extends to section 74A the scheme of Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST dated 9 February 2018

concepts.subsection: Rules 9A and 14A — Three-day registration and the simplified scheme
concepts.statement: The Central Goods and Services Tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2025 — Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025, in force from 1 November 2025 — opened two new routes into registration. Rule 9A lets the system grant registration electronically within three working days of the application, on its own data analysis and risk parameters, with an officer stepping in only where a risk parameter is flagged. Rule 14A is an optional simplified scheme a small supplier may choose: he qualifies where his total output tax liability — central tax, State or Union territory tax, integrated tax and cess together — on supplies made to registered persons does not exceed ₹2,50,000 in a month, and where Aadhaar is authenticated for the primary authorised signatory and at least one promoter or partner. That ₹2,50,000 is a monthly output tax figure on business-to-business supplies; it is neither a turnover limit nor the section 22 registration threshold. A person registered under rule 14A in one State cannot take a second rule 14A registration on the same PAN in another State.

citation.ref: Rules 9A and 14A, inserted by the Central Goods and Services Tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2025, Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025, with effect from 1 November 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 109(8) and rule 110A — When a single Member hears a GST appeal
concepts.statement: An appeal before the Appellate Tribunal is normally heard by two Members, one Judicial and one Technical. Section 109(8) carves out an exception: where the tax or input tax credit involved, or the fine, fee or penalty determined by the order appealed against, does not exceed ₹50 lakh, and the appeal involves no question of law, it may be heard by a single Member with the President's approval, and subject to such further conditions as may be prescribed on the Council's recommendations. So three things must hold together: the amount is within ₹50 lakh, no question of law arises, and the President has approved. Rule 110A, in force from 22 September 2025, settles how the amount is counted: the ₹50 lakh is read cumulatively across every issue and every tax period the order covers, not issue by issue.

citation.ref: Section 109(8), read with Rule 110A of the CGST Rules, 2017, inserted by Notification No. 13/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 18(1B) — Time limit for finalising a provisional customs assessment
concepts.statement: A provisional assessment under section 18(1) of the Customs Act once had no outer date; the Finance Act, 2025 gave it one. Section 18(1B) requires the proper officer to finalise within two years from the date of the provisional assessment, and its first proviso lets the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs extend that by one further year on sufficient cause recorded in writing. The Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2025 — Notification No. 55/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 12 September 2025 — work the detail: the proper officer calls for the documents and information he needs within fifteen days of the provisional assessment, the importer or exporter has two months to supply them with extensions possible, and the assessment is finalised within three months of the documents arriving or the enquiry ending. Certain periods stand outside the two years and the clock restarts when the reason ends — a stay by a court or tribunal, a direction of the Board, a pending request to a foreign authority, a matter before the Settlement Commission. Where a provisional assessment was already pending on 29 March 2025, the two years run from that date, not from the original assessment.

citation.ref: Section 18(1B) with its first proviso, inserted by the Finance Act, 2025, read with the Customs (Finalisation of Provisional Assessment) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 55/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 12 September 2025

concepts.subsection: RoDTEP and section 51B — The electronic duty credit ledger
concepts.statement: Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products gives an exporter back the embedded central, State and local taxes no other scheme refunds — value added tax and excise on the fuel his transport burns, mandi tax, electricity duty, stamp duty on export documents. It is a remission of taxes actually borne, not a bounty, and that is what keeps it inside India's obligations at the World Trade Organization; it replaced the Merchandise Exports from India Scheme for the same reason. The claim is made in the shipping bill at the time of export and the benefit arrives as duty credit in the electronic duty credit ledger that section 51B of the Customs Act, 1962 creates, issued as an e-scrip under the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger Regulations, 2021. Three limits carry the marks. The credit pays only the duties of customs specified in the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 — basic customs duty — and never the integrated tax or compensation cess collected at import. The e-scrip is valid for two years from its creation in the ledger, a period the 2022 amendment raised from one year, and anything unused at the end lapses and is not regenerated. And an e-scrip transfers to another Importer-Exporter Code holder only whole: part transfer is not permitted, and the transfer leaves the two years running as they were. Who may claim it has moved as well. The scheme opened to eligible exports from Domestic Tariff Area units, and Advance Authorisation holders, Export Oriented Units and Special Economic Zone units were shut out of it; they were brought in later, and Notification No. 35/2025 dated 30 September 2025 followed by Notification No. 74/2025-26 dated 31 March 2026 carry the scheme for all four classes up to 30 September 2026. So an Advance Authorisation holder asking whether RoDTEP is open to him is asking a question whose answer changed: it is, and the older position that it is not is the misconception to watch for.

citation.ref: Section 51B, read with regulations 6 and 7 of the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger Regulations, 2021, as amended by the Electronic Duty Credit Ledger (Amendment) Regulations, 2022, Notification No. 79/2022-Customs (N.T.) dated 15 September 2022

concepts.subsection: Entries 36C to 36E — Individual life and health insurance exempted
concepts.statement: Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 put three entries into the exemption notification, Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), with effect from 22 September 2025. Entry 36C exempts services of life insurance business provided by an insurer to the insured where the insured is not a group — a contract covering an individual, or an individual and his family. Entry 36D does the same for health insurance business on the same terms. Entry 36E exempts reinsurance of the services covered by 36C and 36D. What sits outside stays taxable at eighteen per cent: a group term policy, a group credit life policy, a group health policy an employer takes for his staff. The exemption follows the description of the service and the identity of the insured, not the size of the premium — and because it is an exemption rather than zero rating, it breaks the insurer's input tax credit chain on those supplies instead of preserving it.

citation.ref: Serial numbers 36C, 36D and 36E, inserted by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Rule 7 — The composition rate, and the turnover it applies to
concepts.statement: Section 10 settles who may compound; rule 7 settles at what rate, and on what. A manufacturer, other than of goods the Government has kept out of the scheme, pays one per cent — half central tax, half State tax — of the turnover in State or turnover in Union territory. A restaurant not serving alcohol pays five per cent of that same turnover in State. Any other supplier eligible under section 10(1) and 10(2), which in practice means a trader, also pays one per cent, but of the turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in State — and that difference is the whole point of the rule. A trader dealing partly in exempt goods leaves the exempt turnover out of his base; the manufacturer's one per cent runs on the entire turnover in State, exempt supplies included. A supplier of services under the section 10(2A) scheme pays six per cent of turnover in State. In every case the amount comes out of the supplier's own pocket: section 10(4) forbids him to collect it from his customer, and he takes no input tax credit.

citation.ref: Rule 7, read with sections 10(1), 10(2A) and 10(4) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Section 148A — Track and trace, and the section 122B penalty
concepts.statement: The Finance Act, 2025 built an enabling frame for marking goods that are easy to evade tax on. Section 148A lets the Government notify goods, and the persons or classes of persons in possession of or dealing with them, and require a unique identification marking to be affixed and the prescribed information about it to be stored and shared electronically. Section 2(116A) defines that marking — a digital stamp, digital mark or similar marking that is unique, secure and non-removable. Section 148A by itself carries no punishment; section 122B, in force from 1 October 2025, supplies it. A person covered by clause (b) of section 148A(1) who acts in contravention pays a penalty of ₹1,00,000 or ten per cent of the tax payable on those goods, whichever is higher, and that amount is in addition to any penalty under Chapter XV or under the penalty chapter itself, not a substitute for it.

citation.ref: Sections 148A and 122B with the definition in section 2(116A), inserted by the Finance Act (No. 7) of 2025, section 122B in force from 1 October 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 18A — Voluntary revision of an entry after clearance
concepts.statement: Before the Finance Act, 2025 an importer who found his own mistake after clearance had no clean way to correct it: section 149 amended a document, and anything touching the assessment waited for the department to issue a notice under section 28. Section 18A now lets the importer, the exporter or an authorised person voluntarily revise an entry already made in a bill of entry, shipping bill or bill of export after the goods are cleared, and the revised entry is treated as a self-assessment. Where the revision shows duty short paid, he pays it with interest, no penalty attaches and no notice under section 28 issues. Where it shows duty paid in excess, the application is itself treated as a claim for refund under section 27, so no separate refund application is needed. The route is closed in defined cases — where an audit, search, seizure or investigation has already been started and intimated, and where the entry has already been reassessed under section 17, 18 or 84. The Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 70/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 30 October 2025 and in force from 1 November 2025, prescribe an electronic application filed at the port where the duty was paid, with a fee of ₹1,000.

citation.ref: Section 18A, inserted by the Finance Act, 2025, read with the Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 70/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 30 October 2025, and Circular No. 26/2025-Customs dated 31 October 2025

concepts.subsection: Sections 37(4), 39(11), 44(2) and 52(15) — Three years and the return is barred
concepts.statement: A late GST return was once late for ever and could still be filed, with late fee and interest. The Finance Act, 2023 shut that door by inserting a sub-section into each of the four return provisions — section 37(4) for the statement of outward supplies, section 39(11) for the return, section 44(2) for the annual return and section 52(15) for the electronic commerce operator's statement — barring the furnishing of any of them after three years from the due date. Those sub-sections came into force on 1 October 2023 under Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023, and the portal began enforcing the bar from 1 October 2025. The three years runs from the due date of that return itself, not from the end of the financial year and not from the annual return's due date. Each of the four sub-sections carries a proviso letting the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, notify conditions on which a barred return may still be furnished — so the bar is hard, not absolute.

citation.ref: Sections 37(4), 39(11), 44(2) and 52(15) with their provisos, inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 and brought into force with effect from 1 October 2023 by Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023

concepts.subsection: Second proviso to section 16(2) and rule 37 — Paying the supplier within 180 days
concepts.statement: Credit taken on an invoice the recipient has not paid does not stay taken. The second proviso to section 16(2) says that where the recipient fails to pay the supplier the value of the supply together with the tax within 180 days from the date of the invoice, an amount equal to the credit availed is added to his output tax liability, with interest. Rule 37, as substituted with effect from 1 October 2022, works out how much and when: the reversal is proportionate to the amount left unpaid, it goes into the return for the tax period immediately following the 180 days, and interest runs on it under section 50. When the recipient later pays, rule 37(4) lets him take the credit back, and that re-availment is expressly outside the section 16(4) time limit. Supplies on which tax is payable under reverse charge sit outside the proviso altogether, because there is no supplier's tax to hand across.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 16(2), read with rule 37 of the CGST Rules, 2017 as substituted by Notification No. 26/2022-Central Tax dated 26 December 2022 with effect from 1 October 2022

concepts.subsection: Sections 100 and 101 — Appeal against an advance ruling
concepts.statement: An advance ruling under section 98 is not the end of the road. Section 100 gives an appeal to the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling — to the applicant, or to the concerned officer or the jurisdictional officer who disagrees with the ruling — within thirty days from the date the ruling is communicated, and the proviso lets the Appellate Authority allow a further thirty days where it is satisfied the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause. Section 101(2) requires the Appellate Authority to pass its order within ninety days of the appeal being filed. Section 101(3) holds the trap: where the two members of the Appellate Authority differ on any point, it is deemed that no advance ruling can be issued on that point. There is no casting vote and no further appeal — the applicant is left exactly where he began. The Advance Ruling Authority below must itself pronounce within ninety days of receiving the application.

citation.ref: Sections 100(2) with its proviso, 101(2) and 101(3), read with section 98(6)

concepts.section: Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
concepts.subsection: Section 25(4A) — Two-year sunset on a conditional customs exemption
concepts.statement: Section 25(1) lets the Central Government exempt goods from customs duty by notification in the public interest — a general exemption, open to anyone importing those goods. Section 25(2) is a different power: it exempts goods of a strategic or secret nature, or goods for a charitable purpose, by special order made in each individual case, and needs no notification. Section 25(4A), inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, puts a clock on the first kind wherever it carries conditions. A conditional exemption granted under section 25(1) ceases to have effect on the 31st day of March falling immediately after two years from the date it was granted, unless the notification itself specifies otherwise or the Government varies or rescinds it sooner. For conditional exemptions already in force when the provision came in, the two years count from 1 February 2021. Section 25(4B) keeps whole classes outside the sunset, among them exemptions flowing from a multilateral or bilateral trade agreement and from obligations under international agreements, treaties or conventions. An unconditional exemption is not touched by the sunset at all.

citation.ref: Sections 25(4A) and 25(4B), inserted by the Finance Act, 2021, read with sections 25(1) and 25(2)

concepts.subsection: Rule 96A — Export under bond or LUT, and the two clocks
concepts.statement: An exporter who chooses to export without payment of integrated tax furnishes a bond or a Letter of Undertaking under rule 96A, undertaking to pay the tax with interest if the export does not in fact happen. Two different clocks then run, and they measure different things. For goods, the tax falls due within fifteen days after three months from the date the export invoice was issued, if the goods have not left India by then — or such further period as the Commissioner allows. For services the test is money, not movement: the tax falls due within fifteen days after one year from the invoice date if payment has not been received in convertible foreign exchange, again subject to extension by the Commissioner. Missing either date costs more than tax and interest — the facility of exporting under bond or Letter of Undertaking is withdrawn until the amount is paid, and restored once it is. Non-receipt of payment does not by itself set off the goods clock; for goods the only question is whether they were exported.

citation.ref: Rule 96A(1)(a) and 96A(1)(b), read with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017 and Circular No. 37/11/2018-GST dated 15 March 2018

concepts.section: Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
concepts.subsection: IGCR Rules, 2022 — One year for the end use, and a quarterly statement
concepts.statement: An importer claiming a concessional rate of duty that depends on what he does with the goods runs on the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022. He files a one-time prior intimation estimating quantity and value, obtains an identification number, executes a continuity bond, and accounts for the goods in a prescribed record. Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2025, in force from 2 February 2025, loosened two periods. The time within which the imported goods must be put to the intended purpose, and the time within which unutilised or defective goods may be re-exported or cleared on payment of the differential duty, both became one year in place of six months. And the statement in Form IGCR-3 became quarterly — a quarter being three consecutive calendar months ending in March, June, September or December — in place of the monthly statement the rules first demanded. Failing the end use does not undo the import: it makes the differential duty payable, with interest.

citation.ref: Rules 6, 7 and 10 of the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022, as amended by Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2025 with effect from 2 February 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 20 as substituted — Input Service Distributor becomes compulsory
concepts.statement: Until 31 March 2025 the Input Service Distributor route was a choice: a head office receiving common input services for its branches could distribute the credit through an ISD registration or cross-charge the service to them as a distinct person. From 1 April 2025 the choice is gone. Section 2(61) and section 20, as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024, say that an office receiving tax invoices for input services for or on behalf of distinct persons shall distribute the credit through the ISD mechanism, and section 24(viii) makes a separate ISD registration compulsory for that office. Two things widened with the substitution. The definition now expressly takes in invoices for services on which tax is payable by the recipient under section 9(3) or section 9(4), so a reverse-charge input service received on a branch's behalf goes through the ISD as well — the office pays that tax under its ordinary registration and then distributes the credit through its ISD registration. And distribution now covers central tax, State or Union territory tax and integrated tax, with rule 39 saying which head goes out as which. The word that changed is one syllable and decides everything: may became shall.

citation.ref: Sections 2(61) and 20, as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025, read with section 24(viii) and rule 39 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 65 and rule 101 — Audit by the tax authorities, and when the clock starts
concepts.statement: The Commissioner or an officer authorised by him may undertake the audit of any registered person for a financial year or part of it. Section 65(3) requires not less than fifteen working days' prior notice in FORM GST ADT-01. Section 65(4) then gives three months from the commencement of the audit to complete it, and lets the Commissioner — nobody lower — extend that by a further period not exceeding six months, for reasons recorded in writing. The whole difficulty sits in the Explanation to section 65(4), which fixes what commencement means: the date on which the records and other documents called for by the tax authorities are made available by the registered person, or the actual institution of audit at the place of business, whichever is later. An officer who walks in before the records arrive has not started the clock. Findings, the reasons for them and the rights and obligations of the registered person are communicated within thirty days in FORM GST ADT-02, and where the audit shows tax unpaid, short paid, wrongly refunded or credit wrongly availed, the officer may proceed under section 74A.

citation.ref: Sections 65(3), 65(4) with its Explanation and 65(6), read with rule 101 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST ADT-01 and ADT-02

concepts.subsection: Section 66 and rule 102 — Special audit by a nominated accountant
concepts.statement: A special audit is not an audit the taxpayer arranges. At any stage of scrutiny, inquiry, investigation or other proceedings, an officer not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner who, having regard to the nature and complexity of the case and the interest of revenue, is of the opinion that the value has not been correctly declared or that credit availed is not within the normal limits, may — with the prior approval of the Commissioner — direct the registered person in FORM GST ADT-03 to get his records examined and audited by a chartered accountant or a cost accountant as may be nominated by the Commissioner. The report is due within ninety days, extendable by a further ninety days on an application by the registered person or the accountant, or for material and sufficient reason. Section 66(3) makes the power available notwithstanding that the accounts have already been audited under any other provision of this Act or under any other law, so a company audit is no shield. Section 66(4) guarantees an opportunity of being heard on any material gathered and proposed to be used. Section 66(5) puts the expenses of the examination and audit, including the accountant's remuneration, on the Commissioner, and makes his determination final.

citation.ref: Sections 66(1) to 66(6), read with rule 102 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST ADT-03 and ADT-04

concepts.subsection: Section 67 and rule 140 — Seizure, the six months, and provisional release
concepts.statement: Section 67(1) lets an officer not below the rank of Joint Commissioner, on reasons to believe recorded by him, authorise in writing in FORM GST INS-01 an inspection of any place of business of a taxable person, of a person engaged in transporting goods, or of the owner or operator of a warehouse or godown. Section 67(2) carries that to search and seizure where goods liable to confiscation, or documents, books or things useful to the proceedings, are secreted; where seizure is not practicable the proper officer may instead serve a prohibition order in FORM GST INS-03 forbidding removal without his permission. Two consequences matter more than the machinery. Section 67(7) returns the seized goods to the person from whom they were seized if no notice is given within six months of the seizure, a period the proper officer may extend on sufficient cause by a further period not exceeding six months and no more. And section 67(6) keeps a door open throughout — seized goods are released provisionally on execution of a bond and furnishing of security, which rule 140 fixes as a bond for the value of the goods in FORM GST INS-04 together with a bank guarantee equal to the applicable tax, interest and penalty. Goods of a perishable or hazardous nature may be disposed of at once under section 67(8).

citation.ref: Sections 67(1), 67(2), 67(6) and 67(7), read with rules 139 and 140 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST INS-01, INS-03 and INS-04

concepts.subsection: Section 69 — Who may authorise an arrest, and what the five crore line decides
concepts.statement: The power to authorise an arrest under GST sits in one office. Section 69(1) lets the Commissioner, where he has reasons to believe that a person has committed an offence specified in clause (a), (b), (c) or (d) of section 132(1) which is punishable under clause (i) or clause (ii) of that sub-section, or under section 132(2), authorise by order any officer of central tax to arrest that person. No officer below the Commissioner may give that authorisation, and the contrast with section 67 — where a Joint Commissioner authorises an inspection or a search — is the usual place candidates slip. What the amount decides is not whether an arrest may happen but what follows it. Section 132(5) makes the listed offences cognizable and non-bailable only where the amount of tax evaded, or credit wrongly availed or utilised, or refund wrongly taken, exceeds five crore rupees; section 132(4) leaves every other offence non-cognizable and bailable. Where the offence is cognizable and non-bailable, section 69(2) requires the arresting officer to inform the person of the grounds of arrest and produce him before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours. Where it is not, section 69(3) requires the Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner to admit him to bail or forward him to the custody of the Magistrate, with the same powers as an officer in charge of a police station.

citation.ref: Sections 69(1), 69(2) and 69(3), read with sections 132(4) and 132(5)

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Sections 125 and 126 — The residual penalty and the minor-breach relief
concepts.statement: Section 125 is the sweeper. Any person who contravenes a provision of the Act or the rules for which no penalty is separately provided is liable to a penalty which may extend to twenty-five thousand rupees — a ceiling, not a fixed amount, and available only where nothing else fits. Section 126 runs the other way. Sub-section (1) forbids any officer to impose a penalty for minor breaches of tax regulations or procedural requirements, and in particular for any omission or mistake in documentation which is easily rectifiable and made without fraudulent intent or gross negligence. Its Explanation supplies both tests: a breach is minor where the amount of tax involved is less than five thousand rupees, and a documentation omission is easily rectifiable where it is an error apparent on the face of record. Sub-section (2) requires any penalty to be commensurate with the degree and severity of the breach; sub-section (3) forbids a penalty without notice and an opportunity of being heard; sub-section (5) lets voluntary disclosure before discovery be treated as a mitigating factor. And sub-section (6) is the trap that decides most questions: the whole of section 126 does not apply where the penalty specified under the Act is either a fixed sum or expressed as a fixed percentage.

citation.ref: Sections 125 and 126(1) with its Explanation, 126(2), 126(3), 126(5) and 126(6)

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Section 138 — Compounding an offence, and the one offence that cannot be compounded
concepts.statement: Section 138(1) lets the Commissioner compound an offence under the Act, on payment of the compounding amount, either before or after the institution of prosecution — but only after the tax, interest and penalty involved in the offence have been paid. The proviso carves out cases, and the sharpest of them is the offence under clause (b) of section 132(1), issuing an invoice or bill without any supply of goods or services, which cannot be compounded at all. Section 138(2) fixes the amount at not less than twenty-five per cent and not more than one hundred per cent of the tax involved, a band that replaced the earlier fifty to one hundred and fifty per cent range with its rupee floors. Section 138(3) gives compounding its point: on payment of the compounding amount no further proceedings shall be initiated under the Act against the accused in respect of the same offence, and any criminal proceeding already instituted stands abated. Compounding settles the criminal side alone; it does not touch proceedings under any other law, and it does not wipe out the tax.

citation.ref: Sections 138(1) with its provisos, 138(2) and 138(3), read with section 132(1)(b) and rule 162 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rules 27, 30 and 31 — The ladder when transaction value fails
concepts.statement: Section 15(1) gives transaction value only where the supplier and the recipient are not related and the price is the sole consideration for the supply. Fail either limb and section 15(4) sends the valuation to Chapter IV of the rules. Rule 27 governs a consideration not wholly in money and works down in order — the open market value of the supply; failing that, the sum of the consideration in money and the money equivalent of the non-monetary part, where that equivalent is known at the time of supply; failing that, the value of a supply of like kind and quality; and failing that, rule 30 or rule 31. Rule 30 values the supply at one hundred and ten per cent of the cost of production or manufacture, the cost of acquisition of the goods, or the cost of provision of the services, whichever limb fits. Rule 31 is the residual — value determined by reasonable means consistent with the principles and general provisions of section 15 and of this Chapter. For goods the order is strict, rule 30 before rule 31. For services it is not: the proviso to rule 31 lets the supplier of a service opt for rule 31 disregarding rule 30 altogether.

citation.ref: Rules 27, 30 and 31 with the proviso to rule 31, read with sections 15(1) and 15(4) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 34 — The rate of exchange, and why goods and services differ
concepts.statement: A supply priced in a foreign currency has to be turned into rupees before any tax can be computed, and rule 34 gives two different answers depending on what was supplied. Rule 34(1) says the rate of exchange for determining the value of taxable goods is the applicable rate of exchange notified by the Board under section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, for the date of the time of supply of those goods. Rule 34(2) says the rate for determining the value of taxable services is the applicable rate of exchange determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles for the date of the time of supply of those services. Two things follow. The converting date is the date of the time of supply in both cases — never the invoice date as such, never the date the money is received, and never the date the service was performed, except so far as one of those events happens to fix the time of supply under section 12 or section 13. And the customs rate notified by the Board reaches goods only; a service converts at the accounting rate even where a customs rate for the same day exists and differs.

citation.ref: Rules 34(1) and 34(2), read with sections 12 and 13 of the CGST Act, 2017 and section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962

concepts.subsection: Rule 35 — Backing the tax out of a tax-inclusive price
concepts.statement: A retail price marked as including all taxes is not a taxable value, and treating it as one taxes the tax. Rule 35 supplies the arithmetic. Where the value of a supply is inclusive of integrated tax or, as the case may be, of central tax, State tax, Union territory tax and cess, the tax amount for a head is the value inclusive of taxes multiplied by the rate of tax in per cent for that head, divided by one hundred plus the sum of all the applicable rates in per cent. On an intra-State supply at eighteen per cent the denominator is one hundred and eighteen, and the numerator is nine for central tax and nine again for State tax, so each head takes nine one-hundred-and-eighteenths of the marked price and the taxable value is what remains. Running the whole eighteen through the same denominator gives the total tax on the sale, which is a useful check but is not the figure for any one head. The rates to use are the live ones — five, eighteen and forty per cent since 22 September 2025; the twelve and twenty-eight per cent slabs were abolished that day and a denominator built on them is wrong before the arithmetic starts.

citation.ref: Rule 35, read with section 15(1) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 43 — Capital goods credit spread over sixty months
concepts.statement: Rule 42 apportions credit on inputs and input services; rule 43 does the same job for capital goods, and it does it over time. Credit on a capital good used exclusively for non-business purposes or exclusively for exempt supplies is not credited to the electronic credit ledger at all. Credit on one used exclusively for taxable supplies, zero-rated supplies included, is credited in full. What is left is the common capital goods credit, denoted A for each item and aggregated as Tc. Rule 43 fixes the useful life of a capital good at five years, so the common credit attributable to a tax period is Tm equal to Tc divided by sixty. The part of that monthly slice attributable to exempt supplies is Te equal to E divided by F multiplied by Tm, where E is the aggregate value of exempt supplies during the tax period and F is the total turnover in the State during that tax period. Te is added to the output tax liability of the registered person for every tax period of the useful life, along with interest. Where a capital good used at first exclusively for exempt supplies or non-business purposes is later put to common use, A is arrived at by reducing the input tax by five per cent for every quarter or part of a quarter that has passed.

citation.ref: Rule 43(1), clauses (a) to (h), read with sections 17(1) and 17(2) of the CGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 35 and rules 56 to 58 — Records, and what unaccounted goods cost
concepts.statement: Section 35(1) requires every registered person to keep and maintain, at his principal place of business as mentioned in the certificate of registration, a true and correct account of production or manufacture, of inward and outward supplies, of stock, of input tax credit availed, of output tax payable and paid, and of such other particulars as are prescribed; where more than one place of business is on the certificate, the accounts relating to each place are kept at that place. Section 35(2) reaches beyond registration — every owner or operator of a warehouse, godown or other place used for storage, and every transporter, must maintain records of the consigner, the consignee and the goods, whether or not he is registered. Rules 56 to 58 supply the detail, including serial numbering of manual records, scoring out with attestation rather than erasure, and a log of every electronic entry edited or deleted. Two points carry the marks. Section 35(5), which had required accounts to be audited by a chartered accountant or a cost accountant above a turnover limit, was omitted with effect from 1 August 2021, and FORM GSTR-9C is now a self-certified reconciliation statement. And section 35(6) says that where the registered person fails to account for goods or services, the proper officer shall determine the tax payable on them as if they had been supplied by that person, and proceed under section 74A.

citation.ref: Sections 35(1), 35(2) and 35(6), with section 35(5) as omitted with effect from 1 August 2021, read with rules 56, 57 and 58 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Rule 89(5) — What Net ITC means in an inverted duty refund
concepts.statement: Section 54(3) allows a refund of accumulated credit in two cases only, and where the case is an inverted duty structure the amount is not the accumulation itself but a figure rule 89(5) computes. The whole weight of that computation sits in one defined term. The Explanation to rule 89(5) says Net ITC means input tax credit availed on inputs during the relevant period, other than credit for which refund is claimed under sub-rules (4A) or (4B). Inputs are defined by section 2(59) as any goods other than capital goods used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business. Two whole categories therefore never enter Net ITC: the credit on input services, and the credit on capital goods. Both remain perfectly good credit, usable against output tax without limit — they are simply outside the refund. The Supreme Court settled the point in Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India (P) Ltd, holding the exclusion of input services from the formula to be within the rule-making power and not discriminatory. The practical consequence is that a manufacturer whose ledger swells on credits for services will find his inverted refund much smaller than his balance, and the gap is not an error.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) with its Explanation, read with section 54(3) and section 2(59) of the CGST Act, 2017, and Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India (P) Ltd

concepts.subsection: Export Goods Valuation Rules, 2007 — Valuing an export, and the method that does not exist
concepts.statement: Section 14(1) of the Customs Act makes the value of export goods the transaction value, that is the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export from India for delivery at the time and place of exportation, where the buyer and seller are not related and price is the sole consideration. The proviso that adds cost of transport, loading, unloading, handling and insurance belongs to imported goods; an export is valued at the place of exportation, so ocean freight and insurance beyond that point are never added. Where the declared value is rejected — rule 8 lets the proper officer do that where he has reason to doubt its truth or accuracy, after asking the exporter for an explanation — the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 run in order. Rule 4 compares the transaction value of goods of like kind and quality exported at or about the same time to the same destination, adjusted for differences in nature, quality and quantity. Rule 5 builds a computed value from the cost of production, manufacture or processing, the charges for design or brand, and an amount towards profit. Rule 6 falls back on reasonable means consistent with the principles of the rules and of section 14(1), and says in terms that the local market price of the export goods shall not be the basis. There is no deductive value method for exports; that belongs to the import rules.

citation.ref: Section 14(1) with its proviso, read with rules 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007

concepts.subsection: Sections 53 to 56 — Transit, transhipment, and where the duty falls
concepts.statement: The two words are not interchangeable and the difference is physical. Transit under section 53 is goods that arrive in a conveyance, are mentioned in the arrival manifest as for transit, and continue in the same conveyance to a place outside India or to another customs station; they are allowed to pass without payment of duty. Transhipment under section 54 is goods moved onto a different conveyance, and it needs a document — a bill of transhipment presented to the proper officer, or, where the transhipment is under an international treaty or bilateral agreement, a declaration for transhipment. Section 54(2) allows transhipment to a place outside India without payment of duty; section 54(3) allows transhipment to another customs station in India without payment of duty at the port of arrival, subject to the conditions prescribed for the due arrival of the goods at the destination. Section 55 then decides where the duty falls — goods transited under section 53 or transhipped under section 54(3) to a customs station are treated, on arrival there, as if they had been imported into that station, so assessment and duty happen at the destination and not at the port of entry. Section 52 keeps baggage, goods imported by post and stores outside the chapter altogether.

citation.ref: Sections 52, 53, 54(1), 54(2), 54(3), 55 and 56, read with the Goods Imported (Conditions of Transhipment) Regulations, 1995

concepts.subsection: Section 65 and the MOOWR Regulations, 2019 — Manufacture inside a bonded warehouse
concepts.statement: Section 65(1) of the Customs Act lets the owner of warehoused goods carry on any manufacturing process or other operations in relation to them inside the warehouse, with the permission of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs. The Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse Regulations, 2019 work it — one application to the jurisdictional Commissioner for a licence under section 58 and permission under section 65 together, a one-time bond under section 59, digital accounts of the goods received and consumed, and a monthly return. The point of the scheme is deferment, not exemption. Nothing is paid when the goods enter. When the resultant goods are exported, the deferred import duty on the warehoused goods used in them is never collected at all. When the resultant goods are cleared into the domestic tariff area, the import duty on the warehoused goods contained in them becomes payable at that moment, and goods and services tax is charged on the domestic supply of the resultant product. Section 65(2)(a) settles waste — remitted where the resultant goods are exported, charged where they go into home consumption. And section 61(1)(a) gives capital goods in such a warehouse a warehousing period running till their clearance and other goods a period running till their consumption or clearance, so the ninety-day interest clock in section 61(2), which belongs to ordinary goods under section 61(1)(c), never starts.

citation.ref: Sections 65(1) and 65(2), read with sections 58, 59, 61(1)(a) and 61(2), and the Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse (No. 2) Regulations, 2019, Notification No. 69/2019-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 October 2019

concepts.section: Classification of Imported and Export Goods
concepts.subsection: Heading 9801 and the Project Imports Regulations, 1986
concepts.statement: Project imports is a classification device, not an exemption. Everything imported for the initial setting up, or for the substantial expansion, of a specified project is classified under a single heading — 9801 of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 — and assessed at one uniform rate, whatever heading each turbine, cable, pump or steel section would carry if imported on its own. The specified projects are an industrial plant, an irrigation project, a power project, a mining project, a project for the exploration of oil or other minerals, and any other project the Central Government notifies. Industrial plant is defined narrowly and expressly leaves out a hospital, hotel, photographic studio, film processing laboratory, photocopying studio, laundry, garage and workshop, as well as a single machine or a composite machine dressed up as a plant. The Project Imports Regulations, 1986 attach the conditions. The contract must be registered with the proper officer at the port of import before any goods are cleared, on the recommendation of the sponsoring authority certifying that the goods are required for the project. Spare parts, raw materials and consumable stores are covered only up to ten per cent of the value of the goods registered, and only if the contract shows them. After the last consignment clears, a statement of the goods actually imported is filed and the contract is finalised.

citation.ref: Heading 9801 of the First Schedule, read with regulations 4, 5, 6 and 7 of the Project Imports Regulations, 1986

concepts.subsection: Section 9A, Customs Tariff Act — Anti-dumping duty and the lesser duty rule
concepts.statement: Where an article is exported to India at less than its normal value, section 9A(1) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 lets the Central Government impose an anti-dumping duty not exceeding the margin of dumping, that being the difference between the normal value and the export price. That cap is not the levy. Rule 4 of the Anti-dumping Rules, 1995 requires the designated authority to recommend the amount of duty which, if less than the margin of dumping, would be adequate to remove the injury to the domestic industry — the lesser duty rule — so the duty imposed is the lower of the dumping margin and the injury margin. Section 9A(2) allows a provisional duty on a preliminary finding, which shall not remain in force for more than six months, extendable by the Central Government to nine months on a request from exporters accounting for a significant percentage of the trade. Section 9A(5) ends a final duty five years from the date of imposition unless revoked earlier, and lets the Government extend it by a further five years after a sunset review, with the duty continuing pending a review begun before expiry for up to one year. Section 9A(2A) keeps the duty off imports by a hundred per cent export-oriented undertaking or a unit in a special economic zone unless the notification specifically applies it, and section 9B forbids both anti-dumping and countervailing duty on the same article to compensate for the same situation.

citation.ref: Sections 9A(1), 9A(2), 9A(2A) and 9A(5), read with rule 4(d) of the Customs Tariff (Identification, Assessment and Collection of Anti-dumping Duty on Dumped Articles and for Determination of Injury) Rules, 1995, and section 9B

concepts.subsection: Section 8B, Customs Tariff Act — Safeguard measures and the developing-country carve-out
concepts.statement: Anti-dumping answers unfair pricing; a safeguard answers a surge. Section 8B, as substituted, is headed as a power to apply safeguard measures rather than merely to levy a safeguard duty, and the measures it allows are a safeguard duty, a tariff-rate quota, and such other measure as may be prescribed. The trigger is that an article is imported into India in such increased quantities and under such conditions as to cause or threaten to cause serious injury to the domestic industry. A provisional measure may be applied on a preliminary determination and stays in force for not more than two hundred days. A final measure ceases four years from the date of imposition unless revoked earlier, and even with extensions the total period may not exceed ten years. Two carve-outs decide most questions. A safeguard measure does not apply to an article originating in a developing country so long as that country's share of the imports of that article into India does not exceed three per cent; and where the article comes from more than one developing country each with less than three per cent, the measure reaches none of them so long as their imports together do not exceed nine per cent of the total imports of that article. And the measure does not apply to articles imported by a hundred per cent export-oriented undertaking or a unit in a special economic zone unless it is specifically made applicable to them.

citation.ref: Section 8B as substituted — the power to apply safeguard measures, the two hundred day provisional measure, the four-year life with a ten-year outer limit, and the developing country carve-out — read with the Customs Tariff (Identification and Assessment of Safeguard Measures) Rules, 2021

concepts.subsection: Section 16(1)(b) IGST — Supplying an SEZ, and the authorised-operations test
concepts.statement: Section 16(1) of the IGST Act zero-rates two things: an export of goods or services, and a supply of goods or services to a Special Economic Zone developer or unit for authorised operations. Those last three words were added by the Finance Act, 2021 and settled an argument. A zone is deemed to be outside the customs territory of India for the purposes of authorised operations, and no further — a supply into a zone that has nothing to do with the unit's letter of approval is an ordinary inter-State supply on which integrated tax is charged in the normal way. It is not exempt, and it is not zero-rated; the distinction matters because exemption breaks the supplier's credit chain while zero rating preserves it, and an ordinary taxable supply does neither. The endorsement of the specified officer of the zone is what evidences authorised operations when a refund is claimed. Movement the other way is not a supply by the unit at all: section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 treats a clearance from a zone into the domestic tariff area as an import, so the domestic buyer files a bill of entry and pays customs duty together with integrated tax under section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and the unit charges nothing on an invoice.

citation.ref: Sections 16(1)(b) and 16(3), read with section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, rule 89(2)(f) of the CGST Rules, 2017, and section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

concepts.subsection: Section 147 and Notification 48/2017 — Deemed exports, and why they are not zero-rated
concepts.statement: Section 147 lets the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, notify certain supplies of goods as deemed exports, where the goods supplied do not leave India, payment is received in Indian rupees or in convertible foreign exchange, and the goods are manufactured in India. Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017 notified four categories: goods supplied by a registered person against an Advance Authorisation; capital goods supplied against an Export Promotion Capital Goods Authorisation; goods supplied to an Export Oriented Unit; and gold supplied by a bank or a notified Public Sector Undertaking against an Advance Authorisation. Three limits define the concept. Section 147 speaks only of goods, so a service can never be a deemed export however the recipient is described. A deemed export is not a zero-rated supply under section 16 of the IGST Act, so it cannot be made under a bond or LUT — the tax is charged and paid, and relief comes afterwards. And the third proviso to rule 89(1) lets the refund of that tax be claimed either by the recipient or by the supplier, the conditions in Circular No. 14/14/2017-GST governing which, including that where the supplier claims it the recipient must not have availed the input tax credit and must say so.

citation.ref: Section 147, read with Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017, the third proviso to rule 89(1) of the CGST Rules, 2017, and Circular No. 14/14/2017-GST dated 6 November 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 7 — What counts as a supply, and the club that cannot plead mutuality
concepts.statement: Section 7(1) is the gate every question about GST has to pass. Clause (a) covers all forms of supply of goods or services or both — sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal — made or agreed to be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business. Clause (aa), inserted by the Finance Act, 2021 with effect from 1 July 2017, covers the activities or transactions by a person, other than an individual, to its members or constituents or the other way about, for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, and its Explanation deems the person and its members to be two separate persons and the supply to take place from one to the other, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law or in any judgment, decree or order of any court. That last phrase is aimed at the doctrine of mutuality and at the decision in State of West Bengal v. Calcutta Club Ltd, which is displaced for GST. Clause (b) brings in the import of services for a consideration whether or not in the course or furtherance of business, and clause (c) the activities in Schedule I made without a consideration. Section 7(1A) then does the classifying and nothing more — where an activity constitutes a supply under section 7(1) it shall be treated as a supply of goods or of services as referred to in Schedule II. The old section 7(1)(d), which let Schedule II create a supply by itself, was omitted by the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017. Section 7(2) puts Schedule III and notified activities of a government or a local authority outside supply altogether, and section 7(3) lets the Government notify a supply of goods to be treated as a supply of services and the reverse.

citation.ref: Sections 7(1)(a), 7(1)(aa) with its Explanation, 7(1)(b), 7(1)(c), 7(1A), 7(2) and 7(3), read with Schedules I, II and III, the Finance Act, 2021 and the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018

concepts.subsection: Section 2(31) — Consideration, and the deposit that is not one yet
concepts.statement: Consideration in relation to the supply of goods or services or both includes any payment made or to be made, whether in money or otherwise, in respect of, in response to, or for the inducement of the supply, whether by the recipient or by any other person; and it includes the monetary value of any act or forbearance, in respect of, in response to, or for the inducement of the supply. Two carve-outs sit inside the definition. A subsidy given by the Central Government or a State Government is excluded, so such a subsidy is neither consideration under section 2(31) nor an inclusion in value under section 15(2)(e). And the proviso says a deposit given in respect of the supply shall not be considered as payment made for the supply unless the supplier applies the deposit as consideration for the said supply. The word that carries the proviso is "applies". Money sitting as security is outside the levy however long it sits; the moment the supplier appropriates it against the price it becomes consideration and the tax attaches then. Two further points follow from the words. Consideration may come from a person who is not the recipient, so a payment made by a third party still funds a taxable supply. And it need not be money at all — an act or a forbearance counts at its monetary value, which is what sends a consideration not wholly in money into rule 27.

citation.ref: Section 2(31) with its proviso, read with section 15(2)(e) and section 7(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Sections 2(17), 2(84) and 2(107) — Business, person, and who is a taxable person
concepts.statement: Three definitions decide whether a transaction is inside GST at all. Section 2(84) says who a person is, and the list is wide — an individual, a Hindu Undivided Family, a company, a firm, a limited liability partnership, an association of persons, a co-operative society, a local authority, a government, a trust, and every artificial juridical person. Section 2(107) says a taxable person means a person who is registered or liable to be registered under section 22 or section 24. Section 2(17) says what business means, and it is far broader than trade. It takes in any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure, wager or any other similar activity, whether or not it is for a pecuniary benefit; any activity or transaction in connection with or incidental or ancillary to it; any such activity or transaction whether or not there is volume, frequency, continuity or regularity; the provision by a club, association, society or any such body of the facilities or benefits to its members; and the admission of persons to any premises for a consideration. What none of the three does is make everything a registered person touches taxable. Section 7(1)(a) needs the supply to be made in the course or furtherance of business, so a person's disposal of something he holds privately, on which no input tax credit was ever taken and which never formed part of the assets of the business, is not a supply, and his registration does not change that. The registration decides who must account for tax on his supplies; it does not decide what a supply is.

citation.ref: Sections 2(17), 2(84), 2(105) and 2(107), read with section 7(1)(a) and paragraph 1 of Schedule I

concepts.subsection: Schedule II paragraph 4 — Transfer of business assets, and the going-concern carve-out
concepts.statement: Paragraph 4 of Schedule II deals with business assets and has three limbs, each with a different answer. Clause (a) — where goods forming part of the assets of a business are transferred or disposed of by or under the directions of the person carrying on the business so as no longer to form part of those assets, that is a supply of goods by him, whether or not for a consideration. Clause (b) — where goods held or used for the purposes of the business are put to any private use or are made available to any person for use for any purpose other than a purpose of the business, by or under the directions of the person carrying on the business, the usage or making available is a supply of services. Clause (c) — where any person ceases to be a taxable person, any goods forming part of the assets of any business carried on by him shall be deemed to be supplied by him in the course or furtherance of his business immediately before he ceases to be a taxable person, unless the business is transferred as a going concern to another person, or the business is carried on by a personal representative who is deemed to be a taxable person. The trap is the machinery around it. Since the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 substituted section 7(1A) and omitted the old section 7(1)(d), both with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017, Schedule II can only classify something that is already a supply under section 7(1); it cannot create one. Paragraph 4 survives that change because its clauses are written as deeming provisions in their own right and because paragraph 1 of Schedule I independently makes the permanent transfer or disposal of business assets on which input tax credit has been availed a supply even without consideration.

citation.ref: Paragraph 4 of Schedule II, read with section 7(1A), paragraph 1 of Schedule I, and the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 omitting section 7(1)(d) with effect from 1 July 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 10(1)(c), (d), (e) and 11 IGST — Place of supply where nothing moves, and where it is installed
concepts.statement: Section 10(1)(a) of the IGST Act answers the ordinary case where the supply involves movement of goods, and the answer is the location of the goods at the time at which the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient. The rest of section 10 handles the cases it does not reach. Clause (c) — where the supply does not involve movement of goods, whether by the supplier or by the recipient, the place of supply is the location of such goods at the time of the delivery to the recipient. Clause (d) — where the goods are assembled or installed at site, the place of supply is the place of such installation or assembly. Clause (e) — where the goods are supplied on board a conveyance, including a vessel, an aircraft, a train or a motor vehicle, the place of supply is the location at which such goods are taken on board. Section 11 handles the border: the place of supply of goods imported into India is the location of the importer, and the place of supply of goods exported from India is the location outside India. Two habits cause errors. Clause (d) is written on a physical fact — where the thing ends up bolted down — and not on whose name is on the invoice or where the recipient is registered; the recipient's location governs services under section 12(2), never goods. And once the place of supply is fixed, the character of the supply follows section 7 or section 8 of the IGST Act by comparing it with the location of the supplier, so a supplier and a place of supply in two different States make it an inter-State supply on which integrated tax is charged.

citation.ref: Sections 10(1)(c), 10(1)(d) and 10(1)(e), and section 11, read with sections 7(1) and 8(1) of the IGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Vouchers — what is taxed when a voucher changes hands
concepts.statement: A voucher is an instrument that carries an obligation to accept it as consideration for a supply, and the difficulty has always been that three different things happen around it: the voucher is created and sold, it is passed down a chain of distributors, and it is finally redeemed against goods or services. The settled position, taken by the GST Council at its 55th meeting and put into words by Circular No. 243/37/2024-GST, separates them. Where the voucher is a pre-paid instrument recognised by the Reserve Bank of India it is money, and a transaction in money is excluded from the definitions of goods in section 2(52) and of services in section 2(102), so the transaction in the voucher itself is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services. Where the voucher is not such an instrument it is an actionable claim, and Schedule III keeps actionable claims other than the specified ones outside supply. Distribution of vouchers on a principal-to-principal basis is therefore not a supply either. What is a supply is the service: where a distributor or an agent earns a commission, a fee or a discount for distributing or marketing the vouchers, that is a supply of services by him to the issuer and it is taxable. Unredeemed vouchers — breakage — are not consideration for any supply, because no supply is ever made against them. The redemption is taxed on its own terms, as the supply of whatever the voucher buys. Sections 12(4) and 13(4), which used to fix the time of supply of a voucher, and rule 32(6), which valued one, were taken out as part of the same exercise.

citation.ref: Circular No. 243/37/2024-GST dated 31 December 2024, read with sections 2(52) and 2(102) and paragraph 6 of Schedule III, and with the omission of sections 12(4) and 13(4) and rule 32(6)

concepts.subsection: Section 49(5) and rule 88A — The order in which the credit ledger is spent
concepts.statement: Section 49(5) fixes the order in which the electronic credit ledger is used, and rule 88A, inserted with effect from 29 March 2019, loosens one part of it. Integrated tax credit is applied first towards integrated tax, and the balance may then go towards central tax and State or Union territory tax in any order and in any proportion — that freedom is rule 88A's contribution, and it replaced a rigid sequence that made the balance go to central tax first. Section 49B with rule 88A then adds the gate: the whole of the integrated tax credit must be exhausted before any central tax or State tax credit is used at all. Central tax credit is applied towards central tax and then towards integrated tax; State tax credit towards State tax and then towards integrated tax; and clauses (e) and (f) of section 49(5) forbid the two ever crossing — central tax credit shall not be utilised towards payment of State tax, and State tax credit shall not be utilised towards payment of central tax. The practical consequence is that the choice rule 88A gives away is worth money. Splitting the leftover integrated tax credit unevenly between the central and State heads can leave a stranded balance on one head and a cash payment on the other, while splitting it so that both heads finish together can leave nothing to pay in cash. Rule 86B separately restricts how much of the output liability a person above a prescribed monthly turnover may discharge from the credit ledger, but it caps the proportion; it does not change the order.

citation.ref: Sections 49(5)(a) to 49(5)(f), 49A and 49B, read with rules 88A and 86B of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 49(3), 49(4) and 49(8) — The three ledgers, and what each one may pay
concepts.statement: Three registers sit on the portal and each one has a job the others cannot do. The electronic cash ledger under section 49(1) and rule 87 is credited by every deposit made by challan in FORM GST PMT-06, and section 49(3) lets the amount in it be used for payment of tax, interest, penalty, fees or any other amount payable under the Act or the rules. The electronic credit ledger under section 49(2) and rule 86 is credited with the input tax credit self-assessed in the return, and section 49(4) lets it be used for making any payment towards output tax and nothing else. Output tax is defined in section 2(82) as the tax chargeable on taxable supplies made by a person or by his agent, but excluding tax payable by him on a reverse charge basis, so three liabilities can never come out of the credit ledger: tax under reverse charge, and interest, and penalty or fee. Those go in cash. The electronic liability register under rule 85 is the third, and it simply records what is due. Section 49(8) fixes the order in which a payment is set against liabilities — self-assessed tax and other dues of previous tax periods first, then self-assessed tax and other dues of the current tax period, and only then any other amount payable, including any amount determined under section 73, 74 or 74A. Section 49(10) lets a registered person transfer an amount lying in the cash ledger from one head or major head to another, and from one registration to another registration of the same person having the same Permanent Account Number, by filing FORM GST PMT-09; nothing similar exists for the credit ledger.

citation.ref: Sections 49(1) to 49(4), 49(8) and 49(10), with section 2(82), read with rules 85, 86 and 87 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST PMT-06 and PMT-09

concepts.subsection: Section 17(5)(b) and (h) — Free samples, gifts, and what an employer must provide by law
concepts.statement: Section 17(5) blocks credit in a closed list, and two of its clauses catch ordinary business spending. Clause (h) blocks input tax credit in respect of goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off or disposed of by way of gift or free samples. The words carry two consequences. Giving goods away free is not a supply for want of consideration, so no output tax arises — but the credit taken on those goods has to go, and it goes under clause (h) rather than under any apportionment rule. And a write-off in the books, with no theft and no gift, blocks the credit just as squarely; the clause does not need anything to have gone wrong. Clause (b) blocks credit on food and beverages, outdoor catering, beauty treatment, health services, cosmetic and plastic surgery, leasing or renting or hiring of motor vehicles, vessels and aircraft whose own credit is blocked, life insurance and health insurance, and membership of a club, health and fitness centre, and travel benefits extended to employees on vacation such as leave or home travel concession. The relief inside it is the proviso, and it is where marks are won: input tax credit in respect of such goods or services or both shall be available where it is obligatory for an employer to provide the same to its employees under any law for the time being in force. The test is a legal obligation, not a contractual one and not a company policy — a canteen a factory must run under the Factories Act qualifies, a canteen it chooses to run does not. Clause (b) also allows credit where the inward supply is used for making an outward taxable supply of the same category, or as an element of a taxable composite or mixed supply.

citation.ref: Sections 17(5)(b) with its provisos and 17(5)(h), read with section 7(1)(a) and paragraph 1 of Schedule I

concepts.section: Tax Invoice, Credit and Debit Notes
concepts.subsection: Section 31(3) and rule 55 — Which document goes with which event
concepts.statement: Section 31(3) names a different document for each event, and using the wrong one is a contravention on its own. A registered person supplying exempted goods or services, or paying tax under the composition levy in section 10, issues a bill of supply instead of a tax invoice — rule 49 governs its particulars and it carries no tax. On receipt of an advance payment he issues a receipt voucher, rule 50, evidencing receipt of the payment. Where he has issued a receipt voucher and afterwards no supply is made and no tax invoice is issued, he issues a refund voucher against that payment, rule 51. Where he is liable to pay tax under section 9(3) or section 9(4) he issues an invoice to himself in respect of goods or services received from an unregistered supplier on the date of receipt — the self-invoice under clause (f). And on making payment to that supplier he issues a payment voucher, rule 52, at the time of making the payment. The two documents in the reverse charge case are separate and both are required: the self-invoice records the inward supply, the payment voucher records the money going out. Rule 55 adds the document that is not an invoice at all — a delivery challan, in lieu of an invoice, for the supply of liquid gas where the quantity at the time of removal is not known, for the transportation of goods for job work, for the transportation of goods for reasons other than by way of supply, and in other notified cases, including goods sent in a semi-knocked-down or completely-knocked-down condition where the invoice goes with the first consignment and a delivery challan with each of the rest.

citation.ref: Sections 31(3)(c), 31(3)(d), 31(3)(e), 31(3)(f) and 31(3)(g), read with rules 49, 50, 51, 52 and 55 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 2(117), 37(4) and 39(10) — A valid return, and the order the returns must go in
concepts.statement: Section 2(117) defines a valid return as a return furnished under section 39(1) on which self-assessed tax has been paid in full. The definition carries weight because a return filed without paying the self-assessed tax is not a valid return, and a chain of consequences hangs on the word — most directly the recipient's credit, since section 16(2)(c) and (d) need the tax to have been paid to the Government and the return to have been furnished. The returns then run in a fixed order and each provision locks a door behind it. Section 37(1) requires the details of outward supplies in FORM GSTR-1 for a tax period, and section 37(4) says a registered person shall not be allowed to furnish those details for a tax period if the details for any of the previous tax periods have not been furnished. Rule 59(6) blocks it from the other side — GSTR-1 cannot be furnished where the return in FORM GSTR-3B for the preceding tax period has not been furnished. Section 39(10) closes the loop: a registered person shall not be allowed to furnish a return under section 39 for a tax period if the return for any of the previous tax periods, or the details of outward supplies under section 37 for the said tax period, has not been furnished. So GSTR-1 for a month must precede GSTR-3B for that same month, GSTR-3B for the preceding month must precede GSTR-1 for this one, and nothing can be skipped and picked up later. Section 44 then requires the annual return, which reconciles what the monthly returns said; it does not replace any of them, and filing it does not cure a month that was never filed.

citation.ref: Sections 2(117), 37(1), 37(4), 39(1), 39(7) and 39(10), read with rule 59(6) of the CGST Rules, 2017 and section 16(2)(c)

concepts.subsection: Sections 61 to 64 — Scrutiny, best judgement, the unregistered person and the summary order
concepts.statement: Four sections sit between the return and the demand, and picking the wrong one is the usual error. Section 61 is scrutiny: the proper officer may scrutinise the return and the particulars furnished to verify their correctness, inform the registered person of the discrepancies noticed in FORM GST ASMT-10 and seek his explanation, and where the explanation in ASMT-11 is found acceptable he informs him in ASMT-12 and takes no further action. Where no explanation is furnished within the prescribed period, or the explanation is not satisfactory, or the person does not take corrective measures after accepting the discrepancy, the officer may launch audit under section 65 or 66, inspection under section 67, or proceedings under section 73, 74 or 74A. Section 62 is best judgement assessment and it reaches only a registered person who fails to furnish a return even after a notice under section 46; the officer assesses to the best of his judgement using the material available, and the order stands withdrawn if the person afterwards furnishes a valid return within the period the section allows, though interest and late fee continue. Section 63 is the one for the person outside the net — a taxable person who fails to obtain registration though liable, or whose registration has been cancelled but who was liable to pay tax, may be assessed to the best of the officer's judgement within five years from the date the annual return for the relevant financial year was due, and only after a show cause notice and an opportunity of being heard. Section 64 is summary assessment, allowed only where the officer has evidence of a liability and sufficient grounds to believe that delay will adversely affect the interest of revenue, and only with the previous permission of the Additional Commissioner or Joint Commissioner; section 64(2) lets the taxable person apply within thirty days for it to be withdrawn.

citation.ref: Sections 61, 62, 63 and 64 with section 64(2), read with rules 98 to 100 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORMS GST ASMT-10, ASMT-11 and ASMT-12

concepts.subsection: Sections 78, 79 and 80 — The three months, the six modes of recovery, and instalments
concepts.statement: Section 78 sets the clock. Any amount payable in pursuance of an order passed under the Act shall be paid within three months from the date of service of the order, and if it is not, recovery proceedings shall be initiated. The proviso lets the proper officer require payment within a shorter period, where it is expedient in the interest of revenue, for reasons to be recorded in writing. Section 79 then lists the modes and the officer may proceed by one or more of them. He may deduct the amount from any money owing to the person which is under his control or under the control of any other specified officer. He may detain and sell any goods belonging to the person which are under his control. He may issue a notice in writing to any other person from whom money is due or may become due to the defaulter, or who holds or may hold money for or on account of him, requiring that person to pay — and where that third person fails to comply, he is deemed to be a defaulter in respect of the amount and is liable to be proceeded against himself. He may distrain any movable or immovable property belonging to the person and detain it until the amount is paid, selling it if the amount is not paid within thirty days. He may prepare a certificate and send it to the Collector of the district, who shall recover the amount as an arrear of land revenue. Or he may apply to the appropriate Magistrate, who shall proceed to recover the amount as if it were a fine imposed by him. Section 80 is the safety valve: on an application, the Commissioner may extend the time for payment or allow payment in monthly instalments not exceeding twenty-four months, with interest, but never for the amount due as per the liability self-assessed in any return — and a default in one instalment makes the whole outstanding balance payable at once.

citation.ref: Sections 78 with its proviso, 79(1)(a) to 79(1)(f) with section 79(4), and 80, read with rules 143 to 155 and rule 158 of the CGST Rules, 2017

concepts.subsection: Sections 2(91), 5 and 6 — Who is a proper officer, and the bar on parallel proceedings
concepts.statement: Section 2(91) says a proper officer, in relation to any function to be performed under the Act, means the Commissioner or the officer of the central tax who is assigned that function by the Commissioner in the Board. Two things follow. There is no such thing as "the proper officer" in the abstract — the answer is always relative to a function, and the same officer may be the proper officer for one function and not for another. And the assignment is made by the Commissioner, so the source of an officer's authority is a circular or an order assigning functions, not his rank alone. Section 5 works the powers. Sub-section (1) gives an officer of central tax the powers conferred and duties imposed on him, subject to conditions and limitations. Sub-section (2) lets an officer exercise the powers and discharge the duties conferred or imposed on any other officer of central tax who is subordinate to him — a senior officer may always do what his junior may do, never the reverse.
