concepts.statement: Section 110(1) lets a proper officer who has reason to believe that any goods are liable to confiscation seize them, and where it is not practicable to seize them, order that the owner shall not remove or deal with them without permission. Seizure is a holding step, not a punishment, and the law puts a clock on it. Section 110(2) provides that where no notice under section 124(a) is given within six months of the seizure of the goods, the goods shall be returned to the person from whose possession they were seized. The proviso lets the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs extend that period by a further six months, for reasons to be recorded in writing, and the person concerned must be informed before the original period expires. Miss both and the goods go back by operation of the sub-section, with no application needed. What returning the goods does not do is end the case: the department may still issue a notice and adjudicate confiscation and penalty later, it simply no longer holds the goods while it does. Documents and things seized are governed separately, and section 110A supplies the middle course throughout — pending the order of the adjudicating authority, goods, documents or things seized or bank accounts provisionally attached may be released to the owner on taking a bond, with such security and conditions as the adjudicating authority requires.

citation.ref: Sections 110(1) and 110(2) with the proviso, read with sections 110A and 124

concepts.subsection: Section 26A — Import duty back on goods that were not what was ordered
concepts.statement: Section 26A is the customs answer to a bad delivery. Where imported goods on which duty has been paid and which have been cleared for home consumption are found to be defective, or otherwise not in conformity with the specification agreed upon between the importer and the supplier, the duty is refunded — but the section fences the relief with conditions and each of them is a possible exam point. The goods must not have been worked, repaired or used after importation, except where such use was indispensable to discover the defect or to test whether the goods conform to the specification. The goods must be identified to the satisfaction of the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner as the goods that were imported. The importer must not claim drawback on them. And the goods must be exported, or the importer must relinquish his title to them and abandon them to customs, or they must be destroyed or rendered commercially valueless in the presence of the proper officer, within the period the section allows from the date of clearance, extendable on sufficient cause. The refund claim itself is filed within the further period prescribed. The section does not apply at all to perishable goods, to goods that have exceeded their shelf life or their recommended storage-before-use period, or to goods against which an offence appears to have been committed under the Act or any other law. Distinguish it from section 74, which is drawback on re-export of duty-paid goods generally, and from section 27, which refunds duty paid in excess of what was due.

citation.ref: Section 26A(1) with its provisos and section 26A(3)

concepts.subsection: Sections 128, 129A and 129DD — The three orders the Tribunal cannot hear
concepts.statement: A customs appeal has an ordinary route and an exception, and the exception is the examinable part. The ordinary route — any person aggrieved by a decision or order passed by an officer of customs lower in rank than the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) within sixty days of communication, extendable by a further thirty days on sufficient cause shown; from the Commissioner (Appeals), or from an order passed by a Principal Commissioner or Commissioner as adjudicating authority, an appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal under section 129A. The exception is the first proviso to section 129A(1), which says no appeal shall lie to the Appellate Tribunal in respect of an order relating to any goods imported or exported as baggage, any goods loaded in a conveyance for importation into India but not unloaded at their place of destination or short-landed, or the payment of drawback as provided in Chapter X and the rules made under it. Those three go instead to the Central Government by revision application under section 129DD, filed within three months, and the Central Government's order is the end of that road but for a writ. Beyond the Tribunal, section 130 gives an appeal to the High Court on a substantial question of law, and section 130E an appeal to the Supreme Court — but any question relating to the rate of duty or to the value of goods for assessment goes to the Supreme Court and never to the High Court.

citation.ref: First proviso to section 129A(1), read with sections 128, 129DD, 130 and 130E

concepts.subsection: Social Welfare Surcharge — What it is charged on
concepts.statement: The Social Welfare Surcharge replaced the education cesses on imported goods and is levied by section 110 of the Finance Act, 2018 to finance education, health and social security. Its character decides every question asked about it: it is a surcharge on duty, not a duty on value. The surcharge is calculated at the prescribed rate on the aggregate of duties, taxes and cesses which are levied and collected by the Central Government under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962 and any other law for the time being in force as an addition to, and in the same manner as, a duty of customs — so the assessable value never enters the computation, and where the basic customs duty is nil the surcharge on it is nil too. Three levies are expressly kept out of that base: the integrated tax charged on imports under section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, the goods and services tax compensation cess under section 3(9), and the safeguard, countervailing and anti-dumping duties under sections 8B, 9 and 9A of that Act. The surcharge is collected as a duty of customs, and all the machinery provisions of the Customs Act on refunds, exemptions, interest, recovery and penalties apply to it. Because it is not the integrated tax, it is not creditable — like the basic customs duty it rides on, it is a cost.

citation.ref: Section 110 — Social Welfare Surcharge on imported goods, read with sections 3(7) and 3(9) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

concepts.subsection: Section 7 of the FTDR Act — The Importer-Exporter Code, and who does not need one
concepts.statement: Section 7 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 says that no person shall make any import or export except under an Importer-Exporter Code number granted by the Director General of Foreign Trade or an officer authorised by him. It is the licence to trade across the border and the first thing an exporter obtains, before any scheme, scrip or authorisation. The code is now the Permanent Account Number of the person, issued in the format of an IEC by the DGFT on an online application, so one entity holds one code across all its branches, and the details must be updated electronically every year even where nothing has changed — an IEC not updated is liable to be deactivated. Two classes of person are outside the requirement. A Ministry or department of the Central Government or of a State Government, and other categories the policy notifies, may import and export without one. And goods imported or exported for personal use, not connected with trade, manufacture or agriculture, need no code — which is what lets a traveller bring in a personal effect and a person import equipment for a family member without registering as a trader. Import and export by categories such as notified charitable institutions are similarly relieved. The code is a permission to trade and not a benefit: holding it confers no exemption and no duty concession by itself.

citation.ref: Section 7, read with the Importer-Exporter Code provisions of the Foreign Trade Policy and the exempt categories notified under them

concepts.subsection: Local delivery — out of entry 18 and into section 9(5)
concepts.statement: Two notifications of 17 September 2025, both effective 22 September 2025, moved local delivery in one step. Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) added an Explanation to entry 18 of the exemption notification: the exemption for transportation of goods does not apply to local delivery services provided by an electronic commerce operator, or through one. Notification No. 17/2025-Central Tax (Rate) then added local delivery to the services notified under section 9(5), so the operator pays the tax as if it were the supplier — except where the person supplying through the operator is himself liable for registration under section 22(1), in which case that supplier pays in the ordinary way. Read together: the first instrument decides that the service is taxable at all, and the second decides whose liability it is. A delivery rider below the registration threshold delivering through a platform is the case both were written for.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by Notification No. 17/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025, read with entry 18 of Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Omnibus under section 9(5) — and the company that falls out of it
concepts.statement: Passenger transport by omnibus was notified under section 9(5) with effect from 22 September 2025, and it carries an exception the other passenger-transport entry does not. Where the person supplying the omnibus service through the electronic commerce operator is a company, the tax is not payable by the operator: the company pays it itself. Every other omnibus supplier through a platform leaves the liability with the operator. The radio-taxi entry beside it is drawn the other way — it covers a motorcab, maxicab, motorcycle or any other motor vehicle and expressly excludes an omnibus, so the two entries divide the vehicles between them rather than overlapping. The test is therefore two questions in order: which vehicle, and then, if it is an omnibus, is the supplier a company.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by Notification No. 17/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 16 — Input tax credit conditions
concepts.statement: Input tax credit needs every section 16(2) condition together — a tax invoice, receipt of the goods or services, the detail appearing in GSTR-2B, the tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier, and the return filed. Holding a valid invoice while the supplier has not paid the tax defeats the credit.

citation.ref: Section 16(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 9(3) — Reverse charge
concepts.statement: For notified supplies — legal services from an advocate to a business entity among them — the recipient, not the supplier, is liable to pay the tax, and pays it in cash rather than through input tax credit.

citation.ref: Section 9(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 22 — Registration
concepts.statement: Registration becomes compulsory when aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh for a supplier of services. The ₹40 lakh limit is for suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States, and special category States carry lower limits.

citation.ref: Section 22

concepts.subsection: Section 10 — Composition levy
concepts.statement: A composition taxpayer cannot make inter-State outward supplies of goods. The scheme trades a small turnover-based levy for staying local; crossing the State line with outward supplies forfeits eligibility.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)

concepts.subsection: Customs valuation
concepts.statement: Additions to the transaction value of imported goods include selling commissions, and cost of transport and insurance to the place of importation — but buying commission, paid to the importer's own agent for representing him abroad, is not added.

citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 16(4) — Time limit for input tax credit
concepts.statement: Input tax credit for an invoice cannot be taken after the thirtieth of November following the end of the financial year the invoice belongs to, or the filing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. A valid, eligible credit dies purely of lateness.

citation.ref: Section 16(4)

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Place of supply of goods
concepts.statement: Where a supply involves movement of goods, the place of supply is the location where the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient. Who arranges the transport does not decide it; where the goods end up does.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Time of supply — advances
concepts.statement: An advance received for a supply of services is taxable when received. For goods, suppliers other than composition taxpayers pay tax only on issue of the invoice — advances for goods were taken out of the tax net by notification. The same rupee of advance is taxed on one side of the goods-services line and not the other.

citation.ref: Section 12 and 13, with Notification 66/2017-CT

concepts.subsection: Section 15 — Value of supply
concepts.statement: A discount given after the supply reduces the taxable value only if it was agreed before or at the time of supply and can be linked to the specific invoices, and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. A goodwill discount invented after the event changes the price, not the tax.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)

concepts.subsection: Section 50 — Interest on delayed payment
concepts.statement: Interest on delayed payment of tax runs at 18 per cent, and on the portion paid through the electronic cash ledger it is charged only on that net cash amount where the return is filed late — the credit-covered portion carries no interest. Wrongly availed and utilised credit draws its own interest.

citation.ref: Section 50(1) proviso and 50(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 143 — Job work
concepts.statement: Inputs sent for job work must return, or be supplied from the job worker's premises, within one year; capital goods within three years. Miss the window and the original despatch is deemed a supply from the day the goods went out, with tax and interest reaching back to it.

citation.ref: Section 143(3) and 143(4)

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Zero-rated supply
concepts.statement: Exports and supplies to SEZ units are zero-rated, not exempt: the output carries no tax, yet input tax credit survives. The exporter either supplies under a letter of undertaking without paying tax and claims refund of unutilised credit, or pays IGST and claims refund of the tax paid.

citation.ref: Section 16

concepts.subsection: Rule 138 — E-way bill
concepts.statement: An e-way bill is generated before movement of goods worth more than fifty thousand rupees in a consignment. The obligation attaches to the movement, not the sale — stock transfers, job work despatches and sales returns all need one, and some States set higher intra-State limits.

citation.ref: Rule 138

concepts.section: Offences and Penalties and Ethical Aspects under GST
concepts.subsection: Section 129 — Detention of goods in transit
concepts.statement: Goods moved in contravention — typically without a valid e-way bill or invoice — are detained, and release requires a penalty of two hundred per cent of the tax payable where the owner comes forward. Detention is a transit consequence and runs independently of whether the tax on the supply itself was ever evaded.

citation.ref: Section 129(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Schedule I — Supply without consideration
concepts.statement: Four transactions are supplies even without consideration — permanent transfer of business assets on which credit was taken, supplies between related or distinct persons in business, goods moved through agents who undertake to supply or receive on the principal's behalf, and imported services from a related person for business. Employer gifts to an employee stay out up to fifty thousand rupees a year.

citation.ref: Schedule I

concepts.subsection: Schedule III — Neither goods nor services
concepts.statement: Schedule III lists what GST cannot touch at all — an employee's services to the employer in the course of employment, sale of land and of completed buildings, actionable claims other than specified ones, funeral services, and duties of courts and MPs. These are not exempt supplies; they are not supplies, so they never enter aggregate turnover.

citation.ref: Schedule III

concepts.subsection: Section 54 — Refunds
concepts.statement: A refund claim is filed within two years from the relevant date, and the relevant date moves with the ground of the claim — export shipment dates for goods exported, the date payment lands for export of services, the judgment's date where tax was paid under a later-reversed demand. Miss the window and the money stays with the Government however good the ground was.

citation.ref: Section 54(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 10(2A) — Composition for service providers
concepts.statement: A supplier of services outside the restaurant category, ineligible for the ordinary composition scheme, may opt for the special scheme where aggregate turnover in the preceding year stayed within fifty lakh rupees, paying six per cent. The ordinary scheme's goods-centred gates do not decide this one.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A)

concepts.subsection: Section 17(5) — Blocked credits
concepts.statement: Input tax credit on motor vehicles for transporting persons with seating capacity up to thirteen (including the driver) is blocked — unless the vehicle is used for further supply of such vehicles, transporting passengers, or driving training. Vehicles above thirteen seats and goods-transport vehicles are outside the block, and services of insurance, repair and maintenance follow the vehicle they attach to.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 13 — Time of supply of services
concepts.statement: For services, time of supply is the earlier of invoice and payment where the invoice issues within the thirty-day limit; where it does not, the earlier of the date the service is provided and the payment. The clock decides which tax period the liability lands in — issuing the invoice late does not push the liability later.

citation.ref: Section 13(2)

concepts.subsection: Customs — Duty drawback on re-export
concepts.statement: Section 74 refunds up to ninety-eight per cent of import duty when the imported goods themselves are re-exported within two years, identified as the same goods. Goods that were used before re-export get tapering rates by period of use. Section 75 is the other drawback — for duty on inputs consumed in manufacturing exported goods — and the two never apply to the same claim.

citation.ref: Section 74

concepts.subsection: IGST — Place of supply for immovable property services
concepts.statement: Services directly relating to immovable property — architects, surveyors, engineers, hotel accommodation, letting, construction-linked services — are supplied where the property sits, whatever the locations of supplier and recipient. The property anchors the tax, and if it lies outside India the default recipient-location rule takes over.

citation.ref: Section 12(3)

concepts.subsection: Schedule II — Works contract as a service
concepts.statement: A works contract — a contract for building, construction, fabrication or similar work on immovable property involving transfer of property in goods — is deemed wholly a supply of services by Schedule II. One levy, one classification: the old VAT-plus-service-tax split of a single contract is gone, and works contract input credit has its own restrictions in section 17(5).

citation.ref: Schedule II, para 6(a)

concepts.subsection: Customs valuation — Transaction value
concepts.statement: Customs duty is assessed on transaction value — the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India — plus prescribed additions, at the time and place of importation. A relationship between buyer and seller displaces that price only where it influenced it; a related-party price the importer shows to be at arm's length stands.

citation.ref: Section 14

concepts.subsection: Section 15(2) — Inclusions in value
concepts.statement: The value of supply includes taxes other than GST itself, amounts the supplier was liable to pay but the recipient paid, incidental expenses like packing and commission charged by the supplier, interest or penalty for delayed payment of consideration, and subsidies directly linked to price from anyone other than the Government. Each inclusion widens the base beyond the bare price.

citation.ref: Section 15(2)

concepts.subsection: IGST — Export of services definition
concepts.statement: A service is exported only when all five conditions hold: supplier in India, recipient outside India, place of supply outside India, payment received in convertible foreign exchange (or INR where RBI permits), and supplier and recipient not merely two establishments of one person. Failing any one, the supply is not an export and zero-rating is lost.

citation.ref: Section 2(6)

concepts.section: Tax Invoice, Credit and Debit Notes
concepts.subsection: Section 34 — Credit and debit notes
concepts.statement: A supplier who has charged too much tax — goods returned, deficient supply, price revised down — issues a credit note and reduces output liability, but only up to the thirtieth of November following the financial year of supply (or the annual return, if earlier), and only if the incidence of tax has not been passed to someone who bears it. A commercial credit note without GST can issue any time, adjusting price but not tax.

citation.ref: Section 34(2)

concepts.subsection: IGST on imported goods
concepts.statement: Import of goods is taxed as inter-State supply, but the IGST is levied and collected as customs duty — under the Customs Tariff Act, on the value determined under the Customs Act at the point of importation, together with basic customs duty. The importer generally takes credit of the IGST so paid; basic customs duty is never creditable.

citation.ref: Section 5(1) proviso

concepts.subsection: Section 25 — Distinct persons
concepts.statement: Registrations of one entity in different States are distinct persons, and supplies between them — stock transfers, services of one office to another — are taxable supplies even without consideration, valued under the rules with full input credit typically flowing. One legal person, several taxable persons: the design keeps each State's revenue whole.

citation.ref: Section 25(4) with Schedule I

concepts.subsection: Customs — Pilferage and remission
concepts.statement: Goods pilfered after unloading but before clearance attract no duty from the importer — unless restored — and the custodian pays instead; goods lost or destroyed before clearance earn remission on the Assistant Commissioner's satisfaction, and goods relinquished before clearance drop the duty too. Pilferage is automatic by the section's operation; remission must be sought and shown.

citation.ref: Sections 13 and 23

concepts.subsection: E-commerce — TCS and section 9(5)
concepts.statement: An e-commerce operator collects tax at source on the net value of supplies made through it by others — a collection mechanism, not a levy. For the notified services section 9(5) goes further: the operator is liable to pay the tax as if it were the supplier, and the actual supplier's registration position changes accordingly. TCS and 9(5) never apply to the same supply. Six categories are notified — passenger transport by radio-taxi and similar motor vehicles; passenger transport by omnibus, unless the supplier through the operator is a company, in which case the company pays; accommodation; housekeeping; restaurant service other than at specified premises; and local delivery. Accommodation, housekeeping and local delivery each fall out of section 9(5) where the supplier through the operator is itself liable for registration under section 22(1).

citation.ref: Sections 52 and 9(5), read with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended

concepts.subsection: Exempt, nil-rated, non-taxable and zero-rated
concepts.statement: Four different fates: a nil-rated supply is taxable at zero in the tariff; an exempt supply is freed by notification and includes nil-rated and non-taxable supplies for definition purposes; a non-taxable supply is outside the levy itself, like alcohol for human consumption; zero-rated means exports and SEZ supplies — taxable in principle, taxed at zero, with input credit preserved. Only zero-rating keeps the credit; exemption breaks the credit chain.

citation.ref: Sections 2(47), 2(78) and IGST 16

concepts.subsection: Advance ruling — binding scope
concepts.statement: An advance ruling binds only the applicant who sought it and the jurisdictional officers in respect of that applicant — not other taxpayers, however identical their facts, and not other States' authorities. It holds unless law, facts or circumstances change, and a ruling obtained by fraud or suppression is void from the start. Other taxpayers may read it as persuasive weather, never as shelter.

citation.ref: Section 103

concepts.subsection: Section 51 — Tax deduction at source
concepts.statement: Government departments, local authorities and notified entities deduct tax at source at two per cent from payments to suppliers where a contract's taxable value exceeds two and a half lakh rupees — the deduction tested contract-wise, on value excluding GST. No deduction where the supplier's State and the place of supply differ from the recipient's State. The deductee takes the amount as cash ledger credit, not as input tax.

citation.ref: Section 51

concepts.subsection: Section 54(3) — Refund of unutilised input tax credit
concepts.statement: Accumulated input tax credit is refundable in exactly two cases: zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, and the inverted duty structure — input tax rates exceeding output rates. Credit piling up because sales are slow, or because outputs are exempt, earns no refund; the inverted-structure refund runs on the rule's formula and excludes input services from the computation.

citation.ref: Section 54(3)

concepts.section: Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
concepts.subsection: Customs — Date for rate of duty
concepts.statement: The rate of duty and tariff valuation for imports is taken on the date of filing the bill of entry for home consumption — or, for warehoused goods, the date of the ex-bond bill of entry when the goods leave the warehouse for home consumption. A rate change while goods sit in bond therefore lands on the importer; the vessel's arrival date matters only where the bill was filed in advance.

citation.ref: Section 15(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 24 — Compulsory registration
concepts.statement: Certain persons register regardless of turnover: inter-State taxable suppliers of goods, persons liable under reverse charge, casual taxable persons with no fixed place in the State, non-resident taxable persons, e-commerce operators, TDS deductors, and agents supplying for others. The threshold exemption belongs to section 22; section 24's list overrides it — though inter-State suppliers of services enjoy a notified threshold relaxation the goods side never got.

citation.ref: Section 24

concepts.subsection: Foreign trade policy — EPCG
concepts.statement: The Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme imports capital goods at zero customs duty against an export obligation of six times the duty saved, to be discharged over six years from authorisation — with the goods installed and put to use, and the obligation over and above the average of past exports. Default surrenders proportionate duty with interest; the scheme buys machinery cheap with a promise, and the promise is enforced.

citation.ref: EPCG scheme (export obligation 6x duty saved in 6 years)

concepts.subsection: IGST — Bill-to-ship-to supplies
concepts.statement: Where goods are delivered to one person on the instruction of another, the law sees two supplies: supplier to the instructing buyer, and instructing buyer to the actual recipient — with the first leg's place of supply deemed to be the instructing buyer's principal place of business, wherever the goods physically went. Tax type on each leg follows its own deemed geography, and each leg carries its own invoice.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(b)

concepts.section: Classification of Imported and Export Goods
concepts.subsection: Customs — General rules of interpretation
concepts.statement: Tariff classification walks the General Interpretative Rules in order: headings and their notes first; incomplete articles classify as complete if they have the essential character; mixtures and composites classify by the material giving essential character; and only when goods remain equally classifiable under two headings does the later heading win. The specific description always beats the general one before any tie-breaker is reached.

citation.ref: General Rules for Interpretation 1-4

concepts.subsection: Rule 32(5) — Margin scheme for second-hand goods
concepts.statement: A dealer in second-hand goods, selling them as such after at most minor processing that does not change their nature, may pay GST only on the margin — selling price less purchase price, with a negative margin ignored — provided no input tax credit was taken on the purchase. Buying from unregistered consumers is the scheme's habitat; take credit on the inward side and the whole selling price becomes taxable.

citation.ref: Rule 32(5)

concepts.subsection: Rule 33 — Pure agent
concepts.statement: Costs a supplier incurs as a pure agent of the recipient stay out of the value of supply when every condition holds: the supplier contracts as the recipient's authorised agent for that payment, the recipient alone uses what was procured, the actual amount is separately indicated on the invoice and recovered without markup, and it is in addition to the supplier's own services. Mark it up, or bundle it, and the exclusion is gone.

citation.ref: Rule 33

concepts.subsection: Section 8 — Composite and mixed supplies
concepts.statement: A composite supply bundles naturally — two or more taxable supplies ordinarily supplied together with one principal supply — and takes the principal supply's rate. A mixed supply is an artificial bundle for a single price whose parts could be sold separately, and it takes the highest rate among them. Natural bundling is tested by trade practice: what buyers expect to come together.

citation.ref: Sections 2(30), 2(74) and 8

concepts.subsection: Actionable claims and specified activities
concepts.statement: Actionable claims are goods by definition, yet Schedule III keeps them outside GST — except the specified ones: lottery, betting, gambling, and since the 2023 amendments, online money gaming, which are taxable, valued on their own rules. An unsecured debt assigned, an insurance claim transferred — outside the levy; a lottery ticket sold — squarely inside it.

citation.ref: Schedule III with section 2(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 50(3) — Interest on wrongly availed credit
concepts.statement: Interest on wrongly availed input tax credit runs only where the credit is also utilised — credit that sat unused in the electronic credit ledger until reversal costs nothing. The same mercy governs delayed payment interest under section 50(1): where the return is late but the tax was paid by balance in the cash ledger, interest applies on the portion paid through cash late, computed on the net cash liability. Both rules arrived as retrospective corrections of harsher readings.

citation.ref: Section 50(1) proviso and 50(3)

concepts.subsection: Customs refunds — unjust enrichment
concepts.statement: A customs duty refund is paid to the claimant only on proof that the duty's incidence was not passed on to any other person; otherwise the refund is sanctioned but credited to the Consumer Welfare Fund. The presumption runs against the claimant — passing on is assumed until displaced by evidence such as a chartered accountant's certificate and unchanged prices. Captive consumption and duty paid under protest walk the same test.

citation.ref: Section 27

concepts.subsection: Import of services — reverse charge
concepts.statement: Services imported for business bear IGST in the recipient's hands under reverse charge — the foreign supplier is beyond the levy's practical reach, so the Indian recipient self-assesses, pays in cash, and takes credit where eligible. Import by an individual for personal purposes stays outside as not being in the course of business — except OIDAR services, which are taxed even to consumers with the foreign supplier itself required to register.

citation.ref: Section 5(3) with 2(11)

concepts.subsection: OIDAR services
concepts.statement: Online information and database access or retrieval services — streaming, cloud storage, e-books, online advertising, essentially automated digital delivery with minimal human intervention — are taxed in India even when supplied to unregistered consumers. The foreign supplier (or its appointed person) registers under the simplified scheme and pays; for registered business recipients, ordinary reverse charge applies instead. The 2023 amendments deleted the minimal-human-intervention escape arguments by tightening the definition.

citation.ref: Section 2(17) and 14

concepts.section: Tax Invoice, Credit and Debit Notes
concepts.subsection: E-invoicing
concepts.statement: Registered persons with aggregate annual turnover above five crore rupees (in any year from 2017-18) must report B2B invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an IRN and QR code — without which the invoice is not a valid invoice at all. B2C supplies, and notified exclusions like banks, insurers, GTAs and passenger transporters, stay outside. The e-invoice auto-populates GSTR-1 and travels with the e-way bill system.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4) (₹5 crore threshold from 1 August 2023)

concepts.subsection: FTP — Advance authorisation
concepts.statement: Advance authorisation imports inputs duty-free for physical incorporation in export products, on actual user condition — the inputs and the resulting goods cannot be sold domestically until the export obligation is discharged. The scheme demands minimum value addition (generally fifteen per cent) and export within the specified period, with inputs quantified by standard input-output norms or self-declaration. It frees inputs; EPCG frees capital goods — parallel schemes, different subject matter.

citation.ref: Advance Authorisation scheme

concepts.subsection: Goods transport agencies — the two routes
concepts.statement: A GTA's services are taxed one of two ways: reverse charge at five per cent paid by the specified recipient with the GTA taking no input credit, or forward charge by the GTA's own annual declared option — at five per cent without credit or eighteen per cent with full credit. The credit-preserving rate was twelve per cent until 21 September 2025 and became eighteen per cent on 22 September 2025, when the twelve per cent slab went. Services to unregistered persons largely ride exemptions. The declaration binds for the financial year; recipients must know which regime their transporter elected, since the liability moves with it.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with the notified GTA options, the forward-charge rate with credit raised to eighteen per cent by Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — concurrent audit, its appointment and its reporting
concepts.statement: Concurrent audit is the examination of a bank's transactions as they happen or as near to it as possible, and it is treated as part of the bank's early warning system rather than as a second statutory audit. Four things about it are examinable and none of them is about technique. Its scope and the coverage of business and branches are left to the discretion of the head of internal audit with the due prior approval of the Audit Committee of the Board, and risk sensitive areas identified by the bank's own business model must be brought inside it. Who does it is the bank's choice between its own officials and external auditors; where its own officials are used they must be experienced, well trained and sufficiently senior, and they must be independent of the branch being audited. How long they may do it is fixed at two levels: the Audit Committee of the Board decides the maximum tenure of external concurrent auditors, which generally is not more than five years on a continuous basis with the bank, and no concurrent auditor may continue with a branch or business unit for more than three years. And where the findings go is fixed too — major deficiencies go at once to the branch and the controlling office in a special note, a quarterly review of key features goes before the Audit Committee of the Board along with zone-wise reporting and an annual appraisal of the system, minor irregularities are rectified in a timely manner while serious ones go to the controlling or head offices for immediate action, and a fraudulent transaction is reported immediately to the Inspection and Audit Department at head office, to the Chief Vigilance Officer and to the branch managers concerned, unless the branch manager is himself involved. Where an external firm is appointed and serious acts of omission or commission are noticed in its working, the appointment may be cancelled and the fact reported to the Reserve Bank and to the Institute. Terms of appointment and remuneration of external firms are fixed by the Audit Committee of the Board, and the bank reviews the effectiveness of the whole system once a year.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — concurrent audit: the scope left to the head of internal audit with the prior approval of the Audit Committee of the Board, the choice between the bank's own officials and external auditors, the maximum tenure of five years with the bank and three years with a branch or business unit, the quarterly review and zone-wise reporting to the Audit Committee, and the immediate reporting of fraudulent transactions to the Inspection and Audit Department, the Chief Vigilance Officer and the branch managers concerned

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 200 — audit risk and its three components
concepts.statement: Audit risk is the risk of expressing an inappropriate audit opinion on financial statements that are materially misstated, and it is the product of three separate risks. Inherent risk is the susceptibility of an assertion to a misstatement that could be material, individually or when aggregated with others, assuming there are no related controls; it is addressed both at the financial statement level and at the assertion level. Control risk is the risk that the entity's system of internal control will not prevent, or detect and correct on a timely basis, a misstatement that could be material, and some control risk will always exist because every system of internal control has inherent limitations. Detection risk is the risk that the auditor will not detect a misstatement that exists, and it is the only one of the three the auditor controls; it arises from selecting an inappropriate audit procedure, from misapplying an appropriate one, and from misinterpreting the results of one. The relationships are fixed. Audit risk is inherent risk multiplied by control risk multiplied by detection risk. Inherent risk and control risk together are the risk of material misstatement, which is the risk that the statements are misstated before the audit begins and which exists independently of the audit. Audit risk is therefore the risk of material misstatement multiplied by detection risk, and the acceptable level of detection risk for a given level of audit risk bears an inverse relationship to the assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level — the higher the assessed risk, the less detection risk the auditor may accept and the more persuasive the evidence he must obtain. Audit materiality is also inversely related to audit risk.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — audit risk as the product of inherent risk, control risk and detection risk, the risk of material misstatement as inherent risk multiplied by control risk, the inverse relationship between the combined inherent and control risk and detection risk, and the inverse relationship between audit materiality and audit risk

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — assertions and the two levels at which risk is assessed
concepts.statement: Assertions are the representations by management, explicit or otherwise, that are embodied in the financial statements, and the auditor uses them to consider the different types of potential misstatement that may occur. They fall into three categories and the names are not interchangeable. About classes of transactions and events for the period under audit there are five — occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cut-off and classification. About account balances at the period end there are four — existence, rights and obligations, completeness, and valuation and allocation. About presentation and disclosure there are four — occurrence and rights and obligations, completeness, classification and understandability, and accuracy and valuation. Separately, risk is assessed at two levels, and the difference decides what the auditor does about it. A risk at the overall financial statement level relates pervasively to the statements as a whole and potentially affects many assertions, so it is answered by an overall response rather than by a procedure on one balance; an incompetent chief accountant is the standard example, because the errors that follow will not be confined to one balance or to one assertion. A risk at the assertion level is identified with a particular class of transactions, account balance or disclosure, and an assessment is made for each individual assertion — the valuation of payables may be a low risk in the same audit in which the valuation of obsolescent inventory is a high one.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the three categories of assertions used by the auditor and the assertions named in each, and the difference between assessing the risks of material misstatement at the overall financial statement level and at the assertion level

concepts.subsection: SA 300 — the audit programme, how it is drawn up and when it is altered
concepts.statement: The audit programme is the document that allocates work to the members of the engagement team. It contains the audit objectives for each area and enough detail to serve both as a set of instructions to the assistants and as a means of controlling the proper execution of the work, and spelling out the objective for each area is what links the procedures to a purpose. Six matters are considered in formulating it: the nature of the business the organisation is engaged in, the overall plan, the system of internal control and the accounting procedures, the size of the organisation and the structure of its management, information about the organisation of the business, and the accounting and management policies followed. The overall plan governs — if drawing the programme makes a divergence from the overall plan necessary, the plan is modified first and only then is the specific matter taken into the programme. On a first appointment the programme is developed in three stages: a broad outline is drawn up to begin with; the details are filled in after the internal and accounting procedures have been reviewed, on a consideration of the deficiencies in the system of internal control; and after the detailed checking procedure is over the extent of the special first-time and opening balance procedures is determined. At each subsequent engagement the programme is reviewed and modified on account of the experience gained during previous audits, important changes in the business, and the evaluation of internal control made for the current year. Four circumstances in particular force an alteration during the audit: the volume of turnover has substantially increased beyond what the procedures were designed for, or there have been significant changes in the accounting organisation, procedures or personnel; it is discovered that the internal control procedures were not as effective as assumed when the programme was framed; there has been an extraordinary increase in book debts or in the value of stocks compared with the previous year; and a suspicion has arisen, or information has been received, that assets have been misappropriated.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — formulating an audit programme and the matters to be considered, the three stages in which a programme is developed on a first appointment, the grounds on which it is reviewed and modified at each subsequent engagement, and the circumstances in which it has to be suitably altered during the audit

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: SA 265 — the letter of weakness and what it does not excuse
concepts.statement: The letter of weakness, also called the management letter, is how the auditor communicates deficiencies in internal control in writing. Four things are said about it and they pull in different directions. It lists the areas of weakness in the system and offers suggestions for improvement. It must clearly indicate that it discusses only the weaknesses that came to the auditor's attention as a result of his audit, and that his examination was not designed to determine the adequacy of internal control for management's own purposes. It serves as a reference document management can use to revise the system and to insist on its strict implementation. And it may serve to minimise the auditor's legal liability in the event of a major defalcation or other loss resulting from a weakness in internal control — in one reported case an auditor was acquitted of a charge of negligence over an employee's fraud precisely because he had already informed the client about the unsatisfactory state of specific areas and had suggested improvements that the management did not act upon. But the letter is not a substitute for the report. By writing to the management about the weaknesses in the system the auditor is not absolved from his duty to report the shortcomings in the accounts by way of qualification where the defects have not been corrected to his satisfaction, weighing the materiality of the weaknesses and their impact.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the letter of weakness: what it lists, the statement it must carry that it discusses only weaknesses noticed during the audit and that the examination was not designed to determine the adequacy of internal control for management, its value as a reference document and in minimising legal liability, and the rule that writing it does not absolve the auditor from qualifying the report where the defects are uncorrected

concepts.subsection: SA 570 (Revised) — the additional procedures and the cash flow forecast
concepts.statement: Where events or conditions have been identified that may cast significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence to determine whether a material uncertainty exists, and he does it by performing additional audit procedures including a consideration of mitigating factors. The module's list is the examinable one: analysing and discussing cash flow, profit and other relevant forecasts with management; analysing and discussing the entity's latest available interim financial statements; reading the terms of loan agreements and determining whether any have been breached; reading the minutes of meetings of shareholders, those charged with governance and the relevant committees for reference to financing difficulties; inquiring of the entity's legal counsel about litigation and claims and the reasonableness of management's assessment of their outcome and financial implications; confirming the existence, legality and enforceability of arrangements to provide or maintain financial support with related and third parties, and assessing the financial ability of those parties to provide additional funds; performing procedures on subsequent events that either mitigate or otherwise affect the ability to continue; confirming the existence, terms and adequacy of borrowing facilities; requesting management to make its assessment where it has not yet done so; and evaluating management's plans for future action, whether their outcome is likely to improve the situation and whether they are feasible in the circumstances. Where the entity has prepared a cash flow forecast and the analysis of that forecast is a significant factor in considering the future outcome, the auditor does two specific things — he evaluates the reliability of the underlying data generated to prepare the forecast, and he determines whether there is adequate support for the assumptions underlying it. Where management is unwilling to make or to extend its assessment, the auditor considers the implications for his report. And where approval of the financial statements is delayed, he inquires into the reasons and, if he believes the delay relates to the going concern events or conditions, performs the additional procedures and considers the effect on his conclusion.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — the additional audit procedures where events or conditions casting significant doubt on the ability to continue as a going concern have been identified, the two things done where a cash flow forecast has been prepared, the position where management is unwilling to make or extend its assessment, and the inquiry into a delay in the approval of the financial statements

concepts.subsection: SA 600 — acceptance as principal auditor and the other auditor's competence
concepts.statement: Before accepting the work as principal auditor, the auditor considers four matters: the materiality of the portion of the financial information which he himself audits; his own degree of knowledge regarding the business of the components; the risk of material misstatement in the financial information of the components audited by the other auditors; and the performance of the additional procedures the Standard sets out regarding those components, which may result in his having significant participation in that audit. Two further points govern the relationship afterwards. Where the statute confers on him a right to visit a component and examine its books and records, and another auditor has been appointed for that component, the principal auditor would normally be entitled to rely upon the work of that auditor unless there are special circumstances that make a visit or an examination essential. And when planning to use the work of another auditor he should consider the other auditor's professional competence in the context of the specific assignment if the other auditor is not a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India — the other auditor may in some circumstances not be a professionally qualified auditor at all, as where a component is in a foreign country whose law permits it. The documentation runs the same way: the principal auditor documents the components audited by other auditors, the procedures performed and the conclusions reached, and the results of his discussions and of his review of the written summary of the other auditor's procedures, but he need not document the reasons for limiting his procedures where he has previously obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence that acceptable quality control policies and procedures are complied with in the conduct of the other auditor's practice.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — acceptance as principal auditor and the four matters considered, the right to visit and examine the books of a component and the entitlement to rely on the component's auditor absent special circumstances, the consideration of the professional competence of an other auditor who is not a member of the Institute, and the documentation requirement with its exception where quality control compliance has been established

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — deciding whether an auditor's expert is needed at all
concepts.statement: SA 620's first question is not how to use an expert but whether to use one. An auditor who is not an expert in a relevant field other than accounting or auditing may nevertheless be able to obtain a sufficient understanding of that field to perform the audit without an auditor's expert, and the understanding may come from experience in auditing entities that require such expertise, from education or professional development in the field including formal courses, or from discussion with auditors who have performed similar engagements. Such a discussion is a different thing from consultation with an auditor's expert about a specific set of circumstances on the engagement, where the expert is given all the relevant facts so that he can give informed advice on the particular matter. Where the auditor does decide he needs one, the considerations include whether management has used a management's expert in preparing the financial statements, the nature and significance of the matter including its complexity, the risks of material misstatement in it, and the expected nature of the procedures to respond to the identified risks together with the availability of alternative sources of audit evidence. An expert may be needed to help with obtaining an understanding of the entity and its internal control, identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement, determining and implementing overall responses at the financial statement level, designing and performing further audit procedures at the assertion level, or evaluating the sufficiency and appropriateness of the evidence obtained. The nature, timing and extent of the auditor's own procedures on the expert's work turn on the nature of the matter, the risk of material misstatement in it, the significance of the expert's work in the context of the audit, the auditor's knowledge of and experience with that expert's previous work, and whether that expert is subject to the firm's quality control policies and procedures. Four things in particular suggest the need for different or more extensive procedures: the work relates to a significant matter involving subjective and complex judgments; the auditor has not previously used that expert and has no prior knowledge of his competence, capabilities and objectivity; the expert is performing procedures integral to the audit rather than being consulted for advice on an individual matter; and the expert is an external expert and is therefore not subject to the firm's quality control policies and procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — determining the need for an auditor's expert, the ways in which an auditor who is not an expert may obtain a sufficient understanding of the field without one, the considerations when deciding whether to use an expert, the matters governing the nature, timing and extent of the auditor's procedures, and the four factors suggesting more extensive procedures

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — a report whose wording is prescribed, and a report under two sets of standards
concepts.statement: Two situations take the auditor's report out of the layout SA 700 (Revised) itself sets out, and in both the question is the same: may the report still say the audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing? Where law or regulation applicable to the entity requires a specific layout or wording, the report may refer to the Standards on Auditing only if it includes, at a minimum, each of thirteen elements — a title; an addressee as required by the circumstances of the engagement; an Opinion section containing an expression of opinion on the financial statements and a reference to the applicable financial reporting framework used to prepare them; an identification of the entity's financial statements that have been audited; a statement that the auditor is independent of the entity in accordance with the relevant ethical requirements relating to the audit and has fulfilled his other ethical responsibilities, which refers to the Code of Ethics issued by ICAI; where applicable a section addressing and not inconsistent with the reporting requirements of SA 570; where applicable a Basis for Qualified or Adverse Opinion section; where applicable a section including the information required by SA 701 or additional information about the audit prescribed by law that is not inconsistent with it; a description of management's responsibilities together with an identification of those responsible for the oversight of the financial reporting process; a reference to the Standards on Auditing and to the law or regulation with a description of the auditor's responsibilities; the auditor's signature; the place of signature; and the date. What is not on the list is as examinable as what is: the Other Information section, the location of the description of the auditor's responsibilities and the other reporting responsibilities section are all absent from it. The second situation is an audit conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing and also the International Standards on Auditing or the auditing standards of another jurisdiction. The report may refer to both only if there is no conflict between the two sets of requirements that would lead the auditor to form a different opinion, or not to include an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph that in the circumstances is required by the Standards on Auditing; and only if the report includes at a minimum each of the same thirteen elements. Where the report does refer to both, it clearly identifies them, including the jurisdiction of origin of the other auditing standards.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 700 (Revised): an auditor's report prescribed by law or regulation may refer to the Standards on Auditing only if it carries the thirteen listed minimum elements, and a report on an audit conducted in accordance with both the Standards on Auditing and the International Standards on Auditing or the standards of another jurisdiction may refer to both only where no conflict would lead the auditor to a different opinion or to omitting a required Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — supplementary information presented with the financial statements
concepts.statement: Information not required by the applicable financial reporting framework is often printed alongside the audited financial statements, and SA 700 (Revised) makes the auditor decide whether his opinion covers it. He evaluates whether, in his professional judgement, the supplementary information is nevertheless an integral part of the financial statements because of its nature or because of how it is presented. Where it is an integral part, it shall be covered by the auditor's opinion, and no label saying otherwise changes that. Where it is not an integral part, he evaluates whether it is presented in a way that sufficiently and clearly differentiates it from the audited financial statements; if it is not, he asks management to change how the unaudited supplementary information is presented, and if management refuses he identifies the unaudited supplementary information and explains in his report that it has not been audited. The module's two examples are the ones to hold. A note to the financial statements explaining or reconciling the extent to which the financial statements comply with another financial reporting framework may be supplementary information that cannot be clearly differentiated from them, and the opinion would also cover notes or supplementary schedules that are cross-referenced from the financial statements. An additional profit and loss account disclosing specific items of expenditure, presented as a separate schedule included as an appendix, may be supplementary information that can be clearly differentiated from them.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 700 (Revised): supplementary information not required by the applicable financial reporting framework that is an integral part of the financial statements by its nature or by how it is presented shall be covered by the auditor's opinion, and where it is not an integral part but is not sufficiently and clearly differentiated the auditor asks management to change the presentation and, on refusal, identifies it and explains in his report that it has not been audited

concepts.subsection: SA 710 — comparative financial statements, and an opinion that has changed
concepts.statement: SA 710 offers two approaches and the reporting consequences are opposite. Under corresponding figures the auditor's opinion on the financial statements refers to the current period only. Under comparative financial statements the auditor's opinion refers to each period for which financial statements are presented, and that is what makes the prior period live again. Two rules follow from it. When reporting on the current period's audit, if the auditor's opinion on the prior period financial statements differs from the opinion he previously expressed on them, he shall disclose the substantive reasons for the different opinion in an Other Matter paragraph in his report — the changed opinion goes in the opinion, the reasons for the change go in the paragraph. And if he concludes that a material misstatement is present in previously audited figures on which a predecessor auditor reported, he shall report it to the appropriate level of management and request that the predecessor auditor be informed; if the prior period statements are then amended and the predecessor auditor agrees to issue a new report on them, the auditor shall report only on the current period. The treatment common to both approaches is unchanged: where the prior period was audited by a predecessor auditor and the auditor is permitted to refer to that report, he states the fact, the type of opinion the predecessor expressed and the date of that report; where the prior period was not audited at all, he says so, and saying so does not relieve him of obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the opening balances contain no misstatement materially affecting the current period.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 710: with comparative financial statements the auditor's opinion refers to each period presented; where the opinion on the prior period differs from the opinion previously expressed the substantive reasons are disclosed in an Other Matter paragraph; and where a material misstatement is found in previously audited figures the auditor reports it to management and requests that the predecessor auditor be informed, reporting only on the current period if the prior statements are amended and the predecessor issues a new report

concepts.subsection: SA 720 (Revised) — the contents of the Other Information section
concepts.statement: Whether the Other Information section appears at all is one question; what goes inside it is another, and SA 720 (Revised) fixes five things. The section shall include a statement that management is responsible for the other information; an identification of the other information, if any, obtained by the auditor prior to the date of his report and, for an audit of the financial statements of a listed entity, of the other information, if any, expected to be obtained after the date of his report; a statement that the auditor's opinion does not cover the other information and that accordingly he does not express, or will not express, an audit opinion or any form of assurance conclusion on it; a description of the auditor's responsibilities relating to reading, considering and reporting on the other information as required by the standard; and, where other information has been obtained prior to the date of the report, either a statement that the auditor has nothing to report or, where he has concluded that there is an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information, a statement that describes it. Where the auditor expresses a qualified or adverse opinion under SA 705 (Revised), he considers the implications of the matter giving rise to the modification for that statement. And where law or regulation requires him to refer to the other information using a specific layout or wording, the report may refer to the Standards on Auditing only if it includes at a minimum three things: an identification of the other information obtained prior to the date of the report, a description of the auditor's responsibilities with respect to it, and an explicit statement addressing the outcome of the auditor's work for this purpose.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — SA 720 (Revised): the five contents of the Other Information section, and the three elements a report must carry at a minimum where law or regulation prescribes the layout or wording of the reference to other information

concepts.subsection: SA 800 — planning a special purpose audit, and describing the framework in the report
concepts.statement: Between accepting a special purpose engagement and writing the alert, SA 800 makes three adjustments that are routinely missed. On materiality, SA 320's judgements about what is material to users are ordinarily based on the common financial information needs of users as a group; in an audit of special purpose financial statements those judgements are based on the financial information needs of the intended users. And where management has agreed with the intended users on a threshold below which misstatements identified during the audit will not be corrected or otherwise adjusted, the existence of that threshold does not relieve the auditor from the requirement to determine materiality in accordance with SA 320 for the purpose of planning and performing the audit. On communication, SA 260 (Revised) requires the auditor to determine the appropriate persons within the entity's governance structure with whom to communicate, and where the entity also prepares a complete set of general purpose financial statements, those responsible for the oversight of the special purpose financial statements may not be the same as those charged with governance responsible for the oversight of the general purpose ones. On the report, the auditor's report shall describe the purpose for which the financial statements are prepared and, if necessary, the intended users, or refer to a note in the special purpose financial statements that contains that information; and if management has a choice of financial reporting frameworks, the explanation of management's responsibility shall also refer to its responsibility for determining that the applicable financial reporting framework is acceptable in the circumstances. Where the auditor also considers it appropriate to indicate that his report is intended solely for the specific users, the paragraph alerting readers may be expanded to include those other matters and the heading modified accordingly.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 800: materiality judgements based on the financial information needs of the intended users and an agreed correction threshold that does not relieve the auditor of determining materiality under SA 320; the persons responsible for oversight of the special purpose financial statements who may not be those charged with governance for the general purpose statements; the report describing the purpose and the intended users and management's responsibility for determining the framework is acceptable; and the alerting paragraph expanded, with the heading modified, to restrict distribution or use

concepts.subsection: SA 805 — accepting and planning an audit of a single financial statement or a specific element
concepts.statement: SA 805 asks a question before it asks anything else: is an audit of this in accordance with the Standards on Auditing practicable at all? SA 200 requires the auditor to comply with all SAs relevant to the audit, and that applies whether or not he is also engaged to audit the entity's complete set of financial statements — so where he is not, he shall determine whether the audit of the single financial statement or of the specific element in accordance with the SAs is practicable. It may not be, and the standard says why: he often does not have the same understanding of the entity and its environment, including its internal control, as an auditor who also audits the complete set; he does not have audit evidence about the general quality of the accounting records or other accounting information that such an audit would acquire; he may therefore need further evidence to corroborate audit evidence acquired from the accounting records; and in the case of a specific element certain SAs require audit work that may be disproportionate to the element being audited. If he concludes it may not be practicable, he may discuss with management whether another type of engagement might be more practicable. Acceptability of the financial reporting framework is decided on the same narrow ground: whether applying it will result in a presentation that provides adequate disclosures to enable the intended users to understand the information conveyed in the financial statement or the element, and the effect of material transactions and events on it. In planning and performing the audit he adapts all relevant SAs. Where he audits the element alongside the complete set he may use audit evidence obtained in that audit, but the SAs still require him to plan and perform the audit of the element to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on which to base the opinion on it. Because the statements and many of the elements, including their notes, are interrelated, he may not be able to consider the element in isolation and may need to perform procedures on the interrelated items. And the materiality determined for the element may be lower than that for the complete set, which affects the nature, timing and extent of the procedures and the evaluation of uncorrected misstatements.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 805: determining whether an audit in accordance with the SAs is practicable where the auditor is not also engaged on the complete set, the acceptability of the framework turning on adequate disclosures to the intended users, the use of evidence from the audit of the complete set without displacing the requirement to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on the element, the interrelated items, and materiality for the element which may be lower than for the complete set

concepts.subsection: SA 810 — the report on summary financial statements, its date, and auditor association
concepts.statement: The report on summary financial statements is short and almost every line of it is prescribed. Its introductory paragraph identifies the summary financial statements on which the auditor is reporting including the title of each statement; identifies the audited financial statements; refers to the auditor's report on those statements, the date of that report and, where that report carried no modification, Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph, the fact that an unmodified opinion was expressed; states, if the report on the summary is dated later than the report on the audited financial statements, that the summary financial statements and the audited financial statements do not reflect the effects of events that occurred subsequent to the date of the report on the audited financial statements; and states that the summary financial statements do not contain all the disclosures required by the financial reporting framework applied in the preparation of the audited financial statements and that reading them is not a substitute for reading the audited financial statements. The addressee gets its own rule: where the addressee of the summary financial statements is not the same as the addressee of the report on the audited financial statements, the auditor evaluates the appropriateness of using a different addressee, having regard to the terms of the engagement, the nature of the entity and the purpose of the summary. The report is dated no earlier than the later of two dates — the date on which the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate evidence on which to base the opinion, including evidence that the summary financial statements have been prepared and that those with the recognised authority have asserted that they have taken responsibility for them, and the date of the auditor's report on the audited financial statements. Association is the last requirement and it works in two directions. Where the entity plans to state in a document containing the summary financial statements that the auditor has reported on them but does not plan to include his report, he requests management to include it, and if management does not, he determines and carries out other appropriate actions designed to prevent management from inappropriately associating him with the summary financial statements in that document. Where he was engaged to report on the financial statements but not on the summary, and the entity plans to refer to him and to the fact that the summary is derived from statements he audited, he must be satisfied that the reference is made in the context of his report on the audited financial statements and that the statement does not give the impression that he has reported on the summary; if not, he requests management to change the statement or not to refer to him, and if management does neither he advises management that he disagrees with the reference and carries out other appropriate actions to prevent an inappropriate reference.

citation.ref: Ch. Specialised Areas — SA 810: the elements of the auditor's report on summary financial statements including the statement required where that report is dated later than the report on the audited financial statements, the report dated no earlier than the later of the date evidence was obtained on the summary and the date of the report on the audited financial statements, and the auditor association requirements where the entity refers to the auditor without including his report

concepts.subsection: SRS 4400 — agreeing the terms of an agreed-upon procedures engagement
concepts.statement: An agreed-upon procedures engagement is defined by what was agreed, so SRS 4400 spends its opening on the agreement. The auditor should ensure with representatives of the entity and, ordinarily, the other specified parties who will receive copies of the report of factual findings, that there is a clear understanding regarding the agreed procedures and the conditions of the engagement. Five matters are to be agreed: the nature of the engagement, including the fact that the procedures performed will not constitute an audit or a review and that accordingly no assurance will be expressed; the stated purpose for the engagement; the identification of the financial information to which the agreed-upon procedures will be applied; the nature, timing and extent of the specific procedures to be applied; and the limitations on distribution of the report of factual findings — and where such a limitation would be in conflict with the legal requirements, if any, the auditor would not accept the engagement. It is in the interests of both the client and the auditor that the auditor sends an engagement letter documenting the key terms of the appointment: it confirms his acceptance of the appointment and helps avoid misunderstanding about the objectives and scope of the engagement, the extent of his responsibilities and the form of reports to be issued, and it includes a listing of the procedures to be performed as agreed between the parties and a statement that distribution of the report of factual findings would be restricted to the specified parties who have agreed to the procedures. The procedures applied may include inquiry and analysis; recomputation, comparison and other clerical accuracy checks; observation; inspection; and obtaining confirmations. The report of factual findings is addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority. A person performing related services need not necessarily be the auditor of the entity's financial statements.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4400: the five matters to be agreed including limitations on distribution, with the auditor not accepting the engagement where such a limitation would conflict with legal requirements; the matters included in the engagement letter; the procedures that may be applied; and the report of factual findings addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority

concepts.subsection: SRS 4410 — what a compilation engagement is, and the terms it cannot begin without
concepts.statement: SRS 4410 deals with the practitioner's responsibilities when engaged to assist management with the preparation and presentation of historical financial information without obtaining any assurance on that information, and to report on the engagement. A compilation engagement is one in which a practitioner applies accounting and financial reporting expertise to assist management in the preparation and presentation of financial information of an entity in accordance with an applicable financial reporting framework, and issues a report. It is not an assurance engagement: it does not require the practitioner to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management for the compilation, or otherwise to gather evidence to express an audit opinion or a review conclusion. Management retains responsibility for the financial information and for the basis on which it is prepared and presented, including the judgement required for its preparation, the selection and application of appropriate accounting policies and, where needed, the development of reasonable accounting estimates. Because it is a non-assurance engagement the independence requirements do not apply, although laws or regulations may specify requirements or disclosure rules pertaining to independence; the relevant ethical requirements do apply, and threats to compliance with them are identified and appropriately addressed. SQC 1 applies to the firm in respect of its compilation engagements, because it applies to all Engagement Standards.
