Acceptance is conditional: the practitioner shall not accept the engagement unless he has agreed the terms of engagement with management, and the engaging party if different, including the intended use and distribution of the financial information and any restrictions on either; the identification of the applicable financial reporting framework; the objective and scope of the engagement; the responsibilities of the practitioner including the requirement to comply with relevant ethical requirements; the responsibilities of management for the financial information and its preparation and presentation under an acceptable framework, for such internal control as management determines is necessary, for the accuracy and completeness of the records, documents, explanations and other information provided, and for the judgements needed in preparing and presenting the information; and the expected form and content of the practitioner's report. The agreed terms are recorded in an engagement letter or other suitable form of written agreement prior to performing the engagement.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement and does not require the practitioner to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management, management retains responsibility for the information and its basis, independence requirements do not apply unless law or regulation specifies them, and the engagement shall not be accepted unless the listed terms are agreed and recorded in an engagement letter or other written agreement before the engagement is performed

concepts.subsection: SRS 4410 — proposing amendments, withdrawing, and the practitioner's report
concepts.statement: A compilation engagement gives the practitioner no opinion to modify, so everything he can do about a defect he does before the report is issued. He obtains an understanding of the entity's business and operations, including its accounting system and accounting records, and of the applicable financial reporting framework including its application in the entity's industry; he compiles the information using the records, documents, explanations and other information, including significant judgements, provided by management; he discusses with management or those charged with governance the significant judgements for which he has provided assistance; and prior to completion he reads the compiled financial information in the light of his understanding. Where what management has provided is incomplete, inaccurate or otherwise unsatisfactory, he brings that to management's attention and requests the additional or corrected information; where he is unable to complete the engagement because management has failed to provide it, he withdraws from the engagement and informs management and those charged with governance of the reasons. Where he becomes aware that the compiled financial information does not adequately refer to or describe the applicable financial reporting framework, that amendments are required for it not to be materially misstated, or that it is otherwise misleading, he proposes the appropriate amendments to management; if management declines or does not permit them, he withdraws and informs management and those charged with governance of the reasons; and if withdrawal is not possible he determines the professional and legal responsibilities applicable in the circumstances. He obtains an acknowledgement from management or those charged with governance that they have taken responsibility for the final version of the compiled financial information. The report is in writing and is not a vehicle to express an opinion or conclusion in any form. It carries the title; the addressee as required by the terms of the engagement; a statement that the practitioner has compiled the financial information based on information provided by management; a description of management's responsibilities; the identification of the applicable financial reporting framework and, where a special purpose framework is used, a description of it or a reference to its description; the identification of the financial information including the title of each element and the date or period; a description of the practitioner's responsibilities, including that the engagement was performed in accordance with the standard and that he has complied with relevant ethical requirements; a description of what a compilation engagement entails; explanations that since a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement the practitioner is not required to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management and that accordingly he does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion on whether the financial information is prepared in accordance with the applicable framework; where a special purpose framework is used, an explanatory paragraph describing the purpose for which the information is prepared and, if necessary, the intended users, or referring to a note that discloses it, and drawing readers' attention to the fact that the information is prepared in accordance with a special purpose framework and may not be suitable for other purposes; the date of the report; the practitioner's signature; and the place of signature. The documentation holds the significant matters arising and how they were addressed, a record of how the compiled financial information reconciles with the underlying records, documents, explanations and other information provided by management, and a copy of the final version of the compiled information for which responsibility was acknowledged together with the practitioner's report.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: proposing amendments where the compiled information does not adequately describe the framework, requires amendment not to be materially misstated or is otherwise misleading, withdrawing and informing management and those charged with governance where amendments are declined or where management fails to provide what was requested, the elements of the practitioner's report including the two explanations and the special purpose framework paragraph, and the three documentation requirements

concepts.subsection: SRE 2400 (Revised) — the factors against acceptance, and the preconditions
concepts.statement: SRE 2400 (Revised) applies where the practitioner performing the review is not the auditor of the entity's financial statements, and it keeps two separate gates in front of the engagement. The first is a list of circumstances in which, unless required by law or regulation, he shall not accept the engagement at all. He shall not accept it if he is not satisfied that there is a rational purpose for the engagement — and it may be unlikely that there is one where there is a significant limitation on the scope of work, where he suspects association of his name with the financial statements in an inappropriate manner, or where the engagement is intended to meet compliance requirements of a law or regulation that requires the financial statements to be audited. He shall not accept it if he is not satisfied that a review engagement would be appropriate in the circumstances; where it would not be, he may recommend another type of engagement, an audit where that is more appropriate, or, where the circumstances preclude an assurance engagement altogether, a compilation or other accounting services engagement. He shall not accept it if he has reason to believe that relevant ethical requirements, including independence, will not be satisfied; if his preliminary understanding indicates that the information needed to perform the review is likely to be unavailable or unreliable; if he has cause to doubt management's integrity such that it is likely to affect proper performance of the review; or if management or those charged with governance impose a limitation on the scope of his work in the terms of the proposed engagement such that he believes it will result in his disclaiming a conclusion. The second gate is the preconditions. Before accepting, he shall determine whether the financial reporting framework applied is acceptable, including, for special purpose financial statements, obtaining an understanding of the purpose for which they are prepared and of the intended users; and he shall obtain management's agreement that it acknowledges and understands its responsibilities for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with that framework, for such internal control as is necessary to enable their preparation free from material misstatement, and to provide him with access to all relevant information, with additional information he may request, and with unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom he determines it necessary to obtain evidence. If he is not satisfied as to a precondition he discusses the matter with management or those charged with governance, and if changes cannot be made he shall not accept the engagement unless required by law or regulation to do so — an engagement conducted in those circumstances does not comply with the standard, so he shall not include any reference in his report to the review having been conducted in accordance with it. If he discovers after acceptance that a precondition is not satisfied, he discusses it and determines whether the matter can be resolved, whether it is appropriate to continue with the engagement, and whether and how to communicate the matter in his report.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): the factors affecting acceptance, including the absence of a rational purpose where law or regulation requires the financial statements to be audited, and the preconditions, with the consequence that an engagement accepted without them because law or regulation requires it carries no reference to the review having been conducted in accordance with the standard

concepts.subsection: SRE 2400 (Revised) — materiality in a review, and the written representations
concepts.statement: Two things in a review are not scaled down to match the assurance. Materiality is the first. The practitioner shall determine materiality for the financial statements as a whole and apply it in designing the procedures and in evaluating the results obtained from them, and his judgement about what is material in relation to the financial statements as a whole is the same regardless of the level of assurance obtained as the basis for expressing the conclusion. He shall revise it if he becomes aware of any information during the review that would have caused him to determine a different amount initially. Written representations are the second. He shall request management to provide a written representation that it has fulfilled its responsibilities described in the agreed terms, which shall include that management has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with the applicable framework, including where relevant their fair presentation, and has provided him with all relevant information and access as agreed, and that all transactions have been recorded and are reflected in the financial statements. He shall also request written representations that management has disclosed to him the identity of the entity's related parties and all the related party relationships and transactions of which it is aware; significant facts relating to any frauds or suspected frauds known to it that may have affected the entity; known actual or possible non-compliance with laws and regulations whose effects affect the financial statements; all information relevant to the use of the going concern assumption; that all subsequent events requiring adjustment or disclosure have been adjusted or disclosed; material commitments, contractual obligations or contingencies affecting the financial statements including disclosures; and material non-monetary transactions or transactions for no consideration in the period. Where law or regulation requires management to make written public statements about its responsibilities and those statements provide some or all of the required representations, the matters they cover need not be repeated. If management does not provide one or more of the requested representations, he discusses the matter with management and those charged with governance, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the effect on the reliability of representations and evidence in general, and takes appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the conclusion. And he shall disclaim a conclusion on the financial statements, or withdraw where withdrawal is possible under applicable law or regulation, if he concludes that there is sufficient doubt about the integrity of management such that the written representations are not reliable, or if management does not provide the required representations about its responsibilities for the preparation of the financial statements and the recording of all transactions.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): materiality determined for the financial statements as a whole, the practitioner's judgement about what is material being the same regardless of the level of assurance obtained, with revision where later information would have changed it; and the written representations, with a disclaimer of conclusion or withdrawal where management does not provide those about its responsibilities or where its integrity is in sufficient doubt

concepts.subsection: SRE 2410 — a limitation on scope, and a material uncertainty about going concern
concepts.statement: A limitation on scope ordinarily prevents the auditor from completing an interim review, and SRE 2410 answers it differently depending on where the limitation came from. Where it is imposed by management, the auditor does not accept the engagement at all if his preliminary knowledge indicates that he would be unable to complete the review because of it. Where management imposes it after acceptance, he requests its removal; if management refuses, he is unable to complete the review and express a conclusion, and he communicates in writing to the appropriate level of management and to those charged with governance the reason why the review cannot be completed — and if a matter has come to his attention causing him to believe that a material adjustment to the interim financial information is necessary, he communicates that too. He then considers his legal and regulatory responsibilities, including whether he is required to issue a report; where he is, he disclaims a conclusion and provides in the report the reason why the review cannot be completed, again communicating any material adjustment he believes necessary. Where the limitation arises from circumstances other than management, he is ordinarily unable to complete the review and express a conclusion; but in some rare circumstances, where the limitation is clearly confined to one or more specific matters that, while material, are not in his judgement pervasive to the interim financial information, he modifies the report by indicating that, except for the matter described in an explanatory paragraph, the review was conducted in accordance with the standard, and qualifies the conclusion. Going concern is answered on the state of the disclosure rather than on the state of the entity. Where a material uncertainty comes to his attention that may cast significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern and adequate disclosure is made in the interim financial information, he modifies the report by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph. Where he had already added such a paragraph to a prior audit or review report and the material uncertainty still exists with adequate disclosure made, he modifies the current report by adding a paragraph to highlight the continued material uncertainty. Where the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, he should express a qualified or adverse conclusion as appropriate, and the report should include specific reference to the fact that there is such a material uncertainty.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2410: a limitation on scope imposed by management, with a disclaimer of conclusion and the reason given where a report is required, against a limitation arising otherwise and clearly confined to specific matters that are not pervasive, which is met by an explanatory paragraph and a qualified conclusion; and going concern, where adequate disclosure of a material uncertainty is met by an emphasis of matter paragraph and inadequate disclosure by a qualified or adverse conclusion

concepts.section: Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services
concepts.subsection: SAE 3402 — what the standard covers, and what a type 1 and a type 2 report each comprise
concepts.statement: SAE 3402 applies only when the service organisation is responsible for, or otherwise able to make an assertion about, the suitable design of controls. It does not deal with assurance engagements to report only on whether controls at a service organisation operated as described, nor with engagements to report only on controls other than those related to a service that is likely to be relevant to user entities' internal control as it relates to financial reporting — controls affecting a user entity's production or quality control, for example. Within that scope, each report is built of three components and the difference between the two is a date against a period. A type 1 report comprises the service organisation's description of its system; a written assertion by the service organisation that, in all material respects and based on suitable criteria, the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented at the specified date and the controls related to the control objectives stated in the description were suitably designed as at the specified date; and a service auditor's assurance report conveying reasonable assurance about those matters. A type 2 report comprises the description; a written assertion with three limbs rather than two — that the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented throughout the specified period, that the controls related to the stated control objectives were suitably designed throughout the specified period, and that those controls operated effectively throughout the specified period; and a service auditor's assurance report that conveys reasonable assurance about those matters and includes a description of the tests of controls and the results thereof. The service auditor's opinion is expressed in the positive form, and in a type 1 report the report also carries a statement that the service auditor has not performed any procedures regarding the operating effectiveness of controls and that therefore no opinion is expressed on it.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3402: the standard applies only where the service organisation is responsible for or able to assert the suitable design of controls and does not deal with engagements to report only on whether controls operated as described or only on controls unrelated to user entities' financial reporting; and the three components of a type 1 and of a type 2 report, the type 2 assertion running throughout the specified period with a third limb on operating effectiveness and the report including a description of the tests of controls and their results

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — who the Order applies to, and the five exempt classes
concepts.statement: Paragraph 1 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 applies the Order to every company including a foreign company as defined in clause (42) of section 2 of the Companies Act, and then exempts five classes and no others. A banking company as defined in clause (c) of section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. An insurance company as defined under the Insurance Act, 1938. A company licensed to operate under section 8 of the Companies Act. A One Person Company as defined under clause (62) of section 2 and a small company as defined under clause (85) of section 2. And a private limited company, not being a subsidiary or holding company of a public company, which passes three money tests at once — a paid up capital and reserves and surplus not more than one crore rupees as on the balance sheet date, total borrowings not exceeding one crore rupees from any bank or financial institution at any point of time during the financial year, and a total revenue as disclosed in Schedule III to the Companies Act including revenue from discontinuing operations not exceeding ten crore rupees during the financial year as per the financial statements. Four things about that last exemption decide most questions on it. It is conjunctive, so failing any one condition puts the company back inside the Order. Being a subsidiary or a holding company of a public company defeats it however small the figures are. The borrowing test is measured at any point of time during the year and not at the balance sheet date, so a limit repaid before the year end still counts. And the revenue test is total revenue including revenue from discontinuing operations, not turnover. Paragraph 2 then fixes what the Order does: every report made by the auditor under section 143 of the Companies Act on the accounts of every company audited by him to which the Order applies shall in addition contain the matters specified in paragraphs 3 and 4 — an addition to the section 143 report rather than a report of its own — and the Order shall not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3.

citation.ref: paragraph 1 on the companies to which the Order applies and the classes it exempts, including the private limited company that is not a subsidiary or holding company of a public company and passes the paid up capital and reserves and surplus, borrowings and total revenue tests, read with paragraph 2 on the matters every report under section 143 shall in addition contain and on the Order's application to a report on consolidated financial statements

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(vi)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(vi) of paragraph 3 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 asks two questions in one sentence: whether maintenance of cost records has been specified by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 148 of the Companies Act, and whether such accounts and records have been so made and maintained. The two are asked in order, because the second only arises if the first is answered yes. Three confusions follow from reading it as one question. The clause is not about a cost audit. Section 148 carries both the power to specify that cost records be kept and the power to direct that they be audited, and clause 3(vi) reaches only the first; whether a cost auditor was appointed and whether the cost audit was carried out are not what this clause states on. The clause is not skipped where the Central Government has specified nothing, because paragraph 3 requires the auditor's report to include a statement on the matters specified rather than a statement only where something is wrong — the answer is simply that maintenance of cost records has not been specified for the company, and the second limb does not arise. And where either limb is answered unfavourably, paragraph 4(a) requires the report to state the basis for that answer, which a bare "no" does not do.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(vi) — whether maintenance of cost records has been specified by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 148 of the Companies Act and whether such accounts and records have been so made and maintained — read with paragraph 3 and paragraph 4(a)

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(viii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(viii) of paragraph 3 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 requires the auditor to state whether any transactions not recorded in the books of account have been surrendered or disclosed as income during the year in the tax assessments under the Income Tax Act, 1961, and if so, whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books of account during the year. It is a two-limb clause and the second limb is where companies fail: money surrendered to the tax authorities is very often left out of the accounts, on the view that the tax has been paid and the matter is closed. The clause says otherwise — the question is whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books of account during the year, and an unfavourable answer carries paragraph 4(a) with it, so the report states the basis for it. Two things the clause does not do are as examinable as what it does. It does not decide whether the unrecorded transactions were a fraud; that is answered under section 143(12) with Rule 13 and, inside the Order itself, under clause 3(xi), and it is possible for clause 3(viii) to be answered in the affirmative with no fraud reported at all. And it does not reach a surrender made after the year end, because it asks about what has been surrendered or disclosed during the year.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(viii) — whether any transactions not recorded in the books of account have been surrendered or disclosed as income during the year in the tax assessments under the Income Tax Act, 1961 and whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books of account during the year — read with paragraph 4(a) and paragraph 3(xi)

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xii) of paragraph 3 of the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 applies to a Nidhi company and carries three separate questions, each of which is answered on its own. Sub-clause (a) asks whether the Nidhi company has complied with the Net Owned Funds to Deposits in the ratio of 1:20 to meet out the liability — so deposits of more than twenty times net owned funds breach it, and the test is a ratio rather than an absolute amount, which is why a growing Nidhi can fail it without any single deposit being irregular. Sub-clause (b) asks whether the Nidhi company is maintaining ten per cent unencumbered term deposits as specified in the Nidhi Rules, 2014 to meet out the liability; the word that decides it is unencumbered, since a term deposit pledged against a borrowing is not available to meet the liability. Sub-clause (c) asks whether there has been any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof for any period and, if so, for the details — and "for any period" means a default that has since been made good is still reported. All three are answered whatever the answers are, because paragraph 3 requires a statement on the matters specified, and an unfavourable answer to any of them carries paragraph 4(a), so the report states the basis for it.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xii)(a), (b) and (c) — the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20, the ten per cent unencumbered term deposits specified in the Nidhi Rules, 2014, and any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof for any period — read with paragraph 4(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 143(3)(j) and Rule 11 — the other matters the report must carry
concepts.statement: Clause (j) of section 143(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the auditor's report to state such other matters as may be prescribed, and Rule 11 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 is what prescribes them. Six matters sit there and they are a list to be known as a list. Whether the company has disclosed the impact, if any, of pending litigations on its financial position in its financial statement. Whether the company has made provision, as required under any law or accounting standards, for material foreseeable losses, if any, on long term contracts including derivative contracts. Whether there has been any delay in transferring amounts, required to be transferred, to the Investor Education and Protection Fund by the company. The funding chain, which has three sub-limbs and is the one most often stated wrongly: whether management has represented that no funds have been advanced or loaned or invested by the company in any other persons or entities including foreign entities, the Intermediaries, with the understanding that the Intermediary shall directly or indirectly lend or invest in other persons or entities identified by or on behalf of the company, the Ultimate Beneficiaries, or provide any guarantee, security or the like on their behalf; whether management has represented that no funds have been received by the company from any persons or entities including foreign entities, the Funding Parties, with the understanding that the company shall directly or indirectly lend or invest in Ultimate Beneficiaries identified by or on behalf of the Funding Party or provide any guarantee, security or the like on their behalf; and, based on such audit procedures as the auditor has considered reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances, whether anything has come to their notice that has caused them to believe that those two representations contain any material mis-statement. Whether the dividend declared or paid during the year by the company is in compliance with section 123 of the Companies Act, 2013. And whether the company has used such accounting software for maintaining its books of account as has a feature of recording audit trail, whether the same has been operated throughout the year for all transactions recorded in the software, whether the audit trail feature has not been tampered with, and whether the audit trail has been preserved by the company as per the statutory requirements for record retention. Separately from Rule 11, section 197(16) requires the auditor to make a statement in his report under section 143 as to whether the remuneration paid by the company to its directors is in accordance with the provisions of that section, whether remuneration paid to any director is in excess of the limit laid down under it, and such other details as may be prescribed; ICAI's advisory of 9 September 2019 places that statement, for auditors of public companies, under the section headed "Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements".

citation.ref: Rule 11, prescribing the other matters to be included in the auditor's report under clause (j) of sub-section (3) of section 143 — pending litigations, provision for material foreseeable losses on long term contracts including derivative contracts, delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, the representations on Intermediaries and Funding Parties with the auditor's own statement on them, compliance of dividend with section 123, and the accounting software's audit trail — read with section 197(16) on directors' remuneration

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: Internal control — the five international frameworks and what each counts
concepts.statement: Five internal control frameworks are followed internationally and the module names each with the counts that identify it. The Internal Control - Integrated Framework issued by the Committee of the Sponsoring Organisations of the Treadway Commission, the COSO Framework, was introduced in 1992; it articulates seventeen principles across five components — control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring — every one of which must be present and functioning for a system of internal control to be effective, and it lists three categories of objectives: operations objectives, reporting objectives and compliance objectives. The Guidance on Assessing Control published by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, the Criteria of Control or CoCo framework, was developed to improve organisational performance and decision making with better controls, risk management and corporate governance, and includes twenty criteria for effective control in four areas: purpose or direction, commitment or identity and values, capability or competence, and monitoring and learning or evolution. Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology, COBIT, was created by ISACA for IT governance and management and has thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives in four domains: planning and organisation, acquisition and implementation, delivery and support, and monitoring and evaluation. Internal Control: Guidance for Directors on the Combined Code, published by the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales and known as the Turnbull Report, says that the board should maintain a sound system of internal control to safeguard shareholders' investment and the company's assets, that the directors should at least annually conduct a review of the effectiveness of the group's system of internal control covering financial, operational and compliance controls and risk management and report to shareholders that they have done so, and that companies which do not have an internal audit function should from time to time review the need for one. And section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of the United States of America mandates that all publicly-traded companies establish internal controls and procedures for financial reporting and document, test and maintain them; it was followed by the constitution of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, and under the SEC rules and the PCAOB standard management performs a formal assessment of its controls over financial reporting and includes an assessment of internal control over financial reporting in its annual report, while the external auditors provide two opinions as part of a single integrated audit — an independent opinion on the effectiveness of the system of internal control over financial reporting, and the traditional opinion on the financial statements. The COSO framework itself acknowledges that internal control has limitations and provides reasonable assurance, not absolute assurance.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the international internal control frameworks: COSO's seventeen principles across five components and its three categories of objectives, CoCo's twenty criteria in four areas, COBIT's thirty-four high-level processes and two hundred and ten control objectives in four domains, the Turnbull Report's key principles, and Sarbanes-Oxley section 404 with the two opinions of a single integrated audit

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: Internal control — the questionnaire, the check list and the flow chart
concepts.statement: Three techniques are used to evaluate a system of internal control, and the examinable part is what separates them rather than what each looks like. An internal control questionnaire is a set of questions framed in an organised manner about each functional area, with the purpose of evaluating the effectiveness of control and detecting its weaknesses; it is intended to be filled in by the company executives in charge of the various areas, questions are framed so that generally a "No" answer reflects a weakness, and answers are given as Yes, No or Not applicable. A check list is a series of instructions or questions on internal control which the auditor must follow or answer, and it is more in the nature of a reminder to the auditor about the matters to be checked. The three distinctions the module draws between them are the answer to most questions on this: the questionnaire incorporates a large number of detailed questions while the check list generally contains questions relating to the main control objective within the area under review; in a questionnaire the questions are usually answered by company executives while in a check list they are answered by the auditor or his staff; and a "No" in a questionnaire indicates a weakness but not the significance of that weakness, whereas in a check list a specific statement is required where an apparent weakness may prove to be material in relation to the accounts as a whole. A flow chart is a graphic presentation of internal controls drawn to show the controls in each section or sub-section; it provides the most concise and comprehensive way of reviewing internal controls and gives a bird's eye view of the system. Two periods go with the techniques. For the first year of an engagement, issue of a questionnaire is necessary; for subsequent years the auditor may instead ask the client to confirm whether the control system has changed, but it is good practice in a continuing engagement to issue a questionnaire irrespective of any change every third year, which alerts the client to unnoticed changes and makes it more control- conscious. And where the auditor is already aware of the features and efficacy of the controls through a continuing relationship, he may review only the changes in the intervening period, but a comprehensive review in such cases must be made at an interval of about three years. The review is ordinarily undertaken as a distinct phase of the audit before finalisation of the audit programme, though where the size of operations is rather small it can be undertaken in conjunction with other audit procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the techniques of evaluation of internal control: the internal control questionnaire and its basic assumptions, the check list, the flow chart, the three distinctions between a questionnaire and a check list, the issue of a questionnaire in the first year and every third year, and the comprehensive review of the system at an interval of about three years

concepts.section: Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control
concepts.subsection: Internal control — the internal check system
concepts.statement: An internal check system is the organisation of the overall system of book-keeping and the arrangement of staff duties in such a way that no one person can carry through a transaction and record every aspect of it. It is part of the overall control system and operates as a built-in device so far as the organisation and job-allocation aspects of control are concerned, providing checks on the day-to-day transactions which operate continuously as part of the routine, whereby the work of each person is either proved independently or made complementary to the work of another. Its objectives are to detect errors and frauds with ease, to avoid and minimise the possibility of errors and frauds being committed by any member of the staff, to increase the efficiency of the staff working within the organisation, to locate the responsibility area or the stage where an actual fraud or error occurs, to protect the integrity of the business by ensuring that the accounts are always subject to proper scrutiny and check, and to prevent and avoid the misappropriation or embezzlement of cash and the falsification of accounts. The effectiveness of an efficient system of internal check depends on four considerations: clarity of responsibility, so that the responsibility of the different persons engaged in the various operations is properly identified, for which a well-integrated organisational chart helps; division of work, segregated so that the free flow of work is not interrupted and the work of one person is complementary to that of another, with rotation of employees through the various components of the job; standardisation of the entire accounting process by suitable policies commensurate with the nature of the business; and appraisal, a periodic review of the chain of operations and workflow, which may be carried out by preparing an audit flow chart. The general conditions of the system are a list in their own right: no single person should have complete control over any important aspect of the business operation and every employee's action should come under the review of another person; staff duties should be rotated so that members do not perform the same function for a considerable length of time; every member of the staff should be encouraged to go on leave at least once a year; persons having physical custody of assets must not be permitted to have access to the books of account; there should be an accounting control for each class of assets together with periodical inspection to establish their physical condition; mechanical devices should be used wherever practicable to prevent loss or misappropriation of cash; budgetary control should be exercised and wide deviations reconciled; for inventory taking at the close of the year trading activities should if possible be suspended and the count done by staff belonging to several sections of the organisation; financial and administrative powers should be distributed judiciously among different officers with the manner of their exercise reviewed periodically; and procedures should be laid down for the periodical verification and testing of the accounting records.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the internal check system: its meaning, its six objectives, the four considerations its effectiveness depends on, and the general conditions including rotation of duties, compulsory leave, the separation of custody of assets from access to the books, and the suspension of trading during inventory taking

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Public sector audit — compliance audit, and where it sits beside the other two
concepts.statement: Compliance audit is the independent assessment of whether a given subject matter is in compliance with the applicable criteria, carried out by assessing whether activities, financial transactions and information comply in all material respects with the regulatory and other rules which govern the audited entity. It is concerned with two things at once. Regularity, which is the adherence of the subject matter to the formal criteria emanating from relevant laws, regulations and agreements applicable to the entity. And propriety, which is the observance of the general principles governing sound financial management and the ethical conduct of public officials. Regularity is emphasised in compliance auditing, but propriety is equally pertinent in the public sector context, where there are certain expectations concerning financial management and the conduct of officials — so a transaction that satisfies every rule can still be a compliance audit finding. Compliance auditing is part of a combined audit that may also include other aspects, and it is generally conducted in one of three ways: in relation with the audit of financial statements, or separately as individual compliance audits, or in combination with performance auditing. When it is part of a performance audit, compliance is seen as one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness, and non-compliance may be the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of the state of the activities that are the subject matter of the performance audit. Its process runs from general principles and an annual compliance audit plan, through planning the individual audits, performing them and gathering evidence, evaluating evidence and forming conclusions, to reporting — with documentation, communication and quality control running alongside all of it.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — compliance audit: its concern with regularity and with propriety, the three ways in which it is generally conducted, and its relation to performance auditing where compliance is one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness

concepts.section: Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings
concepts.subsection: Public sector audit — the C&AG's report on undertakings, and the Audit Board
concepts.statement: The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General on the audit of public sector undertakings are presented to Parliament in several parts, and there are four of them: an introduction containing a general review of the working results of Government companies, deemed Government companies and corporations; the results of comprehensive appraisals of selected undertakings conducted by the Audit Board; a resume of the company auditors' reports submitted by them under the directions issued by the C&AG and of his comments on the accounts of the Government companies; and the significant results of audit of the undertakings not taken up for appraisal by the Audit Board. For certain specified states the C&AG submits a separate audit report on commercial matters to the legislature, while for other States and Union Territories with a legislature there is a commercial chapter in the main audit report; a state audit report carries both the results of the audit appraisal of the performance of selected companies and corporations and important individual instances of financial irregularities, wasteful expenditure and system deficiencies noticed by the statutory auditors. The Audit Board is a unique feature of the audit conducted by the Indian Audit and Accounts Department: it is constituted for conducting comprehensive audit appraisals of the working of public sector enterprises in diverse sectors, associates with itself experts in the disciplines relevant to the appraisal, and discusses its findings and conclusions with the managements of the enterprises and with their controlling ministries and departments before finalisation, so that their view points are ascertained first. Two things about its standing are examinable and easy to get wrong: the Audit Boards have no separate legal entity, and they work under the supervision and control of the Comptroller and Auditor General. Behind all of it sits section 143(5) of the Companies Act, 2013: in the case of a Government company the C&AG has the power to direct the auditor as to the manner in which the accounts are to be audited, and the auditor shall submit an audit report which includes the directions issued by the C&AG, the action taken on them and their impact on the accounts and financial statements of the company.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the parts of the C&AG's audit report on public sector undertakings, the constitution and standing of the Audit Boards which have no separate legal entity and work under the supervision and control of the C&AG, and the directions under section 143(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 with the action taken on them and their impact reported by the auditor

concepts.section: Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
concepts.subsection: BRSR — who files it, from when, and the three sections of the questionnaire
concepts.statement: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report arrived at the end of a decade of widening requirements, and the dates and the ranks are the examinable part. In 2012 SEBI required the top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation to file a Business Responsibility Report. In 2015 the BRR became part of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations and the top 500 listed companies by market capitalisation were required to file it. In 2017 SEBI advised the top 500 listed companies which were required to prepare a BRR to adopt Integrated Reporting on a voluntary basis from the financial year 2017-18. In 2019, by the fifth amendment to the Listing Regulations and with effect from 26 December 2019, the annual report of the top 1,000 listed entities based on market capitalisation was required to contain a business responsibility report. And in 2021 SEBI introduced the new reporting requirements on ESG parameters called the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, which seeks disclosures on performance against the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct. Reporting under BRSR is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23; disclosure was voluntary in the financial year 2021-22. The reporting questionnaire is divided into three sections and each has its own content. Section A, General Disclosures, contains the details of the listed company, its products, services and operations, employee related details, and its holding, subsidiary and associate companies. Section B, Management Process and disclosures, contains the questions related to policy and management processes, governance, leadership and oversight. Section C, Principle-wise performance disclosures, is where companies report key performance indicators in alignment with the nine principles, classified into essential indicators which are mandatory and leadership indicators which are voluntary. The point of the whole design is comparability: the BRSR is intended to have quantitative and standardised disclosures on ESG parameters so that companies, sectors and periods can be compared, and it is expected to become the single means of disclosing sustainability related information in India.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the evolution of ESG reporting in India from the top 100 listed companies in 2012 to the top 500 and then the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation, the introduction of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report in 2021, its mandatory application from the financial year 2022-23 after a voluntary year, and the three sections of the reporting questionnaire

concepts.subsection: Digital auditing — a digital audit against auditing digitally
concepts.statement: Two phrases in this chapter sound alike and mean opposite things, and telling them apart is the first thing the chapter asks for. A digital audit is placing assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems implemented in an organisation — the IT systems are the subject matter, and the work exists because organisations must review their technology-related controls to identify gaps and risks, to improve continuously and to ensure regulatory compliance. Auditing digitally is using advancements in technology for conducting an effective and efficient audit — the technology is the tool, and the subject matter is whatever the audit was about anyway; using a sampling tool to select a sample from a population based on materiality, or a bot to analyse compliance with statutory payments, is auditing digitally. The features of a digital audit are that it encourages the auditee to embrace technological advancement and gives it confidence to stay updated, improves the quality of the opinion and so leads to a more reliable audit report, saves time, cost and human effort which can be spent on more productive tasks, allows processes to be standardised and controls to be implemented to mitigate risk, helps the organisation gain a comprehensive overview of end-to-end processes, and helps the auditee make informed decisions. Its advantages are enhanced effectiveness and efficiency, better audit quality, lower costs, better analytics and improved risk assessment. And its considerations are cautionary rather than promotional: know what business benefits the organisation wants from automation; think people first and do not underestimate how difficult change is; target the right processes, which is the key to successful automation; ensure the process works and is standardised before automating it, because bots do not easily adapt to process change; treat automation as part of a broader digitalisation strategy rather than a stand-alone solution; and do not forget governance and data security in the risk framework.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — a digital audit as placing assurance on the effectiveness of the IT systems implemented in an organisation against auditing digitally as using advancements in technology to conduct an effective and efficient audit, with the features and advantages of a digital audit and the considerations and challenges that go with automation

concepts.subsection: Digital auditing — the five IT dependencies and the three areas of general IT controls
concepts.statement: IT dependencies are created when IT is used to initiate, authorise, record, process or report transactions or other financial data for inclusion in the financial statements, and identifying them is what tells the auditor where the entity actually relies on IT, what risks arise from that reliance, which general IT controls are related, and therefore what an effective and efficient audit approach looks like. There are five types. Automated controls, designed into the IT environment to enforce business rules — a purchase order approved by workflow, a format check, an existence check that a duplicate customer number cannot exist, a reasonableness check on a maximum payment amount. Reports, being information generated by IT systems, often used in the entity's execution of a manual control such as a business performance review, or used by the auditor himself when selecting items for testing or performing substantive procedures — a vendor master report, a customer ageing report. Calculations, being accounting procedures performed by an IT system instead of a person, such as the system applying the straight-line formula to compute depreciation or computing an invoice by multiplying price by quantity shipped. Security, including segregation of duties, enabled by the IT environment to restrict access to information and to separate the roles and responsibilities that would allow an employee to perpetrate and conceal errors or fraud. And interfaces, being programmed logic that transfers data from one IT system to another, such as an interface transferring data from a payroll sub-ledger to the general ledger. Management responds to the risks arising from those dependencies by implementing information technology general controls, and the module groups them into three areas, each with its own control objective. Access security, whose objective is to ensure that access to programs and data is authenticated and authorised to meet financial reporting objectives — access requests reviewed and authorised, a terminated user's access removed on a timely basis, access rights periodically monitored for appropriateness, transactions of administrative and sensitive generic IDs monitored, security policies maintained, and access to the operating system and database restricted. Program change, whose objective is to ensure that modified systems continue to meet financial reporting objectives — a change management policy, development, testing and production environments segregated, changes tracked and recorded, changes tested and approved before migration into production, emergency changes approved, and segregation of duties maintained between developer and implementor. And data centre and network operations, whose objective is to ensure that production systems are appropriately backed up to meet financial reporting objectives — backup and recovery policies, data backed up and recoverable, restoration testing performed, service level agreements monitored, and batch job schedules monitored for failures with access restricted. The consequence is the part that decides audit work: the auditor scopes general IT controls into testing where IT dependencies are identified, and if the controls around the IT environment are not implemented or are not operating effectively, the general IT controls cannot be relied upon, which means the IT dependencies cannot be relied upon either.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — the five types of IT dependency, being automated controls, reports, calculations, security and interfaces, and the three areas of general IT controls with their control objectives, being access security, program change, and data centre and network operations, read with the consequence that ineffective general IT controls leave the IT dependencies unrelied upon

concepts.subsection: Digital auditing — remote audit
concepts.statement: A remote or virtual audit is one in which the auditor uses online or electronic means to conduct the audit, either partially or completely, engaging technology to obtain audit evidence or to perform documentation review with the participation of the auditee. The auditor must develop tailored strategies so that the remote audit meets the requirements and delivers results equivalent to a traditional onsite audit, and the module groups what he considers under three heads. Feasibility and planning — agreeing the audit timelines, the meeting platform to be used for audit sessions, the data exchange mechanisms and any access authorisation requests, and determining that the technology is available and that auditors and auditees have the competencies for it; the execution phase involves video or tele conferencing with auditees, and the documentation for audit evidence is transferred through a document sharing platform. Confidentiality, security and data protection — access to the document sharing platform is sufficiently restricted and secured by encrypting the data sent across the network, information once reviewed and documented is removed from the platform and stored according to the applicable archiving standards and data protection requirements, legislation and regulations may require additional agreements from both sides, the auditor should not take screenshots of auditees and any screenshot of a document or record used as evidence should be previously authorised by the audited organisation, and access to the auditee's IT system should be through a virtual private network, which creates a safe and encrypted online connection. And risk assessment — the risks to achieving the audit objectives are identified, assessed and managed, and the assessment of whether a remote audit would be sufficient to achieve the audit objectives is made and documented for each audit, involving all members of the audit team and the audited organisation's representative. Its advantages are no travel time or cost, comfort and flexibility for the team, evidence gathering spread over several weeks instead of concentrated into a short period that takes personnel away from their daily activities, first-hand evidence directly from the IT system where direct access is given, and a wider selection of auditors from a global network of experts. Its disadvantages are interrupted meetings from network issues, limited or no ability to see the facility, the culture of the organisation or the body language of the auditees, time zone problems, security and confidentiality violations, remote access to sensitive IT systems not being allowed, cultural challenges and a lack of knowledge of local laws, the impossibility of physical verification of assets and stock taking, and — the one with a consequence attached — an increased opportunity to present doctored documents and to omit relevant information, which may call for additional planning and some additional or different audit procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — remote or virtual audit: the three considerations of feasibility and planning, confidentiality, security and data protection, and risk assessment, including the restriction and encryption of the document sharing platform, the prior authorisation of screenshots used as evidence and the use of a virtual private network, together with the advantages and the disadvantages including the increased opportunity to present doctored documents

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — who appoints the auditor, and what is settled before the audit starts
concepts.statement: A bank's auditor is appointed by a different body according to what the bank is, and in either case the Reserve Bank must approve first. The auditor of a banking company is appointed at the annual general meeting of the shareholders; the auditor of a nationalised bank is appointed by the bank acting through its Board of Directors; and in either case approval of the Reserve Bank is required before the appointment is made. Most nationalised and public sector banks appoint four or more firms of chartered accountants to act jointly as statutory central auditors, while a statutory branch audit is carried out by a single firm. The appointment letter of a statutory central auditor carries the period of appointment, the particulars of the other central auditors and of the previous auditors, the procedural requirements for accepting, a statement of the division of work among the joint auditors in a nationalised bank, and the scope including any special reports or certificates; a branch auditor's letter is on similar lines except for the particulars of other auditors and the division of work. Before the audit starts, three things are settled. The Reserve Bank has advised banks to obtain from the auditor a declaration of indebtedness, a written confirmation that the auditor, the firm, its partners and their family members have not been declared wilful defaulters by any bank or financial institution, and this is in addition to the declaration about the absence of the disqualifications in section 141 of the Companies Act. An audit firm should not undertake a statutory audit assignment while it is associated with internal assignments in the bank during the same year. And under SA 210 the terms of the engagement are agreed with the bank and documented before significant portions of fieldwork begin.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — audit of accounts and appointment of auditor: four or more firms as statutory central auditors, a single firm for a branch, the contents of the appointment letter, the annual general meeting for a banking company and the Board for a nationalised bank with the Reserve Bank's approval in either case; Stage I initial considerations: the declaration of indebtedness, internal assignments in the same year, and the terms of the engagement under SA 210

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — verifying the statutory liquidity ratio and compiling the demand and time liabilities
concepts.statement: The Reserve Bank requires the statutory central auditors of a bank to verify compliance with the statutory liquidity ratio requirements on 12 odd dates in different months of the fiscal year, not being Fridays, and the resulting report goes to the top management of the bank and to the Reserve Bank. The two things verified are the correctness of the compilation of the demand and time liabilities position and the maintenance of liquid assets under section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act. The branch auditors send weekly trial balances as on Fridays, consolidated at head office into the position for every reporting Friday; the central auditor asks the branch auditors to verify the trial balances on the dates he selects and to examine the cash balance at the branch on those dates, and he examines the consolidation on a test basis and the valuation of securities against the Reserve Bank's guidelines. In compiling the liabilities he checks that the excluded items have been excluded — paid-up capital, reserves, any credit balance in the profit and loss account, loans from the Reserve Bank, refinance from EXIM Bank, NHB, SIDBI and NABARD, part recoveries of debts considered bad and doubtful, and margins held in sundry deposits for funded facilities — and that the included items have been included: the net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts, and borrowings from abroad, which are liabilities to others and are taken at gross, so that an adverse balance in the Nostro mirror account is a liability to others, unlike liabilities towards the banking system in India, which may be netted against assets towards that system.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — compliance with CRR and SLR requirements: 12 odd dates in different months not being Fridays, the report to top management and the Reserve Bank, the weekly Friday trial balances and their consolidation, the items excluded from and included in the demand and time liabilities, and borrowings from abroad taken at gross as liabilities to others

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — drawing power, temporary deficiencies, unreviewed limits and quick mortality
concepts.statement: Four rules decide whether a working capital account is merely irregular or has become non-performing. Drawing power is calculated net of the stipulated margin, on the stock and the eligible book debts, and in a consortium the calculation and allocation made by the lead bank bind the member banks; for a construction company the work in progress must be valued consistently and the mobilisation advance received is reduced in arriving at it, and a stock audit including book debts is carried out for every account whose funded exposure exceeds the stipulated limit. A bank does not classify an account as non-performing merely because of deficiencies that are temporary in nature — the non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement, the balance temporarily exceeding the limit, or the non-renewal of limits on the due date. But the stock statements relied on for drawing power must not be older than 3 months, and the outstanding based on drawing power calculated from a stock statement older than 3 months is irregular. And an account whose regular or ad hoc limit is not reviewed within 180 days from the due date or the date of the ad hoc sanction is treated as non-performing, the auditor also checking that ad hoc or short reviews are not done repetitively. Among the accounts the auditor selects for examination are quick or early mortality cases: an advance that slips to non-performing within 12 months of its sanction.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — drawing power calculated net of margin, the lead bank's calculation binding in a consortium, mobilisation advances in construction and the stock audit; accounts with temporary deficiencies not classified as non-performing; stock statements not older than 3 months; limits not reviewed within 180 days treated as non-performing; quick or early mortality within 12 months of sanction

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — Basel III, the two tiers of capital and the 9 per cent ratio
concepts.statement: Basel III is the global standard on the capital adequacy of banks, stress testing and market liquidity risk, and it aims at three things: improving the banking sector's ability to absorb shocks arising from financial and economic stress whatever their cause, improving risk management and governance, and strengthening banks' transparency and disclosure. In India the Reserve Bank has prescribed since 1992 a uniform methodology for scheduled commercial banks other than regional rural banks. Capital is split for supervisory purposes into two tiers by quality: Tier I consists mainly of share capital and disclosed reserves and is the bank's highest quality capital because it is fully available to cover losses; Tier II consists of certain reserves and certain types of subordinated debt and has a lower loss absorption capacity. The capital to risk-weighted assets ratio is eligible total capital funds divided by risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items, multiplied by 100, and the Reserve Bank requires a minimum of 9 per cent on an ongoing basis. Each exposure is weighted before it enters the denominator — a secured housing loan up to ₹75 lakh at 50 per cent subject to conditions, above ₹75 lakh at 75 per cent, commercial real estate at 100 per cent, so a housing loan of ₹60 lakh contributes ₹30 lakh — and a non-performing asset purchased from another bank carries a 100 per cent weight. The authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, including its disclosures and the other ratios in the notes, is one of the certificates the statutory central auditors give beside the main report.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — Basel III framework: its three aims, the uniform methodology of 1992, Tier I and Tier II capital, the CRAR formula with risk-weighted assets and off-balance-sheet items in the denominator, the minimum of 9 per cent, the housing loan risk-weight example, the 100 per cent weight on purchased non-performing assets, and the authentication of the capital adequacy ratio among the certificates

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — deposits, inoperative accounts, non-resident accounts and window-dressing
concepts.statement: Deposits are of two kinds, repayable on demand — current and savings accounts — and repayable after a fixed term, including recurring deposits. Savings accounts are opened for individuals, Hindu undivided families and some approved institutions, never for a business or professional concern, whose transactions run through current accounts; no interest is generally paid on a current account, and a debit balance in a current account is not netted on the liabilities side but shown under advances. A savings or current account with no transactions for over two years is inoperative or dormant, a high-risk area for fraud, and it may be revived only with proper authority. On term deposits the auditor checks that receipts are issued serially, that the correct rate has been offered on bulk deposits of ₹2 crore and above for scheduled commercial banks, that the foreclosure penalty has been deducted on premature closure, and that interest has been paid on the basis of 360 days in a year. Foreign currency non-resident deposits are opened by non-resident Indians as fixed deposits only and are converted at the rate notified by head office, the difference going to the profit and loss account. NRE accounts may be opened by non-resident Indians and persons of Indian origin and are repatriable; NRO accounts may be opened by all non-residents and are not repatriable except for all current income subject to conditions; both are in rupees and may be savings, current, recurring or fixed. Deposits must not be inflated for presentation: overdrafts granted near the balance sheet date and placed back as deposits, with further advances on their security, inflate both deposits and advances, and where that window-dressing is indicated the auditor considers a suitable qualification in the main audit report.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — deposits: current and savings accounts, no savings account for a business concern, debit balances shown under advances, inoperative accounts after two years revived only with proper authority, bulk deposits of ₹2 crore and above, the foreclosure penalty, interest on the basis of 360 days, FCNR accounts as fixed deposits, NRE and NRO accounts and repatriability, and window-dressing calling for a qualification in the main report

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the nationalised bank's report to the Central Government and the certificates beside it
concepts.statement: The auditor of a nationalised bank reports to the Central Government on five matters: whether in his opinion the balance sheet is a full and fair balance sheet containing all the necessary particulars and properly drawn up so as to exhibit a true and fair view of the affairs of the bank; whether the profit and loss account shows a true balance of profit or loss for the period; where he called for any explanation or information, whether it was given and whether it is satisfactory; whether or not the transactions of the bank which came to his notice have been within the powers of that bank; and whether or not the returns received from the offices and branches have been found adequate for the purpose of his audit; with any other matter he considers should be brought to the notice of the Central Government. Beside the report, the terms of appointment require a long form audit report and a set of reports and certificates: on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls over financial reporting, on compliance with the statutory liquidity ratio requirements, on whether income recognition, asset classification and provisioning follow the Reserve Bank's guidelines, on any serious irregularity needing immediate attention in line with section 143(12), a certificate on the custody and utilisation of unused Bank Receipt forms, the authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, the status of compliance with the Ghosh Committee's recommendations on frauds and malpractices and the Jilani Committee's on internal control and inspection, instances of adverse credit-deposit ratio in rural areas, asset liability management, the corporate governance certificate for a listed bank, and certification of claims of interest subsidies and subventions.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — auditor's report of a nationalised bank to the Central Government: the balance sheet and profit and loss account, explanations called for, transactions within the powers of the bank, adequacy of branch returns, other matters; and the reports and certificates required by the terms of appointment beside the long form audit report

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — the 15 per cent capital ratio, and when an asset is sub-standard or lost
concepts.statement: Every applicable non-banking financial company maintains a minimum capital ratio, consisting of Tier I and Tier II capital, of not less than 15 per cent of its aggregate risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and of the risk-adjusted value of its off-balance-sheet items; each asset is multiplied by its risk weight and the aggregate is what the ratio is measured against, so a ratio computed on the balance sheet alone overstates the position. Alongside the ratio sits the classification of assets. A sub-standard asset includes an asset whose terms as to interest or principal have been renegotiated, rescheduled or restructured after the commencement of operations, and it stays sub-standard until the expiry of one year of satisfactory performance under the new terms. A loss asset is one identified as such by the company, by its internal or external auditor or by the Reserve Bank on inspection, to the extent not written off, and also an asset adversely affected by a potential threat of non-recoverability due to erosion in the value of the security, the non-availability of security, or any fraudulent act or omission on the part of the borrower. The auditor checks compliance with the prudential norms as a whole — income recognition, accounting for investments, classification, provisioning, capital adequacy, the prohibition on loans against the company's own shares, and the norms for concentration of credit and investments — and that the Board of a company granting demand or call loans has framed and implemented a policy for them.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — prudential norms: the minimum capital ratio of 15 per cent of aggregate risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and risk-adjusted off-balance-sheet items; sub-standard assets including renegotiated or restructured assets until one year of satisfactory performance; the definition of a loss asset; the prohibition on loans against own shares; the demand and call loan policy

concepts.section: Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies
concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — a downgraded credit rating, matured deposits and what counts as a fraud
concepts.statement: A deposit-taking non-banking financial company's ceiling on public deposits is tied to a credit rating from an approved agency, and the auditor checks that the rating is in force and that the company has informed the Reserve Bank of any revision. Where the rating is downgraded below the minimum investment grade, an investment and credit company or a factor regularises the excess deposits in a fixed way: with immediate effect it stops accepting fresh public deposits and renewing existing ones, all existing deposits run off to maturity, and it reports the position within 15 working days to the concerned Regional Office of the Reserve Bank where it is registered; and no matured public deposit is renewed without the express and voluntary consent of the depositor. The auditor's report on such a company says whether it is accepting public deposits without a minimum investment grade rating, whether deposits in excess of the permissible quantum have been regularised in the manner provided, and whether the capital adequacy ratio in the return to the Reserve Bank is correctly determined. On frauds, the company's classification runs from misappropriation and criminal breach of trust through fraudulent encashment, unauthorised credit facilities for reward, negligence and cash shortages, cheating and forgery, irregularities in foreign exchange transactions, and any other fraud. Negligence and cash shortages, and foreign exchange irregularities, are reported as fraud where an intention to cheat is suspected or proved; where it is not, a cash shortage is still treated and reported as fraud if it exceeds ₹10,000, or exceeds ₹5,000 and was detected by management, the auditor or an inspecting officer and not reported on its occurrence by the person handling the cash.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — Acceptance of Public Deposits Directions: the credit rating ceiling, the procedure on downgrade below investment grade with the report within 15 working days, no renewal of a matured deposit without express and voluntary consent, the audit report items for a deposit-taking company; Monitoring of Frauds Directions: the classes of fraud and the ₹10,000 and ₹5,000 cash-shortage lines

concepts.section: Professional Ethics and Liabilities of Auditors
concepts.subsection: Section 2(2), Regulation 191 and sections 24 and 25 — who is in practice, and who is punished for pretending
concepts.statement: A member is deemed to be in practice under section 2(2) when, individually or in partnership with chartered accountants in practice or with members of the other prescribed professions, for remuneration received or to be received, he engages in the practice of accountancy; offers to perform or performs services involving the auditing or verification of financial transactions, books, accounts or records, or the preparation, verification or certification of financial accounting and related statements, or holds himself out to the public as an accountant; renders professional services or assistance on matters of accounting procedure or the recording, presentation or certification of financial facts; or renders such other services as in the opinion of the Council may be rendered by a chartered accountant in practice, under which the Council permits the entire range of management consultancy and other services. A person is in practice not only when he serves clients but when he offers to: setting up an establishment offering accounting services is practice though no client has been served, and a member rendering service with the armed forces is deemed in practice.
