options.misconception: subtracts one spot rate from the other, when the two rates cover different lengths of time and must be compounded out
options.why: 8 − 6 = 2 per cent treats the rates as though they were amounts. They are returns over different periods — one over a year, one over two — so the shorter has to be compounded out of the longer by dividing the growth factors, 1.1664 / 1.06, giving about 10.04 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: The one-year spot rate is 6 per cent and the two-year spot rate is 8 per cent, both annually compounded.

items.stem: What can the shape actually be taken to mean?

options.text: It always means the market expects interest rates to rise
options.misconception: takes the expectations theory as the only explanation of the shape, when a term premium produces the same upward slope with no change in rates expected
options.why: That is the expectations theory's reading and it is one of three. Liquidity preference says part of the slope is payment for tying money up rather than a forecast, and market segmentation says it can come from nothing more than heavy demand for short paper. A curve that has sloped up for most of recorded history cannot have been forecasting rising rates the whole time.

options.text: Liquidity preference explains it by long bonds being more liquid and so yielding less
options.misconception: inverts the premium, when the theory says the lender must be paid more for longer paper whose price swings further when rates change
options.why: Liquidity preference runs the other way. A long bond's price moves far more for a given change in rates, and the lender's money is committed for longer, so he demands extra yield to hold it. That extra is the term premium, and it pushes long yields up rather than down.

options.text: Market segmentation theory explains it by making the long rate the average of expected short rates
options.misconception: attaches the expectations theory's mechanism to market segmentation, which holds the opposite — that each maturity is priced by its own supply and demand
options.why: Market segmentation says the maturities are separate markets. Banks want short paper, insurers and pension funds want long paper, and each bucket's rate is set by who is buying and selling in it — the rates need not be linked by any average at all. Averaging expected short rates is the expectations theory.

options.text: Under the expectations theory it says short rates are expected to rise; under liquidity preference it may slope up on a term premium alone, with rates expected to stay flat
options.why: The expectations theory reads the long rate as the average of the short rates the market expects, so an upward slope is a forecast of rising rates. Liquidity preference adds that a lender parting with money for longer must be paid a term premium for the price risk he takes on, which tilts the curve upwards even when no change in rates is expected. The same shape supports both readings, which is why the curve alone settles nothing.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: The yield curve slopes upwards — three-month paper yields less than one-year paper, which yields less than ten-year paper. Two analysts read the same curve and reach different conclusions.

items.stem: What spot rate does the international Fisher effect imply for a year from now?

options.text: ₹80.00, unchanged, since the exchange rate has nothing to do with interest rates
options.misconception: treats the interest difference as a free gain, when the expected currency movement is exactly what the effect says removes it
options.why: If the rate stayed at ₹80, a dollar investor could borrow at 4 per cent, lend at 12 per cent in rupees and pocket the 8 per cent interest difference for nothing. The international Fisher effect exists to describe why that is not expected to work — the rupee is expected to weaken to about ₹86.15 and give the difference back.

options.text: About ₹86.15 to the dollar
options.why: The international Fisher effect puts the expected spot rate at today's spot times one plus the home nominal interest rate over one plus the foreign one: 80 × 1.12 / 1.04 = ₹86.15. The currency of the higher nominal interest rate is expected to weaken by about the difference, so a lender who chases the 12 per cent rupee rate expects to hand the gain back on the exchange rate.

options.text: About ₹86.40 to the dollar
options.misconception: applies the interest difference as a simple percentage of the spot rate instead of taking the ratio of the two growth factors
options.why: 80 × 1.08 = ₹86.40 adds the 8 percentage point difference straight to the spot rate. The relationship is a ratio, not a difference: 1.12 / 1.04 = 1.0769, which is a 7.69 per cent movement and gives ₹86.15. The approximation is close at small differences and drifts as they widen.

options.text: About ₹74.29 to the dollar
options.misconception: puts the two rates the wrong way round, so the high interest currency is expected to strengthen — the reverse of what the effect states
options.why: 80 × 1.04 / 1.12 = ₹74.29 has the rupee appreciating. The international Fisher effect says the opposite: a high nominal interest rate carries high expected inflation inside it, and the currency of the higher rate is expected to weaken, not strengthen. The home rate goes on top of the fraction.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: One-year nominal interest rates are 12 per cent in India and 4 per cent in the United States. The spot rate is ₹80 to the dollar.

items.stem: What is the initial outlay on the replacement?

options.misconception: deducts the whole sale price and forgets the tax the sale itself triggers on the excess over written-down value
options.why: 12,00,000 − 5,00,000 = ₹7,00,000 assumes every rupee of the sale price stays with the company. It sold for ₹1,00,000 more than the written-down value, and 30 per cent of that excess goes in tax, so only ₹4,70,000 is left to set against the new machine.

options.misconception: treats the replacement as a fresh purchase, ignoring that disposing of the old machine funds part of the new one
options.why: ₹12,00,000 is the new machine's price with no credit for the old one. A replacement is an incremental decision — the company would not be selling this machine but for the replacement, so its net proceeds of ₹4,70,000 belong in the initial outlay, bringing it to ₹7,30,000.

The old machine brings in ₹5,00,000, out of which tax of 0.30 × (5,00,000 − 4,00,000) = ₹30,000 goes on the excess over its written-down value, so ₹4,70,000 is actually recovered. The initial outlay is therefore 12,00,000 − 4,70,000 = ₹7,30,000. Everything in a replacement decision is measured this way, on incremental cash flows — what changes because the old machine goes and the new one arrives.

options.misconception: sets off the old machine's book value instead of what it actually fetched, when book value is not cash and the buyer's cheque is
options.why: 12,00,000 − 4,00,000 = ₹8,00,000 uses the written-down value of ₹4,00,000. That book value is the tax records' view of the machine, not money. What reduces the outlay is the ₹5,00,000 the buyer pays, less the ₹30,000 of tax on the excess.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company is replacing a machine whose written-down value is ₹4,00,000. A buyer will pay ₹5,00,000 for it today. The new machine costs ₹12,00,000. Take it that the excess of the sale price over the written-down value is taxed at 30 per cent in the year of sale.

items.stem: What is the project's NPV today?

options.text: About ₹20 lakh
options.misconception: rolls the tree back correctly but never discounts the year-one expected value to today
options.why: 100 − 80 = ₹20 lakh treats ₹100 lakh arriving at the end of year 1 as though it were in hand today. At 10 per cent its present value is 100 / 1.10 = ₹90.91 lakh, so the NPV is ₹10.91 lakh. Rolling a decision tree back gives values at the node where they stand, and each still has to be discounted to today.

options.text: About ₹10.91 lakh
options.why: Roll the decision tree back from the far end. In a good market the second stage is worth 320 − 200 = ₹120 lakh, so that node is worth 40 + 120 = ₹160 lakh at the end of year 1. In a bad market the second stage is worth 150 − 200 = −₹50 lakh, so the company does not spend, and the node is worth ₹40 lakh. Weighting the two chance branches equally gives 0.5 × 160 + 0.5 × 40 = ₹100 lakh at the end of year 1, whose present value is 100 / 1.10 = ₹90.91 lakh, and the NPV is 90.91 − 80 = ₹10.91 lakh.

options.text: About ₹65.45 lakh
options.misconception: values the project on the favourable branch alone, ignoring the equal chance that the market turns out badly
options.why: 160 / 1.10 − 80 = ₹65.45 lakh plans on the good market arriving. It has only an even chance of doing so, and the bad branch is worth ₹40 lakh, not ₹160 lakh. The two must be weighted by their probabilities at the chance node before anything is discounted, which brings the year-1 figure to ₹100 lakh.

options.text: About minus ₹11.82 lakh
options.misconception: forces the second stage at both nodes, when the whole reason for staging is that the company may walk away after a bad result
options.why: Spending the ₹200 lakh in a bad market too gives 40 + 150 − 200 = −₹10 lakh at that node, so the expected value falls to 0.5 × 160 + 0.5 × (−10) = ₹75 lakh, a present value of 75 / 1.10 = ₹68.18 lakh and an NPV of −₹11.82 lakh. Nobody is compelled to spend after a bad result. At a decision node the better branch is taken and the other dropped, which is what makes the node worth ₹40 lakh rather than minus ₹10 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company spends ₹80 lakh today on the first stage of a project. That stage returns ₹40 lakh at the end of year 1 whatever happens. Also at the end of year 1 the market is revealed, with an equal chance of being good or bad. At that point, and only then, the company may spend a further ₹200 lakh on the second stage. In a good market the later flows from that second stage are worth ₹320 lakh measured at the end of year 1; in a bad market they are worth ₹150 lakh on the same basis. The discount rate is 10 per cent.

items.stem: What money rate should be used, and what is the project's NPV?

options.text: A money rate of 13.4 per cent, giving an NPV of about minus ₹7.03 lakh
options.misconception: uses the money rate on cash flows still stated in today's prices, so inflation is charged in the discount rate while never being credited to the receipts
options.why: Discounting the uninflated ₹50 lakh at 13.4 per cent gives 50 / 1.134 = ₹44.09 lakh and 50 / 1.285956 = ₹38.88 lakh, a total of ₹82.97 lakh and an NPV of minus ₹7.03 lakh. The money rate belongs with the money cash flows. Charging inflation in the denominator while leaving today's prices in the numerator penalises the project for a rise in prices it is never given credit for.

options.text: A money rate of 13.0 per cent, giving an NPV of about minus ₹0.37 lakh
options.misconception: adds the real rate and the inflation rate instead of compounding them, which leaves out the inflation earned on the real return itself
options.why: 8 + 5 = 13 per cent understates the rate, because inflation applies to the real return as well as to the principal. Compounding gives 1.08 × 1.05 − 1 = 13.4 per cent. At 13 per cent the inflated flows discount to 52.50 / 1.13 = ₹46.46 lakh and 55.125 / 1.2769 = ₹43.17 lakh, a total of ₹89.63 lakh and an NPV of minus ₹0.37 lakh — too kind by nearly half a lakh.

options.text: A money rate of 13.4 per cent, giving an NPV of about ₹5.87 lakh
options.misconception: inflates the cash flows and then discounts them at the real rate, counting the price rise in the receipts while never charging it in the rate
options.why: 52.50 / 1.08 = ₹48.61 lakh and 55.125 / 1.1664 = ₹47.26 lakh come to ₹95.87 lakh, an NPV of ₹5.87 lakh, and the project appears worth doing. It is the mirror of the other mixing error — the money cash flows have been discounted at the real rate, so inflation lifts the numerator and is never charged in the denominator. Matched properly the NPV is about minus ₹0.84 lakh and the project is rejected.

options.text: A money rate of 13.4 per cent, giving an NPV of about minus ₹0.84 lakh
options.why: The money rate compounds the two, 1.08 × 1.05 − 1 = 13.4 per cent. The cash flows in actual rupees are 50 × 1.05 = ₹52.50 lakh and 50 × 1.05² = ₹55.125 lakh, whose present values at 13.4 per cent are 52.50 / 1.134 = ₹46.30 lakh and 55.125 / 1.285956 = ₹42.87 lakh, a total of ₹89.16 lakh against an outlay of ₹90 lakh — an NPV of about minus ₹0.84 lakh. Leaving the flows at ₹50 lakh and discounting at the real rate of 8 per cent gives the identical ₹89.16 lakh, which is the check that the two routes agree.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A project costs ₹90 lakh today and is expected to produce ₹50 lakh a year for two years, stated in today's prices. Prices are expected to rise by 5 per cent a year and the company's real required return is 8 per cent a year.

items.stem: What cost of equity should the project be given?

options.text: 14.0 per cent
options.misconception: stops at the asset beta and never releveres it, which prices the project as though it were funded entirely by equity
options.why: 6 + 1.00 × 8 = 14.0 per cent uses the asset beta of 1.00 as though it were the equity beta. The asset beta describes the business with no debt at all. This project carries ₹20 crore of debt against ₹80 crore of equity, and putting that back gives an equity beta of 1.175 and a cost of equity of 15.4 per cent.

options.text: 19.6 per cent
options.misconception: uses the comparable's equity beta unchanged, importing its gearing along with its business risk when the two companies are geared quite differently
options.why: 6 + 1.70 × 8 = 19.6 per cent borrows the comparable's equity beta whole. That 1.70 describes a company financed half by debt; the project is financed one part debt to four parts equity and so carries far less financial risk. The business risk may be borrowed; the gearing has to be stripped out and the project's own put back, giving 1.175.

options.text: 14.5 per cent
options.misconception: leaves the one minus tax rate factor out of both the unlevering and the relevering, overstating how much risk a rupee of debt adds
options.why: Without the tax factor the asset beta is 1.70 / (1 + 50 / 50) = 0.85 and the relevered beta is 0.85 × (1 + 20 / 80) = 1.0625, giving 6 + 1.0625 × 8 = 14.5 per cent. Interest is deductible, so each rupee of debt loads the shareholders with only 0.70 of a rupee of extra risk. Carrying that 0.70 through both steps gives 1.175 and 15.4 per cent.

options.text: 15.4 per cent
options.why: Strip the comparable's gearing first. Its asset beta is 1.70 / (1 + 0.70 × 50 / 50) = 1.70 / 1.70 = 1.00. Put the project's own gearing back on it: 1.00 × (1 + 0.70 × 20 / 80) = 1.175. The cost of equity is then 6 + 1.175 × 8 = 15.4 per cent. The tax factor of 0.70 belongs in both steps, because interest is deductible and the taxman carries part of the risk that gearing adds.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: A listed company in the same business has an equity beta of 1.70, with debt of ₹50 crore and equity of ₹50 crore at market values. A company appraising a project in that business will fund it with debt of ₹20 crore and equity of ₹80 crore. The tax rate is 30 per cent, the risk-free rate is 6 per cent and the market risk premium is 8 per cent. Take the debt beta as zero.

items.stem: What actually separates an active mandate from a passive one?

options.text: How often the portfolio is traded — a fund that trades daily is active and one that trades yearly is passive
options.misconception: takes turnover as the definition when it is only a symptom, since an index fund tracking a fast-changing benchmark can trade more than a patient stock-picker
options.why: Turnover follows from the mandate; it does not define it. An index fund tracking a benchmark that changes often will trade more than a patient active manager who buys ten companies and holds them for years. The question is whether a return above the benchmark is being sought, not how busy the dealing desk looks.

options.text: Active management wins whenever the manager's gross return beats the index
options.misconception: compares gross returns, when research fees and dealing costs come out of the investor's return and the passive alternative carries far less of both
options.why: The gross return is not what the investor receives. Active management carries research fees and dealing costs that the passive alternative largely avoids, and the excess has to cover all of them before the investor is any better off. A manager who beats the index by less than his own costs has lost the argument.

options.text: A passive manager buys and holds and never trades again, while an active one trades
options.misconception: confuses buy-and-hold with tracking a stated benchmark, which forces trades whenever the index changes its constituents or new money arrives
options.why: A passive fund does trade. The index changes its constituents, companies are taken over, weights shift, and money coming in has to be put to work in the right proportions. What makes it passive is that every one of those trades is dictated by the benchmark rather than by a view, so buy-and-hold is a different thing altogether.

options.text: Whether a return above the benchmark is being sought at all — and an active manager has to earn that excess after his higher costs and turnover, not before
options.why: A passive mandate accepts the benchmark's return and competes on cost and on how faithfully it tracks. An active mandate sets out to beat the benchmark by selecting securities or timing the market, and research and dealing make it dearer to run. The comparison that decides the question is the return after those costs and that turnover, because the investor is paid net and not gross.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: An investment committee is choosing between a manager who promises to beat the index and one who promises only to reproduce it at low cost.

items.stem: What are the most this position can gain, the most it can lose, and its break-even?

options.text: Maximum gain ₹40, maximum loss ₹60, break-even ₹1,060
options.misconception: charges the full premium of the bought call and never credits the premium received on the call that was sold
options.why: Treating the position as costing ₹60 gives a maximum loss of ₹60, a break-even of 1,000 + 60 = ₹1,060 and a gain of 100 − 60 = ₹40. The ₹25 premium received on the sold call is real money that came in on day one, so the position cost ₹35 net, and every one of the three figures shifts accordingly.

options.text: Maximum gain ₹100, maximum loss ₹35, break-even ₹1,035
options.misconception: takes the gap between the two strikes as the profit and forgets that the net premium was paid out of it
options.why: The gap between the strikes, 1,100 − 1,000 = ₹100, is what the position collects at expiry when the share finishes above ₹1,100. The net premium of ₹35 was paid to get there and has to come off it, leaving ₹65. Notice the consistency check the option fails — a break-even of ₹1,035 and a cap at ₹1,100 can only be ₹65 apart.

options.text: Maximum gain ₹65, maximum loss ₹35, break-even ₹1,035
options.why: The net premium paid is 60 − 25 = ₹35, and that is the maximum loss, suffered whenever the share finishes at or below the lower strike of ₹1,000. Above ₹1,100 the written call gives back everything the bought call earns beyond that point, so the gain stops at (1,100 − 1,000) − 35 = ₹65. The break-even is the lower strike plus the net premium, 1,000 + 35 = ₹1,035.

options.text: Maximum gain unlimited, maximum loss ₹35, break-even ₹1,035
options.misconception: prices the bought call and ignores the written one, which is precisely what puts a ceiling on the position
options.why: A bought call on its own does have an unlimited gain. This investor has also sold a call at ₹1,100, and above that level every rupee the bought call earns is owed on the written one. Surrendering the gain above ₹1,100 is what the ₹25 premium was received for, and it caps the maximum gain at ₹65.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹1,000. An investor who expects a moderate rise buys a three-month call at a strike of ₹1,000 for a premium of ₹60 and sells a three-month call on the same share and expiry at a strike of ₹1,100 for a premium of ₹25.

items.stem: When is early exercise worth considering?

options.text: Never for either, since an American option is always worth more alive than exercised
options.misconception: extends the call's rule to the put, missing that exercising a put brings in the strike money and that interest on it can outweigh the time value surrendered
options.why: The rule holds for the call and not for the put. Exercising a deep in the money put hands over the share and brings in the strike at once, and the interest earned on that money can be worth more than the time value surrendered. That possibility is exactly why an American put is worth more than a European one on the same terms.

options.text: For both, as soon as they are in the money, since intrinsic value in hand is certain and the rest is speculation
options.misconception: treats the time value still in the option as speculation rather than as money the market will pay for it today
options.why: Time value is not a hope; it is a price somebody will pay right now. An option in the money with two months to run trades above its intrinsic value, so exercising it hands that difference away for nothing. Selling the option realises both parts, which is why early exercise of a call on a share paying no dividend is never right.

options.text: Never for a call on a share paying no dividend, since selling the option fetches more than exercising it; but a put can be worth exercising early, because the strike money comes in at once
options.why: Exercising a call surrenders whatever time value remains, and the option can always be sold in the market for its intrinsic value plus that time value, so on a share paying no dividend early exercise is never right. A put is different — exercising brings in the strike, and once the share has fallen far enough the interest on that money can be worth more than the time value given up.

options.text: Never for a call in any circumstances, dividend or no dividend
options.misconception: states the no-dividend rule without its condition, when a dividend just ahead can make exercising a call worthwhile because the option holder receives no dividend
options.why: A dividend is the exception. The holder of a call receives no dividend, and the share price drops when it goes ex-dividend, so exercising just before that date buys the share in time to collect it. Where the dividend is larger than the time value being surrendered, early exercise of the call is the better move.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: An investor holds an American call and an American put on shares of two different companies, and both are well in the money with two months still to run.

items.stem: What will the importer end up paying?

options.text: ₹8.30 crore, the spot value, since the two premiums cancel and the options offset each other
options.misconception: reads equal premiums as equal and opposite positions, when the two options sit at different strikes and bite at different rates
options.why: Equal premiums make the structure cost nothing; they do not make it do nothing. The two strikes differ — the call is struck at ₹85 and the put at ₹81 — so they bite at quite different rates and the position is not offset at all. Only a call and a put bought and sold at one and the same strike would leave the importer at 1 million × 83 = ₹8.30 crore.

options.text: Between ₹8.10 crore and ₹8.50 crore — at a spot of ₹86.50 it pays ₹8.50 crore, and at a spot of ₹79.50 it pays ₹8.10 crore
options.why: Above ₹85 the importer exercises its bought call and buys dollars at ₹85, so at a spot of ₹86.50 it pays 1 million × 85 = ₹8.50 crore. Below ₹81 the written put is exercised against it and it must buy at ₹81, so at a spot of ₹79.50 it pays ₹8.10 crore. Between the two strikes both options lapse and it buys at spot. The rate paid therefore lives inside a band, which is the whole point of a range forward.

options.text: Never more than ₹85, and it keeps the whole benefit of any fall in the dollar
options.misconception: prices the bought call and forgets the written put, which is what pays for the cap and is the price of the structure costing nothing
options.why: A cap with the whole downside kept is a plain bought option, and it costs a premium. This structure costs nothing because the importer sold a put at ₹81, and that written put is what pays for the cap at ₹85 — the benefit of a fall below ₹81 is surrendered. There is no free protection; the premium is paid in opportunity rather than in cash.

options.text: At a spot of ₹79.50 it pays ₹7.95 crore, since it would let both options lapse and buy in the market
options.misconception: assumes the importer can abandon the option it sold, when a written option is exercised by the counterparty and not by the hedger
options.why: The importer may abandon the call it bought, but a written option is never his to abandon. At a spot of ₹79.50 the counterparty holding that put exercises it and the importer must buy dollars at ₹81, paying ₹8.10 crore rather than the ₹7.95 crore the market would have charged. That surrendered ₹0.15 crore is what bought the protection above ₹85.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian importer owes one million dollars in six months. The spot rate is ₹83 to the dollar. It buys a six-month dollar call at a strike of ₹85 and sells a six-month dollar put at a strike of ₹81, the two premiums being equal so the structure costs nothing on the day it is put on.

items.stem: What should the treasurer do?

options.text: Sell 12 contracts
options.misconception: matches the principal alone and ignores that a six-month borrowing carries twice the interest a three-month contract covers
options.why: 60 / 5 = 12 contracts match the ₹60 crore principal against a ₹5 crore notional. But the borrowing runs for six months and each contract covers a three-month interest period, so twelve contracts hedge only half the interest at risk. Scaling by 6 / 3 gives the 24 contracts the exposure actually needs.

options.text: Sell 24 contracts
options.why: A borrower loses when rates rise, and a rise in rates drives the futures price down, so the hedge is a short position — he sells. The number of contracts is the exposure over the contract size, 60 / 5 = 12, scaled by the exposure period against the period the contract covers, 6 / 3 = 2, giving 12 × 2 = 24 contracts. The second step matters because a three-month contract hedges only three months of interest however large the principal.

options.text: Sell 6 contracts
options.misconception: divides by the ratio of the two periods instead of multiplying by it, halving a hedge that needed doubling
options.why: 12 divided by 2 gives 6 and turns the adjustment upside down. The borrowing period of six months is longer than the three months a contract covers, so more contracts are needed, not fewer — 12 × 2 = 24. Dividing leaves three-quarters of the interest exposure uncovered.

options.text: Buy 24 contracts
options.misconception: takes the long position, which gains when the futures price rises and so loses at exactly the moment the borrowing gets dearer
options.why: The contract count is right and the direction is wrong. The price is quoted as one hundred minus the rate, so a rise in rates makes the futures price fall. A buyer would lose on the futures at the very moment his borrowing became dearer, doubling the damage instead of offsetting it. A borrower sells.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A treasurer will borrow ₹60 crore in three months' time, for a period of six months, and fears that rates will have risen by then. On this exchange an interest rate futures contract has a notional principal of ₹5 crore, covers a three-month interest period, and is quoted as one hundred minus the rate.

items.stem: How much of next year's cash flow reaches the parent?

options.text: ₹5.40 crore
options.misconception: allows for the blocked funds but forgets the tax the host country deducts on the amount actually remitted
options.why: 6 million units × ₹9 = ₹5.40 crore keeps the 4 million units of blocked funds out, which is right, and then stops. The host country deducts 10 per cent of the amount remitted, so 5.4 million units cross the border rather than 6 million, and ₹4.86 crore reaches the parent.

options.text: ₹4.86 crore
options.why: Only 10 million × 0.60 = 6 million units may be remitted. The withholding tax takes 10 per cent of that, leaving 5.4 million units, which converts at ₹9 to 48.6 million rupees — ₹4.86 crore. The other 4 million units belong to the project but never reach the parent next year, and the difference between the two views is why a foreign project is appraised twice.

options.text: ₹8.10 crore
options.misconception: deducts the withholding tax but treats the whole cash flow as remittable, when only 60 per cent of it may leave the country
options.why: 10 million × 0.90 × 9 = ₹8.10 crore applies the withholding tax to everything the project earns. The restriction bites first — only 6 million units may be remitted at all — and the tax then applies to that 6 million, not to the full 10 million.

options.text: ₹9.00 crore
options.misconception: values the whole of the project's cash flow, ignoring both the limit on remittance and the tax deducted on what is sent
options.why: 10 million × 9 = ₹9.00 crore is the project's own cash flow converted at the expected rate. It is the right figure for judging the subsidiary and the wrong one for judging the investment, because 40 per cent of it cannot be remitted at all and the rest suffers a withholding tax on the way out.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company's foreign subsidiary will generate 10 million units of local currency as after-tax cash flow next year. Under the terms of the investment approval only 60 per cent of it may be remitted, and the balance must stay in the host country where it earns nothing. The host country deducts a withholding tax of 10 per cent on the amount remitted. The expected exchange rate is ₹9 to the unit.

items.stem: What is the bond worth today?

options.text: About ₹966.20
options.misconception: treats a half-yearly bond as an annual one, so the first half of each year's interest is made to arrive six months later than it does
options.why: A ₹100 coupon for two years at 12 per cent gives 100 × 1.690051 = ₹169.01 plus 1,000 × 0.797194 = ₹797.19, that is ₹966.20. It ignores that half of each year's interest arrives six months early, and money that arrives sooner is worth more. Working in half-yearly periods gives ₹965.35.

options.text: About ₹787.39
options.misconception: doubles the number of periods but leaves the rate at the full annual figure, charging twelve per cent for each half year
options.why: Discounting four periods at 12 per cent each gives 50 × 3.03735 = ₹151.87 plus 1,000 × 0.635518 = ₹635.52, that is ₹787.39. Twelve per cent is the annual figure; the rate per period is half of it. Doubling the periods without halving the rate compounds the required return twice over and undervalues the bond by nearly ₹180.

options.text: About ₹960.30
options.misconception: halves the rate and doubles the periods correctly but leaves the coupon annual, so the interest is made to arrive once a year instead of twice
options.why: 100 / 1.06² + 100 / 1.06⁴ + 1,000 / 1.06⁴ = 89.00 + 79.21 + 792.09 = ₹960.30 gets the rate per period right and the timing of the coupon wrong. The bond pays ₹50 at the end of each of the four half years, not ₹100 at the end of each year, and interest arriving sooner is worth more, which lifts the value to ₹965.35.

options.text: About ₹965.35
options.why: Move the whole calculation to a half-yearly period. The coupon is ₹50 every six months, there are four periods, and the rate per period is 6 per cent. The annuity factor is (1 − 1.06 to the power minus 4) / 0.06 = 3.4651, so the coupons are worth 50 × 3.4651 = ₹173.26, and the face value is worth 1,000 × 0.792094 = ₹792.09. Together they come to ₹965.35.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of face value ₹1,000 carries interest at 10 per cent a year, paid half-yearly, and has exactly two years left to maturity. The required return is 12 per cent a year, compounded half-yearly.

items.stem: What is the share worth today?

options.text: About ₹120.74
options.misconception: discounts the terminal value for three years, when it already stands at the end of year two and discounting it again charges one year twice
options.why: 151.20 / 1.15³ = ₹99.42 pushes the terminal value one year too far back. Capitalising the year-3 dividend at the required return less growth produces a value as at the end of year 2, not the end of year 3, so it is discounted for two years and gives ₹114.33. The extra year costs almost ₹15 a share.

options.text: About ₹105.00
options.misconception: applies the constant growth model straight off at the long-run rate, ignoring the two years of high growth altogether
options.why: 10 × 1.05 / (0.15 − 0.05) = ₹105.00 runs the constant growth model from tomorrow at 5 per cent. The company is expected to grow at 20 per cent for two years first, and those two years lift every dividend that follows — which is why the terminal value is computed off ₹15.12 rather than off ₹10.50.

options.text: About ₹135.65
options.why: The high-growth dividends are 10 × 1.20 = ₹12.00 in year 1 and ₹14.40 in year 2. The first dividend of the stable phase is 14.40 × 1.05 = ₹15.12, so the terminal value at the end of year 2 is 15.12 / (0.15 − 0.05) = ₹151.20. Discounting all three at 15 per cent gives 12 / 1.15 = ₹10.43, 14.40 / 1.3225 = ₹10.89 and 151.20 / 1.3225 = ₹114.33, a total of about ₹135.65.

options.text: About ₹130.21
options.misconception: uses the last high-growth dividend in the terminal value formula instead of the first dividend of the stable phase
options.why: 14.40 / 0.10 = ₹144.00 capitalises the year-2 dividend. The perpetuity formula needs the dividend of the year after the one at which it stands, so the terminal value is built on 14.40 × 1.05 = ₹15.12 and comes to ₹151.20. The difference works through to ₹135.65 rather than ₹130.21.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company has just paid a dividend of ₹10 a share. Dividends are expected to grow at 20 per cent a year for the next two years and at 5 per cent a year for ever after. The required return is 15 per cent.

items.stem: What is the growth rate, and what is the share worth?

options.text: Growth of 10.8 per cent, giving a value of about ₹211.05
options.why: The retention ratio is 1 − 0.40 = 0.60, so growth is 0.60 × 18 = 10.8 per cent. The dividend just paid was 40 per cent of ₹20, that is ₹8, and next year's is 8 × 1.108 = ₹8.864. The value is 8.864 / (0.15 − 0.108) = 8.864 / 0.042 = about ₹211.05.

options.text: Growth of 10.8 per cent, giving a value of about ₹190.48
options.misconception: puts the dividend just paid into the formula instead of next year's, which understates the value by one year of growth
options.why: 8 / 0.042 = ₹190.48 uses the ₹8 dividend just paid. The buyer of the share today does not receive it; the first dividend he receives is 8 × 1.108 = ₹8.864. The growth rate is right and the numerator is a year stale, which costs about ₹20 a share.

options.text: Growth of 7.2 per cent, giving a value of about ₹109.95
options.misconception: multiplies the return on equity by the payout ratio instead of the retention ratio, so a generous dividend appears to be the source of growth
options.why: 0.40 × 18 = 7.2 per cent uses the payout ratio. Money paid out as dividend leaves the company and earns nothing more for it; it is the 60 per cent retained that is reinvested at 18 per cent. Using the retention ratio gives 10.8 per cent and a value of ₹211.05 instead of ₹109.95.

options.text: Growth of 18 per cent, at which the model gives no finite value
options.misconception: takes the return on equity itself as the growth rate, forgetting that the 40 per cent paid out as dividend is not reinvested and cannot grow anything
options.why: Only the profit kept back is put to work, so growth is the retention ratio times the return on equity, 0.60 × 18 = 10.8 per cent. Setting growth at 18 per cent puts it above the required return of 15 per cent, the denominator turns negative and the model collapses — which is itself the signal that the growth rate has been overstated.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company earns a return on equity of 18 per cent and pays out 40 per cent of its earnings as dividend. Earnings per share for the year just ended were ₹20 and the required return is 15 per cent. Growth is expected to continue at the rate the company can fund from its own profits.

items.stem: What is the 10 per cent holding worth?

options.text: ₹27.50 crore
options.misconception: adds the two discounts together and applies 45 per cent to the whole figure, when the second discount applies to what is left after the first
options.why: 50 × (1 − 0.45) = ₹27.50 crore adds 20 and 25 as though they applied to the same base. They do not — the second discount applies to the ₹40 crore that survives the first, so the combined effect is 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60 and the answer is ₹30 crore. Adding discounts always overstates the fall.

options.text: ₹30 crore
options.why: Ten per cent of ₹500 crore is ₹50 crore before any adjustment. The minority discount of 20 per cent takes it to 50 × 0.80 = ₹40 crore, and the discount for lack of marketability of 25 per cent then takes that to 40 × 0.75 = ₹30 crore. Each discount bites on what is left after the other, which is why they are applied one after the other rather than added.

options.text: ₹50 crore
options.misconception: takes the arithmetic share of the whole-company value, when a small holding in an unlisted company neither controls it nor can be sold at will
options.why: ₹50 crore is a tenth of the whole. The whole carries control and the tenth does not, and a value drawn from listed comparables assumes a market the buyer of an unlisted holding does not have. The minority discount and the discount for lack of marketability are what carry the figure from ₹50 crore to ₹30 crore.

options.text: ₹40 crore
options.misconception: applies the minority discount and stops, treating an unlisted holding as though it could be sold as readily as a listed one
options.why: 50 × 0.80 = ₹40 crore applies the minority discount and allows for the holder having no control. It says nothing about his being unable to find a buyer. The two discounts answer different questions — one is about control and the other about liquidity — and both apply to a minority stake in an unlisted company, bringing it to ₹30 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A valuer values the whole of an unlisted company at ₹500 crore using multiples drawn from listed comparables. He is now asked to value a 10 per cent holding in it. The engagement terms specify a minority discount of 20 per cent and a discount for lack of marketability of 25 per cent, to be applied one after the other.

items.stem: What do the two methods give, and what does the difference represent?

options.text: Net assets ₹80 crore and capitalised earnings ₹120 crore, and the company is worth the lower of the two
options.misconception: takes the lower figure as a rule of prudence, when the two methods answer different questions and the going concern basis is the one the sale is on
options.why: Both figures are right and the conclusion is not. The net asset figure of ₹80 crore is what the business is worth broken up; a going concern earning ₹12 crore a year is worth what those earnings support, ₹120 crore. Taking the lower of the two by habit would hand the buyer the goodwill for nothing.

options.text: Net assets ₹80 crore and capitalised earnings ₹120 crore, the ₹40 crore gap being goodwill
options.why: The net asset method gives 120 − 40 = ₹80 crore, what the assets would realise less what is owed. The earnings method gives 12 / 0.10 = ₹120 crore, the maintainable profit capitalised at the rate for the risk. The ₹40 crore between them is goodwill — what the business earns over and above what its assets on their own would justify, and the reason a going concern is worth more than a breaking-up one.

options.text: Net assets ₹80 crore and capitalised earnings ₹1.20 crore
options.misconception: multiplies the maintainable profit by the capitalisation rate instead of dividing by it, which values a permanent income stream at a tenth of one year of it
options.why: 12 × 0.10 = ₹1.20 crore multiplies the maintainable profit by the rate. Capitalising means asking what sum, earning 10 per cent, would produce ₹12 crore a year — which is 12 / 0.10 = ₹120 crore. The answer must be far larger than one year's profit, never a fraction of it, and a figure below the annual earnings is the signal that the division has been inverted.

options.text: Both ₹120 crore, since the assets and the earnings agree
options.misconception: reads the gross asset figure as the value of the business, forgetting that the lenders are paid before the shareholders see anything
options.why: The ₹120 crore of assets is not the shareholders' to keep — ₹40 crore of it answers to the creditors, so the net asset method gives ₹80 crore. That it coincides with the capitalised earnings figure of ₹120 crore is a coincidence of these numbers, and treating them as agreeing hides the ₹40 crore of goodwill sitting between the two.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company's assets would realise ₹120 crore and it owes ₹40 crore. It earns a maintainable profit after tax of ₹12 crore a year, and the capitalisation rate for a business of this kind is 10 per cent. It is being sold as a going concern.

items.stem: How is the ₹12 crore shortfall borne?

options.text: The equity tranche loses its ₹5 crore and the senior tranche absorbs the remaining ₹7 crore, the mezzanine being untouched
options.misconception: skips the mezzanine tranche, when losses climb through every class below the senior one before the senior is reached at all
options.why: Losses climb one rung at a time. Once the equity tranche's ₹5 crore is gone the next rung is the mezzanine tranche, which has ₹15 crore standing between the loss and the senior paper. A ₹12 crore shortfall never reaches the senior tranche — it would take a loss above ₹20 crore to do that.

options.text: The senior tranche is paid ₹80 crore in full, the mezzanine receives ₹8 crore and loses ₹7 crore, and the equity tranche is wiped out
options.why: Collections run down the waterfall from the top. The senior tranche takes its ₹80 crore first, leaving ₹8 crore. The mezzanine tranche is next and takes all ₹8 crore of it against its ₹15 crore entitlement, so it loses ₹7 crore. Nothing is left for the equity tranche, which loses its whole ₹5 crore. Losses climb from the bottom, and 5 + 7 = ₹12 crore is the whole shortfall.

options.text: Each tranche bears the loss in proportion to its size — senior ₹9.6 crore, mezzanine ₹1.8 crore and equity ₹0.6 crore
options.misconception: shares the loss pro rata, which is what tranching exists to abolish, since equal ranking is precisely what the senior tranche is paying to avoid
options.why: 12 × 0.80, 12 × 0.15 and 12 × 0.05 spread the loss by size. That is how a single class of paper would behave, and it is exactly what tranching removes. The senior tranche accepts a lower return in exchange for being paid first, and it is untouched here because the junior classes below it absorb the entire ₹12 crore.

options.text: The senior tranche takes ₹80 crore and the mezzanine ₹15 crore in full, with the equity tranche bearing the whole ₹12 crore
options.misconception: loads the entire shortfall on the equity tranche, when that tranche is only ₹5 crore and cannot absorb more loss than its own size
options.why: The equity tranche is ₹5 crore, so ₹5 crore is the most it can lose. Paying the senior and the mezzanine in full would need 80 + 15 = ₹95 crore against collections of ₹88 crore, so the arithmetic cannot stand either. The excess loss climbs to the mezzanine tranche, which takes ₹8 crore of its ₹15 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: A pool of receivables of ₹100 crore is funded by a senior tranche of ₹80 crore, a mezzanine tranche of ₹15 crore and an equity tranche of ₹5 crore. Collections from the pool come to ₹88 crore.

items.stem: What separates internal credit enhancement from external?

options.text: Credit enhancement lifts the rating of every tranche in the deal equally
options.misconception: reads enhancement as adding safety to the whole structure, when subordination lifts the senior paper precisely by pushing loss onto the junior paper below it
options.why: Subordination moves risk about rather than adding safety. The senior tranche is rated higher because the junior tranches stand in front of it, and those junior tranches are rated lower for the same reason. What lifts one class is what depresses another, so an equal lift across the deal is not what happens.

options.text: An external guarantee makes the senior paper risk-free, since the guarantor rather than the pool stands behind it
options.misconception: forgets that an external enhancement substitutes the guarantor's credit standing for part of the pool's and can never be better than the guarantor
options.why: A guarantee is only as good as the guarantor. External enhancement swaps part of the pool's risk for the credit standing of the party giving the guarantee or the letter of credit, so the paper is capped by that party's own rating and falls with it. That dependence is the standing objection to external enhancement and the reason internal devices are preferred.

options.text: Internal enhancement uses the deal's own material — a pool larger than the paper issued, junior tranches, excess spread and a cash collateral account; external enhancement is a third party's promise, such as a guarantee or a letter of credit
options.why: Internal credit enhancement is built out of the transaction itself. Overcollateralisation transfers a pool worth more than the paper issued, junior tranches take loss first, excess spread is the surplus of pool interest over what the paper pays, and a cash collateral account is money set aside inside the structure. External enhancement brings in a third party by guarantee or letter of credit, and the paper then depends on that party staying solvent.

options.text: Overcollateralisation means the vehicle holds cash equal to the securities it has issued
options.misconception: confuses overcollateralisation with a cash reserve, when it means the receivables transferred are worth more than the paper issued against them
options.why: Overcollateralisation is about the pool, not about cash. Receivables worth more than the securities issued are transferred to the vehicle, so ordinary losses are absorbed by the surplus before any investor is touched. Cash set aside is a separate device, the cash collateral account, and holding cash equal to the paper would defeat the purpose of raising it.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: An originator wants the senior paper from a securitisation rated above its own corporate rating, and is offered several ways of achieving it.

items.stem: What has the plan produced?

options.text: 1,000 units at an average cost of ₹24.75
options.misconception: buys the same number of units each month rather than investing the same sum, which lands the investor exactly on the simple average of the prices
options.why: Buying 250 units a month gives 1,000 units for 250 × (30 + 25 + 20 + 24) = ₹24,750, an average cost of ₹24.75. That is the simple average of the prices, and it is what a fixed number of units produces. A fixed sum buys more units when the price is low, which is what drags the average cost down to ₹24.24.

options.text: 990 units, and the plan cannot lose, because buying more units when prices fall guarantees a gain
options.misconception: mistakes a lower average cost for a guaranteed profit, when averaging only beats the simple average of the prices and does nothing to make the price recover
options.why: What averaging guarantees is that the average cost, ₹24.24, comes out below the simple average of the prices paid, ₹24.75. It guarantees nothing about where the price ends up. Here it ends at ₹24, below the average cost, and the plan is ₹240 down despite the averaging having worked exactly as advertised.

options.text: 990 units at an average cost of about ₹24.24, and a holding worth ₹23,760 — a loss of ₹240
options.why: The instalments buy 6,000 / 30 = 200 units, then 240, then 300, then 250 — 990 units in all for ₹24,000, an average cost of 24,000 / 990 = ₹24.24. That is below the simple average of the four net asset values, (30 + 25 + 20 + 24) / 4 = ₹24.75, because more units were bought when the price was low. At ₹24 the holding is worth 990 × 24 = ₹23,760, so the plan is ₹240 down.

options.text: 990 units, and the investor is ahead, since the closing value of ₹24 is above the ₹20 paid at the low point
options.misconception: judges the plan against its best instalment rather than against the average cost of all four
options.why: The ₹20 instalment was one of four. What the investor paid on the whole holding is the average cost of ₹24.24, and the closing net asset value of ₹24 is below it, so he is ₹240 down. Measuring against the cheapest purchase would make almost every plan look successful.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: An investor puts ₹6,000 into a scheme on the first of each month for four months. The net asset values on those four dates are ₹30, ₹25, ₹20 and ₹24, and the value on the last of them is also the value at which the holding stands today.

items.stem: How does the loss fall under each form of consideration?

options.text: Under the cash deal Q Ltd's shareholders lose ₹11.25 crore of the price they were promised
options.misconception: attaches the share exchange's loss to the cash alternative, when a cash price is fixed on signing and the seller has no further exposure to the outcome
options.why: ₹11.25 crore is what Q Ltd's shareholders lose under the share exchange, where they still own a slice of the combined company. Under the cash deal they were paid ₹180 crore and walked away, so whatever happens afterwards is nothing to do with them and the entire ₹30 crore falls on P Ltd's shareholders.

options.text: The two are identical, since both hand Q Ltd's shareholders ₹180 crore
options.misconception: reads the share offer as a fixed amount, when it is a fixed proportion whose value moves with whatever the combined company turns out to be worth
options.why: The two are identical only if the combined company really is worth ₹800 crore. Cash fixes an amount; a share exchange fixes a proportion, and 22.5 per cent of ₹750 crore is ₹168.75 crore rather than ₹180 crore. The moment the outcome differs from the forecast the two forms of consideration part company.

options.text: Under the share exchange P Ltd's shareholders bear the whole ₹50 crore shortfall, since shares once issued cannot be taken back
options.misconception: reverses the effect of issuing shares, which is precisely what makes the incoming shareholders share the disappointment rather than escape it
options.why: Issuing shares is what spreads the loss. Q Ltd's shareholders now own 22.5 per cent of the combined company, so 22.5 per cent of every rupee of disappointment is theirs — ₹11.25 crore of it. P Ltd's shareholders carry ₹18.75 crore. It is the cash deal, where nothing is shared, that leaves the acquirer holding the whole ₹30 crore.

options.text: Under cash P Ltd's shareholders lose the whole ₹30 crore; under the share exchange they lose ₹18.75 crore and Q Ltd's shareholders lose ₹11.25 crore
options.why: With cash, Q Ltd's shareholders take ₹180 crore and go, leaving P Ltd's shareholders with 750 − 180 = ₹570 crore against ₹600 crore standalone, a loss of ₹30 crore. Under the share exchange, Q Ltd's shareholders hold 22.5 per cent of ₹750 crore, that is ₹168.75 crore, so they lose ₹11.25 crore of the ₹180 crore forecast, and P Ltd's shareholders keep ₹581.25 crore and lose ₹18.75 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: P Ltd is worth ₹600 crore on its own and Q Ltd ₹150 crore on its own. P Ltd forecasts a combined value of ₹800 crore. It offers Q Ltd's shareholders either ₹180 crore in cash, or shares giving them 22.5 per cent of the combined company — which on the forecast is also worth ₹180 crore. In the event no synergy at all arrives and the combined company is worth only ₹750 crore.

items.stem: How does the study material classify the two approaches?

options.text: The first is technical analysis and the second is fundamental analysis
options.misconception: swaps the two labels
options.why: The labels run the other way round. Reading growth, inflation, an industry's demand and a company's margins is fundamental analysis; reading a chart of price and traded volume is technical analysis.

options.text: Both are technical analysis, since both work from published data
options.misconception: separates the two by where the number was published rather than by what the number is about
options.why: Fundamental analysis uses published financial and economic data; technical analysis uses market data alone — price, volume and open interest. What separates them is the subject matter, not whether somebody printed the figures.

options.text: Only the first is analysis; the second is guesswork with no stated method
options.misconception: dismisses technical analysis instead of describing it
options.why: Technical analysis has three stated principles — the market discounts everything, price moves in trends, and history tends to repeat itself — and the study material sets it out as one of the two approaches to security analysis. Whether it works is a separate argument from what it is.

options.text: The first is fundamental analysis and the second is technical analysis
options.why: Fundamental analysis works from the economy to the industry to the company to reach an intrinsic value, and recommends buying where the market price sits below it. Technical analysis reads price and volume alone, on the assumptions that price discounts everything, that prices move in trends and that history tends to repeat itself.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: Two analysts study the same share. The first works through the country's growth rate and inflation, then the industry's demand supply gap, then the company's margins and net worth. The second looks only at a chart of the share's daily price and traded volume over two years.

items.stem: Which type of risk does this illustrate?

options.text: Compliance risk
options.misconception: reaches for the regulatory label wherever a company suffers a loss
options.why: Compliance risk is the risk of failing the rules and regulations a business must live under, and it bites hardest when a company enters a new state or a new line of business under laws it does not know. No rule was broken here.

options.text: Financial risk
options.misconception: calls the money consequence the risk itself
options.why: Financial risk is unexpected change in financial conditions — prices, exchange rates, interest rates, credit standing. The collapse in sales is what the strategic failure cost, not a movement in a financial variable.

options.text: Strategic risk
options.why: Strategic risk is a strategy becoming less effective so the company struggles to reach its goals — technological change, a new competitor, a shift in customer demand. Shelving its own digital camera is the study material's own worked example of exactly this.

options.text: Operational risk
options.misconception: files a failure of direction under a failure of daily running
options.why: Operational risk is people and process going wrong in the day-to-day running — the clerk who pays ₹1,00,000 where ₹10,000 was due. Nothing in the running failed here; the running was fine and the direction was not.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: A camera maker builds a working digital camera in its own laboratory and shelves it, because selling it would eat into the film business that pays for everything. Ten years on, rivals sell digital cameras, film sales collapse and the company never recovers.

items.stem: Which structure fits?

options.text: An interval scheme
options.misconception: reads a periodic window as continuous access
options.why: An interval scheme opens for purchase and redemption only during pre-specified intervals — monthly, quarterly, annually. Between those windows the investor is locked in, and "at any time" is precisely what he said he needed.

options.text: An open-ended scheme
options.why: An open-ended scheme lets the investor enter and exit at any time. Its capital is unlimited and its redemption period indefinite, and the fund itself buys the units back at a price based on NAV — which is both conditions he asked for.
keywords: enter and exit at any time

options.text: Any of the three, since every mutual fund buys its own units back on demand
options.misconception: assumes redemption on demand is a feature of all mutual funds
options.why: Only the open-ended structure buys its own units back on demand. That single difference is what the functional classification of mutual funds is drawn on, and it is why the question has an answer at all.

options.text: A close-ended scheme
options.misconception: treats a listing on an exchange as the same thing as redemption by the fund
options.why: A close-ended scheme has a fixed life and a fixed corpus. Before maturity the only way out is to sell to another buyer on the stock exchange at whatever the market offers, which can sit well below NAV. The fund is not the counterparty.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: An investor says he may need his money at any time and wants a scheme that will buy his units back itself, at a price tied to the value of what the fund holds.

items.stem: Which source of startup finance is built for exactly this position?

options.text: Crowdfunding
options.misconception: picks the best-known modern source instead of the one that matches the shortage
options.why: Crowdfunding gathers small amounts of capital from a large number of individuals through social media and crowdfunding websites to finance a new business initiative. It funds an idea over weeks of campaigning; it does not put material into a supplier's hands against one confirmed order.

options.text: Purchase order financing
options.why: Purchase order financing exists for the startup that has found a large new order and lacks the cash to produce and deliver against it. The financier advances the funds directly to the supplier so the goods can be made, and is repaid out of the transaction the order completes.

options.text: Microloans
options.misconception: takes a small-ticket source to a need sized by the order
options.why: Microloans are small loans given at lower interest rates by an individual, or by several individuals each contributing a portion. The small size is the whole point of them, and an order large enough for the bank to refuse is not what they are for.

options.text: Factoring of accounts receivable
options.misconception: funds money already earned when what is needed is money for production not yet done
options.why: Factoring advances most of an amount already outstanding on a credit sale and pays the balance when the customer settles. Here nothing has been delivered, so there is no receivable to sell — the cash is needed before the invoice can exist.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A two-year-old manufacturer has just won its largest ever order from a retail chain. It has no cash to buy the raw material and produce the goods, and the bank has refused a working capital limit for want of a track record. Nothing has been delivered and no invoice has been raised.

items.stem: What do the two findings together say about this market's efficiency?

options.text: Semi-strong efficient, but not weak form efficient
options.misconception: treats the three forms as independent tests rather than nested ones
options.why: The levels nest. Semi-strong includes everything the weak form covers, because past prices are themselves public information, so no market can pass the higher test and fail the lower one. This combination cannot exist.

options.text: Nothing, since efficiency is about whether prices are fair and not about whether anyone can profit
options.misconception: separates efficiency from the returns it is actually defined by
options.why: Efficiency is tested exactly by whether abnormal returns can be earned from a stated set of information after adjusting for risk. That is what the serial correlation, run and filter rule tests measure at the weak level, and what the announcement studies measure at the semi-strong level.

options.text: Strong form efficient
options.misconception: jumps to the top level on evidence about the bottom one
options.why: Strong form efficiency means price reflects all information, private as well as public, so even corporate insiders would earn nothing extra. The finding here is that even public information still pays, which is two levels short of that.

options.text: Weak form efficient, but not semi-strong efficient
options.why: Weak form efficiency means price already reflects everything in the record of past prices and volumes, so chart study pays nothing — which is the first finding. The semi-strong level adds all other publicly available information, and an earnings announcement is public, so a trader still profiting from it says that level has not been reached.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A researcher finds two things in the same market. A trader who studies past price charts and volumes earns nothing above the market after adjusting for risk. A trader who acts on an earnings announcement in the minutes after it is published still earns an abnormal return.

items.stem: What did the analysis leave out?

options.text: The economy and industry stages, which come before company analysis
options.why: Fundamental analysis is three concentric circles worked from the outside in — economy analysis, then industry analysis, then company analysis. A company's fortunes are tied to its industry and the industry's to the economy, so a contracting economy and a demand supply gap in the industry sink a good company along with a bad one.

options.text: Nothing — a low price earnings ratio against peers is a complete case on its own
options.misconception: treats one ratio as the whole of company analysis
options.why: The study material warns that the price earnings ratio should in theory be alike for two similar companies and in practice never is, and that EPS cannot be the sole basis of an investment decision. A low multiple is a question to be answered, not the answer.

options.text: The quality of management, which is the only company factor that matters
options.misconception: elevates one company-level factor above the framework it belongs to
options.why: Quality of management is one company-level factor among many — net worth, growth record, competitive advantage, corporate governance, marketability of the shares — and it is the one thing the analyst did look at. Naming it as the answer leaves the economy and the industry out for a second time.

options.text: Technical analysis, since a price chart would have shown the fall coming
options.misconception: replaces the missing layers of one method with a different method altogether
options.why: A chart might well have shown a downtrend, but the gap sits inside fundamental analysis itself — two of its three layers were never worked. Technical analysis is the alternative approach, not the missing stage of this one.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: An analyst decides a company is well run and cheap on its price earnings ratio against its peers, and buys. The economy is contracting and the industry is running with heavy surplus capacity. The share falls anyway.

items.stem: What does the advanced role of the CFO now cover?

options.text: Nothing beyond that list, which already describes the whole role
options.misconception: keeps the CFO inside the role the material calls traditional
options.why: Governance, compliance, controls and business ethics are named as the traditional role and are still carried. The point of the chapter is what has been added on top of them, driven by globalisation, the growth of information and communications, and the pandemic.

options.text: A new objective, since wealth maximisation for shareholders is no longer the goal
options.misconception: reads a widened job as a changed objective
options.why: Wealth maximisation is still the objective. What the chapter says has changed is the range of responsibilities used to reach it, and it adds that the value creation is now expected to be sustainable over a longer period. The goal held still; the work did not.

options.text: Day-to-day marketing and product design, since finance pays for them
options.misconception: stretches the expanded role into functions the material never gives it
options.why: The expansion named is into risk, the supply chain, mergers and sustainability financing — places where money is the deciding constraint. Funding a function is not running it, and the chapter puts marketing at the functional level of strategy rather than on the CFO's desk.

options.text: The risk management framework, the financial viability of the supply chain, mergers and restructuring, and ESG financing
options.why: The four areas the role has grown into are the overall risk management framework of the organisation, the financial viability of the supply chain, mergers and corporate restructuring, and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) financing — the shift from traditional financing to sustainability financing. Together they make the CFO a leader in value creation.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

items.scenario: A board is rewriting its CFO's job description after the pandemic. It already lists governance, compliance, controls, business ethics and financial reporting, and asks what the study material says has been added to that in recent years.

items.stem: What does a technical analyst expect near ₹125, and what would a clean move above it mean?

options.text: A move above ₹125 confirms the range, so the share should return towards ₹100
options.misconception: treats a breakout as evidence that the old band still holds
options.why: A breach is the evidence against the range, not for it. Once the price passes the resistance level convincingly, the analyst stops expecting the old band and starts looking for newer levels to form.

options.text: Selling pressure at ₹125, which is the resistance level; a clean breach signals a departure from the range and an attempt at new levels
options.why: The peak a price falls away from becomes the resistance level, because every holder who failed to sell at the high is keen to liquidate there. The trough it rebounds from becomes the support level. A breach of either indicates a distinct departure from the status quo and an attempt to set newer levels.

options.text: Nothing in particular, since support and resistance are one line described twice
options.misconception: collapses two levels doing opposite jobs into a single idea
options.why: They are two different prices doing opposite work. ₹100 is the support level below, where buying appears; ₹125 is the resistance level above, where selling appears. The price is expected to travel between them.

options.text: Buying pressure at ₹125, since a rising price draws buyers in
options.misconception: reads momentum into a level the pattern says is made of supply
options.why: Momentum is not what the level is built from. ₹125 is where the holders who wish they had sold last time will sell, and that supply is exactly what has turned the price back before.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A share fell from a peak of ₹125, traded down to ₹100 and rebounded, and for two months has moved between those two prices. It is now at ₹123 and rising.

items.stem: Which obstacle is this, and what does the study material say about it?

options.text: Lack of standardisation, of which the duty is a symptom
options.misconception: relabels a tax cost as a documentation problem
options.why: Lack of standardisation is that every originator follows its own format for documentation and administration, so no two deals read alike and each has to be understood from scratch. It slows the market; it is not what a stamp office charges for.

options.text: Stamp duty, and a pass through certificate escapes it because it evidences a receivable rather than a debt
options.why: Stamp duty on a mortgage debt under the Transfer of Property Act is named first among the problems holding securitisation back in India. The material adds that a pass through certificate does not evidence any debt but only a receivable, so it is exempt, and that some states have reduced the duty on securitised instruments.

options.text: Ineffective foreclosure laws, which are the reason the duty is charged
options.misconception: joins two separate obstacles into a cause and an effect
options.why: Foreclosure laws are a separate item on the same list. Weak ones make it hard for a lender to take the property when a borrower defaults, which makes mortgage backed securities less attractive to investors. They have nothing to do with why a transfer attracts duty.

options.text: Taxation, and the SPV will certainly be taxed as an entity on the pool's whole income
options.misconception: turns an unsettled tax question into a settled rule
options.why: Taxation is on the list precisely because it is unsettled. There is no specific provision for securitised instruments, and expert opinion divides between taxing the SPV in a representative capacity and taxing the investors on their share. Certainty is what nobody has here.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: A finance company in India wants to securitise a pool of housing loans. Its counsel warns that transferring the mortgage debt to the special purpose vehicle will attract a duty running into double digits as a percentage in some states, and asks whether the instrument chosen changes that.

items.stem: At which level of strategy does each decision sit?

options.text: All three are corporate, because the group board approved all three
options.misconception: reads the level of strategy off who signed rather than off what was decided
options.why: The level is a property of the question, not of the approver. Senior management decides strategy, middle management tactics and line management operations, but a board approving a departmental system does not turn that system into a decision about which businesses to be in.

options.text: Corporate, functional and business unit, in that order
options.misconception: swaps the last two levels
options.why: Pricing against a rival to hold share is competitive advantage for one unit's products, which is business unit level. A treasury system is a departmental process, which is functional level. Reversing them puts a departmental process above a competitive decision.

options.text: Corporate, business unit and functional, in that order
options.why: Corporate level strategy selects the businesses a company competes in and coordinates that portfolio, so cement against chemicals is corporate. Business unit level strategy is about sustaining competitive advantage for one unit's products, which is the paints pricing question. Functional level strategy sits in the operating divisions and departments, and a treasury system is exactly that.

options.text: Business unit, business unit and functional, since a group of divisions has no corporate level
options.misconception: denies the corporate level to a group that is organised into divisions
options.why: The corporate level is exactly what a group of several divisions has, and its whole job is which businesses to be in and how the portfolio fits together. Selling one division to enter a different industry is that decision and no other.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

items.scenario: One group board meeting settles three things. Whether to sell the cement division and enter speciality chemicals. How the paints unit should price against its nearest rival to hold share. Whether the treasury department should move to a new cash-pooling system.

items.stem: How does the Dow Theory classify the three, and what can it tell the investor?

options.text: The four-week fall ended the bull market, because the direction reversed
options.misconception: reads a secondary movement as a change in the primary one
options.why: A secondary movement is opposite in direction to the primary by definition — that is what makes it a correction rather than a reversal. Under the theory the trend turns when successive highs and successive lows are both lower, not when one four-week fall happens.

options.text: Primary movement, secondary movement and daily fluctuations — and it gives direction only, never how far
options.why: The primary movement is the main trend, running from a year to thirty-six months or longer, and it is what bull or bear names. The secondary movement is shorter and runs opposite to it. The daily fluctuations are the narrow day-to-day moves. The theory's stated purpose is to say where the market is and where it is going, although not how far or high.

options.text: It will give the level the index should reach before the primary movement ends
options.misconception: expects a magnitude from a theory that offers only direction
options.why: The theory determines where the market is and where it is going, and the material says plainly that it does not say how far or high. Direction without magnitude is the limit of what it claims, and reading a target out of it is reading something that is not there.

options.text: The daily moves carry the signal, since they are the most recent evidence
options.misconception: prefers the freshest data to the trend the theory is actually built on
options.why: The daily fluctuations are explicitly no part of the Dow Theory's interpretation of the market. They are watched only because they add up to the longer movement; on their own they say nothing about where the market is going.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A market index has risen for eighteen months. Inside that stretch there was a four-week fall of 12 per cent, and there have been moves of about a per cent either way almost every day throughout.

items.stem: What pattern is this, and what does a fall below ₹150 imply?

options.text: A head and shoulders top; a fall below the neckline is a sell signal, with a drop of about ₹70 expected
options.why: The left shoulder at ₹180, the head at ₹220 and the right shoulder at ₹182 form a head and shoulders top, the single most important pattern for a reversal of trend. The neckline joins the points where head and shoulders meet, here ₹150, and the drop expected equals the distance from the top of the head to it — ₹220 less ₹150.

options.text: A triangle or coil, so the direction cannot be predicted
options.misconception: reaches for the pattern of uncertainty instead of reading the one on the chart
options.why: A triangle or coil is the formation the material describes as a pattern of uncertainty, where it is difficult to predict which way the price will break out. Three peaks around a higher middle one is not that shape; it is the reversal pattern with the clearest published reading of the lot.

options.text: A double top, complete at ₹182, so the level at ₹150 does not matter
options.misconception: names a two-peak pattern where there are three, and drops the level the signal depends on
options.why: A double top has two peaks of about the same height; this has three, with the middle one clearly highest, which is the head. And the price movement after the second shoulder is precisely what is crucial — the signal is the break of the level at ₹150, not the shoulder.

options.text: An inverse head and shoulders, so the fall below ₹150 confirms a coming rise
options.misconception: applies the inverted pattern's reading to the upright one
options.why: An inverse head and shoulders has its head as the lowest point between two higher troughs, and there it is a rise above the neck line that signals a purchase. Here the head is the highest point of the three, so this is the top formation and its signal runs downward.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A share chart shows a rise to ₹180, a fall to ₹150, a rise to ₹220, a fall back to ₹150, and a rise to ₹182 followed by a decline. The line joining the two troughs sits at ₹150.

items.stem: How does the study material classify these four?

options.text: Only the last is financial risk; the other three are operational risks
options.misconception: narrows financial risk down to a shortage of cash
options.why: Operational risk is people and process inside the company — a payment made for the wrong amount. A government blocking remittances, a customer defaulting and a rate resetting are all changes in financial conditions arriving from outside, which is what the chapter means by financial risk.

options.text: They are four separate risk types, so none of them is financial risk
options.misconception: treats the sub-categories as rivals to the heading above them
options.why: Financial risk is the heading and these are its categories, not alternatives to it. The chapter's other headings — strategic risk, compliance risk and operational risk — sit beside financial risk, and not one of these four belongs under them.

options.text: The conversion restriction is currency risk rather than political risk
options.misconception: files a government action under the exposure that action happens to touch
options.why: Currency risk is exchange rate movement changing cash flows. A restriction on converting the local currency is an adverse action by the host government, which the chapter lists under political risk beside confiscation, rationing of remittance and price control of products.

options.text: Political, counter party, interest rate and liquidity risk — all four are categories of financial risk
