options.why: Overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality is where SA 220 (Revised) starts, not where it stops. The standard asks that direction, supervision and review be responsive to the nature and circumstances of the engagement, so a protocol identical for a dormant company and for a goodwill impairment worked by an article assistant fails by never varying.
keywords: overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality
responsive to the nature and circumstances

options.text: Only the timing of the report — how work is reviewed is a matter for the firm's system of quality management under SQC 1, not for this engagement
options.misconception: pushes engagement-level direction, supervision and review up into the firm's system, when SA 220 places it on the engagement partner
options.why: SQC 1 governs the firm's system and SA 220 (Revised) governs this audit. The requirements on direction, supervision and review sit on the engagement partner for this engagement, and delegating the work never delegates the responsibility for quality on it.

options.text: Three things — the hardest judgements were worked by a less experienced team member without direction, supervision and review by more experienced ones; the partner reviewed no documentation on those judgements himself; and the report was dated before the engagement quality review was complete
options.why: SA 220 (Revised) requires direction, supervision and review to be planned and performed on the basis that the work of less experienced engagement team members is directed, supervised and reviewed by more experienced engagement team members, and it requires the engagement partner to review the audit documentation relating to significant matters and significant judgements, including difficult or contentious matters, and the conclusions reached. A flat manual that sends every file through the same review has stopped responding to the nature and circumstances of the engagement. And where an engagement quality review is required, the auditor's report is not dated until the partner is notified that it is complete.
keywords: nature and circumstances of the engagement

citation.ref: para 13, with the requirements on direction, supervision and review and on the completion of an engagement quality review before the auditor's report is dated

items.scenario: A firm's manual gives every audit file the same review: the manager reviews all working papers, the partner reviews the manager's memo and the draft report, and nothing else. On this engagement the goodwill impairment model, a disputed ₹22 crore tax position and the revenue cut-off conclusion were all worked and concluded by a first-year article assistant, and the manager's memo says "no exceptions". The partner signs the report the same evening the engagement quality reviewer receives the file.

items.stem: What does SA 299 (Revised) require?

options.text: A had to communicate the scrap sale to both B and C in writing before the audit was completed, and he is not bound by the majority — a joint auditor in disagreement expresses his own opinion in a separate audit report
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) makes coordination a written duty: a joint auditor who comes across matters relevant to the areas of responsibility of other joint auditors, or requiring discussion with or the application of judgement by them, communicates those matters to all the other joint auditors in writing prior to the completion of the audit — and a telephone call to one of the three is neither in writing nor to all of them. On the opinion the joint auditors are not a committee. A joint auditor is not bound by the views of the majority, and where he disagrees he expresses his opinion in a separate audit report.
keywords: in writing prior to the completion of the audit
not bound by the views of the majority

options.text: A's call to C discharged the coordination duty, C owning the related party listing and A's only obligation running to the auditor whose area the matter touched
options.misconception: narrows a communication owed to all the other joint auditors down to one of them, and drops the requirement that it be in writing
options.why: The requirement runs to all the other joint auditors, not to whichever one seems closest, and it is a communication in writing prior to the completion of the audit. B audits the south plants, where the same vendor may well appear, and an oral mention leaves nothing on any file.
keywords: in writing prior to the completion of the audit

options.text: A should press for a qualification, but responsibility for the missed related party is C's alone, the head office having been divided to him
options.misconception: uses the division of work to move a matter one joint auditor actually found onto the auditor in whose area it fell
options.why: Division fixes who performs the work, and each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to him. It does not excuse a joint auditor who has himself come across a matter deserving the others' attention from communicating it, and it does not decide the opinion, which each joint auditor forms for himself.

options.text: A must sign the common report — joint auditors issue one report, and a dissent that splits it defeats the purpose of appointing joint auditors
options.misconception: makes the common report compulsory, when SA 299 provides for a separate report precisely where the joint auditors disagree
options.why: The common report is what joint auditors issue when they agree. SA 299 (Revised) provides for the other case in terms: where the joint auditors are in disagreement with regard to the opinion or any matters to be covered by the audit report, the dissenting joint auditor expresses his opinion in a separate audit report.

citation.ref: the coordination requirement to communicate in writing to all the other joint auditors prior to the completion of the audit, and the separate audit report on disagreement, read with the division of responsibility at para 13 and para 14

items.scenario: Three firms are joint auditors of a company and the work is divided by location: A takes the north plants, B the south plants, C the head office and the financial statements. Working at a north plant, A finds a ₹34 crore scrap sale routed through a vendor that C's related party listing does not carry, and mentions it to C on a telephone call. At the report stage B and C are satisfied with an unmodified opinion; A believes a qualification is required. B and C tell A that two out of three settles it and that he must sign the common report.

items.stem: Which of the three may the auditor rely on as it stands?

options.text: The invoice test — fifty items traced to despatch notes with no exceptions is sufficient appropriate audit evidence over receivables
options.misconception: reads sufficiency as curing a relevance failure, when a procedure that does not test the assertion answers nothing however many items it covers
options.why: Sufficiency is the measure of quantity and appropriateness the measure of quality, and quality begins with relevance. A test running from the recorded population outwards can never reach an unrecorded sale, so five hundred items would answer completeness no better than fifty.

options.text: The customer statements — they originated outside the entity, and evidence from an independent external source is the most reliable category there is
options.misconception: keeps the external-source generalisation while ignoring that the document reached the auditor as a photocopy and through the client's own hands
options.why: Evidence from independent sources outside the entity is more reliable, but that generalisation sits beside two others: evidence obtained directly by the auditor is more reliable than evidence obtained indirectly, and an original document is more reliable than a photocopy. A statement downloaded by the credit controller and handed over as a photocopy has lost both.

options.text: None of them — the invoice test is not relevant to completeness, the ageing report is information produced by the entity whose accuracy has not been tested, and a photocopy routed through the client is neither an original nor obtained directly by the auditor
options.why: Relevance is the connection between the procedure and the assertion. Selecting from the sales ledger and tracing outwards tests occurrence, because a sale never recorded is not in the population sampled from, so it cannot test completeness. Agreeing an ageing report's total to the trial balance says nothing about whether the buckets are right, and SA 500 requires the auditor using information produced by the entity to obtain audit evidence about the accuracy and completeness of the information and to evaluate whether it is sufficiently precise and detailed. And evidence obtained directly by the auditor is more reliable than evidence obtained indirectly, while an original document is more reliable than a photocopy.

options.text: The ageing report — it came out of the system rather than from a person, and a system-generated report needs no further testing
options.misconception: treats a report as reliable because a system printed it, when the report is still information produced by the entity
options.why: A report is information produced by the entity whether a clerk typed it or the system generated it. Its reliability turns on the controls over that system and on the parameters the report was run with, and SA 500 asks for audit evidence about its accuracy and completeness before it is used.

citation.ref: para 7 and para 9

items.scenario: To test whether trade receivables are complete, the senior selects fifty invoices from the sales ledger and traces each to a despatch note. To support the ageing, he takes the ageing report the client's system printed on 2 April, ties its grand total to the trial balance, and does nothing further with it. To confirm three large balances he accepts photocopies of customer statements that the client's credit controller downloaded from the customers' portals.

items.stem: What does SA 505 require?

options.text: Accept the documents offered — contracts, despatch records and the ledger are alternative procedures, and performing them deals with the refusal
options.misconception: stops at the alternative procedures and drops the inquiry into the reasons and the evaluation of what the refusal itself means
options.why: Alternative audit procedures are one of the three steps, not all of them. The refusal is itself audit evidence about the risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and here it sits on top of an undisclosed related party — which is exactly what the evaluation step exists to catch.

options.text: Send the requests anyway — the auditor controls the confirmation process, and management has no standing to withhold permission
options.misconception: reads control over the process as a power to override the entity's refusal, which SA 505 answers with a procedure instead
options.why: The auditor does control the external confirmation process — determining the information to be confirmed, selecting the confirming party, designing the requests and sending them. Control does not extend to writing to a customer over the entity's objection. SA 505 answers a refusal by inquiring, evaluating and performing alternative audit procedures, and by taking an unreasonable refusal to those charged with governance.

options.text: Inquire into the reasons and seek evidence as to their validity and reasonableness, evaluate what the refusal does to your risk assessment, perform alternative procedures — and, the brother's directorship making the refusal look unreasonable, communicate with those charged with governance and determine the implications for the opinion
options.why: SA 505 sets three steps on a refusal: inquire as to management's reasons for the refusal and seek audit evidence as to their validity and reasonableness; evaluate the implications of the refusal on the assessment of the relevant risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and on the nature, timing and extent of other audit procedures; and perform alternative audit procedures designed to obtain relevant and reliable audit evidence. Where the auditor concludes that the refusal is unreasonable, or the alternative procedures do not deliver, he communicates with those charged with governance and determines the implications for the audit and for the auditor's opinion.

options.text: Treat the refusal as a management-imposed limitation and disclaim an opinion at once, ₹47 crore being material
options.misconception: jumps from a refusal to a disclaimer, skipping the alternative procedures and the grading of the possible effects
options.why: A refusal may well end in a modified opinion, but not before the alternative audit procedures have been attempted and the effect graded. SA 705 (Revised) disclaims only where the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive; ₹47 crore of receivables in an entity of unstated size has not been shown to be pervasive, and a qualification may be the answer.

citation.ref: para 8 and para 9

items.scenario: You select eleven customers for positive confirmation. The finance director refuses to let you write to two of them — ₹47 crore between them — saying both are in commercial negotiations and a letter would sour the relationship. He offers the sales contracts, the despatch records and the ledger for both instead. Your inquiries then establish that one of the two is a company in which the finance director's brother is a director, a fact that appears nowhere in the related party disclosures.

items.stem: What does SA 540 (Revised) require you to do with that pattern?

options.text: Evaluate whether the judgements and decisions management made, even though each is individually reasonable, are indicators of possible management bias, and evaluate the implications for the audit
options.why: SA 540 (Revised) runs two evaluations. One asks whether the accounting estimates and related disclosures are reasonable in the context of the applicable financial reporting framework or are misstated. The other asks whether the judgements and decisions made by management in making those estimates, even if they are individually reasonable, are indicators of possible management bias — and four changes in one year all moving profit the same way is what that second question exists for. Where such indicators are identified the auditor evaluates the implications for the audit, and an intention to mislead makes the bias fraudulent in nature.

options.text: Treat the four as misstatements and accumulate them under SA 450, an indicator of bias being a misstatement by definition
options.misconception: converts an indicator of possible bias into a misstatement, when the standard says such indicators do not themselves constitute misstatements for concluding on individual estimates
options.why: SA 540 (Revised) says indicators of possible management bias do not themselves constitute misstatements for the purpose of drawing conclusions on the reasonableness of individual accounting estimates. Each of these four amounts sits inside a supportable range, so there is no difference to accumulate; what the pattern changes is the assessment of risk, not the schedule of uncorrected misstatements.

options.text: Report a suspected fraud to the Central Government under section 143(12), management bias being fraud by another name
options.misconception: leaps from an indicator of possible bias to a fraud report, without the intention to mislead the standard requires or the reason to believe an offence of fraud the section requires
options.why: Management bias becomes fraudulent in nature where there is an intention to mislead, and nothing here has established one — four favourable judgements are a reason to look, not a conclusion. Section 143(12) is engaged where the auditor has reason to believe that an offence of fraud is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees, which is a higher and separate finding.
keywords: reason to believe that an offence of fraud

options.text: Nothing — each estimate falls inside a supportable range and is backed by a memo, so each is reasonable and the audit's question about them has been answered
options.misconception: stops at the reasonableness of each estimate taken alone, which is the evaluation the standard deliberately puts a second one beside
options.why: Reasonableness of the individual estimates is one evaluation, and the standard adds another precisely because judgements can be individually reasonable and still be indicators of possible management bias. Answering only the first question guarantees the pattern is never seen, because the pattern does not live inside any one estimate.

citation.ref: the evaluation of whether management's judgements and decisions are indicators of possible management bias, read with the retrospective review at para 14

items.scenario: Profit before tax fell 60 per cent this year. Four things happened in the accounts. The warranty provision was set at ₹2.1 crore, the bottom of a supportable range of ₹2.1 crore to ₹3.4 crore, having sat at the top of that range for three years. The useful life of the moulding line was extended from eight years to twelve. An impairment indicator on a subsidiary was acknowledged and the test deferred to the first quarter of next year. The expected credit loss rate on the oldest receivable bucket was cut from 40 per cent to 25 per cent. Each change is supported by a management memo you find reasonable, and each amount sits inside a range you can support.

items.stem: Has the opinion been formed as SA 700 (Revised) requires?

options.text: No, but only the title needs fixing — the policy and the disaggregation are presentation choices belonging to management, not to the auditor
options.misconception: hands the appropriateness of accounting policies and the adequacy of disclosure back to management, when SA 700 makes both part of the auditor's own evaluation
options.why: Management prepares the financial statements; the auditor evaluates them. SA 700 (Revised) requires the auditor to evaluate whether the accounting policies selected and applied are consistent with the framework and are appropriate, and whether adequate disclosures enable users to understand the effect of material transactions and events. Neither question is answered by calling it management's choice.

options.text: Yes — the procedures are complete and the uncorrected misstatement is far below materiality, which is what forming an opinion means
options.misconception: treats the conclusions on evidence and on uncorrected misstatements as the whole of forming an opinion, dropping the evaluation of the financial statements themselves
options.why: Those two conclusions are steps in SA 700 (Revised), not the whole of it. The auditor also evaluates whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, including the qualitative aspects of the entity's accounting practices. A file with no open points can still sit under a set of financial statements that do not comply.
keywords: qualitative aspects of the entity's accounting practices

options.text: No, but the answer is an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing users' attention to the accounting policy and to the single-line revenue disclosure
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter where the matter is a departure from the framework, which is a misstatement calling for a modified opinion
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and SA 706 (Revised) allows one only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter. A depreciation policy the framework does not permit is a departure from that framework, and inadequate disclosure of ₹210 crore of contract revenue is a misstatement — both go to the opinion.

options.text: No — forming the opinion includes evaluating the qualitative aspects of the entity's accounting practices, and a policy the framework does not permit, disclosure that does not let users understand material transactions, and an inappropriate financial statement title are all failures of that evaluation
options.why: SA 700 (Revised) does not let the opinion rest on the evidence file alone. The auditor evaluates whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the requirements of the applicable financial reporting framework, and that evaluation includes consideration of the qualitative aspects of the entity's accounting practices. It names the tests: whether the accounting policies selected and applied are consistent with the framework and are appropriate; whether adequate disclosures enable users to understand the effect of material transactions and events; and whether the terminology used, including the title of each financial statement, is appropriate.
keywords: qualitative aspects of the entity's accounting practices
understand the effect of material transactions and events

citation.ref: para 11 to para 15

items.scenario: The file is complete. Every planned procedure was performed, no exception is open, and the only uncorrected misstatement is ₹4 lakh against a materiality of ₹90 lakh. The entity's balance sheet is headed "Statement of Assets and Liabilities"; its depreciation policy is disclosed but is not one the framework permits for that class of asset; and ₹210 crore of contract revenue appears as a single line with no disaggregation. The manager says the opinion is unmodified, there being nothing left to test and nothing material uncorrected.

items.stem: Which of the three may carry an Emphasis of Matter paragraph?

options.text: All three — an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is available for any matter of importance, and the qualification and the key audit matter get their own sections in any event
options.misconception: reads the paragraph as free-standing, when SA 706 makes it unavailable where the matter drives a modification or has been determined to be a key audit matter
options.why: The two conditions are written into the requirement itself. A matter that requires the auditor to modify the opinion, and a matter determined to be a key audit matter, are both outside what an Emphasis of Matter paragraph may carry, however important either of them is.

options.text: Only the early adoption — the litigation is barred because it has been determined to be a key audit matter, and the write-down is barred because you are required to modify the opinion as a result of it
options.why: SA 706 (Revised) allows an Emphasis of Matter paragraph only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion under SA 705 (Revised) as a result of the matter and, where SA 701 applies, only where the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter to be communicated in the auditor's report. The early adoption is presented and disclosed in the financial statements, is fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements, and fails neither gate.

options.text: The write-down and the early adoption — an Emphasis of Matter paragraph beside the qualification shows the reader where the disclosure sits, and only the key audit matter is excluded
options.misconception: adds an Emphasis of Matter paragraph on the very matter causing the modification, which the first condition excludes
options.why: The first condition excludes exactly that: the paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter. The place for the ₹18 crore is the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, which already describes the matter and its effects.

options.text: The litigation and the early adoption — a key audit matter and an Emphasis of Matter paragraph do different jobs, so one matter may appear as both
options.misconception: puts a determined key audit matter into an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, which SA 706 rules out where SA 701 applies
options.why: They do different jobs, and SA 706 (Revised) still makes you choose: where SA 701 applies, an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is available only if the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter to be communicated in the auditor's report. This is a listed company, so SA 701 applies and the litigation belongs in the Key Audit Matters section alone.
keywords: has not been determined to be a key audit matter

citation.ref: para 8(a) and para 8(b)

items.scenario: A listed company, with three matters in front of you. A ₹120 crore litigation, fully disclosed, which you have determined to be a key audit matter. An inventory write-down of ₹18 crore that management has disclosed but measured on a basis the framework does not permit — you are qualifying the opinion for it. And an unusually large early adoption of a new accounting standard, fully and accurately disclosed, which you consider fundamental to users' understanding. The partner wants an Emphasis of Matter paragraph for all three.

items.stem: What does SA 720 require next?

options.text: Modify the opinion on the financial statements — a ₹410 crore export claim beside ₹190 crore of audited export revenue is a material misstatement
options.misconception: modifies the opinion for a misstatement sitting in the other information rather than in the financial statements the opinion covers
options.why: The opinion covers the financial statements, and you are satisfied those are right. What exists here is a material misstatement of the other information, which SA 720 addresses in the Other Information section of the auditor's report, not by modifying an opinion on financial statements that are not wrong.
keywords: material misstatement of the other information

options.text: Obtain a written representation that the Board's Report is consistent with the financial statements, and file it
options.misconception: substitutes a representation from the party that has already refused to correct for the action SA 720 requires
options.why: A written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own, and the management giving it has already declined to correct the figure. SA 720 asks for a request to correct, escalation to those charged with governance, and then consideration of the implications for the auditor's report.

options.text: Communicate the matter with those charged with governance and request that the correction be made, and if it is still not corrected take appropriate action — considering the implications for your report and telling them how you plan to address the misstatement in it, or withdrawing where that is possible
options.why: Having concluded that a material misstatement of the other information exists, SA 720 requires the auditor to request management to correct it and, where management refuses, to communicate the matter with those charged with governance and request that the correction be made. If other information obtained before the date of the auditor's report remains uncorrected, the auditor takes appropriate action, including considering the implications for the auditor's report and communicating with those charged with governance about how he plans to address the material misstatement, or withdrawing from the engagement where withdrawal is possible under applicable law or regulation.
keywords: material misstatement of the other information

options.text: Nothing further — you express no opinion on the other information, so an error management will not fix is management's error alone
options.misconception: reads "no opinion on the other information" as no responsibility for it, when SA 720 sets out a chain of actions ending at the auditor's own report
options.why: Expressing no opinion or conclusion on the other information is true, and it is not the end of the auditor's involvement. SA 720 requires him to request a correction, to escalate a refusal to those charged with governance and, where the misstatement stands, to consider the implications for the auditor's report.
keywords: no opinion or conclusion on the other information

citation.ref: para 17 and para 18

items.scenario: The draft Board's Report you receive four days before signing claims that "exports grew 34 per cent and now contribute ₹410 crore". The audited financial statements show export revenue of ₹190 crore, down 8 per cent, and you are satisfied the financial statements are right. You raise it. The chief financial officer says the ₹410 crore is an order book figure, that the Board's Report is management's document and not audited, and declines to change it.

items.stem: What is the position under SA 810?

options.text: You may accept, provided you first perform enough procedures on the underlying audited financial statements to satisfy yourself about them
options.misconception: treats the precondition as work that can be made up after the event, when SA 810 requires the engagement to audit the source financial statements
options.why: The precondition is about the engagement, not about effort. SA 810 requires that the auditor has been engaged to conduct an audit of the financial statements from which the summary financial statements are derived, and re-performing procedures over someone else's audit does not create that engagement.

options.text: You may accept and give an unmodified opinion on the highlights, the other firm's qualification being a matter for its own report
options.misconception: severs the report on the summary from the modification in the auditor's report on the audited financial statements, which SA 810 requires it to describe
options.why: The report on summary financial statements identifies the audited financial statements and the date of the auditor's report on them, and where that report contained a modified opinion, it says so. A qualification on inventory in the source cannot be left behind by summarising the numbers it attaches to.

options.text: You cannot accept — SA 810 permits a report on summary financial statements only where the auditor has been engaged to audit the financial statements they are derived from — and the opinion asked for is the wrong one in any case
options.why: SA 810 does not allow the engagement to be taken at all unless the auditor has been engaged to conduct an audit, in accordance with the Standards on Auditing, of the financial statements from which the summary financial statements are derived. Nor does the standard offer a true and fair view opinion on a summary. The opinion says either that the summary financial statements are consistent, in all material respects, with the audited financial statements in accordance with the applied criteria, or that they are a fair summary of the audited financial statements in accordance with the applied criteria.

options.text: You may accept and give a true and fair view opinion, a condensed balance sheet and statement of profit and loss being financial statements like any others
options.misconception: treats summary financial statements as a complete set, when they omit disclosures the framework requires and carry their own form of opinion
options.why: Summary financial statements contain less detail than the audited financial statements and do not contain all the disclosures required by the financial reporting framework applied in preparing them — which is why the report says exactly that, and says that reading them is not a substitute for reading the audited financial statements. The opinion is on consistency with, or fair summarisation of, the audited financial statements.
keywords: do not contain all the disclosures
not a substitute for reading the audited financial statements

citation.ref: the precondition of having been engaged to audit the financial statements from which the summary financial statements are derived, and the two permitted forms of opinion

items.scenario: A company's annual report carries a two-page "Financial Highlights" set — a condensed balance sheet and statement of profit and loss with no notes — derived from financial statements audited by another firm, whose report carried a qualified opinion on inventory. The board asks you, who did not audit those financial statements, to report on the highlights, and asks for wording saying that they give a true and fair view.

items.stem: How should the report be read?

options.text: The gap is closed by the service organisation's own written assertion, which covers the whole of the service it delivers to your client
options.misconception: stretches the assertion beyond the description it attaches to, when a carved-out subservice organisation's controls sit outside that description
options.why: The written assertion is about the fair presentation of the description, the suitability of the design of the controls and, in a type 2 report, their operating effectiveness — all of them measured against the description, which here excludes the custody provider's controls. An assertion cannot assert about controls its own description leaves out.

options.text: As a carve-out, not a qualification — the description identifies the subservice organisation's services but excludes its control objectives and controls, so the report covers the service organisation's own controls and you must obtain assurance about the carved-out controls separately
options.why: SAE 3402 allows the description of the system to deal with a subservice organisation by the carve-out method, under which the description identifies the nature of the services performed by the subservice organisation but excludes its control objectives and related controls, and the service auditor's procedures do not extend to them. That is a permitted presentation and not a modification of the opinion. The consequence falls on the user auditor, who has to obtain assurance about the custody reconciliation controls by some other means.

options.text: As an inclusive-method report, since the description names the custody provider and the services it performs
options.misconception: takes naming the subservice organisation as inclusion, when the inclusive method requires its control objectives and controls to be in the description and within the service auditor's procedures
options.why: Naming the provider is what the carve-out method itself calls for — the description identifies the nature of the services performed by the subservice organisation. The inclusive method goes further: the subservice organisation's control objectives and related controls sit in the description and the service auditor's procedures extend to them, which this report expressly says they do not.

options.text: The manager is right — a report whose opinion excludes a set of controls is a modified report and cannot support any reliance
options.misconception: reads a carve-out as a modification, when SAE 3402 provides for it as one of two ways of describing a subservice organisation
options.why: A carve-out narrows what the report covers; it does not qualify the opinion on what it does cover. The alternative permitted presentation is the inclusive method, under which the description includes the subservice organisation's control objectives and related controls and the service auditor's procedures extend to them.

citation.ref: the inclusive and carve-out methods of dealing with a subservice organisation, and the service organisation's written assertion

items.scenario: Your client's fund accounting is done by a service organisation, which has itself outsourced its custody reconciliations to a second provider. The service organisation's type 2 report describes the nature of the custody reconciliation service but sets out no control objectives or controls for it, and the service auditor's opinion is expressed "excluding the controls at the custody provider". Your manager reads that as a scope qualification and proposes to reject the report.

items.stem: What does SAE 3400 permit?

options.text: Both, this being a forecast built on management's best-estimate assumptions, and a forecast carrying a higher level of assurance than a projection
options.misconception: calls a hypothetical assumption a best estimate, and invents a difference in assurance level between a forecast and a projection
options.why: A forecast is prepared on the basis of best-estimate assumptions as to events management expects to take place; a plant not yet ordered running at 96 per cent from its first month is a hypothetical assumption, which makes this a projection. Either way the assurance is the same — negative assurance on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis, with an opinion on preparation and presentation.

options.text: Both, provided the report states that the projection is management's and adds a disclaimer of liability
options.misconception: treats a disclaimer as curing an opinion the standard does not offer and assumptions it says to refuse
options.why: A disclaimer added underneath does not change what the report says above it. Assumptions that are clearly unrealistic go to acceptance of the engagement, and an assurance that projected profits will be achieved is unavailable on any assumptions, because prospective financial information relates to events that may not occur.

options.text: A positive opinion on the assumptions is available, but not a statement that the results will be achieved
options.misconception: upgrades the assurance on the assumptions from negative to positive, when the standard gives negative assurance on that limb
options.why: The two limbs of the report are graded differently. On the assumptions the auditor gives negative assurance as to whether they provide a reasonable basis for the prospective financial information; the positive opinion is on whether that information is properly prepared on the basis of those assumptions and presented in accordance with the relevant financial reporting framework.
keywords: properly prepared on the basis of those assumptions

options.text: Neither — where the assumptions are clearly unrealistic the engagement should not be accepted, and even on acceptable assumptions the report gives negative assurance on whether they provide a reasonable basis, never an assurance that the results will be achieved
options.why: SAE 3400 says the auditor should not accept, or should withdraw from, an engagement when the assumptions are clearly unrealistic, and a first-month utilisation above the industry best and 38 points above the company's own is that. Nor does the standard offer what the board is asking for. The report expresses negative assurance as to whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis for the prospective financial information, an opinion on whether that information is properly prepared on the basis of those assumptions and presented in accordance with the relevant financial reporting framework, and a caveat that actual results are likely to be different.
keywords: actual results are likely to be different

citation.ref: the definitions of a forecast and a projection, the elements of the report, and the requirement not to accept an engagement where the assumptions are clearly unrealistic

items.scenario: A company preparing a rights issue asks you to examine a five-year projection built on the assumption that a plant not yet ordered will be commissioned in eighteen months and will run at 96 per cent capacity from its first month — against an industry best of 71 per cent and the company's own current 58 per cent. The board wants a report saying the projected profits will be achieved, and a positive opinion on the assumptions.

items.stem: What does SRS 4400 permit in that report?

options.text: A negative conclusion — nothing has come to your attention — since seven procedures over a defined population is at least a limited assurance engagement
options.misconception: upgrades agreed-upon procedures to a review, whose negative conclusion rests on procedures the practitioner designed for that purpose
options.why: A negative conclusion belongs to a review engagement, where the practitioner designs inquiry and analytical procedures sufficient to support limited assurance. In an agreed-upon procedures engagement the procedures come from the parties rather than from the practitioner's own assessment, and the report expresses no assurance at all.

options.text: A report of factual findings and no conclusion of any kind, distribution restricted to the bank and the borrower, and a statement in the report that you are not independent
options.why: An agreed-upon procedures engagement expresses no assurance, so the practitioner reports the factual findings — the procedures performed and what they showed — and the users draw their own conclusions. "Fairly stated except as noted" is a conclusion and is not available. Distribution is restricted to the parties that have agreed to the procedures, because others who do not know what was agreed may misinterpret the results. And independence is not a requirement for an agreed-upon procedures engagement: where the practitioner is not independent, a statement to that effect is made in the report.
keywords: restricted to the parties that have agreed to the procedures

options.text: You must decline the engagement outright, a partner's shareholding making the firm ineligible
options.misconception: applies an audit independence requirement to an engagement where SRS 4400 does not impose one
options.why: Independence is not a requirement for an agreed-upon procedures engagement. Where the terms or objectives of the engagement, or national standards, do require it, that requirement governs; otherwise the practitioner may accept and states in the report of factual findings that he is not independent.

options.text: The report may go to the two other lenders, the borrower being your client and entitled to decide who sees his own report
options.misconception: treats distribution as the client's to decide, when the restriction protects readers who never saw the procedures that were agreed
options.why: The restriction exists because the report means something only to those who know what was agreed. SRS 4400 restricts distribution to the parties that have agreed to the procedures, and the report says so; a lender who did not agree them cannot tell what the seven procedures did and did not cover.
keywords: restricts distribution to the parties that have agreed to the procedures

citation.ref: the report of factual findings and the statement that no assurance is expressed, the restriction of distribution to the parties that have agreed to the procedures, and the position on independence

items.scenario: A bank and a borrower jointly engage you to perform seven specified procedures on the borrower's stock and receivables statements — footing them, matching a sample to invoices, and confirming ten balances. Three invoices totalling ₹1.4 crore do not match. The borrower asks for a report concluding that the statements are "fairly stated except as noted", and asks that a copy go to two other lenders who did not agree the procedures. He also points out that your firm's partner holds shares in the borrower.

items.stem: What does section 139(2) allow?

options.text: N & Associates may be appointed — the bar attaches to the firm that held the office, and a separate firm is a separate person however its partners overlap
options.misconception: stops at the outgoing firm, missing the proviso that reaches a firm sharing a common partner with it
options.why: Section 139(2) has a proviso aimed at exactly this arrangement: as on the date of appointment, no audit firm having a common partner or partners with the outgoing audit firm, whose tenure has expired in a company immediately preceding the financial year, shall be appointed as auditor of the same company for a period of five years. Two shared partners out of four is a common partner.

options.text: M & Co must also give up its other listed audits, rotation being a limit on how long a firm may audit listed companies at all
options.misconception: turns a company-by-company tenure limit into a ceiling on the firm's listed practice
options.why: Rotation under section 139(2) runs against the company. The firm is capped at two terms of five consecutive years as auditor of that company, and nothing in the section touches its appointments elsewhere; the separate ceiling on the number of company audits a person may hold sits in section 141(3)(g).
keywords: two terms of five consecutive years

options.text: M & Co may be reappointed for one year, the cap being on terms of five years and a one-year appointment not being a term
options.misconception: reads the cap as counting five-year blocks, when the ineligibility runs against re-appointment in the same company for five years however short the proposed term
options.why: The proviso does not bar a third five-year term; it bars re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years from the completion of the two terms. A one-year appointment made inside that window is exactly what it prohibits.
keywords: re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years

options.text: Neither firm may be appointed — a firm that has completed two terms of five consecutive years is ineligible for re-appointment in the same company for five years, and a firm with a common partner with the outgoing firm is barred for five years too — while M & Co's other audits are untouched
options.why: Section 139(2) caps an audit firm at two terms of five consecutive years in a company, and its proviso makes a firm that has completed two such terms ineligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years from the completion of those terms; a one-year transition is a re-appointment and runs into the same bar. A further proviso catches N & Associates: as on the date of appointment, no audit firm having a common partner or partners with the outgoing audit firm, whose tenure has expired in a company immediately preceding the financial year, shall be appointed as auditor of the same company for a period of five years. The cap runs company by company, so M & Co's other engagements are unaffected.
keywords: two terms of five consecutive years
re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years

citation.ref: Section 139(2) with its provisos on ineligibility for re-appointment for five years and on a firm having a common partner with the outgoing audit firm

items.scenario: A listed company's auditor is the firm M & Co, appointed at the 2016 annual general meeting and again at the 2021 annual general meeting, each time for five years; its term ends at the 2026 annual general meeting. The audit committee proposes N & Associates, a firm in which two of M & Co's four partners are also partners. A director asks whether M & Co could instead be reappointed for one year as a transition, and whether M & Co must now give up its other listed audits.

items.stem: How many of those four things are wrong?

options.text: Two — the signature and the representative are wrong, but circulating the annual report to every member satisfies the reading requirement, and the auditor may speak on any item
options.misconception: treats circulation of the report as equivalent to reading the qualifications before the meeting, and reads the right to be heard as unlimited
options.why: Section 145 requires the qualifications to be read before the company in general meeting; sending members a document is not reading it before the meeting, and the section separately requires that they be open to inspection by any member. And the right under section 146 is to be heard on any part of the business which concerns him as the auditor, not on whatever is tabled.
keywords: read before the company in general meeting
open to inspection by any member

options.text: Three — everything except the signature, a firm being free to decide which of its partners signs on its behalf
options.misconception: treats the choice of signatory as internal to the firm, when section 141(2) restricts it to partners who are chartered accountants
options.why: The choice is not the firm's to make. Section 141(2) provides that where a firm including a limited liability partnership is appointed as an auditor, only the partners who are chartered accountants shall be authorised to act and sign on behalf of the firm, and section 145 ties the signing of the report to that provision.
keywords: only the partners who are chartered accountants
act and sign on behalf of the firm

options.text: All four — only a partner who is a chartered accountant may sign, the qualifications must be read before the general meeting, the representative must himself be qualified to be an auditor, and the right to be heard covers only business concerning him as auditor
options.why: Section 145 requires the auditor to sign the report in accordance with section 141(2), under which only the partners who are chartered accountants are authorised to act and sign on behalf of a firm. The same section requires that qualifications, observations or comments on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company be read before the company in general meeting and be open to inspection by any member. Section 146 lets the auditor attend through an authorised representative who shall also be qualified to be an auditor, and gives him a right to be heard on any part of the business which concerns him as the auditor — the board's dividend proposal is not that.
keywords: only the partners who are chartered accountants
read before the company in general meeting

options.text: One — only the signature, since section 145 governs signing and nothing else, and attending a general meeting is a courtesy rather than a duty
options.misconception: reduces section 145 to a signing rule and treats attendance under section 146 as optional when it is cast as a duty
options.why: Section 145 carries the reading requirement as well as the signing rule. And section 146 says the auditor shall, unless otherwise exempted by the company, attend any general meeting either himself or through his authorised representative — an obligation, subject only to the company exempting him.
keywords: unless otherwise exempted by the company

citation.ref: Section 145 read with section 141(2), and section 146

items.scenario: A company's audit report carries two qualifications, one on a ₹31 crore related party advance. The audit firm's managing partner, a cost accountant and not a chartered accountant, signs the report on the firm's behalf. At the annual general meeting the company does not read the qualifications out, saying every member received the annual report anyway. The firm sends its senior manager, a semi-qualified employee, to attend, and he tries to raise a question about the board's dividend proposal.

items.stem: What is wrong with that drafting?

options.text: The clause asks whether you took into consideration the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditor, and he raised two — the answer is that you considered them, not that none existed
options.why: Clause 3(xviii) has the auditor state whether there has been any resignation of the statutory auditors during the year and, if so, whether he has taken into consideration the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors. Those are the concerns the outgoing auditor actually raised, not what his Form ADT-3 chose to say, and here he raised a revenue cut-off issue and a refusal of access. Having looked into both and satisfied yourself, the honest answer is that you considered them, with the position stated; a report saying no issues were raised is untrue.
keywords: resignation of the statutory auditors during the year
taken into consideration the issues, objections or concerns

options.text: Nothing, since you concluded the cut-off was right, and a concern that turns out to be unfounded is not a concern to report
options.misconception: reads "taken into consideration" as covering only concerns the incoming auditor ends up agreeing with
options.why: The clause reports what you did with the concerns, not whether they survived. Having taken the issues, objections or concerns into consideration is the reportable act, and concluding after work that the cut-off is right is that consideration — not a reason to say nothing was raised.
keywords: taken the issues, objections or concerns into consideration

options.text: Nothing under CARO, but you were required to obtain the outgoing auditor's no-objection certificate before accepting the appointment
options.misconception: invents a no-objection certificate in place of the written communication Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule actually requires
options.why: What the Chartered Accountants Act requires is communication. Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule makes it misconduct to accept a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him in writing; the predecessor's consent is not a condition and no no-objection certificate is prescribed.
keywords: Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule

options.text: Nothing — the clause is answered from the Form ADT-3 the outgoing auditor filed, that being the statutory record of why he left
options.misconception: substitutes the outgoing auditor's filing for the concerns he actually raised with the incoming auditor
options.why: Form ADT-3 is what section 140(2) requires a resigning auditor to file with the company and the Registrar within thirty days. Clause 3(xviii) asks about the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors, and a letter to you naming a ₹26 crore cut-off issue raises them whatever the form says.
keywords: issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xviii)

items.scenario: You are appointed in October to fill a casual vacancy after the previous auditor resigned in August. His Form ADT-3 says he resigned "for personal reasons". When you write to him he replies at length, describing an unresolved ₹26 crore revenue cut-off issue and management's refusal to give him the customer contracts. You look into both, and satisfy yourself on evidence he never saw that the cut-off is right. You draft clause 3(xviii) as: "The previous auditor resigned during the year; his stated reason was personal, and no issues were raised."

items.stem: How does clause 3(xx) get reported?

options.text: Neither limb is satisfied, the whole ₹3 crore having had to reach a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the year end
options.misconception: applies the Schedule VII route to an ongoing project, which section 135(6) sends to a special account instead
options.why: An ongoing project is the exception. Section 135(6) has the amount unspent pursuant to an ongoing project transferred to a special account within thirty days from the end of the financial year, to be spent on that project within three financial years; only if it is still unspent at the end of those three years does it go to a Fund specified in Schedule VII, within thirty days of the end of the third financial year.

options.text: Fully complied — both amounts are unspent corporate social responsibility money and both have been moved out of the company's working funds into a dedicated account
options.misconception: treats one ring-fenced account as satisfying two limbs that have two different destinations
options.why: Ring-fencing is not the test. Clause 3(xx)(a) asks whether the amount was transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII to the Companies Act; clause 3(xx)(b) asks whether it was transferred to a special account under section 135(6). An account the company opened for itself answers only the second.

options.text: The clause cannot be reported yet, both windows still being open on the date of the audit report
options.misconception: treats both limbs as running on the six-month clock, when the ongoing-project transfer is due within thirty days of the year end
options.why: Only clause 3(xx)(a) runs on six months. The section 135(6) transfer for an ongoing project is due within thirty days from the end of the financial year, so that window closed on 30 April and the position on it is already fixed and reportable.
keywords: thirty days from the end of the financial year

options.text: Clause 3(xx)(b) is satisfied for the ₹1.8 crore, but clause 3(xx)(a) is not — an unspent amount relating to other than an ongoing project must go to a Fund specified in Schedule VII, not into an account the company itself controls
options.why: The two limbs have different destinations. Section 135(6) sends the amount unspent pursuant to an ongoing project to a special account, the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account, within thirty days from the end of the financial year, and 20 May meets that for the ₹1.8 crore. The second proviso to section 135(5) sends the unspent amount in respect of other than ongoing projects to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within a period of six months of the expiry of the financial year, and money still sitting in an account the company controls has not gone there.
keywords: thirty days from the end of the financial year
six months of the expiry of the financial year

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xx)(a) and 3(xx)(b), with the second proviso to section 135(5) and section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A company's corporate social responsibility obligation for the year ended 31 March was ₹8 crore; it spent ₹5 crore. Of the ₹3 crore unspent, ₹1.8 crore relates to a school building the board had identified as an ongoing project, and ₹1.2 crore relates to a one-off donation programme that was simply not run. On 20 May the company moved the whole ₹3 crore into one separate bank account it opened and labelled "CSR Unspent Account". The finance head says the money is ring-fenced either way and asks you to report clause 3(xx) as fully complied.

items.stem: What does clause 3(xiii) require you to report?

options.text: Only the consultancy contract — the flat is below any threshold section 188 prescribes, so no reporting arises on it
options.misconception: answers a disclosure failure with a section 188 threshold, when the clause's disclosure limb has no threshold at all
options.why: Whether the flat crosses a section 188 threshold decides whether it needed approval under that section. It does not decide disclosure: the clause asks whether the details have been disclosed as required by the applicable accounting standards, and a related party transaction is disclosed under that standard whatever the Companies Act thresholds say.
keywords: disclosed as required by the applicable accounting standards

options.text: A non-compliance on the consultancy contract, which needed audit committee approval whatever its pricing, and on the flat, whose details were not disclosed as the applicable accounting standard requires
options.why: Clause 3(xiii) asks whether all transactions with related parties are in compliance with sections 177 and 188 where applicable, and whether the details have been disclosed in the financial statements as required by the applicable accounting standards. Being in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis takes a transaction outside the approval regime of section 188; it does not take it outside the audit committee's approval under section 177, so the ₹12 crore contract fails the first limb. The flat was approved but never disclosed, so it fails the second, and the arm's length pricing of the ₹96 crore purchases does nothing for either.
keywords: ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis

options.text: Nothing — two of the three are at arm's length and in the ordinary course of business, and the third was approved by both the audit committee and the board
options.misconception: treats arm's length pricing and approval as answering a clause that also asks about disclosure
options.why: The clause has a disclosure limb of its own: whether the details have been disclosed in the financial statements as required by the applicable accounting standards. An ₹80 lakh sale of a flat to a director's spouse that appears nowhere in the notes fails that limb however well it was approved.

options.text: Only the flat — the consultancy contract is in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length, and so falls outside sections 177 and 188 alike
options.misconception: extends the section 188 carve-out for ordinary-course arm's length transactions to the audit committee's approval under section 177
options.why: That carve-out belongs to section 188. Section 177 requires the audit committee's approval of related party transactions, and a ₹12 crore consultancy contract with a director's firm needed it whether or not it was in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis.
keywords: ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xiii), with sections 177 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 and disclosure as required by the applicable accounting standards

items.scenario: A listed company with an audit committee has three related party transactions. Raw material purchases of ₹96 crore from a promoter-owned supplier, on standard terms and at prices matching two unrelated suppliers, approved by the audit committee and disclosed in the notes. A ₹12 crore consultancy contract with a director's firm, in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length, never placed before the audit committee, disclosed in the notes. And an ₹80 lakh sale of a flat to a director's spouse at book value, approved by the audit committee and by the board, disclosed nowhere in the notes. The manager plans a clean clause 3(xiii) because the two big ones are at arm's length.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The Institute must finish first, the Board of Discipline and the Disciplinary Committee being the forums the Chartered Accountants Act creates for a member's misconduct
options.misconception: gives the earlier statute priority, when the later section expressly displaces the other forum
options.why: Sections 21A and 21B do create those forums, and section 132(4) carves this class of case out of them. Where the Authority has initiated an investigation, no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in the same matter, and the Institute's forums act only where the Authority has not taken it up.

options.text: Neither may proceed, the Authority's jurisdiction covering only the company, and any action against an individual member remaining with the Institute
options.misconception: limits the Authority to entities, when section 132(4) names members and firms of chartered accountants in terms
options.why: Section 132(4) is written about people. It gives the Authority power to investigate matters of professional or other misconduct committed by any member or firm of chartered accountants registered under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, and lets it debar a member or a firm for a minimum period of six months and up to ten years.
keywords: any member or firm of chartered accountants

options.text: Both may proceed, the Authority looking at the audit and the Institute at the member's conduct, since they enforce different statutes
options.misconception: reads the two forums as running in parallel, when the proviso to section 132(4) stops one of them
options.why: They do enforce different statutes, and Parliament still chose one forum for a given matter of misconduct. The proviso bars any other institute or body from initiating or continuing proceedings in such matters once the Authority has initiated an investigation.

options.text: The Institute must stop — once the Authority has initiated an investigation, no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in the same matter of misconduct
options.why: Section 132(4) gives the National Financial Reporting Authority power to investigate, either suo motu or on a reference made to it by the Central Government, matters of professional or other misconduct committed by a member or firm of chartered accountants, and its proviso settles the overlap in terms: where the Authority has initiated an investigation, no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct. Which statute came first does not enter into it.
keywords: no other institute or body shall initiate or continue

citation.ref: Section 132(4) with its proviso

items.scenario: A complaint about the audit of a large listed company is filed with the Institute against the engagement partner. Two months later the National Financial Reporting Authority begins its own investigation into the same audit, on a reference from the Central Government. The Institute's Director (Discipline) proposes to carry on with his own examination so that the member is not judged twice on incomplete facts, and the member's counsel says the Institute must finish first because the Chartered Accountants Act came earlier.

items.stem: How does the Code of Ethics have this dealt with?

options.text: Disclosure in the engagement letter is enough — a threat the client knows about and accepts is no longer a threat to independence
options.misconception: treats the client's knowledge as a safeguard, when independence in appearance is judged by a reasonable and informed third party rather than by the client
options.why: The test is not what the client will accept. An acceptable level is the level at which a reasonable and informed third party would be likely to conclude that the accountant complies with the fundamental principles, and for an audit engagement he must be independent both in mind and in appearance. A disclosure tells the reader a threat exists; it does not reduce it.
keywords: independent both in mind and in appearance

options.text: Rotate the engagement partner and stop the consulting work, after which the fee concentration and the chairman's warning need no separate response, safeguards having been applied
options.misconception: applies safeguards to two threats and declares the other two answered, when each threat is evaluated and addressed on its own
options.why: Rotating the partner addresses the familiarity threat and stopping the consulting work addresses the self-review threat, and neither touches the other two. The framework has each threat identified, evaluated against an acceptable level and addressed; a fee concentration of twenty-eight per cent and an explicit warning that other engagements will be withdrawn are separate threats needing their own answers.

options.text: Identify each threat by its category, evaluate whether each is at an acceptable level, and address those that are not by eliminating the circumstances or applying safeguards — and where no safeguard can bring a threat to an acceptable level, decline or end the engagement rather than disclose it
options.why: The conceptual framework requires the professional accountant to identify threats to compliance with the fundamental principles, to evaluate whether they are at an acceptable level, and to address those that are not by eliminating the circumstances that create the threat, by applying safeguards, or by declining or ending the professional activity. These are four different threats — a familiarity threat from eleven years on the engagement, a self-review threat from auditing a system the firm designed and still maintains, a self-interest threat from twenty-eight per cent of total fees, and an intimidation threat from the chairman's warning — and disclosure is not one of the three permitted responses.

options.text: Only the fee concentration matters — the other three are relationships rather than financial interests, and independence is about money
options.misconception: reduces independence to self-interest, when the Code names five categories of threat and only one of them is financial
options.why: Self-interest is one category of five. A long association is a familiarity threat, auditing the firm's own system is a self-review threat, and a warning that three audits will be lost is an intimidation threat, each arising without any additional money changing hands.

citation.ref: the conceptual framework — identify, evaluate and address threats to compliance with the fundamental principles — and the five categories of threats, with independence in mind and in appearance for an audit engagement

items.scenario: Four facts about one audit. The engagement partner has been on the client for eleven years. The firm designed and implemented the client's revenue recognition system three years ago and its consulting arm still maintains it. Twenty-eight per cent of the firm's total fees come from this client and its group. And the client's chairman has told the partner that if the inventory write-down is insisted upon, the group's other three audits will move elsewhere. The partner proposes to disclose all four in the engagement letter and carry on.

items.stem: Is that reasoning available under SA 200?

options.text: Yes, provided the omission and the reason for it are documented under SA 230 and a written representation is obtained from management about the balance
options.misconception: treats documentation and a written representation as substitutes for the evidence that was never obtained
options.why: Writing down that a procedure was skipped records the gap; it does not fill it. And a written representation is audit evidence but is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about any of the matters it deals with, so it cannot stand in for the confirmation the partner dropped.

options.text: No — the inherent limitations are not a basis for being satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive, and the difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for omitting a procedure for which there is no alternative
options.why: Every sentence the partner quotes is in SA 200 and none of them does the work he wants. The standard says in terms that the inherent limitations of an audit are not a basis for the auditor to be satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive, and that the matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for omitting an audit procedure for which there is no alternative. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance and the auditor still has to obtain it, complying throughout with relevant ethical requirements, including those pertaining to independence.

options.text: Yes — reasonable assurance is not absolute assurance, and an audit conducted within a reasonable period of time and at a reasonable cost cannot chase every balance
options.misconception: turns the reason assurance is not absolute into a licence to omit the procedure that would have produced the evidence
options.why: The reason an audit gives reasonable assurance rather than absolute is not a permission to obtain less of it. Cost and time are named in SA 200 as a source of the inherent limitations of an audit, and named again as something that is not in itself a valid basis for omitting a procedure. The same paragraph that gives the excuse takes it away.

options.text: No, but only because the balance is material — for an immaterial balance the fee position would justify the omission
options.misconception: reads the rule as a materiality test, when the standard bars cost as a basis for omitting a procedure for which there is no alternative
options.why: Materiality decides which balances need a procedure at all. Once a procedure is needed and there is no alternative to it, SA 200 does not let the difficulty, time or cost involved be the reason it is not performed. The two questions are separate and the answer here does not turn on the second.

citation.ref: para 14 with para 5, read with the inherent limitations of an audit and the rule that they are not a basis for being satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive

items.scenario: The engagement is running well over budget. The partner tells the team to drop the external confirmation of a material balance for which no other source of evidence exists, and to rely on the ledger and management's word instead. His reasoning, written in the file, is that an audit gives reasonable assurance and not absolute assurance, that it must be completed within a reasonable period of time and at a reasonable cost, and that the inherent limitations of an audit are recognised by SA 200 itself.

items.stem: What has the manager got wrong under SA 240?

options.text: Nothing — a risk factor is not evidence that fraud has occurred, and primary responsibility for the prevention and detection of fraud rests with those charged with governance and management
options.misconception: uses the correct allocation of primary responsibility to relieve the auditor of the risk assessment the standard puts on him
options.why: Both halves are true and neither answers the point. The primary responsibility for the prevention and detection of fraud does rest with those charged with governance and management, and a fraud risk factor is indeed not proof of anything. SA 240 nevertheless makes the auditor identify and assess the risks of material misstatement due to fraud, and fraud risk factors are the information he does it with.
keywords: primary responsibility for the prevention and detection of fraud
those charged with governance and management

options.text: He should have reported the matter to the Central Government under section 143(12) at once, unapproved journals to revenue being an offence involving fraud
options.misconception: jumps from a fraud risk factor to a statutory fraud report, when nothing has yet been identified or suspected
options.why: Section 143(12) is engaged where the auditor has reason to believe that an offence involving fraud is being or has been committed. A condition that provides an opportunity is not that belief. The step SA 240 asks for first is the assessment; a fraud identified or suspected is what starts the reporting machinery.

options.text: The three observations are the incentive or pressure, the perceived opportunity and the ability to rationalise that SA 240 describes as generally present when fraud occurs — they are fraud risk factors feeding his risk assessment, and the inquiries the standard requires are a set of topics, not the single question whether fraud has occurred
options.why: A bonus and a covenant riding on profit are an incentive or pressure; a system that lets one man post unapproved journals to revenue is a perceived opportunity; "everybody does it" is the ability to rationalise the act. Those are fraud risk factors and SA 240 has the auditor use them in identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement due to fraud. The required inquiries are wider than one question too — management's own assessment of the risk of fraud, its process for identifying and responding to those risks, its communications to those charged with governance and to employees, and knowledge of any actual, suspected or alleged fraud.

options.text: He should have obtained a written representation that management has disclosed its assessment of the risk of fraud, which cures the gap in the file
options.misconception: substitutes a written representation SA 240 requires in addition for the risk assessment work it never replaces
options.why: SA 240 does require that written representation, and it is required on top of the inquiries and the assessment, not instead of them. A representation about management's assessment of the risk of fraud is management's word about management's own process, which is precisely the thing the auditor is meant to be evaluating.
keywords: assessment of the risk of fraud

citation.ref: the three conditions generally present when fraud occurs and the required inquiries of management, read with the presumed risk in revenue recognition at para 26 and management override at para 31

items.scenario: The finance head's variable pay turns on reported profit, and a bank covenant is measured on the same figure. The revenue system lets him post manual journals to revenue after the cut-off with no second approval. In a planning meeting he remarks that "every company in this trade bills a little early in March and reverses it in April". The manager records all three observations and writes in the file: "Asked the finance head whether any fraud has occurred. He confirmed none. No fraud identified."

items.stem: What is the position under SA 250?

options.text: Give the assurance for laws fundamental to the operating aspects of the business but not for those that determine the reported figures, since the auditor's procedures on the first category are the wider ones
options.misconception: inverts the two categories of law, and would produce a compliance opinion neither category supports
options.why: It is the other way round. The higher duty attaches to laws with a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures; for laws fundamental to the operating aspects of the business the auditor performs only specified procedures to help identify non-compliance. Neither category ends in an opinion that the company has complied.

options.text: Add the line — a written representation on compliance is one SA 250 requires the auditor to obtain, and having obtained it he may report what it says
options.misconception: turns a representation the auditor obtains into a conclusion he is entitled to express
options.why: The representation is evidence the auditor collects; it is not a finding he publishes. SA 580 adds that a written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about any of the matters it deals with, so it could not support the sentence even if the auditor were entitled to make it.

options.text: Decline the report wording, but treat the representation and the certificate as the audit evidence for compliance with the laws that determine the reported amounts and disclosures
options.misconception: lets a representation and an internal certificate stand as the evidence SA 250 requires the auditor to obtain for the first category of laws
options.why: For laws generally recognised to have a direct effect on the determination of material amounts and disclosures, SA 250 requires the auditor to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding compliance. A certificate prepared inside the company is information produced by the entity, and management's own representation is the weakest form of evidence there is about management's own conduct.

options.text: Decline — compliance is management's responsibility, with the oversight of those charged with governance; you are not responsible for preventing non-compliance and cannot be expected to detect non-compliance with all laws and regulations; and whether an act constitutes non-compliance is ultimately a matter for legal determination by a court
options.why: SA 250 puts the duty to ensure the entity's operations are conducted in accordance with laws and regulations on management, with the oversight of those charged with governance. It then limits the auditor expressly: he is not responsible for preventing non-compliance and cannot be expected to detect non-compliance with all laws and regulations.
