options.text: No written representations are needed where every component has been audited, since the component auditors' reports already cover the same ground
options.misconception: assumes component audits answer questions that only exist at the group level
options.why: A component auditor reports on that component's own financial statements. He says nothing about whether every component has been included in the consolidation, about the group's reportable segments, or about the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments — which are exactly the matters the parent's management is asked to confirm.

options.text: A representation that the consolidation is arithmetically accurate, which discharges the auditor's work on the consolidation adjustments
options.misconception: treats a representation as evidence that removes the need for the procedures it describes
options.why: A written representation is audit evidence, but it is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about any of the matters it deals with. It does not relieve the auditor of the procedures on the completeness of components, on the consolidation adjustments or on related parties that he would otherwise perform.

options.text: A representation from each component's management that its own financial statements are free from material misstatement, in place of representations from the parent
options.misconception: pushes the representation down to the components and leaves the group-level matters unrepresented
options.why: The written representations in an audit of consolidated financial statements are obtained from the management of the parent, because it is the parent's management that is responsible for preparing and presenting those statements — for identifying components, obtaining their financial information, making the consolidation adjustments and harmonising accounting policies.

options.text: Completeness of the components included in the consolidated financial statements; identification of reportable segments for segmental reporting; identification of related parties and related party transactions for reporting; and the appropriateness and completeness of the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments, including the elimination of intra-group transactions
options.why: Those four are the standard examples of representations obtained from the parent's management on matters material to the consolidated financial statements, alongside the acknowledgement of its responsibility for a true and fair presentation and its approval of those statements. The completeness of the components is the one the auditor can least easily establish alone, because a component left out of the consolidation leaves no trace inside it.
keywords: matters material to the consolidated financial statements

citation.ref: Ch. Group Audits — written representations from the parent's management on the completeness of components, the identification of reportable segments, the identification of related parties and related party transactions, and the appropriateness and completeness of the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments including the elimination of intra-group transactions, read with SA 580

items.scenario: You are completing the audit of a group's consolidated financial statements and are drafting the written representations to be obtained from the parent's management on matters material to those statements.

items.stem: Which statement is correct?

options.text: He is appointed by the Central Government and holds office at its pleasure, his reports being submitted to the Ministry of Finance
options.misconception: makes a constitutional authority an appointee of the executive whose accounts he audits
options.why: The appointment is by the President under Article 148, and removal is possible only by a special procedure on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity — not at anyone's pleasure. His audit reports go to the President or the Governor, who causes them to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislative Assembly, not to a ministry.

options.text: The form in which the accounts of the Union and the States are kept is prescribed by Parliament by statute, the Comptroller and Auditor General having no say in it
options.misconception: moves the power over the form of the accounts to the legislature and drops his advisory role
options.why: Article 150 provides that the President prescribes the form in which the accounts of the Union and the States shall be kept, and he does so on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor General. The advice is part of the office's constitutional position, not an omission from it.

options.text: His duties and powers are settled by the Constitution alone, no statute having been made under Article 149
options.misconception: stops at the Constitution and misses the statute that actually defines the duties and powers
options.why: Article 149 provides that he shall perform such duties and exercise such powers as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament, and the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 is that law, defining his functions and powers in detail and fixing his tenure.

options.text: He is appointed by the President under Article 148 and may be removed only by a special procedure on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity; under the 1971 Act he holds office for six years or up to the age of sixty-five, whichever is earlier; and under Article 151 his reports are laid before Parliament or the State Legislature
options.why: Article 148 provides for appointment by the President and for a special procedure for removal, only on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity, with salary and conditions of service determined by Parliament. The Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 provides a term of six years or up to the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier. Article 151 requires his reports to be submitted to the President or the Governor, who causes them to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislative Assembly.
keywords: six years or up to the age of sixty-five

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — Articles 148 to 151 of the Constitution and the term of six years or up to the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, under the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971

items.scenario: A trainee asks what protects the independence of the Comptroller and Auditor General, given that the Government whose accounts he audits is also the executive he works alongside.

items.stem: Which committee is this, and what marks it out?

options.text: An Audit Board, constituted by the Comptroller and Auditor General with experts in the relevant disciplines to conduct comprehensive audit appraisals
options.misconception: confuses the C&AG's own appraisal machinery with a committee of the legislature
options.why: An Audit Board is part of the Comptroller and Auditor General's own machinery for comprehensive audit appraisals of public sector enterprises: it associates experts, discusses findings with the enterprise and its ministry, has no separate legal entity and works under his supervision and control. It is not a committee of Parliament, and Parliament's committees are where the reports land afterwards.

options.text: The Public Accounts Committee, whose duty is to satisfy itself that the moneys were disbursed legally on the purpose to which they were applied and that the expenditure was authorised
options.misconception: names the committee whose subject is the regularity of expenditure when the question describes an appraisal of commercial performance
options.why: The Public Accounts Committee satisfies itself that moneys were disbursed legally on the service or purpose to which they were applied, that the expenditure incurred was authorised, and that re-appropriation was made in accordance with the provisions made. That is the regularity of spending, not whether an undertaking is run on prudent commercial practices.

options.text: The Estimates Committee, which reports what economies and improvements in efficiency may be effected and may suggest alternative policies
options.misconception: picks the committee that works on the estimates before the money is spent rather than on the working of an undertaking
options.why: The Estimates Committee examines the estimates to report what economies, improvements in organisation, efficiency or administrative reform may be effected consistently with the policy underlying them, to suggest alternative policies, and to suggest the form in which the estimates shall be presented. It does not comment on a policy approved by Parliament, and its subject is the estimates, not the appraisal of a public undertaking's performance.

options.text: The Committee on Public Undertakings, which exercises over public sector undertakings the same financial control the Public Accounts Committee exercises over Government departments, and whose examination takes the form of a comprehensive appraisal of the undertaking's performance
options.why: The Committee on Public Undertakings examines the reports and accounts of public undertakings, examines the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General on them, and examines their autonomy and efficiency and whether they are being managed in accordance with sound business principles and prudent commercial practices. It exercises the same financial control over public sector undertakings that the Public Accounts Committee exercises over the functioning of Government departments, and its examination takes the form of a comprehensive appraisal of performance.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the Committee on Public Undertakings, the Public Accounts Committee and the Estimates Committee and their respective functions, and the Audit Boards constituted by the Comptroller and Auditor General for comprehensive appraisals

items.scenario: A committee of Parliament has taken up a public sector power company. It is examining the company's reports and accounts, the Comptroller and Auditor General's reports on it, and whether the undertaking is being managed in accordance with sound business principles and prudent commercial practices. Its examination is taking the form of a comprehensive appraisal of the company's performance, including its policies and its programmes.

items.stem: How is this engagement classified?

options.text: As no assurance engagement at all, since there is no assertion by the entity for the auditor to test
options.misconception: treats an entity assertion as a precondition of every assurance engagement, which direct reporting engagements exist to disprove
options.why: A public sector audit has three parties — the auditor, the responsible party and the intended users — and it does not require the responsible party to have made an assertion first. In a direct reporting engagement the auditor measures the subject matter against the criteria himself, and it is a full engagement with the same elements as any other.

options.text: As a financial audit, since every audit conducted for the Comptroller and Auditor General is an attestation engagement on financial information
options.misconception: collapses the three types of public sector audit into the one that is always an attestation engagement
options.why: Financial audit expresses an opinion on financial statements and is always an attestation engagement, but the audit of public enterprises is not restricted to financial and compliance audit; it extends to performance, which examines the economy, efficiency and effectiveness with which the entity operates and fulfils its objectives.

options.text: As a direct reporting engagement, in which the auditor himself measures or evaluates the subject matter against the criteria; performance and compliance audits are generally direct reporting engagements, while financial audits are always attestation engagements because they rest on financial information presented by the responsible party
options.why: In a direct reporting engagement it is the auditor who measures or evaluates the subject matter against the criteria. In an attestation engagement the responsible party measures the subject matter against the criteria and presents the subject matter information, and the auditor gathers evidence to express a conclusion on it. Financial audits are always attestation engagements, and performance and compliance audits are generally direct reporting engagements — which is why a performance audit reports findings and recommendations rather than an opinion.

options.text: As an attestation engagement, because the auditor attests to the criteria he has drawn from the programme's objectives
options.misconception: locates the attestation in the criteria rather than in who measured the subject matter against them
options.why: What makes an engagement an attestation engagement is that the responsible party measured the subject matter against the criteria and presented the subject matter information, leaving the auditor to gather evidence about it. Criteria are the benchmarks used for the evaluation, and who identified them does not change who performed the measurement.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the three parties to a public sector audit, the subject matter, criteria and subject matter information, and the distinction between attestation engagements and direct reporting engagements, with financial audits always attestation and performance and compliance audits generally direct reporting

items.scenario: A chartered accountant firm has been engaged for a performance audit of a State electricity distribution company. There is no statement by the company of its own economy, efficiency and effectiveness; the team will measure the company's performance against criteria drawn from the objectives of the programme. A colleague argues that because the team is measuring rather than checking someone's assertion, this cannot be a proper audit engagement at all.

items.stem: Is the company required to appoint an internal auditor?

options.text: Yes, and because the company is required to appoint an internal auditor, its statutory auditor may not use the internal audit function's work in the audit
options.misconception: turns a statutory obligation to have internal audit into a bar on the statutory auditor using its work
options.why: Whether the company must have an internal auditor is settled by section 138 with Rule 13. Whether the statutory auditor may use the internal audit function's work is settled by SA 610 (Revised) and by nothing else, and the existence of the function does not decide that question either way.

options.text: No — its borrowings of thirty crore rupees are well below one hundred crore, and borrowings are the operative test for a private company
options.misconception: picks one of the two private-company tests and treats it as the only one
options.why: A private company has two tests and either brings it in: turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more during the preceding financial year, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding one hundred crore rupees at any point of time during that year. The borrowings test fails here; the turnover test does not.

options.text: No — its paid-up share capital is only forty lakh rupees, far below the fifty crore threshold, so none of the criteria is met
options.misconception: applies a threshold that belongs to unlisted public companies to a private company, and reads alternative tests as if they were cumulative
options.why: The paid-up share capital test of fifty crore rupees applies to an unlisted public company, not to a private company, which is tested only on turnover and on borrowings. And the tests are alternatives joined by "or", so failing one of them is not an answer where another is met.

options.text: Yes — its turnover in the preceding financial year is two hundred crore rupees or more, and for a private company that test alone brings it in; it must comply within six months of the commencement of applicability
options.why: A private company must appoint an internal auditor if it had a turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more during the preceding financial year, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding one hundred crore rupees at any point of time during the preceding financial year. Turnover in the preceding financial year here is two hundred and sixty crore, so the company is caught, and an existing company that gets covered must comply within six months of the commencement of such applicability.

citation.ref: Section 138 read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 — a private company with turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more during the preceding financial year or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding one hundred crore rupees, and compliance within six months of the commencement of applicability

items.scenario: A private limited company has paid-up share capital of forty lakh rupees, reserves of nine crore fifty lakh rupees, outstanding borrowings from a bank of thirty crore rupees, and turnover in the three financial years immediately preceding the year under audit of forty-nine crore, one hundred and forty-five crore and two hundred and sixty crore rupees respectively. It has no internal audit system, and management says the requirement does not apply because its capital is small.

items.stem: What does SIA 370 require?

options.text: A statement that the internal audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Internal Audit must be included in every report, whether or not it can be substantiated
options.misconception: makes a compliance statement automatic when the Standard conditions it on evidence
options.why: The statement that the internal audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Internal Audit is included where the internal audit was in fact so conducted and the internal auditor can substantiate that with supporting evidence and documentation. A claim of compliance that cannot be substantiated is not a report element the Standard asks for.

options.text: No internal audit report may be issued in final form unless a written draft has previously been shared with the auditee; the assignment report goes to the auditee with copies to local and executive management, and it is the Chief Internal Auditor's periodic comprehensive report that goes to the audit committee at the close of a plan period
options.why: SIA 370 makes it absolute that no internal audit report shall be issued in final form unless a written draft of the report has previously been shared with the auditee. Reporting runs in two stages: the assignment-level Internal Audit Report is issued to the auditee with copies shared with local and executive management as agreed during planning, and separately the Chief Internal Auditor prepares a periodic comprehensive report of all internal audit activities, normally quarterly, for the highest governing authority, generally the audit committee.

options.text: The draft may be skipped where the findings are clear, since SIA 370 mandates the content of the report but leaves the process of issuing it to professional judgement
options.misconception: extends the discretion the Standard gives over format into the one step it makes mandatory
options.why: The Standard does mandate no particular format or list of contents, because how and what to report is a matter of the internal auditor's professional judgement in consultation with the auditee. That discretion is about form. The requirement that a written draft be shared with the auditee before the report is issued in final form is not discretionary.

options.text: The report must be issued to the audit committee first in every case, since the internal auditor reports to the audit committee and not to management
options.misconception: reads the reporting line for the function as the addressee of every assignment report
options.why: The internal audit function's independence comes from reporting to the audit committee, but that is not the addressee of an assignment report. At the end of a particular audit assignment the Internal Audit Report is issued to the auditee, with copies to local and executive management; the audit committee receives the periodic comprehensive report.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 370, Reporting Results
citation.ref: the two stages of reporting internal audit results, the elements of the Internal Audit Report, the absence of any mandated format, and the rule that no report is issued in final form unless a written draft has previously been shared with the auditee

items.scenario: An internal auditor has finished an assignment on the procurement function and has drafted his report. The chief financial officer, who owns the process reviewed, asks him to issue the report straight to the audit committee in final form without circulating a draft, to save time before the quarterly meeting.

items.stem: What does SIA 390 require?

options.text: He records the four items as unresolved and takes no further step, since he has already reported them once and management has been informed
options.misconception: stops at the first report, when the Standard makes the follow-up a continuing duty
options.why: Monitoring and reporting means the periodic tracking of prior issues, evaluating the corrective action taken, and reporting open and pending matters to management and those charged with governance. Where no action is taken within a reasonable time the internal auditor draws management's attention to it, and where recommendations were not implemented he ascertains the reasons.

options.text: He may implement the four action plans, since closing a control gap is in the entity's interest and the internal auditor is part of the management team
options.misconception: lets urgency override the one separation that makes the next review meaningful
options.why: Implementing a control and then reviewing it are the two things one person cannot do. The responsibility to implement the action plans remains with management, and an internal auditor who builds the control cannot afterwards give an independent view on whether it works.

options.text: The Chief Internal Auditor monitors the closure of prior audit issues and reports open and pending matters through an Action Taken Report, but the responsibility to implement the action plans remains with management
options.why: The Chief Internal Auditor is responsible for continuously monitoring the closure of prior audit issues through the timely implementation of the action plans, using a formal monitoring process pre-agreed with management and those charged with governance, and the internal auditor's responsibility usually takes the form of an Action Taken Report on previous audits. The responsibility to implement the action plans remains with management, so the internal auditor monitors, evaluates and reports rather than implementing.

options.text: He removes the four items from the follow-up list, since a control gap that management has chosen not to close is a matter of management's risk appetite and not an audit issue
options.misconception: converts management's inaction into an acceptance of risk that ends the auditor's duty to report it
options.why: An open issue stays open and is reported as open. The internal auditor reports any open and pending matters to management and to those charged with governance, generally the audit committee, and highlights the recommendations that have not been implemented fully or partly; management's silence does not close a finding.
keywords: not been implemented fully or partly

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 390, Monitoring and Reporting of Prior Audit Issues
citation.ref: the Chief Internal Auditor's responsibility for continuously monitoring the closure of prior audit issues, the Action Taken Report on previous audits, and the rule that the responsibility to implement the action plans remains with management

items.scenario: Last year's internal audit reported eleven control gaps in the stores function. Management agreed action plans for all eleven; six months later, four remain open. The head of stores asks the internal auditor to implement the four himself, since he knows what is needed and it will close the point faster.

items.stem: What is wrong here?

options.text: The internal auditor should not hold an opening meeting with stakeholders, since advance notice of the areas to be tested destroys the value of the testing
options.misconception: imports a surprise-inspection idea into an engagement the Standards plan openly
options.why: The internal auditor holds an opening meeting with key stakeholders before the engagement starts and states the information and system access he needs, and he schedules the work in advance. Sampling and analytical procedures under the Standards on Internal Audit are what address the risk of a process being dressed up, not secrecy about the engagement.

options.text: The audit scope must be approved by the audit committee and the Board, not by the management whose process is being examined; only once approved does the internal auditor share the detailed plan, schedule the work and hold the opening meeting
options.why: Planning is the second of the five steps of an internal audit engagement, performed under SIA 310, and the gate inside it is that the audit scope must be approved by the audit committee and the Board. A scope approved by the manager whose process is to be reviewed is the manager setting the limits of his own examination. Only once approved does the internal auditor share the detailed audit plan with key managerial personnel, schedule the work in advance and hold the opening meeting.

options.text: The detailed work plan should have been prepared before the understanding of the business was obtained, so that the fieldwork can begin at once
options.misconception: reverses the order of steps the engagement is required to follow
options.why: The five steps are performed in sequence: obtain knowledge of the business and its environment, perform audit planning, gather the required information, perform the audit checks, and report the issues. The detailed work plan is prepared after the major risks in the process under review have been evaluated, which cannot happen before the business is understood.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since the chief financial officer is senior management and the audit committee will see the results in any case
options.misconception: treats after-the-fact visibility as equivalent to approval of the scope beforehand
options.why: Seeing the results afterwards does not answer the question of what was allowed to be looked at. The scope is approved by the audit committee and the Board precisely so that the managers whose work is examined do not set the boundaries of the examination.
keywords: approved by the audit committee and the Board

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — the five steps of an internal audit engagement performed in sequence, and the approval of the audit scope by the audit committee and the Board under SIA 310 before the detailed plan is shared and the fieldwork begins

items.scenario: An internal auditor has obtained an understanding of the entity and drafted a scope for a review of the purchase-to-pay cycle. The chief financial officer approves the scope, tells him the audit committee will be shown the results afterwards, and asks him to begin fieldwork the same week.

items.stem: How should the account stand in the year-end financial statements?

options.text: Standard, because the post-year-end instalment cured the overdue position
options.misconception: uses a later receipt to rewrite the balance sheet date
options.why: Classification is tested as at the reporting date. The week-later payment is next year's recovery — evidence for upgrade in due course, not an eraser for the year-end position.

options.text: Doubtful, since any default this size shows the loan is unlikely to be repaid
options.misconception: skips the ladder's first rung
options.why: Doubtful status is earned by remaining substandard for twelve months, not by the auditor's pessimism on day one. Over-classifying misstates provisions exactly as under-classifying does.

options.text: Standard — the security cover means the bank will lose nothing
options.misconception: lets collateral answer a question asked about repayment
options.why: Security affects how much is provided, not whether the asset performs. An account can be fully secured and fully non-performing at once; the ninety-day clock reads payments, not valuations.

options.text: Substandard NPA, with the accrued interest reversed — record of recovery decides, not security or reputation
options.why: Past ninety days overdue at the balance sheet date, the classification is automatic and borrower-wise reputation, group standing and security value have no vote — the norms look at the record of recovery alone. A fresh NPA starts as substandard, and unrealised interest on it comes out of income.

citation.ref: Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning

items.scenario: As branch auditor you find a term loan whose last instalment was received 100 days before year-end, shown as standard with interest accrued to income. The branch manager explains the borrower is a reputed group, the security comfortably covers the loan, and one further instalment arrived a week after year-end.

items.stem: Has the auditor discharged his reporting duty?

options.text: Yes — the LFAR is the designated channel for advances-related findings
options.misconception: routes by subject matter instead of by severity
options.why: The LFAR is where advances findings go when they inform rather than distort. Once the numbers themselves are materially wrong, the opinion on those numbers must say so.

options.text: No, but the fix is a longer LFAR with quantified impact
options.misconception: cures the wrong document
options.why: Quantification helps, in the report that carries the opinion. An unqualified opinion sitting beside a devastating LFAR is exactly the contradiction the rule against substitution prevents.

options.text: Yes, since NPA classification is RBI's supervisory concern, not the auditor's opinion
options.misconception: hands the true and fair view to the regulator
options.why: Provisioning driven by classification lands in the profit and loss the auditor opines on. RBI's interest adds a reader; it subtracts nothing from the opinion.

options.text: No — a matter affecting the true and fair view must qualify the audit report itself; the LFAR is a supplement, not a substitute
options.why: The two documents answer different questions to different readers. Shareholders and the public read the audit report's opinion on the true and fair view; a material misclassification of advances falsifies that opinion however fully the LFAR describes it. The finding belongs in both places — described in the LFAR, and qualifying the opinion.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks

items.scenario: A branch auditor finds systemic failure in the branch's NPA identification — dozens of accounts past ninety days still standard, with material impact on the branch's results. He writes it up thoroughly in the LFAR's advances section and issues an unqualified branch audit report, satisfied the matter is on record for RBI and the central auditors.

items.stem: On the two frauds alone, what does Meera do?

options.text: Both frauds are reported by the route the rules fix, and neither waits for the scheduled meeting. The dye invoices are a fraud on the company by an employee of 1 crore rupees or more, so Meera goes to the Board or the audit committee first — not later than 2 days from the day she knew — and asks them to reply within 45 days. Their reply, her report and her comments on it then go to the Central Government inside 15 days of that reply landing; if 45 days pass in silence she sends her report on anyway, with a note pointing back to the first one. It travels sealed, on the firm's letterhead, as the statement Form ADT-4 prescribes. The 30 lakh rupees of yarn sits below the threshold, so it goes to the audit committee inside the same 2 days, with the nature of the fraud described, the rough amount and who was involved, and the company then carries it in the Board's report. Recovery cancels neither report.
options.why: Sub-section (12) is written for this situation exactly: an auditor doing her job comes to believe that somebody inside the company has defrauded it. Rule 13 puts the dividing line at 1 crore rupees, taken fraud by fraud, and lays out two roads. Neither road starts at the Central Government. Above the line, the auditor tells the Board or the audit committee first, not later than 2 days from the day the fraud became known to her, and asks for their reply or observations within 45 days. Once that reply arrives she passes it to the Central Government along with her own report and her comments on what they said, inside 15 days of the reply reaching her; where nothing comes back in the 45 days she sends her report anyway, with a note giving the details of what she sent earlier. It goes to the Secretary of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, sealed, by registered or speed post with an email behind it, on the firm's letterhead, signed with seal and membership number, as the statement Form ADT-4 prescribes. Below the line nothing is excused: the fraud goes to the audit committee set up under section 177, or to the Board where there is none, inside the same 2 days, with the nature of the fraud described, the rough amount and the people involved, and the company puts those details in the Board's report. Whether the money will be recovered, and when the committee happens to sit next, are not conditions the rule contains. In short, the 1.8 crore rupees fraud goes first to the Board or audit committee not later than 2 days from knowledge with a reply asked within 45 days and then to the Central Government in Form ADT-4, and the yarn goes to the audit committee inside the same 2 days.

options.text: The manager is right. A fraud of a crore or more is reported straight to the Central Government in the prescribed form, and the audit committee is informed at its scheduled meeting; the yarn fraud, being under a crore and recovered, needs no report.
options.misconception: A fraud of a crore or more goes directly to the Central Government, and a smaller one goes nowhere.
options.why: The route under rule 13 begins with the Board or the audit committee within 2 days, and the Central Government receives the report only after their reply or after 45 days without one; a fraud under 1 crore rupees still goes to the audit committee within 2 days and into the Board's report, recovered or not.

options.text: Neither fraud is reported under sub-section (12), which is about fraud by the company; these are frauds against it by staff, so Meera reports both under clause (xi) of the Order and considers a qualification, and nothing goes to the Board, the committee or the Central Government.
options.misconception: Section 143(12) covers fraud by the company, and fraud against it by employees is only a CARO matter.
options.why: Sub-section (12) is written for fraud committed against the company by its officers or employees, which is exactly these two; clause (xi) of the Order is a further report on fraud noticed during the year, not a substitute for the route under rule 13.

options.text: The finance head's proposal is accepted. The fraud is placed before the audit committee at its meeting in five weeks with the recovery position, and the yarn fraud, being under a crore and already recovered, is noted in the management letter only.
options.misconception: A fraud the company will recover, or one under a crore, needs no report from the auditor beyond a management letter.
options.why: The rule says immediately but not later than 2 days of the auditor's knowledge of the fraud, not the committee's next meeting; and a fraud under 1 crore rupees is reported to the audit committee within the same 2 days with its nature, amount and parties, and disclosed in the Board's report, recovery or no recovery.

citation.ref: section 143(12) with rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014: a fraud against the company by its officers or employees of 1 crore rupees or above is reported to the Board or audit committee immediately but not later than 2 days of knowledge, seeking a reply within 45 days, and then to the Central Government within 15 days of the reply in Form ADT-4; a fraud below 1 crore rupees is reported to the audit committee or Board within 2 days and disclosed in the Board's report

items.scenario: Kapoor & Sethi are the statutory auditors of Beas Textiles Limited, an unlisted public company at Ludhiana with a revenue of 310 crore rupees and a dyeing unit at Panipat that is a branch audited by another firm. Meera Kapoor is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026, and three matters have reached her in the last week of the audit. First, the team has established that the purchase manager, working with a dye supplier, raised invoices for 1.8 crore rupees of dyes that were never delivered and had them paid in full during the year, and that a storekeeper separately removed yarn worth 30 lakh rupees, which the company found and recovered in January 2026. The finance head accepts both, says the company will recover the 1.8 crore rupees from the supplier, and asks that the matter be placed before the audit committee at its scheduled meeting in five weeks; on the yarn, he says that anything under a crore is not the auditor's business to report anywhere. The audit manager's view is that a fraud above a crore goes straight to the Central Government and the committee can be told afterwards. Second, the ledger shows an advance of 4 crore rupees, interest-free, to a partnership firm of the managing director's brother against a mortgage of land whose title deed the company has never held; 60 lakh rupees of club subscriptions and the expenses of a family wedding charged to business promotion; and shares of a listed company bought during the year for 2.1 crore rupees and sold in March 2026 to a group company for 1.4 crore rupees. The finance head says these are matters the auditor merely looks into under sub-section (1) of section 143 and never reports on, so the report stays as it is whatever she finds; the manager says the report must answer each of the six matters one by one, the way it answers the clauses of the Order. Third, the company has refused the team's request for the minutes of the remuneration committee and the change log of the vendor master, calling both confidential; the Panipat branch auditor's report has not been sent to the firm; and one director was disqualified under sub-section (2) of section 164 in June 2025 through another company's default, which the finance head says is that company's auditor's concern. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the three ledger entries alone, what does Meera do?

options.text: The manager is right. The six matters in sub-section (1) are answered one by one in a separate paragraph of the report, favourable or not, in the way the clauses of the Order are answered, so the report will carry six statements.
options.misconception: The six inquiry matters are a checklist reported clause by clause, like the Order.
options.why: Nothing about these six reaches the report unless the auditor has something particular to say, and where she is satisfied the report reads exactly as it would have; only an adverse answer is reported, and there is no clause-by-clause paragraph.

options.text: The finance head is right. Sub-section (1) is a duty of inquiry and nothing more: Meera looks into the advance, the expenses and the share sale, records her inquiry in the working papers, and the report stays as it is whatever she finds.
options.misconception: Section 143(1) is a duty to inquire with no reporting consequence at all.
options.why: The auditor is not required to report on the sub-section (1) matters unless he has special comments to make, and an adverse answer is a special comment reported to the members; the working papers are where a satisfied inquiry rests, not an adverse one.

options.text: The three entries are frauds by the managing director against the company, so they leave sub-section (1) and are reported to the Central Government under sub-section (12) within the prescribed time, and the audit report itself says nothing about them.
options.misconception: An adverse answer under section 143(1) is automatically a fraud to be reported under section 143(12).
options.why: Sub-section (1) asks whether an advance is properly secured or on prejudicial terms, whether personal expenses sit in revenue and whether securities were sold below cost, none of which is a finding of fraud; an adverse answer on these is reported to the members, and the route under sub-section (12) needs reason to believe an offence of fraud by an officer or employee, which the inquiry has not established.

options.text: Meera inquires into each of the three and reports only where the answer is adverse, which here is all three. Her duty under sub-section (1) is to inquire into six named matters, and three of them meet these facts: a secured loan or advance that is not truly covered by its security, or lent on terms that work against the company or its members; private spending put through the revenue account; and securities that left the company for less than it paid for them. She is not required to report on any of them where the inquiry satisfies her, and the report then stays exactly as it is. But an interest-free advance against land the company holds no title to, a wedding charged to business promotion and shares sold to a group company for 70 lakh rupees less than they cost are each an answer in adverse, so she reports each to the members. The finance head is right that inquiry is not reporting and wrong that the report never changes; the manager is wrong that the six are answered clause by clause.
options.why: Sub-section (1) hands the auditor a duty to ask, not a duty to announce, and the chapter sets out six things she must ask about: whether money lent against security is genuinely covered by it and whether the terms of the lending run against the company or its members; whether transactions existing only as book entries hurt the company; whether a company that is neither an investment nor a banking one let shares, debentures and other securities go for less than it paid; whether loans have been dressed up as deposits; whether somebody's private spending has been put through the revenue account; and whether cash actually came in for shares said to have been issued for cash. What follows from all that is settled by the Research Committee opinion the chapter carries. She need say nothing about these six where the asking leaves her satisfied, and then the wording of her report is unchanged; but she must put each question and think about what the answer gives her before deciding that nothing needs saying. Where an answer comes back in adverse, she makes a report to the members on it. An interest-free advance to the managing director's brother's firm, mortgaged on land whose title deed the company has never held, is neither truly covered nor on terms that leave the company unharmed; club subscriptions and a family wedding sitting in business promotion are private spending in the revenue account; shares that cost 2.1 crore rupees and went to a group company for 1.4 crore rupees left for less than the company paid. Each is something particular to say. In short, Meera must inquire into the six matters, is not required to report on them where satisfied, and reports to the members on each answer she finds in adverse, which here is all three.

citation.ref: section 143(1): a duty to inquire into six named matters — among them whether a secured loan or advance really is secured and whether its terms work against the company or its members, whether securities went out for less than they cost, and whether personal spending has been put through the revenue account — with nothing said in the report about them unless the auditor has something particular to say, and a report to the members on any answer found in adverse

items.scenario: Kapoor & Sethi are the statutory auditors of Beas Textiles Limited, an unlisted public company at Ludhiana with a revenue of 310 crore rupees and a dyeing unit at Panipat that is a branch audited by another firm. Meera Kapoor is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026, and three matters have reached her in the last week of the audit. First, the team has established that the purchase manager, working with a dye supplier, raised invoices for 1.8 crore rupees of dyes that were never delivered and had them paid in full during the year, and that a storekeeper separately removed yarn worth 30 lakh rupees, which the company found and recovered in January 2026. The finance head accepts both, says the company will recover the 1.8 crore rupees from the supplier, and asks that the matter be placed before the audit committee at its scheduled meeting in five weeks; on the yarn, he says that anything under a crore is not the auditor's business to report anywhere. The audit manager's view is that a fraud above a crore goes straight to the Central Government and the committee can be told afterwards. Second, the ledger shows an advance of 4 crore rupees, interest-free, to a partnership firm of the managing director's brother against a mortgage of land whose title deed the company has never held; 60 lakh rupees of club subscriptions and the expenses of a family wedding charged to business promotion; and shares of a listed company bought during the year for 2.1 crore rupees and sold in March 2026 to a group company for 1.4 crore rupees. The finance head says these are matters the auditor merely looks into under sub-section (1) of section 143 and never reports on, so the report stays as it is whatever she finds; the manager says the report must answer each of the six matters one by one, the way it answers the clauses of the Order. Third, the company has refused the team's request for the minutes of the remuneration committee and the change log of the vendor master, calling both confidential; the Panipat branch auditor's report has not been sent to the firm; and one director was disqualified under sub-section (2) of section 164 in June 2025 through another company's default, which the finance head says is that company's auditor's concern. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the refused documents, the branch report and the disqualified director alone, what does Meera's report state?

options.text: The report says nothing about the two documents. Board and committee papers are the company's to withhold as confidential, and a refused paper affects the report only if Meera concludes the resulting limitation is material, in which case it appears as a scope paragraph and not otherwise.
options.misconception: Management may withhold papers as confidential and the report stays silent unless the auditor decides the gap is material.
options.why: Clause (a) of sub-section (3) has the report state whether all the information and explanations necessary for the audit were obtained and, if not, the details thereof and the effect on the financial statements; the company's view of confidentiality does not change what the clause requires the report to say.

options.text: The report answers each of the three under sub-section (3), and a refusal is reported, not absorbed. It says whether Meera asked for and got every piece of information and explanations her audit needed and, where she did not, what was withheld and what the gap does to the financial statements — so the minutes and the vendor master change log are named, with their effect. It says whether the Panipat branch report, made under sub-section (8) by another firm, reached her and what she did with it in building her own. And it says whether any director of Beas is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2), which is answered for Beas's own director whichever company's default caused it. Confidentiality is an answer to none of the three.
options.why: Sub-section (3) lists what the report shall state, and three of its clauses land on these facts. Clause (a) is about what the auditor was given: did she ask for all the information and explanations her audit needed, on her own honest judgement of what it needed, and did she get them — and where she did not, the report has to name what was missing and say what the gap does to the financial statements. A company that keeps back its remuneration committee minutes and the change log of its vendor master has not given the auditor what she judged necessary, and the clause wants that written down with its effect rather than quietly worked around by narrowing the audit. Clause (c) is about a branch somebody else audited under sub-section (8): did that firm's report come to her, and what did she do with it in building her own? A branch report that never arrived is answered in those same terms. Clause (g) asks whether a director of the company is disqualified from being appointed as a director, on the grounds section 164(2) sets out; it asks about this company's own board, and a disqualification triggered by another company's default disqualifies the director all the same. In short, the report states whether the information and explanations needed were obtained and, where they were not, what is missing and to what effect; whether the branch report under sub-section (8) reached her and how she dealt with it; and whether a director of Beas is disqualified from being appointed as a director on the grounds section 164(2) sets out.
keywords: disqualified from being appointed as a director

options.text: The Panipat branch is another auditor's work. Its report belongs to that firm and to the branch, so Meera's report on the company does not mention whether it was received, and she audits the branch figures herself if it does not arrive.
options.misconception: A branch audited by another auditor is outside the company auditor's report.
options.why: Clause (c) has the company auditor's own report say whether a branch report made under sub-section (8) by another firm reached her and what she did with it, so an absent branch report is stated rather than silently worked around.

options.text: The disqualification is answered by the auditor of the defaulting company, whose report carries the director. Meera's report on Beas states nothing on the director, because Beas itself has not defaulted.
options.misconception: Director disqualification is reported only by the auditor of the company where the default occurred.
options.why: Clause (g) asks whether any director of this company is disqualified from being appointed as a director under section 164(2); it is this company's own board that is being asked about, whatever company's default produced the disqualification.

citation.ref: section 143(3): the report says whether every piece of information and explanations the audit needed was asked for and given and, where it was not, what is missing and what that does to the financial statements; whether a branch report made under sub-section (8) by somebody else reached the auditor and how it was used; and whether any director stands disqualified under section 164(2)

items.stem: On the receivable and the tunnel fire alone, can either matter go in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph?

options.text: The receivable can, because the note is complete and the paragraph will say the opinion is not modified; the fire cannot, because it is a key audit matter.
options.misconception: Applies the key audit matter gate and forgets the modification gate.
options.why: The second half is right and the first is the mistake the module names: management's disclosure through the notes does not remove the auditor's duty to modify where evidence is lacking, and an emphasis of matter is not a substitute for a modification of opinion. The paragraph's statement that the opinion is not modified would be untrue.

options.text: Neither. The paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter, and the receivable is a matter on which the file says a qualification is required; a complete note does not change that, because an emphasis of matter is not a substitute for a modification. The tunnel fire fails the other gate: where SA 701 applies, a matter already determined to be a key audit matter is not placed in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph as well.
options.why: Two conditions sit on this paragraph, and the two matters fail one each. The first is that the matter must not be one that leaves the auditor required to modify the opinion under SA 705 (Revised). The second, where SA 701 is in play, is that the matter must not already have been settled on as a key audit matter for the report. The receivable runs into the first, and it is the very trap the module warns of: management presses for an unmodified opinion on the ground that the notes tell the whole story, but the auditor still has to judge whether disclosure by itself will do or the report has to be modified, and the paragraph is not a substitute for a modification. The module adds that this paragraph is used only where sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the matter is already in hand, and the firm holds none on whether the 38 crore rupees will be recovered. So the opinion is qualified for the evidence the firm could not get, the note is pointed to inside the basis for that qualification, and the matter stays out of a paragraph that announces an unmodified opinion. The fire runs into the second gate: the team has already settled on it as a key audit matter, and the module's table on how the two relate says such a matter is described in the key audit matters section rather than lit up a second time here. In short, a matter that forces a modification is shut out because this paragraph is not a substitute for one, and a matter already settled on as a key audit matter is shut out by the other gate.

options.text: The fire can, because a key audit matter of that importance may be highlighted twice; the receivable cannot, because it requires a qualification.
options.misconception: Applies the modification gate and forgets the key audit matter gate.
options.why: The second gate is that, where SA 701 is in play, the matter must not already have been settled on as a key audit matter, and the module's table on the two says emphasis paragraphs used freely weaken what they are meant to carry; a key audit matter is described in the key audit matters section and is not emphasised on top of that.

options.text: Both. The purpose of the paragraph is to draw attention to matters fully disclosed in the notes, which both are, and a qualification would be disproportionate where management has hidden nothing.
options.misconception: Treats a complete note as curing a limitation on evidence.
options.why: Full disclosure is the entry condition for the paragraph, not the whole test; the module requires that the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter and that it is not a key audit matter. A qualification for an inability to obtain evidence turns on the evidence, not on candour, and the module says the paragraph is not a substitute for a modification.

citation.ref: SA 706 (Revised) puts two gates on an Emphasis of Matter paragraph: the matter must not be one that leaves the auditor required to modify the opinion under SA 705 (Revised), and, where SA 701 is in play, it must not already have been settled on as a key audit matter for the report; the paragraph is no stand-in for a modification

items.scenario: Iyer & Lakhani audit Betwa Hydro Power Limited, a listed company at Jabalpur with revenue of 1,150 crore rupees from three run-of-river stations. Radhika Iyer is the engagement partner and the draft report for the year ended 31 March 2026 is on her desk with three requests from the chief financial officer. First, a receivable of 38 crore rupees from a state distribution company has been under dispute for two years; the note describes the dispute in full, but the firm has been unable to obtain evidence about its recoverability and Radhika's file concludes that a qualification is required; the chief financial officer asks for an Emphasis of Matter paragraph instead, "since the note is complete and your opinion need not change", and asks that the same paragraph also cover the fire in the headrace tunnel at the Bargi station, which the team has already determined to be a key audit matter for its impairment assessment. Second, the accounts of the three stations are audited by three branch auditors, whose reports have been furnished to the firm, and the stations account for total assets of 610 crore rupees and revenue of 290 crore rupees; the manager proposes to say nothing of this in the report "because the Companies Act lets us rely on branch auditors anyway", while the chief financial officer suggests that if it must be mentioned it belongs under Emphasis of Matter "as it is important". Third, the manager's draft places under a single heading "Emphasis of Matter" both the company's early application, where permitted, of an amendment to an accounting standard that has a material effect and is disclosed in a note, and the fact that the comparative figures for the previous year were audited by another firm which issued an unmodified opinion.

items.stem: On the branch auditors alone, what does the report say about the three stations, and where?

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph, because the stations are more than half the company's assets and a matter of that importance must be emphasised, with a statement that the opinion is not modified.
options.misconception: Chooses the paragraph by how important the matter is rather than by what it is about.
options.why: Importance is not the test between the two paragraphs; subject matter is. The module's Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and the fact that other auditors audited the stations is not presented in them. A matter relevant to understanding the audit takes an Other Matter paragraph.

options.text: Nothing. The branch auditors' reports are the principal auditor's evidence and the Act permits reliance on them; a paragraph would suggest the firm's opinion is weaker than it is.
options.misconception: Reads statutory permission to rely as a reason not to disclose the reliance.
options.why: The module's own illustration of the Other Matter paragraph is the branch paragraph, and its text says the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter; the paragraph informs the reader who audited what, which is a matter relevant to understanding the audit, and the reliance the Act permits is what it records.

options.text: An Other Matter paragraph, in a separate section under that heading, and not an Emphasis of Matter paragraph: that the firm did not audit the financial statements of three stations reflecting total assets of 610 crore rupees and revenue of 290 crore rupees, that they were audited by branch auditors whose reports have been furnished to the firm, and that the opinion so far as it relates to those amounts and disclosures is based solely on those reports. The paragraph is available because it is not prohibited by law or regulation and the matter is not a key audit matter; the Companies Act's leave to rely on the branch auditors is why the opinion is unmodified, not a reason to be silent about it.
options.why: The module gives the rule and then this very paragraph as its worked illustration. The rule: where the auditor judges that a reader needs to be told something the accounts do not carry — something bearing on the audit itself, on what the auditor answered for, or on the report — an Other Matter paragraph is where it goes, so long as no law or regulation forbids it and, where SA 701 is in play, the matter has not already been settled on as a key audit matter; and it goes in a separate section, headed "Other Matter" or whatever other heading fits. The illustration is a company whose branches were audited by branch auditors, and the paragraph there gives the branches' assets and revenue, says their statements were audited by those auditors and that their reports have reached the principal firm, says the opinion so far as it touches those amounts and disclosures is based solely on those reports, and adds that the opinion is not modified. What that reports is the audit and who performed it — which is exactly why it can never be emphasised instead: an emphasis may take in only what the accounts themselves carry, and how the audit work was split between firms is not in them, however large the stations are. The manager has it backwards: the statute's leave to rely on other auditors is what makes the reliance sound, and the paragraph is how the reader learns the reliance happened. Where such a paragraph is expected, its wording goes to those charged with governance beforehand. In short, the branch paragraph is an Other Matter paragraph in a separate section, open because it is not prohibited by law or regulation, and it tells the reader that the opinion on those amounts is based solely on the branch auditors' reports.
keywords: not prohibited by law or regulation

options.text: A qualified opinion, because the firm did not itself audit assets of 610 crore rupees and cannot take responsibility for figures it has not examined.
options.misconception: Treats reliance on another auditor's report as a limitation on scope.
options.why: The branch auditors' reports have been furnished and the module's illustration treats reliance on them as consistent with an unmodified opinion, recorded in an Other Matter paragraph that states the opinion is based solely on those reports; there is no inability to obtain evidence and no misstatement, so nothing under SA 705 (Revised) is engaged.

citation.ref: SA 706 (Revised) on the Other Matter paragraph: it carries something the accounts do not, which the auditor judges a reader needs in order to grasp the audit, the auditor's duties or the report; it is open where no law or regulation forbids it and where the matter has not already been settled on as a key audit matter, and it sits in its own section under that heading; the module's illustration is the branch paragraph

items.scenario: Iyer & Lakhani audit Betwa Hydro Power Limited, a listed company at Jabalpur with revenue of 1,150 crore rupees from three run-of-river stations. Radhika Iyer is the engagement partner and the draft report for the year ended 31 March 2026 is on her desk with three requests from the chief financial officer. Third, the manager's draft places under a single heading "Emphasis of Matter" both the company's early application, where permitted, of an amendment to an accounting standard that has a material effect and is disclosed in a note, and the fact that the comparative figures for the previous year were audited by another firm which issued an unmodified opinion.

items.stem: On the manager's single heading alone, is the draft right to put both matters under Emphasis of Matter?

options.text: Yes. Both matters are important to a reader of the report and neither modifies the opinion, which is all an Emphasis of Matter paragraph requires; two headings for two short matters would clutter the report.
options.misconception: Uses importance as the test instead of subject matter.
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph may take in only what the statements themselves carry, and the identity of last year's auditor is not among that; it is a fact bearing on a reader's understanding of the audit and takes an Other Matter paragraph in its own section. Importance to the reader is not the dividing line.

options.text: No; the two matters take two paragraphs. The early application of the amendment is presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and the module lists it among the occasions for an Emphasis of Matter paragraph — which may refer only to information the statements themselves carry, with a pointer to the note and a line saying the opinion is not modified. That another firm audited the comparatives is nowhere in the accounts; it bears on a reader's understanding of the audit and of this firm's report, so it goes in a separate Other Matter paragraph.
options.why: What separates the two paragraphs is the subject, not the size. One of them is for something the accounts themselves already say — a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements which a reader must grasp to make sense of them — and where the auditor uses it, the paragraph may refer only to information the statements carry, must point to the note that describes the matter, and must say the opinion is not modified. Adopting an amendment early, where that is permitted, when it bites materially and is disclosed in a note, is on the module's own list of occasions for such a paragraph, and this company's note is that case. The other paragraph is for something the accounts do not say at all: a fact bearing on a reader's understanding of the audit, of what the auditor answered for, or of the report itself, and it sits in its own section headed "Other Matter" or under whatever other heading fits. Who audited last year's figures appears nowhere in the accounts. It is a fact about the audit, and about what this firm's report does and does not reach, so it cannot be filed under a heading whose paragraph may refer only to information inside the statements. One heading over both is not a small drafting slip: it files a statement about the audit inside a paragraph defined as being about the accounts. In short, the amendment is presented or disclosed in the financial statements and takes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, which may refer only to information in them, while the previous auditor bears on a reader's understanding of the audit and takes an Other Matter paragraph.
keywords: presented or disclosed in the financial statements

options.text: No; both belong under Other Matter, because neither concerns a figure in the accounts and each is about the circumstances of this year's reporting.
options.misconception: Sends a disclosed accounting matter to the paragraph reserved for matters about the audit.
options.why: The early application of the amendment is disclosed in a note and has a material effect on the financial statements, which is a matter presented or disclosed in them and one the module lists among the circumstances for an Emphasis of Matter paragraph; only the previous auditor is a matter outside the financial statements and relevant to users' understanding of the audit.

options.text: No; the comparatives audited by another firm should not be mentioned at all, because that firm's opinion was unmodified and mentioning it implies doubt, while the amendment is correctly under Emphasis of Matter.
options.misconception: Confuses an Other Matter paragraph with an expression of doubt.
options.why: The amendment is rightly emphasised, but the module's Other Matter paragraph exists for a matter not presented in the financial statements that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit or the auditor's report, and which firm audited the comparatives is that; telling the reader is the purpose, and it implies no doubt where the paragraph reports an unmodified opinion.

citation.ref: SA 706 (Revised) on the two paragraphs beside the opinion: one is for a matter the accounts already present or disclose which is fundamental to reading them, and it may take in only what the statements themselves carry; the other is for a matter the statements do not carry, bearing on a reader's grasp of the audit, of the auditor's duties or of the report; and early application of a new standard with a material effect is on the module's own list of occasions for the first

items.stem: On property, plant and equipment alone, what does the report state?

options.text: The land is not reported, because the company occupies it and pays its tax and is its owner in substance; only the revaluation is stated, since a change of twelve per cent crosses the line, and the dies are left to next year's write-off.
options.misconception: Beneficial ownership and possession satisfy the title-deed clause.
options.why: Clause (i)(c) asks in whose name the title deed is held and, where not the company's, asks for the details in the format including the reason and whether in dispute; ownership in substance is not the question, and the discrepancy is reported under (i)(b) as noticed and not dealt with.

options.text: Since there is no dispute and the promoter holds the land for the company, Lakshmi takes a written confirmation from him and reports the deed as held for the company; the dies go to a qualification of the opinion rather than to the Order.
options.misconception: A promoter's confirmation converts his name into the company's for the title-deed clause.
options.why: Clause (i)(c) asks whether the deed is held in the name of the company, not for whom it is held, and a confirmation does not change the name on the deed; the discrepancy is stated under (i)(b) whatever the opinion paragraph does about it.

options.text: The revaluation needs no statement because the note to the accounts already discloses it and the clause asks only whether a revaluation took place; the missing dies are not a discrepancy until they are written off, so only the land is reported.
options.misconception: A note in the accounts discharges the revaluation clause, and a discrepancy exists only once written off.
options.why: Clause (i)(d) asks whether the revaluation is based on the valuation by a Registered Valuer and requires the amount of change to be specified when it is 10% or more, which the auditor states whatever the note says; and a discrepancy is what the verification noticed, with the write-off being the dealing the clause asks about.

options.text: Three statements, none of them the finance head's. Under clause (i)(c) the report states that the title deed of the factory land is not held in the name of the company and gives the details in the prescribed format: the description, the gross carrying value of 14 crore rupees, whose name it stands in, that he is a promoter and director, the period since 2009, the reason, and that it is not in dispute; the property tax changes nothing. Under clause (i)(d) it states that the company revalued its plant and machinery during the year, that the revaluation is not based on the valuation by a Registered Valuer, and specifies the amount of change, because twelve per cent is 10% or more of the net carrying value of that class. Under clause (i)(b) it states that material discrepancies were noticed on physical verification and that they have not been properly dealt with in the books of account.
options.why: Each of the three sub-clauses asks a question of fact and the report answers it as a fact. Clause (i)(c) asks whether the title deeds of all immovable properties disclosed in the financial statements are held in the name of the company, and if not asks for the details in a format whose columns are the description, the gross carrying value, the name the deed is held in, whether that person is a promoter, director or their relative or employee, the period held, the reason for its not being held in the name of the company, and whether it is in dispute; a deed standing in a promoter-director's name since 2009 is answered no, with every column filled, and who pays the property tax is not a column. Clause (i)(d) asks whether the company has revalued its property, plant and equipment during the year and, if so, whether the revaluation is based on the valuation by a Registered Valuer, and asks the auditor to specify the amount of change if the change is 10% or more in the aggregate of the net carrying value of the class; a chief engineer is not a Registered Valuer, twelve per cent clears the 10% line for the plant and machinery class, and a note in the accounts is the company's disclosure, not the auditor's statement. Clause (i)(b) asks whether any material discrepancies were noticed on verification and, if so, whether they have been properly dealt with in the books of account; dies and moulds of 1.2 crore rupees that could not be found and still stand in the books were noticed and not dealt with, and an intention to write them off next year is the answer no, not the absence of a discrepancy. In short, the report states that the deed is not held in the name of the company with the format's details, that the revaluation is not based on a Registered Valuer with the amount of change, and that material discrepancies were noticed and not properly dealt with in the books of account.
keywords: held in the name of the company
properly dealt with in the books of account
