items.scenario: Krishnan & Pillai are the statutory auditors of Bhavani Pumps Limited, an unlisted public company at Coimbatore with a revenue of 310 crore rupees, and Lakshmi Krishnan is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Her report under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order is in draft and the finance head has answered three of its clauses in writing. First, on property, plant and equipment: the title deed of the factory land, with a gross carrying value of 14 crore rupees, has stood since 2009 in the name of the promoter-director, who says he holds it for the company, and there is no dispute; the plant and machinery was revalued in March 2026 by the company's own chief engineer, raising the net carrying value of that class by twelve per cent, and a note to the accounts says so; and the management's verification of assets in January 2026 could not find dies and moulds of 1.2 crore rupees, which remain in the books because the finance head intends to write them off next year. His answer is that property tax paid by the company makes the land the company's, that a note in the accounts is enough for the revaluation, and that a shortfall to be written off next year is not a discrepancy. Second, on loans: the company lent 18 crore rupees to its subsidiary, on which interest of 1.1 crore rupees was more than 120 days overdue at the year end; 7 crore rupees to a partnership owned by the managing director's brother, repayable on demand with no terms of repayment; and 5 crore rupees to a dealer, which fell due in September 2025 and was extended by a year on the same day. His answer is that the board approved each loan under section 186, so the clause has nothing to report. Third, on corporate social responsibility: of the obligation for the year ended 31 March 2025, 50 lakh rupees not tied to any project was never transferred to any fund, and 30 lakh rupees of it was spent on new projects during the year under audit; of the current year's obligation, 80 lakh rupees unspent on an ongoing school building was transferred to the special account the company opened for it. His answer is that the report should say the company has complied with section 135, because spending is better than transferring and the school money went where it should. Lakshmi has to settle what each clause says.

items.stem: On the three loans alone, what does the report state?

options.text: Only the loan to the partnership is reported, because it is the one to a related party; the subsidiary's loan and the dealer's loan are ordinary commercial loans with repayment schedules and need no mention.
options.misconception: Clause (iii) is a related-party clause.
options.why: The related-party amount is one column of sub-clause (f), not the scope of the clause; interest overdue for more than ninety days is reported under (d) and a loan renewed or extended after falling due under (e), whoever the borrower is.

options.text: The overdue interest is reported only if it is still overdue on the date of the report, and because the dealer's loan was extended on the very day it fell due nothing ever fell overdue on it, so nothing is stated under the renewal sub-clause.
options.misconception: An extension granted on the due date is not a renewal, and overdue amounts are judged at the report date.
options.why: Sub-clause (d) asks the total amount overdue for more than ninety days at the balance sheet date, and sub-clause (e) asks whether a loan that has fallen due during the year has been renewed or extended, which an extension on the due date is; the overdue question and the renewal question are different sub-clauses.

options.text: Section 186 is the question of clause (iv); clause (iii) asks its own, and each of the three loans answers one. The report gives the aggregate amount granted during the year and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, with the 18 crore rupees to the subsidiary shown apart from the loans to parties other than subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates; states whether the terms of each are prejudicial to the company's interest; states that on the subsidiary's loan interest of 1.1 crore rupees is overdue for more than ninety days and whether reasonable steps have been taken for its recovery; states that the dealer's loan of 5 crore rupees, which fell due during the year, was renewed or extended, with the aggregate and its percentage of the loans granted during the year; and states that 7 crore rupees to the partnership is repayable on demand without terms of repayment, with the aggregate, its percentage of the total loans, and the amount of it granted to related parties.
options.why: Board approval under section 186 answers clause (iv), which asks whether sections 185 and 186 have been complied with, and it answers nothing in clause (iii), which is a set of factual questions about the loans themselves. Sub-clause (a) asks the aggregate during the year and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, separately for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and for other parties, so the subsidiary's loan is the first line of the answer and not outside it. Sub-clause (b) asks whether the terms of all loans are not prejudicial to the company's interest, which is stated for each. Sub-clause (d) asks, if the amount is overdue, the total amount overdue for more than ninety days and whether reasonable steps have been taken for recovery of the principal and interest; interest of 1.1 crore rupees overdue for more than 120 days at the year end is overdue for more than ninety days and is stated with the steps taken. Sub-clause (e) asks whether any loan which has fallen due during the year has been renewed or extended, and if so the aggregate so renewed or extended and its percentage of the total loans granted during the year; a loan that fell due in September 2025 and was extended by a year on that day is exactly that, and the extension being prompt does not take it out. Sub-clause (f) asks whether any loans repayable on demand or without specifying terms or period of repayment have been granted, and if so the aggregate, its percentage of the total loans, and the amount granted to promoters and related parties; a loan to the managing director's brother's partnership repayable on demand with no terms fills every column. In short, the report states the amounts by class of borrower, the terms, the interest overdue for more than ninety days with the recovery steps, the dealer's loan renewed or extended with its percentage, and the partnership's loan repayable on demand with the related-party amount.
keywords: overdue for more than ninety days

options.text: The finance head is right: each loan was approved by the board under section 186, so the clause is answered favourably, and the subsidiary's loan is in any case outside it as a loan within the group.
options.misconception: Board approval under section 186 disposes of clause (iii), and group loans are outside it.
options.why: Section 186 is clause (iv)'s question; clause (iii)(a) asks the aggregate and balance outstanding to subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates by name, so a group loan is the first thing reported, and the overdue interest, the extension and the demand loan are each a separate sub-clause.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(iii) asks, where the company has granted loans or advances in the nature of loans, the aggregate during the year and the balance outstanding to subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and to other parties; whether the terms are not prejudicial to the company's interest; whether a schedule of repayment has been stipulated and the repayments are regular; the total amount overdue for more than ninety days and whether reasonable steps have been taken for recovery; whether a loan fallen due during the year has been renewed or extended, with the aggregate and its percentage; and whether loans repayable on demand or without terms have been granted, with the aggregate, the percentage and the amount to promoters and related parties

items.stem: On the corporate social responsibility money alone, what does the report state?

options.text: Because the ongoing project's money reached the special account, the clause is answered favourably as a whole; the 50 lakh rupees belongs to the previous year's obligation and was a matter for the previous year's report.
options.misconception: Clause (xx) is one answer, and last year's unspent amount belongs to last year's report.
options.why: The two limbs are answered separately, and the six months for the previous year's unspent amount expired on 30 September 2025, within the year under audit, so the failure to transfer to a Fund specified in Schedule VII is a fact of this year's report whatever last year's said.

options.text: Spending the money on corporate social responsibility is a better outcome than parking it in a fund, so the 30 lakh rupees spent satisfies the clause for that part and only the 20 lakh rupees still lying with the company is reported as not transferred.
options.misconception: Later spending on projects substitutes for the transfer to a Schedule VII fund.
options.why: Limb (a) asks whether the unspent amount was transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the expiry of the financial year; spending after that date is not a transfer, and the unspent amount the limb asks about is the whole 50 lakh rupees.

options.text: Corporate social responsibility is the board's matter under section 135 and is reported in the board's report; the auditor's report under the Order carries it only where the company has no corporate social responsibility committee at all.
options.misconception: Corporate social responsibility is for the board's report, not the auditor's.
options.why: Paragraph 3 of the Order has the auditor's report include a statement on every listed matter for a company to which the Order applies, and clause (xx) asks about the transfer to a Fund specified in Schedule VII and to the special account without any condition about a committee.

options.text: Two statements, one unfavourable and one favourable, and neither of them is that the company has complied with section 135. Under clause (xx)(a) the report states that, in respect of other than ongoing projects, the company has not transferred the unspent amount of 50 lakh rupees to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within a period of six months of the expiry of the financial year to which it relates, and that spending 30 lakh rupees of it on new projects afterwards is not that transfer. Under clause (xx)(b) the report states that the amount remaining unspent pursuant to an ongoing project, 80 lakh rupees, has been transferred to the special account in compliance with section 135(6); a favourable answer is still a statement, not a silence.
options.why: Clause (xx) has two limbs with two destinations, and the report answers each in its own words. Limb (a) asks whether, in respect of other than ongoing projects, the company has transferred the unspent amount to a Fund specified in Schedule VII to the Companies Act within a period of six months of the expiry of the financial year, in compliance with the second proviso to section 135(5); the 50 lakh rupees for the year ended 31 March 2025 was tied to no project, six months from the expiry of that year ran out on 30 September 2025, inside the year under audit, and no transfer was made, so the answer is no with the amount, and the later spending of 30 lakh rupees on new projects is a use of the money and not the transfer the limb asks about. Limb (b) asks whether any amount remaining unspent under section 135(5) pursuant to any ongoing project has been transferred to the special account in compliance with section 135(6); the 80 lakh rupees for the school building was, so the answer is yes, and the Order asks for the statement on every matter in paragraph 3, favourable or not, with reasons required only where the answer is unfavourable. A single line that the company has complied with section 135 is neither limb and is wrong on the first. In short, the report states that the unspent amount for other than ongoing projects was not transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months, and that the ongoing project's unspent amount was transferred to the special account.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xx)(a) asks whether, in respect of other than ongoing projects, the company has transferred the unspent amount to a Fund specified in Schedule VII to the Companies Act within a period of six months of the expiry of the financial year in compliance with the second proviso to section 135(5); 3(xx)(b) asks whether any amount remaining unspent under section 135(5) pursuant to any ongoing project has been transferred to the special account in compliance with section 135(6)

items.stem: On the chief financial officer's list alone, which matters are key audit matters and why?

options.text: Whichever matters the chief financial officer selects, since key audit matters are chosen from matters communicated with management and management is best placed to say which were significant to the company.
options.misconception: Hands the selection of key audit matters to management.
options.why: The module's starting pool is the matters communicated with those charged with governance, and the judgment of which required significant auditor attention and which were of most significance is the auditor's professional judgment. Significance to the company is not the test; significance in the audit is.

options.text: The contract revenue and the plant impairment, and not the other three. Key audit matters are determined from the matters communicated with those charged with governance as those that required significant auditor attention, judged by higher assessed risk or significant risks, significant auditor judgments on areas of significant management judgment and estimation uncertainty, and significant events; from those the auditor selects the matters of most significance. Routine work that went through without difficulty does not qualify, however many items the company would like listed.
options.why: The module defines the term and then the funnel. Key audit matters are those matters that, in the auditor's professional judgment, were of most significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period, and they are selected from matters communicated with those charged with governance. The auditor shall determine, from those matters, the ones that required significant auditor attention in performing the audit, taking into account areas of higher assessed risk of material misstatement or significant risks identified in accordance with SA 315, significant auditor judgments relating to areas in the financial statements that involved significant management judgment including accounting estimates identified as having high estimation uncertainty, and the effect on the audit of significant events or transactions that occurred during the period. Revenue on long-term contracts and the impairment of a plant are the module's own examples of key audit matters, and the senior's paper records them as the significant risks that took the team's judgment. A register reconciliation, a tax reconciliation and bank confirmations that went through without difficulty required no significant attention, and the number of matters is the outcome of the judgment, not an input to it. In short, the two matters that were communicated with those charged with governance, required significant auditor attention and were of most significance are the key audit matters.
keywords: communicated with those charged with governance

options.text: None of them should be described. Naming the contract revenue and the impairment would amount to separate opinions on those two balances, which SA 701 forbids.
options.misconception: Reads the "no separate opinion" sentence as a bar on communicating key audit matters.
options.why: The introductory language the module prescribes says that the matters were addressed in the context of the audit as a whole and that the auditor does not provide a separate opinion on them; that sentence is how a key audit matter is described without becoming a separate opinion, not a reason to describe none.

options.text: All five. A key audit matter is any area the audit covered in depth, and listing more of them increases the transparency the standard is designed to give the reader.
options.misconception: Treats a key audit matter as anything audited carefully rather than what required significant attention.
options.why: Transparency is the purpose the module states, but the selection rule is the module's funnel: matters communicated with those charged with governance that required significant auditor attention, and among those the ones of most significance. Routine procedures that went through without difficulty fail the first test, and a longer list dilutes rather than increases the communicative value.

citation.ref: key audit matters are those that in the auditor's professional judgment were of most significance in the audit of the current period, determined from the matters communicated with those charged with governance as those that required significant auditor attention, taking into account areas of higher assessed risk of material misstatement or significant risks, significant auditor judgments on areas involving significant management judgment including estimates with high estimation uncertainty, and the effect of significant events or transactions

items.scenario: Menon & Saxena are the statutory auditors of Bhima Wind Components Limited, an unlisted public company at Coimbatore that fabricates towers for wind turbines, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Revenue is 720 crore rupees. The company's lenders asked for a report that names the matters the auditors spent most of their effort on, and the engagement letter records the firm's decision to communicate key audit matters. Three matters are open before signing. First, the chief financial officer has sent the partner a list of five matters he wants shown as key audit matters, "because five shows how thorough the audit was": revenue on long-term tower contracts, impairment of the Tuticorin plant, the reconciliation of the fixed asset register, GST reconciliations, and the year-end bank confirmations. The senior's working paper records that the contract revenue and the impairment were significant risks that took most of the team's judgment and time, and that the other three were routine and went through without difficulty. Second, the company breached the debt-to-equity covenant on a 150 crore rupee term loan at the year end, the lender has not yet waived it, and note 38 discloses the breach and the resulting material uncertainty about going concern completely and accurately; the partner has drafted a key audit matter headed "Liquidity and covenant compliance" and intends to use it in place of a going concern section "so the report does not carry a heading the lenders dislike". Third, the managing director has written that the company is not listed, that SA 701 therefore cannot apply to it, and that the whole Key Audit Matters section must be dropped from the report.

items.stem: On the covenant breach alone, may the partner report it as a key audit matter instead of under going concern?

options.text: Neither. Because note 38 already discloses the uncertainty completely and accurately, nothing further is required in the auditor's report; the auditor reports on the financial statements, not on what the notes already say.
options.misconception: Assumes an adequate note discharges the auditor's own going concern reporting.
options.why: Adequate disclosure by management is the condition for an unmodified opinion, not a reason to say nothing: the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section exists to draw attention to that very note. The module also says a key audit matter is no substitute for the disclosures the framework requires, and the reverse is equally true.

options.text: No. Communicating a key audit matter is not a substitute for reporting under SA 570 when a material uncertainty exists. The breach and its consequence go under a separate Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, drawing attention to note 38, and the Key Audit Matters section carries a reference to that section rather than a description of the matter under a heading of the partner's choosing.
options.why: The module lists what communicating key audit matters is not, and the third item is the answer. It is not a substitute for reporting in accordance with SA 570 (Revised) when a material uncertainty exists relating to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on an entity's ability to continue as a going concern, just as it is not a substitute for a modified opinion under SA 705 or for the disclosures management is required to make. A covenant breach with no waiver on a 150 crore rupee loan, disclosed by the company itself as a material uncertainty, is exactly the SA 570 case, and the reporting it calls for is the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section. The module's own illustration then shows how the two sections sit together: the Key Audit Matters section says that, except for the matter described in the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, no other key audit matters were determined, which is a reference, not a description. The lenders' dislike of a heading is not a consideration the standard admits, and a report that hid the going concern section behind a liquidity label would give them less than the standard requires. In short, a key audit matter is not a substitute for the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, and the key audit matters section carries a reference to it.
keywords: Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern

options.text: Yes. The matter took significant auditor attention and involved significant judgment, so it meets the definition of a key audit matter, and the heading is the auditor's to choose.
options.misconception: Lets the definition of a key audit matter override the separate reporting SA 570 requires.
options.why: A matter can meet the definition and still not be described in the Key Audit Matters section: the module says communicating key audit matters is not a substitute for reporting in accordance with SA 570, and the illustration has the section refer to the going concern section rather than describe the matter. Meeting the definition is why the reference is there; it is not a licence to relabel.

options.text: Yes, provided the key audit matter description also explains that a material uncertainty exists; a description that says the same thing as a going concern section is equivalent to it.
options.misconception: Treats matching content under a different heading as compliance with SA 570.
options.why: The module rules out the substitution in terms, whatever the words used, because the reader is entitled to find a material uncertainty under the heading the standards give it. The going concern section is required, and the key audit matters section refers to it.

citation.ref: communicating key audit matters is not a substitute for reporting in accordance with SA 570 when a material uncertainty exists relating to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern, nor for a modified opinion under SA 705, nor for disclosures required of management; the illustrated section refers to the Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section and states that no other key audit matters were determined

The senior's working paper records that the contract revenue and the impairment were significant risks that took most of the team's judgment and time, and that the other three were routine and went through without difficulty. Second, the company breached the debt-to-equity covenant on a 150 crore rupee term loan at the year end, the lender has not yet waived it, and note 38 discloses the breach and the resulting material uncertainty about going concern completely and accurately; the partner has drafted a key audit matter headed "Liquidity and covenant compliance" and intends to use it in place of a going concern section "so the report does not carry a heading the lenders dislike". Third, the managing director has written that the company is not listed, that SA 701 therefore cannot apply to it, and that the whole Key Audit Matters section must be dropped from the report.

items.stem: On the managing director's objection alone, does SA 701 apply to this report?

options.text: Yes. The standard is mandatory for listed entities, but it also applies in circumstances when the auditor otherwise decides to communicate key audit matters, and when law or regulation requires it. The firm decided, and recorded the decision in the engagement letter, so the section stays and the standard governs it in full. The only bar the module names is a report in which the auditor disclaims an opinion, and that is not this report.
options.why: The module sets out three circumstances in which SA 701 applies to an audit of a complete set of general purpose financial statements: listed entities; circumstances when the auditor otherwise decides to communicate key audit matters in the auditor's report; and when required by law or regulation to communicate key audit matters in the auditor's report. Being unlisted removes the first road, and the managing director stops reading there. The second road is the one this firm took, at the lenders' request and in the engagement letter, and once the auditor decides to communicate key audit matters the standard applies to how they are determined and described exactly as it would for a listed company. The module adds the one prohibition: SA 705 (Revised) prohibits the auditor from communicating key audit matters when the auditor disclaims an opinion on the financial statements, unless such reporting is required by law or regulation. This report expresses an opinion, so the prohibition does not bite. In short, SA 701 applies beyond listed entities to the case where the auditor otherwise decides, and the section comes out only where the auditor disclaims an opinion.

options.text: No. SA 701 is confined to listed entities, and an auditor who includes a Key Audit Matters section in an unlisted company's report is reporting outside the standard's scope, so the section must be dropped.
options.misconception: Reads the listed-entity requirement as the whole scope of the standard.
options.why: The module's second circumstance is exactly an auditor who otherwise decides to communicate key audit matters, in an entity where the standard does not require it. That decision brings the audit within SA 701, and the section is prepared under it.

options.text: It applies, but because the company is unlisted the section may be limited to a statement that key audit matters were considered, without naming or describing any.
options.misconception: Invents a reduced form of the section for a voluntary adopter.
options.why: Once SA 701 applies, its requirements for determining and describing key audit matters apply without a lighter form for unlisted entities; where matters are determined they are described, and a statement that there are none is used only when the auditor has determined that there are none.

options.text: It applies only if the lenders' request is written into a loan covenant, because a requirement imposed by a third party is the "law or regulation" limb of the standard's scope.
options.misconception: Mistakes a contractual request for the law-or-regulation limb of the standard.
options.why: A lender's request is not law or regulation; what it did here was prompt the auditor's own decision, and the module's second circumstance, where the auditor otherwise decides, is met by that decision recorded in the engagement letter, covenant or no covenant.

citation.ref: SA 701 applies to audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, to circumstances when the auditor otherwise decides to communicate key audit matters in the auditor's report, and when required by law or regulation; SA 705 prohibits communicating key audit matters when the auditor disclaims an opinion, unless such reporting is required by law or regulation

items.stem: QUESTION 1 OF 3 — turns on the deposits at the Rourkela branch. The balance sheet placement and the investment book are noise for this one. On the deposits alone, what does Sujata conclude?

options.text: Every one of the six is wrong. A savings account is not opened for a business or professional concern, so the rice mill's turnover belongs in a current account. An overdrawn current account is never set off against deposits; the two crore rupees must be included under the head advances instead. An account with no transactions for over two years is inoperative, so the forty-one are misclassified and the revival on an unwritten instruction was not made with proper authority. The four crore rupee deposit is a bulk deposit, two crore rupees and above, and needed the bulk rate verified. Interest accrued but not due goes under other liabilities and provisions, not inside the term deposits figure. And the March round trip inflates both deposits and advances, which is window dressing; for that Sujata should consider a suitable qualification in the main audit report. In short, the netted overdrafts must be included under the head advances, the dormant accounts are those with no transactions for over two years, and the March reversal calls for a suitable qualification in the main audit report.
options.why: The chapter settles each of the six separately. A trading or professional business does not bank in a savings account; its turnover runs through a current account. Where such an account is overdrawn the bank does not shrink its deposits by that amount — the overdraft is an asset and is included under the head advances, so both the deposits figure and the advances figure here are wrong by two crore rupees. An account is treated as inoperative or dormant when there are no transactions for over two years, and an inoperative account is revived only with proper authority — a telephone instruction nobody recorded is not that, and the chapter marks inoperative accounts as a high-risk area of fraud. Bulk deposits are two crore rupees and above for scheduled commercial banks presently, so the correct rate had to be verified rather than the retail card rate applied. Interest accrued but not due on deposits is shown under other liabilities and provisions and not clubbed with the deposits. And the module's own example of window dressing is this exact round trip — overdrafts near the balance sheet date, the overdrawn money placed as deposits, further advances against those deposits, reversed after the close of the year — for which the auditor should consider making a suitable qualification in the main audit report besides other applicable reporting.
keywords: no transactions for over two years
suitable qualification in the main audit report

options.text: The March overdraft-to-deposit round trip is a presentation matter only, and since the transactions were reversed on 4 April it is enough to disclose it as a subsequent event without touching the audit report.
options.misconception: Treating a transaction reversed shortly after the year end as self-correcting, when what is being tested is the figure that stood on the balance sheet date and the intention that put it there.
options.why: The reversal is the evidence of window dressing, not the cure for it. The balance sheet at 31 March carries inflated deposits and inflated advances, and where the figures point to window dressing the chapter asks the auditor to weigh a suitable qualification in the main audit report, on top of whatever else he has to report.

options.text: The netting of the three overdrawn current accounts is correct, because the same customer's debit and credit balances at one branch are two sides of one relationship and the net figure is the true liability of the bank.
options.misconception: Carrying the offsetting rule for a customer's several accounts over from an ordinary company's books, where a net receivable is normal, into a balance sheet whose form is fixed by the Third Schedule.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite in terms. An overdrawn balance is not allowed to shrink the deposits shown on the liabilities side; it crosses over and is included under the head advances. Netting understates deposits and understates advances at the same time, which is why the rule is written as a prohibition rather than a preference.

options.text: The forty-one accounts are not yet inoperative, because an account becomes dormant only after three years without a transaction, and the revival in January restarted that clock in any event.
options.misconception: Borrowing the three-year period from unclaimed deposits and the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund and applying it to the inoperative-account test, which is a different and shorter clock.
options.why: The period in the chapter is over two years, not three, so all forty-one were already inoperative at the year end. And a revival does not cure the earlier misclassification — it is itself the risk the rule is aimed at, which is why an inoperative account may be revived only with proper authority and why a large fall in the balance of such an account calls for the withdrawal authorisation to be examined.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — audit of deposits: savings accounts and business concerns, debit balances in current accounts, inoperative accounts, bulk deposits, interest accrued but not due, and deposits inflated for balance sheet presentation.

items.scenario: Mahapatra & Sahu are a firm of chartered accountants at Bhubaneswar, and Sujata Mahapatra is the partner in charge of the audit of a nationalised bank, where her firm is one of four appointed jointly as statutory central auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters reach her in the week the branch returns are being consolidated. First, the deposits at the Rourkela branch. A savings account has been opened in the name of a rice-milling partnership firm and the whole of that firm's business turnover has passed through it. Three current accounts at the branch were overdrawn at the year end by two crore rupees between them, and the branch has shown its deposits figure on the liabilities side net of that overdrawn amount. Forty-one savings and current accounts in which nothing at all has moved since February 2024 are still being counted as operative, and one of them was revived in January and emptied a week later on a telephone instruction nobody wrote down. A term deposit of four crore rupees placed in November was given the rate the bank publishes for its retail depositors. Interest accrued but not due on term deposits, seven crore rupees, has been added into the term deposits figure itself. And in the last week of March the branch sanctioned overdrafts to four borrowers, the overdrawn money came back the same day as fresh term deposits, further advances were drawn against the security of those deposits, and the whole arrangement was reversed on 4 April. Second, where three balances sit in the balance sheet. The inter-office adjustments account is in credit by twelve crore rupees at the year end and the bank has set that credit off against advances. Advances are shown at their gross figure, with provisions of three hundred and forty crore rupees disclosed separately on the liabilities side. And a contractor's claim, on which the High Court passed a decree against the bank in February that the bank has decided not to appeal, is still listed among claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts. Third, the investment book. In December the bank moved securities of a face value of nine hundred crore rupees from available for sale to held to maturity; the shift was cleared by the investment committee and by the asset liability committee, and the finance head says that is the competent authority because the Board delegated investment decisions to those committees years ago. On one security the interest has been in arrears since 12 November 2025 and the bank has gone on taking the coupon to income, because the issuer is a state undertaking and the finance head expects the money. Sujata has to settle all three before the consolidated statements go up.

items.stem: QUESTION 2 OF 3 — turns on where the three balances sit in the balance sheet. The branch's deposits and the investment book are noise for this one. On the placement alone, what does Sujata require?

options.text: Only the decree must move. The inter-office set-off and the gross presentation of advances are both acceptable, because the Third Schedule fixes the heads of the balance sheet and not the arithmetic that produces the figure under each head.
options.misconception: Reading a prescribed form as a list of captions to be filled in however the entity likes, when for a bank the form carries the measurement and the offsetting rules with it.
options.why: The chapter fixes the arithmetic as well as the heads. A credit on the inter-office adjustments account, if in credit at the year end, has a home of its own under Other Liabilities and Provisions, and what is shown for advances and for investments already excludes provisions against them. Both of the two treatments the bank has adopted are therefore wrong on their own, before the decree is reached.

options.text: The provisions of three hundred and forty crore rupees are correctly shown as a separate liability, because showing advances net of provisions would hide the size of the bank's bad loan book from the reader of the balance sheet.
options.misconception: Letting a sound instinct about transparency override a prescribed presentation, when the same information is required to reach the reader by a route the form already provides.
options.why: The concern is real and the Third Schedule answers it elsewhere, through the disclosures and the notes, not by grossing up the face of the balance sheet. The rule in the chapter is flat: a bank presents both advances and investments net, with the provisions held against them — tested and accepted by its auditors — already taken off the figure that reaches the reader.

options.text: All three must move. A balance standing on the inter-office adjustments account, if in credit, has its own home under Other Liabilities and Provisions and cannot be set off against advances. What a bank shows for its advances and its investments already excludes provisions held against them, tested to the auditors' satisfaction, so the three hundred and forty crore rupees comes off the advances figure instead of standing as a separate liability. And a decree the bank has decided not to appeal is no longer contingent: the disclosed contingent liabilities must not include crystallised liabilities of the nature of a loss or expense, which require a provision to be made instead. In short, an inter-office adjustments account, if in credit, belongs under Other Liabilities and Provisions, the advances figure excludes provisions made to the auditors' satisfaction, and crystallised liabilities come out of the contingent list and into a provision.
options.why: Each of the three is a placement rule and none of them is a matter of judgement. The Third Schedule requires bills payable, inter-office adjustments (net), interest accrued and others including provisions to be disclosed under Other Liabilities and Provisions, and the chapter places the balance on the inter-office adjustments account, if in credit, squarely under that same head; netting it off against advances understates both sides of the balance sheet at once. On the asset side the chapter is equally flat: what a bank shows for advances and for investments already excludes provisions against them, tested to the auditors' satisfaction, so those figures are presented net and the provision never surfaces as a liability of its own. And among the representations the auditor obtains on contingent liabilities is that the disclosed contingent liabilities do not include any crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense, which require the creation of a provision or adjustment — an unappealed decree is exactly such a liability, and leaving it in the contingent list keeps a real charge off the face of the accounts.
keywords: inter-office adjustments account, if in credit

options.text: The contractor's decree stays where it is until the appeal period expires and the bank actually pays, since until money leaves the bank the amount remains a claim against the bank not acknowledged as a debt.
options.misconception: Tying recognition to the cash going out rather than to the point at which the obligation stopped being contingent, which is the whole distinction between a provision and a contingent liability.
options.why: The bank has decided not to appeal, so the liability has crystallised and the label no longer fits — the bank does acknowledge the debt. The representation the auditor obtains is that the disclosed contingent liabilities do not include crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense, which require a provision. Payment is when the provision is used, not when it arises.

citation.ref: Third Schedule, Form A — Other Liabilities and Provisions, the inter-office adjustments balance in credit, advances and investments stated net of provisions, and contingent liabilities.

items.stem: QUESTION 3 OF 3 — turns on the investment book. The branch's deposits and the balance sheet placement are noise for this one. On the investments alone, what does Sujata conclude?

options.text: Both are wrong. Moving a security out of available for sale and into held to maturity is a step the bank's own board has to sanction: it is duly approved by the Board of Directors and by nobody below them, however wide the standing delegation the investment committee or the asset liability committee holds. Those committees are competent to fix a category on the day the security is bought, which is a different decision altogether. And a coupon in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days makes it a non-performing investment, so from the second week of February the bank should have stopped reckoning income and made provision for the depreciation in its value; the identity of the issuer and the finance head's expectation of payment change nothing. In short, the shift out of available for sale needed approval duly approved by the Board of Directors, and interest in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days makes it one of the bank's non-performing investments.
options.why: The chapter separates the two decisions on purpose. Which category a security enters on the day it is bought turns on what the bank meant to do with it, and the proof of that intention is a decision by a competent authority — the board, but a committee will do. Shifting one out of a category later is the tighter rule, and there the auditor looks for a move duly approved by the Board of Directors itself; a delegation handed to two committees years ago is not that approval. On the arrears the test is mechanical rather than a matter of judgement. An investment goes bad for this purpose once either the interest or the principal has stood in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days. From that point the security sits among the bank's non-performing investments, the income stops being taken to the profit and loss account, and a provision is made for the fall in its value. Ninety days from 12 November 2025 runs out in the second week of February, so the coupon taken to income after that date should not have been.
keywords: duly approved by the Board of Directors
in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days

options.text: The security is not yet a non-performing investment, because the issuer is a state undertaking and payments backed by a state government are not treated as being in arrears while recovery is expected.
options.misconception: Importing the comfort of a government-linked borrower into a rule that was deliberately written to be counted rather than judged.
options.why: There is no such carve-out in the chapter. The test is the age of the arrears alone: an investment is non-performing once either sum has sat in arrears and remains unpaid for more than 90 days. Who the issuer is and what management expects have no place in it, which is the point of writing the test as a number of days.

options.text: The shift is properly approved. The chapter names the Board, the asset liability committee and the investment committee as competent authorities for the categories of the investment portfolio, and both committees cleared this one.
options.misconception: Reading one list of competent authorities as though it governed every decision about the investment book, when the chapter attaches it to the acquisition decision and puts a higher bar on the shift.
options.why: Those three bodies are named for classification at the time of acquisition, where the question is what the bank intended when it bought the security. Shifting an existing holding out of available for sale into held to maturity carries its own requirement, and the chapter states it separately: the auditor examines whether the shift is duly approved by the Board of Directors of the bank.

options.text: The bank may go on taking the coupon to income so long as it makes provision for the depreciation in the value of the investment, because the provision already reflects the loss and stopping the income as well would count the same thing twice.
options.misconception: Treating a provision as a substitute for stopping accrual, which leaves an uncollected coupon sitting in the profit and loss account of the year it was never earned in.
options.why: The chapter requires both, not a choice between them: in the case of a non-performing investment banks have not to reckon income on the securities and are required to make provisions for depreciation in the value of the investment. Income recognition and valuation are separate consequences of the same classification, and the second does not buy off the first.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — examination of classification and shifting between HTM, HFT and AFS, the approval required for a shift out of available for sale, and non-performing investments.

items.stem: On the planning memo alone, what must Zeenat do before the strategy is set?

options.text: Nothing further. Acceptance is a one-time decision that was taken and documented before the appointment, and planning under SA 300 begins with the overall audit strategy; the tax partner's work is a firm-level matter for the firm's quality control, not the engagement.
options.misconception: Treats acceptance as a tender-stage event rather than a beginning-of-engagement activity.
options.why: The module places the acceptance and continuance procedures, the ethical evaluation including independence, and the terms of the engagement at the beginning of the current audit engagement, as preliminary engagement activities that precede the strategy, and makes the engagement partner responsible for being satisfied with the conclusions. A partner's new work for the promoter is a threat the engagement's own independence evaluation must consider.

options.text: Evaluate independence and issue the firm's own engagement letter, but the acceptance procedures need not be repeated because the company was accepted at the tender and nothing in the standard requires them twice.
options.misconception: Keeps two of the three preliminary activities and drops the first.
options.why: The module's first activity at the beginning of the current audit engagement is the SA 220 procedures on acceptance and continuance, and their content includes significant matters that have arisen since; a tender-stage review months earlier does not satisfy an activity the standard places at the start of the engagement itself.

options.text: Perform the three preliminary engagement activities at the beginning of the current audit engagement, whatever was done at the tender: the acceptance procedures SA 220 requires, covering the integrity of the owners and management, the team's competence and time, the firm's ability to meet ethical requirements and significant matters arising; an evaluation of compliance with ethical requirements including independence, which the tax partner's new work for the promoter now demands; and an understanding of the terms of the engagement under SA 210 in the firm's own engagement letter, not another firm's letter renamed.
options.why: The module lists the activities and fixes their timing. The auditor shall undertake the following activities at the beginning of the current audit engagement: performing the procedures required by SA 220 regarding the continuance of the client relationship and the specific audit engagement, which on the combined reading of SA 220 and SQC 1 turn on the integrity of the principal owners, key management and those charged with governance, whether the engagement team is competent and has the necessary capabilities, expertise, time and resources, whether the firm and the team can comply with relevant ethical requirements, and significant matters that have arisen during the current or previous audit engagement; evaluating compliance with ethical requirements, including independence, as required by SA 220; and establishing an understanding of the terms of the engagement as required by SA 210. The module calls acceptance and continuance very important preliminary engagement activities and says the engagement partner should be satisfied that the procedures have been followed and that the conclusions are appropriate. A tender in February is not the beginning of the engagement, and what has changed since is exactly what the activities exist to catch: a partner of the firm now working for the promoter personally is a matter for the independence evaluation, and the terms of the engagement are the firm's own to establish and record. In short, the activities are done at the beginning of the current audit engagement, independence is evaluated afresh, and the terms of the engagement are established in the firm's own letter.
keywords: beginning of the current audit engagement

options.text: Use the previous auditors' engagement letter as it stands, since the terms of a statutory audit are fixed by law and do not change with the auditor, and record the acceptance and independence work after the strategy so that fieldwork is not delayed.
options.misconception: Borrows another firm's terms and reorders the preliminary activities behind the strategy.
options.why: The module requires the auditor to establish an understanding of the terms of the engagement as required by SA 210, an understanding between this firm and the entity, and places all three activities at the beginning of the current audit engagement, before the strategy is set, not after.

citation.ref: at the beginning of the current audit engagement the auditor performs the procedures required by SA 220 regarding acceptance and continuance of the client relationship and the specific audit engagement, evaluates compliance with relevant ethical requirements including independence as required by SA 220, and establishes an understanding of the terms of the engagement as required by SA 210

items.scenario: Rao & Farooqui were appointed statutory auditors of Chambal Auto Castings Limited, an unlisted public company at Bhilwara with revenue of 640 crore rupees, for the year ended 31 March 2026, after the previous auditors completed their term. Zeenat Farooqui is the engagement partner and three matters are open at the planning stage. First, the manager's planning memo opens with the overall audit strategy and records that "acceptance was completed at the tender stage in February 2026, so no further preliminary work is needed"; since then the firm's tax partner has begun advising the promoter on his personal tax affairs, and no engagement letter has been issued because the manager intends to reuse the previous auditors' letter with the firm's name changed. Second, the senior proposes to accept the opening balances as they stand, "because last year was audited by a firm of standing and the closing figures are in the signed accounts", and the chief financial officer has said that opening balances are last year's problem and this year's audit should start from 1 April. Third, the previous auditors' report for the year ended 31 March 2025 carried a qualified opinion because they could not attend the physical count of inventory of 22 crore rupees at the Bhilwara foundry, which is the opening inventory for this year and has flowed into this year's cost of sales; the chief financial officer wants the new report to say in an Other Matter paragraph that the previous year was audited by another firm whose report was qualified, and nothing more.

items.stem: On the senior's proposal alone, what does SA 510 require of the new auditors for the opening balances?

options.text: Evidence, not acceptance. The auditor reads the most recent financial statements and the predecessor auditor's report, determines whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward, determines whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies, and performs audit procedures on opening balances to obtain evidence that they contain no misstatement materially affecting this year. A prior audit by a firm of standing is a source to read, not evidence in itself, and the year does not start on 1 April for the auditor.
options.why: The module frames the objective and lists the procedures. An initial audit engagement is one in which the prior period's financial statements were not audited or were audited by a predecessor auditor, and the auditor's objective is sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether the opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements and whether appropriate accounting policies are consistently applied. The auditor shall read the most recent financial statements and the predecessor auditor's report; determine whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward; determine whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies; perform audit procedures on opening balances; and, if the current period's financial statements are misstated due to a misstatement in the opening balances, communicate with management or those charged with governance. Nothing in that list is satisfied by the standing of the previous firm, and the module's own worked example is a new auditor with a lingering doubt about opening inventory who is asked whether any responsibility exists, which is the senior's question in different words. Opening balances are the current year's problem because they sit inside the current year's statements. In short, the auditor reads the predecessor auditor's report, checks that the closing balances were correctly brought forward, and performs audit procedures on opening balances.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the opening balances are correct, which discharges the responsibility because the previous year's accounts were approved by the members.
options.misconception: Substitutes a representation and a shareholder vote for audit procedures.
options.why: A representation is not among the procedures the module lists, and approval by the members is not audit evidence; the auditor performs audit procedures on opening balances and checks the balances brought forward and the policies applied.

options.text: Accept them. Opening balances audited by a predecessor are outside the current engagement, and the new auditor's responsibility begins with the transactions of the current year; the predecessor's report is the evidence.
options.misconception: Treats the predecessor's audit as the current auditor's evidence.
options.why: The module's SA 510 exists for exactly this engagement and requires audit procedures on opening balances, not acceptance of them; the predecessor's report is read, and the closing balances are checked as brought forward, but the evidence about misstatement in the opening balances is the current auditor's to obtain.

options.text: Re-audit the previous year in full, because an initial engagement makes the new auditor responsible for the prior period's statements as well as the current one.
options.misconception: Overshoots from procedures on opening balances to a second audit of last year.
options.why: The module's objective is evidence about whether the opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period, obtained by reading the prior statements and report, checking the balances brought forward, checking the policies and performing audit procedures on opening balances; it is not an opinion on the prior year, and no re-audit is called for.

citation.ref: in an initial audit engagement the auditor reads the most recent financial statements and the predecessor auditor's report, determines whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward, determines whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies, performs audit procedures on the opening balances, and where the current period's statements are misstated by a misstatement in the opening balances communicates with management or those charged with governance

Zeenat Farooqui is the engagement partner and three matters are open at the planning stage. First, the manager's planning memo opens with the overall audit strategy and records that "acceptance was completed at the tender stage in February 2026, so no further preliminary work is needed"; since then the firm's tax partner has begun advising the promoter on his personal tax affairs, and no engagement letter has been issued because the manager intends to reuse the previous auditors' letter with the firm's name changed. Second, the senior proposes to accept the opening balances as they stand, "because last year was audited by a firm of standing and the closing figures are in the signed accounts", and the chief financial officer has said that opening balances are last year's problem and this year's audit should start from 1 April. Third, the previous auditors' report for the year ended 31 March 2025 carried a qualified opinion because they could not attend the physical count of inventory of 22 crore rupees at the Bhilwara foundry, which is the opening inventory for this year and has flowed into this year's cost of sales; the chief financial officer wants the new report to say in an Other Matter paragraph that the previous year was audited by another firm whose report was qualified, and nothing more.

items.stem: On the predecessor's qualification alone, does an Other Matter paragraph settle the new auditors' report?

options.text: Yes. The qualification belongs to the previous auditors and the previous year; an Other Matter paragraph referring to it is the module's own device for a predecessor's report, and this year's opinion is on this year's figures.
options.misconception: Lets a reference to the predecessor's qualification stand in for the current auditor's own.
options.why: The module requires the auditor to evaluate the effect of the predecessor's modification on the current period and, where it is relevant and material to the current period's financial statements, to modify the current period audit report. Opening inventory in this year's cost of sales makes last year's matter this year's, and a paragraph about another firm's report does not replace the auditor's own modification.

options.text: Yes, provided the Other Matter paragraph also states that the new auditors place no reliance on the opening inventory; a disclaimer of reliance is the same as a modification.
options.misconception: Confuses words of non-reliance with a modified opinion.
options.why: A statement of non-reliance in an Other Matter paragraph is not a modification of the opinion, and the module requires the current period audit report to be modified where the predecessor's modification is relevant and material; where the opening balances cannot be verified that means a qualified opinion or a disclaimer under SA 705, not a paragraph.

options.text: No; the new auditors must give an adverse opinion, because a qualification on inventory that remains unresolved has become pervasive by carrying into a second year.
options.misconception: Reaches for an adverse opinion on a limitation rather than a known misstatement.
options.why: The module's rows turn on the kind of problem, not on how many years it has lasted: an inability to obtain audit evidence regarding opening balances brings a qualified opinion or a disclaimer, and the qualified-or-adverse row is for a misstatement found in the opening balances and not properly presented. Nothing here has found a misstatement.

options.text: No. Where the predecessor's report was modified, the auditor evaluates the effect of the matter on this year's statements, and if the modification is relevant and material to them the auditor must modify the current period audit report. Unverified opening inventory that has flowed into this year's cost of sales is that case unless the new auditors can now obtain evidence on it themselves; if they cannot, the result is a qualified opinion or a disclaimer for opening balances they could not verify, and a paragraph recording what another firm said does not discharge it.
options.why: The module's reporting column for SA 510 has three rows and the third answers this. On the predecessor's modification: if there is a modification in the predecessor auditor's report, the auditor evaluates the effect of the matter giving rise to that modification with respect to the current period's financial statements, and if the modification is relevant and material to the current period's financial statements the auditor shall modify the current period audit report. Opening inventory of 22 crore rupees that nobody counted is the opening figure in this year's cost of sales, so the matter is both relevant and material this year, and the only way out of the modification is for the new auditors to obtain evidence about that opening inventory themselves, by procedures on the opening balances. If they cannot, the module's first row applies: where the auditor is unable to obtain audit evidence regarding opening balances, the opinion is qualified or disclaimed; the qualified-or-adverse row is for opening balances found to contain a misstatement not properly presented or disclosed, which is not yet this. The chief financial officer's paragraph would tell the reader that another firm qualified last year while this year's opinion stays clean on a figure this firm has not verified either, which is the reverse of what the standard requires. In short, a modification that is relevant and material to this year means the auditor must modify the current period audit report, and unverifiable opening balances bring a qualified opinion or a disclaimer.
keywords: modify the current period audit report

citation.ref: where the predecessor auditor's report was modified, the auditor evaluates the effect of the matter giving rise to the modification on the current period's financial statements and, if the modification is relevant and material to the current period's financial statements, modifies the current period audit report; where the auditor is unable to obtain audit evidence regarding opening balances the opinion is qualified or disclaimed, and where opening balances contain a misstatement not properly presented or disclosed the opinion is qualified or adverse

items.scenario: Rao & Farooqui were appointed statutory auditors of Chambal Auto Castings Limited, an unlisted public company at Bhilwara with revenue of 640 crore rupees, for the year ended 31 March 2026, after the previous auditors completed their term. Zeenat Farooqui is the engagement partner and three matters are open at the planning stage. First, the manager's planning memo opens with the overall audit strategy and records that "acceptance was completed at the tender stage in February 2026, so no further preliminary work is needed"; since then the firm's tax partner has begun advising the promoter on his personal tax affairs, and no engagement letter has been issued because the manager intends to reuse the previous auditors' letter with the firm's name changed. Second, the senior proposes to accept the opening balances as they stand, "because last year was audited by a firm of standing and the closing figures are in the signed accounts", and the chief financial officer has said that opening balances are last year's problem and this year's audit should start from 1 April. Third, the previous auditors' report for the year ended 31 March 2025 carried a qualified opinion because they could not attend the physical count of inventory of 22 crore rupees at the Bhilwara foundry, which is the opening inventory for this year and has flowed into this year's cost of sales; the chief financial officer wants the new report to say in an Other Matter paragraph that the previous year was audited by another firm whose report was qualified, and nothing more.

items.stem: On the warranty provision alone, can the audit senior close the area on the chief financial officer's signed statement?

options.text: Yes, provided the statement is included in the formal representation letter signed by both the managing director and the chief financial officer rather than as a separate note.
options.misconception: Treats the form of the representation as the source of its evidential weight.
options.why: Who signs and where the words sit change nothing about what a representation is. The module says representations do not provide sufficient appropriate evidence on their own about any matter they deal with, and that is as true of a line in the full letter as of a separate statement.

options.text: No, because a written representation is not audit evidence at all; SA 580 requires the letter only as a formality of the engagement, and nothing in the audit file may rest on it.
options.misconception: Swings from "enough by itself" to "worth nothing".
options.why: The module calls written representations necessary audit evidence, and SA 580's second objective is to support other evidence relevant to the financial statements or specific assertions by means of them. They are evidence; what they are not is sufficient on their own. The conclusion is right and the reason is not.

options.text: Yes, because a warranty provision is an accounting estimate and estimates are management's responsibility; the auditor's only evidence about them is management's own assertion that the assumptions are reasonable.
options.misconception: Confuses whose responsibility the estimate is with whose evidence supports it.
options.why: That management makes the estimate is why the auditor tests it, not a reason to take management's word. The module is explicit that a reliable representation does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence obtained about specific assertions; the claims history, the assumptions and the payments made in the year are all evidence the auditor obtains herself.

options.text: No. A written representation is necessary audit evidence but is not sufficient appropriate evidence on its own about any matter it deals with, and a reliable representation does not reduce the other evidence the auditor must obtain about the assertion. The provision has to be tested against the claims history, the assumptions and the year's 9 crore rupees of payments; the statement supports that work and does not replace it.
options.why: The module states SA 580's position in two sentences: although written representations provide necessary audit evidence, they do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters with which they deal; and the fact that management has provided reliable written representations does not affect the nature or extent of other audit evidence that the auditor obtains about the fulfilment of management's responsibilities or about specific assertions. A representation that the assumptions behind an estimate are reasonable is one of the standard representations, and it is obtained in addition to the auditor's own procedures on the estimate, never instead of them. A 6 crore rupees provision against 9 crore rupees of claims paid in the year is exactly the kind of figure whose basis the auditor must examine for herself. In short, the statement is not sufficient on its own, and having it does not reduce the testing the estimate needs.

citation.ref: written representations provide necessary audit evidence but do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters with which they deal, and the fact that management has provided reliable written representations does not affect the nature or extent of the other audit evidence the auditor obtains about specific assertions

items.scenario: Chenab Auto Components Private Limited makes wiring harnesses at Chakan for three vehicle makers. Its revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was 310 crore rupees and its profit before tax 21 crore rupees. Fernandes & Sethi are the statutory auditors, and the partner intends to sign the report on 28 August 2026. Three things stand between her and the signature. First, the provision for warranty claims is 6 crore rupees, against 9 crore rupees of claims paid in the year; the chief financial officer has signed a statement that the provision is adequate and the assumptions behind it reasonable, and the audit senior proposes to close the area on that statement alone, "since a signed representation from the CFO is audit evidence". Second, the firm asked for a written representation that all related party relationships and transactions known to management have been disclosed to the auditors; the managing director, whose brother owns the company's largest wire supplier, has struck that line out of the draft letter, saying "you have been told everything that matters, and I will not sign a line that reads like an accusation". Third, the audit found that for eight months of the year one accounts executive raised purchase orders, approved supplier invoices and released the payments, with nobody reviewing what she released, across 140 crore rupees of purchases; the chief financial officer says a second person was hired in July 2026 to split the work and asks that "nothing be put in writing about a problem that no longer exists".

items.stem: On the struck-out line alone, what does SA 580 require of the partner now?

options.text: Qualify the opinion "except for" the related-party disclosures in the note, since the refusal concerns one disclosure and its effect is confined to that note.
options.misconception: Reads a refusal about completeness of information as a misstatement of one disclosure.
options.why: The representation refused is not about one note; it is that all related party relationships and transactions known to management have been disclosed to the auditors, a statement about the completeness of what the auditor has been given. The auditor cannot say what else is missing, so the possible effects are not confined to one item, and a qualification of one note does not describe the position.

options.text: Nothing further. The managing director has given the information orally, and SA 580 accepts oral representations from the person responsible for the financial statements.
options.misconception: Treats an oral statement as satisfying a requirement for a written one.
options.why: SA 580 is about written representations, and the module's response to one not provided is to discuss, re-evaluate integrity and act under SA 705. An oral assurance from the very person whose family connection is in question is not the representation the auditor asked for, and a refusal to put it in writing is itself evidence about integrity.

options.text: Discuss the refusal with the managing director, re-evaluate the integrity of management and what that does to every other representation and piece of evidence, and take appropriate action on the report under SA 705. The line refused is about the completeness of the information given to the auditor, which goes to the whole audit rather than one balance, so a persisting refusal leads to a disclaimer of opinion, not an "except for" qualification of the related-party note.
options.why: The module sets out the response to a requested written representation not provided: the auditor shall discuss the matter with management, re-evaluate the integrity of management, and take appropriate actions including the impact on the audit report under SA 705. A managing director whose brother is the largest supplier refusing to confirm that related party relationships have been disclosed is the strongest possible reason to re-evaluate integrity, and a doubt about integrity spreads to every other representation and to the reliability of evidence generally. What is refused is a representation about the completeness of the information provided to the auditor, one of the representations SA 580 itself requires about management's responsibilities; the possible effects of not having it are not confined to one account, so the SA 705 consequence of a refusal that persists is a disclaimer of opinion rather than a qualification of one note.

options.text: Drop the line and sign, provided the partner performs additional procedures on the supplier owned by the brother; extra evidence on the known relationship makes the representation unnecessary.
options.misconception: Assumes evidence on the known relationship can stand in for a representation about unknown ones.
options.why: Procedures on the one relationship the auditor happens to know about do not answer the question the representation asks, which is whether there are others. Written representations about management's responsibilities, including the completeness of the information provided, are required by SA 580 regardless of what other evidence exists, and the module's response to their refusal is re-evaluation of integrity and action under SA 705, not substitution.

citation.ref: where a requested written representation is not provided, the auditor discusses the matter with management, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the reliability of other representations and evidence, and takes appropriate action including the effect on the auditor's report under SA 705; a representation refused about the completeness of the information provided to the auditor goes to the whole audit, and SA 580 has the auditor disclaim the opinion where that representation is not given
