items.stem: On the payments clerk alone, what does SA 265 require, and what must the communication contain?

options.text: One person raising orders, approving invoices and releasing 140 crore rupees of payments with no review is a significant deficiency identified during the audit, and it is communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis, and in writing to management, whether or not it has since been fixed. The letter describes the deficiency and explains its potential effects, and says that the audit's purpose was an opinion on the financial statements, that internal control was considered to design procedures and not to give an opinion on its effectiveness, and that only deficiencies identified and judged to merit reporting are included.
options.why: SA 265, as the module sets it out, has the auditor determine whether deficiencies identified on the basis of the audit work are, individually or in combination, significant, and then communicate significant deficiencies in internal control identified during the audit in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis, and also in writing to management at an appropriate level of responsibility. The duty attaches to a deficiency identified during the audit; a hire in July that splits the work is the response to the communication, not a reason to withhold it, and the eight months over which one person controlled ordering, approval and payment are what the financial statements were prepared under. The written communication must contain a description of the deficiencies and an explanation of their potential effects, and sufficient information for the reader to understand the context, namely that the purpose of the audit was for the auditor to express an opinion on the financial statements, that the audit included consideration of internal control in order to design audit procedures appropriate in the circumstances and not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control, and that the matters reported are limited to those deficiencies identified during the audit and concluded to be of sufficient importance to merit reporting. The letter is there to describe and explain, not to give an opinion on its effectiveness.
keywords: not to give an opinion on its effectiveness

options.text: Report it orally to the chief financial officer, who is the appropriate level of management, and record the conversation in the audit file; a written letter is only for deficiencies management disputes.
options.misconception: Invents a written-only-if-disputed rule and stops at management.
options.why: The module says the communication of significant deficiencies to those charged with governance is in writing, and the communication to management of those same deficiencies is also in writing unless it would be inappropriate to communicate directly with management. Whether management agrees has nothing to do with the form.

options.text: Nothing in writing is required. The deficiency has been remedied before the report date, and SA 265 is concerned only with deficiencies that still exist when the auditor reports.
options.misconception: Reads a remedy after the year end as cancelling the duty to report the year's deficiency.
options.why: The module's rule is that significant deficiencies identified during the audit are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis. It is the identification during the audit that triggers the duty; the standard nowhere excuses a deficiency because management says it has since been fixed, and the auditor has not tested the July arrangement in any case.

options.text: Communicate it in writing to the audit committee, and include in the letter an opinion that the company's internal control over purchases was ineffective for the year, so that the board understands the seriousness.
options.misconception: Turns the letter of weakness into an opinion on internal control, which it disclaims.
options.why: The written communication does the reverse of that. Among the things SA 265 requires it to explain is that the audit included consideration of internal control in order to design audit procedures, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control. The letter describes the deficiency and its potential effects; it does not carry an opinion on the control system.

citation.ref: significant deficiencies in internal control identified during the audit are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis, and in writing to management at an appropriate level; the written communication describes the deficiencies and explains their potential effects, and gives the context — the purpose of the audit was an opinion on the financial statements, internal control was considered to design procedures and not to express an opinion on its effectiveness, and the matters reported are limited to those identified and judged to merit reporting

items.stem: On the manager's weekend alone, was he right that no auditor's expert is needed?

options.text: No. The route the standard allows without an expert is a sufficient understanding of the field gained through experience of auditing such entities, education or professional development, or discussion with auditors who have done similar engagements; a weekend's reading and a call to a friend is none of those, and a geologist consulted on this reserve would himself be an auditor's expert. Every consideration for engaging one points the same way: management has used a management's expert, the matter is significant and complex, the risk of misstatement is high after a one-fifth cut, and there are no alternative sources of audit evidence for a reserve in the ground.
options.why: The module answers both halves of the manager's note. An auditor who is not an expert in a relevant field other than accounting or auditing may nevertheless obtain a sufficient understanding of that field to perform the audit without an auditor's expert, and it may come through experience in auditing entities that require such expertise, through education or professional development in the field including formal courses, or through discussion with auditors who have performed similar engagements; the module adds that discussion of that kind differs from consultation with an auditor's expert about a specific set of circumstances encountered on the engagement, where the expert is given all the relevant facts to give informed advice on the particular matter. A call to a geologist about this reserve is the second thing, not the first, and it makes the geologist an auditor's expert whose work then has to be evaluated under the standard. Whether to use one is decided on the module's considerations: whether management has used a management's expert in preparing the financial statements, the nature and significance of the matter including its complexity, the risks of material misstatement in the matter, and the expected nature of the procedures to respond to the risks including the availability of alternative sources of audit evidence. The company's engineer is a management's expert, which is a reason for the auditor to consider an expert of the auditor's own, not a reason against; the reserve drives the amortisation of 310 crore rupees of assets and has moved by a fifth; and no ledger or confirmation can tell the team how much ore is underground. The module's own examples of fields for an auditor's expert include the estimation of oil and gas reserves. In short, a weekend is not a sufficient understanding of the field, management's expert is a reason to consider the auditor's own, and there are no alternative sources of audit evidence for the reserve.

options.text: Yes, provided the manager's reading is documented and the geologist he calls is given the drilling data, because SA 620 lets an auditor obtain the understanding through discussion with individuals possessing expertise in the field.
options.misconception: Dresses a consultation on the engagement's facts as professional development.
options.why: The module draws exactly this line: discussion with individuals in the field to enhance the auditor's own capacity differs from consultation with an auditor's expert about the specific circumstances of the engagement, where the expert is given the relevant facts to advise on the particular matter. A geologist handed this company's drilling data to say whether this reserve holds is an auditor's expert, and the standard's requirements on competence, agreement and evaluation then apply.

options.text: No; the auditor must engage an expert whenever management has, because SA 620 requires the auditor's expert to match management's expert field for field.
options.misconception: Turns a judgement on the considerations into a mechanical rule.
options.why: The module lists management's use of an expert as one consideration among the nature and significance of the matter, the risks of material misstatement and the availability of alternative evidence; there is no rule of matching, and an auditor with a sufficient understanding of the field may proceed without an expert. The conclusion here is right on the considerations, not on a rule that does not exist.

options.text: Yes. The reserve was prepared by a qualified mining engineer, and where management has used an expert the auditor's task under SA 500 is to evaluate that expert's competence and work, not to hire a second expert to do it again.
options.misconception: Treats management's expert as a substitute for the auditor's own.
options.why: The module lists whether management has used a management's expert among the considerations for deciding whether the auditor needs an expert of the auditor's own, and evaluating a mining engineer's reserve model is itself work in a field other than accounting or auditing that the team has no sufficient understanding of; the management's expert's competence is evaluated under SA 500, and that evaluation does not supply the auditor with geology.

citation.ref: an auditor who is not an expert in a field other than accounting or auditing may obtain a sufficient understanding of that field without an auditor's expert through experience, education or professional development, or discussion with auditors who have performed similar engagements, which differs from consultation with an expert on a specific set of circumstances; the considerations in deciding whether to use an auditor's expert include whether management has used a management's expert, the nature and significance of the matter including its complexity, the risks of material misstatement, and the expected nature of procedures including the availability of alternative sources of audit evidence

items.scenario: Venkatesh & Bose audit Damodar Ferro Alloys Limited, an unlisted public company at Rourkela with revenue of 860 crore rupees, which mines its own manganese ore under a lease. Mine development assets of 310 crore rupees are amortised on the units-of-production method over the ore reserve, and the reserve estimate, prepared for the company by a mining engineer on its staff, was cut by a fifth this year after new drilling. Priya Venkatesh is the engagement partner and three things happen in the course of the audit. First, the audit manager records that the team will assess the reserve estimate itself, "after reading up on reserve estimation over a weekend and a phone call to a geologist I know", and that no auditor's expert is needed because the company's engineer is qualified and the figure is his. Second, when Priya overrules him and engages Dr Anjali Sethi, an independent geologist who has never worked with the firm, the manager briefs her by telephone: "look at the reserve and tell us if it holds", hands her the company's drilling logs and the engineer's model, and puts nothing in writing, saying a written engagement would "slow things down and she is a professional". Third, when Dr Sethi's report supports the reduced reserve, the chief financial officer asks that the auditor's report name her and her firm "so the lenders can see an independent expert stood behind the number", and the manager suggests adding the words "in reliance on the report of Dr Sethi" to the opinion paragraph to limit the firm's own exposure.

items.stem: On the telephone briefing alone, what should have passed between the firm and Dr Sethi before she began?

options.text: A written representation from Dr Sethi that she has no interest in or relationship with the company, which settles her objectivity, after which the work can proceed on the oral briefing.
options.misconception: Substitutes the objectivity check for the agreement on the work.
options.why: A representation about interests and relationships goes to the module's separate evaluation of the expert's objectivity and may be appropriate, but it is not the agreement the module requires on the nature, scope and objectives of the work, the roles, the communication and the confidentiality requirements, and it does not replace it.

options.text: Nothing more than the briefing given. An auditor's external expert is engaged for her expertise and the standard leaves the terms of the work to the expert's own professional standards; a written scope would amount to directing her judgement.
options.misconception: Confuses agreeing the scope of the work with directing the expert's conclusions.
options.why: The module requires the auditor to agree with the expert, in writing when appropriate, on the nature, scope and objectives of the work, the roles, the communication and the confidentiality requirements; agreeing what is to be done is what makes the later evaluation of the work's adequacy possible, and it is not directing the expert's judgement within that scope.

options.text: An agreement, and in writing here, on four matters: the nature, scope and objectives of her work, so that "tell us if it holds" becomes a defined task the firm can later evaluate; the respective roles and responsibilities of the firm and of her; the nature, timing and extent of communication between them, including the form of the report she will give; and the need for her to observe confidentiality requirements, because the drilling logs are the company's confidential information and an external expert is not bound by the firm's professional duty merely by being engaged. Writing is appropriate because she is external, new to the firm, working on a complex matter and holding sensitive data.
options.why: The module places an agreement between the decision to use an expert and the start of her work, and says what it must cover. The auditor shall agree, in writing when appropriate, with the auditor's expert on the nature, scope and objectives of that expert's work; the respective roles and responsibilities of the auditor and that expert; the nature, timing and extent of communication between them, including the form of any report to be provided by the expert, on which the module notes that where the work relates to the auditor's conclusions on a significant risk both a formal written report at the end and oral reports as the work progresses may be appropriate; and the need for the auditor's expert to observe confidentiality requirements, because it is necessary for the confidentiality provisions of the ethical requirements that apply to the auditor also to apply to the expert, with any further requirements law, regulation or the entity itself imposes. The telephone briefing covers none of the four: the scope is a sentence, roles are unstated, the form of report is unagreed, and a geologist outside the firm has been handed the company's drilling logs with no undertaking about them. The module also requires the auditor to obtain a sufficient understanding of the expert's field precisely in order to determine the nature, scope and objectives of the expert's work and to evaluate its adequacy afterwards, so an undefined scope makes the later evaluation impossible as well. The manager's reason, that she is a professional, is the point rather than the answer: her professional standards are her own, and the agreement is what binds her work to the auditor's purposes. In short, the firm agrees with her in writing on the nature, scope and objectives of the work, the roles, the communication and report, and the confidentiality requirements she must observe.

options.text: A written agreement on the fee and the timetable, since those are the only terms that differ from one expert to another; the scope is self-evident from the matter and confidentiality follows from her professional status.
options.misconception: Assumes confidentiality away, which the module names as the matter to be agreed.
options.why: The module's four matters are the scope and objectives, the roles, the communication and form of report, and the confidentiality requirements; it says in terms that the confidentiality provisions binding the auditor must be made to apply to the expert, which an external geologist's own professional status does not do on its own.

citation.ref: the auditor shall agree, in writing when appropriate, with the auditor's expert on the nature, scope and objectives of that expert's work, the respective roles and responsibilities of the auditor and the expert, the nature, timing and extent of communication including the form of any report, and the need for the expert to observe confidentiality requirements; the confidentiality provisions that apply to the auditor must also apply to the expert

items.scenario: Venkatesh & Bose audit Damodar Ferro Alloys Limited, an unlisted public company at Rourkela with revenue of 860 crore rupees, which mines its own manganese ore under a lease. Mine development assets of 310 crore rupees are amortised on the units-of-production method over the ore reserve, and the reserve estimate, prepared for the company by a mining engineer on its staff, was cut by a fifth this year after new drilling. Priya Venkatesh is the engagement partner and three things happen in the course of the audit. First, the audit manager records that the team will assess the reserve estimate itself, "after reading up on reserve estimation over a weekend and a phone call to a geologist I know", and that no auditor's expert is needed because the company's engineer is qualified and the figure is his. Second, when Priya overrules him and engages Dr Anjali Sethi, an independent geologist who has never worked with the firm, the manager briefs her by telephone: "look at the reserve and tell us if it holds", hands her the company's drilling logs and the engineer's model, and puts nothing in writing, saying a written engagement would "slow things down and she is a professional". Third, when Dr Sethi's report supports the reduced reserve, the chief financial officer asks that the auditor's report name her and her firm "so the lenders can see an independent expert stood behind the number", and the manager suggests adding the words "in reliance on the report of Dr Sethi" to the opinion paragraph to limit the firm's own exposure.

items.stem: On the request to name the geologist alone, can the report refer to Dr Sethi?

options.text: No, because an expert's report is not audit evidence at all and can never be mentioned in any auditor's report; the firm must obtain its own evidence on the reserve by other means.
options.misconception: Denies the expert's work its status as evidence in order to reach the right answer.
options.why: The module says the auditor may accept the expert's findings or conclusions as appropriate audit evidence once the work is found adequate, and it contemplates a reference where law or regulation requires one and in a modified report where relevant; the reason the firm does not name Dr Sethi here is that nothing requires it, not that her work is worthless.

options.text: No, to both. The firm has sole responsibility for the opinion and using Dr Sethi's work does not reduce it, so the words "in reliance on" would be untrue as well as improper; and the report shall not refer to the work of an auditor's expert where the opinion is unmodified unless required by law or regulation to do so, which nothing here requires. Where such a reference is required, the report must state that it does not reduce the auditor's responsibility, which is the opposite of what the manager wants it to do.
options.why: The module sets the responsibility first and the rule on the report second. The auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion expressed, and that responsibility is not reduced by the auditor's use of the work of an auditor's expert; what the standard permits is that, having followed it and concluded that the expert's work is adequate for the auditor's purposes, the auditor may accept the expert's findings or conclusions in the expert's field as appropriate audit evidence. That makes Dr Sethi's report evidence in the file, not a shared signature on the opinion. On the report itself the module is categorical: the auditor shall not refer to the work of an auditor's expert in an auditor's report containing an unmodified opinion unless required by law or regulation to do so, and if such a reference is required the auditor shall indicate in the report that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility for the audit opinion. The module's note is that such a requirement arises in some cases for transparency in the public sector, which a private manganese miner is not. The chief financial officer's reason, that lenders would take comfort from an expert's name, is the reason the rule exists in that direction: a reference the reader takes as a second guarantor, or as a limit on the first, misdescribes who is answerable for the opinion. The manager's phrase is worse than a mention, because it is written to reduce a responsibility the standard says cannot be reduced. In short, the auditor has sole responsibility that the expert's work does not reduce, and an unmodified report does not refer to the expert unless required by law or regulation, in which case it says the reference does not reduce that responsibility.
keywords: unless required by law or regulation

options.text: Yes to both, provided the report also states that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility, which is the form SA 620 prescribes for a reference to an expert.
options.misconception: Reads the mandatory rider as permission to refer.
options.why: The module's statement that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility is what the report must say when law or regulation requires a reference; it is not a formula that unlocks a voluntary one, and the words "in reliance on" in the opinion paragraph contradict it in the same sentence.

options.text: Yes to the chief financial officer's request, because naming an independent expert increases the transparency of the report and the lenders are its users; no to the manager's phrase, because it limits responsibility.
options.misconception: Treats the public-sector transparency exception as a general licence.
options.why: The module permits no reference to the work of an auditor's expert in a report with an unmodified opinion unless required by law or regulation, and transparency is the reason the module gives for such a legal requirement in the public sector, not a ground on which the auditor may add one. The second half is right; the first is the prohibited case.

citation.ref: the auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion and that responsibility is not reduced by the use of the work of an auditor's expert; the auditor shall not refer to the work of an auditor's expert in a report containing an unmodified opinion unless required by law or regulation, and where such a reference is required the report indicates that it does not reduce the auditor's responsibility for the opinion

Third, when Dr Sethi's report supports the reduced reserve, the chief financial officer asks that the auditor's report name her and her firm "so the lenders can see an independent expert stood behind the number", and the manager suggests adding the words "in reliance on the report of Dr Sethi" to the opinion paragraph to limit the firm's own exposure.

items.stem: On the bank's letter and the internal auditor's request alone, what does Meera do?

options.text: Nothing goes to the bank on the finance head's telephone call. Information acquired in the course of the engagement is disclosed to a person other than the client only with the consent of the client or as required by law, and for a company that consent is given by the Board of Directors by resolution, or by the Managing Director where the Board's powers are delegated to him widely enough to include it; a finance head on the telephone is neither, so Meera asks the company for that consent before any note on the supplier leaves the firm. The working papers are a different matter: she is not required to give the bank, the client or the internal auditor access to her working papers at all, and may at her discretion give the client extracts of them.
options.why: The clause has two doors and the finance head's call opens neither. Disclosure of information acquired in the course of the engagement to any person other than the client is misconduct unless it is with the consent of the client or is required by law, and a lender's letter is a request, not a requirement of law. The consent has to come from a person competent to give it: in a company, by section 179 of the Companies Act, that is the Board of Directors, so the consent is by a resolution of the Board of Directors, or from the Managing Director if the Board's powers are delegated to him comprehensively enough to include the power to give it; a finance head speaking on the telephone is not that person and a note to the bank on his word would be disclosure without consent. Working papers stand apart from information: the Code says the auditor is not required to provide the client or other auditors of the same enterprise access to his audit working papers, that the term auditor includes the internal auditor, and that he may at his discretion make extracts available to the client, so neither the bank's copies nor the internal auditor's access is owed, and the finance head's consent, if it were valid, would change nothing on that. In short, information leaves only with the consent of the client given by the Board of Directors or a managing director it has empowered, and nobody, bank, client or internal auditor, has a right of access to her working papers.

options.text: Once the Board of Directors consents, Meera must send both the note and the working papers, because a valid consent removes every restriction and refusing the papers would then be a breach of her duty to the client.
options.misconception: A valid consent obliges the auditor to hand over the working papers as well.
options.why: Consent of the client opens the door for information; it creates no right of access to the auditor's working papers, which the Code says the auditor is not required to provide and may give in extract at his own discretion.

options.text: The bank is a lender with 40 crore rupees at stake, so its request is a disclosure required by law in substance; the note and the working papers go to the bank, and the internal auditor, being part of the client, has access to the working papers as of right.
options.misconception: A lender's request for information about its borrower is disclosure required by law.
options.why: A lender's interest is not a requirement of law, and the clause's only doors are the consent of the client and a legal requirement; the Code says the auditor is not required to give other auditors access to his working papers and that the term includes the internal auditor.

options.text: The finance head's telephone consent is enough, since he is the officer who deals with the auditor day to day; the working papers, however, are the property of the company and go to whoever the company names, including the bank and the internal auditor.
options.misconception: The officer who deals with the auditor can consent for the company, and working papers belong to the client.
options.why: Consent must come from a person competent to give it, which for a company is the Board of Directors by resolution or a managing director with delegated powers wide enough; and the working papers are the auditor's, to which the Code gives the client and other auditors no right of access.

citation.ref: Clause (1) of Part I of the Second Schedule: a chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he discloses information acquired in the course of his professional engagement to any person other than his client so engaging him without the consent of his client or otherwise than as required by any law for the time being in force; the Code adds that for a company the consent comes from the Board of Directors, and that an auditor is not required to give the client or other auditors access to his working papers

items.scenario: Bhargava & Iyer are a firm of chartered accountants at Panchkula with two partners, Meera Bhargava and Rohit Iyer, and Meera is the engagement partner on the statutory audit of Ghaggar Foods Limited, an unlisted public company with a revenue of 180 crore rupees. Three matters sit on her desk in the first week of September 2026. First, the inspection team of the bank that has lent 40 crore rupees to Ghaggar Foods has written directly to the firm asking for a note on the company's purchases from a supplier owned by a director's brother and for copies of the firm's working papers on the stock count; the company's finance head has said on the telephone that the bank may have whatever it asks for, and in the same week the company's internal auditor has asked for access to the firm's working papers on debtors for his own review. Second, three engagements have been offered to the firm: the audit of a charitable trust that runs two schools, of which Rohit is a trustee; the audit of a management college where Meera teaches two evenings a week as a part-time lecturer; and a certificate of stock and debtors for a bank on behalf of a trading partnership in which Rohit is a partner, on which Rohit says the clause is about opinions and not certificates and that Meera, not he, will sign. Third, a shareholder of Ghaggar Foods has filed a complaint with the Institute on two counts: that in the previous year the firm certified the company's export turnover for a government incentive from a printout of the sales management information system without examining the books of account, and that in the current year the firm signed its audit report forty days after the date the company needed it to meet a statutory filing, because the firm's staff were engaged elsewhere; Rohit's answer is that the certified figure later proved right, that the company lost nothing, and that nobody has alleged dishonesty, so there is nothing to answer. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the three engagements offered to the firm alone, what does Meera decide?

options.text: None of the three is taken as offered. The clause bars a member from expressing his opinion on the financial statements of any business or enterprise in which he, his firm, or a partner in his firm has a substantial interest, and the Council has decided that a chartered accountant should not by himself or in his firm name accept the auditorship of a trust where his partner is a trustee of the trust, nor of a college where he works as a part-time lecturer. The certificate is caught too: financial statements in this clause cover reports and certificates and every attest function, the clause reaches a partner in his firm and not only the signer, and a member who is a partner in a trading firm shall not audit or certify its statements, so Meera signing instead of Rohit cures nothing.
options.why: The clause is written for the firm, not the signature. It bars the expression of an opinion on the financial statements of any business or enterprise in which the member, his firm, or a partner in his firm has a substantial interest, and the Code says the words financial statements cover both reports and certificates usually given after an examination of accounts and any attest function under any enactment, with the Council adding that the requirement applies equally to certificates and audits for banks. On the trust, the Council has decided that a chartered accountant should not by himself or in his firm name accept the auditorship of a trust where his partner is either an employee or a trustee of the trust, and Rohit is a trustee. On the college, the same decision says he should not accept the auditorship of a college if he is working as a part-time lecturer in the college, and Meera teaches there two evenings a week. On the trading partnership, the Council's view is that the holding of interest in a business or enterprise not being a company by a member as a partner affects his independence of mind and the member shall not audit its financial statements; that bar runs to the firm and to every partner in his firm, so moving the signature from Rohit to Meera moves the engagement nowhere. In short, a trust where a partner is a trustee, a college where the member is a part-time lecturer, and a partnership in which a partner in his firm holds an interest are all outside what the firm may certify or audit.

options.text: Only Rohit's two engagements are affected, because it is Rohit who is a trustee and a partner; Meera's lecturing is teaching, not a financial interest, so the college audit may be accepted in her own name.
options.misconception: A teaching post is not an interest that bars the college's audit.
options.why: The Council has decided that a chartered accountant should not by himself or in his firm name accept the auditorship of a college if he is working as a part-time lecturer in the college, which is exactly Meera's position.

options.text: The trust and the college audits may be accepted provided the relationship is disclosed in the report, since disclosure is what independence rules ask for; only the certificate for the partnership is barred outright.
options.misconception: Disclosing the relationship in the report cures a substantial-interest bar.
options.why: The clause bars the expression of the opinion itself and the Council's decisions are that the auditorship should not be accepted, in the member's own name or in his firm name; nothing in the clause or the decisions is satisfied by a disclosure.

options.text: The certificate for the bank is outside the clause because a certificate of stock and debtors is not an opinion on financial statements, and it is safe if Rohit does not sign it; the trust and the college are the two to refuse.
options.misconception: Clause (4) is about audit opinions, not certificates.
options.why: The Code says financial statements in this clause cover reports and certificates and any attest function, the Council emphasises that the requirement applies to certificates and audits for banks, and the clause reaches a partner in his firm whoever signs.

citation.ref: Clause (4) of Part I of the Second Schedule: a chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he expresses his opinion on financial statements of any business or enterprise in which he, his firm, or a partner in his firm has a substantial interest; financial statements cover reports and certificates and any attest function, and the Council has decided that a member should not by himself or in his firm name accept the auditorship of a college where he is a part-time lecturer or of a trust where his partner is a trustee

Three matters sit on her desk in the first week of September 2026. Second, three engagements have been offered to the firm: the audit of a charitable trust that runs two schools, of which Rohit is a trustee; the audit of a management college where Meera teaches two evenings a week as a part-time lecturer; and a certificate of stock and debtors for a bank on behalf of a trading partnership in which Rohit is a partner, on which Rohit says the clause is about opinions and not certificates and that Meera, not he, will sign. Third, a shareholder of Ghaggar Foods has filed a complaint with the Institute on two counts: that in the previous year the firm certified the company's export turnover for a government incentive from a printout of the sales management information system without examining the books of account, and that in the current year the firm signed its audit report forty days after the date the company needed it to meet a statutory filing, because the firm's staff were engaged elsewhere; Rohit's answer is that the certified figure later proved right, that the company lost nothing, and that nobody has alleged dishonesty, so there is nothing to answer. Meera has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the complaint's two counts alone, what does Meera tell Rohit the firm faces?

options.text: The late report is misconduct because a statutory date was missed, but the certificate is not, because an auditor is a watchdog and not a bloodhound and may rely on the company's own system report unless something excites suspicion.
options.misconception: Watchdog not bloodhound means the auditor may certify from management's reports.
options.why: The watchdog passage says the auditor is not bound to approach his work with suspicion; it does not let him certify figures without examining the books of account, which the Code's own case holds to be a failure to exercise due diligence and gross negligence.

options.text: The certificate is misconduct, but the late report is a matter between the firm and its client under the engagement letter and not professional misconduct, since the Institute does not police delivery dates.
options.misconception: Missing an audit deadline is a contractual matter, not professional misconduct.
options.why: The Code's case is a member who had not completed his audit work and had not submitted his report in due time to enable the company to comply with a statutory requirement, held guilty of professional misconduct under Clause (7); the date is the client's statutory one, and the clause reaches it.

options.text: Neither count can stand, because gross negligence needs either dishonesty or a loss to somebody, and here the figure was right and the company lost nothing; at most the Institute writes to the firm asking for more care in future.
options.misconception: Gross negligence needs dishonesty or a loss.
options.why: The clause is attracted whenever it has to be judged whether the accountant honestly and reasonably discharged his duties, and the Code's cases under it found misconduct with no dishonesty and no loss alleged; the letter asking for more care is for minor errors and lapses, which a certificate given without examining the books is not.

options.text: Both counts are answerable under the clause, and Rohit's three points answer neither. The clause is failing to exercise due diligence or being grossly negligent in the conduct of professional duties, and it needs no dishonesty and no loss; certifying a turnover figure from a management information system printout without examining the books of account is the very case of failing to exercise due diligence, whatever the figure later proved, and not completing the audit and submitting the report in due time to let the company meet a statutory requirement is misconduct under the same clause. What the clause does not reach is a minor error or lapse, which is brought to the member's attention rather than taken to the Disciplinary Committee.
options.why: The clause asks whether the accountant honestly and reasonably discharged his duties, and the Code says it is attracted whenever that has to be judged; negligence under it runs from the frontiers of fraud to minor negligence, so an absence of dishonesty is not a defence, and nothing in the clause requires a loss to anybody. On the first count the Code's own case is a member who certified circulation figures from a management information report without examining the books of account, held to have failed to exercise due diligence and to be grossly negligent because certification of figures from statistical information without cross verification with the financial records is exactly that; an export turnover certified from a sales system printout is the same act, and that the figure later proved right does not supply the examination that was never made. On the second count the Code's case is a member who had not completed his audit work and had not submitted his audit report in due time to enable the company to comply with a statutory requirement, held guilty under this clause; a report signed forty days after the date the company needed it, because staff were engaged elsewhere, is that case. What the Code keeps outside the clause is the minor error or lapse, which the Council brings to the member's attention so that greater care is taken, and neither count is of that kind. In short, a certificate given without examining the books of account and a report not submitted in due time are each a failure to exercise due diligence, and neither dishonesty nor a loss is an element of the clause.
keywords: without examining the books of account

citation.ref: Clause (7) of Part I of the Second Schedule: a chartered accountant in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he does not exercise due diligence, or is grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties; the Code treats certifying figures from a management information report without examining the books of account, and not completing the audit and submitting the report in due time to let the company meet a statutory requirement, as within the clause, and minor errors and lapses as outside it

items.stem: On the opening stock alone, can the senior take the 48 crore rupees on the predecessor's unmodified report?

options.text: Yes. An unmodified report from a qualified predecessor is sufficient appropriate evidence about the opening balances, and the new auditor's responsibility begins with the transactions of the year of appointment.
options.misconception: Treats the predecessor's report as evidence about the opening balances rather than as a document the new auditor reads on the way to obtaining evidence.
options.why: The new auditor's objective under SA 510 is evidence about whether the opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements, which is not met by reading another auditor's opinion. The module lists reading the predecessor auditor's report as one step among several, followed by audit procedures on the opening balances themselves.

options.text: No, and because the predecessor's working papers are unavailable the opening inventory is unauditable, so the opinion must be qualified for a scope limitation on opening stock without further work.
options.misconception: Jumps to a modified opinion before performing the procedures that could produce the evidence.
options.why: The working papers are one possible source of evidence, not the only one. The module's additional procedures for opening inventory, reconciling the current count to the opening quantities and testing the valuation of the opening inventory, do not depend on the predecessor. A qualified or disclaimed opinion is the result where the auditor is unable to obtain the evidence after trying, not the starting point.

options.text: Yes, provided the year-end count agrees with the books; a clean closing count proves the stock system works and so proves the opening figure the same system produced.
options.misconception: Assumes a closing count carries evidence backwards to the opening balance.
options.why: This is the reasoning the module rejects in terms: the current period's audit procedures on the closing inventory balance provide little audit evidence regarding inventory on hand at the beginning of the period. A count at 31 March 2026 says what was there on that day, not what was there twelve months earlier.

options.text: No. Reading the predecessor auditor's report and the prior statements is the first step, not the evidence. The firm must obtain evidence of its own that the opening inventory contains no misstatement that materially affects this year's figures, and this year's count gives little audit evidence about stock on hand at 1 April 2025; so it performs additional procedures, such as reconciling the current count back to the opening quantities through the year's movements and testing the valuation of the opening inventory.
options.why: The module sets out the auditor's procedures in an initial audit engagement: read the most recent financial statements and the predecessor auditor's report, determine whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward and reflect appropriate accounting policies, and perform audit procedures on the opening balances. The objective is sufficient appropriate evidence about whether the opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements, and the auditor evaluates whether the current period's procedures provide evidence relevant to the opening balances or whether specific procedures are needed. The module then says of inventories in particular that the current period's procedures on the closing balance provide little audit evidence regarding inventory on hand at the beginning of the period, so additional procedures may be necessary, and names observing a current physical count and reconciling it to the opening quantities and performing procedures on the valuation of the opening inventory. A predecessor's unmodified report is read, not relied on in place of that work; his silence about his working papers does not change the objective. In short, the predecessor auditor's report is read, the current count gives little audit evidence about the opening inventory, and the firm does its own procedures on it.

citation.ref: in an initial audit engagement the auditor reads the most recent financial statements and the predecessor auditor's report and performs audit procedures on the opening balances; the current period's procedures on the closing inventory balance provide little audit evidence regarding inventory on hand at the beginning of the period, so additional procedures may be necessary, such as observing a current physical count and reconciling it to the opening quantities and performing procedures on the valuation of the opening inventory

items.scenario: Godavari Frozen Foods Private Limited freezes and stores vegetables at a cold-storage plant near Nashik and sells to retail chains. Kulkarni & Menon were appointed its statutory auditors in September 2025 for the year ended 31 March 2026, after the previous auditor, a sole practitioner, retired from practice; his report on the year ended 31 March 2025 was unmodified. Revenue for the year was 380 crore rupees and profit before tax 19 crore rupees. The partner has three notes from the senior on her desk. First, opening stock at 1 April 2025 was 48 crore rupees of frozen produce, the firm attended no count at that date, the retired auditor has not answered two letters asking for his working papers, and the senior proposes to accept the opening figure "on the strength of a clean report from a qualified predecessor". Second, trade receivables at the year end are 65 crore rupees, of which 40 crore rupees is owed by five retail chains; the managing director has refused to let the firm send confirmation requests to those five, saying "the chains resent audit letters and it costs us shelf space", and has offered instead statements of account which his sales team will collect from the chains and hand to the firm. Third, the company revalued the cold-storage plant at 31 March 2026 from 70 crore rupees to 120 crore rupees on a valuer's report; the firm engaged its own chartered engineer, who has twenty years in refrigeration plant, and he has returned a two-page opinion agreeing with 120 crore rupees, resting on a remaining useful life of twenty-five years and on a replacement cost taken from a 2019 supplier quotation which the company gave him. The senior has filed the opinion as the evidence for the revaluation, "since an engineer with twenty years' experience has signed it".

items.stem: On the refused confirmations alone, what does SA 505 require of the firm?

options.text: Inquire into the reasons for the refusal and seek evidence that they are valid and reasonable; evaluate what the refusal does to the assessed risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and to the other procedures; and perform alternative audit procedures on the 40 crore rupees, such as subsequent receipts and shipping documents. Statements collected by the sales team are received indirectly and are not confirmations. If the refusal is found unreasonable, the firm communicates with those charged with governance and considers the implications for the audit and the opinion.
options.why: The module's table for SA 505 gives the three steps when management refuses to allow a confirmation request to be sent: inquire as to management's reasons for the refusal and seek audit evidence as to their validity and reasonableness; evaluate the implications of the refusal on the assessment of the relevant risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and on the nature, timing and extent of other audit procedures; and perform alternative audit procedures designed to obtain relevant and reliable audit evidence. It adds that if the refusal is unreasonable the auditor communicates with those charged with governance and considers the implications for the audit and the auditor's opinion. Control of the confirmation process, from choosing the party to receiving the reply, belongs to the auditor, and the module names a response received by the auditor indirectly as a factor that raises doubt about its reliability; a statement carried in by the client's own sales staff is that case exactly. In short, the firm asks the reasons for the refusal, performs alternative audit procedures, and takes an unreasonable refusal to those charged with governance.

options.text: Accept the managing director's offer. A statement of account signed by the customer is external evidence whoever carries it, and for a private company the confirmation process is a matter for management's convenience.
options.misconception: Treats a document that originated outside the company as an external confirmation regardless of who handled it on the way.
options.why: The confirmation process is controlled by the auditor, including sending the request and receiving the reply directly, and the module names a response received indirectly as a reason to doubt its reliability. A statement handed over by the client's sales team gives the auditor no assurance that it came from the chain unaltered, and nothing in SA 505 turns on whether the company is private.

options.text: Treat the refusal as a scope limitation imposed by management and disclaim the opinion, since 40 crore rupees is over half of receivables and confirmations were necessary.
options.misconception: Moves straight from a refusal to a disclaimer without the inquiry and the alternative procedures SA 505 requires first.
options.why: The module's steps come before any conclusion on the opinion: inquire into the reasons, evaluate the risk implications, and perform alternative audit procedures. Only if the refusal is unreasonable does the auditor communicate with those charged with governance and consider the implications for the opinion, and even then the form of any modification depends on whether alternative procedures produced the evidence.

options.text: Send the confirmation requests regardless, since the auditor controls the confirmation process and management cannot forbid it; a refusal is noted in the letter of weakness.
options.misconception: Reads the auditor's control of the process as a power to override the client rather than a responsibility for how requests are handled.
options.why: SA 505 recognises that management may refuse and prescribes what the auditor does then, which is inquiry, evaluation, alternative procedures and, for an unreasonable refusal, communication with those charged with governance. Writing to a customer over the client's objection is not among the steps, and the letter of weakness is about control deficiencies, not this.

citation.ref: where management refuses to allow the auditor to send a confirmation request the auditor inquires as to management's reasons for the refusal and seeks audit evidence as to their validity and reasonableness, evaluates the implications of the refusal on the assessment of the relevant risks of material misstatement including the risk of fraud and on the nature, timing and extent of other audit procedures, and performs alternative audit procedures; if the refusal is unreasonable the auditor communicates with those charged with governance and considers the implications for the audit and the auditor's opinion

items.stem: On the valuer's report alone, is the engineer's signed opinion the evidence for the 120 crore rupees?

options.text: Yes, but the auditor's report must refer to the engineer by name and state that the revaluation was verified by him, so that responsibility for the figure is shared.
options.misconception: Believes referring to an expert in the report divides responsibility for the opinion.
options.why: SA 620 says the auditor's responsibility for the opinion is not reduced by using an expert, and the report does not refer to the expert unless law or regulation requires it, in which case it states that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility. There is no sharing of responsibility, and naming the engineer does not replace evaluating his work.

options.text: No, because an auditor may not use an expert on a matter that management has already had valued; the firm must obtain a third valuation from an independent valuer chosen jointly with the company.
options.misconception: Invents a bar on using an auditor's expert alongside a management's expert.
options.why: Nothing in SA 620 bars an auditor's expert where management used an expert of its own; the two are different things and the standard exists for exactly this use. What the module requires is the evaluation of the auditor's expert's work, its assumptions and methods and source data, not a further valuation.

options.text: Yes. Once the firm has satisfied itself about the expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity, his conclusion in his own field is audit evidence, and second-guessing an engineer on refrigeration plant would be the auditor acting outside her competence.
options.misconception: Stops at the expert's qualifications and treats the evaluation of his work as beyond the auditor.
options.why: Competence, capabilities and objectivity are assessed before the expert is used; the module then requires the auditor to evaluate the adequacy of the work itself, including the assumptions and methods and the source data. Asking whether a 2019 quotation is complete and accurate for a 2026 value, or whether the findings are consistent with other evidence, is not engineering, and the auditor's sole responsibility for the opinion is not reduced by the expert's signature.

options.text: Not yet. The engineer's competence is the entry ticket, not the evaluation. The firm must evaluate whether his work is adequate for its purposes: whether his findings are relevant and reasonable and consistent with other evidence, whether the twenty-five-year life and the replacement-cost approach are relevant and reasonable as assumptions and methods, and whether a 2019 quotation supplied by the company is relevant, complete and accurate source data for a 2026 value. The firm keeps sole responsibility for the opinion; using an expert does not reduce it.
options.why: The module states that the auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion expressed and that this responsibility is not reduced by the auditor's use of the work of an auditor's expert; the expert's findings may be accepted as appropriate evidence only after the auditor, having followed SA 620, concludes that the work is adequate for the auditor's purposes. That evaluation covers the relevance and reasonableness of the expert's findings or conclusions and their consistency with other audit evidence; where the expert's work involves significant assumptions and methods, the relevance and reasonableness of those assumptions and methods in the circumstances; and where it involves source data that is significant to the work, the relevance, completeness and accuracy of that source data. A twenty-five-year remaining life and a replacement-cost method are significant assumptions and methods, and a seven-year-old quotation handed over by the company is source data whose relevance, completeness and accuracy have to be checked before a 50 crore rupees uplift rests on it. In short, the assumptions and methods and the source data are evaluated by the firm, which keeps sole responsibility for the opinion.

citation.ref: the auditor has sole responsibility for the audit opinion and that responsibility is not reduced by the use of an auditor's expert; the auditor evaluates the adequacy of the expert's work for the auditor's purposes, including the relevance and reasonableness of the findings and their consistency with other evidence, the relevance and reasonableness of significant assumptions and methods, and the relevance, completeness and accuracy of source data significant to the work

items.scenario: Godavari Frozen Foods Private Limited freezes and stores vegetables at a cold-storage plant near Nashik and sells to retail chains. Kulkarni & Menon were appointed its statutory auditors in September 2025 for the year ended 31 March 2026, after the previous auditor, a sole practitioner, retired from practice; his report on the year ended 31 March 2025 was unmodified. Revenue for the year was 380 crore rupees and profit before tax 19 crore rupees. The partner has three notes from the senior on her desk. First, opening stock at 1 April 2025 was 48 crore rupees of frozen produce, the firm attended no count at that date, the retired auditor has not answered two letters asking for his working papers, and the senior proposes to accept the opening figure "on the strength of a clean report from a qualified predecessor". Second, trade receivables at the year end are 65 crore rupees, of which 40 crore rupees is owed by five retail chains; the managing director has refused to let the firm send confirmation requests to those five, saying "the chains resent audit letters and it costs us shelf space", and has offered instead statements of account which his sales team will collect from the chains and hand to the firm. Third, the company revalued the cold-storage plant at 31 March 2026 from 70 crore rupees to 120 crore rupees on a valuer's report; the firm engaged its own chartered engineer, who has twenty years in refrigeration plant, and he has returned a two-page opinion agreeing with 120 crore rupees, resting on a remaining useful life of twenty-five years and on a replacement cost taken from a 2019 supplier quotation which the company gave him. The senior has filed the opinion as the evidence for the revaluation, "since an engineer with twenty years' experience has signed it".

items.stem: On the four uncertainties alone, what does Aparna settle?

options.text: Aparna disclaims an opinion on the financial statements as a whole because of the way the four uncertainties interact, and gives the clean opinion on the statement of cash flows in the same report, since none of the four touches it and the reader is better served by knowing which part of the statements is sound.
options.misconception: Reading the bar on a piecemeal opinion as a matter of usefulness to the reader, rather than a contradiction the standard forbids outright.
options.why: The opinion is right and the addition undoes it. A report that disclaims, or gives an adverse opinion, on the statements as a whole may not also carry a clean opinion beside it — same framework, one statement, or particular elements, accounts or items — because the two things contradict each other inside one document. A reader told that no opinion can be formed on the statements, and then told that one of those statements is fine, will take the second sentence and read the first as a formality. The four uncertainties also reach the cash flow statement through the recallable borrowing, whatever the finance head says.

options.text: Aparna gives a qualified opinion with all four matters set out in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section. She has sufficient appropriate audit evidence about every one of them and no single matter is pervasive, so the statements are true and fair except for the four, and the clean opinion on the statement of cash flows is left out as unnecessary.
options.misconception: Treating pervasiveness as a test applied to each matter one at a time, so four non-pervasive matters can only add up to a qualification.
options.why: Adding up four matters that are each not pervasive does not settle whether the statements as a whole can be reported on, and that is the judgement the standard asks for. A qualified opinion is a statement that everything outside the named matters is true and fair. She cannot make that statement here, because the four matters are not separate exceptions to an otherwise settled picture — the licence decides the plant, the plant decides the borrowing, and the possible cumulative effect runs through every figure. The standard provides for precisely this: where the auditor has evidence about each individual uncertainty and still cannot form an opinion because of the potential interaction of the uncertainties, the opinion is disclaimed.

options.text: Aparna gives an unmodified opinion with four emphasis of matter paragraphs, one for each uncertainty, since all four are disclosed in the notes and she has evidence about each. Drawing the reader's attention to them is what the reporting standards provide for when a matter is properly disclosed and the auditor has no disagreement with the accounting.
options.misconception: Using emphasis of matter as a way of reporting doubt, when it decorates an opinion the auditor is still able to express.
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph leaves the opinion unmodified, and the opinion is the thing in doubt. It is used where the auditor can say the statements are true and fair and wants the reader to notice something that is already disclosed. Here she cannot say that, because the potential interaction of the uncertainties and their possible cumulative effect make it impossible to form the opinion at all. Four paragraphs of attention attached to a clean opinion would tell the reader the statements can be relied on subject to being read carefully, which is a stronger assurance than she is in a position to give.

options.text: Aparna disclaims an opinion, and refuses the clean opinion on the one statement. Holding enough evidence on each uncertainty separately does not settle the question. What she cannot form a view on is the potential interaction of the uncertainties — the licence decides the plant, the plant decides the borrowing, the borrowing is already recallable, and the arbitration and the tax demand sit on top of all of it — and the possible cumulative effect that interaction has across every figure. That is the case the standard reserves for extremely rare circumstances and answers with a disclaimer, not with a qualified opinion carrying four limbs and not with four emphasis of matter paragraphs. And once the opinion on the whole is disclaimed, the report cannot carry a clean opinion beside it under the same framework on one statement or on specific elements, accounts or items, so the statement of cash flows does not get one.
options.why: The finance head's two proposals both assume the difficulty is a list of separate problems, and it is not. A qualified opinion says the statements are true and fair except for named matters, which requires the auditor to know what the rest of the statements look like once those matters are set aside; here she does not, because each uncertainty changes what the others are worth. That is why the standard has a second route to a disclaimer beside the ordinary one. The ordinary route is an inability to obtain evidence whose possible effects are material and pervasive. The second route is written for exactly this case, and the standard calls it extremely rare: the auditor holds enough evidence on every uncertainty taken by itself, and an opinion is still beyond her because of the potential interaction of the uncertainties — what each of them does to the others — and the possible cumulative effect of the four together. Emphasis of matter paragraphs fail for a further reason: they draw attention to something disclosed while leaving the opinion unmodified, and an unmodified opinion is the one thing she cannot give. The last part follows from the first. A disclaimer on the statements as a whole and a clean opinion on the cash flow statement in the same report would contradict each other, which is why the standard bars a clean opinion, under the same framework, on one statement or on specific elements, accounts or items alongside it. In short, she disclaims because of the potential interaction of the uncertainties and of the possible cumulative effect of the four together, and she does not add a clean opinion on specific elements, accounts or items to the same report.

citation.ref: the second route the standard gives to a disclaimer — evidence held on every uncertainty taken singly, an opinion still beyond reach because of how the uncertainties would work on one another and what they might come to together, and the standard calling that extremely rare — together with its bar on a report that disclaims, or gives an adverse opinion, on the statements as a whole also carrying a clean opinion beside it under the same framework, whether on one statement or on specific elements, accounts or items

items.scenario: Sinha & Varma are a firm of chartered accountants at Lucknow, and Aparna Sinha is the engagement partner on the audit of Gomti Polymers Limited, a listed company, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters are open in the week the report is to be signed. First, four uncertainties. An arbitration on a terminated supply contract, where the award is reserved and the claim against the company is 210 crore rupees; a tax demand of 96 crore rupees under appeal; a covenant on a borrowing of 340 crore rupees that the company breached in December 2025 and that lets the lender recall the whole amount on notice; and the renewal of the manufacturing licence for the company's only plant, pending with the state authority since October 2025. Aparna has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about each of the four on its own, and no one of them taken alone is pervasive; what she cannot see is how the four would work out together, since each turns on the others and their possible cumulative effect runs through every figure in the statements. The finance head proposes a qualified opinion carrying four separate limbs, or failing that an emphasis of matter paragraph for each, and adds that since the statement of cash flows is untouched by any of the four she should give a clean opinion on that one statement inside the same report. Second, the annual report. The board's report, which she received before the date of her own report, puts segment revenue for the speciality division at 480 crore rupees where the audited statements show 380 crore rupees, and repeats the higher figure twice more in the management discussion. She asked for the correction; management refused; she wrote to the audit committee, which also declined, saying the board's report is a management document that nobody audits. The finance head's position is that her opinion does not cover the other information at all, so the most she may do is say that she read it. Third, the shape of the report itself. The finance head has sent back a redrafted report in which a two-page background to the arbitration comes first, then the basis on which the audit was conducted, then the two responsibilities sections, with the opinion paragraph at the very end, where he says a reader will finally have the context to understand it; he has kept the heading Opinion over that paragraph, and has left standing the sentence saying that the financial statements have been audited. Aparna has to settle all three before she signs.

items.stem: On the figure in the board's report alone, what does Aparna settle?

options.text: Aparna modifies her opinion on the financial statements for the misstatement in the board's report. A figure a hundred crore rupees away from the audited revenue, repeated three times, is material, and once management and those charged with governance have both refused to correct it the only instrument left to the auditor is a qualification.
options.misconception: Reaching for the opinion because it is the strongest instrument, when the misstatement is outside what the opinion covers.
options.why: The opinion is on the financial statements, and the financial statements are not wrong — the audited segment revenue is 380 crore rupees and stays 380 crore rupees. The misstatement is in the other information, which the opinion does not cover, and the standard gives it its own place in the report for that reason: a statement in the Other Information section that describes the uncorrected material misstatement. Qualifying the opinion would tell readers something untrue about the statements, and it would also hide the real point, which is that the board's report and the audited figures do not agree.

options.text: Aparna has already done the two things that come first — she asked management to correct it and, on the refusal, took it to those charged with governance and asked them to correct it. What follows now is not silence. She weighs the implications for the auditor's report and tells those charged with governance how she plans to address the misstatement in it, and because the board's report reached her before the date of her own report, the Other Information section must carry a statement that describes the uncorrected material misstatement instead of a statement that she has nothing to report. Resigning the engagement is the other action open to her where the law allows it. The finance head is right that her opinion does not cover the other information, and the section says so in terms; that is a different thing from having nothing to say about it.
options.why: The finance head has taken a true sentence and drawn the wrong conclusion from it. The auditor's opinion does not cover the other information, and the Other Information section says exactly that — that management is responsible for it and that no opinion or assurance conclusion is expressed on it. But the same section also reports the outcome of the auditor's reading of it, and that outcome is not optional. Where the other information was obtained before the date of the report, the section ends either with a statement that the auditor has nothing to report or, where a material misstatement has been left uncorrected, with one that describes the uncorrected material misstatement. Saying only that she read it would be the first of those two endings, which would be untrue. The steps before that point have all been taken: the request to management, then the same request put to those charged with governance. What the standard requires once they too refuse is that she weigh the implications for the auditor's report and tell them how she plans to address the matter in it, and it names resigning the engagement, where the law permits it, as the other course. In short, the matter goes to those charged with governance, she weighs the implications for the auditor's report, and the Other Information section describes the uncorrected material misstatement rather than reporting nothing.

options.text: Aparna accepts that nothing further is open to her. She read the other information and found the inconsistency, she asked for a correction and she escalated it, which is the whole of the duty; her opinion does not cover the board's report, so the Other Information section states that management is responsible for it and that no opinion is expressed on it, and stops there.
options.misconception: Reading the escalation as the whole of the duty, so the report says nothing about what the escalation failed to fix.
options.why: Three of the steps are right and the report is where it goes wrong. The section that says the opinion does not cover the other information is the same section that must report what came of reading it. Where the other information was obtained before the date of the report, that section ends either with a statement that the auditor has nothing to report or with one that describes the uncorrected material misstatement. Stopping after the responsibility sentence leaves the reader with the first of those by implication, and the reader is the person the whole exercise is for — a segment revenue figure a hundred crore rupees above the audited one, repeated three times, is what the section exists to surface.

options.text: Aparna signs the report with a statement in the Other Information section that describes the uncorrected material misstatement, and treats the matter as closed with that. Since the audit committee has already been told and has declined, there is nothing to be gained by writing to them again about what the report will say.
options.misconception: Treating the earlier request for a correction as the same communication as telling governance how the report will address the matter.
options.why: The statement in the report is right and the step left out is the one that gives those charged with governance a last chance to act. The standard asks her to weigh what the misstatement means for her report and then to tell governance how the report is going to deal with it — a different communication from the earlier request to correct the figure. A board that has refused a correction in the abstract often behaves differently when it is told, before the report is signed, what the report is going to say. Skipping it also leaves the auditor without a record that the outcome was put to them.

citation.ref: what the standard asks once a material misstatement of the other information is found — the request to management, then the same request to those charged with governance on a refusal; and where the other information came in before the report is dated and is still wrong, the auditor weighs the implications for the auditor's report, tells governance how the report is going to deal with it, and may resign where the law allows it — together with the two ways the Other Information section can end for information obtained before that date: nothing to report, or a statement describing the material misstatement left uncorrected
