items.stem: On the Bhavani Rice Mills account alone, is the branch right to show it as regular, and what does the auditor do?

options.text: Yes. Drawing power is the bank's own computation on its own sanction terms, and the branch auditor checks only that the arithmetic from the statement on file is right
options.misconception: confines the auditor to checking the branch's arithmetic, when the module asks him to test the basis of the drawing power including the age of the statement
options.why: Recomputing the drawing power from the latest stock and book-debt statement is part of the auditor's own work on advances — net of the stipulated margin, net of creditors for goods, net of bills discounted against book debts — and the age of the statement is the first thing that computation tests. An auditor who checks the arithmetic of a four-month-old statement has verified the branch's sum and not the borrower's security, and the module's three-month rule is written for exactly that gap.

options.text: Yes. The outstanding has stayed within the drawing power all year and every stock statement on file supports it, so the account is regular
options.misconception: treats a drawing power computed once as valid until replaced, when the module ties its validity to the age of the stock statement it rests on
options.why: The drawing power on file was computed from a statement dated 30 November 2025, and the module is direct that statements relied upon for drawing power should not be older than three months, with an outstanding based on an older one considered irregular. A limit that rests on stock nobody has declared for four months is not a limit the borrower has today; the stock may have been sold, pledged or eaten by creditors for goods since. Staying under a stale figure proves nothing about the security now.

options.text: No. A drawing power worked out from a stock statement older than three months does not make the outstanding regular, so the account is irregular; the auditor calls for the latest stock statement, recomputes the drawing power, and does not classify the account as NPA merely for this deficiency while it is temporary
options.why: The module holds two rules side by side. A bank should not classify an advance as NPA merely because of a deficiency that is temporary in nature, and it names drawing power not being available on the latest stock statement as one of those deficiencies. But the stock statements a bank relies on for drawing power should not be older than three months, and an outstanding based on a drawing power calculated from a statement older than three months is considered irregular. Bhavani's statement is four months old at the year end, so the 2.55 crore rupees is irregular whatever the branch's returns say — being inside a stale figure is not being inside a drawing power. What the auditor does is what the deficiency asks for: obtain the latest statement, recompute the drawing power net of margin and creditors for goods, and judge the account on that. Irregular is the finding; NPA is not, unless the recomputed figure or the conduct of the account takes it there.

options.text: No. A stock statement more than three months old means the security cannot be verified at all, so the account is classified NPA from the day the statement went stale
options.misconception: turns every irregularity into an NPA, when the module keeps a temporary deficiency and non-performance apart
options.why: The module says the opposite in terms: a bank should not classify an account as NPA merely due to deficiencies which are temporary in nature, and it lists non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement as one. A stale statement makes the outstanding irregular and sends the auditor to get a fresh one; it does not on its own crystallise a date of NPA. The account becomes non-performing on the conduct of the account, not on the age of a piece of paper.

citation.ref: Chapter 14, audit of advances — accounts with temporary deficiencies; stock statements relied on for drawing power not to be older than three months, and an outstanding based on an older one treated as irregular

items.scenario: Kaveri Bank is a nationalised bank, and Rao & Bhat are the statutory branch auditors of its Hosur industrial branch for the year ended 31 March 2026. Advances at the branch are 96 crore rupees and three matters stand out from the review. First, Bhavani Rice Mills holds a cash credit limit of 3 crore rupees against stock and book debts. The latest stock statement on the branch file is dated 30 November 2025, the drawing power of 2.7 crore rupees was worked out from it, and the outstanding of 2.55 crore rupees has stayed within that figure all year, so the branch's returns show the account as regular. Second, Deccan Forgings has a term loan of 5 crore rupees whose instalment due on 15 December 2025 is still unpaid, and a cash credit of 2 crore rupees that has run within its limit with regular credits all year; a letter of credit opened for Deccan devolved in February 2026 and the 40 lakh rupees the branch paid under it sits in a separate account. The branch has classified the term loan alone as non-performing. Third, a loan of 4 crore rupees to a housing scheme carrying a guarantee of the Central Government has been overdue since August 2025; the branch has not invoked the guarantee, has kept the account standard, and has credited 32 lakh rupees of interest on it to income for the year.

items.stem: The branch has classified Deccan Forgings' term loan alone as non-performing. How do Deccan's facilities stand at 31 March 2026?

options.text: All of Deccan's facilities are non-performing from 31 March 2026, the date on which the auditor found the overdue instalment
options.misconception: dates the NPA from the audit rather than from the day the ninety days ran out, which moves the provision and the income reversal
options.why: The facilities are all non-performing, but the date is wrong, and the date decides the provision and the reversal of income. The account became non-performing when the instalment had stayed overdue for more than ninety days, which is in March 2026 counted from 15 December 2025, not on the day of the auditor's visit or the balance sheet date. The module asks the auditor to verify that the bank's system crystallises the date of NPA accurately and to compare the date of NPA with the previous year's; an NPA dated by discovery rather than by default is exactly what that check is for.

options.text: The term loan is non-performing and the cash credit stays standard, since it has run within its limit with regular credits and each facility is judged on its own conduct
options.misconception: classifies facility by facility on each account's own conduct, when the module requires the borrower's facilities to move together
options.why: This is the branch's classification and it is the one the module names as wrong. Asset classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise; all the facilities granted to a borrower are treated as NPA when one of them becomes irregular. The cash credit's regular credits are a fact about that account's operations, and the norm is deliberately blind to them: a borrower in default on one facility is a borrower whose every exposure carries the doubt.

options.text: Both facilities are non-performing, and the 40 lakh rupees stays as a separate standard account because a devolved letter of credit is a crystallised contingent liability, not an advance
options.misconception: keeps a devolved letter of credit outside the borrower's classification because it sits in a separate account, when the module folds it into the principal account
options.why: Half right, and the half that is wrong is the half the separate account was designed to hide. The module says in terms that debits arising out of the devolvement of a letter of credit or invoked guarantees kept in a separate account are treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the purpose of the prudential norms on asset classification, income recognition and provisioning. The money the branch paid under Deccan's letter of credit is money Deccan owes the bank; it takes the classification of Deccan, which is non-performing.

options.text: All of Deccan's facilities are non-performing — the term loan, the cash credit and the 40 lakh rupees of the devolved letter of credit — because classification is borrower-wise and the separate account is part of the borrower's principal account for the prudential norms
options.why: A term loan whose instalment has stayed unpaid for more than ninety days is non-performing, and the 15 December instalment is more than a hundred days overdue at the year end. The module then asks the auditor to ensure that asset classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise: all the facilities granted by a bank to a borrower have to be treated as NPA, not only the particular facility that has become irregular. The cash credit's good conduct does not rescue it — it belongs to a borrower who cannot service his term loan. And the module adds the point the branch's bookkeeping hides: where debits arising from the devolvement of a letter of credit or an invoked guarantee are kept in a separate account, the outstanding balance is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for asset classification, income recognition and provisioning. So the 40 lakh rupees is an NPA balance of Deccan's, not a standalone entry.

citation.ref: Chapter 14, audit of advances — asset classification to be borrower-wise and not facility-wise; debits from a devolved letter of credit kept in a separate account treated as part of the borrower's principal account

items.stem: The housing scheme loan is guaranteed by the Central Government, has been overdue since August 2025, and the guarantee has not been invoked. What is the auditor's position on its classification, on the 32 lakh rupees of interest, and on his report?

options.text: The account is non-performing, with the interest reversed and provision made, because it has been overdue for more than ninety days and the guarantee has not been invoked
options.misconception: applies the ninety-day rule to a Central Government guaranteed advance, when the module reserves NPA status for repudiation of the guarantee
options.why: More than ninety days overdue is the general rule, and the module carves Central Government guaranteed advances out of it: they are treated as NPA only when the Central Government repudiates the guarantee when invoked. Not invoking the guarantee is a reason for the auditor to ask why and to report it in the LFAR; it is not the event that makes the account non-performing. The State Government version of this answer would be right — that exception does not apply to State Government guaranteed advances, which are NPA when overdue for more than ninety days — but the guarantee here is the Centre's.

options.text: The account becomes non-performing on the day the bank invokes the guarantee, so the auditor insists that the branch invoke it now and classify the account from that date
options.misconception: makes invocation the event that creates the NPA, when the module makes it repudiation, and puts the auditor in the bank's seat on whether to invoke
options.why: Invocation is not the trigger; repudiation is. The module's words are that the facility can be treated as NPA only when the Central Government repudiates its guarantee, when invoked — a guarantee that is invoked and honoured leaves a standard account that has been repaid. Nor does the auditor decide when the bank invokes its guarantees; where the amount is overdue for long and the guarantee has not been invoked, his role is to obtain the reasoning and report it in the LFAR, while reversing the interest the branch has booked and not received.

options.text: The account stays standard and the interest stays in income, because a sovereign guarantee secures both the principal and the interest and removes the doubt about recovery
options.misconception: stretches the classification exemption for Central Government guarantees to income recognition, when the module confines it to asset classification
options.why: The classification is right and the income is wrong. The module is explicit that for the purpose of income recognition, interest on a government guaranteed advance that has become NPA is not to be taken to income unless it is realised, and that the classification exemption is not available in respect of the income recognition norms. A guarantee is a promise to pay on default; it is not a receipt. Interest booked on the strength of it and not received is reversed.

options.text: The account stays standard for classification and provisioning, because a Central Government guaranteed advance becomes NPA only when the Central Government repudiates the guarantee on invocation; but the 32 lakh rupees of unrealised interest is reversed, since the exemption does not extend to income recognition; and the branch's reason for not invoking the guarantee is obtained and reported in the LFAR
options.why: The module splits this advance three ways and the branch has got one of the three right. Classification: a credit facility backed by a Central Government guarantee, though overdue, can be treated as NPA only when the Central Government repudiates its guarantee when invoked; the guarantee has not been invoked, so repudiation has not arisen, and the branch is correct not to apply the NPA norms for provisioning. Income: that exemption is not available for income recognition — interest on a government guaranteed advance that has become NPA is not taken to income unless it is realised, so the 32 lakh rupees credited to income and not recovered is reversed. Report: where the bank has not invoked the Central Government guarantee though the amount is overdue for long, the reasoning is obtained and duly reported in the LFAR, the long form audit report. Standard, reversed, reported — three different answers to what looked like one question.

citation.ref: Chapter 14, audit of advances — Central Government guaranteed advances treated as NPA only on repudiation of the guarantee when invoked; the exception not available for income recognition; the reason for not invoking a long-overdue guarantee reported in the LFAR

items.stem: QUESTION 1 OF 3 — turns on the terms in the appointment letter. The warehouse report and last year's open issues are noise for this one. On those terms alone, what does Ananya tell the company before she signs?

options.text: Refuse the automation role but accept the receivables assignment, since the redesign was delivered fourteen months ago and a completed past engagement no longer affects the firm's objectivity.
options.misconception: Believes a self-review threat expires with the passage of time rather than with a change of the activity being reviewed.
options.why: Time does not dissolve a self-review. The receivables process on this year's plan is the very process the firm built, so any finding about it is a finding about the firm's own work, and the temptation not to make it is exactly what the rule against reviewing an activity you were previously responsible for is there to remove. The gap of fourteen months changes nothing about who designed the controls being tested.

options.text: Accept both extra responsibilities, because the module expressly allows the internal auditor to give advisory inputs on matters such as automation of activities and process re-engineering.
options.misconception: Reads permission to advise as permission to own the operational responsibility and later audit it.
options.why: Being asked for a view is not the same as being handed the job. The module does allow the internal auditor to offer advice on how a process is run, and automation is one of the places it says so. Advice ends where ownership begins. Take charge of the automation and he becomes answerable for an operational area; test a process his own firm designed and he is marking his own work, which is the whole reason the module keeps him away from anything he was previously responsible for.

options.text: The terms have to change. The internal audit function must sit outside the functions it audits and report directly to the audit committee, because independence has to hold not only in mind but also in appearance; the audit committee or the board settles the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology after talking to the internal auditor, and one executive cannot settle it alone; and since nobody may sit in judgement on work he was himself previously responsible for, the firm can take neither the automation role nor this year's receivables assignment.
options.why: Putting the head of internal audit under the chief financial officer places him beneath the very officer whose function he examines. Freedom from pressure is the first thing the module asks of him, and it sets the test twice over: the independence has to be real and it has to be visible, not only in mind but also in appearance. A line that merely looks compromised has already failed. Where the company is listed, the reporting is expected to run past the executives and land with those charged with governance, so the committee rather than a finance officer is who the head of internal audit answers to, and the function is meant to sit clear of anything it examines. Rule 13(2) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 then hands the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology to the audit committee, or to the board, after they have talked it over with the internal auditor — one executive deciding it alone is not what the rule describes. Automating purchase to pay is an operational job, and deciding how an area works before auditing that area is the conflict the module warns of; the receivables assignment is the same fault in a cleaner form, because the firm would be marking work it was previously responsible for. In short, independence must hold not only in mind but also in appearance, the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology are the committee's to settle, and nobody audits what he was previously responsible for.
keywords: not only in mind but also in appearance

options.text: Accept the reporting line as drafted, and ask instead that the audit committee ratify the year's scope after the work is finished, which restores the committee's authority without disturbing the company's management structure.
options.misconception: Treats a later sign-off by the audit committee as curing a reporting line that runs into the finance function.
options.why: Ratification after the event is not the same thing as formulation before it. Under rule 13(2) the year's scope, its periodicity and the method are settled at the start, by the committee or the board and in consultation with the internal auditor; a committee told afterwards what was covered cannot decide what should have been covered. And the reporting line is the larger problem, because it is what the outside world sees.

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — integrity, objectivity and independence of the internal auditor, the position and reporting of the chief internal auditor within the organisation structure, rule 13(2) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 on who formulates the scope, and the conflict in reviewing an activity the auditor was previously responsible for.

items.scenario: Basu & Kanungo are a firm of chartered accountants at Ranchi, and Ananya Basu is the partner who leads its internal audit practice. The firm has been offered the internal audit of a listed steel fabrication company for the year ending 31 March 2027, as an outside service provider, and three parts of the arrangement reach her in the week the engagement is being set up. First, the terms in the appointment letter. It says the head of internal audit will report to the chief financial officer, that the chief financial officer alone will settle the scope, the periodicity and the methodology for the year, and that the audit committee will be told what was covered once the work is finished. Beneath that, two further responsibilities are offered to the firm: taking charge of automating the company's purchase to pay process, and owning the redesign of the receivables process, which this same firm was paid fourteen months ago to redesign and which stands on this year's internal audit plan. The chief financial officer says those two pieces are worth more in fees than the audit itself. Second, the reporting. The plan for the year holds eleven assignments, the first of them the Jamshedpur warehouse. Ananya's team will finish the warehouse work in November, and the company wants the findings held back until the whole year is done so that one report goes up in April. Warehouse management has asked not to be copied on anything, on the ground that the plant head will pass on whatever matters. The chief financial officer has also asked her to confirm in writing that the standard her firm follows on reporting results governs the comprehensive report on the entity as a whole, because the audit committee has begun asking for one every quarter and nobody in the company wants to write it. Third, what became of last year's findings. The previous internal auditor's files list thirty-four issues raised in the year just ended. Nineteen of them carry a management action plan with a named owner and a date; twenty-two are still open. The chief financial officer's position is that the internal auditor raised them and the internal auditor should therefore close them, and he has asked Ananya's team to do the remediation work on nine of the nineteen for a separate fee. On six others the management accepted the recommendation, began the work and then stopped, and nobody has asked why. There is no agreed process for tracking any of this, and the audit committee has never been told that anything is open. Ananya has to settle all three before the engagement letter is signed.

items.stem: QUESTION 2 OF 3 — turns on the reporting arrangement. The appointment letter's terms and last year's open issues are noise for this one. On the reporting arrangement alone, what does Ananya settle with the company?

options.text: Issue the warehouse report in November but send it only upwards, to executive management and the audit committee, since the warehouse is the audited unit and should not receive the findings against it.
options.misconception: Thinks the auditee is a party to be reported about rather than the party the report is addressed to.
options.why: This inverts the addressee. The Internal Audit Report is issued to the auditee — the unit whose area was examined — with copies going to local and executive management as agreed during the planning phase. Withholding a report from the people whose processes it describes leaves nobody positioned to correct anything.

options.text: There are two reports and neither absorbs the other. One is written at the end of a particular audit assignment, goes to the unit that was audited, and is copied to local and executive management on terms fixed while the work was being planned — so the warehouse findings go out in November and warehouse management is copied; the report covering the whole plan period is a separate document, normally quarterly, sent up by the engagement partner to the audit committee; and she cannot sign the confirmation asked for, because the Standard reaches only the first type of reports.
options.why: Results are normally reported in two stages, and the company is trying to fold them into one. The narrow report comes first: it takes one area, one function or one part of the business, is written at the end of a particular audit assignment, says how the work was done and what was found, goes to the unit that was audited, and is copied to local and executive management on terms fixed while the assignment was being planned. That is why warehouse management cannot opt out of a copy, and why sitting on November's findings until April drains the report of any use. The wider report comes second: it covers everything internal audit did across the plan period, is written by the chief internal auditor — or by the engagement partner where the work is outsourced, as here — comes round quarterly as a rule, and goes up to the body that answers for internal audit, which will usually be the audit committee. The Standard says in its own scope that it reaches only the first type of reports and leaves the entity-wide one alone, so the confirmation the chief financial officer wants would be a false statement. In short, the assignment report is written at the end of a particular audit assignment and copied to local and executive management, the entity-wide report is a separate quarterly one for the audit committee, and the Standard governs only the first type of reports.
keywords: at the end of a particular audit assignment
only the first type of reports

options.text: Give the written confirmation, because a Standard on reporting results necessarily governs every report an internal auditor signs, including the quarterly one for the entity.
options.misconception: Assumes a Standard named for an activity covers every instance of that activity, without reading its stated scope.
options.why: The Standard fixes its own boundary and says so: it deals with the internal auditor's responsibility to issue the assignment report, not the periodic reporting for the whole entity under the annual or quarterly plan. Signing a confirmation that it governs the quarterly report would misstate the Standard, and it would also hand the firm a duty the company is trying to avoid writing itself.

options.text: Agree to the single report in April, since the audit committee is the body that internal audit results are owed to and one complete report serves it better than eleven partial ones.
options.misconception: Treats the audit committee as the only real recipient and the assignment report as an optional interim step.
options.why: The assignment report is not a draft of the periodic report; it is a report in its own right, owed to the auditee at the end of the assignment so that the people who run the area can act on the findings while acting still helps. Waiting until April means the warehouse carries a known weakness for five months. The committee's quarterly report is a separate obligation and does not discharge this one.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 370, Reporting Results
citation.ref: The two stages in which internal audit results are reported — the report that closes one assignment and who receives a copy of it, the periodic report for the whole plan period and who it goes up to — and which of the two the Standard itself governs.

items.stem: QUESTION 3 OF 3 — turns on the thirty-four issues raised in the year just ended. The appointment letter's terms and the warehouse report are noise for this one. On those prior issues alone, what does Ananya do?

options.text: Report all twenty-two open issues to the audit committee once, in writing, and treat the prior year as closed, since follow-up is discharged by reporting the position.
options.misconception: Confuses a single act of reporting with the continuing duty to monitor until issues are actually closed.
options.why: One report is a snapshot, and the duty is a continuing one: the chief internal auditor monitors closure through a formal process, periodically reviews the manner and extent of implementation where recommendations were accepted, and keeps reporting what remains open. Declaring the prior year closed while twenty-two items are open is the outcome the standard exists to prevent.

options.text: Decline the remediation work and build the monitoring instead. The responsibility to implement the action plans remains with the management, so the firm cannot take over the nine items; what she owes is a formal monitoring process whose elements are pre-agreed with management and those charged with governance, and an Action Taken Report of previous audits; and on the six where the recommendation was accepted and the work then stopped, she reviews the manner and extent of implementation and reports those which have not been implemented fully or partly.
options.why: Monitoring the closure of prior audit issues is a continuing duty of the chief internal auditor, carried out through a formal monitoring process whose elements are pre-agreed with management and those charged with governance. That process is exactly what is missing here, and its absence is why the audit committee has heard nothing about twenty-two open items. But monitoring is not doing: the responsibility to implement the action plans remains with the management, so taking the remediation of nine issues for a fee would put the firm in the position of auditing its own work next year. What the internal auditor owes is usually an Action Taken Report of previous audits, which tracks the issues raised and evaluates the corrective action the auditee actually took. Where no action has been taken within a reasonable time, he should draw management's attention to it and ascertain the reasons; where management accepted the recommendations and began work, he should periodically review the manner and the extent of implementation and report the recommendations which have not been implemented fully or partly, which is precisely the position of the six that stalled. In short, the responsibility to implement the action plans remains with the management, the internal auditor's product is an Action Taken Report of previous audits, and he reports the recommendations which have not been implemented fully or partly.
keywords: responsibility to implement the action plans remains with the management
Action Taken Report of previous audits
not been implemented fully or partly

options.text: Take the nine remediation items for the separate fee but ring-fence them with a different team inside the firm, since remediation is consulting rather than audit and the firm is an outside service provider in any case.
options.misconception: Believes an internal wall between teams removes a self-review threat that sits at the level of the firm.
options.why: A second team does not make the firm a second firm. Next year's internal audit would be testing controls this firm installed, and the standard places implementation squarely with management for that reason. Being an outside service provider changes who employs the internal auditor, not whose job it is to fix a finding.

options.text: Drop the fifteen issues that carry no management action plan, because an issue with no named owner and no agreed date was never accepted by management and so cannot be monitored.
options.misconception: Reads a missing management action plan as management having rejected the issue, and rejection as closure.
options.why: The absence of an action plan is itself a finding to report, not a reason to let an issue go. Where management has not acted on a recommendation or has not implemented it, the internal auditor is to draw management's attention to it and ascertain the reasons — which presumes the issue stays on the list until somebody explains it away.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 390, Monitoring and Reporting of Prior Audit Issues
citation.ref: Continuous monitoring by the chief internal auditor of the closure of prior audit issues through a formal process whose elements are pre-agreed with management and those charged with governance, the management's retained responsibility to implement the action plans, and the Action Taken Report of previous audits.

items.stem: On the senior's plan alone, what does SA 250 require of the auditor for the effluent limits and discharge hours, as against tax deducted at source and provident fund?

options.text: The same thing for all of them. Every law the company must obey can produce a fine that hits the statements, so the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance with each, exactly as the senior proposes.
options.misconception: Collapses the two categories into one because both can end in a fine.
options.why: A fine can indeed have a material effect, and that is why the second category has procedures at all; but the module limits the auditor's responsibility for laws without a direct effect on the amounts to specified audit procedures of inquiry and inspecting correspondence, not to evidence of compliance with each condition.

options.text: Two different things. Tax deducted at source and provident fund are laws with a direct effect on the amounts and disclosures in the statements, and for those the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about compliance. The effluent limits and discharge hours are laws fundamental to the operating aspects of the business, and for those the auditor's responsibility is limited to specified audit procedures: inquiring of management and, where appropriate, those charged with governance, and inspecting correspondence with the regulator, while staying alert to what the rest of the audit turns up.
options.why: The module draws the line the senior's plan erases. SA 250 sorts laws into two categories and gives the auditor a different job in each. In the first sit the laws everybody accepts as feeding straight into the figures and the notes — tax and labour law are the module's examples. In the second sit laws that do not move the figures at all, but which the entity has to obey if it is to keep operating, stay in business, or avoid a penalty large enough to matter; the module's examples there are an operating licence, a regulatory solvency requirement, and environmental rules. Category one calls for sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the entity has complied. Category two calls for less, and the module says exactly how much less: a short list of specified audit procedures aimed at surfacing a breach big enough to affect the statements, being a question put to management, and where it fits to those charged with governance, about whether the entity is obeying the law, and a reading of any correspondence with the licensing or regulatory authority. Beyond that list, the auditor stays alert to a breach that some other procedure happens to expose. The chief financial officer is right about the plan and wrong about the conclusion: the auditor is not a pollution inspector, and the auditor still asks and still reads the regulator's letters. In short, direct effect laws get evidence of compliance; the consent conditions get the specified audit procedures of inquiry and inspecting correspondence with the regulator.

options.text: The reverse of the plan. Environmental law is where the material penalties are, so it takes full evidence of compliance, while tax deducted at source and provident fund are routine deductions that need only inquiry.
options.misconception: Sorts the categories by penalty size instead of by effect on the statements.
options.why: Tax and labour laws are the module's examples of laws with a direct effect on the amounts and disclosures, for which evidence of compliance is obtained; environmental regulations are its example of the other category, for which the specified audit procedures apply. The size of a possible penalty does not move a law from one category to the other.

options.text: Nothing for the effluent limits and discharge hours. They are operating matters outside the financial statements, so the auditor has no responsibility for them at all and the plan should drop them.
options.misconception: Reads "limited responsibility" as no responsibility.
options.why: The module keeps a responsibility for the second category, limited but real: the auditor performs the specified audit procedures of inquiring of management and those charged with governance and inspecting correspondence with the regulator, and remains alert, because non-compliance with a licence condition can have a material effect on the statements or on going concern.

citation.ref: the two categories the standard separates. Where a law has a direct effect on the amounts and disclosures a set of statements carries — tax and labour law are the examples — the auditor gathers sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the entity has complied. Where it has no such effect, but obeying it is fundamental to keeping the business running — an operating licence, environmental rules — the duty shrinks to specified audit procedures: asking management, and where it fits those charged with governance, and inspecting correspondence with the licensing or regulatory authority, while staying alert to whatever else the audit turns up

items.scenario: Varma & Qureshi are the statutory auditors of Kosi Speciality Chemicals Limited, a listed maker of dyes and intermediates with its plant at Dahej, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Revenue is 980 crore rupees and the company operates under a consent to operate from the state pollution control board that fixes effluent limits and discharge hours. Farah Qureshi is the engagement partner, and three matters are open in the last week of fieldwork. First, the senior's plan for laws and regulations treats every law alike: it proposes to test compliance with the effluent limits and the discharge hours "the same way we test tax deducted at source and provident fund, by obtaining evidence of compliance with each condition", and the chief financial officer has objected that the auditors are not pollution inspectors. Second, a newspaper report in March 2026 disclosed that the pollution control board had fined the company 6 crore rupees in December 2025 for an effluent breach; the fine was paid and booked, but nobody had told the auditors, and the chair of the audit committee has written to ask why the audit "did not catch a breach of this size" and to say that the board expects the audit report to confirm that the company now complies with all environmental laws. Third, the audit has since found a plant log showing that the managing director personally authorised discharge outside the permitted hours on three nights in November 2025 to meet a shipment; the company's lawyers have advised on further penalties the auditors understand could reach 40 crore rupees, and the chief financial officer has refused to let the auditors see the board's correspondence with the pollution control board or the lawyers' opinion, saying "regulatory letters are not audit evidence and we are not obliged to show them".

items.stem: On the audit committee chair's letter alone, how should Farah answer the question and the expectation?

options.text: Compliance is the responsibility of management, watched over by the board and its committee; preventing a breach is no part of the auditor's job and the auditor cannot be expected to detect every breach of every law, least of all one that lives in plant records outside the financial reporting systems and was kept from the auditors. And the report cannot confirm compliance with environmental law, because whether an act is a breach at all is a legal determination for a court, not a conclusion an auditor expresses.
options.why: The module answers the question with the allocation of responsibility and the expectation with the limits of an audit. Keeping the entity's operations inside the law is management's job, watched over by those charged with governance, and the module goes on to list the machinery an entity may put behind that job — tracking what the law requires, keeping a register of the laws that matter to it, logging complaints. Preventing a breach is no part of the auditor's job, and the auditor cannot be expected to detect every breach of every law; what the auditor owes is reasonable assurance that the statements taken as a whole hold no material misstatement. The module then explains why an audit is an especially blunt instrument here, and gives three reasons. A great many laws bear on how a business is run day to day rather than on anything its financial reporting systems record. A breach is often hidden on purpose. And whether an act is a breach at all is in the end for a court to decide. A December fine for an effluent breach that management never mentioned is the first two reasons in one, and the third answers the chair's expectation: an auditor's report does not certify that the company complies with environmental law, and the written representation the auditor obtains about known breaches is evidence, not a conclusion the auditor may hand back. In short, compliance is the responsibility of management, the auditor cannot be expected to detect every breach, and compliance is a legal determination the report does not make.

options.text: Answer that the auditor relies on management's written representation that all known non-compliance has been disclosed, so the omission is management's breach of that representation, and give the confirmation of compliance on the strength of a fresh representation.
options.misconception: Turns a written representation into a certificate of compliance.
options.why: The representation is evidence the auditor obtains about known instances of non-compliance, and the module treats it as such and as a matter bearing on the reliability of other representations; it is not a basis on which the auditor confirms compliance, which remains a legal determination by a court and not the auditor's conclusion.

options.text: Decline both, on the ground that environmental law is outside the audit entirely; the auditor reports on the financial statements and has no responsibility of any kind for laws that do not determine the figures.
options.misconception: Overshoots from "not responsible for detecting all" to "no responsibility at all".
options.why: The module keeps a limited responsibility for laws fundamental to the operations, through specified audit procedures, and requires the auditor to respond to non-compliance that comes to light, evaluate its effect on the statements, and communicate it to those charged with governance. "No responsibility of any kind" overstates the answer and would mislead the committee.

options.text: Accept the criticism. A fine of 6 crore rupees is material to the audit, so failing to find it is an audit failure, and the report should carry the confirmation the board asks for once the auditors have re-tested compliance since the fine.
options.misconception: Treats the size of a fine as proof of an audit failure and a licence to certify compliance.
options.why: Materiality of a fine does not make its detection the auditor's responsibility: the module puts prevention outside the auditor's job altogether and says the auditor cannot be expected to detect every breach of every law, then gives its reasons. And no re-testing produces a confirmation of compliance, because that is a legal determination by a court, outside what an auditor's report expresses.

citation.ref: keeping the entity's operations inside the law is management's job, watched over by those charged with governance; preventing a breach is no part of the auditor's job, and the auditor cannot be expected to detect every breach of every law — the more so because a great many laws bear on how a business is run rather than on what its reporting systems record, because a breach is often hidden on purpose, and because whether an act is a breach at all is in the end for a court to decide

items.stem: On the plant log and the refused letters alone, to whom does Farah take the matter, and what does the refusal do to the opinion?

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement. Once management refuses evidence about a breach the managing director authorised, the auditor cannot continue and resignation is the only response the standard allows.
options.misconception: Jumps to resignation past the reporting steps the standard sets out.
options.why: The module's responses are communication to the next higher level of authority, legal advice where the communication may not be acted upon, and a qualified opinion or a disclaimer on the basis of a limitation on the scope. Withdrawal is not the response SA 250 prescribes for a refusal of evidence, and taking it first would leave the audit committee untold.

options.text: Discuss it with the managing director as the head of management, obtain his written representation that no further penalty is expected, and give an unmodified opinion; the 6 crore rupee fine is already booked and the rest is speculation.
options.misconception: Takes a representation from the person implicated as the evidence the standard wants.
options.why: Discussion with management is the module's first step for suspected non-compliance, but where management itself is involved the communication goes to the next higher level of authority, and a representation from the person on the plant log cannot replace the evidence that has been withheld. The module treats a management-imposed inability to obtain evidence about possibly material non-compliance as a scope limitation, not as speculation.

options.text: Qualify or give an adverse opinion for the 40 crore rupee penalty as an unrecorded liability, because the auditors have a lawyer's figure and the company has not provided for it.
options.misconception: Uses the misstatement branch when the problem is withheld evidence.
options.why: The qualified-or-adverse branch is for non-compliance the auditor concludes has a material effect that is not adequately reflected. Here the auditors have not seen the lawyers' opinion or the regulator's letters; what they have is a refusal, and the module's answer to being precluded from the evidence is a qualified opinion or a disclaimer for a limitation on the scope, after the matter has gone to the audit committee.

options.text: Because the managing director is involved, the matter goes to the next higher level of authority at the company, the audit committee, and if Farah believes that communication will not be acted upon she considers legal advice. The refusal is a different matter with its own consequence: the auditor has been precluded by management from obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence about non-compliance that may be material, so the opinion is qualified or disclaimed for a limitation on the scope.
options.why: The module deals with the two halves separately. On communication: a breach that comes to the auditor's attention is told to those charged with governance unless it is clearly inconsequential, and told at once where it looks deliberate and material. Where suspicion falls on management itself, or on those charged with governance, the module sends the matter up instead — to whatever authority sits above them inside the entity, an audit committee or a supervisory board — and where no such authority exists, or a message to it looks unlikely to be acted on, or the auditor cannot tell who should be told, legal advice is to be considered. A plant log carrying the managing director's own authorisation is that case, and a listed company has the committee. On the opinion: being shut out by management, or by those charged with governance, from the evidence needed to judge whether a breach that could be material to the statements has happened or probably has, leaves the auditor qualifying the opinion or disclaiming it for a limitation on the scope, under SA 705. The regulator's letters and the lawyers' opinion are the evidence about a penalty the auditors understand could reach 40 crore rupees, the chief financial officer has withheld them, and the module's other branch, a qualified or adverse opinion, is for non-compliance whose material effect is known and not reflected, which is not yet this. items.stem: On the Sahu Traders account alone, what is the position at 31 March 2026 and what does the partner do about it?

options.text: Nothing is wrong. Drawing power is a sanction-stage figure; once the account is within limit and credits are regular, the age of the stock statement has no bearing on regularity.
options.misconception: Treats drawing power as fixed at sanction rather than as a figure that moves with the stock statements.
options.why: Drawing power is recomputed from each stock statement, which is why the module fixes the age of the statement that may be relied on at three months; an outstanding measured against a drawing power older than that is irregular by the module's own words, whatever the credits look like.

options.text: The outstanding is irregular, because the drawing power rests on a stock statement older than three months, and the branch's register overstates the cover. That deficiency is temporary in nature, so the account is not classified as NPA merely on that ground; the partner reports the irregularity, ensures the branch calls for current statements and recomputes drawing power, and looks at the operation of the account on its other parameters before deciding its classification.
options.why: The module gives both halves of this rule side by side. Stock statements relied upon by the bank for determining drawing power should not be older than three months, and the outstanding in the account based on drawing power calculated from stock statements older than three months is considered irregular; the auditor ensures adherence to that guideline. At the same time, banks should not classify an advance as NPA merely due to deficiencies that are temporary in nature, and the module names non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement as the first example of such a deficiency, alongside the balance exceeding the limit temporarily and non-renewal of limits on the due date. A November statement in a March balance sheet is four months old, so the drawing power of 5.9 crore rupees on the register is not one the branch may rely on, and the account is irregular from the day the statement went out of date; but weekly credits and an outstanding within limit are exactly the other parameters the module tells the auditor to consider before calling the account non-performing. In short, the statement is older than three months, the outstanding is irregular, and the deficiency is temporary rather than a reason on its own for NPA.

options.text: The partner substitutes her own drawing power from the year-end physical stock she inspects, and if the outstanding is within that figure the account is regular and nothing is reported.
options.misconception: Puts the auditor in the branch's seat as the maker of drawing power.
options.why: The auditor checks the branch's calculation against the guidelines; she does not make a drawing power of her own, and a figure computed on a statement older than three months is irregular whether or not a later inspection would have covered the balance. The irregularity is reported and the branch obtains current statements.

options.text: The account is NPA. Four months without a stock statement means four months without valid drawing power, and an account without drawing power is out of order for that whole period.
options.misconception: Collapses "irregular" into "non-performing" and skips the temporary-deficiency rule.
options.why: The module says in terms that a bank should not classify an advance as NPA merely because of deficiencies temporary in nature, and its first example is non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement. The account is irregular, which is a different finding from non-performing, and the classification is decided on the account's other parameters.

items.scenario: Joshi & Karandikar are the statutory branch auditors of the Kolhapur main branch of Malaprabha Bank, a public sector bank, for the year ended 31 March 2026. The branch has advances of 410 crore rupees, and the partner has three matters open on the last day of the visit. First, Sahu Traders, a jaggery wholesaler, has a cash credit limit of 6 crore rupees with an outstanding of 5.7 crore rupees at the year end; the drawing power of 5.9 crore rupees on the branch's register was computed from the stock statement for November 2025, the last one the borrower submitted, and the branch manager says the account "operates like a textbook, with credits every week, so the missing statements are a paperwork matter". Second, Warna Fabrics has a term loan of 8 crore rupees whose instalments and interest are paid on the day they fall due, and a cash credit limit of 3 crore rupees that is within limit; a letter of credit of 1.2 crore rupees opened for its yarn supplier devolved on the branch on 12 December 2025, the branch parked the amount in a separate "LC devolvement" account, and nothing has been paid into it since; the branch has classified all of Warna's facilities as standard, on the ground that "the term loan and the cash credit are regular, and the devolved LC is a separate account with its own history". Third, the branch manager asks the partner to keep both matters out of the branch audit report and to "put them in the LFAR, where such things belong and where head office will see them in due course", and mentions in passing that the original title deeds of the factory mortgaged by Warna Fabrics are held at the regional office and not at the branch.

items.stem: On the Warna Fabrics facilities alone, is the branch's classification right?

options.text: No. The devolvement debit kept in a separate account is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the prudential norms, and it has been unpaid for more than ninety days at the year end. Classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise, so all the facilities of Warna Fabrics, the term loan and the cash credit included, become non-performing together, and interest on them not realised is reversed rather than taken to income.
options.why: The module states two rules that together dispose of the branch's argument. Asset classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise, so all the facilities granted by a bank to a borrower have to be treated as NPA and not the particular facility which has become irregular. And if debits arising out of devolvement of a letter of credit or an invoked guarantee are kept in a separate account, the outstanding balance is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the purpose of the prudential norms on asset classification, income recognition and provisioning. A devolvement on 12 December 2025 with nothing paid by 31 March 2026 is an overdue of more than ninety days sitting in the borrower's principal account, whatever ledger the branch opened for it, and the punctual term loan does not rescue the borrower any more than the devolved LC could be quarantined from him. Income recognition follows: the module says interest on a non-performing advance is not taken to income unless realised and income to the extent not recovered is reversed. In short, the devolvement is part of the borrower's principal account, the norms are borrower-wise and not facility-wise, and all the facilities are NPA.
keywords: part of the borrower's principal account

options.text: Yes, because a devolved letter of credit is a contingent liability that has crystallised, not an advance, and contingent items are outside the prudential norms on asset classification.
options.misconception: Keeps a crystallised commitment in the contingent column after the bank has paid it.
options.why: Once the letter of credit devolves the bank has paid the beneficiary and the borrower owes the bank; the module treats the devolvement debit as part of the borrower's principal account for asset classification, income recognition and provisioning, which is the opposite of outside the norms.

options.text: No, but only the devolved amount of 1.2 crore rupees is classified as NPA and provided for; the term loan and the cash credit continue as standard because their own dues are current.
options.misconception: Accepts the devolvement as an overdue but still classifies facility by facility.
options.why: This halves the rule. The devolvement debit is part of the borrower's principal account, and the consequence the module draws from a borrower-wise classification is that all the facilities become NPA, not that the overdue piece alone is marked.

options.text: Yes. Each facility is classified on its own record; the devolved LC account is the only irregular one and may be classified as substandard by itself while the term loan and the cash credit stay standard.
options.misconception: Classifies each account on its own history instead of the borrower as a whole.
options.why: This is facility-wise classification, and the module says classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise: all the facilities granted to the borrower are treated as NPA, not only the one that has become irregular.

items.stem: On the branch manager's request and the title deeds alone, what is the LFAR for, and does the request work?

options.text: The LFAR is a confidential report from the branch auditor direct to RBI, so putting the matters there is stronger than the branch report, and the branch manager's request should be accepted on that ground.
options.misconception: Mistakes the LFAR's eventual copy to RBI for a direct confidential channel.
options.why: The module's route is branch auditor to statutory central auditors, consolidation at head office, the audit committee, and only then a copy to RBI within 60 days with the board's views. It is a questionnaire to the central auditors, not a direct line to the regulator, and it does not displace the branch report.

options.text: The request works. The LFAR is the branch auditor's channel to head office for irregularities in advances, and the main branch report is reserved for the true and fair view of the branch's balance sheet, which two accounts out of 410 crore rupees do not touch.
options.misconception: Treats the LFAR as the home for anything about advances and the main report as untouched by them.
options.why: The module presents the LFAR as furnished besides the statutory report, and a misclassified borrower alters the branch's asset classification returns, provisions and income, which are the figures the main report speaks to. Whether two accounts are material is the auditor's judgement to make on the figures, not a rule that moves them out of the report.

options.text: Title deeds held at the regional office are outside the branch auditor's remit altogether; she verifies only what is at the branch and need not mention the deeds anywhere.
options.misconception: Limits the branch auditor's responsibility to documents physically in the branch.
options.why: The module says the opposite: where title deeds are held at head office or another location, the branch auditor obtains a written representation from branch management and brings the fact to the notice of the central statutory auditor through a mention in the report and in the LFAR.

options.text: The LFAR is a questionnaire the branch auditor answers for the statutory central auditors, furnished besides the branch audit report and not in place of it; it is consolidated at head office, placed before the audit committee with the action taken, and sent to RBI within 60 days. So the request fails: a matter that changes classification and figures goes in the main report, and the LFAR carries it as well. The title deeds at the regional office are covered by a written representation from the branch and a mention in both the report and the LFAR.
options.why: The module describes the long form audit report as something the terms of appointment require the auditors to furnish besides the statutory audit report. For branch auditors it is in the form of a questionnaire on which observations and comments are given on cash, balances with banks, investments, advances, deposits and other matters, submitted by the statutory branch auditors to the statutory central auditors; consolidation happens at head office, the central auditors submit the bank's LFAR to management, it is placed before the audit committee of the board with the action taken or proposed on the irregularities in it, and a copy with the agenda note and the board's views goes to RBI within 60 days. Nothing in that makes it a substitute for the branch report: an irregular drawing power and a borrower wrongly kept standard bear on the branch's returns and figures, and belong in the main report, with the LFAR answering its own questions on them as well. For the title deeds the module is specific: where they are held at head office or some other location the branch auditor obtains a written representation to that effect from branch management and brings the fact to the notice of the central statutory auditor through a suitable mention in the report, and also in the LFAR. In short, the LFAR is a questionnaire for the statutory central auditors that sits beside the main report, not under it.

items.stem: On the write-up and the letterheads alone, what does Lakshmi settle?

options.text: Almost all of the write-up has to come out. The fastest growing claim and the turnaround boast are exaggerated claims for the services offered; the comparison with every other firm in the city is an unsubstantiated comparison to the work of others; the two paragraphs of praise are testimonials or endorsements and they name clients, and the standard tax audit fee is the fees charged, all three of which the guidelines shut out by name; the magazine's award is an achievement, and the exception runs only to awards given by the Central or State Governments or Regulatory bodies; the rising sun is a monogram, which is not permissible in any form; the firm registration number is mandatory and cannot be dropped; and eighteen point breaks the cap of 14. On the letterheads the two lines go opposite ways: Registered Valuer stays, because a member empanelled as one may mention it on his visiting card and letter head, while Serving coastal Andhra since 1994 comes off, because a letterhead may not carry the date of setting up of practice.
options.why: The growth partner has read the proviso and stopped there. A write-up describing what the firm does and who its people are is indeed allowed — but only on the Council's terms, and this draft misses eight of them. Honesty is the first term, and the fastest growing line fails it because nothing supports the claim. Two more terms deal with boasting: exaggerated claims about the service or about a partner's qualifications are shut out, and so, separately, is any comparison with another firm's work that cannot be backed up — which is what beating every other firm in the city is. Praise quoted from a client breaks three terms in one go: it is a testimonial, it names the client, and the paragraph beside it prints the fee. The award has an exception written into it, and a business magazine is neither a government nor a regulator. Monograms are shut out in every form, the firm registration number has to be there, and 14 is the largest type allowed. Letterheads run on a different rule and the two lines split under it. A title the Central Government recognises may be shown, which is why a partner empanelled as a Registered Valuer or an Insolvency Professional may say so beside his name. Founding year is different again: a write-up may give it, a letterhead may not, and Serving coastal Andhra since 1994 is printed on a letterhead. In short, the draft carries exaggerated claims, testimonials or endorsements and much else the guidelines shut out, while on the letterheads Registered Valuer stays and the date of setting up of practice goes.
keywords: date of setting up of practice

options.text: The write-up is corrected throughout and both lines come off the letterheads. Clause (7) restrains a member from using any designation or expression other than Chartered Accountant on letter heads, and Registered Valuer is plainly another designation, so it cannot stand however genuinely the partner holds the empanelment.
options.misconception: Reading the designation restraint without the exception attached to it, so a recognised title is treated the same as a boast.
options.why: The write-up half is right and the reading of the clause is too flat. Not every designation is shut out. The clause carries an exception, and three things fall inside it: a degree from a university India's law set up or the Central Government recognises, a title that shows membership of the Institute, and a title from another institution the Central Government or the Council recognises. That exception is why a partner empanelled as an Insolvency Professional or a Registered Valuer may show it beside his name. The line that must go is the other one, which nothing excepts: a letterhead may not carry the date of setting up of practice.

options.text: Nothing in the write-up needs changing. Clause (7) bans advertising, but the proviso expressly lets a firm publish a write-up about the work it does and the details of the practice, and everything in the draft is either work the firm does or a detail of the practice. Only the two letterhead lines are in question, and both of those come off.
options.misconception: Reading the write-up proviso as the whole permission, when it is expressly subject to guidelines that decide the contents.
options.why: A write-up is permitted only on the Council's terms, and it is those terms rather than the proviso that decide what may go inside one. They speak to this draft point by point: nothing exaggerated, no comparison with another firm that cannot be backed up, no testimonial, no client named, no fee printed, no award unless a government or a regulator gave it, no monogram, the firm registration number compulsory, and 14 the largest type. Treating the proviso as a permission that stands on its own turns a narrow opening into a general licence to advertise, which is the one thing the clause exists to prevent. The letterheads then go the other way from the answer given: Registered Valuer is expressly permitted and stays.

options.text: The write-up is corrected as far as the exaggerated claims, the comparison, the testimonials, the client names, the fee and the award, and the monogram, the missing firm registration number and the font size are all fixed, and both letterhead lines are left as printed. Registered Valuer is a designation the member actually holds and the year the firm started is a detail of the practice, which a write-up is allowed to give.
options.misconception: Treating what a write up may contain and what a letterhead may carry as one list, when they are two different rules with different contents.
options.why: The write-up half is right and one of the two letterhead lines is wrong. Founding year is indeed among the details a firm may put in a write-up — and a letterhead is not a write-up. Stationery runs on the older rule inside the clause itself, which shuts out the date of setting up of practice, so Serving coastal Andhra since 1994 comes off. Registered Valuer is the line that stays, because a partner empanelled as one may show it beside his name. Carrying a permission across from the write-up rules to the letterhead rules is the trap in this matter.

citation.ref: Clause (7) of Part I of the First Schedule — the misconduct of advertising one's own attainments, and of putting a designation other than Chartered Accountant on the firm's stationery — together with the proviso that opens the door to a write-up, and the Council's Advertisement Guidelines, 2008, which set the conditions that door is subject to: honesty, no exaggerated claims, no unsubstantiated comparisons, no testimonials or endorsements, no client names, no fees, awards only from government or a regulator, no monogram, a compulsory firm registration number and a font size cap of 14

items.scenario: Rao & Iyer are a firm of chartered accountants at Vijayawada, and Lakshmi Rao is the managing partner. Three matters come to her in the same week, all of them raised by the partner who looks after the firm's growth. First, the marketing. He has drafted a write-up for a business magazine that calls the firm the fastest growing audit practice in coastal Andhra, says its goods and services tax work is turned around quicker than that of any other firm in the city, quotes two paragraphs of praise from the finance heads of two listed clients naming both companies, states the fee the firm charges for a standard tax audit, and carries a Best Emerging Firm award given by that same magazine in 2024. It is set in eighteen point type over a monogram of a rising sun that he had drawn for the firm, and it leaves out the firm registration number because he thinks it clutters the page. He has also had new letterheads printed. They carry the words Registered Valuer under the name of the partner who is empanelled as one, and beneath the firm's name the line Serving coastal Andhra since 1994. Second, the number of company audits. The firm has four partners. One of them holds a certificate of practice and is in full-time employment with a sugar company; another is a part-time practising partner who comes in three days a week. The firm's register shows ninety- six company audits in hand, and inside that figure are six one person companies, four dormant companies, and one client whose head office and eleven branches are each written up as a separate line. A third partner holds nine more company audits in his own name through his proprietary firm. The growth partner has worked out that four partners at thirty each gives one hundred and twenty, so the firm can take twenty-four more before it has to think about it. Third, three arrangements about fees. A firm of company secretaries at Guntur sends the firm work, and in return Rao & Iyer have agreed to take twenty per cent of the fees the company secretaries earn on the assignments Rao & Iyer send the other way. A management consultant with no professional qualification of any kind introduced a large manufacturing client last year, and the growth partner has agreed to pay him fifteen per cent of the audit fee from that client every year the firm holds the audit. And a chartered accountant in practice at Rajahmundry has offered the firm a referral fee for a client passed to Rao & Iyer, which the growth partner has refused because he believes any payment between firms for a client is barred. Lakshmi has to settle all three before the write-up goes to the magazine.

items.stem: On the number of company audits alone, what does Lakshmi settle?

options.text: The ceiling is sixty because only two partners count, and the firm holds ninety-six against it, so it must give up thirty-six audits before it may accept anything at all. What the register records is what the firm holds, and a guideline about counting cannot make audits it is actually performing disappear.
options.misconception: Taking the firm's own register as the count, when the guideline defines what an assignment is and what is left out of it.
options.why: The ceiling is right and the count is the firm's own register rather than the guideline's. The guideline decides what goes into the specified number, and it takes two things out. One person companies and dormant companies are excepted by name, so the ten of them here are not counted at all. And where one firm audits a company's head office and its branches, or several branches of that same company, all of it is regarded as one audit assignment — so the twelve lines for that client are one. The firm is doing every bit of that work and it still holds seventy-five assignments for this purpose, because the guideline counts assignments and not lines in a register.

options.text: The ceiling is sixty and the firm holds seventy-five, so it is over; but the third partner's nine proprietary audits are his own affair and sit outside this calculation entirely, since they are held in the name of a different firm with a different registration number.
options.misconception: Treating a separate proprietary firm as a separate ceiling, when the guideline aggregates every assignment held in relation to the same member.
options.why: The ceiling and the count are right and the last part is the proviso the guideline wrote for exactly this arrangement. Audits a partner takes personally, or under the name of a proprietary firm of his own, are gathered up with everything held by the firms he belongs to, and the whole lot has to fit inside one specified number. A separate registration number is what makes the proviso necessary rather than what defeats it — it exists so that a member cannot double his own ceiling by holding a second firm. So the nine count against him, and the position is worse than the seventy-five suggests.

options.text: The growth partner has the ceiling right at one hundred and twenty but the count of what is held wrong. All four are partners of the firm and each carries his own thirty; what he missed is that the six one person companies and four dormant companies come out and that the head office and eleven branches are one assignment, so the firm holds seventy-five and has forty-five in hand.
options.misconception: Counting every partner of the firm, when the guideline names two kinds of partner who do not count towards the firm's ceiling.
options.why: Both corrections to what is held are right and the ceiling is the half that is wrong. The guideline names two kinds of partner who do not lift a firm's specified number, and this firm has one of each: a partner holding a job elsewhere, full-time or part-time, and a part time practising partner. Two partners count, so the ceiling is sixty. Getting the numerator right and the denominator wrong turns a firm that is already over into a firm with forty-five audits of room, which is the more dangerous of the two errors because it is the one that leads to accepting more.

options.text: The firm is already over the line, not twenty-four short of it. Two of the four partners do not count at all — a chartered accountant in full-time employment elsewhere is not counted for determining the firm's specified number, and a part time practising partner is not taken into account for reckoning the firm's assignments — so the ceiling is 30 audit assignments per partner on two partners, which is sixty. Against that, the ninety-six on the register are not ninety-six: the six one person companies and dormant companies come out because they are excepted by name, and the head office and eleven branches of the one client are regarded as one audit assignment rather than twelve. That leaves seventy-five held against a ceiling of sixty. The nine audits the third partner holds through his proprietary firm make it worse rather than better, because the total for all the firms in relation to him and by him has to stay inside the specified number in the aggregate.
options.why: Every step of the growth partner's arithmetic is a rule he has not read. He counted four partners; the guideline is choosy about which partners raise a firm's ceiling. A partner who is employed elsewhere, whether that job is full-time or part-time, adds nothing to it, and neither does a part time practising partner. The partner working at the sugar company and the partner who comes in three days a week both drop out, so two countable partners at 30 audit assignments per partner give sixty rather than one hundred and twenty. He also counted what the firm holds wrongly, and here the guideline helps him twice. One person companies and dormant companies sit outside the count altogether. And a single client's head office with its branches, however many lines a register spends on them, is regarded as one audit assignment. Ninety-six less the ten excepted companies, less eleven of the twelve lines written for the one client, is seventy-five. Seventy-five against sixty means the firm is already holding more than it may, before it takes on anything new. The third partner's nine proprietary audits do not sit outside the arithmetic either: what he holds personally is added to the firm's tally and measured against the same specified number. In short, the ceiling is 30 audit assignments per partner on the partners who count, one person companies and dormant companies come out of what is held, a head office and its branches are regarded as one audit assignment, and the firm is over.
keywords: one person companies and dormant companies

citation.ref: Chapter VIII, the specified number of audit assignments — the ceiling of 30 audit assignments per partner and the five things that decide the sum: one person companies and dormant companies are outside the count; a head office with its branches, or several branches of the same company, is regarded as one audit assignment; the partner count is taken on the date the assignment is accepted; a partner employed elsewhere full-time or part-time, and a part time practising partner, do not add to the firm's ceiling; and a partner's own audits, held personally or through a proprietary firm, are aggregated with the firm's against the same specified number
