items.stem: On the three fee arrangements alone, what does Lakshmi settle?

options.text: The company secretaries arrangement is permitted and so is the payment to the management consultant, since Clause (3) governs only what a member accepts from a non-member and says nothing about what he chooses to pay out of fees that are already his own. Only the refusal of the Rajahmundry referral fee needs putting right.
options.misconception: Looking only at the clause about accepting a share, and missing that paying one out is a separate clause with its own list.
options.why: The first and third are right and the middle one ignores the clause written for it. Money going out has a rule of its own. Under Clause (2) a member is guilty the moment he parts with a share, commission or brokerage out of his professional fees — whether he pays it himself or lets somebody else route it — unless the recipient is a fellow member, a partner, a retired partner, the legal heir of a partner who has died, a member of another professional body, or somebody holding the prescribed qualifications. That the fee was the firm's own before it was split is the situation the clause describes, not an answer to it. A consultant with no professional qualification of any kind is on none of those lists.

options.text: The payment to the consultant has to stop and the Rajahmundry referral fee may be taken, but the company secretaries arrangement has to go too. The proviso covers a member entering into partnership or sharing his own fees with a member of a prescribed body; it does not stretch to taking a cut of what that other professional earns from his own clients.
options.misconception: Restricting the prescribed-bodies proviso to fees the member pays out, when it is written into the clause about fees he receives.
options.why: Two right and one distinction that the clause does not draw. The proviso sits inside Clause (3) itself — the clause about money a member takes from somebody else's professional earnings — and what it permits is a profit sharing or similar arrangement with a member of a prescribed body, receiving a share, commission or brokerage out of that person's fees included. Receiving is the word the proviso uses. The Council prescribed those bodies precisely so that a chartered accountant who works alongside a company secretary, a cost accountant, an advocate, an architect or an actuary is not forced to keep the two practices at arm's length over money.

options.text: All three arrangements have to go. A member may not take a share of the profits of the professional work earned by an outsider, and a firm of company secretaries are outsiders; he may not pay any share of his own fees to an outsider either, which disposes of the consultant; and the growth partner was right about the third, since a payment made for handing over a client is a commission whoever receives it.
options.misconception: Reading both clauses as a flat ban on money crossing the firm's boundary, without the prescribed-bodies proviso or the position on referral fees.
options.why: The consultant is right and the other two are read without their provisos. Clause (3) does not stop at the outsider: a proviso follows it, opening the clause to members of the bodies the Council has prescribed and to others holding the qualifications Clause (2) refers to, and company secretaries are on that list. Referral fees are settled expressly the other way — one member in practice may charge another for passing a client across. Refusing money the profession permits costs the firm and teaches the partner the wrong rule for next time.

options.text: One of the three is allowed, one is not, and the one he refused should have been taken. Taking a fifth of the company secretaries' fees is permitted: the bar on accepting a share of the profits of the professional work done by an outsider carries a proviso for a member of a prescribed professional body, and the Institute of Company Secretaries of India is one of the bodies the Council has prescribed. Paying the management consultant fifteen per cent of the audit fee is not permitted, because that is a share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of the firm's professional business going to a person who is neither a member of the Institute nor a member of any prescribed body nor a partner, retired partner or legal representative of a deceased partner. And the offer from Rajahmundry was refused for a reason that does not exist: referral fees between one member in practice and another in relation to referring a client are not prohibited at all.
options.why: The growth partner has one rule in his head and it is doing all three jobs badly. There are two clauses here and they point in opposite directions. Clause (3) watches money coming in: a member may not take a slice of the profits of the professional work earned by somebody outside the Institute. Clause (2) watches money going out: out of his own professional fees a member may not hand anyone a share, commission or brokerage unless that person is on a short list — a fellow member, a partner, a retired partner, the legal heir of a partner who has died, or a member of a body the Council has prescribed. Both clauses open the same door, and Regulation 53A says who may walk through it: company secretaries, cost accountants, advocates, architects and actuaries. The Guntur firm are company secretaries, so the incoming share sits inside the proviso and may be taken. The management consultant holds no professional qualification at all, so he stands on none of those lists; a fifteen per cent slice of the audit fee every year is exactly the share, commission or brokerage the clause names, and calling it an introduction rather than a commission changes nothing, because the clause reaches an indirect payment as readily as a direct one. The third arrangement breaches nothing: a member in practice may charge another member in practice referral fees for passing a client across, and by refusing them the firm has given up money it was entitled to. In short, a share of the profits of the professional work done by a prescribed body's member may be taken here because company secretaries are such a body, the payment to the consultant is a barred share, commission or brokerage, and referral fees between members are allowed.

citation.ref: Clause (3) of Part I of the First Schedule — money coming in, where a member takes a share of the profits of the professional work of an outsider — read with its proviso for a prescribed body; Clause (2) of the same Part — money going out, where a member parts with a share, commission or brokerage out of his own professional fees — read with the list of people to whom that may be paid; Regulation 53A, for the bodies the Council has prescribed, being the company secretaries, the cost accountants, the Bar Council, the architects and the actuaries; and the settled position on referral fees passing between two members in practice

items.stem: On the branch, the depot and the struck-out paragraph alone, what does the report say?

options.text: Because the Jaipur branch was audited by another firm, Priya has no duty on it beyond attaching that firm's report; the branch auditor answers for the branch and the company auditor's report is silent on it.
options.misconception: A branch audited by another auditor is outside the company auditor's report.
options.why: Clause (c) has the company auditor state whether the branch report has been sent to him and the manner in which he has dealt with it in preparing his report; the branch report is dealt with, not attached, and the company auditor's report says so.

options.text: The missing depot returns are a limitation on scope, so Priya gives a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements as a whole and drops the separate statements under section 143(3), which are absorbed by the disclaimer.
options.misconception: A modified opinion replaces the statements section 143(3) requires.
options.why: The statements under section 143(3) are required of every company audit report and are not absorbed by the opinion paragraph; the missing returns are stated under the books clause and their effect on the opinion is a separate judgement, which on 22 crore rupees of one line is a qualification, not a disclaimer on the whole.

options.text: Three statements, each required. The report says the Jaipur branch office was audited by another firm, that its report was sent to her and how she dealt with it in preparing her own. On the Surat depot the report states that proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit have not been received from a branch not visited by her, whatever the company calls a place that keeps its own books of stock and sales, and says so under the books clause. And the paragraph on internal financial controls goes back in: the exemption from that clause is for certain private companies, and Luni Ceramics is a public company, so being unlisted takes nothing away.
options.why: Section 143(3) is a list of statements the report shall make, and none of the three can be dropped by a finance head. Clause (c) has the auditor state whether the report on the accounts of any branch office audited under sub-section (8) by a person other than the company's auditor has been sent to him and the manner in which he has dealt with it in preparing his report, which is exactly the Jaipur position and is stated as a fact. Clause (b) has the report state whether proper books of account have been kept and proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit have been received from branches not visited by him; the Surat depot keeps its own books of stock and sales, it was not visited, and no returns came, so the report states that the returns were not received, and the word the company uses for the place does not change the substance of what the clause asks. Clause (i) has the report state whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and the operating effectiveness of such controls, and the chapter's note excludes only a private company that is a one person company or a small company, or whose turnover is below fifty crore rupees with borrowings below twenty-five crore rupees; a public company with 260 crore rupees of revenue is outside every limb of that note, and whether its shares are listed is not the test. In short, the report states the branch office report and how it was dealt with, states that proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit were not received from the depot, and reports on internal financial controls because the exemption does not reach a public company.
keywords: proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit

options.text: The finance head is right on two of the three. A depot is not a branch office, so the returns clause is satisfied by the books at Morbi, and the internal financial controls clause is a listed-company requirement; only the Jaipur branch report needs a statement in the report.
options.misconception: Internal financial controls reporting is a listed-company matter and a depot is outside the branch clause.
options.why: The returns clause asks whether proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit were received from branches not visited, and a place keeping its own books of stock and sales is such a branch whatever it is called; and the exemption from the internal financial controls clause is for certain private companies, not for unlisted ones.

citation.ref: section 143(3)(b) has the report state whether proper books of account as required by law have been kept and proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit have been received from branches not visited by him; (c) whether the report of a branch office audited by another person has been sent to him and the manner in which he has dealt with it; (i) whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements and their operating effectiveness, a clause from which only certain private companies are exempt

items.scenario: Mehta & Rao are the statutory auditors of Luni Ceramics Limited, an unlisted public company at Morbi with a revenue of 260 crore rupees, and Priya Mehta is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters stand between her and the signing of the report. First, the company's Jaipur branch was audited by another firm under the Act and its report reached Priya in May, while the Surat depot, which keeps its own books of stock and sales, sent no returns at all for the year because the finance head says a depot is not a branch; the same finance head has struck the paragraph on internal financial controls out of the draft report on the ground that the company is unlisted and the clause applies only to listed companies. Second, three items sit unanswered in the draft under the matters prescribed by rule: a goods and services tax demand of 9 crore rupees under appeal since 2024 appears nowhere in the financial statements, the unclaimed dividend of 2018 was transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund eleven months after it fell due, and an interim dividend of 6 crore rupees was paid in December 2025 on which the file holds no working of any kind on whether it complied with section 123; the finance head's position is that these are matters for a management representation letter and not for the auditor's report. Third, Priya's report will carry a qualification on the stock at the Surat depot, which she could not verify and which is 22 crore rupees of the 60 crore rupees of inventories; the company secretary has planned that the chairman will summarise the auditor's report at the annual general meeting in September without reading the qualification, and has drafted a reply to a shareholder who asked to inspect the full report saying that the report is available to the board and will be filed with the Registrar in due course. Priya has to settle each of the three before the report is signed.

items.stem: On the three items under the prescribed matters alone, what does Priya do?

options.text: The GST demand and the late transfer are disclosed in the notes at Priya's insistence and the dividend is left to the directors' report; once the notes are corrected the rule 11 matters fall away because there is nothing left to comment on.
options.misconception: Rule 11 matters need a comment only when the financial statements remain wrong.
options.why: Correcting the notes settles what the financial statements say, but the rule asks the auditor to state his views and comments in the report, including on the delay in transfer to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, which was a fact of the year and is not undone by a note, and on the dividend's compliance with section 123, which is the auditor's statement and not the directors'.

options.text: Since the demand of 9 crore rupees is under appeal and the company expects to win, it is not a pending litigation with an impact on financial position, so only the delayed transfer and the dividend call for a comment.
options.misconception: A litigation the company expects to win is not a pending litigation for rule 11.
options.why: The rule asks whether the company has disclosed the impact, if any, of pending litigations on its financial position; an appeal is a pending litigation whatever the company expects of it, and the auditor comments on whether its impact was disclosed, not on whether the company will win.

options.text: The finance head's approach is acceptable. The prescribed matters are answered on management's representation, and the report need only state that management has represented each of them and that nothing has come to the auditor's notice to the contrary.
options.misconception: Every rule 11 matter is reported on the strength of a management representation.
options.why: The representation form belongs to the two funding limbs alone, where the rule itself asks what management has represented; on pending litigations, the Investor Education and Protection Fund and section 123 the rule asks for the auditor's own views and comments, which a representation cannot supply.

options.text: All three go into the auditor's report as her own views and comments, not into a representation letter. She states that the company has not disclosed the impact of pending litigations on its financial position, naming the 9 crore rupees demand under appeal; states that there has been a delay of eleven months in transferring the unclaimed dividend to the Investor Education and Protection Fund; and does her own work on the interim dividend before stating whether it was paid in compliance with section 123, since a representation is not a view.
options.why: Clause (j) of section 143(3) has the report state such other matters as may be prescribed, and rule 11 prescribes them in words that leave the finance head no room: the auditor's report shall also include their views and comments on the listed matters. A management representation letter is evidence the auditor obtains; it is not a view of the auditor and it is not in the report, so the proposal answers a reporting requirement with a filing. On the first matter the rule asks whether the company has disclosed the impact, if any, of pending litigations on its financial position in its financial statement; a 9 crore rupees demand under appeal is a pending litigation, it appears nowhere, and the report says so. On the second the rule asks whether there has been any delay in transferring amounts required to be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund; eleven months is a delay and the report states it, the transfer having been made does not erase the lateness the rule asks about. On the third the rule asks whether the dividend declared or paid during the year is in compliance with section 123, which is a conclusion the auditor reaches from his own procedures on the source of the dividend and the manner of its declaration, and a file that holds no working cannot yet support either answer, so the work is done first and the statement follows. In short, the report carries the auditor's own views and comments on the undisclosed pending litigations, on the delay in transfer to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, and on compliance of the dividend with section 123.

citation.ref: section 143(3)(j) has the report state such other matters as may be prescribed, and rule 11 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 has the report include the auditor's views and comments on whether the company has disclosed the impact of pending litigations on its financial position, whether there has been any delay in transferring amounts required to be transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, and whether the dividend declared or paid during the year is in compliance with section 123

items.scenario: Mehta & Rao are the statutory auditors of Luni Ceramics Limited, an unlisted public company at Morbi with a revenue of 260 crore rupees, and Priya Mehta is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters stand between her and the signing of the report. First, the company's Jaipur branch was audited by another firm under the Act and its report reached Priya in May, while the Surat depot, which keeps its own books of stock and sales, sent no returns at all for the year because the finance head says a depot is not a branch; the same finance head has struck the paragraph on internal financial controls out of the draft report on the ground that the company is unlisted and the clause applies only to listed companies. Second, three items sit unanswered in the draft under the matters prescribed by rule: a goods and services tax demand of 9 crore rupees under appeal since 2024 appears nowhere in the financial statements, the unclaimed dividend of 2018 was transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund eleven months after it fell due, and an interim dividend of 6 crore rupees was paid in December 2025 on which the file holds no working of any kind on whether it complied with section 123; the finance head's position is that these are matters for a management representation letter and not for the auditor's report. Third, Priya's report will carry a qualification on the stock at the Surat depot, which she could not verify and which is 22 crore rupees of the 60 crore rupees of inventories; the company secretary has planned that the chairman will summarise the auditor's report at the annual general meeting in September without reading the qualification, and has drafted a reply to a shareholder who asked to inspect the full report saying that the report is available to the board and will be filed with the Registrar in due course. Priya has to settle each of the three before the report is signed.

items.stem: On the general meeting and the shareholder's request alone, what does Priya tell the company?

options.text: Both plans are contrary to section 145. A qualification on 22 crore rupees of stock she could not verify is a qualification on a matter with an adverse effect on the functioning of the company, and the section requires that such qualifications be read before the company in general meeting; a summary that leaves it out does not do that. The same section makes the report open to inspection by any member of the company, so the shareholder who asked is entitled to inspect it now, and neither the board's possession of it nor a later filing with the Registrar answers the request.
options.why: Section 145 has two limbs after the signing rule, and the company secretary's plan defeats both. The section says that the qualifications, observations or comments on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company mentioned in the auditors' report shall be read before the company in general meeting; a qualification on stock of 22 crore rupees that the auditor could not verify is the plainest case of such a qualification, and the section's word is read, not summarised, so a chairman's summary that omits it leaves the requirement unmet. The section then says those matters shall be open to inspection by any member of the company; the shareholder is a member, the request is for inspection, and a reply that the report is with the board and will be filed later offers neither the inspection nor the timing the section provides, since availability at the Registrar is a different right under a different provision. Priya's part is to tell the company, in writing, that the qualification is to be read before the company in general meeting and that the report is open to inspection by any member, and to be present at the meeting where her report is read. In short, a qualification with an adverse effect on the functioning of the company is read before the company in general meeting and is open to inspection by any member, and a summary and a deferred filing satisfy neither.
keywords: read before the company in general meeting
open to inspection by any member

options.text: Since the report will be filed with the Registrar and become a public document, the shareholder's right is met by the filing, and Priya need only insist that the chairman read the qualification at the meeting.
options.misconception: Filing the report with the Registrar discharges the member's right of inspection.
options.why: Section 145 makes the qualifications open to inspection by any member of the company as a right of the member against the company, and a later public filing is a different matter under a different provision; the request to inspect is met by inspection, and the qualification is read before the company in general meeting as well.

options.text: How the report is presented at the meeting and who may see it are matters of company administration for the board and the secretary, not for the auditor; Priya's duty ends with signing a report that carries the qualification.
options.misconception: What happens to the auditor's report after signing is no concern of the auditor.
options.why: Section 145 itself attaches the reading and inspection requirements to the qualifications in the auditor's report, so they follow from what the auditor signed; the auditor who knows the qualification will not be read before the company in general meeting or opened to inspection by any member does not leave the matter to administration.

options.text: The qualification is on inventories, which is a balance sheet matter and not a financial transaction with an adverse effect on the functioning of the company, so the reading requirement does not reach it; only the inspection request must be met.
options.misconception: Only qualifications about transactions, not balances, have to be read at the meeting.
options.why: The section speaks of qualifications, observations or comments on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company, and a qualification because 22 crore rupees of stock could not be verified is such a matter; it is read before the company in general meeting and open to inspection by any member.

citation.ref: under section 145 the person appointed as auditor signs the auditor's report, and the qualifications, observations or comments on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company mentioned in the auditor's report shall be read before the company in general meeting and shall be open to inspection by any member of the company

items.stem: On the Angul receivable alone, whose responsibility is the Angul work, and must Deshpande & Rao re-perform it?

options.text: The Angul receivables work, including the procedures that missed the insolvency, is the responsibility of Bhattacharya & Sen alone, because it was allocated to them. Deshpande & Rao are entitled to assume that the other joint auditors carried out their part in accordance with the Standards, and it is not necessary for them to review or test that work; re-performing it is not required. The provision now needed is a matter brought to all three firms' notice, and its treatment in the statements and the report is a shared responsibility.
options.why: Responsibility here follows the allocation. A firm handed a unit answers for that unit alone — for getting and weighing the information and explanations it needs there, and for running its procedures properly. Angul and trade receivables went to Bhattacharya & Sen, so a confirmation that stopped short of the customer's insolvency is their execution and their lapse. The module then says what the other firms may take for granted: each of them is entitled to assume that the rest did their share to the Standards on Auditing, and no firm has to go back over another's papers or run tests of its own to find out whether it was done that way. So "so that we are covered" asks for work nobody is obliged to do; it is not necessary, and doing it would move the responsibility nowhere. What all three firms do share, once the receivable is known to every one of them, is the joint and several responsibility for a matter brought to their notice and agreed on, for how the statements present and disclose it, and for the report itself. In short, the work allocated to Bhattacharya & Sen stays theirs, the other firms are entitled to assume it was done to the Standards, and it is not necessary for Deshpande & Rao to do it again.

options.text: All three firms are jointly and severally responsible for the Angul receivable, because joint auditors sign one report and the law does not divide liability by plant; Deshpande & Rao should re-perform the work before signing.
options.misconception: Reads a common report as common responsibility for every allocated area.
options.why: The module's joint and several responsibility is a listed set: work not divided, common planning decisions, matters brought to notice and agreed, statutory compliance, presentation and disclosure, and the report. Work allocated to one joint auditor is that auditor's responsibility only, and the others are entitled to assume it was properly done without reviewing or testing it.

options.text: Nobody is responsible for it as auditors, because the balance was confirmed by the customer and a confirmation is the evidence the Standards ask for on a receivable; the insolvency is a valuation question for management.
options.misconception: Treats a confirmation as the end of the receivables work.
options.why: Proper execution of the audit procedures for an allocated area is the allocated joint auditor's responsibility, and a confirmation that establishes existence does not answer recoverability. The lapse is Bhattacharya & Sen's, not nobody's.

options.text: Bhattacharya & Sen are responsible, but since the fault has come to light Deshpande & Rao must now review the whole Angul file and test the receivables, because the entitlement to assume proper work falls away once one lapse is found.
options.misconception: Invents a trigger that converts one firm's allocated work into everybody's.
options.why: The module states the entitlement and the absence of any duty to review or test without a condition of that kind. What a discovered matter does create is a joint responsibility for its treatment once it is brought to the notice of all the joint auditors and agreed; it does not transfer the allocated work.

citation.ref: SA 299 (Revised) on divided work: a firm answers for the area allocated to it and for running its procedures there properly; the other firms may take it that it did its part to the Standards on Auditing, and none of them has to go back over that firm's work or test it to find out whether it was done that way

items.scenario: Mahanadi Steel Limited, a listed steel maker with plants at Rourkela, Angul and Kalinganagar and revenue of 4,800 crore rupees, is audited for the year ended 31 March 2026 by three joint auditors. The signed work allocation gives Rourkela and treasury to Deshpande & Rao, Angul and trade receivables to Bhattacharya & Sen, and Kalinganagar and inventory to Kulkarni Associates; compliance with the statutes, presentation and disclosure, and the audit report were left undivided. Meera Deshpande is the engagement partner at Deshpande & Rao, and three matters are open a week before the signing date the company has fixed. First, a 30 crore rupee receivable from an Angul customer that entered insolvency in February 2026 carries no provision, and Bhattacharya & Sen's file shows the balance was confirmed but the insolvency was not picked up; the chief financial officer found it after the draft reports circulated, and Meera's senior asks whether Deshpande & Rao must now re-perform the Angul receivables work "so that we are covered". Second, during the treasury work Deshpande & Rao found that a 90 crore rupee loan to a company owned by the promoter's family, booked at Kalinganagar, has been reclassified as an advance to a supplier; Meera told Kulkarni's partner about it on the telephone and treats that as done, and she wants the opinion qualified for the classification, while the other two firms consider an Emphasis of Matter paragraph enough and say that two firms against one settles the common report. Third, Deshpande & Rao's engagement quality control reviewer has not completed his review, Meera has not yet read the file on the loan classification herself, and her manager proposes that she sign on the agreed date on the strength of the manager's review, with the partner's review and the quality control review "to follow within the week".

items.stem: On the Kalinganagar loan alone, has Meera done what SA 299 asks of her, and does two against one settle the report?

options.text: Not yet, and no. A matter one firm meets that falls in another's area goes to every other firm, in writing, before the audit closes, so a telephone call to one of them is not the communication the standard asks for. On the opinion, Meera is not bound by the views of the majority: if the disagreement survives the firms talking their conclusions over, she gives her own opinion in a separate audit report, and each report points at the other under an Other Matter paragraph.
options.why: Two rules answer the two halves. Take coordination first. When a firm, doing its own work, runs into something belonging to another firm's area — something that deserves their attention, or has to be disclosed, or needs talking over or judging by them — that something goes to every other firm, in writing, before the audit closes. A loan to a promoter's company booked at Kalinganagar and relabelled as a supplier advance sits squarely in Kulkarni's area and in the disclosure all three firms answer for. What happened instead was one partner, on the telephone: one firm rather than every firm, spoken rather than written, and Bhattacharya & Sen have heard nothing at all. Now reporting. One report signed by all of them is the ordinary outcome, and the standard provides for the other one beside it: where the firms cannot agree on the opinion, or on anything else the report has to cover, each puts its own view in its own report, the two reports point at each other in an Other Matter paragraph as per SA 706, and Meera is not bound by the views of the majority. Before any of that the firms talk their conclusions over and pass them between themselves, so the disagreement is tested rather than assumed — but if she still lands on a qualification, counting firms settles nothing. In short, the matter goes to every other firm in writing, Meera is not bound by the views of the majority, and a firm that still disagrees signs a separate audit report.
keywords: not bound by the views of the majority

options.text: Yes, and yes. Telling the joint auditor whose area it is discharges the duty of coordination, and joint auditors resolve a difference on the opinion by majority so that the entity receives a single report, which is the purpose of a joint audit.
options.misconception: Imports voting into a standard that provides for separate reports instead.
options.why: The duty runs to every other firm, in writing, before the audit closes — not to the one firm concerned, by telephone. And the standard holds no majority rule: a firm that disagrees is not bound by the views of the majority and puts its differing opinion in a separate audit report, with the two reports pointing at each other.

options.text: Meera has no duty to communicate at all, because the loan sits in Kulkarni's area and each joint auditor is responsible only for the work allocated to them; whether to qualify is therefore Kulkarni's call alone.
options.misconception: Stretches the division of work into a division of the opinion.
options.why: Allocated responsibility limits who performs the work, not who must be told. The module requires a joint auditor who comes across a matter relevant to another's area to communicate it to all the other joint auditors in writing, and the opinion is a matter on which every joint auditor forms and, if necessary, separately expresses their own view.

options.text: Not yet on communication, but on the report Meera must fall in with the other two: the standard requires a common audit report, and a joint auditor who cannot agree with it should withdraw rather than issue a second report.
options.misconception: Reads "common report" as absolute and misses the separate-report provision beside it.
options.why: The common report is the ordinary case, and the exception sits in the very same sentence: firms that cannot agree on the opinion each express their own in a separate audit report. Withdrawal is nowhere in it.

citation.ref: SA 299 (Revised) on coordination and on reporting: a matter one firm meets that falls in another's area goes to every other firm, in writing, before the audit closes; the firms issue one report, but a firm that cannot agree on the opinion, or on anything else the report must cover, gives its own report instead, is not held to what the others think, and the reports point at each other in an Other Matter paragraph as per SA 706

items.stem: On the signing date alone, may Meera sign on the manager's review with her own review and the quality control review to follow?

options.text: No, but only because of the quality control review; the partner may rely on the manager's review of the loan file, since the standard allows review to be performed by a more experienced member of the team.
options.misconception: Takes the team's layered review as a substitute for the partner's own.
options.why: Work of less experienced members being reviewed by more experienced ones is the team's layering; it does not remove the module's requirement that review of audit documentation before issue of the report is the engagement partner's responsibility, and that sufficient appropriate audit evidence supports the conclusions before the report is issued.

options.text: Yes, provided the three joint auditors sign together, because in a joint audit the quality control review by any one of the firms covers the common report.
options.misconception: Lets a joint audit pool one firm's quality control across the others.
options.why: SA 220 attaches to each firm's own engagement and its own partner: it is Deshpande & Rao's reviewer whose review must be complete before Meera dates the report, and the partner's own review of documentation is not transferred to another firm by a joint appointment.

options.text: Yes. The partner's responsibility for quality is discharged through the team, the manager's review is the firm's review, and the quality control review is a firm-level monitoring step that may be completed after the report is dated.
options.misconception: Confuses the engagement quality control review with the firm's monitoring after the fact.
options.why: Direction, supervision, performance and the reading of the documentation before the report goes out are the partner's own, and the standard says in terms that at a listed entity no date goes on the report until the engagement quality control review has finished. That is a condition on dating, not monitoring after the fact.

options.text: No. Direction, supervision and the performance of the engagement are the partner's, and so is reading the audit documentation before the report goes out; a manager's review does not stand in for her own on a judgment as significant as the loan classification. Before she dates the report she has to be satisfied that sufficient appropriate audit evidence sits behind the conclusions drawn, and at a listed company she may put no date on it until the engagement quality control review has finished. The company's chosen date yields to both.
options.why: Engagement performance sits on the partner herself. She directs the engagement, oversees it and performs it to the professional standards and the law that govern it; the report being right for the circumstances is hers to answer for; and reading the audit documentation before the report goes out is hers too, as is being satisfied that sufficient appropriate audit evidence stands behind what the report concludes. A partner who has not read the file on a 90 crore rupee related-party classification cannot say that of her own report, and handing the reading to the manager hands over the work without handing over the answerability. Then the rule that attaches at a listed company: the partner establishes that a quality control reviewer is in place, talks the significant matters through with him, and puts no date on the report until the engagement quality control review has finished. A review "to follow within the week" means a report dated ahead of its own review, which is the one thing that rule shuts out. In short, direction, supervision and review belong to the partner, the report is dated only once sufficient appropriate audit evidence supports it, and never before the engagement quality control review is done.

citation.ref: SA 220 (Revised) on the engagement partner's own job: directing, supervising and performing the engagement, and reading the audit documentation before the report goes out, satisfied that sufficient appropriate audit evidence stands behind what was concluded; and, at a listed entity, no date on the report before the engagement quality control review has finished

items.stem: On the bank's report on the financial statements alone, what does Radhika do?

options.text: Radhika does not sign on the strength of the finance head's papers, and she may engage the chartered accountant at Anand. Clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule makes it misconduct to certify or submit in her name or in the name of the firm a report of an examination of financial statements unless the examination of such statements and the related records has been made by the member or by a partner or an employee in his firm or by another chartered accountant in practice. The company's accounts staff and a consultancy of commerce graduates are none of those, however carefully she reads their schedules, so the firm examines the statements and the related records itself. The Anand unit may be examined by another chartered accountant in practice, which the clause allows, and the report then rests on that examination and her own.
options.why: The clause names four pairs of hands and no others: the member, a partner or an employee in his firm, or another chartered accountant in practice. The chapter says why: the clause restrains a member from subscribing to a report on a financial statement so long as it has not been examined by him or by a partner or an employee of his firm or by another chartered accountant in practice, so that the work entrusted to him has been carried out by the member directly or under his supervision before he renders his report. The client's own accounts staff are the people whose figures are being reported on, and a consultancy of commerce graduates is nobody the clause recognises; reading their working papers is not making the examination, and a firm that is short of staff this month is short of a report this month. The exception the chapter explains is the one the finance head has stumbled on for the wrong reason: the examination may be carried out by another chartered accountant in practice, which is what enables two or more members to accept a joint assignment or a member to carry out the examination with the assistance of another member in practice. So the Anand records may be examined by the Anand member, and the rest by the firm, and the report in the firm's name then stands on examinations the clause accepts. In short, the report may rest only on an examination of the statements and the related records made by the member, a partner or an employee in his firm, or another chartered accountant in practice, and the finance head's examiners are none of these.
keywords: a partner or an employee in his firm

options.text: Radhika signs, but the report states in a paragraph that the examination of the records was carried out by the company's staff and an outside consultancy and that the firm relied on their work, so that the bank is not misled about who did what.
options.misconception: A report may rest on any examiner provided the report discloses who it was.
options.why: The clause has no disclosure exception; a report of an examination made by anybody outside the four permitted hands is misconduct whether or not the report says so, and telling the bank who examined does not turn the consultancy into an employee of the firm.

options.text: Radhika signs after reading the papers. The clause is about the quality of the examination, the finance head's staff and the consultancy have produced complete working papers, and a partner who has read and questioned them has supervised the work in the sense the clause requires.
options.misconception: Reading another examiner's working papers carefully is the same as making the examination.
options.why: The clause turns on who made the examination, not on how good the papers look: it must be made by the member, a partner or an employee in his firm, or another chartered accountant in practice, and reading somebody else's schedules is not making it.

options.text: Radhika cannot engage the Anand member either. The clause requires the examination to be made within her own firm, so every record, including the Anand unit's, must be examined by her, her partner or the firm's employees before the report is signed.
options.misconception: Every part of the examination must be made inside the member's own firm.
options.why: The clause expressly accepts an examination made by another chartered accountant in practice, and the chapter explains that this exception is what allows joint assignments and assistance from another member in practice.

citation.ref: clause (2) of Part I of the Second Schedule: a member in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he certifies or submits in his name or in the name of his firm a report of an examination of financial statements unless the examination of such statements and the related records has been made by him or by a partner or an employee in his firm or by another chartered accountant in practice

items.scenario: Desai & Trivedi are a firm of chartered accountants at Vadodara, and Radhika Desai is the partner in charge of Mahi Agro Processors Private Limited, a client that is seeking a term loan of 40 crore rupees from a bank for a second plant at Anand. Three matters have come to her from the company's finance head, a retired bank manager with a management degree who is not a member of the Institute. First, the bank wants a report from the firm on the company's financial statements for the three years to 31 March 2026, with the stock and receivables examined. The finance head has had the records examined by his own accounts staff and by a consultancy of commerce graduates that he engaged for the purpose, has sent the firm their working papers and schedules, and asks Radhika to certify the report in the firm's name after reading them, since the firm has no staff to spare this month; for the Anand unit's records, which sit at Anand, he suggests that the firm engage a chartered accountant in practice there to examine them. Second, the bank wants a five-year projection of profits. The company's own team has prepared it, Radhika has reviewed the assumptions on prices, yields and interest and found them reasonable, and the loan proposal that the company has printed carries on its cover the words "Projections certified by Desai & Trivedi, Chartered Accountants"; the finance head says the word is deserved because the review was careful, and that the bank is used to seeing it. Third, the finance head proposes to join the firm as a partner from October 2026, bringing with him the loan-syndication work of a dozen companies he knows, and Radhika's friend, an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of Gujarat, has asked at the same time to join the firm as a partner to handle its tax litigation. Radhika's own partner, Nikhil Trivedi, says a partner who brings work is worth more than a rule, and that in any case the advocate belongs to a recognised profession and so does the banker. Radhika has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the five-year projection alone, what does Radhika do?

options.text: The word "certified" comes off the cover before the proposal goes, and the firm's report on the projection says what the projection is. Clause (3) of Part I of the Second Schedule makes it misconduct to permit her name or the firm's name to be used in connection with an estimate of earnings contingent upon future transactions in a manner which may lead to the belief that she vouches for the accuracy of the forecast. The Council's opinion is that a chartered accountant can participate in preparing profit or financial forecasts and can review them, provided the report indicates clearly the sources of information, the basis of the forecasts and the major assumptions made in arriving at them, and so long as she does not vouch for the accuracy. A careful review does not change what a reader takes from "certified"; the test is what the document invites the bank to believe.
options.why: The clause does not forbid a member to work on a forecast. The chapter reproduces the Council's opinion, taken when it finalised the guidance on accountants' reports on profit and financial forecasts: a chartered accountant can participate in the preparation of profit or financial forecasts and can review them, provided he indicates clearly in his report the sources of information, the basis of forecasts and the major assumptions made in arriving at the forecasts, and so long as he does not vouch for the accuracy of the forecasts; the same applies to projections built on hypothetical assumptions about future events and management actions. What the clause punishes is the manner in which the name is used: a manner which may lead to the belief that the member vouches for the accuracy of the forecast. A loan proposal whose cover says the projections are certified by the firm says exactly that to a bank, whatever the assumptions were and however carefully Radhika went through them, because the clause looks at what the document invites the reader to believe and not at the quality of the work behind it. The chapter's own case is a member who issued projection statements for individuals on which a bank lent, and who was held guilty under clause (3) among others. So the firm's report on the projection names the sources of information, the basis and the major assumptions, states that it does not vouch for the outcome, and the cover is corrected. In short, the firm may review the forecast and say so, indicating the sources of information, the basis and the major assumptions, but may not let its name be used in a manner which may lead to the belief that it vouches for the accuracy, and "certified" does exactly that.

options.text: The word stays. Radhika reviewed the assumptions on prices, yields and interest and found them reasonable, so the firm can stand behind the projection, and a certificate that rests on careful work is not the mischief the clause was written for.
options.misconception: Careful work on a forecast entitles the member to certify it.
options.why: The clause turns on the manner in which the name is used and whether it may lead to the belief that the member vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, not on how careful the review was; the Council's opinion permits review only so long as the member does not vouch for the accuracy.

options.text: The word stays because the reader is a bank. A lender's credit department knows that a projection is an estimate, so no belief that the firm vouches for its accuracy can arise, and the clause is aimed at documents put before the public.
options.misconception: A sophisticated reader cures a forecast the firm has called certified.
options.why: The clause asks whether the manner of use may lead to the belief that the member vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, and the chapter's own case of projection statements issued to a bank ended in a finding of misconduct; the reader's expertise is not the test.

options.text: The firm withdraws from the projection altogether. A chartered accountant's name may not be connected with an estimate of future earnings in any form, so Radhika's review is withdrawn and the company sends the projection to the bank without any reference to the firm.
options.misconception: A chartered accountant may not be associated with a forecast or projection at all.
options.why: The Council's opinion is that a member can participate in the preparation of forecasts and can review them, provided the report indicates the sources of information, the basis and the major assumptions and does not vouch for the accuracy; the clause bars a manner of use, not the association.

citation.ref: clause (3) of Part I of the Second Schedule: permitting his name or the name of his firm to be used in connection with an estimate of earnings contingent upon future transactions in a manner which may lead to the belief that he vouches for the accuracy of the forecast; the Council's opinion is that a member can participate in preparing and can review profit or financial forecasts provided he indicates clearly the sources of information, the basis of forecasts and the major assumptions, and does not vouch for their accuracy

items.scenario: Desai & Trivedi are a firm of chartered accountants at Vadodara, and Radhika Desai is the partner in charge of Mahi Agro Processors Private Limited, a client that is seeking a term loan of 40 crore rupees from a bank for a second plant at Anand. Three matters have come to her from the company's finance head, a retired bank manager with a management degree who is not a member of the Institute. First, the bank wants a report from the firm on the company's financial statements for the three years to 31 March 2026, with the stock and receivables examined. The finance head has had the records examined by his own accounts staff and by a consultancy of commerce graduates that he engaged for the purpose, has sent the firm their working papers and schedules, and asks Radhika to certify the report in the firm's name after reading them, since the firm has no staff to spare this month; for the Anand unit's records, which sit at Anand, he suggests that the firm engage a chartered accountant in practice there to examine them. Second, the bank wants a five-year projection of profits. The company's own team has prepared it, Radhika has reviewed the assumptions on prices, yields and interest and found them reasonable, and the loan proposal that the company has printed carries on its cover the words "Projections certified by Desai & Trivedi, Chartered Accountants"; the finance head says the word is deserved because the review was careful, and that the bank is used to seeing it. Third, the finance head proposes to join the firm as a partner from October 2026, bringing with him the loan-syndication work of a dozen companies he knows, and Radhika's friend, an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of Gujarat, has asked at the same time to join the firm as a partner to handle its tax litigation. Radhika's own partner, Nikhil Trivedi, says a partner who brings work is worth more than a rule, and that in any case the advocate belongs to a recognised profession and so does the banker. Radhika has to settle each of the three.

items.stem: On the two proposed partners alone, what does Radhika decide?

options.text: Both may join. Banking and law are recognised professions, the clause was written to keep unqualified people out of a chartered accountant's practice, and a retired branch manager with a management degree and an enrolled advocate are each qualified in their own field.
options.misconception: Any recognised profession qualifies its member for partnership with a chartered accountant.
options.why: The clause admits only a Chartered Accountant in practice or a member of a professional body prescribed by the Council, and Regulation 53B lists company secretaries, cost accountants, advocates, engineers, architects and actuaries; a management degree and a banking career are on no list, and even the advocate waits for the Council's guidelines on multi-disciplinary partnerships.

options.text: The banker cannot be a partner, and the advocate not yet. Clause (4) of Part I of the First Schedule makes it misconduct to enter into partnership, in or outside India, with any person other than a Chartered Accountant in practice or such other person who is a member of another professional body having such qualifications as may be prescribed. A retired bank manager with a management degree is a member of no prescribed body, and the work he brings is no answer to the clause. An advocate enrolled with the Bar Council is on the list in Regulation 53B, with company secretaries, cost accountants, engineers, architects and actuaries; but the Council's note is that members cannot form Multi-Disciplinary partnerships till the regulators of those other professionals also permit partnership with chartered accountants and the Council issues guidelines, so the advocate waits on that.
options.why: The clause is a closed list. A member in practice may enter into partnership with a Chartered Accountant in practice, or with such other person who is a member of any other professional body having such qualifications as may be prescribed, including a resident who but for residence abroad would be entitled to be registered as a member or whose qualifications the Central Government or the Council recognises for the purpose; nobody else, in or outside India. The Council has prescribed the bodies in Regulation 53B: a company secretary who is a member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, a cost accountant who is a member of the Institute of Cost and Works Accountants of India, an advocate who is a member of the Bar Council of India, an engineer who is a member of the Institution of Engineers or holds an engineering degree from a recognised university or institution, an architect who is a member of the Indian Institute of Architects, and an actuary who is a member of the Institute of Actuaries of India. A retired banker with a management degree is on no such list, and Nikhil's point that he brings work is not a point the clause hears; the work of a dozen companies is precisely what a partnership with a non-member would be sharing. The advocate is a member of a prescribed body, and that is where the chapter adds its caution: a chartered accountant in practice is not permitted to enter into partnership with any person other than a Chartered Accountant in practice or such other persons as the Council prescribes, and members cannot form Multi-Disciplinary partnerships till the regulators of those other professionals also permit partnership with chartered accountants and guidelines are issued by the Council. In short, partnership is open only to a Chartered Accountant in practice or a member of a body prescribed in Regulation 53B, the banker is neither, and even a prescribed member waits until Multi-Disciplinary partnerships are permitted on both sides.

options.text: Neither may ever join. A chartered accountant in practice may be in partnership only with other chartered accountants in practice, so the advocate is refused on the same footing as the banker and the firm stays as it is.
options.misconception: Clause (4) allows partnership with chartered accountants in practice and nobody else.
options.why: The clause itself extends to members of other professional bodies having such qualifications as may be prescribed, and Regulation 53B prescribes advocates among others; the advocate is refused for now because of the Council's note on multi-disciplinary partnerships, not because the clause bars him.

options.text: The banker may join and the advocate may not. A partner who brings syndication work and will never sign an audit report is outside the mischief of the clause, while a lawyer in the partnership would put the firm in litigation, which a chartered accountant's firm may not carry on.
options.misconception: A non-member partner who does not sign reports is outside clause (4).
options.why: The clause turns on who the partner is, not on what he signs: a person who is neither a Chartered Accountant in practice nor a member of a prescribed body is barred whatever his role; and an advocate is on the Regulation 53B list, held back only by the Council's note on multi-disciplinary partnerships.

citation.ref: clause (4) of Part I of the First Schedule: entering into partnership, in or outside India, with any person other than a Chartered Accountant in practice or such other person who is a member of any other professional body having such qualifications as may be prescribed; Regulation 53B prescribes company secretaries, cost accountants, advocates, engineers, architects and actuaries, and members cannot form multi-disciplinary partnerships till the regulators of those professionals also permit them and the Council issues guidelines

items.stem: On the two fee arrangements alone, how does Meenakshi answer Vikram?

options.text: Both are in order. Suresh Rao is being paid for bringing business, which is consultancy, and an office allowance is an expense of the firm rather than a share of its fees; the company secretary did half of the work and is paid for that half.
options.misconception: Treating the label on a payment as settling its character, when the Council looks at the substance of the transaction and has already held an office allowance to a non-member to be a share of profits.
options.why: The clause catches any share, commission or brokerage paid directly or indirectly out of the fees or profits of the professional business, and the Council has held that a payment to a non-member labelled office allowance was in substance a share of profits; what the firm writes in its ledger does not decide what the payment is. The company secretary is in order for a different reason, that his body is prescribed under Regulation 53A.

options.text: The 10 per cent to Suresh Rao is professional misconduct under Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule whatever the ledger calls it, and the share with the company secretary is in order. The clause bars paying or allowing any share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of the professional business to anyone other than a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner, a deceased partner's legal representative, or a member of a professional body prescribed by the Council; a garment exporter is none of those, and it is the substance of the transaction that is looked into, not the name entered against it. A company secretary is a member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, a body prescribed under Regulation 53A, so a fee may be shared with him.
options.why: The clause polices the outflow of fees, and it lists exactly who may receive a part of them: a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner, the legal representative of a deceased partner, or a member of another professional body or a person holding a qualification that the Council has prescribed. Suresh Rao is a tax client with no qualification, so the 10 per cent is a share, commission or brokerage in the fees paid to a person outside every category, and the fact that it bought the introduction is the very thing the clause exists to stop. The ledger entry does not rescue it: the Council decided the case of a chartered accountant who gave half of his audit fees to a non-member under the nomenclature of office allowance for years, and held that in substance he had shared his profits, because it is not the nomenclature of a transaction that is material but the substance of the transaction. The company secretary stands on the other side of the same line. The Council has prescribed, in Regulation 53A of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988, the professional bodies whose members a practising member may share fees with, and the Institute of Company Secretaries of India is on that list, as are cost accountants, advocates, architects and actuaries; so sharing the secretarial fee with him is expressly in order. In short, the payment to the exporter is a share, commission or brokerage judged on the substance of the transaction and is misconduct, and the share with the company secretary is permitted under Regulation 53A.

options.text: Both are professional misconduct. Clause (2) permits a share of fees only to a member of the Institute or a partner, so a company secretary is as much outside the clause as a garment exporter, and the firm must recover both payments.
options.misconception: Reading the clause as ending at members and partners, and missing the prescribed professional bodies and qualifications added by the Council under Regulation 53A.
options.why: The clause itself extends to a member of any other professional body or a person with such other qualification as may be prescribed, and the Council has prescribed under Regulation 53A the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, the cost accountants' institute, the Bar Council, the architects' institute and the actuaries' institute, and a list of qualified persons besides; the share with the company secretary is expressly allowed.

options.text: The 10 per cent is in order because it is a one-time payment for a single introduction rather than a continuing arrangement, and the company secretary must be paid a fixed fee rather than a percentage, because a percentage is what the clause forbids.
options.misconception: Inventing a distinction between a one-off commission and a continuing one, and a rule about percentages, neither of which is in the clause; the clause turns on who receives the share, not on how often or in what form.
options.why: The clause is broken by paying or allowing, or agreeing to pay or allow, any share, commission or brokerage to a person outside its list, and it draws no line between a single payment and a continuing one; and it forbids nothing about the form of a payment to a person inside its list, so a company secretary may be paid a share of the fee for the work he did.

citation.ref: Clause (2) of Part I of the First Schedule bars paying or allowing any share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of the professional business to any person other than a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner, the legal representative of a deceased partner, or a member of a professional body or a person with a qualification prescribed by the Council under Regulation 53A; the Council looks at the substance of the transaction, not the name given to it

items.scenario: Iyer & Bhonsle, a firm of two partners at Hyderabad, leaves the firm's own compliance to Meenakshi Iyer, and three things reach her desk in April 2026. First, the firm's largest new audit client of the year came through Suresh Rao, a garment exporter who is himself a tax client of the firm and holds no professional qualification of any kind; Vikram Bhonsle, the other partner, has agreed to pay him 10 per cent of the first year's audit fee from that client, entered in the firm's ledger as an office allowance, and in the same month has agreed to share the fee from a secretarial compliance assignment with a company secretary in whole- time practice who did half of that work. Second, Meenakshi has accepted a seat on the board of Golconda Foods Limited, a listed company the firm has never audited, as an ordinary director holding no executive office, and Vikram became a working partner in his brother's granite export business on 1 April 2026 and filed his application for the Council's permission on 20 April. Third, while Meenakshi was abroad from 6 to 18 April, the firm's audit manager, a chartered accountant of nine years' standing who holds a power of attorney from both partners, signed and issued the audit report of a private company client and a net worth certificate for its bank, and in the same fortnight signed the audit queries on two other audits and the letters forwarding draft observations to their managements. Vikram's view is that a power of attorney and nine years of experience settle the third matter, that the ledger description settles the first, and that a permission applied for is as good as one granted.

items.stem: On the directorship and the granite business alone, where does each partner stand?

options.text: Both need the Council's specific permission before they begin. A directorship is an occupation other than the profession like any other, and Vikram's application of 20 April protects him from that date onward, so only Meenakshi is presently in breach.
options.misconception: Reading the clause without its proviso, and treating an application as if it were the approval, when the module's illustration holds a member guilty for the days between taking up the office and applying.
options.why: The proviso to Clause (11) takes an ordinary directorship out of the clause altogether where the member is not managing director or a whole time director and neither he nor a partner is interested in the company as an auditor, so Meenakshi needs no permission; and an application does not protect anyone, because the clause requires the Council's specific and prior approval, and Vikram was engaged without it from 1 April.

options.text: Neither needs anything. An interest in a family business is within the Council's general permission because it came through the family, and a seat on a board is not an occupation at all, so neither partner has engaged in anything the clause reaches.
options.misconception: Stretching the Council's concession for an inherited and passive family interest to cover a member who is actively working in a relative's business.
options.why: The Council's indulgence for a family business is for an interest that devolved on the member by inheritance, succession or partition, in a business he did not create and is not actively engaged in carrying on; Vikram joined his brother's business as a working partner, which is active engagement in a business concern and needs the specific and prior approval of the Council. Meenakshi is safe, but by the proviso, not because a board seat is nothing.

options.text: Meenakshi may hold the seat only after obtaining the Council's specific permission, because Golconda Foods is a listed company, while Vikram is safe because he applied within thirty days of joining the business, which is the time the Council allows.
options.misconception: Adding a listing test and a grace period that the clause does not contain; the only tests are executive office, audit interest, and approval before the engagement begins.
options.why: The proviso to Clause (11) draws its line at managing director or whole time director and at the firm being interested in the company as an auditor, and says nothing about listing; and there is no thirty-day window anywhere in the clause or the Council's resolutions, the approval has to be specific and prior, and the module holds a member guilty for the nine days between taking office and applying.

options.text: Meenakshi needs no permission, and Vikram is guilty of professional misconduct for the days before he applied. The proviso to Clause (11) does not disentitle a chartered accountant from being a director of a company, not being managing director or a whole time director, unless he or any of his partners is interested in such company as an auditor, and the firm has never audited Golconda Foods. A working partnership in a business is not within the Council's general permission; it needs the specific and prior approval of the Council, so from 1 April to 20 April Vikram was engaged in another business without permission, and an application filed afterwards does not reach back over those days.
options.why: Clause (11) forbids a member in practice to engage in any business or occupation other than the profession of chartered accountant unless permitted by the Council, and its own proviso then carves out one thing: nothing in it disentitles a chartered accountant from being a director of a company, not being managing director or a whole time director, unless he or any of his partners is interested in such company as an auditor. Meenakshi's seat is an ordinary directorship with no executive office at a company the firm has never audited, so she is inside the proviso and needs nobody's leave; that the company is listed adds nothing, because the proviso does not ask. Vikram is outside every permission. The Council's general permission, for which no application is needed, covers a listed set of occupations: employment under chartered accountants in practice, private tutorship, authorship, honorary office in charitable bodies, editorship of professional journals, owning agricultural land and farming it, and the like. A working partnership in a granite export business is none of them; employment or partnership in a business concern sits in the Council's specific resolution, where the specific and prior approval of the Council is required in each case. The module's own illustration is a member who took over as executive chairman of a company on the first of a month and applied on the tenth: he was engaged in another occupation for those days without the Council's permission and was guilty under Clause (11) for them, and Vikram's 1 April to 20 April is the same gap. In short, an ordinary director who is not managing director or a whole time director needs no permission unless the firm is interested in the company as an auditor, and a partnership in a business needs the Council's specific and prior approval before it begins.

citation.ref: Clause (11) of Part I of the First Schedule bars a member in practice from any business or occupation other than the profession unless the Council permits it, with a proviso that nothing disentitles him from being a director of a company not being managing director or a whole time director unless he or any of his partners is interested in such company as an auditor; employment or partnership in a business concern is outside the Council's general permission and needs its specific and prior approval in each case

items.stem: On what the audit manager signed alone, what does Meenakshi conclude?

options.text: The audit report is misconduct but the net worth certificate is not, because the clause names a balance sheet, a profit and loss account, a report and financial statements, and a certificate to a bank is none of those four.
options.misconception: Reading the word report narrowly as the audit report alone, when the module reads it as any expression of a professional opinion, and holds a certificate signed by a member who is not a partner to be within the clause.
options.why: A report for the purposes of the clause is any document arising out of a professional assignment whose subject matter is the expression of a professional opinion, whether financial or non-financial, and a certificate of net worth is exactly that; the module's illustration of an assistant chartered accountant signing a stock certificate for a bank on the absent member's instruction ends in misconduct under Clause (12).

options.text: Nothing is misconduct. The manager is a chartered accountant, so section 26 of the Act is satisfied, and a power of attorney from both partners makes his signature the firm's own for every document on the list.
options.misconception: Stopping at section 26's requirement that the signatory be a member, and missing the clause's second limb that the signatory must be a partner; authority does not travel by power of attorney.
options.why: Section 26 is the floor, not the whole rule: Clause (12) adds a second limb that bars a member not being his partner from signing a balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements for the firm, and the module's illustration of a power of attorney given to an employee chartered accountant ends in a finding of misconduct under Clause (12) and under the Second Schedule for section 26 as well.

options.text: The audit report and the net worth certificate are professional misconduct under Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule, and the rest is not. A chartered accountant in practice may not allow a person not being a member of the Institute in practice, or a member not being his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements; the manager is a member but not a partner, and the power of attorney changes nothing, because the clause reaches a member who is not a partner whatever authority he holds, and section 26 of the Act compounds it. Audit queries and letters forwarding draft observations are routine documents on which no professional opinion is expressed, and the Council has said their signing may be delegated.
options.why: Clause (12) has two limbs and the second is the one that catches this manager. The first limb bars a person who is not a member of the Institute in practice from signing; the second bars a member not being his partner, so a chartered accountant employed by the firm, however senior and however long in the profession, may not sign a balance sheet, a profit and loss account, a report or financial statements on the firm's behalf. A report here means one arising out of a professional assignment and expressing a professional opinion, whether financial or non-financial, so the net worth certificate for the bank is inside the clause exactly as the audit report is; the module's own illustration is a member abroad who directed his assistant, also a chartered accountant, to sign and issue a stock certificate to a bank, and he was guilty. A power of attorney is no answer: the module's other illustration is a practising member who gave power of attorney to an employee chartered accountant to sign reports and financial statements, and he was guilty under Clause (12) and also under Clause (1) of Part II of the Second Schedule for contravening section 26, which says that no person other than a member shall sign any document on behalf of a chartered accountant in practice or a firm in his or its professional capacity. What the clause leaves alone is the paperwork of an audit that carries no opinion: the Council has clarified that the power to sign routine documents on which a professional opinion or authentication is not required may be delegated, and its list begins with the issue of audit queries during the course of audit and includes letters forwarding draft observations or financial statements, so the manager's second fortnight of signing is in order. The Council adds that where signing is delegated, the fact that a document was not signed by a chartered accountant is no defence to the firm in an enquiry. In short, a member not being his partner may not sign a report or a certificate for the firm and a power of attorney does not change that, while audit queries and forwarding letters are routine documents whose signing may be delegated.

options.text: Everything the manager signed is misconduct, the audit queries and the forwarding letters included, because nothing may leave a firm of chartered accountants in its professional capacity over a signature other than a partner's.
options.misconception: Reading Clause (12) as covering every document of the firm, when the Council has listed the routine documents whose signing may be delegated and audit queries are the first of them.
options.why: The Council has clarified that the power to sign routine documents on which a professional opinion or authentication is not required may be delegated without attracting Clause (12), and its list names the issue of audit queries during the course of audit and letters forwarding draft observations or financial statements; the clause is about documents that carry an opinion outward, not about correspondence.

citation.ref: Clause (12) of Part I of the First Schedule bars a member in practice from allowing a person not being a member of the Institute in practice, or a member not being his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements, read with section 26 of the Act; a report means one expressing a professional opinion, financial or non-financial; the Council has listed the routine documents on which no opinion is expressed whose signing may be delegated
