items.stem: On the turnover alone, was the company required to have an internal auditor for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Yes. A private company is covered when its turnover in the preceding financial year is two hundred crore rupees or more, and the 236 crore rupees of the year ended 31 March 2025 is the preceding year for this audit; the borrowings limit is a separate, alternative test. The company had six months from the applicability commencing to comply.
options.why: Rule 13 lists two tests for a private company, either of which brings it in: turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more during the preceding financial year, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions exceeding one hundred crore rupees at any point during the preceding financial year. For the year ended 31 March 2026 the preceding financial year is the one ended 31 March 2025, and its turnover of 236 crore rupees meets the first test whatever the borrowings were. The rules add that an existing company that becomes covered complies with the requirement within six months of the applicability commencing, so the company should have had an internal auditor well before the year end.

options.text: No. The managing director is right that a private company is covered only through its bank borrowings, and the turnover test in rule 13 applies to unlisted public companies.
options.misconception: Carries the private company's exemption from two of the four public-company tests over to all of them.
options.why: Rule 13 gives private companies two tests of their own, turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more and bank borrowings exceeding one hundred crore rupees, either being enough. What a private company is spared is the paid-up capital and deposits tests, which apply only to unlisted public companies.

options.text: Not yet. Turnover is measured over the year being audited, so the 251 crore rupees of the year ended 31 March 2026 brings the company in only from the year that follows.
options.misconception: Reads the test as applying to the current year's figures.
options.why: Every test in rule 13 is stated for the preceding financial year, not the year under audit. The preceding year for this audit is the one ended 31 March 2025, and its turnover was 236 crore rupees; the requirement had already attached, and the six months allowed to comply ran from then.

options.text: No, because the tests are cumulative: a private company must exceed both the turnover figure and the borrowings figure, and this one fails the borrowings limb.
options.misconception: Reads the rule's "or" as "and".
options.why: The tests are alternatives joined by "or", and the module's own case study brings a private company in on turnover alone with borrowings far below the limit. Meeting the turnover test in the preceding year is sufficient on its own.

citation.ref: section 138 read with rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 — every private company having turnover of two hundred crore rupees or more, or bank or public financial institution borrowings exceeding one hundred crore rupees at any point, during the preceding financial year; an existing company that becomes covered complies within six months of the applicability commencing

items.scenario: Prithvi Packaging Private Limited makes corrugated boxes at two plants near Nashik. Its paid-up share capital is 8 crore rupees, its borrowings from banks never exceeded 60 crore rupees in any year, and it has never accepted deposits. Its turnover was 172 crore rupees in the year ended 31 March 2024, 236 crore rupees in the year ended 31 March 2025, and 251 crore rupees in the year ended 31 March 2026, and it has never had an internal auditor. Verma & Goel are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026, and the engagement partner has three matters in front of him. First, when the audit senior raised internal audit, the managing director said that "internal audit is for public companies, and for private ones only when bank loans cross a hundred crore, and ours are nowhere near". Second, to close the point, the board in February 2026 named the company's own finance manager, a chartered accountant who left practice six years ago and has been an employee since, as internal auditor; the audit senior objects that an internal auditor must be a chartered accountant in practice and cannot be an employee of the company. Third, the firm is short of staff for the year-end count, and the partner plans to have the finance manager's two-person internal audit team do three things for the statutory audit: attend and test-count the box stock at both plants, assess the risk of material misstatement in revenue for the audit plan, and evaluate the provision for slow-moving stock, which is the largest estimate in the accounts.

items.stem: On the finance manager alone, is the audit senior's objection to the appointment right?

options.text: Partly. An employee may be internal auditor, but only a chartered accountant may hold the post, so a cost accountant or any other professional would have been ineligible.
options.misconception: Narrows the eligible professions to chartered accountants only.
options.why: The section names chartered accountants and cost accountants alike, and then adds such other professional as may be decided by the Board. The employee point is right and the qualification point is wrong.

options.text: Yes on both counts. The internal auditor must hold a certificate of practice, and an employee cannot audit the company that pays him.
options.misconception: Imports the statutory auditor's independence rules into an appointment the Act deliberately leaves open to employees.
options.why: Section 138 says the opposite on both points: a chartered accountant or cost accountant whether engaged in practice or not, and the internal auditor may or may not be an employee. In-house internal audit departments are the ordinary case the section contemplates.

options.text: Yes, because a person who has left practice for more than five years has lost the eligibility that section 138 attaches to being a chartered accountant.
options.misconception: Invents a currency-of-practice condition the section does not contain.
options.why: Nothing in section 138 turns on years since leaving practice; the words are "whether engaged in the practice or not". A chartered accountant who has been an employee for six years is as eligible as one who is in practice.

options.text: No. Section 138 allows a chartered accountant or a cost accountant whether in practice or not, or such other professional as the Board decides, and the internal auditor may or may not be an employee of the company; a chartered accountant in the company's employment is eligible.
options.why: The module states section 138 in those terms: the internal auditor shall either be a chartered accountant or a cost accountant, whether engaged in practice or not, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board, and the internal auditor may or may not be an employee of the company. Both limbs of the senior's objection, that the appointee must be in practice and cannot be an employee, are wrong. Whether an employee who runs finance can be objective about his own department is a different question, and one the statutory auditor weighs under SA 610 before relying on his work, not a bar on the appointment itself.
keywords: may or may not be an employee

citation.ref: section 138 — the internal auditor shall be a chartered accountant or a cost accountant, whether engaged in practice or not, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board; the internal auditor may or may not be an employee of the company

items.stem: On the partner's plan alone, which of the three tasks may the internal auditors be given as direct assistance?

options.text: The test-counting and the risk assessment, but not the provision; risk assessment is planning rather than evidence, so the judgement rule does not reach it.
options.misconception: Excludes planning judgements from the significant-judgement rule.
options.why: Assessing the risks of material misstatement is the first item in the module's list of significant judgements that the external auditor must make himself, precisely because the whole audit plan rests on it. It cannot be handed to the internal auditors any more than the estimate can.

options.text: None of them. Internal auditors employed by the company can never provide direct assistance to the statutory auditor, whatever the task.
options.misconception: Reads the limits on direct assistance as a ban on it.
options.why: SA 610 (Revised) permits direct assistance, and sets out how to decide its nature and extent: the amount of judgement involved, the assessed risk of material misstatement, and the threats to the internal auditors' objectivity and their competence. A test-count under the external auditor's direction and review is within what may be assigned.

options.text: All three, provided the partner reviews the internal auditors' working papers and the firm's own staff re-perform a sample of each task.
options.misconception: Treats supervision as a substitute for the external auditor making the significant judgements himself.
options.why: Review and re-performance do not open the door that SA 610 closes. The prohibition on using internal auditors for procedures that involve significant judgements, such as assessing the risks of material misstatement and evaluating significant accounting estimates, is absolute, because those judgements are the external auditor's own.

options.text: Only the test-counting, and only after the partner has evaluated threats to the internal auditors' objectivity and their competence and obtained the written agreements. Assessing the risk of material misstatement and evaluating the slow-moving stock provision are significant judgements that stay with the external auditor, who has sole responsibility for the opinion.
options.why: SA 610 does not let the external auditor use internal auditors for direct assistance on procedures that involve making significant judgements in the audit, and the module's list of those judgements includes assessing the risks of material misstatement and evaluating significant accounting estimates; the reason given is that the external auditor has sole responsibility for the opinion expressed and so must make those judgements himself. A routine test-count is the kind of work that may be assigned, but only after the external auditor has evaluated the existence and significance of threats to the internal auditors' objectivity and their level of competence, and with written agreements from the entity and the internal auditors, all of which go into the audit documentation along with who reviewed the work.

citation.ref: the external auditor shall not use internal auditors to provide direct assistance on procedures that involve making significant judgements in the audit, which include assessing the risks of material misstatement and evaluating significant accounting estimates, because the external auditor has sole responsibility for the opinion; evaluation of threats to objectivity and competence, and written agreements, before any direct assistance

items.stem: On the payroll alone, what does Kavita require of the plan?

options.text: The controls testing was the wrong choice. On a fully automated payroll the auditor cannot rely on controls at all and should have planned a full substantive audit of the 62 crore rupees from the start, so the plan is replaced rather than added to.
options.misconception: Automated processing means controls cannot be relied on and only substantive work counts.
options.why: A highly automated process is the case the chapter gives for the opposite conclusion, that substantive procedures alone may not be sufficient and controls must be tested; the tests done here support reliance, and the fault in the plan is only the missing substantive floor, not the reliance.

options.text: Substantive procedures on payroll go back into the plan. The strong automated controls, tested and found clean, let the firm rely on them and reduce the substantive work on the 62 crore rupees, but the standard requires substantive procedures for each material class of transactions irrespective of the assessed risks, so a material balance is never left to tests of controls alone; the senior scales the substantive procedures down, not to nothing.
options.why: The senior has confused reducing substantive work with removing it. SA 330 lets the auditor rely on the operating effectiveness of controls when he has tested them, and the cleaner the tests the more the substantive procedures can be scaled back in nature, timing and extent; that is the reward for the control testing done here, and it is a real one. But the same standard then says that irrespective of the assessed risks of material misstatement the auditor shall design and perform substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance and disclosure. Payroll at 62 crore rupees is a material class of transactions, and the assessed risk, however low the control tests have made it, is what the floor is written to be irrespective of. The reason is the one the chapter gives for control risk itself: every system of internal control has inherent limitations, and evidence about a control operating is not evidence about the amounts it processed. So the plan keeps the reliance and adds a reduced set of substantive procedures on payroll, such as an analytical procedure on cost against headcount and rate and a test of details on a small sample of the year's payments. In short, substantive procedures are performed on payroll because they are required for each material class of transactions irrespective of the assessed risks, and excellent controls reduce them without removing them.

options.text: The senior's plan stands. Where the automated controls and the change controls around them have been tested without deviation, the control tests are themselves sufficient appropriate evidence on the payroll balance and substantive procedures would only duplicate them.
options.misconception: Excellent controls make substantive procedures unnecessary on a material balance.
options.why: Tests of controls give evidence that a control operated, not evidence about the amounts it processed, and the standard requires substantive procedures for each material class of transactions irrespective of the assessed risks; clean control tests reduce the substantive work and cannot replace it.

options.text: Because payroll is material and no substantive procedures have been done, the position is a limitation on scope, and Kavita records that the payroll balance will have to be qualified in the report unless management supplies further evidence.
options.misconception: A gap in the audit plan is a scope limitation to be reported rather than corrected.
options.why: Nothing has been refused or lost; the audit is at the planning stage and the auditor designs the substantive procedures the standard requires and performs them, and a modified opinion answers an inability to obtain evidence, not a plan that has not yet been carried out.

citation.ref: irrespective of the assessed risks of material misstatement, the auditor shall design and perform substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance, and disclosure; tests of controls are performed where the auditor intends to rely on their operating effectiveness, and the more persuasive the evidence needed the greater the reliance placed on a control

items.scenario: Desai & Mathur are the statutory auditors of Sabarmati Textiles Limited, an unlisted public company at Ahmedabad with a revenue of 420 crore rupees, and Kavita Desai is the engagement partner for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters come out of the planning file and the interim work. First, the company's payroll of 62 crore rupees runs entirely on an enterprise resource planning system, with attendance captured from biometric devices, rates locked by the human resources head, and every month's payroll computed and posted without manual intervention; the firm tested the automated controls and the change controls around them and found no deviation, and the audit senior has planned no substantive procedures on payroll at all, on the ground that the controls are excellent and any further work would be a waste of the client's fee. Second, in July 2025 the company began selling finished garments through a large online marketplace, which now carries 48 crore rupees of the year's revenue, on terms allowing the customer to return the garment within thirty days, with the marketplace computing and remitting a net settlement after returns, commission and promotional deductions; in planning, Kavita identified revenue on these sales as a significant risk, and the senior has planned the same sales cut-off and invoice vouching as for the company's dealer sales, with no work on the company's own process for estimating returns or reconciling the marketplace settlement statements. Third, the tests of controls over purchase approvals found six deviations in the forty purchase orders examined, each an order above the approval limit signed by a junior officer during the three months from October 2025 when the purchase head had resigned and the post lay vacant; the senior proposes to keep the preliminary assessment of control risk as low and to keep the substantive procedures on purchases at the reduced level planned on it, because the deviations are explained by the vacancy and the post has since been filled. Kavita has to decide what the file needs on each of the three matters before the final audit begins.

items.stem: On the marketplace revenue alone, what does Kavita require of the plan?

options.text: The plan for this revenue is rewritten. A significant risk is one requiring special audit consideration, so the standard procedures used for dealer sales do not answer it; the firm first obtains an understanding of the company's related controls over the returns estimate and the settlement reconciliation, and then designs procedures that directly address the risk, such as testing the returns estimate against actual returns after the year end and reconciling the marketplace statements to recorded revenue for the 48 crore rupees.
options.why: Identifying a significant risk in planning is a commitment, not a label. The chapter lists among the auditor's planning tasks identifying the significant risks that require special audit consideration and those risks for which substantive procedures alone are not sufficient, and says that the planned audit procedures should directly address these risks. Marketplace sales are new this year, carry a thirty-day return right that makes revenue depend on an estimate, and are settled net by a third party whose deductions the company does not compute, so Kavita was right to name the risk; what the senior has done is plan for it exactly as for the risk-free dealer sales, which is the one response the standard rules out. The first step the standard requires for a significant risk is an understanding of the entity's related controls, here the process by which the company estimates returns and the reconciliation of the marketplace settlement statements, because that understanding decides whether controls can be relied on and what the substantive procedures must do. The procedures then follow the risk rather than the standard programme: the estimate is tested against returns actually received after the year end, the settlement statements are agreed to recorded revenue and the deductions examined, and an element of unpredictability is built in. In short, a significant risk requires special audit consideration, an understanding of the related controls over it, and planned procedures that directly address it, none of which the dealer-sales programme provides.

options.text: Since the marketplace computes the settlement, the evidence lies with the marketplace; Kavita obtains a report from the marketplace's own auditor on its settlement controls and treats that as the response to the significant risk.
options.misconception: A third party's report substitutes for the auditor's own response to a significant risk.
options.why: The marketplace is a customer channel, not a service organisation processing the company's transactions on its behalf, and even a report on a service organisation would not address the company's own returns estimate; the response is the firm's own understanding of the related controls and procedures that directly address the risk.

options.text: The senior's plan is adequate. Sales cut-off and invoice vouching are the recognised substantive procedures for revenue, and the marketplace channel is revenue like any other; the significant risk label affects the sample size, not the kind of procedure.
options.misconception: A significant risk changes how much of the standard programme is done, not what is done.
options.why: A significant risk is one requiring special audit consideration and the planned procedures must directly address it; the risk here lies in the returns estimate and the net settlement, which cut-off and vouching of invoices do not touch at any sample size.

options.text: Because the risk is significant, the firm does not rely on controls at all and goes straight to substantive testing of every marketplace invoice, so the missing work on the company's returns process and settlement reconciliation is no defect in the plan.
options.misconception: A significant risk is answered by testing more invoices and controls can be ignored.
options.why: For a significant risk the standard requires the auditor to obtain an understanding of the related controls before deciding the response, and the returns estimate is not tested by vouching invoices however many are examined; skipping the understanding leaves the procedures unable to directly address the risk.

citation.ref: the auditor identifies the significant risks that require special audit consideration and those risks for which substantive procedures alone are not sufficient, considers the nature of the internal control in place and its effectiveness in mitigating the risk, and plans audit procedures that directly address those risks

items.stem: On the purchase approvals alone, what does Kavita require of the plan?

options.text: The assessment of control risk on purchases is revised upward and the substantive procedures on purchases are enlarged to match. Six deviations in forty mean the preliminary assessment of control risk is not supported for the year, whatever their cause; a higher control risk raises the risk of material misstatement, which lowers the detection risk the firm may accept, so the nature, timing and extent of the planned substantive procedures on purchases change to obtain more persuasive evidence, covering in particular the three months the post was vacant.
options.why: The senior has treated an explanation as a cure. The chapter is direct: where deviations are found the auditor makes specific inquiries, and where on the basis of them he concludes that the preliminary assessment of control risk is not supported, he amends that assessment unless other tests of control support it, and having revised the assessed level of control risk he modifies the nature, timing and extent of his planned substantive procedures. The vacancy explains why the control failed; it does not mean the control operated, and for three months of the year orders above the limit went through without the approval the firm planned to rely on. Audit risk is inherent risk multiplied by control risk multiplied by detection risk, and the auditor controls only the last: with control risk now higher, the risk of material misstatement on purchases is higher, the detection risk the firm may accept is lower, and SA 330 requires more persuasive audit evidence the higher the assessed risk. So the substantive procedures on purchases go up from the reduced level, in nature as well as extent, with the vacant months tested directly, and the chapter adds that the tests of control themselves should cover such a period of change. In short, the preliminary assessment of control risk is not supported, it is revised, and the nature, timing and extent of the substantive procedures on purchases are modified to obtain more persuasive evidence.

options.text: Six deviations in forty show that the purchase approval control cannot be relied on for the year, so the firm abandons the control approach entirely and audits purchases by substantive procedures alone at the full level, without further inquiry into the cause.
options.misconception: Any deviation in a test of controls means reliance on the control is lost for the whole year.
options.why: The chapter has the auditor make specific inquiries into deviations first, and the answer here is that the control operated for nine months and failed for three; the response is to revise the assessment and modify the nature, timing and extent of the substantive procedures to the period and extent of the failure, not to discard evidence the tests of control legitimately provide for the rest of the year.

options.text: Kavita extends the tests of controls to another forty purchase orders drawn from the months after the post was filled; if those are clean, the control risk assessment is confirmed and the planned substantive procedures on purchases need no change.
options.misconception: Further control tests on a later period can restore reliance for a period in which the control failed.
options.why: Clean results from the months after the vacancy say nothing about the three months in which the control did not operate; the assessment is not supported for those months however the later sample turns out, and the substantive procedures on purchases must be modified to obtain more persuasive evidence for that period.

options.text: The senior's proposal stands. The deviations all fall in a three-month vacancy that has ended and is explained, so they are an anomaly rather than a control failure, and the preliminary assessment of control risk and the reduced substantive procedures built on it remain appropriate.
options.misconception: Deviations with a known cause do not count against the control risk assessment.
options.why: An explained deviation is still a deviation; the control did not operate for a quarter of the year, so the preliminary assessment of control risk is not supported for that year and must be revised, with the nature, timing and extent of substantive procedures modified to obtain more persuasive evidence for the period affected.

citation.ref: where deviations found in tests of control lead the auditor to conclude that the preliminary assessment of control risk is not supported, he amends that assessment and modifies the nature, timing and extent of the planned substantive procedures, obtaining more persuasive audit evidence the higher the assessed risk

items.stem: On the income pattern alone, what must the auditors' report to the board say?

options.text: That the company must surrender its certificate before the accounts are signed, and the audit report on the financial statements must be qualified until it does.
options.misconception: Turns a regulatory statement to the board into a condition on the audit opinion.
options.why: The auditor's duty is to state in the report to the board whether the company is entitled to continue to hold the certificate, with reasons where the statement is unfavourable, and to report the matter to the Reserve Bank; what the company then does with its registration is between it and the Reserve Bank, and an unfavourable statement on this point does not by itself modify the opinion on the financial statements.

options.text: That the company remains entitled to hold its certificate, because the assets test is the one that decides principal business and 58 per cent passes it comfortably.
options.misconception: Takes the assets limb alone as the principal business test.
options.why: The module states both criteria together and says a company qualifies when it fulfils both. Passing the assets test while income from financial assets is 44 per cent of gross income is not fulfilling both, so the statement on entitlement to continue is unfavourable and the reasons must be given.

options.text: That the company is not entitled to continue to hold its certificate of registration on the principal business criteria as at 31 March 2026, with reasons: both tests must be met, and income from financial assets at 44 per cent of gross income fails the income test even though the assets test is passed.
options.why: The module's principal business criteria have two limbs, financial assets more than 50 per cent of total assets net of intangibles and the income test, income from financial assets more than 50 per cent of gross income, and a company which fulfils both tests qualifies as an NBFC. The auditor's report to the board of every NBFC must include a statement on whether a company holding a certificate of registration is entitled to continue to hold it in terms of the principal business criteria as on 31 March of the year, and where the statement is unfavourable the report states the reasons. A certificate granted in 2019 does not answer a question the Directions ask afresh at every year end.

options.text: Nothing on this point. Registration was examined by the Reserve Bank when the certificate was granted, and the auditor's statement on registration is required only of a company that holds no certificate.
options.misconception: Treats the certificate as settling the matter once, when the entitlement to hold it is tested every year end.
options.why: The report to the board has two registration statements, not one: whether a company doing non-banking financial business has obtained a certificate, and, for a company that holds one, whether it is entitled to continue to hold it on the principal business criteria as at 31 March. The second is the one this company fails.

citation.ref: NBFC principal business criteria — financial assets more than 50 per cent of total assets net of intangibles and income from financial assets more than 50 per cent of gross income, both to be fulfilled; the auditor's report to the board states whether a company holding a certificate of registration is entitled to continue to hold it in terms of those criteria as on 31 March

items.scenario: Sahyadri Finvest Limited holds a certificate of registration from the Reserve Bank as a non-deposit-taking investment and credit company, granted in 2019, and its total assets at 31 March 2026 are 320 crore rupees. Mathur & Bhatt are its statutory auditors, and the engagement partner has three notes from the field work. First, the company has grown a warehousing and logistics arm alongside its lending: by the audited figures for the year, financial assets are 58 per cent of total assets after netting off intangibles, but income from financial assets is 44 per cent of gross income because warehouse rents and freight fees now earn more than interest does. The chief financial officer says the certificate obtained in 2019 "settled the registration question for good". Second, a demand loan of 9 crore rupees was called in November 2024 and nothing has been received since; it was shown as a non-performing asset at 31 March 2025, but this year the company has moved it back to standard because the borrower "has promised to settle by Diwali", and has credited 1.1 crore rupees of interest on it to profit and loss for the year. Third, the board passed its usual resolution in April 2025 that the company would not accept public deposits, but in December 2025 the company accepted 3 crore rupees of public deposits from forty members of the public, repayable in eighteen months. The partner intends to mention the deposits in the report to the board and consider the matter closed there.

items.stem: On the called loan alone, what should the auditors require?

options.text: Leave the classification to management's judgement of the borrower, since asset classification in an NBFC is a matter of the company's credit policy rather than the auditor's, and confine the audit to checking that the interest arithmetic is right.
options.misconception: Treats NPA classification as a management policy choice rather than a prescribed rule the auditor verifies.
options.why: The module makes it the auditor's task to assess whether the NBFC has complied with the prudential norms and in particular to verify that advances have been properly classified as standard, sub-standard, doubtful or loss with proper provision under the Directions. The classification is prescribed, and the arithmetic of interest that should never have been accrued is beside the point.

options.text: Accept the standard classification, because a demand loan has no fixed instalments and so cannot be overdue, but ask for a provision against the interest in case the promise fails.
options.misconception: Believes a demand loan cannot become an NPA.
options.why: A demand or call loan is expressly one of the Directions' categories of non-performing asset once it has remained overdue from the date of demand, and this one was called in November 2024 and has paid nothing since. Its classification is settled by the Directions, not by whether it has instalments, and income on it is recognised on realisation only.

options.text: Keep the loan as a non-performing asset but leave the interest in profit and loss, since the borrower remains liable for it and the company has a legal right to receive it.
options.misconception: Separates the NPA classification from the income recognition rule that follows from it.
options.why: A legal right to interest is what accrual would rest on, and the Directions take exactly that route away for non-performing assets: unrealised income on them is not taken to profit and loss on an accrual basis and is accounted for on realisation only. The classification and the income treatment go together.

options.text: The loan stays a non-performing asset: an account that was an NPA last year continues as one unless it has become regular under the Directions, and a promise is not a payment. The 1.1 crore rupees of accrued interest comes out of profit and loss, because income on an NPA is recognised on realisation only.
options.why: The module's audit procedures on prudential norms say the auditor checks that all accounts classified as NPAs in the previous year continue to be shown as such, and where one is not, specifically examines it to see whether it has become regular and can be treated as performing under the Directions; a called demand loan on which nothing has been received for seventeen months continues as an NPA and has not become regular. They also say unrealised income on NPAs is not taken to profit and loss on an accrual basis and is accounted for on realisation only, so the interest credited must be reversed.

citation.ref: NBFC prudential norms — an account classified as NPA in the previous year continues to be shown as such unless the auditor specifically examines it and finds it has become regular under the Directions; unrealised income on NPAs is not taken to profit and loss on accrual and is accounted for on realisation only

Mathur & Bhatt are its statutory auditors, and the engagement partner has three notes from the field work. First, the company has grown a warehousing and logistics arm alongside its lending: by the audited figures for the year, financial assets are 58 per cent of total assets after netting off intangibles, but income from financial assets is 44 per cent of gross income because warehouse rents and freight fees now earn more than interest does. Third, the board passed its usual resolution in April 2025 that the company would not accept public deposits, but in December 2025 the company accepted 3 crore rupees of public deposits from forty members of the public, repayable in eighteen months. items.stem: On the deposits alone, is the partner right that the report to the board closes the matter?

options.text: No. Because the deposits were taken in breach of the board's own resolution, the auditors must qualify the opinion on the financial statements, and that qualification is the report the Reserve Bank receives.
options.misconception: Uses the audit opinion as the channel to the regulator, when the Directions prescribe a separate report.
options.why: Whether the financial statements are misstated is a separate question from the regulatory statements, and the Reserve Bank is reached by the exception report the Directions require, not by the audit opinion. The route is the unfavourable statement with reasons in the report to the board, and then the exception report to the regional office.

options.text: No. The statement on whether the company accepted public deposits is unfavourable and the report to the board must give the reasons, and the auditors are then obliged to send an exception report to the Reserve Bank's regional office of the Department of Non-Banking Supervision, containing only the contraventions.
options.why: For an NBFC not accepting public deposits, the Directions require the report to the board to state whether the board has passed a resolution for non-acceptance and whether the company has accepted any public deposits during the year; where a statement is unfavourable the report states the reasons. Where any statement is unfavourable or qualified, or the auditor thinks the company has not complied with the Acceptance of Public Deposits Directions, it is the auditor's obligation to make an exception report of those matters to the regional office of the Department of Non-Banking Supervision under whose jurisdiction the registered office lies, and that report contains only the contraventions, with no statement about compliance.

options.text: Yes. The auditors report to the company, and it is the company's own duty to tell the Reserve Bank what it has done; an auditor who wrote to the regulator would breach the confidentiality owed to the client.
options.misconception: Reads the report to the board as the end of the auditor's regulatory duty.
options.why: The Directions place the duty on the auditor, not the company: where a statement in the report to the board is unfavourable or the auditor finds non-compliance with the Public Deposits Directions, the auditor is obliged to make an exception report to the Reserve Bank's regional office. A report the law requires is not a breach of confidentiality.

options.text: No, but the further step is a full copy of the report to the board sent to the Reserve Bank, so that the regulator sees every statement, favourable and unfavourable, in one place.
options.misconception: Confuses the exception report with a copy of the full report to the board.
options.why: The Directions say the opposite about the content: the exception report is to contain the details of the unfavourable or qualified statements and the non-compliance, and it shall not contain any statement with respect to compliance with those provisions. It is a report of contraventions only, not a copy of the whole.

citation.ref: Non-Banking Financial Companies Auditor's Report (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2016 — for a company not accepting public deposits, the report to the board states whether the board passed a resolution for non-acceptance and whether any public deposits were accepted; reasons for an unfavourable statement; obligation to submit an exception report to the regional office of the Department of Non-Banking Supervision, containing only the contraventions

items.stem: On the three holdings and the seat alone, what does Anjali decide about the firm's reappointment?

options.text: All three pass. The brother's holding is worth 90,000 rupees, which is under the one-lakh relief; an independent director is not part of the management the sub-clause is aimed at; and a partner's 2,000 rupees is too small to compromise anyone's independence.
options.misconception: The relative's limit is a market-value test, independent directors are outside section 141(3)(f), and a partner's small holding is below some threshold.
options.why: The relief for a relative is stated in face value, not market value, so 1,50,000 rupees of shares are over it; section 141(3)(f) asks whether the relative is a director, with no exception for an independent one; and the one-lakh relief is written for a relative only, so a partner holding any security or interest in the holding company is caught whatever the amount.

options.text: Only the brother's holding disqualifies, as the one over the lakh line; the father's directorship is a matter for the board's own independence rules rather than the auditor's, and Vikram's shares are in the holding company, which section 141(3)(d) does not reach.
options.misconception: Section 141(3)(d) reaches only the company being audited, and a relative's directorship is the board's problem.
options.why: Section 141(3)(d)(i) names the company, its subsidiary, its holding or associate company and a subsidiary of such holding company, so a security of the holding company is within it; and section 141(3)(f) is the auditor's own disqualification where a relative of the member is a director of the company.

options.text: The three facts attach to Anjali and to Vikram as individuals and not to Nair & Menon, so the firm may be reappointed provided the partner whose facts are in question stays off the engagement: Vikram signs, and Anjali's brother and father are then no concern.
options.misconception: A disqualification is personal to one partner and is cured by another partner signing.
options.why: Section 141(3)(d)(i) is triggered by a holding of the person, his relative or his partner, so each partner is caught through the other, and Vikram is in any case disqualified by his own holding in the holding company; there is no partner left who is clean.

options.text: The firm cannot be reappointed on any of the three, and the finance head's three answers each miss the test. The brother's shares are securities of face value exceeding one lakh rupees: the relief for a relative is measured by face value, so 1,50,000 rupees of shares are over it whatever the market says of them. The father's seat is caught because a relative of the member is a director of the company, and section 141(3)(f) asks whether the relative is a director, not whether he is independent or in management. Vikram is caught because a partner holds any security or interest in the holding company, which section 141(3)(d)(i) names alongside the company and its subsidiary, and the one-lakh relief is written for a relative, not for the member or a partner, so 2,000 rupees is enough. With each partner disqualified in her or his own right, Anjali declines to sign the consent.
options.why: Section 141(3)(d)(i) makes a person ineligible to be appointed auditor where he, or his relative or partner, is holding any security of or interest in the company or its subsidiary, or of its holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company. The one relief is for a relative, who may hold security or interest in those companies of face value not exceeding one lakh rupees; the line is drawn on face value, so shares of face value exceeding one lakh rupees disqualify Anjali through her brother even though their market value has fallen below it. There is no such relief for the member or a partner: a partner who holds any security or interest, of any face value, in the holding company is within the sub-clause, so Vikram's two hundred shares disqualify him, and a broker's error is the story of how he came to hold them and not an answer. Section 141(3)(f) makes a person ineligible where a relative of the member is a director of the company or is in its employment as a director or key managerial personnel; the sub-clause turns on the relative holding the office, and whether the director is independent is a question for the board's composition and not for the auditor's eligibility. Each of the three facts alone would disqualify the partner it attaches to, and with both partners disqualified the firm has nobody who can sign. In short, the brother's shares are of face value exceeding one lakh rupees, a relative of the member is a director, and a partner holds any security or interest in the holding company, so the firm does not accept the reappointment.
keywords: relative of the member is a director

citation.ref: section 141(3)(d)(i) makes a person ineligible where he, or his relative or partner, is holding any security of or interest in the company or its subsidiary, or of its holding or associate company or a subsidiary of such holding company, with the proviso, through rule 10 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, that a relative may hold security or interest of face value not exceeding one lakh rupees; section 141(3)(f) makes a person ineligible whose relative is a director or is in the employment of the company as a director or key managerial personnel

items.scenario: Nair & Menon, a two-partner firm at Kochi, are the statutory auditors of Sharavati Marine Foods Limited, an unlisted public company with a revenue of 240 crore rupees, whose shares are held by Sharavati Holdings Private Limited and which itself owns Sharavati Cold Chain Private Limited. Anjali Nair is the engagement partner, the firm's reappointment for the year ending 31 March 2027 is on the agenda of the annual general meeting in September 2026, and three matters have come to her before she signs the consent. First, three facts about the firm's people: Anjali's brother holds shares in Sharavati Marine Foods of a face value of 1,50,000 rupees whose market value has fallen to 90,000 rupees; her father, a retired banker, was appointed an independent director of the company in January 2026; and her partner Vikram Menon holds two hundred shares in Sharavati Holdings of a face value of 2,000 rupees, bought years ago through a broker's error he never corrected. The finance head's view is that a holding worth less than a lakh in the market is within the limit, that an independent director is not management, and that two thousand rupees is too small to count. Second, the audit committee's minutes propose to engage Nair & Menon, alongside the audit, for the internal audit of Sharavati Cold Chain at a fee of 12 lakh rupees, for the design and implementation of the financial module of the new enterprise software at Sharavati Holdings, and for tax advisory to Sharavati Marine Foods itself; the finance head says section 144 speaks of the company alone, so services to the subsidiary and the holding company are outside it, and that an internal audit is audit work the statutory auditor is best placed to do. items.stem: On the three services alone, what does Anjali tell the audit committee?

options.text: All three are refused. An auditor cannot take any non-audit engagement from the group it audits, because section 144 exists to keep the auditor to the audit, and tax advisory to the company is as much a non-audit service as the other two.
options.misconception: Section 144 bars every non-audit service to an audit client.
options.why: Section 144 lists the services that cannot be rendered and expressly permits other services approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee; tax advisory is not listed, so it is a permitted other service on that approval.

options.text: Two of the three are refused and the third may be taken with the committee's approval. Section 144 bars the listed services whether rendered directly or indirectly to the company or its holding company or subsidiary company, so the finance head's reading that it speaks of the company alone is wrong on its own words: the internal audit of Sharavati Cold Chain is internal audit for a subsidiary company and the financial module at Sharavati Holdings is design and implementation of any financial information system for the holding company, and both are refused however the fee is set. Tax advisory is not on the list, so it may be provided to the company as an other service, on the approval of the Board of Directors or the audit committee, which the minutes supply.
options.why: Section 144 has two limbs. The first is that the auditor provides to the company only such other services as are approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee. The second is a list of services those approvals cannot reach, and it reaches them whether rendered directly or indirectly to the company or its holding company or subsidiary company; a service to the subsidiary or to the holding company is therefore within the bar in terms, and the finance head's reading stops at the first word of a phrase that goes on. Internal audit is the second item on the list, and it is on the list because it is audit work: the statutory auditor cannot review internal audit work that the firm itself performed. Design and implementation of any financial information system is the third item, and the financial module of an enterprise system is such a system. Tax advisory is not among the listed services, so it falls under the first limb and may be rendered to the company once the Board of Directors or the audit committee approves it, which the minutes do. In short, internal audit and design and implementation of any financial information system are refused for the holding company or subsidiary company as much as for the company, and tax advisory goes ahead on the committee's approval.
keywords: design and implementation of any financial information system

options.text: The finance head is right on scope: section 144 governs services to the company whose auditor the firm is, so the subsidiary's internal audit and the holding company's system are outside it; only a service to Sharavati Marine Foods itself would need testing against the list.
options.misconception: Section 144 reaches only the audited company and not its holding company or subsidiary company.
options.why: Section 144's list applies to the services whether rendered directly or indirectly to the company or its holding company or subsidiary company; the holding company and the subsidiary company are named in the section, and the internal audit and the system design are on the list.

options.text: The internal audit may be taken, because it is audit work and the statutory auditor is the person best placed to do it; only the design of the financial module is refused as the building of a system the firm would then audit, and the tax advisory needs no approval because it is professional work of a chartered accountant.
options.misconception: Internal audit is audit work and so open to the statutory auditor, and professional services need no approval.
options.why: Internal audit is the second item on section 144's list and is barred whatever the auditor's competence for it; and every other service, tax advisory included, is provided only as approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee.

citation.ref: section 144 provides that an auditor shall provide to the company only such other services as are approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee, which shall not include, whether rendered directly or indirectly to the company or its holding company or subsidiary company, accounting and book keeping services, internal audit, design and implementation of any financial information system, actuarial services, investment advisory services, investment banking services, rendering of outsourced financial services, management services, and any other prescribed service

items.stem: On the audit trail alone, what does the report state?

options.text: Because the switch-off was for performance and not to alter any entry, the feature was not tampered with, and the report answers all four questions favourably on the strength of a written representation from management that no entry was changed during the eleven days.
options.misconception: A benign reason for switching the feature off, backed by a representation, keeps the statement favourable.
options.why: Whether the feature has not been tampered with is one question and whether it was operated throughout the year for all transactions is another; eleven days in which it did not run answer the second question no whatever the motive, and a representation is not a record from which the auditor can trace from the general ledger to the source document.

options.text: The rule asks four questions, and the finance head has answered one of them for half a year. The report states that from April to September 2025 the company used accounting software for maintaining its books which did not have a feature of recording audit trail (edit log); that in the software used from 1 October 2025 the feature was not operated throughout the year for all transactions recorded in the software, because it was switched off for eleven days in March 2026 during the year-end close; and that the audit trail of the software used until September 2025 has not been preserved by the company, because its data was not retained after the migration. That the new software has the feature is the answer to the first question for the second half of the year, and it is not the answer to the other three.
options.why: Rule 11 has the auditor's report state four things about the company's accounting software: whether the company has used such software for maintaining its books of account which has a feature of recording audit trail (edit log) facility; whether the same has been operated throughout the year for all transactions recorded in the software; whether the audit trail feature has not been tampered with; and whether the audit trail has been preserved by the company as per the statutory requirements for record retention. An audit trail is the step-by-step sequential record by which the auditor can trace from the general ledger to the source document, and the four questions are about the year as a whole and not about the software in use on the date of the report. For April to September the software had no such feature, so the first question is answered no for that period. For the new software the feature existed but was switched off for eleven days in March 2026, so it was not operated throughout the year for all transactions recorded in the software, and the transactions of the close, the ones most worth tracing, ran without it. The data of the old software, with whatever trail it kept, was not retained, so the audit trail has not been preserved by the company as per the statutory requirements for record retention. Each is stated as a fact; the finance head's sentence answers the first question for the second half of the year and nothing else. In short, the report states that the software used until September had no audit trail (edit log) feature, that in the new software the feature was not operated throughout the year for all transactions, and that the old software's audit trail has not been preserved.
keywords: operated throughout the year for all transactions

options.text: The report states that the company uses accounting software with an audit trail feature, as the finance head says; the rule is about the software the company has, and the company has it.
options.misconception: The audit trail statement is only that the software has the feature.
options.why: Whether the software has the feature is the first of four questions; the rule also has the report state whether the feature was operated throughout the year for all transactions, whether it was not tampered with, and whether the audit trail has been preserved as per the statutory requirements for record retention, and the year here fails the second and the fourth and the first for six months.

options.text: Only the new software is reported on, because a migration starts the statement afresh: the old software and its data belong to the period before the company had an audit trail at all, and the eleven days are reported as a matter of internal control in the letter to those charged with governance, not in the report.
options.misconception: A change of software resets the audit trail statement, and a short gap is a control point rather than a reporting one.
options.why: The rule asks whether the feature was operated throughout the year for all transactions recorded in the software and whether the audit trail has been preserved, so the six months without the feature and the data not retained are answered in the report, and eleven days off is a period in the year in which the feature did not operate.

citation.ref: section 143(3)(j) read with rule 11 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, which has the auditor's report state whether the company has used such accounting software for maintaining its books of account which has a feature of recording audit trail (edit log) facility, whether the same has been operated throughout the year for all transactions recorded in the software, whether the audit trail feature has not been tampered with, and whether the audit trail has been preserved by the company as per the statutory requirements for record retention

items.stem: On the capitalised repairs alone, is the senior right that the opinion must be adverse?

options.text: Neither. Because the finance director has refused to reverse the entry, the partner has been prevented from obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence and should disclaim an opinion.
options.misconception: Confuses management's refusal to correct with a limitation on the auditor's evidence.
options.why: The evidence is complete; the firm knows exactly what was spent and what it did. A refusal to correct a known misstatement is a disagreement about the financial statements, which is modified for misstatement, not an inability to obtain evidence, which is the road to a disclaimer.

options.text: Yes. Any misstatement that moves the profit by more than a quarter is pervasive by definition, and an adverse opinion is required whenever the reader would be misled about the result for the year.
options.misconception: Uses a profit percentage as the test for pervasiveness.
options.why: Pervasiveness is defined by where the effects reach, not by a percentage of profit. The module's three limbs are confinement to specific elements, substantial proportion of the financial statements, and disclosures fundamental to users' understanding, and a single overstated plant addition fails all three.

options.text: Yes, but only because the company is listed; for a listed company every material misstatement left uncorrected is treated as pervasive so that the market is warned.
options.misconception: Invents a listed-company rule that hardens every qualification into an adverse opinion.
options.why: SA 705 draws no distinction between listed and unlisted companies in choosing between a qualified and an adverse opinion. The choice rests on the module's pervasiveness test in every case, and a listed company with a confined misstatement receives a qualified opinion like any other.

options.text: No. The misstatement is material, but it is confined to plant and to repairs expense, and 18 crore rupees against 900 crore rupees of assets and 1,150 crore rupees of revenue is not a substantial proportion of the financial statements; its effects are not pervasive. The partner expresses a qualified opinion, with the misstatement described and its financial effects quantified in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section.
options.why: The module's rule turns on pervasiveness, not on the size of the number against the profit. A qualified opinion is expressed when the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements, individually or in the aggregate, are material but not pervasive to the financial statements; an adverse opinion when they are both material and pervasive. Pervasive effects are those that in the auditor's judgment are not confined to specific elements, accounts or items of the financial statements, or if so confined represent or could represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements, or in relation to disclosures are fundamental to users' understanding. The module then gives the very picture: a problem localised to inventory has no impact on receivables, plant, loans or payables, and is not pervasive. Capitalised repairs are localised in the same way. Plant is overstated and profit is overstated by one figure, every other caption is properly supported, and one figure of 18 crore rupees in a balance sheet of 900 crore rupees is not a substantial proportion of the financial statements. The senior's percentage of profit measures materiality, which is settled, not pervasiveness, which is the question. In short, the effect is confined and not a substantial proportion, so the opinion is a qualified opinion rather than an adverse one.

citation.ref: a qualified opinion is expressed when misstatements, individually or in the aggregate, are material but not pervasive, and an adverse opinion when they are both material and pervasive; pervasive effects are those not confined to specific elements, accounts or items of the financial statements, or that if so confined represent or could represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements, or that in relation to disclosures are fundamental to users' understanding

items.scenario: Pillai & Ghosh are the statutory auditors of Sindhu Ceramics Limited, a listed maker of floor tiles at Morbi, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Revenue is 1,150 crore rupees, profit before tax is 62 crore rupees and total assets are 900 crore rupees. The partner has three matters open in the week before signing. First, the company has capitalised 18 crore rupees spent during the year on relining and repairing its kilns as additions to plant, though the work restored the kilns to their existing condition and extended nothing; the audit evidence is complete, the effect is confined to plant and to the repairs line in the statement of profit and loss, and the finance director refuses to reverse it. The senior's note reads "eighteen out of sixty-two is twenty-nine per cent of the profit, so this has to be adverse". Second, about forty per cent of the company's despatches are carried by a transport company owned by the managing director's brother, at a freight cost of 70 crore rupees for the year; the firm has the contracts, the invoices and the ownership records, and the financial statements carry no related party disclosure of the relationship or the transactions at all. The managing director says "put it in your report if you must, but we are not writing it in the notes". Third, the chair of the audit committee has written to the partner asking to be "told the outcome on the day the report is signed rather than sent drafts", and the partner's plan is to inform the committee at the signing meeting that "there will be a qualification" and to hand over the signed report at the same meeting.

items.stem: On the missing related party disclosure alone, what does the Basis for Opinion section carry, and what happens before it is written?

options.text: A missing note is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about related parties, so the section gives the reasons for that inability and the opinion is qualified for a scope limitation.
options.misconception: Confuses an omitted disclosure with a limitation on the auditor's evidence.
options.why: Nothing is missing from the auditor's evidence; the firm holds the contracts, invoices and ownership records. What is missing is the disclosure in the financial statements, which is a material misstatement, and the module's treatment for it is to describe the nature of the omitted information and include the omitted disclosures, not to give reasons for an inability that does not exist.

options.text: The partner first discusses the non-disclosure with those charged with governance. The Basis for Qualified Opinion section then describes the nature of the omitted information, and, since the firm holds the contracts, invoices and ownership records and nothing in law prohibits it, the partner must also include the omitted disclosures themselves: the relationship and the 70 crore rupees of transactions. The managing director's offer to have it in the report instead of the notes does not make the notes complete.
options.why: The module gives an omitted disclosure its own three-step treatment, distinct from a wrong number and from a misstated narrative. If there is a material misstatement of the financial statements that relates to the non-disclosure of information required to be disclosed, the auditor shall discuss the non-disclosure with those charged with governance, describe in the Basis for Opinion section the nature of the omitted information, and, unless prohibited by law or regulation, include the omitted disclosures, provided it is practicable to do so and the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the omitted information. Both provisos are met here: the firm has the evidence, and a related party relationship with one transport contractor and one year's freight figure is practicable to set out. So the reader gets, in the auditor's report, what the company would not put in its notes. That does not cure the financial statements, which remain materially misstated for want of the disclosure and are qualified for it; the module's point is that the auditor's report does not leave the reader without the information as well. In short, the partner discusses it with those charged with governance, describes the nature of the omitted information, and includes the omitted disclosures in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section.

options.text: Because the managing director has agreed that the matter may appear in the auditor's report, the disclosure there satisfies the requirement and the opinion need not be modified.
options.misconception: Lets a disclosure in the auditor's report stand in for the one the financial statements must carry.
options.why: Information required to be disclosed in the financial statements is missing from them, and that is a material misstatement whatever the auditor's report says. Including the omitted disclosures in the Basis for Opinion section is part of how the modification is written, not a way of avoiding it.

options.text: The Basis for Qualified Opinion section states only that a required related party disclosure has been omitted; supplying the missing figures would make the auditor the author of the company's notes, which is management's job.
options.misconception: Treats including the omitted disclosure in the report as trespassing on management's responsibility.
options.why: The module requires more than a bare statement of omission: the nature of the omitted information is described, and the omitted disclosures are included where practicable and evidenced and not prohibited by law. Setting out in the auditor's report what the notes should have said is exactly what the standard asks for; it does not make the notes management's any less.

citation.ref: where a material misstatement relates to the non-disclosure of information required to be disclosed, the auditor discusses the non-disclosure with those charged with governance, describes in the Basis for Opinion section the nature of the omitted information, and, unless prohibited by law or regulation, includes the omitted disclosures, provided it is practicable to do so and he has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the omitted information

items.stem: On the audit committee chair's request and the partner's plan alone, what does SA 705 require?

options.text: The partner need only communicate that a modification is expected; the wording is the auditor's alone and sharing a draft would let the board negotiate the opinion.
options.misconception: Reads the communication requirement as the fact of a modification without its wording.
options.why: The module's sentence names the wording of the modification as one of the two things communicated. Sharing it does not hand the opinion to the board; the standard says the auditor discusses and deliberates the findings with them, and agreement is not a condition of modifying.

options.text: The chair's request governs. Those charged with governance decide how they wish to be communicated with, and telling them the outcome at signing meets SA 705 as long as they hear it from the auditor before anyone else.
options.misconception: Lets those charged with governance waive a communication the standard imposes on the auditor.
options.why: SA 705 fixes what the auditor communicates and when: the circumstances and the wording of the expected modification, once the auditor expects to modify. A preference of the committee for less cannot cut down a requirement laid on the auditor.

options.text: Once the partner expects to modify the opinion, she communicates to those charged with governance the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification, and discusses the findings and the type of misstatements with them. That happens before the report is signed, so that the matters can still be deliberated; a sentence at the signing meeting that "there will be a qualification", followed by the signed report, gives the committee neither the circumstances nor the wording in time.
options.why: The module states the requirement in one sentence and it has two objects. When the auditor expects to modify the opinion in the auditor's report, the auditor shall communicate with those charged with governance the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification; and the auditor is required to discuss and deliberate with those charged with governance the audit findings and the type of misstatements. The trigger is the expectation, which the partner already has in the week before signing, not the signature. The content is the circumstances and the wording, which means the draft sentences of the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and the qualified opinion itself, not an announcement that a qualification is coming. And the purpose is deliberation, which cannot happen once the report is in the chair's hands. The chair's preference for no drafts does not alter what the standard requires of the auditor; the partner explains that and sends the circumstances and the proposed wording ahead of the meeting. In short, the partner expects to modify, so the circumstances and the wording of the modification go to those charged with governance before signing, for discussion.

options.text: If the committee is told in advance and disagrees with the qualification, the partner must withhold the modification until the disagreement is resolved, so it is safer to tell them at signing.
options.misconception: Treats advance communication as giving governance a veto over the opinion.
options.why: Nothing in SA 705 makes the modification depend on the committee's agreement; the communication exists so that the findings are deliberated and misstatements can be corrected, and if they are not the opinion is modified as the auditor concluded. Timing the communication to avoid the discussion defeats the requirement.

citation.ref: when the auditor expects to modify the opinion in the auditor's report, the auditor shall communicate with those charged with governance the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification, and is required to discuss and deliberate with them the audit findings and the type of misstatements

items.stem: QUESTION 1 OF 3 — turns on the four field findings and the company's answer that every rupee was sanctioned by an empowered officer under rules in force. Where the three papers go and the three engagements out of the Accountant General's office are noise for this one. On the field findings alone, what does Rukmini conclude?

options.text: None of the four goes in the report. Each sanction was passed by an officer who held the power, under rules that were in force at the time, so the spending is regular; whether it was wise is for the company's management to worry about and not for its auditor.
options.misconception: Treating a valid sanction as the end of the enquiry, which is the habit a private-sector statutory audit builds and which propriety audit was created to reach past.
options.why: This is the position chapter 15 is written against. Propriety audit exists because regularity and propriety are two different tests, and clearing the first says nothing at all about the second. If a valid sanction settled the matter the C&AG would have no reason to apply both.

options.text: Rukmini should hand all four to the management for correction and keep them out of her reporting, because the chapter puts the duty of enforcing economy in public spending on the executive departments rather than on the auditor.
options.misconception: Reading a division of labour as a transfer of the whole duty, so the sentence naming who must fix a problem is taken to excuse the auditor from reporting that it exists.
options.why: The chapter splits that work in two and gives the auditor the second half. Departments do the enforcing; the auditor's part is to put the waste, and the spending that was improper or avoidable or pointless, in front of the authorities who can act on it. A private list handed to the management does neither of those things.

options.text: Only the locked hostel goes in. The other three ask the auditor to second-guess commercial judgement, and the chapter warns that a decision has to be weighed against the circumstances of the day rather than with hindsight, so Rukmini should leave them where they are.
options.misconception: Widening a caution meant to keep the auditor fair about commercial risk into a general licence to skip the propriety standards, which are stated rules rather than opinions.
options.why: That warning shields a manager who took a risk under uncertainty and was unlucky. It does not reach these three, each of which is measured against a standard written down long before the decision was taken — a sanction that must not enrich the person passing it, funds that must not be narrowed to one group, and benefits that must stay inside approved terms. None of the three asks the auditor to guess at a business call.

options.text: All four belong in the report, and the company is answering a question nobody asked. A regularity audit asks whether a rule was broken. Propriety asks the next question: did the money buy anything, and would a careful person have parted with it that way? Spending can clear every rule the company has and still be waste. A hostel finished and then left locked is infructuous expenditure — it bought a building nobody uses. Each of the other three breaks one of the standards of financial propriety: nobody may sanction a payment he stands to gain from, however far around the corner the gain sits; money voted for a whole class of workers may not be narrowed to one contractor's men; and staff take what their approved terms give them and nothing beside. In short, a building left locked is infructuous expenditure, a clean sanction file settles the regularity audit and nothing further, and the remaining three findings each break one of the standards of financial propriety.
options.why: The company's answer disposes of the regularity audit and stops there. Chapter 15 sets propriety beside regularity as a separate test, and its whole point is that the two can part company: a transaction may be faultless on every formality and still be money thrown away. A hostel handed over three years ago and locked ever since bought nothing at all, which is what makes it infructuous expenditure rather than merely an unwise choice. The remaining three are weighed against the principles the Audit Code lays down as the standards of financial propriety — that an officer should be as sparing with public money as he would be with his own and spend no more than the occasion calls for; that nobody may pass an order he benefits from, directly or at one remove; that funds meant for a group are not diverted to a favoured slice of it; and that nothing reaches management outside the terms already agreed. The consultancy sanction, the welfare grant and the summer arrangement fail the second, the third and the fourth of those in turn.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — propriety audit as a test distinct from regularity, the principles of financial propriety drawn from the Audit Code, and the division of work between the executive and the auditor once waste has been found.

items.scenario: Ambekar & Nabar are a firm of chartered accountants at Nagpur, and Rukmini Ambekar is the partner in charge of the audit of a state government owned company that mines lignite and burns it at two power stations of its own, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters reach her in the same fortnight. First, four findings from the field inspection, to every one of which the company answers that the money was sanctioned by the officer empowered to sanction it, under rules in force on the day.
