Third, the managing director wants that last sentence of note 41 struck, keeping the events and the plans, "because the plans are in the note and the sentence reads like an obituary".

items.stem: On the managing director's edit alone, if the last sentence of note 41 is struck and the board approves the accounts without it, what happens to the auditor's report?

options.text: The separate going concern section falls away and the opinion is modified. Without the clear statement that a material uncertainty exists and that the company may be unable to realise its assets and discharge its liabilities in the normal course, the uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, so the auditor expresses a qualified or adverse opinion as appropriate and states in the basis for opinion paragraph that a material uncertainty exists and that the financial statements do not adequately disclose it.
options.why: The module defines adequate disclosure in two parts, the principal events or conditions and management's plans, and a clear statement that there is a material uncertainty related to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern and that the entity may be unable to realise its assets and discharge its liabilities in the normal course of business. Striking the last sentence removes the second part, and events and plans alone are not adequate disclosure. The module's table then gives the road: where the use of the going concern basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and adequate disclosure is not made, the auditor expresses a qualified or adverse opinion as appropriate and mentions the matter in the basis for opinion paragraph. The separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" exists only for the case where disclosure is adequate, so it cannot be used to repair a note that is not. In short, the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, the opinion is qualified or adverse, and the basis for opinion paragraph says why.

options.text: An adverse opinion in every case, because omitting a going concern statement means the going concern basis has become inappropriate.
options.misconception: Confuses inadequate disclosure of a material uncertainty with inappropriate use of the going concern basis.
options.why: The basis has not changed; the partner's conclusion that it is appropriate stands. What has changed is the adequacy of the disclosure, and for that the module's road is a qualified or adverse opinion as appropriate, the choice depending on how pervasive the omission is. The adverse opinion in every case belongs to the different road where the basis itself is inappropriate.

options.text: Nothing changes. The events and the plans are still in note 41, the reader can draw the conclusion for herself, and the auditor's own separate going concern section says the uncertainty exists, which cures whatever the note leaves out.
options.misconception: Treats the auditor's report as a place to supply a disclosure the financial statements should have made.
options.why: The module's definition of adequate disclosure requires the clear statement itself, in the financial statements, not a reader's inference from events and plans. The separate section is written only where adequate disclosure is made and draws attention to the note; it does not stand in for words the note lacks, and the road for inadequate disclosure is a modified opinion.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an emphasis of matter paragraph that supplies the missing sentence, since an emphasis of matter is the auditor's tool for drawing attention to what the accounts say too quietly.
options.misconception: Uses an emphasis of matter to fill a gap in disclosure, which is the one thing it can never do.
options.why: An emphasis of matter refers only to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and here the disclosure is not adequate, so the paragraph cannot be used at all. The module's road is a qualified or adverse opinion with the matter in the basis for opinion paragraph.

citation.ref: adequate disclosure of a material uncertainty includes a clear statement that there is a material uncertainty and that the entity may be unable to realise its assets and discharge its liabilities in the normal course of business; where the use of the going concern basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and adequate disclosure is not made in the financial statements, the auditor expresses a qualified or adverse opinion as appropriate and mentions it in the basis for opinion paragraph

items.stem: The confirmation from Sundar Metals reached the team through the finance controller rather than direct. What is that reply worth, and what does the team do now?

options.text: It is not reliable confirmation evidence, because the route was out of the auditors’ hands — the team investigates the reliability of what came back, sends a fresh request asking Sundar Metals to reply direct, and if the company will not permit that, inquires into the reasons, evaluates what the refusal does to the assessed risks including the risk of fraud, and performs alternative procedures
options.why: Control of the external confirmation process belongs to the auditor: determining what is to be confirmed, selecting the confirming party, designing the request so that it asks for a reply direct to the auditor, and sending it. A reply that travelled through the client has left that control, whoever wrote it, so its reliability is in doubt and the auditor obtains further evidence to resolve the doubt. If the company then refuses to let a direct request go out, SA 505 treats the refusal neither as fatal nor as the end of the matter: the auditor inquires into management’s reasons and seeks evidence of their validity, evaluates the implications for the assessed risks of material misstatement including fraud and for the nature, timing and extent of other procedures, and performs alternative procedures. Only if the refusal is unreasonable, or the alternatives do not produce relevant and reliable evidence, does he communicate with those charged with governance under SA 260 and determine the implications for the opinion under SA 705 (Revised).
keywords: external confirmation process belongs to the auditor

options.text: It is good evidence, because the supplier did write it and the controller only passed it on
options.misconception: treats the origin of the document as the test, when the test is whether the auditor kept control of the route it came by
options.why: The test is not who composed the document, it is whether the auditor kept control of the route it travelled. A reply that passes through the client can be altered, replaced or selected before it arrives, and the auditor cannot tell from the reply itself that none of that happened. That is exactly why SA 505 has the request ask for a response sent directly to the auditor, and why a response arriving by any other route raises a question about its reliability that has to be answered with more evidence.

options.text: The balance is unconfirmed, so the team should modify the opinion for a limitation on scope
options.misconception: goes straight to the opinion, when SA 505 puts alternative procedures before any question of modification
options.why: This skips two steps SA 505 requires first. A doubt about the reliability of a response is answered by obtaining further audit evidence, and where a confirmation cannot be obtained the auditor performs alternative procedures designed to produce relevant and reliable evidence — inspecting later payments, goods received notes and supplier invoices for this balance would do a great deal here. A modification is what follows when those procedures fail, not what replaces them.

options.text: Ask the finance controller to obtain a fresh confirmation from Sundar Metals and pass it on once it arrives
options.misconception: leaves the process in management’s hands, which is the very thing that made the first reply unreliable
options.why: This repeats the fault rather than curing it. The reason the first reply is doubtful is that the company stood between the supplier and the auditor, and asking the company to fetch the second one leaves it standing there. The request has to go from the auditor and the reply has to come back to the auditor; if management will not permit that, the refusal itself is the finding, and SA 505 says what to do about it.

citation.ref: para 7 and para 8, read with para 10 and para 11 on doubts over the reliability of a response

items.scenario: Tarangini Alloys Limited is a listed company making steel castings, and Bhatia & Rao are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. The audit is at the completion stage and the report has not been signed. Three things sit on the manager's desk. The team sent a balance confirmation request to Sundar Metals, a supplier carrying a year-end balance of 3.4 crore rupees, and the request asked for the reply to be sent directly to the auditors; the reply reached the team by email, forwarded by Tarangini's own finance controller, who explained that the supplier had sent it to the company by mistake. On 12 May 2026 a fire destroyed the Raipur warehouse and the stock inside it, all of which had been bought and moved there after the year end, and management has quantified the loss and does not want to say anything about it in the financial statements. And the managing director has proposed that the firm's fee for the year be settled at 5 per cent of a sales tax refund the company expects from an appeal now pending, on the argument that the firm's work on the year's records is what will support the claim.

items.stem: The Raipur fire happened on 12 May, before the report is signed. What does SA 560 require of the auditor, given what management wants to do?

options.text: Nothing is adjusted, because the stock did not exist at 31 March and the condition arose after it — but a material event of this kind has to be disclosed, the auditor is squarely in the window where he must actively look for such events, and if management will not disclose it he discusses the matter with those charged with governance and modifies the opinion
options.why: SA 560 divides the timeline. Between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor’s report the auditor actively performs procedures to catch events needing adjustment or disclosure, and this fire falls inside that window. Which of the two it needs is settled by when the condition arose: the destroyed stock was bought and moved after the year end, so nothing at 31 March is misstated and no figure is adjusted. It is a material event after the reporting period all the same, and the framework requires its nature and an estimate of its financial effect to be disclosed. Management refusing that leaves the financial statements materially misstated, which the auditor takes to those charged with governance and, if it stands, to a modified opinion.
keywords: date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor’s report

options.text: The auditor draws attention to the fire in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph and leaves the financial statements as they are
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter paragraph to stand in for a disclosure that is missing from the financial statements
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter already presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and it is not a substitute for a disclosure the framework requires or for a modification the circumstances call for. With management declining to disclose the event there is nothing in the statements for the paragraph to point at, and using one here would let a missing disclosure pass as a matter merely worth noticing.

options.text: The closing stock and the loss must be brought into the 31 March figures, because the event happened before the report was signed
options.misconception: treats every event before the report date as adjusting, when the test is whether the condition existed at the balance sheet date
options.why: The date of the report decides what the auditor must LOOK for; it does not decide what is adjusted. Adjustment belongs to events giving evidence of conditions that existed at the balance sheet date. This stock was bought after the year end and was never in the 31 March balance sheet, so adjusting for its loss would put an event of the next year into the accounts of this one and misstate them in the other direction.

options.text: Nothing further is required, because the auditor’s duty to search for subsequent events ends once the audit work is complete
options.misconception: reads the rule for the second window into the first, when the report is not yet signed
options.why: That is the rule for the OTHER window. The duty to perform procedures ends at the date of the auditor’s report, and this report has not been signed, so the auditor is still in the active window and this event is one of the things he is looking for. Even past that date SA 560 does not go quiet: a fact coming to the auditor’s knowledge before the statements are issued, which would have changed the report, must be discussed and pursued.

citation.ref: para 6 and para 10, read with the reporting framework on events after the reporting period

items.scenario: Tarangini Alloys Limited is a listed company making steel castings, and Bhatia & Rao are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. The audit is at the completion stage and the report has not been signed. Three things sit on the manager's desk. The team sent a balance confirmation request to Sundar Metals, a supplier carrying a year-end balance of 3.4 crore rupees, and the request asked for the reply to be sent directly to the auditors; the reply reached the team by email, forwarded by Tarangini's own finance controller, who explained that the supplier had sent it to the company by mistake. On 12 May 2026 a fire destroyed the Raipur warehouse and the stock inside it, all of which had been bought and moved there after the year end, and management has quantified the loss and does not want to say anything about it in the financial statements. And the managing director has proposed that the firm's fee for the year be settled at 5 per cent of a sales tax refund the company expects from an appeal now pending, on the argument that the firm's work on the year's records is what will support the claim.

items.stem: The managing director wants the year’s audit fee settled at 5 per cent of the expected sales tax refund. What is the firm’s position?

options.text: The firm must refuse, because a fee contingent on the findings or results of the professional employment is misconduct unless the engagement is one of the few Regulation 192 names, and a company’s statutory audit is not among them
options.why: Clause 10 of Part I of the First Schedule makes a member in practice guilty of professional misconduct if he charges or offers to charge, accepts or offers to accept, fees which are based on a percentage of profits or which are contingent upon the findings or results of the professional employment, except as permitted by regulation. Regulation 192 is that exception and it is a closed list: a receiver or liquidator on a percentage of realisation or disbursement of assets, the auditor of a co-operative society on paid-up capital, working capital, gross or net income or profits, a valuer for direct taxes on the value of the property valued, and certain management consultancy, fund raising, debt recovery and cost optimisation services the Council has permitted. A statutory audit fee riding on a tax refund is outside every one of them.
keywords: contingent upon the findings or results

options.text: It is acceptable so long as the basis is set out in the engagement letter and reported to those charged with governance
options.misconception: treats disclosure as a cure, when the clause forbids the basis rather than the secrecy
options.why: Clause 10 bars the BASIS of the fee, not the concealment of it. Nothing in the clause turns on whether the arrangement is written down or told to anybody, and a term recorded in an engagement letter is still a fee contingent on the result of the employment. Disclosure is the answer to several other threats to independence; it is not an answer to a rule that forbids the arrangement itself.

options.text: It is acceptable, because Regulation 192 permits a percentage basis for debt recovery services and recovering a refund from the department is debt recovery
options.misconception: carries one permitted service’s exception across to a different engagement
options.why: The permission attaches to the SERVICE, not to the money the client hopes to receive. What the Council has permitted on a percentage or contingent basis are certain management consultancy, fund raising, debt recovery and cost optimisation services — separate engagements with their own scope. This fee is for the statutory audit of the year’s financial statements, which is not one of them, and a permitted service cannot lend its exception to a different engagement merely because both are billed to the same client.

options.text: It is acceptable if the firm caps the amount, so that 5 per cent can never exceed what it would have charged on a time basis
options.misconception: thinks a ceiling changes the basis, when it only changes the amount
options.why: A ceiling changes how much the fee can be; it does not change what the fee depends on. Under the capped arrangement the firm still earns more if the appeal succeeds and less if it fails, so its reward still moves with the result of the work, which is the thing Clause 10 names. The self- interest threat the clause exists to remove survives the cap untouched.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 10, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: Tarangini Alloys Limited is a listed company making steel castings, and Bhatia & Rao are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. The audit is at the completion stage and the report has not been signed. Three things sit on the manager's desk. The team sent a balance confirmation request to Sundar Metals, a supplier carrying a year-end balance of 3.4 crore rupees, and the request asked for the reply to be sent directly to the auditors; the reply reached the team by email, forwarded by Tarangini's own finance controller, who explained that the supplier had sent it to the company by mistake. On 12 May 2026 a fire destroyed the Raipur warehouse and the stock inside it, all of which had been bought and moved there after the year end, and management has quantified the loss and does not want to say anything about it in the financial statements. And the managing director has proposed that the firm's fee for the year be settled at 5 per cent of a sales tax refund the company expects from an appeal now pending, on the argument that the firm's work on the year's records is what will support the claim.

items.stem: On the senior's plan alone, may negative confirmations be the only substantive procedure on receivables?

options.text: Yes, provided every non-reply is followed up with alternative procedures such as subsequent receipts, which converts each silence into evidence.
options.misconception: Mends the wrong procedure instead of choosing the right one.
options.why: Following up every silence with alternative procedures is what a positive request requires on non-response; it is not the design of a negative request, and it would not make the negative request a suitable sole procedure for a large disputed balance that fails the module's four conditions in the first place.

options.text: Yes for the whole ledger. A negative confirmation is a recognised form of external confirmation, the retailer population plainly qualifies, and a chain the size of Kirana Mart would certainly reply if it disagreed with 46 crore rupees.
options.misconception: Assumes a large customer's silence is a reply.
options.why: The module's conditions are tested against the population the request is sent to, and a single large disputed balance is not a large number of small, homogeneous transactions with a very low expected exception rate; the module also warns that a party is less likely to reply when the information is in its favour, which a customer holding back deductions may consider it to be.

options.text: No for the whole ledger. Negative confirmations provide less persuasive evidence than positive ones and can only ever supplement positive requests, so positive confirmations must go to a sample of the retailers as well.
options.misconception: Denies the sole-procedure use the module expressly permits.
options.why: The module allows negative confirmation as the sole substantive procedure where its four conditions are met, and the retailer ledger meets them on the file: low assessed risk with effective controls, a large number of small, homogeneous balances, a very low expected exception rate and no reason to expect the requests to be disregarded.

options.text: For the retailers, yes; for Kirana Mart, no. Negative requests may be the sole substantive procedure only where the assessed risk is low and controls are effective, the population is a large number of small, homogeneous balances, a very low exception rate is expected and nothing suggests recipients would ignore the request, which the file supports for the 3,400 retailers. A single balance of 46 crore rupees with a live dispute fails every one of those conditions, and a silence from it would be the least persuasive evidence the standard knows; it needs a positive confirmation or equivalent procedures.
options.why: The module lists four conditions and all four must hold for negative confirmations to stand alone. The auditor is to use negative confirmation as the sole substantive audit procedure when the assessed risk of material misstatement is low and relevant controls are effective, the population comprises a large number of small, homogeneous transactions, a very low exception rate is expected, and the auditor is not aware of circumstances that would cause recipients of negative confirmation requests to disregard them. The senior's reason is the reason the conditions exist: the module says that a failure to receive a response to a negative request does not indicate receipt of the request or verification of the information in it, that such a failure provides significantly less persuasive evidence than a response to a positive request, and that confirming parties are more likely to reply when the information is not in their favour and less likely otherwise. Silence therefore proves little, which is tolerable only across a population where the four conditions make misstatement unlikely and small. The retailer ledger is that population on the file's own findings. Kirana Mart is one balance of 46 crore rupees, a large part of the receivables, with 4 crore rupees in dispute, so the risk is not low, the balance is neither small nor homogeneous with the rest, an exception is expected rather than rare, and a customer in a dispute has every reason to let a negative request lie. In short, negative confirmations may be the sole substantive procedure for the small, homogeneous retailer balances where a very low exception rate is expected, and not for the one large disputed balance.

citation.ref: the auditor may use negative confirmation requests as the sole substantive audit procedure only when the assessed risk of material misstatement is low and relevant controls are effective, the population comprises a large number of small, homogeneous transactions, a very low exception rate is expected, and the auditor is not aware of circumstances that would cause recipients to disregard the requests; a failure to respond to a negative request provides significantly less persuasive evidence than a response to a positive request

items.scenario: Kulkarni & Hegde audit Tungabhadra Consumer Products Limited, an unlisted public company at Hubballi with revenue of 540 crore rupees, which distributes packaged foods to about 3,400 small retailers and to one modern-trade chain, Kirana Mart, which owes 46 crore rupees at the year end and is disputing 4 crore rupees of promotional deductions. Nandita Kulkarni is the engagement partner and three things happen on receivables. First, the senior's plan is to send negative confirmation requests to the whole receivables ledger, Kirana Mart included, as the only substantive procedure on receivables, "because the small ones never reply anyway and a silence saves us the follow-up"; the file records that for the retailer balances the assessed risk is low, the credit controls were tested and found effective, the balances are small and alike, and past years produced almost no exceptions. Second, when Nandita insists on a positive confirmation for Kirana Mart, the chief financial officer refuses to let it be sent, saying the chain's terms are under renegotiation and "a letter from auditors will spook them", and offers instead the signed supply agreement and a representation that the balance is correct. Third, at completion the chief financial officer hands over a written representation letter that specifically confirms the recoverability of all receivables and the adequacy of the provision for slow-moving inventory, and the manager proposes to halve the year-end sample on both "now that management has put it in writing and we have no reason to doubt them".

items.stem: On the refused confirmation alone, what does the standard require of Nandita?

options.text: Send the confirmation anyway, because the auditor's right of access under the Companies Act cannot be restricted by management, and treat any attempt to stop it as a limitation on scope.
options.misconception: Skips the evaluation of the reason and the alternative procedures.
options.why: The module's first step is to inquire into the reason and seek evidence of its validity and reasonableness, and a reasonable commercial reason is contemplated; the response to an unreasonable refusal is to communicate with those charged with governance and consider the implications for the opinion, after alternative procedures, not to override management on the first day.

options.text: Accept the refusal, because a confirmation request cannot be sent without the client's consent, and take the signed supply agreement together with the representation as sufficient appropriate evidence for the balance.
options.misconception: Treats the client's consent as the end of the auditor's duty on the balance.
options.why: The module does not let a refusal end the matter: the auditor tests the reason, evaluates the effect on risk including fraud, and performs alternative audit procedures. A supply agreement evidences terms rather than a year-end balance, and a representation is management's assertion, so neither replaces the third-party evidence lost.

options.text: Three steps, and the agreement and representation are not a substitute for any of them: inquire into the reason given and seek evidence as to its validity and reasonableness, which means testing whether a renegotiation is in fact under way; evaluate what the refusal does to the assessed risk on this balance, including the risk of fraud, and to the other procedures; and perform alternative audit procedures on the 46 crore rupees, such as subsequent receipts, dispatch records and the deduction correspondence. If the reason does not hold up, the refusal is unreasonable, and Nandita communicates with those charged with governance and considers the effect on the opinion.
options.why: The module's column on a refusal has exactly this sequence. When management refuses to allow the auditor to send a confirmation request, the auditor inquires as to management's reasons for the refusal and seeks audit evidence as to their validity and reasonableness; evaluates the implications of the refusal on the assessment of the relevant risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and on the nature, timing and extent of other audit procedures; and performs alternative audit procedures designed to obtain relevant and reliable audit evidence. If the refusal is unreasonable, the auditor communicates with those charged with governance and considers the implications for the audit and the auditor's opinion. A commercial reason may be a real one, which is why the first step is to test it rather than to accept or reject it: correspondence with the chain about new terms would support it, and its absence would not. What the chief financial officer offers in exchange is evidence of a different thing. A supply agreement shows the terms of trade, not what is owed at the year end, and a representation is management's own assertion about a balance the auditor was prevented from confirming with the one party who knows; neither is the third-party evidence the confirmation would have been, and the alternative procedures have to reach for records that are, such as cash received after the year end against specific invoices. The disputed deductions make the fraud-risk limb more than a formality, because a refusal that keeps the auditor from the customer is the shape of a balance that would not survive the customer's answer. In short, the auditor seeks evidence of the reason's validity and reasonableness, performs alternative audit procedures on the balance, and if the refusal is unreasonable communicates with those charged with governance and considers the opinion.

options.text: Report the refusal to those charged with governance immediately and qualify the opinion, since a refusal to permit a confirmation is by definition an imposed limitation on the scope of the audit.
options.misconception: Reaches for the last step before performing the first three.
options.why: The module makes communication with those charged with governance the response to a refusal that proves unreasonable after the reason has been tested, and it requires alternative audit procedures first; where those procedures yield sufficient appropriate evidence there is no limitation, and where they do not the effect on the opinion is considered then.

citation.ref: where management refuses to allow the auditor to send a confirmation request, the auditor inquires as to management's reasons and seeks audit evidence as to their validity and reasonableness, evaluates the implications of the refusal on the assessment of the risks of material misstatement including the risk of fraud and on the nature, timing and extent of other audit procedures, and performs alternative audit procedures designed to obtain relevant and reliable evidence; if the refusal is unreasonable the auditor communicates with those charged with governance and considers the implications for the audit and the opinion

items.stem: On the completion letter alone, may the manager halve the samples?

options.text: No, because a representation on specific assertions is not permitted at all; SA 580 allows only the general representations on management's responsibilities, so the letter should be returned and the samples run in full.
options.misconception: Reaches the right sample size by denying the letter's proper role.
options.why: The module's objectives include supporting other audit evidence relevant to specific assertions by means of written representations, so a specific representation is proper and is obtained; the samples run in full because the representation is not sufficient on its own, not because it should never have been asked for.

options.text: Yes for inventory, no for receivables, because the provision for slow-moving stock is a management estimate on which management's own view is the best evidence available.
options.misconception: Carves out estimates from a rule the module applies to every matter.
options.why: The module's rule applies to any of the matters the representations deal with, an estimate included; the auditor's evidence on an inventory provision is ageing, subsequent sales and physical condition, and the representation supports that evidence without reducing it.

options.text: Yes. A specific written representation on an assertion is audit evidence under SA 500, and evidence obtained from one source reduces the amount needed from another; the module calls the letter necessary evidence for that reason.
options.misconception: Treats a representation as interchangeable with evidence from outside management.
options.why: The module calls written representations necessary audit evidence and in the same sentence says they are not sufficient appropriate evidence on their own about any matter they deal with, and that reliable representations do not affect the nature or extent of other evidence the auditor obtains on specific assertions; the letter's role is to support that evidence, not to reduce it.

options.text: No. The letter is necessary audit evidence and the auditor obtains it, but written representations do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters they deal with, and the fact that management has provided reliable representations does not affect the nature or extent of other audit evidence the auditor obtains about specific assertions. The samples on recoverability and on slow-moving inventory are the same size after the letter as before it; the letter supports that evidence, it does not replace half of it.
options.why: The module states the rule in both directions. SA 580 deals with the auditor's responsibility to obtain written representations from management and, where appropriate, those charged with governance, and the module says that although written representations provide necessary audit evidence, they do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters with which they deal; furthermore, the fact that management has provided reliable written representations does not affect the nature or extent of other audit evidence that the auditor obtains about the fulfilment of management's responsibilities or about specific assertions. The module's stated objectives for the auditor put the letter in its place: to obtain representations that management believes it has fulfilled its responsibilities for the financial statements and for the completeness of information given to the auditor, and to support other audit evidence relevant to specific assertions by means of written representations. Support is the word, and the manager's proposal turns support into substitution. Recoverability of receivables and the adequacy of an inventory provision are judgements a management has every reason to hold, so a letter saying management holds them adds nothing to what the auditor already knew when the sample was designed. The module's own test question makes the point in the negative by listing "written representation provides sufficient appropriate audit evidence" as the statement that is not a pillar of the standard. In short, the letter is necessary audit evidence, it is not sufficient on its own about any matter it deals with, and it does not change the nature or extent of other audit evidence.
keywords: nature or extent of other audit evidence

citation.ref: written representations provide necessary audit evidence but do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters with which they deal; the fact that management has provided reliable written representations does not affect the nature or extent of other audit evidence the auditor obtains about the fulfilment of management's responsibilities or about specific assertions

items.stem: On the dealership alone, what does Meenakshi settle?

options.text: Meenakshi agrees with the finance head. Capital and reserves of 80 lakh rupees, bank borrowing of 40 lakh rupees and turnover of 9.2 crore rupees are each inside the limits on the balance sheet date, and a division closed in December 2025 is no part of the year's turnover, so the company is exempt and the annexure can be left off.
options.misconception: Reading all three money tests as balance sheet date readings, when only the capital test is, and treating a discontinued division as outside turnover.
options.why: Every figure in this answer is read on the balance sheet date, and only one of the three tests is written that way. Capital and reserves and surplus is measured as on the balance sheet date, so 80 lakh rupees is correctly inside the limit. The borrowing test is not: it asks about borrowings at any point of time during the financial year, which is what makes the August cash credit of 1.3 crore rupees decisive and the March figure of 40 lakh rupees beside the point. The revenue test is not either: the Order says total revenue as disclosed in Schedule III, including revenue from discontinuing operations, which is written precisely to stop a closed division being dropped. And before any of that, the exception is only open to a private company that is not a subsidiary of a public company.

options.text: Meenakshi says no separate annexure is needed for the dealership, because it is a wholly owned subsidiary of Vaigai Auto Limited and the group's position under the Order will be answered in the annexure attached to the consolidated financial statements of the parent.
options.misconception: Treating the Order as something answered once for a group, when it is answered by each company's own auditor in that company's own report.
options.why: The Order attaches to an auditor's report on a company's own financial statements, and each company covered by it gets its own annexure from its own auditor. Nothing in the Order lets a subsidiary's answers be given in the parent's report, and the consolidated report is the one place the Order almost entirely fails to reach: paragraph 2 keeps it out of a consolidated auditor's report altogether except clause (xxi), which only collects what the component auditors themselves qualified. So this answer would leave the dealership's own report without the annexure the Order requires and would put nothing in the consolidated report to replace it.

options.text: Meenakshi tells him the exemption is not open to this company at all, and that even if it were, two of his three tests fail. The exemption describes a private company that is neither a subsidiary or holding company of a public company, and this dealership is a wholly owned subsidiary of a listed company, so the description stops there whatever the figures are. Taking the figures anyway: capital and reserves of 80 lakh rupees is inside the one crore rupees limit, but bank borrowing has to stay under a crore at any point of time during the year, and the cash credit stood at 1.3 crore rupees in August 2025, so it fails on a figure the year end does not show; and the third test is Schedule III total revenue, including revenue from discontinuing operations, which puts 9.2 crore rupees and 1.1 crore rupees together at 10.3 crore rupees and above the ten crore rupees limit. The tests are cumulative, so failing one is enough. The annexure under the Order goes with the report.
options.why: Paragraph 1 covers companies generally and then lifts out a list of classes, and the private company class is a single description to be answered whole rather than a set of thresholds to be scored. The description opens by ruling out any company that is a subsidiary or holding company of a public company; a wholly owned subsidiary of a listed company is exactly that, so the dealership falls outside the exception before a rupee is looked at. The figures then confirm it twice over. Borrowing is not a balance sheet reading. The question is whether a crore was ever exceeded with a bank or a financial institution at any point of time during the year, and a festival cash credit of 1.3 crore rupees in August 2025 is such a point, so bringing it down to 40 lakh rupees by March 2026 changes nothing. Revenue is written with the same care: Schedule III total revenue, including revenue from discontinuing operations, which is why the closed spare-parts division cannot be dropped, and 9.2 crore rupees with 1.1 crore rupees is 10.3 crore rupees against a ten crore rupees limit. Only the capital and reserves test is met, and the conditions are joined by "and", so one failure ends the claim. In short, the company is a subsidiary or holding company of a public company and so outside the exception, its borrowings exceed the limit at any point of time during the year, and its revenue including revenue from discontinuing operations crosses ten crore rupees.
keywords: subsidiary or holding company of a public company
at any point of time during the year

options.text: Meenakshi says the Order applies, and the reason is the turnover alone. Adding the spare-parts division takes revenue to 10.3 crore rupees, above the ten crore rupees limit. Had that division not been there, the company would have been exempt, because the other two limits are met on the balance sheet date.
options.misconception: Stopping at the first failed test and treating the others as met, so the year end reading of the borrowing limit survives.
options.why: The conclusion is right and the reasoning would mislead him the next time. The revenue test is indeed failed, and for the reason given. But it is not the only test failed, and it is not the first thing that answers the question. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of a listed company, so the private company exception never opens for it, whatever the turnover. And the borrowing test is failed as well, because it is written on any point of time during the year and the cash credit was 1.3 crore rupees in August 2025. Saying the company would otherwise have been exempt teaches him to read the borrowing limit at the year end, which is the mistake the Order's wording exists to prevent.

citation.ref: paragraph 1 — the Order covers companies generally, and among the classes lifted out is the private company that is not a subsidiary or holding company of a public company and clears all three money tests: capital together with reserves and surplus no higher than one crore rupees, read on the balance sheet date; borrowing from a bank or a financial institution no higher than one crore rupees at any point of time during the year; and Schedule III total revenue, counting revenue from discontinuing operations, no higher than ten crore rupees for the year

items.scenario: Raman & Iyer are a firm of chartered accountants at Madurai, and Meenakshi Raman is the partner on three audits for the year ended 31 March 2026 that all sit inside one group headed by Vaigai Auto Limited, a listed company. Three matters have reached her from the group's finance head in the week the reports are to be signed. First, Vaigai Motors Private Limited, a dealership that is a wholly owned subsidiary of Vaigai Auto Limited, has paid-up capital and reserves and surplus of 80 lakh rupees at the balance sheet date; its cash credit from a bank stood at 1.3 crore rupees in August 2025 during the festival stocking and was brought down to 40 lakh rupees by March 2026; and its revenue as disclosed in Schedule III is 9.2 crore rupees from the dealership together with 1.1 crore rupees from a spare-parts division that was closed in December 2025 and is shown as a discontinued operation. The finance head says the company is exempt from the Order on all three money tests, being a private company with capital under a crore, bank borrowing under a crore at the year end and turnover under ten crore rupees, so the Order's annexure can be left off its report. Second, Vaigai Nidhi Limited, a Nidhi company in the group, has net owned funds of 2 crore rupees and deposits from members of 46 crore rupees; it holds term deposits of 4.6 crore rupees with a scheduled bank, of which 3 crore rupees are pledged against an overdraft taken in the company's name; and in November 2025 six depositors whose deposits had matured were repaid two months late, with the interest for the delay paid in January 2026. Its managing director says the clause on Nidhi companies is about the deposit ratio and nothing else, that the term deposits are there in the bank whatever the pledge, and that a delay made good with interest is not a default for the report. Third, on Vaigai Auto Limited's consolidated financial statements, the audit manager has drafted a full annexure under the Order for the group, answering every clause for the parent and its four Indian subsidiaries taken together, since the group is what the consolidated statements present; one of those subsidiaries is a small company outside the Order, and the auditor of another has qualified his own report under the Order on clause (vii) for statutory dues of 60 lakh rupees in dispute, which the finance head asks to be left out of the consolidated report as immaterial to a group with revenue of 900 crore rupees. Meenakshi has to settle each of the three before the reports are signed.

items.stem: On the Nidhi company alone, what does Meenakshi settle?

options.text: Meenakshi says the ratio limb is satisfied and the other two are not. Deposits of 46 crore rupees are twenty-three times net owned funds of 2 crore rupees, which is more than the twenty times the rule asks a Nidhi to carry, so the cover is comfortable; the pledge and the late repayment are the two matters to report.
options.misconception: Treating the 1:20 ratio as a minimum a Nidhi should exceed rather than a ceiling it must stay under.
options.why: This reads the ratio backwards. Net Owned Funds to Deposits in the ratio of 1:20 is a limit on how much a Nidhi may owe its members for the funds it has of its own, so it is satisfied when deposits are twenty times the funds or less and broken when they are more. Carrying twenty-three times is not comfortable cover, it is three times the funds too much, and it is the first thing the clause asks about. The other two conclusions in this answer are right, which is what makes it easy to accept.

options.text: Meenakshi says the ratio and the pledge are to be reported but the repayment is not. The six depositors were paid in full, the interest for the two months of delay was paid in January 2026, and a delay made good with compensation before the year ended leaves no default outstanding on the balance sheet date to report.
options.misconception: Reading the default limb as a balance sheet date question, so any delay cured during the year disappears from the report.
options.why: The third limb is not written about what is outstanding at the year end. It reaches a default in paying interest, or in repaying a deposit, for any period at all — and for any period is the phrase that catches a default that began and ended inside the year. Two months late is such a period, six deposits are the details the clause then calls for, and paying interest for the delay is a consequence of the default rather than a cure for it. A student who reports only what is unpaid on the balance sheet date will miss every default a company clears before March.

options.text: Meenakshi says the term deposit limb is met and the other two are not. The company holds 4.6 crore rupees of term deposits against member deposits of 46 crore rupees, which is exactly ten per cent, and the money sits in a scheduled bank whether or not a lien is noted against it, so the pledge is a matter between the company and its bank.
options.misconception: Reading the ten per cent as a quantity of term deposits held, ignoring the word unencumbered and so the lien that makes them unavailable.
options.why: The clause does not ask for ten per cent term deposits, it asks for ten per cent unencumbered term deposits, and the whole point of the limb is that this money must be free to meet out the liability to depositors. A deposit pledged against the company's own overdraft cannot be drawn on for that purpose while the overdraft stands, so 3 crore rupees of the 4.6 crore rupees does not count and 1.6 crore rupees is what is left against a requirement of 4.6 crore rupees. Reading the limb as a balance in a bank rather than a balance available to depositors is the mistake the word unencumbered is in the clause to prevent.

options.text: Meenakshi tells the managing director that all three limbs of the clause are answered unfavourably. The first limb is the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20, and 2 crore rupees against 46 crore rupees is 1:23, so the deposits carried are more than twenty times the funds and the ratio is broken. The second is the ten per cent of unencumbered term deposits the Nidhi Rules, 2014 require, and of the 4.6 crore rupees held, 3 crore rupees are pledged against an overdraft, leaving 1.6 crore rupees free against a requirement of 4.6 crore rupees. The third reaches any default, for any period, in paying interest on deposits or in repaying them, so six matured deposits repaid two months late is a default however it was made good, and the details of it go in the report with the reasons.
options.why: Clause (xii) has three limbs and the facts fail each one. The first is a ceiling and not a floor. A Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20 lets a Nidhi carry deposits up to twenty times its own funds, so 2 crore rupees of funds support 40 crore rupees at most, and 46 crore rupees is past that at 1:23. The second limb turns on one word. The ten per cent the Nidhi Rules, 2014 require is ten per cent of unencumbered term deposits, and a deposit pledged against the company's own overdraft is encumbered, so only 1.6 crore rupees of the 4.6 crore rupees counts and the ten per cent is not held. The third limb was written to take away exactly the argument offered: it catches a default in paying interest, or in repaying a deposit, for any period at all, so a repayment two months late is a default of two months, and paying the interest afterwards cures the depositor's loss without curing the report's answer. Paragraph 4(a) then requires the reasons to be stated wherever the answer is unfavourable or qualified. In short, the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio is breached, the ten per cent unencumbered term deposits are not held once the pledge is counted, and a late repayment is a default for any period and goes in with its details.

citation.ref: paragraph 3 clause (xii), the three limbs asked about a Nidhi — the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20 it must keep to; the ten per cent of unencumbered term deposits the Nidhi Rules, 2014 require it to hold against what it owes depositors; and any default, for any period, in paying interest on deposits or in repaying them, with the details where there has been one

items.scenario: Raman & Iyer are a firm of chartered accountants at Madurai, and Meenakshi Raman is the partner on three audits for the year ended 31 March 2026 that all sit inside one group headed by Vaigai Auto Limited, a listed company. Three matters have reached her from the group's finance head in the week the reports are to be signed. First, Vaigai Motors Private Limited, a dealership that is a wholly owned subsidiary of Vaigai Auto Limited, has paid-up capital and reserves and surplus of 80 lakh rupees at the balance sheet date; its cash credit from a bank stood at 1.3 crore rupees in August 2025 during the festival stocking and was brought down to 40 lakh rupees by March 2026; and its revenue as disclosed in Schedule III is 9.2 crore rupees from the dealership together with 1.1 crore rupees from a spare-parts division that was closed in December 2025 and is shown as a discontinued operation. The finance head says the company is exempt from the Order on all three money tests, being a private company with capital under a crore, bank borrowing under a crore at the year end and turnover under ten crore rupees, so the Order's annexure can be left off its report. Second, Vaigai Nidhi Limited, a Nidhi company in the group, has net owned funds of 2 crore rupees and deposits from members of 46 crore rupees; it holds term deposits of 4.6 crore rupees with a scheduled bank, of which 3 crore rupees are pledged against an overdraft taken in the company's name; and in November 2025 six depositors whose deposits had matured were repaid two months late, with the interest for the delay paid in January 2026. Its managing director says the clause on Nidhi companies is about the deposit ratio and nothing else, that the term deposits are there in the bank whatever the pledge, and that a delay made good with interest is not a default for the report. Third, on Vaigai Auto Limited's consolidated financial statements, the audit manager has drafted a full annexure under the Order for the group, answering every clause for the parent and its four Indian subsidiaries taken together, since the group is what the consolidated statements present; one of those subsidiaries is a small company outside the Order, and the auditor of another has qualified his own report under the Order on clause (vii) for statutory dues of 60 lakh rupees in dispute, which the finance head asks to be left out of the consolidated report as immaterial to a group with revenue of 900 crore rupees. Meenakshi has to settle each of the three before the reports are signed.

items.stem: On the consolidated financial statements alone, what does Meenakshi settle?

options.text: Meenakshi lets the manager's annexure stand. Consolidated financial statements present the group as one economic entity, so the clauses of the Order are properly answered for the parent and its subsidiaries taken together, and answering them all gives the reader more than clause (xxi) alone would.
options.misconception: Treating the consolidated statements as one company's statements, so the whole Order is thought to apply to the group.
options.why: Paragraph 2 decides this in words, and it decides it the other way: a consolidated auditor's report is outside the Order but for clause (xxi). The reason is that almost every clause of the Order is about one company's own records, registers, dues, loans and statutory compliance, none of which exists at the level of a consolidation. Answering them for a group means inventing group answers to company questions, and a reader cannot tell which company any answer belongs to. More reporting than the Order asks for is not a safe error here; it is an annexure purporting to be given under an Order that does not reach the report it is attached to.

options.text: Meenakshi has the annexure cut back to clause (xxi) and answered in one line, saying that qualifications have been reported by the auditors of certain components included in the consolidated financial statements. Naming the companies would single out one subsidiary's auditor, which the clause does not require.
options.misconception: Answering clause (xxi) as a yes or no question and dropping the details and paragraph numbers that follow the yes.
options.why: The first half of this is right and the second half leaves out the part of the clause that has the work in it. A yes to qualifications or adverse remarks is where clause (xxi) starts rather than where it stops: the companies then have to be named and the paragraph numbers carrying the remarks given. A reader is meant to be able to go from the consolidated report to the exact paragraph of the exact component auditor's annexure, and a sentence saying certain components had qualifications gives him nowhere to go. Paragraph 4(a) points the same way, requiring reasons wherever an answer is unfavourable or qualified.

options.text: Meenakshi has the manager's annexure withdrawn and one clause put in its place. Paragraph 2 keeps the Order off a consolidated auditor's report altogether except clause (xxi), so answering every clause for the group is reporting the Order does not ask for. Clause (xxi) asks the group auditor to look across the CARO reports of the companies consolidated, say whether their own auditors made any qualifications or adverse remarks, and where they did, name those companies and give the paragraph numbers carrying the remarks. The subsidiary that is a small company has no CARO report of its own, so it brings nothing. The subsidiary whose auditor qualified clause (vii) for 60 lakh rupees of disputed statutory dues has to be named, with the paragraph number of his annexure, and the size of the group is no reason to leave it out.
options.why: Two sentences of the Order settle this, and the manager has used neither. The first is in paragraph 2: what the Order asks sits on top of the section 143 report, and it is kept off a consolidated auditor's report altogether except clause (xxi). A group-wide annexure answering every clause is therefore work the Order does not ask for and an answer no clause authorises. The second is clause (xxi) itself, which collects rather than tests. It sends the group auditor across the CARO reports of the companies consolidated to say whether their own auditors made any qualifications or adverse remarks, and where they did, to name those companies and give the paragraph numbers carrying the remarks. That is a report about other auditors' reports, so a component with no CARO report of its own contributes nothing, which is why the small company outside the Order simply does not appear. And the clause carries no threshold at all: it is answered by what another auditor wrote, not by what the group auditor thinks it is worth, so 60 lakh rupees against 900 crore rupees of revenue is not a reason to drop it. In short, the Order reaches the consolidated report only except clause (xxi), that clause collects qualifications or adverse remarks made by the component auditors, and it is answered with the companies named and the paragraph numbers given.

options.text: Meenakshi agrees with the finance head that the qualification can be left out. Clause (xxi) is answered on what is material to the consolidated financial statements, and disputed statutory dues of 60 lakh rupees against group revenue of 900 crore rupees would not change any reader's view, so the clause is answered in the negative.
options.misconception: Reading a materiality filter into clause (xxi), when the clause reports what other auditors wrote rather than what the group auditor considers significant.
options.why: Clause (xxi) has no materiality test in it. Whether a component auditor put qualifications or adverse remarks in his own CARO report is a fact about what he wrote, and once the answer is yes the clause wants his company named and his paragraph numbers given. The group auditor is collecting, not re-deciding: the component auditor already applied his own judgement when he qualified his report, and nothing in the clause invites that judgement to be overturned by comparing the figure with group revenue. Answering the clause in the negative when a component auditor did qualify is a false answer to a factual question, and paragraph 4(a) would require the reasons for an unfavourable answer that is never given.

citation.ref: paragraph 2, which keeps the Order off a consolidated auditor's report altogether except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3; and clause (xxi) itself, which asks the group auditor to look across the CARO reports of the companies consolidated, say whether their own auditors made any qualifications or adverse remarks, and where they did, name those companies and give the paragraph numbers carrying the remarks

items.stem: Assume the representation letter and the misstatements are resolved. On the going concern matter alone, what does the auditor's report say?

options.text: A qualified opinion, because significant doubt about going concern exists at the date of the report
options.misconception: treats the presence of a going concern uncertainty as a fault in the financial statements, when the fault would be failing to disclose it
options.why: The existence of doubt is not a misstatement. SA 570 modifies the opinion when the financial statements fail — when the disclosure of a material uncertainty is inadequate, which is a qualified or adverse opinion under SA 705, or when the going concern basis itself is inappropriate, which is adverse. Here the basis is agreed to be appropriate and the note is adequate, so there is nothing to qualify. The report's job is to point at the note, and the separate section does that without touching the opinion.

options.text: An adverse opinion, because a bank has recalled the company's only working capital facility and the replacement is not yet approved
options.misconception: reads the severity of the event as the test, when the test is whether the going concern basis is appropriate and whether the uncertainty is disclosed
options.why: An adverse opinion follows when management has prepared the statements on the going concern basis and the auditor judges that basis inappropriate — the company will not be able to realise its assets and discharge its liabilities in the normal course. The engagement partner has concluded the opposite: the basis is appropriate, with a material uncertainty attached. A recall and a pending replacement are exactly the kind of events that create an uncertainty rather than settle the question, and the standard's answer to an adequately disclosed uncertainty is an unmodified opinion with the separate section.

options.text: An unmodified opinion, with a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" that draws attention to the note and states that a material uncertainty exists and that the opinion is not modified in respect of it
options.why: When the auditor concludes that management's use of the going concern basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists, SA 570 asks two things of the financial statements: that they adequately disclose the principal events or conditions and management's plans to deal with them, and that they disclose clearly that a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern. Vellore's note does both — the recall, the term sheet, the directors' assessment, and the sentence about significant doubt. Where the disclosure is adequate the auditor expresses an unmodified opinion and the report carries a separate section under the heading "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern", which draws attention to the note and states that these events or conditions indicate that a material uncertainty exists and that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter. The uncertainty is real; the report says so; the opinion is clean because the statements tell the truth about it.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph referring to the going concern note
options.misconception: uses the pre-revision Emphasis of Matter road, when SA 570 (Revised) prescribes a separate section with its own heading
options.why: This is the shape the report had under the old SA 570, and it is the answer most often written from memory. The revised standard replaced it: a material uncertainty that is adequately disclosed is reported in a separate section under the prescribed heading "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern", not in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph. The heading is the point — a reader searching the report finds the going concern matter by name.

citation.ref: para 18 and para 22 — basis appropriate, material uncertainty adequately disclosed, separate section under the heading Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern

items.scenario: Vellore Textiles Limited is an unlisted spinning company, and Menon & Iyer are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. The audit is at the completion stage and the report is due to be signed on 20 June 2026. Three matters are open. In February 2026 the company's bank recalled its working capital line of 38 crore rupees after two covenant breaches, and the company has since been running on supplier credit; management has a signed term sheet from a second bank for a replacement facility, subject to that bank's credit committee, and has drafted a note to the financial statements that sets out the recall, the term sheet, the directors' assessment, and states plainly that a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the company's ability to continue as a going concern. The engagement partner agrees that the going concern basis is appropriate. Second, the managing director has returned the written representation letter unsigned, with a note saying the company gave the auditors every record they asked for and will not sign "a form letter that treats us as suspects"; the paragraph he objects to is the one on the completeness of the information provided. Third, the team's schedule of misstatements found during the audit totals 22 lakh rupees, all of it overstated revenue from cut-off errors, against an overall materiality of 1.2 crore rupees, and the finance controller has declined to correct any of it because "it is nowhere near material".

items.stem: The managing director will not sign the representation on the completeness of the information provided. What does the auditor do, and where does it end if he holds his position?

options.text: Qualify the opinion for a limitation on scope confined to the matters the representation would have covered
options.misconception: treats a missing completeness representation as a bounded scope limitation, when it undermines the evidence as a whole
options.why: A qualification confines the doubt to identified matters. A refusal to represent that the information provided was complete leaves nothing confined: it casts doubt over the whole body of evidence, since every procedure rested on the information the auditor was given. That is why SA 580 names the disclaimer rather than a qualification for this representation and for the one on management's responsibility, and why the auditor also re-evaluates integrity rather than just the paragraph.

options.text: Record the managing director's oral assurance in the working papers and sign the report, since every record requested was in fact produced
options.misconception: treats records produced as proof of completeness, when completeness is exactly what only management can represent and must represent in writing
options.why: Written representations are audit evidence in their own right about matters the auditor cannot otherwise verify — chief among them whether the information provided was complete, which by its nature only management can assert. SA 580 requires that assertion in writing, and an oral assurance recorded by the auditor is not the management's written representation. The fact that everything asked for was produced says nothing about what was not asked for because the auditor did not know it existed.

options.text: Discuss the refusal with management, re-evaluate management's integrity and the reliability of every other representation and of audit evidence generally, and if the representation is still withheld, disclaim an opinion on the financial statements
options.why: SA 580 sets out the road when a requested written representation is not provided: the auditor discusses the matter with management, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the effect that may have on the reliability of representations, oral or written, and of audit evidence in general, and takes appropriate action including determining the effect on the opinion under SA 705. For most representations that ends in a judgement. For two it does not: the representations that management has fulfilled its responsibility for the financial statements and that it has provided the auditor with all relevant information and access are ones the audit cannot be completed without, and where management does not provide them the auditor disclaims an opinion. The managing director's objection is to precisely the completeness representation, so if the discussion does not move him, the report is a disclaimer. Having given every record asked for is not a substitute for saying so in writing — the written representation is what turns "we think we had everything" into evidence.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement immediately, since a refusal to sign is evidence of management fraud
options.misconception: jumps from refusal to fraud and from fraud to withdrawal, skipping the discussion and re-evaluation SA 580 requires
options.why: SA 580 asks first for a discussion and a re-evaluation of integrity, not a conclusion. A refusal may come from misunderstanding, pride or advice as easily as from concealment, and the standard's response is measured: discuss, reassess, and if the representation is still not given, disclaim. Withdrawal is a possibility the auditor considers where law and the engagement permit and where continuing is untenable; it is not the prescribed first step, and a refusal to sign is not in itself evidence of fraud.

citation.ref: para 19 and para 20 — requested written representations not provided; the representations on responsibility and on completeness of information, and the disclaimer of opinion

items.scenario: Vellore Textiles Limited is an unlisted spinning company, and Menon & Iyer are its statutory auditors for the year ended 31 March 2026. The audit is at the completion stage and the report is due to be signed on 20 June 2026. Three matters are open. In February 2026 the company's bank recalled its working capital line of 38 crore rupees after two covenant breaches, and the company has since been running on supplier credit; management has a signed term sheet from a second bank for a replacement facility, subject to that bank's credit committee, and has drafted a note to the financial statements that sets out the recall, the term sheet, the directors' assessment, and states plainly that a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the company's ability to continue as a going concern. The engagement partner agrees that the going concern basis is appropriate. Second, the managing director has returned the written representation letter unsigned, with a note saying the company gave the auditors every record they asked for and will not sign "a form letter that treats us as suspects"; the paragraph he objects to is the one on the completeness of the information provided. Third, the team's schedule of misstatements found during the audit totals 22 lakh rupees, all of it overstated revenue from cut-off errors, against an overall materiality of 1.2 crore rupees, and the finance controller has declined to correct any of it because "it is nowhere near material".

items.stem: The finance controller will not correct the 22 lakh rupees of overstated revenue. What does SA 450 require of the team before the report is signed?

options.text: Request correction, and when it is refused, evaluate whether the 22 lakh rupees is material individually or in aggregate with other uncorrected misstatements, considering size, nature and circumstances; communicate the uncorrected misstatements individually to those charged with governance with their effect on the opinion; and obtain a written representation that their effects are immaterial, with the schedule attached
options.why: SA 450 does not let a number below materiality end the matter. The auditor communicates accumulated misstatements to management on a timely basis and requests correction; where management refuses, the auditor obtains an understanding of its reasons and takes that into account in evaluating whether the financial statements as a whole are free of material misstatement. The evaluation is of each misstatement and of the aggregate, and it considers the size and nature of the misstatements and the circumstances — revenue overstated by cut-off error, all in one direction, in a year the company is negotiating a facility with a bank, is a nature and a circumstance, not just 22 lakh rupees against 1.2 crore. The uncorrected misstatements are then communicated to those charged with governance, individually, with the effect they may have on the opinion, and a written representation is obtained that management believes their effects to be immaterial individually and in aggregate, with a list of them attached to the letter.

options.text: Compare the 22 lakh rupees with performance materiality, and if it is within that lower figure, treat the schedule as cleared
options.misconception: uses performance materiality, a planning figure, as the test for uncorrected misstatements at completion
options.why: Performance materiality is set below overall materiality to reduce the chance that the aggregate of undetected and uncorrected misstatements exceeds materiality; it shapes the extent of testing. It is not the yardstick for evaluating misstatements found. SA 450 evaluates uncorrected misstatements against materiality for the financial statements as a whole, revised if need be in the light of the misstatements found, and considers the nature and circumstances as well as the size. Clearing a schedule against performance materiality confuses the planning tool with the completion judgement.

options.text: Qualify the opinion, because management has refused to correct a known misstatement
options.misconception: treats management's refusal as the trigger for modification, when the trigger is materiality of the uncorrected misstatements
options.why: The opinion is modified when uncorrected misstatements are material, individually or in aggregate, to the financial statements as a whole — not because management declined a correction. If the auditor's evaluation, after considering size, nature and circumstances, concludes that 22 lakh rupees is immaterial, the opinion is unmodified and the matter is handled by communication to those charged with governance and the written representation. Refusal is a reason to look harder at the evaluation; it is not by itself a ground for qualifying.

options.text: Note the amount in the working papers and take no further action, since 22 lakh rupees is well under the materiality of 1.2 crore rupees
options.misconception: treats overall materiality as a threshold below which nothing need be done, when SA 450 requires evaluation, communication and representation regardless
options.why: Below overall materiality is where SA 450 begins, not where it ends. The standard requires the uncorrected misstatements to be evaluated in aggregate and for their nature and circumstances, communicated to those charged with governance with their effect on the opinion, and covered by a written representation with the list attached. A misstatement that is quantitatively small can still matter for what it does — here it inflates revenue in a year the company is showing its accounts to a new lender — and management's refusal to correct it is itself something the auditor considers.

citation.ref: para 8, para 11, para 12 and para 14 — request to correct, evaluation individually and in aggregate, communication to those charged with governance, and the written representation
