items.stem: On the tax demand alone, may the partner include an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, and what would it have to say?

options.text: Yes, if in her judgement the matter is fundamental to users' understanding: the demand is appropriately disclosed in note 34, she has sufficient appropriate evidence and the opinion is not modified by it, and an uncertainty over exceptional litigation is one of the circumstances SA 706 names. The paragraph refers to note 34, states that the opinion is not modified, and its wording goes to the audit committee first; it may not be used if the matter is a key audit matter.
options.why: SA 706 lets the auditor include an Emphasis of Matter paragraph for a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements that, in the auditor's judgement, is fundamental to users' understanding of them, on two provisos: the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion under SA 705 as a result of the matter, and, since SA 701 applies to a listed company, the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter. The module's list of circumstances that may call for one begins with an uncertainty relating to the future outcome of exceptional litigation or regulatory action, which a disputed 18 crore rupees demand before a tribunal is. The paragraph sits under a heading that includes the term Emphasis of Matter, refers to the matter and to where note 34 discloses it, refers only to what the financial statements themselves present, and states that the opinion is not modified; and because the auditor expects to include one, she communicates that expectation and the wording to those charged with governance. The audit committee's wish to have nothing said does not bind her.

options.text: Yes, but because the company is listed the matter must be placed in the Key Audit Matters section under an Emphasis of Matter sub-heading rather than in a paragraph of its own.
options.misconception: Merges the two paragraphs SA 706 keeps apart.
options.why: SA 706 puts an Emphasis of Matter in a separate section of the report with its own heading, and its second proviso is that the matter has NOT been determined to be a key audit matter. The two are alternatives for a given matter, not a nesting; a key audit matter is described in the Key Audit Matters section under SA 701, and a matter that is one cannot also be the subject of an Emphasis of Matter.

options.text: No. Because the note already discloses the demand, drawing further attention to it would amount to a second disclosure by the auditor, which SA 706 forbids.
options.misconception: Reads the condition that the matter be disclosed as a bar rather than a precondition.
options.why: The opposite is the rule. An Emphasis of Matter can only ever refer to a matter that IS presented or disclosed in the financial statements; a matter the notes do not disclose cannot be the subject of one. Disclosure in note 34 is what makes the paragraph possible, not what bars it.

options.text: No. The outcome of the appeal is uncertain, and an uncertainty the auditor cannot resolve requires a qualified opinion for a limitation on scope, not an Emphasis of Matter.
options.misconception: Confuses uncertainty about a future event with an inability to obtain evidence.
options.why: An uncertainty about how litigation will end is not a limitation on the auditor's evidence. The partner has read the appeal papers and counsel's opinion and agrees the disclosure is right; sufficient appropriate evidence about the disclosure exists, and the module names exactly this kind of uncertainty as a circumstance that may call for an Emphasis of Matter.

citation.ref: an Emphasis of Matter paragraph draws attention to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is fundamental to users' understanding of them, provided the opinion need not be modified as a result of the matter and, where SA 701 applies, the matter is not a key audit matter; an uncertainty about the outcome of exceptional litigation or regulatory action is a circumstance that may call for one; the paragraph refers to the note, states that the opinion is not modified, and its wording is communicated to those charged with governance

items.scenario: Vindhya Ceramics Limited, listed on the National Stock Exchange, makes floor tiles at Morbi. For the year ended 31 March 2026 its revenue was 1,150 crore rupees, profit before tax 64 crore rupees, total assets 900 crore rupees and trade receivables 210 crore rupees. Iyer & Rao are the statutory auditors, and the engagement partner is settling the report with three matters in front of her. First, a goods and services tax demand of 18 crore rupees, raised in 2024 on the classification of a range of vitrified tiles, is under appeal before the tribunal; note 34 discloses it as a contingent liability with the basis of the demand and the company's grounds, senior counsel has advised in writing that the demand is unlikely to survive, the partner has read the appeal papers and the counsel's opinion and agrees with the treatment, and the audit committee asks that the report "say nothing about it, since the note says it all". Second, a receivable of 12 crore rupees from Kesar Trading, the company's largest distributor, has been outstanding since September 2025; a resolution professional was appointed over Kesar in January 2026, the debt is unsecured, and the company has made no provision; note 38 sets out these facts and management's view that the amount is recoverable in full, and the chief financial officer says that "the note discloses it fully, so an Emphasis of Matter pointing at the note is the most you need". Third, to keep the report clean for the exchange, the partner is minded to describe the Kesar receivable as a key audit matter, setting out the procedures performed and the judgement involved, in place of any qualification.

items.stem: On the Kesar receivable alone, is the chief financial officer right that an Emphasis of Matter pointing at note 38 is the most the report needs?

options.text: Yes. Note 38 discloses every fact the auditor knows, and where the financial statements themselves tell users the position, the auditor's role is to draw attention to the note, not to second-guess management's view of recoverability.
options.misconception: Treats a note as curing the misstatement it describes.
options.why: Disclosure of a fact does not cure the misstatement of a figure. The auditor's opinion is on whether the financial statements are materially misstated, and a receivable carried at full value against an unsecured counterparty in insolvency is misstated whatever the note says; the module says in terms that an Emphasis of Matter is not a substitute for modification.

options.text: No. An unsecured 12 crore rupees debt from a distributor under a resolution professional, carried at full value with no provision, is a material misstatement, and a note describing it does not cure it. The effect is confined to one item and is not pervasive, so the opinion is qualified, "except for" the effects of the matter set out in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section. An Emphasis of Matter is not a substitute for that modification and is only for a matter appropriately presented.
options.why: The module deals with this case directly: management may insist on no modification because the notes disclose the full facts and its own assessment, but the auditor must judge whether disclosure alone suffices or the opinion must be modified, and it is clarified that an Emphasis of Matter is not a substitute for modification of the opinion. An Emphasis of Matter is confined to something appropriately presented for which the auditor has sufficient appropriate evidence; a receivable carried at 12 crore rupees against a counterparty in insolvency with no security is not appropriately presented, however fully note 38 describes it. Under SA 705 the auditor expresses a qualified opinion where misstatements are material but not pervasive, and pervasive effects are those not confined to specific elements of the financial statements; this one is confined to a single receivable, so the opinion is qualified, stating that except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section the statements give a true and fair view, with the matter and its quantified effect set out in that section.

options.text: No, but the right report is a disclaimer of opinion, because until the insolvency process ends nobody can obtain evidence of how much of the 12 crore rupees will be recovered.
options.misconception: Mistakes uncertainty about the amount recoverable for an absence of evidence.
options.why: A disclaimer is for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence whose possible effects could be both material and pervasive. Here the auditor has the evidence: an unsecured debt, a resolution professional appointed, no provision. That evidence supports a conclusion that the figure is misstated, which is a material misstatement confined to one item, not a scope limitation across the statements.

options.text: No, and the opinion must be adverse: 12 crore rupees is close to a fifth of profit before tax, which makes the misstatement both material and pervasive.
options.misconception: Reads "material and pervasive" as "large".
options.why: Pervasiveness is not a matter of the size of the misstatement against profit. The module defines pervasive effects as those not confined to specific elements, accounts or items, or that represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements, or that are fundamental to users' understanding; one receivable out of 210 crore rupees on a balance sheet of 900 crore rupees is confined to a single item. The right modification is a qualified opinion.

citation.ref: a qualified opinion where misstatements are material but not pervasive, expressed "except for" the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section; pervasive effects are those not confined to specific elements of the financial statements; an Emphasis of Matter is not a substitute for modification of the opinion and is only for a matter appropriately presented, and management's insistence that the notes disclose the full facts does not remove the need to modify

items.scenario: Vindhya Ceramics Limited, listed on the National Stock Exchange, makes floor tiles at Morbi. For the year ended 31 March 2026 its revenue was 1,150 crore rupees, profit before tax 64 crore rupees, total assets 900 crore rupees and trade receivables 210 crore rupees. Iyer & Rao are the statutory auditors, and the engagement partner is settling the report with three matters in front of her. First, a goods and services tax demand of 18 crore rupees, raised in 2024 on the classification of a range of vitrified tiles, is under appeal before the tribunal; note 34 discloses it as a contingent liability with the basis of the demand and the company's grounds, senior counsel has advised in writing that the demand is unlikely to survive, the partner has read the appeal papers and the counsel's opinion and agrees with the treatment, and the audit committee asks that the report "say nothing about it, since the note says it all". Second, a receivable of 12 crore rupees from Kesar Trading, the company's largest distributor, has been outstanding since September 2025; a resolution professional was appointed over Kesar in January 2026, the debt is unsecured, and the company has made no provision; note 38 sets out these facts and management's view that the amount is recoverable in full, and the chief financial officer says that "the note discloses it fully, so an Emphasis of Matter pointing at the note is the most you need". Third, to keep the report clean for the exchange, the partner is minded to describe the Kesar receivable as a key audit matter, setting out the procedures performed and the judgement involved, in place of any qualification.

items.stem: On the partner's idea alone, can describing the Kesar receivable as a key audit matter take the place of a qualification?

options.text: No. SA 701 applies to this listed company, and it says in terms that communicating key audit matters is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when SA 705 requires one. A matter that requires a qualification is dealt with in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section; the Key Audit Matters section cannot be used to keep the report clean.
options.why: SA 701 applies to audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and its scope paragraph, set out in the module, says that communicating key audit matters in the auditor's report is not a substitute for disclosures the framework requires management to make, not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when the circumstances require it under SA 705, not a substitute for reporting under SA 570 on a material uncertainty about going concern, and not a separate opinion on individual matters. The key audit matters section adds information about how the audit was conducted in the context of an opinion already formed on the statements as a whole; it does not change what that opinion has to be. Where the facts call for a qualification, the matter is described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and the opinion is qualified, and the wish to present a clean report to the exchange is not a consideration SA 701 recognises.

options.text: Yes. For a listed company the Key Audit Matters section is the place where matters of most significance are reported, and a matter fully described there with the procedures performed need not also modify the opinion.
options.misconception: Treats the key audit matters section as an alternative form of modification.
options.why: Being of most significance in the audit is what makes a matter a key audit matter; it is not what decides the opinion. SA 701's scope paragraph excludes exactly this use: describing a matter as a key audit matter is not a substitute for a modified opinion when SA 705 requires one. The two operate together, not in place of each other.

options.text: No, because a matter that gives rise to a modified opinion can never be mentioned anywhere else in the report, so the Key Audit Matters section must stay silent about the receivable.
options.misconception: Reaches the right answer through an invented rule of silence.
options.why: The bar is on substitution, not on mention. What SA 701 forbids is using the key audit matters section instead of the modified opinion the circumstances require; the matter is described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and the opinion is qualified. The conclusion that the partner's plan fails is right, but the reason given, a rule of total silence, is not in the standard.

options.text: Yes, provided the description in the Key Audit Matters section quantifies the possible loss and states that the auditor disagrees with management, which gives users the same information as a qualification.
options.misconception: Assumes the content of a paragraph can do the work of the opinion.
options.why: A key audit matter description is not a separate opinion on an individual matter, and SA 701 says so; the auditor does not express disagreement with management inside it. Giving users "the same information" is not the test. If the statements are materially misstated the opinion itself must say so, in the form SA 705 prescribes.

citation.ref: applies to audits of listed entities; communicating key audit matters is not a substitute for disclosures the framework requires, for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when SA 705 requires it, for reporting under SA 570 on a material uncertainty, nor is it a separate opinion on individual matters

items.stem: On the liabilities compilation alone, what does Anjali settle?

options.text: Anjali corrects all four entries in the liabilities statement — the branch adjustment credit balance goes in, the borrowings from abroad go in at gross level, the accrued interest goes in and the NABARD refinance stays out — and accepts the twelve Fridays as satisfying the liquidity ratio verification, since Friday is the reporting day the whole system is built on.
options.misconception: Treating the Friday reporting cycle as the audit test dates, when the requirement is written to fall away from it.
options.why: The liabilities are right and the dates are not, and the reason given is the reason the requirement exists. Friday is the reporting day for the weekly trial balances from the branches and for the liabilities position consolidated at head office. The auditor's verification of compliance with the liquidity ratio is set on twelve odd dates in different months of the year that are not Fridays, so that the dates tested are not the dates the bank already prepares for. Accepting a Friday compilation as the verification means the bank has been checked only on the days it was ready to be checked, and the report to the top management and the Reserve Bank would say compliance was verified when it was not.

options.text: Anjali tells him one of the four entries is right and the liquidity ratio work has not started. Leaving out the refinance from NABARD is correct; refinance from NABARD, SIDBI, the National Housing Bank and EXIM Bank is excluded. The net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts is not an internal item that cancels itself — it is included in liabilities. Borrowings from abroad are reported at gross level as liabilities to others; only liabilities towards the banking system in India may be set off against assets with that system, and a bank abroad is not that system. The 26 crore rupees of interest that had accrued by the reporting date goes in whether or not the books had caught up with it. And the twelve Fridays are the wrong dates: compliance is verified on twelve odd dates in different months of the year that are not Fridays, the Friday statements being the basis on which the liabilities position is struck, not the basis of the verification. Her report goes to the top management and to the Reserve Bank, and says how many branches were unaudited and that she relied on their returns.
options.why: Three of the general manager's four readings turn on the same mistake, which is treating a liability as something the bank owes to an outsider on the balance sheet date. The Reserve Bank's list works the other way round. The exclusions are named one by one, and refinance from NABARD is on that list, which is why leaving it out is right. What is not on the list stays in. The net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts is money the bank holds unsquared between its own offices, and it is included; calling it internal does not make it disappear. Borrowings from abroad are the clearest case: the netting permitted for liabilities towards the banking system in India is permitted because both sides of it are inside the same system, so a borrowing from a bank abroad is reported at gross level as a liability to others and nothing is set off against it. Interest that has accrued by the reporting date is a liability from that date, and the bank's habit of writing it into the books at the quarter end is a bookkeeping rhythm, not a rule about when it is owed. The liquidity ratio dates are a separate error of the same family: the weekly Friday trial balances are how the liabilities position is determined, while the auditor's compliance verification is deliberately set on dates the bank cannot anticipate. In short, the net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts is included in liabilities, borrowings from abroad are reported at gross level, and the verification is done on twelve odd dates in different months of the year that are not Fridays.
keywords: net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts

options.text: Anjali corrects the branch adjustment accounts and the accrued interest, both of which go into liabilities, and accepts the rest. The refinance from NABARD is rightly excluded, the borrowings from abroad are dealings between banks and may be set off against the balances held with banks abroad, and a compilation on twelve Fridays through the year meets the verification requirement.
options.misconception: Reading the netting allowed within the banking system in India as a netting allowed between any two banks, and treating the Friday reporting rhythm as the verification dates.
options.why: Two of the three are right and the two that are wrong are the ones the general manager most wants agreement on. Netting is allowed only for liabilities towards the banking system in India against assets with that same system; borrowings from abroad by banks in India are outside it and are shown as liabilities to others at their full amount, so setting the balances abroad against them understates the liabilities on which both ratios are worked. And the twelve Fridays are the dates on which the liabilities position is struck, not the dates on which compliance is verified — the Reserve Bank asks for odd dates in different months that are not Fridays precisely so that the bank cannot arrange itself for them.

options.text: Anjali corrects only the borrowings from abroad, which are shown at their full amount as liabilities to others. The branch adjustment accounts are internal and net to nothing outside the bank, interest not yet written into the books is not yet a liability, the NABARD refinance is rightly out, and the twelve Fridays are the required verification dates.
options.misconception: Treating internal accounts and unposted accruals as outside liabilities, so only the item owed to an identifiable outsider on a posted date is counted.
options.why: The one correction made is correct, and three of the four things left alone are wrong. A net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts is included in liabilities; it is an unsquared amount the bank holds, and the fact that both sides of the entry are its own offices is not a reason to leave it out. Interest accrued by the reporting date is included even though the bank records it periodically, because the accrual and the posting are two different dates and the liability follows the first. And the compliance verification is done on odd dates in different months of the year that are not Fridays, which is a different set of dates from the Friday trial balances the liabilities position is built on.

items.scenario: Kelkar & Deshmukh are a firm of chartered accountants at Nagpur, and Anjali Kelkar is the partner in charge of the statutory central audit of Wainganga Bank Limited, a scheduled commercial bank, for the year ended 31 March 2026. Three matters have come to her from the general manager (accounts) in the week the report is to be signed. First, the compilation of demand and time liabilities. The bank's statement leaves out a refinance of 300 crore rupees taken from NABARD; it also leaves out a net credit balance of 42 crore rupees in the branch adjustment accounts, which the general manager calls an internal account that cancels against itself; it shows borrowings from abroad of 180 crore rupees netted against the bank's own balances with banks abroad, on the footing that both are dealings with the banking system; and it omits 26 crore rupees of interest that had accrued on deposits by the reporting date but was written into the books only at the following quarter end. For the statutory liquidity ratio, he has handed her a compilation prepared as on twelve Fridays spread through the year and says the verification is complete. Second, the head other assets. Interest accrued of 55 crore rupees includes 9 crore rupees on bills purchased and discounted that are long overdue, where the branch's own note records that recovery is uncertain, and the general manager's position is that interest accrues by contract whether or not anybody collects it. A suspense account carries 7 crore rupees, of which 4.2 crore rupees are entries more than three years old for which no reason for the delay is on record, and he says a suspense balance is temporary by definition and so needs no provision. And a building taken over in 2019 from a defaulting borrower in satisfaction of a debt of 12 crore rupees stands in the books at 12 crore rupees, though its net realisable value on the date it was taken over was 9.5 crore rupees; he says the bank will sell it at a profit one day. Third, the reports beyond the audit report itself. The general manager suggests that the long form audit report for the bank is a management document, so it should go before the board only if the board asks for it and nothing about it need reach the Reserve Bank; and he asks whether authentication of the capital adequacy ratio and the report on the conduct of treasury operations belong to this engagement at all, or are a separate assignment the bank would have to commission. Anjali has to settle each of the three before the report is signed.

items.stem: On the other assets alone, what does Anjali settle?

options.text: Anjali takes the interest out and examines the suspense entries, and leaves the building at 12 crore rupees. The asset was taken over in full and final settlement of a debt of that amount, so 12 crore rupees is what the bank gave up for it, and the realisable value matters only when it is sold.
options.misconception: Measuring an asset taken in satisfaction of a claim at the amount of the claim, and deferring the shortfall to the sale.
options.why: A non-banking asset acquired in satisfaction of claims is recorded at the lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired, measured when it is taken over, so the figure is 9.5 crore rupees. The claim given up is not the cost, because the bank did not choose this asset as an investment — it took what was available for a debt that was not being paid, and the rule exists so that the shortfall is recognised then rather than carried as an asset until a sale finally proves it. Since 2019 the difference has sat in other assets as a profit the bank still expects.

options.text: Anjali requires the suspense account to be examined entry by entry and the building to be brought down to 9.5 crore rupees, but leaves the interest accrued alone. Interest on bills purchased and discounted accrues under the contract and the bills have not been written off, so the whole 55 crore rupees stands until the advances themselves are treated as bad.
options.misconception: Treating a contractual accrual as income until the underlying advance is written off, instead of testing what can be realised.
options.why: The interest is the item the head exists to test. Other assets carries interest accrued only to the extent that can be realised in the ordinary course of business, which does not wait for the advance to be written off; it is the accounting rule that revenue is not recognised where there is significant uncertainty about collectability, and the branch's own note that recovery is uncertain is precisely that. Leaving the 9 crore rupees in overstates both the asset and the year's income, and it does so in the head where such an amount is least likely to be asked about again.

options.text: Anjali requires all three to change. Interest accrued is carried only to the extent that can be realised in the ordinary course of business, so the 9 crore rupees on long overdue bills, where the branch's own note records the doubt, comes out; a contractual right to interest is not revenue where collection is significantly uncertain. On the suspense account she asks for the details of the old outstanding entries with the reasons for the delay, and where a balance calls for a provision or a write-off she examines whether it has been made — 4.2 crore rupees standing over three years unexplained is the reason the head is looked at at all. And the building came in at the wrong figure: an asset acquired in satisfaction of claims is recorded at the lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired, which is 9.5 crore rupees and not 12. She also reads the terms of the settlement, checks that ownership is legally vested in the bank, and looks at section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, since the asset is held to be disposed of and has been there since 2019.
options.why: Each of the three answers is the same idea in a different place: other assets is the head where an amount that will never be collected can sit for years looking like an asset, so each item in it is tested against what the bank will actually get. Interest accrued is included only to the extent that can be realised in the ordinary course of business, which is the accounting rule that revenue is not recognised where there is significant uncertainty about collectability; the branch's own note is that uncertainty in writing, so the 9 crore rupees is not carried whatever the contract says. The suspense account is examined by obtaining the details of the old outstanding entries and the reasons for the delay, because the age is the evidence — an entry nobody has been able to explain in three years is not a temporary parking of a receipt, and where the balance requires a provision or a write-off the auditor sees whether one has been made rather than accepting that the head is temporary by nature. The building is measured by a rule written for this exact hope: an asset taken in satisfaction of claims is recorded at the lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired, so the shortfall is taken when the asset comes in and is not carried as a future profit. In short, interest goes in only to the extent that can be realised in the ordinary course of business, the old outstanding entries in suspense are obtained with their reasons and provided for where needed, and the building enters at the lower of the net book value of the advance or the net realisable value of the asset acquired.
keywords: realised in the ordinary course of business
net book value of the advance or the net realisable value

options.text: Anjali takes the 9 crore rupees of interest out and brings the building down to 9.5 crore rupees, and accepts the suspense account as it stands. A suspense balance is a holding place for entries awaiting classification, so its age is a housekeeping matter for the bank rather than something the audit provides against.
options.misconception: Reading the suspense account as a housekeeping matter because of what it is called, rather than examining the old entries for a provision.
options.why: Two right and the third is where the loss usually hides. The suspense account is examined by obtaining the details of the old outstanding entries and the reasons for the delay, and where a balance requires a provision or a write-off the auditor examines whether it has been made. An entry more than three years old with no reason on record is not awaiting classification; it is an amount nobody can account for, and treating the head as temporary by definition is what lets it stay. Age is the evidence here, not the excuse.

items.stem: On the reports after the audit report alone, what does Anjali settle?

options.text: Anjali agrees that the certificates, authentication of the capital adequacy ratio among them, are part of this engagement, and accepts that the long form audit report is addressed to the management. Once she has given it to the management the bank decides what to do with it, and whether it goes further is the board's affair.
options.misconception: Treating the report as delivered when it reaches management, so the stages after that are read as the bank's own business.
options.why: The first half is right and the second stops one step too early. The long form audit report is submitted to the management, and it does not stop there: it is placed before the Audit Committee of the Board with the action taken or proposed, and a copy of it with the relative agenda note and the Board's views goes to the Reserve Bank within 60 days. Those stages are not the bank's discretion, and they are the reason the report is worth writing — a report that reaches only the people it comments on is a report with no reader who can act on it.

options.text: Anjali says the long form audit report goes to the management, before the Audit Committee of the Board and to the Reserve Bank within 60 days with the agenda note and the Board's views. On the second question she agrees with the general manager: authentication of the capital adequacy ratio and the report on treasury operations are certificates outside the statutory audit, which the bank engages an auditor for separately.
options.misconception: Reading a bank audit as a company audit plus optional extras, so the regulatory certificates look like separate assignments.
options.why: The route of the report is right and the second half misreads what a bank audit includes. The statutory central auditor of a bank gives a list of reports and certificates as part of the same engagement, and authentication of the capital adequacy ratio and the report on whether treasury operations were conducted in accordance with the Reserve Bank's instructions are both on it, beside the liquidity ratio report, the income recognition and asset classification report and the Ghosh and Jilani committee reports. Treating them as separate work would leave the regulator without figures it depends on the statutory auditor to certify, and would make the engagement look like a company audit with an opinion and nothing else.

options.text: Anjali says both parts of his suggestion are wrong. The long form audit report is not a paper that waits to be asked for: it goes from her to the management, it is placed before the Audit Committee of the Board with the action taken or proposed on each matter in it, and a copy of it with the relative agenda note and the Board's views is submitted to the Reserve Bank within 60 days. And the certificates are not a separate assignment for the bank to commission — authentication of the capital adequacy ratio and the report on whether treasury operations were conducted in accordance with the Reserve Bank's instructions are among the reports the statutory central auditor gives as part of this engagement, along with the report on compliance with the liquidity ratio, the report on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning, and the reports on the Ghosh and Jilani committee recommendations.
options.why: The general manager has read both things as favours the bank may decline. Neither is. The long form audit report has a route written for it, and every stage of that route is somebody else's check on the bank: management first, then the Audit Committee of the Board, which must record what is being done about each matter, and then the Reserve Bank, which receives the report together with the agenda note and the Board's own views within 60 days. Making it depend on the board asking would break the route at the point where it stops being internal. The second half is a mistake about what a bank audit is. A company audit ends at an opinion on the financial statements; a bank audit carries a list of reports and certificates alongside it, because the regulator relies on the auditor for figures it cannot verify itself — the capital adequacy ratio is authenticated by her, treasury operations are reported against the Reserve Bank's instructions, and the liquidity ratio, income recognition and asset classification and the Ghosh and Jilani committee reports sit in the same list. In short, the long form audit report goes to management, then before the Audit Committee of the Board, and to the Reserve Bank within 60 days with the agenda note and the Board's views, and authentication of the capital adequacy ratio is part of this engagement rather than a separate one.

options.text: Anjali says the long form audit report goes to the management, then before the Audit Committee of the Board with the action taken or proposed, and that a copy reaches the Reserve Bank; the bank sends it with its other returns whenever those are due, there being no separate time limit. The certificates, including authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, are part of this engagement.
options.misconception: Remembering the route the report takes but not that it carries a time limit of its own.
options.why: Everything here is right except the timing, and the timing is the part that decides whether the report is of any use. A copy of the long form audit report together with the relative agenda note and the Board's views is submitted to the Reserve Bank within 60 days. Letting it travel with whatever return happens to be due next means the regulator reads the auditor's observations on a year that is already well past, and it also removes the pressure that makes the Board record its views at all.

items.stem: Which facts block the appointment?

options.text: All three — any financial connection with an audit client disqualifies
options.misconception: replaces the statutory thresholds with a zero-tolerance rule
options.why: Parliament drew money lines precisely so trivial connections would not bar appointment. Reading them as zero makes the limits in the rule meaningless.

options.text: B's loan and C's guarantee — only the relative's shareholding is tolerated
options.misconception: forgets the guarantee has its own threshold
options.why: The guarantee disqualifies only beyond one lakh rupees. At ₹90,000 it is inside the line; the only fact past its ceiling is the ₹6 lakh debt.

options.text: None — the interests belong to a spouse, a borrower on market terms, and a guarantor, not the auditors themselves
options.misconception: shrinks the provision to the signing partner's own name
options.why: The section speaks of the person, the relative and the partner, and the rule prices each connection. B's own debt crosses its line regardless of the loan's fairness.

options.text: Only B's loan — the spouse's holding and C's guarantee sit within their limits
options.why: A relative's securities are permitted up to one lakh rupees face value, so ₹80,000 passes. The guarantee limit is one lakh, so ₹90,000 passes. Indebtedness has a five-lakh ceiling and B's ₹6 lakh crosses it — market terms do not matter — and one disqualified partner disqualifies the firm.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(d) read with Rule 10

items.scenario: A firm is proposed as auditor of a company. Partner A's spouse holds shares of the company of face value ₹80,000. Partner B owes the company ₹6 lakh on a car loan taken on market terms. Partner C has guaranteed his friend's ₹90,000 dues to the company.

items.stem: What does clause 3(xi) actually require here?

options.text: Report both frauds with nature and amount — the clause covers any fraud on the company, noticed or reported, whoever committed it
options.why: CARO 2020 widened the clause to any fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year. The outsider's ₹1.2 crore is a fraud on the company, and its being reported to the police is exactly what makes it "reported". Nature and amount go into the report for each.

options.text: Report both, but omit amounts to avoid prejudicing the pending investigations
options.misconception: lets litigation caution trim a prescribed disclosure
options.why: The clause asks for nature and amount in terms. The auditor reports what was noticed; investigations run on their own track and are not compromised by a statutory report stating the figure involved.

options.text: Report only the stores officer — outsider frauds are police matters, not audit matters
options.misconception: carries the old officers-and-employees limit into the 2020 order
options.why: The 2016 order's wording was narrower; the 2020 clause dropped the limitation. An auditor answering the old question in the new report under-reports by ₹1.2 crore.

options.text: Report neither, since clause 3(xi) is triggered only by frauds the auditor discovers himself
options.misconception: reads "noticed or reported" as "noticed by the auditor"
options.why: Noticed or reported during the year — by anyone. Frauds surfacing through management, police complaints or whistle-blowers are squarely inside the words.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xi)

items.scenario: During the year, a company's stores officer was caught inflating supplier invoices for ₹40 lakh, and an outside gang defrauded the company of ₹1.2 crore through a fake vendor registration. Writing the CARO report, the audit senior drafts clause 3(xi) to cover only the stores officer, reasoning that CARO concerns frauds by the company's own people, and the vendor fraud was reported to the police, not to the auditor.

items.stem: Can the report be signed today?

options.text: No — for a listed entity the quality review must be completed before the report is dated
options.why: SQC 1 makes the engagement quality control review a gate, not a debrief: an objective look at the significant judgments and conclusions, finished before the report's date. A review conducted after signing can no longer change the one thing it exists to test.

options.text: Yes — the review is the firm's internal process and the report is the engagement's
options.misconception: files a signing condition under housekeeping
options.why: The review is internal in who performs it, not in what it protects. Its position before the report date is what gives the reviewer's objections any force.

options.text: Yes, provided the reviewer belongs to the engagement team and already knows the file
options.misconception: staffs the review with the people it is meant to check
options.why: The reviewer's value is distance — someone outside the team evaluating the team's judgments. A team member reviewing his own conclusions is the engagement grading itself.

options.text: No, unless the engagement partner documents that he considered the open issues himself
options.misconception: substitutes self-review for the second pair of eyes
options.why: The partner's own consideration is the thing under review. His memo cannot stand in for the objective evaluation SQC 1 assigns to another qualified person.

citation.ref: Engagement quality control review requirements

items.scenario: The audit of a listed company is nearly done. The engagement partner, under deadline pressure, proposes signing the report today and having the firm's quality control reviewer go through the significant judgments next week, arguing the review is an internal formality that does not concern the client.

items.stem: Is the clean audit a substitute for due diligence?

options.text: Yes for the financials, with diligence confined to legal and operational matters
options.misconception: carves financial diligence out on the audit's authority
options.why: Financial due diligence reads the same numbers with a buyer's eyes — quality of earnings, sustainability, normalisation. The audit did none of that, and a deal is priced on exactly that.

options.text: No, because audits performed by the target's own auditor are inherently unreliable
options.misconception: wins the right conclusion by slandering the wrong party
options.why: The reputed firm's work needs no doubting for the lawyer to be right. Even a flawless audit is a different exercise; the argument is scope, not competence.

options.text: Yes — a true and fair view certified by auditors is the highest assurance available
options.misconception: ranks assurance levels instead of matching scope to purpose
options.why: The opinion's assurance is high on the question it answered. A buyer's losses come overwhelmingly from matters outside that question — commitments, dependencies, liabilities that are disclosed correctly yet deadly.

options.text: No — the audit answered a different question for a different audience, and the rumour needs an investigation alongside the diligence, not instead of it
options.why: The audit opined that the statements fairly present the past under a framework — it never priced the business, tested contract terms, tax exposures or customer concentration, and it owed its opinion to shareholders, not to a buyer. Due diligence asks the buyer's questions. The promoter rumour is a specific suspicion — an investigation's job — and it runs beside the diligence with its own depth.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

items.scenario: A client acquiring a rival says: "The target's accounts carry a clean audit opinion from a reputed firm, so due diligence would duplicate work already done. If anything, just investigate the promoter's rumoured side-dealings." His lawyer insists a full due diligence is still needed.

items.stem: What does propriety audit make of an unimpeachable file?

options.text: Nothing, unless a rule specifically caps renovation rates
options.misconception: demands a broken rule before any audit comment
options.why: Propriety supplies the standard where rules run out — that is its function. Waiting for a rate cap turns the auditor into a rule-checker for a class of loss rules cannot foresee.

options.text: The transaction fails — sanctioned extravagance in a relative's favour is exactly what propriety audit exists to catch
options.why: Regularity audit reads the file and finds every rule followed; propriety audit reads the bargain and asks whether a prudent person would pay triple his own money to a relative of the decision-maker. The standards of prudence, economy and no personal advantage condemn it however complete the sanctions.

options.text: The auditor may only report the relationship, not question the price
options.misconception: shrinks propriety to conflict disclosure
options.why: Economy is a propriety canon in its own right. Triple market rate fails it with or without the relative; the relationship adds the personal-advantage failure on top.

options.text: The transaction passes — audit tests compliance, and compliance is total
options.misconception: stops at the regularity rail
options.why: If sanction ended the enquiry, the surest waste would be waste with the best paperwork. Government audit added propriety precisely because public money can be lost lawfully.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

items.scenario: A public sector company buys office renovation services at triple the market rate from a vendor who is the purchasing director's relative. Every step carried proper sanction: budget approval, tender committee sign-off, board ratification. Management tells the government auditor the file is unimpeachable.

items.stem: Do the objections hold?

options.text: Neither — the review tests the firm's systems on sample files, not the client's accounts, and access to attestation working papers is inherent in the framework
options.why: Nothing about the client reopens: the reviewer asks whether the firm's quality controls, documentation and standards compliance operated on that engagement. The confidentiality objection fails because the peer review framework itself provides for the reviewer's access with confidentiality obligations of his own — a member cannot plead the client against the profession's oversight of the member.

options.text: The confidentiality objection holds — client consent is needed for each file shown
options.misconception: puts a consent gate where the framework put an obligation
options.why: The reviewer stands under his own duty of confidentiality within the review's structure. Engagement-by-engagement client vetoes would let firms curate their own review.

options.text: Both — completed audits are closed files in every sense
options.misconception: confuses reviewing the auditor with reopening the audit
options.why: Closed for the client is not closed for the firm's own quality trail. The completed file is precisely the evidence of how the firm's systems behaved when it mattered.

options.text: Both fail, but only because peer review reports are never made public
options.misconception: right result hung on secrecy instead of scope
options.why: The objections fail on what review is — systems examination of the practice unit — not on who reads the outcome. Publicity is beside the point.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control

items.scenario: A peer reviewer examining an audit firm selects a completed statutory audit as a sample. The firm's managing partner objects on two grounds: the client's financial statements were approved long ago and cannot be reopened, and client confidentiality bars an outsider from the working papers.

items.stem: Who appoints the first auditor now?

options.text: The Registrar of Companies, on the company's application
options.misconception: imports a government-company style default into an ordinary company
options.why: The C&AG-then-Comptroller cascade belongs to government companies. For others the statute keeps the appointment inside the company — board, then members.

options.text: The board — statutory timelines for internal appointments are directory, not mandatory
options.misconception: keeps a lapsed power alive by calling the deadline soft
options.why: The section's structure is a handover: board first, members on the board's failure. Reading the deadline away erases the members' role the provision creates.

options.text: The members, in an extraordinary general meeting within ninety days
options.why: The board's thirty-day window from registration closed on 30 April; section 139(6) hands the power to the members, who appoint at an EGM within ninety days. The appointee serves until the first AGM concludes — the same tenure the board's appointee would have had.

options.text: No one — the company must wait for the first annual general meeting
options.misconception: leaves the company auditor-less for up to a year
options.why: The first auditor's whole purpose is covering the stretch before the first AGM. The ninety-day EGM route exists so the office never waits that long.

citation.ref: Section 139(6)

items.scenario: A private company incorporated on 1 April has a board that never appoints a first auditor. On 20 May the promoters realise the lapse. One director suggests the board can still appoint, being only a few days late; another says the power is gone and the Registrar now appoints; a third says the members must do it.

items.stem: What must change for the engagement to be forensic?

options.text: Nothing — audit methodology is the profession's standard for all engagements
options.misconception: stretches assurance methodology over investigation
options.why: Audit method is built for reasonable assurance about statements taken as a whole. Pointed at a suspected fraud, its materiality and reliance shortcuts are the hiding places.

options.text: Everything named — targeted procedures over materiality sampling, corroborated evidence over explanations, findings of fact over an opinion
options.why: A fraudster hides below sampling thresholds, so forensic scoping follows suspicion, red flags and data analytics across the whole population of interest. Management's word is a lead to verify, not evidence — the output may face a courtroom, where chain of custody and corroboration decide weight. And the deliverable reports what was found, quantified and attributed; assurance opinions belong to a different species of engagement.

options.text: The engagement should simply be declined — accountants cannot investigate
options.misconception: vacates a field the profession has standardised
options.why: ICAI issued the FAIS precisely because members do this work. The discipline is doing it under the right standards, not abstaining.

options.text: Only the sampling — deeper samples with the same reliance and opinion suffice
options.misconception: fixes coverage while keeping the wrong evidence bar and output
options.why: Full coverage of uncorroborated explanations proves nothing a tribunal will accept, and an opinion on fairness answers a question nobody in the fraud asked.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting

items.scenario: Engaged to investigate suspected procurement fraud, a forensic accountant is pressed by the audit-trained team to plan the work like a statutory audit: sample the vendors on materiality, accept management's explanations recorded in file notes, and conclude with an opinion that the procurement function presents fairly.

items.stem: Which of the colleague's two positions fail?

options.text: Both — regulatory requirements rise sharply up the layers, and the statutory auditor has direct reporting duties to RBI
options.why: Scale-based regulation is graduated by design: the upper layer carries prudential and governance requirements approaching a bank's, so the audit programme that fits a base-layer lender tests a fraction of what the housing financier must comply with. And the auditor's exception reporting to RBI is the auditor's own statutory duty — discharging it through management is not discharging it.

options.text: Only the reporting point — audit programmes standardise across any lender
options.misconception: concedes the rare duty and keeps the daily error
options.why: Programmes derive from what the entity must comply with. Two layers apart, the compliance universes differ in capital, concentration, governance and disclosure — the programmes cannot match.

options.text: Only the identical programmes — reporting to RBI is indeed management's channel
options.misconception: keeps the duty on the wrong desk
options.why: The exception-reporting framework names the statutory auditor. An auditor who found non-compliance and told only the client has kept the regulator blind exactly as the duty forbids.

options.text: Neither — NBFC prudential norms are uniform and reporting flows through the entity
options.misconception: audits the label instead of the layer
options.why: Uniformity is what the scale-based framework replaced. The audit scales with the regulation, and the direct reporting duty bypasses the entity deliberately.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies

items.scenario: You are auditing two NBFCs: a small base-layer lender, and an upper-layer housing financier that RBI's list places two layers higher. A colleague plans identical audit programmes for both, reasoning that an NBFC is an NBFC, and adds that any RBI Act non-compliance found is management's problem to report to the regulator.

items.stem: Can the two paragraphs go?

options.text: Yes — an unqualified opinion implies every subsidiary matter is satisfactory
options.misconception: folds express statutory answers into implication
options.why: Parliament asked for statements, not inferences. Readers — and regulators inspecting reports — check the answers as given, and an implied yes is a blank.

options.text: The books paragraph stays but the directors one goes — auditors cannot certify board matters
options.misconception: mistakes a written-representation-based statement for a certification
options.why: The auditor reports on 164(2) status on the strength of representations received from the directors, which is exactly how the section contemplates it. Difficulty of verification does not delete the duty.

options.text: Both go if the audit committee approves the shortened format
options.misconception: lets governance approve away statute
options.why: No committee controls the contents of a statutory report. The audit committee oversees the auditor's independence and work, not the statute's checklist.

options.text: No — each 143(3) matter is a statutory reporting duty answered expressly, clean opinion or not
options.why: The opinion answers true and fair; section 143(3) asks its own list of questions, and the report states the answer to each — proper books, information obtained, agreement of accounts with books, standards compliance, director disqualifications, and the rest. They are not commentary the drafter may trim; a missing answer is a non-compliant report however healthy the accounts.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)

items.scenario: Finalising a company audit report, the senior deletes two paragraphs as clutter: the statement on whether proper books of account were kept, since the opinion already covers the accounts; and the statement on directors' section 164(2) disqualification, since board matters are the secretary's field. The financial statements themselves are clean.

items.stem: Can the April test carry the year?

options.text: No — broken change management means the control tested in April may not be the control that ran in September
options.why: Reliance on an automated control across a period rests on general controls proving the application stayed as tested. Unapproved production changes and shared administrator access mean anyone could have altered or bypassed the match at any time, unlogged. The foundation failed, so the single test supports April at best — the auditor extends testing or goes substantive.

options.text: Yes for amounts below materiality, with manual testing above it
options.misconception: slices control reliance by transaction size
options.why: A compromised control is compromised for every rupee through it. Materiality shapes how much substantive work replaces the reliance, not a size-band where broken controls still count.

options.text: Yes — automated controls are consistent by nature, which is their audit advantage
options.misconception: quotes the benchmark while its condition lies broken
options.why: The consistency argument assumes the program is unchanged. That assumption is precisely what change management evidences, and here it evidences the opposite.

options.text: No, and the IT weaknesses also mean the financial statements must be qualified
options.misconception: jumps from control weakness to opinion modification
options.why: Control failure changes the audit approach — more substantive evidence — and earns a management letter, and IFC reporting where applicable. The opinion qualifies only if sufficient evidence cannot be obtained or misstatements stand.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance

items.scenario: An auditor tests the billing application's automated three-way match in April and finds it works perfectly, planning to rely on it for the whole year. Later he learns the IT team shares one administrator login, developers push changes straight to production without approval, and the change log for the year is unreliable.

items.stem: Which engagements does section 144 permit?

options.text: None — an auditor may render no other service of any kind
options.misconception: reads the prohibited list as a total ban
options.why: The section bars its listed services and routes the rest through approval. Tax audits, certifications and representations live lawfully beside statutory audits across the profession.

options.text: Only the tax representation — the spouse's bookkeeping is the auditor acting indirectly, and internal audit of the subsidiary is expressly barred
options.why: The prohibited list covers accounting and book keeping and internal audit, and it applies to the company, its holding company and its subsidiaries alike. "Directly or indirectly" was defined to reach exactly the spouse's-consultancy route. Tax representation is outside the prohibited list and stands with the audit committee's approval it received.

options.text: All three — only services to the audited company itself are restricted
options.misconception: stops the section at the company's own boundary
options.why: The section names the holding and subsidiary companies in the same breath. Auditing the parent while internally auditing the child is auditing one's own feeder work.

options.text: The bookkeeping and the tax work — a spouse's separate firm is a separate person
options.misconception: takes the corporate veil at face value against an anti-avoidance definition
options.why: The Explanation to section 144 defines indirect rendering through relatives and connected entities. The separate registration is the arrangement the definition was written to see through.

citation.ref: Section 144

items.scenario: An audit firm holds a company's statutory audit. During the year: the partner's spouse's consultancy takes over the company's bookkeeping; the firm itself accepts the internal audit of the company's subsidiary; and the firm provides tax representation before the tribunal for the company, approved by the audit committee.

items.stem: What report does this engagement actually support?

options.text: No report at all — assurance-less engagements are not reportable
options.misconception: confuses no assurance with no deliverable
options.why: The factual findings report is the deliverable, and banks run covenant monitoring on such reports daily. It reports facts and disclaims assurance — both on purpose.

options.text: The positive opinion is fine, since the bank chose the procedures it trusts
options.misconception: lets the user's procedure list widen the practitioner's conclusion
options.why: The bank chose procedures, not an opinion. A conclusion beyond the work performed is unsupported whoever designed the work.

options.text: A limited assurance review conclusion in negative form
options.misconception: upgrades the engagement one rung instead of none
options.why: Even negative assurance needs the inquiry-and-analytics fabric of a review across the statements. Three covenant procedures support findings, not any form of assurance on the statements.

options.text: Factual findings of the specified procedures, no assurance expressed — the drafted opinion claims an audit nobody performed
options.why: Agreed-upon procedures deliver what was agreed: this ratio recomputed, that balance confirmed, findings stated, conclusions left to the bank. A true-and-fair opinion asserts reasonable assurance over the statements as a whole — evidence three procedures cannot carry. The generous-sounding report is the dangerous one: it promises the bank an audit's comfort at a procedures engagement's depth.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services (SRS 4400), read with Ch. Review of Financial Information (SRE 2400)

items.scenario: A bank asks a CA firm to verify three specific covenant ratios in a borrower's quarterly figures using procedures the bank itself lists. The firm performs exactly those procedures and drafts a report concluding that "the quarterly statements present a true and fair view", reasoning that a positive conclusion serves the bank better than a dry list of findings.

items.stem: Is he exposed under the CA Act?

options.text: No, provided he declares the receipts in his income tax return
options.misconception: launders misconduct through tax compliance
options.why: Tax law asks whether income was declared; the conduct rule asks whether it should exist. A disclosed kickback is a documented one.

options.text: Yes, but only if the company proves it paid above-market fees
options.misconception: makes employer loss an ingredient
options.why: The clause requires acceptance of the share, nothing more. Loss aggravates; its absence does not absolve.

options.text: Yes — Part II of the First Schedule reaches members in service, and accepting a share of the employer's lawyer's fees is its named misconduct
options.why: The Part exists because the practice-only reading he relies on was too convenient: a member in employment who accepts any part of the fees of a lawyer, CA, broker or agent engaged by the employer commits professional misconduct in terms. Market-rate fees do not cure it — the kickback corrupts his judgment about whom to engage, which is the mischief whether or not the price moved.

options.text: No — the CA Act's schedules govern practice, and employment is outside them
options.misconception: the exact belief Part II was written to defeat
options.why: The Part is titled for members in service. Membership carries the discipline into employment; only the applicable clauses change.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part II

items.scenario: A chartered accountant employed as a company's finance head engages a law firm for the company's litigation. The law firm, grateful for the steady work, credits him personally 10 per cent of its fees each quarter. He reasons that the conduct rules bind only members in practice, and that his employer suffers no loss since the legal fees are market rate.

items.stem: What should the forms actually be?

options.text: 3CB for both, as prepared — one uniform form simplifies compliance
options.misconception: chooses forms by convenience instead of by the other-law audit test
options.why: Rule 6G's split is the whole point of having two forms. A 3CB on a company asserts an opinion this engagement never formed, over an audit that already exists.

options.text: 3CD alone for both — the particulars are what the department reads
options.misconception: ships the annexure without its report
options.why: 3CD is a statement of particulars, certified by the report that covers it. Without 3CA or 3CB there is no auditor's report at all, and the filing is invalid.

options.text: 3CA with 3CD for the company; 3CB with 3CD for the proprietorship
options.why: The company's accounts already carry a Companies Act audit opinion, so the tax auditor reports in Form 3CA, referencing that audit and certifying the particulars in 3CD. The proprietorship has no other audit, so Form 3CB applies and this engagement itself opines on the accounts' true and fair view. "Fuller is safer" would have the tax auditor re-opining on statements another auditor signed.

options.text: 3CA for both, since a chartered accountant's involvement makes any audit statutory
options.misconception: reads "audited under any other law" as "audited by anyone"
options.why: The proprietorship's accounts are audited under no law but 44AB itself. With no other statutory audit to lean on, 3CA would reference an opinion that does not exist.

citation.ref: Section 44AB with Rule 6G

items.scenario: A CA accepts two tax audits: a private limited company whose statutory audit another firm completed last month, and a proprietorship trading firm with ₹4 crore turnover whose accounts nobody else audits. His article assistant prepares Form 3CB for both, reasoning that 3CB is the fuller form and fuller is safer, with Form 3CD attached to each.

items.stem: What does CARO 2020 require of the auditor here?

options.text: Nothing — CARO concerns the financial statements, and the books are correct
options.misconception: audits only the shareholder-facing set
options.why: The clause's subject is the bank-facing set. Correct books beside inflated bank statements is precisely the reportable condition, not a defence to it.

options.text: Report under clause 3(ii)(b) that the quarterly returns do not agree with the books, with details of the differences
options.why: Limits above five crore sanctioned against current assets put the company squarely in the clause, and its question is exactly this comparison. Padded stock statements inflate drawing power — borrowing against inventory that is not there — and the clause was inserted after bank frauds built on that habit. The explanation is the finding: management admits the two sets differ.

options.text: Qualify the audit opinion, since a 20 per cent difference is material
options.misconception: escalates a CARO disclosure into an opinion modification
options.why: The books — and so the financial statements — are right; the opinion has no misstatement to qualify. The CARO report carries the finding, and the banker reading it learns what the drawing power was built on.

options.text: Report only if the bank itself has complained of the difference
options.misconception: waits for the victim to notice
options.why: The clause asks the auditor to compare, not to await grievances. The banker's ignorance of the padding is the reason the auditor's comparison exists.

citation.ref: Clause 3(ii)

items.scenario: A company enjoys ₹40 crore of sanctioned working capital limits against stock and debtors. Comparing the quarterly stock statements filed with the bank against the books, the auditor finds the bank statements consistently report inventory 20 per cent higher. Management explains the bank figures are "estimates for drawing power" and the audited books are what matters.

items.stem: What does the performance audit examine that the department's defence does not touch?

options.text: Nothing — clean transactions at good prices exhaust an auditor's mandate
options.misconception: caps government audit at the voucher
options.why: That cap would grade every failed scheme by its bookkeeping. The C&AG's performance mandate asks what the public got, not only what the department spent.

options.text: Fraud — such waste must mean embezzlement to find
options.misconception: assumes failure implies theft
options.why: Programmes fail honestly through poor design and worse execution. Performance audit documents that failure and recommends redesign; investigation waits for indicators of dishonesty, absent here.

options.text: Efficiency and effectiveness — output per rupee and outcomes against the programme's purpose — where regular, economical spending can still fail
options.why: The defence covers regularity and one E, economy. Performance audit's other two Es are the ones bleeding: 30 per cent coverage measures poor efficiency of conversion from money to canals, and unchanged yields measure ineffectiveness against the objective the outlay was voted for. Cheap pipes to nowhere are the case the three-E framework exists to name.

options.text: The policy choice of irrigation itself, which the audit should condemn
options.misconception: audits the legislature's choice instead of the executive's delivery
options.why: Policy objectives belong to government; audit takes them as given and measures delivery against them. The line protects both the auditor's neutrality and the report's authority.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings

items.scenario: A state irrigation programme spent exactly its budget, every rupee sanctioned and vouched, buying pipes at good prices — but five years on, the canals reach 30 per cent of the intended farmland and crop yields in the command area are unchanged. A performance audit is criticised by the department: "every transaction was regular and economical; there is nothing left to audit."

items.stem: What does SRE 2410 require here?

options.text: Report the margin jump as a key audit matter in the review report
options.misconception: borrows the audit report's furniture for a review
options.why: KAMs belong to audit reports under SA 701. The review concludes in negative assurance — after the doubt is resolved — or carries a modification if it cannot be.

options.text: Resign the review and demand a full audit of the quarter
options.misconception: escalates past the standard's own answer
options.why: The standard's answer is extension, proportionate to the doubt. Most anomalies resolve in a day of targeted work; abandoning the engagement is for impasses, not first responses.

options.text: Extend procedures until the margin doubt resolves — a possible material misstatement suspends the lighter routine
options.why: Inquiry and analytics are the review's floor, not its ceiling. A fifteen-point margin jump is precisely the anomaly the analytics exist to surface, and once a possible material misstatement comes to the auditor's attention the standard requires additional procedures — corroborating the mix claim against sales data, testing cut-off, whatever the doubt demands. Timetables yield to unresolved doubts, or the conclusion does.

options.text: Accept the explanation — limited assurance means limited scepticism
options.misconception: scales scepticism down with the assurance level
options.why: The assurance level scales the planned procedures, never the auditor's duty to chase what those procedures find. Negative assurance over a known open doubt is a false statement in negative form.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information (SRE 2410)

items.scenario: During a quarterly limited review, analytical procedures show the quarter's gross margin jumping from 24 to 39 per cent with no price change the auditor knows of. The CFO's explanation is one line: "better product mix." The review timetable allows two days. The audit senior proposes accepting the explanation since limited reviews are built on inquiry, and confirmations would exceed the engagement's scope.

items.stem: What does the NOCLAR framework require of you?

options.text: Resign quietly as the partner suggests — exit ends the involvement
options.misconception: the silent exit the framework was written to prevent
options.why: A resignation that leaves the discharge running and the successor unwarned protects only the resigner. NOCLAR obliges a response proportionate to the harm, and this harm is bodily.

options.text: Escalate to those charged with governance, press for rectification, and if the response fails, weigh public-interest disclosure to the authority — quiet resignation alone is the barred response
options.why: The framework's sequence has begun and cannot stop at a CFO who calls the crime a cost. Governance must be engaged formally; their answer here is apparently the same, which pushes the member to the further-action stage: assessing whether the public interest — a poisoned river against a client relationship — requires disclosure to the regulator, which the Code's confidentiality rule expressly permits for NOCLAR. Resignation may eventually accompany the response; it cannot substitute for it.

options.text: Maintain confidentiality absolutely — the auditor's duty is to the client alone
options.misconception: reads confidentiality without its NOCLAR gate
options.why: The Code itself carves the gate: disclosure in accordance with the NOCLAR provisions is not a breach. Confidentiality protects clients' affairs, not their continuing crimes against third parties.

options.text: Report the matter to the police immediately, before any internal step
options.misconception: skips the sequence in the other direction
options.why: The framework starts with management and governance because rectification is the best outcome and they may yet deliver it. External disclosure is the assessed last resort, not the reflex first step.

citation.ref: Responding to Non-Compliance with Laws and Regulations

items.scenario: Mid-audit, you find your client has been discharging untreated effluent for years, concealed by falsified pollution-control reports — a criminal offence endangering a river town. The CFO, confronted privately, says the board knows and considers the penalties cheaper than the treatment plant, and reminds you that client information is confidential. A partner suggests quietly resigning the engagement after this year's report.

items.stem: What does clause 3(iii) actually surface here?

options.text: Prejudicial terms, the on-demand share to related parties, and the March renewals settling old loans — the clause was drafted for this exact pattern
options.why: Interest-free and term-free lending to group entities is what "terms prejudicial to the company's interest" describes. The clause separately demands the percentage of loans repayable on demand or without terms, related-party share included — a disclosure that does not care that no default has technically occurred — and its renewal limb asks precisely whether fresh loans settled existing ones. The no-overdue defence answers one sub-clause of several.

options.text: A qualification of the audit opinion for the interest foregone
options.misconception: turns a CARO disclosure into a misstatement
options.why: Foregone interest is a commercial choice reported through CARO and related-party disclosures; the accounts are not misstated by it. The opinion qualifies for accounting failures, not generous lending.

options.text: Only a going concern doubt about the borrowers
options.misconception: relocates a lender-side reporting duty to the borrowers' health
options.why: The clause reports the company's own lending conduct. Borrower distress may matter elsewhere; the prejudicial terms and rollovers report here even if every borrower is solvent.

options.text: Nothing — loans repayable on demand carry no schedule to breach
options.misconception: the technical defence the sub-clauses outflank
options.why: The clause was amended to catch evergreen demand loans: their share must be disclosed regardless of default, and the renewal question exposes the March rollovers directly.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii)

items.scenario: A company's books show ₹25 crore lent to group entities: interest-free, no written terms, repayable "on demand" — a demand never made in four years. Each March, fresh loans to the same parties retire the oldest balances. Management assures the auditor that demand loans cannot be overdue, so clause 3(iii) has nothing to report.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 110 conclude about power over each investee?

options.text: Power over neither until the investor can also point to a contractual arrangement, a board majority or a shareholders' agreement
options.misconception: demands a documented route to power when voting rights on their own can supply it
options.why: Contractual arrangements are one of the things an investor considers where the voting picture is inconclusive. They are not a precondition. Requiring one would make the guidance on holdings below a majority unusable.

options.text: Power over both, since in each company the investor is the largest single shareholder
options.misconception: stops at being the largest holder without asking how easily the others can combine against the investor
options.why: Relative size matters because of what it implies about outvoting. Six holders of 10 per cent need only meet once to outvote a 40 per cent holder; thousands of 1 per cent holders with no means of consulting each other realistically cannot. Being largest is evidence, not an answer.

options.text: Power over Alpha Ltd on the size of the holding relative to the others, without further evidence; over Beta Ltd the holding alone settles nothing and other facts must be weighed
options.why: Power can rest on voting rights that fall well short of a majority. Where the relevant activities are directed by a majority vote, one investor holds sufficiently more voting rights than any other, and the other shareholdings are widely dispersed, the absolute size of that holding and the relative size of the other holdings can settle the question on their own — 45 per cent against thousands of holders none above 1 per cent is the standard's own example of that. Where six other holders own 10 per cent each, the number of parties required to outvote the investor is small, so size alone is not conclusive and the investor must go on to weigh potential voting rights, rights from other contractual arrangements and the remaining facts and circumstances.

options.text: No power over either, because neither holding carries more than half the votes
options.misconception: reads control as a head count of votes, when the standard asks whether the investor can in practice direct the relevant activities
options.why: A majority of votes is the easiest route to power, not the only one. If it were the only one, an investor facing thousands of unconnected 1 per cent holders would control nothing while directing everything the company does, which is the position Ind AS 110 was written to catch.

citation.ref: para B41 to B45, read with the definition of power in para 10 and the assessment in para 7
