items.scenario: An acquirer pays ₹100 crore for a subsidiary whose identifiable net assets have an acquisition date fair value of ₹65 crore, so goodwill of ₹35 crore is recognised. The tax authority allows no deduction for that goodwill at any time, including when the subsidiary later disposes of the underlying business, so the goodwill's tax base is nil. Two years later the acquirer writes the goodwill down by ₹9 crore for impairment, which the tax authority does not allow either, so the taxable temporary difference on the goodwill falls to ₹26 crore.

items.stem: What does the company do about the ₹80 lakh at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Recognise a liability when the obligation arises, to the extent the contributions payable will not be available as a refund or as a reduction in future contributions after they are paid into the plan; the liability increases the defined benefit liability so that no gain or loss is expected
options.why: The company's general point is ordinarily right — a requirement to contribute does not affect the measurement, because once paid the contributions become plan assets and the additional net liability is nil. The Appendix to Ind AS 19 identifies the case where that breaks down. Where an entity has an obligation under a minimum funding requirement to pay contributions covering an existing shortfall for services already received, it must ask whether those contributions will be available as a refund or as a reduction in future contributions after they are paid in. To the extent they will not, a liability is recognised when the obligation arises, and it increases the defined benefit liability so that no gain or loss is expected when the money is actually paid.
keywords: no gain or loss is expected

options.text: Nothing at 31 March 2026, because the asset ceiling applies only where the plan is in surplus and this plan is in deficit
options.misconception: reads the whole Appendix as being about the ceiling, when it also asks when a funding requirement creates a liability
options.why: The ceiling limits a surplus, and there is no surplus here. The Appendix addresses three issues, and the third is when a minimum funding requirement might give rise to a liability — which does not depend on the plan being in surplus at all. A deficit plan whose contributions are irrecoverable is exactly the case it was written for.

options.text: Nothing — the company is right, because a contribution becomes a plan asset on payment and so leaves the net defined benefit liability unchanged
options.misconception: applies the general position to the one case the Appendix carves out of it
options.why: The reasoning holds only while the money remains the company's in some form once it is in the plan, whether as a refund it can draw or as contributions it will not have to make later. Here the rules allow no refund and the actuary has found no reduction in future contributions, so the ₹80 lakh leaves the company and never comes back in any shape. That is a cost the company is already committed to, and it belongs on the balance sheet now.

options.text: Disclose the ₹80 lakh as a contractual commitment, since it is a future contribution and Ind AS 19 requires disclosure of expected contributions for the next annual period
options.misconception: answers a recognition question with the disclosure that sits beside it
options.why: Expected contributions for the next annual reporting period are indeed disclosed, and that disclosure exists alongside the recognition rule rather than instead of it. Where the contributions payable to meet an existing shortfall will not be available afterwards, the Appendix requires a liability to be recognised, and a note cannot stand in for an amount the standard says goes on the face of the statements.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para 23 and 24, read with the asset ceiling in para 64

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company's defined benefit plan is in deficit on the Ind AS 19 measurement. A statutory minimum funding requirement obliges the company to pay ₹80 lakh of contributions during the year to 31 March 2027 to make good a shortfall for past service measured on the minimum funding basis. The plan rules permit no refund to the company in any circumstances, and the actuary determines that once these ₹80 lakh are in the plan they will not reduce the contributions the company must make for future service either. The company's view is that a contribution can never affect the measurement of a defined benefit liability, because the money becomes a plan asset the moment it is paid.

items.stem: How is the ₹100 crore attributed between the owners of the parent and the non-controlling interests?

options.text: ₹90 crore to the owners of the parent and ₹10 crore to the non-controlling interests
options.misconception: carries the potential-voting-rights test from the question of power across to the question of attribution, where the standard excludes it
options.why: Potential voting rights are weighed in deciding whether an investor has power over an investee, and that is where their work ends. Attribution is on present ownership interests alone. Counting the options twice would give the parent 90 per cent of a profit on which it has no present claim, and would leave the minority carrying a share of the results of shares they still own.

options.text: ₹65 crore to the owners of the parent and ₹35 crore to the non-controlling interests
options.why: The proportion of profit or loss and changes in equity allocated to the parent and the non-controlling interests is determined solely on the basis of present ownership interests and does not reflect the possible exercise or conversion of potential voting rights and other derivatives. The 25 per cent of options therefore change nothing in the attribution, however certain their exercise looks, and the instruments themselves are accounted for under Ind AS 109. The exception is narrow — where an entity has, in substance, an existing ownership interest as a result of a transaction that currently gives it access to the returns associated with an ownership interest, the proportion allocated is determined by taking that eventual exercise into account. The 5 per cent contract is that case, so P Ltd is attributed 65 per cent.

options.text: ₹65 crore to the owners of the parent and ₹35 crore to the non-controlling interests, with the 25 per cent of options presented within non-controlling interests in the consolidated balance sheet
options.misconception: treats an instrument conferring no present ownership as a component of the equity attributable to non-controlling interests
options.why: The split of the profit is right and the balance sheet is not. Non-controlling interest is the equity in a subsidiary not attributable to the parent, and an option that entitles its holder to nothing until exercise is not equity of the subsidiary held by anybody. Ind AS 109 governs the options, which is what the attribution rule expressly leaves them to.

options.text: ₹60 crore to the owners of the parent and ₹40 crore to the non-controlling interests
options.misconception: applies the general rule to both instruments and misses the in-substance ownership exception that reaches the second one
options.why: Ignoring the options is right and ignoring the 5 per cent contract is not. The exception asks whether the transaction currently gives the entity access to the returns associated with an ownership interest, and a contract that hands over the dividends today does exactly that. Where it applies, Ind AS 109 is not applied to the instrument at all.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B89 and B90

items.scenario: P Ltd holds 60 per cent of the ordinary shares of S Ltd and consolidates it. P Ltd also holds currently exercisable options over a further 25 per cent of S Ltd's ordinary shares, deeply in the money, which carry no right to any dividend or to any share of net assets until they are exercised; the options were counted in concluding that P Ltd has power over S Ltd. Separately, P Ltd has a contract over another 5 per cent of S Ltd's shares which, from today, entitles it to the dividends and other returns on those shares. S Ltd's profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹100 crore and it has no other comprehensive income.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 112 require of the note?

options.text: The significant judgements and assumptions behind the conclusion on the type of joint arrangement, and information presented separately for each class of interest with an explanation of how interests have been aggregated
options.why: An entity discloses the significant judgements and assumptions it has made in determining the nature of its interest in another entity or arrangement and the type of joint arrangement in which it has an interest. An arrangement carried on through a separate vehicle is a joint venture unless the legal form, the contractual terms or other facts give the parties rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities, so concluding that this one is a joint operation is exactly the kind of judgement a reader cannot reconstruct from the figures. The Standard also requires information to be presented separately for interests in subsidiaries, joint ventures, joint operations, associates and unconsolidated structured entities, and requires the entity to disclose how it has aggregated its interests in similar entities.

options.text: The judgement disclosure is needed only where the conclusion is that the arrangement is a joint venture, that being the outcome that keeps assets off the balance sheet
options.misconception: makes the disclosure turn on which answer was reached rather than on a judgement having been made at all
options.why: The requirement attaches to the judgement, not to its outcome. A joint operation puts the company's share of the assets and liabilities on its own balance sheet and a joint venture puts one equity-accounted line there, so a reader needs the reasoning whichever way the classification went.

options.text: Nothing at all for the structured entity, since the company does not control it and it is therefore outside the group the note describes
options.misconception: reads Ind AS 112 as reaching only what is consolidated
options.why: Unconsolidated structured entities are one of the classes the Standard names, and they are the class it was most concerned to bring into view — an interest that carries risk without appearing in the consolidated figures is precisely what a reader cannot otherwise see. The scope covers interests in subsidiaries, joint arrangements, associates and unconsolidated structured entities alike.

options.text: One combined table is enough, provided every interest the company holds appears somewhere in it
options.misconception: aggregates across the five classes the Standard requires to be presented separately
options.why: Aggregation is allowed within a class of similar entities and is not allowed across the classes. Information is presented separately for subsidiaries, joint ventures, joint operations, associates and unconsolidated structured entities, because the risks a reader is being told about differ completely between them, and the entity must say how it aggregated whatever it did aggregate.

citation.ref: para 7, read with the requirement to present information separately by class of interest and to disclose how interests have been aggregated

items.scenario: A company has three sets of interests. It and one other party jointly control an arrangement carried on through a company incorporated for the purpose, and after weighing the legal form, the contractual terms and the other facts it has concluded that the arrangement is a joint operation rather than a joint venture. It holds interests in two associates. And it holds an interest in a structured entity that it does not consolidate. The draft note sets out one combined table headed "interests in other entities", and says nothing about how the joint arrangement came to be classified, on the ground that Ind AS 111 already gives the test.

items.stem: What stands between the fund and the definition of an investment entity?

options.text: The perpetual debt alone — an exit strategy is needed for debt that has the potential to be held indefinitely but not for the five-year bonds, and having one investor and two investments does not by itself disqualify the fund
options.why: An investment entity shall have an exit strategy documenting how it plans to realise capital appreciation from substantially all of its equity investments and non-financial asset investments, and shall also have an exit strategy for any debt instruments that have the potential to be held indefinitely, for example perpetual debt investments. Debt with a fixed maturity cannot be held indefinitely, so the five-year bonds need none. More than one investment, more than one investor and investors who are not related parties are typical characteristics of an investment entity, and the absence of one or more of these typical characteristics does not necessarily disqualify an entity but indicates that additional judgement is required.

options.text: Nothing — the equity exit strategies are documented and debt repays itself, so the fund already meets the definition
options.misconception: treats every debt instrument as self-liquidating, when perpetual debt has no maturity to rely on
options.why: A fixed-maturity bond does repay itself and needs no plan. Perpetual debt does not, which is why the requirement names it. Without an exit strategy for it the fund is holding an investment it has no documented intention of ever realising, which is the opposite of what an investment entity does.

options.text: Nothing, because an exit strategy is required only for equity investments and both debt holdings are outside the requirement
options.misconception: stops at the equity limb of a requirement that reaches debt with no maturity as well
options.why: The requirement runs to substantially all equity and non-financial asset investments and then, expressly, to debt instruments that have the potential to be held indefinitely. Reading it as equity-only would let a fund hold perpetual paper forever and still call itself an investment entity.

options.text: The single investor and the two investments — those are conditions of the definition and the fund fails them outright
options.misconception: turns the typical characteristics into conditions of the definition
options.why: The definition has three elements — obtaining funds from investors to provide them with investment management services, committing to invest solely for capital appreciation or investment income, and measuring and evaluating performance on a fair value basis. The typical characteristics sit beside those elements, and their absence indicates that additional judgement is required rather than settling the matter.

citation.ref: para 27 and 28, read with the application guidance in Appendix B on exit strategies and on the typical characteristics of an investment entity

items.scenario: A fund obtains money from investors, provides them with investment management services, commits in its offering document to invest solely for capital appreciation and investment income, and measures and evaluates every holding on a fair value basis. It has documented how it plans to realise each of its equity investments within five to eight years. It also holds perpetual debt issued by one investee, for which it has no exit plan, and five-year bonds issued by another, for which it also has no exit plan. The fund has one investor and two investments, both substantial.

items.stem: What must the finished statement show?

options.text: The ₹20 lakh in profit or loss, being the excess of what the parent paid over the carrying amount of the interest it acquired
options.misconception: routes a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners through performance
options.why: Buying out a minority that the parent already controlled is a dealing between the owners of a business, not a purchase of one. It has its own named line inside transactions with owners, and nothing about it reaches the year's result.

options.text: One combined adjustments line is enough, both amounts arising under Ind AS 8 and both landing in equity
options.misconception: merges two adjustments the standard requires to be shown separately from each other
options.why: A change in accounting policy and a correction of an error say different things about the company. One is a decision about how to report; the other is an admission that an earlier report was wrong. The requirement to show them separately, component by component and period by period, exists so that a reader can tell which happened.

options.text: The ₹60 lakh and the ₹15 lakh shown separately by component of equity as adjustments to the opening balances, for each prior period and at the beginning of the period, and the ₹20 lakh inside transactions with owners as a change in ownership interest that does not result in a loss of control
options.why: The statement of changes in equity must disclose the total adjustment to each component of equity resulting from changes in accounting policies and, separately, from corrections of errors, and those adjustments are disclosed for each prior period and at the beginning of the period. Retrospective adjustments and retrospective restatements are not changes in equity of this year at all — they are adjustments to the opening balance of retained earnings, or of another component where an Ind AS requires it, which is where the ₹15 lakh on the revaluation surplus belongs. The reconciliation for each component then discloses separately the changes resulting from transactions with owners in their capacity as owners, showing separately contributions by and distributions to owners and changes in ownership interests in subsidiaries that do not result in a loss of control.

options.text: Both adjustments among this year's movements, with the ₹20 lakh correctly placed inside transactions with owners
options.misconception: gets the ownership change right and leaves retrospective adjustments in the wrong period
options.why: The half that is right does not save the half that is not. A retrospective adjustment restates the opening balance of the earliest period presented; showing ₹75 lakh as movements of the year to 31 March 2026 would make this year look ₹75 lakh worse and leave the earlier periods still reported on the old basis.

citation.ref: para 110, read with para 106(b) and 106(d)

items.scenario: For the year ended 31 March 2026 a company does three things. It changes an accounting policy retrospectively, which reduces the opening retained earnings of the earliest period presented by ₹60 lakh. It corrects a prior period error, which reduces the opening revaluation surplus by ₹15 lakh. And it buys a further 10 per cent of a subsidiary from the minority, ₹20 lakh of the price being taken directly to equity attributable to the owners of the parent. The draft statement of changes in equity shows a single line called "adjustments" of ₹75 lakh among this year's movements and puts the ₹20 lakh inside profit for the year.

items.stem: Over which periods must the segment information be presented?

options.text: For the nine months and its comparative alone, since interim information is reported on a year-to-date basis
options.misconception: reads the year-to-date basis as replacing the interim period rather than accompanying it
options.why: Year-to-date describes the basis of the cumulative column, not the whole requirement. The current interim period is presented as well, and without it the movement inside the latest three months is invisible.

options.text: For the three months and the nine months, with a comparative for the year ended 31 March 2025 rather than for the corresponding periods
options.misconception: compares an interim period against a full prior year instead of against the comparable interim period
options.why: The comparative for a statement of profit and loss is the comparable interim period of the immediately preceding financial year. Only the balance sheet takes the end of the immediately preceding financial year as its comparative, and it does so because a balance sheet is a position at a date rather than a performance over a stretch of time.

options.text: For the three months and its comparative alone, as drafted, a quarterly report being about the quarter
options.misconception: drops the cumulative year-to-date columns that sit alongside the interim period
options.why: A quarter on its own can be flattered or spoiled by timing. The cumulative figures exist so that a reader can see the year as it has actually run, which is why the standard asks for both and not for a choice between them.

options.text: For the three months ended 31 December 2025 and cumulatively for the nine months to that date, each with a comparative for the corresponding periods of the previous financial year
options.why: Interim information is normally reported on a financial year-to-date basis, and the periods rule requires statements of profit and loss for the current interim period and cumulatively for the current financial year to date, with comparative statements of profit and loss for the comparable interim periods, current and year-to-date, of the immediately preceding financial year. The interim segment disclosure follows those periods, so the note needs four columns and not two.

citation.ref: para 20, read with the interim segment disclosure in para 16A(g)

items.scenario: A listed company with a 31 March year end publishes quarterly interim reports and discloses segment information in its annual financial statements under Ind AS 108. It is preparing the report for the quarter ended 31 December 2025, its third quarter. The draft gives segment revenue and a measure of segment result for the three months ended 31 December 2025, with a comparative for the three months ended 31 December 2024, and nothing further.

items.stem: Which of the four enter the disclosure?

options.text: The lease liabilities, the swap and the overdraft, an overdraft being borrowed money like any other
options.misconception: treats an overdraft that forms part of cash management as a financing liability
options.why: Where a bank overdraft is repayable on demand and forms an integral part of an entity's cash management, it is included as a component of cash and cash equivalents. The balance swings between positive and negative as part of one cash position, and no cash flow from financing activities arises on it at all.

options.text: The lease liabilities alone, since the disclosure is about liabilities and a derivative asset cannot enter it
options.misconception: reads the heading and misses the express extension to financial assets that hedge those liabilities
options.why: The heading is a description, not the boundary. The requirement is extended in terms to changes in financial assets where the cash flows from them run through financing activities, and the example the standard itself gives is an asset that hedges a financing liability. Leaving the swap out would show the borrowing moving with exchange rates and hide the instrument that offsets it.

options.text: All four, since every one of them will be settled in cash sooner or later
options.misconception: makes eventual cash settlement the test, when the test is how that cash flow is classified
options.why: Everything on a balance sheet is settled in cash eventually. What decides membership is the classification of the cash flow — financing, operating or investing — and trade payables for raw materials are operating however certainly they will be paid.

options.text: The lease liabilities and the swap; the overdraft and the trade payables stay out
options.why: Liabilities arising from financing activities are liabilities for which cash flows were, or future cash flows will be, classified in the statement of cash flows as cash flows from financing activities. That takes in the lease liabilities and leaves out trade payables, whose payments are operating. The requirement also applies to changes in financial assets, for example assets that hedge liabilities arising from financing activities, if cash flows from those financial assets were, or future cash flows will be, included in cash flows from financing activities, which is why the swap belongs in the reconciliation whichever side of the balance sheet it happens to sit on. The overdraft is a component of cash and cash equivalents, so its movements are inside the balance being explained rather than a financing cash flow to be reconciled.

citation.ref: para 44A and 44C, read with the definition of cash equivalents in para 8

items.scenario: A company is drawing up the disclosure on liabilities arising from financing activities and argues over four balances. Its lease liabilities, on which the cash payments are presented as financing cash flows. A bank overdraft repayable on demand which forms an integral part of the company's cash management and is included in cash and cash equivalents. Trade payables for raw materials. And a cross-currency swap taken out to hedge a dollar borrowing, whose settlements are presented within financing cash flows.

items.stem: Is the consultant right?

options.text: No, but Company B measures in the most advantageous market instead, the exchange being closed to it
options.misconception: reaches for the fallback when the entity does have a principal market of its own
options.why: The most advantageous market answers only in the absence of a principal market. Company B has one — the regional market is the market with the greatest volume and level of activity that B can access — so the fallback is never reached and no comparison of net proceeds across markets is made.

options.text: Yes for a commodity traded on an exchange, though Company B would use its own market for an asset that had no exchange at all
options.misconception: makes access relevant only where no larger market exists, when it qualifies the identification of the principal market in every case
options.why: Whether a market is an exchange or not changes nothing. The question in every case is which market with the greatest volume and level of activity the entity can access, and an exchange the entity cannot deal on fails that question exactly as a closed private market would.

options.text: Yes — fair value is a market-based measurement, so the deepest market for the commodity fixes one price for every holder
options.misconception: reads a market-based measurement as one that ignores which markets the holder can actually reach
options.why: Market-based means the measurement uses the assumptions market participants would use rather than the entity's own intentions. It does not mean the entity is priced in a market it cannot trade in. Access at the measurement date is written into the identification of the principal market for that reason.

options.text: No — the exchange is Company A's principal market and the regional market is Company B's, so the two properly report different fair values for the same commodity
options.why: Fair value is measured in the principal market, and the principal market is the market with the greatest volume and level of activity for the asset that the entity can access at the measurement date. A market the entity cannot enter cannot be its principal market, whatever its size. There could be different principal markets for different reporting entities even if they belong to the same group, and the assessment is made separately for different assets as well, so two holders of the same commodity reaching different fair values is the expected outcome rather than an inconsistency to be fixed.

citation.ref: para 16 and 19

items.scenario: Two unrelated companies each hold the same commodity at 31 March 2026. Company A is a member of the national exchange, which has by far the greatest volume and level of activity for the commodity, and deals there routinely. Company B is not a member, cannot become one before the reporting date, and can deal only in a regional market with much lower volumes, where it has always transacted. A consultant tells Company B that fair value is a property of the asset, so B must measure at the exchange price too.

items.stem: Does either contract contain a significant financing component?

options.text: The retention contract only, a customer who withholds money being in substance lent it back
options.misconception: reads a performance-protection retention as consideration deferred for the sake of finance
options.why: The money is withheld because the work may prove defective, and the amount withheld is proportional to that risk rather than to the passage of time. That is the difference arising for reasons other than the provision of finance, which the standard names as taking the contract outside the financing rules.

options.text: Both of them, since the one-year practical expedient is unavailable and more than a year passes in each case
options.misconception: treats the length of the gap as the whole test, when the overriding provision is reached first
options.why: The practical expedient removes the adjustment where the gap is a year or less. Failing the expedient does not create a financing component; it only means the entity must go and ask whether one exists, and the overriding provision answers that neither of these has one.

options.text: Neither of them
options.why: Ind AS 115 carries an overriding provision. A contract would not have a significant financing component where the customer paid for the goods or services in advance and the timing of the transfer of those goods or services is at the discretion of the customer — the prepaid mobile card is the standard's own example — or where the difference between the promised consideration and the cash selling price arises for reasons other than the provision of finance and is proportional to the reason for the difference, the example given being payment terms that protect one party from the other failing to complete its obligations. A defect retention is that second case. Neither contract is adjusted for the time value of money.
keywords: reasons other than the provision of finance

options.text: The prepaid card only, since the customer parts with cash before receiving anything at all
options.misconception: makes advance payment by itself decisive, which is the very case the discretion limb removes
options.why: Advance payment is what makes the question worth asking, not what answers it. Where the customer decides when the service is taken, the entity is not being financed by the delay — the customer is choosing it — and the standard removes such a contract by name.

citation.ref: para 62(a) and 62(c), read with para 60 and the practical expedient in para 63

items.scenario: Two contracts are under review. In the first, a construction company is paid by milestones that coincide with its performance, and the customer retains 10 per cent of each milestone payment until one year after completion as protection against defects. In the second, a telecom company sells prepaid cards; the customer pays now and decides when, within a stated band of time, to use the minutes. In both contracts more than a year passes between some of the cash and the related performance, so the one-year practical expedient is unavailable.

items.stem: How does the operator recognise its consideration for the construction services?

options.text: Wholly an intangible asset, since the operator must run the metro for twenty-five years before it earns anything at all
options.misconception: reads the obligation to operate as making every entitlement contingent
options.why: Having to perform is not the same as having to hope. The annuity is payable whatever the ridership, so once the operator performs, the amount is not contingent on anything the public does. Only the fare entitlement carries demand risk.

options.text: Wholly a financial asset, the authority having guaranteed part of the return under a single arrangement with a single grantor
options.misconception: lets a partial guarantee carry the whole consideration into a financial asset
options.why: A financial asset arises only so far as the operator has an unconditional right to receive cash. Nothing is guaranteed on the fare side, so the operator carries the ridership risk on ₹500 crore of its consideration, and that risk is precisely what the split exists to show.

options.text: Split it, recognising a financial asset for the guaranteed portion and an intangible asset for the fare-based portion, each component measured initially at the fair value of the consideration received or receivable
options.why: Where the operator is paid for the construction services partly by a financial asset and partly by an intangible asset, it is necessary to account separately for each component of the operator's consideration, and the consideration received or receivable for both components is recognised initially at the fair value of the consideration received or receivable. The guaranteed annuity gives an unconditional contractual right to receive cash from or at the direction of the grantor, which is a financial asset. The fare entitlement is a right to charge users of a public service whose amounts are contingent on the extent to which the public uses that service, which is an intangible asset.

options.text: Split, but with the intangible asset taken as the residual once the financial asset has been recognised at the present value of the guaranteed annuity
options.misconception: applies a residual method the Appendix does not use
options.why: Each component is recognised initially at the fair value of the consideration received or receivable for it. A residual would make the intangible asset absorb every error in measuring the other component, and would make the two halves of one contract measured on two different bases.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 18, read with para 16 and 17

items.scenario: An operator builds a metro line for a state authority under a twenty-five-year concession, spending ₹1,200 crore. Under the contract the authority pays a guaranteed annuity whatever the ridership, and the operator additionally collects fares from passengers, with no guarantee of any kind on the fare side and no shortfall made good. On the model both parties used to price the bid, ₹700 crore of the consideration for the construction services is attributable to the guaranteed annuity and ₹500 crore to the fare entitlement.

items.stem: May the company take the low-value recognition exemption on both head leases?

options.text: On neither — an intermediate lessor may take no recognition exemption at all
options.misconception: overstates a bar that reaches the low-value election and leaves the short-term one standing
options.why: The short-term exemption survives a sublease. Where the head lease is a short-term lease that the entity has accounted for under that exemption, the sublease is simply classified as an operating lease. It is the low-value election alone that a sublease closes off.

options.text: On the first only — a lessee that subleases an asset, or expects to sublease it, cannot account for that head lease as a lease of a low-value asset
options.why: If a lessee subleases an asset, or expects to sublease an asset, the head lease does not qualify as a lease of a low-value asset. The bar applies to the intermediate lessor whatever the underlying asset is worth, so a right-of-use asset and a lease liability are recognised on the second head lease. That matters beyond the balance sheet, because a sublease is classified by reference to the right-of-use asset arising from the head lease, and while the exemption is being taken there is no such asset to measure the sublease against.

options.text: On both, provided the sublease itself turns out to be an operating lease
options.misconception: makes the bar depend on how the sublease is classified, when it bites before the classification is reached
options.why: Classification comes later and depends on the right-of-use asset the head lease creates. The bar operates first, on the fact of subleasing or expecting to sublease, and it is what brings that right-of-use asset into existence in the first place.

options.text: On both — the low-value election is available asset by asset, and an item does not stop being of low value because somebody else uses it
options.misconception: applies the low-value election to a head lease the standard removes from it
options.why: The election is indeed made asset by asset, and that is not the point. The standard takes a subleased head lease out of the election altogether, before the value of the underlying item is ever considered, because the lessee has stopped being a user and become a lessor.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B7, read with para 5 and 6 and the sublease classification in para B58

items.scenario: A company takes two head leases on the same day, each of a single item of office furniture that is of low value when new, each for three years, and neither carrying a purchase option. It intends to use the first item itself. At the same time it subleases the second item to a tenant for the whole three years.

items.stem: How does the company account for the ₹90 crore?

options.text: Add the ₹90 crore to the cost and take the ₹50 crore to other comprehensive income against the revaluation surplus
options.misconception: applies the revaluation-model route to an asset carried at cost, and to an impairment rather than to the liability change
options.why: Two things go wrong at once. The revaluation route in the Appendix applies only where the related asset is measured using the revaluation model, and this one is not; and even there it governs the liability change itself, not an impairment loss arising afterwards. There is also no revaluation surplus on this asset for the amount to sit in.

options.text: Add the ₹90 crore to the cost of the refinery and depreciate ₹210 crore over eight years, an increase in a provision not being an impairment indicator
options.misconception: takes the addition to cost as the end of the matter, when the Appendix names it as the trigger to look further
options.why: The Appendix does not leave this to the general list of impairment indicators; it makes the addition to cost itself the thing the entity must consider. The reason is plain enough — a bigger obligation to clean up does not make the plant more valuable, so a carrying amount that has just been raised by one is exactly where recoverability is in doubt.

options.text: Add it to the cost of the refinery, then test the asset for impairment because the addition is an indication that the new ₹210 crore carrying amount may not be fully recoverable, recognise a ₹50 crore impairment loss and depreciate the remaining ₹160 crore over eight years
options.why: Under the cost model a change in a decommissioning, restoration or similar liability is added to, or deducted from, the cost of the asset in the current period, and the provision is adjusted to match. The Appendix then requires that if the change and the resulting adjustment result in an addition to the cost of an asset, the entity shall consider whether this is an indication that the new carrying amount of the asset may not be fully recoverable — and if it is such an indication, shall test the asset for impairment by estimating its recoverable amount and account for any impairment loss in accordance with Ind AS 36. Here ₹210 crore against a recoverable amount of ₹160 crore gives an impairment loss of ₹50 crore, and what is left is depreciated over the eight years that remain.

options.text: Recognise the ₹90 crore as an expense of the year, since it arises from a regulation and a rate change rather than from anything the refinery gained
options.misconception: expenses a change the Appendix capitalises under the cost model
options.why: Under the cost model the change is added to, or deducted from, the cost of the asset. Only a decrease that exceeds the asset's carrying amount reaches profit or loss, and separately the periodic unwinding of the discount is a finance cost. Expensing the increase would leave the asset and the provision measured on different bases from the same estimate.

citation.ref: Appendix A, para 5(a) and 5(c), read with Ind AS 36

items.scenario: A refinery carried under the cost model has a carrying amount of ₹120 crore at 31 March 2026 and a remaining useful life of eight years. A new regulation and a fall in the market discount rate raise the present value of the decommissioning obligation by ₹90 crore at that date. The refinery's recoverable amount at 31 March 2026, measured under Ind AS 36, is ₹160 crore. There is no revaluation surplus in existence for this asset.

items.stem: What deferred tax asset does the parent recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: None
options.why: An entity recognises a deferred tax asset for all deductible temporary differences arising from investments in subsidiaries, branches and associates and interests in joint ventures, to the extent that, and only to the extent that, it is probable that the temporary difference will reverse in the foreseeable future and that taxable profit will be available against which the temporary difference can be utilised. Both limbs must hold. The signed agreement satisfies the first and the absence of any forecast taxable profit defeats the second, so nothing is recognised however certain the reversal is.

options.text: ₹14 crore, because a deductible temporary difference is always recognised in full, the restrictions in Ind AS 12 on investments applying only to taxable temporary differences
options.misconception: reads the investment rules as reaching deferred tax liabilities alone
options.why: Both sides are addressed. Taxable temporary differences on such investments give a liability unless a two-part exception is met, and deductible temporary differences give an asset only where a two-part condition is met. The second rule exists because an investor may have no way of turning a book loss on an investment into a tax deduction it can use.

options.text: ₹14 crore, the binding agreement making reversal in the foreseeable future certain
options.misconception: takes the reversal condition as the whole test, when the recognition rule joins two conditions with "and"
options.why: Reversal only creates the deduction; it does not create anything to deduct it from. A company with no taxable profit gets no benefit from a deductible amount, and a deferred tax asset is an asset precisely because a benefit is expected. Both conditions are required together.

options.text: None, because a deductible temporary difference on an investment in a subsidiary can never be recognised
options.misconception: turns a test with two conditions into a prohibition
options.why: It is recognised whenever both conditions are met, and they often are — a committed sale producing a deduction against expected taxable profit is exactly the case the rule was written to allow. What defeats it here is the absence of taxable profit, not the fact that the investment is in a subsidiary.

citation.ref: para 44

items.scenario: A parent's investment in a foreign subsidiary carries an amount of ₹180 crore in the consolidated financial statements against a tax base of ₹250 crore, a deductible temporary difference of ₹70 crore. The parent has signed a binding agreement to sell the subsidiary in the year ending 31 March 2027, so the difference will certainly reverse. The parent has, however, a long record of tax losses in the jurisdiction where the relief would arise and its forecasts show no taxable profit there in any year covered by them. The rate the parent is told applies to such a deduction is 20 per cent.

items.stem: How are the three amounts treated?

options.text: The ₹80 lakh deducted from equity and the other two charged to profit or loss, a buy-back being a use of cash rather than an equity transaction
options.misconception: leaves a reacquisition of the entity's own shares outside the meaning of an equity transaction
options.why: Reacquiring the entity's own equity instruments is an equity transaction as surely as issuing them is — the consideration paid is deducted from equity and no gain or loss on the instruments reaches profit or loss. The costs of doing it follow the transaction they belong to.

options.text: The whole ₹117 lakh to profit or loss, costs of raising or returning capital being period costs like any other
options.misconception: treats the cost of a transaction with owners as an operating expense of the business
options.why: These costs buy nothing that is used in trading. They are the cost of a movement in the company's own capital, so they are set against that movement rather than against the year's results, which is what deducting them from equity does.

options.text: The whole ₹117 lakh deducted from equity, the abandoned issue included, since an equity transaction was intended in every case
options.misconception: deducts from equity a cost that produced no equity transaction at all
options.why: The deduction attaches to an equity transaction that happens. Where the issue is abandoned there is no movement in equity for the cost to attach to, and the standard says in terms that the costs of an equity transaction that is abandoned are recognised as an expense.

options.text: The ₹80 lakh and the ₹12 lakh are deducted from equity, with any related income tax dealt with under Ind AS 12, and the ₹25 lakh on the abandoned issue is an expense; the amount taken out of equity is disclosed separately
options.why: The transaction costs of an equity transaction are accounted for as a deduction from equity to the extent they are incremental costs directly attributable to the equity transaction that otherwise would have been avoided, and issuing and acquiring the entity's own equity instruments are both equity transactions, so the buy-back costs go the same way as the issue costs. The costs of an equity transaction that is abandoned are recognised as an expense. Income tax relating to transaction costs of an equity transaction is accounted for in accordance with Ind AS 12, and the amount of transaction costs accounted for as a deduction from equity in the period is disclosed separately.

citation.ref: para 37 and 39, read with para 35A

items.scenario: A company incurs three lots of costs during the year ended 31 March 2026. It pays ₹80 lakh of merchant banker and legal fees on a rights issue that completes. It pays ₹25 lakh on a second issue that it abandons after market conditions turn, so no shares are ever issued. And it pays ₹12 lakh of stamp duty and brokerage on buying its own shares back through the exchange. The finance head proposes to charge the whole ₹117 lakh to profit or loss as professional and regulatory expenses.

items.stem: What does the company recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹40 lakh in other comprehensive income, and then an immediate reclassification of ₹15 lakh out of the reserve into profit or loss, leaving ₹25 lakh in the reserve
options.why: The cash flow hedge reserve is adjusted to the lower, in absolute amounts, of the cumulative loss on the hedging instrument at ₹40 lakh and the cumulative change in the present value of the hedged expected future cash flows at ₹42 lakh, so ₹40 lakh goes to other comprehensive income and there is no ineffectiveness to recognise. But where the amount accumulated in the reserve is a loss and the entity expects that all or a portion of that loss will not be recovered in one or more future periods, it shall immediately reclassify the amount that is not expected to be recovered into profit or loss as a reclassification adjustment. Waiting for the forecast sales would defer a loss the company already knows it will bear.

options.text: ₹15 lakh left in the reserve and ₹25 lakh reclassified to profit or loss, the unrecoverable part being the effective portion
options.misconception: reverses which part of the accumulated loss is reclassified
options.why: The amount reclassified is the amount that is not expected to be recovered, which is the ₹15 lakh. What stays in the reserve is the part that still relates to cash flows the forecast sales will produce, and it will move to profit or loss when they do.

options.text: ₹40 lakh in other comprehensive income and nothing in profit or loss until the forecast sales occur, as the finance head proposes
options.misconception: applies the ordinary timing rule to a loss the standard requires to be taken now
options.why: The reserve is normally reclassified to profit or loss in the periods during which the hedged expected future cash flows affect profit or loss, and that is the rule the finance head has in mind. It carries an exception written in mandatory terms for a loss that will not be recovered, and the company has already concluded that ₹15 lakh will not be.

options.text: ₹42 lakh in other comprehensive income, being the cumulative change in the hedged item, with ₹2 lakh of ineffectiveness in profit or loss
options.misconception: takes the higher of the two cumulative amounts, when the reserve is set at the lower in absolute amounts
options.why: The test is a lower-of test taken in absolute amounts, and ₹40 lakh is the smaller. An under-hedge leaves part of the hedged item's movement unhedged rather than creating ineffectiveness to book, so there is nothing for the ₹2 lakh to be.

citation.ref: para 6.5.11(a), (b) and (d)(iii)

items.scenario: A company designated a forward contract as the hedging instrument in a cash flow hedge of highly probable forecast dollar sales expected in the year ending 31 March 2027. Every qualifying criterion is met. At 31 March 2026 the cumulative loss on the hedging instrument since inception is ₹40 lakh and the cumulative change in the present value of the hedged expected future cash flows since inception is ₹42 lakh. The forecast sales remain highly probable, but the company has assessed that ₹15 lakh of the accumulated loss will not be recovered in any future period. The finance head proposes to leave the whole ₹40 lakh in the cash flow hedge reserve until the sales occur.

items.stem: Are the terms substantially different, and how do the two fees enter the answer?

options.text: Yes — only the ₹3 crore paid to the lender enters the test, giving ₹353 crore against ₹395 crore and a difference of about 10.6 per cent, so the old loan is extinguished, and both fees are then recognised as part of the gain or loss on the extinguishment
options.why: In determining the fees paid net of any fees received for the 10 per cent test, a borrower includes only fees paid or received between the borrower and the lender, including fees paid or received by either the borrower or the lender on the other's behalf. The law firm is neither party, so the ₹5 crore stays out of the test — ₹350 crore plus the lender's ₹3 crore is ₹353 crore against ₹395 crore, a difference of about 10.6 per cent, which makes the terms substantially different and the modification an extinguishment. Where an exchange or modification is accounted for as an extinguishment, any costs or fees incurred are recognised as part of the gain or loss, and at that stage both fees count.

options.text: Yes, but only the ₹3 crore paid to the lender enters the gain or loss, the ₹5 crore of legal advice being a period expense
options.misconception: carries the test's restriction forward into the measurement of the gain or loss, where it does not apply
options.why: The restriction to fees between the borrower and the lender belongs to the test alone, where it exists so that a borrower cannot manufacture a 10 per cent difference by hiring advisers. On extinguishment, any costs or fees incurred are recognised as part of the gain or loss, which takes in the law firm's ₹5 crore as well.

options.text: No, because a renegotiation with the same lender on the same principal can never be substantially different, nothing having been exchanged
options.misconception: reads the rule as reaching only an exchange of instruments, when a substantial modification of terms is treated the same way
options.why: An exchange between an existing borrower and lender of debt instruments with substantially different terms is accounted for as an extinguishment, and a substantial modification of the terms of an existing financial liability is accounted for in the same way, whether or not it is attributable to the financial difficulty of the debtor. Who the lender is settles nothing; the test does.

options.text: No — both fees belong in the test, giving ₹358 crore against ₹395 crore and a difference of about 9.4 per cent, so the loan survives and both fees adjust its carrying amount
options.misconception: puts a third party's fee into a test the standard confines to fees between the borrower and the lender
options.why: The costs counted for the test are not the costs counted once the answer is known. For the test the standard names only fees paid or received between the borrower and the lender; it is afterwards, and only where the modification does not result in derecognition, that any costs or fees incurred adjust the carrying amount and are amortised over the remaining term of the modified liability.

citation.ref: para 3.3.2 and 3.3.3, with the 10 per cent test and the fees included in it in Appendix B, para B3.3.6

items.scenario: A company renegotiates a term loan with the same lender on 1 October 2025. Its carrying amount is ₹400 crore. The company pays the lender an amendment fee of ₹3 crore and pays an independent law firm ₹5 crore for advice on the amendment. Discounted at the original effective interest rate, the remaining cash flows of the old loan have a present value of ₹395 crore, and the cash flows under the new terms, before any fee, have a present value of ₹350 crore.

items.stem: What is open to each company?

options.text: The first may take it if it translates the previous GAAP carrying amounts into the new functional currency at the transition-date rate
options.misconception: tries to cure a closed gate with a translation, when the condition is that the functional currency has not changed at all
options.why: The condition is absolute — the election is available where there is no change in functional currency on the date of transition. Translating old amounts into a new functional currency is exactly the exercise the condition exists to prevent, because those amounts were never measured on that basis.

options.text: The first may not take the election at all; the second may, and may take it for its investment property too
options.why: The election to continue with the carrying value of all of its property, plant and equipment as measured under previous GAAP and to use that as deemed cost is available only where there is no change in the entity's functional currency on the date of transition to Ind AS. That gate is closed for the first company, which is left with retrospective application or with fair value at the date of transition as deemed cost. For the second company the gate is open, and the same measurement option can be applied to investment property.

options.text: The first may take it, and the second may not extend it to investment property, the election being written for property, plant and equipment alone
options.misconception: inverts both limbs of the answer
options.why: The functional currency condition is what stops the first company, and the option is expressly available for investment property as well, so the second company is the one with the wider choice rather than the narrower.

options.text: Both may take it, a change in functional currency being a translation matter that does not touch the deemed cost election
options.misconception: misses the condition the election opens with
options.why: The condition is the first thing the election says. It exists because previous GAAP amounts were measured in the old functional currency, and carrying them forward once the currency of measurement has changed would give a starting cost expressed in a currency the entity no longer reports in.

citation.ref: para D7AA

items.scenario: Two companies adopt Ind AS from 1 April 2026, with 1 April 2025 as the date of transition. The first company's functional currency changes on the date of transition from the rupee to the dollar, and it wants to continue with the previous GAAP carrying amounts of all its property, plant and equipment as deemed cost. The second company's functional currency does not change, and it wants the same treatment for all its property, plant and equipment and for its investment property as well.

items.stem: What do the 2021 amendments to Division II require?

options.text: The benami and virtual currency disclosures only, the surrendered income being covered by the current tax note
options.misconception: lets the tax note absorb a disclosure Schedule III asks for by name
options.why: The tax note explains the charge for the year. This disclosure exists because income was surrendered and never entered the books at all, which is a fact about the reliability of the records rather than about the tax computation, and Schedule III asks for it separately for that reason.

options.text: Only the ratio note — the other three are income-tax and regulatory matters that sit outside the financial statements
options.misconception: reads the 2021 amendments as a ratio note and nothing else
options.why: The amendments were written precisely to bring matters of this kind onto the face of the notes, where an auditor sees them and a reader can find them. A prescribed disclosure does not stop being one because the underlying subject is also dealt with by another regulator.

options.text: All three, but in the Board's report rather than in the notes to the financial statements
options.misconception: moves a prescribed note into the directors' report
options.why: Schedule III prescribes the format and content of the financial statements, and what it requires goes in them. The Board's report carries its own list under the Companies Act, and reporting something there does not discharge a Schedule III requirement.

options.text: All three carry their own disclosure alongside the ratio note — details of the benami proceedings, the income surrendered and not recorded in the books, and the dealings in the virtual currency
options.why: The 2021 amendments added a block of additional information to Division II of which the ratio note is one item among several. Others require details of any proceedings initiated or pending against the company for holding any benami property, disclosure of any income surrendered or disclosed in a tax assessment that has not been recorded in the books of account, and details of any crypto currency or virtual currency traded or invested in during the year. Each is a prescribed note, and a company cannot select among them.
keywords: not been recorded in the books

citation.ref: Schedule III Division II — additional regulatory information inserted by the 2021 amendments

items.scenario: A company preparing its financial statements under Division II of Schedule III has three matters on the table. Proceedings have been initiated against it under the law prohibiting benami transactions. It surrendered income during a search assessment which has not been recorded in its books of account. And it bought and sold units of a virtual digital currency during the year. The chief financial officer says the ratio note is the only thing the 2021 amendments added, so none of the three needs anything in the notes.

items.stem: Under which provision, if any, can he be held guilty?

options.text: Clause 2 of Part II of the Second Schedule — being an employee of any company, firm or person, disclosing confidential information acquired in the course of his employment, the only exceptions being disclosure required by law and disclosure permitted by the employer
options.why: Part II of the Second Schedule holds four clauses and binds a member of the Institute whether in practice or not. Its clause 2 makes a member guilty where, being an employee of any company, firm or person, he discloses confidential information acquired in the course of his employment, except as and when required by any law for the time being in force or except as permitted by the employer. Neither exception is available here — no law required the file to be handed over and the employer permitted nothing. Whether the file carried a marking is not the test; the clause turns on the information being confidential and having been acquired in the course of employment.
keywords: Part II of the Second Schedule

options.text: Clause 1 of Part I of the Second Schedule, for disclosing information acquired in the course of his professional engagement without his client's consent
options.misconception: charges a member in employment under a clause written for a member in practice
options.why: Part I of the Second Schedule is headed professional misconduct in relation to Chartered Accountants in practice, and its clause 1 speaks of information acquired in the course of a professional engagement and of the consent of a client. This member has an employer, not a client, and holds no certificate of practice.

options.text: No clause reaches him, since he certified nothing and expressed no opinion
options.misconception: assumes professional misconduct requires an audit, a report or a certificate
options.why: Part II of the Second Schedule reaches members of the Institute generally, and none of its four clauses asks whether the member reported on anything. Clause 2 is written for the member who is somebody's employee, which is exactly what he is.

options.text: Clause 4 of Part II of the Second Schedule, for defalcating money received in his professional capacity
options.misconception: reaches for the wrong clause of the right Part
options.why: Clause 4 covers a member who defalcates or embezzles money received in his professional capacity. No money moved here; what left the company was information, and clause 2 of the same Part addresses that by name.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, clause 2

items.scenario: A Chartered Accountant employed as a group financial controller, holding no certificate of practice, gives a friend at a rival company a copy of his employer's customer pricing file. He says two things in his defence. He certified nothing and expressed no opinion, so no clause of the Schedules reaches him. And the file carried no confidentiality marking, so his employer's permission was not needed.

items.stem: How many of the four offend the principle of confidentiality?

options.text: All four, but only the partner and the manager can be answerable, an articled assistant not being a member of the Institute
options.misconception: locates the duty in the assistant alone when the accountant who controls him carries it
options.why: Whether the assistant is a member is not the question the principle asks. The accountant shall take reasonable steps to ensure that personnel under the accountant's control respect the accountant's duty of confidentiality, so a firm that told him nothing has failed that requirement in its own right.

options.text: Two — a prospective client is owed nothing until the engagement is accepted, and a family conversation is private
options.misconception: makes the duty start with the engagement letter and stop at the front door
options.why: Both limbs are written out expressly. Information disclosed by a prospective client is covered, which is why a firm that declines an engagement may not trade on what it learned while considering it; and the accountant must be alert to inadvertent disclosure in a social environment and particularly to an immediate or close family member.

options.text: Three — the file passed inside the firm is not a breach, the duty running to outsiders
options.misconception: reads confidentiality as a wall around the firm rather than around the information
options.why: The principle names confidentiality within the firm or employing organisation as its own requirement. A client hands information to the accountant for a purpose, and a colleague with no part in that purpose is as much a stranger to it as anybody outside the door.

options.text: All four
options.why: The principle requires an accountant to be alert to the possibility of inadvertent disclosure, including in a social environment and particularly to a close business associate or an immediate or a close family member; to maintain confidentiality of information within the firm or employing organisation; to maintain confidentiality of information disclosed by a prospective client or employing organisation; and to take reasonable steps to ensure that personnel under the accountant's control, and individuals from whom advice and assistance are obtained, respect the accountant's duty of confidentiality. None of the four is helped by the circumstances that override confidentiality, because none is required by law, authorised by the client, or a professional duty or right to disclose.

citation.ref: Section 114 — Confidentiality, sub-paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (g)

items.scenario: Four things happen in one firm in a month. A partner describes a client's forthcoming results at a family dinner to his brother, who has no connection with the client. A manager forwards a client's file to a colleague in another service line who has no need of it. A prospective client's projections are discussed with an outsider after the firm decides not to accept the engagement. And an articled assistant, who has been told nothing about confidentiality, mentions a client's name at a college reunion.

items.stem: Which of them may use the relief?

options.text: The first and the third, and the second for its transactions with the department alone
options.misconception: splits the relief transaction by transaction, when it attaches to the status of the reporting entity
options.why: The relief is available to a reporting entity that is itself government-related, and it then covers that entity's dealings with the government and with other entities under the same government. An entity that is not government-related has nothing to be relieved of, since a customer relationship generated no disclosure in the first place.

options.text: The first and the third only
options.why: A government-related entity is an entity that is controlled, jointly controlled or significantly influenced by a government. Significant influence over the first is enough and the third is controlled outright, so both qualify. The second does not, because selling to a government department makes that department a customer, and a customer with whom an entity transacts a significant volume of business is not a related party simply by virtue of the resulting economic dependence — there is no related party relationship for the relief to relieve.

options.text: All three, any entity whose fortunes depend on a government being government-related
options.misconception: reads economic dependence as the test, when the definition names control, joint control and significant influence
options.why: Dependence is a commercial fact rather than a relationship the standard recognises. Ind AS 24 says in terms that departments and agencies of a government that does not control, jointly control or significantly influence the reporting entity are not related parties simply by virtue of their normal dealings with it.

options.text: The third only, the relief being written for entities a government controls
options.misconception: drops joint control and significant influence out of a definition that names all three
options.why: The definition lists control, joint control and significant influence together, and the relief follows the definition. A government holding significant influence over a listed company can still produce the very problem the relief was written for — dealings with a long list of other entities under the same government.

citation.ref: para 9 definition of a government-related entity, and para 11(d) and (e), read with para 25

items.scenario: Three companies want to use the relief Ind AS 24 offers to government-related entities. The first is a listed company in which a state government holds 26 per cent and has the right to appoint two of its nine directors; the government is treated as having significant influence over it. The second sells the whole of its output to a central government department under an annual tender and has no government shareholding of any kind. The third is wholly owned by a municipal corporation.

items.stem: Do the Ind AS 103 business combination principles apply on the formation of this joint operation?

options.text: Yes, and the same answer would follow even if A Ltd, B Ltd and C Ltd were companies under the common control of one group
options.misconception: ignores the carve-out that sends a common control transaction to Appendix C of Ind AS 103 instead
options.why: The first half is right and the second half is not. Where the transaction is a common control transaction as defined in Ind AS 103, the entity does not apply these requirements at all — it applies the accounting specified in Appendix C of Ind AS 103 instead. These three companies are unrelated, so the carve-out is not reached, but the answer would change if they were not.

options.text: No — the requirements apply only where every party to the joint operation contributes a business, and here two of the three contribute assets
options.misconception: turns "one of the parties" into "all of the parties" and reads the exclusion backwards
options.why: The exclusion is drafted the other way round. The requirements do not apply if ALL of the parties that participate in the joint operation only contribute assets or groups of assets that do not constitute businesses. Requiring every party to bring a business would make the exclusion say nothing, since a single contributed business is what makes the formation the acquisition of a business in the first place.

options.text: No — the Ind AS 103 principles reach a joint operation only when an entity buys an interest in one that already exists, and a formation is by definition not an acquisition
options.misconception: reads the provision as covering purchases alone and misses the sentence that extends it to a formation
options.why: The extension to a formation is written into the Standard in terms, and it is not an afterthought — it is the reason a party cannot escape business combination accounting by arranging for the business to be dropped into a new vehicle instead of sold into an old one. What is true is that a formation has no previously held interest to worry about, so the question of remeasuring one does not arise here at all.

options.text: Yes — they apply to the formation of a joint operation if, and only if, an existing business is contributed on formation by one of the parties, and A Ltd's terminal is that contribution
options.why: The requirements that bring the Ind AS 103 principles across to an interest in a joint operation whose activity is a business also apply to the formation of a joint operation if, and only if, an existing business as defined in Ind AS 103 is contributed to the joint operation on its formation by one of the parties that participate in it. One party is enough — the gate asks whether a business came in, not whether every party brought one. The mirror of the rule is written beside it: these requirements do not apply to the formation of a joint operation if all of the parties only contribute assets or groups of assets that do not constitute businesses. B Ltd's plot of land and C Ltd's cash are that kind of contribution, but A Ltd's terminal is not, so the gate opens.

citation.ref: para 21A read with Appendix B paras B33A and B33D, and the common control carve-out to Appendix C of Ind AS 103

items.scenario: Three unrelated companies form a joint operation on 1 April 2026 to run a port terminal, each taking a one-third interest and the three sharing joint control. On formation, A Ltd transfers into the arrangement an existing terminal it has been operating for years, with its berths, cranes, staff, customer contracts and operating processes, which everybody agrees is a business as defined in Ind AS 103. B Ltd contributes a plot of adjoining land and nothing else. C Ltd contributes cash. The activity of the joint operation itself constitutes a business. The finance teams disagree about whether the Ind AS 103 principles come into play at all on a formation, as opposed to on a later purchase of an additional interest.

items.stem: Which of the three balances is, in substance, part of the net investment in S Ltd?

options.text: All three, since every one of them is a monetary balance with a foreign operation that has in practice stayed outstanding
options.misconception: treats a balance that happens to persist as a balance nobody plans to settle
options.why: Persisting is not the test, and the Standard excludes trade receivables and trade payables by name so that a rolling trading balance cannot be dressed up as permanent funding. Each year's invoices here ARE expected to be paid in the ordinary course; what stays constant is the level of trading, not the debt.

options.text: Only the third — the trade receivable is excluded whatever its age, the twelve-year loan does not qualify merely for being long, and the loan routed through T Ltd qualifies whatever currency it is denominated in
options.why: A monetary item receivable from or payable to a foreign operation forms part of the net investment only if settlement is neither planned nor likely to occur in the foreseeable future, and such items may include long-term receivables or loans but do not include trade receivables or trade payables. Age does not change that, so the six-year-old trading balance stays out. A long-term loan with a fixed maturity does not automatically qualify simply because it is of a long duration, unless management has expressed its intention to renew the loan at maturity so that the period of repayment is not foreseeable — and that intention must be documented by auditable evidence such as board minutes, which is exactly what is missing. The loan T Ltd made qualifies because, from the group's point of view, the funding relates to an investment in a foreign operation, and this is the case irrespective of the currency in which the loan is denominated.

options.text: The second and the third, a twelve-year maturity being long enough that repayment is not in the foreseeable future
options.misconception: reads duration as a substitute for the absence of a planned settlement
options.why: A fixed maturity is a plan. In the absence of management's intention to renew, the loan's maturity date implies that its settlement is planned in the foreseeable future, however far off that date is. Ten to fifteen years is the very example the study material uses to make the point, and the intention to renew has to be evidenced, not assumed.

options.text: Only a loan made by the parent itself can be part of the parent's net investment, so none of the three qualifies
options.misconception: requires the lender to be the reporting entity, when the consolidated statements look at the group's position
options.why: The funding here was arranged by P Ltd and provided by T Ltd on its direction, and in the consolidated financial statements the exchange difference on it goes to other comprehensive income because from the group's point of view the funding relates to an investment in a foreign operation. Which group company wrote the cheque does not change what the money is.

citation.ref: para 15 and 15A, with the study material's worked examples on a rolling trading balance and on funding routed through a fellow subsidiary

items.scenario: An Indian parent P Ltd is preparing consolidated financial statements and has three balances with its foreign subsidiary S Ltd. The first is a trade receivable for inventory P Ltd sells to S Ltd; the balance has stood on the books at every year end for six years running, though each year's invoices are expected to be paid in the ordinary course. The second is a loan from P Ltd to S Ltd with a fixed maturity twelve years away, on which the board has minuted no intention one way or the other about renewal. The third is a loan to S Ltd made, on P Ltd's direction, by T Ltd, another subsidiary of P Ltd, which nobody expects to be repaid and which is denominated in T Ltd's own functional currency, a third currency.

items.stem: How should the restated figures be translated into rupees?

options.text: All amounts — assets, liabilities, equity items, income and expenses — at the closing rate at the date of the most recent balance sheet, but the comparative column is left as the amounts previously presented as current year amounts in the prior year's statements
options.why: Where an entity's functional currency is that of a hyperinflationary economy, all amounts, being assets, liabilities, equity items, income and expenses including comparatives, are translated at the closing rate at the date of the most recent balance sheet. Average rates have no place here, because the restated figures are already expressed in one measuring unit and putting a different rate on income and expenses would undo that. The exception is the comparative column: when amounts are translated into the currency of a non-hyperinflationary economy, comparative amounts are those that were presented as current year amounts in the relevant prior year financial statements, not adjusted for subsequent changes in the price level or subsequent changes in exchange rates. The rupee is such a currency, so last year's column is left exactly as it was reported.
keywords: closing rate at the date of the most recent balance sheet
subsequent changes in the price level

options.text: All amounts including the comparatives at the closing rate at 31 March 2026, so that both columns are stated in the same rupees
options.misconception: applies the general rule and misses the carve-out for a non-hyperinflationary presentation currency
options.why: This is the rule as it stands for translation into the currency of another hyperinflationary economy, and the words "except that" immediately following it are what this answer drops. Translating into a non-hyperinflationary currency, the comparative amounts are those presented as current year amounts in the relevant prior year financial statements. Restating them again would move a figure the reader has already seen reported, for a price-level change that has nothing to do with the rupee.

options.text: Assets and liabilities at the closing rate, income and expenses at the average rate for the year, with the comparatives re-translated at this year's closing rate
options.misconception: applies the ordinary translation method to a hyperinflationary operation and then restates the comparatives it should have left alone
options.why: Both halves fail. The ordinary method, closing rate for assets and liabilities and transaction or average rates for income and expenses, is displaced where the functional currency is that of a hyperinflationary economy, and every amount goes at the closing rate at the date of the most recent balance sheet instead. And the comparatives translated into a non-hyperinflationary currency are not adjusted for subsequent changes in exchange rates at all.
