options.text: No reversal at all, because the unit's original loss fell first on goodwill and a goodwill impairment cannot be reversed
options.misconception: extends the bar on reversing goodwill to every other asset in the same unit
options.why: The bar is on goodwill and nothing else. The patent, the plant and the building each carry a loss that the standard requires to be reversed once the estimates behind recoverable amount have changed, and ₹34 lakh of it can be.

options.text: ₹42 lakh allocated pro rata on carrying amounts, being ₹7 lakh on the patent and ₹17.5 lakh on each of the plant and the building
options.misconception: applies the pro rata step without the ceiling that sits on each individual asset
options.why: Pro rata on ₹18, ₹45 and ₹45 lakh does give those figures, and every one of them breaches its own ceiling — the patent would reach ₹25 lakh against a ₹22 lakh limit and the plant and building ₹62.5 lakh against ₹60 lakh. A reversal may not carry an asset above where it would have stood had it never been impaired.

options.text: ₹42 lakh, taking the unit to its ₹150 lakh recoverable amount, with the ₹8 lakh the individual ceilings block credited back to goodwill
options.misconception: reverses an impairment loss recognised for goodwill, which the standard prohibits outright
options.why: Goodwill is the one asset whose impairment loss is never reversed, because any later increase in its recoverable amount is likely to be internally generated goodwill, which cannot be recognised. The ₹8 lakh simply is not recognised, and the unit stops at ₹142 lakh.

citation.ref: para 122 and 123, with the bar on reversing goodwill in para 124

items.scenario: A cash-generating unit was impaired two years ago, and the loss was large enough to write its goodwill down to nil. At 31 March 2026 it carries a patent at ₹18 lakh, plant at ₹45 lakh and a building at ₹45 lakh, ₹108 lakh in all. Recoverable amount has risen to ₹150 lakh and the indicators for a reversal are clearly met. Had no impairment loss ever been recognised, the carrying amounts net of depreciation at this date would have been ₹22 lakh for the patent, ₹60 lakh for the plant and ₹60 lakh for the building.

items.stem: How is the ₹9 crore treated?

options.text: Recognised in profit or loss as incurred, while the acquired brand itself stays on the balance sheet at ₹60 crore
options.why: Subsequent expenditure on brands, mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and items similar in substance is always recognised in profit or loss as incurred, whether the item was externally acquired or internally generated, because such expenditure cannot be distinguished from the cost of developing the business as a whole. The acquisition gave the brand a cost, measured in a transaction with a third party. The campaign gives it none, and the acquired asset is unaffected either way.
keywords: recognised in profit or loss as incurred
developing the business as a whole

options.text: Recognised in profit or loss, and the ₹60 crore brand written off as well, since brands cannot sit on a balance sheet
options.misconception: extends the bar on internally generated brands to a brand acquired in a business combination
options.why: The bar is on internally generated brands. A brand acquired as part of a business combination is recognised separately from goodwill where it is identifiable, and its acquisition-date fair value is its cost. Only the spending that follows is expensed.

options.text: Capitalised into the brand's carrying amount, the brand being a recognised asset already
options.misconception: applies the ordinary subsequent-expenditure test to a class of item the standard singles out by name
options.why: Ordinary subsequent expenditure on an intangible can be capitalised where it meets the recognition criteria. Brands and their cousins are carved out of that, precisely because nobody can tell where spending on the brand ends and spending on the business begins.

options.text: Capitalised to the extent an independent valuer certifies that the brand's value has risen by at least ₹9 crore
options.misconception: substitutes a valuation for a recognition rule
options.why: A valuer can price the brand, and the answer changes nothing. Recognition is settled before measurement is reached, and here the standard settles it against capitalisation whatever the value has done.

citation.ref: para 20, read with para 63

items.scenario: A company acquires a business and, as part of it, recognises an acquired brand at its ₹60 crore acquisition-date fair value. Over the following year it spends ₹9 crore on advertising, sponsorship and a repositioning campaign aimed squarely at that same brand. The marketing director says the ₹9 crore should be added to the brand's carrying amount, because it plainly makes the brand stronger and the brand is already an asset on the balance sheet.

items.stem: What is wrong with the accounting, and how does the plant stand at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — an asset still physically capable of use is depreciated whatever its classification, and the classification stands
options.misconception: keeps depreciating an asset whose carrying amount is now to be recovered by sale rather than by use
options.why: Depreciation allocates cost over the period an asset's benefits are consumed in use. Once recovery is through a sale transaction, there is no consumption to allocate, which is why the standard stops the charge at the classification date.

options.text: The plant is written up to ₹24 lakh, fair value less costs to sell now exceeding its carrying amount
options.misconception: reads the measurement rule as a two-way test rather than as a ceiling
options.why: The rule takes the lower of the two figures, so it can only ever write an asset down. Fair value above carrying amount changes nothing, and a gain is recognised only to the extent of impairment losses previously recognised on that asset.

options.text: The ₹5 lakh of depreciation should never have been charged; the plant remains classified as held for sale and is carried at ₹20 lakh
options.why: A non-current asset is not depreciated while it is classified as held for sale, because it is being recovered through sale rather than through use, so the ₹5 lakh comes back. The one-year period is extended where the delay is caused by events or circumstances beyond the entity's control and there is sufficient evidence that the entity remains committed to its plan to sell, and contamination found by a buyer's inspection is precisely that. Measurement stays at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, so ₹20 lakh stands.

options.text: The depreciation is rightly reversed, but classification must cease because the sale did not complete within one year
options.misconception: applies the one-year period as absolute, ignoring the extension for delays outside the entity's control
options.why: The one-year expectation is tested at classification, and the standard then provides for exactly this — a delay caused by circumstances beyond the entity's control, with the entity still committed to its plan. Declassifying here would reverse the presentation and restart depreciation on an asset that is genuinely for sale.

citation.ref: para 25 for depreciation, with the extension to the one-year period in Appendix B, para B1

items.scenario: A plant was classified as held for sale on 1 April 2025, when the criteria were plainly met. It then had a carrying amount of ₹20 lakh, fair value less costs to sell of ₹24 lakh, and four years of useful life left. The company went on charging depreciation of ₹5 lakh through the year. In February 2026 a committed buyer withdrew after its inspection found contamination nobody had known about; the company began remediation at once, is still actively marketing the plant and expects to sell within the following year. Fair value less costs to sell at 31 March 2026 is still ₹24 lakh.

items.stem: At what amounts are the two measured, and in which levels do the measurements sit?

options.text: The shares at ₹22.50 but still as a Level 1 measurement, the input remaining an exchange price for the identical share
options.misconception: keeps the Level 1 label on a measurement whose quoted price has been adjusted
options.why: The amount is right and the label is not. Level 1 is defined by quoted prices, unadjusted, in active markets for identical assets, and the word unadjusted does the work. The moment judgement is applied to the quote, the measurement drops out of that level.

options.text: The shares at ₹22.50 as a Level 2 measurement, and the unlisted security as a Level 3 measurement
options.why: A quoted price in an active market is used without adjustment whenever it is available, but a quoted price may fail to represent fair value where a significant event occurs on the measurement date after the close of trading. The non-approval was a condition of the asset existing at the measurement date and the ₹22.50 opening price shows how market participants priced it, so the closing price is adjusted, and once adjusted the measurement is no longer a Level 1 measurement. Where an observable input requires an adjustment using an unobservable input and that adjustment moves the result significantly, the measurement is categorised within Level 3.

options.text: The shares at ₹36 as a Level 1 measurement, an exchange closing price being used unadjusted, and the unlisted security as a Level 2 measurement
options.misconception: applies the unadjusted-quoted-price rule to a price that no longer reflects a condition existing at the measurement date, and ignores what a significant unobservable adjustment does to the level
options.why: The unadjusted rule holds while the quote is faithful. Here the market had not yet been told what the regulator had decided, so the closing price values a drug that had already failed. And an observable starting point does not keep a measurement in Level 2 once an unobservable adjustment is what drives it.

options.text: The shares at ₹36, with the fall disclosed as a non-adjusting event after the reporting period, and the unlisted security as a Level 3 measurement
options.misconception: treats the regulator's decision as an event after the reporting period, when it was a condition of the asset existing at the measurement date
options.why: The decision was taken and communicated on 31 March. What arrived afterwards was the market's reaction to it, and a reaction is evidence of a condition that already existed rather than a new event.

citation.ref: para 77 and 79, read with the level determination in para 73 and 75

items.scenario: A company holds listed shares in a biotechnology firm and measures them at fair value at 31 March 2026. The shares closed at ₹36 that day. After trading closed on 31 March the drug regulator told the firm that its lead drug had not been approved, the firm put out a press release that evening, and the shares opened at ₹22.50 on the next trading day. The company also holds an unlisted security priced from the quoted price of a similar traded instrument, reduced by a significant adjustment for a restriction on sale that no market data supports.

items.stem: How does the lessor classify this lease?

options.text: A single finance lease over the whole property, the thirty-year term covering the major part of the building's economic life
options.misconception: treats land and buildings as one unit when the land element is far from immaterial
options.why: A lessor may treat them as a single unit only where the amount for the land element is immaterial to the lease, in which case the building's economic life stands for the whole. Land worth ₹80 crore against a building worth ₹120 crore is not immaterial by any reading.

options.text: A single finance lease, because payments over one title cannot be split between the two elements
options.misconception: reaches for the fallback that applies where allocation is unreliable, when the scenario says the split can be made reliably
options.why: The fallback is real — where the lease payments cannot be allocated reliably the whole lease is a finance lease, unless it is clear that both elements are operating leases. It is reached only when allocation fails, and here the relative fair values are given.

options.text: The two elements are assessed separately — the building element is a finance lease and the land element an operating lease
options.why: For a lease that includes both land and buildings, the lessor assesses the classification of each element separately, given that land normally has an indefinite economic life. The lease payments are allocated between them in proportion to the relative fair values of the leasehold interests at the inception date, which is 60 to 40 here. Thirty years over a thirty-year building whose fair value is substantially recovered transfers substantially all the risks and rewards, so that element is a finance lease. Thirty years over land that will still be there afterwards transfers nothing like all of them, so that element is an operating lease.

options.text: A single operating lease over the whole property, land of indefinite life never transferring substantially all the risks and rewards
options.misconception: lets the land element decide the classification of the building element as well
options.why: The conclusion about land is right and it does not travel. Assessing the elements separately exists so that a building whose value is substantially recovered is recognised as sold on credit, whatever the ground it stands on.

citation.ref: para 55 and 56, read with the classification criteria in para 63

items.scenario: A lessor grants a thirty-year lease of a plot with a factory building standing on it. The building's remaining economic life is thirty years; the land's is indefinite. At the inception date the leasehold interests are worth ₹120 crore for the building and ₹80 crore for the land, and the annual rent can be reliably allocated in that proportion. The present value of the payments allocated to the building amounts to substantially all of the building's fair value.

items.stem: What deferred tax is recognised on the land?

options.text: None, because land is a non-depreciable asset and non-depreciable assets give rise to no temporary differences
options.misconception: denies that a difference exists at all, when one plainly does and it is the exception rather than its absence that blocks recognition
options.why: A temporary difference is the gap between carrying amount and tax base, and ₹50 crore against nil is a gap whether the asset depreciates or not. Getting the right answer from the wrong premise fails the moment the same land is revalued or sold under a regime that does allow a deduction.

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹12.5 crore, being 25 per cent of the ₹50 crore difference
options.misconception: applies the general rule to a difference the initial recognition exception carves out
options.why: The general rule is real and it has three exceptions written into the same paragraph. This transaction falls squarely inside the second of them, so the arithmetic is right and the recognition step never opens.

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹12.5 crore, with the matching debit added to the cost of the land
options.misconception: grosses up the asset, which is the outcome the exception was written to prevent
options.why: Carrying the land at ₹62.5 crore would report a plot at more than anyone paid for it, and then depreciate or impair that inflated figure. The standard names this and refuses it.

options.text: None, even though a ₹50 crore taxable temporary difference plainly exists
options.why: A deferred tax liability is recognised for all taxable temporary differences except where the liability arises from the initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction that is not a business combination and that, at the time of the transaction, affects neither accounting profit nor taxable profit. Both conditions hold on this purchase, so the exception bites and nothing is recognised. The alternative would be to gross up the cost of the land itself, which the standard says would make the financial statements less transparent.
keywords: neither accounting profit nor taxable profit

citation.ref: para 15(b) and para 22, read with the deferred tax asset mirror in para 24

items.scenario: A company buys a plot of land for ₹50 crore in a transaction that is not a business combination. Under the tax law the land carries no depreciation allowance and no deduction of any kind, on purchase or on eventual sale, so its tax base is nil. The purchase affects neither accounting profit nor taxable profit at the time it happens. The tax rate is 25 per cent. The finance team proposes a deferred tax liability of ₹12.5 crore on the ₹50 crore taxable temporary difference.

items.stem: What goes to profit or loss and what goes to other comprehensive income?

options.text: ₹38.4 crore charged to profit or loss and a ₹17 crore gain in other comprehensive income
options.why: Net interest is found by applying the discount rate to the net defined benefit liability, so 7 per cent of the ₹120 crore deficit is ₹8.4 crore, and that with the ₹30 crore of current service cost gives ₹38.4 crore in profit or loss. The return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest is a remeasurement, and the amount included in net interest is 7 per cent of the ₹500 crore of plan assets, being ₹35 crore. The actual return of ₹52 crore, already stated after the costs of managing plan assets, exceeds that by ₹17 crore, and the excess is recognised in other comprehensive income.

options.text: ₹38.4 crore charged to profit or loss and a ₹19 crore gain in other comprehensive income, adding back the ₹2 crore spent on managing the plan assets
options.misconception: treats the costs of managing plan assets as a separate expense, when the return on plan assets is defined net of them
options.why: The return on plan assets is interest, dividends and other income together with realised and unrealised gains, less the costs of managing plan assets and any tax payable by the plan itself. The ₹52 crore is already that net figure, so adding the ₹2 crore back counts it twice.

options.text: ₹30 crore charged to profit or loss, with the whole ₹52 crore earned on the plan assets credited there as investment income
options.misconception: puts the entire actual return through profit or loss, when only the part measured at the discount rate belongs there
options.why: Splitting the return at the discount rate is the whole design. The part the entity could have expected from the passage of time sits in profit or loss inside net interest; the part that depends on how markets happened to move is a remeasurement and stays out of the operating result.

options.text: ₹38.4 crore charged to profit or loss and nothing in other comprehensive income, there having been no actuarial gain or loss this year
options.misconception: reads remeasurements as meaning actuarial gains and losses alone
options.why: Remeasurements are three things and not one — actuarial gains and losses, the return on plan assets outside net interest, and any change in the effect of the asset ceiling outside net interest. The obligation was quiet this year and the assets were not.

citation.ref: para 123 and 127, with the definition of the return on plan assets in para 8 and the profit or loss and OCI split in para 120

items.scenario: At 1 April 2025 a company's gratuity plan holds plan assets with a fair value of ₹500 crore against a defined benefit obligation of ₹620 crore, and the discount rate at that date is 7 per cent. Through the year the plan assets earn ₹52 crore after ₹2 crore of costs of managing them. Current service cost is ₹30 crore. There were no contributions, no benefits paid, no plan amendment and no change in any actuarial assumption, and the timing of cash flows within the year may be ignored.

items.stem: What is provided for at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Nothing — neither the ₹4 crore fitting cost nor any fine, because no present obligation exists at the reporting date for either
options.why: Only obligations arising from past events existing independently of an entity's future actions are recognised as provisions. The company can avoid the fitting cost entirely by its own future actions — by changing its method of operation, or by closing or selling the factory — so there is no present obligation for it. The fine has a different obligating event, which is operating the factory without filters once the law bites, and that has not happened yet.

options.text: ₹4 crore, since the law is already enacted and the company cannot lawfully run the factory without filters
options.misconception: reads an enacted law as the obligating event, when the entity can still avoid the expenditure by changing what it does
options.why: Enactment fixes what will be required of anyone who chooses to operate; it does not oblige this company to operate. A law that can be sidestepped by the entity's own future decisions creates no liability today, however certain the company is that it will comply.

options.text: Nothing for the fitting, but a provision for the fines expected from 1 June 2026 onwards
options.misconception: provides for a penalty whose obligating event, operating without filters, has not yet occurred
options.why: A fine for unlawful operation is a genuine obligation once the unlawful operation happens, which is why penalties and clean-up costs for damage already caused are provided. Here nothing has been operated unlawfully at the reporting date.

options.text: Nothing recognised, but the ₹4 crore is disclosed as a contingent liability
options.misconception: calls a future cost the entity can avoid a contingent liability, when there is no possible obligation arising from a past event at all
options.why: A contingent liability is a possible obligation arising from past events whose existence depends on uncertain future events. There is no past event here. Future expenditure the entity controls is not disclosed as a contingency; it is simply next year's cost.

citation.ref: para 19, read with the recognition conditions in para 14 and the definition in para 10

items.scenario: A law taking effect on 1 June 2026 requires factories of a certain type to be fitted with smoke filters. At 31 March 2026 a company's factory has no filters and none has been ordered. Fitting them will cost ₹4 crore. A factory that operates after 1 June 2026 without filters attracts a fine. The company intends to keep the factory running and has not decided when it will fit them.

items.stem: How does Ind AS 32 classify the three instruments?

options.text: All three are equity, since none of the triggering events is within the issuer's control
options.misconception: inverts the rule — an event outside the issuer's control is what makes the instrument a liability, not what saves it
options.why: Control by the issuer is what would allow it to avoid payment. Where the issuer cannot avoid the settlement because the trigger is beyond its control, the obligation is real and the instrument is a liability.

options.text: The first is a financial liability; the second and third are equity
options.why: A contingent settlement provision that could require the issuer to deliver cash on the occurrence of an uncertain future event beyond the control of both the issuer and the holder makes the instrument a financial liability, and a revenue test is exactly such an event. Two exceptions rescue the others. An obligation that can arise only on liquidation of the issuer does not create a liability, and neither does a part of the provision that is not genuine, meaning one with no commercial substance.

options.text: The first is equity because the revenue test may never be met, and the second and third are liabilities
options.misconception: classifies on how likely the trigger is rather than on whether a contingent obligation exists
options.why: Probability plays no part. The question is whether the issuer has an obligation it cannot avoid should the event occur, and a revenue test the company cannot control is such an obligation whether it fires or not.

options.text: All three are financial liabilities, each of them being redeemable in cash on some event
options.misconception: applies the contingent settlement rule without the two exceptions written into it
options.why: The rule and its exceptions sit in one paragraph. Without them, every perpetual instrument would become a liability the moment somebody wrote a liquidation clause into it, and an absurd trigger would carry the same weight as a real one.

citation.ref: para 25, read with the exception for obligations arising on liquidation in para 16(b) and the definition in para 11

items.scenario: A company issues three instruments. The first must be redeemed in cash if the company's revenue falls below ₹500 crore in any of the next five years, an outcome neither the company nor the holders control. The second must be redeemed in cash only if the company goes into liquidation. The third carries a redemption clause triggered if a named director's grandchild is born on 29 February, a possibility both parties accept has no commercial substance whatever.

items.stem: Where is the simplified approach compulsory and where is it a choice?

options.text: Compulsory only for the 45-day receivables; for the other two, lifetime expected credit losses are an accounting policy the company may adopt but need not
options.why: The simplified approach is mandatory for trade receivables and contract assets that result from transactions within the scope of Ind AS 115 and contain no significant financing component. Where a trade receivable does contain a significant financing component, and for lease receivables, the entity may choose as its accounting policy to measure the loss allowance at lifetime expected credit losses; if it does not, the general three-stage model governs those balances. The policy is elected separately for trade receivables and for lease receivables.

options.text: Compulsory for all three, since the simplified approach exists precisely so that receivables need no staging assessment
options.misconception: reads the simplified approach as covering every receivable, when its mandatory limb is confined to those without a significant financing component
options.why: The convenience is real and its scope is not unlimited. Once a receivable carries a financing component it starts to behave like a loan, which is why the standard offers the simplification there instead of imposing it.

options.text: Compulsory for the first two and unavailable for the lease receivables, leasing being outside the scope of Ind AS 115
options.misconception: reads the scope of Ind AS 115 as the boundary of the election, when the standard extends it separately to lease receivables under Ind AS 116
options.why: Lease receivables are named in their own limb of the same paragraph, with their own election. And the second set is not compulsory, because its financing component is exactly what moves it into the optional limb.

options.text: Compulsory for none of them — the simplified approach is an election available across all three
options.misconception: turns a mandatory rule into an election
options.why: For plain trade receivables there is no choice at all. The word used is that an entity shall always measure the loss allowance at lifetime losses for them, which is why a provision matrix is the ordinary practice rather than an option.

citation.ref: para 5.5.15, read with the general model in para 5.5.3 and 5.5.5

items.scenario: A company holds three sets of balances at 31 March 2026. The first are trade receivables from ordinary 45-day sales with no financing element in them. The second are trade receivables on a three-year deferred-payment arrangement that does contain a significant financing component. The third are finance lease receivables from equipment the company lets out. The credit controller says the simplified approach must be applied to all three, since all three are receivables.

items.stem: What happens to each reserve balance?

options.text: All three are reclassified in full to profit or loss, each being a disposal of part of the group's interest
options.misconception: treats every reduction in a holding as a disposal of the whole foreign operation
options.why: Full reclassification belongs to a full disposal, or to a partial one that costs the group control. A 10 per cent sale that leaves control intact is a transaction with the group's own co-owners and never touches profit or loss.

options.text: All three balances stay in equity until the last share of each operation has been sold
options.misconception: waits for a complete exit before anything is recycled
options.why: The first operation has been sold outright, so its balance is recycled now, and the associate's proportionate share follows the interest that has gone. Only the subsidiary where control is retained keeps its balance inside equity, and even there it moves across to the non-controlling interests.

options.text: The first is reclassified in full to profit or loss, and both partial disposals are re-attributed to non-controlling interests
options.misconception: applies the re-attribution to an associate, which carries no non-controlling interest in the group's accounts
options.why: There is nothing to re-attribute to. An associate is equity accounted rather than consolidated, so no minority interest in it appears in the group balance sheet, and the proportionate share of the reserve goes to profit or loss instead.

options.text: The first is reclassified in full from equity to profit or loss; 10 per cent of the second is re-attributed to non-controlling interests; one-seventh of the third is reclassified to profit or loss
options.why: On disposal of a foreign operation, the cumulative exchange differences recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity are reclassified from equity to profit or loss when the gain or loss on disposal is recognised. On the partial disposal of a subsidiary that includes a foreign operation where control is retained, the entity instead re-attributes the proportionate share of the cumulative amount to the non-controlling interests, so nothing reaches profit or loss. In any other partial disposal only the proportionate share is reclassified to profit or loss, and 5 over 35 is one-seventh.
keywords: reclassified from equity to profit or loss

citation.ref: para 48, 48A, 48C and 48D

items.scenario: A group makes three moves in the year ended 31 March 2026. It sells its entire holding in a wholly owned foreign subsidiary. It sells 10 per cent of a second wholly owned foreign subsidiary and keeps control. It sells 5 percentage points of its 35 per cent stake in a foreign associate and keeps significant influence. Each of the three foreign operations has a credit balance standing in the foreign currency translation reserve.

items.stem: Where does each ₹12 crore gain go?

options.text: The first to profit or loss because the reason is evidenced, and the second to capital reserve because it is not
options.misconception: invents a profit-or-loss route for the evidenced case, which is the one that goes through other comprehensive income
options.why: Evidence changes the route, not the destination. With it the gain travels through other comprehensive income; without it, straight into equity. Neither reaches profit or loss.

options.text: Both to profit or loss on the acquisition date
options.misconception: applies the IFRS 3 treatment where the Indian text carves it out
options.why: IFRS 3 does take a bargain purchase gain to profit or loss, and that is the classic trap in an Ind AS paper. The Indian standard keeps an acquisition-day windfall out of earnings entirely.

options.text: The first through other comprehensive income, accumulated in equity as capital reserve; the second recognised directly in equity as capital reserve
options.why: The gain is recognised in other comprehensive income on the acquisition date and accumulated in equity as capital reserve where there exists clear evidence of the underlying reasons for classifying the business combination as a bargain purchase. A regulator's forced-sale order, on file, is that evidence. Where no clear evidence exists, the gain is recognised directly in equity as capital reserve instead, so it never passes through other comprehensive income at all.

options.text: Both through other comprehensive income into capital reserve, the destination being the same either way
options.misconception: takes the other comprehensive income route as the single Indian answer, missing the condition attached to it
options.why: The two routes end in the same place on the balance sheet and take different paths to it, and the path is what the statement of profit and loss and other comprehensive income shows. Without evidence of why the bargain arose, nothing is presented as income at all.

citation.ref: para 34 and 36, read with the reassessment requirement in para 36

items.scenario: A group makes two acquisitions in the same year, and after the reassessment the standard requires, each still shows a bargain purchase gain of ₹12 crore. In the first, a competition regulator had ordered the seller to dispose of the division within a fixed timetable, and the order and correspondence are on file. In the second, the deal team can point to no reason at all for the discount beyond a hard negotiation.

items.stem: Which of these may be measured at the proportionate share?

options.text: None of them — the choice is open only where the acquirer holds less than 75 per cent
options.misconception: invents a shareholding threshold on an election that has none
options.why: There is no percentage anywhere in the election. What matters is the character of the instrument the outsiders hold, not how much of the company the acquirer bought.

options.text: Only the 25 per cent of ordinary shares; the employee options and the preference shares are measured at their acquisition-date fair values
options.why: The choice between fair value and the proportionate share is offered only for components of non-controlling interest that are present ownership interests and that entitle their holders to a proportionate share of the entity's net assets in the event of liquidation. The ordinary shares are; the options confer no present ownership and the preference shares confer no share of net assets on liquidation. All other components of non-controlling interests are measured at their acquisition-date fair values unless another Ind AS requires a different basis.

options.text: All three, the election being made once for the whole business combination and then applied to everything the group does not own
options.misconception: reads the election as covering everything that carries the label non-controlling interest
options.why: The election is made for each business combination and it reaches only one kind of component. Anything else the acquiree has issued to outsiders sits outside it and comes in at fair value.

options.text: Only the preference shares, being the component whose proportionate share is easiest to measure
options.misconception: picks the component by ease of measurement rather than by the present-ownership test
options.why: Ease is not a criterion, and the preference shares are the clearest exclusion of the three, since they carry no entitlement to net assets on liquidation at all. Measuring them at a proportionate share of net assets would give them a share of something they have no claim on.

citation.ref: para 19, read with the measurement principle in para 18

items.scenario: An acquirer takes 75 per cent of a company. The other 25 per cent of the ordinary shares is held by outsiders and entitles them to a proportionate share of net assets on liquidation. The acquiree has also issued share options to its own employees, none of them yet exercisable, and a class of preference shares held by outsiders that carries no entitlement to any share of net assets on liquidation. The group controller proposes to measure all three at the proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets.

items.stem: What should the parent have done?

options.text: Treat both sales as equity transactions, since the parent still controlled the subsidiary when the first contract was signed
options.misconception: leaves the loss of control out of the accounting altogether
options.why: Control did leave, and when it does the group derecognises the subsidiary's assets, liabilities and non-controlling interests and recognises the resulting gain or loss in profit or loss. Keeping everything inside equity would record the exit of a business as a movement between owners.

options.text: Treat both sales as a loss of control, remeasuring the retained interest to fair value in March and again in April
options.misconception: recognises the loss-of-control gain twice on one disposal
options.why: Control is lost once. Treating the arrangements as a single transaction means one derecognition, one remeasurement of anything retained, and one gain, recognised when control actually goes.

options.text: Account for the two sales as a single transaction, control being lost on the combined disposal
options.why: A parent may lose control of a subsidiary in two or more arrangements, and circumstances sometimes indicate that the multiple arrangements should be accounted for as a single transaction. The indicators are all here — the arrangements were entered into in contemplation of each other, they form a single transaction designed to achieve an overall commercial effect, and neither is economically justified on its own. Splitting them would let a parent choose how much of the gain ever reaches profit or loss, and in which year.

options.text: Exactly what the accountant did — two separate contracts on two dates, with control genuinely passing only in April
options.misconception: takes the legal form of separate contracts as decisive, when the standard tests the substance across the arrangements
options.why: Two signatures on two days are easy to arrange and that is the problem. The standard asks whether the arrangements were designed together, and a second contract already agreed when the first was signed answers it.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B97 and B98, read with the loss-of-control accounting in para 25 and B98

items.scenario: A parent holds 80 per cent of a subsidiary. On 15 March 2026 it sells 25 per cent to a buyer, and on 12 April 2026 it sells the remaining 55 per cent to the same buyer. The two contracts were negotiated together, the second was already agreed when the first was signed, and neither price makes commercial sense without the other. The group accountant treats the March sale as an equity transaction taken inside equity and the April sale as the loss of control, so the whole gain falls in the year ending 31 March 2027.

items.stem: Which project should the company take, and on what figures?

options.text: Project X, at an equivalent annual value of about ₹3.79 lakh against Project Y's ₹3.18 lakh
options.why: Dividing each net present value by the annuity factor for its own life turns a total into an equivalent annual value: 12.00 / 3.170 = ₹3.79 lakh a year for X and 15.50 / 4.868 = ₹3.18 lakh a year for Y. Because the winner is repeated for ever, the annual figure is the only fair comparison, and on a benefit the higher one wins — the mirror of the rule on costs, where the lower equivalent annual cost wins.

options.text: Project X, at ₹3.00 lakh a year against Project Y's ₹2.21 lakh, dividing each net present value by the number of years
options.misconception: divides by the plain count of years rather than by the annuity factor, which throws away the time value the factor carries
options.why: 12.00 / 4 = ₹3.00 lakh and 15.50 / 7 = ₹2.21 lakh. Both understate the annual figure, because a rupee due in year seven is not a rupee due in year one. It is the annuity factor — 3.170 and 4.868 — that converts a present value back into a level annual amount, giving ₹3.79 lakh and ₹3.18 lakh. Here the same project wins either way, which is luck, not method.

options.text: Project Y, because its net present value of ₹15.50 lakh is the larger of the two totals
options.misconception: compares totals earned over lives of different lengths, which credits the longer project for simply running more years
options.why: Y's total is bigger partly because it covers seven years against X's four. Put on the same footing — value per year of project life — X earns ₹3.79 lakh a year and Y only ₹3.18 lakh. Over any common horizon, repeating X beats repeating Y.

options.text: Project Y, at an equivalent annual figure of ₹3.18 lakh against Project X's ₹3.79 lakh, the lower annual figure being preferred
options.misconception: applies the equivalent annual cost rule, where the lower figure wins, to a stream of benefits, where the higher one does
options.why: The arithmetic is right and the rule has been read upside down. A low annual charge is good when the figure is a cost. Here the figure is what the project earns each year, so ₹3.79 lakh beats ₹3.18 lakh and Project X is chosen.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company can take Project X or Project Y, not both, and whichever it takes it will repeat indefinitely on the same terms. Project X has a net present value of ₹12.00 lakh over a four-year life. Project Y has a net present value of ₹15.50 lakh over a seven-year life. The cost of capital is 10 per cent; the annuity factors are 3.170 for four years and 4.868 for seven years.

items.stem: What is the incremental annual cash flow after tax from the replacement?

options.misconception: takes the operating saving gross, leaving out both the tax on it and the depreciation shield that partly offsets that tax
options.why: A saving of ₹3,00,000 raises taxable profit, so the company keeps only ₹2,10,000 of it. Against that, the extra depreciation shelters ₹1,60,000 of profit and saves ₹48,000 of tax. Both belong in the figure, and together they give ₹2,58,000.

options.misconception: claims the whole of the new machine's depreciation shield and forgets that the old machine would have gone on earning a shield of its own
options.why: 3,00,000 × 0.70 + 2,40,000 × 0.30 = ₹2,82,000 credits the replacement with the entire ₹72,000 shield on the new machine. Keeping the old one would still have produced ₹80,000 of depreciation and ₹24,000 of tax saved, so only the ₹48,000 difference is caused by the replacement.

The cost saving is taxed, leaving 3,00,000 × 0.70 = ₹2,10,000. The depreciation shield is incremental too — the new machine's ₹2,40,000 less the ₹80,000 the old machine would have gone on claiming — so (2,40,000 − 80,000) × 0.30 = ₹48,000 is added. Together that is ₹2,58,000. The same figure arrives the long way: profit before tax rises by 3,00,000 − 1,60,000 = ₹1,40,000, tax takes 30 per cent leaving ₹98,000, and adding back the ₹1,60,000 of extra depreciation gives ₹2,58,000.

options.misconception: stops at profit after tax and never adds back depreciation, which is a charge in the accounts and not a payment of money
options.why: (3,00,000 − 1,60,000) × 0.70 = ₹98,000 is the rise in profit after tax. Depreciation of ₹1,60,000 was deducted to reach it and no money left the company, so it is added back: 98,000 + 1,60,000 = ₹2,58,000. A replacement is appraised on cash, not on profit.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A new machine will cut cash operating costs by ₹3,00,000 a year. Depreciation on the new machine is ₹2,40,000 a year on a straight line basis. Had the old machine been kept, it would have gone on charging depreciation of ₹80,000 a year. The tax rate is 30 per cent.

items.stem: What is the present value of the interest tax shield to be added in the adjusted present value?

options.text: ₹3.60 lakh
options.misconception: adds the three years of tax saved without discounting, treating money in year three as money today
options.why: Total interest is 6 + 4 + 2 = ₹12 lakh and 30 per cent of that is ₹3.60 lakh — the right shields, never brought to today. Discounting them at 10 per cent gives about ₹3.08 lakh, and the ₹0.52 lakh difference is what waiting costs.

options.text: About ₹4.48 lakh
options.misconception: charges interest on the full ₹60 lakh for all three years, forgetting that a repayment loan carries a falling balance
options.why: A constant shield of ₹1.80 lakh over the three-year annuity factor of 2.487 gives ₹4.48 lakh. It assumes ₹60 lakh is owed throughout. Two-thirds of the loan has been repaid by the start of year three, and interest — and so the shield — falls with it.

options.text: ₹18.00 lakh
options.misconception: applies the perpetual-debt shortcut, debt times the tax rate, to a loan that is repaid inside three years
options.why: 60 × 0.30 = ₹18 lakh is the value of the shield when the debt is never repaid, because a perpetuity of interest at the cost of debt discounts back to the amount borrowed. This loan is gone in three years, so only three years of shrinking shields exist, worth about ₹3.08 lakh.

options.text: About ₹3.08 lakh
options.why: Interest falls as the loan is repaid: ₹6.00 lakh in year one on ₹60 lakh outstanding, ₹4.00 lakh in year two on ₹40 lakh, ₹2.00 lakh in year three on ₹20 lakh. The tax shield is 30 per cent of each — ₹1.80, ₹1.20 and ₹0.60 lakh — and discounting gives 1.80 × 0.909 = ₹1.64 lakh, 1.20 × 0.826 = ₹0.99 lakh and 0.60 × 0.751 = ₹0.45 lakh, a total of about ₹3.08 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A project is part funded by a term loan of ₹60 lakh at 10 per cent interest. The principal is repaid in three equal instalments of ₹20 lakh at the end of each of the three years, so interest is charged on the amount outstanding at the start of each year. The tax rate is 30 per cent and the tax shield is discounted at the 10 per cent cost of the debt. Discount factors at 10 per cent are 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751.

items.stem: What is the project's net present value under the certainty equivalent method?

options.text: About ₹3.72 lakh
options.why: Each expected flow is first shrunk to its certain equivalent: 25 × 0.90 = ₹22.50 lakh, 25 × 0.80 = ₹20.00 lakh and 25 × 0.70 = ₹17.50 lakh. Those are then discounted at the risk-free rate, because the risk has already been taken out in the numerator — 22.50 × 0.943 = ₹21.22 lakh, 20.00 × 0.890 = ₹17.80 lakh and 17.50 × 0.840 = ₹14.70 lakh, a total of ₹53.72 lakh. Less the ₹50 lakh outlay, the net present value is about ₹3.72 lakh.

options.text: About ₹16.83 lakh
options.misconception: discounts the full expected cash flows at the risk-free rate, so no allowance for risk is made anywhere in the working
options.why: 25 × (0.943 + 0.890 + 0.840) = ₹66.83 lakh, giving ₹16.83 lakh. The risk-free rate belongs with certainty equivalents, not with risky expected flows. Skipping the coefficients strips the risk adjustment out of the numerator without putting anything back in the denominator.

options.text: About minus ₹3.06 lakh
options.misconception: shrinks the cash flows for risk and then discounts them at the risk-adjusted rate as well, so the same risk is charged twice
options.why: Discounting the certain amounts at 14 per cent gives 22.50 × 0.877 + 20.00 × 0.769 + 17.50 × 0.675 = about ₹46.93 lakh and a negative answer. The coefficients have already priced the risk. Using a rate that also carries a risk premium counts it a second time, which is exactly the double counting the method exists to avoid.

options.text: ₹10.00 lakh
options.misconception: applies the certainty equivalent coefficients but never discounts, so money three years out is treated as money today
options.why: 22.50 + 20.00 + 17.50 = ₹60 lakh less ₹50 lakh gives ₹10 lakh. Certainty equivalents remove risk; they do nothing about time. The second step of the method is to discount them at the risk-free rate, which brings ₹60 lakh down to ₹53.72 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A project costs ₹50 lakh today and is expected to bring in ₹25 lakh at the end of each of three years. The management's certainty equivalent coefficients are 0.90 for year one, 0.80 for year two and 0.70 for year three. The risk-free rate is 6 per cent and the company's risk-adjusted cost of capital is 14 per cent. Discount factors at 6 per cent are 0.943, 0.890 and 0.840.

items.stem: What is year one's net operating cash flow in money terms, before tax?

options.text: ₹45.00 lakh
options.why: Revenues and costs carry their own rates and are inflated separately: sales become 100 × 1.08 = ₹108 lakh and costs become 60 × 1.05 = ₹63 lakh, leaving ₹45 lakh. Inflating the net figure by any single rate is wrong whenever the two sides move at different speeds, and the gap widens every year the project runs.

options.text: ₹40.00 lakh
options.misconception: leaves the flows in today's prices while discounting at a rate that already contains an inflation premium, so inflation is charged and never credited
options.why: ₹40 lakh is the margin at today's prices. The 12 per cent rate is a money rate — it demands a return that covers inflation — so the receipts it is applied to must be money receipts as well. Matching a money rate with today's prices penalises the project for a price rise it is never given credit for.

options.text: ₹43.20 lakh
options.misconception: inflates the net margin by the revenue rate, which credits the higher rate to the costs as well
options.why: 40 × 1.08 = ₹43.20 lakh applies 8 per cent to the whole ₹40 lakh margin. Only the sales side rises at 8 per cent; the costs rise at 5 per cent, so they eat less of the revenue than this working assumes and the true money margin is ₹45 lakh.

options.text: ₹42.00 lakh
options.misconception: inflates the net margin by the cost rate, which holds selling prices down to the slower of the two rates
options.why: 40 × 1.05 = ₹42 lakh applies 5 per cent to everything. That understates the sales, which are expected to rise at 8 per cent. Handled side by side the answer is 108 − 63 = ₹45 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A project's first year, stated in today's prices, shows sales of ₹100 lakh and cash operating costs of ₹60 lakh. Selling prices are expected to rise by 8 per cent a year while these costs rise by 5 per cent a year. The discount rate of 12 per cent already carries an inflation premium.

items.stem: What annual rate does the market imply for the two years running from the end of year two to the end of year four?

options.text: About 23.29 per cent a year
options.misconception: quotes the whole two-year forward return as though it were an annual rate, so two years of growth are charged to one year
options.why: 1.4116 / 1.1449 − 1 = 23.29 per cent is right as a total for the two years together and far too high for one of them. Spread evenly it is the square root of 1.2329, about 11.04 per cent a year, and compounding that twice gives the 23.29 per cent back.

options.text: About 11.65 per cent a year
options.misconception: halves the two-year return instead of taking its square root, which ignores that the first of the two years earns interest the second year then earns on
options.why: 23.29 / 2 = 11.65 per cent divides the growth as though it were simple interest. The second year earns on the first year's earnings too, so the split is a square root, not a halving — 11.04 per cent, and 1.1104 squared comes back to 1.2329.

options.text: About 11.04 per cent a year
options.why: Lending for four years must pay the same as lending for two and rolling into the forward period: 1.4116 / 1.1449 = 1.2329 is the growth over those last two years together. Because the answer is wanted as an annual rate, the square root is taken — the square root of 1.2329 is 1.1104, so about 11.04 per cent a year. Any other rate would let somebody borrow one way and lend the other for a certain profit.

options.text: 9.00 per cent a year
options.misconception: reads the four-year spot rate as the rate for the later years, when a spot rate is the average return over the whole period it covers
options.why: The 9 per cent covers all four years, and the first two of them earn only 7 per cent. The later years must therefore earn more than 9 per cent to lift the average that far, which is what the 11.04 per cent forward rate is saying.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: The two-year spot rate is 7 per cent and the four-year spot rate is 9 per cent, both annually compounded. Take 1.07 squared as 1.1449 and 1.09 to the fourth power as 1.4116.

items.stem: Which yield should the investor price this bond on?

options.text: About 13.33 per cent, the yield to call, since the call date is nearer
options.misconception: assumes the call will be exercised whenever one exists, when the option belongs to the issuer and is used only where it pays the issuer to use it
options.why: A call is worth exercising when the issuer can refinance more cheaply, which is what a price above par signals. This bond trades at ₹880 on an 8 per cent coupon — cheap money the issuer wants to keep. Calling it would mean paying ₹1,020 for a liability the market values at ₹880, so the yield of 13.33 per cent describes an event that will not happen.

options.text: About 9.79 per cent, the yield to maturity
options.why: The approximate yield to maturity is [80 + (1,000 − 880)/10] ÷ [(1,000 + 880)/2] = 92 / 940 = 9.79 per cent, and the yield to call is [80 + (1,020 − 880)/3] ÷ [(1,020 + 880)/2] = 126.67 / 950 = 13.33 per cent. Yield to worst is the lower of the two, and here it is the maturity figure. That matches the sense of it: the bond stands below par because its coupon is below the market, so the issuer is holding a cheap liability and will not pay ₹1,020 to be rid of it.

options.text: About 11.56 per cent, the average of the two yields
options.misconception: averages the two yields instead of taking the worse one, as though the outcome were half a call and half a redemption at maturity
options.why: (9.79 + 13.33) / 2 = 11.56 per cent. Only one of the two things will happen, and which one is the issuer's choice, not a coin toss. The convention is to price on the worse outcome for the investor — the yield to worst — which is 9.79 per cent here and would be the call figure on a bond trading at a premium.

options.text: Neither can be used until the issuer states whether it intends to call
options.misconception: treats the issuer's discretion as making the bond unpriceable, when yield to worst is precisely the convention that settles it
options.why: No issuer announces its intentions years ahead, which is why the convention exists. The investor computes both yields and quotes the lower — 9.79 per cent — so that whatever the issuer does, the return is at least what was quoted.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of ₹1,000 face value carries an 8 per cent annual coupon and has 10 years to maturity. It trades at ₹880. The issuer may redeem it at ₹1,020 at the end of year 3. Use the approximate yield formula — annual coupon plus the annual amortisation of the discount or premium, over the average of the price paid and the amount receivable.

items.stem: What is the premium payback period on this convertible?

options.text: 1.00 year
options.misconception: divides the premium by the coupon alone, forgetting that converting would have brought dividends the holder is giving up by staying in the debenture
options.why: 100 / 100 = 1.00 year counts the whole ₹100 coupon as the advantage of holding on. Somebody who converted today would collect ₹30 of dividends on the 25 shares, so only ₹70 of the coupon is an advantage, and the payback is 1.43 years.

options.text: About 1.43 years
options.why: The conversion value is 25 × ₹36 = ₹900, so the buyer is paying a conversion premium of 1,000 − 900 = ₹100 for the right to wait. What he gets for waiting is the extra income the debenture pays over the shares: a coupon of ₹100 against dividends of 25 × ₹1.20 = ₹30, so ₹70 a year. The premium payback period is 100 / 70 = about 1.43 years — how long the income advantage takes to repay what was paid over conversion value.

options.text: About 12.86 years
options.misconception: puts the conversion value in the numerator instead of the premium, so it measures how long the income takes to repay the shares rather than the extra paid for them
options.why: 900 / 70 = 12.86 years asks how long the income advantage takes to repay the whole ₹900 of conversion value. Only the ₹100 above that value is at risk of being lost if the share never rises, and it is that ₹100 the payback period is measured on.

options.text: About 3.33 years
options.misconception: divides the premium by the dividends given up rather than by the income advantage, which measures what is lost and not what is gained
options.why: 100 / 30 = 3.33 years divides by the ₹30 of dividends the holder does not receive. The dividends are the deduction, not the recovery. What repays the premium is the ₹70 by which the coupon exceeds them.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A convertible debenture of ₹1,000 face value carries a 10 per cent coupon and converts into 25 equity shares. The share trades at ₹36 and pays a dividend of ₹1.20 a share. The convertible itself trades at ₹1,000.

items.stem: What is the comparable's asset beta?

options.text: About 0.95
options.misconception: drops the debt term, which is the short form that only holds when the debt beta is zero — and here the question says it is not
options.why: 1.40 × 60/88 = 0.955 uses the familiar short formula. It is the full formula with the second term struck out, and striking it out is only allowed when lenders bear no market risk at all. These lenders bear a beta of 0.20, and their share of the business risk, 0.064, belongs in the asset beta.

options.text: About 0.81
options.misconception: applies the tax factor to the equity instead of to the debt, shrinking the wrong side of the ratio
options.why: Weighting by 60 × 0.70 = 42 against debt of 40 gives 1.40 × 42/82 + 0.20 × 40/82 = 0.81. The tax relief attaches to interest, which is paid on debt; dividends carry no such relief. The factor therefore multiplies the debt and never the equity.

options.text: About 1.02
options.why: With a debt beta that is not zero the asset beta is the weighted average of the two betas, the weights being equity and after-tax debt: debt after tax is 40 × 0.70 = ₹28 crore, so the total is 60 + 28 = ₹88 crore. The asset beta is 1.40 × 60/88 + 0.20 × 28/88 = 0.955 + 0.064 = about 1.02. The business risk is carried partly by the shareholders and partly by the lenders, and both shares belong in the figure.

options.misconception: leaves the one minus tax rate factor out of the weights, overstating how much of the business risk sits with the lenders
options.why: 1.40 × 60/100 + 0.20 × 40/100 = 0.92 weights by the raw debt and equity. Interest is deductible, so the taxman carries part of the gearing and only 0.70 of each rupee of debt counts. Putting that factor in gives weights of 60 and 28 out of 88, and an answer of 1.02.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A quoted comparable has an equity beta of 1.40 and, unusually, its bonds are volatile enough to carry a debt beta of 0.20. At market values its debt is ₹40 crore and its equity ₹60 crore. The tax rate is 30 per cent.

items.stem: What does Fama's decomposition say about this manager?

options.text: Net selectivity is about minus 1.67 per cent although the alpha is positive at 3.7 per cent — the picks were good but did not cover the cost of the risk left undiversified
options.why: Return required for systematic risk is 5 + 0.9 × 7 = 11.3 per cent, so gross selectivity, the same figure as the alpha, is 15 − 11.3 = 3.7 per cent. Return required for total risk is 5 + (30/18) × 7 = 16.67 per cent, so net selectivity is 15 − 16.67 = minus 1.67 per cent. The difference of 5.37 per cent is the diversification cost, and here it swallows the whole of the good stock picking and more.

options.text: Both the gross and the net figures are 3.7 per cent, because a beta of 0.9 is below the market's and a low-beta fund is by definition well diversified
options.misconception: reads a low beta as evidence of good diversification, when beta measures only the part of the risk that moves with the market and says nothing about the rest
options.why: Beta of 0.9 and standard deviation of 30 per cent against a market at 18 per cent is exactly the combination the decomposition is built to expose — little market sensitivity and a great deal of specific risk. The two measures answer different questions, and this fund scores well on one and badly on the other.

options.text: The manager added 3.7 per cent, since Jensen's alpha is the measure of stock selection and Fama adds nothing to it
options.misconception: stops at the return required for systematic risk, which charges for beta alone and lets a badly diversified fund keep the reward for risk it need not have run
options.why: 3.7 per cent is gross selectivity and it is a real measure. Fama's point is that a fund running 30 per cent total risk against the market's 18 has taken on far more than its beta admits, and a return of 16.67 per cent was needed to justify it. Charged for that, the manager is 1.67 per cent short.

options.text: Net selectivity is about minus 1.67 per cent, showing the manager picked stocks badly
options.misconception: reads a negative net selectivity as a verdict on the stock picking, when the picking earned a positive alpha and it was the failure to diversify that cost the money
options.why: The number is right and the diagnosis is not. Measured against beta the manager beat the requirement by 3.7 per cent, so the selection worked. What did not work was holding those picks in a portfolio concentrated enough to run 30 per cent standard deviation. The remedy is more names, not different ones.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Over the year a fund returned 15 per cent with a standard deviation of 30 per cent and a beta of 0.9. The market returned 12 per cent with a standard deviation of 18 per cent. The risk-free rate was 5 per cent.

items.stem: What return can he expect, and how is the portfolio built?

options.text: 17.5 per cent, being 1.25 times the market's 14 per cent
options.misconception: gears into the market and counts the extra return without counting the interest on the money borrowed to get it
options.why: 1.25 × 14 = 17.5 per cent is the return on the geared holding before paying for the borrowing. The 0.25 borrowed costs 6 per cent, which is 1.5 per cent of his own money, and 17.5 − 1.5 = 16 per cent.

options.text: 8 per cent, by putting 25 per cent in the market portfolio and 75 per cent in the risk-free asset
options.misconception: reads the 25 per cent as a weight in the market when it is the standard deviation the investor is willing to bear
options.why: 0.25 × 14 + 0.75 × 6 = 8 per cent is a lending portfolio, and its standard deviation is 0.25 × 20 = 5 per cent, not 25. The investor asked for five times that much risk, which takes him past the market portfolio and into borrowing.

options.text: 14 per cent, since the market portfolio is the best any investor can hold
options.misconception: stops the capital market line at the market portfolio, forgetting that it continues beyond it for anyone willing to borrow
options.why: The market portfolio is the best holding of risky assets, and it is not the end of the line. Combining it with lending gives points below it and combining it with borrowing gives points above it, up to 16 per cent at a standard deviation of 25 per cent.

options.text: 16 per cent, by putting 125 per cent of his money in the market portfolio and borrowing the other 25 per cent at the risk-free rate
options.why: The capital market line runs from the risk-free rate through the market portfolio and onwards: expected return is 6 + [(14 − 6)/20] × 25 = 6 + 0.4 × 25 = 16 per cent. The slope of 0.4 is the reward per unit of risk. A standard deviation of 25 against the market's 20 means holding 25/20 = 1.25 times his own money in the market, and the extra 0.25 is borrowed — a borrowing portfolio. Checking it, 1.25 × 14 − 0.25 × 6 = 16 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: The risk-free rate is 6 per cent. The market portfolio is expected to return 14 per cent with a standard deviation of 20 per cent. An investor is willing to carry a standard deviation of 25 per cent and wants the best return the capital market line offers at that level of risk.

items.stem: What is the combined company's earnings per share?

options.text: ₹4.00, unchanged
options.misconception: sets the exchange ratio on the two earnings per share figures when the offer is stated in terms of market prices
options.why: On earnings per share the ratio would be 3.00 / 4.00 = 0.75, meaning 7.5 lakh new shares and 110 / 27.5 = ₹4.00 — no change at all, which is what swapping on earnings always produces. The deal here is struck on market prices, and the market rates B Ltd's earnings below A Ltd's, so only 5 lakh shares are issued.

options.misconception: puts the combined earnings over the acquirer's own share count, forgetting that shares had to be issued to pay for the target
options.why: 110 / 20 = ₹5.50 counts B Ltd's earnings and none of the cost of getting them. The consideration was 5 lakh new shares, and they dilute the earnings across 25 lakh shares, not 20.

The exchange ratio on market prices is 30 / 60 = 0.5, so B Ltd's 10 lakh shareholders receive 5 lakh new shares in A Ltd. Combined earnings are 80 + 30 = ₹110 lakh over 20 + 5 = 25 lakh shares, giving an earnings per share of ₹4.40 against A Ltd's own ₹4.00 before the deal. The rise is arithmetic: B Ltd's earnings were bought on a multiple of 10 while A Ltd's own shares trade on 15.

options.text: About ₹3.67
options.misconception: adds the target's own share count to the acquirer's instead of the number of shares actually issued in exchange for them
options.why: 110 / 30 = ₹3.67 assumes B Ltd's 10 lakh shares carry over one for one. They are cancelled and replaced at the agreed ratio of 0.5, which is 5 lakh A Ltd shares, so the combined count is 25 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A Ltd has 20 lakh shares, earnings of ₹80 lakh and a market price of ₹60 a share. B Ltd has 10 lakh shares, earnings of ₹30 lakh and a market price of ₹30 a share. A Ltd will absorb B Ltd and the shares are to be exchanged on the basis of the two market prices. Earnings are simply added, with no synergy.

items.stem: What is the most the acquirer can pay for the target?

options.text: ₹215 crore
options.why: The savings are worth 25 × (1 − 0.28) = ₹18 crore a year after tax, and in perpetuity at 12 per cent that is 18 / 0.12 = ₹150 crore. The integration cost of ₹25 crore is a cost of the acquisition and comes off, leaving net synergy of ₹125 crore. The ceiling is the target's own standalone value plus that net synergy: 90 + 125 = ₹215 crore.

options.text: About ₹273 crore
options.misconception: capitalises the savings before tax, valuing money the taxman will take
options.why: 25 / 0.12 = ₹208.33 crore, less ₹25 crore and plus ₹90 crore, gives ₹273 crore. Only ₹18 crore of each year's ₹25 crore stays in the business; the other ₹7 crore is extra tax on the higher profit the saving creates. Capitalising the pre-tax figure overstates the ceiling by nearly ₹60 crore.

options.text: ₹90 crore
options.misconception: refuses any premium at all, when the synergy is precisely the fund a premium can be paid out of
options.why: Paying the standalone value and not a rupee more would leave the acquirer with the whole ₹125 crore of net synergy, and no seller would accept it. The ceiling is not where the acquirer's gain is largest but where it runs out, and that is at ₹215 crore.

options.text: ₹240 crore
options.misconception: capitalises the savings and never deducts what it costs to achieve them, when the integration spend is as much a part of the deal as the price
options.why: 90 + 150 = ₹240 crore treats the ₹150 crore of savings as free. Somebody has to pay the ₹25 crore of integration cost, and it is the acquirer, out of the same pocket as the purchase price. Net of it the synergy is ₹125 crore and the ceiling is ₹215 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A target is worth ₹90 crore as an independent company. The acquirer expects the merger to produce cost savings of ₹25 crore a year before tax, for ever. Integrating the two businesses will cost ₹25 crore, payable at once. The tax rate is 28 per cent and the relevant cost of capital is 12 per cent.

items.stem: What money multiple does the sponsor earn on exit?

options.text: 3.25 times
options.misconception: credits the whole exit enterprise value to the sponsor, forgetting that the lenders are repaid before the equity sees anything
options.why: 780 / 240 = 3.25 times skips the debt. ₹360 crore is still owed on the day of sale and the lenders take it off the top; only the ₹420 crore beneath it belongs to the sponsor.

options.text: 2.50 times
options.misconception: values the exit at the multiple the sponsor paid on entry, so the deal is credited with growth it achieved and spared the fall in the multiple it did not control
options.why: 120 × 8.0 = ₹960 crore less ₹360 crore gives ₹600 crore and 2.50 times. The exit multiple is set by whoever is buying, and here it is 6.5, not 8.0. That contraction costs the sponsor ₹180 crore of enterprise value and three-quarters of a turn of return.

options.text: About 0.98 times
options.misconception: applies the change in enterprise value to the sponsor's stake in proportion, which is the arithmetic of an ungeared holding
options.why: Enterprise value did fall from ₹800 crore to ₹780 crore, and 780 / 800 gives 0.975. But the sponsor never owned the enterprise — it owned a ₹240 crore slice sitting beneath ₹560 crore of debt, and that slice grows as the debt above it shrinks. That is the whole point of leverage, and it works in the sponsor's favour here.

options.text: 1.75 times
options.why: Exit enterprise value is 120 × 6.5 = ₹780 crore, and the debt still outstanding comes off first: 780 − 360 = ₹420 crore of equity. Against the ₹240 crore put in that is 420 / 240 = 1.75 times. The ₹200 crore of debt repaid and the 20 per cent EBITDA growth together outweighed the fall in the exit multiple from 8.0 to 6.5, but only just.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A sponsor buys a company at 8.0 times an EBITDA of ₹100 crore, so ₹800 crore, funded with ₹560 crore of debt and ₹240 crore of its own equity. Five years later EBITDA is ₹120 crore, debt outstanding is ₹360 crore, and buyers are only willing to pay 6.5 times EBITDA.

items.stem: What one-year rupee interest rate is consistent with the international Fisher effect?

options.text: About 0.72 per cent
options.misconception: divides by the expected rate instead of multiplying, which has the rupee strengthening when the quoted numbers say it weakens
options.why: 1.045 × 80/83 = 1.0072 puts the ratio upside down. Going from ₹80 to ₹83 a dollar means more rupees per dollar, which is a weaker rupee, so the multiplier is 83/80 and the rupee rate has to be the higher of the two, not the lower.

options.text: 4.50 per cent, the same as the dollar rate
options.misconception: assumes the two currencies must pay the same nominal rate, when it is the expected currency movement that equalises them and not the rates themselves
options.why: If both paid 4.5 per cent while the rupee was expected to fall to ₹83, no rupee investor would lend in rupees. What the effect equalises is the return after the expected exchange movement, and that needs a rupee rate of about 8.42 per cent.

options.text: About 8.42 per cent
options.why: The international Fisher effect says one plus the rupee rate equals one plus the dollar rate times the expected change in the rate of exchange: 1.045 × 83/80 = 1.045 × 1.0375 = 1.0842, so about 8.42 per cent. Put in money, a dollar investor with ₹80 could earn 4.5 per cent at home, and for the two routes to leave him equally well off the rupee must pay enough to cover both that and the ₹3 the rupee is expected to lose.

options.text: 8.25 per cent
options.misconception: adds the expected depreciation to the foreign interest rate instead of compounding them, leaving out the depreciation suffered on the interest itself
options.why: 83/80 is a fall of 3.75 per cent and 4.5 + 3.75 = 8.25 per cent. The rupee weakens on the interest as well as on the principal, so the two multiply: 1.045 × 1.0375 = 1.0842. The approximation is close at these numbers and drifts as the rates widen.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: The spot rate is ₹80 to the dollar and the market expects it to be ₹83 to the dollar in a year. The one-year nominal interest rate in the United States is 4.5 per cent.

items.stem: What does leading and lagging tell the company to do?

options.text: Lag the payable and lead the receivable, the standard action when the home currency is expected to strengthen
options.misconception: reads a single direction for the rupee when it is expected to move differently against the two currencies in the question
options.why: The rupee is not simply strengthening. It is expected to weaken against the dollar and strengthen against the euro, and each exposure is judged against its own currency. Lagging the dollar payable is the one action here that loses money on both counts.

options.text: Delay both, to keep the money inside the business for as long as possible
options.misconception: treats leading and lagging as a cash-management preference rather than a view on currencies, so it gives the same answer whatever the rates are expected to do
options.why: Holding cash longer is worth something, and it is not what this tool is for. Lagging the dollar payable means buying dollars after they have become dearer, and lagging the euro receivable means converting euros after they have become cheaper — losing on both sides to gain three months of float.

options.text: Lead the payable and lag the receivable, because payables are always settled early and receivables collected late
options.misconception: applies a fixed rule by the type of item, when the rule depends entirely on which way the currency in question is expected to move
options.why: Half right by accident. If the euro were expected to strengthen against the rupee the receivable should indeed be lagged — but here the rupee is expected to strengthen against the euro, so waiting costs money. There is no rule about payables and receivables, only about currencies.

options.text: Settle the dollar payable early and press for the euro receivable early — lead both
options.why: Leading means paying or collecting before the due date and lagging means after it, and the choice turns on which way the currency is expected to move. Dollars are expected to cost more rupees in three months, so the payable is settled now while they are cheap. Euros are expected to fetch fewer rupees in three months, so the receivable is collected now while it is worth more. Both point the same way here, which is why reading the currency rather than the type of item is the whole skill.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian company has a payable of one million dollars and a receivable of one million euros, both due in three months. It expects the rupee to weaken against the dollar over those three months and to strengthen against the euro. Both counterparties are group companies and will accept early settlement.

items.stem: What is the effective annual cost of this borrowing in rupees?

options.text: About 3.41 per cent
options.misconception: counts the currency movement but treats the front-end fee as an expense outside the loan, when it reduces the money the borrower ever had the use of
options.why: 1.06 × 80/82 − 1 = 3.41 per cent is the cost of a dollar loan with no fee. Here ₹16.4 lakh was taken off the top, so the company services a one million dollar loan on 990,000 dollars of money. Dividing by what was received rather than by what was signed for gives 4.46 per cent.

options.text: About 4.46 per cent
options.why: The company actually receives 990,000 × ₹82 = ₹8,11,80,000. In a year it must repay 1.06 million dollars at ₹80, which is ₹8,48,00,000. The cost is 36,20,000 / 8,11,80,000 = about 4.46 per cent. The strengthening rupee cuts the cost well below the 6 per cent coupon, and the front-end fee claws part of that saving back by shrinking what was received.

options.text: About 3.56 per cent
options.misconception: subtracts the expected currency gain from the coupon instead of compounding the two, and drops the front-end fee as well
options.why: ₹82 to ₹80 is a fall of 2.44 per cent, and 6 − 2.44 = 3.56 per cent. The rupee gain applies to the interest as well as to the principal, so the two compound rather than subtract, and the fee has still to come out. Both corrections together give 4.46 per cent.

options.text: 6.00 per cent
options.misconception: quotes the foreign coupon as the cost, ignoring both the movement in the exchange rate and the fee deducted at drawdown
options.why: 6 per cent is what the loan costs in dollars. The company earns and reports in rupees, and in rupees it borrowed ₹8.12 crore and will repay ₹8.48 crore. That works out at 4.46 per cent, and the difference is a real gain, not a presentation.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company borrows one million dollars for one year at 6 per cent interest. A front-end fee of 1 per cent of the loan is deducted at drawdown, so only 990,000 dollars are received. The spot rate is ₹82 to the dollar and the company expects ₹80 to the dollar in a year.

items.stem: What is the result on the futures position?

options.text: A gain of ₹7,50,000
options.misconception: applies the three-month fraction twice, once to the interest period and once again to the whole position
options.why: 30,00,000 × 3/12 = ₹7,50,000 scales an answer that has already been scaled. The 3/12 belongs inside the value of one contract and nowhere else; after that the twenty contracts are simply added up.

options.text: A loss of ₹30,00,000
options.misconception: forgets that the price is quoted as one hundred minus the rate, so it reads a rise in rates as a rise in the futures price and puts the seller on the losing side
options.why: Rates rose, and because the quote is 100 minus the rate the price fell from 94.00 to 92.80. Somebody who sold at 94.00 buys back at 92.80 and gains. That is exactly why a borrower sells: the futures gain arrives at the same moment the borrowing becomes dearer.

options.misconception: applies the rate change to the notional principal for a full year, when the contract prices only three months of interest
