options.why: 20 × 5,00,00,000 × 0.0120 = ₹1.20 crore charges a whole year of interest on the notional. These contracts settle a three-month period, so the move is multiplied by 3/12 and each contract is worth ₹1,50,000, not ₹6,00,000.

options.text: A gain of ₹30,00,000
options.why: The price moved 1.20, which is 120 basis points, and the treasurer is short, so the fall is a gain. Each contract is worth 5,00,00,000 × 0.0120 × 3/12 = ₹1,50,000, because the contract covers only a three-month interest period however large the notional principal is. Twenty contracts give ₹30,00,000, which is set against the extra interest the treasurer now pays on the actual borrowing.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A treasurer sells 20 interest rate futures contracts at a price of 94.00. Each contract has a notional principal of ₹5 crore and covers a three-month interest period, and the price is quoted as one hundred minus the rate. At settlement the reference rate is 7.20 per cent, so the futures price is 92.80.

items.stem: At what index level would the trader first face a margin call?

options.misconception: has the direction of the loss the wrong way round, treating a seller of futures as somebody who loses when the index falls
options.why: 22,000 − 1,100 = 20,900 is where a buyer would be called. This trader sold, so a falling index credits the account and a rising one debits it. The danger is above, at 23,100.

options.misconception: counts the lot size of one contract when two are open, so it doubles the number of points the cushion can absorb
options.why: 55,000 / 25 = 2,200 points prices the move on a single lot. Two contracts are open, so every index point moves ₹50 through the account, not ₹25, and the cushion runs out in half the distance — 1,100 points.

options.misconception: measures the fall against the whole initial margin, when the call is triggered as soon as the balance drops through the maintenance level
options.why: 2,20,000 / 50 = 4,400 points is where the account would be emptied altogether. The maintenance margin exists precisely so that nobody gets that far: the call comes at ₹1,65,000, which is ₹55,000 or 1,100 points below the start.

A short position loses when the index rises. The cushion is the initial margin less the maintenance margin, 2,20,000 − 1,65,000 = ₹55,000, and each index point costs 2 × 25 = ₹50. So 55,000 / 50 = 1,100 points may be lost before the balance touches the maintenance line, which puts the trigger at 22,000 + 1,100 = 23,100. Once it is breached the call restores the full initial margin, not merely the shortfall.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A trader sells 2 index futures contracts at 22,000, with a lot size of 25 units per contract. The initial margin on the two contracts together is ₹2,20,000 and the maintenance margin is ₹1,65,000. Nothing else moves in the account.

items.stem: What is the best estimate of the option's price after those five days?

options.text: About ₹14.54
options.misconception: counts the gain from rising volatility and forgets that five days of life have been consumed as well
options.why: 14.00 + 0.54 = ₹14.54 leaves out theta. Every day that passes takes ₹0.06 off a long option whatever else is happening, and five of them have gone: ₹0.30. Both effects apply at once, leaving ₹14.24.

options.text: About ₹13.70
options.misconception: counts the time decay and treats vega as irrelevant because the share price did not move, when vega prices expected future movement and not past movement
options.why: 14.00 − 0.30 = ₹13.70 is the price if nothing but the calendar changed. Volatility did change, from 24 to 27, and an option is worth more when the market expects a wider range of outcomes — whether or not anything has happened yet. That adds ₹0.54.

options.text: About ₹14.24
options.why: Theta takes 5 × 0.06 = ₹0.30 out for the five days that have passed, and vega puts 3 × 0.18 = ₹0.54 back for the three percentage points volatility has risen. The net change is plus ₹0.24, so the estimate is ₹14.24. The share never moved, which is what makes this a clean reading of the two: a bought option can gain on a still day if the market's view of future movement widens enough.

options.text: About ₹13.16
options.misconception: treats a rise in volatility as a loss to the option holder, which is the writer's position and not the buyer's
options.why: 14.00 − 0.30 − 0.54 = ₹13.16 subtracts the vega effect. Rising volatility helps the buyer of either a call or a put, because the option's downside is capped at the premium while its upside is not. It is the writer who loses when volatility climbs.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A call option is priced at ₹14.00. Its theta is minus 0.06 a day and its vega is 0.18 for each percentage point of volatility. Over the next five days the share price does not move, but implied volatility rises from 24 per cent to 27 per cent.

items.stem: What annual return did the unit holder earn?

options.text: 16.0 per cent
options.why: The holding period return is (27.50 − 25.00 + 0.50) / 25.00 = 3.00 / 25.00 = 12.0 per cent for the nine months. Stated on an annual basis that is 12.0 × 12/9 = 16.0 per cent, because the money was at work for three quarters of a year and a yearly figure has to cover four quarters.

options.text: 9.0 per cent
options.misconception: multiplies by nine twelfths instead of twelve ninths, scaling a part-year return down when it should be scaled up
options.why: 12.0 × 9/12 = 9.0 per cent shrinks a return the holder earned in less than a year. The fraction goes the other way: a year is twelve ninths of nine months, so the annual figure is 12.0 × 12/9 = 16.0 per cent.

options.text: About 13.3 per cent
options.misconception: annualises the change in net asset value alone and leaves the dividend out, when the cash paid out is part of what the holder earned
options.why: (27.50 − 25.00) / 25.00 = 10.0 per cent, annualised to 13.3 per cent, counts the price rise and forgets the ₹0.50 taken in cash. That ₹0.50 came out of the fund's own assets and is exactly why the closing figure is not higher still.

options.text: 12.0 per cent
options.misconception: reports the nine-month return as though it were an annual one, so a shorter holding is quietly compared with a longer one
options.why: 12.0 per cent is what the holder earned in nine months, and it is the right first step. Left there it understates the scheme, because anyone comparing it with a fund that took a year to earn 12 per cent would rank the two the same when this one was a quarter faster.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A unit holder bought units of a scheme at a net asset value of ₹25.00 and sold them exactly nine months later at ₹27.50. During those nine months the scheme paid a dividend of ₹0.50 a unit, taken in cash. Returns are to be stated on a simple annual basis.

items.stem: What is the share worth today?

options.text: About ₹59.21
options.misconception: discounts the capitalised value for four years because the first dividend falls in year four, when the formula already places that value one year ahead of the dividend it uses
options.why: 100 / 1.6890 = ₹59.21 charges one year of discounting twice. Dividing a dividend by the required return less growth produces a value as at the end of the year before that dividend — year three here — so three years of discounting is the whole of it.

options.text: About ₹67.50
options.why: Capitalising the ₹8 dividend gives 8 / (0.14 − 0.06) = ₹100, and that figure stands one year before the dividend inside it — at the end of year three. Discounting three years back, 100 / 1.4815 = ₹67.50. Nothing else is added, because there is no dividend in years one to three to discount.

options.misconception: stops at the capitalised figure and never brings it back to today, quoting a value that stands three years out as if it were a price now
options.why: ₹100 is what the share will be worth at the end of year three, when the first dividend is one year away. Money three years out is not money today; at 14 per cent it is worth 100 / 1.4815 = ₹67.50.

options.text: About ₹71.55
options.misconception: grows the ₹8 by another year before capitalising it, when ₹8 is already the first dividend of the growing phase
options.why: 8 × 1.06 / 0.08 = ₹106, discounted three years, gives ₹71.55. The growth rate applies from the first dividend onwards, so ₹8 goes into the formula as it stands. Growing it once more assumes a dividend in year three that the company has said it will not pay.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company will pay no dividend at all for the next three years while it builds capacity. Its first dividend, of ₹8 a share, will be paid at the end of year four, and dividends will grow at 6 per cent a year for ever after that. The required return is 14 per cent. Take 1.14 cubed as 1.4815 and 1.14 to the fourth as 1.6890.

items.stem: What is the investor's position?

options.text: The total interest he ever collects can come to less than the ₹40 crore he paid, so he can lose money even holding to the end
options.why: Interest is charged on principal that is still outstanding. When borrowers repay early the principal disappears and the interest stops with it, so the strip's cash flows do not merely arrive later — some of them never arrive at all. That is what makes an Interest Only strip unusual: an ordinary bond held to maturity returns its face value, and this instrument carries no such promise.

options.text: The strip gains, because a lower discount rate raises the present value of every future payment
options.misconception: applies the ordinary bond rule that prices rise when rates fall, missing that the strip's own cash flows shrink at the same time
options.why: Falling rates do lift the value of a fixed stream. This stream is not fixed: the same fall in rates is what sends borrowers off to refinance, and the interest they would have paid is cancelled. The loss of cash flow outweighs the gentler discounting.

options.text: His loss is limited, since the principal still outstanding is returned to him at the end
options.misconception: reads a principal claim into an instrument that was defined by having none
options.why: The strip pays interest and nothing else — the principal goes to the Principal Only holder by construction. There is no redemption amount to fall back on, which is why these instruments are described as highly volatile and are the least preferred by investors.

options.text: He is unaffected, because early repayment of principal is the Principal Only holder's concern and the interest schedule is fixed
options.misconception: assumes the strip has a fixed payment schedule, when the schedule is whatever the borrowers choose to do
options.why: The schedule is not fixed on either strip. Prepayment shortens the life of the whole pool, and the two halves feel it in opposite ways — the Principal Only holder gets his money sooner and gains, while the Interest Only holder simply stops being paid.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: An investor pays ₹40 crore for the Interest Only strip on a pool of housing loans. Market interest rates then fall sharply and a large part of the pool is repaid early by borrowers refinancing elsewhere.

items.stem: Is the fund asking for this at the right point?

options.text: No — the exit plan is the sixth stage and belongs at the end of the holding period, once the state of the market is actually known
options.misconception: reads the order of the list as the order in which each matter is decided, when the exit is settled at the outset and only carried out at the end
options.why: What happens at the end is the exit itself. What happens at the beginning is the agreement about it — which routes are open and on what terms. Leaving that to be argued six years later is how a fund ends up locked into a company it cannot leave.

options.text: No — the six stages end at post investment activity, and an exit plan is a commercial preference rather than a stage of the process
options.misconception: drops a stage from the list, treating the exit as something outside the process when it is the sixth stage of it
options.why: The exit plan is the sixth and last of the named stages, not an optional extra. A venture fund exists to put money in and take it out again within a set life, so how it leaves is structural to the investment rather than a matter of taste.

options.text: No — this is post investment activity, which starts the moment the term sheet is signed
options.misconception: starts post investment activity at signature rather than at investment, and misplaces the exit discussion into it
options.why: Post investment activity begins once the money is actually in, and it is where the fund puts its nominee on the board and monitors the milestones. Nothing has been invested here; terms are still being agreed, which is deal structuring.

options.text: Yes — the exit plan is named last among the six stages, but the fund settles it at the time of investing, because that is when it has the leverage to insist
options.why: The six stages are deal origination, screening, due diligence, deal structuring, post investment activity and exit plan. The list names the stages; it does not say every one of them is decided only when its turn arrives. The exit plan is spelled out at the time of investing, while the founder still needs the money — afterwards the fund is a minority holder asking a favour.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A venture fund has finished checking a founder's claims and is now settling terms. Before it signs, it requires the promoter to set out in writing how the fund will eventually get its money back out of the company — even though the fund expects to stay invested for six years or more.

items.stem: What are these three questions called?

options.text: Suitability, acceptability and feasibility — acceptability being the resource question and feasibility the stakeholder one
options.misconception: has the right three names and swaps the last two, so the resource count is filed under stakeholder satisfaction
options.why: The three names are right and two of them have changed places. Feasibility is the resource question — what kind and how many are needed to formulate and implement the strategy. Acceptability is the stakeholder question, and it runs to financial and non-financial satisfaction both.

options.text: Financial resources, financial tools and financial goals — the three components of financial planning
options.misconception: reaches for the other triad in the same chapter, which describes planning rather than testing a strategy
options.why: Those three do sit in the same chapter, as Financial Planning = FR + FT + FG. They describe what financial planning is made of — the money available, the instruments used and the targets set. They are not the tests a corporate level strategy is put through.

options.text: Corporate, business unit and functional — the three levels of strategy
options.misconception: names the three levels at which strategy is set in place of the three tests one strategy has to pass
options.why: Those are the levels a strategy sits at, not the questions asked of it. The proposal here is already known to be a corporate level one — it is about which businesses to be in. The three questions are what that corporate level strategy is then tested against.

options.text: Suitability, feasibility and acceptability — the three questions a corporate level strategy has to answer
options.why: Corporate level strategy is tested on three questions and these are they. Suitability asks whether the strategy would work for the accomplishment of the common objective of the company. Feasibility determines the kind and number of resources required to formulate and implement it. Acceptability is concerned with the stakeholders' satisfaction, and the material adds that it can be financial and non-financial — which is why the last question was put in both those terms.

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

items.scenario: A board is weighing a proposal to sell its cement division and enter speciality chemicals. It puts three questions to the proposal. Would this actually get the company to the common objective it has set? What kind of resources, and how many, would formulating and running it take? And would the people with a stake in the company wear it, in money terms and otherwise?

items.stem: What does the sustainable growth model say about the finance director's argument?

options.text: The model has nothing to say about it, since the sustainable growth rate is a real-terms measure by construction
options.misconception: exempts the model from inflation, when the chapter names inflation as one of the two sources of growth it handles
options.why: The chapter names growth from increased volume and growth from inflation side by side and works through what inflation does to the funding requirement and to the debt to equity ratio. It is inside the model, not outside it.

options.text: He is right — an inflationary rise in sales and assets funds itself, so only the five points of volume growth need new money
options.misconception: treats a price-driven rise in the value of assets as though it arrived with the cash to pay for it
options.why: The rise in the value of stock and equipment is a rise in what the company must spend to hold them, not a rise in cash. Somebody has to fund the extra rupees tied up, and the model says plainly that this inflationary increase must be financed as though it were real growth.

options.text: Inflation raises the sustainable growth rate, because a higher money return on equity raises the amount retained each year
options.misconception: counts the nominal lift in the return on equity while ignoring that the assets it must fund have risen by the same inflation
options.why: Retained earnings do come out larger in money terms, and so do the assets they have to finance. What tips the balance the other way is the historical cost measurement: the debt rises with today's prices while the book equity carries yesterday's, so the ratio drifts up and, if it must be held constant, growth has to come down.

options.text: He is wrong — the inflationary increase in assets has to be financed as though it were real growth, and on historical cost books that pushes the debt to equity ratio up, so inflation lowers the sustainable growth rate
options.why: Growth comes from two sources, increased volume and inflation, and the model treats them alike: the inflationary increase in assets must be financed as though it were real growth, because the company still has to find the money to replace stock and equipment at the new prices. Inflation therefore increases the amount of external financing required and raises the debt to equity ratio when that ratio is measured on a historical cost basis — the debt is fresh and the equity is stale. If creditors require that ratio to stay constant, inflation lowers the firm's sustainable growth rate rather than leaving it alone.
keywords: financed as though it were real growth
lowers the firm's sustainable growth rate

citation.ref: Ch. Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy

items.scenario: A company's sales are set to grow 9 per cent next year. Four of those points are price rises that simply follow inflation; five points are extra volume. The finance director argues that only the five points of real volume growth has to be funded, because the inflation part pays for itself — prices and asset values are rising together. The company's assets are carried in the books at historical cost, and its lenders insist the debt to equity ratio measured on those book figures does not move.

items.stem: What is this technique called, what are the three sets of figures called, and what does the material suggest when they conflict?

options.text: It is the anticipatory survey approach, which is another name for the same thing
options.misconception: joins two separate techniques for economic analysis into one
options.why: An anticipatory survey is a different technique. It gathers expert opinion on construction activity, spending on plant and machinery and inventory levels, along with the future spending habits of consumers. Its own weakness is that the intentions surveyed may never materialise. Reading indicator series is the barometer approach and sits beside it.

options.text: The barometer or indicator approach — leading, roughly coincidental and lagging indicators — and a diffusion or composite index combining several indicators into one
options.why: The barometer or indicator approach reads the future of the economy off series that move with it at different times. Leading indicators reach their high and low points in advance of economic activity; roughly coincidental indicators reach their peaks and troughs at approximately the same time as the economy; lagging indicators turn only after the economy has turned already. Because the measures can give conflicting signals, the material suggests a diffusion or composite index, combining several indicators into one to measure the strength or weakness in the movement of a set of them.

options.text: All three are leading indicators, since every series used to forecast the economy leads it by definition
options.misconception: reads the purpose the analyst puts a series to as the classification the material gives it
options.why: What makes a series leading is when it turns, not what it is used for. Only the machinery orders reach their turning points in advance. Employment turns with the economy and the length of unemployment turns after it, which is precisely why the three are told apart.

options.text: Sorting them decides nothing, because properly chosen indicators cannot conflict
options.misconception: assumes agreement among indicators, when the material warns of conflicting signals and offers a remedy for them
options.why: The material says in terms that the various measures obtained from such indicators may give conflicting signals about the future direction of the economy. That is the stated reason the diffusion or composite index is suggested at all — and it does not eliminate irregular movements even then.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: An analyst doing the economy stage watches three sets of figures. New orders for machinery, which turn up or down some months before the economy does. Total employment, which turns at about the same time as the economy. And the average length of unemployment, which only turns after the economy already has. On this occasion the three point in different directions.

items.stem: How does Charles Dow's own account of a primary uptrend read this?

options.text: Accumulation by the far-sighted investors is the third move, since the knowledgeable buy last, once the case is proven
options.misconception: turns the sequence around, so the informed buyers arrive after the crowd instead of before it
options.why: Accumulation by the far-sighted, knowledgeable investors is the first move up, before the good earnings are reported at all. They are also the first out, near the end of the third move. Buying early and selling early is the whole of what the word far-sighted is doing in Dow's account.

options.text: This is the third move up — widespread reports of financial well-being, with rampant speculation — and the far-sighted investors selling is what starts the first move down of the downtrend
options.why: Dow proposed that a primary uptrend has three moves up. The first is accumulation of shares by the far-sighted, knowledgeable investors. The second comes with the arrival of the first reports of good earnings by corporations. The third comes with widespread report of financial well-being, and it also sees rampant speculation. Towards the end of that third stage the far-sighted investors, realising the high earnings levels may not be sustained, start selling — and that is the first move down of the downtrend.

options.text: This is the second move up, which is the one caused by the first reports of good earnings
options.misconception: places widespread good news at the stage where the first reports of it arrive
options.why: The second move up is caused by the arrival of the first reports of good earnings — the news is fresh and narrow. What is described here is news that has spread everywhere, together with rampant speculation, which is the third move.

options.text: The Dow Theory names only the primary movement, the secondary movement and the daily fluctuations, and says nothing about stages inside a trend
options.misconception: stops at the three movements and misses the three-stage description of the primary trend itself
options.why: The three movements are how the theory sorts what is happening at any moment. Separately from that, Dow described the primary uptrend as running in three moves up and the downtrend in three moves down, each with its own cause. Both descriptions are his.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A market has been in a primary uptrend for two years. The newspapers are full of reports of companies doing well across the board, small investors are borrowing to buy, and prices are running far above anything earnings justify. Quietly, a handful of large long-standing investors are selling.

items.stem: How does the study material treat these two objections?

options.text: The material answers both by pointing to the empirical evidence for the random walk hypothesis, which supports technical analysis
options.misconception: files the random walk evidence among the defences when the material lists it among the attacks
options.why: The random walk evidence runs the other way. The material names it as one of the detractors' arguments — the evidence in support of the random walk hypothesis casts its shadow over the usefulness of technical analysis, because a price series with no memory cannot be charted into a forecast.

options.text: Both are arguments in favour — trends persist under crowd psychology, so a tool that spots them early pays
options.misconception: hands the advocates' case to the detractors, so the reason the method might work is offered as the reason it might not
options.why: Crowd psychology making trends persist is one of the three arguments in favour, along with shifts in demand and supply being gradual rather than instantaneous and fundamental information being assimilated by the market over a period of time. The two objections here are from the other list.

options.text: Both are on its own list of the detractors' arguments, and it neither adopts nor dismisses them — it concludes technical analysis may not work well in a rational, well ordered and efficient market but may help in a real one that is not
options.why: The material sets the detractors' arguments out itself, and these are two of the four: that by the time an uptrend or downtrend has been signalled it may already have taken place, and that technical analysis must ultimately be a self-defeating proposition, since with more and more people employing it the value of such analysis tends to decline. The other two are that most technical analysts cannot offer a convincing explanation for their tools, and that the empirical evidence for the random walk hypothesis casts a shadow over the whole exercise. Against those it sets three arguments in favour and then concludes that in a rational, well ordered and efficient market technical analysis may not work very well, while with the imperfection and irrationality of the real world it may be helpful, especially used alongside fundamental analysis.

options.text: The material rejects both, since it treats technical analysis as one of the two proper approaches to security analysis
options.misconception: reads the material's willingness to teach a method as a defence of it against every criticism
options.why: It teaches the method and it prints the case against it in the same section, under the heading of evaluation. Setting out four criticisms in the author's own words is not rejecting them. What it does instead is say when the method may help and when it may not.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: Two objections are put to a chartist. The first is that his tools may work now but will stop working, because the more people who use them the less they are worth. The second is that by the time his charts have signalled an uptrend, the uptrend has already happened.

items.stem: What is the security's expected return under the Arbitrage Pricing Theory?

options.text: 12.8 per cent
options.why: Expected return is the risk free rate plus each factor's sensitivity multiplied by that factor's own risk premium, added up. Market gives 1.2 × 5 = 6.0 per cent. GDP growth gives 0.5 × 2 = 1.0 per cent. Inflation gives 0.4 × −3 = −1.2 per cent: a negative premium means the market does not reward that exposure but discounts it, so the term is carried through with its minus sign and comes off the required return. So 7 + 6.0 + 1.0 − 1.2 = 12.8 per cent.

options.text: 5.8 per cent
options.misconception: adds up the three factor terms and never puts the risk free rate underneath them
options.why: 6.0 + 1.0 − 1.2 = 5.8 per cent is the total compensation for bearing the three exposures. Compensation for risk is paid on top of the riskless rate, not instead of it, which is why the formula opens with the risk free rate. Adding the 7 per cent gives 12.8 per cent.

options.text: 13.0 per cent
options.misconception: uses the market factor alone, which is the single-factor CAPM answer and not an Arbitrage Pricing Theory one
options.why: 7 + 1.2 × 5 = 13.0 per cent is what CAPM would say, because CAPM has only the one factor. The point of the multi-factor model is that the other two exposures are priced as well — the GDP term adding 1.0 and the inflation term taking off 1.2.

options.text: 15.2 per cent
options.misconception: takes the size of the inflation premium and drops its minus sign, so an exposure the market discounts is paid for instead
options.why: 7 + 6.0 + 1.0 + 1.2 = 15.2 per cent adds the inflation term instead of subtracting it. The premium given is minus 3 per cent, and multiplying it by a sensitivity of 0.4 gives minus 1.2 per cent. Signs are the whole difference between 12.8 and 15.2 here.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: A security is priced against three factors. The market factor carries a risk premium of 5 per cent and the security's sensitivity to it is 1.2. The GDP growth factor carries a premium of 2 per cent at a sensitivity of 0.5. The inflation factor carries a premium of minus 3 per cent at a sensitivity of 0.4. The risk free rate is 7 per cent.

items.stem: Which of the obstacles named in the study material is this?

options.text: None of them — securitisation turns an illiquid pool into tradable paper, so the paper itself must be liquid
options.misconception: assumes the liquidity created for the originator is the same liquidity available to the investor afterwards
options.why: Securitisation does give the originator its money at once, by selling the pool. Whether the securities issued against that pool can then be traded is a separate question, answered by the market they trade in — and the material names the inadequate debt market in India as an obstacle for exactly that reason.

options.text: Weak credit enhancement, since better enhancement would have made the paper easy to sell
options.misconception: reaches for a feature of the deal's structure to explain a shortage of buyers in the market around it
options.why: Credit enhancement changes who bears the pool's losses — through overcollateralisation, subordination, excess spread or an outside guarantee. It cannot manufacture a buyer. Even paper enhanced to the highest grade needs a market with people in it before it can be sold on.

options.text: The accounting obstacle, since unsettled accounting makes the paper hard to price
options.misconception: applies an obstacle that sits in the originator's own books to a difficulty an outside investor has in finding a buyer
options.why: The accounting concern is about how the originator reports securitised assets in its books — securitisation is slated to be off balance sheet and the receivables really are removed, and the problem is sharpest where the assets are transferred without recourse. It is a question for the seller's accounts, not for the depth of the market the buyer sells into.

options.text: The inadequate debt market — India has no well-developed debt market, so there is no deep secondary market for securitised or asset backed securities to be resold into
options.why: Lack of the existence of a well-developed debt market in India is one of the six obstacles named, and it is the one that hinders the growth of the secondary market of securitised or asset backed securities. The others bite when a deal is being put together; this one bites afterwards, on the investor who wants to leave early, and it is why he is quoted a discount rather than a price.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: An investor bought asset backed securities out of an Indian issue two years ago. He now wants out before maturity and finds there is barely anybody to sell to — no screen, no regular quotes, and the few buyers he can find want a large discount for taking the paper off him.

items.stem: What does the study material say the expense ratio covers?

options.text: It is inside — that is what the word total means in Total Expense Ratio
options.misconception: reads a name as a guarantee of completeness, when the material names one cost the ratio leaves out
options.why: Total Expense Ratio, or Management Expense Ratio, are alternative names for the same figure, not a promise that nothing is missing from it. The material states the exclusion directly: brokerage costs for trading the portfolio are outside the ratio.

options.text: Neither is inside — the expense ratio is the fund manager's fee and nothing more
options.misconception: shrinks the ratio to a single line when the material lists six kinds of cost inside it
options.why: Management and advisory fees are only the first item. Travel costs, audit fees, custodian fees, registrar fees and consultancy fees all sit inside the ratio too. The one thing named as outside it is the brokerage paid on trading the portfolio.

options.text: It is inside, and so is any exit load the investor pays on the way out
options.misconception: mixes an annual charge on the fund's assets with a one-off deduction made from one investor's redemption
options.why: An exit load is a different animal. It is deducted from the NAV at the time an investor redeems or transfers, it is paid by that investor and not by the fund's assets year on year, and many schemes charge none at all once the units have been held for a stipulated period.

options.text: It is not inside — the ratio covers management and advisory fees, travel costs, audit fees, custodian fees, registrar fees and consultancy fees, and expressly excludes brokerage costs for trading the portfolio
options.why: The expense ratio is the percentage of the assets spent to run the scheme, and the material lists what goes into it: management and advisory fees, travel costs, audit fees, custodian fees, registrar fees and consultancy fees. It then says the expense ratio does not include brokerage costs for trading the portfolio. So a heavily traded fund carries a drag the quoted ratio never shows, which is why the material also warns the ratio can run as high as 2 to 3 per cent and seriously undermine performance.
keywords: brokerage costs for trading the portfolio

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A scheme reports an expense ratio of 1.8 per cent. Its fund manager traded heavily during the year and paid a great deal of brokerage on buying and selling the portfolio. An investor wants to know whether that brokerage is already inside the 1.8 per cent.

items.stem: Is the distributor right, and how does this structure actually differ from a close-ended one?

options.text: No — it is an open-ended scheme, since the fund itself buys the units back at a price based on NAV
options.misconception: takes redemption by the fund at NAV as the test, when the test is whether that redemption is available at any time
options.why: The fund does buy the units back at NAV based prices, which is why an interval scheme is called a combination of the two structures. But an open-ended scheme lets the investor enter and exit at any time, with an indefinite redemption period. Three months of being locked in is not that.

options.text: No — it is an interval scheme, and it differs on three points: it need not be listed on a stock exchange because it carries its own redemption window, it can issue fresh units during the specified interval at NAV based prices, and its maturity period is not defined
options.why: An interval scheme is a combination of the open-ended and close-ended structures, open for purchase and redemption during pre-specified intervals — monthly, quarterly, annually — at prevailing NAV based prices. The material then names three differences from a close-ended scheme. It is not required to be listed on the stock exchanges, as it has an in-built redemption window. It can make a fresh issue of units during the specified interval period. And its maturity period is not defined, where a close-ended scheme has a limited life at the end of which the corpus is liquidated.

options.text: Yes — a scheme that is shut most of the time is close-ended in substance, whatever it is called
options.misconception: judges the structure by how often the window is open rather than by the three things the window changes
options.why: Being shut most of the time is what an interval scheme and a close-ended one have in common, and it is not what separates them. What separates them is that a close-ended scheme has a fixed life and a fixed corpus and must be listed for its investors to get out at all, while an interval scheme has no defined maturity, needs no listing and can take in new money each window.

options.text: Yes, and like every close-ended scheme it must be listed on an exchange and cannot issue further units after its offer closes
options.misconception: applies the listing requirement and the closed corpus to a structure the material exempts from both
options.why: Those are the two points the material uses to tell an interval scheme apart from a close-ended one. An interval scheme is not required to be listed, because the redemption window is built into it, and it can make a fresh issue of units during that window at prevailing NAV based prices.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A scheme opens for both purchase and redemption for one week every quarter, at prices based on the prevailing NAV, and is shut the rest of the time. A distributor tells an investor it is simply a close-ended scheme with a convenience window bolted on.

items.stem: Which financial option does the study material liken each of these three to?

options.text: The comparison is decorative, since real options are valued by methods of their own and not by option pricing methods
options.misconception: treats real options as a separate valuation family, when the material uses the same three methods on both
options.why: The methods employed to value real options are the same ones used for financial options — the binomial model, the risk neutral method and the Black-Scholes model. What is harder is identifying the value of certain inputs, since the underlying is a project that is not traded, which is also why real options are said to be valued rather than priced.

options.text: The growth option to a European call, the abandonment option to an American put, and the timing option to an American call
options.why: A growth option is a project with a negative or insignificant NPV of its own, taken because it opens considerable profitability later — research spending, heavy advertising, a first investment in a foreign market — and the material likens it to a European call option. The abandonment option, exercised when the value from the project's assets exceeds the present value of continuing, is similar to an American put option. The timing option, the third choice of delaying until better information or ideas arrive, is like an American call option.

options.text: The growth option to an American call and the timing option to a European call, since research can be cashed in whenever it succeeds
options.misconception: swaps which of the two rights to invest may be taken up at any moment
options.why: The labels are the other way round. The material likens the growth option to a European call and the timing option to an American call — the option of when to invest is precisely the one exercised at a moment of the holder's choosing, as better information arrives.

options.text: All three to call options, since every real option is a right to invest that the firm may or may not take up
options.misconception: files a right to get out under rights to get in, missing that abandonment is a right to sell
options.why: Two of them are rights to invest and one is not. Abandoning is disinvesting — the right to sell at some future date at a certain or zero price, the flexibility to exit a business. That is a put, and it is why the material calls it an American put.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A company holds three pieces of flexibility. It has spent heavily on research that has no payoff of its own but would let it enter a new market later. It can walk away from a running plant and sell the assets if conditions sour. And it can put off a solar installation for a year to see which way electricity tariffs move.

items.stem: Which of the model's stated assumptions has she broken?

options.text: The assumption that the variance of the return is constant over the life of the option, since a dividend makes the price jump
options.misconception: names a real assumption of the model that this particular event does not break, when a nearer one is broken outright
options.why: The constant variance assumption is about how widely the return scatters, not about a known, scheduled drop in the price. The dividend breaks the assumption written for it — that stocks do not pay dividend — and there is no need to reach past it.

options.text: None — the model says nothing about dividends, and only assumes a volatility and a risk-free rate
options.misconception: mistakes the model's two disputable inputs for the whole of what it assumes
options.why: Volatility and the risk-free rate are the two things investors have to agree on before they can agree on the option's value, which is a different point. The list of assumptions accompanying the model runs to seven, and no dividend is one of them, stated in those words.

options.text: That stocks do not pay dividend
options.why: The seven assumptions printed with the model are that European options are considered, that there are no transaction costs, that short term interest rates are known and constant, that stocks do not pay dividend, that the stock price movement is similar to a random walk, that stock returns are normally distributed over a period of time, and that the variance of the return is constant over the life of the option. A dividend paid before expiry breaks the fourth of those directly, and it matters because the share price drops by roughly the dividend on the ex-date, taking the call's value down with it while the formula is looking the other way.

options.text: The no-transaction-costs assumption, since paying a dividend costs the company money
options.misconception: reads an assumption about the cost of dealing in the option as an assumption about the company's own outgoings
options.why: The no-transaction-costs assumption is about what it costs to trade and hedge — brokerage, spreads, the cost of running the hedge the writer must keep. What the company pays its shareholders is not a transaction cost of the option, and it is covered by its own separate assumption.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A dealer prices a six-month call on a share using Black-Scholes exactly as the formula stands. The company has announced that it will pay a substantial dividend in four months, before the option expires. The dealer changes nothing in her inputs.

items.stem: How does the study material describe a currency swap's three stages, and what is that middle stage?

options.text: The middle stage is a single forward contract covering the whole five years, settled once at maturity alongside the principal
options.misconception: collapses a run of dated forward contracts into one, so the intervening payment dates disappear
options.why: The interest is exchanged at settlement dates through the term, which is why the material calls it a series of forward foreign exchange contracts rather than one. Each payment date has its own contract in effect, all struck at the same opening rate.

options.text: There is no exchange of principal at the outset — only the interest streams are swapped, and the principal is re-exchanged at maturity
options.misconception: drops the first of the three stages, leaving each party without the currency it entered the swap to obtain
options.why: The spot exchange of principal at the start is the first of the three stages, and it is the reason each party ends up holding the currency it wanted. Without it the swap would deliver interest in a currency neither side has the principal in.

options.text: A spot exchange of principal, then a continuing exchange of interest payments through the term, then a re-exchange of principal on maturity — and the middle stage is a series of forward foreign exchange contracts, typically fixed at the same exchange rate as the spot rate used at the outset
options.why: The material sets a currency swap out in three stages. First a spot exchange of principal, which forms part of the agreement because a similar effect could be had in the spot foreign exchange market. Then the continuing exchange of interest payments during the term, and this is described as a series of forward foreign exchange contracts running through the life of the swap, the contract typically fixed at the same exchange rate as the spot rate used at the outset. Then the re-exchange of principal on maturity. So the interest leg is hedged for the whole term, not only the principals.
keywords: series of forward foreign exchange contracts

options.text: The same three stages, except that each interest payment is converted at whatever the spot rate happens to be on that date, so the interest flows carry currency risk even though the principals do not
options.misconception: leaves the interest leg floating, when the material describes it as a run of forward contracts struck at the outset
options.why: If the interest legs repriced at each date's spot rate the company would still be exposed on five years of payments, which is most of what it entered the swap to avoid. The material describes that leg as a series of forward foreign exchange contracts, typically at the opening spot rate — so it is fixed, like the principals.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: A treasurer is shown a five-year rupee-dollar currency swap and asked to describe what her company is actually signing up to, stage by stage. She is particularly unsure what the middle part — the interest payments running across the five years — amounts to in market terms.

items.stem: What is the project's net present value in rupees?

options.text: ₹160 crore, and both consistent routes give it
options.why: Route one keeps everything in dollars: 132 / 1.10 = $120 million, less the $100 million put in, is $20 million, converted at today's spot rate of ₹80 to ₹1,600 million, that is ₹160 crore. Route two keeps everything in rupees: the inflow converts at the forward rate, 132 × 88 = ₹11,616 million, discounted at the rupee rate of 21 per cent gives ₹9,600 million, less the outlay of 100 × 80 = ₹8,000 million, is ₹1,600 million again. The two agree because the forward rate and the two discount rates carry the same currency expectation.

options.text: ₹256 crore
options.misconception: converts at the forward rate and then discounts at the dollar rate, so the expected currency gain is credited while the rupee's higher required return is never charged
options.why: 11,616 / 1.10 = ₹10,560 million, less ₹8,000 million, gives ₹2,560 million or ₹256 crore. Rupee cash flows have to meet the rupee required return of 21 per cent. Using 10 per cent on them takes the currency gain built into the ₹88 forward rate and never pays for it.

options.text: About ₹73 crore
options.misconception: discounts dollar cash flows at the rupee rate and converts at spot, so the currency premium is charged without the compensating appreciation ever being credited
options.why: 132 / 1.21 = $109.09 million, less $100 million, is $9.09 million, converted at ₹80 to about ₹727 million or ₹73 crore. The 21 per cent rate carries the rupee's expected slide inside it; dollar cash flows do not. Charging that premium against flows that never receive the matching appreciation manufactures a poor answer out of a good project.

options.text: ₹176 crore
options.misconception: converts the dollar net present value at the one-year forward rate instead of at spot, so a figure already stated in today's money is moved a year forward
options.why: $20 million × 88 = ₹1,760 million or ₹176 crore. The $20 million is already a present value — money as at today — so it converts at today's rate of ₹80, giving ₹160 crore. The ₹88 rate belongs to a cash flow arriving in a year's time, and the year-one inflow has already used it in the other route.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company is appraising a one-year US project. It puts in $100 million today and takes out $132 million in a year. The spot rate is ₹80 per dollar. The required return in rupees is 21 per cent and in dollars 10 per cent, and the international parity conditions hold, so the one-year forward rate works out at 80 × 1.21 / 1.10 = ₹88 per dollar.

items.stem: When should the machine be abandoned, and what is the project worth?

options.text: At the end of year 1, for an NPV of about ₹15.45 lakh
options.misconception: discounts the operating cash flow of year 1 but takes the sale proceeds at face value, though both fall due on the same date
options.why: −100 + 50 × 0.9091 + 70 = ₹15.45 lakh leaves the ₹70 lakh undiscounted. The sale happens at the end of year 1, exactly when the ₹50 lakh arrives, so both are multiplied by 0.9091: 120 × 0.9091 = ₹109.09 lakh, and the NPV is ₹9.09 lakh.

options.text: At the end of year 2, for an NPV of about ₹7.44 lakh
options.misconception: stops one year late, taking the last date at which the sale still fetches something rather than the date at which the sale beats carrying on
options.why: −100 + 50 × 0.9091 + (40 + 35) × 0.8264 = ₹7.44 lakh, which is better than running to the end but worse than stopping a year earlier. Year 2's salvage of ₹35 lakh plus that year's ₹40 lakh comes to ₹75 lakh, worth ₹68.18 lakh at the end of year 1 — less than the ₹70 lakh on offer there. The test is the sale proceeds against the value of continuing, at every date.

options.text: The project should be rejected, since running it to the end gives an NPV of about minus ₹6.46 lakh
options.misconception: judges the project on the static NPV of running it to the end, which prices the freedom to stop early at exactly zero
options.why: −₹6.46 lakh is what the machine is worth if nobody is allowed to sell it. The right to stop is worth 9.09 − (−6.46) = ₹15.55 lakh here, and it turns a rejection into an acceptance. A project is not rejected until the best of its stopping points has been valued.

options.text: At the end of year 1, for an NPV of about ₹9.09 lakh
options.why: Work out the NPV of each stopping point and take the best. Abandoning at the end of year 1 gives −100 + (50 + 70) × 0.9091 = ₹9.09 lakh. Abandoning at the end of year 2 gives −100 + 50 × 0.9091 + (40 + 35) × 0.8264 = ₹7.44 lakh. Running the full three years gives −100 + 45.45 + 33.06 + 15.03 = −₹6.46 lakh. The same answer falls out of the rule directly: at the end of year 1 the abandonment value of ₹70 lakh beats the ₹68.18 lakh that carrying on to the end of year 2 is then worth, so the machine goes.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A machine costs ₹100 lakh now. It brings in ₹50 lakh at the end of year 1, ₹40 lakh at the end of year 2 and ₹20 lakh at the end of year 3. It can be sold for ₹70 lakh at the end of year 1, for ₹35 lakh at the end of year 2, and for nothing at the end of year 3. Every figure is known with certainty. The discount rate is 10 per cent, so the present value factors are 0.9091, 0.8264 and 0.7513.

items.stem: What is the chance this project ends in a loss, and what is its expected NPV?

options.text: A 70 per cent chance of a loss, and an expected NPV of about ₹18.33 lakh
options.misconception: averages the three end values equally, when the branches they sit on are not equally likely
options.why: (−5 + 80 − 20) ÷ 3 = ₹18.33 lakh gives the ₹80 lakh outcome the same standing as the other two. It occurs 30 per cent of the time and the failed pilot 40 per cent, so each end value must be multiplied by the chance of reaching it: the answer is ₹16 lakh.

options.text: A 70 per cent chance of a loss, and an expected NPV of ₹25 lakh
options.misconception: averages the two demand outcomes without weighting them by the chance of ever getting past the pilot, so a branch reached 60 per cent of the time is treated as certain
options.why: 0.50 × 80 + 0.50 × (−20) = ₹30 lakh, less the ₹5 lakh pilot, gives ₹25 lakh. That figure assumes the plant always gets built. It gets built only when the pilot succeeds, which is 60 per cent of the time, so each demand branch carries 0.60 × 0.50 = 0.30, not 0.50, and the expected NPV is ₹16 lakh.

options.text: A 30 per cent chance of a loss, and an expected NPV of ₹16 lakh
options.misconception: counts only the low-demand outcome as a loss and writes the failed pilot off as money already spent rather than as an outcome of the project
options.why: The failed pilot is one of the three ways this project can end, and it ends at minus ₹5 lakh. It happens 40 per cent of the time. Adding it to the 30 per cent chance of low demand gives 70 per cent. Money already committed does not stop being a loss because it was committed first.

options.text: A 70 per cent chance of a loss, and an expected NPV of ₹16 lakh
options.why: Read the tree forwards to get the three end points and the chance of reaching each. Pilot fails, 0.40, worth −₹5 lakh. Pilot succeeds and demand is high, 0.60 × 0.50 = 0.30, worth ₹80 lakh. Pilot succeeds and demand is low, 0.30, worth −₹20 lakh. Two of the three end points are losses and together they carry 0.40 + 0.30 = 0.70 of the probability. The expected NPV is 0.40 × (−5) + 0.30 × 80 + 0.30 × (−20) = −2 + 24 − 6 = ₹16 lakh. A project can be worth taking and still lose money most of the time.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company spends ₹5 lakh on a pilot. There is a 40 per cent chance the pilot fails, in which case the company stops and the project's NPV is minus ₹5 lakh. There is a 60 per cent chance it succeeds, and the company then builds the plant. Once built, demand is high with a 50 per cent chance, giving an NPV of ₹80 lakh, and low with a 50 per cent chance, giving an NPV of minus ₹20 lakh. Every NPV is already stated in today's money.

items.stem: At what buyback price would EPS come out exactly unchanged at ₹12?

options.text: It depends on how many shares are bought — ₹200 if ten lakh are bought, ₹100 if twenty lakh are
options.misconception: assumes the size of the buyback moves the point of balance, when the number of shares cancels out of both sides of the comparison
options.why: The number cancels. Twenty lakh shares at ₹200 costs ₹4,000 lakh, profit falls to ₹960 lakh over 80 lakh shares, and EPS is again ₹12.00. At ₹100 for twenty lakh shares the cost is ₹2,000 lakh, profit is ₹1,080 lakh over 80 lakh shares and EPS rises to ₹13.50. The balance point is a price, ₹200, and it holds at any size.

options.text: ₹150 a share
options.misconception: charges the forgone income at the 8 per cent gross rate, when the company was only ever keeping 75 paise in the rupee of it
options.why: 12 ÷ 0.08 = ₹150 uses the pre-tax return. Only 6 per cent of the cash ever reached profit after tax. At ₹150, ten lakh shares cost ₹1,500 lakh, profit falls by ₹90 lakh to ₹1,110 lakh over 90 lakh shares, and EPS rises to ₹12.33 — so ₹150 is a price at which the buyback still helps, not the point of balance.

options.text: ₹200 a share
options.why: The cash earns 8 per cent before tax and 8 × 0.75 = 6 per cent after tax, so every ₹100 spent takes ₹6 of profit away. Buying n shares at price P removes 0.06 × nP of profit and n shares. EPS holds still when the profit given up per share cancelled equals the old EPS, that is when 0.06P = 12, so P = ₹200. Check it: 10 lakh shares at ₹200 costs ₹2,000 lakh, profit falls to 1,200 − 120 = ₹1,080 lakh over 90 lakh shares, and 1,080 ÷ 90 = ₹12.00. Below ₹200 EPS rises and above it EPS falls, because the earnings yield on the price paid, 12 ÷ 200 = 6 per cent, is exactly what the cash was earning after tax.

options.text: There is no such price — cutting the share count always lifts EPS, whatever is paid
options.misconception: counts only the benefit of the buyback and never the after-tax income the cash surrendered, which is the whole reason a price can be too high
options.why: The cash leaves with its earnings. At ₹300 a share, ten lakh shares cost ₹3,000 lakh, profit falls by ₹180 lakh to ₹1,020 lakh over 90 lakh shares, and EPS drops to ₹11.33. Paying too much for a share buys back too little earning power per rupee, and EPS falls.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A company earns profit after tax of ₹1,200 lakh on 100 lakh shares, so EPS is ₹12. It holds surplus cash earning 8 per cent a year before tax and pays tax at 25 per cent. It intends to buy shares back with that cash, and the board wants to know the price above which the buyback would start to pull EPS down.

items.stem: What does the acquisition actually cost A Ltd's own shareholders?

options.text: Nothing — 10 lakh shares at ₹100 each is ₹1,000 lakh, exactly what B Ltd was worth
options.misconception: prices the shares given away at yesterday's market price, when the shares handed over are shares in a company the merger has already made more valuable
options.why: ₹100 is A Ltd's price before the merger, and the buyer is not handing over pre-merger shares. Once the ₹500 lakh of gains are in, each of the 50 lakh shares is worth 5,500 ÷ 50 = ₹110, so the 10 lakh issued are worth ₹1,100 lakh. Measuring the cost at the old price makes every share-financed deal look free.

options.text: ₹1,100 lakh — the value of the shares A Ltd hands over
options.misconception: reports the price paid rather than the cost, which is the price paid less the value of what was bought
options.why: ₹1,100 lakh is what changes hands, not what it costs. A Ltd receives a business worth ₹1,000 lakh on its own in exchange, so only the ₹100 lakh of excess is a cost to its shareholders. Cost is always the consideration less the standalone value of the thing acquired.

options.text: ₹100 lakh, being ₹1,100 lakh handed over less B Ltd's ₹1,000 lakh standalone value
options.why: The combined company is worth 4,000 + 1,000 + 500 = ₹5,500 lakh and has 40 + 10 = 50 lakh shares. B Ltd's shareholders hold 10 of those 50, that is 20 per cent, worth 0.20 × 5,500 = ₹1,100 lakh. They brought in ₹1,000 lakh, so the true cost is ₹100 lakh, and A Ltd's own shareholders keep 500 − 100 = ₹400 lakh of the gain. Shares handed over carry a slice of the gains with them, which is why the cost is not what those shares were worth yesterday.

options.text: ₹500 lakh — the whole of the expected gain passes to B Ltd's shareholders
options.misconception: assumes the target captures the entire gain, when it captures only the part attaching to the proportion of the combined company it receives
options.why: B Ltd's shareholders receive 20 per cent of the combined company, so they receive 20 per cent of the ₹500 lakh of gains — ₹100 lakh. The other ₹400 lakh stays with A Ltd's own shareholders. They would take the whole ₹500 lakh only if they ended up owning the whole thing.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A Ltd has 40 lakh shares trading at ₹100, so it is worth ₹4,000 lakh. B Ltd has 20 lakh shares trading at ₹50, so it is worth ₹1,000 lakh. A Ltd expects the merger to create gains with a present value of ₹500 lakh. It offers one of its own shares for every two B Ltd shares, so it will issue 10 lakh new shares.

items.stem: Which form of restructuring is this?

options.text: A sell-off of all four divisions, since each has left the company
options.misconception: assumes a division leaving must have been sold, when a sell-off needs an outside buyer paying consideration
options.why: A sell-off transfers a division to a third party for cash or securities. There is no buyer here and no consideration. The divisions go to the people who already owned them, which is the opposite of a sale.

options.text: A spin-off, since shares in a new company go to the existing shareholders in proportion
options.misconception: reads the pro rata distribution alone and misses that a spin-off separates a part while the parent carries on with the rest
options.why: A spin-off does hand shares to the same shareholders in the same proportion, and it raises no cash either. What it does not do is end the parent. One division leaves and the company keeps the others. Here all four leave and nothing is left to keep.

options.text: An equity carve-out, since four new companies have been floated
options.misconception: confuses the creation of new companies with the sale of shares in one of them to outside investors
options.why: A carve-out sells part of a subsidiary's equity to the public, so it brings cash in and the parent keeps a controlling stake in a company it still owns. Neither happens here — nobody new subscribes, not a rupee is raised, and the parent does not remain to control anything.

options.text: A split-up — the whole firm is broken into separate companies and the parent does not survive
options.why: A split-up is a series of separations done at once, covering the entire firm. Four divisions become four companies with full legal status, the shareholders own all four in their old proportions, and the original company is wound up. It is the parent's disappearance that marks it out: in every other form of divestment the parent is still there afterwards.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A company has four divisions. Each one is put into a newly incorporated company of its own, and every existing shareholder receives shares in all four in the same proportion as before. No outside investor subscribes and no cash is raised. The original company is then wound up and ceases to exist.

items.stem: What is he worth afterwards under each of the three things he can do?

options.text: ₹36,000 if he subscribes and ₹36,000 if he sells his rights, but only ₹33,300 if he lets them lapse
options.why: Subscribing: he takes 100 new shares for 100 × 84 = ₹8,400, holds 400 shares at ₹111 = ₹44,400, and 44,400 − 8,400 = ₹36,000. Selling: the right is worth 111 − 84 = ₹27 per new share, or ₹9 per share held, so he keeps 300 × 111 = ₹33,300 and collects 300 × 9 = ₹2,700, again ₹36,000. Letting them lapse: he keeps ₹33,300 and collects nothing. The price falls to ₹111 whatever he does; only acting recovers what the fall took.

options.text: ₹36,000 in all three cases — the ex-rights price adjustment protects him whether he acts or not
options.misconception: treats the price fall as self-correcting, when the fall happens to every holder and only exercising or selling hands back the value it took
options.why: The drop from ₹120 to ₹111 hits his 300 shares no matter what he does — that is ₹2,700 gone. What subscribing or selling does is give him ₹2,700 back, as new shares bought below their worth or as cash for the rights. Doing nothing keeps the fall and takes back nothing, leaving ₹33,300.

options.text: He gains ₹2,700 by subscribing, buying at ₹84 shares that are worth ₹111
options.misconception: counts the discount on the new shares as a gain and ignores that the fall in the old ones is exactly what paid for it
options.why: The 100 new shares are indeed worth 100 × 27 = ₹2,700 more than he pays. His 300 old shares have fallen from ₹120 to ₹111 at the same time, which is 300 × 9 = ₹2,700 lost. The two cancel to the rupee, which is why a rights issue leaves a subscribing shareholder exactly where he was.

options.text: ₹44,400 if he subscribes, a gain of ₹8,400 on the ₹36,000 he started with
options.misconception: values the shares held after the issue without deducting the money paid to acquire them
options.why: ₹44,400 is 400 shares at ₹111, and he had to pay ₹8,400 to get to 400 shares. Netting that off leaves ₹36,000, the figure he started with. Reading the holding without the cheque that bought it turns his own money into a profit.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A company's shares trade cum-rights at ₹120. It announces a 1-for-3 rights issue — one new share for every three held — at a subscription price of ₹84. The theoretical ex-rights price works out at ₹111. A shareholder holds 300 shares, worth ₹36,000 before the announcement.

items.stem: What does Walter's model price the share at, and what would paying the whole ₹12 out do to that price?

options.text: ₹60 now, and cutting the dividend to nil would raise it further
options.misconception: assumes retention always compounds value, when it does so only where the firm earns more on the money than the shareholders' own required return
options.why: At a dividend of nil, P = [0 + (0.10/0.15) × 12] / 0.15 = 8 / 0.15 = ₹53.33 — lower, not higher. Retention adds value only when the return on it beats the cost of equity. Here it is 10 per cent against 15 per cent, so holding cash back destroys value and the price falls.

options.text: ₹20, capitalising the ₹3 dividend at 15 per cent
options.misconception: values the share on its dividend alone and drops the retained earnings term, though the ₹9 held back is still working inside the company
options.why: 3 / 0.15 = ₹20 throws away the ₹9 a share the company keeps. That ₹9 earns 10 per cent, and Walter's formula prices it at (0.10/0.15) × 9 = ₹6 before capitalising. The numerator is ₹9, not ₹3, and the price is ₹60.

options.text: ₹60 now, rising to ₹80 if the whole ₹12 were paid out
options.why: P = [D + (r/Ke)(E − D)] / Ke = [3 + (0.10/0.15) × 9] / 0.15 = [3 + 6] / 0.15 = ₹60. At a dividend of ₹12 nothing is retained, so P = 12 / 0.15 = ₹80. The firm earns 10 per cent on money the shareholders could put to work at 15 per cent, which is its cost of equity, so every rupee it keeps back is worth less inside the company than outside it and the price climbs as the payout climbs.

options.text: ₹60 now, and the payout makes no difference to the price under Walter's model
options.misconception: applies the irrelevance result, which under Walter holds only in the single case where the return on retention equals the cost of equity
options.why: Payout is irrelevant under Walter only when r equals Ke, because then the bracket collapses to E whatever D is. Here r is 10 per cent and Ke is 15 per cent, and the price runs from ₹53.33 at nil payout to ₹80 at full payout — a spread of ₹26.67 that the payout decides.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A company has EPS of ₹12 and pays a dividend of ₹3 a share. It earns 10 per cent on what it retains, and its cost of equity is 15 per cent.

items.stem: What does each of the three term structure theories make of a curve shaped like this?

options.text: Liquidity preference cannot account for an inverted curve at all, so this shape rules that theory out
options.misconception: reads the theory's claim that the normal shape is upward sloping as a claim that a downward one is impossible
options.why: Liquidity preference says a premium for tying money up tilts the curve upwards, which is why an upward slope is the ordinary shape. It does not forbid the other one. When the market expects rates to fall by more than the premium is worth, the curve inverts and the theory says so — it simply reads a larger expected fall out of the same shape than the expectations theory does.

options.text: Expectations reads it as short rates being expected to fall; liquidity preference reads the expected fall as larger still, because a term premium is pushing the long end the other way
options.why: Under the expectations theory the long rate is the average of the short rates the market expects, so a long rate below the short one is a forecast that rates will come down. Under liquidity preference a lender parting with money for longer must be paid something extra for the price risk, which tilts the curve upwards; for the curve to have fallen anyway, the expected drop in rates must be big enough to swallow that term premium and still leave the long end lower. The same inverted curve therefore implies a sharper fall under the second theory than under the first.

options.text: Expectations reads it as short rates being expected to rise, the long end having been pulled down by heavy buying
options.misconception: reverses the expectations theory, which ties the long rate to the average of the short rates the market expects rather than to demand for long paper
options.why: If short rates were expected to rise, their average over ten years would sit above today's short rate and the long end would be higher, not lower. Heavy buying of long paper is a preferred habitat explanation, not an expectations one, and the two must not be mixed together.

options.text: Preferred habitat says the curve must slope upwards, since long lenders always have to be coaxed out of short paper
options.misconception: treats one segment's preference as universal, when the theory lets any segment be the one short of funds and so permits any shape
options.why: Preferred habitat says each maturity has its own buyers and sellers, and whichever segment is short of funds must pay more to pull players out of their own habitat. That can be the short end as easily as the long. The theory allows a curve sloping upward, falling or flat, and settles none of them by itself.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: The yield curve has inverted. Three-month paper yields 7.5 per cent, one-year paper 7.0 per cent and ten-year paper 6.2 per cent, so the long end pays less than the short end.

items.stem: How many runs are in this series, and what does the count suggest?

options.text: Twenty runs — one for each daily change
options.misconception: counts every change as a run, when a run is a stretch of consecutive changes sharing a sign and may be one change long or many
options.why: A run ends only when the sign differs from the one before it. Here the sign changes three times over twenty days, so there are four stretches, not twenty. Twenty runs would arise only if the sign alternated every single day.

options.text: Four runs — far fewer than the eleven expected, so the changes do not look independent
options.why: A run is an unbroken stretch of changes carrying the same sign, and a new run starts the moment the sign flips. The series breaks into five rises, four falls, five rises and six falls: four runs. Four against about eleven means the signs arrive in long blocks rather than shuffling, which is what a trending series looks like. Independence is what the weak form claims, so a count this far below expectation is evidence against it for this series.

options.text: Four runs — and since eleven were expected, a count of four shows the series is more random than chance would give
options.misconception: reads a low run count as more randomness, when few runs mean long unbroken stretches and stretches are the opposite of randomness
options.why: Randomness shows up as frequent sign flips, which produce many short runs. Long blocks of one sign produce few. Four runs in twenty days means the price kept going the same way once it started, and a market where yesterday's direction predicts today's is not behaving independently.

options.text: Two runs — one covering the rises and one covering the falls
options.misconception: groups the changes into two buckets by sign, when a run is defined by consecutive position and not by which sign it carries
options.why: The ten rises are not one run; they come in two separate blocks with four falls between them. Position is what counts, not the sign taken across the whole series. Five, four, five, six — four runs.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: Twenty consecutive daily price changes are marked by sign, in order — five rises, then four falls, then five rises, then six falls. There are ten rises and ten falls in all. A researcher is told that a purely random series of this length and composition would be expected to throw up about eleven runs.

items.stem: Which fund ends the year ahead, and why?

options.text: The fund that does nothing, since trading costs money and the market ended where it began
options.misconception: assumes an unchanged index means an unchanged portfolio, ignoring that the two trading policies took money out of the swings on the way
options.why: Buy and hold ends where it started, because nothing was bought or sold. Its pay-off is a straight line and it sits between the other two, beaten by constant mix in a market like this and beaten by CPPI in a sustained fall. Doing nothing is a policy, and here it is the middling one.

options.text: The CPPI fund, because the floor protects it through every fall
options.misconception: takes the protection CPPI gives in a sustained fall as an advantage in a market that keeps reversing, when the same rule sells low and buys high on each swing
options.why: CPPI shrinks the equity holding as the cushion shrinks, so it sells after a fall and buys after a rise — the wrong way round when the market comes back each time. The floor is worth having in a market that keeps going down. In one that swings and returns, CPPI performs poorly, and the study material says so.

options.text: The constant mix fund, because restoring the split makes it buy after every fall and sell after every rise
options.why: A market that swings and comes back rewards anyone who trades against the swing. Constant mix does exactly that: a fall leaves shares under their target weight so it buys, and a rise leaves them over so it sells. Each round trip banks a small gain, and the gains pile up over the year even though the market itself went nowhere. This is why the study material puts constant mix ahead in a flat market.

options.text: All three end level, since the market itself ended level
options.misconception: reads the outcome off the market's start and end points, when two of the three policies traded along the way and the path is what they were paid for
options.why: The path is the point. Constant mix bought low and sold high at every swing and is ahead; CPPI sold low and bought high at the same swings and is behind; only the fund that did nothing is level. Three portfolios holding the same shares can end a flat year in three different places.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Over a year the market swings sharply up and then sharply down, several times over, and ends the year at the level it started. Three funds hold the same opening mix of shares and bonds. One does nothing all year. One restores a fixed 60:40 split after every move. One runs constant proportion portfolio insurance with a floor and a multiplier.

items.stem: What mix minimises risk, and what is the risk of that mix?

options.text: 60 per cent in A and 40 per cent in B, with a risk of exactly nil
options.why: The covariance is −1 × 12 × 18 = −216. The weight of A is B's variance less the covariance, over the sum of the two variances less twice the covariance: (324 + 216) ÷ (144 + 324 + 432) = 540 ÷ 900 = 0.60. The variance is then 0.36 × 144 + 0.16 × 324 + 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × (−216) = 51.84 + 51.84 − 103.68 = 0. At a correlation of minus one, and only there, the two swings cancel completely and the weights come out as the plain ratio of the standard deviations, 18 ÷ 30 = 0.60.

options.text: 50 per cent in each, with a risk of 3 per cent
options.misconception: assumes perfect opposition cancels risk at any split, when it cancels only at the one split where the two swings are equal in size
options.why: An equal split gives 0.25 × 144 + 0.25 × 324 − 2 × 0.25 × 216 = 36 + 81 − 108 = 9, a standard deviation of 3 per cent. Half of B's 18 per cent swing is 9 and half of A's 12 per cent swing is 6, so 3 per cent is left over. Matching them takes 60 per cent in A against 40 per cent in B.

options.text: About 69 per cent in A and 31 per cent in B, with a risk of about 10 per cent
options.misconception: leaves the covariance term out of both the weights and the variance, which is the answer for uncorrelated shares rather than perfectly opposed ones
options.why: Dropping the covariance gives 324 ÷ (144 + 324) = 0.692 and a variance of 0.479 × 144 + 0.095 × 324 = 99.7, a standard deviation near 10 per cent. That is what these two shares would do if they moved independently. They do not — they move in exact opposition, and the covariance of −216 both shifts the weights to 60:40 and wipes the risk out.

options.text: 40 per cent in A and 60 per cent in B, with a risk of 6 per cent
options.misconception: puts the larger weight on the more volatile share, when cancelling two opposed swings needs more money in the quieter one
options.why: At 40:60 the variance is 0.16 × 144 + 0.36 × 324 − 2 × 0.4 × 0.6 × 216 = 23.04 + 116.64 − 103.68 = 36, a standard deviation of 6 per cent. It is low but it is not nil. Only one mix cancels exactly, and because B swings one and a half times as far as A, it takes the smaller share of the money, not the larger.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Share A has a standard deviation of 12 per cent and Share B one of 18 per cent. The correlation between them is exactly minus one — whenever one is above its average the other is below it, in strict proportion.

items.stem: How much goes into each?

options.text: ₹15 lakh into P and ₹5 lakh into R, leaving ₹80 lakh uninvested
options.misconception: reports the raw Z values as though they were percentages, skipping the step that scales them to add to one
options.why: 0.15 and 0.05 are the unscaled figures, and there is no reason for two of them to add to one. Dividing each by their total of 0.20 turns them into 75 per cent and 25 per cent, which is the step that makes sure every rupee of the ₹100 lakh is placed.
