options.text: About ₹57 lakh into P and ₹43 lakh into R, in proportion to their excess returns to beta
options.misconception: splits the money in proportion to the ranking ratios themselves, which decide who gets in but not how much each one takes
options.why: 8 ÷ (8 + 6) = 57 per cent uses the ratio that ranked the securities. The amount invested turns on something the ranking never looked at: how far each ratio clears the cut-off, and how much company-specific risk comes with it. P clears by 3 against R's 1, which is what drives the split to 75:25.

options.text: ₹50 lakh into each, since both cleared the cut-off
options.misconception: treats clearing the cut-off as an all-or-nothing admission, when the model sizes each holding by how far it clears and by its unsystematic variance
options.why: Clearing the cut-off decides whether a security is in. It does not decide how much. P clears by 3 percentage points and R by 1, on similar amounts of company-specific risk, so P deserves three times the money — ₹75 lakh against ₹25 lakh.

options.text: ₹75 lakh into P and ₹25 lakh into R
options.why: For each selected security work out Z, the beta over the unsystematic variance, multiplied by the amount its excess return to beta clears the cut-off by. For P that is (1.5 ÷ 30) × (8 − 5) = 0.05 × 3 = 0.15. For R it is (1.0 ÷ 20) × (6 − 5) = 0.05 × 1 = 0.05. The two come to 0.20, and each security's share is its own Z over that total: 0.15 ÷ 0.20 = 75 per cent and 0.05 ÷ 0.20 = 25 per cent. Dividing by the total is what forces the whole ₹100 lakh to be placed.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Under Sharpe's single index model two securities have cleared the cut-off rate of 5 per cent. Security P has a beta of 1.5, an excess return to beta of 8 per cent, and unsystematic variance — the part of its variance the market index does not explain — of 30. Security R has a beta of 1.0, an excess return to beta of 6 per cent, and unsystematic variance of 20. A fund has ₹100 lakh to place.

items.stem: What does the copper effectively cost him a tonne?

options.text: ₹8,60,000 — the spot price on the day he buys
options.misconception: prices the purchase in the physical market and leaves the futures leg out of the reckoning altogether
options.why: ₹8,60,000 a tonne is what he pays the seller, and it is what an unhedged refiner would have been left with. The long futures position gained ₹40,000 a tonne as prices rose, and that gain belongs in the effective cost, bringing it to ₹8,20,000.

options.text: ₹8,05,000 — the spot price on the day he put the hedge on
options.misconception: assumes a hedge freezes today's spot price, when what a futures hedge fixes is the futures price, which already carries the cost of holding the metal until delivery
options.why: Today's spot of ₹8,05,000 is the price of copper for someone taking it away today. The refiner wants it in June, and June copper is quoted at ₹8,20,000 — the difference is the cost of financing and storing it in between. No hedge gets him June metal at today's price.

options.text: ₹8,20,000 — and the same figure would have come out whatever day he closed the hedge
options.misconception: treats the exactness of this hedge as automatic, when it comes from closing on the day the contract expires and from nothing else
options.why: The figure is right and the reason is wrong. Away from expiry the futures price and the spot price need not agree, and the effective cost is the futures price paid plus whatever that gap turns out to be — unknowable in advance. It is only because the contract dies on the day he buys that the gap is nil and the entry price holds exactly.

options.text: ₹8,20,000 — the futures price he paid, exactly
options.why: The contract expires on the very day he buys, and at expiry the futures price and the spot price converge, so the futures settles at ₹8,60,000 too. He pays 500 × 8,60,000 = ₹43 crore in the market and gains 500 × (8,60,000 − 8,20,000) = ₹2 crore on the futures, an effective ₹41 crore, or ₹8,20,000 a tonne. Matching the hedge to the contract's own expiry is what removes the basis and turns an approximate hedge into an exact one.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A refiner will buy 500 tonnes of copper on 30 June. Today copper spot is ₹8,05,000 a tonne and the June futures contract, which expires on 30 June, trades at ₹8,20,000. He buys June futures covering the full 500 tonnes and holds them to expiry. On 30 June copper spot is ₹8,60,000.

items.stem: What happens on settlement?

options.text: The seller pays ₹20 crore and the bank keeps the bonds
options.misconception: pays par without taking delivery, which would leave the buyer better off than if there had been no default at all
options.why: That would hand the bank ₹20 crore in cash plus bonds worth ₹7 crore — ₹27 crore against a ₹20 crore exposure. Protection restores the loss; it does not pay a profit on it. Par is paid only against delivery of the bonds.

options.text: The bank delivers the ₹20 crore of bonds to the seller and receives ₹20 crore in cash
options.why: Physical settlement is the older of the two methods: the protection buyer hands over the defaulted bonds and the seller pays their par value. The bank gives up paper worth ₹7 crore in the market and takes ₹20 crore, so it ends whole and the seller is left holding the defaulted debt and whatever it eventually recovers on it.

options.text: The seller pays ₹13 crore and the bank keeps the bonds
options.misconception: describes cash settlement, where the seller pays the shortfall against par and the buyer is left holding the paper
options.why: ₹20 crore less the 35 per cent the bonds are still worth is ₹13 crore, and that is precisely what a cash-settled contract pays. The bank would then keep bonds worth ₹7 crore, coming to the same ₹20 crore. Both routes leave the buyer whole; they differ over who is left holding the defaulted paper.

options.text: The seller pays ₹7 crore, the market value of what the bonds are still worth
options.misconception: pays the recovery rather than the loss, inverting the amount a credit default swap is written to cover
options.why: ₹7 crore is what the bank still has, not what it lost. The loss is the other ₹13 crore, and that is the cash settlement figure. Under physical settlement the seller does not pay a difference at all — it pays the full ₹20 crore and takes the bonds.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A bank holds ₹20 crore face value of X Ltd bonds and has bought credit default swap protection on them. X Ltd defaults. The bonds now trade at 35 per cent of face value. The contract between the bank and the protection seller is written for physical settlement.

items.stem: What does each company end up paying on the funding it actually wanted?

options.text: X pays 5 per cent on dollars and Y pays 12 per cent on rupees, the swap changing the currency but not the cost
options.misconception: treats the swap as a pure exchange of currencies, missing that the saving comes from each side borrowing where its own advantage is widest
options.why: Those are the rates with no swap at all. The gain is real: the two together pay 9 + 6.5 = 15.5 per cent to the market instead of the 5 + 12 = 17 per cent they would have paid borrowing directly. That 1.5 per cent is what they are dividing.

options.text: X pays 8.25 per cent and Y pays 5.75 per cent
options.misconception: takes each company's half share off the rate it actually borrowed at rather than off the rate it would have paid for the currency it wanted
options.why: 9 − 0.75 and 6.5 − 0.75 measure the saving against the wrong benchmark. X borrowed rupees only as a step on the way to dollars; the question is what dollars now cost it, against the 5 per cent it could have had directly. That is 4.25 per cent, and for Y rupees cost 11.25 per cent against 12.

options.text: X pays 4.25 per cent on dollars and Y pays 11.25 per cent on rupees
options.why: Each borrows where its edge is widest — X takes rupees at 9 per cent, Y takes dollars at 6.5 per cent — and they swap the streams. Half of the 1.5 per cent is 0.75 per cent each, and each company's saving is measured against what it would have paid for the currency it wanted. X wanted dollars and would have paid 5 per cent, so it ends at 5 − 0.75 = 4.25 per cent. Y wanted rupees and would have paid 12 per cent, so it ends at 12 − 0.75 = 11.25 per cent. The two effective rates add to 15.5, which is the 9 plus 6.5 actually paid out.

options.text: X pays 3.5 per cent on dollars and Y pays 10.5 per cent on rupees
options.misconception: gives each company the whole 1.5 per cent, when 1.5 per cent is the total between them and splitting it equally leaves 0.75 per cent each
options.why: 3.5 and 10.5 would add to 14 per cent, but 15.5 per cent is being paid to the outside world — 9 on the rupee loan and 6.5 on the dollar loan. A swap cannot manufacture 3 per cent of saving out of a 1.5 per cent gap. Each side keeps 0.75 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: Indian company X can borrow rupees at 9 per cent and dollars at 5 per cent. American company Y can borrow rupees at 12 per cent and dollars at 6.5 per cent. X wants dollar funding and Y wants rupee funding. X's edge over Y is 3 per cent in rupees and 1.5 per cent in dollars, so 1.5 per cent in all is available, and the two agree to split it equally with no dealer in between.

items.stem: Under the study material's four principles of an active strategy, what is each of the three doing?

options.text: Sector rotation, market timing and security selection — three of the four principles, the fourth being the use of a specialised investment concept
options.why: Sector rotation shifts the weight given to industries on a view of their outlook, which is exactly overweighting pharmaceuticals against steel. Market timing departs from the long-run asset mix on a forecast of the general market, which is what moving between shares and cash is. Security selection is the search for an under-priced security. The fourth principle, which none of the three is following, is the use of a specialised investment concept — concentrating on growth stocks, or neglected stocks, or cyclicals.

options.text: All three are security selection, since every active decision ends in a decision about what to hold
options.misconception: collapses four distinct principles into one, when the study material separates them by what the manager is forecasting — an industry, the whole market, or one company
options.why: They end in a holding, but they start in different forecasts, and the forecast is what the study material names. An industry outlook is sector rotation, a view on the general market is market timing, and a view on one company being mispriced is security selection. A manager good at one is not thereby good at another.

options.text: The first two are passive, because neither one picks individual shares
options.misconception: takes stock picking as the definition of active management, when departing from the benchmark on any forecast — of a sector or of the whole market — is active
options.why: A passive manager holds the benchmark's constituents in the benchmark's weights. Both the first two are deliberately away from those weights on a forecast of their own, one by industry and one by asset class, so both are active. Neither is buying an index and following it.

options.text: Market timing, sector rotation and the use of a specialised investment concept
options.misconception: names the fourth principle in place of the third, when a specialised concept means committing to a style such as growth or cyclical stocks rather than hunting a mispriced share
options.why: The third manager is looking for shares whose price is below what he thinks they are worth, which is security selection. A specialised investment concept is something else — settling on one kind of investment, growth stocks or neglected stocks or asset stocks, and mastering it. Its danger, the study material says, is that the concept can become obsolete.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Three fund managers describe what they do. The first overweights pharmaceuticals and underweights steel because he expects pharmaceuticals to do better over the coming year. The second moves money between shares and cash according to where he thinks the whole market is heading. The third hunts for individual shares he believes are under-priced.

items.stem: What does the study material tell him to look at instead?

options.text: The company's own financial ratios and the prospects of its industry
options.why: The study material puts the risk of default second among the four things to weigh when choosing a fixed income avenue, and says to look at the credit rating of the bond — then adds that if no credit rating is available the relevant financial ratios of the firm have to be examined, such as debt equity, interest coverage and earning power, along with the general prospects of the industry the firm belongs to. A rating is the convenient route to that judgement, not the only one.

options.text: The yield to maturity, which is the first of the four things the material says to weigh
options.misconception: names a real selection criterion but the wrong one, when yield to maturity measures the return if the bond is paid and says nothing about whether it will be
options.why: Yield to maturity is indeed first on the material's list, and it answers a different question: what the investor earns if he holds the bond to maturity and everything is paid. The chance of everything being paid is the second item on the same list, and that is the one he is asking about.

options.text: Nothing — an unrated instrument cannot be assessed and should simply be refused
options.misconception: treats a rating as the only possible route to a view on default risk, when the material gives a named fallback for exactly this case
options.why: Rating agencies did not invent credit analysis; they industrialised it. The ratios an agency works from are on the company's own published accounts and the investor can read them. What he loses without a rating is a second opinion and a comparable grade, not the ability to form a view at all.

options.text: Its liquidity — whether the debenture can be turned into cash at short notice
options.misconception: substitutes the risk of not being able to sell for the risk of not being paid, when the material lists the two separately and they can point in opposite directions
options.why: Liquidity is the fourth item on the same list of four, and it is a real question. It is not this question. A debenture that trades freely can still default, and one that nobody trades can still pay every rupee on the day. Being able to get out early is not the same as being paid.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: An investor is offered the debentures of a company whose issue no agency has rated. He wants to know how likely he is to be paid.

items.stem: How does the study material classify these four, and what does it say about the one holding paper?

options.text: All four are index funds under another name, since an exchange traded fund must track an index
options.misconception: takes the commonest kind for the whole class, when the material says most ETFs are index funds and then names three other kinds that are not
options.why: Most exchange traded funds are index funds, and the material says so — which is a statement about how many, not about what they must be. A fund holding gold tracks the price of gold, not an index of shares, and it is an exchange traded fund all the same.

options.text: Index, commodity, bond and currency exchange traded funds — and bond ETFs tend to do well in a recession, so their performance may point to broader economic conditions
options.why: The study material lists four kinds of exchange traded funds. Index ETFs, which are most of them, hold securities to replicate a stock market index. Commodity ETFs invest in commodities such as precious metals and futures. Bond ETFs invest in bonds and thrive during a recession, because investors pull money out of the stock market and into government or strong corporate paper — which is why their performance may be indicative of broader economic conditions. Currency ETFs are total return products giving the investor the spot change, local institutional interest rates and a collateral yield.

options.text: The currency one is not an exchange traded fund at all, since a currency is not a holding that can be valued
options.misconception: assumes an exchange traded fund must hold securities, when the material lists currency ETFs among the four and describes what their return is built from
options.why: Currency ETFs are on the material's own list. It describes them as total return products where the investor gets access to the foreign exchange spot change, local institutional interest rates and a collateral yield — three components, all of them measurable, which is precisely what makes the unit valuable day to day.

options.text: Index, commodity, bond and currency exchange traded funds — and bond ETFs do worst in a recession, since a downturn is when borrowers default
options.misconception: reads a recession as a credit event for a bond fund, when the material says the opposite — money moves into bonds in a downturn and bond ETFs thrive
options.why: Defaults do rise in a downturn, but that is not what the material says drives a bond fund's price. Money leaves the stock market for government paper and financially stable issuers, and that demand lifts the fund. The classification is right in this option and the direction is upside down.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: An investor is shown four exchange traded funds. One tracks a stock market index, one holds precious metals, one holds government and corporate paper, and one gives him exposure to a foreign currency.

items.stem: What does market value added support, and what does it not?

options.text: A high market value added means the share is cheap
options.misconception: reads a high figure as an opportunity, when the material says companies with a higher market value added become market favourites and eventually pricey
options.why: The material runs it the other way: companies with a higher market value added naturally become the darlings of the share market and would eventually become pricey from a pure pricing perspective. A big surplus says the market already believes in the company. Whether that belief is overdone is a separate question the figure does not answer.

options.text: It is economic value added measured once, so the two are interchangeable
options.misconception: treats a market perception of the whole life as the same thing as a derived figure for one year, when the study material separates them precisely on that point
options.why: Economic value added is derived from the accounts for a period — the return earned above the charge for the capital employed in that period. Market value added is what the market perceives, across the whole of the company's future. The material calls the second the true value added as perceived by the market and the first a derived value added for the more discerning investor.

options.text: It is a per-share figure, so dividing ₹500 crore by the number of shares gives the price
options.misconception: turns a whole-firm surplus into a per-share value, when the ₹500 crore is already inside the market price the shares are quoted at
options.why: Market value added is the market value of the whole firm less the whole of the capital employed. The market's opinion of the company is already in the quoted share price; the surplus is the gap between that price and the money put in, and adding it to the price again would count the same optimism twice.

options.text: It gauges how well the enterprise has used the capital it was given, judged by the market — but it gives no basis for valuing a share
options.why: The study material is explicit that market value added does not itself give any basis of share valuation. What it gives is an alternative way to gauge the performance efficiency of an enterprise from a market capitalisation point of view, on the logic that the market will fairly discount what management has done. It is a verdict on the capital already put in, not a price for a share going out.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A board is told the company's market value added is ₹500 crore, the highest in its industry. A director who wants to sell a block of his own shares proposes using that figure to argue for a price.

items.stem: What is wrong with that valuation, and what does the study material do instead?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — a discounted cash flow valuation already prices the risk through its discount rate
options.misconception: assumes the discount rate carries the risk of failure, when the rate was estimated from companies that are operationally and financially sound
options.why: The rate in the valuation came from healthy companies in the industry. The material says in terms that such rates reflect companies which are operationally as well as financially sound and have to be adjusted for the probabilities of failure before they can be used on a distressed one. A rate borrowed from a firm that will survive prices a risk this firm does not merely bear more of — it bears a different one.

options.text: The company is worthless, so no valuation is needed
options.misconception: reads a missed payment as the end of value, when the material says a company that cannot service its debt is not thereby entirely worthless
options.why: The material opens the topic by saying the opposite: although a company may not be making payments on some or all of its debt obligations, there may still be value remaining in the instruments held. Somebody buys distressed debt, and what he pays is a valuation. Declaring it nil is a refusal to do the work, not a result.

options.text: A terminal value assuming an infinite life is the wrong assumption for a firm that may not survive; the material deflates each period's cash flow by the chance of failure, taking expected cash flow as cash flow times one minus the probability of distress
options.why: A discounted cash flow valuation values a firm as a going concern, and its terminal value rests on an infinite life with ever-growing cash flows — an assumption the material says may not be relevant for a distressed firm with negative cash flows. Its modified method estimates a probability of distress for each period and uses expected cash flow equal to cash flow times one minus that probability. The discount rate is rebuilt too, because rates taken from sound companies have to be adjusted for the chance of failure.

options.text: Drop the cash flow method and use a price-earnings multiple from comparable companies
options.misconception: reaches for the multiple the material says often cannot be used at all on a distressed firm, when it turns instead to revenue and EBITDA multiples marked down against the industry
options.why: Price-earnings and price-to-book often cannot even be used on a distressed firm — earnings are negative and book equity may be too. The material's relative-valuation route uses revenue and EBITDA multiples, and marks them down against the industry average: if the average firm trades at two times revenue, a distressed one might be taken at one and a quarter.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company's score puts it firmly in the distress zone — it has already missed payments on part of its borrowing. An analyst nevertheless values it by projecting five years of cash flows and adding a terminal value on the usual assumption of perpetual growth, discounted at the cost of capital used for healthy companies in the industry.

items.stem: What does the 70 per cent stake cost?

options.text: ₹70 crore
options.why: 70 per cent of 20 lakh shares is 14 lakh shares. The controlling stake premium lifts the price per share from ₹400 to 400 × 1.25 = ₹500. So 14,00,000 × 500 = ₹70 crore. The premium is paid because a parcel that carries control is worth more than the same shares bought a few at a time, which is the mirror of the discount a minority parcel attracts.

options.text: ₹56 crore
options.misconception: prices a controlling block at the price of a small parcel, when the study material lists a controlling stake premium precisely because control is worth paying for
options.why: 14,00,000 × 400 = ₹56 crore values the block at the price at which a few shares change hands. Those trades buy no say in the dividend, the strategy or a sale, and this block buys all three. The 25 per cent premium is what the parties agreed that difference is worth, and it takes the figure to ₹70 crore.

options.text: ₹42 crore
options.misconception: applies a discount where the material lists a premium, when a discount belongs to a small parcel or an unlisted holding and control moves the price the other way
options.why: 14,00,000 × 300 = ₹42 crore takes 25 per cent off instead of adding it. The study material's list runs both ways — a market share premium, a controlling stake premium and a brand value premium on one side, a small player discount and an unlisted company discount on the other. Control is on the premium side.

options.text: ₹100 crore
options.misconception: applies the controlling price to every share in issue, when the buyer is paying for 70 per cent and the other 30 per cent stays where it is
options.why: 20,00,000 × 500 = ₹100 crore is what the whole company would cost at the controlling price. The buyer is taking 14 lakh shares, not 20 lakh. The remaining 6 lakh shares stay with holders who are now the minority, and they are not being bought at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A company has 20 lakh shares in issue. Trades in small parcels, and the multiples of listed comparables, both put the value at ₹400 a share. A buyer wants 70 per cent of the company — enough to control it — and the parties agree a controlling stake premium of 25 per cent.

items.stem: Which model can value this option properly, and why?

options.text: Neither, since no model can value an option whose exercise date is unknown
options.misconception: treats an unknown exercise date as a dead end, when testing every possible date is precisely what a tree does
options.why: An unknown exercise date is what the tree is built to handle. It does not guess the date; it works backwards from expiry and, at each node, takes the higher of exercising now and holding on. The date falls out of that comparison rather than being assumed at the start.

options.text: Black-Scholes, after adding the present value of the dividend back into the share price
options.misconception: patches the dividend but leaves the real limitation untouched, since the model still prices at expiry alone and cannot see an early exercise point before it
options.why: Adjusting the share price for a dividend is a sensible repair to one Black-Scholes assumption and it does not touch the other. The model would still be computing a single value at expiration, with nothing in it that can notice that exercising in month eleven beat holding to month twelve. That noticing is what the tree does at every node.

options.text: Black-Scholes, because it is far faster and the difference on one dividend is small
options.misconception: trades away the one feature that decides an American option's value, when Black-Scholes computes the price at a single point of time and never looks at the steps along the way
options.why: Speed is Black-Scholes' real advantage — it prices a great many options in very little time. Its stated limitation is that it cannot accurately price options with an American-style exercise, because it calculates the price at one point of time only, at expiration, and does not consider the steps along the way where early exercise might happen. Here those steps are the whole question.

options.text: The binomial tree, because it can test at every step whether exercising is worth more than holding and reset the option's value at that step to the intrinsic value where it is
options.why: The binomial tree's advantage over Black-Scholes is exactly that it prices American options accurately, because at every step of the tree it is possible to check for the possibility of early exercise — a put deep in the money whose price at that point, with a dividend coming, is below its intrinsic value. Where such a point is found the holder is assumed to exercise, the value at that node is set to the intrinsic value, and that flows back up the tree into every value above it.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A dealer must value an American put on a share that will go ex-dividend a month before the option expires. She has a Black-Scholes calculator and a binomial tree, and the two give different answers.

items.stem: What will the exporter receive if the spot rate in six months is ₹88, and what if it is ₹79?

options.text: ₹8.30 crore at ₹88, and ₹8.10 crore at ₹79
options.misconception: caps the exporter at today's spot rate, when the cap sits at the strike of the call he wrote and not at the rate ruling when he wrote it
options.why: 1 million × 83 = ₹8.30 crore assumes a zero-cost structure must give up everything above today's rate. It gives up everything above ₹86, because that is where the written call is struck. Choosing that strike is how the two premiums were made equal, and the ₹3 of room between ₹83 and ₹86 is what the exporter kept.

options.text: ₹8.60 crore at ₹88, and ₹8.10 crore at ₹79
options.why: An exporter's range forward is the importer's turned round: he buys the option that protects a seller, a put, and writes the one that pays for it, a call. At ₹88 the written call is exercised against him and he must sell dollars at ₹86, so 1 million × 86 = ₹8.60 crore. At ₹79 he exercises his bought put and sells at ₹81, so ₹8.10 crore. Between ₹81 and ₹86 both lapse and he sells at spot.

options.text: ₹8.60 crore at ₹88, and ₹7.90 crore at ₹79
options.misconception: forgets the bought put, which is the leg the exporter may choose to exercise and the only reason a fall below ₹81 does not reach him
options.why: 1 million × 79 = ₹7.90 crore is what the market would pay, and it is not what he gets. He holds a put struck at ₹81 and exercises it, taking ₹8.10 crore. The bought leg is the one he controls; the written leg is the one controlled against him, and this option has them the wrong way round.

options.text: ₹8.80 crore at ₹88, and ₹8.10 crore at ₹79
options.misconception: forgets the written call, which is exercised against the exporter and is the whole reason the protection cost nothing
options.why: 1 million × 88 = ₹8.80 crore assumes the exporter keeps the gain above ₹86. He sold that gain: the call he wrote is the counterparty's to exercise, and at ₹88 the counterparty exercises it and takes the dollars at ₹86. Keeping the whole upside would have meant buying the put outright and paying a premium in cash.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian exporter will receive one million dollars in six months. The spot rate is ₹83 to the dollar. It puts on a range forward that costs nothing: it buys a six-month dollar put struck at ₹81 and sells a six-month dollar call struck at ₹86, the two premiums being equal.

items.stem: In each of those first three years, what does the project earn and what reaches the parent?

options.text: The project earns ₹50 crore, and nothing reaches the parent
options.misconception: leaves the royalty out of the project's costs and forgets that it is a route out for the parent's money that a dividend block does not close
options.why: ₹50 crore is what the subsidiary makes before paying anybody, and the royalty is one of the things it pays — so the project's figure is ₹42 crore. And the parent is not empty-handed: the block is on dividends, not on royalties, and ₹8 crore a year comes out under the technology agreement. That is why such agreements are written.

options.text: The project earns ₹50 crore, and ₹8 crore reaches the parent
options.misconception: gets the parent's receipt right but never charges the royalty against the project, counting the same 8 million units in both answers
options.why: The parent's ₹8 crore is right. The project's ₹50 crore counts those same units a second time, because the money the parent receives is money the subsidiary paid out. Take it off once and the project stands at ₹42 crore, which with the parent's ₹8 crore accounts for the 50 million units exactly.

options.text: The project earns ₹42 crore, and ₹42 crore reaches the parent
options.misconception: assumes the two views of a foreign investment must produce the same figure, when the whole reason for appraising it twice is that they need not
options.why: Charging the royalty against the project is right; handing the whole result to the parent is not. Only ₹8 crore may leave the country in these three years. The remaining ₹34 crore belongs to the project and sits in the host country, which is exactly the gap that can make a foreign project worth doing on its own numbers and not worth doing on the parent's.

options.text: The project earns ₹42 crore, and ₹8 crore reaches the parent
options.why: The royalty is an expense of the subsidiary, so the project's own cash flow is 50 − 8 = 42 million units, or ₹42 crore at ₹10 to the unit. To the parent the same 8 million units are a return, ₹8 crore, and because royalties may be remitted they are the only money that actually crosses the border while dividends are blocked. The study material says it plainly: management and royalty payments are returns to the parent firm.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company's foreign subsidiary will generate 50 million local units a year of operating cash flow before paying anything to its parent. Under the technology agreement it pays the parent a royalty of 8 million units a year, and the host country allows royalties to be remitted freely. Dividends, however, may not be remitted for the first three years. The exchange rate is ₹10 to the unit.

items.stem: What has he been quoted, and what happens if it expires in the money?

options.text: A right, exercisable in five years, to enter a two-year swap
options.misconception: reads the two figures the wrong way round, when the first names how long the option runs and the second the term of the swap it opens
options.why: The convention is the wait first and the swap second. Reversing them changes both the date the treasurer is protected from and the length of the protection — here from five years of cover starting in two into two years of cover starting in five, which is a different hedge for a different loan.

options.text: A right that can be taken up only by actually entering the swap, since a swaption is a right to a contract and not a claim for cash
options.misconception: misses that swaptions can be cash-settled, when the study material says they are marked to market at expiry off the applicable forward curve and the difference is settled in cash
options.why: Entering the swap is one way to settle and not the only one. The material states that swaptions can be cash-settled: at expiry the swap is valued against the forward curve prevailing then and one side simply pays the other the difference. That is what lets a treasurer who has decided not to borrow after all still collect what the option is worth.

options.text: A right, exercisable in two years, to enter a five-year swap as the payer of fixed — the two years being the option period, and cash settlement meaning the swap is marked to market against the forward curve then and the difference paid over in cash
options.why: The first figure is the wait and the second is the swap's own term: a three-month into five-year swaption is an option to enter a five-year swap three months from now, so a two-year into five-year one is the same thing two years out, entered as the payer of fixed. The time between the deal and expiry is the option period. Swaptions can be cash-settled, so at expiry they are marked to market off the applicable forward curve and the difference is settled in cash — no swap need ever be entered. A payer swaption is also called a call swaption.

options.text: A seven-year interest rate swap starting today
options.misconception: adds the two periods into a single instrument and loses the optionality, when the point of a swaption is that nothing is entered unless the buyer chooses
options.why: Two and five are not added. The treasurer has entered nothing today except the option itself, for which he pays 35 basis points. If rates have fallen in two years he walks away and borrows at the market rate; a seven-year swap struck today would bind him from the first day and through the whole seven years.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A treasurer is quoted a two-year into five-year payer swaption at a premium of 35 basis points, and is told it may be cash settled at expiry.

items.stem: What total does the scheme make available to write off the accumulated losses and the over-valued assets?

options.text: ₹450 lakh
options.why: The reduction in equity capital is 4 lakh × ₹75 = ₹300 lakh and the reduction in preference capital is 1 lakh × ₹40 = ₹40 lakh. The debenture interest waiver adds ₹20 lakh and the creditors' waiver 200 × 0.25 = ₹50 lakh, giving ₹410 lakh of reduced liabilities. The revaluation of land and building adds a further ₹40 lakh, for ₹450 lakh in all. It matches what has to be written off — accumulated losses and fictitious assets of ₹360 lakh, and the ₹90 lakh by which plant is written down — because that is how a workable scheme is drawn.

options.text: ₹540 lakh
options.misconception: counts the write-down of plant as a source of credit, when it is one of the things the scheme's credit is being used to absorb
options.why: The ₹90 lakh by which plant falls from ₹250 lakh to ₹160 lakh is on the other side of the exercise. Assets written up create credit; assets written down consume it, alongside the accumulated losses and the fictitious assets. Adding it to the ₹450 lakh counts a debit as a credit and makes the scheme look ₹90 lakh better funded than it is.

options.text: ₹410 lakh
options.misconception: counts only what the claimants give up and leaves out the upward revaluation, when writing an asset up releases exactly the same kind of credit
options.why: ₹410 lakh is the sum of the four sacrifices — equity, preference, debenture interest and creditors. Bringing land and building to its realistic value of ₹190 lakh releases another ₹40 lakh of credit that the losses can equally be written off against, and the material's own working lists the appreciation on revalued assets beside the reduction in liabilities for that reason.

options.text: ₹550 lakh
options.misconception: cancels the equity capital altogether rather than writing it down, when the shares survive at ₹25 each and only the ₹75 written off is available
options.why: Taking the whole ₹400 lakh of equity capital assumes the shareholders are wiped out. They are not: they keep 4 lakh shares of ₹25 each, so ₹100 lakh of capital remains and only ₹300 lakh has been given up. Reading a capital reduction as a cancellation overstates the credit by exactly the capital that survives.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A company's scheme of reconstruction provides that its 4 lakh equity shares of ₹100 each be reduced to ₹25 each fully paid; its 1 lakh preference shares of ₹100 each be reduced to ₹60 each; the debenture holders forgo ₹20 lakh of accrued interest; the trade creditors, owed ₹200 lakh, forgo 25 per cent of their claim; land and building standing at ₹150 lakh be revalued at ₹190 lakh; and plant and machinery standing at ₹250 lakh be written down to ₹160 lakh.

items.stem: What must the promoter pay to take the fund out?

options.text: ₹9.60 crore
options.misconception: applies the rate once and not to each of the four years the fund's money was locked in
options.why: 8 × 1.20 = ₹9.60 crore is one year's growth. The fund has been in for four, and the whole point of a rate agreed at entry is that it runs for however long the exit takes. Four years at 20 per cent multiplies the money by 2.0736, giving ₹16.59 crore.

options.text: ₹14.40 crore
options.misconception: treats the pre-agreed rate as simple interest on the original sum, when a rate of return earns on what has already accrued as well as on the capital
options.why: 8 + 8 × 0.20 × 4 = ₹14.40 crore charges 20 per cent of the original ₹8 crore in each of the four years. An internal rate of return is what the money has to grow at, year on year, so the second year's 20 per cent is charged on ₹9.60 crore and not on ₹8 crore. The gap over four years is more than ₹2 crore.

options.text: ₹8.00 crore
options.misconception: reads a buy-back as a return of the capital put in, when the commitment is given at a pre-agreed rate of return and not at cost
options.why: Returning the ₹8 crore would leave the fund with four years and nothing to show for them, which no fund would sign. The commitment is at a pre-agreed rate, and that rate is what makes the buy-back a real exit rather than a formality. The same deal-structuring stage often adds a tag-along clause, requiring the promoter to sell part of his own stake alongside the fund so that a trade sale can actually be delivered.

options.text: ₹16.59 crore
options.why: A pre-agreed internal rate of return compounds, so the sum due is 8 × 1.20 to the fourth power. 1.20 squared is 1.44 and 1.44 squared is 2.0736, so 8 × 2.0736 = ₹16.5888 crore, about ₹16.59 crore. The study material puts the pre-agreed rate on such a buy-back generally between an internal rate of return of 18 and 25 per cent, and makes the promoter buy-back the route taken when an initial public offering or a third-party sale does not happen.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A venture fund put ₹8 crore into a company exactly four years ago. There has been no listing and no trade buyer has appeared. The agreement gives the fund a buy-back commitment from the promoter at a pre-agreed internal rate of return of 20 per cent a year, and the promoter holds the first right of buy-back.

items.stem: What is the arbitrage-free futures price?

options.misconception: charges the interest on the money tied up but forgets that holding the stock also pays a dividend, so it prices the futures as if the two positions earned the same
options.why: 220 + 8.25 = ₹228.25 counts only the cost of carrying the stock. A person who buys the stock instead of the futures receives ₹2.50 that the futures holder never sees, and that receipt reduces the premium the futures can fairly command, bringing the fair price to ₹225.75.

The cost-of-carry model is futures price equals spot price plus carrying cost less returns. The carrying cost for three months is 220 × 0.15 × 0.25 = ₹8.25, and the ₹2.50 dividend is a return the stockholder collects and the futures holder does not, so it comes off: 220 + 8.25 − 2.50 = ₹225.75. That is the theoretical minimum price at which the contract can trade without opening an arbitrage.

options.misconception: adds the dividend to the carrying cost instead of deducting it, treating a receipt as though it were another expense of holding the stock
options.why: 220 + 8.25 + 2.50 = ₹230.75 puts the dividend on the wrong side. The formula is spot plus carrying cost less returns, and a dividend is a return. Adding it makes holding the stock look dearer than it is and pushes the fair futures price ₹5 too high.

options.misconception: applies a full year of interest to a three-month contract, ignoring that the carrying cost runs only for the life of the contract
options.why: 220 × 0.15 = ₹33 is a year's interest, giving 220 + 33 − 2.50 = ₹250.50. The contract runs three months, so the rate is pro-rated by 0.25, which is ₹8.25. Charging four times the carry puts the futures ₹24.75 above where arbitrage would hold it.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A stock trades at ₹220 on 31 December. Three-month futures on it are available. Money is borrowed and lent at 15 per cent a year. The company will pay a dividend of ₹2.50 a share before the futures contract expires, and the holder of the stock — not the holder of the futures — will receive it.

items.stem: What does the fund do in the futures market?

options.text: Sell 96 contracts
options.misconception: uses the target beta itself as the hedge ratio instead of the difference between the target and the beta the portfolio already has
options.why: 0.8 × ₹12 crore ÷ ₹10 lakh = 96 contracts hedges an exposure of 0.8, leaving an effective beta of 1.2 − 0.8 = 0.4 — half of what was asked for. The calculation works on the gap between where the portfolio is and where it is wanted, which is 0.4.

options.text: Sell 144 contracts
options.misconception: computes a full hedge when only part of the beta is to be removed, which leaves the portfolio short of the market rather than lightly exposed to it
options.why: 1.2 × ₹12 crore ÷ ₹10 lakh = 144 contracts takes the beta all the way to zero. The fund asked for 0.8, not nought, so only the 0.4 of beta it wants to shed is hedged. Selling 144 would leave it hoping the market falls.

options.text: Buy 48 contracts
options.misconception: gets the number right and the direction backwards, so the trade raises the portfolio's market sensitivity instead of lowering it
options.why: Long futures add market exposure. Buying 48 contracts takes the effective beta from 1.2 up to 1.6, moving away from the 0.8 target rather than towards it. Lowering a beta means selling futures; raising one means buying them.

options.text: Sell 48 contracts
options.why: The number of contracts is the change in beta wanted, times the portfolio value, divided by the contract value. (0.8 − 1.2) × ₹12 crore = −₹4.8 crore of market exposure to shed, and ₹4.8 crore ÷ ₹10 lakh = 48 contracts. The sign is negative, so they are sold.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A fund holds a ₹12 crore equity portfolio with a beta of 1.2. It does not want to come out of the market; it wants the portfolio to behave as though its beta were 0.8. Index futures trade at 20,000 with a lot size of 50, so one contract is worth ₹10 lakh.

items.stem: What is that put worth?

options.misconception: rearranges the identity with the wrong signs, adding the share and subtracting the present value of the strike instead of the other way round
options.why: 150 + 12 − 148.15 = ₹13.85 is the identity turned inside out. Parity says call minus put equals share minus present value of strike, so the share is subtracted from the put's side, not added to it: −150 + 12 + 148.15 = ₹10.15.

Put-call parity in the study material's form is value of put = minus value of share, plus value of call, plus present value of the exercise price. The present value of the exercise price is 160 ÷ 1.08 = ₹148.15, so the put is −150 + 12 + 148.15 = ₹10.15. The identity holds whatever the share's volatility, because it is enforced by arbitrage rather than by a valuation model.
keywords: present value of the exercise price

options.misconception: puts the strike into the identity at its face amount instead of its present value, ignoring that the strike is paid a year from now and not today
options.why: −150 + 12 + 160 = ₹22.00 uses the undiscounted strike. The parity portfolio lends only ₹148.15 today so that it grows to ₹160 by expiry. The ₹11.85 of interest between the two is the whole difference between ₹22.00 and ₹10.15.

options.misconception: assumes a call and a put on the same share, strike and expiry must cost the same, when they are equal only where the share price equals the present value of the strike
options.why: The two premiums are equal only in the special case where the share stands exactly at the present value of the strike. Here the share is ₹150 and that present value is ₹148.15, so the call is dearer by exactly ₹1.85 and the put is ₹10.15.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹150 and pays no dividend. A one-year European call at a strike of ₹160 costs ₹12. The one-year risk-free rate is 8 per cent. A European put on the same share, at the same strike and expiry, is not quoted anywhere.

items.stem: What is the one-step binomial value of the put?

options.misconception: computes the expected payoff correctly and then quotes it as the price, forgetting that the payoff arrives one period from now
options.why: ₹6.67 is what the put is expected to be worth at the end of the period, not what it is worth today. Dividing by the risk-free growth factor of 1.10 brings it back to ₹6.06, and the 61 paise is the interest on the money over the period.

options.misconception: prices the option on what exercising it today would fetch, when an option's value comes from what it may be worth at expiry and not from its intrinsic value now
options.why: The share is at ₹100 and the strike is ₹100, so exercising today gains nothing. That is the intrinsic value, not the price. There is a real chance the share falls to ₹80, and what the put is worth today is the discounted value of that chance, ₹6.06.

With u = 1.25 and d = 0.80, the risk-neutral probability is p = (1.10 − 0.80) ÷ (1.25 − 0.80) = 0.30 ÷ 0.45 = 0.6667. The put pays nothing at ₹125 and 100 − 80 = ₹20 at ₹80, so the expected payoff is 0.3333 × 20 = ₹6.67, and discounting that at 1.10 gives ₹6.06.

options.misconception: values the call rather than the put, taking the payoff on the up move where a put pays on the down move
options.why: 0.6667 × (125 − 100) ÷ 1.10 = ₹15.15 is the call. Check the pair against put-call parity: call minus put should equal share minus the discounted strike, 100 − 100 ÷ 1.10 = ₹9.09, and 15.15 − 6.06 = ₹9.09. The two are consistent, and only ₹6.06 answers what was asked.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trading at ₹100 will move in one period to either ₹125 or ₹80. The risk-free growth factor for the period is 1.10. A European put on the share has a strike of ₹100.

items.stem: How many puts does it buy, and why is that not 20,000?

options.text: 8,000 puts
options.misconception: multiplies the shares by the delta where the sizing divides, which is the arithmetic for hedging an option position with shares run backwards
options.why: 20,000 × 0.4 = 8,000 is the calculation for the opposite problem — how many shares hedge a written option. Here the options are the hedging instrument, so the share exposure is divided by each option's delta: 20,000 ÷ 0.4 = 50,000.

options.text: 50,000 puts
options.why: The shares carry a position delta of plus 20,000, one for each share held. Each put contributes minus 0.4, so the number needed is 20,000 ÷ 0.4 = 50,000. A put's delta is negative, which is what makes it a hedge for a long holding, and it is smaller than one in size, which is why the hedge needs more puts than there are shares.

options.text: 33,333 puts
options.misconception: divides by one minus the size of the delta, a figure that belongs to no hedge at all
options.why: 20,000 ÷ 0.6 = 33,333 uses 0.6 where 0.4 belongs. The hedge ratio is the delta itself, so the divisor is 0.4 and the answer is 50,000. At 33,333 puts the position still loses about ₹6,667 on a ₹1 fall.

options.text: 20,000 puts
options.misconception: matches one option to one share, ignoring that each put offsets only 0.4 of a share's move
options.why: On a ₹1 fall the shares lose ₹20,000 while 20,000 puts gain only 0.4 × 20,000 = ₹8,000. Three-fifths of the exposure would still be open. It takes 50,000 puts for the two sides to cancel.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A fund holds 20,000 shares of a company and wants protection against a small fall without selling them. It will buy put options on the same share, each option covering one share. The puts have a delta of minus 0.4.

items.stem: Over what range does this position make money, and how bad can each of its two sides get?

options.text: It makes money outside the range ₹460 to ₹540, and the most it can lose is the ₹40 received
options.misconception: describes the buyer's position rather than the writer's, so it hands the writer the buyer's profit region and the buyer's capped loss
options.why: Making money outside the range and losing at most the premium is the position of whoever bought this straddle. The writer took the ₹40 in and makes money when the share stays inside the range; his loss is the buyer's gain, and it is not capped.

options.text: It makes money between ₹460 and ₹540; above ₹540 the loss has no ceiling, while below ₹460 it stops at ₹460 a share
options.why: The break-even points are the same ₹460 and ₹540 as for the buyer, because a written straddle is the buyer's position seen from the other side — the two are mirror images and what one loses the other makes. Above ₹540 the written call's loss grows rupee for rupee with the share and nothing stops it. Below ₹460 the written put's loss also grows, but a share cannot fall below zero, so the worst case there is ₹500 of intrinsic value less the ₹40 received, that is ₹460.

options.text: It makes money between ₹482 and ₹522, and the most it can make is ₹40
options.misconception: charges each side only the premium of the option that finishes in the money, when the writer received both premiums whatever the share does
options.why: 500 − 18 = ₹482 and 500 + 22 = ₹522 apply one premium on each side. The writer took in ₹40 on day one and keeps it whichever way the share moves, so the cushion either side of the strike is the full ₹40 and the break-evens are ₹460 and ₹540.

options.text: It makes money between ₹460 and ₹540, and the loss has no ceiling in either direction
options.misconception: reads a written put as carrying unlimited loss like a written call, when a share price cannot go below zero and so that side is bounded
options.why: The break-evens are right and the downside is not. A call's loss is unbounded because a share can rise without limit. A put's loss stops where the share stops, at zero, so the most that side can cost is ₹500 of intrinsic value less the ₹40 premium — ₹460 a share. Large, and finite.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹500. A trader who expects it to stay where it is writes a three-month call at a strike of ₹500 for a premium of ₹22 and writes a three-month put at the same strike for a premium of ₹18. He receives ₹40 on day one.

items.stem: What does the position make?

options.text: A profit of ₹45
options.why: The bought call finishes 1,080 − 1,000 = ₹80 in the money. The written call struck at ₹1,100 finishes out of the money and expires worthless, so nothing is owed on it. The net premium paid on day one was 60 − 25 = ₹35, and 80 − 35 = ₹45. The maximum gain of ₹65 has not been reached, because the share has not passed the higher strike where the ceiling begins.

options.text: A profit of ₹80
options.misconception: reports the bought call's intrinsic value as the profit, charging none of the premium the position cost to put on
options.why: ₹80 is what the bought call is worth at expiry, not what the position made. ₹35 of net premium went out on day one and has to be recovered before anything is profit, which leaves ₹45.

options.text: A profit of ₹65
options.misconception: assumes the position is already at its cap, when the cap applies only from the higher strike upward and the share is ₹20 short of it
options.why: ₹65 is the most this spread can make and it is reached only at or above ₹1,100. At ₹1,080 the bought call is worth ₹80 rather than ₹100, so the profit is 80 − 35 = ₹45. The last ₹20 of the share's climb would have been worth another ₹20 to the position.

options.text: A profit of ₹20
options.misconception: charges the full ₹60 premium of the bought call and never credits the ₹25 received on the call that was sold
options.why: 80 − 60 = ₹20 treats the spread as costing ₹60. The ₹25 received on the written call is real money that came in on day one, so the position cost ₹35 net and the profit is ₹45. Ignoring that credit understates every figure in the strategy.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: An investor built a bull call spread on a share: bought a three-month call at a strike of ₹1,000 for a premium of ₹60, and sold a three-month call on the same share and expiry at a strike of ₹1,100 for a premium of ₹25. At expiry the share finishes at ₹1,080.

items.stem: How does the money market hedge run, and roughly what rate does it lock in?

options.text: ₹87.36 per dollar
options.misconception: grosses the spot rate up for the rupee borrowing but forgets that the dollars bought today sit on deposit and earn interest over the same six months
options.why: 84 × 1.04 = ₹87.36 charges the rupee interest and credits nothing for the dollar deposit. Because the dollars earn 2 per cent over the half year, fewer of them need to be bought today, and the effective rate is 84 × 1.04 ÷ 1.02 = ₹85.65.

options.text: ₹82.35 per dollar
options.misconception: credits the interest the dollars earn but never charges the cost of the rupees borrowed to buy them, taking only the half of the calculation that helps
options.why: 84 ÷ 1.02 = ₹82.35 is what the dollars cost today once the deposit interest is allowed for. Those rupees are borrowed at 8 per cent, so six months of interest has to be added back, bringing the locked rate to ₹85.65.

options.text: Borrow dollars now, convert at spot, and invest the proceeds in rupees — locking roughly ₹85.65 per dollar
options.misconception: runs the exporter's version of the hedge on an importer's exposure, building a dollar liability where the importer already has one
options.why: Borrowing dollars manufactures a dollar debt. The importer already owes dollars; what the hedge must build is a dollar asset maturing when the payment falls due. The rate quoted happens to be right because interest rate parity fixes it either way, but the trade described leaves the exposure doubled rather than covered.

options.text: Borrow rupees now, convert at spot, and place the dollars on deposit — locking roughly ₹85.65 per dollar
options.why: The dollar deposit has to grow to exactly $5,00,000 in six months, so 5,00,000 ÷ 1.02 = $4,90,196 goes in today. At ₹84 that costs ₹4,11,76,470, which is borrowed in rupees and repaid six months later with 4 per cent for the half year, as ₹4,28,23,529. Divided by the $5,00,000 it settles, that is about ₹85.65 a dollar — the same figure as 84 × 1.04 ÷ 1.02.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An importer must pay $5,00,000 in six months. The spot rate is ₹84 per dollar. Dollar deposits earn 4 per cent a year and rupee borrowing costs 8 per cent a year. The importer will not use the forward market.

items.stem: What cross rate does the bank quote?

options.why: On its bid the bank buys sterling and pays rupees, so it buys the pound at 1.2500 dollars and sells those dollars at 83.20: 1.2500 × 83.20 = ₹104.00. On its offer it takes the other side of each leg, 1.2520 × 83.30 = ₹104.29. Chaining two quotes always widens the spread, because the bank takes the worse half of both.

options.text: ₹104.15, quoted both ways
options.misconception: works the cross from the mid rates and hands the customer a quote with no spread in it, which is not a price any dealer makes
options.why: 83.25 × 1.2510 = ₹104.15 is the mid cross. It is a useful reference number and it is not a quote — a dealer who buys and sells at the same price earns nothing on either side and loses on both legs of his own cover.

options.misconception: pairs each bid with the other quote's offer, which narrows the chained spread when chaining can only widen it
options.why: 1.2500 × 83.30 = ₹104.13 and 1.2520 × 83.20 = ₹104.17 mix the sides. A six-pip spread and a ten-paisa spread cannot combine into a four-paisa one; the bank would be quoting a tighter cross than either market it covers in, and a customer could deal both ways against it and take the difference.

options.misconception: divides the rupee quote by the sterling quote instead of multiplying, which is the arithmetic for a cross whose two quotes share a base currency
options.why: 83.20 ÷ 1.2520 = ₹66.45 and 83.30 ÷ 1.2500 = ₹66.64. Division is what you use when both quotes are against the same base. Here the dollar is the base in one and the counter in the other, so the two chain by multiplication and the pound is worth about ₹104, not ₹66.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: A Mumbai bank quotes USD/INR at 83.20 / 83.30 and is quoted GBP/USD at 1.2500 / 1.2520 by its London correspondent. In each pair the first figure is the bid and the second the offer. A customer asks the bank for a two-way GBP/INR quote.

items.stem: What rate does relative purchasing power parity say today's should be, and what does the gap mean?

options.text: ₹49.50, so the market is close enough and there is no real movement to speak of
options.misconception: applies Indian inflation alone and forgets that American prices rose too, so the whole 10 per cent is charged to the rupee instead of only the 8 point gap
options.why: 45.00 × 1.10 = ₹49.50 assumes US prices stood still. They rose 2 per cent, so the rate moves on the ratio 1.10 ÷ 1.02, which is ₹48.53. Getting the parity rate wrong by ₹0.97 hides two-thirds of the real movement the comparison exists to expose.

options.text: ₹41.73, so the dollar has depreciated in real terms
options.misconception: inverts the ratio, putting foreign inflation on top, which makes the currency with the faster inflation strengthen — the opposite of what the theory says
options.why: 45.00 × 1.02 ÷ 1.10 = ₹41.73 is the formula upside down. A currency whose prices rise 10 per cent against another's 2 per cent buys less, so the rupee must weaken and the parity rate must sit above ₹45.00, not below it.

options.text: ₹48.53, and the ₹1.47 gap is a real appreciation of the rupee of 3.27 per cent
options.misconception: computes the parity rate correctly and then names the wrong currency as the one that gained, reading a rise in a direct quote as strength in the home currency
options.why: The parity rate is right. In a direct quote of rupees per dollar, a higher number means more rupees are needed for one dollar, so the dollar is the currency that gained. The rupee has depreciated in real terms by that same ₹1.47.

options.text: ₹48.53, and the ₹1.47 gap is a real appreciation of the dollar of 3.27 per cent
options.why: The same formula runs forward from last year: 45.00 × 1.10 ÷ 1.02 = ₹48.53. The market is at ₹50.00, so the dollar buys ₹1.47 more than inflation on its own explains. Measured against the ₹45.00 it started from, that is 1.47 ÷ 45.00 = 3.27 per cent of real appreciation, and it is explained by factors other than inflation.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: A year ago the exchange rate was ₹45.00 per US dollar. Over the year that has passed, inflation was 10 per cent in India and 2 per cent in the United States. Today the rate stands at ₹50.00 per dollar.

items.stem: Which exposure is this, and does any cash move because of it?

options.text: Transaction exposure, because dollar amounts had to be converted into rupees
options.misconception: reads an accounting conversion as a settlement, when transaction exposure needs an amount actually received or paid across currencies
options.why: Transaction exposure arises on a receivable, a payable or a committed amount that is settled at a rate different from the one assumed. Nothing here was settled; the dollars stayed in the subsidiary and only the reporting arithmetic changed.

options.text: No exposure at all, since the subsidiary's business is unchanged and no money was lost
options.misconception: treats an exposure as real only when it moves cash, when a translation effect changes reported net worth, gearing and any covenant written on them
options.why: It costs no cash and it is still an exposure. The consolidated figures are what lenders read covenants against and what shareholders judge the group by, and a rate move can breach a gearing covenant without a single rupee changing hands.

options.text: Translation exposure, and no cash moves — the change is in the arithmetic of consolidation
options.why: Translation exposure is the parent's restatement of a foreign subsidiary's accounts into the reporting currency. Nothing in the subsidiary's trading changed and no amount was settled at a worse rate, so no cash flow arises from it — what changed is the rupee number the consolidation reports.

options.text: Economic exposure, because the group is worth less in rupees than it was
options.misconception: applies economic exposure to a balance sheet restatement, when it is about future operating cash flows and competitive position
options.why: Economic exposure is the effect of a rate move on the present value of future operating cash flows — harm that reaches a company through its prices, its customers and its rivals. This subsidiary's customers and margins are unchanged; only the closing rate used to restate it moved.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian parent owns a US subsidiary whose assets and liabilities are all in dollars. This year the subsidiary traded exactly as before — same customers, same margins, same dollar profit — and settled nothing across a border. The rupee strengthened against the dollar, and the group's consolidated balance sheet now shows a smaller rupee figure for the subsidiary's net assets than last year.

items.stem: What is the settlement amount, and who pays whom?

options.text: The seller pays the buyer about ₹7,34,394
options.why: The formula is notional times the excess of the reference rate over the forward rate times the day fraction, the whole divided by one plus the reference rate for that same fraction. The gross difference is ₹20 crore × 0.015 × 90/360 = ₹7,50,000. Because an FRA settles at the start of the borrowing period rather than at its end, that figure is discounted at the actual rate now prevailing: 7,50,000 ÷ (1 + 0.085 × 0.25) = ₹7,34,394. The market fixed above the agreed rate, so the seller owes the buyer.

options.text: The seller pays the buyer about ₹7,37,101
options.misconception: discounts the difference at the agreed contract rate instead of the actual rate now prevailing, when it is the rate the market is offering that the money can be put to work at
options.why: 7,50,000 ÷ (1 + 0.07 × 0.25) = ₹7,37,101 uses the contract rate. The study material is explicit that the differential is discounted at the post-change actual rate, because that is what the buyer earns on the money over the period he now holds it early. At 8.5 per cent the answer is ₹7,34,394.

options.text: The seller pays the buyer ₹30,00,000
options.misconception: applies the rate difference to the notional for a whole year, when a 3x6 contract fixes a rate for a three-month period only
options.why: ₹20 crore × 0.015 = ₹30,00,000 is a year of the difference. A 3x6 FRA covers the three months beginning three months from now, so the day fraction of 90/360 applies and the gross figure is ₹7,50,000 before discounting.

options.text: The seller pays the buyer ₹7,50,000
options.misconception: settles the gross interest difference without discounting it, forgetting that the money changes hands at the start of the period while the extra interest it compensates for is suffered at the end
options.why: ₹7,50,000 is what the extra 1.5 per cent costs over the three months, but it is a cost borne at the end of the period. The FRA pays at the beginning, so the amount is brought back by one quarter's interest, giving ₹7,34,394. Paying the full figure early would over-compensate the buyer.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A treasurer buys a 3x6 forward rate agreement on a notional of ₹20 crore at an agreed forward rate of 7 per cent. On the settlement date the three-month reference rate fixes at 8.5 per cent. The day count is 90 days over a 360-day year.

items.stem: How much is there in total for the two of them to share through a swap, and where does it come from?

options.text: 1.0 per cent a year in total
options.why: A's advantage over B in the fixed market is 11.5 − 10 = 1.5 per cent; in the floating market it is only 1.0 − 0.5 = 0.5 per cent. The quality spread differential, 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 per cent, is the whole surplus available. It exists because A's advantage is larger in the market it does not want, so each borrows where its own edge is greatest and they swap the streams.

options.text: 2.0 per cent a year
options.misconception: adds the two market gaps instead of subtracting them, counting the same company's advantage twice over
options.why: 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 per cent adds an advantage A has in one market to an advantage A has in the other. Both belong to the same company; the swap can only monetise the amount by which one exceeds the other, which is 1.0 per cent.

options.text: 0.5 per cent a year
options.misconception: takes the gap in the floating market alone, which is the smaller of the two advantages rather than the difference between them
options.why: 0.5 per cent is A's edge in the floating market — the market A actually wants, and therefore the edge it could have used with no counterparty at all. What the swap is worth is the difference between the two edges, 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 per cent.

options.text: 1.5 per cent a year
options.misconception: takes A's advantage in the fixed market as the gain, when that advantage is partly matched in the floating market and only the excess can be shared
options.why: 1.5 per cent is how much cheaper A borrows fixed than B does. B is not helpless in the floating market either — it is only 0.5 per cent behind there — so 0.5 of the 1.5 is available to A without any swap at all. Only the 1.0 per cent difference between the two gaps is created by the swap.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: Company A can borrow fixed at 10 per cent or floating at MIBOR plus 0.5 per cent. Company B can borrow fixed at 11.5 per cent or floating at MIBOR plus 1 per cent. A wants floating-rate debt and B wants fixed-rate debt.

items.stem: What does the cap pay after each of those two resets?

options.text: Nothing after either reset — a cap limits the rate charged on the loan rather than paying cash
options.misconception: assumes a cap attaches to the loan and rewrites its interest rate, when it is a separate contract with a separate counterparty that settles in cash
options.why: The lender is not a party to the cap. The borrower still pays the lender at 10.5 per cent and separately receives ₹37.5 lakh from the cap seller, and it is the two together that hold the effective cost at 9 per cent.

options.text: ₹1.5 crore after the first reset, and nothing after the second
options.misconception: applies the rate difference for a whole year to a contract that resets and pays quarterly
options.why: ₹100 crore × 0.015 = ₹1.5 crore is a year of the excess. The reset covers 90 days, so the day fraction of 90/360 applies and the payment is ₹37.5 lakh. The annual figure would be reached only if the benchmark stayed at 10.5 per cent through all four quarters.

options.text: ₹37.5 lakh after the first reset, and ₹50 lakh paid away after the second
options.misconception: treats a bought cap as a swap that settles in both directions, when the buyer paid a premium precisely so that he owes nothing when rates fall
options.why: ₹100 crore × (0.090 − 0.070) × 90/360 = ₹50 lakh is what a swap struck at 9 per cent would cost the borrower at 7 per cent. A cap is an option and is exercised only when it helps; the premium paid up front is the whole of what its buyer ever gives up.

options.text: ₹37.5 lakh after the first reset, and nothing after the second
options.why: The cap pays the notional times the excess of the actual rate over the cap rate times the day fraction: ₹100 crore × (0.105 − 0.090) × 90/360 = ₹37.5 lakh, paid on the payment date at the end of that period. At 7 per cent the benchmark is below the strike, and a cap is an option, so the payment is the greater of nought and the difference — which is nothing.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A borrower buys an interest rate cap on a notional of ₹100 crore with a cap rate of 9 per cent, reset quarterly on a 90-day over 360-day basis. At the first reset the benchmark fixes at 10.5 per cent. At the next reset it fixes at 7 per cent.

items.stem: What are its Macaulay duration and its modified duration?

options.text: Both are 2 years
options.misconception: reads duration off the maturity, which is true only of a zero-coupon bond because only there does every rupee arrive at the end
options.why: A coupon-bearing bond's duration is always less than its maturity, because ₹100 comes back at the end of year one and does not wait for redemption. That early rupee pulls the weighted average down to 1.909 years, and modified duration is lower again at 1.736.

options.text: Macaulay 1.5 years
options.misconception: averages the two years without weighting them by the present value arriving in each, so a ₹100 coupon counts as heavily as a ₹1,100 redemption
options.why: (1 + 2) ÷ 2 = 1.5 years gives the two years equal billing. Ninety-one per cent of the bond's value arrives in year two, and the weights have to reflect that, which pulls the answer to 1.909 years — far closer to two than to one.

options.text: Macaulay 1.909 years, modified 1.736
options.why: Macaulay duration is the weighted average time at which the money comes back. The year-one cash flow of ₹100 has a present value of ₹90.91 and the year-two cash flow of ₹1,100 has a present value of ₹909.09, so weighting each year by its share of the ₹1,000 price gives (1 × 90.91 + 2 × 909.09) ÷ 1,000 = 1.909 years. Modified duration divides that by one plus the yield, 1.909 ÷ 1.10 = 1.736, and it is the figure that estimates the percentage price move per one per cent change in yield.

options.text: Macaulay 1.736 years, modified 1.909
options.misconception: swaps the two, when modified duration is Macaulay divided by one plus the yield and so is always the smaller of the pair
options.why: The two figures are right and they are the wrong way round. Modified duration is Macaulay duration divided by 1.10, so it can only be smaller. The Macaulay figure is 1.909 years and the modified figure is 1.736.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of ₹1,000 face value carries a 10 per cent annual coupon and has exactly two years left to maturity. Its yield to maturity is 10 per cent, so it trades at ₹1,000. The discount factors at 10 per cent are 0.9091 for year one and 0.8264 for year two.

items.stem: In what proportions should the fund hold them, and what does that achieve?

options.text: 40 per cent in P and 60 per cent in Q
options.why: A portfolio's duration is the weighted average of the durations of what it holds, so w × 2 + (1 − w) × 7 = 5 gives 7 − 5w = 5 and w = 0.4. At a portfolio duration of five years, matching the horizon, the price loss and the reinvestment gain from a rate move cancel on the date the money is needed, which is what immunisation means.

options.text: All of it in Bond Q, whose 7-year duration is the nearer of the two to the horizon
options.misconception: picks the single closest bond instead of blending, when a mix can hit the horizon exactly and one bond alone cannot
options.why: Bond Q is nearer — two years out against Bond P's three — and near is not matched. A portfolio of duration seven against a five-year liability loses more on a rate rise than the extra reinvestment income makes up. Blending the two hits five exactly.

options.text: 50 per cent in each
options.misconception: assumes the midpoint of two durations must be the answer, when the target of five is not the midpoint of two and seven
options.why: 0.5 × 2 + 0.5 × 7 = 4.5 years. An equal split lands halfway between the two durations, which is 4.5 and not 5. The target sits three-fifths of the way from 2 towards 7, so the weight on Q is 0.6.

options.text: 60 per cent in P and 40 per cent in Q
options.misconception: reports the weights the wrong way round, giving a portfolio duration a year short of the horizon
options.why: 0.6 × 2 + 0.4 × 7 = 4.0 years, a year short of five. A portfolio whose duration is below its horizon is exposed to rates falling, because the reinvestment income it was counting on does not arrive. Reading which weight belongs to which bond is half the calculation.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A fund must pay a fixed sum in exactly five years. Only two bonds are available: Bond P, whose duration is 2 years, and Bond Q, whose duration is 7 years.

items.stem: What does the convexity-adjusted estimate give on the fall, and what does the pair of answers show?

options.text: ₹1,136 — a 13.6 per cent gain, larger than the 10.4 per cent loss an equal rise causes
options.why: The duration term is plus 6 × 0.02 = 12 per cent and the convexity term is 0.5 × 80 × 0.02 × 0.02 = 1.6 per cent. The convexity term is added on a fall exactly as it is added on a rise, because it turns on the square of the yield change and a square is positive either way. That is the asymmetry a bondholder is paying for: 13.6 per cent up against 10.4 per cent down, on moves of the same size.

options.text: ₹1,152 — a 15.2 per cent gain
options.misconception: drops the one-half, doubling a correction that comes from the second-order term of the expansion the estimate is built on
options.why: Using 80 × 0.02 × 0.02 = 3.2 per cent instead of half of it gives 15.2 per cent and ₹1,152. The one-half belongs to the second-order term and does not go away; with it the estimate is ₹1,136.

options.text: ₹1,104 — a 10.4 per cent gain, the same size as the loss on an equal rise
options.misconception: subtracts the convexity correction on a fall, in the belief that it is added only on a rise, which makes the price response symmetric when convexity is exactly what breaks the symmetry
options.why: 12 − 1.6 = 10.4 per cent gives ₹1,104 and makes the gain and the loss mirror each other. The correction carries the square of the yield change, so it is positive whichever way the yield went, and it is always added. The right answer is 12 + 1.6 = 13.6 per cent.

options.text: ₹1,120 — a 12 per cent gain, the duration estimate with convexity left out
options.misconception: uses the straight-line duration estimate alone, which understates the gain on a fall just as it overstates the loss on a rise
options.why: Plus 6 × 0.02 = 12 per cent gives ₹1,120. The straight line is the same in both directions and the real price curve is not. Leaving the 1.6 per cent correction out costs ₹16 of estimated value here, and far more on a larger move.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation
