items.scenario: A bond priced at ₹1,000 has a modified duration of 6 years and a convexity of 80. Its yield falls by 200 basis points. On an equal rise of 200 basis points the convexity-adjusted estimate is a fall of 10.4 per cent.

items.stem: What is the effective annual yield, and why is it not 10 per cent?

options.text: 10.00 per cent
options.misconception: reads the coupon rate as the return actually earned, treating a bond that pays twice a year as though the whole ₹100 arrived at the year end
options.why: 10 per cent would be right if the ₹100 came once, at the end of the year. It comes as ₹50 after six months and ₹50 after twelve, and the first ₹50 can be put to work for the remaining half year. That is what lifts the effective figure to 10.25 per cent.

options.text: 10.38 per cent
options.misconception: compounds four times a year when the bond pays twice, applying quarterly mechanics to a half-yearly instrument
options.why: 1.025 to the fourth power, less one, is 10.38 per cent — the effective rate for a bond paying ₹25 every quarter. This one pays ₹50 every six months, so the rate per period is 5 per cent and there are two periods, giving 10.25 per cent. More frequent payment would indeed be worth more; it is not what the terms say.

options.text: 10.25 per cent
options.why: At par the yield for each half-yearly period is the coupon over the price, 50 ÷ 1,000 = 5 per cent. Two such periods compound inside the year: 1.05 × 1.05 − 1 = 0.1025, so the effective annual yield is 10.25 per cent. The 10 per cent on the certificate is a nominal rate quoted per annum, and the extra 25 basis points is what the first half-year's ₹50 earns over the rest of the year.

options.text: 5.00 per cent
options.misconception: quotes the rate per period as though it were the annual figure, halving a return instead of compounding it
options.why: 5 per cent is what the bond yields over six months, not over a year. Two of those periods make a year, and compounding rather than merely adding them gives 1.05 × 1.05 − 1 = 10.25 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of ₹1,000 face value pays interest at 10 per cent a year in two half-yearly instalments of ₹50 each. It is quoted at par, ₹1,000. An investor reads the coupon and says his return is 10 per cent a year.

items.stem: What is the portfolio's standard deviation, and what does that tell him?

options.text: 10 per cent, because the two partly cancel each other as any two assets do
options.misconception: applies the uncorrelated formula, dropping the cross term that a correlation of +1 makes largest
options.why: That is the answer when the correlation is zero: 0.36 × 0.01 + 0.16 × 0.04 = 0.01, whose square root is 10 per cent. Here the correlation is +1, so the cross term 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 0.10 × 0.20 × 1 must be added, and it is what carries the answer up to 14 per cent. Assuming assets always partly cancel is the error this case exists to catch.

options.text: 15 per cent, the average of 10 and 20
options.misconception: averages the two standard deviations without weighting them, ignoring that only 40 per cent sits in the riskier asset
options.why: A weighted average is right here, but the weights are 60 and 40, not 50 and 50: 0.6 × 10 + 0.4 × 20 = 14 per cent. 15 per cent is the answer to a question about an equal split, and the gap between the two is the whole value of reading how much sits where.

options.text: About 14.83 per cent, from the weighted average of the two variances
options.misconception: averages the variances and takes the square root, which is not the same as averaging the standard deviations
options.why: 0.6 × 0.01 + 0.4 × 0.04 = 0.022, whose square root is 14.83 per cent. Weighting variances rather than squaring the weights themselves is a different sum, and it happens to sit close enough to the right answer to look convincing. The weights enter the variance formula squared, not raw.

options.text: 14 per cent — exactly the weighted average of the two, so the mix has bought him nothing
options.why: When two assets are perfectly positively correlated the cross term is at its largest and the variance collapses to a perfect square, so the portfolio standard deviation is the plain weighted average of the two: 0.6 × 10 + 0.4 × 20 = 14 per cent. There is no diversification benefit anywhere on this line — every mix of the two sits on the straight line joining them, and he could have reached 14 per cent by holding cash against A alone.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Asset A has a standard deviation of 10 per cent and Asset B one of 20 per cent. This time the two are perfectly positively correlated. An investor puts 60 per cent of his money into A and 40 per cent into B.

items.stem: Which form of efficiency does this market reach, and which does it fail?

options.text: It satisfies only the weak form
options.misconception: stops at the lowest level and ignores the finding on published accounts, which is precisely the semi-strong test being met
options.why: The weak form covers past prices and volumes. Published annual results are other public information, which is the semi-strong level, and the study found that they too paid nothing. The market therefore reaches semi-strong, one rung above weak.

options.text: It fails all three forms, since somebody is beating the market
options.misconception: treats any profitable trading as proof of inefficiency at every level, when each level is defined against a stated set of information
options.why: Efficiency is always tested against a named information set. Insiders profiting says only that private information is not yet in the price. Two of the three tests were passed here, and passing the semi-strong one necessarily means passing the weak one beneath it.

options.text: It satisfies the semi-strong form and fails the strong form
options.why: The strong form says price reflects all information, private as well as public, so not even an insider could earn an abnormal return. Directors dealing on unpublished information are earning exactly that, so the strong form fails. Charts paying nothing is the weak form holding, and published results paying nothing is the semi-strong form holding — and because the levels nest, the higher of the two that holds is the market's grade.

options.text: It satisfies the strong form, since prices did move once the insiders traded
options.misconception: reads price movement after a trade as evidence of efficiency, when the test is whether anyone could earn an abnormal return from the information beforehand
options.why: Prices moving after insiders buy is the market slowly discovering what they already knew. Strong form efficiency would mean the price had moved before they could act, leaving them nothing to earn. They earned a consistent premium, so it had not.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A study of one market finds three things. Trading rules built on past prices and volumes earn nothing above the market once risk is allowed for. Trading on published annual results earns nothing either. But directors dealing in their own companies' shares before an announcement is made public earn a consistent abnormal return.

items.stem: Which of the four is the financial risk?

options.text: All four, since every one of them costs the company money
options.misconception: sorts risks by whether they hurt the accounts rather than by where they come from, which would make every risk a financial risk and empty the classification of meaning
options.why: Every risk on any list ends up in the accounts somewhere; that is not what the heading means. The chapter separates strategic, compliance, operational and financial risk by their source, so that each can be owned by whoever is in a position to act on it.

options.text: The customer's default alone — the other three are operational, compliance and strategic risk in turn
options.why: Financial risk is an unexpected change in financial conditions, and a customer failing to honour its obligation is counter party risk, one of its categories. The mis-keyed payment is operational risk, which is people and process inside the company. The missed filing is compliance risk. Losing in a market the board chose to enter is strategic risk.

options.text: The missed filing and the customer default, since both end in a demand for money
options.misconception: pulls compliance risk under financial risk because a penalty is payable, when the penalty is the consequence and the source is a rule that was not followed
options.why: A missed filing is compliance risk — the failure to meet a requirement of law or regulation. What it costs is not what classifies it. Only the customer's default is financial risk here.

options.text: The mis-keyed payment, since it is a payment and money left the company
options.misconception: files a risk under the department where it happens to land rather than under what caused it
options.why: A clerk keying the wrong figure is a failure of process and control inside the company, which is operational risk however large the amount. The financial risk in this list is the customer's default, because it is an outside party failing to honour what it owes.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: Four things go wrong at a manufacturer in one month. A clerk keys a supplier payment as ₹50 lakh instead of ₹5 lakh. A new environmental notification requires a filing that nobody made. The expansion into a new market that the board chose last year is losing badly to a bigger rival. And a customer defaults on a ₹2 crore bill.

items.stem: What are the borrowers called in this structure, and what is the NBFC now doing?

options.text: The borrowers are the investors, since it is their instalments that pay the securities
options.misconception: confuses who supplies the cash flow with who buys the paper, which are opposite ends of the same structure
options.why: The investors are the people who bought the securities the SPV issued, and they receive the money. The borrowers pay it in. They are the obligors, and their instalments are the asset the securities are backed by.

options.text: The borrowers are the obligors, and the NBFC is acting as the servicer — an administrative role sub-contracted back to it, which does not undo the sale
options.why: The obligors are the parties who owe the money, and their payments are the root of the whole securitisation, which is why the pool is assessed on their credit quality. The servicer collects what is due from the obligors, passes it to the SPV and follows up on defaults; the chapter notes that this administration is generally sub-contracted back to the originator or an associate of it.

options.text: The NBFC still owns the receivables, since it is still the one collecting them
options.misconception: reads possession of the collection process as ownership of the asset, when the true sale transferred both legal and beneficial interest to the SPV
options.why: The true sale moved legal as well as beneficial interest to the SPV, which is what takes the assets off the NBFC's balance sheet and puts them beyond its own creditors. Who physically collects the money is an administrative arrangement, and the SPV can replace the servicer without the sale being affected.

options.text: The NBFC is the credit enhancer, because the collections are still coming through it
options.misconception: reads a collection agency's work as a guarantee of payment, when enhancement is a separate and separately sized commitment
options.why: Credit enhancement is a stated commitment — over-collateralisation, a cash collateral account, or a third party's support — that absorbs losses up to a capped amount. Collecting and forwarding instalments is servicing and carries no such promise; the NBFC bears nothing if a borrower stops paying.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: An NBFC sells its car-loan receivables to an SPV in a true sale. The borrowers go on paying their instalments at the NBFC's branches exactly as before, and the NBFC forwards every collection to the SPV for a fee. It also chases anyone who falls behind, and takes legal action where it has to.

items.stem: Which stage of venture capital funding is this?

options.text: The second round
options.misconception: places a profitable company in the stage meant for one that is selling product but has not yet reached profit
options.why: The second round is working capital for early-stage companies that are selling product but are not yet profitable. This company turned profitable already, so it has passed that stage and sits at the third round.

options.text: The third round, also called mezzanine financing
options.why: The third round is expansion money for a newly profitable company, and it is the stage the study material also names mezzanine financing. The fourth round, called bridge financing, is the money that finances the going public — and the company has said that is expressly not what it is raising yet.

options.text: The fourth round, also called bridge financing
options.misconception: reaches for the stage nearest the exit because the company is now profitable, when bridge financing is specifically the money raised to fund the going public
options.why: The fourth round exists to carry a company to a public issue. This one has ruled that out for now and wants capacity instead, which is the third round, or mezzanine financing.

options.text: Seed money
options.misconception: names the first stage of the list for a company several stages past it, reading a new expansion as though it were a new idea
options.why: Seed money is the low-level financing needed to prove a new idea, before there is a product or a customer. This company has two years of commercial production behind it and a profit, which puts it four stages further on.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A company has been in commercial production for two years and has just turned profitable. It now wants money to expand capacity. It says clearly that it is not yet raising the money that will carry it to a public issue.

items.stem: What is its enterprise value?

options.text: ₹350 crore
options.misconception: subtracts net debt instead of adding it, running the bridge in the direction that goes from enterprise value to equity value
options.why: 500 − 150 = ₹350 crore is the bridge run backwards. Subtracting net debt is how you get from enterprise value down to equity value; starting at equity value, the net debt is added, which gives ₹650 crore.

options.text: ₹700 crore
options.misconception: adds gross borrowings without crediting the cash the buyer also acquires, so the company is charged for its debt and given nothing for the money sitting against it
options.why: 500 + 200 = ₹700 crore ignores the ₹50 crore of cash. That cash passes to the buyer and can repay part of the borrowing on day one, so the bridge runs on net debt of ₹150 crore and the answer is ₹650 crore.

options.text: ₹650 crore
options.why: The bridge runs from equity value to enterprise value by adding net debt. Borrowings of ₹200 crore less cash of ₹50 crore is net debt of ₹150 crore, and 500 + 150 = ₹650 crore. A buyer of the whole company takes on the borrowings and also gets the cash, which is why only the net figure is added.

options.text: ₹500 crore
options.misconception: takes market capitalisation as enterprise value, when capitalisation prices only the shareholders' claim and enterprise value prices the whole business
options.why: ₹500 crore is what the shares are worth. Somebody buying the business outright also has to deal with ₹200 crore of borrowings, against which ₹50 crore of cash comes with the company. The enterprise is therefore worth ₹650 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A listed company's market capitalisation is ₹500 crore. Its balance sheet shows borrowings of ₹200 crore and cash and cash equivalents of ₹50 crore.

items.stem: What does SA 200 say the auditor's overall objectives are, and what follows when an objective in a relevant SA cannot be achieved?

options.text: There are two overall objectives, but an objective in an individual SA that cannot be achieved is answered by documenting the departure and issuing an unmodified opinion
options.misconception: treats documentation of a departure as a substitute for evaluating what the failure does to the overall objectives
options.why: Documentation records a decision; it does not make the decision correct. The standard asks the auditor to evaluate the effect on the overall objectives, and an unmodified opinion is the one outcome that evaluation cannot produce where material evidence is missing.

options.text: Withdrawal is the only course open where an objective cannot be achieved, an audit falling short of reasonable assurance being incapable of supporting any report at all
options.misconception: makes withdrawal the sole remedy, when the standard names modification of the opinion beside it
options.why: The standard offers two courses and leaves the choice to the circumstances. A modified opinion tells the reader exactly what could not be audited, which is often more use to him than an auditor who has left.

options.text: There is one overall objective, reasonable assurance, so an auditor who has not obtained it has nothing to report and may hand the engagement back in silence
options.misconception: drops the second overall objective, which is to report on the financial statements and communicate as required by the SAs
options.why: Silence is not one of the routes the standard offers. The obligation to report and to communicate is stated as an objective in its own right, which is why an auditor who cannot obtain evidence still has to say so rather than disappear.

options.text: There are two overall objectives — to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, and to report on the financial statements and communicate as required by the Standards on Auditing in accordance with the auditor's findings — and where an objective in a relevant SA cannot be achieved, the auditor evaluates whether that prevents him from achieving the overall objectives and therefore requires him to modify the opinion or withdraw from the engagement
options.why: SA 200 states two overall objectives, not one. The first is to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error. The second is to report on the financial statements and communicate as required by the Standards on Auditing in accordance with the auditor's findings, and that second objective survives the failure of the first. Where an objective in a relevant SA cannot be achieved, the auditor evaluates whether this prevents him from achieving the overall objectives and thereby requires him to modify the opinion or withdraw from the engagement.

citation.ref: the overall objectives of the auditor, read with the requirement where an objective in a relevant SA cannot be achieved

items.scenario: Three weeks before the deadline you accept that you cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about a material investment in an unlisted company, and that the objective of SA 501 on that item cannot be achieved. The engagement partner's view is that an auditor has one objective, to obtain reasonable assurance, and that having failed to obtain it he simply has nothing to deliver — the firm will return the engagement letter and say nothing further.

items.stem: Are the preconditions for an audit present?

options.text: Yes — the acknowledgement of responsibilities is the whole of the preconditions, and an unsuitable basis of preparation is a matter for the opinion at the end of the audit
options.misconception: reduces the preconditions to the acknowledgement, dropping the acceptability of the framework
options.why: The framework is the yardstick the opinion is measured against. Accepting an engagement whose yardstick is unusable leaves the auditor performing an audit that has nothing to conclude for or against, which is why SA 210 settles the question before acceptance.

options.text: No — establishing whether the preconditions are present has two parts, and the first is determining whether the financial reporting framework to be applied in the preparation of the financial statements is acceptable; management's willingness answers only the second, so the auditor shall not accept the engagement
options.why: SA 210 puts two questions at the acceptance stage. The auditor determines whether the financial reporting framework to be applied in the preparation of the financial statements is acceptable, and he obtains management's agreement that it acknowledges its responsibilities. A basis invented by the entity, capitalising selling costs and omitting deferred tax, is not an acceptable framework, and where the preconditions are not present the auditor shall not accept the proposed engagement unless required by law or regulation.
keywords: financial reporting framework to be applied

options.text: No, and the bar is absolute — the auditor may never accept an engagement on a framework he considers unacceptable, whatever any law or regulation may say
options.misconception: removes the exception the standard makes where law or regulation requires the auditor to accept
options.why: The standard's own words are that the auditor shall not accept unless required by law or regulation to do so. Statutes do sometimes compel an audit on a framework the auditor would not have chosen, and the standard then routes the problem into the terms of the engagement and the report rather than into a refusal.

options.text: Yes, provided the auditor includes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph describing the basis of preparation so that readers are not misled
options.misconception: uses a paragraph in the report to cure a defect the standard deals with at the acceptance stage
options.why: A paragraph can draw attention to a disclosure; it cannot supply a framework. And an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter, which is not this case.

citation.ref: para 6 on establishing whether the preconditions for an audit are present, read with the requirement not to accept where they are not

items.scenario: A prospective client proposes that its financial statements be prepared on a basis of its own devising, under which selling costs are capitalised and carried forward, deferred tax is left out entirely, and the statements are nevertheless headed as presenting a true and fair view. Management is entirely willing to acknowledge in writing its responsibility for the financial statements, for internal control and for giving you access to everything you ask for. No law or regulation requires you to take the engagement.

items.stem: What does SA 230 require the file to record about the work performed?

options.text: Nothing further — the conclusion is what a later reader needs, and the list of customers is a scratch paper discarded when the final file is assembled
options.misconception: treats the record of what was tested as working material rather than as part of the documentation the standard requires
options.why: A conclusion nobody can re-perform is an assertion. The identifying characteristics exist so that a reviewer or an inspector can go back to the same thirty balances, and a sample that cannot be reconstructed cannot be re-examined by anyone.

options.text: The identifying characteristics of the specific items or matters tested, who performed the audit work and the date such work was completed, and who reviewed the audit work performed and the date and extent of such review
options.why: SA 230 states the three things exactly. In documenting the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures performed, the auditor records the identifying characteristics of the specific items or matters tested — here, which thirty customers — and who performed the audit work and the date such work was completed, and who reviewed the audit work performed and the date and extent of such review. A bare conclusion satisfies none of them.
keywords: the date and extent of such review

options.text: Everything in the first option, and in addition a signed statement from each confirming customer's finance head that the reply was genuine
options.misconception: adds a requirement the standard does not carry, and moves the auditor's documentation onto the confirming party
options.why: Documentation is a record of what the auditor did. A confirmation reply is already external evidence, and asking the sender to authenticate his own letter would start a chain with no end.

options.text: Only the identifying characteristics; who did the work and who reviewed it are matters of firm policy rather than requirements of the standard
options.misconception: leaves two of the three elements to firm policy, when the standard states all three together
options.why: Responsibility is part of the record. Who performed the work fixes whether it was done by someone competent to do it, and the date and extent of the review fix whether the review happened before the report or after somebody asked a question.

citation.ref: para 9

items.scenario: The receivables section of an audit file holds one working paper. It reads in full, "Confirmations sent to a sample of 30 customers. Replies agreed to the ledger. No exceptions." It does not say which thirty customers were selected. It is unsigned and undated. A partner's initials appear in the top corner with no date beside them and nothing about how much of the work the initials cover.

items.stem: What is missing from that understanding?

options.text: Only monitoring of controls; the control environment, the risk assessment process and the information system belong to those charged with governance rather than to the entity's internal control
options.misconception: moves three components outside internal control on the footing that governance owns them
options.why: Governance participates in the control environment; it does not remove it from internal control. The standard lists all five as components of the entity's system of internal control, whoever inside the entity happens to operate them.

options.text: Four of the five components of internal control — the control environment, the entity's risk assessment process, the information system and communication, and monitoring of controls — each of which the auditor obtains an understanding of, alongside control activities
options.why: Internal control has five components and the file holds one. The auditor obtains an understanding of the control environment, the entity's risk assessment process, control activities, the information system and communication, and monitoring of controls. Each carries its own audit meaning: a weak control environment undermines every activity beneath it, and monitoring of controls is what tells the auditor whether a control that worked in April is still working in November.

options.text: Nothing — control activities are the only component that operates at the assertion level, so understanding them is the whole of the requirement
options.misconception: keeps the one component that maps onto assertions and drops the four that condition it
options.why: Control activities are where a transaction is caught, and the other four decide whether they are designed sensibly, staffed honestly, fed with the right information and checked over time. Reading only the activities is reading the last line of the argument.

options.text: Nothing is missing in substance, but the four components must be tested for operating effectiveness rather than merely understood
options.misconception: converts an understanding requirement into a test of controls the auditor is not required to perform
options.why: Obtaining an understanding is one thing and testing operating effectiveness is another, and the second is a response decided under SA 330 on the controls the auditor intends to rely on. The file's problem is that four components were never understood at all, not that they were not tested.

citation.ref: the requirement to obtain an understanding of each component of internal control — control environment, the entity's risk assessment process, control activities, the information system and communication, and monitoring of controls

items.scenario: The internal control section of a file runs to forty pages. All of it describes controls inside the sales, purchases and payroll cycles — approvals, matches, reconciliations, segregation of duties. Nothing in the file records how the entity identifies and responds to its business risks, how management and those charged with governance set the tone, how financial information is captured and communicated, or how the entity checks over time that its controls are still working. The senior says misstatements are prevented at the transaction level, so the rest is background reading.

items.stem: What does SA 330 require?

options.text: Nothing further, provided the chief financial officer gives a written representation that the financial statements agree with the books of account
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for a procedure the auditor can perform himself
options.why: A written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about the matter it deals with, and agreeing a set of statements to the ledgers is work the auditor can simply do. Asking management to certify the arithmetic of its own pack is the weakest available answer.

options.text: Nothing further — audited balances plus arithmetic cannot produce a misstatement, so the conversion step carries no audit risk
options.misconception: treats the assembly of the financial statements as arithmetic, when it is where adjustments and disclosures are made outside the accounting system
options.why: The step is not arithmetic. It is where balances are regrouped, where consolidation and reclassification entries are posted and where the notes are written, and none of it is visible in the ledgers the team has already tested.

options.text: Nothing further, because the journal entry testing that SA 240 requires for the risk of management override already covers the closing process
options.misconception: reads a fraud-driven procedure as discharging a requirement SA 330 imposes on every audit whatever the fraud risk
options.why: The two look alike and ask different questions. SA 240's testing selects entries on fraud-risk criteria to address management override; SA 330's requirement is unconditional and includes agreeing the statements and their disclosures back to the records, which no selection of journals does.

options.text: Substantive procedures related to the financial statement closing process — agreeing or reconciling the information in the financial statements, including the disclosures, with the underlying accounting records, and examining material journal entries and other adjustments made during the course of preparing the financial statements
options.why: SA 330 requires substantive procedures related to the financial statement closing process in every audit, and this spreadsheet is that process. The auditor agrees or reconciles the information in the financial statements with the underlying accounting records, disclosures included, and examines material journal entries and other adjustments made while the statements were being prepared. Seventeen top-level adjustments that never touch the accounting system are precisely what the requirement was written to reach.

citation.ref: para 20

items.scenario: Every material class of transactions and account balance in a company's books has been tested substantively and cleared. The last step of the year is the conversion of the trial balance into the financial statements. That happens in a spreadsheet kept by the group reporting team: seventeen top-level adjustments are posted in it, the disclosure notes are typed in by the chief financial officer's assistant, and nothing from the spreadsheet goes back into the accounting system. The manager plans no work at all on that step, since every balance feeding it has already been audited.

items.stem: What does SA 501 require?

options.text: Nashik is impracticable, so alternative audit procedures are performed and the opinion is modified if they do not work; the February count needs nothing, the auditor having no responsibility for a period he did not observe
options.misconception: calls a temporary obstruction impracticability and leaves the intervening period unaudited
options.why: Impracticability is about a count the auditor cannot attend at all, not one he cannot attend on the day. And the whole point of a count before the year end is that the roll forward has to be audited, because it is the roll forward that produces the balance sheet figure.

options.text: A certificate from management as to quantities answers both, the auditor having been kept out of one location and the other having been counted before he arrived
options.misconception: accepts a representation in place of evidence the auditor could still obtain by attending later and testing the intervening period
options.why: A written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own, and here the evidence was available: the road opened, and the perpetual records for the intervening month exist and can be tested.

options.text: Neither location needs attendance, since a count conducted by management under its own instructions is management's assertion and the auditor's job is to test the records that follow from it
options.misconception: reads attendance out of the standard on the footing that the count belongs to management
options.why: The count is management's and the attendance is the auditor's. He attends to evaluate management's instructions, observe the count being performed, inspect the inventory and perform test counts, none of which the records afterwards can show him.

options.text: At Nashik, make or observe some physical counts on an alternative date and perform audit procedures on the intervening transactions, the blockade having lifted so that attendance was never impracticable; and for the February count, perform audit procedures to obtain evidence about whether changes in inventory between the count date and the date of the financial statements are properly recorded
options.why: SA 501 separates the two situations. Where the auditor is unable to attend physical inventory counting due to unforeseen circumstances, he makes or observes some physical counts on an alternative date and performs audit procedures on the intervening transactions — a month-long blockade that then lifts is an unforeseen circumstance, not impracticability. Where the counting is conducted at a date other than the date of the financial statements, he performs audit procedures to obtain evidence about whether changes in inventory between the two dates are properly recorded.

citation.ref: para 5 on a count conducted at a date other than the date of the financial statements and para 6 on being unable to attend due to unforeseen circumstances, read with para 4 and para 7

items.scenario: Inventory is material. The count at the Nashik plant is fixed for 31 March; on that morning a protest blocks the approach road and the site is inaccessible. The blockade is lifted a month later and the plant is then reachable. At a second location the company counts its entire inventory on 28 February and rolls the figure forward to 31 March using its perpetual records. The manager proposes to treat Nashik as a case of impracticability and take a management certificate for it, and to do nothing at all on the February count because a count is a count.

items.stem: How does SA 530 have you treat the three situations?

options.text: Drop the destroyed invoice from the sample as unavailable and select a replacement for it as well, since neither item can be tested as selected
options.misconception: treats an item the auditor cannot reach as though the procedure were merely inapplicable, when the standard makes it a misstatement
options.why: The two are opposites. A cancelled entry is simply outside what the procedure was designed to test; an invoice that cannot be produced is evidence that is missing, and replacing it would let a population of unavailable records test perfectly clean.

options.text: Treat the destroyed invoice as a misstatement, because you were unable to apply the designed procedure to it; perform the procedure on a replacement item for the cancelled entry, because the procedure is not applicable to that item; and investigate the nature and cause of the five errors, where the shared branch may lead you to identify every item in the population with that feature and extend procedures to them
options.why: SA 530 gives the two situations opposite answers on purpose. If the audit procedure is not applicable to the selected item, the auditor performs the procedure on a replacement item. If he is unable to apply the designed procedure to a selected item, he treats that item as a misstatement in the case of tests of details. He then investigates the nature and cause of any deviations or misstatements identified, and a common feature such as one branch is a lead to be followed rather than a coincidence.

options.text: Treat the five tax errors as an anomaly and exclude them from the projection, since they all come from one branch and so are not representative of the population
options.misconception: calls a pattern an anomaly, when an anomaly is a misstatement the auditor has demonstrated is not representative of the population
options.why: A shared branch is a reason to look for more of them, not fewer. An anomaly requires a high degree of certainty that the misstatement is not representative, and five errors on one branch's invoices point the other way.

options.text: All the errors found are simply projected across the population and nothing else follows, projection being the response SA 530 prescribes to a sample result
options.misconception: stops at projection, which is one requirement among several, and leaves the untestable item and the inapplicable item unresolved
options.why: Projection is what the auditor does with misstatements once he has decided which items are misstatements. That decision is what the destroyed invoice and the cancelled entry turn on, and the investigation of cause is a separate requirement again.

citation.ref: para 10, para 11 and para 12

items.scenario: You select sixty purchase invoices for a test of details. One of the sixty was in a records room destroyed by flooding; the company cannot produce it by any route and neither can the supplier. Another of the sixty turns out to be a duplicate entry that was cancelled and reversed the same day, so the procedure you designed does not apply to it. On five others the procedure runs and each shows the wrong rate of tax applied, and all five come from the same branch office.

items.stem: What is missing from the letter?

options.text: Nothing — representations are requested on whatever matters the auditor chooses to ask about, and this auditor chose three
options.misconception: treats every representation as discretionary, when two of them are required in every audit
options.why: The specific representations are chosen; the two general ones are not. They exist because the whole premise of an audit is that management accepts those responsibilities, and the letter is where management says at the end that it did.

options.text: Nothing is missing, because the two general matters are already set out in the engagement letter, which management signed at the start of the year
options.misconception: reads the engagement letter's description of responsibilities as a representation that they were afterwards fulfilled
options.why: The engagement letter records what management undertakes to do. The representation records that it did it, twelve months later and with the audit finished, which is a different statement made at a different time.

options.text: The two representations required in every audit — that management has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements, and that it has provided the auditor with all relevant information and access and that all transactions have been recorded and are reflected in the financial statements — and the letter must be for all the financial statements and periods referred to in the auditor's report
options.why: SA 580 asks for two representations whatever else the audit threw up. Management confirms that it has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with the applicable framework, and that it has provided the auditor with all relevant information and access agreed in the terms of the engagement and that all transactions have been recorded and are reflected in the financial statements. The written representations are also for all the financial statements and periods referred to in the auditor's report, so a letter confined to the current year is short by a year.
keywords: fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation
all the financial statements and periods

options.text: Only the period point; the two general representations become unnecessary once specific representations on the significant matters have been obtained
options.misconception: lets specific representations displace the two the standard requires unconditionally
options.why: Specific representations sit on top of the two general ones and never in place of them. Confirming three matters says nothing about whether anything was withheld on the other matters nobody asked about.

citation.ref: para 10 and para 11 on the written representations required in every audit, read with the requirement that they cover all the financial statements and periods in the auditor's report

items.scenario: The representation letter on your file deals with three matters, each of them a point the team raised during the audit: contingent liabilities, related party transactions and events after the reporting date. It says nothing about management's responsibility for the financial statements and nothing about whether everything relevant was given to you. It is dated the same day as your report and states that it covers the year ended 31 March 2026, although your report also covers the comparative figures for the previous year.

items.stem: What does SA 600 require of the principal auditor beyond the statement in the report?

options.text: Advise the other auditor of the use to be made of his work and report and make sufficient arrangements for coordination — the areas requiring special consideration, the procedures for identifying inter-component transactions and the timetable — and then consider the significant findings of the other auditor, which may be done by discussing the audit procedures applied or by reviewing a written summary of his procedures and findings
options.why: SA 600 puts work at both ends. Before the other auditor starts, the principal auditor advises him of the use to be made of his work and report and coordinates the areas needing special consideration, the identification of inter-component transactions and the timetable. After it, the principal auditor considers the significant findings of the other auditor, and may discuss the audit procedures applied or review a written summary of the other auditor's procedures and findings, in the form of a completed questionnaire or checklist.
keywords: use to be made of his work

options.text: Re-audit the three branches himself, since he cannot state a division of responsibility for work whose quality he has not established
options.misconception: replaces a review of another auditor's work with a second audit the standard does not require
options.why: The principal auditor is normally entitled to rely upon the work of the other auditor unless special circumstances make it essential for him to visit the component or examine its books. Re-auditing every branch would make the division of work pointless.

options.text: Obtain the other auditors' complete working paper files in every case and re-perform a selection of their tests before signing
options.misconception: turns an exceptional step into the routine requirement
options.why: Visiting the component and examining its records is available where special circumstances call for it. As a standing practice it ignores the ordinary route the standard sets out — discussion of procedures, or a written summary of them and of the findings.

options.text: Nothing — a signed report from a member of the same profession is itself the evidence, and the statement of division in the report is what tells the reader where responsibility sits
options.misconception: treats receipt of another auditor's report as the whole of the principal auditor's work
options.why: The statement of division tells the reader how much of the audit was somebody else's. It does not tell the principal auditor anything, and he is the one who has to conclude on the financial statements as a whole.

citation.ref: the principal auditor's procedures — advising the other auditor of the use to be made of his work, coordination, and consideration of the other auditor's significant findings — read with the statement of division of responsibility

items.scenario: You are the principal auditor of a company with three branches audited by other firms. You never told those firms what use you would make of their work, what areas needed special attention, how inter-branch transactions were to be identified, or when you needed their reports. Each firm sent you a signed audit report on its branch in due course. You have filed all three, read none of the reasoning behind them, asked no questions, and drafted your report stating the division of responsibility and the magnitude of the divided portion.

items.stem: What is missing from the Basis for Opinion section?

options.text: A reference to the section of the auditor's report that describes the auditor's responsibilities under the Standards on Auditing, and a statement that the auditor is independent of the entity in accordance with the relevant ethical requirements and has fulfilled his other ethical responsibilities, referring to the Code of Ethics issued by ICAI
options.why: The Basis for Opinion section carries four things and the draft has two. It states that the audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing, refers to the section of the report describing the auditor's responsibilities under those standards, includes a statement that the auditor is independent of the entity and has fulfilled his other ethical responsibilities — referring to the Code of Ethics issued by ICAI — and states whether the auditor believes the evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate.

options.text: A description of the audit procedures performed on each material account balance, so that the reader can judge whether the evidence really was sufficient
options.misconception: turns the basis section into an account of the audit programme, which no standard requires
options.why: The report says whether the auditor believes the evidence is sufficient and appropriate; it does not set out the evidence. Where a matter of most significance needs describing, that is done in the Key Audit Matters section and only where SA 701 applies.

options.text: Nothing — the two sentences present are the whole of what the standard asks for under that heading
options.misconception: keeps the two elements everyone remembers and drops the cross-reference and the independence statement
options.why: The independence statement is the part a reader cannot get anywhere else in the report, and it is required in every report rather than only where independence has been in question. The section is short, and it is not two sentences short.

options.text: The key audit matters, which belong inside the Basis for Opinion section because they are the matters the opinion actually rests on
options.misconception: puts key audit matters inside the basis section, when SA 701 gives them a section of their own
options.why: Key audit matters have their own section, later in the report, and the standard states in terms that the auditor does not provide a separate opinion on them. Folding them into the basis would read as though the opinion turned on those matters alone.

citation.ref: the Basis for Opinion section, directly following the Opinion section

items.scenario: A draft auditor's report on a company's financial statements carries an Opinion section and then a Basis for Opinion section which reads, in full, "We conducted our audit in accordance with the Standards on Auditing. We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion." Nothing else appears under that heading.

items.stem: What does SA 701 require?

options.text: Keep the section and state under the Key Audit Matters heading that the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate in the report
options.why: The section stays. Where the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate, the report carries a Key Audit Matters heading and says so in terms. The point is that a reader of a listed company's report knows the section is required, so its absence would read as an omission and its presence with that sentence is a positive statement the auditor is standing behind.
keywords: no key audit matters to communicate

options.text: Leave the section out — a heading with nothing under it conveys less than silence, and the requirement is to communicate matters, not to announce their absence
options.misconception: reads the requirement as conditional on there being something to say
options.why: Silence and a statement look identical to a reader and mean opposite things. One of them says the auditor considered the question and reached an answer; the other could equally mean the section was forgotten.

options.text: Move the statement into the Basis for Opinion section, which is where the report explains what the opinion rests on
options.misconception: relocates a required section into another, when each carries its own heading
options.why: The Basis for Opinion section has its own four elements and this is not among them. A reader looking for the Key Audit Matters heading in a listed company's report would not find it.

options.text: Determine a key audit matter from the largest balance in the financial statements so that the section is not empty
options.misconception: fills the section by size, when the determination runs on matters that required significant auditor attention
options.why: A balance being large is not a reason it required significant auditor attention. Manufacturing a matter tells the reader that something was of most significance in the audit when nothing was, which misdescribes the audit.

citation.ref: the presentation where the auditor has determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate

items.scenario: A listed company has had an uneventful year. There are no higher assessed risks of material misstatement, no significant management judgements, no unusual transactions and no going concern question. Working through the matters communicated with those charged with governance, you conclude honestly that none of them was of most significance in the audit. The partner proposes to leave the Key Audit Matters heading out of the report altogether, on the ground that an empty heading looks like an oversight.

items.stem: Which of the two may be left out of the Key Audit Matters section?

options.text: Both, since describing either would damage the company and the auditor is not required to harm the entity he audits
options.misconception: reads commercial harm as a general licence to omit, when the second exception is extremely rare and closed once the entity has itself disclosed
options.why: Damage to the entity is the beginning of the enquiry, not the end. The exception asks whether the adverse consequences would outweigh the public interest benefits, and a company that has already told the stock exchange has answered that itself.

options.text: Neither — a matter determined to be a key audit matter is described in the report without exception, which is what makes the section reliable
options.misconception: denies the two exceptions the standard states in the same requirement
options.why: The exceptions are written into the requirement. The first exists because an auditor cannot be asked to break a statute in order to comply with a standard, and the second exists for the extremely rare case where publication would do more harm than good.

options.text: Only the regulatory investigation, because law precludes public disclosure about the matter; the customer dispute must be described, because the extremely rare adverse-consequences exception does not apply where the entity has itself publicly disclosed information about the matter
options.why: SA 701 describes every key audit matter in the report unless one of two things is true. Either law or regulation precludes public disclosure about the matter, which the governing statute here does; or, in extremely rare circumstances, the auditor determines that the adverse consequences of communicating would reasonably be expected to outweigh the public interest benefits — and that second exception is expressly unavailable where the entity has publicly disclosed information about the matter, which this stock exchange filing did.

options.text: Only the customer dispute — commercial damage is the plainer case for omission, while a regulator's investigation is a matter of public interest that must be described
options.misconception: inverts the two exceptions, omitting the one the standard closes and describing the one law forbids
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both. The statute settles the investigation without any weighing at all, and the company's own filing removes the dispute from the only exception that could have covered it.

citation.ref: para 14

items.scenario: Two matters in a listed company's audit have been determined to be key audit matters. The first is a confidential regulatory investigation into the company, which the governing statute forbids anybody from disclosing publicly until it concludes. The second is a dispute with the company's largest customer; management argues that any public mention would wreck the renegotiation now under way, though the company itself has already filed a disclosure with the stock exchange naming the customer and the amount at stake.

items.stem: What does SA 706 require of the paragraph?

options.text: Only a heading — the wording inside is the auditor's own, and pointing at the note is a courtesy to the reader rather than a requirement
options.misconception: treats the reference to the disclosure as optional, when the standard requires the paragraph to point at where the matter is fully described
options.why: The reference is what keeps the paragraph tied to the financial statements. Without it the auditor is telling the reader about something the reader cannot go and read, which is the opposite of drawing attention to a disclosure.

options.text: The placement is right — the Basis for Opinion section is where a matter of this importance belongs, so that the reader meets it immediately after the opinion
options.misconception: puts the paragraph inside another required section, when the standard asks for a separate section of its own
options.why: The Basis for Opinion section has its own contents and a fire is none of them. Burying an emphasis inside it also removes the heading a reader scans for.

options.text: The paragraph is right in substance, and the auditor's own doubt about recoverability is exactly what an Emphasis of Matter paragraph exists to convey
options.misconception: uses the paragraph to introduce the auditor's own view, when it refers only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements
options.why: The paragraph points at the entity's disclosure and adds nothing to it. A doubt about recoverability that the financial statements do not carry is either a matter for the opinion or a matter to be disclosed by the entity, and in neither case does it belong in an emphasis.

options.text: A separate section with a heading that includes the term "Emphasis of Matter"; a clear reference to the matter being emphasised and to where the relevant disclosures that fully describe it can be found in the financial statements, referring only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements; and an indication that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter
options.why: SA 706 states three things. The paragraph goes in a separate section of the report under a heading that includes the term Emphasis of Matter. It carries a clear reference to the matter and to where the relevant disclosures fully describing it can be found, and it refers only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements. And it indicates that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter emphasised, without which a reader cannot tell the paragraph from a qualification.

citation.ref: the requirements when the auditor includes an Emphasis of Matter paragraph — separate section with an appropriate heading, clear reference to the matter and to the relevant disclosures, and an indication that the opinion is not modified

items.scenario: A fire destroyed a company's Nashik plant after the year end. It is fully and correctly disclosed in note 34, no modification of the opinion is required as a result of it, and SA 701 does not apply to this audit. You have decided an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is proper. The draft puts a single sentence inside the Basis for Opinion section, reading, "Attention is drawn to the fire at the Nashik plant, which in our view casts doubt on the recoverability of the related insurance claim." There is no reference to note 34 and nothing about the opinion.

items.stem: What does section 141 require?

options.text: The firm vacates the office of auditor now — a person whose relative is in the employment of the company as a director or key managerial personnel is disqualified, one disqualified partner disqualifies the firm, and a disqualification incurred after appointment obliges the auditor to vacate, the vacancy so caused being deemed a casual vacancy
options.why: Two provisions run together. A person whose relative is a director or is in the employment of the company as a director or key managerial personnel is not eligible for appointment as auditor, and where a firm is appointed the disqualification of any partner disqualifies the firm. Section 141 then deals with the disqualification arising later: where a person appointed as auditor incurs any of the disqualifications after his appointment, he shall vacate his office and such vacation shall be deemed to be a casual vacancy in the office of the auditor.

options.text: The engagement partner steps aside and the second partner signs, the disqualification attaching to the individual rather than to the firm
options.misconception: builds a wall inside the firm, when the statute disqualifies the firm on any partner's disqualification
options.why: Where a firm is appointed as auditor, the disqualification of a partner is the firm's disqualification. Moving the signature changes who holds the pen and not who is appointed.

options.text: Nothing happens this year — the eligibility tests are applied on the date of appointment, and a fact arising afterwards is dealt with by not seeking reappointment
options.misconception: reads section 141 as a test applied once, when the section deals expressly with a disqualification incurred after appointment
options.why: The section has a sub-section written for exactly this sequence. If eligibility were tested only at appointment, an auditor could become as interested as he liked the day after and still sign the report.

options.text: The firm may continue for the remainder of the year if the audit committee records that it is satisfied with the firm's independence
options.misconception: lets a governance body approve past a statutory disqualification
options.why: The audit committee recommends and oversees; it cannot make an ineligible person eligible. The statute names the disqualifications and no committee is given a power to waive them.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(f) read with Section 141(3) proviso on firms and Section 141(4)

items.scenario: A firm is appointed auditor of a company in August and is clean on every test on that date. In January the engagement partner's brother is appointed chief financial officer of the same company and is designated as its key managerial personnel. The firm proposes to complete the year's audit and simply not offer itself for reappointment, on the footing that the disqualification tests in section 141 are applied as at the date of appointment. A second partner offers to sign the report instead, having no relative anywhere near the company.

items.stem: What must the report state?

options.text: Both, but they belong in the report under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order rather than in the auditor's report under section 143
options.misconception: moves two statutory statements from the section that requires them into an Order that does not
options.why: The Order adds matters to the auditor's report; it does not take any away. These two are section 143(3) clauses and are answered in the auditor's report itself.

options.text: Both of the omitted matters — whether proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit have been received from the branches not visited by him, and whether the report on the accounts of each branch office audited by a person other than the company's auditor has been sent to him and the manner in which he has dealt with it in preparing his report
options.why: Section 143(3) asks its own list of questions and two of them are about branches. The books-of-account clause continues into whether proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit have been received from the branches not visited by him, and a separate clause asks whether the report on the accounts of any branch office audited under section 143(8) by a person other than the company's auditor has been sent to him and the manner in which he has dealt with it in preparing his report.
keywords: proper returns adequate for the purposes of his audit
the manner in which he has dealt with it

options.text: Only the branch returns statement; what passed between the company's auditor and a branch auditor is a professional matter between the two of them
options.misconception: keeps the clause about returns and drops the clause about the branch auditor's report, which the section states separately
options.why: The section asks in terms whether the branch auditor's report reached him and how he dealt with it, which is precisely the reader's interest — the principal auditor's opinion covers the whole company including branches he never saw.

options.text: Neither — those statements are required only where the auditor has something adverse to say about a branch, and here he has not
options.misconception: reads the section 143(3) matters as exception reporting, when each is answered expressly in every report
options.why: They are statements, not exceptions. A reader checks the answers as given, and a blank where an answer should be tells him nothing about whether the question was even asked.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(b) and Section 143(3)(c), read with Section 143(8)

items.scenario: A company has eleven branch offices. You visited two of them. Four branches were audited under section 143(8) by other chartered accountants, whose reports reached you before you signed. Your draft report states that proper books of account as required by law have been kept by the company so far as appears from your examination of those books, and stops there. You have left out any mention of the branches you did not visit and any mention of the branch auditors' reports, on the footing that the branch auditors answer for their own work and any reader may read their reports for himself.

items.stem: Which of the three breach section 144?

options.text: The first and the second — for a firm the section reaches services rendered through any entity in which the firm or any partner has significant influence or control and through any entity whose name, trade mark or brand is used by the firm or any of its partners, and the prohibition covers services to the holding company as well as to the company
options.why: The Explanation to section 144 defines rendering services directly or indirectly, and for a firm it reaches services rendered by itself, by any of its partners, by its parent, subsidiary or associate entity, by any entity in which the firm or any partner of the firm has significant influence or control, and by any entity whose name or trade mark or brand is used by the firm or any of its partners. Design and implementation of a financial information system and actuarial services are both on the prohibited list, and the list applies to the company, its holding company and its subsidiary company alike.

options.text: Only the second — a separately registered foreign entity is a separate person, however similar its name, and control is the only connection the section recognises
options.misconception: reads the brand limb out of the Explanation, leaving a network that shares a name outside the section
options.why: The Explanation names the shared name, trade mark or brand as a connection in its own right, precisely because a network can be built without any shareholding at all. Ignoring that limb leaves the easiest arrangement untouched.

options.text: None — the prohibition binds the appointed auditor, and neither the brand-sharing entity nor the controlled associate is the appointed auditor of this company
options.misconception: confines the section to the appointed auditor, when the Explanation exists to reach services rendered indirectly
options.why: If the section stopped at the appointed auditor it would be answered by incorporating a second entity. The Explanation was written to say who else counts, and both of these entities are inside it.

options.text: All three — any service rendered to an audit client by anyone connected with the auditor is prohibited once the audit is held
options.misconception: reads the prohibition as covering every service, when the section bars a named list and routes the rest through approval
options.why: The section bars nine categories and says the auditor may provide such other services as are approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee. Representation before a tax authority is not on the list and it had the approval the section contemplates.

citation.ref: the Explanation to Section 144 on services rendered directly or indirectly in the case of a firm, read with the prohibited list and its extension to the holding company and the subsidiary company

items.scenario: A firm is the statutory auditor of a company. During the year three things happen. An entity registered in another country, which is not a partner of the Indian firm but trades under the same brand name that the firm and its partners use, designs and implements the company's new financial information system. An entity in which the audit firm holds control provides actuarial services to the company's holding company. And a partner of the firm, in his personal capacity, appears for the company before the goods and services tax appellate authority, an engagement the audit committee approved in advance.

items.stem: Who appoints the first auditor now, and how long does the appointee hold office?

options.text: The members, at an extraordinary general meeting, the Board's own window having passed — and the appointee holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting, not for a term of five years
options.why: Section 139(7) sets a cascade for a government company and each step opens only when the one before it fails. The Comptroller and Auditor-General appoints first; on his failure the Board appoints within its own window; on the Board's failure the company informs the members, who appoint the first auditor at an extraordinary general meeting. Whoever makes the appointment, the first auditor holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting, which is what makes him the first auditor rather than an auditor with a term.

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor-General, whose power over a government company's audit cannot lapse whatever period the section names
options.misconception: treats the constitutional auditor's role as making the statutory period ornamental
options.why: The Comptroller and Auditor-General's powers over a government company are wide and this particular one is time-bound. The section says what happens if he does not appoint within the period, which it would not need to say if the power never lapsed.

options.text: The Board, whose power revives once the Comptroller and Auditor-General has failed and is not limited by any period
options.misconception: keeps a lapsed power alive by reading the Board's window as open-ended
options.why: The Board's power is the second step of a cascade and it carries its own period. Reading that period away would delete the members' step entirely, and the section would then have no way of ever producing an auditor if the Board did nothing.

options.text: The members, and the appointee holds office for five years, subject to ratification by the members at each annual general meeting
options.misconception: gives the first auditor the five-year term of a subsequent auditor and revives a ratification requirement that has been omitted from the Act
options.why: The first auditor's office ends at the conclusion of the first annual general meeting, which is where the ordinary appointment machinery takes over. The requirement of annual ratification was omitted from the Act and is no part of the answer either way.

citation.ref: Section 139(7), read with Section 139(6)

items.scenario: A government company within the meaning of section 2(45) is registered on 1 April. The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India does not appoint a first auditor within the sixty days the section allows him from the date of registration. The Board then lets its own thirty-day window pass without appointing anybody either. It is now 15 July and the company still has no auditor. The company secretary advises the Board that on the Comptroller and Auditor-General's failure the power simply reverts to the Board with no time limit on it, and that whoever is appointed will hold office for five years like any other auditor.

items.stem: What does clause 3(i) require the auditor to report?

options.text: That the company is not maintaining proper records showing full particulars, including quantitative details and situation, of Property, Plant and Equipment, nor proper records of intangible assets; that Property, Plant and Equipment have not been physically verified by the management at reasonable intervals; and that proceedings are pending against the company for holding benami property, together with whether the company has appropriately disclosed the details in its financial statements
options.why: Clause 3(i) is a set of separate questions and three of them are answered badly here. It asks whether the company is maintaining proper records showing full particulars, including quantitative details and situation, of Property, Plant and Equipment, and proper records of intangible assets. It asks whether those assets have been physically verified by the management at reasonable intervals. And it asks whether any proceedings have been initiated or are pending against the company for holding any benami property, and if so whether the company has appropriately disclosed the details in its financial statements.

options.text: Nothing — the title deeds are all in the company's name and there was no revaluation during the year, so the clause is answered clean
options.misconception: answers the two sub-clauses the auditor remembers and leaves the records, the verification and the benami sub-clauses unread
options.why: Title deeds and revaluation are two sub-clauses of five. A clean answer on those says nothing about whether the company can tell anybody what assets it owns or where they are.

options.text: The record-keeping and verification failures, but not the benami proceedings, which are a legal matter for the company's own disclosure and not for the auditor to raise
options.misconception: hands a named CARO reporting duty to the company's disclosure and off the auditor's report
options.why: The sub-clause asks the auditor two things about the proceedings — that they exist, and whether the company has appropriately disclosed the details. The second question only makes sense because the first is his to report.

options.text: Only the physical verification point, the maintenance of registers being a matter of internal record-keeping and the benami notice being sub judice
options.misconception: reduces three reportable findings to one, on grounds the clause does not recognise
options.why: The clause asks about the records in terms, and it asks about proceedings that have been initiated or are pending — which is what a pending proceeding is. Neither is excused by being internal or by being before an authority.

citation.ref: Clause 3(i)(a), Clause 3(i)(b) and Clause 3(i)(e)

items.scenario: A company's fixed asset register shows only the total cost of each class of plant. It carries no quantitative details and no situation, and the company's intangible assets appear in no register at all. Property, plant and equipment have not been physically verified by anybody for four years. The Initiating Officer under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 has issued a notice to the company in respect of a warehouse and those proceedings are pending; the notes to the accounts say nothing about them. Every title deed is in the company's own name and there was no revaluation during the year.

items.stem: What does clause 3(ii) require?

options.text: Report under clause 3(ii)(a) on whether physical verification was conducted at reasonable intervals by the management and whether, in the auditor's opinion, the coverage and procedure of such verification is appropriate — the part coverage and the walk-through both speak to that — and report that discrepancies of 10% or more in the aggregate for a class of inventory were noticed and how they were dealt with in the books of account; clause 3(ii)(b) does not arise, no working capital limits having been sanctioned
options.why: Clause 3(ii)(a) asks three things: whether physical verification of inventory has been conducted at reasonable intervals by the management, whether in the opinion of the auditor the coverage and procedure of such verification is appropriate, and whether any discrepancies of 10% or more in the aggregate for each class of inventory were noticed and if so whether they have been properly dealt with in the books of account. Clause 3(ii)(b) is triggered only where the company has been sanctioned working capital limits in excess of five crore rupees on the security of current assets, and none were.
keywords: properly dealt with in the books of account

options.text: Report under clause 3(ii)(b) as well, since the sub-clause applies to every company that finances inventory, whether or not limits were sanctioned
options.misconception: applies the quarterly-returns sub-clause to a company with no sanctioned working capital limits against current assets
options.why: That sub-clause has its own trigger — working capital limits in excess of five crore rupees sanctioned at any point in the year on the basis of security of current assets. With no limits there are no quarterly returns to compare with anything.

options.text: Nothing at all — the discrepancy was written off before the year end, so the books are right and the accounts carry no misstatement
options.misconception: reads a disclosure clause as though it asked whether the accounts are wrong
options.why: Correcting the books is the second half of the sub-clause, not an escape from it. The clause asks whether the discrepancy was noticed and how it was dealt with, and a write-off is the answer to the second question rather than a reason to skip the first.

options.text: Report the discrepancy only — how much of the inventory management chose to count and by what method are management's own arrangements, on which the auditor expresses no view
options.misconception: drops the auditor's own opinion on coverage and procedure, which the sub-clause asks for by name
options.why: The sub-clause says in terms, in the opinion of the auditor. Coverage of sixty-two per cent and an estimate in place of a count for work in progress is exactly the fact pattern that question exists to surface.

citation.ref: Clause 3(ii)(a), read with Clause 3(ii)(b)

items.scenario: A company counts its inventory once a year, on 31 March. This year management's team counted only the two largest of its five warehouses, which hold sixty-two per cent of the value, and used a walk-through estimate rather than a count for work in progress. In one of the warehouses counted, the shortfall in a class of raw material was fourteen per cent of that class in the aggregate; the shortfall was written off in the books before the year end. The company has never been sanctioned working capital limits by any bank or financial institution.

items.stem: What does clause 3(ix) require?

options.text: Only the pledge, since it is the single arrangement on which any default has actually occurred
options.misconception: uses default as the trigger for sub-clauses whose triggers are the transaction itself
options.why: The short-term-for-long-term sub-clause and the subsidiary-obligation sub-clause are triggered by the utilisation and by the taking of the funds. Default appears only inside the pledge sub-clause, as an extra question once a pledge is reported.

options.text: Three separate reports — that funds raised on short term basis have been utilised for long term purposes, with the nature and amount; that funds were taken to meet the obligations of its subsidiaries, with the nature of the transaction and the amount; and that a loan was raised on the pledge of securities held in a joint venture, with details and with the default in repayment of that loan
options.why: Clause 3(ix) is six questions and the company has answered the first three cleanly and the last three badly. A cash credit facility repayable on demand spent on a warehouse is funds raised on short term basis have been utilised for long term purposes, and the nature and amount are to be indicated. The borrowing to pay the subsidiary's instalment is funds taken to meet the obligations of its subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures. And the sub-clause on a loan raised on the pledge of securities held in its subsidiaries, joint ventures or associate companies asks for details and asks separately whether the company has defaulted in repayment of such loans.
