options.text: Nothing — there was no default on any borrowing of the company's own, it is not a wilful defaulter, and every term loan went where it was meant to go
options.misconception: answers the first three sub-clauses of the clause and treats them as the whole of it
options.why: Those are three sub-clauses and there are six. The three the company fails are about where the money came from and what it was pledged against, which no amount of punctual repayment touches.

options.text: All three, and the auditor must in addition report the company as a wilful defaulter, two missed instalments being a default deliberately made
options.misconception: has the auditor make a declaration the clause asks him only to report if a lender has made it
options.why: The sub-clause asks whether the company is a declared wilful defaulter by any bank or financial institution or other lender. The declaration is theirs to make and the auditor's to report; he does not reach the conclusion himself from missed instalments.

citation.ref: Clause 3(ix)(d), Clause 3(ix)(e) and Clause 3(ix)(f)

items.scenario: During the year a company draws ₹12 crore on its cash credit facility, repayable on demand, and builds a new warehouse with it. It borrows ₹8 crore from a non-banking finance company expressly to pay an instalment falling due on its subsidiary's loan. And it raises a ₹20 crore loan by pledging the shares it holds in its joint venture, and has since missed two instalments on that loan. On its own term loans the company has never defaulted, every rupee was spent on the purpose for which it was raised, and it is not a declared wilful defaulter.

items.stem: Where does Clause 7 of Part I of the First Schedule bite?

options.text: On all three, a letterhead being a professional document and everything printed on it a statement about the member
options.misconception: treats every fact on a letterhead as an advertisement, when the objection is to attainments and to the practice date rather than to the firms' names
options.why: The clause reads what is being said. Firm names identify where the member practises; a date of establishment is a claim of standing, which is why one is permitted and the other is not.

options.text: On none — the member did not write the offer document and a letterhead is not published to the world at large
options.misconception: excuses the member from a publication he is named in, when the Council places on him the duty to see that it does not advertise his attainments
options.why: The Council's position is that the member concerned has to take the necessary steps. It is his name and his attainments in the document, and a member who lets them appear has not taken them.

options.text: On the offer document and on the practice date — a description of the member's expertise and specialisation in a company's offer document is misconduct and he must take steps to see that it does not appear, and a member is not permitted to specify the date of setting up of practice on a letterhead; naming all three firms on his personal letterhead is permitted
options.why: The Council has stated that where a company in which a chartered accountant in practice is a director issues a prospectus or announcement describing his expertise, specialisation and knowledge in a field, it is misconduct, and the member has to take the necessary steps to ensure that it does not advertise his professional attainments. Separately, a member is not permitted to specify the date of setting up of practice or establishment of the firm on letterheads. There is no prohibition on printing the names of all the firms in which a member holding a certificate of practice is a partner on his personal letterhead.
keywords: date of setting up of practice

options.text: On the offer document alone — a letterhead advertises nothing once it carries no description of services
options.misconception: reads the clause as reaching only descriptions of services, when it separately restrains claims a member may not print
options.why: The practice date describes no service and still says something about the member's attainments. That is why the position on letterheads is stated separately from the position on write-ups describing services.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 7, read with the Council's decisions on a prospectus of a company in which a member is a director and on what a letterhead may carry

items.scenario: CA Bhatt holds a certificate of practice and is a partner in three firms. He is also a director of a listed company, and that company's offer document names him as a director and sets out his areas of specialisation and his standing in the profession. His own personal letterhead names all three firms in which he is a partner. Beneath the names, the letterhead adds the line "In practice since 1998".

items.stem: Where does Clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule bite?

options.text: On CA P — failing to complete the work and submit the report in time, so that the company could not meet its statutory requirement, is a failure to exercise due diligence; CA Q's slip is one of the minor errors and lapses which do not amount to gross negligence and do not constitute professional misconduct
options.why: The clause catches a member who does not exercise due diligence or is grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties, and delivering late so that the client cannot comply with a statute is a want of due diligence even where the work itself was sound. At the other end, negligence per se would not amount to gross negligence in the case of minor errors and lapses, which do not constitute professional misconduct — the Council brings such matters to members' attention rather than referring them.

options.text: On both — the clause reaches negligence of every degree, and each member fell short of the care his client was entitled to
options.misconception: flattens a clause that distinguishes minor lapses from gross negligence into a single standard
options.why: The expression negligence covers a wide field and extends from the frontiers of fraud to collateral minor negligence. Professional misconduct occupies the serious end of it, and a ₹4,000 slip the member found and fixed himself is at the other end.

options.text: On CA Q alone — an arithmetical error is a failure of care, while a missed deadline is a matter of the engagement letter rather than of professional conduct
options.misconception: sends a want of due diligence into the contract and treats a self-corrected slip as the misconduct
options.why: It is the wrong way round. A slip the member caught himself is evidence that his review worked, and delay that costs the client its statutory compliance is the classic instance of the clause.

options.text: On neither — no set of accounts was misstated in either case, so nobody was misled and there is nothing for the clause to punish
options.misconception: measures the clause by whether the financial statements ended up wrong, when it asks whether the member brought reasonable skill, care and caution to his duties
options.why: The test is the skill, care and caution a reasonably competent, careful and cautious auditor would use. A report that arrives too late to be used has failed the client whatever the accounts said.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 7

items.scenario: Two members are complained against. CA P accepted a company audit, did not complete his work and did not submit his audit report in time, so the company could not comply with the statutory requirement that depended on it; nothing he did do is criticised as wrong. CA Q, auditing a manufacturer, made an arithmetical slip in one schedule which overstated a note by ₹4,000; he found it himself and corrected it before the report was signed, and no other part of his file is criticised.

items.stem: Where does Clause 9 leave him?

options.text: Not guilty — Clause 9 applies where an auditor is appointed in place of a retiring auditor at an annual general meeting, and a vacancy arising mid-year is outside it
options.misconception: narrows the clause to one route of appointment, when the duty to ascertain runs on any appointment as auditor of a company
options.why: The clause speaks of accepting an appointment as auditor of a company, with no route excluded. The Council's own guidance sets out the checks for a first auditor, for an appointment after a resignation or removal, and for a joint auditor not reappointed.

options.text: Not guilty — a casual vacancy caused by a resignation is filled by the Board alone, so there were no general meeting records for him to inspect in the first place
options.misconception: stops at the Board's power to fill a casual vacancy, when an appointment to fill a vacancy caused by resignation must also be approved by the company at a general meeting
options.why: The Board fills the vacancy, and where the vacancy arose from a resignation the appointment must also be approved by the company in general meeting. Those are precisely the records the incoming auditor should have seen and was refused.

options.text: Guilty — to ascertain means to find out for certain, so a certificate from the management is not sufficient; the incoming auditor verifies the company's relevant records himself, and where the company will not allow that verification he should not accept the audit assignment
options.why: The Council has spelt out what the clause asks of an incoming auditor. The word ascertain means to find out for certain, so it would not be sufficient for the incoming auditor to accept a certificate from the management that the provisions have been complied with; he must verify the relevant records of the company. If the company is not willing to allow him to verify those records, the incoming auditor should not accept the audit assignment. Iyer did the opposite of both.
keywords: should not accept the audit assignment

options.text: Not guilty — a written certificate from the company is exactly the ascertainment from the company that the clause calls for, and he obtained it before accepting
options.misconception: reads ascertaining from the company as receiving the company's own assurance, when the Council requires verification of the records
options.why: The clause exists because the company is the party whose compliance is in question. Taking its word for it would make the duty circular, which is why the Council put the word ascertain under a microscope.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 9, read with the Council's guidelines on the records an incoming auditor is to verify and with Section 139(8) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: CA Iyer is offered the audit of a company whose previous auditor resigned in the middle of the year. He asks the company whether the appointment provisions have been complied with, and the managing director hands him a signed certificate saying that all the requirements of sections 139 and 140 have been duly complied with. Iyer then asks to see the board minutes and the notice and resolution of the general meeting. The company refuses, saying the certificate should be enough for anybody. Iyer accepts the appointment.

items.stem: What do section 138 and Rule 13 say?

options.text: Covered, and the general manager may be appointed, and as internal auditor he settles the scope, functioning and periodicity of the internal audit himself
options.misconception: leaves the scope with the internal auditor, when the Audit Committee or the Board formulates it in consultation with him
options.why: Consultation is not delegation. An internal auditor who sets his own scope decides which parts of the company will never be looked at, which is the one decision the rule takes away from him.

options.text: Not covered — the tests for an unlisted public company are paid-up share capital and turnover, and this company is under both
options.misconception: reads the unlisted public company criteria as two, when borrowings and deposits stand beside capital and turnover
options.why: There are four criteria and any one of them brings the company in. Deposits sit there because a company holding public money has depositors with an interest in its controls whatever its size on the other measures.

options.text: Covered, but the appointment is invalid — an internal auditor must be a chartered accountant in practice and must not be an employee of the company he audits internally
options.misconception: imports the independence conditions of a statutory audit into an office the rule expressly opens to employees and to members not in practice
options.why: The rule says the opposite twice over. It names a cost accountant as eligible, it says whether engaged in practice or not, and it says the internal auditor may or may not be an employee of the company.

options.text: The company is covered, because an unlisted public company with outstanding deposits of twenty-five crore rupees or more at any point of time during the preceding financial year is caught by that test alone; the appointment is valid, because the internal auditor may be a chartered accountant or a cost accountant whether engaged in practice or not and may or may not be an employee of the company; but the Audit Committee or the Board formulates the scope and periodicity, in consultation with him
options.why: An unlisted public company is tested on four criteria joined by "or", and outstanding deposits of twenty-five crore rupees or more at any point of time during the preceding financial year is one of them, so thirty-one crore brings the company in whatever capital and turnover do. The internal auditor shall either be a chartered accountant or a cost accountant, whether engaged in practice or not, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board, and he may or may not be an employee of the company. The Audit Committee of the company or the Board shall, in consultation with the Internal Auditor, formulate the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology for conducting the internal audit.
keywords: whether engaged in practice or not
may or may not be an employee

citation.ref: Section 138 read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 — the unlisted public company criteria including outstanding deposits, who may be appointed as internal auditor, and the formulation of the scope by the Audit Committee or the Board

items.scenario: An unlisted public company has paid-up share capital of twelve crore rupees, turnover of ninety crore rupees, no borrowings at all from banks or public financial institutions, and outstanding deposits of thirty-one crore rupees at one point during the preceding financial year. It proposes to appoint its own general manager (finance) as internal auditor. He is a cost accountant, he is an employee of the company, and he is not in practice. The managing director says internal audit does not apply because capital and turnover are both under the limits, and that in any event an employee cannot be an internal auditor. He adds that if it does apply, the general manager will settle the scope and periodicity himself.

items.stem: Where do these three sit under SA 220 (Revised)?

options.text: Only the shareholding is his — the competence of the team is a staffing decision for whoever allocates people, and continuance was settled when the engagement was accepted
options.misconception: drops the assignment of engagement teams from the engagement partner's list and treats continuance as a one-off decision
options.why: The assignment of engagement teams is one of the heads the standard names, and continuance is a conclusion revisited rather than a door that shuts at acceptance. A partner who cannot say who on his team can audit a derivative book has not discharged either.

options.text: The engagement partner's responsibility is the review of the audit documentation before the report is issued, so all three are premature
options.misconception: confines the engagement partner to engagement performance, which is one head among several
options.why: Review is the last of the partner's responsibilities, not the whole of them. By the time the file reaches him, an independence breach and an under-skilled team have already shaped every working paper he is reading.

options.text: All three are the engagement partner's own responsibility — he identifies the threat to independence that safeguards may not be able to eliminate or reduce to an acceptable level and reports it to the relevant persons within the firm so that the activity or interest creating it can be eliminated or the firm can withdraw where withdrawal is legally permitted; he satisfies himself that the conclusions reached on acceptance and continuance of the client relationship are appropriate; and he ensures that the engagement team and any auditor's expert who is not part of the team collectively have the appropriate competence and capabilities to perform the engagement
options.why: The standard describes the engagement partner's responsibilities under named heads, and only one of them is engagement performance. On ethics, the partner identifies a threat to independence and reports it to the relevant persons within the firm, so the activity or interest can be eliminated or the firm can withdraw where legally permitted. On acceptance and continuance, the conclusions reached about the client relationship are his to be satisfied about, not the risk partner's alone. And on the assignment of the engagement team, he ensures the team together with any auditor's expert outside it collectively have the appropriate competence and capabilities for the work.

options.text: All three belong to the firm's system of quality control, and the engagement partner is entitled to rely on that system, so nothing here is for him to do
options.misconception: treats the firm's system of quality control as discharging the engagement partner's own engagement-level responsibilities
options.why: An engagement team may rely on the firm's system, but that reliance ends the moment information in front of the team says otherwise — and a shareholding, a missing competence and an unresolved integrity doubt are exactly such information. The system sets the policy; the partner applies it to this engagement.

citation.ref: the engagement partner's responsibilities for relevant ethical requirements, for acceptance and continuance of the client relationship, and for the assignment of engagement teams

items.scenario: Three things surface in the third week of an audit. A senior on the engagement team has bought shares in the client, and the engagement partner cannot see any safeguard that would reduce the threat. The client has opened a derivative book during the year and nobody on the team, and no expert engaged by the firm, has ever audited one. And the doubts about the promoter's integrity that were raised when the firm decided to continue the relationship were never taken any further. The manager's view is that all three belong to the firm's risk partner, and that the engagement partner's own responsibility begins with the review of the file at the end.

items.stem: What does SQC 1 require on each of the three?

options.text: Nothing turns on any of the three because the firm audits no listed entity, SQC 1's requirements on independence and leadership applying to firms with listed clients
options.misconception: reads a listed-entity scope into SQC 1, which applies to the firm in respect of all its assurance and related services engagements
options.why: SQC 1 applies to the firm across all its audits and reviews of historical financial information and its other assurance and related services engagements. Only the engagement quality control review carries a listed-entity trigger, and that is one part of one element.

options.text: Only the independence confirmation is a requirement — how a firm balances deadlines against quality is a matter of its own commercial judgement, and who the engagement partner is concerns the firm and not the client
options.misconception: treats the leadership and human resources elements as aspiration rather than requirement
options.why: All six elements are requirements in the same sense. The leadership element exists precisely because a firm's own commercial judgement is the pressure it has to be insulated from, and the client is told who the engagement partner is so that the person answerable is known outside the firm as well as inside it.

options.text: A three-yearly confirmation from partners is enough, staff being covered by the partners' supervision, and the rest is a matter for the engagement quality control reviewer
options.misconception: shortens the annual confirmation and narrows it to partners, and pushes the firm-level elements onto the engagement quality control review
options.why: The confirmation is annual and it reaches all personnel required to be independent. The engagement quality control review sits inside engagement performance and looks at one engagement's judgements; it was never the place where a firm's independence policy or its leadership policy is discharged.

options.text: The firm's policies must be such that commercial considerations do not override the quality of the work performed; written confirmation of compliance with the firm's policies and procedures on independence must be obtained at least annually from all firm personnel required to be independent; and the identity and role of the engagement partner are communicated to the client's management and to those charged with governance
options.why: Each of the three is a stated requirement of a different element. Leadership responsibility means the firm assigns its management responsibilities so that commercial considerations do not override the quality of the work performed — a deadline that beats a quality step is the failure the element was written against. Ethical requirements carry the rule that the firm obtains written confirmation of compliance with its independence policies at least annually, and from all personnel required to be independent, not from partners alone. And human resources carries the requirement that the identity and role of the engagement partner are communicated to the client's key management and to those charged with governance.
keywords: identity and role of the engagement partner

citation.ref: the leadership responsibilities, ethical requirements and human resources elements — commercial considerations not overriding quality, the annual written confirmation of independence from all personnel, and communication of the engagement partner's identity and role to the client

items.scenario: A firm's quality control manual says three things. Where a quality step would cost a reporting deadline the deadline wins, because the managing partner's business plan sets the targets. Written independence confirmations are taken from the partners once every three years and are never taken from staff at all. And the identity of the engagement partner is recorded in the firm's internal allocation sheet but is never told to the client.

items.stem: What follows a qualified peer review report?

options.text: The Quality Review Board issues the certificate, the Peer Review Board's role ending with the appointment of the reviewer
options.misconception: swaps the two bodies, which have different constitutions and different functions
options.why: The Peer Review Board is constituted by the Council of the Institute and runs the peer review process end to end. The Quality Review Board is set up by the Central Government to review the quality of services, recommend to the Council and guide members — it issues no peer review certificate.

options.text: The certificate is issued in every case once the review is complete, the qualification being recorded on the file for the next review to pick up
options.misconception: treats the certificate as an attendance record rather than the outcome of an unqualified report
options.why: A certificate that issued whatever the reviewer found would say nothing. It is the unqualified report that the certificate reports, which is why a qualified one produces a follow-on review instead.

options.text: A peer review certificate is issued only where the reviewer's report is unqualified — on a qualified report the practice unit is informed that the certificate cannot be issued, told the reasons, and given the due date for a follow-on review as decided by the Peer Review Board, which is constituted by the Council of the Institute; the Quality Review Board is a separate body set up by the Central Government
options.why: The outcome turns on the report. Where the peer reviewer issues an unqualified report a peer review certificate is issued. Where the report is qualified the practice unit is informed that the certificate cannot be issued along with the reasons, and is told the due date for conducting a follow-on review as the Board may decide. The body doing this is the Peer Review Board, constituted by the Council of the Institute; the Quality Review Board is set up by the Central Government and works on a risk-based approach through technical reviewers, which is a different mechanism altogether.

options.text: A qualified report means the practice unit's attestation reports for the review period must be withdrawn and reissued
options.misconception: turns a review of the unit's systems into a re-audit of its clients
options.why: The review examines the systems and procedures the practice unit has put in place, not the accounts of any auditee. Nothing in the process reaches back into a report already issued to a client.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — the Peer Review Board, the peer review certificate on an unqualified report, and the follow-on review where the report is qualified

items.scenario: A practice unit has been through a peer review and the reviewer's report is qualified. The managing partner's position is that the review is now over, that the certificate follows as a matter of course because the unit submitted to the process, and that in any event it is the Quality Review Board and not the Peer Review Board that issues it.

items.stem: What do SA 240's risk assessment procedures require beyond the questionnaire?

options.text: The margin movement is a matter for SA 520 alone, to be investigated as an analytical difference and not as a fraud consideration
options.misconception: treats an unexplained analytical result as belonging to one standard only, when SA 240 requires it to be evaluated for fraud risk as well
options.why: The same fluctuation is read twice for two purposes. SA 520 asks whether the difference is explained; SA 240 asks what an unexpected relationship says about the risk of material misstatement due to fraud, and a nine-point margin jump in one division answers both.

options.text: Nothing more on the inquiries — management's own assessment of the risk of fraud is the matter SA 240 puts the question to, and the chief financial officer speaks for management
options.misconception: collapses four risk assessment activities into one inquiry of one officer
options.why: Management's assessment is one topic among several and management is one source among several. Asking only the officer with the most to lose from an answer is the shape of inquiry the standard was written to widen.

options.text: Inquiries of management and of others within the entity; an understanding of how those charged with governance exercise oversight of management's processes for identifying and responding to the risks of fraud and of the internal control management has established to mitigate those risks; and an evaluation of unexpected relationships identified in performing analytical procedures which may indicate a risk of material misstatement due to fraud
options.why: The standard names four risk assessment activities and the questionnaire is a fragment of one. Inquiries run to management and to others within the entity — legal counsel, internal audit, and the people who initiate, process or record the unusual transactions are exactly who is meant. Separately the auditor obtains an understanding of how those charged with governance exercise oversight of management's fraud processes and of the internal control established to mitigate the risks. And unexpected relationships identified in performing analytical procedures are evaluated for what they say about the risk of fraud, which is why the margin jump could not simply be handed back to management.
keywords: those charged with governance exercise oversight

options.text: Those charged with governance need not be approached at the risk assessment stage — they are communicated with later, and only if a fraud is actually identified or suspected
options.misconception: confuses the risk assessment understanding of governance oversight with the later communication of an identified fraud
options.why: Two different requirements sit at two different points. The understanding of how governance exercises oversight is obtained while risks are being assessed; the communication of an identified or suspected fraud comes afterwards and does not replace it.

citation.ref: the risk assessment procedures — inquiries of management and others within the entity, the understanding of how those charged with governance exercise oversight of management's fraud processes, and the evaluation of unexpected relationships identified in performing analytical procedures

items.scenario: The whole of a team's fraud risk assessment is a questionnaire signed by the chief financial officer. The audit committee was asked nothing. The in-house legal counsel, the head of internal audit and the operating staff who process the unusual year-end rebate credits were never approached. And an analytical procedure threw up a nine-point jump in one division's gross margin that was left where it lay, the senior noting that margins are a management matter.

items.stem: What more does SA 260 require for a listed entity?

options.text: The independence communication is required only where the auditor has identified a threat he could not reduce to an acceptable level
options.misconception: makes an unconditional listed-entity requirement conditional on a problem having been found
options.why: The communication happens whether or not a threat was found; its purpose is to let those charged with governance form their own view rather than to report the auditor's. A clean position still has to be shown.

options.text: Oral communication is sufficient throughout provided the audit committee raises no objection, documentation being needed only for written communications
options.misconception: reverses the documentation rule, which exists precisely for the matters communicated orally
options.why: Where a communication is written the auditor retains a copy; where it is oral he records the matter, the date and the persons in the audit documentation. The oral route is the one that needs the note, because nothing else survives it.

options.text: A statement that the engagement team and others in the firm as appropriate, the firm and, where applicable, network firms have complied with relevant ethical requirements regarding independence; all relationships and other matters between the firm, the network firms and the entity that may reasonably be thought to bear on independence, including the total fees charged for audit and non-audit services, allocated to categories that help those charged with governance assess the effect on independence; and the safeguards applied — and where any matter is communicated orally the auditor includes it in the audit documentation with when and to whom it was communicated
options.why: For a listed entity the independence communication is a set of four things, not a sentence. It states the compliance of the engagement team, the firm and the network firms with the relevant ethical requirements on independence; it names all relationships and other matters that may reasonably be thought to bear on independence; it gives the total fees charged for audit and non-audit services by the firm and the network firms, allocated to categories so that those charged with governance can weigh the effect; and it sets out the safeguards applied. Separately, a matter communicated orally goes into the audit documentation together with when and to whom it was communicated, which is why a conversation nobody recorded fails even where its content was right.

options.text: Nothing further — a statement of independence is the requirement, and the fees of network firms are their own commercial affair rather than a matter for this audit committee
options.misconception: treats network firms as outside the independence communication, when the requirement names them expressly
options.why: Network firms are inside the communication for the same reason they are inside the independence rules — what a sister firm bills the client bears on whether the auditor is independent in appearance, and the committee cannot assess that without the figure.

citation.ref: the communication of auditor independence to those charged with governance of a listed entity, and the documentation of matters communicated orally

items.scenario: The auditor of a listed company communicated the planned scope and timing of the audit, and his findings, to the audit committee's chairman over lunch. His file records neither the date of that conversation nor who was present. On independence he handed across one line — that the firm is independent — and nothing about the group's three network firms, which billed the company substantial consulting fees during the year.

items.stem: What does SA 320 require?

options.text: Revise materiality — the trigger includes a change in the auditor's understanding of the entity as a result of performing further audit procedures, not only a change in the entity's results — and select an appropriate benchmark, total cost or net cost being the example given for a public utility programme, profit before tax from continuing operations being the benchmark for a profit-oriented entity and gross profit or total revenues where profit before tax is volatile
options.why: Materiality is revised on new information, on a change in circumstances during the audit, and on a change in the auditor's understanding of the entity as a result of performing further audit procedures. The third trigger is the one at work here: nothing about the undertaking changed, the auditor's grasp of it did. On the benchmark, the factors include the nature of the entity and the items on which the attention of its users tends to be focused, and the worked examples run profit before tax from continuing operations for a profit-oriented entity, gross profit or total revenues where that figure is volatile, total cost or net cost for a public utility programme, and assets where the entity has custody of assets.

options.text: Raise materiality to whatever figure makes the firm's computed sample sizes workable, since the audit cannot be performed at fifty-five thousand rupees
options.misconception: sets materiality from the convenience of the audit rather than from what could influence the decisions of users
options.why: Materiality is a judgement about the users of these financial statements, and sample sizes follow from it rather than the other way round. A figure reverse-engineered from a workload has stopped measuring anything.

options.text: Apply five per cent of total assets, that being the benchmark prescribed for any entity not run for profit
options.misconception: turns the illustrative benchmarks into a prescribed rule and ignores what the users of this entity actually look at
options.why: The standard gives factors and examples, not a table to look a figure up in. Assets are the example where the entity has custody of assets; a water supply scheme funded by a grant is judged on what it costs to run.

options.text: Keep the fifty-five thousand rupee figure — materiality is determined at planning, and a benchmark once chosen is held so that the audit is not designed around its own answer
options.misconception: treats the planning figure and the benchmark as fixed, when the standard names a change in the auditor's understanding as a trigger for revision
options.why: Holding a figure that was built on a misunderstanding is not discipline. The standard asks the auditor to revise on information that would have led him to a different amount initially, and a benchmark that was wrong from the start is exactly that.

citation.ref: the revision of materiality as the audit progresses, read with the factors affecting the identification of an appropriate benchmark and the examples of benchmarks

items.scenario: A manager sets materiality for a municipal water supply undertaking at five per cent of profit before tax. The undertaking is not run for profit; its surplus for the year is eleven lakh rupees, so materiality comes out at fifty-five thousand rupees and every sample size the firm's software computes is unworkable. Half way through the audit he understands for the first time that the undertaking's income is a fixed municipal grant and that what its users and its funders look at is what the scheme costs to run. He proposes to leave materiality where it is, on the ground that it was set at planning and that the benchmark, once chosen, is not revisited.

items.stem: What must the user auditor be satisfied about before using a type 1 or type 2 report?

options.text: The service auditor's professional competence and his independence of the service organisation, and the adequacy of the standards under which the type 1 or type 2 report was issued — and, for a type 2 report, the adequacy of the time period covered by the tests of controls and the time elapsed since they were performed, which here leaves six months of the year untested
options.why: Before a service auditor's report becomes evidence in someone else's audit, the user auditor satisfies himself about the service auditor's professional competence and independence from the service organisation, and about the adequacy of the standards under which the report was issued — an unnamed framework answers neither. Where the report is type 2, he also evaluates the adequacy of the time period covered by the tests of controls and the time elapsed since they were performed. A report stopping on 30 September says nothing about the six months that follow it.
keywords: time period covered by the tests of controls

options.text: That the service organisation has agreed in writing that the user auditor may rely on the report, reliance being a matter of the service organisation's consent
options.misconception: substitutes a permission from the service organisation for the auditor's own evaluation of the report
options.why: Consent is not evidence. Nothing the service organisation agrees to changes whether its auditor was competent, independent, working to adequate standards, or testing the right months.

options.text: Nothing beyond the type of the report — a type 2 report reports on operating effectiveness over a period, and that is what makes it usable
options.misconception: treats the type of the report as the whole test, ignoring who wrote it, under what standards, and over which period
options.why: The type tells you what the report set out to do. Whether it did it turns on the competence and independence of the person who wrote it, the standards he worked to, and whether the period he tested is the period you are auditing.

options.text: That the gap between 30 September and the year end is covered by a written representation from the client's management about the service organisation's controls
options.misconception: uses a representation from the user entity to fill an evidence gap about controls operating elsewhere
options.why: A user entity's management cannot represent about the operation of controls it does not run and cannot see. The gap is closed by tests of controls at the service organisation, by a report covering the period, or by substantive work — not by a sentence in a letter.

citation.ref: the user auditor's evaluation of a type 1 or type 2 report — the service auditor's professional competence and independence, the adequacy of the standards under which the report was issued, and the time period covered by the tests of controls

items.scenario: A service organisation hands your client a type 2 report covering 1 April to 30 September. Your client's year ends on 31 March. The report is signed by a firm you have never heard of and does not say under what standards it was prepared. Your manager plans to rely on it for the whole year because it is a type 2 report and type 2 reports cover operating effectiveness.

items.stem: What does SA 500 require where information used as audit evidence has been prepared using the work of a management's expert?

options.text: Engage an auditor's expert of the firm's own to re-perform the actuarial valuation, an auditor being unable to evaluate work in a field outside his competence
options.misconception: makes a second expert the only route, when the standard asks for an understanding sufficient to evaluate the work
options.why: A second expert is sometimes the right response and it is never the required first step. What the standard asks for is an understanding of the field sufficient to evaluate the work, which is a lower bar than doing the work again.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the actuary is independent, which settles the objectivity question
options.misconception: substitutes management's assertion about the expert for the auditor's own evaluation of him
options.why: Management's view of its own expert is the very thing under examination. A representation may be obtained, but the evaluation of competence, capabilities and objectivity remains the auditor's work.

options.text: Only the appropriateness of the work matters — the expert's relationships and fee sources are the entity's affair, since it is the entity and not the auditor who engaged him
options.misconception: drops objectivity from the three matters the standard names, on the ground that the expert was engaged by the entity
options.why: That the entity engaged him is the reason objectivity is in the list, not the reason it is out of it. A valuation prepared to please the person who pays for it is unreliable however the arithmetic checks.

options.text: Evaluate the competence, capabilities and objectivity of that expert — objectivity is one of the three, and a close family relationship with the finance director together with a dependence on the group's fees goes directly to it — and obtain an understanding of the work of that expert sufficient to evaluate its appropriateness as audit evidence for the relevant assertion
options.why: The standard puts three things in front of the auditor and objectivity is the third of them: he evaluates the competence, capabilities and objectivity of the management's expert. Family relationships with the entity's officers and financial dependence on the entity are the circumstances that erode objectivity, and no amount of technical skill answers them. The second requirement is that the auditor obtains an understanding of the work of that expert — not that he re-performs it, and not that he defers to it, but that he understands it well enough to evaluate whether it is appropriate as audit evidence.

citation.ref: the requirements where information to be used as audit evidence has been prepared using the work of a management's expert — evaluating his competence, capabilities and objectivity and obtaining an understanding of his work

items.scenario: The actuary who valued a company's gratuity and leave encashment liabilities is the finance director's brother-in-law, and roughly four-fifths of his professional income comes from the group. The audit senior says objectivity is beside the point because SA 500 is about the work rather than the person, and that no understanding of the actuary's work is possible in any event since actuarial science is outside the auditor's own field.

items.stem: What does SA 501 have the auditor do here?

options.text: Where information is obtained that raises doubt about the integrity and objectivity of the third party, perform other audit procedures instead of, or in addition to, confirmation — attending, or arranging for another auditor to attend, the third party's physical counting of inventory if practicable; obtaining another auditor's or a service auditor's report on the adequacy of the third party's internal control for ensuring that inventory is properly counted and adequately safeguarded; and inspecting documentation regarding inventory held by third parties
options.why: Confirmation from the custodian is the first route the standard offers, and it is the route that stops working when the custodian is the problem. Where information raises doubt about the integrity and objectivity of the third party, the auditor performs other procedures instead of or in addition to the confirmation, and the standard names them: attending the count himself or arranging for another auditor to attend, obtaining another auditor's or a service auditor's report on the adequacy of the third party's internal control over counting and safeguarding, and inspecting documentation regarding the inventory held.
keywords: arranging for another auditor to attend

options.text: Nothing further — the confirmation came directly from the custodian rather than through the client, which is the requirement the standard sets
options.misconception: treats directness as the whole test of a confirmation, ignoring the reliability of the party confirming
options.why: A confirmation is only as good as the party writing it. Directness removes one risk, that the client edited the reply, and leaves untouched the risk that the custodian's own word is worth nothing.

options.text: Qualify the opinion at once for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, no procedure being available where a custodian is under investigation
options.misconception: goes to the report before performing the alternative procedures the standard names
options.why: The standard supplies three further procedures before any question of the opinion arises. A modification that skipped them would be reporting the auditor's convenience rather than a limitation.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from the client's management confirming the quantities and condition of the inventory lying with the custodian
options.misconception: replaces evidence about inventory held elsewhere with an assertion from management that has no better access to it
options.why: Management is no closer to the goods than the auditor is, and its representation adds no knowledge. The requirement is evidence about existence and condition, which is obtained by going to where the goods are or by testing the controls of whoever holds them.

citation.ref: inventory under the custody and control of a third party — confirmation, and the other audit procedures where information raises doubt about the third party's integrity and objectivity

items.scenario: A material part of your client's inventory sits with a third-party custodian. During the year the tax authorities raided that custodian over a fake-invoicing scheme and its proprietor is in custody. A confirmation nevertheless comes back directly from the custodian's office confirming the quantities and condition of everything held. Your manager treats the confirmation as obtained directly and closes the point.

items.stem: What does SA 520 require when a result differs from the expected value by a significant amount?

options.text: Reduce the extent of the tests of details on revenue and receivables, the analytical result being favourable in both cases
options.misconception: reads an unexplained favourable movement as assurance rather than as a risk indicator
options.why: A movement in the direction management would have wanted is not a comfort. Both of these are the classic signatures of revenue recorded early and receivables netted off, which is why the standard sends the auditor towards the difference rather than away from it.

options.text: Treat the two movements as a scope limitation, management having failed to substantiate them, and modify the opinion
options.misconception: jumps from an unexplained difference to the report without performing the other audit procedures the standard requires
options.why: A difference the auditor has not yet investigated is not a limitation on his scope. It becomes one only after the further procedures have been performed and have failed.

options.text: Record management's explanation, which is what inquiry of management means, and move on where the explanation is plausible on its face
options.misconception: stops at the inquiry and drops the evidence relevant to the response, which is the other half of the same requirement
options.why: Plausibility is the quality a fabricated explanation is designed to have. The standard asks for evidence relevant to the response for that reason, and a product-mix claim is testable against the sales ledger in an afternoon.

options.text: Investigate the difference by inquiring of management and obtaining appropriate audit evidence relevant to management's responses, and by performing other audit procedures as necessary in the circumstances — the need for other procedures arising where management cannot explain, or where the explanation together with the evidence obtained relevant to it is not adequate
options.why: The requirement has two halves and the senior has done the first. Where analytical procedures identify fluctuations or relationships inconsistent with other relevant information, or differing from expected values by a significant amount, the auditor inquires of management and obtains appropriate audit evidence relevant to management's responses. An explanation on its own is a statement, not evidence. Beyond that he performs other audit procedures as necessary, which is what happens where management cannot explain the movement or where the explanation and the evidence together still do not answer it.
keywords: appropriate audit evidence relevant to management's responses

citation.ref: investigating the results of analytical procedures — inquiring of management and obtaining appropriate audit evidence relevant to management's responses, and performing other audit procedures as necessary in the circumstances

items.scenario: The analytical procedures performed near the end of an audit throw up two results well outside expectation: gross margin nine percentage points above last year, and debtor days forty days shorter. The finance head explains both in one sentence — a better product mix. The senior records the sentence in the file and closes the point, the explanation having been obtained from the person best placed to give it.

items.stem: What does SA 550 require of you now?

options.text: Obtain audit evidence that the transaction has been appropriately authorised and approved, and evaluate whether the terms of the transaction are consistent with management's explanations to you and whether the transaction has been properly accounted for and disclosed in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework
options.why: Inspecting the contract and testing the business rationale is one part of the response to a significant related party transaction outside the normal course of business, and three parts remain. The auditor obtains audit evidence that the transaction has been appropriately authorised and approved — a sale of an asset of this kind with no board minute and no members' resolution fails that at once. He evaluates whether the terms are consistent with management's explanations, which a price thirty per cent below the term sheet is not. And he evaluates whether it has been properly accounted for and disclosed, which a gain routed to reserves without a note is not.

options.text: Nothing further on the audit side — report the absence of board approval to those charged with governance and leave the accounting to management
options.misconception: turns a set of audit requirements into a communication, and hands the accounting question back to the party being audited
options.why: Communication with those charged with governance sits alongside the work; it does not replace it. And whether the gain is correctly presented is an audit conclusion, not a preference management is entitled to.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from management that the sale was on terms equivalent to those prevailing in an arm's length transaction, which answers the price point and the approval point together
options.misconception: substitutes an arm's length representation for the separate requirements on authorisation, on consistency with explanations and on accounting
options.why: An arm's length assertion is itself an assertion to be audited, and it says nothing about whether the board approved the sale or whether the gain was accounted for correctly. Three separate requirements cannot be answered by one sentence about price.

options.text: Treat the price difference as a matter for the valuation of the brand alone, the term sheet being a negotiating document with no evidential value
options.misconception: dismisses the inconsistency between the terms and management's own explanation, which the standard requires to be evaluated
options.why: The term sheet matters here not as a valuation but as what management told you. A transaction whose terms contradict the explanation given for it is the specific thing the standard asks the auditor to evaluate.

citation.ref: identified significant related party transactions outside the entity's normal course of business — evidence of appropriate authorisation and approval, consistency of the terms with management's explanations, and proper accounting and disclosure

items.scenario: A manufacturer sells its oldest brand to an entity owned by the promoter's family. You have identified the sale as a significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business, inspected the assignment deed, and satisfied yourself that the stated rationale — exiting a line the company no longer makes — is genuine. Three things are still open. The board minutes for the year do not mention the sale and no members' resolution was passed. The price in the deed is thirty per cent below the figure in the term sheet management showed you. And the gain has been credited straight to reserves with no note.

items.stem: What procedures does SA 560 require between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report?

options.text: Interim financial statements prepared for a bank are outside the audit and need not be read, being unaudited and prepared for a single user
options.misconception: excludes the latest subsequent interim financial statements, which the standard names among the required procedures
options.why: The standard asks for the entity's latest subsequent interim financial statements without any qualification about who they were prepared for. They are read as a source of subsequent events, not as a statement anyone is opining on.

options.text: Only the written representation is required in this window; active procedures begin only where something comes to the auditor's notice
options.misconception: reverses the two windows, applying the reactive duty of the post-report window to the period before the report
options.why: The reactive duty belongs after the report is signed. Before that date the auditor performs procedures designed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence that subsequent events have been identified, and a representation is the last step of that work rather than a substitute for it.

options.text: Obtain an understanding of any procedures management has established to ensure that subsequent events are identified; inquire of management and, where appropriate, of those charged with governance whether any subsequent events have occurred which might affect the financial statements; read the minutes of meetings of the entity's owners, management and those charged with governance held after the date of the financial statements; and read the entity's latest subsequent interim financial statements — with written representations that all subsequent events have been adjusted or disclosed
options.why: In this window the auditor is actively looking, and the standard lists what looking means. He obtains an understanding of any procedures management has established for identifying subsequent events. He inquires of management and, where appropriate, of those charged with governance. He reads the minutes of meetings of owners, management and those charged with governance held after the date of the financial statements — which is why stopping at 31 March misses the whole point. He reads the entity's latest subsequent interim financial statements. And he requests written representations that all subsequent events have been adjusted or disclosed.

options.text: Reading the board minutes up to the date of the financial statements is the requirement, minutes after that date relating to the following year
options.misconception: reads minutes only up to the balance sheet date, when the requirement is for meetings held after it
options.why: A meeting held in May is precisely where an insolvency, a fire or a settlement occurring in April will be recorded. Reading only up to 31 March closes the file on the window the standard opens.

citation.ref: the procedures required between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report, read with the written representation on subsequent events

items.scenario: A company's year ended on 31 March and the report is to be signed on 20 June. The subsequent events section of the file holds two things: a note that the board minutes were read up to 31 March, and the signed representation letter. Nobody asked management or the audit committee anything; the minutes of the April and May board meetings were never called for; and the interim accounts the company prepared for its bankers in April and May were not read.

items.stem: What does SA 700 (Revised) require in that section, and what does it permit?

options.text: The sentence is sufficient — the section states what the auditor did, and the limitations of an audit are a matter of professional knowledge rather than of the report
options.misconception: treats the description of reasonable assurance and materiality as background rather than as required content of the section
options.why: The section is written for a reader who has no professional knowledge. Telling him that reasonable assurance is not a guarantee, and what makes a misstatement material, is the work the section does.

options.text: The section must state that reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with SAs will always detect a material misstatement when it exists, and that misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, they could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of these financial statements — and the fuller description may be located in an appendix to the auditor's report, or, where law, regulation or national auditing standards expressly permit, replaced by a reference to a website of an appropriate authority whose description addresses and is not inconsistent with it
options.why: The one sentence in the draft states the conclusion and omits the two things the section exists to say. It must state that reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with SAs will always detect a material misstatement when it exists, and it must state that misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, they could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users taken on the basis of these financial statements. On placement the standard is more generous than the partner was told: the detailed description may sit in an appendix to the report, and where law, regulation or national auditing standards expressly permit, a reference to a website of an appropriate authority may take its place.

options.text: The section may be shortened to a cross-reference to the Standards on Auditing themselves, since the responsibilities are set out there in full
options.misconception: replaces the required statements with a citation of the standards, which is not one of the permitted routes
options.why: A reference to the standards is not a reference to a website of an appropriate authority carrying the description, and it leaves the reader with nothing. The permitted shortcuts are the appendix and, where expressly permitted, the named website.

options.text: The whole description must appear in the body of the report, an appendix or a website reference being a dilution of the auditor's own statement of his responsibilities
options.misconception: denies the placement options the standard expressly allows
options.why: The standard permits the material to be located in an appendix, and permits a website reference where law, regulation or national auditing standards expressly allow it and the description there is not inconsistent. Neither route changes what the auditor is responsible for.

citation.ref: the required content of the Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements section, and the permission to locate the description in an appendix or, where expressly permitted, on a website of an appropriate authority

items.scenario: A draft auditor's report carries, under the heading Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements, a single sentence: "We audited the financial statements in accordance with the Standards on Auditing and obtained reasonable assurance that they are free from material misstatement." The partner wants to move the fuller description out of the body of the report, and has been told that an appendix is not permitted and that pointing the reader at a regulator's website is never allowed.

items.stem: Which of the matters in the proviso do these four engage?

options.text: None — the proviso creates a duty to inquire and the auditor reports nothing under it, all his reporting obligations being in section 143(3)
options.misconception: reads the absence of routine reporting as an absence of any reporting, when an adverse finding is stated
options.why: Nothing is said where the inquiry is satisfied, which is not the same as nothing being said at all. Where the inquiry produces an adverse answer the auditor reports it to the members, and four adverse answers are what these facts produce.

options.text: Only the sale of securities below cost, the other three being matters for CARO 2020 rather than for section 143(1)
options.misconception: moves three of the proviso's own matters into CARO, which is a separate reporting order
options.why: CARO adds reporting; it does not remove the proviso's matters from section 143(1). Loans shown as deposits and shares allotted for cash without cash are named in the proviso itself and are answered there.

options.text: All four, and each must also be positively confirmed in the auditor's report every year along with the other two matters in the proviso
options.misconception: turns the proviso into an annual positive-assurance report, when only adverse findings are stated
options.why: The duty is to inquire and to apply the mind; the report speaks only where an answer is adverse. An auditor who prints six clean answers every year has told the reader nothing about which years the answer was tested.

options.text: All four — whether loans and advances made on the basis of security have been properly secured and whether the terms on which they have been made are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members; whether so much of the assets as consist of shares, debentures and other securities have been sold at a price less than that at which they were purchased, the company not being an investment company or a banking company; whether loans and advances made by the company have been shown as deposits; and, where the books state that shares have been allotted for cash, whether cash has actually been received
options.why: The proviso names six matters and the manager has remembered two of them. A loan on a second charge over land already fully charged, at two per cent for twelve years, goes to whether it was properly secured and whether the terms are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members. Securities costing seven crore sold for three crore goes to the matter about assets consisting of shares, debentures and other securities sold below their purchase price, which applies because this company is neither an investment company nor a banking company. Loans described as security deposits go to whether loans and advances have been shown as deposits. And shares recorded as allotted for cash where no cash arrived goes to the last matter in the proviso.

citation.ref: Section 143(1), proviso clauses (a), (c), (d) and (f)

items.scenario: Four things come out of an unlisted manufacturing company's books. Eighteen crore rupees lent against a second charge on land already fully charged to a bank, carrying two per cent interest and repayable after twelve years. Quoted securities that cost seven crore rupees sold to a promoter entity for three crore; the company is neither an investment company nor a banking company. Five crore rupees of loans to a supplier shown in the balance sheet under the heading "security deposits". And nine crore rupees of shares recorded in the books as allotted for cash, against which the bank statements show nothing received. The manager says the proviso to section 143(1) is about book entries and personal expenses, neither of which arises.

items.stem: Is the reporting requirement met?

options.text: Yes — the reporting requirement is that the software has the feature and that the feature operated throughout the year, both of which hold
options.misconception: stops at the operation limb and drops both the tampering limb and the preservation limb
options.why: Operation is one of three limbs. A trail that anybody could edit and that is thrown away after a year fails the other two, whatever the switch said all year.

options.text: No — the requirement has a third limb, that the audit trail has been preserved by the company as per the statutory requirements for record retention, which a twelve-month backup cycle does not satisfy; and whether the feature was tampered with is tested through the controls over the trail itself, which fail here on shared user IDs, on unrestricted access with no access logs, and on unauthorised changes to the audit trail's configuration
options.why: The reporting requirement asks three things and the manager has answered one. The third is whether the audit trail has been preserved by the company as per the statutory requirements for record retention, and a company that overwrites its logs after twelve months has not preserved them. Tampering is not established by nobody having alleged it either: the controls the auditor examines are that the feature cannot be disabled or deactivated, that access to the audit trail is restricted with access logs maintained, that user IDs are assigned to each individual and not shared, that changes to the audit trail's configuration are authorised and logged, and that periodic backups are taken and archived for the statutory period.

options.text: The access controls, the shared logins and the retention of backups are matters for the internal financial controls reporting and have no bearing on this requirement
options.misconception: separates the audit trail reporting from the controls that make the trail reliable, when those controls are how the tampering limb is tested
options.why: The two reports overlap and neither swallows the other. A trail anybody can edit is how the auditor answers whether the feature was tampered with, so those controls are read for this requirement whether or not they are read again elsewhere.

options.text: No, and the consequence is a qualification of the opinion on the financial statements, since books maintained without a preserved audit trail are not proper books of account
options.misconception: converts a separate reporting requirement into a modification of the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: This is a reporting requirement answered in its own place, and answering it adversely is not the same as concluding the financial statements are misstated. The books can be complete and accurate while the trail over them is not preserved.

citation.ref: Rule 11 — the auditor's reporting on the use of accounting software with an audit trail feature, its operation throughout the year without being tampered with, and its preservation as per the statutory requirements for record retention

items.scenario: A company's accounting software had the audit trail feature switched on for the whole year. Four other things are true. The database administrators share one login between them. Anyone in the finance team can open and edit the table the log is written to, and no record is kept of who opened it. The log's configuration was changed twice during the year without anyone's approval. And the logs for the two earlier years are gone, the company keeping backups for twelve months. The manager proposes a clean report: the feature was on all year and nobody has alleged tampering.

items.stem: What else does clause 3(xi) require?

options.text: Nothing — sub-clause (b) is answered only where a report was actually filed, and sub-clause (c) is answered only where the company refers a whistle-blower complaint to the auditor
options.misconception: treats both sub-clauses as conditional, when each is answered every year and the second requires the auditor to obtain the complaints
options.why: Both are standing questions. A nil answer on Form ADT-4 is still an answer, and the second sub-clause places the initiative on the auditor rather than on whoever happens to forward him a complaint.

options.text: The thirty lakh fraud must in any event be reported in Form ADT-4, and sub-clause (b) then answered in the affirmative
options.misconception: ignores the threshold in rule 13 that decides whether the report goes to the Central Government or to the audit committee
options.why: Rule 13 splits the route by amount: at or above the prescribed figure the report goes to the Central Government in Form ADT-4, and below it to the audit committee or the Board. The CARO answer follows what the rule actually required, not what would be tidier.

options.text: The other two sub-clauses — whether any report under section 143(12) has been filed by the auditors in Form ADT-4 as prescribed under rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 with the Central Government, which is answered even where the answer is that none was filed; and whether the auditor has considered whistle-blower complaints, if any, received during the year by the company, which requires him to obtain them and consider them
options.why: The clause has three sub-clauses. Sub-clause (b) asks whether any report under section 143(12) has been filed by the auditors in Form ADT-4 as prescribed under rule 13 with the Central Government — a question the auditor answers about his own conduct, and answers even when the answer is that no such report was filed. Sub-clause (c) asks whether the auditor has considered whistle-blower complaints, if any, received during the year by the company, which cannot be answered by an auditor who never called for them; three complaints alleging invoice inflation in one division are exactly what the sub-clause was written to reach.

options.text: The whistle-blower complaints are covered by clause 3(xiv) on the internal audit system, the vigil mechanism being part of that system
options.misconception: moves the whistle-blower question to a different clause, when clause 3(xi)(c) names it
options.why: Clause 3(xiv) asks about the internal audit system and whether its reports were considered. Whistle-blower complaints are named in clause 3(xi)(c) and are answered there, alongside the frauds and the Form ADT-4 question they sit with.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xi)(b) and clause 3(xi)(c), read with rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: During the year the auditor found one fraud, of thirty lakh rupees, and reported it to the audit committee because the amount fell below the threshold for reporting to the Central Government. No report in Form ADT-4 was therefore filed. Separately, the company's vigil mechanism received nine complaints, three of them alleging invoice inflation in the same division; the audit senior never asked for them, on the view that the vigil mechanism belongs to the audit committee. He drafts clause 3(xi) covering the thirty lakh fraud and nothing else.

items.stem: What does section 143(3)(i) require the report to state?

options.text: Two things — whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place, and the operating effectiveness of such controls — so a control that was not performed for four months is reported however the financial statements came out, the internal financial controls opinion being a separate opinion from the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: The clause asks whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and it asks about the operating effectiveness of such controls. Design and operation are two questions, and a control that exists on paper and was not performed for a third of the year fails the second whatever the closing figures show. The auditor's substantive work is what kept the financial statements right; it is not evidence that the company's own control operated. The internal financial controls opinion is a separate opinion and is reached on its own evidence.
keywords: adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements

options.text: A modified opinion on the financial statements, since an internal financial controls failure of this size cannot leave the opinion on the financial statements unqualified
options.misconception: ties the opinion on the financial statements to the internal financial controls opinion, when the two are formed separately
options.why: The two opinions travel separately. An adverse conclusion on internal financial controls does not by itself modify the opinion on financial statements that the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate evidence about by other means.

options.text: That adequate internal financial controls are in place — operating effectiveness being demonstrated by the absence of any uncorrected misstatement in the financial statements
options.misconception: reads a clean set of financial statements as evidence that the company's controls operated
options.why: A clean set of financial statements can be the product of the audit rather than of the entity's controls, which is exactly what happened here. Operating effectiveness is tested on the control, not inferred from the outcome.

options.text: Nothing on this control — the failure is a deficiency to be communicated to those charged with governance, and the clause reports only on the design of the system as a whole
options.misconception: narrows the clause to design and pushes an operating failure into a communication
options.why: Communicating the deficiency is required and it is not a substitute. The clause names operating effectiveness in terms, so a control that did not operate is answered in the report and not only in a letter.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(i) — whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and the operating effectiveness of such controls

items.scenario: An unlisted public company with a turnover of nine hundred crore rupees is audited. The control over revenue cut-off — a review of despatch documents against invoices at each month end — was simply not performed for four months of the year. Your own substantive work found the errors it would have caught, management corrected all of them, and the financial statements carry no uncorrected misstatement. The manager proposes to state that the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and that such controls were operating effectively, because the numbers ended up right.

items.stem: How should the three accounts stand?

options.text: All three are non-performing, since each departs in some way from the terms of sanction
options.misconception: collapses the distinction between a temporary deficiency and a weakness in the credit itself
options.why: If every departure from sanction made an account non-performing, the norms would not have named temporary deficiencies separately. The purpose of the distinction is that a stock statement arriving late and a borrower who has vanished are not the same event.

options.text: The first two require the account to be treated as non-performing unless the branch obtains a fresh stock statement and a renewal sanction before the accounts are signed
options.misconception: makes classification turn on post-year-end paperwork rather than on whether the deficiency is temporary
options.why: Whether the deficiency is temporary is judged on the position at the balance sheet date, not on how quickly the branch can produce documents afterwards. Curing the paperwork later changes nothing about the classification on the date it is made.

options.text: The other way round — the first two are temporary deficiencies, and an account is not classified as non-performing merely because drawing power based on the latest stock statement is unavailable, because the balance outstanding exceeded the limit temporarily, or because limits were not renewed on the due date; the third indicates inherent weakness and is deemed non-performing whatever the position on the limit
options.why: The norms separate a deficiency in paperwork from a weakness in the credit. An account is not to be classified as non-performing merely because of temporary deficiencies such as the non-availability of drawing power based on the latest stock statement, a balance outstanding exceeding the limit temporarily, or limits not renewed on the due date — the first two accounts are that and nothing more. Where an account indicates inherent weakness, it is deemed non-performing, and a shut factory with an untraceable borrower is the plainest case of it even though no instalment has fallen due.

options.text: The branch manager is right on all three — a missing stock statement and an expired limit are irregularities in the account, while an account within its limit with nothing overdue cannot be non-performing
options.misconception: treats every documentary irregularity as an NPA trigger and treats "nothing overdue" as conclusive against one
