options.why: The record of recovery is the ordinary test and inherent weakness is the exception written beside it. Paperwork that is late does not make a good account bad, and a limit that has not yet been breached does not make a dead one good.

citation.ref: Ch. Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies — accounts with temporary deficiencies, and accounts indicating inherent weakness

items.scenario: Three cash credit accounts at a branch on 31 March. In the first, the borrower has not submitted his latest stock statement, so drawing power on the latest statement could not be worked out; the outstanding is inside the sanctioned limit and every interest debit has been served. In the second, the limit expired on 15 February and the renewal proposal is with the sanctioning authority; the account operates regularly and is within the old limit. In the third, the borrower's factory has been shut for seven months and he is untraceable, though nothing is overdue and the outstanding is inside the limit. The branch manager classifies the first two as non-performing and the third as standard.

items.stem: How does Clause 1 of Part I of the Second Schedule answer the three?

options.text: All three may be answered in full once the member records in his file that disclosure is in the client's own commercial interest
options.misconception: invents an exception for the member's own view of the client's interest, which the clause does not contain
options.why: The clause admits two exceptions and neither is the member's judgement about what would suit the client. A note in a file is not consent and it is not a law.

options.text: He is not required to give the client, or other auditors of the same enterprise or of a related enterprise such as a parent or a subsidiary, access to his audit working papers, though he may at his discretion make portions of or extracts from them available; sharing working papers and sharing information are different things, and information may be given to the client or to a regulatory body after obtaining the client's consent; and for a company that consent comes from the Board of Directors by resolution, unless the Board's powers have been delegated to the managing director comprehensively enough to include it
options.why: Three different rules answer the three requests. An auditor is not required to provide the client or other auditors of the same enterprise or its related enterprises, such as a parent or a subsidiary, access to his audit working papers, and the main auditor has no right of access to a branch auditor's papers either; he may make portions or extracts available if he chooses. Information is a separate question from working papers, and information may be given to the client or to a regulatory body once the client's consent has been obtained. And in the case of a company the consent must come from the Board of Directors by resolution, unless the Board's powers have been delegated to the managing director widely enough to cover it.

options.text: The holding company's auditor is entitled to the working papers, a group audit being one audit, and the managing director's instruction binds the member because he is the company's chief executive
options.misconception: creates a right of access for another auditor and treats an officer's instruction as the company's consent
options.why: The other auditor may rely on the member's work without ever seeing his papers, which is the arrangement the profession works on. And consent belongs to the company, expressed the way the company expresses decisions, not to whichever officer asks.

options.text: Nothing may go to the regulator either, because a request that is not backed by legal compulsion cannot be answered whatever the client says
options.misconception: forgets that consent is the other door out of the duty, alongside legal compulsion
options.why: The clause bars disclosure without the client's consent or otherwise than as required by law. Consent is a door in its own right, so a client that wants the regulator informed can open it.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 1 — access to audit working papers, the difference between sharing working papers and sharing information, and who may give the client's consent

items.scenario: Three requests land on a practising member in one week. The auditor of his client's holding company asks for his audit working papers on the subsidiary, so that the group opinion can be supported. The client's managing director, whose board has passed no resolution delegating the point to him, asks him to send those working papers to the company's banker. And a regulator writes asking for information about the client's export incentive claims; the client is entirely willing for the information to go.

items.stem: Which of the three does Clause 4 of Part I of the Second Schedule bar?

options.text: Only the second — a certificate for a tax assessment is an attest function, while a net worth certificate for a bank is a private commercial document outside the clause
options.misconception: reads "financial statements" narrowly and excludes certificates given after an examination of the accounts
options.why: A net worth certificate given after an examination of the accounts is precisely a report or certificate of the kind the clause names. Who asked for it does not change what it is.

options.text: None, because twenty-six per cent of voting power is below the threshold at which a member is deemed to have a substantial interest
options.misconception: misplaces the threshold, which is reached at shares carrying not less than twenty per cent of the voting power
options.why: A member is deemed to have a substantial interest in a company where shares carrying not less than twenty per cent of the voting power at any time during the relevant years are beneficially owned by him or by the persons named with him. Twenty-six is above that, not below it.

options.text: All three, because the clause reaches every document a member with a substantial interest signs, whatever it is for and whoever sees it
options.misconception: ignores the carve-out for statements prepared by a member in employment purely for his employer
options.why: The carve-out exists because such a pack is not an opinion offered to anyone outside. It is also prepared for a different company altogether, in which the member's shareholding is not in issue at all.

options.text: The first two — the words "financial statements" in this clause cover both reports and certificates usually given after an examination of the accounts or the financial statement and any attest function under any statutory enactment or for the purposes of income-tax assessments — while the third is outside it, statements prepared by members in employment purely for the information of their employers in the normal course of their duties and not meant to be submitted to any outside authority not being caught
options.why: The clause is not confined to a document headed "financial statements". Its words cover reports and certificates usually given after an examination of the accounts or the financial statement, and any attest function under any statutory enactment or for the purposes of income-tax assessments — so both the net worth certificate and the tax certificate fall inside it. What falls outside is the third: statements prepared by members in employment purely for the information of their employers in the normal course of their duties and not meant to be submitted to any outside authority. Twenty-six per cent of the voting power is beyond the twenty per cent at which substantial interest is reached under Appendix 9 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 4 — the meaning of "financial statements" for the clause, read with the definition of substantial interest in Appendix 9 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: A member holds shares carrying twenty-six per cent of the voting power in a private company. Three documents are put in front of him. A net worth certificate on that company for its banker, given after an examination of its accounts. A certificate accompanying that company's income-tax return, an attest function for the purposes of the assessment. And a monthly management accounts pack that he prepares as a salaried employee of an entirely different company, purely for that employer's own information and never sent outside it.

items.stem: Which of the four need the Council's permission, and what else follows?

options.text: Editorship of professional journals, and owning agricultural land and carrying out agricultural activity, are within the general permission and need no specific permission; part-time or full-time lectureship for courses other than the Institute's, and tutorship under an educational institution other than the Institute's coaching organisation, need the specific and prior approval of the Council — and the permission is subject to the direct teaching hours taken together not exceeding 25 hours a week if he is to undertake attest functions
options.why: The Council has passed two resolutions and the answer turns on which list an activity falls in. The general permission covers, among other things, private tutorship, authorship of books and articles, editorship of professional journals, acting as a notary public, holding public elective office, acting as surveyor and loss assessor under the Insurance Act, 1938, recovery consultancy in the banking sector, and owning agricultural land and carrying out agricultural activity. The specific and prior approval of the Council is needed for employment in business or non-business concerns, for the office of managing director or whole-time director, for interest in family business concerns, for editorship of journals other than professional journals, and for lectureship and tutorship outside the Institute's own coaching organisation. On top of that sits the condition that direct teaching hours taken together must not exceed 25 hours a week for the member to be able to undertake attest functions.

options.text: None needs permission, because none of the four is a business — teaching, farming and editing are professional or personal pursuits rather than trade
options.misconception: reads Clause 11 as reaching only business, when it reaches any business or occupation other than the profession
options.why: The clause covers any business or occupation other than the profession of accountancy. A lectureship is an occupation, which is why the Council had to name it in the list requiring specific approval.

options.text: Only the lectureship needs permission, and the hours he teaches are a private matter that affects nothing
options.misconception: drops the tutorship outside the Institute's coaching organisation and drops the hours condition attached to the permission
options.why: Tutorship under an educational institution other than the Institute's coaching organisation is on the specific list beside the lectureship, and the permission is granted subject to the 25-hour condition. Thirty hours a week puts his attest work in question.

options.text: All four need specific permission, the proviso to Clause 11 saving only a directorship simpliciter and nothing else
options.misconception: ignores the Council's general resolution, which permits a listed set of occupations without any application
options.why: The proviso about a directorship is one thing and the Council's general permission is another. Editing a professional journal and farming one's own land are on the general list and need no application at all.

citation.ref: Regulation 190A with the Council's general and specific resolutions in Appendix 9, read with Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

items.scenario: A practising member takes on four things in one year and asks nobody about any of them. He edits a professional journal. He owns agricultural land and farms it. He accepts a full-time lectureship at a private college. And he takes a part-time tutorship at a private coaching institute that has nothing to do with the Institute's own coaching organisation. Between the last two he teaches thirty direct hours a week, and he continues to sign audit reports.

items.stem: Which of the four breach Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule?

options.text: The company secretary, the advocate and the commerce graduate — fees may be shared only with a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner or a deceased partner's legal representative
options.misconception: stops at the four categories in the clause and omits the members of other professional bodies and prescribed persons the Council has added
options.why: The clause itself names a member of any other professional body and such other persons having such qualifications as may be prescribed. Regulation 53A is where those are prescribed, and it is why a company secretary and an advocate are inside the line.

options.text: Only the referral fee to the other chartered accountant, a payment for the introduction of work being the very thing the clause was written against
options.misconception: confuses the outflow of fees to a non-member with a referral fee between two members, which is permitted
options.why: Clause 2 polices where the fee went, and a fellow member in practice is the one recipient nobody has ever doubted. The introduction that offends is the one by a person outside the permitted lists.

options.text: Only the payment to the commerce graduate — the Council has prescribed under Regulation 53A the professional bodies and the persons qualified in India with whom fees may be shared, and they include a Company Secretary, a Cost Accountant, an Actuary and holders of a Bachelor in Engineering, Technology, Architecture or Law and a Master in Business Administration, alongside the Bar Council of India and the other named bodies; a Bachelor of Commerce appears on neither list, and a referral fee between two members in practice is not prohibited at all
options.why: The clause bars payment of any share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of the professional business to anyone outside a named set, and the Council has prescribed that set under Regulation 53A. The professional bodies are the Institute of Company Secretaries of India, the Institute of Cost and Works Accountants of India, the Bar Council of India, the Indian Institute of Architects and the Institute of Actuaries of India. The persons qualified in India are a Company Secretary, a Cost Accountant, an Actuary, and a Bachelor in Engineering, in Technology, in Architecture or in Law, and a Master in Business Administration. A commerce graduate is on neither list, and it is not prohibited for a member in practice to charge a referral fee from another member in practice.

options.text: All four, since a share of professional fees may never leave the firm's own partners
options.misconception: reads the clause as an absolute bar, when it names permitted recipients and the Council has prescribed more
options.why: Sharing with another member of the Institute or with a firm of chartered accountants is in order on the face of the clause, and the referral fee between two members in practice is expressly not prohibited.

citation.ref: Regulation 53A(1) and Regulation 53A(3), read with Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

items.scenario: A firm makes four payments out of its professional fees during the year. A share to a practising company secretary who worked with it on a secretarial due diligence. A share to an advocate enrolled with the Bar Council of India who worked on the same file. A share to a commerce graduate who introduced the assignment and did none of the work. And a referral fee to another chartered accountant in practice for passing on an assignment.

items.stem: Which of the four are professional misconduct under Clause 10 of Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: The third and the fourth — an advance received against services to be rendered does not fall under the clause, and moneys received for expenses intended to be spent within a reasonably short time need not be put in a separate bank account; but moneys received for expenses that are not intended to be spent within a reasonably short time should be put in a separate bank account immediately, and moneys received in the capacity of trustee, executor or liquidator must be put in a separate bank account immediately
options.why: The Council has drawn four lines through this clause. An advance received against services to be rendered is the member's own money on account and does not fall under it. Moneys received for expenses to be incurred which are intended to be spent within a reasonably short time — stamp paper, prescribed statutory fees — need not go into a separate bank account. Moneys for expenses not intended to be spent within a reasonably short time should be put in a separate bank account immediately, which the eight lakh rupees sitting from April to December plainly is. And moneys received in the capacity of trustee, executor or liquidator must be put in a separate bank account immediately, whatever the amount and whatever the intention.
keywords: advance received against services to be rendered

options.text: Only the fourth, moneys received as liquidator being trust moneys, while everything received from a client in the course of practice is the member's to hold in his office account
options.misconception: treats every client receipt other than a fiduciary one as the member's own money
options.why: The duty attaches to moneys of the client, and eight lakh rupees held for eight months to meet a duty demand is client money in every sense. Only the fee advance and the short-term float are outside the duty.

options.text: None, provided the office account never falls below the total held and every payment is eventually made on time
options.misconception: treats a sufficient balance and an eventual payment as a substitute for a separate banking account
options.why: The offence is the mixing, not the shortfall. Keeping enough in a common account does not separate the client's money from the firm's, which is the whole of what the clause asks for.

options.text: All four — client moneys of every description must be kept in a separate banking account, the clause admitting no distinction
options.misconception: ignores the exclusions the clause and the Council both draw, for fees and for money meant to be spent shortly
options.why: The clause itself excepts fees or remuneration and money meant to be expended, and the Council has said in terms that a fee advance and a short-term expense float are outside it. A rule with no exceptions would make a stamp-paper float misconduct.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 10, read with the Council's suggestions on fee advances, short-term expense moneys and moneys received as trustee, executor or liquidator

items.scenario: Four receipts reach a practising member's office in one month, and all four are put into the firm's office account. Two lakh rupees as an advance against next year's audit fee. Fifteen thousand rupees to buy stamp paper and pay filing fees that week. Eight lakh rupees handed over in April to meet a duty demand that falls due in December. And forty lakh rupees received by him in his capacity as liquidator of a company.

items.stem: Where does he stand under Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: Clause 9 reaches both — the clause is failing to invite attention to any material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit applicable to the circumstances, and the circulation certification carries a special procedure the member accepted in writing and undertook to report any lapse of; and the failure to perform a statutory duty in the manner required is not excused merely by giving a qualification or reservation in the auditor's report, so the sentence about the unverified cash does not save him
options.why: Clause 9 is about the audit's own method rather than about the figures. It catches a failure to invite attention to any material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit applicable to the circumstances, and what is generally accepted takes its content from the Institute's own pronouncements — engagement and quality control standards, statements, guidance notes and the rest. Certifying circulation for the Audit Bureau of Circulations carries its own special procedure, which members accept in writing and undertake to report any lapse of, so a silent departure from it is squarely within the clause. And a bare disclosure does not cure the first failure, because the failure to perform a statutory duty in the manner required is not excused merely by giving a qualification or reservation in the auditor's report; where he does qualify, he would be well advised to say why he could not follow the accepted procedure.
keywords: not excused merely by giving a qualification

options.text: Neither is misconduct — the cash position was disclosed in the report, which is all the Schedule asks, and a circulation certificate is not an audit of financial statements
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing the omitted procedure, and treats a special-purpose certification as outside the accepted-procedure clause
options.why: Disclosure is not performance. And a certification with its own prescribed procedure is exactly where the clause bites, because the accepted procedure in those circumstances is the one the member agreed in writing to follow.

options.text: Both, but under Clause 7 for gross negligence, Clause 9 applying only where the auditor departs from a Standard on Auditing that expressly binds him
options.misconception: narrows generally accepted procedure of audit to the Standards on Auditing alone
options.why: What constitutes generally accepted audit procedure depends on the facts, and guidance comes from the whole body of the Institute's pronouncements and from the special rules governing particular certifications. Clause 7 may run alongside; it does not displace Clause 9.

options.text: Only the cash, and under Clause 8 rather than Clause 9, the failure being a failure to obtain sufficient information necessary for expression of an opinion
options.misconception: reads the cash failure only as an evidence failure and misses the departure from accepted procedure that Clause 9 addresses
options.why: Clause 8 is about the evidence behind the opinion and it is engaged here too, but it says nothing about the circulation certificate. Clause 9 is the clause that reaches a departure from the method itself, in both engagements.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 9 — material departure from the generally accepted procedure of audit, and the rule that a failure to perform a statutory duty is not excused by a qualification in the report

items.scenario: An auditor did not verify cash balances of one crore forty lakh rupees held at three depots, in circumstances where verification was necessary, feasible and material. He performed no alternative procedure and wrote one sentence in his report: "We have not verified the cash balances at the depots." In the same year he certified a magazine's circulation for the Audit Bureau of Circulations, departing from the special procedure he had accepted in writing, and said nothing about the departure. His position is that having disclosed the first in his report he is safe, and that the second is a private arrangement with a trade body.

items.stem: What does SA 330 require of the response?

options.text: The substantive procedures must include tests of details, the approach to this significant risk consisting only of substantive procedures
options.why: SA 330 adds a condition where the auditor's approach to a significant risk consists only of substantive procedures: those procedures shall include tests of details. A substantive analytical procedure on its own does not satisfy it, however carefully the expectation is built, so the plan has to add work on the cut-off itself — the despatch and acceptance documents on either side of the year end.

options.text: Tests of controls over cut-off must be performed, a significant risk always obliging the auditor to test the controls that address it
options.misconception: turns the duty to understand the controls relevant to a significant risk into a duty to test their operating effectiveness
options.why: The auditor obtains an understanding of the entity's controls relevant to a significant risk, but he tests their operating effectiveness only where he intends to rely on them in setting the nature, timing and extent of substantive procedures. Here he does not.

options.text: Nothing more — a substantive analytical procedure is a substantive procedure, so a response made of them is responsive to the risk
options.misconception: reads the requirement as "some substantive work of any kind" and misses the extra condition attaching to a substantive-only approach
options.why: The requirement to perform substantive procedures specifically responsive to a significant risk is one sentence and the condition on a substantive-only approach is the next one. Both have to be met, and the second one names tests of details.

options.text: The assessment must be revised downwards, a substantive-only approach being open only for a risk that is not significant
options.misconception: invents a bar on responding to a significant risk with substantive procedures alone
options.why: A substantive-only approach is perfectly available for a significant risk. What the standard controls is the content of those substantive procedures, not whether the approach may be taken at all.

citation.ref: Substantive procedures related to a significant risk, read with the requirement to test controls only where reliance is intended

items.scenario: Revenue cut-off at a project engineering company is a significant risk. You do not intend to rely on any control over cut-off, so the whole response is substantive. The senior's plan holds one procedure: a month-by-month comparison of gross margin against the prior year, with an acceptable difference set in advance. He says analytical procedures are substantive procedures, so a response made only of them is specifically responsive to the risk and the standard asks for nothing more.

items.stem: What does SA 705 (Revised) require?

options.text: Express an unmodified opinion with an Other Matter paragraph recording that the receivables were not circularised
options.misconception: treats an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence as something a paragraph can disclose away
options.why: An Other Matter paragraph is never a substitute for a modification. The auditor has no evidence over the largest balance in the financial statements, and no paragraph converts that into a basis for an opinion.

options.text: Disclaim an opinion on the financial statements, withdrawal before issuing the report being neither practicable nor possible
options.why: Where the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive, SA 705 (Revised) sends the auditor down a two-step branch: withdraw from the audit where that is practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation and, if withdrawal before issuing the auditor's report is not practicable or possible, disclaim an opinion on the financial statements. The regulator's directive closes the first step here, so the second is the one that operates.

options.text: Withdraw at once, the standard preferring withdrawal to a disclaimer wherever the effects are pervasive
options.misconception: reads the preference for withdrawal as an instruction and drops the condition attached to it
options.why: Withdrawal is offered only where it is practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation. On these facts it is neither, and an auditor who leaves anyway breaches the directive rather than complying with the standard.

options.text: Qualify the opinion, setting out the receivables you were unable to verify in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
options.misconception: applies the material-but-not-pervasive branch to effects the auditor has already concluded are pervasive
options.why: A qualification is the answer where the possible effects could be material but not pervasive. Seventy-two per cent of total assets is the paradigm of pervasive, and the standard says in terms that a qualification would then be inadequate to communicate the gravity of the situation.

citation.ref: Consequence of an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence due to a management-imposed limitation after the auditor has accepted the engagement

items.scenario: Six weeks before the report on a listed company is due, management refuses to let you circularise trade receivables of ₹640 crore, being 72 per cent of total assets, and refuses the ageing behind them. You request that the limitation be removed; management refuses. You communicate the refusal to the audit committee and attempt alternative procedures, which produce nothing you can rely on. You conclude that the possible effects on the financial statements of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive. Your counsel confirms that the Securities and Exchange Board of India's directive on the resignation of an auditor does not permit you to leave without issuing the report for the period.

items.stem: What does SA 700 (Revised) require beyond the checklist?

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the netting and to the single expense line
options.misconception: uses a paragraph to flag a presentation failure the auditor is required to evaluate and, if it is material, to modify for
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter draws attention to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed. These are matters the auditor has concluded are not appropriately presented, which is a different road entirely.

options.text: Nothing beyond the checklist — compliance with the framework's requirements is what forming an opinion means
options.misconception: collapses a fair presentation framework into a compliance framework
options.why: Under a compliance framework the question stops at whether the requirements were met. Under a fair presentation framework the standard adds the further evaluation in terms, which is the whole reason the two kinds of framework are distinguished.

options.text: Only a check that the financial statements adequately refer to or describe the applicable financial reporting framework
options.misconception: takes one element of the evaluation and treats it as the whole of it
options.why: Whether the statements adequately refer to or describe the framework is one item on the list. It sits alongside the accounting policies, the estimates, the disclosures, the terminology and the fair presentation evaluation, and none of them stands in for the others.

options.text: An evaluation of whether the financial statements achieve fair presentation — the overall presentation, structure and content, and whether they represent the underlying transactions and events in a manner that achieves it
options.why: SA 700 (Revised) has the auditor form an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, and where that framework is a fair presentation framework it adds a second evaluation: whether the financial statements achieve fair presentation. That evaluation has two named inputs — the overall presentation, structure and content of the financial statements, and whether the financial statements, including the related notes, represent the underlying transactions and events in a manner that achieves fair presentation. A completed checklist of named disclosures answers neither.

citation.ref: Forming an opinion on the financial statements — the additional evaluation under a fair presentation framework

items.scenario: A company reports under a fair presentation framework. Every disclosure the framework names is present, every accounting policy is one the framework permits, and there are no uncorrected misstatements. The balance sheet nonetheless sets ₹180 crore receivable from one customer group against ₹176 crore payable to the same group and shows the ₹4 crore difference as a single line, and "other expenses" of ₹640 crore carries no breakdown anywhere in the notes. The manager says the framework's disclosure checklist is complete, so the opinion is unmodified.

items.stem: What does SA 240 require of you on withdrawing?

options.text: Send the resignation and stop there — the standard permits withdrawal and says nothing about how it is done
options.misconception: treats the permission to withdraw as the whole of the requirement and skips the two steps attached to it
options.why: The standard attaches both a determination and a discussion to a withdrawal in these circumstances. Silent departure is exactly the outcome those two steps exist to prevent, because it leaves the fraud with nobody outside the boardroom knowing why the auditor left.

options.text: Continue the engagement and qualify the opinion, the standard never permitting withdrawal where the members made the appointment
options.misconception: invents a bar on withdrawal drawn from who appointed the auditor
options.why: SA 240 contemplates withdrawal in exactly these circumstances and says so. Who made the appointment bears on whom the auditor may have to report the withdrawal to, not on whether he may withdraw.

options.text: File the report on the fraud under section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 and treat that as discharging everything the standard asks on withdrawal
options.misconception: lets a statutory fraud report stand in for the standard's own requirements about leaving the engagement
options.why: A report under section 143(12) may well be required on these facts, and it runs alongside SA 240 rather than instead of it. It is not a discussion with those charged with governance about the withdrawal, and it does not answer whether the person who made the appointment must be told.

options.text: Determine the professional and legal responsibilities in the circumstances, including whether there is a requirement to report to the person or persons who made the audit appointment or to regulatory authorities — and discuss the withdrawal and the reasons for it with the appropriate level of management and with those charged with governance
options.why: SA 240 does not leave withdrawal as a private act. The auditor first determines the professional and legal responsibilities applicable in the circumstances, including whether there is a requirement to report to the person or persons who made the audit appointment or, in some cases, to regulatory authorities. He then discusses with the appropriate level of management and with those charged with governance the withdrawal from the engagement and the reasons for the withdrawal. A one-line letter discharges neither, and the managing director is not the person who decides which of them applies.

citation.ref: The auditor unable to continue the engagement — determining responsibilities and communicating the withdrawal

items.scenario: You have established that the promoter-directors routed ₹18 crore through three vendors with no premises and no employees. You communicated the matter to those charged with governance in writing. The audit committee will not act and the board has resolved that the payments were commercial. You conclude that exceptional circumstances have arisen that bring into question your ability to continue the engagement, and you decide to withdraw. The managing director asks you to send in a one-line resignation and say nothing to anyone, since the members appointed you and the members can be told at the next general meeting.

items.stem: What has the senior still not considered under SA 520?

options.text: That an analytical procedure may never be the sole substantive procedure for a material balance, so tests of details are required on both
options.misconception: turns a judgement about suitability into an absolute bar the standard does not contain
options.why: A substantive analytical procedure may be the only substantive procedure for a balance where it is suitable and the expectation is precise enough. The depreciation charge is a fair example; the objection here is to the professional fees, not to the technique.

options.text: Nothing — reliability of the data and an acceptable difference are the two requirements, and both were met
options.misconception: takes the two limbs the senior did satisfy as the whole of the requirement
options.why: Four things are required before a substantive analytical procedure is relied on: suitability for the assertion, reliability of the data, precision of the expectation, and the amount of acceptable difference. Two of the four have been done.

options.text: That the expectation must be built by management from its own records and then tested by the auditor for reasonableness
options.misconception: hands the auditor's own expectation to the entity, which would make the test circular
options.why: The expectation is the auditor's. An expectation supplied by the entity being audited tells the auditor only that the entity's records agree with themselves.

options.text: The suitability of the particular procedure for the assertion — analytical procedures being generally more applicable to large volumes of transactions that tend to be predictable over time — and whether the expectation is sufficiently precise to identify a misstatement that may be material
options.why: SA 520 makes the auditor determine the suitability of particular substantive analytical procedures for given assertions, taking account of the assessed risks and of any tests of details on the same assertion. Analytical procedures are generally more applicable to large volumes of transactions that tend to be predictable over time, which the depreciation charge is and the professional fees plainly are not. The standard separately has him evaluate whether the expectation is sufficiently precise to identify a misstatement that, individually or when aggregated with others, may cause a material misstatement — and a comparison with last year's number on an unpredictable balance produces no such precision.

citation.ref: Substantive analytical procedures — suitability for the assertion and precision of the expectation

items.scenario: Two balances are to be tested by substantive analytical procedures alone. The first is depreciation on a fleet of delivery vans: opening cost, additions and disposals are verified elsewhere, the rate is fixed by policy, and an expected charge can be built to within ₹40,000. The second is consultancy and professional fees of ₹9 crore — eighty-one invoices from thirty-one unrelated suppliers, none of them recurring, with no operating driver in the business that predicts the total. Performance materiality is ₹1.1 crore. The senior plans a comparison with last year's figure for both, and has evaluated the reliability of the data and fixed an acceptable difference in each case.

items.stem: What does SA 530 make the sample size turn on?

options.text: Nothing that has to be reasoned, once a non-statistical approach is chosen and the firm's manual gives a number
options.misconception: reads "non-statistical" as "unreasoned", when it means only that the size is not computed by a statistical formula
options.why: A non-statistical approach uses judgement in place of a formula, and the judgement is over the same three inputs. A number taken from a manual with none of them considered is not a sample size the standard recognises.

options.text: A fixed proportion of the population, so that a larger population always draws a larger sample
options.misconception: makes sample size a percentage of the population, which SA 530 does not do
options.why: For a large population the size of the population itself has almost no effect on the sample size needed. What drives it is how much risk the auditor will accept and how far the tolerable rate sits from the expected rate.

options.text: The level of sampling risk the auditor is willing to accept, the tolerable rate of deviation and the rate of deviation he expects to find — the size being one sufficient to reduce sampling risk to an acceptably low level, whether the approach is statistical or non-statistical
options.why: SA 530 requires the auditor to determine a sample size sufficient to reduce sampling risk to an acceptably low level. What moves that size is the level of sampling risk the auditor is willing to accept, the tolerable rate of deviation for a test of controls or the tolerable misstatement for a test of details, and the rate of deviation or the misstatement he expects to find. Sampling risk is the risk that the conclusion drawn from a sample differs from the conclusion the same procedure would reach on the whole population. The reasoning is owed whether the approach is statistical or non-statistical: the approach changes how the size is arrived at, not whether it must be arrived at.

options.text: Non-sampling risk, which the auditor reduces by taking more items
options.misconception: swaps the two risks, and attaches to sample size the one no sample size can touch
options.why: Non-sampling risk is the risk of an erroneous conclusion for any reason not related to sampling — a badly designed procedure, a misread document. Enlarging the sample does nothing about it; only better procedures and supervision do.

citation.ref: Sample size and the factors influencing it, read with the definitions of sampling risk and non-sampling risk

items.scenario: Two seniors argue about the sample size for a test of the purchase authorisation control. One says the sample must be at least a tenth of the population, because a larger population needs a proportionately larger sample. The other says the firm's standard number is enough and that, because he is using a non-statistical approach, the size needs no reasoning behind it at all. Neither has written down the rate of deviation he would tolerate, nor the rate he expects to find, nor how much risk of a wrong conclusion he is prepared to run.

items.stem: What does SA 620 require before the expert's work is used?

options.text: Objectivity is evaluated only for a management's expert, the auditor's own expert being answerable to the auditor
options.misconception: reverses the two, when the requirement to evaluate competence, capabilities and objectivity is written for the auditor's expert
options.why: SA 620 governs the auditor's expert, and the evaluation of competence, capabilities and objectivity is its requirement. A management's expert is dealt with under SA 500, where the auditor evaluates that expert's competence, capabilities and objectivity as well.

options.text: An evaluation of whether the expert has the necessary competence, capabilities and objectivity — inquiring of the entity about interests and relationships including financial interests, business and personal relationships and other services the expert provides it, and obtaining a written representation from the expert about them
options.why: Competence, capabilities and objectivity are evaluated before the expert's work is relied on, and they are a separate and earlier question from whether the work itself turns out to be adequate. Where the expert is an external expert the auditor inquires of the entity about interests and relationships that may create a threat to objectivity — financial interests, business and personal relationships, and the provision of other services by the expert to the entity — and it is appropriate to obtain a written representation from the expert about any such interest or relationship, and to discuss with him whether any safeguards are adequate. An eleven-year retainer, a fee, and a brother in the entity's management are precisely what that evaluation exists to surface.

options.text: Nothing before the work arrives — objectivity is judged from the report, and a report that stands up is a report from an objective expert
options.misconception: pushes an entry test to the end of the work, where the answer can no longer change what was relied on
options.why: The evaluation comes before reliance because it decides whether the work may be relied on at all. Work that happens to look sound is not evidence that the person who produced it was free of a threat to his objectivity.

options.text: The expert may not be engaged at all, a retainer with the entity and a relative inside it being an absolute bar
options.misconception: converts a threat the auditor must evaluate into a prohibition the standard does not impose
options.why: SA 620 does not bar an expert with a relationship to the entity. It requires the relationships to be identified, the threats evaluated, and safeguards considered — and an expert engaged by the entity is common enough that the standard sets out how to handle it.

citation.ref: Competence, capabilities and objectivity of the auditor's expert, and the inquiry into interests and relationships

items.scenario: You propose to engage an actuary as an auditor's expert on a company's gratuity and pension liability. He is an external expert, not part of your firm. His own firm has been the company's retained actuarial adviser for eleven years and draws a fee from the company for that retainer, and his brother is the company's head of human resources. Your manager says none of this matters, because the objectivity question is about the audit firm rather than the expert, and in any case the work will be evaluated for adequacy when it arrives.

items.stem: What does SA 620 say about naming the expert there?

options.text: Name the expert and state that responsibility for the valuation of the investment rests with him
options.misconception: uses the reference to divide a responsibility the standard says is undivided
options.why: The auditor has sole responsibility for the opinion expressed, and that responsibility is not reduced by his use of the work of an auditor's expert. A sentence apportioning it to the expert states the opposite of the standard.

options.text: The reference may be made, being relevant to an understanding of the modification — and the report must then indicate that the reference does not reduce your responsibility for the opinion
options.why: SA 620 keeps the auditor's expert out of a report containing an unmodified opinion unless law or regulation requires the reference. Where the auditor refers to the work of an auditor's expert because that reference is relevant to an understanding of a modification to the opinion, the standard permits the reference and attaches a condition to it: the report shall indicate that the reference does not reduce the auditor's responsibility for that opinion. The same condition applies where law or regulation requires the reference to be made.

options.text: The reference is permitted here and needs no further wording, the disclaimer itself making clear that nothing has been concluded
options.misconception: makes the reference and drops the sentence the standard requires to accompany it
options.why: The added sentence is a requirement, not a courtesy. Without it a reader may take the mention of a specialist as a division of responsibility, which is the exact misreading the sentence exists to close off.

options.text: The expert may never be named in an auditor's report in any circumstances
options.misconception: takes the default silence for an absolute rule and loses the two exceptions written next to it
options.why: Silence is the default, not the rule. Law or regulation may require the reference, and the auditor may make it where it is relevant to understanding a modification.

citation.ref: Reference to the auditor's expert in the auditor's report

items.scenario: You disclaim an opinion on a company's financial statements because you could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the fair value of an unlisted investment. To make the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion section understandable you want to describe the work of the auditor's expert you engaged on that valuation and why it did not resolve the matter.

items.stem: What has he left out of the engagement quality control review?

options.text: Review of selected audit documentation relating to the significant judgments the engagement team made and the conclusions it reached, discussion of significant matters with the engagement partner, and — the client being a listed entity — consideration of the engagement team's evaluation of the firm's independence in relation to the engagement
options.why: SQC 1 makes an engagement quality control review an objective evaluation of the significant judgments made by the engagement team and of the conclusions reached in formulating the auditor's report, and it names what that evaluation involves: discussion of significant matters with the engagement partner, review of the financial statements and the proposed auditor's report, review of selected audit documentation relating to the significant judgments made and the conclusions reached, and evaluation of the conclusions reached in formulating the report. For a listed entity the reviewer also considers the engagement team's evaluation of the firm's independence in relation to the engagement, whether appropriate consultation has taken place on differences of opinion and other difficult or contentious matters, and whether the documentation selected reflects the work performed on the significant judgments.

options.text: Only the independence point, the review of working papers belonging to the engagement partner rather than to the reviewer
options.misconception: hands the documentation review back to the engagement partner, whose own judgments are the thing being reviewed
options.why: The engagement partner reviews the file as part of directing the engagement. The reviewer looks at selected documentation precisely because his subject is the significant judgments the partner and the team made, and he cannot evaluate those from the finished statements alone.

options.text: He should have re-performed the significant audit procedures himself, a review being worth nothing unless the work is done again
options.misconception: turns an objective evaluation of judgments into a second audit
options.why: SQC 1 asks for an objective evaluation of the significant judgments and the conclusions, not a re-performance. The reviewer reads selected documentation to test the reasoning; he does not redo the testing.

options.text: Nothing — the review is of the judgments and the report, and both were read before the report was dated
options.misconception: treats the output of the audit as the whole subject of the review and drops the documentation behind it
options.why: Reading the statements and the proposed report is one of four named steps. Without the selected documentation behind the significant judgments, the reviewer has nothing against which to test whether those judgments were sound.

citation.ref: The nature, timing and extent of an engagement quality control review, and the additional considerations for the audit of a listed entity

items.scenario: The engagement quality control reviewer on a listed company's audit reads the draft financial statements and the proposed auditor's report, is satisfied with both, and signs off before the report is dated. He opens no working paper, saying the engagement partner has already reviewed the file and a second reading of the same papers adds nothing. He also does not look at the engagement team's conclusion on the firm's independence, saying independence is settled centrally by the firm and is not an engagement matter.

items.stem: What does clause 3(xxi) actually reach?

options.text: The clause requires the opinion on the consolidated financial statements to be modified for the two component qualifications
options.misconception: reads a signpost as a modification, and a component's qualification as automatically material to the group
options.why: Clause 3(xxi) points the reader at where a component's own report already carries a qualification. Whether that matter is material to the consolidated financial statements as a whole is a separate evaluation under SA 705 (Revised), and it may well not be.

options.text: Only the components that are themselves covered by the Order — so the three Indian subsidiaries, of which two carry remarks to be reported; the small company, the banking subsidiary, the foreign subsidiary and the limited liability partnership contribute nothing to the clause and are not reported as clean either
options.why: Clause 3(xxi) asks whether there have been any qualifications or adverse remarks by the respective auditors in the CARO reports of the companies included in the consolidated financial statements, and where there have been, the auditor indicates the details of those companies together with the paragraph numbers of the reports containing them. A component with no CARO report supplies nothing to answer. The Order does not apply to a banking company, to a small company or to a section 8 company, and it does not reach an entity that is not a company under the Act at all, so a foreign body corporate and a limited liability partnership are outside it too — and saying they carry no adverse remarks asserts something the auditor has not examined.
keywords: companies included in the consolidated financial statements

options.text: Every component included in the consolidation, each answered clause by clause, since the reader of the consolidated statements is entitled to the same information as the reader of a standalone one
options.misconception: reads the one clause that survives consolidation as a licence to run the whole Order over the group
options.why: Only clause 3(xxi) operates on a report on consolidated financial statements. The other clauses attach to the auditor's report on the standalone financial statements of the companies the Order covers.

options.text: All seven components, with the four outside the Order reported as carrying no adverse remarks so that the clause is complete
options.misconception: fills a gap in the clause with a positive statement about entities that have no CARO report at all
options.why: A clean answer is an assertion. For a component the Order never touched there is no CARO report and no examination behind such an assertion, so the honest position is that the clause does not reach it.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xxi), read with the paragraph of the Order listing the companies to which it does not apply

items.scenario: The consolidated financial statements you are reporting on include three Indian subsidiaries covered by CARO 2020, one Indian subsidiary that is a small company, a banking subsidiary, a subsidiary incorporated outside India, and a limited liability partnership joint venture. Two of the three CARO-covered subsidiaries have qualifications in their CARO reports. Your manager proposes to state under clause 3(xxi) that the small company, the banking subsidiary, the foreign subsidiary and the limited liability partnership carry "no adverse remarks".

items.stem: What else does clause 3(iii) require to be reported?

options.text: The split between related and other borrowers is asked only of a company whose principal business is to give loans, so a manufacturer reports one aggregate
options.misconception: reverses the carve-out, which takes lending companies out of that sub-clause instead of confining it to them
options.why: The words in brackets exempt a company whose principal business is to give loans from sub-clause (a), and from the renewal disclosure in sub-clause (e). A manufacturer is squarely inside both.

options.text: The aggregate during the year and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date shown separately for subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates and for other parties; whether the schedule of repayment of principal and interest is stipulated and whether the receipts are regular; and the total amount overdue for more than ninety days with whether reasonable steps have been taken for recovery
options.why: Sub-clause (a) asks for the aggregate amount during the year and the balance outstanding at the balance sheet date, split between subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates on one side and other parties on the other, so one figure of ₹55 crore does not answer it. Sub-clause (c) asks separately whether a schedule of repayment of principal and interest has been stipulated and whether the receipts are regular — a schedule that exists and is not being met fails the second half. And where any amount is overdue, sub-clause (d) asks for the total amount overdue for more than ninety days and whether reasonable steps have been taken by the company for recovery of the principal and interest, which on these facts is nothing at all.

options.text: The overdue limb does not arise, a schedule having been stipulated and only one borrower being late
options.misconception: reads the overdue disclosure as a consequence of having no schedule, when it is triggered by the amount being unpaid
options.why: Sub-clause (d) is triggered by an amount being overdue, whatever the paperwork says. One hundred and forty days is beyond ninety, so the amount and the steps taken both have to be stated.

options.text: Nothing more — the terms are not prejudicial, and that is the judgement the clause exists to draw out
options.misconception: answers one sub-clause and reports the whole of clause 3(iii) as satisfied
options.why: Whether the terms are prejudicial is sub-clause (b). It sits beside the amounts, the schedule, the overdue position, the renewals and the on-demand loans, and each of those is answered on its own.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii)(a), clause 3(iii)(c) and clause 3(iii)(d)

items.scenario: A manufacturing company, whose principal business is not to give loans, granted ₹40 crore of loans to two subsidiaries and ₹15 crore to unrelated parties during the year. Every loan carries a written schedule for repayment of principal and interest. ₹6 crore of the subsidiary loans fell due and has been unpaid for one hundred and forty days, and the company has done nothing about it. The audit senior drafts clause 3(iii) as a single aggregate of ₹55 crore with a sentence that the terms are not prejudicial to the company's interest.

items.stem: Is the senior right?

options.text: No, and the whole consolidation must be rebuilt from the original acquisition date as though the 85 per cent had been held throughout
options.misconception: turns a fresh determination on the new tranche into a restatement of every earlier year
options.why: What is redone is the determination of goodwill or capital reserve and of the amount attributable to the non-controlling interests, on the new tranche and from its own date. Prior periods are not rewritten to pretend the holding was always 85 per cent.

options.text: No — permanent consolidation adjustments are made on the first occasion and again on any subsequent occasion on which there is a change in the shareholding of a consolidated entity, so the further 15 per cent reopens the determination of goodwill or capital reserve and of the amount attributable to the non-controlling interests
options.why: Permanent consolidation adjustments are those made only on the first occasion, or on subsequent occasions on which there is a change in the shareholding of a particular entity which is consolidated, and they are two: the determination of goodwill or capital reserve, and the determination of the amount of equity attributable to the minority or non-controlling interests. A purchase of a further 15 per cent is such a change. The auditor gives particular attention to the determination of the pre-acquisition reserves of the component, for which the dates of investment matter, and examines whether those reserves have been allocated appropriately between the parent and the non-controlling interests.

options.text: Yes — permanent adjustments take their name from being made once, on the first occasion of consolidation, and never revisited
options.misconception: keeps half the definition and drops the second trigger written into it
options.why: The definition has two occasions in it, not one: the first consolidation, and any later change in the shareholding. "Permanent" describes an adjustment that is not remade every year, not one that is never remade.

options.text: Yes, because the change happened part-way through the year rather than on the first day of it, so it falls into next year's consolidation
options.misconception: makes the trigger a date in the calendar rather than the change in shareholding itself
options.why: The trigger is the change in shareholding, and the date of investment is what fixes the pre-acquisition reserves to be allocated. A mid-year purchase is dealt with in the year it happens.

citation.ref: Ch. Group Audits — permanent consolidation adjustments and current period consolidation adjustments

items.scenario: A parent has held 70 per cent of a subsidiary for five years. On 1 October this year it bought a further 15 per cent, taking its holding to 85 per cent. The consolidation senior proposes to carry goodwill and the non-controlling interests' share of net assets forward at the figures computed on the original acquisition, on the ground that permanent consolidation adjustments are made only on the first occasion of consolidation, and to treat the intra-group eliminations as the only work of this year.

items.stem: What is the position under section 129?

options.text: Nothing need be attached about the subsidiaries, the consolidated statements already carrying their figures; and the consolidated statements are audited but are not laid before the members
options.misconception: assumes consolidation absorbs the component disclosure, and stops the audit short of adoption
options.why: Consolidation merges the numbers and hides the individual entities, which is why the separate statement of salient features exists. And section 129(4) carries the whole preparation, adoption and audit regime across, laying included.

options.text: The consolidated financial statements are prepared for information only, so no audit of them is required and Form AOC-1 replaces them
options.misconception: treats consolidated statements as a voluntary annexure rather than as statements the Act requires and the auditor reports on
options.why: Section 129(3) requires the consolidated financial statements themselves, and section 129(4) brings the audit requirement with them. Form AOC-1 sits beside them and replaces nothing.

options.text: The full financial statements of every subsidiary must be attached to the company's own financial statements
options.misconception: reads a statement of salient features as a requirement to annex the components entire
options.why: What is attached is a separate statement of the salient features in the prescribed form, not each subsidiary's complete financial statements.

options.text: A separate statement containing the salient features of the financial statement of each subsidiary must be attached in Form AOC-1; and the provisions of the Act on the preparation, adoption and audit of the financial statements of a holding company apply, mutatis mutandis, to the consolidated financial statements
options.why: The proviso to section 129(3) requires the company to attach along with its financial statement a separate statement containing the salient features of the financial statement of its subsidiaries, in Form AOC-1, and for this purpose the word subsidiary includes an associate company and a joint venture. Section 129(4) then provides that the provisions of the Act applicable to the preparation, adoption and audit of the financial statements of a holding company shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to the consolidated financial statements — so they are audited, adopted and laid before the members exactly as the standalone statements are.

citation.ref: Proviso to Section 129(3) with Rule 5 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, and Section 129(4)

items.scenario: A listed company with four subsidiaries and one associate is preparing consolidated financial statements for the first time. The company secretary asks two things: whether anything about the individual subsidiaries has to be attached to the financial statements, and whether the consolidated financial statements themselves have to be audited, adopted and laid before the members in the way the company's own financial statements are.

items.stem: What breaches Regulation 18?

options.text: Only the marketing director's membership — the expertise requirement and the chairperson's attendance are recommendations of good practice rather than requirements
options.misconception: sorts one requirement into the binding column and two identically worded ones into the advisory column
options.why: All three sit in the same sub-regulation and are worded the same way. Nothing marks the expertise requirement or the attendance requirement as advisory.

options.text: Nothing — three independent directors out of four satisfies the two-thirds test, and the rest of Regulation 18 is best practice
options.misconception: stops at the arithmetic of composition and treats every qualitative requirement as optional
options.why: The arithmetic is the part that passes. What fails is the set of qualifications and duties attaching to the members and to the chairperson, which the Regulation states as requirements.

options.text: Only the chairperson's absence — financial literacy is left to the board's judgement and the Regulation prescribes no expertise requirement
options.misconception: drops the two qualifications Regulation 18(1) states in terms and keeps only the attendance rule
options.why: Both qualifications are written into the Regulation, and financial literacy is even defined in it, so neither is a matter of the board's judgement.

options.text: Three things — every member must be financially literate, at least one member must have accounting or related financial management expertise, and the chairperson must be present at the annual general meeting to answer shareholder queries
options.why: Regulation 18(1) requires that all members of the audit committee shall be financially literate, meaning able to read and understand a balance sheet, a statement of profit and loss and a statement of cash flows, and that at least one member shall have accounting or related financial management expertise. It separately requires that the chairperson of the committee shall be an independent director and shall be present at the annual general meeting to answer shareholder queries. The counting is fine here: four directors with three independent clears the two-thirds test, and five meetings inside ninety-day gaps clears Regulation 18(2).
keywords: accounting or related financial management expertise

citation.ref: Regulation 18(1) — financial literacy of every member, accounting or related financial management expertise of at least one, and the chairperson's presence at the annual general meeting

items.scenario: A listed entity's audit committee has four directors, three of them independent, and met five times during the year with no gap longer than ninety days. Its chairperson is an independent director but did not attend the annual general meeting, the company having routed every shareholder question through the managing director. One member, the marketing director, says openly that he cannot read a statement of cash flows, and no member has any accounting or related financial management background.

items.stem: What do sections 177(5) and 177(6) allow the committee?

options.text: The chairman is right on both — the committee's investigative jurisdiction begins with a reference from the Board, and access to records and to outside advisers runs through the Board
options.misconception: reads the Board's reference as the only gateway, when the section gives two and neither depends on the Board
options.why: The section reads "in relation to the items specified in sub-section (4) or referred to it by the Board". Capital work in progress goes to the financial statement and to internal financial controls, both of which are in the terms of reference, so the committee is already inside its own jurisdiction.

options.text: To investigate any matter in relation to the items specified in the terms of reference or referred to it by the Board, with power to obtain professional advice from external sources and full access to information contained in the records of the company; and to call for the comments of the auditors about internal control systems and the scope of audit including their observations, and to review the financial statement before its submission to the Board
options.why: Section 177(6) gives the audit committee authority to investigate into any matter in relation to the items specified in sub-section (4) or referred to it by the Board, and for that purpose the power to obtain professional advice from external sources and full access to information contained in the records of the company. A reference from the Board is one way in, not the only way, and neither the outside advice nor the records need the Board's leave. Section 177(5) lets the committee call for the comments of the auditors about internal control systems, the scope of audit including the observations of the auditors, and review of the financial statement before their submission to the Board, and discuss any related issues with the internal and statutory auditors and with the management.

options.text: The committee may call for the auditors' comments but may not review the financial statement before it goes to the Board, review being the Board's own function
options.misconception: takes review of the financial statement out of a sub-section that names it
options.why: Section 177(5) names review of the financial statement before their submission to the Board as one of the things the committee may take up with the auditors. The Board's own review comes after, not instead.

options.text: The committee may investigate and may take outside advice, but access to the records is a matter for management, the committee being a committee of the Board rather than an authority over the company
options.misconception: grants the power and withholds the access the same sub-section grants alongside it
options.why: Full access to information contained in the records of the company is written into the same sub-section as the power to investigate and the power to take external advice. An investigation without the records would be the power without its subject.

citation.ref: Sections 177(5) and 177(6)

items.scenario: An audit committee suspects that ₹22 crore of capital work in progress at a plant is fictitious. The chairman of the Board tells the committee that it may look only into what the Board refers to it, that it cannot engage an outside forensic firm without the Board's sanction, and that the company's records are the Board's to release. The committee separately wants the statutory auditor's comments on the internal control systems and on the scope of the audit, and wants to review the financial statement before it goes to the Board.

items.stem: How do the four sit across the control types?

options.text: The first three are general IT controls — access security, program change, and data centre and network operations in that order — and the fourth is an application control inside the sales system
options.why: General IT controls govern the environment and are grouped by objective. Access security is about access to programs and data being authenticated and authorised to meet financial reporting objectives, and removing a terminated user's access on a timely basis sits there. Program change is about modified systems continuing to meet those objectives, and covers segregating development from production and having changes tested and approved before migration. Data centre and network operations is about production systems being backed up and monitored, and batch job schedules being monitored for failures. A validation that refuses an invoice with no customer code lives inside one system and tests one transaction, which is what an application control is.

options.text: All four are general IT controls, because every one of them is a failure of the company's information technology
options.misconception: sorts by where the failure happened rather than by what the control does
options.why: The split is not between technology and business. General controls hold the environment steady; application controls test individual transactions inside one system, which is exactly what the customer-code validation does.

options.text: The first is an application control and the fourth a general IT control, access being granted inside the application and a validation rule being part of the platform
options.misconception: reverses the two clearest cases by looking at where a setting is typed rather than at what it governs
options.why: Access provisioning is a general control however it is administered, because it governs who may reach the programs and the data. A field validation inside the sales system governs one transaction, so it is an application control.

options.text: All four are application controls, since each one is a rule the company's software was supposed to enforce
options.misconception: reads anything a computer does as an application control
options.why: User access administration, change management and batch scheduling are not features of one application. They are the environment every application on the platform runs inside.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance — the control objectives and controls for each area of general IT controls

items.scenario: Four weaknesses come out of one company's information technology environment. A terminated employee's login was still active four months after he left. A change to the pricing master was migrated into production without testing and without approval. The overnight batch job failed twice in March and nobody was told. And the sales system accepts and posts an invoice that carries no customer code.

items.stem: How many of the Board's four instructions match how an investigation actually runs?

options.text: The materiality instruction and the timetable, an investigation still being bound by the same thresholds and the same reporting cycle as the audit it grows out of
options.misconception: carries the audit's sampling and reporting rhythm into a probe that is defined by not having them
options.why: Materiality and a fixed reporting cycle belong to an audit, which uses test checking and sampling to form an opinion. An investigation requires a detailed study and examination of the facts and figures in the selected area, on whatever period the question needs.

options.text: All four — an investigation by a chartered accountant follows the same materiality, evidence and reporting discipline as an audit, only aimed at a narrower question
options.misconception: treats an investigation as an audit with a smaller scope, when the evidence standard and the reporting audience both change
options.why: Narrowness of subject is only one of the differences. The evidence sought is conclusive rather than persuasive, nothing is taken on a stated fact, the period is open, and the report goes to whoever commissioned it.

options.text: The reporting instruction only, because an investigation ordered by the Board of a company must ultimately be reported to the members who own it
options.misconception: routes the report to the owners because the entity is a company, when the subject is who commissioned the work
options.why: An audit's outcome is reported to the owners of the business entity. An investigation's outcome goes to the person or persons on whose behalf it was carried out, and even a third party may appoint an investigator.

options.text: None of the four — an investigation seeks conclusive evidence rather than persuasive, does not accept a stated fact until it is substantiated, is not limited by a rigid time frame and may cover several years, and reports to the person or persons on whose behalf it is carried out
options.why: The differences from an audit are what the examiner asks for. An investigation seeks substantive and in some cases conclusive evidence, where an audit is mainly concerned with prima facie or persuasive evidence. An investigator does not accept a stated fact as correct until it is substantiated, while an auditor relies on stated facts in the absence of suspicious circumstances. The work is not limited by a rigid time frame and may cover several years, because the outcome is not certain at the start. And the outcome is reported to the person or persons on whose behalf the investigation is carried out — here the Board that ordered it, not the shareholders in general meeting.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — audit versus investigation

items.scenario: The Board asks you to establish whether the head of procurement took kickbacks over the last four years. It hands you four instructions with the engagement letter: work only to the current year's audit materiality; accept the procurement head's written explanations where nothing on the file contradicts them; present your findings to the shareholders at the annual general meeting; and finish inside the statutory audit's timetable.

items.stem: What is the position under sections 22A and 22G?

options.text: Both may appeal, an appellate body existing to hear anyone dissatisfied with the decision below
options.misconception: assumes a general right of appeal for a complainant, which section 22G does not create
options.why: The section names who may appeal, and a complainant is not on the list. A general right of appeal for anybody dissatisfied would have to be written in, and it is not.

options.text: The Director (Discipline) may appeal where the Council so authorises him and the complainant company may not, the appeal lying to a member aggrieved by an order and to the Director (Discipline) alone — and the Authority is a person who is or has been a judge of a High Court as Chairperson, two members nominated by the Council from among its own members, and two members nominated by the Central Government
options.why: Section 22A has the Central Government constitute an Appellate Authority consisting of a person who is or has been a judge of a High Court as Chairperson, two members nominated by the Council from among its own members, and two members nominated by the Central Government from among persons of ability, integrity and standing having special knowledge of law, economics, business, commerce or accountancy. Section 22G opens the appeal to a member of the Institute aggrieved by an order of the Board of Discipline or of the Disciplinary Committee, and by a proviso to the Director (Discipline) where the Council so authorises him. A complainant is neither of those, so the company has no appeal to the Authority.

options.text: The complainant may appeal and the Director (Discipline) may not, an officer of the Institute having no standing to challenge the Institute's own Committee
