options.misconception: inverts both halves of the section
options.why: It is the other way round. The member and the Director (Discipline) have the appeal; the complainant does not.

options.text: Neither may appeal, the Authority hearing only a member on whom a penalty has been imposed, so an officer of the Institute has no standing
options.misconception: keeps the member's right and loses the proviso that gives the Director (Discipline) his
options.why: The proviso to section 22G is exactly the answer to that: the Director (Discipline) may also appeal against a decision of the Board of Discipline or the Disciplinary Committee, if so authorised by the Council.

citation.ref: Section 22A on the constitution of the Appellate Authority, and Section 22G with its proviso on who may prefer an appeal

items.scenario: The Board of Discipline finds a member not guilty and closes a complaint. The complainant, a company, wants to take the closure to the Appellate Authority. In an unrelated matter the Council considers an order of the Disciplinary Committee far too lenient and wants the Director (Discipline) to challenge it. A member sitting in on both asks who actually sits on the Authority.

items.stem: Which of the four is professional misconduct under Clause 10?

options.text: All four, Clause 10 admitting no exception once a fee moves with an outcome
options.misconception: reads the clause without the words that carry the exception into Regulation 192
options.why: The clause itself says "except as permitted under any regulation made under this Act". Three of the four sit inside those permitted cases, which is the whole point of reading the clause and the regulation together.

options.text: The second and the fourth — a percentage of working capital is a percentage of profits under another name
options.misconception: treats a permitted base for a co-operative society audit as if it were the prohibited profit base
options.why: Regulation 192 names the paid-up capital, the working capital, the gross or net income and the profits, all four, as permitted bases for the auditor of a co-operative society. Working capital is on the list in terms.

options.text: Only the fourth
options.why: Clause 10 bars fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon the findings or results of the professional employment, except as permitted under any regulation made under the Act, and the exception is Regulation 192. That regulation permits a valuer for the purposes of direct taxes and duties to charge on a percentage of the value of the property valued, and permits the auditor of a co-operative society to charge on a percentage of the paid-up capital, the working capital, the gross or net income or the profits. The Council has separately permitted a percentage or contingent basis for debt recovery services, alongside certain management consultancy services, fund raising services and cost optimisation services. A certification fee that rises with the credit limit a bank chooses to sanction is outside every one of those cases, and it is contingent on the result of the very work certified.
keywords: percentage of the value of the property valued

options.text: None, Regulation 192 permitting a percentage fee wherever the client has agreed to one in writing
options.misconception: turns a closed list of permitted engagements into a consent rule
options.why: Regulation 192 permits particular engagements on a percentage basis, and consent is not one of the conditions. A client's agreement cannot bring an engagement inside a list it is not on.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 10, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: A member in practice takes four engagements in one year, each on a percentage basis agreed in writing. As a valuer of a factory building for the purposes of direct taxes, at a stated percentage of the value he determines. As auditor of a co-operative society, at a stated percentage of its working capital. Providing a debt recovery service to a manufacturer, at a stated percentage of the debt actually recovered. And certifying a company's turnover for its bankers, at a stated percentage of the credit limit the bank goes on to sanction.

items.stem: What happens next?

options.text: Neither is right — the Director (Discipline) places all the information and the complaint before the Board of Discipline whatever Schedule was invoked, and the Board either agrees with him and closes the matter or disagrees, in which case it may advise him to investigate further, proceed with the matter itself where it is allied to the First Schedule, or refer it to the Disciplinary Committee where it is allied to the Second Schedule or to both
options.why: Which Schedule the clause sits in decides the forum only where the prima facie opinion is that the member is guilty. Where the Director (Discipline) is of the opinion that the member is not guilty, he submits all the information and complaints to the Board of Discipline whatever the clause complained of, and it is the Board that decides what happens. If it agrees, the matter is closed. If it disagrees, it may advise the Director (Discipline) to further investigate the matter, may proceed with the matter itself if it is allied to the First Schedule, or may refer the matter to the Disciplinary Committee if it is allied to the Second Schedule or to both the Schedules.

options.text: The complainant is right — a Second Schedule allegation goes to the Disciplinary Committee whatever the Director (Discipline) thinks of it
options.misconception: applies the guilty routing to a not-guilty opinion, so that the Schedule decides the forum in every case
options.why: The routing by Schedule operates on a prima facie opinion of guilt. On a not-guilty opinion there is one destination whatever the Schedule, and that is the Board of Discipline.

options.text: The complaint goes to the Appellate Authority, which is where a complainant dissatisfied with the closure of his complaint takes it
options.misconception: reaches for the appeal route before the first-instance body has even seen the matter
options.why: The Appellate Authority hears appeals against orders of the Board of Discipline and the Disciplinary Committee, from a member on whom a penalty was imposed or from the Director (Discipline) where the Council authorises him. Nothing has yet reached it, and a complainant has no appeal to it in any case.

options.text: The member is right — a prima facie opinion that he is not guilty closes the file, the Director (Discipline) being the officer the Act charges with forming it
options.misconception: gives the Director's opinion a finality the Act deliberately withholds
options.why: The Director (Discipline) forms the opinion; he does not dispose of the complaint. A not-guilty opinion goes to the Board of Discipline for it to accept or reject, which is what stops one officer from closing complaints alone.

citation.ref: Section 21 read with the Chartered Accountants (Procedure of Investigations of Professional and Other Misconduct and Cases) Rules, 2007 — the route where the prima facie opinion is not guilty

items.scenario: A complaint against a member alleges gross negligence in the conduct of his professional duties, which is a clause of Part I of the Second Schedule. The Director (Discipline) examines it and forms a prima facie opinion that the member is not guilty. The complainant insists the matter must still go to the Disciplinary Committee, because the clause complained of sits in the Second Schedule. The member insists the Director's opinion ends the matter there and then.

items.stem: Are the two a network, and what follows for P?

options.text: No — a network requires common ownership, control or management, and two firms with no common partner cannot have it
options.misconception: reads one alternative test as the essential one, so that separate ownership settles the question
options.why: Common ownership, control or management is again one entry among six. Separate partners, separate profits and separate deeds do not undo a network built on any of the others.

options.text: Yes, but the consequence stops at disclosure — P discloses the relationship to those charged with governance and continues
options.misconception: substitutes disclosure for the independence requirement that membership of a network actually attracts
options.why: Membership of a network makes the independence requirements applying to an audit client of the firm apply to the network firm too. A material financial interest in the audit client is not a matter that disclosure cures.

options.text: Yes — a larger structure aimed at co-operation that shares common quality control policies and procedures, or that shares a common business strategy, is a network on either of those tests standing alone, so Q's shareholding is treated as though P held it and P is not independent of the audit client
options.why: A network is a larger structure aimed at co-operation between firms which also does any one of a list of things: shares profits or costs, has common ownership, control or management, shares common quality control policies and procedures, shares a common business strategy, uses a common brand name, or shares a significant part of professional resources. Each of those tests stands on its own, so a quality control manual applied across both firms with cross review, or a signed common business strategy, makes a network with no brand, no shared people and no shared money anywhere in the arrangement. The consequence is the reason the definition exists: the independence requirements that apply to an audit client of the firm apply to a network firm too, so a financial interest that is material to Q is treated as though P held it.

options.text: No — a network needs a common brand name or a significant part of the professional resources shared, and neither is present
options.misconception: takes two of the alternative tests as the only two, when the list is disjunctive
options.why: The brand and the shared resources are two entries on a list of six, and any one entry is enough. Two other entries are met here in terms.

citation.ref: The definition of a network and of a network firm, and the application to a network firm of the independence requirements for an audit client of the firm

items.scenario: Two firms practise in different cities under different names. They share no brand, no letterhead, no office, no staff, no specialists and no profits or costs; they have no common partner and no common ownership, control or management. What they do share is one written quality control manual adopted by both, under which each reviews a sample of the other's engagements, and a signed three-year business plan setting common target sectors and a common pricing policy. Firm P audits a listed company. Firm Q holds a shareholding in that same company which is material to Q.

items.stem: What does the Code require?

options.text: Both may be assigned, the Code's provisions running only the other way — on a partner or employee leaving the firm for the client
options.misconception: keeps only the outward movement and misses that the Code answers both directions separately
options.why: The Code deals with both directions. Going out, a former partner joining the client raises a familiarity or intimidation threat unless no significant connection remains with the firm. Coming in is the case here, and it has its own rule.

options.text: The first may not be assigned to the audit team at all, his employment having occurred during the period covered by the audit report; the second may be, the threats from his earlier service being evaluated and addressed, for example by having an appropriate reviewer review the work he performs
options.why: Where an individual who was a director or officer of the audit client, or an employee in a position to exert significant influence over the preparation of the client's accounting records or financial statements, joins the firm, he shall not be assigned to the audit team if that service or employment occurred during the period covered by the audit report. That is a bar rather than a threat to be weighed, and no reviewer cures it, because the individual would be auditing records he himself prepared. Where the service was before the period covered by the report, the firm evaluates the self-interest, self-review and familiarity threats and addresses those that are not at an acceptable level, and having an appropriate reviewer review the individual's work is one of the actions available.
keywords: period covered by the audit report

options.text: Both may be assigned, the reviewing partner being the safeguard the Code asks for in either case
options.misconception: treats an outright bar as a threat that a safeguard can bring to an acceptable level
options.why: For service during the period covered by the report the Code does not offer safeguards; it says the individual shall not be assigned to the team. Safeguards belong to the other case, where the service predates that period.

options.text: Neither may be assigned, anybody who has ever worked for the client being barred from its audit team
options.misconception: extends the bar to any past employment, losing both the timing test and the significant-influence test
options.why: The bar is drawn by two conditions: the individual's role at the client, and whether the service fell within the period covered by the audit report. A treasury employee of three years ago meets neither.

citation.ref: Employment with an audit client — an individual who has served with the client joining the firm

items.scenario: Two recruits join an audit firm in April. One was until March the financial controller of a listed audit client of the firm and personally prepared the accounting records for the year now under audit. The other left the same client's treasury department three years ago and was never in a position to exert significant influence over the preparation of its accounting records or its financial statements. The engagement partner proposes to put both on that client's audit team, with a second partner reviewing whatever they do.

items.stem: What provision do the three actually require?

options.text: ₹30 lakh on A, ₹12.5 lakh on B and ₹45 lakh on C
options.misconception: treats pending recovery proceedings as a reason to hold a loss asset at a part provision
options.why: A loss asset is one where loss has been identified but the amount has not been written off. So long as it stays on the books the whole outstanding is provided; the recovery proceedings do not scale the provision down.

options.text: ₹12 lakh on A, ₹12.5 lakh on B and ₹90 lakh on C
options.misconception: nets the ECGC cover off the outstanding before applying the substandard rate, which the norm forbids in terms
options.why: The 15 per cent on a substandard asset is computed on the total outstanding without any allowance for ECGC guarantee cover or for securities available. Deducting the cover first is the single commonest error on this norm.

options.text: ₹30 lakh on A, ₹7.5 lakh on B and ₹90 lakh on C
options.misconception: applies the same 15 per cent to a secured and an unsecured substandard exposure
options.why: An unsecured exposure identified as substandard carries an additional 10 per cent over the general provision, taking it to 25 per cent. On ₹50 lakh that is ₹12.5 lakh, not ₹7.5 lakh.

options.text: ₹30 lakh on A, ₹12.5 lakh on B and ₹90 lakh on C
options.why: A substandard asset carries a general provision of 15 per cent of the total outstanding, and the norm says in terms that it is made without making any allowance for ECGC guarantee cover and securities available — so A needs 15 per cent of the whole ₹200 lakh, which is ₹30 lakh, and the branch is short by ₹18 lakh. An exposure identified as substandard that is unsecured carries an additional 10 per cent, 25 per cent in all, so B needs ₹12.5 lakh. A loss asset should be written off, and where it is permitted to remain on the books 100 per cent of the outstanding is provided, so C needs the whole ₹90 lakh.
keywords: 15 per cent of the total outstanding

citation.ref: Prudential norms on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning — the provisioning norms for substandard assets and for loss assets

items.scenario: A branch has three advances at the year end. Advance A of ₹200 lakh is classified substandard and is fully secured; it also carries ECGC guarantee cover of ₹120 lakh, and the branch has provided ₹12 lakh, being 15 per cent of the ₹80 lakh left after deducting that cover. Advance B of ₹50 lakh is classified substandard and is wholly unsecured; the branch has provided ₹7.5 lakh. Advance C of ₹90 lakh has been identified as a loss asset and remains on the books while recovery proceedings run; the branch has provided ₹45 lakh.

items.stem: What else must the additional report cover?

options.text: Whether the company is engaged in the business of a non-banking financial institution and, on its asset pattern and income pattern, is entitled to continue to hold the certificate; whether the Board has passed the resolution the directions require for a company not accepting public deposits and whether any have in fact been accepted; whether the prudential norms on income recognition, accounting standards, asset classification and provisioning have been complied with; and, where it applies, whether the capital adequacy ratio has been correctly determined and reported
options.why: The directions the Reserve Bank issues to auditors of non-banking financial companies set out the matters the additional report to the Board must carry, and holding a certificate of registration granted under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 is only the first of them. Continued entitlement to hold that certificate turns on the asset pattern and the income pattern as at the year end. For a company that does not accept public deposits, the board resolution to that effect and whether any deposits were in fact accepted are separate matters. Compliance with the prudential norms on income recognition, accounting standards, asset classification and provisioning is another, and where the requirement applies to the company, the correct determination and reporting of the capital adequacy ratio is another again.

options.text: Nothing else — the certificate of registration is the whole subject of the additional report, everything else being covered by the report under section 143
options.misconception: shrinks a report with a named list of matters down to its first item
options.why: The directions list the matters, and registration is one of several. The report under section 143 is on the financial statements and answers a different question for different readers.

options.text: The capital adequacy ratio and the prudential norms only, the registration and deposit matters applying to deposit-taking companies alone
options.misconception: assumes the deposit-related matters drop out for a company that takes no deposits, when they are precisely the matters it must report on
options.why: For a company not accepting public deposits the directions ask exactly that: whether the Board has passed the required resolution and whether the company has nonetheless accepted any. The duty exists because the company says it takes none.

options.text: A summary of the observations in the report under section 143, the additional report being the regulator's copy of the statutory one
options.misconception: treats the additional report as a duplicate rather than as a separate report on separate matters
options.why: The additional report is a distinct report to the Board on matters the directions specify. It is not a précis of the opinion on the financial statements, and most of what it covers appears nowhere in that opinion.

citation.source: Reserve Bank of India directions to auditors of non-banking financial companies
citation.ref: The matters to be included in the auditor's additional report to the Board of Directors, read with section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

items.scenario: You are drafting the additional report to the Board of Directors of a non-banking financial company that does not accept public deposits. Your assistant has covered one matter only — whether the company holds a certificate of registration — and says everything else belongs in the report on the financial statements under section 143, because the Board already sees that.

items.stem: Which of the three positions does the Act support?

options.text: Only the refusal of inspection — the qualifications go before the general meeting and no further, and the auditor has a standing right to attend whether or not notice reaches him
options.misconception: swaps the two limbs, denying the inspection section 145 gives and inventing a right to attend that does not depend on the notice the company must send
options.why: Section 145 makes the qualifications open to inspection by any member as well as read before the meeting, and section 146 requires the notices to be forwarded to the auditor.

options.text: Only the exemption — the company may exempt the auditor from attending, but the notice of the meeting must still be forwarded to him, and the qualifications in his report are open to inspection by any member
options.why: Section 146 requires that all notices of, and other communications relating to, any general meeting be forwarded to the auditor, and that he shall attend the meeting either himself or through his authorised representative unless otherwise exempted by the company. So the exemption is the company's to give and the notice is not its to withhold. Section 145 separately requires the qualifications, observations or comments on financial transactions or matters which have any adverse effect on the functioning of the company to be read before the company in general meeting and to be open to inspection by any member of the company.
keywords: unless otherwise exempted by the company
open to inspection by any member

options.text: All three — attendance is the auditor's own choice, so no notice is needed, and inspection of an audit report is a matter between the company and the Registrar
options.misconception: treats attendance as the auditor's discretion, when section 146 makes it a duty that only the company can waive, and treats the member's inspection right as if it did not exist
options.why: The notice is forwarded to the auditor as a matter of right under section 146, and section 145 gives every member inspection of the qualifications. Neither depends on what the auditor would prefer to do.

options.text: None — the notice must be sent, the company has no power to excuse the auditor from attending, and the member is entitled to inspect
options.misconception: reads the attendance duty in section 146 as absolute and misses the words "unless otherwise exempted by the company" sitting inside it
options.why: Two of the three limbs here are right, which is what makes the option tempting, but the section does allow the company to exempt the auditor from attending.

citation.ref: Section 146 read with section 145

items.scenario: A company is preparing for its annual general meeting. It does not send the notice of the meeting to its auditor, saying he has no business at a meeting of shareholders. Its board separately passes a resolution exempting the auditor from attending this year's meeting and writes to tell him so. After the meeting a member asks the company to let him inspect the two qualifications carried in the auditor's report, and is refused on the ground that inspection of an audit report is a matter for the Registrar.

items.stem: How does the financial due diligence treat them?

options.text: All three are deducted in arriving at normalised earnings, because each will reduce the profits the buyer earns after completion
options.misconception: runs a one-off structural exposure through an earnings multiple, which prices a single event as though it recurred every year
options.why: Normalisation strips out what will not recur and puts in the costs the business will bear year after year; a one-time acceleration or a lost lease is neither.

options.text: None — a contingency that has not crystallised is outside a due diligence, which reports on the figures the accounts actually carry
options.misconception: confuses due diligence with an audit of the past, when the assignment is to price what the buyer is acquiring going forward
options.why: The report states findings of fact about the target's whole position for the party who engaged it, and a term that fires on completion is part of that position.

options.text: All three are reported as liabilities the transaction itself will trigger — they sit outside the historical accounts and outside the earnings adjustment, and they drive the price, the warranties and the indemnities, and the consents to be obtained before completion
options.why: A due diligence works out what the buyer is actually buying rather than verifying last year's profit, so a lease, a borrowing or a customer contract carrying a change-of-control clause that the transaction itself will trigger is exactly the kind of hidden liabilities the assignment exists to find. None of them is an adjustment to normalised earnings, because none describes the sustainable trading of the business; they change what the buyer must pay, promise or obtain, which is why they feed the price, the warranties and the indemnities.

options.text: Only the loan, which is added to net debt because it becomes repayable; the lease and the customer contract are ordinary commercial risks the buyer simply accepts and no report is needed on them
options.misconception: reports one of the three and drops the two that can destroy the value being bought, when all three are triggered by the same event
options.why: Net debt collects what is debt-like at completion on the existing terms. Whether the acceleration is shown there or as a hidden liability, the lease and the customer contract still have to be reported, because each can remove what the buyer is paying for.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — hidden liabilities identified in a financial due diligence, including guarantees, onerous contracts and change-of-control clauses that the transaction itself triggers

items.scenario: On a share purchase of a manufacturer, the diligence turns up three things the audited accounts show nothing about. The factory lease lets the landlord terminate on a change in the target's controlling shareholder. A term loan becomes immediately repayable on a change of control. And the target's largest customer contract lets the customer walk away if the target is acquired by a competitor, which the buyer is. The seller says none of them is a liability today, so none belongs in the report.

items.stem: What is the defect in what the team did?

options.text: Nothing of substance — the copies carry the same content as the originals, and the content is what the findings rest on
options.misconception: treats forensic evidence as information, when what makes it evidence is that its handling can be proved from the moment it was taken
options.why: A perfect copy whose handling cannot be traced proves nothing about where it came from, which is the first question it will be asked.

options.text: The team should have obtained the suspect's written consent before examining the laptop, without which nothing found on it may be used
options.misconception: invents a consent precondition; the failing here is the record of handling, not permission to look at a machine the entity itself owns
options.why: The investigator's problem is not that he looked. It is that he cannot show what he did with what he found.

options.text: The chain of custody is broken and nothing records who held the evidence when — a gap of that kind lets the evidence be challenged or makes it inadmissible, and deleting the originals destroys the source the copies would have to be proved against
options.why: A forensic engagement produces evidence meant to stand where it will be read, so the team must be able to show a clear chain of custody until the evidence is presented in court. Where evidence is inconclusive, or where there are gaps in the chain of custody, it may be challenged in court or even become inadmissible. Copying to a personal device with no record of handling, and deleting the originals from the machine they came from, leaves findings that may well be true sitting on evidence nobody can rely on.

options.text: Only that the laptop was returned too soon; the copying and the deletion were sound precautions against tampering by the suspect
options.misconception: calls destruction of the source a precaution, when removing the original is the one step that cannot be undone and is the suspect's strongest argument
options.why: Preserving the original and imaging it is how tampering is guarded against; deleting it removes the only thing the copy could ever be checked against.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — collecting evidence that can be used in court and keeping a clear chain of custody, gaps in which may leave the evidence challengeable or inadmissible

items.scenario: Investigating a suspected procurement fraud, the team takes the suspect's laptop, copies the folders it wants onto a team member's personal pen drive, deletes those folders from the laptop so the suspect cannot alter them, and returns the laptop the same evening. No record is kept of who held the laptop, the pen drive or the files at any point. The findings that come out of the copies are clear, and the team writes them up.

items.stem: What has to happen before the working paper's claim to a complete population can stand?

options.text: The 4 per cent difference should be projected across the flagged exceptions so that its effect on the financial statements can be measured
options.misconception: projects from a sample when the problem is that the population was never obtained; projection answers a sampling question, not a completeness one
options.why: There is nothing to project from here. The missing records were never tested, so no conclusion about them can be extrapolated from the ones that were.

options.text: The extraction has to be reconciled to a control total in the accounting records and the parameters it was run with have to be checked — here the date range is a month short and the extracted total does not agree to the trial balance, so the analytic covered part of the population and the coverage claim is unsupported
options.why: Data extracted from the entity's systems is information produced by the entity, so the auditor obtains audit evidence about its accuracy and completeness before relying on anything run over it — reconciling the extraction to the general ledger or to another control total, and checking the parameters the extraction was run with. A date range ending in February leaves March out, and a total below the trial balance says records are missing. Until both are resolved, one hundred per cent describes the extract and not the population.
keywords: parameters the extraction was run with

options.text: A written representation from management that the download given to the team was complete and accurate
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for evidence about information the entity itself produced, which is the one thing a representation cannot supply
options.why: A representation is not audit evidence about the accuracy of the very data the entity handed over, and the reconciliation that would settle it is available in the file.

options.text: Nothing — the analytic ran over every record the system returned, and what the system returns is the population
options.misconception: treats the extract as the population, when the extract is only what somebody asked the system for on the parameters he happened to type
options.why: The system returned what it was asked for. Whether that was the population is the question the reconciliation answers.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance, read with SA 500 on information produced by the entity

items.scenario: The team asks the client's IT department for a download of all sales invoices for the year and runs an analytic over it looking for credit notes issued to the same customer within seven days of the invoice. The working paper records that the population tested was complete. Two things sit in the file that nobody has looked at: the extraction request names a date range running from 1 April to 28 February, and the total of the invoices extracted is 4 per cent below the revenue figure in the trial balance.

items.stem: Has the team put the disclosures in the right sections?

options.text: No — all three are in the wrong place. Section A carries the general description of the entity, Section B carries the policy and management process disclosures, and Section C carries the performance against the nine principles
options.why: The report has three sections and each has its own content. Section A is general disclosures about the entity, its products, operations, employees and group companies. Section B is management process and policy disclosures covering governance, leadership and oversight. Section C is principle-wise performance disclosures against the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct, and Section C alone is the one that splits into essential and leadership indicators.

options.text: Only the policy disclosures are misplaced; product and employee details belong in Section C alongside the performance figures
options.misconception: pulls the entity's general description into the performance section, which reports against the nine principles rather than describing the company
options.why: Products, operations and employee numbers are the general disclosures Section A asks for. Section C reports what the entity did against each principle.

options.text: Yes — the prescribed format leaves the ordering to the entity so long as every required disclosure appears somewhere in the report
options.misconception: treats a prescribed format as a checklist with no structure, when the three sections are what make one company's report comparable with another's
options.why: Each section is defined by what belongs in it, and a reader looking for the entity's governance policies goes to Section B because that is where the format puts them.

options.text: No, but only because Section B has been left empty — Sections A and C may be completed in either order
options.misconception: invents an ordering freedom the format does not give, and misses that Section A's own content has been moved out of it
options.why: Section B is not empty here; the policy disclosures that belong in it have been put in Section A, and Section A's own content has gone to Section C.

citation.ref: Regulation 34(2)(f) read with the prescribed BRSR format, Sections A, B and C

items.scenario: A listed company is drafting its first Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. Its team puts the details of the company's products, its plant locations and its employee numbers into Section C; its policy on responsible business conduct and how the board oversees that policy into Section A; and its principle-wise performance figures into Section B.

items.stem: Under which principles do the two disclosures belong?

options.text: The first under Principle 5, respect for and promotion of human rights, privacy being a right; the second under Principle 2, safe and sustainable goods and services
options.misconception: sends a consumer disclosure to the human rights principle and a life-cycle environmental disclosure to the design principle, leaving Principles 6 and 9 with nothing to report
options.why: Principle 5 is human rights read against the Constitution, national law and the International Bill of Human Rights, and Principle 2 is about design, production methods and reduce, reuse and recycle. Neither is where these two disclosures sit.

options.text: The first under Principle 1, ethics, transparency and accountability, data handling being a governance matter; the second under Principle 8, inclusive growth and equitable development
options.misconception: treats every disclosure about conduct as Principle 1 and every environmental harm to communities as Principle 8, which is how candidates collapse nine principles into two
options.why: Principle 1 carries the anti-bribery and disclosure machinery, and Principle 8 carries inclusive growth including land acquisition and displacement. Neither reaches these facts.

options.text: The first under Principle 9, providing value to consumers responsibly; the second under Principle 6, protection and restoration of the environment
options.why: Principle 9 is providing value to consumers responsibly — reducing negative impacts, not restricting freedom of choice, disclosing adverse impacts accurately, and respecting the customer's right to privacy when handling customer data. Principle 6 is protection and restoration of the environment across the whole life cycle of the product, with measurement of pollution, waste, energy and land use and a contribution to climate resilience in line with India's commitments including the Paris Agreement.

options.text: Both under Principle 6, since electronic waste and customer data are both things the product leaves behind
options.misconception: reads Principle 6 as covering everything a product leaves behind, when personal data is not an environmental impact and has its own principle
options.why: Principle 6 is measured in pollution, waste, energy and land use. Data privacy is disclosed under the consumer principle.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — Principle 6 on protection and restoration of the environment across the life cycle of the product and Principle 9 on providing value to consumers responsibly

items.scenario: A consumer electronics company is mapping two disclosures to the principles for Section C of its report. The first sets out how it handles the personal data its customers give it and how it avoids restricting a customer's freedom to choose between its own accessories and other makers'. The second sets out the environmental impact of the product across the whole of its life, from the materials drawn in to the electronic waste left at the end, together with the company's contribution to India's commitments under the Paris Agreement.

items.stem: How does section 27 treat the two new offices?

options.text: Raipur complies and the second Nagpur office fails, because an exemption cannot be claimed where no member has been named at all
options.misconception: treats the exemption as something claimed by naming somebody, when it removes the requirement of a second member altogether
options.why: Where the exemption applies, both offices may be under the same charge and no second member is needed. Raipur is the office that fails, because the man named is neither a partner nor an employee nor actually in charge.

options.text: Both comply — the Nagpur office is in the same city and Raipur has a member of the Institute named as in charge, which is all the section asks for
options.misconception: reads "a member of the Institute" on its own and drops the requirement that he be a partner or in whole-time employment, and that he actually be in charge
options.why: The words are met on their face and the substance is not: a monthly visitor with his own separate practice is not in separate charge of the office.

options.text: Both fail — the Council's exemptions relieve only a second office in the same premises, and every office anywhere else needs its own member
options.misconception: shortens the exemptions to the same-premises case and drops the same-city limb and the prescribed-distance limb sitting beside it
options.why: The exemptions cover the same premises, the same city, and a distance from the municipal limits that the Council's guidelines prescribe.

options.text: The second Nagpur office is covered by the Council's exemption for an office in the same city, so it needs no second member; Raipur fails, because the member in charge of a firm's office must ordinarily be a partner or in the firm's whole-time employment and must actually be in charge
options.why: Section 27 requires each office of a member or a firm in India to be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute, and the Council's general exemptions relieve that where the second office is in the same premises or in the same city as the first. Naming an outside practitioner does not satisfy the section: the member in separate charge must ordinarily be either a partner of the firm or a member in whole-time employment with it, and he is expected to be actually in charge, attending the office rather than merely named on a letter.

citation.ref: Section 27, read with the Council's general exemptions from separate charge of a second office and the requirement that the member in separate charge of a firm's office be a partner or in whole-time employment with the firm

items.scenario: A firm has its head office in Nagpur. It opens a second office across the same city, and a third in Raipur. For Raipur it names CA Deshpande, a member of the Institute who is neither a partner of the firm nor in its employment; he runs his own practice elsewhere, has agreed to let his name be given as the member in charge, and visits once a month. For the second Nagpur office it names nobody at all.

items.stem: Which of the three disclosures is within Clause 2 of Part II of the Second Schedule?

options.text: Only the first — the board's written authorisation is the employer's permission; her own view that the study is harmless is not an exception, and the customer's consent cannot release her because the confidence is not the customer's to waive
options.why: Clause 2 of Part II of the Second Schedule makes it professional misconduct for a member, being an employee, to disclose confidential information acquired in the course of his employment, except as and when required by any law for the time being in force or except as permitted by the employer. Two doors lead out and there is no third. The board's written authorisation is the second of them. A member's own judgement that a disclosure is harmless is not a door, and a customer's consent is not the employer's permission.
keywords: acquired in the course of his employment

options.text: None — an employee may never disclose information acquired in the course of his employment, the clause admitting no exception at all
options.misconception: drops both exceptions the clause writes out, one of which is the employer's own permission
options.why: The clause names two exceptions on its face, and the board's written authorisation is squarely inside one of them.

options.text: The first and the third — consent from the person the information is about releases the member in either case
options.misconception: borrows the consent rule from the confidentiality clause that binds a member in practice, where it is the client's consent that counts, and applies it to information the employer holds
options.why: The practice clause sits in Part I and turns on the client's consent. This one sits in Part II and turns on the employer's permission, and the two are not interchangeable.

options.text: The first and the second — a disclosure that harms nobody and serves the whole industry is outside the mischief the clause is aimed at
options.misconception: reads a harm test into a clause that has none; the clause turns on permission and on legal compulsion, not on consequences
options.why: Whether the benchmarking study hurts anyone is not the question the clause asks. It asks whether a law required the disclosure or the employer permitted it.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 2

items.scenario: CA Nandini is the financial controller of a manufacturing company. Three disclosures come up in one month. Her board authorises her in writing to give the company's product costing data to a prospective joint-venture partner. A trade body asks her for the same data for an industry benchmarking study; she judges the study harmless and useful to the whole industry, and sends it. And a customer whose pricing data the company holds writes to her consenting to her sharing that data with the customer's own bank; the company knows nothing of this.

items.stem: Is Bhatt exposed under Clause 3 of Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: No — he wrote a correct report, and the brochure is the company's document; a member answers only for words he wrote himself
options.misconception: reads the clause as being about authorship, when what it prohibits is permitting the use of the name
options.why: The clause is aimed at the name, not the draft. A member who watches his name being used that way and does nothing has allowed it.

options.text: Yes — knowing of the brochure and letting it run is permitting his name to be used in a manner that may lead the reader to believe he vouches for the forecast, and his own report does not travel with the brochure
options.why: Clause 3 catches a member who permits his name or the name of his firm to be used in connection with an estimate of earnings contingent upon future transactions in a manner which may lead to the belief that he vouches for the accuracy of the forecast. Permitting is not confined to drafting the words: a member who is shown the document, understands what it says about him and allows it to keep circulating has permitted it. The test is the impression the document as it stands invites, and a report the reader never sees cannot correct that impression.

options.text: Yes, but only from the moment the projections turn out to be wrong, until which no reader has been misled
options.misconception: dates the misconduct from the outcome, when the breach is complete the moment the name is lent in that manner
options.why: Whether the forecast comes true is not the test. The clause looks at what the document invited the reader to believe when he read it.

options.text: No — the brochure says only "reviewed", which is a weaker word than certified and carries no warranty of the numbers
options.misconception: hunts for a forbidden word, when the clause tests the impression the document creates as a whole
options.why: A professional name printed beside a profit chart with nothing else on the page is the impression the clause is about, whatever single word was chosen.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 3

items.scenario: CA Bhatt gives a company a carefully worded report on its five-year projections, saying that the assumptions provide a reasonable basis for the projection and that actual results are likely to differ. The company then prints a fundraising brochure carrying only the line "Projections reviewed by CA S. Bhatt" beside a chart of the projected profits, with every caveat left out. Bhatt is sent a copy, sees what has been done with his name, decides that his own report is on file and says nothing. The brochure circulates for four months.

items.stem: Does Part II of the First Schedule reach the arrangement?

options.text: Yes, but the misconduct is cured once the company is told about it and raises no objection
options.misconception: treats the employer as the person wronged and free to waive it, when what the clause protects is the standing of the profession
options.why: No consent by the employer appears anywhere in the clause, and the misconduct is complete on the payment.

options.text: No — Part II catches only what he receives from his employer's lawyers, brokers and agents; what he does with his own salary is his own affair
options.misconception: keeps the accepting limb of Part II and drops the paying limb sitting immediately beside it
options.why: The Part holds both limbs. Paying away a share of his emoluments is the first of them.

options.text: Yes — a member in employment who pays any person a share of the emoluments of his employment commits professional misconduct, and it makes no difference that the money is his own or that his employer has lost nothing
options.why: Part II of the First Schedule binds a member in service, and its first limb is the paying limb: he is guilty of professional misconduct if he pays any person a share of the emoluments of his employment. The clause does not ask whether the employer was out of pocket or whether the recipient did any work. The profession's fee-sharing discipline follows the member into service and runs in both directions — paying out of his emoluments, and accepting a share of the fees of a lawyer, chartered accountant, broker or agent engaged by his employer.

options.text: No — the schedules bind a member in practice, and a member in employment answers to his contract of service rather than to the Institute
options.misconception: the practice-only reading that Part II exists to defeat; it binds a member in service in terms
options.why: Part II is headed for members in service precisely because the discipline does not stop at the door of a practice.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part II

items.scenario: CA Mehra is employed as a company's group financial controller. A former colleague introduced him to the company, and under a private arrangement Mehra pays him 5 per cent of his own monthly salary as thanks. The colleague is not a member of the Institute, does no work for the company and has no dealings with it. The company knows nothing about the arrangement. Mehra says his salary is his own money to do with as he likes.

items.stem: Which of the three does the framework reach?

options.text: All three — a member who becomes aware of any breach of law at a client, or by any of its directors, is inside the framework
options.misconception: drops both exclusions, which would push every trivial filing default and every director's private affair through an escalation built for matters that damage the entity or the public
options.why: The framework names its own boundaries so that the escalation it requires is reserved for the matters that need it.

options.text: Only the third — the framework reaches non-compliance and suspected non-compliance in the conduct of the client's business, and it puts outside itself matters that are clearly inconsequential and personal misconduct unrelated to the business
options.why: The framework is engaged by non-compliance or suspected non-compliance with laws and regulations at the client, and it excludes two things by its own terms: a matter that is clearly inconsequential, which a late filing settled by a nominal fee is, and personal misconduct unrelated to the business activities of the client, which the managing director's own rental income is. Two sets of production records kept for three years to under-declare output is neither of those, and it is material to the financial statements besides.
keywords: personal misconduct unrelated to the business

options.text: The first and the third — a managing director's own tax evasion goes to his integrity, which bears directly on the audit
options.misconception: integrity may well matter to the auditor's risk assessment, but the framework itself excludes personal misconduct unrelated to the business activities of the client
options.why: What the auditor does with a doubt about integrity is a separate question from whether this framework is engaged, and on that question the exclusion is express.

options.text: The second and the third, a late statutory filing being the plainest case of non-compliance there is
options.misconception: reads "non-compliance" without the filter of consequence, when a breach that is clearly inconsequential does not start the response at all
options.why: The filing was late and was paid for. Nothing about it calls for the member to escalate, press for rectification or weigh a disclosure in the public interest.

citation.ref: Responding to Non-Compliance with Laws and Regulations — the scope of the framework, and its exclusion of matters that are clearly inconsequential and of personal misconduct unrelated to the business activities of the client

items.scenario: Auditing a mid-sized company, a member comes across three things. The managing director has been under-reporting the rent from a private property of his own that has nothing to do with the company. The company filed one statutory return eleven days late and paid the nominal fee for it. And the company has for three years kept two sets of production records so as to under- declare its output to an excise authority, which if unwound would materially change the financial statements. The engagement partner asks which of the three engages the NOCLAR framework.

items.stem: Is that advice right?

options.text: No — the clause bars a member in practice from entering into partnership, in or outside India, with anyone other than a chartered accountant in practice or a member of a body the Council has notified, so where the firm sits does not save it
options.why: Clause 4 of Part I of the First Schedule reaches a partnership entered into in or outside India, and those words are in the clause itself rather than read into it. The permitted co-partners are a chartered accountant in practice and a person belonging to a professional body the Council has notified, subject to the Council's conditions. A foreign qualification outside that list is not one of them, and neither the location of the firm nor the absence of Indian clients is a condition the clause carries.
keywords: professional body the Council has notified

options.text: Yes, provided he intimates the Institute of the foreign partnership and the firm takes no Indian assignments
options.misconception: invents an intimation cure; the clause admits permitted categories of partner, not permitted disclosures about a partner who is not one of them
options.why: Telling the Institute about an arrangement the clause forbids does not make the arrangement permitted.

options.text: Yes — the Chartered Accountants Act governs conduct in India, and a partnership formed and operating abroad is outside its reach
options.misconception: the territorial argument the clause answers on its own face by naming a partnership entered into in or outside India
options.why: The Act follows the member rather than the firm's address, and the clause says so in as many words.

options.text: No — and the same bar would catch a plain fee-sharing referral arrangement with the same Singapore accountant, Clause 4 reaching every commercial link with a non-member
options.misconception: stretches Clause 4 beyond partnership; a fee-sharing arrangement is dealt with by the clauses on paying out and on accepting a share of profits, not by the partnership clause
options.why: Clause 4 is about entering into partnership. A referral or fee-sharing arrangement is governed by different clauses of the same Part.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 4

items.scenario: CA Sharma, in practice in Chennai, is invited to become a partner in a professional firm in Singapore. The proposed co-partner is a Singapore-qualified accountant who is not a member of the Institute and does not belong to any professional body the Council has notified. Sharma's Indian practice will continue unchanged, and the Singapore firm will take no Indian work. He is advised that the First Schedule stops at the Indian border.

items.stem: Does Clause 1 of Part I of the First Schedule permit the arrangement?

options.text: No — the person allowed to practise in the member's name must be a chartered accountant in practice and be in partnership with him or employed by him, and Fernandes, running an independent practice, meets the first requirement and not the second
options.why: Clause 1 makes it professional misconduct for a member in practice to allow any person to practise in his name as a chartered accountant unless that person is also a chartered accountant in practice and is in partnership with or employed by him. Both conditions have to hold at once. Fernandes holds a certificate of practice, so the first is satisfied; he is neither a partner nor an employee, so the second fails, and two independent practices cannot lend each other a name however well qualified each of them is.
keywords: in partnership with or employed by him

options.text: No — and it would fail just as surely if Fernandes were Kulkarni's salaried employee, because a member may practise only in his own name
options.misconception: reads the clause as an absolute bar, when it expressly permits a chartered accountant in practice who is a partner or an employee to practise in the member's name
options.why: The clause opens the door for exactly that case. What it shuts out is the person who is not in practice, or not a partner or employee.

options.text: Yes — the mischief the clause is aimed at is an unqualified person working in a member's name, and Fernandes is fully qualified
options.misconception: keeps the qualification condition and drops the partnership-or-employment condition standing beside it
options.why: The clause protects the public's ability to know whose judgement stands behind the work, and that needs a relationship the Institute can trace, not only a qualification.

options.text: Yes, provided Kulkarni reviews and signs everything issued from the Hubli office
options.misconception: offers supervision in place of the relationship the clause requires, when the clause names partnership or employment and nothing else answers it
options.why: Supervision is not one of the two things the clause asks for, and a member cannot supply by arrangement what the clause requires by status.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 1

items.scenario: CA Kulkarni practises in Belgaum and has built a name there. CA Fernandes, also a chartered accountant holding a certificate of practice, runs his own firm in Hubli. They agree that Fernandes may hold out and work in Kulkarni's firm name at Hubli while keeping his own clients, his own fees and his own separate firm. No partnership deed is signed and neither employs the other. Kulkarni is content, since Fernandes is a fully qualified practising member.

items.stem: What does Clause 3 of Part I of the First Schedule say about the two offers?

options.text: Clause 3 is the receiving side — it bars accepting a share of the profits of the professional work of a person who is not a member — so the tax-return preparer's offer is misconduct, while the company secretaries' arrangement falls inside the Council's carve-out
options.why: Clause 3 catches a member in practice who accepts or agrees to accept any part of the profits of the professional work of a person who is not a member of the Institute; what a member pays out of his own professional fees is the subject of the clause before it. An unqualified tax-return preparer is not a member, so a fixed share of that practice's profits is squarely inside it. The Council has made a carve-out for prescribed arrangements with the professional bodies it has notified, and a firm of company secretaries in practice is within that carve-out.

options.text: Neither offer concerns him — Clause 3 is about a member paying a share of his own fees to an outsider, so nothing he receives is caught by it
options.misconception: runs Clause 3 in the wrong direction; paying out is the neighbouring clause, and Clause 3 is about what the member takes in
options.why: The two clauses sit next to each other and face opposite ways. Reading only one of them is how the first offer gets missed.

options.text: Both are permitted, since Iqbal does none of the referred work himself and so shares in nothing he has earned
options.misconception: makes the member's own effort the test, when the clause bars accepting a share of another person's professional profits precisely because he did not earn it
options.why: Doing none of the work is the reason the clause bites, not a reason it does not.

options.text: Both are misconduct — Clause 3 admits no exception, so a share of profits from any firm outside the Institute is barred
options.misconception: drops the Council's carve-out for the professional bodies it has notified, which sits in the clause as a proviso
options.why: The clause carries a limited exception for prescribed reciprocal arrangements with certain other recognised professional bodies, and that is the second offer.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 3

items.scenario: CA Iqbal, in practice, is offered two arrangements. An unqualified tax-return preparer with a large local following offers him a fixed one-third of the profits of the preparer's own practice in return for Iqbal being available to him for advice. Separately, a firm of company secretaries in practice offers him a share of the profits of work referred between the two firms, under an arrangement of the kind the Council has permitted with the professional bodies it has notified. Iqbal believes Clause 3 is about what he pays out, so he thinks neither offer concerns him.

items.stem: What does SIA 370 say about the two decisions?

options.text: The fraud may wait for the report, but the effective controls must go in, since the report has to be balanced
options.misconception: gets the balance rule right and the urgent one wrong, which is the more expensive half of the pair
options.why: Five weeks is five weeks in which the stock keeps moving. That is why the Standard takes the fraud out of the reporting timetable altogether.

options.text: The fraud must be reported at once to the audit committee rather than to management, and the effective controls may be left out
options.misconception: sends the immediate report to the wrong recipient and keeps the one-sided draft
options.why: SIA 370 has the matter brought to management's attention immediately. The audit committee receives the Chief Internal Auditor's periodic comprehensive report at the close of a plan period.

options.text: Both are wrong — a suspected fraud goes to management at once rather than waiting for the report, and the report's conclusions rest on everything found, with controls that worked acknowledged rather than passed over
options.why: Where the internal auditor comes across any actual or suspected fraud or other misappropriation of assets, he brings it to management's attention immediately and does not wait for the report at all. And the report's conclusions are based on all the findings rather than on a few deviations, which is why controls found to be operating effectively are acknowledged: a report that lists only failures misdescribes the entity it is describing.

options.text: Both are right — the report is the internal auditor's channel to management, and a report that dwells on working controls wastes the reader's time
options.misconception: treats the assignment report as the only channel, when a suspected misappropriation is the one finding that cannot wait for it
options.why: The report is the ordinary channel and the fraud is the exception to it, and the balance rule exists because a one-sided report is a misleading one.

citation.source: Standard on Internal Audit (SIA) 370, Reporting Results
citation.ref: the immediate reporting of an actual or suspected fraud to management, and conclusions based on all the findings with controls operating effectively acknowledged

items.scenario: Halfway through an internal audit of a warehouse, the internal auditor finds what looks like a systematic misappropriation of stock by a storekeeper. He notes it for the report he will issue at the end of the assignment, five weeks away. In drafting that report he also decides to list only the failures, leaving out the three controls he tested and found operating effectively, on the view that a report exists for problems.

items.stem: What must the Central Government do in each case?

options.text: In the first it must order an investigation, the section leaving it no discretion where a court or the Tribunal so orders; in the second it may order one, the special resolution being a ground on which it forms its own opinion
options.why: Section 210 puts the Central Government on two different footings. On the receipt of a report of the Registrar or of an inspector under section 208, on the intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated, or in the public interest, it may order an investigation where it is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so. But where a court or the Tribunal, in any proceeding before it, orders that the affairs of a company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall order an investigation. In every case it is the Central Government that appoints one or more persons as inspectors.
keywords: appoints one or more persons as inspectors

options.text: It must refer both to the Tribunal under section 213, the Tribunal being the only forum that may order an investigation into a company's affairs
options.misconception: section 213 is the Tribunal's route on an application by members or another person; section 210 is the Central Government's own and does not pass through the Tribunal
options.why: The two sections differ in who moves. Section 210 needs no application and no Tribunal order, except in the one case where a court or the Tribunal has already given one.

options.text: It must order an investigation in both, a special resolution of the members binding the Government as firmly as a court's order does
options.misconception: raises the special resolution from a ground to a command, when the section leaves the Government its own opinion on that ground
options.why: The resolution opens the door; whether to walk through it is still the Central Government's judgement.

options.text: It may decline in both, the section saying only that the Central Government may order an investigation
options.misconception: reads the discretionary limb across the whole section and misses the court-or-Tribunal limb, which says shall
options.why: The section carries both words, and which one applies depends on where the case came from.

citation.ref: Section 210 — the grounds on which the Central Government may order an investigation, and its duty to order one where a court or the Tribunal directs

items.scenario: In a proceeding before it, a court records that the affairs of a company ought to be investigated and orders accordingly. In a different company and on separate facts, the members pass a special resolution that the company's affairs ought to be investigated, and the resolution is intimated to the Central Government, which takes the view that nothing in it merits appointing an inspector.

items.stem: Which of the three must stop?

options.text: Only the State economic offences wing — the bar reaches another investigating agency proceeding in respect of an offence under the Companies Act, so it does not touch an investigation under a different statute or a review the company itself commissioned
options.why: Section 212(2) provides that once a case has been assigned to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office, no other investigating agency of the Central Government or of any State Government shall proceed with an investigation in that case in respect of an offence under this Act, and an investigation already initiated is not proceeded with further, its relevant documents and records being transferred to the SFIO. The bar is bounded by those words, so a money-laundering investigation under another statute continues, and a forensic review commissioned by the company is not an investigating agency at all.

options.text: None — the section asks agencies to coordinate rather than to stop, and each keeps the documents it gathered
options.misconception: softens a prohibition into a request, and ignores the requirement that the relevant documents and records be handed over to the SFIO
options.why: The section stops the other agency and moves its papers, which is the opposite of running in parallel.

options.text: The State wing and the Directorate of Enforcement — once the SFIO has the case every other agency stands down, so that one investigation runs
options.misconception: reads the bar as a general takeover of the company, when it is confined by its own words to an offence under the Companies Act
options.why: A separate statute creates separate offences, and the section says nothing about them.

options.text: All three, the company's own forensic review included, since parallel work would compromise the evidence the SFIO is gathering
options.misconception: extends a bar written for investigating agencies of the Central or a State Government to a private engagement the section does not touch
options.why: A firm engaged by the audit committee is not an investigating agency of any Government, so the section does not reach it.

citation.ref: Section 212(2) — the bar on any other investigating agency proceeding in respect of an offence under the Act once a case is assigned to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office

items.scenario: The Central Government assigns a case to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office. Three other bodies are already looking at the same company. A State economic offences wing is investigating the same facts as offences under the Companies Act. The Directorate of Enforcement is investigating them as offences under a separate money-laundering statute. And the company's own audit committee has engaged a firm of chartered accountants to run a forensic review of the same transactions.

items.stem: Where do the three sit under the scale-based framework?

options.text: A housing finance company sits outside the scale-based framework altogether, being regulated as a housing lender rather than as an NBFC
options.misconception: leaves housing finance companies outside a framework they were expressly brought inside
options.why: A housing finance company is placed in the middle or the upper layer like any other covered NBFC, and the layer decides the prudential requirements the audit must test against.

options.text: All three follow asset size alone — the small deposit taker in the base layer, and the other two in the upper layer if they are large enough
options.misconception: reduces a framework built on size, activity and perceived riskiness to a single size test, which is exactly what the activity-based placements override
options.why: Some placements are fixed by what the NBFC does rather than by how large it is, and the deposit taker and the housing financier are both of that kind.

options.text: Each company decides its own layer and reports it, the Reserve Bank publishing only the top layer
options.misconception: gives the entity a choice it does not have; the upper layer is a list the Reserve Bank identifies and the top layer is one it populates
options.why: Placement is not a self-assessment. The auditor confirms it against the framework and the Reserve Bank's own identification.

options.text: A deposit-taking NBFC is in the middle layer whatever its size; a housing finance company is in the middle or the upper layer and never in the base layer; and a Government-owned NBFC is placed in the base or the middle layer, and not in the upper layer until the Reserve Bank says otherwise
options.why: Under scale-based regulation the layer is fixed by the framework and by the Reserve Bank, not by the entity or by its auditor. All deposit-taking NBFCs sit in the middle layer irrespective of asset size. A housing finance company is included in the middle layer or the upper layer as the case may be, and not in the base layer. Government-owned NBFCs are placed in the base layer or the middle layer and will not be placed in the upper layer till further notice. The upper layer itself comprises those NBFCs the Reserve Bank specifically identifies as warranting enhanced regulatory requirement.

citation.ref: Ch. Special Features of Audit of Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies — the four layers of scale-based regulation and the placement of deposit-taking, housing finance and Government-owned NBFCs

items.scenario: Three NBFCs come up in a firm's planning meeting. One is a deposit-taking NBFC with a small balance sheet. One is a housing finance company. One is a large Government-owned NBFC that the audit senior expects to find in the upper layer because of its size. The senior proposes to put the first in the base layer because it is small, and to take the other two companies' own view of where they belong.

items.stem: What may the Authority order, and where does an appeal lie?

options.text: A monetary penalty, and debarment of the member or the firm from being appointed as an auditor or internal auditor, from undertaking any audit or internal audit of any company or body corporate, or from performing any valuation under section 247, for at least six months and at most ten years; an appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal
options.why: Where misconduct is proved, section 132 lets the Authority impose a monetary penalty and debar the member or the firm from being appointed as an auditor or internal auditor, or from undertaking any audit or internal audit of any company or body corporate, or from performing any valuation under section 247, for a minimum period of six months and up to a maximum of ten years. An appeal against such an order lies to the Appellate Tribunal, and not to the Appellate Authority constituted under the Chartered Accountants Act.

options.text: It may impose a monetary penalty but it cannot debar, debarment being reserved to the Disciplinary Committee of the Institute
options.misconception: keeps half the power and gives the rest away, when debarment is named in section 132 itself
options.why: Debarment from audit, internal audit and valuation under section 247 is written into the Authority's own powers.

options.text: It may debar permanently, and its order is final, the section providing no appeal
options.misconception: removes both the floor and the ceiling the section sets, and the appeal it provides
options.why: The section fixes a minimum of six months and a maximum of ten years, and an appeal lies against the order.

options.text: It may only recommend action to the Institute, which passes the order, with an appeal to the Appellate Authority under the Chartered Accountants Act
options.misconception: makes the Authority an advisory body, when section 132 gives it the power to penalise and to debar in its own right
options.why: The Authority investigates and orders. The Institute's own forums are the ones the proviso to section 132(4) stops from running alongside it.

citation.ref: Section 132 — monetary penalty and debarment for a minimum of six months and a maximum of ten years, with an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal

items.scenario: The National Financial Reporting Authority finds professional misconduct proved against an audit firm and its engagement partner in the audit of a large listed company. The firm asks what the Authority can actually order against it, and where it can go if it disagrees with the order.

items.stem: What are the three parties, and where has the trainee gone wrong?

options.text: The auditor, the responsible party and the intended users — and the department is the responsible party, not the intended user; the criteria are the benchmarks the subject matter is measured against, and the subject matter information is the outcome of that measurement
options.why: Every public sector audit has three parties. The auditor, a role filled by the Supreme Audit Institution of India. The responsible party, whose responsibilities are determined by constitutional or legislative arrangement, generally the auditable entity and those charged with its governance. And the intended users, the individuals or organisations for whom the auditor prepares the report. The department whose procurement is examined is the auditable entity, and so the responsible party. The subject matter is what is measured or evaluated, the criteria are the benchmarks used to evaluate it, and the subject matter information is the outcome of measuring the subject matter against those criteria.

options.text: The auditor, the responsible party and the intended users — and the trainee is right, an entity being the intended user of a report addressed to it
options.misconception: gets the three roles and then collapses two of them into one
options.why: The party responsible for the subject matter and the users for whom the report is prepared are distinct roles, which is what gives the engagement its structure.

options.text: The auditor, the entity and the legislature — and the trainee is right, since the department reads the report and acts on it
options.misconception: names the reader of the day instead of the role, when the entity being examined is the responsible party whatever it does with the report afterwards
options.why: The three roles are auditor, responsible party and intended users, and the legislature is one intended user among others rather than a party in its own name.

options.text: There are only two parties in a compliance audit, the auditor and the entity; the three-party structure belongs to attestation engagements alone
options.misconception: confines the three-party structure to one type of engagement, when it is common to every public sector audit
options.why: What separates attestation from direct reporting is who measures the subject matter against the criteria, not how many parties there are.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the three parties to a public sector audit, and the subject matter, the criteria and the subject matter information

items.scenario: A team is planning a compliance audit of a State department's procurement. The planning file has to name the three parties to the engagement and identify the subject matter, the criteria and the subject matter information. A trainee writes that the intended user is the department being audited, since the report will be addressed to it.

items.stem: Which statement corrects him?

options.text: Only the second half is wrong; his purview is confined to bodies in which Government holds equity, financing alone giving no right of audit
options.misconception: makes equity the only gateway, when substantial financing from Union or State revenues is itself a ground of audit purview
options.why: Both halves of what the trainee was told are wrong, and the financing ground is the one this option keeps out.

options.text: Nothing needs correcting — an audit purview fixed by the Constitution cannot extend to a body the Government neither owns nor controls
options.misconception: leaves out the financing ground, when a body substantially financed from Union or State revenues is within the purview even where it is neither owned nor controlled
options.why: Money voted by a legislature is followed by that legislature's auditor, whoever owns the body that spends it.

options.text: Only the first half is wrong; the appraisals are indeed his officers' alone, the Audit Boards being advisory committees of Parliament
options.misconception: moves the Audit Boards to Parliament, when they are constituted within the Indian Audit and Accounts Department
options.why: The Boards have no separate legal entity and work under the Comptroller and Auditor General's supervision and control.
