options.misconception: gives the Financial Stability Board's creation the wrong name
options.why: What the Financial Stability Board created in 2015 is the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures, aimed at companies that predominantly handle financial-related interests, such as banks and insurance firms.

options.text: It is the body the IFRS Foundation Trustees announced on 3 November 2021 to deliver a comprehensive global baseline of sustainability-related disclosure standards
options.misconception: gives the Value Reporting Foundation the announcement and the mandate that belong to the International Sustainability Standards Board
options.why: That announcement created the International Sustainability Standards Board, whose purpose is a comprehensive global baseline of sustainability-related disclosure standards for investors and other capital market participants. It is a different body from the merged foundation, and it came later.

options.text: It is the result of the merger of the Global Reporting Initiative and the Carbon Disclosure Project
options.misconception: merges the two bodies whose names come up most often rather than the two that actually merged
options.why: The Global Reporting Initiative is an independent international organisation based in Amsterdam and remains one; the Carbon Disclosure Project collects environmental performance data and reports to investors, buyers and other stakeholders. Neither was part of this merger.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the Value Reporting Foundation as the result of the merger between the SASB Foundation and the International Integrated Reporting Council

items.scenario: Reading about the consolidation among sustainability bodies, a colleague comes across the Value Reporting Foundation and asks you what it is and where it came from.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: It is the better of the two approaches, since numbers in a sustainability section invite challenge that narrative does not
options.misconception: prefers the form that cannot be checked, when the material says the mixed approach adds the most to the quality of the disclosure
options.why: Being hard to challenge is not a virtue in a disclosure. Metrics and key performance indicators are what let a reader see progress against goals, and a mixed approach that combines them with the narrative adds the maximum value.

options.text: It is qualitative ESG reporting, which describes strategy and policy; quantitative reporting carries metrics and key performance indicators linked to each area to measure progress against goals; and a mixed approach using both tends to add the maximum value to the quality of the disclosures
options.why: ESG reporting can be both quantitative and qualitative in nature. A qualitative report describes the company's strategy or policy around the relevant topics, which is what this board has produced. A quantitative approach carries metrics and key performance indicators linked to each area, so progress against goals can be measured and achievements reported. A mixed approach that uses both tends to add the maximum value to the quality of the disclosures, so the answer is to add the numbers rather than to replace the words.

options.text: It is quantitative reporting, a stated policy being a measurable commitment in itself
options.misconception: calls a policy a measure, when the quantitative form is defined by the metrics and indicators attached to it
options.why: A policy states an intention. Quantitative reporting is the metrics and key performance indicators linked to each area, which is precisely what this section does not have.

options.text: It is not ESG reporting at all, ESG reporting being by definition the disclosure of metrics and key performance indicators
options.misconception: recognises only the quantitative half of ESG reporting and dismisses the qualitative half the same material describes
options.why: Reporting on strategy and policy in words is one of the two recognised forms. It is incomplete on its own, which is a different criticism from saying it is not ESG reporting.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — qualitative and quantitative ESG reporting and the value of a mixed approach

items.scenario: A company's ESG section describes its climate policy, its supplier code and its diversity policy in words. It carries no numbers, no targets and no measures of progress. The board asks whether what it has produced counts as ESG reporting, and whether it should be doing something else instead.

items.stem: Which list is it?

options.text: Banks and insurance, energy, transportation, materials and buildings, agriculture, food, and forestry products
options.why: In developing the understanding of an entity the auditor includes the consideration of climate-related risks and how they may be relevant to the audit, and those risks could be more relevant in certain sectors or industries — banks and insurance, energy, transportation, materials and buildings, agriculture, food, and forestry products. The list is a starting point for where to look, not a boundary on the requirement.

options.text: Listed entities in any sector, and no unlisted entity in any sector
options.misconception: turns a question about the nature of a business into a question about whether its shares are traded
options.why: Listing determines what an entity must disclose. It does not determine whether a warming climate affects its assets, its liabilities or its estimates, which is what makes the risk relevant to the audit.

options.text: None — climate-related risks sit outside the auditor's understanding of the entity in every sector
options.misconception: excludes from the understanding of the entity a risk the material puts expressly inside it
options.why: The consideration of climate-related risks is part of developing the understanding of the entity and its environment. The sector list says where it bites hardest, not whether it applies at all.

options.text: Energy and mining alone, climate-related risk being a question about carbon emissions and nothing else
options.misconception: reduces climate-related risk to the emitting industries and misses the financing, transport, construction and food sectors the material names
options.why: Emissions are one route by which climate reaches the financial statements. Financing exposure, transport assets, building materials and agricultural output are others, and the sectors named cover all of them.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the sectors in which climate-related risks could be more relevant to the audit

items.scenario: A firm is deciding where in its client portfolio to build climate-related risk into the understanding of the entity first. A partner asks which sectors the study material actually names as ones where climate-related risks could be more relevant to an audit.

items.stem: Which Social Audit Standards govern the three?

options.text: SAS 200, SAS 1300 and SAS 1100 respectively
options.why: The series runs by the field the social enterprise works in. SAS 200 covers promoting health care including mental healthcare, sanitation and making available safe drinking water. SAS 1300 covers the promotion of financial inclusion. SAS 1100 covers slum area development, affordable housing and other interventions to build sustainable and resilient cities.

options.text: None of them — the Social Audit Standards govern the audit of a social enterprise's financial statements rather than an assessment of its impact
options.misconception: reads the series as a financial audit series, when each Standard guides the Social Auditor in an independent impact assessment engagement
options.why: Each Standard guides the Social Auditor in an independent impact assessment engagement of a Social Enterprise working in a particular field, and sets out the audit steps and procedures for conducting the social impact assessment. The financial statements of the enterprise are a separate matter.

options.text: SAS 500, SAS 800 and SAS 1000 respectively
options.misconception: sends a water and sanitation programme to the environmental standard, financial inclusion to the incubator standard and housing to the livelihoods standard
options.why: SAS 500 is environmental sustainability and climate change including forest and wildlife conservation; SAS 800 is supporting incubators of social enterprises; SAS 1000 is promoting livelihoods for the rural and urban poor. None of the three matches the engagements described.

options.text: SAS 100 governs all three, the later numbers merely elaborating the general standard it lays down
options.misconception: treats the first number in the series as a general standard the rest expand on, when each Standard is tied to its own field
options.why: SAS 100 is itself a field standard — eradicating hunger, poverty, malnutrition and inequality. There is no general standard sitting above the series; the number follows the work the social enterprise does.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the Social Audit Standards SAS 100 to SAS 1600 and the fields to which each of them applies

items.scenario: Your firm takes on three impact assessment engagements in the same month. The first is for a social enterprise running rural sanitation and safe drinking water programmes. The second is for one working on the promotion of financial inclusion. The third is for one carrying out slum area development and affordable housing.

items.stem: How do the Council's guidelines answer him, and under which clause would a breach be charged?

options.text: The wife's debt is outside the guideline, which reaches only the member's own indebtedness; but the fee taken in full before the report was signed is indebtedness and bars him
options.misconception: drops the relative from a bar that names her and turns a permitted progressive recovery of fees into a debt
options.why: Both halves are the wrong way round. The guideline names a relative of the member or of a partner in terms, so the wife's ₹4,00,000 is squarely within it, and fees recovered as and when a part of the work is done are not a debt owed to the client at all.

options.text: Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines bars a member in practice, a partner of a firm in practice, the firm, or a relative of such member or partner from accepting appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it beyond the limit fixed in the statute or, in other cases, ₹1,00,000 — a partnership firm is a concern and the wife is a relative, so the appointment is barred — while fees recovered on a progressive basis are not indebtedness; and a breach is misconduct under Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule
options.why: Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines, 2008 is written far wider than section 141. It reaches a member in practice, a partner of a firm in practice, the firm itself, and a relative of such member or partner; it applies to a concern of any kind and not only to a company; and the ceiling is the limit fixed in the statute where a statute fixes one and ₹1,00,000 in other cases. On the fee, the Research Committee's opinion is that a member who recovers his fees on a progressive basis as and when a part of the work is done, without waiting for the completion of the whole job, cannot be said to be indebted to the client at any stage. Because the source of the bar is a Council guideline, the charge for breaching it is Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule, which makes contravention of any guidelines issued by the Council professional misconduct.
keywords: a relative of such member or partner
Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule

options.text: Nothing bars him — section 141(3)(d) is the only rule on an auditor's indebtedness, it applies to companies, and a partnership firm engagement falls outside it altogether
options.misconception: treats the Companies Act as the only source of the indebtedness bar, missing the Council guideline that applies to a concern of any kind
options.why: Section 141(3)(d) is one rule and the Council General Guidelines are another, and the second is the wider of the two. It bars accepting appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it, and a partnership firm is a concern. A member who is outside the Companies Act is not therefore outside the guidelines.

options.text: Both facts bar him, because any money moving between an auditor and his client before the report is signed is indebtedness
options.misconception: reads every pre-report receipt as indebtedness, when a fee earned as the work is done is payment and not a loan
options.why: A fee is money the client owes the auditor, not money the auditor owes the client, and the Research Committee has said that progressive recovery does not make the member indebted at any stage. What bars this appointment is the ₹4,00,000 the wife owes the firm.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 1, read with Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines, 2008 on appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it

items.scenario: CA Bhatia is asked to become the auditor of Sahaj Traders, a partnership firm. At the date he is asked, his wife owes the firm ₹4,00,000 on an interest-free advance she took to buy a car. He says that section 141 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs an auditor's indebtedness, that it applies to companies and not to a partnership firm, and that in any case the debt is his wife's and not his. On a separate engagement he has been recovering his fee on a progressive basis as parts of the work were completed, and had received the whole fee before he signed, which he now worries about.

items.stem: What does the Council's guidance on the relative size of fees require of the firm?

options.text: The trading company requires disclosure, the proportion being far past any trigger; the exemption for a small practice goes to the size of the fee and cannot answer a question about the proportion
options.misconception: reads the exemption out of the guidance by treating it as answering a different question from the one the trigger asks
options.why: An exemption exists precisely to take a case outside a trigger that would otherwise be met. The guidance exempts a firm whose total fees do not exceed the specified amount from the provision altogether, and a proportion computed inside an exempt practice is not reported.

options.text: No disclosure in either case — the exemption for a firm whose total fees do not exceed the specified amount answers the first, and the exemption for the audit of a nationalised bank, and generally where the appointment of the auditor is made by the Government, answers the second; and where the guidance does bite, the trigger is a higher proportion for an entity that is not a public interest entity than for one that is, in each case for two consecutive years
options.why: The guidance has a differentiated trigger and then two exemptions, and this firm is inside both exemptions. The trigger differs by the kind of client: disclosure is called for where, for two consecutive years, the gross annual professional fees from an audit client exceed a stated proportion of the total fees of the firm, and that proportion is set higher for a client that is not a public interest entity than for one that is. The first exemption is for a practice whose total fees do not exceed the specified amount, which this firm's do not. The second is for the audit of government companies, public undertakings, nationalised banks, public financial institutions and regulators, and generally where appointments of auditors are made by the Government.

options.text: Only the bank audit requires disclosure, a regulated entity's auditor being held to the stricter public interest entity proportion whatever the exemptions say
options.misconception: applies the stricter trigger to an appointment the guidance expressly exempts, so the exemption is never reached
options.why: The order of the questions is the point. A case that falls inside an exemption never reaches the trigger at all, and the audit of a nationalised bank whose auditors are appointed by the Government is one of the cases the guidance exempts by name.

options.text: Both require disclosure — the exemptions cover government companies alone, and a nationalised bank is a banking company rather than a government company
options.misconception: reads the exemption list too narrowly, missing that it names nationalised banks and, more widely, appointments made by the Government
options.why: The list is longer than government companies. It names public undertakings, nationalised banks, public financial institutions and regulators, and it extends to any case where the appointment of the auditor is made by the Government — which is how this bank's auditors were appointed.

citation.ref: the Council's guidance on Fees–Relative Size — the differentiated disclosure requirement for public interest entities and other entities where the gross annual professional fees from an audit client exceed the stated proportion of the firm's total fees for two consecutive years, and the exemptions for a firm whose total fees do not exceed the specified amount and for government companies, public undertakings, nationalised banks, public financial institutions, regulators and appointments made by the Government

items.scenario: A four-partner firm has two clients that worry a new partner. The first is an unlisted trading company, not a public interest entity, which has for two consecutive years produced well over half of the firm's gross annual professional fees. The second is a nationalised bank whose auditors are appointed by the Government, and the fees from it also run far above the proportion at which the Council's guidance on the relative size of fees would otherwise call for disclosure. The firm's total fees for the year are below the amount at which the guidance's exemption for a small practice stops applying.

items.stem: What does the Code have the firm evaluate, and how does it then address what it finds?

options.text: Whether the client is content with the two individuals, and whether any error has been found in the nine years, an unblemished record showing that objectivity has survived
options.misconception: measures a familiarity threat by the client's satisfaction and by hindsight, rather than by the factors the Code names
options.why: A familiarity threat is measured before the damage, not after it. The client's contentment is not one of the factors, and an absence of errors found is at least as consistent with a threat having taken effect as with its absence.

options.text: There is nothing to weigh — the Code's fixed rotation and cooling-off requirement applies to every audit client, and both individuals are already past it
options.misconception: extends the prescribed rotation and cooling-off, which the Code writes for a public interest entity, to every audit client
options.why: The Code does two different things in the same section. For a public interest entity it prescribes a term and a cooling-off period. For every other audit client it requires the firm to evaluate the familiarity and self-interest threats and to address them, which is why the factors exist at all.

options.text: The nature and length of the individual's relationship with the client, his role on the engagement team, the extent to which the client's management has changed, and the nature or complexity of the client's accounting and reporting issues — and it then addresses what it finds by rotating the individual off the team, changing his role, having an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team review the work, or an independent internal or external quality review of the engagement
options.why: Where the Code leaves long association to evaluation rather than prescribing a term, it names what the evaluation weighs: the nature and length of the individual's relationship with the client, the individual's role on the engagement team, the extent to which the client's management has changed, and the nature or complexity of the client's accounting and reporting issues. Nine years on a company whose management has not changed and whose accounting is simple reads differently from nine years on one that has been through both. The actions that follow are also named — rotating the individual off, changing his role, an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team, or an independent quality review.

options.text: Only the length of service — the Code's factors are all ways of measuring time on the engagement, so the nine years and the seven years answer the question by themselves
options.misconception: reduces a four-factor evaluation to the one factor that can be counted, so the client's own circumstances never enter it
options.why: Length is one factor of four. The individual's role, how far the client's management has changed, and how complex the client's accounting and reporting issues are all bear on whether the relationship has made him too sympathetic or too accepting, and two of those have nothing to do with the calendar.

citation.ref: the long association provisions — the evaluation of the familiarity and self-interest threats created by long association, the factors that evaluation weighs, and the actions by which the firm addresses the threat where the client is not a public interest entity

items.scenario: Kesari Mills is an unlisted family company and is not a public interest entity. The senior manager has been on its audit for nine years and the engagement partner for seven. The firm accepts that a familiarity threat exists and that no fixed rotation requirement applies to a client of this kind. The audit manager asks what the firm is actually supposed to weigh before deciding what to do.

items.stem: Under which head does each fall?

options.text: Iyer falls under Second Schedule Part III and Rao under First Schedule Part IV — she went to prison and he did not
options.misconception: measures by the sentence served, so the heavier charge follows the person the court treated more harshly rather than the graver offence
options.why: This reads the two Schedules off the sentences, which is exactly the swap they are drafted to prevent. Both Schedules describe an offence punishable with imprisonment for a stated term, and neither asks what punishment the court chose within its powers.

options.text: Rao falls under Second Schedule Part III and Iyer under First Schedule Part IV — the line is drawn by the term of imprisonment the offence carries, not by the sentence the court actually awarded
options.why: Second Schedule Part III catches a member held guilty by any civil or criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months, and Rao's offence carries up to seven years however lightly he was dealt with. First Schedule Part IV catches an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, and Iyer's does, however long she was actually inside. The term of imprisonment the offence carries is what the Schedules measure; the sentence awarded is what the court decided about the person, and it moves nothing.
keywords: term of imprisonment the offence carries

options.text: Rao falls under Second Schedule Part III and Iyer under neither — a fine or a short sentence is too small a matter to engage other misconduct at all
options.misconception: adds a threshold of seriousness the Schedules do not contain, when First Schedule Part IV exists precisely for the lighter offence
options.why: There is no floor. First Schedule Part IV is written for the offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, so a conviction of that kind is other misconduct and goes before the Board of Discipline rather than falling out of the code altogether.

options.text: Both fall under Second Schedule Part III — an offence carrying seven years in one case and an actual term of imprisonment served in the other
options.misconception: puts an offence punishable with up to six months into the Second Schedule because the sentence happened to be custodial
options.why: Rao belongs there and Iyer does not. Her offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, which is First Schedule Part IV, and serving four months of that term does not enlarge the offence.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part IV, and Second Schedule, Part III — the dividing line being the term of imprisonment the offence is punishable with

items.scenario: Two members come before the Institute. Mr Rao is convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years; the magistrate takes a lenient view of his circumstances and imposes a fine of ₹5,000, with no imprisonment at all. Mrs Iyer is convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of up to six months, and is sentenced to four months, which she serves.

items.stem: Which of the four is a safeguard as the Code of Ethics uses that word?

options.text: None — a self-review threat can never be reduced by a safeguard, so the only answer is to decline or end the professional activity
options.misconception: turns the Code's last resort into a rule about a whole category of threat, when declining follows from the facts rather than from the label
options.why: Declining or ending the activity is one of three ways of addressing a threat, and it is reached where the circumstances creating the threat cannot be eliminated and no safeguard is capable of being applied. That is a conclusion on facts. A self-review threat is not in a class of its own, and the Code offers a reviewer who was not on the team as an action that might address it.

options.text: All four — anything that makes an improper conclusion less likely is a safeguard, and the four together are stronger than any one of them
options.misconception: treats every favourable feature of the environment as a safeguard, so nothing is ever left to be done about the threat
options.why: Counting the environment as a safeguard is how a threat gets talked down without anything changing. A certification and a regulator existed before the threat arose and will exist after it; the Code asks what the accountant did about this threat.

options.text: The first three — a safeguard is something already in place before the engagement begins, and a review carried out after the work is done comes too late to be one
options.misconception: puts a timing condition on the word that the Code does not, and rules out the very example the Code gives
options.why: The Code names having an appropriate reviewer review the work performed as an action that might address a self-review threat, and a review is by its nature after the work. What matters is whether the action effectively reduces the threat, not when in the engagement it falls.

options.text: Only the last — a safeguard is an action, individually or in combination, that the accountant takes and that effectively reduces a threat to an acceptable level, and an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team reviewing the work is one of the Code's own examples; the other three are conditions, policies and procedures that might affect the evaluation of whether a threat is at an acceptable level, and are not themselves safeguards
options.why: The Code defines the word narrowly on purpose. Safeguards are actions, individually or in combination, that the accountant takes and that effectively reduce threats to an acceptable level, and its examples are all things somebody does — assigning additional time and qualified personnel to required tasks; having an appropriate reviewer, who was not a member of the team, review the work performed or advise as necessary; using different partners and engagement teams with separate reporting lines for non-assurance services; involving another firm to perform or re-perform part of the engagement; and separating teams when dealing with confidential matters. A certification, a regulator and a training requirement are conditions, policies and procedures in the environment: they might affect the evaluation of whether a threat is at an acceptable level, and none of them is an action taken against this threat.

citation.ref: the conceptual framework — addressing threats by eliminating the circumstances, applying safeguards, or declining or ending the professional activity, with the definition of safeguards as actions the accountant takes and the examples of such actions

items.scenario: A team has identified a self-review threat and is listing what it will rely on to bring it to an acceptable level. The list has four entries: the firm's ISO certification; the fact that the client is a regulated entity that files with a regulator; the profession's continuing education requirements; and having an appropriate reviewer, who was not a member of the team, review the work performed.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: No — Clause 3 of Part II of the Second Schedule names the Quality Review Board among the bodies to which the information, statement, return or form may be submitted, alongside the Institute, the Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee and the Appellate Authority
options.why: Clause 3 does not stop at the Institute. It catches a member who includes in any information, statement, return or form to be submitted to the Institute, the Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board or the Appellate Authority any particulars knowing them to be false. The Board being set up by the Central Government rather than by the Council changes nothing, because the clause lists it by name.

options.text: No, but only if the false statement affected the Board's conclusion on the quality of the engagement
options.misconception: adds a consequence the clause does not require, when the wrong is complete on including particulars known to be false
options.why: The clause is complete when the member includes particulars knowing them to be false. Whether anyone was misled goes to what the Disciplinary Committee makes of it, not to whether the clause is engaged.

options.text: Yes — Clause 3 reaches the Institute and its own organs, and a false statement to the Quality Review Board is a matter for that Board's own procedures and for nobody else
options.misconception: reads the clause as protecting the Institute's own machinery only, when it lists the bodies it protects and the Board is one of them
options.why: The clause is a list, and reading the list settles it. The Quality Review Board appears in it expressly, so a knowing falsehood in a submission to the Board is professional misconduct whatever the Board itself decides to do about the review.

options.text: No, but the charge is Clause 2 of Part III of the First Schedule, for not complying with the requirements asked for by the Quality Review Board
options.misconception: picks the clause about silence when the member spoke, and spoke falsely, which is what moves the case into the Second Schedule
options.why: Clause 2 of Part III punishes a member who does not supply the information called for or does not comply with the requirements asked for. This member complied and lied while doing it, and knowledge of the falsity is exactly what carries the case across into the Second Schedule.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 3 — the bodies to which a statement, return or form carrying particulars known to be false may be submitted

items.scenario: A member's firm is selected for a review by the Quality Review Board. In the information he submits to the Board he states that a second partner reviewed the engagement file before the report was signed, knowing that nobody did. When this is put to him he says that Clause 3 speaks of information submitted to the Institute, and that the Quality Review Board is a separate body set up by the Central Government, so the clause cannot reach him.

items.stem: Which clause reaches these two, and before which forum?

options.text: Clause 3 of Part III of the First Schedule reaches both — it catches a member who gives information knowing it to be false while inviting professional work from another chartered accountant, and equally while advertising through a write-up — and being a First Schedule matter, the Board of Discipline hears it
options.why: Clause 3 of Part III polices three routes at once: inviting professional work from another chartered accountant, responding to tenders or enquiries, and advertising through a write-up or anything provided for in items (6) and (7) of Part I. The letter to the larger firm is the first route and the circulated write-up is the third, and both carried information the member knew to be false. Because Part III sits in the First Schedule, the Board of Discipline hears the case.
keywords: inviting professional work from another chartered accountant

options.text: Only the write-up, under Clause 7 of Part I, because it advertises the firm's attainments; a letter between two members is a private commercial approach and outside the Schedules
options.misconception: files a knowing falsehood under the advertising clause and treats an approach to another member as beyond the disciplinary code
options.why: Clause 7 of Part I is about advertising attainments and about designations, and it would be engaged by a write-up whether or not anything in it was false. What is wrong here is the knowledge, and the clause that turns on knowledge across all three routes — the letter included — is Clause 3 of Part III.

options.text: Only the letter — Clause 3 names inviting work from another chartered accountant, while a write-up is governed by the Council's write-up guidelines, and a departure from a guideline is not misconduct
options.misconception: takes the write-up route out of a clause that names it, and treats a Council guideline as advisory
options.why: The clause names advertising through a write-up in the same breath as inviting work from another chartered accountant. And a guideline is not advisory in any event: Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule makes contravention of any guidelines issued by the Council professional misconduct in itself.

options.text: Neither — Clause 3 catches false information only in a response to a tender or an enquiry from a user of professional services, and neither a letter to another chartered accountant nor a write-up is that
options.misconception: shrinks a clause with three named routes down to one of them, so the two routes the profession opened up go unpoliced
options.why: Tenders and enquiries are one of the three routes the clause names. Inviting professional work from another chartered accountant is another, and advertising through a write-up is the third, and the clause treats a knowing falsehood on any of them alike.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part III, Clause 3 — false information given while inviting professional work from another chartered accountant, while responding to tenders or enquiries, or while advertising through a write-up

items.scenario: CA Sengupta writes to a larger firm offering to take sub-contracted certification work, stating that his firm holds an ISO certification and has branch offices in two cities, knowing that it has neither. Separately he circulates a write-up describing his services, in which he states that his firm has completed more than two hundred bank audits, knowing the true number is under thirty.

items.stem: Which of the two breaches Clause 2 of Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: Neither — in both cases the examination was made by a chartered accountant, which is the whole of what the clause requires
options.misconception: reads the clause as requiring a chartered accountant, when it requires one of four specified relationships to the member
options.why: A chartered accountant in the client's whole-time employment is neither in practice nor an employee in his firm, and the clause names relationships rather than qualifications. Reading it as a qualification test would let the client audit itself and have the member sign.

options.text: Only the first — an outsider is an outsider, and the fourth permitted person means a chartered accountant to whom the whole engagement has been sub-contracted with the client's consent
options.misconception: adds a consent condition the clause does not contain, and reads the fourth permitted person almost out of existence
options.why: The clause says another chartered accountant in practice and stops there. It asks nothing about the client's consent and nothing about whether the whole engagement or only the examination was passed on.

options.text: Only the second — Clause 2 permits the examination to be made by the member himself, by a partner, by an employee in his firm, or by another chartered accountant in practice, and CA Pillai is the fourth of those; the client's own accounts department is none of the four, and the qualification of the person heading it does not put him inside the list
options.why: Clause 2 names four pairs of hands and CA Pillai is one of them: another chartered accountant in practice, engaged for the work, is expressly permitted, and it makes no difference that he is outside the firm. The client's accounts head fails on both halves of the test — he is not an employee in his firm, being employed by the client, and he is not in practice at all. Being a chartered accountant is not the qualification the clause asks about; whose chartered accountant he is, is.

options.text: Both — the examination has to be made inside the firm, by the member himself, by a partner or by an employee of the firm, and anybody else is an outsider
options.misconception: drops the fourth permitted person from a list of four, so a lawful arrangement is condemned along with an unlawful one
options.why: The list has four entries and the fourth is another chartered accountant in practice. The clause was drafted that way so that a firm may bring in a practising member for work it cannot do itself, which is what happened in the first engagement.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 2 — the four persons by whom the examination of the financial statements and the related records may be made

items.scenario: Two certification engagements are reviewed. In the first, the firm engaged CA Pillai, a chartered accountant in practice on his own account who is neither a partner of the firm nor employed by it, to carry out the examination of the financial statements and the related records; the engagement partner then signed the certificate. In the second, the examination was carried out entirely by the client's own accounts department, whose head is a chartered accountant in the client's whole-time employment, and the engagement partner signed after reading their file.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: Yes, because responding to an empanelment is expressly permitted, and what a partner pays outside the engagement is a matter between him and the officer
options.misconception: reads the permission to respond to a tender or an enquiry as covering the means by which the response was made to succeed
options.why: The permission is to answer an invitation, not to buy the outcome. Nothing in it touches how the member conducted himself while the decision was being made, which is precisely what the second limb of Clause 5 reaches.

options.text: Yes — Clause 5's first limb names a person who is not an employee or a partner, so where the member acts himself there is nobody to bring the clause into play
options.misconception: reads a two-limbed clause as though it had only its first limb, so a member who does the improper thing himself escapes
options.why: Reading only the first limb would mean a member could do personally what he may not pay an agent to do. The second limb exists for that case: it is about the means and not about the hands.

options.text: No, but the charge is Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule, for paying a share of professional fees to a person who is not a member of the Institute
options.misconception: reaches for the fee-sharing clause when the money was not a share of any fee but a payment made to procure the work
options.why: Clause 2 polices the outflow of professional fees — a share, commission or brokerage out of the fees earned. A lump sum paid to an officer to obtain an empanelment is not a share of the fees on the work, and the clause that fits what was done is Clause 5's second limb.

options.text: No — Clause 5 has a second limb, securing any professional business by means which are not open to a chartered accountant, and that limb asks how the work was obtained rather than who obtained it; a private payment to the officer who controls the empanelment is such a means
options.why: Clause 5 has two limbs and either one is enough. The first asks who brought the work in — a person who is not an employee of the member and not his partner. The second limb asks by what means it was secured, and it catches means which are not open to a chartered accountant whoever employed them, the member himself included. A payment made privately to the officer who decides the empanelment is the paradigm case, and the firm's own hands on it make it worse rather than safer.
keywords: means which are not open to a chartered accountant

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 5 — the second limb, securing professional business by means which are not open to a chartered accountant

items.scenario: A firm wants a place on a state undertaking's audit panel. No outsider is involved at any stage: the managing partner meets the undertaking's finance director himself and pays him ₹2,00,000 privately to have the firm's name put on the panel. The firm is empanelled and takes the work. The partner's position is that Clause 5 is aimed at touts and agents, and that since nobody outside the firm brought the work in, the clause cannot be engaged.

items.stem: Who may lawfully sign?

options.text: CA Shah and CA Dutt — firms in one network share quality control and standards, so a network firm's partner signs as a partner for this purpose
options.misconception: treats network membership as partnership, when the network's consequence is for independence and not for who may sign
options.why: A network exists for other purposes: where a firm is a network firm the independence requirements that apply to an audit client of one apply to the other. It does not make the partners of one firm the partners of another, and Clause 12 asks about partnership in this firm.

options.text: None of the three — nobody who did not himself perform the examination may sign the report, and none of them did
options.misconception: merges the clause about who may sign with the clause about who may make the examination, and misreads the second one as well
options.why: Two different clauses answer two different questions. Clause 12 fixes who may sign, and Clause 2 of Part I of the Second Schedule fixes who may make the examination — permitting the member, a partner, an employee in his firm, or another chartered accountant in practice. A partner may therefore sign on work done by the firm's employees.

options.text: CA Shah and CA Menon — a retired partner belongs to the firm's own circle, and the room he keeps shows the connection has not been broken
options.misconception: treats a continuing association with the firm as partnership, when the clause turns on whether the person is a partner now
options.why: The clause asks one question about status. A member who has retired is not a partner, and the courtesy of an office is not a partnership deed. His signature on the firm's report would say that somebody is answerable for it who is not.

options.text: Only CA Shah — Clause 12 bars a member not being his partner from signing on the firm's behalf, and a retired partner and a partner of a network firm are both members who are not partners of this firm; CA Shah having done no work on the audit does not disqualify him, because the clause fixes who may sign and not who must have done the work
options.why: Clause 12 makes it misconduct to allow a person not being a member of the Institute in practice, or a member not being his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements. A retired partner is no longer a partner, and a partner of a network firm is a partner of a different firm however close the two are, so both are members not being his partner. CA Shah is a partner, which is what the clause asks. Who made the examination is a separate question answered by Clause 2 of Part I of the Second Schedule, and that clause permits the work to be done by a partner or an employee of the firm.
keywords: a member not being his partner

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 12 — the second limb, a member not being his partner

items.scenario: The firm's sole signing partner is in hospital and an audit report falls due. Three people offer to sign it on the firm's behalf. CA Menon retired from the firm's partnership two years ago and still keeps a room in its office. CA Dutt is a partner of another firm belonging to the same international network as this one. CA Shah is a partner of this firm who took no part at all in this audit.

items.stem: In which audit is the presumption properly rebutted?

options.text: Only the first — a single type of simple revenue transaction is the example SA 240 gives of circumstances in which the presumption is not applicable, while a complex revenue structure with a lack of controls over revenue recognition is where the risk is at its highest, and past honesty is no reason at all
options.why: SA 240 permits the presumption to be rebutted where it is not applicable in the circumstances of the engagement, and the Standard's own example is a single type of simple revenue transaction — leasehold revenue from a single unit rental property. The second file inverts the test. Where there is a complex revenue structure, or a lack of controls over revenue recognition, there is a high probability of fraud risk in revenue recognition, so those facts are reasons for the presumption to stand. Management's honesty in previous years is not among the circumstances the Standard contemplates, and the auditor keeps his skepticism regardless of it.
keywords: single type of simple revenue transaction

options.text: In both — the rebuttal is the auditor's own judgement, and a documented reason is all SA 240 asks for
options.misconception: treats the documentation requirement as the whole test, so any recorded reason is as good as any other
options.why: Documentation records a conclusion; it does not make one. What SA 240 asks the auditor to conclude is that the presumption is not applicable in the circumstances of the engagement, and a note saying management is honest does not reach that conclusion however carefully it is filed.

options.text: In neither — a rebuttal is open only where the entity has no revenue at all, which is why the Standard treats the risk as presumed
options.misconception: sets the bar at no revenue, when the Standard's own example is an entity that does have revenue of a single simple kind
options.why: An entity with no revenue would have nothing to presume about. The Standard's example is an entity with revenue of one simple kind, and the first audit here is exactly that.

options.text: In the second only — that auditor identified the complexity and the control weakness and dealt with them, while the first did no analysis of his revenue streams at all
options.misconception: reverses the test, treating complexity and weak controls as grounds for rebuttal rather than as the reasons the presumption stands
options.why: Identifying complexity and a lack of controls is the finding that keeps the presumption alive, not the finding that retires it. And the first auditor's revenue is a single lease, so there is one stream to analyse and he has analysed it.

citation.ref: para 26 and 47, with the example of circumstances in which the presumption of a risk of fraud in revenue recognition is not applicable

items.scenario: Two audits are reviewed. In the first, the entity's only revenue is rent from a single let property under one lease, invoiced monthly on fixed terms, and the file records that the presumed fraud risk in revenue recognition was rebutted. In the second, the entity earns revenue from four streams including corporate bookings, the team has itself found that the controls over revenue recognition are not designed to catch improper cut-off, and the file records that the presumption was rebutted because management has been honest in all previous years.

items.stem: What does SA 210 say about that paragraph?

options.text: It comes out, and so does the fresh engagement letter — a changed engagement continues to run under the letter originally signed
options.misconception: drops the requirement to record the changed terms, which SA 210 states separately from the rule about the report
options.why: The paragraph comes out and the letter stays. Where the terms are changed, the auditor and management agree on and record the new terms of the engagement in an engagement letter or other suitable form of written agreement.

options.text: It stays — the more a reader knows about the work behind a report, the better informed he is, and the change in terms ought to be disclosed to him
options.misconception: treats extra information as always helpful, when the extra information here invites reliance the review conclusion cannot carry
options.why: What the paragraph adds is not information about the review; it is a suggestion that the review rests on audit work. SA 210 keeps the two apart precisely so that a limited assurance conclusion is read as one.

options.text: It stays, because the change here had a reasonable justification; a paragraph of that kind is improper only where the engagement was downgraded without one
options.misconception: makes the rule about the reference depend on why the terms were changed, when it holds whatever the justification was
options.why: Justification and reporting are two separate requirements. A change with no reasonable justification is not agreed to at all; where it is agreed to, the report on the related service still carries no reference to the original engagement or its procedures.

options.text: It comes out — the report on the related service does not include reference to the original engagement or to any procedures performed in it, the one exception being an engagement changed to agreed-upon procedures, where reference to the procedures performed is a normal part of the report
options.why: SA 210 is careful about what the new report may say, because a review report that recites audit work invites the reader to take more comfort than the engagement now provides. The report on the related service does not include reference to the original engagement, nor to any procedures performed in the original audit engagement. The single exception is where the engagement has been changed to agreed-upon procedures, because there a description of the procedures performed is a normal part of the report and the reader is told in terms that no assurance is expressed.

citation.ref: para 16 and para 17, with the requirement that the report on the related service make no reference to the original engagement or to the procedures performed in it, except where the engagement is changed to agreed-upon procedures

items.scenario: Nine weeks into a voluntary audit the entity's circumstances change: a proposed listing is abandoned and the board now needs only a review for its bankers. You are satisfied that this is a change in circumstances affecting the entity's requirements, you agree to the change, and you and management record the new terms in a fresh engagement letter. Your manager then drafts the review report and, to show the depth of what was done, adds a paragraph stating that the engagement began as an audit and describing the audit procedures already performed.

items.stem: What does SA 260 require?

options.text: The three matters must be communicated, but the timing is a matter for the auditor, SA 260 fixing no date for any communication
options.misconception: reads the absence of a fixed date as an absence of any requirement about timing
options.why: No date is fixed and a standard is set instead: the auditor communicates with those charged with governance on a timely basis. A communication that arrives too late for the body to act on it fails that standard whatever the calendar says.

options.text: Circumstances that affect the form and content of the auditor's report are one of the significant findings communicated to those charged with governance, so the intended qualification, the key audit matters and the going concern paragraph all go to the audit committee — and the communication is made on a timely basis, which a draft produced as the meeting opens is not
options.why: SA 260's list of significant findings from the audit names circumstances that affect the form and content of the auditor's report, and all three of these do: a qualification changes the opinion, a Key Audit Matters section is a part of the report, and a going concern paragraph is another. The committee is the body that oversees the financial reporting process, and it can only oversee something it hears about while it can still act. That is why the auditor communicates with those charged with governance on a timely basis rather than at the moment the report is signed.
keywords: form and content of the auditor's report

options.text: Nothing — the report is the auditor's own statement, and SA 260's list deals with matters arising in the audit rather than with what the report will eventually say
options.misconception: treats the report as outside the communication, when the standard's list names circumstances that affect its form and content
options.why: The list says otherwise in terms. Circumstances that affect the form and content of the auditor's report is one of the significant findings the standard requires to be communicated, and it is there because a governing body reading a qualification for the first time in the signed report has been deprived of its function.

options.text: Only the qualification needs to be communicated — key audit matters and a going concern paragraph do not modify the opinion, so they do not affect the form and content of the report
options.misconception: reads "form and content" as meaning a modification of the opinion alone, when it covers everything the report will contain
options.why: Form and content are wider than the opinion. A Key Audit Matters section and a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern paragraph both change what the report looks like and what it tells a reader, and both are matters the committee needs to know are coming.

citation.ref: para 16 and para 21 — circumstances that affect the form and content of the auditor's report as one of the significant findings from the audit, communicated on a timely basis

items.scenario: The audit will end with a qualified opinion on inventory, a Key Audit Matters section naming revenue recognition, and a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern paragraph. The engagement partner proposes to hand the audit committee the draft report on the morning of the board meeting at which the accounts are to be adopted, saying that what goes into the auditor's report is the auditor's own affair and that the committee will see it soon enough.

items.stem: What does SA 540 (Revised) require to be documented?

options.text: The indicators must be documented, but in summary only, the standard requiring documentation of significant judgements rather than of every observation made along the way
options.misconception: invents a summary standard, when the requirement names the indicators identified and the implications for the audit
options.why: The requirement is specific about two things: the indicators of possible management bias identified during the audit, and the implications for the audit. A summary that names neither leaves the reviewer no way of telling what was seen.

options.text: The indicators need be documented only where the auditor concludes that the estimates are misstated, since it is then that they explain the modification
options.misconception: makes the documentation requirement follow the outcome, when it follows the identification of the indicators
options.why: If the requirement ran only where the estimates were misstated it would never reach the case it was written for. The standard's own point is that judgements can be individually reasonable and still be indicators of possible management bias, and that is exactly the file this senior wants to leave silent.

options.text: The indicators of possible management bias identified during the audit and the implications for the audit both go into the audit documentation, whatever the conclusion reached on the reasonableness of the estimates
options.why: The requirement follows the identification, not the outcome. SA 540 (Revised) has the auditor include in the audit documentation the indicators of possible management bias identified during the audit and the implications for the audit, which is what allows anyone reading the file to see that the pattern was noticed and weighed rather than missed. A conclusion recorded with the reasoning stripped out of it does not show how it was reached, and the indicators are the reasoning here.

options.text: Only the conclusion — indicators that did not turn into misstatements are not audit evidence and have no place in the file
options.misconception: treats what was considered and set aside as not worth recording, when the file is meant to show how the conclusion was reached
options.why: Documentation records the work as well as the result. The indicators are what the auditor weighed in reaching the conclusion that the estimates are reasonable, and a file that shows only the conclusion cannot be reviewed against the judgement that produced it.

citation.ref: the audit documentation requirement — indicators of possible management bias identified during the audit and the implications for the audit

items.scenario: You identified a pattern of accounting estimates all leaning the same way, evaluated it, and concluded that every estimate falls inside a supportable range and that the financial statements are not misstated in respect of them. The senior proposes to record in the file only the conclusion that the estimates are reasonable, saying that indicators of bias which led nowhere would only invite questions from a reviewer or a regulator later on.

items.stem: What comes first, and why is the engagement team told at all?

options.text: Nothing happens until management confirms the relationship, since management identifies related parties and the auditor's role is to test what it has identified
options.misconception: leaves the determination to the party whose own list is in question
options.why: The list was silent about this party, which is the whole difficulty. The determination whether the underlying circumstances confirm the existence of the relationship is the auditor's, and management is then asked to identify all transactions with the party for his further evaluation.

options.text: The team is told so that the extra work can be shared out and the additional procedures properly staffed before the deadline
options.misconception: reads a risk-assessment communication as a resourcing message, so the point of telling the team is lost
options.why: Staffing follows, but it is not why the standard requires the communication. The reason given is that the other members may need to reconsider what their own procedures have already produced, because a related party discovered late can change what earlier work is worth.

options.text: First determine whether the underlying circumstances confirm the existence of the related party relationship or transaction, an arrangement that merely suggests one not yet being one — and the prompt communication to the other members of the engagement team is made so that they can determine whether the information affects the results of, and the conclusions drawn from, risk assessment procedures already performed, including whether the risk of material misstatement needs to be reassessed
options.why: SA 550 puts a threshold in front of the steps. Where the auditor identifies arrangements or information that suggests the existence of related party relationships or transactions management has not previously identified or disclosed, he shall determine whether the underlying circumstances confirm the existence of those relationships or transactions — a similar name is a reason to look, not yet a related party. The standard also states why the engagement team is told: to assist the other members of it in determining whether this information affects the results of, and the conclusions drawn from, risk assessment procedures already performed, including whether the risk of material misstatement needs to be reassessed.

options.text: The six steps begin at once — SA 550 sets no threshold, and a suspicion strong enough to notice is strong enough to act on
options.misconception: skips the determination the standard puts first, so the steps run on a resemblance that may turn out to be nothing
options.why: There is a threshold and it is stated. The auditor determines whether the underlying circumstances confirm the existence of the relationship or transaction, and the steps that follow — requesting management, inquiring into the controls, substantive procedures — are for a party the circumstances have confirmed.

citation.ref: para 22 — the determination whether the underlying circumstances confirm the existence of the relationship or transaction, and the purpose of the prompt communication to the other members of the engagement team

items.scenario: Inspecting bank confirmations you see a guarantee the company has given for a loan taken by Meghna Enterprises, a name that appears nowhere on management's related party list. The name resembles that of a business the managing director's spouse is said to run, but you have nothing yet beyond the resemblance. The senior proposes to start the SA 550 steps at once — write to the engagement team, ask management for all transactions with Meghna Enterprises, and inquire why the controls failed to identify it.

items.stem: Which engagement fits what the company has described?

options.text: An audit — anything short of reasonable assurance is of no practical use to a lender, and the company's preference for a negative conclusion cannot lower the standard
options.misconception: treats the audit as the only engagement worth having, when the framework provides a middle rung for exactly this need
options.why: Lenders use review reports routinely for interim and half-yearly figures. The question is what level of assurance the user needs and is asking for, and here the user has said what it needs and it is less than an audit.

options.text: A review, but with the conclusion expressed positively, since what the lender ultimately wants to know is that the statements are right
options.misconception: keeps a review's procedures and borrows an audit's form of conclusion, so the report says more than the work supports
options.why: The negative form is not a stylistic habit; it is what limited assurance can honestly carry. A positive conclusion asserts that the practitioner has obtained enough evidence to say the statements are right, which inquiry and analytical procedures alone do not provide.

options.text: An agreed-upon procedures engagement — it is the cheapest of the three, and the report can be worded so that nothing came to the practitioner's attention
options.misconception: buys the cheapest engagement and then borrows a review's wording for it, which is the misdescription the ladder exists to prevent
options.why: The wording is not free to move between engagements. An agreed-upon procedures report states factual findings on named procedures and says expressly that it is not an audit or a review and that no assurance is expressed; a sentence borrowed from a review would promise the lender something the work never produced.

options.text: A review — it gives limited assurance on the financial statements as a whole, is built mainly on inquiry and analytical procedures, and its conclusion is expressed in the negative form; an agreed-upon procedures engagement gives no assurance at all and says nothing about the statements as a whole, and an audit's reasonable assurance is more than the company has asked for
options.why: The three engagements sit on a ladder and the company has described the middle rung. A review gives limited assurance across the financial statements, working mainly through inquiry and analytical procedures, and it concludes in the negative form — nothing has come to our attention that causes us to believe the statements are not prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the framework. An agreed-upon procedures engagement gives no assurance at all and reports factual findings on the specified procedures only, so it can say nothing about the statements as a whole. An audit would answer the need, and would cost more than the need.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services, read with Ch. Review of Financial Information — the level of assurance and the form of conclusion in a review and in an agreed-upon procedures engagement

items.scenario: A company must give its lender comfort on a full set of half-yearly financial statements. No statute requires those statements to be audited. The company wants the least expensive engagement that still lets the lender take a view on the statements as a whole, and it has told the lender it will accept a conclusion worded in the negative.

items.stem: What is required?

options.text: The opinion is not modified by the CARO answer — the CARO report is a separate statement annexed to the auditor's report, and whether the opinion is modified is decided under SA 570 and SA 705 — but where the answer to any CARO question is unfavourable or qualified, the auditor's report must also state the basis for that answer, so a bare "no" will not do
options.why: Two documents and two questions. The CARO report is a separate statement annexed to the auditor's report, and answering one of its clauses unfavourably is not itself a modification of the opinion; whether the opinion is modified is settled under SA 570 and, if it comes to it, SA 705, and here the disclosure is adequate so the opinion stands unmodified with the Material Uncertainty section. What CARO adds is that where the answer to any of its questions is unfavourable or qualified, the auditor's report shall also state the basis for such unfavourable or qualified answer.

options.text: The opinion stands unmodified and a bare "no" is enough — CARO calls for an answer to each question, not for the auditor's reasons
options.misconception: answers the clause and stops, missing the requirement that an unfavourable answer carry its basis
options.why: The first half is right and the second is not. CARO requires that where the answer to any of its questions is unfavourable or qualified, the report shall also state the basis for that answer, which is what makes the annexure readable by anyone but its author.

options.text: An unfavourable answer to clause 3(xix) requires the opinion to be qualified, the clause and the going concern conclusion being about the same thing
options.misconception: treats a CARO answer as though it were part of the opinion, so one unfavourable clause drags the opinion with it
options.why: They are not the same thing and they do not sit in the same document. Clause 3(xix) asks its own question on its own named inputs and is answered in an annexure; the opinion on the financial statements is formed under the standards and is modified only when they require it.

options.text: The clause cannot be answered unfavourably at all where the going concern basis has been found appropriate, since a company that is a going concern is by definition capable of meeting its liabilities
options.misconception: collapses the clause into the SA 570 conclusion, when the clause asks a differently worded question anchored to the balance sheet date
options.why: The going concern basis being appropriate and no material uncertainty existing are different findings — SA 570 provides for a Material Uncertainty section precisely for the case where both an appropriate basis and a material uncertainty exist together. Clause 3(xix) asks whether the auditor is of the opinion that no material uncertainty exists that the company is not capable of meeting its liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet as they fall due within one year of that date, and that question can be answered unfavourably on an appropriate going concern basis.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xix), read with paragraph 4 requiring the auditor's report to state the basis for any unfavourable or qualified answer

items.scenario: You conclude under clause 3(xix) that a material uncertainty does exist. Separately, under SA 570 you conclude that the going concern basis is appropriate and that the disclosure of the uncertainty in the notes is adequate, so you include a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section and your opinion is unmodified. The engagement partner asks whether an unfavourable answer to the clause forces the opinion to be modified, and whether a bare "no" in the CARO annexure is enough.

items.stem: What does clause 3(xx) actually report on?

options.text: Report both limbs adversely, clause 3(xx) covering compliance with section 135 as a whole
options.misconception: reads a two-limbed clause about transfers as a general compliance check on the whole of section 135
options.why: The clause is narrower than the section it sits under. It has exactly two questions, both about the transfer of an unspent amount to a stated destination within a stated window, and neither is a general audit of how the money was spent.

options.text: Report clause 3(xx)(b) adversely, because money handed to an unregistered implementing agency has not reached its ongoing project and is therefore unspent for the purpose of section 135(6)
options.misconception: converts a spending irregularity into an unspent amount, when the second limb asks only whether an amount remaining unspent pursuant to an ongoing project reached the special account
options.why: Section 135(6) deals with an amount remaining unspent at the end of the financial year in respect of an ongoing project, which is transferred to the special account within thirty days of the year end. Money paid out to an agency has been spent, well or badly, and the second limb has nothing to say about the choice of agency.

options.text: Report clause 3(xx)(a) adversely — money spent on an activity outside Schedule VII is in substance unspent corporate social responsibility money, whatever the cash book shows
options.misconception: rewrites improper spending as an unspent amount, so a clause about a transfer is used to report a different failure
options.why: Clause 3(xx)(a) asks whether an unspent amount was transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII. The company transferred nothing because it had nothing unspent, and deeming the misspent money to be unspent would make the clause report something it never asks about.

options.text: Neither limb has anything to report — both ask only whether an unspent amount was transferred, one to a Fund specified in Schedule VII and the other to the special account, and nothing here was unspent; the propriety of the spending is a section 135 compliance question answered elsewhere in your reporting, not inside clause 3(xx)
options.why: Read the two limbs as they are written. Clause 3(xx)(a) asks whether, in respect of other than ongoing projects, the unspent amount was transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the expiry of the financial year. Clause 3(xx)(b) asks whether any amount remaining unspent pursuant to an ongoing project was transferred to the special account under section 135(6). Both are questions about whether an unspent amount was transferred, and a company that spent everything has no unspent amount to transfer. That the money went to the wrong activity and through an unregistered agency is a real failure, but the propriety of the spending is not what either limb asks about; it belongs where compliance with section 135 is reported.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xx)(a) and 3(xx)(b), with the second proviso to section 135(5) and section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A company met its whole corporate social responsibility obligation in cash during the year, so nothing at all was left unspent. On examination you find that a large part of the money was spent on a programme that is not an activity specified in Schedule VII, and that a further part went to an implementing agency which is not registered as the CSR Rules require. The audit committee asks whether clause 3(xx) must therefore be reported adversely.

items.stem: Is that right?

options.text: No — the first limb asks whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature of its business, and a system run by an outside firm covering every location on a defined cycle is such a system; who employs the internal auditor is not what the limb asks about
options.why: The clause asks about a system and about its fit, not about a payroll. An internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature of the business can be staffed by the company's own employees, by an outside firm engaged for the purpose, or by a mixture, and the question in every case is whether the coverage matches what this company is and does. Here it does. Who employs the internal auditor decides nothing under this limb, and answering "no" would tell a reader something about the company that is not true.
keywords: internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature

options.text: No, but the second limb must then be answered "no" as well, since the reports of an outside firm are not reports of the Internal Auditors
options.misconception: reads "Internal Auditors" in the second limb as meaning employees, so a properly considered set of reports goes unreported
options.why: The second limb asks whether the reports of the Internal Auditors for the period under audit were considered by the statutory auditor. The outside firm is the internal auditor here, its reports cover the period under audit, and they are on the file and have been read.

options.text: Yes — an internal audit system means a function inside the company, and an engagement bought from an outside firm is a professional service rather than a system
options.misconception: reads "internal" as describing who is employed rather than what is examined
options.why: Internal describes the subject matter, not the contract of employment. The function examines the company's own activities as a service to the company, and it does that whether the people performing it are on the payroll or engaged from outside.

options.text: No — and because the arrangement is an outsourced one, the first limb is answered by the scope set out in the outside firm's engagement letter, without any separate test of whether the coverage matched the company's size and nature
options.misconception: substitutes the contracted scope for the judgement about fit that the limb actually calls for
options.why: An engagement letter says what was promised. The limb asks whether what the company has is commensurate with the size and nature of its business, which is answered by looking at the coverage delivered against the operations that exist, whoever wrote the scope.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xiv)(a) and 3(xiv)(b)

items.scenario: A company has no internal audit department of its own. Its internal audit is carried out by an outside firm of chartered accountants engaged for the purpose, which covers every location on a defined cycle; its reports for the whole of the period under audit are on your file and you have read them. The audit senior proposes to answer clause 3(xiv)(a) "no", on the ground that a company which employs no internal auditor has no internal audit system.

items.stem: What must the parent's auditor obtain from those component auditors before that reliance?

options.text: The component auditors' complete working paper files, since the parent's auditor cannot rely on a report he has not verified for himself
options.misconception: turns reliance on another auditor into re-performance of his audit, which is not what the framework asks for
options.why: The parent's auditor is not required to re-audit the components, and his opinion in respect of them is expressly stated to be based solely on the other auditors' reports. What he obtains are confirmations and the information he needs for the consolidation and the disclosures.

options.text: Nothing further — the reports have been furnished, and the Other Matter paragraph records that the opinion in respect of those amounts rests solely on them
options.misconception: treats the disclosure of reliance as the justification for it, so the paragraph does the work the confirmations were meant to do
options.why: Recording a reliance and being entitled to it are two different things. The confirmations as to independence and compliance with the code of ethics are what make the other auditors' reports usable, and the paragraph tells the reader what was done, not whether it was proper.

options.text: Confirmations from the component auditors as to their independence and their compliance with the code of ethics, together with the information required for the consolidation and for the disclosure requirements — the Other Matter paragraph discloses how the work was divided and does not by itself create the entitlement to rely on another auditor's report
options.why: A report arriving through the client's post room is not, by itself, a basis for an opinion. The parent's auditor obtains certain confirmations from the component auditors — as to their independence and their compliance with the code of ethics, and the information required for the consolidation and for the disclosure requirements. Only then does his opinion, in so far as it relates to those components, rest on their reports. The Other Matter paragraph is the disclosure that follows; it records how the work was divided and cannot supply what the division depends on.
keywords: compliance with the code of ethics

options.text: A written representation from the management of the holding company that the component auditors were independent and complied with ethical requirements
options.misconception: takes from management a confirmation that only the component auditors themselves can give
options.why: Management does not know whether another firm was independent and cannot be the source of that assurance. The confirmations come from the component auditors, and a representation from the parent's management about somebody else's independence is worth nothing on the point.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
