options.why: Who enjoys a benefit and whose business earned it are two questions. The benefit arose from Meridian's dealings with its supplier, and what Meridian then does with it is a separate matter between the company and its directors.

options.text: The value is charged, but under the same provision that charges the ₹5,00,000 waiver of interest
options.misconception: pushes a fresh benefit into the provision that reaches back to a deduction allowed in an earlier year
options.why: That provision operates on a liability for which a deduction was already allowed, which is what the interest waiver is. The holiday answers to no earlier deduction; it is a benefit arising from business in the year it was given.

options.text: Nothing is charged, no money having been received and the holiday not being capable of being turned into money
options.misconception: reads the charge as reaching money alone, when the clause names a benefit whether convertible into money or not
options.why: The clause says in terms that convertibility does not matter. It was drafted that way because a supplier can reward a distributor with a holiday as easily as with a cheque, and the reward is worth the same either way.

citation.ref: Section 28(iv), read with Section 41(1)

items.scenario: Meridian Ltd distributes air-conditioners. Its supplier runs a sales incentive and gives Meridian a fully paid foreign holiday for two of its directors, worth ₹8,00,000, for crossing an annual target. Meridian pays nothing for it, cannot exchange it for money, and records nothing in its books. Separately, a bank waives ₹5,00,000 of interest that Meridian had claimed and been allowed as a deduction in an earlier year.

items.stem: What follows for him from assessment year 2026-27?

options.text: He is out of section 44AD for five years, but the audit requirement does not reach him, his turnover being below the section 44AB limit throughout
options.misconception: reads the audit duty as arising only from turnover, when section 44AD imposes one of its own on a departing assessee
options.why: The audit requirement written into section 44AD stands on its own feet and turns on the total income exceeding the maximum amount not chargeable to tax, not on turnover. That is why it was put inside section 44AD rather than left to the turnover test.

options.text: He is shut out of section 44AD for five assessment years, and for those years he must keep books under section 44AA and get them audited under section 44AB
options.why: Section 44AD(4) shuts an eligible assessee out of the section for five assessment years subsequent to the assessment year in which he declared profit otherwise than in accordance with the presumptive sub-section. Section 44AD(5) adds that where that happens and the total income exceeds the maximum amount which is not chargeable to income-tax, he must keep and maintain books of account under section 44AA and get them audited. Both consequences follow from the single departure in assessment year 2025-26.
keywords: maximum amount which is not chargeable to income-tax

options.text: He may go back to section 44AD in any later year he chooses, the scheme being an annual option exercised year by year
options.misconception: treats the scheme as a free annual choice, when the section locks a departing assessee out for a fixed run of years
options.why: It was an annual option until he stepped out of it. The lock-out exists so that nobody can use the presumptive figure in the good years and his books in the lean ones.

options.text: He is out of section 44AD permanently, a departure from the presumptive scheme being irreversible once made
options.misconception: turns a lock-out the section counts in years into a permanent bar
options.why: The sub-section counts five assessment years and stops. A permanent bar would punish one honest year of low profit for the rest of a working life, which is not what the words say.

citation.ref: Section 44AD(4) and Section 44AD(5), read with Section 44AA(2) and Section 44AB

items.scenario: Mr Deo is a resident individual running a retail business. He declared income under section 44AD for assessment years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25. For assessment year 2025-26 his books show a genuinely lower profit and he declares that lower figure instead of the presumptive one. His turnover stays inside the section's limit in every one of those years, and his total income in every year exceeds the maximum amount which is not chargeable to income-tax.

items.stem: What written down value does the machine carry?

options.text: ₹10,00,000 reduced by depreciation only for the years in which she actually earned professional receipts
options.misconception: makes the deeming depend on the year's results, when the section attaches it to the asset being used for the purposes of the profession
options.why: The section speaks of an asset used for the purposes of the profession and of each of the relevant assessment years. It asks nothing about what the profession earned in any of them.

options.text: Nil — every deduction is deemed to have been given full effect to under the presumptive scheme, so no cost survives at all
options.misconception: turns a deemed year-by-year depreciation into a complete write-off of the asset
options.why: What is deemed allowed is the depreciation for each year at the rate the asset carries, not the whole cost in one go. The value runs down over the years exactly as it would have under an ordinary computation.

options.text: ₹10,00,000 — depreciation that was never claimed is depreciation that was never allowed, so nothing has reduced the cost
options.misconception: reads the written down value as a record of what was actually claimed, when the section deems the depreciation to have been claimed and allowed
options.why: The presumptive figure already stands in place of every expense, depreciation among them. Leaving the cost untouched would let one asset be written off twice, once inside the presumption and once again on sale.

options.text: The value left after deducting depreciation for every one of those years, which the section deems to have been claimed and allowed
options.why: Section 44ADA deems every deduction allowable under sections 30 to 38 to have been given full effect to, and it goes on to say that the written down value of any asset used for the purposes of the profession is deemed to have been calculated as if the assessee had claimed and had been actually allowed the deduction for depreciation for each of the relevant assessment years. So the machine's value has fallen every year even though nothing was ever claimed on paper.
keywords: each of the relevant assessment years

citation.ref: Section 44ADA(2) and Section 44ADA(3)

items.scenario: Dr Ahuja has declared her professional income under section 44ADA for four years running. She bought a diagnostic machine in the first of those years for ₹10,00,000 and has never claimed depreciation on it anywhere, because her income was presumptive throughout and no computation of expenses was ever made. She now sells the machine and asks what value it carries for working out the consequence of the sale.

items.stem: Can he compute his income under section 44AE?

options.text: No — the two vehicles held on hire purchase count as his, so he held more than ten goods carriages during the year
options.why: Section 44AE is open only to an assessee who owns not more than ten goods carriages at any time during the previous year, and its Explanation says that an assessee in possession of a goods carriage, whether taken on hire purchase or on instalments and for which the whole or any part of the amount payable is still due, is deemed to be the owner of that carriage. Nine and two make eleven before the December vehicle is counted at all.
keywords: not more than ten goods carriages

options.text: Yes — only nine carriages are registered in his name, and registration is what ownership means for this purpose
options.misconception: makes the registration certificate the test of ownership, when the Explanation deems a possessor under hire purchase to be the owner
options.why: A registration certificate names whoever the finance company's paperwork requires. The Explanation was written because the person running the vehicle and earning from it is the person the section is aimed at.

options.text: Yes — the ceiling is tested on the last day of the previous year, and by then the extra December vehicle had already been sold
options.misconception: tests the ceiling on a single date, when the section says at any time during the previous year
options.why: The words are at any time during the previous year, so one day above the line is enough. A year-end test would let an assessee run a large fleet and sell down in March.

options.text: No, but for a different reason — a carriage held on hire purchase is outside the scheme altogether, so no presumed income can be computed for those two
options.misconception: shuts out of the scheme vehicles the Explanation expressly brings into it
options.why: The Explanation brings them in rather than keeping them out; in an eligible case they are counted and earn the presumed income like any other vehicle. What defeats Mr Sohal is the number he holds, not the arrangement he holds them under.

citation.ref: Section 44AE(1) and clause (b) of the Explanation to Section 44AE

items.scenario: Mr Sohal runs a goods transport business. Throughout previous year 2025-26 he held nine goods carriages registered in his own name and two more taken on hire purchase from a finance company; instalments on those two are still being paid and the finance company stays the registered owner until the last instalment is met. For a fortnight in December he also held a further registered vehicle before selling it.

items.stem: Can the carried-forward loss be set off in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Yes, but only half of it, a late return costing the assessee the balance of the carried-forward amount
options.misconception: invents a proportionate penalty for a late return that the Act nowhere imposes
options.why: The Act's answers to a late return are the forfeiture in section 80, a fee and interest. It nowhere scales a carried-forward loss down by a fraction.

options.text: No — a carried-forward loss may be set off only against the income of a year for which the return itself was furnished within the due date
options.misconception: transplants the filing condition that governs the loss year onto the year of set off
options.why: There is no such condition anywhere in the Act. If there were, one late return years later would destroy a loss already determined and already carried, which is far more than section 80 says.

options.text: No — the loss lapsed the moment the later return went in late, and it cannot be revived in any subsequent year either
options.misconception: treats a late return in a later year as extinguishing a loss that was already determined on a timely return
options.why: A loss once determined on a return filed in time travels for the number of years the Act allows it. A late return in one of those years does not consume what has already been carried.

options.text: Yes — the timely return is a condition of the year in which the loss is determined, not of the year in which it is set off
options.why: Section 80 bars the carry forward and set off of a loss which has not been determined in pursuance of a return filed in accordance with section 139(3). It fixes on the return of the loss year, and Marut filed that one in time. Nothing in section 80 or in section 72 makes the set off in a later year depend on the return of that later year being furnished by its due date.
keywords: determined in pursuance of a return

citation.ref: Section 80 read with Section 139(3) and Section 72(1)

items.scenario: Marut Ltd incurred a business loss in previous year 2023-24 and furnished that year's return within the due date under section 139(1), so the loss was determined and carried forward. In previous year 2025-26 it earns a business profit and wants to set the carried-forward loss against it. It furnishes the return for previous year 2025-26 four months after the due date for that year.

items.stem: Whose loss is deemed to be a speculation loss?

options.text: Company P's alone — the deeming carries its own exclusion for a company whose principal business is dealing in shares
options.why: The Explanation to section 73 deems a company to be carrying on a speculation business where any part of its business consists in the purchase and sale of shares of other companies. The same Explanation excludes two kinds of company, and one of them is a company the principal business of which is the business of trading in shares or banking or the granting of loans and advances. Company Q sits inside that exclusion and Company P does not.

options.text: Neither — the Explanation stands omitted, so no company's share loss is deemed speculative any longer
options.misconception: reports as removed an Explanation that is still in the section and still operating
options.why: The Explanation is still there and still works. What has changed over the years is the list of companies it excludes, which now names a company whose main trade is dealing in shares.

options.text: Company Q's alone — the more heavily a company deals in shares, the more plainly the deeming applies to it
options.misconception: reverses the exclusion, reading the scale of the dealing as the test when the Explanation exempts the company that does it as its main trade
options.why: The Explanation was aimed at a company using a side line in shares to manufacture losses against its real business. A company that does nothing else has no other business to shelter.

options.text: Both — the Explanation reaches any company at all that buys and sells the shares of other companies
options.misconception: applies the deeming and stops before the exclusions written into the same Explanation
options.why: The exclusions sit in the same sentence as the deeming. A company whose whole trade is shares is not speculating on the side, and the side dealing is the mischief the Explanation was aimed at.

citation.ref: The Explanation to Section 73, read with Section 73(1) and Section 43(5)

items.scenario: Two companies each make a loss from buying and selling shares of other companies during previous year 2025-26. Company P manufactures pumps, and the share dealing is what it does with its surplus funds alongside that business. Company Q's principal business is the business of trading in shares, and it carries on nothing else of any size. Neither is a banking company, neither grants loans and advances, and neither has a gross total income consisting mainly of income under the heads interest on securities, house property, capital gains and other sources.

items.stem: Which of the three keeps its carried-forward business loss?

options.text: All three — the section reaches only a change of ownership brought about in order to traffic in losses, and none of these was
options.misconception: reads a purpose test into a section that operates on the arithmetic of shareholding
options.why: The section never asks why the shares moved. It counts voting power and then lists the changes it forgives, which is a far narrower thing than forgiving every honest change of hands.

options.text: S alone — the insolvency exception is statutory, while an inheritance is only a change the officer may overlook on the facts
options.misconception: turns one of the section's own written exceptions into a matter of the officer's discretion
options.why: Both exceptions sit in the same sub-section and neither depends on anybody's view of the facts. A death is a change the shareholder did not choose, which is exactly why the section names it.

options.text: R and S — a death and a change under an approved resolution plan are both written into the section as exceptions
options.why: Section 79 bars the set off of a carried-forward loss where shares carrying not less than fifty-one per cent of the voting power are no longer beneficially held by the same persons. Its second sub-section then lifts that bar in named cases, two of which are a change consequent upon the death of a shareholder and a change pursuant to a resolution plan approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 after a reasonable opportunity of being heard has been given to the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner. Company T's ordinary sale is inside the bar.

options.text: R alone — the insolvency exception protects a company only for the year in which the resolution plan is approved, and not for the years after it
options.misconception: reads a limit of time into an exception the sub-section states without one
options.why: Nothing in the sub-section confines the relief to one year. It takes that change of shareholding out of the section's reach, and the loss then travels for the years the Act otherwise allows it.

citation.ref: Section 79(2), read with Section 79(1)

items.scenario: Three closely held companies each carry forward a business loss, and in each of them more than half the voting power changes hands during previous year 2025-26. In company R the shares moved because a shareholder died and his holding passed to his son. In company S the change came about pursuant to a resolution plan approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner having been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. In company T the shares were simply sold to an unconnected investor for cash.

items.stem: How much is charged under section 56(2)(x)?

options.text: ₹2,00,000 — the exclusion covers gifts on the occasion of the marriage of the individual himself, and his sister's marriage is not that occasion
options.why: The proviso to section 56(2)(x) lists the receipts the clause does not touch, and one of them is a sum received on the occasion of the marriage of the individual. It is the marriage of the individual receiving the money that must be the occasion. His own wedding gifts fall outside the charge; the money given at his sister's wedding does not, so ₹2,00,000 is charged.
keywords: on the occasion of the marriage of the individual

options.text: ₹6,00,000 — the exclusion is for gifts received from a relative, and not one of these friends is a relative
options.misconception: collapses a list of separate exclusions into the first item on it, when the marriage limb stands on its own feet
options.why: The proviso lists several exclusions and each runs separately. A gift from a friend at the individual's own marriage is excluded by the marriage limb even though the friend is nobody's relative.

options.text: ₹2,00,000, with the ₹4,00,000 charged instead under the residuary head, an exclusion from one clause not being an exemption from tax
options.misconception: sends an excluded receipt to the residuary head, when the exclusion means there is no charge on it at all
options.why: The residuary head charges income, and a gift is not income except where a clause makes it so. Once the proviso takes the receipt out of that clause, nothing else in the Act brings it back in.

options.text: Nothing — both sets were given at a wedding, and money given at a wedding is outside the clause
options.misconception: reads the exclusion as covering any wedding at all, when it names the marriage of the individual who receives the money
options.why: The words fix the occasion to the recipient's own marriage. A relative's wedding is a happy occasion and it is not the one the proviso names.

citation.ref: Clause (II) of the proviso to Section 56(2)(x), read with Section 56(2)(x)(a)

items.scenario: Mr Raghav received two sets of gifts of money from friends during previous year 2025-26, none of the givers being a relative. ₹4,00,000 was given on the occasion of his own marriage in November 2025, and ₹2,00,000 was given on the occasion of his younger sister's marriage in February 2026. Each of the two aggregates is above the threshold the clause fixes for money received without consideration.

items.stem: How much of the house property loss can be set off against his salary?

options.text: None — under the default regime a loss under the head income from house property may not be set off against any other head at all
options.why: Section 115BAC computes total income without set off of any loss under the head Income from house property with any other head of income. The ₹2,00,000 ceiling in section 71(3A) belongs to the computation an assessee reaches by opting out. Under the default regime the set off against salary is not reduced to a ceiling, it is refused outright.
keywords: without set off of any loss

options.text: The whole ₹3,00,000 — the restriction applies to a self-occupied house, and this house is let out
options.misconception: confines the restriction to self-occupied property, when it is drafted about the head of income rather than about the use of the house
options.why: The restriction is written about the head, not about how the owner uses the property. Letting a house out changes how its annual value is computed; it does not decide whether a loss under that head may travel to another head.

options.text: ₹2,00,000, being the ceiling the Act fixes for setting a house property loss against other heads
options.misconception: applies the ceiling that governs the regime the assessee has not chosen
options.why: That ceiling belongs to the computation an assessee reaches by opting out of the default regime. Under the default regime the prohibition comes first, and there is nothing left for a ceiling to limit.

options.text: None this year, and the loss cannot be carried forward either, the default regime refusing both
options.misconception: reads a bar on setting the loss off against other heads as a bar on carrying it forward as well
options.why: What is barred is the set off against another head in the same year. The loss still travels forward to be set off against income from house property in later years, in the ordinary way the carry forward provision allows.

citation.ref: Section 115BAC(2), read with Section 71(3A) and Section 71B

items.scenario: Mr Wadia has salary income and one house, which is let out throughout previous year 2025-26. After the interest on the housing loan the house produces a loss of ₹3,00,000 for the year. He has not opted out of section 115BAC, so his total income for assessment year 2026-27 falls to be computed under the default regime. He asks how much of the loss can come off his salary.

items.stem: How does the Act answer those three points?

options.text: A clarifying Explanation makes royalty include the consideration whether or not the payer has possession or control, whether or not he uses the thing directly, and whether or not it is in India
options.why: Explanation 5 to section 9(1)(vi) was inserted to remove exactly these arguments. It clarifies that royalty includes and has always included consideration in respect of any right, property or information, whether or not the possession or control of it is with the payer, whether or not it is used directly by the payer, and whether or not the location of it is in India. Each of the non-resident's three facts is a limb the Explanation names and disposes of.

options.text: The Explanation settles the question for good, so the treaty between India and the non-resident's country need not be looked at
options.misconception: lets an Explanation to the Act close a question the treaty may answer more favourably for the payee
options.why: The Explanation settles what the Act deems. Where a treaty applies, its own definition governs to the extent it is more beneficial, and Indian courts have repeatedly held that an amendment to the Act does not by itself widen a treaty definition.

options.text: Only the argument about location fails; possession by the payer and direct use by him remain conditions of a royalty
options.misconception: takes one limb of a three-limb Explanation and leaves the other two standing
options.why: The Explanation lists the three matters together and treats them alike. A reading that keeps two of them alive would leave the clarification doing a third of the work it was written to do.

options.text: The three points are good answers, a payment being royalty only where the payer holds the thing paid for, uses it himself and finds it in India
options.misconception: reads into the definition of royalty a set of requirements that the clarifying Explanation was inserted to remove
options.why: If those were requirements, almost no cross-border licence would ever be royalty, because the owner keeps the property and the servers usually sit abroad. The Explanation says so in terms, and says it for the past as well as the future.

citation.ref: Explanation 5 to Section 9(1)(vi), read with Explanation 2 to Section 9(1)(vi) and Section 90(2)

items.scenario: Orbit Ltd, an Indian company, pays a non-resident for the use of a database of technical drawings. The servers holding the database stand outside India. Orbit's staff never take possession or control of the drawings. The day-to-day access is used by a contractor Orbit engages rather than by Orbit itself. The non-resident says those three facts between them leave nothing for section 9(1)(vi) to catch.

items.stem: To which of the two Indian companies does section 94B apply?

options.text: Both — the guarantee catches each of them, and the exclusion for banking and insurance describes the lender rather than the borrower
options.misconception: reads the exclusion as being about the lender, when the sub-section describes the borrower the section does not apply to
options.why: The sub-section says nothing in this section applies to an Indian company engaged in the business of banking or insurance, and the section speaks throughout to the borrower who claims the interest. What the lender does was never the test.

options.text: Kalinga alone — the guarantee makes the bank's loan a debt issued by an associated enterprise, and an insurance company is taken out of the section by name
options.why: Section 94B deems a debt to have been issued by an associated enterprise where the lender is not associated but an associated enterprise either provides an implicit or explicit guarantee to that lender or deposits a corresponding and matching amount of funds with it, so the parent's guarantee brings the bank's loan inside the section. A separate sub-section says nothing in the section applies to an Indian company or a permanent establishment of a foreign company engaged in the business of banking or insurance, which takes the sister company out.

options.text: Kalinga alone, and only because the guarantee was explicit — had the parent merely given the bank an implicit comfort, the section would not have reached the loan
options.misconception: distinguishes an implicit guarantee from an explicit one, when the section names both in the same breath
options.why: The words are an implicit or explicit guarantee. They were drafted that way because a parent's letter of comfort can carry as much weight with a bank as a formal guarantee does.

options.text: Neither — both loans came from a bank that is not an associated enterprise, and the section reaches only interest paid to an associated enterprise
options.misconception: stops at the identity of the lender, when the section deems a guaranteed loan from an unrelated lender to be associated enterprise debt
options.why: The deeming exists because a guarantee does the same work as the loan itself. Without it any group could put an unrelated bank between itself and its Indian subsidiary and step outside the section entirely.

citation.ref: Section 94B(2) and Section 94B(3), read with Section 94B(1)

items.scenario: Kalinga Ltd, an Indian company that manufactures valves, pays interest of ₹9 crore in previous year 2025-26 to a foreign bank which is not its associated enterprise. Kalinga's foreign parent gave that bank an explicit guarantee for the loan. In the same group, Kalinga's Indian sister company is engaged in the business of insurance and pays similar interest to the same bank on the same kind of guaranteed loan.

items.stem: Must Zephyr furnish a return of income in India?

options.text: Yes — a return is the only route to the treaty rate, and a non-resident who does not file loses the treaty benefit
options.misconception: makes the treaty rate depend on filing a return, when the payer may apply the treaty at the time of deduction
options.why: The treaty rate is applied when the tax is deducted, on the strength of the residency certificate and the prescribed information. The relief assumes exactly that — the tax has already been taken at the right rate.

options.text: No — where a non-resident's total income is only of the kinds this section covers and tax has been deducted at a rate not lower than the section's own rate, no return need be furnished
options.why: Section 115A carries its own relief from filing. It is not necessary for the assessee to furnish a return under section 139(1) if his total income consisted only of the dividend, interest, royalty or fees for technical services the section covers, and the tax deductible at source under Chapter XVII-B has been deducted from that income at a rate not less than the rate specified in the section. Zephyr satisfies both limbs.
keywords: not less than the rate specified

options.text: Yes — the relief from filing in this section covers dividend and interest alone, and royalty was never brought within it
options.misconception: confines the filing relief to the first of the two clauses of income it actually covers
options.why: The relief refers to income under either clause of the section's first sub-section, and royalty and fees for technical services sit in the second of them. It was widened deliberately, so that a payee with nothing else here is not made to file for a tax already collected in full.

options.text: No, and Zephyr would still not have had to file even if it had earned business profits here as well, the whole of its Indian tax having been withheld at source
options.misconception: extends the relief past the condition that the total income consist only of the incomes the section names
options.why: The relief has two limbs, and the first is about what the total income consists of. Add a rupee of business profit and that condition fails, whatever was deducted from the rest.

citation.ref: Section 115A(5), read with Section 115A(1) and Section 139(1)

items.scenario: Zephyr Ltd is a foreign company with no permanent establishment in India. Its only Indian income in previous year 2025-26 is royalty from an Indian payer under an agreement made after 31 March 1976. Tax was deducted at source from the whole of that royalty, and the rate of deduction was not lower than the rate section 115A specifies for such income. Zephyr's adviser says a return must be furnished in India in every case where a non-resident has Indian income.

items.stem: What is the position in February 2027?

options.text: Processing is in time so long as it raises no demand, the period applying only to an intimation that asks for money
options.misconception: confines the time limit to intimations raising a demand, when the proviso speaks of any intimation under the sub-section
options.why: The proviso says no intimation shall be sent after the period, and it draws no line by outcome. A refund or a nil result is an intimation too, and the same period governs it.

options.text: Processing is out of time, and in any event the acknowledgement of her return has already been deemed to be the intimation
options.why: A proviso to section 143(1) says that no intimation shall be sent after the expiry of nine months from the end of the financial year in which the return is made, which for a return made in financial year 2025-26 means 31 December 2026. The same sub-section provides that where no sum is payable by or refundable to the assessee and no adjustment has been made, the acknowledgement of the return is deemed to be the intimation. Sarita has had her intimation without anything arriving in the post.
keywords: nine months from the end of the financial year

options.text: Processing is in time, the period running from the end of the assessment year rather than from the end of the financial year in which the return was made
options.misconception: measures the period from the assessment year, when the proviso measures it from the financial year in which the return is made
options.why: A return for one assessment year can be furnished across more than one financial year, so the Act ties the clock to the filing. Reading it the other way would give two returns processed side by side different deadlines for no reason.

options.text: Processing is out of time, and because nothing was ever sent to her no intimation exists at all, leaving her nothing she could take on appeal
options.misconception: treats silence as the absence of an intimation, when the sub-section deems the acknowledgement to be one
options.why: The Act closes that gap itself. In a case like hers the acknowledgement is deemed to be the intimation, which is what gives her something to be aggrieved by should she ever need it.

citation.ref: The provisos to Section 143(1), read with Section 143(1)(a)

items.scenario: Sarita furnished her return for assessment year 2025-26 on 12 July 2025, so the return was made in financial year 2025-26. It needed no adjustment of any kind, nothing was payable by her and nothing was refundable to her. The Centralised Processing Centre sent her nothing at all. In February 2027 an officer proposes to process the return under section 143(1) and to send her an intimation making an adjustment to it.

items.stem: What is wrong with what the Panel has done?

options.text: Both parts — the Panel may confirm, reduce or enhance a variation but may not set one aside or send it back for further enquiry, and every direction it issues binds the officer
options.why: Section 144C says the Dispute Resolution Panel may confirm, reduce or enhance the variations proposed in the draft order so, however, that it shall not set aside any proposed variation or issue any direction for further enquiry and passing of the assessment order. Another sub-section says that every direction issued by the Panel shall be binding on the Assessing Officer, so nothing it issues is a recommendation he may weigh.

options.text: Only the second part — a remand is open to the Panel, that being how any appellate body deals with a record it finds thin
options.misconception: gives the Panel a power that the same sentence of the section expressly withholds from it
options.why: An appellate body ordinarily may remand, and this one was denied that power on purpose. The Panel sits inside the assessment, and a remand would defeat the short timetable the section builds around it.

options.text: Only the remand — the Panel's views have always been advice the Assessing Officer weighs, which is why it is he and not the Panel who signs the assessment
options.misconception: reads a direction the Act calls binding as advice, because the Assessing Officer is the one who passes the final order
options.why: Who signs the order and who decides the point are different questions. The Act says the direction binds him, and that is what makes the Panel a decision-maker rather than a reviewer.

options.text: Neither — the Panel may do both, and the assessee's remedy is an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against the final order
options.misconception: answers a question about what the Panel may lawfully do with the existence of an appeal later on
options.why: An appeal afterwards does not make an order lawful when it is made. The section sets out what the Panel may and may not do, and a remand falls on the forbidden side of that line.

citation.ref: Section 144C(8) and Section 144C(10), read with Section 144C(5) and Section 144C(13)

items.scenario: An eligible assessee objects in time to a draft order before the Dispute Resolution Panel. Having heard the matter, the Panel takes the view that the record is thin and that the Transfer Pricing Officer ought to make fresh enquiries. It therefore issues a direction setting the proposed variation aside and sending the matter back for a fresh assessment. On a second variation it tells the Assessing Officer that its view is a recommendation he may depart from if he disagrees with it.

items.stem: How does section 153 treat the special audit period?

options.text: The period is excluded, but the order must be passed on the very day the exclusion ends, there being no further extension
options.misconception: applies the exclusion and drops the proviso that guarantees a minimum period after it
options.why: An exclusion that handed the officer back a single day would be worth nothing. The proviso exists because the excluded period usually eats the tail of the limitation, and it puts a fixed stretch of days back.

options.text: The period from the direction to the last date for furnishing the report is excluded, and if fewer than sixty days then remain, the remaining period is extended to sixty days
options.why: Explanation 1 to section 153 excludes, in computing the period of limitation, the period commencing on the date the Assessing Officer directs the assessee to get his accounts audited under section 142(2A) and ending with the last date on which the assessee is required to furnish a report of that audit. A proviso adds that where, immediately after that exclusion, the period available for making the order is less than sixty days, the remaining period is extended to sixty days.
keywords: last date on which the assessee is required to furnish

options.text: The whole limitation period starts afresh from the date the audit report is furnished
options.misconception: converts an exclusion of a period into a fresh start of the entire period
options.why: An exclusion stops the clock and then lets it run on from where it stopped. Restarting it would hand the department a whole fresh year every time a special audit was ordered.

options.text: Nothing is excluded — the officer chose to order the audit, and limitation is not extended by a step the department itself takes
options.misconception: makes the exclusion depend on whose decision caused the delay, when the Explanation excludes the period by description alone
options.why: The Explanation lists periods and says nothing about fault. A special audit is ordered because the accounts are complex, and the officer cannot be made both to wait for it and to be out of time when it arrives.

citation.ref: Explanation 1 to Section 153 with the proviso following it, read with Section 153(1) and Section 142(2A)

items.scenario: An assessment under section 143(3) on Neelkanth Ltd must ordinarily be completed by 31 March 2027. On 5 February 2027 the Assessing Officer directs the company under section 142(2A) to get its accounts audited by a nominated accountant, and the last date on which the report of that audit is required to be furnished is 5 June 2027. The company argues that the assessment is barred from 1 April 2027, the special audit having been the officer's own choice.

items.stem: Which of the four may furnish an updated return?

options.text: All four — an updated return is open to any person for any year inside the window, which is the whole point of the scheme
options.misconception: reads the window as the only condition, when the sub-section adds a list of persons it shuts out
options.why: The window says how long and the list says who. The scheme is for a person volunteering before the department has reached him, so a search, a survey or a prosecution closes it.

options.text: D alone — a survey, an updated return already furnished and prosecution proceedings already initiated each bar the return
options.why: Section 139(8A) carries a list of persons who may not furnish an updated return, and three of them are in this scenario. A person on whom a survey has been conducted under section 133A other than sub-section (2A) of that section is barred, so is a person who has already furnished an updated return for the relevant assessment year, and so is a person against whom any prosecution proceedings under Chapter XXII have been initiated before the date of furnishing. Nothing on that list touches D.

options.text: A, B and D — only the prosecution bars an updated return, the other two being matters left to the officer's discretion
options.misconception: reduces a list of statutory bars down to the one item on it that sounds most serious
options.why: Every bar is written into the sub-section and none of them turns on anybody's discretion. A second updated return for one year is barred by name, which stops the scheme being used as a rolling correction.

options.text: D alone, and D must also show a reasonable cause for having left the receipt out of his original return
options.misconception: adds a reasonable cause test that the sub-section does not contain
options.why: The sub-section asks nothing about why the income was left out. A person may furnish an updated return whether or not he furnished a return before, and the additional tax is the price rather than the excuse.

citation.ref: The provisos to Section 139(8A), read with Section 139(8A) and Section 140B

items.scenario: Four people want to furnish an updated return for assessment year 2024-25 in June 2026, and the time window for that year is still open. A had a survey conducted on him under section 133A in March 2026, and it was not a survey under sub-section (2A) of that section. B has already furnished one updated return for assessment year 2024-25. C has had prosecution proceedings under Chapter XXII initiated against him for that year before the date he wants to file. D simply forgot a bank interest receipt and has had nothing of the kind happen to him.

items.stem: Is Coral Ltd resident in India for previous year 2025-26?

options.text: No — the management test is the substance test, and substance beats the place where a company happens to be registered
options.misconception: treats the management test as one that can displace incorporation, when the section makes them two independent routes to residence
options.why: The test was brought in to catch a foreign company run from India, not to release an Indian company run from abroad. Incorporation in India is a route to residence in its own right and nothing takes it away.

options.text: No, unless the Board has issued guiding principles that bring a company like Coral within the management test
options.misconception: makes an Indian company's residence depend on guidance written for deciding where a foreign company is managed
options.why: Those guiding principles help decide where a foreign company is effectively managed. Coral never reaches that question, because the first limb of the sub-section has already answered it.

options.text: Yes, but only its Indian income is charged, the management of the company being wholly outside India
options.misconception: gives a resident company the scope of total income that belongs to a non-resident
options.why: Residence and scope are two steps, and the second follows the first. A resident is charged on its global income, and where its managers sit does not narrow the reach of that charge.

options.text: Yes — a company is resident if it is an Indian company, and the management test is reached only for a company that is not one
options.why: Section 6(3) says a company is resident in India in any previous year if it is an Indian company, or if its place of effective management in that year is in India. The two limbs are alternatives, so an Indian company is resident whatever its place of effective management may be. The second limb only ever has work to do for a foreign company.

citation.ref: Section 6(3), read with Section 2(26) and Section 5(1)

items.scenario: Coral Ltd is incorporated in India under the Companies Act, 2013. Every one of its directors lives in Dubai, all board meetings are held there, and the whole of the company's management and commercial decision-making happens in Dubai. It has no office and no staff in India, and its only Indian connection is its certificate of incorporation. It claims to be a non-resident for previous year 2025-26 because its place of effective management is plainly outside India.

items.stem: What does section 44AB require of the company?

options.text: Nothing at all — section 44AB does not reach a company, whose accounts are audited under the Companies Act, 2013 in any case
options.misconception: reads the statutory audit as taking a company outside section 44AB, when the section turns on turnover and not on the form of the entity
options.why: Section 44AB applies to every person carrying on business whose turnover crosses the limit, company or not. The statutory audit changes how the requirement is met, not whether it applies at all.

options.text: The Companies Act audit is enough as the audit itself, but the company must still furnish that audit report and a further report in the form prescribed under section 44AB, by the specified date
options.why: The proviso to section 44AB says that where a person is required by or under any other law to get his accounts audited, it shall be sufficient compliance if he gets the accounts audited under that other law before the specified date and furnishes by that date the report of the audit required under that other law and a further report in the form prescribed under section 44AB. So the company does not sit through a second audit of the same accounts, and it does not escape the second report either.

options.text: A fresh audit of the same accounts under section 44AB, the proviso being available only to a person who is not a company
options.misconception: confines the proviso to non-corporate assessees, when it speaks of any person required by or under any other law to get his accounts audited
options.why: The proviso is written for a person required by or under any other law to get his accounts audited, and a company audited under the Companies Act, 2013 is the plainest example of one. Nothing in it turns on the form of the assessee.

options.text: Nothing more — an audit under the Companies Act, 2013 discharges section 44AB completely, report and all
options.misconception: reads the proviso as excusing the section 44AB report as well, when it excuses only the second audit of the same accounts
options.why: The proviso relieves the assessee of a duplicate audit. The report in the form section 44AB prescribes carries particulars the Companies Act audit report does not, and the proviso requires it in terms alongside the other law's report.

citation.ref: Proviso to Section 44AB, read with Section 44AB(a) and the Explanation defining the specified date

items.scenario: Konark Cements Ltd is a company. Its turnover for previous year 2025-26 is above the limit at which section 44AB requires a person carrying on business to get his accounts audited. Its accounts for that year have been audited by its statutory auditor under the Companies Act, 2013, and that audit was completed well before the specified date. The finance head takes the view that the statutory audit is the end of the matter and that nothing further is owed under section 44AB.

items.stem: Which of the two amounts does section 43B(h) push out of previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Neither — both were paid on 30 June 2026, before the due date for furnishing the return, which preserves the deduction for previous year 2025-26
options.misconception: applies the first proviso to section 43B, which rescues the other clauses but was not extended to clause (h)
options.why: The first proviso to section 43B saves a deduction where the sum is paid on or before the due date for furnishing the return. Clause (h) was deliberately left out of that rescue, so a payment in June does nothing for the year that ended in March.

options.text: Only the ₹18,00,000, the larger sum being the one the clause was aimed at
options.misconception: sizes the disallowance by the amount owed rather than by the class the supplier is registered in
options.why: Clause (h) has no monetary floor and no ceiling. What decides it is whether the supplier is a micro or small enterprise and whether the sum is outstanding beyond the section 15 time limit at the year end.

options.text: Only the ₹9,00,000 owed to Anand Tools
options.why: Section 43B(h) covers any sum payable by the assessee to a micro or small enterprise beyond the time limit specified in section 15 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006. A medium enterprise is not named in the clause, so the ₹18,00,000 owed to Suraj Components stays outside it and is deducted on accrual. The ₹9,00,000 owed to Anand Tools is past the agreed forty-day term and still unpaid at the year end, so it waits for previous year 2026-27, the year of actual payment.

options.text: Both amounts, the payment discipline of the MSMED Act running to every enterprise registered under it
options.misconception: extends clause (h) to a medium enterprise, which the clause does not name, when the MSMED Act's own registration covers all three sizes
options.why: Registration under the MSMED Act, 2006 is one thing and the class of supplier clause (h) names is another. The clause names a micro or small enterprise and stops there, which is why the size of the supplier has to be read off the registration before anything else.

citation.ref: Section 43B(h) with the first proviso to Section 43B, read with Section 15 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006

items.scenario: Vindhya Ltd bought goods on 5 December 2025 from two suppliers, under written agreements fixing payment within forty days of delivery in each case. It owes ₹18,00,000 to Suraj Components, which is registered under the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 as a medium enterprise, and ₹9,00,000 to Anand Tools, registered under the same Act as a small enterprise. Both amounts are unpaid at 31 March 2026 and both are paid on 30 June 2026. The company's return for assessment year 2026-27 is due on 31 October 2026.

items.stem: How much of the ₹50,00,000 is deductible under section 37(1)?

options.text: ₹18,00,000 — the amounts covered by section 80G and section 35CCD, allowed through section 37(1)
options.misconception: routes the two other reliefs through the residuary section, when each is a claim under its own section with its own computation
options.why: A deduction under section 80G is made from gross total income and a deduction under section 35CCD is a business deduction under its own section. Neither becomes a section 37(1) claim, and the arithmetic of ₹12,00,000 plus ₹6,00,000 belongs to those sections.

options.text: ₹32,00,000 — everything except the two sums that find relief elsewhere
options.misconception: nets the other reliefs out of section 37(1), when Explanation 2 disallows the whole corporate social responsibility spend under that section and the others stand on their own
options.why: Explanation 2 is not a rule about double deduction. It removes the whole class of spending from section 37(1), so there is no residue to allow under that section after the other claims are taken out.

options.text: ₹50,00,000 — the spending is compulsory under the Companies Act, so it is laid out wholly and exclusively for the business
options.misconception: argues from the compulsion, when Explanation 2 deems the expenditure not to be for the business whatever made the company incur it
options.why: Compulsion under another statute is what created the class of expenditure, and Parliament answered it directly. The Explanation deems the spending not to be for the purposes of the business, which settles the wholly and exclusively test before it is reached.

options.text: Nothing under section 37(1), although ₹12,00,000 may still be claimed under section 80G and ₹6,00,000 under section 35CCD
options.why: Explanation 2 to section 37(1) says that any expenditure incurred by an assessee on the activities relating to corporate social responsibility referred to in section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 shall not be deemed to be expenditure incurred for the purposes of the business or profession. That shuts section 37(1) on the whole ₹50,00,000. The other two claims survive because section 80G and section 35CCD are separate provisions with their own conditions, and the Explanation speaks only to the residuary section.
keywords: activities relating to corporate social responsibility
shall not be deemed to be expenditure incurred

citation.ref: Explanation 2 to Section 37(1), read with Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, Section 80G and Section 35CCD

items.scenario: Bharat Alloys Ltd spends ₹50,00,000 in previous year 2025-26 discharging its corporate social responsibility obligation under section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013. Of that, ₹12,00,000 was a contribution to a fund for which a deduction under section 80G is available to the company, and ₹6,00,000 was spent on a skill development project of the kind section 35CCD covers, whose conditions the company satisfies. The whole ₹50,00,000 is debited to the profit and loss account and claimed under section 37(1).

items.stem: How do the reach of the standards and the conflict work out?

options.text: They bind Mr Bose and Coral Ltd but not Ms Anita, and where a standard conflicts with the Act the Act prevails
options.why: The standards notified under section 145(2) apply to a person following the mercantile system of accounting, and only for income computed under the heads profits and gains of business or profession and income from other sources. They do not apply to an individual or Hindu undivided family who is not required to get his accounts audited under section 44AB. Ms Anita has neither head and keeps cash accounts, so nothing in them reaches her. On the second question the standards themselves say that where there is a conflict the provisions of the Act shall prevail to that extent.
keywords: profits and gains of business or profession
the provisions of the Act shall prevail

options.text: They bind Coral Ltd alone, a company being the only assessee section 145(2) reaches
options.misconception: confines the standards to companies, when they turn on the method of accounting and the head of income rather than on the form of the assessee
options.why: Section 145(1) speaks of income chargeable under profits and gains of business or profession or income from other sources being computed in accordance with the cash or mercantile system regularly employed by the assessee. Mr Bose is squarely within it.

options.text: They bind Mr Bose and Coral Ltd, and on a conflict the standard prevails, that being the point of notifying them
options.misconception: gets the reach right and inverts the conflict rule, reading the standards as an override rather than a computation aid
options.why: The standards exist to detach the tax computation from accounting choices, not to displace the charge. The conflict rule runs the other way and the Act governs.

options.text: They bind all three as notified standards of general application, and on a conflict the later notification prevails over the Act
options.misconception: gives a notification precedence over the statute it was issued under, when the standards say the opposite in their own terms
options.why: A standard notified under section 145(2) draws its whole force from the section. It cannot displace the Act, and it says so, which is why the conflict question has only one answer.

citation.ref: Sections 145(1) and 145(2), read with the preamble and scope of the notified Income Computation and Disclosure Standards I to X

items.scenario: Three assessees ask whether the income computation and disclosure standards apply to them for previous year 2025-26. Ms Anita has only salary income and income from house property and keeps her personal accounts on the cash basis. Mr Bose carries on a business, follows the mercantile system and is required to get his accounts audited under section 44AB. Coral Ltd follows the mercantile system and has business income and interest income. Separately, Coral Ltd finds one requirement in a standard that cannot stand with an express provision of the Act.

items.stem: How does section 2(47) treat what she did?

options.text: Nothing in section 2(47) reaches it — a flat moves for tax purposes only on a registered conveyance, and none was executed
options.misconception: reads section 2(47) as needing a conveyance, when the definition is inclusive and clause (vi) was written for exactly the route taken here
options.why: Section 2(47) opens with the word includes and then names relinquishment, extinguishment of rights, compulsory acquisition, part performance and the arrangement in clause (vi) alongside a sale. A conveyance is one route into the definition, not the gate to it.

options.text: Clause (v) reaches it — the buyer was let into possession of the flat in part performance of a contract
options.misconception: reaches for the part-performance clause, which needs a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act for the immovable property itself
options.why: Clause (v) is about possession of immovable property allowed to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. What was contracted for and sold here was the shares, and clause (vi) is the limb that catches an arrangement of that shape.

options.text: Nothing in section 2(47) reaches it, and the ₹95,00,000 is a capital receipt not chargeable to tax
options.misconception: reads the absence of a conveyance as the absence of any transfer, when the sale of the shares is itself a transfer under clause (i)
options.why: A sale of shares is the sale of a capital asset and is a transfer under clause (i) of section 2(47) whatever else is true of the flat. Clause (vi) is what closes the further argument that the immovable property did not move.

options.text: Clause (vi) reaches it — a transaction which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of immovable property, including by acquiring shares in a co-operative society
options.why: Clause (vi) of section 2(47) covers any transaction, whether by way of becoming a member of or acquiring shares in a co-operative society, company or other association of persons, or by way of any agreement or arrangement or in any other manner whatsoever, which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of any immovable property. Handing over the shares handed over the flat, and the clause was written so that the society's ownership of the building answers nothing.
keywords: acquiring shares in a co-operative society

citation.ref: Section 2(47)(vi), read with Section 2(47)(i), Section 2(47)(v) and Section 45(1)

items.scenario: Mrs Rao holds shares in a co-operative housing society which carry with them the right to occupy flat 12B in the society's building. In January 2026 she sells those shares to a buyer for ₹95,00,000 and the buyer moves into the flat. The flat itself is never conveyed to anyone; the society's records simply show a new shareholder in her place, and the building stays in the society's name throughout. She says no immovable property was transferred by her at all.

items.stem: What arises in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: A short-term capital gain of ₹2,00,000, a depreciated item having no cost left to set against it
options.misconception: treats the whole consideration as gain, when section 50(1) sets it against the opening written down value of the block before anything is left over
options.why: The block, not the individual item, is the unit of computation. Section 50(1) subtracts the opening written down value of the whole block, which is ₹9,00,000, so there is nothing for the ₹2,00,000 to exceed.

options.text: No capital gain and no capital loss — the ₹2,00,000 comes off the block and depreciation runs on the reduced written down value of ₹7,00,000
options.why: Section 50 operates in two cases and no others. Section 50(1) creates a short-term capital gain only where the consideration exceeds the aggregate of the transfer expenditure, the opening written down value and the actual cost of any asset acquired during the year, and section 50(2) creates a gain or loss only where the block ceases to exist. Neither happens here: ₹2,00,000 is well below ₹9,00,000 and assets remain in the block. The money received is simply deducted from the written down value under section 43(6)(c), leaving ₹7,00,000 to depreciate.
keywords: deducted from the written down value

options.text: A short-term capital loss of ₹7,00,000, being the written down value less the consideration
options.misconception: strikes a loss on a block that survives, when section 50(2) reaches only the case where the block ceases to exist at the end of the year
options.why: A loss under section 50(2) needs every asset in the block to have gone. While assets remain, the shortfall is not a loss at all; it stays inside the block as written down value and is recovered through depreciation over the following years.

options.text: No capital gain, and no depreciation either for the year, an asset having gone out of the block during it
options.misconception: reads a sale out of a block as stopping depreciation, when depreciation continues on whatever written down value the block still carries
options.why: Depreciation under section 32 is computed on the written down value of the block as it stands after the year's additions and deductions. A sale reduces that value; it does not switch the allowance off.

citation.ref: Sections 50(1) and 50(2), read with Section 43(6)(c) and Section 32(1)

items.scenario: Nilgiri Associates, a firm, has one block of furniture and fittings. The written down value of the block on 1 April 2025 is ₹9,00,000. Nothing is bought for the block during previous year 2025-26. One item out of the block is sold in October 2025 for ₹2,00,000, with no expenditure on the transfer. Several items remain in the block on 31 March 2026. The partner preparing the computation wants to strike a short-term capital loss on the sale.

items.stem: What is charged in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Business profit of ₹20,00,000 on the plot sold, being ₹26,00,000 less the indexed cost of ₹6,00,000, and no capital gain
options.misconception: collapses the two charges into one, when section 45(2) splits the surplus at the fair market value on the date of conversion
options.why: The rise up to the date of conversion accrued to him as the owner of a capital asset and stays under capital gains with its indexation and its long-term character. Only the rise after conversion was earned as a trader.

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹14,00,000 and business profit of ₹6,00,000, on the one plot alone
options.why: Section 45(2) charges the capital gain in the previous year in which the stock-in-trade is sold or otherwise transferred, so only the plot actually sold is charged and the other three wait for the years in which they go. On that plot the fair market value on the date of conversion, ₹20,00,000, is the deemed full value of consideration, and against the indexed cost of ₹6,00,000 it gives ₹14,00,000. The excess of the ₹26,00,000 sale price over that same ₹20,00,000 is business profit of ₹6,00,000.
keywords: in which the stock-in-trade is sold
fair market value on the date of conversion

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹14,00,000 in previous year 2023-24 and business profit of ₹6,00,000 in previous year 2025-26
options.misconception: charges the capital gain in the year of conversion, when section 45(2) postpones it to the year the stock is sold
options.why: Conversion is a transfer under section 2(47)(iv), which is why a capital gain arises at all, but section 45(2) exists to move the charge to the year of sale. Nothing is taxable in 2023-24.

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹56,00,000 on all four plots and business profit of ₹6,00,000 on the one sold
options.misconception: charges the gain on the whole of the converted stock in the year any part of it is sold, when section 45(2) is applied plot by plot as each is sold
options.why: The charge is tied to the sale of the stock-in-trade, and three plots have not been sold. Their gain is computed on the same conversion-date value when their turn comes, in the year each of them goes.

citation.ref: Section 45(2) read with Section 2(47)(iv) and Section 48

items.scenario: Mr Sinha bought four identical plots in 2010. On 1 July 2023 he converted all four into stock-in-trade of his property business, when the fair market value of each plot was ₹20,00,000. The indexed cost of acquisition of each plot, taken up to the year of conversion, is ₹6,00,000. In previous year 2025-26 he sold one of the four plots for ₹26,00,000. The other three are still held as stock on 31 March 2026.

items.stem: In which previous year is the ₹9,00,000 charged under the head capital gains?

options.text: Previous year 2026-27, but under income from other sources rather than capital gains, her entitlement not being final
options.misconception: moves an interim payment of compensation to another head, when section 56(2)(viii) sends only the interest on compensation there
options.why: Section 56(2)(viii) puts interest received on compensation or on enhanced compensation under income from other sources. The compensation itself, interim or final, is deemed by section 45(5) to be income under capital gains.

options.text: In the previous year in which the final order of the High Court is made, so neither previous year 2025-26 nor previous year 2026-27
options.why: The proviso to section 45(5) says that any amount of compensation received in pursuance of an interim order of a court, Tribunal or other authority shall be deemed to be income chargeable under the head capital gains in the previous year in which the final order of such court, Tribunal or other authority is made. Receipt is the test for enhanced compensation under clause (b), and this proviso is the one exception to it, because money paid under an interim order can still be taken back.
keywords: chargeable under the head capital gains

options.text: Previous year 2026-27, section 45(5)(b) charging enhanced compensation in the year it is received
options.misconception: applies the receipt rule in clause (b) without its proviso, which is written for a payment made under an interim order
options.why: Clause (b) does charge enhanced compensation in the year of receipt, and that is the right rule for money paid under a final decree. The proviso carves out the interim payment precisely because the entitlement to it is not yet settled.

options.text: Previous year 2025-26, the year in which the interim order was made
options.misconception: takes the date of the interim order as the charging event, when the proviso points at the final order and not at the interim one
options.why: The proviso names the previous year in which the final order is made. The interim order is what triggers the proviso; it is not the date the proviso fixes.

citation.ref: Proviso to Section 45(5), read with Section 45(5)(b) and Section 56(2)(viii)

items.scenario: Ms Fernandes's land was compulsorily acquired and she went to court for more compensation. On 12 March 2026, with the appeal still pending, the High Court made an interim order directing the acquiring authority to pay her ₹9,00,000 against her claim for enhancement. The ₹9,00,000 reached her on 20 May 2026. The final order in the appeal had still not been made by 31 March 2027, and the authority may yet recover the money if the appeal fails.

items.stem: Is the transaction a slump sale under section 2(42C)?

options.text: Yes, but only because the consideration is wholly in shares; had any part of it been cash the definition would have failed
options.misconception: makes the form of the consideration the test, when the clause asks only that it be a lump sum with no values assigned to individual assets and liabilities
options.why: Cash, shares or a mixture of the two are all capable of being a lump sum consideration. What the clause forbids is the assignment of values to the individual assets and liabilities, which is what would turn the deal into an itemised sale.

options.text: No — a slump sale needs a sale, and shares issued in exchange for an undertaking are not a sale
options.misconception: reads the clause as it stood before the 2021 amendment, which replaced the requirement of a sale with a transfer by any means
options.why: Before 2021 the clause spoke of the transfer of an undertaking as a result of the sale, and a slump exchange was argued to be outside it. The amendment was made to end that argument and it did.

options.text: No — the land was valued at ₹8 crore, so values were assigned to individual assets and the definition fails
options.misconception: counts a stamp duty valuation as an assignment of values, which Explanation 2 to the clause says it is not
options.why: A stamp duty valuation is forced on the parties by another law and says nothing about how they priced the undertaking between themselves. Explanation 2 was written so that complying with the stamp law does not cost the transaction its character.

options.text: Yes on both points — the clause now covers a transfer by any means, and a valuation made only for stamp duty is not an assignment of values
options.why: Section 2(42C) defines a slump sale as the transfer of one or more undertaking, by any means, for a lump sum consideration without values being assigned to the individual assets and liabilities. The words by any means were put into the clause in 2021 to bring an exchange, and every other mode of transfer, inside it. Explanation 2 to the clause then says that the determination of the value of an asset or liability for the sole purpose of payment of stamp duty, registration fees or other similar taxes or fees shall not be regarded as assignment of values to individual assets or liabilities.
keywords: sole purpose of payment of stamp duty

citation.ref: Section 2(42C) with Explanation 2, as amended by the Finance Act, 2021, read with Section 50B

items.scenario: Kaveri Ltd transfers its packaging undertaking to Nila Ltd as a going concern. Nila Ltd pays no cash; it issues its own equity shares to Kaveri Ltd for the undertaking. The agreement fixes no value for any individual asset or liability of the undertaking, but the land inside it was separately valued at ₹8 crore for the sole purpose of working out the stamp duty on the conveyance. Kaveri Ltd says this cannot be a slump sale: there was no sale, only an exchange, and in any case a value was assigned to the land.

items.stem: What is the annual value of the four unsold flats for those two years?

options.text: Nil for both years — the relief runs for two years from the end of the financial year in which the completion certificate was obtained
options.why: Section 23(5) says that where the property consists of any building or land appurtenant thereto which is held as stock-in-trade and is not let during the whole or any part of the previous year, the annual value shall be taken as nil for the period up to two years from the end of the financial year in which the certificate of completion of construction of the property is obtained. The certificate came on 10 September 2024, inside financial year 2024-25, so the period runs to 31 March 2027 and covers both previous years.

options.text: Nil in both years and in every later year as well, a building held as stock-in-trade being a trading asset outside the head altogether
options.misconception: reads section 23(5) as putting stock-in-trade outside house property, when it is a time-limited relief written inside the head
options.why: The sub-section sits in section 23, which computes annual value under the head income from house property, and it fixes the annual value at nil only for the stated period. Once that period ends, section 23(1) applies to the unsold flats again.

options.text: The expected rent in both years — the company is the owner and section 23(1)(a) taxes the sum for which the property might reasonably be let
options.misconception: applies the general rule in section 23(1)(a) without section 23(5), which was inserted for a builder's unsold stock
options.why: Section 23(1)(a) is the default and would tax an empty flat on what it might fetch. Section 23(5) suspends that default for a limited period so that a builder is not taxed on rent he never had while the stock is still fresh.

options.text: Nil for previous year 2025-26 and the expected rent for previous year 2026-27, the two years running from the date of the certificate
options.misconception: measures the two years from the date of the certificate, when the sub-section runs them from the end of the financial year in which it was obtained
options.why: Running from the date would end the relief on 10 September 2026 and split previous year 2026-27 in half. The sub-section avoids that by measuring from the end of the financial year, so the relief ends on a 31 March.

citation.ref: Section 23(5), read with Section 22 and Section 23(1)(a)

items.scenario: Meru Developers Ltd builds flats for sale and holds them as stock-in-trade of its business. The certificate of completion of construction for one building was obtained from the local authority on 10 September 2024. Four flats in that building were unsold and were not let at any time during previous year 2025-26 or previous year 2026-27. The Assessing Officer proposes to tax a notional annual value on the four flats in both years.

items.stem: How much of the ₹6,00,000 is clubbed with Mr Deshmukh for previous year 2025-26, and under which head?

options.text: Nothing — once the money is put into her own business the income is her business income and section 64(1)(iv) has nothing to work on
options.misconception: reads the change of form as ending the clubbing, when Explanation 3 was written for exactly that change
options.why: Section 64(1)(iv) speaks of income arising directly or indirectly from the transferred asset, and Explanation 3 spells out what that means when the asset has been folded into a business. Changing the form of the money does not release it.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, as business income
options.why: Explanation 3 to section 64(1) says that where an asset transferred to the spouse is invested in a business, the income to be clubbed is that part of the business income which bears the same proportion to it as the value of the asset invested bears to the total investment in the business as on the first day of the previous year. ₹5,00,000 against ₹20,00,000 is one fourth, and one fourth of ₹6,00,000 is ₹1,50,000. Clubbed income keeps the head it bore in the transferee's hands, so it comes to him as business income.
keywords: first day of the previous year

options.text: ₹6,00,000, as business income — the gift was without consideration, so the whole income of the business it funded clubs with him
options.misconception: clubs the whole business income, when Explanation 3 clubs only the proportion the transferred asset bears to the total investment
options.why: Fifteen lakh rupees of the capital in the business was never his. Explanation 3 exists to apportion the income so that only what the transferred money earned comes back to the transferor.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, but as income from other sources in his hands
options.misconception: changes the head on clubbing, when section 64 brings the income into the transferor's total income under the head it already bore
options.why: The proportion is right. Section 64 moves income between persons, not between heads, so business income of the wife comes to him as business income and is set off and computed accordingly.

citation.ref: Explanation 3 to Section 64(1), read with Section 64(1)(iv)

items.scenario: On 1 May 2024 Mr Deshmukh gifted his wife ₹5,00,000 for nothing in return. On 1 August 2024 she put the whole ₹5,00,000 into her own proprietary trading business as capital. Her total investment in that business on 1 April 2025 was ₹20,00,000, of which the gifted money is part. The business earned a profit of ₹6,00,000 in previous year 2025-26. They are married throughout and are not living apart under any agreement.

items.stem: For which of the two does partial integration operate?

options.text: For neither — agricultural income is exempt under section 10(1) and can never touch the rate on anything else
options.misconception: reads the exemption as putting agricultural income out of sight for every purpose, when the rate schedule brings it back for the rate alone
options.why: Section 10(1) keeps agricultural income out of total income, and the aggregation in the rate schedule never taxes it. It only decides which slabs the rest of the income sits in, which is why the exemption survives the exercise intact.

options.text: For Mr Prakash alone
options.why: Partial integration is a rate device carried in the Finance Act's rate schedule, and it is written for an individual, a Hindu undivided family, an association of persons or body of individuals and an artificial juridical person. A firm is charged at a flat rate on the whole of its income, so there are no lower slabs for the farm income to push its business income out of and the device has nothing to work on. Mr Prakash is taxed on a slab scale, so it works on him.

options.text: For both — the gates are net agricultural income above ₹5,000 and non-agricultural income above the basic exemption limit, and each assessee clears them
options.misconception: applies the two gates without first asking whether the assessee belongs to a class the scheme is written for
options.why: Those two gates are real and they come second. The first question is whether the assessee is one of the persons the rate schedule applies the scheme to, and a firm is not.

options.text: For Ganga Traders alone — its partners are individuals, so the farm income integrates at the firm's level on their behalf
options.misconception: looks through the firm to its partners, when a firm is a separate person assessed on its own income at its own rate
options.why: A firm is its own assessee under the Act and its income is not the partners' income. What the partners receive from it is dealt with by section 10(2A) and section 28(v), not by the firm's rate computation.

citation.ref: Section 10(1) read with the rate schedule in the Finance Act, 2025 providing for aggregation of agricultural income

items.scenario: Two assessees for previous year 2025-26. Ganga Traders is a partnership firm with business income of ₹30,00,000 and net agricultural income of ₹9,00,000. Mr Prakash is a resident individual with business income of ₹30,00,000 and net agricultural income of ₹9,00,000. Both ask whether the agricultural income affects the rate at which their non-agricultural income is taxed.

items.stem: What can he do?

options.text: He may switch between the two regimes every year, the choice being made afresh with each year's return
options.misconception: applies the year-by-year choice, which belongs to a person with no business income, to a person who has it
