options.text: In person before the committee constituted for his region, with a right to be heard orally
options.misconception: assumes the appellate practice of a hearing in a room, which the scheme was built to remove
options.why: An appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) grew out of a hearing across a table. Section 245MA(3) was drafted from the other end, and the first object it names is the removal of the interface between the committee and the assessee.

options.text: By the Commissioner (Appeals), who sits as the Dispute Resolution Committee for cases in his charge
options.misconception: merges the committee with the appellate authority it was created to stand beside
options.why: Section 245MA(1) requires the Central Government to constitute one or more Dispute Resolution Committees. It is a separate body, and its powers to reduce or waive penalty and to grant immunity from prosecution are what make it worth choosing over an appeal.

citation.ref: Section 245MA(3) read with Section 245MA(1) and the e-Dispute Resolution Scheme, 2022

items.scenario: Mr Sequeira's application to a Dispute Resolution Committee has been admitted. He lives in Mangalore and the committee is not constituted in his state. He asks his adviser when he will have to travel to appear before it, whether he may take counsel with him, and what happens if he cannot attend on the day.

items.stem: Can the assessment be attacked on that ground even though section 144 was rightly invoked?

options.text: Yes, and the assessment is a nullity, so no fresh assessment can be made for the year at all
options.misconception: turns a defective estimate into a want of jurisdiction, which is a different defect with a different consequence
options.why: Jurisdiction to assess under section 144 was properly assumed on an admitted default. What is wrong is the quantum, and an appellate authority may reduce it or set the assessment aside so that a fresh estimate is made on material.

options.text: No, an assessee who has failed to comply cannot afterwards question the officer's estimate
options.misconception: treats the default as taking away the right of appeal against the order that follows it
options.why: The default is what lets the officer estimate at all. It does not put the resulting order outside section 246A, and an appeal against an assessment made under section 144 lies like an appeal against any other assessment.

options.text: Yes, because the power to assess to the best of judgement carries a duty to make an honest and fair estimate on such material as there is
options.why: A best judgement assessment always involves an element of guesswork, and the Supreme Court in Kachwala Gems held that the authority must make an honest and fair estimate and must not act dishonestly, vindictively or capriciously. Here the invoking of section 144 stands and the estimate does not, because the order rests on no material and states a purpose of punishing the assessee. The figure can be challenged in appeal even though the default is admitted.

options.text: No, the only remedy against the figure is an application to the Joint Commissioner under section 144A
options.misconception: makes a direction power that operates before the order the sole remedy against the order
options.why: Section 144A lets a Joint Commissioner issue directions to the Assessing Officer, on his own motion or on the assessee's application, and it works while the assessment is being made. It sits alongside the appeal and does not replace it once the order has been passed.

citation.ref: Section 144(1) read with Section 246A and Kachwala Gems v. Joint Commissioner of Income Tax (SC)

items.scenario: Ganjam Traders answered no notice and produced no book. Section 144 was rightly invoked. The Assessing Officer estimated the turnover at ten times the highest figure in any of the three preceding years and applied a net profit rate of sixty per cent, recording in the order that the firm deserved to be taught a lesson. He held no material supporting either figure and referred to none.

items.stem: What happens to the two pending proceedings?

options.text: The pending scrutiny assessment abates and is absorbed into the block assessment; the pending appeal is untouched and goes on
options.why: Section 158BA(2) provides that an assessment or reassessment pending on the date of initiation of the search or of the requisition, for any assessment year falling in the block period, shall abate. The scrutiny for assessment year 2023-24 is such a proceeding and it abates by force of the sub-section. Abatement is written for proceedings before the Assessing Officer, so an appeal already before the Commissioner (Appeals) against a completed assessment continues.

options.text: The scrutiny abates only if the Assessing Officer records that it does in the block assessment order
options.misconception: makes abatement an order somebody passes, when the sub-section makes it happen by itself
options.why: The words are that the pending assessment shall abate. Nothing has to be ordered and no notice withdrawing the scrutiny is issued; the proceeding simply ceases on the date the search is initiated.

options.text: Neither abates, the block assessment simply running alongside the pending scrutiny
options.misconception: allows two assessments of the same year to run at once, which abatement exists to prevent
options.why: If the scrutiny went on beside the block assessment the same income could be assessed twice and two officers could reach two answers. The sub-section removes the pending proceeding so that the block assessment does the work for those years.

options.text: Both abate, everything touching the block period being drawn into the block assessment
options.misconception: extends abatement to appellate proceedings, which the sub-section does not reach
options.why: Abatement is a rule about assessments and reassessments, which are proceedings before the Assessing Officer. An appellate authority already seised of a completed assessment is not divested by a search that happens afterwards.

citation.ref: Section 158BA(2) read with Section 158BC

items.scenario: A search under section 132 is initiated at Nadir Exports on 5 February 2026. On that date two proceedings are alive. A scrutiny assessment for assessment year 2023-24 is pending before the Assessing Officer, taken up on a notice under section 143(2). An appeal against the completed assessment for assessment year 2021-22 is pending before the Commissioner (Appeals). Both years fall inside the block period.

items.stem: What interest is payable by him under section 234A?

options.text: Interest for five months on the whole ₹5,00,000
options.misconception: ignores both the payment and the credit for tax deducted at source in fixing the base
options.why: Even where tax is genuinely outstanding, the base begins with the tax on total income as reduced by the ₹50,000 deducted at source and by anything already paid. Neither reduction has been made here.

options.text: None, because nothing remained unpaid on the due date and section 234A charges interest on the tax outstanding rather than a fee for a late return
options.why: Section 234A(1) charges interest on the amount of the tax on total income as reduced by tax deducted at source, advance tax and the other credits it names, and where nothing is left unpaid on the due date the base of that charge is nil. The Supreme Court in Prannoy Roy held the levy to be compensatory rather than penal, so a person who had already paid before the due date pays no interest under the section however late the return.

options.text: None under section 234A and none under section 234B either, a payment made before the due date counting as advance tax
options.misconception: converts self-assessment tax paid after the previous year ended into advance tax
options.why: Advance tax is what is paid during the previous year on the instalment dates in section 211. Money paid on 25 July 2026 is self-assessment tax under section 140A, and section 234B measures the advance tax actually paid during the previous year against ninety per cent of the assessed tax.

options.text: Interest for five months on ₹4,50,000, that being how late the return was
options.misconception: charges interest on tax already paid, treating section 234A as a penalty for delay in filing
options.why: The section works on an amount outstanding. Once the ₹4,50,000 went in on 25 July 2026 there was nothing left for interest to run on, and the lateness of the return does not create a base where the section provides none.

citation.ref: Section 234A(1) read with Section 140A and Commissioner of Income Tax v. Prannoy Roy (SC)

items.scenario: Mr Vaz's tax on total income for assessment year 2026-27 is ₹5,00,000. Tax of ₹50,000 was deducted at source. He paid the whole balance of ₹4,50,000 as self-assessment tax on 25 July 2026, before his due date under section 139(1) of 31 July 2026. He then forgot the return and furnished it only on 10 December 2026.

items.stem: Does holding the securities as stock in trade keep section 14A away?

options.text: Yes, because section 14A reaches an investment and stock in trade is not an investment
options.misconception: reads a word into the section, which speaks of expenditure in relation to exempt income and never of investments
options.why: Section 14A(1) disallows expenditure incurred in relation to income which does not form part of total income. It says nothing about how the asset is classified in the accounts, and the classification cannot decide whether the exempt income arose.

options.text: No, the purpose for which the securities were acquired does not matter, and what is disallowed is the expenditure relating to the exempt interest
options.why: The Supreme Court in Maxopp Investment held that the dominant purpose for which an assessee acquired the securities is irrelevant to section 14A, which asks only whether expenditure was incurred in relation to income that does not form part of total income. Where they are held as stock in trade the exempt income still arises, so the section applies and what is disallowed is the part of the expenditure attributable to that income, not the cost of the trading operation as a whole.

options.text: Yes, because the interest was incidental, so no expenditure was incurred in relation to it
options.misconception: revives the dominant purpose argument that Maxopp Investment answered
options.why: That was the theory of dominant purpose and it was rejected. The exempt income arose, expenditure was incurred in earning the whole receipt, and a part of that expenditure relates to the part which bears no tax.

options.text: No, and the whole of the expenditure on the trading operation is disallowed
options.misconception: turns an apportionment provision into a total disallowance
options.why: Only so much of the expenditure as relates to the exempt income goes. Section 14A is an apportionment provision, and Rule 8D supplies the method where the Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the assessee's own working.

citation.ref: Section 14A(1) read with Maxopp Investment Ltd v. Commissioner of Income Tax (SC)

items.scenario: Merit Securities Ltd deals in securities. Part of its holding is tax-free bonds whose interest is exempt under section 10(15), and it holds those bonds as stock in trade, buying and selling them in the ordinary course of its trade. It earned ₹9,00,000 of exempt interest on them while they were held during previous year 2025-26. It says section 14A cannot touch it, because it bought the bonds to trade in them and the exempt interest reached it only incidentally.

items.stem: Is the interest deductible under section 36(1)(iii)?

options.text: Yes, if the advance was made as a measure of commercial expediency, the test being whether the borrowing served the assessee's own business and not whether the money was spent inside it
options.why: Section 36(1)(iii) allows interest on capital borrowed for the purposes of the business. The Supreme Court in S.A. Builders held that where borrowed money is advanced interest-free to a sister concern the deduction turns on commercial expediency, so that the interest is allowed if the advance was made for the assessee's own business purpose even though the money left its hands. A subsidiary building a plant to supply the parent's raw material is that purpose stated plainly.

options.text: Yes, and no enquiry into the purpose of the advance is needed once the borrower is a subsidiary
options.misconception: turns commercial expediency into an automatic rule for companies in one group
options.why: The relationship is not the test. The facts have to show that the advance served the assessee's business, and an advance to a subsidiary for something unconnected with the assessee fails as surely as an advance to a stranger would.

options.text: No, money lent away cannot have been capital borrowed for the purposes of the assessee's own business
options.misconception: reads the words for the purposes of the business as requiring the money to be spent inside the business
options.why: The words look at purpose, not at where the money ends up. An advance that secures the assessee's supply, protects its market or keeps its subsidiary alive is made for its business, and the Supreme Court has said as much.

options.text: No, unless the subsidiary is charged interest at the rate the bank charges Pallav Ltd
options.misconception: makes the deduction depend on a matching receipt, which the section nowhere requires
options.why: Section 36(1)(iii) does not ask what the borrower earns on the money. Where the advance answers a business purpose the interest is allowed whether or not anything comes back on it.

citation.ref: Section 36(1)(iii) read with S.A. Builders Ltd v. Commissioner of Income Tax (SC)

items.scenario: Pallav Ltd borrows ₹2,00,00,000 from a bank at 10 per cent a year and lends the whole of it to its wholly owned subsidiary free of interest. The subsidiary uses the money to build a plant that will make the main raw material Pallav Ltd buys. The Assessing Officer disallows the ₹20,00,000 of interest, holding that money handed to another company was not borrowed for the purposes of Pallav Ltd's own business.

items.stem: What does section 9B do on these facts?

options.text: It charges the ₹12,00,000 in the firm's hands as capital gains
options.misconception: puts every section 9B charge under capital gains, when the head follows what was actually transferred
options.why: Section 9B(2) charges the profits or gains under the head profits and gains of business or profession, or under capital gains, according as what was transferred was stock in trade or a capital asset. Cloth held for sale is stock, so the business head applies.

options.text: It deems the firm to have transferred the stock in trade at its fair market value of ₹42,00,000, and the ₹12,00,000 is charged as profits and gains of business
options.why: Section 9B(1) applies where a specified person receives any capital asset or stock in trade or both from a specified entity on its dissolution or reconstitution. Section 9B(2) deems the fair market value of what was transferred, on the date it is received, to be the full value of the consideration, giving ₹42,00,000 against a cost of ₹30,00,000. Because what moved was stock in trade, the ₹12,00,000 is chargeable in the firm's hands under the head profits and gains of business or profession rather than as capital gains.

options.text: Nothing, section 9B reaching only a capital asset received by a partner
options.misconception: reads half the words of sub-section (1), which names stock in trade beside a capital asset
options.why: The sub-section says capital asset or stock in trade or both. Leaving trading stock out would have let a firm settle a retiring partner in goods and pay nothing on the way out, which is the gap the section was written to close.

options.text: It defers the charge to the year in which the retiring partner sells the cloth
options.misconception: postpones a charge that section 9B fixes to the year the asset is received
options.why: Section 9B(3) charges the income in the previous year in which the capital asset or stock in trade is received by the specified person. The firm's liability is settled by the handing over, whatever the partner afterwards does with the goods.

citation.ref: Sections 9B(1), 9B(2) and 9B(3)

items.scenario: On the retirement of a partner from Kaveri Textiles the firm hands him finished cloth out of its trading stock in part settlement of his account. The cloth cost the firm ₹30,00,000 and its fair market value on the date it is handed over is ₹42,00,000. No capital asset changes hands. The firm's accountant reports nothing, on the footing that section 9B is a capital gains provision and no capital asset moved.

items.stem: Is the rent taxable as Mr Rustom's income?

options.text: No, a benefit taken back by the transferor is a matter for section 64 and not for the sections on revocable transfers
options.misconception: sends the case to the spouse and minor child provisions, which do not reach a nephew
options.why: Section 64 clubs the income of a spouse, a son's wife and a minor child on the transfers it names. A trust for an adult nephew is nowhere inside it, and the proviso to section 62(1) is what decides this case.

options.text: Yes, but only so much of the rent as was actually spent for his benefit
options.misconception: apportions the income to the benefit taken, when the proviso withdraws the shelter for the whole of it
options.why: The proviso is a condition on the exemption and not a measure of it. Once the transferor derives a benefit from the income, section 62 stops applying to the transfer and section 61 restores the whole of the income to him.

options.text: Yes, because the shelter section 62 gives an irrevocable trust is conditional on the transferor deriving no direct or indirect benefit from the income
options.why: Section 62(1) takes a transfer by way of trust which is not revocable during the lifetime of the beneficiary out of section 61, so the irrevocable deed would ordinarily hold the rent away from Mr Rustom. The proviso attaches a condition to that shelter, which is that the transferor derives no direct or indirect benefit from such income. Paying his club subscription and his children's school fees out of the rent is an indirect benefit from the income itself, so section 62 does not protect the settlement and section 61 restores the ₹9,00,000 to him.

options.text: No, the deed not being revocable during the nephew's lifetime, section 62 protects it whatever is done with the money afterwards
options.misconception: reads the first limb of section 62(1) and stops before the proviso that qualifies it
options.why: The limb is satisfied and satisfying it is not enough. The proviso is a separate condition written to catch the arrangement where the transferor gives away the title and keeps the enjoyment.

citation.ref: The proviso to Section 62(1), read with Sections 61 and 63

items.scenario: Mr Rustom settles a let-out property on a trust for his adult nephew by a deed which is not revocable during the nephew's lifetime. The rent of ₹9,00,000 a year is received and kept by the nephew. Under a side arrangement made at the same time, the trustees pay Mr Rustom's club subscription and the school fees of his own children each year out of that rent.

items.stem: Is that ceiling right for a buy-back?

options.text: Yes, and anything above accumulated profits is a return of capital, which can never be income
options.misconception: applies the company law character of a buy-back to a clause that deems the payment to be income
options.why: A buy-back is in commercial terms a return of capital, and that is exactly why a deeming clause was needed to tax it. The clause overrides the character of the receipt and calls the whole of it dividend.

options.text: Yes, every limb of section 2(22) is capped by accumulated profits
options.misconception: treats the ceiling as a feature of the definition as a whole rather than of the particular clauses that carry it
options.why: The ceiling is written into clauses (a) to (e) one clause at a time, and it is missing from the clause that covers a buy-back. Where the words are absent the cap is absent, and no general ceiling sits in the opening words of the definition.

options.text: No, but only the part matching accumulated profits bears tax and the balance is exempt
options.misconception: invents an exemption for the part of the receipt above accumulated profits
options.why: Nothing in the clause exempts anything. The whole payment is dividend and the whole of it is charged at the rates applying to that shareholder, which is why the amount of the reserves decides nothing here.

options.text: No, clause (f) of section 2(22) carries no accumulated profits ceiling, so the whole ₹1,50,00,000 is dividend
options.why: Each of clauses (a) to (e) of section 2(22) contains the words to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits, and that is where the ceiling comes from. Clause (f) was written without them. It deems any payment by a company on purchase of its own shares from a shareholder to be dividend, so the whole ₹1,50,00,000 is dividend whatever the company's reserves happen to be.

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(f) read with Section 2(22)(a) to (e)

items.scenario: Sundar Ltd, an unlisted company whose accumulated profits stand at ₹40,00,000, buys back shares from one of its shareholders in January 2026 for ₹1,50,00,000. The shareholder's adviser accepts that the whole receipt is dividend in principle, but says the amount cannot exceed ₹40,00,000, because a deemed dividend is always capped by what the company has in accumulated profits.

items.stem: Is that addition sustainable?

options.text: No, an issue of shares is a transaction on capital account from which no income arises, and Chapter X computes income rather than creating it
options.why: The Bombay High Court in Vodafone India Services held that the issue of shares at a premium by an Indian company to its non-resident holding company is a transaction on capital account, that no income arises from it, and that Chapter X is machinery which presupposes income and cannot bring a receipt into charge. There is therefore nothing for an arm's length price to be applied to. The one provision that ever taxed a share premium in the issuing company's hands, section 56(2)(viib), stands omitted from assessment year 2025-26.

options.text: No, but the shortfall is a deemed advance by the company to its parent, carrying imputed interest
options.misconception: reaches for the secondary adjustment machinery, which needs a primary adjustment that can stand
options.why: A secondary adjustment under section 92CE follows a primary adjustment that has been made and has become final. Where the primary adjustment itself cannot be made, nothing follows from it.

options.text: Yes, and the shortfall is charged in the company's hands under section 56(2)(viib)
options.misconception: applies a clause omitted from assessment year 2025-26, and in the opposite direction to the one it ran in
options.why: That clause charged a premium received above fair market value, not a premium the company failed to charge. It pointed the other way, and it is gone in any event from assessment year 2025-26.

options.text: Yes, an issue of shares to an associated enterprise is an international transaction, so its price must be at arm's length
options.misconception: stops at the definition of an international transaction without asking whether any income arises to be computed
options.why: The definition can be satisfied and the charge still absent. Sections 92 to 92F compute the income arising from an international transaction, and where the transaction is on capital account and produces no income there is nothing for them to work on.

citation.ref: Sections 92 and 92C read with Section 56(2)(viib) omitted w.e.f. assessment year 2025-26, and Vodafone India Services Pvt Ltd v. Union of India (Bombay High Court)

items.scenario: Estuary Devices Pvt Ltd, an unlisted Indian company in which the public are not substantially interested, issues equity shares to its non-resident holding company during previous year 2025-26 at ₹100 a share. The Transfer Pricing Officer values the shares at ₹260 each, treats the ₹160 a share not charged as a shortfall in the price of an international transaction, and adds the aggregate shortfall to the company's income.

items.stem: Does section 115BBI apply to it?

options.text: Yes, but only if it also obtains registration under section 12AB
options.misconception: makes the two routes cumulative when the sub-section lists them as alternatives
options.why: A body that holds approval under section 10(23C) does not additionally register under section 12AB, and section 115BBI does not ask it to. The list in the opening words is a list of alternatives, and satisfying any one of them brings the charge in.

options.text: No, an institution approved under section 10(23C) is dealt with by section 115TD instead
options.misconception: confuses the charge on accreted income when a body leaves the regime with the annual charge on specified income
options.why: Section 115TD taxes accreted income when a trust or institution ceases to be eligible, or merges, or dissolves without transferring its assets properly. Section 115BBI is an annual charge on the specified income of a body that carries on, and both provisions name section 10(23C) institutions and registered trusts together.

options.text: Yes, section 115BBI names an institution referred to in section 10(23C) alongside a trust registered under section 12AA or section 12AB
options.why: Section 115BBI(1) opens by naming the assessees it applies to, and the list covers a fund, trust, institution, university or other educational institution, hospital or other medical institution referred to in section 10(23C) as well as a trust or institution registered under section 12AA or section 12AB. Approval and registration are two routes to the same shelter, and the charge on specified income was drafted to follow both of them.

options.text: No, the section reaches only a trust or institution registered under section 12AA or section 12AB
options.misconception: reads half the list of assessees in the opening words of sub-section (1)
options.why: Both routes are named in the same breath in the opening words. Confining the section to registered trusts would leave every approved university and hospital outside a charge written for the same behaviour.

citation.ref: Section 115BBI(1) read with Section 10(23C) and Section 12AB

items.scenario: Vidya Foundation runs a college and is approved under sub-clause (vi) of clause (23C) of section 10. It is not registered under section 12AB and has never applied to be. During previous year 2025-26 part of its income is found to be specified income. Its adviser says section 115BBI is a section for trusts registered under section 12AB and cannot reach an institution that took the approval route instead.

items.stem: Is that right?

options.text: Yes on the car and no on the scrap, a motor vehicle being goods like any other
options.misconception: folds the separate motor vehicle provision into the general goods provision that was omitted
options.why: A motor vehicle has a sub-section of its own, written before the general goods provision existed and untouched by its removal. Scrap likewise has its own home in the list in sub-section (1).

options.text: Yes, the whole of section 206C ceased to apply to sales of goods from 1 April 2025
options.misconception: reads the omission of one sub-section as the repeal of the section it sat in
options.why: Only that sub-section went. The section continues to carry collection on the goods listed in sub-section (1), on a licence or lease in sub-section (1C), on a motor vehicle in sub-section (1F) and on remittances and tour packages in sub-section (1G).

options.text: No, but on the scrap it is the buyer who must now deduct under section 194Q instead
options.misconception: substitutes the buyer's deduction for a seller's collection that still stands on its own footing
options.why: Section 194Q excludes a transaction on which tax is collectible under section 206C other than sub-section (1H) of it. Scrap is collectible under sub-section (1), so section 194Q stands aside and the seller collects as before.

options.text: No, only sub-section (1H) was omitted; section 206C(1) still applies to the sale of scrap and section 206C(1F) to the sale of a motor vehicle
options.why: The omission with effect from 1 April 2025 took away sub-section (1H) alone, which was the collection on a sale of goods generally. Section 206C(1) has stood since the section was enacted and covers alcoholic liquor, tendu leaves, timber, other forest produce, scrap and minerals. Section 206C(1F) covers the sale of a motor vehicle. Both survive untouched, so each of these two sales still carries a collection.

citation.ref: Sections 206C(1) and 206C(1F), read with Section 206C(1H) omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2025 and Section 194Q

items.scenario: During previous year 2025-26 Kesar Metals makes two sales. It sells scrap arising from its manufacturing process to a fabricator, and it sells a company car to an individual buyer. Its accountant has read that tax collection at source on a sale of goods was withdrawn with effect from 1 April 2025, and proposes to collect nothing on either sale.

items.stem: On which of the two must the dealer collect tax under section 206C(1G)?

options.text: On the State Government remittance only
options.misconception: reverses both carve-outs, collecting from the buyer the section names and relieving the one it does not
options.why: It is the other way round in each case. A Government buyer is expressly outside the sub-section, and a buyer who has already deducted under another provision is expressly relieved of the collection.

options.text: On both, the exclusions applying only to a remittance for education or for medical treatment
options.misconception: confines the carve-outs to the purposes that carry a lower rate of collection
options.why: Purpose decides the rate at which collection is made. The provisos decide whether the sub-section applies to the buyer at all, and they are not written by reference to what the money is for.

options.text: On neither, a State Government being outside the sub-section and a buyer who is liable to deduct under another provision and has deducted being relieved of it
options.why: The provisos to section 206C(1G) carve out two classes of buyer. One is a buyer who is liable to deduct tax at source under any other provision of the Act and has deducted such amount, because the same money would otherwise bear a deduction and a collection at once. The other is a buyer who is the Central Government, a State Government, an embassy, a High Commission, a legation, a consulate, the trade representation of a foreign State, a local authority or any other person notified by the Central Government.

options.text: On Mr Talwar's remittance only, a deduction under Chapter XVII-B being unable to answer a collection under Chapter XVII-BB
options.misconception: treats the deduction and collection chapters as sealed off from each other, when the proviso reads across
options.why: The proviso refers in terms to a buyer liable to deduct tax at source under any other provision of this Act. Section 195 is such a provision, and a deduction actually made under it switches the collection off.

citation.ref: Section 206C(1G) with its provisos, read with Section 195

items.scenario: An authorised dealer handles two remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme during previous year 2025-26, each of ₹22,00,000 and each for a purpose that is neither education nor medical treatment. The first is remitted by a State Government department. The second is remitted by Mr Talwar, a resident individual, to a non-resident consultant, and Mr Talwar has already deducted tax on the whole sum under section 195 and paid it over.

items.stem: What is wrong with the way it was built?

options.text: Each comparable's entry should be the weighted average of its margins for the current year and the two immediately preceding years, where it carried on such transactions in those years
options.why: Rule 10CA(2) provides that where the most appropriate method is the transactional net margin method, the resale price method or the cost plus method, and the comparable enterprise undertook similar comparable uncontrolled transactions in the two financial years immediately preceding the current year, the price for that enterprise is the weighted average of the prices or margins of all those transactions across those years. Each of the seven entered the dataset as a single-year figure, so the dataset is built on the wrong base however sound the comparables are.

options.text: Nothing in the base, the multiple-year rule applying to the tested party's own results rather than to the comparables
options.misconception: turns a rule about the enterprises entering the dataset into one about the enterprise being tested
options.why: The sub-rule speaks of the enterprise undertaking the comparable uncontrolled transactions, which is the comparable. The tested party's own result for the year is what is then measured against the range that dataset produces.

options.text: Nothing, earlier years being used only where the current year's data is not available
options.misconception: makes multiple-year data a fallback, when for these three methods the rule makes it the ordinary construction
options.why: What the availability of data changes is how many years go into the average. It does not turn a single year into the rule for a method the sub-rule names.

options.text: Each comparable's entry should be the simple arithmetic mean of its margins for the three years
options.misconception: substitutes a simple average for the weighted average the sub-rule names
options.why: The sub-rule says weighted average, and the weights are the denominators of the profit level indicator, which is the cost, the sales or the assets as the case may be. A comparable with a larger base therefore counts for more than one with a smaller base.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(2) read with Rule 10CA(3)

items.scenario: Vantage Precision Pvt Ltd applies the transactional net margin method for previous year 2025-26 and selects seven comparable companies. For each of the seven it takes the margin of the current year alone and builds its dataset from those seven figures. Each of the seven carried on the same comparable activity in the two years before as well. The Transfer Pricing Officer does not quarrel with the choice of comparables; he objects to the way the dataset was built.

items.stem: Are those two claims allowed?

options.text: Neither, no deduction being allowed in computing total income and no credit being allowed to the company or to anyone else
options.why: Section 92CE(2B) provides that the tax paid on the excess money is the final payment of tax in respect of it and that no further credit shall be claimed by the assessee or by any other person. Section 92CE(2C) provides that no deduction under any other provision of this Act shall be allowed in respect of the amount on which that tax has been paid. What the company does get in exchange is sub-section (2D), under which it need make no secondary adjustment and compute no interest from the date the tax was paid.

options.text: The deduction is refused but the credit is allowed, the amount having gone in as tax
options.misconception: assumes that anything paid as tax must be creditable against the regular liability
options.why: The additional tax is not paid on the company's total income. It is paid on money left with the associated enterprise, as a settlement of that money once and for all, which is why credit for it is shut out by name.

options.text: Both are refused, and the company must go on imputing interest on the money still abroad
options.misconception: keeps the imputation running after the option has been exercised and paid for
options.why: Ending the imputation is the whole point of the option. Once the tax is paid, no secondary adjustment is made and no interest is computed from the date of that payment.

options.text: Both, the additional tax being a cost of the transfer pricing adjustment like any other
options.misconception: treats a tax on income as an expense incurred in earning it
options.why: Section 40(a)(ii) already keeps a tax on profits out of the computation of business income, and this part of section 92CE says the same thing again for this particular tax in terms.

citation.ref: Sections 92CE(2B), 92CE(2C) and 92CE(2D), read with Section 92CE(2A)

items.scenario: A primary adjustment made on Cendrel India Pvt Ltd has become final and the excess money was not repatriated within the time prescribed. The company exercises the option to pay the one-time additional tax on the excess money and pays it. In computing its total income for the year it then claims that tax as a deduction, and in its return it also claims credit for it against its regular tax liability.

items.stem: Can it have the benefit of the safe harbour rules?

options.text: Yes, but the margin is raised to the floor of thirty per cent that section 94A(5) sets
options.misconception: mixes the deduction at source floor in section 94A with the profit margin under the safe harbour rules
options.why: Thirty per cent in section 94A(5) is a floor for the rate at which tax is deducted on a payment to a person located in a notified jurisdictional area. It is not a profit margin and it has nothing to say to safe harbour.

options.text: Yes, Form 3CEFA having been filed at the specified margin, the declared price must be accepted
options.misconception: treats the filing of the form as the whole of the qualification, when the rules exclude certain counterparties outright
options.why: The option is exercised by filing the form, and the rules then decide whether it could be exercised at all. Where the associated enterprise is in a notified jurisdictional area the answer is that it could not.

options.text: No, because an information technology enabled service is not an eligible international transaction
options.misconception: attacks a condition the scenario states is satisfied, instead of the one that actually fails
options.why: Information technology enabled services are among the transactions the safe harbour rules were written for. What defeats this claim is where the associated enterprise is, not what the service is.

options.text: No, the rules do not apply to a transaction with an associated enterprise located in a country notified under section 94A or in a no tax or low tax territory
options.why: Rule 10TF takes the safe harbour rules away from an eligible international transaction entered into with an associated enterprise located in any country or territory notified under section 94A, and from one entered into with an associated enterprise located in a no tax or low tax country or territory. Answering the description of an eligible assessee and filing Form 3CEFA does not help where the counterparty sits in such a place, and the price falls to be determined under section 92C in the ordinary way.

citation.ref: Rule 10TF read with Section 92CB(1) and Section 94A of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: Estrela Analytics Pvt Ltd provides information technology enabled services to its associated enterprise, which is located in a country the Central Government has notified as a notified jurisdictional area under section 94A. The company answers the description of an eligible assessee, the transaction answers the description of an eligible international transaction, and the company files Form 3CEFA for previous year 2025-26 at the margin the rules specify.

items.stem: Which of the three is deemed to accrue or arise in India?

options.text: The advertisement revenue only, data being an asset rather than an operation carried out in India
options.misconception: takes one of the three limbs of the Explanation for the whole of it
options.why: The Explanation names three things and gives them equal standing: advertisement aimed at customers here, the sale of data collected from here, and the sale of goods or services made using that data. The second and third are as much inside it as the first.

options.text: The advertisement revenue and the data revenue but not the American software revenue, only income attributable to the specified operations being deemed to accrue here
options.why: Explanation 3A to section 9(1)(i) says that the income attributable to the operations carried out in India includes income from an advertisement which targets a customer who resides in India or who accesses the advertisement through an internet protocol address located in India, income from the sale of data collected from a person who resides in India or who uses such an address, and income from the sale of goods or services using data so collected. A business connection deems only so much of the income as is attributable to the operations carried out in India, so the software sold to American customers stays outside.
keywords: attributable to the operations carried out in India

options.text: All three, a business connection bringing the whole of a non-resident's income into charge in India
options.misconception: reads a business connection as making the non-resident resident here
options.why: Section 9(1)(i) deems only so much of the income as is reasonably attributable to the operations carried out in India. A business connection is a rule about the source of income, not a rule about residence.

options.text: None of the three, the significant economic presence limb needing a place of business in India, which the company has none
options.misconception: reads a physical requirement into a limb that was written to work without one
options.why: Explanation 2A provides that the transactions or activities constitute a significant economic presence whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business in India or renders services in India. Having no premises here is the case the limb exists for.

citation.ref: Explanation 3A to Section 9(1)(i), read with Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i)

items.scenario: Lumen Analytics Inc is resident in a country with which India has no double taxation avoidance agreement, so no treaty is available to it. It has no office or server in India and it crosses the significant economic presence thresholds. Its receipts for the year are of three kinds: payments from advertisers for advertisements targeted at customers who reside in India, payments from a European buyer for data collected from users in India, and payments from customers in the United States for software that has no Indian connection at all. The Assessing Officer proposes to tax the whole of its worldwide receipts.

items.stem: What may the Assessing Officer do about the relief already allowed?

options.text: Withdraw the relief for later years only, the year in which it was allowed being closed
options.misconception: reads the withdrawal as prospective, when the sub-section reaches back to the year the relief was given
options.why: The words are that the benefit shall be deemed to have been wrongly allowed, which looks at the year it was allowed in. That is precisely why a power to recompute that year's income had to be attached to them.

options.text: Reopen the assessment for that year under section 148, a wrongly allowed relief being income that escaped assessment
options.misconception: reaches for reassessment when the section supplies a rectification route of its own
options.why: The sub-section directs the amendment to be made as if section 154 applied, which is a rectification with its own clock counted from the failure. Choosing reassessment instead ignores the route the section actually gives.

options.text: Treat it as wrongly allowed and recompute that year's total income, the amendment being made as if section 154 applied and the four years running from the end of the year in which the failure occurred
options.why: Section 115JH(3) covers exactly this. Where a benefit, exemption or relief has been claimed and granted under a notification issued under sub-section (1) and there is afterwards a failure to comply with any condition in it, the benefit is deemed to have been wrongly allowed, and the Assessing Officer may recompute the total income of that previous year and make the necessary amendment as if the provisions of section 154 applied. The period of four years in section 154(7) is then counted from the end of the previous year in which the failure took place, not from the year in which the relief was given.

options.text: Nothing, relief granted by a notification of the Central Government not being open to an Assessing Officer to withdraw
options.misconception: treats the notification as beyond the officer, when the same section hands him the recomputation
options.why: The notification sets the conditions and the section says what happens when they are broken. The sub-section that says it names the Assessing Officer and gives him the power itself.

citation.ref: Section 115JH(3) read with Sections 115JH(1) and 154(7)

items.scenario: Baltra Logistics BV is incorporated in the Netherlands and had never been resident in India before. For previous year 2025-26 its place of effective management is found to be in India, so it is resident here, and the relief in the Central Government's notification is applied to it for that year on the conditions the notification carries. Two years later it is found that the company did not comply with one of those conditions.

items.stem: Is that reasoning right?

options.text: No, but the deduction on the gain is made under section 195 rather than under section 196B
options.misconception: falls back on the general section for a payment that a special section already covers
options.why: Section 195 applies to any other sum chargeable to a non-resident, which is what makes it the residual provision. Where section 196B names the payment, section 196B is what operates on it.

options.text: No, and section 196B reaches a short-term capital gain on those units too
options.misconception: widens the section past the long-term gain it names
options.why: The words are long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of such units. A short-term gain on the same units is outside that section and falls back on section 195.

options.text: Yes, a payer cannot know the cost of acquisition, so no deduction section can reach a capital gain
options.misconception: turns a reason given for one particular exclusion into a rule covering all of the sections
options.why: An exclusion for capital gains is written where Parliament wanted one and left out where it did not. Sections 196B and 196C put long-term capital gains inside the duty to deduct in as many words.

options.text: No, section 196B requires deduction from the long-term capital gains on the transfer of those units as well as from the income in respect of them
options.why: Section 196B is written to cover income in respect of units referred to in section 115AB and, by name, long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of such units. Section 196C is drafted the same way for the bonds and global depository receipts referred to in section 115AC. A capital gain is therefore not outside the deduction sections as a class; where a section names the gain, the gain is deducted from.

citation.ref: Section 196B read with Sections 196C, 115AB and 195

items.scenario: Cascade Offshore Fund holds units referred to in section 115AB. During previous year 2025-26 it earns income in respect of those units, and it also makes a long-term capital gain on transferring some of them. The person making the payments proposes to deduct on the income in respect of the units and to deduct nothing on the gain, reasoning that a deduction section never reaches a capital gain.

items.stem: What does section 286 require of Solvent India Pvt Ltd?

options.text: It must furnish the country-by-country report in India itself, the parent's country having no agreement with India for exchanging the report
options.why: Section 286(4) requires a constituent entity resident in India whose parent is not resident here to furnish the report itself where the parent is resident in a country with which India has no agreement providing for the exchange of the report, or where there has been a systemic failure of that country to exchange it and the failure has been intimated to the entity. Filing at home does not help where the report has no way of travelling to India.

options.text: Nothing beyond the intimation about the parent, the report itself being the parent's obligation wherever it is resident
options.misconception: reads the ordinary rule and stops before the local filing exception written under it
options.why: The ordinary rule is that the parent files at home and the report reaches India through an exchange agreement. The sub-section that follows is the answer to the case where there is no agreement for it to travel under.

options.text: It must furnish the master file in Form 3CEAA instead, local filing of the country-by-country report being outside section 286
options.misconception: substitutes the master file obligation for the country-by-country one
options.why: The master file and the country-by-country report are separate obligations with separate triggers and separate forms. Whether the master file is due here turns on Rule 10DA, and it does not answer the question section 286 asks.

options.text: It must furnish the report only if the parent designates it as the alternate reporting entity
options.misconception: makes local filing wait on a designation, when the sub-section fastens on the Indian entity by itself
options.why: Designating an alternate reporting entity is a route the group may choose for its own convenience. Local filing does not wait for the group to choose anything; it applies because there is no agreement.

citation.ref: Section 286(4) read with Sections 286(1) and 286(2)

items.scenario: Solvent Group is headquartered in a country with which India has no agreement providing for the exchange of country-by-country reports. Its consolidated group revenue for the accounting year is ₹9,000 crore, which is above the threshold for a report. Its only constituent entity in India is Solvent India Pvt Ltd, which is not the parent and has not been designated an alternate reporting entity. The parent files the report with its own tax authority.

items.stem: What does section 94A(4) require of him?

options.text: The sum is deemed to be his income in any event, the sub-section admitting of no explanation
options.misconception: reads the deeming as absolute when it is conditional on the explanation failing
options.why: The deeming is prefaced by the word unless. A satisfactory explanation of where the payer got the money keeps the sum out of the recipient's income altogether.

options.text: Nothing further, the receipt having been traced to the payer's bank account, after which the burden is the department's
options.misconception: applies the ordinary rule about a traced receipt to a sub-section that deliberately reverses it
options.why: The sub-section exists because the department cannot look behind an account held in a notified area. It puts the burden on the recipient and pushes it one step further back than the ordinary rule does.

options.text: He must satisfactorily explain the source of that money in the hands of the payer, failing which the ₹35,00,000 is deemed to be his own income
options.why: Section 94A(4) provides that where an assessee receives any sum from a person located in a notified jurisdictional area, then unless the assessee satisfactorily explains the source of such money in the hands of the payer, or in the hands of the beneficial owner where the payer is not the beneficial owner, the sum shall be deemed to be the income of the assessee. Showing that the money arrived is not the same as showing where the payer got it, so the bank advice does not discharge the burden.

options.text: The sub-section applies only where the payer is an associated enterprise of the recipient
options.misconception: carries the deemed association in an earlier sub-section into one that asks nothing about the relationship
options.why: Deeming the parties to a transaction to be associated enterprises belongs to the transfer pricing limb of the section. This is a separate charge, and its only trigger is that the payer is located in a notified jurisdictional area.

citation.ref: Section 94A(4) read with Sections 94A(1) and 94A(2)

items.scenario: Mr Bharadwaj receives ₹35,00,000 during previous year 2025-26 from Corvina Ltd, a company located in a country the Central Government has specified as a notified jurisdictional area under section 94A(1). He produces the bank advice showing that the money came out of Corvina's own account, and says his burden ends there because the receipt is fully traced.

items.stem: What does Article 6 of the Multilateral Instrument do to that argument?

options.text: It inserts a limitation on benefits article setting out objective tests of who may claim the treaty
options.misconception: confuses the preamble article with the simplified limitation on benefits provision, which is optional
options.why: A limitation on benefits test asks who the claimant is, by objective tests of ownership and activity, and the Convention offers a simplified version of it as an option. The preamble article changes what the treaty says it is for, and the principal purpose test is a separate article again.

options.text: It applies only between parties that have both adopted the arbitration part of the Convention
options.misconception: ties a minimum standard to an optional part of the Convention that few parties took
options.why: The arbitration part is optional and was adopted by a minority. The preamble article stands on its own and reaches every covered tax agreement, whatever a party did about arbitration.

options.text: Nothing, Article 6 being an optional provision that a party may reserve out of
options.misconception: treats a minimum standard of the Convention as one of its optional provisions
options.why: The preamble article and the principal purpose test are the minimum standard, and a party cannot simply reserve out of them. A reservation is available only where the party's own agreement already contains equivalent preamble language.

options.text: It rewrites the preamble of the covered tax agreement to say that the parties intend to eliminate double taxation without creating opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through treaty shopping
options.why: Article 6(1) is part of the minimum standard, so it applies to every covered tax agreement. It writes into the preamble that the parties intend to eliminate double taxation without creating opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through tax evasion or avoidance, including through treaty shopping arrangements. A purposive reading of a treaty is measured against its preamble, so the argument that the treaty is silent on avoidance no longer holds.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Article 6(1) read with Section 90(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: A treaty between India and another country is a covered tax agreement modified by the Multilateral Instrument. A taxpayer claiming a benefit under it argues that the treaty's only purpose is to allocate taxing rights between two states, that nothing in its text speaks against arrangements set up to obtain a benefit under it, and that a purposive reading therefore has nothing to bite on.

items.stem: Does the withdrawal of the levies help the company?

options.text: No, but the amount is recoverable as tax under the Income-tax Act, 1961 rather than under the Finance Act, 2016
options.misconception: moves the charge into the wrong statute
options.why: The equalisation levy was never a charge under the Income-tax Act. It lives in a chapter of a Finance Act, which carries its own machinery for the statement, the assessment, the interest, the penalty and the appeal.

options.text: Yes, because section 10(50) exempts the receipt in the non-resident's hands
options.misconception: points at the recipient's exemption, which says nothing about the payer's own duty to pay the levy
options.why: Section 10(50) kept the non-resident's income outside the Income-tax Act where the equalisation levy had been paid on it. It is a relief given to the recipient and it does not discharge the Indian payer's obligation to pay the levy in the first place.

options.text: No, each withdrawal operates from its own date and leaves untouched a liability that had already arisen on consideration paid before that date
options.why: The six per cent levy on online advertisement ceased on consideration paid or payable on or after 1 April 2025, and the two per cent levy on e-commerce supply or services ceased on consideration received or receivable on or after 1 August 2024. Neither withdrawal was made retrospective, so a payment made in March 2024 was chargeable when it was made, and the machinery for the statement, the interest and the penalty in Chapter VIII of the Finance Act, 2016 continues to apply to it.
keywords: Chapter VIII of the Finance Act, 2016

options.text: Yes, a levy that no longer exists cannot be collected from anybody
options.misconception: reads the removal of a charge as wiping out liabilities that had already accrued under it
options.why: A charge is tested on the day the taxable event happened. Removing it stops the levy from reaching later consideration and it does not undo a liability that had already arisen on earlier consideration.

citation.ref: Chapter VIII, Sections 165 and 165A, levies withdrawn w.e.f. 1-8-2024 and 1-4-2025, read with Section 10(50) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: Marlin Retail Ltd paid a non-resident for online advertisement space in March 2024 and deducted no equalisation levy on the payment. In 2026 the department raises the point. The company answers that both equalisation levies have since been withdrawn, so nothing can now be demanded from it on a levy that has ceased to exist.

items.stem: Is the notice under section 148 good?

options.text: Yes, because section 148A does not apply at all where the information reached the officer under the section 135A scheme, and the approval that section 148 requires in that very case was obtained
options.why: Section 148A(4) provides that the provisions of that section shall not apply to income escaping assessment in the case of an assessee where the Assessing Officer has received information under the scheme notified under section 135A. There is therefore no notice to show cause to serve and no order under section 148A(3) to pass. Section 148 supplies the safeguard instead, by making it a condition of its own notice that where the officer has received information under that scheme, the prior approval of the specified authority is obtained. Section 151 names the specified authority as the Additional Commissioner or the Additional Director or the Joint Commissioner or the Joint Director, so the approval taken here answers it and the notice stands.

options.text: No, section 148A must be complied with before every notice under section 148, whatever the source of the information
options.misconception: treats the pre-notice stage as universal, missing the sub-section that takes information received under the section 135A scheme out of the section altogether
options.why: The exclusion is written into section 148A itself and not into some proviso elsewhere. Where the information came to the Assessing Officer under the scheme notified under section 135A, the section says in terms that its provisions shall not apply, and what stands in place of the hearing for that case is the approval demanded by section 148.

options.text: No, the approval is bad, an approval for a reassessment notice having to come from the Principal Commissioner or the Principal Chief Commissioner
options.misconception: reaches for the senior ranks that approve a special audit, when section 151 fixes the specified authority at the Additional or Joint level
options.why: Section 151 defines the specified authority for the purposes of sections 148 and 148A as the Additional Commissioner or the Additional Director or the Joint Commissioner or the Joint Director, as the case may be. Nobody of higher rank is named in it, and the approval here came from one of the four.

options.text: Yes, and no approval was needed either, the whole of the pre-notice machinery falling away once section 148A is out of the picture
options.misconception: reads the carve-out as carrying off the section 151 approval too, when section 148 imposes that approval precisely in the section 135A case
options.why: The approval is not part of the section 148A stage and does not travel with it. Section 148 sets out the conditions for its own notice, and one of them is that where the Assessing Officer has received information under the scheme notified under section 135A, the prior approval of the specified authority is obtained. The carve-out removes the hearing and leaves the approval standing, and that approval is then the only thing between the assessee and a notice nobody outside the officer's room has looked at.

citation.ref: Section 148A(4) read with Section 148 and Section 151

items.scenario: For assessment year 2024-25 the Assessing Officer receives information about Sanchit Textiles under the scheme notified in respect of faceless collection of information under section 135A. He serves no notice to show cause, takes no reply and passes no order under section 148A(3). He obtains the prior approval of the Additional Commissioner and issues the notice under section 148. The firm objects that the whole pre-notice stage was skipped.

items.stem: Is the reassessment validly begun?

options.text: No, because the show-cause notice is timed by a sub-section of its own, which allowed only three years and ran out before it was issued
options.why: Section 149 runs two clocks. Section 149(2) governs the notice to show cause under section 148A and allows three years from the end of the relevant assessment year, stretching to five years only where the escaped income, as per the information with the Assessing Officer, amounts to or is likely to amount to fifty lakh rupees or more. Assessment year 2023-24 ended on 31 March 2024, so with ₹22,00,000 at stake the show-cause notice had to be issued by 31 March 2027, and 20 May 2027 is outside that. The three years and three months the officer relied on belongs to section 149(1), which times the section 148 notice alone and cannot rescue a show-cause notice that was already late.
keywords: three years from the end of the relevant assessment year

options.text: Yes, because a show-cause notice under section 148A may be issued up to five years in every case, the fifty lakh test governing only the section 148 notice
options.misconception: reads the extended limb of sub-section (2) as unconditional, when it carries a fifty lakh test of its own
options.why: Both sub-sections carry the fifty lakh test, and each reaches its longer period only when that test is met — five years under sub-section (2) and five years and three months under sub-section (1). The two tests are not worded alike, and that is worth holding on to. Sub-section (1) needs books of account or other documents or evidence in the Assessing Officer's possession showing the escaped income, while sub-section (2) asks only what the information with him suggests. Here ₹22,00,000 fails both, so neither extension opens.

options.text: No, but it is the section 148 notice that is late, three years from the end of the relevant assessment year having run out on 31 March 2027
options.misconception: swaps the two sub-sections, applying the show-cause notice's three years to the section 148 notice
options.why: The bare three years belongs to sub-section (2) and to the show-cause notice. The section 148 notice is given three years and three months by sub-section (1), which runs to 30 June 2027, so 25 June 2027 is inside its own limit. What sinks this reassessment is the stage before it, not the notice itself.

options.text: Yes, section 149 fixing a single period of three years and three months, inside which both notices comfortably fall
options.misconception: collapses section 149 into one clock, missing that sub-section (2) times the show-cause notice on its own
options.why: Section 149(1) provides the time limit up to which a notice under section 148 can be issued for the relevant assessment year, and section 149(2) provides the time limit up to which the show-cause notice under section 148A can be issued. Two notices, two sub-sections, two dates, and a reassessment has to survive both of them.

citation.ref: Section 149(2) read with Section 149(1) and Section 148A

items.scenario: For assessment year 2023-24 the Assessing Officer has information suggesting that ₹22,00,000 of Harivadan Enterprises' income has escaped assessment. Nothing he holds puts the figure anywhere near fifty lakh rupees. He issues the notice to show cause under section 148A on 20 May 2027, considers the firm's reply, passes the order under section 148A(3) and issues the notice under section 148 on 25 June 2027. He records that he is inside the three years and three months section 149 allows, which run to 30 June 2027.

items.stem: At what rates is surcharge levied on his income-tax?

options.text: 37% on the whole of the income-tax, because total income exceeds ₹2 crore and he is not a company
options.misconception: reaches for the 37% tier, which does not exist under the default regime and needs income above ₹5 crore outside it
options.why: Under the default regime of section 115BAC the highest surcharge is 25%. The 37% tier survives only for a person who has opted out of the default regime, and even then it needs income excluding the specified portion above ₹5 crore.

options.text: 25% on the whole of the income-tax, because total income exceeds ₹2 crore
options.misconception: applies the top tier to the whole tax and forgets the 15% cap on dividend and specified capital gains
options.why: The 25% tier is measured on total income excluding the dividend and section 111A, 112 and 112A portion, and the surcharge on that portion never exceeds 15%. Applying 25% across the board overstates the surcharge on ₹1 crore of income.

options.text: 15% on the whole of the income-tax, because the dividend and capital gains cap governs the whole return
options.misconception: extends the 15% cap from the dividend and capital gains portion to all income
options.why: The cap belongs to the portion of income-tax on dividend and section 111A, 112 and 112A gains. The other ₹2.2 crore carries the tier its own size earns, which is 25%.

options.text: 25% on the income-tax on the ₹2.2 crore of other income, and 15% on the income-tax on the ₹1 crore of dividend and section 112A gains
options.why: Total income excluding dividend and capital gains under sections 111A, 112 and 112A is ₹2.2 crore, which exceeds ₹2 crore, so the 25% tier applies to the income-tax on that portion. The surcharge on the income-tax attributable to the dividend and capital gains portion is capped at 15% whatever the total income. Two rates, one return.

citation.source: Finance Act, 2025 — Part I of the First Schedule with section 115BAC
citation.ref: Surcharge tiers on the default regime and the 15% cap on dividend and specified capital gains

items.scenario: Mr Bhaskar, a resident individual paying tax under the default regime for the previous year 2025-26, has a total income of ₹3.2 crore, of which ₹60 lakh is dividend income and ₹40 lakh is long-term capital gain chargeable under section 112A; the remaining ₹2.2 crore is business income.

items.stem: What is her tax including surcharge, before cess, after marginal relief?

options.text: ₹12,54,000 — surcharge at 10% on ₹11,40,000 with no adjustment
options.misconception: levies the surcharge and forgets marginal relief at the ₹50 lakh threshold
options.why: Marginal relief exists so that earning ₹1 lakh more than ₹50 lakh cannot cost more than ₹1 lakh in tax. Without it the extra ₹1,00,000 of income would cost ₹1,44,000, which is exactly the outcome the relief prevents.

options.text: ₹11,40,000 — no surcharge, because marginal relief cancels it entirely when income is within ₹1 lakh of the threshold
options.misconception: treats marginal relief as a waiver of surcharge rather than a ceiling on the increase
options.why: Relief caps the increase in tax at the increase in income; it does not remove the surcharge. Here ₹1,00,000 of the surcharge survives inside the ₹12,10,000 ceiling, and only ₹44,000 is relieved.

options.text: ₹12,21,000 — surcharge at 10% on the ₹1,00,000 of income above ₹50 lakh only
options.misconception: applies the surcharge to the slice of income above the threshold instead of to the income-tax
options.why: Surcharge is a percentage of income-tax on the whole total income once the threshold is crossed, not a levy on the slice above it. The slice-only reading is what marginal relief approximates, but the law does it by a ceiling, not by a different base.

options.text: ₹12,10,000 — the lower of ₹11,40,000 plus 10% surcharge (₹12,54,000) and ₹11,10,000 plus the ₹1,00,000 by which income exceeds ₹50 lakh
options.why: Total income exceeds ₹50 lakh, so surcharge at 10% applies: ₹11,40,000 plus ₹1,14,000 = ₹12,54,000. Marginal relief limits the tax with surcharge to the tax on ₹50 lakh plus the excess income: ₹11,10,000 plus ₹1,00,000 = ₹12,10,000. The lower figure, ₹12,10,000, is the liability before cess, and the marginal relief is ₹44,000.

citation.source: Finance Act, 2025 — Part I of the First Schedule
citation.ref: Marginal relief where total income exceeds ₹50 lakh — the lower of tax plus surcharge and tax on ₹50 lakh plus the excess

items.scenario: Ms Devika, a resident individual on the default regime, has a total income of ₹51,00,000 for the previous year 2025-26, none of it dividend or capital gains. Her income-tax before surcharge on ₹51,00,000 comes to ₹11,40,000 and on ₹50,00,000 to ₹11,10,000 under the slabs she is given.

items.stem: At what basic rates are they taxed, and what surcharge applies?

options.text: Alpha at 25% and Beta at 30%, with surcharge at 12% for both because total income exceeds ₹1 crore
options.misconception: uses the 12% surcharge, which needs total income above ₹10 crore
options.why: Surcharge is 7% where total income exceeds ₹1 crore but does not exceed ₹10 crore, and 12% only above ₹10 crore. At ₹5 crore both companies are in the 7% band.

options.text: Alpha at 30% and Beta at 25%, because the test is turnover in the current previous year 2025-26
options.misconception: applies the ₹400 crore test to the current year's turnover
options.why: The Finance Act fixes the reference year for the rate: the previous year 2023-24 for the assessment year 2026-27. A company that has grown past ₹400 crore since keeps the 25% rate for this year, and one that has shrunk does not gain it.

options.text: Alpha at 25% and Beta at 30%, because the test is turnover in the previous year 2023-24; both bear surcharge at 7%
options.why: The concessional 25% rate turns on total turnover or gross receipts in the previous year 2023-24 not exceeding ₹400 crore — the current year's turnover is irrelevant. Alpha's ₹390 crore qualifies; Beta's ₹410 crore does not, so Beta pays 30%. Both have total income above ₹1 crore and not above ₹10 crore, so surcharge is 7% of income-tax for each.

options.text: Both at 22%, because every domestic company is now taxed at 22%
options.misconception: treats the section 115BAA rate as the default for all domestic companies
options.why: 22% is the rate for a company that has exercised the option under section 115BAA and given up the listed deductions and losses. Neither company has opted, so the ordinary 25% or 30% rate applies by the turnover test.

citation.source: Finance Act, 2025 — Part I of the First Schedule
citation.ref: Domestic company rate by the ₹400 crore turnover test for the previous year 2023-24; surcharge at 7% between ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore

items.scenario: Two domestic companies have not opted for section 115BAA or 115BAB. Alpha Ltd had a total turnover of ₹390 crore in the previous year 2023-24 and ₹520 crore in 2025-26. Beta Ltd had a turnover of ₹410 crore in 2023-24 and ₹300 crore in 2025-26. Both have a total income of ₹5 crore for the assessment year 2026-27, with no capital gains.

items.stem: What is the tax payable before cess, and the marginal relief?

options.text: ₹3,36,33,600, with no marginal relief because relief is available only at the ₹1 crore threshold
options.misconception: allows marginal relief at ₹1 crore but not at ₹10 crore
options.why: Marginal relief accompanies both company thresholds. At ₹10 crore the comparison is with the tax and surcharge on ₹10 crore plus the excess income, exactly as at ₹1 crore with the tax on ₹1 crore.

options.text: ₹3,21,00,000, with marginal relief of ₹15,33,600
options.misconception: caps the tax at the ₹10 crore figure and forgets to add the excess income
options.why: The ceiling is the tax with surcharge on ₹10 crore plus the amount of income exceeding ₹10 crore. Leaving out the ₹1,00,000 of excess income makes the extra rupee of income free of tax, which is not what the relief does.

options.text: ₹3,22,00,000, with marginal relief of ₹14,33,600
options.why: Above ₹10 crore the surcharge is 12%, giving ₹3,36,33,600. Marginal relief limits the tax with surcharge to the tax with surcharge on ₹10 crore, ₹3,21,00,000, plus the ₹1,00,000 by which income exceeds ₹10 crore — ₹3,22,00,000. The relief is the difference, ₹14,33,600, and cess at 4% is added to ₹3,22,00,000 afterwards.

options.text: ₹3,32,00,000, with marginal relief of ₹4,33,600, comparing against tax at 12% on ₹10 crore
options.misconception: computes the ceiling with the 12% surcharge instead of the 7% that applies at exactly ₹10 crore
options.why: At a total income of exactly ₹10 crore the surcharge is 7%, not 12%, because the 12% band begins only when income exceeds ₹10 crore. The ceiling therefore uses ₹3,21,00,000, as the module's own illustration does.

citation.source: Finance Act, 2025 — Part I of the First Schedule
citation.ref: Marginal relief for a domestic company at the ₹10 crore threshold — the module's illustration on ₹10,01,00,000

items.scenario: Gamma Ltd, a domestic company taxed at 30% and not under section 115BAA, has a total income of ₹10,01,00,000 for the assessment year 2026-27 with no capital gains. Tax at 30% with 12% surcharge works out to ₹3,36,33,600; tax at 30% with 7% surcharge on ₹10 crore is ₹3,21,00,000.

items.stem: What relief does section 91 give her?

options.text: No relief, because section 91 applies only where India has an agreement under section 90 with the country
options.misconception: inverts the two sections — section 90 is for agreement countries, section 91 for the rest
options.why: Section 91 exists precisely for income from a country with which India has no agreement; the absence of an agreement is one of its six conditions. Where there is an agreement, relief follows the agreement under section 90.

options.text: A deduction of ₹1,60,000 — 20% of ₹8,00,000 at the Indian rate, since Indian tax is what is being relieved
options.misconception: uses the Indian rate although the foreign rate is lower
options.why: Section 91 takes the lower of the two rates. Relieving at the Indian rate would refund ₹40,000 of Indian tax that no foreign country ever collected, turning relief into a subsidy for the foreign income.

options.text: A deduction of ₹1,20,000 — 15% of ₹8,00,000, being the foreign rate, which is lower than the Indian rate of 20%
options.why: All six conditions hold: resident, income accruing outside India, not deemed to accrue in India, taxed abroad, tax paid, and no agreement. The relief is a deduction from Indian income-tax of the doubly taxed income at the Indian rate of tax or the rate of tax of the foreign country, whichever is lower. The foreign rate is ₹1,20,000 on ₹8,00,000, that is 15%, against the Indian rate of 20%, so the deduction is 15% of ₹8,00,000 = ₹1,20,000.

options.text: A deduction of ₹8,00,000 from her total income, exempting the foreign income altogether
options.misconception: treats unilateral relief as an exemption of the income rather than a deduction from the tax
options.why: Section 91 gives a deduction from the Indian income-tax payable, computed on the doubly taxed income at a rate. The income itself stays in total income; only the tax on it is relieved, and only to the extent of the lower rate.

citation.ref: Section 91(1) — deduction at the lower of the Indian rate and the foreign rate on doubly taxed income

items.scenario: Ms Anjali, resident in India, earned ₹8,00,000 from a lecture tour in a country with which India has no tax agreement, and paid tax of ₹1,20,000 there on it. Her Indian income-tax on her total income, after every relief under the Act but before any double taxation relief, works out to an average rate of 20%.

items.stem: Which of the officer's two positions is correct?

options.text: Only the first — a disputed foreign tax is not tax paid until the dispute ends
options.misconception: makes the finality of the foreign assessment a condition, which section 91 does not contain
options.why: Section 91 asks whether the income was taxed abroad and the tax paid; it does not ask whether the foreign assessment is final. If the refund is later granted, the position is revisited then.

options.text: Both — relief needs a final foreign assessment and the Indian rate is a net figure
options.misconception: adds a finality condition and a net-of-relief rate, neither of which the section contains
options.why: Section 91's conditions are six and finality is not among them, and its Explanation computes the Indian rate before double taxation relief, not after.

options.text: Only the second — the Indian rate must reflect the net tax actually borne in India
options.misconception: computes the Indian rate after double taxation relief, which the Explanation excludes
options.why: The Explanation to section 91 fixes the Indian rate at the tax after relief under the Act but before double taxation relief. Net of double taxation relief the rate would depend on the answer it is meant to produce.

options.text: Neither — tax deducted at source abroad is tax paid, and the Indian rate is computed after relief under the Act but before double taxation relief
options.why: The condition is that the income has been subjected to income-tax in the foreign country and that the assessee has paid tax on it there; deduction at source is payment of tax, and a pending refund claim does not undo it. And the Explanation defines the Indian rate of tax as the Indian income-tax after deduction of any relief due under the Act but before deduction of any double taxation relief, divided by total income — computing it after the very relief being measured would be circular.
