keywords: before deduction of any double taxation relief

citation.ref: Section 91(1) conditions and the Explanation defining the Indian rate of tax and the rate of tax of the foreign country

items.scenario: A tax officer denies section 91 relief to a resident on income from a non-agreement country, because the foreign income was assessed there but the foreign tax, though deducted at source by the payer, is still under a refund dispute abroad; separately, the officer says the "Indian rate of tax" must be computed after deducting the double taxation relief itself.

items.stem: Is the company right?

options.text: No — section 90(2A) applies Chapter X-A to the assessee even if its provisions are not beneficial to him
options.why: Section 90(2) gives the assessee the more beneficial of the Act and the agreement, but section 90(2A) carves the general anti-avoidance rule out of that comparison: the provisions of Chapter X-A apply to the assessee even if such provisions are not beneficial to him. A treaty is a shield against double taxation, not against a finding that the arrangement was impermissible, and section 90(1)(b) itself says agreements are for avoiding double taxation without creating opportunities for non-taxation through treaty-shopping.

options.text: No — because a company can never claim treaty benefits under section 90, which is for individuals
options.misconception: invents a limit on who may claim treaty benefits
options.why: Section 90 benefits any assessee to whom an agreement applies, companies included. The company loses here because of Chapter X-A, not because of what it is.

options.text: Yes, unless India first renegotiates the treaty to include an anti-abuse clause
options.misconception: makes the override depend on the treaty's text, when the Act applies it regardless
options.why: The override is in the Act, in section 90(2A), and applies to every agreement under section 90 or 90A. Whether the treaty carries its own anti-abuse article is a separate matter.

options.text: Yes — section 90(2) is unqualified, and the residency certificate settles entitlement to the treaty
options.misconception: reads section 90(2) without the carve-out in section 90(2A)
options.why: Section 90(2A) was inserted precisely so that the beneficial-provision rule could not be used to escape the general anti-avoidance rule. The certificate proves residence; it does not neutralise Chapter X-A.

citation.ref: Section 90(2A) — Chapter X-A applies even where not beneficial; section 90(1)(b) — avoidance of double taxation without treaty-shopping

items.scenario: A Mauritius-resident company routes an investment into India through an arrangement the Assessing Officer finds to be an impermissible avoidance arrangement under Chapter X-A. The company holds a valid tax residency certificate and argues that under section 90(2) the India-Mauritius treaty, being more beneficial, must prevail over the general anti-avoidance rule.

items.stem: Which item does not belong?

options.text: The uniform rate — section 90(1) names relief, avoidance, exchange of information and recovery, and no more
options.why: Section 90(1) lists four purposes: granting relief in respect of income taxed in both countries or chargeable under both laws to promote mutual economic relations, trade and investment; avoiding double taxation without creating opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through evasion or avoidance; exchange of information for the prevention of evasion or avoidance or investigation of such cases; and recovery of income-tax under both laws. Rates are what each treaty negotiates article by article; uniformity across treaties is not a purpose the section names.

options.text: Exchange of information — that belongs to the tax information exchange agreements, not section 90
options.misconception: separates information exchange from section 90, which names it in clause (c)
options.why: Section 90(1)(c) provides for exchange of information for the prevention of evasion or avoidance and the investigation of such cases; an agreement can be made for that purpose alone.

options.text: Relief for doubly taxed income — relief is given by section 91, not by an agreement
options.misconception: confuses unilateral relief under section 91 with the relief clause of section 90(1)(a)
options.why: Section 90(1)(a) provides for agreements granting relief for income on which tax has been paid in both countries. Section 91 is the fallback for countries with no agreement.

options.text: Recovery of income-tax — that is a matter for domestic collection machinery, not a treaty
options.misconception: drops recovery, which section 90(1)(d) names expressly
options.why: Clause (d) of section 90(1) provides for agreements for recovery of income-tax under the Act and under the corresponding law of the other country. Assistance in collection is a standing treaty purpose.

citation.ref: Section 90(1)(a) to (d) — the four purposes of an agreement

items.scenario: A student lists the purposes for which the Central Government may enter into an agreement under section 90(1): relief for doubly taxed income, avoidance of double taxation, exchange of information against evasion or avoidance, recovery of income-tax, and the fixing of a uniform rate of tax on non-residents across all treaty countries.

items.stem: May they?

options.text: No — under section 245RR, once a resident applicant's application is made, no income-tax authority or the Tribunal shall take any decision on that issue
options.why: Section 245RR provides that where a resident applicant has applied to the Board for Advance Rulings on an issue, no income-tax authority or the Appellate Tribunal shall take any decision in respect of that issue. The Commissioner (Appeals) and the Assessing Officer are both income-tax authorities, so both are stopped on the royalty question; a resident cannot run an appeal and a ruling application on the same issue at once.

options.text: Yes — section 245RR restricts only the Tribunal, not the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Assessing Officer
options.misconception: reads the section as reaching the Tribunal alone
options.why: The section names both: no income-tax authority or the Appellate Tribunal. The Commissioner (Appeals) and the Assessing Officer are income-tax authorities under section 116.

options.text: The application itself is invalid, because a resident can never apply where an appeal on the issue is pending
options.misconception: applies the pendency bar of section 245R(2) to a notified resident, whom it excepts
options.why: Section 245R(2) lets a notified resident applicant seek a ruling even where the question is pending before an authority, the Tribunal or a court. Once that application is made, section 245RR is what stops the other proceedings.

options.text: Yes — the Board's ruling binds only the future, so the earlier year's appeal may proceed
options.misconception: limits the freeze to future years, when section 245RR speaks of the issue, not the year
options.why: The restriction is on any decision in respect of the issue on which the ruling is sought. Section 245RR does not carve out earlier years; the point of it is that one question is decided on one road.

citation.ref: Section 245RR read with the proviso to section 245R(2) for a notified resident applicant

items.scenario: Sarovar Ltd, an Indian company and a notified resident applicant, applies to the Board for Advance Rulings on whether a payment to a foreign supplier is royalty. While the application is pending, the Commissioner (Appeals) proposes to decide the same question in Sarovar's appeal against its assessment for an earlier year, and the Assessing Officer proposes to decide it in the current year's assessment.

items.stem: Is the ruling invalid?

options.text: No — section 245P provides that a proceeding before, or a ruling by, the Board is not invalid merely because of a vacancy or defect in its constitution
options.why: Section 245P says that no proceeding before, or pronouncement of advance ruling by, the Board for Advance Rulings shall be questioned or be invalid on the ground merely of the existence of any vacancy or defect in the constitution of the Board. The ruling stands; the remedy against a ruling the Principal Commissioner dislikes is the appeal to the High Court under section 245W, not a constitutional objection.

options.text: No, because the Principal Commissioner has no standing to challenge a ruling at all
options.misconception: denies the Revenue any remedy, when section 245W gives the Revenue an appeal too
options.why: The Revenue has an appeal to the High Court against a ruling under section 245W; what it cannot do is attack the ruling for a vacancy on the Board, because section 245P forbids that ground.

options.text: Yes — a ruling by an improperly constituted Board is a nullity
options.misconception: applies a general nullity rule the Act displaces for the Board
options.why: The Act displaces the general rule expressly in section 245P, so that rulings are not unsettled by staffing gaps.

options.text: Yes, but only if the applicant objects; the Revenue cannot raise the point
options.misconception: invents a one-sided rule, when section 245P bars the objection from anyone
options.why: The section says the proceeding or ruling shall not be questioned on that ground — by either side.

citation.ref: Section 245P — vacancies not to invalidate proceedings; section 245W — the appeal

items.scenario: A ruling is pronounced by the Board for Advance Rulings at a time when one of its two member posts had fallen vacant and the sitting was held with a defect in its constitution. The Principal Commissioner argues that the ruling is void on that ground alone.

items.stem: Which Vienna Convention principle does the treaty partner's position offend?

options.text: None — India is not a party to the Vienna Convention, so its principles cannot be invoked against a treaty partner
options.misconception: treats India's non-membership as making the Convention irrelevant
options.why: The Supreme Court in Ram Jethmalani held that although India is not a party, the Convention contains principles of customary international law that guide treaty interpretation in India; the Delhi High Court in AWAS Ireland applied Articles 26, 27 and 31 with Article 51(c) of the Constitution.

options.text: Article 29 — a treaty binds each party in respect of its entire territory
options.misconception: picks the territorial article for a question about internal law
options.why: Article 29 concerns the geographic reach of a treaty. Nothing here turns on territory.

options.text: Article 28 — treaties do not have retrospective effect
options.misconception: confuses the retrospective domestic amendment with the non-retroactivity of the treaty itself
options.why: Article 28 says the treaty does not bind a party as to facts before it entered into force. The complaint here is the reverse: a domestic law reaching back to defeat a treaty already in force, which is Article 27's ground.

options.text: Article 27 — a party may not invoke the provisions of its internal law as justification for its failure to perform a treaty
options.why: Article 27 provides that a party may not invoke the provisions of its internal law as justification for its failure to perform a treaty, and the module's own gloss is that contracting states should not dishonour their commitments by retrospectively amending their domestic tax laws or by not abiding by the treaty terms. It sits with Article 26, pacta sunt servanda, under which every treaty in force is binding on the parties and must be performed in good faith.

citation.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969
citation.ref: Articles 26 and 27; Ram Jethmalani v. Union of India; AWAS Ireland v. DGCA

items.scenario: A treaty partner amends its domestic law with retrospective effect so that a payment the treaty exempts becomes taxable at source, and says the amendment must prevail because its Parliament is supreme.

items.stem: Which reading follows Article 31?

options.text: Neither — under Article 32 the preparatory work decides the meaning of every term
options.misconception: promotes the supplementary means of Article 32 to the general rule
options.why: Article 32's preparatory work and circumstances of conclusion are supplementary means, used to confirm the Article 31 meaning or where that meaning is ambiguous, obscure or absurd. They do not displace the general rule.

options.text: The second — Article 31 interprets in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning of the terms in their context and in the light of the object and purpose, giving the ordinary meaning first
options.why: Article 31's general rule is that a treaty shall be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to its terms in their context and in the light of its object and purpose. The module reads it as the basic principle that treaties are interpreted by first giving the ordinary meaning to the language, and only if that meaning is ambiguous or leads to illogical results is the purpose considered. Context means the text with its preamble and annexes and any agreement made between all the parties in connection with its conclusion.

options.text: The second, but context is limited to the article in which the term appears
options.misconception: narrows context to the article, when Article 31 defines it as the whole text with preamble, annexes and related agreements
options.why: The context for interpretation comprises the text including its preamble and annexes, together with any agreement relating to the treaty made between all the parties in connection with its conclusion.

options.text: The first — a purposive reading always governs a treaty because treaties are political instruments
options.misconception: puts purpose ahead of the words, which Article 31 orders the other way
options.why: Purpose is part of the rule, but as the light in which the ordinary meaning is read, not as a substitute for it. Starting from purpose lets the reader write the term he wants.

citation.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969
citation.ref: Article 31 — the general rule of interpretation and the meaning of context; Article 32 — supplementary means

items.scenario: Two advisers disagree on how to read a treaty term. One says the object and purpose of the treaty should be consulted first and the words read to serve it; the other says the words are read in their ordinary meaning first and purpose is reached only if that meaning is ambiguous or leads to an illogical result.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The State Y protocol is not binding on the State X treaty, but where the language is the same it may be referred to for the intention of the parties — and the Indian courts are not consistent on the point
options.why: The module's treatment of provisions in parallel tax treaties: the interpretation or explanation in treaty X is not binding while interpreting treaty Y, but if the language is similar between the two, one can make a reference to the clearer treaty for understanding the intention of the contracting parties — and the views of the Indian judiciary are not consistent, with contradictory judgments of courts and the Tribunal. Other treaties in pari materia are one of Starke's extrinsic aids, usable in case of doubt provided clear words are not contradicted.

options.text: No reference is permissible — each treaty is a closed text and extrinsic material is barred
options.misconception: shuts out extrinsic aids, which Article 32 and the module expressly admit
options.why: Article 32 admits supplementary means, and the module lists protocols, subsequent agreements, subsequent conduct and treaties in pari materia as aids, subject only to the rule that clear words are not thereby contradicted.

options.text: The State Y protocol binds the State X treaty, because a protocol is part of every Indian treaty on the same subject
options.misconception: extends one treaty's protocol to another treaty
options.why: A protocol is a supplement to the treaty it belongs to and forms part of that treaty alone. It has no force in a different treaty, though it may inform the reading of the same words.

options.text: The State Y protocol governs, because the later of two treaties always controls the earlier
options.misconception: invents a later-in-time rule between treaties with different partners
options.why: There is no such rule between treaties with different counterparties; each binds only its own parties. Reference to a parallel treaty is an aid to intention, not a rule of priority.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
citation.ref: Provisions in parallel tax treaties; treaties in pari materia as an extrinsic aid; protocol as part of its own treaty

items.scenario: India's treaty with State X uses the same words on fees for technical services as its treaty with State Y, but the treaty with State Y carries a protocol spelling out that the words require the services to "make available" technical knowledge. An assessee dealing with State X asks whether the State Y protocol can be used to read the State X treaty.

items.stem: How do these three sources stand as aids to interpretation?

options.text: All three are recognised extrinsic aids — commentaries as classic sources, a subsequent agreement under Article 31(3), and subsequent conduct as evidence of the parties' intention
options.why: The module lists, after Starke, a subsequent agreement between the parties regarding the interpretation or application of the treaty, which Article 31(3) of the Vienna Convention brings into the context, and the subsequent conduct of the state parties as evidence of their intention and their conception of the treaty; and it names the commentaries of Philip Baker and Klaus Vogel as classic sources of interpretation for tax treaties, as the Andhra Pradesh High Court used international material in CIT v. Visakhapatnam Port Trust. All three may be resorted to provided clear words are not contradicted.

options.text: Only the commentary — governments cannot alter a treaty's meaning by later letters or practice
options.misconception: treats a subsequent agreement as an amendment rather than as context under Article 31(3)
options.why: Article 31(3) makes any subsequent agreement between the parties regarding interpretation or application part of the context in which the treaty is read. It is not an amendment; it is evidence of what the parties meant.

options.text: Only the exchange of letters — a private author's commentary and administrative practice have no place in interpreting a treaty
options.misconception: excludes commentaries and conduct, both of which the module lists as aids
options.why: Commentaries are treated as authoritative sources, as Kanga and Palkhivala are in domestic tax, and subsequent conduct is one of Starke's four aids. Neither is binding, but both are admissible.

options.text: None — Article 31 confines interpretation to the treaty text and its preamble
options.misconception: reads Article 31 as excluding everything outside the text, forgetting Article 31(3) and Article 32
options.why: Article 31(3) takes in subsequent agreements and practice, and Article 32 admits supplementary means including preparatory work. The text comes first; it does not come alone.

citation.source: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 with ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties
citation.ref: Article 31(3) — subsequent agreement and practice; Starke's extrinsic aids; commentaries as classic sources; CIT v. Visakhapatnam Port Trust

items.scenario: In reading a treaty article, a Tribunal relies on the commentary of Klaus Vogel, on a later exchange of letters between the two governments agreeing how the article applies, and on the way both tax administrations have applied the article for a decade.

items.stem: Is the share taxable in Mr Prakash's hands?

options.text: Yes, as to 40% of the firm's book profit, with the deduction under section 80-IAC re-claimed by the partner in his own return
options.misconception: passes a firm's Chapter VI-A deduction through to its partners
options.why: Chapter VI-A deductions belong to the assessee that earns them; a partner does not claim the firm's section 80-IAC in his return. The share is simply exempt under section 10(2A).

options.text: Yes — section 10(2A) exempts only the partner's share of the firm's taxable total income, which is nil
options.misconception: reads "total income" in section 10(2A) as the firm's post-deduction figure, the reading the Circular rejects
options.why: That is exactly the argument the Circular was issued to close. A firm's income is taxed once, in the firm, and a deduction the firm earned does not turn its distributed profit into the partner's income.

options.text: No, because a partner's share of profit is charged in the firm's hands under section 28(v)
options.misconception: confuses section 28(v), which charges the partner's salary and interest, with the share of profit
options.why: Section 28(v) charges in the partner's hands the interest, salary, bonus, commission or remuneration he receives from the firm, to the extent allowed to the firm under section 40(b). The share of profit is a different stream and is exempt under section 10(2A).

options.text: No — under Circular 8/2014 the entire profit credited to a partner is exempt even where the firm's taxable income is nil after an exemption or deduction
options.why: The CBDT clarified in Circular No. 8/2014 that the income of a firm is to be taxed in the hands of the firm only and can under no circumstances be taxed in the hands of its partners; the entire profit credited to the partners' accounts is exempt under section 10(2A) even if the income chargeable to tax becomes nil in the firm's hands on account of an exemption or deduction. The officer's reading would tax in the partner's hands an income the Act chose not to tax in the firm's.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A); CBDT Circular No. 8/2014

items.scenario: Mr Prakash is a partner with a 40% share in a firm whose whole income is from a unit claiming deduction under section 80-IAC, so the firm's taxable income for the year is nil. The firm credits ₹18,00,000 to his account as his share of profit. The Assessing Officer taxes the ₹18,00,000 in his hands, reasoning that section 10(2A) exempts a share of "total income" and the firm's total income after deduction is nil.

items.stem: How much of the ₹2,40,000 is exempt under section 10(2)?

options.text: ₹90,000 — only receipts that are not out of income are exempt, because the income part was already taxed in the family
options.misconception: inverts the rule, exempting the non-income receipt and taxing the income distribution
options.why: The income distribution is the one the family already paid tax on and the one section 10(2) exempts. A receipt out of borrowed funds is outside the clause.

options.text: ₹2,40,000 — every sum a member receives from his HUF is exempt
options.misconception: reads section 10(2) as exempting any receipt from the family, not only receipts out of its income
options.why: The clause is tied to the source of the payment. A distribution of borrowed money or of capital is not a payment out of the income of the family, and the exemption does not reach it.

options.text: Nil — the HUF is a separate person, so a member's receipt from it is income from other sources in his hands
options.misconception: forgets that section 10(2) exists precisely to stop the family's income being taxed twice
options.why: The family pays tax on its income as a person; section 10(2) then keeps the same income from being taxed again when it reaches a member. The ₹1,50,000 out of rental income is exempt for that reason.

options.text: ₹1,50,000 — section 10(2) exempts only what a member receives out of the income of the family or of an impartible estate belonging to it
options.why: The exemption applies only in respect of a payment made by the HUF to its member out of the income of the family or out of the income of the impartible estate belonging to the family. ₹1,50,000 comes out of the family's rental income and is exempt; ₹90,000 out of a bank loan is not a payment out of income at all, so section 10(2) says nothing about it and its character is decided on its own facts.
keywords: out of the income of the family

citation.ref: Section 10(2) — payments out of the income of the family or of an impartible estate

items.scenario: Mr Vinod, a coparcener, receives ₹2,40,000 during the year from his HUF. ₹1,50,000 is paid out of the family's rental income for the year and ₹90,000 is his share of a sum the karta borrowed from a bank in the family's name and distributed among the members.

items.stem: Can the society claim exemption under sub-clauses (iiiad) and (iiiae) of section 10(23C)?

options.text: No — an institution can claim section 10(23C) only after approval by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, whatever its receipts
options.misconception: applies the approval requirement of sub-clauses (vi) and (via) to the small-receipts sub-clauses, which need none
options.why: Sub-clauses (iiiad) and (iiiae) exempt small institutions without any approval; approval is the route of sub-clauses (iv), (v), (vi) and (via). The society fails here on the ₹5 crore aggregate, not for want of approval.

options.text: Yes, for the colleges only — the ₹5 crore ceiling applies to educational institutions, and hospitals are exempt without limit
options.misconception: gives hospitals an unlimited exemption when sub-clause (iiiae) carries the same ₹5 crore ceiling
options.why: Sub-clause (iiiae) exempts a hospital or institution existing solely for philanthropic purposes only where aggregate annual receipts do not exceed ₹5 crore, and the aggregation rule pulls the colleges' receipts into the same test.

options.text: Yes — the colleges at ₹3.2 crore and the hospital at ₹2.4 crore are each within ₹5 crore, and each sub-clause is tested on its own
options.misconception: tests the ₹5 crore ceiling per activity when the section aggregates across the person's universities and hospitals
options.why: The ceiling is on the person's aggregate annual receipts, and the section says in terms that the exemptions do not apply where the aggregate from universities and hospitals together exceeds ₹5 crore.

options.text: No — where one person has receipts from universities and hospitals both, the exemptions fail if the aggregate of all of them exceeds ₹5 crore, and ₹5.6 crore does
options.why: Sub-clauses (iiiad) and (iiiae) each require aggregate annual receipts of the person not exceeding ₹5 crore, and where the person has receipts from universities or educational institutions as well as from hospitals or institutions, the exemptions would not apply if the aggregate of annual receipts from all of them exceeds ₹5 crore. The colleges' ₹3.2 crore and the hospital's ₹2.4 crore aggregate to ₹5.6 crore, so neither sub-clause is available; the society must seek approval under sub-clause (vi) or (via).

citation.ref: Section 10(23C)(iiiad) and (iiiae) — the ₹5 crore aggregate receipts ceiling across universities and hospitals

items.scenario: Sahyadri Education Society runs two colleges and a charitable hospital, all solely for their purposes and not for profit, with no government financing and no approval under section 10(23C). For the year the colleges' aggregate receipts are ₹3.2 crore and the hospital's are ₹2.4 crore.

items.stem: Is its income exempt under section 10(23C)(iiiac) as an institution substantially financed by the Government?

options.text: No — its receipts of ₹40 crore exceed ₹5 crore, so it needs approval under sub-clause (via)
options.misconception: applies the ₹5 crore ceiling of sub-clause (iiiae) to a government-financed hospital under sub-clause (iiiac)
options.why: The ₹5 crore ceiling belongs to sub-clauses (iiiad) and (iiiae) for institutions that are neither government-financed nor approved. A substantially government-financed hospital is under sub-clause (iiiac), which has no receipts ceiling.

options.text: Yes, but only if the grant is at least 50% of receipts in each of the three preceding years as well
options.misconception: adds a three-year test the Explanation does not contain
options.why: The test is for the relevant previous year alone: the institution is substantially financed for that previous year if the grant in that year exceeds 50% of that year's receipts. Each year stands on its own figures.

options.text: No — substantially financed means wholly financed, and ₹18 crore of the receipts came from elsewhere
options.misconception: equates "substantially" with "wholly"
options.why: The sub-clause reads "wholly or substantially financed", and the Explanation defines substantially by a single number: a grant exceeding 50% of total receipts in the year.

options.text: Yes — the government grant of ₹22 crore exceeds 50% of total receipts of ₹40 crore, so it is substantially financed by the Government for that previous year
options.why: The Explanation fixes the test: if the government grant to the hospital during the relevant previous year exceeds 50% of its total receipts including voluntary contributions, it is considered substantially financed by the Government for that previous year. ₹22 crore is 55% of ₹40 crore, so sub-clause (iiiac) applies without any receipts ceiling or approval.

citation.ref: Section 10(23C)(iiiac) with the Explanation — grant exceeding 50% of total receipts in the previous year

items.scenario: Godavari Government-aided Hospital exists solely for philanthropic purposes and not for profit. For the year its total receipts, including voluntary contributions, are ₹40 crore, of which ₹22 crore is a grant from the State Government.

items.stem: What is chargeable to tax in his hands?

options.text: Nothing — the business profit is income from a source in Sikkim and the bond interest is interest on securities, and section 10(26AAA) exempts both
options.why: Section 10(26AAA) exempts, in the hands of a Sikkimese individual, income from any source in the State of Sikkim and income by way of dividend or interest on securities. The ₹2,25,000 business profit falls in the first limb. The ₹55,000 is interest on securities, and the second limb carries no geographic test, so it does not matter that the bonds were issued by the Government of Rajasthan.
keywords: any source in the State of Sikkim

options.text: ₹55,000 — the Rajasthan bond interest arises outside Sikkim and only income from a source in Sikkim is exempt
options.misconception: reads a Sikkim-source condition into the dividend and interest limb
options.why: The second limb of section 10(26AAA) exempts dividend and interest on securities without asking where the security was issued. Only the first limb is tied to a source in Sikkim.

options.text: Both amounts — section 10(26AAA) was struck down and Sikkimese individuals are taxed like any other resident
options.misconception: invents a repeal; the clause is in the Act and the module
options.why: Section 10(26AAA) is in force and the module works this very example to a nil answer. The two limbs cover both of his incomes.

options.text: ₹2,25,000 — business income is never exempt under section 10(26AAA), which covers only investment income
options.misconception: narrows the exemption to passive income, leaving out the first limb
options.why: The first limb exempts income from any source in the State of Sikkim, and a business located in Sikkim is such a source. Both limbs apply to him.

citation.ref: Section 10(26AAA) — income from any source in Sikkim, and dividend or interest on securities

items.scenario: Mr Gaitonde, born and brought up in Sikkim and a Sikkimese individual, has a net profit of ₹2,25,000 from a business located in Sikkim and interest of ₹55,000 on bonds issued by the Government of Rajasthan.

items.stem: What is exempt under section 10(26)?

options.text: None — Mizoram is not among the areas specified in the Constitution, so section 10(26) does not reach her
options.misconception: reads only the Sixth Schedule districts and misses the named States
options.why: Section 10(26) names, besides the specified districts, the States of Manipur, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram and Nagaland, and Ladakh. A tribe member residing in Mizoram is squarely within it.

options.text: ₹6,00,000 only — the dividend comes from a Mumbai company, which is not a source in Mizoram
options.misconception: applies the geographic test to the dividend limb
options.why: Dividend and interest on securities form a separate limb of section 10(26) with no geographic condition; where the paying company is located does not matter.

options.text: All three — a Scheduled Tribe member residing in Mizoram is exempt on her whole income
options.misconception: treats section 10(26) as a personal exemption rather than one tied to the source of income
options.why: The exemption is on income from a source in the specified areas or States, plus dividend and interest on securities. Income earned from a source outside those areas, like a consultancy carried on in Bengaluru, stays taxable.

options.text: ₹6,00,000 and ₹1,20,000 — income from a source in Mizoram and dividend from anywhere are exempt; the Bengaluru consultancy is not
options.why: Section 10(26) exempts a member of a Scheduled Tribe residing in Mizoram on income arising or accruing from any source in the specified areas or States, and on income by way of dividend or interest on securities. The Aizawl shop is a source in Mizoram, and the dividend is exempt wherever the company sits. The Bengaluru consultancy is neither a source in a specified area nor dividend or interest on securities, so it is taxable.
keywords: any source in the specified areas

citation.ref: Section 10(26) — the specified districts, the five named States and Ladakh; the two limbs of the exemption

items.scenario: Ms Lalrinpuii, a member of a Scheduled Tribe, resides in Mizoram. She earns ₹6,00,000 from a shop in Aizawl, ₹1,20,000 as dividend on shares of a Mumbai-listed company, and ₹3,00,000 from a consultancy she carries on in Bengaluru, where she spends four months a year.

items.stem: What is exempt under section 10(30)?

options.text: ₹11,20,000 — 40% of the Tea Board subsidy, because only 40% of tea income is business income under Rule 8
options.misconception: runs the exempt subsidy through the Rule 8 split
options.why: Rule 8 splits the income from growing and manufacturing tea between agricultural and business income. A subsidy exempt under section 10(30) is outside total income altogether and is not part of the income Rule 8 apportions.

options.text: Nil — a subsidy is a revenue receipt taxable under section 2(24)(xviii) and section 10(30) was made redundant by that clause
options.misconception: lets the general definition of income override a specific exemption
options.why: Section 2(24)(xviii) brings subsidies into income generally, but section 10 takes named items out of total income, and section 10(30) still names the Tea Board replantation subsidy.

options.text: ₹37,00,000 — every subsidy received by a tea grower is exempt
options.misconception: extends section 10(30) to any subsidy a tea business receives
options.why: The clause is confined to a subsidy from or through the Tea Board under a notified replantation, replacement, rejuvenation or consolidation scheme. A general capital subsidy from another body takes its ordinary treatment.

options.text: ₹28,00,000 only — a Tea Board subsidy under a notified replantation or rejuvenation scheme, backed by the Board's certificate, is wholly exempt; the packing-line subsidy is not from the Tea Board
options.why: Section 10(30) exempts wholly a subsidy received by an assessee growing and manufacturing tea in India through or from the Tea Board, on two conditions: the subsidy is under a scheme for replantation or replacement of bushes or rejuvenation or consolidation of tea areas notified by the Central Government, and the assessee furnishes the Tea Board's certificate of the amount to the Assessing Officer. The ₹28,00,000 meets both. The ₹9,00,000 comes from a State department for a packing line, which is neither the Tea Board nor a replantation scheme, so it is outside the clause.
keywords: through or from the Tea Board

citation.ref: Section 10(30) — the notified scheme and the Tea Board certificate

items.scenario: Nilgiri Estates Ltd grows and manufactures tea in India. During the year it received ₹28,00,000 from the Tea Board under a notified replantation scheme, holds the Board's certificate for that amount, and also received ₹9,00,000 from a State industries department as a general capital subsidy for a new packing line.

items.stem: Is the subsidy exempt under section 10(31)?

options.text: No — section 10(31) covers rubber and coffee only, and cardamom is not a specified commodity
options.misconception: leaves cardamom out of a clause that names it
options.why: Section 10(31) names rubber, coffee, cardamom or any other commodity notified by the Central Government, and the Spices Board is one of the Boards it lists.

options.text: Yes, as to 35% of it, the balance being agricultural income under Rule 7B
options.misconception: apportions an exempt subsidy under the coffee rule, which does not apply to cardamom or to subsidies
options.why: Rule 7B splits income from growing and curing coffee; it does not apply to cardamom, and no apportionment rule applies to a subsidy that section 10(31) takes out of total income wholly.

options.text: Not as things stand — section 10(31) covers a Spices Board subsidy for replacement of cardamom plants, but the exemption requires the Board's certificate of the amount to be furnished to the Assessing Officer
options.why: Section 10(31) exempts a subsidy received from or through the Rubber Board, Coffee Board, Spices Board or any other commodity Board by an assessee growing and manufacturing rubber, coffee, cardamom or another notified commodity, under a scheme for replantation, replacement, rejuvenation or consolidation. Both conditions must be met, and the second is that the assessee furnishes a certificate from the Board as to the amount of subsidy received during the previous year to the Assessing Officer. Without it the exemption is not established; with it, the ₹6,00,000 is wholly exempt.

options.text: Yes — the certificate is a matter of procedure and cannot defeat a substantive exemption
options.misconception: treats the certificate as optional when the section makes it a condition
options.why: The module lists the certificate as one of the two conditions of section 10(31), beside the notified-scheme condition. It is what proves the amount and the source, and the exemption is written to depend on it.

citation.ref: Section 10(31) — the commodity Boards, the notified scheme and the certificate condition

items.scenario: Malabar Spices Ltd grows and manufactures cardamom in Kerala. It received ₹6,00,000 from the Spices Board under a notified scheme for replacement of cardamom plants, but did not obtain the Board's certificate of the amount received and did not furnish one to the Assessing Officer.

items.stem: What is Mr Arun's gross total income?

options.text: ₹7,30,000 — because both spouses have income, the salary is clubbed with the one whose other income is lower
options.misconception: invents a lower-income rule; the both-substantial-interest rule points to the higher other income, and it does not arise here
options.why: Only Mr Arun has a substantial interest, so the salary is clubbed with him. Where both spouses have a substantial interest, the income goes to the spouse whose total income excluding it is higher, not lower.

options.text: ₹7,30,000 — salary is her own earning from her own work and cannot be clubbed
options.misconception: treats remuneration as outside clubbing altogether
options.why: Section 64(1)(ii) exists for exactly this remuneration — salary, commission or fees to a spouse from a concern in which the individual has a substantial interest — and lifts it only where the spouse's own qualification earns it.

options.text: ₹10,75,000 — her salary of ₹4,20,000 less the ₹75,000 standard deduction is clubbed with his ₹7,30,000 under section 64(1)(ii)
options.why: Mr Arun has a substantial interest in the company, holding 20% or more of the voting power, and his wife's salary from it is not attributable to any technical or professional qualification, so section 64(1)(ii) includes it in his total income. The salary is computed as it would be in her hands — ₹4,20,000 less the standard deduction of ₹75,000 under section 16(ia) — giving ₹3,45,000, and with his other income of ₹7,30,000 his gross total income is ₹10,75,000. Her gross total income is her own ₹4,20,000.

options.text: ₹11,50,000 — the full ₹4,20,000 is clubbed, because the standard deduction belongs to the salary earner and not to the person it is clubbed with
options.misconception: clubs the gross salary without the deduction the head allows
options.why: What is clubbed is the income computed under the head, and the standard deduction is part of computing salary income. The module's own working takes ₹4,20,000 less ₹75,000.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(ii) with Explanation 2 on substantial interest — the module's illustration on Mr Arun and Mrs Anamika

items.scenario: Mr Arun holds shares carrying 55% of the voting power in MNO Pvt Ltd. His wife, Mrs Anamika, works there as a software programmer at ₹35,000 a month but holds no qualification for the job. Their other incomes are ₹7,30,000 and ₹4,20,000 respectively, and both are on the default regime.

items.stem: Is the officer right?

options.text: Yes — the exception needs a technical or professional qualification from a recognised body, which a model does not hold
options.misconception: reads "qualification" as a formal degree, the narrow reading R. Bharati rejected
options.why: The court held that the words do not necessarily connote a qualification conferred by a university after a course of study; the term is given a wide meaning and skill and experience in a profession suffice.

options.text: Yes — a proprietor holds 100% of the concern, and the professional exception is available only in a company
options.misconception: limits the exception to companies when the proviso applies to any concern
options.why: Section 64(1)(ii) applies to a concern of any kind, with substantial interest measured by 20% of profits for a non-company, and the proviso for a professionally qualified spouse applies to every concern alike.

options.text: No — because the salary was allowed as a deduction to Naresh, clubbing it would tax the same sum twice
options.misconception: treats the deduction to the payer as a bar to clubbing in the payer's hands
options.why: Clubbing and deduction are separate questions; the officer's admission that the salary is deductible does not decide section 64. What decides it here is the proviso, satisfied because her income is attributable to her own professional skill.

options.text: No — following CIT v. Smt. R. Bharati, "professional qualification" takes a wide meaning covering the skill, experience and competence a line of work needs, so a model's remuneration is attributable to her own profession and is not clubbed
options.why: The Madras High Court in CIT v. Smt. R. Bharati held that "professional qualifications" and "knowledge" in the proviso to section 64(1) do not require a degree from a recognised university; qualification refers to the qualities a person must possess to perform the work, so long as the work is technical or professional, and a person having skill, experience and competence in a line of work is professionally qualified. Modelling is such a line, so the exception applies and the salary is assessed in her hands.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 64(1)(ii); CIT v. Smt. R. Bharati (1999) 240 ITR 697 (Mad)

items.scenario: Mr Naresh, a fashion designer, owns his whole business and pays his wife, a working model with years of experience and no formal degree, ₹10,000 a month for modelling his designs. The Assessing Officer allows the salary as a deduction to Naresh but clubs it in his hands under section 64(1)(ii), saying she holds no professional qualification.

items.stem: How much is clubbed with Mrs Radha for the assessment year 2026-27?

options.text: Nil — a gift from a wife to her husband is between relatives and section 56(2)(x) exempts it
options.misconception: confuses the tax on the gift in the recipient's hands with the clubbing of the income it earns
options.why: Section 56(2)(x) is not attracted because the gift came from a relative, and that is a separate question. Section 64(1)(iv) clubs the income the gifted money earns, and only a bona fide loan instead of a gift would have kept the clubbing away.

options.text: ₹2,69,231 — 7/13 of ₹5,00,000, taking his capital as the ₹6,00,000 he started with
options.misconception: uses the opening capital of the earlier year and ignores the loss that reduced it
options.why: The proportion is taken on the first day of the previous year in which the income arises, 1 April 2025, when his capital was ₹3,00,000 after the loss. The 6:7 ratio uses a figure that no longer existed on that day.

options.text: ₹3,50,000 — profit apportioned by capital on 1 April 2025, ₹3,00,000 of his own against ₹7,00,000 from the gift, so 7/10 of ₹5,00,000
options.why: Under section 64(1)(iv) with Explanation 3, where an asset transferred without adequate consideration to a spouse is invested by the spouse in a business, the proportionate income is clubbed, the proportion being the value of the transferred asset to the total investment on the first day of the previous year. On 1 April 2025 his capital was ₹3,00,000, being ₹6,00,000 less the ₹3,00,000 loss, and the gift ₹7,00,000, a ratio of 3:7. So 7/10 of the ₹5,00,000 profit, ₹3,50,000, is clubbed with Mrs Radha.
keywords: first day of the previous year

options.text: ₹5,00,000 — the whole profit, because the business would have collapsed without her gift
options.misconception: clubs the entire income when the Explanation clubs only the proportionate part
options.why: Explanation 3 confines the clubbing to the income proportionate to the transferred asset's share of the total investment. His own ₹3,00,000 earned its share, which stays with him.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(iv) with Explanation 3 — the module's illustration on Mr Rahul and Mrs Radha

items.scenario: Mr Rahul started a proprietary business on 1 April 2024 with ₹6,00,000 of his own and lost ₹3,00,000 in 2024-25. On 1 April 2025 his wife, Mrs Radha, gifted him ₹7,00,000, which he put into the business the same day. The business earned ₹5,00,000 in 2025-26.

items.stem: Is she right?

options.text: Yes — clubbing under section 64 applies only to transfers made directly to a spouse, a son's wife or a minor child, and TPS Co Ltd is none of them
options.misconception: misses clauses (vii) and (viii), which reach transfers to anyone for the benefit of a spouse or son's wife
options.why: Clauses (vii) and (viii) were written for the indirect route: an asset given to a third person or association with the income earmarked for the spouse or the son's wife. The transferee's identity does not matter; the beneficiary's does.

options.text: No — section 64(1)(viii) includes in the transferor's income the income from an asset transferred without adequate consideration to any person, to the extent it is used for the benefit of the transferor's son's wife
options.why: Section 64(1)(viii) is attracted on a transfer of any asset, directly or indirectly, otherwise than for adequate consideration, to any person or association of persons, to the extent the income from the asset is for the immediate or deferred benefit of the transferor's son's wife. The ₹42,000 meant for her daughter-in-law is included in Mrs Komal's total income; that she no longer owns the property is the reason the section exists, not an answer to it.

options.text: No — the entire rental income of the property is clubbed with Mrs Komal, not only ₹42,000
options.misconception: clubs the whole income when clause (viii) reaches only the part used for the son's wife
options.why: The section includes income "to the extent" it is used for the benefit of the son's wife. ₹42,000 is that extent; the rest of the rent is TPS Co Ltd's own income.

options.text: Yes — the ₹42,000 is taxed in the son's wife's hands as income from other sources, which is where the benefit lands
options.misconception: taxes the beneficiary instead of the transferor
options.why: Clubbing puts the income in the transferor's hands, not the beneficiary's. The daughter-in-law receives the benefit; Mrs Komal bears the tax on it.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(viii) — the module's illustration on Mrs Komal and TPS Co Ltd

items.scenario: Mrs Komal transferred an immovable property to TPS Co Ltd without consideration, on the condition that ₹42,000 a year out of the rental income be used for the benefit of her son's wife. She says the ₹42,000 cannot be taxed in her hands because she no longer owns the property.

items.stem: How is the interest on the deposits taxed?

options.text: Nothing is clubbed — neither brother transferred anything to his own wife, and section 64(1)(iv) speaks only of a transfer to one's own spouse
options.misconception: reads the section literally and misses the indirect-transfer route the Supreme Court closed
options.why: Section 64(1)(iv) reaches assets transferred directly or indirectly to a spouse, and Keshavji Morarji holds that inter-connected transfers adopted as a device to evade tax make each person the indirect transferor to his own spouse.

options.text: The interest on ₹5.2 lakh is clubbed with Mr Madan alone, because his gift came first and started the arrangement
options.misconception: clubs the whole arrangement with one party by order of dates
options.why: Each brother is the indirect transferor to his own wife, so each is clubbed with the interest on ₹5.2 lakh in his own wife's deposit. The order of the gifts does not make one brother the transferor of both.

options.text: The interest on the full ₹6.5 lakh is clubbed with Mr Madan's brother and on ₹5.2 lakh with Mr Madan
options.misconception: clubs the whole of the larger gift instead of the extent of the mutual consideration
options.why: Only ₹5.2 lakh of the ₹6.5 lakh is consideration for the return gift. The excess ₹1.3 lakh was a gift to the brother's wife with nothing coming back for it, and its interest is hers.

options.text: The interest on ₹5.2 lakh is clubbed with each brother, as the deemed transferor to his own wife; the interest on the remaining ₹1.3 lakh stays with Mr Madan's brother's wife
options.why: The two gifts are cross transfers, so intimately connected that they form a single transaction with each as consideration for the other, and under CIT v. Keshavji Morarji the clubbing provisions apply to the circuitous route as if each brother had transferred to his own spouse. The clubbing goes only to the extent of the cross transfer, ₹5.2 lakh: interest on ₹5.2 lakh is clubbed with Mr Madan and with his brother respectively, and the interest on the ₹1.3 lakh by which Mr Madan's gift exceeded the return gift is taxed in his brother's wife's own hands.

citation.ref: Cross transfers under section 64(1); CIT v. Keshavji Morarji (1967) 66 ITR 142 (SC) — the module's illustration on Mr Madan

items.scenario: On 14 June 2025 Mr Madan gifted ₹6.5 lakh to his brother's wife. On 12 July 2025 his brother gifted ₹5.2 lakh to Mr Madan's wife. Both wives put the money in bank fixed deposits at 9% on 1 August 2025.

items.stem: What must the Assessing Officer establish before clubbing the house rent with B and the dividend with A?

options.text: That the two transfers are so intimately connected as to form part of a single transaction, each constituting consideration for the other, by being mutual or otherwise
options.why: Cross transfers are clubbed in the hands of the deemed transferor only if the transfers are so intimately connected that they form part of a single transaction and each transfer constitutes consideration for the other, by being mutual or otherwise. The simultaneous, equal, reciprocal gifts to persons who are not the donors' own relatives show that each was the price of the other and that the circuitous method was adopted to get round section 64. The rent then goes to B and the dividend to A, assuming A's income exceeds his wife's.

options.text: That the assets transferred are of exactly equal value, without which there is no consideration
options.misconception: makes equality of value a condition, when clubbing runs to the extent of the mutual consideration whatever the values
options.why: Unequal cross transfers are still clubbed, to the extent of the smaller amount; the module's own illustration clubs ₹5.2 lakh out of a ₹6.5 lakh gift. Equality is not the test, connection is.

options.text: That A and B intended to evade tax, proved by their own admission or correspondence
options.misconception: demands proof of subjective intent when the test is the objective connection of the transactions
options.why: Keshavji Morarji looks at whether the transactions are inter-connected parts of the same transaction so that the circuitous method can be said to be a device to evade tax. The connection is inferred from the transfers themselves, not from a confession.

options.text: That each transfer was for inadequate consideration on its own facts, taking the deeds at their word
options.misconception: examines each gift alone, which is the framing the cross transfer was designed to survive
options.why: Read singly, each is a gift to a stranger's relative and section 64 says nothing. The question is whether the two are one transaction in which each gift is the consideration for the other.

citation.ref: Cross transfers — the module's example of A and B; CIT v. Keshavji Morarji (1967) 66 ITR 142 (SC)

items.scenario: A transfers ₹50,000 to the wife of his brother B, who uses it to buy a house. On the same day B transfers shares in a foreign company worth ₹50,000 to A's minor son. Each deed recites that it is made out of natural love and affection, and the two have no other dealings.

items.stem: Is the officer's action valid?

options.text: Yes — under section 65 the transferor is always the person liable, and the transferee can never be asked to pay
options.misconception: inverts section 65, which is what lets the transferee be asked to pay the attributable portion
options.why: Section 65 provides the opposite: the notice of demand in respect of tax on clubbed income, or on income of a deemed owner under section 27, may be served on the transferee, who is then liable for that portion of the transferor's tax.

options.text: No — once the property is gifted, the entire income belongs to the donees, and the demand should be served on Mrs Ravi and Mrs Divya for their shares
options.misconception: ignores section 27(i), which keeps the wife's share in the transferor's hands
options.why: The wife's share is Mr Ravi's income by deeming, and the demand for it may be served on him. Section 65 merely allows it to be served on the transferee as well; it does not move the liability off him.

options.text: Only in part — Mr Ravi is deemed owner under section 27(i) of the share gifted to his wife, and section 65 lets the demand for that portion be served on her too; the daughter's share is taxed in her own hands and cannot be demanded from him
options.why: Under section 27(i) an individual who transfers a house property without adequate consideration to his spouse, or to a minor child not being a married daughter, is deemed its owner. Mr Ravi is deemed owner of the share transferred to his wife, and that half of the income is his under the head house property; section 65 allows the notice of demand for the tax attributable to it to be served on Mrs Ravi as the person holding the property. A married daughter is outside section 27(i) and outside section 64, so the income from her share is taxable in her hands, and a demand on Mr Ravi for the entire income is not valid.

options.text: Yes — a person who gifts his only house to relatives remains liable for the tax on all of its income
options.misconception: extends deemed ownership to every donee relative
options.why: Deemed ownership under section 27(i) reaches a spouse and a minor child other than a married daughter, and no one else. A gift to a married daughter transfers the income with the property.

citation.ref: Sections 27(i) and 65 — the module's illustration on Mr Ravi

items.scenario: Mr Ravi gifted his only house property in equal shares to his wife, Mrs Ravi, and to his married daughter, Mrs Divya. The house is let. The Assessing Officer serves a notice of demand on Mr Ravi for the tax on the whole of the rental income.

items.stem: How is the income from the converted property dealt with for 2025-26?

options.text: After partition the property is no longer HUF property, so section 64(2) ceases and each member is taxed on his or her own share
options.misconception: treats partition as the end of section 64(2), when the section provides for partition expressly
options.why: Section 64(2) deals with the partitioned case in terms: the spouse's share on partition is deemed an indirect transfer from the converting member, and its income stays with him.

options.text: The income from his wife's share is included in Mr Suresh's income as a deemed indirect transfer to her, the son's share is the son's, and a clubbed loss is set off in Mr Suresh's computation because income includes loss
options.why: Section 64(2) continues to include in the converting member's income the income from property he converted into HUF property after 31 December 1969, and where the converted property has been partitioned, the income from the share received by the spouse is deemed to arise from an indirect transfer by him to her and is included in his income. The adult son's share is neither his spouse nor a minor child, so it is the son's. And Explanation 2 to section 64 says income includes loss for both section 64(1) and 64(2), so a loss on the clubbed portion is taken into his computation.

options.text: The whole income from all three shares is clubbed with Mr Suresh, since he converted the whole property
options.misconception: clubs the son's share, which section 64(2) does not reach after partition
options.why: After partition the section follows the spouse's share only. A share falling to an adult son is outside section 64 altogether, and the son is taxed on it.

options.text: The dividend on the wife's share is clubbed, but the loss on the debentures stays with the family because clubbing carries income, never loss
options.misconception: forgets Explanation 2 to section 64
options.why: Explanation 2 provides that "income" in section 64 includes loss, and the module notes it applies to both section 64(1) and 64(2). The clubbed loss reduces Mr Suresh's total income like any other loss of his.

citation.ref: Section 64(2) on conversion and partition; Explanation 2 to section 64 — income includes loss

items.scenario: Mr Suresh threw his self-acquired shares into the common stock of his HUF in 2022. In 2025-26 the family partitioned, and the shares fell one-third each to Mr Suresh, his wife and their adult son. In that year the shares yielded a dividend, and a separate block of converted debentures produced a net loss.

items.stem: What is his aggregate turnover, and what is his turnover in the State of Gujarat?

options.text: ₹39 lakh for both figures, turnover in a State meaning aggregate turnover under another name
options.misconception: treats turnover in State as a synonym rather than the narrower measure it is
options.why: Section 2(112) measures the turnover of supplies made from a particular State by a taxable person. It is used where a rule has to work State by State, and it can equal the all-India figure only where the person supplies from one State and no other.

options.text: ₹36 lakh, exempt supplies belonging to turnover in a State but not to aggregate turnover
options.misconception: swaps the two definitions, dropping exempt supplies out of the wider one
options.why: Both definitions take in exempt supplies. Section 2(6) names them in terms, and section 2(112) is built on the same idea narrowed to one State. Neither definition leaves them out, which is why a person selling mostly exempt goods can still be pulled over a line.

options.text: ₹25 lakh, each registration being a distinct person whose turnover is computed on its own
options.misconception: reads section 25 as splitting the definition, when distinct persons still share one PAN
options.why: Section 25(4) makes separately registered establishments distinct persons for the charge, and section 2(6) still measures across everything under the same Permanent Account Number. The two provisions work together, and the second is not undone by the first.

options.text: Aggregate turnover ₹39 lakh, computed for the whole PAN; turnover in Gujarat ₹14 lakh
options.why: Section 2(6) computes aggregate turnover on an all India basis for persons having the same Permanent Account Number, so the two registrations are added together — ₹22 lakh plus ₹3 lakh plus ₹14 lakh. Section 2(112) defines turnover in State separately, as the turnover of supplies made from that State alone, which is ₹14 lakh. Being distinct persons changes who files a return; it does not split the definition.

citation.ref: Sections 2(6) and 2(112), read with section 25(4)

items.scenario: A person holds one Permanent Account Number and two registrations, one in Maharashtra and one in Gujarat. Supplies made from Maharashtra for the year are taxable ₹22 lakh and exempt ₹3 lakh. Supplies made from Gujarat are taxable ₹14 lakh. There is nothing else. He argues that the two registrations are distinct persons under section 25, so each State's figure stands alone.

items.stem: How do the four lines classify?

options.text: Only the liquor is exempt; the rice is taxable, a nil rate being a rate like any other
options.misconception: separates a nil rate from exemption when section 2(47) puts them in the same definition
options.why: A nil rate is a rate, but the very first words of section 2(47) name a supply attracting nil rate of tax as an exempt supply. Nil rated and exempt part company when a rate is being quoted and travel together when credit is being worked out.

options.text: Rice and land are exempt supplies; liquor and the export are outside GST altogether
options.misconception: puts land inside the definition and pushes a zero-rated export outside the Act
options.why: Land is kept out by Schedule III, so it never becomes an exempt supply. The export is squarely inside the Act — section 16 of the IGST Act makes it a zero-rated supply, which is a taxable supply carrying a rate of zero rather than an escape from the levy.

options.text: All four are exempt supplies, none of them carrying any tax
options.misconception: uses the absence of tax as the test, when the definition works through nil rate, exemption and non-taxability
options.why: Tax can be absent for more than one reason. Land escapes because it is not a supply, and the export escapes because it is zero-rated with credit. Neither of those is an exemption, and calling them one costs the company the credit on its exports.

options.text: Rice exempt; liquor a non-taxable supply and so exempt as well; land not a supply at all; the export a taxable supply that is zero-rated
options.why: Section 2(47) defines an exempt supply as one attracting nil rate of tax or wholly exempt under section 11, and it includes a non-taxable supply. Alcoholic liquor for human consumption sits outside the charge, so it is swept in that way. The sale of land is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services under Schedule III, so the definition never reaches it. The export is taxable at a rate of zero with the credit chain left intact.

citation.ref: Sections 2(47) and 2(78), read with Schedule III and section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: Four lines sit in one company's accounts for the year — sale of fresh unbranded rice, which bears a nil rate; sale of alcoholic liquor for human consumption; sale of a plot of land it had held for years; and export of software services. The accountant must mark each one.

items.stem: Which movement is a supply even though nothing was received for it?

options.text: The movement to the warehouse operator, possession having passed to him
options.misconception: uses transfer of possession as the test, which describes a bailment rather than the agency entry
options.why: Possession passes in a bailment too, and a bailment is not what entry 3 is about. The entry turns on who undertakes to supply the goods onward to the customer, and on these facts that is the consignment agent and not the warehouse.

options.text: Both, goods having left the manufacturer's premises without consideration in each case
options.misconception: makes the movement of the goods the test, when entry 3 asks who undertakes to supply them onward
options.why: Goods moving is not enough, or every despatch to a transporter would be taxed. Entry 3 needs the person receiving them to have undertaken to supply them on the principal's behalf, and a warehouse operator storing goods for a fee has undertaken nothing of the kind.

options.text: The movement to the consignment agent
options.why: Entry 3 of Schedule I treats a supply of goods by a principal to his agent as a supply made without consideration where the agent undertakes to supply such goods on behalf of the principal. Raising the invoice in his own name is what shows the consignment agent has undertaken that. The warehouse operator raises no invoice and supplies nothing onward, so he is a bailee holding goods for a fee and the movement to him is not a supply.

options.text: Neither, because entry 3 needs the agent to have paid something for the goods
options.misconception: puts a consideration back into an entry whose whole purpose is to deem a supply without one
options.why: Schedule I is the list of activities treated as a supply even if made without consideration. Requiring a payment would leave entry 3 with no work at all to do, since an agent who paid for the goods would be an ordinary buyer.

citation.ref: Entry 3 of Schedule I, read with section 7(1)(c) and Circular No. 57/31/2018-GST

items.scenario: A manufacturer moves goods to two places and receives nothing for either movement. The first lot goes to a consignment agent who stores the goods and sells them to customers under invoices he raises in his own name. The second lot goes to a public warehouse operator who holds the goods for a storage fee and hands them over to customers against invoices the manufacturer raises.

items.stem: What does the law require of him?

options.text: He may supply on his Rajasthan registration, the goods being his own and moved to his own stall
options.misconception: treats a registration in one State as covering supplies made from another
options.why: Registration under section 25(1) is State-wise. Supplies made from the Mumbai stall are made in Maharashtra and need a registration obtained there, whatever registrations the person holds elsewhere.

options.text: Nothing — his turnover is below the threshold and a ten-day stall is too small to matter
options.misconception: applies the section 22 threshold to a category section 24 places outside it
options.why: Section 24 opens with words overriding the threshold, and a casual taxable person is on its list. The ₹6 lakh gives him no protection at all once he starts supplying from the stall.

options.text: Registration in Maharashtra as a casual taxable person whatever his turnover, applied for before the fair begins
options.why: Section 24(ii) makes registration compulsory for a casual taxable person notwithstanding the threshold in section 22, and section 2(20) describes such a person as one who occasionally supplies in a State where he has no fixed place of business. The proviso to section 25(1) requires him to apply at least five days prior to the commencement of business.

options.text: A regular Maharashtra registration, the casual category being open only to a person unregistered everywhere
options.misconception: makes the casual category depend on being unregistered elsewhere rather than on having no fixed place of business in that State
options.why: Section 2(20) asks one question — whether the person has a fixed place of business in the State where he is supplying. His existing Rajasthan registration neither helps him nor disqualifies him from registering as a casual taxable person in Maharashtra.

citation.ref: Sections 24(ii) and 2(20), read with section 25(1) and its proviso

items.scenario: A Jaipur furniture maker with a turnover of ₹6 lakh takes a stall at a ten-day trade fair in Mumbai and will sell from it. He has no fixed place of business anywhere in Maharashtra. He is registered in Rajasthan.

items.stem: How does section 23 treat him?

options.text: Not an agriculturist at all, since he uses hired labour rather than working the land himself
options.misconception: narrows section 2(7), which expressly covers hired labour under personal supervision
options.why: Section 2(7) covers cultivation of land by the person's own labour, by the labour of his family, and by servants on wages or by hired labour under his personal supervision or that of a family member. Hiring help does not take him out of the definition.

options.text: Outside registration altogether, an agriculturist being relieved for everything he supplies
options.misconception: attaches the relief to the person when the clause attaches it to a described supply
options.why: The clause reads to the extent of supply of produce out of cultivation of land. It relieves a kind of supply, so any other business the same man carries on is looked at separately and on its own facts.

options.text: Outside registration for both lines, produce being produce and the neighbours' crops agricultural too
options.misconception: attaches the relief to the nature of the goods rather than to who cultivated them
options.why: The words are produce out of cultivation of land, meaning cultivation by the agriculturist himself. That the goods are agricultural does not carry the relief across to a trader who bought them from somebody else.

options.text: Outside registration for his own produce, but the trading in other farmers' produce stands on its own footing
options.why: Section 23(1)(b) relieves an agriculturist, to the extent of supply of produce out of cultivation of land. Section 2(7) covers an individual or a Hindu Undivided Family who undertakes cultivation of land, including by hired labour under personal supervision, so he qualifies as one. The words to the extent of confine the relief to what he grew, and buying a neighbour's crop and reselling it is not produce out of cultivation of land by him.

citation.ref: Sections 23(1)(b) and 2(7)

items.scenario: A man cultivates his own land using hired labour working under his personal supervision, and sells the crop. In the same year he also buys produce from neighbouring farmers and sells it on at a margin. He holds no registration and says section 23 covers everything he does.

items.stem: What must he still file, and by when?

options.text: A final return, within three months of the date of cancellation or the date of the order, whichever is later
options.why: Section 45 requires every registered person whose registration is cancelled to furnish a final return within three months of the date of cancellation or the date of the order of cancellation, whichever is later. The order of 20 May 2026 is the later of the two dates here, so the three months are counted from it and not from 31 March 2026.

options.text: Nothing — cancellation ends the duty to file, returns hanging on the registration
options.misconception: reads cancellation as ending every filing duty, when section 45 creates one that arises because of it
options.why: Section 45 is written for this exact person. The obligation it creates comes into existence on cancellation, so it cannot be escaped by pointing at the cancellation as the reason for not filing.

options.text: The annual return for the year, which serves as the final return for a person leaving the system
options.misconception: substitutes the annual return under section 44 for the separate final return under section 45
options.why: They are different returns under different sections. The annual return under section 44 is filed by a registered person for a financial year; the final return under section 45 is filed once, by a person whose registration has been cancelled.

options.text: A final return, within three months of the date of cancellation, the date of the order being irrelevant
options.misconception: takes the first of the two dates section 45 names instead of the later of them
options.why: The section names both dates and then says whichever is later. Where the cancellation takes effect from a date earlier than the order, as here, it is the order that starts the three months running.

citation.ref: Section 45, read with sections 29 and 44

items.scenario: A registered person applies for cancellation because he has closed his business. The order of cancellation is passed on 20 May 2026 and the cancellation is given effect from 31 March 2026. He assumes that once the registration is gone he has nothing further to file.

items.stem: What happens to the input tax credit?

options.text: Both credits go — clause (h) names destruction and writing off alongside gifts
options.why: Section 17(5)(h) blocks input tax credit in respect of goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off or disposed of by way of gift or free samples. Destruction by flood and a write-off in the books are two of the five events listed there, so both credits must go. An insurance settlement is money received from an insurer and does not enter the clause at all.

options.text: Only the destroyed goods lose the credit; a write-off is a book entry and the goods are still there
options.misconception: treats writing off as reversible bookkeeping when the clause names it as an event in its own right
options.why: The clause says written off, without asking whether the goods survived the entry. Once the person has written them off in his books the credit goes, and what he does with the goods afterwards is a separate question with its own answer.

options.text: Both credits stand, the insurance settlement having made the company whole
options.misconception: makes the credit turn on whether the loss was made good, which clause (h) never asks
options.why: Clause (h) asks what became of the goods, not who ended up bearing the cost. Insurance is a contract with an insurer and has no place in the input tax credit computation on either side.

options.text: Neither goes, clause (h) being aimed at gifts and free samples, and a casualty is not a giving away
options.misconception: reads clause (h) as though it named only voluntary disposals
options.why: The clause lists five events and only two of them are voluntary. Goods lost, stolen or destroyed sit inside it as squarely as goods given away, which is why an ordinary stock loss carries a credit reversal with it.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(h), read with section 16(1)

items.scenario: A manufacturer's godown floods. Finished goods that had carried input tax credit on their inputs are destroyed. In the same year the company writes off in its books a quantity of slow-moving raw material which is still physically lying in stock. An insurance settlement is received for the flood loss.

items.stem: What does section 49 permit?

options.text: Any credit may pay any liability, all three being taxes under one system collected together
options.misconception: treats the three heads as a single pool, which section 49(5) keeps deliberately apart
options.why: The three are levied by different statutes and the money is shared between different governments. Section 49(5) sets out head by head what each credit may be used for, and the central and the State heads never meet.

options.text: Central tax credit may pay State tax so long as the integrated tax credit has been exhausted first
options.misconception: reads the ordering rule in section 49A as if it also lifted the bar between the central and State heads
options.why: Section 49A governs the order in which credits are taken up, not what each of them may pay. Exhausting the integrated tax credit first does not unlock a set-off that section 49(5) never permitted in the first place.

options.text: The order of utilisation is the taxpayer's to choose, rule 88A having made section 49A optional
options.misconception: reads rule 88A as removing the ordering rule when it only relaxes it inside the integrated tax credit
options.why: Rule 88A lets integrated tax credit be applied towards central tax and State tax in any order and in any proportion once the integrated tax liability is met. The requirement to exhaust that credit before touching the other two survives untouched.

options.text: Integrated tax credit must be used up first and may go against any head; central tax credit can never be set against State tax
options.why: Section 49A requires the credit of integrated tax to be utilised fully towards integrated tax, central tax and State tax before central tax credit or State tax credit may be used at all. Section 49(5) then allows central tax credit against central tax and integrated tax only, and State tax credit against State tax and integrated tax only, so the cross set-off he proposes is barred and some cash will have to be paid.

citation.ref: Sections 49(5), 49A and 49B, read with rule 88A of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: For one month a registered person owes integrated tax ₹1 lakh, central tax ₹1 lakh and State tax ₹1 lakh. His electronic credit ledger holds integrated tax credit ₹1.5 lakh, central tax credit ₹1 lakh and State tax credit ₹0.2 lakh. To avoid paying anything in cash he proposes to set his central tax credit against the State tax liability.

items.stem: What must he pay, and what becomes of that balance?

options.text: Nothing at all, the credit having been validly taken when the goods were bought and the option operating only from April
options.misconception: treats a valid original credit as immune to a later change of status
options.why: Section 18(4) exists because the goods will now be used to make supplies taxed under the composition levy, where no credit is allowed. What triggers the payment is the change of status, not any defect in the credit when it was taken.

options.text: An amount equal to the credit on the stock and on the capital goods worked out as on 31 March 2027, and the balance left in the ledger lapses
options.why: Section 18(4) requires a registered person who opts to pay tax under section 10 to pay an amount equivalent to the credit of input tax on inputs held in stock, on inputs contained in semi-finished or finished goods held in stock, and on capital goods, on the day immediately preceding the date of exercising the option. Rule 44 works the capital goods figure out on the remaining useful life.
