The supplier is registered in Gujarat and the place of supply, worked out under the IGST Act, is also Gujarat. The department's accounts office proposes to deduct tax at source from the payment.

items.stem: Is the supply an export of services?

options.text: Yes — the payment condition is satisfied by rupees wherever the Reserve Bank of India permits them
options.why: The fourth condition in section 2(6) asks for payment in convertible foreign exchange or in Indian rupees wherever permitted by the Reserve Bank of India. Those closing words were put in for exactly this kind of trade, so a rupee receipt the central bank allows satisfies the condition and all five conditions hold.

options.text: No — section 2(6) requires payment in convertible foreign exchange and nothing else will do
options.misconception: reads the fourth condition without the words about rupees that were added to it
options.why: That was the condition as first enacted, and it stranded exporters to neighbours who settle in rupees under arrangements the central bank itself approves. The words now sit in the definition.

options.text: No, because a supply to Nepal is a supply within the region and cannot be an export
options.misconception: invents a regional carve-out that neither the IGST Act nor the definition contains
options.why: The definition asks where the recipient is and where the place of supply is, and Nepal is outside India on both counts. No provision treats a neighbouring country differently for the export of services.

options.text: Yes, and being an export it is exempt, so no input tax credit may be taken on it
options.misconception: gets the export right and then treats a zero-rated supply as an exempt one
options.why: An export of services is a zero-rated supply under section 16 of the IGST Act, and section 16(2) preserves the credit on inputs used to make it. Exemption is what breaks a credit chain; zero-rating is what keeps it.

citation.ref: Section 2(6), clause (iv), read with section 2(6) as a whole and sections 16(1) and 16(2)

items.scenario: An Indian consultancy advises an unrelated Nepalese company. The supplier is in India, the recipient is in Nepal, and the place of supply worked out under section 13 is outside India. The client pays in Indian rupees through banking channels, an arrangement the Reserve Bank of India permits for this trade. The consultancy is told it has no export because no foreign currency came in.

items.stem: On whom may a penalty under section 112 be imposed?

options.text: The importer alone, section 112 reaching only the person who made the entry
options.misconception: reads the first limb of section 112 as the whole of it and drops the second
options.why: If the section stopped at the person who made the entry, everyone downstream who knowingly handled smuggled goods would be untouchable. The second limb was written for the storekeeper, the carrier and the dealer who know what they are handling.

options.text: The importer and the warehouse keeper, but not the transporter
options.why: Section 112 has two limbs. The first reaches a person who does or omits to do an act which renders the goods liable to confiscation, or abets it — that is the importer. The second reaches a person concerned in carrying, removing, depositing, harbouring, keeping, concealing, selling or purchasing goods which he knows or has reason to believe are liable to confiscation — the keeper knew, and the transporter did not.
keywords: renders the goods liable to confiscation
knows or has reason to believe

options.text: The importer and the transporter, a carrier who physically moved the goods being concerned in their removal whatever he believed
options.misconception: applies the second limb without its knowledge requirement, which is the condition the limb turns on
options.why: Carrying and removing are indeed the acts named, and the limb qualifies them with knows or has reason to believe. A transporter with clean-looking paperwork and no cause for suspicion falls outside it.

options.text: All three, the goods themselves being liable to confiscation and everyone who handled them answering for it
options.misconception: attaches the personal penalty to the goods when section 112 attaches it to conduct and, in its second limb, to knowledge
options.why: Confiscation is a proceeding against the goods; section 112 is a proceeding against a person. The second limb carries a knowledge requirement precisely so an innocent carrier is not penalised for a consignment he had no reason to doubt.

citation.ref: Section 112, clauses (a) and (b), read with sections 111(d) and 111(m)

items.scenario: A consignment is smuggled past customs by a fraudulent declaration. Three people are before the adjudicating officer: the importer who signed the declaration; a warehouse keeper who stored the goods afterwards knowing how they had come in; and a transporter who moved them from the port believing the paperwork to be in order.

items.stem: What must be added to the transaction value?

options.text: Neither — an item supplied free of charge cannot be part of a price the buyer never paid
options.misconception: reads the transaction value as the invoice figure when rule 10 exists to add what the invoice leaves out
options.why: The invoice is low precisely because the buyer bore those costs himself. Rule 10 brings them back so that two importers of identical goods pay the same duty whichever way they arranged the supply of the tooling.

options.text: The value of the dies, but not the Pune drawings
options.why: Rule 10(1)(b) adds the value, apportioned as appropriate, of goods and services supplied by the buyer free of charge or at reduced cost for use in producing the imported goods — materials and components, tools and dies and moulds, materials consumed, and engineering, development, art work, design work, plans and sketches. The last of those four carries the words undertaken elsewhere than in India, so design work done in Pune is not added.

options.text: The drawings, but not the dies, design work being an intangible that enters the value while tooling is a separate import
options.misconception: inverts the rule, adding the one category the rule qualifies and dropping one it adds unconditionally
options.why: Tools, dies and moulds used in producing the imported goods are added by name and without qualification. Design work is the qualified category, and the qualification runs against adding it here.

options.text: Both the dies and the drawings, everything the buyer contributed to making the goods being an addition
options.misconception: applies the buyer-supplied rule across all four categories and misses the geographical limit on the fourth
options.why: Three of the four categories are added wherever they came from. The engineering and design category alone is qualified by the words undertaken elsewhere than in India, so Indian design work stays out.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(b), clauses (i) to (iv), read with rule 10(1)(a) and rule 3

items.scenario: An importer's foreign supplier makes a machine to the importer's specification. The importer supplied the supplier, free of charge, with a set of dies made abroad and with engineering drawings prepared by a design firm in Pune. The invoice price reflects neither. The importer says a free supply is by definition not part of any price.

items.stem: How does rule 3 settle the classification?

options.text: By rule 2(a) — the shaver is a complete article and rule 2 governs complete articles
options.misconception: reaches for rule 2(a), which extends a heading to incomplete or unassembled articles, in a case about which of two headings applies
options.why: Rule 2(a) widens a heading to take in an incomplete, unfinished or unassembled article. It says nothing about choosing between two headings that both cover a finished one, which is rule 3's work.

options.text: By rule 3(a) — the heading naming shavers and clippers is the most specific description and wins before any tie-breaker is reached
options.why: Rule 3 runs in order and rule 3(a) comes first: the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description. A heading naming the article beats one describing a class it happens to fall in, and only goods that remain equally classifiable reach the later rules at all.

options.text: By rule 3(c) — where two headings compete, the one occurring last in numerical order prevails
options.misconception: reaches the last tie-breaker while an earlier limb of rule 3 still decides the question
options.why: Rule 3(c) is the end of the sequence and it applies only when the goods cannot be classified by reference to rule 3(a) or rule 3(b). Here rule 3(a) answers, so the numerical order never comes into play.

options.text: By rule 3(b) — the component giving the article its essential character decides it, and that is the shaving head
options.misconception: uses the essential character test, which rule 3(b) reserves for mixtures, composite goods and retail sets that rule 3(a) cannot place
options.why: Rule 3(b) is for mixtures, composite goods made up of different components, and goods put up in sets for retail sale. It is reached only where rule 3(a) fails, and rule 3(a) has not failed here.

citation.ref: General Rules for the Interpretation of the First Schedule, rule 3(a), (b) and (c), read with rules 1 and 2(a)

items.scenario: An electric shaver with a built-in hair trimmer is imported. One heading covers shavers and hair clippers with a self-contained electric motor by name. Another, later in the tariff, covers electro-mechanical domestic appliances with a self-contained electric motor in general terms. The importer wants the later heading, and points to rule 3(c).

items.stem: Which of the three qualifies under heading 9801?

options.text: The fertiliser plant and the machining centre, a machine that performs several operations being a composite plant
options.misconception: treats a composite machine as a plant, which the definition expressly refuses
options.why: The definition excludes a single machine, and it excludes a composite machine as well, precisely so that a versatile machine cannot be dressed up as a plant. The heading is for a project, not for a piece of equipment.

options.text: Only the fertiliser plant
options.why: Heading 9801 covers goods imported for the initial setting up or substantial expansion of a specified project — an industrial plant, an irrigation project, a power project, a mining project, a project for the exploration of oil or other minerals, and any other project notified. Industrial plant is defined so as to leave out a hotel, and to leave out a single machine or a composite machine, so only the first applicant is inside.

options.text: The fertiliser plant and the hotel, a hotel being an establishment with plant and machinery of its own
options.misconception: reads industrial plant on its ordinary meaning and misses the establishments the definition expressly excludes
options.why: The definition names the exclusions — a hotel, a hospital, a photographic studio, a film processing laboratory, a photocopying studio, a laundry, a garage and a workshop. Whatever machinery such an establishment installs, it is not an industrial plant for this heading.

options.text: All three, heading 9801 turning on the value of the contract rather than on the kind of project
options.misconception: invents a value test when the heading works by a list of specified projects
options.why: There is no value threshold in the heading. It names the projects it covers, and the conditions in the Regulations are about registration and documentation rather than about size.

citation.ref: Heading 9801 of the First Schedule with the definition of industrial plant, read with regulations 3 and 4 of the Project Imports Regulations, 1986

items.scenario: Three importers apply to register contracts under the project imports scheme. The first is setting up a fertiliser plant. The second is building a five-star hotel and wants its kitchens, lifts and laundry equipment covered. The third is importing one large computer-controlled machining centre for an existing factory and calls it a plant because it performs several operations.

items.stem: What import duty falls on that wristwatch, and when?

options.text: None at all — the goods take the export exit out of the warehouse, so no clearance for home consumption ever happens
options.why: Section 71 lets warehoused goods leave a warehouse only by a permitted route, and the levy follows the exit the goods take rather than the contract of sale. A sale to a departing passenger sends the watch out of India, so the goods are cleared for export and there is no clearance for home consumption on which import duty could fall.

options.text: Import duty falls at the rate in force on the date of sale, section 15(1)(b) applying to any removal from a warehouse
options.misconception: reads section 15(1)(b) as covering every removal, when it dates only a clearance for home consumption under section 68
options.why: Section 15(1)(b) fixes the rate by the date the bill of entry for home consumption in respect of warehoused goods is presented under section 68. A removal for export is a different exit and does not put that sub-clause in play.

options.text: Import duty falls on the day the passenger pays, the sale being the taxable event
options.misconception: makes the counter sale the taxable event, when the exit route out of the warehouse is what the levy follows
options.why: The contract of sale decides nothing about the duty. What decides it is which of section 71's exits the goods take, and here they take the export one.

options.text: Import duty falls, but at the rate in force on the date the shop first imported the watch
options.misconception: assumes duty must fall somewhere and then reaches for section 15(1)(a) to date it
options.why: Section 15(1)(a) dates the rate for goods entered for home consumption on first import. Nothing here is entered for home consumption at all, so there is no rate date to find.

citation.ref: Sections 71 and 69, read with sections 68 and 15(1)(b)

items.scenario: A passenger flying out of Mumbai to Frankfurt buys a wristwatch at the departure duty-free shop after clearing immigration. The shop's stock sits in a licensed warehouse and the wristwatch was imported months earlier and deposited there. The passenger boards with it.

items.stem: May those four containers be unloaded?

options.text: Not until the manifest is amended or supplemented with the proper officer's permission, which he may give if satisfied there was no fraudulent intention
options.why: Section 32 is an independent bar on every conveyance — no imported goods shall be unloaded unless they are mentioned in the arrival manifest, import manifest or import report for that conveyance. Entry inwards does not cure it. Section 30(4) supplies the way out: the proper officer may permit the document to be amended or supplemented where he is satisfied it is incorrect or incomplete and there was no fraudulent intention.

options.text: Yes — entry inwards has been granted for the vessel, and that covers everything aboard her
options.misconception: treats entry inwards as a blanket permission when section 32 tests each consignment against the manifest
options.why: Entry inwards under section 31 unlocks unloading from a vessel; section 32 then asks, of each consignment, whether it is mentioned in the manifest. The two requirements sit side by side and one does not satisfy the other.

options.text: No, and the position cannot be retrieved — an omission from the manifest is final and the goods must go back on the vessel
options.misconception: treats an incomplete manifest as beyond repair, ignoring the amendment power in section 30(4)
options.why: Section 30(4) exists precisely for the incorrect or incomplete manifest. What it asks of the officer is satisfaction that there was no fraudulent intention, not that the document was right first time.

options.text: Yes, because the bill of lading proves what the goods are, and that is what the manifest is for
options.misconception: substitutes a commercial document for the statutory one that section 32 names
options.why: Section 32 names the arrival manifest, the import manifest and the import report, and nothing else. A bill of lading may well persuade the officer to permit an amendment, but it does not stand in the manifest's place.

citation.ref: Section 32, read with sections 30(4) and 31

items.scenario: A vessel has been granted entry inwards at Kandla. While unloading, the dock staff find four containers aboard that appear nowhere in the arrival manifest. The steamer agent says a clerical error at the loading port left them off the list, produces the bill of lading for each, and asks that they be landed now and the paperwork sorted afterwards.

items.stem: On whose imports is the anti-dumping duty payable?

options.text: On none of the three, because a final anti-dumping duty is levied on the exporter and not on any importer
options.misconception: puts the incidence on the foreign exporter, when the duty is collected on import like any other duty of customs
options.why: The duty answers the exporter's pricing but it is collected from the importer on import, as an addition to and in the same manner as a duty of customs. Nobody sends a bill abroad.

options.text: On the domestic manufacturer and the export-oriented undertaking, a special economic zone being outside the customs territory of India
options.misconception: reaches for the zone's deemed-foreign status when the exemption comes from section 9A(2A) and covers both categories alike
options.why: Section 9A(2A) names the export-oriented undertaking and the special economic zone unit in one breath and treats them the same. Splitting them puts the answer on the wrong provision and gets one of the two wrong.

options.text: On the domestic manufacturer's alone — the duty does not reach the export-oriented undertaking or the special economic zone unit unless the notification specifically applies it to them
options.why: Section 9A(2A) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 keeps anti-dumping duty off articles imported by a hundred per cent export-oriented undertaking or by a unit in a special economic zone unless the notification imposing the duty specifically makes it applicable to them. Silence in the notification therefore means no duty on those two, while the ordinary domestic importer pays.

options.text: On all three, an anti-dumping duty being a duty of customs that follows the goods and not the importer
options.misconception: applies the duty by the goods alone and misses the identity-based carve-out in section 9A(2A)
options.why: The duty does follow the article as a general matter, and section 9A(2A) is the express exception written into the same section. Who imports decides the answer for these two categories.

citation.ref: Section 9A(2A), read with sections 9A(1) and 9A(5)

items.scenario: A final anti-dumping duty is in force on a chemical. Three importers bring in the same chemical from the same exporter: a domestic manufacturer clearing it for home consumption, a hundred per cent export-oriented undertaking importing it for use in its own production, and a unit in a special economic zone importing it for its authorised operations. The notification imposing the duty says nothing about either of the last two.

items.stem: What is wrong with the way the value was rejected?

options.text: Rule 8 lets him reject a declared value only after asking the exporter to explain, giving him a hearing, and recording his reasons in writing
options.why: Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 gives the proper officer a power to doubt and a procedure he must use before acting on the doubt. He asks the exporter to furnish further information, intimates the grounds of his doubt, gives a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and records his reasons in writing. Skipping all three steps makes the rejection bad however sound the officer's data was.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — rule 8 gives the officer an untrammelled power to reject a value he has reason to doubt
options.misconception: reads the power in rule 8 without the conditions the same rule attaches to its exercise
options.why: The power and the procedure are in the same rule. A rejection that skips the procedure is not an exercise of the power at all, and appellate forums set such assessments aside without reaching the valuation.

options.text: He should have gone straight to the residual method in rule 6, comparison under rule 4 being available only where the exporter agrees
options.misconception: invents a consent requirement for rule 4 and inverts the order the rules lay down
options.why: The rules run in order and rule 4 comes before rule 6. The exporter's agreement is not a condition of using comparison; his hearing is a condition of rejecting his own declared value.

options.text: He should have taken the local market price of the leather goods, that being the only objective figure available
options.misconception: uses the one basis rule 6 expressly forbids for export goods
options.why: Rule 6 says in terms that the local market price of the export goods shall not be the basis for determining the value. It is the one figure the rules put out of reach.

citation.ref: Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007, read with rules 4 and 6 and section 14(1)

items.scenario: A proper officer doubts the declared free on board value of a consignment of leather goods. He forms his view from contemporaneous export data, rejects the declared value the same afternoon, redetermines it under rule 4 and lets the goods go. The exporter is told nothing until he receives the assessed shipping bill, and no reasons are recorded anywhere.

items.stem: What can he do about each?

options.text: Revise the first entry and then file a separate refund application under section 27 within the ordinary limitation; the second may also be revised, an intimation not being a bar
options.misconception: adds a second application section 18A dispenses with, and misses the case in which the route is closed
options.why: The whole convenience of the route is that the revised entry does the refund claim's work. And an intimated investigation is one of the express bars, not a formality that leaves the route open.

options.text: Both can be revised, and the excess is credited to the importer's account automatically without any claim being made
options.misconception: turns a deemed refund claim into an automatic credit, and ignores the bar on the second consignment
options.why: Being treated as a claim under section 27 means the refund machinery runs, including the test of unjust enrichment. It does not mean money moves by itself.

options.text: Revise the first entry, and the revision is itself treated as a refund claim under section 27; the second is outside section 18A because an investigation was started and intimated
options.why: Where a revised entry under section 18A shows duty paid in excess, the application is treated as a claim for refund under section 27, so no separate refund application is filed. The route is closed in defined cases, and one of them is where an audit, search, seizure or investigation has already been started and intimated to the person, which is what happened on the second consignment.
keywords: treated as a claim for refund

options.text: Neither can be revised — section 18A works only where duty was short paid, excess payments going to section 27 from the start
options.misconception: reads section 18A as a one-way street when it deals with both directions of error
options.why: Section 18A covers duty short paid and duty paid in excess alike. Short payment brings duty with interest; excess payment turns the application into a refund claim.

citation.ref: Section 18A, read with section 27 and the Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025

items.scenario: An importer's own review in July 2026 finds two things about bills of entry cleared in February 2026. On one, an exemption he was entitled to was never claimed, so ₹3,00,000 of duty was paid in excess. On another, covering a different consignment, the department had already issued him an intimation in May 2026 that an investigation had been started.

items.stem: What are the answers?

options.text: The surcharge is payable on the integrated tax, which is what remains after the basic customs duty was exempted
options.misconception: puts into the base the one levy the provision expressly keeps out of it
options.why: The integrated tax under section 3(7), the compensation cess under section 3(9) and the trade-remedy duties are all excluded from the surcharge's base by name.

options.text: The surcharge is payable on the assessable value, an exemption from basic customs duty not being an exemption from the surcharge
options.misconception: gives the surcharge a value base of its own when it has none
options.why: The surcharge has no base but the duties. Exempting the duty leaves the surcharge with nothing to be a percentage of, which is a different thing from exempting the surcharge.

options.text: No surcharge is payable, and any surcharge paid on other consignments is creditable as input tax alongside the integrated tax
options.misconception: gets the first half right and then puts a customs levy into the GST credit chain
options.why: Only the integrated tax charged on the import enters the input tax ledger. The surcharge is collected as a duty of customs and has no credit mechanism at all.

options.text: No surcharge is payable, because it is a percentage of a nil duty; and had any been payable it would have been a cost, not a credit
options.why: The surcharge is charged on the aggregate of the duties of customs, so where the basic customs duty is nil the surcharge on it is nil too — the assessable value never enters the computation. And because it is not the integrated tax, it is not creditable; like the basic customs duty it rides on, it is a cost.

citation.ref: Section 110 — Social Welfare Surcharge on imported goods, read with sections 3(7) and 3(9) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

items.scenario: A registered manufacturer imports a machine whose basic customs duty is fully exempt under a notification, so no basic customs duty is payable. Integrated tax under section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act is charged at the port and paid. His accountant asks two questions: is Social Welfare Surcharge payable, and is it creditable if it is.

items.stem: How do the Baggage Rules treat the television?

options.text: It is an Annexure-I article, so it is outside rule 3 altogether and outside the General Free Allowance as well, and duty is payable on it
options.why: Rule 3 clears used personal effects and travel souvenirs with no value ceiling, but it takes out the articles listed in Annexure-I, and a television is one of them. Rule 5's General Free Allowance is given for articles outside Annexure-I, so it cannot cover the television either. Being cheap does not help — the exclusion is by description, not by value.

options.text: It is free of duty because the passenger arrived by air rather than by land, and the arrival route is what the rules turn on
options.misconception: reads the by-land distinction as the whole of the rules when it only decides which allowance a passenger gets
options.why: Arriving other than by land is what entitles a passenger to a General Free Allowance at all; a passenger arriving by land gets used personal effects only. Neither branch reaches an Annexure-I article.

options.text: It is covered by the General Free Allowance along with the camera, since the two together are worth less than the allowance
options.misconception: tests an Annexure-I article by value when the allowance is given only for articles outside Annexure-I
options.why: The allowance and the annexure work in sequence, not in competition. An article on the annexure never reaches the value test, so the arithmetic never begins.

options.text: It is a used personal effect once the passenger has unpacked and used it, and rule 3 clears it with no ceiling
options.misconception: tries to bring an Annexure-I article back through rule 3 by calling it a personal effect
options.why: Rule 3's own words carve out the Annexure-I articles, so no amount of personal use puts a television back inside it. The worn clothing is the personal effect here.

citation.ref: Rules 3 and 5 of the Baggage Rules, 2026 with Annexure-I (Notification No. 14/2026-Customs (N.T.) dated 01.02.2026, in force 02.02.2026)

items.scenario: A resident lands at Bengaluru from Singapore in June 2026 carrying his own worn clothing, a television set bought abroad, and a camera bought abroad. Take the General Free Allowance applicable to him as given at ₹75,000, and take it as given that the television and the camera together are worth less than that.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of the admission?

options.text: India — an event held in more than one country including India is placed wholly in India
options.why: Section 13(5) of the IGST Act puts admission to, and organisation of, an event at the place where the event is actually held. Its proviso deals with the split case: where the event is held in more than one country including India, the place of supply is India. The ticket is not apportioned between the two legs.

options.text: Singapore, that being where the greater part of the event is held and where the organiser sits
options.misconception: apportions by where most of the event happens, which is the test the proviso replaces
options.why: The proviso does not weigh the legs against each other. Once any part of the event is held in India, the whole place of supply is India.

options.text: Gujarat, being the location of the registered recipient under the general rule in section 13(2)
options.misconception: falls back to the default in section 13(2) when a specific sub-section covers events
options.why: Section 13(2) applies only where none of the specific sub-sections does. Section 13(5) covers admission to an event by name, so the default never comes into play.

options.text: Split between Singapore and India in the ratio of the days spent in each, under section 13(7)
options.misconception: applies the apportionment rule for a service supplied in more than one State to a service supplied in more than one country
options.why: Apportionment under section 13(7) operates once the place of supply is India and the service is supplied in more than one State or Union territory. It does not divide a supply between India and a foreign country.

citation.ref: Section 13(5) with its proviso, read with sections 13(2) and 13(7)

items.scenario: A Singapore company runs a two-leg trade exhibition — three days in Singapore and two days in Mumbai, sold as one event on one ticket. It sells admission to an Indian company registered in Gujarat. The supplier is outside India and the recipient is in India, so section 13 governs rather than section 12.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: No, but only because the paper physically crosses a customs boundary into the zone, which makes it an export of goods
options.misconception: turns a deemed inter-State supply into an export, which would send the supplier to a shipping bill
options.why: A supply to a zone is zero-rated, not an export of goods out of India. No shipping bill is filed and the goods never leave the country.

options.text: No — a supply to a Special Economic Zone unit is an inter-State supply whatever the two locations are, so integrated tax is the levy in question
options.why: Section 7(5)(b) of the IGST Act says that a supply of goods or services to a Special Economic Zone developer or unit shall be treated as a supply in the course of inter-State trade or commerce. The two locations do not enter it. Being for authorised operations, the supply is then zero-rated under section 16(1)(b), so the supplier makes it under a Letter of Undertaking or pays integrated tax and claims it back.

options.text: Yes for goods, no for services — section 7(5)(b) covers services to a zone alone
options.misconception: splits a provision that names goods and services together
options.why: Section 7(5)(b) speaks of a supply of goods or services or both to a Special Economic Zone developer or unit. Nothing in it turns on which of the two is supplied.

options.text: Yes — supplier and recipient are in the same State, so the supply is intra-State and central tax and State tax are correct
options.misconception: applies the ordinary location test to a supply the statute deems inter-State by description
options.why: The ordinary test compares the supplier's location with the place of supply. Section 7(5)(b) overrides that comparison for a Special Economic Zone by deeming the supply inter-State.

citation.ref: Section 7(5)(b), read with section 16(1)(b)

items.scenario: A stationery supplier registered in Karnataka supplies printer paper to a Special Economic Zone unit that is also in Karnataka, a few kilometres away, for the unit's authorised operations. The supplier charges central tax and State tax, saying both parties are in the same State so the supply cannot be inter-State.

items.stem: What are his choices for the first month's PMT-06?

options.text: He may defer the whole payment to the quarterly return, monthly payment being expected but not required under QRMP
options.misconception: reads the scheme as quarterly for both the return and the payment, which is the half of it the scheme does not give
options.why: The scheme is quarterly return and monthly payment. The deposit in each of the first two months of the quarter is required, and the scheme's name carries both halves.

options.text: He must deposit ₹90,000, the deposit being a payment of the month's tax and therefore exactly the liability
options.misconception: treats the monthly deposit as an assessment of the month when it is a deposit against the quarter's liability
options.why: The tax for the quarter is assessed in the quarterly GSTR-3B. What goes in Form GST PMT-06 each month is a deposit on account, which is why a fixed sum method can exist at all.

options.text: Deposit ₹1,40,000 under the fixed sum method, or deposit his self-assessed liability after setting off the credit — the scheme lets him pick either
options.why: The scheme gives two methods for the monthly deposit in Form GST PMT-06 and the taxpayer chooses. The fixed sum method takes 35 per cent of the tax paid in cash in the preceding quarter, which on the given figures is ₹1,40,000. The self-assessed method takes his own working for the month, and the credit in his electronic credit ledger is available against it. Neither method is compulsory.

options.text: He must use the fixed sum method, the self-assessed route being open only to a taxpayer in his first quarter in the scheme
options.misconception: makes one of two optional methods compulsory and invents a first-quarter condition for the other
options.why: Both methods are open every month. The fixed sum route is a convenience for a taxpayer who does not want to work the month out, not an obligation on anyone.

citation.ref: Rule 61A read with the proviso to section 39(7) and Notification No. 84/2020-Central Tax dated 10.11.2020

items.scenario: A dealer inside the QRMP scheme filed a quarterly GSTR-3B for the quarter just ended, having paid ₹4,00,000 of tax in cash for that quarter. Take as given that the fixed sum method for Form GST PMT-06 is 35 per cent of the tax paid in cash in the preceding quarter, and that PMT-06 is due by the 25th of the following month. In the first month of the new quarter his actual liability works out at ₹90,000, and he has ₹60,000 of credit in his electronic credit ledger.

items.stem: What is the correct course?

options.text: A fresh e-way bill must be generated for the balance journey, an expired bill being incapable of revival
options.misconception: treats expiry as final when the rule provides for extension around the moment of expiry
options.why: Generating a fresh bill would break the link with the original consignment and its Part A details. The rule keeps one bill for one movement and lets its validity be extended instead.

options.text: No action is needed — validity is suspended automatically while the vehicle is stationary for reasons outside the transporter's control
options.misconception: invents an automatic suspension where the rule requires a positive act by the transporter
options.why: Nothing suspends itself. The extension has to be made in the system, within the window, with the reason stated, or the consignment is moving on an expired e-way bill.

options.text: The consignor must apply to the Commissioner for an extension, an extension of validity being an officer's decision
options.misconception: sends a system-driven extension to an officer who has no part in it
options.why: The extension is made by the transporter in the e-way bill system. The Commissioner's powers over e-way bills lie elsewhere and are not engaged by a delayed truck.

options.text: The transporter updates Part B in the e-way bill system within the permitted window and states the reason, and the same e-way bill continues with a fresh validity
options.why: Rule 138(10) lets the validity period be extended in exceptional circumstances where the goods cannot be transported within the original period. The transporter updates the details in Part B, gives the reason, and the same e-way bill continues. A landslide holding up the truck is exactly the circumstance the extension exists for.

citation.ref: Rule 138(10) with its proviso on extension of validity

items.scenario: An e-way bill for a road consignment expires at 11 p.m. on 12 June 2026 while the truck is still 90 kilometres short of its destination, held up by a landslide on the highway. Take as given that the rule allows an extension to be made within eight hours before or after the expiry. The consignor asks whether a fresh e-way bill must now be generated.

items.stem: Does either movement need an e-way bill?

options.text: Both do — an inter-State job-work despatch by a principal and an inter-State movement of handicraft goods by an unregistered exempt person need one whatever the consignment is worth
options.why: Rule 138(1) sets the fifty-thousand line and then carries two provisos that put certain movements inside the rule irrespective of the value of the consignment. One is goods sent by a principal to a job worker in another State. The other is handicraft goods moved from one State to another by a person exempted from obtaining registration. Both movements here fall inside one of the two.

options.text: Only the job-work despatch does, an unregistered person having no obligation under rule 138 at all
options.misconception: assumes an unregistered person is outside the e-way bill machinery, when the handicraft proviso is written for exactly such a person
options.why: The handicraft proviso names a person exempted from obtaining registration. It exists because such a person is outside registration, not in spite of it.

options.text: Only the handicraft movement does, a job-work despatch not being a supply and therefore outside the rule
options.misconception: ties the e-way bill to a supply, when the rule is triggered by causing the movement of goods
options.why: Rule 138 attaches to movement, including movement for reasons other than supply. A despatch to a job worker is inside it on that footing alone, and the proviso then removes the value floor for the inter-State case.

options.text: Neither does, both consignments being below the fifty-thousand line the rule sets
options.misconception: reads the value threshold as the whole of rule 138(1) and misses the provisos beneath it
options.why: The threshold is the general rule and the provisos are the exceptions written under it. Two named movements are inside the rule at any value at all.

citation.ref: Rule 138(1) with the provisos on movements requiring an e-way bill irrespective of value

items.scenario: Two movements start on the same morning. A registered principal in Ludhiana sends components worth ₹22,000 to a job worker in Ambala, in another State. A craftsman in Jaipur, exempt from registration and not registered, sends handicraft goods worth ₹18,000 to a buyer in Delhi. Both are below fifty thousand rupees.

items.stem: Is the auditor right?

options.text: Yes for the card payments only, since a code that was never used cannot have been made available
options.misconception: assumes the relief is lost once the customer pays by another route, when the notification provides for exactly that case
options.why: The notification deals with the other-mode payment separately, and asks only for a cross-reference of that payment on the invoice. Paying by card does not put the chain in default.

options.text: No, and no code or cross-reference is needed at all, because the chain reports its invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal and that code is enough
options.misconception: uses the static Portal code to answer a requirement written for a payment instruction
options.why: The Portal's code identifies an invoice; a dynamic code lets a consumer pay. And business-to-consumer invoices are outside rule 48(4) and are never uploaded to the Portal at all.

options.text: Yes — rule 46 requires the code to be printed on the invoice itself, and a screen at the till is not an invoice
options.misconception: reads the requirement as being about ink on paper when the notification is about the customer being able to pay
options.why: What the requirement is for is the customer's ability to scan and pay. The notification says in terms that a digital display plus a cross-reference on the invoice discharges it.

options.text: No — the requirement is treated as met where the code is made available through a digital display and the invoice carries a cross-reference of the payment, and where payment is by another mode the cross-reference of that payment suffices
options.why: Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax treats the Dynamic Quick Response code requirement as complied with where the supplier makes the code available to the recipient through a digital display and the invoice carries a cross-reference of the payment made using it. Where payment is made by any other mode, the invoice must instead carry a cross-reference of that payment. Both of the chain's counters are inside one of the two.

citation.ref: Rule 46 with Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax and its provisos on compliance, read with rule 48(4)

items.scenario: A retail chain above the notified turnover shows the payment code on a screen at the till. Some customers scan it and pay; some pay by card at the same counter. In both cases the printed invoice handed over carries a cross-reference of the payment made. The chain's auditor says every one of those invoices is defective because the code itself is not printed on the paper.

items.stem: What can the department do about the ruling?

options.text: Nothing, unless the company first applies for a fresh ruling on the correct composition
options.misconception: puts the initiative on the applicant when section 104 gives the power to the Authority
options.why: The power to declare a ruling void sits with the Authority or the Appellate Authority and is exercised on their own finding. It waits on no application from the person who obtained the ruling.

options.text: Nothing — a ruling binds the jurisdictional officer under section 103 until the law changes, and the law has not changed
options.misconception: treats section 103's binding force as absolute, when section 104 removes the ruling itself in a fraud case
options.why: Section 103 binds an officer to a ruling that stands. Section 104 is about whether it stands at all, and a ruling obtained on false facts can be taken away from underneath the binding rule.

options.text: Nothing for the past, but the ruling ceases to bind from the date the misstatement is discovered
options.misconception: gives the declaration prospective effect, when the words of section 104 are void ab initio
options.why: Void ab initio means void from the beginning. A prospective cessation would leave the benefit of the fraud with the applicant for two years, which is the opposite of what the section does.

options.text: Declare it void ab initio, so it is treated as if it had never been made and the intervening period is open to demand
options.why: Section 104 lets the Authority or the Appellate Authority declare a ruling void ab initio where it finds the ruling was obtained by fraud or suppression of material facts or misrepresentation of facts. All the provisions of the Act then apply to the applicant as if the ruling had never been made, after he is given an opportunity of being heard.
keywords: as if the ruling had never been made

citation.ref: Section 104, read with sections 103(1) and 103(2)

items.scenario: A company obtained an advance ruling in its own favour on the classification of a product, describing the product's composition in its application. Two years later the department finds that the composition stated in the application was not the composition of the product the company actually makes, and that the difference was known to the company when it applied.

items.stem: What did the department leave out, and what was it entitled to do?

options.text: The findings, the reasons for them and his rights and obligations had to be communicated within thirty days in FORM GST ADT-02; the demand itself is properly raised under section 74A
options.why: Section 65(6) requires the proper officer, on conclusion of the audit, to inform the registered person within thirty days of the findings, the reasons for those findings, and his rights and obligations, and the communication goes in FORM GST ADT-02. Where the audit shows tax unpaid, short paid, wrongly refunded or credit wrongly availed, the officer may then proceed under section 74A, so the demand route is right even though the intimation was skipped.

options.text: Nothing was left out — an audit report is an internal document and the taxpayer sees the case for the first time in the notice
options.misconception: treats the audit findings as internal when the section requires them to be communicated
options.why: The section makes the communication a step in the audit itself, not a courtesy. The taxpayer is told the findings and the reasons before any demand is framed.

options.text: The findings had to be communicated, and because they were not, no demand can be raised on them at all
options.misconception: turns a procedural default into a complete bar on the demand
options.why: The intimation is required and its omission is a defect the taxpayer can press. It does not take away the power to determine tax on what the audit found.

options.text: The findings had to be communicated within thirty days, and the demand should have gone under section 73 as no fraud is alleged
options.misconception: reaches for section 73, which stops at FY 2023-24, instead of section 74A
options.why: Sections 73 and 74 govern up to FY 2023-24. From FY 2024-25 onwards section 74A is the single demand provision whether or not fraud is alleged, and section 65(6) sends the officer to it.

citation.ref: Section 65(6), read with rule 101 of the CGST Rules, 2017, FORM GST ADT-02 and section 74A

items.scenario: An audit under section 65 is completed on 10 August 2026. The audit team's working papers show that credit of ₹14 lakh was wrongly availed. Nothing is communicated to the registered person, and in December 2026 he receives a notice determining that amount, the first he hears of the finding.

items.stem: What must happen before the material is used?

options.text: The company must be given an opportunity of being heard on the material gathered in the special audit and proposed to be used against it
options.why: Section 66(4) guarantees the registered person an opportunity of being heard in respect of any material gathered on the basis of the special audit and proposed to be used in any proceedings under the Act. Material the company has never seen cannot become the basis of a determination until that hearing is given.

options.text: The report must first be sent to the Commissioner for approval, his prior approval being needed at every stage of a special audit
options.misconception: repeats the prior approval required for directing the audit and attaches it to the use of the report
options.why: The Commissioner's prior approval is a condition of the direction under section 66(1). The condition on using the material is the hearing in section 66(4).

options.text: The company must first be allowed to appoint its own accountant to answer the report, the special audit being one-sided
options.misconception: invents a right of counter-audit where the section gives a right to be heard
options.why: The accountant is nominated by the Commissioner and paid by him, and the company neither picks nor pays. What it gets is a hearing on the material, not an audit of its own.

options.text: Nothing more — the report of an accountant nominated by the Commissioner is evidence in itself and the company's remedy is an appeal
options.misconception: treats the report as self-proving and postpones the hearing to the appellate stage the section brings forward
options.why: The section puts the hearing before the material is used, not after the demand. Sending the taxpayer to appeal instead is what section 66(4) was written to prevent.

citation.ref: Section 66(4), read with sections 66(1), 66(2) and rule 102 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A special audit under section 66 is directed and the nominated cost accountant submits his report, which relies on costing working papers the accountant obtained from the company's overseas parent. The officer proposes to determine tax on the strength of that material. The company has never seen the working papers.

items.stem: Can he?

options.text: The transfer order is appealable but the prosecution sanction is not, an internal reallocation of work affecting his rights
options.misconception: keeps one of the two listed matters appealable because it feels administrative rather than penal
options.why: Both appear on the same list. Section 121 names the transfer of proceedings first and the sanction of prosecution third, and gives neither a different treatment.

options.text: Neither is appealable — both are on the list in section 121, and his remedy against an arbitrary order of either kind is a writ, not an appeal
options.why: Section 121 shuts out an appeal against an order directing the transfer of proceedings from one officer to another, and against an order sanctioning prosecution under the Act. Both are steps in the administration of a case rather than determinations of liability. The bar is on an appeal and not on every remedy, so a writ to the High Court remains available.

options.text: Both are appealable, since section 107 lets any person aggrieved by any decision or order appeal to the Appellate Authority
options.misconception: reads section 107(1) without section 121, which opens with words overriding every other provision
options.why: Section 121 begins notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any provision of the Act. The wide words in section 107(1) do not survive it for the matters section 121 lists.

options.text: Neither is appealable, and neither can be revised either, but only because the Revisional Authority has no power over a Commissioner's own order
options.misconception: explains the revisional bar by rank when it comes from section 108(1) being made subject to section 121
options.why: It is true that neither can be revised, and the reason is that section 108(1) opens subject to the provisions of section 121. Rank has nothing to do with it.

citation.ref: Section 121 clauses (a) and (c), read with sections 107(1) and 108(1)

items.scenario: A taxpayer receives two communications on the same day. One is an order of the Commissioner transferring his case from the officer who had been hearing it to another officer in a different range. The other is an order sanctioning prosecution against him under the Act. He wants to appeal against both to the Appellate Authority.

items.stem: May he revise it on 1 June 2026?

options.text: Yes — no appeal has been filed, and the only bar in section 108(2) is an order that has been the subject of an appeal
options.misconception: reads clause (a) of section 108(2) as the whole of the sub-section, when it shuts four doors
options.why: The appeal bar is the first of four. Clause (b) adds a floor and a ceiling in time, clause (c) shuts out an order already taken for revision, and clause (d) an order itself passed in revision.

options.text: No, and he can never revise it, because a revision may only follow an appellate order
options.misconception: makes an appeal a precondition of revision, when revision is the department's look at an order nobody has appealed
options.why: Revision exists precisely for the unappealed order. What clause (b) does is make the Authority wait for the appeal window to close first.

options.text: No — he must wait until the section 107(2) period has expired, so not before 1 September 2026, and in any event not after three years from the order
options.why: Section 108(2)(b) puts two limits on the same power. The Revisional Authority shall not exercise it where the period specified under section 107(2) has not yet expired — that period is the department's own window to direct an appeal, six months on the given facts — or where more than three years have expired after the order sought to be revised was passed. A revision on 1 June 2026 falls inside the first bar.

options.text: Yes, provided he first stays the operation of the order, which cures the timing objection
options.misconception: uses the power to stay, which section 108(1) gives, as if it lifted the bar in section 108(2)
options.why: Staying the order is part of how a revision is conducted once it may be begun. It says nothing about whether it may be begun, which clause (b) decides.

citation.ref: Section 108(2)(b), read with sections 108(1), 108(2)(a) and 107(2)

items.scenario: An adjudicating officer passes an order on 1 March 2026 and it is communicated the same day. Nobody appeals. On 1 June 2026 the Revisional Authority, having read the file, considers the order erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of revenue and proposes to revise it at once. Take as given that the period specified in section 107(2) is six months from communication.

items.stem: What is the position on limitation and on who hears the appeal?

options.text: The appeal is in time, since limitation runs from the date the Tribunal passed the order and not from communication, and a single Judge may hear it
options.misconception: starts the clock at the order rather than at communication, and drops the requirement of a two-Judge Bench
options.why: Limitation runs from the date the order is communicated to the person. And the appeal is heard by a Bench of not less than two Judges, so the composition is wrong as well.

options.text: The appeal does not lie to the High Court at all, an order of a State Bench of the Tribunal going directly to the Supreme Court
options.misconception: extends the direct-to-Supreme-Court route, which is for the Principal Bench and for place-of-supply differences, to an ordinary State Bench order
options.why: A direct appeal to the Supreme Court lies from an order of the Principal Bench, and from an order relating to a difference of views on the place of supply. An ordinary valuation dispute decided by a State Bench goes to the High Court on a substantial question of law.

options.text: The appeal is barred outright, the one hundred and eighty days being an absolute limit the High Court cannot relax
options.misconception: reads the period without the express power to admit a late appeal on sufficient cause
options.why: The section gives the period and, in the same breath, the power to admit an appeal filed after it where the Court is satisfied there was sufficient cause. An absolute reading takes that power away.

options.text: The appeal is late against the one hundred and eighty days allowed, but the Court may admit it on sufficient cause; and once admitted it is heard by a Bench of not less than two Judges
options.why: An appeal to the High Court is filed within one hundred and eighty days of the order being communicated, and the Court may admit an appeal after that period on being satisfied there was sufficient cause for not filing it in time. Counsel's illness is the kind of cause the Court weighs. The appeal is then heard by a Bench of not less than two Judges, which decides by majority, so a single Judge cannot dispose of it.

citation.ref: Sections 117(2), 117(3) and 117(5), read with section 117(1) and section 118

items.scenario: A State Bench of the Appellate Tribunal decides an ordinary valuation dispute, with no difference of views between States about the place of supply. The order is communicated to the taxpayer on 1 April 2026. He files an appeal to the High Court on 1 December 2026, explaining that his counsel was ill for four months. A single Judge takes up the admission.

items.stem: Can it rectify without hearing him?

options.text: No — where the rectification adversely affects any person, the principles of natural justice must be followed, and this one cuts his refund
options.why: The third proviso to section 161 says that where the rectification adversely affects any person, the principles of natural justice shall be followed by the authority carrying it out. A transposed digit is indeed an error apparent on the face of record and is within the section, but reducing a refund from ₹9,00,000 to ₹90,000 plainly affects him adversely, so he must be heard first.

options.text: No, and the order cannot be rectified at all — a change in the amount of a refund is a review, which section 161 does not permit
options.misconception: calls an arithmetical correction a review, when the section is written for exactly this kind of slip
options.why: Section 161 will not reopen a debatable question or a fresh appreciation of evidence. A transposed digit is neither; it is the clerical or arithmetical error the section exists to put right.

options.text: Yes, provided the correction is made within six months, because the six-month limit is the only condition the section imposes
options.misconception: treats the first proviso's time limit as the section's only condition and overlooks the safeguard in the third
options.why: Time is one condition and natural justice is another. Being inside six months does not excuse an unheard rectification that takes money away.

options.text: Yes — an error apparent on the face of record is corrected on the record itself and no hearing is contemplated by the section
options.misconception: reads the power in section 161 without the third proviso that conditions its exercise
options.why: The section corrects the record and the third proviso decides when the person must be heard first. Whether the error is obvious is a different question from whether the correction hurts him.

citation.ref: Section 161 with its third proviso, read with its first and second provisos

items.scenario: An order allowed a refund of ₹9,00,000. Two months later the authority notices that a figure in its own computation was transposed and that the correct refund is ₹90,000. It proposes to rectify the order under section 161 and issue a corrected one, without hearing the taxpayer, on the footing that a transposed digit needs no argument.

items.stem: How is the lathe's sale valued, and what happens to the shortfall?

options.text: The lathe carries no taxable value at all, and the negative margin is simply ignored — the other machine is still taxed on its full ₹1,00,000 margin
options.why: Rule 32(5) values the supply at selling price less purchase price, and a negative margin is ignored. So the lathe bears no value and no tax, and the shortfall does not travel: it is not a loss to be set against the margin on any other supply, so the other machine is taxed on its own ₹1,00,000.

options.text: The lathe is taxed on its full selling price of ₹5,20,000, the margin scheme being unavailable where the dealer sells at a loss
options.misconception: reads a loss as disqualifying the supply from the scheme, when the rule provides for it by ignoring the negative margin
options.why: Nothing about a loss puts the supply outside rule 32(5). The conditions are that the goods are second-hand, sold as such after at most minor processing that does not change their nature, and that no input tax credit was taken.

options.text: The lathe is outside the scheme because cleaning and testing is processing, so the whole ₹5,20,000 is taxable
options.misconception: treats any work on the goods as processing that changes their nature, which the rule allows so long as the nature is unchanged
options.why: The rule tolerates minor processing that does not change the nature of the goods. Cleaning and testing a lathe leaves it the same lathe.

options.text: The lathe carries a negative value of ₹80,000, which reduces the other machine's margin to ₹20,000
options.misconception: pools the margins across supplies, when the rule values each supply on its own
options.why: The rule fixes a value for the supply in front of it. There is no pooling of margins across a dealer's stock and no net margin for the month.

citation.ref: Rule 32(5) with its proviso on the negative margin

items.scenario: A dealer in second-hand machinery buys a lathe from an unregistered owner for ₹6,00,000, takes no input tax credit, cleans and tests it without altering its nature, and sells it for ₹5,20,000 because the market has moved against him. He asks whether the ₹80,000 shortfall can be set against the margin on another machine sold the same month for a ₹1,00,000 margin.

items.stem: May the principal supply the goods directly from the job worker's premises?

options.text: No, and no declaration can help — goods can only ever be supplied from a place named on the principal's own registration at the time the inputs were sent out
options.misconception: treats the additional place of business as impossible to add, when declaring it is exactly the route the proviso offers
options.why: The declaration is the way through, not a closed door. Once the job worker's premises is on the principal's registration as an additional place of business, the supply may go from there.

options.text: Yes, freely — section 143 permits supply from the job worker's premises within the one year and asks nothing further
options.misconception: reads the permission in section 143(1)(b) without the proviso that conditions it
options.why: The one year is the time limit and the proviso is the condition. Both have to be satisfied, and the time limit alone does not open the job worker's shed as a despatch point.

options.text: Yes, because the job worker being unregistered means the premises is treated as the principal's own by default
options.misconception: inverts the proviso, which excuses the declaration where the job worker is registered and requires it where he is not
options.why: Registration of the job worker is what removes the need to declare. An unregistered job worker is the case in which the declaration is required.

options.text: Not as things stand — he must first declare the job worker's premises as his own additional place of business, the job worker being unregistered and the goods not notified
options.why: Section 143(1)(b) lets the principal supply the goods from the place of business of a job worker, but its proviso stops him unless he declares that place as his additional place of business. The proviso excepts two cases only — where the job worker is registered under section 25, or where the principal supplies goods of a class notified by the Commissioner — and neither applies here.

citation.ref: Section 143(1)(b) with its proviso, read with sections 143(3) and 25

items.scenario: A principal in Nashik sends inputs to a job worker in Aurangabad and, well inside the one year, finds a buyer who wants the finished goods shipped straight from the job worker's shed. The job worker is not registered under GST, and the principal has not declared the shed as anything on his own registration certificate. The goods he makes are not of any class notified by the Commissioner.

items.stem: Until when must those records be kept?

options.text: Until 31 December 2029 — seventy-two months are counted from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the year, not from the end of the year itself
options.why: Section 36 requires the accounts and records to be retained for seventy-two months from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the year they relate to. On the given date of 31 December 2023, seventy-two months run to 31 December 2029, so nothing may be cleared out in the early part of that year.

options.text: Until 31 December 2029, but only for the accounts, invoices and other documents being free to go after five years
options.misconception: splits the retention obligation between records and documents, which section 36 does not do
options.why: Section 36 speaks of the accounts and records required by section 35, and holds them all for one period. There is no shorter clock for the underlying documents.

options.text: Until 31 March 2029 — seventy-two months from the end of the financial year 2022-23
options.misconception: counts from the close of the financial year, which is the anchor the section does not use
options.why: The end of the year is the natural place to start counting and it is not the one section 36 names. The section anchors the period to the due date of the annual return, which falls later.

options.text: Until 31 December 2028 — sixty months from the due date of the annual return
options.misconception: substitutes a sixty-month period for the seventy-two months the section prescribes
options.why: Section 36 fixes seventy-two months. Sixty is the period the earlier indirect tax laws used and it has no place here.

citation.ref: Section 36, read with sections 35(1) and 44

items.scenario: A registered person is clearing out storage in 2029 and wants to know when his records for the financial year 2022-23 may go. Take as given that the annual return for 2022-23 was due to be furnished on 31 December 2023. No appeal, revision, other proceeding or investigation touches that year.

items.stem: Are they right?

options.text: The transporter is right and the godown owner is not, storage being a supply of service while transport of the goods of others is not
options.misconception: decides the obligation by whether the person makes a taxable supply, when section 35(2) turns on what he handles
options.why: Section 35(2) names the transporter and the owner or operator of a warehouse or godown side by side. Whether either makes a taxable supply is not what the sub-section asks.

options.text: Both are right, because an unregistered person can be asked for records only through a notice under section 71 to enter and inspect
options.misconception: confuses the power to access premises with the standing duty section 35(2) imposes to keep the records in the first place
options.why: Access to a place of business is a separate power. Section 35(2) imposes the duty to maintain the records, and that duty exists before any officer asks to see them.

options.text: No — section 35(2) reaches every owner or operator of a warehouse or godown and every transporter, whether or not he is registered
options.why: Section 35(1) is indeed written for a registered person, but section 35(2) reaches beyond registration. Every owner or operator of a warehouse, godown or other place used for storage of goods, and every transporter, must maintain records of the consigner, the consignee and other prescribed particulars of the goods, irrespective of whether he is registered under the Act.

options.text: Yes — nobody outside registration owes an obligation under Chapter VIII, and the department must approach the registered supplier instead
options.misconception: reads the whole of section 35 as applying to registered persons, when sub-section (2) is written for unregistered ones
options.why: The sub-section exists because goods pass through hands that are not registered, and the trail would break there. It says in terms that it applies whether or not the person is registered.

citation.ref: Section 35(2), read with section 35(1) and rule 58 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A transport company and the owner of a godown are both asked by the department for records of the consignors, the consignees and the goods handled over a period. Neither is registered under GST — the transporter because his own turnover is small, the godown owner because he only rents out space and makes no taxable supply. Both reply that section 35 is written for registered persons and does not reach them.

items.stem: Which of the two streams is exempt?

options.text: Only the fees from her own patients; what she bills the hospital is a service to a business and taxable
options.misconception: makes the identity of the person paying the bill decide the exemption, when the entry asks what service was supplied and by whom
options.why: Who pays is not the test. The entry asks whether health care services were supplied by one of the three persons it names, and both streams answer yes.

options.text: Neither, because the exemption reaches only a hospital run as a registered institution
options.misconception: adds a registration condition the entry does not contain
options.why: Nothing in the entry conditions the exemption on the supplier being an institution or on any registration of the premises. Most of what a doctor does bears no tax.

options.text: Both — the entry names an authorised medical practitioner as well as a clinical establishment, so the exemption follows her into either place
options.why: Entry 74 exempts health care services by a clinical establishment, an authorised medical practitioner or para-medics. A qualified doctor treating patients is an authorised medical practitioner whether she does it in her own room or in someone else's ward, and what she bills the hospital for treating its patients is health care services just as much as what she bills the patient across her own desk.

options.text: Only what she bills the hospital, the exemption belonging to the clinical establishment that treats the patient
options.misconception: reads the entry as covering institutions alone and drops the practitioner from the list of three
options.why: The entry names three suppliers and the practitioner is the second of them. A doctor needs no institution behind her to be inside it.

citation.ref: Entry 74, read with the definitions of health care services, clinical establishment and authorised medical practitioner in paragraph 2 of the notification

items.scenario: A qualified doctor runs a single-room clinic of her own and charges patients a consultation fee. The same doctor also attends a nearby hospital twice a week as a visiting consultant and raises a monthly bill on the hospital for treating its in-patients. She is not an employee of the hospital.

items.stem: How much of that is right?

options.text: All of it — the Council is a forum of the States, and the Centre attends it as a guest
options.misconception: treats the Council as a body of the States alone, when the Article seats the Union at its head
options.why: The Union is not a guest. It holds the chair and a second seat, and its vote carries a fixed share of the weight when the Council decides anything.

options.text: Only the part about the chair — the Centre and the States take it in turn
options.misconception: invents a rotation, which the Article does not provide for at any point
options.why: There is no rotation anywhere in Article 279A. The chair is fixed on one office and stays there.

options.text: None of it — the Union Finance Minister is the Chairperson, the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance is a member, and the State members choose one of themselves as Vice-Chairperson
options.why: Article 279A(2) constitutes the Council with the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson, the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance, and the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation or any other Minister nominated by each State Government. Article 279A(3) then has the State members choose one of their number as Vice-Chairperson, for such period as they decide. All three statements in the newsletter are wrong.

options.text: Only the part about the Vice-Chairperson — the office exists but the Union fills it
options.misconception: puts the Union in an office the Article reserves for the State members to fill from among themselves
options.why: The office exists, and the Article gives it to the States. They choose one of their own members to hold it, and the Union has no part in that choice.

citation.ref: Article 279A(2) read with Article 279A(3)

items.scenario: A trade newsletter reports a GST Council meeting and says three things about it. That the Council was chaired by a State finance minister on rotation. That the Union Minister of State for Finance has no place on it. And that no post of Vice-Chairperson exists.

items.stem: What is actually charged on the petrol and the diesel?

options.text: Only the State's sales tax, the Union's power to tax petroleum having gone with the 101st Amendment
options.misconception: assumes the amendment stripped the Union of its excise power over goods it deliberately left outside GST
options.why: The Union kept its excise power over exactly these goods and over tobacco. Stripping it would have left a hole in the revenue on the day GST began.

options.text: Nothing at all — petroleum left the old system in 2017 and has not yet entered the new one
options.misconception: mistakes a postponed entry into GST for an escape from tax altogether
options.why: The old levies were never lifted from these goods. They are among the most heavily taxed things sold in the country, which is the practical reason the date keeps being deferred.

options.text: GST, because Article 246A reaches every supply of goods made in India
options.misconception: reads Article 246A as self-executing over petroleum, when Article 279A(5) holds the levy back until a date is recommended
options.why: Article 246A gives the power. Article 279A(5) postpones its exercise over these five goods until a date is recommended, and until then the older levies hold the ground.

options.text: Central excise duty and the State's own sales tax — the five petroleum products sit inside the GST definition but the tax on them begins only from a date the Council recommends
options.why: Article 279A(5) says the Council shall recommend the date on which GST is to be levied on petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel. No such date has been recommended, so those five carry central excise duty and the State's sales tax as before, while everything else the refinery sells, lubricants included, is under GST.

citation.ref: Article 279A(5), read with Article 246A and Article 366(12A)

items.scenario: A refinery sells lubricants and greases at its depot, and petrol and high speed diesel at its pumps. Its new accountant says that since 1 July 2017 everything a refinery sells bears GST and nothing else.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: No — an undertaking covers one export invoice, so a fresh one was needed for every shipment even in 2025-26
options.misconception: cuts the undertaking down to a single consignment, which would make the facility unusable
options.why: One undertaking covers every export the exporter makes in that year. Requiring one per shipment would put a fresh filing behind every container.

options.text: No — a Letter of Undertaking covers the financial year in which it is furnished, and a fresh one is needed for 2026-27
options.why: The Letter of Undertaking furnished under rule 96A is valid for the whole financial year in which it is tendered, and no longer. A fresh one has to be furnished for each financial year in which the exporter wants to export without payment of tax, and shipping in May 2026 on last year's undertaking leaves the export uncovered.

options.text: Yes, provided his turnover and his export profile have not changed since April 2025
options.misconception: makes the undertaking's life depend on the exporter's circumstances rather than on the calendar
options.why: Nothing about turnover or profile keeps an undertaking alive. It expires with the year whether the business has changed or not.

options.text: Yes — an undertaking runs until the department cancels or withdraws it
options.misconception: treats the undertaking as open-ended, when its life is fixed by the year it is tendered in
options.why: Withdrawal is what happens when the exporter defaults on the amount due. It is not what ends an undertaking that has simply reached the end of its year.

citation.ref: Rule 96A, read with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017 and Notification No. 37/2017-Central Tax

items.scenario: An exporter of engineering goods furnished a Letter of Undertaking in April 2025 and exported through 2025-26 without paying integrated tax. In May 2026 he ships again under the same Letter of Undertaking, saying one that has been accepted and never withdrawn goes on working.

items.stem: What happens to the ₹840?

options.text: No refund is paid, and the balance lapses at the end of the financial year
options.misconception: invents a lapse, when nothing in the ledger expires with the year
options.why: A cash ledger balance carries forward without limit. There is no year-end sweep of the ledger anywhere in the Act or the rules.

options.text: The refund must be paid, the floor applying only to a refund of unutilised input tax credit
options.misconception: confines the floor to credit refunds when it is written across the sanction of any refund
options.why: The floor is not written for one kind of claim. It bars payment of any refund below the amount named, and a cash ledger balance is claimed through the same machinery as the rest.

options.text: No refund is paid, and the ₹840 stays in the ledger to be set against a later liability
options.why: Section 54(14) puts a floor under a refund, and ₹840 is below it, so nothing is paid out. The money is not lost by that. It sits in the electronic cash ledger as the trader's own deposit and can be debited against tax, interest, penalty or fee whenever the next liability arises.

options.text: The refund must be paid, because money in the cash ledger is his own deposit and no bar can reach it
options.misconception: treats the character of the money as putting it outside a provision that governs the payment of refunds generally
options.why: It is his own deposit, and that is why it stays available to him. It does not follow that a small balance must be paid out; it follows that nothing is taken away from him.

citation.ref: Section 54(14), read with sections 49(6) and 54(1)
