items.scenario: A small trader deposited a little more than he needed on a challan and has ₹840 sitting unused in his electronic cash ledger. He wants it paid back into his bank account. Take it as given that section 54(14) bars payment of a refund where the amount is less than ₹1,000.

items.stem: Is the trust carrying on a business for GST?

options.text: Yes, but only because it sells to the public rather than to its own beneficiaries
options.misconception: makes the identity of the customer the test, when the definition turns on the nature of the activity
options.why: Who buys does not decide it. Selling to members or beneficiaries alone would still be trade within the definition, and the trust would still be in business.

options.text: No, because it is a charitable trust and charity sits outside GST altogether
options.misconception: confuses the definition of business with the separate exemption for charitable activities
options.why: Whether a supply is exempt is a different question, decided by a notification and by what the activity actually is. It is reached only after the transaction has been found to be a supply made in the course of business, which is what this question asks.

options.text: Yes — the definition covers trade whether or not it is for a pecuniary benefit, so the absence of profit changes nothing
options.why: Section 2(17)(a) says business includes any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, vocation, adventure, wager or any other similar activity, whether or not it is for a pecuniary benefit. Buying handicrafts and selling them on is trade, and the words in the definition were put there to stop exactly this argument.

options.text: No — an activity carried on without a profit motive is not business, business meaning an activity carried on to earn
options.misconception: reads a profit motive into a definition whose own words say it is not needed
options.why: The ordinary meaning of business does carry a profit motive, and the definition displaces it in seven words. Reading the motive back in would leave those words with nothing to do.

citation.ref: Section 2(17)(a), read with section 7(1)(a)

items.scenario: A charitable trust runs a shop on its campus selling handicrafts made by village artisans. It buys the goods from the artisans, sells them at a mark-up and passes every rupee of the surplus back to the artisans, keeping nothing for itself. It has no profit motive of any kind.

items.stem: Is that right?

options.text: No — a composition supplier bears no reverse charge liability at all, the scheme being a complete substitute for the ordinary law
options.misconception: treats the option as an exit from the Act rather than an alternative way of paying tax on his own supplies
options.why: Nothing in the section excuses him as a recipient. A person who opts in stays a registered person under the same Act, and the reverse charge provisions apply to him as to anyone else.

options.text: Yes — a composition supplier pays his percentage on everything that passes through his books
options.misconception: reads the composition levy as a tax on the whole of the business rather than a substitute for the charge on outward supplies
options.why: The scheme replaces one charge and one only. Inward supplies on which the recipient is made liable are outside the substitution altogether.

options.text: No — the composition amount stands in place of the tax on his own outward supplies only, and what he owes as a recipient is payable at the rate applicable to those supplies, in cash
options.why: Section 10(1) lets him pay an amount in lieu of the tax payable under section 9(1), which is the charge on his own outward supplies. It says nothing about section 9(3), so his liability as a recipient under reverse charge survives untouched, is computed at the rate those supplies actually carry, and is paid in cash because section 10(4) leaves him no credit to set against anything.

options.text: No — he must pay at the rate those supplies carry, but may set his input tax credit against it
options.misconception: gives a composition supplier a credit the scheme expressly denies him
options.why: A composition supplier is not entitled to any credit of input tax. There is nothing in his credit ledger to spend, so the reverse charge liability is met in cash.

citation.ref: Sections 10(1) and 10(4), read with sections 9(1), 9(3) and 49(4)

items.scenario: A trader in Nagpur pays tax under the composition levy. In one quarter he pays freight to a goods transport agency and takes advice from an advocate. Both are supplies on which the recipient answers for the tax under reverse charge. He proposes to add their value to his own turnover and pay his composition percentage on the whole.

items.stem: May it?

options.text: No — the head office should keep the credit and cross-charge Pune for the architect's service
options.misconception: reaches for a cross-charge where the distribution mechanism already covers the facts
options.why: A cross-charge is a fresh supply between two registrations and a fresh invoice with tax on it. Here the credit simply has to be distributed to the branch it belongs to.

options.text: No — such an invoice cannot go through the distributor at all, and the architect must bill the Pune branch directly
options.misconception: reads the mechanism as confined to services benefiting every unit, when it handles a single-recipient service by giving that recipient the lot
options.why: The mechanism handles both cases. A service attributable to one unit is distributed to that unit, and nothing in the rules sends the supplier back to reissue his invoice.

options.text: Yes — an Input Service Distributor always distributes by turnover, that being the only method the rules give
options.misconception: treats the turnover ratio as the single rule when it is the rule for common credit only
options.why: The ratio answers one question, which is how to split a credit that serves several units. Applying it to a service used by one unit would move that unit's credit to three others that never received the service.

options.text: No — credit attributable to one recipient is distributed only to that recipient, and the turnover ratio is for credit that serves more than one
options.why: Rule 39 sorts the credit before it apportions anything. Where the input service is attributable to a single recipient of credit, the whole of that credit goes to that recipient. The turnover ratio is the rule for common credit — services that benefit more than one unit — and it never reaches a service used by one branch alone.

citation.ref: Rule 39(1), read with section 20 of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A company's head office is registered as an Input Service Distributor for four branches. It receives an architect's invoice for redesigning the Pune branch alone. Nothing in the work touches the other three. The head office proposes to spread that credit across all four branches by turnover, as it does with every other invoice.

items.stem: When is he liable to be registered?

options.text: From 12 June 2026, the date of the succession, whatever his own turnover has been
options.why: Section 22(3) says that where a business carried on by a registered taxable person is transferred, whether on account of succession or otherwise, to another person as a going concern, the transferee or the successor is liable to be registered with effect from the date of the transfer or succession. The threshold in section 22(1) has already been crossed by the business, and the successor steps into that position on the day he takes it over.

options.text: From the date the Registrar of Companies gives effect to the transfer
options.misconception: applies section 22(4), which is written for a transfer under a court-sanctioned scheme, to a plain succession
options.why: Sub-section (4) fixes that date for a transfer pursuant to a sanctioned scheme of amalgamation or demerger of two companies. A son taking over his late father's proprietary shop involves no Registrar and no scheme.

options.text: Never, so long as he continues to use his father's registration for the same shop
options.misconception: treats a registration as attaching to the business when it is granted to a person
options.why: Registration is granted to a person, not to a shop. The father's registration is cancelled on his death and cannot be carried on by anybody else.

options.text: Only when his own turnover crosses the threshold, each person being tested on his own supplies
options.misconception: tests the successor afresh under section 22(1) when section 22(3) fixes his liability by the succession itself
options.why: Sub-section (1) is the general test and sub-section (3) is a specific one written over it. A successor who had to build a turnover from nothing would run a registered shop unregistered for months.

citation.ref: Section 22(3), read with sections 22(1) and 22(4)

items.scenario: A registered trader dies on 12 June 2026 and his son takes over the shop the same week and carries it on unchanged. The son has never been in business before and has no turnover of his own. He proposes to wait until the business crosses the threshold again in his own hands before registering.

items.stem: What is his position?

options.text: The balance is refunded automatically when the registration expires, the deposit having served its purpose
options.misconception: treats the expiry of the registration as completing the claim when the statute makes the returns the condition
options.why: Expiry ends the registration; it does not sanction a refund. Until the returns are filed nobody knows what the true liability for the period was.

options.text: The refund may be made now and the returns filed afterwards, the two being separate obligations
options.misconception: separates two things the sub-section joins with the word unless
options.why: The sub-section is written as a bar with one way past it. It is precisely the sequence the trader wants to reverse.

options.text: No refund until he has furnished all the returns for the whole period the registration was in force
options.why: Section 54(13) says the advance tax deposited by a casual taxable person shall not be refunded unless he has furnished all the returns required under section 39 for the entire period for which the certificate of registration was granted. The condition is a condition of the refund, not a penalty, and the balance stays where it is until the returns are in.

options.text: Nothing is refundable at all — advance tax once deposited is the price of the casual registration
options.misconception: reads the deposit as a fee rather than as tax paid in advance against an estimated liability
options.why: The deposit is tax, estimated in advance. Whatever is left after the actual liability is met belongs to the trader and comes back to him once the condition is satisfied.

citation.ref: Section 54(13), read with sections 27(2) and 39

items.scenario: A trader registered as a casual taxable person for a Jaipur trade fair deposited advance tax before the fair. Sales were poorer than he expected, and ₹1,20,000 of the deposit is still unused when the registration expires. He has not filed his returns for the period and asks for the balance back at once.

items.stem: On what amount does the operator collect tax at source for the month?

options.misconception: deducts the returns correctly but sweeps the section 9(5) service into a base that expressly leaves it out
options.why: On a notified service the operator is deemed to be the supplier and pays the tax itself. Collecting at source on the same supply would put the operator on both sides of one transaction.

options.misconception: adds everything that passed through the platform and deducts nothing
options.why: Two separate rules are ignored at once. The returns come out, and the notified service was never in.

Tax is collected on the net value of taxable supplies, which the Explanation to section 52(1) defines as the aggregate value of taxable supplies made through the operator by registered persons, other than services notified under section 9(5), reduced by the supplies returned to the suppliers during the month. ₹50,00,000 less the ₹6,00,000 returned gives ₹44,00,000, and the passenger transport never enters because the operator pays that tax as the supplier.

options.misconception: uses the gross value and forgets that returns are deducted in the very month they come back
options.why: The word net is doing work. Returns are subtracted in the same month, so that the operator does not collect on a sale the customer sent back.

citation.ref: Section 52(1) with its Explanation, read with section 9(5)

items.scenario: In one month an operator's platform carries ₹50,00,000 of goods supplied by registered sellers through it, of which ₹6,00,000 worth is returned to those sellers in the same month. The platform separately carries ₹10,00,000 of passenger transport, a service notified under section 9(5) on which the operator itself pays the tax.

items.stem: What happens to the drawback he was paid?

options.text: It is cut down proportionately to whatever part of the proceeds did come in
options.misconception: reads the proviso as scaling the drawback when it withdraws it for the unrealised part outright
options.why: Where nothing at all is realised there is nothing to scale. The deeming operates on the drawback allowed in respect of the goods whose proceeds did not come in.

options.text: Nothing — drawback refunds duty paid on inputs, and whether the buyer pays is a matter between the exporter and his customer
options.misconception: separates drawback from the realisation of export proceeds, which the proviso joins
options.why: The two are joined in the section itself. Drawback exists to make an export competitive, and an export that brings no foreign exchange back has not done what the relief was granted for.

options.text: It stands, because realisation of proceeds is a condition of the GST refund on exports and of nothing else
options.misconception: assumes only the GST side cares about the money coming in, when the customs proviso says the same thing
options.why: Both regimes care. Rule 96A does it for the integrated tax and this proviso does it for drawback, and neither borrows the condition from the other.

options.text: It is deemed never to have been allowed, and the amount is recovered from him
options.why: The second proviso to section 75(1) says that where drawback has been allowed and the sale proceeds are not received in India within the time allowed under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, the drawback shall be deemed never to have been allowed. The rules made under section 75(2) then prescribe how the amount is recovered or adjusted. The drawback rides on the export being a real export that brought money in.
keywords: deemed never to have been allowed

citation.ref: The second proviso to section 75(1), read with section 75(2) and the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An exporter shipped goods in 2025 and was paid drawback under section 75 at the All Industry Rate. The foreign buyer never paid for the consignment, the period allowed under the Foreign Exchange Management Act for realising the sale proceeds has gone by, and the Reserve Bank has granted no extension.

items.stem: Which of the two can be provisionally assessed under section 60?

options.text: Only the officer's, since it is the officer who assesses and the taxpayer's objection cannot stop him
options.misconception: reads the officer's role in passing the order as a power to begin the process
options.why: The officer passes the order, and he passes it on a request. Nothing in the section lets him begin without one.

options.text: Both — an officer in doubt may order it, and any doubt about liability is a good enough reason
options.misconception: turns a facility the taxpayer asks for into a power the officer exercises, and widens its grounds past the two the section names
options.why: The section names who asks and what he may ask about, and both answers are narrow. An officer who doubts a classification has the assessment and audit provisions to work with instead.

options.text: Neither — the section starts with the taxable person's own written request and reaches only an inability to fix the value or the rate
options.why: Section 60(1) opens with the taxable person being unable to determine the value of the supply or the rate of tax applicable to it, and requires him to request the proper officer in writing giving reasons. An officer cannot start it, and a doubt about whether something is taxable at all is neither of the two grounds. Section 60(2) then allows provisional payment only against a bond with such surety or security as the officer thinks fit.

options.text: Only the taxpayer's, since he asked; whether the doubt is about value, rate or liability makes no difference
options.misconception: gets the person right and drops the two grounds, which are the other half of the sub-section
options.why: Asking is necessary and not sufficient. The request has to be about the value or the rate, and a doubt about whether a receipt is taxable at all is a question for a ruling or for the adjudication that follows a notice.

citation.ref: Sections 60(1) and 60(2)

items.scenario: Two things happen in one division. An officer doubts a taxpayer's classification of a new product and proposes to assess him provisionally until the doubt is settled; the taxpayer objects and wants a final assessment. Elsewhere a taxpayer who is sure of his value and his rate but doubts whether a receipt is taxable at all asks for provisional assessment.

items.stem: Is that the whole of the obligation?

options.text: Yes — the section asks for a marking and nothing beyond it
options.misconception: reads one limb of the obligation and treats it as the whole
options.why: A mark on a carton proves nothing on its own. The mechanism only works if what was marked, and when, can be read back out of the dealer's records.

options.text: No — the section requires the marking to go on the goods or packages as the notification says, and it also requires the equipment, the records and the information the notification prescribes
options.why: Section 148A empowers the Government to notify a class of goods and the persons dealing in them, and the obligation it creates has several limbs. The unique identification marking goes on the goods or the packages as notified, the machinery and equipment for affixing it have to be in place, the prescribed records have to be kept and the prescribed information furnished. A marking with no records behind it does not let anyone trace anything, which is what the mechanism is for.

options.text: No — the section reaches every registered person, so any dealer in any goods must mark every consignment
options.misconception: reads an enabling provision as a general one, when it bites only on notified goods and notified persons
options.why: The section works through a notification that names the goods and the persons. A dealer outside that notification has no marking obligation at all.

options.text: No, but the only thing he owes beyond the marking is the prescribed amount for the system
options.misconception: picks up the payment limb and drops the record-keeping and reporting limbs
options.why: Paying for the system is one of the things required and it does not stand in for keeping records or furnishing information.

citation.ref: Section 148A, inserted by the Finance Act, 2025, read with section 122B

items.scenario: A dealer in a class of goods notified under section 148A puts the unique identification marking on the outer carton of each consignment as it leaves, keeps no separate record of the markings and files nothing about them, saying the section asks for a marking and the marking has been made.

items.stem: Can it?

options.text: No, not under section 122; the trader can only be reached by the residual penalty in section 125
options.misconception: reaches for the residual penalty when a specific one has been enacted for this very person
options.why: Section 125 applies where no penalty is separately provided. A penalty is separately provided here, and it is measured by the amount involved rather than capped at a small fixed sum.

options.text: Yes — section 122(1A) penalises the person who retains the benefit of such a transaction and at whose instance it is conducted, in an amount equal to the tax evaded or the credit availed
options.why: Section 122(1A) was written for the beneficiary rather than the doer. It reaches a person who retains the benefit of a transaction covered by the fake-invoice and wrongful-credit clauses of section 122(1) and at whose instance that transaction is conducted, and it fixes the penalty at an amount equivalent to the tax evaded or the input tax credit availed of or passed on. Both limbs are satisfied here.

options.text: Only as an abettor under section 122(3), which carries a much smaller ceiling
options.misconception: puts the principal beneficiary in the aiding-and-abetting sub-section, which was written for third parties around the fraud
options.why: Sub-section (3) is for the person who helps somebody else's contravention along. The trader here is the one the transaction was run for, which is the description in sub-section (1A).

options.text: No — section 122 penalises the person who does the listed act, and issuing the invoice is the act
options.misconception: reads section 122 as ending at sub-section (1), which is exactly the gap sub-section (1A) was inserted to close
options.why: Sub-section (1) does work that way, and by itself it would leave the person who ordered the fraud and pocketed it untouched. Sub-section (1A) sits immediately after it for that reason.

citation.ref: Section 122(1A), read with clauses (i), (ii), (vii) and (ix) of section 122(1) and sections 122(3) and 125

items.scenario: An investigation finds that a supplier issued invoices without any supply behind them, and did it at the instance of a trader who took the credit on those invoices and kept the benefit of it. The supplier is penalised under section 122(1). The trader says he issued no invoice and did none of the acts section 122(1) lists, so section 122 cannot reach him.

items.stem: Is the claim in time?

options.text: Yes, and in fact no limitation applies to a section 77 refund at all
options.misconception: turns a favourable relevant date into an absence of limitation
options.why: Section 54(1) applies to this refund like any other. What section 77 changes is when the clock starts, not whether there is one.

options.text: No — the two years run from the date the department held the supply to be inter-State
options.misconception: anchors the clock to the finding rather than to the payment the clause names
options.why: The finding is what makes the payment necessary, and the clause fixes on the payment. It is a date that can be proved from a challan rather than argued about from an order.

options.text: No — the two years run from the original payment in June 2023 and expired in June 2025
options.misconception: uses the general relevant date for tax paid and misses the clause written for a section 77 claim
options.why: The right to this refund does not exist until the supply is held to be inter-State and the integrated tax is paid. Counting from the wrong-head payment would extinguish a claim before it was born.

options.text: Yes — for a section 77 refund the two years run from the date he paid under the correct head, so from 10 August 2025
options.why: Section 54(1) counts two years from the relevant date, and the relevant date for a person claiming refund under section 77 is the date of payment of the tax under the correct head. That payment was made on 10 August 2025, so the claim in March 2027 is well inside the two years. Any other reading would let the window shut before the refund could even arise.

citation.ref: Section 77, read with section 54(1) and the relevant-date clause in Explanation (2) to section 54 for a refund claimed under section 77

items.scenario: A supplier paid central tax and State tax in June 2023 on a supply he treated as intra-State. The department later held the supply to be inter-State, and he paid the integrated tax on 10 August 2025. He applies in March 2027 for refund of the central and State tax under section 77. The department says the two years ran out in June 2025.

items.stem: On what value is the integrated tax charged?

options.misconception: adds the surcharge and leaves the basic customs duty out, on the view that a duty cannot be part of the base for another tax
options.why: One tax being charged on a base that includes another is exactly what the sub-section provides for, and the basic customs duty is the first thing it names.

options.misconception: adds the basic customs duty and stops, treating the surcharge as something other than a customs duty on the goods
options.why: The surcharge is levied as a duty of customs and collected in the same manner as one, so the words of the sub-section take it in along with the basic duty.

options.misconception: charges the integrated tax on the bare assessable value, as if it were a levy on the goods standing apart from the duties
options.why: The base is built up, not taken as it comes. Charging on the bare value would leave the imported article taxed more lightly than the same article bought in India, which is what the loading is there to prevent.

Section 3(8) of the Customs Tariff Act builds the base for the integrated tax out of the value determined under section 14 of the Customs Act plus any duty of customs chargeable on the article and any sum chargeable on it in the same manner as a duty of customs. That is the assessable value plus the basic customs duty plus the surcharge, and it comes to ₹22,20,000.

citation.ref: Sections 3(7) and 3(8), read with section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962

items.scenario: A consignment is imported with an assessable value of ₹20,00,000 under section 14 of the Customs Act. Basic customs duty of ₹2,00,000 is charged, and the social welfare surcharge on it works out to ₹20,000. No other duty applies. The importer's clerk says integrated tax is a tax on the goods, so it must be charged on the ₹20,00,000.

items.stem: What is missing?

options.text: The previous sanction of the Commissioner for the prosecution, which no other officer can give
options.why: Section 132(6) says a person shall not be prosecuted for any offence under that section except with the previous sanction of the Commissioner. The authorisation of an arrest under section 69(1) is a separate decision taken earlier and on a different question, so it cannot stand in for the sanction, and an Additional Commissioner cannot supply it.

options.text: Nothing — the Commissioner authorised the arrest, and that authorisation carries the prosecution with it
options.misconception: treats one decision of the Commissioner as covering a second decision the Act requires separately
options.why: The two decisions answer different questions at different stages. One asks whether a person should be taken into custody during an investigation; the other asks whether the completed investigation should go to a criminal court.

options.text: Nothing — sanction is needed only where the offence is cognizable and non-bailable
options.misconception: reads the sanction requirement as attaching to the graver offences alone, when the sub-section covers any offence under the section
options.why: The sub-section says any offence under the section. The cognizable and non-bailable line decides how the person is dealt with on arrest, and it does not sort prosecutions into those that need sanction and those that do not.

options.text: Nothing is missing except that the complaint has to be signed by the Commissioner himself
options.misconception: converts a requirement of sanction into a requirement that the Commissioner file the complaint
options.why: The Commissioner sanctions; the complaint is filed by the officer taking the case forward. What the file must show is his approval, not his signature on the complaint.

citation.ref: Section 132(6), read with sections 69(1) and 132(1)

items.scenario: An investigation into a fake-invoice racket is complete. The arrest was authorised by the Commissioner and the investigation was run by an Additional Commissioner, who now directs that a complaint be filed in the criminal court against the accused. Nothing on the file records any further approval.

items.stem: How much may the bank take for the month?

options.text: ₹36 lakh
options.why: Section 17(4) lets the bank avail fifty per cent of the eligible input tax credit for the month, and the word eligible does the sorting. Tax that section 17(5) blocks is never eligible credit at all, so the ₹8 lakh drops out first and the fifty per cent is taken of the remaining ₹72 lakh.

options.text: ₹28 lakh
options.misconception: removes the blocked credit twice, once before the halving and once after it
options.why: The ₹8 lakh comes out once. Taking it away again after the fifty per cent has been worked out charges the bank for the same disallowance twice over.

options.text: ₹72 lakh
options.misconception: removes the blocked credit correctly and then confines the fifty per cent to input services alone
options.why: The sub-section applies the fifty per cent to the eligible credit on inputs, capital goods and input services together. There is nothing in it that spares two of the three.

options.text: ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: halves the whole input tax and so lets half of a wholly blocked credit through
options.why: Halving a blocked credit still leaves half of it in the ledger. A credit section 17(5) disallows is disallowed entirely, whichever route under section 17 the bank is on.

citation.ref: Section 17(4), read with section 17(5)(a)

items.scenario: A banking company on the fifty per cent route under section 17(4) has input tax of ₹80 lakh for a month. Of that, ₹8 lakh is the tax on motor cars bought for its executives' personal use, a credit section 17(5) blocks outright. Nothing comes from another registration under the same PAN.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: Yes — consideration must move from the recipient, and a payment by a stranger to the contract is not consideration
options.misconception: carries the contract-law rule that consideration must move from the promisee into a definition that says the opposite in terms
options.why: The definition settles it with five words. Without them a supplier could be paid in full by a group company and argue that nothing was received for the supply.

options.text: No — a payment made by any other person in respect of the supply is consideration, so the parent's payment is consideration for the supply to the subsidiary
options.why: Section 2(31)(a) takes in any payment made or to be made in respect of, in response to, or for the inducement of the supply, whether by the recipient or by any other person. The money came in respect of this supply, so it is consideration, and who handed it over does not matter. The subsidiary stays the recipient under section 2(93), being the person liable to pay.

options.text: No — the supply is one made without consideration between related persons and is caught by Schedule I instead
options.misconception: reaches for the schedule for supplies without consideration when consideration was in fact paid
options.why: Schedule I is the route for a supply where nothing is received at all. Here money was received in respect of the supply, so the general charge is satisfied on its own and the schedule is never needed.

options.text: No — but the supply is then made to the parent, which paid, and the invoice must be raised on it
options.misconception: makes the payer the recipient, when section 2(93) fixes the recipient as the person liable to pay the consideration
options.why: Section 2(93) names the recipient as the person liable to pay, and the agreement puts that liability on the subsidiary. Someone else settling the bill does not move the supply to him.

citation.ref: Section 2(31)(a), read with sections 2(93) and 7(1)(a)

items.scenario: A software firm licenses its product to a subsidiary company, which is the one that will use it and the one named in the agreement as liable to pay. The subsidiary is short of cash, so its parent company pays the whole invoice straight to the software firm. The subsidiary pays nothing at any stage. The firm's accountant says that with the recipient having paid nothing, there is no consideration and so no supply.

items.stem: Can he furnish them now?

options.text: Yes — the three-year bar is in section 39(11) and catches only the monthly return, the outward supply statement having no such limit
options.misconception: treats the bar as sitting in one sub-section when the Finance Act, 2023 put the same three years on each of the returns and statements separately
options.why: Section 39(11) does carry it for the return, and it is one of four such bars inserted at the same time. The outward supply statement has its own, in section 37(5), in the same words.

options.text: No — the outward supply details are barred three years after their own due date, so the door closed in October 2025
options.why: Section 37(5) forbids a registered person furnishing the details of outward supplies for a tax period after the expiry of three years from the due date of furnishing those details. The due date was 11 October 2022, so three years ran out in October 2025. The bar is on the statement itself and a willingness to pay the late fee does not reach it.

options.text: Yes, once he pays the late fee, a delayed statement of outward supplies carrying a fee and nothing worse
options.misconception: reads a fee for lateness as buying a right to file after the bar has fallen
options.why: A late fee prices lateness up to the point where filing is still permitted. Past three years the filing is not permitted at all, and there is nothing for a fee to buy.

options.text: No, but only because his monthly return for that period is unfiled; filing that first would reopen the statement
options.misconception: mistakes the sequencing rule between the two filings for the three-year bar, which is about age rather than order
options.why: The sequencing rules do block one filing until another is made, and they operate within the period when filing is still open. Nothing in them revives a statement that has aged out.

citation.ref: Section 37(5), inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 and brought into force with effect from 1 October 2023, read with section 39(11)

items.scenario: A registered person never furnished the details of his outward supplies for September 2022, which were due on 11 October 2022. In February 2026 a buyer chases him for them so that the credit can appear in the buyer's statement, and he is willing to pay whatever late fee is asked.

items.stem: Who has to register and pay the integrated tax on those supplies?

options.text: The Indian consumers, each paying under reverse charge on his own subscription
options.misconception: applies the ordinary import-of-services reverse charge to consumers, which is the very thing the scheme was built to avoid
options.why: Reverse charge works where the recipient is a registered person who files returns. Millions of unregistered individuals cannot self-assess, and the whole scheme exists to move the duty away from them.

options.text: The Indian representative — it must register and pay the tax on behalf of the supplier
options.why: Section 14(2) of the IGST Act gives the foreign supplier a single registration under the simplified scheme, and its first proviso then says that any person located in the taxable territory representing such supplier for any purpose in the taxable territory shall get registered and pay integrated tax on behalf of the supplier. Once there is a representative here, the duty moves to him.

options.text: Nobody — with no physical presence in India there is nothing to register
options.misconception: treats physical absence as putting the supplier outside the levy, when absence is the premise of the scheme rather than an escape from it
options.why: The scheme was written for suppliers with no presence here. Absence is what it assumes, not what excuses it.

options.text: The foreign supplier itself, through the simplified single registration, a representative in India making no difference
options.misconception: reads the simplified scheme as the only route and misses the proviso that displaces it where a representative exists
options.why: The simplified scheme is the route where the supplier has nobody here. The proviso exists because a person already present in India is easier to register and easier to collect from.

citation.ref: Section 14(2) with its provisos, read with sections 2(17) and 14(1)

items.scenario: A foreign company supplies online information and database access services to unregistered individuals in India. It has no office and no server here, but it does have an Indian agency that represents it in India for marketing and customer support and holds itself out as its representative.

items.stem: May he?

options.text: Yes — an exemption is a relief, and any relief may be waived by the person it is meant to benefit
options.misconception: treats an exemption from the levy as a personal benefit the supplier may decline, rather than as something that removes the tax from the supply
options.why: The notification does not confer a benefit on a person; it takes the supply out of charge. There is nothing for the supplier to waive, because the tax never arises on that supply at all.

options.text: Yes, provided he tells the department in writing that he is not availing the exemption
options.misconception: invents an opting-out procedure, which exists for a conditional exemption and not for an unconditional one
options.why: Where an exemption is conditional the supplier may simply not satisfy the condition, and then it does not apply to him. An unconditional one leaves him nothing to decline and no form on which to decline it.

options.text: No — an unconditional exemption operates on the levy itself, so there is no tax on the supply for him to charge
options.why: A notification under section 11(1) exempts the supply from tax, and where it is unconditional the supplier has no choice in the matter. Section 32(2) forbids a registered person collecting any amount as tax except in accordance with the Act, and section 76 makes every amount collected as tax payable to the Government whether or not the supply was taxable. He would be paying it over without any of it becoming credit in his customers' hands.

options.text: No, but he keeps his input tax credit even so, an exemption on the output side not being a reason to reverse it
options.misconception: gets the answer on charging right and then keeps a credit that an exempt supply breaks
options.why: Section 17(2) confines credit to the part attributable to taxable supplies, and an exempt supply is not one. Losing the credit chain is the real cost of an exemption and is why the supplier wanted to charge in the first place.

citation.ref: Section 11(1), read with sections 32(2), 76 and 17(2)

items.scenario: A notification under section 11(1) exempts a described service absolutely, with no condition attached. A supplier of that service would rather keep charging tax on his invoices, so that his customers keep taking credit and his own input tax credit chain stays alive. He proposes to carry on charging and to pay over everything he collects.

items.stem: From what date does interest run on that ₹4,00,000?

options.text: No interest at all, the delay in finalising having been the department's
options.misconception: makes the interest depend on whose delay it was, when the sub-section fixes it on the shortfall alone
options.why: Whose fault the delay was does not enter section 18(3). What the deadline in section 18(1B) answers is how long the department may take; what section 18(3) answers is what the shortfall costs.

options.text: From 12 March 2026, the date the goods were actually assessed provisionally
options.misconception: takes the date of the assessment itself, which is the near miss the sub-section deliberately avoids by naming the month
options.why: The sub-section does not use the date of the assessment. It reaches back to the first day of the month containing it, which is a coarser and simpler rule to administer across thousands of bills of entry.

options.text: From 20 November 2026, the date of the final assessment order
options.misconception: treats the shortfall as arising only when it is quantified, which is the very thing the sub-section is written to prevent
options.why: Quantification is not creation. The duty was short from the outset, and starting the clock at the order would hand the importer an interest-free loan for the length of the enquiry.

options.text: From 1 March 2026 — the first day of the month in which the duty was provisionally assessed
options.why: Section 18(3) makes the importer liable to interest on any amount payable consequent to the final assessment, at the rate fixed under section 28AA, from the first day of the month in which the duty is provisionally assessed till the date of payment. The provisional assessment was made in March 2026, so the clock starts on the first day of that month and runs to 30 November 2026.

citation.ref: Section 18(3), read with sections 18(1), 18(1B) and 28AA

items.scenario: A consignment was assessed provisionally on 12 March 2026 while the declared value was under enquiry, the importer having furnished the security the proper officer asked for. The assessment was finalised on 20 November 2026 and ₹4,00,000 of further duty was found payable. The importer paid it on 30 November 2026.

items.stem: Which of the four is an adjudicating authority as the Act defines it?

options.text: The Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Authority, both of them deciding the taxpayer's liability
options.misconception: reads the definition as covering everyone who decides, when section 2(4) names the Appellate Authority in its exclusion
options.why: Deciding is not the test the definition uses. The Appellate Authority decides a great deal and is still named in the words that follow "but does not include", so it is outside the expression however much it looks like an authority that adjudicates.

options.text: The Assistant Commissioner and the Authority for Advance Ruling, a ruling being an order under the Act
options.misconception: keeps the advance ruling authority in, when it is one of the bodies section 2(4) expressly names as out
options.why: A ruling binds the applicant and the officer, and it is still not an adjudication for this purpose. Both the Authority for Advance Ruling and the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling sit in the excluded list.

options.text: The Assistant Commissioner alone
options.why: Section 2(4) defines an adjudicating authority as any authority appointed or authorised to pass any order or decision under the Act, and then takes a list back out of it — the Board, the Revisional Authority, the Authority for Advance Ruling, the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling, the Appellate Authority, the Appellate Tribunal and the Anti-profiteering Authority. The other three on his list are all inside that exclusion, so only the officer who decided the demand at first instance is left.

options.text: All four, an adjudicating authority being anyone who passes an order under the Act
options.misconception: stops at the opening words of section 2(4) and never reaches the exclusion that follows them
options.why: The opening words are wide and the closing words cut them down. A definition that ends "but does not include" is a definition whose second half decides most questions, and here it removes three of the four.

citation.ref: Section 2(4)

items.scenario: A taxpayer lists four people who have passed something against him in the last two years: the Assistant Commissioner who decided his demand, the Appellate Authority who heard his first appeal, the Authority for Advance Ruling who answered his application, and the Commissioner exercising his revisionary power.

items.stem: How do the two services sit under GST?

options.text: The first is exempt and the second is taxable, the consignment note being evidence of a small carrier
options.misconception: has the two the wrong way round and treats the consignment note as a mark of informality
options.why: The consignment note brings a carrier inside the levy rather than out of it. It is the document by which an agency takes charge of the goods, and it is the reason the agency is the exception to an otherwise exempt entry.

options.text: The first is a goods transport agency service; the second is transport of goods by road and is exempt
options.why: A goods transport agency is defined as a person who provides service in relation to transport of goods by road and issues a consignment note, by whatever name called. The document is the definition, not the lorry. Transport of goods by road is otherwise exempt except where it is supplied by a goods transport agency or a courier agency, so the truck owner who issues no consignment note stays outside the levy altogether.

options.text: Both are exempt, road transport of goods being an exempt service in every form
options.misconception: reads the exemption for transport of goods by road without the exception written into it
options.why: The exemption carries its own exception and the exception is the whole point of it. A goods transport agency and a courier agency are lifted out of the entry, and the first transporter is one of them.

options.text: Both are goods transport agency services, since both carry goods by road for a fee
options.misconception: makes the carrying of goods the test, when the definition turns on the document the carrier issues
options.why: Carrying goods for a fee is what every road transporter does. What separates a goods transport agency from the rest is the consignment note, which is why the definition names it and nothing else.

citation.ref: Entry 18, read with the definition of goods transport agency in paragraph 2 of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate)

items.scenario: A trader hires two road transporters in the same week. The first hands him a consignment note for the load and takes responsibility for it until delivery. The second is a truck owner who simply drives the goods across and gives a receipt for the hire, issuing no consignment note at all.

items.stem: Which of the two premiums bears GST?

options.text: Only the factory's group policy
options.why: Entry 36C exempts services of life insurance business provided by an insurer to the insured where the insured is not a group. The salaried man's endowment policy is exactly that — one person, or a person and his family — so it is exempt. A group term policy is a policy over a group, which the entry's own words keep outside, so it stays taxable.

options.text: Neither, life insurance being exempt as a class since September 2025
options.misconception: reads the entry as a class exemption for life insurance and drops the words that keep a group out
options.why: The entry is not written over life insurance at large. Every word of it after "insurer" is about who the insured is, and an employer buying cover over four hundred workers is the case those words exclude.

options.text: Only the endowment policy, the savings portion inside it being investment rather than insurance
options.misconception: splits an individual policy into a risk part and a savings part, when the entry exempts the life insurance business as supplied to that insured
options.why: There is no splitting to do once the entry applies. It exempts the service supplied to an insured who is not a group, and an endowment policy issued to one man is such a service whatever mixture of risk and saving sits inside it.

options.text: Both, the exemption reaching only health insurance and not life insurance
options.misconception: gives health cover an exemption that life cover has as well, under the entry that sits immediately before it
options.why: Two entries were inserted side by side. One covers life insurance business and the next covers health insurance business, on the same terms and with the same words about a group, so an individual policy of either kind is exempt.

citation.ref: Serial number 36C, inserted by Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025, read with serial number 36D

items.scenario: In July 2026 a life insurer issues two policies. One is an endowment policy taken by a salaried man on his own life, with his wife as nominee. The other is a group term policy taken out by a factory over its four hundred workers, the factory paying the whole premium.

items.stem: How does paragraph 4 of Schedule II classify the two?

options.text: Both are supplies of goods, the same asset being involved in each case
options.misconception: classifies by what the asset is rather than by whether it left the business for good
options.why: The asset is a red herring in both clauses. What separates them is whether the goods have stopped being assets of the business, which the guillotine has and the camera has not.

options.text: Both are supplies of services, neither having been sold for money
options.misconception: treats the absence of a sale as making the transaction a service, when clause (a) applies whether or not for a consideration
options.why: Clause (a) says in terms that it applies whether or not for a consideration. A free disposal is inside it, and it produces a supply of goods.

options.text: The guillotine is a supply of goods and the camera is a supply of services
options.why: Clause (a) covers goods forming part of the assets of a business that are transferred or disposed of so as no longer to form part of those assets, and calls that a supply of goods, whether or not for a consideration — the guillotine has gone for good. Clause (b) covers goods held for the business that are put to any private use or made available for a purpose other than a purpose of the business, and calls the usage a supply of services — the camera came back, so what was supplied was its use and not the thing.

options.text: Neither is a supply, because no consideration passed in either case
options.misconception: requires a consideration where paragraph 4 is written as a set of deeming provisions that do not need one
options.why: Paragraph 4 exists to catch exactly these two cases. Both clauses are deeming provisions that work without any money changing hands, and the credit taken on the goods is why they were written.

citation.ref: Clauses (a) and (b) of paragraph 4 of Schedule II, read with section 7(1A)

items.scenario: A printing firm does two things with equipment on which it had taken input tax credit. It gives an old guillotine away to a school, for nothing. And it lets its proprietor take the office camera home for his son's wedding for a fortnight, after which the camera comes back to the shop floor.

items.stem: What does section 49 actually allow?

options.text: Storage in any warehouse with space, public or private, the section caring only that the goods are secure
options.misconception: treats the two kinds of warehouse as interchangeable, when the section names only one of them
options.why: A private warehouse is licensed for the goods of the person who holds the licence. The section sends goods that cannot be cleared to a public warehouse, and that word is doing work rather than describing.

options.text: Storage in a public warehouse, but only with the permission of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner
options.misconception: puts the first permission at the rank that the section reserves for extending the period
options.why: The senior officer appears later in the section, on the extension of the period, not at the start. The permission to store is given at the level of the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner.

options.text: Storage in a public warehouse, on his application, if the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner is satisfied the goods cannot be cleared within a reasonable time
options.why: Section 49 has three conditions written into its opening lines and he has missed two of them. The permission is that of the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner, not any officer to hand; it follows an application by the importer and a satisfaction that the goods cannot be cleared within a reasonable time; and the place named is a public warehouse.

options.text: Nothing — an importer who cannot pay must warehouse the goods under section 60 instead
options.misconception: sends him to the warehousing chapter, which is what section 49 exists to spare him
options.why: Warehousing under section 60 needs a bill of entry for warehousing and a bond, and it moves the rate of duty. Section 49 is the door for an importer who has already entered his goods for home consumption and simply needs time.

citation.ref: Section 49

items.scenario: An importer has entered a consignment for home consumption and cannot pay the duty for another few weeks. He asks the customs house to let the goods sit in his own private bonded warehouse down the road, which has space, and says the Superintendent on the docks can sign it off.

items.stem: To which of these do the transit and transhipment provisions in Chapter VIII apply?

options.text: To the cargo and to the stores, stores also continuing in the same conveyance
options.misconception: reasons from the fact that the stores stay aboard, which is true and is not what decides it
options.why: Stores do continue in the same conveyance and are still excluded by name. They are governed by their own sections on consumption aboard and on supply without payment of duty, not by the transit provisions.

options.text: To everything aboard, the chapter following the conveyance rather than the goods
options.misconception: reads the chapter as attaching to the ship, when its first section removes three classes of goods from it
options.why: The chapter is about goods and not about vessels. Its opening section names three classes it does not apply to, and all three of them are aboard this ship.

options.text: To the cargo and the postal parcels, both being goods brought into an Indian port for onward movement
options.misconception: keeps goods imported by post inside a chapter that names them in its exclusion
options.why: Goods imported by post are one of the three named exclusions and have a separate chapter of their own. Being onward-bound does not put them back into Chapter VIII.

options.text: Only the cargo containers
options.why: Section 52 opens the chapter by taking three things out of it — baggage, goods imported by post, and stores. Each of those has its own chapter elsewhere in the Act, so the suitcases, the parcels and the ship's fuel and provisions are all outside sections 53 to 56, and the manifested cargo is the only consignment those sections reach.

citation.ref: Section 52, read with sections 53, 54 and 55

items.scenario: A vessel calls at Kochi on its way to Male. Aboard it are cargo containers manifested for Male, the ship's own fuel and provisions declared as stores, a passenger's suitcases, and a sack of parcels for delivery to addresses in India through the post.

items.stem: Can he, and what does the summons let him do?

options.text: No, because a summons may only require attendance to give evidence and never the production of documents
options.misconception: halves the power, which names giving evidence and producing a document as alternatives
options.why: The sub-section names both. It reaches a person whose attendance is considered necessary either to give evidence or to produce a document or any other thing, and an officer may ask for either or for both.

options.text: Yes, and the summons also lets him go to the office and take the ledgers if the accountant does not bring them
options.misconception: reads a summons as authorising the entry and seizure that only an authorisation under section 67 can permit
options.why: A summons produces a person and a paper across a table. Going to the premises and taking the books is a search and a seizure, and it needs the written authorisation and the recorded reason to believe that section 67 requires.

options.text: No — without material suggesting an offence he has no power to call for anything at all
options.misconception: imports section 67's threshold into section 70, when the summons power is exercisable in any inquiry
options.why: The threshold he is thinking of belongs to search and seizure. The summons power exists during an inquiry and does not wait for a suspicion of an offence, which is what makes it the ordinary opening move of an investigation.

options.text: Yes — a summons needs no reason to believe and no authorisation, but it compels a person and a document and does not let him enter or seize anything
options.why: Section 70 and section 67 are different instruments. A summons compels a named person to attend and to produce a document in an inquiry, and it needs neither a reason to believe nor a written authorisation. What it does not carry is any power to enter premises, to search them or to seize what is found there — that is section 67, and it is fenced with the conditions this officer has not met.

citation.ref: Section 70(1), read with section 67(1) and section 67(2)

items.scenario: An officer wants a taxpayer's purchase ledgers and the delivery challans behind them. He has no material suggesting an offence, and no written authorisation from a Joint Commissioner. He proposes to issue a summons to the accountant requiring him to bring the records.

items.stem: Is the adviser right on either point?

options.text: No on both — the penalty is ten per cent of the profiteered amount, and none is leviable if that amount is deposited within thirty days of the order
options.why: Section 171(3A) fixes the penalty at ten per cent of the profiteered amount, so the base is the money he kept and not his turnover. Its proviso then says no penalty shall be leviable if the profiteered amount is deposited within thirty days of the date of passing of the order, which leaves the manufacturer a month in which the penalty can still be avoided altogether.

options.text: Right on the second — the penalty is measured on turnover, the profiteering being spread across sales
options.misconception: puts the penalty on turnover when the sub-section measures it on the amount not passed on
options.why: Turnover is nowhere in the sub-section. It fixes the penalty as a percentage of the profiteered amount, which is the sum the order says should have come off the price and did not.

options.text: No on both, and in any case the amount is recovered as a demand of tax with interest under the demand provisions
options.misconception: routes the recovery through the demand sections, when the amount was never tax
options.why: The money is the recipient's, not the Government's. It is returned to him with interest, or sent to the Consumer Welfare Fund where he cannot be identified, and it does not travel through the demand provisions at all.

options.text: Right on the first — the penalty follows the order automatically and nothing he does afterwards touches it
options.misconception: misses the proviso, which makes the penalty avoidable by paying within a fixed window
options.why: The sub-section has a proviso and the proviso is the useful half. Depositing the profiteered amount inside the window written into it means no penalty is leviable at all.

citation.ref: Section 171(3A) with its proviso, read with sections 171(1) and 171(3)

items.scenario: An order finds that a manufacturer kept ₹40 lakh of a rate reduction to himself and directs him to return it. His adviser tells him two things: that a penalty will follow whatever he does now, and that the penalty is charged on his turnover for the period.

items.stem: When is the time of supply for that ₹700?

options.text: There is no time of supply, an amount not covered by an invoice not being consideration for any supply
options.misconception: treats an unbilled overpayment as outside the levy, when the proviso exists precisely because it is inside it
options.why: Money received against a taxable supply is consideration whether or not an invoice covers it yet. The proviso would have nothing to do if the excess were outside the levy; it is there to say when the tax on it falls due.

options.text: The date of issue of the invoice for the excess, and the supplier has no say in it
options.misconception: reads a relief the supplier may take as a rule he must follow
options.why: The words "at the option of the said supplier" are in the proviso. It is a concession he may use, not a mandatory shift of the time of supply, and a supplier who finds it simpler to tax the excess on receipt may do that.

options.text: At the architect's option, the date on which he issues the invoice relating to the excess
options.why: The proviso to section 13(2) covers a supplier who receives an amount up to one thousand rupees in excess of the amount indicated in the tax invoice. For that excess the time of supply shall, at the option of the said supplier, be the date of issue of invoice relating to it. The relief is optional, so he may take the excess into tax on receipt if he prefers, and the proviso simply spares him from having to.

options.text: The date of receipt, without exception, every rupee received against a service being taxable when it comes in
options.misconception: applies the general rule in section 13(2) and never reaches the proviso sitting under it
options.why: Receipt is the general rule and the proviso is written as an exception to it for small overpayments. Ignoring the proviso makes an architect account for tax on seven hundred rupees of rounding in the month it arrives.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 13(2), read with the corresponding proviso to section 12(2)

items.scenario: An architect invoices a client ₹47,300 for a design. The client rounds the transfer up and pays ₹48,000 in the same month, ₹700 more than the invoice. The extra ₹700 is not returned and will be set against the next job.

items.stem: Is the fee outside GST, and is the consultant's reason right?

options.text: Outside, but by section 7(2)(b) and the notification under it, not by Schedule III
options.why: Section 7(2) has two clauses and they work differently. Clause (a) sends you to Schedule III, which is a fixed list in the Act. Clause (b) covers such activities or transactions undertaken by the Central Government, a State Government or any local authority in which they are engaged as public authorities as may be notified by the Government on the recommendations of the Council. A municipality is a local authority and this activity has been notified, so it is clause (b) that keeps the fee out.

options.text: Outside, because a local authority is not a person and cannot make a supply at all
options.misconception: denies a local authority the status the definition of person expressly gives it
options.why: A local authority is named in the definition of person, and a government is too. Both can and do make taxable supplies; what takes this one out is the notification, not the identity of the supplier.

options.text: Outside, and Schedule III is the right reason, since Schedule III is where everything outside supply is listed
options.misconception: treats Schedule III as the only door out of supply, when section 7(2)(b) is a second and separate one
options.why: Schedule III is a closed list written into the Act and it does not mention this activity. The second clause of section 7(2) is a standing power to notify, and it is by a notification under that power that the activity is outside.

options.text: Inside GST, because a fee is a consideration and the municipality supplied something for it
options.misconception: applies section 7(1)(a) without reading section 7(2), which overrides it
options.why: Section 7(2) opens with words that make it prevail over sub-section (1). An activity it covers is not a supply however neatly it fits the definition in clause (a).

citation.ref: Section 7(2)(b), read with section 7(2)(a), section 2(84) and Notification No. 14/2017-Central Tax (Rate)

items.scenario: A municipality carries out an activity in relation to a function entrusted to it under the Constitution, and charges the residents a fee for it. That activity has been notified by the Government on the Council's recommendation. The municipality's consultant says the fee is outside GST, and puts it down to Schedule III.

items.stem: Is the consultant right, and what still has to happen?

options.text: Wrong, because an exporter who pays integrated tax on exports has no refund at all and must set it against domestic output tax
options.misconception: denies the second of the two routes section 16 gives an exporter
options.why: Section 16 offers two routes and this is the second of them — pay the integrated tax and claim it back. An exporter with no domestic output tax would otherwise have nothing to set it against.

options.text: Right, and nothing else is needed, the shipping bill being complete in itself the moment it is filed
options.misconception: takes the deeming and stops before the conditions that decide when the deemed application is filed
options.why: The deeming and its timing are in the same rule. Until the manifest or report is filed and the return is furnished, there is no application on foot and nothing for the system to process.

options.text: Right — the shipping bill is deemed to be the refund application, but it is treated as filed only once the export manifest or report is filed and a valid return is furnished
options.why: Rule 96(1) deems the shipping bill filed by an exporter of goods to be an application for refund of the integrated tax paid on the goods exported, so no separate application is made. The same rule then holds that deemed application back until two things happen — the person in charge of the conveyance files an export manifest or an export report covering the shipping bill, and the exporter furnishes a valid return.

options.text: Wrong — a refund of integrated tax paid on exports is claimed like any other refund, on an application to the proper officer
options.misconception: puts the payment route through the ordinary refund application, which is what rule 96 replaces for goods
options.why: The ordinary application belongs to the letter of undertaking route, where unutilised credit is refunded. Where the tax was paid on the export invoice, the shipping bill itself is the application and the refund is worked out from the customs system.

citation.ref: Rule 96(1), read with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: An exporter chooses the second route and pays integrated tax on his export invoices rather than going under a letter of undertaking. He asks his consultant when to file the refund application on the common portal, and is told the shipping bill has already done that job.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: No, but the only consequence is a general penalty, the invoices themselves remaining valid
options.misconception: separates the requirement from rule 48(5), which is what gives the requirement its bite
options.why: Rule 48(5) says a document required to be issued in the manner rule 48(4) prescribes, and issued otherwise, shall not be treated as an invoice. That is a heavier consequence than a penalty and it reaches the refund and the recipient as well.

options.text: Yes — an overseas buyer has no registration and no input tax credit, so nothing turns on the number
options.misconception: reasons from the recipient's credit, when the requirement follows the class of supply and not what the buyer can claim
options.why: The buyer's credit is why the rule matters for a domestic sale; it is not why the rule applies. The sub-rule names exports on its own account, and the exporter's own refund runs on documents that have to be valid.

options.text: No — the rule covers supplies to a registered person and exports alike, and a supply to a special economic zone unit is inside it too
options.why: Rule 48(4) names supplies to a registered person and supplies for export in the same breath, so an export invoice needs an Invoice Reference Number exactly as a domestic business invoice does. A supply to a unit in a special economic zone is treated the same way. The consequence in rule 48(5) follows the requirement, so the invoices he has not reported are not valid invoices.

options.text: Yes for exports, no for the special economic zone unit, which is a registered person in India
options.misconception: gets the second half right for the wrong reason and keeps exports out, when the sub-rule names them expressly
options.why: Both are in, and exports are in by name rather than by any argument about registration. It is the class of supply the sub-rule lists that decides, and it lists exports.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4), read with rule 48(5)

items.scenario: An exporter well above the turnover line issues three kinds of invoice: to Indian registered customers, to buyers abroad against shipping bills, and to a unit inside a special economic zone. He has been reporting only the first kind to the Invoice Registration Portal, on the view that the requirement is for supplies to registered persons in India.

items.stem: What does section 126 require of the officer?

options.text: To make the penalty commensurate with the degree and severity of the breach, and to consider the voluntary disclosure as a mitigating factor
options.why: Section 126(2) requires the penalty imposed to be commensurate with the degree and severity of the breach, so a maximum imposed without regard to the facts is not a penalty the sub-section allows. Section 126(5) then says that where a person voluntarily discloses the circumstances of a breach to the officer prior to its discovery, the officer may consider that as a mitigating factor when quantifying the penalty.

options.text: Nothing — the officer fixes the penalty within the statutory range and the taxpayer's conduct afterwards is irrelevant
options.misconception: reads the range as the whole of the discretion, when the section directs how the discretion is to be exercised inside it
options.why: The range is where the section starts, not where it ends. Two sub-sections tell the officer how to choose within it, one on proportionality and one on disclosure before discovery.

options.text: To cancel the penalty altogether, a voluntary disclosure before discovery being a complete defence
options.misconception: turns a mitigating factor into an immunity, which the sub-section does not give
options.why: The words are that the officer may consider the disclosure as a mitigating factor. That lightens the penalty and does not remove it, and the section keeps the power to impose one.

options.text: To impose no penalty, because a breach the taxpayer found himself is by definition a minor breach
options.misconception: pulls in the minor-breach bar, which turns on the amount of tax and on the error being apparent on the face of record
options.why: Minor is defined in the Explanation by the amount of tax involved, and easily rectifiable by the error being apparent on the face of record. Who found the breach does not enter either test.

citation.ref: Sections 126(2) and 126(5), read with section 126(1) and its Explanation

items.scenario: A registered person finds a contravention in his own records and tells the officer about it before any audit or scrutiny has reached it. The contravention carries no fixed penalty and no fixed percentage, so the penalty has to be worked out. The officer proposes to impose the maximum, saying the facts of the disclosure are none of his concern.

items.stem: Will that application succeed?

options.text: No, because a person with a place of business in two States cannot use rule 14A at all
options.misconception: turns a bar on a second rule 14A registration into a bar on the scheme for anyone with two States
options.why: Having two States does not shut him out. He keeps the rule 14A registration he has and takes the second one by the ordinary route; what he cannot have is the scheme twice.

options.text: Yes, provided the two States' monthly output tax figures are added and the total stays within the ceiling
options.misconception: invents an aggregation test, when the obstacle is the second registration itself and not the arithmetic
options.why: There is no adding to do. The monthly output tax test is applied to the applicant in the State he is applying in, and it is not the test that defeats this application.

options.text: Yes — registration is State-wise, so each State is looked at separately and both may be under rule 14A
options.misconception: applies the general State-wise principle of registration to a scheme that has its own bar written across States
options.why: Registration is State-wise and this scheme is not. The bar is written on the permanent account number, which is what makes it reach across a State line that ordinary registration never crosses.

options.text: No — a person registered under rule 14A in one State cannot take a second rule 14A registration on the same permanent account number in another State
options.why: Rule 14A is a one-per-person scheme. A person who has been granted registration under it in any State or Union territory cannot obtain another rule 14A registration on the same permanent account number elsewhere, and satisfying the monthly output tax test and the Aadhaar condition in the second State does not get round it. The Maharashtra registration is still open to him by the ordinary route.

citation.ref: Rule 14A, inserted by Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025 with effect from 1 November 2025

items.scenario: A supplier already registered under rule 14A in Madhya Pradesh opens a second place of business in Maharashtra on the same permanent account number. His monthly output tax on supplies to registered persons in Maharashtra will be small, and Aadhaar is authenticated for the signatory and for one partner. He applies for the Maharashtra registration under rule 14A as well.

items.stem: Is the adviser right?

options.text: No — where no certificate is required from the authority, the Explanation lets a registered architect, a chartered engineer or a licensed surveyor be the competent authority
options.why: The carve-out in paragraph 5(b) is drafted as a completion certificate issued "where required" by the competent authority, and the Explanation then defines competent authority as the Government or any authority authorised to issue such a certificate under any law and, where no such certificate is required from that authority, an architect registered with the Council of Architecture, a chartered engineer registered with the Institution of Engineers, or a licensed surveyor of the local body. The engineer's certificate therefore starts the clock, and the entire consideration came afterwards.

options.text: Yes, unless the flats had also been first occupied, first occupation being the only event available where no certificate is issued
options.misconception: makes first occupation the sole fallback and leaves the Explanation's list of substitute authorities out of account
options.why: First occupation is the other event and it works on its own. It is not the only route open where the local body issues nothing, because the Explanation supplies a competent authority for exactly that situation.

options.text: No, and for the further reason that a small block is not construction within paragraph 5(b) at all
options.misconception: reads construction narrowly, when the Explanation stretches it to additions, alterations, replacements and remodelling
options.why: Size does not come into it, and the definition runs the other way. Construction is defined to include additions, alterations, replacements or remodelling of any existing civil structure, so the expression is wider than a new building rather than narrower.

options.text: Yes — without a certificate from the local body the carve-out cannot be satisfied at all
options.misconception: reads the certificate as having to come from the authority in every case, past the words where required
options.why: The words "where required" are what save this builder. A place where no certificate is required is exactly the case the Explanation was written for, and it names three professionals who may issue one instead.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II with the Explanation to paragraph 5

items.scenario: A builder finishes a small block in a village where the local body issues no completion certificate for buildings of that size. He obtains a certificate of completion from a chartered engineer registered with the Institution of Engineers and sells every flat afterwards, taking not a rupee before that certificate. A buyer's adviser says paragraph 5(b) still catches the sales because no competent authority issued anything.

items.stem: Is the sale a deemed export?

options.text: No — section 147 reaches only goods manufactured in India, and these were imported and resold as they were
options.why: Section 147 lets the Government notify supplies as deemed exports where the goods supplied do not leave India, where payment is received in Indian rupees or in convertible foreign exchange, and where such goods are manufactured in India. The first two are satisfied here and the third is not, so the notification cannot reach this sale however the recipient is described.

options.text: No, because a deemed export requires the goods to leave India and these do not
options.misconception: inverts the condition, which requires precisely that the goods do not leave India
options.why: Goods that leave India are an export and are zero-rated. The whole idea of a deemed export is that the goods stay here, which is why the section says so in terms.

options.text: Yes, provided he pays the tax and does not go under a letter of undertaking, the origin of the goods being irrelevant
options.misconception: gets the tax mechanics right and drops the manufacture condition, which is the one that decides this case
options.why: Paying the tax rather than using a letter of undertaking is right for a deemed export and is beside the point here. The supply never becomes a deemed export in the first place because the pumps were not made in India.

options.text: Yes — the recipient is an Export Oriented Unit, which is one of the notified categories, and that is what the notification turns on
options.misconception: reads the notified category as the whole test and skips the conditions section 147 sets before any notification can bite
options.why: The notification works inside the section that authorises it. Section 147 states three conditions and the goods must satisfy all of them before a notified category has anything to attach to.

citation.ref: Section 147, read with Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017

items.scenario: A registered trader imports finished pumps, pays the customs duties on them and clears them for home consumption.
