options.misconception: gives the first auditor the five-year term section 139(1) gives an auditor appointed at an annual general meeting
options.why: The first auditor holds office only till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting. The term of five consecutive years in section 139(1) belongs to an auditor the members appoint at an annual general meeting, and the first auditor's office ends exactly where that appointment starts.

options.text: The Board had sixty days, and on its failure the Registrar appoints the auditor
options.misconception: mistakes the period and hands the appointment to an authority the section never names
options.why: The period in section 139(6) is thirty days from the date of registration, and the fallback is the members at an extraordinary general meeting. The Registrar has no power to appoint an auditor of a company; the only outside appointer in section 139 is the Comptroller and Auditor-General, and that is for a government company under section 139(7).

options.text: The Board had thirty days from registration; having failed, it must inform the members, who appoint the first auditor at an extraordinary general meeting within ninety days, and he holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting
options.why: Section 139(6) requires the first auditor of a company other than a government company to be appointed by the Board of Directors within thirty days from the date of registration of the company. On the Board failing to do so, it shall inform the members, who shall within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting appoint the first auditor, and he shall hold office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting.

options.text: Nothing yet — the first auditor is appointed by the members at the first annual general meeting, and until then the company simply has none
options.misconception: leaves a company without an auditor until its first annual meeting
options.why: The first annual general meeting is where the first auditor's term ENDS, not where it begins. A company registered in March would otherwise trade for the better part of two years with nobody appointed to examine its books.

citation.ref: Section 139(6), read with sections 139(1) and 139(7)

items.scenario: A company which is not a government company is registered on 3 March 2026. Its Board never gets round to appointing an auditor. On 20 June 2026 the promoters ask what should have happened, and what has to happen now.

items.stem: What does section 140(4) require of the company?

options.text: The company may decline to circulate the representation or to read it, since it alone decides what goes to its members
options.misconception: gives the company a discretion the Act gives only to the Tribunal
options.why: The only escape is by order. The Tribunal may, on the application of the company or of any other aggrieved person, direct that the representation need not be sent out and need not be read out, if satisfied that the right is being abused to secure needless publicity for defamatory matter. That is the Tribunal's judgement, not the board's.

options.text: Nothing — an auditor who is not being reappointed has no standing to address the members
options.misconception: treats an auditor at the end of his term as a stranger to the meeting
options.why: The one moment an auditor most needs to be heard is when he is being replaced, because a board that dislikes his findings has an obvious motive. Section 140(4) is what gives him the floor at that moment.

options.text: The representation must be circulated to the members whatever the delay, and the meeting adjourned until it has been
options.misconception: converts a right to be heard into a right to postpone the meeting
options.why: The section provides for exactly this failure rather than punishing it with a delay. Where the copy could not be sent because the representation came too late, the auditor may require it to be read out at the meeting, and the meeting goes ahead.

options.text: The representation must be read out at the meeting, and the fact that a representation has been made must be stated in the notice of the resolution given to the members
options.why: On special notice of a resolution appointing an auditor other than the retiring auditor, section 140(4) requires the company to send a copy to the retiring auditor, who may make a representation in writing and request its notification to the members. The company shall state the fact of the representation having been made in any notice of the resolution given to the members and send a copy of it to every member to whom notice of the meeting is sent. Where a copy is not sent because the representation was received too late or because of the company's default, the auditor may require that it be read out at the meeting.

citation.ref: Section 140(4), read with section 115

items.scenario: A company proposes to appoint a firm other than its retiring auditor at the coming annual general meeting, and special notice of the resolution has been received. The retiring auditor sends a written representation and asks that it be notified to the members. It reaches the company four days before the meeting, too late to be posted with anything. The company proposes to say nothing about it at the meeting.

items.stem: What does section 55(2) require?

options.text: The partly paid shares cannot be redeemed until they are fully paid, and the ₹4 crore redeemed out of profits must be matched by a transfer of an equal nominal amount to the capital redemption reserve account
options.why: Section 55(2) allows redemption only on the conditions written into it. No shares shall be redeemed unless they are fully paid, so the ₹3 crore tranche cannot be touched. Where shares are redeemed out of profits, a sum equal to the nominal amount of the shares redeemed shall be transferred to a reserve called the capital redemption reserve account, and the provisions relating to reduction of share capital then apply to that reserve as if it were paid-up share capital. The reserve stands in the place of the capital that has gone, which is why it cannot simply be dispensed with.

options.text: Nothing is wrong on the reserve, because the transfer is required only where the redemption is funded by a fresh issue of shares
options.misconception: reverses the condition, requiring the reserve in the one case that does not need it
options.why: The transfer is required precisely where the redemption comes out of profits, because that is where capital leaves and nothing new replaces it. A redemption funded by a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose needs no transfer, the fresh issue being the replacement.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — a company may redeem partly paid shares provided it redeems only the paid-up portion of them
options.misconception: splits a share into paid and unpaid halves that the section treats as one thing
options.why: A share is redeemed or it is not. Section 55(2) refuses redemption of a share that is not fully paid, because redeeming it would hand money back to a member who still owes money to the company.

options.text: The partly paid shares may be redeemed once the Tribunal permits it
options.misconception: invents a dispensation the section does not carry
options.why: The Tribunal's part in section 55 is in sub-section (3), where a company unable to redeem shares already due for redemption may be permitted to issue further redeemable preference shares to the consenting holders. It cannot excuse a company from the requirement that a share be fully paid before it is redeemed.

citation.ref: Section 55(2) with its provisos, read with section 55(3)

items.scenario: A company proposes to redeem two tranches of preference shares — ₹4 crore that are fully paid, and ₹3 crore on which a call remains unpaid. It will fund the ₹4 crore out of profits which would otherwise be available for dividend, and proposes to transfer nothing to any reserve, on the reasoning that capital is simply being returned to the people who put it in.

items.stem: How does the Tribunal treat the silence and that creditor?

options.text: The silence is presumed to be no objection, but the ₹6 crore must still be discharged, determined, secured, or the creditor's consent obtained, before the reduction can be confirmed
options.why: Section 66(2) requires the Tribunal to give notice of the application to the Central Government, the Registrar, the Securities and Exchange Board in the case of a listed company, and the creditors of the company, and where no representation is received within three months it shall be presumed that they have no objection. Section 66(3) is a separate condition on the order itself — the Tribunal may confirm the reduction only if satisfied that the debt or claim of every creditor has been discharged or determined or has been secured or his consent is obtained. A creditor who says nothing has not thereby been paid.

options.text: The creditor must be paid in full in cash before the application can even be made
options.misconception: narrows to one the four ways section 66(3) allows a claim to be dealt with
options.why: The sub-section names four — discharged, determined, secured, or consent obtained. A security or a consent will do, and so will a determination of a disputed claim. Cash in advance is one route among them and not a precondition of applying.

options.text: The creditor's position is irrelevant, because only a member may be heard on a reduction of the capital he subscribed
options.misconception: shuts out the class section 66 names first
options.why: Section 66(2) names the creditors expressly among those the Tribunal notifies, and section 66(3) makes the Tribunal's satisfaction about every creditor a condition of its order. Reducing capital thins the fund creditors look to, which is the whole reason they are heard.

options.text: The silence disposes of both points — a creditor who does not object inside three months is taken to have accepted that his debt goes unpaid
options.misconception: reads a presumption about objections as a discharge of the debt
options.why: The presumption in section 66(2) is about the representation, and nothing more. Section 66(3) puts a second and independent condition on the Tribunal, and it asks about the debt itself rather than about whether anybody complained.

citation.ref: Sections 66(2) and 66(3)

items.scenario: A company applies to the Tribunal to confirm a reduction of its share capital. It has accepted no deposits, and its auditor has certified that the proposed accounting treatment conforms to the accounting standards. A trade creditor owed ₹6 crore has neither been paid nor given his consent, and three months have passed since the Tribunal's notice with no representation from the Central Government, the Registrar or any creditor.

items.stem: Which of the two payments needed the members' prior permission?

options.text: Only the ₹3 crore, since it is by far the larger of the two payments
options.misconception: measures the need for permission by the size of the payment rather than by the section it is made under
options.why: Size is what decides the question under section 181 and it decides nothing under section 183, which puts no ceiling on the amount at all. What section 183(2) does add is a duty to disclose the total contributed to that Fund in the profit and loss account.

options.text: Neither of them
options.why: The proviso to section 181 asks for prior permission of the company in general meeting only where the aggregate of contributions to bona fide charitable and other funds in a financial year exceeds five per cent of the average net profits for the three immediately preceding financial years, and five per cent of ₹20 crore is ₹1 crore. The ₹80 lakh is under the line. Section 183(1) then lets the Board contribute such amount as it thinks fit to the National Defence Fund or any other Fund approved by the Central Government for the purpose of national defence, notwithstanding sections 180, 181 and 182, so that ₹3 crore never enters the aggregate at all.

options.text: Only the ₹80 lakh, because a contribution to a charitable fund of any size needs the members' permission
options.misconception: reads the proviso as removing the Board's power altogether
options.why: The main limb of section 181 gives the power to the Board, and the proviso takes it back only above five per cent of the three-year average. Below the line the Board acts on its own.

options.text: Both, because together they come to ₹3.8 crore, far past five per cent of ₹20 crore
options.misconception: aggregates a payment that a later section takes out of the aggregate
options.why: Section 183 opens with the words "notwithstanding anything contained in sections 180, 181 and 182", which is how Parliament takes a defence contribution outside the very arithmetic the aggregation depends on. What remains inside the five per cent line is the ₹80 lakh alone.

citation.ref: Section 181 with its proviso, read with sections 183(1) and 183(2)

items.scenario: A company's average net profits for the three immediately preceding financial years are ₹20 crore — take that figure as given. During the year the Board resolves on two payments without asking the members for anything: ₹80 lakh to a bona fide charitable trust running schools, and ₹3 crore to the National Defence Fund.

items.stem: How many of the three may be paid under section 202?

options.text: None of them
options.why: Section 202(2) lists the cases in which no payment shall be made, and these three are on it. Where the office of the director is vacated under section 167, A is out. Where the director has been guilty of fraud or breach of trust in relation to, or of gross negligence in or gross mismanagement of, the conduct of the affairs of the company, B is out. And where the director resigns otherwise than on a reconstruction of the company or its amalgamation, C is out. Compensation is for a loss the director did not bring on himself.

options.text: Only B, because gross negligence is a matter for the company to weigh rather than a bar written into the Act
options.misconception: turns a listed disqualification into a discretion of the board
options.why: Gross negligence in or gross mismanagement of the conduct of the company's affairs is one of the cases section 202(2) names, alongside fraud and breach of trust. The board's view of how serious it was does not reopen the question.

options.text: Only C, a voluntary resignation being the one clean departure of the three
options.misconception: reads a resignation outside a reconstruction as a case the section allows
options.why: Section 202(2) names that exact case and refuses payment for it. A director who walked out has lost no office; he gave one up, and the section pays for losses rather than for changes of mind.

options.text: All three, provided each payment stays inside the ceiling of the unexpired term or three years, whichever is shorter
options.misconception: applies the ceiling to payments the section forbids outright
options.why: Section 202(3) fixes how much may be paid where a payment may be made at all. Section 202(2) decides whether it may, and a payment it bars does not become lawful by being kept small.

citation.ref: Sections 202(2) and 202(3), read with section 167

items.scenario: Three managing directors leave three companies in one group in the same quarter. A's office was vacated under section 167 because he had been absent from all meetings of the Board held during twelve months without obtaining leave — take the vacation as established. B was found by his Board to have been guilty of gross negligence in the conduct of the company's affairs. C resigned of his own accord to join a competitor, no reconstruction or amalgamation being involved. Each claims compensation for loss of office.

items.stem: What does section 236 require of the money?

options.text: Any unclaimed amount goes to the Investor Education and Protection Fund at once and the shareholder loses it
options.misconception: collapses the trust in section 236(6) into an immediate transfer out of the shareholder's reach
options.why: Section 236(6) has the company continue to hold the amount in trust for a shareholder who has not come forward, and pay him when he claims it. Section 125 moves money to the Investor Education and Protection Fund on its own conditions and its own clock, and even then a claimant may apply for a refund.

options.text: The whole amount goes into a separate bank account operated by the transferor company for at least one year, is disbursed within sixty days, and anything unclaimed is held in trust for the shareholder
options.why: Section 236(4) requires the majority shareholders to deposit an amount equal to the value of the shares to be acquired in a separate bank account, to be operated by the transferor company for at least one year for payment to the minority shareholders, and that amount shall be disbursed to the entitled shareholders within sixty days. Section 236(5) makes the transferor company act as a transfer agent for receiving and paying the price and for the surrender of the certificates. Section 236(6) keeps the money the shareholder's — where he does not come forward, the company continues to hold the amount in trust for him.

options.text: Nothing in particular — the valuer fixes the price and how the acquirer pays it is a matter between the parties
options.misconception: treats the payment machinery as a private arrangement
options.why: The minority is losing its shares whether it likes it or not, so the Act does not leave the money with the person doing the acquiring. It is deposited, held by the transferor company, and paid out on a clock.

options.text: The money must be deposited with the Tribunal, which disburses it on each shareholder's application
options.misconception: sends the money to a forum the section never involves in the payment
options.why: The account is operated by the transferor company, which also acts as transfer agent. The Tribunal has no role in section 236's payment machinery at all.

citation.ref: Sections 236(4), 236(5) and 236(6), read with section 125

items.scenario: An acquirer holding 94 per cent of the issued equity share capital has made the offer under section 236 at a price determined by a registered valuer. It proposes to pay each minority shareholder out of its own current account as and when he surrenders his certificates, and to keep whatever nobody claims.

items.stem: Is counsel right?

options.text: No, but the Depository Receipts limb is open only where the transferee is the foreign company
options.misconception: reads a limb open in both directions as open in one
options.why: Section 234(2) allows a foreign company to merge into an Indian company or the reverse, and its proviso speaks of payment to the shareholders of the merging company without caring which side of the border the transferee sits on.

options.text: Yes — an amalgamation under the Act is a share-for-share exchange, and cash consideration turns it into a sale of the undertaking
options.misconception: imports a tax test into a question of company law
options.why: Whether the shareholders of the amalgamating company become shareholders of the amalgamated one is what section 2(1B) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 asks, and it decides whether the merger is tax neutral. Section 234 is not written to that test, and its proviso names cash in terms.

options.text: No — the scheme may provide for consideration in cash, in Depository Receipts, or partly in each
options.why: The proviso to section 234(2) says that the terms and conditions of a scheme of merger between an Indian company and a company incorporated in a notified jurisdiction may provide, among other things, for the payment of consideration to the shareholders of the merging company in cash, or in Depository Receipts, or partly in cash and partly in Depository Receipts. Nothing in section 234(2) confines the consideration to shares of the transferee.

options.text: Yes, unless the Reserve Bank of India specifically permits cash in the approval it grants
options.misconception: makes a permission the Act already grants depend on the regulator
options.why: The prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India is required for the merger itself under section 234(2). The permission to pay in cash is in the proviso to that sub-section — it is in the Act, and the regulator is not its source.

citation.ref: Section 234(2) with its proviso

items.scenario: A company incorporated in a jurisdiction the Central Government has notified merges into an Indian company, and the prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India is in hand. The scheme proposes to pay the shareholders of the merging foreign company partly in cash and partly in Depository Receipts issued by the Indian transferee. Counsel objects that the Companies Act allows consideration only in shares of the transferee company.

items.stem: What has gone wrong?

options.text: Only the service point is wrong; a company incorporated abroad need display nothing in India, its name being registered elsewhere
options.misconception: reads incorporation abroad as an exemption from Chapter XXII
options.why: Section 379(1) applies sections 380 to 386 and sections 392 and 393 to every foreign company that has a place of business in India, and section 382 is squarely inside that range. Registration abroad is what makes the Chapter apply, not what excuses it.

options.text: A return of the alteration had to reach the Registrar within thirty days; the name and the country of incorporation must both be exhibited outside the office and stated on its business papers; and service at the address last delivered to the Registrar is good service
options.why: Section 380(3) requires a foreign company, where any alteration is made in the documents delivered to the Registrar, to deliver a return of the particulars of the alteration within thirty days. Section 382 requires it to conspicuously exhibit outside every office or place where it carries on business in India the name of the company and the country in which it is incorporated, in letters easily legible in English and in the local language, and to state the same on every prospectus, business letter, bill head and notice. Section 383 makes a document sufficiently served where it is addressed to the person whose name and address were delivered to the Registrar and left at or posted to that address.
keywords: country in which it is incorporated

options.text: Everything except the display, which the name alone satisfies — the country of incorporation is required only where the liability of the members is limited
options.misconception: confuses the display of the country with the separate notice about limited liability
options.why: Section 382 requires the name and the country in which the company is incorporated together, wherever the name is exhibited or stated. Limited liability is a separate requirement in the same section — where the liability of the members is limited, notice of that fact must be given in every prospectus and in all its business papers, and exhibited outside every place of business.

options.text: Only the display is wrong; the Registrar's records catch up at the next annual filing, and service at a stale address is bad service
options.misconception: pushes an event-driven return into an annual filing and puts the cost of a stale address on the person serving
options.why: Section 380(3) attaches to the alteration itself and runs thirty days from it, not from any year end. Section 383 then puts the consequence of a stale address squarely on the company, which is exactly why the return is required so quickly.

citation.ref: Sections 380(3), 382 and 383, read with section 379(1)

items.scenario: A foreign company already registered under section 380 changes the address of its principal place of business in India and replaces the person resident in India authorised to accept service on its behalf. Six months later it has told the Registrar neither thing. The board outside its Mumbai office carries the company's name only, and its Indian invoices show the name without anything else. A summons is then served at the old address.

items.stem: Can it apply now?

options.text: Yes, provided the members pass a special resolution, the shift of office and the sale being ordinary acts of a company winding itself down
options.misconception: treats the resolution as the whole of what the application needs
options.why: The special resolution, or the consent of seventy-five per cent of the members in terms of paid-up share capital, is what section 248(2) asks for. Section 249 asks something else entirely — what the company has been doing in the last three months — and it names a disposal for gain and a shift of the registered office among the disqualifying acts.

options.text: Yes — the liabilities are extinguished, which is the only condition section 248(2) attaches to the company's own application
options.misconception: reads section 248(2) without section 249 standing in front of it
options.why: Extinguishing the liabilities is a condition and not the only one. Section 249 is a separate gate, and it exists so that a company cannot rearrange itself and then disappear before anybody has had a chance to look at what it did.

options.text: No — an application is barred where, in the previous three months, the company has shifted its registered office or disposed of property held for gain in the normal course of trading
options.why: Section 248(2) lets a company, after extinguishing all its liabilities, apply to the Registrar for removing its name from the register, by a special resolution or with the consent of seventy-five per cent of its members in terms of paid-up share capital. Section 249 then refuses that application where at any time in the previous three months the company has changed its name or shifted its registered office, or has made a disposal for value of property or rights held for the purpose of disposal for gain in the normal course of trading or otherwise carrying on business. Both of this company's acts fall inside the three months.

options.text: No, and the bar runs for twelve months from the date of the disposal
options.misconception: lengthens a period the section fixes at three months
options.why: The period in section 249 is the previous three months. The company here need only wait out the balance of it, which is a different answer from being shut out for a year.

citation.ref: Sections 248(2) and 249

items.scenario: A company has stopped trading and has paid off every creditor. Two months ago it sold its last remaining warehouse at a profit, and in the same month it shifted its registered office to another city. It now wants to file its own application with the Registrar to have its name removed from the register.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The offence cannot be compounded while the investigation is pending; and had it been compounded, the company would have had to intimate the Registrar within seven days
options.why: The proviso to section 441(1) says that any offence covered under that sub-section by a company or its officer shall not be compounded if the investigation against such company has been initiated or is pending under this Act. That is a bar on the offence rather than on the forum, so no authority may compound it while the investigation runs. Section 441(4) separately requires the company, where an offence is compounded, to give intimation of the compounding to the Registrar within seven days from the date on which it is so compounded.

options.text: It can be compounded and nothing more is needed, the order of compounding being the end of the matter
options.misconception: drops the intimation the Act puts on the company after a compounding
options.why: Section 441(4) puts a seven-day intimation to the Registrar on the company itself, and section 441(5) makes the Registrar bring a compounding done after prosecution has begun to the notice of the court, on which the company or officer is discharged. The order does not work itself into the record.

options.text: It can be compounded, the three-year repeat bar being the only bar in the section and no earlier offence having been compounded
options.misconception: treats the repeat bar as the whole of what section 441 forbids
options.why: The repeat bar in section 441(2) is one of two. The proviso to section 441(1) shuts out an offence of a company under investigation, and it does so whether or not anything has ever been compounded before.

options.text: It can be compounded, but only by the Tribunal, an investigation taking the matter out of the Regional Director's hands
options.misconception: turns a bar on compounding into a change of forum
options.why: The ceiling on the maximum fine is what chooses between the Regional Director and the Tribunal. A pending investigation stops the compounding itself, so there is no forum left to choose between.

citation.ref: Section 441(1) with its proviso, and sections 441(4) and 441(5)

items.scenario: A company has committed an offence punishable with fine only, and no similar offence of its has ever been compounded. An inspection under section 206 has since ripened into an investigation into the company's affairs, and that investigation is pending. The company applies for compounding and asks what it must do if the application succeeds.

items.stem: What are the two things to say about this order?

options.text: The company had to be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before any penalty was imposed; and on a repeat inside three years the penalty is twice the amount the provision lays down
options.why: Section 454(4) requires the adjudicating officer, before imposing any penalty, to give the company or the officer in default or any other person a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Section 454A then provides that where a company or an officer or any other person, having already been subjected to a penalty for a default, again commits the same default within a period of three years from the date of the order imposing the first penalty, it or he is liable to twice the amount of penalty provided for that default under the relevant provision.

options.text: The earlier penalty is irrelevant; the amount is fixed by the provision that was breached and nothing multiplies it
options.misconception: overlooks section 454A altogether
options.why: Section 454A exists exactly for the repeat offender and doubles the penalty provided for the default. A penalty that never moved would make the second default cheaper than the first in real terms.

options.text: The order stands, because adjudication is an administrative act and the hearing comes on appeal before the Regional Director
options.misconception: postpones to the appeal a hearing the section puts before the penalty
options.why: Section 454(4) puts the opportunity of being heard before the penalty is imposed. The appeal under section 454(5) is a second look at an order that ought already to have been made after hearing the person penalised, not the first chance to speak.

options.text: The doubling applies only where the repeat happens within one year, and two years is outside the window
options.misconception: shortens the period section 454A names
options.why: The period in section 454A is three years from the date of the order imposing the first penalty. Two years is comfortably inside it.

citation.ref: Sections 454(4) and 454A, read with section 454(5)

items.scenario: An adjudicating officer issues an order imposing a penalty on a company for a filing default without issuing it any notice or hearing it at all. The same company had been penalised by an order of the adjudicating officer for the same default two years earlier.

items.stem: What does section 36 say about the three the former management left out?

options.text: Only the trademark, ownership being the test and the company owning the mark outright
options.misconception: reads ownership as excluding an asset somebody else holds security over
options.why: Section 36(3) names encumbered assets in terms. A charge gives its holder a claim on the proceeds of the asset; it does not make the charge holder the owner, and it does not take the asset out of the estate.

options.text: The warehouse only once the bank relinquishes its security, and the receivable only once it is collected
options.misconception: postpones an asset's entry into the estate until it has been turned into money
options.why: The estate is formed at the outset out of what the corporate debtor owns. Section 52 lets a secured creditor choose between relinquishing its security to the liquidation estate and realising it, and section 36(3) separately brings in all proceeds of liquidation as and when they are realised. The asset goes in first and the proceeds follow it.

options.text: None of the three, the estate being limited to what the liquidator can physically take charge of
options.misconception: measures the estate by possession rather than by ownership
options.why: The sub-section says assets that may or may not be in possession of the corporate debtor. A receivable is nowhere to be seized and is in the estate all the same, which is the point of writing possession out of the test.

options.text: All three are in the estate — an encumbered asset, an intangible asset and an asset not in the corporate debtor's possession are each named as included
options.why: Section 36(3) puts into the liquidation estate the assets over which the corporate debtor has ownership rights, assets that may or may not be in possession of the corporate debtor including encumbered assets, tangible assets whether movable or immovable, and intangible assets including intellectual property and contractual rights. A mortgaged warehouse, a registered trademark and an uncollected receivable each sit squarely on that list. Section 36(2) then makes the liquidator hold the estate as a fiduciary for the benefit of all the creditors, which is why he cannot drop an asset because one creditor has a charge over it.

citation.ref: Sections 36(2) and 36(3), read with section 52

items.scenario: A liquidator is told by the corporate debtor's former management that only three things can be in the liquidation estate — the factory land the company owns free of any charge, the plant on the shop floor, and the cash in its bank accounts. The company also holds a registered trademark, a warehouse mortgaged to a bank which has not moved on its security, and ₹4 crore of trade receivables that have not been collected.

items.stem: Where is he wrong?

options.text: On both — the liquidation commenced on 5 May, and the company is dissolved only from the date of the Adjudicating Authority's order, a copy of which goes to the registering authority within fourteen days
options.why: Section 59(5) deems the voluntary liquidation proceedings to have commenced from the date of passing of the resolution, subject to the creditors' approval — the approval is a condition of the process, not the starting line. Section 59(7) requires the liquidator, where the affairs have been completely wound up and the assets completely liquidated, to apply to the Adjudicating Authority for the dissolution of the corporate person; section 59(8) has the Adjudicating Authority order that the corporate person shall be dissolved from the date of that order; and section 59(9) requires a copy of that order to be forwarded within fourteen days to the authority with which the corporate person is registered.
keywords: date of passing of the resolution

options.text: On neither — a solvent company's liquidation is a private affair needing no order, dissolution following when the Registrar strikes the name off
options.misconception: routes a dissolution under the Code through the Companies Act
options.why: Section 59 puts the dissolution of a corporate person in voluntary liquidation in the hands of the Adjudicating Authority. Strike off under section 248 of the Companies Act is a different door, and a company that has gone into voluntary liquidation under the Code is not walking through it.

options.text: Only on the commencement date; a final report filed with the Board does end the corporate person's existence
options.misconception: lets a filing with the regulator do the work of an order of the Adjudicating Authority
options.why: The Board here is the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, and the liquidator does file with it under the regulations. Dissolution is an order under section 59(8), and a company is not dissolved by a report written about it.

options.text: Only on the dissolution; commencement does run from the creditors' approval, the resolution being conditional on it
options.misconception: reads a condition as moving the date it is attached to
options.why: Section 59(5) deems the commencement to be the date of passing of the resolution and makes the creditors' approval a condition attached to it. Once the approval arrives the clock is read back to the resolution, which is why the members' date and not the creditors' date is the one that counts.

items.scenario: A solvent company has met every condition in section 59(3) correctly. The special resolution to liquidate was passed on 5 May 2026 and creditors representing two-thirds in value of the debt approved it on 9 May 2026. The liquidator has now realised all the assets and paid everybody. He proposes to date the commencement of the liquidation from 9 May, and to treat the company as dissolved from the day he files his final report with the Board.

items.stem: What is the cost auditor's position?

options.text: He should take it to the audit committee whatever the amount, because only a statutory auditor's report ever reaches the Central Government
options.misconception: keeps the Central Government route for one professional and gives the others the committee route
options.why: The two routes turn on the amount involved, not on which professional found the fraud. Because section 143(14) carries the section across as it stands, a fraud above the prescribed amount goes from him to the Central Government in the same manner, through the Board or the audit committee, as it would from the statutory auditor.

options.text: He may report only once the company releases him from the confidentiality clause, since the Act does not override a contract freely made
options.misconception: treats a statutory duty as something a contract can switch off
options.why: Section 143(13) is written the other way round — no duty to which an auditor is subject is contravened by a report made honestly under sub-section (12). A confidentiality clause cannot turn lawful reporting into a breach, and the duty does not wait on the company's permission to report the company.

options.text: He carries the reporting duty himself, and a report made honestly cannot be treated as a breach of any duty he owes
options.why: Section 143(14) says the provisions of the section shall apply mutatis mutandis to a cost accountant in practice conducting cost audit under section 148 and to a company secretary in practice conducting secretarial audit under section 204, so the duty in section 143(12) is his own and not the statutory auditor's alone. Section 143(13) then says that no duty to which an auditor of a company may be subject shall be regarded as having been contravened by reason of his reporting the matter, if it is done in good faith. The confidentiality point is answered by the statute rather than by the engagement letter.

options.text: The duty is the statutory auditor's alone, so his only course is to hand the finding to him and let him decide whether to report it
options.misconception: reads section 143(12) as a duty attached to the office of statutory auditor
options.why: Section 143(14) extends the whole section, sub-section (12) included, to the cost accountant conducting cost audit and to the company secretary conducting secretarial audit. Passing the finding along would leave a duty the statute puts on him personally undischarged, and the statutory auditor may never have seen the scrap ledger at all.

citation.ref: Sections 143(13) and 143(14), read with section 143(12), section 148 and section 204

items.scenario: A cost accountant in practice is conducting the cost audit of a manufacturing company under section 148. He finds that a general manager has been diverting scrap sales to a firm the manager himself owns, and the amount involved is above the limit at which a fraud has to be reported to the Central Government — take that as given. The company's counsel tells him that section 143(12) binds the statutory auditor and nobody else, and warns him that reporting anything outside the company would breach the confidentiality clause in his engagement letter.

items.stem: Which of the four carries a full CARO 2020 report?

options.text: Only the consolidated financial statements, because the group is listed and CARO follows a listing
options.misconception: thinks listing is what brings CARO in
options.why: Listing is not a test anywhere in paragraph 1(2), and the consolidated report is the one place the Order is expressly held back. Paragraph 2 excludes the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements save for the clause on qualifications in the component auditors' reports.

options.text: None of them — the first three are outside the Order altogether, and on the consolidated financial statements only the single clause about qualifications in the component companies' CARO reports is given
options.why: Paragraph 1(2) of the Order puts a banking company, an insurance company, a company licensed to operate under section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, a One Person Company and a small company outside CARO altogether, whatever their size. Paragraph 2 then says the Order shall not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3, which asks whether any qualification or adverse remark appears in the CARO reports of the companies included in the consolidation. So no full report is due on any of the four.

options.text: All four, because CARO applies to every audit report signed under section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013
options.misconception: reads CARO as universal
options.why: CARO is an order made under section 143(11) and it carries its own scope. Paragraph 1(2) excludes five classes of company by name, adds a size test for private companies, and paragraph 2 excludes the consolidated report, so a great many reports under section 143 carry no CARO paragraph at all.

options.text: Only the One Person Company, since the exclusions in paragraph 1(2) are for banking, insurance and section 8 companies alone
options.misconception: leaves the One Person Company and the small company off the list of excluded companies
options.why: Paragraph 1(2) names a One Person Company and a small company alongside the banking, insurance and section 8 companies. Being small, or having one member, is enough on its own; the financial limits in the same paragraph are a separate route out for a private company that is not a subsidiary or holding company of a public company.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 1(2) and 2 with clause (xxi) of paragraph 3, read with section 143(11) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: An audit firm signs four reports in one week — for a banking company, for a company licensed under section 8 to promote education, for a One Person Company, and on the consolidated financial statements of a listed manufacturing group whose standalone report carried the full CARO 2020 paragraph. A junior asks which of the four had to carry a CARO report.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 1 require of each?

options.text: Both are acceptable — twelve months from the date the statements are approved is the horizon, and a note explaining the decision to close cures the basis
options.misconception: measures the twelve months from the wrong date and treats a note as a substitute for changing the basis
options.why: The standard measures the period from the end of the reporting period, which for a 31 March 2026 year end reaches 31 March 2027. And where the intention is to liquidate or to stop trading, the going concern basis is not available at all, so a note beside it merely explains a basis the entity was not entitled to use.

options.text: Neither has a problem, because the going concern question belongs to the auditor under SA 570 rather than to management under Ind AS 1
options.misconception: hands management's own assessment to the auditor
options.why: Ind AS 1 puts the assessment on management when it prepares the financial statements. SA 570 requires the auditor to evaluate that assessment; it does not make it for him, and an assessment that was never properly made is itself something the auditor has to deal with.

options.text: Meridian must look forward at least twelve months from the end of the reporting period, and Calder may not use the going concern basis at all — it discloses that fact, the basis actually used and the reason it is not regarded as a going concern
options.why: Ind AS 1 requires management, in making its assessment, to take into account all available information about the future, which is at least, but is not limited to, twelve months from the end of the reporting period. The clock therefore starts at 31 March 2026 and not at the date of approval, and six months is short of it. Where management intends to liquidate the entity or to cease trading, or has no realistic alternative but to do so, the entity does not prepare its financial statements on a going concern basis; it discloses that fact, together with the basis on which the statements are prepared and the reason why the entity is not regarded as a going concern.

options.text: Meridian is fine because six months is a reasonable commercial horizon, and Calder must use the liquidation basis that Ind AS 1 prescribes for such cases
options.misconception: shortens the assessment period and invents a prescribed liquidation basis
options.why: The standard sets the floor at twelve months and does not leave the horizon to what management finds reasonable. It also prescribes no particular alternative basis — it requires the entity to disclose the basis actually used and the reason it is not regarded as a going concern, which is a disclosure requirement rather than a named framework.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 25 and 26

items.scenario: Two companies are finalising financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. At Meridian Ltd management's going concern assessment looks forward only to 30 September 2026, six months from the date the statements are being approved, and the finance head says that is as far as anybody can see. At Calder Ltd the board has resolved to cease trading and realise the assets piecemeal, and its finance head proposes to keep preparing the statements on a going concern basis with a note explaining the board's decision.

items.stem: How does section 143(3)(i) apply to this?

options.text: The statement is clean, because substantive testing proved the financial statements right and a control weakness that caused no misstatement is not reportable
options.misconception: measures the controls by their consequences instead of by their operation
options.why: A control that did not operate is a deficiency whether or not anything went wrong behind it. The opinion on the financial statements and the statement on internal financial controls answer different questions, and one of them coming out clean does not clean the other.

options.text: The clause asks two questions and only one has been answered — design and operation are separate findings, and a control nobody performed for four months has to be evaluated as a deficiency in operation
options.why: Section 143(3)(i) requires the auditor to state whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and the operating effectiveness of such controls. Those are two findings inside one clause, and a control that existed on paper but was not performed for a third of the year fails on the second whatever the first shows. The absence of a misstatement answers neither question, because the controls statement reports on the controls and not on the numbers.

options.text: The statement is clean, because the control was adequately designed and adequacy is what the clause asks about
options.misconception: reads the clause as a question about design alone
options.why: The clause names the operating effectiveness of the controls as well as their adequacy. Reporting on design alone would leave a company free to write excellent procedures and never run them, which is the state of affairs the second half of the clause exists to catch.

options.text: The gap goes to those charged with governance and nowhere else, because section 143(3)(i) concerns only the controls the Board has laid down
options.misconception: sends a statutory reporting requirement into a private communication with management
options.why: Section 143(3)(i) puts the auditor's own statement on internal financial controls into the report to the members. Communicating deficiencies to those charged with governance is a separate duty that runs alongside it and does not discharge it.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(i)

items.scenario: A company's control over the authorisation of purchase orders is well designed and fully documented. For the first four months of the year, while the financial controller's post lay vacant, nobody performed the authorisation step at all; it ran properly for the remaining eight months and a new controller has been in post since. Substantive testing found no misstatement. The chief financial officer says the control is adequate, so the auditor's statement on internal financial controls should be a clean one.

items.stem: Which of the four may he accept?

options.text: All four, because the client agreed the basis in writing and a fee freely negotiated cannot be misconduct
options.misconception: treats agreement between the parties as the test
options.why: Clause 10 makes the basis of the fee itself the misconduct, and no agreement can license it. The exceptions come from a regulation made under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, not from what a client is willing to sign.

options.text: The first three — each falls inside an exception the Council has prescribed, and the statutory audit fee does not
options.why: Clause 10 of Part I of the First Schedule makes it misconduct for a member in practice to charge or accept fees which are based on a percentage of profits, or which are contingent upon the findings or results of the work, except as permitted under any regulation made under the Act. Regulation 192 is that permission, and it names among others a receiver or liquidator, whose fees may be based on a percentage of the realisation or disposal of the assets; an auditor of a co-operative society, whose fees may be based on a percentage of the paid-up capital, the working capital or the gross or net income or profits; and a valuer in a direct taxes matter, whose fees may be based on a percentage of the value of the property valued. A statutory audit is on none of those lists.

options.text: None of them, because a percentage fee is prohibited outright and the regulations only reduce the punishment
options.misconception: reads the exceptions out of the clause
options.why: The clause carries the words "except as permitted under any regulation made under this Act" on its face. The exceptions are part of the prohibition rather than a mitigation of it, so an engagement inside one of them is not misconduct at all.

options.text: Only the liquidator's fee, that being the single exception the regulations allow
options.misconception: remembers one exception and treats the list as closed at it
options.why: The regulation sets out several cases and not one. Beside the receiver or liquidator it covers an auditor of a co-operative society, a valuer in a direct taxes matter and certain other engagements, each with the base on which the percentage may be taken written into it.

citation.ref: Clause 10 of Part I of the First Schedule, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: Four engagements are offered to a chartered accountant in practice in one month, each on a fee linked to a percentage. As liquidator of a company, a fee based on a percentage of the realisation of assets. As auditor of a co-operative society, a fee based on a percentage of its working capital. As valuer of a property in a client's direct tax matter, a fee based on a percentage of the value of the property valued. And as statutory auditor of a private company under the Companies Act, 2013, a fee based on a percentage of that company's net profit.

items.stem: What is wrong with the two appointments?

options.text: Mr Q cannot be an alternate at all, and the seat filled after the death has to be put to the members at the immediate next general meeting
options.why: Section 161(2) lets the Board appoint an alternate director for a director absent from India for not less than three months, but not a person who is holding any alternate directorship for any other director in the company; his term cannot extend beyond that of the original director, and he vacates the office when the original director returns to India. Section 161(4) lets the Board fill a casual vacancy in the office of a director appointed by the company in general meeting, and requires that appointment to be subsequently approved by the members in the immediate next general meeting.

options.text: Only the filled vacancy is wrong, and the cure is a fresh appointment by the members at any general meeting held within a year
options.misconception: relaxes the meeting at which the members' approval must be taken
options.why: The words are that the appointment shall be subsequently approved by the members in the immediate next general meeting, not at some meeting within a year. And the alternate appointment is defective on its own footing, quite apart from this one.

options.text: Only the alternate appointment is wrong, and the defect is the eight months — an alternate may be appointed only where the original director will be away for less than three months
options.misconception: inverts the three-month condition in the sub-section
options.why: The sub-section requires the original director to be absent from India for not less than three months, so an eight-month absence is comfortably inside it. The defect is that the person appointed already holds an alternate directorship for another director of the same company.

options.text: Both are sound — the articles allow the Board to appoint alternates and to fill vacancies, and section 161 does no more than confirm the power
options.misconception: reads the articles as the source of the power and the section as a formality
options.why: Section 161 is where each power comes from, and it carries its own conditions. The articles must authorise the Board, but the eligibility bar on a person already holding an alternate directorship and the members' approval of a filled vacancy do not come from the articles and cannot be dispensed with by them.

citation.ref: Sections 161(2) and 161(4)

items.scenario: A public company's Board makes two appointments at one meeting, the articles authorising both. Director P leaves India for eight months, and the Board appoints Mr Q as his alternate — Mr Q is already the alternate director of another director of the same company. Separately, director R, who had been appointed by the members at the last annual general meeting, dies, and the Board fills his seat and records that nothing further is needed because the articles let it fill vacancies.

items.stem: Which of them may the company appoint?

options.text: Only candidate A, since insolvency alone is a statutory bar and the other two matters were private arrangements between a man and his creditors
options.misconception: keeps the insolvency limb and drops the composition limb beside it
options.why: The composition limb sits in the same sub-section as the insolvency limb and is a separate bar in its own words. A person who has at any time suspended payment to his creditors, or has made a composition with them, is caught whether or not any court was ever involved.

options.text: Only candidate C, a sentence of four months not reaching the line the section draws, while the other two are each caught by a limb written to reach back over a whole life
options.why: Section 196(3) says no company shall appoint or continue the employment of any person as its managing director, whole-time director or manager who is an undischarged insolvent or has at any time been adjudged an insolvent; who has at any time suspended payment to his creditors or makes, or has at any time made, a composition with them; or who has at any time been convicted by a court of an offence and sentenced for a period of more than six months. Paying the creditors afterwards does not undo the composition, and the words "at any time" leave no room for the passage of years. Four months is short of the line, so candidate C is outside the clause.

options.text: All three, because the disqualifications in section 196(3) are spent once the underlying difficulty has been resolved
options.misconception: reads a disqualification written with the words "at any time" as one that expires
options.why: Two of the three clauses say "has at any time been adjudged an insolvent" and "has at any time made a composition". The sub-section is written to reach back without limit, and paying the creditors afterwards is not a discharge of the bar it creates.

options.text: None of them, because a conviction of any kind bars a person from the office whatever the sentence was
options.misconception: drops the length of the sentence out of the clause
options.why: The clause is a conviction and a sentence for a period of more than six months, both together. A conviction carrying a shorter sentence, or a fine alone, does not engage the words the sub-section actually uses.

citation.ref: Section 196(3)

items.scenario: A public company has three candidates for the office of managing director, all aged fifty-five, all with the members behind them. Candidate A was adjudged an insolvent four years ago and that bankruptcy has not been annulled. Candidate B suspended payment to his creditors two years ago and made a composition with them, and every one of those creditors has since been paid in full. Candidate C was convicted by a court six years ago and sentenced to imprisonment for four months, which he served.

items.stem: Which of the three documents is correctly signed?

options.text: Company A's and Company B's, since a company secretary who prepared the Board's report may sign it
options.misconception: lets the person who drafted the report be the person who signs it
options.why: Section 134(6) names the chairperson where authorised, or at least two directors one of whom shall be a managing director, or the director where there is one director. The company secretary signs the financial statement under section 134(1) where he is appointed, which is a different document.

options.text: Only Company B's — Company A needed the managing director among its two signing directors, and Company C's Board's report had to be signed by the chairperson where authorised, and otherwise by at least two directors one of whom is the managing director
options.why: Section 134(1) requires the financial statement to be signed on behalf of the Board at least by the chairperson of the company where he is authorised by the Board, or by two directors out of which one shall be the managing director, if any, and by the Chief Executive Officer, the Chief Financial Officer and the company secretary wherever they are appointed; its proviso says that in the case of a One Person Company the financial statement shall be signed by only one director. Section 134(6) requires the Board's report and any annexures to it to be signed by its chairperson where he is authorised by the Board, and where he is not so authorised, by at least two directors one of whom shall be a managing director, or by the director where there is one director.

options.text: Only Company A's, because a One Person Company must still find a second signatory and a report signed by the secretary is enough where he is key managerial personnel
options.misconception: refuses the One Person Company the proviso written for it
options.why: The proviso to section 134(1) says that in the case of a One Person Company the financial statement shall be signed by only one director. And Company A is the defective one of the three, its two signing directors not including the managing director the sub-section requires where there is one in office.

options.text: All three, because the Act asks only that the documents be approved by the Board and the manner of signing is internal practice
options.misconception: treats signing as a formality the Board may arrange as it pleases
options.why: Both sub-sections say who shall sign, and they name particular officers. Approval by the Board is the earlier step; the signatures are how the statute puts named people behind what was approved, which is why it does not leave the choice open.

citation.ref: Sections 134(1) with its proviso and 134(6)

items.scenario: Three companies present their signed documents. Company A is a public company with a managing director in office; its financial statements are signed by two directors, neither of them the managing director, and by its chief financial officer and its company secretary. Company B is a One Person Company whose sole director has signed the financial statements alone. Company C's Board's report is signed by its company secretary alone, on the footing that he drafted it.

items.stem: Which of the three refusals is good in law?

options.text: Alpha's and Gamma's — the section does not apply to a private company at all, and it reaches the contract of service of a managing or whole-time director rather than the appointment of a non-executive director; Beta's is bad
options.why: Section 190(4) says the provisions of this section shall not apply to a private company, so Alpha owes its member nothing under it. Section 190(1) requires the company to keep at its registered office a copy of the contract of service with a managing or whole-time director, or a written memorandum setting out its terms where the contract is not in writing, which is why a non-executive director's letter of appointment falls outside it. Keeping the document in another city and offering to email it does not answer a section that fixes the place where it must be kept.

options.text: All three, because the right of inspection belongs to the Board and the auditor rather than to individual members
options.misconception: takes the inspection right away from the members the section names
options.why: The copies kept under the section are open to inspection by any member of the company without payment of fee. Two of these three refusals are good for reasons outside that right — one company sits outside the section and one document does — and the third is simply bad.

options.text: Only Alpha's, because a public company must show any member any document relating to any of its directors
options.misconception: widens the section into a general right to the Board's papers
options.why: The section names the contract of service with a managing or whole-time director, or a memorandum of its terms. A non-executive director's appointment letter is not that document, and no general right of access to board papers is created anywhere in it.

options.text: Only Beta's is bad, on the address, and Alpha must comply as well, a private company being a company for every purpose of the Act
options.misconception: overlooks an exemption written into the section itself
options.why: The Act does exempt private companies in places, and this is one of them. Section 190(4) says in terms that the provisions of the section shall not apply to a private company, so Alpha's refusal is good however the document is described.

items.scenario: Three companies refuse a member. Alpha Private Ltd will not show a member the managing director's contract of service. Beta Ltd, a public company, keeps its whole-time director's contract at its corporate office in another city rather than at the registered office, and offers to email a scan instead. Gamma Ltd, a public company, refuses to show a member the letter of appointment of a non-executive director who sits on its Board and draws sitting fees.

items.stem: Which of them is a small company?

options.text: Only the second and the fourth, a section 8 company being a private company for this purpose
options.misconception: brings a section 8 company back in through its private status
options.why: A company registered under section 8 is excluded by the proviso in terms, and being a private company as well does not rescue it. The proviso operates precisely on companies that would otherwise have qualified on the opening words and the figures.

options.text: Only the fourth — the definition opens by excluding every public company, and the proviso then excludes a section 8 company and a company governed by any special Act
options.why: Section 2(85) defines a small company as a company, other than a public company, whose paid-up share capital and turnover do not exceed the prescribed amounts, so an unlisted public company is outside it however few members it has and however small it is. The proviso excludes a holding company or a subsidiary company, a company registered under section 8, and a company or body corporate governed by any special Act. Only the fourth company answers the definition and escapes every limb of the proviso.

options.text: The first and the fourth, since the exclusions are about group membership and neither of those two sits in a group
options.misconception: reduces the proviso to its holding and subsidiary limb
options.why: The proviso has three limbs and the group limb is only one of them. A company registered under section 8 and a company governed by any special Act are excluded whatever their group position, and the opening words keep every public company out before the proviso is even reached.

options.text: All four, because the definition is a size test and the prescribed limits are met in each case
options.misconception: reads the numbers as the whole of the definition
options.why: The numbers are the second half of it. The first half says "a company, other than a public company", and the proviso then takes out three further classes by name. A company can be tiny and still fall outside the definition entirely.

citation.ref: Section 2(85) with its proviso

items.scenario: Four companies each have paid-up share capital and turnover comfortably inside the limits prescribed for a small company — take that as given in every case. The first is an unlisted public company with eleven members. The second is a private company licensed under section 8 to promote education. The third is a company governed by a special Act of Parliament. The fourth is a private company with no holding company and no subsidiary.

items.stem: How do the Rules actually apply to the four?

options.text: Only the banking company is outside, the exemption being for regulated financial institutions and not for a Government company
options.misconception: shortens the list of exempt classes
options.why: Four classes are named, and a Government company as defined in the Act is one of them, sitting beside the banking company, the systemically important non-banking financial company and the insurance company.

options.text: All four chains must come down to two layers, because the restriction lives in section 2(87) of the Act and a rule cannot exempt anybody from what the Act says
options.misconception: forgets that the proviso to section 2(87) prescribes the restriction through the Rules themselves
options.why: The proviso to section 2(87) says a company shall not have layers of subsidiaries beyond such numbers as may be prescribed. What is prescribed is the 2017 Rules, exempt classes and grandfathering included, so the exemptions are part of the restriction rather than an escape from it.

options.text: The three exempt companies are outside, and the manufacturing company must cut its chain back to two layers within the period the Rules allow
options.misconception: reads the transitional provision as an unwinding order
options.why: The Rules do not require an existing chain to be cut back. A company in excess on the commencement date files a return disclosing its layers and is frozen where it stands, and if it later reduces the layers it may not climb back above the reduced number.

options.text: They do not apply to the banking company, the insurance company or the Government company at all; the manufacturing company keeps the layers it already had but may add no further layer
options.why: Rule 1(2) says the Rules shall not apply to a banking company, to a non-banking financial company registered with the Reserve Bank of India and considered systemically important by it, to an insurance company and to a Government company, so the two-layer restriction never reaches those chains however deep they run. A company outside those classes that was already in excess of the limit when the Rules commenced is not made to unwind — it files the prescribed return with the Registrar and shall not have any additional layer of subsidiaries over and above the layers existing on that date.

citation.ref: Rules 1(2) and 2 of the Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules, 2017, read with the proviso to section 2(87)

items.scenario: A group secretary reviews four Indian chains. A banking company holds a chain of four subsidiaries, one below the other. An insurance company in the same group holds three layers. A Government company holds four. A manufacturing company in the group, which is none of those things, has held three layers since before the Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules, 2017 came into force and now wants to add a fourth. The secretary tells all four to collapse their chains to two layers.

items.stem: What is the position of the two loans?

options.text: The manufacturing company may not lend at all while the deposit default subsists, however compliant the rest of it is; and the housing finance company needs no special resolution
options.why: Section 186(8) says no company which is in default in the repayment of any deposits accepted by it or in payment of interest thereon shall give any loan or give any guarantee or provide any security or make an acquisition till such default is subsisting. It is a flat bar, and the limits, the resolution and the rate do not answer it. Section 186(11) then says that nothing in the section except sub-section (1) shall apply to a loan made, a guarantee given or a security provided by a banking company, an insurance company or a housing finance company in the ordinary course of its business, or by a company established with the object of and engaged in the business of financing industrial enterprises or of providing infrastructural facilities.

options.text: Neither may lend — the first is barred by the default and the second because a housing finance company is a company like any other for section 186
options.misconception: reads section 186 as applying to every company without exception
options.why: The exempt cases are named in the section. A housing finance company making a loan in the ordinary course of its business is one of them, and only sub-section (1), the restriction on layers of investment companies, continues to apply to it.

options.text: Both loans are fine — the first is inside the limits with a special resolution and a lawful rate, and the second needs the resolution the secretary asks for
options.misconception: treats compliance with the limits as compliance with the whole section
options.why: The deposit default is a separate bar that a company cannot satisfy by getting everything else right, and it stands until the default is cleared. And the housing finance company's ordinary-course lending is taken out of the section except for sub-section (1), so the resolution is not required of it at all.

options.text: The first is fine because a deposit default is a matter under sections 73 to 76 and has nothing to do with section 186, and the second needs the resolution
options.misconception: keeps the consequences of a deposit default inside the deposit chapter
options.why: The bar is written inside section 186 itself and makes a subsisting deposit default a disqualification from lending, guaranteeing, securing or acquiring. The consequences under the deposit provisions run alongside it rather than instead of it.

citation.ref: Sections 186(8) and 186(11)

items.scenario: A manufacturing company is in default in the repayment of deposits it accepted three years ago, and the default is continuing. Its Board proposes a fresh loan of ₹5 crore to an unrelated body corporate, well inside the section 186 limits, with a special resolution taken anyway and interest fixed above the prevailing yield on government securities. Separately a housing finance company in the same group proposes a loan of ₹100 crore in the ordinary course of its business, and the group secretary tells it to pass a special resolution because the amount is above the limits.

items.stem: What is the position on the old contract and on the fresh resolution?

options.text: Ratification is still open, because the section allows it at any time before the contract has been performed
options.misconception: reads ratification as open-ended where the section puts a clock on it
options.why: The clock runs three months from the date on which the contract or arrangement was entered into, not from its performance and not from its discovery. Once it runs out the company's remedy shifts from ratifying the contract to avoiding it.

options.text: Nothing can be done about the old contract, because a contract made without approval is void and a void contract can be neither ratified nor avoided
options.misconception: turns a voidable contract into a void one
options.why: The section says the contract shall be voidable at the option of the Board or of the shareholders. Voidable means the company chooses — a third party who dealt with the company is not left with nothing — and the company keeps its recovery route against the director or employee who entered into it.

options.text: Ratification is out of time, so the contract is voidable at the option of the Board and the directors concerned must indemnify the company; and the related party shareholder may not vote on the fresh resolution
options.why: Section 188(3) gives three months from the date on which the contract or arrangement was entered into for the Board or, as the case may be, the shareholders to ratify a contract made without the consent the section requires. Four months later that window has closed, the contract is voidable at the option of the Board, and where it is with a related party to any director the directors concerned shall indemnify the company against any loss. Section 188(4) separately leaves the company free to proceed against the director or employee who made it to recover what it lost. The second proviso to section 188(1) is a flat bar of its own — no member of the company shall vote on the resolution to approve such a contract if that member is a related party.

options.text: The related party shareholder may vote, because his shares carry voting rights and the restriction exists only for a listed entity under the listing regulations
options.misconception: thinks the bar on a related party voting lives only in the listing regulations
options.why: The Companies Act, 2013 carries its own bar in the proviso to section 188(1), and it applies to every company that has to put a related party contract to its members. The listing regulations add to it for a listed entity; they are not the only place it lives.

citation.ref: Sections 188(3) and 188(4), read with the second proviso to section 188(1)

items.scenario: A public company entered into a five-year supply contract with a firm in which a director's brother is a partner, at prices well above the market, and no Board resolution was ever taken for it. The Board discovers this four months after the contract was signed and wants to put it right. In the same week the company plans to put a fresh related party contract to its members for approval, and the shareholder who is the related party, holding forty per cent, intends to vote in favour of it.

items.stem: What has the company failed to do?

options.text: It should have consolidated the two subsidiaries into the statement sent to the members, which is all the section asks about a subsidiary
options.misconception: confuses the duty to consolidate with the duty to circulate
options.why: Consolidation is section 129(3). Section 136 is about what is put in front of the members, and it asks for the separate accounts of each subsidiary on the website and on demand — separate being the whole point, since consolidation is where a subsidiary's own figures disappear into the group's.

options.text: It had to place the separate audited accounts of each subsidiary on its website and give the member the copy he asked for, and for the foreign subsidiary it may place unaudited financial statements with a translation into English
options.why: The provisos to section 136(1) require every company having a subsidiary or subsidiaries to place separate audited accounts in respect of each subsidiary on its website, if any, and to provide a copy of the separate audited financial statements in respect of each subsidiary to any shareholder of the company who asks for it. Where the subsidiary is incorporated outside India and is not required under the law of its country to get its financial statements audited, the holding company places and provides the unaudited financial statements, and where those are not in English a translated copy in English goes with them.

options.text: It was right to refuse the member, because the audited accounts of a subsidiary belong to that subsidiary and to its own members
options.misconception: reads the shareholder's right as one he must exercise against the subsidiary
options.why: The proviso gives the right to any shareholder of the company that has the subsidiary, and puts the duty to provide the copy on that company. Whose accounts they are is not the test the proviso applies.

options.text: Nothing — a listed company that sends the salient features statement has discharged the section for itself and for its group
options.misconception: treats the salient features route as covering the subsidiaries as well
options.why: The salient features route answers what has to go to the members about the company's own accounts. The subsidiary duties sit in their own provisos to the same sub-section and are separate obligations about separate documents.

citation.ref: The provisos to section 136(1)

items.scenario: A listed holding company has two subsidiaries. One is Indian.
