The other is incorporated in a country whose law does not require its financial statements to be audited, and its accounts are drawn up in that country's language. Before the annual general meeting the company sends its members the salient features statement in the prescribed form and puts its own annual report on its website. It puts nothing about either subsidiary anywhere, and when a member writes asking for the Indian subsidiary's audited accounts he is told to buy them from the subsidiary.

items.stem: What does the application have to disclose to the Tribunal?

options.text: By affidavit, all material facts relating to the company — its latest financial position, the latest auditor's report on its accounts, and the pendency of any investigation or proceedings against it — together with the reduction of share capital included in the scheme
options.why: Section 230(2) requires the company, or any other person by whom an application is made, to disclose to the Tribunal by affidavit all material facts relating to the company, such as the latest financial position of the company, the latest auditor's report on the accounts of the company and the pendency of any investigation or proceedings against the company, together with a reduction of share capital of the company, if any, included in the compromise or arrangement. A pending investigation is a material fact the sub-section names by itself, and confidentiality is not a ground it recognises.

options.text: Only that the scheme is fair and that the requisite majorities have been obtained, the rest being for the meetings to consider
options.misconception: leaves the disclosure duty to the creditors' meeting
options.why: The disclosure is made to the Tribunal, by affidavit, at the time the application is made and before any meeting is called. The meetings decide whether to accept the scheme; the affidavit is what lets the Tribunal decide whether to call them at all.

options.text: Nothing about the capital reduction, since a reduction is dealt with under section 66 and needs a separate application of its own
options.misconception: separates a reduction that sits inside a scheme from the scheme carrying it
options.why: The sub-section requires a reduction of share capital included in the compromise or arrangement to be disclosed in the same affidavit. The scheme carries the reduction, and the Tribunal is told about it when the application is made rather than later and separately.

options.text: The financial position and the auditor's report, but not the investigation, which stays confidential until it produces a report
options.misconception: reads confidentiality into a list the sub-section wrote out in full
options.why: The sub-section names the pendency of any investigation or proceedings against the company as one of the material facts to be disclosed. It is the pendency that has to be told to the Tribunal, not the contents of anybody's file.

citation.ref: Section 230(2)

items.scenario: A company applies to the Tribunal under section 230 for a compromise with its creditors. The affidavit filed with the application says only that the scheme is fair and that the members support it. The company is at that moment the subject of an investigation ordered under section 210, and the scheme itself includes a reduction of its share capital. The company secretary says the investigation is confidential and that the reduction need not be mentioned because section 66 will be complied with separately.

items.stem: What may the Tribunal do in each case?

options.text: In the first, on the trustee's petition, impose such restrictions on the incurring of further liabilities by the company as it thinks necessary; in the second, on an application by the debenture-holders or the trustee, direct the company to redeem the debentures forthwith on payment of principal and interest due
options.why: Section 71(9) lets the debenture trustee, where he comes to a conclusion that the assets of the company are insufficient or are likely to become insufficient to discharge the principal amount as and when it becomes due, file a petition before the Tribunal, and the Tribunal may after hearing the company and any other interested person impose such restrictions on the incurring of any further liabilities by the company as it thinks necessary in the interests of the debenture-holders. Section 71(10) says that where a company fails to redeem the debentures on the date of their maturity or fails to pay interest when it is due, the Tribunal may, on the application of any or all of the debenture-holders or of the debenture trustee and after hearing the parties, direct by order that the company redeem the debentures forthwith on payment of principal and interest due.

options.text: In both cases the Tribunal may only order the company to be wound up, that being the consequence the Act attaches to a failure on debentures
options.misconception: jumps to winding up where the section provides a targeted order
options.why: Both orders are aimed at protecting the debenture-holders while the company carries on — restraining the incurring of further liabilities in the one case and compelling redemption in the other. Neither sub-section mentions winding up.

options.text: Nothing in the first, a trustee having no standing until a default has occurred, and in the second the debenture-holders must sue as ordinary creditors
options.misconception: makes an actual default the condition of every remedy the section gives
options.why: The first power is written for the case before the default — the words are "insufficient or are likely to become insufficient". And the second gives the Tribunal power to order redemption forthwith, which is exactly why a suit is not the debenture-holders' only route.

options.text: In the first it may order the company to create additional security, and in the second it may award interest only, redemption being a matter of contract between the parties
options.misconception: invents one power and shrinks another
options.why: The order the first sub-section contemplates is a restriction on the incurring of further liabilities, not a direction to create security. And the second says the Tribunal may direct the company to redeem the debentures on payment of principal and interest due, so redemption is precisely what the order compels.

citation.ref: Sections 71(9) and 71(10)

items.scenario: Two matters reach the Tribunal. In the first, a debenture trustee has concluded from the accounts and a valuation that the company's assets are likely to become insufficient to discharge the principal amount when it falls due; the company is still paying interest on time, and its finance head says the trustee can do nothing until an actual default happens. In the second, a company has failed to redeem its debentures on the date of their maturity, and its finance head says the debenture-holders' only remedy is to sue for the money.

items.stem: What may the Tribunal's order do?

options.text: Only the buy-out, because the Tribunal's power is confined to relieving the minority of its shareholding
options.misconception: shrinks a wide list of remedies down to the best-known one
options.why: The purchase of shares is one clause among many. The same list reaches agreements with the managing director, the conduct of the affairs of the company in future, the removal of the managing director or a director, and the recovery of undue gains made by them.

options.text: The first two, but keeping the man out of office in future is a matter for the members when they next appoint a managing director
options.misconception: makes a statutory bar a matter of shareholder choice
options.why: The bar is put in the statute itself and only the Tribunal may lift it, by leave. The members cannot vote it away, and a company that appoints him in breach exposes both him and itself to the penalty the section carries.

options.text: All three are open to it — it may set aside or modify an agreement with the managing director, may order the purchase of members' shares by the company itself with the consequent reduction of capital, and a person whose agreement is so terminated is then barred for five years without the Tribunal's leave
options.why: Section 242 sets out what an order may provide for, and the list is a long one — the regulation of the conduct of the affairs of the company in future, the purchase of the shares or interests of any members by other members or by the company itself and, in the case of a purchase by the company, the consequent reduction of its share capital, and the termination, setting aside or modification of any agreement between the company and the managing director or any other director or the manager. Section 243 then says that a person whose agreement is terminated or set aside shall not, without the leave of the Tribunal, serve as the managing director or other director or manager of the company for five years from the date of that order.

options.text: None of them without the company's consent, because the Tribunal cannot rewrite a contract or a capital structure the members themselves approved
options.misconception: treats an order under section 242 as needing the company's agreement
options.why: The whole purpose of the section is to override what the majority has arranged where the affairs are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to members or to the public interest. The order may provide for the termination, setting aside or modification of an agreement, and a certified copy of an order altering the memorandum or articles is filed with the Registrar.

citation.ref: Sections 242 and 243, read with section 241

items.scenario: The Tribunal has heard a petition under section 241 and is satisfied that the company's affairs are being conducted in a manner prejudicial to the interests of some of its members. The petitioners ask it to set aside the managing director's five-year service agreement, to order the company itself to buy their shares with the consequent reduction of its capital, and to keep the removed managing director out of office in future. The company's counsel says the Tribunal's only power is to order the majority shareholders to buy the minority out.

items.stem: How should the Authority answer the three?

options.text: It can do none of the three until the Central Government makes a reference, that power being a delegated one
options.misconception: makes a reference from the Central Government a precondition to acting
options.why: The words are "either suo motu or on a reference made to it by the Central Government". They are alternatives, and the first of them lets the Authority begin on its own once it is satisfied that the matter is one of misconduct by a member or a firm.

options.text: It may take up the auditor without waiting for anybody, but it cannot penalise the directors — its investigating power reaches professional or other misconduct by a member or a firm of chartered accountants
options.why: Section 132(4)(a) gives the Authority the power to investigate, either suo motu or on a reference made to it by the Central Government, into matters of professional or other misconduct committed by any member or firm of chartered accountants registered under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. That is who the power reaches, so directors who falsified the accounts answer elsewhere and to other authorities, and re-opening or revising the filed accounts is a matter for the sections that deal with those accounts. Section 132(2) separately gives the Authority its functions — recommending accounting and auditing policies and standards to the Central Government, monitoring and enforcing their compliance, and overseeing the quality of service of the professions associated with ensuring such compliance.

options.text: It may penalise the directors but not the auditor, because the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has exclusive jurisdiction over its own members
options.misconception: hands the auditor to the Institute and the directors to the Authority, reversing both
options.why: The power is about misconduct by a member or a firm of chartered accountants, which is the auditor and not the directors. Where the Institute stands once the Authority has begun is settled by the proviso to the same sub-section, and it is not a rule of exclusivity in the Institute's favour.

options.text: It can do all three, because section 132 makes the Authority the regulator of financial reporting and of everyone involved in it
options.misconception: reads a regulator's subject matter as the list of persons it may penalise
options.why: The subject matter is financial reporting, but the persons named in the investigating power are a member or a firm of chartered accountants. What may be done to a company about its accounts is a different question, answered by the sections that govern re-opening and revision.

citation.ref: Sections 132(2) and 132(4)(a)

items.scenario: A company's directors are found to have falsified its revenue. The National Financial Reporting Authority opens a file. The company writes to it asking three things — that it impose a penalty on the two directors who did it, that it direct the company to restate its filed accounts, and that it confirm it cannot act at all unless the Central Government makes a reference to it.

items.stem: What does section 10 require?

options.text: An ordinary resolution of the members will do, and a partnership needs only the consent of the managing partner who signs the application
options.misconception: lowers both of the thresholds the sub-section fixes
options.why: The words are a special resolution passed by the shareholders and a resolution passed by at least three-fourths of the total number of partners. Neither of them is satisfied by a simple majority or by one partner's signature.

options.text: A special resolution of the shareholders, or a resolution of at least three-fourths of the total number of partners, approving the filing must be furnished with the books and the proposed professional's name; and an incomplete application gets a notice to rectify the defect within seven days before it can be rejected
options.why: Section 10(3) requires the corporate applicant to furnish its books of account and such other documents relating to such period as may be specified, the name of the resolution professional proposed to be appointed as interim resolution professional, and the special resolution passed by the shareholders of the corporate debtor or the resolution passed by at least three-fourths of the total number of partners of the corporate debtor approving the filing of the application. The proviso to section 10(4) then requires the Adjudicating Authority, before rejecting the application, to give a notice to the applicant to rectify the defect in his application within seven days from the date of receipt of that notice.

options.text: A Board resolution is enough, because section 10 is the corporate debtor's own route and the Board is the corporate debtor's mind
options.misconception: leaves out the shareholder or partner approval the sub-section requires
options.why: The sub-section names the special resolution of the shareholders, or the resolution of at least three-fourths of the total number of partners, as a document that must be furnished. Putting a company into insolvency is not left to the Board alone, which is why the owners' approval has to be on the file.

options.text: An incomplete application is rejected without more, the chance to cure being available only to a financial creditor applying under section 7
options.misconception: confines a cure provision to one of the sections that carries it
options.why: The proviso to section 10(4) carries its own notice to rectify, as do the provisos to section 7(5) and section 9(5). A corporate applicant gets the same chance to complete its file before the application can be thrown out.

citation.ref: Sections 10(3) and 10(4) with its proviso

items.scenario: A company's Board resolves to file an application under section 10 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The managing director files it with the books of account and the name of a proposed insolvency professional, but with no resolution of the members, saying the Board's own resolution is enough because the Board manages the company. A partnership firm in the same group also wants to file, and its managing partner signs the application alone. Both applications turn out to be incomplete in one respect, and the Adjudicating Authority is minded to reject them.

items.stem: Is he right about the length of his term?

options.text: Yes, and the powers of the Board revive on the thirtieth day until a resolution professional is appointed
options.misconception: gives the suspended Board its powers back in a gap that does not exist
options.why: There is no gap for the Board to fill. The interim resolution professional is carried through to the appointment under section 22, and the management of the affairs of the corporate debtor stays vested in him for as long as he holds office.

options.text: No, but only because the committee's delay extends his term — had the committee met in time his term would still have ended at thirty days
options.misconception: keeps the old thirty-day rule alive as a default that delay merely postpones
options.why: The term is defined by the appointment under section 22 and not by a period at all. Whether the committee is quick or slow, he holds office until the resolution professional is appointed and not for any fixed number of days.

options.text: Yes — his term is thirty days from his appointment, after which he may act only with the Adjudicating Authority's leave
options.misconception: applies the sub-section as it stood before it was substituted
options.why: The thirty-day term was replaced. The sub-section now runs his term to the date of appointment of the resolution professional under section 22, with no gap in between and no application for leave to be made.

options.text: No — his term continues till the date of appointment of the resolution professional under section 22, so he stays in office until the committee's appointment takes effect
options.why: Section 16(5) as it now stands says the term of the interim resolution professional shall continue till the date of appointment of the resolution professional under section 22. The thirty-day limit he is relying on was in the sub-section as originally enacted and was substituted in 2018, precisely so that a corporate debtor is not left with nobody in charge while the committee has yet to make its appointment. Section 16(2) is what put him there — where the applicant proposes a professional and no disciplinary proceeding is pending against him, that is the person the Adjudicating Authority appoints.

citation.ref: Sections 16(2) and 16(5), read with section 22

items.scenario: A financial creditor's application is admitted on 3 August 2026. The creditor had proposed a named insolvency professional against whom no disciplinary proceeding is pending, and the Adjudicating Authority appoints him as interim resolution professional the same day. By 2 September the committee of creditors has not met and has appointed nobody as resolution professional. The interim resolution professional stops work that day, saying his term was thirty days and has run out, and the suspended directors say the company is now left with nobody in charge.

items.stem: How does section 3 of the Competition Act, 2002 apply to the two?

options.text: Only the export agreement, because section 3(5) is about trade with other countries and says nothing about intellectual property
options.misconception: keeps one limb of the sub-section and drops the other
options.why: The sub-section has two limbs. The first preserves the right to restrain infringement of, and to impose reasonable conditions necessary for protecting, rights conferred under the intellectual property statutes it lists; the second is the export limb.

options.text: Both may fall outside section 3 — the first if the condition is a reasonable one necessary for protecting the patent rights, and the second because the agreement relates exclusively to the production, supply, distribution or control of goods for export from India
options.why: Section 3(5) says nothing in section 3 shall restrict the right of any person to restrain any infringement of, or to impose reasonable conditions as may be necessary for protecting any of his rights conferred upon him under the statutes it lists, which include the Patents Act, 1970 — so the protection runs only as far as the conditions are reasonable and necessary, and an unreasonable clause loses it. The same sub-section preserves the right of any person to export goods from India to the extent to which the agreement relates exclusively to the production, supply, distribution or control of goods or provision of services for such export.

options.text: Neither is saved — a market-sharing agreement is presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition, and a patent gives no immunity from the Act
options.misconception: reads the exemption in section 3(5) out of the section it sits in
options.why: Section 3(5) is written into section 3 itself and it does carve out both cases. Market sharing is presumed anti-competitive when it bites, but the export limb asks first whether the agreement relates exclusively to exports, and if it does the presumption is never reached.

options.text: Both are saved outright — a patent holder may impose any condition he chooses, and an exporters' agreement is beyond the Act altogether
options.misconception: turns a qualified exemption into an absolute one
options.why: The words are "reasonable conditions as may be necessary for protecting" the rights, so a condition going beyond that is not saved at all. And the export limb applies only to the extent the agreement relates exclusively to exports, so a clause reaching the Indian market falls straight back inside section 3.

citation.ref: Section 3(5)

items.scenario: Two agreements come before the Competition Commission of India. A patentee licenses its patent to a single manufacturer on condition that the licensee makes no competing generic during the term of the licence, and says the condition is necessary to protect the patent. Separately, two Indian tile makers agree to divide the markets of three foreign countries between them for their export sales; their agreement says nothing at all about India.

items.stem: What does Regulation 7(1) require of the two of them?

options.text: Both, but within thirty days, which is the period Regulation 7 allows for any initial disclosure
options.misconception: applies the one-time period in Regulation 7(1)(a) to a later appointment
options.why: Thirty days is the period in Regulation 7(1)(a), which governed the one-time disclosure by promoters, key managerial personnel and directors when the Regulations took effect. A person appointed or becoming a promoter afterwards falls under the next clause, and that clause carries seven days.

options.text: Only the chief financial officer, since a promoter is outside Regulation 7 until he is also a director or key managerial personnel
options.misconception: leaves promoters out of the initial disclosure
options.why: The sub-regulation names a person upon becoming a promoter or a member of the promoter group alongside a key managerial personnel and a director. The obligation attaches to becoming one of those, not to holding an office in the company.

options.text: Each had to disclose his holding of securities of the company as on the date of his appointment or of becoming a promoter, within seven days, and the ₹10 lakh figure has nothing to do with this obligation
options.why: Regulation 7(1)(b) requires every person on appointment as a key managerial personnel or a director of the company, or upon becoming a promoter or a member of the promoter group, to disclose his holding of securities of the company as on the date of appointment or of becoming a promoter, to the company within seven days of it. It is an initial disclosure of a position rather than a report of a transaction, so it falls due whether or not he trades and whatever the value happens to be. The ₹10 lakh line belongs to the continual disclosure in Regulation 7(2), which is a different obligation entirely.

options.text: Neither has anything to disclose, because Regulation 7 is triggered by trading and neither of them has traded since
options.misconception: reads every disclosure in Regulation 7 as a report of a trade
options.why: The first sub-regulation asks for a holding as at a date, not for a transaction. The second is the trading disclosure, and it is the one that aggregates value traded over a calendar quarter.

citation.ref: Regulations 7(1)(a) and 7(1)(b)

items.scenario: A listed company appoints a new chief financial officer on 1 September 2026. He already holds shares of the company worth ₹3 lakh, bought years earlier, and discloses nothing — the value is below ₹10 lakh, he says, and in any case the obligation begins only when he trades. In the same month, on 12 September, another person becomes a promoter of the company. He discloses nothing either.

items.stem: What does Regulation 30 require?

options.text: The first is disclosed without applying the materiality criteria at all, being deemed material; only the second is judged against those criteria, and the board's policy cannot override a deeming provision
options.why: Regulation 30(2) says the events specified in Para A of Part A of Schedule III are deemed to be material events and the listed entity shall make disclosure of such events. Regulation 30(3) says the events specified in Para B of that Part shall be disclosed based on application of the guidelines for materiality, which are the criteria set out in Regulation 30(4). The policy the board frames operates under those criteria, so it operates on Para B alone.

options.text: Both are disclosed, because every event in Schedule III is deemed material and the criteria in Regulation 30(4) are guidance rather than a test
options.misconception: collapses the two Paras into a single list
options.why: Part A of Schedule III is deliberately split in two. Para A carries the deeming provision; Para B is tested against the criteria, and an event that fails those criteria is not disclosed under this Regulation.

options.text: Neither is disclosed, because the materiality policy the board framed governs every event and neither crosses its thresholds
options.misconception: applies the board's materiality policy to events the Regulations deem material
options.why: A deemed material event is not put to the policy for a decision at all. Disclosure of every event in Para A is required by the Regulation itself, and the policy the board frames applies to the events in Para B.

options.text: The first is disclosed only if the board considers it material, and the second never is, Para B being a list of events the Regulations exclude
options.misconception: reverses the roles of the two Paras
options.why: Para A is the deemed list and Para B is the tested list; neither of them is a list of exclusions. The events in Para B become disclosable as soon as the materiality criteria are met.

citation.ref: Regulations 30(2), 30(3) and 30(4), read with Part A of Schedule III

items.scenario: A listed entity faces two disclosures in one week. The first is an event set out in Para A of Part A of Schedule III to the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 — take that classification as given. The second is an event set out in Para B of the same Part — again, take that as given. Neither event crosses any of the value thresholds in the board's own policy for determination of materiality. The company secretary proposes to disclose neither, saying the board's policy is what decides both.

items.stem: What is the correct position on the three points?

options.text: There is no period for compounding, a compounded contravention may still be adjudicated where the sum looks low, and the penalty ceiling is twice the sum involved
options.misconception: removes the clock from the compounding provision and the bar that follows a compounding
options.why: The compounding provision fixes one hundred and eighty days from the receipt of the application. The next sub-section then closes the matter, and the ceiling in the penalty provision is thrice, not twice, the sum involved where the amount is quantifiable.

options.text: The contravention is to be compounded within one hundred and eighty days of the application; no proceeding may be initiated or continued on a contravention that has been compounded; and the penalty could have run up to thrice the sum involved
options.why: Section 15(1) says any contravention under section 13 may, on an application made by the person committing it, be compounded within one hundred and eighty days from the date of receipt of the application by the authorities the section specifies. Section 15(2) says that where a contravention has been compounded, no proceeding or further proceeding, as the case may be, shall be initiated or continued against the person in respect of the contravention so compounded. Section 13(1) sets the penalty at up to thrice the sum involved where the amount is quantifiable and up to two lakh rupees where it is not, with a further penalty which may extend to five thousand rupees for every day after the first day during which the contravention continues.

options.text: The period is one hundred and eighty days, but compounding settles only the money and leaves the Directorate free to prosecute the same contravention
options.misconception: reads compounding as a settlement of the amount rather than a closure of the matter
options.why: The words are that no proceeding or further proceeding shall be initiated or continued against the person in respect of the contravention so compounded. Compounding closes the contravention, which is the whole reason a person applies for it.

options.text: No penalty could have been imposed at all, because a FEMA contravention is a civil matter and the Act provides only for compounding
options.misconception: mistakes a civil penalty regime for the absence of any penalty
options.why: The Act has its own penalty provision, and compounding is the alternative to it rather than a replacement for it. What the 1999 Act did was replace the criminal regime of the earlier law with a civil penalty, and that penalty runs up to thrice the sum involved where the amount is quantifiable.

citation.ref: Sections 13(1), 15(1) and 15(2)

items.scenario: A company has contravened a provision of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999. The sum involved is quantifiable and is ₹80 lakh — take that as given. The company applies for compounding. Six months pass with no order made, and its adviser says there is no time limit binding the authority. After an order is eventually made and the sum paid, the Directorate of Enforcement proposes to open an adjudication on the same contravention, thinking the compounding sum too low. The company also asks what the maximum penalty could have been had it not compounded at all.

items.stem: Who formulates the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology of the internal audit?

options.text: The statutory auditor, as part of the audit plan he draws up for the year
options.misconception: hands one professional's engagement to the holder of a different office
options.why: The statutory auditor is appointed under section 139 and reports to the members. He has no power to fix another professional's terms of engagement, and the Rule names the audit committee or the Board.

options.text: Nobody in the company — the Rules themselves prescribe the scope and a fixed quarterly cycle for every company covered
options.misconception: expects the Rules to write the audit programme rather than to say who writes it
options.why: Rule 13 says which companies must have an internal audit and who may conduct it. It deliberately leaves the scope, the periodicity and the method to be settled company by company, because a trading company past the turnover line and a manufacturer of the same size need different work.

options.text: The internal auditor alone, since anybody else setting his agenda would destroy his independence
options.misconception: reads independence as a freedom to write one's own terms of reference
options.why: Independence protects what he reports and to whom, not what he is asked to look at. The Rule gives him a voice and not a veto — the audit committee or the Board formulates the work in consultation with him, which is a conversation neither side can hold alone.

options.text: The audit committee, in consultation with the internal auditor — and in a company that has no audit committee, the Board does it
options.why: Rule 13(2) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 says the Audit Committee of the company or the Board shall, in consultation with the Internal Auditor, formulate the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology for conducting the internal audit. So it is neither the internal auditor's own brief nor the statutory auditor's plan. He is heard before it is settled, and the body he reports to settles it.

citation.ref: Section 138(2) read with Rule 13(2) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A company covered by section 138 appoints a cost accountant already on its payroll as its internal auditor. He asks who decides what he is to examine and how often. The chief financial officer tells him he writes his own brief, because independence means nobody may tell an internal auditor what to look at. The company secretary disagrees and says the statutory auditor settles it as part of his audit plan. The company has an audit committee.

items.stem: What is the answer on the two points?

options.text: The company may act, but only by removing his access to the mechanism; and the unlisted company routes complaints to its company secretary
options.misconception: invents a remedy the Rule does not give and fills the second gap with an officer the Rule does not name
options.why: The Rule's remedy is action against the concerned director or employee, including reprimand; nothing in it lets a company cut a person out of the mechanism. And where there is no audit committee it is a director nominated by the Board, not an officer of the company, who receives the concerns.

options.text: Where complaints are repeatedly frivolous, the audit committee or the nominated director may take suitable action against the complainant; and a covered company with no audit committee has its Board nominate a director to play that role
options.why: Rule 7 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014 says that in case of repeated frivolous complaints being filed by a director or an employee, the audit committee or the director nominated may take suitable action against the concerned person, including reprimand. The same Rule says that a company which is not required to constitute an audit committee shall have its Board nominate a director to play the role of the audit committee for the purpose of the vigil mechanism. Neither answer touches the safeguard against victimisation, which protects the honest user of the mechanism and not the serial one.

options.text: Nothing can be done about the complainant, because any action against him would be the victimisation the section forbids
options.misconception: reads the protection against victimisation as covering a complainant proved to be abusing the mechanism
options.why: The safeguard is against victimisation for using the mechanism. A person whose complaints are found baseless one after another is not being victimised when the pattern itself is acted on, and the Rule says so in terms.

options.text: The unlisted company owes nothing at all, because the vigil mechanism belongs to section 177 and section 177 is about the audit committee
options.misconception: ties the vigil mechanism to the existence of an audit committee
options.why: Section 177(9) requires the prescribed classes of companies to establish a vigil mechanism whether or not they are required to have an audit committee, and the Rule exists precisely to fill that gap by making the Board nominate a director to play the committee's role.

citation.ref: Sections 177(9) and 177(10), read with Rule 7 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A listed company's vigil mechanism is overseen by its audit committee. One employee has filed eleven complaints in a year; every one was investigated and every one was found to be baseless, and the latest names a colleague he is in a personal dispute with. The head of human resources asks whether anything can be done about him, or whether a complainant is untouchable for good. In the same group, an unlisted company that is covered by the requirement has no audit committee at all, and asks who is supposed to receive complaints there.

items.stem: Which of the three is an inactive company?

options.text: Only R, because the definition is satisfied when a company fails all three tests together
options.misconception: reads three alternative limbs as cumulative conditions
options.why: The word between the limbs is "or". Reading them together would leave the definition reaching almost nobody, and would defeat the third limb, which was written for the company that has simply stopped filing.

options.text: None of them — whether a company is inactive is for the Registrar to decide on the facts, and the Explanation is only guidance
options.misconception: turns a statutory definition into an administrative discretion
options.why: The Explanation defines the expression for the section, and a company either answers it or does not. What the Registrar decides is a separate question — whether to grant the status of a dormant company applied for, or to place a company on the register himself.

options.text: Only P and R, since a company that is trading cannot be inactive whatever it has failed to file
options.misconception: drops the filing limb from the definition
options.why: The third limb asks about filings and not about business, and it stands on its own. That is also why the Registrar may put a company that has not filed for two financial years consecutively on the register of dormant companies after giving it notice.

options.text: All three — the Explanation gives three tests joined by "or", and each company satisfies at least one of them
options.why: The Explanation to section 455(1) says an inactive company means a company which has not been carrying on any business or operation, or has not made any significant accounting transaction during the last two financial years, or has not filed financial statements and annual returns during the last two financial years. The three limbs are alternatives, so P is caught by the first, Q by the third, and R by the first and the second together. Filing everything on time does not rescue a company that does nothing, and trading hard does not rescue one that files nothing.

citation.ref: Explanation (i) to section 455(1), read with section 455(4)

items.scenario: Three unlisted companies are compared. P was incorporated in 2019 to hold a patent, has never carried on any business, and has filed its financial statements and its annual returns on time every year. Q trades normally and profitably but has filed neither financial statements nor annual returns for the last two financial years. R has done no business for four years and has made no significant accounting transaction in that time. Each asks whether it answers the description of an inactive company.

items.stem: Which of the associate's four does section 15(1) actually require?

options.text: Only the closing date — the penalties live in the Code and need not be repeated in a newspaper
options.misconception: treats a required disclosure as surplus because the law is public
options.why: Section 15(1) requires the penalties for false or misleading claims to be stated in the announcement itself. The announcement is read by suppliers and employees who will never open the Code, and the warning is part of what makes the claims process work.

options.text: The penalties for a false or misleading claim, and the date on which the process shall close
options.why: Section 15(1) sets out what the public announcement shall contain — the name and address of the corporate debtor, the name of the authority with which it is incorporated or registered, the last date for submission of claims, the details of the interim resolution professional vested with the management and responsible for receiving claims, the penalties for false or misleading claims, and the date on which the corporate insolvency resolution process shall close. The amount of the default is on none of that list, and the liquidation value is not even known at this stage.
keywords: penalties for false or misleading claims
last date for submission of claims

options.text: All four, since a creditor deciding whether to file needs the scale of the default and the value of the company
options.misconception: adds to a list the sub-section wrote out in full
options.why: The section names its contents exhaustively. A creditor files on what he is owed, not on what somebody else is owed, and the two valuations are confidential and reach only the committee, and only after resolution plans have come in.

options.text: Only the amount of the default, which is what the Adjudicating Authority has just found
options.misconception: puts the admission order's finding into an announcement aimed at creditors generally
options.why: The announcement invites the whole world of creditors to come in with their own claims. The default that got the application admitted is one creditor's debt, and stating it would say nothing to anybody else about what to file or by when.

citation.ref: Section 15(1), read with sections 13(1)(b) and 13(2)

items.scenario: An interim resolution professional drafts the public announcement. His draft carries the corporate debtor's name and address, the name of the authority with which it is registered, the last date for the submission of claims, and his own details. His associate says four things are still missing — the amount of the default admitted by the Adjudicating Authority, the liquidation value of the company, the penalties for a false or misleading claim, and the date on which the corporate insolvency resolution process shall close.

items.stem: Which of the four cannot be made under the Scheme?

options.text: None of the four — the Scheme permits anything at all so long as the annual ceiling is not crossed
options.misconception: reads the ceiling as the Scheme's only condition
options.why: The ceiling is about the amount and the prohibitions are about the purpose, and they work independently. A remittance for margins to an overseas exchange, for trading in foreign exchange abroad, or to a country identified by the Financial Action Task Force as non-cooperative is barred whatever the sum involved.

options.text: The medical treatment, because a remittance for medical treatment is governed by Schedule III to the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 and not by the Scheme
options.misconception: treats a facility that also exists outside the Scheme as barred inside it
options.why: Schedule III is what allows a remittance for medical treatment beyond the Scheme's ceiling, on the estimate of a doctor or a hospital. It does not push the payment out of the Scheme; within the annual ceiling it may be made freely.

options.text: The gift to his sister, because a gift is not a transaction the Scheme was made for
options.misconception: reads the Scheme as a facility for the remitter's own expenses only
options.why: A gift to a relative resident outside India is a permissible current account transaction and is one of the commonest uses of the Scheme. What the Scheme limits is the total, not who benefits from it.

options.text: The margin money placed with the overseas exchange
options.why: The Scheme covers any permissible current or capital account transaction, so a gift to a relative abroad, the purchase of immovable property abroad and medical treatment are all inside it. What it shuts out is a remittance for margins or margin calls to overseas exchanges and counterparties and for trading in foreign exchange abroad, alongside the transactions Schedule I to the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 prohibits outright — remittance out of lottery winnings, the purchase of lottery tickets and banned publications, and remittances to countries identified by the Financial Action Task Force as non-cooperative.

citation.ref: Schedule I to the FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, read with the Reserve Bank's Master Direction on the Liberalised Remittance Scheme

items.scenario: A resident individual plans four remittances in 2026-27, and the four together are comfortably inside the annual ceiling under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme. He wants to send a gift to his sister who lives in Canada; to pay part of the price of a flat he is buying in Dubai; to place margin money with an overseas exchange where he intends to trade currency futures; and to pay for his mother's medical treatment abroad.

items.stem: How do the three requests stand under Rule 12?

options.text: The widow takes only the four thousand that had vested, since nothing else had accrued to her husband
options.misconception: reads the death provision as carrying across only what had already vested
options.why: The Rule says all the options granted to him till such date shall vest in the legal heirs or nominees. Death accelerates the vesting rather than freezing it, which is the whole point of writing a separate consequence for it.

options.text: Everything lapses in both cases — options are personal to the employee, so death and resignation each end the whole holding
options.misconception: reads the personal character of an option as ending it on every exit
options.why: Options are personal, which is why they cannot be sold to the brother. It does not follow that they die with the employee: the Rule accelerates vesting on death and passes the whole holding to the legal heirs or nominees, and it preserves vested options after a resignation.

options.text: The widow takes all ten thousand; the employee who resigned keeps only what had vested, to be exercised within the scheme's period, and the unvested options expire; and the transfer to the brother is not permitted at all
options.why: Rule 12 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 says the option granted to employees shall not be transferable to any other person and shall not be pledged, hypothecated, mortgaged or otherwise alienated, and that no person other than the employee to whom the option is granted is entitled to exercise it. On the death of the employee while in employment, all the options granted to him till that date vest in his legal heirs or nominees. On resignation or termination, all options not vested as on that day expire, while the vested ones may still be exercised on the terms the scheme lays down.

options.text: The transfer to the brother is permissible if the Board approves it and the scheme is amended to allow transfers
options.misconception: treats a bar written into the Rules as a term the company may relax
options.why: The Board may vary the terms of a scheme in the ways the Rules allow, but it cannot approve what the Rules forbid. Non-transferability is not a term of this company's scheme; it is a condition of every option scheme under the Rules.

citation.ref: Rule 12 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, read with section 62(1)(b)

items.scenario: A company's employee stock option scheme is running normally. Three questions reach the company secretary in one week. An employee has died in service holding four thousand vested and six thousand unvested options, and his widow asks for all ten thousand. A second employee has resigned holding three thousand vested and five thousand unvested options and wants to keep both lots. A third wants to transfer two thousand of his vested options to his brother, who is willing to pay him for them.

items.stem: What does section 92(3) require of this company?

options.text: Neither, because a return filed with the Registrar is already a public document and the company owes no separate disclosure
options.misconception: treats a filing with the Registrar as discharging a duty owed to the members
options.why: The filing and the placing are separate duties in separate sub-sections. Section 92(3) is aimed at the member or the lender who wants to read the return without paying for a copy from the Registrar's portal.

options.text: The annual return on the website, and nothing in the Board's report
options.misconception: reads the first half of the sub-section and stops
options.why: The sub-section has two limbs and the second is the one that reaches the reader: the web link is to be disclosed in the Board's report, so a member reading the report knows the return exists and where it sits.

options.text: The extract in Form MGT-9 annexed to the Board's report, exactly as before
options.misconception: carries forward a requirement the amended sub-section removed
options.why: The extract was the old form of the same idea — giving members the substance of the return without making them go and find it. The sub-section now does that with a link to the full return instead of a summary of it.

options.text: A copy of the annual return placed on the company's website, if it has one, with the web link disclosed in the Board's report — and the extract in Form MGT-9 is no longer required at all
options.why: Section 92(3) as it now stands says every company shall place a copy of the annual return on the website of the company, if any, and that the web link of such annual return shall be disclosed in the Board's report. The extract the Board's report used to carry went when that sub-section was substituted, so annexing Form MGT-9 answers a requirement that has ceased to exist while leaving the one that has replaced it unmet.

citation.ref: Section 92(3), as substituted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017

items.scenario: A company secretary is assembling the Board's report for 2025-26. He proposes to annex the extract of the annual return in Form MGT-9, as the firm has done every year since 2015, and says the company's website need carry nothing, because the annual return is filed with the Registrar and anybody who wants it can pay for a copy there.

items.stem: Which of the four are operational creditors?

options.text: The employees and the supplier — a tax department is a creditor of a different kind altogether and stands outside the Code's two classes
options.misconception: leaves government dues outside a definition that names them
options.why: There is no third class. Section 5(21) puts a debt in respect of dues arising under any law and payable to the Central Government, a State Government or a local authority squarely inside operational debt, which is why tax departments appear regularly as applicants under section 9.

options.text: Only the supplier, since operational debt means what a company owes its trade suppliers
options.misconception: shrinks operational debt to trade payables
options.why: Goods are one limb of three. The sub-section names services, says "including employment" in terms, and adds dues payable to a Government or a local authority under any law.

options.text: All four, because anybody a company owes money to is an operational creditor unless he holds security
options.misconception: makes security the line between financial and operational debt
options.why: The line is what the money was for, not what secures it. An unsecured term loan is still financial debt, because it was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and a secured supplier is still an operational creditor.

options.text: The employees, the State Government and the supplier — each of them holds operational debt; the bank holds financial debt and its route is section 7
options.why: Section 5(21) defines an operational debt as a claim in respect of the provision of goods or services including employment, or a debt in respect of the payment of dues arising under any law for the time being in force and payable to the Central Government, any State Government or any local authority. Unpaid salary is the employment limb, the tax is the statutory dues limb and the supplier's bill is the goods limb, so each of the three is an operational creditor under section 5(20) and applies under section 9. The bank's term loan was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, which puts it in section 5(8) and sends it to section 7 instead.

citation.ref: Sections 5(20) and 5(21), read with sections 5(8), 7 and 9

items.scenario: A company has stopped paying everybody. It owes unpaid salary to its own employees, goods and services tax to a State Government, a term loan to a bank, and the price of raw material to a supplier. Each of the four amounts is above the minimum notified under section 4, none of them is disputed, and all four want to move the Adjudicating Authority.

items.stem: What is wrong with the two decisions?

options.text: The point about the rights issue is right, but the shares may be held, since destruction is a SEBI requirement that binds listed companies alone
options.misconception: moves a Companies Act condition into the SEBI regulations
options.why: Section 68(7) sits in the Act and applies to every company that buys back its own shares, listed or unlisted. The SEBI regulations add to it for a listed company; they are not the source of it.

options.text: The shares had to be extinguished and physically destroyed within seven days of the last date of completion of the buy-back, so they cannot be held for resale; and no further issue of the same kind of shares may be made within six months, which catches the rights issue
options.why: Section 68(7) requires a company that has bought back its own shares to extinguish and physically destroy them within seven days of the last date of completion of the buy-back, which is why treasury shares are not an outcome the section allows. Section 68(8) then bars a further issue of the same kind of shares or other specified securities within a period of six months of the completion, and it names the further issue under section 62(1)(a) among the issues it stops. Its exceptions are a bonus issue and the discharge of subsisting obligations such as the conversion of warrants, a stock option scheme, sweat equity, or the conversion of preference shares or debentures into equity shares.

options.text: The point about the shares is right, but the rights issue is free because section 68(8) stops only a fresh public issue
options.misconception: reads "further issue of the same kind" as a public issue
options.why: The sub-section speaks of a further issue of the same kind of shares or other specified securities and mentions the allotment of new shares under section 62(1)(a) in terms. A rights issue of equity after a buy-back of equity is exactly what it stops.

options.text: Nothing — once the buy-back has been lawfully completed the section has no more to say
options.misconception: treats completion as the end of the section's conditions
options.why: Two of the conditions are written to bite after completion. One destroys the shares so that capital is actually reduced, and the other stops the company putting the same capital back within six months, which would make the whole exercise a device for supporting the price.

citation.ref: Sections 68(7) and 68(8), read with section 62(1)(a)

items.scenario: A company completes a buy-back of forty lakh equity shares on 12 June 2026, every condition of section 68 having been satisfied on the way in. The board then decides to keep the bought-back shares in the company's own name so that they can be sold when the price recovers, and three months later resolves on a rights issue of equity shares to fund a new plant. The company secretary sees no difficulty: the buy-back is over and its conditions were met.

items.stem: Is the chief financial officer right on either proposal?

options.text: On neither — section 129(4) applies the provisions on preparation, adoption and audit to the consolidated financial statements mutatis mutandis, and section 129(5) puts the disclosure of a deviation, its reasons and its financial effects on the company itself
options.why: Section 129(4) says the provisions of the Act applicable to the preparation, adoption and audit of the financial statements of a holding company shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to the consolidated financial statements, so they are audited, laid before the annual general meeting and adopted exactly as the standalone statements are. Section 129(5) then says that where the financial statements do not comply with the accounting standards, the company shall disclose the deviation, the reasons for it and the financial effects, if any, arising out of it — a duty of the company, discharged in its own statements.

options.text: On both — consolidated statements are prepared for information and the auditor is the proper person to flag a departure
options.misconception: treats the consolidated statements as a supplementary schedule rather than as financial statements
options.why: Section 129(4) exists to stop exactly that reading. Once a company has to prepare consolidated statements they carry the whole apparatus of the Act — audit, laying, adoption, filing — and the company's own disclosure duty under section 129(5) runs on them as well.

options.text: Right on the audit only — the consolidated statements need no separate opinion, but the company must disclose the deviation itself
options.misconception: keeps half of section 129(4)
options.why: The sub-section carries preparation, adoption and audit across together; it does not split them. A consolidated statement that nobody has audited is one nobody has tested, and it is the statement on which the group's true picture depends.

options.text: Right on the deviation only — the auditor's report is where non-compliance with an accounting standard is reported
options.misconception: moves the company's own disclosure duty onto its auditor
options.why: The auditor reports under section 143(3)(e) whether, in his opinion, the financial statements comply with the accounting standards. That is his obligation and it does not relieve the company of the separate disclosure section 129(5) requires it to make.

citation.ref: Sections 129(4) and 129(5), read with section 143(3)(e)

items.scenario: A holding company prepares consolidated financial statements for the year. Its chief financial officer proposes that they be sent to members for information but not put to the annual general meeting for adoption and not audited, since the standalone statements already carry an audit opinion. He also proposes that a departure from one accounting standard in a group measurement be left for the auditor to describe in his report, rather than mentioned by the company anywhere in its own statements.

items.stem: What has the board missed?

options.text: The committee is needed, but the managing director may chair it, since he is the person answerable to shareholders
options.misconception: puts an executive at the head of a committee the section reserves for a non-executive
options.why: Section 178(5) says the chairperson shall be a non-executive director. The committee exists to look at the company's dealings with its own security holders from outside the executive line, which is why the section names the class of director rather than the office.

options.text: Nothing — grievances about transfers and dividends are administrative and belong with the company secretary
options.misconception: treats a statutory committee as an optional layer over an existing process
options.why: The section makes it a committee of the Board once the count of security holders is crossed, and puts a non-executive director at its head, so that the people whose grievances are being answered are not answered by the management they are complaining about.

options.text: The committee is needed only where the company has securities listed on a stock exchange
options.misconception: reads a Companies Act committee as a listing requirement
options.why: The trigger in section 178(5) is a count of shareholders, debenture holders, deposit holders and other security holders, and it says nothing about listing. An unlisted company past that count owes the committee.

options.text: A Stakeholders Relationship Committee chaired by a non-executive director, to consider and resolve the grievances of the security holders; and that the chairperson of each committee constituted under section 178, or a member he authorises, must attend the general meetings
options.why: Section 178(5) requires the Board of a company which consists of more than one thousand shareholders, debenture holders, deposit holders and any other security holders at any time during a financial year to constitute a Stakeholders Relationship Committee, whose chairperson shall be a non-executive director. Section 178(6) gives that committee the work of considering and resolving the grievances of the security holders. Section 178(7) requires the chairperson of each of the committees constituted under the section, or in his absence a member of the committee authorised by him, to attend the general meetings.

items.scenario: A company has about fourteen hundred shareholders and three hundred debenture holders. Its board has an audit committee and a nomination and remuneration committee, and says nothing further is needed. Complaints about share transfers and unpaid dividends go to the company secretary, who answers to the managing director. At the last annual general meeting the chairperson of the audit committee did not attend and sent nobody, and the chairman of the meeting told a member that a committee chairperson has no business at a general meeting.

items.stem: Is counsel right?

options.text: No, but no offer is needed here because the rights come out of an agreement rather than out of shares
options.misconception: reads control as something only shares can carry
options.why: Regulation 2(1)(e) names shareholders agreements and voting agreements inside the definition itself, precisely so that control acquired on paper is treated the same as control acquired by buying votes.

options.text: No, but the trigger is Regulation 3(1), because acquiring control is deemed to be an acquisition of twenty-five per cent of the voting rights
options.misconception: invents a deemed shareholding to force control into a percentage trigger
options.why: Nothing is deemed. Regulation 3(1) is about crossing twenty-five per cent of the voting rights, and Regulation 4 stands beside it for the acquirer who takes control without crossing anything.

options.text: No — Regulation 4 requires an open offer for the acquisition of control irrespective of the acquisition or holding of any shares or voting rights
options.why: Regulation 4 of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 says that irrespective of acquisition or holding of shares or voting rights in a target company, no acquirer shall acquire, directly or indirectly, control over such target company unless he makes a public announcement of an open offer. Regulation 2(1)(e) defines control to include the right to appoint a majority of the directors or to control the management or policy decisions, exercisable by shareholding, management rights, shareholders agreements, voting agreements or in any other manner. The right to appoint a majority of the board is control on the face of that definition, and the percentage is beside the point.

options.text: Yes — the Regulations are a set of shareholding thresholds and he has crossed none of them
options.misconception: reads the code as being about percentages alone
options.why: The percentage triggers are one route to an open offer and the acquisition of control is a separate one, written in its own regulation and opening with the words "irrespective of acquisition or holding of shares or voting rights".

citation.source: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
citation.ref: Regulation 4, read with Regulation 2(1)(e) and Regulation 3(1)

items.scenario: An investor holds nine per cent of the voting rights of a listed company and does not propose to buy a single further share. Under a shareholders' agreement signed on 1 September 2026 he obtains the right to appoint a majority of the board of directors and a veto over the annual business plan. His counsel advises that no open offer arises, because the takeover code works on shareholding percentages and nine per cent is nowhere near any of them.

items.stem: What is wrong with what he has told the Adjudicating Authority?

options.text: The one hundred and twenty days is right, but within it the plan may be filed whenever the resolution professional is ready
options.misconception: reads a single deadline where the section sets two
options.why: Section 54D sets an outer limit for the process and an earlier one for the submission of the approved plan, so that the Adjudicating Authority has time to consider it inside the outer limit rather than on its last day.

options.text: The timetable could have been extended by the committee of creditors on a sixty-six per cent vote, so nothing is lost
options.misconception: borrows the extension in section 12(2) for a chapter that has none
options.why: Section 12(2) lets the committee resolve to extend a corporate insolvency resolution process beyond one hundred and eighty days. Chapter III-A has no equivalent — its answer to a process that has run out of time is termination under section 54D(3), not extension.

options.text: Both clocks have already run out — the process had to be completed within one hundred and twenty days of the commencement date, and the approved plan had to be submitted to the Adjudicating Authority within ninety days of it
options.why: Section 54D(1) requires the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process to be completed within a period of one hundred and twenty days from the pre-packaged insolvency commencement date, so a process that commenced on 1 April 2026 was over at the end of July. Section 54D(2) separately requires the resolution professional to submit the resolution plan as approved by the committee of creditors to the Adjudicating Authority within ninety days from that date. Section 54D(3) is what happens when he cannot: he files an application for termination of the process the day after that period expires.

options.text: Nothing — the one hundred and eighty days runs for every process the Code creates
options.misconception: carries the section 12 timetable into Chapter III-A
options.why: The one hundred and eighty days belongs to section 12 and to the corporate insolvency resolution process. Chapter III-A was written to be faster because the debtor stays in possession and the plan is largely settled before the process begins, and section 54D carries its own two clocks.

citation.ref: Sections 54D(1), 54D(2) and 54D(3), read with section 12

items.scenario: A pre-packaged insolvency resolution process for an eligible micro enterprise commences on 1 April 2026. On 20 August 2026 the resolution professional tells the Adjudicating Authority that the committee of creditors approved a resolution plan on 15 August and that he will file it in the next few weeks. He adds that there is no hurry, because the pre-packaged process has the same one hundred and eighty day outer limit as an ordinary corporate insolvency resolution process, with the same extension available on a vote of the committee.

items.stem: How do the two stand under section 4?

options.text: The matched discount is protected by the Explanation to section 4(2)(a), which takes out a discriminatory condition or price adopted to meet the competition; cutting output and shelving the upgrade is abuse under section 4(2)(b)
options.why: Section 4(2)(a) makes it an abuse to impose an unfair or discriminatory condition or price in the purchase or sale of goods or services, and its Explanation says that this shall not include such discriminatory condition or price which may be adopted to meet the competition. A discount confined to the one customer a rival has quoted for, and still above cost, is that case exactly. Section 4(2)(b) is a separate limb and it is where the second act lands: limiting or restricting production of goods or provision of services, or technical or scientific development relating to goods or services, to the prejudice of consumers.

options.text: Neither is an abuse — a producer decides its own output and its own research priorities, and matching a rival's price is ordinary trade
options.misconception: treats output and research as commercial freedoms a dominant enterprise keeps intact
options.why: They are freedoms for everybody else. Section 4(2)(b) names limiting or restricting production and technical or scientific development to the prejudice of consumers as an abuse precisely because a dominant enterprise's restraint is felt by the whole market rather than absorbed by it.

options.text: Both are abuses, because a dominant enterprise may never charge two customers different prices
options.misconception: reads section 4(2)(a) without the Explanation attached to it
options.why: The Explanation is part of the same provision and it says the discriminatory price does not include one adopted to meet the competition. Without it a dominant firm could never respond to a rival's quote at all, which would protect the rival rather than the customer.

options.text: The discount is an abuse and the output cut is not, since discrimination between customers is the clearest case the section contains
options.misconception: keeps the general words of section 4(2)(a) and ignores both its Explanation and section 4(2)(b)
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both halves. The Explanation takes the matched discount out, and section 4(2)(b) puts the output cut in.

citation.ref: Sections 4(2)(a) with its Explanation and 4(2)(b), read with section 4(1)

items.scenario: An enterprise that is dominant in the supply of industrial gas does two things in the same quarter. In one city a new rival quotes a lower price to a large hospital, and the enterprise offers that hospital — and nobody else — a matching discount, which still leaves its price above its own cost of production. Separately it cuts back output of the small cylinder size hospitals prefer, so that buyers move to its larger and costlier size, and shelves a purification upgrade its engineers had ready for release.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: Section 273(1) gives the Tribunal five courses, an interim order and a provisional liquidator among them; an order under that sub-section must be made within ninety days of the presentation of the petition; and before appointing a provisional liquidator the Tribunal must give the company notice and a reasonable opportunity to make representations, unless it records special reasons in writing for dispensing with the notice
options.why: Section 273(1) lets the Tribunal dismiss the petition with or without costs, make any interim order it thinks fit, appoint a provisional liquidator of the company till the making of a winding up order, make an order for winding up with or without costs, or make any other order it thinks fit — five courses and not two. Its first proviso requires the order to be made within ninety days from the date of presentation of the petition. Its second proviso is the safeguard the Registrar is asking the Tribunal to skip: notice to the company and a reasonable opportunity to make its representations before a provisional liquidator is appointed, unless for special reasons recorded in writing the Tribunal dispenses with it.

options.text: A provisional liquidator may be appointed at once and without notice as a matter of course, since urgency is the whole reason the power exists
options.misconception: reads an exception as if it were the rule
options.why: The exception exists and it is conditional. The Tribunal may dispense with the notice only for special reasons recorded in writing, and a dispensation given as a matter of course would swallow the safeguard the second proviso was written to create.

options.text: The company is right — the Tribunal either winds the company up or dismisses the petition, and it has no timetable
options.misconception: reads the jurisdiction as all or nothing and reads the provisos out of the sub-section
options.why: Interim orders and the appointment of a provisional liquidator are clauses (b) and (c) of the same sub-section, and the first proviso puts a ninety-day limit on the decision. A petition that can neither be disposed of nor policed in the meantime would be the worst of both.

options.text: The ninety days is directory only, and in any case no interim order may be made, because an interim order in a winding up would prejudge the petition
options.misconception: treats an interim order as a partial final order
options.why: An interim order preserves the position while the petition is decided, which is the opposite of deciding it. The Act contemplates it in clause (b) of section 273(1) and puts the outer limit on the decision in the proviso that follows.

citation.ref: Section 273(1) with both its provisos, read with section 272(1)

items.scenario: The Registrar presents a petition for the winding up of a company on 5 January 2026, with the previous sanction of the Central Government. At the first hearing he asks the Tribunal to appoint a provisional liquidator at once and without notice, because the directors are said to be moving assets out. The company replies that the Tribunal's only choice on a winding up petition is to order a winding up or to dismiss the petition, that it may take as long as it likes to decide, and that a provisional liquidator cannot be appointed before the order.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Section 192 catches it — the section covers a director, or a person connected with him, acquiring assets from the company for consideration other than cash just as it covers the company acquiring from him, so prior approval by a resolution in general meeting was needed, with the value of the assets calculated by a registered valuer set out in the notice
options.why: Section 192(1) has two halves. Clause (a) covers the case where a director of the company or of its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or a person connected with him, acquires or is to acquire assets for consideration other than cash from the company; clause (b) covers the company acquiring such assets from him. A flat going to the whole-time director's son against shares is clause (a), and a son is a relative within section 2(77) and plainly a person connected with him. Section 192(2) then requires the notice for the resolution to include the particulars of the arrangement along with the value of the assets involved, duly calculated by a registered valuer.

options.text: The section does not apply, because the son is not a director of the company or of any company in its group
options.misconception: drops the connected person from a sub-section that names him
options.why: Section 192(1) names a director of the company or of its holding, subsidiary or associate company, "or a person connected with him". Without those words the section could be avoided by routing every arrangement through a relative, which is exactly what has happened here.

options.text: The section applies, but a Board resolution with the audit committee's note is enough where the counterparty is not the director himself
options.misconception: substitutes a board approval for the general meeting the section requires
options.why: Section 192(1) requires prior approval by a resolution of the company in general meeting, and it makes no distinction between the director and a person connected with him. The Board cannot approve for the members what the section reserves to them.

options.text: The section does not apply, because it catches only assets the company acquires from a director
options.misconception: reads one half of section 192(1) and stops
options.why: The sub-section is written in both directions on purpose. A company handing a valuable asset to a director's family against paper is the mischief just as much as a company buying an asset from him at a price nobody outside has tested.

citation.ref: Sections 192(1)(a) and 192(2), read with section 2(77) and section 247

items.scenario: A company owns a flat it no longer uses. It transfers the flat to the son of its whole-time director and, instead of taking money, accepts from the son shares he holds in an unlisted company. The Board approves the transfer at a meeting and the audit committee notes that the son holds no office in the company and that the flat is not worth very much. Nothing is put to any general meeting and no valuation is obtained from outside the company.

items.stem: What has been left out?

options.text: Nothing after the sanction — filing the certified copy of the order with the Registrar within thirty days completes everything the company owes
options.misconception: treats registration of the order as the end of the scheme's compliance
options.why: Section 232(5) does require the certified copy to be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of receipt of the order, and section 232(7) then runs for as long as the scheme takes to implement, with a certified annual statement to the Registrar each year until it is completed.

options.text: Nothing — the scheme itself and a valuation report are what a member needs in order to vote
options.misconception: treats the notice requirements as a matter for the companies to judge
options.why: Section 232(2) writes the list out and does not leave it to be judged. The directors' own report is the item that matters most to a small holder, because it is where the effect on his class, as against the promoters' class, has to be spelled out.

options.text: The notice had to carry a confirmation that a copy of the draft scheme had been filed with the Registrar, a directors' report explaining the effect of the compromise on each class of shareholders, key managerial personnel, promoters and non-promoter shareholders, and a supplementary accounting statement because the transferor's last annual accounts are more than six months old; and a certified statement has to be filed with the Registrar every year until the scheme is completed
