options.why: The default is what the notice demands payment of; the fourteen days are counted from the service of that notice, and they exist to give the guarantor a last chance to pay before an insolvency application is filed against him.

citation.ref: Sections 95(1) and 95(4), read with sections 60(2) and 94

items.scenario: A bank wants to move against the personal guarantor of a corporate debtor. It serves a notice of demand on him on 1 June 2026 and files an application under section 95 on 8 June 2026, through a resolution professional it has engaged for the purpose. The guarantor's counsel raises two objections: that a creditor must exhaust its remedies against the corporate debtor before touching the guarantor, and that a creditor may apply only in his own name and not through a professional.

items.stem: What may the Adjudicating Authority do?

options.text: Order a contribution from the director, but leave it unsecured, section 66 ending with the direction to contribute and giving no power to attach anything
options.misconception: overlooks section 67, which exists to give the order teeth
options.why: Section 67(1) is written for exactly this. It lets the Adjudicating Authority direct that the liability be a charge on the debts the corporate debtor owes that person or on the security he holds over its assets, so a director cannot set off his own claim against the contribution he has been ordered to make.

options.text: Order a contribution from all three, section 66(2) reaching every person who was in charge of and responsible to the corporate debtor for the conduct of its business
options.misconception: imports a formula from other statutes into a sub-section that names a director or a partner
options.why: That formula belongs to provisions such as section 48 of the Competition Act, 2002 and section 179 of the Companies Act's penal scheme. Section 66(2) says director or partner, and the professional who wants to reach a shadow controller has to prove the intent section 66(1) requires.

options.text: Order a contribution from the director and the chief financial officer, an officer in default being treated as a director for this purpose
options.misconception: stretches "officer in default" into "director" where the Code names the office
options.why: Officer in default is a Companies Act concept used for penalties under that Act. Section 66(2) does not use it, and a chief financial officer who is not on the board is not a director however senior he is.

options.text: Order a contribution from the director alone, wrongful trading being directed at a director or a partner of the corporate debtor; the chief financial officer and the holding company could only be reached under the fraudulent trading limb, which needs an intent that is not made out — and the Authority may make the contribution a charge on what the corporate debtor owes the director or on any security he holds over its assets
options.why: Section 66(2) opens on an application by the resolution professional and lets the Adjudicating Authority direct a director or a partner of the corporate debtor to make a contribution — the persons it names hold that legal status and no others are within it. Section 66(1) is the wider net, reaching any persons who were knowingly parties to carrying on the business with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose, but that intent has to be proved and the facts here disclose none. Section 67(1) then lets the Authority give directions for giving effect to an order under section 66, and in particular provide for the liability of the person under the order to be a charge on any debt or obligation due from the corporate debtor to him, or on any mortgage or interest in a mortgage on the assets of the corporate debtor held by him.

citation.ref: Sections 66(1), 66(2) and 67(1)

items.scenario: On the resolution professional's application the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that the business was carried on after there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding the process. Three respondents are named: an executive director of the company; the chief financial officer, who held no directorship; and the foreign holding company, which gave day-to-day instructions but held no office. There is no evidence of any intention to defraud anybody. The professional asks for a contribution from all three and for it to be secured.

items.stem: Which of them needs registration as an investment adviser?

options.text: The insurance agent and the fourth, since a recommendation to buy a unit linked insurance plan is a recommendation about a security
options.misconception: treats the agent's insurance products as securities and drops the exemption written for him
options.why: The exemption covers an insurance agent or broker offering investment advice solely on insurance products. The moment he advises on shares or mutual funds as well he is outside it, but an agent who stays with insurance stays inside it.

options.text: The fourth and the portfolio manager, because a person already registered with SEBI in one capacity must take a second registration before advising at all
options.misconception: reads the incidental-advice exemption as unavailable to an existing SEBI registrant
options.why: The Regulations do the opposite: a stock broker, portfolio manager or merchant banker giving advice incidental to the activity for which he is registered is named in the exemption, because his conduct in that activity is already regulated.

options.text: All four, because Regulation 4 postpones registration for the exempted persons rather than removing the requirement
options.misconception: reads an exemption as a deferment
options.why: Regulation 4 says such persons are not required to seek registration for the advice it describes. It is not a transitional provision, and nothing in it starts a clock.

options.text: Only the fourth — the Regulations exempt an advocate whose investment advice is incidental to his legal practice, an insurance agent offering advice solely on insurance products, and a portfolio manager whose advice is incidental to the activity he is already registered for
options.why: Regulation 4 of the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 exempts a list of persons from the requirement to register, and one thread runs through the whole list: the advice is incidental to something else the person is already doing. It names an insurance agent or insurance broker offering investment advice solely on insurance products; an advocate, solicitor or law firm giving investment advice incidental to legal practice; a stock broker, portfolio manager or merchant banker giving advice incidental to the activity for which he holds his own registration; and a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India or of the other named professional bodies whose advice is incidental to his professional service. Regulation 3(1) bites on the fourth because his advice is incidental to nothing — it is the business itself.

citation.ref: Regulation 4, read with Regulation 3(1)

items.scenario: Four people advise on securities and none of them holds a certificate of registration as an investment adviser. An advocate, while settling a family arrangement for a client, advises him to sell one listed holding and buy another. An insurance agent recommends insurance products and nothing else. A portfolio manager registered with SEBI advises his own portfolio management clients as part of that service. And a fourth man runs a paid advisory desk whose only business is telling subscribers which shares to buy.

items.stem: What is the position under section 130?

options.text: The application lies, the income-tax authorities being named among those who may make it, but on the grounds the section states and no others; 2016-17 is out of reach, no order being permitted for a period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year; notice must go to the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board, any other statutory regulatory body and any person concerned, whose representations are considered before an order is made; and accounts revised under an order are final
options.why: Section 130(1) allows a company to re-open its books and recast its financial statements only on an order of a court of competent jurisdiction or of the Tribunal, made on an application by the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board, any other statutory regulatory body or authority, or any person concerned — and only on one of two grounds: that the relevant earlier accounts were prepared in a fraudulent manner, or that the affairs of the company were mismanaged during the relevant period casting a doubt on the reliability of the financial statements. Its proviso requires notice to those authorities and to any other person concerned and their representations to be taken into consideration before any order is passed. Sub-section (2) makes accounts so revised final, and sub-section (3) bars an order in respect of any period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year.

options.text: The application lies and no notice is needed, the Tribunal being entitled to act on the material the applicant places before it
options.misconception: drops the proviso that makes the hearing a wide one
options.why: The proviso to section 130(1) requires notice to the Central Government, the income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board or any other statutory regulatory body or authority concerned and to any other person concerned, and their representations to be considered. Re-opened accounts change what several regulators have already acted upon, which is why they are all called.

options.text: The application does not lie at all, a company's filed accounts being re-openable only on the company's own application to the Tribunal
options.misconception: takes the directors' voluntary route as the only route
options.why: The voluntary route is section 131 and it belongs to the directors. Section 130 is the route others take against the company, and it names the income-tax authorities in its own list of applicants.

options.text: The application lies and both years are within reach, section 130 setting no outer limit — the look-back restriction belongs to the voluntary route instead
options.misconception: strips section 130 of a limit it has and gives its limit to the other section
options.why: Both sections have limits and they are different. Section 130(3) bars an order for any period earlier than eight financial years preceding the current one; section 131(1) allows a voluntary revision for any of the three preceding financial years.

citation.ref: Sections 130(1) with its proviso, 130(2) and 130(3), read with section 131(1)

items.scenario: In the financial year 2026-27 the income-tax authorities apply to the Tribunal for an order re-opening a company's books and recasting its financial statements for two years, 2016-17 and 2021-22, saying the accounts of both were prepared in a fraudulent manner. The company answers that only it can ask for its own accounts to be re-opened, that nobody else need be heard on the application, and that in any case accounts once revised can always be revised again later.

items.stem: What does section 207 provide?

options.text: The duty to produce the books and papers and to render all assistance is on every director, officer and other employee of the company; and a director or officer convicted of disobeying it is not merely punished — on and from the date of conviction he is deemed to have vacated his office and is disqualified from holding office in any company
options.why: Section 207(1) makes it the duty of every director, officer or other employee of the company to produce to the Registrar or the inspector all books and papers of the company which are in their custody or power, to furnish any statement, information or explanation relating to the affairs of the company, and to render all assistance in connection with the inspection. Section 207(4) punishes a director or officer who disobeys, and then adds the consequence that no fine carries: where a director or an officer of the company has been convicted of an offence under the section, he shall on and from the date on which he is so convicted be deemed to have vacated his office as such and shall be disqualified from holding an office in any company.

options.text: The duty is the company's alone; an inspector who wants documents from an individual must summon him as a witness under the civil court powers the section confers
options.misconception: reads the power to summon as the only route to an individual
options.why: Section 207(1) puts the duty directly on every director, officer and other employee. The civil court powers in section 207(3) are an additional tool for the inspector, not a substitute for a duty the sub-section before it has already imposed.

options.text: An employee is outside the section, which names directors and officers only, so the warehouse manager was right to say nothing
options.misconception: drops the words "or other employee" from the duty
options.why: The sub-section names every director, officer or other employee. Records are usually in the custody of people well below board level, which is why the duty is written to reach whoever actually holds them.

options.text: The conviction carries a fine and no more; a disqualification from holding office in other companies arises only under section 164
options.misconception: overlooks the vacation and disqualification section 207(4) attaches to a conviction under it
options.why: Section 164 lists the general disqualifications, and section 207(4) adds one of its own for this offence: the office is deemed vacated from the date of conviction and the person is disqualified from holding an office in any company.

citation.ref: Sections 207(1) and 207(4), read with sections 206(5) and 207(3)

items.scenario: An inspector appointed by the Central Government under section 206(5) calls on a director and on the warehouse manager to produce the stock records and explain them. The director refuses, saying that only the company is bound to produce anything and that an employee owes an inspector nothing at all. He is later prosecuted and convicted for the refusal, and asks whether the conviction touches the two other boards he sits on.

items.stem: What may the Commission do?

options.text: Withdraw the benefit only for the false evidence limb; a disclosure that turns out to add nothing is still a disclosure honestly made
options.misconception: drops the vitality requirement written into the section's own words
options.why: The section asks for a disclosure that is full, true and vital, and the proviso names a disclosure found not to be vital as its own ground. Leniency is bought with information the Commission did not already have.

options.text: Nothing — a disclosure made before the Director General's report is protected, and the benefit once claimed cannot be withdrawn
options.misconception: reads the timing cut-off as the only condition the section imposes
options.why: Timing is the first gate and not the last. The section describes the disclosure that earns the benefit as full, true and vital, and attaches conditions of continuing cooperation, which is why a proviso exists to take the benefit away.

options.text: Impose the penalty the company would otherwise have been liable to, the section allowing the benefit to be withdrawn where the applicant does not comply with the conditions on which it was granted, gives false evidence, or the disclosure is found not to be vital
options.why: Section 46 of the Competition Act, 2002 lets the Commission impose a lesser penalty on a member of a cartel who makes a full, true and vital disclosure, and a proviso to it provides that where such an applicant does not comply with the conditions on which the lesser penalty was imposed, or gives false evidence, or the disclosure made is found not to be vital, he shall be liable to the penalty to which he would otherwise have been liable. Two of the three limbs are made out here: continuing to exchange prices with a rival is a failure to comply with the condition that the applicant cease to participate in the cartel, and a disclosure that adds nothing to what the Commission already had is not vital. Applying before the Director General's report is what gets an applicant through the door; it is not what keeps him inside.

options.text: Reduce the extent of the reduction it would otherwise have allowed, but not withdraw the benefit, since the company did disclose the existence of the cartel
options.misconception: treats the benefit as something scaled to the quality of the disclosure rather than as conditional
options.why: Where the conditions are broken the section restores the penalty the applicant would otherwise have been liable to. The graduated reduction is how much relief a compliant applicant gets; it is not the remedy for one who has broken the terms.

citation.ref: Section 46 with its provisos, as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023

items.scenario: A cartel member applies for a lesser penalty well before the Director General's report and makes a disclosure. As the inquiry runs it emerges that the company went on exchanging prices with one rival for months after the application, and that most of what it disclosed was already on the Commission's file and added nothing to the case. The company says the benefit cannot be taken back now: the disclosure was made in good faith and in time.

items.stem: Where is the chief financial officer wrong?

options.text: On the second — section 129A applies of its own force once a company is above the turnover figure prescribed for it, whatever is listed
options.misconception: gives an enabling section a trigger the Central Government has not yet prescribed
options.why: Section 129A does not work off any figure. It requires the Central Government to prescribe the class of unlisted companies, the periodical basis, the form and the manner of the audit or limited review before anything is due under it.

options.text: On the first — and the obligation that bites is Regulation 33, a listed entity being a listed entity and the results chapter applying to all of them
options.misconception: ignores that the LODR's chapters are keyed to the kind of security listed
options.why: Regulation 33 belongs to the chapter for an entity with listed specified securities. An entity whose only listed securities are non-convertible ones takes its obligations from Chapter V, where Regulation 52 states the results requirement written for it.

options.text: On none of the three — the company is not a listed entity, section 129A is not in force for it, and nothing is due to anybody
options.misconception: makes the listing of equity the test of a listed entity
options.why: The definition turns on any of the designated securities being listed, and non-convertible securities are on that list. A company that has raised money from the public debt market is answerable to the exchange for its results, whoever owns its equity.

options.text: On the first and so on the third — the Regulations apply to a listed entity that has listed any of the designated securities, and non-convertible securities are among them, so the company is a listed entity and must submit periodical financial results to the exchange under the chapter that governs entities with listed non-convertible securities; he is right about section 129A
options.why: The SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 apply to a listed entity which has listed any of the designated securities, and non-convertible securities are designated securities — so listing the debentures makes the company a listed entity even though its equity is unlisted. What changes is which chapter applies. Regulation 33 sits in the chapter written for an entity with listed specified securities, so it does not reach this company; Chapter V holds the obligations of an entity with listed non-convertible securities, and Regulation 52 there requires financial results to be submitted to the recognised stock exchange for each period it prescribes. Section 129A is a different question altogether and he is right about it: it is an enabling power that operates only on a class of unlisted companies the Central Government prescribes.

citation.source: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
citation.ref: Regulation 52 in Chapter V of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, read with Regulation 33 and section 129A of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A company whose equity shares are not listed anywhere has listed its non-convertible debentures on the debt segment of a recognised stock exchange. Its chief financial officer tells the audit committee three things: that the SEBI (LODR) Regulations do not touch the company at all because the equity is unlisted; that section 129A has not been brought to bear on any class of unlisted companies; and that the company therefore has no duty to publish periodical financial results to anybody.

items.stem: Is the resolution applicant right?

options.text: Yes — a plan approved under section 31 binds all stakeholders including the stock exchange and the regulator, so no listing condition survives it
options.misconception: reads section 31's binding effect as a repeal of continuing obligations the plan is silent about
options.why: Section 31 binds the stakeholders to what the plan provides, which settles the claims and the terms the plan deals with. It does not decide questions the plan never took up, and a company that goes on being listed goes on owing the exchange what every listed company owes it.

options.text: Yes on the exemption at least, since Regulation 3(2) applies to any resolution plan approved under section 31, whatever the plan provides
options.misconception: drops the condition attached to the carve-out
options.why: The carve-out is for a delisting made pursuant to such a plan — a plan providing for the delisting or for an exit to the existing public shareholders at a specified price. A plan that keeps the company listed never engages the Delisting Regulations, so there is nothing for the exemption to remove.

options.text: No — the exemption is for a plan that delists the shares or gives the public shareholders an exit at a specified price, and this plan does neither; a company that stays listed carries the minimum public shareholding requirement, and the timetable the exchange has stated is the one it has to meet
options.why: Regulation 3(2) of the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 takes those Regulations off a delisting made pursuant to a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. It is a carve-out from the delisting machinery for a plan that takes the shares off the exchange, and it says nothing about a plan that leaves them on it. A company whose shares remain listed is bound by the minimum public shareholding requirement in Rule 19A of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957 and Regulation 38 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, and Rule 19A itself fixes the period within which a company whose public shareholding has fallen below the minimum on the implementation of a resolution plan must restore it. Section 31 binds the stakeholders to the terms of the plan; it does not repeal a listing condition the plan never addressed.

options.text: No, but the company may apply to have the requirement waived, minimum public shareholding being a matter of the regulator's discretion in a rescue
options.misconception: treats a continuing listing condition as waivable on request
options.why: The requirement is in a Rule made under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 and is restored on a timetable rather than waived. What a rescued company gets is time, which is why Rule 19A carries its own period for a fall caused by the implementation of a resolution plan.

citation.ref: Regulation 3(2), read with Rule 19A of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957, Regulation 38 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 and section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

items.scenario: A resolution plan approved on 3 August 2026 leaves the company listed. The new owner takes ninety-two per cent of the equity and the public shareholding falls to eight per cent. The stock exchange writes to the company saying the public holding must be raised to at least ten per cent within twelve months and to twenty-five per cent within three years of the fall. The resolution applicant answers that the Delisting Regulations exempt a plan approved under section 31 from everything, and that section 31 makes the plan binding on the exchange as much as on anybody else.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: Everything is in order — the cap was not crossed, and a company that returns the application money in full owes nothing further
options.misconception: treats repayment as a cure regardless of when it happens
options.why: Repayment is not the test; the date of it is. Section 42(6) gives sixty days to allot and a further fifteen days to repay, and once both have gone the company repays with interest at twelve per cent a year measured from the expiry of the sixtieth day, not from the day it finally paid.

options.text: The placement is void because 237 persons were offered the securities, and the return of the money on 10 July cures nothing
options.misconception: counts every offeree, ignoring the two classes the Rules take out of the count
options.why: The arithmetic is right and the law is not. Rule 14 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 leaves qualified institutional buyers and employees offered securities under a stock option scheme out of the two hundred, which is why companies place with institutions without spending the cap.

options.text: The cap was never crossed, because qualified institutional buyers and employees under a stock option scheme are excluded from the count, leaving 195; but the money was due to be repaid within fifteen days of the sixty days running out, and because it was not, interest runs on it at twelve per cent a year from the day the sixtieth day expired
options.why: Section 42 caps a private placement at two hundred identified persons in a financial year, and Rule 14 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 excludes qualified institutional buyers and employees to whom shares are offered under a scheme of employees stock option from that count, so only the 195 identified persons are counted and the cap holds. Section 42(6) is what is broken: the company had to allot within sixty days from the receipt of the application money, and having failed, to repay within fifteen days from the expiry of those sixty days; a repayment after that carries interest at twelve per cent per annum from the expiry of the sixtieth day. Repaying on 10 July without interest does not answer it.

options.text: The allotment simply lapsed and the money had to go back within sixty days of the offer letter, which it did not, so the company must refund with interest from the date of the offer letter
options.misconception: measures both clocks from the offer letter instead of from the receipt of the money
options.why: Section 42(6) runs from the receipt of the application money and not from the date of the offer letter — sixty days to allot, fifteen more to repay, and interest thereafter from the expiry of the sixtieth day. The offer letter starts no clock of its own for this purpose.

citation.ref: Section 42(2) and section 42(6), read with Rule 14 of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: During 2026-27 an unlisted public company makes a private placement to 195 identified persons, to 30 qualified institutional buyers, and to 12 of its own employees under its stock option scheme. No offer is advertised, and every rupee comes through banking channels into a separate account. All the application money is received on 1 April 2026. The allotment is not made, and the money is returned to the applicants on 10 July 2026 without any interest. The finance head says the placement failed the moment the offerees crossed two hundred, and that returning the money is a complete answer to everything else.

items.stem: Is the company secretary right?

options.text: No on both, and no special resolution is needed for either, because a valuation report by a registered valuer is what section 62(1)(c) substitutes for the members' approval
options.misconception: treats the valuer's report as an alternative to the special resolution rather than an addition to it
options.why: Section 62(1)(c) requires both. The issue must be authorised by a special resolution and the price must be determined by the valuation report of a registered valuer; the report tells the members what they are approving, it does not stand in their place.

options.text: No on the investor, but yes on the loan — a conversion increases subscribed capital and so must be offered to existing shareholders first, whatever was resolved earlier
options.misconception: ignores section 62(3), which disapplies the whole section to an approved conversion
options.why: Section 62(3) exists precisely because a conversion does increase subscribed capital. It says nothing in the section applies where the terms of the loan were approved by a special resolution passed before the loan was raised, so the lender's option is honoured without going back to the members a second time.

options.text: Yes — section 62(1)(a) applies to every further issue, and an outside investor may be reached only through the renunciation of an existing shareholder
options.misconception: reads clause (a) as the whole of section 62 and drops clauses (b) and (c)
options.why: Section 62(1) opens with three clauses in the alternative — to existing shareholders under clause (a), to employees under a stock option scheme under clause (b), and to any persons on a special resolution under clause (c). Renunciation is a right of a shareholder inside clause (a); it is not the only door to an outsider.

options.text: No — a further issue to any persons on a special resolution and a valuer's report is its own route under section 62(1)(c), and a conversion of a loan whose terms were approved by special resolution before the loan was raised is taken outside section 62 altogether by section 62(3)
options.why: Section 62(1)(a) is the rights route, but section 62(1)(c) is an alternative: shares may be offered to any persons, if it is authorised by a special resolution, whether or not those persons are existing shareholders, at a price determined by the valuation report of a registered valuer and subject to Rule 13 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014. Section 62(3) then says nothing in the section applies to the increase of subscribed capital caused by the exercise of an option attached to debentures issued or a loan raised, where the terms of the issue or the loan were approved by a special resolution before the loan was raised. Neither route touches the pre-emptive offer.

citation.ref: Sections 62(1)(a), 62(1)(c) and 62(3), read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A company wants to do two things. It wants to issue fresh equity to a strategic investor who is not a member at all, at a price supported by a registered valuer's report and with a special resolution of the members. It also wants to convert a term loan into equity, the terms of the loan having been approved by the members by special resolution before the loan was raised. The company secretary advises that section 62 makes every further issue of share capital a rights issue first, so both must be offered to the existing shareholders before anybody else may be reached.

items.stem: Do the exceptions cover these two loans?

options.text: The second is covered and the first is not, because a loan from a holding company to its wholly owned subsidiary is outside section 185 whatever the money is spent on
options.misconception: applies the wholly owned subsidiary exception without its utilisation proviso
options.why: The proviso to section 185(3) requires that a loan made to a wholly owned subsidiary be utilised by the subsidiary for its principal business activities. A subsidiary that parks the money in listed shares has not done that, and the exception falls away.

options.text: Both are covered — a lending company and a wholly owned subsidiary are the two clearest exceptions in section 185(3) and neither carries any further condition
options.misconception: reads the exceptions as covering a class of lender rather than a class of loan
options.why: Each exception in section 185(3) carries its own condition inside it — a rate of interest for the lending company, and utilisation for the principal business activities for the subsidiary. Take the condition away and the exception does not apply, however the lender is described.

options.text: The first is covered and the second is not, because a lending company in the ordinary course of its business may lend at whatever rate its board approves
options.misconception: drops the interest-rate condition attached to the ordinary-course exception
options.why: The rate is the whole of the condition. Section 185(3) allows the ordinary-course lender the exception only where an interest is charged at a rate not less than the prevailing yield of the Government security closest to the tenor of the loan, which is there to stop a soft loan to a director's company being dressed as ordinary business.

options.text: Neither loan is covered — the lending company's exception applies only where interest is charged at not less than the prevailing yield of the Government security closest to the tenor of the loan, and the holding-to-subsidiary exception applies only where the subsidiary uses the money for its principal business activities
options.why: Section 185(3) is not a list of persons but a list of conditions. The exception for a company which in the ordinary course of its business provides loans requires that interest be charged at a rate not less than the rate of prevailing yield of one year, three year, five year or ten year Government security closest to the tenor of the loan, and eleven per cent below that yield fails it. The exception for a loan made by a holding company to its wholly owned subsidiary carries a proviso that the loan be utilised by the subsidiary for its principal business activities, and buying listed shares as an investment is not that.

citation.ref: Section 185(3) with its proviso, read with sections 185(1) and 185(2)

items.scenario: A non-banking finance company whose business is lending advances ₹5 crore to a body corporate in which one of its directors holds a controlling stake, charging eleven per cent a year, which is below the prevailing yield of the Government security closest to the tenor of that loan. Separately, a holding company lends ₹20 crore to its wholly owned subsidiary, which uses the money to buy listed equity shares as an investment rather than for the trade it was set up to carry on. Both boards say section 185 does not reach them because each falls inside an exception.

items.stem: What does section 180(1)(c) require?

options.text: Neither needs a special resolution because the ceiling in section 180(1)(c) is the paid-up share capital and free reserves alone, which the company has not been shown to exceed
options.misconception: leaves the securities premium account out of the aggregate the section names
options.why: The aggregate in section 180(1)(c) is the paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium taken together, and the securities premium of ₹10 crore is part of it. Leaving it out would give ₹70 crore, which the existing borrowings already match, so the omission changes the answer in the other direction too.

options.text: Neither facility needs a special resolution, because both are loans from the company's own bankers taken in the ordinary course of its business
options.misconception: reads the carve-out as covering any bank borrowing rather than only a temporary one
options.why: The carve-out is for temporary loans obtained from the company's bankers in the ordinary course of business, and the Explanation says what temporary means — repayable on demand or within six months, and never a loan raised for financial expenditure of a capital nature. A five-year loan to build a plant is the very thing the Explanation excludes.

options.text: Both facilities count, so the total of ₹95 crore exceeds ₹80 crore and one special resolution must cover the pair
options.misconception: brings the temporary bank facility into a computation the section keeps it out of
options.why: Section 180(1)(c) says apart from temporary loans obtained from the company's bankers in the ordinary course of business. A cash credit line repayable on demand is the example the Explanation itself gives, so it never enters the ₹95 crore figure.

options.text: The ₹5 crore cash credit is left out of the computation as a temporary loan from the company's bankers, but the ₹20 crore term loan counts and takes total borrowings past the ₹80 crore aggregate, so a special resolution is needed before it is taken
options.why: Section 180(1)(c) requires a special resolution where the money to be borrowed, together with the money already borrowed, will exceed the aggregate of the company's paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium — here ₹80 crore — apart from temporary loans obtained from the company's bankers in the ordinary course of business. The Explanation defines a temporary loan as one repayable on demand or within six months, such as a short-term cash credit arrangement, but expressly excludes loans raised for the purpose of financial expenditure of a capital nature. The cash credit is out; the plant loan is in, and ₹70 crore plus ₹20 crore is ₹90 crore.

citation.ref: Section 180(1)(c) with its Explanation, read with section 180(2)

items.scenario: A public company has paid-up share capital of ₹40 crore, free reserves of ₹30 crore and securities premium of ₹10 crore. It has already borrowed ₹70 crore. Its board now resolves, without going to the members, to take two further facilities from its bankers — a ₹5 crore cash credit line for working capital, repayable on demand, and a ₹20 crore five-year term loan to build a new plant. The chief financial officer says neither needs a special resolution, because both are bank facilities taken in the ordinary course of business.

items.stem: Which of these amounts are deposits?

options.text: The brother's ₹60 lakh and the ₹40 lakh advance — the relative's exclusion is available only to a private company, and an advance for goods stops being excluded once it has gone unappropriated beyond three hundred and sixty-five days; only the director's ₹1 crore stays out
options.why: Rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014 excludes an amount received from a person who at the time of receipt was a director of the company, or a relative of the director of the private company, where he furnishes a written declaration that the amount is not being given out of funds acquired by borrowing or accepting loans or deposits from others. The words attach the relative limb to a private company alone, so in a public company a brother's money is a deposit whatever he declares. The same Rule excludes an advance for the supply of goods only where it is appropriated against that supply within three hundred and sixty-five days from the date of acceptance, and eighteen months is past that.
keywords: relative of the director of the private company

options.text: Only the ₹40 lakh advance, the two declarations being enough for both the director and his brother because the Rule speaks of a director or his relative without distinguishing companies
options.misconception: reads the relative limb without the words that tie it to a private company
options.why: The Rule reads "a director of the company or a relative of the director of the private company", and those last three words are doing work. In a public company the exclusion reaches the director and stops there, which is why this is a favourite point in a case study.

options.text: All three — a public company may accept deposits from its members alone, so money from a director, from his brother and from a customer are all deposits from the public
options.misconception: collapses the director's own exclusion into the general bar on public deposits
options.why: A director's own money, supported by the written declaration the Rule requires, is excluded from the meaning of deposit altogether, so it is not a deposit from anybody. The bar on accepting deposits from the public applies to money that is a deposit in the first place.

options.text: None of them — the two declarations cover the first two sums and a trade advance is a commercial receipt that never becomes a deposit
options.misconception: extends the relative exclusion to a public company and treats a trade advance as permanently excluded
options.why: The declaration does its work only for the persons the Rule names, and for a relative that is a relative of the director of a private company. A trade advance is excluded conditionally, not absolutely — it must be appropriated against the supply within three hundred and sixty-five days, and an advance that outlives that period falls into the definition of deposit.

citation.ref: Sections 73(1) and 73(2), read with Rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: An unlisted public company that is not an eligible company receives three sums during 2026-27. ₹1 crore comes from one of its directors, who gives a written declaration that the money is his own and not borrowed. ₹60 lakh comes from that director's brother, who gives exactly the same declaration. ₹40 lakh comes from a customer as an advance against a supply of goods, and eighteen months later the goods have still not been supplied and the advance has not been appropriated. The company secretary records none of the three as deposits.

items.stem: What is the position of Mr P's office?

options.text: His office has become vacant twice over — section 167(1)(b) vacates the office of a director who absents himself from all the meetings of the Board held during a period of twelve months whether or not he took leave of absence, and section 164(3) lets a private company's articles add grounds of disqualification of their own
options.why: Section 167 vacates an office on grounds of its own and is not limited to a disqualification under section 164. Section 167(1)(b) says the office of a director shall become vacant where he absents himself from all the meetings of the Board of Directors held during a period of twelve months with or without leave of absence, so the leave he took is beside the point and five missed meetings in a row exhaust the ground. Section 164(3) separately allows a private company to provide by its articles for any disqualifications for appointment as a director in addition to those in sub-sections (1) and (2), which is where the shareholding condition takes effect.
keywords: with or without leave of absence

options.text: The article is fatal but the absence is not, because leave of absence granted by the Board preserves a director's office however many meetings he misses
options.misconception: reads leave of absence as saving an office that section 167(1)(b) vacates regardless
options.why: The words of section 167(1)(b) are "with or without leave of absence". They were put there to stop a board keeping an absent director in office by granting him leave, so the leave he was given makes no difference at all.

options.text: Nothing has happened, because section 167 vacates an office only where a director has incurred a disqualification under section 164 and he has incurred none
options.misconception: treats section 167 as attached to section 164 rather than carrying independent grounds
options.why: Section 167(1)(a) is the clause tied to section 164, and it is only the first of several. Clause (b) on absence from meetings, and the other clauses on contravening section 184, on conviction and sentence, and on a court order, all vacate an office without any section 164 disqualification behind them.

options.text: The absence is fatal but the article is not, because a company's articles cannot add a ground of disqualification to a list Parliament has written
options.misconception: denies a private company the extra grounds section 164(3) expressly permits
options.why: Section 164(3) says a private company may by its articles provide for any disqualifications for appointment as a director in addition to those specified in sub-sections (1) and (2). The statute invites the articles in, for a private company, which is what makes reading the articles part of the answer here.

citation.ref: Sections 167(1)(b) and 164(3), read with sections 164(1) and 167(1)(a)

items.scenario: Mr P is a director of a private company. Between 1 July 2025 and 30 June 2026 the board met five times and he attended none of them, having taken leave of absence for every one. The company's articles also provide that a director who ceases to hold at least one thousand equity shares of the company shall vacate his office, and Mr P sold his entire holding in May 2026. The company's financial statements and annual returns are all filed and up to date, and Mr P is under no personal incapacity. The board says nothing has happened, because section 164 lists neither absence from meetings nor a shareholding requirement.

items.stem: Where is the counsel wrong?

options.text: Only on the creditor — the reliefs are correctly stated, because once a resolution has been passed the members' remedy is confined to damages against the directors
options.misconception: limits section 245 to compensation and ignores the declaratory and restraining orders in it
options.why: Damages under section 245(1)(g) are the last of the orders, not the only one. The section was drafted to let a class stop something as well as be paid for it, which is why declaring the resolution void and restraining the directors from acting on it are both on the list.

options.text: On the reliefs and on the creditor — section 245(1) lets the Tribunal declare void a resolution altering the memorandum or articles where it was passed by suppression of material facts and restrain the company and its directors from acting on it, but the application may be made only by members or depositors or any class of them, so the supplier has no standing
options.why: Section 245(1) is not confined to damages. Its list of orders begins with restraining the company from committing an act ultra vires the memorandum or articles, and includes declaring a resolution altering the memorandum or articles void where the resolution was passed by suppression of material facts or obtained by mis-statement, and restraining the company and its directors from acting on such a resolution. Who may ask is the other half of the section, and it names the requisite number of members or depositors, or any class of them. A trade creditor is neither, so he cannot join.

options.text: On nothing — the members' only route against a resolution passed by suppression of facts is an application for oppression and mismanagement under sections 241 and 244
options.misconception: sends a class action down the oppression route the Act keeps separate from it
options.why: Sections 241 and 244 give a remedy for affairs conducted in a manner prejudicial or oppressive, and they run against the company and its management. Section 245 is a separate remedy with its own list of orders and its own class of applicants, and the members here may use it.

options.text: Only on the reliefs — the supplier may join, because a class action is open to any class of persons whose interests are prejudiced by the conduct of the company's affairs
options.misconception: reads "any class of them" as opening the section to persons other than members and depositors
options.why: The words "or any class of them" attach to the members and the depositors already named; they widen how those two groups may come, not who may come. A creditor's remedy lies elsewhere — in his own suit, or under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 — and not in section 245.

citation.ref: Section 245(1), contrasted with sections 241 and 244

items.scenario: An unlisted public company passed a special resolution altering the objects clause of its memorandum, having kept from the members a material fact about the promoter's interest in the new business. A group of members well above the number the Rules require, joined by a trade supplier the company owes money to, wants the Tribunal to declare the resolution void and to stop the directors acting on it. The company's counsel says a class action lies only for damages after the loss has been suffered, that a resolution already passed cannot be touched, and that a creditor stands in the same shoes as a member.

items.stem: What is the correct position on the two questions?

options.text: The managing director is right about the valuation, which belongs to the Board under section 179, and the committee's remit is confined to the financial statements and the auditors
options.misconception: reads the committee's terms of reference as ending at the accounts
options.why: Section 177(4) reaches well past the accounts — scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments, valuation of undertakings or assets of the company wherever it is necessary, evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems, and monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers are all in the list.

options.text: The recommendation does not bind the Board and nothing need be said about it anywhere, the committee's views being internal to the company
options.misconception: leaves out the disclosure section 177(8) requires when a recommendation is refused
options.why: Section 177(8) is the whole answer to a Board that departs from its audit committee. The Board's report must disclose the composition of the committee and, where a recommendation has not been accepted, that fact with the reasons, so the members read the disagreement before they vote.

options.text: The recommendation does not bind the Board, but section 177(8) requires the Board's report to disclose that a recommendation of the audit committee was not accepted and the reasons for it; and the valuation of undertakings or assets of the company, wherever it is necessary, is inside the committee's terms of reference under section 177(4)
options.why: Section 139(1) makes the appointment of the auditor an act of the members at the annual general meeting on the Board's proposal, so the audit committee recommends and does not decide. What the Act does instead is make the disagreement visible: section 177(8) requires the Board's report to disclose the composition of the audit committee and, where the Board has not accepted any recommendation of the committee, to disclose that along with the reasons for it. Section 177(4) then lists the committee's terms of reference and valuation of undertakings or assets of the company, wherever it is necessary, is one of them.

options.text: The recommendation binds the Board, because section 177(4) puts the recommendation for appointment and remuneration of auditors in the committee's hands
options.misconception: turns a power to recommend into a power to appoint
options.why: Section 177(4) gives the committee the recommendation and section 139(1) gives the members the appointment. The Act deals with a Board that overrides the committee by making it say so in its report under section 177(8), not by taking the decision away from it.

citation.ref: Sections 177(4) and 177(8), read with section 139(1)

items.scenario: A listed company's audit committee, properly constituted, recommends against proposing the existing audit firm for reappointment, giving its reasons in writing. The Board disagrees and puts the firm to the members at the annual general meeting anyway. Separately, the Board proposes to have an undertaking of the company valued for a possible sale, and the managing director tells the committee that a valuation is a Board matter with which it has no concern. The company secretary advises that the committee's recommendation binds the Board and that the valuation is indeed outside its remit.

items.stem: What does section 90 require the company itself to do?

options.text: It must apply to the Tribunal at once for an order restricting the shares, the empty register being enough on its own
options.misconception: skips the notice and the reply period the section places before any application
options.why: The application is the last step and not the first. Section 90(7) allows it only where the person noticed under section 90(5) fails to give the information within the thirty days section 90(6) allows, or gives information that is not satisfactory, and it must then be made within fifteen days of the expiry of that period.

options.text: It must go and find him — section 90(4A) puts the company under a duty to take steps to identify a significant beneficial owner, section 90(5) lets it give notice in Form BEN-4, the recipient has thirty days to reply, and on no reply or an unsatisfactory one the company must apply to the Tribunal within fifteen days for an order restricting the shares
options.why: Section 90(4A) requires every company to take necessary steps to identify an individual who is a significant beneficial owner in relation to it and to require him to comply with the section, so the duty does not wait on a declaration. Section 90(5) lets the company give notice in Form BEN-4 to any person it knows or has reasonable cause to believe to be a significant beneficial owner or to have knowledge of one. Section 90(6) gives that person thirty days to give the information. Where no information is given or the information given is not satisfactory, section 90(7) requires the company to apply to the Tribunal within fifteen days of the expiry of that period for an order restricting the shares, which the Tribunal passes within sixty days under section 90(8).

options.text: It must report the body corporate to the Registrar, who then investigates and identifies the individual behind it
options.misconception: hands the company's own enquiry to the Registrar
options.why: The Registrar is not the enquiring authority here. Section 90 puts the enquiry on the company — identify under sub-section (4A), notice under sub-section (5), reply under sub-section (6) — and the forum for an unanswered notice is the Tribunal under sub-section (7), not the Registrar.

options.text: Nothing until a declaration is filed — the obligation in section 90(1) is on the individual, and the company's part is to file Form BEN-2 once it has a declaration to file
options.misconception: reads the company's role as passive, which section 90(4A) was inserted to end
options.why: Section 90(1) does put a declaration on the individual and the company does file Form BEN-2 once it has one. Section 90(4A) was inserted afterwards precisely because that left a company free to know nothing, and it now requires the company to take necessary steps to identify the individual itself.

citation.ref: Sections 90(4A), 90(5), 90(6), 90(7) and 90(8), read with Rule 2(1)(h) of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018

items.scenario: An unlisted public company's register of members shows a body corporate holding eighteen per cent of its equity. The company's directors know that the body corporate is controlled by an individual, but nobody has declared anything and the register of significant beneficial owners is empty. The company secretary says the company's duty begins only when a declaration in Form BEN-1 arrives, and that until an individual comes forward there is nothing the company can do.

items.stem: What does section 197 permit?

options.text: The excess is his unless the company sues for it, and a special resolution at any later general meeting can put the matter beyond doubt
options.misconception: treats the excess as the director's money and the waiver as available without a time limit
options.why: Section 197(9) makes him hold the sum in trust for the company until he refunds it, so it is the company's money in his hands. Section 197(10) then puts a two-year limit on any waiver, measured from the date the sum becomes refundable, and a resolution outside that window cannot waive anything.

options.text: The company may waive recovery by an ordinary resolution, a waiver being a matter of ordinary business once the excess has been disclosed in the accounts
options.misconception: downgrades the special resolution section 197(10) requires
options.why: Section 197(10) names a special resolution and nothing less. The excess arose because the limits themselves may be exceeded only on a special resolution, so letting a simple majority forgive it afterwards would undo the section.

options.text: He must refund it and holds it in trust for the company until he does; the company may waive recovery only by a special resolution passed within two years from the date the sum became refundable, and because a default to a public financial institution is running, that lender's prior approval must be obtained before the members are asked
options.why: Section 197(9) says a director who draws remuneration in excess of the limits shall refund the sum to the company and, until it is refunded, hold it in trust for the company, so the money is the company's from the start and not his. Section 197(10) forbids the company to waive recovery unless approved by special resolution within two years from the date the sum becomes refundable, which puts the outer date at 30 September 2028 and makes a September 2028 meeting the last chance. Its proviso requires that where the company has defaulted in payment of dues to any bank or public financial institution or non-convertible debenture holder or other secured creditor, the prior approval of that creditor be obtained before the shareholders are asked.

options.text: The lender's approval is irrelevant, and Central Government approval is what section 197 requires before any excess remuneration may be retained
options.misconception: revives the Central Government approval abolished in 2018 and drops the lender's prior approval
options.why: Central Government approval for remuneration beyond the section 197 limits was removed by the 2017 amendment with effect from 2018, and what replaced it is the members' special resolution. The proviso to section 197(10) then adds the lender, requiring the prior approval of the bank, public financial institution, non-convertible debenture holder or other secured creditor whose dues are in default.

citation.ref: Sections 197(9) and 197(10) with its proviso, read with section 197(1)

items.scenario: A public company's managing director drew remuneration for 2025-26 that exceeded the limit section 197 allows, and no special resolution was passed at any time. The excess became refundable on 30 September 2026. The company has defaulted in repaying a term loan to a public financial institution, and that default is continuing. The Board wants to let the managing director keep the excess and proposes to put a special resolution to the members at the annual general meeting in September 2028, taking the view that the money is his until the members say otherwise and that the lender has no say in the company's remuneration decisions.

items.stem: Is the finance head right on either point?

options.text: On neither — Rule 4(3) exempts all three from cost audit on those facts and not on which Table the industry sits in, and the exemption is from the audit alone, the duty to maintain cost records under Rule 3 continuing unaffected
options.why: Rule 4(3) of the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014 exempts from the requirement of cost audit a company whose revenue from exports in foreign exchange exceeds seventy-five per cent of its total revenue, a company operating from a special economic zone, and a company engaged in the generation of electricity for captive consumption through a captive generating plant. Each of the three answers one of those descriptions on its own facts. The Tables decide coverage and thresholds, not exemption, and Rule 3 keeps the cost records requirement running for a covered company whether or not its accounts are audited.

options.text: Right on the records but wrong on the Tables — the three exemptions apply across both Tables, and a company exempt from cost audit is relieved of maintaining cost records as well
options.misconception: reads an exemption from the audit as an exemption from the records
options.why: Rule 4 is headed by the audit and Rule 3 by the records, and the exemption in Rule 4(3) is expressed as an exemption from the requirement of cost audit. A covered company continues to include the particulars of cost in its books under section 148(1) and Rule 3.

options.text: Right on the Tables but wrong on the records — the export exemption applies only to a company in the non-regulated sector, because a regulated industry is audited on public interest grounds
options.misconception: attaches a sector condition to an exemption Rule 4(3) writes without one
options.why: Rule 4(3) names three descriptions of company and attaches no sector condition to any of them. The regulated and non-regulated split in the Tables governs which industries are covered and at what turnover, and it stops there.

options.text: On both — Table A companies are in the regulated sector and can never be exempt, while a Table B company that is exempt from cost audit keeps no cost records
options.misconception: makes the exemption turn on the Table and treats records and audit as one duty
options.why: Rule 4(3) is written by reference to what the company does with its revenue and where it operates, and it applies across both Tables. Rule 3 imposes the record-keeping duty separately, and nothing in Rule 4(3) touches it — a company exempt from the audit still writes the records the audit would have examined.

citation.ref: Rule 4(3) of the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014, read with Rule 3 of those Rules and sections 148(1) and 148(2) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: Three companies sit in industries listed in the Tables to the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014 and each crosses the turnover threshold for cost audit. The first earns eighty per cent of its total revenue from exports in foreign exchange. The second operates wholly from a special economic zone. The third generates electricity solely for its own captive consumption. Their common finance head says the exemption depends entirely on whether the industry sits in Table A or Table B, and that in any case a company exempt from cost audit need keep no cost records either.

items.stem: What has the plan missed?

options.text: Three things — a notice of the proposed scheme inviting objections or suggestions from the Registrar, the Official Liquidator and persons affected by the scheme, within thirty days; a declaration of solvency filed by each company with the Registrar; and the cancellation of the shares the transferee holds in the transferor, which it may not keep in its own name
options.why: Section 233(1)(a) requires a notice of the proposed scheme inviting objections or suggestions from the Registrar and Official Liquidators where the registered offices of the companies are situated, and from persons affected by the scheme, within thirty days. Section 233(1)(b) requires each of the companies to file a declaration of solvency with the Registrar before convening the meeting. Section 233(11) then says the transferee company shall not on merger or amalgamation hold any shares in its own name or in the name of any trust, and all such shares shall be cancelled or extinguished, so treasury shares are not an outcome the section allows.

options.text: Only the notice — a declaration of solvency is required only in a members' voluntary winding up, and a transferee may hold shares in the transferor as an investment once the merger is registered
options.misconception: borrows the winding-up context for the declaration and ignores section 233(11)
options.why: Section 233(1)(b) writes the declaration of solvency into the merger itself, in the prescribed form and filed with the Registrar. Section 233(11) is equally express that the transferee shall not hold shares in its own name or in the name of any trust and that all such shares shall be cancelled or extinguished.

options.text: Nothing — with more than ninety per cent of total shares and nine-tenths in value of creditors, section 233 asks for nothing more from anybody outside the two companies
options.misconception: treats the two approval thresholds as the whole of section 233
options.why: The thresholds are only sub-clauses (c) and (d). Sub-clause (a) puts the scheme in front of the Registrar, the Official Liquidator and persons affected by it for thirty days, and sub-clause (b) requires a declaration of solvency, both before the approvals are taken.

options.text: Only the shares — the notice and the declaration of solvency belong to a scheme under section 232 before the Tribunal, and section 233 exists to dispense with them
options.misconception: assumes the fast track dispenses with every formality rather than with the Tribunal
options.why: What section 233 dispenses with is the Tribunal, not the scrutiny. The notice under section 233(1)(a) and the declaration of solvency under section 233(1)(b) are the fast track's own requirements, and objections raised on that notice are what can send the scheme to the Tribunal under section 233(5).

items.scenario: A holding company proposes to absorb its wholly owned subsidiary under section 233. It has the members' approval by more than ninety per cent of the total number of shares and written approval from creditors representing more than nine-tenths in value. It has told nobody outside the two companies, has filed no declaration of solvency, and proposes on the merger to keep the shares it holds in the subsidiary alive in its own name so that they can be sold later. Its lawyers say the whole point of the fast track is that nobody outside the companies has to be consulted.

items.stem: How should the two objections be dealt with?

options.text: Both fail — section 5(7) makes a person to whom a financial debt has been legally assigned or transferred a financial creditor in his own right, and the acknowledgement in the signed balance sheet starts a fresh three-year period, so the application filed on 1 June 2026 is in time
options.why: Section 5(7) defines a financial creditor as any person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes a person to whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred, so the assignee stands exactly where the bank stood. On limitation, section 238A applies the Limitation Act, 1963 to proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority; the three-year period under Article 137 runs from the date of default, but section 18 of that Act starts it afresh on an acknowledgement of liability made in writing and signed before the period expires, and an entry in a signed balance sheet can be such an acknowledgement. Three years from 15 July 2024 had not run out on 1 June 2026.

options.text: Both succeed — an assignee has bought a claim rather than disbursed money for the time value of money, and limitation runs from the default and cannot be restarted under the Code
options.misconception: reads the disbursement test as personal to the original lender and treats section 238A as excluding acknowledgement
options.why: The disbursement test in section 5(8) describes the debt, not the holder of it, and section 5(7) says in terms that an assignee is a financial creditor. Section 238A brings in the whole Limitation Act, 1963 and not merely its periods, so section 18 on acknowledgement applies along with Article 137.

options.text: The assignment objection fails but the limitation objection succeeds, because section 238A allows no acknowledgement to extend a period that runs from the date of default
options.misconception: applies the limitation period without the section that restarts it
options.why: Section 238A makes the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963 apply as far as may be, and section 18 of that Act is one of them. An acknowledgement of liability signed before the period expires starts a fresh period from the date of the acknowledgement.

options.text: The limitation objection fails but the assignment objection succeeds, so the asset reconstruction company must first have the assignment confirmed by a civil court before it can apply
options.misconception: adds a confirmation step the Code does not require of an assignee
options.why: Section 5(7) needs no confirmation from anybody. A person to whom the debt has been legally assigned or transferred is a financial creditor for the purposes of the Code, and he applies under section 7 in that character.

citation.ref: Sections 5(7), 5(8) and 238A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, read with Article 137 and section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963

items.scenario: A bank's term loan to a manufacturing company fell into default on 1 March 2022, in an amount well above the sum notified under section 4. On 1 October 2023 the bank assigned the debt to an asset reconstruction company for value. The corporate debtor's audited balance sheet for the year ended 31 March 2024, signed on 15 July 2024, records the loan as payable. The asset reconstruction company files an application under section 7 on 1 June 2026. The corporate debtor resists on two grounds — that only the original lender who parted with the money is a financial creditor, and that the claim is time-barred because more than three years have gone by since the default.

items.stem: How do these three claims rank against the ₹9 crore?

options.text: The government's ₹10 crore ranks ahead of the ₹15 crore shortfall, statutory dues having priority over a private debt under the general law
options.misconception: imports a Crown priority the Code's ranking has displaced
options.why: Section 53(1) opens by overriding anything to the contrary in any other law, and inside it the government dues for the two years preceding the liquidation commencement date rank equally with the unpaid balance of a secured creditor that enforced its own security. Neither is ahead of the other.

options.text: The ₹15 crore shortfall ranks with the relinquishing secured creditors alongside the workmen in clause (b), because a secured creditor keeps its rank whether it relinquishes or enforces
options.misconception: gives the enforcing secured creditor the rank the Code reserves for one that relinquishes
options.why: The choice under section 52 is the whole point of the ranking. A secured creditor that relinquishes its security into the estate is put with the workmen in section 53(1)(b); one that enforces its own security keeps what it realises and takes any shortfall down to section 53(1)(e), alongside the government.

options.text: All ₹6 crore of workmen's dues rank ahead, then the ₹15 crore shortfall, then the government dues, because workmen come first in the waterfall whatever the period they relate to
options.misconception: ignores the twenty-four month window that defines the workmen's dues in clause (b)
options.why: Clause (b) is not "workmen's dues"; it is workmen's dues for the period of twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date. Anything older is a debt of the company like any other and joins the residual class in section 53(1)(f).

options.text: The ₹4 crore of recent workmen's dues is paid first; the ₹15 crore shortfall of the enforcing secured creditor ranks with the ₹10 crore of government dues below it and shares what is left rateably; and the ₹2 crore of older workmen's dues drops below both of them
options.why: Section 53(1)(b) covers workmen's dues for the period of twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date, and that is where the ₹4 crore sits. A secured creditor that declines to relinquish and realises its security under section 52 is dealt with by section 53(1)(e), which ranks any amount unpaid to it following the enforcement equally with government dues for the two years preceding that date, so the ₹15 crore and the ₹10 crore share what survives the workmen. Workmen's dues falling outside the twenty-four month window are not in clause (b) at all and fall into the residual class in section 53(1)(f), behind both.

citation.ref: Sections 53(1)(b), 53(1)(e) and 53(1)(f), read with section 52

items.scenario: A company is in liquidation under the Code. A secured creditor owed ₹50 crore chose not to relinquish its security and realised ₹35 crore by enforcing it, leaving ₹15 crore unpaid. Workmen are owed ₹6 crore in all, of which ₹4 crore relates to the twenty-four months before the liquidation commencement date and ₹2 crore to earlier periods. Government dues for the two years preceding that date are ₹10 crore. The liquidator has ₹9 crore in the estate after paying process and liquidation costs in full.

items.stem: Is the bidder eligible?

options.text: Yes, and for the committee's reason — section 29A(c) looks only at the account of the resolution applicant itself and of the corporate debtor, so an account of a different company is irrelevant
options.misconception: reads clause (c) without Explanation I, which extends it to connected persons
options.why: Clause (c) is expressly extended by Explanation I, which is what makes section 29A a promoter test rather than a company test. It reaches the person in management or control of the applicant and the holding, subsidiary, associate and related party of that person, so a sister company's account is squarely in.

options.text: Yes, because section 240A switches off clause (c) wherever the resolution applicant is the promoter of the business rather than an outside investor
options.misconception: reads section 240A as a promoter relaxation when it is an MSME relaxation
options.why: Section 240A switches off clauses (c) and (h) only where the corporate debtor is a micro, small or medium enterprise, and this corporate debtor is not one. Nothing in the Code relaxes section 29A because the bidder happens to be a promoter.

options.text: No, and nothing can be done — once an account connected to the applicant has been a non-performing asset for over a year, clause (c) is an absolute bar and no payment cures it
options.misconception: applies clause (c) without the proviso that lets the applicant clear the account
options.why: The first proviso to clause (c) exists to let a bidder buy his way back to eligibility. Paying all overdue amounts with interest and charges on the non-performing asset accounts before the plan is submitted lifts the disqualification, and the timing of the payment is what matters.

options.text: Not on the committee's reasoning — section 29A(c) reaches a connected person, and Explanation I brings in the person in management or control of the resolution applicant and the companies he controls; but the proviso to clause (c) makes the bidder eligible if it pays all the overdue amounts with interest and charges before submitting the plan, which it proposes to do
options.why: Section 29A(c) disqualifies a person, or any other person acting jointly or in concert with him, whose account or an account of a corporate debtor under his management or control has been classified as a non-performing asset with at least one year gone from the classification to the insolvency commencement date, and Explanation I defines a connected person to include the person who is or shall be in management or control of the business of the corporate debtor during the implementation of the plan and the holding, subsidiary, associate or related party of such a person. The promoter's second company is caught that way. The first proviso to clause (c) is the cure: the person is eligible if he makes payment of all overdue amounts with interest and charges relating to the non-performing asset accounts before submission of the resolution plan.
keywords: before submission of the resolution plan

citation.ref: Section 29A(c) with its first proviso and Explanation I, read with sections 30(4) and 240A

items.scenario: A bidder company wants to submit a resolution plan for a corporate debtor that is not a micro, small or medium enterprise. The bidder's own accounts have never been irregular. Its promoter, who controls it and would control the corporate debtor while the plan was implemented, also controls a second company whose account was classified as a non-performing asset four years before the insolvency commencement date and remains overdue. Before submitting the plan the bidder offers to pay every overdue amount on that account with interest and charges. The committee of creditors says the bidder is clean because the bad account is neither its own nor the corporate debtor's.

items.stem: Are these preferential transactions?

options.text: Neither is — the supplier payment falls inside the exclusion for a transfer made in the ordinary course of the business or financial affairs of both the corporate debtor and the transferee, and the mortgage secured new value advanced at the same time rather than an antecedent debt
options.why: Section 43(3)(a) takes out of the section a transfer made in the ordinary course of the business or financial affairs of the corporate debtor or the transferee, and the Supreme Court in Anuj Jain read that "or" as "and", so a payment that is ordinary for both sides is excluded — which this one is. The mortgage fails the section at its foundation: section 43(2) requires the transfer to be for the benefit of a creditor on account of an antecedent debt, and money advanced on the same day is not antecedent. Section 43(3)(b) says the same thing from the other side by excluding a transfer creating a security interest in property acquired by the corporate debtor to the extent that the security interest secures new value.

options.text: Both are — once a transfer inside the look-back puts a creditor in a better position than he would have been in under section 53, section 43 catches it
options.misconception: applies the better-position test without the antecedent debt requirement or the exclusions
options.why: The better-position test in section 43(2)(b) is the last of several conditions, not the first. The transfer must also be to a creditor, surety or guarantor on account of an antecedent debt, and it must survive the exclusions in section 43(3), and both transactions fail the section before the comparison with section 53 is reached.

options.text: Only the supplier payment is, because an ordinary trade payment prefers one unsecured creditor over the others, while a bank's registered charge is beyond challenge
options.misconception: reverses the two exclusions, treating registration rather than new value as what saves the mortgage
