options.why: Registration is a condition of the exclusion, not the reason for it — what saves the mortgage is that it secures new value rather than an antecedent debt. And the supplier payment is protected by section 43(3)(a) precisely because it was ordinary for both sides.

options.text: Only the mortgage is, because a security interest granted while the company was sliding into insolvency prefers a secured creditor over every unsecured one
options.misconception: treats the effect of a security interest as decisive and ignores section 43(3)(b)
options.why: Section 43(3)(b) was written for exactly this transaction — a security interest in property the corporate debtor acquired, to the extent it secures new value given at the time of or after the security agreement and used to acquire that property. The effect on unsecured creditors is not the test where the exclusion applies.

citation.ref: Sections 43(2), 43(3)(a) and 43(3)(b), read with section 43(4) and section 44

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process commences on 1 July 2026. Two transactions from March 2026 are put to the resolution professional, and both are well inside the one-year look-back. The first is a payment of ₹3 crore to a raw-material supplier on the sixty-day credit terms the two have used for years, made in the ordinary way of business on both sides. The second is a mortgage the corporate debtor gave a bank over a machine, the bank having advanced the purchase money for that machine on the same day under a security agreement signed then, with the charge registered within thirty days of the debtor receiving the machine. The resolution professional says both are preferences because each left one creditor better off than the rest.

items.stem: What are the limits on the two orders?

options.text: The third party is protected, but only because the transfer is outside the two-year relevant period in section 46(1), and section 51 is limited to restoration
options.misconception: applies the section 45 look-back to a section 49 application and understates section 51
options.why: The relevant period in section 46(1) governs an application about an undervalued transaction under section 45. Section 49 is deliberately outside it, and what protects the purchaser is the good-faith limit written into section 49 itself.

options.text: The section 49 order cannot prejudice an interest in property acquired in good faith, for value and without notice of the relevant circumstances, so the third party keeps the plot; and section 51 lets the Authority do far more than restore — set aside the whole or part of the debt, modify the terms, order repayment of amounts received, and require any security to be released
options.why: Section 49 has no relevant period, which is what makes it reach an old transfer, but it has its own limit: an order under it shall not affect any interest in property which was acquired from a person other than the corporate debtor in good faith, for value and without notice of the relevant circumstances. A purchaser who paid full value and knew nothing answers that description. Section 51 then lists the orders for an extortionate credit transaction and restoration is only the first — the Authority may also set aside the whole or part of any debt created by the transaction, modify its terms, require any party to repay amounts received, and require any security interest created as part of it to be relinquished.
keywords: without notice of the relevant circumstances

options.text: The third party loses the plot because a transferee takes no better title than his transferor, but the section 51 point is right and only restoration is available
options.misconception: applies the general rule on title where the Code has written an express protection
options.why: The general rule would indeed follow the property, which is why the Code wrote an exception to it. The order under section 49 must not prejudice an interest acquired in good faith, for value and without notice, and section 51 in any event allows setting aside the debt, modifying the terms, ordering repayment and releasing a security.

options.text: Neither has a limit — section 49 carries no relevant period and therefore no defence, and section 51 confines the Authority to restoring the position
options.misconception: reads the absence of a look-back period as the absence of any protection, and reads section 51 too narrowly
options.why: Section 49 trades a look-back period for a good-faith defence: the order shall not prejudice an interest acquired in good faith, for value and without notice of the relevant circumstances. Section 51 is a menu of five kinds of order, of which restoring the position is one.

citation.ref: Sections 49 and 51, read with sections 45(2), 46(1) and 50(1)

items.scenario: Two questions come before the Adjudicating Authority in one liquidation. First, an application under section 49 concerns a plot the corporate debtor transferred at a gross undervalue to keep it away from a decree-holder; the original transferee has since sold the plot to a third party who paid full market value, knew nothing of the corporate debtor's affairs, and bought before any application was made. Second, the liquidator has established an extortionate credit transaction and asks what the Authority may do about it beyond putting the parties back where they were. The lender argues that section 49 sets aside the transfer wherever it can be traced, and that the only order available for an extortionate transaction is restoration.

items.stem: What are the thresholds?

options.text: Sixty-six per cent for all three, the committee being a single body that votes on one standard
options.misconception: applies the higher threshold to every decision instead of only the ones the Code names
options.why: The Code sets one general threshold and then raises it for named matters. Section 21(8) is the general rule at fifty-one per cent, and sixty-six per cent applies where section 28(3) or section 30(4) says so, which is to the listed actions and to the resolution plan.

options.text: Fifty-one per cent for all three, since section 21(8) is the general provision on how the committee decides and no other provision displaces it
options.misconception: applies the general threshold where two specific provisions raise it
options.why: Section 21(8) itself opens by saying it applies save as otherwise provided in the Code, and section 28(3) and section 30(4) are two such provisions. Both require sixty-six per cent, one for the actions listed in section 28(1) and the other for a resolution plan.

options.text: Seventy-five per cent for the resolution plan, sixty-six per cent for the security interest and fifty-one per cent for the administrative matter
options.misconception: uses the seventy-five per cent threshold the Code carried before the 2018 amendment
options.why: Seventy-five per cent was the original threshold and it was reduced to sixty-six per cent by the 2018 amendment, which also created the fifty-one per cent general rule. Section 30(4) now reads sixty-six per cent, the same as section 28(3).

options.text: Sixty-six per cent for the resolution plan and sixty-six per cent for the security interest, but fifty-one per cent for the administrative matter
options.why: Section 30(4) requires the committee to approve a resolution plan by a vote of not less than sixty-six per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors. Creating a security interest over the assets of the corporate debtor is one of the actions listed in section 28(1), and section 28(3) requires the prior approval of the committee by a vote of sixty-six per cent for any of them. Everything else runs on section 21(8), under which the committee takes its decisions by a vote of not less than fifty-one per cent of the voting share, so an ordinary administrative matter carries at fifty-one per cent.

items.scenario: A committee of creditors has three matters before it at one meeting. It must approve a resolution plan. It must decide whether to let the resolution professional create a security interest over the corporate debtor's assets to support a fresh facility. And it must settle an ordinary administrative matter, the scale of expenses the resolution professional may incur. The resolution professional tells the committee that every decision it takes needs sixty-six per cent of the voting share.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The staff are discharged but the liquidator may sue, because the deemed discharge in section 33(7) is absolute and only the bar on proceedings has an exception
options.misconception: takes the exception out of section 33(7) while keeping the proviso to section 33(5)
options.why: Both provisions carry a qualification and section 33(7)'s is the more important of the two here. It excepts the case where the business is continued during the liquidation process by the liquidator, which is exactly what he has decided to do.

options.text: The deemed discharge does not operate, because section 33(7) excepts the case where the business is continued during the liquidation process by the liquidator; and the liquidator may sue, because the proviso to section 33(5) lets a proceeding be instituted by the liquidator on behalf of the corporate debtor with the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority
options.why: Section 33(7) deems the liquidation order to be a notice of discharge to the officers, employees and workmen of the corporate debtor, except where the business of the corporate debtor is continued during the liquidation process by the liquidator — and the plant is running, so the exception applies and the letters are wrong. Section 33(5) does bar the institution of a suit or other legal proceeding by or against the corporate debtor, but its proviso allows a suit or other legal proceeding to be instituted by the liquidator on behalf of the corporate debtor with the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority, so the ₹4 crore is recoverable.
keywords: prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority

options.text: The staff are not discharged and the liquidator may sue without asking anybody, section 33(5) applying only to proceedings against the corporate debtor
options.misconception: reads the bar as one-directional and drops the requirement of prior approval
options.why: Section 33(5) bars a suit or other legal proceeding by or against the corporate debtor, in both directions. What the proviso gives the liquidator is not freedom but a route, and the route runs through the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority.

options.text: Both the human resources head and the former managing director are right — the order discharges the staff and shuts the company out of court altogether
options.misconception: reads section 33(7) and section 33(5) without the exception and the proviso inside them
options.why: Section 33(7) carries its own exception for a business continued by the liquidator, and section 33(5) carries its own proviso letting the liquidator sue with the Adjudicating Authority's prior approval. A liquidator who could neither keep staff nor sue a debtor could not sell an undertaking as a going concern at all.

citation.ref: Sections 33(5) with its proviso and 33(7), read with sections 34(1) and 35(1)(e)

items.scenario: A liquidation order is passed on 1 September 2026 and the resolution professional continues as liquidator. He decides to keep the plant running so that the undertaking can be sold whole, and it runs without a break. On the strength of the order the human resources head issues termination letters to every workman and officer, saying the Code has discharged them all automatically. The liquidator separately wants to sue a customer who owes the company ₹4 crore, and the former managing director tells him section 33(5) bars any proceeding by or against the company, so the receivable must simply be written off.

items.stem: What has the company got wrong under the Regulations?

options.text: Two things — Regulation 17(1C) required the members' approval at the next general meeting or within three months of the appointment, whichever is earlier, so 20 September was too late; and Regulation 17(2) allows a maximum gap of one hundred and twenty days between two board meetings, which the gap from 5 November 2026 to 20 March 2027 exceeds
options.why: Regulation 17(1C) requires the listed entity to ensure the approval of shareholders for the appointment of a person on the board of directors at the next general meeting or within a time period of three months from the date of appointment, whichever is earlier. Three months from 1 April 2026 is 1 July 2026, which comes first, so an approval in September is out of time however section 161(1) would have read on its own. Regulation 17(2) requires the board to meet at least four times a year with a maximum time gap of one hundred and twenty days between any two meetings, and 5 November 2026 to 20 March 2027 is a longer gap than that.

options.text: Only the appointment — four board meetings in a financial year satisfy Regulation 17(2), which counts meetings rather than the intervals between them
options.misconception: counts the meetings and ignores the maximum gap the Regulation also imposes
options.why: Regulation 17(2) imposes two conditions in one sentence — at least four meetings in a year and a maximum gap of one hundred and twenty days between any two of them. Four meetings bunched at the ends of the year fail the second even while they satisfy the first.

options.text: Only the meeting gap — the appointment is in order because a general meeting held within the same financial year satisfies Regulation 17(1C)
options.misconception: keeps the general meeting limb of Regulation 17(1C) and drops the three-month limb
options.why: Regulation 17(1C) says the next general meeting or three months from the date of appointment, whichever is earlier. Where the general meeting is more than three months away, the three months governs, and here it expired on 1 July 2026.

options.text: Nothing — section 161(1) governs an additional director's tenure and four meetings were held, so both the Act and the Regulations are satisfied
options.misconception: answers a Regulation question out of the Companies Act, where the Regulation is stricter
options.why: A listed entity has to satisfy both, and where they differ the stricter one decides. Regulation 17(1C) shortens the approval window to the earlier of the next general meeting and three months, and Regulation 17(2) polices the gap between meetings as well as their number.

citation.ref: Regulations 17(1C) and 17(2), read with sections 161(1) and 173(1) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A listed company's board appoints an additional director on 1 April 2026 and proposes to put his appointment to the members at the annual general meeting on 20 September 2026, relying on section 161(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, under which an additional director holds office up to the date of the next annual general meeting. The board met four times during 2026-27 — on 1 April 2026, 15 July 2026, 5 November 2026 and 20 March 2027. The company secretary certifies that the company has complied with both the Act and the Regulations.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: A special resolution is still needed, because Regulation 24(5) admits of no exception once the holding falls to fifty per cent or less
options.misconception: applies Regulation 24(5) without the carve-out for a court or tribunal approved scheme
options.why: The carve-out is written into the Regulation. Where the transaction is under a scheme of arrangement duly approved by a court or tribunal, or under a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Code, the special resolution is not required and a disclosure to the exchanges within one day of the approval takes its place.

options.text: No special resolution is needed, and the managing director is right about the audit committee, whose remit under the Regulations stops at the listed entity's own accounts
options.misconception: confines the audit committee to the listed entity and ignores Regulation 24(2)
options.why: Regulation 24 is built to follow the money down into the group. Regulation 24(2) requires the audit committee of the listed entity to review the financial statements and in particular the investments made by the unlisted subsidiary, and Regulations 24(3) and 24(4) bring the subsidiary's minutes and significant transactions up to the listed board.

options.text: No special resolution and no disclosure either, a scheme sanctioned by the Tribunal being a matter of public record from which the exchanges take their own notice
options.misconception: reads the carve-out as removing the disclosure along with the approval
options.why: The carve-out replaces one obligation with another. The listed entity is relieved of the special resolution but must disclose the event to the stock exchanges within one day of the approval, so the market learns of it on the entity's own initiative.

options.text: No special resolution is needed, because the requirement is carved out where the transaction is under a scheme of arrangement duly approved by a court or tribunal, but the event must be disclosed to the stock exchanges within one day of the approval; and the parent's audit committee is required to review the financial statements and in particular the investments made by the unlisted subsidiary
options.why: Regulation 24(5) requires a special resolution before a listed entity disposes of shares in a material subsidiary so as to reduce its holding to fifty per cent or less or to cease to exercise control, and Regulation 24(6) does the same for a sale of more than twenty per cent of the subsidiary's assets. Both are carved out where the transaction is made under a scheme of arrangement duly approved by a court or tribunal, or under a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, in which case the event is disclosed to the stock exchanges within one day of the approval. Regulation 24(2) separately requires the audit committee of the listed entity to review the financial statements, and in particular the investments made, of the unlisted subsidiary.

citation.ref: Regulations 24(2), 24(5) and 24(6), read with Regulations 24(3) and 24(4)

items.scenario: A listed parent has an unlisted Indian subsidiary that is material within the meaning of the Regulations. Under a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the Tribunal, the parent's holding in that subsidiary will fall from a hundred per cent to forty per cent. The parent's company secretary asks whether a special resolution of the parent's shareholders is still needed, and what if anything must be told to the stock exchanges. The managing director separately tells the parent's audit committee that it has no business reviewing an unlisted subsidiary's investments, those being the subsidiary board's affair.

items.stem: What is wrong with this quarter's submission?

options.text: Only the coverage point — the audit committee's role is advisory and the board may approve results it has not seen, and the chief financial officer is right that a review and an audit give the same assurance
options.misconception: makes the audit committee's review optional and equates two different levels of assurance
options.why: Regulation 33(2) makes the audit committee's review a step in the process and not a courtesy. And the two engagements differ by design — a limited review under SRE 2410 expresses a conclusion in the negative form, while an audit expresses an opinion under SA 700 (Revised) on the strength of reasonable assurance.

options.text: Nothing — the results were filed in time, and coverage and committee review are annual requirements that do not apply to a quarter
options.misconception: treats the consolidation coverage and the audit committee review as annual-only duties
options.why: The eighty per cent coverage rule is written for the quarterly consolidated results in terms, and Regulation 33(2) requires board approval after audit committee review of the financial results, quarterly as well as annual. Neither waits for the year end.

options.text: Only the audit committee point — the coverage is satisfied because the entity reviewed more than half of its consolidated revenue and more than half of its consolidated assets
options.misconception: reads the coverage test as a simple majority instead of the eighty per cent the Regulation sets
options.why: The test is at least eighty per cent of each of consolidated revenue, assets and profits, taken separately. Sixty per cent of revenue and fifty-five per cent of assets both fall short, and failing any one of the three limbs is enough.

options.text: Two things and a misunderstanding — at least eighty per cent of each of consolidated revenue, assets and profits must have been audited or subjected to limited review, and sixty and fifty-five per cent fall short; the results had to be approved by the board after review by the audit committee; and a limited review is a lower level of assurance than an audit, not the same one
options.why: For quarterly consolidated results a listed entity must ensure that at least eighty per cent of each of the consolidated revenue, assets and profits respectively has been subjected to audit or, in case of unaudited results, subjected to limited review. Regulation 33(2) requires the financial results to be approved by the board of directors after being placed before and reviewed by the audit committee, and it draws no distinction between a quarter and a year. A limited review under SRE 2410 consists of inquiry and analytical procedures and ends in a negative-form conclusion that nothing has come to the practitioner's attention, which is not the reasonable assurance behind an opinion under SA 700 (Revised).

citation.ref: Regulations 33(2) and 33(3), read with SRE 2410 and SA 700 (Revised)

items.scenario: A listed entity with six subsidiaries submits its quarterly consolidated financial results within the time allowed. Components making up sixty per cent of consolidated revenue and fifty-five per cent of consolidated assets were subjected to limited review; the rest are unreviewed management figures. The results were approved by the board of directors, but the audit committee did not see them first, because the chief financial officer took the view that the committee reviews only annual accounts. He adds that a limited review gives the same assurance as an audit, so the coverage cannot matter.

items.stem: Who may proceed and who may not?

options.text: All three may proceed — the first two are persons resident in India and the third is receiving property from a relative, which the Rules permit
options.misconception: treats residence as answering every question and reads the relative gift rule without its exclusions
options.why: Residence answers the German national's case and no more. The nationality bar operates whatever the person's residential status, and the gift permission for an Overseas Citizen of India covers immovable property other than agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property — which is precisely what is being given here.

options.text: The German national may buy, having become a person resident in India from the day he came here for employment; the Chinese national needs the Reserve Bank's prior permission whatever his residential status; and the Overseas Citizen of India may not take the farm house by gift at all, a farm house reaching him only by inheritance from a person resident in India
options.why: Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 includes a person who has come to or stays in India for taking up employment, so the German national is a person resident in India from his arrival and may acquire immovable property here. The Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 separately require the prior approval of the Reserve Bank for the acquisition of immovable property by a citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Nepal, Bhutan, Macau, Hong Kong or the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, whatever his residential status. Those Rules let an Overseas Citizen of India acquire any immovable property other than agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property, and allow such property to come to him only by inheritance from a person resident in India, so a gift of a farm house is outside the permission.
keywords: prior approval of the Reserve Bank

options.text: The German national must wait until he has spent more than one hundred and eighty-two days in India, the Chinese national may buy freely as a long-standing resident, and the Overseas Citizen of India may take the gift
options.misconception: reduces section 2(v) to the day count and drops the nationality bar and the farm house exclusion
options.why: Section 2(v) opens with the day count and then overrides it, including a person who has come to India for employment from the day he arrives. The nationality bar in the Rules is expressly independent of residential status, and a farm house may reach an Overseas Citizen of India only by inheritance from a person resident in India.

options.text: None may proceed — a foreign national needs the Reserve Bank's prior approval to acquire immovable property in India in every case
options.misconception: applies the prior-approval requirement to every foreign national instead of to a person resident outside India and the listed nationalities
options.why: The prior approval requirement attaches to a person resident outside India who is neither a Non-Resident Indian nor an Overseas Citizen of India, and separately to the listed nationalities whatever their residence. A German national who has become a person resident in India under section 2(v) is in neither category.

citation.ref: Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, read with the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019

items.scenario: Three people want to buy property in India. A German national arrived on 1 May 2026 on a five-year employment contract with an Indian company and now lives in Bengaluru; he wants to buy a flat there. A Chinese national has lived and worked in India for nine unbroken years and is plainly a person resident in India by any day count; he wants to buy a flat in Pune. An Overseas Citizen of India living in Toronto wants to accept a farm house in Coimbatore as a gift from his brother, who is a person resident in India. Their common adviser says all three may go ahead, because residence is settled by counting days and each of the first two is resident while the third is taking property from a relative.

items.stem: Where is the chief financial officer wrong?

options.text: On neither — nine months is the period for every exporter and Rule 96A gives one year from the invoice for the money to arrive in every case
options.misconception: applies the general nine-month period and the services limb of Rule 96A to a warehouse export of goods
options.why: Regulation 9(1) itself carves out goods exported to a warehouse established outside India and gives them fifteen months from the date of shipment, because the goods are sold after they arrive. Rule 96A puts its one-year receipt-of-payment condition on services; for goods it measures the export of the goods themselves.

options.text: Only on the exchange period — fifteen months applies, but the letter of undertaking has indeed failed, because payment for any export under a letter of undertaking must be received within one year of the invoice
options.misconception: carries the services condition in Rule 96A across to an export of goods
options.why: Rule 96A has two limbs and they measure different things. For goods the undertaking is that the goods be exported out of India within fifteen days after the expiry of three months from the date of issue of the export invoice; the one-year receipt of payment in convertible foreign exchange is the condition for a supply of services.

options.text: On both — goods exported to a warehouse established outside India carry fifteen months from the date of shipment, so the exchange obligation ran to 10 July 2027 and was met; and for goods the condition attached to the letter of undertaking is that the goods leave India within the period the rule allows from the invoice, so when the money arrived does not bear on it
options.why: Regulation 9(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015 gives all exporters nine months from the date of export, but gives goods exported to a warehouse established outside India fifteen months from the date of shipment, and money received on 1 June 2027 is inside fifteen months from 10 April 2026. Rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 puts the one-year condition on the receipt of payment only for a supply of services; for goods the undertaking is that the goods are exported out of India within fifteen days after the expiry of three months from the date of issue of the export invoice, which happened on 10 April 2026. For goods the tax clock measures the shipment and the exchange clock measures the money.

options.text: Only on the letter of undertaking — the tax position is safe, but fifteen months applies only where the Reserve Bank has granted an extension on an application, and none was made here
options.misconception: turns a period the Regulation itself gives into a discretionary extension
options.why: The fifteen months is written into Regulation 9(1) for goods exported to a warehouse established outside India and needs no application to anybody. An extension is a separate facility, and it is not what is being relied on here.

citation.ref: Regulation 9(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015, read with section 8 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 and Rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An exporter ships goods out of India on 10 April 2026 to its own warehouse established in the Netherlands, from which the goods are sold as buyers are found. The export invoice is dated 5 April 2026 and the shipment goes under a letter of undertaking without payment of integrated tax. The money reaches India on 1 June 2027. The chief financial officer says the exchange obligation was breached on 10 January 2027, nine months from shipment, and that the letter of undertaking has also failed because the payment came in more than a year after the invoice.

items.stem: Which of the four are specified orders he may take to a Dispute Resolution Committee?

options.text: All four, since none is based on a search, a survey or information under section 90 or section 90A
options.misconception: treats the three negative conditions as the whole test, when they only filter orders that have already answered the definition
options.why: Freedom from search, survey and treaty information is one of three conditions attached to an order that already falls within one of the five categories. It cannot pull in a Panel-directed assessment or a section 154 order that reduces the assessed income, neither of which is within any category at all.

options.text: The section 143(1) intimation and the section 201 order only
options.why: An intimation under section 143(1) is a specified order where the assessee objects to the adjustments made in it, and an order under section 201 deeming a person to be an assessee-in-default for failure to deduct tax is a specified order in its own right. The other two are excluded by their own limbs. An order of assessment is a specified order except an order passed in pursuance of directions of the Dispute Resolution Panel, which is precisely what the second one is. And a rectification order under section 154 qualifies only where it has the effect of enhancing the assessment or reducing the loss; one that reduces the assessed income by ₹40,000 gives him nothing to dispute.
keywords: in pursuance of directions of the Dispute Resolution Panel
enhancing the assessment or reducing the loss

options.text: The section 143(1) intimation only, an order under section 201 being a recovery order rather than an assessment
options.misconception: leaves out the fifth category of specified order, which is written for exactly this default
options.why: The definition names an order made under section 201, or under section 206C(6A), deeming a person to be an assessee-in-default for failing to deduct or collect tax at source or to remit it, as a specified order. The definition even goes on to say how the variation in such an order is measured, which it would not do if the order were outside it.

options.text: The section 143(1) intimation, the assessment order passed on the Panel's directions and the section 201 order — all three being within the ₹10,00,000 and ₹50,00,000 limits
options.misconception: applies the two monetary tests and misses that an assessment passed in pursuance of the Dispute Resolution Panel's directions is excluded from the definition whatever the figures
options.why: The ₹10,00,000 and ₹50,00,000 tests are applied after an order has got through the definition, not instead of it. The third limb of the definition reads an order of assessment or reassessment, except an order passed in pursuance of directions of the Dispute Resolution Panel, so the Panel-directed order never becomes a specified order however small the variation is.

citation.ref: Explanation (b) to section 245MA read with Rule 44DAD(ii) — an intimation under section 143(1) objected to and an order under section 201 are specified orders, an assessment passed in pursuance of directions of the Dispute Resolution Panel is excluded, and a section 154 order qualifies only where it enhances the assessment or reduces the loss

items.scenario: Four orders reach Mr Sabharwal in the same fortnight. One is an intimation under section 143(1) making an adjustment of ₹6,00,000 that he objects to. One is an order of assessment passed by the Assessing Officer in pursuance of the directions of the Dispute Resolution Panel, carrying variations of ₹7,00,000. One is a rectification order under section 154 that reduces his assessed income by ₹40,000. One is an order under section 201 deeming him an assessee-in-default on ₹3,00,000 of professional fees on which he did not deduct tax. His returned income for every year concerned is ₹44,00,000, and none of the four is founded on a search, a survey or information received under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A.

items.stem: Is this a specified order that may be taken to a Dispute Resolution Committee?

options.text: No — the variation is the ₹11,20,000 on which tax was not deducted, which is more than ₹10,00,000, even though the returned income of ₹47,00,000 is within ₹50,00,000
options.why: The definition says in terms how a variation is measured for this kind of order: the variation in a specified order relating to a default in deduction or collection of tax at source refers to the amount on which tax has not been deducted or collected in accordance with the Act. That amount is ₹11,20,000, not the tax on it. The aggregate of variations must not exceed ₹10,00,000, so the first condition fails and the second one being satisfied cannot save it.
keywords: amount on which tax has not been deducted

options.text: Yes — the variation is the ₹1,12,000 of tax not deducted, which is well within ₹10,00,000
options.misconception: measures the variation by the tax short-deducted rather than by the amount on which tax was not deducted
options.why: That is the natural reading and the Explanation forecloses it. For an order under section 201 or section 206C(6A) the variation is the amount on which tax has not been deducted or collected, which here is the ₹11,20,000 of fees. Measuring it by the tax would let almost every tax deduction default through, because the tax is a small percentage of the payment.

options.text: Yes — the variation is ₹1,33,000, being the tax of ₹1,12,000 together with the interest of ₹21,000 charged under section 201(1A)
options.misconception: adds the interest to the tax and still measures the variation by the demand rather than by the payment
options.why: Interest under section 201(1A) is a consequence of the default, not part of the variation. And the variation is not the demand at all: it is the amount on which tax was not deducted, which is ₹11,20,000.

options.text: No — an order under section 201 can never be a specified order, because the assessee has not been assessed on any income by it
options.misconception: reads the specified order categories as confined to orders determining income, when the fifth category is written for a deductor
options.why: The fifth category is an order under section 201 or section 206C(6A) deeming a person to be an assessee-in-default, and it is the reason the Explanation troubles to define what the variation means in such a case. This order fails on the ₹10,00,000 limit, not because the section is closed to it.

citation.ref: Explanation (b) to section 245MA read with Rule 44DAD(ii) — an order under section 201 is a specified order, the variation being the amount on which tax has not been deducted, tested against the ₹10 lakh limit on aggregate variations and the ₹50 lakh limit on returned income

items.scenario: Vetri Interiors was served an order under section 201 for previous year 2024-25. It had failed to deduct tax under section 194J on professional fees of ₹11,20,000, and the order works out the tax not deducted at ₹1,12,000 with interest under section 201(1A) of ₹21,000. Its return for the relevant assessment year showed a total income of ₹47,00,000. No search, survey or treaty-information is involved.

items.stem: Is that advice right?

options.text: Yes — a person against whom any penalty has been levied under the Income-tax Act, 1961 is outside the specified conditions until the penalty is paid or set aside
options.misconception: invents a penalty condition, when the conditions are about detention, conviction and prosecution and not about penalty at all
options.why: Nothing in the Explanation to section 245MA or in Rule 44DAD mentions a penalty under the Income-tax Act. Reading one in would close the route to most of the small taxpayers it was written for, since a variation in an assessment order very often carries a penalty with it.

options.text: Yes — accepting a loan in cash in breach of section 269SS is itself an offence, and a person who has committed an offence under the Act cannot be a specified person
options.misconception: turns a penalty provision into an offence and then treats a supposed offence as equal to a prosecution and a conviction
options.why: Section 269SS is enforced by a penalty under section 271D, not by prosecution. And even where an income-tax authority has actually initiated a prosecution the condition speaks of that initiation or a conviction following it, not of a breach nobody has prosecuted.

options.text: No — the levy of a penalty under income-tax law is not among the specified conditions at all, so it does not disqualify her
options.why: The specified conditions are a closed list about detention under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, conviction after prosecution under the six named Acts, prosecution initiated by an income-tax authority, and notification under the Special Court Act, 1992, with the Black Money Act condition added by the rules. Non-levy of a penalty under income-tax law is nowhere among them, so a penalty under section 271D for a breach of section 269SS leaves her a specified person and she may apply.

options.text: No, but only because the penalty is under Chapter XXI; a prosecution instituted under any law would have disqualified her even without a conviction
options.misconception: drops the conviction requirement from the second specified condition, where institution of prosecution alone is not enough
options.why: The condition about the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the five other named Acts needs both limbs — prosecution instituted AND a conviction under one of those Acts. A prosecution that has not ended in a conviction under those Acts does not shut the door.

citation.ref: Explanation (a) to section 245MA read with Rule 44DAD(iii) — the specified conditions are a closed list of detention, conviction, prosecution by an income-tax authority and notification under the Special Court Act, 1992, and a penalty levied under income-tax law is not among them

items.scenario: Mrs Kulkarni has received a scrutiny assessment order enhancing her total income, and the order is a specified order on the figures. No order of detention has ever been made against her and no prosecution has been initiated or instituted against her under any law. A penalty under section 271D has, however, been levied on her for accepting a loan in cash in breach of section 269SS, and she has not yet paid it. She is told she cannot approach a Dispute Resolution Committee while a penalty under the Income-tax Act stands against her.

items.stem: May he make the application?

options.text: No — the Black Money Act proceedings for the same assessment year shut him out, while the money-laundering prosecution does not, because it ended in an acquittal
options.why: Rule 44DAD(iii) requires that proceedings under the Black Money Act, 2015 have not been initiated for the assessment year for which resolution of the dispute is sought, and they have been initiated for that very year. The condition about the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 needs a prosecution instituted and a conviction under it; an acquittal leaves that condition satisfied.

options.text: No — a prosecution having been instituted against him under the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 is by itself enough, whatever the outcome
options.misconception: stops at institution of the prosecution and drops the conviction the condition also requires
options.why: The words are that prosecution has been instituted and he has been convicted of an offence punishable under one of those Acts. Both halves are needed. An assessee acquitted after a prosecution under that Act still satisfies this condition.

options.text: Yes — neither matters, since the specified conditions look only at prosecutions initiated by an income-tax authority
options.misconception: collapses four separate conditions into the third one and ignores the extra condition the rules add
options.why: Prosecution by an income-tax authority is only one of the conditions. Detention under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, conviction under six named Acts, and notification under the Special Court Act, 1992 are others, and Rule 44DAD(iii) adds the Black Money Act condition on top of all of them.

options.text: Yes — Black Money Act proceedings bar an application only where they relate to an assessment year other than the one in dispute
options.misconception: inverts the rule, which bars an application where the proceedings relate to the very year for which resolution is sought
options.why: The rule reads the other way round. What disqualifies him is that proceedings under the Black Money Act have been initiated for the assessment year for which resolution of the dispute is sought, which is assessment year 2024-25 in both cases here.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAD(iii) read with Explanation (a) to section 245MA — no Black Money Act, 2015 proceedings initiated for the assessment year for which resolution is sought, and a prosecution under the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 barring an applicant only where it has led to a conviction

items.scenario: Mr Fernandes wants to take a specified order for assessment year 2024-25 to a Dispute Resolution Committee. Two things sit in his file. A prosecution was once instituted against him under the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 and it ended in his acquittal. And proceedings under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 have been initiated against him for assessment year 2024-25 itself.

items.stem: What is his position now?

options.text: He has no appeal left, the time limit under section 246A having expired while the committee was considering the application
options.misconception: counts the calendar without the exclusion the rule gives for the time the committee spent deciding admission
options.why: That is the outcome the exclusion exists to prevent. The days the committee spent deciding whether to admit the application do not count against him, so the appeal period has not in fact run out.

options.text: He may appeal only with the condonation of the Commissioner (Appeals) on proof of sufficient cause, the exclusion being a matter of discretion
options.misconception: turns an automatic exclusion of time into a discretionary condonation of delay
options.why: The exclusion is not discretionary and does not depend on anybody being persuaded. The period taken in deciding on the admission is simply left out of the reckoning, so there is no delay to condone.

options.text: He may still appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals), because the period the committee took in deciding on the admission is excluded from the time available to file that appeal
options.why: The rule says so in terms. Where the committee rejects the application the assessee may file an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals), and the period taken by the committee in deciding on the admission has to be excluded from the period available to file such appeal. The route was designed so that trying it costs nothing, and an assessee who lost his appeal by applying would be a reason never to apply.

options.text: He may apply afresh to the same committee, a rejection at the admission stage not being a decision on the merits
options.misconception: reads a rejection as leaving the application alive, when the rule sends a rejected applicant to the appellate route
options.why: The rule provides one consequence for a rejection and it is the appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) with the exclusion of time. Nothing allows a second application on the same specified order.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — an assessee whose application is rejected may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals), and the period taken by the Dispute Resolution Committee in deciding on the admission is excluded from the period available to file that appeal

items.scenario: Mr Bhatt applied to a Dispute Resolution Committee instead of appealing. The committee served a show-cause notice, considered his reply and rejected the application. Three months have passed since the specified order was served on him and the ordinary period for appealing to the Commissioner (Appeals) has run out on the face of the calendar. He is told he gambled and lost.

items.stem: How does the rule treat this?

options.text: The committee must extend the time on its own motion before rejecting, the specified date being indicative only
options.misconception: turns an extension available on the assessee's own application into something the committee must grant unasked
options.why: An extension of time is available on the basis of an application made in that behalf to the committee. Nothing requires the committee to extend time nobody asked it to extend.

options.text: The committee must give a personal hearing before rejecting an application, whether or not the assessee asks for one
options.misconception: makes the hearing automatic and in person, when it follows a request and is conducted electronically
options.why: The rule ties the hearing to a request from the assessee, and the scheme is written to eliminate the interface between the committee and the assessee so far as technology allows. Where the assessee stays silent the committee may reject the application on that footing.

options.text: The committee may reject the application where no response is furnished, and a hearing arises only if the assessee asks for one, in which case it is given through video telephony or video conferencing to the extent technologically feasible
options.why: Two separate things are being run together. The rule allows the committee, where no response is furnished by the assessee, to reject the application. And the opportunity of being heard is granted on a request from the assessee, not automatically, and when it is granted it is through video telephony or video conferencing to the extent technologically feasible. A personal appearance was never on offer.

options.text: The committee may not reject the application for silence alone; it must decide the application on its merits and record why the assessee's case fails
options.misconception: reads silence as leaving the committee with a duty to decide the merits, when the rule makes silence itself a ground for rejection
options.why: The rule is explicit that where no response is furnished by the assessee the committee may reject the application. It is not obliged to construct a case for a person who did not answer its notice.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — a show-cause notice before rejection, an opportunity of being heard on the assessee's request through video telephony or video conferencing to the extent technologically feasible, extension of time on an application made in that behalf, and rejection where no response is furnished

items.scenario: A Dispute Resolution Committee doubts that an application should be admitted. It sends the assessee a show-cause notice setting a date and time for a response. The assessee neither responds nor asks for anything. His counsel later says the committee could not lawfully reject the application without first hearing him in person.

items.stem: By when must the committee have passed its order, and by when must the Assessing Officer act on it?

options.text: The committee by 14 November 2026 and the Assessing Officer by 9 January 2027, each period running from the date of the event
options.misconception: runs both periods from the date of admission and the date of receipt, when each runs from the end of the month in which the event falls
options.why: Neither period is measured from a date. The committee's six months and the Assessing Officer's one month both start at the end of the month in which the triggering event happened, which pushes each deadline out to a month end.

options.text: The committee by 31 May 2027, being six months from the end of the assessment year, and the Assessing Officer by 31 January 2027
options.misconception: attaches the committee's period to the end of the assessment year rather than to the month of admission
options.why: The committee's period is tied to its own admission of the application and to nothing about the assessment year. Six months from the end of May 2026 is 30 November 2026.

options.text: The committee by 30 November 2026, being six months from the end of the month in which the application was admitted, and the Assessing Officer by 31 January 2027, being one month from the end of the month in which he received the order
options.why: Both clocks run from the end of a month rather than from a date. The committee has six months from the end of the month in which the application for dispute resolution is admitted by it, so from 31 May 2026, which is 30 November 2026. Section 245MA(2A) then gives the Assessing Officer one month from the end of the month in which the committee's order is received, so from 31 December 2026, which is 31 January 2027.
keywords: six months from the end of the month
one month from the end of the month

options.text: The committee by 30 November 2026, and the Assessing Officer by 8 January 2027, being thirty days from receipt
options.misconception: gets the committee's clock right and then swaps the Assessing Officer's month for a thirty-day period counted from receipt
options.why: Section 245MA(2A) says a period of one month from the end of the month in which the order is received, not thirty days from receipt. On these facts that is 31 January 2027.

citation.ref: Section 245MA(2A) read with Rule 44DAB — the committee's order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is admitted, and the Assessing Officer's conforming or modified order within one month from the end of the month in which the committee's order is received

items.scenario: A Dispute Resolution Committee admitted an application on 14 May 2026. It passed its order of resolution and served a copy on the Assessing Officer, who received it on 9 December 2026.

items.stem: What can he do about the variations now?

options.text: He may make a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel, the draft order under section 144C(1) having remained a draft order throughout
options.misconception: leaves the Panel route open after the committee has acted, when the two are alternatives for an eligible assessee
options.why: Once the committee has dealt with a specified order that was a draft order under section 144C(1), the assessee is not eligible to file a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel against the modified order. The Assessing Officer passes an order of assessment in conformity with the committee's order, and that is the end of it.

options.text: Nothing — no appeal or revision lies against the modified order, and having gone to the committee he can neither make a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel nor appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) against it
options.why: The rule closes both doors. No appeal and no revision lie against the modified order. And where the specified order was that of an eligible assessee referred to in section 144C(1), he is not eligible to file a reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel or an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) against the modified order. An eligible assessee chooses between the Panel and the Committee at the start and does not get both.

options.text: He may seek revision under section 264, which is not an appeal and so is untouched by the bar
options.misconception: reads the bar as covering appeals only, when the rule shuts out revision in the same breath
options.why: The words are that no appeal or revision would lie against the modified order. Section 264 is a revision and is shut out with the rest.

options.text: He may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals), because an order making no modification to the variations is prejudicial to his interest and the bar applies only to an order in his favour
options.misconception: assumes an order that changes nothing is prejudicial, when all three decisions open to the committee are treated as not prejudicial to the assessee
options.why: All three outcomes are treated as orders not prejudicial to the interest of the assessee — a modification not prejudicial to him, a refusal to modify coupled with waiver and immunity, and a plain disposal with no modification. The bar on appeal does not turn on which of the three he got.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB read with section 245MA(2A) — the three decisions open to the committee, each treated as an order not prejudicial to the interest of the assessee, no appeal or revision against the modified order, and no reference to the Dispute Resolution Panel or appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) by an eligible assessee under section 144C(1)

items.scenario: A Dispute Resolution Committee has heard an eligible assessee whose specified order was a draft order under section 144C(1). It decides to make no modification at all to the variations, but to waive the penalty and grant immunity from prosecution. The Assessing Officer passes his order in conformity and serves it with a notice of demand. The assessee wants to take the variations further.

items.stem: What may the committee grant?

options.text: Neither, since a prosecution launched before the application makes the whole of Rule 44DAC unavailable to him
options.misconception: extends a bar written only for immunity so that it also swallows the waiver of penalty
options.why: The bar is written about immunity alone. Waiver of the penalty imposable and immunity from prosecution are separate reliefs and the committee may grant either or both; only the second is closed by a prosecution already begun.

options.text: Both, provided the prosecution is withdrawn by the income-tax authority before the committee passes its order
options.misconception: invents a cure by withdrawal, when the rule fixes the position by reference to the date the application was received
options.why: The rule fixes the point in time at the date of receipt of the application. What happens to the prosecution afterwards does not reopen an immunity the rule has already closed.

options.text: Both, the prosecution being irrelevant once the committee has resolved the dispute and the demand has been paid
options.misconception: treats resolution and payment as curing everything, and misses the one express bar in the rule
options.why: Resolution and payment are what open the reliefs, not what override the exception. Where the prosecution was initiated before the committee received the application, immunity cannot be granted at all.

options.text: Waiver of the penalty, but not immunity, because prosecution proceedings had been initiated before the date on which it received his application
options.why: The two reliefs are granted on the same conditions — payment of the tax due on the returned income in full where such tax is available, co-operation with the committee, and confirmation that the demand has been paid — and he satisfies all three. But there is one separate bar and it goes only to immunity: no immunity is granted where proceedings for the prosecution of an offence have been initiated before the date of receipt of the application for dispute resolution. The penalty waiver is unaffected.
keywords: tax due on the returned income
before the date of receipt of the application

citation.ref: Rule 44DAC read with section 245MA(2) — waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution on confirmation of payment of the demand where the tax on the returned income has been paid in full and the assessee has co-operated, and no immunity where prosecution proceedings were initiated before the date of receipt of the application

items.scenario: An application has been resolved and the assessee has paid the demand and confirmed the payment to the Dispute Resolution Committee. He had also paid in full the tax due on the income he had returned, and he answered every notice the committee sent. He asks for waiver of the penalty and immunity from prosecution. The department points out that a prosecution for an offence under the Act was launched against him two months before he applied to the committee.

items.stem: What is the effect on the immunity and the waiver?

options.text: The immunity stands withdrawn, and the provisions of the Act then apply as if the immunity or waiver had never been granted at all
options.why: The rule makes the grant conditional and says exactly what a breach does. An immunity granted to a person stands withdrawn if he fails to comply with any of the conditions subject to which it was granted, and on such withdrawal the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961 apply as if such immunity or waiver had never been granted. It is not a prospective withdrawal; the relief is treated as never having existed.
keywords: as if such immunity or waiver had never been granted

options.text: Nothing happens to the immunity, which once granted is final; the breach of the condition can only be visited with a fresh penalty
options.misconception: treats the grant as unconditional, when the rule lets the committee attach conditions and provides for withdrawal on breach
options.why: The committee grants the relief subject to such conditions as it thinks fit, for reasons recorded in writing, and a failure to comply with any of them withdraws the immunity.

options.text: The immunity is withdrawn only for the future, so a prosecution may be launched for anything done after the breach but the earlier period stays protected
options.misconception: makes the withdrawal prospective, when the rule undoes the grant from the beginning
options.why: The words are that the Act applies as if the immunity or waiver had never been granted. There is no protected earlier period left behind.

options.text: The waiver of penalty survives and only the immunity from prosecution falls, the rule speaking of immunity alone
options.misconception: reads the withdrawal as touching only one of the two reliefs, when the rule restores the position as if neither had been granted
options.why: The withdrawal provision ends by saying that the provisions of the Act apply as if such immunity or waiver had never been granted, which names both.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAC — waiver or immunity granted subject to conditions for reasons recorded in writing, withdrawn on failure to comply with any of them, with the Act applying as if the immunity or waiver had never been granted

items.scenario: A Dispute Resolution Committee granted an assessee immunity from prosecution and waived the penalty, recording its reasons in writing and imposing a condition on him. Eighteen months later he has failed to comply with that condition.

items.stem: What must it do, and what happens next?

options.text: It may terminate the proceedings for reasons recorded in writing and after giving him an opportunity of being heard, and it then intimates the income-tax authority so that the action the Act provides for may be taken
options.why: Concealment of a particular material to the proceedings or the giving of false evidence is one of the four grounds on which the committee may decide to terminate at any stage. Two safeguards run with the power — reasons to be recorded in writing and an opportunity of being heard — and where the proceedings are terminated the committee has to intimate the income-tax authority for taking necessary action as per the provisions of the Act.
keywords: reasons to be recorded in writing

options.text: It may terminate at once and without a hearing, an assessee who has given false evidence having forfeited the right to be heard
options.misconception: drops the opportunity of being heard, which the rule requires before termination on any of the four grounds
options.why: The rule attaches the safeguard to the power itself, without exception for the seriousness of the ground. The committee terminates for reasons to be recorded in writing and after giving an opportunity of being heard to the assessee.

options.text: It must reject the application, since false evidence goes to admission and a rejected application never reaches the merits
options.misconception: confuses rejection at the admission stage with termination, which is what the rule provides for a proceeding already admitted
options.why: Rejection belongs to the screening stage and is decided on the application itself. Once the application has been admitted the committee's power is to terminate the proceedings, and false evidence is one of the four listed grounds for doing so.

options.text: It must pass an order of resolution making no modification, which is the only order it is permitted to pass once an application has been admitted
options.misconception: treats the three decisions on the merits as the committee's only exits, when termination is a separate route out
options.why: The three decisions are what the committee does when it disposes of an admitted application on the merits. Termination is a distinct power exercisable at any stage of the proceedings on one of four grounds, and it ends the proceeding rather than deciding it.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — termination of dispute resolution proceedings where the assessee has concealed a material particular or given false evidence, for reasons recorded in writing and after an opportunity of being heard, with intimation to the income-tax authority

items.scenario: A dispute resolution proceeding is well past the admission stage. The committee finds that the assessee has given false evidence on a point material to the proceedings. It wishes to end the proceeding.

items.stem: In which of the four may the committee terminate the proceedings?

options.text: The first and the fourth only, non-payment of the demand being a matter for recovery rather than for the committee
options.misconception: leaves out the fourth ground, which the rule states in terms
options.why: Failure to pay the demand as required in the notice of demand is itself listed as a ground for termination, and it has to be, because waiver and immunity under Rule 44DAC depend on confirmation that the demand has been paid.

options.text: The first, the third and the fourth — a disagreement with what the committee proposes is not one of the four grounds
options.why: The grounds are a closed list of four: failure to co-operate during the proceedings, failure to respond to or submit information in response to a notice, satisfaction that the assessee has concealed a material particular or given false evidence, and failure to pay the demand as required in the notice of demand. Ignoring notices, not paying the demand and ceasing to attend are the first, fourth and again the first of those. Saying in writing that he disagrees is participation, not a ground.

options.text: All four, since the committee may terminate at any stage if it considers it necessary
options.misconception: reads the opening words as a free-standing discretion, when they are followed by an exhaustive list of grounds
options.why: The power is exercisable at any stage of the proceedings, but only if one of the four listed things has happened. An assessee who argues his case has done none of them.

options.text: The third only, the other three being matters the committee must decide against the assessee on the merits rather than grounds for termination
options.misconception: treats non-cooperation as something to be weighed in the decision instead of a listed ground for ending the proceeding
options.why: Failure to co-operate and failure to respond to a notice are each a listed ground. The rule does not require the committee to construct a decision on the merits out of an assessee's silence.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — the four grounds for terminating a dispute resolution proceeding, being failure to co-operate, failure to respond to or submit information in answer to a notice, concealment of a material particular or false evidence, and failure to pay the demand

items.scenario: Four things happen in four different admitted proceedings. In the first the assessee ignores two notices calling for information. In the second the assessee tells the committee in writing that he disagrees with the modification it proposes and asks it to think again. In the third the assessee does not pay the demand raised by the notice of demand. In the fourth the assessee stops attending altogether and answers nothing.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: No application under section 245C can be made on or after 1 February 2021, the Commission having ceased to operate from that date, and the applications pending as on 31 January 2021 were sent to seven Interim Boards for Settlement constituted by Notification No. 91 of 2021 dated 10 August 2021
options.why: The Settlement Commission ceased to operate with effect from 1 February 2021 and no application under section 245C for settlement of a case can be made on or after that date. To dispose of the applications pending as on 31 January 2021 the Central Government constituted seven Interim Boards for Settlement by Notification No. 91 of 2021 dated 10 August 2021.

options.text: Pending applications were transferred to the Dispute Resolution Committees, which took over the Commission's work
options.misconception: treats the Committee as the Commission's successor, when it is a separate forward-looking route with its own narrow limits
options.why: The Dispute Resolution Committee is not the Settlement Commission's successor. It hears a dispute arising from a variation in a specified order within the ₹10 lakh and ₹50 lakh limits, and the old settlement applications went to the Interim Boards instead.

options.text: The Commission ceased to operate from 1 April 2021, and pending applications lapsed with it
options.misconception: borrows the date on which the Dispute Resolution Committee scheme began and assumes the pending applications died
options.why: 1 April 2021 is when the new scheme of dispute resolution took effect. The Commission ceased on 1 February 2021, and the applications pending on the day before did not lapse — seven Interim Boards were set up precisely so that they could be disposed of.

options.text: Applications may still be made under section 245C, but they are heard by the Interim Boards rather than by the Commission
options.misconception: turns the Interim Boards into a continuing forum, when they exist only to clear a closed set of applications already pending
options.why: The Interim Boards were constituted to dispose of the applications pending as on 31 January 2021 and nothing else. The door to new applications under section 245C shut on 1 February 2021.

citation.ref: Section 245C read with Chapter XIX-AA — the Income-tax Settlement Commission ceasing to operate from 1 February 2021, seven Interim Boards for Settlement constituted by Notification No. 91 of 2021 dated 10 August 2021 for applications pending as on 31 January 2021, and the Dispute Resolution Committee scheme with effect from 1 April 2021

items.scenario: A client has heard that the Income-tax Settlement Commission still takes applications and wants to make one for a case that has been running for years. He also wants to know what happened to the applications that were pending when the Commission stopped.

items.stem: What is the answer, and why?

options.text: It does not, because a company is not a person the Board may specify for dispute resolution under Chapter XIX-AA at all
options.misconception: rules the company out on its status when what actually rules it out is the size of the variation and of the returned income
options.why: The Chapter operates in the case of such persons or class of persons as the Board may specify, and it does not exclude companies as a class. What defeats this company is the arithmetic — ₹40,00,000 of variations and ₹9 crore of returned income.

options.text: It does, the Dispute Resolution Committee having inherited the Settlement Commission's jurisdiction over any case a taxpayer wishes to settle
options.misconception: reads the Committee as a replacement of the Settlement Commission rather than a differently designed and much narrower route
options.why: Nothing was inherited. The Commission's pending work went to the Interim Boards, and the Committee was created separately, with effect from 1 April 2021, for small and medium taxpayers on a specified order.

options.text: It does, provided the company withdraws any appeal, since the monetary limits apply only to non-corporate assessees
options.misconception: invents a corporate exemption from the two monetary tests, which are written without reference to the kind of assessee
options.why: The ₹10 lakh limit on variations and the ₹50 lakh limit on returned income are conditions on the order and the return, not on the status of the assessee. Withdrawing an appeal is a step after admission and cannot cure a failure of the limits.

options.text: It does not, because the new scheme was formulated to give early tax certainty to small and medium taxpayers and reaches only a specified order within the ₹10 lakh and ₹50 lakh limits, neither of which this company meets
options.why: The purpose is written into the reason the Chapter exists — to prevent tax disputes in future and settle issues at the initial stage, providing early tax certainty to small and medium taxpayers. The limits follow from that purpose: the aggregate of variations must not exceed ₹10 lakh and the returned income must not exceed ₹50 lakh. Variations of ₹40,00,000 on a returned income of ₹9 crore fail both.

citation.ref: Chapter XIX-AA with section 245MA and the Explanation defining a specified order — the scheme formulated with effect from 1 April 2021 to give early tax certainty to small and medium taxpayers, confined to variations not exceeding ₹10 lakh on a returned income not exceeding ₹50 lakh

items.scenario: A large company with variations of ₹40,00,000 in its assessment order, and a returned income of ₹9 crore, asks whether Chapter XIX-AA gives it the sort of one-stop settlement the Settlement Commission once offered.

items.stem: How are the four classified?

options.text: Tax planning, tax management, tax avoidance and tax evasion, in that order
options.misconception: treats a wrong classification of an asset as lawful planning gone too far, when it is a false particular
options.why: The generator is not at the factory. Describing it as plant fitted there so as to claim a higher rate of depreciation is furnishing of false particulars in an attempt to evade tax, which is the module's own classification of this fact pattern, and not avoidance.

options.text: Tax planning, tax management, tax evasion and tax evasion, in that order
options.why: Depositing in a term deposit to claim a deduction the statute offers is tax planning — full advantage of a relief the Act permits, without violating anything. Keeping a register so that deductions are deposited on time reduces no liability at all and is tax management, which is compliance. Recording a generator at the chairman's farmhouse as factory plant is a misstatement of fact that unjustifiably raises the depreciation from 10 per cent to 15 per cent, and furnishing false particulars to reduce tax is evasion. A credit note recording a commission that moves ₹80,000 to a person who will pay nothing on it is a fictitious transaction, and reducing liability by recording one is evasion too.

options.text: Tax planning, tax planning, tax avoidance and tax avoidance, in that order
options.misconception: folds compliance into planning and then treats two misstatements of fact as avoidance, which is lawful in form
options.why: Tax management is a separate label from tax planning: the register saves no tax and exists to meet an obligation. And avoidance means methods which technically satisfy the requirements of law while circumventing it. Neither the generator entry nor the credit note satisfies the requirements of law even technically; both misstate what happened.

options.text: Tax management, tax management, tax evasion and tax planning, in that order
options.misconception: calls an ordinary deduction claim compliance, and calls a fictitious commission planning because the recipient's rebate is itself lawful
options.why: A section 80C deduction claimed on a real deposit is the textbook example of planning, not management. And the fact that the daughter's own rebate under the default regime is lawful does not make the company's credit note lawful; the transaction it records did not happen.

citation.ref: Section 270A read with the Direct Taxes Enquiry Committee (Wanchoo Committee) distinction between tax evasion and tax avoidance — planning as full advantage of permitted reliefs, tax management as compliance, and false particulars and fictitious transactions as evasion

items.scenario: Four things happened at Kadam Textiles Ltd during previous year 2025-26. Its promoter put ₹1,50,000 into a five-year bank term deposit to claim a deduction under section 80C. The accounts department kept a monthly register of every payment liable to deduction of tax at source so that nothing was deposited late. A generator installed at the chairman's farmhouse was recorded in the fixed asset register as plant in the factory, so that depreciation ran at 15 per cent instead of the 10 per cent that furniture and fittings attract. And a credit note for commission of ₹80,000 was raised in favour of the chairman's daughter, whose total income under the default regime stays within ₹12,00,000 and who therefore pays nothing on it, while the company's income fell by the same amount.

items.stem: How does the module treat these two failures?

options.text: Both are evasion but the penalty is 50 per cent, which is the rate for a case where income has not been correctly returned
options.misconception: applies the under-reporting rate to conduct the Act classifies as misreporting
options.why: Fifty per cent is the rate for under-reporting. Conduct in the list of common forms of evasion is misreporting, and misreporting carries 200 per cent.

options.text: Only the unrecorded receipt is evasion; a failure to report a specified domestic transaction is a reporting default and carries its own separate penalty instead
options.misconception: separates the transfer pricing reporting default from evasion, when the module puts it in the same list as suppression of a receipt
options.why: A separate penalty for a reporting default does not take the failure out of the list. The module names the failure to report a specified domestic transaction under Chapter X as one of the common forms of tax evasion alongside the suppression of a receipt.

options.text: Both are named among the common forms of tax evasion, and both amount to misreporting of income carrying penalty at 200 per cent
options.why: The list of common forms of tax evasion has six entries and these are two of them — failure to record any receipt in the books of account having a bearing on total income, and failure to report any international transaction or deemed international transaction or specified domestic transaction under Chapter X. The module says of the whole list that these constitute misreporting of income attracting penalty at 200 per cent under section 270A.

options.text: Both are tax avoidance rather than evasion, since neither involves a false document
options.misconception: requires a forged document before conduct can be evasion, when suppression and non-reporting are themselves listed forms of it
options.why: Evasion is described as a manoeuvre involving deceit, misrepresentation of facts, falsification of accounting calculations or downright fraud, and the list of its common forms begins with misrepresentation or suppression of facts. No document need be forged.

citation.ref: Section 270A read with the module's list of common forms of tax evasion — failure to record a receipt bearing on total income and failure to report an international, deemed international or specified domestic transaction under Chapter X, both constituting misreporting of income at 200 per cent

items.scenario: Two failures come to light in a scrutiny. The company failed to record in its books a receipt that bore on its total income. Separately, it failed to report a specified domestic transaction under Chapter X, which its finance head says is a transfer pricing compliance matter and nothing to do with evasion of tax.

items.stem: Which proposition actually emerges from the module's account of the case law?

options.text: Neither — where a transaction is genuine its form governs and not its substance, and it is only where the transaction is colourable or a mere device that the question becomes one between appearance and truth, at which point the authorities may pierce the corporate veil
options.why: The principles are stated as a pair.
