When a transaction is arranged in one form known to law it attracts tax accordingly, and if it is entered into in another equally lawful form it may not, so the form put through is what is considered. That rule applies only to genuine transactions; where the transaction is not genuine but colourable or a mere device the question is not one between form and substance but between appearance and truth, and it is then open to the authorities to pierce the corporate veil and look behind the legal facade.

options.text: The officer is right — Duke of Westminster survives untouched in India, so no arrangement may ever be looked through
options.misconception: ignores the departure Mc Dowell made from the earlier Indian decisions following Westminster
options.why: The Supreme Court in Mc Dowell expressly disassociated itself from the earlier observations echoing the Westminster principle, listed the evil consequences of avoidance, and held that it is for the court to expose sophisticated legal devices for what they are.

options.text: The partner is right — Mc Dowell established that substance prevails over form in every case, so a genuine transaction may be recharacterised whenever it results in less tax
options.misconception: reads Mc Dowell as abolishing the form rule rather than confining it to genuine transactions
options.why: Mc Dowell held that tax planning may be legitimate provided it is within the framework of law and that colourable devices cannot be part of tax planning. The Gujarat High Court in Minal Rameshchandra read it as directed at artificial and transparent devices and sham practices, and held that where an arrangement cannot be dismissed as an artificial device the subject is taxed by the strict letter of the law.

options.text: The proposition that survives is Kharwar's — that the legal effect of a transaction may be displaced by probing into its substance
options.misconception: keeps the one sentence of Kharwar that Mc Dowell expressly disapproved and drops the one that survives
options.why: Kharwar said the opposite of that: the legal effect of a transaction cannot be displaced by probing into the substance of the transaction, though the authority is bound to determine the true legal relation and may unravel a device. It is that sentence which has since been expressly disapproved in Mc Dowell.

citation.ref: Mc Dowell and Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1985) 154 ITR 148 (SC) read with CIT v. Motor and General Stores (P) Ltd. (1967) 66 ITR 692 (SC), CIT v. B.M. Kharwar (1969) 72 ITR 603 (SC) and CIT v. Smt. Minal Rameshchandra (1987) 61 CTR 80 (Guj) — form governs a genuine transaction, and appearance against truth governs a colourable one

items.scenario: A partner in a firm argues before an Assessing Officer that after Mc Dowell the substance of a transaction always prevails over its form, so the officer may look through any arrangement he dislikes. The officer argues that Mc Dowell changed nothing, and that Duke of Westminster still governs India without qualification.

items.stem: How did the Supreme Court deal with an arrangement of this shape?

options.text: It held that a validly incorporated subsidiary is a separate legal person, so the transfer had to be respected in the absence of direct evidence of motive
options.misconception: treats separate legal personality as conclusive, which is the argument the Court declined to accept
options.why: The Court accepted that there was no direct evidence that the subsidiary was formed as a device, and decided against the holding company anyway, on the footing that the true state of affairs was there to be found behind the structure.

options.text: It declined to interfere, holding that a dispute about a payment under welfare legislation is not a tax matter and the tax reasoning had no place in it
options.misconception: assumes the reasoning is confined to tax, when the Court applied it to a welfare statute in terms
options.why: The case was about a payment of bonus rather than about tax, and that is the point of citing it. The Court applied the same reasoning it had laid down in Mc Dowell, and said the duty arises where ingenuity is expended to avoid liability to taxation and to welfare legislation alike.

options.text: It held that the arrangement was tax avoidance and applied the General Anti-Avoidance Rules to disregard the subsidiary
options.misconception: reads a 1986 decision as an application of Chapter X-A, which came into force from assessment year 2018-19
options.why: The decision is from 1986 and the General Anti-Avoidance Rules took effect from assessment year 2018-19. What the case supplies is the judicial reasoning that Chapter X-A later codified, not an application of it.

options.text: It held on the facts that the transfer was a device to reduce the gross profits, and that it is the duty of the court to get behind the smoke screen and discover the true state of affairs wherever ingenuity is expended to avoid a liability
options.why: This is Associated Rubber Industries. The subsidiary had no asset except the transferred investments and no income except the dividend on them, and the Court held that the purpose of the transfer was to reduce the gross profits of the holding company and so the payment due under the Payment of Bonus Act. The absence of direct evidence did not save it: the Court said it is its duty in every case where ingenuity is expended to avoid a liability to taxation or to welfare legislation to get behind the smoke screen and discover the true state of affairs.

citation.ref: Associated Rubber Industries (1986) 157 ITR 77 (SC) read with Mc Dowell and Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1985) 154 ITR 148 (SC) — a subsidiary holding nothing but transferred investments treated as a device, and the duty of the court to get behind the smoke screen

items.scenario: A holding company forms a wholly owned subsidiary that has no assets of its own except a block of investments transferred to it by the holding company, and no income of its own except the dividend on those investments. The effect is to reduce the holding company's gross profits and with them a liability it owes under welfare legislation. There is no direct evidence that the subsidiary was formed for that purpose.

items.stem: Which of these is a tax benefit for the purpose of section 96?

options.text: All except the treaty-driven refund, tax benefit being defined by reference to amounts payable under the Act alone
options.misconception: drops the two limbs that are written specifically about a tax treaty
options.why: Two of the six limbs are written about a treaty — a reduction, avoidance or deferral that would be payable as a result of a tax treaty, and an increase in a refund as a result of a tax treaty. Chapter X-A was drafted to reach treaty benefits, so leaving them out would empty it.

options.text: Only those arising in the relevant previous year; the deferral and the unused loss arise in a later year and so are outside the definition
options.misconception: confines the definition to the year under examination, when it says the relevant previous year or any other previous year
options.why: The closing words of the definition are in the relevant previous year or any other previous year, which is what lets a deferral into a later year and an unused loss count.

options.text: Only the reduction in total income, the other three producing no reduction in the tax eventually payable
options.misconception: reads a tax benefit as a permanent saving of tax, when the definition covers deferral and an increase in a loss as well
options.why: The definition does not ask whether tax is permanently saved. It names deferral in the same breath as reduction and avoidance, and names an increase in a loss separately, precisely because those two produce no immediate saving.

options.text: All four, section 102(10) covering a deferral, an increase in a loss, an increase in a refund as a result of a tax treaty and a reduction in total income
options.why: The definition has six limbs and these fall within four of them. A reduction, avoidance or deferral of tax or other amount payable under the Act; an increase in a refund; the same two again where they arise as a result of a tax treaty; a reduction in total income; and an increase in a loss — in the relevant previous year or in any other previous year. So a pure deferral qualifies with no permanent saving at all, and an unused loss qualifies before it has been used.

citation.ref: Section 102(10) read with section 96 — the six limbs of a tax benefit including deferral, an increase in a refund, treaty-driven reduction or refund, a reduction in total income and an increase in a loss, in the relevant previous year or any other previous year

items.scenario: Four results are put to an Assessing Officer who is considering whether the purpose test in Chapter X-A is met. An arrangement defers tax by three years without reducing the total tax ever paid. An arrangement increases a business loss that has not yet been set off against anything. An arrangement increases a refund because of a tax treaty. An arrangement reduces total income without reducing the rate.

items.stem: Is that argument good?

options.text: Yes — an impermissible avoidance arrangement is an arrangement, so the whole reorganisation must be struck down or none of it
options.misconception: treats the arrangement as indivisible, which is the reading section 95 and Rule 10UA exist to defeat
options.why: Nothing has to be struck down as a whole. A single step may be declared impermissible and the consequences confined to it, leaving the other six steps and their tax treatment alone.

options.text: No, but only if the fourth step is itself a separate agreement; a step within a single agreement is not an arrangement
options.misconception: makes the definition turn on how many documents there are, when it covers a step whether or not the understanding is even enforceable
options.why: An arrangement means any step in, or a part or whole of, any transaction, operation, scheme, agreement or understanding, whether enforceable or not. Whether the step sits inside one document or several decides nothing.

options.text: No — section 95 says the Chapter may be applied to any step in, or a part of, an arrangement as it applies to the arrangement, and Rule 10UA then confines the tax consequences to that part
options.why: The Chapter was drafted against exactly this argument. Section 95 provides that its provisions may be applied to any step in, or a part of, the arrangement as they are applicable to the arrangement, and section 102(1) defines an arrangement to include any step in a transaction. Rule 10UA completes it: where a part of an arrangement is declared to be an impermissible avoidance arrangement, the consequences in relation to tax are determined with reference to such part only.

options.text: Yes, unless the sixth other steps are also shown to lack commercial substance, since the purpose test applies to the arrangement as a whole
options.misconception: requires the purpose test to be satisfied for the whole arrangement when the section allows it to be applied to a step
options.why: The section applies the Chapter to a step exactly as it applies to an arrangement, and that includes the purpose test. The question is whether the main purpose of that step is a tax benefit, not whether the reorganisation as a whole was commercially motivated.

citation.ref: Sections 95, 102(1) and 102(9) read with Rule 10UA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — Chapter X-A applied to any step in or part of an arrangement, with the tax consequences determined with reference to that part only

items.scenario: A commercial reorganisation runs through seven steps. Six of them have obvious business reasons. The fourth step routes a payment through an entity that does nothing else and exists only to change where the receipt is taxed. The assessee argues that Chapter X-A is written about arrangements, that this reorganisation is plainly a genuine commercial arrangement taken as a whole, and that the Chapter therefore cannot touch any part of it.

items.stem: Can the arrangement be deemed to lack commercial substance?

options.text: Yes — it involves round trip financing, which is judged without any regard to whether the funds can be traced, to the time or sequence in which they moved, or to the means by which they moved
options.why: Section 97 deems an arrangement that involves round trip financing to lack commercial substance, and defines round trip financing as any arrangement in which funds are transferred among the parties through a series of transactions with no substantial commercial purpose other than obtaining the tax benefit. It then removes the obvious defence by saying the test is applied without having any regard to whether the funds can be traced to any funds transferred to or received by any party, to the time or sequence in which they were transferred or received, or to the means, manner or mode of transfer. The subsidiary does nothing else, so the interest may be taxed in Meghna Ltd's hands by disregarding it.

options.text: No — round tripping requires the funds to come back to the person who put them out, and here they cannot be traced to Meghna Ltd at all
options.misconception: reads a tracing requirement into round trip financing, which the section removes in terms
options.why: The definition says the test applies without having any regard to whether the funds involved can be traced to any funds transferred to or received by any party in connection with the arrangement. Untraceability is the ordinary state of affairs in these structures and is why the words were written.

options.text: Only if the tax benefit exceeds ₹3 crore in the year and the subsidiary is a connected person of Tarun Ltd
options.misconception: adds a connected-person requirement that the section does not impose for round trip financing
options.why: The ₹3 crore floor in Rule 10U is real, but nothing in the round trip financing limb requires any party to be a connected person. That requirement does not even attach to an accommodating party, who may be connected or not.

options.text: No — the loan is at a commercial rate of 11 per cent to an unrelated borrower, so the arrangement is at arm's length and no tainted element is present
options.misconception: answers the first tainted element, non-arm's-length dealings, and leaves the third one untouched
options.why: Arm's length pricing answers a different limb. The third tainted element is that the arrangement lacks commercial substance or is deemed to, and an arrangement involving round trip financing is deemed to lack it however commercial the interest rate is.

citation.ref: Section 97(1)(b)(i) with section 97(2) — round trip financing deemed to make an arrangement lack commercial substance, judged without regard to tracing, to the time or sequence of transfers or to the means, manner or mode of transfer

items.scenario: Meghna Ltd, an Indian company, incorporates a subsidiary in a low tax jurisdiction with equity of ₹5 crore. The subsidiary lends ₹5 crore to Tarun Ltd, an unrelated Indian company, at 11 per cent a year, and Tarun Ltd claims the interest as a deduction. The subsidiary has no other activity of any kind. The department cannot trace the money Tarun Ltd pays back to Meghna Ltd.

items.stem: What weight do those three facts carry?

options.text: The payment of taxes under the arrangement is conclusive, since an arrangement on which tax has been paid has by definition produced no tax benefit
options.misconception: reads payment of some tax as proof that no benefit arose, when a benefit is measured against the alternative course
options.why: Tax having been paid under an arrangement is expressly one of the relevant but insufficient factors. A tax benefit is the difference between the liability under the arrangement and the liability under the alternative course available, and paying some tax says nothing about that difference.

options.text: Each is a relevant factor and none is sufficient — section 97(4) names the period of existence, the payment of taxes and the provision of an exit route as relevant but not sufficient
options.why: Section 97(4) lists the three in terms as factors which are relevant but not sufficient for determining whether an arrangement lacks commercial substance: the period or time for which the arrangement including the operations in it exists, the fact of payment of taxes directly or indirectly under the arrangement, and the fact that an exit route including a transfer of any activity or business or operations is provided by it. All three point the assessee's way and none of them decides the question.

options.text: An arrangement that has existed for more than five years is outside the General Anti-Avoidance Rules, so the first fact is decisive
options.misconception: turns a relevant factor into the five-year safe period that the Board was asked for and refused to give
options.why: The Board was asked to provide a definite timeline of five to ten years of existence during which the rules would not apply, and answered that the period for which an arrangement exists is only a relevant factor and not a sufficient factor under section 97(4).

options.text: None of the three has any bearing, section 97 listing only the deeming limbs and nothing else
options.misconception: overlooks section 97(4), which exists precisely to say what these three facts are worth
options.why: Section 97(4) is part of the section and names all three. They are relevant, and an assessee is entitled to rely on them; what he cannot do is treat any of them as settling the matter.

citation.ref: Section 97(4) read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — the period of existence, the payment of taxes and an exit route as relevant but not sufficient factors, and the refusal to fix a five to ten year period outside the rules

items.scenario: An assessee resists a finding that his arrangement lacks commercial substance on three grounds. It has been in place for eight years. Tax has been paid under it every year. And it contains an exit route allowing the business to be transferred out.

items.stem: Is that the limit of the consequences?

options.text: No — section 98 illustrates consequences including treating equity as debt, reallocating a receipt or an expenditure among the parties, treating the situs of an asset as being elsewhere, and disregarding a corporate structure altogether
options.why: The consequence may be determined in such manner as is deemed appropriate in the circumstances, and section 98 gives illustrations that go far beyond a denial. Steps may be disregarded, combined or re-characterised; the arrangement may be treated as if it had never been entered into; an accommodating party may be disregarded or merged with another; connected persons may be deemed one person; accruals, receipts, expenditure, deductions, relief and rebates may be reallocated among the parties; the place of residence of a party or the situs of an asset or transaction may be treated as elsewhere; and any corporate structure may be looked through. It adds expressly that equity may be treated as debt or the reverse.

options.text: Yes as regards recharacterisation, but a receipt may be reallocated between parties only where they are connected persons
options.misconception: attaches a connected-person condition to the reallocation power that the section does not carry
options.why: Reallocation is available among the parties to the arrangement. Treating connected persons as one and the same person is a separate illustration in the same list, not a precondition for the reallocation one.

options.text: Yes — the only consequence the Chapter provides is denial of the tax benefit under the Act or under a tax treaty
options.misconception: stops at the opening words of section 98 and ignores the illustrations that follow them
options.why: Denial of the benefit is where the section starts, not where it ends. It goes on to say the consequence may be determined in such manner as is deemed appropriate and then lists seven kinds of manner.

options.text: No, but a re-characterisation may only reduce a deduction; income of a capital nature can never be treated as revenue
options.misconception: denies one of the three re-characterisations the section states in terms
options.why: The section says any accrual or receipt of a capital nature may be treated as of a revenue nature or the reverse, alongside treating equity as debt and re-characterising any expenditure, deduction, relief or rebate.

citation.ref: Section 98 with section 98(2) — consequences including disregarding, combining or re-characterising a step, treating the arrangement as never entered into, reallocation among the parties, relocation of residence or situs, looking through a corporate structure, and treating equity as debt or a capital receipt as revenue

items.scenario: An arrangement has been declared an impermissible avoidance arrangement. The assessee accepts that the tax benefit claimed under it must be denied, but says that is the limit of what may be done: the department cannot rewrite the transaction, move anybody's residence or reallocate receipts between the parties.

items.stem: What is the Board's position on that request?

options.text: A corresponding adjustment will not be made in the hands of the other participant, because Chapter X-A is an anti-avoidance provision with deterrent consequences and matching adjustments across taxpayers would blunt the deterrence
options.why: The Board was asked to clarify that where a consequence is applied in the hands of one participant there would be a corresponding adjustment in the hands of another, and it declined. Its answer is that adequate procedural safeguards ensure the rules are invoked in a uniform, fair and rational manner, but that in the event of a particular consequence being applied in the hands of one of the participants, a corresponding adjustment in the hands of another participant will not be made, because corresponding tax adjustments across different taxpayers could militate against deterrence.

options.text: A corresponding adjustment must be made, since taxing the same receipt twice would be double taxation of one amount
options.misconception: assumes symmetry follows from fairness, which is exactly the request the Board refused
options.why: The clarification is explicit that no corresponding adjustment will be made. The consequence is deliberately asymmetric, and that asymmetry is described as part of the deterrent.

options.text: A corresponding adjustment is made automatically wherever both participants are resident in India, the asymmetry being intended only for cross-border cases
options.misconception: confines the Board's answer to cross-border arrangements, when it is written about participants generally
options.why: The answer is not limited by residence. It speaks of a consequence applied in the hands of one participant and of corresponding adjustments across different taxpayers, without distinguishing domestic arrangements from cross-border ones.

options.text: A corresponding adjustment is available only on an application to the Approving Panel, which may direct it while issuing its directions
options.misconception: invents a route to symmetry through the Approving Panel, which issues directions about the declaration rather than adjustments in another taxpayer's hands
options.why: The Approving Panel issues directions on whether the arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement and for which previous years. Nothing gives it a power to make an adjustment in another participant's assessment, and the Board's answer is that no such adjustment is made at all.

citation.ref: Sections 98 and 99 read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — no corresponding adjustment in the hands of another participant where a consequence is applied to one, corresponding adjustments being treated as militating against deterrence

items.scenario: An arrangement between two Indian companies has been declared impermissible, and a receipt has been reallocated so that it is taxed in the hands of the first company. The second company, which had already offered the same receipt to tax, asks for a corresponding adjustment reducing its own income by the same amount.

items.stem: Which of these is protected by the grandfathering in Rule 10U(1)(d)?

options.text: The original shares, the split shares and the bonus shares, but neither the aircraft lease nor the loan
options.why: The grandfathering covers income arising from the transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017. The Board has clarified that shares brought into existence by way of split or consolidation of a grandfathered holding, and bonus shares issued in respect of shares acquired before that date in the hands of the same investor, are eligible. It has equally clarified that on accounting principles an investment is an asset held for income by way of dividends, interest or rentals and for capital appreciation, and that lease contracts and loan arrangements are by themselves not investments, so grandfathering is not available for them.

options.text: All four, since each was entered into before 1 April 2017 and the rule protects everything of that vintage
options.misconception: reads the grandfathering as covering anything dated before 1 April 2017, when it is confined to income from the transfer of investments
options.why: The words of the rule are income from transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017. A lease and a loan are not investments, so their date does not help them, and an arrangement of any other kind is expressly still within the Chapter for a benefit obtained on or after that date.

options.text: None, the grandfathering having lapsed because the Chapter applies to any arrangement irrespective of the date on which it was entered into
options.misconception: reads the sentence that keeps old arrangements inside the Chapter as cancelling the investment grandfathering, when it is expressly subject to it
options.why: That sentence begins by excepting the grandfathered investments. It says the provisions apply to any arrangement other than the one specified in that clause, irrespective of the date on which it was entered into, for a tax benefit obtained on or after 1 April 2017.

options.text: The original shares alone, the split and the bonus shares having come into existence after 1 April 2017
options.misconception: dates the investment by when the new share certificates appeared rather than by when the underlying investment was made
options.why: The clarification deals with exactly that. Shares brought into existence by split or consolidation, and bonus shares issued on shares acquired before 1 April 2017 in the hands of the same investor, are grandfathered, because the investment behind them was made before the date.

citation.ref: Rule 10U(1)(d) read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — grandfathering of income from the transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017, extended to splits, consolidations, bonus issues and compulsorily convertible instruments, and denied to lease contracts and loan arrangements

items.scenario: An investor holds four things acquired before 1 April 2017 and disposes of them in previous year 2025-26. Shares of an Indian company bought in January 2016. Shares that came out of a split of that same holding in 2019. Bonus shares issued in 2021 on the January 2016 holding, still in his own hands. And his rights under an aircraft lease and under a loan he advanced, both entered into in 2016.

items.stem: How do the two objections stand?

options.text: Both succeed, the two objections reinforcing each other because a pre-2017 arrangement is tested only against the benefit of the assessee actually assessed
options.misconception: combines both misreadings, and adds a rule about who is assessed that appears nowhere in the exclusion
options.why: Neither objection stands on its own and putting them together does not help. The Chapter reaches an old arrangement for a new benefit, and the floor is an aggregate across the parties for the relevant assessment year.

options.text: The date objection succeeds — an arrangement entered into before 1 April 2017 is outside the Chapter altogether
options.misconception: extends the grandfathering of investments to arrangements, which the rule expressly separates
options.why: Only income from the transfer of investments made before 1 April 2017 is protected by date. For everything else the rule says the opposite in terms, applying the Chapter irrespective of when the arrangement was entered into so long as the benefit is obtained on or after that date.

options.text: The threshold objection succeeds — the ₹3 crore limit is applied taxpayer by taxpayer, and none of the three crossed it
options.misconception: divides an aggregate limit among the parties, which the rule and the Board both refuse
options.why: The exclusion is written about the tax benefit arising in aggregate to all the parties to the arrangement, and the Board has answered a request to read it per taxpayer by saying the limit cannot be read in respect of a single taxpayer only.

options.text: Both fail — the Chapter applies to an arrangement irrespective of the date it was entered into for a tax benefit obtained on or after 1 April 2017, and the ₹3 crore floor is tested on the aggregate benefit to all the parties in the relevant assessment year
options.why: The date objection is answered by the rule itself, which applies the provisions to any arrangement other than a grandfathered investment irrespective of the date on which it was entered into, in respect of a tax benefit obtained on or after 1 April 2017. The threshold objection is answered by the words of the exclusion: it applies where the tax benefit arising in the relevant assessment year, in aggregate to all the parties to the arrangement, does not exceed ₹3 crore. The Board has confirmed that the limit cannot be read in respect of a single taxpayer only. Here the aggregate is ₹4 crore.
keywords: in aggregate to all the parties

citation.ref: Rule 10U(1)(a) and the proviso to Rule 10U(1) read with CBDT Circular No. 7 of 2017 dated 27 January 2017 — the ₹3 crore floor measured on the aggregate tax benefit to all parties in the relevant assessment year, and the Chapter applying irrespective of the date the arrangement was entered into for a benefit obtained on or after 1 April 2017

items.scenario: An arrangement was entered into in 2014. It produces a tax benefit for the first time in previous year 2025-26, and the benefit that year comes to ₹4 crore spread over three parties to the arrangement, no single one of whom gets more than ₹2 crore. The assessee says the arrangement predates the Chapter and that in any case no party crossed ₹3 crore.

items.stem: Which of the five are virtual digital assets?

options.text: The crypto token, the non-fungible token and the gift voucher, a voucher being a digital representation of value exchanged for consideration
options.misconception: keeps the voucher inside the first limb and misses that it has been notified out of the definition
options.why: A gift card or voucher, being a record that may be used to obtain goods or services or a discount on them, is one of the three things expressly excluded from the definition by notification.

options.text: All five, the definition covering anything of value that can be transferred, stored or traded electronically
options.misconception: applies the width of the first limb without the exclusions the Central Government has notified under the same section
options.why: The definition is wide, and the section then lets the Central Government exclude digital assets by notification. Three classes have been excluded — vouchers and gift cards, reward and loyalty points, and subscriptions — precisely because the first limb would otherwise have swallowed them.

options.text: The crypto token only, a non-fungible token being outside the definition unless it is issued by a regulated exchange
options.misconception: adds a regulated-issuer condition to the non-fungible token limb, which turns instead on notification and on what the token carries
options.why: A non-fungible token is a limb of the definition in its own right, and the Central Government has specified a token which qualifies to be a virtual digital asset as one. Who issued it is not the test.

options.text: The crypto token and the non-fungible token only
options.why: A crypto-asset that relies on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or similar technology to validate and secure transactions is a virtual digital asset in its own limb of section 2(47A), and a notified non-fungible token is another. The other three were taken out by notification: gift cards and vouchers usable to obtain goods or services or a discount on them; mileage points, reward points and loyalty cards given without direct monetary consideration under an award, reward, benefit, loyalty, incentive, rebate or promotional programme and redeemable only for goods, services or a discount; and a subscription to a website, platform or application.

citation.ref: Section 2(47A) read with CBDT Notification No. 74/2022 dated 30 June 2022 — the crypto-asset and non-fungible token limbs of the definition, and the exclusion of gift cards and vouchers, mileage, reward and loyalty points, and subscriptions to a website, platform or application

items.scenario: A client lists five things he holds and asks which of them the Act treats as a virtual digital asset. A crypto token recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger. A gift voucher from a department store, usable only against goods there. Airline mileage points earned under a loyalty programme and redeemable only for flights. A twelve-month subscription to a streaming platform. And a non-fungible token that carries no claim to anything physical.

items.stem: How does the notification on non-fungible tokens treat the two?

options.text: The first is a non-fungible token and so a virtual digital asset; the second is not, because its transfer results in the transfer of ownership of an underlying tangible asset and that transfer of ownership is legally enforceable
options.why: The Central Government specified a token which qualifies to be a virtual digital asset as a non-fungible token, with one carve-out: it does not include a non-fungible token whose transfer results in transfer of ownership of an underlying tangible asset where the transfer of ownership of that underlying tangible asset is legally enforceable. The artwork token carries no such title and stays inside; the warehouse token carries an enforceable title and falls out, so its transfer is dealt with under the ordinary provisions instead.

options.text: Both are non-fungible tokens and so virtual digital assets, the carve-out applying only to tokens representing immovable property registered under the Registration Act
options.misconception: narrows the carve-out to registered immovable property, when it is written about any underlying tangible asset
options.why: The carve-out speaks of an underlying tangible asset and of a legally enforceable transfer of ownership in it. It is not confined to any particular class of property or to any register.

options.text: The second is a virtual digital asset and the first is not, since only a token backed by something real has inherent value
options.misconception: inverts the carve-out by assuming backing by a real asset is what brings a token in
options.why: Backing by a real asset is what takes the token out, not what brings it in, provided the transfer of ownership in that asset is legally enforceable. A token with nothing behind it stays inside the definition.

options.text: Neither is a virtual digital asset, a non-fungible token being covered only if the Central Government notifies each token individually
options.misconception: reads the notification as requiring token-by-token specification rather than a class notification with a carve-out
options.why: The notification specifies a class — a token which qualifies to be a virtual digital asset — and then carves out the enforceable-title case. No individual token has to be named.

citation.ref: Section 2(47A)(b) read with CBDT Notification No. 75/2022 dated 30 June 2022 — a token qualifying as a virtual digital asset specified as a non-fungible token, excluding one whose transfer results in a legally enforceable transfer of ownership of an underlying tangible asset

items.scenario: Two tokens are sold in the same week. The first is a token representing a piece of digital artwork; nothing physical passes and no title to any physical thing is created. The second is a token whose transfer transfers ownership of a warehouse, and the transfer of that ownership is legally enforceable against the seller.

items.stem: What is the tax on the income from the virtual digital asset?

options.text: ₹1,91,880 — being 31.2 per cent of ₹6,15,000, after allowing the ₹35,000 of exchange and brokerage charges as a cost of transfer
options.misconception: allows the cost of transfer, when the section allows the cost of acquisition and nothing else
options.why: The words are that no deduction is allowed in respect of any expenditure or allowance except the cost of acquisition. Brokerage and exchange charges are expenditure on the transfer and are outside that single exception, which is what makes this head harsher than capital gains.

options.text: ₹2,02,800 — being 30 per cent of ₹6,50,000 plus cess, the ₹35,000 of charges not being deductible and the business loss not being available against this income
options.why: Section 115BBH allows no deduction under any provision of the Act in respect of any expenditure or allowance except the cost of acquisition, so the income is ₹8,10,000 less ₹1,60,000, which is ₹6,50,000, and the ₹35,000 of charges is simply lost. No set off of any loss is allowed against that income, so the business loss cannot touch it and is carried forward instead. Tax at 30 per cent on ₹6,50,000 is ₹1,95,000, and cess at 4 per cent brings it to ₹2,02,800.
keywords: No set off of any loss

options.text: ₹1,95,000 — 30 per cent of ₹6,50,000, no cess being chargeable on a special rate under section 115BBH
options.misconception: exempts a special-rate income from health and education cess, which applies to income-tax however computed
options.why: The computation of the income is right and the cess is not optional. The module's own worked illustrations under this section apply the rate as 31.2 per cent, being 30 per cent with cess at 4 per cent on it.

options.text: ₹1,40,400 — being 31.2 per cent of ₹4,50,000, after setting off the business loss of ₹2,00,000
options.misconception: sets a business loss against income taxed under section 115BBH, which the section forbids
options.why: The section says no set off of any loss shall be allowed against income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset. The business loss of ₹2,00,000 has to be carried forward for set off against business income of a later year instead.

citation.ref: Section 115BBH — income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset taxed at 30 per cent, with no deduction for any expenditure or allowance except the cost of acquisition and no set off of any loss against that income

items.scenario: Mr Pathak, aged 34, transferred a virtual digital asset during previous year 2025-26 for ₹8,10,000. It had cost him ₹1,60,000 and he paid ₹35,000 of exchange and brokerage charges on the sale. He also has a business loss of ₹2,00,000 for the year, which he wants set off. Take health and education cess at 4 per cent and ignore surcharge and any other income.

items.stem: What is taxable, and what happens to the loss?

options.text: ₹90,000 is taxable, and the ₹40,000 loss may be set off against her other income of the year because only set off against virtual digital asset income is barred
options.misconception: reads the bar as one-directional, when the section blocks the loss against income computed under any provision of the Act
options.why: There are two separate prohibitions. One stops other losses coming into this income. The other stops this loss going out — it is not allowed to be set off against income computed under any provision of the Act.

options.text: ₹50,000 is taxable, losses and gains on virtual digital assets being netted against each other before the rate is applied
options.misconception: assumes an intra-head netting, when the section forbids the set off of any loss against this income including a loss on another such asset
options.why: There is no netting. The section allows no set off of any loss against this income and does not make an exception for a loss on another virtual digital asset, which is why each transfer is computed on its own.

options.text: ₹90,000 is taxable, but the ₹40,000 loss may be carried forward for eight assessment years for set off against gains on virtual digital assets
options.misconception: gets the current year right and then borrows the capital loss carry-forward rule, which this section expressly denies
options.why: The section says the loss shall not be allowed to be carried forward to succeeding assessment years. There is no eight-year window and no future gain it can be used against.

options.text: ₹90,000 is taxable, and the ₹40,000 loss is neither set off against the gain nor carried forward to any later year
options.why: The bar is written twice over and it catches this. No set off of any loss is allowed against income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset, and a loss from the transfer of a virtual digital asset is not allowed to be set off against income computed under any provision of the Act nor allowed to be carried forward to a succeeding assessment year. So the gain of ₹90,000 is taxed in full at 30 per cent and the ₹40,000 dies in the year it arose.
keywords: No set off of any loss
not allowed to be set off

citation.ref: Section 115BBH(2) — no set off of any loss against income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset, and a loss from such a transfer neither set off against income computed under any provision of the Act nor carried forward to a succeeding assessment year

items.scenario: During previous year 2025-26 Ms Devika made a gain of ₹90,000 on the transfer of one virtual digital asset and a loss of ₹40,000 on the transfer of another. She proposes to offer ₹50,000 to tax, and to carry the loss forward if the department disagrees.

items.stem: Who has to deduct tax under section 194S, and how much?

options.text: Mr Harsh need not deduct, his consideration of ₹48,000 being within the ₹50,000 threshold for a specified person; Corniche Ltd must deduct ₹120, being 1 per cent of ₹12,000, the threshold for any other person being ₹10,000
options.why: The section has two thresholds. For a specified person — an individual or Hindu undivided family with no income under the head profits and gains of business or profession, or whose turnover did not exceed ₹1 crore in business or ₹50 lakh in a profession in the preceding financial year — the aggregate consideration must exceed ₹50,000 in the financial year before any deduction is due, and Mr Harsh is inside it. For anybody else the figure is ₹10,000, which Corniche Ltd has crossed, so it deducts at 1 per cent.

options.text: Both must deduct at 1 per cent, the single threshold under section 194S being ₹10,000 for everybody
options.misconception: applies one threshold to both, missing the higher figure the section gives a specified person
options.why: The section sets out a table with two rows. A specified person has a threshold of ₹50,000 and every other person a threshold of ₹10,000, and Mr Harsh is inside the higher one.

options.text: Neither must deduct, both being below the ₹50,000 threshold that applies to a transfer of a virtual digital asset
options.misconception: applies the specified person's threshold to a company, which gets the lower one
options.why: The ₹50,000 figure is available only to a specified person, which is an individual or a Hindu undivided family answering the turnover or no-business-income test. A company is in the other row, where the threshold is ₹10,000.

options.text: Mr Harsh must deduct ₹480 but cannot, having no tax deduction account number; Corniche Ltd must deduct ₹120
options.misconception: puts Mr Harsh over a threshold he is under, and treats the absence of a deduction account number as an obstacle when the section disapplies that requirement for him
options.why: Mr Harsh is below his ₹50,000 threshold, so nothing is due from him at all. And if he had been over it, the want of a deduction account number would not have stopped him: section 203A does not apply to a specified person under this section.

citation.ref: Section 194S with the table of thresholds and the disapplication of section 203A — deduction at 1 per cent, ₹50,000 for a specified person being an individual or Hindu undivided family with turnover within ₹1 crore in business or ₹50 lakh in a profession or with no business income, and ₹10,000 for any other person

items.scenario: Two buyers pay for virtual digital assets during financial year 2025-26. Mr Harsh is salaried, has no income under the head profits and gains of business or profession, and pays ₹48,000 in the year for an asset bought from a resident. Corniche Ltd, a company, pays ₹12,000 in the year for an asset bought from a resident.

items.stem: What is the answer to the three questions?

options.text: Deduction is on ₹5,00,000 excluding the goods and services tax but including the ₹6,000 of platform charges, which are part of what the buyer paid
options.misconception: excludes the tax but keeps the deductor's own service charge, when the clarification excludes both
options.why: The clarification is that the withholding is on the net consideration after excluding the goods and services tax and the charges levied by the deductor for rendering the service. Both come out.

options.text: Deduction is on the consideration net of the goods and services tax and the charges levied by the deductor, section 194Q does not apply once tax has been deducted under section 194S, and the payment gateway need not deduct where the person required to deduct has done so
options.why: The Board's guidelines answer all three. The tax required to be withheld under section 194S is on the net consideration after excluding the goods and services tax and the charges levied by the deductor for rendering the service. Once tax is deducted under section 194S, tax is not required to be deducted under section 194Q, and the Board declined to decide whether a virtual digital asset is goods at all. And a payment gateway is not required to deduct on a transaction where the person required to make the deduction has already done so, and may take an undertaking to that effect.

options.text: Deduction is on the gross ₹5,96,000, section 194Q applies in addition because a virtual digital asset is goods, and the payment gateway must also deduct
options.misconception: takes the gross figure and then stacks three deductions on one payment, which is the outcome the guidelines were issued to prevent
options.why: Every limb is answered the other way. The deduction is on the net consideration, section 194Q is displaced once section 194S has been applied, and the payment gateway is relieved where the payer has deducted.

options.text: Deduction is on the net consideration, but where tax is deductible under section 194-O as well the deduction is made under section 194-O and not under section 194S
options.misconception: reverses the priority between the two sections, which the Act settles in favour of section 194S
options.why: The section says that in a case where tax is deductible under section 194-O along with section 194S, the tax shall be deducted under section 194S and not section 194-O.

citation.ref: Section 194S with CBDT Circular No. 13/2022 dated 22 June 2022 and Circular No. 14/2022 dated 28 June 2022 — deduction on the consideration net of goods and services tax and the deductor's charges, section 194S in preference to section 194-O, section 194Q displaced once section 194S has been applied, and no deduction by a payment gateway where the payer has deducted

items.scenario: A company buys a virtual digital asset from a resident dealer for ₹5,00,000 plus goods and services tax of ₹90,000, and the platform charges the buyer ₹6,000 for the service of executing the trade. The payment is routed through a payment gateway. The company's tax head asks whether tax is to be deducted on ₹5,96,000, whether section 194Q applies because the asset might be goods, and whether the payment gateway must deduct as well.

items.stem: Which form does each report go in, and what opinion does the tax auditor give in each?

options.text: Form 3CA for both, Form 3CB being used only where the accounting year differs from the financial year
options.misconception: turns the one situation the module singles out for Form 3CB into the only situation it covers
options.why: A company whose accounting year differs from the financial year does have to prepare and audit accounts for the financial year and report in Form 3CB, but that is a particular case, not the rule. Form 3CB is used wherever no other law requires an audit.

options.text: Form 3CB for the company and Form 3CA for the firm, the more demanding form being reserved for the corporate assessee
options.misconception: reverses the two forms by assuming the choice turns on the status of the assessee rather than on whether another law already requires an audit
options.why: The choice turns on one fact only — whether the accounts are already required to be audited under another law. It is a company that usually is, which puts it in Form 3CA, the form where the tax auditor gives the fewer opinions because somebody else has already given the other one.

options.text: Form 3CD for both, Forms 3CA and 3CB being alternative annexures to it
options.misconception: inverts the relationship, when Form 3CD is the statement of particulars annexed to whichever report is used
options.why: Form 3CD is the statement of particulars required under section 44AB and is annexed to the audit report, which is in Form 3CA or Form 3CB. The report is not annexed to the particulars.

options.text: Form 3CA for the company, where the tax auditor gives no true and fair opinion and only says whether the Form 3CD particulars are true and correct; Form 3CB for the firm, where he gives the true and fair opinion on the balance sheet and the profit and loss account as well
options.why: Form 3CA is used where the accounts of the business or profession have been audited under any other law, such as the Companies Act, 2013 or the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008. There the tax auditor is not required to give his opinion on whether the accounts give a true and fair view; he annexes the audited accounts and the statutory auditor's report and opines only on the particulars in Form 3CD. Form 3CB is for a person whose accounts are not required to be audited under any other law, and there he opines that the balance sheet shows the state of affairs as at the last date of the accounting year and the profit and loss account the profit or loss for that year, as well as on the Form 3CD particulars.

citation.ref: Rule 6G with Circular No. 561 dated 22 May 1990 — Form 3CA where the accounts are audited under another law and the tax auditor gives no true and fair opinion, Form 3CB where they are not and he does, and Form 3CD annexed to whichever report is used

items.scenario: Two clients need a tax audit report for previous year 2025-26. One is a private company whose accounts are audited under the Companies Act, 2013. The other is a partnership firm whose accounts no other law requires to be audited.

items.stem: What does Rule 6G(3) permit here?

options.text: A revised report may be issued by the same auditor at any time up to the completion of the assessment, the assessment year limit applying only to the original report
options.misconception: stretches the deadline for a revision to the completion of the assessment
options.why: The rule fixes the outer date for the revised report itself: it has to be furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year for which the report pertains.

options.text: No revision is possible once the report has been uploaded; the payment can only be dealt with in the return
options.misconception: treats a signed report as final, when the rule provides expressly for this one situation
options.why: This is the situation Rule 6G(3) was written for. A payment made after the report which changes a section 40 or section 43B disallowance is the ground of revision the rule names.

options.text: A revised report may be issued by any chartered accountant, and there is no time limit because the rule places no limit on the number of revisions
options.misconception: reads the absence of a limit on the number of revisions as the absence of a time limit and of a rule about who may revise
options.why: There is no restriction on how many times a report may be revised, and there are restrictions on who and when. The same tax auditor does the revision, and the revised report goes in before the end of the relevant assessment year.

options.text: A revised report may be issued, because a payment has been made after the report which necessitates recalculation of the disallowance under section 43B, but it has to be issued by the same tax auditor and furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year
options.why: Rule 6G(3) allows a revision where there is a payment by the person after the report was furnished which necessitates recalculation of the disallowance under section 40 or section 43B, and requires the revised report to be furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year. Revision of a tax audit report has to be done by the same tax auditor who did the original audit and not by another. The revised report must carry a reference to the earlier report, be signed on the current date, and be issued under a fresh unique document identification number.
keywords: before the end of the relevant assessment year

citation.ref: Rule 6G(3) — a revised tax audit report where a payment after the report necessitates recalculation of a disallowance under section 40 or section 43B, furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year, by the same tax auditor, with a reference to the earlier report and a fresh unique document identification number

items.scenario: A tax audit report for previous year 2025-26 was signed and uploaded in September 2026. In November 2026, before filing the return, the assessee paid a sum covered by section 43B whose payment changes the disallowance the report had computed. He asks a second chartered accountant to issue a revised report, saying the original auditor is unavailable.

items.stem: What penalty may the Assessing Officer direct under section 271B?

options.text: Nothing, because section 273B keeps a penalty under section 271B out wherever the assessee is otherwise compliant
options.misconception: reads section 273B as a general exemption rather than a defence that has to be made out on reasonable cause
options.why: Section 273B says no penalty shall be imposed if the person proves that there was reasonable cause for the failure. It is a defence to be established, and on these facts there is no explanation at all.

options.text: ₹8,50,000, being the fixed sum of ₹1,50,000 in addition to one half of one per cent of turnover
options.misconception: adds the two figures, when the section offers them as alternatives and takes the lesser
options.why: The two figures are alternatives, not cumulative. The Assessing Officer directs payment of a sum equal to the percentage or to ₹1,50,000, whichever is less.

options.text: ₹1,50,000, being lower than one half of one per cent of the ₹14 crore turnover
options.why: The penalty is one half of one per cent of the total sales, turnover or gross receipts in business, or ₹1,50,000, WHICHEVER IS LESS. Half a per cent of ₹14 crore is ₹7,00,000, which is the larger of the two, so the penalty is the flat ₹1,50,000. The percentage only ever bites where turnover is below ₹3 crore.
keywords: one half of one per cent

options.text: ₹7,00,000, being one half of one per cent of the turnover of ₹14 crore
options.misconception: takes the percentage as the penalty, when the section directs the lower of the percentage and the fixed sum
options.why: The section ends with the words whichever is less. Where the percentage works out above ₹1,50,000 it is the fixed sum that applies, so a large business never pays more than ₹1,50,000 under this section.

citation.ref: Section 271B read with section 273B — penalty of one half of one per cent of total sales, turnover or gross receipts or ₹1,50,000, whichever is less, and no penalty where reasonable cause for the failure is proved

items.scenario: Sarvesh Traders had turnover of ₹14 crore for financial year 2025-26 and did not get its accounts audited under section 44AB at all. It has no explanation to offer. Ignore any other default.

items.stem: What follows for the company and for the chartered accountant?

options.text: The company is not in default at all, since each business is tested separately and neither crossed the ₹10 crore limit on its own
options.misconception: tests the threshold business by business, when the aggregate sales, turnover and gross receipts of all businesses are taken
options.why: The aggregate sales, turnover or gross receipts of all businesses carried on by the assessee are taken in deciding whether the prescribed limit has been exceeded. On ₹18 crore it plainly has been.

options.text: The company is in default and the penalty is computed on the whole ₹18 crore, the report furnished for part of the turnover being of no effect
options.misconception: ignores that a report was in fact furnished for the larger business when fixing the base of the penalty
options.why: The example in the module is exactly this. The Assessing Officer wanted to charge on ₹18 crore and the answer is that, the report having been furnished for ₹15 crore, the penalty is invoked only on the ₹3 crore left uncovered.

options.text: The company is in default because the turnovers of all its businesses are aggregated to ₹18 crore, but the section 271B penalty is computed on the ₹3 crore for which no report was furnished; the chartered accountant is liable to ₹10,000 under section 271J for that certificate
options.why: Where an assessee carries on more than one business activity the results of all of them are clubbed, so the threshold is tested on ₹18 crore and section 44AB was attracted for the whole. The module's own example then limits the penalty base: since the assessee has already furnished the report for ₹15 crore, the penalty is invoked only on the turnover of ₹3 crore and not on ₹18 crore. Section 271J is a separate charge on the accountant, of ₹10,000 for each report or certificate in which incorrect information is furnished.

options.text: The company is in default, but section 271J has no application to the chartered accountant because it is confined to a registered valuer
options.misconception: confines section 271J to one of the several persons it names
options.why: Section 271J reaches an accountant, a merchant banker and a registered valuer alike, and charges ₹10,000 for each report or certificate in which incorrect information is furnished under the Act or the Rules.

citation.ref: Section 271B read with section 44AB and section 271J — the turnover of all businesses aggregated for the threshold, the penalty computed only on the turnover for which no report was furnished, and ₹10,000 for each report or certificate carrying incorrect information

items.scenario: Nandini Ltd runs two businesses, one with turnover of ₹15 crore and the other with turnover of ₹3 crore, all receipts and payments being through banking channels. It prepared financial statements only for the first, got them audited and furnished the report in time, believing the second business too small to matter. Its chartered accountant separately furnished a certificate under the Act carrying information he had not verified and which turned out to be incorrect.

items.stem: Which form does each need?

options.text: Form 10B or 10BB for the trust, Form 29B for the company, Form 3CEA for the slump sale and Form 15CB for the remittance
options.why: Section 12A(1)(b) requires a trust or institution to have its accounts audited and to furnish Form 10B or Form 10BB before the specified date to claim exemption under section 11 or section 12. A company to which section 115JB applies furnishes Form 29B certifying the correctness of the computation of book profit. A slump sale under section 50B needs Form 3CEA certifying the net worth of the undertaking or division. And a remittance to a non-resident chargeable under the Act needs a certificate in Form 15CB where the remittance, or the aggregate of such remittances, exceeds ₹5 lakh during the financial year, which ₹7,00,000 does.

options.text: Form 10B or 10BB for the trust, Form 29C for the company, Form 10CCB for the slump sale and Form 15CB for the remittance
options.misconception: swaps the minimum alternate tax form for the alternate minimum tax one and uses the profit-linked deduction form for a slump sale
options.why: Form 29C is for a person to whom alternate minimum tax under section 115JC applies, not a company under section 115JB, which uses Form 29B. Form 10CCB is the audit report for a deduction under sections 80-IA to 80-IE, prescribed by Rule 18BBB, and has nothing to do with a slump sale.

options.text: Form 3CD for all four, being the statement of particulars required under the Act
options.misconception: treats one form as covering every report, when each provision prescribes its own
options.why: Form 3CD is the statement of particulars annexed to a tax audit report under section 44AB. Each of the other provisions prescribes a form of its own.

options.text: Form 10B or 10BB for the trust, Form 29B for the company, Form 3CEA for the slump sale, and no form for the remittance, which is below the ₹10 lakh limit for a Form 15CB
options.misconception: raises the Form 15CB limit to ₹10 lakh, when it is ₹5 lakh in the financial year
options.why: The certificate is required where the remittance or the aggregate of such remittances exceeds ₹5 lakh during the financial year and the remittances are chargeable under the Act. A remittance of ₹7,00,000 is over that.

citation.ref: Sections 12A(1)(b), 115JB, 115JC, 50B and 80-IA(7) with Rules 18BBB and 37BB — Form 10B or 10BB for a trust, Form 29B for minimum alternate tax, Form 29C for alternate minimum tax, Form 3CEA for the net worth on a slump sale, Form 10CCB for a deduction under sections 80-IA to 80-IE, and Form 15CB where a remittance or the aggregate of remittances exceeds ₹5 lakh in the financial year

items.scenario: A practice is preparing four filings. A trust claiming exemption under section 11. A company to which minimum alternate tax under section 115JB applies. An assessee who has sold an undertaking by way of a slump sale under section 50B. And a client remitting ₹7,00,000 to a non-resident, the remittance being chargeable under the Act.

items.stem: How does each fare under Part I of the Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949?

options.text: Both are guilty, an incorrect report being professional misconduct whatever the accountant does afterwards
options.misconception: makes the misconduct strict, when what the clauses ask about is diligence and the sufficiency of the information obtained
options.why: The clauses are about conduct, not outcome. The second accountant's report was wrong and he was held not guilty, because on discovering the error he withdrew it and informed the assessee immediately, which is what due diligence required of him at that point.

options.text: The first is guilty under clauses (7) and (8), and the second is not guilty, having withdrawn his report as soon as he knew and told the assessee at once
options.why: Clause (7) covers a failure to exercise due diligence or gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties and clause (8) a failure to obtain sufficient information necessary for the expression of an opinion. Given the nature of the business the onus was on the first to extend his verification to cash payments, mere reliance on a management certificate is not acceptable, and certifying that there were no such instances against ₹30 crore of them attracts both clauses. The second acted the moment he knew — he withdrew the report in Form 10CCB, informed the assessee, who filed a revised return withdrawing the claim — and was held not guilty under clause (7).

options.text: The first is guilty under clause (7) only, clause (8) being confined to a statutory audit under the Companies Act, 2013
options.misconception: confines clause (8) to company audits, when it applies to the expression of any opinion by a chartered accountant in practice
options.why: Clause (8) applies to a chartered accountant in practice who fails to obtain sufficient information necessary for the expression of an opinion, and it was applied alongside clause (7) in the tax audit case.

options.text: Neither is guilty, since the first carried out test checks and held a certificate from the management, which is the evidence an auditor is entitled to rely on
options.misconception: treats test checks and a management certificate as sufficient regardless of what the business is and what the sums involved are
options.why: The contention that test checks did not reveal the violations was held not tenable. Considering the nature of the business the onus was on the chartered accountant to verify the position, such payments can be identified independently of bank transactions, and mere reliance on a certificate issued by the management is not acceptable.

citation.ref: Clauses (7) and (8) of Part I of the Second Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, read with section 40A(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Rule 18BBB with Form 10CCB — want of due diligence and failure to obtain sufficient information, and withdrawal of a report on discovery of the error with immediate communication to the assessee

items.scenario: Two chartered accountants are before the Disciplinary Committee. The first certified in Form 3CD that there were no payments in breach of section 40A(3) by a jewellery business, when such payments in fact ran to ₹30 crore; his defence is that his test checks did not reveal them and that he relied on a certificate from the management. The second issued Form 10CCB for a deduction under section 80-IA, later discovered that the ten year period had already expired, withdrew his report at once and told the assessee, who filed a revised return giving up the claim.

items.stem: Which of the four are agricultural income?

options.text: The seedlings and the sub-tenant's rent only
options.why: Explanation 3 to section 2(1A) deems income derived from saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery to be agricultural income whether or not the basic operations were carried out on land, so the ₹75,000 qualifies. Rent from agricultural land in India is agricultural income and ownership is not one of the conditions, so rent received by an original tenant from a sub-tenant qualifies too. The house rent fails on Explanation 2, which takes out income derived from a building used for any purpose other than agriculture, including letting for residential purposes. And poultry farming is one of the activities the module says the term agriculture cannot be stretched to.

options.text: The sub-tenant's rent only, income from a nursery being business income unless the basic operations were carried out on the land
options.misconception: applies the pre-Explanation case law and misses the deeming provision that settles it
options.why: That was the position under Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy, and Explanation 3 was inserted to settle it the other way. Income from saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery is deemed agricultural whether or not the basic operations were carried out on land.

options.text: The house rent, the seedlings and the sub-tenant's rent
options.misconception: treats rent from a building standing on agricultural land as agricultural income whatever the building is used for
options.why: Explanation 2 to section 2(1A) says that income derived from any building from its use for any purpose other than agriculture, including letting for residential purposes or for a business or profession, is not agricultural income. Houses occupied by industrial workers as homes are that use exactly.

options.text: The seedlings only, rent being agricultural income only in the hands of the owner of the land
options.misconception: reads ownership of the land into the first limb, which asks only that the rent be derived from land in India used for agriculture
options.why: Three conditions have to hold — rent or revenue derived from land, land situated in India, and land used for agricultural purposes — and ownership is not among them. Rent received by an original tenant from a sub-tenant is agricultural income.

citation.ref: Section 2(1A) with Explanations 2 and 3 read with section 10(1) — rent from land in India used for agriculture without any requirement of ownership, a building used for a non-agricultural purpose taken out by Explanation 2, nursery saplings and seedlings deemed agricultural by Explanation 3, and poultry farming outside the term agriculture

items.scenario: Four receipts for assessment year 2026-27. Rent of ₹60,000 from tenants living in houses built on land used for agriculture, the tenants being workers at a nearby factory who occupy them as homes. ₹75,000 from the sale of seedlings raised in a nursery without carrying out all the basic operations on land. ₹2,40,000 of rent received by an original tenant of agricultural land in India from his sub-tenant. And ₹4,00,000 from a poultry farm run on the same holding.

items.stem: How are the three treated?

options.text: Only the potted plants are agricultural income, Explanation 3 covering anything grown in a container
options.misconception: stretches the nursery deeming provision to plants that were never part of a nursery operation
options.why: Explanation 3 is about saplings or seedlings grown in a nursery. It does not turn every plant raised in a pot into agricultural produce; the module keeps the pot-grown case on the other side of the line.

options.text: The store house income is agricultural, the Sri Lankan orchard income is fully taxable, and the potted plants grown directly in pots do not give agricultural income
options.why: Income from a farm building is agricultural where the building is on or in the immediate vicinity of the land and the cultivator requires it as a dwelling house or store house by reason of his connection with the land, and both conditions hold. The land has to be situated in India, so income from agricultural land in a foreign country is taxable in full. And on Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy the basic operations must be performed on the land before income can be agricultural, so income derived from the sale of plants grown directly in pots is not agricultural income.

options.text: All three are agricultural income, the source in each case being the growing of a crop
options.misconception: ignores the requirement that the land be in India and the basic operations rule for plants never grown on land
options.why: Two of the three fail. Land in a foreign country takes the income entirely outside the exemption, and plants raised directly in pots never involve the basic operations on land that Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy requires.

options.text: The store house income and the Sri Lankan orchard income are agricultural, and only the potted plants are taxable, since exemption follows the nature of the activity and not the place
options.misconception: drops the requirement that the land be situated in India from the definition
options.why: The definition names the place expressly. Rent or revenue must be derived from land situated in India and used for agricultural purposes, and if the agricultural land is situated in a foreign country the entire income is taxable.

citation.ref: Section 2(1A) read with CIT v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy (1957) 32 ITR 466 (SC) — the farm building conditions of immediate vicinity and connection with the land, the requirement that the land be situated in India, and the basic operations test for plants grown directly in pots

items.scenario: A grower keeps a store house on the edge of the field where his crop is cleaned and bagged, and he needs it as a store house because of his connection with the land. In the same year he also earns ₹9,00,000 from an orchard he owns in Sri Lanka, and he sells potted ornamental plants grown directly in pots on a terrace, with no operations of any kind carried out on land.

items.stem: What are his business income and his agricultural income?

options.text: Business income ₹6,40,000 and agricultural income ₹9,60,000, applying the 40 and 60 per cent split
options.misconception: uses the tea and roasted-coffee percentages for rubber
options.why: Forty per cent business and 60 per cent agricultural is Rule 8 for tea, and Rule 7B for coffee that is also roasted and ground. Rubber under Rule 7A is 35 and 65.

options.text: Business income ₹5,60,000 and agricultural income ₹10,40,000, being 35 per cent and 65 per cent of the ₹16,00,000 of profit on sale
options.why: Rule 7A applies to income derived from the sale of centrifuged latex manufactured from field latex obtained from rubber plants grown by the seller in India, and it splits the PROFIT, not the sale proceeds. The profit is ₹52,00,000 less ₹22,00,000 of growing cost less ₹14,00,000 of manufacturing cost, which is ₹16,00,000. Thirty-five per cent of that, ₹5,60,000, is business income and the balance 65 per cent, ₹10,40,000, is agricultural income and exempt.

options.text: Business income ₹18,20,000 and agricultural income ₹33,80,000, being 35 per cent and 65 per cent of the ₹52,00,000 of sale proceeds
options.misconception: applies the percentages to the sale proceeds rather than to the profit on sale
options.why: The rule speaks of profits on sale. Applying the split to turnover would tax him on business income of ₹18,20,000 when the whole enterprise made ₹16,00,000.

options.text: Business income ₹10,40,000 and agricultural income ₹5,60,000, being 65 per cent and 35 per cent of the profit
options.misconception: reverses the two percentages, giving the taxable share the larger figure
options.why: Under Rule 7A it is 35 per cent that is taxable as business income and 65 per cent that is agricultural and exempt. The exempt share is the larger one, which is the point of the rule.

citation.ref: Rule 7A of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — 35 per cent of the profit on sale of centrifuged latex manufactured from field latex obtained from rubber plants grown by the seller in India taxable as business income, and the balance 65 per cent agricultural income

items.scenario: Mr Nilekani grows rubber plants in India and manufactures centrifuged latex from the field latex obtained from them. The latex is sold for ₹52,00,000. Growing the rubber plants cost him ₹22,00,000 and manufacturing the latex cost him ₹14,00,000.

items.stem: What is the business income of each?

options.text: ₹8,00,000, ₹5,00,000 and ₹8,00,000 respectively, roasting and grinding being a further agricultural process that increases the exempt share
options.misconception: swaps the two coffee percentages by assuming more processing makes more of the profit agricultural
options.why: More manufacturing makes more of the profit business income, not less. Coffee grown and cured is 25 per cent business; coffee also roasted and ground is 40 per cent business, because the extra processing is a manufacturing activity.

options.text: ₹7,00,000, ₹7,00,000 and ₹8,00,000 respectively, coffee being 35 per cent business income however it is processed
options.misconception: uses the rubber percentage for coffee and collapses the two coffee cases into one
options.why: Thirty-five per cent is Rule 7A for rubber. Coffee has two figures of its own — 25 per cent where it is grown and cured, and 40 per cent where it is also roasted and ground.

options.text: ₹5,00,000, ₹8,00,000 and ₹8,00,000 respectively, being 25 per cent, 40 per cent and 40 per cent of the profit
options.why: Rule 7B gives 25 per cent as business income for coffee grown and cured by the seller in India, leaving 75 per cent agricultural, and 40 per cent for coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground by the seller in India with or without chicory or other flavouring ingredients, leaving 60 per cent agricultural. Rule 8 gives 40 per cent for tea grown and manufactured by the seller in India, leaving 60 per cent agricultural. Applied to ₹20,00,000 those are ₹5,00,000, ₹8,00,000 and ₹8,00,000.

options.text: ₹5,00,000, ₹8,00,000 and ₹12,00,000 respectively, tea being 60 per cent business income
options.misconception: inverts the tea split, which gives 40 per cent to business and 60 per cent to agriculture
options.why: Rule 8 taxes 40 per cent of the profit on sale of tea grown and manufactured by the seller in India as business income and leaves the balance 60 per cent as agricultural income.

citation.ref: Rules 7B and 8 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 — 25 per cent of the profit taxable as business income on coffee grown and cured by the seller in India, 40 per cent on coffee also roasted and ground with or without chicory, and 40 per cent on tea grown and manufactured by the seller in India

items.scenario: Three growers in India each made a profit of ₹20,00,000 on sale in previous year 2025-26. The first grew and cured coffee. The second grew, cured, roasted and ground coffee, mixing chicory into it. The third grew tea leaves and manufactured tea from them.

items.stem: Is stopping the analysis at section 9B correct?

options.text: Yes — once section 9B taxes the land, section 45(4) does not apply again to the same reconstitution
options.misconception: treats the two sections as alternatives rather than cumulative charges
options.why: The sections tax different components of the same event: 9B taxes the asset transfer, 45(4) taxes the excess over the capital account. Both can apply to a single reconstitution without double-taxing the same rupee.

options.text: No — but the liability falls on partner A personally, not on the firm
options.misconception: shifts the charge to the retiring partner
options.why: Both section 9B and section 45(4) tax the entity — the firm, AOP or BOI — not the partner receiving the assets. The partner's own capital gains, if any, arise separately on disposal of what was received.

options.text: No — section 45(4) must also be tested, taxing any excess of money plus the fair market value of assets received by A over A's capital account balance, as the firm's capital gains
options.why: The two sections operate in sequence on the same event: 9B taxes the deemed transfer of the capital asset at fair market value; 45(4) separately catches any excess consideration — in cash or assets — over the partner's capital account, taxable as capital gains for the firm. Skipping 45(4) misses this second charge.
