options.misconception: uses the forty per cent foreign company rate that ceased to apply from assessment year 2025-26
options.why: Case 1 is right and Case 2 uses a rate that no longer exists. The rate for a foreign company was reduced from forty per cent to thirty-five per cent by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from assessment year 2025-26, so the figure is ₹21,00,000.

options.text: Case 1 — ₹20,00,000, being 20 per cent of the gross ₹1,00,00,000 under section 115A; Case 2 — ₹21,00,000, being 35 per cent of the net ₹60,00,000 under section 44DA
options.why: With no permanent establishment, section 115A charges the gross receipt at twenty per cent with no deduction for expenditure, giving ₹20,00,000. Where the royalty is effectively connected with a permanent establishment, section 115A steps aside and section 44DA taxes ₹1,00,00,000 less ₹40,00,000, that is ₹60,00,000, at the ordinary foreign company rate of thirty-five per cent, giving ₹21,00,000.

options.text: ₹20,00,000 in both cases — section 115A charges royalty at 20 per cent on the gross amount whether or not there is a permanent establishment
options.misconception: overlooks section 44DA, which takes effectively connected royalty out of section 115A altogether
options.why: The whole point of section 44DA is that effective connection with a permanent establishment moves the income to the business head, taxed net at the ordinary rate, with books required under section 44AA and an audit report in Form 3CE. Section 115A(1) itself excludes such income.

options.text: Case 1 — ₹10,00,000 at 10 per cent on the gross amount; Case 2 — ₹21,00,000 at 35 per cent on the net amount
options.misconception: uses the ten per cent section 115A rate that applied before assessment year 2024-25
options.why: Case 2 is right. The section 115A rate on royalty and fees for technical services was doubled from ten per cent to twenty per cent with effect from assessment year 2024-25, so Case 1 is ₹20,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 115A(1)(b) and Section 44DA(1) with its provisos, read with Section 90(2) and Rule 6GA (Form 3CE)

items.scenario: Lyra GmbH, a foreign company, receives royalty of ₹1,00,00,000 from an Indian company during previous year 2025-26 under an agreement made after 31 March 1976. In Case 1 it has no permanent establishment in India. In Case 2 the agreement is effectively connected with its permanent establishment in India, and it has incurred ₹40,00,000 of expenditure wholly and exclusively for that permanent establishment. Ignore surcharge, cess and any treaty relief.

items.stem: Which state does Article 4(2) treat him as a resident of, and by which test?

options.text: India, on the habitual abode test — he spent more nights in India than in Country Y during the year
options.misconception: jumps to the habitual abode test while the centre of vital interests test is still capable of deciding
options.why: Habitual abode is the third test and is reached only where a centre of vital interests cannot be determined. Here it plainly can, and where the sequence decides earlier the later tests are simply not applied.

options.text: Whichever state he is a national of, nationality being the test the Article applies where a person has a home in both states
options.misconception: promotes nationality, which is the fourth test, above the centre of vital interests and habitual abode
options.why: Nationality comes fourth, after permanent home, centre of vital interests and habitual abode, and it is reached only where he has an habitual abode in both states or in neither. If he is a national of both or of neither, the competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement.

options.text: India — section 6(1) makes him a resident of India, and a treaty cannot displace a residential status conferred by the Act
options.misconception: denies the treaty any effect on residence, when section 90(2) lets the assessee take whichever of the Act and the treaty is more beneficial
options.why: Section 90(2) is what makes Article 4(2) operate at all. He remains a resident under section 6 for the Act's own purposes, but for the treaty's purposes he is treated as a resident of one state only, and that decides which state may tax what.

options.text: Country Y, on the centre of vital interests test — a permanent home is available in both, so the tie is broken by his closer personal and economic relations, which are in Country Y
options.why: Article 4(2) is worked in order and stops at the first test that decides. The permanent home test does not decide because a home is available in both states, so the next test applies: the centre of vital interests, being the state with which his personal and economic relations are closer. His family and his only business are in Country Y, so the tie breaks there and the habitual abode test is never reached.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital
citation.ref: Article 4(2), as adopted in India's double taxation avoidance agreements, read with Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: Mr Sethi is a resident of India for previous year 2025-26 under section 6(1), having stayed 190 days in India, and is at the same time a resident of Country Y under Country Y's own law. India and Country Y have a treaty carrying the standard Article 4(2) tie-breaker. He owns and keeps available a permanent home in both countries. His wife, children and his only business are in Country Y, though he spent more nights in India than in Country Y during the year.

items.stem: How is the ₹2,00,00,000 of undisclosed income of the block period charged to tax?

options.text: At the slab rates applicable to Mr Batra as an individual, the undisclosed income being added to his other income of the years concerned
options.misconception: assesses undisclosed income year by year at ordinary rates instead of as one block at the section 113 rate
options.why: Block assessment exists precisely so that undisclosed income found in a search is not folded back into each year's ordinary computation. It is assessed as one figure for the block period and charged at the flat rate section 113 sets.

options.text: 60 per cent on the undisclosed income of the part-period from 1 April 2025 to the date of the search only, the six preceding years being reopened by separate notices under section 148 and taxed at ordinary rates
options.misconception: splits the block period, when section 158BC assesses the whole of it in a single block assessment
options.why: The part-period from the first day of April of the year of search is part of the block period, not a separate assessment. Everything inside the block period is determined together under section 158BC, which is what makes a separate reassessment for those years unnecessary.

options.text: ₹1,20,00,000 — a flat 60 per cent under section 113, applied to the undisclosed income of the whole block period as one, whatever Mr Batra's status
options.why: Section 113 charges the total undisclosed income of the block period determined under section 158BC at sixty per cent, and sixty per cent of ₹2,00,00,000 is ₹1,20,00,000. The rate is flat and does not vary with the assessee's status, and it is increased by the surcharge levied by the Central Act applicable in the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the search was initiated.

options.text: ₹1,50,00,000 — 60 per cent tax of ₹1,20,00,000 plus a mandatory surcharge of 25 per cent on that tax
options.misconception: imports the twenty-five per cent surcharge that section 115BBE carries for unexplained credits into the section 113 charge
options.why: The sixty per cent is right; the surcharge is borrowed from the wrong section. Section 113 adds the surcharge levied by the Central Act for the relevant year, not the fixed twenty-five per cent that rides on section 115BBE.

citation.ref: Sections 158B(b), 158BA and 158BC read with Section 113, as inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 September 2024

items.scenario: A search under section 132 is initiated at Mr Batra's premises on 10 December 2025. The block assessment under section 158BC determines the total undisclosed income of the block period at ₹2,00,00,000. Mr Batra's other income for the years in the block period was returned and assessed in the ordinary way and is not in dispute. Ignore surcharge and cess.

items.stem: By when must the section 143(2) notice be served, and by when must the section 143(3) order be passed?

options.text: Notice by 30 September 2027 and order by 31 March 2028
options.misconception: uses the six-month period for a section 143(2) notice that the Finance Act, 2021 cut to three months
options.why: The order date is right. The notice period was reduced from six months to three months from the end of the financial year in which the return is furnished with effect from 1 April 2021, so the last date is 30 June 2027.

options.text: Notice by 30 June 2027 and order by 31 December 2027
options.misconception: uses the nine-month completion period that applied to assessment years before 2022-23
options.why: The notice date is right. For assessment year 2022-23 and every year after it the section 153(1) period is twelve months from the end of the assessment year, not nine, so the order date is 31 March 2028.

options.text: Notice by 30 January 2027 and order by 31 March 2028
options.misconception: counts the three months from the date the return was filed instead of from the end of the financial year in which it was filed
options.why: Three months from 30 October 2026 would indeed be 30 January 2027, and that is the wrong starting point. Section 143(2) runs from the end of the financial year in which the return is furnished, which is 31 March 2027.

options.text: Notice by 30 June 2027 and order by 31 March 2028
options.why: The return was furnished in financial year 2026-27, which ends on 31 March 2027, and section 143(2) allows three months from that end, giving 30 June 2027. Assessment year 2026-27 also ends on 31 March 2027, and section 153(1) allows twelve months from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable, giving 31 March 2028.
keywords: twelve months from the end of the assessment year

citation.ref: Section 143(2) proviso as amended by the Finance Act, 2021, and Section 153(1)

items.scenario: Cobalt Ltd furnishes its return of income for assessment year 2026-27 on 30 October 2026, within the due date under section 139(1). The Assessing Officer wishes to take the case up for scrutiny. No reference is made to the Transfer Pricing Officer and no other extension applies.

items.stem: Can Mr Nair take the order to a Dispute Resolution Committee under section 245MA?

options.text: Yes — the variations of ₹9,00,000 are within ₹10,00,000 and the returned income of ₹46,00,000 is within ₹50,00,000, so it is a specified order; the committee may also reduce or waive the penalty and grant immunity from prosecution
options.why: A specified order is one where the aggregate of the variations does not exceed ₹10,00,000 and the returned income does not exceed ₹50,00,000, and both tests are satisfied here. What makes this route worth taking is the relief no appellate authority can give: the committee may grant a reduction or waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution, and must pass its order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is admitted.

options.text: No — his returned income of ₹46,00,000 exceeds the ₹10,00,000 limit the section sets for eligibility
options.misconception: applies the ₹10 lakh variation limit to the returned income and drops the separate ₹50 lakh income limit
options.why: The section has two different figures for two different things. Ten lakh rupees is the cap on the aggregate variations; fifty lakh rupees is the cap on the returned income. Reading one into the other rules out cases the section was written for.

options.text: Yes on the figures, but the committee has no power to touch the penalty, which he must contest separately before the Commissioner (Appeals)
options.misconception: denies the committee the penalty and prosecution powers section 245MA expressly gives it
options.why: The power to grant a reduction or waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution, exercised in accordance with Rule 44DAC, is the distinguishing feature of the Dispute Resolution Committee. Without it the route would offer nothing an appeal does not.

options.text: No — an assessment order can only be challenged by an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 246A
options.misconception: treats the appellate route as exclusive, when section 245MA offers an alternative for a specified order
options.why: Section 245MA was inserted to give a small taxpayer an option other than appeal. It is confined to a specified order and excludes search, survey and treaty-information cases, but within those limits it stands beside section 246A.

citation.ref: Section 245MA with the Explanation defining a specified order, read with Rule 44DAC and the e-Dispute Resolution Scheme, 2022

items.scenario: Mr Nair returned an income of ₹46,00,000 for assessment year 2026-27. The assessment order proposes variations aggregating ₹9,00,000 and initiates penalty. The order is an ordinary scrutiny assessment — it is not founded on a search or survey, and no information under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A is involved. He would rather not appeal.

items.stem: What is taxable in the company's hands on this issue of shares?

options.text: ₹40,00,000 is taxable, but in the hands of the subscribers under section 56(2)(x) rather than in the company's hands
options.misconception: confuses the two provisions — section 56(2)(x) taxes a recipient who pays below fair market value, not one who pays above it
options.why: Section 56(2)(x) charges a person who receives property for less than its fair market value. These subscribers paid ₹500 for shares worth ₹300, which is more than fair market value, so nothing arises to them either.

options.text: Only the premium attributable to the non-resident subscribers is taxable, resident subscribers having always been outside the charge
options.misconception: reverses the position — the charge originally covered resident subscribers and was extended to non-residents in 2023, and the whole clause is now gone
options.why: Section 56(2)(viib) applied to resident subscribers from the start and was extended to non-residents with effect from assessment year 2024-25. Both limbs went together when the clause was omitted, so the distinction decides nothing now.

options.text: Nothing — section 56(2)(viib) was omitted with effect from assessment year 2025-26, so the ₹40,00,000 of premium above fair market value is not chargeable at all
options.why: The excess is ₹200 a share over the ₹300 fair market value on 20,000 shares, which is ₹40,00,000, and before the omission that whole amount would have been income from other sources. Section 56(2)(viib) was omitted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from assessment year 2025-26, so nothing arises in previous year 2025-26. Section 68 would still be open had the subscribers not been established, but on these facts it is not.

options.text: ₹40,00,000 is taxable as income from other sources, being the consideration received in excess of the fair market value of the shares
options.misconception: applies section 56(2)(viib), which stands omitted from assessment year 2025-26
options.why: The arithmetic is the arithmetic of a provision that no longer exists. Two hundred rupees a share on 20,000 shares is ₹40,00,000, and that figure had a charge on it up to assessment year 2024-25 and none after.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(viib) omitted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025 (A.Y. 2025-26), read with Sections 68 and 56(2)(x)

items.scenario: Ardent Systems Pvt Ltd, an unlisted company in which the public are not substantially interested, issues 20,000 equity shares during previous year 2025-26 at ₹500 each to a mix of resident and non-resident investors. The fair market value determined under Rule 11UA is ₹300 a share. The company can establish the identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of every subscriber.

items.stem: How is the ₹12,00,000 charged under section 115BBI?

options.text: At the maximum marginal rate rather than at 30 per cent, because income applied for the benefit of a specified person forfeits exemption
options.misconception: applies the maximum marginal rate that section 164(2) once carried, when section 115BBI now prescribes a rate of its own
options.why: Section 115BBI names thirty per cent for specified income and that rate displaces the older maximum marginal rate reasoning. Surcharge and cess ride on top of the thirty per cent but they do not turn it into the maximum marginal rate.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — 30 per cent of ₹10,00,000, the ₹2,00,000 of expenditure incurred in earning the income being deductible first
options.misconception: allows a deduction for expenditure against specified income, which section 115BBI(2) expressly forbids
options.why: The rate is right and the base is not. Sub-section (2) is the operative bar: no expenditure, no allowance and no set-off of loss may reduce specified income, so the ₹2,00,000 stays in.

options.text: ₹3,60,000 — 30 per cent of the whole ₹12,00,000, with no deduction for the ₹2,00,000 of expenditure and no set-off of the brought forward deficit
options.why: Income applied for the benefit of a person referred to in section 13(3) is specified income, and section 115BBI(2) allows no deduction for any expenditure, allowance or set-off of loss against it. The charge is therefore on the gross ₹12,00,000 at thirty per cent, which is ₹3,60,000. The trust's remaining income continues to be governed by sections 11 to 13 in the ordinary way.

options.text: The whole of the trust's income for the year loses exemption and is charged at 30 per cent, not merely the ₹12,00,000
options.misconception: treats a section 13 violation as forfeiting the trust's exemption entirely, when section 115BBI isolates only the specified income
options.why: Section 115BBI takes out the specified income and taxes it separately. Income applied for the charitable objects keeps its exemption under sections 11 and 12, which is what makes the section a targeted charge rather than a cancellation of registration.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBI(1) and 115BBI(2) with the Explanation, read with Sections 11(5) and 13(3)

items.scenario: A trust registered under section 12AB applies ₹12,00,000 of its income during previous year 2025-26 for the benefit of a person referred to in section 13(3). It incurred ₹2,00,000 of expenditure in earning the income so applied, and it has a brought forward deficit it wishes to set off. Its remaining income is applied wholly for its charitable objects. Ignore surcharge and cess.

items.stem: What is its gross total income for previous year 2025-26, and what is carried forward?

options.text: Gross total income nil, with ₹1,00,000 of unabsorbed depreciation carried forward indefinitely
options.why: Current year depreciation goes first, leaving business income of ₹7,00,000. The brought forward business loss of ₹5,00,000 goes next, leaving ₹2,00,000. The unabsorbed depreciation of ₹6,00,000 then absorbs that ₹2,00,000 and, being deemed part of the current year's allowance, a further ₹3,00,000 against house property income, leaving ₹1,00,000 to be carried forward indefinitely.

options.text: Gross total income ₹3,00,000, with ₹4,00,000 of unabsorbed depreciation carried forward
options.misconception: confines unabsorbed depreciation to business income, when section 32(2) lets it be set off against income under any head except salaries
options.why: The order of set-off is handled correctly here, which is what makes the slip convincing. Unabsorbed depreciation is deemed part of the current year's allowance and can meet income under any head other than salaries, so it takes the ₹3,00,000 of house property income and only ₹1,00,000 remains.

options.text: Gross total income ₹5,00,000, the unabsorbed depreciation of previous year 2016-17 having lapsed after eight years
options.misconception: applies the eight-year carry-forward limit for a business loss to unabsorbed depreciation, which is carried forward without any time limit
options.why: Section 32(2) sets no time limit. The eight-year limit belongs to section 72 and governs the business loss of previous year 2019-20, which is still within time in assessment year 2026-27.

options.text: Gross total income ₹3,00,000, with ₹4,00,000 of business loss carried forward
options.misconception: sets off unabsorbed depreciation before the brought forward business loss, stranding the loss it should have absorbed first
options.why: Taking the ₹6,00,000 of depreciation against the ₹7,00,000 leaves only ₹1,00,000 for the business loss, so ₹4,00,000 of it is stranded and the house property income stays taxable because a business loss cannot reach it. The settled order puts the business loss ahead precisely to avoid that.

citation.ref: Section 32(2) read with Sections 72(2), 72(3) and 80

items.scenario: For previous year 2025-26 Meridian Ltd has business profits of ₹15,00,000 before depreciation, current year depreciation of ₹8,00,000, and income from house property of ₹3,00,000. It carries forward a business loss of ₹5,00,000 from previous year 2019-20 and unabsorbed depreciation of ₹6,00,000 from previous year 2016-17. All returns were filed within the time allowed by section 139(1).

items.stem: What is the disallowance under section 14A read with Rule 8D?

options.text: ₹10,50,000 — ₹1,50,000 of direct expenditure plus 1 per cent of ₹9,00,00,000; the absence of exempt income during the year is no answer
options.why: Rule 8D adds the expenditure directly relating to the exempt income to one per cent of the annual average of the monthly averages of the investment balances, so ₹1,50,000 plus ₹9,00,000 gives ₹10,50,000. That is below the ₹18,00,000 of total expenditure claimed, so the rule's own ceiling does not bite. The Explanation inserted by the Finance Act, 2022 makes the section apply whether or not exempt income accrued during the year.

options.text: ₹9,00,000 — 1 per cent of the annual average of the monthly averages of the investment balances
options.misconception: applies only the one per cent limb of Rule 8D and drops the direct expenditure limb
options.why: Rule 8D has two limbs and both are added. Leaving out the ₹1,50,000 that relates directly to the exempt investments understates the disallowance by exactly that amount.

options.text: ₹1,50,000 — only the expenditure directly relating to the investments, the 1 per cent limb applying only in a year when exempt income is actually earned
options.misconception: makes the one per cent limb of Rule 8D conditional on exempt income having been earned, a condition neither the rule nor section 14A contains
options.why: Neither limb of Rule 8D is switched off by the absence of exempt income. Once the Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the assessee's own working, the rule is applied in full and both limbs are added.

options.text: Nothing — no exempt income was earned in the year, so there is no income in relation to which expenditure could have been incurred
options.misconception: relies on the pre-2022 case law that no disallowance arises in a year without exempt income, which the Explanation to section 14A now overrides
options.why: That argument won for years and was closed by statute. The Finance Act, 2022 added a non-obstante clause and an Explanation saying the disallowance is made whether or not such exempt income has accrued or arisen or been received during the previous year.

citation.ref: Section 14A(1) with its Explanation inserted by the Finance Act, 2022, read with Rule 8D(2) and 8D(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Halcyon Ltd claims total expenditure of ₹18,00,000 in computing its business income for previous year 2025-26. Of that, ₹1,50,000 relates directly to investments the income from which does not form part of total income. The annual average of the monthly averages of the opening and closing balances of those investments is ₹9,00,00,000. The company received no dividend and no other exempt income during the year. The Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the company's claim that nothing should be disallowed.

items.stem: Which of the three gains is long-term?

options.text: Only the listed shares are long-term; gold needs 36 months and the unlisted shares 24 months
options.misconception: keeps the thirty-six month category that was withdrawn on 23 July 2024
options.why: Gold did sit in a thirty-six month class until 23 July 2024, and on that reading 30 months would fall short. That class no longer exists — every asset outside the listed-security group is now long-term after twenty-four months, so the jewellery qualifies.

options.text: All three are long-term, shares of any company being long-term after 12 months
options.misconception: extends the twelve-month period for a listed security to shares of an unlisted company
options.why: The twelve-month period is given to a security listed on a recognised stock exchange in India, to a unit of an equity oriented fund, to a unit of the Unit Trust of India and to a zero coupon bond. Shares of an unlisted private company are none of those and take the twenty-four month period.

options.text: The listed shares and the gold jewellery are long-term; the unlisted shares are short-term
options.why: After the rationalisation of 23 July 2024 section 2(42A) leaves two periods only. A security listed on a recognised stock exchange is long-term after twelve months, so 14 months qualifies. Every other capital asset is long-term after twenty-four months, so the gold at 30 months qualifies and the unlisted shares at 20 months do not.

options.text: Only the gold jewellery is long-term; the 12-month period went when indexation went, leaving a single 24-month test for every asset
options.misconception: reads the rationalisation as collapsing everything into one period, when two survive
options.why: The amendment reduced three periods to two, not to one. The listed shares held 14 months are long-term on the twelve-month test, and the unlisted shares held 20 months remain short-term.

citation.ref: Section 2(42A) as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 23 July 2024

items.scenario: Mr Anand makes three sales during previous year 2025-26, all of them after 23 July 2024. He sells equity shares of a company listed on a recognised stock exchange in India that he had held for 14 months, gold jewellery he had held for 30 months, and equity shares of an unlisted private company he had held for 20 months. None of the three is a market linked debenture or a specified mutual fund.

items.stem: Is the gain long-term or short-term?

options.text: Short-term, the thirty-six month period still applying to a transfer made before 23 July 2024
options.why: The rationalisation of section 2(42A) reaches a transfer made on or after 23 July 2024. This transfer is three weeks earlier, so the position before it governs, and gold sat in the thirty-six month class. Thirty months falls short of it.

options.text: Long-term, twenty-four months being the period for every asset outside the listed-security group
options.misconception: states the rule correctly and applies it to a transfer it does not reach
options.why: Twenty-four months is right for a transfer made on or after 23 July 2024. This transfer was made before it, and an amendment cannot reach backwards over a sale already made.

options.text: Long-term — the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 governs the whole of previous year 2024-25, so the twenty-four month period applies to every transfer in it
options.misconception: applies the amendment across the entire previous year instead of from the date the amendment itself names
options.why: An amendment to a holding period is not applied by previous year but by the date named in it, and this one names 23 July 2024 for the transfer. A sale on 1 July 2024 and a sale on 1 December 2024 fall on opposite sides of the same previous year.

options.text: Neither — jewellery is a personal effect, so it is not a capital asset and no capital gain arises
options.misconception: forgets that jewellery is written out of the personal effects exclusion by name
options.why: Personal effects are indeed excluded from the meaning of a capital asset, but jewellery is named as an exception to that exclusion and stays a capital asset. So a gain does arise, and the only question is which period it is measured against.

citation.ref: Section 2(42A) as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 23 July 2024, read with the exclusion of personal effects in section 2(14) and the exception for jewellery within it

items.scenario: Ms Deepa sells gold jewellery on 1 July 2024. She had held it for 30 months. She holds nothing else that is sold in that year.

items.stem: What is the tax on the long-term capital gain?

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — the lower of 12.5 per cent on the unindexed gain of ₹30,00,000 and 20 per cent on the indexed gain of ₹15,00,000
options.why: The proviso to section 112(1) lets a resident individual transferring land or a building acquired before 23 July 2024 take the lower of the two packages. Without indexation the gain is ₹40,00,000 less ₹10,00,000, that is ₹30,00,000, and 12.5 per cent of it is ₹3,75,000. With indexation the gain is ₹40,00,000 less ₹25,00,000, that is ₹15,00,000, and 20 per cent of it is ₹3,00,000. The lower figure stands.

options.text: ₹1,87,500 — 12.5 per cent of the indexed gain of ₹15,00,000
options.misconception: mixes the two limbs, taking the new rate on the indexed base when the proviso offers rate and base only as a pair
options.why: Both halves of this figure exist in the section and neither belongs with the other. The choice is between 12.5 per cent without indexation and 20 per cent with it; nobody is given indexation at the lower rate.

options.text: ₹6,00,000 — 20 per cent of the unindexed gain of ₹30,00,000
options.misconception: keeps the pre-amendment twenty per cent rate while dropping the indexation that went with it
options.why: This is the worst of both regimes and is nowhere in the section. Twenty per cent is available only on the indexed gain of ₹15,00,000, and on the unindexed gain the rate is 12.5 per cent.

options.text: ₹3,75,000 — 12.5 per cent of the unindexed gain of ₹30,00,000, indexation having been withdrawn for every transfer made on or after 23 July 2024
options.misconception: overlooks the proviso preserving the comparison for a resident individual or HUF on land or a building acquired before 23 July 2024
options.why: The general rule is stated correctly and one exception has been missed. Indexation is gone as a general matter, but the proviso keeps the twenty per cent computation alive purely as a ceiling for this narrow class of taxpayer and asset.

citation.ref: Section 112(1) with its proviso, as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 23 July 2024

items.scenario: Mr Bhatia, a resident individual, sells on 1 December 2025 a plot of land he bought in June 2010 for ₹10,00,000. The sale consideration is ₹40,00,000, and the stamp duty value is lower than that. The indexed cost of acquisition, if indexation were applied, would be ₹25,00,000. Ignore surcharge and cess, and assume he claims no exemption under section 54EC or section 54F.

items.stem: What is the tax on the long-term capital gain?

options.text: ₹5,00,000 — twelve and a half per cent of the unindexed gain, with no comparison available
options.why: The proviso to section 112(1) is open to a resident individual and a Hindu undivided family and to nobody else. A firm gets the general rule alone: the gain is ₹60,00,000 less ₹20,00,000, that is ₹40,00,000, and twelve and a half per cent of it is ₹5,00,000. The date of purchase and the fact that the asset is land, which would matter for an individual, decide nothing here.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — twenty per cent of the indexed gain of ₹15,00,000, indexation surviving for a firm
options.misconception: treats the withdrawal of indexation as something the proviso took away rather than the general rule
options.why: Indexation was withdrawn for every transfer made on or after 23 July 2024, whoever makes it. The proviso does not preserve indexation for anyone; it gives a resident individual or Hindu undivided family a ceiling computed as though indexation had survived.

options.text: ₹8,00,000 — twenty per cent of the unindexed gain of ₹40,00,000
options.misconception: keeps the pre-amendment rate while dropping the indexation that went with it
options.why: Twenty per cent never applies to an unindexed gain. It survives only inside the proviso, and only on the indexed figure, and only for a resident individual or Hindu undivided family.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 — the lower of the two computations, as for any resident selling land bought before 23 July 2024
options.misconception: reads the proviso as turning on the asset and the date alone, when it also names who may use it
options.why: The asset and the date are two of the three conditions and this firm meets both. The third is the taxpayer, and the proviso names a resident individual and a Hindu undivided family. A firm, a company, an association of persons, a body of individuals and a non-resident are all outside it.

citation.ref: Section 112(1) with its proviso, as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 23 July 2024 — the proviso being available to a resident individual or Hindu undivided family only

items.scenario: A partnership firm resident in India sells on 1 December 2025 a plot of land it bought in June 2010 for ₹20,00,000. The sale consideration is ₹60,00,000 and the stamp duty value is lower. The indexed cost of acquisition, if indexation were applied, would be ₹45,00,000. Ignore surcharge and cess, and assume no exemption is claimed.

items.stem: What is charged, under which head, and in which previous year?

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹21,00,000 in previous year 2023-24 and business profit of ₹12,00,000 in previous year 2025-26
options.misconception: charges the capital gain in the year of conversion instead of the year the stock is sold
options.why: Both amounts are computed correctly and one is put in the wrong year. Conversion is a transfer, but section 45(2) postpones the charge to the previous year in which the stock-in-trade is actually sold, which is the whole purpose of the sub-section.

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹21,00,000 and business profit of ₹12,00,000, both in previous year 2025-26
options.why: Section 45(2) charges the capital gain in the year the stock is sold, so both figures fall in previous year 2025-26. The fair market value on the date of conversion is the deemed full value of consideration, giving ₹30,00,000 less the indexed cost of ₹9,00,000, that is ₹21,00,000. The surplus of the sale price over that same fair market value, ₹42,00,000 less ₹30,00,000, is business profit of ₹12,00,000.
keywords: fair market value on the date of conversion

options.text: Long-term capital gain of ₹33,00,000 in previous year 2025-26 and no business profit
options.misconception: takes the actual sale price as the full value of consideration for the capital gain, when section 45(2) deems the fair market value on the date of conversion to be it
options.why: Using ₹42,00,000 against the indexed cost of ₹9,00,000 gives ₹33,00,000 and taxes the whole rise as capital gain. The split exists because everything above the conversion-date value was earned as a trader, not as an investor.

options.text: Business profit of ₹37,00,000 in previous year 2025-26 and nothing under capital gains
options.misconception: treats the entire surplus over the original cost as business income, denying the split section 45(2) creates
options.why: Taking ₹42,00,000 less the original ₹5,00,000 produces ₹37,00,000 and loses both the indexation and the concessional long-term rate. The gain up to the date of conversion accrued to her as owner of a capital asset and stays under capital gains.

citation.ref: Section 45(2) read with Section 2(47)(iv) and Section 48

items.scenario: Ms Chitra acquired a plot in 2012 for ₹5,00,000. On 10 May 2023 she converted it into stock-in-trade of her real estate business, when its fair market value was ₹30,00,000. She sold the plot from that stock on 20 June 2025 for ₹42,00,000. The indexed cost of acquisition, taken up to the year of conversion, is ₹9,00,000.

items.stem: What is taxable in previous year 2025-26, and what happens to the earlier forfeiture?

options.text: ₹4,00,000 is income from other sources in previous year 2025-26, both forfeitures being taxed in the year the second one occurred
options.misconception: applies section 56(2)(ix) to an advance received before 1 April 2014, which the section does not reach
options.why: The charge attaches to the sum received on or after 1 April 2014. The ₹1,00,000 of 2010-11 was never within it, and pulling it into this year taxes an amount that is already destined to reduce the cost of the house.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 is taxable as capital gain in previous year 2025-26, forfeiture being the extinguishment of the buyer's right in the house
options.misconception: forces the receipt into capital gains when there is no transfer by the owner and the statute places it under other sources
options.why: Mr Deshpande still owns the house and has transferred nothing, so no capital gain can arise to him. Parliament settled the head by naming the receipt in section 56(2)(ix), which sits in the income from other sources chapter.

options.text: ₹3,00,000 is income from other sources in previous year 2025-26; the ₹1,00,000 forfeited in 2010-11 is not taxed now and will reduce the cost of acquisition when the house is sold
options.why: Section 56(2)(ix) taxes a forfeited advance received on or after 1 April 2014 as income from other sources in the year of forfeiture, so the ₹3,00,000 is charged in previous year 2025-26 and the proviso to section 51 keeps it out of the cost computation. The ₹1,00,000 was received before that date, so section 51 alone governs it and it is deducted from the cost of acquisition whenever the house is eventually transferred.

options.text: Nothing is taxable in previous year 2025-26; both amounts reduce the cost of acquisition when the house is sold
options.misconception: applies the pre-2014 section 51 treatment to a current forfeiture, ignoring the proviso that now excludes it
options.why: That was the law for the ₹1,00,000 and it is no longer the law for the ₹3,00,000. Once section 56(2)(ix) taxes a forfeited sum, the proviso to section 51 stops it being deducted from cost as well, so it is not taxed twice and not relieved twice.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(ix) inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 with effect from assessment year 2015-16, read with Section 51 and its proviso

items.scenario: Mr Deshpande bought a house in 2005 for ₹20,00,000. In financial year 2010-11 he received an advance of ₹1,00,000 from a buyer and forfeited it when that negotiation failed. In previous year 2025-26 he received an advance of ₹3,00,000 from a second buyer and forfeited that too when the second negotiation also failed. He still owns the house at the end of previous year 2025-26.

items.stem: Can the Assessing Officer refer the valuation to a Valuation Officer under section 55A?

options.text: No — clause (a) allows a reference only where the value claimed is less than fair market value, and here the assessee has claimed more
options.misconception: uses the pre-1 July 2012 wording of section 55A(a), which was one-directional
options.why: That was the law until 1 July 2012 and it made the clause useless against exactly this device, since a seller inflating a 2001 value always claims more rather than less. The Finance Act, 2012 substituted the words to close it.

options.text: Yes, under clause (a) — since 1 July 2012 the clause is triggered where the registered valuer's value is at variance with fair market value, and a value that is too high is as much a variance as one that is too low
options.why: Section 55A(a) applies where the value claimed is in accordance with a registered valuer's estimate and the Assessing Officer is of opinion that it is at variance with its fair market value. Those words replaced "is less than the fair market value" with effect from 1 July 2012, and that amendment is precisely what allows an inflated claim to be referred.
keywords: at variance with its fair market value

options.text: No — section 55A reaches only the sale consideration, so an inflated cost of acquisition can be attacked only by reopening the assessment under section 147
options.misconception: confines section 55A to the consideration, when it operates on any fair market value needed for the capital gains Chapter
options.why: The section opens with the words "with a view to ascertaining the fair market value of a capital asset for the purposes of this Chapter", which covers a value adopted as the cost of acquisition as much as one adopted as consideration.

options.text: No — clause (b) requires the Assessing Officer to be of opinion that fair market value exceeds the value claimed, and his opinion here is the opposite
options.misconception: goes to clause (b) when the presence of a registered valuer's report puts the case squarely in clause (a)
options.why: Clause (b) is correctly described and is the wrong clause. It governs a case not supported by a registered valuer's report; where such a report exists, as it does here, the case falls under clause (a) and the one-directional test does not apply.

citation.ref: Section 55A(a) as amended by the Finance Act, 2012 with effect from 1 July 2012, read with Section 55A(b) and Rule 111AA

items.scenario: Mr Elias sells during previous year 2025-26 a house he has owned since 1995. In computing his capital gain he substitutes the fair market value of the house as on 1 April 2001, which he puts at ₹60,00,000, supported by the report of a registered valuer. The Assessing Officer is of opinion that the true fair market value on that date was about ₹25,00,000, and that the assessee's figure has been inflated to enlarge the cost of acquisition.

items.stem: What is her tax liability for assessment year 2026-27?

options.misconception: tests the section 87A rebate on gross salary of ₹12,75,000 instead of on total income after the standard deduction
options.why: This is ₹60,000 of tax plus four per cent cess, arrived at by denying the rebate. The twelve lakh rupee limit in section 87A is a limit on total income, and total income is struck after the deduction under section 16(ia).

options.text: Nil
options.why: The standard deduction of ₹75,000 under section 16(ia) brings total income to ₹12,00,000. On the section 115BAC(1A) slabs the tax is nil on the first ₹4,00,000, ₹20,000 on the next ₹4,00,000 at 5 per cent and ₹40,000 on the next ₹4,00,000 at 10 per cent, which is ₹60,000. The section 87A rebate of ₹60,000 is available because total income does not exceed ₹12,00,000, so the tax is wiped out and no cess arises.

options.misconception: denies the standard deduction inside the new regime, which section 16(ia) allows there at ₹75,000
options.why: Taking total income at ₹12,75,000 produces tax of ₹71,250 — ₹20,000, ₹40,000 and ₹11,250 on the last ₹75,000 at 15 per cent — with no rebate and cess of ₹2,850. The standard deduction is one of the few allowances the default regime keeps, and it is the larger figure of ₹75,000 there.

options.misconception: computes under the old regime, which since assessment year 2024-25 applies only to someone who has opted out
options.why: On the old slabs, with a ₹50,000 standard deduction, the tax on ₹12,25,000 is ₹1,80,000 plus cess of ₹7,200. Section 115BAC is now the default, and Ms Farida has not opted out of it.

citation.ref: Section 115BAC(1A) and Section 87A as amended by the Finance Act, 2025 for assessment year 2026-27, read with Section 16(ia)

items.scenario: Ms Farida, a resident individual aged 40, has gross salary of ₹12,75,000 for previous year 2025-26 and no other income. She claims no exempt allowance and no deduction under Chapter VI-A, and she does not opt out of section 115BAC.

items.stem: What is his income from house property for previous year 2025-26?

options.misconception: computes the thirty per cent allowance on gross annual value instead of on net annual value
options.why: Thirty per cent of ₹3,60,000 is ₹1,08,000, which over-deducts by ₹9,000 and gives ₹1,22,000. The allowance is calculated after municipal taxes have been taken off, which is what makes the intermediate figure worth writing down.

Expected rent is the higher of municipal value and fair rent, ₹3,40,000, capped by standard rent at ₹3,20,000; actual rent of ₹3,60,000 is higher, so gross annual value is ₹3,60,000. Only the ₹30,000 of municipal taxes actually paid during the previous year comes off, giving net annual value of ₹3,30,000. Thirty per cent of that is ₹99,000, and interest of ₹1,00,000 follows, leaving ₹1,31,000.
keywords: actually paid during the previous year

options.misconception: deducts the repairs actually incurred instead of the flat thirty per cent section 24(a) gives
options.why: Substituting the ₹50,000 spent for the statutory allowance leaves ₹1,80,000. Section 24(a) is a flat thirty per cent of net annual value and takes no account of what was really spent, whether that is more or less.

options.misconception: deducts the municipal taxes charged for the year rather than only those actually paid during it
options.why: Taking the whole ₹40,000 gives a net annual value of ₹3,20,000, thirty per cent of ₹96,000 and an answer of ₹1,24,000. The first proviso to section 23 allows only what was borne by the owner and paid in the year, and the ₹10,000 paid in May 2026 will be deductible in the following previous year.

citation.ref: Section 23(1) with its first proviso, and Section 24(a) and 24(b)

items.scenario: Mr Gokhale owns a house that is let throughout previous year 2025-26. Its municipal value is ₹3,00,000, its fair rent ₹3,40,000 and its standard rent under the rent control law ₹3,20,000. The rent actually received for the year is ₹3,60,000. Municipal taxes for the year are ₹40,000, of which he paid ₹30,000 on 20 January 2026 and the balance ₹10,000 on 10 May 2026. Interest on the loan taken to buy the house is ₹1,00,000 for the year, and he actually spent ₹50,000 on repairs.

items.stem: What is chargeable under section 41(1) in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: ₹6,00,000 only, and it is chargeable even though that business no longer exists
options.why: A deduction was allowed for the trade payable, so its remission is deemed to be profits and gains of business of the year of remission, and section 41(1) says in terms that this applies whether or not the business is in existence in that year. The waived term loan is different — the borrowing was a capital receipt for which no deduction was ever allowed, so neither section 41(1) nor section 28(iv) reaches it.
keywords: whether or not the business is in existence

options.text: Nothing, because the business to which the trade payable related was discontinued in 2021
options.misconception: reads a continuing business as a condition of section 41(1), which the sub-section expressly removes
options.why: Discontinuance was a defence under the older case law and Parliament closed it. The words "whether the business or profession in respect of which the allowance or deduction has been made is in existence in that year or not" sit inside section 41(1) itself.

options.text: ₹6,00,000, but by rectifying assessment year 2019-20 in which the deduction was allowed
options.misconception: reopens the year of the deduction, when section 41(1) charges the year in which the benefit is obtained
options.why: Nothing about the earlier assessment was wrong when it was made. Section 41(1) charges the previous year in which the amount is obtained or the remission occurs, which is previous year 2025-26.

options.text: ₹8,00,000, both the trade payable and the term loan being liabilities that have ceased
options.misconception: brings a capital loan waiver into section 41(1) when no deduction was ever allowed for the borrowing
options.why: Section 41(1) is the mirror of a deduction already taken, so it can only recapture what was once claimed. The Supreme Court in Mahindra and Mahindra held that a waived loan taken to buy a capital asset falls outside both section 41(1) and section 28(iv).

citation.ref: Section 41(1) with Explanation 1, read with Commissioner of Income Tax v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd (2018) 404 ITR 1 (SC)

items.scenario: Helios Ltd discontinued one of its two businesses in 2021 and has not carried it on since. In previous year 2025-26 two things happen. A supplier of that discontinued business waives ₹6,00,000 of a trade payable for goods bought in 2018, for which a deduction was allowed in assessment year 2019-20. Separately, a lender waives ₹2,00,000 of a term loan the company had taken to buy machinery, and the company writes that ₹2,00,000 back in its accounts.

items.stem: How much of the interest for previous year 2025-26 is deductible under section 36(1)(iii)?

options.text: ₹1,00,000 is deductible and ₹3,50,000 is added to the actual cost of the machine
options.why: Interest for the year is nine months on ₹50,00,000 at 12 per cent, that is ₹4,50,000. The proviso disallows the part from the date of borrowing to the date the asset is first put to use, which is 1 July 2025 to 31 January 2026, seven months, or ₹3,50,000; Explanation 8 to section 43(1) capitalises it. The remaining two months, ₹1,00,000, is deductible.

options.text: Nothing is deductible; the whole ₹4,50,000 is capitalised
options.misconception: runs the capitalisation to the end of the previous year instead of stopping on the date the asset is first put to use
options.why: The proviso ends on the date the asset was first put to use, which is 1 February 2026 and not 31 March 2026. Interest for February and March is ordinary business interest and is allowed.

options.text: ₹2,00,000 is deductible and ₹2,50,000 is added to the actual cost of the machine
options.misconception: stops the capitalisation on the date of delivery and installation rather than on the date of first use
options.why: Counting from 1 December 2025 gives four months of deductible interest and five months capitalised. The statutory test is the date on which the asset was first put to use, which here is two months later than the date it arrived.

options.text: The whole ₹4,50,000 is deductible, the machine being for an existing line and not for any extension of the business
options.misconception: uses the pre-2016 wording of the proviso, which was confined to borrowing for extension of an existing business
options.why: That limitation was real until assessment year 2016-17 and was then removed. The proviso now reaches any asset acquired out of borrowed money, whether the business is being extended or simply re-equipped.

citation.ref: Section 36(1)(iii) with its proviso as amended with effect from assessment year 2016-17, read with Explanation 8 to Section 43(1)

items.scenario: Indus Ltd borrows ₹50,00,000 on 1 July 2025 at 12 per cent a year to buy a machine for its existing manufacturing line. The machine is delivered and installed on 1 December 2025 and is first put to use on 1 February 2026. Interest is paid regularly. The company closes its accounts on 31 March.

items.stem: What is its deduction under section 80JJAA for assessment year 2026-27?

options.misconception: ignores the monthly emoluments ceiling and counts the six workmen paid ₹28,000 a month
options.why: Adding their ₹20,16,000 of annual emoluments to ₹79,20,000 gives ₹99,36,000 and thirty per cent of ₹29,80,800. A person whose total emoluments are more than ₹25,000 for a month is not an additional employee at all for that month.

Only the thirty workmen qualify. The six paid ₹28,000 a month are excluded because emoluments exceed ₹25,000 a month, and the four who joined in November are excluded because they worked fewer than 240 days. Additional employee cost is 30 times ₹22,000 times twelve months, that is ₹79,20,000, and thirty per cent of it is ₹23,76,000.

options.misconception: applies the 150-day relaxation to a company outside the apparel, footwear and leather businesses
options.why: Counting the four November joiners adds ₹4,40,000 of emoluments and produces this figure. The relaxed period of 150 days is given only to a business manufacturing apparel, footwear or leather products; every other employer needs 240 days.

options.misconception: deducts the additional employee cost itself instead of thirty per cent of it
options.why: The qualifying additional employee cost is identified correctly and then not scaled. Section 80JJAA allows thirty per cent of that cost, in each of three assessment years, not the whole of it once.

citation.ref: Section 80JJAA(1) and (2) with Explanation, read with Rule 19AB (Form 10DA)

items.scenario: Jupiter Engineering Ltd, whose accounts are audited under section 44AB, takes on 40 new workmen during previous year 2025-26. Thirty of them are paid ₹22,000 a month and worked 300 days in the year. Six are paid ₹28,000 a month and also worked 300 days. The remaining four are paid ₹22,000 a month but joined on 1 November 2025 and worked 151 days. All emoluments are paid by bank transfer, all forty participate in a recognised provident fund, and there is a net increase in the total number of employees. The company does not manufacture apparel, footwear or leather products, and it furnishes Form 10DA in time.

items.stem: What deduction is allowed to it under section 80M?

options.text: Nil
options.misconception: believes section 80M died with the dividend distribution tax, when it was reinserted by the Finance Act, 2020
options.why: The old section 80M was dropped when dividend distribution tax was introduced and a new one was inserted by the Finance Act, 2020 with effect from assessment year 2021-22, at the moment dividend became taxable in the shareholder's hands again.

options.misconception: treats section 80M as an exemption for inter-corporate dividend rather than a deduction capped by what is passed on
options.why: The deduction cannot exceed the dividend the company itself distributes within the time allowed. Money kept in the company is taxed in the company, and only ₹18,00,000 was passed on in time.

Section 80M allows a deduction only for dividend distributed on or before one month prior to the due date under section 139(1). That due date is 31 October 2026, so the cut-off is 30 September 2026, and only the ₹18,00,000 paid on 15 September 2026 counts. The ₹9,00,000 paid on 20 October 2026 is after the cut-off and is not deductible in this year.
keywords: one month prior to the due date

options.misconception: measures the distribution against the due date itself instead of one month before it
options.why: Both distributions fall before 31 October 2026, which is why this figure is tempting. The statute deliberately pulls the deadline back by a month so that the deduction is settled before the return is filed.

citation.ref: Section 80M with its proviso, inserted by the Finance Act, 2020 with effect from assessment year 2021-22

items.scenario: Kalinga Ltd, a domestic company, receives dividend of ₹30,00,000 from another domestic company during previous year 2025-26. Its due date for furnishing the return under section 139(1) for assessment year 2026-27 is 31 October 2026. It distributes dividend of its own of ₹18,00,000 on 15 September 2026 and a further ₹9,00,000 on 20 October 2026.

items.stem: What tax and penalty does the addition attract?

options.text: Tax of ₹23,40,000 on ₹30,00,000 after setting off the brought forward loss, and penalty of ₹1,80,000
options.misconception: sets off a brought forward loss against income charged under section 115BBE, which sub-section (2) forbids
options.why: The arithmetic is right for a base of ₹30,00,000 and the base is wrong. The bar on set-off was put into sub-section (2) with effect from assessment year 2017-18 precisely because taxpayers were sheltering additions of this kind behind old losses.

options.text: Tax of ₹24,00,000 and penalty of ₹2,40,000
options.misconception: applies the sixty per cent rate alone and forgets the flat twenty-five per cent surcharge and the cess
options.why: The rate and the penalty are right and the surcharge is missing. Where total income includes income referred to in section 115BBE, the Finance Act charges surcharge at twenty-five per cent of that tax whatever the level of income, and cess follows on the total.

options.text: Tax of ₹31,20,000 with no set-off of the loss, and penalty of ₹2,40,000 under section 271AAC
options.why: Section 115BBE(2) allows no set-off of any loss against income assessed under section 69, so the base stays ₹40,00,000. Tax at sixty per cent is ₹24,00,000, surcharge at twenty-five per cent of that tax is ₹6,00,000 and cess at four per cent on ₹30,00,000 is ₹1,20,000, giving ₹31,20,000. Section 271AAC charges ten per cent of the section 115BBE(1)(i) tax of ₹24,00,000, that is ₹2,40,000.

options.text: Tax of ₹31,20,000 and penalty of ₹12,00,000 under section 270A for under-reporting
options.misconception: levies the section 270A penalty on income charged under section 115BBE, which section 271AAC(2) excludes
options.why: Fifty per cent of the ₹24,00,000 of tax produces this penalty, and section 271AAC(2) says no penalty under section 270A shall be imposed on income of this kind. The penalty is the flat ten per cent that section 271AAC fixes.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBE(1) and 115BBE(2), and Section 271AAC(1) and 271AAC(2)

items.scenario: In the assessment of Mr Lal for assessment year 2026-27 the Assessing Officer adds ₹40,00,000 as unexplained investment under section 69. Mr Lal had not shown that amount in his return of income and had paid no tax on it. He asks that a brought forward business loss of ₹10,00,000 be set off against the addition first. Ignore his other income.

items.stem: How is the firm assessed for assessment year 2026-27?

options.text: The ₹15,00,000 is disallowed to the firm and is still taxable in the partners' hands as business income under section 28(v)
options.misconception: taxes the partners on an amount the firm was not allowed to deduct, which the proviso to section 28(v) prevents
options.why: Section 28(v) charges interest and remuneration received by a partner, and its proviso excludes so much of it as has not been allowed as a deduction to the firm. Otherwise the same money would be taxed twice.

options.text: It is still assessed as a firm, but the whole ₹15,00,000 is disallowed under section 185, and the partners are not taxed on it either
options.why: Specifying the individual shares of the partners in the instrument is a condition in section 184(1), and it has not been met. Section 185 does not change the firm's status; it denies the deduction for interest, salary, bonus, commission or remuneration to any partner, so all ₹15,00,000 is added back. The proviso to section 28(v) then keeps the same amount out of the partners' hands.

options.text: The remuneration is allowed to the extent section 40(b) permits, and only the excess is disallowed; interest at 12 per cent is within the limit and is fully allowed
options.misconception: applies the section 40(b) limits as though section 184 had been complied with, when section 185 removes the claim before any limit can operate
options.why: Section 40(b) is a ceiling on a deduction that is otherwise available. Section 185 is a prior gate, and once it closes there is nothing left for the ceiling to cut down.

options.text: It is assessed as an association of persons, the deed not satisfying section 184
options.misconception: reads a section 184 failure as changing the assessee's status, when section 185 keeps it a firm and removes the deduction instead
options.why: Before 1993 a failure of this kind did cost a firm its status. Section 185 as it now stands says the firm shall be so assessed and then attaches a single consequence, which is the disallowance.

citation.ref: Sections 184(1) and 185, read with the proviso to Section 28(v)

items.scenario: Zenith and Co, a firm, pays its two working partners remuneration of ₹12,00,000 and interest on capital of ₹3,00,000 at 12 per cent a year during previous year 2025-26. Its book profit before those payments is ₹40,00,000. The partnership is evidenced by a written deed and a certified copy accompanied the return, but the deed does not specify the individual shares of the partners.

items.stem: In whose hands are the debenture interest and the shop rent taxable for previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Both are Mr Menon's — the ₹4,00,000 of interest under section 60 and the ₹6,00,000 of rent under section 61
options.why: Section 60 includes transferred income in the transferor's total income where the asset producing it has not been transferred, and it says in terms that this applies whether the transfer is revocable or not revocable, so the irrevocable deed is no defence to the ₹4,00,000 of interest. The shop itself was transferred, but the right to take it back makes the transfer revocable under section 63, and section 61 puts the rent back with him.
keywords: whether the transfer is revocable or not revocable

options.text: Both are his, but the rent only from the year in which he actually takes the shop back
options.misconception: applies the section 62 deferral, which is for a transfer not revocable during the lifetime of the transferee, to a transfer revocable after a fixed term
options.why: Section 62 postpones section 61 only for a trust not revocable during the beneficiary's lifetime or a transfer not revocable during the transferee's lifetime. A right to take the shop back after twelve years is neither, so the rent is his from previous year 2025-26.

options.text: Neither is his — the interest deed is irrevocable and the shop was genuinely transferred to his brother
options.misconception: reads section 60 as reaching only a revocable transfer of income
options.why: Irrevocability defeats section 61 in some cases and never defeats section 60. Section 60 asks one question only, which is whether the asset went with the income, and here the debentures did not.

options.text: The rent is his under section 61, but the interest belongs to his son, the deed being irrevocable
options.misconception: applies section 61's revocability test to a case governed by section 60, where revocability is irrelevant
options.why: Half the answer is right, which is what makes it tempting. Section 61 is about a transfer of assets and turns on revocability; section 60 is about a transfer of income alone and does not.

citation.ref: Sections 60, 61, 62(1) and 63

items.scenario: Mr Menon holds 8 per cent debentures of ₹50,00,000. On 1 April 2025 he executes an irrevocable deed directing the company to pay all future interest on them to his major son, keeping the debentures himself. Separately, he transfers a let-out shop to his brother under a deed which entitles Mr Menon to take the shop back after twelve years. Rent from the shop for previous year 2025-26 is ₹6,00,000, and the son and the brother have each received the money.

items.stem: What interest is payable under sections 234A and 234B?

options.text: ₹8,000 under section 234A and ₹16,000 under section 234B
options.why: Assessed tax is ₹6,00,000 less the ₹1,00,000 deducted at source, that is ₹5,00,000, and the advance tax of ₹3,00,000 is below ninety per cent of it, so section 234B applies on the shortfall of ₹2,00,000 from 1 April 2026 to 15 November 2026, eight months at one per cent, giving ₹16,000. Section 234A runs on the same ₹2,00,000 from 1 August 2026 to 15 November 2026, which is three months and a part, counted as four months, giving ₹8,000.

options.text: ₹8,000 under section 234A and ₹40,000 under section 234B
options.misconception: charges section 234B on the whole assessed tax instead of on the shortfall of advance tax
options.why: Eight months at one per cent on ₹5,00,000 gives ₹40,000, and it ignores the ₹3,00,000 already paid. Section 234B(1) charges interest on the assessed tax as reduced by the advance tax paid, so the base is ₹2,00,000.

options.text: ₹8,000 under section 234A and nothing under section 234B, advance tax having been paid
options.misconception: treats any payment of advance tax as escaping section 234B, when the test is ninety per cent of assessed tax
options.why: Ninety per cent of ₹5,00,000 is ₹4,50,000 and he paid ₹3,00,000, so the section applies. Only a payment of at least ninety per cent of assessed tax keeps section 234B away.

options.text: ₹6,000 under section 234A and ₹16,000 under section 234B
options.misconception: counts only the completed months from 1 August to 31 October and drops the part month of November
options.why: Both sections charge for every month or part of a month, so the fifteen days of November count as a full month. Three months would be ₹6,000; the correct count is four.

citation.ref: Section 234A(1) and Section 234B(1) with Explanation 1

items.scenario: Mr Nambiar's tax on total income for assessment year 2026-27 is ₹6,00,000. Tax of ₹1,00,000 was deducted at source from his income. He paid advance tax of ₹3,00,000 on 15 March 2026. His due date for furnishing the return under section 139(1) was 31 July 2026. He paid the balance of his tax and furnished the return on 15 November 2026.

items.stem: What interest is payable to her under section 244A?

options.misconception: starts the period at 1 April of the assessment year even though the return was furnished after the due date
options.why: Fifteen months from 1 April 2026 to 20 June 2027 at ₹2,000 a month gives ₹30,000. The proviso to section 244A(1)(a) reserves that starting point for a return furnished on or before the due date, and hers was nearly five months late.

Because the return was not furnished on or before the due date under section 139(1), interest on a refund out of tax deducted at source runs from the date of furnishing the return and not from 1 April of the assessment year. December 2026 to June 2027 is seven months, and half a per cent a month on ₹4,00,000 is ₹2,000 a month, giving ₹14,000.

options.text: Nothing
options.misconception: reads section 244A as paying interest only where the delay was the department's fault
options.why: Interest is payable as of right on a refund; section 244A(2) merely excludes any period of delay attributable to the assessee, and the late filing is dealt with by moving the starting date rather than by refusing interest altogether.

options.misconception: pays interest at the one per cent a month the taxpayer is charged under sections 234A and 234B
options.why: The period of seven months is counted correctly and the rate is doubled. Section 244A pays half a per cent for every month or part of a month, which is half of what the department charges.

citation.ref: Section 244A(1)(a) with its proviso and Section 244A(2)

items.scenario: Ms Oberoi is due a refund of ₹4,00,000 for assessment year 2026-27, arising wholly out of tax deducted at source from her income. Her due date for furnishing the return under section 139(1) was 31 July 2026, and she furnished it on 20 December 2026. The refund is granted to her on 20 June 2027. No part of the delay is attributable to her after she filed.

items.stem: What can he obtain under section 270AA?

options.text: He can have immunity from the section 270A penalty but must still face prosecution
options.misconception: splits the immunity, when section 270AA(1) covers the penalty and the prosecution together
options.why: The application is for immunity from imposition of penalty under section 270A and from initiation of proceedings under section 276C or section 276CC. Where it is granted the two go together, and where it is refused neither is available.

options.text: His application had to be made by 12 June 2026, one month from the date of the order, and is now out of time
options.misconception: counts one month from the date the order was received rather than from the end of the month in which it was received
options.why: The section says within one month from the end of the month in which the order was received. For an order received on 12 May 2026 that end is 31 May 2026, so the last date is 30 June 2026 and not 12 June 2026.

options.text: Immunity must be granted, both conditions in section 270AA(1) having been satisfied
options.misconception: treats payment of the demand and non-filing of an appeal as sufficient, when section 270AA(3) adds a third requirement
options.why: Those two conditions open the door and do not decide what is behind it. Sub-section (3) withholds immunity in a misreporting case, which is the one category Parliament thought undeserving of it.

options.text: He may apply in Form 68 up to 30 June 2026, but immunity cannot be granted, the proceedings being for misreporting
options.why: The application is due within one month from the end of the month in which the order was received, so the last date is 30 June 2026. Paying the demand and not appealing satisfies section 270AA(1), but section 270AA(3) directs the Assessing Officer to grant immunity only where the penalty proceedings are not for misreporting under section 270A(9). Misreporting is outside the scheme however well the other two conditions are met.
keywords: one month from the end of the month

citation.ref: Sections 270AA(1), 270AA(2) and 270AA(3), read with Section 270A(9) and Rule 129 (Form 68)

items.scenario: Mr Pillai receives an assessment order for assessment year 2025-26 on 12 May 2026. The order makes an addition and records that penalty proceedings under section 270A are initiated for misreporting of income within the meaning of section 270A(9). He pays the tax and interest specified in the notice of demand within the time allowed there, and he files no appeal against the order.

items.stem: What penalties can be imposed?

options.text: ₹35,000 under section 271D, ₹35,000 under section 271E and ₹2,50,000 under section 271DA
options.why: Accepting a cash loan of ₹20,000 or more breaches section 269SS and section 271D charges a penalty equal to the amount taken; repaying it in cash breaches section 269T and section 271E charges the same again. The ₹2,50,000 breaches section 269ST because it was received in respect of a single transaction, and section 271DA charges a penalty equal to the amount received.

options.text: ₹35,000 under section 271D and ₹35,000 under section 271E, but nothing under section 271DA, no single day's receipt reaching ₹2,00,000
options.misconception: reads section 269ST as a per-day test alone, ignoring its single transaction and single event limbs
options.why: The section forbids receiving ₹2,00,000 or more in aggregate from a person in a day, or in respect of a single transaction, or in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion. The three limbs are alternatives, so splitting one invoice across five days defeats nothing.

options.text: ₹35,000 under section 271D only, repayment in cash carrying no penalty
options.misconception: overlooks section 269T and section 271E, which mirror the acceptance rule on repayment
options.why: One cash loan taken and repaid in cash is penalised twice, once on the way in and once on the way out. Section 269T is a separate prohibition with its own penalty in section 271E.

options.text: Nothing at all, ₹35,000 being far below the ₹2,00,000 cash limit and the loan being genuine
options.misconception: applies the ₹2,00,000 section 269ST limit to a loan, which section 269SS restricts at ₹20,000
options.why: Two different limits govern two different things. A loan, deposit or specified sum is restricted at ₹20,000 by section 269SS, and genuineness is no defence — only reasonable cause under section 273B is.

citation.ref: Sections 269SS, 269T and 269ST, read with Sections 271D, 271E, 271DA and 273B

items.scenario: Mr Qureshi, who is in business, accepts a cash loan of ₹35,000 from a friend on 10 June 2025 and repays the whole of it in cash on 20 March 2026. Separately, he receives ₹2,50,000 in cash from one customer against a single invoice, taken in five instalments of ₹50,000 each on five different days. Neither party is a bank, a co-operative bank, a post office savings bank or a government body, and no reasonable cause is pleaded.

items.stem: Can the prosecution be launched?

options.text: No — the proviso bars prosecution because the return was furnished before the end of the assessment year, whatever the amount of tax involved
options.why: Assessment year 2026-27 ends on 31 March 2027, and the return was furnished on 20 February 2027. Clause (ii)(a) of the proviso to section 276CC says a person shall not be proceeded against for a failure under section 139(1) if he has furnished the return before the end of the relevant assessment year, and it sets no ceiling on the tax involved.
keywords: before the end of the relevant assessment year

options.text: No — section 278E puts the burden on the department to prove that the failure was wilful
options.misconception: reverses section 278E, which makes the court presume a culpable mental state and puts the burden of disproving it on the accused
options.why: The conclusion is right for the wrong reason, which is worse than a wrong conclusion here. Section 278E directs the court to presume the existence of a culpable mental state and requires the accused to prove its absence beyond reasonable doubt.

options.text: Yes — imprisonment of three months to two years, this being an ordinary late filing
options.misconception: misses both the proviso and, on its own reasoning, the ₹25,00,000 threshold that would have governed the sentence
options.why: Two errors sit on top of each other. The proviso stops the prosecution, and had it not, tax of ₹80,00,000 would have put the case in the six months to seven years band and not this one.

options.text: Yes — rigorous imprisonment of six months to seven years, the tax sought to be evaded exceeding ₹25,00,000
options.misconception: reads the punishment band without the proviso, which bars the prosecution altogether
options.why: The band is quoted correctly and never comes into play. The proviso is a bar on proceeding at all, so the question of which sentence applies does not arise once the return is in before 31 March 2027.

citation.ref: Section 276CC with its proviso, read with Section 278E

items.scenario: Mr Raghavan, a proprietor whose accounts are subject to audit under section 44AB, was required to furnish his return for assessment year 2026-27 by 31 October 2026 and did not do so. He furnished it on 20 February 2027. The tax sought to be evaded, had the failure not been discovered, would have been ₹80,00,000. The department proposes to prosecute him under section 276CC.

items.stem: What is the position of the deductor?

options.text: The certificate covers the whole of previous year 2025-26, so the customer must refund the tax it deducted between May and August
options.misconception: treats a section 197 certificate as retrospective to the start of the year, when it operates from the date of issue
options.why: A deductor cannot return tax it has already deposited against the payee's account. The certificate is prospective, and the earlier deduction is simply credit that Mr Sundaram sets against his liability when he files.

options.text: The Form 15G declaration was enough, a resident with no taxable income being entitled to nil deduction on any payment
options.misconception: reads section 197A as a general self-declaration route, when it is confined to the sections that provision names
options.why: Form 15G works for the limited list in section 197A, which covers payments such as interest under section 194A and rent under section 194-I. Payments to a contractor under section 194C are outside it, and the only route for them is a certificate under section 197.

options.text: Nothing needed at all — a payee heading for a loss is outside section 194C, which reaches only income
options.misconception: confuses the payee's final liability with the deductor's duty, which attaches to the sum credited or paid
options.why: Section 194C deducts from any sum credited or paid to a resident contractor for carrying out work, whatever the payee's eventual profit or loss. That is exactly the mismatch section 197 exists to correct, and it is corrected by a certificate rather than by the deductor's own judgement.

options.text: The Form 15G declaration had no effect and the deductions to August were correct; the customer stops deducting from 1 September 2025, and the tax already deducted is recovered by Mr Sundaram as a refund on his own return
options.why: Section 197A lists the sections for which a declaration works and section 194C is not one of them, so Form 15G was of no effect and the customer was right to keep deducting. The section 197 certificate operates from the date it is issued, which is 1 September 2025, and it does not reach back over deductions already made; those are claimed as a refund on his return.
keywords: from the date it is issued

citation.ref: Section 197(1) read with Rule 28AA and Rule 28 (Form 13), and Sections 197A(1A) and 197A(1C)

items.scenario: Mr Sundaram, a resident contractor, expects a loss for previous year 2025-26 and does not want tax deducted under section 194C from his running bills. On 1 May 2025 he gives his customer a declaration in Form 15G and asks it to deduct nothing. The customer deducts tax anyway from the bills paid in May to August 2025. He then applies in Form 13 and receives a certificate under section 197 for nil deduction, issued on 1 September 2025.

items.stem: What is included in his total income for previous year 2025-26?

options.text: ₹6,00,000 — the salary alone
options.misconception: treats a not ordinarily resident as a non-resident and drops the business-controlled-from-India limb
options.why: This is the correct answer for a non-resident, for whom only the receipt and accrual limbs in section 5(2) apply. A not ordinarily resident carries one more limb, and the Singapore business controlled from Pune falls inside it.

options.text: ₹16,50,000 — all four amounts
options.misconception: applies the resident and ordinarily resident scope to a not ordinarily resident, taxing all foreign income
options.why: Adding every figure gives ₹16,50,000 and is the answer for a resident and ordinarily resident only. The proviso to section 5(1) exists precisely to cut a not ordinarily resident's foreign income down to the business controlled in or profession set up in India.

options.text: ₹10,00,000 — the salary and the Singapore profit
options.why: The salary is for services rendered in India and so is deemed to accrue in India, which catches a not ordinarily resident under section 5(1) whatever the place of payment. The Singapore profit accrues outside India but the business is controlled from India, which is the single extra limb the proviso to section 5(1) adds. The Dubai interest accrues outside India from no Indian-controlled business and is out.
