options.why: Three years is the period after which arbitration may be initiated, not the window for departing from its result. The departure window is six months. And the articles address juridical double taxation only.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital, 2017 and United Nations Model Double Taxation Convention between Developed and Developing Countries, 2021
citation.ref: Article 25B(5) of the UN Model and Articles 23A and 23B of the two Models — a six-month window for the competent authorities to depart from an arbitration decision, with no such provision in the OECD Model, and relief confined to juridical double taxation with economic double taxation left to bilateral negotiation

items.scenario: An arbitration decision under a treaty on Alternative B of the UN Model's Article 25 has been communicated to both competent authorities, and both would like to depart from it. In a separate matter the same taxpayer complains that profits of a company are taxed in the source State in the company's hands and the dividend out of them is taxed again in the residence State in the shareholder's hands.

items.stem: Which line is right?

options.text: It was established in 2015 alongside the final BEPS package and has 139 members
options.misconception: dates the Framework to the year the fifteen Action Plans were delivered and takes the count of countries that joined the October 2021 Statement for its membership
options.why: 2015 is the year the fifteen Action Plans were delivered, a year before the Framework was set up, and 139 is the number of countries and jurisdictions that joined the 8 October 2021 Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution, not the membership of the Framework.

options.text: It was established in 2013 when the OECD published its report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting, with 65 members
options.misconception: dates it to the first BEPS report and takes the number of countries at the first MLI signing ceremony for its membership
options.why: February 2013 is when the report Addressing Base Erosion and Profit Shifting was published, three years before the Framework existed, and more than 65 countries is the number that signed the Multilateral Instrument at Paris on 7 June 2017.

options.text: It was established in July 2021, when 134 of its members agreed the two-pillar solution
options.misconception: takes the agreement the Framework reached for the moment the Framework itself was created
options.why: In July 2021, 134 members of the Inclusive Framework, representing more than 90 per cent of worldwide GDP, reached the historic agreement on a two-pillar solution. That the Framework already had 134 members that month is itself the answer to whether it was founded then.

options.text: It was established in June 2016 at Kyoto in Japan with an initial membership of 89 countries and jurisdictions, and as at 28 May 2024 it had 147 members
options.why: The idea came out of the strong interest developing countries had shown in the BEPS Project. Drawing on the experience of the Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes, the OECD and G20 countries decided in early 2016 to design a more inclusive framework in which countries participate on an equal footing, and in June 2016, at the request of the G20, the Inclusive Framework was established at Kyoto in Japan with an initial membership of 89 countries and jurisdictions. As at 28 May 2024 it includes 147 members, who on an equal footing monitor the implementation of the BEPS measures and contribute to their development.

citation.ref: The establishment of the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS at Kyoto in June 2016 with an initial membership of 89 countries and jurisdictions, and 147 members as at 28 May 2024

items.scenario: A briefing note has to state, in one line each, when and where the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS was established, how many members it began with and how many it has on the latest count in the study material.

items.stem: Which description is right?

options.text: Pillar One has two parts — Amount A, the framework for reallocating taxing rights over the residual profits of large and highly profitable groups, and Amount B, a simplified transfer pricing approach for baseline distribution activity; Pillar Two also has two — the GloBE Rules, a minimum tax framework in each jurisdiction, and the Subject to Tax Rule, which lets a source jurisdiction tax back a payment that bears a low nominal rate in the residence jurisdiction
options.why: Both Pillars are built in two complementary halves and it is worth holding them as four things rather than two. Amount A is the international framework for reallocation of taxing rights over profits of large and highly profitable multinationals; Amount B is the simplified transfer pricing approach for baseline distribution activity. The Global Anti-Base Erosion Rules establish a minimum tax framework in each jurisdiction where a large group operates, and the Subject to Tax Rule allows a source jurisdiction to tax back where taxing rights have been ceded under a tax treaty and a payment is subject to a low nominal rate in the residence jurisdiction.

options.text: Pillar One is Amount A alone; Amount B belongs to the transfer pricing guidelines and forms no part of the Two-Pillar Solution
options.misconception: treats Amount B as ordinary transfer pricing work outside the agreement
options.why: Amount B is described by the Inclusive Framework as a critical component of Pillar One, and the final package on Pillar One is the text of a Multilateral Convention for Amount A together with a framework for Amount B. It simplifies transfer pricing, but it is part of the Pillar.

options.text: Amount A and Amount B are both parts of Pillar Two, and the GloBE Rules and the Subject to Tax Rule are both parts of Pillar One
options.misconception: keeps the four parts and attaches each pair to the wrong Pillar
options.why: Amount A and Amount B belong to Pillar One; the GloBE Rules and the Subject to Tax Rule belong to Pillar Two.

options.text: Pillar One is the global minimum tax on the profits of large groups and Pillar Two is the reallocation of taxing rights to market jurisdictions
options.misconception: swaps the two Pillars
options.why: Pillar One is the reallocation and Pillar Two is the minimum tax. Pillar One is designed to deliver a fairer distribution of taxing rights over the largest and most profitable groups; Pillar Two exists so that groups pay a minimum level of tax wherever they operate.

citation.ref: The Statement on a Two-Pillar Solution of 8 October 2021 — Pillar One as Amount A and Amount B, and Pillar Two as the Global Anti-Base Erosion Rules and the Subject to Tax Rule

items.scenario: A note for a client describes the Two-Pillar Solution agreed on 8 October 2021 and has to set out what each Pillar is made of before it goes any further.

items.stem: Which of the four groups is in scope of Amount A?

options.text: Group I and Group IV
options.misconception: applies the turnover and profitability tests correctly and forgets that extractives are carved out whatever their size
options.why: Group IV passes both quantitative tests and is still out, because extractives and regulated financial services are excluded from the scope of Amount A.

options.text: Group I and Group III
options.misconception: treats high profitability as enough without the turnover threshold
options.why: Group III is very profitable at 25 per cent and is far short of the turnover threshold at 15 billion euros. Amount A is aimed at the largest and most profitable groups, which means both, not either.

options.text: Group I only
options.why: In-scope companies are multinationals with global turnover above 20 billion euros and profitability above 10 per cent, profitability being profit before tax divided by revenue, and extractives and regulated financial services are out of the scope. Group I clears both numbers at 26 billion and 14 per cent and is in a sector that is not carved out. Group II fails on profitability, Group III fails on turnover, and Group IV, which passes both numbers, is an extractives group and is excluded for that reason alone.

options.text: Group I, Group II and Group IV
options.misconception: treats turnover alone as the scope test, dropping the profitability limb
options.why: Group II is over the turnover line at 26 billion euros and under the profitability line at 7 per cent. Both tests have to be passed, and Group IV is excluded by its sector in any event.

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount A — global turnover above 20 billion euros and profitability above 10 per cent measured as profit before tax over revenue, with extractives and regulated financial services out of scope

items.scenario: Four multinational groups are tested against the scope of Amount A. Group I has global turnover of 26 billion euros and profit before tax of 14 per cent of revenue, and sells consumer goods. Group II has global turnover of 26 billion euros and profit before tax of 7 per cent of revenue. Group III has global turnover of 15 billion euros and profit before tax of 25 per cent of revenue. Group IV has global turnover of 40 billion euros and profit before tax of 20 per cent of revenue, and its business is oil and gas extraction.

items.stem: How much profit is reallocated to market jurisdictions as Amount A?

options.text: 750 million euros
options.why: Amount A is 25 per cent of the residual profit, and residual profit is defined as profit in excess of 10 per cent of revenue. Ten per cent of revenue is 3,000 million euros, so the residual profit is 6,000 less 3,000, that is 3,000 million euros, and Amount A is 25 per cent of that, 750 million euros. The 10 per cent is doing a second job here that is worth naming: it is the same figure as the profitability threshold that decides whether the group is in scope at all, and it is also the routine return the group keeps before anything is reallocated.

options.text: 600 million euros
options.misconception: reads the 10 per cent as the share of profit reallocated rather than as the routine return that defines the residual
options.why: Ten per cent of the profit before tax is 600 million euros, but 10 per cent is not a share of anything that moves. It is a percentage of revenue, and it marks the line above which profit becomes residual.

options.text: 3,000 million euros
options.misconception: reallocates the whole residual profit and drops the 25 per cent share
options.why: 3,000 million euros is the residual profit itself. Only a quarter of it is reallocated; the rest stays where the ordinary rules put it.

options.text: 1,500 million euros
options.misconception: applies the 25 per cent to the whole profit before tax rather than to the residual profit
options.why: Twenty-five per cent of 6,000 million euros is 1,500 million, but the base is wrong. Amount A reaches only the residual — the profit above a routine return of 10 per cent of revenue — and never the whole profit.

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount A — 25 per cent of the residual profit, residual profit being the profit in excess of 10 per cent of revenue, allocated to market jurisdictions with nexus using revenue-based allocation keys

items.scenario: A group is in scope of Amount A. For the year its revenue is 30,000 million euros and its profit before tax is 6,000 million euros.

items.stem: Which of the two countries has nexus for Amount A?

options.text: Both, since each exceeds 250,000
options.misconception: applies the lower threshold to every jurisdiction regardless of its GDP
options.why: 250,000 applies only where annual GDP is below 40 billion. Country Y's GDP is 60 billion, so its threshold is 1 million.

options.text: Neither, since neither reaches 1 million
options.misconception: applies the higher threshold to every jurisdiction regardless of its GDP
options.why: 1 million applies only where annual GDP is 40 billion or more. Country X's GDP is 25 billion, so its threshold is 250,000 and it clears it comfortably.

options.text: Country Y only, because it is the larger economy
options.misconception: reads the GDP figure as the thing being tested, when it only selects which revenue threshold applies
options.why: The GDP figure does not decide nexus; it decides which revenue bar the market revenue is measured against. Being the larger economy raises Country Y's bar rather than clearing it.

options.text: Country X only
options.why: The market revenue threshold is 1 million or more for a jurisdiction with annual GDP of 40 billion or more, and 250,000 or more for a jurisdiction with annual GDP below 40 billion. Country X, with GDP of 25 billion, is measured against 250,000 and its 600,000 clears it. Country Y, with GDP of 60 billion, is measured against 1 million and its 800,000 falls short. The smaller economy has the lower bar, which is the design: nexus is meant to reach markets that would otherwise be too small to register.

citation.ref: The special-purpose nexus rule for Pillar One Amount A — market revenue of at least 1 million for a jurisdiction with annual GDP of 40 billion or more and at least 250,000 for one with annual GDP below 40 billion, applying solely for Amount A and altering nexus for no other purpose

items.scenario: An in-scope group has applied the revenue sourcing rules and finds market revenue of 600,000 in Country X, whose annual GDP is 25 billion, and market revenue of 800,000 in Country Y, whose annual GDP is 60 billion.

items.stem: How is the transaction priced?

options.text: By the matrix, and then adjusted towards the internal comparable uncontrolled price under the data availability mechanism
options.misconception: uses the data availability mechanism as a general adjustment when it exists for a different problem
options.why: The data availability mechanism provides upward adjustments where there is no or insufficient data in the global dataset for a particular tested party jurisdiction and there is evidence that the jurisdiction could reasonably be considered higher risk. It is not a route for reconciling the matrix to a comparable the taxpayer already has.

options.text: By the Amount B pricing matrix, which overrides any comparable once the transaction is in scope
options.misconception: treats the Amount B approach as mandatory for every in-scope transaction
options.why: Step 2 says an in-scope transaction is priced using the Amount B pricing framework unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price is available. The exception is written into the step itself.

options.text: Neither — a transaction for which an internal comparable uncontrolled price exists can never be in scope at step 1
options.misconception: moves the comparable-price test from step 2 back into the step 1 scoping test
options.why: Step 1 asks only whether the tested party is involved in a qualifying transaction meeting the scoping criteria. The comparable uncontrolled price is a step 2 question, and the two steps do different work.

options.text: By the internal comparable uncontrolled price, which displaces the pricing matrix, the operating expense cross-check and the data availability mechanism
options.why: The pricing step applies only unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price is available, so where one is, the whole of the three-sub-step framework falls away — the pricing matrix, the operating expense cross-check that tests the matrix result against the tested party's operating expense level, and the data availability mechanism. That ordering makes sense of what Amount B is for: it approximates an arm's length return where local comparables are absent, which is why it is aimed at low-capacity jurisdictions in the first place. Where a reliable comparable exists there is nothing to approximate.
keywords: unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price

citation.ref: Pillar One Amount B — step 1 scoping and step 2 pricing, the pricing framework applying unless a reliable internal Comparable Uncontrolled Price is available, with the pricing matrix, the operating expense cross-check and the data availability mechanism as its three sub-steps

items.scenario: A distributor in a low-capacity jurisdiction carries on baseline marketing and distribution for its group and is in scope of Amount B at step 1, being party to a qualifying transaction that meets the scoping criteria. The group also has a reliable internal comparable uncontrolled price for the same transaction.

items.stem: Which statement is right?

options.text: Both are refreshed annually, so the matrix percentages change every year
options.misconception: collapses the same two cadences into the shorter of the two
options.why: The annual review is of the financial data and other datapoints. The analysis behind the matrix itself is on a five-year cycle, unless a significant change in market conditions warrants an interim update — which is what keeps the approach usable as a simplification.

options.text: Amount B was published in December 2021 with the GloBE Model Rules, and every figure in it is refreshed annually
options.misconception: dates Amount B to the release of the Pillar Two rules, which are a different Pillar and two years earlier
options.why: December 2021 is when the GloBE Model Rules for the minimum tax were released, and those are Pillar Two. The Amount B report came on 19 February 2024 and the pending design aspects on 17 June 2024.

options.text: Both the analysis behind the pricing matrix and the underlying financial data are updated every five years, with no annual review
options.misconception: collapses two different cadences into the longer of the two
options.why: There are two cadences on purpose. The analysis supporting the pricing matrix and the operating expense cap-and-collar rates is updated every five years; the financial data and other datapoints are reviewed annually and updated where necessary.

options.text: The Inclusive Framework reported on Amount B on 19 February 2024 and published the pending design aspects on 17 June 2024; the analysis behind the pricing matrix and the cap-and-collar rates is updated every five years unless a significant change in market conditions warrants an interim update, while the financial data and other datapoints are reviewed annually
options.why: Those are the two dates and the two cadences. The report of 19 February 2024 was aimed at simplifying and streamlining the application of the arm's length principle to in-country baseline marketing and distribution activities, with a particular focus on the needs of low-capacity jurisdictions, and the pending design aspects followed on 17 June 2024. The analysis behind the matrix and the cap-and-collar rates is on a five-year cycle, updated every five years unless a significant change in market conditions warrants an interim update, while the financial data and other datapoints are reviewed annually and updated where necessary. The split cadence exists to simplify compliance: a matrix that moved every year would be no simpler than a benchmarking study.

citation.ref: The Inclusive Framework's report on Pillar One Amount B of 19 February 2024 and its pending design aspects of 17 June 2024 — the pricing matrix and operating expense cap-and-collar analysis updated every five years unless market conditions warrant an interim update, with the financial data reviewed annually

items.scenario: A firm is briefing a client on how settled the Amount B figures are — when the Inclusive Framework published them, and how often they will change.

items.stem: Is the group within the scope of the GloBE Rules for the tested fiscal year?

options.text: No — the test looks at the fiscal year immediately preceding the tested year, in which revenue was 640 million euros
options.misconception: reads the test as a one-year test, so a single year below the line takes the group out
options.why: The immediately preceding year is only one of the four the test looks at. It is precisely because a single year can fall below the line that the test is written as two of four.

options.text: No — the threshold must be met in each of the four preceding fiscal years
options.misconception: reads the two-of-four test as a test that must be satisfied in all four years
options.why: The rule says at least two of the four, not all four. A four-year requirement would take almost every group out of scope in the year after a bad year.

options.text: Yes, but because the average of the four years exceeds 750 million euros
options.misconception: satisfies the test by averaging the four years rather than by counting how many of them clear the threshold
options.why: The average here is 755 million euros, so the answer comes out the same, and that is what makes the method dangerous: it will give the wrong answer whenever one very large year carries three small ones. The rule counts years over the threshold; it does not average them.

options.text: Yes — the test is annual revenue of 750 million euros or more in at least two of the four fiscal years immediately preceding the tested year, and two of these four reach it
options.why: The GloBE Rules apply to Constituent Entities of a multinational group that has annual revenue of 750 million euros or more in the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Ultimate Parent Entity in at least two of the four fiscal years immediately preceding the tested fiscal year. Here the 900 and the 780 reach it, which is two of the four, so the group is in scope. The design of the test is what matters: a single year over the line does not bring a group in, and a single year under it does not take a group out.
keywords: at least two of the four

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — annual revenue of 750 million euros or more in the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Ultimate Parent Entity in at least two of the four fiscal years immediately preceding the tested fiscal year

items.scenario: A group's annual revenue in the consolidated financial statements of its Ultimate Parent Entity, for the four fiscal years immediately preceding the tested fiscal year, was 900 million euros in the earliest of them, then 700 million euros, then 780 million euros, and 640 million euros in the fiscal year immediately preceding the tested year.

items.stem: What does the Excluded Entity status of the pension fund do to the group?

options.text: The whole group is out of scope, because the Ultimate Parent Entity is an Excluded Entity
options.misconception: reads the exclusion of the parent as an exclusion of everything beneath it
options.why: The rules say in terms that this exclusion does not affect the multinational group owned by such entities, which remains in scope of the GloBE Rules if the group as a whole otherwise meets the consolidated revenue threshold.

options.text: A pension fund is not an Excluded Entity at all; only government entities and international organisations are
options.misconception: truncates the list of Excluded Entities to its first two members
options.why: The list runs wider than that: government entities, international organisations, non-profit organisations, and pension funds or investment funds that are Ultimate Parent Entities, plus holding vehicles used by them.

options.text: The pension fund is not subject to the rules and its revenue is left out of the consolidated revenue test as well
options.misconception: extends the exclusion from liability to the measurement of the threshold
options.why: The rules separate the two questions. An Excluded Entity is not subject to the charge; its revenue is nevertheless still taken into account for the purposes of the consolidated revenue test.

options.text: The pension fund and the holding vehicle it uses are not themselves subject to the rules, but the fund's revenue still counts for the consolidated revenue test and the group it controls stays in scope
options.why: Excluded Entities are government entities, international organisations, non-profit organisations, and pension funds or investment funds that are Ultimate Parent Entities of a group, together with any holding vehicles used by such entities, organisations or funds. Two things follow and they pull in opposite directions, which is why this is examinable. The excluded entity is not subject to the rules. But its revenue is still taken into account for the purposes of the consolidated revenue test, and the exclusion does not affect the group it owns, which remains in scope if the group as a whole meets the threshold. The exclusion protects sovereign, non-profit and charitable entities and the policy of not adding a layer of tax between the investment and the investor; it is not a way out for the operating group.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — Excluded Entities being government entities, international organisations, non-profit organisations and pension or investment funds that are Ultimate Parent Entities together with their holding vehicles, whose revenue is still counted for the consolidated revenue test and whose exclusion leaves the group they control in scope

items.scenario: A pension fund is the Ultimate Parent Entity of a group. Beneath it sit a holding vehicle used by the fund and a chain of operating companies in several countries. Taken as a whole the group is well above the revenue threshold.

items.stem: What is the effective tax rate for Country B, and what would it be if B Co had instead made a GloBE loss of 5,000,000 euros?

options.text: 20 per cent on the facts, being the tax measured against C Co's income alone, and 20 per cent again on the loss facts
options.misconception: computes the effective tax rate entity by entity rather than on a jurisdictional blend
options.why: The effective tax rate is calculated on a jurisdictional basis, not per entity. The denominator is the Net GloBE Income of the jurisdiction, which is 15,000,000 euros on the first set of facts.

options.text: 13.3333 per cent on the facts, and unchanged if B Co made the loss, since a loss-making entity is left out of the computation
options.misconception: leaves a loss-making entity out of the jurisdictional figure instead of netting its loss against the other entity's income
options.why: Jurisdictional blending allows all the profits, losses and taxes of the constituent entities located in the same jurisdiction to be blended for the effective tax rate calculation. Net GloBE Income is the GloBE income of all constituent entities less the GloBE losses of all of them, so a loss reduces the denominator rather than dropping out of it.

options.text: 13.3333 per cent on the facts, and 40 per cent if B Co made the loss
options.why: The Effective Tax Rate is the total of the Adjusted Covered Taxes of each constituent entity located in the jurisdiction divided by the Net GloBE Income of that jurisdiction. Net GloBE Income here is 5,000,000 plus 10,000,000, that is 15,000,000 euros, so the rate is 2,000,000 over 15,000,000 or 13.3333 per cent, below the 15 per cent minimum. If B Co had made a loss of 5,000,000 instead, jurisdictional blending would net that loss against C Co's 10,000,000, leaving Net GloBE Income of 5,000,000 euros, and the rate would be 2,000,000 over 5,000,000, that is 40 per cent. Note which way it moves: a loss in the jurisdiction raises the effective tax rate, because the taxes are being spread over less income.

options.text: 13.3333 per cent on the facts, and nil if B Co made the loss, because a net GloBE loss means no effective tax rate need be computed
options.misconception: applies the net-loss rule to a jurisdiction that is still in net profit after the blend
options.why: It is true that where there is a net GloBE loss the effective tax rate need not be calculated and in most cases no top-up tax is due. But the blend here is 10,000,000 less 5,000,000, which is a net income of 5,000,000 euros, not a loss. The rule bites only when the jurisdiction as a whole is in loss.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — Effective Tax Rate as the Adjusted Covered Taxes of the jurisdiction over its Net GloBE Income, Net GloBE Income being the GloBE income of all constituent entities less the GloBE losses of all of them on a jurisdictional blending basis, against a 15 per cent minimum rate

items.scenario: In Country B an in-scope group has two constituent entities. B Co has GloBE income of 5,000,000 euros and C Co has GloBE income of 10,000,000 euros. The adjusted covered taxes of the two taken together are 2,000,000 euros.

items.stem: Who bears the top-up tax attributable to the Country C subsidiary?

options.text: The subsidiaries in Countries A and B, under the Undertaxed Payment Rule, because the priority runs domestic minimum top-up tax first, then the Income Inclusion Rule at the parent, and the Undertaxed Payment Rule only where neither of the first two applies
options.why: The model rules prescribe a priority ranking. Where Country C imposes a Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax the jurisdictional top-up tax is imposed on the Country C subsidiary itself. Where it does not, the Ultimate Parent Entity in Country X pays an amount equal to its allocable share of that subsidiary's top-up tax under the Income Inclusion Rule, provided Country X has implemented it. Where neither happens, and Countries A and B have implemented the Undertaxed Payment Rule, those two subsidiaries bear the top-up tax in their own jurisdictions by a denial of deductions or an equivalent adjustment. The rule transfers the levy to the group's other constituent entities located where the GloBE rules are in force.

options.text: Nobody — with no domestic minimum top-up tax in Country C and no Income Inclusion Rule in Country X, the top-up tax falls away
options.misconception: stops at the first two rules and forgets that the third exists as a backstop
options.why: The Undertaxed Payment Rule is triggered precisely where the Ultimate Parent Entity's jurisdiction does not implement the Income Inclusion Rule or does not adopt the GloBE rules. It is the backstop, and its whole purpose is that the top-up tax does not fall away.

options.text: The Country C subsidiary, because the low-tax jurisdiction always has the first right to collect
options.misconception: applies the domestic minimum top-up tax to a jurisdiction that has not enacted one
options.why: A Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax gives the low-tax jurisdiction the right to collect the jurisdictional top-up tax by introducing the charge in its own domestic tax laws. Country C has not introduced it, so there is no charge for it to collect under.

options.text: The parent in Country X, under the Income Inclusion Rule, whether or not Country X has adopted the GloBE rules
options.misconception: applies the Income Inclusion Rule in a jurisdiction that has not implemented the GloBE rules
options.why: The Income Inclusion Rule reaches a constituent entity that is the Ultimate Parent Entity located in a GloBE implementing jurisdiction. Country X has not adopted the rules, so there is nothing there to charge the parent with, and that is exactly the gap the third rule exists to close.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — the priority ranking of the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax, then the Income Inclusion Rule imposing tax on the parent equal to its allocable share, then the Undertaxed Payment Rule as backstop where the parent's jurisdiction has not implemented the Income Inclusion Rule or adopted the rules

items.scenario: The Ultimate Parent Entity of a group is in Country X and it has three wholly owned subsidiaries, in Countries A, B and C. Country C is a low-taxed jurisdiction. Country C has not introduced a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax. Country X has not adopted the GloBE rules at all. Countries A and B have both implemented the Undertaxed Payment Rule.

items.stem: How is the jurisdictional top-up tax arrived at?

options.text: The percentage is applied to the Net GloBE Income of 15,000,000 euros, the substance-based exclusion being a deduction from the tax rather than from the profit
options.misconception: applies the top-up tax percentage to the wrong base, treating the carve-out as a credit against tax
options.why: The carve-out reduces the profit, not the tax. Excess Profit is defined as Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion, and it is the Excess Profit that the percentage is applied to.

options.text: The full 15 per cent minimum rate is applied to the excess profit, the effective tax rate being relevant only to deciding whether the jurisdiction is low-taxed
options.misconception: charges the whole minimum rate a second time, ignoring the tax the jurisdiction has already collected
options.why: The effective tax rate does two jobs, not one. It decides whether the jurisdiction is low-taxed, and it is then subtracted from the minimum rate to give the percentage charged. Charging the full 15 per cent would tax the same profit twice over.

options.text: The percentage is the effective tax rate itself, 13.333 per cent, applied to the excess profit
options.misconception: charges the effective tax rate rather than the shortfall between it and the minimum
options.why: The Top-up Tax Percentage is the minimum rate less the effective tax rate. It is a shortfall, which is why it is described as a positive percentage point difference.

options.text: The Top-up Tax Percentage is the minimum rate less the effective tax rate, 15 less 13.333, that is 1.6667 per cent, and it is applied not to the Net GloBE Income but to the Excess Profit, which is 15,000,000 less 1,500,000, that is 13,500,000 euros
options.why: The Jurisdictional Top-up Tax is the Top-up Tax Percentage multiplied by the Excess Profit, plus any Additional Current Top-up Tax, less any Domestic Top-up Tax. The Top-up Tax Percentage is the positive percentage point difference between the minimum rate and the effective tax rate. The Excess Profit is the Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion. The two bases are deliberately different: the percentage is worked out on the aggregate profits, the Net GloBE Income, but it is applied to the excess income after the substance carve-out, so that groups keep the benefit of incentives on substantive activity.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — Jurisdictional Top-up Tax as the Top-up Tax Percentage on the Excess Profit plus additional current top-up tax less domestic top-up tax, the percentage being the minimum rate less the effective tax rate and the Excess Profit being Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion

items.scenario: For Country B a group has Net GloBE Income of 15,000,000 euros and an effective tax rate of 13.333 per cent. The substance-based income exclusion for the jurisdiction is 1,500,000 euros. There is no additional current top-up tax and no domestic top-up tax.

items.stem: Which answer is right?

options.text: The de-minimis exclusion applies automatically wherever average revenue is below 10 million euros, whatever the income, and no election is needed
options.misconception: drops the second limb of the de-minimis test and the election that switches it on
options.why: Both limbs have to be satisfied — average revenue below 10 million euros and average income or loss that is a loss or is below 1 million euros — and the exclusion is provided at the election of the Filing Constituent Entity rather than applying of its own force.

options.text: The exclusion is 5 per cent of payroll costs only, tangible assets carrying no carve-out; and the de-minimis exclusion applies where average revenue is below 1 million euros
options.misconception: drops the tangible-asset half of the carve-out and swaps the two de-minimis figures
options.why: The exclusion has two halves — a payroll carve-out and a tangible asset carve-out — and the de-minimis figures are 10 million euros of average revenue and 1 million euros of average income, not the other way round.

options.text: The exclusion is 5 per cent of the carrying value of eligible tangible assets in the jurisdiction plus 5 per cent of the payroll costs of employees performing activities there, with a ten-year transition starting at 8 per cent of tangible assets and 10 per cent of payroll and phasing down to 5 per cent; and the de-minimis exclusion, at the filing entity's election, applies where the jurisdiction's Average GloBE Revenue is less than 10 million euros and its Average GloBE Income or Loss is a loss or is less than 1 million euros
options.why: The substance-based income exclusion for a jurisdiction is the sum of the payroll carve-out and the tangible asset carve-out for each constituent entity there, equal to 5 per cent of the carrying value of tangible assets located in the jurisdiction and 5 per cent of the payroll costs for employees who perform activities there. There is a ten-year transition period in recognition of the impact on existing incentives and investment, during which the figures are 8 per cent of the carrying value of eligible tangible assets and 10 per cent of eligible payroll costs, both phasing down to 5 per cent over the ten years. The de-minimis exclusion has two limbs and both must be met, and it operates at the election of the Filing Constituent Entity — average revenue below 10 million euros and average income or loss that is a loss or below 1 million euros. Its purpose is to avoid a full effective tax rate computation where the top-up tax would not justify the compliance cost.

options.text: The transition starts at 10 per cent of tangible assets and 8 per cent of payroll
options.misconception: has both transitional percentages and attaches each to the wrong carve-out
options.why: It is 8 per cent of the carrying value of eligible tangible assets and 10 per cent of eligible payroll costs. The payroll figure is the higher of the two.

citation.ref: The GloBE Model Rules — the substance-based income exclusion at 5 per cent of the carrying value of tangible assets and 5 per cent of payroll costs with a ten-year transition from 8 per cent and 10 per cent, and the de-minimis exclusion at the Filing Constituent Entity's election where average GloBE revenue is below 10 million euros and average GloBE income or loss is a loss or below 1 million euros

items.scenario: A client asks two questions about the GloBE rules. What is the substance-based income exclusion worth, now and during the transitional period? And when may a jurisdiction be left out of the computation altogether?

items.stem: What may Country A do under the Subject to Tax Rule?

options.text: It keeps its 5 per cent withholding and may impose an additional tax of 3 per cent of the covered income
options.why: The specified rate is 9 per cent less the nominal rate applied in the resident State, further reduced by any source taxation already allocated to the source jurisdiction in accordance with other articles of the treaty. Here that is 9 less 5 less 1, which is 3 per cent. The payor jurisdiction retains its 5 per cent withholding right and imposes the additional 3 per cent on top, so the total tax on the payment reaches the 9 per cent the rule is aimed at.

options.text: It may charge nothing, because the Subject to Tax Rule applies only where the residence State taxes the payment at nil
options.misconception: reads "subject to tax" as requiring the income to bear no tax at all in the residence State
options.why: The rule bites wherever the recipient is subject to a nominal corporate income tax rate below 9 per cent. A nominal 1 per cent is below 9 per cent, so the rule engages; it is not a rule about untaxed income.

options.text: It may charge an additional 8 per cent, being 9 per cent less the 1 per cent nominal rate in Country B
options.misconception: takes only one of the two reductions, forgetting the source taxation the treaty has already allocated
options.why: The specified rate is the difference between 9 per cent and the nominal rate in the resident State, further reduced by any source taxation already allocated to the source jurisdiction under other articles of the treaty. Country A already has 5 per cent, and that 5 per cent comes off too.

options.text: It may charge 9 per cent in place of the 5 per cent withholding the treaty gives it
options.misconception: treats the 9 per cent as a fresh rate that replaces the treaty rate rather than as a ceiling the source State tops up to
options.why: The 9 per cent is not a rate the source State charges. It is the level below which the residence State's nominal taxation triggers the rule, and the specified rate is the gap between it and what has already been taxed.

citation.ref: The Subject to Tax Rule of Pillar Two — the specified rate being 9 per cent less the nominal rate applied in the resident State and further reduced by source taxation already allocated to the source jurisdiction under other articles of the treaty

items.scenario: Company A is resident in Country A, a developing country, and pays a royalty to Company B, its group company resident in Country B, for a licence to use a trademark. The treaty between the two countries lets Country A withhold tax at 5 per cent on royalty payments. Country B taxes the royalty at a nominal rate of 1 per cent.

items.stem: Does the Subject to Tax Rule apply to this payment?

options.text: Yes — every condition of the rule is satisfied
options.misconception: works through the payment, the threshold and the connection and misses the developing-country test the rule opens with
options.why: Three of the four conditions are satisfied, which is what makes this tempting. The one that is not is the first: the rule applies to covered payments by an entity in a developing country, and developing country is defined by a gross national income per capita of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019.

options.text: No, because the covered income of 400,000 falls below the 1 million threshold
options.misconception: applies the higher covered-income threshold to a country whose GDP is below 40 billion
options.why: The threshold is 250,000 or 1 million a year depending on whether the source country's GDP is above or below 40 billion. This country's GDP is 30 billion, so its threshold is 250,000, and 400,000 exceeds it.

options.text: No, because a management service fee is not a covered payment
options.misconception: reads the list of covered payments as confined to passive income
options.why: Covered payments are interest, royalties, payments for distribution rights for a product or service, insurance or reinsurance premiums, guarantee or financing fees, rentals for industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, and payments for services. Service fees are expressly in.

options.text: No — the payer's country is not a developing country for this rule, which defines one as having gross national income per capita of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019 on the World Bank Atlas method
options.why: The Subject to Tax Rule exists to prevent base erosion in developing countries, and it defines them: a gross national income per capita, calculated using the World Bank Atlas method, of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019, a figure to be regularly updated. At 14,000 dollars the payer's country is outside that. Everything else here is satisfied — the parties are connected persons, since connection is direct or indirect ownership of more than 50 per cent of the interests or a de facto control relationship and the holding is 60 per cent; a payment for services is a covered payment; 400,000 exceeds the 250,000 threshold that applies where the source country's GDP is below 40 billion; and a nominal 4 per cent is below 9 per cent. The first condition still fails, and it fails on its own.

citation.ref: The Subject to Tax Rule of Pillar Two — applicable to covered payments by an entity in a developing country, defined as one with gross national income per capita of 12,535 US dollars or less in 2019 on the World Bank Atlas method, made to connected persons at more than 50 per cent of the interests, where covered income in the source country exceeds 250,000 or 1 million by reference to a GDP of 40 billion

items.scenario: A payment is made by an entity in a country whose gross national income per capita on the World Bank Atlas method was 14,000 US dollars in 2019, to a group company that holds 60 per cent of its interests. The payment is a management service fee. The total covered income arising in that source country is 400,000 a year, and the source country's annual GDP is 30 billion. The recipient's country taxes the fee at a nominal 4 per cent.

items.stem: Which of these four are BEPS minimum standards?

options.text: Actions 5 and 13 only
options.why: There are four minimum standards in the whole BEPS package and they are Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14. Two of them appear in this list, so two of these four are binding. Action 3 on controlled foreign company rules and Action 12 on mandatory disclosure are best practices, which the OECD defines as an optional recommendation for States to follow rather than a standard; guidance drawn from best practices is what supports countries proposing to act on mandatory disclosure initiatives or CFC legislation.

options.text: Actions 3 and 12, being the ones a country has to legislate for in its own domestic law
options.misconception: reverses which two bind, on the footing that the domestic-law Actions must be the compulsory ones
options.why: Both minimum standards and best practices can call for domestic legislation, so that is not the dividing line. What makes an Action a minimum standard is that non-implementation would produce negative spill-overs on other countries, including on competitiveness, and Actions 3 and 12 are expressly not minimum standards.

options.text: Actions 5, 6, 13 and 15
options.misconception: puts the multilateral instrument among the minimum standards in place of Action 14 on dispute resolution
options.why: Action 15 is the machinery for putting treaty measures into existing treaties, not a standard of its own. The fourth minimum standard is Action 14, making dispute resolution more effective.

options.text: All four
options.misconception: treats every Action Plan as carrying the same level of commitment
options.why: The Actions carry three different levels of commitment, and that is a distinction the OECD draws in terms: a new minimum standard, a revision of an existing standard, and a best practice. Only four Actions are minimum standards.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The 2015 BEPS package — Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14 as the four minimum standards subject to peer review, against a revision of an existing standard and a best practice, with the controlled foreign company rules of Action 3 and the mandatory disclosure rules of Action 12 as best practice only

items.scenario: A country is deciding what it is obliged to legislate for and what it may leave alone. Four Action Plans are on the table: Action 3 on controlled foreign company rules, Action 5 on countering harmful tax practices, Action 12 on disclosure of aggressive tax planning arrangements, and Action 13 on transfer pricing documentation.

items.stem: What reason does the study material give for that?

options.text: Because controlled foreign company rules are treaty measures, and a minimum standard can only be a domestic-law measure
options.misconception: classifies CFC rules as treaty measures when they are domestic legislation taxing a resident shareholder
options.why: Controlled foreign company rules are domestic legislation. They tax income in the parent country even where it has not been repatriated, which is a purely domestic charge on a resident shareholder.

options.text: Because CFC rules were superseded by the Income Inclusion Rule under Pillar Two
options.misconception: reads a later development back into a report that predates it by six years
options.why: Action 3 was delivered in 2015 and the GloBE Model Rules came in December 2021. The two coexist; nothing in Action 3 was written by reference to a rule that did not yet exist.

options.text: Because too few countries had CFC rules at the time for a peer review process to be workable
options.misconception: invents a practical obstacle where the study material gives a disagreement of principle
options.why: The obstacle recorded is disagreement about what a CFC regime is for, not the number of countries that had one. CFC rules had been in use for decades before the BEPS Project.

options.text: Because there was fundamental disagreement over the policy of CFC regimes, in particular whether a State should use its regime to protect other States' tax bases from earnings stripping
options.why: The Final Report does not propose a minimum standard for CFC regimes. The OECD regards them as important in tackling base erosion and profit shifting and made a series of best practice recommendations on the building blocks of an effective regime, but the reason it was unable to provide more than best practice was fundamental disagreement over the policy of CFC regimes — in particular whether states should use the regime to protect other states' tax bases from earnings stripping. It is a disagreement about purpose, not about technique.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: BEPS Action Plan 3 on strengthening controlled foreign company rules — the Final Report declining to propose a minimum standard because of fundamental disagreement over the policy of CFC regimes, and offering best practice recommendations on the building blocks instead

items.scenario: A student notices that the OECD calls controlled foreign company rules important in tackling base erosion and profit shifting, and yet Action 3 produced only best practice recommendations on the building blocks of an effective regime.

items.stem: Which statement is right?

options.text: Peer review covers all fifteen Actions, so that implementation of the whole package can be monitored
options.misconception: extends peer review from the four minimum standards to the entire package
options.why: Peer review attaches to the minimum standards, because those are the ones every member has committed to implement. Monitoring of the wider package takes the form of assessment reports on what countries have done, which is a different thing from a peer review with a standard to measure against.

options.text: The Actions are grouped on coherence, substance and transparency, with Actions 1 and 15 horizontal across all three; and each of the four minimum standards is subject to peer review, which every member of the Inclusive Framework commits to take part in
options.why: The Action Plans are structured round three fundamental pillars — coherence, substance and transparency — with Action 1 on the digital economy and Action 15 on the multilateral instrument sitting horizontally across them. Action 5 appears twice, its preferential-tax- regimes component under substance and its exchange-of-rulings component under transparency. And each of the four minimum standards is subject to peer review in order to ensure timely and accurate implementation and safeguard the level playing field, with all members of the Inclusive Framework committing both to implementing the minimum standards and to participating in the peer review.

options.text: The Actions are grouped by whether each is a treaty measure or a domestic-law measure
options.misconception: substitutes a plausible classification for the one the OECD actually used
options.why: The grouping is by objective, not by instrument. The three fundamental pillars are introducing coherence in domestic rules affecting cross-border activities, reinforcing substance requirements so that taxation aligns with value creation, and improving transparency and tax certainty.

options.text: Action 1 belongs to the coherence pillar and Action 15 to the transparency pillar
options.misconception: forces the two horizontal Actions into pillars when the classification places them across all three
options.why: Action 1 on the digital economy and Action 15 on the multilateral instrument are classified as horizontal. Both cut across the whole package rather than serving one objective, which is why Action 15 is called the machinery Action.

citation.source: OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project
citation.ref: The classification of the fifteen BEPS Action Plans on coherence, substance and transparency with Actions 1 and 15 horizontal, and the peer review to which each of the four minimum standards is subject

items.scenario: A note groups the fifteen Action Plans and describes how compliance with them is checked. Only one of the four statements in it is accurate.

items.stem: Does the company have a significant economic presence in India?

options.text: Yes, and the whole of the company's global income is then deemed to accrue or arise in India
options.misconception: gets the trigger right and ignores the attribution limit written into the same provision
options.why: The provision ends with a limit: where a business connection is established by reason of significant economic presence, only so much of the income as is attributable to the transactions or activities referred to in the two limbs is deemed to accrue or arise in India.

options.text: No — with no office, employee or agent in India there can be no business connection at all
options.misconception: requires a physical presence, which is the very thing the provision was written to do without
options.why: The provision says the opposite in terms: the transactions or activities constitute a significant economic presence whether or not the agreement is entered into in India, whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business in India, and whether or not he renders services in India.

options.text: Yes — the two limbs are alternatives, and although the payments of ₹1.6 crore fall short of the ₹2 crore limb, systematic and continuous soliciting of business or interaction with at least 3 lakh users is the second limb and 4.2 lakh users satisfies it
options.why: Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i) gives significant economic presence two limbs. The first is transactions in respect of goods, services or property carried out by a non-resident with any person in India, including the provision of download of data or software in India, where the aggregate of payments during the previous year exceeds ₹2 crore. The second is systematic and continuous soliciting of business activities or engaging in interaction with users in India, where the number of users is at least 3 lakh. Either is enough, and the second is met here. Both apply whether or not the agreement is entered into in India and whether or not the non-resident has a residence or place of business here — and only the income attributable to those activities is deemed to accrue or arise in India.

options.text: No — the aggregate of payments has to exceed ₹2 crore before there can be a significant economic presence, and ₹1.6 crore falls short
options.misconception: reads the two limbs of the definition as cumulative when they are alternatives
options.why: The definition sets out two separate kinds of transaction, each with its own condition, and satisfying either is enough. The payments limb is not a gateway the user limb has to pass through.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) — significant economic presence as either payments exceeding ₹2 crore in the previous year from transactions in goods, services or property including downloads of data or software, or systematic and continuous soliciting or interaction with at least 3 lakh users, applying whether or not the agreement is entered into in India, with only the attributable income deemed to accrue or arise in India

items.scenario: A non-resident company has no office, employee or agent in India. During previous year 2025-26 it receives ₹1.6 crore from customers in India for downloads of its software, and its platform is used by 4.2 lakh users in India with whom it interacts systematically and continuously. The agreements with the Indian customers are all signed outside India.

items.stem: Which mapping is right?

options.text: All three options were adopted as a single measure, the equalisation levy, which remains in force
options.misconception: collapses three separate Indian provisions into one and misses that the levy has been withdrawn
options.why: Three separate provisions answer the three options, and the equalisation levy is no longer one of them: the 2 per cent levy on e-commerce supply or services was withdrawn by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 and the 6 per cent levy on specified services by the Finance Act, 2025.

options.text: Significant economic presence answers the withholding tax option and section 194-O answers the virtual fixed place of business option
options.misconception: has both provisions and attaches each to the wrong OECD option
options.why: Significant economic presence is a nexus rule — it makes a non-resident's presence a business connection — which is what the virtual fixed place option was about. Section 194-O is a deduction of tax at source, which is the withholding option.

options.text: Significant economic presence under Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i) answers the virtual fixed place of business option; section 194-O, at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount of the sales or services facilitated by an e-commerce operator, answers the withholding tax option; and the equalisation levy answered the third, and is the one India has withdrawn
options.why: The OECD offered three options and recommended none, leaving countries to act in their own domestic law. India acted on all three. The concept of significant economic presence, which the study material itself describes as similar to the virtual fixed place permanent establishment recommended in the 2015 Action 1 report, was introduced by Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i). Section 194-O answers the option of a final withholding tax on payments for digital goods or services: an e-commerce operator that facilitates the sale of goods or provision of services of an e-commerce participant through its digital or electronic facility or platform deducts tax at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount. The third option was the equalisation levy, and it is the one India has abandoned in both its forms.

options.text: Section 194-O answers the withholding tax option, at 1 per cent of the gross amount of the sales or services facilitated
options.misconception: states the section 194-O rate as 1 per cent
options.why: The rate in section 194-O is 0.1 per cent of the gross amount of the sales or services or both. The mapping is otherwise right, which is what makes the wrong figure worth catching.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to Section 9(1)(i) and Section 194-O, read against the three options offered under BEPS Action Plan 1 — a modified permanent establishment rule, a virtual fixed place of business, and a final withholding tax or an equalisation levy, with tax deducted at 0.1 per cent of the gross amount by an e-commerce operator

items.scenario: A firm is mapping the options the OECD offered for the direct tax challenges of the digital economy under Action Plan 1 against the provisions India actually enacted.

items.stem: Does the Multilateral Instrument apply to either treaty?

options.text: To the Country M treaty only, notification by India being the operative act
options.misconception: makes the Instrument apply on the strength of one party's own notification
options.why: It is the only one of the two where notification is not matched, so it is the clearer failure of the two. Each country has to notify its treaty with the other while depositing its instrument with the OECD.

options.text: To both, since India has notified each of them
options.misconception: treats one side's notification as enough to make a treaty a covered tax agreement
options.why: Article 2 requires each party to have notified the agreement to the Depositary as a listed agreement. That is the matching principle, and it needs both.

options.text: To the Country N treaty only, because matched notification is what matters and ratification is a formality
options.misconception: reduces ratification to a formality, when it is what starts the entry-into-force clock
options.why: Ratification is the act that makes the Convention enter into force for a country, and until it has entered into force for both Contracting States its provisions cannot have effect for their treaty. Matched notification decides what the Instrument could modify; ratification decides whether it modifies anything yet.

options.text: To neither — the matching principle needs both parties to notify before a treaty is a Covered Tax Agreement, which fails for Country M; and for Country N the Instrument has not entered into force, since entry into force follows the deposit of an instrument of ratification
options.why: Two different conditions fail in the two cases. Article 2 defines a Covered Tax Agreement as an agreement for the avoidance of double taxation that is in force between parties and which each party has notified to the Depositary as a listed agreement — the matching principle — so India-Country M is not a Covered Tax Agreement at all, the same position as India-Mauritius, where India notified and Mauritius did not. For Country N the notification is matched but the Instrument applies only to countries which have signed it and have ratified, accepted or approved it under domestic law and deposited that instrument with the OECD depositary. That is the India-Italy position in the study material: Italy notified its treaty with India as a Covered Tax Agreement and has not ratified, so the Instrument does not apply to that treaty.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Article 2 and Article 34 of the Convention — a Covered Tax Agreement being one notified to the Depositary by each party as a listed agreement, and the Convention applying only to countries that have signed and have ratified, accepted or approved it and deposited that instrument with the OECD depositary

items.scenario: Two situations are put to an adviser. India and Country M have both signed and ratified the Multilateral Instrument; India has notified its treaty with Country M as a covered tax agreement, but Country M has not notified its treaty with India. Separately, India and Country N have each notified their treaty with the other, but Country N has not ratified the Instrument under its own law.

items.stem: When did the Convention enter into force for India, and from when could its provisions first take effect here?

options.text: 1 October 2019, being the first day of the month following the expiry of three calendar months beginning on 25 June 2019, with the earliest effect in India on 1 April 2020, six calendar months later
options.why: On deposit of the instrument of ratification the Convention enters into force on the first day of the month following the expiry of three calendar months beginning on the date of deposit. Three calendar months from 25 June 2019 expires in September, so the first day of the following month is 1 October 2019. For taxes other than withholding taxes the provisions have effect for a taxable period beginning on or after the expiration of six calendar months from the later of the entry-into-force dates, which for India is 1 April 2020 — the earliest date on which the Convention could take effect here. The Central Government notified the Convention under section 90(1) by Notification No. 57/2019 dated 9 August 2019.

options.text: 1 July 2019 and 1 January 2020, the withholding tax rule applying to every kind of tax
options.misconception: shortens the entry-into-force period and applies the withholding-tax effective date rule to all taxes
options.why: Two errors compound. The period before entry into force is three calendar months, not a few days. And the calendar-year rule — the first day of the next calendar year beginning on or after the later entry-into-force date — is the rule for withholding taxes only; for other taxes the period is six calendar months and it runs to the start of a taxable period.

options.text: 25 September 2019 and 25 March 2020, both counted forward from the date of deposit itself
options.misconception: counts three and six months forward from the day of deposit instead of to the first day of the month that follows
options.why: Entry into force is not three months from the date of deposit. It is the first day of the month following the expiry of three calendar months beginning on that date, which is what moves it from late September to 1 October.

options.text: 1 October 2019 for both, entry into force and entry into effect being one event
options.misconception: collapses the two clocks into one, when the Convention runs them separately
options.why: They are two separate clocks and the second starts only when the first has finished for both Contracting States. Entry into force is when a country becomes a party; entry into effect is when the modified provisions actually begin to govern a taxable period.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Articles 34 and 35 of the Convention, read with Section 90(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Notification No. 57/2019 dated 9 August 2019 — entry into force on the first day of the month following the expiry of three calendar months from deposit, effect for withholding taxes from the first day of the next calendar year and for other taxes after six calendar months, with India depositing on 25 June 2019, entering into force on 1 October 2019 and taking effect from 1 April 2020

items.scenario: India signed the Multilateral Instrument at Paris on 7 June 2017 and deposited its instrument of ratification with the OECD depositary on 25 June 2019.

items.stem: Which summary is right?

options.text: It replaces each covered tax agreement, the text of the treaty ceasing to have effect once the Instrument enters into force
options.misconception: reads the Instrument as superseding the treaty rather than applying alongside it
options.why: The Instrument modifies tax treaties not by amending their text but by being applied together with the relevant treaty. It does not make the existing agreement otiose; it operates alongside it and modifies the application of some clauses on the later-in-time principle.

options.text: It has 7 parts and 39 articles, of which Articles 3 to 17 are the substantive provisions; a party may reserve out of provisions that do not reflect a BEPS minimum standard and may withdraw the reservation later; and of the four BEPS minimum standards only Actions 6 and 14 are minimum standards inside the Instrument, Actions 5 and 13 being implemented in domestic law
options.why: The Instrument runs to 7 parts and 39 articles: scope and interpretation in Articles 1 and 2, hybrid mismatches in 3 to 5, treaty abuse in 6 to 11, avoidance of permanent establishment status in 12 to 15, improving dispute resolution in 16 and 17, arbitration in 18 to 26, and final provisions in 27 to 39, with Articles 3 to 17 recognised as the substantive provisions. A reservation is a unilateral statement by which a State excludes or modifies the legal effect of certain provisions, and jurisdictions have the possibility to opt out only of provisions that do not reflect a BEPS minimum standard, with the possibility to withdraw the reservation and opt in later. Of the four minimum standards under the BEPS package, Actions 6 and 14 are the ones specifically provided as minimum standards under the Instrument.

options.text: It has 7 parts and 39 articles, and no reservation of any kind is permitted, the whole Instrument being a minimum standard
options.misconception: gets the structure right and treats every provision as compulsory, when the reservation mechanism is the reason countries signed
options.why: The structure is right and the rest is not. The Instrument provides flexibility in three ways — a choice among alternative provisions, a choice whether to apply optional provisions such as mandatory binding arbitration, and the right to reserve out. Without that flexibility the tax policies of the signatories would never have converged enough for them to sign.

options.text: All four BEPS minimum standards are minimum standards inside the Instrument as well
options.misconception: assumes the four BEPS minimum standards carry over unchanged into the Instrument
options.why: Only two do. Action 6 on treaty abuse and Action 14 on dispute resolution are specifically provided as minimum standard provisions under the Instrument; the solutions for Action 5 and Action 13 are incorporated under domestic laws instead, which is why they cannot be minimum standards in a treaty instrument.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: The structure of the Convention in 7 parts and 39 articles with Articles 3 to 17 as the substantive provisions, the reservation mechanism limited to provisions that do not reflect a BEPS minimum standard, and Actions 6 and 14 as the minimum standards inside the Instrument with Actions 5 and 13 implemented in domestic law

items.scenario: A firm is summarising the Multilateral Instrument for a training note — how it is built, how much a country may opt out of, and how the BEPS minimum standards sit inside it.

items.stem: Is the Assessing Officer right about section 131(3)?

options.text: Yes — recording reasons is good practice but the section imposes no condition, and the 15-day period runs only after the assessee asks for the books back
options.misconception: turns a statutory condition into practice and makes the clock start on the assessee's request rather than on the impounding
options.why: The recording of reasons is a condition the section states in terms for these three officers, not a matter of practice, and the period is measured from the retention itself. Nothing in section 131(3) makes it depend on the assessee asking.

options.text: No — the outer limit is 30 days from the date the books were produced, and no approval can extend it
options.misconception: puts the limit at 30 days and treats it as absolute, when the figure is 15 days excluding holidays and an approval lifts it
options.why: Thirty days is the outer limit in a different provision — section 132(8), which says seized books cannot be kept more than 30 days after the assessment proceedings are completed even with approval. Under section 131(3) the number is 15 days, holidays are excluded, and the approval of a senior authority carries it further.

options.text: Yes — the restriction bites only where the books were seized in a search, and books produced voluntarily in a proceeding may be retained indefinitely
options.misconception: reads the impounding power as available only after a search, when section 131(3) is about books produced before an authority in an ordinary proceeding
options.why: Section 131(3) is written for exactly this situation — books produced before an authority in any proceeding under the Act. A search is not needed to trigger it and is not what the time limit turns on.

options.text: No — the words he is relying on are unrestricted only for the other authorities; an Assessing Officer, an Assistant Director or a Deputy Director must record his reasons for impounding and must obtain prior approval to retain the books for more than 15 days, holidays excluded
options.why: Section 131(3) does say the authority may impound and retain books for such period as it thinks fit, and for a Commissioner or a Chief Commissioner that is the whole of the rule. The section then subjects three officers to two conditions. The Assessing Officer, the Assistant Director and the Deputy Director must record their reasons for impounding, and if they wish to keep the books for a period exceeding 15 days, excluding holidays, they must first obtain the approval of a Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director. Both are missing here.

citation.ref: Section 131(3) — the power to impound and retain books produced in a proceeding, unrestricted except for the Assessing Officer, Assistant Director and Deputy Director, who must record reasons and obtain prior approval to retain for more than 15 days excluding holidays

items.scenario: In the course of a scrutiny proceeding the Assessing Officer requires a firm to produce its ledgers, and when they are produced he keeps them. He writes nothing on the file about why. He still has them forty days later, having taken nobody's approval, and tells the partner that section 131(3) lets him retain books for such period as he thinks fit.

items.stem: Is the order good, and what could the Director General have done instead?

options.text: The order is bad — section 131(1A) carries only the four Civil Court powers in section 131(1), which stop at discovery and inspection, attendance and examination on oath, production of books and issuing commissions, and none of them is a power to seize; to reach the ₹50,00,000 he must authorise a search under section 132(1)
options.why: Section 131(1A) does two things and only two. It names the investigation wing, and it lets those officers exercise the powers conferred by section 131(1) even where no proceeding is pending against the person. Those powers are the four a Civil Court has under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — discovery and inspection, enforcing the attendance of any person including an officer of a banking company and examining him on oath, compelling the production of books of account and documents, and issuing commissions. Seizure is not among them and never has been. A Director General is, however, one of the authorities who may authorise a search under section 132(1) on the strength of information in his possession that a person holds money representing undisclosed income, and it is that route, not section 131(1A), that reaches the cash.
keywords: even where no proceeding is pending

options.text: The order is good as to the cash but bad as to procedure — he should first have issued a summons under section 131(1) and seized the ₹50,00,000 only on a failure to comply
options.misconception: treats a failure to comply with a summons as converting a section 131 power into a power of seizure
options.why: A failure to produce books after a summons under section 131(1) is one of the three limbs of reason to believe that lets a search be authorised under section 132(1). It does not turn section 131 itself into a seizure power, and it is the authorisation under section 132(1) that does the work either way.

options.text: The order is bad, and there is nothing else the Director General can do himself — a search may be authorised only by a Principal Chief Commissioner or a Principal Commissioner, so he must refer the information onward
options.misconception: leaves a Director General off the list of authorities who may authorise a search under section 132(1)
options.why: The first half is right and the second is not. Section 132(1) names the Principal Director General, the Director General, the Principal Director and the Director alongside the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner and Commissioner, so the Director General can authorise the search himself.

options.text: The order is good — section 131(1A) exists precisely so that the investigation wing can act where no proceeding is pending, and a power to enquire into ₹50,00,000 of concealed cash without a power to hold it would be worthless
options.misconception: reads the removal of the pending-proceeding requirement as an enlargement of the powers themselves
options.why: What section 131(1A) removes is the requirement that a proceeding be pending. The list of powers it lets those officers exercise is unchanged, and it is the section 131(1) list. A power can be usefully exercised without a proceeding and still not include seizure.

citation.ref: Sections 131(1) and 131(1A) read with section 132(1) — the four Civil Court powers available to the investigation wing even where no proceeding is pending, none of which is a power of seizure, and the authorities competent to authorise a search

items.scenario: A Director General of Income-tax receives information that a person holds ₹50,00,000 of unaccounted cash. No proceeding of any kind is pending against that person. The Director General passes an order invoking section 131(1A) and directing that the ₹50,00,000 be seized.

items.stem: How does the challenge stand?

options.text: It fails on its own terms but the search has a different defect — a Joint Commissioner may authorise a search if the Board has empowered him, and where he is the authorising officer the officer he may name is confined to an Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner or Income-tax Officer, so a Joint Director cannot be the authorised officer on his warrant
options.why: Section 132(1) has two rungs. A Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director, Director, Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may authorise a search, and each of them may name a Joint Director, Joint Commissioner, Additional Director, Additional Commissioner, Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner or Income-tax Officer. An Additional Director, Additional Commissioner, Joint Director or Joint Commissioner may also authorise a search, but only if empowered by the Board, and the officer he may then name is confined to an Assistant Director, Deputy Director, Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner or Income-tax Officer. So the flat proposition that a Joint Commissioner cannot authorise a search is wrong, and the pairing on this warrant is wrong.
keywords: only if empowered by the Board

options.text: It fails entirely — any authority above the rank of Income-tax Officer may authorise a search where he holds information, and the rank of the officer who conducts it is an internal matter
options.misconception: treats the authorising ladder as a general seniority test and the identity of the authorised officer as administrative
options.why: Both halves of section 132(1) are statutory. The authorising officers are named, the officers each of them may authorise are named, and the pairing is part of the condition on which the search is lawful rather than an internal allocation of work.

options.text: It succeeds — section 132(1) lists eight authorising officers and a Joint Commissioner is not among them in any circumstances
options.misconception: reads the list of authorising officers as closed, ignoring the second rung available to an Additional or Joint officer empowered by the Board
options.why: The section carries a second rung expressly. An Additional Director, Additional Commissioner, Joint Director or Joint Commissioner may authorise a search if he is empowered by the Board to do so, and what changes is the seniority of the officer he may send in.

options.text: It succeeds because the Joint Commissioner did not disclose the information in his possession to Ganesh before signing, which the section requires him to do
