A crypto-asset for this purpose is the digital representation of value defined in section 2(47A)(d), which relies on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger or similar technology to validate and secure transactions.

citation.ref: Sections 285BAA(1) to 285BAA(4) read with section 2(47A)(d) — the crypto-asset statement, 30 days to rectify a defect after which the Act applies as if inaccurate information had been furnished, a notice of not more than 30 days where nothing is filed, and ten days to correct a discovered inaccuracy

items.scenario: A platform through which people buy and sell digital tokens is a prescribed reporting entity for the purposes of the crypto-asset statement. It files its statement, is told on 10 September that the statement is defective, and lets three months pass. A month after that its own audit finds that two users' transactions were reported at the wrong values.

items.stem: Which of them may be authorised as the company's representative under section 288?

options.text: CA Sundar and CA Prakash — the loan is his brother's rather than his own, and the disqualification reaches only the accountant himself
options.misconception: confines the indebtedness test to the accountant, when the list reads a person who, or his relative or partner, is indebted
options.why: The words are a person who, or his relative or partner, is indebted to the company or its group in excess of ₹5,00,000. A brother is a relative and ₹7,00,000 is over the line.

options.text: CA Sundar and CA Tanvi — a fraud conviction is spent after five years and a shareholding of ₹800 is trivial, while the loan and the number of audits both disqualify
options.misconception: puts the fraud disqualification at five years, when the list requires ten to have elapsed
options.why: The period is ten years from the date of conviction, and six have gone. Everything else in the option is right, which is what makes the wrong figure decide the answer.

options.text: None of them — a chartered accountant may never appear for a company before an appellate authority, that being work reserved for a legal practitioner
options.misconception: reads appearance before an income-tax authority as advocacy reserved to lawyers, when section 288 names an accountant among those who may appear
options.why: Section 288 names both. A legal practitioner entitled to practise in any Civil Court in India may appear, and so may an accountant, and it is only the section 141(3) disqualifications that thin the field.

options.text: CA Sundar alone — a relative may hold security or interest in the company of a face value not exceeding ₹1,000, while indebtedness of a relative above ₹5,00,000, holding appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies, and a fraud conviction where ten years have not elapsed each disqualify
options.why: The definition of accountant in section 288 excludes, for a company assessee, a person who is not eligible for appointment as its auditor under section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. That list disqualifies a person whose relative or partner is indebted to the company or its group in excess of ₹5,00,000, so CA Prakash's brother's ₹7,00,000 loan is fatal; a person who at the date of appointment already holds appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies, which catches CA Rehana at 22; and a person convicted by a court of an offence involving fraud where a period of ten years has not elapsed, which catches CA Tanvi at six years. The footnote to the same list permits a relative to hold security or interest in the company of a face value not exceeding ₹1,000, and CA Sundar's wife holds ₹800.

citation.ref: Section 288 with the Explanation defining accountant, read with section 141(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 — a relative or partner indebted in excess of ₹5 lakh, appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies and a fraud conviction within ten years disqualifying, while a relative may hold security of face value not exceeding ₹1,000

items.scenario: A company looks for someone to appear for it before the Commissioner (Appeals). Four names come up. CA Prakash, whose brother has taken a loan of ₹7,00,000 from the company. CA Rehana, who is already the statutory auditor of 22 companies. CA Sundar, whose wife holds shares in the company of a face value of ₹800. And CA Tanvi, who was convicted of an offence involving fraud six years ago.

items.stem: What are the three answers?

options.text: He may not appear for the trust; nobody may attend a section 131 examination for the client; and a valuation question must be argued by an accountant because a registered valuer is a witness rather than a representative
options.misconception: gets the section 131 point right and both others wrong, treating a registered valuer as incapable of appearing
options.why: Section 287A says in terms that a taxpayer entitled or required to attend on a matter relating to the valuation of an asset may attend by a registered valuer. And the rider in section 288 lets the partner appear for the trust despite being unable to audit it.

options.text: He may not appear for the trust, because a contribution of ₹75,000 exceeds the ₹50,000 substantial contribution limit and the disqualification runs to representation as well as to audit
options.misconception: carries the audit disqualification into representation, which the rider in section 288 exists to prevent
options.why: The rider was written for this. Being unable to audit an assessee or to sign a report or certificate for him does not stop an accountant appearing for him in a proceeding as authorised representative.

options.text: He may appear for the trust; the firm may also attend the section 131 examination provided it holds a written authority; and a registered valuer may appear only with the Assessing Officer's leave
options.misconception: allows a representative to stand in for a personal examination on oath and adds a permission requirement to section 287A
options.why: Section 288(1) opens with the words otherwise than when required under section 131 to attend personally for examination on oath or affirmation, which is an exception no written authority can cure. And section 287A gives the taxpayer the right to attend by a registered valuer without anybody's leave.

options.text: He may appear for the trust, because ineligibility to audit or to furnish a report or certificate does not make an accountant ineligible to attend as authorised representative; nobody may attend in place of a person required under section 131 to attend personally for examination on oath; and on a question of valuation the taxpayer may attend by a registered valuer under section 287A
options.why: Section 288 carries a rider in exactly these words — the ineligibility for carrying out any audit or furnishing any report or certificate in respect of an assessee shall not make an accountant ineligible for attending an income-tax proceeding referred to in section 288(1) as authorised representative on behalf of that assessee. So the ₹75,000 contribution, which is above the ₹50,000 that makes a person a substantial contributor and bars him from auditing the trust, does not bar him from appearing for it. Section 288(1) itself excepts the case where a person is required under section 131 to attend personally for examination on oath or affirmation, which nobody may do for him. And section 287A lets a taxpayer who is required to attend on a matter relating to the valuation of an asset attend by a registered valuer, subject to the same section 131 exception.
keywords: shall not make an accountant ineligible
attend personally for examination on oath

citation.ref: Section 288(1) and the rider to the Explanation defining accountant, read with section 287A — appearance by an authorised representative except where section 131 requires personal attendance on oath, the ₹50,000 substantial contribution that bars an audit of a trust but not an appearance for it, and appearance by a registered valuer on a valuation matter

items.scenario: Three questions come to a firm on the same morning. Its partner is not eligible to audit a charitable trust because he gave it ₹75,000 last year, and the trust asks whether he can nonetheless appear for it in an assessment. A client summoned under section 131 to be examined on oath asks whether the firm can go in his place. And another client, whose only dispute is the value of a factory building, asks who may appear on that.

items.stem: How many of the four may apply?

options.text: All four — the ₹100,00,00,000 notification sets the fee band rather than the class of applicant, and any resident may ask about his own liability
options.misconception: confuses the ₹100 crore notification defining the class of resident applicant with the transaction slabs that fix the fee
options.why: Two different figures do two different jobs. The notification of 28 November 2014 makes a resident an applicant only where his transactions total ₹100,00,00,000 or more, and Rule 44E separately uses ₹100,00,00,000 and ₹300,00,00,000 to fix the fee for an applicant who is already qualified.

options.text: Three — Alpha Inc, Bharat Ltd and Mr Dev; Chandra Ltd cannot, because a resident may seek a ruling on his own tax liability only if he falls in a class notified by the Central Government, and the notified class is a resident whose transactions total ₹100,00,00,000 or more
options.why: Section 245N(a) gives an advance ruling five limbs and section 245N(b) gives each of them its applicant. A non-resident may ask about a transaction he has undertaken or proposes to undertake, which covers Alpha Inc. A resident may ask about the tax liability of a non-resident arising out of a transaction he has undertaken or proposes to undertake with that non-resident, which covers Bharat Ltd. Any person, resident or non-resident, may ask whether an arrangement proposed to be undertaken is an impermissible avoidance arrangement referred to in Chapter X-A, which covers Mr Dev. A resident asking about his own tax liability must fall within a class notified by the Central Government, and Notification No. 73/2014 dated 28 November 2014 notifies a resident in relation to his tax liability arising out of one or more transactions valuing ₹100,00,00,000 or more in total, so ₹40,00,00,000 leaves Chandra Ltd out.

options.text: Two — only Alpha Inc and Bharat Ltd, because the whole chapter is written for the tax liability of a non-resident and a resident's own affairs are outside it in every case
options.misconception: reads advance rulings as available only where a non-resident's liability is in question
options.why: Two of the five limbs are about a resident's own position. A notified resident may ask about his own tax liability, and any person, resident or non-resident, may ask whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement.

options.text: Three — Alpha Inc, Bharat Ltd and Chandra Ltd; Mr Dev cannot, because a question of impermissible avoidance is for the Approving Panel under Chapter X-A and never for a Board for Advance Rulings
options.misconception: sends the avoidance question to the Approving Panel, when section 245N(a) expressly makes it a limb of advance ruling
options.why: Section 245N(a) names it as a limb in its own words — a determination or decision whether an arrangement proposed to be undertaken by any person, resident or non-resident, is an impermissible avoidance arrangement referred to in Chapter X-A. It is the one limb open to everybody, and it is Chandra Ltd that fails on the ₹100,00,00,000 test.

citation.ref: Sections 245N(a) and 245N(b) with Notification No. 73/2014 dated 28 November 2014 — the five limbs of advance ruling and their applicants, including the notified resident whose transactions total ₹100 crore or more and the impermissible avoidance question open to any person

items.scenario: Four people want a ruling from a Board for Advance Rulings. Alpha Inc, a non-resident, on the tax effect of a transaction it proposes to undertake in India. Bharat Ltd, a resident, on the tax liability of a non-resident arising out of a supply contract Bharat Ltd proposes to enter into with that non-resident. Chandra Ltd, a resident and not a public sector company, on its own tax liability arising out of transactions totalling ₹40,00,00,000. And Mr Dev, a resident individual, on whether an arrangement he proposes to undertake is an impermissible avoidance arrangement.

items.stem: Which of those is right?

options.text: All except the last — the two remedies may be pursued together, because an advance ruling only clarifies a question and an appeal decides a dispute
options.misconception: allows a resident applicant to run an appeal and an application at once, which section 245RR forbids
options.why: Section 245RR exists to stop exactly that. Where a resident applicant has made an application in respect of an issue for the decision of a Board, no income-tax authority or Tribunal may take any decision on that issue.

options.text: All except the third — a Board may call for the Commissioner's records but has no power over a third party such as a bank, which can only be reached by the Assessing Officer
options.misconception: confines the Board's powers to the departmental record, when section 245U gives it the powers of a Civil Court over any person
options.why: Section 245U names the banking company specifically. The Board may enforce the attendance of any person, including any officer of a banking company, examine him on oath and compel the production of books of account and other documents.

options.text: All of them — three Boards for Advance Rulings have given rulings since 1 September 2021, each of two members who are officers not below the rank of Chief Commissioner; a vacancy or defect in the constitution does not make a proceeding or ruling open to question; a Board has the powers of a Civil Court including compelling the production of books and examining on oath; and section 245RR stops any income-tax authority or the Tribunal deciding an issue on which a resident applicant has applied
options.why: Section 245-OB lets the Central Government constitute Boards for Advance Rulings, and three have been constituted for giving rulings on or after 1 September 2021, two with their headquarters in Delhi and one in Mumbai; every such Board consists of two members, each an officer not below the rank of Chief Commissioner nominated by the Board. Section 245P says a proceeding before, or a ruling by, a Board is not questioned or invalid merely because of a vacancy or a defect in its constitution. Section 245U gives it all the powers of a Civil Court in respect of discovery and inspection, enforcing the attendance of any person including an officer of a banking company and examining him on oath, issuing commissions and compelling the production of books of account. And section 245RR provides that where a resident applicant has applied on an issue, no income-tax authority or Tribunal shall take any decision on it, so the two remedies cannot be run together.
keywords: not below the rank of Chief Commissioner

options.text: Only the last — a Board consists of three members of whom one is a retired judge, and a defect in its constitution invalidates whatever it has done
options.misconception: describes the Dispute Resolution Committee's three-member composition and denies the protection section 245P gives
options.why: Three members, two of them retired officers, is Rule 44DAA and the Dispute Resolution Committee. A Board for Advance Rulings has two members, each an officer not below the rank of Chief Commissioner, and section 245P protects its proceedings against a vacancy or defect.

citation.ref: Sections 245-OB, 245P, 245RR and 245U with Notification No. 96/2021 dated 1 September 2021 — three Boards of two members each not below the rank of Chief Commissioner, a vacancy not invalidating a proceeding, the Civil Court powers, and the bar on an authority or the Tribunal deciding an issue a resident applicant has taken to a Board

items.scenario: A resident applicant is told three things by his adviser and doubts all of them. That the body which will hear him is not a tribunal of judges but a bench of two serving revenue officers. That a vacancy on that bench would not upset its ruling. And that the same bench can compel a bank to produce records and can examine a person on oath. He also asks whether, having applied, he can keep his appeal on the same issue alive before the Tribunal.

items.stem: What fee accompanies each application?

options.text: ₹5,00,000 for both, since the fee follows the value of the transactions and the public sector company's amounts are the larger
options.misconception: applies the transaction slabs to every applicant, when Rule 44E confines them to sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iia) and puts everyone else at ₹10,000
options.why: The slabs are written only for an applicant referred to in sub-clause (i), (ii) or (iia) of clause (b) of section 245N. Any other applicant, however large the sums in issue, pays ₹10,000 in all cases.

options.text: ₹10,00,000 for the non-resident and ₹10,000 for the public sector company, the top slab applying to anything above ₹1,00,00,00,000
options.misconception: collapses the middle slab, treating everything above ₹100 crore as attracting the ₹10 lakh fee
options.why: There are three slabs, not two. The ₹10,00,000 fee applies only where the transactions exceed ₹3,00,00,00,000, and ₹2,50,00,00,000 sits in the middle slab at ₹5,00,000.

options.text: ₹10,000 for both, because section 245Q(2) fixes the fee at ₹10,000 and Rule 44E only prescribes the form of the application
options.misconception: reads section 245Q(2) as fixing a flat fee, when its words are ₹10,000 or such fee as may be prescribed, whichever is higher
options.why: The section itself contemplates a higher prescribed fee. Its words are a fee of ₹10,000 or such fee as may be prescribed, whichever is higher, and Rule 44E prescribes the slabs that are higher for the applicants it names.

options.text: ₹5,00,000 for the non-resident, its transactions exceeding ₹1,00,00,00,000 but not ₹3,00,00,00,000, and ₹10,000 for the public sector company, which pays that in all cases
options.why: Section 245Q(2) says the application shall be made in quadruplicate and be accompanied by a fee of ₹10,000 or such fee as may be prescribed, whichever is higher, and Rule 44E prescribes the higher fees only for an applicant falling in sub-clause (i), (ii) or (iia) of clause (b) of section 245N. For that applicant the fee is ₹2,00,000 where the transactions do not exceed ₹1,00,00,00,000, ₹5,00,000 where they exceed ₹1,00,00,00,000 but do not exceed ₹3,00,00,00,000, and ₹10,00,000 where they exceed ₹3,00,00,00,000. Any other applicant, which includes the notified public sector company, pays ₹10,000 in all cases.

citation.ref: Section 245Q(2) with Rule 44E — the fee of ₹10,000 or the prescribed fee whichever is higher, and the slabs of ₹2 lakh, ₹5 lakh and ₹10 lakh against ₹100 crore and ₹300 crore for an applicant under sub-clause (i), (ii) or (iia) of section 245N(b), with ₹10,000 for any other applicant

items.scenario: Two applications are being prepared on the same day. One is by a non-resident falling in sub-clause (i) of section 245N(b), on transactions in respect of which the ruling is sought totalling ₹2,50,00,00,000. The other is by a public sector company notified for the purpose, on an issue pending before the Appellate Tribunal, where the amounts involved are far larger.

items.stem: Which of them may the Board allow, and how long has it to rule?

options.text: The second, the third and the fourth — a valuation question may be answered because section 245U gives the Board the powers of a Civil Court, and only a genuinely pending question is excluded
options.misconception: reads the Board's procedural powers as enlarging the questions it may answer, when the fair market value ground is a separate bar
options.why: Powers of procedure and jurisdiction over a question are different things. The determination of the fair market value of any property is named as a question the Board shall not allow, whatever powers it holds to gather evidence.

options.text: The third and the fourth — the pending question and the fair market value question are grounds on which the Board shall not allow an application, while the avoidance ground has its own exception for a question whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement; and where an application is allowed the ruling must be pronounced within six months from the receipt of the application
options.why: Section 245R lists three questions the Board shall not allow. One already pending before any income-tax authority, the Appellate Tribunal or any court, though a notified resident may ask even then and this applicant is not one. One involving the determination of the fair market value of any property. And one relating to a transaction or issue designed prima facie for the avoidance of income-tax, except in the case of a notified resident applicant or where a resident or non-resident asks whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement, which is exactly the third application. No application is rejected without an opportunity of being heard and the order must give the reason. Where an application is allowed, the Board pronounces its ruling within six months from the receipt of the application by the Board.

options.text: Only the fourth — an avoidance transaction is barred without exception, and the Board has twelve months from admission to pronounce
options.misconception: drops the exception written into the avoidance ground and doubles the time limit while measuring it from admission
options.why: The avoidance ground carries its own exception for the question whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement, which is one of the five limbs of advance ruling. And the time limit is six months from the receipt of the application, not twelve from its admission.

options.text: All four — the three grounds are matters the Board takes into account in framing its ruling rather than reasons for refusing to hear a case at all
options.misconception: turns mandatory grounds of rejection into considerations, when the section says the Board shall not allow such an application
options.why: The words are that the Board shall not allow an application where the question raised is one of the three. They govern admission, not the content of a ruling.

citation.ref: Section 245R — the three grounds on which the Board shall not allow an application, the exceptions for a notified resident and for the impermissible avoidance question, the opportunity of being heard before rejection, and the six-month limit for pronouncing a ruling

items.scenario: Four applications reach a Board for Advance Rulings. The first raises a question already pending before the Appellate Tribunal in the applicant's own case, and the applicant is not a notified resident. The second asks the Board to fix the fair market value of a plant in Kerala. The third relates to a transaction the Board considers to be designed prima facie for the avoidance of income-tax, and the applicant is a non-resident asking whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement. The fourth raises an ordinary question of law on a proposed transaction.

items.stem: What is the position in the three cases?

options.text: The withdrawal is too late because it must be sought within 30 days of the Board sending the application to the Commissioner; the 60 days for an appeal cannot be extended; and a void ruling simply falls away with no adjustment of time limits
options.misconception: measures the withdrawal window from a later event, denies the extension the proviso gives, and drops the exclusion of the intervening period
options.why: All three figures are in the sections. Thirty days runs from the date of the application, the High Court may add 30 days on sufficient cause, and the period between the ruling and the order declaring it void is excluded so that the department is not shut out by limitation.

options.text: The withdrawal is open to him only with the Board's leave; the further period the High Court may grant is 60 days rather than 30; and where a ruling is void the exclusion runs from the date of the application rather than the date of the ruling
options.misconception: adds a leave requirement to the withdrawal, doubles the extension and starts the exclusion at the application
options.why: Withdrawal within 30 days is the applicant's own right and needs nobody's leave. The further period is 30 days, and the excluded period begins with the date of the advance ruling and ends with the date of the order declaring it void.

options.text: The withdrawal is open to him; the appeal against a ruling lies to the Appellate Tribunal rather than the High Court, so the 60 days does not apply; and a void ruling stands until set aside by a court
options.misconception: sends the appeal to the Tribunal, when section 245W takes a ruling of a Board straight to the High Court
options.why: A ruling pronounced or an order passed by a Board for Advance Rulings is appealable before the High Court under section 245W. And the Board itself declares a ruling void ab initio under section 245T, without anybody having to go to court.

options.text: The withdrawal is open to him because it was sought within 30 days from the date of the application; the High Court may grant a further period of 30 days beyond the 60 days where it is satisfied that sufficient cause prevented the appeal; and where a ruling is declared void the Act applies as if it had never been made, excluding the period from the date of the ruling to the date of that order
options.why: Section 245Q(3) lets an applicant withdraw within 30 days from the date of the application, and 3 April to 1 May is inside that. Section 245W(1) gives an applicant aggrieved by a ruling or order 60 days from its communication to appeal to the High Court, and the proviso lets the High Court grant a further period of 30 days where it is satisfied on an application that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from presenting it in time. Section 245T lets the Board declare a ruling void ab initio where it finds, on a representation by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or otherwise, that it was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts, and the Act then applies to the applicant as if the ruling had never been made, after excluding the period beginning with the date of the advance ruling and ending with the date of the order under that section.
keywords: within 30 days from the date of the application
as if the ruling had never been made

citation.ref: Sections 245Q(3), 245T and 245W(1) with its proviso — withdrawal within 30 days from the date of the application, a ruling declared void ab initio for fraud or misrepresentation with the intervening period excluded, and an appeal to the High Court within 60 days extendable by a further 30 days on sufficient cause

items.scenario: A non-resident applied to a Board for Advance Rulings on 3 April 2025 and changed his mind on 1 May 2025, when he asked to withdraw. A different applicant received a ruling and wants to take it to the High Court, but the sixty days ran out while his counsel was ill. And in a third case the Board has found that the ruling it gave was obtained by misrepresentation of facts and has declared it void ab initio.

items.stem: What is chargeable under the Black Money Act, and when?

options.text: ₹90,00,000 in the previous year 2025-26 at 30 per cent, giving ₹27,00,000 of tax, with no deduction for the ₹4,00,000 of fees and no set-off of the loss
options.why: The proviso to section 3(1) settles the year: an undisclosed asset located outside India is charged to tax on its value in the previous year in which such asset comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer, so the year of acquisition is beside the point and 2025-26 is the year of charge. Section 3(1) fixes the rate at 30 per cent of the undisclosed foreign income and asset, and 30 per cent of ₹90,00,000 is ₹27,00,000. Section 5(1) is written to stop exactly the two claims Mr Anand makes — no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance and no set-off of any loss is allowed in computing the total undisclosed foreign income and asset, whether or not the Income-tax Act, 1961 would have allowed it.
keywords: comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer

options.text: Nothing — the asset was acquired in the previous year 2011-12, so any charge belongs to that year and no assessment for it can now be made
options.misconception: charges an undisclosed foreign asset in the year of acquisition, when the proviso moves it to the year it comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer
options.why: The proviso to section 3(1) is what makes this Act work on old assets at all. The value is charged in the previous year in which the asset comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer, however long ago it was acquired.

options.text: ₹90,00,000 in the previous year 2025-26, but taxed at the slab rates applicable to Mr Anand under the Income-tax Act, 1961 because the Black Money Act contains no rate of its own
options.misconception: reads the Black Money Act as borrowing the Income-tax Act's rates, when section 3(1) carries its own flat rate
options.why: Section 3(1) carries its own rate in its own words — every assessee is liable to tax at 30 per cent in respect of his undisclosed foreign income and asset of the previous year. And section 4 keeps that income out of total income under the Income-tax Act altogether.

options.text: ₹86,00,000 in the previous year 2025-26 at 30 per cent, giving ₹25,80,000, the custody and management fees being an allowable expense against the value of the holding
options.misconception: allows expenditure against the value of an undisclosed foreign asset, which section 5(1) refuses whether or not the Income-tax Act would have allowed it
options.why: Section 5(1) says no deduction in respect of any expenditure or allowance shall be allowed in computing the total undisclosed foreign income and asset, and adds that this holds irrespective of whether it is allowable under the Income-tax Act, 1961.

citation.source: Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015
citation.ref: Section 3(1) with its proviso, section 4(c) and section 5(1) — tax at 30 per cent, an undisclosed foreign asset charged in the previous year in which it comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer, and no deduction for expenditure or allowance and no set-off of loss

items.scenario: Mr Anand has been resident and ordinarily resident throughout. He acquired shares in a foreign company in the previous year 2011-12 out of sources he cannot explain, and the Assessing Officer comes to know of them during the previous year 2025-26, when their fair market value determined under Rule 3 is ₹90,00,000. Mr Anand says the charge, if any, arose in 2011-12 and is long dead; that in any event he should be allowed the ₹4,00,000 of custody and management fees he has paid on the holding over the years; and that he has a foreign capital loss to set against it.

items.stem: What amount is chargeable to tax under the Black Money Act?

options.text: ₹60,00,000 — the cost of ₹80,00,000 less the ₹20,00,000 already assessed, the charge being on what the asset cost rather than on what it is now worth
options.misconception: charges the historical cost of an undisclosed foreign asset instead of its value in the year it comes to notice
options.why: The charge is on value, not on cost. The proviso to section 3(1) charges an undisclosed foreign asset on its value in the previous year in which it comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer, and the cost enters only as the denominator of the proportion in section 5(2).

options.text: ₹2,00,00,000 — no deduction is available, because section 5(1) refuses every deduction in computing the total undisclosed foreign income and asset
options.misconception: reads the bar on expenditure and set-off in section 5(1) as removing the deduction section 5(2) gives for income already taxed
options.why: The two sub-sections do different jobs. Section 5(1) refuses expenditure, allowances and losses; section 5(2) allows a reduction for income already assessed or assessable to tax, on evidence that the asset was acquired out of it.

options.text: ₹1,80,00,000 — the ₹20,00,000 that has already suffered tax is deducted from the ₹2,00,00,000, since a person cannot be taxed twice on the same money
options.misconception: deducts the assessed amount at its historical figure instead of scaling it to the asset's present value
options.why: Section 5(2) does not deduct the historical figure. For immovable property it scales the assessed income up in the same proportion that it bore to the total cost, which is what gives ₹50,00,000 rather than ₹20,00,000 on these numbers.

options.text: ₹1,50,00,000 — the deduction for immovable property is proportionate, so it is ₹2,00,00,000 multiplied by ₹20,00,000 over ₹80,00,000, which is ₹50,00,000, and that comes off the ₹2,00,00,000
options.why: Section 5(2) fixes the size of the deduction where the income already assessed relates to immovable property. The deduction bears to the value of the asset as on the first day of the financial year in which it comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer the same proportion as the assessable or assessed foreign income bears to the total cost of the asset. Here the value on 1 April 2025 is ₹2,00,00,000, the assessed income is ₹20,00,000 and the total cost is ₹80,00,000, so the deduction is ₹2,00,00,000 multiplied by 20 over 80, which is ₹50,00,000, and the amount chargeable is ₹1,50,00,000.

citation.source: Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015
citation.ref: Section 5(2) with the proviso to section 3(1) — the deduction for income already assessed where the asset is immovable property, computed in the same proportion to the value on the first day of the financial year in which it comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer as the assessed income bears to the total cost of the asset

items.scenario: A house property outside India was acquired by Mrs Bhatia in the previous year 2013-14 for a total cost of ₹80,00,000. Of that investment, ₹20,00,000 had already been assessed to tax in her total income for that year and earlier years under the Income-tax Act, 1961, and she can furnish evidence of it to the Assessing Officer's satisfaction. The asset comes to the notice of the Assessing Officer during the previous year 2025-26, and its value on 1 April 2025 is ₹2,00,00,000.

items.stem: What penalty does section 43 come to?

options.text: ₹20,00,000 — ₹10,00,000 for each of the two failures, the accounts being one and the flat another
options.misconception: multiplies the penalty by the number of assets, when section 43 fixes one sum for the failure
options.why: Section 43 directs the assessee to pay, by way of penalty, a sum of ₹10,00,000. It is a single figure for the failure and not a rate per asset.

options.text: Nil — the aggregate value of everything he failed to report is what the ₹20,00,000 proviso measures, and on that footing the accounts are below it while the flat is a single asset he has always owned openly
options.misconception: aggregates only the assets that suit the relief and reads immovable property as capable of falling inside it
options.why: Immovable property is put outside the relief by the words of the proviso, which speaks of an asset or assets other than immovable property. No aggregation brings a flat inside it.

options.text: ₹10,00,000 — the proviso relieves an asset or assets other than immovable property whose aggregate value does not exceed ₹20,00,000, so the two accounts at ₹18,00,000 would have been covered on their own, but the flat is immovable property and is outside the relief altogether
options.why: Section 43 charges a penalty of ₹10,00,000 on a resident other than a not ordinarily resident who fails to furnish, in his return of income, information about an asset located outside India held by him as beneficial owner or otherwise, or in respect of which he was a beneficiary, or about income from a source outside India. The proviso to sections 42 and 43 says the penalty shall not apply in respect of an asset or assets, other than immovable property, where the aggregate value of such asset or assets does not exceed ₹20,00,000. The two bank accounts total ₹18,00,000 and would have been inside it; the flat is immovable property, which the proviso excepts from the relief in its own words, so the penalty stands at ₹10,00,000.

options.text: Three times the tax computed on the value of the flat, section 41 being the penalty that applies wherever an undisclosed foreign asset is found
options.misconception: reaches for the section 41 penalty on computed tax where the default is a reporting failure under section 43
options.why: Section 41 applies where tax has been computed in respect of undisclosed foreign income and asset, and it is three times that tax. Section 43 is the separate penalty for failing to furnish information about a foreign asset in the return, and it is ₹10,00,000.

citation.source: Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015
citation.ref: Sections 41 and 43 with the proviso to sections 42 and 43 — a penalty of ₹10 lakh for failing to furnish information about a foreign asset, not applying to assets other than immovable property whose aggregate value does not exceed ₹20 lakh, against the section 41 penalty of three times the tax computed

items.scenario: Mr Chetan has been resident and ordinarily resident throughout. He filed his return under section 139(1) on time but gave no information in it about two foreign bank accounts holding ₹18,00,000 between them, or about a flat abroad worth ₹60,00,000 of which he is the beneficial owner. His adviser says the ₹20,00,000 relief in the Black Money Act covers him because the accounts are under it.

items.stem: What follows on the two matters?

options.text: No prosecution lies against Mrs Devi, because section 49 is not attracted where the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year; and the ₹4,00,000 penalty needs no approval of the Joint Commissioner, since approval is required where an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner levies a penalty exceeding ₹5,00,000, while a wilful attempt to evade tax under section 51 carries rigorous imprisonment of not less than three years extending to ten years and a fine
options.why: Section 49 punishes a wilful failure to furnish the return required under section 139(1) in due time by a resident other than a not ordinarily resident who holds a foreign asset or has foreign income, with rigorous imprisonment of not less than six months extending to seven years and a fine, and then carves out the escape Mrs Devi has taken — prosecution would not be attracted if he furnishes such return before the expiry of the assessment year. On the penalty, section 46(4) requires the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner or Joint Director where the penalty exceeds ₹1,00,000 and the authority levying it is an Income-tax Officer, or exceeds ₹5,00,000 and the authority is an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner or an Assistant or Deputy Director, so ₹4,00,000 levied by an Assistant Commissioner is below the line. Section 51 punishes a wilful attempt to evade tax, penalty or interest with rigorous imprisonment of not less than three years extending to ten years and a fine.
keywords: before the expiry of the assessment year
three years extending to ten years

options.text: Mrs Devi can still be prosecuted because the return was late whatever she did afterwards; the ₹4,00,000 penalty needs approval because the limit for every authority is ₹1,00,000; and section 51 carries six months to seven years like the other offences
options.misconception: denies the escape section 49 gives, applies the ₹1 lakh approval limit to every rank, and levels the sentence for evasion down to the reporting offences
options.why: All three figures are in the sections. Section 49 excludes prosecution where the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year, section 46(4) has two limits by rank, and section 51 is the heaviest of the offences at three to ten years.

options.text: No prosecution lies against Mrs Devi; the penalty needs approval because any penalty over ₹1,00,000 does; and a wilful attempt to evade payment of tax carries the same three to ten years as an attempt to evade tax
options.misconception: uses the ₹1 lakh limit for an Assistant Commissioner and gives evasion of payment the same sentence as evasion of tax
options.why: The ₹1,00,000 limit belongs to a penalty levied by an Income-tax Officer, and for an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner the figure is ₹5,00,000. And section 51 splits the two — three to ten years for a wilful attempt to evade tax, penalty or interest, and three months to three years for a wilful attempt to evade payment of it.

options.text: No prosecution lies against Mrs Devi and no approval is needed for the penalty, but a prosecution under section 51 may be launched by the Assessing Officer without anybody's sanction once the penalty order is made
options.misconception: drops the sanction section 55 requires before a prosecution under sections 49 to 53 is begun
options.why: Section 55 says a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence under sections 49 to 53 except with the sanction of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner or the Commissioner (Appeals). The first two halves of the option are right and this one is not.

citation.source: Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015
citation.ref: Sections 46(4), 49, 51 and 55 — prior approval of the Joint Commissioner or Joint Director where a penalty exceeds ₹1 lakh levied by an Income-tax Officer or ₹5 lakh levied by an Assistant or Deputy Commissioner, no prosecution under section 49 where the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year, rigorous imprisonment of three to ten years under section 51, and the sanction required by section 55

items.scenario: Mrs Devi, resident and ordinarily resident, holds a foreign account and did not file her return by the due date under section 139(1). She files it before the end of the relevant assessment year and discloses everything. In a separate matter Mr Eshwar is charged with a wilful attempt to evade tax under the Act, and a penalty of ₹4,00,000 is proposed against him by an Assistant Commissioner.

items.stem: What are the answers under section 245MA and the rules made under it?

options.text: A committee of three members, being two retired officers of the Indian Revenue Service who have held the post of Commissioner of Income-tax or an equivalent or higher post for five years or more and one serving officer not below the rank of Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, deciding by majority; a fee of ₹1,000; one month from the receipt of the specified order; and proof of withdrawal of the appeal within 30 days of the communication that the application is admitted
options.why: Rule 44DAA requires the Central Government to constitute a Dispute Resolution Committee for every region of a Principal Chief Commissioner, consisting of three members — two retired officers from the Indian Revenue Service (Income-tax) who have held the post of Commissioner of Income-tax or any equivalent or higher post for five years or more, and one serving officer not below the rank of Principal Commissioner or Commissioner as specified by the Board — appointed for a period of three years and deciding by majority. Rule 44DAB requires the application in the prescribed form accompanied by a fee of ₹1,000. The time to file is one month from the receipt of the specified order where no appeal is pending, and where an appeal is already pending before the Commissioner (Appeals) it is such time from the constitution of the committee as the Board specifies. And within 30 days of receiving the communication that the application is admitted the assessee must submit proof of withdrawal of the appeal filed under section 246A or of the application before the Dispute Resolution Panel, or say that no such proceeding is pending, failing which the committee may reject the application.

options.text: A committee of three serving officers of the rank of Commissioner or above; no fee, the route being meant for a small taxpayer; one month from the receipt of the specified order; and the appeal may be kept alive because the committee's order is not a decision on the merits
options.misconception: makes the committee wholly serving and fee-free and lets the assessee run the appeal alongside the application
options.why: Two of the three members are retired officers, which is what gives the committee its independence, the application carries a fee of ₹1,000 under Rule 44DAB, and the appeal must be withdrawn with proof furnished within 30 days of the admission.

options.text: A single Commissioner sitting as the committee; a fee of ₹10,000; six months from the receipt of the specified order; and the appeal lapses automatically on admission
options.misconception: turns the committee into one officer, borrows the advance ruling fee, stretches the filing period and assumes the appeal lapses without the assessee doing anything
options.why: Every figure is wrong. Three members under Rule 44DAA, ₹1,000 under Rule 44DAB, one month from the receipt of the specified order, and a positive duty on the assessee to furnish proof of withdrawal within 30 days of the admission.

options.text: A committee of three members with two of them retired; a fee of ₹1,000; but the application may be filed at any time before the appeal period under section 246A expires, and no withdrawal is needed because the two proceedings run in parallel
options.misconception: replaces the one-month filing period with the appeal period and lets both proceedings run at once
options.why: The composition and the fee are right and the last two are not. The time is one month from the receipt of the specified order, and the committee may reject the application where the assessee does not produce proof of withdrawal of a section 246A appeal or a Dispute Resolution Panel application within 30 days of the communication admitting it.

citation.ref: Rules 44DAA and 44DAB read with section 245MA(1) — a three-member committee of two retired Indian Revenue Service officers who have held the post of Commissioner or higher for five years or more and one serving officer not below the rank of Principal Commissioner, deciding by majority, a fee of ₹1,000, an application within one month of the specified order, and proof of withdrawal of a section 246A appeal within 30 days of admission

items.scenario: An assessee has received a specified order and wants to take it to a Dispute Resolution Committee rather than appeal. He asks four things. Who will actually hear him. What the application costs. How long he has to file it, no appeal having been filed anywhere. And what he must do if the committee admits the application while an appeal of his under section 246A is pending on the same order.

items.stem: Is he entitled to the section 54 exemption?

options.text: No, but he can claim it under section 54F instead
options.misconception: swaps in the section that runs in the opposite direction
options.why: Section 54F exempts gains on assets other than a residential house when the proceeds buy a residential house. Here the sale was residential and the purchase was not — the wrong way round for both sections.

options.text: Yes, because the amount invested exceeds the capital gain
options.misconception: reads the quantum condition and skips the nature-of-asset condition
options.why: The amount decides how much of the gain is exempt once the conditions are met. It cannot substitute for the condition that the new asset be a residential house.

options.text: Yes, if the shop is let out for residential use by the tenant
options.misconception: lets the tenant's use recharacterise the property
options.why: The character of the asset purchased is what it is — commercial premises. What a tenant does inside it does not turn a shop into a residential house for section 54.

options.text: No — the reinvestment must be in a residential house in India
options.why: Section 54 is an exemption for keeping capital in residential housing. Both ends of the transaction must be residential: the asset sold and the asset bought. A shop fails the second condition however large the investment.

citation.ref: Section 54

items.scenario: An individual sells a residential house in June 2025, earning a long-term capital gain of ₹65 lakh. Within a year he invests ₹70 lakh in a commercial shop, arguing the whole gain is exempt because the reinvestment exceeds the gain.

items.stem: Is a tax audit under section 44AB required?

options.text: Yes, because turnover exceeds ₹1 crore
options.misconception: applies the base limit without testing for the digital-transactions proviso
options.why: ₹1 crore is the starting rule, and the proviso is the examinable part: heavy banking- channel usage lifts the limit tenfold precisely to spare businesses like this one.

options.text: Yes, because the limit for firms is ₹50 lakh
options.misconception: applies the professional gross-receipts limit to a business
options.why: ₹50 lakh is the threshold for a profession's gross receipts. A trading firm is a business and takes the business limits.

options.text: No, because audit under section 44AB applies only to companies
options.misconception: confuses tax audit with statutory audit under the Companies Act
options.why: Section 44AB turns on turnover, not on the form of the entity. Individuals, firms and companies are all within it; companies separately face statutory audit regardless.

options.text: No — the enhanced ₹10 crore limit applies because cash stays within 5 per cent
options.why: Where both cash receipts and cash payments are within 5 per cent of their totals, the audit threshold is ₹10 crore, not ₹1 crore. At ₹8 crore of largely digital turnover, no audit is required.

citation.ref: Section 44AB

items.scenario: A trading firm has turnover of ₹8 crore for the year. Its cash receipts are 3 per cent of total receipts and cash payments are 2 per cent of total payments; everything else moves through banking channels.

items.stem: What is the MAT position of this company?

options.text: MAT applies at the standard rate on book profit, payable if higher
options.misconception: runs the MAT comparison out of habit for every company
options.why: The compare-and-pay-higher routine belongs to companies under the normal regime. For a 115BAA company there is nothing to compare — the computation itself is switched off.

options.text: MAT does not apply to it at all
options.why: Opting into 115BAA takes the company outside MAT entirely — section 115JB(5A) says the book profit provisions do not apply. The bargain is a lower flat rate in exchange for the incentives, and MAT has no role because there are no incentives left to claw back.

options.text: MAT applies, but unused MAT credit can be set off against it
options.misconception: keeps MAT credit alive inside a regime that has no MAT
options.why: Old MAT credit lapses on opting in — one of the real costs of the choice. There is no future MAT liability for the credit to meet.

options.text: MAT applies only if book profit exceeds taxable income by 20 per cent
options.misconception: invents a threshold test for when MAT switches on
options.why: No such trigger exists anywhere in the Act. Under the normal regime MAT is always computed; under 115BAA it never is.

citation.ref: Section 115BAA read with Section 115JB(5A)

items.scenario: A domestic company opted for section 115BAA two years ago. This year its book profit is high while its taxable income is modest, and the tax team begins computing MAT on book profit as a comparison.

items.stem: What is the due date?

options.text: 30 November 2026
options.misconception: extends the transfer pricing date to every company
options.why: 30 November applies only where a report under section 92E is required — international or specified domestic transactions. This company has none.

options.text: 30 September 2026
options.misconception: recalls the pre-amendment audit due date
options.why: 30 September was the audit-case date years ago and survives in old material. The current date is 31 October.

options.text: 31 July 2026
options.misconception: applies the no-audit individual due date to a company
options.why: 31 July belongs to taxpayers with no audit requirement. A company never files by this date.

options.text: 31 October 2026
options.why: A company is an audit case by definition for this purpose, and the due date for audit cases is 31 October of the assessment year.

citation.ref: Section 139(1)

items.scenario: A private limited company with no international or specified domestic transactions asks for the last date to file its income-tax return for assessment year 2026-27.

items.stem: Which statement describes the section 112A treatment?

options.text: Taxed with indexation benefit at the general long-term rate
options.misconception: applies the section 112 computation that 112A displaces
options.why: Indexation is the general regime's feature. Section 112A trades it away for the lower rate and the annual exempt slab.

options.text: Taxed above an annual exemption threshold at the special rate, without indexation
options.why: Section 112A carves listed STT-paid equity out of the general LTCG regime: a slab of gain each year is exempt, the excess is taxed at the concessional rate, and no indexation is available against it.

options.text: Taxed at normal slab rates like any other income
options.misconception: ignores the special regime entirely
options.why: Listed equity LTCG never meets slab rates while 112A stands; the section exists to give it its own rate and threshold.

options.text: Fully exempt, because STT was paid at both purchase and sale
options.misconception: remembers the pre-2018 section 10(38) exemption as still alive
options.why: The blanket exemption ended when 112A arrived. STT payment is now the condition for the concessional regime, not for exemption.

citation.ref: Section 112A

items.scenario: An investor sells listed equity shares after two years, through the exchange with STT paid, realising a long-term gain. She asks how the gain is taxed.

items.stem: Who can use section 44AD here?

options.text: The LLP can, because presumptive schemes exist for entities without detailed books
options.misconception: reasons from the scheme's purpose instead of its words
options.why: Whatever the purpose suggests, the definition decides — and it names the LLP only to shut it out.

options.text: The firm can; the LLP cannot
options.why: Section 44AD is open to a resident individual, HUF or firm — and the definition expressly excludes a limited liability partnership. The firm declares 6 per cent on its banked turnover; the LLP keeps books and computes profit normally.

options.text: Neither, because turnover above ₹1 crore requires audited books
options.misconception: applies the 44AB audit limit to a presumptive filer
options.why: Declaring under 44AD is precisely what makes the audit requirement fall away within the scheme's turnover limit. The two sections are alternatives, not a ladder.

options.text: Both, since their turnover and business are identical
options.misconception: tests eligibility by size and trade rather than by the person
options.why: The scheme's gate is the kind of person, not the kind of business. Identical turnover does not bring an excluded entity inside.

citation.ref: Section 44AD

items.scenario: A resident partnership firm runs a retail business with turnover of ₹1.8 crore, received almost entirely through UPI and bank transfer. An LLP in the same market, with the same turnover, asks to declare profit the same presumptive way.

items.stem: What survives to be carried forward?

options.text: Only the ₹80 lakh unabsorbed depreciation
options.why: Section 80 forfeits the carry forward of a business loss claimed in a late return, so ₹2.2 crore is gone. Unabsorbed depreciation is carried under section 32(2), which stands outside that condition — it survives the late filing, and with no eight-year limit either.

options.text: The whole ₹3 crore, since the return was filed with a valid explanation
options.misconception: believes an explained delay preserves the loss
options.why: Section 80 has no explanation clause. The due date is the condition, and missing it is the consequence, however good the reason.

options.text: The whole ₹3 crore, but for four years instead of eight
options.misconception: invents a penalty of a shortened period rather than a forfeiture
options.why: Section 80 does not shorten the window; it shuts the door. The loss either carries for its full period or, filed late, does not carry at all.

options.text: Nothing at all, because the return was late
options.misconception: extends the section 80 forfeiture to depreciation it does not touch
options.why: The forfeiture reaches what is carried under sections 72 and its siblings. Depreciation travels under section 32(2), a different vehicle the late return does not stop.

citation.ref: Section 72 read with Section 80

items.scenario: A company incurs a business loss of ₹3 crore, of which ₹80 lakh is unabsorbed depreciation. It files the loss year's return four months after the due date.

items.stem: How much is taxable under section 56(2)(x)?

options.text: ₹25,000 — the amount by which the friends' gifts exceed fifty thousand
options.misconception: taxes the excess over the threshold instead of the whole
options.why: Fifty thousand is a trigger, not an exemption slab. One rupee past it and the entire aggregate is income — the cliff is the examinable feature.

options.text: ₹3,75,000 — all gifts, since the aggregate crossed the threshold
options.misconception: pulls relatives' gifts into the aggregate once the threshold breaks
options.why: Relatives' gifts are excluded from the section altogether, not merely from the trigger. The uncle's money neither counts toward the fifty thousand nor becomes taxable when the line is crossed.

options.text: Nothing, because each individual gift is below fifty thousand
options.misconception: applies the threshold gift by gift instead of in aggregate
options.why: The section aggregates all such receipts in the year. Splitting a sum across givers or occasions does not defeat it — ₹40,000 plus ₹35,000 is ₹75,000 against one limit.

options.text: ₹75,000 — the friends' gifts in full; the uncle's gift is exempt as from a relative
options.why: The friends' gifts aggregate to ₹75,000, past the fifty-thousand line, and the section then taxes the whole aggregate, not the excess. The mother's brother is within the definition of relative, so his ₹3 lakh never enters the computation.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x)

items.scenario: During the year an individual receives ₹40,000 from one friend and ₹35,000 from another, both as birthday gifts, and ₹3 lakh from his mother's brother for no particular occasion.

items.stem: What does section 44ADA actually permit?

options.text: She must declare the actual ₹42 lakh, since presumptive income cannot be below truth
options.misconception: reads the presumption as a minimum-of-actual rule
options.why: The presumption replaces the actual computation; that is its point. The words "or a higher amount claimed" give her the option of more, never the obligation.

options.text: She may declare ₹30 lakh only if she also maintains full books as a safeguard
options.misconception: attaches the books requirement to the scheme instead of to leaving it
options.why: Books and audit are the price of declaring BELOW the presumptive rate, not of using it. Inside the scheme, freedom from books is the principal benefit.

options.text: Declaring 50 per cent of receipts — ₹30 lakh — is permitted as her deemed income, even if the true profit is higher
options.why: The section deems 50 per cent or such higher sum as the assessee claims; declaring the floor is the scheme working as designed. The bargain runs the other way too — with true profit above the deemed figure, the law still accepts the 50 per cent declaration.

options.text: Nothing — architecture is not a specified profession for this section
options.misconception: shrinks the section 44AA list that 44ADA borrows
options.why: The section covers the legal, medical, engineering, architectural, accountancy, technical consultancy and interior decoration professions. Architecture is named in it.

citation.ref: Section 44ADA

items.scenario: A practising architect has gross receipts of ₹60 lakh, received almost entirely by bank transfer. Her actual expenses are low and true profit is around ₹42 lakh. She asks whether she can declare ₹30 lakh under section 44ADA and keep the difference untaxed.

items.stem: What did section 194-IA require?

options.text: Deduction of ₹18,000 — 1 per cent of the amount above ₹50 lakh
options.misconception: taxes the excess over the threshold instead of the whole
options.why: Fifty lakh is a trigger, not a slab. Once crossed, the deduction runs on the full consideration from the first rupee.

options.text: Nothing, because the buyer is an individual not liable to tax audit
options.misconception: imports the audit-linked exemption from other TDS sections into this one
options.why: Sections like 194C spare small individual payers; 194-IA deliberately does not. Property purchases were pulled in precisely because ordinary buyers are the payers.

options.text: Nothing, because TDS on property applies only when the seller is a non-resident
options.misconception: swaps in section 195 and discards the resident-seller section
options.why: A non-resident seller invokes section 195 at different rates. Resident sellers are the very case 194-IA exists for.

options.text: Deduction of ₹68,000 — 1 per cent of the whole consideration — with no TAN needed
options.why: The section binds any buyer, business or not, once consideration or stamp duty value reaches ₹50 lakh, and it charges 1 per cent on the entire amount. It was built for exactly this buyer: the form works on PAN alone, no TAN required.

citation.ref: Section 194-IA

items.scenario: An individual buys a flat for ₹68 lakh from a resident seller. At registration the buyer pays the full amount without deducting anything, saying he has no TAN and is not in business, so TDS provisions cannot apply to him.

items.stem: Is he resident for the year?

options.text: Yes — 123 days this year and 365 in the preceding four satisfies the second condition
options.misconception: applies the ordinary 60-plus-365 limb to a departing employee
options.why: That limb is exactly what the explanation switches off for this taxpayer. Applying it taxes a departing worker's global income for the very year he left — the outcome the carve-out exists to prevent.

options.text: No, because employment abroad automatically makes anyone non-resident from the date of departure
options.misconception: turns a day-count adjustment into an automatic exemption
options.why: The carve-out changes the threshold, not the method. Leave in February after 200 days and the same employee is resident, employment abroad notwithstanding.

options.text: No — for a citizen leaving for employment, only the 182-day test applies, and 123 fails it
options.why: The explanation to section 6(1) replaces the 60-day limb with 182 for a citizen leaving India for employment abroad. His four-year history becomes irrelevant; 123 days against a 182-day test makes him non-resident.

options.text: Yes, because an Indian citizen is always resident unless he stays out a full year
options.misconception: attaches residence to citizenship rather than days
options.why: Residence under the Act is arithmetic on days, not passport. Citizenship enters only to select which day-count applies.

citation.ref: Section 6(1)

items.scenario: An Indian citizen left India on 1 August 2025 to take up employment in Dubai, after being in India for 123 days of the year. Over the four preceding years he was in India throughout. His accountant applies the 60-plus-365 test and calls him resident.

items.stem: How is the minor's income taxed?

options.text: Both incomes club with the father, as the natural guardian
options.misconception: picks the parent by guardianship instead of income
options.why: The section names the parent whose total income is greater. Guardianship has no role in the choice.

options.text: Both incomes club with the mother, as she earns more
options.misconception: clubs talent income along with passive income
options.why: The skill-and-talent exclusion exists because that income is genuinely the child's earning, not a parental arrangement wearing the child's name. The chess money is assessed in the minor's own hands.

options.text: Neither clubs, since the source money came from grandparents, not parents
options.misconception: tests clubbing by who gave the capital
options.why: Section 64(1A) clubs a minor's income regardless of where the underlying funds came from. The giver matters under other provisions; here only the child's age does.

options.text: Interest of ₹2,38,500 clubs with the mother; the chess winnings stay the minor's own
options.why: Passive income clubs with the higher-earning parent — the mother — after the ₹1,500 exemption. Chess prize money is income from the minor's skill and talent, which section 64(1A) leaves out of clubbing altogether.

citation.ref: Section 64(1A) read with Section 10(32)

items.scenario: A fourteen-year-old earns ₹2.4 lakh in bank interest on money gifted by grandparents, and ₹3 lakh in prize money from national-level chess tournaments. The father's income is ₹30 lakh and the mother's ₹42 lakh.

items.stem: How much of the loss reduces his other income this year?

options.text: The full ₹5.6 lakh, since let-out property interest has no ceiling
options.misconception: confuses the uncapped interest deduction with uncapped set-off
options.why: Both statements are true separately and the trap is joining them. Interest is fully deductible in computing the property loss; the loss then hits the two-lakh gate on its way to the salary.

options.text: ₹2 lakh now; ₹3.6 lakh carries forward against house property income for eight years
options.why: Section 71(3A) caps the inter-head set-off at two lakh however large the computed loss. The remainder is not lost — it carries forward — but it waits for house property income, which for many taxpayers means it waits a long time.

options.text: Nothing, because losses from let-out property cannot touch salary at all
options.misconception: overreads the cap into a prohibition
options.why: The set-off exists — section 71 permits it — and the 2017 amendment only capped it. Two lakh of this loss reduces the salary income this year.

options.text: ₹2 lakh now, with the balance carrying forward against any head of income
options.misconception: carries the loss forward with wider set-off rights than it left with
options.why: Carried-forward house property loss narrows, not widens — in later years it meets only house property income. The inter-head window exists in year one alone, capped.

citation.ref: Section 71(3A)

items.scenario: An individual's let-out property produces a loss of ₹5.6 lakh this year, driven by home loan interest. His salary income is ₹28 lakh, and he expects the whole loss to reduce his salary tax this year.

items.stem: In which year is the ₹22 lakh deductible?

options.text: Next year — the due-date escape does not apply to MSME dues, so payment year governs
options.why: Clause (h) was built without the proviso that rescues other 43B items. The February bill on 30-day terms was payable beyond the MSMED window at the year end, so the deduction waits for the year of actual payment, the return's due date notwithstanding.

options.text: This year, since payment preceded the due date of filing the return
options.misconception: applies the general 43B proviso to the one clause carved out of it
options.why: The proviso's absence for clause (h) is the whole design — Parliament wanted MSMEs paid in days, not by October. The familiar rule is the trap laid for the well-prepared.

options.text: This year, because the liability was incurred when the goods were supplied
options.misconception: answers from the mercantile system that 43B overrides
options.why: Accrual is exactly what section 43B suspends for its listed sums. Incurring the liability starts the story; only payment finishes it.

options.text: Never, as delayed MSME payments are disallowed permanently as a penalty
options.misconception: converts a timing provision into a permanent disallowance
options.why: Section 43B defers, it does not confiscate. The deduction arrives with the payment year — the cost of delay is timing and the MSMED interest, not the deduction itself.

citation.ref: Section 43B(h)

items.scenario: At 31 March a trader owes ₹22 lakh to a registered micro enterprise for goods supplied in February on 30-day terms. He pays on 25 July, well before filing his return on 31 October, and claims the deduction this year, citing the familiar rule that payment before the return's due date preserves it.

items.stem: What consideration does section 50C adopt for each sale?

options.text: ₹100 lakh and ₹96 lakh — the stamp value always prevails when higher
options.misconception: applies the deeming without the tolerance band
options.why: The 110 per cent tolerance exists exactly for genuine small gaps like the first sale. Deeming there taxes a difference Parliament chose to ignore.

options.text: ₹92 lakh and ₹88 lakh — the second sale is deemed at exactly 110 per cent
options.misconception: caps the deeming at the tolerance line instead of the stamp value
options.why: The tolerance is a gate, not a ceiling. Once crossed, the full stamp value of ₹96 lakh becomes the consideration; ₹88 lakh is only where the gate stood.

options.text: ₹92 lakh for the first sale; ₹96 lakh for the second
options.why: The first sale's stamp value of ₹100 lakh sits within 110 per cent of ₹92 lakh (₹101.2 lakh), so the tolerance protects the actual price. The second sale's ₹96 lakh exceeds 110 per cent of ₹80 lakh (₹88 lakh), so the deeming replaces the consideration in full — not merely the excess.

options.text: ₹92 lakh and ₹80 lakh — actual consideration governs capital gains
options.misconception: ignores the deeming provision entirely
options.why: Section 50C exists because understated property prices are the oldest trick in the book. Outside the tolerance, the stamp value is the consideration whether or not more money moved.

citation.ref: Section 50C

items.scenario: An individual sells a plot for ₹92 lakh. The stamp duty authority values it at ₹100 lakh for registration. In a second sale the same year, another plot fetches ₹80 lakh against a stamp value of ₹96 lakh.

items.stem: What is the consequence in the firm's computation?

options.text: The full ₹20 lakh is disallowed until the default is made good
options.misconception: applies the old full-disallowance rule or the non-resident clause
options.why: Hundred per cent disallowance is the pre-2014 history of this clause and remains the rule for payments abroad under 40(a)(i). For residents, Parliament softened it to thirty.

options.text: ₹6 lakh is disallowed permanently as the price of the default
options.misconception: reads a timing disallowance as a forfeiture
options.why: The clause's second limb restores the amount in the payment year. The cost of default is deferral and interest under the TDS chapter, not permanent loss.

options.text: ₹6 lakh is disallowed this year, and returns as a deduction in the year the TDS is paid
options.why: Section 40(a)(ia) disallows thirty per cent of the sum on which tax went undeducted, and the disallowance is temporary — the year the tax is finally deposited, the thirty per cent comes back. Genuineness of the expense never enters this section's arithmetic.

options.text: Nothing is disallowed, since the expense is genuine and evidenced
options.misconception: treats genuineness as answering a withholding default
options.why: The section polices deduction of tax, not the truth of the expense. The most genuine payment in the books still loses thirty per cent for the default.

citation.ref: Section 40(a)(ia)

items.scenario: A firm pays ₹20 lakh as contract charges to a resident contractor during the year and deducts no tax at source. The books are otherwise clean and the expense is genuine and fully evidenced.

items.stem: How much 54EC exemption does she actually get?

options.text: ₹65 lakh — the whole land gain, since she invested more than that
options.misconception: accepts the asset gate but misses the monetary cap
options.why: Right asset, right window, but the section counts only fifty lakh of the investment. The remaining ₹15 lakh of gain is taxed at the long-term rate.

options.text: ₹1.35 crore — the full amount invested within six months
options.misconception: reads the six-month window as the only condition
options.why: Timing is necessary, not sufficient. The asset-class gate and the fifty-lakh cap operate on top of it, and here they cut the claim by more than half.

options.text: ₹1 crore — fifty lakh against each of the two gains
options.misconception: applies the cap per asset instead of per financial year
options.why: The fifty-lakh ceiling is on investment in the financial year, not per transfer — and the share gain was never eligible, whatever the cap.

options.text: ₹50 lakh, against the land gain only
options.why: Two gates close most of the claim: 54EC covers only gains from land or building, so the share gain is out entirely, and the investment that counts is capped at fifty lakh in a financial year. Of the ₹65 lakh land gain, ₹50 lakh is exempt and the rest is taxed.

citation.ref: Section 54EC

items.scenario: An individual sells listed shares in June, realising a long-term gain of ₹70 lakh, and a plot of land in July, realising a long-term gain of ₹65 lakh. In September she invests ₹1.35 crore in NHAI-class 54EC bonds and claims exemption for both gains in full.

items.stem: What does opting into 115BAA actually cost the company?

options.text: All three go — the incentives are surrendered, and with MAT inapplicable the MAT credit lapses
options.why: The concessional rate is bought by giving up the specified incentives, unabsorbed additional depreciation and profit-linked deductions among them. MAT not applying sounds like relief but also means the accumulated credit has nothing to set against — which is why companies with large credits often wait before opting.

options.text: Only a timing cost — the option can be dropped in a lean year and retaken later
options.misconception: treats an irrevocable option as an annual election
options.why: Once exercised, the option applies to that year and all subsequent years. Walking out in a lean year is exactly the flexibility the section withholds.

options.text: The deductions go, but the MAT credit survives to offset the new liability
options.misconception: keeps a credit born of a levy the company has left
options.why: MAT credit exists to smooth MAT paid against regular tax. Under 115BAA there is no MAT at all, and the credit cannot cross into a regime that never charges it.

options.text: Nothing — the lower rate and the incentives run together
options.misconception: prices the option at zero
options.why: Parliament's bargain is rate for incentives. A company keeping both would make the regular regime pointless for everyone.

citation.ref: Section 115BAA

items.scenario: A manufacturing company weighing the 115BAA option has ₹12 crore of unabsorbed additional depreciation, sizeable MAT credit carried forward, and a claim under a profit-linked deduction. The CFO believes the company can opt in, enjoy twenty-two per cent, and still use all three.

items.stem: What survives the change in ownership?

options.text: Neither — every carried-forward claim dies with the change in control
options.misconception: sweeps depreciation into a section that never mentions it
options.why: Section 79 speaks of "loss". Unabsorbed depreciation merges into the next year's depreciation under its own section and survives ownership changes untouched.

options.text: Both, provided the new owners continue the same line of business
options.misconception: imports the old business-continuity idea into a shareholding test
options.why: Continuity of business matters in other places; section 79's test is continuity of voting power. Running the identical trade with new owners fails it just the same.

options.text: Only the ₹4 crore of unabsorbed depreciation — section 79 kills the business loss
options.why: With 70 per cent changing hands, the 51 per cent continuity test fails and the business loss cannot be carried forward and set off. Unabsorbed depreciation travels under section 32(2), not section 79, and courts have consistently kept it outside the shareholding test — which is why acquirers price the two very differently.

options.text: Both — losses belong to the company, and the company has not changed
options.misconception: stops at separate legal personality
options.why: Separate personality is exactly what section 79 overrides for closely held companies. The section exists because buying a shell for its losses is trading in tax attributes, and Parliament closed that market.

citation.ref: Section 79

items.scenario: A closely held trading company has ₹10 crore of carried-forward business loss and ₹4 crore of unabsorbed depreciation. During the year, promoters holding 70 per cent sell their entire stake to a new investor group. The new owners plan to set both amounts off against this year's profits.

items.stem: Who is right?

options.text: The adviser — a treaty overrides domestic law without further formality
options.misconception: quotes the override while skipping the statutory condition on it
options.why: The override itself flows through section 90, and Parliament wrote the TRC condition into the same section. The gate and the door come as a set.

options.text: Neither — the company must always pay the higher of the two rates
options.misconception: inverts the beneficial-provision rule
options.why: Section 90(2) says the treaty applies to the extent it is more beneficial. Higher-of-the -two is the one reading the section forbids.

options.text: The adviser, provided the company files an Indian return declaring residence in Singapore
options.misconception: substitutes self-declaration for the other state's certificate
options.why: The certificate must come from the government of the residence country — that is the point of it. Form 10F supplements a TRC; nothing the taxpayer signs replaces one.

options.text: The officer — section 90(4) makes the TRC a condition for claiming any treaty benefit
options.why: The beneficial-treaty rule in section 90(2) is real, but subsection (4) hangs a key on the door: a certificate of residence from the other government. Without it the company cannot invoke the treaty at all, and the Act's rate applies until the certificate is obtained.
