citation.ref: Section 90(2) and (4)

items.scenario: A Singapore company earns fees from India that the treaty taxes at 10 per cent but the Act taxes at a higher rate. It has no tax residency certificate. Its adviser says the treaty rate applies automatically because treaties override the Act; the tax officer says treaty benefit is barred without the certificate.

items.stem: Can the addition under section 68 stand?

options.text: Yes, but taxed at normal slab rates with business losses set off
options.misconception: adds the income but forgets 115BBE's special regime
options.why: Section 115BBE exists to make unexplained money expensive: sixty per cent plus surcharge, and no deduction or loss set-off. Slab treatment would make an addition under section 68 cheaper than declaring the income honestly.

options.text: No, because money received by cheque can never be a cash credit
options.misconception: confuses the credit's mode with its explanation
options.why: Section 68 speaks of any sum credited; the cheque is merely how it travelled. Unexplained money does not launder itself by passing through one bank account.

options.text: Yes — for closely held share capital, the resident investor's own source must also satisfy the officer
options.why: The proviso to section 68 makes the source of the source part of the company's burden for share application money from residents. A banking trail that begins with unexplained cash explains nothing; the addition stands and 115BBE prices it at sixty per cent plus surcharge, with no losses set off against it.

options.text: No — identity, genuineness and creditworthiness were all evidenced
options.misconception: applies the classic three-limb test without the share-capital proviso
options.why: The three limbs remain the law for ordinary credits. For closely held companies' share capital, Parliament added the fourth question, and the cash deposit is where this explanation dies.

citation.ref: Section 68 read with 115BBE

items.scenario: A closely held company shows ₹2 crore of fresh share capital from a resident investor. Asked to explain, it produces the investor's confirmation, PAN and bank statement showing the cheque — but the investor's account received ₹2 crore in cash days before investing, and he offers no explanation of where that came from. The company argues its own burden ended with identity, genuineness and the banking channel.

items.stem: How does the clubbing fall in year two?

options.text: Nothing clubs — the gift was genuine and she is assessed on her own deposits
options.misconception: treats a genuine gift as adequate consideration
options.why: Genuineness was never the issue; consideration is. Love and affection make a gift real and still leave it without adequate consideration, which is the very case the section taxes to the transferor.

options.text: Both amounts club with the husband — everything traces back to his gift
options.misconception: follows the money forever instead of following the asset
options.why: The section stops at income from the transferred asset. Income on accumulated income is one step beyond its words, and the settled reading leaves it with the transferee.

options.text: Both amounts are the wife's, but the husband loses ₹30 lakh from his capital
options.misconception: imagines clubbing ends once the transfer is complete
options.why: The transfer is complete in property law; tax law keeps the income tethered to the transferor for as long as the marriage and the asset both subsist.

options.text: The ₹2.4 lakh on the gifted money clubs with the husband; the ₹18,000 on the reinvested interest is the wife's
options.why: Section 64(1)(iv) clubs income arising from the transferred asset — the ₹30 lakh — so its interest belongs to the husband year after year. The first year's interest, once earned, is the wife's own money; what it earns in turn is income from her asset, outside the clubbing.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(iv)

items.scenario: A husband gifts his wife ₹30 lakh, which she puts in a fixed deposit earning ₹2.4 lakh interest in year one. She reinvests that interest in a second deposit, which itself earns ₹18,000 in year two. In year two, whose income is what?

items.stem: What does section 44AE actually presume for the year?

options.text: The same rates, but skipping the five workshop months
options.misconception: reads "per month" as per operating month
options.why: The words are months of ownership, and the scheme's bargain is bluntness. An assessee wanting his idle months recognised must leave the presumption, keep books and be audited.

options.text: ₹16,000 a month for each heavy vehicle and ₹7,500 for each light one, for all twelve months of ownership
options.why: The presumption runs on ownership, not operation: 16MT × ₹1,000 = ₹16,000 per heavy vehicle per month or part, ₹7,500 per light vehicle, for every month the vehicle was owned. The workshop months count in full — the section trades exactness for simplicity, in both directions.

options.text: ₹7,500 per vehicle across the fleet, heavy or light
options.misconception: misses the separate tonnage rate for heavy vehicles
options.why: The 2018 amendment split the rates: heavy goods vehicles earn the presumption by the ton. Flat-rating a 16MT lorry understates each heavy vehicle by more than half.

options.text: Nothing — six lorries make him ineligible, since the limit is five
options.misconception: shrinks the ten-carriage ceiling
options.why: Eligibility runs to ten goods carriages at any time during the year. Six is comfortably inside.

citation.ref: Section 44AE

items.scenario: A transporter owned six lorries all year — two heavy vehicles of 16MT gross weight each and four light ones. One heavy vehicle stood in the workshop for five months after an accident. He computes presumptive income counting only the months each vehicle actually ran.

items.stem: Does GAAR reach this borrowing?

options.text: Yes — a tax benefit above three crore whose purpose test is met is automatically impermissible
options.misconception: collapses the two-limb test into the threshold
options.why: The three-crore line in Rule 10U is a floor below which GAAR is not invoked, not a trigger above which it applies. Above it, the tainted-element limb still has to be proved.

options.text: No — a real loan on arm's-length terms carries no tainted element, and choosing the tax-efficient route is permissible planning
options.why: GAAR needs both limbs: the main-purpose tax benefit and a tainted element. Genuine borrowing at market terms from a real lender, deployed in the business, misuses nothing and lacks no commercial substance. The Act itself makes interest deductible; using a provision as intended is planning, not avoidance, whatever the amount saved.

options.text: No, because GAAR applies only to cross-border arrangements
options.misconception: confines a general rule to international transactions
options.why: The chapter reaches any arrangement, domestic or foreign. This borrowing escapes on the merits — the missing tainted element — not on geography.

options.text: Yes, because the company admits tax drove the choice of debt over equity
options.misconception: makes motive alone sufficient
options.why: Every rational taxpayer weighs tax; section 96 demands more — dealings not at arm's length, misuse of provisions, absence of substance, or abnormal means. An ordinary loan exhibits none.

citation.ref: Sections 95-96, Rule 10U

items.scenario: To fund expansion, a company chooses to borrow rather than issue equity because interest is deductible and dividends are not, saving ₹20 crore of tax over the loan's life. The assessing officer invokes GAAR: the financing was chosen mainly for the tax benefit, which exceeds three crore rupees.

items.stem: Is CUP the most appropriate method here?

options.text: No method applies — a transaction with no comparables is outside transfer pricing
options.misconception: reads absence of a comparable price as absence of an arm's length price
options.why: The methods exist to approximate arm's length outcomes precisely where direct prices are missing. Escaping the regime for want of comparables would exempt every captive arrangement — the core of what the regime polices.

options.text: Yes, because captive sales to a parent can never be tested by profit-based methods
options.misconception: excludes profit methods from exactly the situation they were designed for
options.why: A captive routine supplier is where transactional net margin thrives — its comparables are independent companies with similar functions, not identical products.

options.text: No — with no true comparable, a net margin method fits a routine manufacturer better than a heavily adjusted CUP
options.why: CUP's directness depends entirely on comparability; when adjustments do the real work, the method's precision is an illusion. Rule 10B asks for the most appropriate method, not the most direct-sounding — and a routine, intangible-free manufacturer is the textbook case for testing net margins against comparable companies.

options.text: Yes — the law ranks CUP first, so it applies whenever any comparison can be constructed
options.misconception: imports a hierarchy the Indian rules never adopted
options.why: Section 92C lists methods without ranking them. The selection standard is appropriateness to the transaction and data; a constructed comparison fails that test exactly when the adjustments dominate.

citation.ref: Section 92C read with Rule 10B

items.scenario: An Indian subsidiary manufactures components sold only to its foreign parent; nothing identical trades between independents, and the subsidiary performs routine functions with no unique intangibles. The transfer pricing officer insists on the comparable uncontrolled price method as "the most direct", using a broadly similar product's price with heavy adjustments.

items.stem: What does the company actually pay, and what happens to the difference?

options.text: ₹6 crore — tax follows total income as computed under the Act
options.misconception: computes tax as if MAT did not exist
options.why: MAT exists because companies with healthy book profits and skilful deductions were paying near zero. The book-profit floor is precisely for this fact pattern.

options.text: ₹6 crore now, with ₹9 crore payable only if book profits persist three years
options.misconception: invents an averaging test the section does not contain
options.why: The comparison is annual and unconditional: each year stands alone, higher of the two numbers, no waiting period.

options.text: About ₹15 crore — fifteen per cent of book profit — with the ₹9 crore excess carried as MAT credit for up to fifteen years
options.why: Section 115JB compares regular tax with fifteen per cent of book profit and collects the higher. The extra ₹9 crore is not lost: it rides forward as credit, usable in years when regular tax exceeds MAT, for fifteen assessment years — a prepayment, provided the company stays in the MAT regime long enough to use it.

options.text: ₹15 crore, gone for good — MAT is a penalty for excessive deductions
options.misconception: reads a timing levy as a punishment
options.why: The credit mechanism is the section's other half. MAT accelerates tax; over the cycle the credit hands the acceleration back against future regular liability.

citation.ref: Section 115JB

items.scenario: A company under the regular regime reports book profit of ₹100 crore but, thanks to accelerated depreciation and deductions, total income of just ₹20 crore. Regular tax on ₹20 crore comes to about ₹6 crore. The CFO budgets ₹6 crore for the year's tax.

items.stem: How does section 270A actually apply to the two additions?

options.text: No penalty on either if the company pays the tax and interest demanded
options.misconception: stretches 270AA immunity over misreporting
options.why: Payment-and-no-appeal immunity exists for under-reporting cases. The provision expressly withholds it where the penalty arises from misreporting — the bogus bills stay exposed.

options.text: Fifty per cent on both, since both were disclosed somewhere in the books
options.misconception: lets book entries of fake bills count as disclosure
options.why: Recording a false invoice is not disclosing a fact; it is the false entry itself — the statute's own example of misreporting. Disclosure saves the debatable claim, not the fabricated one.

options.text: The disclosed debatable claim may escape penalty entirely; the bogus bills draw two hundred per cent
options.why: A claim made with full disclosure and a bona fide explanation sits in the section's carve-outs from under-reported income — losing a debatable point is not under-reporting. False entries are named misreporting, and misreporting is priced at two hundred per cent with no 270AA immunity available.

options.text: Two hundred per cent on both — every addition sustained is misreporting
options.misconception: erases the section's central two-tier design
options.why: The section splits honest-but-wrong from dishonest, at fifty and two hundred per cent, with carve-outs before either. Flattening it to the top rate restores the arbitrariness the old penalty regime was replaced to end.

citation.ref: Sections 270A and 270AA

items.scenario: Two additions survive a company's assessment: ₹1 crore disallowed because the officer read a genuinely debatable provision differently, with the company's claim fully disclosed in the return's notes; and ₹60 lakh of purchases that proved to be bogus bills from a non-existent vendor. The officer proposes two hundred per cent penalty on the tax on both.

items.stem: Can the revision stand?

options.text: No — after real enquiry, a possible view is not erroneous, and prejudice alone cannot carry a revision
options.why: Section 263 needs error and prejudice together. The officer asked, received, weighed and reasoned; that his conclusion favoured the assessee makes it prejudicial in the Commissioner's eyes, but a plausible view after enquiry is not error. Revision on preference would make every assessment provisional.

options.text: Yes — any order that collects less tax than it might is prejudicial, which suffices
options.misconception: reads one condition where the section writes two
options.why: Prejudice without error covers half the section's text. Both limbs are conditions, and the enquiry on record defeats the first.

options.text: Yes, because share premium acceptance is inherently a high-risk error
options.misconception: substitutes the issue's risk profile for the order's actual defect
options.why: Risk explains why enquiry was needed; the record shows it happened. Section 263 reviews what the officer did, not how dangerous the topic sounds.

options.text: No, because the Commissioner can never revise a completed assessment
options.misconception: denies the power instead of its limits
options.why: The power is real and regularly used — above all where the officer made no enquiry at all. This order survives on its record, not on any immunity.

citation.ref: Section 263

items.scenario: An assessing officer examined a large share premium during assessment — issued a questionnaire, received valuation reports and investor confirmations, discussed them in the order — and accepted the premium. The Commissioner, reviewing later, would have added it, and invokes section 263 on the ground that the acceptance cost the revenue tax.

items.stem: What does section 94B actually do to the ₹40 crore?

options.text: All ₹40 crore deducts if the loan's interest rate is proven arm's length
options.misconception: answers a thin-cap section with a transfer pricing defence
options.why: Section 94B assumes the rate is fine and attacks the quantum of debt instead. Arm's length pricing answers 92C; the EBITDA cap applies on top of it.

options.text: Nothing deducts — interest to related non-residents above one crore is disallowed outright
options.misconception: turns the threshold into a cliff
options.why: One crore is the gate below which the section ignores you, not a line beyond which everything falls. Past the gate, the EBITDA formula does the limiting.

options.text: ₹30 crore deducts this year; ₹10 crore carries forward up to eight years; TDS runs on the full ₹40 crore regardless
options.why: The cap is thirty per cent of EBITDA — ₹30 crore — and the excess is not lost but parked, deductible within the cap in the next eight years. The section only limits the payer's deduction; the interest is still paid, still the non-resident's income, and still bears withholding in full.

options.text: ₹30 crore deducts and TDS applies only to that deductible portion
options.misconception: lets the payer's cap shrink the payee's income
options.why: Withholding follows the payment, not the deduction. The disallowed ₹10 crore is still interest paid to a non-resident, taxable in its hands and withheld on accordingly.

citation.ref: Section 94B

items.scenario: An Indian subsidiary pays ₹40 crore interest to its foreign parent. Its EBITDA is ₹100 crore. The CFO fears the entire ₹40 crore is lost as a deduction; the tax head counters that at least the section leaves TDS obligations lighter on the disallowed part.

items.stem: Does SEP catch the platform?

options.text: No, because digital services can never have an Indian business connection
options.misconception: right answer, mistaken ground
options.why: Domestically, SEP creates exactly that business connection — thresholds crossed, the hook holds. What saves the platform is the treaty override, not any gap in section 9.

options.text: Yes, because streaming into India constitutes a virtual permanent establishment
options.misconception: invents a PE category the treaty does not contain
options.why: PE under the treaty means fixed places, dependent agents and the like. Virtual presence concepts live in domestic law and multilateral proposals, not in the operative treaty text.

options.text: No — the treaty's permanent establishment article governs a treaty resident, and SEP cannot override it
options.why: Section 90(2) lets the taxpayer take the treaty where more beneficial, and the treaty taxes business profits only through a permanent establishment — which needs more than users and revenue. SEP rewrote the domestic definition of business connection, not the treaty; its practical reach is non-treaty jurisdictions, and this platform is not one.

options.text: Yes — SEP was enacted precisely to tax digital businesses like this one
options.misconception: reads the purpose while skipping the treaty ceiling
options.why: The purpose is real and the domestic hook now exists — but a treaty resident claims the treaty, and business profits without a PE stay untaxed here until the treaty itself changes.

citation.ref: Section 9(1)(i) with Explanation 2A

items.scenario: A US-based streaming platform with no office, server or staff in India earns large subscription revenue from Indian users, crossing the significant economic presence thresholds. The platform is entitled to the India-US tax treaty. The assessing officer taxes its profits, holding that the SEP amendment overrides treaties as later domestic law.

items.stem: What can the trust actually do about the ₹25 lakh shortfall?

options.text: Carry it forward as next year's application, netting against next year's 85 per cent
options.misconception: invents inter-year set-off in the wrong direction
options.why: The regime tests each year's application against each year's income. The route forward for this year's surplus is 11(2) accumulation, not a credit against a future year's obligation.

options.text: Nothing — unspent income above fifteen per cent is taxable, full stop
options.misconception: reads section 11(1) without 11(2)
options.why: The five-year accumulation exists precisely for lumpy charitable projects like building wings. The accountant's rule is the default, not the last word.

options.text: Simply resolve to spend it eventually — charitable intention protects charitable money
options.misconception: substitutes intention for the statutory conditions
options.why: The shelter is procedural on purpose: stated purpose, filed statement, specified investments, five years. An unminuted intention satisfies none of them and the exemption fails.

options.text: Accumulate it for the hospital wing under section 11(2) — a specific purpose, the prescribed statement, and a five-year clock
options.why: Eighty-five per cent of ₹1 crore is ₹85 lakh; ₹60 lakh is applied and ₹15 lakh rides the standing accumulation, leaving ₹25 lakh exposed. Section 11(2) shelters it: name the specific purpose, file the statement before the return's due date, invest in specified modes, and spend within five years. Miss those conditions and the amount falls back into tax.

citation.ref: Section 11(1) and 11(2)

items.scenario: A registered charitable trust earns ₹1 crore in the year and spends ₹60 lakh on its school by 31 March. The trustees plan a hospital wing and want to keep the remaining ₹40 lakh for it, without tax. The accountant says the shortfall below eighty-five per cent is simply taxable and nothing can be done after the year has run.

items.stem: What is the correct capital gain?

options.text: ₹60 crore long-term — FMV of ₹130 crore as deemed consideration, less ₹70 crore net worth ignoring the revaluation
options.why: Two corrections: since the 2021 amendment, consideration is the higher rule-computed fair market value, ₹130 crore, not the ₹120 crore price; and net worth expressly ignores revaluation, so cost is ₹70 crore. Fifteen years of holding makes the gain long-term — the undertaking's age governs, depreciable contents notwithstanding.

options.text: Itemised gains asset by asset, since a lump sum must be allocated to compute anything
options.misconception: dissolves the slump sale into the piecemeal sale it is defined against
options.why: The absence of item-wise values is the definition of a slump sale, and section 50B exists to tax exactly that. Allocation would recreate the valuation disputes the lump-sum route avoids.

options.text: ₹60 crore, but short-term — the plant inside was depreciated, and depreciable assets always yield short-term gains
options.misconception: applies section 50's asset-level rule to an undertaking-level transfer
options.why: A slump sale taxes one capital asset — the undertaking. Its holding period, past thirty-six months, sets the character; the deeming for depreciable assets stays with itemised transfers.

options.text: ₹25 crore — price received less book net worth as stated
options.misconception: accepts both the stale consideration and the revalued cost
options.why: Each error flatters the taxpayer: revaluation inflates cost by ₹25 crore and the FMV deeming lifts consideration by ₹10 crore. The section blocks both doors by its terms.

citation.ref: Section 50B

items.scenario: A company sells its fifteen-year-old bottling division as a going concern for ₹120 crore lump sum. The division's net worth per the prescribed computation is ₹70 crore; its books show ₹95 crore after a recent upward revaluation of land. Rule-based fair market value of the undertaking is ₹130 crore. The CFO computes long-term gain of ₹25 crore (120 − 95).

items.stem: Is the tax team right?

options.text: Yes — TDS provisions apply only where money is paid or credited
options.misconception: states the pre-2022 gap the section was written to close
options.why: That reasoning is why dealer incentives escaped for years. Section 194R's words cover any benefit or perquisite, in cash or in kind or partly both.

options.text: No TDS, but each distributor must self-declare the trip's value in the return
options.misconception: relies on the recipient honesty the section stopped relying on
options.why: The benefit is taxable in the distributor's hands with or without 194R; the section exists because self-declaration of free trips was rare. The collection duty now sits with the provider.

options.text: No — section 194R reaches benefits in kind, and the company must ensure tax on ₹3 lakh per distributor is paid before the trip
options.why: The section was enacted for exactly this: benefits arising from business relationships that never touch a bank account. Each trip crosses the twenty-thousand threshold fifteen times over, and for a benefit wholly in kind the provider's duty is to ensure the tax is deposited — by collecting it from the distributor or bearing it grossed up — before release.

options.text: TDS applies, but on the company's cost of the trip after group discounts, at 2 per cent
options.misconception: right obligation, invented rate
options.why: The rate is ten per cent of the benefit's value. Valuation questions are real at the margin, but a fifth of the correct rate is not a valuation position.

citation.ref: Section 194R

items.scenario: A pharma company sends its top thirty distributors on a fully paid foreign conference trip worth ₹3 lakh each. No cash changes hands — the company books the travel directly. Its tax team sees no TDS obligation: nothing was paid to the distributors, and TDS attaches to payments.

items.stem: What does section 35 actually allow this year?

options.text: ₹2 crore only — capital expenditure must travel through depreciation
options.misconception: denies the section's central acceleration
options.why: Full-year deduction of capital research spend is precisely what distinguishes section 35 from ordinary depreciation. The equipment deducts now, once, entirely.

options.text: ₹7 crore — revenue and capital research expenditure in full, but nothing for the land
options.why: The salaries and materials deduct as revenue research expenditure, and the equipment deducts fully in the year despite being capital — that acceleration is the section's gift. Land is its stated exception: however research-bound, it neither deducts under 35 nor depreciates. The weighted era is over; one hundred per cent is the ceiling.

options.text: ₹10.5 crore — the 150 per cent weighting applies to the revenue portion
options.misconception: claims a sunset benefit
options.why: The weighted deductions were legislated down to one hundred per cent. Nostalgia for 150 per cent is now an excess claim inviting disallowance and penalty.

options.text: ₹10 crore — everything spent in the direction of research qualifies
options.misconception: reads the capital allowance without its land exception
options.why: The section says expenditure of a capital nature excluding land. Land appreciates and waits; Parliament declined to fund patience.

citation.ref: Section 35(1) and (2)

items.scenario: A manufacturing company spends during the year on in-house research related to its business: ₹2 crore on scientists' salaries and materials, ₹5 crore on laboratory equipment, and ₹3 crore on land beside the factory for a future research block. The CFO claims ₹10 crore under section 35, recalling that research once earned a weighted 150 per cent, and hoping at least 100 per cent survives for all of it.

items.stem: Where is the company's POEM?

options.text: In India, but only its Indian-sourced income becomes taxable
options.misconception: gives residence the consequences of source
options.why: Residence brings worldwide income within reach, subject to treaty relief. Source-only taxation is the regime the company just lost.

options.text: In Singapore — the board is the organ of management and it met there
options.misconception: reads the minutes as the management
options.why: Formal authority matters when actually exercised. POEM was adopted precisely to see through boards that convene abroad to bless decisions made at home.

options.text: Nowhere taxable — a subsidiary's decisions naturally involve its parent, which cannot create residence
options.misconception: stretches shareholder oversight into a safe harbour
options.why: Guidance distinguishes a parent's governance influence from the subsidiary's own decisions being taken by the parent's officers. Selecting this company's suppliers and prices is the latter.

options.text: In India — decisions are made in substance in Mumbai, and Singapore's minutes record ratification, not management
options.why: The test asks where key management and commercial decisions are in substance made. A board that rubber-stamps Mumbai's emails has moved the venue of signatures, not of management; the effective decisions travel with the CFO. The company is resident, and its global income enters the Indian net for the year.

citation.ref: Section 6(3)

items.scenario: A Singapore-incorporated trading subsidiary of an Indian group holds all board meetings in Singapore, minuted meticulously. The evidence shows every significant decision — supplier selection, pricing, financing — is made by the group CFO in Mumbai and emailed to the Singapore directors, who approve without discussion. The company claims non-resident status on the strength of its meeting venue.

items.stem: What can the Commissioner (Appeals) lawfully do?

options.text: Enhance by the ₹3 crore after a show-cause opportunity — but not remand; the appeal must be decided
options.why: Section 251 arms the first appellate authority with enhancement, so an appeal can leave the taxpayer worse off — counsel's floor does not exist, though the power runs only after a reasonable opportunity to show cause. The remand power was deliberately removed: the file's quality is the Commissioner's problem to cure by enquiry and decision, not to return to sender.

options.text: Enhance immediately — the taxpayer invited full scrutiny by appealing
options.misconception: skips the mandatory hearing
options.why: Enhancement without a show-cause opportunity fails the section's own condition and natural justice with it. The power is real; the process is not optional.

options.text: Neither — an appellate authority is confined to the grounds the taxpayer raised
options.misconception: shrinks the first appeal to the appellant's agenda
options.why: The first appeal is a re-look at the assessment, with the assessment's subject matter open. Enhancement on connected matters within it is the statute's express grant.

options.text: Both — appellate powers include everything the assessing officer could do
options.misconception: keeps the abolished remand alive
options.why: The set-aside-and-remand power was taken away by amendment. Deciding, with enquiry where needed, is now the only route through.

citation.ref: Sections 250-251

items.scenario: Appealing a ₹2 crore addition, a taxpayer's counsel is confident: at worst the addition stands. Reviewing the file, the Commissioner (Appeals) notices a related deduction the assessing officer allowed that looks untenable, worth another ₹3 crore, and also considers sending the whole case back for a fresh assessment given the file's poor quality.

items.stem: How is the December 2025 buy-back actually taxed for her?

options.text: Capital gains of ₹8 lakh — consideration less cost, like any share sale
options.misconception: taxes the buy-back as an ordinary transfer
options.why: The deeming intercepts the consideration and calls all of it dividend. The capital gains computation still runs, but with nil consideration — yielding a loss, not the ₹8 lakh gain.

options.text: Dividend of ₹8 lakh — the deeming nets off her cost first
options.misconception: imports a cost deduction the provision denies
options.why: The dividend is the entire sum received; cost has no place in dividend taxation. Its only outlet is the engineered capital loss on the side.

options.text: Exempt in her hands — the company discharges the buy-back tax under section 115QA
options.misconception: applies the pre-October 2024 regime
options.why: Section 115QA and the shareholder exemption ceased for buy-backs from 1 October 2024. Answering the old law on a December 2025 buy-back is the error this change was bound to produce.

options.text: The full ₹20 lakh is her dividend income at slab rates, and the ₹12 lakh cost becomes a capital loss usable only against capital gains
options.why: From 1 October 2024 the exemption and the company-level tax are both gone: the whole consideration is deemed dividend under section 2(22)(f), with TDS and slab taxation, and no cost deduction against it. The cost is preserved separately — consideration deemed nil produces a ₹12 lakh capital loss to set off or carry forward against capital gains alone, never against the dividend.

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(f) (Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024)

items.scenario: In December 2025 a listed company buys back shares at ₹1,000 each. An investor tenders 2,000 shares bought years ago at ₹600. Remembering the old regime, she expects the ₹20 lakh receipt to be exempt in her hands with the company paying the buy-back tax, and asks only whether her ₹12 lakh cost still matters.

items.stem: Does section 2(22)(e) bite?

options.text: No — the recipient is the firm, and dividends can only accrue to shareholders
options.misconception: reads the section without its concern limb
options.why: The concern limb exists because sole reliance on direct loans made avoidance trivial. The deemed dividend is assessed in the hands the provision names, detour notwithstanding.

options.text: No, because a repaid loan was never income in substance
options.misconception: lets subsequent events rewrite the taxable event
options.why: The mischief is shareholders enjoying company profits as untaxed loans. A rotating loan — drawn, repaid, redrawn — would otherwise deliver dividends perpetually tax free.

options.text: Yes, but only ₹2 crore times his 40 per cent shareholding
options.misconception: apportions a deeming that attaches to the payment
options.why: The deemed dividend is the payment itself, capped by accumulated profits — not a pro-rata slice of it. His shareholding qualifies the trigger; it does not dilute the amount.

options.text: Yes — a loan to a concern in which the substantial shareholder is substantially interested is deemed dividend, and repayment does not erase it
options.why: The provision expressly reaches payments to any concern in which such a shareholder holds substantial interest — routing through the firm is the oldest detour it closed. The deeming operates when the loan is made, to the extent of accumulated profits; repayment seven months later no more undoes it than returning a dividend would. Market interest helps commercial optics, not the statutory deeming.

citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e)

items.scenario: A private company with ₹5 crore of accumulated profits lends ₹2 crore to a partnership firm in which its 40 per cent shareholder is a partner with a substantial interest. The loan carries market interest and is repaid in full within seven months. The shareholder argues no dividend can arise: the money went to the firm, not to him, and it came back.

items.stem: Is the set-off valid?

options.text: Yes, against the futures profit at least — both involve the stock market
options.misconception: matches by market instead of by statutory character
options.why: The futures profit is expressly non-speculative; the share loss is deemed speculative. Statutory characters, not trading venues, decide who may meet whom — and these two are on opposite sides.

options.text: Yes — delivery-based share trading is never speculation, so the loss is ordinary business loss
options.misconception: applies section 43(5) and skips the company-specific Explanation
options.why: For individuals that is the end of it. For companies the Explanation adds a deeming on top of the definition, and this company fits none of its exceptions.

options.text: No — the Explanation deems the company's share-trading loss speculative, and speculation loss cannot touch the distribution profit or even the F&O profit
options.why: Delivery normally saves a transaction from being speculative, but the Explanation to section 73 deems a company's share-dealing business speculation regardless of delivery, unless the company is in the carved-out classes. The loss can meet only speculation profit — and the index futures profit is statutorily not speculative, being eligible exchange-traded derivatives. The ₹50 lakh waits, four years at most, for a speculation profit that may never come.

options.text: No set-off ever — deemed speculation losses lapse the same year
options.misconception: denies the carry-forward the section grants
options.why: The loss survives four assessment years, usable against any speculation profit arising in them. Restrictive is not the same as extinguished.

citation.ref: Section 73 with section 43(5)

items.scenario: A trading company (not an investment or banking company) has three results this year: ₹50 lakh loss from its business of buying and selling listed shares with delivery; ₹20 lakh profit from exchange-traded index futures; and ₹80 lakh profit from its commodities distribution business. It sets the share loss against the distribution profit.

items.stem: Who is right about the ₹8 lakh?

options.text: The colleague — aggregation means the whole ₹20 lakh bears tax
options.misconception: converts a rate device into a charge
options.why: Taxing farm income is beyond Parliament's chosen scheme — agriculture is the States' field. The two-step computation deducts the farm slice back out, leaving only the rate effect.

options.text: The scheme applies, but only if agricultural income exceeds the business income
options.misconception: invents a proportionality condition
options.why: The gates are five thousand rupees of farm income and other income above the basic exemption — both crossed here. Relative size is nowhere in the test.

options.text: The accountant — exempt means the ₹8 lakh never enters any computation
options.misconception: reads the exemption as invisibility
options.why: Total invisibility would let a large landowner's modest business income enjoy the lowest slabs. The rate integration exists to price ability to pay without taxing the exempt source.

options.text: Neither — the farm income is not taxed, but it fixes the rate: tax on ₹20 lakh, less tax on the agricultural income plus the exemption limit
options.why: Partial integration threads between the two errors. Aggregating ₹20 lakh pushes the business income into the slabs it would occupy if the taxpayer's true capacity were visible; the deduction of tax on agricultural income plus the exemption limit then returns what would have fallen on the farm income itself. The exemption holds; only the rate feels the farm.

citation.ref: Section 10(1) with Finance Act rate schedule

items.scenario: An individual under the old regime has business income of ₹12 lakh and net agricultural income of ₹8 lakh. His accountant computes tax on ₹12 lakh alone, citing the exemption of agricultural income; a colleague objects that the ₹8 lakh must be added and taxed like any other income.

items.stem: What does section 43B allow this year?

options.text: The GST and the interest — the bank's acceptance of the conversion discharged the liability
options.misconception: treats novation as payment
options.why: The liability was rearranged, not extinguished by outflow; not a rupee left the company. The Explanation names this arrangement and denies it.

options.text: All three — mercantile accounting deducts what accrues
options.misconception: reads the books where the section reads the bank statement
options.why: Section 43B exists to override accrual for exactly these sums, which taxpayers accrued for decades and paid never. The non obstante clause beats the method of accounting.

options.text: Only the GST — the late bonus waits for its payment year, and the conversion of interest into a loan is statutorily not payment
options.why: Payment by the due date of the return preserves accrual-year deduction, which saves the GST. The bonus missed that date, so it deducts in the year actually paid. The interest is the trap the Explanations closed in terms: conversion into a loan or borrowing is not actual payment, and the deduction arrives only as the converted loan is repaid.

options.text: The GST and the bonus — employee dues enjoy a grace period until actually paid
options.misconception: invents a bonus concession beyond the due-date proviso
options.why: The proviso's grace runs to the return's due date for every 43B sum alike. A March payment is eleven months past it; the deduction simply shifts years.

citation.ref: Section 43B

items.scenario: At year-end a company's books accrue: GST of ₹80 lakh, paid in full in May, well before the return's due date; bonus of ₹40 lakh, paid the following March, after the return was filed; and ₹1.2 crore of interest owed to its bank, which the bank agreed to convert into a fresh term loan in February. The company claims all three this year.

items.stem: What is the correct withholding position on these purchases?

options.text: Both deduct and collect, at 0.1 per cent each, as the sections literally overlap
options.misconception: revives the overlap the omission dissolved
options.why: Even in the overlap era the buyer's TDS took precedence and switched the TCS off. Now there is no second provision at all.

options.text: The buyer deducts 0.1 per cent on ₹1.4 crore — seller-side TCS on goods is gone, and the buyer's duty stands alone
options.why: Turnover above ten crore makes the manufacturer a specified buyer, and purchases beyond fifty lakh from one seller trigger deduction on the excess — ₹1.4 crore here, a modest ₹14,000 of tax but a serious obligation. The TCS the accountant is waiting for was omitted from 1 April 2025; nobody else is collecting, and the failure prices itself through the 30 per cent expense disallowance.

options.text: The seller collects TCS at 0.1 per cent, and the buyer rightly does nothing
options.misconception: relies on the omitted collection provision
options.why: That was the fallback half of an overlap that ended in April 2025. Waiting for a repealed section to act is how withholding defaults happen in transition years.

options.text: Nothing applies — goods purchases below ₹5 crore are outside withholding entirely
options.misconception: invents a threshold from the turnover test
options.why: Ten crore tests the buyer's size; fifty lakh tests the purchases per seller. Both are crossed, and no five-crore line exists anywhere in the section.

citation.ref: Section 194Q (TCS on goods omitted w.e.f. 1 April 2025)

items.scenario: In FY 2025-26 a manufacturer with ₹60 crore turnover buys ₹1.9 crore of steel from one resident supplier. Its accountant deducts nothing, reasoning that the seller will collect TCS on the sale as sellers always did, and that double taxation must be avoided.

items.stem: Is the full exemption right?

options.text: No — 54F works on net consideration, so investing ₹1.5 crore of ₹3 crore exempts only half the gain, ₹60 lakh
options.why: The adviser has computed section 54, which reinvests the gain — but that section is for selling a house. For shares, section 54F demands the net consideration be invested, exempting proportionately: 1.5/3 of the ₹1.2 crore gain, ₹60 lakh. The one existing house is within the not-more-than-one gate, so the claim survives — at half strength.

options.text: Yes, provided the shares' gain is otherwise taxable under section 112A
options.misconception: hangs the exemption on the levy section
options.why: 54F asks about the asset sold and the house bought, not which rate section would have taxed the gain. The proportionate formula still gives only ₹60 lakh.

options.text: Yes — a house costing more than the gain always absorbs it fully
options.misconception: applies section 54's gain-based formula to a 54F asset
options.why: The two sections' formulas differ by design: house-to-house asks the gain; anything-to-house asks the whole consideration, since otherwise sale proceeds could be enjoyed while a sliver bought exemption.

options.text: No exemption — owning any other house on the transfer date kills 54F
options.misconception: tightens the one-house gate to zero
options.why: The disqualification reads more than one residential house other than the new one. A single existing house is expressly tolerated.

citation.ref: Section 54F

items.scenario: An individual sells listed shares held six years for ₹3 crore (indexed cost irrelevant here; the long-term gain is ₹1.2 crore) and buys a residential flat for ₹1.5 crore. He owns one other house already. His adviser computes full exemption of the ₹1.2 crore gain since the flat's price exceeds the gain.

items.stem: What can an updated return do for him in June 2026?

options.text: Declare the omitted income with fifty per cent additional tax — but never the loss; an updated return cannot reduce liability
options.why: June 2026 sits in the second year after AY 2024-25's end, so the confession costs the tax and interest plus fifty per cent of them — the price of the second twelve months. The loss half of his hope is structurally barred: section 139(8A) refuses any updated return that shows a loss, lowers the liability, or raises a refund. The window's four-year reach (Finance Act 2025) changes when he may file, not what direction the numbers may move.

options.text: Both — an updated return replaces the original in full
options.misconception: treats ITR-U as a fresh return
options.why: It is a one-way instrument built to collect more tax with immunity from the worst consequences. Returns that cut both ways closed with the revised-return deadline.

options.text: Nothing — the window for AY 2024-25 shut twenty-four months after it ended
options.misconception: applies the pre-2025 window
options.why: The Finance Act 2025 stretched the window to forty-eight months, with the sixty and seventy per cent bands pricing the added years. AY 2024-25 remains open well past June 2026.

options.text: The income at twenty-five per cent additional tax, since he is volunteering
options.misconception: reads the first-year rate as the volunteer's rate
options.why: The bands run on the clock, not on virtue: twenty-five per cent belonged to the first twelve months, which ended in March 2026. His candour arrives in the fifty per cent band.

citation.ref: Section 139(8A) with 140B (Finance Act 2025)

items.scenario: In June 2026 a consultant realises he omitted ₹18 lakh of foreign consulting receipts from his return for assessment year 2024-25. He also realises that including them converts his year into a small loss position on another business, and hopes an updated return can both confess the income and claim the loss, paying whatever surcharge applies.

items.stem: What is the correct ceiling, and does the ₹15 lakh survive?

options.text: Nothing — partner remuneration is never deductible, being profit distribution
options.misconception: states the pre-1993 world
options.why: Working partner remuneration within the ceiling is expressly deductible and taxed in the partners' hands instead. Total denial double-counts what the scheme deliberately splits.

options.text: ₹12.3 lakh on the old slabs, disallowing ₹2.7 lakh
options.misconception: applies the pre-2024 limits the accountant memorised
options.why: The old first-slab of three lakh and floor of ₹1.5 lakh were doubled. Stale limits under-allow by exactly the amendment Parliament passed.

options.text: ₹13.8 lakh — 90 per cent of the first ₹6 lakh plus 60 per cent of ₹14 lakh — so ₹1.2 lakh of the claim disallows
options.why: The Finance Act 2024 rewrote the slab from AY 2025-26: the first six lakh of book profit earns the higher of three lakh or ninety per cent (₹5.4 lakh here), and the remaining ₹14 lakh earns sixty per cent (₹8.4 lakh) — ₹13.8 lakh in all. The deed authorises ₹15 lakh, but the statute caps the deduction; the excess ₹1.2 lakh is disallowed in the firm's hands.

options.text: ₹15 lakh in full — the deed's authorisation is the only condition
options.misconception: reads the deed as the ceiling
options.why: The deed is the first gate; the statutory formula is the second. Remuneration beyond the formula is disallowed however solemnly the deed promises it.

citation.ref: Section 40(b) (Finance Act 2024) with 194T

items.scenario: For FY 2025-26 a firm's book profit is ₹20 lakh, and its deed authorises remuneration of ₹15 lakh to its two working partners, which the firm pays and claims. The accountant computes the deductible ceiling using the limits he memorised years ago: ₹1.5 lakh or 90 per cent on the first ₹3 lakh, and 60 per cent beyond.

items.stem: How do the write-off and the later recovery fare?

options.text: The write-off deducts on the book entry alone — irrecoverability need not be proved — and the ₹30 lakh is income of the year it arrives
options.why: Since the 1989 amendment the condition is that the debt is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts, not established as such — the Supreme Court settled that the officer cannot demand proof the debt died. The balancing safeguard is section 41(4): what returns is taxed when it returns, so the ₹30 lakh lands in the recovery year's income.

options.text: The disallowance stands — a live customer means a live debt
options.misconception: applies the pre-1989 establish-it-first test
options.why: That evidentiary battle is what the amendment ended. Commercial judgment recorded in the books carries the deduction; the recovery rule protects the revenue if the judgment proves pessimistic.

options.text: The write-off deducts, and the ₹30 lakh recovery is a tax-free windfall
options.misconception: takes the deduction and forgets its mirror
options.why: Section 41(4) exists precisely for this sequence. A deduction taken and cash later received without tax would make pessimistic write-offs a planning device.

options.text: The write-off deducts only after filing a recovery suit that fails
options.misconception: adds a litigation condition the section dropped
options.why: Requiring futile suits was the old regime's waste. The books' write-off is the statutory event; suing a hopeless debtor is commerce, not a tax condition.

citation.ref: Section 36(1)(vii) with 41(4)

items.scenario: A manufacturer writes off ₹90 lakh owed by a struggling customer, passing the entry before year-end. The assessing officer disallows it: the customer is still in business, recovery suits were never filed, and the debt might yet be paid. Two years later the customer, recovering, pays ₹30 lakh of the written-off amount.

items.stem: How does ICDS treat the two claims?

options.text: The contract loss deducts as prudence, the MTM waits as speculation
options.misconception: lets one anticipated loss through on sentiment
options.why: Prudence is the accounting reason for the provision — and anticipation of losses is exactly what the construction ICDS declines to import into tax.

options.text: Both wait — expected contract losses are not anticipated under ICDS, and speculative MTM losses are generally not deductible until settlement
options.why: Section 145(2)'s standards govern the computation whatever the books say: ICDS on construction contracts recognises losses as incurred by the percentage of completion, refusing the upfront ₹15 crore that Ind AS prudence demands; and ICDS I's general rule denies marked-to-market losses except where a specific ICDS allows them. The books stay Ind AS; the return adjusts both items out and reverses them over time.

options.text: Both deduct — audited accounts bind the assessing officer
options.misconception: promotes book profits into taxable profits
options.why: The computation standards exist precisely to detach tax from accounting prudence. Book-tax differences of this kind are the daily work of the computation.

options.text: Neither deducts ever — ICDS disallows provisions permanently
options.misconception: reads a timing standard as a prohibition
options.why: ICDS moves recognition, it does not extinguish it. The contract loss deducts as completion progresses, and the forward loss on settlement — later, not never.

citation.ref: Section 145(2) with ICDS I-X

items.scenario: A construction company's Ind AS accounts recognise a ₹15 crore provision for the expected total loss on an onerous contract in year one of three, and also book a ₹4 crore mark-to-market loss on open forward contracts held for a speculative position. The tax computation claims both, the CFO reasoning that audited Ind AS accounts are the last word for tax too.

items.stem: What does section 115BBC actually charge each?

options.text: Neither — donations to registered trusts are exempt income
options.misconception: lets registration absorb the anonymous-donation charge
options.why: Sections 11-12 exempt applied income; 115BBC carves anonymous receipts out of that comfort for secular trusts. Registration is the precondition of the regime, not immunity from this section.

options.text: The hospital pays 30 per cent on ₹55 lakh — the cushion of ₹25 lakh spares the rest — and the temple pays nothing under this section
options.why: The hospital's cushion is the higher of ₹1 lakh or 5 per cent of total donations (₹25 lakh), so ₹55 lakh of the anonymous ₹80 lakh bears the flat 30 per cent. The temple stands wholly outside: religious institutions' anonymous offerings are the section's express exception, Parliament recognising that hundi donations are anonymous by devotion, not design.

options.text: Both pay 30 per cent on their full anonymous receipts
options.misconception: misses both the cushion and the religious exception
options.why: The section's two mercies are its most examinable features. Charging the temple's hundi would tax a practice as old as the temples.

options.text: The hospital on ₹55 lakh, the temple on whatever exceeds its own ₹16 lakh cushion
options.misconception: gives the temple a cushion it does not need
options.why: The cushion mechanics never reach the temple — wholly religious institutions are excluded from the section before any computation begins.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC

items.scenario: A charitable hospital trust receives ₹5 crore of donations in the year, of which ₹80 lakh arrived in collection boxes with no donor records. Separately, a temple trust — wholly religious — counts ₹3 crore of anonymous hundi offerings. Both fear the 30 per cent anonymous-donation levy on their unrecorded receipts.

items.stem: What does section 35D actually allow?

options.text: ₹1.6 crore a year for five years — the full ₹8 crore amortised
options.misconception: spreads the whole spend and skips the five per cent cap
options.why: The cap is the section's binding constraint here: only ₹5 crore enters the amortisation at all. Instalments divide the capped pool, not the invoice total.

options.text: Nothing — preliminary expenses are permanently capital
options.misconception: states the pre-35D common law as the whole answer
options.why: That harsh default is real, and section 35D is its legislated exception for the listed expenses. Denying the ₹5 crore ignores the section outright.

options.text: ₹1 crore a year for five years — the pool caps at ₹5 crore (five per cent of the project), and the excess ₹3 crore earns nothing
options.why: Pre-commencement expenditure is capital in nature and undeducible but for this section, which rations its mercy twice: the qualifying pool cannot exceed five per cent of project cost — ₹5 crore here — and even that spreads over five equal instalments from commencement. The ₹3 crore beyond the cap simply perishes; neither this section nor section 37 rescues pre-business spending.

options.text: ₹8 crore in year one — expenses of starting up deduct when business starts
options.misconception: converts capital pre-commencement spending into revenue
options.why: Before the business exists there is no business to deduct against, which is the very gap 35D fills — on its own instalment and cap terms, not on the claimant's.

citation.ref: Section 35D

items.scenario: Before commencing its ₹100 crore plant, a company spends ₹8 crore on feasibility studies, project reports and incorporation-related legal work — all within the specified list. In year one of operations the CFO claims the entire ₹8 crore, calling it revenue expenditure of setting up.

items.stem: Which of the three arrangements does Clause 1 permit?

options.text: Mr Iyer's and Mr Rao's — Mr Rao has completed articleship and works under Verma's supervision, which is what the clause is aimed at
options.misconception: reads supervision and training as a substitute for membership, when the clause asks only whether the person is a chartered accountant in practice
options.why: Nothing in Clause 1 turns on how well supervised the person is. It asks whether he is a chartered accountant in practice, and a semi-qualified assistant is not, however capable he is and however closely Verma watches the Nashik desk.

options.text: All three, provided Verma signs every report himself and the three men only meet clients and prepare files
options.misconception: confuses Clause 1, which is about practising in the member's name, with Clause 12, which is about who may sign
options.why: Clause 12 is the clause about signing, and Verma keeping the pen would answer that one. Clause 1 is about a different mischief — a person holding himself out to the public as practising in the member's name — and meeting clients in the firm's name at a desk in another town is exactly that.

options.text: Only Mr Iyer's — he alone satisfies both conditions, being a chartered accountant in practice and employed by Verma
options.why: Clause 1 permits a member to allow another person to practise in his name only where that person is also a chartered accountant in practice and is in partnership with or employed by him. Both conditions have to hold at once. Mr Iyer holds a certificate of practice and is employed, so he passes both. Mr Rao is not a member at all. Mr Sen is a member but, holding no certificate of practice, he is not a chartered accountant in practice, so his employment answers only the second condition and the first defeats him.
keywords: in partnership with or employed by him

options.text: Mr Iyer's and Mr Sen's — both are members of the Institute and both are on Verma's payroll
options.misconception: treats membership of the Institute as the same thing as being in practice, and so ignores the certificate of practice
options.why: Membership and practice are two different states. A member who has not taken out a certificate of practice is not a chartered accountant in practice, and the clause names the second, not the first. Mr Sen's employment satisfies half the test and the missing half is the half that matters.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 1

items.scenario: CA Verma runs a sole practice. To cover three towns he makes three arrangements. Mr Rao, who cleared the Intermediate examination and completed articleship but is not a member, runs the Nashik desk in the firm's name and meets clients there. Mr Iyer is a chartered accountant who holds a certificate of practice and is Verma's salaried employee; he works in the firm's name at Pune. Mr Sen is a chartered accountant employed by Verma who has never taken out a certificate of practice; he works in the firm's name at Nagpur.

items.stem: Which of the three breaches Clause 5, and does any other clause come into it?

options.text: Only Mr Khanna's arrangement, and only under Clause 2 — Clause 5 is about advertising, not about agents
options.misconception: collapses Clause 5 into the advertising and solicitation clauses, missing that it polices who brought the work in
options.why: Advertising is Clause 7 and solicitation is Clause 6. Clause 5 is a separate provision about how the business was secured, and its first limb names the person who is not an employee or a partner. Charging only under Clause 2 answers where the money went and leaves the procurement itself unanswered.

options.text: Mr Khanna's arrangement and the manager's calls — any canvassing for work is business secured by means not open to a chartered accountant
options.misconception: reads the second limb so widely that it swallows the first limb's careful exclusion of the member's own employees and partners
options.why: The clause's own words exclude an employee of such chartered accountant. A firm's salaried manager speaking to the firm's existing clients is the firm speaking, and reading the second limb to catch that would make the first limb's exclusion meaningless.
keywords: an employee of such chartered accountant

options.text: Only Mr Khanna's arrangement — and it breaches Clause 2 as well, because the share of fees also went to a non-member
options.why: Clause 5 catches a member who secures professional business through the services of a person who is not an employee of such chartered accountant or who is not his partner. Mr Khanna is neither, so the first limb is breached the moment he brings work in. The salaried manager is an employee, which is precisely the person the clause leaves alone, and responding to a tender is expressly outside the solicitation bar in Clause 6. The commission is a second, separate wrong — Clause 2 forbids paying any share of professional fees to a person who is not a member of the Institute — so one arrangement breaches two clauses, one about how the work was secured and one about where the fee went.

options.text: All three — a tender response is soliciting work from the public, however the tender was worded
options.misconception: forgets the proviso that lets a member respond to tenders and enquiries issued by users of professional services
options.why: The solicitation clause carries a proviso permitting a member to respond to tenders or enquiries issued by users of professional services and to secure work as a consequence. A bank that floats a tender has invited the offer, so the member is answering rather than soliciting.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 5, read with Clauses 2 and 6

items.scenario: A practising firm signs three arrangements in one year. It retains Mr Khanna, a business development consultant who is neither a partner nor an employee, on a monthly retainer plus two per cent of the fees of every certification engagement he introduces. It asks its own salaried manager, an employee of the firm, to call on existing clients about the firm's new transfer pricing practice. And it responds to a tender floated by a public sector bank for concurrent audit and is selected.

items.stem: Where does Bose stand?

options.text: Not guilty — whether the company complied with the Companies Act is the company's own affair and its officers' liability, not the incoming auditor's
options.misconception: treats compliance with the appointment provisions as owed only by the company, when Clause 9 makes the incoming auditor's failure to ascertain it his own misconduct
options.why: The company's default is the company's, but Clause 9 creates a duty on the member — to ascertain from the company, before accepting, whether the requirements have been duly complied with. His misconduct is not the removal; it is accepting without asking.

options.text: Not guilty — he communicated with the outgoing auditor in writing and received a clear reply, which is the whole of the incoming auditor's duty
options.misconception: treats Clause 8 as the only pre-acceptance duty, so a clean reply from the outgoing auditor is read as clearance for the appointment itself
options.why: Clause 8 is about a conversation between two professionals. Clause 9 is about the lawfulness of the appointment, and the outgoing auditor's silence cannot cure a removal that never went through section 140(1). Two duties, and he performed one.

options.text: Guilty under Clause 9 — writing to the outgoing auditor discharged Clause 8 and nothing else, and Clause 9 required him to ascertain that the requirements for the appointment had been duly complied with
options.why: Clause 8 and Clause 9 are two separate duties on the same appointment, and satisfying one says nothing about the other. Clause 8 asks for a letter to the outgoing auditor; Clause 9 asks the incoming auditor to ascertain from the company whether the requirements governing the appointment have been duly complied with. A removal before the expiry of the term needs a special resolution and the previous approval of the Central Government under section 140(1), and Bose never asked whether either existed. The letter he did write is therefore beside the point.

options.text: Guilty under Clause 8 as well, because a removal in dispute means the outgoing auditor's no-objection was needed before acceptance
options.misconception: converts the communication required by Clause 8 into a permission the outgoing auditor can withhold
options.why: Clause 8 requires communication in writing and nothing more; an outgoing auditor has never been able to veto his successor. Bose wrote, so Clause 8 is answered, and adding a second charge here would punish him for a duty that does not exist.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 9, read with section 140(1) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A company's board tells CA Bose that the existing auditor has been removed with immediate effect and offers him the appointment. Bose writes to the outgoing auditor, who replies that he has nothing to add, and Bose accepts. It emerges later that the removal was before the expiry of the auditor's term and that the company obtained neither the previous approval of the Central Government nor the special resolution of the members. Bose says he did everything the profession asked of him.

items.stem: Which signatures may lawfully be given on the firm's behalf?

options.text: The fellow partner's and the manager's — the manager is a chartered accountant employed by the firm, which is what the clause requires
options.misconception: reads the clause as though employment by the firm were enough, when its second limb excludes a member who is not a partner
options.why: Employment is enough under Clause 1, which governs practising in the member's name. It is not enough here, because Clause 12 names a member not being his partner as a person who may not sign. The two clauses draw their lines in different places on purpose.

options.text: All three — a certificate of net worth is not a balance sheet, a profit and loss account or a report, so the articled assistant's signature is outside the clause
options.misconception: reads the list of documents narrowly and forgets that a member may not allow a non-member to sign for the firm at all
options.why: The clause names a balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements, and a net worth certificate is a report on financial information issued in the firm's name. Reading the list as a loophole for certificates would let the least qualified person in the office sign the documents the public relies on most.

options.text: Only the fellow partner's — Clause 12 bars a member who is not his partner as firmly as it bars a non-member
options.why: Clause 12 makes it misconduct to allow a person not being a member of the Institute in practice, or a member not being his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm, any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements. The manager is a member, but he is not a partner, so the second limb catches him. The articled assistant is not a member at all. Only the fellow partner is inside both limbs, and the absent partner's email and the client's resolution change nothing, because authority to sign is not something either of them can confer.
keywords: balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements

options.text: The fellow partner's and the manager's, because the written authority and the client's board resolution together supply the authority
options.misconception: assumes signing authority can be delegated by agreement, when the clause fixes who may sign regardless of what anyone consents to
options.why: Neither an absent partner nor a client can widen the class of people Clause 12 allows. A resolution recording that the client is content proves only that the client is content. The prohibition runs against the member who allows the signature, not against the client who receives it.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 12

items.scenario: The signing partner of a firm is abroad when three documents fall due. He emails written authority for his manager, a chartered accountant in whole-time employment with the firm, to sign the audit report of a company; he asks his fellow partner to sign the audit report of a second company; and he asks an articled assistant to sign a net worth certificate. The client of the first company also passes a board resolution recording that it accepts the manager's signature.

items.stem: Which heads of misconduct do the three facts attract, and before which forum?

options.text: All three — Clause 1 for acting as a fellow, Clause 2 for not supplying the information called for, and Clause 3 for false information in a tender, all in Part III of the First Schedule, and so all before the Board of Discipline
options.why: Part III of the First Schedule binds every member. Clause 1 catches a member who, not being a fellow of the Institute, acts as a fellow of the Institute, which is what "FCA" on an associate's letterhead does. Clause 2 catches a member who does not supply the information called for by the Director (Discipline), and the merits of the complaint are no answer to it. Clause 3 catches false information given while responding to tenders. All three sit in the First Schedule, so the case goes before the Board of Discipline.

options.text: Only the silence, since a letterhead is a private matter between the member and his stationer and a tender is a commercial negotiation
options.misconception: treats representations made to clients and to tendering authorities as outside the disciplinary code because no audit opinion was involved
options.why: Part III applies to a member whether in practice or not and is not confined to audit work. Holding out as a fellow and overstating a firm's standing to a tendering authority are both representations the public relies on, and both are named in the Schedule.

options.text: All three, but before the Disciplinary Committee, because giving false information knowingly is a Second Schedule matter
options.misconception: assumes that dishonesty always routes a case to the heavier forum, when the routing follows the Schedule the clause sits in
options.why: Knowledge does move some charges to the Second Schedule, but only where a Second Schedule clause covers the facts. False information in a tender is named in Clause 3 of Part III of the First Schedule, so the routing follows that Schedule and the Board of Discipline hears it.

options.text: The letterhead under Clause 7 of Part I, the tender under Clause 3 of Part III, and nothing for the silence
options.misconception: files the false fellowship under the designation clause and treats silence towards the Institute's own machinery as no misconduct at all
options.why: Clause 7 of Part I is about advertising attainments and about designations other than chartered accountant; claiming a grade of membership the member does not hold is dealt with by Clause 1 of Part III. And silence is expressly misconduct — the clause names not supplying the information called for as the wrong itself.
keywords: not supplying the information called for

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part III, Clauses 1, 2 and 3

items.scenario: CA Menon is an associate of the Institute. His letterhead reads "CA S. Menon, FCA". The Director (Discipline), examining a complaint against him, writes three times asking for the working papers of one engagement; Menon does not reply, saying privately that the complaint is malicious and he will answer when it reaches a hearing. In the same year he bids for a government empanelment and states in the tender that his firm has four partners and eleven years of standing, knowing it has two partners and six.

items.stem: Which head does each fall under, and which forum hears it?

options.text: All three go before the Disciplinary Committee, because other misconduct is the graver charge and the Board of Discipline handles only clause-by-clause professional misconduct
options.misconception: treats other misconduct as a single grave head, when it is split across the two Schedules and routed like anything else
options.why: Other misconduct is not one head but two, and the routing works exactly as it does for professional misconduct. A matter under First Schedule Part IV goes before the Board of Discipline; only Second Schedule Part III reaches the Disciplinary Committee.

options.text: A and B are other misconduct under First Schedule Part IV and go before the Board of Discipline; C is other misconduct under Second Schedule Part III and goes before the Disciplinary Committee
options.why: First Schedule Part IV covers a conviction for an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months and, separately, an action that in the opinion of the Council brings disrepute to the profession or the Institute, whether or not related to professional work. A's three-month offence and B's disrepute both land there, so the Board of Discipline hears them. C's offence is punishable with imprisonment exceeding six months, which is Second Schedule Part III, so the Disciplinary Committee hears it. The dividing line is the term the offence carries, not the sentence awarded.

options.text: A and C are other misconduct; B is not, because a conviction by a court is what the head requires
options.misconception: reads both limbs of First Schedule Part IV as needing a court's finding, when the second limb turns only on the opinion of the Council
options.why: Part IV has two limbs and only the first needs a conviction. The second asks whether, in the opinion of the Council, the member brings disrepute to the profession or the Institute, and a member acquitted or never charged can still fall within it.

options.text: None of them — the Schedules punish professional misconduct, and nothing here arose out of professional work
options.misconception: assumes the Schedules reach only work done as a chartered accountant, missing that other misconduct is a separate head that expressly need not relate to professional work
options.why: Other misconduct exists precisely for conduct outside the practice. First Schedule Part IV says in terms that the action may be one whether or not related to his professional work, and a conviction under either Schedule needs no connection with an engagement.
keywords: whether or not related to his professional work

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part IV, and Second Schedule, Part III

items.scenario: Three members come before the Institute in the same month. A is convicted by a magistrate of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of up to three months and is let off with a fine. B is not convicted of anything, but a widely reported brawl at a housing society meeting leads the Council to form the opinion that his conduct has brought disrepute to the profession. C is convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of two years. None of the three facts arose out of professional work.

items.stem: Which clause is the cleanest charge, and why does the partner's review not save it?

options.text: Clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule alone — the failure is gross negligence, and Clause 2 is about disclosure of information
options.misconception: reaches for the negligence clause and misremembers Clause 2 of the Second Schedule as the confidentiality provision
options.why: Confidentiality is Clause 1 of that Part, not Clause 2. Gross negligence may well be present too, but Clause 2 fits these facts precisely, because it asks the one question the scenario answers — whose hands made the examination.

options.text: No clause is breached, because the firm used an expert's work and satisfied itself about the expert's competence and the relevance of the findings
options.misconception: borrows the auditor's use of an expert, which applies to a field outside accounting and auditing, to justify outsourcing the accounting examination itself
options.why: Using an expert covers expertise in a field other than accounting and auditing — a valuer, an actuary, a geologist. An examination of financial statements and the related records is the member's own field, and Clause 2 names exactly who may perform it.

options.text: No clause is breached, provided the consultancy worked under the firm's written supervision and its files were retained by the firm
options.misconception: treats supervision and file custody as making outside workers into employees in his firm
options.why: Supervision does not change who the workers are. The clause permits an employee in his firm, and a contracted consultancy is not that however closely it is instructed or however completely its papers end up in the firm's cabinet.

options.text: Clause 2 of Part I of the Second Schedule — the examination was made by none of the four permitted persons, and reading a summary is not making the examination
options.why: Clause 2 forbids certifying or submitting, in his name or the name of his firm, a report of an examination of financial statements unless the examination of such statements and the related records has been made by him or by a partner or an employee in his firm or by another chartered accountant in practice. The outside consultancy is none of those four. The partner's questions may show diligence, but the clause asks who made the examination, and on these facts nobody inside the permitted circle did.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 2

items.scenario: A firm is asked to certify a company's claim for an export incentive, which requires an examination of the financial statements and the related shipping and costing records. To meet the deadline the firm engages an outside consultancy of commerce graduates, none of them members of the Institute and none employed by the firm, to carry out the entire examination. The engagement partner reads their summary memorandum, asks two questions, and signs the certificate in the firm's name.

items.stem: Has the firm breached Clause 3 of Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: No — the assumptions genuinely were reasonable and the file proves it, so there was nothing false in the presentation
options.misconception: tests the clause by the quality of the underlying work rather than by the belief the wording invites
options.why: The clause does not ask whether the work was good. It asks whether the name was used in a manner which may lead to the belief that he vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, and a firm with an immaculate file can still lend its name to a sentence that promises the future.
keywords: vouches for the accuracy of the forecast

options.text: Yes — a chartered accountant may not associate his name with projected figures at all, whatever words are used
options.misconception: turns a rule about how the name is used into a ban on working with prospective financial information
options.why: Members report on prospective financial information regularly and properly. What Clause 3 controls is the manner of the association, so a report on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis, with a plain warning that actual results are likely to differ, is permitted work.

options.text: Yes — the words used lead the reader to believe the firm vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, and careful work on the assumptions does not answer that
