Para 17 gives an intangible asset where the operator receives a right to charge users of the public service, since those amounts are contingent on the extent that the public uses the service. Para 22 then recognises borrowing costs as an expense unless the operator has a contractual right to an intangible asset, in which case they are capitalised during the construction phase.

options.text: The road is the operator's property, plant and equipment under both versions, depreciated over the twenty-year concession, with the ₹70 crore capitalised into its cost either way
options.misconception: reads physical possession and operation of the infrastructure as control of it
options.why: Para 11 answers this directly — infrastructure within the scope of the Appendix shall not be recognised as property, plant and equipment of the operator, because the arrangement does not convey the right to control its use. The operator has access to operate the road on behalf of the grantor on the contract's terms, which makes it a service provider rather than an owner.

options.text: A financial asset under both versions, since the operator will be paid for its construction services either way, with the ₹70 crore expensed under both
options.misconception: reads any expectation of cash as the unconditional contractual right para 16 requires
options.why: Para 17 answers version two — a right to charge users of the public service is not an unconditional right to receive cash, because the amounts are contingent on the extent that the public uses the service. Traffic risk sits with the operator there, so it holds an intangible asset, and para 22 then capitalises the borrowing costs during construction rather than expensing them.

options.text: An intangible asset under both versions, because the operator's real asset in either case is the twenty-year concession right, with the ₹70 crore capitalised under both
options.misconception: treats the concession licence as the asset regardless of who carries the demand risk
options.why: The Appendix classifies by the nature of the consideration the grantor gives, not by the label on the contract. Para 16 recognises a financial asset where the grantor contractually guarantees to pay specified or determinable amounts, which is version one, and para 22 then requires those borrowing costs to be recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 11, 16, 17 and 22

items.scenario: An operator builds a 60 km toll road for a state authority under a twenty-year concession, spending ₹900 crore and finishing on 31 March 2026, and must operate and maintain the road for the whole term. Two versions of the contract are under discussion. Under version one the authority contractually guarantees a specified annual amount whatever the traffic. Under version two the operator's only entitlement is to collect tolls from road users for twenty years, with no guarantee of any kind. The operator incurred ₹70 crore of borrowing costs during construction on loans raised for the project.

items.stem: How much borrowing cost does the company capitalise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹65.04 crore — the same ₹47.04 crore on general borrowings, but ₹18 crore on the specific loan without deducting the ₹1.5 crore earned on the deposits
options.misconception: ignores para 12's deduction of investment income on the temporary investment of specific borrowings
options.why: Para 12 determines the amount eligible for capitalisation on a specific borrowing as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any investment income on the temporary investment of those borrowings. The ₹1.5 crore earned on the idle ₹40 crore is not a separate windfall to be left out of the calculation; it reduces the cost carried into the asset.

options.text: ₹65.09 crore — a single 9.571 per cent rate, the weighted average of every borrowing including the specific loan, applied to the whole ₹680 crore of expenditure
options.misconception: builds the capitalisation rate from all borrowings, when para 14 excludes those made specifically for the asset
options.why: Para 14 defines the capitalisation rate as the weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to the borrowings of the entity that are outstanding during the period, other than borrowings made specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset. Folding the specific loan into the pool counts it twice, because para 12 has already dealt with that loan directly and at its own rate.

options.text: ₹63.54 crore — ₹16.5 crore on the specific loan and ₹47.04 crore from applying a 9.8 per cent capitalisation rate to the ₹480 crore of expenditure not met from it
options.why: Para 12 makes the amount eligible on funds borrowed specifically the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing less any investment income on the temporary investment of those borrowings, so ₹18 crore less ₹1.5 crore is ₹16.5 crore. Para 14 applies a capitalisation rate to the expenditure met from general borrowings, the rate being the weighted average of the borrowing costs applicable to the entity's borrowings outstanding during the period other than those made specifically for a qualifying asset — ₹33 crore plus ₹16 crore over ₹500 crore, or 9.8 per cent — which on ₹480 crore gives ₹47.04 crore. The ₹63.54 crore total sits below the ₹67 crore actually incurred, so the para 14 ceiling does not bite.

options.text: ₹67 crore — the whole of the borrowing costs incurred during the year, since the plant is a qualifying asset and every borrowing helped to fund it
options.misconception: reads the para 14 cap as the amount to capitalise rather than as a ceiling on it
options.why: The sentence saying the amount an entity capitalises during a period shall not exceed the amount of borrowing costs it incurred during that period is a ceiling, not a measure. Para 14 measures the amount by applying the capitalisation rate to the expenditure on the asset, and ₹480 crore at 9.8 per cent plus ₹16.5 crore under para 12 gives ₹63.54 crore, comfortably inside the ceiling.

citation.ref: para 12 and 14

items.scenario: A company is constructing a plant, a qualifying asset, throughout the year ended 31 March 2026. It raised a ₹200 crore term loan specifically for the plant at 9 per cent, of which ₹40 crore sat in deposits for part of the year and earned ₹1.5 crore. Its general borrowings, outstanding all year, are ₹300 crore of debentures at 11 per cent and a ₹200 crore working capital loan at 8 per cent. Expenditure on the plant averaged ₹680 crore over the year, of which ₹200 crore was met from the specific loan.

items.stem: What basic earnings per share does the company report for the year ended 31 March 2026, and what happens to the comparative?

options.text: ₹13.80 for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the comparative restated from ₹12.50 to ₹10.00
options.misconception: treats the whole rights issue as a bonus issue, when only its bonus element is retrospective
options.why: Counting all 50,00,000 shares from the start of both years gives ₹13.80 and ₹10.00, and treats money that arrived on 1 October 2025 as though it had always been there. Appendix A para A2 isolates the gift from the fresh money through the factor of fair value per share immediately before the exercise of rights over the theoretical ex-rights fair value per share, and only that factor is retrospective.

options.text: ₹14.76 for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the comparative for the year ended 31 March 2025 restated from ₹12.50 to ₹11.50
options.why: Para 27(b) treats a rights issue priced below fair value as containing a bonus element. Appendix A para A2 multiplies the shares outstanding before the issue by the fair value per share immediately before the exercise of rights over the theoretical ex-rights fair value per share. That theoretical ex-rights price is ₹92 — ₹40,00,00,000 of existing value plus ₹6,00,00,000 of proceeds, over the 50,00,000 shares outstanding afterwards — so the factor is 100 over 92. The 40,00,000 shares of the first half year become 43,47,826 and weight to 21,73,913, the 50,00,000 of the second half weight to 25,00,000, and ₹6,90,00,000 over 46,73,913 shares is ₹14.76. The same factor restates the prior year to ₹11.50.

options.text: ₹14.76 for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the ₹12.50 comparative left as published because the rights issue happened after that year had ended
options.misconception: applies the adjustment factor to the current year only, when a bonus element is applied to every period presented
options.why: The current year is computed correctly and the comparative is not. Appendix A para A2 says the adjusted number of shares is used in calculating basic and diluted earnings per share for all periods before the rights issue, which is what moves the comparative from ₹12.50 to ₹11.50. Leaving it alone would show growth that is an artefact of the share count.

options.text: ₹15.33 for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the ₹12.50 comparative left exactly as published
options.misconception: treats a rights issue as an ordinary issue for cash, ignoring the bonus element para 27(b) identifies
options.why: An issue at full fair value brings in resources in proportion to the shares issued and needs no retrospective adjustment, which is why simply weighting 40,00,000 for six months and 50,00,000 for six gives ₹15.33. But a rights issue priced at ₹60 against a fair value of ₹100 hands existing shareholders part of the value for nothing, and para 27(b) treats that part as a bonus element, which by its nature is applied to every period presented.

citation.ref: para 27(b), with Appendix A, para A2

items.scenario: A company had 40,00,000 equity shares in issue throughout the year ended 31 March 2025 and reported basic earnings per share of ₹12.50 for that year on a profit of ₹5,00,00,000. On 1 October 2025 it made a rights issue of one new share for every four held, at ₹60, when the fair value of a share immediately before the exercise of the rights was ₹100. All the rights were taken up. Profit attributable to equity holders for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹6,90,00,000.

items.stem: What income tax expense does the company recognise in each of the two quarters?

options.text: ₹20.8 crore in the first quarter and ₹33.2 crore in the second, being the ₹54 crore year-to-date charge at 30 per cent less the ₹20.8 crore already taken, with the first quarter left as reported
options.why: Para 30(c) recognises income tax expense in each interim period on the best estimate of the weighted average annual income tax rate expected for the full financial year, and adds that amounts accrued in one interim period may have to be adjusted in a subsequent interim period of that financial year if the estimate of the annual rate changes. Para 28 makes the measurement year-to-date, so the half year carries ₹180 crore at 30 per cent, being ₹54 crore, and the second quarter absorbs the whole ₹33.2 crore difference. Para 36 leaves the amounts reported in the first quarter alone.
keywords: weighted average annual income tax rate

options.text: Nothing in the first quarter and ₹54 crore in the second, since the annual tax rate can only be estimated reliably once the year is further advanced
options.misconception: defers the interim tax charge until the annual rate firms up, when para 30(c) asks for a best estimate each period
options.why: Para 30(c) asks for the best estimate of the weighted average annual income tax rate expected for the full financial year, not for certainty. Waiting would leave the first quarter's profit looking untaxed and the second quarter's looking disproportionately taxed, which is exactly the distortion the year-to-date measurement in para 28 exists to prevent.

options.text: ₹24 crore for the first quarter, its published statements restated at the revised rate, and ₹30 crore in the second
options.misconception: restates a published interim period, which para 36 refuses
options.why: The revised estimate is dealt with inside the year, not backwards. Para 36 says the amounts reported in prior interim periods are not retrospectively adjusted, and para 30(c) puts the correction into the subsequent interim period instead. So the first quarter keeps its ₹20.8 crore and the catch-up lands in the second.

options.text: ₹20.8 crore in the first quarter and ₹30 crore in the second, applying the revised 30 per cent rate to the second quarter's own ₹100 crore
options.misconception: measures a quarter as a discrete standalone period instead of on the year-to-date basis para 28 requires
options.why: This is the discrete period approach, and Ind AS 34 does not use it. Para 28 says the frequency of an entity's reporting shall not affect the measurement of its annual results, and that to achieve that objective measurements for interim reporting purposes shall be made on a year-to-date basis. Taxing only the quarter's own profit at the new rate would leave the first quarter's ₹80 crore taxed for ever at 26 per cent.

citation.ref: para 30(c), read with para 28 and para 36

items.scenario: A company reports quarterly. At the end of the first quarter, 30 June 2025, it expects a weighted average annual income tax rate of 26 per cent for the year ending 31 March 2026, taking into account a tax holiday on part of its income; profit before tax for that quarter is ₹80 crore. By the end of the second quarter, 30 September 2025, the expected annual rate has risen to 30 per cent, and profit before tax for the half year is ₹180 crore, of which ₹100 crore arose in the second quarter.

items.stem: What must the company disclose beyond its single segment's figures?

options.text: Nothing beyond the single segment's own figures, because paragraphs 32 to 34 are aimed at entities that have more than one reportable segment
options.misconception: reads the entity-wide disclosures as segment disclosures, when para 31 applies them to single-segment entities too
options.why: Para 31 opens with exactly this point — paragraphs 32 to 34 apply to all entities subject to this Ind AS including those entities that have a single reportable segment. The only relief it gives is that the information need not be repeated where it has already been provided as part of the reportable segment information, and here it has not.

options.text: Revenue and non-current assets broken out for India and for each of the ten foreign countries individually, plus the major customer disclosure
options.misconception: reads para 33 as a country-by-country schedule, when it asks for domicile, all foreign countries in total, and material individual countries only
options.why: Para 33 asks for revenues attributed to the entity's country of domicile and to all foreign countries in total, with an individual foreign country disclosed separately only where its revenues are material. The United Arab Emirates at ₹250 crore of ₹1,000 crore is material and is shown; the nine countries sharing ₹130 crore are not each broken out, and para 33 permits but does not require subtotals for groups of countries.

options.text: Revenue for India and for all foreign countries in total with the United Arab Emirates shown separately as material, the same split for non-current assets, and the fact that one customer contributed ₹140 crore together with the segment reporting it, but not that customer's name
options.why: Para 31 applies paragraphs 32 to 34 to all entities subject to this Ind AS, including those that have a single reportable segment, so one segment is no escape. Para 33 requires revenues from external customers attributed to the entity's country of domicile and to all foreign countries in total, disclosing any individual foreign country separately where its revenues are material, with the same split for non-current assets. Para 34 requires the fact of a single external customer at 10 per cent or more of revenues, the total revenue from each such customer and the identity of the reporting segment, while stating that the entity need not disclose the identity of a major customer.

options.text: The geographical and product information, and the fact of the ₹140 crore customer together with the customer's name, since a reader cannot judge the concentration without knowing who it is
options.misconception: reads para 34 as requiring the major customer to be named
options.why: Para 34 requires the fact, the total amount of revenues from each such customer, and the identity of the segment or segments reporting those revenues. It then says in terms that the entity need not disclose the identity of a major customer or the amount each segment reports from that customer. What it does add is that a group of entities known to be under common control counts as a single customer.

citation.ref: para 31, 33 and 34

items.scenario: A company has concluded, correctly, that it has a single reportable segment. Revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was ₹1,000 crore, made up of ₹620 crore from India, ₹250 crore from the United Arab Emirates and ₹130 crore spread across nine other countries. One external customer, a state electricity board, accounted for ₹140 crore of that revenue. Non-current assets other than financial instruments and deferred tax assets stand at ₹700 crore in India and ₹90 crore in the United Arab Emirates. None of this information appears in the segment note.

items.stem: What expense does the company recognise for the year ended 31 March 2027?

options.text: ₹80 lakh — the ₹40 lakh original charge plus the whole ₹40 lakh of incremental fair value recognised at once on 1 April 2026, the repricing being complete on that date
options.misconception: recognises the incremental fair value immediately, which B43(a) does only where the modification occurs after vesting date
options.why: Para B43(a) recognises the incremental fair value granted immediately only where the modification occurs after vesting date. This repricing happened on 1 April 2026, inside the vesting period, so the incremental amount is included in the measurement of services received over the period from the modification date until the modified equity instruments vest — two years, at ₹20 lakh a year.

options.text: ₹40 lakh, unchanged, because the ₹45 fair value after the repricing is still well below the ₹80 fair value at which the options were granted
options.misconception: nets the repricing benefit against the fall in value since grant, when B43(a) measures both fair values at the modification date
options.why: Para B43(a) compares the modified instrument with the original instrument, both estimated as at the date of the modification, and never against the grant date figure. The fall from ₹80 to ₹25 is the market moving, which the grant date measurement has already absorbed once and for all. The ₹20 an option the board handed over on 1 April 2026 is a fresh benefit and is recognised in addition.

options.text: ₹60 lakh — the ₹40 lakh annual charge based on the ₹80 grant date fair value, plus ₹20 lakh being half of the ₹40 lakh incremental fair value spread over the two years to vesting
options.why: Para 27 requires the entity to recognise, as a minimum, the services received measured at the grant date fair value of the equity instruments granted, irrespective of any modification, and in addition to recognise the effects of modifications that increase the total fair value of the arrangement. Appendix B para B43(a) measures the incremental fair value granted as the difference between the fair value of the modified equity instrument and that of the original equity instrument, both estimated as at the date of the modification — ₹45 less ₹25, being ₹20 an option or ₹40 lakh over 200,000 options — and includes it over the period from the modification date until the modified instruments vest, which is two years, alongside the original charge over the remainder of the original vesting period.

options.text: A credit of ₹12.5 lakh for the year, remeasuring the whole award at the ₹45 post-modification fair value so that the cumulative charge becomes ₹67.5 lakh against the ₹80 lakh already recognised
options.misconception: remeasures an equity-settled award at a later fair value, when para 27 fixes a minimum at grant date fair value
options.why: An equity-settled award is measured once, and para 27 says the entity shall recognise as a minimum the services received measured at the grant date fair value of the instruments granted, irrespective of any modification. Only the incremental fair value is added on top. Remeasuring downward to ₹45 would let a repricing that benefited employees reduce the total expense, which is precisely what that minimum prevents.

citation.ref: para 27, with Appendix B, para B43(a)

items.scenario: On 1 April 2024 a company granted 1,000 share options to each of 200 employees, vesting on 31 March 2028 subject to continued service, with a grant date fair value of ₹80 an option. By 1 April 2026 the share price had fallen badly and the board repriced the options, leaving the number of options and the vesting date unchanged. Immediately before the repricing an option's fair value was ₹25 and immediately afterwards it was ₹45. All 200 employees are still expected to remain until vesting.

items.stem: What does the company present to satisfy the disclosure on liabilities arising from financing activities?

options.text: A reconciliation from ₹500 crore to ₹633 crore showing ₹120 crore of financing cash flows, the ₹40 crore of borrowings assumed with the subsidiary being counted as a drawdown alongside the ₹200 crore
options.misconception: treats an assumed liability as a cash movement, when para 43 keeps non-cash transactions out of the statement of cash flows altogether
options.why: No cash moved on the ₹40 crore. Para 43 excludes investing and financing transactions that do not require the use of cash or cash equivalents from the statement of cash flows, and para 44B(b) gives that amount its own line as a change arising from obtaining or losing control of subsidiaries or other businesses. Putting it in the cash column would overstate financing cash flows and leave the cash flow statement disagreeing with the bank.

options.text: A reconciliation from ₹500 crore to ₹580 crore covering only the ₹200 crore drawn and the ₹120 crore repaid, the rest being movements no cash passed through
options.misconception: reads the disclosure as a restatement of the financing section of the cash flow statement, when para 44A expressly reaches the non-cash movements as well
options.why: Para 44A asks for changes in liabilities arising from financing activities including both changes arising from cash flows and non-cash changes. A disclosure confined to the cash would be an exact copy of the financing section already presented and would tell a reader nothing new. It also fails to reach the closing balance sheet figure of ₹633 crore, which is the whole point of the reconciliation.

options.text: A single reconciling line of ₹133 crore between opening and closing borrowings, since the Standard asks for the movement and not for its causes
options.misconception: gives the total movement without the five-way split para 44B requires
options.why: Para 44B lists what an entity shall disclose to the extent necessary to satisfy para 44A — changes from financing cash flows, changes arising from obtaining or losing control of subsidiaries or other businesses, the effect of changes in foreign exchange rates, changes in fair values, and other changes. A one-line movement hides that ₹53 crore of the increase never involved cash, and para 44E adds that where the disclosure is combined with other assets and liabilities these changes must still be shown separately.

options.text: A reconciliation from ₹500 crore to ₹633 crore, showing ₹80 crore of financing cash flows and ₹53 crore of non-cash movements split as ₹15 crore of exchange effect, ₹40 crore from obtaining control of a subsidiary, ₹10 crore negative from fair values and ₹8 crore of other changes
options.why: Para 44A requires disclosures that let users evaluate changes in liabilities arising from financing activities, including both changes arising from cash flows and non-cash changes, and para 44D names a reconciliation between the opening and closing balance sheet amounts as one way to fulfil it. Para 44B fixes the five buckets, so the ₹200 crore drawn less the ₹120 crore repaid is the ₹80 crore of financing cash flows, and the ₹15 crore exchange effect, the ₹40 crore assumed on obtaining control of a subsidiary, the ₹10 crore fair value fall and the ₹8 crore of other changes are the non-cash changes. Five hundred plus eighty plus fifteen plus forty less ten plus eight is ₹633 crore.

citation.ref: para 44A, 44B and 44D, with para 43

items.scenario: A listed company's borrowings stood at ₹500 crore on 1 April 2025. During the year ended 31 March 2026 it drew fresh loans of ₹200 crore in cash and repaid ₹120 crore in cash. An exchange loss of ₹15 crore arose on a dollar-denominated loan. It acquired a subsidiary and assumed the subsidiary's borrowings of ₹40 crore, no cash passing for those borrowings. A borrowing designated at fair value through profit or loss fell in value by ₹10 crore, and ₹8 crore of capitalised transaction costs were amortised into the carrying amount of the loans.

items.stem: What must the manufacturer disclose for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: Nothing this year, because the supplier finance requirements apply to annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026 and the company's first affected year is the one ending 31 March 2027
options.misconception: pushes the Indian application date out by a year
options.why: The effective date section of Ind AS 7 says an entity shall apply the supplier finance amendments, which added paragraphs 44F to 44H, for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025. The year ended 31 March 2026 began on 1 April 2025 and is therefore the first year in which the disclosure is required, with the transition relief covering only comparatives, certain opening figures and interim periods in that first year.

options.text: The reverse factoring balance must be reclassified out of trade payables into borrowings, and the cash outflow moved from operating to financing activities
options.misconception: turns a disclosure requirement into a reclassification rule, which paras 44F to 44H never make
options.why: Para 44H(b)(i) asks for the carrying amounts and the associated line items presented in the balance sheet, which presupposes that the entity has already decided where the liability sits and simply has to say where. Whether the liability remains a trade payable or has become a borrowing turns on derecognition and the substance of the arrangement under Ind AS 109 and Ind AS 1, not on the new disclosure, and the same is true of where the outflow sits in the statement of cash flows.

options.text: Only the reverse factoring is a supplier finance arrangement, and for it the company gives the terms and conditions, opening and closing carrying amounts with their balance sheet line items, how much of that the bank has already paid the suppliers, the range of payment due dates against comparable trade payables, and the non-cash changes — the year ended 31 March 2026 being the first year the requirement applies
options.why: Para 44G describes a supplier finance arrangement as one where a finance provider offers to pay amounts the entity owes its suppliers and the entity agrees to pay at the same date or later, which is the reverse factoring exactly. The same paragraph says arrangements that are solely credit enhancements, such as letters of credit used as guarantees, and instruments used to settle directly with a supplier, such as credit cards, are not supplier finance arrangements. Para 44H then lists the terms and conditions, the carrying amounts and associated line items at the beginning and end of the period, the amounts for which suppliers have already received payment from the finance providers, the range of payment due dates against comparable trade payables, and the non-cash changes. The Indian application date is annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025.

options.text: All three are supplier finance arrangements, since each of them involves a bank standing between the company and its suppliers, and all three are disclosed in aggregate
options.misconception: reads any bank involvement in the payables cycle as a supplier finance arrangement, ignoring the two exclusions written into para 44G
options.why: Para 44G excludes two things by name. Arrangements that are solely credit enhancements for the entity, financial guarantees including letters of credit used as guarantees among them, are not a supplier finance arrangement, because the bank never takes the entity's place as the payer. Nor are instruments the entity uses to settle directly with a supplier, credit cards being the example given. Only the reverse factoring extends the entity's payment terms in the way the definition describes.

citation.ref: para 44F, 44G and 44H, with the Indian application date in the effective date section

items.scenario: For the year ended 31 March 2026 a manufacturer has three arrangements with its bankers. Under the first, a bank pays the manufacturer's suppliers on the invoice due date and the manufacturer pays the bank ninety days later; the manufacturer calls it reverse factoring and the balance sits in trade payables. Under the second, the bank issues letters of credit that guarantee the manufacturer's payment to certain suppliers but never pays them itself. Under the third, the company settles small supplier bills directly using corporate credit cards.

items.stem: In what order must management work, and what may it use?

options.text: The Framework's definitions first, because they are the conceptual foundation, and only where the Framework is silent may an Ind AS on a similar and related issue be used
options.misconception: inverts the two limbs of para 11, putting the Framework above the analogous Standard
options.why: Para 11 lists the requirements in Ind ASs dealing with similar and related issues at (a) and the definitions, recognition criteria and measurement concepts in the Framework at (b), in that order and expressly in descending order. An analogy to a Standard the Board has already worked through beats a first-principles reading of the Framework, because the Standard is the Framework already applied to a related problem.

options.text: Any of the four may be picked, so long as the policy chosen gives information that is relevant and reliable, which is the only test para 10 sets
options.misconception: reads para 10's relevance and reliability objective as the whole of the rule and drops the mandatory hierarchy in para 11
options.why: Para 10 sets the objective and para 11 says how it is reached. Para 11 opens with the words in making the judgement described in paragraph 10, management shall refer to, and consider the applicability of, the following sources in descending order. Shall and descending order are both doing work. A free choice among four sources would let the answer be picked first and the authority found afterwards.

options.text: Ind AS 37 first as an Ind AS dealing with a similar and related issue, then the Framework's definitions and recognition criteria; only after those may it look to the recent pronouncement of the International Accounting Standards Board, and to the United States rule only in the absence of an IASB pronouncement and only where nothing conflicts with the first two
options.why: Para 11 makes management refer to, and consider the applicability of, two sources in descending order — the requirements in Ind ASs dealing with similar and related issues, and then the definitions, recognition criteria and measurement concepts for assets, liabilities, income and expenses in the Framework. Para 12 is permissive and comes after it, and the Indian text orders it too: management may also first consider the most recent pronouncements of International Accounting Standards Board and in absence thereof those of the other standard-setting bodies that use a similar conceptual framework, other accounting literature and accepted industry practices, to the extent that these do not conflict with the sources in paragraph 11.

options.text: The United States rule may be adopted straight away, since para 12 lets management consider the pronouncements of other standard-setting bodies and accepted industry practice
options.misconception: treats para 12's optional sources as free-standing, missing both the precedence given to IASB pronouncements and the bar on conflicting with para 11
options.why: Para 12 is subordinate twice over. It says management may also first consider the most recent pronouncements of International Accounting Standards Board and in absence thereof those of the other standard-setting bodies — so an IASB pronouncement on the same fact pattern comes ahead of the United States rule — and it ends by confining all of it to the extent that these do not conflict with the sources in paragraph 11. Convenience is not one of the criteria.

citation.ref: para 10, 11 and 12

items.scenario: A company enters a novel arrangement for which no Ind AS applies specifically. Its finance team finds that Ind AS 37 deals with a closely similar and related issue, that the Framework's definitions of a liability and of an expense speak directly to the arrangement, that the International Accounting Standards Board has issued a recent pronouncement on almost the same fact pattern, and that the United States standard setter has a long-standing rule that would give a different and more convenient answer.

items.stem: What is the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹40 crore — ₹20 crore on the airframe, ₹15 crore on the engines and ₹5 crore on the remainder
options.why: Para 43 requires each part of an item of property, plant and equipment with a cost that is significant in relation to the total cost of the item to be depreciated separately, and para 44 gives the airframe and engines of an aircraft as its own example. Four hundred over twenty is ₹20 crore and one hundred and fifty over ten is ₹15 crore. Para 46 then says that to the extent an entity depreciates separately some parts of an item, it also depreciates separately the remainder of the item, the remainder consisting of the parts that are individually not significant, so the ₹50 crore over ten years adds ₹5 crore.
keywords: significant in relation to the total cost

options.text: ₹60 crore, depreciating the whole ₹600 crore over the ten-year life of the shortest-lived significant part
options.misconception: applies the shortest component life to the entire asset instead of a life to each part
options.why: Para 43 asks for a separate charge for each part with a cost significant in relation to the total cost of the item, and para 50 allocates each depreciable amount over its own useful life. Writing the airframe off in ten years understates the carrying amount of an asset the airline will still be flying in year fifteen, and prudence is not a reason to do it.

options.text: ₹35 crore — ₹20 crore on the airframe and ₹15 crore on the engines, the ₹50 crore of fittings staying at cost because no part of it is individually significant
options.misconception: leaves the remainder undepreciated once the significant parts are stripped out, when para 46 requires it to be depreciated too
options.why: Para 46 is written for exactly this: to the extent that an entity depreciates separately some parts of an item of property, plant and equipment, it also depreciates separately the remainder of the item, and the remainder consists of the parts of the item that are individually not significant. Where expectations for those parts vary, approximation techniques may be used, which is what the ten-year average is. Nothing lets the remainder sit at cost.

options.text: ₹30 crore, depreciating the whole ₹600 crore over the twenty-year life of the aircraft as a single asset
options.misconception: treats the aircraft as one asset with one useful life, which is exactly what para 43 forbids
options.why: Para 43 makes separate depreciation of significant parts a requirement, not a refinement. Using twenty years for the engines would carry them for a decade after they have been replaced, and para 44 gives the airframe and engines as the illustration precisely because their consumption patterns differ.

citation.ref: para 43, 44 and 46, with para 50

items.scenario: An airline buys an aircraft on 1 April 2025 for ₹600 crore. Of that, ₹400 crore is the airframe, with a useful life of twenty years; ₹150 crore is the two engines, with a useful life of ten years; and the remaining ₹50 crore is made up of seats, galleys, avionics and cabin fittings, no one of which has a cost significant in relation to the total cost of the aircraft, and which the airline expects to consume over ten years on average. Residual values are nil throughout and the airline depreciates on a straight-line basis.

items.stem: How does the company account for the year's movements on the plant and the provision?

options.text: Charge the ₹6 crore unwinding to profit or loss and deduct the whole ₹50 crore from the plant, leaving it at a negative carrying amount of ₹15 crore to be absorbed by future additions
options.misconception: ignores the cap in Appendix A para 5(b), which stops the deduction at the asset's carrying amount
options.why: Para 5(b) says in terms that the amount deducted from the cost of the asset shall not exceed its carrying amount, and that if a decrease in the liability exceeds the carrying amount of the asset, the excess shall be recognised immediately in profit or loss. A negative carrying amount is not an outcome the Standard contemplates, and the ₹15 crore is a gain the company has already earned, not one to be held back against future spending.
keywords: recognised immediately in profit or loss

options.text: Charge the ₹6 crore unwinding to profit or loss as a finance cost, then deduct the ₹50 crore fall in the liability from the plant only as far as its ₹35 crore carrying amount, taking the plant to nil and the remaining ₹15 crore immediately to profit or loss
options.why: Appendix A para 8 recognises the periodic unwinding of the discount in profit or loss as a finance cost as it occurs and says capitalisation under Ind AS 23 is not permitted, so the provision goes from ₹80 crore to ₹86 crore before the re-estimate and the fall to ₹36 crore is ₹50 crore. Para 4 sends changes from the estimated amount of the outflow or from the discount rate to paras 5 to 7. Para 5(a) deducts the change from the cost of the related asset and para 5(b) caps the amount deducted at the asset's carrying amount, so ₹35 crore comes off the plant and the excess of ₹15 crore is recognised immediately in profit or loss.
keywords: recognised immediately in profit or loss

options.text: Add the ₹6 crore unwinding to the carrying amount of the plant as a borrowing cost on a qualifying asset, and deduct ₹50 crore from the resulting ₹41 crore, leaving the plant at nil and ₹9 crore in profit or loss
options.misconception: capitalises the unwinding of the discount, which Appendix A para 8 forbids outright
options.why: Para 8 gives no room for judgement — the periodic unwinding of the discount shall be recognised in profit or loss as a finance cost as it occurs, and capitalisation under Ind AS 23 is not permitted. Capitalising it would inflate the base against which the fall in the liability is netted and would understate this year's finance cost by ₹6 crore.

options.text: Charge the ₹6 crore unwinding to profit or loss and recognise the ₹50 crore decrease in other comprehensive income as an increase in the revaluation surplus on the plant
options.misconception: applies the revaluation model treatment in Appendix A para 6 to an asset carried under the cost model
options.why: Para 6 opens with the words if the related asset is measured using the revaluation model, and only then does a decrease in the liability increase the revaluation surplus through other comprehensive income. This plant is on the cost model, so para 5 governs, and there is no revaluation surplus in existence for the credit to sit in.

citation.ref: Appendix A, para 4, 5, 6 and 8

items.scenario: A chemicals company carries a plant under the cost model. At 1 April 2025 the plant's carrying amount was ₹35 crore and the decommissioning provision recognised as part of its original cost stood at ₹80 crore. During the year ended 31 March 2026 the unwinding of the discount on that provision was ₹6 crore. At 31 March 2026 a new engineering study and a rise in the market discount rate cut the estimated present value of the decommissioning obligation to ₹36 crore. No borrowing costs are being capitalised on any qualifying asset.

items.stem: How much is capitalised as an intangible asset at 31 March 2026 and how much is expensed?

options.text: ₹150 lakh capitalised and ₹130 lakh expensed, the whole of the post-1 October spend going into the asset because the criteria were met throughout that period
options.misconception: capitalises every rupee spent after the criteria were met, missing the para 67 exclusions
options.why: Meeting the para 57 conditions opens the door; it does not decide what walks through it. Para 66 confines the cost to directly attributable costs necessary to create, produce and prepare the asset to be capable of operating in the manner intended by management, and para 67 names selling, administrative and other general overhead expenditure among the items that are not components of that cost. The ₹15 lakh is expensed.

options.text: ₹135 lakh capitalised and ₹145 lakh expensed
options.why: Para 57 recognises an intangible asset arising from development if, and only if, the entity can demonstrate all six conditions, which happened on 1 October 2025. Para 65 makes the cost the sum of expenditure incurred from the date when the intangible asset first meets the recognition criteria, so the ₹40 lakh of research under para 54 and the ₹90 lakh spent before the criteria were met stay in expense. Para 67 keeps selling and administrative overheads out of the cost of an internally generated intangible asset, so ₹15 lakh of the ₹150 lakh is expensed and ₹135 lakh is capitalised, leaving ₹145 lakh in profit or loss.

options.text: ₹225 lakh capitalised and ₹55 lakh expensed, the ₹90 lakh spent on the chosen candidate being brought back into the cost of the asset once the criteria were met
options.misconception: reinstates expenditure already recognised as an expense, which para 71 prohibits outright
options.why: Para 71 says expenditure on an intangible item that was initially recognised as an expense shall not be recognised as part of the cost of an intangible asset at a later date, and para 65 points at para 71 for exactly this reason. The ₹90 lakh was spent while the entity could not demonstrate the availability of resources to complete the asset, so it was an expense when incurred and it stays one.

options.text: Nothing capitalised and the whole ₹280 lakh expensed, since a pharmaceutical project cannot be shown to generate probable future economic benefits until regulatory approval is granted
options.misconception: reads para 57 as requiring certainty of outcome rather than demonstration of the six conditions
options.why: Para 57 asks the entity to demonstrate how the intangible asset will generate probable future economic benefits, and para 60 says that is assessed using the principles in Ind AS 36. Probable is not certain, and para 58 records that in the development phase an entity can in some instances identify an intangible asset and demonstrate that it will generate probable future economic benefits. Treating every development cost as research collapses the distinction para 54 and para 57 draw.

items.scenario: A pharmaceutical company runs one internal project through the year ended 31 March 2026. It spent ₹40 lakh between April and June investigating alternative compounds, with no candidate identified. It spent ₹90 lakh between July and September on a chosen candidate, during which it could not demonstrate that it had the finance to complete the work and had not fixed on whether to sell or licence the result. On 1 October 2025 it secured funding and board approval, and from that date every one of the six conditions in paragraph 57 was met. It spent ₹150 lakh between October and March, of which ₹15 lakh was identified selling and general administrative overhead that did not contribute to preparing the asset for its intended use.

items.stem: How are the four properties classified and measured at 31 March 2026?

options.text: The fourth property becomes owner-occupied property for the two years of refurbishment, because it is not earning rentals while the work is going on, and returns to investment property afterwards
options.misconception: reads a pause in rental income as owner-occupation, which para 58 rules out
options.why: Para 58 says that if an entity begins to redevelop an existing investment property for continued future use as investment property, the property remains an investment property and is not reclassified as owner-occupied property during the redevelopment. Owner-occupation under para 57(a) means the entity itself using the property for the production or supply of goods or services or for administrative purposes, and refurbishing it is not that.

options.text: The first and second are transferred at their ₹140 crore fair value, with the ₹40 crore difference on each taken to profit or loss on the date of the change in use
options.misconception: applies the IAS 40 fair value model transfer rules, which India has not adopted
options.why: Para 56 requires every investment property to be measured after initial recognition in accordance with Ind AS 16's requirements for the cost model, other than one classified as held for sale. The paragraphs of IAS 40 that revalue a property on transfer appear in Ind AS 40 as paragraphs 60 to 65 marked as not adopted, and para 59 says instead that a transfer changes neither the carrying amount nor the cost of the property for measurement or disclosure purposes. There is no gain to recognise.

options.text: The third property becomes inventories on 1 March 2026, because a property held for sale is stock in trade whatever it was held for before
options.misconception: treats a decision to sell as a change in use, when para 57(b) requires development with a view to sale
options.why: Para 57(b) makes the trigger the commencement of development with a view to sale, and para 58 spells out the consequence for a property being sold as it stands: when an entity decides to dispose of an investment property without development, it continues to treat the property as an investment property until it is derecognised, and does not treat it as inventory. The property leaves the balance sheet as investment property.
keywords: development with a view to sale

options.text: The first becomes owner-occupied property and the second becomes inventories, both at ₹100 crore; the third and fourth stay investment property at ₹100 crore, and no gain is recognised on any of them
options.why: Para 57 makes a transfer to or from investment property when, and only when, there is a change in use: para 57(a) on commencement of owner-occupation and para 57(b) on commencement of development with a view to sale, which covers the first two. Para 58 says that when an entity decides to dispose of an investment property without development it continues to treat the property as an investment property until it is derecognised, and that a property being redeveloped for continued future use as investment property remains investment property. Para 59 then settles the measurement — transfers between investment property, owner-occupied property and inventories do not change the carrying amount of the property transferred.
keywords: do not change the carrying amount

citation.ref: para 56, 57, 58 and 59

items.scenario: A real estate company holds four properties at 31 March 2026, each carried at ₹100 crore. It moved its head office into the first on 1 January 2026, having previously let it out. It began building flats for sale on the second, which it had held to earn rentals. It resolved on 1 March 2026 to sell the third exactly as it stands, with no development at all, and expects to find a buyer within the year. It began a two-year refurbishment of the fourth, which it will go on letting out afterwards. Fair values at 31 March 2026 are ₹140 crore for each property.

items.stem: At what amount are the inventories carried at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹550 lakh
options.misconception: excludes every storage cost, missing the carve-out in para 16(b) for storage necessary before a further production stage
options.why: This strips out the ₹12 lakh of maturation cellar cost along with the ₹8 lakh of finished goods storage. Para 16(b) excludes storage costs unless those costs are necessary in the production process before a further production stage. Maturing the spirit is a required stage before bottling, so that ₹12 lakh is a cost of bringing the inventory to its present condition and belongs in cost.

options.text: ₹562 lakh
options.why: Para 11 makes the costs of purchase the purchase price plus import duties and other taxes not subsequently recoverable plus transport and handling, so ₹500 lakh, ₹30 lakh and ₹20 lakh go in. Para 18 takes the ₹40 lakh difference between the ₹540 lakh paid and the ₹500 lakh normal credit price out as a financing element recognised as interest expense over the period of the financing. Para 16(b) excludes storage costs unless those costs are necessary in the production process before a further production stage, which the ₹12 lakh of maturation cellar cost is, so it stays in and the ₹8 lakh of finished goods storage does not. Para 16(a), (c) and (d) take out the abnormal wastage, the administrative overheads and the selling costs, leaving ₹562 lakh.

options.text: ₹602 lakh
options.misconception: capitalises the deferred settlement premium, which para 18 makes interest expense
options.why: This uses the ₹540 lakh invoiced rather than the ₹500 lakh normal credit price. Para 18 says that when an arrangement effectively contains a financing element, that element, for example a difference between the purchase price for normal credit terms and the amount paid, is recognised as interest expense over the period of the financing. Carrying the ₹40 lakh in inventory would move a finance cost into gross margin.

options.text: ₹577 lakh
options.misconception: includes abnormal wasted materials in cost, which para 16(a) names as an exclusion
options.why: This is ₹562 lakh plus the ₹15 lakh silo failure. Para 16(a) lists abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour or other production costs among the costs excluded from the cost of inventories and recognised as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. Normal wastage is absorbed in the conversion cost; an abnormal loss is not a cost of bringing anything to its present location and condition.

citation.ref: para 11, 16 and 18

items.scenario: A distillery buys a consignment of grain in the year ended 31 March 2026. The supplier's price on normal credit terms was ₹500 lakh, but the distillery took twelve months to pay and the invoiced amount was ₹540 lakh. It paid non-refundable import duties of ₹30 lakh and inward freight of ₹20 lakh. It incurred ₹15 lakh of abnormal wastage when a silo failed, ₹12 lakh of cellar costs storing part-processed spirit for the maturation that the process requires before bottling, ₹8 lakh storing finished bottles awaiting despatch, ₹9 lakh of head office administrative overhead that did not contribute to bringing the inventory to its present location and condition, and ₹7 lakh of selling costs. All of the inventory is unsold at 31 March 2026 and net realisable value is well above cost.

items.stem: How does the media group recognise revenue on the two licences?

options.text: The brand licence is a right to access, satisfied over time across the five years; the film licence is a right to use, satisfied at a point in time once the service can use and benefit from the film; and the royalty is recognised only as the subscriptions arise
options.why: Para B58 makes a licence a right to access where the customer reasonably expects activities that significantly affect the intellectual property, the licence directly exposes the customer to their effects, and the activities do not themselves transfer a good or service — all true of the brand. Para B59A adds that the benefit from a brand is often dependent on the entity's ongoing activities, while completed media content usually has significant stand-alone functionality. Para B60 makes the brand licence a performance obligation satisfied over time and para B61 makes the film a right to use satisfied at a point in time, with no revenue before the customer is able to use and benefit from the licence. Para B63 recognises a sales-based or usage-based royalty only at the later of the sale or usage occurring and the performance obligation being satisfied.

options.text: Both are rights to access satisfied over time, since each gives the customer the use of the group's intellectual property throughout a stated licence period
options.misconception: reads the passage of a licence period as performance over time, when B58 turns on the entity's own continuing activities
options.why: A licence term is not a measure of performance. Para B58 requires activities by the entity that significantly affect the intellectual property, and para B59A says that where the property has significant stand-alone functionality — software, drug formulas and completed media content are the examples given — the customer's benefit is not significantly affected unless those activities change its form or functionality. The film is finished, so para B61 makes it a right to use.

options.text: The film royalty is estimated at contract inception and included in the transaction price, constrained to the amount that is highly probable not to reverse
options.misconception: applies the general variable consideration constraint to a sales-based royalty on a licence, which B63 overrides
options.why: Para B63 opens with the words notwithstanding the requirements in paragraphs 56 to 59, which are the variable consideration and constraint paragraphs, and then says a sales-based or usage-based royalty promised in exchange for a licence of intellectual property is recognised only when the later of the subsequent sale or usage occurring and the satisfaction of the performance obligation happens. No estimate is made at inception.

options.text: Both are rights to use recognised in full on 1 October 2025, because the licences were granted and the customers could start using them that day
options.misconception: ignores the entity's continuing activities on the brand, which B58 and B59A make decisive
options.why: Para B59A says an entity's activities significantly affect the intellectual property where the customer's ability to obtain benefit is substantially derived from or dependent upon them, and it names a brand as the example. The clothing maker is exposed to the group's marketing and sponsorship, so the three criteria in para B58 are met and para B60 spreads the brand revenue over the five years.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B58, B59A, B60, B61 and B63

items.scenario: A media group signs two contracts on 1 October 2025, each licence being a separate performance obligation. Under the first it licenses its sports brand to a clothing maker for five years; the group runs a continuous marketing and sponsorship programme that the licensee expects and on which the value of the brand plainly depends, and the licensee is exposed to how well that programme goes. Under the second it licenses a completed feature film to a streaming service for three years; the film is finished and the group will do nothing further to it. The film licence carries a royalty of two per cent of the streaming service's subscription revenue.

items.stem: How does the company account for the ₹105 lakh?

options.text: Treat both warranties as performance obligations and allocate the ₹105 lakh across three of them, giving the one-year warranty its own slice of revenue
options.misconception: makes an assurance-type warranty a performance obligation, when B30 sends it to Ind AS 37
options.why: Para B30 is the test the one-year warranty fails: if a customer does not have the option to purchase a warranty separately, the entity accounts for it under Ind AS 37 unless the warranty, or part of it, provides a service in addition to the assurance that the product complies with agreed-upon specifications. This one promises performance to specification and nothing more, so it is a cost provision and not revenue deferred.

options.text: Allocate ₹100 lakh to the machine at its stand-alone selling price and the residual ₹5 lakh to the extended warranty
options.misconception: uses a residual approach where an observable stand-alone selling price exists, and so drops the ₹7 lakh discount entirely onto one obligation
options.why: Para 76 allocates the transaction price in proportion to the stand-alone selling prices of all the performance obligations, and para 81 requires a discount to be allocated proportionately to all of them unless the para 82 criteria for allocating it to only some are met. The extended warranty has an observable stand-alone selling price of ₹12 lakh, so the residual approach in para 79(c) is not available and the ₹7 lakh discount is shared.

options.text: Allocate ₹93.75 lakh to the machine, recognised on delivery, and ₹11.25 lakh to the extended warranty, recognised across the three years, with the one-year warranty provided for under Ind AS 37
options.why: Para B29 says that if a customer has the option to purchase a warranty separately, the warranty is a distinct service and is accounted for as a performance obligation, which the extended warranty is. Para B30 sends a warranty the customer cannot buy separately, and which only assures that the product complies with agreed-upon specifications, to Ind AS 37 as a provision. Para 74 and para 76 then allocate the transaction price on a relative stand-alone selling price basis and para 81 spreads the discount proportionately, so ₹105 lakh times ₹100 lakh over ₹112 lakh is ₹93.75 lakh and ₹105 lakh times ₹12 lakh over ₹112 lakh is ₹11.25 lakh.
keywords: option to purchase a warranty separately

options.text: Recognise the whole ₹105 lakh on delivery of the machine and provide for both warranties under Ind AS 37, since a warranty is a cost of selling a machine rather than a thing sold
options.misconception: sends a separately purchasable warranty to Ind AS 37, which B29 makes a distinct service
options.why: Para B29 is explicit that where the warranty is priced or negotiated separately the entity promises a service in addition to the product, so the warranty is a distinct service and a performance obligation with a share of the transaction price allocated to it. Booking the whole ₹105 lakh on delivery would recognise three years of servicing revenue on day one.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B29 and B30, with para 74, 76 and 81

items.scenario: A machine tool maker sells a machine with a one-year warranty that it will perform to the agreed specifications. That warranty is not priced separately and no customer can decline it. The company also sells a three-year extended warranty covering wear and consumables, which any customer may buy on its own for ₹12 lakh. A customer buys one machine and the extended warranty together for ₹105 lakh. The stand-alone selling price of the machine is ₹100 lakh and of the extended warranty ₹12 lakh. The machine is delivered on 1 April 2025.

items.stem: How does the company, as intermediate lessor, classify and account for the two subleases?

options.text: The office sublease is a finance lease, tested against the right-of-use asset from the head lease rather than the building, so the right-of-use asset is derecognised and a net investment recognised, discounted at the head lease rate adjusted for initial direct costs; the warehouse sublease is an operating lease
options.why: Para B58(b) classifies a sublease by reference to the right-of-use asset arising from the head lease, rather than by reference to the underlying asset, and eighteen of the nineteen remaining years is substantially all of that right-of-use asset. Para B58(a) makes a sublease an operating lease where the head lease is a short-term lease the entity has accounted for applying para 6, which is the warehouse. Para 68 lets an intermediate lessor that cannot readily determine the interest rate implicit in the sublease use the discount rate used for the head lease, adjusted for any initial direct costs associated with the sublease, to measure the net investment.

options.text: The office sublease is an operating lease, because eighteen years is nowhere near the fifty-year economic life of the building, so the company keeps its right-of-use asset and recognises sublease income on a straight-line basis
options.misconception: classifies the sublease against the underlying asset, which B58(b) expressly refuses
options.why: Para B58(b) says the sublease shall be classified by reference to the right-of-use asset arising from the head lease, rather than by reference to the underlying asset, giving the item of property, plant or equipment that is the subject of the lease as the example of what not to use. What the intermediate lessor holds is nineteen years of use, not the building, and it has passed on eighteen of them.

options.text: Both subleases are finance leases, since in each case the sublease covers most of what remains of the head lease
options.misconception: applies the general B58(b) test to a sublease of a short-term head lease, which B58(a) settles first
options.why: Para B58(a) comes first and admits no comparison: if the head lease is a short-term lease that the entity, as a lessee, has accounted for applying paragraph 6, the sublease shall be classified as an operating lease. Having taken the recognition exemption the company has no right-of-use asset on the warehouse to measure the sublease against.

options.text: The office sublease is a finance lease but the company keeps the head lease right-of-use asset on its balance sheet alongside the net investment, since it remains liable to the head lessor
options.misconception: confuses the continuing head lease liability with the right-of-use asset, which is what the sublease transfers
options.why: The head lease liability does stay, because the sublease does not release the intermediate lessor from anything owed to the head lessor. What goes is the asset: on a finance sublease the intermediate lessor has passed substantially all the risks and rewards of the right-of-use asset to the sublessee and recognises a net investment in the sublease in its place. Holding both would count the same right of use twice.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B58, with para 68

items.scenario: A company holds two head leases as lessee. The first is a twenty-year lease of an office building whose economic life is fifty years; nineteen years of the head lease term remain and the company subleases the whole building to a third party for eighteen of those nineteen years. The second is a nine-month lease of a warehouse, on which the company took the short-term lease recognition exemption; it subleases the warehouse for six months. The rate implicit in the office sublease cannot be readily determined.

items.stem: What additional current tax liability does the company recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹10.5 crore, using the expected value of the deduction of ₹58 crore
options.why: Para 9 asks whether it is probable the taxation authority will accept the treatment and para 11 governs where it is not. Para 11(b) uses the expected value, being the sum of the probability-weighted amounts in a range of possible outcomes, where the outcomes are neither binary nor concentrated on one value, which describes a 25, 45 and 30 per cent spread. One hundred at a quarter, sixty at forty-five per cent and twenty at thirty per cent is ₹58 crore, so ₹42 crore is disallowed and the tax on it at 25 per cent is ₹10.5 crore.

options.text: ₹10 crore, using the most likely amount of the deduction of ₹60 crore
options.misconception: uses the most likely amount where the range of outcomes calls for the expected value under para 11(b)
options.why: Para 11(a) offers the most likely amount, the single most likely amount in a range of possible outcomes, and says it may better predict the resolution of the uncertainty if the possible outcomes are binary or are concentrated on one value. Three outcomes spread at 25, 45 and 30 per cent are neither, so para 11(b)'s expected value is the method that better predicts the resolution, and it gives ₹58 crore rather than ₹60 crore.

options.text: ₹25 crore, disallowing the whole ₹100 crore claim because acceptance is not probable
options.misconception: reads a failure of the probable test as a total disallowance, when para 11 measures the effect of the uncertainty rather than assuming the worst
options.why: Para 11 says that where acceptance is not probable the entity shall reflect the effect of uncertainty by using either the most likely amount or the expected value. Neither method produces a full disallowance on these facts, since a 25 per cent chance of full allowance and a 45 per cent chance of ₹60 crore both carry weight. Para 11 is a measurement rule, not a switch between all and nothing.

options.text: Nothing, because no notice has been issued and the company thinks the claim will not be picked up for scrutiny
options.misconception: builds the chance of not being detected into the measurement, which para 8 forbids
options.why: Para 8 requires the entity to assume that a taxation authority will examine amounts it has a right to examine and have full knowledge of all related information when making those examinations. Detection risk is deliberately assumed away, so the odds of the claim going unnoticed cannot reduce the liability, and the absence of a notice is not a reason to recognise nothing.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 8, 9 and 11

items.scenario: A company claimed a deduction of ₹100 crore in its return for the year ended 31 March 2026. Its tax counsel advises that it is not probable the assessing officer will accept the claim in full. The possible outcomes are a full allowance of ₹100 crore with a 25 per cent probability, an allowance of ₹60 crore with a 45 per cent probability, and an allowance of ₹20 crore with a 30 per cent probability. The applicable tax rate is 25 per cent. No notice has yet been issued and the company believes the claim is unlikely to be picked up for scrutiny.

items.stem: What can the undertaking leave out and what must it still give?

options.text: It may leave out everything about related parties, key management personnel compensation included, because the whole of Ind AS 24 gives way to the government-related exemption
options.misconception: reads para 25 as a blanket exemption from the Standard rather than from paragraph 18 alone
options.why: Para 25 exempts the entity from the disclosure requirements of paragraph 18 and names no other paragraph. Key management personnel compensation sits in paragraph 17 and the parent and ultimate controlling party disclosure sits in paragraph 13; neither is touched, and para 26 adds requirements rather than removing them.

options.text: It must give the full paragraph 18 detail for every transaction with every other government-controlled entity, since the exemption covers only transactions with the government itself
options.misconception: reads para 25 as reaching only the government, when para 25(b) covers fellow entities under the same government
options.why: Para 25(b) extends the exemption to another entity that is a related party because the same government has control or joint control of, or significant influence over, both the reporting entity and the other entity. That limb exists precisely because a state-owned entity would otherwise have to catalogue its dealings with every other state-owned entity in the country.

options.text: It may use the exemption and give nothing in its place, the relief in para 25 being unconditional
options.misconception: takes the exemption without the substitute disclosures para 26 makes the price of it
options.why: Para 26 opens with the words if a reporting entity applies the exemption in paragraph 25, it shall disclose the following, and then lists the name of the government, the nature of the relationship, the nature and amount of each individually significant transaction and an indication of the extent of the others. Para 27 adds that the level of detail turns on the closeness of the relationship, the size of the transaction and whether it was carried out on non-market terms.

options.text: It may leave out the paragraph 18 detail for the power and coal transactions, but must name the government and the nature of its relationship, give the nature and amount of the ₹4,000 crore power purchase as an individually significant transaction and an indication of the extent of the ₹150 crore of coal purchases, and must still disclose the ₹9 crore of key management personnel compensation and the relationship with its subsidiary
options.why: Para 25 exempts a reporting entity from the disclosure requirements of paragraph 18 in relation to transactions and outstanding balances with a government that has control, joint control or significant influence over it and with another entity that is a related party because the same government controls, jointly controls or significantly influences both. Para 26 replaces those with the name of the government and the nature of its relationship, the nature and amount of each individually significant transaction, and for the rest a qualitative or quantitative indication of their extent. The exemption reaches paragraph 18 and nothing else, so key management personnel compensation and the parent and subsidiary relationships stand.

citation.ref: para 25, 26 and 27

items.scenario: A central public sector undertaking is controlled by the Government of India. During the year ended 31 March 2026 it bought power worth ₹4,000 crore from another central public sector undertaking under the same government, bought coal worth ₹150 crore in aggregate from four others, paid its key management personnel ₹9 crore, and has a wholly owned subsidiary of its own. It wishes to use the relief Ind AS 24 offers to government-related entities.

items.stem: How is the ₹1,000 lakh split on initial recognition?

options.text: A financial liability of ₹711.80 lakh, being the present value of the redemption amount, and an equity component of ₹288.20 lakh
options.misconception: leaves the present value of the coupon stream out of the liability component
options.why: The liability component is the fair value of a similar liability without the conversion option, and a similar liability pays interest as well as principal. Para 32 measures it as the whole of that instrument's cash flows discounted at the market rate, so the ₹192.14 lakh present value of the ₹80 lakh coupons belongs in the liability. Dropping it overstates the equity component threefold.
keywords: fair value of a similar liability

options.text: A financial liability of ₹1,000 lakh and no equity component, since the company is obliged to redeem at par if the holders do not convert
options.misconception: classifies the whole convertible as a liability, missing the conversion option that para 29 identifies as equity
options.why: Para 28 requires the issuer of a non-derivative financial instrument to evaluate its terms to determine whether it contains both a liability and an equity component and to classify them separately. Para 29 gives a bond convertible by the holder into a fixed number of ordinary shares as the example of a compound financial instrument, the option to convert being an equity instrument because it will be settled in a fixed number of the entity's own shares. The redemption obligation is the liability component, not the whole.

options.text: An equity component of ₹150 lakh valued directly by an option pricing model and a financial liability of ₹850 lakh taken as the balance
options.misconception: measures the equity component first and leaves the liability as the residual, reversing the order para 31 fixes
options.why: Para 31 puts the residual on the equity side and only there: the equity component is assigned the residual amount after deducting from the fair value of the instrument as a whole the amount separately determined for the liability component. Valuing the option first would make the liability depend on an option model rather than on the fair value of a similar liability, and para 32 says the liability is determined first.

options.text: A financial liability of ₹903.94 lakh and an equity component of ₹96.06 lakh
options.why: Para 32 says the issuer of a bond convertible into ordinary shares first determines the carrying amount of the liability component by measuring the fair value of a similar liability that does not have an associated equity component. Eighty lakh of annual interest times the 2.4018 annuity factor is ₹192.14 lakh and ₹1,000 lakh times 0.7118 is ₹711.80 lakh, giving a liability of ₹903.94 lakh. Para 31 then assigns the equity component the residual amount after deducting the liability from the fair value of the instrument as a whole, which is ₹96.06 lakh, and records that no gain or loss arises from initially recognising the components separately.
keywords: fair value of a similar liability

citation.ref: para 28, 29, 31 and 32

items.scenario: On 1 April 2025 a company issues debentures with a face value of ₹1,000 lakh at par. They carry interest of 8 per cent payable annually in arrears and are redeemable at par in three years. Each debenture may be converted at the holder's option, at maturity, into a fixed number of the company's own equity shares. The market rate of interest for a similar debenture without a conversion option is 12 per cent. The three-year annuity factor at 12 per cent is 2.4018 and the present value factor for the third year at 12 per cent is 0.7118.

items.stem: What does the company disclose for liquidity and market risk?

options.text: A maturity analysis of non-derivative financial liabilities at ₹2,340 crore of contractual undiscounted cash flows, the ₹300 crore of guarantees entering at their maximum amount in the earliest time band, a separate analysis for derivative financial liabilities, a description of how liquidity risk is managed, and a sensitivity analysis showing the effect on profit or loss and equity of changes reasonably possible at 31 March 2026, with a statement that the year-end exposure is unrepresentative
options.why: Para 39(a) and (b) require maturity analyses for non-derivative and for derivative financial liabilities showing the remaining contractual maturities, and para B11D says the contractual amounts disclosed are the contractual undiscounted cash flows, which differ from the balance sheet figure because that is based on discounted cash flows. Para B11C(c) allocates the maximum amount of an issued financial guarantee contract to the earliest period in which the guarantee could be called. Para 39(c) adds the description of how liquidity risk is managed, para 40 requires the sensitivity analysis for each type of market risk against changes reasonably possible at the reporting date, and para 42 requires the entity to say so where the year-end exposure makes that analysis unrepresentative.

options.text: The same maturity analysis but leaving out the ₹300 crore of financial guarantees, none of which the company expects to be called
options.misconception: applies an expected-outflow filter to issued financial guarantee contracts, which B11C(c) does not permit
options.why: Para 39(a) names issued financial guarantee contracts inside the maturity analysis of non-derivative financial liabilities, and para B11C(c) says that for issued financial guarantee contracts the maximum amount of the guarantee is allocated to the earliest period in which the guarantee could be called. Expectation is not the test; the worst-case timing and amount are, because that is what liquidity risk means.

options.text: A maturity analysis built on the ₹2,000 crore carrying amount of the borrowings, since that is the figure the balance sheet and the rest of the note are reconciled to
options.misconception: uses balance sheet carrying amounts in the maturity analysis where B11D requires contractual undiscounted cash flows
options.why: Para B11D says the contractual amounts disclosed in the maturity analyses required by paragraph 39(a) and (b) are the contractual undiscounted cash flows, and it adds that such undiscounted cash flows differ from the amount included in the balance sheet because the amount in the balance sheet is based on discounted cash flows. A liquidity table is about what has to be paid and when, so the ₹340 crore of future interest cannot be left out.

options.text: A sensitivity analysis run on the largest floating-rate exposure the company carried at any point in the year, since the year-end figure understates the risk
options.misconception: substitutes a peak exposure for the reporting date exposure, when para 40 fixes the date and para 42 handles the distortion by disclosure
options.why: Para 40(a) requires a sensitivity analysis for each type of market risk to which the entity is exposed at the end of the reporting period, showing how profit or loss and equity would have been affected by changes in the relevant risk variable that were reasonably possible at that date. Where the year-end exposure does not reflect the exposure during the year, para 42 requires the entity to disclose that fact and the reason, rather than to change the base of the analysis.

citation.ref: para 39, 40 and 42, with Appendix B, para B11C and B11D

items.scenario: A non-banking finance company is preparing its financial instruments note for the year ended 31 March 2026. Its borrowings of ₹2,000 crore carrying amount will require ₹2,340 crore of contractual payments including future interest. It has issued financial guarantees of ₹300 crore for a group company, none of which it expects to be called, callable on demand. It has floating-rate borrowings whose exposure at 31 March 2026 was smaller than at any point during the year.

items.stem: What may the parent do in its separate financial statements?

options.text: It cannot equity account anything; it must carry all three subsidiaries either at cost or under Ind AS 109, applying one of those consistently to that category, and it recognises the whole ₹20 crore dividend in profit or loss when its right to receive it was established
options.why: Para 10 gives two routes when an entity prepares separate financial statements — at cost, or in accordance with Ind AS 109 — and requires the entity to apply the same accounting for each category of investments.
