options.why: Proportionate carry-over is the treatment for transactions that keep control. Crossing from control to influence changes what is owned — a business became a shareholding — and the standard prices that change through fair value.

citation.ref: para 25

items.scenario: A parent holds 80 per cent of a subsidiary whose net assets it carries at ₹500 crore (NCI ₹100 crore). It sells a 50 per cent stake for ₹450 crore, keeping 30 per cent whose fair value is ₹270 crore, and control passes to the buyer. The group accountant computes the gain as ₹450 crore received less book value sold, and carries the retained 30 per cent at its old consolidated book value.

items.stem: Where do the two credits actually belong?

options.text: The uplift to OCI, but the surplus recycles to profit or loss on sale like a cash flow hedge reserve
options.misconception: assumes all OCI recycles
options.why: Recycling is item-specific. Revaluation surplus is in the never-recycled family — para 41's route is a direct transfer to retained earnings, bypassing profit or loss entirely.

options.text: The uplift belongs in OCI as revaluation surplus, and on sale the surplus moves straight to retained earnings, never through profit or loss
options.why: Para 39 sends revaluation increases to other comprehensive income — profit or loss sees an uplift only to the extent it reverses a decrease previously charged there. And the surplus's exit is a transfer within equity: crediting it to profit on disposal would let a company manufacture earnings by revaluing and selling, which is the precise loop the standard closes. The gain on sale compares proceeds with the revalued carrying amount.

options.text: Both credits belong in profit or loss — gains are gains
options.misconception: books unrealised and recycled gains alike as earnings
options.why: The first credit is an unrealised valuation movement; the second would count the same value a second time. OCI and the equity transfer exist to keep both out of the earnings line.

options.text: Both to revaluation surplus, where the amount stays forever
options.misconception: right destination, missing the disposal transfer
options.why: On derecognition the surplus may move to retained earnings — it has served its purpose once the asset is gone. Freezing it overstates the revaluation reserve against assets no longer held.

citation.ref: para 39-40

items.scenario: A company revalues its factory upward by ₹40 crore, crediting the gain to profit or loss to lift a weak year. Two years later it sells the factory, and proposes to route the accumulated ₹40 crore revaluation surplus through profit or loss as part of the gain on sale — "realising" it at last.

items.stem: Which warehouse's copper writes down?

options.text: Neither — raw materials always stay at cost until consumed
options.misconception: hardens the exception into immunity
options.why: The exception's own second sentence writes materials down when the finished product's cost has crossed its NRV. The loss-making line is exactly that case.

options.text: Only the second — materials hold at cost while their finished products sell at or above cost
options.why: Para 32 is the exception the accountant missed: raw materials are not written below cost when the finished goods they enter will sell at or above cost, because the materials' value is recovered through the product, not the metals market. The loss-making line fails that test, so its copper writes down — to replacement cost, ₹650, as the practical measure of its NRV.

options.text: Both, but only to the average of cost and market
options.misconception: splits a difference no rule splits
options.why: Where a write-down applies, it goes to NRV — approximated by replacement cost for materials — not halfway. Where it does not apply, cost holds in full.

options.text: Both — market price below cost is the definition of an NRV write-down
options.misconception: applies the finished-goods rule to inputs directly
options.why: NRV for materials is not their resale price; the maker is not in the copper-selling business. Recovery runs through cables, and profitable cables recover the ₹800.

citation.ref: para 32

items.scenario: A cable maker holds copper bought at ₹800 a kilo whose market price has fallen to ₹650. Finished cables made from this copper still sell above their total cost. The accountant writes the copper down by ₹150 a kilo, citing prudence and the lower-of-cost-or-NRV rule. In a second warehouse, copper feeds a loss-making cable line whose finished cost now exceeds selling price.

items.stem: How does Ind AS actually measure the three?

options.text: All three at fair value — agriculture is wholly a fair value standard
options.misconception: misses the bearer-plant amendment
options.why: That was the pre-amendment world, and revaluing mature plantations yearly is exactly the burden the carve-out removed. The trees now depreciate like machines for making latex.

options.text: All three at cost — prudence forbids recognising unrealised farm gains
options.misconception: extends the bearer-plant relief to the produce
options.why: The carve-out was drawn precisely between the tree and what grows on it. Produce markets price latex daily; the standard trusts that price over an accumulation of input costs.

options.text: Trees at cost under Ind AS 16 as bearer plants; growing latex at fair value less costs to sell; harvested latex into inventory at harvest-date fair value as its cost
options.why: The scope carve-out sends bearer plants — assets that exist to grow produce, like these rubber trees — to Ind AS 16's cost-and-depreciation world, which suits the accountant halfway. The produce on the trees stays biological: fair value less costs to sell with movements in profit or loss. At harvest the measurement freezes into Ind AS 2 as deemed cost, and ordinary inventory rules take over.

options.text: Trees and growing latex at fair value, harvested latex at selling price with profit booked on harvest day
options.misconception: books the sale before the buyer
options.why: Harvest fixes deemed cost, not revenue. The gain to that point came through the biological asset's remeasurement; the trading margin waits for an actual sale under Ind AS 115.

citation.ref: para 12-13 and scope

items.scenario: A plantation company carries three things: its rubber trees, decades-old and producing; the latex accumulating in this season's tapping; and harvested latex sitting in tanks awaiting sale. The accountant measures all three at historical cost, arguing that valuing living things is speculation and cost is prudent.

items.stem: What does Schedule III require of the ratio note?

options.text: Whichever ratios the company's industry customarily reports
options.misconception: substitutes industry practice for the prescribed list
options.why: The list is fixed so companies cannot curate flattering metrics. Industry measures may be added; the eleven cannot be subtracted.

options.text: The ratios, but explanations only where management considers the change material
options.misconception: replaces the bright-line trigger with discretion
options.why: Twenty-five per cent is the Schedule's own line, chosen to remove exactly this judgment. Management explains every crossing, however comfortable the story.

options.text: All eleven named ratios with their computation elements, and an explanation for any ratio that moved more than twenty-five per cent
options.why: The 2021 amendments made the ratios a prescribed disclosure, not an analyst courtesy — including numerators and denominators so readers see what was computed. Both flagged movements are far past the twenty-five per cent trigger, and the explanation requirement exists because the numbers famously do not speak: a doubled debt-equity could be expansion or distress, and the note must say which.

options.text: Nothing — ratio analysis is voluntary supplementary information
options.misconception: treats a Schedule III item as investor relations
options.why: The Schedule's general instructions list the ratios by name. Deleting them is non-compliance with the statements' own prescribed format, which the auditor must then report.

citation.ref: Schedule III Division II (2021 amendments)

items.scenario: Reviewing draft statements, a CFO deletes the ratio note — "analysts compute their own ratios" — and, when overruled, restores it but omits explanations for the debt-equity ratio doubling and the receivables turnover halving, reasoning that the numbers speak for themselves.

items.stem: How much loss does the equity method actually recognise?

options.text: ₹25 crore — the equity carrying amount alone absorbs losses
options.misconception: leaves the in-substance investment out of the base
options.why: A loan with no realistic repayment terms funds the associate exactly as capital does, and para 38 counts it. Stopping at ₹25 crore overstates the loan's recoverability by the ₹10 crore the losses have consumed.

options.text: ₹35 crore — the equity value and the in-substance loan absorb losses to zero, and the last ₹5 crore goes unrecognised absent any obligation
options.why: Para 38's interest includes long-term interests that are in substance part of the net investment, so the loan extends the loss-absorbing base to ₹35 crore. Below zero, a shareholder with no guarantee or constructive obligation has nothing more to lose — negative carrying amounts would book other shareholders' problems. The unrecognised ₹5 crore waits: future profits are first applied against it before any profit share returns.

options.text: ₹35 crore now and the ₹5 crore the moment next year's losses continue
options.misconception: defers past zero instead of stopping
options.why: Zero is a floor, not a queue. Further losses accumulate off-books against future profits; they never enter the accounts unless an obligation arises.

options.text: ₹40 crore as booked — accounts must reflect the associate's full deterioration
options.misconception: recognises losses beyond the investor's exposure
options.why: Reality for a non-guaranteeing shareholder is that loss stops at the investment. The negative ₹5 crore is a liability the investor does not have.

citation.ref: para 38-39

items.scenario: An investor carries a 30 per cent associate at ₹25 crore and has also extended it a ₹10 crore loan repayable "whenever convenient, if ever" — in substance part of the net investment. The associate's losses assign the investor a ₹40 crore share over two years. The investor books ₹40 crore of losses, driving the investment ₹5 crore negative, "to reflect reality". It has guaranteed nothing.

items.stem: Does the ₹20 crore belong in the transaction price now?

options.text: Include ₹11 crore — 55 per cent of the bonus as its expected value
options.misconception: stops at estimation and skips the constraint
options.why: Expected value is a permitted estimation method, but para 56 then constrains the estimate. An all-or-nothing bonus at 55 per cent leaves any included amount exposed to a significant reversal; the constraint trims it to nil for now.

options.text: Yes — more likely than not is the recognition standard for uncertain amounts
options.misconception: imports the provisions-style probable test into revenue
options.why: Revenue's constraint sets a higher bar on purpose: overstated revenue reversed later misleads worse than delayed revenue. "Highly probable of no significant reversal" is stricter than 51 per cent.

options.text: No revenue at all until the contract completes, bonus or base
options.misconception: swings from optimism to abstinence
options.why: The fixed ₹100 crore is not variable and recognises over time as performance progresses. The constraint disciplines the uncertain slice only.

options.text: No — a 55 per cent chance cannot make a significant reversal highly improbable, so the bonus stays out until the uncertainty narrows
options.why: The constraint in para 56 is deliberately asymmetric: include variable amounts only to the extent it is highly probable that cumulative revenue will not significantly reverse. A near-coin-flip bonus of this size fails that test plainly — a 45 per cent chance of unwinding ₹20 crore is the significant reversal the rule guards against. As milestones pass and the risk factors resolve, the assessment updates and the bonus enters when the bar is cleared.

citation.ref: para 56

items.scenario: A contractor's ₹100 crore contract carries a ₹20 crore early-completion bonus. Management rates the chance of earning it at 55 per cent — weather and approvals could go either way — and includes the full ₹20 crore in revenue as work progresses, since more likely than not means probable enough.

items.stem: Which classifications are right?

options.text: The T-bill yes; the old bond and the shares no; and the swinging overdraft belongs inside cash and cash equivalents
options.why: The three-month test runs from acquisition, so the T-bill qualifies and the bond bought three years ago never did — nearing maturity now does not reclassify it. Listed shares fail the known-amount test however liquid: an hour's notice does not fix the price. And an on-demand overdraft integral to daily cash management is a component of cash equivalents under para 8, not financing.

options.text: All four as classified — liquidity is the only test
options.misconception: substitutes marketability for the definition's three limbs
options.why: Convertible to a known amount, insignificant value risk, short maturity from acquisition: the shares fail the first two, the bond the third, and the overdraft was misplaced entirely.

options.text: Everything except the overdraft, which is always financing
options.misconception: half-remembers the general rule past its exception
options.why: Bank borrowings are generally financing — para 8 then carves out on-demand overdrafts woven into cash management. A balance swinging daily with collections is that carve-out described.

options.text: The bond joins the T-bill — two months to maturity is under three
options.misconception: measures maturity from the reporting date
options.why: The standard counts from the date of acquisition, screening out instruments that spent years exposed to value swings before happening to near maturity.

citation.ref: para 7-8

items.scenario: Preparing the cash flow statement, an accountant classifies as cash equivalents: a 91-day treasury bill bought on issue day; a 5-year government bond maturing in two months, bought three years ago; a portfolio of blue-chip listed shares "liquid enough to sell in an hour"; and excludes the company's overdraft, repayable on demand and swinging daily with collections, as a financing item.

items.stem: What do the consolidation procedures actually require?

options.text: No elimination — the sale really happened and both entities recorded it
options.misconception: consolidates by addition alone
options.why: Addition without elimination counts internal churn as revenue and stuffs profit into inventory the group still holds. The eliminations are what make the totals mean anything.

options.text: The 80 per cent eliminations are right — the minority's share was genuinely sold
options.misconception: treats NCI as an outsider customer
options.why: NCI are owners within the group, not counterparties outside it. The single- entity fiction eliminates the whole transaction and then shares results with NCI by allocation.

options.text: Eliminate the ₹50 crore sale and the ₹5 crore unrealised profit in full, and restate the property to group policy before consolidating
options.why: B86 eliminates intragroup transactions and unrealised profits in full — the group sold nothing to outsiders, so no fraction of the ₹50 crore or of the ₹5 crore in inventory survives; NCI bears its 20 per cent share of the profit elimination through allocation, not through partial elimination. And para 19 demands uniform policies: the subsidiary's fair-valued property is restated to the group's basis before its lines join the group's.

options.text: Full elimination, but each entity's own policies are preserved as its management chose them
options.misconception: consolidates policies as a federation
options.why: One reporting entity cannot measure identical assets two ways in one balance sheet. Uniformity is a stated accounting requirement, with restatement as its mechanism.

citation.ref: para 19 and B86

items.scenario: A parent owns 80 per cent of a subsidiary. During the year the subsidiary sold goods costing ₹40 crore to the parent for ₹50 crore, and half remain in the parent's closing inventory. The subsidiary also carries investment property at fair value under a policy the group does not use. The group accountant eliminates 80 per cent of the intragroup sale and ₹4 crore of the unrealised profit, and consolidates the subsidiary's property figures as reported.

items.stem: How do the three stand under Chapter 6?

options.text: All three are eligible; the ₹1 crore figure is a Board of Approval guideline rather than a condition, and net foreign exchange is tested only at exit
options.misconception: dissolves both the floor and the test
options.why: The floor is a condition of establishment, and the Board's power is to allow a lower one, which is not the same as the figure being advisory. Net foreign exchange is monitored by the Unit Approval Committee through the life of the unit, not first examined when it leaves.

options.text: All three fail — the first and second on the ₹1 crore investment floor, and the third on the year-four shortfall
options.misconception: applies the investment floor to every applicant and reads the NFE test annually
options.why: The floor has a list of exceptions written beside it, and units in an EHTP, STP or BTP are on that list along with handicrafts, agriculture, information technology and services. The first promoter fails for a different reason entirely, and the third fails on nothing yet, because the test is not annual.

options.text: The first fails because it is a trading unit, the second is fine because the ₹1 crore floor does not apply to STP units, and the third is not yet in default because the test is a cumulative five-year block
options.why: Chapter 6 says in terms that trading units are not covered by these schemes, so no investment figure saves the first promoter — the scheme buys export production, not export trading. The minimum investment of one crore rupees in plant and machinery does not apply to units in an EHTP, STP or BTP, so ₹60 lakh is no obstacle to the second. And net foreign exchange is computed cumulatively in blocks of five years from the commencement of production, so a single negative year is answered by the rest of its block; where the shortfall is caused by a restriction on export of a product in the letter of permission, the Board of Approval may extend the block period besides.
keywords: one crore rupees in plant and machinery
cumulatively in blocks of five years

options.text: The first is fine because it exports its entire production, the second fails on investment, and the third must apply to the Board of Approval within thirty days
options.misconception: treats exporting everything as the whole eligibility test
options.why: Exporting the entire production is the undertaking a unit gives, not the definition of who may give it. A trading unit exporting everything it buys is still a trading unit, and Chapter 6 excludes it by name. There is no thirty-day application of this kind in the paragraph.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 6.00(a), 6.04 and 6.06 of Chapter 6

items.scenario: A Coimbatore promoter puts ₹80 lakh into plant and machinery to set up a unit that will buy finished pumps from local makers and export them, and applies for EOU status. A second promoter puts ₹60 lakh into machinery for a software development unit in an STP. A third runs an existing EOU which earned negative net foreign exchange in its fourth year of production after its main buyer's country restricted the product, and has been told by its consultant that the shortfall in year four is a default.

items.stem: What is wrong with the second half of that assumption?

options.text: The extension is not available at all — the Board may extend the block only where an export product has been prohibited or restricted
options.misconception: sees one extension ground and misses the second
options.why: There are two grounds, side by side. A prohibition or restriction on an export product named in the letter of permission may extend the block suitably; adverse market conditions or any ground of genuine hardship may extend it by up to one year, on a case-to-case basis.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; duty repayment with interest is the whole of the consequence and the letter of permission runs until its own expiry
options.misconception: treats the undertaking as a tax obligation rather than a licence condition
options.why: The letter of permission is construed as an authorisation for all purposes, and the undertaking is what it stands on. Chapter 6 attaches cancellation and penal action to a breach precisely because the exemptions were given against a promise.

options.text: The block period cannot be extended once it has begun, so the application will be returned without consideration
options.misconception: reads the five-year block as fixed
options.why: The block is the ordinary measuring period, not an immovable one. Chapter 6 gives the Board of Approval express power to extend it, and the whole reason the test is cumulative is to absorb bad years rather than to punish them.

options.text: Failing the net foreign exchange undertaking exposes the unit to penal action under the FT (D&R) Act and to cancellation of its letter of permission, on top of any duty
options.why: The unit executes a legal undertaking with the Development Commissioner, and Chapter 6 says that failure to ensure positive net foreign exchange or to abide by the terms of the letter of permission renders the unit liable to penal action under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, without prejudice to action under any other law, and to cancellation or revocation of the letter. The extension he is asking for is real — the Board may extend the block by up to one year for adverse market conditions or genuine hardship, case by case — but a refusal costs more than money.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 6.04 and 6.05(c) of Chapter 6

items.scenario: An EOU making industrial valves is three years into its second five-year block. A slump in its export market has left it certain to close the block negative unless something changes. Its finance head proposes to write to the Board of Approval for an extension of the block period on the ground of adverse market conditions, and assumes that if refused, the only consequence is that the duty exemptions already taken become repayable.

items.stem: Which of these four can it do while its net foreign exchange is negative?

options.text: None of the four — every domestic clearance by an EOU requires positive net foreign exchange
options.misconception: reads one condition across all four exceptions
options.why: Paragraph 6.07 does not carry one condition. Two of its clearances say in terms that they are not subject to achievement of net foreign exchange, and the services entitlement is written as a percentage cap rather than as a condition on the unit's overall position.

options.text: The rejects, the scrap and the services — but not the finished components
options.why: Sale of finished goods into the domestic tariff area is expressly subject to fulfilment of positive net foreign exchange, so the ₹40 lakh clearance is barred this year. Sale of rejects up to five per cent of the free-on-board value of exports is not subject to achievement of net foreign exchange, and ₹6 lakh against ₹200 lakh is three per cent. Scrap, waste and remnants arising out of the production process are likewise not subject to achievement of positive net foreign exchange. And the services cap is a proportion — up to fifty per cent of the free-on-board value of exports or of the foreign exchange earned — which 30 per cent is inside.

options.text: All four — the net foreign exchange test bites only at the end of the five-year block
options.misconception: confuses the timing of the block with the condition on a sale
options.why: The block is how the earning is measured; the domestic sale condition is a separate gate that asks whether the unit is positive when it clears the goods. A unit mid-block and negative cannot clear finished goods on the strength of years still to come.

options.text: The finished components and the rejects only; scrap and services both need positive NFE
options.misconception: inverts which two escape the test
options.why: It is exactly the other way round on the first pair. Finished goods carry the condition and rejects within five per cent do not, and scrap, waste and remnants are relieved of it by name in the same paragraph.

citation.ref: Paragraph 6.07(a), (b), (d) and (e) of Chapter 6

items.scenario: An EOU manufacturing moulded plastic components has, in the current year, negative net foreign exchange. It wants to clear four things into the domestic tariff area: finished components worth ₹40 lakh, rejects worth ₹6 lakh against exports of ₹200 lakh free on board, grinding scrap arising in production, and — through its software division — data processing services worth 30 per cent of that division's export earnings.

items.stem: What has the accountant left out?

options.text: Nothing — the exemption was lawfully availed and the GST on clearance is the whole liability
options.misconception: treats an export-conditioned exemption as unconditional once availed
options.why: The exemption on an EOU's inputs is conditioned on the output being exported. The paragraph that permits the domestic sale is the same one that requires the reversal, and it is written as a single condition, not as an option.

options.text: The customs duties availed as exemption on the inputs must be reversed, and an amount equal to the anti-dumping duty leviable at import is payable on those inputs besides
options.why: Paragraph 6.07(a) requires payment of goods and services tax and compensation cess along with reversal of the duties of customs availed as exemption on the inputs used in making the goods now cleared, computed on the standard input output norms. The exemption was given because the goods were going abroad; when they stay, it is unwound. Separately, an amount equal to the anti-dumping duty leviable at the time of import is payable on the goods used to make what is cleared into the domestic tariff area.
keywords: reversal of the duties of customs

options.text: The goods must first be exported and re-imported, since an EOU cannot clear finished goods domestically at all
options.misconception: denies an entitlement the chapter grants
options.why: Chapter 6 permits the sale outright where the goods are freely importable under the policy, are specified in the letter of permission and the unit is net foreign exchange positive. There is no round trip; there is a price.

options.text: Only basic customs duty on the inputs need be reversed; the integrated tax and cess were never exempt in the first place
options.misconception: half-right on the reversal and wrong on what was exempt
options.why: An EOU's imports come in without the customs duty under the First Schedule and without the additional duties, and without integrated tax and compensation cess under the revenue notification. The reversal is of the duties of customs availed as exemption, and the anti-dumping element sits beside it; narrowing it to basic customs duty understates it.

citation.ref: Paragraph 6.07(a)(i) and (iv) of Chapter 6

items.scenario: An EOU with comfortably positive net foreign exchange clears finished goods into the domestic tariff area. Its accountant pays goods and services tax and compensation cess on the clearance and treats that as the end of the matter, reasoning that the customs duty on the imported inputs was validly exempt at the time of import and that the exemption is not undone by a later domestic sale.

items.stem: Is the exemption claim good?

options.text: Yes — the unit remains an EOU in law until the final exit order, so every entitlement runs
options.misconception: reads status as the test when the paragraph names a moment
options.why: The chapter does not leave this to inference from status. It fixes the cut-off at the No Dues Certificate, which is the point at which the unit's liabilities have been settled on the footing that it is going.

options.text: Yes, but only for inputs and not for capital goods, since capital goods carry the depreciation question
options.misconception: splits a bar that the paragraph writes across both
options.why: The words are "capital goods or inputs", together. Depreciation is a separate matter and goes to the duty on disposal into the domestic tariff area, available only where the unit is net foreign exchange positive after taking that depreciation into account.

options.text: No — between the No Dues Certificate and the final exit order the unit may claim no exemption for procuring capital goods or inputs, though an advance authorisation, a DFIA or drawback stay open to it
options.why: Paragraph 6.17(e) closes exactly this window. Once customs have issued the No Dues Certificate the unit shall not be entitled to claim any exemption for procurement of capital goods or inputs, and it waits for the Development Commissioner's final exit order, which issues within seven working days where nothing is pending under the FT (D&R) Act. What the paragraph leaves open in the same breath is the schemes any exporter may use: an advance authorisation, a duty free import authorisation, or duty drawback as per its eligibility.

options.text: No — and the advance authorisation and drawback routes are equally closed until final exit
options.misconception: over-reads the bar into schemes the paragraph preserves
options.why: The paragraph says the opposite in terms: the unit can claim an advance authorisation, a duty free import authorisation or duty drawback as per its eligibility. What it loses is the exemption that belonged to being an EOU.

citation.ref: Paragraph 6.17(e) of Chapter 6

items.scenario: An EOU has decided to leave the scheme. It has achieved positive net foreign exchange over its blocks. It intimates the Development Commissioner and customs in writing, assesses its own duty on the capital goods it will retain, pays, and obtains a No Dues Certificate. While waiting for the final exit order it places an order for imported inputs and claims the EOU exemption on them, on the footing that it is still an EOU until the order issues.

items.stem: Is the consultant right about either?

options.text: Right on both — conversion makes them EOU capital goods and the exit price attaches to the unit
options.misconception: prices the unit rather than the history of the goods
options.why: The exit charge is on the duty foregone, and neither set of goods had duty foregone under the EOU scheme. The chapter follows the goods, not the label on the unit at the moment of removal.

options.text: Wrong on the first and right on the second — the EPCG obligation revives on exit from the EOU scheme
options.misconception: revives a discharged obligation
options.why: An export obligation completely fulfilled is spent. Nothing in Chapter 6 revives it on a later exit, and the paragraph says so by relieving those very goods of customs duty on removal.

options.text: No, on both — duty-paid machines carried into an EOU and EPCG goods whose obligation was fully discharged before conversion both come out without customs duty
options.why: Paragraph 6.17(f) covers both cases by name. Where a unit was first established as a domestic unit with machines procured on payment of applicable import duty or duty of excise and was afterwards converted into an EOU, removal of those capital goods into the domestic tariff area on exit is without payment of duty — the duty was paid once already. And where a domestic unit imported capital goods under the EPCG scheme and got converted into an EOU after completely fulfilling the export obligation, no customs duty is charged on those goods at the time of removal on exit.
keywords: after completely fulfilling the export obligation

options.text: Right on the first and wrong on the second — a duty-paid machine is still relieved of duty on entering an EOU
options.misconception: inverts the two limbs of the paragraph
options.why: It is the first that is exempt for the plainest reason of all: the duty was paid at import and never refunded. The EPCG limb needs the extra fact that the export obligation was completely fulfilled before conversion, and it has it here.

citation.ref: Paragraph 6.17(f) of Chapter 6

items.scenario: Two units are exiting. The first was a domestic unit that bought its machines from abroad on payment of full import duty, converted to an EOU three years later, and is now leaving and taking those same machines into the domestic tariff area. The second imported capital goods under EPCG as a domestic unit, discharged its export obligation completely, then converted to an EOU, and is now leaving with those goods. A consultant tells both that customs duty is payable on removal because they are EOU capital goods today.

items.stem: Which parts of the plan hold?

options.text: The sale holds only after the export obligation is discharged; until then the DFIA is untransferable like an advance authorisation
options.misconception: imports a discharge condition into a post-export scheme
options.why: There is no obligation left to discharge — a duty free import authorisation is issued on a post-export basis, against exports already made. The transferability is not waiting on anything.

options.text: The sale holds, because a DFIA is transferable; the integrated tax assumption does not, because a DFIA exempts basic customs duty alone
options.why: The Regional Authority issues a transferable duty free import authorisation with a validity of twelve months from the date of issue, so selling it on is exactly what the scheme contemplates — and it is the sharpest difference from an advance authorisation, which carries the actual user condition and is not transferable even after the export obligation is completed. But the authorisation is exempted only from payment of basic customs duty, so the integrated tax and compensation cess at import are paid.

options.text: Both hold — a DFIA is transferable and carries the same duty exemptions as an advance authorisation
options.misconception: assumes the two schemes exempt the same duties
options.why: They do not. The narrower exemption is the price of transferability: a scrip that can be sold to anyone cannot carry the whole family of duties an actual-user authorisation does. Paragraph 4.25 confines it to basic customs duty in terms.

options.text: Neither holds — a DFIA carries the actual user condition and cannot be sold
options.misconception: carries the advance authorisation's actual user condition across
options.why: The actual user condition belongs to the advance authorisation, where it survives even the completion of the export obligation. The duty free import authorisation is issued transferable, which is why it is issued only after export and only against notified norms.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 4.25(i), 4.28(viii) and 4.16(i) of Chapter 4

items.scenario: An exporter of engineering goods has completed a shipment and wants to recover the duty cost of the inputs that went into it. His options are a duty free import authorisation or, for future shipments, an advance authorisation. He plans to take a duty free import authorisation and then sell it to an importer friend for cash, and separately assumes that whichever he takes, the integrated tax at import will be exempt.

items.stem: How do the two propositions stand?

options.text: The norms point holds but only for sensitive items; for an ordinary chemical a self-declaration is accepted
options.misconception: reads the sensitive-items declaration as the whole norms rule
options.why: The sensitive-items list requires an extra declaration of technical characteristics, quality and specification in the shipping bill. It is an addition for those inputs, not a relaxation of the requirement that notified norms exist before a DFIA can issue at all.

options.text: The norms point fails but the value addition is fine, since twenty per cent applies only to the gems and jewellery sector
options.misconception: displaces the general floor onto a sector
options.why: Twenty per cent is the general minimum for this scheme. The gems and jewellery sector has its own value addition rules in the Handbook of Procedures, and tea and spices have their own figures under the advance authorisation, but none of that lifts the twenty here.

options.text: Both hold — the self-ratification route covers unnotified norms and fifteen per cent is the floor
options.misconception: carries the advance authorisation's norms and value addition into the DFIA
options.why: The self-ratification scheme belongs to Chapter 4's advance authorisation provisions, and the fifteen per cent figure is that scheme's floor. The duty free import authorisation is written with its own norms requirement and its own higher floor.

options.text: Both fail — a DFIA issues only for products with notified norms, and its minimum value addition is twenty per cent, not fifteen
options.why: Paragraph 4.26 says a duty free import authorisation shall be issued only for products for which standard input output norms have been notified, so there is no self-declaration route into this scheme; separate authorisations issue for each set of norms. And paragraph 4.27 fixes the minimum value addition of twenty per cent for it. Seventeen per cent clears the fifteen per cent floor of an advance authorisation, which is where the figure he was given comes from, and falls short here.
keywords: minimum value addition of twenty per cent

citation.ref: Paragraphs 4.26(i), 4.27 and 4.29(a) of Chapter 4, read with paragraph 4.09(i)

items.scenario: An exporter of a speciality chemical wants a duty free import authorisation. There are no standard input output norms notified for his export product, and he proposes to apply on a self-declaration of the inputs consumed, as an applicant for an advance authorisation may in certain cases. He also expects to achieve value addition of about seventeen per cent, which he has been told clears the scheme's floor.

items.stem: What is wrong with that advice?

options.text: The advice is right on the benefit but wrong on the label — it is a deemed export under the policy, which carries no benefits of its own
options.misconception: grants the label and denies the consequences
options.why: The label is what the benefits hang on. Paragraph 7.03 attaches three of them to supplies qualifying as deemed exports under the policy, and paragraph 7.04 sets out which categories get which.

options.text: It answers a policy question out of the GST list — the FTP has its own categories, and supply of capital goods against an EPCG authorisation is one of them
options.why: Chapter 7 draws the distinction itself. For the policy, a deemed export is a transaction where the goods do not leave the country, payment is in rupees or free foreign exchange and the goods are manufactured in India; for GST, deemed exports mean only the supplies notified under section 147. Two lists, one phrase. Supply of capital goods against an EPCG authorisation is category (c) of paragraph 7.02, so the policy's benefits — an advance authorisation or DFIA, deemed export drawback, and refund of terminal excise duty where applicable — are in issue whatever section 147 says.
keywords: only the supplies notified under section 147

options.text: Nothing — section 147 is the single definition of deemed exports in Indian law and the policy follows it
options.misconception: collapses two definitions into one
options.why: The policy expressly separates them, and says in paragraph 7.01(ii) that deemed exports for GST purposes would include only what is notified under section 147. It would not need to say so if the two lists were the same.

options.text: It is wrong because the goods left the manufacturer's premises, and any movement of goods for consideration is an export in the policy's sense
options.misconception: makes movement the test
options.why: The defining feature of a deemed export is the opposite — the goods do not leave the country. Movement within India is what puts the transaction in Chapter 7 rather than Chapter 2.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 7.01 and 7.02(c) of Chapter 7, read with section 147 of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A manufacturer supplies capital goods to a domestic buyer holding an EPCG authorisation. The goods never leave India and payment comes in rupees. His tax consultant checks section 147 of the CGST Act and the notification issued under it, finds that this supply is not in that list, and advises that the transaction is therefore not a deemed export and no benefit of any kind is available on it.

items.stem: Which of the three supplies qualify as deemed exports under the policy?

options.text: The EOU supply and the multilateral-agency supply, since the funding source is what matters
options.misconception: treats the agency's notification as the whole condition
options.why: Being on the Department of Economic Affairs list makes the project eligible; it does not make every supply to it a deemed export. The paragraph requires the supply itself to be under international competitive bidding in accordance with those agencies' procedures.

options.text: The EOU supply and the nuclear supply, since the certificate and national bidding are enough
options.misconception: reads the procedural conditions and misses the capacity threshold
options.why: National competitive bidding is permitted for a nuclear project, and the Joint Secretary's certificate is required, but both sit on top of a capacity threshold the paragraph states in figures. A 300 MW project does not reach it.

options.text: Only the supply to the EOU
options.why: Supply of goods by a manufacturer to an EOU, STP, EHTP or BTP is category (b) of paragraph 7.02 and needs no bidding condition. The nuclear project fails on capacity — the paragraph requires a project of 440 MW or more, and 300 MW is short of it however good the certificate and the tender. The multilateral-agency supply fails because those supplies must be made under international competitive bidding in accordance with the funding agency's procedures, and a negotiated award is not that.

options.text: All three, because in each case the goods stay in India and payment is in rupees
options.misconception: takes the general definition as sufficient without the category
options.why: Paragraph 7.01 describes what deemed exports are; paragraph 7.02 says which supplies are regarded as such. A transaction must land in one of the seven categories with its own conditions met, and staying in India is only the starting point.

citation.ref: Paragraph 7.02(b), (d) and (g) of Chapter 7

items.scenario: A sub-contractor supplies equipment to a nuclear power project of 300 MW, tendered through national competitive bidding with the Department of Atomic Energy certificate in place. A second supplier, a manufacturer, supplies goods to an EOU. A third supplies goods to a project funded by a notified multilateral agency, but the contract was awarded on a negotiated basis rather than through international competitive bidding.

items.stem: What is its specific export obligation?

options.text: ₹300 lakh
options.misconception: applies the reliefs to the average export obligation, leaving the specific one untouched
options.why: It is the other way round. Each of these paragraphs cuts the SPECIFIC obligation and each of them says, in the same breath, that there shall be no change in the average export obligation. Nothing here reduces the average.

options.text: ₹42.19 lakh
options.misconception: multiplies the three reliefs together, when the policy allows exactly one of them
options.why: Taking a quarter off for domestic sourcing, then three quarters of that for green technology, then a quarter of that for Assam gives ₹42.19 lakh, and it is the answer the arithmetic invites. Paragraph 5.04(l) shuts it: only one benefit is admissible, so they are a choice and not a stack.

options.text: ₹75 lakh
options.why: The base figure is six times the duty saved, that is ₹300 lakh. Three reliefs are open to this unit and paragraph 5.04(l) allows only ONE of them, so it takes the largest. For a manufacturing unit in Assam the specific obligation is twenty-five per cent of the base figure, which is ₹75 lakh, against ₹225 lakh under either of the other two.

options.text: ₹225 lakh
options.misconception: reads the North East relief as taking twenty-five per cent off rather than reducing to twenty-five per cent
options.why: Twenty-five per cent less and twenty-five per cent of are different instructions, and Chapter 5 uses both in neighbouring paragraphs. Domestic sourcing is twenty-five per cent LESS, which leaves ₹225 lakh; a unit in Assam gets twenty-five per cent OF, which leaves ₹75 lakh.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 5.01(b), 5.04(d), 5.04(l), 5.08, 5.10 and 5.11 of Chapter 5

items.scenario: A manufacturing unit in Assam holds an EPCG authorisation. It sources the capital goods from a domestic manufacturer against an invalidation letter, and the notional duties, taxes and cess saved on the free-on-rail value work out to ₹50 lakh. It exports green technology products listed for the purpose.

items.stem: Where does he stand?

options.text: The balance is condoned only once the sixth year has run out
options.misconception: reads the half-period test as a waiting time rather than as a deadline to beat
options.why: Half or less than half the original period is the LATEST point by which the performance must be shown, not the earliest at which relief may be claimed. Waiting for the sixth year would defeat a paragraph whose stated purpose is accelerating exports.

options.text: The balance is condoned and the domestic sourcing reduction stands as well, being a reduction in the obligation rather than a benefit under the policy
options.misconception: separates the sourcing reduction from the list of benefits, when 5.04(l) names it first
options.why: Paragraph 5.04(l) lists paragraphs 5.04(d), 5.09, 5.10 and 5.11 together and allows one benefit out of the four. The domestic sourcing reduction is 5.04(d) and is the first name on that list.

options.text: Nothing yet — the incentive needs the whole specific obligation to have been discharged
options.misconception: reads an incentive for early performance as a reward for complete performance
options.why: Discharging the whole obligation needs no condonation, so a paragraph requiring it would do nothing. The threshold is seventy-five per cent or more of the specific obligation, met early, and the point of it is to release him from the rest.

options.text: The balance of the specific obligation is condoned and the authorisation redeemed, but he cannot also keep the domestic sourcing reduction
options.why: Paragraph 5.09 condones the remainder where seventy-five per cent or more of the specific obligation and one hundred per cent of the average obligation to date have been met in half or less than half the original period, and three years of six is half. Paragraph 5.04(l) then names 5.04(d) and 5.09 in the same list of which only one benefit is admissible, so the condonation and the domestic sourcing reduction are alternatives.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 5.04(d), 5.04(l) and 5.09 of Chapter 5

items.scenario: An EPCG authorisation was issued with a six year export obligation period. The capital goods were sourced from a domestic manufacturer. Three years in, the holder has fulfilled eighty per cent of his specific export obligation and the whole of his average export obligation to date.

items.stem: What is his average export obligation, and how much counts towards the specific obligation?

options.text: An average of ₹100 lakh a year to be met across the six years as a whole, so nothing is due yet
options.misconception: spreads a yearly obligation over the whole period, which is what the paragraph rules out
options.why: The average export obligation shall be fulfilled every financial year until the export obligation is completed. A shortfall in year one is a shortfall in year one; it is not answered by a better year five.

options.text: An average of ₹100 lakh, and the whole ₹150 lakh counts towards the specific obligation
options.misconception: treats the two obligations as running side by side, when one is measured net of the other
options.why: They are not independent. Exports over and above the average shall ONLY be considered for fulfilment of the export obligation, so the first ₹100 lakh is spent on the average and only ₹50 lakh reaches the specific obligation.

options.text: An average of ₹100 lakh, of which ₹50 lakh counts towards the specific obligation
options.why: The average is the arithmetic mean of the three preceding licensing years for the same and similar products, that is ₹100 lakh, and it has to be met every financial year. Exports over and above the average are the only ones considered for fulfilment of the specific obligation, so ₹150 lakh less ₹100 lakh leaves ₹50 lakh.

options.text: An average of ₹120 lakh, of which ₹30 lakh counts
options.misconception: takes the best of the three years as the benchmark rather than their mean
options.why: The best year is not the test. Paragraph 5.04(c) says the average would be the arithmetic mean of export performance in the preceding three licensing years, which is ₹100 lakh here.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5.04(c) of Chapter 5

items.scenario: An EPCG holder exported the same and similar products worth ₹80 lakh, ₹100 lakh and ₹120 lakh in the three licensing years before his authorisation was issued. In the first financial year of the export obligation period he exports ₹150 lakh of those products. He is in no sector relieved of maintaining an average.

items.stem: What average export obligation does he carry, and may he sell the looms once he has exported enough?

options.text: No average on the looms, an average on the trawler, and the looms may not be transferred for five years from the date of import even after the obligation is met
options.why: Handlooms are one of the thirteen categories relieved from maintaining an average export obligation. That relief is expressly withdrawn for the import of fishing trawlers, boats, ships and other similar items, so the trawler carries one. And goods other than tools imported by those categories may not be transferred for five years from the date of import even where the export obligation has been fulfilled.
keywords: five years from the date of import

options.text: No average on either, since the exporter is in a relieved sector
options.misconception: makes the sector the only test, when the policy also carves out particular items
options.why: The sector opens the relief and the item can close it again. Paragraph 5.12(b) withdraws it for fishing trawlers, boats, ships and other similar items, whoever imports them.

options.text: An average on both, the relief cutting the specific obligation and not the average
options.misconception: swaps which of the two obligations paragraph 5.12 is about
options.why: Paragraph 5.12 is headed exemption from maintenance of average export obligation and does exactly that. It is paragraphs 5.04(d), 5.10 and 5.11 that cut the specific obligation, and each of those leaves the average alone.

options.text: No average on the looms, and they are freely transferable once the export obligation is discharged
options.misconception: lets the transfer bar end with the obligation, when it is written to outlast it
options.why: The bar runs for five years from the date of import and applies even in cases where export obligation has been fulfilled. Tools are the only thing taken out of it.
keywords: five years from the date of import

citation.ref: Paragraphs 5.12(a), 5.12(b) and 5.12(c) of Chapter 5

items.scenario: A handloom exporter takes two EPCG authorisations. Under the first he imports looms; under the second he imports a fishing trawler for a separate line of business.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: It may be revalidated for a further twelve months on payment of the prescribed fee
options.misconception: carries over the revalidation practice of other authorisations to the one that excludes it
options.why: Revalidation is ordinary enough elsewhere, which is why the policy bothers to shut it here in terms: revalidation of an EPCG authorisation shall not be permitted.

options.text: It stays valid for import throughout the six year export obligation period
options.misconception: runs the import window and the export obligation period off the same clock
options.why: Two clocks start on the same day and stop at different times. Twenty-four months is the window for bringing the capital goods in; six years is the period for exporting against them.

options.text: The import window closed after twenty-four months and revalidation is not permitted, so the balance cannot come in under this authorisation
options.why: An EPCG authorisation is valid for import for twenty-four months from the date of issue, and the policy says in the next sentence that revalidation of an EPCG authorisation shall not be permitted. There is nothing to extend.

options.text: It was valid for eighteen months and lapsed in October 2025
options.misconception: shortens the import window, which is a figure the paragraph states plainly
options.why: The figure is twenty-four months from the date of issue of the authorisation, so the window ran to March 2026 and the part already imported was in time.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5.01(d) of Chapter 5

items.scenario: An EPCG authorisation is issued on 1 April 2024 with a six year export obligation period. The holder imports part of the capital goods by March 2026 and applies in May 2026 to revalidate the authorisation so that he can bring in the rest.

items.stem: May he sell it?

options.text: No — the actual user condition runs until the obligation is completed and the certificate is granted
options.why: Paragraph 5.03 sets both events, not one: imported capital goods are subject to the actual user condition till export obligation is completed AND the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate is granted. Performing in fact is half of it; the certificate is the other half.

options.text: No, and he never may — the actual user condition on capital goods imported at zero duty is permanent
options.misconception: reads a condition with a stated end as having none
options.why: It has an end and the paragraph states it: the actual user condition runs till the export obligation is completed and the certificate is granted. After that the machine is his to deal with.

options.text: Yes — the obligation has been discharged in fact, and the certificate only records it
options.misconception: stops at the first of the two events the paragraph names
options.why: The paragraph names two events joined by an and. An Export Obligation Discharge Certificate that merely recorded the past would not need naming at all. Until it is granted the condition is still on the machine.

options.text: Yes, provided he pays proportionate duty with interest on the sale
options.misconception: reaches for the remedy for default when there has been no default
options.why: Proportionate duty with interest is what a holder pays when he does NOT meet the obligation. This holder met it, and what he is waiting for is the Export Obligation Discharge Certificate, not a way of buying his way out.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5.03 of Chapter 5

items.scenario: An EPCG holder has exported enough to meet six times the duty saved and has met his average export obligation every year. He has applied for his Export Obligation Discharge Certificate but it has not yet been granted. A buyer offers to take the imported machine off his hands now.

items.stem: What is the deferred tax balance on the machine at 31 March 2026?

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹13.20 lakh
options.misconception: stops at the temporary difference and never applies the tax rate to it
options.why: ₹13.20 lakh is the temporary difference itself. Deferred tax is the tax on that difference, so the rate of 25 per cent still has to be applied, which brings it to ₹3.30 lakh.

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹3.30 lakh
options.misconception: gets the difference right and the sign wrong, reading an asset carried above its tax base as producing a deferred tax asset
options.why: The ₹13.20 lakh is right. The direction is not. When an asset's carrying amount is higher than its tax base, the future deductions left in the tax system are smaller than the benefits the company will report, so future tax payments will be larger, and larger future payments are a liability.
keywords: future tax payments will be larger

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹1.05 lakh
options.misconception: reports the year's movement, which is the deferred tax expense, in place of the balance the balance sheet carries
options.why: At 31 March 2025 the carrying amount was ₹105 lakh against a tax base of ₹96 lakh, a liability of ₹2.25 lakh. The balance has moved to ₹3.30 lakh, so ₹1.05 lakh is the charge for the year. The balance sheet carries the balance, not the movement.
keywords: carries the balance, not the movement

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹3.30 lakh
options.why: Two years of straight line depreciation at ₹15 lakh a year leave a carrying amount of ₹90 lakh. Tax depreciation is ₹24 lakh in the first year and ₹19.20 lakh in the second, so the tax base is ₹76.80 lakh. The carrying amount of the asset exceeds its tax base by ₹13.20 lakh, which makes the difference taxable rather than deductible, and 25 per cent of ₹13.20 lakh is ₹3.30 lakh of deferred tax liability.

citation.ref: the definition of the tax base of an asset and the requirement that a taxable temporary difference multiplied by the applicable rate gives a deferred tax liability

items.scenario: A company bought a machine on 1 April 2024 for ₹120 lakh. In its books it depreciates the machine on the straight line basis over eight years with no residual value. The tax law allows depreciation on the written down value at 20 per cent a year. The applicable tax rate is 25 per cent and no change to it has been announced. The company is preparing its balance sheet at 31 March 2026, and its finance executive has written down four possible figures for the deferred tax on this machine.

items.stem: What deferred tax balance does the provision carry at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Nothing — the provision is disallowed for tax, so there is no deferred tax on it
options.misconception: reads a timing difference as a permanent one because the deduction is refused this year
options.why: The deduction is not refused, it is postponed to the year of payment, and a postponed deduction is exactly what a temporary difference is. A permanent difference is one where the deduction never arrives at all.
keywords: postponed to the year of payment

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹10 lakh
options.why: The tax base of a liability is its carrying amount less any amount that will be deductible in future periods. The whole ₹40 lakh will be deductible when paid, so the tax base is nil and the deductible temporary difference is the full ₹40 lakh. At 25 per cent that is a deferred tax asset of ₹10 lakh, and it is recognised because the company expects taxable profits to use it against.
keywords: less any amount that will be deductible in future periods

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹10 lakh
options.misconception: flips the sign, treating a liability whose carrying amount exceeds its tax base as producing a deferred tax liability
options.why: For a liability the direction is the reverse of an asset's. A carrying amount above the tax base means deductions still to come that have not yet been taken, so future tax payments will be smaller, and that is an asset.
keywords: future tax payments will be smaller

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹3.75 lakh
options.misconception: reports the year's movement in the deferred tax asset in place of the balance
options.why: The opening provision of ₹25 lakh carried a deferred tax asset of ₹6.25 lakh, and the closing one carries ₹10 lakh, so ₹3.75 lakh is the credit for the year. It is the movement, and the balance sheet asks for the balance.
keywords: the balance sheet asks for the balance

citation.ref: the definition of the tax base of a liability as its carrying amount less any amount that will be deductible for tax purposes in respect of that liability in future periods

items.scenario: A company gives a two-year warranty with its products. Its warranty provision stood at ₹25 lakh at 31 March 2025 and at ₹40 lakh at 31 March 2026. The tax law allows a deduction for warranty costs only in the year the company actually pays them, and every rupee in the provision is expected to be paid and deducted in a later year. The tax rate is 25 per cent. The company is profitable and expects to remain so.

items.stem: What deferred tax arises in the consolidated financial statements on the goods still held?

options.text: Nothing — the profit is eliminated on consolidation, so there is nothing left to tax-effect
options.misconception: treats the consolidation adjustment as removing the difference, when the adjustment is what creates it
options.why: Before the elimination the group's books and the tax return agreed. It is the elimination that pulls the carrying amount below the tax base, so the adjustment creates the temporary difference rather than removing it.
keywords: It is the elimination that pulls the carrying amount below the tax base

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹3.6 lakh
options.why: In the consolidated balance sheet the unsold goods are carried at what they cost the group, 40 per cent of ₹60 lakh, which is ₹24 lakh. Their tax base is what the subsidiary paid for them, 40 per cent of ₹90 lakh, which is ₹36 lakh. The tax base is higher, so the ₹12 lakh difference is deductible and gives a deferred tax asset of ₹3.6 lakh at 30 per cent. The same figure arrives from the other direction, since the unrealised profit is 40 per cent of the ₹30 lakh mark-up.
keywords: carried at what they cost the group
Their tax base is what the subsidiary paid

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹3.6 lakh
options.misconception: flips the sign, reading the elimination of profit on consolidation as something that raises future tax
options.why: The group has paid tax early, on a profit its own accounts have not yet reported. What is coming is relief, not a further charge, so the balance is an asset.

options.text: A deferred tax asset of ₹9 lakh
options.misconception: tax-effects the whole intra-group profit instead of the part still sitting in inventory
options.why: ₹9 lakh is 30 per cent of the entire ₹30 lakh mark-up. Sixty per cent of the goods have left the group, so that much of the profit is realised and there is no longer any difference between the group's books and the tax return on it. Only the ₹12 lakh still in inventory is a temporary difference.
keywords: that much of the profit is realised

citation.ref: the example of a deductible temporary difference arising where unrealised profits on intragroup transactions are eliminated from the carrying amount of inventory with no equivalent adjustment for tax purposes

items.scenario: A parent sold goods to its wholly owned subsidiary during the year ended 31 March 2026 for ₹90 lakh. Those goods had cost the parent ₹60 lakh. By 31 March 2026 the subsidiary had sold 60 per cent of them to outside customers and still held the rest. Both companies are taxed by the same taxation authority at 30 per cent and both expect to make taxable profits. The parent has already been taxed on its profit on the sale.

items.stem: What is the deferred tax asset at 31 March 2027, and what is the deferred tax movement for that year?

options.text: No asset at all, and a deferred tax expense of ₹9 lakh for the year
options.misconception: treats any sale outside the group as realising the whole of the intra-group profit
options.why: A quarter of the goods have not left the group. The profit inside them is still unrealised and still carries a difference between the consolidated carrying amount and the tax base, so ₹2.25 lakh of asset survives into the following year.

options.text: An asset of ₹2.25 lakh, and deferred tax income of ₹6.75 lakh for the year
options.misconception: gets the balance right and the direction of the movement wrong
options.why: The asset has shrunk, and a shrinking asset is a charge. Deferred tax income would mean the balance had grown, which happens in the year of the intra-group sale, not in the year the goods are sold on.
keywords: a shrinking asset is a charge

options.text: An asset of ₹2.25 lakh, and a deferred tax expense of ₹6.75 lakh for the year
options.why: At 31 March 2026 the whole ₹30 lakh mark-up was unrealised and the asset was ₹9 lakh. A year later a quarter of the goods remain, so the unrealised profit is ₹7.5 lakh and the asset is ₹2.25 lakh. The balance has fallen by ₹6.75 lakh, and a fall in a deferred tax asset is a deferred tax expense in the year the goods are sold on — which is exactly the year the group reports the profit the tax was paid on.
keywords: a fall in a deferred tax asset is a deferred tax expense

options.text: An asset of ₹6.75 lakh, and a deferred tax credit of ₹2.25 lakh for the year
options.misconception: swaps the balance and the movement, taking the realised part as the closing balance
options.why: ₹6.75 lakh is the part that has been realised and so has gone; ₹2.25 lakh is what is left. The two figures are right and they are in each other's places.
keywords: the part that has been realised

citation.ref: the example of a deductible temporary difference on unrealised intragroup profit eliminated from inventory, read with the requirement that the deferred tax balance is remeasured at each reporting date and the movement recognised in the period

items.scenario: In the year ended 31 March 2026 a parent sold goods costing it ₹50 lakh to its wholly owned subsidiary for ₹80 lakh, and none of them had been sold outside the group by the year end. In the year ended 31 March 2027 the subsidiary sold three-quarters of those goods to outside customers and still holds the rest. Both companies are taxed by the same taxation authority at 30 per cent throughout and both are profitable.

items.stem: What deferred tax arises on the acquisition, and what goodwill does the acquirer recognise?

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹15 crore, and goodwill of ₹35 crore
options.why: The three uplifts total ₹60 crore of taxable temporary difference, so the deferred tax liability is ₹15 crore, recognised as one of the liabilities assumed at the acquisition date. Net assets at fair value are ₹180 crore plus ₹60 crore less ₹15 crore, which is ₹225 crore, and goodwill is ₹260 crore less ₹225 crore. No deferred tax is recognised on the goodwill itself.
keywords: recognised as one of the liabilities assumed
No deferred tax is recognised on the goodwill itself

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹23.75 crore, and goodwill of ₹35 crore
options.misconception: recognises deferred tax on the initial recognition of goodwill as well as on the fair value uplifts
options.why: ₹23.75 crore is 25 per cent of the ₹60 crore uplift plus 25 per cent of the ₹35 crore goodwill. The standard refuses deferred tax on the initial recognition of goodwill, and the reason is visible in the arithmetic — the liability would reduce net assets, which would raise goodwill, which would raise the liability again.
keywords: refuses deferred tax on the initial recognition of goodwill

options.text: A deferred tax liability of ₹15 crore, and goodwill of ₹5 crore
options.misconception: recognises the deferred tax liability but adds it to the identifiable net assets instead of deducting it
options.why: A liability assumed reduces what the acquirer has bought. Adding ₹15 crore takes net assets to ₹255 crore and understates goodwill by ₹30 crore, which is twice the deferred tax.
keywords: reduces what the acquirer has bought

options.text: No deferred tax, and goodwill of ₹20 crore
options.misconception: leaves the fair value uplifts out of the deferred tax computation because they never touch the acquiree's own books
options.why: It is precisely because the uplifts never reach the tax computation that they are temporary differences. The consolidated figures carry the assets at ₹240 crore while the tax system still carries them at ₹180 crore, and that gap is taxable.

citation.ref: the requirement that deferred tax arising in a business combination is recognised as an identifiable asset or liability at the acquisition date and so affects goodwill, and the exception for the initial recognition of goodwill

items.scenario: On 1 April 2025 an acquirer bought the whole of a company for ₹260 crore in cash. The acquiree's identifiable net assets stood in its own books at ₹180 crore, and those book values equal their tax bases. The fair value exercise raised land by ₹30 crore and plant by ₹20 crore, and recognised a brand worth ₹10 crore that the acquiree had never carried. None of the three changes anything in the acquiree's tax computation, and nothing about the goodwill will ever be deductible for tax. The rate expected to apply to the reversals is 25 per cent.

items.stem: What goodwill does H Ltd recognise on the acquisition of S Ltd?

options.text: ₹3.5 crore
options.why: The uplifts total ₹10 crore, so the deferred tax liability is ₹2.5 crore and net assets at fair value are ₹52 crore plus ₹10 crore less ₹2.5 crore, which is ₹59.5 crore. The non-controlling interest at fair value is 1 crore shares at ₹15, which is ₹15 crore. Goodwill is ₹48 crore plus ₹15 crore less ₹59.5 crore.

options.text: ₹3.375 crore
options.misconception: measures the non-controlling interest at its proportionate share of net assets when the group's policy is fair value
options.why: A quarter of ₹59.5 crore is ₹14.875 crore, which is what the proportionate share basis would give. The group has elected fair value, and the quoted price of ₹15 a share puts the non-controlling interest at ₹15 crore instead.
keywords: the proportionate share basis would give
The group has elected fair value

options.text: ₹16.5 crore
options.misconception: applies the tax rate to the whole of the net assets rather than to the temporary differences on them
options.why: 25 per cent of ₹62 crore is ₹15.5 crore, which would be the tax on selling the business rather than the deferred tax on the differences inside it. Only the ₹10 crore of uplift is a temporary difference; the ₹52 crore of book net assets already agrees with its tax base.
keywords: Only the ₹10 crore of uplift is a temporary difference

options.text: ₹1 crore
options.misconception: omits the deferred tax on the fair value uplifts, leaving net assets overstated by the whole liability
options.why: Without the ₹2.5 crore liability net assets come out at ₹62 crore and goodwill at ₹1 crore. Goodwill moves rupee for rupee with the deferred tax, which is why leaving it out is visible in the answer.
keywords: Goodwill moves rupee for rupee with the deferred tax

citation.ref: the recognition of deferred tax on fair value adjustments as part of the acquisition accounting, read with Ind AS 103 paragraph 19 on measuring the non-controlling interest at fair value or at the proportionate share of identifiable net assets

items.scenario: On 1 April 2025 H Ltd paid ₹48 crore in cash for 75 per cent of S Ltd. S Ltd has 4 crore equity shares in issue and its shares were quoted at ₹15 each on that date. H Ltd's stated policy is to measure the non-controlling interest in every acquisition at its acquisition-date fair value, using the quoted price where one exists. S Ltd's own books showed net assets of ₹52 crore, equal to their tax bases. The fair value exercise raised property by ₹8 crore and inventory by ₹2 crore, with no equivalent adjustment for tax. The rate expected to apply is 25 per cent.

items.stem: What deferred tax liability does the company recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹20 crore
options.misconception: applies the new rate to everything, including the reversal that happens before the new rate takes effect
options.why: 25 per cent of ₹80 crore is ₹20 crore. The cut applies to income arising on and after 1 April 2027, so the ₹20 crore reversing in 2026-27 is still taxed at 30 per cent.
keywords: is still taxed at 30 per cent

options.text: ₹16.76 crore
options.misconception: discounts the deferred tax balance to present value because the reversals are spread over four years
options.why: Discounting ₹6 crore, ₹5 crore, ₹5 crore and ₹5 crore at the factors given produces ₹16.76 crore, and the standard forbids it in terms. Deferred tax liabilities and assets are not discounted, which is why detailed scheduling of reversal dates is needed for the rate and never for the timing.
keywords: Deferred tax liabilities and assets are not discounted

options.text: ₹21 crore
options.why: Deferred tax is measured at the rates expected to apply to the period in which each difference reverses. The ₹20 crore reversing in 2026-27 falls before the change and goes at 30 per cent, giving ₹6 crore. The ₹60 crore reversing in the three years after that goes at 25 per cent, giving ₹15 crore. The cut counts because it is substantively enacted by the reporting date, and no discounting is permitted.
keywords: the rates expected to apply to the period in which each difference reverses
substantively enacted by the reporting date

options.text: ₹24 crore
options.misconception: uses the rate in force at the reporting date for everything, ignoring a change that is already substantively enacted
options.why: 30 per cent of ₹80 crore is ₹24 crore. The test is not the rate in force today but the rate expected to apply when each difference reverses, and a substantively enacted cut is exactly the kind of thing that changes that expectation.
keywords: not the rate in force today

citation.ref: the requirement to measure deferred tax at the rates expected to apply to the period of reversal based on rates enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period, and the prohibition on discounting deferred tax liabilities and assets

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company has taxable temporary differences of ₹80 crore, which will reverse evenly at ₹20 crore a year over the four years beginning 2026-27. The rate in force is 30 per cent. Before 31 March 2026 the government announced a cut to 25 per cent for income arising on and after 1 April 2027, and in this jurisdiction such an announcement is regarded as having the substantive effect of enactment. The company's treasurer suggests discounting the liability, and offers present value factors at 10 per cent of 0.9091, 0.8264, 0.7513 and 0.6830.

items.stem: What is the liability after the rate change, and where does the increase go?

options.text: ₹36 crore, the new rate being applied only from the following year
options.misconception: waits for the new rate to take effect before remeasuring, when the test is the rate expected to apply on reversal
options.why: The balance is measured at the rate expected to apply when the differences reverse, and those reversals are all after the change. Waiting would report a liability the company knows is too small.
keywords: the rate expected to apply when the differences reverse

options.text: ₹42 crore, with the whole ₹6 crore taken to other comprehensive income
options.misconception: sends the whole effect of a rate change outside profit or loss because part of the balance sits there
options.why: Only ₹12 crore of the ₹36 crore relates to the revaluation. The ₹24 crore on accelerated depreciation was always a charge in profit or loss and its ₹4 crore increase stays there.
keywords: was always a charge in profit or loss

options.text: ₹42 crore, with the whole ₹6 crore charged to profit or loss
options.misconception: sends every effect of a rate change to profit or loss, because the rate change itself has nothing to do with the revaluation
options.why: The rule looks at what the balance relates to, not at what caused it to move. ₹2 crore of the increase relates to a surplus sitting in other comprehensive income and follows it there.
keywords: looks at what the balance relates to

options.text: ₹42 crore, with ₹4 crore charged to profit or loss and ₹2 crore to other comprehensive income
options.why: Restating at 35 per cent takes ₹36 crore to ₹42 crore. A change in rates is recognised in profit or loss except to the extent that it relates to items previously recognised outside profit or loss, so the part of the increase attaching to the revaluation, ₹12 crore restated to ₹14 crore, follows the revaluation into other comprehensive income and the rest goes through profit or loss.
keywords: except to the extent that it relates to items previously recognised outside profit or loss
follows the revaluation into other comprehensive income

citation.ref: the requirement that deferred tax resulting from a change in tax rates is recognised in profit or loss except to the extent that it relates to items previously recognised outside profit or loss, whether in other comprehensive income or directly in equity

items.scenario: Before adjusting for a change in rates, a company's deferred tax liability at 31 March 2026 stands at ₹36 crore, measured at 30 per cent. ₹12 crore of it arose on a revaluation of property whose surplus was recognised in other comprehensive income, and the deferred tax on it was recognised there too. The remaining ₹24 crore arose on accelerated tax depreciation, and was charged to profit or loss. A rise in the rate to 35 per cent, applying to every one of these reversals, was substantively enacted before 31 March 2026.

items.stem: What deferred tax asset may the company recognise on the unused losses?

options.text: ₹8.75 crore
options.misconception: counts only the taxable temporary differences and treats the evidenced future profit as too soft to count
options.why: The test is written with two limbs joined by "or" — sufficient taxable temporary differences, or convincing other evidence that sufficient taxable profit will be available. A signed contract is the second limb, and it counts.

options.text: ₹5 crore
options.misconception: counts only the evidenced future profit and forgets that taxable temporary differences are themselves future taxable amounts
options.why: A taxable temporary difference reversing in the right period is a future taxable amount by construction — that is what makes it taxable — so it is the first thing to look at, not something outside the test.
keywords: a future taxable amount by construction

options.text: ₹13.75 crore
options.why: Where an entity has a history of recent losses, a deferred tax asset on unused tax losses is recognised only to the extent of sufficient taxable temporary differences, or convincing other evidence that sufficient taxable profit will be available.
