Audit of Banks — the audit procedures for Stationery and Stamps and for Inter-Office Adjustments under Other Assets, including the confinement of the head to exceptional items valued at cost, the physical verification of security stationery at the year end, and the reporting of the year-end status of inter-branch accounts with the dates reconciled and the outstanding debit and credit entries

items.scenario: Two items in a bank's Other Assets schedule are being discussed at the closing meeting. The first is Stationery and Stamps of ₹41 crore, which the finance team has built by carrying forward the whole of the year's unconsumed stationery at every branch, including ordinary printed forms supplied by head office. The second is Inter-Office Adjustments, where the central reconciliation is complete only to a date four months before the year end and a large number of entries remain outstanding on both sides. The finance head says the outstanding entries will clear in the normal course and that a bare figure in the schedule is all a reader needs.

items.stem: What is wrong?

options.text: Only the partly paid investments. Derivative contracts belong with guarantees given on behalf of constituents, and bills for collection belong with acceptances and endorsements
options.misconception: keeps the items but merges them into neighbouring heads, which defeats the point of a prescribed breakdown
options.why: Outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts have their own head, and bills for collection are not a contingent liability at all — they are shown separately because the bank holds the bills as an agent rather than owing anything on them.
keywords: holds the bills as an agent

options.text: Nothing, provided management represents that all off-balance sheet transactions have been accounted for and all year-end contingent liabilities disclosed
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for the disclosure it is meant to support
options.why: The representation is one of the auditor's procedures and covers, among other things, that all off-balance sheet transactions have been accounted for as and when entered into and that all year-end contingent liabilities have been disclosed. It does not decide which heads the disclosure carries; the Third Schedule does.
keywords: It does not decide which heads

options.text: All three. The liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts and the liability for partly paid investments are each separate heads of contingent liabilities under the Third Schedule, and bills for collection are shown separately rather than within any contingent liability head
options.why: The heads are prescribed and there are six of them — claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts, liability for partly paid investments, liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts, guarantees given on behalf of constituents within and outside India, acceptances, endorsements and other obligations, and other items for which the bank is contingently liable. Bills for collection sit apart from all six, because the bank holds those bills as an agent.
keywords: liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts

options.text: Only the bills for collection, since derivative positions carried at fair value and unpaid calls on investments are both recognised in the balance sheet and disclosing them again would double count
options.misconception: assumes recognition in the balance sheet displaces the contingent liability disclosure, when both are prescribed heads of that disclosure
options.why: The Third Schedule names both as heads of contingent liabilities in their own right. The disclosure is of the exposure, not a second recognition of an amount already booked, which is why the auditor's concern is that all contingent liabilities are identified and properly valued.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the heads of contingent liabilities disclosed under the Third Schedule, including liability for partly paid investments and liability on account of outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts, and the separate disclosure of bills for collection

items.scenario: A bank's draft disclosure of contingent liabilities lists claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts, guarantees given on behalf of constituents, and acceptances, endorsements and other obligations. Three things have been left out. Outstanding forward exchange contracts and derivative contracts, on the view that these are trading positions carried at fair value in the books and so are already in the balance sheet. Liability for partly paid investments, on the view that the unpaid amount is a commitment rather than a liability. And bills held for collection on behalf of customers, which have been added into acceptances, endorsements and other obligations to keep the disclosure short.

items.stem: What does the auditor seek in the management representation on contingent liabilities?

options.text: That all off-balance sheet transactions have been accounted for as and when entered into, after following the due procedure laid down and supported by the underlying documents — which is the whole of the representation on contingent liabilities
options.misconception: names three real limbs of the representation and treats them as its entirety
options.why: Those three are in the representation and they are not all of it. The representation runs on to the disclosure of all year-end contingent liabilities, to crystallised liabilities, to AS 29 estimates, to guarantees on behalf of directors and section 20, and to the justification for treating an outcome as remote.
keywords: they are not all of it
the justification for treating an outcome as remote

options.text: That the estimated financial effects have been computed under AS 29, which answers all three, since a decreed claim, a director-related guarantee and a remote claim are all matters of estimation
options.misconception: folds three separate representations into the one about measurement, when only one of them is about estimating an amount
options.why: The AS 29 representation is that the estimated amounts of the financial effect of the contingent liabilities are based on best estimates, including consideration of the possibility of any reimbursement. It says nothing about whether a crystallised liability has been wrongly left in the disclosure, about section 20, or about a remote classification.

options.text: A representation is not sought on contingent liabilities at all, because a written representation is not audit evidence and the auditor must verify each item against the underlying documents
options.misconception: rejects a representation the chapter expressly directs the auditor to obtain, on a proposition about representations generally
options.why: The auditor is directed to obtain a representation from management on these matters, alongside his other procedures on the identification and valuation of contingent liabilities. The representation supplements the work on the underlying documents rather than replacing it.

options.text: That the disclosed contingent liabilities do not include any crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense, which require a provision or adjustment instead; that where guarantees have been issued on behalf of the bank's directors, arrangements exist for the commitment to be met out of the party's own resources so that no violation of section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 arises; and that management's justification is given for liabilities not disclosed because their outcome is remote
options.why: The representation covers each of the three. It states that the disclosed contingent liabilities do not include any crystallised liabilities which are of the nature of loss or expense and which therefore require creation of a provision or adjustment in the financial statements. It states that in the case of guarantees issued on behalf of the bank's directors, adequate and effective arrangements have been made so that the commitment would be met out of the party's own resources, that the bank will not be called upon to grant a loan or advance on invocation, and that no violation of section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 has arisen. And it states that contingent liabilities not disclosed because the possibility of their outcome is remote include management's justification for that decision.
keywords: met out of the party's own resources
section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the management representation obtained on contingent liabilities, including that crystallised liabilities of the nature of loss or expense are not shown as contingent, that estimated financial effects are best estimates in terms of AS 29 including any reimbursement, that guarantees issued on behalf of the bank's directors raise no violation of section 20 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and that management's justification is given where an outcome is treated as remote

items.scenario: You are auditing a bank's contingent liabilities. Three matters come up. A claim against the bank in a consumer dispute was decreed against it in February and the bank has decided not to appeal; the amount remains inside claims not acknowledged as debts. A guarantee has been issued on behalf of a company in which two of the bank's directors are interested, and nothing on the file shows what would happen if it were invoked. And a group of claims has been left out of the disclosure entirely on the ground that the possibility of any outflow is remote, with no note of why management takes that view.

items.stem: How is the question decided?

options.text: By the test on assets and income taken from the last audited balance sheet — financial assets more than 50 per cent of total assets netted off by intangible assets, and income from financial assets more than 50 per cent of gross income — and the company meets both, so it is a non-banking financial company and required to register
options.why: Both the asset pattern and the income pattern are considered, as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet, to decide the company's principal business. The company is treated as a non-banking financial company where its financial assets constitute more than 50 per cent of the total assets netted off by intangible assets, and income from financial assets constitutes more than 50 per cent of the gross income. Here the assets are ₹300 crore against ₹480 crore and the income is ₹38 crore against ₹60 crore, so both limbs are met, and a company which fulfils both criteria would require to be registered.
keywords: as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet
more than 50 per cent of the total assets
more than 50 per cent of the gross income

options.text: By the objects in the memorandum of association, which state what the company's principal business is; a company whose objects are trading is not a non-banking financial company however its balance sheet looks
options.misconception: answers a question of fact from the constitutional documents, when the test is quantitative and taken from the accounts
options.why: The principal business is identified from the asset pattern and the income pattern as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet. What the memorandum says the company was set up to do does not enter the test.
keywords: asset pattern and the income pattern

options.text: By whether the lending is to outside parties. Lending confined to group companies is treasury management within a group and is excluded from financial assets for the purpose of the test
options.misconception: invents an exclusion for intra-group lending that the test does not contain
options.why: The test looks at financial assets and at income from financial assets. It does not ask who the borrower is, and nothing in it carves out lending to group companies.
keywords: does not ask who the borrower is

options.text: By the asset test alone. Financial assets above half of total assets makes the company a non-banking financial company, and the income figures are a cross-check rather than a condition
options.misconception: keeps one limb of a two limb test and demotes the other to corroboration
options.why: Both criteria must be fulfilled. The company is treated as a non-banking financial company where financial assets are more than 50 per cent of total assets netted off by intangible assets AND income from financial assets is more than 50 per cent of gross income, and a company which fulfils both these criteria qualifies.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the identification of a non-banking financial company from both the asset pattern and the income pattern as evidenced by the last audited balance sheet, with financial assets more than 50 per cent of total assets netted off by intangible assets and income from financial assets more than 50 per cent of gross income

items.scenario: You have been appointed auditor of a company that describes itself in its memorandum as a trading company and has never held a certificate of registration from the Reserve Bank. Its last audited balance sheet shows total assets of ₹500 crore, of which intangible assets are ₹20 crore and financial assets — loans given to group companies and to unrelated borrowers, and investments in securities — are ₹300 crore. Its gross income for that year was ₹60 crore, of which ₹38 crore was interest and dividend income from those financial assets. The directors say the company cannot be a non-banking financial company because lending is not what the company was set up to do and because most of the lending is to group companies.

items.stem: What does the auditor have to do about it in his report?

options.text: Answer clause 3(xvi)(a) but only after the company has applied for registration, since until then it is not established that registration was required
options.misconception: makes the auditor's answer wait on the company's application, when the requirement to register is decided by the test and not by the application
options.why: Whether registration is required is answered by the principal business test on the last audited balance sheet, and the company meets both limbs. The auditor answers the clause on the position as it is, and an application not yet made is part of what makes the answer unfavourable.
keywords: answered by the principal business test
part of what makes the answer unfavourable

options.text: Nothing in the report. Registration is regulatory and the auditor's remedy is to report the matter to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank under the directions issued to auditors of non-banking financial companies
options.misconception: routes the matter to a reporting duty that belongs to the auditor of a registered non-banking financial company, and drops the CARO clause that applies here
options.why: The additional report to the Board and the exception report to the Regional Office are duties under the directions the Reserve Bank issues to auditors of non-banking financial companies. This company is not registered and this auditor's duty on these facts is the CARO clause, which asks exactly this question of every company the Order covers.

options.text: Modify the opinion on the financial statements, because carrying on the business of a non-banking financial institution without a certificate of registration is a contravention of law
options.misconception: converts a non-compliance into a modification without asking whether the financial statements are misstated
options.why: A modification requires a material misstatement of the financial statements or an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Non-compliance is reported where the law requires it to be reported, and here that is the CARO clause; whether the opinion is modified turns on the effect of the non-compliance on the financial statements.
keywords: turns on the effect of the non-compliance

options.text: Answer clause 3(xvi)(a) of the Order, which asks whether the company is required to be registered under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and, if so, whether the registration has been obtained — and state the basis for the unfavourable answer
options.why: The Order puts the question directly to the auditor. Clause 3(xvi)(a) asks whether the company is required to be registered under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and if so whether the registration has been obtained. On these facts the answer is that it is required and has not been, which is an unfavourable answer, and paragraph 4(a) requires the report to state the basis for it.
keywords: required to be registered under section 45-IA
whether the registration has been obtained

citation.ref: clause 3(xvi)(a) on whether the company is required to be registered under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and if so whether the registration has been obtained, read with paragraph 4(a) on stating the basis for an unfavourable or qualified answer

items.scenario: The company in the previous engagement meets both limbs of the principal business test and has never registered. It is covered by the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020. The audit manager proposes to raise the matter with the directors, note it in the working papers, and leave the auditor's report alone on the ground that registration is a matter between the company and the Reserve Bank.

items.stem: What should the answer to clause 3(xvii) say?

options.text: That the company has incurred cash losses in the financial year and in the immediately preceding financial year, with the amount of the cash losses stated for each — ₹2.10 crore and ₹1.45 crore
options.why: The clause asks two things at once. It asks whether the company has incurred cash losses in the financial year and in the immediately preceding financial year, and it then says that if so, the auditor is to state the amount of the cash losses. Both years are inside the question, so both amounts go into the answer, and a bare "Yes" leaves out the half of the clause that asks for the figure.
keywords: in the financial year and in the immediately preceding financial year
state the amount of the cash losses

options.text: That the company has incurred cash losses of ₹2.10 crore in the financial year; the preceding year is outside the scope of the current year's report
options.misconception: confines the clause to the year under audit, when its words carry it back one year
options.why: The clause says in terms that it covers the financial year and the immediately preceding financial year. The report is for the current year but the question it answers spans two, and dropping the earlier year answers only half of it.
keywords: the financial year and the immediately preceding financial year

options.text: That the company has incurred operating losses of ₹1.60 crore and ₹0.70 crore in the two years
options.misconception: reports the operating loss, which is a different figure from the one the clause names
options.why: The clause names cash losses. The operating loss is another figure in the same schedule and answering with it means the reader of the CARO annexure is given a number the Order did not ask for.
keywords: a number the Order did not ask for

options.text: That the company has incurred a loss of ₹5.40 crore in the financial year, being the loss before tax shown by the statement of profit and loss
options.misconception: answers with the loss in the profit and loss account, treating a cash loss as though it were the reported loss
options.why: The loss before tax and the cash loss are different figures, which is why the schedule carries both. The clause asks for the cash loss, and it asks about the preceding year too, which this answer leaves out altogether.
keywords: asks about the preceding year too

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xvii)

items.scenario: You are the statutory auditor of a company to which the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 applies, for the year ended 31 March. The company has had two poor years. Its schedules, which you have verified, give the following for the year under audit and for the year before it. Turnover was ₹63 crore and ₹71 crore. The debit balance in the profit and loss account stood at ₹9.30 crore at the year end. The loss before tax was ₹5.40 crore and ₹3.90 crore. The operating loss was ₹1.60 crore and ₹0.70 crore. The cash loss was ₹2.10 crore and ₹1.45 crore. Your audit manager has drafted the CARO annexure and has answered clause 3(xvii) with the single word "Yes".

items.stem: What should the answer say?

options.text: That the company has not incurred cash losses in the financial year or in the immediately preceding financial year
options.why: The clause asks about cash losses, not about the loss in the statement of profit and loss, and those are different figures. Where the verified position is that no cash loss arose in either year, that is the answer, and the figures from the statement of profit and loss do not belong in it. The clause is still answered rather than left blank.
keywords: still answered rather than left blank

options.text: Nothing. Where the answer is in the negative the clause is not applicable and the annexure omits it
options.misconception: treats the clause as exception reporting, when paragraph 3 requires a statement on each specified matter
options.why: Paragraph 3 says the auditor's report shall include a statement on the matters specified. Every clause that applies to the company is answered, and an omitted clause tells the reader nothing about whether the question was even asked.
keywords: shall include a statement on the matters specified
an omitted clause tells the reader nothing

options.text: That the company has incurred losses of ₹8.40 crore and ₹7.10 crore, since the clause is intended to alert the reader to a loss-making company
options.misconception: replaces the figure the clause names with the one the answerer thinks the clause was for
options.why: What the clause is for is not the test; its words are. It asks whether cash losses were incurred and, if so, for the amount of the cash losses. A reader who wants the loss before tax has the statement of profit and loss.
keywords: the amount of the cash losses

options.text: That the company has not incurred cash losses, together with a statement of the basis on which that answer is given, as paragraph 4 of the Order requires
options.misconception: attaches the basis requirement to a favourable answer, when paragraph 4 attaches it to an unfavourable or qualified one
options.why: Paragraph 4(a) requires the basis to be stated where the answer to a paragraph 3 question is unfavourable or qualified. A plain negative answer to this clause is neither, so no basis is called for.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xvii), read with paragraph 3 and paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: A company to which the Order applies carries a very large depreciation charge on a plant commissioned three years ago. Its statement of profit and loss shows a loss before tax of ₹8.40 crore this year and ₹7.10 crore last year. The workings you have verified show that the company incurred no cash loss in either year. The audit senior's draft answers clause 3(xvii) by saying that the company has incurred losses of ₹8.40 crore and ₹7.10 crore in the two years, on the view that a loss is a loss and the clause cannot have meant to let a loss-making company answer in the negative.

items.stem: What does the Order require?

options.text: Answer for both years using the preceding auditor's report, and state that the preceding year's answer is based solely on that report
options.misconception: substitutes another auditor's report for evidence on a matter this auditor must state, without the Order providing for such reliance
options.why: The previous year's audit report carries an opinion on the previous year's financial statements; it does not answer this clause for the auditor now signing. Where he cannot form his own view he says so and gives the reasons, which is what the Order provides for.

options.text: Answer for the current year only. A clause cannot require an auditor to report on a year he did not audit, and the previous auditor's report covers that year
options.misconception: reads a limit into the clause from who signed the earlier report, when the clause's words look at the company's position in both years
options.why: The clause asks about the company, not about the auditor's own engagements. The immediately preceding financial year is inside the question whoever audited it, and the Order supplies a route for an auditor who cannot answer rather than an exemption from answering.
keywords: a route for an auditor who cannot answer

options.text: The clause covers both years, so the preceding year must be addressed; and where the auditor is unable to express an opinion on a specified matter his report shall indicate that fact together with the reasons why he cannot
options.why: The clause asks about the financial year and the immediately preceding financial year, and nothing in it turns on who audited the earlier year. Where the auditor cannot answer, the Order provides for that too: where he is unable to express any opinion on any specified matter, his report shall indicate such fact together with the reasons as to why it is not possible for him to give his opinion on the same. Silence is the one answer the Order does not allow.
keywords: indicate such fact together with the reasons

options.text: Answer for both years and, since the position for the earlier year is unknown, modify the audit opinion on the current year's financial statements for a limitation on scope
options.misconception: escalates an unanswerable CARO clause into a modification of the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: The CARO annexure and the opinion are different reports answering different questions. An inability to answer a clause of the Order is dealt with inside the Order, by indicating the fact with reasons; it does not by itself say anything is missing from the evidence supporting the current year's financial statements.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xvii), read with paragraph 4(b)

items.scenario: You have been appointed statutory auditor of a company for the year ended 31 March. It is your first year on the engagement. The company has incurred a cash loss this year and the amount is not in dispute. The preceding year was audited by another firm, which has since ceased practice; you have the previous year's signed financial statements but the schedule reconciling the previous year's cash position was never prepared and the underlying records for part of that year were destroyed in a flood before you were appointed. You have performed what alternative procedures you can and cannot satisfy yourself one way or the other about whether a cash loss arose in the preceding year. Your partner's instinct is to answer the clause for the current year only and say nothing about the earlier one.

items.stem: What does paragraph 4 of the Order add?

options.text: Nothing. Clause 3(xvii) asks for the amount and the amount has been given, and paragraph 4 applies only where the auditor qualifies his opinion on the financial statements
options.misconception: reads paragraph 4 as attaching to a qualified audit opinion, when it attaches to an unfavourable or qualified answer inside the annexure
options.why: Paragraph 4 is about the answers to the paragraph 3 questions, not about the opinion on the financial statements. An unfavourable answer inside the annexure triggers it whether or not the opinion itself is modified.
keywords: about the answers to the paragraph 3 questions
whether or not the opinion itself is modified

options.text: Paragraph 4 requires the basis only where the auditor is unable to express an opinion, so it reaches the statutory dues clause but not the cash losses clause
options.misconception: collapses the two limbs of paragraph 4 into one, dropping the limb about unfavourable and qualified answers
options.why: Paragraph 4 has two limbs. Sub-paragraph (a) requires the basis where the answer is unfavourable or qualified. Sub-paragraph (b) is the separate case where the auditor is unable to express any opinion, and then his report indicates that fact together with the reasons.

options.text: Paragraph 4 requires the auditor to modify his opinion on the financial statements wherever an answer under paragraph 3 is unfavourable
options.misconception: turns a requirement to explain an answer into a requirement to change the opinion
options.why: It requires the basis for the answer to be stated, and nothing more. Whether the opinion is modified is decided under SA 705 (Revised) on the audit evidence about the financial statements, and many unfavourable CARO answers sit beside an unmodified opinion.
keywords: requires the basis for the answer to be stated

options.text: Where the answer to any of the paragraph 3 questions is unfavourable or qualified, the report shall also state the basis for that answer — so both clauses need the basis stated, and the rule is general rather than particular to one clause
options.why: Paragraph 4(a) is written across the whole of paragraph 3. Where, in the auditor's report, the answer to any of the questions referred to in paragraph 3 is unfavourable or qualified, the report shall also state the basis for such unfavourable or qualified answer. A pair of amounts with no basis, and an unpaid statutory due with no explanation, both fall short of it.
keywords: any of the questions referred to in paragraph 3

citation.ref: paragraph 4(a) and paragraph 4(b), read with paragraph 3(xvii) and paragraph 3(vii)

items.scenario: A company to which the Order applies incurred cash losses in both the year under audit and the year before it, and the amounts are established and agreed. The audit manager's draft annexure answers clause 3(xvii) with the two amounts and nothing else. The engagement partner asks whether anything more is needed, and separately whether the same treatment applies to clause 3(vii) on statutory dues, where the draft records an unpaid amount without saying anything about why it is unpaid.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Repeat the clause 3(xvii) answer in the consolidated annexure, because the consolidated statements include the subsidiary and its losses are part of the group's result
options.misconception: applies the whole Order to the consolidated report, when paragraph 2 applies only one clause of it there
options.why: Consolidation brings the subsidiary's figures into the group statements; it does not bring the Order's clauses into the group report. The Order shall not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi).
keywords: does not bring the Order's clauses

options.text: Answer clause 3(xvii) in the consolidated annexure and add the emphasis of matter paragraph, since both draw attention to a matter properly disclosed in the consolidated financial statements
options.misconception: adds a paragraph on top of a clause that does not apply, and treats a component's CARO answer as a matter disclosed in the group statements
options.why: The clause does not apply to that report at all, so there is nothing to answer. And an emphasis of matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements; a statement made in another company's CARO annexure is not one, and clause (xxi) is the route the Order provides.
keywords: does not apply to that report
presented or disclosed in the financial statements

options.text: The Order does not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi), so there is no clause 3(xvii) answer to give there; what the consolidated report carries under the Order is the clause (xxi) statement about qualifications or adverse remarks in the CARO reports of the companies included in the consolidation
options.why: Paragraph 2 of the Order says that it shall not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3. Clause 3(xvii) therefore has no place in the consolidated annexure. The route by which a group reader learns of a component's CARO position is clause (xxi), which asks whether there have been any qualifications or adverse remarks in the CARO reports of the companies included in the consolidated financial statements and, if so, for the details.
keywords: no place in the consolidated annexure

options.text: Give no answer under the Order at all in the consolidated report, since the holding company itself has incurred no cash losses
options.misconception: reaches the right silence on clause 3(xvii) for the wrong reason, and drops the one clause that does apply
options.why: The reason there is no clause 3(xvii) answer is that the Order does not apply to a report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi), not that the holding company's own position is clean. Clause (xxi) still has to be answered in that annexure.
keywords: does not apply to a report on consolidated financial statements

citation.ref: paragraph 2, that the Order shall not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3, read with paragraph 3(xvii) and paragraph 3(xxi)

items.scenario: A holding company to which the Order applies has one Indian subsidiary, also covered by the Order. The subsidiary has incurred cash losses in both the year under audit and the preceding year; the holding company itself has not. You are the auditor of the holding company and are signing both the standalone and the consolidated financial statements. The subsidiary's own auditor has reported the cash losses under clause 3(xvii) in the subsidiary's CARO annexure. The audit manager wants to repeat that statement in the CARO annexure to your report on the consolidated financial statements, so that a reader of the group accounts is not left unaware of it, and separately proposes an emphasis of matter paragraph in the consolidated report drawing attention to the subsidiary's losses.

items.stem: Is CA Ranade right?

options.text: Yes — section 6 requires a certificate of practice only for the work that is reserved to chartered accountants, and tax representation is open to anybody the client authorises
options.misconception: treats the certificate as a licence for reserved work only, when section 6 bars a member from practising at all without it
options.why: Section 6 says no member shall be entitled to practise unless he holds a certificate of practice; it does not list the services. A member not in practice is precluded from accepting any engagement to render the services normally rendered by a chartered accountant even where the service needs no special qualification, and that is exactly the case of representation before an assessing officer.

options.text: Yes, provided he appears as an ordinary authorised representative and does not describe himself as a chartered accountant before the assessing officer
options.misconception: thinks the misconduct lies in the designation used, so that dropping the letters cures it
options.why: The Council's view is about capacity, not description. A member has no capacity in which to practise that is separable from his membership, so the appearance is one in his capacity as a chartered accountant whatever he calls himself at the hearing. Dropping the designation is a Clause (7) question; this is a section 6 one.

options.text: No, but only because he surrendered the certificate voluntarily — had he kept it through the suspension he could have continued the representation work
options.misconception: reads the surrender as the operative fact, when the suspension itself is what bars practice
options.why: Suspension from practice is the bar, and the surrender of the certificate follows from it rather than causing it. A suspended member cannot practise in any capacity during the period, and holding on to a piece of paper that the Council has suspended the right behind would change nothing.

options.text: No — a member has no other capacity, separable from his capacity as a member of the Institute, in which to take up such work, so he cannot appear before the tax authorities for the period he remains suspended, and he is guilty of professional misconduct
options.why: Once a person becomes a member of the Institute he is bound by the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and its Regulations, and when he appears before the income-tax authorities he does so only in his capacity as a chartered accountant and a member. The Council's view, carried into the module's own illustration of a member suspended for six months, is that having bound himself by the Act he cannot set it at naught by contending that, though suspended, he may practise in some other capacity — he has no other capacity. A member not holding a certificate of practice cannot take up any other such work for the period he remains suspended, and the representation assignments are professional misconduct.

citation.ref: Section 6(1), read with the Council's view that a member of the Institute can have no other capacity in which he can take up practice separable from his capacity to practise as a member, and Illustration 1 in chapter 19 of ICAI's Study Material — a member suspended for six months who undertook representation assignments before the income-tax authorities

items.scenario: The Disciplinary Committee suspends CA Ranade from practice for six months and he surrenders his certificate of practice for the period. He declines every audit that comes his way during those months. He does, however, keep appearing before the income-tax authorities for eight long-standing clients whose assessments are in progress, filing their replies and attending hearings as their authorised representative. His position is that representation is not an audit, that no certificate of practice is needed to appear before an assessing officer, and that a suspension from practice as a chartered accountant does not touch work he could have done had he never qualified at all.

items.stem: What is his position?

options.text: His name has been removed from the Register under section 20 for non-payment of a prescribed fee, so he must first apply for re-entry and pay the arrears before any certificate can exist
options.misconception: confuses the fee for the certificate of practice with the membership fee whose non-payment removes a name under section 20
options.why: Section 20 concerns the Register of Members and the prescribed fee for membership; what lapsed here is the annual fee for the certificate of practice under section 6(2), and the consequence of that lies in Regulation 10, which reaches the certificate and not the membership. Removal of the name is a separate event with its own ground.

options.text: The certificate became liable to cancellation when the fee stayed unpaid past 30 September; on an application in the approved form with the fee, received by the Secretary before the expiry of the relevant year, the Council may restore it with effect from the date on which it was cancelled
options.why: Regulation 10 lists non-payment of the annual fee for the certificate till the 30th day of September of the relevant year among the grounds on which a certificate of practice is liable for cancellation — the fee still unpaid on 30 September is the trigger — and section 6(2) fixes the fee as payable on or before 1 April. Regulation 11 answers the second half: for a certificate cancelled for non-payment of the fee, the Council may restore it with effect from the date on which it was cancelled, on an application complete in all respects with the fee, received before the expiry of the relevant year. January is inside the year, so the door is still open.
keywords: before the expiry of the relevant year
date on which it was cancelled

options.text: Nothing has happened to the certificate, because a certificate of practice can be cancelled only by an order of the Council after a hearing, and no such order has been made
options.misconception: applies the hearing that Regulation 10 attaches to the false-information ground to every ground
options.why: Regulation 10 gives four grounds and attaches the opportunity of being heard to one of them — a certificate issued on incorrect, misleading or false information or by mistake. Non-payment of the fee by 30 September is its own ground, and the module's own words are that the certificate shall be liable for cancellation on it.

options.text: The certificate stood cancelled on 1 April, the day the fee fell due, and restoration is possible only by a fresh application as if he had never held one
options.misconception: collapses the due date into the cancellation date and forgets that Regulation 11 restores from the cancellation date
options.why: The fee is due on or before 1 April, but the ground for cancellation is non-payment till 30 September; the six months between are the grace the Regulation gives. And a certificate cancelled for non-payment is restored under Regulation 11 with effect from the date of cancellation, not issued afresh, provided the application reaches the Secretary before the relevant year is out.

citation.ref: Regulation 10 (a certificate of practice liable for cancellation where the annual fee is not paid till the 30th day of September of the relevant year) and Regulation 11 (restoration with effect from the date of cancellation on an application received before the expiry of the relevant year), read with section 6(2) of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 fixing the fee as payable on or before 1 April

items.scenario: CA Bhaskar, a sole practitioner, forgot the annual fee for his certificate of practice for the year and paid nothing by 1 April, nothing by 30 September, and nothing since. In January of the following calendar year, still inside the same relevant year, his bank asks him for a certificate on a client's stock statement, and he notices the lapse. He asks whether the certificate has gone, and if so what he must do and from what date his position is regularised.

items.stem: Whose name may be entered?

options.text: Only Chetan's — insolvency, discharged or not, is a permanent disability, and Amol's age is cured by the time the Council meets to consider the application
options.misconception: reads insolvency as permanent and the age test as of the Council's meeting rather than the application
options.why: The section names an undischarged insolvent, and separately a discharged insolvent who lacks the court's certificate; a discharged insolvent who has the certificate is not debarred at all. The age test is applied at the time of the application for the entry of the name, in the words of the section, so an applicant of twenty years and nine months fails it whatever the calendar does afterwards.

options.text: All three, provided each discloses the fact on the application, because the only misconduct section 8 creates is the failure to disclose a disability
options.misconception: mistakes the disclosure rule for the whole of the section, when disclosure is an additional duty and the disabilities themselves bar entry
options.why: The module records two consequences side by side. The disabilities debar a person from having his name entered in or borne on the Register, and separately a failure to disclose that one suffers from a disability constitutes professional misconduct. Disclosure does not admit an applicant who is debarred; Amol is debarred by his age however candid the form.

options.text: Only Bina's — a conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude is a bar that no executive order can lift, and Amol is under age
options.misconception: forgets the two express escapes from the conviction bar, a pardon and a written order of the Central Government
options.why: Section 8 states the conviction bar with its own exception: unless in respect of the offence the person has either been granted a pardon or, on an application made by him, the Central Government has by an order in writing removed the disability. Chetan's order is exactly that, and the disability is gone.

options.text: Bina's and Chetan's, but not Amol's until he attains the age of 21 years — a discharged insolvent with the court's certificate of misfortune, and a convict whose disability the Central Government has removed by written order, are both outside section 8
options.why: Section 8 debars a person who has not attained the age of 21 years at the time of his application, so Amol must wait. It debars a discharged insolvent only where he has not obtained from the court a certificate that his insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part; Bina holds that certificate of misfortune. And it debars a person convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude unless he has been granted a pardon or the Central Government has, on his application, by order in writing removed the disability; Chetan has that order, and his disability was removed by written order.

citation.ref: Section 8, clauses (i), (iv) and (v) — the age of 21 years at the time of the application, a discharged insolvent without a certificate that the insolvency was caused by misfortune without misconduct, and a conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude unless pardoned or the disability removed by a written order of the Central Government

items.scenario: Three people who have passed the final examination and completed their training apply to have their names entered in the Register of Members in the same month. Amol is twenty years and nine months old on the date of his application. Bina was adjudged insolvent four years ago, has since been discharged, and holds a certificate from the court stating that her insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on her part. Chetan was convicted six years ago of an offence involving moral turpitude punishable with imprisonment, and the Central Government has since, on his application, removed the disability by an order in writing.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The Council may remove her name from the Register, because a person found to have been subject to a section 8 disability when the name was entered, or to have become subject to one since, may be removed under section 20, and her failure to disclose it was itself professional misconduct
options.why: Section 20 lets the Council remove the name of a member who is found to have been subject, at the time when his name was entered in the Register, or at any time thereafter, to any of the disabilities mentioned in section 8. An undischarged insolvent is one of those, and a discharged insolvent without the court's certificate of misfortune is another, so she was subject to a section 8 disability at entry and, on her own account, still is. The module adds that failure to disclose a disability constitutes professional misconduct, and the blank column is that failure.

options.text: Her name can be removed only for the specified period that the Disciplinary Committee fixes, and only after that period may the Council act under section 20
options.misconception: imports the specified-period rule for removal on inquiry into a removal for a disability, which needs no period
options.why: The specified-period rule belongs to the disability of having been removed from membership on being found guilty on inquiry: such a person cannot re-enter the Register until the period expires. Removal for a disability that existed at entry is a distinct ground under section 20, and nothing in it waits on a period fixed by anyone.

options.text: Nothing can be done, since her discharge ended the insolvency and section 8 speaks only of an undischarged insolvent
options.misconception: stops at the first insolvency clause and misses the second, which reaches a discharged insolvent without the court's certificate
options.why: Section 8 has two insolvency clauses. The first debars an undischarged insolvent; the second debars a discharged insolvent who has not obtained from the court a certificate stating that the insolvency was caused by misfortune without any misconduct on his part. Devika never obtained that certificate, so discharge alone did not lift the disability.

options.text: The Council may cancel her certificate of practice under Regulation 10 but may not disturb her membership, because the Register can only be altered at the member's own request or on death
options.misconception: reads section 20 as if it had only its first two grounds, and treats the certificate as the outer limit of the Council's reach
options.why: Section 20 gives four grounds — death, the member's own request, non-payment of a prescribed fee, and a section 8 disability found to have existed at entry or arisen since — and a fifth, mandatory removal on an order under the Act. The certificate does go with the name under Regulation 10, but it goes because the name goes, not instead of it.

citation.ref: Section 20 — removal from the Register of a member found to have been subject, at the time his name was entered or at any time thereafter, to any of the disabilities in section 8 — read with section 8 clauses (iii) and (iv) and the rule that failure to disclose a disability constitutes professional misconduct

items.scenario: When CA Devika applied for membership eleven years ago she was an undischarged insolvent and left the relevant column of the form blank. She was discharged two years later, never obtained any certificate from the court, and has practised without incident since. A former partner, now in dispute with her, writes to the Institute setting out the history. Devika's reply is that the disability, if it ever was one, ended with her discharge nine years ago, that she has been a member in good standing for over a decade, and that the Council has no power to touch a name that has stood on the Register that long.

items.stem: How does his answer stand?

options.text: It is valid — KYC norms bind banks and financial institutions under their own regulators, and the Council has issued none of its own for chartered accountants
options.misconception: stops at the industry the norms came from and misses that the Council adopted norms for members in practice
options.why: The financial services industry's obligation is the background the module gives; the foreground is that, keeping in mind the standards of the profession in India, the Council of ICAI issued KYC norms to be observed by members in practice. They exist, and they are the ones the agency is entitled to find on his file.

options.text: It is valid — the norms apply to assignments pertaining to attestation functions, and consultancy, compilation and an ERP set-up are none of those
options.misconception: reads the attestation sentence as a licence to hold nothing on a non-audit client, against the module's own answer to this very case
options.why: The module states that the norms apply in all assignments pertaining to attestation functions and, in the same chapter, holds this member to them for consultancy and a compilation engagement, calling his contention invalid. He is examined from ICAI's material, and ICAI's answer is that the information should have been kept.

options.text: It is not valid, but only because he should have obtained a copy of the last audited financial statement — the directors' particulars are the company's registrar's concern, not a consultant's
options.misconception: keeps the general block and drops the regulatory block that the corporate client alone carries
options.why: The regulatory information is the part of the norms that exists only for a corporate entity: the company's PAN, its CIN, and the directors' names, addresses and DINs. It is precisely what an agency investigating a group of companies would ask a member for, and it is on the list the module reproduces in answering this case.

options.text: It is not valid — the Council's KYC norms are mandatory in nature, and for a corporate client he should have kept the name and address, business description, the name of the parent company, a copy of the last audited financial statement, the type of engagement, and the company's PAN, CIN and its directors' names, addresses and DINs
options.why: This is the module's own case, answered its own way. The Council of ICAI approved KYC norms to be observed by members in practice, mandatory in nature, and the module holds a member who gave consultancy, a compilation engagement and advisory services to a corporate client to have been bound to keep the information for a corporate entity: the general block with the name of the parent company, the engagement block, and the regulatory block of the company's PAN, its CIN and the directors' names, addresses and DINs. His contention that he was not supposed to keep any information is not valid.

citation.source: Council of ICAI — KYC Norms for members in practice
citation.ref: The KYC norms approved by the Council, mandatory in nature, as applied in ICAI's Study Material, chapter 19, to a member who gave GST consultancy, a compilation engagement and ERP advisory services to a company found to be part of a money-laundering group — the general, engagement and regulatory information required for a corporate entity

items.scenario: CA Farhan gave GST consultancy to Meridian Traders Pvt Ltd for two years, carried out a compilation engagement on its historical financial information, and helped it set up an ERP system. He never audited it. An investigating agency now finds that Meridian is one of a group of companies used for money laundering and asks Farhan for the particulars he holds about the company, its parent and its directors. He has almost nothing on file and answers that he gave only consultancy and a compilation engagement, that he never certified anything, and that he was therefore not supposed to keep any information about the company.

items.stem: Which is the right division?

options.text: One list for all clients is right, because the norms are mandatory and a mandatory norm cannot vary with the client
options.misconception: equates mandatory with uniform, when the norms are mandatory and differ by client type
options.why: Mandatory says the norms must be followed; it says nothing about their content being the same for a proprietor and a company. The Council set out three lists precisely because the identifying documents of a person, a firm and a company are different things.

options.text: The directors' names, addresses and DINs, the Company Identification Number and the company's PAN form a regulatory block required for a corporate entity only; an individual is identified by PAN or Aadhaar; and a non-corporate entity gives a copy of its PAN and its partners' names and addresses with their PAN, Aadhaar or DIN
options.why: The norms give three lists. For an individual or proprietor: name, PAN or Aadhaar number, business description, last audited financial statement, and the type of engagement. For a corporate entity the general and engagement blocks are joined by a regulatory block for the corporate entity only — the company's PAN, its CIN and its directors' names, addresses and DINs. For a non-corporate entity: name and address, a copy of the PAN, business description, the partners' names and addresses with their PAN, Aadhaar or DIN, and the last audited financial statement, with the type of engagement.

options.text: The name of the parent company is required of every client, so that the firm can trace any group the client belongs to
options.misconception: makes the parent-company line universal, when it is asked only of a corporate client that is a subsidiary
options.why: The parent company appears once in the norms, in the corporate entity's general information, and only in case of a subsidiary. A proprietor has no parent company and a partnership firm is not asked for one; tracing a group is exactly what the corporate list is built to do.

options.text: Directors' DINs are needed for a company and for a partnership firm alike, since the partners of a firm may hold DINs
options.misconception: carries the directors' block across to the non-corporate client, where the norms ask for the partners' particulars instead
options.why: For a non-corporate entity the norms ask for the partners' names and addresses with their PAN, Aadhaar or DIN, and a DIN there is one of three acceptable identifiers for a partner. The block that is specific to a corporate client is the regulatory one — directors' names, addresses and DINs alongside the company's PAN and CIN — and it is asked of a company because a company has directors.

citation.source: Council of ICAI — KYC Norms for members in practice
citation.ref: The three lists in the Council's KYC norms — individual or proprietor, corporate entity, non-corporate entity — as set out in ICAI's Study Material, chapter 19, paragraph 4.7

items.scenario: A firm is designing a client-acceptance form to satisfy the Council's KYC norms. The junior who drafts it proposes one list for every client: name and address, business description, copy of the last audited financial statement, type of engagement, PAN, the client's own Aadhaar number, and the names, addresses and DINs of its directors. A partner points out that the firm's clients include sole proprietors, partnership firms and companies, and asks which of these lines belong to which client.

items.stem: What do the norms require here?

options.text: The engagement must be refused, because a certification is an attestation function and the norms cannot be satisfied without an audited financial statement
options.misconception: turns a line of information to be kept into a condition of acceptance
options.why: The norms list what a member keeps about a client; they do not say that a client who has never been audited cannot be acted for. A certification is squarely an attestation function and the norms apply to it, which is why the member records the name, the identifier, the business description and the type of engagement, and notes that no audited statement exists.

options.text: Nothing is required, because the norms apply to corporate and non-corporate entities and an individual is neither
options.misconception: overlooks that the first of the three client types in the norms is the individual or proprietor
options.why: The norms open with the individual or proprietor, before the corporate and the non-corporate entity, and give him his own list. A sole trader asking for a certificate is the first case the norms provide for.

options.text: Both PAN and Aadhaar are required for an individual, so the trader must supply his PAN before any work starts
options.misconception: reads the norms' "or" as "and"
options.why: The norms say PAN No. or Aadhar Card No. of the individual. One identifier is the requirement, and a trader who gives his Aadhaar number has given it.

options.text: For an individual the norms ask for the name, the PAN number or Aadhaar number, a business description and a copy of the last audited financial statement, with the type of engagement; Aadhaar satisfies the identity line, and the audited-statement line can only be met with one that exists
options.why: The individual's list reads PAN number or Aadhaar number of the individual, printed there as PAN No. or Aadhar Card No., so either identifier meets it and the assistant's insistence on PAN over Aadhaar has no footing in the norms. The list also asks for a copy of the last audited financial statement, and a trader who has never been audited has none to copy; the norms are a record of what the client is, not a bar on acting for a client who has never been audited. The type of engagement, a certification, is the engagement line.

citation.source: Council of ICAI — KYC Norms for members in practice
citation.ref: The KYC norms for a client who is an individual or proprietor — name, PAN or Aadhaar number, business description, copy of the last audited financial statement, and the type of engagement — ICAI's Study Material, chapter 19, paragraph 4.7

items.scenario: A sole practitioner is asked by an individual trader to certify a net-worth statement. The trader offers his name, a one-line description of the business and his Aadhaar number, and says that as he has never been audited there is no financial statement to give. The practitioner's assistant wants to insist on the trader's PAN as well, on the ground that the norms name PAN first, and to refuse the engagement until an audited financial statement is produced.

items.stem: What should the engagement partner conclude instead, and on what?

options.text: That control risk alone is elevated, the other two being unaffected because the organisation is small and its transactions are simple
options.misconception: reads size as a proxy for inherent risk, when the scenario's own facts raise it independently of scale
options.why: A small organisation can carry high inherent risk, and this one does: foreign funds, crowdfunding against the constitution, a contested field, the integrity of the people concerned and an unaudited prior year. Detection risk is elevated too, on the plainest fact in the scenario — nobody has audited this body before.

options.text: That the partner is right on inherent risk and wrong only on detection risk, because an organisation with no profit motive has no reason to misstate its accounts
options.misconception: treats the absence of a profit motive as the whole of inherent risk, when the module locates the risk in the funds, the field and the people rather than in an incentive to inflate earnings
options.why: The incentive to overstate a profit is one source of inherent risk and not the definition of it. What raises inherent risk here is the field the organisation works in, the receipt of foreign funds, crowdfunded money that may not match the constitution, the standing of the people behind the body, and a prior year nobody has audited.

options.text: That the audit should not be accepted at all, since an organisation facing public accusations cannot be audited to an acceptable level of risk
options.misconception: converts a high assessed risk into a refusal, when the assessment exists to drive the nature, timing and extent of the work
options.why: Assessing risk as high is the beginning of the audit and not the end of it. The assessment tells the auditor where to look and how hard, and drives the nature, timing and extent of the procedures. Refusal is a separate question with its own tests, and nothing in the scenario reaches them.

options.text: That all three components are elevated — inherent risk from the field, the foreign funds, the crowdfunding seen against the organisation's own constitution, the standing of the people behind it and the unaudited prior year; control risk from a sudden inflow into a body that is unlikely to have formal controls, where non-compliance can cost it the certificate; and detection risk from this being a first engagement
options.why: Audit risk is assessed on all its components, and here each of them has something pointing at it. An organisation working in a political and social field can have its activities made inherently risky by that alone; crowdfunded donations have to be seen in relation to the constitution of the organisation, which may make them risky; receipt of foreign funds makes transactions inherently risky; the credibility and integrity of the persons behind it are important, since such bodies can be involved in money laundering or in misutilising donors' funds; and the prior year being unaudited raises inherent risk through the probable effect of any misstatement in it. Because activities were small last year and the donations are substantial this year, formal controls may not be in place, and their absence can lead to non-compliance with laws whose consequence here is cancellation of the certificate, so control risk could be high. And a first-year engagement carries a lack of understanding of what the organisation does, which raises detection risk through inappropriate sampling or a faulty application of the procedures chosen.
keywords: crowdfunded donations have to be seen in relation to the constitution
credibility and integrity of the persons
formal controls may not be in place

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the components of audit risk in the audit of a non-governmental organisation working in a political and social field: the field itself, crowdfunded donations seen in relation to the constitution, receipt of foreign funds, the credibility and integrity of the persons behind the organisation and the unaudited prior year as sources of inherent risk; the absence of formal controls after a sudden increase in donations, with cancellation of the foreign contribution certificate as the consequence of non-compliance, as the source of control risk; and the first-year engagement as the source of detection risk

items.scenario: A firm has just been appointed auditor of a non-governmental organisation working in the field of upholding democracy, and this is the first year anybody has audited it. Until last year the organisation ran on a small scale and its accounts were never audited. This year it has received substantial donations, a large part of them from abroad, and it has begun raising money from the public through a crowdfunding platform. The Government now has the legislative power to cancel the organisation's certificate for the receipt of foreign contributions. Because the work sits where political and social questions meet, accusations and counter-accusations about the organisation and the people who run it are being traded in public. The engagement partner's first note on the file reads that the audit risk is ordinary, since the organisation has no commercial pressure to overstate a profit and nobody stands to gain from the accounts.

items.stem: How should the auditor treat the three appeals?

options.text: Treat the crowdfunded receipts as a source of inherent risk and test them against the society's own constitution, the second appeal in particular being money raised for a purpose the deed does not authorise
options.why: Crowdfunding donations have to be seen in relation to the constitution of the body, which may make them risky, and that is a matter for the auditor's risk assessment rather than for the committee alone. The flood relief appeal raised money for a purpose the objects do not carry and the open-ended appeal has been credited to a general fund without anybody asking what the donors were told, so both raise the question of whether the receipt and its application are properly recorded and disclosed. That the platform can name every donor goes to the existence of the receipts and not to this.
keywords: seen in relation to the constitution

options.text: Report the second appeal to the platform and treat the other two as ordinary donations, because the platform is the party that permitted an appeal outside the objects
options.misconception: hands the auditor's own risk assessment to a third party and leaves the open-ended appeal unexamined
options.why: The auditor's question is what the society's financial statements say and how risky its receipts are; whom the platform should have checked is not his to pursue. And the open-ended appeal is not ordinary — money solicited for unspecified work and taken to a general fund is exactly where the constitution has to be read.

options.text: Accept all three as vouched, since the platform's records are external evidence of who gave what and the application of funds is a matter for the committee
options.misconception: stops at the existence of the receipt, when the risk in crowdfunded money is whether the body was constituted to raise and hold it at all
options.why: Tracing a receipt answers whether the money came in, not whether it should have. The module puts the question the other way round: crowdfunding donations may have to be seen in relation to the constitution of the organisation, which may make these risky. A complete donor list does not cure an appeal the objects do not authorise.

options.text: Treat all three as high control risk rather than high inherent risk, since the failure is that nobody at the society checked the appeals against the deed before they were launched
options.misconception: files the risk under the wrong component, when what the module identifies here is the susceptibility of the receipt itself
options.why: The absence of a check is a control matter and it is real, but the module locates crowdfunded donations seen against the constitution among the things that make the body's activities inherently risky. The two are assessed separately, and answering with only the control component leaves the susceptibility of the receipts unassessed.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — crowdfunding donations to be seen in relation to the constitution of the organisation, which may make them risky, as a source of inherent risk in the audit of a not-for-profit body

items.scenario: A charitable society's trust deed states its objects as the running of two primary schools and a library in one district. During the year the society ran three crowdfunding appeals on a public platform. The first raised money for school books and is plainly within the objects. The second raised money for flood relief in a neighbouring state, which the deed does not mention at all. The third was open-ended, asking donors to support "the society's work", and the money has been credited to the general fund. The treasurer tells the auditor that the platform holds a record of every donor and every rupee, that the receipts are therefore fully vouched, and that what the money was raised for is a question for the managing committee and not for the audit.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Revise the control risk assessment, carry the revision through to the assessment of the risks of material misstatement, and modify the nature, timing and extent of the planned substantive procedures
options.why: The chain is the answer. Deviations from established controls may lead the auditor to conclude that control risk needs to be revised; the revision of the control risk assessment is likely to lead to a revision in the risks of material misstatement; and it may also result in a modification of the nature, timing and extent of planned substantive procedures. That a serious violation of the delegation of powers has been found in half the grants sampled is a finding about how the controls actually operate, and the executive director's explanation that no money has been lost answers a different question from the one the auditor asked.
keywords: control risk needs to be revised

options.text: Leave the programme as planned and report the deviations in the management letter, the testing having shown a governance weakness rather than a misstatement
options.misconception: treats a failed test of controls as a matter for the management letter only, when the assessment the plan was built on has just been shown to be wrong
options.why: A test of controls is performed to support an assessment, so a test that fails withdraws the support. The deviations from established controls may lead the auditor to conclude that control risk needs to be revised, and leaving the programme untouched carries on auditing to a level of assurance the evidence no longer justifies.

options.text: Withdraw the reliance on controls entirely and issue a modified opinion, since controls that are not operating as laid down mean the financial statements cannot be relied upon
options.misconception: jumps from a control failure to a reporting outcome, skipping the revision of procedures that stands between them
options.why: A control deviation is not itself a misstatement. What follows is a revised assessment and a modified programme; whether the opinion is affected depends on what that programme then finds. Reporting first is answering a question the audit has not yet reached.

options.text: Extend the sample of grants and payments until enough compliant items are found to support the original assessment
options.misconception: treats sampling as a search for a result, when a deviation rate found in a sample is evidence about the population
options.why: Enlarging a sample to look for the answer already written down is the opposite of testing. The deviations found are evidence about how the controls operate, and the assessment moves to meet the evidence rather than the evidence being gathered until it meets the assessment.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — where a procedure relating to delegation of powers has not been followed and appointments or sanctions have been made in violation of laid down procedures, the deviations from established controls may lead the auditor to conclude that control risk needs to be revised, the revision is likely to lead to a revision in the risks of material misstatement, and it may result in a modification of the nature, timing and extent of planned substantive procedures

items.scenario: At the planning stage the auditor of a charitable institution assessed the risks of material misstatement as low, on the strength of a written delegation of powers under which every grant above a stated amount has to be sanctioned by the governing council and every payment above a stated amount needs two signatures. Testing during the audit tells a different story. Of ten large grants sampled, five were sanctioned by the executive director alone; of twelve large payments, four carry a single signature; and in three cases the supporting file was created after the payment. The executive director explains that the council meets only twice a year, that the delegation is unworkable in a relief organisation, and that no money has been lost. The audit senior proposes to note the deviations in the management letter and to leave the planned programme as it is, since the tests were of controls and not of amounts.

items.stem: How should the auditor treat what he has found?

options.text: As matters for the society's governing body rather than for the audit, since the honorary secretary is right that the auditor's function is not investigation
options.misconception: reads a raised risk assessment as an investigation, when it is the ordinary consequence of what the auditor has learnt about the entity
options.why: The auditor is not being asked to prove anything against anybody. He is being asked what the risk of material misstatement is, and the standing of the people running the body, its foreign receipts and an unexplained flow of money straight out again are exactly the matters the module tells him to weigh.

options.text: As a control risk matter only, the failure being that the society has no procedure for vetting its office bearers or its vendors
options.misconception: files a susceptibility of the entity's transactions under the control component, when what has been found goes to the character of the transactions themselves
options.why: The absence of vetting is a control weakness and it can be reported. But the receipt of foreign funds, the possibility of misutilisation and the standing of the persons behind the body are matters the module places in inherent risk, and answering with only the control component leaves that assessment unmade.

options.text: As grounds for reporting the society to the authority that regulates foreign contributions before any further audit work is done
options.misconception: reaches for an external report on suspicion alone, before the auditor has done the work that would tell him whether there is anything to report
options.why: Nothing has yet been established beyond a set of facts that make the audit riskier. What follows first is a raised assessment and the work that answers it; whether anything has to be reported outside the entity is a question the auditor reaches after he knows what he has, not before.

options.text: As matters going to inherent risk that raise the assessment for the audit as a whole — the credibility and integrity of the persons behind the body are relevant, bodies of this kind can be used for money laundering or for misutilising donors' funds, and the receipt of foreign funds makes transactions inherently risky in itself
options.why: The module names each of these as a source of inherent risk in this setting. The credibility and integrity of the persons behind the organisation is important; shady organisations can be involved in money laundering activities and may be involved in misutilising funds from donors; and since the body is in receipt of foreign funds, that may make its transactions inherently risky. Raising the assessment is not an accusation and does not turn the audit into an investigation — it decides where the work goes and how persuasive the evidence has to be before the auditor is satisfied.
keywords: credibility and integrity of the persons

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the credibility and integrity of the persons behind a not-for-profit body, the possibility of involvement in money laundering or in misutilising funds from donors, and the receipt of foreign funds, as sources of inherent risk in assessing audit risk for such a body

items.scenario: An auditor is planning the first audit of a society that receives foreign contributions. Three things come out of his enquiries. Two of the four office bearers were, until eighteen months ago, office bearers of another society whose registration for foreign contributions was withdrawn. A substantial part of this year's foreign receipts arrived from a single overseas body in four instalments, and the same overseas body is named in the society's own annual report as its "programme partner". And the society's bank statements show a pattern of large receipts being followed within days by transfers to three vendors whose invoices describe the work only as "programme support". The society's honorary secretary says the auditor is straying into a criminal investigation, which is not the auditor's function, and that in any event none of this has anything to do with the truth and fairness of the accounts.

items.stem: What is wrong with the partner's position?

options.text: The inexperience is a detection risk matter and it has already produced its two consequences — a programme designed for a different kind of entity and a sampling method chosen without regard to where this body's risk sits
options.why: A first engagement raises detection risk because the auditor may lack an understanding of what the body actually does, and the module identifies the two ways that shows up: inappropriate sampling procedures, and a faulty application of the audit procedures chosen. Both are on the file already. A programme built for a manufacturing client does not ask the questions a grant-funded body raises — whether restricted donations were spent on their programme, whether receipts are complete, whether the objects authorise the spending — and an interval selection over a payments register cannot find those either.

options.text: The problem is control risk, because an institution running seven programmes across four states cannot have controls the auditor can rely on
options.misconception: assumes a control conclusion from the shape of the entity, without any evidence about the controls themselves
