options.why: Nothing in the scenario says anything about the institution's controls. What it describes is how the audit has been planned and by whom, which is the auditor's side of the equation and therefore the detection component.

options.text: Nothing — inexperience is met by supervision and review, and a systematic selection from every register gives each programme proportionate coverage
options.misconception: treats the team's unfamiliarity as a staffing question alone, when the module places a first engagement's lack of understanding inside detection risk
options.why: Supervision and review matter and do not answer this. Where the audit has been accepted for the first time there may be a lack of understanding of the activities of the body, and the module says in terms that this may lead to higher detection risk through inappropriate sampling procedures or a faulty application of audit procedures — which is what a programme copied from a manufacturer and a mechanical interval selection produce.

options.text: The inexperience raises inherent risk, since a team that does not understand a charity will not see the transactions a charity is susceptible to
options.misconception: puts the auditor's own limitation into the entity's component of risk, when inherent risk is the susceptibility of the assertion before any audit work is contemplated
options.why: Inherent risk is about the entity and its assertions, not about the audit team. What the team knows and how it selects its samples determine whether the auditor will fail to detect a misstatement that exists, and that is detection risk.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — where the audit of a not-for-profit body has been accepted for the first time there may be a lack of understanding of its activities, which may lead to a higher detection risk due to inappropriate sampling procedures or a faulty application of audit procedures

items.scenario: A firm has taken on the audit of a charitable institution none of its partners has worked with before. The institution runs seven programmes across four states, funds them from a mixture of grants, general donations and programme-specific donations, and accounts for each programme separately. The audit team has three members, none of whom has audited a charity. The manager plans the work by taking last year's programme for a manufacturing client and adjusting the account names, and proposes to select samples of vouchers by taking every twentieth item from each programme's payments register. The engagement partner is content, on the footing that a voucher is a voucher whatever the entity does, and that any risk the team's inexperience creates is a matter for supervision rather than for the risk assessment.

items.stem: What is missing from the file, and why does it matter?

options.text: Nothing of substance — the standards require evidence of the work performed, and a complete record of procedures and findings is a stronger file than one carrying a superseded plan
options.misconception: treats the plan as a draft made redundant by the work, when the standard requires the plan and every significant change to it with the reasons
options.why: The requirement is not satisfied by the record of what was done. The auditor documents the overall audit plan and the significant changes made to it during the engagement, together with the reasons for those changes, and a file that shows only the outcome cannot show that the work was planned rather than improvised.

options.text: The plan is missing but it does not matter here, because the extended procedures were more rigorous than the plan would have required and no assurance was lost
options.misconception: measures the documentation requirement by the quality of the work, when what it secures is the ability to show the work was planned and reviewed
options.why: More work is not the same as planned work. The record exists so that somebody other than the auditor can see what was intended, what changed and why, and can review and approve the procedures before they are performed — and none of that is available from a file that starts at the results.

options.text: The audit plan and the record of the change to it — the auditor must document the plan and the significant changes made during the engagement together with the reasons, and the plan is also the record that the procedures were properly planned and could be reviewed and approved before they were performed
options.why: The documentation of the audit plan is a record of the planned nature, timing and extent of risk assessment procedures and of further audit procedures at the assertion level in response to the assessed risks, and it serves as a record of the proper planning of the procedures so that they can be reviewed and approved prior to their performance. The change here is exactly the kind the standard has in mind: extensive procedures on the verification of foreign contributions in place of what was originally envisaged, which needs to be documented along with the reason for it. Failure to document the plan carries the risk of not having conducted the audit according to professional standards in a qualitative manner.
keywords: reviewed and approved prior to their performance

options.text: Only the reason for the change, the plan itself being implicit in the programme she followed
options.misconception: keeps half the requirement, when the plan and the change and the reason are three separate things the standard asks for
options.why: The standard asks for the audit plan, for the significant changes made to it and for the reasons for those changes. The programme actually followed evidences none of the three, and reconstructing a plan from the work afterwards is what the documentation requirement exists to make unnecessary.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — SA 300 requires the auditor to document the audit plan and the significant changes made to it during the engagement together with the reasons; the documentation is a record of the planned nature, timing and extent of risk assessment procedures and further audit procedures at the assertion level and of the proper planning of the procedures so that they can be reviewed and approved prior to their performance; illustrated by extended procedures on the verification of foreign contributions to rule out round-tripping

items.scenario: An auditor is conducting the audit of a society that promotes awareness of the internet among disadvantaged communities and is registered under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 for the receipt of foreign contributions. Her original programme allowed a light check on those receipts. During the audit she becomes uneasy about the route by which some of the money arrived and embarks on far more extensive procedures than she first envisaged, tracing receipts back through the remitting institutions to rule out round-tripping. She documents every procedure she performed and every finding it produced, and the file is thorough on both. She does not write down how she planned the audit in the first place, on the view that a plan is a private working note superseded by what was actually done, and that a file recording the work in full cannot be criticised for lacking a record of what was once intended.

items.stem: Is the colleague right, and why?

options.text: Yes, but only because foreign contributions are involved; for an ordinary class of receipts the size could properly be left to the field team
options.misconception: makes a general requirement about the audit plan turn on the subject matter of one class of transactions
options.why: The requirement is about what an audit plan contains and it does not vary with the kind of receipt. Foreign contributions are where this trust's risk is concentrated, so the sizes there matter most, but the plan must describe the extent of every planned procedure.

options.text: Yes — the audit plan must describe the nature, timing and extent of the procedures, and the extent includes deciding the sample sizes to be tested, so the sizes belong in the plan
options.why: The plan has to state the extent of the procedures as well as their nature and timing, and the extent of audit procedures includes deciding about the sample sizes to be tested for performing them. Leaving the sizes to be settled at the moment each procedure is performed leaves the plan incomplete on one of its three limbs. Nothing stops the size being changed later — a change to the plan is expected and is documented with its reason — but it has to have been planned before it can be changed.

options.text: No — the plan is complete because it names the procedures, the timing and the staff, and sample size is a matter of professional judgement exercised during performance
options.misconception: reads the extent of a procedure as something separate from the plan, when the extent is one of the three things the plan must describe
options.why: Sample size is a matter of judgement and it is still part of the extent, which is what the plan must describe. A plan naming the procedure and the date but not how much of the population will be tested has not said how far the work goes.

options.text: No — sample sizes are a documentation matter rather than a planning matter, and it is enough that the senior records the size actually used
options.misconception: swaps a planning requirement for a recording one, so that the size is only ever known after the event
options.why: Recording what was done is a separate obligation and does not discharge this one. The point of putting the extent in the plan is that it can be reviewed and approved before the procedures are performed, which a size chosen on the day and written down afterwards cannot be.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — SA 300 states that the audit plan shall include a description of the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures, and the extent of audit procedures includes deciding about the sample sizes to be tested, so an approach that defers sample size to the time of performance is not proper

items.scenario: A partner is planning the audit of a trust that receives foreign contributions. He lists, in order, the procedures he intends to perform on each class of receipt and payment, sets out when in the year each will be done and by whom, and records the assertions each is aimed at. On sample sizes he writes that these will be settled by the senior on the ground at the time each procedure is performed, because the right number depends on what the records look like when they are opened and it would be artificial to fix it in advance. He shows the plan to a colleague, who says the approach is not proper.

items.stem: What should the auditor do?

options.text: Abandon the plan and audit the remaining balances substantively without a written programme, since a plan overtaken by events is worse than none
options.misconception: reads the need to change a plan as a reason to work without one
options.why: The requirement is to reconsider the plan, not to discard it. Working without one loses the record of the planned nature, timing and extent of the procedures and the ability to have them reviewed and approved before they are performed.

options.text: Ask the society to reconstruct the missing grant agreements so that the planned procedure can be performed as approved
options.misconception: preserves the procedure by having the evidence created, which produces a document made for the auditor rather than evidence of what happened
options.why: A document assembled after the fact to satisfy a test is not evidence that the control operated. The control did not operate for three quarters of the year, and that is a finding the audit has to respond to by changing what it does, not by restoring the paperwork the plan assumed.

options.text: Reconsider the plan and the programme in the light of what the review of internal control and the procedures have shown, and document the changes with the reasons for them
options.why: The audit plan and the related programme should be reconsidered as the audit progresses, and such reconsideration is based on the auditor's review of internal control, his preliminary evaluation of it and the results of his compliance and substantive procedures. A control the plan relied on has stopped operating and a planned procedure has become impossible, which is precisely the case the rule is written for. The changes and the reasons for them are then documented, so that the file shows both what was planned and why it moved.

options.text: Complete the approved programme and set the difficulties out in the completion memorandum, the plan being the engagement partner's approved instruction
options.misconception: treats an approved plan as fixed, when the plan and the programme are reconsidered as the audit progresses
options.why: The plan is not a permission slip. The audit plan and the related programme should be reconsidered as the audit progresses, on the basis of the auditor's review of internal control, his preliminary evaluation of it and the results of his compliance and substantive procedures. All three have moved here, so the plan has to move with them.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — the audit plan and related programme should be reconsidered as the audit progresses, such reconsideration being based on the auditor's review of internal control, his preliminary evaluation thereof and the results of his compliance and substantive procedures, read with the requirement to document significant changes to the plan and the reasons for them

items.scenario: The audit of a society receiving foreign contributions is half done. The plan was built on the assumption that the society's receipts function had a working control: every foreign remittance was to be matched by the accounts officer to a signed grant agreement before it was recognised. The auditor's review of internal control and his preliminary evaluation of it now show that the accounts officer left in the first quarter, that the matching stopped when she did, and that three quarters of the year's remittances have been recognised without any agreement on file. The auditor also finds that two payments he had planned to test by inspecting the contract can only be tested by tracing them to the bank. The audit manager objects that the plan was approved by the engagement partner at the start of the audit and cannot now be rewritten, and that the proper course is to complete the approved programme and describe the difficulties in the completion memorandum.

items.stem: What is wrong with the approach, in terms of what a plan is for?

options.text: The plan has to be built on this year's assessed risks — new funders, spending routed through implementing partners and a change of accounting system each change what the procedures must respond to, and the plan is the record of that response
options.why: A plan is the record of the planned nature, timing and extent of the risk assessment procedures and of the further audit procedures at the assertion level in response to the assessed risks, and it is the record that the procedures were properly planned so that they could be reviewed and approved prior to their performance. Two new funders change the verification of receipts, implementing partners in other states change where the spending has to be traced to, and a new accounting system changes the controls being relied on. A plan that does not mention any of them cannot be a response to them.
keywords: further audit procedures at the assertion level
reviewed and approved prior to their performance

options.text: The approach is wrong because a second-year engagement is still an initial audit engagement and needs a fresh plan on that ground
options.misconception: misuses the definition of an initial audit engagement, which turns on whether the prior period was audited and by whom
options.why: An initial audit engagement is one where the prior period financial statements were not audited or were audited by a predecessor auditor. This firm audited last year, so this is not one. The plan needs rebuilding because the risks have changed, which is a different reason and the right one.

options.text: The approach is wrong only because a plan must be signed afresh each year, the form of the document being what the standard is concerned with
options.misconception: makes the requirement a formality about signatures, when what the standard asks is that the plan answer this year's risks
options.why: Re-signing last year's plan changes nothing about whether the procedures answer this year's risks. The requirement bites on the content: the plan describes the nature, timing and extent of the procedures responding to the risks that have been assessed now.

options.text: Nothing, provided the fieldwork covers the new funders and the implementing partners, since a plan is a means to the work and the work is what produces the evidence
options.misconception: reduces the plan to a scheduling device, when it is the record of the response to the assessed risks at the assertion level
options.why: The documentation of the audit plan is a record of the planned nature, timing and extent of risk assessment procedures and of further audit procedures at the assertion level in response to the assessed risks. A plan carried over from a year with different funders, different delivery arrangements and a different system is not a response to this year's risks at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — the documentation of the audit plan as a record of the planned nature, timing and extent of risk assessment procedures and further audit procedures at the assertion level in response to the assessed risks, and as a record of the proper planning of the procedures so that they can be reviewed and approved prior to their performance

items.scenario: A society registered for the receipt of foreign contributions is audited by a firm for the second year. The engagement partner tells the team that because last year's file is complete and the society's activities have not changed, this year's plan can be last year's plan with the dates altered, and that the time saved should go into the fieldwork instead. During the year, however, the society has taken on two new overseas funders, has begun routing part of its programme spending through three implementing partners in other states, and has changed its accounting software. A team member points out these three changes; the partner answers that they are matters of detail that the fieldwork will pick up, and that a plan is a plan.

items.stem: What does the auditor have to do about the opening balances?

options.text: Report on the current year and state in the report that the opening balances were not audited by the firm, which discharges the responsibility
options.misconception: substitutes a disclaimer of responsibility for the work the standard requires on opening balances
options.why: A sentence in the report is not a procedure. The auditor has an objective in respect of the opening balances — whether they contain misstatements that materially affect this year — and he has to do work to reach a conclusion on it before he decides what the report says.

options.text: Ask the institution to have the prior year audited by another firm before this year's audit can be completed
options.misconception: makes a prior-year audit a precondition, when the standard is written for exactly the case where there was none
options.why: The definition of an initial audit engagement expressly covers the case where the prior period was not audited. The standard tells the auditor what to do in that situation rather than requiring the situation to be removed.

options.text: Read the most recent financial statements, determine whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward, determine whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies, and perform audit procedures on the opening balances themselves
options.why: An initial audit engagement is one in which the financial statements for the prior period were either not audited or were audited by a predecessor auditor, and this is the first kind. The auditor's objective is to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether the opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements and whether appropriate accounting policies are consistently applied. The procedures are to read the most recent financial statements and the predecessor's report where there is one, determine whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward, determine whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies, and perform audit procedures on the opening balances.
keywords: perform audit procedures on the opening balances

options.text: Confine the work to the corpus and the earmarked funds, since those are the balances a charitable institution's donors care about, and accept the remaining opening figures as carried forward
options.misconception: selects among the opening balances by subject matter, when the test is whether a misstatement in them would materially affect the current period
options.why: The question the standard asks is whether the opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements, and land and buildings taken in at an unexplained valuation and an uncounted stock of teaching materials are as capable of doing that as the funds are.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 510 on initial audit engagements, being engagements in which the prior period financial statements were not audited or were audited by a predecessor auditor: the objective in respect of opening balances and the procedures of reading the most recent financial statements and the predecessor's report, determining whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward, determining whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies, and performing audit procedures on the opening balances

items.scenario: A firm is appointed in July to audit a charitable institution for the year just ended. The institution's accounts have never been audited. Its balance sheet at the start of the year carries a corpus fund, three earmarked funds, land and buildings taken in at a valuation nobody can now explain, and a stock of teaching materials the institution says was counted at the year end but for which no count sheet survives. The treasurer's position is that the firm has been appointed for this year and can only report on this year, that the opening figures are last year's business, and that if the firm is uncomfortable it should simply say in its report that the opening balances were not audited by it and leave the matter there.

items.stem: How is each of the two dealt with in the report?

options.text: Both are dealt with the same way, as a single qualification covering the opening balances as a whole
options.misconception: merges a misstatement found with an inability to obtain evidence, which the standard keeps apart because they lead to different wording and different tests
options.why: They are two different matters. One is a misstatement the auditor has established, the other is evidence he could not obtain, and the standard on opening balances gives each its own consequence. Even the wording differs: a modification for a misstatement is expressed as "except for the effects", one for missing evidence as "except for the possible effects".

options.text: The fund misstatement calls for a disclaimer because it arose in a period the auditor did not audit, and the teaching materials call for an adverse opinion because the records are absent
options.misconception: swaps the two consequences, attaching the evidence remedy to the established misstatement and the misstatement remedy to the gap in evidence
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both. A disclaimer belongs to the case where evidence could not be obtained, and an adverse opinion to a misstatement so pervasive that a qualification would not convey it. Here the misstatement is established and the missing evidence is confined.

options.text: The fund misstatement calls for a qualified or adverse opinion; the teaching materials call for a qualified opinion or a disclaimer, and on these facts the effect is material but not pervasive, so a qualification
options.why: The standard on opening balances splits exactly this way. If the auditor concludes that the opening balances contain a misstatement that materially affects the current period's financial statements, or that policies are not consistently applied or a change is not properly accounted for, presented and disclosed, the opinion is qualified or adverse. If the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances, the opinion is qualified or a disclaimer is issued. Which of each pair applies then turns on pervasiveness, and here the missing evidence is confined to one line of expenditure rather than running across the statements.
keywords: unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: Neither affects the opinion, both matters belonging to a prior period on which this auditor expresses no opinion, and both should be set out in an Other Matter paragraph
options.misconception: treats an opening balance as outside the current opinion, when the whole point of the standard is that a misstated opening balance carries into this year
options.why: The auditor's objective is stated in terms of the current period: whether the opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements. A fund misstated at the opening carries into this year's statement of funds, and an unverifiable opening stock carries into this year's expenditure.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 510 audit conclusions and reporting on opening balances: a qualified opinion or a disclaimer where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances, and a qualified or adverse opinion where the opening balances contain a misstatement materially affecting the current period or are not properly presented and disclosed, read with the distinction in Ch. Reporting between a misstatement and an inability to obtain evidence and with the meaning of pervasive

items.scenario: The same first audit reaches its conclusion with two separate problems on the opening balances. On the earmarked funds, the auditor has been able to do enough work: he has traced the movements and satisfied himself that a material part of one fund was spent during the prior year on a purpose the donor did not authorise and was never disclosed, and the misstatement carries into this year's opening balance and this year's fund statement. On the teaching materials, the auditor has been able to do nothing at all: there is no count sheet, no subsequent sale to trace, and the materials were consumed during the year, so no alternative procedure exists and the possible effect on this year's expenditure is material but confined to that one line. The institution will not amend the fund statement.

items.stem: What should the auditor do with the offer?

options.text: Accept the certificate as the evidence available, since a representation from the person responsible is the only evidence such receipts admit of
options.misconception: treats a written representation as a substitute for other evidence, when the standard says it does not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own
options.why: A written representation is necessary audit evidence and it is not enough by itself. Although written representations provide necessary audit evidence, they do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own, and the fact that management has provided reliable representations does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains.

options.text: Take the certificate but rely on the controls over the collections instead, whether or not any exist, since controls are the only source of evidence for a receipt with no external document
options.misconception: assumes controls can be relied on without testing whether they exist and operate, when here there is not even a written procedure
options.why: Controls are the right place to look for evidence about the completeness of an unvouched receipt, and they can only be relied on if they exist and are shown to operate. The trust has no written procedure at all, so there is nothing to test and reliance is not available.

options.text: Refuse the certificate as worthless and qualify the opinion at once, since a receipt that cannot be vouched at source can never be audited
options.misconception: goes straight from the absence of a source document to a modification, skipping the representation the auditor is required to obtain and the controls he is required to consider
options.why: The representation is still to be obtained; the standard requires it and calls it necessary evidence even though it is not sufficient on its own. And whether the opinion is modified depends on whether the completeness of the receipts can be supported another way, which is a question about the controls and has to be answered before the report is written.

options.text: Take the representation, but treat it as one piece of evidence and not the answer — test what controls exist over the collection, counting and banking of the cash, and where sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the completeness of these receipts still cannot be obtained, determine the effect on the opinion as a limitation on scope
options.why: The representation is obtained and is necessary, and it does not do the work: written representations do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters they deal with, and a reliable representation does not affect the nature or extent of the other evidence the auditor obtains. For a receipt with no external counterpart the evidence that remains is the control operating over the collection itself, so that is what the auditor examines and tests. Where even that is absent and no alternative procedure reaches the completeness of the receipts, the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and what follows is a scope limitation whose effect on the opinion depends on how material and how pervasive the possible misstatement is.
keywords: do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 580, that although written representations provide necessary audit evidence they do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own and that reliable representations do not affect the nature or extent of other audit evidence obtained, read with Ch. Audit Evidence on obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence and with Ch. Reporting on a modification arising from an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

items.scenario: A charitable trust raises a substantial part of its income in ways that leave no counterpart outside the trust. Sealed collection boxes are placed at four temples and opened monthly by two volunteers. Cash is collected at public events and handed to a volunteer coordinator, who brings it to the office a few days later. Anonymous donations are dropped at the office and entered in a day book by whoever is at the desk. There are no counterfoils, no donor names for these receipts and no external record of any kind. The auditor asks how the trust satisfies itself that everything collected is banked, and is told there is no written procedure. The managing trustee offers to sign a certificate stating that all collections have been fully accounted for, and says that with that certificate on file the auditor has what he needs.

items.stem: How should the auditor answer?

options.text: That cost cannot decide it — difficulty, time or cost is not in itself a valid basis to omit a procedure for which there is no alternative or to accept evidence that is less than persuasive; if a genuine alternative procedure gives sufficient appropriate evidence it may be used, and if none does, the limitation goes to the report
options.why: The standard forecloses the argument the trustee is making. The matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for the auditor to omit an audit procedure for which there is no alternative or to be satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive. That leaves two honest routes. If some other procedure would give sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the completeness of the drive's receipts, the auditor may perform that instead — it is the sufficiency of the evidence and not the price of it that decides. If nothing does, the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on a material matter, and that is a limitation whose effect on the opinion has to be determined.
keywords: unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: Accept the summary statements because the trust's own committee has accepted them, the committee being those charged with governance
options.misconception: treats acceptance by those charged with governance as evidence, when their acceptance is not a substitute for the auditor's own conclusion
options.why: Who else is satisfied is not the test. The auditor has to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence himself, and an internal body's acceptance of a weaker document does not make it stronger.

options.text: Accept the summary statements, since the cost of the alternative is out of proportion to the amount at stake and an auditor must have regard to the reasonableness of the work he imposes
options.misconception: lets cost decide the extent of the work, which is the reasoning the standard rules out in terms
options.why: The matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for the auditor to omit an audit procedure for which there is no alternative, or to be satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive. Cost may inform how a procedure is designed; it cannot be the reason for settling for weaker evidence.

options.text: Perform the full reconciliation regardless, since a material class of receipts must always be verified to source and no alternative procedure is ever adequate
options.misconception: hardens the rule into a bar on alternative procedures, when what it bars is dropping a procedure because it is expensive where no alternative exists
options.why: The standard's words are that cost is not a valid basis to omit a procedure for which there is no alternative. Where an alternative procedure does give sufficient appropriate audit evidence it is available, and the auditor chooses between procedures on what they prove rather than on a rule that only one route can ever do.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 200 as reproduced there, that the matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for the auditor to omit an audit procedure for which there is no alternative or to be satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive, with the position that where a procedure is impracticable alternative audit procedures may provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence and that where they cannot, the scope limitation goes to the opinion

items.scenario: The same trust has one further class of receipts: money collected in a rural fundraising drive by two hundred volunteers, each of whom issued handwritten slips. The slips exist but are held at four district offices, unsorted, and the drive's total is material to the income statement. The auditor proposes to visit the district offices, sort the slips and reconcile them to the amounts banked. The managing trustee objects that the exercise would take three weeks, that the trust would have to pay for the auditor's travel and time, that the cost would exceed a tenth of what the drive raised, and that in a charity every rupee spent on audit is a rupee not spent on beneficiaries. He asks the auditor to accept the district offices' summary statements instead, which are less persuasive but far cheaper, and points out that the trust's own committee has accepted them.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a separate section drawing attention to the closure and the liquidator's appointment, since the facts are fully known to the reader once the auditor points to them
options.misconception: reaches for the treatment reserved for an adequately disclosed uncertainty, where here nothing is disclosed and the basis of preparation is itself wrong
options.why: A separate section drawing attention to a matter presupposes that the financial statements say something for the auditor to draw attention to, and that the basis of accounting is appropriate. Neither holds. There is no note at all, and the question is not whether an uncertainty exists but whether the entity may still be presented as a going concern.

options.text: An adverse opinion — the statements have been prepared on a basis that is no longer appropriate, and that affects everything in them rather than any one balance
options.why: Where the financial statements have been prepared using the going concern basis of accounting but, in the auditor's judgment, management's use of that basis is inappropriate, the auditor shall express an adverse opinion. It is not a question of degree here: the plant has closed, the workforce has gone, the members have resolved on a voluntary winding up and a liquidator is in control of the assets, so the entity is not going to continue in operational existence. That the company has not yet been struck off answers a legal question and not an accounting one. Because the wrong basis runs through every asset and every deferral rather than being confined to specific elements, the effects are pervasive and a qualification would not convey the position.

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because until the liquidator has realised the assets nobody can say what they are worth and the auditor cannot form a view
options.misconception: turns a misstatement the auditor has identified into an inability to obtain evidence, which is the other of the two circumstances entirely
options.why: The two circumstances requiring a modification are a material misstatement and an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and this is the first. The auditor is not short of evidence; he knows the plant has closed, the workforce has gone and a liquidator is in control. Uncertainty about the eventual realisation is a normal feature of a break-up basis, not a reason to disclaim.

options.text: A qualified opinion, the misstatement being confined to the carrying amounts of the plant, the inventory and the deferred expenditure
options.misconception: treats a wrong basis of preparation as a set of individual valuation errors, when it is a matter affecting the statements as a whole
options.why: A qualified opinion is for a misstatement that is material but not pervasive. Pervasive effects are those not confined to specific elements, accounts or items, and a basis of accounting that should not have been used at all is the clearest case of that — it decides how every asset and every liability in the statements has been measured and presented.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — the implications for the auditor's report where the use of the going concern basis of accounting is inappropriate: the auditor shall express an adverse opinion, read with SA 705 (Revised) on the two circumstances requiring a modification and on the meaning of pervasive effects as those not confined to specific elements, accounts or items of the financial statements

items.scenario: A company's only manufacturing plant stopped work in November and has not restarted. In December its workforce was paid off. In February the members passed a resolution to wind the company up voluntarily, and in March a liquidator was appointed and took control of the assets. The financial statements for the year ended 31 March have been drawn up exactly as in previous years: plant and machinery at cost less depreciation, inventory at cost, deferred expenditure carried forward and amortised over four more years, and no note anywhere about the resolution, the liquidator or the closure. The managing director tells the auditor that the winding up is not complete, that the company legally exists until it is struck off, and that it would be wrong to write anything down before the liquidator has actually sold it.

items.stem: How should the auditor's report deal with this?

options.text: A qualified opinion, because an uncertainty of this size means the auditor cannot say the statements give a true and fair view without reservation
options.misconception: treats the existence of an uncertainty as a reservation, when the opinion is modified only if the uncertainty is not adequately disclosed
options.why: A qualified opinion arises from a material misstatement or from missing evidence, and there is neither. The company has disclosed the claim, the range of outcomes and the doubt itself; the auditor has concluded the basis is appropriate. Where adequate disclosure of the material uncertainty is made, the opinion is unmodified.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with the matter reported in the Key Audit Matters section, since it is plainly among the matters of most significance in the audit
options.misconception: substitutes the key audit matters section for a reporting requirement that stands on its own and applies whether or not that section exists
options.why: Whether the matter is also a key audit matter is a separate question and does not answer this one. The separate section on a material uncertainty related to going concern is required in its own right, and the key audit matters section is confined in scope to particular audits and is not a substitute for it.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with the matter set out in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, that being the paragraph the report uses to point at something already disclosed
options.misconception: uses the general paragraph for drawing attention to a disclosed matter, where a specific and separately headed section is prescribed for this one
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph is for a matter appropriately presented or disclosed that is fundamental to users' understanding, and it is not the vehicle here. Reporting on a material uncertainty about going concern has its own separate section with its own heading and its own two required statements, and the specific requirement displaces the general one.

options.text: An unmodified opinion, with a separate section under its own heading drawing attention to the note and stating that a material uncertainty exists and that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter
options.why: Where the use of the going concern basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and adequate disclosure of it is made in the financial statements, the auditor expresses an unmodified opinion and the report includes a separate section under the heading "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" which draws attention to the note in the financial statements that discloses the matter and states that these events or conditions indicate that a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern and that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter. Adequate disclosure is what makes the opinion unmodified; the separate section is what makes the reader see it.
keywords: Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern
not modified in respect of the matter

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — going concern implications for the auditor's report where the basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and adequate disclosure is made: an unmodified opinion with a separate section under the heading "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern" drawing attention to the note and stating that a material uncertainty exists and that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter

items.scenario: A company faces a claim under labour legislation covering nine years of alleged underpayment across three plants. The matter is before a tribunal and the company's counsel cannot predict the outcome. If the claim succeeds in full, the amount would exceed the company's net worth and the company would not be able to pay it out of its own resources. The company is otherwise trading profitably and its bankers have renewed all its facilities for a further year. Note 10 to the accounts sets out the claim, its history, the range of possible outcomes and the company's reasons for resisting it; Note 11 states that these conditions indicate a material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt on the company's ability to continue as a going concern. The auditor is satisfied that the going concern basis is appropriate, that a material uncertainty exists and that the disclosure is adequate.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because until the refinancing is settled nobody can know whether the company will continue and the auditor cannot form a view
options.misconception: converts an uncertainty about the future into an inability to obtain evidence about the present
options.why: A disclaimer belongs to an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The auditor here is not short of evidence; he knows the facilities expire, that four lenders have been approached and that the notes are incomplete. What he has found is a misstatement, and a misstatement is answered by a qualification or an adverse opinion.

options.text: A qualified opinion, with the Basis for Qualified Opinion section stating that a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the company's ability to continue as a going concern and that the financial statements do not adequately disclose the matter
options.why: Where the use of the going concern basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and adequate disclosure of it is not made in the financial statements, the auditor expresses a qualified or adverse opinion as appropriate and states in the Basis for Qualified Opinion or Basis for Adverse Opinion section that a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern and that the financial statements do not adequately disclose this matter. The statements here are materially misstated by the inadequacy of the disclosure, and because that effect is material but not pervasive the modification is a qualification.

options.text: An adverse opinion, since financial statements that do not tell the reader the company may be unable to continue are misleading as a whole
options.misconception: escalates to the outcome reserved for a pervasive misstatement, on facts the auditor has assessed as confined
options.why: An adverse opinion is expressed where the misstatement is both material and pervasive. Pervasive effects are those not confined to specific elements, accounts or items, or which represent a substantial proportion of the statements, or which are fundamental to users' understanding in relation to disclosures. The auditor has assessed this as confined to one incomplete disclosure, so the qualification is the proportionate answer.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a separate section on the material uncertainty, the notes having disclosed the expiry and the amounts involved
options.misconception: treats partial disclosure as adequate disclosure, when what is missing is the consequence the reader needs
options.why: The unmodified route is available only where adequate disclosure of the material uncertainty is made. These notes give the magnitude, the expiration and the total but do not discuss the impact or the availability of refinancing, so the fact of the uncertainty is not fully disclosed and the statements are materially misstated by the omission.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — going concern implications where the basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and adequate disclosure is not made: a qualified or adverse opinion as appropriate in accordance with SA 705 (Revised), with the Basis for Qualified or Adverse Opinion section stating that a material uncertainty exists and that the financial statements do not adequately disclose the matter, read with the illustration of a company unable to renegotiate or obtain replacement financing whose notes do not discuss the impact or the availability of refinancing

items.scenario: A company financed its fixed capital with long-term borrowing and its working capital with short-term lines. Both mature within four months of the year end. The company has approached four lenders and has not been able to renegotiate the existing arrangements or obtain replacement financing, and it has told the auditor that if nothing is arranged it may be unable to realise its assets and discharge its liabilities in the normal course of business. The notes to the financial statements set out the magnitude of the financing arrangements, the dates on which they expire and the total sum involved. They say nothing about what would follow if the money is not replaced and nothing about whether refinancing is available. The auditor accepts that the going concern basis is still appropriate, and considers that the effect of what is missing from the notes, while material, is confined to this one disclosure.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Accept the nine-month assessment supported by the sanction letter, since the limits are in place and the auditor may not require management to do work it considers unnecessary
options.misconception: lets the refusal settle the matter, when the standard treats an unwillingness to make or extend the assessment as something the auditor has to respond to
options.why: A sanction letter for existing limits answers whether facilities exist today, not whether the company can meet its obligations over the period the assessment must cover. Management's unwillingness to extend the assessment when requested is expressly a situation the auditor is required to respond to rather than one he may accept.

options.text: Prepare his own cash flow forecast from the company's records, since the assessment is ultimately about facts the auditor can establish for himself
options.misconception: moves the assessment from management to the auditor, when the responsibility to make it is management's and the auditor's job is to evaluate it
options.why: The assessment is management's responsibility and the auditor's responsibility is to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about it and to conclude on the appropriateness of management's use of the basis. An auditor who builds the forecast himself has audited his own work, and he still has no assessment from those responsible for making one.

options.text: Consider the implications for his report, management being unwilling to extend its assessment when requested to do so
options.why: The implications table gives three outcomes and this is the third of them: if management is unwilling to make or extend its assessment when requested to do so by the auditor, the auditor shall consider the implications for the auditor's report. The refusal does not by itself decide that the basis is inappropriate or that a material uncertainty exists — it leaves the auditor without evidence he asked for, and what follows depends on whether he can conclude without it. He would also perform the additional procedures open to him, evaluate management's plans for future action and request written representations about the feasibility of those plans.
keywords: unwilling to make or extend its assessment

options.text: Express an adverse opinion, a refusal to look twelve months ahead being an admission that the going concern basis cannot be supported
options.misconception: reads a refusal as a conclusion about the basis of accounting, when the standard reserves the adverse opinion for a case where the auditor judges the basis inappropriate
options.why: An adverse opinion on this ground follows only where the financial statements have been prepared on the going concern basis and, in the auditor's judgment, management's use of that basis is inappropriate. Nothing here establishes that yet. The refusal is a limitation on what the auditor has been given, and the standard directs him to consider its implications rather than to treat it as a finding about the basis.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 570 (Revised): the additional procedures where events or conditions casting significant doubt have been identified, including requesting management to make its assessment, evaluating management's plans of future action, analysing the cash flow forecast and requesting written representations on the plans and their feasibility, and the position where management is unwilling to make or extend its assessment, in which case the auditor shall consider the implications for the auditor's report

items.scenario: An auditor identifies several conditions during the audit of a company whose year ended on 31 March: the current ratio and the debt service coverage ratio have both deteriorated sharply, creditors are being paid late, salaries were delayed twice during the year, and the bankers have declined a request for additional facilities. He asks the directors to make their assessment of the company's ability to continue as a going concern. The board's assessment covers the nine months to 31 December only, on the ground that the company's business is seasonal and the December position is the one that matters. The directors decline to extend the assessment to twelve months from the balance sheet date and decline to prepare a cash flow forecast, saying that the auditor already has the bank's sanction letter for the existing limits and that a forecast would be guesswork.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: An unmodified opinion that names the processor and explains that the auditor was unable to examine its controls, so that the reader knows the limit of what was done
options.misconception: treats naming a limitation in the report as a substitute for modifying the opinion, and refers to the service organisation in an unmodified report
options.why: An explanation is not an opinion. Where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence he modifies; describing the gap while giving a clean opinion tells the reader the statements are free from material misstatement when the auditor does not know that. And a user auditor shall not refer to the work of a service auditor in a report containing an unmodified opinion unless law or regulation requires it.

options.text: An adverse opinion, since a material part of the accounting has been carried out where the auditor cannot see it and the statements cannot be said to give a true and fair view
options.misconception: answers missing evidence with the outcome reserved for a misstatement the auditor has established
options.why: An adverse opinion is expressed where the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements are both material and pervasive. Here he has obtained no evidence at all about the payroll processing and has established no misstatement, so the modification arises from an inability to obtain evidence and is expressed as a qualification or a disclaimer.

options.text: A modified opinion — the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the services provided, and because the possible effects are confined to payroll and the balances flowing from it, a qualification rather than a disclaimer
options.why: The user auditor shall modify the opinion in the user auditor's report if he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the services provided by the service organisation relevant to the audit of the user entity's financial statements. That is the position here: no assurance report on the processor's controls, no access to test them, no records at the company that would allow the processing to be tested there, and a user control that reconciles a total to a payment without reaching the master data or the computation. Which modification follows turns on pervasiveness, and the possible effects of undetected misstatements are confined to payroll cost and the balances that flow from it, so they are material but not pervasive and the opinion is qualified using the wording for possible effects.
keywords: unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because a whole accounting function has been placed beyond the auditor's reach and the audit as a whole is therefore incomplete
options.misconception: assumes a disclaimer whenever an entire function cannot be tested, without asking whether the possible effects run across the financial statements
options.why: A disclaimer is for possible effects that are both material and pervasive, so that a qualification would be inadequate to communicate the gravity of the situation. Payroll is one function and everything else in this audit is complete and satisfactory, so the possible effects are confined to specific elements rather than fundamental to the statements as a whole.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402: reporting by the user auditor, who shall modify the opinion in accordance with SA 705 if unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the services provided by the service organisation relevant to the audit of the user entity's financial statements, read with the qualified and disclaimer tests and the meaning of pervasive in Ch. Reporting

items.scenario: A company outsourced its entire payroll to an outside processor two years ago. The processor holds the employee master data, calculates gross pay, statutory deductions and net pay, makes the payments and returns a monthly summary that the company posts as a single journal entry. Payroll is material to the company's results. The auditor asks the processor for an assurance report on its controls and is told none is prepared. He asks to visit and test the processing and is refused. He asks the company for the underlying calculations and is told the company holds only the monthly summaries, having no copy of the master data or of the individual computations. The company's own controls over payroll consist of a finance officer checking that the total in the summary matches the total paid out of the bank, which tests neither the master data nor the calculation. Everything else in the audit is complete and satisfactory.

items.stem: What should go into the report?

options.text: Everything the partner wants, since the custodian's assurance report is audit evidence and a reader is entitled to know the sources the opinion rests on
options.misconception: treats transparency about sources as an entitlement, when the rule exists to stop the reader inferring a shared responsibility
options.why: The report communicates the auditor's opinion and the basis for it, not an inventory of the evidence. The reason a reference is barred in an unmodified report is that it suggests the opinion is partly somebody else's, which is why the only permitted reference carries a statement that it does not diminish the user auditor's responsibility.

options.text: The reference may be included provided the report also states that it does not diminish the auditor's responsibility for the opinion, that statement being what makes any such reference proper
options.misconception: applies the safeguard that accompanies a legally required reference to a reference the auditor has chosen to make
options.why: That statement is required where a reference is required by law or regulation, and it does not create a general permission. Where no law requires the reference, the reference itself is not to be made at all, and adding a disclaimer to it does not cure it.

options.text: The reference should be included in the Other Matter section rather than the Basis for Opinion section, since it explains the conduct of the audit rather than the opinion
options.misconception: solves the question by choosing a paragraph, when the objection is to the reference existing in an unmodified report at all
options.why: Where the reference is not permitted, no section of the report is the right place for it. The rule is about whether the work of a service auditor may be mentioned in a report containing an unmodified opinion, not about where a mention would sit.

options.text: None of it — the auditor shall not refer to the work of a service auditor in a report containing an unmodified opinion unless law or regulation requires it, and the audit committee is told what was done through the communication with those charged with governance instead
options.why: The user auditor shall not refer to the work of a service auditor in the user auditor's report containing an unmodified opinion unless required by law or regulation to do so. If such reference is required by law or regulation, the report shall indicate that the reference does not diminish the user auditor's responsibility for the audit opinion — which is the point of the rule: the opinion is the user auditor's alone and a reference invites the reader to think it is shared. Nothing prevents the partner from telling the audit committee what work was done; that is what the communication with those charged with governance is for.
keywords: shall not refer to the work of a service auditor
unless required by law or regulation

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402: the user auditor shall not refer to the work of a service auditor in the user auditor's report containing an unmodified opinion unless required by law or regulation to do so, and where such reference is required the report shall indicate that the reference does not diminish the user auditor's responsibility for the audit opinion

items.scenario: A company's investment accounting is performed by a custodian. The auditor obtains the custodian's assurance report covering the whole of the financial year, evaluates the professional competence and independence of the firm that issued it, satisfies himself that the controls tested and their results are relevant to the assertions in the company's financial statements, tests the complementary controls at the company, and concludes that he has sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The opinion will be unmodified. The engagement partner, who has spent a fortnight on this part of the audit, wants the report to name the custodian, name the firm that issued the assurance report and describe the work relied on, so that the audit committee can see what was done and so that responsibility is fairly shared. No law or regulation requires any such reference.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Determine which of the four are relevant to the assertions being tested, test those at the company, and treat the assurance report as supporting only the periods and controls where the complementary controls actually operated — obtaining evidence another way for the rest and modifying the opinion if he cannot
options.why: A complementary user entity control is one the service organisation assumes, in the design of its service, will be implemented by user entities and which, if necessary to achieve the control objectives, is identified in the description of the system. When a report is used as audit evidence, the auditor determines whether the complementary controls identified are relevant to the user entity and, if so, obtains an understanding of whether they have been implemented and tests their operating effectiveness. Where they have not operated the provider's controls cannot be assumed effective for that period either, so the auditor needs evidence about pricing and credit exposure from elsewhere — and where he cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the services relevant to the audit, he modifies.

options.text: Ask the provider to reissue its assurance report without the assumption about the company's controls, so that the report the auditor holds stands on its own
options.misconception: tries to remove the condition rather than address it, when the assumption reflects how the service is actually designed
options.why: The assumption is not a drafting choice. The provider's controls are designed on the footing that certain things happen at the user entity, and a report that pretended otherwise would describe a system that does not exist. What the auditor has to do is test those controls where they matter and respond to the ones that failed.

options.text: Treat the assurance report as worthless and audit the year's invoicing entirely substantively, since two of the four assumed controls have failed
options.misconception: discards the whole report because part of what it assumes has failed, when the failures are confined to particular controls and particular periods
options.why: Two of the four complementary controls did operate, and the exception report clearance operated for part of the year. The response is proportionate to what failed and when, not an abandonment of everything the report supports.

options.text: Rely on the assurance report as it stands, since the provider's controls were tested by the service auditor and found effective and the company's own lapses are a separate matter for the management letter
options.misconception: reads the service auditor's opinion as free-standing, when the description itself makes the provider's controls conditional on what the user entity does
options.why: The description says the provider's controls over pricing and credit limits are designed on the assumption that the four controls operate at the company. Where a report is used, the auditor must determine whether the complementary user entity controls identified by the service organisation are relevant to the user entity, and if so obtain an understanding of them and test them. An assumption that has failed cannot be treated as a matter for the management letter.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402 on complementary user entity controls, being controls the service organisation assumes in the design of its service will be implemented by user entities and which are identified in the description of the system, with the requirement when using a type 1 or type 2 report to determine whether those controls are relevant and to obtain an understanding of and test them at the user entity, read with the requirement to modify the opinion where the user auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the services provided

items.scenario: A company's sales invoicing runs on a platform operated by an outside provider. The auditor obtains the provider's assurance report covering the full year. The description of the system states that the provider's controls over pricing and credit limits are designed on the assumption that four things are done at the company: master price lists are approved by the sales director before upload, credit limits are reviewed monthly by the finance controller, exception reports produced by the platform are cleared within seven days, and user access is recertified each quarter. The auditor finds that the price list approval operates, that the access recertification operates, that the monthly credit limit review has never been performed, and that exception reports were cleared until June and then abandoned when the controller left. The audit plan had assumed reliance on the assurance report for the whole year.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because the amount of the eventual liability cannot be known until the appellate authority has ruled
options.misconception: converts an uncertain amount into an inability to obtain evidence, when the auditor holds the demand, the records and counsel's opinion
options.why: A disclaimer follows an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The auditor has the notice, the quantified demand, the company's own monitoring records and counsel's assessment; he is not short of evidence. What he has found is that a material matter is neither provided for nor disclosed, which is a misstatement.

options.text: An adverse opinion, since a company that broke an environmental law for eleven months and then concealed the consequence has presented accounts that are misleading throughout
options.misconception: escalates on the seriousness of the underlying conduct rather than on the pervasiveness of the effect on the financial statements
options.why: The choice between a qualification and an adverse opinion turns on the auditor's judgment about the pervasiveness of the effects on the financial statements, not on how badly the entity behaved. One omitted provision and its disclosure, material against the results and small against the balance sheet total, is confined.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a paragraph drawing attention to the appeal, the outcome of exceptional regulatory action being the classic case for such a paragraph
options.misconception: uses the paragraph for drawing attention to a disclosed matter where nothing has been disclosed and the statements are misstated
options.why: A paragraph drawing attention to a matter is available only where the matter is appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements. These statements neither provide for the penalty nor mention it, so there is nothing to draw attention to and the reason for the modification is a misstatement rather than a matter needing emphasis.

options.text: A qualified opinion — the non-compliance has a material effect on the financial statements and has not been adequately reflected in them, and the effect is confined rather than pervasive
options.why: If the auditor concludes that the non-compliance has a material effect on the financial statements and has not been adequately reflected in them, he shall express a qualified or adverse opinion. Which of the two follows from pervasiveness: the omitted liability and its disclosure are confined to specific elements of the statements and do not represent a substantial proportion of them, so the effects are material but not pervasive and the opinion is qualified. That an appeal is pending goes to the measurement of the liability, not to whether the reader should be told about it at all.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 250, reporting non-compliance in the auditor's report on the financial statements: where the auditor concludes that the non-compliance has a material effect on the financial statements and has not been adequately reflected in them, he shall in accordance with SA 705 express a qualified or adverse opinion, read with the pervasiveness test in Ch. Reporting

items.scenario: A manufacturer discharged effluent above the permitted limit for eleven months of the year. The State pollution control board issued a show-cause notice in January and a demand for a quantified penalty in March; the amount is material to the results though small against the balance sheet total. The company has filed an appeal and has paid nothing. The auditor has the notice, the demand, the company's own internal monitoring records confirming the breaches and an opinion from the company's counsel putting the chance of success on appeal at less than even. The financial statements neither provide for the penalty nor disclose it; the finance director says that providing for it would prejudice the appeal and that the matter is contingent until the appellate authority rules. The auditor has communicated with those charged with governance and they support the finance director.

items.stem: What does the auditor's report say?

options.text: An unmodified opinion, since the auditor is not responsible for detecting non-compliance with every law and cannot be expected to establish whether an offence has occurred
options.misconception: uses the limit on the auditor's responsibility to excuse a limitation deliberately imposed on him
options.why: It is true that the auditor is not responsible for preventing non-compliance and cannot be expected to detect non-compliance with all laws and regulations. That is about the scope of his duty to look, not about what he does when he has looked, has found something material and has been stopped from going further.

options.text: An adverse opinion, the refusal by both management and the audit committee being itself evidence that the payments were improper
options.misconception: treats a refusal as proof of the underlying wrong, and answers missing evidence with the outcome reserved for an established misstatement
options.why: A refusal is not evidence of what the documents would have shown. An adverse opinion requires the auditor to have obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence and concluded that misstatements are material and pervasive, and he has obtained no evidence at all on this point.

options.text: A qualified opinion together with a report of the suspected offence to the enforcement authority, the auditor being obliged to report outside the entity once those charged with governance are themselves involved
options.misconception: states the external reporting duty as automatic, when the standard requires the auditor to determine whether such a responsibility exists
options.why: Where the auditor has identified or suspects non-compliance he shall determine whether he has a responsibility to report it to parties outside the entity — a determination, not a duty that arises by itself. The reporting outcome on the financial statements is the qualification or disclaimer, and whether anything goes outside is a separate question answered against the law that applies.

options.text: A qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion on the basis of a limitation on the scope of the audit, the auditor having been precluded by management and by those charged with governance from obtaining evidence about whether a material non-compliance has occurred
options.why: If the auditor is precluded by management or those charged with governance from obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence to evaluate whether non-compliance that may be material to the financial statements has, or is likely to have, occurred, he shall express a qualified opinion or disclaim an opinion on the basis of a limitation on the scope of the audit. Which of the two follows from whether the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be material but not pervasive, or both material and pervasive. Note who refused: the preclusion came from management and then from those charged with governance, which is what puts the case in this limb rather than in the one for a limitation imposed by circumstances.
keywords: precluded by management or those charged with governance
limitation on the scope of the audit

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 250: where the auditor is precluded by management or those charged with governance from obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence to evaluate whether non-compliance that may be material has or is likely to have occurred, he shall express a qualified opinion or disclaim an opinion on the basis of a limitation on the scope of the audit in accordance with SA 705, read with the requirement to determine whether there is a responsibility to report to parties outside the entity

items.scenario: During the audit of a trading company the auditor notices payments to three overseas intermediaries described only as "facilitation" and totalling a material sum, made in the two months before a large export order was awarded. He asks for the agreements with the intermediaries, the correspondence with the customer's procurement department and the legal advice the company obtained before making the payments. The managing director refuses all three, saying the papers are privileged. The auditor raises it with the audit committee, which meets and resolves that the documents will not be produced to the auditor and that he is not to contact the company's external lawyers. Nothing else in the audit is affected and the auditor cannot tell from anything he does hold whether an offence has been committed.

items.stem: How does the auditor deal with this in the report?

options.text: Request management to remove the limitation and, if it refuses, communicate with those charged with governance and consider withdrawing from the engagement
options.misconception: applies the route built for a limitation management has imposed, where the limitation came from a fire and management has been cooperative
options.why: The request to remove the limitation, the communication with those charged with governance and the possibility of withdrawal belong to a limitation imposed by management after the auditor accepted the engagement. Nobody imposed this one. Asking management to remove a limitation it did not create and cannot lift is a step with nothing behind it.

options.text: Evaluate the effect on the opinion, the limitation having been imposed by circumstances rather than by management or those charged with governance
options.why: If the auditor is unable to determine whether non-compliance has occurred because of limitations imposed by the circumstances rather than by management or those charged with governance, he shall evaluate the effect on the auditor's opinion. The distinction matters because the other limb — a preclusion by management or those charged with governance — carries its own consequences, and management here has been cooperative and has itself tried to obtain duplicates. What the auditor is left with is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on a material matter, and the effect on the opinion is then determined on materiality and pervasiveness in the ordinary way.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: Report the matter to the regulator of that country and delay the report until an answer is received
options.misconception: makes an external enquiry a precondition to reporting, and converts an unanswered request into a duty to report a non-compliance nobody has established
options.why: Nothing has been established to report. Management has already written to the local regulator and had no answer, and an audit report cannot be held open indefinitely against a reply that may never come. The auditor evaluates the effect of the missing evidence on his opinion and reports.

options.text: Give an unmodified opinion, since the loss of records was outside everybody's control and an auditor cannot modify an opinion because of an accident
