options.misconception: treats the innocence of the cause as answering the question, when the report speaks to what the auditor could establish and not to whose fault the gap was
options.why: Why the evidence is missing does not change that it is missing. The reader is told whether the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and a fire that nobody could help leaves the same hole in the evidence as a refusal would.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 250: where the auditor is unable to determine whether non-compliance has occurred because of limitations imposed by the circumstances rather than by management or those charged with governance, he shall evaluate the effect on the auditor's opinion in accordance with SA 705

items.scenario: A company operates a branch in another country. Six weeks before the auditor's visit a fire in the branch office destroyed the correspondence files, the local statutory registers and the supporting documents for the branch's foreign exchange transactions for the whole year. The accounting records themselves survived on a server, but they show only the amounts and dates and not the underlying approvals or filings. The auditor cannot determine whether the branch complied with the exchange control law of that country, and non-compliance would be material. Nobody at the company prevented the auditor from doing anything; management has been cooperative throughout, has written to the local regulator asking for duplicate filings and has received no answer. There is no other source for the documents.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Ask the company to date the financial statements later so that the insolvency falls inside the period covered and can be accounted for as a current-year event
options.misconception: proposes to move the reporting date to fit the event, when the reporting date is fixed and the question is only how an event after it is treated
options.why: The date of the financial statements is the end of the period they cover and is not a matter of choice. What the standard governs is how events after that date are treated, and this one is treated by adjusting the amounts because it evidences a condition that already existed.

options.text: Treat the event as one requiring adjustment of the receivable, and where the company will not adjust, modify the opinion — the financial statements being materially misstated by an unadjusted balance
options.why: The auditor's objective for events occurring between the date of the financial statements and the date of his report is to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether those events requiring adjustment of, or disclosure in, the financial statements are appropriately reflected. This event evidences conditions existing at the reporting date, so what it requires is adjustment rather than disclosure. Management's refusal leaves a material misstatement in the statements, and where the report has not yet been provided the auditor modifies the opinion; whether the modification is a qualification or an adverse opinion depends on whether the effect is confined. He would also obtain a written representation that all events requiring adjustment or disclosure have been adjusted or disclosed.
keywords: conditions existing at the reporting date

options.text: Accept the note, since the event occurred after the reporting date and disclosure is what the financial statements owe the reader in that case
options.misconception: classifies the event by the date it happened rather than by what it proves about the position at the reporting date
options.why: The test is not when the event occurred but what it evidences. This one provides evidence of conditions that existed at the date of the financial statements — defaults to other suppliers before the year end, cheques dishonoured in February, a financial position recited as pre-dating the year end — so it requires adjustment of the amounts, and a disclosure does not discharge that.

options.text: Sign an unmodified report and write to those charged with governance recording the disagreement, so that the matter is on record without disrupting the accounts
options.misconception: substitutes a communication with governance for the modification the misstatement requires
options.why: Communicating with those charged with governance is required and is not an alternative to reporting. A material misstatement the entity refuses to correct is reflected in the opinion; a letter that nobody outside the company reads does not tell the reader of the financial statements anything.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 560: the auditor's objective in respect of events occurring between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report, being to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether those events requiring adjustment of, or disclosure in, the financial statements are appropriately reflected, with the written representation that all such events have been adjusted or disclosed, read with SA 705 on a modification arising from a material misstatement

items.scenario: A company's year ended on 31 March and the audit is nearly complete; the report has not been signed. A customer owing a material sum, shown in full as good in the trade receivables, filed for insolvency on 12 May. The auditor's enquiries establish that the customer had defaulted to three other suppliers before 31 March, that its cheques to this company had bounced twice in February, and that the insolvency petition recites a financial position that existed well before the year end. The auditor asks the company to write the balance down. The finance director refuses, saying that the resolution process may still produce a recovery, that the insolvency happened after the year end and so is a matter for next year's accounts, and that in any case the company has disclosed the filing in a note headed "events after the reporting period".

items.stem: What does the auditor do?

options.text: Take no further step, the events giving rise to the suit having occurred after the reporting date and the auditor's responsibility having ended when the report was signed
options.misconception: reads the date of the report as the end of the auditor's responsibility, when the standard exists precisely for facts that become known afterwards
options.why: The auditor's objective extends to responding appropriately to facts that become known to him after the date of his report which, had they been known at that date, may have caused him to amend the report. That the underlying events post-date the reporting date affects whether the statements are adjusted or the matter disclosed; it does not end the auditor's obligation to respond.

options.text: Resign the engagement and inform the members directly of the judgment, since the board has made clear it will circulate statements the auditor knows to be incomplete
options.misconception: replaces the prescribed sequence with a step of the auditor's own, before the statements have even been issued
options.why: The standard sets out what to do and in what order, and it stops at notifying those charged with governance and then, if the statements are issued anyway, taking appropriate action to prevent reliance on the report. Resigning and approaching the members directly is neither of those and would leave the report standing unqualified in the members' hands.

options.text: Withdraw the report of 15 July and issue a fresh one carrying a modified opinion, since a signed report can always be replaced before the statements are issued
options.misconception: reaches for a modification, which is the route where the report has not yet reached management, and treats withdrawal as freely available
options.why: Modifying the opinion is what the standard directs where the auditor's report has not yet been provided to management. This report has been provided, which puts the case in the other limb: the auditor notifies those charged with governance not to issue the statements before the amendments are made, and acts to prevent reliance if they are issued anyway.

options.text: Notify those charged with governance not to issue the financial statements to third parties before the necessary amendments are made, and if they are issued nevertheless, take appropriate action to prevent reliance on the auditor's report
options.why: Where a fact becomes known to the auditor after the date of his report but before the financial statements are issued, he discusses the matter with management or those charged with governance, determines whether the financial statements need amendment and inquires how management intends to address it. If management does not amend, the response depends on where the report has got to: if the report has not yet been provided to management, the auditor modifies the opinion; if it has already been provided, the auditor notifies management and those charged with governance not to issue the financial statements to third parties before the necessary amendments have been made, and if they are nevertheless issued, takes appropriate action to seek to prevent reliance on the auditor's report.
keywords: not to issue the financial statements to third parties

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 560: facts which become known to the auditor after the date of the auditor's report but before the date the financial statements are issued — discuss with management or those charged with governance, determine whether the financial statements need amendment, inquire how management intends to address the matter; and where management does not amend, modify the opinion if the report has not yet been provided to management, or if it has, notify those charged with governance not to issue the statements to third parties and, if they are still issued, take appropriate action to prevent reliance on the auditor's report

items.scenario: An auditor signed her report on 15 July and delivered it to the company that afternoon. The financial statements have not yet been sent to the members, filed, or given to anybody outside the company. On 18 July the company lost a suit brought by a creditor in a fast-track court and must pay a large sum; the events giving rise to the suit all occurred after the reporting date, but the amount is material and the outcome is now certain. The auditor asks the directors to amend the financial statements to reflect the judgment. On 22 July the board replies that it will not amend them, that the report is already signed, and that it intends to circulate the statements to the members with the notice of the annual general meeting the following week.

items.stem: What report should the auditor issue, and dated when?

options.text: A fresh report dated 20 July, that being the date the directors decided to amend and therefore the date on which the auditor's original reservations were met
options.misconception: dates the report from the decision to amend rather than from the approval of the amended statements
options.why: A decision to amend is not an amendment. The report cannot be dated earlier than the date on which the auditor obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence on which to base his opinion, including evidence that the amended financial statements have been prepared and that those with authority have approved them — and approval came on 25 July.

options.text: Either an amended report carrying an additional date restricted to the amendment, or a new or amended report including a statement in an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph — and the new report cannot be dated earlier than the date the amended financial statements were approved
options.why: Where management amends the financial statements, the auditor carries out the procedures necessary in the circumstances on the amendment and then has two routes: to amend the auditor's report to include an additional date restricted to that amendment, so that the reader can see the original audit was completed earlier and only the amendment was audited to the later date; or to provide a new or amended report including a statement in an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph explaining the reason for the amendment and referring to the earlier report. Whichever is chosen, the report on the amended financial statements shall not be dated earlier than the date of approval of the amended financial statements, which here is 25 July.
keywords: Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter
not be dated earlier than the date of approval

options.text: Keep the original report and its date of 15 July, and issue a separate letter to the members explaining the two amendments
options.misconception: leaves a report standing on financial statements that no longer exist in the form audited, and reports the change outside the report
options.why: The financial statements have changed, so a report bearing the earlier date describes a document nobody will now be reading. And a separate letter is not the auditor's report; the reader of the amended statements has to be able to see, from the report attached to them, what was audited and to what date.

options.text: A fresh report dated 25 July with a modified opinion, since the original report was signed on statements that were materially misstated in two respects
options.misconception: carries the original modification into a report on statements from which the misstatements have been removed
options.why: The opinion is on the financial statements the report accompanies, and both matters have now been reflected in them. Nothing is left to modify for. What the reader is told about the history comes through the additional date or through the Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph, not through an opinion that no longer fits the accounts.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 560: where management amends the financial statements after a fact becomes known to the auditor, the auditor extends the audit procedures and either amends the auditor's report to include an additional date restricted to the amendment or provides a new or amended report including a statement in an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph, the report on the amended financial statements not being dated earlier than the date of approval of the amended financial statements

items.scenario: The same company reconsiders. On 20 July the directors agree to amend the financial statements for the judgment, and while they are at it they also amend them for an earlier matter — a fire that destroyed stock on 27 June, which the auditor had asked them to reflect before the original report was signed and which they had refused. The amended financial statements are approved by the board on 25 July. The auditor extends her audit procedures over both amendments and to the date of the new approval, and is satisfied. She now has to decide what report to issue and what date it should bear. A partner suggests keeping the original date of 15 July, since that is when the audit of the financial statements as a whole was completed.

items.stem: How should the auditor proceed?

options.text: Disclaim an opinion at once, since attendance at the count is the only procedure that gives evidence of the existence of inventory and it can never be replaced
options.misconception: treats attendance as irreplaceable, when the standard provides for alternative procedures where attendance is impracticable
options.why: The standard contemplates alternative procedures precisely for the case where attendance is impracticable, and gives an example of one. Only where those cannot give sufficient appropriate audit evidence does the modification follow, and even then the choice between a qualification and a disclaimer depends on whether the possible effects are pervasive.

options.text: Accept the storekeeper's sheets, supported by a management representation, since attendance was impossible and the cost of anything further is out of proportion to the balance
options.misconception: lets cost decide the extent of the work and treats a representation as filling the gap left by the missing procedure
options.why: The matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for the auditor to omit an audit procedure for which there is no alternative or to be satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive. And a written representation provides necessary audit evidence but does not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own.

options.text: Perform whatever alternative procedures can give sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the existence and condition of the inventory, disregarding the cost objection — and if no alternative can, modify the opinion as a result of the scope limitation
options.why: Where attendance at physical inventory counting is impracticable, the auditor performs alternative audit procedures, for example inspection of documentation of the subsequent sale of specific inventory items acquired or purchased prior to the physical inventory counting, to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about existence and condition. Cost does not enter the decision: the matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for the auditor to omit a procedure for which there is no alternative or to be satisfied with evidence that is less than persuasive. In some cases it may not be possible to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by alternative procedures at all, and in those cases the auditor is required to modify the opinion as a result of the scope limitation.

options.text: Attend a count now and roll the quantities back to 31 March, which is always available and removes the need for any modification
options.misconception: assumes a roll-back is always possible, when the entire closing stock has been consumed and the records will not support the reconciliation
options.why: A count at a later date with a roll-back is a real alternative in many audits and it is not one here: the whole of the closing stock was drawn off and consumed in April and May, and the production records do not reconcile inputs to specific tank withdrawals. A procedure that cannot be performed on these facts is not an answer to them.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 501 on attendance at physical inventory counting: where attendance is impracticable the auditor performs alternative audit procedures such as inspecting documentation of the subsequent sale of specific items, and where it is not possible to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by alternative procedures SA 705 requires the auditor to modify the opinion as a result of the scope limitation, read with SA 200 as reproduced there, that difficulty, time or cost is not in itself a valid basis to omit a procedure for which there is no alternative or to be satisfied with less than persuasive evidence

items.scenario: A firm is appointed in June to audit a chemicals company for the year ended 31 March, so no member of the firm attended the year-end count. The inventory is bulk liquid held in six sealed tanks, material to the financial statements. The company's own count was made by dipping the tanks and applying a density conversion; the working sheets survive but were prepared and signed by one storekeeper alone. The whole of the closing stock was drawn off and consumed in production during April and May, so no item can be identified and traced to a later sale, and the production records do not reconcile inputs to specific tank withdrawals. The auditor proposes to engage an independent engineer to reconstruct the tank movements from the plant's flow meters. The finance director objects that this would cost more than the audit fee, that the exercise would take a month, and that the storekeeper's sheets have been accepted by the company's own management for years.

items.stem: What does the auditor do now?

options.text: Insist on personal attendance and refuse to complete the audit until the operator permits a visit, attendance being the only procedure that establishes existence
options.misconception: treats attendance by the auditor himself as the only route, when the standard names several others including attendance arranged through another auditor
options.why: The standard names alternatives: attending or arranging for another auditor to attend, obtaining a report on the third party's controls, inspecting documentation, and confirming with other parties where the inventory has been pledged. Refusing to move until one particular procedure becomes available leaves the audit stalled where the standard offers routes forward.

options.text: Write the inventory down to nil and issue an unmodified opinion on the restated figures, since stock whose existence cannot be verified should not be carried
options.misconception: has the auditor decide the accounting, and treats unverifiable as equivalent to non-existent
options.why: The auditor does not write down the entity's assets; management prepares the financial statements and the auditor reports on them. And the inability to verify a balance is not evidence that the goods are absent — it is an absence of evidence, which is answered by further procedures and, if those fail, by a modification for a scope limitation.

options.text: Treat the one-line confirmation as sufficient, a reply from an independent third party being external evidence and therefore more reliable than anything generated inside the company
options.misconception: relies on the source of the evidence without weighing what it actually says or what is known about the party who sent it
options.why: External origin raises the reliability of evidence; it does not make a reply evidence of something it does not state. This one gives no quantities, no descriptions and no condition, and the auditor now has information raising doubts about the integrity and objectivity of the party who sent it.

options.text: Perform other procedures — inspecting documentation of subsequent sales, arranging for another auditor to attend or to report on the adequacy of the warehouse's controls over goods held for others — and where sufficient appropriate audit evidence about existence and condition still cannot be obtained, modify the opinion
options.why: Where inventory under the custody and control of a third party is material, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about its existence and condition by requesting confirmation from the third party or by performing inspection or other appropriate procedures. Where information comes to his attention raising doubt about the integrity and objectivity of the third party, he considers performing other procedures: attending or arranging for another auditor to attend the third party's count, obtaining another auditor's report or a service auditor's report on the adequacy of the third party's internal control for ensuring that inventory is properly counted and safeguarded, inspecting documentation regarding inventory held by third parties, and requesting confirmation from other parties where inventory has been pledged. If none of that can give sufficient appropriate audit evidence on a material balance, what is left is a scope limitation and the opinion is modified.
keywords: integrity and objectivity of the third party

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 501 on inventory under the custody and control of a third party: the requirement to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about its existence and condition by confirmation or by inspection or other procedures, and the other procedures to be considered where information raises doubt about the integrity and objectivity of the third party, including attending or arranging for another auditor to attend the count and obtaining a report on the adequacy of the third party's internal control, read with SA 705 on a modification for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

items.scenario: A trading company holds a material part of its stock at an independent warehouse in another state. The auditor sends a confirmation request to the warehouse operator and receives a one-line reply stating that goods are held to the account of the company, without quantities, descriptions or condition. He then learns three things: the warehouse operator has defaulted on its own borrowings and its accounts show a going concern note; two other depositors have complained publicly about shortages at the same premises; and the operator's licence was suspended for a month during the year. The auditor asks to attend a count at the warehouse and is told visits are not permitted under the operator's insurance policy. He asks for a report from the operator's own auditor on the adequacy of its controls over goods held for others, and is told none exists.

items.stem: What does the auditor do?

options.text: Qualify the opinion, the refusal being a limitation on scope that is material but confined to the two matters the paragraphs deal with
options.misconception: treats the refused representations as one more confined limitation, when what is withheld undermines the reliability of everything else management has said
options.why: These two representations are not about a balance; they are about whether the financial statements were prepared as management undertook and whether the auditor was given everything. Doubt about those is not confined, which is why the standard answers this case with a disclaimer rather than leaving it to the ordinary material-but-not-pervasive test.

options.text: Accept the letter as signed, the missing paragraphs being duplicated in the engagement letter and the substantive representations all having been given
options.misconception: treats the engagement letter as carrying the representation, when the two documents do different work at different times
options.why: The engagement letter records what management agrees to do at the start; the written representation is management's confirmation, at the end and covering the period reported on, that it has done it. They are not interchangeable, which is why the representations about management's own responsibilities are asked for separately and why their absence has a consequence of its own.

options.text: Discuss the matter with management, re-evaluate the integrity of management and the effect on the reliability of representations and audit evidence generally, and — these being the representations about management's own responsibilities — disclaim an opinion
options.why: Where management does not provide one or more of the requested representations, the auditor discusses the matter with management, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the effect that may have on the reliability of representations and of audit evidence in general, and takes appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the opinion. Two situations are answered by a disclaimer rather than a qualification, and this is one of them: where management does not provide the representations that it has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements and that it has provided the auditor with all relevant information and access agreed in the terms of the engagement. The history of documents produced only on a third request is exactly what the re-evaluation of integrity is for.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement immediately, since an auditor who cannot obtain the basic representations has no basis on which to continue
options.misconception: makes withdrawal the automatic answer, skipping the discussion and re-evaluation the standard requires and the reporting outcome it prescribes
options.why: Withdrawal is one of the actions that may follow and it is not where the standard starts. The auditor first discusses the matter, re-evaluates management's integrity and the effect on the reliability of the evidence he holds, and then takes appropriate action — which on these facts means disclaiming an opinion.

citation.ref: para 19 and para 20, read with para 14 — where management does not provide one or more of the requested written representations the auditor shall discuss the matter with management, re-evaluate the integrity of management and evaluate the effect that this may have on the reliability of representations and audit evidence in general, and take appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the opinion; and shall disclaim an opinion where management does not provide the representations that it has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements and that it has provided the auditor with all relevant information and access

items.scenario: An audit is complete but for the representation letter. Management signs the representations about related parties, litigation, subsequent events and the valuation of inventory without demur. It strikes out two paragraphs: the one stating that management has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with the applicable framework, and the one stating that it has provided the auditor with all relevant information and access agreed in the terms of the engagement. The managing director's explanation is that the engagement letter already records both, that repeating them is a lawyer's device, and that the board will not sign the same undertaking twice. During the audit the auditor has twice found documents that were requested early and produced only after being asked a third time.

items.stem: What is wrong with the manager's note, and what follows?

options.text: The period is the problem — the auditor should obtain a report covering only the part of the year during which the technology provider was engaged, and rely on the existing report for the rest
options.misconception: reads the gap as a gap in time, when it is a gap in scope that runs through the whole period
options.why: The exclusion is not about dates. The technology provider's controls are outside the description and outside the opinion for the entire period the report covers, so no part of the year is covered in respect of them and slicing the period changes nothing.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the excluded controls are technology controls rather than accounting controls, and the assurance report covers the accounting the company relies on
options.misconception: divides controls by their label rather than by whether they bear on the assertions, when access provisioning and data restoration go directly to completeness and accuracy
options.why: What matters is whether a control bears on the assertions in the company's financial statements, not whether it is called a technology control. User access provisioning decides who can change a fund balance and data restoration decides whether the balances survive a failure intact; both go to completeness and accuracy.

options.text: The report is invalid, since an assurance report that excludes controls the user relies on cannot properly be issued
options.misconception: treats a permitted method of dealing with a subservice organisation as a defect in the report
options.why: The carve-out method is one of the two methods the standard provides for, and a report using it is properly issued so long as the description says what is excluded — which this one does. The problem is not the report; it is what the user auditor concluded from it.

options.text: The description uses the carve-out method, so the excluded provider's controls are outside both the description and the service auditor's opinion — the auditor must obtain evidence about those controls separately, and modify the opinion if he cannot
options.why: Where a service organisation uses a subservice organisation, the description of the system may deal with it by the inclusive method, which brings the subservice organisation's relevant control objectives and controls into the description and into the scope of the engagement, or by the carve-out method, which excludes them from both while describing the nature of the services provided. Under a carve-out the service auditor has expressed no opinion on those controls at all, so an assurance report covering the full year says nothing about them, however long the period. The auditor therefore has to obtain evidence about the excluded controls himself, and where he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the services provided that are relevant to the audit, he modifies the opinion.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3402: the inclusive and carve-out methods of dealing with a subservice organisation in the description of the system, the carve-out method excluding the subservice organisation's relevant control objectives and controls from the description and from the scope of the service auditor's engagement while describing the nature of the services provided, read with SA 402 on the user auditor modifying the opinion where unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the services provided by the service organisation

items.scenario: A company's fund accounting is performed by an administrator, and the auditor obtains the administrator's assurance report for the full year. Reading the description of the system, he finds that the administrator does not itself host the application: the hosting, the database backups and the logical access administration are performed by a separate technology provider, and the description states that the controls at that provider are excluded from the description and from the scope of the service auditor's opinion. The controls excluded include user access provisioning and the restoration of data after a failure, both of which bear directly on the completeness and accuracy of the company's fund balances, which are material. The engagement manager's note reads that the assurance report covers the full year and can therefore be relied on for the whole of the fund accounting.

items.stem: Which opinion does SA 705 (Revised) require, and why?

options.text: An adverse opinion, because the group's most significant asset cannot be supported and the financial statements therefore do not give a true and fair view
options.misconception: applies the misstatement row of the matrix to a matter that is an inability to obtain evidence
options.why: An adverse opinion is expressed where the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements are both material and pervasive. Here no misstatement has been established at all, and the auditor cannot say the statements do not give a true and fair view when he cannot say what the amount ought to be.
keywords: having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: A qualified opinion, using the phrase "except for the possible effects of the matter", since the difficulty is confined to one investment
options.misconception: reads pervasiveness off the number of line items affected rather than off the proportion of the financial statements those items represent
options.why: The first limb of pervasiveness asks whether the effects are confined to specific elements. The second limb answers the case where they are — if so confined, do they represent or could they represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements. More than nine-tenths of net assets is that proportion, so being confined to one investment does not save the qualification.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an other matter paragraph explaining that the joint venture's records were not made available
options.misconception: uses a paragraph that adds information to the report as a way of not answering the opinion question at all
options.why: A paragraph that describes the difficulty leaves the opinion saying the financial statements give a true and fair view, which is precisely what the auditor is unable to say. The inability to obtain evidence drives the opinion itself; no additional paragraph can carry it.

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, because this is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence whose possible effects on the financial statements of undetected misstatements, if any, could be both material and pervasive
options.why: The type of modification is decided by two things together — the nature of the matter, and the auditor's judgement about pervasiveness. The nature here is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, not a known misstatement, so the question is about the possible effects of undetected misstatements, if any. A holding that is more than nine-tenths of the group's net assets means those possible effects could be both material and pervasive, and on that row of the matrix the answer is a disclaimer of opinion, not a qualification. Finding no misstatement is not a finding that there is none.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

citation.ref: para 5 on pervasiveness, read with the requirement to disclaim an opinion where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence on which to base the opinion and concludes that the possible effects on the financial statements of undetected misstatements, if any, could be both material and pervasive

items.scenario: You are the statutory auditor of a power generating company for the year ended 31 March. The company's own operations are small. Its one substantial holding is a joint venture that runs a transmission line, carried in the consolidated balance sheet at an amount representing more than nine-tenths of the group's net assets. Three weeks before you sign, the joint venture's board declines to give you access to its management or to its auditors, and your request for that firm's audit documentation is refused. The joint venture's own audited financial statements are not made available to you either. You perform every alternative procedure you can think of — public filings, the shareholders' agreement, the group's own records of distributions received — and none of them lets you conclude on the group's share of the joint venture's assets, liabilities, income and expenses. Nothing you have seen suggests the carrying amount is wrong. You simply cannot tell. The rest of the group's balances are properly supported and you have no other unresolved matter. Your engagement partner says that since you have found no misstatement, the honest answer is a qualified opinion saying so.

items.stem: What may you do?

options.text: Withdraw only after issuing the audit report for the full year, because the Securities and Exchange Board of India's directive on the resignation of an auditor does not permit withdrawing from the engagement without issuing the report — so in practice the report is issued, and on these facts it disclaims an opinion
options.why: SA 705 (Revised) puts withdrawal first only where withdrawal is practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation, and disclaims where it is not. For a listed company that second branch is the live one. The listing agreement and the Securities and Exchange Board of India's directive on the resignation of auditors do not permit withdrawing from the engagement without issuing the audit or review report, and where limited review reports have been issued for all three quarters the auditor issues the audit report for the full year before resigning. The report he issues on these facts carries a disclaimer of opinion.
keywords: practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation
do not permit withdrawing from the engagement without issuing
the audit report for the full year

options.text: Resign now and say in the resignation letter that the reason is professional pre-occupation, leaving the incoming auditor to deal with the division
options.misconception: reaches for a form of words the Institute has expressly told auditors not to use, on top of a resignation the securities regulator does not permit
options.why: Two things are wrong with it. The resignation itself is not permitted without the report. And the Institute has announced that an auditor of an unlisted company shall not give professional pre-occupation as the reason for resignation and shall state the reasons clearly in the resignation letter, so the sentence proposed here is the one form of words that has been ruled out.

options.text: Issue the audit report with a qualified opinion, since resigning is barred and a disclaimer would be too severe for a single division
options.misconception: lowers the modification because the exit is blocked, when the blocked exit changes only who reports and not what the report says
options.why: The regulator's rule decides whether he may leave, not what his opinion is. The opinion still follows from the conclusion he has reached — possible effects of undetected misstatements that could be both material and pervasive — and that conclusion gives a disclaimer.

options.text: Resign at once without any further report, since the standard directs withdrawal wherever the possible effects could be material and pervasive
options.misconception: reads the withdrawal branch as unconditional, dropping the words that make it conditional on law and regulation
options.why: The direction is conditional on its face. The auditor withdraws where withdrawal is practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation, and disclaims an opinion where withdrawal before issuing the report is not practicable or possible. A rule of the securities regulator that forbids resigning without a report is exactly what makes it not possible.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — where the auditor's withdrawal is not permitted, the Securities and Exchange Board of India circular of 18 October 2019 on the resignation of an auditor and the requirement to issue the audit or limited review report before resigning, read with SA 705 (Revised) para 13 and para 14

items.scenario: You are the statutory auditor of a listed company. Halfway through the audit of the year ended 31 March, management refuses you access to the records of a division that carries a large part of the company's revenue, and refuses again after you ask for the limitation to be removed. You communicate the refusal to the audit committee. No alternative procedure gets you to the revenue of that division, and you conclude that the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive. You have already issued limited review reports for all three quarters of the year. Your partner reads SA 705 (Revised), sees that withdrawal comes before a disclaimer, and proposes to resign from the engagement at once without issuing anything further.

items.stem: What else does SA 705 (Revised) require him to change or remove?

options.text: The statement that the financial statements have been audited becomes a statement that he was engaged to audit them; the cross-reference to the section describing the auditor's responsibilities and the statement that the audit evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate both come out; and the description of the auditor's responsibilities is reduced to three statements — that his responsibility is to conduct an audit in accordance with the Standards on Auditing and issue a report, that because of the matters described in the Basis for Disclaimer of Opinion section he was not able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an opinion, and the statement about independence and other ethical responsibilities
options.why: A disclaimer changes the report in more places than the two headings. The SA 700 statement that the financial statements have been audited is amended to say the auditor was engaged to audit them. Two SA 700 elements are not included at all — a reference to the section where the auditor's responsibilities are described, and a statement about whether the audit evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for the opinion, which would contradict the disclaimer. And the description of the auditor's responsibilities is amended to include only those three statements.
keywords: reference to the section where the auditor's responsibilities are described
sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for the opinion

options.text: Only the description of the auditor's responsibilities, which is shortened; the sentence about the sufficiency of the audit evidence stays, because it describes what he did rather than what he concluded
options.misconception: keeps the evidence sentence by reading it as a description of work done, when it is a statement that the evidence provides a basis for an opinion the auditor is not expressing
options.why: That sentence does not report effort. It states that the audit evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for the auditor's opinion, which is the exact proposition a disclaimer denies, and SA 705 (Revised) directs that a report disclaiming an opinion shall not include it.
keywords: provide a basis for the auditor's opinion

options.text: The whole auditor's responsibilities section is removed, since an auditor who expresses no opinion has no responsibilities to describe
options.misconception: deletes a section the standard reduces, and denies responsibilities that the auditor plainly still carries
options.why: The section is amended, not deleted. It keeps three statements, and one of them exists to say what his responsibility was — to conduct an audit in accordance with the Standards on Auditing and to issue an auditor's report. The independence statement stays as well.

options.text: Nothing else. The Opinion and Basis sections carry the modification and the rest of the report is standard wording that the standard does not touch
options.misconception: treats the modification as confined to the two sections that carry the opinion, when a disclaimer reaches into the responsibilities description and the evidence statement as well
options.why: Leaving the standard wording in place produces a report that disclaims an opinion in one section and asserts in another that the evidence obtained was sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for that opinion. The standard removes the second statement precisely because it contradicts the first.
keywords: disclaims an opinion in one section

citation.ref: the requirement on a disclaimer to state that the auditor does not express an opinion and that because of the significance of the matters described he has not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, to amend the SA 700 (Revised) statement that the financial statements have been audited to say that the auditor was engaged to audit them, to omit the reference to the section describing the auditor's responsibilities and the statement about the sufficiency of the audit evidence, and to amend the description of the auditor's responsibilities to include only the three statements named, read with para 16

items.scenario: An audit senior is preparing a report that will disclaim an opinion because of an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. He has changed the Opinion heading and the Basis heading, and has written the two required sentences in the Opinion section. He has then left the rest of the standard report exactly as it stands for an unmodified opinion — including the full description of the auditor's responsibilities for the audit of the financial statements, the cross-reference to that section, and the sentence saying the audit evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for the opinion.

items.stem: What does SA 705 (Revised) require?

options.text: Both remaining matters are described in the Basis for Adverse Opinion section, with the reasons and their effects, and the sentence about the sufficiency of the audit evidence is amended to include the word "adverse"
options.why: The standard says it in terms. Even where the auditor has expressed an adverse opinion or disclaimed an opinion, he shall describe in the Basis for Opinion section the reasons for any other matters of which he is aware that would have required a modification to the opinion, and the effects thereof. Separately, where the auditor expresses a qualified or adverse opinion he amends the statement about whether the audit evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for the opinion to include the word "qualified" or "adverse" as appropriate.
keywords: any other matters of which he is aware

options.text: The other two matters are left out, because an adverse opinion is the most severe conclusion on a misstatement and already covers everything else
options.misconception: treats the severity of the opinion as absorbing every other matter, when the standard requires each one to be described whatever the opinion says
options.why: Severity is not coverage. A reader of a report with an adverse opinion still needs to know what else was wrong and by how much, which is why the requirement to describe other matters that would have required a modification applies even after an adverse opinion or a disclaimer.

options.text: Only the depreciation matter is described, because it is a known misstatement; the missing confirmations concern evidence, and evidence matters are reported only where they drive the opinion
options.misconception: limits the requirement to known misstatements, when the requirement is about any matter that would have required a modification, from either row of the matrix
options.why: An inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence is one of the two things that require a modification, so a matter of that kind is one that would have required a modification. Where the modification results from an inability to obtain evidence, the Basis for Opinion section carries the reasons for that inability.
keywords: one of the two things that require a modification

options.text: Both matters are described, but the sentence about the sufficiency of the audit evidence is removed altogether, as it is on a disclaimer
options.misconception: applies the disclaimer's removal of that sentence to an adverse opinion, where the standard amends the sentence instead of dropping it
options.why: Removing it is what a disclaimer does. On a qualified or an adverse opinion the auditor has obtained the evidence and reached a conclusion, so the sentence stays and is amended to include the word "qualified" or "adverse" as appropriate.
keywords: Removing it is what a disclaimer does
the sentence stays and is amended

citation.ref: the requirement to amend the statement about whether the audit evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to include the word "qualified" or "adverse", and the requirement that even where an adverse opinion has been expressed or an opinion disclaimed the auditor shall describe in the Basis for Opinion section the reasons for any other matters of which he is aware that would have required a modification and the effects thereof, read with para 20 and para 21

items.scenario: You are signing a report with an adverse opinion, because the company has consolidated a subsidiary it does not control and the effects run through every primary statement. Two other matters remain unresolved. Depreciation on a class of plant has been charged on a basis that you consider wrong, by an amount that would on its own have been material but not pervasive. And you were unable to obtain confirmations for a block of trade receivables, again material but not pervasive on its own. Your manager's view is that once the opinion is adverse the other two matters are absorbed by it and adding them would only confuse the reader. He also proposes to leave the sentence about the sufficiency of the audit evidence exactly as the unmodified template has it.

items.stem: What goes into the Basis for Qualified Opinion section?

options.text: An explanation of how the disclosure is misstated — what the note says, what the applicable framework requires it to say, and in what respect the two differ
options.why: Where a material misstatement relates to narrative disclosures, the auditor includes in the Basis for Opinion section an explanation of how the disclosures are misstated. The requirement to describe and quantify financial effects belongs to a misstatement of specific amounts, and nothing here moves an amount, so the section carries the explanation rather than a figure.
keywords: an explanation of how the disclosures are misstated

options.text: A description and quantification of the financial effects of the misstatement, or a statement that quantification is impracticable
options.misconception: applies the rule for a misstatement of specific amounts to a misstatement that is entirely narrative
options.why: That rule is for a material misstatement relating to specific amounts in the financial statements, including quantitative disclosures in the notes. A narrative disclosure has its own rule, which asks for an explanation of how it is misstated rather than for a number or an excuse for the absence of one.

options.text: Nothing. The Basis section names the matter and the note, and the reader can compare the note with the framework for himself
options.misconception: reduces the Basis section to a cross-reference, which is the one thing the standard says does not amount to a qualification
options.why: The Basis for Opinion section must include a description of the matter giving rise to the modification, stated from the auditor's standpoint. A pointer to management's note leaves the reader with management's account of the matter and none of the auditor's.
keywords: a description of the matter giving rise to the modification

options.text: The disclosure the company should have made, written out by the auditor in full
options.misconception: reaches for the remedy that belongs to an omitted disclosure and applies it to one that exists but is wrong
options.why: Including the omitted disclosures is what the auditor does where the misstatement is a non-disclosure of information required to be disclosed, and even then only where it is not prohibited by law or regulation, it is practicable, and he has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the omitted information. Here a disclosure exists and is inadequate, which is the narrative limb.
keywords: non-disclosure of information required to be disclosed

citation.ref: the requirement that where a material misstatement relates to narrative disclosures the auditor include in the Basis for Opinion section an explanation of how the disclosures are misstated, distinguished from the requirement in para 21 for a misstatement relating to specific amounts

items.scenario: A company has been served with a demand from a regulator that could, on the company's own counsel's assessment, cost it a sum larger than a year's profit. The company treats it as a contingent liability, which you accept, but the note in the financial statements gives only the name of the regulator and the words "the matter is under appeal". It gives no estimate of the financial effect, no indication of the uncertainties, and no statement that an estimate cannot be made. Management will not expand the note. You conclude that the disclosure is materially misstated but that the effect is not pervasive. No amount in the balance sheet or the statement of profit and loss changes as a result.

items.stem: What does SA 705 (Revised) require you to do about the omitted disclosure?

options.text: Discuss the non-disclosure with those charged with governance, describe in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section the nature of the omitted information, and include the omitted disclosures themselves in that section
options.why: Where a material misstatement is the non-disclosure of information required to be disclosed, the standard sets three steps. The auditor discusses the non-disclosure with those charged with governance. He describes in the Basis for Opinion section the nature of the omitted information. And unless prohibited by law or regulation he includes the omitted disclosures, provided it is practicable to do so and he has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the omitted information — all three conditions are met on these facts.
keywords: discusses the non-disclosure with those charged with governance
the nature of the omitted information
unless prohibited by law or regulation

options.text: Include the omitted disclosures only if management first agrees, since a disclosure the company has not made is management's information to publish
options.misconception: makes an auditor's reporting duty conditional on the consent of the party whose omission caused it
options.why: The conditions the standard attaches are that inclusion is not prohibited by law or regulation, that it is practicable, and that the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the omitted information. Management's agreement is not among them, and a rule that needed it would never operate.
keywords: not prohibited by law or regulation
Management's agreement is not among them

options.text: Report the matter as a key audit matter instead, since it is a matter of most significance that you communicated to those charged with governance
options.misconception: moves a matter that requires a modification into the key audit matters section, which the standards say is not a substitute for one
options.why: Communicating key audit matters is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when the circumstances require it. A material non-disclosure that management will not correct requires a modification, and the key audit matters section cannot carry it.
keywords: not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion

options.text: Describe the nature of the omitted information, but do not reproduce the disclosure — putting management's disclosure into the auditor's report would make the auditor the preparer of the financial statements
options.misconception: refuses a step the standard requires, on a principle the standard has already weighed and answered
options.why: The standard expressly directs the auditor to include the omitted disclosures, subject to three conditions, and reproducing them in the Basis for Opinion section does not put them into the financial statements. Management remains the preparer; the auditor is reporting what should have been there.
keywords: expressly directs the auditor to include the omitted disclosures

citation.ref: the requirement that where a material misstatement is the non-disclosure of information required to be disclosed the auditor shall discuss the non-disclosure with those charged with governance, describe in the Basis for Opinion section the nature of the omitted information, and unless prohibited by law or regulation include the omitted disclosures where practicable and where he has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about them

items.scenario: A company's financial statements omit a disclosure that the applicable financial reporting framework requires: the terms and the ageing of amounts owed to a group of related parties. You have the underlying records, you have tested them, and you can set the disclosure out yourself. Management declines to add it, saying the information is commercially sensitive. Nothing in any law or regulation prevents the information being published. You conclude that the non-disclosure is material but not pervasive.

items.stem: How is pervasiveness tested here?

options.text: It cannot be met. Pervasiveness measures the spread of a misstatement across the primary statements, and a defect in one note has no spread
options.misconception: keeps only the first two limbs of the definition and drops the one the standard added for disclosures
options.why: The definition has three limbs, and the third is expressly about disclosures. Reading the test as a measure of spread across the primary statements makes a whole class of misstatements incapable of ever being pervasive, which is not what the standard says.

options.text: By the third limb of the definition — in relation to disclosures, whether the effects are fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements — so an inadequate disclosure can be pervasive even though no amount moves, and the answer turns on how far short the note falls
options.why: Pervasive effects are those that are not confined to specific elements, accounts or items; or, if so confined, represent or could represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements; or, in relation to disclosures, are fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements. The third limb is written for disclosures and asks nothing about amounts. A note that is incomplete gives a qualified opinion where the effect is material but not pervasive; a material uncertainty omitted altogether is fundamental to users' understanding and gives an adverse opinion.

options.text: By whether the going concern basis is still appropriate. It is, so the statements are not materially misstated and no modification arises
options.misconception: confuses the appropriateness of the basis of accounting with the adequacy of the disclosure about the uncertainty
options.why: Two separate questions. The basis of accounting can be appropriate and the financial statements still be materially misstated because the material uncertainty attaching to it is not adequately disclosed. That inadequate disclosure is the misstatement.

options.text: By whether the matter was communicated to those charged with governance and determined to be a key audit matter; if it was, an emphasis of matter paragraph resolves it
options.misconception: routes an uncorrected misstatement through the reporting choices that exist only where no modification is required
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter, and only for a matter appropriately presented or disclosed. A material uncertainty that is not adequately disclosed is neither.
keywords: would not be required to modify the opinion

citation.ref: para 5 on the three limbs of pervasiveness, including effects that in relation to disclosures are fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements, read with para 7(a) and para 8 on the choice between a qualified and an adverse opinion where a material uncertainty is inadequately disclosed

items.scenario: A company's financing arrangements have expired and it has not been able to renegotiate them or find replacement finance. You conclude that a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on its ability to continue as a going concern. The notes describe the size of the facilities and the date they expired, but say nothing at all about the effect of the failure to refinance or about the availability of refinancing, so the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed. Every figure in the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss has been prepared on the going concern basis, which you accept as appropriate. The company will not add to the note. A colleague argues that since no amount is misstated and the disclosure defect touches only one note, the pervasiveness test cannot be met and the most that is available is a qualified opinion.

items.stem: What does SA 705 (Revised) allow you to do?

options.text: Express an adverse opinion, because the combined effect could be so large that the financial statements do not give a true and fair view
options.misconception: converts an inability to form any opinion into a positive opinion that the statements are wrong
options.why: An adverse opinion is a conclusion, reached on sufficient appropriate audit evidence, that misstatements are both material and pervasive. Nothing here says the statements are misstated. The auditor's difficulty is that he cannot say whether they are.

options.text: Express an unmodified opinion with an emphasis of matter paragraph for each of the four matters, since each is properly disclosed and you have the evidence on each
options.misconception: answers the four uncertainties one at a time, which is exactly the reading the multiple-uncertainties provision exists to displace
options.why: Taken one at a time that would be right, and it is why the provision is worded around the interaction of the uncertainties rather than around any of them alone. Where the auditor concludes he cannot form an opinion because of what the combination might do, an unmodified opinion is not available whatever the individual paragraphs say. A widespread use of emphasis of matter paragraphs also diminishes the effectiveness of the communication.

options.text: Qualify the opinion, since each uncertainty on its own is material but not pervasive
options.misconception: adds the individual assessments together arithmetically, when the standard's concern is the interaction between them rather than their sum
options.why: The provision is not about accumulating four material items. It is about the potential interaction of the uncertainties and their possible cumulative effect, which is what makes the outcome unstateable rather than merely large.

options.text: Disclaim an opinion, on the footing that in extremely rare circumstances involving multiple uncertainties the auditor may conclude that, notwithstanding having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding each individual uncertainty, it is not possible to form an opinion because of the potential interaction of the uncertainties and their possible cumulative effect
options.why: There are two routes to a disclaimer and this is the second one. It does not depend on evidence being missing — the standard says notwithstanding having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding each of the individual uncertainties — but on the potential interaction of the uncertainties and their possible cumulative effect making it impossible to form an opinion. Four open matters whose outcomes change each other's meaning is the case it describes.
keywords: notwithstanding having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence

citation.ref: the requirement to disclaim an opinion when, in extremely rare circumstances involving multiple uncertainties, the auditor concludes that notwithstanding having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding each of the individual uncertainties it is not possible to form an opinion because of their potential interaction and possible cumulative effect

items.scenario: You are auditing a construction company for the year ended 31 March. Four things are open at once. A tax authority has raised a demand that the company is contesting, and its counsel puts the outcome at genuinely uncertain. A joint venture partner has begun arbitration seeking to unwind a contract that carries most of the order book, and the tribunal has not been constituted. The company's principal lender has served a notice of default and has not said whether it will call the loan. And a state government has issued a show cause notice that could cancel the licence for the company's largest project. You have obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about each of the four separately — the demand, the pleadings, the notice and the show cause notice are all on your file, and management's disclosures about each are complete and properly presented. What you cannot do is say what the four come to together: the outcome of any one of them changes what the others mean, and the combinations run from no effect at all to the company ceasing to exist.

items.stem: Which describes the two routes to a disclaimer correctly?

options.text: The second route is a disclaimer given where management has imposed a limitation on scope and withdrawal is not practicable
options.misconception: names a third situation that is really the first route reached by a particular path, and mistakes it for the multiple-uncertainties provision
options.why: That is the first route arrived at through a management-imposed limitation: the auditor is still unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and the possible effects could be both material and pervasive. Evidence is missing there, which is what separates it from the multiple-uncertainties case.
keywords: unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: The second route applies whenever there is more than one going concern indicator, so that two or more indicators together always give a disclaimer
options.misconception: turns a rare judgement into a counting rule, and attaches it to one topic the standard does not name
options.why: The provision is not tied to going concern and does not count anything. It applies in extremely rare circumstances, and only where the auditor concludes that the potential interaction of the uncertainties and their possible cumulative effect make it impossible to form an opinion.

options.text: Only one route exists. Every disclaimer follows from an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and a matter about which the auditor has evidence can never produce one
options.misconception: knows the common route and treats it as the only one, which leaves the multiple-uncertainties provision with nothing to do
options.why: If that were so the standard would not separately provide for the case where the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding each of the individual uncertainties and still cannot form an opinion. The provision exists and is worded to make exactly that point.

options.text: One route is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence where the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive; the other needs no missing evidence at all and rests on the auditor being unable to form an opinion because of the potential interaction of multiple uncertainties, in extremely rare circumstances
options.why: Both are in the standard. The first is the familiar one and sits on the second row of the matrix. The second is separate and expressly assumes the evidence was obtained regarding each of the individual uncertainties, the difficulty being their potential interaction and possible cumulative effect. The words extremely rare are the standard's own and mark it as the exception rather than an easier way out of a hard judgement.

citation.ref: the two circumstances in which the auditor shall disclaim an opinion — an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence where the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive, and extremely rare circumstances involving multiple uncertainties where notwithstanding sufficient appropriate audit evidence on each it is not possible to form an opinion

items.scenario: Two audit assistants are arguing about when a disclaimer of opinion may be given. One says a disclaimer always means the auditor did not get the evidence he needed. The other says he has read of a disclaimer where the auditor had all the evidence.

items.stem: What does the auditor do?

options.text: Modify the opinion, expressing it as "except for" the effects of the matter, and state the qualification independently in the report from the auditor's own standpoint, whatever the note says
options.why: The note is management's stand on the matter; the qualification is the auditor's record of his disagreement, and disclosure by management does not discharge him. Where notes of a qualificatory nature appear, all qualifications are stated independently in the report so that a reader can weigh them, and the report must state the matter from the auditor's standpoint and not from management's. The qualification is expressed in a clear and unambiguous manner as "except for" the effects of the matter to which it relates.

options.text: Give the opinion "subject to" the note, which records the disagreement while acknowledging that management has disclosed the facts
options.misconception: accepts a form of words the study material rules out precisely because it is not forceful enough to be read as a qualification
options.why: Phrases such as "subject to" and "with the foregoing explanation" are not sufficiently clear or forceful and are not appropriate in the opinion paragraph. A qualified opinion is expressed as "except for" the effects of the matter to which the qualification relates.

options.text: Leave the opinion unmodified and refer in the report to management's note, since a reference to a note of a qualificatory nature operates as a qualification
options.misconception: treats a cross-reference as doing the work of a qualification, which is the confusion the rule was written to stop
options.why: A reference to the notes to accounts in the auditor's report does not automatically become a qualification. It carries management's account of the matter into a report that is supposed to carry the auditor's.
keywords: does not automatically become a qualification

options.text: Leave the opinion unmodified and add an emphasis of matter paragraph drawing attention to the note, since the matter is now presented in the financial statements
options.misconception: uses an emphasis paragraph in place of a modification, which the standard forbids in terms
options.why: An emphasis of matter is for something appropriately presented and for which the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence. A misstatement management refuses to correct is not appropriately presented, and an emphasis of matter is not a substitute for a modification of the opinion.
keywords: not a substitute for a modification

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — the distinction between notes on accounts and qualifications, the requirement that a qualification be expressed as "except for" in a clear and unambiguous manner, and the rule that a reference to a note does not automatically become a qualification

items.scenario: You have concluded that a company's inventory is overstated because obsolete lines have not been written down. Management disagrees with you on the facts but agrees to add a note setting out its own assessment of the position and recording that the auditors take a different view. The note is full and fair as an account of management's position, and it names the amount in dispute. The finance director then asks you to leave the opinion unmodified, on the footing that a reader now has everything he needs, and offers as a compromise that your report may say the opinion is given "subject to" the note.

items.stem: What is wrong with the report as drafted?

options.text: Nothing, provided the notes referred to are complete and accurate; the report and the financial statements are read together and duplication helps nobody
options.misconception: relies on the completeness of management's notes to supply the auditor's own statement, which no note can do
options.why: Completeness is not the test. The note is management's stand on the matter and the report has to state the matter from the auditor's standpoint; a reference to the notes does not automatically become a qualification however good the notes are.
keywords: does not automatically become a qualification

options.text: The three matters belong in an emphasis of matter section, since they are already disclosed in the notes
options.misconception: moves qualificatory matters into a paragraph reserved for matters that require no modification
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter. The partner has already accepted that these three are qualificatory in nature, which puts them outside it.
keywords: would not be required to modify the opinion

options.text: Three qualifications have not been stated at all. Where notes of a qualificatory nature appear in the accounts, the auditor states all his qualifications independently in his report, from his own standpoint, so that the reader can assess their significance
options.why: A qualification exists only when the auditor makes it. Where notes of a qualificatory nature appear in the accounts, the auditor should state all qualifications independently in his report so that the user can assess the significance of these qualifications, and all qualifications should be contained in the auditor's report. Three sentences pointing at three notes leave the reader with management's account of three matters and the auditor's account of none.
keywords: state all qualifications independently in his report

options.text: The opinion should have been adverse, because four qualificatory matters together are always pervasive
options.misconception: converts a count of matters into a pervasiveness conclusion, which is a judgement about effects and not about number
options.why: Pervasiveness is judged on whether the effects are confined to specific elements, whether if so confined they represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements, or whether in relation to disclosures they are fundamental to users' understanding. How many matters there are does not answer any of those.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — the notes and report relationship, the requirement that all qualifications be stated independently in the auditor's report and be contained in it, and the rule that a reference to a note does not automatically become a qualification

items.scenario: A draft auditor's report on a company runs to four pages. The opinion paragraph is qualified "except for" one matter, which is described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section. Three further matters that the engagement partner accepts are qualificatory in nature have been dealt with by a single sentence at the end of the report reading that attention is drawn to notes 14, 19 and 23. The partner's reasoning is that the notes are complete, that repeating them would make the report unreadable, and that any reader who wants the detail can turn to the accounts.

items.stem: On what does the choice turn?

options.text: On whether the matter can be quantified. An unquantifiable matter cannot support a qualification and can only be emphasised
options.misconception: makes quantification the gate to a qualification, when the standard provides for a matter that cannot practicably be quantified
options.why: Where a misstatement relates to specific amounts the auditor describes and quantifies the financial effects unless it is impracticable, and where it is impracticable he says so in the Basis for Opinion section. Inability to quantify changes what the section says, not whether the opinion is modified.
keywords: not whether the opinion is modified

options.text: On whether management agrees to the paragraph. A matter fully disclosed by management and accepted as accurate by the auditor needs nothing further in the report
options.misconception: lets management's disclosure close a question the auditor is required to answer for himself
options.why: Client and auditor are separate parties and the auditor exercises his own professional judgement here. The whole point of the rule is that management's having disclosed the facts does not tell the auditor what his report should say.

options.text: On the auditor's own judgement about whether disclosure alone suffices — full disclosure by management does not settle it, and where an irregularity amounts to a breach of law the auditor brings it to the notice of the shareholders by properly qualifying his report
