options.why: The study material puts the judgement on the auditor. Management may insist that it has disclosed the full facts, but the auditor assesses whether the disclosure alone would suffice or whether he must also modify his report or add an emphasis of matter, and where the company has committed an irregularity resulting in a breach of law the auditor should bring it to the notice of the shareholders by properly qualifying his report.
keywords: whether the disclosure alone would suffice

options.text: On whether the breach affects the current year. A breach whose consequences fall in a later year is a matter for the next auditor
options.misconception: defers a matter to a later period on the basis of when its cost lands, rather than when the irregularity occurred
options.why: The irregularity was committed during the year under audit and the auditor knows of it. That is what he reports on, and postponing it leaves the shareholders of this year's accounts uninformed about this year's breach.

citation.ref: Ch. Reporting — the auditor's professional judgement on whether disclosure alone suffices, the rule that an emphasis of matter is not a substitute for modification of the opinion, and the direction that a breach of law be brought to the notice of the shareholders by properly qualifying the report

items.scenario: A company has breached a statutory requirement during the year. The breach is not itself a misstatement of any amount, and the directors have disclosed it fully in a note that describes what happened, what it may cost and what the company has done since. The auditor is satisfied the note is accurate and has the evidence to support every sentence in it. He is deciding what, if anything, his report should say.

items.stem: What does SA 705 (Revised) require, and what has been missed?

options.text: Nothing has been missed. The standard requires the auditor to inform those charged with governance that the opinion will be modified, which the note to the audit committee chair did
options.misconception: stops at the fact of the modification, which is the half of the requirement that was met, and drops the wording
options.why: The requirement names two things and the wording of the modification is the second. A board told only that there will be a qualification, and first seeing the sentence in the signed report, has not been given what the standard asks for.

options.text: Where the auditor expects to modify the opinion he communicates to those charged with governance both the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification — so the wording should have gone to the audit committee before the report was signed, and telling the chief financial officer is not telling those charged with governance
options.why: The requirement has two halves and only one of them was met. The auditor communicates the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification, and he is required to discuss and deliberate the audit findings and the type of misstatements with those charged with governance. Management is not those charged with governance, and a one-line note that a qualification is coming is not the wording of the modification.
keywords: the circumstances that led to the expected modification
Management is not those charged with governance

options.text: Nothing has been missed, because the communication was made to the chief financial officer, who is the officer responsible for the financial statements and will brief the board
options.misconception: substitutes a communication to management for one to those charged with governance, and relies on management to relay it
options.why: Communicating with management is a different requirement with a different purpose. The obligation here runs to those charged with governance, and it is not discharged by telling the person whose accounting the modification is about.

options.text: The communication should have waited until the report was signed, because sharing draft wording before signature exposes the auditor to pressure to change it
options.misconception: postpones a communication whose whole purpose is to happen while the matter can still be discussed
options.why: The trigger is the expectation of a modification, not the signature. The communication is made so that the circumstances can be discussed and deliberated with those charged with governance while something can still be done about them.

citation.ref: the requirement that when the auditor expects to modify the opinion he shall communicate with those charged with governance the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification, read with SA 260 (Revised) para 16

items.scenario: Ten days before the board meeting at which a company's accounts are to be approved, you decide that you will have to qualify your opinion over a revenue cut-off matter. You email the chief financial officer setting out the matter and the amount. On the morning of the board meeting you send the audit committee chair a one-line note saying that the report will carry a qualification. The drafted wording of the qualification is not shared with anybody outside the firm until the signed report is tabled.

items.stem: What effect does that have on the opinion?

options.text: The disagreement is itself reported, and the opinion becomes a disclaimer because the auditor and those charged with governance cannot agree on the facts
options.misconception: turns a disagreement about the accounting into an inability to obtain evidence, which is a different row of the matrix
options.why: A disclaimer is for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, or for extremely rare interacting uncertainties. A disagreement about whether an amount is misstated, where the auditor has the evidence, gives a qualified or an adverse opinion depending on pervasiveness.
keywords: an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: The auditor must reconsider and, if the committee's view is reasonable, express an unmodified opinion, since those charged with governance are the body the standard requires him to satisfy
options.misconception: reads a communication duty as a duty to be satisfied by the recipient, which would put the opinion in the hands of the audited
options.why: Nothing in the requirement makes the modification conditional on the committee. An auditor who could be talked out of a modification by the body he reports to would not be expressing an independent opinion at all.

options.text: None. The communication is a requirement about telling and deliberating, not about obtaining agreement, and the opinion continues to follow from the auditor's own conclusion on the audit evidence
options.why: The requirement is that the auditor communicate the circumstances and the wording and discuss and deliberate the findings with those charged with governance. It is not a requirement to obtain their agreement, and their disagreement does not enter the decision. The opinion is modified when the auditor concludes that the financial statements as a whole are not free from material misstatement or that he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence.
keywords: not a requirement to obtain their agreement

options.text: The auditor may treat the communication requirement as met and issue the report without the modification, provided he records the committee's resolution in his working papers
options.misconception: lets documentation of the disagreement stand in for the modification the evidence requires
options.why: Documenting a disagreement records what happened; it does not change what the report must say. The modification follows from the auditor's conclusion on the audit evidence, and a minute cannot displace it.

citation.ref: the requirement to communicate with those charged with governance the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the wording of the modification, read with the circumstances in which a modification is required — a conclusion that the financial statements as a whole are not free from material misstatement, or an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

items.scenario: An audit committee receives the auditor's communication of an expected adverse opinion, together with the proposed wording. It discusses the matter over two meetings, disagrees with the auditor's view, records its disagreement in the minutes, and resolves that in its judgement the financial statements are correct as drawn. It then writes to the auditor stating that, having considered the matter, it does not accept the modification and asking him to proceed on the basis that the communication requirement has been complied with and the outcome settled.

items.stem: Which of the four may be dealt with by an emphasis of matter paragraph?

options.text: Only the fire, because a subsequent event is the one circumstance the standard names for an emphasis of matter
options.misconception: keeps one item off the illustrative list and treats it as the whole of it
options.why: A significant subsequent event is one of four named circumstances, alongside an uncertainty about the outcome of exceptional litigation or regulatory action, early application of a new accounting standard, and a major catastrophe. The list is illustrative rather than exhaustive in either direction.

options.text: All four, since each is important enough that a reader would want to know about it
options.misconception: reads the paragraph as a place for anything important, dropping the requirement that the matter be in the financial statements
options.why: Importance is only half the test. The paragraph refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements, and shall refer only to information presented or disclosed in them. The state of the internal audit function is not disclosed there and so cannot be emphasised, whatever a reader might want.
keywords: appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements

options.text: Only the regulatory proceedings, since the other three are matters of accounting and an emphasis of matter deals with uncertainties alone
options.misconception: narrows the paragraph to uncertainty, when the list includes early application of a standard and a catastrophe, neither of which is an uncertainty
options.why: Early application of a new accounting standard is not an uncertainty and neither is a catastrophe that has already happened. Both are on the list because they are fundamental to users' understanding of statements that are correctly prepared.

options.text: The regulatory proceedings, the fire and the early application of the new standard — each is presented or disclosed in the financial statements and each is on the standard's own list of circumstances; the vacancy in internal audit is not in the financial statements at all
options.why: The illustrative circumstances include an uncertainty relating to the future outcome of exceptional litigation or regulatory action, a significant subsequent event occurring between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report, and early application where permitted of a new accounting standard having a material effect. All three are disclosed in the statements, which an emphasis of matter paragraph requires, since it shall refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements. The internal audit vacancy is nowhere in them.
keywords: refer only to information presented or disclosed

citation.ref: the illustrative circumstances in which the auditor may consider it necessary to include an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, read with para 9 requiring the paragraph to refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements

items.scenario: You are completing the audit of a company that makes industrial chemicals, for the year ended 31 March. Four things sit in your completion file. First, a competition regulator opened proceedings against the company in January that could, on counsel's view, end in a penalty of an amount the company cannot presently estimate; the outcome is genuinely uncertain and note 31 describes the proceedings, the possible range and the uncertainty in full, which you accept. Second, in May, after the balance sheet date and three weeks before you sign, a fire destroyed the company's second-largest plant; the directors have treated it as a non-adjusting event and note 42 sets out the carrying amount lost and the insurance position, which you have tested and accept. Third, the company has applied a new accounting standard a year before it is mandatory, which the standard permits, and the effect on the year's figures is material and is disclosed. Fourth, the company's internal audit function was without a head for eight months of the year; you extended your own procedures and are satisfied, and nothing about it appears in the financial statements. Your opinion will be unmodified, and SA 701 does not apply to this company.

items.stem: Who is right, and why?

options.text: The senior, unless the loss is material, in which case the opinion is qualified for the uncertainty about the insurance recovery
options.misconception: converts a properly accounted uncertainty into a qualification, when the accounting has been accepted
options.why: The recovery has been recognised only to the extent virtually certain and the auditor accepts the treatment, so there is no misstatement to qualify. Materiality decides whether the matter is fundamental to users' understanding, not whether the opinion is modified.

options.text: The partner, but the paragraph must be an other matter paragraph, because the cyclone is an event outside the accounting records
options.misconception: picks the vehicle from where the event happened rather than from whether the matter is presented or disclosed in the financial statements
options.why: An other matter paragraph refers to a matter other than those presented or disclosed in the financial statements. This one is disclosed in note 18, so it takes an emphasis of matter paragraph.
keywords: other than those presented or disclosed

options.text: The partner. A major catastrophe that has had, or continues to have, a significant effect on the entity's financial position is one of the named circumstances, and the paragraph exists precisely for a matter that is correctly accounted for and disclosed
options.why: Correct accounting is the precondition, not the objection. An emphasis of matter refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is fundamental to users' understanding, and the standard names a major catastrophe that has had, or continues to have, a significant effect on the entity's financial position as one of the circumstances in which the auditor may consider such a paragraph necessary.

options.text: The senior. Where a matter is recognised and disclosed there is no gap in the financial statements, so there is nothing an additional paragraph can add
options.misconception: treats the paragraph as a remedy for a defect, when it exists only where there is no defect
options.why: A gap in the financial statements would be a misstatement, which calls for a modification and rules an emphasis of matter out altogether. The paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter.
keywords: would not be required to modify the opinion

citation.ref: the illustrative circumstances in which the auditor may consider an Emphasis of Matter paragraph necessary, including a major catastrophe that has had or continues to have a significant effect on the entity's financial position, read with para 8(a)

items.scenario: A cyclone destroyed a company's coastal warehouse and most of the stock in it two months before the year end. The loss is recognised, the insurance recovery is recognised only to the extent virtually certain, and note 18 describes the event, the assets lost, the recovery expected and the continuing effect on the company's distribution while a replacement is built. You are satisfied with all of it and your opinion will be unmodified. The engagement partner wants an emphasis of matter paragraph. The audit senior objects that since the loss is already recognised in the numbers and fully disclosed, there is by definition nothing left to emphasise.

items.stem: May the report carry both?

options.text: Yes, provided the emphasis of matter paragraph cross-refers to the Key Audit Matters section so that a reader is not misled into thinking there are two matters
options.misconception: solves a presentation problem the standard did not raise, and leaves untouched the proviso that actually forbids the paragraph
options.why: The bar is not about confusing the reader. It is a condition on including the paragraph at all, and no cross-reference satisfies a condition that the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter.
keywords: a condition on including the paragraph
has not been determined to be a key audit matter

options.text: No, and the matter should be moved out of the Key Audit Matters section into an emphasis of matter paragraph, which speaks to users rather than to the auditor's own workload
options.misconception: reverses the priority, discarding a required key audit matter description in favour of an optional paragraph
options.why: Where SA 701 applies, the use of emphasis of matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of the individual key audit matters. A matter determined to be a key audit matter is described in that section, and the emphasis of matter paragraph is what gives way.
keywords: not a substitute for a description of the individual key audit matters

options.text: No. An emphasis of matter paragraph is available only where, when SA 701 applies, the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter — so where it has, the auditor may instead give it prominence within the Key Audit Matters section, for example by placing it first or by adding to its description
options.why: The second gate closes it. The auditor includes an emphasis of matter paragraph provided that, when SA 701 applies, the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter to be communicated in the auditor's report. Where a key audit matter is also fundamental to users' understanding, the way to signal that is to present it more prominently than the other matters in that section, for instance as the first matter, or to include additional information in the description of it.
keywords: has not been determined to be a key audit matter

options.text: Yes. The two paragraphs answer different questions — one about the audit and one about the reader — so a matter that is both may properly appear twice
options.misconception: reasons from the difference between the two tests to a conclusion the standard closes with an express proviso
options.why: The tests are indeed different, which is why a matter can be one without being the other. But the standard resolves the overlap itself with a proviso, and the proviso bars the emphasis of matter paragraph once the matter has been determined to be a key audit matter.
keywords: bars the emphasis of matter paragraph

citation.ref: para 8(b) barring an Emphasis of Matter paragraph where SA 701 applies and the matter has been determined to be a key audit matter, read with the guidance that a key audit matter which is also fundamental to users' understanding may be presented more prominently in the Key Audit Matters section or carry additional information in its description

items.scenario: A listed company discloses in note 9 an uncertainty about the future outcome of a tax proceeding that could cost it a material sum. You have obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the disclosure and accept it. SA 701 applies. You communicated the matter to the audit committee and, on your professional judgement, it was one of the matters of most significance in this year's audit — you assigned your most experienced manager to it and it took four weeks. You have determined it to be a key audit matter and described it in the Key Audit Matters section. Your manager now proposes to add an emphasis of matter paragraph as well, pointing to note 9, on the ground that the matter is both significant to the audit and fundamental to a reader.

items.stem: Which paragraph does this call for, and what does it say?

options.text: An emphasis of matter paragraph, since the branch balances are in the financial statements and the reader's attention is being drawn to them
options.misconception: picks the vehicle from where the amounts sit rather than from what the paragraph is actually about
options.why: The branch amounts are in the statements but the matter being communicated is not. What is being said is who audited what, which is about the audit and the auditor's responsibilities. An emphasis of matter paragraph shall refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements.
keywords: the matter being communicated is not
refer only to information presented or disclosed

options.text: An other matter paragraph, but only if the branch auditors give their consent to being named
options.misconception: invents a consent condition and leaves out the two provisos the standard actually imposes
options.why: The standard's conditions are that the paragraph is not prohibited by law or regulation and that, when SA 701 applies, the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter. Consent from another auditor is not among them.
keywords: not prohibited by law or regulation
not been determined to be a key audit matter

options.text: An other matter paragraph in a separate section headed "Other Matter", naming the branches, the total assets and revenue they account for, that their financial statements were audited by the branch auditors whose reports have been furnished to you, and that your opinion so far as it relates to the amounts and disclosures included in respect of them is based solely on those reports
options.why: The division of responsibility between the principal auditor and the branch auditors is not a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements. It is relevant to users' understanding of the audit and of the auditor's responsibilities, which is what an other matter paragraph is for, and it goes in a separate section with the heading "Other Matter". ICAI's illustration of that paragraph names the branches, gives the total assets and revenue, records that the reports have been furnished, and states that the opinion so far as it relates to those amounts and disclosures is based solely on the branch auditors' reports.
keywords: not a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements
based solely on the branch auditors' reports

options.text: Neither. Reliance on branch auditors is dealt with under the reporting section for other legal and regulatory requirements, so no paragraph under SA 706 arises
options.misconception: assumes a statutory statement about branch returns displaces the standard's own paragraph, when the two co-exist and answer to different readers
options.why: The Companies Act separately asks the auditor to state whether proper returns adequate for his audit were received from branches not visited by him and how he dealt with a branch auditor's report. That statutory statement does not remove the auditor's judgement under SA 706 that users need to know his opinion on those amounts rests solely on another firm's work.
keywords: separately asks the auditor to state
does not remove the auditor's judgement

citation.ref: para 10 on the Other Matter paragraph and its two provisos, with the requirement to include it in a separate section under the heading "Other Matter", read with the illustration of an Other Matter paragraph on branch financial statements audited by branch auditors in Ch. Reporting

items.scenario: A company's standalone financial statements include the returns of five branches whose financial statements were audited by other chartered accountants. Those branches account for a large part of the company's total assets and revenue, their reports have been furnished to you, and you have dealt with them in preparing your report. Your opinion is unmodified. You want the reader to know how far your own work went. SA 701 applies to this company and you have not determined the branch position to be a key audit matter, and nothing in any law or regulation prevents you saying so.

items.stem: What does SA 706 (Revised) allow?

options.text: An emphasis of matter paragraph instead, since the emphasis of matter route is not subject to the prohibition proviso
options.misconception: swaps one paragraph for the other to escape a proviso, when the two are chosen by subject matter and not by convenience
options.why: The choice between them is decided by whether the matter is presented or disclosed in the financial statements. This one is not, so an emphasis of matter paragraph is unavailable, and the paragraph shall refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements.
keywords: presented or disclosed in the financial statements
refer only to information presented or disclosed

options.text: No other matter paragraph. The paragraph is available only where communicating the matter is not prohibited by law or regulation, and that proviso has no equivalent on the emphasis of matter side
options.why: The other matter paragraph carries two provisos and the first is that this is not prohibited by law or regulation. Where a statute forbids the auditor from publishing the information, the condition fails and the paragraph cannot be included however relevant the auditor thinks it is. The emphasis of matter paragraph carries no such proviso, because by definition it repeats only what the financial statements already say.
keywords: not prohibited by law or regulation

options.text: An other matter paragraph, because relevance to users' understanding of the audit is the test and the auditor has applied it
options.misconception: applies the subject-matter test and stops there, missing the two conditions that sit on top of it
options.why: Relevance to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the auditor's report is what the paragraph is about, but the standard then attaches conditions. Failing one of them ends the matter whatever the auditor's judgement on relevance.

options.text: A modified opinion, since the auditor is prevented by law from telling the reader something material about his audit
options.misconception: turns a restriction on what may be published into a limitation on the audit itself
options.why: Nothing has limited the audit. The auditor obtained the evidence and reached his conclusion; what is restricted is publication of one piece of information. A modification requires a material misstatement or an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and neither is present.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

citation.ref: para 10 on the Other Matter paragraph and the proviso that its inclusion is not prohibited by law or regulation, read with para 9 requiring an Emphasis of Matter paragraph to refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements

items.scenario: You are the auditor of an entity in a regulated sector. During the audit you learn something about the entity's dealings with its regulator that you consider genuinely relevant to a reader's understanding of the scope of your audit. It is not presented or disclosed in the financial statements. The sectoral statute contains a provision that forbids an auditor from publishing information of that description in any report. Your view is that a reader who does not know it will misjudge how far your work reached.

items.stem: How do the four divide?

options.text: The pending appeal and the incomplete note both take an emphasis of matter paragraph, since both concern matters disclosed in the financial statements; the other two take an other matter paragraph
options.misconception: applies the subject-matter test alone and skips the first proviso, which asks whether the matter forces a modification
options.why: Being disclosed is necessary but not sufficient. The paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter, and a note the auditor considers materially incomplete, which management will not correct, is a material misstatement.

options.text: The pending appeal takes an emphasis of matter paragraph; the predecessor auditor and the restriction on use both take an other matter paragraph; and the incomplete related party note takes none of them, because it requires a modification of the opinion
options.why: The dividing line is the subject matter. An emphasis of matter refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements; an other matter refers to a matter other than those, relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the auditor's report. Who audited last year and how the report may be used are both about the audit and the report. And an emphasis of matter paragraph is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter, which an uncorrected material misstatement rules out.
keywords: The dividing line is the subject matter
relevant to users' understanding of the audit
would not be required to modify the opinion

options.text: All four take an other matter paragraph, since none of them changes the opinion and the other matter paragraph is the general purpose vehicle for additional communication
options.misconception: treats one of the two paragraphs as a catch-all, and assumes an uncorrected misstatement leaves the opinion alone
options.why: They are not interchangeable and neither is general purpose; each is defined by whether the matter is presented or disclosed in the financial statements. And the incomplete related party note does change the opinion, because a material misstatement management will not correct requires a modification.

options.text: The predecessor auditor is dealt with under SA 710 and needs no paragraph; the restriction on use goes in an emphasis of matter paragraph; the appeal takes an other matter paragraph
options.misconception: reverses the two paragraphs and treats a matter outside the financial statements as one that may be emphasised
options.why: A restriction on the use of the report is not in the financial statements, so it cannot be emphasised — the paragraph shall refer only to information presented or disclosed in them. The appeal is in note 12 and so cannot take an other matter paragraph, which is for matters other than those presented or disclosed.
keywords: refer only to information presented or disclosed
other than those presented or disclosed

citation.ref: para 8 and para 10 on the subject matter of the two paragraphs and their provisos, read with para 9 requiring an Emphasis of Matter paragraph to refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements

items.scenario: Two trainees are preparing a report and have four matters to place. The company's disclosure of a pending appeal, which is in note 12 and which the auditor accepts. The fact that the prior year's financial statements were audited by another firm, which is nowhere in the financial statements. A restriction the auditor wishes to record on the use of his report, which is also nowhere in the financial statements. And a note on a related party transaction that the auditor considers materially incomplete and which management will not expand.

items.stem: How should it be reported?

options.text: In an other matter paragraph, since the auditor is commenting on the significance of the event rather than on its accounting
options.misconception: chooses the paragraph by what the auditor is doing rather than by whether the matter is in the financial statements
options.why: An other matter paragraph refers to a matter other than those presented or disclosed in the financial statements. This one is disclosed in note 40, so the emphasis of matter paragraph is the right vehicle whatever the auditor's purpose in raising it.
keywords: other than those presented or disclosed

options.text: In the Key Audit Matters section, because a matter this important to a reader must have been of most significance in the audit whether or not it took long
options.misconception: reads significance to the audit off importance to the reader, when the two tests are separate and can diverge
options.why: Key audit matters are those that in the auditor's professional judgement were of most significance in the audit of the financial statements, selected from matters communicated with those charged with governance. An event that was verified in a day by reading one agreement did not require significant auditor attention, however large it is.
keywords: of most significance in the audit
did not require significant auditor attention

options.text: Nowhere in the report. The event is disclosed in note 40 and the auditor has accepted the disclosure, so the report has nothing left to add
options.misconception: assumes adequate disclosure exhausts the report, which would leave the emphasis of matter paragraph with no purpose at all
options.why: Adequate disclosure is the condition for an emphasis of matter paragraph, not a reason against one. The paragraph exists to draw users' attention to a matter that is appropriately presented or disclosed and is of such importance that it is fundamental to their understanding.
keywords: the condition for an emphasis of matter paragraph

options.text: In an emphasis of matter paragraph. A matter may be fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements without having required significant auditor attention, and a matter not determined to be a key audit matter for that reason is exactly what the emphasis of matter paragraph is for
options.why: The two tests measure different things. A key audit matter is one that was of most significance in the audit — it is about what required significant auditor attention. An emphasis of matter is about a matter appropriately presented or disclosed that is fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements. A subsequent event of this size is the standard's own example of a matter that can be the second without being the first.

citation.ref: the relationship between Emphasis of Matter paragraphs and key audit matters — that a matter not determined to be a key audit matter because it did not require significant auditor attention may nonetheless be fundamental to users' understanding and be included in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph — read with para 8(a) and para 8(b)

items.scenario: A listed company to which SA 701 applies signed an agreement in April, after the balance sheet date and before the auditor's report, to sell the division that produces two-thirds of its revenue. The directors treat it as a non-adjusting event and disclose it in note 40, which sets out the terms and the expected effect. The auditor's work on it was straightforward: he read the agreement, checked the disclosure against it and was satisfied within a day. It did not require significant auditor attention and he has not determined it to be a key audit matter. He is nonetheless of the view that a reader who missed note 40 would misunderstand the company entirely.

items.stem: What is wrong with the proposal, and what should he do instead?

options.text: He should remove the loan from the Key Audit Matters section so that the emphasis of matter paragraph becomes available, since that paragraph speaks more directly to a reader
options.misconception: engineers the determination backwards from the paragraph he wants, when the determination is made on significance to the audit
options.why: Whether a matter is a key audit matter is a judgement about what was of most significance in the audit, made from the matters communicated with those charged with governance. It is not adjusted to unlock a reporting paragraph, and dropping a genuine key audit matter would leave the section incomplete.
keywords: of most significance in the audit

options.text: He should add an other matter paragraph rather than an emphasis of matter paragraph, since the restriction applies only to the latter
options.misconception: escapes one paragraph's proviso by choosing the other, ignoring that the same key audit matter proviso sits on both
options.why: Both paragraphs carry the key audit matter proviso: an other matter paragraph is included provided that, when SA 701 applies, the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter. And the recoverability of the loan is disclosed in the financial statements, which puts it outside the other matter paragraph in any event.
keywords: Both paragraphs carry the key audit matter proviso

options.text: Where SA 701 applies, the use of emphasis of matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of the individual key audit matters, and a matter determined to be a key audit matter cannot take an emphasis of matter paragraph at all; he should instead present it more prominently within the section, for example as the first matter, or include additional information in its description
options.why: Two rules bite. The emphasis of matter paragraph is barred because, where SA 701 applies, the matter has been determined to be a key audit matter. And the standard says in terms that the use of emphasis of matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of individual key audit matters. The way to signal relative importance is to present the matter more prominently than the others in the Key Audit Matters section, for instance as the first matter, or to include additional information in the description of it.
keywords: not a substitute for a description of individual key audit matters

options.text: Nothing is wrong. The section and the paragraph do different jobs, so a matter that is both significant to the audit and fundamental to the reader may properly carry both
options.misconception: treats the two as independent when the standard has expressly made the emphasis of matter paragraph unavailable once a matter is a key audit matter
options.why: The proviso decides it. An emphasis of matter paragraph may be included provided that, when SA 701 applies, the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter. Here it has, so the paragraph is not available whatever job it would have done.
keywords: has not been determined to be a key audit matter

citation.ref: para 8(b) and para 10 on the key audit matter proviso attaching to both paragraphs, read with the guidance that the use of Emphasis of Matter paragraphs is not a substitute for a description of individual key audit matters and that a key audit matter which is also fundamental to users' understanding may be presented more prominently or carry additional information in its description

items.scenario: An engagement partner on a listed company has determined four key audit matters and described each of them in the Key Audit Matters section. He considers one of the four — the recoverability of a large loan to a joint venture — to be not only the most demanding part of the audit but also fundamental to a reader's understanding of the financial statements. Rather than describe it at length, he proposes to keep all four descriptions short and equal and to add an emphasis of matter paragraph after the section, drawing attention to the loan.

items.stem: Which of the four go in an emphasis of matter paragraph and which in an other matter paragraph?

options.text: None of them. An unmodified opinion with no key audit matters section carries no additional paragraphs at all
options.misconception: ties the two paragraphs to a modified opinion or to SA 701, when both exist precisely for reports that are otherwise clean
options.why: Both paragraphs are for reports where the opinion is not modified. An emphasis of matter is available only where the auditor would not be required to modify the opinion as a result of the matter, and it states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter emphasised.
keywords: would not be required to modify the opinion
the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter

options.text: The early adoption and the fire may take an emphasis of matter paragraph; the position on the predecessor's working papers may take an other matter paragraph; the cured covenant breach takes neither
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements, which the early adoption in note 22 and the fire in note 35 both are. An other matter paragraph refers to a matter not so disclosed but relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the auditor's report, which is what the predecessor's papers are. The cured covenant breach is neither disclosed in the statements nor about the audit, and no disclosure is required, so nothing in the report attaches to it.
keywords: presented or disclosed in the financial statements
relevant to users' understanding of the audit
nothing in the report attaches to it

options.text: The early adoption takes an emphasis of matter paragraph and the other three take an other matter paragraph, since the fire, the predecessor and the covenant are all matters of fact rather than of accounting policy
options.misconception: sorts the matters by whether they concern policy, which is not the distinction the standard draws
options.why: The standard does not divide matters into policy and fact. It divides them by whether they are presented or disclosed in the financial statements. The fire is disclosed in note 35 and so cannot take an other matter paragraph.
keywords: does not divide matters into policy and fact

options.text: All four may take an emphasis of matter paragraph, since the auditor considers each of them worth a reader's attention
options.misconception: makes the auditor's interest the test, when the test is whether the matter is presented or disclosed in the financial statements
options.why: The paragraph shall refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements. Two of these four are not in the statements at all, so no emphasis of matter paragraph can reach them however much attention they deserve.
keywords: refer only to information presented or disclosed
not in the statements at all

citation.ref: para 8 and para 10 on the two paragraphs and the matters each may carry, read with para 9 requiring an Emphasis of Matter paragraph to refer only to information presented or disclosed in the financial statements and to state that the opinion is not modified

items.scenario: You are signing the report of a manufacturing company for the year ended 31 March. Your opinion is unmodified and SA 701 does not apply. Four things remain to be placed. The company's note 22 discloses that it has adopted a new revenue accounting policy a year early, as the standard permits, and quantifies the effect. Your own audit of the opening balances was constrained because the prior year was audited by a firm that has since been wound up and whose working papers you could not obtain; you performed alternative procedures and are satisfied, and nothing about this appears in the financial statements. Note 35 describes a fire at a leased godown in February and the loss recognised. And a covenant on the company's term loan was breached during the year and cured before the year end, which the company has not disclosed anywhere because nothing was outstanding at the year end and you agree no disclosure is required.

items.stem: What does SA 706 (Revised) say about the practice?

options.text: It is right. Since the paragraph states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter, adding one can never mislead a reader and the only cost is length
options.misconception: assumes the disclaimer inside the paragraph removes every consequence of using it, which is the assumption the standard's warning contradicts
options.why: The sentence that the opinion is not modified protects the opinion, not the communication. Nine paragraphs that each say a matter is fundamental to users' understanding tell the reader that none of them is, which is what the standard means by diminishing effectiveness.
keywords: protects the opinion, not the communication

options.text: It is wrong, and the fix is to put the same matters in other matter paragraphs instead, which carry no such warning
options.misconception: moves matters between the two paragraphs to avoid a warning, when the choice is fixed by whether the matter is in the financial statements
options.why: The paragraphs are not interchangeable. An other matter paragraph refers to a matter other than those presented or disclosed in the financial statements, so a matter that is disclosed there cannot be moved into one.
keywords: other than those presented or disclosed

options.text: It is not a safe addition. A widespread use of emphasis of matter paragraphs diminishes the effectiveness of the auditor's communication about such matters, and each paragraph is available only where both gates are passed — no modification required as a result of the matter, and, where SA 701 applies, the matter not determined to be a key audit matter
options.why: The standard warns against the practice in terms: a widespread use of emphasis of matter paragraphs diminishes the effectiveness of the auditor's communication about such matters. And the paragraph is not freely available. The auditor includes one provided he would not be required to modify the opinion in accordance with SA 705 (Revised) as a result of the matter, and provided that, when SA 701 applies, the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter.
keywords: would not be required to modify the opinion
has not been determined to be a key audit matter

options.text: It is wrong, because an emphasis of matter paragraph may be included only where another Standard on Auditing expressly requires one
options.misconception: turns a warning against overuse into a rule that there is no discretion at all, which would delete the auditor's own judgement from the standard
options.why: The auditor's judgement is the trigger. He includes the paragraph if he considers it necessary to draw users' attention to a matter that in his judgement is of such importance that it is fundamental to users' understanding, subject to the two provisos. Other standards do require such paragraphs in particular cases, but they are not the only route.
keywords: The auditor's judgement is the trigger

citation.ref: para 8(a) and para 8(b) on the two provisos, read with para 9 and with the caution that a widespread use of Emphasis of Matter paragraphs diminishes the effectiveness of the auditor's communication about such matters

items.scenario: A firm's reporting manual tells staff that an emphasis of matter paragraph is a safe addition to any report because it changes nothing, and encourages its use whenever an audit team has been worried about something. On one report last year the team added nine of them. The engagement quality reviewer on this year's audit asks whether that is right.

items.stem: What should the firm do about the three?

options.text: Answer the statutory audit tender but quote a fee the firm can justify against the size and manpower of the assignment, and leave the other two alone as work outside a chartered accountant's field
options.misconception: treats the bidder's own quoted fee as the prescribed minimum fee, and reads the reserved areas as the limit of what a member may pursue
options.why: Both halves are the wrong way round. The exception asks who set the floor: a minimum fee for this purpose is prescribed in the tender document itself and must commensurate with the size, value, volume, manpower requirement and nature of the work, so a figure the bidder chose is the very thing the guideline exists to control. And the restriction bites inside the reserved areas, which means it leaves the non-exclusive areas open — the module's own illustration of a permitted response is a firm bidding to computerise land revenue records.

options.text: Answer the grievance portal tender and the company's enquiry, and leave the statutory audit tender alone — the Council's guideline bars a response in an area exclusively reserved for chartered accountants unless the tender document itself prescribes a minimum fee or the area is open to other professionals
options.why: The proviso permits a response to tenders and enquiries, and Council Guidelines No. 1-CA(7)/03/2016 dated 7th April 2016 then carve the reserved areas back out of it: a member in practice shall not respond to any tender issued by an organisation or user of professional services in areas of services which are exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, such as audit and attestation services. The restriction lifts in two situations and only two — where the minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document itself, and where the area is open to other professionals along with chartered accountants. Statutory audit is the reserved area and this document prescribes no minimum fee, so neither escape is open. The grievance portal is not audit or attestation and is open to other professionals, so the guideline never engages. The company's letter is an enquiry rather than a tender, and answering an enquiry is inside the proviso.
keywords: minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document

options.text: Answer all three, since the proviso permits a member to respond to tenders and enquiries issued by users of professional services and to secure work as a consequence
options.misconception: reads the proviso on its own and stops before the Council guideline that narrows it for the reserved areas
options.why: The proviso is where the analysis starts and not where it ends. The Council issued a guideline under the same clause that bars a response in areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, and audit is the example the guideline itself gives. A member who quotes only the proviso is answering the position as it stood before 2016.

options.text: Answer none of them, because bidding for work advertises the firm's services and the clause that governs an advertisement is Clause (7)
options.misconception: files a solicitation question under the advertising clause, which polices attainments and designations rather than the pursuit of work
options.why: Clause (7) is about advertising professional attainments or services and about using a designation other than chartered accountant on professional documents, cards and sign boards. Nothing here concerns what the firm called itself or what it claimed about its record. The pursuit of work is squarely the soliciting limb, and it is Clause (6) that decides it — including the two provisos that let two of these three be answered.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6), second proviso, read with Council Guidelines No. 1-CA(7)/03/2016 dated 7th April 2016 — a member in practice shall not respond to a tender in areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants such as audit and attestation services, the restriction being inapplicable where the minimum fee of the assignment is prescribed in the tender document itself or where the area is open to other professionals

items.scenario: A four-partner firm is deciding what to do about three invitations that reached it in the same week. A State Government undertaking has floated a tender inviting firms of chartered accountants to bid for its statutory audit; the tender document sets out the scope, the branches to be visited and the timetable, and says nothing whatever about what the assignment will pay, each bidder being asked to quote its own fee. A municipal corporation has floated a second tender, for the design and running of a citizens' grievance portal, open to software houses, management consultancies and firms of chartered accountants alike. And a manufacturing company the firm has never acted for has written asking what the firm would charge to carry out an internal audit of its two plants. The managing partner's view is that all three may be answered, because the clause carries a proviso permitting a member to respond to tenders and enquiries issued by users of professional services and to secure professional work as a consequence.

items.stem: How should the firm proceed?

options.text: Proceed as planned on all three — the area is not exclusive to chartered accountants so the firm may respond, a reasonable earnest money deposit is not interfered with, and the costing paper is the cost sheet the Council asks a responding member to maintain so that the Institute may call for it
options.why: Computerisation of land revenue records is not audit or attestation and is open to other professionals, so the guideline's restriction never engages and the second proviso to Clause (6) does the work on its own. On the deposit, the Council's view is that interference with the prevailing practice of requiring an earnest money or security deposit is not required, though on a complaint or instance of an exorbitant deposit the Ethical Standards Board may look into the matter case by case. And the guideline asks a member responding to a tender to maintain a cost sheet incorporating details of the costs being incurred, having regard to the number of persons involved and the hours to be spent, so that the same may be called for by the Institute for perusal — the senior partner's second worry is the opposite of the rule.

options.text: Proceed with the bid and the cost sheet but withdraw the ₹50,000, a member being barred from putting his own money at risk to obtain professional work
options.misconception: invents a bar on deposits, when the Council expressly declined to interfere with the practice and reserved only the exorbitant case to the Ethical Standards Board
options.why: There is no such bar. The Council considered exactly this and said that interference with the practices prevailing for the requirement of an earnest money or security deposit is not required. What it kept for itself is the outlier: on a complaint or instance of an exorbitant deposit the Ethical Standards Board may look at it case by case. A deposit the tender demands of every bidder alike is not that.

options.text: Proceed with the bid and the deposit but destroy the costing paper, since a document recording what the firm will charge and why is client information the Institute has no business seeing
options.misconception: treats a costing paper about the firm's own effort as client information, when the guideline requires it precisely so that the Institute may call for it
options.why: The cost sheet records the firm's own inputs — persons involved and hours to be spent — and nothing about a client, who at that stage does not exist. The Council asks that it be maintained so that the same may be called for by the Institute for perusal, which is the opposite of a document that must be destroyed.

options.text: Withdraw from the tender altogether, a chartered accountant in practice being confined to work that only a chartered accountant may do
options.misconception: reads the reserved areas as the limit of what a member may pursue, when the restriction runs the other way and bites only inside them
options.why: The guideline restricts a response inside the exclusively reserved areas, which means it leaves the non-exclusive areas open. The module's own illustration is this exact assignment: computerisation of land revenue records does not fall within the exclusive areas, so the firm may respond and may pay the deposit.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) read with Council Guidelines No. 1-CA(7)/03/2016 dated 7th April 2016 — the restriction confined to areas exclusively reserved for chartered accountants, the Council's view that interference with the practice of requiring an earnest money or security deposit is not required with exorbitant deposits left to the Ethical Standards Board, and the cost sheet to be maintained by a member responding to a tender

items.scenario: A State Government invites tenders for the computerisation of its land revenue records. Engineering firms, software houses and firms of chartered accountants are all eligible to bid. A firm of chartered accountants decides to bid and takes three steps before the closing date. It pays ₹50,000 as the earnest money deposit the tender document requires of every bidder. It prepares a working paper setting out the number of people it will put on the job, their grades and the hours it expects them to spend, and files that paper with the tender working papers. And it asks a partner to keep a note of the reasons for the fee it has quoted. A senior partner is uneasy on two counts: he thinks a member may not put the firm's own money at risk to obtain work, and he thinks the costing paper is an internal document that ought not to exist in a form anybody outside the firm could ask for.

items.stem: Which of these may stand and which must not be sent?

options.text: Everything may stand, because the firm is already on the panel and a member on a panel is entitled to be given the work the panel exists to allot, and because the cloth merchants are being offered a service rather than being asked for work
options.misconception: reads empanelment as an entitlement to work, and treats an unsolicited offer of services as something other than solicitation
options.why: Being on a panel means the member may be considered; it confers no claim on any assignment, which is why the Institute allows the letter asking the reason and stops the letter asking for the work. And an unsolicited offer is the clause's own language — soliciting clients or professional work directly or indirectly by circular or personal communication.

options.text: All four letters already sent are misconduct and only the draft is safe, since the clause catches a personal communication seeking work whoever it is addressed to, while a general offer of services to a market is an advertisement governed by Clause (7)
options.misconception: applies the clause without its first proviso and then routes the plainest solicitation to the advertising clause
options.why: Both halves fail. The clause carries the proviso inside itself and it is not narrow: applying for, requesting, inviting or securing professional work from another chartered accountant in practice is permitted. And a letter to persons likely to need a chartered accountant is dealt with under Clause (6) itself, where the Council says it amounts to advertisement.

options.text: The two letters to the firm and the letter asking the reason for no allotment may stand; the letter requesting that work be allowed crossed the line, and the draft to the thirty proprietors must not be sent
options.why: The first proviso says in terms that nothing in the clause prevents a chartered accountant from applying or requesting for or inviting or securing professional work from another chartered accountant in practice — the profession may be approached, the public may not. On the panel, the Institute's position is that writing continuous letters to ascertain the reasons for not getting the work is quite alright, but where such a letter amounts to a request for allowing the work the member is liable for professional misconduct under Clause (6). And addressing letters, emails or circulars specifically to persons who are likely to require the services of a chartered accountant amounts to advertisement, which is what a mailing to thirty proprietors chosen by their trade is.
keywords: from another chartered accountant in practice
ascertain the reasons for not getting the work

options.text: Only the two letters to the firm are misconduct, since seeking work from another firm undercuts the relationships that firm already has
options.misconception: inverts the proviso, treating the one approach the clause expressly protects as the one it forbids
options.why: The proviso protects exactly those letters. Nothing in Clause (6) turns on competition between firms, and the module's own illustration is a member who wrote to two firms asking for work and was held to have committed no misconduct at all.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6), first proviso permitting a chartered accountant to apply for, request, invite or secure professional work from another chartered accountant in practice, read with the Council's position on letters to a body maintaining a panel — writing to ascertain the reasons for not getting the work is permissible while a letter amounting to a request for allowing the work is misconduct — and with the head on soliciting professional work by making roving enquiries, under which letters, emails or circulars addressed specifically to persons likely to require the services of a chartered accountant amount to advertisement

items.scenario: A member who set up in practice eight months ago has written four letters and is drafting a fifth. The first two went to an established firm of chartered accountants, asking whether it had any work it could pass on to him. The third went to the Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies, stating that his firm is already on the panel and asking why no audit work has been allotted to it. The fourth went to the same officer a month later, repeating the question and requesting that work now be allowed to the firm. The fifth, still in draft, is addressed to thirty proprietors in the wholesale cloth market near his office, offering to take up their tax work. A friend has told him that all of this is safe because the clause carries a proviso about asking other chartered accountants for work.

items.stem: What is the position of the firm on these four steps?

options.text: All four steps are proper, since a request to be considered for work is not a request for work
options.misconception: collapses the Council's distinction between writing to a panel one knows of and writing to organisations at large
options.why: The Council drew the line inside that very idea. Asking a body known to keep a panel is permitted; broadcasting the same request to organisations chosen because they might have one is a roving enquiry and is not proper. The difference is whether the member is answering a known process or fishing.

options.text: The letter to the bank is proper and so is the fee quoted in reply to a body that asked, but the eleven identical letters and the reminder are roving enquiries and improper
options.why: The Council's position has three parts and this scenario has all three. Where the existence of such a panel is within the knowledge of a member, he is free to write to the concerned organisation with a request to place his name on the panel. It would not be proper for a chartered accountant to make roving enquiries by applying to any such organisation for having his name included in any such panel — eleven letters sent blind, and a reminder chasing one of them, are exactly that. And it is permissible to quote fees on enquiries being received from such bodies which maintain such panels, so the reply to the company that asked is unobjectionable. The engagement partner's note misses that the wrong is in the asking of organisations at large, not in what was asked for.
keywords: existence of such a panel is within the knowledge of a member
quote fees on enquiries being received

options.text: None is proper, because approaching a prospective client in writing is a circular within the meaning of the clause however few copies are sent
options.misconception: treats every letter as a circular, when the clause is read alongside the Council's own permission to write to a body known to maintain a panel
options.why: The clause names a circular among the means of soliciting, and the Council has then said which letters are and are not caught. A single letter to an organisation known to maintain a panel is expressly permitted, so it cannot be a prohibited circular.

options.text: Only the letter to the bank is proper; quoting a fee turns a request to be empanelled into a solicitation of the assignment itself
options.misconception: forbids a quotation given in answer to an enquiry, which the Council expressly allows
options.why: The Council permits a member to quote fees on enquiries being received from bodies which maintain such panels. The firm did not put the number in front of anybody; it answered a question it was asked, and answering is not soliciting.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — application for empanelment for allotment of audit and other professional work: a member may write where the existence of the panel is within his knowledge, roving enquiries by applying to any such organisation are improper, and it is permissible to quote fees on enquiries being received from bodies maintaining such panels

items.scenario: A firm learns from a colleague that a nationalised bank maintains a panel of auditors, and writes to that bank asking that its name be placed on the panel. In the same week it posts an identical letter to eleven Government companies, having no idea whether any of them keeps a panel at all, chosen because they are the largest employers in the district. A month later one of the eleven writes back saying it does maintain a panel, that the firm's name has been added, and asking what the firm would charge for an internal audit; the firm replies with its fee. A second of the eleven does not reply, and the firm sends it a reminder repeating the request. The engagement partner records in the file that no misconduct can arise because the firm has only ever asked to be considered and has never asked for an assignment.

items.stem: How should the episode be classified?

options.text: Two clauses, not one — the invitation to approach the firm and the distribution of cards are soliciting under Clause (6), while calling himself a management expert falls under section 7 read with Clause (7); the explanation of the tax change is what a member is permitted to do from a platform
options.why: The limbs answer different questions. Clause (6) asks whether the member went after work: telling an audience his firm provides services at reasonable rates and inviting them to approach it is solicitation by personal communication, and distributing cards to the audience is misconduct in terms of Clause (6) on its own. Section 7 read with Clause (7) asks what he called himself: management expert is neither a degree of a university established by law in India or recognised by the Central Government nor a title indicating membership of an institution recognised by the Central Government or the Council. And the answer on the tax change is inside the permission — a member may lecture, give his name and describe himself as a chartered accountant, and may give special qualifications directly relevant to the subject matter, provided what he says is an objective professional view of the topic rather than promotion of himself or his firm.

options.text: One clause — Clause (6) alone, because everything he did was aimed at getting work and the designation was only the means
options.misconception: folds the designation limb into the soliciting limb, when ICAI's own answer holds the member guilty under both
options.why: The designation is a wrong in itself whether or not it wins any work. Section 7 and Clause (7) restrain a member from using any designation or expression other than chartered accountant in documents and settings through which his professional attainments come to the notice of the public, and that is breached at the moment the words are spoken.

options.text: No misconduct at all, a member being free to speak at a Government conference, to answer questions on the law and to give his contact details to people who ask for them
options.misconception: reads the permission to appear and be identified as a chartered accountant as a permission to promote the firm from the platform
options.why: The permission is real and it is bounded. A member may appear on television, broadcast or lecture, give his name, describe himself as a chartered accountant and give special qualifications directly relevant to the subject matter. What he may say must be an objective professional view of the topic and not promotional of himself or his firm, and no reference should be made by a member in practice to the name, address or services of his firm.

options.text: One clause — Clause (7) alone, since a speech is a form of advertising professional attainments and the cards were handed out only because the delegates asked
options.misconception: treats a request from the audience as consent that cures the solicitation, when the clause looks at what was pushed and not at who asked first
options.why: The Council's answer names the distribution of cards to the audience as misconduct in terms of Clause (6) without any qualification about who asked. And the invitation to approach the firm for services at reasonable rates was not asked for by anybody in the hall.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — solicitation by personal communication and the distribution of business cards to an audience, read with section 7 of the Act and First Schedule Part I, Clause (7) on the use of a designation other than chartered accountant, and with the Council's position on a member appearing on a platform or in a broadcast

items.scenario: A member in practice is invited to speak at a national conference organised by a Ministry. From the platform he introduces himself as a management expert; explains, in answer to a question from the floor about a change in the tax law, what the change does and why it matters; adds that his firm provides taxation and audit services at reasonable rates and that anyone in the hall is welcome to approach it; and, when several delegates ask him afterwards how to reach him, hands out business cards carrying the firm name and telephone number. A partner reviewing the episode says only one clause is in play, because everything the member did was aimed at one thing, getting work.

items.stem: What must the firm change before the site goes live?

options.text: The monthly email and the page naming clients — the site must run on a pull and not a push model and names of clients may not be given, while the colour, the articles and the contact details may all stay
options.why: The guidelines answer each of the four. There is no restriction on the colours used in the website. The site must be run on a pull model and not a push model so that a person who wishes to locate the firm has access only on a specific pull request, and none of the information may be circulated on the firm's own initiative or by email or by any other mode except on such a request — which is what a monthly mailing is. Names of clients and fees charged cannot be given, the sole exception being a disclosure a regulator requires, which on these facts does not exist. And members may include articles, professional information, bulletin boards and professional updates, while the addresses, telephone numbers and email addresses of the head office and branches are on the permitted list.
keywords: pull model and not a push model
names of clients and fees charged cannot be given

options.text: The monthly email, the page naming clients and the bright green, the colour being a catch device of the kind the Council bars along with monograms
options.misconception: carries the bar on monograms and catch words, which belongs to the Clause (7) write-up guidelines, across to the website guidelines
options.why: The bar on a monogram or any kind of catch word is a condition on the write-up a member may publish under the proviso to Clause (7). The website guidelines say something different and say it plainly: there is no restriction on the colours used in the website.

options.text: The page naming clients only, since emailing the firm's own material to its own contact list is not pushing it at strangers
options.misconception: reads the pull requirement as protecting only strangers, when the guideline bars circulating the content by email to anybody absent a specific request
options.why: The guideline is written in terms of the request and not the recipient: none of the information contained in the website may be circulated by the firm on its own or through email or by any other mode or technique except on a specific pull request. A contact list is not a set of requests.

options.text: The monthly email and the articles, the articles being professional attainments displayed to the public, while the client names may stay because they are a plain fact about work already done
options.misconception: forbids the articles the guidelines expressly permit and permits the client names they expressly forbid
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both. Members may include articles, professional information, bulletin boards, professional updates and other matters of larger importance or of professional interest on the website, and educational videos on topics of professional relevance are permissible. Names of clients and the fees charged are the head the guidelines single out for a bar, with one narrow exception that has to be earned.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the Council's website guidelines: no restriction on the colours used, the websites to be run on a pull and not a push technology with nothing circulated except on a specific pull request, names of clients and fees charged not to be given, and the permission to include articles, professional information, bulletin boards and professional updates

items.scenario: A firm has built a website and asks its ethics partner to look at it before it goes live. The background is a very bright green throughout. The site is configured to email its contents to every address in the firm's contact list on the first of each month. A page headed "Who we work with" lists the names of the partners and, beside them, the names of the firm's six largest clients; no regulator anywhere requires the firm to disclose who its clients are. A second page carries articles the partners have written on recent notifications, and a third gives the firm's addresses, telephone numbers and email addresses. The ethics partner is told that the design studio has already been paid and that only genuine breaches will be changed.

items.stem: What does the firm have to do, and what should it have done at the outset?

options.text: Add the italicised statement naming the regulator and the page may stay, the statement being what makes such a disclosure permissible
options.misconception: reads the italicised statement as the whole of the condition, when it is one of several and cannot extend the period
options.why: The statement explains a disclosure that is otherwise permitted; it does not create the permission. The permission needs a live requirement, and it stops when the requirement stops however the page is labelled — a note naming a rule that no longer exists proves the point rather than curing it.

options.text: Nothing needs to change, a fact once lawfully published not becoming misconduct because a foreign rule was repealed
options.misconception: treats the permission as attaching to the information, when it attaches to the requirement and lapses with it
options.why: The permission is expressly time-bound: it runs only till such period as the member works under the purview of the regulator or the requirement is in force. Once the requirement goes the general bar returns, and what is left on the page is the names of clients on a chartered accountant's website.

options.text: Take the page down now, and it should never have appeared in that form — the exception runs only to the extent of the regulator's requirement and only while it is in force, and it requires a statement in italics immediately below the disclosure naming the regulator, its jurisdiction and the rule requiring it
options.why: The exception is drawn narrowly and every limb of it is a condition. Disclosure of names of clients or fees charged is permissible only where it is required by a regulator, whether or not constituted under a statute, in India or outside India; only to the extent of the requirement of the regulator; and only till such period that the member works under the purview of such regulator or those requirements are in force. Where the disclosure is made, the member or firm shall ensure that it is mentioned on the website in italics, below the disclosure itself, that the disclosure is in terms of the requirement of the named regulator having jurisdiction in the named country or area, under the named rule or directive. A heading of the firm's own choosing is not that statement, and the day the requirement went the general bar came back.
keywords: only to the extent of the requirement

options.text: Take the page down, and it should never have appeared at all, the guidelines allowing no exception for a regulator outside India
options.misconception: confines the exception to Indian regulators, when the guideline says in terms in India or outside India
options.why: The words of the exception are a regulator, whether or not constituted under a statute, in India or outside India. A foreign securities regulator is inside it. What failed here was the italicised statement and the failure to take the page down, not the country the regulator sits in.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (6) — the Council's website guidelines, note to the head on the nature of assignments handled: disclosure of names of clients or fees charged permissible only where required by a regulator in India or outside India, only to the extent of the requirement and only till it is in force, with the italicised statement below the disclosure naming the regulator, its jurisdiction and the rule or directive

items.scenario: A firm audits entities in a country whose securities regulator requires every audit firm on its register to publish the names of its listed audit clients. The firm puts those four names on its own website under a heading it has chosen itself, "Our marquee engagements", with no note explaining why they appear. Two years later the regulator withdraws the requirement. The firm keeps the page up, because it has become the most visited part of the site and two prospective clients have said it was what persuaded them to call. A partner argues that the disclosure was lawful when it was made, that nothing on the page has changed, and that a fact which was properly published cannot become misconduct because a foreign rule was repealed.

items.stem: Which parts of what he has done are misconduct, and is the senior member right about the website?

options.text: The senior member is wrong about the website itself, which is permissible if it follows the Institute's guidelines — but the telephone canvassing, the posts and the tagging of thirty traders, and the naming of existing clients on the site are each misconduct
