options.text: No — second hand capital goods are not permitted under EPCG, though the spares for the capital goods are
options.why: The EPCG scheme allows the import of capital goods for pre-production, production and post-production at zero customs duty, and it does not permit second hand capital goods. Spares, tools, jigs, fixtures, dies and moulds for the capital goods are within the scheme.

options.text: Yes, but the spares would then have to be imported on payment of full duty
options.misconception: reverses which of the two the scheme actually covers
options.why: Spares for the capital goods are expressly within the scheme. It is the second hand machine that is not.

options.text: No — EPCG is a scheme for raw materials and components, not for machinery at all
options.misconception: confuses EPCG with the input schemes
options.why: EPCG stands for Export Promotion Capital Goods and exists for machinery. Duty-free inputs physically incorporated into the export product come under Advance Authorisation instead.

citation.ref: Chapter 5 — EPCG Scheme, paragraph 5.01

items.scenario: A garment exporter wants to bring in, under the EPCG scheme, a reconditioned five-year-old embroidery machine from Italy together with a new set of spares, tools and dies for it.

items.stem: Is the $1,000 part of the value of the imported machine?

options.text: Yes — a payment made by the buyer to a third party to satisfy an obligation of the seller, as a condition of the sale, forms part of the value
options.why: Rule 10(1)(e) adds to the price all other payments actually made or to be made as a condition of sale of the imported goods, by the buyer to the seller or by the buyer to a third party to satisfy an obligation of the seller. That is exactly this $1,000. Section 14(1) reaches the same place from the other side: the value is the price actually paid or payable for the goods, and money routed at the seller's direction is still part of that price.

options.text: No — only the amount invoiced by the seller and paid to him can make up the transaction value
options.misconception: treats the seller's invoice as the ceiling of the value instead of the whole price
options.why: Section 14(1) speaks of the price actually paid or payable, not the price shown on one document. Splitting a single agreed price across two payees does not shrink it.

options.text: Yes, but only as a buying commission added under rule 10(1)(a)(i)
options.misconception: labels a settlement of the seller's debt a commission, which rule 10 does not add
options.why: Rule 10(1)(a)(i) deals with commissions and brokerage, and it expressly leaves out buying commissions. No agent acted for anyone here; the $1,000 is part of the price itself, so it enters under rule 10(1)(e) and not as a commission.

options.text: No — it is a payment to an unrelated third party and so a post-importation charge outside the value
options.misconception: calls a pre-import condition of sale a post-importation charge because of who was paid
options.why: A post-importation charge is one incurred after the goods reach India, such as inland freight or erection at the buyer's site. This payment discharged the seller's own debt and was agreed before the goods shipped, so it is part of the price and not a later expense.

citation.source: Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Section 14(1) and rule 10(1)(e)

items.scenario: An importer buys a machine from a foreign seller for a total of $10,000. Under the contract he pays $9,000 to the seller and, at the seller's written direction, pays the remaining $1,000 to a third party in settlement of a debt the seller owes that party. The contract makes the second payment a condition of the sale.

items.stem: Is the officer right to use the notional figures?

options.text: Yes for insurance and no for freight, since insurance is always taken at the prescribed percentage
options.misconception: applies the fallback to one head of cost and the actual figure to the other, with no basis for the split
options.why: Both heads are worded the same way. Each takes the actual figure when it is ascertainable and the notional one when it is not, so there is no reason to treat insurance differently from freight.

options.text: No — the notional percentages apply only where the cost is not ascertainable, and here both costs are ascertained and evidenced
options.why: Rule 10(2) adds the cost of transport and the cost of insurance to the price actually paid or payable. The percentages the officer reached for sit in provisos, and each proviso opens with the condition that the cost is not ascertainable. A carrier's invoice and a policy make the cost ascertainable, so the actual amount governs and the proviso is never reached.

options.text: Yes — the percentages in rule 10(2) are compulsory and replace whatever the importer actually paid
options.misconception: reads a fallback provision as the main rule
options.why: The main limb of rule 10(2) adds the real cost. The percentages exist only to fill a gap when the real cost cannot be found, and a provision that fills a gap cannot displace a fact that is proved.

options.text: No — neither freight nor insurance is added at all, because the customs value is the FOB price
options.misconception: values imports on an FOB basis, when section 14 values them at the place of importation
options.why: Section 14(1) values the goods for delivery at the time and place of importation, which is why rule 10(2) brings in transport and insurance. Assessment on a bare FOB figure would leave out costs the statute puts in.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2) and its provisos, read with section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962

items.scenario: An importer declares an FOB price of ₹20,00,000. He produces the carrier's invoice for the freight actually paid, ₹1,20,000, and the marine policy for the insurance premium actually paid, ₹15,000. The proper officer ignores both documents and instead adds the notional percentages of the FOB value that the provisos to rule 10(2) lay down, saying those are the figures the rule prescribes.

items.stem: Is the reproduction fee added to the transaction value of the parts?

options.text: Yes — every payment made to the seller in connection with the goods enters the value
options.misconception: treats the identity of the payee as the test, when rule 10(1)(c) tests the condition of sale
options.why: Money reaching the seller is not automatically part of the price. Rule 10(1)(c) adds a royalty only when the buyer is required to pay it as a condition of the sale, and this sale carried no such condition.

options.text: No — charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in India are kept out of the value
options.why: Rule 10(1)(c) adds royalties and licence fees related to the imported goods which the buyer is required to pay, directly or indirectly, as a condition of sale of the goods being valued. The interpretative notes to rule 10 carve two payments out of that: charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in India, and payments for the right to distribute or resell where they are not a condition of the sale. This fee is for the right to reproduce, so it stays outside the value.

options.text: Yes, under rule 10(1)(e), as a payment made as a condition of sale of the imported goods
options.misconception: invokes a clause whose own words require a condition of sale that the facts deny
options.why: Rule 10(1)(e) covers other payments made as a condition of sale of the imported goods. The facts state that the parts would be sold at the same price without the reproduction agreement, so the payment is not a condition of anything.

options.text: No, because the fee is paid after the goods were imported rather than before
options.misconception: makes the timing of payment the test, which rule 10(1)(c) does not
options.why: Rule 10(1)(c) is indifferent to when the royalty is paid; a royalty payable later is still added if it is a condition of the sale. What keeps this fee out is its subject matter — the right to reproduce — not its date.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(c) and the interpretative notes to rule 10

items.scenario: An importer buys moulded plastic parts from a foreign seller at an arm's length price. Under a separate agreement with the same seller he pays a fee for the right to reproduce the imported design in India in his own factory. The sale of the parts is not conditional on that agreement, and the parts would be sold to him at the same price without it.

items.stem: Which date fixes the rate of duty on this export?

options.text: 11 August 2026 — the date the proper officer makes the order permitting clearance and loading
options.why: Section 16(1)(a) fixes the rate of duty and tariff valuation for export goods entered for export as the rate and valuation in force on the date on which the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance and loading of the goods for exportation under section 51. Neither the date the shipping bill went in nor the date the vessel left has any part in it.

options.text: The date the export proceeds are realised in India
options.misconception: confuses a foreign exchange condition with the moment the duty rate is fixed
options.why: Realisation of proceeds matters for export benefits and for zero-rating under GST. It has no bearing on the rate of customs duty, which section 16 pins to a date at the port.

options.text: 3 August 2026, the date the shipping bill was presented
options.misconception: carries the import rule in section 15(1)(a) across to exports
options.why: The date of presentation of the entry is the test for imports under section 15(1)(a). Section 16 chooses a different moment for exports, and it is the officer's order, not the exporter's filing, that fixes the rate.

options.text: 14 August 2026, the date the vessel actually sailed
options.misconception: reads the physical departure as the taxing event, which section 16 does not
options.why: Section 16 stops at the order permitting clearance and loading. What the vessel does afterwards, and how long it waits, cannot move the rate.

citation.ref: Section 16(1)(a) read with section 51

items.scenario: An exporter files a shipping bill for goods carrying an export duty on 3 August 2026. The proper officer makes the order permitting clearance and loading of the goods for exportation on 11 August 2026, and the vessel sails on 14 August 2026. The rate of export duty changes between the first date and the last.

items.stem: What does section 46(3) require of him?

options.text: The bill of entry should have been presented before the end of 11 June 2026, the day before the vessel arrived
options.why: Section 46(3) requires the importer to present the bill of entry before the end of the day, including a holiday, preceding the day on which the vessel, aircraft or vehicle carrying the goods arrives at the customs station at which the goods are to be cleared. The vessel arrived on 12 June, so the last permitted moment was the end of 11 June, and charges for late presentation follow as prescribed.
keywords: before the end of the day

options.text: Nothing — a bill of entry may be presented at any time before the importer seeks clearance
options.misconception: treats the timing of the entry as the importer's choice, when the section sets a deadline
options.why: Section 46(3) sets a fixed outer moment tied to the arrival of the carrier. The importer's own convenience is not the test, which is why a charge attaches to a late entry.

options.text: It may be presented only after entry inwards is granted to the vessel
options.misconception: borrows the deeming rule in section 15 and reads it as a bar on filing
options.why: Section 15 deems a bill of entry presented before entry inwards to have been presented on the date of entry inwards, for the rate of duty. That is a rule about which rate applies, not a rule forbidding an early filing.

options.text: It must be presented within thirty days of the arrival of the vessel
options.misconception: turns the advance-filing window into a period running after arrival
options.why: The thirty days in section 46(3) run the other way — a bill of entry may be presented in advance of the expected arrival of the carrier. There is no thirty-day grace after arrival.

citation.ref: Section 46(3)

items.scenario: The vessel carrying an importer's consignment arrives at the customs station on 12 June 2026. The importer presents his bill of entry for home consumption on 14 June 2026, saying a bill of entry may be filed at any time before he actually wants the goods released.

items.stem: Is the notice good?

options.text: No — the notice had to be served within one year of the relevant date
options.misconception: uses a period the section no longer contains
options.why: One year is not the limit in section 28(1)(a); two years is. The notice fails, but not for this reason.

options.text: Yes — five years is always available for a demand of customs duty
options.misconception: treats the extended period as the ordinary one, rather than a period unlocked by conduct
options.why: Five years is reserved by section 28(4) for cases of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression. Where the department itself says none of those exists, it cannot take the period that depends on them.

options.text: Yes — the mistake was in the importer's own declaration, so the longer period follows
options.misconception: equates an innocent error by the importer with a wilful misstatement
options.why: Section 28(4) needs the misstatement to be wilful or the facts to be suppressed. An arithmetical slip that nobody says was deliberate is neither, so it leaves the two-year period in place.

options.text: No — with none of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression alleged, the notice had to be served within two years of the relevant date
options.why: Section 28(1)(a) requires a notice for duty not levied, short-levied or erroneously refunded to be served within two years from the relevant date. The five years in section 28(4) is open only where the short levy is by reason of collusion, or any wilful misstatement, or suppression of facts. None is alleged, so the longer period is shut and the notice is out of time.

citation.ref: Section 28(1)(a) and section 28(4)

items.scenario: A short levy comes to light that arose from an arithmetical slip in an importer's own declaration. The department accepts that there was no collusion, no wilful misstatement and no suppression of facts, and alleges none. It serves a notice under section 28 three years after the relevant date.

items.stem: From when does the notification take effect?

options.text: From the first day of the month following its issue
options.misconception: borrows a commencement convention the section does not use
options.why: No such rounding appears in section 25(4). The date of issue is the date, whatever day of the month it falls on.

options.text: Only from a date the Government separately notifies, an exemption having no effect until then
options.misconception: treats a default rule as requiring a further step
options.why: The Government may provide otherwise in the notification itself, and sometimes does. Where it says nothing, section 25(4) supplies the answer rather than leaving the notification asleep.

options.text: From 20 July 2026 — the date of its issue by the Central Government for publication in the Official Gazette
options.why: Section 25(4) says that every notification issued under section 25(1) shall, unless otherwise provided, come into force on the date of its issue by the Central Government for publication in the Official Gazette. The date of issue is the date fixed by the statute, so the goods cleared on 22 July are covered.

options.text: From the day the printed Gazette physically reaches the customs house
options.misconception: makes the effect of a notification depend on its distribution
options.why: Section 25(4) fixes the moment at issue for publication. Making it depend on where a printed copy had travelled would give the same notification different dates at different ports.

citation.ref: Section 25(4)

items.scenario: The Central Government issues an exemption notification under section 25(1) of the Customs Act. The notification is issued for publication in the Official Gazette on 20 July 2026 and says nothing about when it takes effect. An importer whose goods were cleared on 22 July argues that it can only bite from the date the printed Gazette actually reached the customs house.

items.stem: May he do those things while the goods remain warehoused?

options.text: Yes, but each act makes the goods deemed cleared for home consumption on that date
options.misconception: invents a deeming clearance that section 64 does not contain
options.why: Clearance for home consumption happens under section 68, on a bill of entry and payment of duty. Nothing in section 64 turns an inspection or a sorting into a clearance.

options.text: Only inspection is allowed; anything that touches the goods is an operation needing permission under section 65
options.misconception: calls ordinary care of goods a manufacturing operation
options.why: Section 65 governs manufacturing processes and other operations carried on in relation to warehoused goods. Sorting stock and handling containers is not manufacture, and section 64 names those acts as the owner's own.

options.text: No — nothing may be done to warehoused goods until the duty on them is paid
options.misconception: reads the deferment of duty as a freeze on the owner's rights over his own goods
options.why: Duty deferment and the owner's rights are separate. Section 64 exists exactly so that goods can be looked after and offered for sale during the warehousing period.

options.text: Yes — the owner of warehoused goods may inspect them, deal with their containers to prevent loss or damage, sort them, and show them for sale
options.why: Section 64 lets the owner of any warehoused goods, after warehousing them, inspect the goods, deal with their containers in such manner as may be necessary to prevent loss or deterioration or damage to the goods, sort the goods, and show the goods for sale. All four sit before any duty is paid, because duty on warehoused goods falls due when they are cleared, not while they rest.

citation.ref: Section 64

items.scenario: Goods lie in a licensed warehouse and no duty has been paid on them. Without clearing them, the owner wants to walk through the stock and inspect it, to sort it and set the damaged pieces aside, and to show the goods to a prospective buyer.

items.stem: What happens to the bond?

options.text: It is discharged, and the Bengaluru warehouse licensee's own bond takes its place
options.misconception: confuses the importer's warehousing bond with the licensee's bond for running a warehouse
options.why: The licensee bonds himself for the conduct of the warehouse. The duty on the goods stays on the importer's own bond, which section 59(3) keeps standing through the move.

options.text: It is discharged, and a fresh bond for the same goods must be executed at Bengaluru
options.misconception: applies the fresh-bond rule for a transfer of ownership to a mere change of warehouse
options.why: A fresh bond is called for where the goods pass to another person. Here the owner is the same and only the warehouse has changed, which is the very case section 59(3) covers.

options.text: It stays alive — the bond continues in force notwithstanding the transfer of the goods to another warehouse
options.why: Section 59(3) provides that the bond executed under that section shall continue to be in force notwithstanding the transfer of the goods to another warehouse. Removal under section 67 changes where the goods sit, not who has undertaken to pay the duty on them, so the importer remains bound.

options.text: It stays alive, but only until the original warehousing period would have expired
options.misconception: ties the life of the bond to a period rather than to the accounting of the goods
options.why: Section 73 cancels the bond when the goods have been cleared for home consumption or exported or otherwise duly accounted for and all amounts due have been paid. The expiry of a period does not release it.

citation.ref: Section 59(3) read with sections 67 and 73

items.scenario: An importer executed a bond under section 59 for goods warehoused at Chennai. He later removes the same goods to a warehouse at Bengaluru under section 67, the ownership of the goods not changing. He says his Chennai bond died the moment the goods left that warehouse.

items.stem: Is the consultant right?

options.text: No — only the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs may permit manufacture in a warehouse
options.misconception: sends the application to the wrong authority
options.why: The Board frames the rules and regulations. The sanction under section 65(1) is given by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs, at the level where the warehouse is.

options.text: No — manufacture in a warehouse needs the sanction of the Principal Commissioner of Customs or the Commissioner of Customs
options.why: Section 65(1) allows the owner of warehoused goods to carry on manufacturing processes or other operations in relation to those goods in the warehouse only with the sanction of the Principal Commissioner of Customs or Commissioner of Customs, subject to prescribed conditions. A licence under section 58 permits the deposit of goods; it says nothing about working on them.
keywords: sanction of the Principal Commissioner of Customs

options.text: No — manufacture inside a bonded warehouse is prohibited outright
options.misconception: turns a permission requirement into a prohibition
options.why: Section 65 is a permitting provision, and manufacture in bond is a well-used facility. What it requires is sanction, not abstention.

options.text: Yes — the section 58 licence covers everything done inside the licensed premises
options.misconception: reads a licence to store as a licence to manufacture
options.why: Section 58 licenses a place for the deposit of dutiable goods without payment of duty. Section 65 is a separate permission for a separate activity, which is why it exists at all.

citation.ref: Section 65(1) read with section 58

items.scenario: A company holds a licence under section 58 for a private bonded warehouse and now wants to start manufacturing operations on the imported goods lying inside it. Its consultant says that once a warehouse licence is held, work done inside the warehouse needs no separate permission.

items.stem: How are such goods dealt with on being entered for warehousing?

options.text: They may be warehoused without being assessed to duty, on the importer declaring that they are to be supplied as stores to foreign-going vessels or aircraft
options.why: Section 85 provides that where imported goods are entered for warehousing and the importer makes and subscribes to a declaration that the goods are to be supplied as stores to foreign-going vessels or aircraft, they may be warehoused without assessment to duty. The assessment is dispensed with because the goods are not expected to enter the country's home consumption at all.

options.text: They cannot be warehoused at all; stores must be kept outside the warehousing system
options.misconception: denies a facility the section grants in terms
options.why: Warehousing is the ordinary way a chandler holds stores until a ship arrives, and section 85 is written for exactly that trade.

options.text: They must be assessed to duty on entry into the warehouse like any other warehoused goods, with a refund when the stores are put on board
options.misconception: assesses first and refunds later, where section 85 dispenses with the assessment
options.why: Section 85 exists precisely to avoid that round trip. No assessment is made on entry, so there is nothing to refund afterwards.

options.text: They may be warehoused without assessment only if the vessel they are meant for has already arrived at the port
options.misconception: adds a condition about the ship's arrival that the section does not impose
options.why: The declaration is about the intended use of the goods, not about a ship standing at the quay. Section 85 does not wait for a particular vessel.

citation.ref: Section 85

items.scenario: A ship chandler imports provisions and lubricating oil intended to be supplied as stores to foreign-going vessels calling at the port. He wants to hold them in a bonded warehouse until the ships arrive, and asks whether the duty must be worked out on them when they go in.

items.stem: What does section 22 give him?

options.text: An abatement — duty is charged in the proportion the damaged value bears to the sound value, so one-fourth of the duty otherwise payable
options.why: Section 22 gives an abatement of duty on damaged or deteriorated goods. Where imported goods are damaged after unloading in India but before examination for assessment, on account of an accident not due to any wilful act, negligence or default of the importer, the duty borne is in the proportion the value of the damaged goods bears to the value in a sound state. Damaged value is one-fourth, so one-fourth of the duty is payable.

options.text: Nothing — duty attaches on importation, and what happens to the goods afterwards is the importer's risk
options.misconception: ignores a section written for exactly this misfortune
options.why: Sections 22 and 23 exist because the statute does not leave every pre-clearance misfortune on the importer. Section 22 covers damage and deterioration in terms.

options.text: Full remission of duty under section 23, the goods having suffered before clearance
options.misconception: applies the provision for goods lost or destroyed to goods that survive in damaged form
options.why: Section 23 remits duty where goods are lost, otherwise than as a result of pilferage, or destroyed before clearance. These goods still exist and can still be cleared, so the statute reduces the duty rather than wiping it out.

options.text: Half the duty, that being the standard abatement for damaged goods
options.misconception: reaches for a fixed fraction where the section prescribes a proportion of value
options.why: There is no standard fraction in section 22. The relief is measured by the ratio of the damaged value to the sound value, which on these facts is one-fourth.

citation.ref: Section 22

items.scenario: A consignment of glassware is damaged in an accident at the port after unloading and before it is examined for assessment. The accident owes nothing to any wilful act, negligence or default of the importer. The value of the goods in their damaged state is one-fourth of their value in a sound state. The importer is told he must pay duty on the full value.

items.stem: What drawback is available under section 74?

options.text: The reduced percentage laid down for goods used for thirty months
options.misconception: treats a period spent unused as a period of use and slides down the scale instead of out of the section
options.why: The reducing scale is for goods that were taken into use after importation. These goods were never used; what defeats the claim is the two-year limit, not a use-based reduction.

options.text: The whole of the duty paid, since the goods are going back to the very seller they came from
options.misconception: reads re-export to the original seller as a cancellation of the import
options.why: Section 74 never returns the whole duty; even a clean and timely re-export leaves a slice behind. And the identity of the buyer abroad changes nothing about the time limit.

options.text: Ninety-eight per cent of the duty, the goods being unused and identifiable
options.misconception: applies the rate for unused goods without first passing the time limit
options.why: The higher rate for unused goods is reached only after section 74(1) is satisfied. The time limit is a gate before the rate, not a factor within it.

options.text: None, unless the Board extends the period, because the goods were not entered for export within two years of the date of payment of duty
options.why: Section 74(1) allows drawback only where the goods are identified to the satisfaction of the proper officer as the goods that were imported and are entered for export within two years from the date of payment of duty on importation, a period the Board may extend on sufficient cause being shown. Thirty months falls outside it, so however clean the identity of the goods the claim fails without an extension.

citation.ref: Section 74(1)

items.scenario: A company imported a laboratory instrument and paid duty on it on 1 March 2024. The instrument was never put to use, it is still readily identifiable as the article that was imported, and it is entered for export back to the seller on 1 September 2026 — thirty months after the duty was paid. No extension of any period has been applied for.

items.stem: Where does the refund go?

options.text: Half to the exporter and half to the Fund, the duty burden being shared
options.misconception: invents an apportionment the section does not contain
options.why: Section 27(2) sends the refund one way or the other. There is no splitting of a refund between the claimant and the Fund.

options.text: To the Consumer Welfare Fund, unless the exporter proves the duty was not passed on to his foreign buyer
options.misconception: applies the passing-on test to a category the proviso exempts from it outright
options.why: The passing-on test decides the ordinary case. Export duty is listed separately in the proviso, so the exporter is paid without having to prove anything about incidence.

options.text: To the exporter — a refund of export duty is one of the categories the statute pays to the applicant instead of to the Fund
options.why: Section 27(2) directs a sanctioned refund into the Consumer Welfare Fund, but its proviso lists the cases in which the amount is instead paid to the applicant. Refund of export duty is one of them, standing beside drawback of duty and duty or interest whose incidence the claimant has not passed on. So the unjust enrichment test is not applied to this claim at all.

options.text: To the Consumer Welfare Fund in every case, the Fund being where all sanctioned refunds are credited
options.misconception: reads the main limb of section 27(2) and stops before its proviso
options.why: If every refund went to the Fund, no importer would ever be paid anything. The proviso names the claims that are paid out, and export duty is on that list.

citation.ref: Section 27(2) and its proviso

items.scenario: An exporter paid export duty on a consignment and later established that no export duty was chargeable on those goods at all. His refund claim is sanctioned. The department proposes to credit the money to the Consumer Welfare Fund, saying every sanctioned refund goes there unless the claimant proves he bore the burden himself.

items.stem: Is a refund of the import duty available under section 26A?

options.text: No — section 26A applies only to goods imported for personal use
options.misconception: misstates the reach of the section
options.why: Section 26A is not confined to personal imports; goods imported for trade or for use in business are within it. What defeats this claim is the state of the goods.

options.text: No — the section shuts out goods that have exceeded their shelf life or their recommended storage-before-use period
options.why: Section 26A(1) allows a refund of import duty on goods found not to be in conformity with the specification, where they are re-exported, abandoned or destroyed within the periods it lays down. Section 26A(3) then says no refund shall be allowed in respect of perishable goods and goods which have exceeded their shelf life or their recommended storage-before-use period. This reagent falls squarely in that exclusion.

options.text: Yes, but only of the basic customs duty and not of any other duty paid
options.misconception: invents a split between heads of duty that section 26A does not draw
options.why: Section 26A speaks of the import duty paid on the goods. The reason this claim fails is the exclusion for goods past their storage period, not a limit on which duty may be refunded.

options.text: Yes — the goods are unused and every time limit has been met, so the refund follows
options.misconception: treats the conditions in section 26A(1) as the only hurdles, ignoring the exclusion in section 26A(3)
options.why: Meeting the conditions in the first sub-section is necessary but not sufficient. Section 26A(3) carves out a class of goods on which no refund is allowed however clean the rest of the claim.

citation.ref: Section 26A(1) and section 26A(3)

items.scenario: A consignment of a chemical reagent is cleared for home consumption on payment of duty and turns out not to conform to the specification ordered. The importer has not used any of it, and he is well inside every period section 26A lays down. The reagent, however, has passed the end of its recommended storage-before-use period.

items.stem: What does section 110A allow the department to do?

options.text: Release the goods only against payment in advance of the full duty and the maximum penalty
options.misconception: converts a bond and security into an upfront payment of amounts not yet adjudged
options.why: Nothing is due until the adjudicating authority has decided. Section 110A asks for a bond with security, which secures the revenue without pre-judging the case.

options.text: Release the goods only once six months have run from the seizure without a notice
options.misconception: confuses provisional release with the return that follows a failure to issue notice
options.why: The return of goods after six months without a notice is section 110(2), and it is automatic rather than conditional. Section 110A is a separate, earlier route that does not wait for that period to run.

options.text: Release the goods to the owner pending adjudication, on his giving a bond with such security and conditions as the adjudicating authority requires
options.why: Section 110A lets goods, documents or things seized, or a bank account provisionally attached, under section 110 be released to the owner or the bank account holder by the adjudicating authority, on taking a bond from him in the proper form with such security and conditions as that authority may require, pending the order of the adjudicating authority.

options.text: Nothing — seized goods can never leave the department's hands before the adjudication order
options.misconception: denies a provisional release the section provides for in terms
options.why: Section 110A was written to cover exactly the gap between seizure and adjudication. Release before the order is the whole point of it.

citation.ref: Section 110A

items.scenario: Goods are seized under section 110 and adjudication will plainly take several months. The owner does not dispute the seizure but wants the goods in his hands meanwhile, and offers to give whatever undertaking the department asks for.

items.stem: Is he right that no duty is now payable?

options.text: No, but the duty is halved because a fine has already been paid
options.misconception: invents a set-off between the fine and the duty
options.why: Section 125(2) makes the duty payable in addition, without reduction. Nothing in it scales the duty to what was paid as a fine.

options.text: Yes — confiscation vests the goods in the Central Government, so no duty can be demanded of him
options.misconception: applies the consequence of an absolute confiscation to goods that were redeemed
options.why: Vesting under section 126 follows a confiscation that stands. Where the fine is paid the goods come back to the owner, and the duty on goods he now holds remains his to pay.

options.text: No — the owner is liable, in addition to the fine, for the duty and charges payable in respect of the goods
options.why: Section 125(1) gives the option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation. Section 125(2) then says that where such a fine is imposed, the owner of the goods, or the person from whom they were seized, shall in addition be liable to any duty and charges payable in respect of such goods. Redeeming the goods hands them back to him; it does not extinguish what was owed on them.

options.text: Yes — the redemption fine is a composite amount that absorbs the duty
options.misconception: reads the fine as covering everything, when the section adds the duty to it
options.why: The fine is the price of redeeming goods that were liable to confiscation. Section 125(2) separates it from the duty in so many words, and the two are payable together.

citation.ref: Section 125(1) and section 125(2)

items.scenario: Goods that are not prohibited are held liable to confiscation. The adjudicating officer gives the owner the option to pay a fine of ₹2,00,000 in lieu of confiscation, and the owner pays it. He then says that with the fine paid the matter is closed, and that the duty on the goods went with the confiscation.

items.stem: How is the box classified?

options.text: Each article separately, under its own heading, since three headings each cover a part
options.misconception: unpacks a retail set that rule 3(b) directs be classified as one thing
options.why: Rule 3(b) applies to goods put up in sets for retail sale precisely so that they are not taken apart at the border. The box is sold as it is imported.

options.text: Under whichever of the three headings carries the highest rate of duty
options.misconception: imports the highest-rate rule from GST valuation into tariff classification
options.why: The interpretative rules contain no highest-rate test. That idea belongs to a mixed supply under section 8(b) of the CGST Act and has no place in classifying goods under the tariff.

options.text: Under the heading that occurs last in numerical order, applying rule 3(c)
options.misconception: jumps to the tie-breaker before the rule that actually resolves the case
options.why: Rule 3(c) is reached only when the goods cannot be classified by reference to rule 3(a) or rule 3(b). Here rule 3(b) settles it, so rule 3(c) never comes into play.

options.text: As a wallet, that being the component which gives the set its essential character
options.why: Rule 3(b) of the General Rules for the Interpretation of the Import Tariff says that goods put up in sets for retail sale, which cannot be classified by reference to rule 3(a), are classified as if they consisted of the material or component which gives them their essential character. The wallet carries the value and the purpose of the box, so the set takes the wallet's heading.

citation.ref: General Rules for the Interpretation of the Import Tariff, rule 3(b)

items.scenario: A gift box is imported, put up for retail sale exactly as it will be sold, containing a leather wallet, a small steel keyring and a printed greeting card. The wallet accounts for the great bulk of the value and is plainly the reason the box sells. Separate headings cover wallets, keyrings and printed matter, and no single heading describes the box as a whole.

items.stem: Can heading 9801 be applied to the consignment?

options.text: No — heading 9801 covers only civil construction and never machinery
options.misconception: misstates what the heading covers
options.why: Heading 9801 is built around machinery, instruments, apparatus and components required for the initial setting up or substantial expansion of a project. Machinery is the ordinary case, not an excluded one.

options.text: No — the concession depends on the contract being registered with the proper officer before the goods are cleared
options.why: Heading 9801 assesses all the goods of an eligible project at one rate instead of item by item, and the Project Imports Regulations, 1986 make that concession conditional. The importer must apply for registration of the contract with the proper officer at the port of importation, and the registration must be in place before the goods are cleared. An unregistered contract is assessed in the ordinary way, heading by heading.

options.text: Yes, provided he registers the contract within thirty days of clearing the goods
options.misconception: invents a grace period after clearance that the regulations do not give
options.why: The registration has to precede the clearance. There is no window afterwards in which a cleared consignment can be brought back under heading 9801.

options.text: Yes — registration is procedural, and a procedural lapse cannot take away a substantive benefit
options.misconception: calls a condition of the concession a mere formality
options.why: Registration is what identifies the contract, the project and the goods that belong to it. Without it the customs house has no way to know which imports are project imports, which is why the regulations make it a precondition and not a filing.

citation.source: Customs Tariff Act, 1975 read with the Project Imports Regulations, 1986
citation.ref: Heading 9801 and the requirement to register the contract before clearance

items.scenario: An importer brings in machinery for setting up a new industrial plant and claims assessment under heading 9801 at the single project rate. He did not register his contract with the customs house before the goods were cleared, saying registration is a formality he can attend to later.

items.stem: What does section 128 allow?

options.text: Sixty days, with the Commissioner (Appeals) free to condone any delay for sufficient cause
options.misconception: reads the condonation power as open-ended when the proviso caps it
options.why: The proviso names a further period of thirty days. A condonation power written with a number in it cannot be exercised beyond that number.

options.text: The appeal was due within sixty days, and the Commissioner (Appeals) may allow a further thirty days on sufficient cause — beyond that he cannot go
options.why: Section 128(1) gives an aggrieved person sixty days from the date of communication of the order to appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) against a decision or order of an officer lower in rank than a Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs. The proviso lets that authority allow a further period of thirty days if he is satisfied the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause. There is no power to condone anything past that.

options.text: No time limit at all, so long as the appeal is filed before the demand is recovered
options.misconception: ties the right of appeal to the progress of recovery rather than to a period
options.why: Section 128 fixes the period by reference to the date the order was communicated. What the department does about recovery in the meantime does not extend it.

options.text: Three months to appeal, with no condonation available at all
options.misconception: uses a period the section does not give and denies a power it does give
options.why: The period is sixty days, not three months, and section 128 expressly contains a condonation power. Both halves of this answer are wrong.

citation.ref: Section 128(1) and its proviso

items.scenario: An order passed by a Deputy Commissioner of Customs is communicated to an importer on 1 June 2026. He wants to appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) but his consultant is ill, and the appeal is finally ready in the last week of August 2026 — a little under three months after the order reached him.

items.stem: Is the second importer right?

options.text: Yes — a ruling on a classification settles that classification for everyone importing the same goods
options.misconception: reads an advance ruling as a precedent of general application
options.why: A ruling is not a judgment of a court and is not a notification. Section 28J deliberately keeps it to the applicant, which is why two importers of the same machine can each need their own ruling.

options.text: No — an advance ruling binds nobody at all, being only the Authority's opinion
options.misconception: strips a ruling of the binding force section 28J gives it
options.why: The ruling does bind, and it binds the department as much as the applicant. What it does not do is reach people who were not party to the application.

options.text: Yes, provided the second importer files a copy of the ruling with his bill of entry
options.misconception: assumes a procedural filing can extend a ruling to a stranger to it
options.why: Nothing is added by producing the document. The binding force of a ruling is defined by who applied for it, not by who shows it to an officer.

options.text: No — the ruling binds only the applicant who sought it, on the transaction it was sought for, and the officers concerned with him
options.why: Section 28J says an advance ruling is binding only on the applicant who sought it, in respect of the matter referred to in the application, and on the officers and the authorities subordinate to them in respect of that applicant. A person who did not apply gets no right out of it, however identical his goods.

citation.ref: Section 28J

items.scenario: The Customs Authority for Advance Rulings gives an importer a ruling classifying a particular machine under a heading he had argued for. A second importer, who brings in the very same machine from the same maker, tells his customs house that the ruling settles his classification too and that no officer may now take a different view of it.

items.stem: What is the position under the Foreign Trade Policy?

options.text: No code is needed at all once the company holds a GST registration
options.misconception: assumes one registration stands in for the other
options.why: GST registration and the Importer-Exporter Code are issued by different authorities for different purposes. A GST number does not let goods across the customs frontier.

options.text: A separate Importer-Exporter Code is issued for each place of business from which goods move
options.misconception: treats the code like a State-wise GST registration
options.why: GST registers a person State by State; the Importer-Exporter Code follows the person, and the person has one Permanent Account Number. Multiple codes for one entity are what the one-to-one rule prevents.

options.text: The company's Permanent Account Number is its Importer-Exporter Code, and only one such code is issued against one Permanent Account Number
options.why: The Foreign Trade Policy provides that the Permanent Account Number is the Importer-Exporter Code. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade issues the code in electronic form against the applicant's Permanent Account Number, and only one IEC is issued against one such number. Branches and additional places are added to the same code rather than given codes of their own.

options.text: A number wholly unconnected with the Permanent Account Number is allotted on application
options.misconception: describes the position before the code was aligned with the Permanent Account Number
options.why: The Policy now equates the two, so there is no separate series of numbers to be allotted from.

citation.ref: Chapter 2 — Importer-Exporter Code, one code against one Permanent Account Number

items.scenario: A newly incorporated company is about to start importing. It asks whether the Importer-Exporter Code it will be given is a fresh number unconnected with its other tax registrations, and whether it should take one code for its head office and a second for its branch factory.

items.stem: Can he claim RoDTEP on shipments already made?

options.text: Yes — a fresh application to the Directorate General of Foreign Trade covers past shipments
options.misconception: assumes a later application can stand in for a declaration made at export
options.why: The scheme runs through the customs system on the strength of the export document. There is no separate later application that revives a claim the shipping bill never made.

options.text: Yes, on producing the bank realisation certificates for those exports
options.misconception: treats proof of realisation as the trigger for the claim
options.why: Realisation of proceeds is a condition attached to a claim that exists. It cannot create a claim that was never made at the time of export.

options.text: No — the intention to claim the benefit has to be declared in the shipping bill at the time of export
options.why: The RoDTEP claim is built into the export document itself. The exporter must declare his intention to claim the benefit in the shipping bill or bill of export when the goods are exported, and the system processes the claim from that declaration. A shipping bill that carried no such declaration cannot be reopened later to add one.

options.text: Yes, because RoDTEP is a rebate of taxes already borne and a rebate cannot be forfeited by a filing lapse
options.misconception: argues from the purpose of the scheme against the procedure the scheme lays down
options.why: The scheme does rebate embedded duties and taxes that no other mechanism refunds. It grants that rebate only through the declaration in the shipping bill, and the purpose does not dispense with the route.

citation.source: Foreign Trade Policy and the RoDTEP scheme notified under section 51B of the Customs Act, 1962
citation.ref: Declaration of the RoDTEP claim in the shipping bill or bill of export

items.scenario: An exporter shipped several consignments during the year and made no mention of the Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products scheme anywhere in the shipping bills. Reading about the scheme afterwards, he now wants to claim the benefit on those completed exports.

items.stem: May the surplus imported fabric be sold on?

options.text: No — material imported against an Advance Authorisation carries the actual user condition and is not transferable even after the export obligation has been fulfilled
options.why: An Advance Authorisation is issued for inputs physically incorporated in the export product, and it is subject to the actual user condition. The Foreign Trade Policy provides that material imported against it shall not be transferable even after the export obligation has been fulfilled. That is the line that separates it from a Duty Free Import Authorisation, which becomes transferable once the obligation is discharged.

options.text: Yes, on payment of a transfer fee to the Directorate General of Foreign Trade
options.misconception: assumes a fee can buy out a condition the Policy states absolutely
options.why: No fee is provided for. The material stays with the actual user, and an exporter with surplus input must use it himself in his own manufacture.

options.text: Yes — the actual user condition falls away the moment the export obligation is complete
options.misconception: reads the condition as lasting only as long as the obligation
options.why: The Policy says the material is not transferable even after the obligation is fulfilled. The two conditions run separately, and completing one does not lift the other.

options.text: Yes — an Advance Authorisation is a freely transferable instrument like a duty credit scrip
options.misconception: confuses an authorisation to import inputs with a tradable duty credit scrip
options.why: A duty credit scrip is issued to be sold on. An Advance Authorisation is issued to a manufacturer for his own inputs, and it carries the actual user condition throughout.

citation.ref: Chapter 4 — Advance Authorisation, actual user condition and non-transferability of material

items.scenario: An exporter imported fabric duty free under an Advance Authorisation and has fully discharged the export obligation attached to it. A quantity of the imported fabric is left over. The exporter proposes to sell that surplus fabric in the domestic market, on the footing that the obligation is behind it.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of the treatment?

options.text: Haryana, because the recipient will carry the benefit of the treatment home with him
options.misconception: substitutes where the benefit is enjoyed for where the service is performed
options.why: Section 12(4) asks one question — where was the service performed. What the recipient does afterwards, and where he goes, does not enter it.

options.text: Kerala only if the recipient is unregistered; a registered recipient takes the supply to his own State
options.misconception: reads a registered-or-not split into a sub-section that contains none
options.why: The split between a registered and an unregistered recipient lives in section 12(2). Section 12(4) applies the performance test to both alike.

options.text: Kerala, being the place where the services are actually performed
options.why: Section 12(4) fixes the place of supply of restaurant and catering services, personal grooming, fitness, beauty treatment and health service, including cosmetic and plastic surgery, as the location where the services are actually performed. The treatment is given in Kerala, so that is the place of supply whatever the recipient's registration says.

options.text: Haryana, the location of the registered recipient
options.misconception: applies the general rule in section 12(2) where a specific sub-section governs
options.why: Section 12(2) opens with the words "save as provided in sub-sections (3) to (14)". Beauty treatment is named in section 12(4), so the general rule is displaced.

citation.source: Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
citation.ref: Section 12(4)

items.scenario: A person registered in Haryana travels to Kerala and takes a course of massage and beauty treatment at a centre registered in Kerala. Both supplier and recipient are in India, and the whole treatment is given at the centre's premises.

items.stem: What is the place of supply on the trader's leg?

options.text: Punjab, but as a supply that involves no movement, so section 10(1)(c) applies
options.misconception: treats goods that physically travelled as goods that did not move
options.why: The goods moved from the manufacturer's premises to the buyer, and that movement is what the trader's supply causes. Section 10(1)(c) is for supplies where nothing travels at all.

options.text: Haryana, because the trader is registered there and raises the invoice from there
options.misconception: fixes the place of supply by where the invoice is raised
options.why: Where a supplier is registered decides the location of the supplier, not the place of supply. For goods that move, section 10(1)(a) looks at where the movement ends.

options.text: Punjab, where the movement of the goods terminates for delivery to the buyer
options.why: Section 10(1)(b) governs only the leg on which goods are delivered on the direction of a third person. The trader's own supply to the buyer is an ordinary supply involving movement, so section 10(1)(a) applies and the place of supply is the location of the goods at the time at which the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient, which is Punjab.

options.text: Haryana, the third person's principal place of business, section 10(1)(b) governing both legs of the chain
options.misconception: applies the third-person rule to the leg on which the third person is himself the supplier
options.why: Section 10(1)(b) is written for the supply made to the person who acts on a third person's direction. On his own onward supply the trader is not a third person at all; he is the supplier.

citation.source: Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
citation.ref: Section 10(1)(a) read with section 10(1)(b)

items.scenario: A Punjab manufacturer despatches goods to a buyer in Punjab on the written instruction of a trader registered in Haryana, who bought them and sold them on to that buyer. The manufacturer's own leg has already been settled under section 10(1)(b). The question is the trader's own invoice to the Punjab buyer.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of these goods?

options.text: The location of the importer, under section 11(a)
options.misconception: uses the clause written for imports on an export
options.why: Section 11(a) fixes the place of supply of goods imported into India as the location of the importer. These goods are going the other way, so section 11(b) is the clause that applies.

options.text: Chennai port, the last place in India the goods were at
options.misconception: stops the enquiry at the customs frontier instead of following the goods out
options.why: The port is where the goods leave, not where they are supplied. Section 11(b) sends the place of supply beyond it.

options.text: The location outside India to which the goods are exported
options.why: Section 11(b) of the IGST Act says the place of supply of goods exported from India shall be the location outside India. Once the goods go out of the country the place of supply follows them, which is what makes the transaction an inter-State supply and so capable of being zero-rated.

options.text: Tamil Nadu, where the supplier is registered
options.misconception: uses the supplier's registration where section 11 names a place outside India
options.why: Section 11 was written to give exports and imports their own answers. For an export it points outside India, and the supplier's State plays no part in it.

citation.source: Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
citation.ref: Section 11(b)

items.scenario: A supplier registered in Tamil Nadu sells goods to a buyer in Kenya. The goods are shipped out of Chennai port and delivered to the buyer at Mombasa.

items.stem: Where does the deducted amount land?

options.text: In the supplier's electronic cash ledger, to be claimed as credit of the tax deducted
options.why: Section 51(5) says the deductee shall claim credit, in his electronic cash ledger, of the tax deducted and reflected in the return furnished by the deductor. The money is tax already paid on his behalf, so it sits in the cash ledger and can be used to discharge his own liability or claimed as a refund. It is not input tax credit and it does not enter the credit ledger.

options.text: Nowhere in his ledgers — the department refunds it to him directly in cash
options.misconception: assumes the deductor returns the money instead of the ledger crediting it
options.why: The deductor pays the money to the Government, not back to the supplier. Section 51(5) is the route by which the supplier gets the benefit of it.

options.text: It stays with the deductor and is adjusted against the next bill raised by the supplier
options.misconception: treats a statutory deduction as a running account between the two parties
options.why: Once deducted, the amount must be paid to the Government within the prescribed time. It is not the deductor's to hold or to set off against later bills.

options.text: In the supplier's electronic credit ledger, as input tax credit
options.misconception: routes a payment of tax into the ledger meant for credit on inward supplies
options.why: The credit ledger holds input tax credit on inward supplies. Tax deducted at source is money paid towards the supplier's own liability, which is what the cash ledger holds.

citation.source: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
citation.ref: Section 51(5)

items.scenario: A Government department correctly deducted ₹40,000 of tax at source from a supplier's payment, paid it to the Government, and furnished its return showing the deduction against that supplier. The supplier asks where the ₹40,000 now shows up for him.

items.stem: May he collect the tax from his customer?

options.text: Yes, provided he collects no more than the composition rate he actually pays
options.misconception: reads the bar as a cap on the amount rather than a prohibition on collecting at all
options.why: Section 10(4) forbids the collection of any tax, not of tax above a figure. The rate he pays does not create a rate he may charge.

options.text: No — a person paying tax under the composition levy is forbidden to collect any tax from the recipient
options.why: Section 10(4) says a taxable person paying tax under section 10 shall not collect any tax from the recipient on supplies made by him. The composition levy is a percentage of his own turnover that he bears himself, not a tax passed down the chain, which is why section 31(3)(c) requires him to issue a bill of supply instead of a tax invoice.

options.text: Yes, if the customer is registered and wants the tax shown so that he can take credit
options.misconception: lets the customer's wish for credit override a statutory bar
options.why: A composition supplier's customer gets no input tax credit on the supply, because no tax is charged on it. Showing tax on the document does not create a credit the law does not give.

options.text: Yes, and the customer may take input tax credit of the amount shown on the invoice
options.misconception: assumes an amount labelled as tax on a document is creditable
options.why: Credit under section 16 needs a tax invoice from a supplier who was entitled to charge tax. A composition supplier is not, so the customer has nothing to take.

citation.source: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
citation.ref: Section 10(4) read with section 31(3)(c)

items.scenario: A trader who pays tax under the composition levy issues a tax invoice to his customer showing GST separately and collects that amount from him, saying tax collected is tax paid and the customer will not mind.

items.stem: How and by when may he put the omission right?

options.text: By filing a revised return for August 2026 in place of the one already furnished
options.misconception: assumes a return once furnished can be replaced, as under some other tax laws
options.why: There is no revised return under section 39. The Act deals with an error by correcting it in a later period's return, which is why section 39(9) is worded as it is.

options.text: In the return for the month in which he noticed it, and no later than 30 November 2027 or the furnishing of the annual return for 2026-27, whichever comes first
options.why: Section 39(9) says that where a registered person discovers an omission or incorrect particulars in a return furnished, otherwise than as a result of scrutiny, audit, inspection or enforcement activity, he shall rectify it in the return to be furnished for the month or quarter in which the omission is noticed. The proviso bars rectification after the thirtieth day of November following the end of the financial year to which the particulars relate, or the furnishing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier.

options.text: Only with the written permission of the proper officer, an error once filed being final
options.misconception: makes self-correction depend on an approval the section does not require
options.why: Section 39(9) casts the rectification as the registered person's own act — he "shall rectify" it in the later return. No officer's leave is called for.

options.text: At any time before the demand for that period becomes time-barred under section 73
options.misconception: borrows the department's limitation period as the taxpayer's own window
options.why: Section 73 governs how long the department has to raise a demand. The taxpayer's window to correct his own return is the shorter one in the proviso to section 39(9).

citation.source: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
citation.ref: Section 39(9) and its proviso

items.scenario: In February 2027 a registered person notices, on his own reconciliation and not because of any scrutiny, audit, inspection or enforcement action, that his return for August 2026 understated output tax. August 2026 falls in the financial year 2026-27, and he has not yet furnished the annual return for that year.

items.stem: How is this single supply treated under section 8?

options.text: As a supply of delivery services, transport being the last element supplied and so the one that fixes the character
options.misconception: picks the element supplied last instead of the element the customer came for
options.why: Section 2(90) defines the principal supply as the predominant element of a composite supply, to which any other supply is ancillary. The customer is buying a table; delivery is ancillary to it, and the order in which the elements happen decides nothing.

options.text: As three separate supplies, the table, the packing and the delivery each carrying its own treatment
options.misconception: splits a bundle the statute deliberately treats as a single supply
options.why: Section 8(a) exists precisely so that a naturally bundled supply is not taken apart. Once the elements are supplied in conjunction with one another for a single price in the ordinary course of business, the law gives them one character.

options.text: As a supply of the table alone, the table being the principal supply, so packing and delivery take the table's treatment
options.why: Section 2(30) calls this a composite supply — two or more taxable supplies naturally bundled and supplied in conjunction with one another in the ordinary course of business, one of which is a principal supply. Section 8(a) then says such a supply shall be treated as a supply of the principal supply. The table is the predominant element, so packing and delivery follow it and nothing is split out.

options.text: As a mixed supply, taxed at the highest of the treatments the table, the packing and the delivery would attract separately
options.misconception: applies section 8(b) to a bundle that is natural rather than assembled by the seller
options.why: A mixed supply under section 2(74) is two or more individual supplies made together for a single price where the combination does not amount to a composite supply. Here the elements are naturally bundled and cannot be bought apart, so section 8(a) governs and the highest-rate rule in section 8(b) never arises.

items.scenario: A furniture manufacturer sells a dining table for a single price of ₹60,000. The price covers the table, its packing, and delivery to the customer's home. The table cannot be bought without delivery, and the three go together in the ordinary course of the trade.

items.stem: Is the manager's work for the company a supply on which GST is payable?

options.text: Yes, but only once the manager's annual salary crosses the registration threshold for a taxable person
options.misconception: reads the threshold as the test, when the transaction never enters the charge at all
options.why: A threshold decides who must register once a person is making supplies. Schedule III has already taken the employee's services out of the meaning of supply, so the size of the salary changes nothing.

options.text: No — services by an employee to the employer in the course of his employment are treated neither as a supply of goods nor as a supply of services
options.why: Section 7(2)(a) says the activities listed in Schedule III shall be treated neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of services, and paragraph 1 of that Schedule is services by an employee to the employer in the course of or in relation to his employment. A salary paid under a contract of employment is therefore outside the levy, and no one charges or pays tax on it.
keywords: course of or in relation to his employment

options.text: Yes — the salary is consideration for a service, so the company must pay tax on it under reverse charge
options.misconception: treats salary as a taxable supply, when Schedule III removes it from supply before any charge can attach
options.why: Reverse charge only decides who pays the tax on a supply. Paragraph 1 of Schedule III means there is no supply here at all, so there is nothing for section 9(3) or section 9(4) to fasten on to.

options.text: No, because a salary is exempted from tax by a notification issued under section 11
options.misconception: confuses an exemption, which presumes a supply, with an exclusion, which denies one
options.why: An exemption under section 11 applies to something that is a supply and would otherwise be taxable. Schedule III works one step earlier — the activity is not a supply at all — so no notification is needed and none exists.

citation.ref: Section 7(2)(a) read with paragraph 1 of Schedule III

items.scenario: A registered company pays a monthly salary to its accounts manager under a contract of employment. He works only for the company and does the accounting work his employment requires.

items.stem: What is the time of supply of these goods?

options.text: 1 August 2026, the day immediately following sixty days from the date of the invoice
options.misconception: carries the sixty-day period that section 13(3) sets for services into the rule for goods
options.why: Sixty days is the period in section 13(3) for services taxed on reverse charge. For goods, section 12(3) uses thirty days, and in any event receipt of the goods on 10 June is earlier than either of those dates.

options.text: 1 June 2026, the date of the supplier's invoice
options.misconception: applies the forward-charge rule in section 12(2), where the invoice date drives the time of supply
options.why: The invoice date drives section 12(2), which governs a forward-charge supply. Section 12(3) is a separate rule for reverse charge and it does not offer the invoice date as a candidate at all — it uses only the day following thirty days from that invoice.

options.text: 20 July 2026, the date the company actually paid the supplier
options.misconception: picks one of the three dates in section 12(3) instead of the earliest of them
options.why: Payment is one candidate under section 12(3), not the answer. The sub-section takes the earliest of the three, and receipt of the goods on 10 June is earlier than payment on 20 July.

options.text: 10 June 2026, the date of receipt of the goods
options.why: Section 12(3) fixes the time of supply of goods taxed on reverse charge as the earliest of three dates: the date of receipt of the goods, the date of payment as entered in the books of account of the recipient or debited in his bank account whichever is earlier, and the date immediately following thirty days from the date of issue of the invoice. Receipt on 10 June beats both the payment in July and the thirty-day date of 2 July.
keywords: date of receipt of the goods

citation.ref: Section 12(3), read with sections 12(2) and 13(3)

items.scenario: A registered company buys goods on which it must itself pay tax under reverse charge. The supplier's invoice is dated 1 June 2026, the company receives the goods on 10 June 2026, and it pays the supplier on 20 July 2026.

items.stem: When may the buyer take the input tax credit on that invoice?

options.text: On receipt of the last lot in July, and not before
options.why: The first proviso to section 16(2) says that where the goods against an invoice are received in lots or instalments, the registered person shall be entitled to take credit upon receipt of the last lot or instalment. The whole credit therefore waits for July, and nothing may be taken on the May or June deliveries.

options.text: In May, June and July, in proportion to the quantity received in each month
options.misconception: prorates a credit the proviso makes all-or-nothing
options.why: The proviso offers no proportion. It says the entitlement arises upon receipt of the last lot, so no part of the credit may be taken until the delivery is complete.

options.text: In May, when the invoice was issued and the first lot arrived, the invoice being one document for one supply
options.misconception: treats possession of the invoice as enough, ignoring the receipt condition in section 16(2)(b)
options.why: Holding the invoice satisfies section 16(2)(a) only. Section 16(2)(b) also requires that the goods have been received, and where they arrive in lots the first proviso says which receipt counts, namely the last one.

options.text: Never on this invoice — a split delivery obliges the supplier to issue a separate invoice for each lot
options.misconception: invents an invoicing requirement to answer a question the proviso already answers
options.why: The proviso is written for exactly this situation and assumes a single invoice against several deliveries. Nothing requires the supplier to re-invoice, and the credit is taken on the original invoice once the last lot arrives.

citation.ref: First proviso to section 16(2), read with sections 16(2)(a) and 16(2)(b)

items.scenario: A registered buyer holds one tax invoice for 100 tonnes of steel. The supplier delivers it in three lots — 40 tonnes in May, 30 tonnes in June and the last 30 tonnes in July. Every other condition in section 16(2) is satisfied throughout.

items.stem: Who may issue the credit note that reduces the tax on this supply?

options.text: The recipient, since it is his input tax credit that is wrong and he must correct it
options.misconception: reverses the direction of section 34, which corrects the supplier's outward liability and lets the recipient's credit follow
options.why: Section 34 works outwards from the supplier. He issues the credit note and declares it in his return, and the recipient reduces his credit in consequence. The reversal is a result of the note, not a substitute for it.

options.text: Either party — a credit note may be raised by whichever of them discovers the error
options.misconception: treats the credit note as an accounting document rather than the statutory instrument section 34 places in the supplier's hands
options.why: Section 34 names one issuer, and it is the supplier. Which party noticed the mistake decides nothing; the section allocates the document, and a note raised by the recipient has no effect on the tax charged.

options.text: Neither — an excess charge can be undone only by a refund claim under section 54
options.misconception: sends a routine invoice correction down the refund route that section 34 exists to avoid
options.why: Section 34 is the ordinary machinery for an invoice that overstates the taxable value or the tax. A refund claim is not needed where the supplier can issue a credit note and adjust his own liability.

options.text: Only the supplier, being the registered person who made the supply
options.why: Section 34(1) says that where one or more tax invoices have been issued and the taxable value or tax charged is found to exceed what is payable, the registered person who has supplied such goods or services or both may issue to the recipient one or more credit notes. The recipient has no such power, and a document he raises does not touch the supplier's output tax.
keywords: who has supplied such goods or services

citation.ref: Section 34(1) read with section 34(2)

items.scenario: A registered supplier issued a tax invoice charging more tax than was due. The registered recipient wants the excess undone, and proposes to raise a credit note himself, on his own stationery, and reduce his input tax credit by that amount.

items.stem: On what value does he charge GST?

options.text: On ₹20,000 only, the ₹5,000 being expenditure incurred as a pure agent
options.why: Rule 33 of the CGST Rules excludes from the value of supply the expenditure a supplier incurs as a pure agent of the recipient, provided he makes the payment on authorisation by the recipient, shows the amount separately in the invoice, and the supplies so procured are in addition to the services he supplies on his own account. All three conditions are met, so only the professional fee is taxed.

options.text: On ₹25,000, since a reimbursement is excluded only under a separate agency agreement registered with the department
options.misconception: adds a registration formality that rule 33 does not contain
options.why: Rule 33 asks for authorisation by the recipient and separate disclosure on the invoice. It requires no registered agency deed and no filing with the department, so adding that condition defeats an exclusion the rule plainly allows.

options.text: On ₹5,000 only, the filing fee being the taxable element and the professional fee a statutory levy
options.misconception: inverts the two amounts, treating the government fee as the supply and the professional service as a levy
options.why: The professional fee is the consideration for his service and is squarely taxable. The filing fee is a government charge he paid as agent for the client, and rule 33 keeps it out of the value. The two cannot be swapped.

options.text: On ₹25,000, because section 15(2)(c) brings in incidental expenses charged to the recipient
options.misconception: applies the general inclusion in section 15(2) to a reimbursement that rule 33 removes before the section can reach it
options.why: Section 15(2)(c) catches incidental expenses the supplier incurs for himself and passes on. Rule 33 carves out a different thing — money paid on the recipient's behalf, as his agent, and recovered at actuals — and where its conditions are met that amount never enters the value.

citation.ref: Rule 33, read with section 15(2) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A practising company secretary bills a client on one invoice: his professional fee of ₹20,000, and ₹5,000 of statutory filing fees he paid to the Registrar of Companies in the client's name, on the client's written authorisation, and recovered at exactly what he paid. Both amounts are shown separately on the invoice.

items.stem: How does the CGST Act treat the two registrations?

options.text: As related persons for valuation under section 15, but not as distinct persons
options.misconception: reaches for the valuation definition when section 25 has already settled who the parties are
options.why: Section 25(4) settles identity and the Explanation to section 15 settles valuation once identity is known. The two registrations are distinct persons first; the valuation rules then apply to supplies between them.

options.text: As distinct persons only where the registrations are in different States; two registrations inside one State remain one person
options.misconception: drops the words "whether in one State or Union territory or more than one" out of section 25(4)
options.why: Section 25(4) says whether in one State or Union territory or more than one. Two registrations within a single State are distinct persons on exactly the same footing as two across States.

options.text: As distinct persons, one for each registration
options.why: Section 25(4) says a person who has obtained or is required to obtain more than one registration, whether in one State or Union territory or more than one State or Union territory, shall in respect of each such registration be treated as distinct persons for the purposes of the Act. A single permanent account number and a single legal entity make no difference.

options.text: As one person, a company being a single legal entity that cannot supply anything to itself
options.misconception: applies company law's single-entity idea where section 25(4) has written a different rule for GST
options.why: Company law is not the test here. Section 25(4) deliberately splits one legal entity into as many persons as it has registrations, so that a State-wise tax can follow goods and services moving between them.

citation.ref: Sections 25(4) and 25(5), read with paragraph 2 of Schedule I
