options.why: Section 18A lets an importer voluntarily revise an entry after clearance, and the revised entry is treated as a self-assessment. Where it shows duty short paid he pays it with interest; no penalty attaches and no notice under section 28 issues. The application is filed electronically at the port where the duty was paid, with a fee of ₹1,000.

options.text: He must wait for the department, since only the proper officer can reopen a completed assessment, by a notice under section 28
options.misconception: states the position before the Finance Act, 2025, which section 18A was inserted to change
options.why: That was the position until section 18A came in. The importer no longer has to wait for a notice under section 28 to correct his own error.

options.text: He should apply under section 149 to amend the bill of entry, which is the only route for correcting a document after clearance
options.misconception: confuses amendment of a document under section 149 with revision of the entry and its assessment under section 18A
options.why: Section 149 amends a document. Section 18A revises the entry and with it the self-assessment, and it is the provision that deals with duty short paid or paid in excess on that revision.

options.text: He may revise, but the short payment carries a penalty as it would on a section 28 demand, because the error was his own
options.misconception: carries the section 28 penalty into a route whose whole purpose is that voluntary correction costs interest and nothing more
options.why: The absence of a penalty is what makes the route worth using. Voluntary revision under section 18A attracts the duty and interest alone.

citation.ref: Section 18A, read with the Customs (Voluntary Revision of Entries Post Clearance) Regulations, 2025, Notification No. 70/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 30 October 2025

items.scenario: An importer's own review in June 2026 finds that a bill of entry cleared in March 2026 classified the goods under the wrong heading and that ₹4,00,000 of duty was short paid. No audit, search, seizure or investigation has been started against him, and the entry has not been reassessed.

items.stem: Can he file it?

options.text: No — the three years from the due date ran out on 20 August 2025 and section 39(11) bars the return
options.why: Section 39(11) forbids a return being furnished after three years from the due date of furnishing it. That due date was 20 August 2022, so the door closed on 20 August 2025. Willingness to pay does not reopen it.

options.text: Yes, because the three years runs from the due date of the annual return for FY 2022-23
options.misconception: borrows the annual return's due date, which anchors the section 74A limitation rather than this one
options.why: The annual return's due date is the anchor for the section 74A limitation on demands. The three-year bar in section 39(11) runs from the due date of the very return being furnished.

options.text: Yes, on paying the late fee and interest, since the Act sets no outer date for filing a return
options.misconception: states the position before the Finance Act, 2023 sub-sections were brought into force
options.why: That was true until 1 October 2023, when the sub-sections inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 came into force under Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax. Late fee buys lateness, not a barred return.

options.text: No, and nothing can ever revive it — the bar admits of no exception
options.misconception: misses the proviso letting the Government, on the Council's recommendation, allow a barred return on notified conditions
options.why: Each of the four sub-sections carries a proviso under which the Government may, on the recommendations of the Council, notify conditions on which a barred return may still be furnished. The bar is hard but not beyond relief.

citation.ref: Section 39(11), inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 and brought into force with effect from 1 October 2023 by Notification No. 28/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023

items.scenario: A registered person never filed his return in FORM GSTR-3B for the month of July 2022, which was due on 20 August 2022. In June 2026 he wants to file it, and is willing to pay the late fee and the interest.

items.stem: What must he do in the return for the tax period following those 180 days?

options.text: Add the whole ₹1,80,000, since the invoice was not paid in full within 180 days
options.misconception: reverses everything, which was the position before rule 37 was substituted with effect from 1 October 2022
options.why: Rule 37 as substituted with effect from 1 October 2022 makes the reversal proportionate to the unpaid amount. Full reversal on a part payment overstates the liability by ₹90,000.

options.text: Add ₹90,000 to his output tax liability, with interest
options.why: Rule 37 makes the reversal proportionate to the amount left unpaid. Half the invoice value with tax is unpaid, so half the credit — ₹90,000 — is added to his output tax liability in the return for the period immediately following the 180 days, with interest under section 50.

options.text: Nothing — the credit stands, and only interest is payable on the unpaid portion
options.misconception: treats the consequence as interest alone, when the proviso adds the credit itself back to output tax liability
options.why: The second proviso to section 16(2) adds an amount equal to the credit availed to his output tax liability. Interest is on top of that, not instead of it.

options.text: Add ₹90,000, and treat that credit as lost for good, because section 16(4) has since closed for a April 2026 invoice
options.misconception: applies the section 16(4) time limit to re-availment, which rule 37(4) expressly frees from it
options.why: Rule 37(4) lets him take the credit back when he pays the supplier, and says the section 16(4) time limit does not apply to that re-availment. The credit is suspended, not destroyed.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 16(2), read with rule 37 of the CGST Rules, 2017 as substituted with effect from 1 October 2022

items.scenario: A registered person receives a supply on an invoice dated 5 April 2026 for ₹10,00,000 plus GST of ₹1,80,000, and takes the full credit of ₹1,80,000. By the 180th day from the invoice he has paid the supplier ₹5,90,000, exactly half of the ₹11,80,000 due, and nothing more. The supply is not one on which tax is payable under reverse charge.

items.stem: What is the outcome?

options.text: The appeal is admitted, and because the members differ it is deemed that no advance ruling can be issued on that point
options.why: Section 100(2) gives thirty days from communication of the ruling, and its proviso allows a further thirty days where the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause, so day forty-seven is within reach. Section 101(3) then says that where the members differ on any point, it is deemed that no advance ruling can be issued on that point.

options.text: The appeal is admitted, and the difference between the members is referred to the Appellate Tribunal for a ruling
options.misconception: assumes an appeal upward exists, when the advance ruling machinery stops at the Appellate Authority
options.why: The advance ruling route ends at the Appellate Authority. Nothing goes on to the Appellate Tribunal, and a difference between the members leaves the applicant where he started.

options.text: The appeal is admitted, and where the members differ the presiding member's casting vote settles the point
options.misconception: imports a casting vote that section 101(3) does not provide
options.why: There is no casting vote in the Appellate Authority. A difference between the two members produces no ruling at all on the point they differ on.

options.text: The appeal is time barred, because the thirty days in section 100(2) cannot be extended
options.misconception: reads the thirty days as absolute and misses the proviso allowing a further thirty
options.why: The proviso to section 100(2) allows a further period of thirty days where the Appellate Authority is satisfied that sufficient cause prevented the appellant from filing in time. Illness proved to its satisfaction is such a cause.

citation.ref: Section 100(2) with its proviso, read with section 101(3)

items.scenario: An advance ruling is communicated to the applicant on 4 May 2026. He files his appeal before the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling on 20 June 2026 — the forty-seventh day — and satisfies the Authority that illness prevented him from filing sooner. The Authority hears the appeal, and its two members then take opposite views on the only point in issue.

items.stem: Until when does the exemption hold?

options.text: Indefinitely, until the Government rescinds it, since section 25(4A) governs only a special order under section 25(2)
options.misconception: puts the sunset on the wrong sub-section; section 25(2) special orders are a different power altogether
options.why: Section 25(4A) applies to a conditional exemption granted by notification under section 25(1). A special order under section 25(2), for goods of a strategic or secret nature or for a charitable purpose, is made case by case and is a separate power.

options.text: Up to 31 March 2029
options.why: Section 25(4A) ends a conditional exemption on the 31st day of March falling immediately after two years from the date it was granted. Two years from 15 July 2026 runs to 15 July 2028, and the 31 March next after that is 31 March 2029.

options.text: Up to 31 March 2027, the end of the financial year in which it was issued
options.misconception: reads the sunset as an annual expiry at each financial year end rather than a two-year run followed by the next 31 March
options.why: There is no annual expiry in section 25(4A). The date is found by running two years from the grant and then taking the 31 March immediately after.

options.text: Up to 14 July 2028, being exactly two years from the date it was granted
options.misconception: stops at the two years and misses that the sunset then falls on the following 31 March
options.why: The two years is only the first step. Section 25(4A) then carries the expiry forward to the 31st day of March falling immediately after that point.

citation.ref: Section 25(4A), read with sections 25(1) and 25(4B)

items.scenario: The Central Government issues a notification under section 25(1) of the Customs Act on 15 July 2026 exempting a class of imported goods from basic customs duty, subject to the importer using them for a specified purpose. The notification says nothing about how long it will last, and the exemption is not one that flows from any trade agreement or international obligation.

items.stem: What must the exporter do?

options.text: Pay the integrated tax with interest by 25 April 2027, and the LUT facility stays withdrawn until he does
options.why: Rule 96A(1)(b) makes the tax payable within fifteen days after one year from the date of the export invoice where payment has not been received in convertible foreign exchange. One year from 10 April 2026 ends on 10 April 2027, so the fifteen days run to 25 April 2027. Until the amount is paid the Letter of Undertaking facility is withdrawn, and it is restored on payment.

options.text: Pay by 25 July 2026 — fifteen days after three months from the invoice
options.misconception: applies the goods clock in rule 96A(1)(a) to an export of services
options.why: Three months is the period for goods, and it measures whether the goods left India. For services rule 96A(1)(b) gives one year and measures receipt of payment instead.

options.text: Pay the tax with interest, but the LUT continues, since it is withdrawn only where fraud is found
options.misconception: misses that the facility is withdrawn on the default itself and restored only when the amount is paid
options.why: No finding of fraud is needed. The export facility under bond or Letter of Undertaking is withdrawn the moment the exporter fails to pay the amount due, and is restored once he pays.

options.text: Nothing is payable, because for services the undertaking is tested by whether the service was performed, not by payment
options.misconception: transplants the goods test onto services, where the rule turns on receipt in convertible foreign exchange
options.why: Performance is not the test for services. Rule 96A(1)(b) asks whether payment has been received in convertible foreign exchange, and non-receipt within the year makes the tax fall due.

citation.ref: Rule 96A(1)(b), read with section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A registered exporter of consultancy services holds a Letter of Undertaking and exports without payment of integrated tax. He issues an export invoice on 10 April 2026. By 10 April 2027 the client has still not paid, no money has come in convertible foreign exchange, and the exporter has asked the Commissioner for no extension.

items.stem: Where does he stand?

options.text: Within time — he has until 19 May 2027 to put the goods to the intended purpose
options.why: Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) substituted one year for six months in the IGCR Rules, 2022 with effect from 2 February 2025, so the period for putting the goods to the intended purpose runs a full year from import. Goods cleared on 20 May 2026 are within time until 19 May 2027.

options.text: Out of time, and the concessional rate is void from the date of import, so the full duty and a penalty are payable
options.misconception: treats a failed end-use condition as voiding the assessment, when the rules simply make the differential duty payable
options.why: Failing the condition does not undo the import or the assessment. The consequence the rules prescribe is that the differential duty becomes payable, with interest.

options.text: Within time, and he need file no statement at all until the goods are actually consumed
options.misconception: drops the periodic reporting, which runs on its own regardless of whether the goods have been used
options.why: The statement in Form IGCR-3 is due quarterly, a quarter being three consecutive calendar months ending in March, June, September or December. It does not wait on consumption.

options.text: Out of time — the six months ran out on 19 November 2026, and the differential duty is now payable with interest
options.misconception: uses the six-month period that Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) replaced with one year
options.why: Six months was the period until 1 February 2025. The amendment substituted one year in both the end-use rule and the rule on re-export of unutilised or defective goods.

citation.ref: Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022, rules 6, 7 and 10, as amended by Notification No. 07/2025-Customs (N.T.) dated 1 February 2025

items.scenario: An importer clears goods on 20 May 2026 at a concessional rate of duty conditional on their use in manufacture, following the IGCR Rules, 2022. On 1 December 2026 a part of the consignment is still lying unused in his factory.

items.stem: What must the head office do?

options.text: Nothing — the credit belongs to whoever the invoice names, so the head office may simply keep it
options.misconception: lets the head office retain credit on services its branches consume, which is what the ISD mechanism exists to prevent
options.why: The head office makes no outward supply of its own against which to use that credit. The Input Service Distributor mechanism exists precisely so the credit reaches the registrations that consumed the service.

options.text: Take an ISD registration and distribute both credits, paying the tax on the legal service first under its own ordinary registration
options.why: From 1 April 2025 section 20 says an office receiving invoices for input services on behalf of distinct persons shall distribute the credit through the Input Service Distributor mechanism, and section 24(viii) makes that registration compulsory. Section 2(61) now takes in invoices for services taxable under section 9(3) or 9(4), so the reverse charge legal service goes through the ISD too — the tax is paid under the ordinary registration and the credit is then distributed.

options.text: Cross-charge both services to the branches by raising a tax invoice on them as distinct persons, as it did before
options.misconception: keeps the pre-April 2025 choice, which the substitution of section 20 removed
options.why: Cross-charge was one of two permitted routes until 31 March 2025. The substituted section 20 changed may to shall, so distribution of common input services through an Input Service Distributor registration is now compulsory.

options.text: Take an ISD registration for the software subscription, but keep the legal service out, since the ISD mechanism covers only forward-charge invoices
options.misconception: applies the old definition of Input Service Distributor, which said nothing about invoices taxable under section 9(3) or 9(4)
options.why: The substituted section 2(61) expressly brings in invoices for services on which tax is payable by the recipient under section 9(3) or section 9(4). Reverse charge input services received for a branch now run through the ISD as well.

citation.ref: Sections 2(61) and 20 as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025, read with section 24(viii)

items.scenario: A company's head office in Bengaluru receives two invoices in FY 2026-27. One is for a pan-India software subscription used by all three of its branches, each separately registered. The other is for legal services from an advocate, taxable in the company's hands under reverse charge, and availed entirely for the Mumbai branch.

items.stem: By when must the audit be completed?

options.text: 9 July 2026, three months from the date the notice called for the records
options.misconception: starts the clock at the notice, which only begins the fifteen working days of notice period
options.why: The date the records were called for starts nothing. Commencement runs from the date those records are actually made available, or from the actual institution of the audit at the place of business, whichever is later.

options.text: 19 September 2026
options.why: Section 65(4) gives three months from the commencement of the audit, and the Explanation fixes commencement as the date the records called for are made available or the date of actual institution of the audit at the place of business, whichever is later. That is 20 June 2026, so the three months run to 19 September 2026, and only the Commissioner may extend, by up to six further months, for reasons recorded in writing.

options.text: 31 August 2026, three months from the day the team actually began work
options.misconception: takes the actual institution of the audit as the start without testing it against the date the records arrived
options.why: Physical institution on 1 June is one of the two dates the Explanation offers, but not automatically the operative one. The Explanation takes whichever is later, and the records were made available on 20 June.

options.text: 19 March 2027, since three months plus the six-month extension is what the section allows
options.misconception: treats the extension as automatic when it must be granted by the Commissioner for reasons recorded in writing
options.why: Six months is the outer extension, not an addition every audit gets. The Commissioner must grant it for reasons recorded in writing, and until he does the audit stands to be completed within three months.

citation.ref: Section 65(4) with its Explanation, read with rule 101 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An audit under section 65 is notified to a registered person in FORM GST ADT-01 on 10 April 2026, calling for records. The audit team arrives at the place of business and begins work on 1 June 2026. The records called for are handed over on 20 June 2026. Nothing is extended by anybody.

items.stem: What is the correct position under section 66?

options.text: The Assistant Commissioner may direct it with the Commissioner's prior approval, the Commissioner nominates and pays the accountant, and the earlier audit is no bar
options.why: Section 66(1) lets an officer not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner direct a special audit with the prior approval of the Commissioner, by a chartered accountant or a cost accountant nominated by the Commissioner. Section 66(5) makes the Commissioner determine and pay the remuneration, and his determination is final. The report is due within ninety days, extendable by a further ninety days.

options.text: The Assistant Commissioner may order it on his own, being the officer conducting the investigation
options.misconception: drops the Commissioner's prior approval, which section 66(1) makes a condition of the direction
options.why: The rank floor of Assistant Commissioner is only half the condition. Section 66(1) also requires the prior approval of the Commissioner before the direction may issue.

options.text: No special audit is possible, because the accounts have already been audited under the Companies Act
options.misconception: reads an existing audit as a bar, which section 66(3) expressly removes
options.why: Section 66(3) gives the power effect notwithstanding that the accounts have been audited under any other provision of this Act or any other law. What the officer weighs is the nature and complexity of the case and the interest of revenue.

options.text: The company appoints a chartered accountant of its own choice and bears the cost, as with any audit
options.misconception: treats a special audit like a statutory audit, where the auditee appoints the auditor and pays him
options.why: The accountant is nominated by the Commissioner, not chosen by the taxpayer, and section 66(5) puts the expenses of the examination and audit, including the remuneration, on the Commissioner. The registered person neither picks nor pays.

citation.ref: Sections 66(1), 66(2), 66(3) and 66(5), read with rule 102 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: During an investigation into a company's declared values, an Assistant Commissioner forms the view that a special audit is needed. The company objects, saying its accounts were already audited under the Companies Act and its reconciliation statement filed, and that if any audit is to happen it will appoint its own chartered accountant and bear the fee.

items.stem: What is the position on 11 December 2026?

options.text: The goods stand confiscated, the six months having passed without a notice
options.misconception: confuses seizure with confiscation, which needs a separate order under section 130
options.why: Failing to issue a notice frees the goods; it does not vest them in the Government. Confiscation rests on section 130 and an order made under it, not on the lapse of the six months in section 67(7).

options.text: The officer may keep extending as often as he needs, the outer limit being the section 74A limitation
options.misconception: makes the extension open-ended, when section 67(7) allows one further period and no more
options.why: Section 67(7) allows a single further period not exceeding six months. The limitation for a demand under section 74A runs on its own track and does not stretch the life of a seizure.

options.text: The goods must be returned unless the proper officer extends the period on sufficient cause, and provisional release on a bond and bank guarantee is open throughout
options.why: Section 67(7) requires seized goods to be returned where no notice is given within six months of the seizure, and lets the proper officer extend that on sufficient cause by a further period not exceeding six months. Section 67(6) with rule 140 keeps a separate door open the whole time — provisional release on a bond for the value of the goods in FORM GST INS-04 and a bank guarantee equal to the applicable tax, interest and penalty.

options.text: Release before the notice is possible only on paying the tax and penalty in cash
options.misconception: turns provisional release into full payment, when section 67(6) works on a bond and security
options.why: Section 67(6) releases seized goods provisionally on execution of a bond and furnishing of security. Rule 140 fixes that security as a bank guarantee equal to the applicable tax, interest and penalty — a guarantee, not a payment.

citation.ref: Sections 67(6) and 67(7), read with rule 140 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: Goods are seized from a dealer's godown on 10 June 2026 in a search authorised under section 67(2). By 11 December 2026 no notice has been issued to him. The officer says he needs longer; the dealer wants his stock back, or failing that wants it released so he can trade.

items.stem: Who may authorise the arrest, and what follows it?

options.text: Only the Commissioner may authorise it, and at ₹3 crore the offence is bailable, so the Deputy or Assistant Commissioner must admit him to bail
options.why: Section 69(1) puts the power to authorise an arrest in the Commissioner alone, by order, on reasons to believe that an offence in clauses (a) to (d) of section 132(1) has been committed. Section 132(5) makes such an offence cognizable and non-bailable only where the amount exceeds ₹5 crore; below that section 132(4) leaves it non-cognizable and bailable, and section 69(3) requires the Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner to admit the person to bail.

options.text: The Joint Commissioner may authorise it, as he may authorise an inspection or a search
options.misconception: carries the Joint Commissioner's authorisation power from section 67 across to section 69, which names the Commissioner
options.why: A Joint Commissioner authorises an inspection or a search under section 67. An arrest under section 69 may be authorised by the Commissioner and by nobody below him.

options.text: The offence is cognizable and non-bailable, so he must be produced before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours and no departmental officer may bail him
options.misconception: treats every section 132 offence as cognizable, when only the listed offences above ₹5 crore are
options.why: The twenty-four hour rule in section 69(2) applies where the offence is cognizable and non-bailable under section 132(5), which needs the amount to exceed ₹5 crore. At ₹3 crore it stays bailable.

options.text: No arrest may be authorised at all, since ₹3 crore is below the ₹5 crore line
options.misconception: reads the cognizability line as an arrest threshold, when it decides bail rather than the power to arrest
options.why: The ₹5 crore line in section 132(5) decides whether the offence is cognizable and non-bailable. An arrest may still be authorised below it, and the difference shows up in bail, not in whether the power exists.

citation.ref: Sections 69(1), 69(2) and 69(3), read with sections 132(4) and 132(5)

items.scenario: An investigation concludes that a supplier made taxable supplies without issuing invoices, with intent to evade tax. The tax evaded is ₹3 crore. The Joint Commissioner heading the investigation proposes to authorise his arrest and to have him produced before a Magistrate.

items.stem: What does section 126 do for him?

options.text: It bars the section 122 penalty, and the documentation error attracts the general penalty under section 125 instead
options.misconception: has the two the wrong way round, and reaches for the residual penalty where a specific one already exists
options.why: Section 125 applies only where no penalty is separately provided. Here the documentation error is the one section 126 protects, while the failure to issue an invoice carries its own fixed penalty and is untouched.

options.text: Nothing — section 126 is guidance for officers and gives the taxpayer no right
options.misconception: reads a mandatory provision as advisory, when section 126(1) says no officer shall impose a penalty for a minor breach
options.why: The words of section 126(1) are that no officer shall impose any penalty for minor breaches. That is a bar, not advice, and it is backed by section 126(3), which forbids any penalty without a notice and an opportunity of being heard.

options.text: It bars any penalty on the mistyped description, and does nothing at all about the section 122 penalty
options.why: Section 126(1) forbids a penalty for a minor breach or for an omission in documentation that is easily rectifiable and made without fraudulent intent, and the Explanation calls a breach minor where the tax involved is less than ₹5,000 and an error easily rectifiable where it is apparent on the face of record. Section 126(6) then shuts the section out entirely where the penalty is a fixed sum or a fixed percentage, which is what section 122(1) prescribes.
keywords: apparent on the face of record

options.text: It bars both penalties, the tax involved in each being under ₹5,000
options.misconception: applies the minor-breach relief to a fixed penalty, which section 126(6) puts outside the section
options.why: Section 126(6) says the section does not apply where the penalty is a fixed sum or is expressed as a fixed percentage. The ₹10,000 floor in section 122(1) is exactly that, so no amount of smallness reaches it.

citation.ref: Sections 126(1) with its Explanation, 126(3) and 126(6), read with sections 122(1) and 125

items.scenario: A registered person makes two slips in June 2026. On one invoice the description of the goods is mistyped, an error apparent on the face of the record, and the tax on that invoice is ₹3,000. Separately he fails to issue an invoice for a supply, a contravention for which section 122(1) prescribes a penalty of ₹10,000 or an amount equal to the tax evaded, whichever is higher.

items.stem: What is the position on compounding?

options.text: Neither may compound, because compounding is available only before a prosecution is instituted
options.misconception: reads compounding as a pre-prosecution option only, when section 138(1) allows it either way
options.why: Section 138(1) allows compounding either before or after the institution of prosecution. What it does not allow is compounding before the tax, interest and penalty involved in the offence have been paid.

options.text: The first may compound, at not less than fifty per cent and not more than one hundred and fifty per cent of the tax
options.misconception: quotes the earlier compounding band, which was replaced by a twenty-five to one hundred per cent range
options.why: Fifty per cent to one hundred and fifty per cent was the old band, with rupee floors attached to each end. Section 138(2) now runs from twenty-five per cent to one hundred per cent of the tax involved.

options.text: Both may compound, since every offence under section 132 is compoundable once the tax is paid
options.misconception: drops the exclusions in the proviso to section 138(1), the sharpest of which is the fake-invoice offence
options.why: The proviso to section 138(1) carves out cases, and issuing an invoice without any supply under section 132(1)(b) is one of them. Paying the tax does not open a door the proviso has shut.

options.text: The first may compound on paying the prescribed compounding amount; the second cannot compound at all
options.why: Section 138(1) lets the Commissioner compound an offence on payment of the compounding amount, before or after prosecution is instituted, once the tax, interest and penalty have been paid. Its proviso keeps out the offence of issuing an invoice without any supply under section 132(1)(b). Section 138(2) fixes the amount at not less than twenty-five per cent and not more than one hundred per cent of the tax involved.

citation.ref: Sections 138(1) with its proviso and 138(2), read with section 132(1)(b)

items.scenario: Two people are being prosecuted out of the same investigation. The first wrongly availed input tax credit of ₹80 lakh and has since paid the tax, the interest and the penalty. The second issued invoices without any supply behind them. Both apply to the Commissioner to compound.

items.stem: Within what limits must the compounding amount be fixed?

options.text: Any amount the Commissioner considers fit, the section leaving the figure to him
options.misconception: reads a discretion inside limits as a discretion without them
options.why: The Commissioner does choose the figure, but only between the two ends the section fixes. A discretion bounded at twenty-five per cent and one hundred per cent of the tax involved is not an open one.

options.text: Not less than ₹20,00,000 and not more than ₹60,00,000
options.misconception: quotes the band that was replaced, which ran from fifty to one hundred and fifty per cent
options.why: Fifty per cent to one hundred and fifty per cent, with rupee floors at each end, was the earlier band. It was substituted, and the range now runs from twenty-five per cent to one hundred per cent of the tax involved.

options.text: Not less than ₹10,00,000, the section fixing a floor but no ceiling
options.misconception: keeps the minimum and drops the maximum, when the section states both
options.why: Both ends are stated. A compounding amount may not exceed one hundred per cent of the tax involved, which on these figures is ₹40,00,000.

options.text: Not less than ₹10,00,000 and not more than ₹40,00,000
options.why: Section 138(2) puts a floor of twenty-five per cent of the tax involved and a ceiling of one hundred per cent of it. On ₹40,00,000 of tax that is ₹10,00,000 at the bottom and ₹40,00,000 at the top. Paying the tax, the interest and the penalty is not part of the compounding amount; it is the condition without which compounding is not allowed at all.

citation.ref: Section 138(2), the compounding amount being not less than twenty-five per cent and not more than one hundred per cent of the tax involved, read with the condition in section 138(1) that the tax, interest and penalty be paid first

items.scenario: A registered person is prosecuted for an offence in which the tax involved is ₹40,00,000. It is not an offence under section 132(1)(b), he has never been allowed compounding before, and he has paid the tax, the interest and the penalty in respect of it. He applies to the Commissioner to compound.

items.stem: How is the value of the supply determined?

options.text: At one hundred and ten per cent of the cost of provision under rule 30, or, the supply being a service, straight to rule 31 by reasonable means
options.why: Rule 27 governs a consideration not wholly in money and works down through open market value, money plus the money value of the non-monetary part, and like kind and quality, before landing on rule 30 or rule 31. Rule 30 gives one hundred and ten per cent of the cost of provision of the service. The proviso to rule 31 then lets a supplier of services disregard rule 30 and go to reasonable means directly.
keywords: one hundred and ten per cent

options.text: Only rule 30 is open; rule 31 may be reached only after rule 30 has failed
options.misconception: applies the goods sequence to a service and misses the proviso that lets a service supplier skip rule 30
options.why: For goods that sequence is right, rule 30 before rule 31. For a service the proviso to rule 31 lets the supplier opt for rule 31 disregarding rule 30, and this is a service.

options.text: At ₹4,00,000, the transaction value under section 15(1), the parties being unrelated
options.misconception: stops at the unrelated-parties test and forgets that section 15(1) also needs price to be the sole consideration
options.why: Section 15(1) gives transaction value only where the supplier and recipient are not related and the price is the sole consideration for the supply. A machine came with the money, so the price is not the sole consideration and section 15(4) sends the valuation to the rules.

options.text: At one hundred and ten per cent of the cost of acquisition of the printing machine
options.misconception: values the consideration received instead of the supply made, and picks the acquisition limb of rule 30 for a service
options.why: Rule 30 values the supply being made, not the thing received for it, and its limbs are the cost of production or manufacture, the cost of acquisition of goods, and the cost of provision of services. A branding service is valued on the last of the three.

citation.ref: Rules 27, 30 and 31 with the proviso to rule 31, read with sections 15(1) and 15(4)

items.scenario: A design studio in Chennai does branding work for an unrelated client and is paid ₹4,00,000 in cash together with a second-hand printing machine whose money value the studio cannot establish at the time of supply. There is no open market value for the service and no supply of like kind and quality can be found. The studio does know what the work cost it to provide.

items.stem: Which rate converts the value into rupees?

options.text: The rate notified by the Board under section 14 of the Customs Act for 5 June 2026
options.misconception: applies the goods rule in rule 34(1) to a supply of services
options.why: Rule 34(1) sends the value of goods to the rate notified under section 14 of the Customs Act. Services run on rule 34(2) and the accounting rate instead, even where a customs rate for the same day exists.

options.text: The accounting rate on 2 June 2026, when the service was completed
options.misconception: uses the date of provision, which is only one input into fixing the time of supply and not the date the rule names
options.why: Completion of the service is one of the events section 13 weighs in fixing the time of supply, but rule 34 converts at the date of the time of supply itself, which the facts put at 5 June 2026.

options.text: The accounting rate on 20 June 2026, when the money actually came in
options.misconception: converts at the settlement date, when the rule fixes the date of the time of supply
options.why: Rule 34(2) fixes the date of the time of supply, not the date of receipt. Any exchange gain or loss after that date is an accounting matter and does not move the value of the supply.

options.text: The rate determined under generally accepted accounting principles for 5 June 2026
options.why: Rule 34(2) values a supply of services at the applicable rate of exchange determined as per the generally accepted accounting principles for the date of the time of supply. That date is 5 June 2026, so that day's accounting rate governs, and the date of payment does not enter it.

citation.ref: Rule 34(2), read with rule 34(1) and section 13 of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A consultancy firm in Hyderabad bills an Indian client in US dollars for a domestic supply of services. The work was finished on 2 June 2026, the invoice is dated 5 June 2026 and the money arrives on 20 June 2026. The time of supply is 5 June 2026. The Board's customs exchange rate for 5 June differs from the firm's own accounting rate for that day.

items.stem: What are the central tax and the State tax on the sale?

options.text: ₹450 each, the taxable value being ₹5,000
options.why: Rule 35 backs the tax out of a price inclusive of taxes — the tax for a head is the value inclusive of taxes multiplied by that head's rate, divided by one hundred plus the sum of the applicable rates. That is 5,900 × 9 ÷ 118 = ₹450 of central tax and the same of State tax, leaving a taxable value of ₹5,000.

options.text: ₹900 of central tax and nothing else
options.misconception: runs the whole eighteen per cent through the formula as one head and forgets that an intra-State supply splits into two
options.why: 5,900 × 18 ÷ 118 = ₹900 is the total tax on the sale, not the central tax. An intra-State supply carries central tax and State tax in equal halves, so the ₹900 splits into ₹450 and ₹450.

options.text: ₹531 each, being nine per cent of ₹5,900
options.misconception: charges the rate on top of a price that already contains the tax, so the tax is itself taxed
options.why: Applying nine per cent to ₹5,900 treats the marked price as the taxable value when it is a price inclusive of taxes. Rule 35 divides by one hundred plus the sum of the rates precisely to strip the tax out first.

options.text: ₹316 each, at the six per cent half of the twelve per cent slab
options.misconception: prices the sale on a slab abolished on 22 September 2025
options.why: There is no twelve per cent slab. The September 2025 rationalisation left five, eighteen and forty per cent with effect from 22 September 2025, so an eighteen per cent supply splits nine and nine.

citation.ref: Rule 35, read with section 15(1) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A retailer in Nagpur sells an appliance for ₹5,900, the price tag saying the amount includes all taxes. The applicable rate is eighteen per cent, made up of nine per cent central tax and nine per cent State tax, and the supply is intra-State.

items.stem: What must he add to his output tax liability for that month?

options.text: ₹72,000, being the exempt share of the whole credit of ₹3,60,000
options.misconception: reverses on the entire credit in one month instead of spreading it over the sixty months rule 43 prescribes
options.why: Applying the exempt ratio to the whole ₹3,60,000 gives ₹72,000 and ignores the spreading. Rule 43 divides the common capital goods credit by sixty and applies the ratio to that monthly slice.

options.text: Nothing — rule 42 apportions inputs and input services, and capital goods credit is taken in full
options.misconception: stops at rule 42 and misses that rule 43 does the same job for capital goods
options.why: Rule 42 does apportion inputs and input services. Rule 43 is the parallel rule for capital goods, and it runs for every tax period of the five-year useful life.

options.text: ₹6,000, the whole of the month's slice
options.misconception: treats every rupee of the monthly slice as attributable to exempt supplies instead of apportioning it
options.why: ₹6,000 is Tm, the whole slice for the month. Only the exempt share of it is added back, found by multiplying by the exempt supplies over the total turnover in the State — one fifth of ₹6,000.

options.text: ₹1,200, with interest
options.why: Rule 43 spreads the common credit on capital goods over the useful life it fixes at five years, so the amount for a tax period is Tm equal to Tc ÷ 60 — that is ₹3,60,000 ÷ 60 = ₹6,000. The part attributable to exempt supplies is Te = (10,00,000 ÷ 50,00,000) × 6,000 = ₹1,200, which rule 43 adds to the output tax liability along with interest.

citation.ref: Rule 43(1), clauses (c) to (h), read with section 17(2) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A registered person buys a machine in June 2026 for ₹20,00,000 plus central tax and State tax of ₹3,60,000 in all. From the month it is received the machine is used for both taxable and exempt supplies. In that month his exempt supplies are ₹10,00,000 and his total turnover in the State is ₹50,00,000.

items.stem: What follows?

options.text: Both — the tax on the stock, and a separate default for not getting the accounts audited under section 35(5)
options.misconception: applies section 35(5), which was omitted with effect from 1 August 2021
options.why: Section 35(5) did require a chartered accountant or a cost accountant to audit the accounts above a turnover limit, and it was omitted with effect from 1 August 2021. There is no such default left to allege.

options.text: The tax must be recovered from whoever removed the goods, not from the company whose records they escaped
options.misconception: looks for a real supplier, when the sub-section fixes the liability on the person required to keep the account
options.why: Section 35(6) fixes the liability on the registered person required to keep the account. Who physically moved the goods is not what the sub-section turns on.

options.text: Tax is determined on the unaccounted goods as though the company had supplied them, and the missing chartered accountant's audit is no default at all
options.why: Section 35(6) requires the proper officer to determine the tax payable on goods not accounted for as if they had been supplied by the registered person, and then to proceed under section 74A. The audit the company is worried about no longer exists — section 35(5) was omitted with effect from 1 August 2021 and FORM GSTR-9C is now a self-certified reconciliation statement.
keywords: as if they had been supplied

options.text: Only a general penalty, since unaccounted stock has not been supplied and there is no taxable event
options.misconception: waits for an actual supply to be proved, when section 35(6) supplies the deeming
options.why: Section 35(6) does not wait for a supply to be proved. It deems the unaccounted goods to have been supplied by the registered person and lets the tax be determined on that footing.

citation.ref: Section 35(6), with section 35(5) as omitted with effect from 1 August 2021

items.scenario: A stock verification in July 2026 finds goods worth ₹8,00,000 that the company's records do not account for. The company, whose turnover crossed ₹5 crore, adds that it has never had its GST accounts audited by a chartered accountant, and asks whether that is a second default.

items.stem: What is his Net ITC for the rule 89(5) formula?

options.text: ₹9,60,000 — inputs and the machine, both being goods
options.misconception: reads inputs as covering every good, when section 2(59) excludes capital goods by definition
options.why: Section 2(59) defines inputs as any goods other than capital goods used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business. The machine is capital goods and is excluded from Net ITC by that definition alone.

options.text: ₹7,20,000 — the credit on inputs alone
options.why: The Explanation to rule 89(5) defines Net ITC as the input tax credit availed on inputs during the relevant period, and section 2(59) defines inputs as goods other than capital goods. Credit on input services and on the machine therefore stays out, and the Supreme Court upheld that exclusion in Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India (P) Ltd.

options.text: ₹11,40,000 — every rupee of credit taken in the month
options.misconception: treats the whole ledger as refundable, which neither section 54(3) nor rule 89(5) allows
options.why: Section 54(3) refunds accumulated credit only in the two cases its proviso names, and even then rule 89(5) works on a formula whose Net ITC is confined to inputs. The machine's credit is capital goods credit and never enters.

options.text: ₹9,00,000 — inputs and input services together
options.misconception: pulls input services into Net ITC, which rule 89(5) confines to inputs
options.why: Input services carry real credit and it stays usable against output tax, but the Explanation to rule 89(5) restricts Net ITC to the credit availed on inputs. That is what makes an inverted refund smaller than the accumulation it leaves behind.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) with its Explanation, read with section 54(3) and section 2(59) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A fabric manufacturer sells at five per cent and buys at eighteen per cent. In one month he takes credit of ₹7,20,000 on inputs, ₹1,80,000 on input services and ₹2,40,000 on a new machine. Every outward supply he makes is the inverted rated supply, and he applies for a refund of the accumulated credit.

items.stem: How is the export value now found?

options.text: By adding ocean freight and insurance to the foreign port, since value must reach the place of delivery
options.misconception: carries the import proviso to section 14(1) into an export, where value is taken at the place of exportation
options.why: The proviso to section 14(1) adds cost of transport, loading, unloading, handling and insurance to the value of imported goods. Export goods are valued for delivery at the time and place of exportation, so freight and insurance beyond that point are not added.

options.text: By comparison under rule 4 first, then a computed value under rule 5, then the residual method under rule 6
options.why: The export valuation rules run in order. Rule 4 compares the transaction value of goods of like kind and quality exported to the same destination at or about the same time. Rule 5 builds a computed value from the cost of production, the charges for design or brand and an amount for profit. Rule 6 falls back on reasonable means, and says in terms that the local market price of the export goods shall not be the basis.

options.text: The declared value must be accepted, section 14(1) making transaction value binding on the officer
options.misconception: treats transaction value as unrebuttable, when rule 8 lets the officer reject a declared value he has reason to doubt
options.why: Section 14(1) makes transaction value the starting point, not the last word. Rule 8 lets the proper officer reject a declared value where he has reason to doubt its truth or accuracy, after asking the exporter to explain.

options.text: By deductive value, working back from the price at which the goods sell in the country of destination
options.misconception: borrows a method from the import valuation rules, which the export rules do not contain
options.why: Deductive value belongs to the rules for imported goods. The export rules offer comparison, a computed value and the residual method, and nothing else.

citation.ref: Rules 4, 5, 6 and 8 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007, read with section 14(1)

items.scenario: An exporter declares an FOB value of ₹40,00,000 for a consignment of handicrafts. The proper officer has reason to doubt the truth of that value, asks for an explanation, and rejects the declared value under rule 8. Goods of like kind and quality were exported to the same destination a fortnight earlier.

items.stem: What duty falls at Chennai, and where is Lot 2 assessed?

options.text: Lot 2 must be assessed and the duty paid at Chennai, that being where the goods entered India
options.misconception: assesses at the port of entry, when section 55 moves the assessment to the customs station of destination
options.why: Section 54(3) lets the goods move on without payment of duty at Chennai, and section 55 applies the Act to them as if they had been imported into the customs station of destination. Kolkata is where the duty falls.

options.text: Lot 1 needs a bill of transhipment like the others, anything not cleared for home consumption needing one
options.misconception: puts a transhipment document on a transit consignment, which travels on the manifest itself
options.why: A bill of transhipment belongs to section 54 and to goods moving onto another conveyance. Transit goods under section 53 travel on the strength of their entry in the arrival manifest.

options.text: None of the three bears duty at Chennai; Lot 1 is transit, Lots 2 and 3 are transhipment, and Lot 2 is assessed at Kolkata
options.why: Section 53 allows goods manifested for transit in the same conveyance to pass without payment of duty, which covers Lot 1. Transhipment under section 54 covers goods moved onto another conveyance — sub-section (2) for a place outside India and sub-section (3) for another customs station in India, both without duty at Chennai. Section 55 then treats Lot 2 as if it had been imported into Kolkata, so it is assessed there.

options.text: All three are transhipment, the conveyance having entered an Indian customs station
options.misconception: ignores that Lot 1 never leaves the vessel, which is what makes it transit rather than transhipment
options.why: Transit under section 53 is goods that continue in the same conveyance. Transhipment under section 54 is goods moved onto another conveyance. Lot 1 stays aboard, so it is transit.

citation.ref: Sections 53, 54(2), 54(3) and 55

items.scenario: A vessel arrives at Chennai carrying three consignments, all shown in its arrival manifest. Lot 1 is for Colombo and stays aboard the same vessel. Lot 2 is to be moved onto a coastal vessel for Kolkata. Lot 3 is to be moved onto an aircraft for Dubai.

items.stem: What duty does it pay, and does interest run on the machinery?

options.text: On the domestic clearance the article is charged as one manufactured in India, so no customs duty arises at all
options.misconception: assesses the resultant product instead of the imported goods contained in it
options.why: The domestic clearance carries the import duty on the imported warehoused goods contained in the resultant product, and goods and services tax on the domestic supply of that product. Manufacture inside the warehouse does not wash the customs duty away.

options.text: Nothing on the imports used in the exported output; on the domestic clearance, the import duty on the raw material contained in it; and no interest on the machinery
options.why: Section 65 defers the duty on goods brought into the warehouse. Where the resultant goods are exported the deferred duty is never collected; where they are cleared into the domestic tariff area the import duty on the warehoused goods contained in them falls due at that point. Section 61(1)(a) gives capital goods in such a warehouse a period running till their clearance, so the ninety-day interest never begins.

options.text: Interest under section 61(2) runs on everything left in the warehouse beyond ninety days
options.misconception: applies the clause (c) interest clock to a section 65 warehouse, whose goods sit in clause (a) instead
options.why: The ninety-day interest under section 61(2) attaches to ordinary warehoused goods under section 61(1)(c). Goods in a warehouse where manufacture is permitted fall under section 61(1)(a), whose period runs till clearance or consumption, so the clock never starts.

options.text: Duty on the whole import is payable when the goods are warehoused and refunded on export
options.misconception: turns a deferment scheme into a pay-and-refund scheme, which is the very thing section 65 avoids
options.why: Nothing is paid at the time of warehousing. Section 65 works by deferring the duty until the goods leave the warehouse, and the deferment lapses altogether when the resultant goods are exported.

citation.ref: Section 65, read with sections 61(1)(a) and 61(2) and the Manufacture and Other Operations in Warehouse (No. 2) Regulations, 2019

items.scenario: A company holds a licence under section 58 and permission under section 65 for its bonded warehouse. It brings in imported raw material and machinery without paying duty, manufactures, exports seventy per cent of the output and clears thirty per cent into the domestic tariff area. The machinery has been in the warehouse for well over a year.

items.stem: How are the goods assessed?

options.text: Registering the contract after clearance is enough, registration being a procedural step
options.misconception: treats a condition precedent as a formality, when the Regulations require registration before any clearance
options.why: The Project Imports Regulations, 1986 make registration of the contract a condition to be satisfied before any goods are cleared. A contract registered afterwards does not bring the earlier clearance under heading 9801.

options.text: Spare parts of any value are covered, so long as the contract lists them
options.misconception: drops the ten per cent cap the Regulations put on spares and consumables
options.why: Listing them in the contract is necessary but not sufficient. The Project Imports Regulations, 1986 cap spare parts, raw materials and consumable stores at ten per cent of the value of the goods registered.

options.text: Each item is assessed under its own heading, the project scheme being only an exemption laid on top
options.misconception: misses that project imports is a classification device rather than an exemption
options.why: Heading 9801 is a classification heading in the First Schedule, and its whole purpose is to put a whole plant under one heading instead of a hundred. It is not an exemption sitting on top of ordinary classification.

options.text: Everything for the initial setting up goes under one heading at one rate, but the contract had to be registered before clearance and the spares are covered only up to ten per cent
options.why: Project imports classify all goods imported for the initial setting up or substantial expansion of a specified project under heading 9801 of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, at a single rate, whatever heading each item would carry alone. The Project Imports Regulations, 1986 require the contract to be registered with the proper officer before any clearance, on the sponsoring authority's recommendation, and cover spare parts only up to ten per cent of the value of the goods registered — the excess is assessed on its own merits.

citation.ref: Heading 9801 of the First Schedule, read with regulations 4, 5 and 6 of the Project Imports Regulations, 1986

items.scenario: A company setting up a new power project imports turbines, control cabling and structural steel under one contract, together with spare parts worth fifteen per cent of the value of the goods in the contract. It files the bill of entry first and applies to register the contract afterwards.

items.stem: What duty may be imposed, and for how long does it run?

options.text: ₹65 per kg, the injury being separate from the dumping
options.misconception: adds the two margins instead of choosing the lower of them
options.why: The two figures measure the same harm from two directions and are never added. The duty is the lower of the margin of dumping and the amount that removes the injury.

options.text: ₹25 per kg, but only for six months, that being the life of an anti-dumping duty
options.misconception: gives a final duty the life of a provisional duty imposed on a preliminary finding
options.why: Six months is the outer life of a provisional duty imposed under section 9A(2) on a preliminary finding, extendable to nine months. A final duty runs for five years under section 9A(5).

options.text: ₹40 per kg, section 9A allowing the full margin of dumping
options.misconception: reads the statutory ceiling as the amount payable and ignores the lesser duty rule in the Rules
options.why: The margin of dumping is a ceiling, not the levy. Where a smaller amount would remove the injury, the lesser duty rule requires that smaller amount to be recommended, and here it is ₹25.

options.text: ₹25 per kg, for five years from imposition unless revoked earlier, extendable by five years after a review
options.why: Section 9A(1) caps the duty at the margin of dumping, here ₹40, but the Anti-dumping Rules, 1995 require the authority to recommend the lower amount that would be adequate to remove the injury — the lesser duty rule — so ₹25 is the duty. Section 9A(5) ends it five years from the date of imposition unless revoked earlier, and lets the Government extend it by a further five years after a review.

citation.ref: Sections 9A(1), 9A(2) and 9A(5), read with rule 4(d) of the Anti-dumping Rules, 1995

items.scenario: The designated authority finds that a chemical is being exported to India at ₹40 per kg below its normal value, and that a duty of ₹25 per kg would be enough to remove the injury to the domestic industry. The Central Government decides to impose a final anti-dumping duty.

items.stem: Whom may the measure reach?

options.text: Every source, and the measure may run indefinitely once serious injury is established
options.misconception: drops the duration limits, which cap a safeguard measure at four years and ten years in all
options.why: A safeguard measure ceases four years from the date of imposition unless revoked earlier, and even with extensions the total period may not exceed ten years. Serious injury does not buy a permanent measure.

options.text: None — a safeguard may take the form only of a duty, and a duty cannot be limited by origin
options.misconception: states the position before section 8B was substituted, when it was confined to a safeguard duty
options.why: Section 8B was substituted to speak of safeguard measures, which include a safeguard duty, a tariff-rate quota and such other measure as may be prescribed. The form is wider than it once was, and the carve-out applies whatever form is chosen.

options.text: Every source, a safeguard being applied to imports of the article as such and not country by country
options.misconception: treats a safeguard as blind to origin, which the developing-country carve-out contradicts
options.why: A safeguard measure is imposed on the article rather than on a particular exporter, but section 8B carves out imports originating in a developing country within the three per cent and nine per cent limits. Origin therefore does matter.

options.text: Only the imports from the developed countries — each developing country is under three per cent and together they are under nine
options.why: Section 8B keeps a safeguard measure off an article originating in a developing country whose share of the imports of that article into India does not exceed three per cent, and where several such countries are each below that figure, off all of them so long as their imports together do not exceed nine per cent. Four countries at two per cent each come to eight per cent, so all four are outside.

citation.ref: Section 8B as substituted — the developing-country carve-out at three per cent individually and nine per cent in the aggregate, and the four-year life with a ten-year outer limit

items.scenario: Imports of a steel product surge and cause serious injury to Indian producers. Four developing countries each account for two per cent of India's imports of that product; the rest comes from developed countries. The Central Government proposes a safeguard measure.

items.stem: How long may the measure run?

options.text: To 28 February 2030 at the outside, ten years from the date it was first applied
options.why: A safeguard measure ceases four years from the date of its application unless revoked earlier, and the Central Government may extend it where the domestic industry is adjusting. The extension is not open-ended: the total period, extensions included, may in no case exceed ten years from the date on which the measure was first applied. That date is 1 March 2020, so the outer limit is 28 February 2030.

options.text: To 2032, the ten years running afresh from the most recent extension
options.misconception: starts the outer limit at the latest extension instead of at the first application
options.why: The ten years run from the date on which the measure was first applied. Counting from each extension would let a measure be renewed for ever, which is the thing the outer limit exists to stop.

options.text: It ceased on 28 February 2024 and could not have been extended
options.misconception: reads the four-year period as the outer limit rather than as the first term
options.why: Four years is where a measure ends if nothing is done, not where it must end. Extension is expressly provided for where the domestic industry has taken steps to adjust; what is capped is the total.

options.text: Indefinitely — a tariff-rate quota limits quantity rather than charging duty, so the time limits on a safeguard duty do not reach it
options.misconception: reads the time limits as attaching to the form of the measure rather than to the measure
options.why: A safeguard measure means a safeguard duty, a tariff-rate quota, or such other measure as the Central Government considers appropriate, and the four-year and ten-year limits are written against the measure, not against any one of its forms.

citation.ref: Section 8B as substituted — a safeguard measure ceases four years from the date of application unless revoked earlier, and the total period including extensions may not exceed ten years from the date it was first applied; a measure may be a safeguard duty, a tariff-rate quota or such other measure as the Central Government considers appropriate

items.scenario: A safeguard measure in the form of a tariff-rate quota is applied to an article with effect from 1 March 2020. It has since been extended twice, the domestic industry having shown each time that it is adjusting. The industry now asks for it to be carried on until 2032.

items.stem: How are the three treated?

options.text: The unit charges integrated tax on the domestic sale, that being an inter-State supply made by it
options.misconception: puts the tax on the supplier when the clearance is taxed as an import in the buyer's hands
options.why: A clearance from a zone into the domestic tariff area is treated as an import. The duty and the integrated tax are collected from the buyer on a bill of entry under the Customs Act, not charged by the unit on a tax invoice.

options.text: The catering is exempt rather than taxable, since supplies into a Special Economic Zone carry no tax
options.misconception: confuses exemption with zero rating, and applies either to a supply that is neither
options.why: An exempt supply carries no tax and breaks the supplier's input tax credit; a zero-rated supply carries no tax and keeps it. The catering is neither — outside authorised operations, it is an ordinary taxable supply on which integrated tax is charged.

options.text: Everything supplied to the unit is zero-rated, a Special Economic Zone being outside the customs territory of India
options.misconception: states the position before the words for authorised operations were put into section 16(1)(b)
options.why: The zone's deemed-foreign status is for customs purposes and never made every supply into it zero-rated. Section 16(1)(b) now says in terms that the supply must be for authorised operations.

options.text: The machinery is zero-rated, the catering is an ordinary taxable inter-State supply, and the domestic sale is an import in the buyer's hands
options.why: Section 16(1)(b) of the IGST Act makes a supply to a Special Economic Zone unit zero-rated only where it is for authorised operations, which the letter of approval and the specified officer's endorsement establish. The catering falls outside and is taxed as an ordinary inter-State supply. Section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 treats a clearance from the zone into the domestic tariff area as an import, so the buyer files a bill of entry and pays customs duty with integrated tax.

citation.ref: Section 16(1)(b), read with section 30 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005 and section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

items.scenario: A supplier in Pune makes two supplies to a Special Economic Zone unit in Mumbai — machinery covered by the unit's letter of approval for its authorised operations, and catering for a staff anniversary party which the letter of approval does not cover. Separately, the unit sells finished goods to a buyer in the domestic tariff area.

items.stem: What is his position?

options.text: The goods are a deemed export, but only the Export Oriented Unit may claim the refund, having borne the tax
options.misconception: fixes the refund on the recipient alone, when the third proviso to rule 89(1) allows either party
options.why: The third proviso to rule 89(1) allows the application to be made by the recipient or by the supplier of deemed export supplies. Where the supplier claims it, the recipient must not have availed the input tax credit and must say so.

options.text: The goods are a deemed export on which tax must be charged and paid, with the refund open to him or to the unit; the services are not a deemed export at all
options.why: Section 147 lets the Government notify supplies of goods as deemed exports, and Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax includes a supply to an Export Oriented Unit. A deemed export is not zero-rated, so it cannot go under bond or LUT and the tax must be paid first; the third proviso to rule 89(1) then lets either the supplier or the recipient claim the refund. Section 147 speaks only of goods, so the design services fall outside it.

options.text: Both are deemed exports, the recipient being an Export Oriented Unit and that being what the notification turns on
options.misconception: reads the notification as covering anything supplied to a listed recipient, when section 147 reaches only goods
options.why: The identity of the recipient is only half the test. Section 147 empowers the Government to notify supplies of goods as deemed exports, and a service can never be one however the recipient is described.

options.text: Both may go under his Letter of Undertaking without payment of tax, as any export may
options.misconception: treats a deemed export like a zero-rated export, when the goods never leave India and the tax must be paid
options.why: A zero-rated export may go under bond or LUT because section 16 of the IGST Act says so. Section 147 zero-rates nothing; the goods stay in India, the tax is charged and paid, and relief comes afterwards as a refund.

citation.ref: Section 147, read with Notification No. 48/2017-Central Tax dated 18 October 2017 and the third proviso to rule 89(1) of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered manufacturer supplies goods to an Export Oriented Unit following the prescribed procedure, and separately supplies design services to the same unit. He wants to make both under his Letter of Undertaking without paying tax, and to claim a refund afterwards.

items.stem: Is the subscription a supply under section 7?

options.text: Yes, as a supply between related persons without consideration under paragraph 2 of Schedule I
options.misconception: reaches for Schedule I when consideration was actually paid, so section 7(1) is satisfied on its own
options.why: Schedule I is the route for a supply made without any consideration. Here a subscription was paid, so the supply falls inside section 7(1)(aa) directly and Schedule I is never needed.

options.text: No — the doctrine of mutuality survives, so there is no supply between a club and its own members
options.misconception: carries the pre-GST mutuality decisions forward past a provision written to override them
options.why: The doctrine of mutuality is exactly what the Explanation to section 7(1)(aa) sets aside, and it says so in terms — notwithstanding anything contained in any other law or in any judgment, decree or order of any court. A decision from the sales tax and service tax era cannot survive a clause aimed at it.

options.text: Yes, but only for subscriptions collected from the date the amending Act came into force, not for earlier years
options.misconception: reads the amendment as prospective when it was given effect from 1 July 2017
options.why: The clause was inserted with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017, the day GST began. There is no window in which the earlier position applied, so the retrospective effect reaches every subscription from the start of the levy.

options.text: Yes — section 7(1)(aa) deems the club and its members to be two separate persons, and it does so with effect from 1 July 2017
options.why: Section 7(1)(aa), inserted by the Finance Act, 2021 with effect from 1 July 2017, brings in the activities of a person other than an individual to its members for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, and its Explanation deems them to be two separate persons notwithstanding anything in any other law or in any judgment, decree or order of any court. Those closing words are what displaces the doctrine of mutuality for GST.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(aa) with its Explanation, as inserted by the Finance Act, 2021 with effect from 1 July 2017

items.scenario: An incorporated members' club collects an annual subscription from each member and lets them use its swimming pool, gymnasium and dining room. It has never charged GST, arguing that a club and its members are one and the same, so it cannot supply anything to itself, and pointing to the Supreme Court's decision on mutuality in the sales tax and service tax era.

items.stem: When, if ever, does the ₹200 become consideration?

options.text: When it is received, as an advance against the supply of goods
options.misconception: treats a deposit as an advance, when the proviso to section 2(31) keeps it outside payment until it is applied
options.why: An advance is money paid towards the price; a deposit is money held as security for the return of the crates. The proviso to section 2(31) keeps a deposit outside payment for the supply until the supplier applies it, so nothing happens on receipt.

options.text: On forfeiture, as a separate supply of agreeing to tolerate the customer's failure to return the crates
options.misconception: invents a second supply out of the forfeiture, when the money simply becomes the price of the original supply
options.why: Forfeiting the security is not a fresh supply of agreeing to tolerate an act. The money is applied against the very supply it was taken for, so it becomes consideration for that original supply, and nothing new is supplied.

options.text: Never — a security deposit is a financial transaction and stays outside GST whatever happens to it
options.misconception: reads the proviso as a permanent exclusion rather than a deferral until the deposit is applied
options.why: The proviso is written as a condition, not an exclusion — the deposit stays outside payment unless the supplier applies it as consideration. Once it is applied it is consideration like any other, and the word unless is what carries that.

options.text: Not when it is taken, but when the manufacturer applies it against the supply on forfeiture
options.why: The proviso to section 2(31) says a deposit given in respect of a supply shall not be considered as payment made for the supply unless the supplier applies such deposit as consideration for the said supply. Holding it as a refundable security is not applying it; appropriating it on forfeiture is, and the tax attaches at that moment.

citation.ref: Section 2(31) with its proviso, read with section 15(1)

items.scenario: A beverage manufacturer supplies drinks in returnable glass crates and takes ₹200 per crate as a refundable security, shown separately on the invoice and credited to a deposit account. Crates returned within six months get the money back. Where a customer does not return the crates, the manufacturer forfeits the security and writes it off against the customer's account.

items.stem: Is the sale of the car a supply on which the consultant must charge GST?

options.text: No — the sale is not made in the course or furtherance of business, so section 7(1)(a) is not satisfied
options.why: Section 7(1)(a) needs the supply to be made in the course or furtherance of business. The car was a private asset, never part of the practice, so the transaction is outside the scope of supply. His being a taxable person under section 2(107) settles who accounts for tax on his supplies; it does not turn a private disposal into one.

options.text: Yes — he is a registered taxable person, and every sale by a taxable person is a supply
options.misconception: reads registration as the test of supply, when registration decides who accounts for tax and section 7 decides what a supply is
options.why: Registration answers a different question. Section 2(107) makes him a taxable person because he is registered, but section 7(1)(a) still has to be satisfied, and it asks whether the transaction was in the course or furtherance of business.

options.text: Yes, but only on the margin, the difference between the sale price and the depreciated value under rule 32(5)
options.misconception: jumps to a valuation rule before deciding whether there is a supply at all
options.why: Rule 32(5) is a valuation rule for a person dealing in buying and selling second-hand goods, and it decides how much a supply is worth. It cannot be reached until there is a supply, and here there is none.

options.text: Yes — paragraph 1 of Schedule I makes the permanent transfer of a business asset a supply even without consideration
options.misconception: applies Schedule I to an asset that was never a business asset and on which no credit was taken
options.why: Paragraph 1 of Schedule I reaches the permanent transfer or disposal of business assets where input tax credit has been availed on them. Neither limb is met — the car was not a business asset and no input tax credit was ever taken.

citation.ref: Sections 7(1)(a), 2(17) and 2(107), read with paragraph 1 of Schedule I

items.scenario: A management consultant is registered under GST for his practice. He sells the family car, which he bought years ago in his own name, used only for personal travel, never entered in the books of the practice, and on which no input tax credit was ever claimed. The buyer is a second-hand car dealer.

items.stem: How does paragraph 4 of Schedule II treat the two of them?

options.text: Neither is deemed to supply anything, but both must reverse the credit taken on the goods still held
options.misconception: replaces the deemed supply with a bare reversal, when section 29(5) sets a higher-of test and the neighbour is out of it altogether
options.why: A bare reversal is not the rule. On cancellation section 29(5) requires payment of the credit on the goods held or the output tax on them, whichever is higher, and the neighbour who transferred his business as a going concern is outside the deeming clause in the first place.

options.text: Both are deemed to supply the goods, since Schedule II makes anything listed in it a supply on its own
options.misconception: uses the pre-2018 reading in which section 7(1)(d) let Schedule II itself create a supply
options.why: Schedule II classifies; it does not create. The old section 7(1)(d) was omitted and section 7(1A) substituted by the CGST (Amendment) Act, 2018 with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017, and the going-concern carve-out inside clause (c) would apply even if it did.

options.text: The proprietor is deemed to supply the goods immediately before he ceases to be a taxable person; the neighbour is not, the business having been transferred as a going concern
options.why: Clause (c) of paragraph 4 deems goods forming part of the assets of a business to be supplied in the course or furtherance of business immediately before the person ceases to be a taxable person, and it carves out two cases — where the business is transferred as a going concern to another person, and where it is carried on by a personal representative who is deemed to be a taxable person.
keywords: ceases to be a taxable person

options.text: Neither is deemed to supply anything, because nothing was sold and no consideration passed
options.misconception: requires a consideration where paragraph 4 is written as a deeming provision that does not need one
options.why: Paragraph 4 is a deeming provision. Clause (a) says so expressly, applying whether or not for a consideration, and clause (c) deems a supply on a person ceasing to be a taxable person without any transaction at all.
keywords: whether or not for a consideration

citation.ref: Paragraph 4(c) of Schedule II, read with section 7(1A) and section 29(5)

items.scenario: A proprietor winds up his trading business and surrenders his registration. Trading stock and a packing machine, on both of which input tax credit was taken, are still lying with him and he keeps them. His neighbour, in the same position a month earlier, had instead sold his entire business to a buyer who carried it on unchanged.

items.stem: What is the place of supply, and which tax is charged?
