options.text: Maharashtra under section 10(1)(a), the movement of the goods terminating on delivery to the buyer named on the invoice
options.misconception: applies the movement rule when a specific clause for installed goods displaces it
options.why: Section 10(1)(a) governs where the supply merely involves movement of goods, and even then it looks at where the movement terminates for delivery, which was Karnataka and not the buyer's registered State. A supply assembled at site falls under clause (d) instead.

options.text: Karnataka, the place of installation, and the supply is inter-State so integrated tax is charged
options.why: Section 10(1)(d) of the IGST Act fixes the place of supply, where goods are assembled or installed at site, as the place of such installation or assembly. That is Karnataka. The supplier is in Gujarat, so under section 7(1) the supply is inter-State and integrated tax is charged.

options.text: Gujarat, the location of the supplier, and the supply is intra-State so central tax and State tax are charged
options.misconception: puts the place of supply at the supplier's location, which is the one thing section 10 never does
options.why: The location of the supplier is one half of the comparison that decides whether a supply is inter-State; it is never itself the place of supply. Treating it as one here would produce an intra-State supply and the wrong two heads of tax.

options.text: Maharashtra, the location of the recipient, and the supply is inter-State
options.misconception: applies the recipient-location rule for services in section 12(2) to a supply of goods
options.why: The location of the recipient is the general rule for a supply of services under section 12(2). Goods are governed by section 10, and section 10(1)(d) looks at the place of installation and not at the registered address on the invoice.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(d), read with sections 7(1) and 8(1) of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A supplier registered in Gujarat sells a packaging line to a buyer registered in Maharashtra. The contract is signed in Mumbai and the invoice is raised on the Maharashtra registration, but the line is shipped to the buyer's factory in Karnataka, where the supplier's engineers assemble and commission it.

items.stem: On which of these does GST fall?

options.text: On the sale of the vouchers to the distributor, at the time the vouchers are issued
options.misconception: taxes the voucher itself, using the time-of-supply rule for vouchers that has since been taken away
options.why: That answer comes from the old time-of-supply rule for vouchers, which fixed the date of issue where the supply was identifiable. Those sub-sections were omitted with effect from 1 October 2025, and the voucher itself is not a supply of goods or of services in the first place.

options.text: On the marketing agency's fee alone — the transactions in the vouchers themselves are not supplies, and the lapsed vouchers are not consideration for anything
options.why: A transaction in a voucher is either money, where it is a pre-paid instrument recognised by the Reserve Bank of India, or an actionable claim, and neither is a supply of goods or of services. Distribution on a principal-to-principal basis is therefore outside the levy, while a commission or fee earned for distributing or marketing vouchers is a supply of services. Vouchers never redeemed are not consideration for any supply, since no supply is made against them.

options.text: On the distributor's margin, treated as a commission for a service of distributing the vouchers
options.misconception: reads a principal-to-principal trading margin as agency commission, which it is not
options.why: The distributor buys and sells on his own account, so his margin is a trading profit on a principal-to-principal basis and not a commission for any service. Only a distributor or agent who is actually paid a fee or commission by the issuer supplies a service.

options.text: On the marketing fee, and also on the lapsed vouchers as an amount retained for tolerating non-redemption
options.misconception: turns breakage into consideration for tolerating an act, when nothing was supplied against those vouchers
options.why: Breakage is money kept where no supply was ever made. It is not consideration for tolerating an act or for anything else, because there is no supply for it to be the price of.

citation.ref: Circular No. 243/37/2024-GST dated 31 December 2024, read with sections 2(52) and 2(102) and paragraph 6 of Schedule III

items.scenario: A retail chain issues gift vouchers redeemable at its own stores. It sells them in bulk to a distributor at a discount to face value; the distributor sells them on to corporate customers on his own account and keeps the difference. A separate marketing agency is paid a fee by the chain for promoting the vouchers. Some vouchers are never redeemed and lapse.

items.stem: On which amounts does GST fall?

options.text: On Q's commission only — the helpdesk is part of the voucher arrangement and follows it outside the levy
options.misconception: lets the voucher's treatment swallow a separate service supplied alongside it
options.why: A voucher being outside the levy says nothing about services supplied around it. The helpdesk is a service the issuer buys and pays for separately, and it is taxable on its own footing.

options.text: On P's margin and on Q's commission, both being the reward for distributing vouchers
options.misconception: treats a trading margin and an agency commission as the same thing because both are earned on distribution
options.why: What they are paid for differs. P buys and sells on his own account and his margin is a trading profit on a principal-to-principal basis, which the voucher's own treatment keeps outside the levy. Q never owns the voucher and is paid a commission by the issuer for a service.

options.text: On none of them, the whole voucher arrangement being outside GST
options.misconception: extends the treatment of the voucher itself to every payment made in connection with it
options.why: What is outside the levy is the transaction in the voucher, because a voucher is money or an actionable claim and neither is a supply of goods or of services. A commission paid for placing it, and a fee paid for a helpdesk, are payments for services and are inside.

options.text: On Q's commission and on Q's helpdesk fee; P's margin is outside the levy
options.why: Trading in vouchers on a principal-to-principal basis is not a supply of goods or of services, so P's margin bears no tax. Where a distributor or agent is paid a commission or fee by the issuer, that commission is consideration for a supply of services and is taxable. A separate service supplied to the issuer around the voucher — a helpdesk, marketing, co-branding — is taxable in its own right on the same reasoning.

citation.ref: Circular No. 243/37/2024-GST dated 31 December 2024 — trading in vouchers on a principal-to-principal basis, commission paid to a distributor or agent, and additional services supplied to the issuer

items.scenario: An issuer of gift vouchers uses two routes to market. P buys vouchers from the issuer at a discount to face value and sells them on his own account, keeping the difference. Q places vouchers with customers as the issuer's agent and is paid a commission by the issuer for each one placed. Q is also paid a separate fee by the issuer for running a helpdesk for voucher holders.

items.stem: Can he, and how?

options.text: Yes — use the central tax and State tax credit against their own heads first, then the integrated tax credit for whatever is left
options.misconception: reverses the mandatory order, when section 49B and rule 88A require the integrated tax credit to be exhausted first
options.why: The order is not the taxpayer's to choose. Section 49B with rule 88A requires the input tax credit of integrated tax to be exhausted first, before the credit of central tax or State tax may be used at all.

options.text: Yes — apply the integrated tax credit to integrated tax first, then split the remaining ₹40,000 as ₹20,000 to central tax and ₹20,000 to State tax
options.why: Section 49(5)(a) applies the integrated tax credit to integrated tax first, leaving ₹40,000, and rule 88A lets that balance go towards central tax and State tax in any order and in any proportion. Splitting it evenly leaves ₹30,000 on each of the two heads, exactly matched by the ₹30,000 of credit on each, so nothing is left to pay in cash.
keywords: any order and in any proportion

options.text: No — the whole ₹40,000 balance of integrated tax credit must go to central tax first, leaving ₹20,000 of State tax to be paid in cash
options.misconception: uses the rigid sequence that applied before rule 88A, which required the integrated tax balance to be set against central tax first
options.why: That was the position before rule 88A, which now lets the balance of integrated tax credit go towards central tax and State tax in any order and in any proportion. Forcing it all onto one head is what strands credit on the other and creates the cash payment.
keywords: any order and in any proportion

options.text: No — the ₹20,000 of central tax credit left over can be used against the State tax shortfall, so the order does not matter
options.misconception: lets central tax credit pay State tax, which clauses (e) and (f) of section 49(5) forbid outright
options.why: Clauses (e) and (f) of section 49(5) say central tax credit shall not be utilised towards payment of State tax and State tax credit shall not be utilised towards payment of central tax. The two heads never cross, which is precisely why the split of the integrated tax balance decides the cash outgo.

citation.ref: Sections 49(5)(a) to 49(5)(f) and 49B, read with rule 88A of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: For a tax period a registered person in Karnataka has credit in his electronic credit ledger of ₹1,00,000 integrated tax, ₹30,000 central tax and ₹30,000 State tax. His output liability is ₹60,000 integrated tax, ₹50,000 central tax and ₹50,000 State tax. He wants to pay nothing in cash.

items.stem: What may he settle out of the credit ledger?

options.text: The output tax and the interest, interest being an amount payable in respect of a tax already covered by credit
options.misconception: attaches interest to the tax it arises on, when the credit ledger is limited to output tax by its own words
options.why: Interest has no such attachment. The credit ledger may be used for making any payment towards output tax, and interest is not output tax however it arose, so it is paid from the cash ledger.

options.text: Only the output tax on his own supplies; the reverse charge tax and the interest must come from the cash ledger
options.why: Section 49(4) lets the electronic credit ledger be used for making any payment towards output tax and nothing else, and section 2(82) defines output tax as the tax chargeable on taxable supplies made by him but excluding tax payable by him on a reverse charge basis. Interest is not output tax at all, so both the reverse charge tax and the interest fall to section 49(3) and the cash ledger.

options.text: All three, the credit ledger being available for any amount payable under the Act
options.misconception: gives the credit ledger the width that section 49(3) gives the cash ledger
options.why: It is section 49(3) that allows payment of tax, interest, penalty, fees or any other amount, and it says so of the electronic cash ledger. Section 49(4) confines the credit ledger to output tax.

options.text: The output tax and the reverse charge tax, both being tax; only the interest needs cash
options.misconception: treats reverse charge tax as output tax, which the definition in section 2(82) expressly excludes
options.why: Section 2(82) defines output tax as the tax chargeable on taxable supplies made by him or by his agent, but excluding tax payable by him on a reverse charge basis. That exclusion is why reverse charge liability is always a cash payment.

citation.ref: Sections 49(3) and 49(4), read with section 2(82) and rules 86 and 87 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered person has a healthy balance in his electronic credit ledger and almost nothing in his electronic cash ledger. For the month he owes output tax on his own supplies, tax on a legal service received from an advocate on which he must pay under reverse charge, and interest on a payment he made late in an earlier month.

items.stem: Which credits stand?

options.text: The canteen credit stands because the law obliges the employer to provide it; the credit on the free samples must go
options.why: The proviso to section 17(5)(b) allows input tax credit where it is obligatory for an employer to provide the goods or services to its employees under any law for the time being in force, and a canteen the Factories Act requires is exactly that. Section 17(5)(h) blocks credit on goods disposed of by way of gift or free samples, so the sample packs lose it.

options.text: Neither stands — outdoor catering is blocked outright, and goods given away are blocked as well
options.misconception: reads clause (b) as an absolute block and misses the proviso for benefits an employer must provide by law
options.why: Clause (b) is not absolute. Its proviso restores the credit where it is obligatory for an employer to provide the same to its employees under any law for the time being in force, and the statutory canteen meets that test.

options.text: The samples credit stands and output tax must be paid on them as a deemed supply; the canteen credit must go
options.misconception: turns a free sample into a taxable supply, when there is no consideration and clause (h) deals with it by blocking the credit instead
options.why: A free sample given to a person who is not related and not an employee carries no consideration, so there is no supply to tax. The Act deals with it on the credit side instead, and clause (h) blocks the credit on goods disposed of by way of gift or free samples.

options.text: Both stand, since the samples build the market and the canteen keeps the workforce, so both are used in the course of business
options.misconception: applies the general business-purpose test where section 17(5) blocks credit regardless of business purpose
options.why: Section 17(5) opens with words that override section 16(1), so a business purpose is not enough. Outdoor catering is blocked by clause (b) unless the proviso applies, and free samples are blocked by clause (h) whatever the commercial reason for giving them.

citation.ref: Sections 17(5)(b) with its proviso and 17(5)(h), read with section 16(1)

items.scenario: A pharmaceutical company distributes physician sample packs free to doctors, and runs a canteen in its factory which the Factories Act requires it to provide because of the number of workers employed there. It has taken input tax credit on the goods made into the samples and on the catering service bought in for the canteen.

items.stem: Which documents does section 31(3) require, and when?

options.text: A receipt voucher on the date of receipt of the service, and a refund voucher if the service is later cancelled
options.misconception: confuses the documents that go with an advance payment received with those that go with a reverse charge inward supply
options.why: A receipt voucher is issued under section 31(3)(d) on receipt of an advance payment, and a refund voucher under section 31(3)(e) where that advance is returned without any supply. Neither belongs to a recipient discharging tax under reverse charge on a service he has received.

options.text: A self-invoice on the date of receipt of the service, and separately a payment voucher at the time of making the payment
options.why: Section 31(3)(f) requires a registered person liable to pay tax under section 9(3) or 9(4) to issue an invoice to himself in respect of goods or services received from an unregistered supplier on the date of receipt. Section 31(3)(g) separately requires him to issue a payment voucher at the time of making payment to the supplier. Both are required and one cannot stand for the other.

options.text: A bill of supply on the date of receipt, the transporter being unregistered and charging no tax
options.misconception: reaches for a bill of supply, which belongs to a supplier making exempt supplies or paying under composition
options.why: A bill of supply is issued under section 31(3)(c) by a registered person supplying exempted goods or services or paying tax under the composition levy. It has nothing to do with a recipient paying under reverse charge.

options.text: A payment voucher alone, since that is the only document the recipient issues under reverse charge
options.misconception: drops the self-invoice, which section 31(3)(f) requires as the document recording the inward supply
options.why: The payment voucher records money going out. The inward supply itself is recorded by the self-invoice which section 31(3)(f) requires on the date of receipt, and without it there is no invoice supporting the credit.

citation.ref: Sections 31(3)(f) and 31(3)(g), read with rule 52 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and rule 47A

items.scenario: A registered manufacturer receives goods transport services from an unregistered transporter and must pay the tax himself under reverse charge. He receives the service on 4 June 2026 and pays the transporter on 30 June 2026. His accountant proposes to raise one document covering both events.

items.stem: What can he actually file?

options.text: Both, because the annual return under section 44 is where the year is reconciled and any gap can be closed there
options.misconception: treats the annual return as a cure for unfiled monthly returns, which it never is
options.why: The annual return under section 44 reconciles what the periodic returns said; it does not replace one that was never filed, and filing it leaves the bar in section 39(10) exactly where it was.

options.text: Neither — rule 59(6) blocks the May GSTR-1 while April's GSTR-3B is unfiled, and section 39(10) blocks the May GSTR-3B for the same reason
options.why: Rule 59(6) bars a registered person from furnishing the details of outward supplies in FORM GSTR-1 where the return in FORM GSTR-3B for the preceding tax period has not been furnished. Section 39(10) bars a return under section 39 for a tax period where the return for any previous tax period has not been furnished. Both doors are shut until April is filed.

options.text: The May GSTR-1 only, since section 37 is about outward supplies and stands apart from the payment of tax
options.misconception: treats the outward supply statement as independent, when rule 59(6) chains it to the previous month's GSTR-3B
options.why: Section 37 does deal with outward supplies, but rule 59(6) makes furnishing them conditional on the previous month's GSTR-3B having been filed, and section 37(4) separately bars furnishing them where any previous period's details are missing.

options.text: Both, so long as he pays the self-assessed tax for May in full, which is what makes a return valid under section 2(117)
options.misconception: reads section 2(117) as permission to skip a month, when it only says what a return already permitted must contain to be valid
options.why: Section 2(117) says what makes a return valid — self-assessed tax paid in full on a return furnished under section 39(1). It does not license filing out of order, and section 39(10) still bars the May return while April is outstanding.

citation.ref: Sections 37(4), 39(10) and 2(117), read with rule 59(6) of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered person has not filed FORM GSTR-3B for April 2026. In June he wants to file GSTR-1 for May 2026 so that his customers get their credit, and to file GSTR-3B for May 2026, saying he will come back to April later when his cash improves.

items.stem: Under which section is he assessed, and what must precede the order?

options.text: Section 63, best judgement assessment of an unregistered person, after a show cause notice and an opportunity of being heard, within five years from the due date of the annual return
options.why: Section 63 covers a taxable person who fails to obtain registration though liable, or whose registration has been cancelled but who was liable to pay tax. The proper officer may assess to the best of his judgement, but only after a show cause notice and an opportunity of being heard, and within five years from the date the annual return for the relevant financial year was due.

options.text: Section 62, best judgement assessment for failing to file returns, after a notice under section 46
options.misconception: applies the non-filer provision to a person who was never registered and so was never required to file
options.why: Section 62 reaches a registered person who fails to furnish a return even after a notice under section 46 is served on him. A person who never registered has no return to file and no notice under section 46 could reach him.

options.text: Section 61, scrutiny of returns, with a discrepancy notice in FORM GST ASMT-10
options.misconception: reaches for scrutiny where there is no return to scrutinise
options.why: Section 61 lets the proper officer scrutinise the return furnished by a registered person and seek an explanation of the discrepancies in FORM GST ASMT-10. With no registration and no return, there is nothing for the section to work on.

options.text: Section 64, summary assessment, the department already holding evidence of the liability
options.misconception: treats holding evidence as enough for a summary order, when the section needs a risk to revenue from delay and a senior officer's prior permission
options.why: Section 64 needs more than evidence — it needs sufficient grounds to believe that any delay will adversely affect the interest of revenue, and the previous permission of the Additional Commissioner or Joint Commissioner. Neither is present here.

citation.ref: Section 63 with its proviso, read with sections 61, 62 and 64

items.scenario: A trader crossed the registration threshold two years ago and never applied for registration. He has filed no returns, because he has none to file. The department now has his bank statements and wants to assess the tax he should have paid.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The notice is invalid, because recovery from a third person is possible only through the District Collector as an arrear of land revenue
options.misconception: reduces section 79 to one mode when it lists several the officer may use singly or together
options.why: Sending a certificate to the District Collector to recover the amount as an arrear of land revenue is one of the modes in section 79, not the only one. Requiring a third person who owes the defaulter money to pay it over is a separate mode standing on its own.

options.text: The notice is valid, the three months under section 78 having passed, and the customer who ignored it is himself deemed a defaulter for the amount
options.why: Section 78 requires payment within three months from the date of service of the order and allows recovery to begin after that, which 5 August is. Section 79(1)(c) lets the officer require any other person from whom money is due to the defaulter to pay it over, and where that person fails to comply he is deemed to be a defaulter in respect of the amount and may be proceeded against himself.

options.text: The notice is valid, but the customer bears no consequence, the liability being the company's alone
options.misconception: misses section 79(1)(c), which makes the third person personally answerable once he disregards the notice
options.why: Section 79(1)(c) makes the third person who fails to comply with the notice deemed to be a defaulter in respect of the amount, and he is then liable to all the consequences under the Act as though it were his own arrear.

options.text: The notice is premature, since recovery may begin only after the time for filing an appeal has expired
options.misconception: ties the start of recovery to the appeal period rather than to the three months in section 78
options.why: Section 78 ties recovery to three months from the service of the order and to nothing else, with a proviso letting the officer demand payment even sooner in the interest of revenue for reasons recorded in writing. The appeal period runs on its own track.

citation.ref: Sections 78 with its proviso and 79(1)(c) with section 79(4)

items.scenario: An order confirming a demand is served on a company on 1 April 2026. Nothing is paid and no appeal is filed. On 5 August 2026 the proper officer writes to one of the company's customers, who owes it money for goods already delivered, requiring the customer to pay that money to the Government instead. The customer ignores the notice and pays the company.

items.stem: May he?

options.text: Yes — the two Acts are separate levies, so each administration may pursue its own tax on the same facts
options.misconception: treats cross-empowerment as absent, when section 6 was written precisely to stop two administrations working the same case
options.why: Cross-empowerment is the whole point of section 6. Sub-section (1) makes State officers proper officers for this Act, and sub-section (2)(b) then stops a second set of proceedings on the same subject matter, so one case is worked by one administration.

options.text: No — section 6(2)(b) bars proceedings under this Act where a proper officer under the State Act has already initiated proceedings on the same subject matter
options.why: Section 6(1) authorises officers appointed under the State GST Act to be proper officers for the purposes of this Act, and section 6(2)(b) then bars the central tax officer from initiating any proceedings on the same subject matter where a proper officer under the State Act has already initiated proceedings on it.

options.text: Yes, provided he obtains the prior approval of his Commissioner, who may assign the function to him under section 2(91)
options.misconception: reads the Commissioner's power to assign functions as a power to override the statutory bar in section 6(2)(b)
options.why: Section 2(91) lets the Commissioner assign a function and so decide who the proper officer is. It says nothing about whether the proceedings may be brought at all, and no assignment can lift the bar that section 6(2)(b) imposes.

options.text: No, but only because a Commissioner may not exercise powers conferred on an officer subordinate to him
options.misconception: inverts section 5(2), which lets a senior officer exercise a subordinate's powers, and applies it to the wrong question
options.why: Section 5(2) runs the other way — an officer may exercise the powers and discharge the duties conferred on any other officer of central tax subordinate to him. The bar here comes from section 6(2)(b) and has nothing to do with rank.

citation.ref: Sections 6(1) and 6(2)(b), read with sections 2(91) and 5(2)

items.scenario: A State tax officer has already issued a notice to a registered person on the wrongful availment of credit for a particular period, and the proceedings are under way. A central tax officer, who has come to the same conclusion from his own analysis, now proposes to issue his own notice on the same credit for the same period.

items.stem: Is he right on either point?

options.text: Right on the second — once goods are confiscated the title vests in the Government and no fine or tax is payable on top
options.misconception: forgets that section 130(3) keeps the tax, penalty and charges payable in addition to any fine
options.why: Section 130(3) says the tax, penalty and charges payable in respect of the goods remain payable in addition to the fine. Confiscation does not settle the liability, and the owner must be offered the option of a fine before it takes effect.

options.text: No on both — section 130 stands on its own grounds, and the officer must offer him the option of a fine in lieu of confiscation
options.why: Section 130(1) lists its own grounds, one of which is not accounting for goods on which the person is liable to pay tax, and the section no longer overrides section 129 alone, so detention in transit is not a precondition. Section 130(2) then requires the officer to give the owner an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation.

options.text: No on both, but the fine may be fixed at any amount the officer thinks fit
options.misconception: treats the fine as unbounded, when section 130(2) sets both a ceiling and a floor
options.why: The fine is bounded at both ends. It shall not exceed the market value of the goods confiscated less the tax chargeable thereon, and the aggregate of the fine and the penalty shall not be less than the penalty equal to hundred per cent of the tax payable on those goods.

options.text: Right on the first — confiscation under section 130 can only follow a detention under section 129
options.misconception: keeps the two sections chained together after the opening words of section 130 were changed to stop it overriding section 129 alone
options.why: The two were pulled apart when the opening words of section 130 were changed so that the section no longer overrides section 129 alone. Each proceeding now rests on its own grounds, and a detention is not a precondition to a confiscation.

citation.ref: Sections 130(1), 130(2) with its provisos and 130(3), read with section 129

items.scenario: A dealer is found holding a large quantity of goods for which he has no account and on which he is liable to pay tax, and the officer records that the goods were kept off the books with intent to evade payment of tax. Proceedings under section 130 are begun. The dealer says confiscation cannot be ordered unless the goods were first detained in transit under section 129, and that in any case the department must simply take the goods.

items.stem: What credit may he take, and how?

options.text: No credit at all; credit on stock is available only to a person registering for the first time
options.misconception: reads section 18(1) as covering only new registrations, when clauses (c) and (d) cover changes of status
options.why: Section 18(1) has four clauses. Two cover a person registering for the first time, and the other two cover a person ceasing to pay under the composition levy and a person whose exempt supply becomes taxable.

options.text: Credit on the stock only; capital goods are outside section 18(1) altogether
options.misconception: carries the rule for a fresh registrant across to a composition taxpayer, forgetting that clause (c) adds capital goods
options.why: Capital goods are outside clauses (a) and (b), which cover a person taking registration for the first time. Clause (c), for a person ceasing to pay under the composition levy, expressly adds credit on capital goods, reduced by the prescribed percentage points.

options.text: Full credit on everything held on 31 August 2026, the one-year bar applying only to a person taking voluntary registration
options.misconception: confines the one-year limit to one clause when section 18(2) governs the whole of sub-section (1)
options.why: Section 18(2) is written across the whole of sub-section (1) — a registered person shall not be entitled to take input tax credit under sub-section (1) in respect of any supply after the expiry of one year from the date of issue of the tax invoice. It does not pick out a clause.

options.text: Credit on the stock and, reduced by the prescribed percentage points, on the van, as on 31 August 2026 — but nothing on an invoice older than one year, and only on a declaration in FORM GST ITC-01
options.why: Section 18(1)(c) gives a person ceasing to pay under the composition levy credit on inputs held in stock, inputs contained in semi-finished or finished goods held in stock, and on capital goods, as on the day immediately preceding the date from which he becomes liable under section 9, with the capital goods credit reduced by the prescribed percentage points. Section 18(2) bars credit on any supply after one year from the date of issue of the tax invoice, and rule 40 requires the declaration in FORM GST ITC-01.

citation.ref: Sections 18(1)(c) and 18(2), read with rule 40 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and FORM GST ITC-01

items.scenario: A trader paying tax under the composition levy crosses the limit and becomes liable to pay tax under section 9 from 1 September 2026. On 31 August 2026 he holds inputs in stock, inputs contained in finished goods in stock, and a delivery van bought two years ago. Some of the stock is covered by invoices dated more than a year before.

items.stem: What must he do, and what does he owe?

options.text: Apply for revocation; the credit question falls away, cancellation ending every liability from that date
options.misconception: reads cancellation as wiping the slate, which section 29(3) expressly denies
options.why: Section 29(3) says cancellation shall not affect the liability to pay tax and other dues for any period prior to the date of cancellation, whether or not they are determined before or after that date, and section 29(5) adds the payment on goods still held.

options.text: Apply for a fresh registration, revocation being available only where the person himself sought the cancellation
options.misconception: inverts section 30, which is available precisely where the officer cancelled on his own motion
options.why: Section 30 is written for the opposite case. It applies where the registration has been cancelled by the proper officer on his own motion, and a person who asked for his own cancellation has nothing to revoke.

options.text: Apply for revocation, and reverse the credit taken on the goods still held, which is all section 29(5) requires
options.misconception: settles for a reversal when section 29(5) prescribes the higher of the credit and the output tax on those goods
options.why: A reversal is only half the test. Section 29(5) requires an amount equal to the credit on the goods held or the output tax payable on them, whichever is higher, and where the goods have appreciated or the credit was small the output tax is the larger figure.

options.text: Apply for revocation under section 30, having first furnished all the pending returns with tax, interest, penalty and late fee; and pay the higher of the credit on the goods held and the output tax on them
options.why: Section 30 lets a person whose registration was cancelled by the officer on his own motion apply for revocation, and rule 23 requires all returns due for the period from the effective date of cancellation to be furnished first, with the tax, interest, penalty and late fee. Section 29(5) then requires payment of an amount equal to the credit on inputs held in stock and on capital goods, or the output tax payable on those goods, whichever is higher.

citation.ref: Sections 29(3), 29(5) and 30, read with rules 22, 23 and 44 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered person's registration is cancelled by the proper officer on his own motion for a long run of unfiled returns. Three weeks later the person wants the registration back so he can resume trading. He also holds inputs in stock and a machine on which credit was taken, and says that since the registration is gone the credit question is gone with it.

items.stem: What must the officer do next, and what did he do at the assessment stage?

options.text: The officer assessed the goods in the first instance, as customs assessment has always worked, so no separate order is needed
options.misconception: uses the pre-self-assessment sequence, in which the proper officer made the assessment and the importer merely made the entry
options.why: That was the older sequence, replaced when self-assessment was introduced. Section 17(1) now puts the assessment on the importer, and what the officer does afterwards is a re-assessment which section 17(5) makes him explain in a speaking order.

options.text: The importer self-assessed under section 17(1) and the officer re-assessed under section 17(4); a speaking order on the re-assessment must follow within fifteen days
options.why: Section 17(1) makes the importer self-assess the duty. Section 17(4) lets the proper officer re-assess on verification or examination, and section 17(5) requires him, where the re-assessment is contrary to the self-assessment and the importer has not confirmed his acceptance in writing, to pass a speaking order within fifteen days from the date of re-assessment of the bill of entry.

options.text: No speaking order is needed because the importer paid the duty, payment amounting to acceptance
options.misconception: treats payment under protest as the written acceptance that would excuse a speaking order
options.why: What excuses the order is the importer confirming his acceptance of the re-assessment in writing. Paying so that the goods can move is not that confirmation, so the speaking order is still due.

options.text: The officer must instead make an order under section 47 permitting clearance, which is itself the assessment order
options.misconception: confuses the clearance order with the assessment, when section 47 only records that the goods are not prohibited and the duty is paid
options.why: Section 47(1) is the clearance step — the proper officer makes an order permitting clearance for home consumption once satisfied that the goods are not prohibited and the duty and charges have been paid. It settles nothing about the classification and is not an assessment order.

citation.ref: Sections 17(1), 17(4) and 17(5), read with sections 46(1) and 47(1)

items.scenario: An importer files a bill of entry for home consumption, self-assessing the goods under a heading that carries a lower rate. The proper officer examines the goods, disagrees, and re-assesses them under a different heading. The importer does not accept the change and says so, but pays under protest so that the consignment can move.

items.stem: What follows?

options.text: Nothing can be recovered at all, the one-year period for a notice having expired
options.misconception: quotes the pre-2016 limitation of one year, which was replaced by two years for an ordinary short-levy
options.why: One year was the earlier period and it is no longer the law; an ordinary short-levy now carries two years from the relevant date. In any event the payment here was voluntary, so limitation never came into it.

options.text: He must also pay a penalty equal to fifteen per cent of the duty for the immunity to apply
options.misconception: imports the pre-notice penalty from a collusion case under section 28(5) into an ordinary short-levy under section 28(2)
options.why: The fifteen per cent penalty belongs to section 28(5), which deals with a case of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. An ordinary short-levy under section 28(1) needs only the duty and the interest.

options.text: A notice must still issue, since the period for a notice in a non-collusion case is two years and eighteen months is inside it
options.misconception: reads the limitation period as compelling a notice, when section 28(2) removes the need for one where the duty and interest are paid voluntarily
options.why: The two years in section 28(1)(a) is the outer limit for serving a notice, not an instruction to serve one. Where the duty and interest are paid voluntarily and the officer is informed, section 28(2) bars a notice for that amount.

options.text: The proper officer shall not serve a notice for the amount paid, though he may still proceed for any part found short paid
options.why: Section 28(2) lets the person pay the duty on his own ascertainment or on the officer's, with interest under section 28AA, and inform the proper officer in writing, and the proper officer shall not serve any notice in respect of the amount so paid. What survives is the officer's right to proceed for any amount found short paid beyond what was paid.

citation.ref: Sections 28(1)(a) and 28(2), read with sections 28(4), 28(5) and 28AA

items.scenario: An importer discovers, eighteen months after clearance, that a consignment was short-levied because of a clerical mistake in his own declaration. There was no collusion and nothing was suppressed. Before any notice reaches him he pays the differential duty with interest and writes to the proper officer telling him so.

items.stem: Which vessel may consume the imported stores without payment of duty?

options.text: The vessel sailing to Singapore, and only for fuel, spare parts being outside the meaning of stores
options.misconception: reads the definition of stores too narrowly, when section 2(38) includes spare parts and equipment expressly
options.why: Section 2(38) defines stores as goods for use in a vessel or aircraft and includes fuel and spare parts and other articles of equipment, whether or not for immediate fitting. Spare parts are inside the definition by its own words.

options.text: The vessel sailing to Singapore, being a foreign-going vessel; the coastal vessel's stores are dutiable in the ordinary way
options.why: Section 87 allows imported stores on board to be consumed without payment of duty while the vessel is a foreign-going vessel, and section 2(21) makes that one engaged in the carriage of goods or passengers between a port in India and a port outside India. A coastal vessel plying between two Indian ports is not one.

options.text: Both, since section 87 speaks of stores consumed on board and says nothing about the voyage
options.misconception: drops the foreign-going condition, which is the only thing section 87 turns on
options.why: Section 87 is conditional in its own words — the consumption is free of duty while the vessel or aircraft is a foreign-going one. Strip that condition out and the section says nothing at all about which stores it covers.

options.text: Neither, until the stores have been warehoused under section 85 and cleared for consumption
options.misconception: makes warehousing a precondition, when section 85 is an option for stores entered for warehousing rather than a step every ship must take
options.why: Section 85 lets imported goods entered for warehousing and intended for use as stores be warehoused without assessment to duty. It is a facility for stores that go into a warehouse, not a precondition to consuming stores already on board under section 87.

citation.ref: Section 87, read with sections 2(21), 2(38) and 85

items.scenario: A shipping company runs two vessels out of an Indian port. One carries cargo between that port and Singapore. The other carries cargo between that port and another Indian port and never leaves Indian waters. Imported fuel and provisions are taken on board both, and are consumed at sea.

items.stem: Does the explanation reach the supplies made before it was issued?

options.text: No — it operates only from the date of the second notification, like any other amendment
options.misconception: reads a section 11(3) explanation as an ordinary prospective amendment when the sub-section gives it always-was effect
options.why: An ordinary amending notification does work prospectively, but section 11(3) is written differently and says so in terms — every such explanation shall have effect as if it had always been part of the first notification. The whole point of the sub-section is to reach back, which is why the power is fenced by a time limit.

options.text: No — an exemption once granted can only be narrowed by withdrawing the notification and issuing a fresh one
options.misconception: denies a clarificatory power that section 11(3) expressly grants
options.why: Withdrawal and re-issue is one route, but it is not the only one. Section 11(3) gives a separate power to clarify the scope or applicability of an existing notification by inserting an explanation into it, and the department is entitled to use that power instead.

options.text: Yes — it was inserted within a year of the parent notification, so it takes effect as though it had been part of it from the start
options.why: Section 11(3) lets the Government insert an explanation in a notification issued under section 11(1) at any time within one year of the issue of that notification, and says every such explanation shall have effect as if it had always been part of the first such notification. Eleven months is inside that window, so the clarification runs back to the parent notification's own effective date of 1 April.
keywords: as if it had always been

options.text: Yes, but only if a special order under section 11(2) is passed for this supplier
options.misconception: confuses the general notification power with the exceptional special-order power that operates case by case
options.why: Section 11(2) is a different instrument altogether — a special order in each case, under circumstances of an exceptional nature to be stated in the order, granting an exemption. It is not a step in making a general notification work, and nothing in section 11(3) calls for one.

citation.ref: Section 11(3), read with section 11(1)

items.scenario: A notification issued under section 11(1) exempts a described category of services with effect from 1 April. Eleven months later the Government issues a second notification inserting an explanation into the first one, saying the description was never meant to cover a particular sub-category. A supplier who treated that sub-category as exempt from April onwards is told he owes tax for the whole period.

items.stem: On which of the three must the company pay GST under reverse charge?

options.text: The sitting fees and the rent, since the recipient in both cases is a body corporate
options.misconception: treats a company recipient as the trigger, when the trigger is a service supplied by a person acting as a director
options.why: The recipient being a body corporate is a condition of entry 6, not the whole of it; the supply must also be made by a director acting as such. Renting out property he owns personally is not that, so the rent stays on the director and no reverse charge arises on the company.

options.text: All three, because each is a payment by a company to its own director
options.misconception: makes the identity of the payee the test when the notification asks in what capacity the service was supplied
options.why: Entry 6 asks what was supplied and in what capacity, not who was paid. Employment is outside supply altogether, and a letting made in the director's own right as a property owner is supplied in a capacity that is not that of a director, so two of the three payments fall outside the entry.

options.text: Only the sitting fees
options.why: The whole-time director's salary is not a supply at all — entry 1 of Schedule III puts services by an employee to the employer in the course of employment outside the scope of supply. The sitting fees are not employment income and fall inside entry 6 of Notification 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), so the company pays under reverse charge in cash. The rent is supplied in the director's personal capacity as owner of the godown, not in his capacity as a director, so entry 6 does not reach it.

options.text: None, because a director is an employee of the company and employment is outside GST
options.misconception: extends the employment exclusion to a non-executive director who has no employment with the company
options.why: A whole-time director is an employee and an independent director is not. The employment exclusion covers the first and cannot be stretched to the second, whose sitting fees are paid for services rendered to the company otherwise than under a contract of employment.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with entry 6 of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), entry 1 of Schedule III, and Circulars 140/10/2020-GST and 201/13/2023-GST

items.scenario: A private limited company makes three payments in a month. It pays a monthly salary to its whole-time director, booked as salary and subjected to tax deduction at source under section 192 of the Income-tax Act. It pays sitting fees to an independent director for attending board meetings, with deduction under section 194J. And it pays rent to another director for a godown he owns personally and has let to the company.

items.stem: Which of the three sales is a supply of services under paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II?

options.text: All three, because a builder selling flats is always supplying a construction service
options.misconception: reads paragraph 5(b) as taxing every sale by a builder rather than as a rule about when the money arrived
options.why: The trade of the seller is not the test. Paragraph 5(b) turns on when the consideration was received, and paragraph 5 of Schedule III keeps a completed building outside GST no matter who sells it.

options.text: None, because the sale of a building is outside GST under Schedule III
options.misconception: reads paragraph 5 of Schedule III without the opening words that make it subject to paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II
options.why: Paragraph 5 of Schedule III is expressly made subject to paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II. It keeps a completed building outside GST, and it surrenders to paragraph 5(b) wherever money came in before completion, which is exactly Flat 1.

options.text: Flat 1 alone
options.why: The carve-out in paragraph 5(b) applies only where the entire consideration has been received after the completion certificate or after first occupation, whichever is earlier. Flat 1 fails it because a booking amount came in before either event, and the whole value then becomes a supply of services. Flat 2 and Flat 3 both satisfy it — for Flat 3 the earlier of the two events was first occupation, and the entire consideration came after that.

options.text: Flats 1 and 3
options.misconception: treats the completion certificate as the only trigger and overlooks that first occupation can come earlier
options.why: The paragraph names two events and takes the earlier of them, and it is the completion certificate that is qualified by the words where required. For Flat 3 the building had already been first occupied when the money came in, so the exception is met and the sale is not a supply of services.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II, read with paragraph 5 of Schedule III

items.scenario: A builder sells three flats in one project. For Flat 1 the buyer paid a small booking amount before the competent authority issued the completion certificate and the rest afterwards. For Flat 2 the buyer paid the whole price after that certificate was issued. Flat 3 was bought by a family who paid the entire price after the building had been first occupied by earlier residents but before the certificate finally came through.

items.stem: Is the chain right about its counter invoices?

options.text: No, but nothing is needed either, since a customer who is unregistered can take no credit
options.misconception: reads the requirement backwards — it applies because the customer is unregistered, not despite it
options.why: Credit is not what the rule is about. The requirement attaches to an invoice issued to an unregistered customer, so the customer's inability to take credit is the reason the rule exists rather than a reason to skip it.

options.text: Yes — one scannable code on the invoice discharges both requirements
options.misconception: treats the electronic-invoicing code and the dynamic code as one obligation when they serve different purposes
options.why: They are two obligations in two different rules, aimed at two different readers. One lets anyone verify that an invoice was reported; the other lets a consumer pay. A code that does the first does not do the second.

options.text: No — a counter invoice needs a Dynamic Quick Response code carrying payment details, which is not what the Portal returns
options.why: The counter invoices go to an unregistered customer, and rule 46 requires such an invoice to bear a Dynamic Quick Response code — a payment instruction the customer can scan and pay with. The code the Portal returns with an Invoice Reference Number is static and identifies the invoice; it does nothing the dynamic code is there to do.

options.text: No — the chain must also report its counter invoices to the Invoice Registration Portal
options.misconception: extends rule 48(4) to business-to-consumer supplies, which it has never covered
options.why: Rule 48(4) covers supplies to a registered person, exports and supplies to a special economic zone. A business-to-consumer invoice is outside it and is never uploaded to the Invoice Registration Portal, which is precisely why the separate dynamic-code requirement exists.

citation.ref: Rule 46 (the Dynamic Quick Response code requirement) with Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax, read with rule 48(4)

items.scenario: A retail chain is above the notified turnover for both electronic invoicing and the code requirement in rule 46. It reports its invoices to registered dealers to the Invoice Registration Portal and receives an Invoice Reference Number with the signed code the Portal returns. It then prints that same Portal-generated code on the counter invoices it hands to walk-in customers, saying an invoice bearing a scannable code satisfies the rule.

items.stem: Which of the two balances can he claim back as a refund?

options.text: Both balances, since section 49(6) covers the cash ledger and the credit ledger alike
options.misconception: reads section 49(6) as a right to a refund when it only routes the claim to section 54, which then restricts credit refunds
options.why: Section 49(6) does mention both ledgers, but it grants nothing by itself — it says the balance may be refunded in accordance with section 54. Section 54(3) is where the credit ledger is cut down to two cases, and neither of them fits a purely domestic supplier.

options.text: The credit ledger balance only, because money once paid into the cash ledger is tax already paid
options.misconception: treats a challan deposit as a payment of tax when it becomes tax only on being debited against a liability
options.why: A challan credits the cash ledger; it does not discharge anything. The amount becomes tax only when it is debited against a liability, and until then it is the taxpayer's money sitting on the portal.

options.text: Neither, because a balance in either ledger can only be set off against future liability
options.misconception: treats both ledgers as carry-forward accounts when the cash ledger holds the taxpayer's own money
options.why: Carrying forward is what happens to the credit balance, and it is a fair description of it. It is not true of the cash ledger, where the money is a deposit the taxpayer made and has never spent, and the proviso to section 54(1) exists to give it back.

options.text: The cash ledger balance only
options.why: Section 49(6) lets a balance be refunded in accordance with section 54, and the proviso to section 54(1) gives the electronic cash ledger balance its own route because that money is a deposit, not tax. The unutilised credit cannot follow it — section 54(3) allows a refund of credit only on zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax or under an inverted duty structure, and he has neither.

citation.ref: Section 49(6) and the proviso to section 54(1), read with section 54(3)

items.scenario: A trader over-deposited on a challan and has ₹4,20,000 sitting unused in his electronic cash ledger. He also has ₹6,00,000 of unutilised input tax credit in his electronic credit ledger. He makes only domestic taxable supplies, all at the same rate as the goods he buys, and he exports nothing.

items.stem: From which date does interest under section 56 run?

options.text: From 10 March 2026, the date of the appellate order
options.misconception: starts the clock at the order when both the main limb and the proviso start it at the receipt of an application
options.why: Neither limb of section 56 mentions the date of an order as a starting point. The main limb runs from the application under section 54(1) and the proviso from the application filed consequent to the order, so the date of the appellate order does no work here.
keywords: the application filed consequent to the order

options.text: No interest is payable, because the refund was never ordered by the proper officer under section 54(5)
options.misconception: overlooks the Explanation deeming an appellate order of refund to be an order under section 54(5)
options.why: The Explanation to section 56 deems an order of refund made by an appellate authority, the Tribunal or a court against an order of the proper officer to be an order passed under section 54(5). The refund is therefore ordered under that sub-section for the purposes of the section, and interest follows.

options.text: From the day after sixty days from 2 April 2026
options.why: The proviso to section 56 applies because the refund arises from an order that has attained finality, and it starts the clock at sixty days from the date of receipt of the application filed consequent to such order. That application is the one dated 2 April 2026, so interest runs from the day immediately after those sixty days until 20 August 2026, at the higher rate the proviso carries.

options.text: From sixty days after the original 2023 refund application
options.misconception: uses the first application when the proviso names the one filed after the order
options.why: The original application was rejected and the proviso does not revive it. It names the application filed consequent to the order that attained finality, and that is the 2026 application, not the 2023 one.
keywords: the application filed consequent to the order

citation.ref: Proviso to section 56 with the Explanation to section 56, read with sections 54(1) and 54(5)

items.scenario: A refund claim filed in 2023 was rejected. The Appellate Authority allowed it by an order dated 10 March 2026, and no further appeal was filed, so the order attained finality. The claimant filed a fresh refund application consequent to that order on 2 April 2026. The department actually paid on 20 August 2026.

items.stem: Which of the two steps was open to the Appellate Authority?

options.text: Both, because an appellate authority has all the powers of the authority whose order it is reviewing
options.misconception: assumes a general appellate power of remand that section 107(11) removes in terms
options.why: The powers of a first appellate authority under GST are the ones section 107(11) gives it, and that sub-section names three — confirming, modifying or annulling — and then takes away a fourth by barring a reference back. There is no residual power to fall back on.

options.text: Neither
options.why: Section 107(11) lets the Appellate Authority pass an order confirming, modifying or annulling the decision appealed against but expressly says it shall not refer the case back to the adjudicating authority, so the remand is outside its power and the contracts had to be examined in its own further inquiry. The first proviso then bars an order enhancing a penalty unless the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed order.

options.text: The remand, but not the enhancement
options.misconception: half-remembers the sub-section, keeping the bar in its first proviso and dropping the bar in its main limb
options.why: The bar on sending the case back sits in the main limb of section 107(11) itself, not in a proviso. Both steps fail, and for different reasons — one for want of power, the other for want of notice.

options.text: The enhancement, because no fresh tax was demanded and the proviso only protects against a demand of tax
options.misconception: reads the first proviso as covering tax alone when it names fee, penalty, fine in lieu of confiscation, refund and credit
options.why: The first proviso to section 107(11) lists an order enhancing any fee or penalty or fine in lieu of confiscation, confiscating goods of greater value, or reducing a refund or input tax credit. A penalty is squarely inside that list, and the second proviso is the one that deals with tax.

citation.ref: Section 107(11) with its first proviso

items.scenario: Hearing a taxpayer's first appeal, the Appellate Authority finds that the adjudicating authority never looked at a bundle of contracts the taxpayer had filed. It sends the matter back to that officer for a fresh order, and in the same order it raises the penalty from the figure the adjudicating authority had imposed, without putting the increase to the appellant.

items.stem: May he do so?

options.text: No — revision lies only where the order is prejudicial to the taxpayer, and this one favoured him
options.misconception: inverts the direction of section 108, which is written for orders prejudicial to the revenue
options.why: Section 108(1) lets the Revisional Authority act where the order is erroneous in so far as it is prejudicial to the interest of revenue. An exemption wrongly allowed is exactly that; a taxpayer aggrieved by an order goes in appeal instead.
keywords: prejudicial to the interest of revenue

options.text: Yes, and with no time limit, because the point is a fresh one the appeal never touched
options.misconception: takes the proviso's permission without the window it is given in
options.why: The proviso grants the power and fixes its outer limit in the same breath — one year from the appellate order or the three years in clause (b), whichever is later. A fresh point buys a longer window, not an unlimited one.

options.text: No — once an order has gone in appeal it is out of the revisional power altogether
options.misconception: applies clause (a) of section 108(2) without reading the proviso that qualifies it
options.why: That is what clause (a) says on its own, and the proviso immediately following it says otherwise for a point which has not been raised and decided in the appeal. Reading the clause without its proviso closes a door the section deliberately leaves open.

options.text: Yes, on the exemption point, within one year of the appellate order or three years of the original order, whichever is later
options.why: Clause (a) of section 108(2) bars revision of an order that has been the subject of an appeal, but the first proviso qualifies it — the Revisional Authority may pass an order on any point which has not been raised and decided in that appeal, before the expiry of one year from the date of the order in the appeal or the three years in clause (b), whichever is later. The exemption is such a point.

citation.ref: Section 108(2)(a) and (b) with the first proviso to section 108(2), read with section 108(1)

items.scenario: A Deputy Commissioner passed an order in April 2024 covering two issues — the classification of a product and an exemption he allowed on a separate supply. The taxpayer appealed on classification alone, and the Appellate Authority decided that issue in November 2025. The Revisional Authority now wants to revise the same April 2024 order on the exemption, which was never argued in the appeal.

items.stem: Can the order still be rectified under section 161?

options.text: No — the first proviso puts an absolute stop at six months from the date of the order
options.misconception: reads the first proviso without the second one that immediately carves an exception out of it
options.why: The six-month limit is real, and the very next proviso says it shall not apply where the correction is of a clerical or arithmetical error. An absolute reading of the first proviso leaves the second with nothing to do.

options.text: Yes — the six-month limit does not apply to a purely arithmetical mistake
options.why: A wrong addition in the summary is an error apparent on the face of record, and the second proviso to section 161 lifts the outer limit where the rectification is purely in the nature of correction of a clerical or arithmetical error arising from any accidental slip or omission. Eight months is therefore no obstacle.
keywords: apparent on the face of record

options.text: No — section 161 corrects a notice or a certificate, and a demand order has to be reopened under the demand provisions instead
options.misconception: narrows section 161 to notices when it names decisions and orders in the same breath
options.why: Section 161 applies to any decision, order, notice, certificate or other document. A demand order is squarely within it, and nothing in the section sends an arithmetical slip back through the demand machinery.

options.text: No — the taxpayer had only three months to bring the error to the authority's notice and that has long gone
options.misconception: treats the affected person's window as the only route when the authority may also act on its own motion
options.why: Three months is the window for the affected person to bring an error to notice, and it is not the limit on the power itself. The authority may rectify on its own motion, and the accountant pointing the mistake out is simply how it came to be noticed.

citation.ref: Section 161 with its first and second provisos

items.scenario: A demand order sets out the computation correctly in its body but adds the figures wrongly in the summary at the end, so the amount demanded is higher than the working supports. The mistake comes to light eight months after the order was issued, when the taxpayer's accountant reconciles the file.

items.stem: Is his argument good under section 171?

options.text: No, and the amount he kept is recovered from him as a demand of tax under section 74A
options.misconception: treats profiteering as unpaid tax when the amount belongs to the recipient and follows its own machinery
options.why: The amount was never tax; it was the recipient's money, collected in a price that should have come down. The order returns it to the recipient with interest, or where he cannot be identified sends it to the Consumer Welfare Fund, and adds a penalty under section 171(3A).

options.text: No — the obligation is measured against the rate reduction itself, not against last quarter's price
options.why: Section 171(1) is triggered by two things only, a reduction in rate of tax and the benefit of input tax credit, and it requires each to be passed on by way of commensurate reduction in prices. Commensurate means matched to that benefit, so a cut funded by a cheaper input leaves the rate reduction still in his hands, and the amount kept is the profiteered amount.

options.text: Yes, because the National Anti-profiteering Authority no longer exists to examine such a case
options.misconception: confuses which body examines a case with whether the obligation in section 171(1) exists at all
options.why: The obligation in section 171(1) sits in the Act and does not depend on which body examines it. The examining authority has moved more than once, most recently to the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal, and a notified cut-off governs fresh requests, but none of that rewrites the duty to pass the benefit on.

options.text: Yes — the section looks at the net price the consumer actually pays, and that price has fallen
options.misconception: reads section 171 as a general price control when it is tied to two named benefits
options.why: Section 171 is not a price control and does not ask whether prices are lower in general. It asks whether the two named benefits reached the recipient, and a saving from some other cause answers a question the section never puts.

citation.ref: Sections 171(1), 171(2) with its proviso and 171(3A), with the Explanation to section 171

items.scenario: The GST rate on a manufacturer's product is reduced. In the same quarter his own raw material became cheaper, and he cut his selling price by an amount that reflects the raw material saving alone, keeping the tax reduction for himself. He argues that his price is lower than it was, so the consumer has been looked after and nothing more is owed.

items.stem: What does section 152 say about that?

options.text: The information could not be used in the proceedings without first giving the taxpayer a hearing
options.why: Section 152(1) has two prohibitions and the second is this one — no information given for the purposes of section 150 or section 151 shall be used for the purposes of any proceedings under this Act without giving an opportunity of being heard to the person concerned. Lawful collection of the information does not carry lawful use with it.

options.text: Nothing — the bar covers information called for under section 151, not an information return under section 150
options.misconception: reads the bar as applying to one of the two sections when section 152 names both
options.why: Section 152(1) opens by naming information given for the purposes of section 150 or section 151. An information return filed by a third party is within the first of those, so the bar applies with full force.

options.text: Nothing — the information was lawfully obtained, so it may be used like any other material on record
options.misconception: treats lawful collection as lawful use when section 152 separates the two
options.why: Section 150 makes the collection lawful and section 152 then restricts what may be done with what was collected. The two sections do different jobs, and satisfying the first says nothing about the second.

options.text: Nothing — section 152 bars publishing such information, not using it in an assessment
options.misconception: reads the publication limb of section 152(1) and stops before the use limb that follows it
options.why: Publication is the first limb. The same sub-section goes on to bar use in any proceedings without a hearing, and it is that second limb the officer has walked past.

citation.ref: Section 152(1), read with sections 150 and 151

items.scenario: The department obtains a taxpayer's transaction figures from an information return a third party filed under section 150. Without putting those figures to the taxpayer or telling him where they came from, the officer relies on them to raise a demand.

items.stem: Must he register?

options.text: Yes, once his turnover crosses the section 22 threshold, since section 23 only helps a small supplier
options.misconception: treats section 23 as a turnover rule when it turns on what a person supplies, not how much
options.why: Section 23 says nothing about turnover. It relieves a person because of what he supplies — goods not liable to tax or wholly exempt — and a large dealer in exempt vegetables is as much within it as a small one.

options.text: No, but only if he first obtains a notification exempting him under section 23(2)
options.misconception: turns an automatic relief in section 23(1) into an application under the separate power in section 23(2)
options.why: Section 23(1) operates by itself and needs no order or application. Section 23(2) is a separate power for the Government to notify further categories, and it is not a condition of the relief the first sub-section already gives.

options.text: No — section 23 now overrides section 24, and he supplies nothing but exempt goods
options.why: Section 23(1)(a) covers a person engaged exclusively in supplying goods wholly exempt from tax, and the Finance Act, 2023 substituted the opening of the sub-section so that it applies notwithstanding section 22(1) or section 24, with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017. The compulsory category for a person liable to pay tax under reverse charge therefore cannot pull him in.

options.text: Yes — section 24 opens with its own overriding words and prevails over section 23
options.misconception: applies the position as it stood before the 2023 substitution, when the two sections were argued against each other
options.why: That was the argument until the Finance Act, 2023 settled it by putting overriding words at the front of section 23(1) naming section 24 itself. After the substitution section 23 prevails, and because it was given retrospective effect the earlier position does not survive for past years either.

citation.ref: Section 23(1)(a) as substituted by the Finance Act, 2023 with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017, read with section 24

items.scenario: A trader deals only in fresh, unbranded and unpackaged vegetables, which are wholly exempt. He makes no other supply. He regularly hires a goods transport agency to move his produce, and tax on that freight is payable by the recipient under reverse charge. His consultant tells him that section 24 makes registration compulsory for a person liable to pay tax under reverse charge.

items.stem: Which of the four can he take in appeal to the Appellate Authority?

options.text: The demand order and the refund rejection
options.why: Section 121 says no appeal shall lie against four kinds of order, and two of the four grievances are on that list — an order passed under section 80, which is the instalments provision, and an order pertaining to the seizure or retention of books of account. The demand and the refund rejection determine liability and remain appealable under section 107(1).
keywords: seizure or retention of books of account

options.text: The demand order, the refund rejection and the retention of books, because retention hurts him most
options.misconception: measures appealability by how much an order hurts rather than by the list in section 121
options.why: Hardship is not the test. Section 121 names an order pertaining to the seizure or retention of books of account, register and other documents, and once a matter is on that list the size of the grievance changes nothing. A writ remains available; an appeal does not.

options.text: All four, since section 107 lets any person aggrieved by any decision or order appeal
options.misconception: reads section 107(1) without section 121, which opens with words overriding every other provision
options.why: Section 107(1) is wide, and section 121 is written to cut into it — notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any provision of the Act, no appeal shall lie against the four matters it lists. The wide words in one section do not survive the overriding words in the other.

options.text: The demand order alone
options.misconception: assumes a refund rejection is an administrative decision when it determines a right to money
options.why: A refund rejection appears nowhere in section 121 and it decides whether the taxpayer gets his money, so it is appealable in the ordinary way. Only the instalments order and the retention of books are shut out.

citation.ref: Section 121 clauses (b) and (d), read with sections 80 and 107(1)

items.scenario: A registered person is unhappy with four things at once. A demand order under section 74A. An order refusing his request to pay that demand in instalments. An order retaining his seized books of account for longer than he thinks proper. And an order rejecting a refund claim.

items.stem: Is the officer right?

options.text: Yes — the bond runs with the warehousing period fixed under section 61 and cannot be released early
options.misconception: ties the bond to a calendar when section 73 ties it to the goods and the money
options.why: Section 61 fixes how long goods may remain warehoused; it says nothing about the life of the bond. Section 73 is the provision that ends the bond, and its two triggers are the goods being accounted for and the amounts due being paid.
keywords: how long goods may remain warehoused

options.text: No, and no order is needed either — the bond lapses of itself the moment the last of the goods leaves the warehouse
options.misconception: skips the proper officer's act of cancellation, which section 73 makes part of the discharge
options.why: The bond does not simply fall away. Section 73 requires the proper officer to cancel it as discharged in full and to deliver it on demand, so there is an act to be done and a document to be handed back.
keywords: cancel it as discharged in full

options.text: No — section 73 requires the bond to be cancelled and returned once the goods are accounted for and the money is paid
options.why: Section 73 says that when the whole of the goods covered by a bond executed under section 59 have been cleared for home consumption or exported or transferred or are otherwise duly accounted for, and all amounts due on account of those goods have been paid, the proper officer shall cancel the bond as discharged in full and shall on demand deliver it back. Both conditions are met here.

options.text: Yes — the bond also covers penalties and fines that may yet be found due, so it can never be given back
options.misconception: reads the bond's coverage as an open-ended liability when section 73 provides for its discharge in full
options.why: A section 59 bond does bind the importer to pay penalties and fines incurred in respect of those goods, and section 73 still provides for its cancellation once all amounts due on account of the goods have been paid. The coverage is wide; it is not perpetual.

citation.ref: Section 73, read with sections 59(1) and 71

items.scenario: An importer warehoused a consignment against a bond executed under section 59. He has since cleared part of the consignment for home consumption on payment of duty and exported the rest, and every amount due on the goods has been paid. He asks for his bond back. The officer says a warehousing bond stays alive until the warehousing period would have expired.

items.stem: What rate applies, and does interest run?

options.text: The rate in force on 20 July, and interest once the free period ended, since the goods were in a warehouse
options.misconception: treats storage in a warehouse building as warehousing, and applies section 15(1)(b) with section 61
options.why: Section 15(1)(b) and the interest in section 61 both apply to warehoused goods, and these are not warehoused goods however they are stored. It is the legal status the section confers, not the building, that decides.

options.text: The rate in force on 1 June, and no interest, because goods stored under section 49 are not warehoused goods
options.why: Section 49 says in terms that goods so stored shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods, so the warehousing chapter never engages. The goods were entered for home consumption, section 15(1)(a) fixes the rate by the date the bill of entry was presented, and the interest in section 61(2) attaches only to warehoused goods.
keywords: shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods

options.text: The rate in force on 1 June, but interest still runs, because the goods physically occupied a warehouse
options.misconception: keeps half of the warehousing consequences after correctly rejecting the other half
options.why: The same sentence produces both answers. Once the goods are not deemed to be warehoused goods, neither the rate rule for warehoused goods nor the interest that attaches to them can apply, and the importer pays only rent and charges for the storage.
keywords: not deemed to be warehoused goods

options.text: The rate in force on the date of entry inwards of the carrying vessel
options.misconception: applies the proviso to section 15(1)(a) about a bill of entry presented before arrival, which is not what happened
options.why: That proviso deems a bill of entry filed ahead of the vessel to have been presented on the date of entry inwards. Here the bill of entry was presented and assessed in the ordinary way after arrival, so the proviso has nothing to bite on.
