citation.ref: Section 49, read with sections 15(1)(a), 15(1)(b) and 61(2)

items.scenario: An importer presented a bill of entry for home consumption on 1 June and was assessed. He could not arrange funds, and on his application the Deputy Commissioner permitted the goods to be stored in a public warehouse under section 49 pending clearance. He paid and took delivery on 20 July. Between the two dates the rate of basic customs duty went up, and he is told interest has also run because his goods sat in a warehouse.

items.stem: How should the Authority deal with the application?

options.text: It must allow it, because an advance ruling concerns goods yet to be imported and the pending appeal concerns a past import
options.misconception: reads the bar as being about the consignment when the proviso speaks of the question raised
options.why: An advance ruling does look forward, and that is why the applicant may apply at all. The bar is a separate filter and it is worded around the question raised in the application, which is identical in both matters.

options.text: It may allow it, and the ruling will then settle the pending appeal as well
options.misconception: gives the ruling a reach section 28J does not, extending it to a forum already seised of the matter
options.why: Section 28J makes a ruling binding on the applicant and on the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs and officers subordinate to him in respect of that applicant. An appellate forum already hearing the matter is not among them.

options.text: It must reject it straight away, without hearing the applicant, since the bar is absolute
options.misconception: skips the hearing the section requires before any rejection, however clear the ground
options.why: The ground is indeed mandatory, but the procedure is not summary. No application may be rejected without giving the applicant an opportunity of being heard, and the order must record the reasons for the rejection.

options.text: It must not allow it — the bar looks at the question, and the same question is pending in his own case
options.why: The proviso to section 28-I(2) says the Authority shall not allow an application where the question raised in it is already pending in the applicant's case before any officer of customs, the Appellate Tribunal or any court. It is the question raised that the bar examines, not the consignment, so a fresh import does not escape it.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 28-I(2), read with sections 28-I(4), 28H(2) and 28J(1)

items.scenario: An importer is already in dispute about the classification of a particular machine — his appeal on an earlier consignment of the identical machine is pending before the Commissioner (Appeals). He now applies to the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings on the classification of the same machine for an import he plans next year, saying a future consignment is a different transaction from a past one.

items.stem: Is the manager right, and if not, when does duty fall?

options.text: He is wrong, but the duty was already paid when the shop imported the camera
options.misconception: confuses warehousing, which defers duty, with clearance for home consumption, which pays it
options.why: Depositing goods in a warehouse is precisely how an importer avoids paying at import. Duty on warehoused goods is paid later, on a bill of entry for home consumption presented under section 68, which is what the sale to the passenger brings about.

options.text: He is right — a duty-free shop is outside the customs frontiers of India
options.misconception: treats a bonded shop inside the terminal as foreign territory rather than as a warehouse under the Act
options.why: The shop stands on Indian soil and is licensed under the Customs Act. Being a bonded warehouse defers the duty on its stock; it does not put the premises outside India or outside the Act.

options.text: He is wrong — the camera was imported and warehoused, and duty falls when it is cleared for home consumption
options.why: A duty-free shop is a licensed warehouse and its stock is warehoused goods on which duty has been deferred, not remitted. Section 71 lets those goods leave only by a permitted route, and a sale to an arriving passenger takes the home-consumption route, so duty falls when the goods are cleared for home consumption under section 68.

options.text: He is wrong, and the duty is charged at the rate in force on the day the shop first imported the camera
options.misconception: applies section 15(1)(a) to goods cleared out of a warehouse, where section 15(1)(b) governs
options.why: For warehoused goods the rate is fixed by section 15(1)(b) — the date on which the bill of entry for home consumption in respect of them is presented under section 68 — so a rate change between the shop's import and the sale counts against the buyer.

citation.ref: Sections 68 and 71, read with section 15(1)(b)

items.scenario: A passenger landing at Delhi from abroad buys a camera at the arrival duty-free shop inside the terminal. The shop's manager assures him that no customs duty can ever arise on it, because the camera was never imported into India at all.

items.stem: Which of the two is added to the transaction value?

options.text: Both, since both are paid to the seller in connection with the imported goods
options.misconception: adds every payment made to the seller and ignores the two explanations that carve exclusions out of the clause
options.why: Payment to the seller is not by itself enough. The clause carries an explanation excluding charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in India, and another excluding payments for the right to distribute or resell where they are not a condition of the sale for export to India.
keywords: a condition of the sale for export

options.text: The running royalty only
options.why: Rule 10(1)(c) adds royalties and licence fees related to the imported goods that the buyer is required to pay as a condition of the sale, and a payment the supplier insists on before shipping meets that test even though it is measured on later domestic sales. The lump sum is left out because an explanation to the clause says charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in India shall not be added.

options.text: Neither, because a royalty measured on domestic sales relates to the finished product rather than to the imported goods
options.misconception: uses the measure of the royalty as the test in place of the condition-of-sale test the rule actually applies
options.why: How a royalty is computed does not decide the question. The rule asks whether it is related to the imported goods and whether the buyer is required to pay it as a condition of the sale, and here the supplier will not ship without it.

options.text: The lump sum only, because it is a fixed amount attributable to the goods while a running royalty is a post-import expense
options.misconception: inverts both limbs, adding the payment the explanation excludes and dropping the one the clause includes
options.why: The clause has no rule about fixed sums against running amounts. It includes a royalty paid as a condition of the sale whenever it falls due, and an explanation expressly keeps out charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in India.
keywords: as a condition of the sale

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(c) with its explanations, read with section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962

items.scenario: An Indian company imports machinery from a foreign supplier and makes two further payments to the same supplier. One is a running royalty on its domestic sales of the finished output, which the supply contract makes a precondition of shipment — the supplier will not ship until the royalty agreement is signed. The other is a lump sum for the right to reproduce the imported design in India. Neither is included in the invoice price.

items.stem: Is he right about the option?

options.text: No — for goods that are not prohibited the officer must offer the option, and the fine is capped
options.why: Section 125(1) gives the officer a discretion to offer a fine in lieu of confiscation where the import or export of the goods is prohibited, and obliges him to offer it in the case of any other goods. These goods are freely importable, so redemption had to be offered, and a proviso caps the fine at the market price of the goods less the duty chargeable on them.

options.text: No, but only because a mis-declaration of value is not a ground of confiscation in the first place
options.misconception: overlooks section 111(m), which reaches goods not corresponding in respect of value with the entry made
options.why: Section 111(m) covers goods which do not correspond in respect of value or in any other particular with the entry made under the Act, so the liability to confiscation stands. What fails is the refusal to offer redemption, not the confiscation itself.

options.text: No, and once the redemption fine is paid no duty is payable, the fine standing in place of it
options.misconception: ignores section 125(2), under which the owner is in addition liable to duty and charges on the goods
options.why: Section 125(2) says that where a fine is imposed the owner shall in addition be liable to any duty and charges payable in respect of the goods. Redemption buys the goods back; it does not extinguish the levy.

options.text: Yes — the option under section 125 is always at the adjudicating officer's discretion
options.misconception: reads the word may across the whole of section 125(1) when the sub-section uses may and shall for two different classes of goods
options.why: The sub-section splits into two. The discretion belongs to prohibited goods; for any other goods the officer shall give the option, and reading a single word across both halves erases the distinction the section is built on.

citation.ref: Section 125(1) with its proviso and section 125(2), read with section 111(m)

items.scenario: A consignment of freely importable goods is held liable to confiscation under section 111(m) because the declared particulars do not correspond in respect of value with the entry made. The adjudicating officer orders absolute confiscation and refuses to offer redemption, saying the option to pay a fine is his to give or withhold as he sees fit.

items.stem: Which cargo may lawfully be unloaded at that moment?

options.text: The aircraft's cargo, but not the vessel's
options.why: Section 31(1) bars the master of a vessel from permitting the unloading of imported goods until the proper officer has passed an order granting entry inwards, and that requirement is written for a vessel alone. Delivering the arrival manifest is a precondition of entry inwards under section 31(2), not a substitute for the order itself.

options.text: Both, once the goods are found to be mentioned in the manifest, entry inwards being needed only for loading export cargo
options.misconception: swaps entry inwards with entry outwards, which is the order a vessel needs before export goods are loaded
options.why: Mention in the manifest is a separate requirement under section 32 and it applies to every conveyance, but it does not replace entry inwards. The order needed before export goods are loaded on a vessel is entry outwards, a different order in a different section.

options.text: Neither, until entry inwards has been granted to each conveyance
options.misconception: extends a requirement written for vessels to aircraft, for which no entry inwards exists
options.why: Section 31 speaks throughout of the master of a vessel. There is no grant of entry inwards for an aircraft, so its cargo may be unloaded once the other conditions, including mention in the manifest, are satisfied.

options.text: Both, because the arrival manifest was delivered before arrival in each case
options.misconception: treats the manifest as the permission to unload when it is only the condition that lets the permission be given
options.why: Section 31(2) makes delivery of the manifest the thing that unlocks the officer's order; it does not make the manifest the order. Until entry inwards is granted, a vessel's cargo stays aboard.

citation.ref: Sections 31(1) and 31(2), read with sections 30(1) and 32

items.scenario: A vessel and an aircraft arrive at the same customs station on the same morning, both carrying imported cargo, and the arrival manifest for each was delivered before arrival. The ground handler begins unloading the aircraft at once. The shipping agent begins unloading the vessel at the same time, saying the manifest was filed and nothing more is needed.

items.stem: What is its aggregate turnover for the year?

options.text: ₹22 lakh
options.misconception: leaves exempt supplies out of aggregate turnover because no tax was charged on them
options.why: Exempt supplies are named in the definition and go in. A person whose sales are mostly exempt can be pushed over the registration line by them, which is the whole reason the definition says so in terms.

options.text: ₹31 lakh
options.why: Section 2(6) counts taxable supplies, exempt supplies, exports and same-PAN inter-State supplies on an all India basis. The value of inward supplies on which the person himself pays tax on a reverse charge basis is expressly taken out, and the taxes are taken out too, so the figure is ₹18 lakh plus ₹9 lakh plus ₹4 lakh.

options.text: ₹34.24 lakh
options.misconception: adds both the reverse-charge inward supplies and the tax charged on outward supplies
options.why: The definition ends by excluding central tax, State tax, Union territory tax, integrated tax and cess. Turnover is measured before the tax, and the inward supplies do not belong in it either.

options.text: ₹34 lakh
options.misconception: adds the inward supplies bearing reverse-charge tax, which the definition excludes
options.why: The ₹3 lakh of legal services is a purchase, not a supply the firm made. Section 2(6) excludes the value of inward supplies on which tax is payable on reverse charge basis precisely so that buying does not inflate turnover.

citation.ref: Section 2(6)

items.scenario: A firm holds one GST registration, in Karnataka, under a single Permanent Account Number. For the year its books show taxable outward supplies of ₹18 lakh, exempt outward supplies of ₹9 lakh, exports of ₹4 lakh, GST of ₹3.24 lakh charged on its outward supplies, and inward legal services of ₹3 lakh on which the firm itself paid tax under reverse charge.

items.stem: Which of these four was subsumed when GST came in?

options.text: Basic customs duty and the CGST and SGST, the integrated tax on imports having replaced the customs duty
options.misconception: reads the integrated tax charged at import as a replacement for basic customs duty rather than a levy sitting beside it
options.why: Integrated tax on an import is charged in addition to basic customs duty, not instead of it, and it is collected under the Customs Tariff Act as if it were a duty of customs. The customs duty was never subsumed.

options.text: Only the last — the other three were left standing
options.why: The 101st Constitution Amendment folded central excise, service tax, VAT and a family of State levies into one tax under Article 246A. It left basic customs duty on imports, stamp duty on instruments, and the State levies on alcoholic liquor for human consumption outside GST altogether, which is why all three are still being paid.

options.text: All four, GST being a comprehensive tax on every supply in the country
options.misconception: takes the word comprehensive literally and forgets the express carve-outs
options.why: Article 366(12A) itself excludes the supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption from the definition of goods and services tax, and imports keep their own customs levy. The tax is broad, not universal.

options.text: Stamp duty and the CGST and SGST, stamp duty being a tax on a transaction
options.misconception: treats stamp duty as a transaction tax of the kind GST replaced
options.why: Stamp duty is a duty on the instrument — the deed itself — and it stayed with the States and the Union under their own entries. A lease attracting GST can attract stamp duty on the same document without any double taxation question arising.

citation.ref: Article 246A with Article 366(12A)

items.scenario: A manufacturer lists the levies it still pays alongside GST — basic customs duty on an imported machine, stamp duty on a lease deed for its warehouse, State excise on liquor bought for its guest house, and CGST and SGST on its input purchases.

items.stem: What is the legal effect of the Council's decision on that State?

options.text: It is a recommendation — it does not by itself bind the State legislature or Government
options.why: Article 279A makes the Council a constitutional body whose function is to make recommendations to the Union and the States. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals the Supreme Court held those recommendations carry persuasive value and are not binding, because Article 246A gives Parliament and the State legislatures simultaneous power to legislate on GST. The exemption takes effect in that State only when its own notification issues.

options.text: It binds every State from the moment it is carried by the prescribed majority
options.misconception: reads the weighted-voting machinery as making the outcome binding rather than as making it representative
options.why: The voting weights decide when the Council has taken a decision; they say nothing about whether that decision commands a legislature. The Court has held in terms that it does not.

options.text: It has no legal standing at all, the Council being an advisory committee outside the Constitution
options.misconception: swings past the recommendatory point into denying the Council its constitutional status
options.why: The Council is created by Article 279A itself and its recommendations are what the GST statutes repeatedly require the Government to act upon before notifying anything. Not binding is a long way from having no standing.

options.text: It binds the Centre but not the States, the Centre having voted for it
options.misconception: splits the binding force by who voted, when the Article makes no such distinction
options.why: Article 279A draws no line between the Union and the States on this. The recommendation is addressed to both and binds neither of its own force.

citation.ref: Article 279A(4) and 279A(9)

items.scenario: At a meeting of the GST Council a proposal to exempt a described service is carried by the prescribed weighted majority — on the figures given to the members, the Centre's vote weighs one third of the votes cast, the States' votes together weigh two thirds, and three fourths of the weighted votes present and voting are needed to carry a decision. One State afterwards declines to issue the matching State tax notification.

items.stem: Which of the two is exempt?

options.text: Neither, surgery being a taxable service in every case
options.misconception: forgets that health care services are exempt at all
options.why: Diagnosis, treatment and care for illness, injury, deformity, abnormality or pregnancy in a recognised system of medicine are squarely within the exemption. Most of what a hospital does bears no tax.

options.text: The reconstruction after the burn injury; the cosmetic reshaping is taxable
options.why: Health care services by a clinical establishment are exempt, but the definition takes out cosmetic or plastic surgery — except where it is undertaken to restore or reconstruct anatomy or functions of the body affected by congenital defects, developmental abnormalities, injury or trauma. A hand disfigured by fire is injury, so the reconstruction stays inside the exemption and the elective reshaping does not.

options.text: Both, provided the hospital charges no separate room rent
options.misconception: makes an unrelated billing detail the test of the exemption
options.why: Whether a room is billed separately has nothing to do with whether a procedure is cosmetic or reconstructive. The carve-out in the definition is about the purpose of the surgery.

options.text: Both, since everything performed inside a hospital is health care
options.misconception: attaches the exemption to the building rather than to the service being supplied
options.why: The exemption follows the service. A hospital's shop rentals, its canteen sales to visitors and its cosmetic work are all taxable in the same premises where its ward is exempt.

citation.ref: Entry 74, with the definition of health care services in paragraph 2 of the notification

items.scenario: A hospital performs two operations in one week. The first reshapes a patient's nose purely for appearance, at the patient's request. The second reconstructs a hand disfigured in a factory fire.

items.stem: How does the agency's GST position differ between the two contracts?

options.text: The school contract is exempt and the college contract is taxable
options.why: Entry 66 exempts services supplied to an educational institution by way of transportation, catering, security, cleaning or house-keeping only where the institution provides education up to higher secondary school or equivalent. A degree college is an educational institution for what it supplies to its own students, but the inward leg of the exemption does not reach it, so cleaning the college bears tax.

options.text: Both are exempt, the recipient being an educational institution in each case
options.misconception: reads clause (b) as covering every educational institution, ignoring the cut-down that limits it to schools
options.why: Being an educational institution is necessary and not sufficient. The clause that exempts bought-in services names the school level expressly, and a degree college falls outside that limb while remaining an educational institution for its own supplies.

options.text: The college contract is exempt and the school contract is not, degree courses being the recognised qualification
options.misconception: inverts the rule by assuming the higher qualification attracts the wider exemption
options.why: The exemption for bought-in services runs the other way and stops at school level. Recognition of a degree matters to whether the college is an educational institution at all, not to whether its cleaning contractor is exempt.

options.text: Both are taxable, house-keeping never being covered by an education exemption
options.misconception: denies the inward-services limb of entry 66 altogether
options.why: The entry lists security, cleaning and house-keeping performed in such institution among the services it exempts. The limit is which institutions, not which services.

citation.ref: Entry 66, clause (b), with the definition of educational institution in paragraph 2

items.scenario: A housekeeping agency signs two cleaning contracts. One is with a school teaching classes up to the twelfth standard. The other is with a private college awarding a degree recognised by law.

items.stem: How is each letting taxed?

options.text: Both are taxable, with the landlord charging GST once his rental receipts cross the registration threshold
options.misconception: leaves the liability with the supplier when the notified entry has moved it to the recipient
options.why: The family letting stays exempt whatever the landlord's receipts are, and on the company letting the tax is not the landlord's to charge — reverse charge takes it off him entirely.

options.text: The letting to the family is exempt; the letting to the company bears GST, which the company pays under reverse charge
options.why: Renting of a residential dwelling for use as residence is exempt except where the recipient is a registered person. Once the tenant is registered the supply leaves the exemption, and the notified entry puts the liability on the recipient under reverse charge — so the company pays in cash even though the landlord is unregistered and has nothing to do.

options.text: Both are exempt, the flat being used as a residence in each case
options.misconception: applies the old form of the entry, which turned only on the dwelling and the use
options.why: That was the position before the entry was amended. It now carries the words except where the recipient is a registered person, so the tenant's status decides it and the use alone no longer does.

options.text: The company's letting is exempt because a person actually lives in the flat, and the family's letting is taxable
options.misconception: keeps the use-as-residence test and inverts the outcome
options.why: The carve-out that survives on residence is narrow and covers a proprietor renting in his personal capacity for his own home. A company housing a director is renting on the account of its business.

citation.ref: Entry 12 as amended, with entry 5AA of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate)

items.scenario: An individual who is not registered under GST owns a flat and lets it in two successive years. In the first year the tenant is a salaried family that lives in it. In the second the tenant is a company registered under GST, which houses its managing director in the flat.

items.stem: Which receipts are exempt from GST?

options.text: Only the counselling receipts
options.why: The exemption is not for a charitable body but for charitable activities as the notification defines them — public health work including care or counselling of persons addicted to a dependence-forming substance, advancement of religion, spirituality or yoga, certain educational and skill programmes for named vulnerable groups, and preservation of environment. Coaching for a competitive examination is none of those, so the trust pays tax on it like anybody else.

options.text: Only the coaching receipts, education being a charitable purpose
options.misconception: imports the Income-tax Act's wider idea of a charitable purpose into a GST definition that is a closed list
options.why: The notification's list of charitable activities does not include education generally. Its educational limb is confined to programmes for abandoned or orphaned children, abused persons, prisoners and the elderly in rural areas.

options.text: Both, the trust's registration under section 12AB exempting everything it earns
options.misconception: treats registration under the Income-tax Act as an exemption from GST in itself
options.why: Registration qualifies the entity and is only the first of two conditions. What the entity supplies has to fall inside the defined list as well, and most trusts have receipts on both sides of that line.

options.text: Neither, GST having no exemption for a trust
options.misconception: denies entry 1 altogether
options.why: Entry 1 exists and exempts services by a 12AA or 12AB entity by way of charitable activities. The counselling described is squarely inside the public health limb of the definition.

citation.ref: Entry 1, with the definition of charitable activities in paragraph 2 of the notification

items.scenario: A trust registered under section 12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 has two streams of receipts. One is from counselling persons addicted to a dependence-forming substance. The other is from a fee-charging coaching class it runs for a competitive examination.

items.stem: What happens to the central and State tax already paid, and does interest run on the integrated tax?

options.text: It is lost, a payment under the wrong head not being a payment of tax at all
options.misconception: treats a misclassified payment as a nullity, which is the opposite of what the section provides
options.why: The section exists to prevent that outcome. It calls the amount taxes so paid and orders their refund, and it also protects the taxpayer from interest on the correct head.

options.text: It is refunded to him, and no interest is payable on the integrated tax
options.why: Section 77 says a registered person who paid central and State tax on a transaction he considered intra-State, which is subsequently held to be inter-State, shall be refunded the amount so paid, and shall not be required to pay any interest on the integrated tax. Section 19 of the IGST Act carries the mirror rule the other way. The money was with the exchequer all along; only the head was wrong.

options.text: It is adjusted against the integrated tax liability automatically, with no refund claim needed
options.misconception: assumes the ledgers move money between heads, when the section provides for a refund
options.why: There is no automatic transfer between the central, State and integrated tax heads. The section gives a refund of what was paid wrongly, and a refund is claimed.

options.text: It is refunded, but interest runs on the integrated tax from its original due date
options.misconception: applies the ordinary section 50 interest rule to a payment the statute expressly relieves
options.why: Section 50 would charge interest on a late payment of tax, and section 77 is the exception that displaces it for exactly this situation. The sub-section on interest is there precisely so this answer is wrong.

citation.ref: Section 77, read with section 19 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A supplier treated a supply as intra-State and paid central tax and State tax of ₹6 lakh in June 2025. In 2026 the department holds that the supply was inter-State. The supplier now pays integrated tax of ₹6 lakh on the same supply.

items.stem: Is the summons valid, and what does the transporter risk if he gives an untrue answer?

options.text: Valid — the power reaches any person whose evidence is thought necessary, and the inquiry is deemed judicial, so an untrue answer carries the consequences of giving false evidence
options.why: Section 70(1) lets the proper officer summon any person whose attendance he considers necessary either to give evidence or to produce a document, and it is not confined to the taxpayer under investigation. Section 70(2) deems every such inquiry a judicial proceeding, which is what puts a false statement inside the ordinary criminal law rather than the penalty provisions.

options.text: Invalid — a summons may be issued only to the registered person under investigation
options.misconception: narrows the words any person to the taxpayer whose affairs are being examined
options.why: The sub-section says any person, and investigations routinely summon suppliers, customers, transporters and bank officials against whom nothing is alleged. Being a witness is not being an accused.

options.text: Valid only after a show cause notice has first been served on the supplier
options.misconception: makes an inquiry power wait for the adjudication it is meant to precede
options.why: The power is exercisable in any inquiry, and an inquiry is what happens before a notice is framed. Requiring the notice first would make the section useless.

options.text: Valid, but the inquiry is administrative, so an untrue answer at worst attracts a general penalty
options.misconception: misses the deeming in section 70(2) and downgrades a criminal consequence to a penalty
options.why: Section 70(2) deems the inquiry a judicial proceeding for the penal provisions on false evidence. That deeming is the whole sanction behind a summons and is what makes a recorded statement worth taking.

citation.ref: Sections 70(1) and 70(2)

items.scenario: An officer investigating a supplier issues a summons to the supplier's transporter, requiring him to appear, give evidence about the consignments carried and produce his records. No proceeding of any kind is pending against the transporter himself.

items.stem: What penalty does section 122(1) fix on these facts?

options.text: Nothing under section 122; the residual penalty in section 125 applies instead
options.misconception: reaches for the residual penalty when the conduct is on the section 122 list
options.why: Section 125 applies only where no penalty is separately provided. Issuing an invoice without a supply is named in section 122(1), so the residual provision never comes into play.

options.misconception: takes the tax involved as the penalty and ignores the floor the sub-section sets beneath it
options.why: The fixed sum is a floor, not an alternative the officer may pass over. Where the tax is smaller, the fixed sum is what applies, which is how a small-value offence still costs something.

options.misconception: adds the two amounts when the sub-section asks which of them is higher
options.why: The words are whichever is higher, and they choose between the two figures. Nothing in the sub-section adds them together.

Section 122(1) sets one formula for all the specified offences it lists, issuing an invoice without a supply among them — the tax evaded or the credit wrongly availed, or the fixed sum the sub-section names, whichever is higher. With ₹7,000 of tax against a ₹10,000 fixed sum, the higher of the two is the fixed sum.

citation.ref: Section 122(1), read with section 125

items.scenario: A supplier issues an invoice without any actual supply of goods and takes input tax credit on it. The tax involved works out to ₹7,000. Take it as given that the fixed sum named in section 122(1) alongside the tax amount is ₹10,000.

items.stem: What is the position in June 2026?

options.text: It continues, and the taxpayer's only route out is to object to the Commissioner and offer a bank guarantee
options.misconception: treats the objection remedy available while the attachment runs as the only exit after it has expired
options.why: Rule 159(5) does give an objection route within seven days, and it matters during the year. It is beside the point once the year has run and the order has spent itself.

options.text: The attachment has already ceased by operation of law, one year having run from the date of the order
options.why: Section 83(1) permits a provisional attachment where proceedings are pending and the Commissioner is of the opinion, recorded in writing, that it is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. Section 83(2) then says every such provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of one year from the date of the order. Nothing has to be applied for and no releasing order is needed.
keywords: protect the interest of the revenue

options.text: It was never valid, an audit under section 65 not being a proceeding that supports an attachment
options.misconception: denies the section one of the proceedings it expressly names as a trigger
options.why: Section 83 lists the chapters whose proceedings support an attachment and audit is among them. The defect here is age, not authority.

options.text: It continues until the audit concludes and a demand is determined
options.misconception: ties the life of the attachment to the proceedings rather than to the statutory year
options.why: Pending proceedings are what allow the attachment to be made in the first place. They do not extend it, because sub-section (2) fixes its life independently.

citation.ref: Sections 83(1) and 83(2)

items.scenario: During an audit under section 65, the Commissioner records in writing his opinion that attaching the taxpayer's bank account is necessary to protect the revenue, and passes an order under section 83 on 1 March 2025. In June 2026 the audit is still running, no demand has been raised, and the bank still refuses to operate the account.

items.stem: Whom may the department recover the ₹12 lakh from?

options.text: From either of them — the transferor and the transferee are jointly and severally liable for dues up to the date of transfer
options.why: Section 85 makes a taxable person transferring a business and the person to whom it is transferred jointly and severally liable, wholly or to the extent of the transfer, for tax, interest or penalty due up to the time of the transfer, whether determined before or after it. A private allocation of liabilities binds the two parties and not the department.
keywords: up to the time of the transfer
whether determined before or after it

options.text: Only from the seller, the liability being personal to the person who incurred it
options.misconception: treats tax liability as staying with the person who earned the income, which is what section 85 displaces
options.why: Chapter XVI exists to attach liability to people other than the original taxable person, and section 85 is its widest provision. A buyer of a business takes the pre-transfer dues with it.

options.text: Only from the buyer, who now owns the business the tax arose in
options.misconception: replaces joint and several liability with a transfer of the liability
options.why: The section makes both liable, not the buyer alone. The department may proceed against either or both, and the seller does not walk away by selling.

options.text: From neither, since the dues were determined after the transfer had already happened
options.misconception: reads the timing of determination as the test when the section fixes on the period the dues relate to
options.why: The sub-section says whether such dues have been determined before the transfer or afterwards. What matters is that they were due up to the time of transfer.

citation.ref: Section 85(1)

items.scenario: A proprietor sells his whole business as a going concern on 30 June. The agreement says the seller keeps all liabilities arising before the sale. Eighteen months later ₹12 lakh of tax for periods before the sale is determined against the business, and the seller has no money.

items.stem: Where does the further appeal lie?

options.text: To the High Court, with a further appeal to the Supreme Court only on the High Court's certificate
options.misconception: imports the certificate route from ordinary civil appeals into a scheme that provides a direct appeal
options.why: Section 118 gives a direct appeal and asks for no certificate. The certificate machinery belongs to other statutes, not to this one.

options.text: To the High Court, place of supply being a question of law like any other
options.misconception: applies the general rule and misses the proviso written for exactly this dispute
options.why: It is a question of law, and it is still excluded. A dispute between two States about which of them the supply belongs to is not one State's High Court's to settle, which is why the proviso exists.

options.text: To the Supreme Court, a place-of-supply difference between States being outside the High Court's reach
options.why: Section 117 gives an appeal to the High Court from an order of the Appellate Tribunal where the Court is satisfied the case involves a substantial question of law, but its proviso excludes an order relating to a matter where two or more States, or a State and the Centre, differ on the place of supply. Section 118 sends that appeal straight to the Supreme Court.

options.text: Nowhere — an order of the Appellate Tribunal on place of supply is final
options.misconception: mistakes an exclusion from one forum for the absence of any appeal
options.why: The proviso removes the High Court and section 118 supplies the Supreme Court in its place. Nothing about the order is made final.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 117(1), read with section 118

items.scenario: The Appellate Tribunal decides an appeal in which the issue was whether the place of supply was Maharashtra or Karnataka, the two States having taken different views. The taxpayer wants to carry the matter further on a question of law.

items.stem: What has that order actually done?

options.text: Reversed the credit permanently, so the taxpayer must re-avail it if he later succeeds
options.misconception: confuses a restriction on debit with a reversal of the credit itself
options.why: The credit stays in the ledger throughout — only the debit is disallowed. When the restriction goes, the balance is there to be used, with no re-availment and no time-limit question.

options.text: Frozen the taxpayer's use of that much credit, without recovering anything, and it lapses one year from the date it was imposed
options.why: Rule 86A lets the Commissioner or an authorised officer, having reasons to believe credit has been fraudulently availed or is ineligible, disallow debit of an equivalent amount from the electronic credit ledger. Disallowing a debit stops the credit being used; it determines and recovers nothing, which still needs a notice and an order. Sub-rule (3) ends the restriction on the expiry of one year from the date of imposing it.

options.text: Nothing, the order being invalid without a demand notice preceding it
options.misconception: makes the rule wait for the adjudication it is designed to protect
options.why: The rule is a protective measure taken while an investigation runs, and it would be pointless if it could only follow a demand. What it does require is the officer's own recorded reasons to believe.

options.text: Recovered the ₹15 lakh, so that a demand notice would now add nothing
options.misconception: treats blocking as a determination of liability when it is only a restriction on use
options.why: Nothing has been recovered and nothing has been determined. A demand still has to be raised under section 73 or 74A, with the hearing those sections carry, before a rupee is due.

citation.ref: Rule 86A(1) and 86A(3)

items.scenario: An officer authorised by the Commissioner records his reasons to believe that ₹15 lakh of credit lying in a taxpayer's electronic credit ledger came from invoices issued by a supplier found to be non-existent, and on 1 May 2025 passes an order under rule 86A disallowing debit of that amount. No show cause notice has been issued.

items.stem: What is the correct course?

options.text: Go straight to the residual method in rule 9, the earlier methods having failed
options.misconception: treats the fallback as available as soon as any method fails, rather than as the last rung
options.why: Only rules 4 and 5 failed here. Rule 9 is reached after rules 7 and 8 have been tried, and jumping to it skips two methods the rules require to be attempted.

options.text: Move down the ladder to rule 7, and the importer's request to take deductive value before computed value is one the rules expressly allow
options.why: Rule 3(4) says that where the value cannot be determined under the transaction value rule, it shall be determined by proceeding sequentially through rules 4 to 9. With no identical or similar goods, rules 4 and 5 fail and the next rung is the deductive value in rule 7. Rule 6 then permits the order of rules 7 and 8 to be reversed at the request of the importer, so choosing between them is his to ask for.
keywords: at the request of the importer

options.text: Restore the declared transaction value, since a rejection that leaves no substitute method is ineffective
options.misconception: assumes a rejection under rule 12 collapses when the next method is not obvious
options.why: Rule 12 rejects the declared value on its own footing, and the ladder always ends somewhere — rule 9 will produce a value using reasonable means if nothing else does.

options.text: Apply computed value first, the sequence being fixed and no request able to alter it
options.misconception: knows the sequence is mandatory and misses the single departure rule 6 permits
options.why: The sequence is mandatory everywhere except between rules 7 and 8, where rule 6 says in terms that the order may be reversed at the importer's request with the proper officer's approval.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 3(4) with rule 6

items.scenario: A proper officer rejects the declared transaction value of a consignment under rule 12, on grounds put to the importer and after hearing him. No imports of identical or of similar goods can be found for comparison. The importer, who sells the goods on in India, asks that the deductive value method be applied before the computed value method.

items.stem: What follows?

options.text: The goods must be returned and no notice may ever be issued about them
options.misconception: reads the return of the goods as extinguishing the department's case
options.why: The consequence written into the sub-section is the return of the goods and nothing more. A notice and an adjudication on confiscation and penalty can still follow.

options.text: The goods must be returned to the person they were seized from, though the investigation and any later notice are untouched
options.why: Section 110(2) says that where no notice under section 124 is given within six months of the seizure, the goods shall be returned to the person from whose possession they were seized. The period can be extended by a further six months by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner for reasons recorded in writing, and none of that happened. Returning the goods ends the seizure, not the case.

options.text: The goods may be kept, the importer's only remedy being provisional release under section 110A on bond and security
options.misconception: offers a route that exists during the six months as the answer once the six months have gone
options.why: Section 110A is a middle course available while the seizure is lawful. Once the period has expired without a notice, the importer does not have to buy his goods back with a bond.

options.text: The department may hold the goods for as long as the investigation continues
options.misconception: treats seizure as open-ended when the sub-section puts a clock on it
options.why: Seizure is a holding step and the six months is the price of holding without alleging. An investigation may carry on; the goods may not be kept while it does.

citation.ref: Section 110(2) with its proviso

items.scenario: Goods are seized by a customs officer on 10 January. By 10 July no notice under section 124 has been issued and no extension of the period has been granted or communicated. The importer asks for the goods back; the department answers that its investigation is still running.

items.stem: Is the refund of import duty available?

options.text: No, because a refund of import duty can only ever arise under section 27
options.misconception: denies section 26A its own field, which is goods that were correctly assessed but wrongly supplied
options.why: Section 27 refunds duty paid in excess of what was due. Section 26A deals with duty correctly paid on goods that turned out to be defective, and it exists precisely because section 27 does not reach that case.

options.text: No — the goods were used, and use going beyond what was indispensable to discover the defect defeats the claim
options.why: Section 26A refunds duty on goods found defective or not in conformity with the specification agreed, but only where the goods have not been worked, repaired or used after importation, except where such use was indispensable to discover the defect or to test conformity. Two weeks of commercial production is use of quite another kind, so the condition fails however punctual the re-export and the claim were.

options.text: Yes, but only to the extent of duty proportionate to the fortnight of use
options.misconception: invents a tapering relief of the kind section 74 gives for used goods and applies it here
options.why: The tapering by period of use belongs to drawback under section 74. Section 26A is all or nothing, and use is a disqualification rather than a deduction.

options.text: Yes — the goods were re-exported and the claim filed in time, which is all the section requires
options.misconception: reads the timing conditions as the whole of section 26A and drops the no-use condition
options.why: Timeliness is one condition among several. The section also requires that the goods be identifiable, that no drawback be claimed, and that the goods not have been worked, repaired or used.

citation.ref: Section 26A(1) with its provisos

items.scenario: A machine cleared for home consumption on payment of duty turns out not to match the specification agreed with the supplier. Take these as given — the importer ran it in commercial production for two weeks before noticing, and then re-exported it and filed his claim, both inside the periods section 26A allows.

items.stem: Which of them may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal?

options.text: None — an order of the Commissioner (Appeals) can only be taken to the High Court
options.misconception: skips the Tribunal altogether in the customs appellate ladder
options.why: Section 129A gives the appeal from the Commissioner (Appeals) to the Tribunal, and the High Court comes later under section 130, on a substantial question of law.

options.text: The classification and the drawback cases, baggage alone being excluded
options.misconception: remembers baggage as the exception and forgets that drawback sits beside it
options.why: Baggage and drawback are both in the proviso, along with short-landed goods. Drawback disputes have gone by revision to the Central Government since the scheme was framed.

options.text: Only the classification case; the baggage and drawback matters go to the Central Government by revision
options.why: The first proviso to section 129A(1) keeps three classes of order out of the Appellate Tribunal — goods imported or exported as baggage, goods short-landed or not unloaded at their destination, and payment of drawback. Section 129DD gives those a revision application to the Central Government instead. A classification dispute is an ordinary customs appeal and goes to the Tribunal.

options.text: All three, the Tribunal being the appellate forum for every customs order
options.misconception: applies the general appellate scheme and misses the proviso that carves three subjects out of it
options.why: The section opens with a general right of appeal and then takes three subjects away from it in its own proviso. Those three have a different forum, not a lesser one.

citation.ref: First proviso to section 129A(1), read with section 129DD

items.scenario: Three importers lose before the Commissioner (Appeals). The first case is about confiscation of goods brought in as baggage. The second is about a drawback claim. The third is about the classification of an imported machine. All three want to go further.

items.stem: On what amount is the Social Welfare Surcharge computed?

options.misconception: includes the integrated tax in the base, which the levy expressly excludes
options.why: Integrated tax under section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act is one of the levies the surcharge provision leaves out of its base, along with the compensation cess and the trade-remedy duties.

options.misconception: treats the surcharge as a duty on the assessable value like the basic customs duty itself
options.why: The value is what basic customs duty is charged on. The surcharge is charged on that duty, so taking the value again would tax the goods twice on the same footing.

The Social Welfare Surcharge is a surcharge on duty, not a duty on value. Its base is the aggregate of the duties levied and collected as duties of customs, which here is the basic customs duty of ₹1,00,000. The assessable value itself never enters the computation, and the integrated tax on the import is expressly kept out of the base.

options.misconception: adds the value and the duty, mixing the two bases together
options.why: The section names the aggregate of the duties as the base. Value plus duty is not a base any customs levy uses.

citation.ref: Section 110 — Social Welfare Surcharge on imported goods

items.scenario: A consignment is assessed at ₹10,00,000. Basic customs duty on it comes to ₹1,00,000, and integrated tax on the import comes to ₹2,00,000. Take the rate of Social Welfare Surcharge as given at ten per cent.

items.stem: Which of them must hold an Importer-Exporter Code?

options.text: None of them, the code having been replaced by the GST registration number
options.misconception: confuses the merger of the code with the Permanent Account Number for a replacement by GST registration
options.why: The code was aligned with the Permanent Account Number, not with GST registration, and it is still granted by the Director General of Foreign Trade under the trade law rather than the tax law.

options.text: Only the trader
options.why: No person may import or export except under an Importer-Exporter Code granted by the Director General of Foreign Trade, and the code is now the person's Permanent Account Number. The exemptions cover exactly the other two situations — a Ministry or department of the Central or a State Government, and goods imported or exported for personal use not connected with trade, manufacture or agriculture. The fabric is for trade.

options.text: All three, the code being needed for every crossing of the border
options.misconception: reads section 7 as absolute and forgets the notified exempt categories
options.why: Government departments and personal-use consignments are relieved. If they were not, every traveller and every ministry would need a trading code.

options.text: The trader and the Government department, personal use alone being exempt
options.misconception: keeps the personal-use exemption and drops the Government one
options.why: A Ministry or department of the Central or a State Government is among the notified categories that may import and export without a code. The department here is importing for its own use.

citation.ref: Section 7, with the exempt categories notified under the Foreign Trade Policy

items.scenario: Three shipments are planned. A trader is importing fabric to sell in India. A department of a State Government is importing equipment for its own use. An individual is importing a wheelchair for a family member's personal use.

items.stem: Who pays the tax on each of the two local delivery services?

options.text: The operator pays on both, section 9(5) making it the supplier for every local delivery through it
options.misconception: reads the entry without its exception, which is where most of the work in section 9(5) is done
options.why: Three of the six notified categories carry the same exception, and local delivery is one of them. A supplier already liable for registration under section 22(1) is left with his own liability, because the mechanism exists to catch supplies that would otherwise go untaxed rather than to move tax off people who are already in the net.

options.text: The operator pays on the rider's service; the logistics firm pays on its own
options.why: Local delivery was notified under section 9(5) with effect from 22 September 2025, so the operator is liable as if it were the supplier — but the entry carves out the case where the person supplying through the operator is himself liable for registration under section 22(1). The unregistered rider is inside section 9(5) and the operator pays for him. The registered logistics firm is outside it and pays in the ordinary way.

options.text: Neither is taxable, local delivery of goods by road being exempt
options.misconception: applies entry 18 as it read before 22 September 2025, missing the Explanation that lifts platform delivery out of it
options.why: That was the position until 22 September 2025. Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate) added an Explanation to entry 18 saying the exemption does not reach local delivery services provided by an electronic commerce operator or through one. The service is out of the exemption before the question of who pays is even reached.

options.text: The rider pays, being the actual supplier, and the operator pays on the logistics firm's service
options.misconception: has the exception the wrong way round and puts the liability on the person the provision exists to leave out
options.why: Section 9(5) works by moving the liability away from a supplier who is often outside the net and onto the platform. Putting it back on the unregistered rider defeats the provision, and the registered firm is the one the exception hands responsibility to.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by Notification No. 17/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025

items.scenario: A delivery platform carries local deliveries for shops in one city. Two people deliver through it in October 2026. The first is an individual rider whose earnings are far below every registration threshold and who is not registered. The second is a logistics firm already registered under section 22(1), which uses the platform to find work.

items.stem: On which of the three is the platform liable to pay the tax?

options.text: Only the company's omnibus, a company being the party the operator collects from
options.misconception: inverts the exception, reading it as naming who the operator pays for rather than who is left out
options.why: The exception says the opposite. Where an omnibus service is supplied through the operator by a company, the tax is not payable by the operator — the company pays it. It is the one case of the three that leaves the platform out.

options.text: Only the two omnibuses, a maxicab being outside the notified services
options.misconception: forgets that the older radio-taxi entry already covered a maxicab, and reads the new omnibus entry as the whole of it
options.why: The maxicab has been inside the notified services since the beginning: the entry names a radio-taxi, motorcab, maxicab, motorcycle or any other motor vehicle. What 22 September 2025 added was the omnibus, which that entry had always excluded.

options.text: The sole proprietor's omnibus and the maxicab, but not the company's omnibus
options.why: The maxicab falls in the entry for passenger transport by a motorcab, maxicab, motorcycle or any other motor vehicle except an omnibus, which carries no company exception at all. The omnibus entry does carry one: where the supplier through the operator is a company, the company pays the tax itself. So the platform pays for the proprietor's omnibus and for the maxicab, and the company pays its own.

options.text: All three, the platform being liable for every passenger transport service booked through it
options.misconception: treats section 9(5) as one rule about passenger transport, when it is two entries with different exceptions
options.why: The list notified under section 9(5) is a list of separately drawn entries, and the omnibus entry was added with an exception the older entry does not have. Reading them as one rule loses the only distinction the amendment made.

citation.ref: Section 9(5) with Notification No. 17/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by Notification No. 17/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025

items.scenario: A booking platform lists three operators for the same route in November 2026. One is a private limited company running omnibuses. One is a sole proprietor running an omnibus. One is a proprietor running a maxicab.

items.stem: Can the company take the ₹7.2 lakh input tax credit?

options.text: No, and the goods must also be returned to the supplier
options.misconception: attaches a consequence to the goods when the defect is in the tax chain
options.why: The purchase itself is untouched — the goods are the company's. What fails is the credit; the company's remedy against the supplier is contractual, not a return of goods.

options.text: Yes — a valid invoice and receipt of goods complete the recipient's obligations
options.misconception: treats the recipient-side conditions as the whole test
options.why: That was the intuition under the old regime and it is the specific thing section 16(2)(c) rejects. The credit is of tax paid, and no tax was paid.

options.text: No — payment of the tax to the Government by the supplier is itself a condition
options.why: Section 16(2)(c) makes the supplier's actual payment a condition of the recipient's credit. Invoice, receipt and GSTR-2B appearance satisfy three conditions of five; all of them must hold together, and the missing one defeats the claim.

options.text: Yes, provisionally, reversible if the supplier stays in default for six months
options.misconception: recalls the provisional-credit mechanism that no longer exists
options.why: Provisional credit was removed from the law. Credit now follows GSTR-2B and the satisfied conditions, with no provisional window to occupy.

citation.ref: Section 16(2)

items.scenario: A company buys raw material worth ₹40 lakh plus ₹7.2 lakh GST, holds a valid tax invoice, has received the goods, and the invoice appears in its GSTR-2B. It then learns the supplier collected the tax but never deposited it with the Government.

items.stem: What is the GST position on these fees?

options.text: The company pays under reverse charge by debiting its input tax credit
options.misconception: discharges a reverse-charge liability through the credit ledger
options.why: Reverse charge must be paid through the cash ledger. The credit ledger can pay output tax on the company's own supplies, not the tax it owes as a recipient.

options.text: The company pays the GST under reverse charge, in cash
options.why: Legal services from an advocate to a business entity are notified under section 9(3), so the liability sits on the recipient. Reverse charge liability is discharged in cash — the company may then take credit of it, but cannot pay it out of credit.

options.text: The advocate should have charged GST on the bill
options.misconception: applies forward charge to a notified reverse-charge supply
options.why: For notified services the supplier neither charges nor collects. A bill without GST is the correct bill here; the tax travels on the company's own liability.

options.text: No GST arises, because legal services are exempt
options.misconception: stretches the small-recipient exemption to every recipient
options.why: The exemption covers advocates serving individuals and small business entities below the registration threshold. A ₹300 crore company is squarely outside it.

citation.ref: Section 9(3)

items.scenario: A manufacturing company with ₹300 crore turnover engages a senior advocate for a High Court matter and pays fees of ₹5 lakh. The advocate's bill shows no GST.

items.stem: Is registration required?

options.text: Yes, because every supplier of services must register from the first rupee
options.misconception: erases the threshold entirely for services
options.why: First-rupee registration applies to specific cases — inter-State taxable supply, e-commerce, reverse-charge recipients — not to services as a class.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹1.5 crore
options.misconception: mistakes the composition ceiling for the registration threshold
options.why: ₹1.5 crore is the composition scheme's eligibility ceiling — a choice available after registration, not a limit before it.

options.text: No, not until turnover reaches ₹40 lakh
options.misconception: applies the goods-only threshold to a service provider
options.why: The ₹40 lakh limit belongs to suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States. One rupee of service supply keeps the ₹20 lakh limit in charge.

options.text: Yes — the services threshold of ₹20 lakh is crossed
options.why: A supplier of services takes the ₹20 lakh aggregate turnover limit, and ₹25 lakh is past it. Registration follows, with tax on supplies from the effective date.

citation.ref: Section 22

items.scenario: A management consultant in Madhya Pradesh, supplying only services within the State, reaches aggregate turnover of ₹25 lakh during the year and asks whether registration is now compulsory.

items.stem: Can he make this supply while remaining in the scheme?

options.text: Yes, because his turnover is within the ₹1.5 crore ceiling
options.misconception: treats the turnover ceiling as the only eligibility condition
options.why: The ceiling is one condition of several. The inter-State bar is separate, and breaching it disqualifies regardless of how modest the turnover is.

options.text: No — inter-State outward supply ends composition eligibility
options.why: Section 10(2) bars a composition taxpayer from inter-State outward supplies. Shipping to Maharashtra means leaving the scheme and paying tax as a regular taxpayer, with the compliance that follows.

options.text: Yes, paying IGST on this order at the composition rate
options.misconception: extends the composition rate across State lines
options.why: There is no composition IGST. The scheme is a local-trade bargain, and the levy it charges exists only for intra-State supply.

options.text: Yes, if the Maharashtra buyer arranges his own transport from Indore
options.misconception: locates the supply by who carries the goods
options.why: Place of supply follows the movement's termination for delivery, not who pays the transporter. Goods bound for Maharashtra make an inter-State supply either way.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)

items.scenario: A composition dealer in Indore, selling hardware with turnover of ₹90 lakh, receives a large order from a buyer in Maharashtra and intends to supply it under the composition scheme.

items.stem: Which of these amounts is not added in arriving at the assessable value?

options.text: The selling commission of $2,000
options.misconception: excludes all commissions instead of only the buying commission
options.why: Selling commission is paid for the seller's benefit and is expressly added. The carve-out is for buying commission alone.

options.text: None of them — all payments connected with the import are added
options.misconception: adds everything rather than testing each payment against the rule
options.why: The rule works addition by addition, and buying commission is its stated exception. Adding everything overstates the value and the duty with it.

options.text: The buying commission of $1,500
options.why: Rule 10(1)(a) adds commissions and brokerage except buying commission. The importer's own agent works for the buyer, and paying him is part of the cost of buying, not part of the price of the goods.

options.text: The freight of $3,000
options.misconception: leaves transport out of a value that is built to the place of importation
options.why: Cost of transport to the place of importation is a Rule 10(2) addition. Assessable value is the landed value, and freight is part of landing the goods.

citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(a)

items.scenario: An importer's invoice shows goods at $50,000, selling commission of $2,000 paid to the exporter's agent, buying commission of $1,500 paid to the importer's own agent abroad, and freight of $3,000 to the Indian port.

items.stem: Can the credit still be taken?

options.text: No, because credit must be taken in the same month as the invoice
options.misconception: shrinks the statutory window to the invoice month
options.why: The law allows credit any time up to the section 16(4) date — often twenty months from an early-year invoice. The failure here is missing a generous window, not a same-month rule.

options.text: Yes, because the annual return for 2025-26 has not yet been filed
options.misconception: reads the two limbs as alternatives that each keep the window open
options.why: The section takes the EARLIER of the two dates. An unfiled annual return cannot extend the November cut-off; it can only close the window sooner.

options.text: No — the window closed on 30 November 2026
options.why: The invoice belongs to financial year 2025-26, so section 16(4) shuts the credit at the thirtieth of November following that year's end. Discovery in December is discovery too late, however eligible the credit was on its merits.

options.text: Yes, at any time within four years, as with other indirect tax refunds
options.misconception: imports a limitation period from refund law into the credit provision
options.why: Refund limitation under section 54 is a different clock for a different claim. Credit has its own guillotine in section 16(4), and it is measured in months, not years.

citation.ref: Section 16(4)

items.scenario: During a December 2026 review, a company discovers an unclaimed input tax credit of ₹6 lakh on a supplier invoice dated 14 February 2026. All section 16(2) conditions are satisfied and the annual return for 2025-26 has not yet been filed.

items.stem: What is the place of supply, and which tax applies?

options.text: Madhya Pradesh, because the buyer arranged the transport himself
options.misconception: lets who carries the goods decide the place of supply
options.why: Movement "whether by the supplier or the recipient" is within the same rule. The statute cares about the destination of the movement, not about whose truck it is.

options.text: Madhya Pradesh — an intra-State supply, since delivery was taken at the factory gate
options.misconception: fixes the place of supply where possession changed hands rather than where movement ends
options.why: Handing over at the gate is how the movement begins, not where it terminates. The section looks at where the goods are going for delivery to the recipient, which is Ahmedabad.

options.text: Gujarat, but as an intra-State supply of Gujarat attracting CGST and SGST
options.misconception: gets the place right and then misreads what inter-State means
options.why: Inter-State or intra-State compares the supplier's location with the place of supply. Supplier in Madhya Pradesh, place of supply Gujarat — that is inter-State, and IGST is the levy.

options.text: Gujarat — an inter-State supply attracting IGST
options.why: The supply involves movement of goods, and the movement terminates for delivery at the Ahmedabad plant. Section 10(1)(a) fixes the place of supply there, and Madhya Pradesh to Gujarat is inter-State, so IGST applies.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(a)

items.scenario: A dealer in Bhopal sells machinery to a buyer registered in Gujarat. The buyer sends its own truck, takes delivery at the Bhopal factory gate, and carries the machinery to its Ahmedabad plant.

items.stem: Who pays GST in March on the advance?

options.text: Neither, because no invoice has been issued by either
options.misconception: makes the invoice the sole trigger for both goods and services
options.why: For services the payment reaches back as a trigger on its own. The software company's liability arises in March with or without an invoice.

options.text: Both, since money received against a taxable supply is taxable when received
options.misconception: applies the services rule across the goods-services line
options.why: That was the position for goods only briefly. The notification removed advances on goods from the net after the compliance burden proved unworkable, and the asymmetry is now the tested point.

options.text: Only the manufacturer, since goods are tangible and the machine is identifiable
options.misconception: reverses the asymmetry
options.why: The rule runs the other way. Tangibility has nothing to do with it — the notification names goods as the excused side.

options.text: Only the software company — advances for services are taxable on receipt; for goods they are not
options.why: Time of supply for services reaches the earlier of invoice and payment, catching the advance in March. For goods, Notification 66/2017 confined the liability to invoice issue, so the manufacturer pays in May with the invoice.

citation.ref: Section 12 and 13, with Notification 66/2017-CT

items.scenario: On 20 March a machine manufacturer receives a ₹10 lakh advance against a machine to be delivered in May, and a software company receives a ₹10 lakh advance against an implementation project starting in May. Both are regular taxpayers.

items.stem: Which discount reduces the value of supply for GST?

options.text: The 2 per cent scheme discount, provided the dealer reverses the proportionate credit
options.why: It was agreed before the supplies, is linkable to specific invoices, and the recipient's credit reversal completes section 15(3)(b). The tax follows the price the parties had genuinely agreed all along.

options.text: Both, since both are genuine discounts actually passed on
options.misconception: treats commercial genuineness as the statutory test
options.why: Genuineness is necessary but the section demands prior agreement and invoice linkage. The goodwill discount was born after the supplies and fails at the first condition.

options.text: Neither, because post-supply discounts never reduce taxable value
options.misconception: reads the pre-supply agreement condition as banning all later discounts
options.why: The section exists precisely to allow post-supply discounts that were pre-agreed. What it shuts out is the discount invented after the event.

options.text: The goodwill discount, since it is unconditional and unilateral
options.misconception: rewards the discount with fewer strings as the cleaner deduction
options.why: Unconditional generosity is exactly what the section will not net off. The strings — prior agreement, linkage, reversal — are the qualification, not the disqualification.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)

items.scenario: A distributor agreement signed in April promises a 2 per cent year-end discount on all purchases if the dealer crosses ₹5 crore. The dealer crosses it, and the distributor issues a credit note for ₹10 lakh plus tax, linked invoice-wise. Separately, the distributor gives another dealer an unplanned ₹4 lakh goodwill discount for staying loyal in a hard year.

items.stem: On what amount does the section 50 interest run?

options.text: On the full ₹20 lakh of the liability
options.misconception: charges interest on the gross liability the way the section originally read
options.why: Gross-liability interest was the original position, litigated hard and then rewritten retrospectively. Answers citing the old position are answering a repealed law.

options.text: On nothing, since the liability was fully discharged at filing
options.misconception: treats the eventual payment as erasing the delay
options.why: The tax was due with the period's return, not four months later. Discharge ends the clock; it does not unwind it.

options.text: On the ₹14 lakh met from credit, since credit was applied late
options.misconception: inverts the proviso and charges the credit portion
options.why: The proviso protects exactly that portion. Credit sitting in the ledger was already tax paid once; charging interest on it would tax the delay twice.

options.text: On the ₹6 lakh paid through the cash ledger
options.why: The proviso to section 50(1) confines interest, where the return is filed late, to the portion discharged through the electronic cash ledger. The ₹14 lakh met by credit was the Government's money in the system all along, and Parliament amended the section retrospectively to say so.

citation.ref: Section 50(1) proviso

items.scenario: A taxpayer files a GSTR-3B four months late. The tax liability of ₹20 lakh for the period was covered ₹14 lakh by input tax credit and ₹6 lakh by cash, both applied on the day of the late filing.

items.stem: What is the position in August 2026?

options.text: Neither, because goods sent for job work are not supplies at all
options.misconception: remembers the concession and forgets its condition
options.why: The tax-free movement is conditional on timely return. Break the condition and the law rewrites history — the despatch becomes a taxable supply from day one.

options.text: The fabric is deemed supplied in June 2026, when the year expired
options.misconception: dates the deemed supply at the breach instead of the despatch
options.why: The deeming is retrospective to the date the goods went out. That is what makes the interest bite — fourteen months of it here, not two.

options.text: The fabric is deemed supplied on 1 June 2025, with tax and interest; the dies have time until June 2028
options.why: Inputs get one year, and the fabric's year ran out in June 2026 — the deeming reaches back to the day of despatch, so interest runs from 2025, not from the breach. Capital goods get three years, so the dies are safely out until 2028.

options.text: Both are deemed supplied, since neither returned within one year
options.misconception: applies the inputs window to capital goods
options.why: The section keeps two clocks. Dies are capital goods on a three-year clock, and treating them on the one-year clock manufactures a liability that does not exist.

citation.ref: Section 143(3) and 143(4)

items.scenario: A manufacturer sent dies worth ₹30 lakh (capital goods) and fabric worth ₹12 lakh (inputs) to a job worker on 1 June 2025 without payment of tax. The fabric is still with the job worker in August 2026; the dies are expected back in 2027.

items.stem: Is the colleague right?

options.text: Yes, unless the exporter pays IGST on exports first and reclaims it
options.misconception: makes the pay-and-refund route the only lawful one
options.why: Paying IGST and claiming it back is one of two routes. The LUT route reaches the same destination without routing ₹18 lakh through the Government and back.

options.text: Partly — credit survives but can only offset future domestic output tax, never refund
options.misconception: allows the credit but denies the refund that makes exporting viable
options.why: An exporter with no domestic sales would accumulate credit forever. Refund of unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies is the section's whole mechanism.

options.text: No — zero-rating keeps the credit alive, and the unutilised ₹18 lakh is refundable
options.why: Zero-rated is a different legal creature from exempt. Section 16 of the IGST Act preserves credit on inputs feeding zero-rated supplies, and the LUT route exists precisely so the exporter can skip charging tax yet recover the input side as a refund.

options.text: Yes — supplies on which no tax is charged are exempt, and exempt supplies block credit
options.misconception: collapses zero-rated into exempt
options.why: For exempt supplies the credit dies; for zero-rated it survives by express provision. The zero on the invoice looks identical and works oppositely, which is why the paper tests it.

citation.ref: Section 16

items.scenario: An exporter of garments buys inputs carrying ₹18 lakh of GST and exports the entire output under a letter of undertaking, charging no tax on the export invoices. A colleague warns that selling without charging tax makes the supplies exempt, killing the input credit.

items.stem: Was an e-way bill required?

options.text: Yes — the bill attaches to movement of goods above fifty thousand rupees, sale or no sale
options.why: Rule 138 is triggered by causing movement of a consignment worth more than ₹50,000, and a branch transfer moves goods as surely as a sale does. The delivery challan takes the place of the invoice; the e-way bill is needed either way.

options.text: No, because both godowns belong to the same legal entity
options.misconception: treats intra-entity movement as outside the rule
options.why: The rule asks what is moving and how much it is worth, not who owns each end of the journey. Same-entity transfers above the limit are squarely inside it.

options.text: Yes, but only if the goods cross the State border
options.misconception: confines the requirement to inter-State movement
options.why: Intra-State movement carries the requirement too, though States may set higher limits for it. Indore to Bhopal is within one State and still within the rule.

options.text: No, because an e-way bill accompanies a tax invoice, and none exists here
options.misconception: ties the bill to the invoice instead of the movement
