options.why: Movements without invoices travel on delivery challans, and the rule expressly covers reasons other than supply. The paperwork changes; the bill does not.

citation.ref: Rule 138

items.scenario: A registered dealer sends goods worth ₹3.2 lakh from its Indore godown to its own Bhopal branch, a stock transfer with no sale and no payment. The despatch clerk skips the e-way bill on the ground that nothing has been sold.

items.stem: What does release under section 129 cost him?

options.text: Nothing beyond a ₹10,000 general penalty, since no tax was evaded
options.misconception: imports the no-evasion leniency into a strict transit provision
options.why: Section 129 is deliberately indifferent to intent. The absent e-way bill is the offence, and courts have upheld the harshness because transit checks are where evasion hides.

options.text: A bond for the goods' value, with the penalty argued later in adjudication
options.misconception: offers the security route available to a non-owner as the owner's escape
options.why: Security in lieu is a route the section provides, but the release price stays the same penalty. The bond defers payment; it does not reduce what unlocks the truck.

options.text: A penalty of ₹3.6 lakh — two hundred per cent of the tax payable
options.why: Where the owner comes forward, section 129(1)(a) prices release at 200 per cent of the tax payable on the goods. The invoice showing tax charged does not soften it — the section punishes the movement's non-compliance, not evasion of the levy.

options.text: The ₹1.8 lakh tax plus a modest general penalty
options.misconception: applies the pre-amendment tax-plus-penalty formula
options.why: The section was rewritten to a pure penalty of 200 per cent. Answers built on the old tax-plus-100-per-cent split describe a provision that no longer exists.

citation.ref: Section 129(1)(a)

items.scenario: A truck carrying taxable goods worth ₹10 lakh (tax ₹1.8 lakh) is intercepted without a valid e-way bill. The consignor owns up, produces the invoice showing tax fully charged, and argues that since the tax is on the invoice and will be paid with the return, only a token fine can apply.

items.stem: What is the GST position on the two transactions?

options.text: Neither is taxable, since GST requires consideration
options.misconception: treats consideration as indispensable to supply
options.why: Consideration is the general rule and Schedule I is the list of exceptions to it. The van is the textbook case — credit was enjoyed on the way in, so the way out is taxed.

options.text: The van is a deemed supply and taxable; the hampers stay outside as gifts within fifty thousand
options.why: Permanent disposal of a business asset that carried credit is Schedule I's first entry — consideration is irrelevant once the credit was taken. Employee gifts have their own carve-out and ₹4,000 sits well inside the fifty-thousand-per-employee-per-year line.

options.text: The van escapes because it went to a charity; the hampers are taxable perquisites
options.misconception: imports an income-tax charity instinct and a perquisite label into GST
options.why: GST has no donee-based relief here — the recipient's character does not undo Schedule I. And perquisite is an income-tax word; for GST the hampers are simply gifts under the fifty-thousand line.

options.text: Both are taxable, since both are supplies without consideration by a business
options.misconception: sweeps the employee-gift carve-out into the deeming
options.why: Gifts up to fifty thousand rupees a year per employee are expressly kept out. Taxing the hampers taxes what the proviso protects.

citation.ref: Schedule I

items.scenario: A company gives away an old delivery van, on which it had claimed input tax credit, free to a charitable school. The accountant books no GST since nothing was received in return. The same month, the company gifts each of its forty employees a festival hamper worth ₹4,000.

items.stem: How do these two sales sit under GST?

options.text: The building is taxable because it was sold by a developer in the course of business
options.misconception: lets the seller's trade override the completion certificate
options.why: Business character brings a transaction into GST only if it is a supply. A completed building with its certificate is out by schedule, developer or not — the tax belongs to under-construction sales.

options.text: Both are exempt supplies, and count toward aggregate turnover
options.misconception: confuses non-supplies with exempt supplies
options.why: Exempt supplies are supplies that a notification relieves; Schedule III transactions never become supplies in the first place. The difference shows up exactly where the accountant worried — turnover computations.

options.text: The land escapes but the building attracts GST at the works contract rate
options.misconception: taxes a completed sale as if construction services were still being supplied
options.why: Works contract rates belong to construction underway for a buyer. After completion and certification there is no service left to tax; what changes hands is immovable property.

options.text: Neither is a supply at all — Schedule III keeps land and completed buildings outside GST
options.why: Sale of land, and of a building after its completion certificate, are Schedule III entries — treated as neither goods nor services. They are not exempt supplies; they are non-supplies, which is why they also stay out of aggregate turnover.

citation.ref: Schedule III

items.scenario: A developer sells a completed office building with its occupancy certificate in hand for ₹48 crore, and separately sells a plot of land for ₹12 crore. His new accountant worries that these sales, being high-value, will attract GST and swell aggregate turnover past every threshold.

items.stem: Is the refund claim within time?

options.text: Yes — where tax was paid under a demand later set aside, the relevant date is the judgment's date
options.why: Section 54's two years run from the relevant date, and the definition assigns judgment-driven refunds the date of the judgment. The clock the department is reading — the payment date — belongs to a different ground of claim.

options.text: No — two years from payment is absolute, and equity cannot extend limitation
options.misconception: reads one relevant date as the only relevant date
options.why: The rigour of the limitation is real, but the statute itself moves the starting line by ground of claim. No equity is needed; the definition does the work.

options.text: Yes, because limitation never applies to tax collected without authority
options.misconception: right result, lawless route
options.why: Even unconstitutional levies travel through the refund machinery with its windows. The claim succeeds here because the statutory clock starts at the judgment, not because clocks stop for good causes.

options.text: No, unless the company had paid the tax under protest in 2024
options.misconception: imports the old excise protest requirement into GST
options.why: Payment under protest shaped refunds under the old law. Section 54's relevant-date definition replaced that scaffolding; the judgment date governs with or without a protest letter.

citation.ref: Section 54(1)

items.scenario: In August 2026 a company wins its writ petition: tax of ₹40 lakh it paid in March 2024 under a demand is held to have been collected without authority. The department resists the refund, arguing the two-year window from the March 2024 payment closed in March 2026.

items.stem: Is the adviser right?

options.text: No — the consultancy can use the ordinary one per cent traders' rate instead
options.misconception: puts the right taxpayer into the wrong scheme
options.why: The ordinary scheme's rates belong to manufacturers, traders and restaurants. A pure service provider enters through 10(2A) and pays that scheme's six per cent, not the traders' one.

options.text: Yes for this year, since eligibility needs current-year turnover below fifty lakh first
options.misconception: tests eligibility on the running year instead of the preceding one
options.why: The gate reads the preceding financial year — ₹42 lakh, inside the line. The current year's growth ends the scheme prospectively when it crosses, never retrospectively.

options.text: Yes — composition remains closed to every service except restaurants
options.misconception: states the pre-2019 law as current
options.why: True until section 10(2A) arrived, and stale ever since. The scheme the adviser denies is sitting in the section he cited.

options.text: No — section 10(2A) gives pure service providers their own scheme at six per cent within fifty lakh
options.why: The adviser's rule described the original section 10. The 2019 insertion built a parallel scheme for exactly this taxpayer — services, preceding-year turnover within fifty lakh, six per cent on turnover, with the same stay-local discipline.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A)

items.scenario: An interior design consultancy with preceding-year turnover of ₹42 lakh wants a simple flat levy instead of regular GST compliance. Its adviser rules out composition entirely, saying the scheme is for traders and restaurants, never for service providers.

items.stem: On which vehicles is the credit good?

options.text: All three — each vehicle is used in the course of business
options.misconception: lets section 16's general test override section 17's specific block
options.why: Business use is the entry condition, and section 17(5) then blocks listed items notwithstanding it. The sedan is genuinely for business and still loses its credit.

options.text: The bus and the van — only the sedan's credit is blocked
options.why: The block in section 17(5)(a) reaches motor vehicles for transporting persons with seating up to thirteen, and the sedan fits none of the three saving uses. The bus escapes on capacity — above thirteen seats — and the van escapes because it transports goods, a category the block never covered.

options.text: None — credit on motor vehicles is blocked for everyone except vehicle dealers
options.misconception: remembers the block without its capacity and goods carve-outs
options.why: The block was drawn narrowly on purpose: passenger vehicles up to thirteen seats. Buses and goods carriages are ordinary creditable business assets.

options.text: The sedan and the bus, since both carry persons; the van fails as it carries no people
options.misconception: inverts the block — reads it as favouring passenger transport
options.why: Carrying persons in a small vehicle is what triggers the block, not what saves from it. The van's goods-carrying character is exactly why its credit flows.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a)

items.scenario: A consulting firm buys three vehicles in a year: a five-seater sedan for partners' travel, a twenty-seater bus to shuttle staff, and a delivery van for moving office equipment between branches. It claims input tax credit on all three.

items.stem: What is the time of supply for each part of the consideration?

options.text: 10 May for everything — liability arises when full payment is received
options.misconception: waits for the last rupee
options.why: Earlier of the events, not latest. Waiting for final payment would let parties schedule their own tax periods, the exact discretion the section removes.

options.text: 25 March for the advance; 20 April for the balance
options.why: The invoice is timely, so the rule is the earlier of invoice and payment, applied to the extent of each amount. The advance's payment date beats the invoice, pulling 40 per cent into March — the earlier tax period. For the balance the invoice of 20 April beats the May payment.

options.text: 5 April for everything — tax follows completion of the service
options.misconception: replaces the statutory comparators with the completion date
options.why: Completion enters the rule only when the invoice misses its thirty-day window. With a timely invoice, the statute reads invoice against payment and never asks when the work finished.

options.text: 20 April for everything, since one invoice covers the whole supply
options.misconception: lets the invoice absorb an advance received earlier
options.why: The provision applies to the extent the invoice or payment covers the supply. Money received in March is taxable by reference to March; the invoice cannot pull it forward into April.

citation.ref: Section 13(2)

items.scenario: A service is completed on 5 April. The client pays an advance of 40 per cent on 25 March, before completion. The invoice is issued on 20 April, within the thirty-day limit, and the balance is paid on 10 May.

items.stem: What does the company actually get?

options.text: ₹39.2 lakh, but only if the re-export happens within six months of import
options.misconception: shrinks the two-year window
options.why: Section 74 allows two years from payment of duty, extendable on sufficient cause. Fourteen months is comfortably inside.

options.text: The full ₹40 lakh, since the machine was never used in India
options.misconception: rounds ninety-eight up to a hundred
options.why: The statute keeps two per cent even for unused goods — the cost of the round trip through customs. Only the tapering rates for used goods fall below that.

options.text: Nothing — drawback requires the goods to have been used in manufacturing exports
options.misconception: knows only section 75 and reads it as the whole of drawback
options.why: That manufacturing route is real but parallel. Section 74 exists for the simpler case — the goods go back out as themselves — and asks only identity and the time window.

options.text: ₹39.2 lakh — ninety-eight per cent under section 74, since the same goods left within two years
options.why: Re-export of the imported goods themselves, identified as such and inside the two-year window, is exactly section 74's case, and the unused-goods rate is ninety-eight per cent. The department's objection describes section 75, which is the drawback for inputs consumed in manufacture — a different section for a different exporter.

citation.ref: Section 74

items.scenario: A company imports a specialised machine paying ₹40 lakh in duty. The buyer's project is cancelled, and fourteen months later the identical machine, unused and identified by the customs authorities as the imported one, is shipped back to the seller. The company claims the whole ₹40 lakh back; the department offers nothing, saying drawback belongs to manufacturer-exporters.

items.stem: Where is the place of supply, and why?

options.text: Maharashtra — services are supplied from where the supplier works
options.misconception: taxes the origin instead of the destination
options.why: GST is a destination tax; the supplier's location matters for identifying the levy, not the place of supply. Where the architect sits is the one place the section never picks.

options.text: Goa — services directly relating to immovable property are supplied where the property is
options.why: Section 12(3) carves property-linked services out of the default: an architect's design for a specific site takes the site's location. The building in Goa anchors the supply, and the recipient's Karnataka registration never enters the analysis.

options.text: Karnataka — the registered recipient's location governs services between registered persons
options.misconception: applies the general rule over the specific carve-out
options.why: Section 12(2)'s default yields wherever a specific sub-section speaks. Property-linked services have their own rule precisely because the consumption happens at the site.

options.text: The firm may choose any of the three states if it discloses the choice on the invoice
options.misconception: makes place of supply elective
options.why: Place of supply is fixed by statute so that the consuming state gets the revenue. An election on the invoice would let suppliers route tax to convenient states.

citation.ref: Section 12(3)

items.scenario: An architect registered in Maharashtra designs a hotel to be built in Goa for a client registered in Karnataka. The firm bills IGST with place of supply Karnataka, using the default rule that services go where the registered recipient is.

items.stem: How does GST actually treat the contract?

options.text: As one supply of services for the whole ₹10 crore — Schedule II deems the entire works contract a service
options.why: The composite construction contract on immovable property is a works contract, and Schedule II declares it a supply of services in its entirety. One classification, one rate for the whole consideration. The VAT-era vivisection of a single contract is the precise mischief the deeming ended.

options.text: As a supply of goods, since materials dominate the contract value
options.misconception: classifies by the larger component instead of by the deeming
options.why: Dominance tests decide unlisted composite supplies. Works contracts never reach that test — the schedule has already answered, and it answered services regardless of the ratio.

options.text: The split is right — goods are goods and services are services, whatever the contract says
options.misconception: carries the pre-GST split into a regime that abolished it
options.why: Under the old twin levies the split was compulsory; under GST the deeming makes it wrong. The embedded steel is not sold as steel — it disappears into an immovable whole.

options.text: Whichever classification yields less tax, at the contractor's option
options.misconception: converts a statutory deeming into a planning choice
options.why: Schedule II exists to remove exactly this election. Classification is fixed by law so that identical contracts cannot be taxed differently by drafting.

citation.ref: Schedule II, para 6(a)

items.scenario: A contractor builds a factory for ₹10 crore, of which ₹6 crore is steel, cement and machinery embedded in the works and ₹4 crore is labour and services. Its accountant splits the invoice — charging goods rates of GST on ₹6 crore and service rates on ₹4 crore — the way the firm did under VAT and service tax.

items.stem: Is the officer's approach correct?

options.text: No — the relationship displaces the price only if it influenced the price, which the importer may disprove
options.why: Section 14 accepts the price actually paid unless the relationship influenced it, and the valuation rules give the importer the chance to show the price approximates arm's-length benchmarks — a discount explicable by volumes or reduced marketing costs can survive. Rejection needs examination, not the mere existence of the relationship.

options.text: Yes — related-party prices are automatically substituted with the catalogue price
options.misconception: converts a rebuttable concern into an automatic rejection
options.why: Automatic substitution would tax corporate structure rather than value. The rules order an examination of the circumstances of sale first, and accept the price where the relationship did not move it.

options.text: No, because customs must always accept the invoice as conclusive
options.misconception: swings to the opposite absolute
options.why: The declared price is the starting point, not scripture. Where the relationship did influence it, the rules walk down the substitute methods — identical goods, similar goods, and onward.

options.text: Yes, unless the parent certifies in writing that the price is fair
options.misconception: lets the interested party certify its own valuation
options.why: A self-serving certificate from the seller proves nothing. What counts is evidence — test values, comparable sales, cost build-ups — examined under the valuation rules.

citation.ref: Section 14

items.scenario: An Indian subsidiary imports components from its foreign parent at a price 8 per cent below the parent's catalogue price to independent distributors. The customs officer rejects the declared value outright, holding that a price between related persons can never be the transaction value.

items.stem: What is the correct value of supply?

options.text: ₹10.35 lakh — the subsidy is included but interest never is
options.misconception: right on the subsidy, wrong on delayed-payment interest
options.why: Clause (d) names interest, late fee and penalty for delayed payment of consideration as part of value. It is taxed when received, but it is taxed.

options.text: ₹10 lakh — everything beyond the price of the machine is a separate matter
options.misconception: reads value as bare price
options.why: The subsection exists to stop exactly this unbundling. Packing and levies are the cost of delivering the supply, and the statute plants them in its value.

options.text: ₹11.05 lakh at the outset — packing, the levy and the subsidy come in — plus the ₹8,000 interest when received
options.why: Section 15(2) sweeps in incidental expenses charged by the supplier, taxes other than GST, and price-linked subsidies from non-Government sources — the state board is a Government body, but the item to test is its character; a board subsidy directly linked to price from other than Central or State Government enters the value. Interest for delayed payment joins the value when it materialises.

options.text: ₹10.20 lakh — only the packing, since the supplier itself rendered it
options.misconception: admits one inclusion and drops the rest of the list
options.why: The subsection is a list, not an example. The municipal levy and the price-linked subsidy stand on the same statutory footing as the packing.

citation.ref: Section 15(2)

items.scenario: A machine is sold for ₹10 lakh. The invoice adds ₹20,000 packing, ₹15,000 municipal levy the supplier must pay on the sale, and the buyer later pays ₹8,000 interest for settling two months late. A state agricultural board also pays the supplier a ₹50,000 subsidy tied to each machine's price. The accountant charges GST on ₹10 lakh alone.

items.stem: Which supply is actually an export of services?

options.text: Neither, because software services are consumed where they are written
options.misconception: invents an origin rule for services
options.why: Place of supply for such services follows the recipient's location. The German client's supply lands outside India and qualifies; the branch supply fails on identity, not on geography.

options.text: Both — each crosses the border and brings in foreign exchange
options.misconception: tests exports by geography and currency alone
options.why: Those are two conditions of five. The merely-establishments clause was written for precisely the branch case, where money moves inside one legal person.

options.text: Only the German one — the Dubai branch is the same person, and a supply to yourself fails the export definition
options.why: Section 2(6)'s fifth condition excludes supplies between establishments of the same person treated as distinct persons. The branch is the company; convertible currency and a foreign address cannot make a transaction with oneself an export. The German supply ticks all five conditions.

options.text: Both, provided the Dubai branch is separately registered in the UAE
options.misconception: lets foreign registration split one legal person
options.why: Registration abroad changes the branch's local compliance, not its identity. The Indian Act's definition looks at whether supplier and recipient are one person, and they are.

citation.ref: Section 2(6)

items.scenario: An Indian software company provides development services to its own branch in Dubai, which pays in dirhams through banking channels. Separately it serves an unrelated German client, paid in euros. The company treats both as zero-rated exports and claims refunds.

items.stem: Does the tax reduction survive scrutiny?

options.text: Yes, if the buyer certifies it has reversed the corresponding input credit
options.misconception: lets reversal on one side reopen a closed window on the other
options.why: The buyer's reversal is a condition of the mechanism working inside the window, not a key to it afterwards. Past the date, the section offers no route back.

options.text: No, and even the commercial credit note is barred after November
options.misconception: extends the tax deadline to the price itself
options.why: Parties may adjust prices between themselves forever; that is contract, not tax. What expires in November is only the right to take GST back from the government.

options.text: No — the window for a January 2026 (FY 2025-26) supply closed on 30 November 2026
options.why: Section 34(2) lets the credit note reduce tax only up to the thirtieth of November following the financial year of the supply. A December 2026 note for an FY 2025-26 supply is out of time: the goods may come back and the price may be refunded, but the tax adjustment is barred — a commercial credit note is all that remains.

options.text: Yes — returns within one year of supply always carry their tax back
options.misconception: invents a rolling one-year window
options.why: The clock is anchored to the financial year's end, not the invoice date. A supply made in March gets eight months; one made in April gets nearly twenty — the statute accepts that unevenness for the sake of closing years.

citation.ref: Section 34(2)

items.scenario: In January 2026 a wholesaler supplied goods with ₹18 lakh GST. In December 2026 the buyer returns a third of the goods. The wholesaler issues a GST credit note for ₹6 lakh of tax and reduces its output liability in the December 2026 return.

items.stem: How much of the ₹29.8 lakh is actually creditable?

options.text: All ₹29.8 lakh — every tax on a business input is creditable under GST
options.misconception: sweeps basic customs duty into a credit system it never joined
options.why: BCD is a customs levy proper, protecting the border, with no credit mechanism. Only the IGST component crosses into the input tax ledger.

options.text: The ₹19.8 lakh IGST — collected by customs but creditable as input tax; only the ₹10 lakh BCD is cost
options.why: The proviso to section 5(1) routes the tax on imported goods through customs machinery for collection, but what is collected is IGST — input tax in the importer's hands, creditable against output liability like any other. Basic customs duty stays outside the credit chain and lands in cost.

options.text: The IGST, but only half now and half next year, as for capital goods under the old law
options.misconception: applies CENVAT's instalment rule to GST
options.why: The fifty-per-cent-per-year split for capital goods died with CENVAT. GST credits capital goods IGST in full in the year of receipt.

options.text: Nothing — duties paid at the port never enter the GST credit stream
options.misconception: classifies the tax by its collector instead of its character
options.why: The collection point is administrative convenience. The levy's character is IGST on an inter-State supply, and the credit provisions treat it exactly so.

citation.ref: Section 5(1) proviso

items.scenario: A registered manufacturer imports machinery: assessable value ₹1 crore, basic customs duty ₹10 lakh, IGST ₹19.8 lakh charged at the port. Its accountant books the entire ₹29.8 lakh as cost, saying taxes collected by customs are customs duties, and no customs duty is ever creditable under GST.

items.stem: What does GST make of the two internal flows?

options.text: Neither — a person cannot make a supply to himself under any tax law
options.misconception: argues from general law against a specific statutory fiction
options.why: The fiction of distinct persons was enacted to override exactly this intuition. Without it, consuming States would lose the tax on everything routed through another State's warehouse.

options.text: Both, but only when the depot actually sells the stock onward
options.misconception: defers the internal supply to the external sale
options.why: The transfer is itself the taxable event, at its own time of supply. The depot's later sale is a second supply with its own tax — two events, two levies, credit linking them.

options.text: The goods yes, the services no — offices only assist, they do not supply
options.misconception: taxes what moves in trucks and misses what moves between offices
options.why: Services between distinct persons sit in the same Schedule I entry. A head office keeping the group's books renders a service the branches would otherwise buy.

options.text: Both are taxable supplies between distinct persons — the stock transfer and the head office services alike
options.why: Each State registration is a distinct person, and Schedule I taxes supplies between them without consideration. The stock transfer bears IGST on its rule-based value, and the head office's centralised services to branches are supplies too. Credit at the receiving end typically neutralises the cash cost — but the compliance is not optional.

citation.ref: Section 25(4) with Schedule I

items.scenario: A company's Maharashtra factory sends finished stock worth ₹2 crore to its own Karnataka depot for sale there. Its Mumbai head office also handles accounting and IT for all branches. The tax head charges no GST on either, reasoning that no one can sell to themselves or invoice their own branches.

items.stem: Who bears the duty on each consignment?

options.text: Neither falls on the importer — the custodian pays for the pilfered goods, and the fire loss earns remission on proof
options.why: Section 13 lifts the importer's duty on goods pilfered between unloading and clearance and section 45 sends the bill to the custodian whose watch failed. Section 23 remits duty on goods lost or destroyed before clearance once the Assistant Commissioner is satisfied — the fire needs proving, but proven, the duty goes.

options.text: Both — importation was complete when the goods entered Indian waters
options.misconception: fixes duty at the moment of import and ignores both relieving sections
options.why: The taxable event may arise on import, but Parliament relieved exactly these casualties. Charging duty on goods the importer never received turns customs into an insurer's windfall.

options.text: The pilferage yes, the fire no — theft is the importer's commercial risk
options.misconception: reverses the two sections
options.why: Pilferage is the automatic relief — no application, duty simply not payable by the importer — because the goods sat with the custodian. It is the fire that needs a satisfaction-based remission order.

options.text: Neither, provided the importer first pays the duty and claims refunds later
options.misconception: routes statutory relief through the refund machinery
options.why: Section 13 means duty is not leviable on the importer at all, and section 23 remits before payment. Pay-first-refund-later imports the cash flow burden the sections spare.

citation.ref: Sections 13 and 23

items.scenario: Two misfortunes strike an importer at the port: one consignment is pilfered from the custodian's warehouse after unloading, before clearance; another is destroyed in a warehouse fire, also before clearance. The department demands full duty on both, saying risk passes to the importer on arrival.

items.stem: How does GST actually split the two streams?

options.text: TCS on both — the app is one platform and one compliance applies
options.misconception: runs the collection mechanism where the liability shift governs
options.why: Section 9(5) overrides for its notified services precisely because chasing thousands of drivers was impractical. Collecting TCS from a supplier the law has already displaced doubles the machinery on the wrong person.

options.text: Neither — platforms are intermediaries outside the tax net entirely
options.misconception: mistakes facilitation for invisibility
options.why: The statute built two regimes specifically for platforms. An operator with no TCS registration and no 9(5) payment is not neutral; it is non-compliant twice.

options.text: The app pays tax on both streams as the deemed supplier of everything it hosts
options.misconception: stretches 9(5) from its notified services to all commerce
options.why: The deeming covers the notified list — transport, accommodation, restaurants, housekeeping. Goods never entered it; the handicraft seller remains the taxable person, minus the TCS slice.

options.text: TCS on the handicraft sales; on the cab rides the app itself pays the tax under section 9(5), with no TCS on them
options.why: Goods sold through the platform take the section 52 route: the supplier remains liable and the operator collects a slice at source. Passenger transport is a notified 9(5) service, so the app is deemed the supplier and pays the tax itself — and since it pays as supplier, there is nothing to collect TCS on. The two regimes are exclusive by design.

citation.ref: Sections 52 and 9(5)

items.scenario: A marketplace app hosts two businesses: a seller of handicrafts shipping goods to buyers, and a network of cab drivers carrying passengers. The app's compliance team plans to collect TCS on both streams and leave the GST liability with each supplier, treating the app as a mere platform throughout.

items.stem: Which line has its input credit wrongly reversed?

options.text: The exports — zero-rated supplies keep their input credit, unlike the other two
options.why: Zero-rating under IGST section 16 is taxability at rate zero with the credit chain deliberately intact — refundable, not reversible. The liquor is non-taxable and the vegetables exempt; input credit attributable to those two does reverse. Calling all three tax-free treats the one favoured category as if it were the penalised ones.

options.text: The vegetables — nil-rated goods are taxable supplies, so their credit stays
options.misconception: reads nil-rated as outside exemption
options.why: Nil-rated is taxable at zero per cent, but the exempt-supply definition sweeps nil-rated in for credit purposes. The credit attributable to them reverses like any exempt supply's.

options.text: None — no tax on the output always means no credit on the inputs
options.misconception: states the exemption rule as if it were universal
options.why: That symmetry is exactly what zero-rating suspends. Exports carry no tax and full credit — the design that keeps Indian goods competitive abroad.

options.text: The liquor — outside GST means GST rules cannot touch its credit
options.misconception: hopes non-taxability shields the inputs too
options.why: The inputs bore GST even though the output escapes it, and the exempt-supply definition includes non-taxable supplies precisely so their input credit reverses. Outside the levy is inside the reversal.

citation.ref: Sections 2(47), 2(78) and IGST 16

items.scenario: A distillery-cum-exporter reviews three revenue lines: liquor for human consumption sold in India; fresh vegetables (nil-rated) traded domestically; and packaged spices exported to Dubai. The accountant lumps all three as "tax-free sales" and reverses input credit proportionately across them all.

items.stem: Can the client stand on the competitor's ruling?

options.text: Yes — a ruling on a product settles that product's rate for everyone in the State
options.misconception: reads a personal ruling as a rate notification
options.why: Rate-setting for all belongs to notifications and the Council. Advance ruling is a private clarification machinery, and its answers travel with the applicant alone.

options.text: No — the ruling binds only its applicant and that applicant's officers; the client needs its own ruling or its own defence
options.why: Section 103 draws the boundary in terms: the applicant who sought it, and the jurisdictional authorities in respect of the applicant. Identical facts earn the competitor's ruling persuasive value in the client's proceedings, but no binding force — the demand must be fought on merits, or pre-empted by the client's own application.

options.text: No, but only because rulings from rival businesses are inadmissible
options.misconception: invents a rivalry bar where the limit is privity
options.why: The competitor's ruling is perfectly admissible as persuasive material. What it lacks is bindingness for anyone but its own applicant — friendship or rivalry beside the point.

options.text: Yes, because officers must treat identical taxpayers identically
options.misconception: converts an equality aspiration into a statutory binding
options.why: Consistency arguments may persuade an appellate forum; section 103's binding force is nonetheless written narrowly, and the officer issuing the demand breaches no provision.

citation.ref: Section 103

items.scenario: A competitor of your client obtained an advance ruling in the same State holding that the very product both companies make attracts 5 per cent GST, not 18. Your client, on identical facts, starts charging 5 per cent, citing the ruling, and its jurisdictional officer issues a demand at 18 per cent.

items.stem: What did the office get wrong?

options.text: Both calls — the ₹2.4 lakh contract is below the contract-wise threshold, and the deduction base excludes GST
options.why: Section 51's two-and-a-half lakh test applies per contract, not per supplier per year; the smaller contract never enters the net. And the deduction runs on the value excluding the tax charged — deducting on GST-inclusive totals takes two per cent of the government's own tax as well.

options.text: Everything, because municipal bodies are outside section 51 entirely
options.misconception: excludes a named deductor category
options.why: Local authorities are in the section's first rank of deductors. The corporation deducts — on the right contract, on the right base.

options.text: Only the GST-inclusive base — aggregation across contracts is correct
options.misconception: half-right, keeping the aggregation error
options.why: The base correction is real, but the smaller contract still escapes: below the line, no deduction at all, whatever its siblings total.

options.text: Nothing — aggregation prevents contract-splitting abuse
options.misconception: imports income-tax style aggregation into a contract-wise test
options.why: The statute chose the contract as the unit, accepting the splitting risk. Reading in aggregation deducts where Parliament said not to.

citation.ref: Section 51

items.scenario: A municipal corporation awards a supplier two separate contracts in the year: one for ₹2.4 lakh taxable value, one for ₹2.8 lakh plus GST. The accounts office deducts two per cent from payments under both, "since together they cross the threshold", computing the deduction on invoice totals including GST.

items.stem: Whose refund applications survive section 54(3)?

options.text: Only the exporter — inverted structure refunds ended with the rate rationalisations
options.misconception: mistakes rate-schedule housekeeping for repeal
options.why: The inverted-structure refund stands in the statute, formula and all. Rationalisation shrinks how often inversion occurs, not the right when it does.

options.text: The fabric maker and the trader — exporters must first charge IGST and claim that route alone
options.misconception: makes the with-payment route mandatory
options.why: Zero-rating offers two routes at the exporter's choice: pay IGST and claim it back, or ship under LUT and refund the input credit. The LUT route is the one built for working-capital-light exporting.

options.text: The fabric maker and the exporter — inverted structure and zero-rating are the only two gates, and slow sales is neither
options.why: The proviso to section 54(3) names its two cases. Inputs at 18 against output at 5 is the inverted duty structure; LUT exports are zero-rated supplies without payment of tax. The trader's credit is real and stays usable, but accumulation from weak demand is outside both gates — the credit waits for sales, and no refund flows.

options.text: All three — unutilised credit is the taxpayer's money and must be returned on demand
options.misconception: converts a ledger balance into a refundable deposit
options.why: Credit is a set-off right, not a bank balance. Parliament opened two narrow doors for structural accumulation; commercial accumulation keeps its value only against future output tax.

citation.ref: Section 54(3)

items.scenario: Three registered businesses carry large unutilised input credit: a fabric maker whose inputs bear 18 per cent while its output cloth bears 5; an exporter shipping under LUT without charging tax; and a tractor-parts trader whose credit built up because sales collapsed this year. All three apply for refunds of the accumulated credit.

items.stem: Which rate applies?

options.text: 15 per cent — for warehoused goods the rate is taken on the date of the ex-bond bill of entry
options.why: Section 15(1)(b) fixes the rate for goods cleared from a warehouse at the date the ex-bond bill of entry for home consumption is filed. Warehousing defers duty, and the deferral carries rate risk both ways: the importer who waits past a Budget waits at the new rate.

options.text: 10 per cent, provided the into-bond bill of entry was assessed before the Budget
options.misconception: promotes the into-bond assessment into a rate lock
options.why: The into-bond bill records the goods entering the warehouse without payment; it fixes identity and value details, not the eventual rate. The operative filing for rate is the ex-bond one.

options.text: The average of the two rates, apportioned by days in bond at each
options.misconception: invents equitable apportionment in a fixed-date statute
options.why: Section 15 names one date per situation, and blending rates appears nowhere. Certainty of the date is the section's whole design.

options.text: 10 per cent — the taxable event and its rate crystallise on the goods' arrival
options.misconception: fuses the taxable event with the rate-determination date
options.why: The levy may attach on import, but Parliament separately fixed when the rate is read, and for bonded goods that is clearance, not arrival. The two dates diverge exactly in warehousing cases.

citation.ref: Section 15(1)

items.scenario: Goods arrive at port on 1 June, when duty is 10 per cent, and go into a bonded warehouse. On 1 August the Budget raises the rate to 15 per cent. On 1 September the importer files the ex-bond bill of entry to clear the goods for home consumption, and demands assessment at 10 per cent, since duty attaches when goods enter India.

items.stem: Who must register despite the threshold?

options.text: The handicrafts maker and the trader — inter-State goods and reverse charge liability compel registration; the services consultant keeps the threshold
options.why: Section 24 overrides the threshold for inter-State suppliers of goods and for persons liable to pay under reverse charge — the maker's first courier across the border and the trader's GTA freight each trigger it at any turnover. Inter-State service providers were notified out of the compulsion up to the threshold, which is what spares the consultant.

options.text: All three — crossing a State line or a reverse charge in any form ends every exemption
options.misconception: misses the services relaxation
options.why: The notification relieving inter-State service suppliers below the threshold is the asymmetry this question turns on. Goods and services parted ways here.

options.text: Only the trader, since reverse charge is the gravest trigger
options.misconception: ranks the list instead of applying it
options.why: Section 24's clauses are parallel, not graded. Inter-State goods supply compels the maker exactly as reverse charge compels the trader.

options.text: None — the threshold protects small suppliers whatever they do
options.misconception: reads section 22 without section 24
options.why: The threshold is the general rule and section 24 the list of exceptions notwithstanding it. The maker's ₹9 lakh does not matter once the goods cross the border.

citation.ref: Section 24

items.scenario: Three small operators, each below the registration threshold: a Jaipur handicrafts maker with ₹9 lakh turnover who has begun couriering goods to buyers in other States; a Delhi consultant with ₹15 lakh in fees serving clients across India; and a Kerala trader with ₹8 lakh local sales who pays freight to a goods transport agency under reverse charge.

items.stem: Which two scheme conditions is the exporter breaching?

options.text: The scheme itself lapsed with GST, so only customs law conditions matter
options.misconception: buries a living FTP scheme
options.why: EPCG runs under the current Foreign Trade Policy alongside GST, with IGST exemption and duty savings intact. Its conditions bind as firmly as ever.

options.text: The obligation is ₹12 crore over and above the maintained average, and uninstalled machines breach the installation condition outright
options.why: Six times the ₹2 crore saved must come as additional exports beyond the ₹30 crore average the exporter must also maintain — counting business-as-usual shipments discharges nothing. And the scheme requires installation and use of the capital goods within the prescribed period; crated machines in year five invite proportionate duty recovery with interest.

options.text: Only the installation delay, curable by an extension application
options.misconception: half-right on the machines, wrong on the arithmetic
options.why: Extensions exist within limits, but the deeper breach is the discharge theory: without exports above the average, year six ends with the full duty plus interest falling due.

options.text: Nothing — ₹30 crore a year dwarfs a ₹12 crore obligation many times over
options.misconception: counts the average toward the additional obligation
options.why: The average-export condition exists to make the obligation incremental. The scheme pays for growth in exports, not for exports that were happening anyway.

citation.ref: EPCG scheme (export obligation 6x duty saved in 6 years)

items.scenario: A garment exporter imports machines under EPCG saving ₹2 crore of duty. Its recent exports average ₹30 crore a year. The CFO plans to treat the existing ₹30 crore annual exports as automatically discharging the obligation, and in year five reports the machines still in their crates awaiting factory expansion.

items.stem: Is the manufacturer's tax choice right?

options.text: There is only one supply — manufacturer to the final customer — and the trader merely arranges it
options.misconception: collapses the chain the section deliberately preserves
options.why: Two contracts, two considerations, two supplies. The trader buys and resells; the law taxes both margins and lets credit flow down the chain.

options.text: No — the first leg's place of supply is Maharashtra by the deeming, so IGST applies even though the goods stayed in Gujarat
options.why: Section 10(1)(b) deems the third-party-delivery supply to have its place of supply at the instructing buyer's principal place of business — Maharashtra. Gujarat to Maharashtra is inter-State: IGST. The trader's onward leg to the Gujarat customer is then Maharashtra to Gujarat, IGST again, with the customer taking credit. Physical movement misleads; the statute follows the instruction chain.

options.text: Yes — goods delivered within Gujarat make an intra-State supply whatever the paperwork says
options.misconception: reads geography off the truck instead of the section
options.why: The deeming exists precisely because delivery and commercial destination split in bill-to-ship-to trades. Without it, the Maharashtra trader could never take credit of Gujarat's CGST-SGST.

options.text: Both legs are exempt as a single continuous movement under one e-way bill
options.misconception: mistakes a logistics convenience for a tax treatment
options.why: The single e-way bill covers the physical journey; the tax invoices remain two, each with its own place of supply and levy. Documentation of movement never decides chargeability.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(b)

items.scenario: A Gujarat manufacturer receives an order from a Maharashtra trader, with instructions to deliver the goods directly to the trader's customer in Gujarat itself. The manufacturer, seeing goods that never leave Gujarat, charges CGST and SGST on its invoice to the Maharashtra trader.

items.stem: How do the interpretative rules settle it?

options.text: As motor cars — an incomplete article with the essential character of the complete one classifies as complete, and taxpayer choice is not a rule
options.why: Rule 2(a) does the work: a kit lacking only tyres has the essential character of a car, so it classifies as the car, parts pricing notwithstanding. The later-heading tie-breaker in rule 3(c) arrives only when goods are genuinely equally classifiable after the earlier rules — and nowhere do the rules offer the importer the cheaper of two answers.

options.text: As neither — incomplete goods await a separate notification for kits
options.misconception: waits for a rule that already exists
options.why: Rule 2(a) is the kit rule, general and standing. Classification never suspends for want of a bespoke entry; the rules exist to place everything somewhere.

options.text: The importer's fallback stands — ambiguity in tax statutes resolves for the taxpayer
options.misconception: imports a construction canon into a classification code
options.why: The GIRs are a self-contained sequence ending in the later heading, not in taxpayer preference. The favour-the-taxpayer canon addresses genuine statutory ambiguity, not a schedule with its own tie-breakers.

options.text: As parts — until assembled, no car exists to classify
options.misconception: classifies the screwdriver's work instead of the shipment
options.why: Essential character at importation governs. If unassembled kits were parts, every car would cross borders in three boxes at parts duty — the exact planning rule 2(a) forecloses.

citation.ref: General Rules for Interpretation 1-4

items.scenario: An importer brings in car bodies, engines and chassis in knocked-down kits, each kit containing everything needed to assemble one car minus the tyres. The importer classifies the kits as parts, at parts' lower duty; the department classifies them as motor cars. The importer's fallback: when two headings compete, the importer may choose the cheaper.

items.stem: How does GST apply to the two cars?

options.text: Neither pays — second-hand goods have already suffered tax once
options.misconception: converts a margin scheme into an exemption
options.why: The scheme narrows the base; it never nils it. Each resale's value addition bears tax — that is the design, not a defect.

options.text: Both on margin — dealing in second-hand goods is itself the qualification
options.misconception: reads the scheme without its no-credit condition
options.why: Margin taxation exists to avoid taxing embedded, uncredited tax twice. Where credit was taken, nothing is embedded, and the concession's reason vanishes with its condition.

options.text: The first pays on ₹70,000, deducting the refurbishment spend from the margin
options.misconception: enlarges the margin formula
options.why: The rule's margin is selling price less purchase price, full stop. Refurbishment costs are the dealer's business expenses, not a statutory deduction from the base.

options.text: The first pays tax on the ₹1 lakh margin; the second lost the scheme with the credit and pays on the full selling price
options.why: The first car is the scheme's textbook case — bought from an unregistered consumer, refurbished without changing its nature, no credit taken — so tax falls on selling price minus purchase price. Rule 32(5) is conditioned on no input tax credit having been availed; the second car's credit forfeits the margin base, and its whole consideration is taxable like any ordinary supply.

citation.ref: Rule 32(5)

items.scenario: A used-car dealer buys a car from an individual for ₹4 lakh, spends ₹30,000 on denting, painting and servicing without taking any credit, and sells it for ₹5 lakh. On another car bought from a registered fleet operator with a tax invoice, the dealer took input credit of the GST charged, and now wants margin-scheme treatment on its resale too.

items.stem: On what value is GST actually due?

options.text: On ₹3,52,000 plus the fee — all recoveries are consideration however structured
options.misconception: erases the pure agent rule entirely
options.why: The rule exists and the duty recovery satisfies it. Taxing statutory duty routed at actuals through an agent would cascade tax on tax — the outcome the rule prevents.

options.text: On ₹62,000 — the fee plus only the storage markup
options.misconception: salvages the failed exclusion for the cost portion
options.why: Rule 33 is all-or-nothing per cost: conditions met, the whole amount stays out; conditions failed, the whole amount comes in. The ₹40,000 does not stay excluded under a rule its billing just broke.

options.text: On ₹50,000 alone — everything paid to third parties passes through untaxed
options.misconception: treats every reimbursement as automatically excluded
options.why: Exclusion is conditional, and the conditions are the discipline: actuals, separate disclosure, agency. A marked-up bundle is trading, not agency.

options.text: On ₹1,02,000 — the fee plus the marked-up, bundled storage; only the duty recovery survives as a pure agent cost
options.why: The customs duty ticks every rule 33 box: paid as the importer's agent, used by the importer alone, recovered at actuals, separately indicated. The storage charges fail twice — a ₹12,000 markup means recovery beyond actuals, and bundling hides the amount — so the entire ₹52,000 joins the taxable value alongside the fee. Failing the conditions taxes the whole recovery, not only the markup.

citation.ref: Rule 33

items.scenario: A customs broker bills an importer: agency fee ₹50,000 plus GST; customs duty of ₹3 lakh paid on the importer's behalf, recovered at actuals and shown separately; and port storage charges of ₹40,000 actually paid, but billed at ₹52,000 inside a single "handling charges" line. The broker charges GST only on the ₹50,000 fee.

items.stem: How does section 8 tax the two bundles?

options.text: Both at weighted average rates of their contents
options.misconception: invents proportional taxation for bundles
options.why: Section 8 chooses one rate per bundle — the principal's or the highest — exactly to avoid valuation games of allocating a single price across rates.

options.text: The laptop bundle at the laptop's rate as a composite supply; the gift box wholly at the highest rate inside it as a mixed supply
options.why: Chargers, cases and installation travel with laptops in the ordinary course of trade — a natural bundle whose principal supply is the laptop, so its rate covers the lot. Chocolates, dry fruits and drinks share nothing but the box: sellable separately, bundled for price alone, the definition of a mixed supply — so the entire ₹5,000 bears the highest rate among the contents, here the 40 per cent on the aerated drinks. One demerit-rated item drags the whole single-priced box up with it. Averages exist in neither definition.

options.text: Both at the highest rate present in each bundle
options.misconception: treats every bundle as mixed
options.why: The composite category exists so natural trade bundles are not punished. Taxing the bundled charger at the aerated-drink logic would tax commercial reality as if it were tax planning.

options.text: Item-wise rates on an itemised invoice, whatever the pricing
options.misconception: unbundles what the parties priced as one
options.why: Itemised supplies at itemised prices are simply separate supplies — real, but a different transaction. Section 8 answers the single-price bundle, and it answers with one rate.

citation.ref: Sections 2(30), 2(74) and 8

items.scenario: An electronics retailer sells two offerings this Diwali: a laptop delivered with its charger, carry case and installation, priced as one; and a festival gift box at a single price of ₹5,000 containing chocolates (5 per cent), dry fruits (5 per cent) and a case of aerated drinks (40 per cent — the demerit rate, and the highest in the box). The owner wants one blended average rate for each offering.

items.stem: How does GST treat the two?

options.text: The gaming is taxable only if adjudged a game of chance rather than skill
options.misconception: litigates a distinction the amendment made irrelevant
options.why: The 2023 entries tax online money gaming without reference to skill or chance — that debate governed the pre-amendment era and the courts. The current levy asks whether money is staked, not how the game is won.

options.text: Both escape — actionable claims are wholly outside GST
options.misconception: reads Schedule III without its specified-claims exception
options.why: The exception predates the platform era for lottery and betting, and 2023 added online money gaming in terms. The blanket reading died with that amendment.

options.text: The receivables assignment is outside GST under Schedule III; the online money gaming is a specified actionable claim and squarely taxable
options.why: Actionable claims are goods that Schedule III then parks outside supply — the assignment of unsecured debt is the paradigm case, untaxed. The carve-out from the carve-out is the specified list: lottery, betting, gambling and, after the 2023 amendments, online money gaming. Stakes on the rummy platform sit inside the levy on the amounts paid or deposited, whatever skill the game involves.

options.text: Both are taxable — anything transferable for money is a supply
options.misconception: erases Schedule III instead of its exception
options.why: Schedule III's exclusions are real law; debt assignments, land sales and employee services stand outside supply by its operation. The rummy platform loses on the exception, not on the rule.

citation.ref: Schedule III with section 2(1)

items.scenario: A finance company assigns a pool of unsecured loan receivables to an ARC for ₹80 crore. The same month, its promoter's other venture — an online rummy platform where users stake money on games — takes legal advice that both activities are outside GST as actionable claims.

items.stem: On which amount does interest actually run?

options.text: Both — wrong availment is the offence and interest is its price
options.misconception: charges the ledger entry instead of the revenue loss
options.why: This was the department's old reading, and Parliament rejected it retrospectively. Interest compensates delayed revenue; an unused entry delayed none.

options.text: Neither, since both errors were voluntarily corrected before any notice
options.misconception: converts voluntary correction into an interest waiver
options.why: Self-correction spares penalty exposure, not interest. The ₹20 lakh enjoyed the exchequer's money from March to June, and that enjoyment is what interest prices.

options.text: Both, but at nine per cent as a concessional self-correction rate
options.misconception: invents a rate the statute does not offer
options.why: The notified rate for these cases is eighteen per cent where interest applies at all. The relief in the law is the utilisation condition, not a discount.

options.text: Only the ₹20 lakh that was utilised — and from utilisation, not availment; the unused ₹30 lakh reverses free of interest
options.why: Section 50(3) charges interest on credit wrongly availed and utilised. An entry sitting unused in the ledger has taken nothing from the exchequer — the money was never applied against a liability — so its reversal carries no interest. The ₹20 lakh crossed the line in March when set off, and interest runs from that utilisation.

citation.ref: Section 50(1) proviso and 50(3)

items.scenario: A company discovers two old errors: ₹30 lakh of credit availed on an ineligible input in January, which sat unused in the credit ledger until reversed in June; and ₹20 lakh of similarly ineligible credit availed in February that was set off against output tax in March. The officer demands eighteen per cent interest on both from availment to reversal.

items.stem: Who gets the ₹2 crore?

options.text: The importer — a duty held illegal must be returned to whoever paid it
options.misconception: stops at the payment and skips the incidence enquiry
options.why: The payer may have been a conduit. Refunding a recovered cost hands the trader the duty twice — once from customers, once from the State — the enrichment the section calls unjust.

options.text: Split — the importer recovers the duty on unsold closing stock only
options.misconception: right instinct on one slice, presented as the whole answer
options.why: Unsold stock indeed cannot have passed duty on, but the enquiry covers the entire claim: the sold goods' incidence is tested on evidence, not surrendered by assumption.

options.text: The Fund, always — traders can never prove absorption
options.misconception: hardens a rebuttable presumption
options.why: The presumption invites rebuttal, and price behaviour against competitors, margin analyses and certificates rebut it in practice. The Fund takes only the unproven cases.

options.text: It depends on incidence, not victory — matching competitors' prices suggests the duty was absorbed, which if evidenced gets the importer paid
options.why: Winning fixes that the duty was excess; section 27 separately asks who ultimately bore it. The presumption of passing on stands until the importer displaces it — and selling at the same price as lower-duty competitors is respectable evidence the excess came out of its own margin, supported by costing records and a CA's certificate. Fail that proof, and the refund is sanctioned to the Fund: the State holds it for consumers rather than enriching whoever charged them.

citation.ref: Section 27

items.scenario: After winning a classification dispute, an importer-trader becomes entitled to ₹2 crore of excess duty refund. During the dispute years it sold the imported goods at the same prices as its competitors who paid the lower duty. The department sanctions the refund but routes it to the Consumer Welfare Fund; the importer protests that it won the case and the money is legally its own.

items.stem: Where does Indian GST land on the three?

options.text: All three bear reverse charge in the recipients' hands
options.misconception: applies the business rule to persons and the wrong person to OIDAR
options.why: Personal imports lack the business element the charge needs, and the OIDAR scheme deliberately moved the duty to the supplier because millions of consumers cannot self-assess.

options.text: None — services from abroad are exports of the foreign supplier, taxed there
options.misconception: reads the transaction from the wrong shore
options.why: GST is destination-based: consumption in India is India's tax base. The foreign supplier's home treatment does not displace the import levy here.

options.text: Only the legal fees, with the director's streaming exempt as personal use
options.misconception: right on two, wrong on the OIDAR carve-in
options.why: Personal use exempts the astrologer but not OIDAR — the digital-delivery category exists precisely to tax consumer imports that would otherwise slip through.

options.text: The company pays IGST on the legal fees under reverse charge; the astrologer escapes; the streaming platform itself owes tax under OIDAR
options.why: The legal advice is a service imported in the course of business — the recipient self-assesses under section 5(3) and claims credit. The astrologer's consultation is a personal import outside the levy — no business, no reverse charge, and no OIDAR since it is human service, not automated delivery. The streaming subscription is OIDAR to a consumer: taxable, with the foreign platform bearing the registration and payment duty, not the director.

citation.ref: Section 5(3) with 2(11)

items.scenario: Three imports of services in one month: an Indian company takes legal advice from a London firm for a business dispute, paying £40,000; the company's director personally engages a foreign astrologer for his family; and the same director personally subscribes to a foreign music streaming platform.

items.stem: What are the company's Indian GST obligations?

options.text: No registration for either — foreign companies without Indian premises are outside Indian GST
options.misconception: hides behind physical absence
options.why: The OIDAR scheme was built for suppliers with no Indian presence; absence is its premise, not an exemption from it.

options.text: Register for both streams and charge Indian GST on all invoices
options.misconception: sweeps the B2B consulting into the supplier's net
options.why: Where the recipient is registered, reverse charge already collects the tax at the Indian end. Supplier-side registration for that stream would duplicate the levy's machinery.

options.text: Register and pay under the OIDAR scheme for the consumer cloud subscriptions; the consulting is the Indian company's reverse charge problem, not the supplier's
options.why: Automated storage with minimal human intervention delivered to unregistered persons is OIDAR to consumers — the foreign supplier registers under the simplified scheme and remits Indian tax. The consulting fails the OIDAR definition (engineers on calls are the opposite of automated) and its recipient is registered, so ordinary import-of-services reverse charge puts the liability on the Indian buyer.

options.text: Neither, because cloud storage involves servers, making it goods
options.misconception: reclassifies a service by its hardware
options.why: The user buys access and retrieval, not the server. OIDAR names exactly this delivery model as a service, and the definition governs.

citation.ref: Section 2(17) and 14

items.scenario: A US software company sells to India: automated cloud storage subscriptions bought online by thousands of individual users; and customised implementation consulting delivered over video calls by its engineers to an Indian GST-registered company. It asks whether it must register in India for either stream.

items.stem: Is the trader within the e-invoicing net, and does it matter to the buyer?

options.text: No — current-year turnover below the line means no current duty
options.misconception: reads a once-crossed threshold as an annual test
options.why: The rule's words reach back to 2017-18 deliberately, so businesses cannot dip under the line and out of the system. One crossing enrols for good.

options.text: Yes for the trader, but the buyer's credit is safe since tax was charged
options.misconception: insulates the recipient from the supplier's document failure
options.why: Credit rides on a valid tax invoice, and validity here includes the IRN. The buyer holding a non-invoice is exactly why recipients now verify QR codes.

options.text: No, because traders are among the notified exclusions
options.misconception: extends the sectoral carve-outs to ordinary trade
options.why: The exclusions name banks, insurers, GTAs and the like. Trading in goods is the scheme's ordinary population, not its exception.

options.text: Yes — one crossing in any year since 2017-18 brings the duty permanently, and without an IRN the document is not a valid invoice, imperilling the buyer's credit
options.why: The threshold tests aggregate turnover in any financial year from 2017-18 onward, so the 2018-19 crossing binds every later year regardless of decline. Rule 48(5) is why the buyer's auditor is right to care: an invoice required to be e-invoiced but issued without IRN is treated as no invoice, and a valid invoice is the first condition of the recipient's input tax credit.

citation.ref: Rule 48(4) (₹5 crore threshold from 1 August 2023)

items.scenario: A trader whose turnover crossed ₹6 crore back in 2018-19 but has hovered near ₹4 crore since issues ordinary tax invoices to its business customers, reasoning that current turnover decides e-invoicing. A buyer's auditor flags the invoices; the trader replies that at worst this is a procedural lapse the buyer need not worry about.

items.stem: What has the exporter done to its authorisation?

options.text: Broken the actual user condition — duty-free inputs cannot be diverted to the domestic market, and meeting the export obligation later does not cure the diversion
options.why: Advance authorisation is a purpose-bound concession: the imported inputs must be physically used in the export product, and the actual user condition bars their transfer until the obligation is discharged. Selling the fabric locally converts a duty-free import into an untaxed trading windfall — the exact arbitrage the condition exists to stop — inviting duty with interest on the diverted inputs and penal action, however punctually the exports later sail.

options.text: Nothing wrong, if the export obligation is ultimately fulfilled in quantity and value
options.misconception: reads the scheme as an outcome test only
options.why: The scheme polices the route as well as the destination. Duty-free inputs that never enter export production defeat the exemption's basis whatever replacement fabric does later.

options.text: No breach, since fabric is fungible and equivalent fabric will be exported
options.misconception: pleads fungibility against an actual user condition
options.why: Fungibility is why the condition exists: without physical tracking discipline, every duty-free import would become domestic stock with paper exports beside it. The norms bind the imported material itself.

options.text: A breach curable by paying GST on the local sale
options.misconception: settles the customs concession with a GST payment
options.why: The local sale's GST was always due; the breach is of the customs exemption's condition, cured only by duty, interest and the scheme's consequences on the diverted quantity.

citation.ref: Advance Authorisation scheme

items.scenario: A garment exporter imports fabric duty-free under advance authorisation. Domestic fabric prices then spike, and the exporter sells half the imported fabric locally at a handsome profit, planning to buy equivalent Indian fabric later for the export orders and arguing the export obligation will still be met in full.

items.stem: How should the factory handle the two bills?

options.text: Demand B re-issue at 12 per cent, the forward-charge rate for a GTA that keeps its input credits
options.misconception: quotes the superseded 12 per cent rate, which the 22 September 2025 rationalisation replaced with 18 per cent
options.why: Twelve per cent was the credit-preserving forward-charge rate for a GTA, and it is the figure most notes still carry. It stopped being the law on 22 September 2025: Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 substituted 18 per cent when the 12 per cent slab was abolished. Five per cent without credit and 18 per cent with credit are the two lawful forward-charge options now, and B chose the credit-preserving one.

options.text: Reverse charge 5 per cent on both, ignoring B's invoice tax
options.misconception: pays the government twice for one carriage
options.why: B's declared forward charge makes B the taxable person; self-paying again creates double tax with a disputed credit. The declaration on the invoice is the recipient's evidence of which regime governs.

options.text: Self-pay 5 per cent on A's freight under reverse charge; pay B's 18 per cent invoice and take the credit — B's declared option shifts the liability back to B
options.why: Transporter A sits in the default reverse-charge regime, so the factory (a specified recipient) pays the 5 per cent in cash and credits it. Transporter B exercised the forward-charge option the notifications allow — 18 per cent with the GTA keeping its input credits — and once declared, the recipient's reverse charge duty for B's services is gone. The credit-preserving rate was 12 per cent until 21 September 2025; Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 raised it to 18 per cent with effect from 22 September 2025, when the 12 per cent slab went. The accountant's one-rule-for-all misses that the regime follows each transporter's election.

options.text: Pay neither tax — freight is exempt in the recipient's hands
options.misconception: stretches the small-service exemptions over commercial freight
options.why: The exemptions cover categories like single-carriage below thresholds and specified goods. Ordinary factory freight is taxable through one of the two routes on every bill.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with the notified GTA options in Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) and Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), the forward-charge rate with credit raised from 12 to 18 per cent by Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 with effect from 22 September 2025

items.scenario: A factory receives freight bills from two transporters in June 2026. Transporter A's invoice shows no tax and a note that GST is payable by the recipient. Transporter B's invoice charges 18 per cent GST, citing its forward-charge declaration for the year. The factory's accountant pays A's bill without tax and disputes B's, insisting all GTA tax is the recipient's to pay at 5 per cent.

items.stem: How should the two advances stand?

options.text: Both are non-performing, each having been overdue beyond ninety days, and the guarantees go only to the provision required
options.misconception: applies the ninety-day rule to a Central Government guaranteed advance, when for that advance classification turns on repudiation of the guarantee on invocation
options.why: The ninety-day rule is where the analysis starts and not where it ends. The prudential norms carve out one exception, and it is narrow: a Central Government guaranteed facility is treated as non-performing only on repudiation of the guarantee when invoked. It is the State Government guaranteed advance that is caught by the ninety days.

options.text: Neither is non-performing, a guarantee of a government being the best security a bank can hold, so the classification and the interest both stand
options.misconception: reads a government guarantee as a substitute for a record of recovery, when the exception is confined to the Central Government and to classification alone
options.why: Nothing in the norms lets a guarantee replace the record of recovery for a State Government advance, and even for the Central Government advance the exception is confined to classification. Income is a separate question, and interest on a government guaranteed advance that has become non-performing is recognised only on realisation.

options.text: The State Government guaranteed advance is non-performing, and the Central Government guaranteed one is not yet — but the reason the guarantee has not been invoked must be obtained and reported, and on both advances the interest cannot be taken to income
options.why: The exception belongs to the Central Government alone and only for asset classification: a credit facility backed by a Central Government guarantee, though overdue, is treated as non-performing only when the Central Government repudiates its guarantee on invocation, and where the bank has not invoked it though the amount has been overdue for long, the reasoning is obtained and duly reported in the long form audit report. The exception does not apply to a State Government guaranteed advance, which is treated as non-performing if it remains overdue for more than 90 days. And for income recognition, whichever government stands behind it, interest on a government guaranteed advance that has become non-performing is not taken to income unless it is realised.

options.text: Both remain standard but the interest already accrued on both is reversed, income recognition and asset classification being governed by the same test
options.misconception: treats income recognition and asset classification as one rule, when the norms answer them separately and the State Government advance fails the classification test on its own
options.why: They are two rules and they can give different answers on the same advance, which is exactly what happens here. The State Government guaranteed advance fails the classification test because it has been overdue beyond ninety days, so reversing the interest and leaving it standard deals with half the problem.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — government guaranteed advances: interest not taken to income unless realised, a Central Government guaranteed facility treated as non-performing only when the guarantee is repudiated on invocation with the reasoning for non-invocation reported in the long form audit report, and a State Government guaranteed advance treated as non-performing if overdue for more than 90 days

items.scenario: Two advances at a branch on 31 March. The first is backed by a guarantee of the Central Government; the instalments have been overdue for two hundred days and the bank has not invoked the guarantee. The second is backed by a guarantee of a State Government and has been overdue for one hundred and forty days. The branch has kept both as standard and has taken the interest on both to income, on the footing that a sovereign guarantee removes the doubt about recovery.

items.stem: What does the asset classification require here?

options.text: The cash credit and the devolved letter of credit account, the term loan standing on its own because it is separately secured and separately serviced
options.misconception: allows separate security and separate servicing to save one facility, when borrower-wise classification takes no account of either
options.why: Borrower-wise classification does not ask how a facility is secured or how it has been served. Once the borrower is non-performing, every facility granted to him is treated as non-performing, and the term loan is not saved by its own conduct.

options.text: The cash credit and the term loan, but not the devolved letter of credit account, which is a non-fund exposure that crystallised and is dealt with under contingent liabilities
options.misconception: keeps a devolved letter of credit outside the borrower's principal account, when the norms bring that outstanding into it
options.why: The letter of credit stopped being a contingent liability the moment it devolved; what is left is money the bank has paid out and is owed. The norms say so directly — a debit arising out of devolvement kept in a separate account is treated as part of the borrower's principal account for the prudential norms.

options.text: Only the cash credit, since classification follows the conduct of each account and a term loan serviced on time is by definition a standard asset
options.misconception: classifies facility by facility, which is the approach the norms specifically direct the auditor to check against
options.why: That is facility-wise classification, and the norms name it as the thing to be guarded against: the auditor ensures that classification is borrower-wise, so once one facility is non-performing every facility granted to that borrower goes with it whatever its own conduct looks like.
