options.why: Membership and technical performance standards are relevant to competence, capabilities and objectivity; they do not displace the evaluation of the work itself, and the auditor's sole responsibility for the opinion is not reduced by his use of an expert however well qualified.

options.text: Whether the expert is internal or external, and nothing else — an internal expert is covered by the firm's own quality control while an external expert is not, which settles the extent of the work in every case
options.misconception: reduces the five matters to one distinction, which would leave a familiar external expert on a routine matter treated exactly like an unknown one on a critical estimate
options.why: It is one of the factors and not the whole of it. On this engagement the expert is external and unknown and the matter is subjective and material and his work is integral to the audit — four separate reasons for more extensive procedures, of which the internal or external question is only one.

options.text: The nature of the matter, the risk of material misstatement in it, the significance of the expert's work in the context of the audit, the auditor's knowledge of and experience with that expert's previous work, and whether the expert is subject to the firm's quality control policies and procedures — and all four of the circumstances calling for more extensive procedures are present here: subjective and complex judgments, an expert not used before, work integral to the audit rather than advice on an individual matter, and an external expert outside the firm's quality control
options.why: The five matters are what the auditor considers in determining the nature, timing and extent of his procedures, and they are why the internal specialist used every year and this actuary cannot be reviewed alike. Four factors are separately named as suggesting the need for different or more extensive procedures than would otherwise be the case, and every one of them is here: the work relates to a significant matter involving subjective and complex judgments; the auditor has not previously used that expert and has no prior knowledge of his competence, capabilities and objectivity; the expert is performing procedures integral to the audit rather than being consulted for advice on an individual matter; and he is an external expert and therefore not subject to the firm's quality control policies and procedures.
keywords: nature, timing and extent of his procedures
not subject to the firm's quality control

options.text: Only the significance of the expert's work in the context of the audit — the other matters go to whether to engage him rather than to what the auditor does about his work afterwards
options.misconception: keeps one of the five matters and assigns the rest to the engagement decision, when all five bear on the nature, timing and extent of the procedures
options.why: Significance is one of five. The nature of the matter, the risk of material misstatement in it, the auditor's knowledge of the expert's previous work and whether the expert falls inside the firm's quality control all bear on the same question, and the last two are exactly what separates a first-time external expert from a familiar internal one.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — the matters the auditor considers in determining the nature, timing and extent of procedures on an auditor's expert's work, and the four factors that may suggest the need for different or more extensive procedures

items.scenario: A firm engages an external actuary it has never used before to value a defined benefit obligation that is the largest single estimate in the accounts and depends on subjective demographic assumptions. The actuary will not merely advise on a question put to him; he will perform procedures that form part of the audit itself. The engagement partner proposes the same review he applies to the internal specialist the firm uses every year, on the ground that both are experts and both have been engaged by the firm.

items.stem: What does SA 240 require here?

options.text: The inconsistent explanations may be left alone, since inquiry is the weakest form of audit evidence and the auditor should simply obtain a document instead
options.misconception: discards inconsistent responses because inquiry is weak evidence, when the inconsistency is itself something the Standard directs the auditor to investigate
options.why: The inconsistency is the finding. Where responses to inquiries of management or of those charged with governance are inconsistent, the auditor investigates the inconsistencies, and here the document that would replace the inquiry is the very thing in question.

options.text: The auditor must treat the challan as forged and report a suspected fraud, an altered document being conclusive of an intention to deceive
options.misconception: jumps from a document that may not be authentic to a conclusion of fraud, when what the Standard requires at this point is further investigation
options.why: What is required is to investigate further, not to conclude. The document may not be authentic or its terms may have been modified without disclosure — either possibility calls for work, and the conclusion comes after that work rather than instead of it.

options.text: Nothing further — an auditor is entitled to accept records and documents as genuine, and nine years of clean audits are the evidence on which that entitlement rests
options.misconception: reads the entitlement to accept documents as genuine as unconditional, when it stands only until there is reason to believe the contrary
options.why: The entitlement carries its own limit in the same sentence. It runs unless the auditor has reason to believe the contrary, and an altered date with an out-of-sequence serial number is such a reason. Past experience of honesty does not answer it; the Standard says skepticism is maintained notwithstanding that experience.

options.text: The auditor may accept records and documents as genuine unless he has reason to believe the contrary — and there is reason here, so where conditions identified during the audit cause him to believe a document may not be authentic or that terms in it have been modified and not disclosed, he investigates further; inconsistent responses to inquiries are themselves investigated; and the engagement team discussion happens notwithstanding the team's belief that management is honest and has integrity
options.why: The permission to take documents at face value is conditional and the condition has failed. The auditor may accept records and documents as genuine unless he has reason to believe the contrary; where conditions identified during the audit cause him to believe that a document may not be authentic or that terms in a document have been modified but not disclosed to him, he shall investigate further. Where responses to inquiries of management or of those charged with governance are inconsistent, he shall investigate the inconsistencies. And professional skepticism is maintained throughout the audit recognising the possibility that a material misstatement due to fraud could exist notwithstanding past experience of the honesty and integrity of management and those charged with governance — which is why the team discussion occurs notwithstanding the members' belief that they are honest.
keywords: unless he has reason to believe the contrary

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — maintaining professional skepticism throughout the audit notwithstanding past experience of the honesty and integrity of management and those charged with governance, accepting records and documents as genuine unless there is reason to believe the contrary, investigating further where a document may not be authentic or its terms modified, investigating inconsistent responses to inquiries, and holding the engagement team discussion notwithstanding the team's beliefs about management

items.scenario: An assistant produces a delivery challan whose date appears to have been altered and whose serial number is out of sequence with those around it. The finance head explains it one way and the storekeeper explains it another. The senior tells him to take the challan at face value, because the firm has audited this client for nine years and has never had a reason to doubt the directors, and to leave it out of the engagement team discussion for the same reason.

items.stem: What does SA 240 require once a misstatement may be fraud involving senior management?

options.text: Add it to the uncorrected misstatements and evaluate it at the end with the others — a misstatement below performance materiality cannot change the audit, whatever caused it
options.misconception: lets the amount decide, when the Standard's trigger is a misstatement whether material or not that may be the result of fraud involving management
options.why: The Standard says whether material or not in terms. A small misstatement that indicates management fraud is evidence about the whole audit, because an instance of fraud is unlikely to be an isolated occurrence and because the reliability of management's representations is now in question.

options.text: Re-evaluate the assessment of the risks of material misstatement due to fraud and the resulting impact on the nature, timing and extent of the audit procedures — the size of the misstatement being irrelevant to that requirement — and consider whether the circumstances indicate possible collusion involving employees, management or third parties when reconsidering the reliability of evidence already obtained
options.why: The requirement is triggered by the character of the misstatement, not by its amount. Where the auditor identifies a misstatement, whether material or not, and has reason to believe that it is or may be the result of fraud and that management, in particular senior management, is involved, he re-evaluates the assessment of the risks of material misstatement due to fraud and its resulting impact on the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures. He also considers whether circumstances or conditions indicate possible collusion involving employees, management or third parties when reconsidering the reliability of evidence previously obtained — which is the point of the clerk who reports to the director.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement — a misstatement caused by fraud involving the finance director is an exceptional circumstance bringing the auditor's ability to continue into question
options.misconception: goes straight to withdrawal, which arises only on exceptional circumstances that bring the ability to continue into question and even then only after determining the responsibilities
options.why: Withdrawal is a separate and later question. Where exceptional circumstances do bring the ability to continue into question, the auditor first determines the professional and legal responsibilities applicable, considers whether withdrawal is legally permitted, and if he withdraws discusses it with management and those charged with governance and determines whether there is a duty to report. Re-evaluating the risk assessment comes first and applies here.

options.text: Obtain a written representation from the finance director explaining the credit note, and rely on it if the explanation is plausible
options.misconception: seeks the explanation from the person the suspicion is about and treats a representation as evidence of the very matter in doubt
options.why: Where the auditor has reason to believe a misstatement is fraud involving management, the reliability of management representations is one of the things he must reconsider, so a representation from the suspected person settles nothing.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — evaluation of audit evidence under SA 240: where the auditor identifies a misstatement, whether material or not, and has reason to believe it is or may be the result of fraud and that management is involved, he re-evaluates the assessment of the risks of material misstatement due to fraud and its impact on the nature, timing and extent of audit procedures, and considers whether the circumstances indicate possible collusion involving employees, management or third parties

items.scenario: Late in the audit you find a single misstatement of ₹4 lakh, well below performance materiality. It arises from a credit note raised on the last day of the year by the finance director himself, backed by no supporting document, and passed for payment by a clerk who reports to him. You have reason to believe it is not an error. The manager proposes to add it to the schedule of uncorrected misstatements and carry on with the programme as planned.

items.stem: How does SA 240 deal with reporting outside the entity?

options.text: Confidentiality is absolute in both — an auditor may never disclose a client's affairs to a third party, and the remedy where governance will not act is to modify the opinion and resign
options.misconception: treats the duty of confidentiality as incapable of being overridden, when legal responsibilities may override it in some circumstances
options.why: The Standard says in terms that although the professional duty of confidentiality may preclude reporting, the auditor's legal responsibilities may override that duty in some circumstances. Treating it as absolute would mean a bank auditor could not perform the statutory duty the module names.

options.text: Both must be reported outside the entity in every case, a fraud being a matter of public interest that displaces the auditor's duty to the client
options.misconception: converts a duty that depends on the auditor's legal responsibilities into a general obligation to report every fraud externally
options.why: Nothing in the Standard makes external reporting automatic. The auditor determines whether he has a responsibility to report, and where he has none the duty of confidentiality is not displaced by the seriousness of what he has found.

options.text: The bank fraud is reportable and the trading company's is not, the difference being that a bank is regulated and an unlisted company is not
options.misconception: makes regulation of the entity the only route to an external report, missing the separate duty that arises where management and governance fail to act
options.why: There are two routes, not one. A statutory duty such as the bank auditor's is one; the other is the duty that may exist in some entities to report misstatements to authorities where management and those charged with governance fail to take corrective action, which is exactly what has happened on the second engagement.

options.text: The auditor determines in each case whether he has a responsibility to report the occurrence or suspicion to a party outside the entity — the professional duty of confidentiality may preclude such reporting, but legal responsibilities may override that duty, and the audit of a bank is the module's own example, the auditor there having a statutory duty to report the occurrence of fraud to the supervisory authority; and in some entities the auditor may have a duty to report misstatements to authorities where management and those charged with governance fail to take corrective action
options.why: Confidentiality is the starting point and not the end of it. If the auditor has identified or suspects a fraud he determines whether there is a responsibility to report the occurrence or suspicion to a party outside the entity; although the professional duty to maintain the confidentiality of client information may preclude such reporting, the auditor's legal responsibilities may override the duty of confidentiality in some circumstances, and the audit of banks is the example given, where the auditor has a statutory duty to report the occurrence of fraud to the Reserve Bank. The second engagement is the other named case: in some entities there may be a duty to report misstatements to authorities where management and those charged with governance fail to take corrective action.
keywords: may override the duty of confidentiality

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — communications to regulatory and enforcement authorities under SA 240: the determination whether there is a responsibility to report the occurrence or suspicion of fraud to a party outside the entity, the professional duty of confidentiality and the circumstances in which legal responsibilities override it with the bank auditor's statutory duty to report fraud to the Reserve Bank as the example, and the duty in some entities to report misstatements where management and those charged with governance fail to take corrective action

items.scenario: Two engagements in the same firm. On the audit of a bank, the team establishes that a branch manager has been rolling over advances to conceal defaults. On the audit of an unlisted trading company, the team finds misstatements arising from a fraud, reports them to those charged with governance, and is told nothing will be done. In both cases the partner says the duty of confidentiality prevents the firm from telling anybody outside the company.

items.stem: Which of the five must be communicated to those charged with governance?

options.text: Only the two key audit matters — SA 701 requires key audit matters to be taken from the matters communicated to those charged with governance, so that is the only one where communication is a precondition
options.misconception: notices the SA 701 route into the report and mistakes it for the whole of SA 260's requirement
options.why: Key audit matters are indeed drawn from what was communicated, but SA 260 lists five circumstances and that is one of them. The other four carry the same communication requirement for the same reason.

options.text: None of them until the report is signed — communicating an expected modification before the audit is complete would compromise the auditor's independence by inviting management to negotiate the wording
options.misconception: treats advance communication as a threat to independence, when the Standard requires it and even suggests sharing a draft report
options.why: The Standard requires the communication in advance and the module suggests going further by providing a draft of the auditor's report to facilitate discussion of how the matters will be addressed. Communicating is not conceding, and the wording remains the auditor's.

options.text: Only the qualification and the going concern uncertainty — those two put the reader on notice of a problem, while key audit matters, an Emphasis of Matter and a comment on other information are presentational
options.misconception: sorts the five by how bad they look rather than by whether they add information to the report, which is the test the Standard uses
options.why: The test is not severity. It is whether the auditor is required or considers it necessary to include additional information in the report, and key audit matters, an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph and an uncorrected misstatement of the other information each do exactly that.

options.text: All five — the circumstances in which the auditor is required or may consider it necessary to include additional information in his report, and for which communication is required, are an expected modification under SA 705, a material uncertainty related to going concern under SA 570, key audit matters under SA 701, an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph under SA 706, and an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information under SA 720 — and it may be useful to give them a draft of the report to facilitate a discussion of how the matters will be addressed
options.why: The list is closed and it has five entries, only one of which touches the opinion. The point of it is that anything which changes the report from its expected form and content is something those charged with governance were entitled to know about in advance, whether or not the opinion moves. The agreed terms of the engagement already refer to the expected form and content of the report, and this communication tells them where it will differ. Providing a draft of the auditor's report is the module's own suggestion for making that discussion work.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — the circumstances in which the auditor is required or may otherwise consider it necessary to include additional information in the auditor's report and for which communication with those charged with governance is required: an expected modification under SA 705, a material uncertainty related to going concern under SA 570, key audit matters under SA 701, an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph under SA 706, and an uncorrected material misstatement of the other information under SA 720, with the suggestion that a draft of the report be provided

items.scenario: Five things are going to change the shape of this year's auditor's report. A qualification is expected on inventory valuation. A material uncertainty related to going concern will be reported. Two key audit matters will be described. An Emphasis of Matter paragraph will draw attention to a pending litigation note. And the annual report contains a statement about order book values that the auditor has concluded is a material misstatement of the other information and that management will not correct. The partner proposes to communicate only the qualification, since only that changes the opinion.

items.stem: What does SA 260 make of the three proposals?

options.text: The significant risks are properly omitted — they are the auditor's working judgement and communicating them before the work is done would prejudge the findings, which are communicated at the end
options.misconception: postpones the significant risks to the findings stage, when the Standard puts them in the overview of the planned scope and timing
options.why: They belong at the planning stage. The auditor communicates an overview of the planned scope and timing of the audit, which includes communicating about the significant risks identified, precisely so that those charged with governance understand why those matters need special consideration.

options.text: Only the omission of the significant risks is wrong — handing over the detailed timings is candour rather than a fault, and letting the committee set the extent of testing is how oversight is exercised
options.misconception: keeps the requirement to communicate significant risks but ignores the predictability caution and the auditor's sole responsibility for the plan
options.why: Both of the other proposals fail on their own terms. Communicating the nature and timing of detailed audit procedures may reduce their effectiveness by making them too predictable, and the extent of substantive testing is part of the plan, which is the auditor's alone.

options.text: The overview of the planned scope and timing must include the significant risks the auditor has identified, so omitting them is wrong; care is necessary in communicating scope and timing so as not to compromise the effectiveness of the audit, particularly where some of those charged with governance are involved in managing the entity, because communicating the nature and timing of detailed procedures may make them too predictable; and the communication does not change the auditor's sole responsibility to establish the overall audit strategy and the audit plan, so the extent of testing is not the committee's to settle
options.why: The three proposals fail in three different ways. Communicating the significant risks helps those charged with governance understand why those matters require special audit consideration and assists them in overseeing the financial reporting process, so they belong in the overview. Care is necessary so as not to compromise the effectiveness of the audit, particularly where some or all of those charged with governance are involved in managing the entity — as the managing director is here — because communicating the nature and timing of detailed audit procedures may reduce their effectiveness by making them too predictable. And while communication may assist the auditor in planning, it does not change his sole responsibility to establish the overall audit strategy and the audit plan, including the nature, timing and extent of procedures necessary to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence.

options.text: All three are acceptable — a two-way communication is the point of SA 260, so the more the committee is told and the more it decides, the better the oversight
options.misconception: treats the two-way communication as unlimited, when the Standard warns against detail that makes procedures predictable and reserves the plan to the auditor
options.why: The Standard sets both a limit and a boundary. The limit is that care is necessary so as not to compromise the effectiveness of the audit; the boundary is that nothing communicated changes the auditor's sole responsibility for the strategy and the plan.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — the planned scope and timing of the audit communicated to those charged with governance including the significant risks identified, the care necessary so as not to compromise the effectiveness of the audit where some or all of those charged with governance are involved in managing the entity, and the rule that the communication does not change the auditor's sole responsibility to establish the overall audit strategy and the audit plan

items.scenario: At a meeting with an audit committee whose members include the managing director, an auditor is about to present his plan. He proposes to hand over the detailed programme with the dates of every surprise cash count and inventory visit, to omit the significant risks he has identified because naming them might alarm the members, and to invite the committee to settle the extent of the substantive testing on receivables.

items.stem: Where does the responsibility for that lapse lie under SA 299 (Revised)?

options.text: With all four jointly and severally — the area was not divided, and the Standard makes the joint auditors jointly and severally responsible for audit work that is not divided among them
options.misconception: stops at the general rule about undivided work and misses the narrowing that separates the agreed decision from its execution
options.why: That rule is real but it is qualified two paragraphs later. On the planning decisions for a common area the joint auditors answer for the appropriateness of what was agreed; the execution of the agreed procedures is the individual responsibility of the joint auditor who performed them.

options.text: With the lead or convening firm, which is responsible for the areas retained in common and for the quality of the work done in them
options.misconception: imports a lead auditor into a joint audit, which SA 299 does not create and which would displace both the joint and the individual responsibility
options.why: SA 299 knows no lead joint auditor. Responsibility is allocated by what was divided, what was agreed in common, and who executed the work, and there is no firm carrying the others.

options.text: With that firm alone — as regards decisions taken by all the joint auditors under audit planning in respect of common audit areas concerning the nature, timing and extent of the procedures, all the joint auditors are responsible only for the appropriateness of those decisions, and the proper execution of the procedures is the individual responsibility of the joint auditor who performed them
options.why: A common area is not a common excuse. The joint auditors are jointly and severally responsible for the audit work that is not divided and is carried out by all of them, and for the decisions taken by all of them under audit planning in respect of common audit areas. But the Standard then narrows the second limb: on those planning decisions the joint auditors are responsible only in respect of the appropriateness of the decisions concerning the nature, timing and extent of the audit procedures agreed among them, and the proper execution of those procedures is the individual responsibility of the joint auditor concerned. Nothing is wrong with the decision here; the execution failed.
keywords: only in respect of the appropriateness

options.text: With all four, but only if the work allocation document did not record who would perform the batch processing tests — the document being what fixes individual responsibility
options.misconception: makes the allocation document the only source of individual responsibility, when execution carries it whether or not the document names the performer
options.why: The allocation document divides the audit areas and is signed by all the joint auditors and communicated to those charged with governance, which avoids disputes about scope. It is not what makes the execution of an agreed procedure in a common area the responsibility of the auditor who performed it; the Standard does that directly.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — responsibility and co-ordination among joint auditors: all joint auditors being responsible only in respect of the appropriateness of the decisions concerning the nature, timing and extent of the audit procedures agreed among them for common audit areas, while the proper execution of those procedures is the individual responsibility of the joint auditor concerned

items.scenario: Four firms audit a public sector bank jointly and have divided the work by zones. Information technology systems and controls was left undivided because of its nature, and all four agreed at planning what would be tested and how — general controls, application controls, controls over batch processing, back-up and data centre security. The testing of the batch processing controls was actually carried out by one firm's team and was done badly. That firm says the area was a common one, so the lapse is everybody's.

items.stem: What does SA 299 (Revised) require before the report is issued?

options.text: Communication of the modification only — an Emphasis of Matter paragraph does not modify the opinion, so there is nothing about it that those charged with governance need to be told in advance
options.misconception: limits the advance communication to matters that change the opinion, when the expectation of an Emphasis of Matter paragraph carries the same requirement
options.why: Both are named. Where the joint auditors expect to include an Emphasis of Matter or an Other Matter paragraph, they communicate that expectation and the proposed wording of the paragraph, exactly as they do for a modification.

options.text: Nothing beyond issuing a common audit report — the communication requirements about a modification belong to SA 705 and bind a sole auditor, a joint audit being governed by SA 299 alone
options.misconception: treats SA 299 as displacing the other Standards, when it repeats the requirement expressly so that it binds the joint auditors together
options.why: SA 299 carries the requirement itself, so that it is the joint auditors together who communicate the circumstances and the proposed wording, to ensure compliance with SA 705 and SA 706 respectively.

options.text: Communication with those charged with governance of the circumstances that led to the expected modification and of the proposed wording of the modification, to ensure compliance with SA 705, and of the expectation of an Emphasis of Matter paragraph together with the proposed wording of that paragraph, to ensure compliance with SA 706 — and, before finalising the report, the joint auditors discuss and communicate with each other their respective conclusions
options.why: The Standard puts both communications on the joint auditors expressly. When the joint auditors expect to modify the opinion they communicate with those charged with governance the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the proposed wording of it; when they expect to include an Emphasis of Matter or an Other Matter paragraph they communicate that expectation and the proposed wording of the paragraph. And before finalising their report the joint auditors discuss and communicate with each other their respective conclusions that would form the content of the report.

options.text: A separate audit report from each firm — where a report will be modified, each joint auditor must express his own opinion so that the reader can see which firm stands behind the qualification
options.misconception: turns an agreed modification into a case for separate reports, when separate reports arise only from disagreement among the joint auditors
options.why: The joint auditors are required to issue a common audit report. Separate reports arise only where they are in disagreement about the opinion or about a matter to be covered by the report, and here all three agree.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — communication with those charged with governance under SA 299: where the joint auditors expect to modify the opinion they communicate the circumstances that led to the expected modification and the proposed wording to ensure compliance with SA 705, and where they expect to include an Emphasis of Matter or Other Matter paragraph they communicate that expectation and the proposed wording to ensure compliance with SA 706, read with the requirement to discuss and communicate their respective conclusions with each other before finalising the report

items.scenario: Three joint auditors have agreed that the report will carry a qualification on revenue cut-off and an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to a note about a tax demand. One of them proposes that they simply issue the report as drafted, on the ground that those charged with governance will read the qualification and the paragraph when the report reaches them, and that showing them the wording beforehand invites an argument.

items.stem: What does SA 320 say about choosing a benchmark and the percentage applied to it?

options.text: Profit before tax is unusable on a loss-making entity, so revenue or gross profit is the benchmark here; the percentage is not carried across, because a percentage applied to profit before tax from continuing operations will normally be higher than a percentage applied to total revenue; and for an entity that has custody of assets, assets may be the appropriate benchmark
options.why: Determining materiality involves professional judgement, and a percentage is applied to a chosen benchmark as a starting point. The choice of benchmark is affected by the elements of the financial statements, whether there are items on which users' attention tends to be focused, the nature of the entity and where it is in its life cycle together with its industry and economic environment, the ownership structure and the way the entity is financed, and the relative volatility of the benchmark. Where the entity has incurred losses, revenue or gross profit may be considered instead. The percentage then has to move with the benchmark: there is a relationship between the percentage and the chosen benchmark, such that a percentage applied to profit before tax from continuing operations will normally be higher than a percentage applied to total revenue. And where an entity has custody of assets, assets may be an appropriate benchmark.

options.text: Revenue is the benchmark, and the percentage applied to revenue will normally be higher than the one applied to profit before tax, revenue being the larger and therefore the safer figure
options.misconception: inverts the relationship between the percentage and the benchmark, which would set materiality far above anything the users of a loss-making company could tolerate
options.why: The relationship runs the other way. A percentage applied to profit before tax from continuing operations will normally be higher than a percentage applied to total revenue, which is why switching benchmark without switching the percentage produces a materiality figure that means nothing.

options.text: Profit before tax stays as the benchmark whatever the result, materiality being about the entity's earning capacity, and the same percentage is applied to whichever figure is used since the percentage expresses the firm's tolerance for error
options.misconception: keeps one benchmark and one percentage for every entity, when the benchmark is chosen for the entity and the percentage moves with the benchmark
options.why: Neither half survives. The benchmark is chosen by reference to the entity, its life cycle, its industry, how it is financed and what its users look at, and a company with two loss years does not offer a usable profit figure. And the percentage is not a fixed tolerance carried between benchmarks — the one applied to profit before tax from continuing operations will normally be higher than the one applied to total revenue.

options.text: Any benchmark may be used provided the same one is used consistently year on year, and for the depository the benchmark must be fee income, because assets held for clients are not the entity's own
options.misconception: makes consistency the governing rule and refuses assets as a benchmark for an entity that holds them for others
options.why: Consistency is not the test — the benchmark is revisited as the entity changes, and materiality itself may be revised during the audit on new information, a change in circumstances or a change in the auditor's understanding. And where an entity has custody of assets, assets may be an appropriate benchmark precisely because that is what its users are watching.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the use of benchmarks in determining materiality for the financial statements as a whole: the factors affecting the identification of an appropriate benchmark, the relationship between the percentage and the chosen benchmark such that a percentage applied to profit before tax from continuing operations will normally be higher than one applied to total revenue, revenue or gross profit where the entity has incurred losses, and assets where the entity has custody of assets

items.scenario: A construction company has made losses in each of the last two years. Revenue for the year is ₹800 crore, gross profit ₹24 crore and the loss before tax ₹6 crore. The manager proposes to keep profit before tax as the benchmark because the firm always uses it, and to apply to revenue, if he has to switch, the same percentage the firm applies to profit before tax. A second engagement in the same office is the audit of a depository that holds clients' assets but earns a small fee income.

items.stem: What does SA 402 give the user auditor to do at this point?

options.text: Nothing but obtain a Type 1 or Type 2 report — where no such report exists the user auditor cannot obtain evidence about controls he has no access to, and the scope limitation is real
options.misconception: treats the service auditor's report as the only source of understanding, when three other routes are named alongside it
options.why: The report is the first of four routes and the only one that depends on somebody else having already done the work. Contacting the service organisation through the user entity, visiting it and using another auditor are all available, and the absence of a report does not by itself create a scope limitation.

options.text: One or more of four things — obtain a Type 1 or Type 2 report if one is available; contact the service organisation, through the user entity, to obtain specific information; visit the service organisation and perform procedures that will provide the necessary information about the relevant controls; or use another auditor to perform such procedures at the service organisation
options.why: A disclaimer is what happens if the evidence cannot be obtained, not the first response to not having it yet. Where the user auditor is unable to obtain a sufficient understanding from the user entity, the Standard gives him four routes and he may use one or more of them: obtaining a Type 1 or Type 2 report if available; contacting the service organisation through the user entity to obtain specific information; visiting the service organisation and performing procedures there; and using another auditor to perform those procedures on his behalf. Note the second route runs through the user entity rather than direct — the service organisation is the client's contractor, not the auditor's.

options.text: Write directly to the service organisation for its control documentation, the user auditor being entitled to deal with it as he would with any third party holding the entity's records
options.misconception: goes direct to the service organisation, when the Standard routes that contact through the user entity
options.why: The route is specified. The user auditor contacts the service organisation through the user entity to obtain specific information, because his engagement and his access both run through the client rather than through the client's contractor.

options.text: Assess the risks at the maximum and perform substantive procedures on payroll, an understanding of controls being needed only where the auditor intends to rely on them
options.misconception: skips the required understanding by assuming the worst, when the understanding is needed to identify and assess the risks at all rather than only to place reliance
options.why: The understanding is not optional. The user auditor obtains an understanding of how the user entity uses the services — their nature and significance, the nature and materiality of the transactions affected, the degree of interaction and the nature of the relationship — in order to provide a basis for identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement, which comes before any question of reliance.

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402: where the user auditor is unable to obtain a sufficient understanding from the user entity, obtaining that understanding by one or more of obtaining a Type 1 or Type 2 report if available, contacting the service organisation through the user entity, visiting the service organisation and performing procedures, or using another auditor to perform procedures at the service organisation

items.scenario: A company has outsourced its entire payroll to a service organisation. The user entity's own staff can describe what they send and what comes back but know nothing about the controls at the service organisation, and no service auditor's report exists. The user auditor concludes he has not obtained a sufficient understanding of the services and their effect on the user entity's internal control to assess the risks of material misstatement. His manager says the only remaining option is to disclaim.

items.stem: What does SA 402 require of him?

options.text: Nothing about the fraud, which is the service organisation's own affair and its own auditor's problem, and an unmodified opinion with an Other Matter paragraph describing the limit of the work done
options.misconception: treats events at the service organisation as outside the audit, and uses a paragraph to describe a limitation instead of modifying for it
options.why: The Standard makes the inquiry a requirement precisely because a fraud or an uncorrected misstatement at the service organisation can affect the user entity's financial statements. And a limitation on obtaining sufficient appropriate audit evidence is answered by modifying the opinion, not by describing it in a paragraph beside an unmodified one.

options.text: Refer to the work of the service auditor in the report so that the reader can see where the limit lies, and issue an unmodified opinion
options.misconception: reaches for a reference to the service auditor's work as a way of explaining the position, when reference is barred in an unmodified report unless law or regulation requires it
options.why: The user auditor shall not refer to the work of a service auditor in a report containing an unmodified opinion unless required by law or regulation to do so; and where a reference is required, or is relevant to understanding a modification, the report must indicate that the reference does not diminish the user auditor's responsibility for the opinion.

options.text: Report the fraud at the service organisation to those charged with governance of the service organisation and obtain a written representation from it that no other matters exist, then proceed
options.misconception: directs the auditor at the service organisation's governance and at a representation from a party that is not his client
options.why: The inquiry is of the management of the user entity, which is his client, and the written representations in an audit come from that entity's management and those charged with governance. The service organisation's governance is not his reporting line.

options.text: Inquire of the management of the user entity whether the service organisation has reported to it, or whether it is otherwise aware of, any fraud, non-compliance with laws and regulations or uncorrected misstatements affecting the financial statements, and evaluate how those matters affect the nature, timing and extent of his further procedures and his conclusions; and modify the opinion under SA 705, because he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the services provided
options.why: Both halves are express requirements. The user auditor inquires of management of the user entity whether the service organisation has reported to the user entity, or whether the user entity is otherwise aware of, any fraud, non-compliance with laws and regulations or uncorrected misstatements affecting its financial statements, and evaluates how such matters affect the nature, timing and extent of his further audit procedures including the effect on his conclusions and his report. And he modifies the opinion in accordance with SA 705 if he is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the services provided by the service organisation. An explanatory paragraph attached to an unmodified opinion does neither.
keywords: inquires of management of the user entity

citation.ref: Ch. General Auditing Principles and Auditors Responsibilities — SA 402: the inquiry of management of the user entity about fraud, non-compliance with laws and regulations and uncorrected misstatements at the service organisation and the evaluation of their effect, and the requirement to modify the opinion under SA 705 where the user auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the services provided, read with the bar on referring to the work of a service auditor in an unmodified report

items.scenario: A user auditor has learned informally that the service organisation processing the company's sales ledger wrote to the company during the year about a fraud by one of its own operators, and about misstatements it had not corrected. He has also been unable, after exhausting the available routes, to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the services provided. He proposes to say nothing about the fraud, since it happened at the service organisation, and to issue an unmodified opinion with a paragraph explaining that part of the processing was outside his reach.

items.stem: What does SA 500 require of the two?

options.text: Only the confirmations need work — an ageing schedule comes from the accounting system that produced the financial statements, so testing it would be testing the same records twice
options.misconception: exempts entity-produced information from evaluation because it comes from the accounting records, which is the reason to test it rather than to trust it
options.why: The accounting records are the thing under audit. When information produced by the entity is used as audit evidence the auditor evaluates its reliability, completeness and accuracy, and an incomplete ageing schedule silently removes items from the population before the sample is drawn.

options.text: Evidence from an external source is not reliable merely because it is external — all responses carry some risk of interception, alteration or fraud whether they arrive on paper or electronically, and cancelled registrations with no fresh ones raise a real question whether the replies came from the intended parties; and information produced by the entity itself has to be evaluated for its reliability, completeness and accuracy before it is used as audit evidence
options.why: The two failures are the same failure at different ends. Even when audit evidence is obtained from sources external to the entity, circumstances may exist that affect its reliability, and all responses carry some risk of interception, alteration or fraud regardless of whether the response is obtained in paper form or by electronic or other medium; factors indicating doubt include a response received indirectly or one that appears not to come from the originally intended confirming party, and businesses whose registrations were cancelled during the year are exactly that question. At the other end, where the auditor uses information produced by the entity he evaluates its reliability, completeness and accuracy, because a sample selected from an unverified schedule tests only what the schedule chose to show.

options.text: Both are acceptable — evidence from an external source is more reliable than evidence generated inside the entity, and an ageing schedule is a working paper rather than audit evidence, so neither needs further work
options.misconception: turns a general statement about relative reliability into a guarantee, and treats entity-produced information used to select a sample as though it were not evidence at all
options.why: External evidence is generally more reliable, which is not the same as reliable. And a schedule the auditor uses to select his sample is information produced by the entity being used as audit evidence, so its reliability, completeness and accuracy have to be evaluated.

options.text: Only the ageing schedule needs work — a confirmation is a direct written response from a third party, which is the most reliable form of audit evidence there is and cannot be improved on
options.misconception: treats the form of a confirmation as settling its reliability, when the question is whether the response actually came from the intended party
options.why: The form is not the point. If the auditor has doubt about the reliability of a response he obtains further audit evidence, and if he determines that a response is not reliable he evaluates the implications for his assessment of the risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and for the nature, timing and extent of other procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 500: even where audit evidence is obtained from sources external to the entity circumstances may exist that affect its reliability, all responses carrying some risk of interception, alteration or fraud whatever the medium, with the factors indicating doubt about a response; and the evaluation of the reliability, completeness and accuracy of information produced by the entity when it is used as audit evidence

items.scenario: Two pieces of evidence go into the file without further work. The first is a set of confirmations that came back within a week from twenty-five creditors, all of whose registrations under the goods and services tax were cancelled during the year and none of whom has a fresh registration; the senior treats them as reliable because they came from outside the entity. The second is an ageing schedule of receivables printed by the company's own system, which the senior uses to select his sample; he has not checked it against anything.

items.stem: Who is right, and why?

options.text: The partner, because a five-year appointment creates a familiarity threat that can never be reduced to an acceptable level, so the work of this expert cannot be used at all
options.misconception: turns a threat into a disqualification, when the auditor evaluates the threats and the adequacy of the safeguards rather than ruling the expert out
options.why: The evaluation is of the threats and of whether the safeguards are adequate. Safeguards cannot eliminate all threats to an expert's objectivity, but the conclusion is a judgement about the evidence rather than an automatic exclusion of the expert.

options.text: The senior, but for a different reason — the evaluation of objectivity is required only for an auditor's expert under SA 620, a management's expert being management's responsibility
options.misconception: confines the objectivity evaluation to the auditor's own expert, when SA 500 requires it for a management's expert too
options.why: SA 500 requires it directly. Where information to be used as audit evidence has been prepared using the work of a management's expert, the auditor evaluates the competence, capabilities and objectivity of that expert, obtains an understanding of his work, and evaluates the appropriateness of that work as audit evidence for the relevant assertion.

options.text: The partner — the auditor evaluates the objectivity of a management's expert whether the expert is employed by the entity or engaged by it; a broad range of circumstances may threaten objectivity, and because the threat created by being an employee of the entity will always be present, an expert employed by the entity cannot ordinarily be regarded as being more likely to be objective than any other employee, while for an engaged expert the auditor discusses the interests and relationships that may create threats — financial interests, business and personal relationships and the provision of other services — and evaluates whether the safeguards are adequate
options.why: Being engaged rather than employed changes the size of some threats, not the duty to look. A broad range of circumstances may threaten objectivity — self-interest, advocacy, familiarity, self-review and intimidation — and safeguards may be created by external structures such as the expert's profession or by his own work environment. Threats such as intimidation may be of less significance to an expert engaged by the entity than to one employed by it, and safeguards such as quality control policies may work better; but because the threat created by being an employee of the entity is always present, an employed expert cannot ordinarily be regarded as more likely to be objective than other employees. Where the expert is engaged, it may be relevant to discuss with management and with him any interests and relationships creating threats — financial interests, business and personal relationships, the provision of other services — and to evaluate whether the safeguards are adequate.

options.text: The senior — an expert engaged by the entity is by definition independent of it, and the auditor's evaluation is confined to the expert's competence and capabilities
options.misconception: reads engagement as independence and drops objectivity from the three things the auditor evaluates
options.why: The auditor evaluates the competence, capabilities and objectivity of a management's expert, and objectivity is not established by the fact of engagement. An expert can be engaged and still carry a self-interest threat from five consecutive years of fees or from other services he provides.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 500: evaluating the objectivity of a management's expert, the range of circumstances that may threaten objectivity and the safeguards created by external structures or by the expert's work environment, the rule that an expert employed by the entity cannot ordinarily be regarded as being more likely to be objective than other employees because that threat is always present, and the interests and relationships to be discussed where the expert is engaged by the entity

items.scenario: A mining company has engaged the same outside valuer for five years running to compute its environmental liabilities and site clean-up provisions, and describes him in its papers as an independent expert. The audit senior, having made inquiries of management, takes the view that because the valuer was engaged rather than employed and is called independent, his objectivity cannot be questioned and needs no evaluation. The audit partner disagrees.

items.stem: What is wrong with management's instructions?

options.text: Five things — the count should be supervised by a responsible officer not from the storage function, preferably from finance, with the storage in-charge present only to assist; inward and outward movement should not be allowed during the count because it distorts the result; the counting teams should be drawn from departments unconnected with storage, with counting and recording separated and serially numbered count sheets, distinctive marks or tags put on completed areas and each sheet signed by every team member; the paddy in silos should be measured with the strain gauges rather than assumed from silo capacity, since paddy may have been drawn from them; and work in progress should be estimated at each stage of production rather than for the plant as a whole
options.why: Evaluating management's instructions and procedures for recording and controlling the results of the count is the first of the four things the auditor does while attending, and every one of these instructions fails it. A man supervising the count of the inventory he is responsible for is checking his own work. Movement of goods during a count is the classic way a quantity is counted twice or not at all. Teams drawn from the storage function have the same problem as the supervisor, and without distinctive marks nobody can show that an area was covered or covered once. Silo capacity is what the silo could hold, not what is in it. And work in progress estimated for the plant as a whole gives an inaccurate picture, because the stage of completion differs at each step.

options.text: Only the supervision — the officer responsible for storage must not supervise, but the rest is acceptable, and where the auditor doubts the result he performs additional test counts of his own
options.misconception: treats extra test counts as a cure for a badly designed count, when a test count checks the records against the count rather than repairing it
options.why: A test count traces items from the physical inventory to management's count records and back; it cannot repair a count in which goods moved, areas went unmarked and silos were estimated from capacity. The instructions are evaluated before the count, which is why the auditor reads them in advance.

options.text: Only the silos and the work in progress — those are measurement errors that produce wrong quantities, while supervision, movement of goods and the composition of the teams are matters of the company's internal organisation
options.misconception: separates measurement from control, when the control failures are what let a wrong quantity through unnoticed
options.why: The control failures are the reason a wrong quantity survives. A supervisor counting his own inventory, goods moving during the count and unmarked areas each produce quantities nobody can test afterwards, and they are named in the same evaluation as the silos and the work in progress.

options.text: Nothing — these are management's instructions and management is responsible for the count; the auditor observes the count, performs test counts and inspects the inventory, and the design of the count is not his to criticise
options.misconception: reduces attendance to observation, when evaluating management's instructions and procedures is one of the four things attendance is for
options.why: Attendance has four purposes and the first of them is to evaluate management's instructions and procedures for recording and controlling the results of the physical inventory counting. The other three — observing the performance of the count procedures, inspecting the inventory and performing test counts — come after it.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 501: evaluating management's instructions and procedures for recording and controlling the results of the physical inventory counting, including the supervision of the count by an officer outside the storage function, the prohibition on inward and outward movement during the count, counting teams from unconnected departments with separate counting and recording on serially numbered sheets, distinctive marks on completed areas and signed count sheets, the measurement of silo quantities by strain gauges rather than capacity, and the estimation of work in progress at each stage of production

items.scenario: Before attending a rice mill's year end count, the auditor is given management's written instructions. The count is to be supervised by the officer responsible for storage. Receiving and despatch are to carry on as usual so that business is not interrupted. Counting is to be done by teams of three drawn from the storage staff, with no instruction about marking areas already counted or about signing the count sheets. Paddy in the steel silos is to be estimated from the capacity of each silo. Work in progress is to be estimated for the plant as a whole.

items.stem: What does SA 510 require about the opening inventory?

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion — where the prior period was not audited at all, sufficient appropriate audit evidence about opening balances cannot be obtained and the limitation is absolute
options.misconception: treats an unaudited prior period as an automatic scope limitation, when the Standard sets out the procedures by which the evidence is obtained
options.why: A qualified opinion or a disclaimer follows only if the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances after performing the procedures. An initial audit engagement includes the case where the prior period financial statements were not audited, and the Standard tells him what to do about it.

options.text: A written representation from management that the opening inventory was correctly stated, that being the only evidence available for a period during which the firm was not the auditor
options.misconception: substitutes a representation for procedures, when representations never provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own
options.why: Written representations do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters with which they deal. The three named procedures — the reconciliation from a current count, work on the valuation of the opening items, and work on gross profit and cut-off — are what produce the evidence.

options.text: The current period's audit procedures on the closing inventory balance provide little audit evidence about the inventory on hand at the beginning of the period, so additional procedures are necessary — observing a current physical inventory count and reconciling it to the opening inventory quantities, performing audit procedures on the valuation of the opening inventory items, and performing audit procedures on gross profit and cut-off
options.why: The auditor evaluates whether the procedures performed in the current period give evidence relevant to the opening balances or whether specific procedures are needed, and inventory is the case where they do not: work on the closing balance provides little audit evidence regarding the inventory on hand at the beginning of the period. The three additional procedures named are observing a current physical inventory count and reconciling it to the opening inventory quantities, performing audit procedures on the valuation of the opening inventory items, and performing audit procedures on gross profit and cut-off.
keywords: reconciling it to the opening inventory quantities

options.text: Nothing more — the closing inventory, the purchases and the production records together fix the opening figure arithmetically, which is stronger evidence than any procedure on a count that has already happened
options.misconception: derives the opening balance from the closing one, when the current period's work on the closing balance gives little evidence about the opening quantities
options.why: The arithmetic assumes the very things under audit: that purchases and production were completely recorded and correctly cut off. That is why the Standard says the current period's procedures on the closing balance provide little audit evidence regarding the opening inventory and names three additional procedures instead.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — SA 510: the current period's audit procedures on the closing inventory balance providing little audit evidence regarding inventory on hand at the beginning of the period, and the additional procedures that may provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence — observing a current physical inventory count and reconciling it to the opening inventory quantities, performing audit procedures on the valuation of the opening inventory items, and performing audit procedures on gross profit and cut-off

items.scenario: A firm is appointed in July 2026 to audit a manufacturer for the year to 31 March 2027. The previous year was not audited at all and material inventories stood in the balance sheet at 31 March 2026. The manager plans to attend the count at 31 March 2027, and says that once the closing inventory is verified the opening figure follows from it, since the two are linked by the year's purchases and production records.

items.stem: What does SA 520 require when the closing analytical procedures show something new?

options.text: Note it for the following year — analytical procedures at the end of the audit are a review step, and reopening completed substantive work at that stage would mean the audit could never be concluded
options.misconception: treats the closing analytical procedures as incapable of changing the audit, when a previously unrecognised risk they reveal forces the assessment and the procedures to be revised
options.why: They are a review step that is also allowed to find things. Where they identify a previously unrecognised risk of material misstatement the risk assessment is revised and the further planned procedures are modified, and an audit that cannot respond to that is an audit whose conclusion is known in advance.

options.text: Where the results identify a previously unrecognised risk of material misstatement, SA 315 requires the auditor to revise his assessment of the risks of material misstatement and to modify the further planned audit procedures accordingly — the closing procedures assist in forming an overall conclusion as to whether the financial statements are consistent with the auditor's understanding of the entity, and they may be similar to those used as risk assessment procedures
options.why: The manager has the purpose right and the consequence wrong. The conclusions drawn from analytical procedures designed and performed near the end of the audit are intended to verify the conclusions formed during the audit of individual components or elements of the financial statements, and they assist the auditor in drawing reasonable conclusions on which to base his opinion. But the results of such procedures may identify a previously unrecognised risk of material misstatement, and in those circumstances SA 315 requires the auditor to revise his assessment of the risks of material misstatement and modify the further planned audit procedures accordingly. The procedures at this stage may be similar to those that would be used as risk assessment procedures, which is exactly why they can find something new.
keywords: similar to those that would be used as risk assessment procedures

options.text: Treat the finding as an uncorrected misstatement and evaluate it with the others at the end, since at this stage of the audit there is no time left to perform further procedures
options.misconception: converts an identified risk into a misstatement, when nothing has yet been quantified and what is required is further work rather than an entry on a schedule
options.why: A relationship pointing to unrecorded sales is a risk, not a measured misstatement, and it cannot go on a schedule of uncorrected misstatements without an amount. What the Standard requires is that the assessment be revised and the further planned procedures modified.

options.text: Investigate the fluctuation by inquiring of management and obtain evidence relevant to their responses, and if the explanation is adequate no more is needed, the risk assessment being fixed at the planning stage
options.misconception: stops at the inquiry and treats the risk assessment as something settled at planning that later evidence cannot move
options.why: The inquiry is right as far as it goes and it is where the investigation starts. But the risk assessment is not fixed at planning: where the results identify a previously unrecognised risk, SA 315 requires it to be revised and the further planned procedures to be modified.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Planning, Strategy and Execution — SA 520: analytical procedures performed near the end of the audit that assist the auditor in forming an overall conclusion, the conclusions drawn from them verifying those formed during the audit of individual components, and the requirement that where their results identify a previously unrecognised risk of material misstatement the auditor revise his assessment under SA 315 and modify the further planned audit procedures

items.scenario: The analytical procedures performed near the end of an audit, after all the substantive work is finished and the file is complete, throw up a relationship between freight cost and despatched volume that nobody noticed at planning and that points to a risk of unrecorded sales. The manager proposes to note it as a matter for next year's planning, on the ground that the procedures at this stage exist to confirm the conclusions already reached rather than to open new ones.

items.stem: What is wrong with what he has done?

options.text: Nothing — 120 items out of 4,000 is a sample, and projecting the misstatements found in a sample to the population is exactly what SA 530 requires for tests of details
options.misconception: treats any examination of part of a population as audit sampling, when sampling requires that every sampling unit have a chance of selection
options.why: Fewer than all the items is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. Audit sampling requires that all the sampling units have a chance of selection, and an entry of ₹4 lakh posted in June had no chance of being picked here at all.

options.text: The selection — high value and key items may not be chosen deliberately, because deliberate selection destroys the randomness the Standard requires and biases the result
options.misconception: forbids the selective examination of specific items, when it is a legitimate way of obtaining audit evidence and only the projection is barred
options.why: Selecting specific items is legitimate and often efficient, and high value or key items and all items over a certain amount are the usual choices. What it cannot do is stand in for a conclusion about the whole population.

options.text: The projection — this is a selective examination of specific items rather than audit sampling, because the items were chosen for what they are and not so that every sampling unit had a chance of selection, so the results cannot be projected to the entire population and give no audit evidence about the remainder; and the approach is subject to non-sampling risk rather than to sampling risk
options.why: Audit sampling is the application of audit procedures to less than 100 per cent of the items within a population of audit relevance such that all the sampling units have a chance of selection, in order to provide a reasonable basis for a conclusion about the entire population. A selective examination of specific items is not that. It can be an efficient way of obtaining audit evidence and the items chosen here are sensibly chosen, but the results cannot be projected to the entire population and provide no audit evidence concerning the remainder of it. Such an approach is subject to non-sampling risk, which is the risk of the auditor reaching an erroneous conclusion for a reason unrelated to sampling — an inappropriate procedure, a misinterpretation of evidence, or a failure to recognise a misstatement or deviation.

options.text: The risk — an examination of specific items carries a higher sampling risk than a random sample of the same size, because the auditor's own judgement decides what is looked at
options.misconception: names the wrong risk, when a selective examination of specific items carries no sampling risk at all and carries non-sampling risk instead
options.why: Sampling risk is the risk that a conclusion based on a sample differs from the conclusion that testing the whole population would give, and it belongs to sampling. A selective examination of specific items is subject to non-sampling risk — an erroneous conclusion for a reason unrelated to sampling.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit Evidence — the selective examination of specific items as a means of obtaining audit evidence: it does not constitute audit sampling, its results cannot be projected to the entire population and it provides no audit evidence concerning the remainder, and it is subject to non-sampling risk, read with the definition of audit sampling as the application of audit procedures to less than 100 per cent of the items such that all the sampling units have a chance of selection

items.scenario: Testing a population of 4,000 journal entries, an auditor picks every entry above ₹25 lakh, every entry posted on the last two days of the year, and every entry touching the litigation provision — 120 entries in all. He examines each one, finds three misstatements totalling ₹9 lakh, and projects that to the remaining 3,880 entries to arrive at his estimate of the misstatement in the population.

items.stem: How does SA 560 have the two events treated?

options.text: The dividend is adjusted because it will be approved and paid out of this year's profits, and the claim is disclosed because the amount was still uncertain at the year end
options.misconception: reverses the two, recognising a dividend for which no obligation existed at the reporting date and refusing to adjust a claim whose condition did exist then
options.why: It is the wrong way round on both. No liability for the proposed dividend exists at the reporting date because there is no obligation to pay at that date, and the uncertainty about the claim at the year end is the very reason the later settlement is evidence about it.

options.text: The insurance claim is adjusted — it is an event providing evidence of a condition that existed at the date of the financial statements, and the settlement gives fresh information about an item already in them, so the ₹1 crore receivable is written down to the ₹45 lakh accepted; the proposed dividend is not adjusted but is disclosed in the notes, being an event providing evidence of a condition that arose after that date, with no obligation existing at the reporting date
options.why: The financial reporting frameworks identify two types of subsequent event and the treatment follows the type. The claim was lodged and outstanding at the year end and the later settlement provides evidence about a condition that existed then, giving fresh information about an item already included in the financial statements, so they are adjusted to reflect it. The dividend is the other type: the proposal came after the reporting period and no liability exists at the reporting date because there is no obligation to pay at that date, so it is not recognised and the auditor verifies instead that it is disclosed in the notes.
keywords: no obligation to pay at that date

options.text: Both are adjusted — each is a subsequent event of which the auditor has become aware before signing, and events known before the report date are reflected in the financial statements
options.misconception: adjusts for everything learned before the report date, when the adjusting type is defined by the date of the condition rather than by when the auditor learned of it
options.why: The dividing line is the date of the financial statements, not the date of the auditor's knowledge. An event providing evidence of a condition that arose after the date of the financial statements is disclosed rather than adjusted, however early the auditor hears of it.

options.text: Both are disclosed and neither is adjusted, as the manager proposes — both events occurred after the year end, and an amount fixed after the year end cannot be recognised in it
options.misconception: classifies by when the event happened instead of when the condition arose, which would leave every post-year-end settlement of a year-end balance unadjusted
options.why: Every subsequent event happens after the year end; that is what makes it subsequent. What divides them is whether the event gives evidence of a condition that existed at the date of the financial statements, and a settlement of a claim outstanding at that date does exactly that.

citation.ref: Ch. Completion and Review — SA 560: the two types of subsequent event, those providing evidence of conditions that existed at the date of the financial statements and those providing evidence of conditions that arose after that date, with the settlement of an insurance claim outstanding at the year end adjusted as fresh information about an item already in the financial statements and a dividend proposed after the reporting period disclosed in the notes because no obligation to pay exists at the reporting date

items.scenario: Two events reach an auditor before he signs, for a year ended 31 March. A claim of ₹1 crore against an insurer for stock damaged by flooding the previous September stands in the balance sheet as a receivable because it was unsettled at the year end; in April the surveyor recommended ₹45 lakh, the company consented, and ₹45 lakh was received on 15 May. Separately, on 17 April the board proposed a dividend of ₹1 crore, being ₹10 a share, which the general meeting is likely to approve months later. The manager proposes to disclose both in the notes and adjust neither.

items.stem: How does SA 610 (Revised) have the threats to their objectivity evaluated?

options.text: None of the three may be used for anything at all — an internal auditor is not independent of the entity, so direct assistance is available only where law or regulation expressly permits it
options.misconception: reads the internal auditors' lack of independence as a bar on direct assistance, when the Standard bars it only where there are significant threats to objectivity or insufficient competence
options.why: Internal auditors are indeed not independent of the entity, which is why the direction, supervision and review must recognise that.
