options.misconception: removes a term the standard requires to be agreed, when the conflict between the agreed restriction and the law is the reason for not accepting at all
options.why: Dropping the term does not resolve the conflict; it hides it. The limitation on distribution is one of the matters to be agreed, and the standard's answer where that limitation would conflict with the legal requirements is that the auditor would not accept the engagement.

options.text: Accept — the matters to be agreed are guidance on good practice, and what actually binds the auditor is the list of contents the report of factual findings must carry
options.misconception: reads the matters to be agreed as advisory, when the standard states them as what must be agreed and attaches a refusal to one of them
options.why: The report's contents are one requirement and the terms are another. The standard sets out the matters to be agreed and then attaches a consequence to the fifth of them, which is that the auditor would not accept the engagement where the limitation on distribution conflicts with the legal requirements.

options.text: Accept, and add a sentence to the report recording that the restriction is subject to any statutory requirement to produce the report
options.misconception: drafts around a conflict the standard answers by refusing the engagement, leaving a restriction in the report that the law can override without the parties having agreed to it
options.why: A saving sentence leaves the parties agreeing to one thing and the law doing another, and the whole force of an agreed-upon procedures report is that the reader knows what was agreed. Where the limitation on distribution would conflict with the legal requirements, the auditor would not accept the engagement.

options.text: Do not accept the engagement — limitations on distribution of the report of factual findings are one of the five matters to be agreed, and where such a limitation would be in conflict with the legal requirements the auditor would not accept the engagement; the other four are the nature of the engagement including that the procedures will not constitute an audit or a review and that accordingly no assurance will be expressed, the stated purpose, the identification of the financial information to which the procedures will be applied, and the nature, timing and extent of the specific procedures
options.why: The standard makes the agreement about distribution a condition of taking the work rather than a clause to be drafted around. Matters to be agreed include limitations on distribution of the report of factual findings, and when such limitation would be in conflict with the legal requirements, if any, the auditor would not accept the engagement. That is the answer to a restriction the law will not allow: the engagement is declined, not accepted with a restriction nobody can honour.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4400: the matters to be agreed, including limitations on distribution of the report of factual findings, and the requirement that the auditor would not accept the engagement where such a limitation would be in conflict with the legal requirements

items.scenario: A bank and its borrower ask you to perform agreed-upon procedures on the borrower's stock statements. The draft terms restrict distribution of the report of factual findings to the two of them. A statute applying to the borrower requires any such report to be laid before a public authority, which the two parties do not want. The relationship manager suggests you accept and simply keep the restriction in the report.

items.stem: What does SRS 4400 require?

options.text: The report of factual findings is addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority; an engagement letter should be sent documenting the key terms, listing the procedures to be performed as agreed between the parties and stating that distribution of the report would be restricted to the specified parties who have agreed to them; and the procedures applied may include inquiry and analysis, recomputation, comparison and other clerical accuracy checks, observation, inspection and obtaining confirmations
options.why: Each of the three assumptions is wrong. The report of factual findings is addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority, not to whichever officer happened to telephone. It is in the interests of both the client and the auditor that an engagement letter is sent: it confirms the auditor's acceptance of the appointment and helps avoid misunderstanding about the objectives and scope, the extent of his responsibilities and the form of the report, and it includes a listing of the procedures agreed and a statement that distribution would be restricted to the specified parties. And the procedures are not confined to inquiry — recomputation, comparison and other clerical accuracy checks, observation, inspection and obtaining confirmations are all among the procedures an agreed-upon procedures engagement may apply.

options.text: No engagement letter is needed for a non-assurance engagement, and the report may be addressed to whoever commissioned it, provided it says no assurance is expressed
options.misconception: reads the absence of assurance as an absence of formality, when the standard asks for an engagement letter and names the appointing authority as the ordinary addressee
options.why: The absence of assurance is exactly why the terms matter: a reader can only judge a report of factual findings if he knows what was agreed. The standard asks for an engagement letter documenting the key terms and names the appointing authority as the ordinary addressee.

options.text: The procedures in an agreed-upon procedures engagement are confined to inquiry and analytical work, examination of records and confirmation being audit procedures that would convert the engagement into an audit
options.misconception: confuses the procedures applied with the assurance given, when the standard's own list includes inspection and confirmations and the engagement still expresses no assurance
options.why: What separates the engagement from an audit is the absence of an opinion, not the absence of audit techniques — the objective is to carry out procedures of an audit nature to which the parties have agreed and to report factual findings. The listed procedures include recomputation, comparison and other clerical accuracy checks, observation, inspection and obtaining confirmations.

options.text: An engagement letter is needed, but the listing of procedures belongs only in the report of factual findings; putting it in the letter commits the auditor before he has seen the records
options.misconception: keeps the letter and strips out the term that gives it its purpose, when the listing of the agreed procedures is one of the matters the standard puts in it
options.why: The letter is where the parties fix what will be done, which is the whole basis of the engagement. The matters included in it are a listing of the procedures to be performed as agreed between the parties and a statement that distribution of the report of factual findings would be restricted to the specified parties who have agreed to those procedures.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4400: the report of factual findings is addressed ordinarily to the appointing authority, the engagement letter includes a listing of the agreed procedures and a statement that distribution would be restricted to the specified parties, and the procedures applied may include inquiry and analysis, recomputation, comparison and other clerical accuracy checks, observation, inspection and obtaining confirmations

items.scenario: A company's finance head asks you over the telephone to perform agreed-upon procedures on its accounts payable and to address the report to him. No engagement letter is sent. Your assistant proposes to confine the work to inquiry of the accounts department and an analysis of the ageing, on the view that anything more would make the engagement an audit.

items.stem: How many of the three are right under SRS 4410?

options.text: Two — independence and quality control, both of which follow from the engagement being performed under a standard issued by the Institute
options.misconception: treats every standard of the Institute as carrying the independence requirements, when they do not apply to a non-assurance engagement unless law or regulation says otherwise
options.why: Quality control does follow, because SQC 1 applies to all Engagement Standards. Independence does not: being a non-assurance engagement, the independence requirements do not apply to a compilation engagement, although laws or regulations may specify requirements or disclosure rules pertaining to independence, and the relevant ethical requirements apply throughout.

options.text: One — the verification point, because a practitioner who puts his name to financial information must have satisfied himself that it is complete
options.misconception: reads the practitioner's name on the report as a warranty of the information, when the standard says the engagement does not require him to verify its accuracy or completeness
options.why: What his name is on is a statement that he compiled the information from what management provided, and the report says in terms that he is not required to verify its accuracy or completeness and does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion. Management retains responsibility for the financial information and for the basis on which it is prepared.

options.text: None — a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement and does not require the practitioner to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management or otherwise to gather evidence to express an audit opinion or a review conclusion; independence requirements do not apply, though laws or regulations may specify requirements or disclosure rules about it and the relevant ethical requirements do apply; and SQC 1 applies to firms in respect of compilation engagements because it applies to all Engagement Standards
options.why: Each statement fails on the face of the standard. A compilation engagement does not require the practitioner to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management for the compilation, or otherwise to gather evidence to express an audit opinion or a review conclusion — so checking that all revenue has been booked is not part of it. Being a non-assurance engagement, the independence requirements do not apply, although laws or regulations may specify requirements or disclosure rules pertaining to independence; the practitioner must still comply with relevant ethical requirements. And SQC 1 is applicable to all Engagement Standards, of which SRS 4410 is one, so it applies to the firm in respect of its compilation engagements too.

options.text: All three — a member of the Institute performing professional work is bound by verification, independence and quality control alike
options.misconception: collapses three different regimes into one obligation of professional work, when the standard answers each of them separately for a compilation engagement
options.why: The standard separates them. Verification is not required at all; independence is not required unless law or regulation says so; quality control does apply, because SQC 1 reaches every Engagement Standard. Ethical requirements other than independence apply in every case.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement and does not require the practitioner to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management or to gather evidence for an audit opinion or a review conclusion, independence requirements do not apply though laws or regulations may specify requirements or disclosure rules about it, and SQC 1 applies to firms in respect of compilation engagements because it applies to all Engagement Standards

items.scenario: Your firm has been engaged to compile the financial statements of a company from a draft trial balance for management's internal use. A team member says three things: that the firm must verify that all the revenue the company should have booked has in fact been booked; that the firm must be independent of the company; and that quality control standards do not reach an engagement of this kind.

items.stem: What does SRS 4410 require before the work begins?

options.text: Management's acknowledgement of responsibility for the accuracy and completeness of the records is the one term that must be settled first; the rest can be agreed as the work proceeds
options.misconception: picks one of management's responsibilities out of a list of terms the standard requires to be agreed before the engagement is accepted at all
options.why: That acknowledgement is one item inside one of the six terms. The practitioner shall not accept the engagement unless he has agreed all of them, including the intended use and distribution of the information, the applicable framework, the objective and scope, his own responsibilities and the expected form and content of his report.

options.text: The practitioner shall not accept the engagement unless he has agreed the terms with management, and with the engaging party where it is different, covering the intended use and distribution of the information and any restrictions on either, the identification of the applicable financial reporting framework, the objective and scope of the engagement, his own responsibilities including compliance with relevant ethical requirements, management's four responsibilities and the expected form and content of his report — and the agreed terms are recorded in an engagement letter or other suitable form of written agreement prior to performing the engagement
options.why: Acceptance is barred until the terms are agreed, and the standard lists them: the intended use and distribution of the financial information and any restrictions on either; the identification of the applicable financial reporting framework; the objective and scope of the compilation engagement; the responsibilities of the practitioner, including the requirement to comply with relevant ethical requirements; the responsibilities of management for the financial information and its preparation and presentation under a framework acceptable in view of the intended use and users, for such internal control as management determines is necessary, for the accuracy and completeness of the records, documents, explanations and other information provided, and for the judgments needed in preparing and presenting it; and the expected form and content of the report. Because a second company is the engaging party, the terms are agreed with it as well as with management, and they are recorded in an engagement letter or other suitable form of written agreement prior to performing the engagement.
keywords: Acceptance is barred until the terms are agreed

options.text: An engagement letter is not required for a compilation engagement, which is a non-assurance service, so an exchange of emails at the end of the work is enough
options.misconception: drops a written agreement the standard requires before the work starts, on the ground that the engagement gives no assurance
options.why: The standard says the opposite and says when: the practitioner shall record the agreed terms of engagement in an engagement letter or other suitable form of written agreement, prior to performing the engagement. Non-assurance describes what the report says, not how the work is taken on.

options.text: The terms are agreed with management alone, the company paying the fee having no standing to settle the scope of work on another entity's financial information
options.misconception: leaves the engaging party out of the agreement, when the standard requires the terms to be agreed with management and the engaging party where the two are different
options.why: The standard names both. The terms are agreed with management, and the engaging party if different — which is exactly this case, where a second company in the group has engaged the firm to compile the client's information.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: the practitioner shall not accept the engagement unless he has agreed the terms with management and the engaging party if different, covering the intended use and distribution and any restrictions, the applicable financial reporting framework, the objective and scope, the practitioner's responsibilities, management's responsibilities and the expected form and content of the report, recorded in an engagement letter or other suitable written agreement prior to performing the engagement

items.scenario: A company's chief financial officer asks your firm to start compiling the company's financial information at once, promising that the terms can be settled when the work is finished. He is willing to say now that management is responsible for the accuracy and completeness of the records it hands over. The information will be sent to a funding body under a grant contract, and a second company in the group, not the client, is paying your fee.

items.stem: What does SRS 4410 require?

options.text: Issue the report with a qualification describing the omitted expenditure, since the practitioner has read the information and can say what is wrong with it
options.misconception: modifies a report that expresses no opinion or conclusion capable of being modified, when the standard's remedy is an amendment and, failing that, withdrawal
options.why: There is nothing to qualify. The practitioner's report is not a vehicle to express an opinion or conclusion on the financial information in any form, so the standard gives him a different remedy: propose the amendments, and withdraw if they are declined.

options.text: Compile what management has provided and leave the disclosure to management, the financial information and its presentation being management's responsibility throughout
options.misconception: reads management's responsibility for the information as removing the practitioner's own requirement to propose amendments and to withdraw if they are declined
options.why: Management does retain responsibility for the financial information and the basis on which it is prepared, and that is why the practitioner proposes rather than imposes the amendments. But the standard does not leave him there: if management declines, he withdraws from the engagement and informs management and those charged with governance of the reasons.

options.text: Issue the report and describe the omission in an explanatory paragraph, so that a reader is told what the compiled information does not show
options.misconception: uses a paragraph to carry a defect the standard requires to be amended or the engagement left, leaving misleading information in circulation with a note beside it
options.why: The paragraphs the report may carry are prescribed and none of them is for this. Where the compiled information is misleading and management will not amend it, the practitioner withdraws and tells management and those charged with governance why.

options.text: Propose the appropriate amendments to management, and where management declines or does not permit them, withdraw from the engagement and inform management and those charged with governance of the reasons for withdrawing — and if withdrawal is not possible, determine the professional and legal responsibilities applicable in the circumstances
options.why: The standard makes the reading of the compiled information the last check and gives it teeth. Where the practitioner becomes aware that the compiled financial information does not adequately refer to or describe the applicable financial reporting framework, that amendments are required for it not to be materially misstated, or that it is otherwise misleading, he shall propose the appropriate amendments to management. If management declines, or does not permit him to make them, he shall withdraw from the engagement and inform management and those charged with governance of the reasons for withdrawing; and if withdrawal is not possible he shall determine the professional and legal responsibilities applicable in the circumstances. The same withdrawal follows where he is unable to complete the engagement because management has failed to provide records, documents, explanations or other information as requested.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: where the practitioner becomes aware that the compiled financial information does not adequately describe the applicable framework, requires amendment not to be materially misstated, or is otherwise misleading, he proposes the appropriate amendments; where management declines he withdraws and informs management and those charged with governance of the reasons; and where withdrawal is not possible he determines the professional and legal responsibilities applicable

items.scenario: You are compiling a company's financial statements. Reading the compiled information before signing, you find that the expenditure on a new unit at Rourkela, paid out of a bank account maintained there, has not been shown under the appropriate heads, so the statements are misleading on the face of them. Management declines to make the amendment you propose. Earlier in the same engagement the company was slow to hand over the bank records and you had to ask twice before they came.

items.stem: What else must the practitioner's report contain?

options.text: A statement of negative assurance, that nothing has come to the practitioner's attention to suggest the compiled information is not prepared in accordance with the framework
options.misconception: puts a review conclusion into a compilation report, when the standard requires the report to say that no such conclusion is being expressed
options.why: Negative assurance is the language of a review under SRE 2400, which rests on inquiry and analytical procedures performed for that purpose. A compilation report has to say the opposite in terms: the practitioner does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion on whether the information is prepared in accordance with the applicable framework.

options.text: The explanations about assurance, but not the special purpose paragraph — the framework is already identified in the report, and identifying it tells the reader all he needs about the basis used
options.misconception: treats identifying the framework as covering the purpose, the intended users and the warning about other uses, which the standard requires as a separate explanatory paragraph
options.why: Identifying the framework says which rules were followed. The explanatory paragraph says why the information was prepared, for whom, and that as a result it may not be suitable for other purposes — which is the thing a reader outside the intended group would otherwise get wrong.

options.text: Explanations that since a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement the practitioner is not required to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management, and that accordingly he does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion on whether the information is prepared in accordance with the applicable framework — and, the framework being a special purpose one, an explanatory paragraph describing the purpose for which the information is prepared and, if necessary, the intended users, or referring to a note disclosing it, and drawing readers' attention to the fact that the information is prepared under a special purpose framework and may not be suitable for other purposes
options.why: Saying nothing about assurance is not the same as saying there is none. The report shall include explanations that, since a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement, the practitioner is not required to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management for the compilation, and that accordingly he does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion on whether the financial information is prepared in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. And where the information is prepared using a special purpose financial reporting framework, the report carries an explanatory paragraph describing the purpose for which it is prepared and, if necessary, the intended users, or containing a reference to a note that discloses this, and drawing the attention of readers to the fact that the information is prepared in accordance with a special purpose framework and that as a result it may not be suitable for other purposes.
keywords: audit opinion or a review conclusion
may not be suitable for other purposes

options.text: Nothing — an important purpose of the report is to communicate the nature of the engagement, and naming the standard it was performed under does that in one line
options.misconception: treats the name of the standard as telling the reader what the engagement was worth, when the report is required to say in terms that no verification and no opinion or conclusion were given
options.why: A reader who does not know the standard learns nothing from its number. That is why the report spells the position out: the practitioner is not required to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management and does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion on it.

citation.ref: Ch. Related Services — SRS 4410: the practitioner's report shall include explanations that since a compilation engagement is not an assurance engagement the practitioner is not required to verify the accuracy or completeness of the information provided by management and accordingly does not express an audit opinion or a review conclusion, and where a special purpose financial reporting framework is used an explanatory paragraph describing the purpose and the intended users and drawing attention to the fact that the information may not be suitable for other purposes

items.scenario: You have compiled financial information for a company on a basis of accounting set out in a grant contract, which is a special purpose framework, and management has acknowledged responsibility for the final version. Your draft report identifies the information and the framework, describes management's responsibilities and yours, and says the engagement was performed in accordance with SRS 4410. A colleague says nothing else is needed, since the report gives no opinion and there is nothing to explain.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require?

options.text: Accept — a review is an assurance engagement performed under a standard of the Institute, so it satisfies a statute that asks for the financial statements to be examined by a professional accountant
options.misconception: treats a review as interchangeable with an audit for a statutory purpose, when a law requiring an audit is the standard's own example of an engagement with no rational purpose
options.why: A review gives limited assurance in a negatively worded conclusion; an audit gives reasonable assurance in a positively worded opinion. Where the law requires the statements to be audited, the standard says there is no rational purpose for the review, and it is not for the practitioner to substitute one engagement for another.

options.text: Decline both points and stop there — where a review is inappropriate the practitioner withdraws from the relationship, recommending an alternative engagement being outside his role
options.misconception: stops at the refusal, when the standard expressly contemplates recommending another type of engagement where a review would not be appropriate
options.why: The standard goes on from the refusal. Where his preliminary understanding indicates that accepting a review would not be appropriate, the practitioner may consider recommending that another type of engagement be undertaken — an audit, or where the circumstances preclude an assurance engagement, a compilation or other accounting services engagement.

options.text: Accept, and manage the difficulty by extending the procedures until they are equivalent to an audit and by expressing the conclusion in positive terms
options.misconception: converts a review into an audit by doing more work, when the level of assurance is a term of the engagement rather than a function of the effort
options.why: A review is a limited assurance engagement and its conclusion is negatively worded; more procedures do not turn it into a reasonable assurance engagement. If an audit is what the circumstances need, the standard has the practitioner recommend an audit, not perform one under a review engagement letter.

options.text: Unless required by law or regulation to do so, do not accept — there is no rational purpose for a review engagement where the engagement is intended to meet compliance requirements of a law or regulation that requires the financial statements to be audited, and a rational purpose may also be absent where the practitioner suspects association of his name with the financial statements in an inappropriate manner; where a review would not be appropriate he may recommend another type of engagement, an audit here, or where the circumstances preclude an assurance engagement, a compilation or other accounting services engagement
options.why: The standard's first gate is whether the engagement has a rational purpose, and it names this exact case: when the engagement is intended to meet compliance requirements of a relevant law or regulation and such law or regulation requires the financial statements to be audited, there is no rational purpose for such a review engagement. It names the second fact too — it may be unlikely that there is a rational purpose where the practitioner suspects association of his name with the financial statements in an inappropriate manner. And where a review would not be appropriate in the circumstances, he may recommend another type of engagement: an audit where that is more appropriate, or a compilation or other accounting services engagement where the circumstances preclude an assurance engagement.
keywords: requires the financial statements to be audited

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): unless required by law or regulation the practitioner shall not accept a review engagement where he is not satisfied that there is a rational purpose for it, there being none where the law requires the financial statements to be audited and none likely where there is a significant scope limitation or where he suspects inappropriate association of his name, and where a review would not be appropriate he may recommend an audit or a compilation or other accounting services engagement

items.scenario: A company whose financial statements a statute requires to be audited asks you, who are not its auditor, to review them instead and give a report the statute will accept. The directors say a review costs less and reaches the same place. Separately you notice that the company's prospectus draft names you in a way that suggests you stand behind the figures generally.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require now?

options.text: Continue and rely on inquiry of the finance department, a review being built primarily on inquiry and analytical procedures in any event
options.misconception: reads the ordinary shape of review procedures as making a restriction on access harmless, when the precondition is unrestricted access to the persons from whom the practitioner determines evidence is needed
options.why: A review is built primarily on inquiry, which is why who may be asked matters so much. The precondition is unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom the practitioner determines it necessary to obtain evidence, and a restriction on it is not cured by asking the people who remain.

options.text: Nothing follows from the preconditions, which are tested once before acceptance; from here the restriction is dealt with as a limitation on the evidence and answered in the conclusion
options.misconception: treats the preconditions as spent on acceptance, when the standard provides expressly for discovering after acceptance that one of them is not satisfied
options.why: The standard deals with the position after acceptance in its own paragraph. If it is discovered after the engagement has been accepted that the practitioner is not satisfied as to any of the preconditions, he discusses the matter and determines whether it can be resolved, whether to continue, and whether and how to communicate it in his report.

options.text: Discuss the matter with management or those charged with governance and determine three things — whether the matter can be resolved, whether it is appropriate to continue with the engagement, and whether and, if so, how to communicate the matter in your report — the precondition being management's agreement to provide access to all relevant information, additional information you may request and unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom you determine it necessary to obtain evidence
options.why: What the managing director has withdrawn is a precondition. Before accepting, the practitioner obtains management's agreement that it acknowledges and understands its responsibilities to provide him with access to all information relevant to the preparation of the financial statements, with additional information he may request, and with unrestricted access to persons within the entity from whom he determines it necessary to obtain evidence. Where it is discovered after acceptance that he is not satisfied as to any precondition, he shall discuss the matter with management or those charged with governance and shall determine whether the matter can be resolved, whether it is appropriate to continue with the engagement, and whether and, if so, how to communicate the matter in his report.
keywords: whether the matter can be resolved
communicate the matter in his report

options.text: Withdraw at once — a precondition that fails after acceptance ends the engagement, there being nothing left to review
options.misconception: jumps to withdrawal, when the standard first has the practitioner discuss the matter and decide whether it can be resolved and whether to continue
options.why: Withdrawal may be where it ends, but the standard sets out the steps before it. He discusses the matter with management or those charged with governance and determines whether it can be resolved, whether it is appropriate to continue, and whether and how to communicate the matter in his report.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): the preconditions include management's agreement to provide access to all relevant information, additional information requested and unrestricted access to persons within the entity, and where it is discovered after acceptance that a precondition is not satisfied the practitioner discusses the matter and determines whether it can be resolved, whether to continue with the engagement, and whether and how to communicate it in his report

items.scenario: You have accepted a review engagement. A month in, the managing director tells you that you may speak to the finance department only and to nobody else in the company, and that certain subsidiary records will not be made available. The engagement is not one that any law or regulation requires.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require on materiality?

options.text: No materiality is determined in a review, the conclusion being expressed in negative form on the financial statements as a whole rather than on individual amounts
options.misconception: reads a negatively worded conclusion as dispensing with a threshold, when the standard requires materiality to be determined and applied in designing the procedures
options.why: The conclusion is about whether the financial statements are materially misstated, so a threshold is unavoidable. The practitioner shall determine materiality for the financial statements as a whole and apply it both in designing the procedures and in evaluating the results obtained from them.

options.text: Set materiality higher for a review, since fewer procedures are performed and a lower figure would demand work the engagement does not provide for
options.misconception: scales the measure of what matters to a reader by the amount of work being done, when the level of assurance changes the procedures and not the threshold
options.why: The threshold belongs to the reader of the financial statements, not to the engagement. The practitioner's judgement about what is material in relation to the financial statements as a whole is the same regardless of the level of assurance obtained as the basis for the conclusion.

options.text: Determine materiality for the financial statements as a whole and apply it in designing the procedures and in evaluating the results — the practitioner's judgement about what is material in relation to the financial statements as a whole being the same regardless of the level of assurance obtained as the basis for expressing the conclusion — and revise it on becoming aware of information during the review that would have caused a different amount to be determined initially
options.why: The standard closes the shortcut in one sentence: the practitioner's judgement about what is material in relation to the financial statements as a whole is the same regardless of the level of assurance obtained by him as the basis for expressing the conclusion. What the level of assurance changes is the procedures, not the threshold at which a misstatement would matter to a reader. He shall determine materiality for the financial statements as a whole and apply it in designing the procedures and in evaluating the results obtained from them, and shall revise it in the event of becoming aware of any information during the review that would have caused him to determine a different amount initially.
keywords: same regardless of the level of assurance

options.text: Determine materiality at the start and leave it there — revising it mid-engagement would change the basis on which procedures already performed were designed
options.misconception: fixes materiality against later information, when the standard requires revision where that information would have produced a different amount initially
options.why: The standard requires the revision precisely because the earlier figure was set without the information. He shall revise materiality for the financial statements as a whole in the event of becoming aware of any information during the review that would have caused him to determine a different amount initially.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): the practitioner determines materiality for the financial statements as a whole and applies it in designing procedures and evaluating results, his judgement about what is material being the same regardless of the level of assurance obtained, and he revises it on becoming aware of information that would have caused a different amount to be determined initially

items.scenario: Planning a review of a company's financial statements, your senior proposes to set materiality at twice the figure the company's auditors used for the annual audit, on the ground that a review gives limited assurance and fewer procedures are performed. Midway through the review a contingent liability comes to light which, had it been known at the start, would have led you to a lower figure.

items.stem: What does SRE 2400 (Revised) require?

options.text: Accept the oral assurance and complete the review, written representations being a matter of form where the finance director has said the same thing
options.misconception: treats an oral assurance as equivalent to the written representation, when the refusal itself is what the standard says may signal that significant issues exist
options.why: A request for written rather than oral representations often prompts management to consider the matters more rigorously, and a refusal to put them in writing may alert the practitioner to the possibility that one or more significant issues exist. That is why the refusal is dealt with and not accommodated.

options.text: Express a qualified conclusion, the missing representations being a limitation whose possible effects are material but not pervasive
options.misconception: answers a refusal of the representations about management's own responsibilities with a qualification, when the standard sends the practitioner to a disclaimer or to withdrawal
options.why: The two representations refused are the ones that underpin everything else — that management prepared the statements under the framework and that all transactions are recorded. The standard does not grade their absence; it requires a disclaimer of conclusion or withdrawal.

options.text: Discuss the matter with management and those charged with governance, re-evaluate the integrity of management and the effect this may have on the reliability of representations and evidence in general, and take appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the conclusion — and because management has not provided the required representations about its responsibilities, disclaim a conclusion on the financial statements or withdraw from the engagement
options.why: The standard treats a refusal of these particular representations as going to the whole engagement rather than to one balance. Where management does not provide one or more of the requested written representations, the practitioner discusses the matter with management and those charged with governance, re-evaluates the integrity of management and evaluates the effect that this may have on the reliability of representations, oral or written, and evidence in general, and takes appropriate actions including determining the possible effect on the conclusion in his report. And he shall disclaim a conclusion on the financial statements, or withdraw from the engagement if withdrawal is possible under applicable law or regulation, where management does not provide the required representations in respect of its responsibilities for the preparation of the financial statements and the recording of all transactions.

options.text: Treat it as a scope limitation confined to the items the representations covered and report on the rest of the financial statements
options.misconception: confines to particular items a refusal that goes to management's responsibility for the statements as a whole and to the recording of all transactions
options.why: These representations are not about particular items. They are that management has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with the framework and that all transactions have been recorded and reflected in them, which is why their absence takes the conclusion on the statements as a whole with it.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2400 (Revised): where management does not provide a requested written representation the practitioner discusses the matter, re-evaluates the integrity of management and the effect on the reliability of representations and evidence, and takes appropriate actions, and he shall disclaim a conclusion or withdraw where management does not provide the required representations about its responsibilities for the preparation of the financial statements and the recording of all transactions

items.scenario: At the end of a review, management refuses to sign the representation that it has fulfilled its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with the applicable framework and that all transactions have been recorded and reflected in them. It offers instead an oral assurance from the finance director. Nothing in the engagement is required by law or regulation, and withdrawal is possible.

items.stem: What does SRE 2410 require?

options.text: Request the removal of the limitation; management having refused, you are unable to complete the review and express a conclusion, and you communicate in writing to the appropriate level of management and to those charged with governance the reason why the review cannot be completed — and since you are required to issue a report, you disclaim a conclusion and provide in the report the reason why the review cannot be completed, communicating also any matter that causes you to believe a material adjustment to the interim financial information is necessary
options.why: Where management imposes a limitation on scope after the engagement is accepted, the auditor requests its removal; if management refuses, he is unable to complete the review and express a conclusion, and he communicates in writing to the appropriate level of management and those charged with governance the reason why the review cannot be completed. He then considers his legal and regulatory responsibilities, including whether there is a requirement for him to issue a report; where there is, he disclaims a conclusion and provides in the review report the reason why the review cannot be completed. If a matter has come to his attention causing him to believe that a material adjustment to the interim financial information is necessary, he communicates that too.
keywords: reason why the review cannot be completed

options.text: Qualify the conclusion, indicating that except for the matter described in an explanatory paragraph the review was conducted in accordance with SRE 2410
options.misconception: uses the treatment reserved for a limitation arising from circumstances and clearly confined to specific matters that are not pervasive, on a limitation imposed by management
options.why: That route exists, and it is for a different limitation. It applies in rare circumstances where the limitation arises otherwise than from management and is clearly confined to one or more specific matters that, while material, are not pervasive. A limitation imposed by management is dealt with by requesting its removal and, where a report is required, disclaiming a conclusion.

options.text: Withdraw from the review without a report, an auditor who cannot complete his work having nothing to say
options.misconception: leaves the users with no report where the auditor is required to issue one and the standard tells him what it must contain
options.why: Where he is required to issue a report he issues one, and the standard fixes its content: he disclaims a conclusion and provides the reason why the review cannot be completed. What he may not do is stay silent about a limitation the reader would otherwise never see.

options.text: Nothing can be done now — the engagement should not have been accepted with such a limitation in prospect, so the position is a matter for the next engagement
options.misconception: applies the pre-acceptance rule to a limitation imposed after acceptance, when the standard deals with the two separately
options.why: The rule about not accepting applies where the auditor's preliminary knowledge indicates that he would be unable to complete the review because of a limitation management will impose. Where the limitation arrives after acceptance, the standard has him request its removal and then follow the steps that end in a disclaimer if a report is required.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2410: where management imposes a limitation on scope after acceptance the auditor requests its removal and, on refusal, is unable to complete the review, communicating in writing to management and those charged with governance the reason, and where he is required to issue a report he disclaims a conclusion and provides that reason in the report

items.scenario: You are the statutory auditor of a listed company and are reviewing its quarterly interim financial information. After you accepted the engagement, management refused you access to the records of a material subsidiary. The listing regulations require you to issue a report on the quarterly results. A colleague suggests a conclusion qualified "except for" the subsidiary.

items.stem: What does SRE 2410 require in each quarter?

options.text: A qualified conclusion in all three quarters, a material uncertainty about going concern being by its nature something the conclusion must be modified for
options.misconception: modifies the conclusion for an uncertainty that is adequately disclosed, when the standard answers adequate disclosure with an emphasis of matter paragraph
options.why: A disclosed uncertainty is information the reader has; there is nothing wrong with the interim information for the conclusion to be modified about. The standard answers it with an emphasis of matter paragraph and keeps the qualified or adverse conclusion for the case where the disclosure is not adequate.

options.text: An emphasis of matter paragraph in all three quarters, the auditor's job being to draw attention to the uncertainty however the company has dealt with it
options.misconception: uses the paragraph where the disclosure is inadequate, when a paragraph cannot supply a disclosure the interim information itself omits
options.why: An emphasis of matter paragraph draws attention to something the information says; it cannot stand in for something the information does not say. Where the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, the auditor should express a qualified or adverse conclusion with specific reference to it.

options.text: Nothing in the first two quarters, going concern being assessed on annual financial statements, and a qualified conclusion in the third only when the annual audit comes round
options.misconception: defers going concern to the annual audit, when the standard deals with a material uncertainty coming to the auditor's attention during an interim review
options.why: The standard addresses going concern and significant uncertainties inside the interim review itself. A material uncertainty that comes to the auditor's attention as a result of inquiries or other review procedures is dealt with in the review report for that period, by paragraph or by conclusion depending on the disclosure.

options.text: First quarter, modify the review report by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph; second quarter, modify the current report by adding a paragraph to highlight the continued material uncertainty; third quarter, express a qualified or adverse conclusion as appropriate, the report including specific reference to the fact that there is such a material uncertainty
options.why: The answer turns on the disclosure, not on the uncertainty. Where a material uncertainty comes to the auditor's attention and adequate disclosure is made in the interim financial information, he modifies the review report by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph. Where he had already added such a paragraph to a prior audit or review report and the material uncertainty still exists with adequate disclosure made, he modifies the current period's report by adding a paragraph to highlight the continued material uncertainty. And where the material uncertainty is not adequately disclosed, he should express a qualified or adverse conclusion as appropriate, with specific reference in the report to the fact that there is such a material uncertainty.

citation.ref: Ch. Review of Financial Information — SRE 2410: a material uncertainty about going concern adequately disclosed is met by adding an emphasis of matter paragraph, a continuing uncertainty adequately disclosed by adding a paragraph highlighting the continued material uncertainty, and an inadequately disclosed uncertainty by a qualified or adverse conclusion with specific reference to the material uncertainty

items.scenario: Reviewing a company's interim financial information, you find a material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt on its ability to continue as a going concern. In the first quarter it is adequately disclosed in the interim information. In the second quarter the uncertainty is unchanged and adequately disclosed again, and your report for the first quarter had carried an emphasis of matter paragraph about it. In the third quarter the disclosure has been dropped from the interim information altogether.

items.stem: What does SAE 3400 require for each?

options.text: For the inadequate disclosure, express a qualified or adverse opinion, or withdraw from the engagement as appropriate; for the procedure that could not be applied, consider either withdrawal or a disclaimer of opinion describing the scope limitation in the report
options.why: The standard gives three different answers to three different failures and these are two of them. Where the auditor believes that the presentation and disclosure of the prospective financial information is not adequate — the module's own example being a failure to disclose adequately the consequences of assumptions which are highly sensitive — a qualified or adverse opinion should be expressed, or withdrawal from the engagement made as appropriate. Where the examination is affected by conditions that preclude application of one or more procedures considered necessary in the circumstances, either withdrawal from the engagement or a disclaimer of the opinion describing the scope limitation in the report is considered.

options.text: A qualified opinion for both, each defect being material but capable of being described in the report
options.misconception: answers a scope limitation with a qualified opinion, when the standard's answer to conditions precluding necessary procedures is withdrawal or a disclaimer describing the limitation
options.why: The qualified opinion belongs on the disclosure side. Where conditions preclude the application of procedures the auditor considered necessary, what the standard has him consider is either withdrawal from the engagement or a disclaimer of the opinion describing the scope limitation in the report.

options.text: Neither is answered by an opinion — the report on prospective financial information carries negative assurance about the assumptions, and negative assurance cannot be qualified
options.misconception: forgets that the report also carries an opinion on whether the information is properly prepared on the basis of the assumptions and presented in accordance with the framework
options.why: The report carries both. It states negative assurance as to whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis, and it also expresses an opinion as to whether the prospective financial information is properly prepared on the basis of the assumptions and is presented in accordance with the relevant financial reporting framework — and it is that opinion which is qualified, made adverse or disclaimed.

options.text: An adverse opinion for both, setting out the reasons in the report, or withdrawal
options.misconception: applies the answer given for significant assumptions that do not provide a reasonable basis to a disclosure failure and to a scope limitation, which the standard answers differently
options.why: The adverse opinion is the answer to a third failure: where one or more significant assumptions do not provide a reasonable basis for the prospective financial information. On these facts the assumptions are not unreasonable so far as they could be examined; a disclosure failure calls for a qualified or adverse opinion or withdrawal, and a scope limitation for withdrawal or a disclaimer.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3400: where the presentation and disclosure of the prospective financial information is not adequate a qualified or adverse opinion should be expressed or withdrawal made, and where the examination is affected by conditions that preclude application of one or more necessary procedures either withdrawal or a disclaimer of opinion describing the scope limitation is considered

items.scenario: You are examining a company's five-year forecast. Two problems remain at the end of the work. The forecast turns on an assumption about a single customer's offtake which is highly sensitive, and the consequences of that sensitivity are not adequately disclosed. Separately, the company would not give you the capacity study on which the production assumption rests, so a procedure you considered necessary could not be applied. The assumptions themselves, so far as you could examine them, are not unreasonable.

items.stem: What does SAE 3402 require?

options.text: Test the controls over the year and give the opinion as asked — the written assertion is the service organisation's own document and does not limit what the service auditor may report on
options.misconception: treats the written assertion as background paperwork, when a type 2 report is built on an assertion covering the whole specified period and the service auditor reports on the matters asserted
options.why: The assertion is the second of the three components of the report, and the service auditor's objective is to obtain reasonable assurance about the matters asserted. An opinion on operating effectiveness throughout a period beside an assertion that speaks only as at a date would report on something nobody has asserted.

options.text: The assertion is a type 1 assertion and will not carry a type 2 report — a type 2 report comprises the description of the system, a written assertion with three limbs running throughout the specified period rather than two limbs at a date, being that the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented throughout the period, that the controls were suitably designed throughout the period and that they operated effectively throughout the period, and a service auditor's assurance report conveying reasonable assurance about those matters which also includes a description of the tests of controls and the results thereof
options.why: The three components are the same in both reports and the difference sits inside the second of them. A type 1 report comprises the description of the system, a written assertion that the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented at the specified date and that the controls were suitably designed as at that date, and an assurance report conveying reasonable assurance about those matters. A type 2 report comprises the description, an assertion running throughout the specified period with a third limb that the controls operated effectively throughout it, and an assurance report that conveys reasonable assurance about those matters and includes a description of the tests of controls and the results thereof. The service auditor reports on the matters asserted, so an assertion pinned to a date cannot support an opinion covering a period.
keywords: description of the tests of controls

options.text: The only difference between the two is the description of the tests of controls, which may simply be attached to a type 1 report to make it a type 2
options.misconception: reduces the distinction to an attachment, when a type 1 report speaks as at a specified date on the description and the design and says nothing at all about operating effectiveness
options.why: A type 1 report speaks as at a specified date about the description and the suitability of the design, and it carries a statement that the service auditor has not performed any procedures regarding the operating effectiveness of controls and that therefore no opinion is expressed on it. Attaching test results to it would contradict its own text.

options.text: Both report throughout a period; a type 1 report simply covers fewer of the control objectives than a type 2
options.misconception: makes the difference one of coverage, when it is one of a date against a period and of design against operating effectiveness
options.why: Coverage is not what separates them. A type 1 report is a report on the description and design of controls as at a specified date; a type 2 report is a report on the description, the design and the operating effectiveness of controls throughout a specified period.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3402: the three components of a type 1 and a type 2 report, the type 1 assertion speaking as at the specified date on the fair presentation of the description and the suitable design of controls and the type 2 assertion running throughout the specified period with a third limb on operating effectiveness, the type 2 assurance report also including a description of the tests of controls and the results thereof

items.scenario: A payroll processing service organisation has asked you, as service auditor, for a type 2 report covering the year to 31 March. The written assertion it has drafted says that, based on suitable criteria, the description fairly presents the system as designed and implemented as at 31 March and that the controls related to the stated control objectives were suitably designed as at that date. Its finance head asks you to test the controls over the whole year and to add your opinion on their operating effectiveness, leaving the assertion as it is.

items.stem: Which of the two is an engagement under SAE 3402?

options.text: Neither — the standard applies only when the service organisation is responsible for, or otherwise able to make an assertion about, the suitable design of controls, and it does not deal with engagements to report only on whether controls operated as described, or to report only on controls other than those related to a service likely to be relevant to user entities' internal control as it relates to financial reporting, such as controls affecting production or quality control
options.why: Each request fails a different limb of the standard's own scope. SAE 3402 applies only when the service organisation is responsible for, or otherwise able to make an assertion about, the suitable design of controls, which the bureau says it cannot; and the standard does not deal with assurance engagements to report only on whether controls at a service organisation operated as described, which is exactly what the bureau has asked for. The manufacturer's controls over production scheduling and quality inspection are the standard's own example of controls other than those related to a service likely to be relevant to user entities' internal control as it relates to financial reporting.

options.text: The manufacturer only, since it both designs and operates its own controls and can therefore make the assertion the standard requires
options.misconception: satisfies the design assertion and forgets the second limb, which excludes controls unrelated to user entities' financial reporting
options.why: Being able to assert the design is necessary and not sufficient. The standard does not deal with engagements to report only on controls other than those related to a service that is likely to be relevant to user entities' internal control as it relates to financial reporting, and production and quality control are its own examples of those.

options.text: The bureau only, since a report on whether controls operated as described is a report on operating effectiveness, which is what a type 2 report gives
options.misconception: equates a report only on whether controls operated as described with a type 2 report, when the standard excludes the first by name
options.why: They are not the same and the standard separates them expressly: it does not deal with assurance engagements to report only on whether controls at a service organisation operated as described. A type 2 report reaches operating effectiveness on top of a fairly presented description and a suitable design, all asserted by the service organisation.

options.text: Both — a service organisation is any third party providing services to user entities, and an assurance report on its controls is what the standard exists for
options.misconception: reads the definition of a service organisation as the whole of the standard's scope, when the scope also turns on the design assertion and on the controls being relevant to financial reporting
options.why: A service organisation is one providing services likely to be relevant to user entities' internal control as it relates to financial reporting, and even then the standard applies only where the service organisation is responsible for or able to assert the suitable design of the controls. Both limbs have to hold.

citation.ref: Ch. Prospective Financial Information and Other Assurance Services — SAE 3402: the standard applies only when the service organisation is responsible for, or otherwise able to make an assertion about, the suitable design of controls, and does not deal with assurance engagements to report only on whether controls operated as described or to report only on controls other than those related to a service likely to be relevant to user entities' internal control as it relates to financial reporting

items.scenario: Two requests reach your firm. A contract manufacturer wants an assurance report on the controls it operates over production scheduling and quality inspection for the companies it supplies. A data processing bureau wants a report only on whether the controls it runs operated as described to it by its parent, which designed them; the bureau will make no assertion about whether they were suitably designed.

items.stem: Does the Order apply to this company?

options.text: No — the borrowing test is failed but the company is still exempt, because two of the three money conditions are met and the exemption turns on the majority of them
options.misconception: reads the private company exemption as a test that can be passed on the balance of its conditions, when all of them must hold together
options.why: There is no balance to strike. The Order describes one class of private company, and it is a company that is not a subsidiary or holding company of a public company and has capital and reserves within ₹1 crore and borrowings within ₹1 crore and revenue within ₹10 crore. Fail one and the description no longer fits.

options.text: Yes — the borrowing test is failed. The exemption needs total borrowings not exceeding ₹1 crore from any bank or financial institution at any point of time during the financial year, and ₹1.20 crore was outstanding during the year even though nothing was outstanding on 31 March
options.why: The three money tests are not all measured the same way, and this is the one that differs. Paid up capital and reserves and surplus are tested as on the balance sheet date, and ₹0.85 crore is inside the one crore rupees. Total revenue is tested for the financial year, and ₹8.40 crore is inside the ten crore rupees. But borrowings are tested at any point of time during the financial year, so the ₹1.20 crore drawn between June and November is what decides it, and repaying before the year end does not undo it. The exemption is conjunctive — every condition has to hold — so failing one puts the company inside the Order.
keywords: at any point of time during the financial year
as on the balance sheet date

options.text: No — every figure is below its limit on 31 March: ₹0.85 crore against ₹1 crore, nil borrowings against ₹1 crore, and ₹8.40 crore against ₹10 crore
options.misconception: measures all three tests at the balance sheet date, when the borrowing test is expressly measured at any point of time during the financial year
options.why: Only the first of the three is measured at the balance sheet date. The Order's words on borrowings are "at any point of time during the financial year", which is what catches a limit drawn and cleared inside the year, and the revenue test runs for the whole financial year as well.

options.text: Yes — but only because the total revenue of ₹8.40 crore is measured against a limit of ₹5 crore for a private limited company
options.misconception: uses the ₹5 crore working capital figure from clause 3(ii)(b) as the revenue limit in the applicability test
options.why: Five crore rupees is the working capital limit inside clause 3(ii)(b), which is one of the matters reported on once the Order applies. The revenue limit in the exemption is a total revenue not exceeding ten crore rupees during the financial year, which ₹8.40 crore is inside.

citation.ref: paragraph 1(2)(v) — a private limited company, not being a subsidiary or holding company of a public company, having a paid up capital and reserves and surplus not more than one crore rupees as on the balance sheet date, which does not have total borrowings exceeding one crore rupees from any bank or financial institution at any point of time during the financial year, and which does not have a total revenue exceeding ten crore rupees during the financial year

items.scenario: A private limited company, which is neither a subsidiary nor a holding company of any public company, closes its year on 31 March. Its paid up capital and reserves and surplus stand at ₹0.85 crore on that date. Its total revenue as disclosed in Schedule III, including revenue from discontinuing operations, is ₹8.40 crore. It had no borrowings at all on 31 March, but a cash credit limit of ₹1.20 crore was drawn from a bank between June and November and repaid in full before the year end. The audit manager has left the CARO annexure out of the report on the footing that all three figures are inside the limits at the balance sheet date.

items.stem: To which of the four does the Order apply?

options.text: The third and the fourth. The insurance company and the section 8 company are two of the five exempt classes; a Government company is not an exempt class at all; and the private company loses the exemption because it is a subsidiary of a public company, whatever its figures
options.why: The Order applies to every company including a foreign company and then exempts five classes: a banking company, an insurance company, a company licensed to operate under section 8, a One Person Company and a small company, and a private limited company meeting the stated conditions. An insurance company and a section 8 company are named outright. A Government company is nowhere in that list, so its size is beside the point. And the private company's exemption opens with the words "not being a subsidiary or holding company of a public company", which this one is, so the ₹0.40 crore and the ₹6 crore never come into it.
keywords: not being a subsidiary or holding company of a public company

options.text: The second, the third and the fourth. A section 8 company is a company like any other and the Order exempts only banking and insurance companies among special classes
options.misconception: shortens the exempt list to the two regulated financial classes, dropping the section 8 company, the One Person Company and the small company
options.why: The list has five entries, not two. A company licensed to operate under section 8 of the Companies Act is named in it alongside the banking company and the insurance company, and so are a One Person Company and a small company.

options.text: None of them. A Government company is audited under directions issued by the Comptroller and Auditor General, and where those directions apply the Order does not
options.misconception: treats the C&AG's directions under section 143(5) as displacing the Order, when the two requirements sit on the same report
options.why: Directions under section 143(5) tell the auditor of a Government company how the audit is to be conducted and are reported on in his report; they do not take the company out of the Order. Paragraph 2 says every report made by the auditor under section 143 on a company to which the Order applies shall in addition contain the matters specified.

options.text: The third only. The fourth is inside every money limit — ₹0.40 crore against ₹1 crore, nil borrowings against ₹1 crore and ₹6 crore against ₹10 crore — so it is an exempt private company
options.misconception: applies the three money tests without the condition that opens the exemption, so a subsidiary of a public company is read as exempt on its figures
options.why: The figures are only reached if the company is one the exemption describes, and the description begins by excluding a subsidiary or holding company of a public company. Being inside all three limits does not help a company that fails the words before them.

citation.ref: paragraph 1 — the Order applies to every company including a foreign company as defined in clause (42) of section 2 of the Companies Act, and exempts a banking company, an insurance company, a company licensed to operate under section 8, a One Person Company and a small company, and a private limited company not being a subsidiary or holding company of a public company which meets the stated conditions

items.scenario: A firm signs four audit reports this season. The first is an insurance company. The second is a company licensed to operate under section 8 of the Companies Act. The third is a Government company with revenue of ₹60 crore. The fourth is a private limited company which is the subsidiary of a public company, with paid up capital and reserves and surplus of ₹0.40 crore, no borrowings at any time in the year and total revenue of ₹6 crore. The article clerk proposes to attach the CARO annexure only to the third, on the view that the other three are all small or special enough to be outside it.

items.stem: What does paragraph 2 of the Order settle?

options.text: That the matters go into the report itself — every report made by the auditor under section 143 on the accounts of every company to which the Order applies shall in addition contain the matters specified in paragraphs 3 and 4 — and the Order applies to every company including a foreign company as defined in clause (42) of section 2 of the Companies Act
options.why: Paragraph 2 makes the Order an addition to the report under section 143 rather than a document of its own, so a separate note addressed elsewhere does not discharge it. And the reach of the Order is settled in paragraph 1, which applies it to every company including a foreign company as defined in clause (42) of section 2 of the Companies Act; the five exempt classes are the only way out, and place of incorporation is not one of them.
keywords: an addition to the report under section 143
place of incorporation is not one of them

options.text: That the Order applies only to companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, a foreign company being governed by its own law of incorporation and reporting under Chapter XXII instead
options.misconception: reads the Order as confined to Indian incorporation, when paragraph 1 names a foreign company inside its scope
options.why: Paragraph 1 begins by applying the Order to every company including a foreign company as defined in clause (42) of section 2. That definition is exactly the point of naming it, and it is a narrower set of exclusions than the auditor is imagining.

options.text: That the CARO answers are a separate report, which is why the Order calls them an annexure — they are signed separately and may be addressed to those charged with governance
options.misconception: reads the word annexure as making the Order's answers a distinct report, when paragraph 2 adds them to the report under section 143
options.why: What the answers are physically attached to is a matter of presentation. Paragraph 2 fixes the substance: the report made under section 143 shall in addition contain the matters specified, so they form part of that report and go to the same addressee.

options.text: That the Order applies to the auditor's report on the consolidated financial statements in full, so the same answers are repeated in both reports
options.misconception: drops the exception in paragraph 2, which confines the Order on a consolidated report to clause (xxi)
options.why: Paragraph 2 says the opposite in its second limb: the Order shall not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3. Repeating the whole annexure there reports under clauses that do not apply to that report at all.

citation.ref: paragraph 2 — every report made by the auditor under section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013 on the accounts of every company audited by him to which the Order applies shall in addition contain the matters specified in paragraphs 3 and 4, and the Order shall not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3, read with paragraph 1 on the application of the Order to every company including a foreign company

items.scenario: A company to which the Order applies has an auditor who proposes to issue his CARO answers as a separate document, signed on the same day as the audit report but addressed to the board rather than to the members, on the view that the Order is a management reporting requirement and not part of the opinion. He also proposes to leave the Order out altogether for a foreign company he audits, on the view that an Order made under the Companies Act cannot reach a company incorporated abroad.

items.stem: What should the answer to clause 3(vi) say?

options.text: That the maintenance of cost records has been specified by the Central Government under section 148(1), and that such accounts and records have not been made and maintained — with the basis for that unfavourable answer stated
options.why: The clause asks two questions in order. Whether maintenance of cost records has been specified by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 148, which here it has. And whether such accounts and records have been so made and maintained, which here they have not. Whether a cost audit is required is a different question under the same section, and it is not what this clause states on. Because the answer is unfavourable, paragraph 4(a) requires the report to state the basis for it.
keywords: has been specified by the Central Government
a different question under the same section

options.text: That the company has not maintained cost records, and nothing more — the first limb is background and only the failure needs stating
options.misconception: answers only the second limb, when the clause asks the specification question in its own right and the basis for an unfavourable answer is separately required
options.why: A reader who is told only that records were not maintained does not know whether they were ever required. The clause asks whether maintenance has been specified by the Central Government under section 148(1) as its own question, and paragraph 4(a) then requires the basis for the unfavourable answer that follows.

options.text: Nothing, correctly — the clause is about cost audit, and a company below the turnover threshold for a cost audit answers it as not applicable
options.misconception: reads clause 3(vi) as a question about cost audit, when it asks whether the maintenance of records has been specified and whether they have been maintained
options.why: Section 148 carries two separate powers, one to specify that cost records be kept and one to direct that they be audited, and the clause reaches only the first. A company can be well below any cost audit threshold and still be one for which cost records have been specified.
