options.text: That the company has not maintained cost records, and that the audit opinion on the financial statements is qualified in consequence
options.misconception: turns an unfavourable answer inside the annexure into a modification of the opinion on the financial statements
options.why: The annexure and the opinion answer different questions. Paragraph 4(a) requires the basis for an unfavourable answer to be stated inside the Order; whether the opinion is modified is decided under SA 705 (Revised) on the evidence about the financial statements, and many unfavourable CARO answers sit beside an unmodified opinion.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(vi), read with paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: A manufacturing company to which the Order applies makes a product for which the Central Government has specified the maintenance of cost records under sub-section (1) of section 148 of the Companies Act. The company keeps no cost records at all. It is below the turnover at which a cost audit would have to be conducted, and no cost auditor has been appointed. The audit manager answers clause 3(vi) with the words "not applicable, no cost audit is required".

items.stem: What does clause 3(vi) require here?

options.text: An affirmative answer on both limbs — the maintenance of cost records has been specified and such accounts and records have been so made and maintained — because the clause asks about the records and not about the cost audit
options.why: Clause 3(vi) asks whether maintenance of cost records has been specified by the Central Government under section 148(1) and whether such accounts and records have been so made and maintained. Both are yes on these facts, so the answer is affirmative, and paragraph 4(a) is not engaged because the answer is neither unfavourable nor qualified. The failure to appoint a cost auditor is a non-compliance with a different limb of section 148, and putting it under this clause tells the reader that the records themselves were not kept, which is untrue.

options.text: An affirmative answer on the records, together with a statement under clause 3(vi) that the company has not appointed a cost auditor, since the reader of the annexure would otherwise be left unaware of it
options.misconception: adds material to a clause because a reader might want it, rather than because the clause asks for it
options.why: What a reader might find useful is not the test; the clause's words are. Clause 3(vi) asks two questions and both are about the records. A matter the Order does not ask about is not reported under a clause that asks about something else.

options.text: No answer at all — a clause answered in the affirmative is a clause with nothing to report, and the annexure carries only the exceptions
options.misconception: treats the annexure as exception reporting, when paragraph 3 requires a statement on each specified matter
options.why: Paragraph 3 says the auditor's report shall include a statement on the matters specified. Every clause that applies to the company is answered whichever way the answer falls, and an omitted clause tells the reader nothing about whether the question was asked.

options.text: An unfavourable answer, since section 148 has been contravened and the clause names section 148 in terms
options.misconception: reads the mention of section 148 as bringing everything in that section inside the clause, when the clause names only the specification of cost records under sub-section (1)
options.why: The clause names sub-section (1) of section 148, which is the power to specify that cost records be kept. It does not ask whether every requirement of the section has been met, and a company that has kept exactly the records specified has answered both limbs affirmatively.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(vi), read with paragraph 3 and paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: Another company to which the Order applies is in a business for which the Central Government has specified the maintenance of cost records, and the company maintains them properly and completely. It was also required to have those records audited and has simply not appointed a cost auditor for the year. The audit senior proposes to answer clause 3(vi) by saying that the company has failed to comply with section 148, and to give the details of the missing cost audit in the annexure under that clause.

items.stem: What should the answer to clause 3(viii) say?

options.text: That transactions not recorded in the books of account, of ₹3.60 crore, were surrendered as income during the year in the tax assessments under the Income Tax Act, 1961, and that the previously unrecorded income has not been properly recorded in the books of account during the year — with the basis for that unfavourable answer stated
options.why: The clause has two limbs and a bare "Yes" answers only the first. It asks whether any transactions not recorded in the books of account have been surrendered or disclosed as income during the year in the tax assessments under the Income Tax Act, 1961, and if so, whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books of account during the year. Paying the tax settles the position with the tax authority and does nothing about the books, so the second limb is unfavourable, and paragraph 4(a) then requires the basis for that answer.
keywords: properly recorded in the books of account during the year

options.text: That the company surrendered ₹3.60 crore in a tax assessment during the year, which answers the clause, the treatment in the books being a matter for the accounting standards rather than for the Order
options.misconception: stops at the first limb, treating the recording of the income as outside the clause when the clause asks about it in terms
options.why: The clause asks about the books in its own words: whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books of account during the year. That the accounting standards also have something to say about it does not remove the question from the Order.

options.text: That the company has surrendered ₹3.60 crore of unrecorded transactions and that a fraud of that amount has been noticed, which follows automatically from income being concealed
options.misconception: reads an affirmative answer under clause 3(viii) as itself establishing a fraud, when whether there was a fraud is decided separately
options.why: Clause 3(viii) reports a fact about unrecorded transactions surrendered in tax assessments and does not decide that a fraud occurred. Whether a fraud has been noticed or reported is answered under clause 3(xi), and reporting to the Central Government is governed by section 143(12) with Rule 13; an affirmative answer here can stand with no fraud reported at all.

options.text: Nothing under this clause — an amount surrendered in a tax assessment is a matter for clause 3(vii) on statutory dues, since it arises out of a tax proceeding
options.misconception: routes the answer to the statutory dues clause because tax is involved, when clause 3(vii) is about depositing dues and 3(viii) is about unrecorded transactions
options.why: Clause 3(vii) asks whether the company is regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues and what is unpaid or disputed. Clause 3(viii) asks about transactions that were never in the books and were surrendered or disclosed as income in the tax assessments. They are different questions and this is the second one.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(viii), read with paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: During the year under audit a company surrendered ₹3.60 crore of sales that had never been entered in its books, as income in an assessment under the Income Tax Act, 1961, and paid the tax demanded. Nothing has been passed through the books of account, the management taking the view that the tax has been paid and the matter is closed. The audit manager's draft answers clause 3(viii) with the single word "Yes".

items.stem: What does clause 3(viii) require?

options.text: Only the ₹1.20 crore is inside the clause, and the answer is unfavourable, because the company had not recorded those transactions when they arose
options.misconception: reads the clause as asking whether the transactions were recorded when they occurred, when it asks whether the previously unrecorded income was recorded during the year
options.why: That the transactions were unrecorded is the premise of the clause, not its failing — the clause exists precisely for transactions that were never in the books. What it then asks is whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded during the year, and here it has.

options.text: Both amounts are reported, and the answer is unfavourable, because the ₹90 lakh is not in the books at the date the auditor signs his report
options.misconception: measures the clause at the date of the report instead of at the year, when both its limbs are expressed for the financial year under audit
options.why: The date of the report is not the period the clause covers. It asks about what was surrendered or disclosed during the year and what was recorded in the books during the year, so a surrender made after the year end belongs to the next year's answer.

options.text: Neither amount is reported, since income surrendered in a tax assessment and brought into the books is no longer unrecorded and the clause reaches only amounts still outside the books
options.misconception: confines the clause to unrecorded income that remains unrecorded, which would leave the second limb with nothing to answer
options.why: If the clause reached only amounts still outside the books, its second limb — whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books during the year — could never be answered in the affirmative. The clause asks about the surrender first and the recording second.

options.text: Only the ₹1.20 crore is inside the clause, and its answer is affirmative on both limbs — the transactions were surrendered as income during the year and the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books during the year; the ₹90 lakh surrendered after the year end is not what the clause asks about
options.why: The clause is tied to the year twice over. It asks whether transactions not recorded in the books have been surrendered or disclosed as income during the year in the tax assessments, and then whether the previously unrecorded income has been properly recorded in the books of account during the year. The ₹1.20 crore satisfies both, so the answer is affirmative and paragraph 4(a) is not engaged. The ₹90 lakh was surrendered after the year end, so it is outside the clause for the year under audit.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(viii)

items.scenario: A company has two matters on file at the year end. In an assessment completed in July of the year under audit it surrendered ₹1.20 crore of transactions that had not been in its books, and it passed the entries in the books in the same month, so the income now sits in the accounts. Separately, in May after the year end and before the audit report is signed, it surrendered a further ₹90 lakh in a fresh assessment. The audit senior proposes to report both amounts under clause 3(viii), and to answer the second limb "no" for both because the ₹90 lakh is not in the books.

items.stem: How do the three sub-clauses of clause 3(xii) come out?

options.text: Two are unfavourable — the ratio and the ten per cent — but the interest default is not reported, having been made good before the year end
options.misconception: reads the default sub-clause as reporting only defaults still outstanding, when it asks about a default for any period
options.why: The sub-clause asks whether there has been any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof for any period. A default paid three months late is a default for a period, and the clause asks for the details of it.

options.text: None is unfavourable — the ratio of 1:20 permits deposits of twenty times Net Owned Funds, being ₹100 crore, and ₹110 crore is within the ten per cent tolerance the Nidhi Rules allow
options.misconception: turns the ten per cent unencumbered term deposit requirement into a tolerance on the deposit ratio
options.why: The ten per cent is a separate requirement about maintaining unencumbered term deposits to meet the liability; it is not a margin on the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio. The ratio allows ₹100 crore against ₹5 crore of Net Owned Funds, and ₹110 crore is outside it.

options.text: One is unfavourable — the ratio of 1:20 means Net Owned Funds must be at least one twentieth of deposits, so ₹5 crore against ₹110 crore fails; the ten per cent and the interest are matters for the Nidhi Rules and not for the Order
options.misconception: keeps the ratio and drops the other two sub-clauses, when all three are inside clause 3(xii)
options.why: Clause 3(xii) has three sub-clauses of its own, and the second names the ten per cent unencumbered term deposits specified in the Nidhi Rules, 2014 while the third names any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment. That the Nidhi Rules are their source is why the clause cites them.

options.text: All three are unfavourable — deposits of ₹110 crore against Net Owned Funds of ₹5 crore exceed the ratio of 1:20, which allows ₹100 crore; unencumbered term deposits of 6 per cent fall short of the ten per cent required; and there was a default in payment of interest on deposits, which is reported for any period even though it has since been paid
options.why: Sub-clause (a) asks whether the Nidhi has complied with the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio of 1:20, so twenty times ₹5 crore is ₹100 crore and ₹110 crore breaches it. Sub-clause (b) asks whether it is maintaining ten per cent unencumbered term deposits as specified in the Nidhi Rules, 2014, and 6 per cent is not. Sub-clause (c) asks whether there has been any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof for any period and, if so, for the details — the words "for any period" catch a default that has since been made good. Each is answered separately, and each unfavourable answer carries paragraph 4(a) with it.
keywords: ten per cent unencumbered term deposits

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xii)(a), (b) and (c), read with paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: A Nidhi company to which the Order applies has Net Owned Funds of ₹5 crore and deposits of ₹110 crore at the year end. Its unencumbered term deposits stand at 6 per cent, against the ten per cent the Nidhi Rules, 2014 require it to maintain. Interest on a group of deposits fell due in November and was paid in January, three months late. The audit manager proposes to answer clause 3(xii) with "the company is a Nidhi and has complied with the applicable requirements".

items.stem: What does clause 3(xii) require?

options.text: The first two sub-clauses are answered affirmatively, and the third is answered with the details of the default — the clause asks whether there has been any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof for any period and, if so, for the details, without any threshold of amount or number
options.why: Each sub-clause is answered on its own facts, so two affirmative answers and one unfavourable answer is a perfectly ordinary shape for this clause. The third sub-clause asks whether there has been any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof for any period, and if so for the details. It sets no threshold of amount or number and does not ask whether a loss was caused, so a single late repayment is reported with its details, and paragraph 4(a) then requires the basis for that answer.
keywords: no threshold of amount or number

options.text: All three are answered affirmatively, with a note that the auditor has applied a materiality threshold to the third sub-clause because a single depositor is immaterial to the financial statements as a whole
options.misconception: imports a financial statement materiality threshold into a clause that asks for the details of any default
options.why: Materiality for the financial statements decides what affects the opinion, not what the Order asks to be stated. The sub-clause asks about any default for any period and calls for the details, and an answer that filters it by materiality answers a different question.

options.text: All three are answered affirmatively — a repayment made a month late and before the year end is not a default, the deposit having been honoured in full
options.misconception: reads a default as failure to pay at all, when the sub-clause reaches a default in repayment for any period
options.why: The sub-clause is about timing as well as amount: a default in repayment for any period is what it names. A maturity paid a month after it fell due is a default for that month, whether or not the money was eventually paid in full.

options.text: The clause is answered affirmatively and the late repayment is reported instead under clause 3(v) on deposits, which is where a company's dealings with its depositors belong
options.misconception: moves a matter clause 3(xii) names expressly into the general deposits clause
options.why: Clause 3(xii) is the clause written for a Nidhi company, and its third sub-clause names a default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof in terms. A matter a clause asks about is answered under that clause.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xii)(c), read with paragraph 3(xii)(a) and (b) and paragraph 4(a)

items.scenario: A Nidhi company complies with the Net Owned Funds to Deposits ratio and maintains unencumbered term deposits well above the ten per cent required. One depositor's maturity amount, due in August, was repaid in September after the depositor complained. The audit senior proposes to answer clause 3(xii) affirmatively and to say nothing about the late repayment, on the view that one depositor out of thousands is not material and no loss was caused.

items.stem: Which set is Rule 11?

options.text: The whole of CARO 2020, since Rule 11 is the rule under which the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order is made
options.misconception: attributes the Order to Rule 11, when the Order is made by the Central Government under section 143(11)
options.why: The Order is issued by the Central Government in exercise of the powers conferred by section 143(11), after consultation with the National Financial Reporting Authority. Rule 11 sits under section 143(3)(j) and prescribes its own six matters.

options.text: The pending litigations, the provision for foreseeable losses on long term contracts and the delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund — the three the Rule originally carried, the later additions being recommendatory
options.misconception: stops at the Rule's three original matters and treats the funding chain, the dividend and the audit trail as optional
options.why: The Rule as it stands carries six matters, and the auditor's report shall include his views and comments on all of them. Nothing in it makes the representations on Intermediaries and Funding Parties, the compliance of the dividend with section 123 or the audit trail recommendatory.

options.text: The adequacy of internal financial controls and their operating effectiveness; whether any director is disqualified under section 164(2); and whether the financial statements comply with the accounting standards
options.misconception: lists three of the statements section 143(3) itself requires as though Rule 11 prescribed them
options.why: All three are in section 143(3) in their own clauses — internal financial controls in clause (i), the disqualification of a director in clause (g) and compliance with the accounting standards in clause (e). Rule 11 is what clause (j) reaches, and it prescribes a different six matters.

options.text: The impact of pending litigations on the financial position; provision for material foreseeable losses on long term contracts including derivative contracts; delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund; the representations on funds advanced to Intermediaries and received from Funding Parties with the auditor's own statement on them; compliance of the dividend with section 123; and the accounting software's audit trail
options.why: Those six are what Rule 11 prescribes under clause (j) of section 143(3), which is the clause allowing other matters to be prescribed: the pending litigations, the provision for material foreseeable losses on long term contracts including derivative contracts, any delay in transferring amounts to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, the funding chain, the dividend under section 123, and the accounting software's audit trail. The internal financial controls statement the senior has already written is clause (i) of section 143(3) itself and not a Rule 11 matter, and CARO comes from section 143(11) and the Order made under it, so neither belongs in this list.

citation.ref: Rule 11, prescribing the other matters to be included in the auditor's report under clause (j) of sub-section (3) of section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: An audit senior is drafting the "Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements" section for an unlisted public company. He has written paragraphs on the company's compliance with CARO 2020 and on the adequacy of internal financial controls, and asks which further matters Rule 11 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 puts into the report.

items.stem: Is that enough under Rule 11?

options.text: No — the representations must also be given by the Ultimate Beneficiaries and the Funding Parties themselves, since they are the persons with knowledge of the understanding
options.misconception: extends the representation requirement to third parties, when the Rule asks about the management of the company under audit
options.why: The Rule speaks of what the management has represented to the best of its knowledge and belief, other than as disclosed in the notes to the accounts. Nothing in it asks the auditor to obtain anything from an Intermediary, a Funding Party or an Ultimate Beneficiary.

options.text: Yes — the Rule asks whether the management has represented, and once the written representations are on file and reproduced, the requirement is discharged
options.misconception: reads the funding chain as two questions about management's representations, dropping the auditor's own sub-limb
options.why: Two of the three sub-limbs are about management's representations and the third is about the auditor. Leaving it out reports what the company said and nothing about whether the auditor did any work on it.

options.text: No — the Rule has a third sub-limb, under which the auditor states whether, based on such audit procedures as he has considered reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances, anything has come to his notice that has caused him to believe that the two representations contain any material mis-statement
options.why: The funding chain in Rule 11 is written in three parts, and only the first two are about what management has represented — that no funds were advanced or loaned or invested in Intermediaries with the understanding that they would lend or invest in Ultimate Beneficiaries, and that no funds were received from Funding Parties with the understanding that the company would do the same. The third is the auditor's own, and it is what makes the requirement more than a transcription: based on such audit procedures as the auditor has considered reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances, nothing has come to his notice causing him to believe that those representations contain any material mis-statement.
keywords: reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances

options.text: No — the auditor must certify that no funds were in fact advanced to any Ultimate Beneficiary through an Intermediary during the year
options.misconception: turns a statement that nothing has come to the auditor's notice into a positive certificate about the facts
options.why: The Rule does not ask for a certificate. It asks whether, based on procedures the auditor considered reasonable and appropriate, anything has come to his notice causing him to believe the representations contain a material mis-statement, which is a different and narrower statement than certifying what happened.

citation.ref: Rule 11(4)(i), (ii) and (iii) — the representation on funds advanced to Intermediaries, the representation on funds received from Funding Parties, and the auditor's statement that, based on such audit procedures as he has considered reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances, nothing has come to his notice causing him to believe that those representations contain any material mis-statement

items.scenario: A company has advanced funds during the year to two intermediary entities, one of them a foreign entity, and has received funds from a third. Management has given the auditor written representations in the terms Rule 11 requires. The audit manager proposes to reproduce those two representations in the report and stop there, saying that the Rule asks whether management has represented and management has represented.

items.stem: How does the Companies Act answer the three?

options.text: A penalty of twenty-five lakh rupees for a listed company and five lakh rupees for any other company; the provisions bind the statutory auditor alone; and confidentiality is preserved only where the fraud is ultimately established
options.misconception: raises both penalties, confines the duty to the statutory auditor and makes the good faith protection depend on the fraud being proved
options.why: The figures are five lakh rupees for a listed company and one lakh rupees for any other company. The duty reaches a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor as well. And section 143(13) protects reporting done in good faith, which is a test about the reporter's state of mind rather than about how the matter turns out.

options.text: No penalty at all where the fraud is below the prescribed amount and was reported to the audit committee; the reach to other auditors is a matter of professional guidance; and confidentiality is displaced only by an order of a court
options.misconception: reads the penalty as attaching only to the Central Government route and treats the extension to other auditors as guidance rather than statute
options.why: The penalty attaches to non-compliance with section 143(12), which covers the reporting of a fraud below the prescribed amount to the audit committee or the Board as much as the reporting of a larger one to the Central Government. The extension to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor is in the Act itself, and the protection in section 143(13) needs no court order.

options.text: A penalty of one lakh rupees whatever the company, the amount being fixed by the section rather than by the class of company; the provisions reach a cost auditor but not a secretarial auditor; and the good faith protection is a defence the auditor must plead
options.misconception: flattens a two-tier penalty into one figure and drops the secretarial auditor from a provision that names both
options.why: The penalty is two-tier and the tier is set by the class of company: five lakh rupees for a listed company, one lakh rupees for any other. And the provision names a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor together, by reference to section 148 and section 204.

options.text: A penalty of five lakh rupees in the case of a listed company and one lakh rupees in the case of any other company; the fraud reporting provisions apply mutatis mutandis to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor performing their duties under sections 148 and 204; and under section 143(13) no duty to which the auditor is subject is regarded as contravened by reason of his reporting the matter if it is done in good faith
options.why: The three answers are in three separate places and each is stated in terms. An auditor, cost accountant or company secretary in practice who does not comply with section 143(12) is liable to a penalty of five lakh rupees in the case of a listed company and a penalty of one lakh rupees in the case of any other company. The provisions regarding fraud reporting apply mutatis mutandis to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor during the performance of their duties under section 148 and section 204 respectively. And section 143(13) safeguards the act of reporting: no duty to which an auditor of a company may be subject shall be regarded as having been contravened by reason of his reporting the matter if it is done in good faith.

citation.ref: Section 143(12) with Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, read with the application of the fraud reporting provisions mutatis mutandis to a cost auditor and a secretarial auditor under sections 148 and 204, the penalty of five lakh rupees in the case of a listed company and one lakh rupees in the case of any other company, and section 143(13) on reporting done in good faith

items.scenario: Three questions come up at a firm's training session. The statutory auditor of a listed company failed to report a fraud of ₹2 crore in the manner section 143(12) and Rule 13 require, and somebody asks what he is liable to. The cost auditor of an unlisted company found a fraud during his work under section 148 and believes the fraud reporting provisions are for statutory auditors only. And a third asks whether an auditor who reports a suspected fraud that later proves to be nothing has broken his duty of confidentiality to the client.

items.stem: What must the report state?

options.text: Both are problems — section 197(16) requires a statement in the report under section 143 as to whether the remuneration paid by the company to its directors is in accordance with the provisions of that section and whether any director's remuneration exceeds the limit laid down, which for auditors of public companies goes under "Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements"; and section 143(4) requires the reasons to be stated where any matter required to be included in the report is answered in the negative or with a qualification
options.why: Section 197(16) was inserted by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017 and requires the auditor to make a statement as to whether the remuneration paid by the company to its directors is in accordance with the provisions of that section, whether remuneration paid to any director is in excess of the limit laid down under it, and such other details as may be prescribed; ICAI's advisory places that statement, for auditors of public companies, under the section headed "Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements". And section 143(4) is general: where any of the matters required to be included in the audit report is answered in the negative or with a qualification, the report shall state the reasons for it, so a bare negative on the branch returns is half an answer.
keywords: Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements
answered in the negative or with a qualification

options.text: Only the remuneration is a problem — reasons under section 143(4) are required only where the audit opinion itself is modified, and this negative answer sits outside the opinion
options.misconception: attaches section 143(4) to a modified opinion, when it attaches to any matter required to be included in the report being answered in the negative or with a qualification
options.why: Section 143(4) is written about the matters required to be included in the audit report, not about the opinion. A negative answer on the branch returns is one of those matters, so the reasons are stated whether or not the opinion is modified.

options.text: Neither is a problem — remuneration is a matter for the company's own disclosures under section 197, and a negative answer under section 143(3) speaks for itself
options.misconception: leaves the remuneration statement to the company and treats a negative answer as needing no reasons
options.why: Section 197(16) puts the statement on the auditor and puts it in his report under section 143. And section 143(4) requires the reasons wherever a matter required to be in the report is answered in the negative or with a qualification, which is exactly what has happened on the branch returns.

options.text: Only the negative answer is a problem — the remuneration statement is required of auditors of listed companies alone, this being a governance disclosure
options.misconception: confines the section 197(16) statement to listed companies, when the advisory addresses auditors of public companies
options.why: Section 197(16) speaks of the auditor of the company, and ICAI's advisory addresses the placement of the statement for auditors of public companies. Nothing confines it to a listed company.

citation.ref: Section 197(16), requiring the auditor to state in his report under section 143 whether the remuneration paid by the company to its directors is in accordance with that section and whether any director's remuneration is in excess of the limit laid down, read with section 143(4) requiring the reasons where any matter required to be included in the audit report is answered in the negative or with a qualification

items.scenario: A public company's draft audit report says nothing at all about the remuneration paid to its directors. Separately, one of the statements required under section 143(3) is answered in the negative — proper returns adequate for the purposes of the audit were not received from two branches not visited by the auditor — and the draft records the negative answer without saying anything more. The engagement partner is asked whether either is a problem.

items.stem: How is the COSO framework actually built?

options.text: Seventeen principles across five components — control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring — each of which must be present and functioning for internal control to be effective, and three categories of objectives: operations, reporting and compliance
options.why: The framework, introduced in 1992, articulates seventeen principles representing the fundamental concepts associated with its five components, and the requirement is strict: the principles are relevant to every entity and must be present and functioning for a system of internal control to be effective. Its objectives are in three categories, and reporting is only one of them — operations objectives relate to the effectiveness and efficiency of operations including safeguarding assets against loss, reporting objectives to internal and external financial and non-financial reporting, and compliance objectives to compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

options.text: Five components and seventeen principles, but the controller is right about the scope — the framework is confined to internal control over financial reporting, which is why Sarbanes-Oxley section 404 was built on it
options.misconception: keeps the structure and narrows the objectives to financial reporting, dropping the operations and compliance categories
options.why: The framework lists three categories of objectives and reporting is one of them. That section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act is about internal control over financial reporting says something about that statute, not about the breadth of the framework.

options.text: Twenty criteria in four areas — purpose, commitment, capability, and monitoring and learning — with three categories of objectives
options.misconception: gives the CoCo framework's structure under the COSO name
options.why: Twenty criteria in those four areas is the Criteria of Control framework developed by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. COSO is seventeen principles across five components.

options.text: Thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives, in four domains
options.misconception: gives COBIT's structure under the COSO name
options.why: Thirty-four high-level processes and two hundred and ten control objectives in four domains is COBIT, created by ISACA for IT governance and management. It is an IT framework rather than a general internal control framework.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework: seventeen principles across the five components of control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication and monitoring, all of which must be present and functioning, and the three categories of operations, reporting and compliance objectives

items.scenario: A group's head office in India is being asked by its overseas parent to map its internal control documentation to the COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework. The finance controller tells the audit team that the framework is built on four components and about thirty principles, and that it deals with financial reporting objectives alone, so the group's operational and compliance controls fall outside the mapping.

items.stem: How many criteria or objectives does each carry, and in how many areas or domains?

options.text: CoCo — twenty criteria in four areas; COBIT — thirty-four control objectives in two hundred and ten processes across four domains
options.misconception: swaps COBIT's processes and control objectives, so the smaller number becomes the larger
options.why: It is thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives, not the other way about. A framework with two hundred and ten processes carrying thirty-four objectives between them would have more processes than things to control.

options.text: CoCo — twenty criteria in four areas, being purpose, commitment, capability, and monitoring and learning; COBIT — thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives in four domains, being planning and organisation, acquisition and implementation, delivery and support, and monitoring and evaluation
options.why: The Criteria of Control framework includes twenty criteria for effective control in four areas of an organisation: purpose or direction, commitment or identity and values, capability or competence, and monitoring and learning or evolution, and each criterion is examined to identify the controls in place to address it. COBIT has thirty-four high-level processes that cover two hundred and ten control objectives categorised in four domains: planning and organisation, acquisition and implementation, delivery and support, and monitoring and evaluation.
keywords: twenty criteria for effective control in four areas
two hundred and ten control objectives

options.text: CoCo — seventeen criteria in five areas; COBIT — twenty processes covering thirty-four control objectives in four domains
options.misconception: carries COSO's seventeen and five onto CoCo and inverts COBIT's two counts
options.why: Seventeen principles across five components belongs to COSO. CoCo is twenty criteria in four areas, and COBIT's thirty-four is the number of high-level processes while two hundred and ten is the number of control objectives they cover.

options.text: CoCo — twenty criteria in four areas; COBIT — four high-level processes covering thirty-four control objectives in two hundred and ten activities
options.misconception: gets CoCo right and then reads COBIT's three numbers in the wrong order
options.why: The order of COBIT's numbers is the point of them: thirty-four high-level processes, two hundred and ten control objectives that those processes cover, and four domains they are categorised in.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the Criteria of Control framework of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants with twenty criteria in the four areas of purpose, commitment, capability and monitoring and learning, and COBIT with thirty-four high-level processes covering two hundred and ten control objectives in four domains

items.scenario: Two frameworks come up in the same meeting. One was developed by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants to improve organisational performance and decision making with better controls, risk management and corporate governance, and stresses that control involves the whole organisation but begins at the level of the individual employee. The other was created by ISACA for IT governance and management, and guides an organisation on how to use its applications, information, infrastructure and people.

items.stem: What do the two frameworks actually say?

options.text: The Turnbull Report is right as the adviser puts it, and section 404 requires the auditors to opine on internal control alone, the opinion on the financial statements being given separately under the auditing standards rather than as part of the same audit
options.misconception: splits the two section 404 opinions into separate engagements, when they are given as part of a single integrated audit
options.why: The two opinions are described as part of a single integrated audit of the company — an independent opinion on the effectiveness of the system of internal control over financial reporting, and the traditional opinion on the financial statements.

options.text: The Turnbull Report requires the review only from companies with no internal audit function, as the adviser says, but under section 404 the auditors do give two opinions
options.misconception: keeps the inversion of the Turnbull principle while correcting the Sarbanes-Oxley one
options.why: The two are separate principles in the guidance. The directors of a company should at least annually review the effectiveness of the system of internal control; a company without an internal audit function should from time to time review the need for one. The second does not qualify the first.

options.text: The Turnbull Report says the directors should at least annually review the effectiveness of the group's system of internal control, covering financial, operational and compliance controls and risk management, and report to shareholders that they have done so — and a company without an internal audit function should from time to time review the need for one; under section 404 the external auditors provide two opinions as part of a single integrated audit, one on the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting and the traditional one on the financial statements
options.why: Both halves of the adviser's account are inverted. The annual review of effectiveness is a duty of the directors of every company under the guidance, and the review should cover all controls including financial, operational and compliance controls and risk management; the internal audit function comes in separately, as the point that a company which does not have one should from time to time review the need for one. And under the SEC rules and the PCAOB standard, management performs its own formal assessment and includes it in the annual report, while the external auditors provide two opinions as part of a single integrated audit of the company.

options.text: Both frameworks leave the review of effectiveness to management, the board's role being confined to receiving the report, and neither requires anything to be said to shareholders
options.misconception: moves the review off the board in both frameworks and drops the report to shareholders that Turnbull requires
options.why: The Turnbull principles put the review on the directors and require them to report to shareholders that they have conducted it. Under section 404 it is management that performs the formal assessment and includes it in the annual report, which is itself a report to shareholders.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the Turnbull Report's key principles, including the annual review of the effectiveness of the system of internal control covering financial, operational and compliance controls and risk management and the report to shareholders, and Sarbanes-Oxley section 404 with management's assessment of internal control over financial reporting and the two opinions given by the external auditors in a single integrated audit

items.scenario: A board is told two things by its adviser. First, that under the guidance the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales issued on the Combined Code, the directors need review the effectiveness of the system of internal control only where the company has no internal audit function, and that the review is confined to financial controls. Second, that under section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act the external auditor gives a single opinion covering the financial statements, management's assessment of internal control being enough on its own.

items.stem: What separates an internal control questionnaire from a check list?

options.text: The questionnaire is answered by the auditor and the check list by the client, the client being the one who knows whether a control was performed
options.misconception: reverses who answers each document
options.why: It is the other way round. The questionnaire is intended to be filled in by the company executives who are in charge of the various areas, and the check list is a set of instructions or points for the auditor or his own staff.

options.text: Three things — the questionnaire carries a large number of detailed questions while the check list generally contains questions relating to the main control objective within the area under review; the questionnaire is usually answered by company executives while the check list is answered by the auditor or his staff; and a "No" in a questionnaire indicates a weakness but not its significance, whereas the check list calls for a specific statement where an apparent weakness may prove to be material in relation to the accounts as a whole
options.why: The two documents are built for different hands and different purposes, and the module draws the distinction in three parts. Volume and level: the questionnaire is detailed while the check list works at the level of the main control objective. Who answers: company executives in charge of the various areas fill the questionnaire, while the check list is for the auditor or his staff to follow, initial or answer. And what a negative answer carries: a "No" in a questionnaire flags a weakness without saying how much it matters, and the check list requires a specific statement where an apparent weakness may prove to be material in relation to the accounts as a whole.

options.text: The questionnaire evaluates the design of controls and the check list tests their operating effectiveness, so the second replaces tests of control
options.misconception: turns two recording and evaluation techniques into the audit procedures themselves
options.why: Both are techniques for evaluating and recording the system of internal control. Neither is a substitute for the tests of control through which the auditor obtains evidence about whether the controls operated effectively.

options.text: Nothing of substance — a check list in question form is a questionnaire, and the two are interchangeable so long as the same ground is covered
options.misconception: reads the similarity in form as an identity of purpose, when who answers and what a negative answer requires differ
options.why: A check list in question form does look like a questionnaire, which is why the distinction is drawn on other ground: who answers it, how detailed it is, and whether a negative answer must be followed by a specific statement about materiality.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the basic distinctions between an internal control questionnaire and a check list: the number and level of the questions, whether the company's executives or the auditor's staff answer them, and the specific statement a check list requires where an apparent weakness may prove to be material

items.scenario: An audit manager has sent the client's purchase department head a long list of detailed questions about the purchase cycle, to be answered Yes, No or Not applicable, and has separately given his own audit staff a shorter set of points to work through and initial as they test the same cycle. A trainee says the two documents are the same thing under different names.

items.stem: What is wrong with the firm's practice?

options.text: Only the questionnaire — a review conducted after the audit programme is settled is better evidence, because the team then knows what the substantive work found
options.misconception: values the review for what it confirms at the end, when its purpose is to decide the nature, timing and extent of the work in the first place
options.why: The review exists to let the auditor form an opinion on the reliance he may place on the system and to locate the areas of weakness so that the audit programme and the nature, timing and extent of procedures can be adjusted. A review after the programme is settled cannot do either.

options.text: Only the timing — the questionnaire practice is sound, but the review must be completed before the audit programme is finalised in every case without exception
options.misconception: gets the timing right and makes it absolute, dropping the exception for small operations
options.why: The review is ordinarily a distinct phase before finalisation of the audit programme, and there is a stated exception: where the size of operations is rather small it can be undertaken in conjunction with other audit procedures and the programme adjusted afterwards.

options.text: Two things — in a continuing engagement it is good practice to issue a questionnaire irrespective of any change every third year, and a comprehensive review must be made at an interval of about three years where the auditor relies on his continuing knowledge; and the review of internal control should ordinarily be undertaken as a distinct phase before finalisation of the audit programme, the exception being where the size of operations is rather small
options.why: For the first year of an engagement a questionnaire is necessary, and for later years the auditor may ask the client to confirm whether the system has changed — but it is good practice in a continuing engagement to issue one every third year even where nothing has changed, which alerts the client to unnoticed changes and makes it more control-conscious. Separately, where the auditor relies on his continuing relationship and reviews only the changes in the intervening period, a comprehensive review in such cases must be made at an interval of about three years. And the review is ordinarily a distinct phase of the audit before finalisation of the audit programme, because its purpose is to shape the programme; only where the size of operations is rather small can it be undertaken in conjunction with other audit procedures.
keywords: an interval of about three years
before finalisation of the audit programme

options.text: Nothing — a questionnaire is required in the first year alone, and where the client confirms each year that nothing has changed the auditor has all the evidence about the system that he needs
options.misconception: treats the first-year questionnaire as the only one ever required, when a continuing engagement issues one every third year and comprehensively reviews the system at about that interval
options.why: The annual confirmation is the ordinary course, not the whole of it. A questionnaire every third year regardless of change, and a comprehensive review at an interval of about three years, exist precisely to catch the unnoticed and unspectacular changes a confirmation would not report.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the issue of an internal control questionnaire in the first year of an engagement and every third year in a continuing engagement, the comprehensive review of the system at an interval of about three years, and the review as a distinct phase of the audit before finalisation of the audit programme except where the size of operations is small

items.scenario: A firm has audited the same client for nine years. It issued an internal control questionnaire in the first year and has never issued one since, taking a written confirmation each year that the control system has not changed. It also reviews the internal controls at the end of the audit, after the audit programme has been settled, because that is when the team has most information. The client's operations are large and complex.

items.stem: What does an internal check system mean, and what does its effectiveness depend on?

options.text: It is the annual examination of the books by an independent person, and its effectiveness depends on the scope the management gives that person
options.misconception: describes internal audit, an independent appraisal function established within the organisation, rather than internal check
options.why: An independent appraisal function established within the organisation to examine and evaluate its activities, whose scope is determined by management, is internal audit. Internal check is not a separate examination at all — it is built into how the work is allocated and operates continuously as part of the routine.

options.text: It is the segregation of duties alone, and it is effective wherever two or more people are involved in a transaction, whatever their roles
options.misconception: reduces internal check to a headcount, dropping the requirement that one person's work be proved independently or made complementary to another's
options.why: Two people who each complete unrelated halves of a job prove nothing about each other's work. The system requires that the work of each person is either proved independently or made complementary to the work of another, which is a statement about how the duties relate rather than how many hands there are.

options.text: It is the arrangement of book-keeping and staff duties so that no one person can carry through a transaction and record every aspect of it, with the work of each person either proved independently or made complementary to another's — and its effectiveness depends on clarity of responsibility, division of work, standardisation and appraisal
options.why: Internal check is a built-in device in the organisation and job-allocation side of control, providing checks on day-to-day transactions which operate continuously as part of the routine. The point of arranging the work that way is that no one person can carry through a transaction and record every aspect of it, and the one man here does the opposite: he takes a transaction from invoice to bank reconciliation with no part of his work proved by anybody else. Its effectiveness rests on four things — clarity of responsibility, so that each person's responsibility is properly identified; division of work, segregated so that the flow is not interrupted and one person's work is complementary to another's, with rotation through the components of the job; standardisation of the accounting process by suitable policies; and appraisal, a periodic review of the chain of operations and workflow.
keywords: no one person can carry through a transaction

options.text: It is the set of controls the statutory auditor tests, and the proprietor is right that the statutory audit supplies the check where the company is too small to divide the work
options.misconception: treats the statutory audit as a substitute for internal check, when the scope of a statutory audit is limited by time and cost
options.why: The scope of a statutory audit is limited by both time and cost, which is why the existence of a system of internal check is increasingly recognised as essential for an audit to be effective, especially in a large organisation. The audit relies on internal check; it does not replace it.

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the internal check system as the arrangement of book-keeping and staff duties so that no one person can carry through a transaction and record every aspect of it, and the four considerations its effectiveness depends on: clarity of responsibility, division of work, standardisation and appraisal

items.scenario: A growing company has one accounts assistant who raises the sales invoice, posts it to the customer ledger, receives the cheque, banks it and prepares the bank reconciliation. The proprietor says this is efficient, that the man has been with him for years, and that the annual statutory audit is the check on him.

items.stem: Which of the general conditions of an internal check system are being broken?

options.text: None — a small company cannot divide duties as a large one can, and the conditions apply only where the organisation is large enough to permit an extensive division of responsibilities
options.misconception: reads an assumption behind the standard questionnaire as a limit on the conditions of internal check
options.why: That organisations permit an extensive division of duties and responsibilities is one of the basic assumptions behind a standardised internal control questionnaire, and it says that the larger the organisation the greater the scope for division. It is not a licence to drop compulsory leave, the separation of custody from the records, or a periodic review of delegated powers.

options.text: Two — the leave and the custody of the securities. The inventory count and the delegation of powers are matters of operational convenience for management rather than conditions of internal check
options.misconception: treats the count and the delegation as management's convenience, when both are named among the general conditions
options.why: Both are named. The conditions say that for inventory taking at the close of the year trading should if possible be suspended and the count done by staff belonging to several sections, and that financial and administrative powers should be distributed judiciously with the manner of their exercise reviewed periodically.

options.text: One — only the custody of the securities, since the other three are recommendations of good practice and carry no control significance
options.misconception: keeps the one condition with an obvious asset at the end of it and dismisses the rest
options.why: The general conditions are a single list and each entry is there for a reason. Uninterrupted leave, a custodian counting his own stores, and a delegation nobody has revisited in six years are each the kind of arrangement under which a loss goes unnoticed for years.

options.text: Four — every member of the staff should be encouraged to go on leave at least once a year; persons having physical custody of assets must not be permitted to have access to the books of account; for inventory taking at the close of the year trading activities should if possible be suspended and the count done by staff belonging to several sections of the organisation; and financial and administrative powers should be distributed judiciously among different officers with the manner of their exercise reviewed periodically
options.why: Each of the three arrangements breaks a stated condition, and the inventory count breaks two. Compulsory leave exists so that a concealment which needs daily attention comes apart while its author is away. Custody of assets and access to the records of those assets are separated so that the man who can take a thing cannot also adjust the record of it. The count is done with trading suspended if possible and by staff from several sections rather than by the custodian himself. And delegated financial and administrative powers are reviewed periodically rather than settled once.
keywords: Custody of assets and access to the records

citation.ref: Ch. Materiality, Risk Assessment and Internal Control — the general conditions of an internal check system, including that no single person should have complete control over any important aspect of the business, that staff duties should be rotated, that every member of staff should be encouraged to take leave at least once a year, that persons having physical custody of assets must not have access to the books of account, that trading should if possible be suspended for the year-end inventory count which is done by staff of several sections, and that financial and administrative powers should be distributed judiciously and their exercise reviewed periodically

items.scenario: A company is writing down its internal check arrangements. Its cashier has taken no leave in four years and keeps the securities in the safe as well as the register recording them. The annual inventory count is done by the storekeeper who has custody of the stores, with trading continuing through the count so that despatches are not delayed. Financial powers were delegated to the branch heads six years ago and have not been looked at since.

items.stem: What is compliance audit concerned with?

options.text: Regularity alone — propriety belongs to propriety audit, which is a separate exercise the C&AG conducts under its own name
options.misconception: puts propriety wholly outside compliance auditing, when compliance auditing is concerned with it as one of its two limbs
options.why: Propriety audit is indeed a named exercise of its own, and that does not take propriety out of compliance auditing. Compliance auditing is concerned with regularity and with propriety, and the public sector context is why the second is equally pertinent.

options.text: Regularity and propriety both — regularity being the adherence of the subject matter to the formal criteria emanating from relevant laws, regulations and agreements, and propriety being the observance of the general principles governing sound financial management and the ethical conduct of public officials; regularity is emphasised, but propriety is equally pertinent in the public sector
options.why: Compliance auditing has two concerns and the team leader has stopped at the first. Regularity is adherence to the formal criteria emanating from the relevant laws, regulations and agreements applicable to the entity, and every purchase here satisfies it. Propriety is the observance of the general principles governing sound financial management and the ethical conduct of public officials, and the module says in terms that while regularity is emphasised in compliance auditing, propriety is equally pertinent in the public sector context, where there are certain expectations concerning financial management and the conduct of officials. Equipment lying unused for two years is what a propriety concern looks like.

options.text: The economy, efficiency and effectiveness of the department's purchasing, which is what makes a stored asset reportable
options.misconception: reaches the right finding through performance audit's three questions, when the finding here comes from compliance auditing's own propriety limb
options.why: Economy, efficiency and effectiveness are the issues a performance audit addresses. A compliance audit reaches this finding through its own propriety limb — and when compliance auditing is conducted in combination with performance auditing, compliance is seen as one of the aspects of those three rather than the other way round.

options.text: Whether the financial statements of the department are free from material misstatement, which is what "in all material respects" means in the definition
options.misconception: reads compliance auditing as a financial audit because its definition uses the words in all material respects
options.why: The words describe the threshold, not the subject matter. Compliance audit assesses whether activities, financial transactions and information comply in all material respects with the regulatory and other rules which govern the audited entity; an opinion on financial statements is what financial audit is for.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — compliance audit as the independent assessment of whether a given subject matter is in compliance with the applicable criteria, and its concern with regularity and with propriety, propriety being equally pertinent in the public sector context

items.scenario: A team is closing a compliance audit of a State department's purchase of medical equipment. Every purchase was made under a sanction issued by the competent authority, within the delegated financial powers, following the tender procedure the rules lay down. The team has also found that equipment worth several crores was bought two years before the building meant to house it was begun, and has been in storage since. The team leader says that since nothing broke a rule, the compliance audit has nothing to report.

items.stem: How is compliance auditing conducted?

options.text: Only as an individual compliance audit, since combining it with another type of audit would confuse two different sets of criteria and two different conclusions
options.misconception: makes the stand-alone compliance audit the only permitted form, when it is one of three
options.why: A separate individual compliance audit is one of the three ways, not the only one. The others are in relation with the audit of financial statements and in combination with performance auditing, and the criteria of each are stated for what they are.

options.text: Only alongside the audit of financial statements, compliance being a question about transactions and therefore inseparable from the accounts in which they are recorded
options.misconception: ties compliance auditing to the accounts, when its subject matter is activities and information as well as financial transactions
options.why: Compliance auditing assesses whether activities, financial transactions and information comply with the rules governing the entity, so much of its subject matter never reaches the accounts at all. It may be conducted separately or in combination with performance auditing.

options.text: In any of the three ways, but where it forms part of a performance audit the non-compliance is reported only if it caused the failure, a non-compliance that merely accompanies poor performance being outside the scope
options.misconception: narrows the relationship to causation, when non-compliance may equally be an explanation for or a consequence of the state of the activities
options.why: The relationship is stated three ways round: non-compliance may be the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of the state of the activities that are the subject matter of the performance audit. Requiring it to be the cause drops two of the three.

options.text: In one of three ways — in relation with the audit of financial statements, or separately as individual compliance audits, or in combination with performance auditing; and where it is part of a performance audit, compliance is seen as one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness, non-compliance being the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of the state of the activities examined
options.why: Compliance auditing is part of a combined audit that may also include other aspects, and the three ways it is generally conducted are exactly those. Nothing has to be carved out here: when compliance auditing is part of a performance audit, compliance is seen as one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness, and non-compliance may be the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of the state of the activities that are the subject matter — which is precisely the relationship between works awarded without tender and works that failed.
keywords: one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness
the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — compliance auditing conducted in relation with the audit of financial statements, separately as individual compliance audits, or in combination with performance auditing, where compliance is seen as one of the aspects of economy, efficiency and effectiveness

items.scenario: A performance audit of a State scheme for rural water supply finds that a third of the works were awarded without the tender process the scheme's own guidelines require, and that those works are the ones that have failed to deliver. The team is unsure whether the tendering failure belongs in the performance audit report at all, or must be carved out into a separate compliance audit, and whether a compliance audit can be run alongside a financial audit in the same engagement.

items.stem: What are the parts of the report?

options.text: Two — the Audit Board's comprehensive appraisals and the introduction, the remaining material going to the Public Accounts Committee separately rather than into the report
options.misconception: routes two parts of the report to a committee, when the committees receive the report itself
options.why: The audit reports and annual accounts stand referred to the specialised committees; the committees are the readers rather than a separate destination for parts of the report. All four parts are in the report presented to Parliament.

options.text: Four — an introduction containing a general review of the working results of Government companies, deemed Government companies and corporations; the results of comprehensive appraisals of selected undertakings conducted by the Audit Board; a resume of the company auditors' reports submitted under the C&AG's directions together with his comments on the accounts; and the significant results of audit of the undertakings not taken up for appraisal by the Audit Board
options.why: Both partners have one part each and are missing the other three. The report is presented to Parliament in several parts: a general review of working results, the results of the Audit Board's comprehensive appraisals of selected undertakings, a resume of the company auditors' reports submitted under the directions issued by the C&AG together with his comments on the accounts of the Government companies, and the significant results of audit of those undertakings not taken up for appraisal. The last of those is what answers the second partner: an undertaking the Audit Board did not appraise is still reported on.

options.text: One — the resume of the company auditors' reports submitted under the C&AG's directions, the C&AG having no audit of his own to report on a Government company whose statutory audit is conducted by a firm
options.misconception: reduces the report to the compilation the first partner expects, when the C&AG conducts supplementary audit, test audit and comprehensive appraisals of his own
options.why: The resume of the company auditors' reports is one part of four, and it travels with the C&AG's own comments on the accounts. The other three parts are his own work: the general review, the Audit Board's comprehensive appraisals, and the results of audit of the undertakings not appraised.

options.text: Four parts, but the significant results of audit of the undertakings not appraised by the Audit Board are given only where a statutory auditor has qualified his report on that undertaking
options.misconception: makes the fourth part conditional on a qualification, when it carries the significant results of audit of those undertakings whatever the statutory auditor said
options.why: The fourth part is the significant results of audit of the undertakings not taken up for appraisal by the Audit Board, and nothing conditions it on what the company's own auditor reported.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the parts of the C&AG's report on the audit of public sector undertakings presented to Parliament: the introduction with a general review of working results, the results of comprehensive appraisals conducted by the Audit Board, the resume of the company auditors' reports under the C&AG's directions with his comments, and the significant results of audit of undertakings not taken up for appraisal

items.scenario: A firm is reading the Comptroller and Auditor General's report on public sector undertakings for the first time and is trying to work out what it will contain. One partner expects it to be a compilation of the audit reports signed by the companies' own statutory auditors and nothing else. Another expects it to carry only the undertakings the Audit Board has appraised in depth, on the view that anything less than a full appraisal would not be worth reporting to Parliament.

items.stem: What is the position of the Audit Board?

options.text: The Audit Board's conclusions are final when signed, the enterprise's view being taken only after the report is laid before Parliament, when the committees call for it
options.misconception: postpones the enterprise's view to the committee stage, when the Board ascertains it before finalisation
options.why: The Board discusses its findings and conclusions with the managements of the enterprises and their controlling ministries and departments to ascertain their view points before finalisation. What happens afterwards before the committees is a further stage, not the first hearing.

options.text: The Audit Board must confine itself to financial and accounting matters, technical questions being outside the Indian Audit and Accounts Department's competence and reserved to the enterprise's own management
options.misconception: accepts the objection about technical competence, when the Boards associate experts in the relevant disciplines with themselves for that purpose
options.why: That is exactly the problem the arrangement solves: the Audit Boards associate with themselves experts in the disciplines relevant to the appraisals, which is what lets a comprehensive appraisal reach capacity utilisation, project formulation and the management of plant and machinery.

options.text: The Audit Boards have no separate legal entity and work under the supervision and control of the C&AG, whose reports carry their appraisals; they associate with themselves experts in the disciplines relevant to the appraisal; and they discuss their findings and conclusions with the managements of the enterprises and their controlling ministries and departments to ascertain their view points before finalisation
options.why: The managing director is right about one thing and wrong about the consequences of it. The Audit Boards have no separate legal entity, which is why they work under the supervision and control of the Comptroller and Auditor General and why the results of their appraisals are incorporated in his reports rather than issued in their own name. His other two points are already met by how the Board works: it associates with itself experts in the disciplines relevant to the appraisals, and it discusses its findings and conclusions with the managements and with the controlling ministries and departments to ascertain their view points before finalisation.

options.text: The Audit Board is a statutory body constituted under the C&AG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 with a legal entity of its own, which is what gives its appraisals their standing
options.misconception: gives the Audit Board a legal personality it does not have
options.why: The Audit Boards have no separate legal entity. Their standing comes from the C&AG, under whose supervision and control they work and in whose reports their appraisals appear.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the Audit Boards constituted for comprehensive audit appraisals, which associate experts in the relevant disciplines, discuss their findings with the managements and controlling ministries before finalisation, have no separate legal entity, and work under the supervision and control of the Comptroller and Auditor General

items.scenario: An Audit Board is appraising the working of a public sector fertiliser enterprise. Its draft findings are severe. The enterprise's managing director asks on what authority the Board acts, and says that a body constituted inside the audit department has no standing to appraise a company incorporated under the Companies Act, that its conclusions cannot be published without the enterprise being heard first, and that the technical judgements in the draft are beyond the competence of accountants.

items.stem: How did the requirement actually widen, and where does it stand now?

options.text: The top 100 in 2012 and the top 500 in 2015, which is where it still stands; the top 1,000 figure belongs to the Integrated Reporting recommendation, which is voluntary
options.misconception: stops the widening at the top 500 and attaches the top 1,000 to Integrated Reporting
options.why: The Integrated Reporting circular of 2017 advised the top 500 listed companies to adopt it on a voluntary basis from the financial year 2017-18. The top 1,000 is the reach of the business responsibility reporting requirement itself from December 2019, and it is not voluntary.

options.text: The top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation in 2012, the top 500 when the Business Responsibility Report became part of the Listing Regulations in 2015, and the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation with effect from 26 December 2019 — and reporting under BRSR is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23, disclosure having been voluntary in 2021-22
options.why: The requirement widened by rank three times and then changed form. In 2012 SEBI required the top 100 listed companies by market capitalisation to file a Business Responsibility Report. In 2015 the BRR became part of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations and the top 500 listed companies by market capitalisation were required to file it. In 2019, by the fifth amendment and with effect from 26 December 2019, the annual report of the top 1,000 listed entities based on market capitalisation had to contain one. In 2021 SEBI introduced the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report, and reporting under it is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23, disclosure having been voluntary in the financial year 2021-22. A company ranked about 800th is inside the top 1,000.

options.text: The top 1,000 listed entities, and reporting under BRSR has been mandatory since the financial year 2021-22, the year SEBI notified the new format
options.misconception: makes the year of notification the first mandatory year, when 2021-22 was the voluntary year
options.why: SEBI introduced the format in 2021 and the first mandatory year is 2022-23. Disclosure was voluntary in 2021-22, which is why a company that filed nothing for that year was not in default.

options.text: The top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation, but reporting under BRSR is voluntary throughout, the format having been introduced in 2021 as a recommendation
options.misconception: gets the rank right and leaves the requirement voluntary, when it is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23
options.why: Reporting under BRSR is mandatory from the financial year 2022-23. The voluntary year was 2021-22, which is the only year in which disclosure was left to the company.

citation.ref: Ch.
