options.text: Items 1, 2, 4 and 5, together with whether any explanation called for was given and was satisfactory and any other matter for the Central Government's notice; items 3 and 6 are separate reports the terms of appointment require beside the main report and the long form audit report
options.why: The auditor of a nationalised bank reports to the Central Government whether the balance sheet is a full and fair balance sheet containing all the necessary particulars and properly drawn up so as to exhibit a true and fair view, whether the profit and loss account shows a true balance of profit or loss, where he called for any explanation or information whether it was given and whether it is satisfactory, whether or not the transactions of the bank that came to his notice have been within the powers of that bank, whether or not the returns received from the offices and branches were adequate for the purpose of his audit, and any other matter he considers should be brought to the notice of the Central Government. The report on compliance with the statutory liquidity ratio requirements and the report on the status of compliance with the Ghosh Committee's recommendations on frauds and the Jilani Committee's on internal control are among the reports and certificates the terms of appointment require besides the audit report and the long form audit report.
keywords: within the powers of that bank

options.text: Items 1 and 2 only — the remaining four are matters for the long form audit report, which is where everything other than the opinion is said
options.misconception: pushes the powers-of-the-bank and adequacy-of-returns matters into the long form audit report, when both are among the matters the statutory report itself must state
options.why: Whether the transactions were within the powers of the bank and whether the branch returns were adequate are express matters of the report to the Central Government, as is whether explanations called for were given and satisfactory.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — auditor's report of a nationalised bank to the Central Government and its matters; the reports and certificates required by the terms of appointment beside the audit report and the long form audit report, including compliance with the statutory liquidity ratio and the Ghosh and Jilani Committee recommendations

items.scenario: A partner drafting the statutory central auditors' report on a nationalised bank lists what it must say: (1) whether the balance sheet is a full and fair balance sheet exhibiting a true and fair view; (2) whether the profit and loss account shows a true balance of profit or loss; (3) whether the bank has complied with the statutory liquidity ratio on the dates tested; (4) whether the transactions of the bank that came to the auditors' notice were within the powers of the bank; (5) whether the returns from the branches were adequate for the audit; (6) the status of compliance with the Ghosh and Jilani Committee recommendations.

items.stem: Which of the five are among the auditors' reports and certificates?

options.text: Two — only the internal financial controls report and the Bank Receipt forms certificate, the rest being for a nationalised bank alone
options.misconception: confines most certificates to nationalised banks, when the terms of appointment of public sector, private sector and foreign banks require them
options.why: The module's list of reports and certificates follows the terms of appointment of auditors of public sector banks, private sector banks and foreign banks; a listed private sector bank gets the corporate governance certificate on top.

options.text: Four — everything but the report on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning, which the director is right to say is the audit opinion itself
options.misconception: merges the prudential norms report into the opinion, when the module lists a report on whether income recognition, asset classification and provisioning follow the Reserve Bank's guidelines as a separate report
options.why: The report on whether income recognition, asset classification and provisioning have been made as per the Reserve Bank's guidelines is in the list of reports and certificates. That the opinion also depends on the norms does not remove the separate report.

options.text: All five — each is listed among the reports and certificates the terms of appointment require, the corporate governance certificate applying to a bank listed on a stock exchange, and the report on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning is a separate report notwithstanding that the opinion also rests on them
options.why: The reports and certificates beside the audit report and the long form audit report include the report on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls over financial reporting, the report on whether income recognition, asset classification and provisioning have been made as per the Reserve Bank's guidelines, the report on any serious irregularity requiring immediate attention, the certificate on the custody of unused Bank Receipt forms and their utilisation, the authentication of the capital adequacy ratio, the Ghosh and Jilani status report, the report on instances of adverse credit-deposit ratio in rural areas, asset liability management, the certificate on corporate governance for banks listed on a stock exchange, and certification of claims of interest subsidies and subventions. The director's objection does not hold: the prudential norms report is listed as a separate report in its own right.

options.text: Three — the corporate governance certificate is for the company secretary and the rural credit-deposit ratio is a matter for the Reserve Bank's own inspection
options.misconception: reassigns two of the listed certificates to others, when the certificate on corporate governance for a listed bank and the report on adverse rural credit-deposit ratios are both among the auditors' certificates
options.why: Both are in the module's list: the certificate on corporate governance in case of banks listed on a stock exchange, and the report on instances of adverse credit-deposit ratio in the rural areas.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — reports and certificates required beside the audit report: internal financial controls, income recognition, asset classification and provisioning, serious irregularities, unused Bank Receipt forms, capital adequacy, Ghosh and Jilani, adverse rural credit-deposit ratio, asset liability management, corporate governance for a listed bank, and interest subsidy and subvention claims

items.scenario: A listed private sector bank asks its statutory central auditors which of the following it may expect from them beside the audit report: a report on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of internal financial controls over financial reporting; a certificate on corporate governance; a report on instances of adverse credit-deposit ratio in rural areas; a certificate on the custody and utilisation of unused Bank Receipt forms; and a report on whether income recognition, asset classification and provisioning follow the Reserve Bank's guidelines. A director says the last of these cannot be a separate report because it is already the substance of the audit opinion.

items.stem: What is the company's capital ratio, and does it meet the minimum?

options.text: 15 per cent — Tier I and Tier II together, ₹180 crore, against the aggregate of risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and the risk-adjusted value of off-balance-sheet items, ₹1,200 crore; that exactly meets the minimum of 15 per cent, with no comfort above it
options.why: Every applicable non-banking financial company maintains a minimum capital ratio, consisting of Tier I and Tier II capital, of not less than 15 per cent of its aggregate risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and of the risk-adjusted value of its off-balance-sheet items. The manager's 18 per cent divides ₹180 crore by the ₹1,000 crore on-balance-sheet figure alone; the ratio measured as the Directions require is ₹180 crore over ₹1,200 crore, which is 15 per cent, the minimum itself.

options.text: 18 per cent, and it meets the minimum — guarantees are contingent and enter the capital ratio only when invoked
options.misconception: leaves off-balance-sheet exposures out until they crystallise, when the Directions measure the ratio against the risk-adjusted value of off-balance-sheet items as well
options.why: The denominator is the aggregate of risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and the risk-adjusted value of off-balance-sheet items. The guarantees enter now, at their risk-adjusted value, and the ratio is 15 per cent.

options.text: 12 per cent, below the minimum — only Tier I capital counts towards the ratio for a company that accepts no deposits
options.misconception: drops Tier II from the numerator, when the minimum capital ratio is defined as consisting of Tier I and Tier II capital
options.why: The ratio consists of Tier I and Tier II capital together, ₹180 crore, against ₹1,200 crore, which is 15 per cent and meets the minimum.

options.text: 15 per cent, but below the minimum, because a middle layer company must hold 18 per cent
options.misconception: invents a higher layer-based minimum, when the Directions set the minimum capital ratio at 15 per cent
options.why: The minimum under the Directions is 15 per cent of the aggregate risk-weighted exposures. At exactly 15 per cent the company meets it, though with nothing to spare.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — capital requirements: a minimum capital ratio of Tier I and Tier II capital of not less than 15 per cent of aggregate risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet and the risk-adjusted value of off-balance-sheet items

items.scenario: A non-banking financial company in the middle layer has Tier I capital of ₹120 crore and Tier II capital of ₹60 crore. Its risk-weighted assets on the balance sheet are ₹1,000 crore and the risk-adjusted value of its off-balance-sheet items, mainly guarantees, is ₹200 crore. Its finance manager reports a capital ratio of 18 per cent and says the company is comfortably above the minimum.

items.stem: How should the two loans be classified?

options.text: X is doubtful and Y is standard, because restructuring is itself evidence of doubt and a missing security is a matter for provisioning, not classification
options.misconception: over-classifies the restructured loan and under-classifies the lost security, when the Directions place a restructured asset in sub-standard and a security-less threatened asset in loss
options.why: Restructuring puts an asset in sub-standard, not doubtful, for the year of performance. The non-availability of security with a threat to recovery is a classification rule making Y a loss asset, and the provisioning follows from that.

options.text: Both are standard — X because the borrower is performing and Y because nothing is overdue, an overdue being the only trigger for downgrading
options.misconception: makes an overdue the sole trigger of classification, when a restructured asset is sub-standard for a year of performance and a loss asset is defined by the threat to recovery, not by arrears
options.why: Neither the year of satisfactory performance nor the loss-asset definition turns on an overdue. X has not completed the year, and Y's security has gone.

options.text: X stays sub-standard, because a renegotiated or restructured asset remains sub-standard until the expiry of one year of satisfactory performance under the new terms and only nine months have run; Y is a loss asset, because an asset adversely affected by a threat of non-recoverability from the non-availability of security or a fraudulent act of the borrower is a loss asset whether or not it is overdue
options.why: A sub-standard asset includes an asset where the terms of the agreement regarding interest or principal have been renegotiated, rescheduled or restructured after the commencement of operations, until the expiry of one year of satisfactory performance under the renegotiated, rescheduled or restructured terms; nine months of performance do not complete the year. A loss asset means an asset identified as such by the company, its internal or external auditor or the Reserve Bank on inspection, to the extent not written off, and also an asset adversely affected by a potential threat of non-recoverability due to erosion in the value of security or non-availability of security or any fraudulent act or omission on the part of the borrower; the disposal of the charged machinery is both the non-availability of security and a fraudulent act, and the absence of an overdue does not keep the loan standard.

options.text: X is standard, because restructuring with the borrower's consent is not a default; Y is sub-standard, since a loss asset must first pass through the doubtful category
options.misconception: treats classification as a ladder every asset must climb, when a loss asset is defined directly by the threat of non-recoverability and a restructured asset is expressly sub-standard for a year
options.why: The definitions are independent: an asset meeting the loss-asset definition is a loss asset without first being doubtful, and a restructured asset is sub-standard until one year of satisfactory performance has expired.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — asset classification: a renegotiated, rescheduled or restructured asset remains sub-standard until the expiry of one year of satisfactory performance; a loss asset as identified by the company, its auditor or the Reserve Bank, or as adversely affected by erosion or non-availability of security or a fraudulent act of the borrower

items.scenario: Two loans in a non-banking financial company's book on 31 March. Loan X was restructured on 1 July with a longer tenor and a lower rate, and the borrower has paid every restructured instalment for the nine months since; the company has moved it back to standard. Loan Y is not overdue, but the company's own inspection found that the machinery charged as security has been sold by the borrower and cannot be traced, and the company has left it as standard because no instalment has been missed.

items.stem: Which parts of the company's conduct comply with the Directions?

options.text: Everything but the late report — a short grace period for pending applications is reasonable and the renewal mandates are the depositors' consent
options.misconception: reads a grace period into "with immediate effect" and a standing mandate as consent, when the stop is immediate and the consent to renew must be express and voluntary at maturity
options.why: The stop on fresh deposits and renewals takes effect immediately on the downgrade, and a matured deposit is renewed only with the depositor's express and voluntary consent. The late report is only one of three failures.

options.text: Only letting the existing deposits run off to maturity — on the downgrade the company had to stop accepting fresh deposits and renewing existing ones with immediate effect, report the position within 15 working days to the concerned Regional Office of the Reserve Bank, and renew no matured deposit without the express and voluntary consent of the depositor, which a standing mandate is not
options.why: In the event of downgrading of the credit rating below the minimum specified investment grade, an investment and credit company or a factor regularises the excess deposits by three steps: with immediate effect it stops accepting fresh public deposits and renewing existing deposits, all existing deposits run off to maturity, and it reports the position within 15 working days to the concerned Regional Office of the Reserve Bank where it is registered. Accepting deposits for three more weeks breaks the first step, and 20 February is well beyond 15 working days from 10 January. And the Directions provide that no matured public deposit is renewed without the express and voluntary consent of the depositor, so a mandate signed at placement does not authorise the February renewals. Only the run-off to maturity is as the Directions require.

options.text: Everything — the company must regularise the excess in an orderly way and the Directions leave the method to its Board
options.misconception: leaves the method of regularisation to the Board, when the Directions prescribe the three steps and the 15 working day report
options.why: The method is prescribed: stop immediately, run off to maturity, report within 15 working days. The company departed from the first and third and renewed deposits it could not renew.

options.text: Nothing — even letting deposits run to maturity is wrong, because all public deposits must be repaid at once on a downgrade
options.misconception: turns the downgrade into an immediate repayment of all deposits, when the Directions have existing deposits run off to maturity
options.why: Existing deposits run off to maturity under the Directions; there is no immediate repayment. That step the company got right.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — Acceptance of Public Deposits Directions on downgrade below the minimum investment grade: stop fresh deposits and renewals with immediate effect, existing deposits run off to maturity, report within 15 working days to the Regional Office, and no matured deposit renewed without express and voluntary consent

items.scenario: A deposit-taking investment and credit company's rating was downgraded below the minimum investment grade on 10 January. The company continued to accept fresh public deposits until 31 January "to let existing customers complete their applications", renewed deposits that matured in February on the footing that the depositors had signed automatic-renewal mandates when the deposits were placed, and wrote to the Reserve Bank's Regional Office on 20 February. The finance head says the excess over the permissible ceiling will be repaid as the deposits mature.

items.stem: Which of the four are reported as frauds under the classification?

options.text: Cases 1 and 2 — where no fraudulent intention is suspected or proved, a cash shortage is still a fraud if it exceeds ₹10,000, or if it exceeds ₹5,000 and was detected by management, the auditor or an inspecting officer and not reported by the person handling the cash; case 3 is under ₹5,000 and case 4 was reported on its occurrence
options.why: Cases of negligence and cash shortages are reported as fraud if the intention to cheat or defraud is suspected or proved. Where it is not, two cases are nevertheless treated as fraud and reported: cash shortages of more than ₹10,000, and cash shortages of more than ₹5,000 if detected by management, the auditor or an inspecting officer and not reported on the occurrence by the persons handling the cash. Case 1 exceeds ₹10,000 and is a fraud whoever reported it; case 2 exceeds ₹5,000, was found by the auditor and was not reported by the cashier; case 3 at ₹4,000 falls below the ₹5,000 line; case 4 at ₹8,000 is above ₹5,000 but was reported on its occurrence by the cashier, so it is not caught.

options.text: Case 2 only — a shortage reported by the cashier is by definition not a fraud, whatever its size
options.misconception: lets the cashier's own report clear any shortage, when a shortage above ₹10,000 is a fraud regardless of who reported it
options.why: The self-report matters only on the ₹5,000 line. Above ₹10,000 the shortage is treated as fraud whether or not the cashier reported it, so case 1 goes in with case 2.

options.text: None — without a suspected or proved intention to cheat, a cash shortage is negligence and is never reported as fraud
options.misconception: stops at the intention test, when the classification goes on to treat two kinds of unintended shortage as fraud on size and non-reporting
options.why: The Directions treat two classes of shortage as fraud even where fraudulent intention is not suspected or proved at the time of detection: above ₹10,000, and above ₹5,000 detected by others and unreported by the cash handler.

options.text: Cases 1, 2 and 4 — every shortage above ₹5,000 is a fraud, the self-report being relevant only below that line
options.misconception: applies the ₹5,000 line without its condition, when between ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 a shortage is a fraud only if detected by management, the auditor or an inspector and not reported by the cash handler
options.why: Case 4 is above ₹5,000 but was reported on its occurrence by the person handling the cash, and it does not exceed ₹10,000, so neither limb catches it.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Non-Banking Financial Companies — Monitoring of Frauds Directions: negligence and cash shortages reported as fraud where intent is suspected or proved; otherwise cash shortages of more than ₹10,000, and of more than ₹5,000 if detected by management, the auditor or an inspecting officer and not reported by the person handling the cash

items.scenario: Four cash shortages at a non-banking financial company's branches during the year, in none of which any intention to cheat is suspected. (1) ₹12,000 short at a branch, reported by the cashier on the day. (2) ₹6,500 short, found by the internal auditor on a surprise count and never reported by the cashier. (3) ₹4,000 short, found by the branch manager and not reported by the cashier. (4) ₹8,000 short, reported by the cashier on the day it occurred. The company proposes to report only case 2 as a fraud.

items.stem: Who has committed an offence, and what does the Act say of each?

options.text: P, Q and R — Q too, because a member in employment who trains articled assistants is holding himself out as in practice without a certificate
options.misconception: reads the training of articled assistants by an employee as a false claim of practice, when the Act deems him in practice for that limited purpose
options.why: The Explanation to section 2(2) exists for Q: a salaried employee of a chartered accountant in practice or of such a firm is deemed to be in practice for the limited purpose of the training of articled assistants. He commits no offence.

options.text: P and R — setting up an establishment offering accounting services is practice though no client has been served, so P, a member without a certificate of practice, represents that he practises and offends section 24; R, not being a member, uses the designation and offends section 24; Q offends nothing, a salaried employee of a firm being deemed in practice for the limited purpose of training articled assistants
options.why: A person is deemed to be in practice not only when actually engaged in the practice of accountancy but when he offers to render accounting services whether or not he does so, and the act of setting up an establishment offering accounting services amounts to being in practice even though no client has been served. Section 24 punishes a member without a certificate of practice who represents that he is in practice or practises, and any person who, not being a member, represents that he is one or uses the designation chartered accountant; on first conviction the fine may extend to ₹1,000, and on a subsequent conviction to imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to ₹5,000 or both. Q is within the Explanation to section 2(2): an associate or fellow who is a salaried employee of a chartered accountant in practice or a firm of such accountants is deemed to be in practice for the limited purpose of the training of articled assistants.

options.text: R only — P has served no client and so is not yet in practice, and Q cannot train articled assistants without a certificate of practice
options.misconception: waits for a client before treating an establishment as practice, and denies the Explanation that lets a salaried employee of a firm train articled assistants
options.why: Offering to render accounting services is practice; the establishment is enough. And the Explanation to section 2(2) deems Q in practice for the limited purpose of training articled assistants notwithstanding his employment.

options.text: P and R, but R's case goes to the Disciplinary Committee of the Institute, which alone punishes misuse of the designation
options.misconception: sends a non-member to the Institute's disciplinary machinery, when section 24 makes the misuse a criminal offence tried by a court with a fine and, on a second conviction, imprisonment
options.why: The Institute's Board of Discipline and Disciplinary Committee act on members. A person who is not a member and uses the designation is prosecuted under section 24, as in the module's case where a magistrate imposed a fine and, in default, rigorous imprisonment.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — section 2(2) and its Explanation on salaried employees training articled assistants; setting up an establishment as practice though no client is served; section 24 on a non-member using the designation and a member without a certificate representing that he practises, with the fine and imprisonment

items.scenario: Three people in one town. Mr. P, an associate member who holds no certificate of practice, has rented an office, put up a board offering accounting and audit services, and printed cards, though no client has yet walked in. Mr. Q, a fellow member, is a salaried employee of a firm of chartered accountants and trains two articled assistants registered under him. Mr. R, who failed the final examination, describes himself as a chartered accountant on his visiting cards and prepares accounts for shopkeepers for a fee.

items.stem: Which of the three is on the wrong side of the Act?

options.text: None — an LLP is a partnership and not a company, and both individual appointments are within practice
options.misconception: takes the LLP's own reading of section 25, when the section expressly brings in a limited liability partnership that has a company as a partner
options.why: For section 25 the term company includes a limited liability partnership which has a company as its partner. The LLP may not practise as chartered accountants and its officers knowingly a party are liable to the fines.

options.text: Sunita and the LLP — mediation is not among the roles Regulation 191 lists, so it needs the Council's specific permission
options.misconception: reads Regulation 191's list literally, when the Ethical Standards Board has read mediator as within arbitrator, which the regulation names
options.why: The Board's decision is that acting as a mediator in court is deemed covered within the meaning of arbitrator, which Regulation 191 permits to members in practice. No specific permission is needed.

options.text: Only the LLP — a limited liability partnership with a company as a partner is a company for section 25 and may not practise as chartered accountants, and every director, manager, secretary or officer knowingly a party is liable to a fine up to ₹1,000 on first conviction and ₹5,000 after; Raj is deemed in practice under Regulation 191 as a secretary not employed on a salary-cum-full-time basis, and Sunita's mediation is within arbitrator, which Regulation 191 permits
options.why: Under Regulation 191, read with section 2(2)(iv), a member is deemed to be in practice if in his professional capacity, and neither personally nor as an employee, he acts as liquidator, trustee, executor, administrator, arbitrator, receiver, adviser or representative for costing, financial or taxation matters, takes up an appointment made by the Central or a State Government, a court or another legal authority, or acts as a secretary unless his employment is on a salary-cum-full-time basis — so Raj's appointment is within his practice. The Ethical Standards Board has decided that a member in practice can act as a mediator in court, mediation being deemed covered within arbitrator. Section 25 provides that no company, wherever incorporated, shall practise as chartered accountants, and for that section the term company includes any limited liability partnership which has a company as its partner; every director, manager, secretary and other officer knowingly a party to the contravention is punishable with a fine up to ₹1,000 on first conviction and up to ₹5,000 on any subsequent conviction.

options.text: Raj and the LLP — a member in practice may not hold the office of secretary of anybody, that being an occupation other than the profession
options.misconception: treats every secretaryship as another occupation under Clause 11, when Regulation 191 deems a member acting as secretary in his professional capacity to be in practice unless employed on a salary-cum-full-time basis
options.why: Regulation 191 names acting as a secretary among the things a member does in practice, with one carve-out: employment on a salary-cum-full-time basis. Raj's appointment is on a fee in his professional capacity and is within his practice.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Regulation 191 and the secretary not on a salary-cum-full-time basis, the Ethical Standards Board's decision on court mediators as within arbitrator, and section 25 on companies including a limited liability partnership with a company partner, with the fines on officers knowingly a party

items.scenario: CA Raj, in practice, is appointed by the Central Government as secretary to a metro project authority in his professional capacity, on a fee and not on a salary-cum-full-time basis. CA Sunita, in practice, is empanelled by a court as a mediator. Advisory Solutions LLP, whose partners are two chartered accountants and a private limited company, starts signing audit reports in the LLP's name; its company-partner's directors say an LLP is not a company and section 25 does not reach it.

items.stem: Which of the four is within the Council's permissions?

options.text: Arun and Charu — a Director Simplicitor draws no salary, so there is no conflict with the firm's audit, and the audit continues
options.misconception: reads the absence of remuneration as removing the auditor conflict, when the general permission for a Director Simplicitor is expressly withdrawn where the member or a partner is the company's auditor
options.why: The general permission to be a Director Simplicitor does not extend to a company in which the member or any of his partners is interested as auditor; the Council prohibits a member from auditing a company of which he is a director whether or not he holds a substantial interest.

options.text: Only Charu — a member may be a promoter or subscriber to the memorandum and be a Director Simplicitor of that company without permission; Arun's firm being Nila's auditor takes his directorship outside the general permission, Bela's signing of Registrar forms is a direct conflict of role, and Dev cannot hold the office of managing director where a relative holds a substantial interest of twenty per cent or more, so the Council will not grant it
options.why: A Director Simplicitor is an ordinary director who is not a managing or whole-time director, is required only at board meetings and is paid nothing but for attending them, and a member in practice is permitted generally to be one in any company including a board-managed company without specific permission — unless he or any of his partners is interested in the company as an auditor, which is Arun's position. The Council has also decided that a member may be a promoter or subscriber to the memorandum and articles of a company and be its Director Simplicitor without specific permission, which is Charu's. The Ethical Standards Board holds that a member in practice who is Director Simplicitor cannot sign the company's Registrar forms, as it is a direct conflict of role. And a member cannot accept and hold the office of managing or whole-time director if he, his partners or his relatives hold a substantial interest in the company; a brother is a relative, and shares carrying not less than twenty per cent of the voting power are a substantial interest.
keywords: interested in the company as an auditor

options.text: Charu and Dev — the substantial interest bar looks at the member's own holding, and Dev holds nothing
options.misconception: confines substantial interest to the member's own shares, when the twenty per cent is counted across the member, his relatives and the concerns in which they hold such an interest
options.why: A member is deemed to have a substantial interest where shares carrying not less than twenty per cent of the voting power are owned by him or by one or more of his relatives, and a brother is a relative. Dev cannot hold the office of managing director in that company.

options.text: Bela and Charu — signing statutory filings is a ministerial act any director may do, and it keeps the member within the Director Simplicitor role
options.misconception: treats the Registrar filings as within the Director Simplicitor role, when the Ethical Standards Board has decided that signing them is a direct conflict of role
options.why: The Board's decision is that a chartered accountant in practice who is a Director Simplicitor cannot sign the company's Registrar forms. A Director Simplicitor is required only at board meetings.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 11: the Director Simplicitor and the general permission withdrawn where the member or a partner is the auditor, the promoter or subscriber as Director Simplicitor, the Ethical Standards Board on signing Registrar forms, the managing director's office barred where relatives hold a substantial interest, relative and the twenty per cent voting test

items.scenario: Four members in practice. CA Arun is a director of Nila Ltd, attends only board meetings, draws sitting fees alone, and his firm is Nila's statutory auditor. CA Bela is a Director Simplicitor of Ravi Pvt Ltd and, being the only chartered accountant on the board, signs the company's annual filings with the Registrar of Companies. CA Charu subscribed to the memorandum of a new company as a promoter and sits on its board as an ordinary director without remuneration beyond sitting fees. CA Dev has been offered the office of managing director of a company in which his brother holds 24 per cent of the voting power, and has applied to the Council.

items.stem: Which of the six need the Council's specific and prior permission, and what else follows?

options.text: Items 2, 4 and 6 — being Karta of a trading business is engaging in business and always needs specific permission
options.misconception: treats the Karta of a family business as always outside the permissions, when the Council allows interest in a family business devolving by partition where the member takes no active part and invests only the family's funds
options.why: Interest in a family business concern, including interest devolving by inheritance, succession or partition, in whose management no active part is taken, is within the Council's resolutions; a Karta who invests only the family's funds and leaves the management alone is within the limit.

options.text: Items 2 and 6 need specific permission, and item 2 also costs her the attest functions because her teaching exceeds 25 hours a week; items 1 and 3 are generally permitted, item 4 is within the limit for a Karta investing family funds without active management, and item 5 needs no permission because equity and currency derivatives in personal capacity are outside Clause 11
options.why: The general resolution permits, without specific permission, part-time tutorship under the coaching organisation of the Institute and the holding of public elective office such as a Member of Parliament or of a legislative assembly. The specific resolution requires the Council's specific and prior approval for part-time or full-time lectureship for courses other than those relating to the Institute's examinations, and for editorship of journals other than professional journals. Whatever the permission, the teaching hours devoted to such activities taken together should not exceed 25 hours a week in order to be able to undertake attest functions, so at 28 hours she loses them. A member in practice engaged as Karta of a Hindu undivided family doing family business is within the limit prescribed by the Council if he makes investments from the funds of the family only, provided he is not actively engaged in the management. And members may transact in equity and currency derivatives in their personal capacity without the permission of the Council, though not in their professional capacity for clients.

options.text: Items 2, 5 and 6 — trading in derivatives is a business, and a member in practice must obtain permission before dealing in them at all
options.misconception: makes derivatives a business needing permission, when the module's answer is that equity and currency derivatives in personal capacity are not violative of Clause 11 and need no permission
options.why: Members in practice may engage in equity and currency derivative transactions in their personal capacity without the Council's permission; what they may not do is transact for clients in their professional capacity.

options.text: Items 1, 2 and 6 — any teaching for a fee is an occupation, and the Institute's own coaching is no exception
options.misconception: puts the Institute's coaching organisation on the same footing as an outside college, when part-time tutorship under the coaching organisation of the Institute is in the general permission
options.why: The general resolution names part-time tutorship under the coaching organisation of the Institute; it is lectureship for other courses and tutorship under other institutions that need specific permission.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 11: the general resolution (tutorship under the Institute's coaching organisation, public elective office), the specific resolution (lectureship for other courses, editorship of non-professional journals), the 25 teaching hours for attest functions, the Karta of a family business, and equity and currency derivatives in personal capacity

items.scenario: A member in practice lists six things she does or means to do: (1) teach part-time under the coaching organisation of the Institute; (2) take a full-time lectureship in a college for a commerce degree, which with her other teaching will take 28 hours a week; (3) sit as a Member of the Legislative Assembly; (4) act as Karta of her family's Hindu undivided family trading business that came to her on partition, investing only the family's funds and leaving the management to her brother; (5) buy and sell equity and currency derivatives in her own name; (6) edit a lifestyle magazine.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The sale of the goodwill of a deceased proprietor's firm to an eligible member is permitted and instalments are allowed where the agreement provides for them; the legal heir must obtain the Council's permission within a year of the death and the sale must be completed within that year, during which the firm name is kept in abeyance; Nair may then practise as a proprietor under the name Mehta & Co.
options.why: The Council considered under Clause 2 whether the goodwill of a proprietary concern of a chartered accountant can be sold after his death to another eligible member and permitted it, payments being allowed in instalments if the sale agreement contains such a provision. Where the proprietor died on or after 30 August 1998 the sale must be completed in all respects within a year of the death, the name of the firm is kept in abeyance — not removed — only up to one year from the death, and the legal heir of the deceased must obtain the permission of the Council within a year of the death. In the module's own illustration a widow selling her husband's practice with the right to use the firm name is in effect selling the goodwill, the act is permissible, and the buyer can continue to practise in that name as a proprietor.
keywords: within a year of the death

options.text: The sale is permitted, but the widow may continue to receive a share of the fees Nair earns under the name, since she is the legal representative
options.misconception: carries the partnership rule on a deceased partner's share across to a proprietorship, where there is no sharing of fees between the legal representative and the purchaser of the goodwill
options.why: In a proprietorship there is no sharing of fees between the legal representative of the single-member firm and the purchaser of the goodwill; the widow's entitlement is the price of the goodwill, in instalments if agreed.

options.text: The sale is permitted but the price must be paid in one sum, and the Institute need not be told until Nair applies to use the name
options.misconception: forbids instalments and lets the permission wait on the buyer, when instalments are allowed under the agreement and the legal heir must obtain the Council's permission within a year of the death
options.why: Payments may be made in instalments provided the sale agreement contains such a provision, and it is the legal heir who has to obtain the permission of the Council within a year of the death of the proprietor.

options.text: The sale is barred — a proprietor's goodwill dies with him, and a firm name can pass only to a partner
options.misconception: denies the Council's decision that the goodwill of a proprietary firm may be sold after the proprietor's death, which is exactly what the module's illustration permits
options.why: The goodwill of a proprietorship firm of a chartered accountant can be sold or transferred to another eligible member after the death of the proprietor, and the buyer may practise in the name as a proprietor.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule: sale of the goodwill of a proprietary firm after the proprietor's death, instalments under the agreement, the sale completed and the Council's permission obtained within a year of the death, the firm name kept in abeyance for a year, and Illustration 6 on the widow's sale with the firm name

items.scenario: CA Mehta, a sole proprietor practising as Mehta & Co., died on 5 May 2026. His widow proposes to sell the practice to CA Nair for ₹8 lakh, the price including the right to use the name Mehta & Co., payable in four half-yearly instalments under the agreement. She asks whether she must involve the Institute, and by when, and whether Nair can then practise as a proprietor under that name.

items.stem: How do the three stand under Clause 2 and the Council's decisions?

options.text: (3) is in time, because the year runs from the date the heir first approaches the Institute and not from the death
options.misconception: starts the one-year clock at the heir's approach, when the name is kept in abeyance up to one year from the death and a dispute extension needs information to the Institute within a year of the death
options.why: The clocks run from the death: the sale completed within a year of it, the Council's permission sought within a year of it, and the name in abeyance up to one year from it. The son has nothing to stand on after fifteen months of silence.

options.text: (1) and (2) are both misconduct, because a share can go to a legal representative only while at least one partner survives to earn it
options.misconception: reads the rule as needing a surviving partner, when the Council's decision applies equally where all partners die at the same time
options.why: The Council's decision on a deceased partner's share applies also where all the partners die at the same time, so the second firm's heirs take their share under the deed; it is the first firm, with no provision in its deed, that is in breach.

options.text: All three are permitted — a widow's share is a matter of goodwill among partners, and the Institute holds a deceased proprietor's name until a buyer appears
options.misconception: leaves the deceased partner's share to the partners' discretion and the firm name open-ended, when the share needs a provision in the deed and the name is held only one year
options.why: The share is permitted only under a provision of the partnership agreement, and the proprietorship name is kept in abeyance only up to one year from the death, the dispute extension needing a report to the Institute within that year.

options.text: (1) is misconduct, because a deceased partner's legal representative may receive a share of the firm only if the partnership agreement so provides; (2) is permitted, because the same rule applies where all the partners die at the same time and this deed provides for it; (3) is too late, because the firm name is kept in abeyance only up to one year from the death unless a dispute as to the heir was reported within that year
options.why: Under Clause 2, where there are two or more partners and one dies, the legal representative of the deceased partner can continue to receive a share of the firm only if the partnership agreement contains such a provision; paying the widow without one is sharing fees with a non-member. The Council's decision applies also in the case of a partnership firm when all the partners die at the same time, so the heirs under the second deed are within it. For a proprietorship, the name of the firm is kept in abeyance only up to a period of one year from the death of the proprietor, and it is only where there is a dispute as to the legal heir and the information is received by the Institute within a year of the death that the name is kept in abeyance till one year from the settlement of the dispute; the son, who reported nothing in fifteen months, has let the year run.
keywords: partnership agreement contains such a provision

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Clause 2 of Part I of the First Schedule: a deceased partner's legal representative receiving a share only under the partnership agreement, the decision applying where all partners die together, the proprietorship name kept in abeyance one year from death, and the extension where a dispute as to the heir is reported within a year

items.scenario: Three situations. (1) CA Iyer, a partner of a three-partner firm, died; the partnership deed says nothing about a deceased partner's share, but the surviving partners, out of regard, pay his widow one-fifth of the profits every year. (2) All three partners of another firm died in the same accident, and their heirs cite the deed, which provides for a deceased partner's family to receive a share for five years. (3) A sole proprietor died fifteen months ago; his son, who is not a chartered accountant, has not approached the Institute, and now asks that the firm name be held for a buyer he expects to find.

items.stem: Which of the four may he accept?

options.text: (1) and (3) — fees recovered progressively as the work is done make him indebted at no stage, and a bank's credit card is within the Board's decision where the outstanding beyond the credit period does not exceed ₹1,00,000; (2) is barred because a relative's indebtedness above ₹1,00,000 to a concern with no statutory limit is caught by Chapter X, and (4) is barred because the Board does not permit a member to audit a bank from which he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit
options.why: Chapter X of the Council General Guidelines provides that a member in practice, a partner of a firm in practice, the firm, or a relative of such member or partner shall not accept appointment as auditor of a concern while indebted to it, or while he has given a guarantee or security for the indebtedness of a third person to it, for the limits fixed in the statute and in other cases for an amount exceeding ₹1,00,000; a sister is a relative, the society has no statutory limit, and ₹1,50,000 exceeds the line. The Research Committee's opinion is that where the auditor recovers his fees on a progressive basis as and when a part of the work is done, he cannot be said to be indebted to the concern at any stage, so the advance is no bar. The Ethical Standards Board has decided that a member may hold the credit card of a bank he audits provided the outstanding does not exceed ₹1,00,000 beyond the prescribed credit period, and that a member is not permitted to accept the audit of a bank where he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit held there.

options.text: (1), (3) and (4) — a loan against his own fixed deposit is fully secured by the bank's own liability to him and is not indebtedness
options.misconception: nets the loan against the deposit, when the Board's decision is that a loan against a fixed deposit in the bank bars the audit of that bank
options.why: The Ethical Standards Board's decision is categorical: a member in practice is not permitted to accept the audit assignment of a bank where he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit held by him in that bank. The security does not save it.

options.text: (2) and (3) — Chapter X looks only at the member's own debts, and an advance of fees is a debt to the client that bars (1)
options.misconception: leaves relatives out of Chapter X and treats every fee advance as indebtedness, when the chapter names relatives and the progressive-fee opinion takes the advance out
options.why: Chapter X expressly extends to a relative of the member or partner, so the sister's ₹1,50,000 loan bars the society audit; and fees recovered progressively under the engagement terms do not make the auditor indebted at any stage.

options.text: (1) only — any dealing with a bank he audits, a credit card included, is a relationship the Board forbids
options.misconception: forbids the credit card outright, when the Board permits it within the indebtedness limit of ₹1,00,000 beyond the credit period
options.why: The Board allows a member to hold the credit card of a bank he audits, provided the outstanding balance does not exceed ₹1,00,000 beyond the prescribed credit period. At ₹80,000 the card is within the line.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Council General Guidelines Chapter X: indebtedness of the member, partner, firm or relative beyond ₹1,00,000 where no statute fixes a limit, the progressive-fee opinion of the Research Committee; Ethical Standards Board decisions on a bank's credit card within ₹1,00,000 and a loan against a fixed deposit

items.scenario: Four appointments offered to CA Om, in practice. (1) Tax audit of a partnership firm that has paid him ₹2,50,000 of fees in advance under an engagement letter providing for fees to be recovered progressively as parts of the work are done. (2) Audit of a co-operative society, governed by no statutory limit on indebtedness, from which his sister has an unsecured loan of ₹1,50,000. (3) Statutory audit of a bank whose credit card he holds, with ₹80,000 outstanding beyond the credit period. (4) Audit of another bank from which he has taken a loan against a fixed deposit he holds there.

items.stem: What must Wali do before accepting, and what of his own books?

options.text: He must obtain a copy of Vani's communication from the Board of Directors and consider it before accepting, and follow any direction of the Council or its committee not to accept in a case of unjustified removal; and he is in breach of Chapter V, which requires a member in practice to keep a cash book and a ledger for his practice whether or not section 44AA applies
options.why: Under the Ethical Standards Board's guidelines, where an auditor resigns or does not offer himself for reappointment he sends a written communication of his professional reasons to the Board of Directors with a copy to the Institute, and it is obligatory on the incoming auditor, before accepting appointment, to obtain a copy of that communication from the Board of Directors and consider it. Chapter XI of the Council General Guidelines requires a member in practice to follow a direction given by the Council or an appropriate committee, to him as incoming auditor, not to accept the appointment in a case of unjustified removal of the earlier auditor. Chapter V requires a member in practice, or the firm of which he is a partner, to maintain proper books of account of the professional practice including a cash book and a ledger, and the module's illustration holds that it does not matter whether section 44AA of the Income-tax Act applies or not.

options.text: He may accept, because a resignation is not a removal and Chapter XI speaks only of removal; his books are a private matter
options.misconception: confines the Board's procedure to removals, when its guidelines expressly cover resignation and non-reappointment and place a duty on the incoming auditor in each
options.why: The Board's guidelines deal with an auditor who resigns, one who is not reappointed though willing, and removals by government and statutory authorities alike, and in each the incoming auditor must obtain and consider the communication. Chapter V makes the books a professional obligation.

options.text: He must obtain a no-objection certificate from Vani under Clause 8 and nothing more; his books are governed by the Income-tax Act alone
options.misconception: reduces the duty to a Clause 8 communication, when the Board's guidelines add the duty to obtain the outgoing auditor's written reasons from the Board of Directors, and misplaces the books rule in the Income-tax Act
options.why: Clause 8 communication stands on its own; the Board's guidelines require in addition that the incoming auditor obtain a copy of the communication of reasons from the Board of Directors and consider it. Chapter V, not section 44AA, requires his cash book and ledger.

options.text: The managing director's assurance is enough, because the Board's procedure binds the outgoing auditor only; and the Income-tax threshold settles his books
options.misconception: places the whole duty on the outgoing auditor and borrows the Income-tax threshold for the Council's books rule, when the incoming auditor must obtain and consider the communication and Chapter V applies regardless of section 44AA
options.why: The obligation to obtain a copy of the resignation communication from the Board of Directors and consider it is placed on the incoming auditor. And Chapter V's cash book and ledger are required of every member in practice whatever the Income-tax Act says.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Ethical Standards Board guidelines on resignation and non-reappointment with the incoming auditor's duty to obtain and consider the communication; Council General Guidelines Chapter XI on directions in unjustified removal and Chapter V on the cash book and ledger regardless of section 44AA

items.scenario: CA Vani resigned as auditor of Tarak Ltd after the board refused to correct a revenue recognition policy, and wrote to the board saying so, with a copy to the Institute. CA Wali is offered the appointment in her place; the managing director tells him the resignation was "personal" and that there is nothing to read. CA Wali also keeps no cash book or ledger for his own practice, reasoning that his receipts are below the limit at which section 44AA of the Income-tax Act requires books.

items.stem: What do the Council's self-regulatory measures say of the two proposals?

options.text: A statutory auditor firm of ten or more members should not conduct the branch audits, which should go to local firms of fewer than ten members, the exceptions being where the branch records are kept at the head office or significant operations are carried on at the branch; and associating a firm of fewer than five members as joint auditor of a large company is to be encouraged, so the senior firm should not object — the measures being recommendatory, with the Council expecting every member to implement them
options.why: The branch audits of a company should not be conducted by its statutory auditors consisting of ten or more members but by local firms of fewer than ten members, without restricting the statutory auditors' right of access to branch accounts under the Companies Act; the restriction may not apply where the accounting records of the branches are maintained at the head office, or where significant operations of the company are carried out at its branch office. Here the books are at the branches, so no exception applies. In large companies the practice of associating a practising firm with fewer than five members as joint auditors should be encouraged, and where a client desires to appoint such a firm the senior firm should not object. The self-regulatory measures are recommendatory, but the Council expects each and every member to implement them.

options.text: Both proposals are prohibited outright, and a breach of either is professional misconduct under the Second Schedule
options.misconception: turns the recommendatory measures into a Schedule offence, when the module describes them as recommendatory measures the Council expects members to implement
options.why: The self-regulatory measures are recommendatory; the Council expects their implementation but the module does not put them in the Schedules. And the joint audit proposal is one the measures encourage, not prohibit.

options.text: The firm may audit the branches because the measures bind only firms of fewer than ten members, and the objection to the small joint auditor is sound
options.misconception: inverts the ten-member line and the joint audit measure, when it is the large firm that is asked to leave branch audits to local firms and not to object to a small joint auditor
options.why: The measure asks statutory auditors of ten or more members to leave branch audits to local firms of fewer than ten, and asks the senior firm not to object to a joint auditor of fewer than five members.

options.text: The firm may audit the branches under the head-office exception, since a statutory auditor always has access to branch accounts
options.misconception: reads the right of access as the exception, when the exception is for branch records actually maintained at the head office and the books here are at the branches
options.why: The right of access to branch accounts is preserved, but it is not the exception. The exception applies where the branch accounting records are maintained at the head office, and here they are kept at the branches.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — recommended self-regulatory measures: branch audits by local firms of fewer than ten members with the head-office and significant-operations exceptions, joint audits with firms of fewer than five members, and the recommendatory nature of the measures

items.scenario: A firm of twelve partners is statutory auditor of a company with nine branches. The company proposes that the firm audit every branch itself, since the branch books are maintained at the branches. Separately, the company's board wants to add a three-partner firm as joint auditor; the twelve-partner firm objects that a firm that small should not sit beside it on a large company.

items.stem: Is the trainee right on either point?

options.text: No on both — the ratio excludes only typists and peons, so 22 count and four members suffice, and other fees need no disclosure of any kind
options.misconception: gets the arithmetic right by accident while keeping articled and audit assistants in the count, and drops the disclosure the Council recommends
options.why: Articled and audit assistants are expressly excluded along with typists and peons, so 12 count, not 22; and the Council recommends disclosure of payments received for other services through a different firm.

options.text: Yes on both — the ratio is one member for every three non-qualified staff, and fees through another concern breach Clause 2 on sharing fees
options.misconception: misstates the ratio and reads the disclosure measure as a Clause 2 sharing bar, when the ratio is one to five and the measure asks only for disclosure of the payments
options.why: The measure is one member for every five non-qualified staff, and what the Council asks about payments received through a different firm of which the auditor is a partner or proprietor is disclosure as a good and healthy practice, not abstention.

options.text: No on the ratio and half-right on the fees — the ratio is at least one member for every five non-qualified staff excluding articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and others not directly engaged in professional work, so 12 count and four members exceed the required three; and the disclosure of payments received for other services through a different firm is a good and healthy practice the Council recommends, not a legal bar
options.why: In the Council's view a practising firm engaged in audit work should have at least one member for every five non-qualified members of the staff, excluding articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and other persons not engaged directly in such professional work. Of the 25, the 8 articled assistants, 2 audit assistants, 2 typists and the peon are excluded, leaving 12; 12 divided by five calls for three members, and the firm has four. On the fees, the Council has decided that as a good and healthy practice auditors should make a disclosure of the payments received by them for other services through the medium of a different firm or firms in which the auditor is a partner or proprietor. It is a recommended disclosure, and the partner should make it, but the trainee is wrong to call the fees unlawful on that ground.

options.text: Yes on the ratio — 25 staff need five members and the firm has four
options.misconception: counts every non-member employee, when articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and others not directly engaged in professional work are excluded from the ratio
options.why: The 25 includes 13 excluded persons. The ratio is measured on the 12 non-qualified staff directly engaged in professional work, and four members are more than the three needed.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — recommended self-regulatory measures: at least one member for every five non-qualified staff excluding articled and audit assistants, typists, peons and others not directly engaged in professional work; disclosure of payments received for other services through a different firm as a good and healthy practice

items.scenario: A four-partner firm engaged in audit work employs 25 non-member staff: 8 articled assistants, 2 audit assistants, 2 typists, 1 peon and 12 semi-qualified audit staff. One partner also receives fees for tax consultancy to audit clients through a separate proprietary concern of his, and has never mentioned it to the firm's clients. A trainee says the firm breaches the staff ratio and that the separate fees are unlawful.

items.stem: How many of the six are permitted under the Board's decisions?

options.text: Five — everything but the messaging, since a trademark attorney's work is advice on intellectual property, which the Board calls routine professional work
options.misconception: merges advising on intellectual property rights with acting as a trademark or patent attorney, when the Board permits the first and forbids the second
options.why: The Board's decision draws the line inside the subject: acting as a trademark or patent attorney is not permitted, while professional advice in relation to intellectual property rights is routine professional work.

options.text: Four — the internal auditor may buy the shares, a member holding a certificate of practice may be on the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank, the firm may register on Udyog Aadhar, and a kiosk is permitted where the services are the professional activities of a practising chartered accountant; the messaging is not permitted, and a member may not act as a trademark or patent attorney though advice on intellectual property rights is routine professional work
options.why: The Board's decisions are that there is no prohibition for the internal auditor of a company to acquire or purchase its shares; that it is permissible for a practising member holding a certificate of practice to become a member of the Board of Management in primary urban co-operative banks, the role being similar to a Director Simplicitor's; that a firm may register itself on Udyog Aadhar; and that a member in practice can provide services through a kiosk only if the services provided are professional activities of a practising chartered accountant permitted under the Act, which tax return filing and certification are. Against these, it is not permissible for a member to use messaging applications to send messages to make people aware of his practice and mention the services provided, and a member in practice cannot act as a trademark or patent attorney, though professional advice on intellectual property rights is routine professional work and permissible.

options.text: Two — only the share purchase and the Udyog Aadhar registration; a co-operative bank board and a kiosk are business, and messaging a list is fine if the message is factual
options.misconception: rejects the co-operative bank board and the kiosk and accepts the messaging, the reverse of the Board's decisions on all three
options.why: The Board permits the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank and a kiosk providing professional services, and it does not permit messaging applications used to make people aware of a member's practice, factual or not.

options.text: Three — the share purchase, the Udyog Aadhar registration and the kiosk; an internal auditor may not, however, buy shares of a company he audits internally
options.misconception: contradicts itself on the shares and drops the co-operative bank board, when the Board finds no prohibition on the internal auditor's purchase and permits the Board of Management
options.why: There is no prohibition on an internal auditor acquiring the company's shares, and the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank is permitted, making four.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Ethical Standards Board decisions: messaging applications not permitted, the Board of Management of primary urban co-operative banks permitted, trademark and patent attorney not permitted but intellectual property advice routine, the internal auditor's share purchase, Udyog Aadhar registration, and kiosks for professional services

items.scenario: Six things members in practice propose. (1) Sending a message on a messaging application to a list of local businesses describing the firm's services. (2) An internal auditor of a listed company buying its shares on the exchange. (3) Sitting on the Board of Management of a primary urban co-operative bank while holding a certificate of practice. (4) Acting as a trademark attorney for clients' brand registrations. (5) Registering the firm on the Udyog Aadhar portal of the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. (6) Running a kiosk in a mall offering tax return filing and certification.

items.stem: Which of the five can proceed as proposed?

options.text: Only Hema — a member in practice may be the authorised representative of a foreign company if he is not its auditor; Farah may hold either the audit or the monitoring agency, not both at once; Girish or his firm may not audit the joint venture of a company of which he is a non-executive director; Ishan may take e-return registration where it does not conflict with his employment but cannot certify the returns; and Jaya cannot exercise a lien over client records for non-payment of fees
options.why: The Board's decisions are that it is not permissible for a member or firm that is the statutory auditor of a bank to accept the assignment of agency for specialised monitoring of a customer of the same bank simultaneously, either assignment being open at one time; that where a member in practice is a non-executive director of a company, he or a firm in which he is a partner should not accept appointment as statutory auditor of a company which is a joint venture of that company, as it would impact independence; that a member in practice can act as authorised representative of a foreign company provided he is not its auditor; that a member in service is allowed to take e-return registration if it does not conflict with his employment obligation but cannot certify the return; and that a chartered accountant cannot exercise a lien over the client's documents or records for non-payment of his fees.

options.text: Hema and Jaya — a lien for unpaid fees is a general right of any professional over papers in his hands
options.misconception: imports the general lien of other professions, when the Board has decided that a chartered accountant cannot exercise a lien over client documents for non-payment of fees
options.why: The decision is specific: a chartered accountant cannot exercise lien over the client documents or records for non-payment of his fees. Jaya must return them.

options.text: Hema, Girish and Ishan — a joint venture is a separate company, and a member in service may certify returns he is registered to file
options.misconception: severs the joint venture from the director's company and lets a member in service certify, when the Board bars the joint venture audit for independence and limits the member in service to registration without certification
options.why: The Board's view is that auditing the joint venture of a company of which the member is a non-executive director would impact independence, and that a member in service may take e-return registration but cannot certify the return.

options.text: Hema and Farah — monitoring a borrower on the bank's behalf is work for the same client, not a conflicting one
options.misconception: sees the monitoring agency as part of the bank audit, when the Board treats the statutory audit of the bank and the monitoring of its customer as assignments a member may hold only one at a time
options.why: The Board does not permit the statutory auditor of a bank to accept the agency for specialised monitoring of a customer of the same bank simultaneously; the member can accept either of the assignments at one time.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional Ethics — Ethical Standards Board decisions: the statutory auditor of a bank and the agency for specialised monitoring of its customer, the non-executive director and the joint venture's audit, the authorised representative of a foreign company not its auditor, e-return registration by a member in service without certification, and no lien over client records

items.scenario: CA Farah, statutory auditor of a bank, is offered appointment as the agency for specialised monitoring of one of that bank's borrowers for the same period. CA Girish, a non-executive director of Hansa Ltd, is offered the statutory audit of Hansa's joint venture company. CA Hema is offered the role of authorised representative in India of a foreign company she does not audit. CA Ishan, in service, wants to register on the tax portal as an e-return intermediary and to certify the returns he files. CA Jaya has kept a former client's books and vouchers until her unpaid fees are settled.

items.stem: Which of the matters SQC 1 lists on the integrity of a client are engaged, and what must Meera's firm do if it still accepts?

options.text: Nearly all of them — indications that the client might be involved in money laundering or other criminal activities, the reasons for the proposed appointment of the firm and the non-reappointment of the previous one, the identity and business reputation of the principal owners, an inappropriate limitation in the scope of work over the stock records, and a client aggressively concerned with keeping the firm's fees as low as possible; if the firm accepts despite the issues it must document how they were resolved
options.why: On the integrity of a client SQC 1 has the firm consider the identity and business reputation of the client's principal owners, key management, related parties and those charged with governance; the nature of the client's operations and business practices; the attitude of those people to aggressive interpretation of accounting standards and the internal control environment; whether the client is aggressively concerned with maintaining the firm's fees as low as possible; indications of an inappropriate limitation in the scope of work; indications that the client might be involved in money laundering or other criminal activities; and the reasons for the proposed appointment of the firm and non-reappointment of the previous firm. The searches, the cash, the penny stocks, the complaint about the last auditor, the fee condition and the closed stock records each land on one of them. And where issues have been identified and the firm decides to accept or continue the client relationship or the engagement, it should document how the issues were resolved.

options.text: The searches and the fees, and the firm must decline — SQC 1 forbids accepting a client against whom any such indication exists
options.misconception: turns the integrity matters into an automatic bar, when SQC 1 has the firm consider them and, if it accepts despite identified issues, document how they were resolved
options.why: SQC 1 does not forbid acceptance; it requires the firm to consider the matters and, where issues have been identified and it still accepts, to document how the issues were resolved. The closed stock records are a further matter, an inappropriate limitation in scope.

options.text: Only the searches — a client's view of fees and of the previous auditor are commercial matters outside the quality control system
options.misconception: strips fees and the previous auditor out of the integrity matters, when SQC 1 names a client aggressively concerned with low fees and the reasons for non-reappointment of the previous firm
options.why: Both are on the list: whether the client is aggressively concerned with maintaining the firm's fees as low as possible, and the reasons for the proposed appointment of the firm and non-reappointment of the previous firm.

options.text: None yet — integrity is judged from the audit evidence once the engagement has begun, and acceptance turns only on whether the firm has the time and staff
options.misconception: postpones the integrity assessment to the fieldwork, when SQC 1 requires the information to be obtained before accepting a new client and lists integrity matters alongside capability
options.why: The firm obtains the information it considers necessary before accepting an engagement with a new client, and integrity is the first of the two heads it considers; capability, competence, time and resources is the second, not the only one.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 acceptance and continuance: the matters on the integrity of a client including money laundering, reasons for non-reappointment of the previous firm, fee pressure and scope limitation, and documenting how identified issues were resolved; Test Your Understanding 3

items.scenario: At a social function a businessman offers CA Meera the tax audits of his five family-owned firms at generous fees, complaining that his present auditor "asks too many questions". Over coffee a week later she learns that the Enforcement Directorate searched his premises a month ago and recovered a large sum in cash, and that the income-tax department has searched them over bogus capital gains on penny stocks. He adds that he does not want the audit fee to be "a rupee more than last year's" and that the stock records at two firms are "not for auditors".

items.stem: What do SQC 1's continuance and withdrawal policies require?

options.text: The manager's course — the continuance policies apply only at the annual renewal of the engagement, and mid-year information waits for it
options.misconception: confines continuance to the annual renewal, when the policies apply the moment the firm obtains information that would have caused it to decline
options.why: The trigger is obtaining information that would have caused the firm to decline the engagement if obtainable earlier, whenever it arrives; the policies then require consideration of reporting responsibilities and of withdrawal.

options.text: Neither course — the firm considers the professional and legal responsibilities that apply, including whether it must report to the person who made the appointment or to regulatory authorities, and the possibility of withdrawing from the engagement or from the client relationship too; if it withdraws it discusses the withdrawal and its reasons with management and those charged with governance, considers whether any requirement obliges it to remain or to report the withdrawal to regulators, and documents the significant issues, consultations and conclusions
options.why: Where the firm obtains information that would have caused it to decline an engagement had it been obtainable earlier, its policies on continuance include consideration of the professional and legal responsibilities that apply, including whether there is a requirement to report to the person or persons who made the appointment or, in some cases, to regulatory authorities, and the possibility of withdrawing from the engagement or from both the engagement and the client relationship. The withdrawal policies address discussing with the appropriate level of management and those charged with governance the action the firm might take; if withdrawal is appropriate, discussing with them the withdrawal and the reasons for it; considering whether there is a professional, regulatory or legal requirement for the firm to remain in place or to report the withdrawal with its reasons to regulatory authorities; and documenting significant issues, consultations, conclusions and the basis for the conclusions. A one-line letter skips the discussion, the reporting question and the documentation; the manager's view denies the possibility of withdrawal that the policies expressly contemplate.

options.text: The firm must withdraw, and must report the promoter to the regulator in every case — SQC 1 makes both mandatory
options.misconception: makes withdrawal and reporting automatic, when SQC 1 requires the firm to consider the possibility of withdrawing and whether a requirement to report exists
options.why: The policies require consideration of the possibility of withdrawal and of whether a professional, regulatory or legal requirement to report exists; neither is automatic, and a requirement to remain in place is itself among the things to consider.

options.text: The partner's course — a firm may withdraw whenever a client's integrity fails, and the less said the better for confidentiality
options.misconception: treats withdrawal as a private act, when the policies require discussion with management and those charged with governance, consideration of reporting to regulators, and documentation
options.why: Withdrawal under SQC 1 is discussed with the appropriate level of the client's management and those charged with governance, with its reasons, and the firm considers whether it must report the withdrawal to regulatory authorities and documents the issues and conclusions.

citation.ref: Ch. Quality Control — SQC 1 continuance where information would have caused the firm to decline: professional and legal responsibilities including reporting to the appointer or regulators, the possibility of withdrawal, and the four withdrawal policies on discussion, reasons, the requirement to remain or report, and documentation
