The finance head proposes to bring the building into investment property at ₹9 crore, route the ₹3 crore difference through other comprehensive income, and carry it at fair value every year after.
written.question: Advise on each part of the proposal, stating the amount at which the building enters investment property and how it is measured afterwards.

points.text: Confirm the reclassification itself. A property is transferred to or from investment property when, and only when, there is a change in use, and the end of owner-occupation is one of the standard's own examples of evidence of a change in use. A change in management's intentions in isolation would not have been enough.

citation.ref: Transfers — evidence of a change in use

points.text: Reject the ₹9 crore. Transfers between investment property, owner-occupied property and inventories do not change the carrying amount of the property transferred and do not change its cost for measurement or disclosure purposes, so the building enters investment property at ₹6 crore.

citation.ref: Para 59 — transfers do not change carrying amount or cost

keywords: do not change the carrying amount

points.text: Reject the ₹3 crore to other comprehensive income. Nothing is remeasured on the transfer, so no gain arises; there is no revaluation surplus because the building was held under the cost model of Ind AS 16 and not the revaluation model.

citation.ref: Para 59 read with the Ind AS 16 cost model

points.text: Reject carrying it at fair value. An entity shall adopt as its accounting policy the cost model for all of its investment property, measured in accordance with the requirements in Ind AS 16 for the cost model, so depreciation continues on the ₹6 crore carrying amount.

citation.ref: Measurement after recognition — cost model as the accounting policy

keywords: cost model for all of its investment property

points.text: Say what the ₹9 crore is for. Entities are required to measure the fair value of investment property for the purpose of disclosure only, even though they follow the cost model.

citation.ref: Measurement after recognition — fair value measured for disclosure

keywords: for the purpose of disclosure only

written.scenario: The Salem unit of Devipur Ltd is a cash-generating unit. At 31 March 20X6 its carrying amounts, in ₹ lakh, are goodwill 100, building 300, plant 150 and a patent 50, a total of 600. An impairment indicator is present and the recoverable amount of the unit is assessed at ₹450 lakh. The patent could be sold on its own for ₹50 lakh with ₹2 lakh of legal costs. The recoverable amounts of the building and the plant cannot be determined individually because neither generates cash inflows that are largely independent.
written.question: Compute the impairment loss and allocate it, showing the carrying amount of each asset after the allocation.

points.text: Compute the loss. The recoverable amount of a unit is the higher of its fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use, and an impairment loss arises only if it is less than the carrying amount. Here ₹600 lakh less ₹450 lakh gives an impairment loss of ₹150 lakh.

citation.ref: Recoverable amount and recognition of an impairment loss for a cash-generating unit

keywords: higher of its fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use

points.text: State the order of allocation, which is where the marks sit: first, to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill allocated to the cash-generating unit; then, to the other assets of the unit pro rata on the basis of the carrying amount of each asset. So goodwill absorbs ₹100 lakh and falls to nil.

citation.ref: Allocation of an impairment loss for a cash-generating unit — order of allocation

keywords: first, to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill
pro rata on the basis of the carrying amount

points.text: Allocate the remaining ₹50 lakh over the other assets, whose carrying amounts total ₹500 lakh — building 50 × 300/500 = ₹30 lakh, plant 50 × 150/500 = ₹15 lakh, patent 50 × 50/500 = ₹5 lakh.

citation.ref: Allocation of an impairment loss pro rata to the other assets of the unit

points.text: Apply the floor. In allocating an impairment loss the carrying amount of an individual asset shall not be reduced below the highest of its fair value less costs of disposal, its value in use, and zero. The patent's fair value less costs of disposal is 50 − 2 = ₹48 lakh, so it can absorb only ₹2 lakh of the ₹5 lakh.

citation.ref: Limit on allocation to an individual asset within a cash-generating unit

keywords: shall not be reduced below the highest of
fair value less costs of disposal

points.text: Reallocate the excess. The ₹3 lakh that would otherwise have been allocated to the patent is allocated pro rata to the other assets of the unit — building 3 × 300/450 = ₹2 lakh, plant 3 × 150/450 = ₹1 lakh.

citation.ref: Reallocation of the unallocated portion of an impairment loss

keywords: allocated pro rata to the other assets

points.text: State the closing position. Goodwill nil, building 300 − 32 = ₹268 lakh, plant 150 − 16 = ₹134 lakh, patent ₹48 lakh, which totals ₹450 lakh and agrees with the recoverable amount of the unit.

citation.ref: Carrying amount of the unit after allocation of the impairment loss

written.scenario: Hansa Ltd sells its warehouse to Ferrum Leasing for cash of ₹20,00,000, which is also the fair value of the warehouse on that date. Immediately before the sale the warehouse is carried in Hansa's books at ₹12,00,000. On the same day Hansa takes the warehouse back on a lease for twelve years at annual rentals payable at each year end; the present value of those rentals, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease, is ₹8,00,000. There is no repurchase option and the transfer meets the requirements of Ind AS 115 for a performance obligation satisfied by transferring control. Hansa does not take the short-term or low-value exemption.
written.question: Show how Hansa Ltd, the seller-lessee, accounts for the transaction on the date of sale, including the journal entry.

points.text: Establish that a sale has occurred. Both parties apply the requirements of Ind AS 115 on when a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of an asset. The existence of a leaseback in isolation does not preclude a sale, because a lease transfers only the right to control the use of the asset; had there been a substantive repurchase option, no sale would have occurred and the whole transaction would have been a financing transaction.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback transactions — assessing whether the transfer is a sale

keywords: in isolation does not preclude a sale

points.text: Check the terms for off-market pricing. Because the consideration of ₹20,00,000 equals the fair value of the asset, no adjustment arises; a sale price below fair value would have been a prepayment of lease payments and one above fair value an additional financing provided by the buyer-lessor.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — adjustments for off-market terms

points.text: Measure the right-of-use asset at the proportion of the previous carrying amount of the asset that relates to the right of use retained by the seller-lessee: (12,00,000 / 20,00,000) × 8,00,000 = ₹4,80,000. It is not measured at fair value and not at the full carrying amount.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — measurement of the right-of-use asset by the seller-lessee

keywords: proportion of the previous carrying amount

points.text: Split the gain. The total gain is fair value ₹20,00,000 less carrying amount ₹12,00,000 = ₹8,00,000, of which the portion relating to the right retained, (8,00,000 / 20,00,000) × 8,00,000 = ₹3,20,000, is not recognised because that right has not been transferred.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — gain restricted to the rights transferred

points.text: Recognise only the amount of the gain that relates to the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor: 8,00,000 − 3,20,000 = ₹4,80,000.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — recognition of the gain on rights transferred

points.text: Give the entry: Cash Dr ₹20,00,000 and Right-of-use asset Dr ₹4,80,000; to Warehouse ₹12,00,000, to Lease liability ₹8,00,000 and to Gain on rights transferred ₹4,80,000. The underlying asset is derecognised in full and the leaseback is then accounted for as any other lease.

citation.ref: Sale and leaseback — seller-lessee accounting on the date of sale

written.scenario: On 20 February 20X6 the board of Girnar Ltd decided to close its Nagpur plant. A detailed plan approved on 10 March 20X6 names the plant, its 240 workmen, the amounts to be spent and a start date of 1 May 20X6. Letters went to the workmen and to customers on 15 March 20X6. The year end is 31 March 20X6. The estimates are: retrenchment compensation ₹9.00 crore; retraining and relocating 60 workmen who move to the Pune plant ₹2.00 crore; marketing the Pune product line ₹1.50 crore; a new IT system at Pune ₹3.00 crore; operating losses of the Nagpur plant for April 20X6 ₹1.20 crore; an expected gain of ₹6.00 crore on selling the Nagpur land. Separately, a non-cancellable contract obliges Girnar to buy 20,000 units of a raw material used only at Nagpur at ₹500 a unit; the material can be resold at ₹430 a unit, and the supplier will release Girnar for ₹18 lakh.
written.question: State whether a restructuring provision is required at 31 March 20X6 and compute the amount, giving your reason for including or excluding each item.

points.text: Set out the test. A constructive obligation to restructure arises only when the entity has a detailed formal plan identifying the business concerned, the principal locations affected, the location, function and approximate number of employees who will be compensated for terminating their services, the expenditures to be undertaken and when the plan will be implemented, and has raised a valid expectation in those affected by starting to implement the plan or announcing its main features to them.

citation.ref: Para 72 — constructive obligation to restructure

points.text: Conclude that the obligation exists. The board decision of 20 February would not by itself have created an obligation, but the letters of 15 March communicated the plan before the end of the reporting period, so a provision is recognised at 31 March 20X6.

citation.ref: Board decision before the reporting date — announcement or implementation required

keywords: before the end of the reporting period

points.text: Measure it on direct expenditures only — those both necessarily entailed by the restructuring and not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity. The retrenchment compensation of ₹9.00 crore meets both tests and goes in.

citation.ref: A restructuring provision includes only direct expenditures

keywords: not associated with the ongoing activities

points.text: Exclude the three costs the standard names. Retraining or relocating continuing staff ₹2.00 crore, marketing ₹1.50 crore and investment in new systems and distribution networks ₹3.00 crore all relate to the future conduct of the business and are recognised as they arise.

citation.ref: Costs excluded from a restructuring provision

points.text: Exclude the other two. Identifiable future operating losses up to the date of a restructuring are not included unless they relate to an onerous contract, so ₹1.20 crore is out; and gains on the expected disposal of assets are not taken into account in measuring the provision even where the sale is part of the restructuring, so the ₹6.00 crore is not netted off.

citation.ref: Future operating losses and gains on expected disposal of assets

keywords: unless they relate to an onerous contract

points.text: Provide separately for the supply contract. It is onerous because the unavoidable costs of meeting the obligations exceed the economic benefits expected to be received, and the unavoidable cost is the least net cost of exiting, being the lower of the cost of fulfilling it, ₹1,00,00,000 − ₹86,00,000 = ₹14 lakh, and the ₹18 lakh penalty for failing to fulfil it. So ₹14 lakh is provided, after first recognising any impairment loss on the assets used in fulfilling that contract.

citation.ref: Onerous contracts — measurement at the lower of fulfilment cost and penalty

written.scenario: Rampur Alloys Ltd has made losses in each of the last three years and carries forward unused tax losses of ₹80 crore. Against the same taxation authority and the same taxable entity it has taxable temporary differences of ₹30 crore that will reverse before the losses expire. The board's five-year plan shows a return to profit from next year, built on a new product yet to be launched. The tax rate is 25%.
written.question: Advise the amount of deferred tax asset that may be recognised and the disclosure that goes with it.

points.text: State the recognition rule. A deferred tax asset shall be recognised for the carry forward of unused tax losses to the extent that it is probable that future taxable profit will be available against which the unused tax losses can be utilised.

citation.ref: Recognition of deferred tax assets for unused tax losses and unused tax credits

keywords: carry forward of unused tax losses
probable that future taxable profit will be available

points.text: Add the caution that decides this case. The existence of unused tax losses is strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available, so where an entity has a history of recent losses it recognises the asset only to the extent that it has sufficient taxable temporary differences or there is convincing other evidence that sufficient taxable profit will be available.

citation.ref: History of recent losses — restriction on recognising a deferred tax asset

keywords: strong evidence that future taxable profit may not be available

points.text: Apply it. The taxable temporary differences of ₹30 crore relate to the same taxation authority and the same taxable entity and reverse before expiry, so a deferred tax asset of 30 × 25% = ₹7.50 crore is recognised. A board plan resting on an unlaunched product is not convincing other evidence, so nothing is recognised on the balance of ₹50 crore.

citation.ref: Assessing whether taxable profit will be available against unused tax losses

points.text: Give the disclosure that goes with a recognition of this kind: the amount of the deferred tax asset and the nature of the evidence supporting its recognition.

citation.ref: Para 82 — disclosure where recognition depends on future taxable profit

keywords: amount of the deferred tax asset
nature of the evidence supporting its recognition

points.text: Close with the reassessment. At the end of each reporting period the entity reassesses unrecognised deferred tax assets and recognises a previously unrecognised asset to the extent it has become probable that future taxable profits will allow it to be recovered.

citation.ref: Reassessment of unrecognised deferred tax assets at each reporting date

written.scenario: A competition regulator orders Vasant Ltd's owners to divest within 90 days. On 1 July 20X6 Arka Ltd acquires 75% of the equity of Vasant Ltd for cash of ₹90 crore. A qualified valuer measures the identifiable net assets acquired, in accordance with Ind AS 103, at ₹128 crore, and the fair value of the 25% non-controlling interest at ₹30 crore. Arka's board is minded to credit the difference to profit for the year and to show part of it as attributable to the non-controlling shareholders.
written.question: Compute the gain under both permitted measurement bases for non-controlling interest, state where it is recognised, and set out the steps Arka must take before recognising it.

points.text: Define the position. A bargain purchase arises in extremely rare circumstances where the value of the identifiable net assets acquired exceeds the consideration transferred plus the amount of any non-controlling interest, and a forced sale in which the seller is acting under compulsion — as here, a regulator's divestment order — is the standard's own example.

citation.ref: Bargain purchase — circumstances in which a gain arises

points.text: Set out the gate before recognition. The acquirer shall determine whether there exists clear evidence of the underlying reasons for classifying the combination as a bargain purchase, and if it does, reassess whether it has correctly identified all of the assets acquired and all of the liabilities assumed, and then review the procedures used to measure the identifiable assets and liabilities, the non-controlling interest, any previously held equity interest and the consideration transferred.

citation.ref: Reassessment required before recognising a gain on a bargain purchase

keywords: clear evidence of the underlying reasons
correctly identified all of the assets acquired
review the procedures used to measure

points.text: Compute with non-controlling interest at fair value: consideration ₹90 crore plus non-controlling interest ₹30 crore is ₹120 crore, against identifiable net assets of ₹128 crore, giving a gain of ₹8 crore.

citation.ref: Measurement of the gain where non-controlling interest is measured at fair value

points.text: Compute with non-controlling interest at its proportionate share of the identifiable net assets: 128 × 25% = ₹32 crore, so ₹90 crore plus ₹32 crore is ₹122 crore and the gain is ₹6 crore. The choice of basis is available for each business combination and changes the size of the gain.

citation.ref: Non-controlling interest measurement choice and its effect on the bargain purchase gain

keywords: proportionate share of the identifiable net assets

points.text: Correct the board on where it goes. Because clear evidence of the reason exists, the gain is recognised in other comprehensive income on the acquisition date and accumulated in equity as capital reserve. It does not go to profit or loss. Had no clear evidence existed, the gain would have been recognised directly in equity as capital reserve.

citation.ref: Recognition of a bargain purchase gain in OCI and accumulation as capital reserve

keywords: accumulated in equity as capital reserve
does not go to profit or loss

points.text: Correct the second error. The gain shall be attributed to the acquirer and there will be no allocation to the non-controlling shareholders.

citation.ref: Attribution of the bargain purchase gain wholly to the acquirer

keywords: no allocation to the non-controlling shareholders

written.scenario: Malwa Ltd holds a subsidiary, an associate and a joint venture, and prepares consolidated financial statements as well as its own separate financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013. Its finance head proposes to carry the subsidiary at cost, the associate under the equity method and the joint venture at fair value through profit or loss in the separate financial statements, and to credit an interim dividend declared by the subsidiary's board in March to the carrying amount of the investment.
written.question: State the measurement options Ind AS 27 permits in separate financial statements, comment on each part of the proposal, and give the reason India departed from IAS 27 here.

points.text: State the options. An entity shall account for investments in subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures either at cost, or in accordance with Ind AS 109, and it shall apply the same accounting for each category of investments.

citation.ref: Para 10 — accounting for investments in separate financial statements

points.text: Reject the equity method for the associate. It is not one of the two options in Ind AS 27 and cannot be used in separate financial statements, whichever category the investment falls in.

citation.ref: Para 10 — the equity method is not available in separate financial statements

keywords: not one of the two options
cannot be used in separate financial statements

points.text: Give the reason for the carve-out from IAS 27, which permits the equity method: the equity method is not a measurement basis like cost and fair value but is a manner of consolidation, and allowing it would lead to inconsistent accounting conceptually.

citation.ref: Appendix 1 — carve-out from IAS 27 on the equity method

points.text: Correct the dividend treatment. A dividend from a subsidiary, an associate or a joint venture is recognised in profit or loss in the separate financial statements when the entity's right to receive the dividend is established, not deducted from the carrying amount of the investment.

citation.ref: Recognition of dividends from subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures

keywords: right to receive the dividend is established

written.scenario: Nandan Ltd will present its first Ind AS financial statements for the year ending 31 March 20X6, with one year of comparative information. There is no change in its functional currency. Management wants to use fair value as deemed cost for two plants where valuations are available, previous GAAP carrying values for the rest of its property, plant and equipment because the old records are incomplete, and fair value for a let-out office block held as investment property. Its subsidiary wants to use fair value for all of its own plant in its standalone financial statements.
written.question: State the date of transition and advise on each of the four proposals.

points.text: Fix the date of transition, which is the beginning of the earliest period for which the entity presents full comparative information — 1 April 20X4 — and that is the date at which the opening Ind AS Balance Sheet is prepared.

citation.ref: Date of transition to Ind AS and the opening Ind AS Balance Sheet

points.text: Confirm the fair value option. An entity may elect to measure an item of property, plant and equipment at the date of transition at its fair value and use that fair value as its deemed cost, and that election may be made on an item-by-item basis.

citation.ref: Para D5 — fair value as deemed cost for property, plant and equipment

keywords: fair value as its deemed cost

points.text: Refuse the mixture. The option to use previous GAAP carrying values as deemed cost has to be applied to all items of property, plant and equipment, so it cannot be taken for some assets while fair value is used for others; management must choose one route for the whole class.

citation.ref: Para D7AA — previous GAAP carrying value applied to all items

keywords: all items of property, plant and equipment
cannot be taken for some assets

points.text: Refuse fair value for the investment property. Ind AS 40 permits only the cost model, so the option of fair value as deemed cost is not available for investment property to a first-time adopter, though the previous GAAP carrying value option does extend to it.

citation.ref: Deemed cost for investment property read with Ind AS 40

points.text: Deal with the subsidiary. Nothing prevents different entities within a group from choosing different bases for their standalone financial statements, but in consolidated financial statements the entire group is treated as one reporting entity, so different bases may not be used there.

citation.ref: Deemed cost elections within a group for consolidated financial statements

keywords: different bases for their standalone financial statements

written.scenario: Sarvodaya Ltd runs a funded defined benefit gratuity plan. At 1 April 20X5 the present value of the obligation is ₹40,00,000 and the fair value of plan assets is ₹34,00,000. The discount rate on high quality corporate bonds is 8%. During the year the current service cost is ₹6,00,000, benefits of ₹3,00,000 are paid out of the fund and the company contributes ₹5,00,000, both on the last day of the year. On 31 March 20X6 the company amends the plan, raising the benefit for past service by ₹2,00,000. The actuary reports the closing obligation at ₹47,50,000 and the closing fair value of plan assets at ₹38,00,000. There is no asset ceiling.
written.question: Compute the amounts to be recognised in profit or loss and in other comprehensive income for the year, and reconcile the opening and closing net defined benefit liability.

points.text: Split the components first. Service cost, comprising current service cost, past service cost and any gain or loss on settlement, and net interest on the net defined benefit liability go to profit or loss; remeasurements of the net defined benefit liability go to other comprehensive income.

citation.ref: Components of defined benefit cost and where each is recognised

keywords: net interest on the net defined benefit liability

points.text: Compute net interest as the discount rate applied to the opening net defined benefit liability of 40,00,000 − 34,00,000 = ₹6,00,000, that is 8% × 6,00,000 = ₹48,000, which is the change during the period that arises from the passage of time.

citation.ref: Net interest on the net defined benefit liability (asset)

points.text: Charge the plan amendment in full. Past service cost is the change in the present value of the obligation for employee service in prior periods resulting from a plan amendment, and it is recognised as an expense at the earlier of the date the amendment occurs and the date related restructuring costs or termination benefits are recognised — so the whole ₹2,00,000 is expensed this year, not spread.

citation.ref: Recognition of past service cost on a plan amendment

points.text: Total the profit or loss charge: current service cost ₹6,00,000 plus past service cost ₹2,00,000 plus net interest ₹48,000 = ₹8,48,000.

citation.ref: Amounts recognised in profit or loss for a defined benefit plan

points.text: Roll the obligation forward to isolate the actuarial gain: 40,00,000 + interest 3,20,000 + 6,00,000 + 2,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹48,20,000 against the actuary's ₹47,50,000, an actuarial gain of ₹70,000 arising from experience adjustments or changes in actuarial assumptions.

citation.ref: Actuarial gains and losses as a component of remeasurements

points.text: Roll the plan assets forward: 34,00,000 + interest income 2,72,000 + contributions 5,00,000 − benefits 3,00,000 = ₹38,72,000 against the actual ₹38,00,000, so the return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest is a loss of ₹72,000.

citation.ref: Return on plan assets as a component of remeasurements

keywords: return on plan assets excluding amounts included in net interest

points.text: Close it out. The net remeasurement is a loss of ₹2,000 in other comprehensive income, which shall not be reclassified to profit or loss in a subsequent period though it may be transferred within equity; and the closing net liability of 47,50,000 − 38,00,000 = ₹9,50,000 agrees with 6,00,000 + 8,48,000 + 2,000 − 5,00,000.

citation.ref: Remeasurements recognised in OCI are not reclassified to profit or loss

keywords: shall not be reclassified to profit or loss

written.scenario: Tapti Ltd issues 5% convertible debentures at par for ₹50,00,000 on 1 April 20X5. Interest is payable annually in arrears. At the end of the third year the holder may either convert each debenture into a fixed number of Tapti's equity shares or take redemption at par. The market rate for an otherwise identical debenture without the conversion option is 10%. Discount factors at 10% are 0.9091, 0.8264 and 0.7513, and the three-year annuity factor is 2.4868.
written.question: Classify the instrument, explain how it is split on initial recognition, and compute the amount of each component.

points.text: Classify it. The instrument is a compound financial instrument because it contains both a liability component, being the contractual obligation to pay interest and to deliver cash on redemption, and an equity component, being the holder's option to convert into a fixed number of the issuer's own equity instruments.

citation.ref: Compound financial instruments — separate presentation of components

points.text: State the method. Measure the liability component first, as the present value of the contractual cash flows of interest and principal discounted at the market rate at inception for a similar liability that does not have an associated equity component, ignoring the possibility of exercise of the conversion option.

citation.ref: Para 31 — split accounting for a compound financial instrument

keywords: similar liability that does not have an associated equity component

points.text: Compute the liability. Present value of the principal is 50,00,000 × 0.7513 = ₹37,56,500 and present value of the interest of ₹2,50,000 a year is 2,50,000 × 2.4868 = ₹6,21,700, giving a liability component of ₹43,78,200.

citation.ref: Para 31 — measurement of the liability component at present value

points.text: Assign the equity component the residual, being the fair value of the instrument as a whole less the amount separately determined for the liability component: 50,00,000 − 43,78,200 = ₹6,21,800. The two components always sum to the fair value of the instrument as a whole and no gain or loss arises from initially recognising the components separately.

citation.ref: Para 31 — equity component measured as the residual amount

written.scenario: Kestrel Foods Ltd had 30,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each outstanding throughout the year ended 31 March 2025 and reported a basic earnings per share of ₹3.20 on a profit of ₹96,00,000 for that year. On 1 July 2025 it made a rights issue of one share for every five held at ₹40 per share, fully taken up, when the market price immediately before the exercise of the rights was ₹64. Profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹1,26,00,000. The finance manager proposes to compute the 2025-26 earnings per share on a simple time-weighted average of 30,00,000 and 36,00,000 shares and to leave last year's ₹3.20 as reported.
written.question: Compute the basic earnings per share for the year ended 31 March 2026 and the restated figure for 2024-25 under Ind AS 33, explaining why the manager's approach is wrong.

points.text: A rights issue below market price carries a bonus element: it is treated as a bonus issue of part of the shares for no consideration plus an issue of the remainder at full market price, so the number of shares outstanding before the issue is adjusted by the fraction fair value immediately before exercise divided by the theoretical ex-rights fair value per share, for the current year and for every prior period presented. A simple time-weighting ignores the bonus element and leaves last year uncomparable.

citation.ref: Rights issue at a discount — the bonus element and the adjustment fraction applied to current and prior periods

points.text: Theoretical ex-rights price: five shares at ₹64 = ₹320 plus one right share at ₹40 = ₹360 for six shares, so ₹60 per share. The adjustment fraction is ₹64 ÷ ₹60 = 16/15, which corresponds to a bonus issue of 1 for 15.

citation.ref: Theoretical ex-rights fair value — outstanding shares at fair value plus rights proceeds, over shares after exercise

points.text: Weighted average for 2025-26: 30,00,000 × 16/15 × 3/12 = 8,00,000 for April to June, plus 36,00,000 × 9/12 = 27,00,000 for July to March, total 35,00,000 shares. Basic earnings per share = ₹1,26,00,000 ÷ 35,00,000 = ₹3.60.

citation.ref: Weighted average number of shares — bonus-adjusted shares before the rights issue, actual shares after

points.text: Restated 2024-25: 30,00,000 × 16/15 = 32,00,000 shares, so ₹96,00,000 ÷ 32,00,000 = ₹3.00, presented in place of the ₹3.20 originally reported; had the fraction been below one, the rights issue would instead be treated as an issue at full market price with no restatement.

citation.ref: Retrospective adjustment of prior period earnings per share for the bonus element of a rights issue

written.scenario: While preparing the financial statements of Sable Engineering Ltd for the year ended 31 March 2026, the accountant finds that depreciation of ₹12,00,000 on a plant commissioned in April 2024 was never charged in 2024-25 because the asset had been left in capital work-in-progress; the amount is material. In the same year the company also revised the remaining useful life of another machine from five years to three because of faster wear, which reduces that machine's carrying amount by ₹4,00,000 more than the old schedule would have. The chief financial officer wants both adjustments booked in 2025-26 as "prior period items", and adds that restating last year is "impracticable because the auditors have already signed it". Ignore tax.
written.question: State how each matter is treated under Ind AS 8, the effect on the comparative figures and opening equity, and whether the impracticability argument holds.

points.text: The omitted depreciation is a prior period error — an omission from prior period financial statements arising from a failure to use reliable information that was available and could reasonably have been obtained. Unless impracticable, a material prior period error is corrected retrospectively in the first financial statements approved for issue after its discovery by restating the comparative amounts for the prior period in which it occurred.

citation.ref: Correction of a material prior period error — retrospective restatement of the comparative period in which it occurred

points.text: So the 2024-25 comparative is restated: depreciation up by ₹12,00,000, profit for 2024-25 down by ₹12,00,000, the plant's carrying amount at 31 March 2025 down by ₹12,00,000, and opening retained earnings at 1 April 2025 reduced by ₹12,00,000 in the statement of changes in equity; nothing of the ₹12,00,000 passes through the 2025-26 profit or loss. The 2025-26 charge is the current year's own depreciation only.

citation.ref: Effect of retrospective restatement — comparative profit, carrying amount and opening equity; no charge in the current year

points.text: The useful life revision is a change in accounting estimate, not an error: it results from new information about the pattern of wear, and is recognised prospectively in profit or loss for 2025-26 and future periods — the ₹4,00,000 higher depreciation is a current year charge with no restatement of 2024-25.

citation.ref: Change in accounting estimate — prospective recognition; distinguished from an error

points.text: The impracticability argument fails. Applying a requirement is impracticable only when the entity cannot apply it after making every reasonable effort — where the effects are not determinable, where restatement would require assumptions about management's intent in that period, or where it needs significant estimates that cannot be objectively separated from hindsight. A signed audit report is none of these; the ₹12,00,000 is determinable from the fixed asset register.

citation.ref: Definition of impracticable — the three limbs; an issued audit report is not one of them

written.scenario: On 1 April 2023 Lumen Glass Ltd bought a furnace for ₹2,00,00,000 with a ten-year life and no residual value, depreciated on the straight-line basis, and received a government grant of ₹40,00,000 towards it on condition that the plant employ at least 200 workers from the district for five years. Lumen presented the grant as deferred income. On 1 April 2026 the district employment fell below the condition and the entire ₹40,00,000 became repayable. The finance head asks whether the repayment is a prior period error and what the numbers would have been had the grant been deducted from the cost of the furnace instead.
written.question: Account for the repayment on 1 April 2026 under both presentations permitted by Ind AS 20, and state the nature of the adjustment.

points.text: A grant that becomes repayable is accounted for as a change in accounting estimate under Ind AS 8, not as a prior period error: the condition was met when the grant was recognised and the entity's reasonable assurance was justified at the time.

citation.ref: Repayment of a government grant — treated as a change in accounting estimate under Ind AS 8

keywords: not as a prior period error

points.text: Deferred income presentation: ₹4,00,000 of the grant has been released to profit or loss each year, so the unamortised deferred income at 1 April 2026 is ₹40,00,000 less three years at ₹4,00,000 = ₹28,00,000. The repayment of ₹40,00,000 is applied first against that ₹28,00,000, and the ₹12,00,000 by which it exceeds the deferred income is recognised immediately in profit or loss.

citation.ref: Repayment — first against unamortised deferred income, the excess recognised immediately in profit or loss

points.text: Deduction-from-asset presentation: the furnace would have been carried at ₹1,60,00,000 and depreciated at ₹16,00,000 a year, giving ₹1,12,00,000 at 1 April 2026; the repayment increases the carrying amount by ₹40,00,000 to ₹1,52,00,000, and the cumulative additional depreciation of three years at ₹4,00,000 = ₹12,00,000 that would have been charged without the grant is recognised immediately as an expense.

citation.ref: Repayment of a grant related to an asset — increase the carrying amount; cumulative additional depreciation recognised immediately

points.text: Under either presentation the charge to 2025-26 profit or loss on repayment is ₹12,00,000 and depreciation from 2026-27 rises to ₹20,00,000 a year on the remaining seven years, so the presentation choice changes where the numbers sit, not the total; Lumen also considers whether the impairment indicators in Ind AS 36 are triggered by the loss of the grant.

citation.ref: Circumstances giving rise to repayment may require consideration of impairment of the asset

written.scenario: On 1 April 2024 Nova Analytics Ltd granted 1,000 share options each to 50 senior engineers, vesting on 31 March 2027 subject to continued employment; the grant-date fair value was ₹30 per option. By 31 March 2025 the share price had fallen and on 1 April 2025 the board reduced the exercise price, which raised the fair value of each option by ₹9 at the modification date. All 50 engineers are expected to and do remain in service. The finance controller proposes to remeasure the whole award at its new fair value and spread it over the remaining two years, and asks separately what would happen if the board had instead cancelled the options on 1 April 2025 and paid each engineer ₹25,000.
written.question: Compute the expense for each of the three years and explain the accounting for the cancellation alternative.

points.text: The controller is wrong: an entity recognises, as a minimum, the services measured at the grant-date fair value as if the award were not modified, and a modification that increases fair value adds only the incremental fair value, spread from the modification date to the vesting date of the modified options. Year 2024-25: 50 × 1,000 × ₹30 × 1/3 = ₹5,00,000.

citation.ref: Modification — minimum of the grant-date cost; incremental fair value recognised over the period from modification to vesting

points.text: Year 2025-26: original award 50 × 1,000 × ₹30 × 2/3 = ₹10,00,000 cumulative less ₹5,00,000 = ₹5,00,000, plus incremental 50 × 1,000 × ₹9 ÷ 2 years = ₹2,25,000, total ₹7,25,000. Year 2026-27: ₹5,00,000 plus ₹2,25,000 = ₹7,25,000. Total over three years ₹19,50,000, being ₹15,00,000 at grant-date value plus ₹4,50,000 incremental.

citation.ref: Expense pattern after a modification — original cost on the original schedule, increment over the remaining period

points.text: Had the modification reduced fair value, the entity would continue to account for the services as if the modification had not occurred; the decrease is ignored, because the grant-date cost is a floor.

citation.ref: A modification that reduces fair value is not taken into account

points.text: Cancellation on 1 April 2025 is an acceleration of vesting: the amount that would have been recognised over the remaining two years, ₹10,00,000, is recognised immediately. The ₹25,000 paid per engineer, ₹12,50,000 in all, is accounted for as a repurchase of an equity interest, deducted from equity, except that any excess of the payment over the fair value of the instruments at the repurchase date is recognised as an expense.

citation.ref: Cancellation or settlement during vesting — acceleration of vesting; payment as a repurchase of equity, excess over fair value as expense

written.scenario: The board of Vesper Retail Ltd proposes three entries for the year ended 31 March 2026: to recognise an asset of ₹50 crore for the "Vesper" brand it has built through advertising over twenty years, at a valuer's estimate; to leave out of the balance sheet a ₹6 crore claim against a supplier on which the company has won at first instance but the supplier has appealed; and to provide ₹8 crore for warranty costs against a best estimate of ₹3 crore, "to be prudent".
written.question: Evaluate each proposal against the Conceptual Framework's definition of an asset, its recognition criteria and its description of prudence.

points.text: An asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events, an economic resource being a right that has the potential to produce economic benefits. The brand may meet that definition, but recognition also requires that it provide relevant information and a faithful representation; the cost of an internally generated brand cannot be separated from the cost of developing the business, a valuer's estimate of it carries measurement uncertainty so high that it would not faithfully represent the asset, and Ind AS 38 accordingly prohibits it.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Definition of an asset; recognition only where relevance and faithful representation result; measurement uncertainty

points.text: The claim is a right arising from a past event, so it is an asset in definition; whether it is recognised turns on relevance — existence uncertainty and a low probability of inflow can make recognition uninformative — and on the specific standard, which treats a contingent asset as recognised only when the inflow is virtually certain. Pending the appeal it is disclosed, not recognised, and the Framework says an unrecognised item may still need to be made visible in the notes.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS with Ind AS 37
citation.ref: Recognition and relevance — existence uncertainty and low probability; contingent assets disclosed until virtually certain

points.text: Prudence is the exercise of caution under uncertainty and supports neutrality: assets and income are not overstated and liabilities and expenses are not understated, but equally it does not allow the overstatement of liabilities or expenses. A ₹8 crore provision against a ₹3 crore best estimate is not prudence but bias, and Ind AS 37 measures a provision at the best estimate.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Prudence supports neutrality and does not permit overstatement of liabilities or expenses

written.scenario: Tarang Ceramics Ltd is an unlisted company and not a holding, subsidiary, joint venture or associate of any Ind AS company. Its audited standalone balance sheet at 31 March 2026 shows paid-up share capital ₹80 crore, securities premium ₹60 crore, general reserve ₹90 crore, revaluation reserve ₹40 crore, capital reserve arising on an amalgamation ₹30 crore, accumulated losses ₹10 crore and miscellaneous expenditure not written off ₹5 crore. The board believes the company must adopt Ind AS because "our reserves cross ₹300 crore". Its sister company, Tarang Tiles Pvt Ltd, has a net worth of ₹40 crore but is a subsidiary of a listed company that reports under Ind AS.
written.question: Compute Tarang Ceramics' net worth under section 2(57), state whether either company must apply Ind AS and from when, and explain what happens if the threshold is crossed later.

points.text: Net worth under section 2(57) is paid-up share capital plus reserves created out of profits and the securities premium account, less accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off, and excludes reserves created out of revaluation of assets, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation. So ₹80 + ₹60 + ₹90 − ₹10 − ₹5 = ₹215 crore; the revaluation reserve and the amalgamation reserve are left out.

citation.source: Companies Act, 2013 with Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015
citation.ref: Section 2(57) — net worth, and the exclusion of revaluation, write-back and amalgamation reserves

points.text: At ₹215 crore Tarang Ceramics is below the ₹250 crore threshold for unlisted companies and is not covered by the roadmap; it continues with the Accounting Standards, though it may adopt Ind AS voluntarily.

citation.ref: Phase II — unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more; voluntary adoption

points.text: Tarang Tiles Pvt Ltd must apply Ind AS despite its ₹40 crore net worth, because the roadmap covers holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies of a company that is covered.

citation.ref: Coverage of holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies of a covered company

points.text: A company that does not meet the criteria reassesses net worth at each balance sheet date; if Tarang Ceramics crosses ₹250 crore in the audited statements for the year ending 31 March 2027, it applies Ind AS for 2027-28 with comparatives for 2026-27, the net worth being taken from the first audited statements in which it meets the threshold.

citation.ref: Reassessment at each balance sheet date; Ind AS from the following year with comparatives

written.scenario: At 31 March 2026 Helix Motors Ltd has four liabilities. A ₹50 crore term loan repayable in June 2027, on which the company breached a debt-service covenant in March 2026 making the loan repayable on demand; on 20 April 2026, before the accounts were approved, the bank waived the breach. A ₹30 crore term loan on identical terms with the same breach, but on which a second bank agreed on 25 March 2026 to a grace period until 30 June 2027 during which it cannot demand repayment. Commercial paper of ₹20 crore maturing on 30 September 2026 which the company expects to roll over under an existing three-year facility at its own discretion. A deferred tax liability of ₹8 crore. The finance controller proposes to show all four as non-current "since none will actually be paid this year".
written.question: Classify each liability under Ind AS 1 with reasons.

points.text: A liability is current when the entity expects to settle it in its normal operating cycle, holds it primarily for trading, it is due to be settled within twelve months after the reporting period, or the entity does not have an unconditional right to defer settlement for at least twelve months after the reporting period; expectation of payment is not the test, the right to defer is.

citation.ref: The four criteria for a current liability

points.text: The ₹50 crore loan is current. A breach on or before the reporting date that makes the loan payable on demand removes the right to defer, and a waiver obtained after the reporting period and before approval of the statements does not change the classification — it is a non-adjusting event to be disclosed.

citation.ref: Breach of a long-term loan covenant — current even if the lender waives after the reporting period

points.text: The ₹30 crore loan is non-current, because the lender agreed by the end of the reporting period to a period of grace ending at least twelve months after it, within which the breach can be rectified and during which the lender cannot demand immediate repayment.

citation.ref: Grace period agreed by the reporting date ending at least twelve months later — non-current

points.text: The commercial paper is non-current only because Helix both expects and has the discretion to roll it over for at least twelve months under an existing facility; had there been no arrangement, the potential to refinance is ignored and the paper is current. The deferred tax liability is always classified as non-current.

citation.ref: Refinancing at the entity's discretion under an existing facility; deferred tax liabilities non-current

written.scenario: The newly appointed accountant of Orion Pharma Ltd, an Ind AS company, drafts its financial statements in a horizontal balance sheet format, recognises a proposed dividend as a liability "because Schedule III has a line for it", drops several Ind AS disclosures as "Schedule III does not ask for them", and reproduces every accounting policy in the standard's own words across forty pages so that "nothing can be said to be missing".
written.question: Comment on each decision by reference to the scope of Schedule III and the best practices in preparing financial statements.

points.text: Schedule III applies through section 129(1) to every company's financial statements and, for Ind AS companies, its Division II prescribes only the vertical format of the balance sheet; no horizontal alternative exists, so the draft must be recast.

citation.source: Companies Act, 2013 — Schedule III, Division II
citation.ref: Scope of Schedule III under section 129(1); vertical format only

points.text: Schedule III does not prescribe accounting treatment: the presence of a line item in its format does not imply that the item can be recognised, and recognition follows the standards — a proposed dividend is not a liability until approved, so it is disclosed and not recognised.

citation.source: Companies Act, 2013 — Schedule III with Ind AS 10
citation.ref: Schedule III prescribes presentation, not recognition; dividends proposed after the reporting date

points.text: The disclosure requirements of Schedule III are in addition to, and not in substitution of, those in the notified standards, so an Ind AS disclosure cannot be dropped because Schedule III is silent on it; the terms used in Schedule III carry the meanings given in the standards.

citation.source: Companies Act, 2013 — Schedule III, General Instructions
citation.ref: Schedule III disclosures are additional to those of the applicable standards

points.text: Forty pages of boilerplate policies is the opposite of best practice: lack of clarity in applying materiality is a main driver of overloaded financial statements, and entity-specific policies, integration of notes and effective use of materiality make the statements more useful, not less complete.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Analysis of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Best practices — materiality as a filter against overloaded statements; entity-specific policies; integration of notes

written.scenario: Ritu, a chartered accountant employed as financial controller of a listed company, faces four situations in one month. A college friend who trades in shares asks her, over dinner, whether the rumoured acquisition of a competitor is going ahead; she knows it is. A court summons requires her to produce board papers in a supplier's suit. The Institute's peer reviewer of her former firm asks for working papers on an engagement she handled there. And she finds that the draft management discussion in the annual report describes a product recall as "voluntary and precautionary" when a regulator had ordered it; her managing director tells her to leave the wording alone.
written.question: Advise Ritu under the Code of Ethics on each situation.

points.text: The Code's five fundamental principles are integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour, and a chartered accountant in service is bound by all five; the first three situations turn on confidentiality and the fourth on integrity and the duty not to be associated with misleading information.

citation.source: ICAI Code of Ethics — Fundamental Principles
citation.ref: The five fundamental principles binding a chartered accountant in service

points.text: The friend: Ritu must not disclose or use confidential information acquired through her employment for the advantage of a third party; the acquisition is material unpublished information, and passing it on is a breach of confidentiality of the insider-trading kind, so she says nothing.

citation.ref: No use or disclosure of confidential information for a third party's advantage; insider trading as a breach

points.text: The summons and the peer reviewer are both within the permitted heads: disclosure is required by law where documents or evidence are produced in legal proceedings, and there is a professional duty or right to disclose, when not prohibited by law, to comply with peer review or quality review of the Institute; the third head is disclosure permitted by law and authorised by the employer.

citation.ref: Circumstances in which disclosure is required, permitted or a professional duty or right

points.text: The recall wording: when she knows or has reason to believe that information she is associated with is misleading, she must take appropriate action to seek to resolve it — discussing it with her superior and the appropriate level of management or those charged with governance and asking that it be corrected, or that users already given it be informed, and consulting the organisation's ethics or whistle-blowing policy; if it is not corrected she considers further steps, including refusing to remain associated with the information.

citation.source: ICAI Code of Ethics — Preparation and Presentation of Information
citation.ref: Addressing information that is or might be misleading — escalation, correction, and disassociation

written.scenario: Zenith Foods Ltd, a group of twelve companies, is choosing how to move its accounting to the cloud. One vendor offers a ready accounting application used through a browser on a subscription; another offers virtual servers and storage on a pay-as-you-go basis onto which Zenith would install its own software; a third offers a development platform on which Zenith's team would build its own consolidation application. The group also wants to automate the monthly collection of trial balances from the twelve companies and the intercompany eliminations, and its board asks what could go wrong once the books are online.
written.question: Identify the cloud service model in each offer, explain how robotic process automation would serve the consolidation, and name the cybersecurity threats the board should plan for.

points.text: The browser-based accounting application on subscription is Software as a Service; the virtual servers and storage on pay-as-you-go are Infrastructure as a Service, letting Zenith scale without physical hardware; the development platform is Platform as a Service, on which applications are built and deployed without managing the underlying infrastructure.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Accounting and Technology
citation.ref: Common applications of cloud computing — SaaS, IaaS and PaaS

points.text: Robotic process automation uses software bots that mimic human interaction with digital systems to automate manual, repetitive tasks: the bots would extract the twelve trial balances, consolidate the data, perform the elimination calculations, generate the reports and check compliance with the standards, improving accuracy and timeliness and freeing the finance team for judgement work.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Accounting and Technology
citation.ref: Robotic process automation in financial reporting — extraction, consolidation, calculation and reporting by bots

points.text: The threats the module names are phishing that tricks users into clicking malicious links or giving up credentials, malware that steals data or disrupts operations, ransomware that encrypts files and demands payment, insider threats from employees with access to sensitive data, and denial of service attacks that overwhelm a system with traffic; automation itself raises the exposure to data breaches, so access controls and backups are part of the move.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Accounting and Technology
citation.ref: Common cybersecurity threats — phishing, malware, ransomware, insider threats, denial of service

written.scenario: A foreign investor's analyst writes to the CFO of Meru Steels Ltd: "Your statements say they comply with Ind AS. Since India has adopted IFRS, please confirm they comply with IFRS as issued by the IASB so we need not reconcile. Also, when IFRS 18 was issued, why did it not apply in India the same day?"
written.question: Explain the difference between convergence and adoption, whether Meru Steels may assert IFRS compliance, and the process by which a new IFRS becomes an Ind AS in India.

points.text: Adoption means a country implements IFRS exactly as issued by the IASB and is fully compliant with it; convergence means the national standard setter adopts IFRS with some exceptions and works with the IASB towards removing them over time. India, like China and Hong Kong, has converged with IFRS; Canada and Bahrain have adopted it. Ind AS therefore carry carve-outs and carve-ins from the corresponding IFRS, made after considering the local regulatory landscape, business practices and tax provisions.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Introduction to Ind AS
citation.ref: Convergence versus adoption of IFRS; carve-ins and carve-outs

points.text: Meru Steels cannot assert compliance with IFRS. An entity asserts IFRS compliance only when it applies IFRS 1 on first-time adoption and applies the IASB's standards in full; an entity that applies IFRS as amended by a local authority cannot assert compliance with IFRS. Ind AS statements comply with Ind AS, and the analyst's reconciliation, if any, is for him to judge from the carve-outs.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Introduction to Ind AS
citation.ref: IFRS 1 and the assertion of compliance with IFRS as issued by the IASB

points.text: A new IFRS reaches India through the Ind AS setting process: the Accounting Standards Board of ICAI prepares a preliminary draft with the requisite carve-ins and carve-outs; circulates it to Council members and specified outside bodies such as MCA, SEBI, the C&AG and CBDT and meets their representatives; issues an exposure draft for public comment; finalises the Ind AS after considering comments and submits it to the Council of ICAI; the Council approves it, modifying it if necessary in consultation with the ASB; the final draft goes to NFRA with ICAI's recommendation, NFRA reviews and gives inputs; and the MCA notifies the Ind AS under the Companies Act in the Gazette with an applicability date. That is why nothing applies in India on the day the IASB issues it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Introduction to Ind AS
citation.ref: Process of development and finalisation of Ind AS — ASB, the Council, NFRA and MCA

written.scenario: A trader began on 1 January 2025 with ₹12,000, held entirely as 6,000 units of a product bought at ₹2 each. During the year he sold all of them at ₹3 each and withdrew ₹6,000. The general price index rose from 100 to 120 over the year; the specific price of the product rose to ₹2.50 a unit. He says he made a profit of ₹6,000 and drew it, so his capital is intact.
written.question: Compute his retained profit under financial capital maintenance in nominal money, in constant purchasing power, and under physical capital maintenance; state what each says about his drawings; and explain which concept of capital suits which users.

points.text: Under financial capital maintenance in nominal monetary units, profit is earned only if the money amount of net assets at the end exceeds that at the beginning after excluding distributions to and contributions from owners. Closing equity is ₹12,000 (₹18,000 of sales less ₹6,000 drawn) against opening equity of ₹12,000, so the profit for the year was ₹6,000 and retained profit after drawings is nil. On this concept the trader is right: he can buy 6,000 units at ₹2 again, so long as prices have not changed.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Concepts of capital maintenance — financial capital maintenance in nominal monetary units; the module's Example 11

points.text: In constant purchasing power units, profit is the increase in invested purchasing power. Opening equity restated at closing prices is ₹12,000 × 120/100 = ₹14,400; closing equity is ₹12,000; retained profit is ₹12,000 − ₹14,400 = (₹2,400). Only the part of a price rise that exceeds the general price rise is profit, and the rest, ₹2,400 here, is a capital maintenance adjustment in equity. The trader has drawn ₹2,400 too much: had he withdrawn ₹3,600 he would hold the ₹14,400 needed to buy 6,000 units at ₹2.40.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Financial capital maintenance in units of constant purchasing power; the module's Example 12

points.text: Under physical capital maintenance, profit is earned only if the physical productive capacity at the end exceeds that at the beginning. Opening capital at closing current cost is 6,000 units × ₹2.50 = ₹15,000, or ₹12,000 × 125/100; closing equity after adjusting for what the stock would now cost is ₹9,000; retained profit is ₹9,000 − ₹15,000 = (₹6,000). All price changes on the assets are treated as capital maintenance adjustments in equity and not as profit. There should have been no drawings at all: the trader needed the whole ₹15,000 to replace 6,000 units at ₹2.50.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Physical capital maintenance and capital maintenance adjustments; the module's Example 13

points.text: The choice follows the users. A financial concept of capital, invested money or purchasing power, is adopted where users are primarily concerned with the maintenance of nominal invested capital or of its purchasing power; a physical concept, operating capability, where their main concern is the entity's productive capacity. The concept chosen is the point of reference from which profit is measured, and it decides which measurement basis, historical cost or a current value, the statements are built on: the physical concept demands current cost, an entry value measured at each measurement date rather than at acquisition.

citation.source: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting under Ind AS
citation.ref: Concepts of capital — financial and physical — and the link to profit and to the measurement bases

written.scenario: Tarang Finance Ltd, a non-banking financial company, and its manufacturing subsidiary Tarang Motors Ltd are preparing their statements of cash flows under Ind AS 7. In the year Tarang Finance paid interest of ₹40 crore on its borrowings and received interest of ₹90 crore on loans it made, and paid a dividend of ₹10 crore. Tarang Motors paid interest of ₹6 crore, received dividends of ₹2 crore, bought a plant for ₹50 crore by assuming the seller's liabilities of ₹42 crore and paying the balance in cash, and imported goods for EUR 10,000 in January at ₹70 which were unpaid and unsold at 31 March when the rate was ₹65. Tarang Motors also bought a further 10% of a subsidiary it already controlled for ₹8 crore, and acquired a new subsidiary for ₹30 crore, of which ₹5 crore was in shares and the subsidiary held ₹3 crore of cash.
written.question: Classify each item in the two companies' statements of cash flows and state the amounts presented, with the reasons Ind AS 7 gives.

points.text: For a financial institution, interest paid and interest and dividends received are cash flows from operating activities, so Tarang Finance shows ₹40 crore paid and ₹90 crore received in operating; dividends paid, ₹10 crore, are financing, being a cost of obtaining financial resources. For other entities, interest paid and dividends paid are financing and interest and dividends received are investing, returns on investments; so Tarang Motors shows ₹6 crore of interest paid in financing and ₹2 crore of dividends received in investing. Interest and dividends received and paid are each disclosed separately.

citation.ref: Interest and dividends — classification for financial institutions and for other entities

points.text: The plant purchase is a non-cash investing transaction to the extent of the ₹42 crore of liabilities assumed, which is excluded from the statement of cash flows and disclosed elsewhere in the financial statements; only the ₹8 crore paid in cash appears, as an investing outflow. The EUR purchase is recorded at ₹7,00,000 at the date of the transaction; the ₹50,000 unrealised gain from restating the payable to ₹6,50,000 is not a cash flow, and under the indirect method it needs no adjustment because profit of ₹50,000, less the ₹7,00,000 increase in inventory, plus the ₹6,50,000 increase in payables, nets to nil operating cash flow.

citation.ref: Non-cash transactions; foreign currency cash flows and unsettled operating monetary items — the module's Examples 3 and Illustration 9

points.text: Buying a further 10% of a subsidiary without losing control is a transaction with owners under Ind AS 110, so the ₹8 crore is a financing outflow, unless the subsidiary were held by an investment entity at fair value through profit or loss. Obtaining control of the new subsidiary is investing: the aggregate is presented separately, net of the cash acquired, so the outflow is ₹25 crore of cash consideration less ₹3 crore of cash held, ₹22 crore, and the ₹5 crore of shares is a non-cash element disclosed but not presented. The disclosure gives the total consideration ₹30 crore, the cash portion ₹25 crore, the cash in the subsidiary ₹3 crore, and its other assets and liabilities by major category; the effects of losing control are never netted against obtaining it.

citation.ref: Changes in ownership interests in subsidiaries — investing on obtaining or losing control, financing without loss of control, net of cash acquired, and the four disclosures

written.scenario: Vajra Gems Ltd cuts diamonds. It sells 90% of its output in the domestic market, where the price of a standard parcel at 31 March is ₹10,00,000, and may export at most 10% under a government cap; the export price for the same parcel is ₹11,50,000. Selling in either market costs 2% in broker's commission, and shipping a parcel to the export hub costs ₹20,000. The CFO proposes to measure closing inventory carried at fair value at the export price, arguing that a rational seller takes the higher price. Vajra also holds shares of a company listed on both BSE and NYSE; the BSE trades far more volume, but the NYSE closing price is higher.
written.question: Determine the fair value of the diamond parcel and of the shares, explaining the market Ind AS 113 requires, the treatment of the commission and the shipping cost, and whose assumptions the measurement uses.

points.text: Fair value is measured in the principal market, the market with the greatest volume and level of activity for the asset, and only in its absence in the most advantageous market, the one that maximises the amount received after transaction costs. Where a principal market exists its price must be used even if another market's price is more advantageous, because the most liquid market gives the most representative input. The domestic market, with 90% of activity, is the principal market; the export market is the most advantageous but irrelevant while a principal market exists. The CFO is wrong.

citation.ref: Principal market and most advantageous market — the module's diamond example

points.text: Transaction costs are a characteristic of the transaction, not of the asset, so the 2% commission is not deducted from the principal-market price; transport costs are different, because location is a characteristic of a commodity, and the price in the principal market is adjusted for the cost of transporting the asset to that market. The parcel is already where the domestic market trades, so no transport adjustment arises and its fair value is ₹10,00,000; had the principal market been the export hub, the ₹20,000 shipping cost would have been deducted and the ₹20,000 of commission would not.

citation.ref: Transaction costs and transport costs — the module's Example 10 and the table comparing the two markets

points.text: The shares are measured at the BSE closing price: the BSE has the greatest volume and activity, so it is the principal market, and the higher NYSE price is ignored. Both measurements use the assumptions market participants would use, independent, knowledgeable and willing parties acting in their economic best interest, not Vajra's own; a quoted price in an active market for an identical asset is a Level 1 input and takes the highest priority in the fair value hierarchy.

citation.ref: The BSE and NYSE example; market participants; the fair value hierarchy and Level 1 inputs

written.scenario: Pravaha Ltd, with the rupee as functional currency, owns 100% of Sora GmbH, whose functional currency is the euro and whose year ends on 31 December, three months before Pravaha's. Goodwill of EUR 2 million arose on the acquisition. During the year Pravaha lent Sora USD 1 million, repayable on demand, which both treat as an ordinary intra-group loan. After the year end Pravaha sells 30% of Sora and keeps control; the board asks what happens to the ₹18 crore credit balance in the foreign currency translation reserve, and what would happen if it instead sold 70%. It also proposes to write Sora's goodwill down and release a matching part of the reserve.
written.question: State how Sora is translated for consolidation, how the reporting-date gap and the loan are dealt with, and the treatment of the translation reserve on each of the three events.

points.text: Sora's assets and liabilities are translated at the closing rate at the reporting date, income and expenses at the rates on the transaction dates or an appropriate average, and cash flows likewise; the resulting exchange differences go to other comprehensive income and accumulate in a separate component of equity, the foreign currency translation reserve, until disposal. Goodwill and fair value adjustments on the acquisition are assets of the foreign operation, so the EUR 2 million goodwill is expressed in euro and retranslated at the closing rate too, its movement also going to the reserve. There is no group functional currency, only a presentation currency.

citation.ref: Translation of a foreign operation; goodwill and fair value adjustments treated as assets of the foreign operation

points.text: Where Sora does not prepare additional statements to 31 March, Ind AS 110 allows a difference of no more than three months, with adjustments for significant transactions or events between the dates; Sora's assets and liabilities are then translated at the rate at Sora's own reporting date, 31 December, and adjustments are made for significant changes in exchange rates up to 31 March. The intra-group loan is eliminated on consolidation but the exchange difference on it is not, because the group has a real exposure; it is recognised in profit or loss unless the loan is a monetary item forming part of Pravaha's net investment in Sora, and a loan repayable on demand is not one, so the difference stays in profit or loss.

citation.ref: Difference in reporting dates; intra-group transactions — exchange differences not eliminated, net investment exception

points.text: Selling 30% and keeping control is a partial disposal of a subsidiary: Pravaha re-attributes the proportionate share of the accumulated exchange differences, 30% of ₹18 crore or ₹5.4 crore, to the non-controlling interest, and nothing is reclassified to profit or loss. Selling 70% and losing control is accounted for as a disposal even though 30% is retained: the entire ₹18 crore is reclassified from equity to profit or loss when the gain or loss on disposal is recognised, while any amount attributed to non-controlling interests is derecognised without reclassification. A write-down of goodwill or of the carrying amount of Sora is not a partial disposal, so no part of the reserve is reclassified on the proposed impairment.

citation.ref: Disposal and partial disposal of a foreign operation — the module's Examples 3 and 4; write-downs are not partial disposals

written.scenario: Kalpa Foods Ltd has five operating segments, each reviewed separately by its chief operating decision maker. For 2025-26 (₹ crore): Segment A revenue 300 (external 200, intersegment 100), profit 60, assets 300. Segment B revenue 90 (all external), loss 30, assets 40. Segment C revenue 50 (all external), profit 5, assets 20. Segment D revenue 40 (all external), profit 2, assets 30. Segment E revenue 45 (all external), profit 1, assets 10. The CFO proposes to report only Segment A, "because B made a loss and the rest are small".
written.question: Apply the quantitative thresholds of Ind AS 108 to each segment, test the result against the 75 per cent floor, and state which segments Kalpa must report and how the rest are shown.

points.text: Revenue test. A segment is reportable if its reported revenue, including both external sales and intersegment sales, is 10 per cent or more of the combined revenue, internal and external, of all operating segments. Combined revenue is 300 + 90 + 50 + 40 + 45 = ₹525 crore, so the line is ₹52.5 crore. A (300) and B (90) pass; C (50), D (40) and E (45) fail.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 108
citation.ref: Quantitative thresholds — revenue test including intersegment sales

points.text: Profit or loss test. A segment is reportable if its reported profit or loss, in absolute amount, is 10 per cent or more of the greater, in absolute amount, of the combined profit of all segments that did not report a loss and the combined loss of all segments that reported a loss. Combined profits are 60 + 5 + 2 + 1 = ₹68 crore; combined losses are ₹30 crore; the greater is 68 and the line is ₹6.8 crore. A (60) passes, and B passes because its loss of 30 is taken in absolute amount; a loss does not disqualify a segment. C, D and E fail.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 108
citation.ref: Quantitative thresholds — profit or loss test, absolute amounts, greater of combined profits and combined losses

points.text: Assets test. A segment is reportable if its assets are 10 per cent or more of the combined assets of all operating segments. Combined assets are 300 + 40 + 20 + 30 + 10 = ₹400 crore, so the line is ₹40 crore. A passes, and B passes at exactly 40 because the test is "10 per cent or more". After the three tests A and B are reportable; C, D and E meet none of them.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 108
citation.ref: Quantitative thresholds — assets test, "10 per cent or more"

points.text: The 75 per cent floor. If the total external revenue of reportable segments is less than 75 per cent of the entity's revenue, additional operating segments are identified as reportable, even if they do not meet the criteria, until at least 75 per cent of the entity's revenue is included. Entity external revenue is 200 + 90 + 50 + 40 + 45 = ₹425 crore; A and B bring ₹290 crore, which is 68.2 per cent, below the floor. Adding Segment C, the largest of the rest, brings reportable external revenue to ₹340 crore, 80 per cent, so Kalpa reports A, B and C.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 108
citation.ref: 75 per cent of entity revenue — additional segments identified until the floor is met

points.text: The rest. D and E, which are not reportable, are combined and disclosed in an "all other segments" category, separately from other reconciling items, with the sources of that revenue described. Kalpa may still report D or E separately if management believes the information would be useful; and because C is newly reportable, the prior-period segment data presented for comparison is restated to show C separately, unless the information is unavailable and the cost to develop it excessive.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 108
citation.ref: All other segments category; management judgement; restatement of comparatives for a newly reportable segment

written.scenario: Nirvaan Infra Ltd issued four instruments during 2025-26. (a) 12 per cent cumulative preference shares of ₹50 crore, redeemable at par after eight years, the dividend being mandatory each year. (b) ₹30 crore perpetual bonds carrying a 9 per cent coupon payable every year with no discretion to skip it; some holders are abroad and each coupon remittance needs the approval of the exchange-control regulator. (c) ₹20 crore preference shares redeemable after five years in cash, or at the issuer's option by transferring a warehouse whose fair value is well above ₹20 crore. (d) ₹10 crore debentures redeemable after ten years, whose 10 per cent interest is payable only if the board declares it. The CFO proposes to present (a), (c) and (d) as equity because preference shares and debentures with discretionary interest "are not loans", and (b) as equity because "there is no repayment"; and says the regulator's approval requirement means the coupons on (b) are not an obligation until approved.
written.question: Classify each instrument under Ind AS 32, saying which components are liabilities and which are equity, and comment on the effect of the regulator's approval requirement.

points.text: The test is substance, not legal form. An instrument is a financial liability if it carries a contractual obligation to deliver cash or another financial asset that the issuer cannot avoid; it is equity only if the issuer has the unconditional right to avoid delivering cash. That share capital is called "preference shares" or that an instrument is not a loan is irrelevant; and an obligation may be established indirectly through the terms and conditions rather than stated in words.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Financial instruments, equity and financial liabilities
citation.ref: Contractual obligation test; unconditional right to avoid delivering cash; Ind AS 32.20 indirect obligations

points.text: (a) Financial liability in its entirety. The instrument provides for mandatory fixed dividend payments and redemption by the issuer for a fixed amount at a fixed future date; there is a contractual obligation to deliver cash for both the dividends and the principal that cannot be avoided, so the ₹50 crore is presented as a liability and the 12 per cent dividend is finance cost.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Financial instruments, equity and financial liabilities
citation.ref: Illustration — redeemable preference shares with mandatory dividend

points.text: (b) The perpetual bonds carry a mandatory interest of 9 per cent that the issuer cannot avoid; that is a contractual obligation to deliver cash and is a financial liability. The absence of a repayment date does not make the instrument equity: the perpetual principal is only the second component, and the coupon obligation alone takes the instrument out of equity.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Financial instruments, equity and financial liabilities
citation.ref: Illustration — perpetual loan with mandatory interest

points.text: (c) Financial liability.
