The issuer can avoid transferring cash only by settling a non-financial obligation, the warehouse, whose value is significantly higher than the cash amount; a settlement alternative of that kind does not give the issuer a way of avoiding the outflow, so the ₹20 crore preference shares are a liability.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Financial instruments, equity and financial liabilities
citation.ref: Illustration — settlement alternative is a non-financial obligation

points.text: (d) A compound instrument, not wholly equity. Mandatory redemption of ₹10 crore at a fixed future date is a contractual obligation to deliver cash and is a financial liability component; the interest payable at the discretion of the issuer is the equity component. Nirvaan presents the liability at the present value of the redemption amount and the residual in equity, not the whole ₹10 crore as equity.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Financial instruments, equity and financial liabilities
citation.ref: Illustration — redeemable debentures with discretionary interest; compound instruments

points.text: The regulator's approval changes nothing. Lack of access to foreign currency, or the need to obtain approval for payment from a regulatory authority, does not negate the entity's contractual obligation or the holder's contractual right under the instrument; the coupons on (b) are an obligation from the day the bonds are issued.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Financial instruments, equity and financial liabilities
citation.ref: Illustration — restriction on the ability of an entity to satisfy a contractual obligation

written.scenario: Arunodaya Pharma Ltd acquired 100 per cent of Tvesha Labs Ltd on 1 July 2025 for cash of ₹80 crore plus two contingent amounts: (i) 10,00,000 further equity shares of Arunodaya if Tvesha's revenue for 2025-26 exceeds ₹100 crore, valued at ₹12 crore on 1 July 2025; and (ii) cash of ₹15 crore if a drug approval is received by 30 June 2026, valued at ₹9 crore on 1 July 2025. At 31 March 2026 the revenue target is almost certain and the share obligation is valued at ₹14 crore; the approval has progressed and the cash obligation is valued at ₹11 crore. In February 2026 the valuers finalised a Tvesha patent at ₹18 crore against the ₹12 crore used provisionally in July 2025, on licensing terms that existed at the acquisition date. In September 2026 a tax demand of ₹3 crore for 2023-24, which existed at the acquisition date, came to light. The CFO wants every change taken to goodwill.
written.question: Compute the consideration transferred on the acquisition date, classify each contingent amount, and state how each later change is accounted for and why.

points.text: Consideration transferred is measured at acquisition-date fair value, and contingent consideration is recognised at its acquisition-date fair value as part of it: ₹80 crore + ₹12 crore + ₹9 crore = ₹101 crore. Goodwill is measured off that figure, not off the ₹80 crore paid in cash.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 103
citation.ref: Contingent consideration recognised at acquisition-date fair value as part of consideration transferred

points.text: Classification follows Ind AS 32. The obligation to issue a fixed number of Arunodaya's own shares carries no obligation to deliver cash and is settled by a fixed number of own equity instruments, so it is equity. The obligation to pay ₹15 crore in cash is a financial liability.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 103
citation.ref: Classification of contingent consideration as liability or equity on the Ind AS 32 definitions

points.text: The equity-classified consideration is not remeasured: the rise from ₹12 crore to ₹14 crore is ignored, and when the shares are issued the settlement is accounted for within equity.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 103
citation.ref: Subsequent measurement — contingent consideration classified as equity shall not be remeasured

points.text: The liability-classified consideration is measured at fair value at each reporting date with the change recognised in profit or loss: the rise from ₹9 crore to ₹11 crore is a ₹2 crore charge for 2025-26. It is not a measurement-period adjustment, because it results from events after the acquisition date, progress towards the approval, not from information about facts that existed on 1 July 2025.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 103
citation.ref: Subsequent measurement — changes from post-acquisition events go to profit or loss, not goodwill

points.text: The patent is a measurement-period adjustment: the information is about facts that existed at the acquisition date and was obtained within one year of it, so the provisional amount is adjusted retrospectively, the patent rises by ₹6 crore to ₹18 crore and goodwill falls by ₹6 crore.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 103
citation.ref: Measurement period — retrospective adjustment of provisional amounts against goodwill, within one year

points.text: The tax demand came to light in September 2026, more than one year after 1 July 2025, so the measurement period has ended. A change after the measurement period for information that existed at the acquisition date is not adjusted against goodwill; it is accounted for as an error under Ind AS 8, and the ₹3 crore is recognised as a liability that way.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 103
citation.ref: Measurement period shall not exceed one year; later changes accounted for as errors under Ind AS 8

written.scenario: Vanshika Holdings Ltd closes its year on 31 March and owns 70 per cent of Ojas Retail Ltd, whose statutory year ends on 31 December because its regulator abroad requires it. Ojas has audited statements to 31 December 2025. Between 1 January and 31 March 2026 Ojas sold a warehouse at a gain of ₹4 crore. In March 2026 Ojas sold goods costing ₹6,00,000 to Vanshika for ₹8,00,000, all still in Vanshika's inventory on 31 March 2026; and Vanshika sold goods costing ₹3,00,000 to Ojas for ₹4,00,000, half of which Ojas still holds. Ojas values inventory on weighted average; the group uses first-in first-out. The finance team proposes to consolidate Ojas's 31 December statements as they stand "because the gap is within three months", to eliminate only 70 per cent of the intra-group profits "because 30 per cent belongs to outsiders", and to leave Ojas's inventory policy alone.
written.question: Comment on each of the three proposals under Ind AS 110, and compute the eliminations for the two intra-group sales showing what is borne by the non-controlling interest.

points.text: The statements used in consolidation shall have the same reporting date. When the subsidiary's date differs, it prepares additional financial information as of the parent's date unless that is impracticable; only then may the parent use the most recent statements, adjusted for the effects of significant transactions or events between the two dates, and the gap shall be no more than three months. Being within three months permits the use of the December statements only if a March cut is impracticable, and never without adjustment.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Consolidation procedures
citation.ref: Reporting period of parent and subsidiary — same date, additional information unless impracticable, three-month ceiling

points.text: The ₹4 crore warehouse gain is a significant event in the gap and must be adjusted into Ojas's figures before consolidation. The length of the periods and the gap between the dates must also stay the same from period to period, so if Ojas moves to a March cut later, the comparatives are restated to equivalent periods.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Consolidation procedures
citation.ref: Adjustment for significant events between the dates; consistency of the gap from period to period

points.text: Intra-group balances, transactions and the resulting unrealised profits are eliminated in full, and the full elimination applies to every consolidated subsidiary even where the group's interest is less than 100 per cent; the 70 per cent proposal is wrong. The intra-group sales of ₹12,00,000 are excluded from consolidated revenue and cost of sales.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Consolidation procedures
citation.ref: Elimination of intra-group transactions in full, including subsidiaries held below 100 per cent

points.text: Sale by Ojas to Vanshika. The whole ₹2,00,000 profit is unrealised because the goods are still in the group; inventory is reduced to ₹6,00,000, cost to the group, and consolidated profit falls by ₹2,00,000. Because the subsidiary made the sale, that reduction is allocated between the parent and the non-controlling interest in the ratio of their interests: ₹1,40,000 to Vanshika and ₹60,000 to the non-controlling interest.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Consolidation procedures
citation.ref: Unrealised profit on inventories — sale by a subsidiary to its parent, reduction shared with non-controlling interest

points.text: Sale by Vanshika to Ojas. Half the goods remain, so the unrealised profit is half of ₹1,00,000, that is ₹50,000; inventory is reduced to ₹1,50,000 and consolidated profit by ₹50,000. Because the parent made the sale, the reduction is allocated entirely to the parent and none of it to the non-controlling interest.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Consolidation procedures
citation.ref: Unrealised profit on inventories — sale by a parent to its subsidiary, reduction allocated entirely to the parent

points.text: A parent prepares consolidated statements using uniform accounting policies for like transactions and events in similar circumstances; where a group member uses other policies, appropriate adjustments are made to its statements on consolidation. Ojas's weighted-average inventory is restated to first-in first-out for the group; the policy is not left alone because it is Ojas's own.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Consolidation procedures
citation.ref: Uniform accounting policies — adjustments to a group member's statements on consolidation

written.scenario: Sagarika Finance Ltd presents its first Ind AS financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2027, with a date of transition of 1 April 2025. The controller proposes four "clean-ups" in the opening Ind AS balance sheet: (i) revise the provision for doubtful loans at 1 April 2025 downwards using the recovery experience of 2025-26, because "hindsight is better information"; (ii) bring back onto the balance sheet a loan portfolio of ₹120 crore securitised to a trust in 2023-24 and derecognised under previous GAAP, because the Ind AS 109 derecognition tests would not have been met; (iii) treat a forward contract taken in March 2025 as a cash-flow hedge of forecast borrowings from 1 April 2025, though it was never designated as a hedge under previous GAAP, and keep the deferred loss on it shown as an asset; (iv) restate the non-controlling interest of a subsidiary that had losses before transition so that it does not show a deficit.
written.question: Advise on each proposal by reference to the mandatory exceptions in Ind AS 101.

points.text: Ind AS 101 prohibits retrospective application of other Ind AS in four areas, and these are mandatory, not choices: estimates, derecognition of financial assets and liabilities, hedge accounting, and non-controlling interests. Each proposal falls under one of them.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 101
citation.ref: Mandatory exceptions to the retrospective application of other Ind AS

points.text: (i) Rejected. Estimates under Ind AS at the date of transition shall be consistent with estimates made for the same date under previous GAAP, after adjusting for any difference in accounting policies, unless there is objective evidence that those estimates were in error. Recovery experience of 2025-26 is later information, not evidence of error at 1 April 2025; Sagarika uses the previous estimate, adjusted only to reflect the Ind AS 109 expected-loss policy where it differs.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 101
citation.ref: Mandatory exception — estimates consistent with previous GAAP unless objective evidence of error

points.text: (ii) Rejected. A first-time adopter applies the derecognition requirements of Ind AS 109 prospectively for transactions occurring on or after the date of transition. A portfolio derecognised under previous GAAP as a result of a transaction before 1 April 2025 is not recognised under Ind AS, unless it qualifies for recognition by a later transaction or event. Sagarika could apply Ind AS 109 derecognition retrospectively from an earlier date of its choosing only if the information needed was obtained at the time of initially accounting for those transactions.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 101
citation.ref: Mandatory exception — derecognition applied prospectively; securitisation before transition

points.text: (iii) Rejected on both counts. At the date of transition all derivatives are measured at fair value and all deferred losses and gains on derivatives reported under previous GAAP as if they were assets or liabilities are eliminated, so the deferred loss cannot stay as an asset. A hedge relationship is reflected in the opening balance sheet only if it is of a type that qualifies under Ind AS 109 and was designated under previous GAAP; transactions entered into before the date of transition shall not be retrospectively designated as hedges, and hedge accounting runs only from the date the qualifying criteria are met.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 101
citation.ref: Mandatory exception — hedge accounting; derivatives at fair value, deferred gains and losses eliminated, no retrospective designation

points.text: (iv) Rejected. A first-time adopter applies prospectively from the date of transition the Ind AS 110 requirements that total comprehensive income is attributed to the owners of the parent and to the non-controlling interests even if this results in the non-controlling interests having a deficit balance, together with the accounting for changes in ownership without loss of control and for loss of control. Pre-transition losses are not re-attributed, and from 1 April 2025 a deficit is allowed to arise.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Ind AS 101
citation.ref: Mandatory exception — non-controlling interests, Ind AS 110 requirements applied prospectively

written.scenario: The notes to Trishul Engineering Ltd's draft financial statements run to 140 pages. The inventory accounting policy sits in note 2, the estimation of net realisable value in note 41, and the inventory balances in note 12; the policy of writing off assets costing under ₹5,000 sits inside the fixed-asset note rather than with the depreciation policy. The company has committed to buy sixty small machines, none of which is individually material but which total ₹38 crore; the draft omits the commitment "as each is immaterial". Its new electric-drive product line is under 5 per cent of revenue but management has told the market it is the future of the company; the draft folds it into "other revenue". Fourteen accounting policies describe transactions the company has never had.
written.question: Using the best practices set out in the ICAI material on preparing financial statements, advise on materiality as a filter, on the capital commitment and the new product line, on the placement of notes, and on the policies to disclose.

points.text: Materiality is the filter for what to disclose and what to omit: information is disclosed only if it is material, and it is material if it could influence users' decisions based on the financial statements. Lack of clarity in applying materiality is one of the main drivers of overloaded financial statements, and 140 pages of notes is the symptom.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Analysis of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Best practices — materiality as the filter in deciding what to disclose and what to omit

points.text: The capital commitment must be disclosed. Individually each purchase is immaterial, but the total of ₹38 crore is a material commitment for the company, so some disclosure is made regarding it; materiality is judged on the aggregate, not item by item.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Analysis of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Best practices — capital commitments example, immaterial individually but material in total

points.text: The electric-drive line should be disclosed separately. Where a company has communicated to stakeholders a strategic intention to focus on a new line, revenue under 5 per cent of the total that has grown rapidly is disclosed as a separate stream under Ind AS 108, even though other streams of similar size are combined into other revenue; materiality is qualitative as well as quantitative.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Analysis of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Best practices — new revenue stream example, separate disclosure below 5 per cent of revenue

points.text: Integrate the notes. The main note for a line item is integrated with its accounting policy and any relevant key estimates and judgements, so the inventory policy, the net realisable value estimate and the balances sit together in one note; notes are grouped into categories with the most critical information placed more prominently; and accounting policies are disclosed in one place, not scattered, so the ₹5,000 write-off policy moves out of the fixed-asset note into the depreciation policy.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Analysis of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Best practices — integration of notes; policies in one place, not scattered

points.text: Disclose only material accounting policies, removing non-material disclosures that add no value; the fourteen policies describing transactions the company has never had go. Disclosures should be relevant, specific to the company and explain how it applies its policies, judged not only on the materiality of the balances affected but also on the nature of the operations.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Analysis of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Best practices — disclosure of material accounting policies only, specific to the company

written.scenario: Devyani, a Chartered Accountant, is the financial controller of Omkar Textiles Ltd. The CFO has sent the bank a quarterly statement showing inventory ₹40 crore higher than the books, to keep a working-capital line open; Devyani's name is on the covering certificate. Separately, she has found that customs duty on an imported line has been under-declared for two years by a scheme her immediate superior, the CFO, designed. When she raised the inventory figure, the CFO said "the bank has it, forget it", and the audit committee chair said he "does not want to know". Devyani is thinking of resigning quietly.
written.question: Set out, under the Code of Ethics, the actions Devyani should take on the misleading statement and on the suspected non-compliance, and comment on resignation.

points.text: Misleading information: when she knows or has reason to believe that information she is associated with is misleading, she shall take appropriate action to seek to resolve the matter, beginning by discussing her concerns with her superior and the appropriate level of management or those charged with governance and requesting that the information be corrected, and, because the bank already has it, that the bank be informed of the correct information.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
citation.ref: Addressing information that is or might be misleading — superior, governance, correction, informing users

points.text: She consults the employing organisation's policies, such as its ethics or whistle-blowing policy, on how to address the matter internally. If the organisation does not take appropriate action, further steps, taken while remaining alert to confidentiality, are consulting the Institute, the internal or external auditor or legal counsel, and determining whether any requirement exists to communicate to third parties including users, or to regulatory and oversight authorities.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
citation.ref: Further actions — whistle-blowing policy, the Institute, auditors, legal counsel, regulators

points.text: If, after exhausting all feasible options, appropriate action has still not been taken and she has reason to believe the information is still misleading, she shall refuse to be or to remain associated with it; withdrawing her name from the certificate comes before any thought of leaving.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
citation.ref: Refusing to be or remain associated with misleading information

points.text: Non-compliance: as a senior Chartered Accountant she is expected to take whatever action is appropriate in the public interest. She would ordinarily discuss the matter with her immediate superior, but because the CFO appears to be involved, she shall take it to the next higher level of authority, and take steps to have it communicated to those charged with governance, comply with any legal provision on reporting to an appropriate authority, have the consequences rectified or mitigated, reduce the risk of recurrence and deter any continuation.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
citation.ref: Senior Chartered Accountant responding to non-compliance — next higher level where the superior is involved; governance; authority

points.text: She shall determine whether disclosure to the external auditor is needed, and assess the response of her superiors and governance. The audit committee chair's refusal to hear, and a superior involved in the scheme, are circumstances that remove confidence in their integrity, so further action may include informing the management of a parent entity if there is one and disclosing the matter to an appropriate authority as the law provides.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
citation.ref: Determining whether further action is needed — loss of confidence in superiors and governance

points.text: Resigning quietly is not the answer. Resignation is not a substitute for the other actions needed to achieve the objectives of the Code; it becomes the course of action only where the further actions available are limited and it is the only one left.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant
citation.ref: Resignation not a substitute for other actions

written.scenario: Yashasvi Retail Ltd has moved its accounts onto an enterprise resource planning system. The internal auditor reports that the quarter-end closing steps were changed twice by a junior analyst without any approval record, that four people share one "finance superuser" login, and that the listing-regulator deadline for quarterly results was missed because nobody had entered it into the closing calendar. The board asks how internal control over financial reporting should be built into the system, and whether a supplier's proposal to record purchase transactions on a blockchain ledger would help the audit.
written.question: Describe the steps for integrating internal control over financial reporting within the ERP that the three findings call for, and set out the impacts of blockchain on financial reporting that bear on the supplier's proposal.

points.text: Integrating internal control over financial reporting with the ERP standardises and automates procedures, reduces manual effort and error, and enables segregation of duties, real-time visibility, comprehensive audit trails and proactive risk mitigation. The first step is to verify that the process identifies and keeps updated the internal and external financial reporting requirements and deadlines, such as the listing regulations on quarterly results, so the closing calendar in the system is aligned with them; the missed deadline is a failure of that step.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Accounting and Technology
citation.ref: Illustrative steps for integrating ICOFR within ERP — identification of reporting requirements and deadlines

points.text: Changes to the closing and reporting process are tracked through the system's change management functionality, with system logs and the audit trail reviewed to confirm that changes follow the defined roles for change control, initiators, approvers and change management teams, and that each change was authorised by a designated individual with the appropriate authority, such as the CFO or finance manager; the change requests, approvals and documentation are reviewed within the system. The analyst's unapproved changes should have been impossible to make and easy to find.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Accounting and Technology
citation.ref: Illustrative steps — change management functionality, system logs, authorisation by designated individuals

points.text: Roles and responsibilities in the closing process are defined within the system and validated by reviewing the user access matrix and system logs against a responsibility assignment matrix, which states who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task; a shared superuser login defeats that matrix and must be replaced by individual accounts. The qualifications and training of the people assigned to reporting roles are also assessed.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Accounting and Technology
citation.ref: Illustrative steps — user access matrix, responsibility assignment matrix, qualifications and training

points.text: Blockchain is a decentralised, immutable ledger. Its impacts on financial reporting include enhanced transparency, improved data integrity because each transaction is verified and unauthorised modification is prevented, streamlined audit processes with auditors verifying transactions directly on the ledger, an enhanced audit trail that is comprehensive and immutable, simplified reconciliation from a single shared source of truth, cost reduction, security and real-time reporting. For the supplier's proposal, the immutable audit trail and direct auditor access are the benefits that bear on the audit.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 — Accounting and Technology
citation.ref: Key impacts of blockchain on financial reporting

written.scenario: Kaveri Exports Ltd, an Indian company, has shipped goods to a buyer in the United States and will receive US$ 5,10,000 exactly three months from today. The treasury desk has the following quotes and rates. Spot: ₹ 83.00 per US$. Three-month forward: ₹ 83.60 per US$. Annual interest rates — in India, deposit 6% and borrowing 9%; in the United States, deposit 4% and borrowing 8%. Ignore transaction costs, brokerage and taxes.
written.question: Show how a money market hedge would be put in place for this receipt, work out the rupee amount it produces on the due date, compare it with a three-month forward contract, and advise which cover the company should take.

points.text: Set out the direction first — the company has a dollar receivable, so a money market hedge means borrow US dollars now, convert the borrowing to rupees at the spot rate, and place the rupees on deposit in India, with the dollar receipt on the due date used to repay the dollar loan.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 11(B)(i) — Money Market Hedging as an external technique

keywords: convert the borrowing to rupees at the spot rate

points.text: Size the dollar borrowing so that principal plus interest equals the receipt. The US borrowing rate is 8% p.a., which is 2% for three months, so the amount to borrow is US$ 5,10,000 ÷ 1.02 = US$ 5,00,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 11(B)(i) read with the worked money market hedge in Test Your Knowledge

keywords: principal plus interest equals the receipt

points.text: Convert the borrowed dollars at the spot rate of ₹ 83.00 — US$ 5,00,000 × 83.00 = ₹ 4,15,00,000 available in rupees today.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 5.2 — spot quotation used for the immediate conversion leg

points.text: Place those rupees on deposit in India at 6% p.a., which is 1.5% for three months, giving ₹ 4,15,00,000 × 1.015 = ₹ 4,21,22,500 on the due date. This is the certain rupee amount under the money market hedge.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 11(B)(i) — the deposit leg of the money market hedge

points.text: Value the alternative: under a forward contract the exporter sells US$ 5,10,000 three months forward at ₹ 83.60, giving 5,10,000 × 83.60 = ₹ 4,26,36,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 12 — Forward Contract

keywords: sells US$ 5,10,000 three months forward at ₹ 83.60

points.text: Conclude on the comparison: the forward yields ₹ 5,13,500 more (4,26,36,000 less 4,21,22,500), and the effective rate under the money market hedge is only ₹ 82.59 per US$ against ₹ 83.60 on the forward, so the company should take the forward contract.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 11(B)(i) — advantages and disadvantages of the money market hedge, against forward cover

keywords: effective rate under the money market hedge is only ₹ 82.59

written.scenario: A bond of Narmada Power Ltd has a face value of ₹ 1,000, carries a coupon of 10% payable annually and matures in four years, when it is redeemed at par. The yield to maturity on comparable bonds is 12%. Use the following discount factors at 12%: year 1 — 0.8929, year 2 — 0.7972, year 3 — 0.7118, year 4 — 0.6355.
written.question: Compute the current price of the bond, its Macaulay duration and its modified duration, and estimate the change in the bond's price if the yield rises by 50 basis points.

points.text: Price the bond as the present value of the three coupons of ₹ 100 and the final flow of ₹ 1,100 — 89.29 + 79.72 + 71.18 + 699.05 = ₹ 939.24.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8 — bond valuation as the present value of coupon and redemption flows

keywords: present value of the three coupons

points.text: Macaulay duration is the weighted average time within which the investor gets back the promised principal and the promised yield, so weight each year's present value by its year number — 89.29 + 159.44 + 213.54 + 2,796.20 = ₹ 3,258.47 — and divide by the price: 3,258.47 ÷ 939.24 = 3.47 years.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8.8(a) — Macaulay Duration

keywords: weight each year's present value by its year

points.text: Modified duration adjusts Macaulay duration for the yield, being Macaulay duration divided by (1 + YTM/n) — here 3.4693 ÷ 1.12 = 3.10, since the coupon is annual and n is 1.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8.8(b) — Modified Duration

points.text: Apply it to the yield move: the percentage price change is minus modified duration times the change in yield, so −3.10 × 0.50% = a fall of about 1.55%, which on ₹ 939.24 is a drop of ₹ 14.55 to roughly ₹ 924.69.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8.8 — duration as the measure of interest rate risk

keywords: minus modified duration times the change in yield

points.text: Add the standing relationships: a higher coupon rate lowers the duration, a higher yield-to-maturity lowers the duration, and a longer time to maturity raises it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 5 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Para 8.8 — factors affecting a bond's duration

keywords: higher coupon rate lowers the duration
longer time to maturity raises it

written.scenario: The share of Chenab Ltd trades at ₹ 200 today. Over the next year the share is expected to be worth either ₹ 250 or ₹ 160, and nothing in between. The risk free rate of interest is 8% per annum. A European call option on the share with an exercise price of ₹ 210 expires in one year.
written.question: Using the binomial model, compute the fair value of the call option today and state the composition of the riskless hedge portfolio at the valuation date.

points.text: Set up the tree: the up factor u = 250/200 = 1.25 and the down factor d = 160/200 = 0.80, giving payoffs Cu = Max (0, 250 − 210) = ₹ 40 and Cd = Max (0, 160 − 210) = nil.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 7.1 — Binomial Model, construction of the price tree and terminal payoffs

points.text: Compute the risk neutral probability p = (r − d) ÷ (u − d) = (1.08 − 0.80) ÷ (1.25 − 0.80) = 0.28 ÷ 0.45 = 0.6222, so the probability of a fall is 1 − 0.6222 = 0.3778.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 7.1 read with Para 7.2 — Risk Neutral Method

points.text: Discount the expected payoff at the risk free rate — (0.6222 × 40) + (0.3778 × 0) = ₹ 24.89, and 24.89 ÷ 1.08 = ₹ 23.05 is the fair value of the call.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 7.1 — valuing the option by discounting the probability-weighted payoff

keywords: Discount the expected payoff at the risk free rate

points.text: State the hedge: delta = (Cu − Cd) ÷ (Su − Sd) = (40 − 0) ÷ (250 − 160) = 40/90 = 0.4444, so 0.4444 of a share is held for every one call option written.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 7.1 — composition of the implied riskless hedge portfolio (Delta)

keywords: for every one call option written

written.scenario: Sutlej Logistics Ltd runs a fleet of delivery vans and replaces them on a continuous cycle. Each van costs ₹ 6,00,000. Operating costs are ₹ 1,50,000 in year 1, ₹ 2,00,000 in year 2 and ₹ 2,60,000 in year 3. The resale value at the end of year 1 is ₹ 4,00,000, at the end of year 2 is ₹ 3,00,000 and at the end of year 3 is ₹ 1,80,000. The cost of capital is 10%. Present value factors at 10% are 0.909, 0.826 and 0.751 for years 1 to 3; the cumulative factors are 0.909, 1.735 and 2.486.
written.question: Determine the optimum replacement cycle for the vans, showing your working.

points.text: Explain why the plain present values will not do: the three cycles run for different lengths, so they are not comparable until each is converted into an Equivalent Annual Cost, which is the present value of cash outflow divided by the PVAF for that cycle.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 3 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Para 5.2 — Optimum Replacement Cycle, formula for EAC

keywords: present value of cash outflow divided by the PVAF

points.text: One-year cycle — −6,00,000 + 0.909 × (4,00,000 − 1,50,000) = −₹ 3,72,750, the resale and the operating cost both falling in year 1.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 3 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Para 5.2, Illustration 13 — NPV of each replacement cycle

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 3 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Para 5.2, Illustration 13 — NPV of each replacement cycle

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 3 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Para 5.2, Illustration 13 — NPV of each replacement cycle

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 3 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Para 5.2 — computation of EAC for each cycle

points.text: Conclude: the lowest Equivalent Annual Cost is ₹ 3,76,801 on the two-year cycle, so the vans should be replaced every two years.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 3 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Para 5.2 — decision rule, replace on the cycle with the least EAC

written.scenario: Godavari Industries Ltd reports for the year (all figures in ₹ lakh) — revenue 2,000; direct costs 800; selling, general and administrative expenses 500, which include a provision for bad and doubtful debts of 30; interest 100. The tax rate is 30%. The balance sheet shows total assets of 2,400, made up on the funding side of equity share capital 900, reserves 400, non-current borrowings 500 and current liabilities and provisions 600. The trade receivables in total assets are already stated net of the same provision of 30. Pre-tax cost of debt is 10% and the cost of equity is 12%.
written.question: Compute the Economic Value Added of Godavari Industries Ltd for the year and say what the figure means.

points.text: Compute NOPAT — EBIT is 2,000 − 800 − 500 = 700; deduct tax at 30% on EBIT, 210; add back the non-cash provision for bad and doubtful debts of 30, giving NOPAT of ₹ 520 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 13 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: Para 6.3, Illustration 5, Step I — computation of NOPAT

points.text: Find the invested capital — total assets 2,400 less non-interest bearing liabilities of 600 gives 1,800, plus the same non-cash adjustment of 30, giving ₹ 1,830 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 13 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: Para 6.3, Illustration 5, Step II — finding out the Invested Capital

keywords: total assets 2,400 less non-interest bearing liabilities of 600

points.text: Compute the WACC on that capital — equity of 1,300 and debt of 500 out of 1,800, so (1,300/1,800 × 12%) + (500/1,800 × 10% × 0.70) = 8.67% + 1.94% = 10.61%.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 13 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: Para 6.3, Illustration 5, Step III — compute the WACC

keywords: equity of 1,300 and debt of 500 out of 1,800

points.text: Finish it — capital charge = 1,830 × 10.61% = ₹ 194.18 lakh, so EVA = 520 − 194.18 = ₹ 325.82 lakh; a positive EVA means the company is producing value from the funds invested in it, over and above the cost of that capital.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 13 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: Para 6.3, Steps IV and V — EVA equals NOPAT less the capital charge

written.scenario: Tapti Cements Ltd will need to borrow ₹ 80 crore for three months, starting six months from today. Fearing a rise in rates, it buys a 6 × 9 Forward Rate Agreement from its banker at 8.40% per annum on a notional principal of ₹ 80 crore. On the settlement date the three-month reference rate turns out to be (i) 9.00% per annum, and separately consider (ii) 7.80% per annum. Take the FRA period as 3/12 of a year.
written.question: Compute the final settlement amount in each case, state who pays whom, and explain what the company has achieved.

points.text: State the formula and the nature of the instrument — settlement is N(RR − FR)(dtm/DY) divided by [1 + RR(dtm/DY)], and the ₹ 80 crore is only notional principal because an FRA involves no transfer of principal and is settled in cash for the interest differential.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 12 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 4.1.2 — Forward Rate Agreements, features and settlement formula

points.text: Case (i), reference rate 9.00% — the numerator is ₹ 80 crore × (9.00% − 8.40%) × 3/12 = ₹ 12,00,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 12 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 4.1.2 — computation of the interest differential on the notional amount

points.text: Discount that differential at the actual reference rate, because an FRA is settled at the beginning of the period and not at the end — 12,00,000 ÷ [1 + 0.09 × 3/12] = 12,00,000 ÷ 1.0225 = ₹ 11,73,594, which the banker as seller pays to Tapti Cements.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 12 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 4.1.2 — the differential is discounted at the post-change actual rate

written.scenario: An investor is choosing between two securities. Security P has an expected return of 18% and a standard deviation of 25%. Security Q has an expected return of 12% and a standard deviation of 15%. The correlation coefficient between the returns of the two securities is +0.30. The investor places 40% of the funds in P and 60% in Q.
written.question: Compute the expected return and the standard deviation of this portfolio, and show how much risk the investor has removed by diversifying rather than holding the two in proportion.

points.text: Portfolio return is the plain weighted average of the two returns — (0.40 × 18%) + (0.60 × 12%) = 7.2% + 7.2% = 14.4%.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 6 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Para 4.4 — expected return of a portfolio as the weighted average of security returns

keywords: weighted average of the two returns

points.text: State the variance formula and work each term — portfolio variance = x1²σ1² + x2²σ2² + 2x1x2r12σ1σ2, giving 0.16 × 625 = 100, then 0.36 × 225 = 81, then 2 × 0.40 × 0.60 × 0.30 × 25 × 15 = 54.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 6 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Para 4.4.2 — portfolio variance of a two security portfolio

points.text: Add and take the root — portfolio variance = 100 + 81 + 54 = 235, so the portfolio standard deviation is the square root of 235 = 15.33%.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 6 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Para 4.4.2 — portfolio standard deviation is the square root of the portfolio variance

points.text: Measure the benefit — had the two been perfectly positively correlated the standard deviation would be the weighted average, (0.40 × 25) + (0.60 × 15) = 19%, so the gap of 3.67 percentage points is the reduction of portfolio risk through diversification.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 6 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Para 4.4.3 and 4.4.3.1 — dilution of risk through diversification, and the perfectly positively correlated case

keywords: reduction of portfolio risk through diversification

written.scenario: Ambar Ltd is considering the acquisition of Beta Ltd by an exchange of shares. Ambar Ltd has 10,00,000 equity shares, earnings per share of ₹ 8 and a market price of ₹ 120 per share. Beta Ltd has 4,00,000 equity shares, earnings per share of ₹ 5 and a market price of ₹ 45 per share. No synergy gains are expected, so the combined earnings will simply be the sum of the two companies' earnings.
written.question: Work out the exchange ratio on the basis of current market prices, the earnings per share of the merged company, the effect on the shareholders of each company, and the highest exchange ratio Ambar Ltd could offer without its own earnings per share falling.

points.text: Exchange ratio on market prices = market price of the target ÷ market price of the acquirer = 45 ÷ 120 = 0.375, so Ambar Ltd issues 4,00,000 × 0.375 = 1,50,000 new shares.

It also holds cash and bank balances of ₹ 15,00,000 and accrued income of ₹ 5,00,000. Against these stand an accrued management fee of ₹ 4,00,000 and other payables of ₹ 6,00,000. The scheme has 25,00,000 units outstanding and carries an exit load of 1%.
written.question: Compute the Net Asset Value per unit as at 31st March, and the amount an investor holding 10,000 units would receive on redeeming them that day.

points.text: State the build-up: net assets of the scheme = market value of investments + receivables + other accrued income + other assets, less accrued expenses, other payables and other liabilities.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 8 — Mutual Funds

written.scenario: On 1st January the equity share of Vidur Ltd is quoting at ₹ 500 in the cash market, while the three-month futures contract on the same share is quoting at ₹ 520. Money can be borrowed at 12% per annum. The company will pay a dividend of ₹ 8 per share before the futures contract expires. Ignore transaction costs and margins.
written.question: Compute the arbitrage free futures price, say whether an arbitrage opportunity exists, and if it does, set out the steps an arbitrageur would take and the profit per share.

points.text: Apply the cost of carry model — futures price = spot price + carrying cost − returns, so 500 + (500 × 12% × 3/12) − 8 = 500 + 15 − 8 = ₹ 507, which is the theoretical minimum or arbitrage free price.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 5 — the cost-of-carry model for futures and forwards

keywords: futures price = spot price + carrying cost − returns

points.text: Compare — the actual futures price of ₹ 520 exceeds the arbitrage free price of ₹ 507, so the futures are overpriced and an arbitrage opportunity exists.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 5 — arbitrage when the traded price departs from the cost-of-carry price

keywords: actual futures price of ₹ 520 exceeds the arbitrage free price of ₹ 507

points.text: Set out the steps — borrow ₹ 500 for three months at 12%, buy the share in the cash market, and at the same time sell the three-month futures; collect the dividend of ₹ 8 and deliver the share against the futures contract on expiry.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 5 — how the arbitrager acts when futures are overpriced

keywords: deliver the share against the futures contract on expiry

points.text: Compute the gain — inflows of 520 + 8 = ₹ 528 against outflows of 500 + 15 = ₹ 515, a riskless profit of ₹ 13 per share, which is exactly the gap between the traded and the arbitrage free price.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 9 — Derivative Analysis and Valuation
citation.ref: Para 5 — the arbitrager's inflows and outflows

written.scenario: The spot rate is ₹ 84.00 per US dollar. Interest rates are 8% per annum in India and 4% per annum in the United States. The market is quoting a six-month forward rate of ₹ 85.00 per US dollar. An arbitrageur can borrow or lend freely in either currency and faces no transaction costs.
written.question: Test whether interest rate parity holds, and if it does not, show the steps by which an arbitrageur starting with a borrowing of US$ 1,00,000 would realise a gain, and compute that gain.

points.text: State the theory — under covered interest rate parity the size of the forward premium or discount should equal the interest rate differential between the two countries, so that F ÷ S = (1 + rD) ÷ (1 + rF) with both rates taken for the six-month period.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 8.1 — Interest Rate Parity, the covered parity equation

keywords: forward premium or discount should equal the interest rate differential

points.text: Compute the parity forward rate — 84.00 × (1.04 ÷ 1.02) = ₹ 85.65 per US dollar, against the quoted forward of ₹ 85.00, so parity does not hold.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 8.1 read with Test Your Knowledge Practical Question 14 — forward rate from the parity equation

points.text: Choose the direction — because the dollar is cheaper forward than parity requires, the rupee route wins, so the arbitrageur should borrow dollars, convert at spot, invest the rupees in India and cover the dollar repayment by buying dollars forward.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 8.1 — covered interest arbitrage where parity does not hold

points.text: Work the legs — borrow US$ 1,00,000 at 4% per annum, so US$ 1,02,000 is repayable in six months; convert at spot to ₹ 84,00,000 and invest at 8% per annum for six months to get ₹ 87,36,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 8.1 — mechanics of covered interest arbitrage

keywords: US$ 1,02,000 is repayable in six months
invest at 8% per annum for six months to get ₹ 87,36,000

points.text: Close the position — buying US$ 1,02,000 forward at ₹ 85.00 costs ₹ 86,70,000, leaving a riskless arbitrage gain of ₹ 66,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 10 — Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
citation.ref: Para 8.1 — the arbitrage gain as the residual after covering the repayment

written.scenario: Bhima Housing Finance Ltd has a book of home loans running to ₹ 900 crore. Its capital is fully deployed and it cannot lend further without raising fresh funds, but it does not wish to add debt to its own balance sheet. Its board has been advised to securitise part of the loan book. A director asks how the money would actually reach the company and who the other parties in such a deal would be.
written.question: Explain the mechanism of securitisation step by step and name the parties involved, saying what each one does.

points.text: Creation of the pool of assets — the originator segregates assets backed by similar mortgages in terms of interest rate, risk, maturity and concentration, so that the pool is homogeneous.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 7 — Securitization
citation.ref: Para 5.1 read with Para 4.1(a) — Creation of Pool of Assets, and the Originator

keywords: Creation of the pool of assets
interest rate, risk, maturity and concentration

points.text: Transfer to the SPV — the pool is sold to a Special Purpose Vehicle created only for this deal, which takes both legal and beneficial title; the object is to remove and ring fence the asset from the balance sheet of the originator, and the SPV makes an upfront payment which is how the money reaches the company.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 7 — Securitization
citation.ref: Para 5.2 read with Para 4.1(b) — Transfer to SPV, and the Special Purpose Vehicle

keywords: remove and ring fence the asset from the balance sheet

points.text: Sale of securitised papers and administration — the SPV designs and issues instruments such as Pass Through Certificates or Pay Through Certificates to the investors, and the administration of the assets is sub-contracted back to the originator, who collects principal and interest as servicer for an agreed fee and passes it to the SPV.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 7 — Securitization
citation.ref: Para 5.3 and 5.4 read with Para 4.2(c) — Receiving and Paying Agent

keywords: Pass Through Certificates or Pay Through Certificates
administration of the assets is sub-contracted back to the originator

points.text: Name the remaining parties — the obligors who owe the money and whose credit standing is paramount, the rating agency which assesses the strength of the cash flow and the credit quality of obligors, the trustee who protects the investors' interest, and the credit enhancer who gives comfort by over collateralization or cash collateral if it is the originator, or by a letter of credit or surety bonds if it is a third party.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 AFM, Chapter 7 — Securitization
citation.ref: Para 4.2 — Secondary Participants (obligors, rating agency, trustee, credit enhancer)

written.scenario: Amber Appliances Ltd earns a return on equity of 18% and pays out 40% of its earnings as dividend. Its board has approved a plan to grow sales by 16% a year for the next three years while keeping the debt-equity ratio and the dividend payout unchanged and issuing no new equity. The chief financial officer is asked whether the plan is financially consistent, and what changes would make it so.
written.question: Compute Amber's sustainable growth rate, test the plan against it, and state what the company must change to grow at 16%.

points.text: The sustainable growth rate is the maximum rate of growth in sales a firm can achieve given its profitability, asset use, dividend payout and leverage, without issuing new equity: SGR = return on equity × (1 − dividend payout ratio) = 18% × (1 − 0.40) = 10.8%.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
citation.ref: Sustainable growth rate (Higgins) — ROE × (1 − dividend payout ratio)

points.text: The plan is inconsistent. The model assumes a target capital structure without new equity, a target payout ratio and sales growing as fast as the market allows; with the only new equity being retained earnings, assets and sales cannot grow faster than retained earnings plus the debt those earnings can support at the target ratio, so 16% against 10.8% cannot be financed on the stated terms.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
citation.ref: The three assumptions of the sustainable growth model and why growth beyond it is unfunded

points.text: To grow at 16% Amber must relax one of the constraints: raise the retention ratio — even a 20% payout gives only 18% × 0.80 = 14.4% — improve return on equity through margin or asset turnover, accept a higher debt-equity ratio, or issue new equity, which removes the financial constraint altogether.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
citation.ref: Levers on the sustainable growth rate — retention, profitability, leverage and new equity

written.scenario: The treasury of Corvid Capital holds an equity portfolio worth ₹5 crore whose daily return has a standard deviation of 1.5%. The risk committee wants the maximum loss the desk could suffer over one trading day and over ten trading days at a 99% confidence level, assuming normally distributed returns, and asks what the number can and cannot be used for.
written.question: Compute the one-day and ten-day value at risk, explain each component of the calculation, and state its applications and its limits.

points.text: Value at risk rests on three components — the time period, the confidence level, generally 95% or 99%, and the loss expressed in percentage or amount — and is a statistical measure built on standard deviation: the z-score for the chosen confidence level, multiplied by the standard deviation, gives the value at risk.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: Features of value at risk — the three components and the z-score on the standard deviation

points.text: Daily volatility in rupees is 1.5% of ₹5 crore = ₹7.5 lakh; at 99% the z-score from the cumulative normal table is 2.33, so the one-day value at risk is ₹7.5 lakh × 2.33 = ₹17.475 lakh, about ₹17.48 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: One-day value at risk — rupee volatility × z-score at 99%

points.text: Over ten trading days the standard deviation scales by the square root of time, so the ten-day value at risk is ₹17.475 lakh × √10 = ₹17.475 lakh × 3.162 = about ₹55.26 lakh; the committee should expect a loss beyond this on about one trading fortnight in a hundred.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: Value at risk over a longer horizon — scaling by the square root of the number of days

points.text: Value at risk measures the maximum possible loss on a portfolio or trading position, is a benchmark for performance, fixes limits for front-office dealers in treasury, guides trading strategy and serves asset-liability management in banks; its limits are that it assumes a normal distribution, says nothing about the size of loss beyond the confidence level, and depends on a historical standard deviation that can shift.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: Applications of value at risk and the normality assumption behind it

written.scenario: Three people advise Priyanka on her equity portfolio. A chartist says his head-and- shoulders and moving-average signals beat the index every year. A fund manager says his team's reading of published annual reports and results announcements gives it an edge. A former director of a listed company says the only sure profit is trading on what the board knows before it is announced. Priyanka asks which of them, if any, is right if the market is efficient, and how the first claim could be tested.
written.question: Explain the three levels of market efficiency, apply each to the three claims, and describe the tests of the weak form.

points.text: Fama's three levels: in weak form efficiency price reflects all information in the record of past prices and volumes; in semi-strong efficiency it also reflects all other publicly available information; in strong form efficiency it reflects all information, public and private.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Analysis
citation.ref: Fama's three levels of market efficiency

points.text: If the market is weak-form efficient the chartist's technical signals, drawn from past prices, carry no information and cannot beat the index consistently; if it is semi-strong efficient the fund manager's edge from published reports is already in the price; only strong form efficiency would defeat the former director, and it is the level least supported by evidence, so his profit is possible but is insider trading, not analysis.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Analysis
citation.ref: Implications of each level of efficiency for technical analysis, fundamental analysis and inside information

points.text: The weak form is tested by the serial correlation test, correlating price changes in one period with those in another and finding none of significance; the run test, marking each change plus or minus and comparing the number of runs with a random series; and the filter rule test, checking whether a mechanical buy-above and sell-below rule earns more than buy and hold.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Analysis
citation.ref: Empirical tests of weak form efficiency — serial correlation, run and filter rule tests

written.scenario: Sarthak Auto Ltd, an Indian company, is appraising a plant in a South American country. The local team has produced a net present value in local currency that comfortably clears the local competitors' returns. The parent will receive royalties and management fees, the host country levies withholding tax on dividends remitted, exchange control rules will hold back part of each year's profits for at least three years, and Sarthak already has ₹40 crore of earlier profits lying in that country which it cannot bring home. The board asks whose cash flows should decide the investment and how the ₹40 crore is treated.
written.question: Distinguish project cash flows from parent cash flows for this appraisal, explain how blocked funds and remittance costs enter the computation, and advise the board.

points.text: Project and parent cash flows differ because of tax rules, exchange controls and the form of returns: management fees and royalties are returns to the parent but costs to the project, profits remitted are taxed in the host country and again in the home country, and the parent's flows bear exchange rate risk on conversion.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: Why project cash flows and parent cash flows diverge — tax, exchange control, royalties and fees, currency risk

points.text: Appraisal on the project's own local-currency cash flows asks whether it competes with local firms and avoids currency conversion, but a foreign project that replaces imports is not a competitor of local firms; from the parent's angle the yardstick is the operating and financial cash flows actually remitted, which fund the dividends to shareholders and the service of debt, and operating flows must not be mixed with financing flows.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: Evaluation on own cash flows against cash flows accruing to the parent

points.text: The ₹40 crore is direct blocked funds — balances held abroad that cannot be remitted because of exchange control — and if the parent can release them into the new plant they reduce the cost of the investment outlay; the withholding tax and local taxes on remittance are indirect blocked funds and reduce the flows that count to the parent.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: Direct and indirect blocked funds — net of the initial investment; remittance taxes as indirect blocking

points.text: The board should decide on the parent's after-tax remitted cash flows, converted at the expected exchange rates, with the profits held back for three years included only when they can leave, and political and exchange risk handled through certainty equivalents or an adjusted discount rate rather than by the local-currency figure alone.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: Adjusting cash flows and discount rate for political and exchange risk

written.scenario: Nimit has a working prototype of a battery-recycling process and a first customer, is selling below cost, and is not yet profitable. A venture capital fund has shown interest and has asked for an investment memorandum. Nimit wants to know which funding stage he is at and how risky the fund will see him, what happens between the memorandum and the money, and how the fund expects to get out.
written.question: Place Nimit's company in the venture capital funding stages, describe the investment process, and explain the exit routes.

points.text: The stages run seed money for proving an idea, start-up for marketing and product development, first round for early sales and manufacturing, second round for working capital while selling but not yet profitable, third round or mezzanine for expanding a newly profitable company, and fourth round or bridge financing for going public. Nimit, selling but not profitable, is at the second round, which the risk matrix rates high, with funds locked in for three to seven years.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Startup Finance
citation.ref: Stages of venture capital funding and the indicative risk matrix

points.text: The process runs deal sourcing, where the investment memorandum sets out the business model, financial plan, exit plan and a tentative valuation; screening by a senior committee of the fund; due diligence by external consultants to verify the documents, usually at the fund's cost; deal structuring, often convertible so the promoter keeps a right to buy back and with a tag-along clause obliging the promoter to sell part of his stake alongside the fund; and post-investment activity, with a nominee director, milestones and reporting.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Startup Finance
citation.ref: The venture capital investment process — sourcing, screening, due diligence, structuring, post-investment

points.text: Exit is spelt out at the time of investing and happens two ways: sale to third parties, by an initial public offering or private placement to other funds; or a promoter buyback commitment at a pre-agreed rate, generally an internal rate of return of 18% to 25%, with the promoter often holding the first right of buyback if no public issue or third-party sale materialises.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Startup Finance
citation.ref: Exit plan — third-party sale or promoter buyback at an 18% to 25% internal rate of return

written.scenario: Vajra Group runs two-wheelers, cement and a small software arm. At one board meeting three things are on the table: whether to enter battery manufacturing and exit software; how the two-wheeler unit should hold its share against a new low-cost rival; and the finance department's plan for raising ₹600 crore for the battery plant while keeping the group's credit rating. The chair asks why the board should treat these three as different kinds of decision, and what questions the battery entry has to answer before it is approved.
written.question: Place each decision at its level in the strategy hierarchy, state the three questions a corporate-level strategy must answer, and explain why finance carries the highest importance among the functional strategies.

points.text: Strategies at different levels are the outcomes of different planning needs, and there are three: corporate level, business unit level, and functional or departmental level. Entering batteries and exiting software is corporate-level strategy, which is concerned with the selection of businesses in which the company should compete and with the development and coordination of that portfolio of businesses.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
citation.ref: Strategy at different hierarchy levels — corporate level strategy

points.text: Corporate-level strategy must answer three questions. Suitability: whether the strategy would work for the accomplishment of the common objective of the company. Feasibility: the kind and number of resources required to formulate and implement it. Acceptability: whether it satisfies the stakeholders, in financial and non-financial terms. The battery entry is approved only when all three are answered.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
citation.ref: Corporate level strategy — suitability, feasibility, acceptability

points.text: Holding the two-wheeler unit's share against the rival is business unit level strategy. A strategic business unit is any profit centre that can be planned independently from the other units, and at this level the strategic issues are the practical coordination of operating units and developing and sustaining a competitive advantage for the products and services produced.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
citation.ref: Business unit level strategy — profit centre planned independently, competitive advantage

points.text: The ₹600 crore funding plan is functional level strategy, the level of operating divisions and departments, whose issues relate to functional business processes and the value chain; functional units provide input upward and translate the higher-level strategy into discrete action plans. Among the functional activities, finance assumes the highest importance during the top-down and bottom-up interaction of planning, because corporate strategy deals with the deployment of resources and financial strategy with mobilising and using money, the most critical resource, with which other resources can be easily mobilised.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
citation.ref: Functional level strategy — finance as the functional activity of highest importance

written.scenario: Sahyadri Textiles Ltd exports to Europe and has just built a plant in an African country under a new government. It has a ₹200 crore loan at a floating rate, euro receivables due in 90 days, a large advance paid to a machinery supplier that has stopped answering calls, and a treasury that has twice missed supplier payments because collections arrive a month after bills fall due. The host country has begun insisting on local labour and has hinted at limits on converting its currency. The board asks for a map of the financial risks it faces, how each would be identified, and what would manage the supplier and host-country exposures.
written.question: Classify each exposure under the categories of financial risk, state the parameters that identify the interest rate and currency risks, and set out the techniques for managing counter party risk and political risk.

points.text: Financial risk is the unexpected change in financial conditions such as prices, exchange rates, credit rating and interest rates; political risk is not a financial risk in the direct sense but is included because an unexpected political change abroad leads to country risk and financial loss. The categories are counter party risk, political risk, interest rate risk, currency risk and liquidity risk.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: Financial risk — definition and categories

points.text: The floating-rate loan is interest rate risk: a change in rates changes the value of assets and liabilities, and a floating-rate borrower pays more when rates rise while a fixed-rate borrower is left paying comparatively more when rates fall. It is identified from the monetary policy of the government, government actions such as demonetisation, economic growth, the release of industrial data, investment by foreign investors and stock market changes.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: Interest rate risk — floating and fixed; parameters that identify it

points.text: The euro receivables are currency risk, which affects cash flows with movements in exchange rates and can be adverse or favourable: as an exporter Sahyadri gains if the rupee depreciates, the reverse of an importer. It is identified from government action, the nominal interest rate through interest rate parity, the inflation rate through purchasing power parity, natural calamities, war or coup, and a change of government.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: Currency risk — exporter and importer; parameters that identify it

points.text: The silent supplier is counter party risk, the non-honouring of obligations by the other party, which covers failure to deliver goods for a payment already made, or the reverse, and default on borrowings; it includes credit risk. The missed supplier payments are liquidity risk, the inability to meet liabilities when they fall due, arising from inadequate cash or a mismatch in the timing of cash flows. Counter party risk is managed by due diligence before dealing, not over-committing to a single entity or group, knowing exposure limits, reviewing limits and credit-approval procedures regularly, rapid action on any likelihood of default, and performance guarantees, insurance or other instruments.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: Counter party risk and liquidity risk — definitions; techniques to manage counter party risk

points.text: The host-country conditions are political risk, identified from insistence on resident investors or labour, restriction on conversion of currency, expropriation of foreign assets and price fixation of products. Sahyadri should assess the country risk from political rankings, the country's macro-economic conditions, the popularity and stability of the government and the advice of its own embassy, and mitigate it by local sourcing of raw materials and labour, joint ventures, local financing and prior negotiations.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Risk Management
citation.ref: Political risk — identification, assessment of country risk, mitigation techniques

written.scenario: Ketaki Polymers Ltd is appraising a plant costing ₹50,00,000 that will produce a net operating cash flow of ₹16,00,000 a year for four years, estimated in today's prices. Inflation is expected at 8 per cent a year and will affect revenues and costs alike. The company's cost of capital, which includes a premium for that inflation, is 14.48 per cent. An analyst discounts the ₹16,00,000 a year at 14.48 per cent, reports a negative net present value, and recommends rejection. Ignore tax.
written.question: Explain why the analyst's result is wrong, compute the net present value in nominal terms and again in real terms, and comment on whether the two approaches must agree.

points.text: The cost of capital contains a premium for anticipated inflation, so it is a nominal rate: investors require the nominal return to equal the required return in real terms plus the rate of inflation. When the discount rate contains an inflation premium, the inflation factor has to be reflected in the projected cash flows; cash flows in today's prices are real, and discounting real flows at a nominal rate mixes the two and understates the project. The analyst's figure is ₹16,00,000 × 2.8853 − ₹50,00,000 = (₹3,83,563), a rejection produced by the mismatch.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Impact of inflation — nominal required rate equals real rate plus inflation; inflation factor reflected in cash flows

points.text: Nominal approach. Nominal cash flow = (1 + inflation rate) × real cash flow, compounded by year: ₹17,28,000, ₹18,66,240, ₹20,15,539 and ₹21,76,782 for years one to four.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Illustration — real cash flows restated as nominal cash flows

points.text: Discounting those at 14.48 per cent: ₹15,09,434 + ₹14,23,994 + ₹13,43,391 + ₹12,67,350 = ₹55,44,169, less the outlay of ₹50,00,000, a net present value of ₹5,44,169. The project is accepted.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Illustration — NPV using the nominal discount rate

points.text: Real approach. The real discount rate is (1 + nominal rate) ÷ (1 + inflation rate) − 1 = 1.1448 ÷ 1.08 − 1 = 6 per cent. Discounting the real flows of ₹16,00,000 at 6 per cent, annuity factor 3.4651, gives ₹55,44,169, and the same net present value of ₹5,44,169.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Illustration — real discount rate from the nominal rate and inflation; NPV using the real rate

points.text: The two approaches must agree when inflation affects all flows alike, because the real rate is derived from the nominal rate by the same inflation factor applied to the flows. They diverge only where some flows do not inflate: depreciation tax shields are based on historical cost and do not move with inflation, and where revenues and costs inflate at different rates each stream is inflated at its own rate and the nominal method is used.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions
citation.ref: Depreciation charges do not keep parity with inflation; different inflation rates for revenue and cost

written.scenario: Over the last twenty months an index has made a series of higher peaks and higher troughs. Three weeks ago it fell 8 per cent over eleven trading days and has since recovered half of that; within those days it moved up and down by half a per cent a session. A newsletter calls the eleven-day fall "the start of a bear market" and tells readers to sell, and says the theory can tell them how far the market will go.
written.question: Using the Dow Theory, classify the three movements described, say whether the newsletter is right, and explain what the theory can and cannot tell an investor.

points.text: The Dow Theory divides the market's movements into three classifications occurring at the same time: the primary movement, the main trend, lasting from one year to thirty-six months or longer and called a bull or bear market; the secondary movement, shorter in duration and opposite in direction, lasting from two weeks to a month or more; and the daily fluctuations, the narrow day-to-day movements.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Analysis
citation.ref: The Dow Theory — primary movement, secondary movement, daily fluctuations and their durations

points.text: The twenty months of higher peaks and higher troughs is the primary movement, and it is a bull market: the theory states that if the cyclical swings of the averages are successively higher and the successive lows are higher, the trend is up. The eleven-day fall of 8 per cent is a secondary movement, opposite to the primary trend and within its two-weeks-to-a-month duration; the half-per-cent sessions are daily fluctuations, which are not part of the theory's interpretation though they must be studied because they make up the longer movements.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Analysis
citation.ref: The Dow Theory — successively higher highs and lows mark a bull market; secondary opposite in direction

points.text: The newsletter is wrong on both counts. A three-week fall against a twenty-month uptrend is a secondary reaction, not the start of a bear market, which would need successive highs and successive lows that are lower. And the theory's purpose is to determine where the market is and where it is going, although not how far or how high; it offers no target.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Analysis
citation.ref: The Dow Theory — purpose is to determine where the market is and where it is going, not how far

points.text: The theory also describes the anatomy of a primary uptrend in three moves up: accumulation by far-sighted investors, then the first reports of good earnings, then widespread reports of corporate well-being with rampant speculation; towards the end of the third move the far-sighted investors begin selling, starting the first move down, confirmed by the second, with the third coming from distress selling. Reading which move the market is in is the theory's use, not a price forecast.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Analysis
citation.ref: The Dow Theory — three moves of a primary uptrend and of a downtrend

written.scenario: Government zero-coupon yields are 7 per cent for one year, 8 per cent for two years and 9 per cent for three years. A treasurer says these mean "interest rates will be 8 per cent next year and 9 per cent the year after", and wants to value a three-year 8 per cent annual-coupon bond of face value ₹1,000 by discounting every cash flow at 9 per cent.
written.question: Derive the one-year forward rates for years two and three from the spot curve, value the bond using the spot rates, and correct the treasurer's two statements.
