points.text: A spot rate is the discount rate applicable to a cash flow receivable at that maturity; the one-year, two-year and three-year spot rates of 7, 8 and 9 per cent are each the yield on a zero-coupon instrument of that term. A forward rate is the current expected estimate of a future one-year spot rate implied by the curve, so that discounting a year-two flow by the two-year spot rate twice is the same as discounting it once at the one-year spot rate and once at the forward rate for year two.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Spot rates and forward rates — definitions; forward rate as the current expected estimate of next year's one-year spot

points.text: Forward rate for year two: (1 + two-year spot)² ÷ (1 + one-year spot) − 1 = 1.08² ÷ 1.07 − 1 = 1.1664 ÷ 1.07 − 1 = 9.01 per cent.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Forward rate derived from the spot rate curve — year two

points.text: Forward rate for year three: (1 + three-year spot)³ ÷ (1 + two-year spot)² − 1 = 1.09³ ÷ 1.08² − 1 = 1.2950 ÷ 1.1664 − 1 = 11.03 per cent. The forward curve therefore rises faster than the spot curve: 7, 9.01 and 11.03 per cent against 7, 8 and 9.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Forward rate derived from the spot rate curve — year three; forward rate curve

points.text: Value of the bond by the spot rates: ₹80 ÷ 1.07 + ₹80 ÷ 1.08² + ₹1,080 ÷ 1.09³ = ₹74.77 + ₹68.59 + ₹833.96 = ₹977.31. Discounting by the product of the one-year spot and the forward rates gives the same figure, because the forward rates are built from the same curve.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Valuing a bond by discounting each cash flow at its spot rate, or by the product of spot and forward rates

points.text: Both statements are wrong. The spot rates for two and three years are not next year's rates; the rates implied for next year and the year after are the forward rates of 9.01 and 11.03 per cent, and while current spot and forward rates are known, future spot rates are not. And discounting every flow at 9 per cent applies the three-year rate to one- and two-year flows; the coupons are worth more at their own lower spot rates, which is why the spot-rate value exceeds the ₹974.69 a flat 9 per cent would give.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Security Valuation
citation.ref: Future spot rates are not known; each cash flow discounted at its own spot rate

written.scenario: A family office holds three funds. Fund P is a pharmaceutical sector fund: return 19 per cent, standard deviation 24 per cent, beta 1.4. Fund Q is a diversified equity fund: return 16 per cent, standard deviation 14 per cent, beta 1.1. Fund R is a diversified large-cap fund: return 13 per cent, standard deviation 9 per cent, beta 0.7. The risk-free rate is 6 per cent and the market returned 14 per cent. The office's newsletter ranks them P, Q, R "on returns".
written.question: Rank the funds by the Sharpe ratio and by the Treynor ratio, explain why the two rankings differ and which measure suits each fund, and compute Jensen's alpha for each.

points.text: The Sharpe ratio measures the risk premium per unit of total risk: (return − risk-free rate) ÷ standard deviation. P: (19 − 6) ÷ 24 = 0.542; Q: (16 − 6) ÷ 14 = 0.714; R: (13 − 6) ÷ 9 = 0.778. Higher is better on a risk-adjusted basis, so the Sharpe ranking is R, Q, P, the reverse of the newsletter's.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Sharpe ratio — risk premium per unit of total risk

points.text: The Treynor ratio is the same idea with systematic risk in the denominator: (return − risk-free rate) ÷ beta, on the premise that unsystematic risk can be diversified away and only market risk should be rewarded. P: 13 ÷ 1.4 = 9.29 per cent; Q: 10 ÷ 1.1 = 9.09 per cent; R: 7 ÷ 0.7 = 10.00 per cent. The Treynor ranking is R, P, Q.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Treynor ratio — risk premium per unit of systematic risk

points.text: The rankings differ because the two measures define risk differently: Sharpe uses the standard deviation, which captures systematic and unsystematic risk together, while Treynor uses beta, which captures systematic risk alone. P overtakes Q under Treynor because P's high total risk is largely sector-specific and Treynor ignores it. For a sector-specific fund like P the Sharpe ratio is the more meaningful measure, since unsystematic risk is present and the investor bears it; for diversified funds like Q and R the unsystematic element is negligible and the Treynor ratio is more apt. The two usually give similar rankings only because most portfolios are fully diversified.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Sharpe against Treynor — total against systematic risk; sector-specific against diversified funds

points.text: Jensen's alpha is the difference between the portfolio's actual return and the return that could have been made on a benchmark portfolio with the same beta; it measures the ability of active management to add return beyond the reward for bearing market risk. The benchmark return is 6 + beta × (14 − 6). P: 6 + 11.2 = 17.2, alpha 1.8 per cent; Q: 6 + 8.8 = 14.8, alpha 1.2 per cent; R: 6 + 5.6 = 11.6, alpha 1.4 per cent.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Jensen's alpha — actual return less the return on a benchmark with the same beta

points.text: All three managers earned a positive alpha, and R earns the best risk-adjusted return on both ratios. The newsletter's ranking on raw return rewards P for taking the most risk, not for managing it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Portfolio Management
citation.ref: Judgement based solely on returns is erroneous; healthy returns with low volatility preferred

written.scenario: Lakshya Finance, a non-banking finance company, wants to securitise a ₹500 crore pool of car loans with maturities spread over six years. Its investment banker reports four demands from investors: some want securities maturing in two, four and six years rather than one instrument; most are worried that borrowers repaying early will hand them cash they did not want; a pension fund wants only the interest stream and a bank only the principal stream; and all of them want comfort about defaults, because they will have no recourse to Lakshya.
written.question: Contrast pass through certificates with pay through securities and say which structure meets the first two demands, explain the instrument that meets the third, and describe how the fourth is met and by whom.

points.text: Under a pass through certificate the originator transfers the entire receipt of cash, interest and principal, from the assets sold; the securities represent a direct claim of the investors on all the securitised assets held by the special purpose vehicle, and investors carry a proportional beneficial interest in them. Because it is a direct route, any prepayment of principal is distributed proportionately among the holders, all the securities terminate together on the final payment, and cash flows are skewed to the early years if principal is repaid before schedule.

citation.ref: Pass through certificates — direct claim, proportional interest, prepayment passed on, single maturity

points.text: A pay through security overcomes the single maturity and the pass-on of every cash flow. The vehicle's debt securities are backed by the assets, so it can restructure different tranches from the varying maturities of the receivables, desynchronising the servicing of the securities from the cash the assets generate; surplus cash from early retirement of receivables can be reinvested for short-term yield rather than passed on. Pay through therefore meets the first two demands: three tranches maturing in two, four and six years, and prepayments absorbed by the vehicle.

citation.ref: Pay through security — tranches of varying maturities, desynchronised servicing, reinvestment of surplus

points.text: The third demand is met by stripped securities, created by dividing the cash flows of the underlying securities into two new securities: interest only securities for the pension fund and principal only securities for the bank.

citation.ref: Stripped securities — interest only and principal only

points.text: The fourth is met by credit enhancement. Investors directly exposed to the underlying assets with limited or no recourse to the originator seek additional comfort, and a credit rating of the securities, which also aids marketability. The originator itself provides it as over-collateralisation or cash collateral; a third party such as a bank provides it as a letter of credit or surety bond. A trustee oversees that all parties perform the agreement in its true spirit and looks after the investors' interest, and the structurer, usually an investment banker, brings the parties together and sees that the deal meets legal, regulatory, accounting and tax requirements.

citation.ref: Credit enhancer — originator's over-collateralisation or cash collateral, third party's letter of credit or surety bond; trustee; structurer

written.scenario: Ishani wants a net return of 12 per cent a year from a new equity scheme whose initial expenses are 4 per cent of the amount invested and whose recurring expenses are 1.5 per cent a year. The scheme charges an exit load of 1 per cent on units redeemed within a year; she may need the money in eight months. She has also been told that the scheme's "total expense ratio covers everything, including brokerage", that the exit load "goes to the fund house", and that its index-fund cousin "has no risk of missing the index".
written.question: Compute the return the scheme must earn to give Ishani 12 per cent, show what she would receive on redeeming a unit with a net asset value of ₹25 after eight months, and correct the three statements.

points.text: The return the scheme must earn is the investor's required return grossed up for the initial expense, plus the recurring expense: 0.12 ÷ (1 − 0.04) + 0.015 = 0.125 + 0.015 = 14 per cent. The initial expense reduces the amount that goes to work, so the investor's return must be earned on a smaller base, and the recurring expense is taken from the return every year.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mutual Funds
citation.ref: Return a scheme must earn — investor's return grossed up for initial expenses plus recurring expenses

points.text: An entry load, where charged, is added to the prevailing net asset value at allotment, so the investor is allotted fewer units; at present no scheme carries an entry load. The exit load is deducted from the net asset value at redemption: on a unit worth ₹25 redeemed within the year she receives ₹25 × 0.99 = ₹24.75, and nothing is deducted if she holds past the stipulated period.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mutual Funds
citation.ref: Entry and exit load — added to and deducted from the net asset value

points.text: The exit load does not go to the fund house. It goes into the pool of funds of the scheme, not to the asset management company, so it accrues to the investors who stay.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mutual Funds
citation.ref: Exit load goes into the pool of funds of the scheme, not to the asset management company

keywords: not to the asset management company

points.text: The expense ratio is the percentage of assets spent to run the fund: management and advisory fees, travel, audit, custodian, registrar and consultancy fees. It does not include brokerage costs for trading the portfolio, so it does not cover everything. It can run as high as 2 to 3 per cent and can seriously undermine a scheme's performance, which is why it deserves close attention.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mutual Funds
citation.ref: Expense ratio — contents; brokerage excluded; 2 to 3 per cent undermines performance

points.text: An index fund does carry tracking error, the divergence or deviation of the fund's return from the return of the benchmark it follows; expenses, cash held for redemptions and the timing of trades all cause it, so a fund can miss its index even while holding the same shares.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mutual Funds
citation.ref: Tracking error — divergence of a fund's return from its benchmark

written.scenario: Prithvi Motors Ltd wants to raise equity abroad and is choosing between an American depository receipt programme and a global depository receipt issue in Luxembourg. Its shares trade at ₹450 in India; it has just paid a dividend of ₹9 per share, expected to grow at 8 per cent a year; each depository receipt would represent three shares; issue costs would be 2 per cent of the proceeds; and it plans to issue 2,00,000 receipts. A director asks what a depository receipt is, how the two kinds differ, why Indian companies have preferred this route, what the issue would cost the company, and what such issues have done to the Indian market.
written.question: Answer each of the director's questions, computing the cost of capital of the issue and the net proceeds.

points.text: A depository receipt is a negotiable certificate, denominated in a currency not native to the issuer, that represents the company's publicly traded local-currency equity shares. It is created when the local shares are delivered to the depository's custodian bank in the country of incorporation, against which the depository bank abroad issues the receipts; the holder is entitled to the same rights and advantages as owners of the underlying shares in the home country.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: Depository receipts — negotiable certificate, custodian and depository, holder's rights

points.text: Receipts issued in the United States are American depository receipts, denominated in dollars, traded like the securities of United States companies and issued under the very stringent provisions of the Securities and Exchange Commission. A global depository receipt is identical in structure, the only difference being that it can be traded in more than one currency and both within and outside the United States; most are denominated in dollars, a few in euro or sterling, and they trade on a foreign exchange, over the counter, or among qualified institutional buyers.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: ADR against GDR — SEC provisions; GDR traded in more than one currency, within and outside the United States

points.text: Indian companies have used depository receipts to tap the global equity market for foreign-currency funds by way of equity, with no repayment of principal and generally lower servicing costs than debt; for a long time no other form of term foreign exchange funding was available; and a global depository receipt issue has been able to fetch higher prices from international investors than a domestic public issue would from Indian investors, even when sold at a discount to the domestic price. Indian issues have taken the global form because they are marketed globally rather than in one country.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: Why Indian companies issue GDRs — foreign currency equity, no repayment of principal, higher prices

points.text: Cost of capital of the issue by the dividend growth model on net proceeds: expected dividend ₹9 × 1.08 = ₹9.72; net proceeds per share ₹450 less 2 per cent = ₹441; cost = 9.72 ÷ 441 + 0.08 = 0.0220 + 0.08 = 10.20 per cent. Net proceeds of the issue: 2,00,000 receipts × 3 shares × ₹441 = ₹26.46 crore.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: Cost of capital of a GDR issue — expected dividend on net proceeds plus growth

points.text: The impact on the Indian market: trading has to some extent shifted from Bombay to Luxembourg; arbitrage is possible between the receipt and the domestic share; the Indian market is no longer independent of the rest of the world, so investors must follow worldwide events; and Indian retail investors are sidelined from such issues.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — International Financial Management
citation.ref: Impact of GDRs on the Indian capital market

written.scenario: Meghdoot Logistics Ltd has a ₹50 crore one-year loan at the benchmark rate plus 1 per cent, reset quarterly. It buys a cap at a strike of 8 per cent for a premium of 0.40 per cent of the notional, and its banker offers to buy from it a floor at 6 per cent for a premium of 0.35 per cent, "to make the protection almost free". In the first quarter (91 days) the benchmark resets at 9 per cent; in the third quarter (92 days) it resets at 5.5 per cent. The treasurer asks what each instrument is, what the company receives or pays in those two quarters if it takes the collar, and what it gives up.
written.question: Explain the cap, the floor and the collar, compute the settlement in each of the two quarters under the collar, and state the cost and the trade-off.

points.text: An interest rate cap is a call-type option: the buyer pays a premium for the right to receive the difference in interest cost on a notional principal whenever the benchmark rises above the cap rate, and bears no obligation if rates fall below it. It is characterised by a notional principal, a benchmark such as MIBOR for a specified maturity, a cap rate equivalent to a strike, and the period of the agreement with its payment and reset dates; payments follow swap-market conventions and are fixed by the benchmark on each reset date.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Cap option — right to receive the difference above the cap rate; four characteristics

points.text: Cap settlement in the first quarter: notional × max(0, benchmark − cap rate) × days ÷ 365 = ₹50 crore × (0.09 − 0.08) × 91 ÷ 365 = ₹12,46,575 received from the seller on the payment date, offsetting the extra 1 per cent Meghdoot pays on the loan.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Cap payment formula — N × max(0, r − rc) × dt ÷ days in a year

points.text: A floor protects its buyer from a fall in rates: when the benchmark is below the floor rate on a reset date the seller pays the buyer the difference, and when it is above the buyer receives nothing and loses the premium. It gives the buyer the right but not the obligation to sell a forward rate agreement, so it is a European put option on an FRA, and a multi-period floor is a bundle of such puts on a succession of FRAs.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Floor option — payoff when the rate falls below the strike; European put on an FRA

points.text: A collar is a bought cap and a simultaneously sold floor, which locks the borrower into a floating rate bounded on the high side and the low side; the settlement is notional × [max(0, r − cap rate) − max(0, floor rate − r)] × days ÷ 365. First quarter: the cap leg pays ₹12,46,575 and the floor leg nothing. Third quarter: the cap leg pays nothing and Meghdoot, as seller of the floor, pays ₹50 crore × (0.06 − 0.055) × 92 ÷ 365 = ₹6,30,137, giving up the benefit of the lower rate below 6 per cent.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Interest rate collar — bought cap and sold floor; combined payment formula

points.text: The collar is cheaper than the cap alone because the premium earned on the floor offsets the cap premium: net cost 0.40 − 0.35 = 0.05 per cent of ₹50 crore, that is ₹2,50,000 against ₹20,00,000 for the cap by itself; had the two premiums been equal it would be a zero-cost collar. The price is that buying a collar limits the borrower's ability to benefit from a significant decline in rates, as the third quarter shows.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Interest Rate Risk Management
citation.ref: Collar less expensive than a cap; zero-cost collar; limits benefit from a decline in rates

written.scenario: Kanchan Tools Ltd reports for 2025-26 (₹ lakh): earnings before interest and tax 600, after charging a bad-debt provision of 30 inside selling and administrative expenses; total assets 3,000 after deducting that provision from receivables; non-interest-bearing current liabilities 800; equity and reserves 1,800; borrowings 400. The pre-tax cost of debt is 10 per cent, the tax rate 30 per cent and the cost of equity 11 per cent. The market capitalisation is 2,700 and the debt trades at book value. The board wants to know whether management "created value", and a director says the share price already answers that.
written.question: Compute the economic value added and the market value added, and explain what each measures and how they differ.

points.text: Net operating profit after tax: EBIT 600 less tax at 30 per cent 180, plus the non-cash bad-debt provision of 30 added back, gives NOPAT of ₹450 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: EVA step I — NOPAT with non-cash expenses added back

points.text: Invested capital: total assets 3,000 less non-interest-bearing liabilities 800 gives 2,200, plus the non-cash adjustment of 30 for the provision deducted from receivables, giving ₹2,230 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: EVA step II — invested capital as total assets less non-interest-bearing liabilities plus non-cash adjustment

points.text: Weighted average cost of capital on the book weights of equity 1,800 and debt 400: 1,800 ÷ 2,200 × 11 per cent + 400 ÷ 2,200 × 10 per cent × (1 − 0.30) = 9.00 + 1.27 = 10.27 per cent. Capital charge = 2,230 × 10.27 per cent = ₹229.1 lakh. Economic value added = NOPAT 450 − 229.1 = ₹220.9 lakh: management earned that much above the hurdle rate on the capital invested.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: EVA steps III to V — WACC, capital charge, EVA as NOPAT less capital charge

points.text: Market value added is the current market value of the firm less the invested capital: market capitalisation 2,700 plus debt 400 gives 3,100, less 2,230, an MVA of ₹870 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: MVA — current market value of the firm less invested capital

points.text: EVA is a derived value added for the discerning investor, showing management's efficiency in generating returns over and above the hurdle rate on invested capital in one year. MVA is the value added as perceived by the market, an attempt to resolve EVA's neglect of value drivers and its reliance on book values, and it gauges performance from a market-capitalisation point of view without itself giving a basis for share valuation. Because MVA carries the market's view of future value creation, a high-MVA company can become pricey and EVA and MVA may briefly move in opposite directions, a gap investors close over time; the director is half right, since the share price measures expectation, not the year's performance.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Business Valuation
citation.ref: EVA against MVA — derived against market-perceived value added; short-term divergence

written.scenario: Rudra Chemicals Ltd finds that Ashwa Industries has quietly built a 14 per cent stake through market purchases and now tells the board that unless it agrees to a change of control, Ashwa will announce an open offer to shareholders. The board's advisers table six responses: issue a large tranche of convertible debentures to existing shareholders, convertible when a bid is made; sell the highly profitable specialty-polymers division; buy back Ashwa's stake at a premium to the market price in return for its withdrawal; contract hefty severance pay for the senior managers; make a counter-bid for Ashwa; and invite Prabhat Group, a friendly company, to acquire Rudra instead.
written.question: Name the takeover strategies Ashwa has used, name and explain each of the six defensive tactics proposed, and comment on the board's overall position.

points.text: A takeover is an unfriendly acquisition: it becomes hostile when the acquirer, after the target's board rejects its offer, approaches the shareholders directly through a public announcement or tender offer. Ashwa's quiet accumulation of 14 per cent before any open offer is a street sweep, which leaves the target little choice; its threat to make an open offer unless the board settles for a change of control is a bear hug. Other strategies include a strategic alliance that disarms the target by offering a partnership and brand power that displaces the target's brands before buying the weakened company.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring
citation.ref: Hostile takeover through tender offer; takeover strategies — street sweep, bear hug, strategic alliance, brand power

points.text: The convertible debentures are a poison pill: a tactic that makes the target unattractive to a bidder, here by issuing substantial convertible debentures to existing shareholders to be converted when a takeover threatens, so that the number of voting shares rises sharply and the bidder's task becomes difficult. A poison put is the related tactic of issuing bonds that holders can cash in at high prices, draining cash from the target.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring
citation.ref: Defensive tactics — poison pill, poison put

points.text: Selling the specialty-polymers division is a divestiture, and because it is the most attractive business it is selling the crown jewels, which reduces the attractiveness of what remains; in some countries such as the United Kingdom the tactic is not allowed once the deal is known and unavoidable. Buying back Ashwa's stake at a premium in return for its withdrawal is greenmail, an incentive offered by the target's management to the bidder for not pursuing the takeover.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring
citation.ref: Defensive tactics — divestiture, crown jewels, greenmail

points.text: The severance contracts are golden parachutes, hefty compensation to managers ousted by a takeover, which reduces the acquirer's interest. The counter-bid for Ashwa is the Pac-man defence, forcing the acquirer to defend itself and perhaps call off its proposal. Inviting Prabhat is the white knight, a friendly acquirer sought to escape a hostile one so that the management is not replaced; a white squire is the variant where shares are sold to a company not interested in the takeover, so that management keeps control.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring
citation.ref: Defensive tactics — golden parachutes, Pac-man defence, white knight, white squire

points.text: Hostile takeovers should be avoided as far as possible because they are more difficult to consummate; a friendly takeover is the better course. Several of the tactics, greenmail and the crown-jewel sale in particular, protect management rather than shareholders, and the board should weigh each against the shareholders' interest rather than its own survival.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring
citation.ref: Hostile takeovers more difficult to consummate; friendly takeover the better course

written.scenario: Anvi has ₹8 lakh of savings and a signed first order from a corporate client that pays sixty days after delivery. She needs a ₹5 lakh machine, her raw-material supplier wants cash on delivery, and her uncle, who sold his own business last year, offers ₹20 lakh for 15 per cent of the company "so you can set up properly". A mentor tells her to bootstrap for the first year and take the uncle's money only when she knows what it is for.
written.question: Explain what bootstrapping means and why the mentor recommends it, set out three bootstrapping methods that fit Anvi's position, and describe what kind of investor the uncle would be and how that differs from venture capital.

points.text: Bootstrapping is starting and building a company from personal finances or from the operating revenues of the new company. Founders commonly overspend on marketing, offices and equipment they cannot afford; more money at inception leads to complacency and wasteful expenditure, while investing one's own savings produces a cautious approach that curbs waste and keeps the promoter on their toes.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Startup Finance
citation.ref: Bootstrapping — personal finances or operating revenues; discipline against wasteful expenditure

points.text: Trade credit: suppliers are reluctant to extend credit to a new business, so Anvi should prepare a well-crafted financial plan and visit the supplier, the owner if it is small or the chief financial officer if it is large, with a reference who can vouch for her; the supplier may give half the order on credit and the balance on delivery, and the aim is to ship and sell the goods before paying for them, which reduces the working capital needed. Factoring: sell the receivable from the corporate client to a commercial finance company, which takes over collection and the paperwork, possibly on a non-notification basis; it frees money otherwise tied up for sixty days and can cost less than maintaining collections in house.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Startup Finance
citation.ref: Bootstrapping methods — trade credit, factoring

points.text: Leasing: take the ₹5 lakh machine on lease rather than buying it, which reduces the capital cost, avoids a lump-sum payment a startup cannot afford, lets the lessee claim the lease rentals for tax and walk away at the end of the term, while the lessor gets depreciation and any capital appreciation.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Startup Finance
citation.ref: Bootstrapping methods — leasing rather than purchasing equipment

points.text: The uncle would be an angel investor: an affluent individual, often from the entrepreneur's family and friends, who injects his own capital into a startup in exchange for ownership equity or convertible debt, as a one-time or ongoing injection, on terms more favourable than other lenders because he invests in the entrepreneur rather than the viability of the business. Venture capitalists, by contrast, manage pooled money from many investors in a strategically managed fund and invest alongside management in young, rapidly growing companies. Angels who seed failures lose everything, so professional angels look for a defined exit through acquisition or initial public offering.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 — Startup Finance
citation.ref: Angel investors — own money, equity or convertible debt, favourable terms; contrast with venture capital funds

written.scenario: Three unrelated situations at three clients. (a) Inventory is overstated by ₹4 crore against a profit of ₹60 crore; management will not adjust. (b) The company has not consolidated its only subsidiary, which is larger than the parent, and no consolidated statements have been prepared. (c) You were appointed after the year end, the company's records for the first half were destroyed in a fire, and no alternative evidence exists for revenue, purchases or inventory for that half.
written.question: For each, state the opinion you would express and the reason, using the two tests the standard sets.

points.text: State the two tests first: whether the matter is a misstatement or an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and whether its effects are material but not pervasive, or material and pervasive.

citation.ref: Determining the type of modification to the auditor's opinion

keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

points.text: (a) Qualified opinion — a misstatement that is material but not pervasive.

citation.ref: Qualified opinion — material but not pervasive misstatement

points.text: (b) Adverse opinion — a misstatement that is both material and pervasive, since omitting consolidation of the dominant subsidiary affects the statements as a whole.

citation.ref: Adverse opinion — material and pervasive misstatement

points.text: (c) Disclaimer of opinion — an inability to obtain evidence whose possible effects are both material and pervasive.

citation.ref: Disclaimer of opinion — pervasive inability to obtain evidence

points.text: Add that each modification carries a "Basis for Modified Opinion" section placed immediately before the opinion section, describing the matter.

citation.ref: Basis for Modified Opinion section

written.scenario: Fernhill Chemicals Ltd is listed. Its impairment testing of a ₹300 crore cash-generating unit involved significant management judgement and took much of your engagement effort. Separately, a fire after the year end destroyed a warehouse; the event is properly disclosed in the notes and needs no adjustment. Your opinion is unmodified. The audit committee asks why one of these will appear in your report as a key audit matter and the other will not.
written.question: Explain how a key audit matter is selected, and distinguish it from an emphasis of matter paragraph.

points.text: Key audit matters are those matters that, in the auditor's professional judgement, were of most significance in the audit of the current period, and they are selected from matters communicated with those charged with governance.

citation.ref: Definition and determination of key audit matters

keywords: communicated with those charged with governance

points.text: Narrow from that population by what required significant auditor attention — areas of higher assessed risk, significant judgements including estimates with high estimation uncertainty, and the effect of significant events or transactions.

citation.ref: Determining key audit matters — matters requiring significant auditor attention

points.text: Communicating key audit matters is not a substitute for a modified opinion, nor for disclosure the framework requires, nor for reporting a going concern material uncertainty.

citation.ref: Key audit matters are not a substitute for other reporting

points.text: An emphasis of matter paragraph draws attention to something already disclosed in the financial statements which is fundamental to users' understanding — so the fire, being properly disclosed and not a matter of audit significance, belongs there if anywhere.

citation.ref: Emphasis of Matter paragraphs

points.text: Note the applicability point: key audit matters are required for listed entities, which Fernhill is.

citation.ref: Scope — audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities

written.scenario: A junior on your team has set materiality for the financial statements as a whole at ₹50 lakh and proposes to use that same figure when designing and performing every audit procedure, and to ignore any misstatement below it entirely.
written.question: Explain what is wrong, defining the three levels the standard requires.

points.text: Materiality for the financial statements as a whole is what the ₹50 lakh is: the level above which misstatements could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users.

citation.ref: Materiality in the context of an audit

keywords: materiality for the financial statements as a whole
influence the economic decisions of users

points.text: Performance materiality is set below that, to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that the aggregate of uncorrected and undetected misstatements exceeds materiality for the statements as a whole. Procedures are designed against this, not against the headline figure.

citation.ref: Definition and determination of performance materiality

points.text: A separate, lower materiality may be needed for particular classes of transactions, balances or disclosures where misstatements of lesser amounts would still influence users — related party transactions and director remuneration being the usual examples.

citation.ref: Materiality levels for particular classes of transactions, balances or disclosures

points.text: Misstatements below materiality are not simply ignored: only those below the clearly trivial threshold need not be accumulated, and the rest are accumulated and evaluated, individually and in aggregate.

citation.ref: Accumulation of identified misstatements — clearly trivial

written.scenario: Inventory of ₹80 crore is material to Ardsley Steel Ltd. The count took place on 31 March at a plant that was under a curfew, and you could not attend. A further ₹12 crore of inventory is held at a third-party warehouse.
written.question: State your responsibilities and what you would do about each.

points.text: Where inventory is material, attendance at physical counting is required — to evaluate management's instructions and procedures, observe the count, inspect the inventory and perform test counts.

citation.ref: Attendance at physical inventory counting

points.text: Where attendance is impracticable, perform alternative audit procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence — not simply accept the balance. Impracticable means impracticable; inconvenience or cost is not the test.

citation.ref: Where attendance is impracticable

points.text: Where it is not possible to do so, modify the opinion for an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence.

citation.ref: Inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

points.text: For inventory held by a third party, obtain confirmation from that party as to quantities and condition, or perform inspection or other procedures appropriate in the circumstances.

citation.ref: Inventory under the custody and control of a third party

written.scenario: Consider four proposed appointments. (a) CA Anand, whose brother holds equity of face value ₹2 lakh in the company. (b) A firm in which a partner is a director of the company's subsidiary. (c) CA Bela, who owes the company ₹6 lakh on a personal loan. (d) A firm already holding audits of nineteen other companies, being offered a twentieth and a twenty-first, one of which is a dormant company.
written.question: Advise on each under section 141.

points.text: (a) A relative may hold securities of face value not exceeding the prescribed limit of ₹1 lakh; ₹2 lakh exceeds it, so the appointment is barred unless the holding is brought within the limit within the corrective window.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(d)(i) read with Rule 10 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014

points.text: (b) A person whose partner is a director or key managerial personnel of the company — and the disqualification extends through the group as the section provides — cannot be appointed.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(f)

points.text: (c) Indebtedness to the company beyond the prescribed limit of ₹5 lakh disqualifies; ₹6 lakh does.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(d)(ii) read with Rule 10

points.text: (d) The ceiling is twenty companies per person, and dormant companies, one person companies, small companies and private companies with paid-up capital below the prescribed threshold are excluded from the count.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(g)

points.text: Add the consequence: a disqualification incurred after appointment vacates the office, and the vacancy is treated as a casual vacancy.

citation.ref: Section 141(4)

written.scenario: The internal audit function at Kelmore Ltd is competent and objective. The engagement partner proposes to use two internal auditors to carry out substantive procedures on trade receivables, and separately to have them evaluate the significant estimate of expected credit losses.
written.question: Advise, stating what direct assistance is permitted and what is not.

points.text: Direct assistance is permitted under the revised standard, provided the auditor first evaluates the internal auditors' objectivity and competence and the existence and significance of threats to that objectivity.

citation.ref: Using internal auditors to provide direct assistance

points.text: Work so used must be directed, supervised and reviewed by the external auditor, who remains solely responsible for the opinion — that responsibility is not reduced.

citation.ref: Directing, supervising and reviewing work performed by internal auditors

points.text: Internal auditors may not be used for work involving significant judgements, for areas of higher assessed risk of material misstatement, or in relation to work they themselves performed and reported internally — so the receivables testing may be permissible and the expected credit loss estimate is not.

citation.ref: Work that cannot be assigned to internal auditors providing direct assistance

keywords: higher assessed risk of material misstatement

points.text: Obtain written agreement from an authorised representative of the entity that the internal auditors will be allowed to follow the auditor's instructions, and from the internal auditors that they will keep confidentiality and inform the auditor of threats to their objectivity.

citation.ref: Written agreements before using direct assistance

written.scenario: A partner tells a junior that working papers are an internal matter, that anything obvious to the team need not be written down, and that the file can be tidied up whenever there is time after the report is signed.
written.question: State the standard's position on each of the three propositions.

points.text: The test is not what the team knows. Documentation must be sufficient to enable an experienced auditor, having no previous connection with the audit, to understand the nature, timing and extent of procedures, their results and the evidence obtained, and the significant matters and conclusions reached.

citation.ref: Form, content and extent of audit documentation — the experienced auditor test

keywords: no previous connection with the audit

points.text: Record the identifying characteristics of the items tested, who performed the work and the date, and who reviewed it and when.

citation.ref: Documentation of the audit work performed and reviewer

points.text: The file is assembled on a timely basis after the date of the auditor's report, ordinarily not more than sixty days after it, and after assembly nothing may be deleted or discarded before the end of the retention period.

citation.ref: Assembly of the final engagement file and retention

points.text: Where anything is added or changed after assembly, record the reason, by whom and when, and who reviewed it.

citation.ref: Changes to documentation after the assembly of the final audit file

written.scenario: A partner at a mid-sized firm says peer review is the Institute checking whether the firm's audit opinions were correct, that it looks at the firm's tax and consulting files as well, and that a firm can be fined as a result of it.
written.question: Correct him, stating what peer review is for and how it runs.

points.text: Peer review examines the systems and procedures by which attestation services are performed — whether the work was carried out in accordance with technical, ethical and professional standards — and does not second-guess the opinion reached.

citation.ref: Objective and scope of peer review

points.text: Its scope is attestation services only. Non-attestation work such as management consultancy, representation before authorities and tax return preparation is outside it.

citation.ref: Attestation services covered

points.text: It runs in stages — planning, execution and reporting — with a sample of engagements selected by the reviewer, and it concludes in a report to the Board, not in a penalty.

citation.ref: Stages of peer review and the reviewer's report

points.text: Disciplinary action is a separate matter under the Chartered Accountants Act; peer review is not a disciplinary proceeding.

citation.ref: Peer review distinguished from disciplinary proceedings

written.scenario: Kavali Textiles Pvt Ltd, a company reportable under CARO 2020, granted an unsecured, interest-free loan of ₹3 crore to its wholly owned subsidiary during the year, repayable on demand. It also advanced ₹50 lakh to an employee, interest free, repayable over five years. A third loan of ₹1.2 crore to a private company in which one of Kavali's directors is interested has been overdue for 95 days at the year end, and no steps have been taken to recover it.
written.question: State the auditor's reporting obligations under CARO 2020 clause 3(iii) for each of these three facts.

points.text: Clause 3(iii) requires reporting whether the company has granted loans, advances in the nature of loans, or given guarantees or security to any person during the year, and, if so, disclosure of the aggregate amount and number of parties, separating loans to subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates from others.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii) — loans, guarantees, security and advances to any person

keywords: advances in the nature of loans
aggregate amount and number of parties

points.text: For each such loan, report whether the terms and conditions are not prejudicial to the company's interest — an interest-free loan is not automatically prejudicial, but the auditor must form and state a view on it, including on the loan to the subsidiary.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii) — terms not prejudicial to the company's interest

keywords: not prejudicial to the company's interest

points.text: Report on the repayment schedule: the subsidiary loan being repayable on demand has no fixed schedule, so this and its regularity of repayment must be separately stated; for the employee loan, report the schedule stipulated and whether receipts have been regular.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii) — repayment schedule stipulated and regularity of repayments or receipts

points.text: For the loan overdue 95 days, being more than ninety days, report the amount overdue and state that no reasonable steps have been taken for recovery — this is an adverse remark to be made, not omitted.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii) — amount overdue for more than ninety days and steps taken for recovery

points.text: Note the separate limb for loans and advances granted to employees, which is reported under the same clause distinctly from loans to other persons.

citation.ref: Clause 3(iii) — loans and advances in the nature of loans to employees

keywords: loans and advances granted to employees

written.scenario: In the branch audit of Suryoday Cooperative Bank you review three borrower accounts as at 31 March. Ganges Foundry Ltd's cash credit account has remained continuously out of order for 95 days — the outstanding balance has stayed above the sanctioned limit with no credit corresponding to interest applied. A term loan account of Malabar Rice Mills has its instalment and interest overdue for 100 days. A third account, already classified sub-standard, has remained in that classification for exactly twelve months as at this date, and is fully secured.
written.question: Classify each account and state the basis for the classification and the provisioning consequence.

points.text: State the definition first: an asset becomes non-performing when it ceases to generate income for the bank, and for a cash credit or overdraft account this is when the account remains "out of order" for a continuous period.

citation.source: RBI Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning
citation.ref: Definition of a non-performing asset and the out-of-order test for cash credit and overdraft accounts

points.text: Ganges Foundry's cash credit account, out of order for 95 days, exceeds the ninety-day threshold and is classified as a non-performing asset.

citation.source: RBI Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning
citation.ref: Ninety-day norm for a continuous out-of-order cash credit or overdraft account

points.text: Malabar Rice Mills' term loan, with instalment and interest overdue 100 days, exceeds the ninety-day threshold applicable to term loans and is likewise classified as a non-performing asset.

citation.source: RBI Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning
citation.ref: Ninety-day norm for overdue instalment or interest on a term loan

points.text: The account already sub-standard for twelve months moves to doubtful classification, an asset remaining in the sub-standard category for that period being reclassified.

citation.source: RBI Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning
citation.ref: Migration from sub-standard to doubtful after twelve months

points.text: State the provisioning consequence: sub-standard and doubtful assets attract prescribed provisioning that varies with the age of the doubtful classification and the extent to which the advance is secured, higher provisioning applying as an asset ages further into doubtful.

citation.source: RBI Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning
citation.ref: Provisioning norms for sub-standard and doubtful assets

written.scenario: Vantage Software Pvt Ltd, a company whose accounts are audited under the Companies Act 2013, and Meherotra Autoparts, a partnership firm not audited under any other law, both cross the turnover threshold under section 44AB for the year and require a tax audit.
written.question: State which report form applies to each and explain the role of Form 3CD.

points.text: Section 44AB requires specified persons to get their accounts audited and obtain the audit report in the form prescribed for the purpose; which of the two forms applies turns on whether the accounts are already audited under another law.

citation.ref: Section 44AB — tax audit and the prescribed report

points.text: Vantage Software Pvt Ltd, being audited under the Companies Act 2013, uses Form 3CA, in which the tax auditor refers to the accounts already audited under that other law rather than expressing a fresh opinion on them.

citation.ref: Prescribed report where the accounts are audited under another law — Form 3CA

points.text: Meherotra Autoparts, not audited under any other law, uses Form 3CB, in which the tax auditor additionally gives an opinion on whether the financial statements show a true and fair view.

citation.ref: Prescribed report where the accounts are not audited under another law — Form 3CB

keywords: not audited under any other law

points.text: Form 3CD is the statement of particulars annexed to both Form 3CA and Form 3CB, common to both, setting out the prescribed clause-wise particulars — method of accounting, disallowances, TDS compliance and the like — on which the tax auditor reports.

citation.ref: Statement of particulars annexed to Form 3CA and Form 3CB — Form 3CD

written.scenario: Alpha & Co and Beta & Co are joint auditors of Rockford Engineering Ltd. Work was divided by area: Alpha & Co covered revenue and receivables, Beta & Co covered inventory and payables. Both firms signed a common, unmodified audit report. It later emerges that a fictitious sale of ₹5 crore was booked using manipulated dispatch documents, within the area allotted to Alpha & Co, and was not detected because the work performed there was clearly inadequate.
written.question: State each joint auditor's responsibility for the failure, and whether Beta & Co is also answerable for it.

points.text: Where work is divided among joint auditors, each is responsible only for the work allocated to it, and is entitled to rely on the work performed by the other joint auditors without further verification, unless there is reason to believe otherwise.

citation.ref: Division of work among joint auditors and reliance on the work of other joint auditors

keywords: responsible only for the work allocated

points.text: Joint and several responsibility attaches only to matters that are not divided among the joint auditors and are covered by all of them jointly, decisions taken jointly by all joint auditors, and matters brought to the notice of a joint auditor that require consideration by all — not to a matter that was validly allotted to one of them alone.

citation.ref: Matters of joint and several responsibility among joint auditors

points.text: Alpha & Co is responsible for the work allotted to it, so the failure to detect the fictitious sale within revenue and receivables falls on Alpha & Co, being the area it was responsible for.

citation.ref: Responsibility of a joint auditor for work allocated to it

keywords: responsible for the work allotted to it

points.text: A joint auditor is not required to review the work performed by the other joint auditors, so Beta & Co is not liable for Alpha & Co's specifically-allotted work merely because the fraud existed, in the absence of anything that ought to have raised Beta & Co's suspicion.

citation.ref: No requirement for a joint auditor to review work performed by another joint auditor

keywords: not required to review the work

points.text: Conclude: Alpha & Co bears the primary responsibility for the undetected fraud within its allotted area; Beta & Co's exposure turns on whether it had reason to doubt Alpha & Co's work, which nothing in the facts shows.

citation.ref: Reporting responsibility of joint auditors

written.scenario: Talwar Retail Ltd has forty branches. Separate branch auditors were appointed for twelve of them, the remaining twenty-eight being audited by the principal auditor's own team. One branch auditor, for a branch contributing about 6% of the company's turnover, issued a qualified report because of a ₹40 lakh stock reconciliation discrepancy that the principal auditor, on review, considers material to that branch but not material to the company as a whole.
written.question: State the principal auditor's responsibilities in using this branch auditor's report, and how the company's audit report should deal with the qualification.

points.text: Where separate branch auditors are appointed, the principal auditor is entitled to rely on the branch auditor's report for that branch, subject to determining how the branch audit results are to be used in forming the opinion on the financial statements as a whole.

citation.ref: Section 143(8) — audit of branch accounts by a person other than the company's auditor

points.text: The principal auditor considers the significant findings of the branch auditor, evaluates the significance of the branch to the entity as a whole, and, where necessary, discusses the matter with the branch auditor or performs further procedures.

citation.ref: Procedures performed by the principal auditor when using the work of another auditor

points.text: The principal auditor determines whether a matter noted by the branch auditor is material to the financial statements as a whole; a matter material only to the branch need not by itself be carried into a qualification of the group report.

citation.ref: Materiality to the financial statements as a whole when using another auditor's report

keywords: material to the financial statements as a whole

points.text: Since the ₹40 lakh discrepancy is, on the principal auditor's evaluation, not material to the company as a whole, the principal auditor's own report need not be qualified on that matter, though the position may still be discussed with those charged with governance.

citation.ref: Reporting considerations where another auditor's report is qualified

keywords: not material to the company as a whole

written.scenario: During the audit of Devendra Plastics Ltd you note three matters. First, the person who authorises purchase orders is the same person who approves supplier payments. Second, an unusual manual journal entry of ₹15 lakh posted at the year end was not independently reviewed by anyone before posting. Third, petty cash reconciliations are not performed every month.
written.question: Classify each matter and state your reporting responsibility for it.

points.text: Define a significant deficiency in internal control as one that, in the auditor's professional judgement, is of sufficient importance to merit the attention of those charged with governance.

citation.ref: Definition of a significant deficiency in internal control

keywords: merit the attention of those charged with governance

points.text: The absence of segregation of duties between authorising purchase orders and approving payments, and the lack of independent review of a significant unusual manual journal entry, are indicators of significant deficiencies because of the fraud risk each creates.

citation.ref: Indicators of significant deficiencies in internal control

points.text: Communicate significant deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis.

citation.ref: Communicating significant deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance

points.text: The petty cash reconciliation lapse, being a lesser deficiency, is communicated to management at an appropriate level of responsibility on a timely basis, and need not be communicated to those charged with governance unless management has already been told and taken no action.

citation.ref: Communicating other deficiencies in internal control to management

written.scenario: Larkspur Distributors Ltd's trade receivables of ₹22 crore comprise a large number of small, homogeneous retail-dealer balances. The combined assessed risk of material misstatement is low and controls over the receivables process are operating effectively. The audit senior proposes to confirm the entire balance using negative confirmation requests, without further consideration of whether the approach is appropriate.
written.question: State whether negative confirmation requests may be used here, and the conditions attaching to their use.

points.text: A negative confirmation request asks the respondent to reply only if they disagree with the stated information, so the absence of a reply does not, by itself, provide the strong evidence a positive confirmation would — a non-reply may equally mean the request was never received or read.

citation.ref: Negative confirmation requests — nature and limitation of a non-reply as evidence

points.text: Negative confirmation requests may be used as the sole substantive procedure only where a combination of conditions is met: the assessed risk of material misstatement is low, controls relevant to the assertion are operating effectively, the population comprises a large number of small, homogeneous balances, and a low exception rate is expected.

citation.ref: Conditions for using negative confirmation requests as the sole substantive procedure

keywords: assessed risk of material misstatement is low

points.text: The senior must not simply proceed on the population's description — the auditor evaluates whether the stated conditions are actually satisfied in substance before relying on negative confirmations alone, rather than accepting the proposal without that evaluation.

citation.ref: Auditor's evaluation of whether the conditions for using negative confirmations are met

points.text: Investigate any exceptions received, and where a positive confirmation would otherwise be required for balances presenting a significant risk, apply alternative procedures rather than treating a non-reply as satisfactory.

citation.ref: Investigating exceptions and non-replies to confirmation requests

written.scenario: CA Meera is appointed as first-time auditor of Whitfield Ceramics Ltd for the current year; the prior year's financial statements were audited by another firm, which issued an unmodified opinion. Meera is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the opening inventory balance of ₹4 crore, because the predecessor's working papers on the physical count are missing and no records survive that would let her perform alternative procedures.
written.question: State her responsibilities regarding opening balances, and the effect on her report given the evidence gap on opening inventory.

points.text: Obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about whether the opening balances contain misstatements that materially affect the current period's financial statements.

citation.ref: Audit procedures regarding opening balances

points.text: Read the most recent financial statements and the predecessor auditor's report for relevant information, and evaluate whether accounting policies were consistently applied in the current period and, if changed, properly accounted for and disclosed.

citation.ref: Consistency of accounting policies and reading the predecessor auditor's report

points.text: Where the prior period was audited, evidence about opening balances is ordinarily obtained by reviewing the predecessor auditor's working papers, but the sufficiency of this depends on the predecessor's professional competence and independence.

citation.ref: Reliance on the predecessor auditor's working papers for opening balances

points.text: Where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about opening balances, the opinion is modified as a qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion as appropriate — here, inventory being material and no alternative procedures being possible, Meera must assess whether the effect is pervasive.

citation.ref: Effect on the auditor's opinion of inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about opening balances

keywords: unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

points.text: State the modification is an inability to obtain evidence about the opening balance carried forward into the current period, distinct from a finding that the balance is actually misstated.

citation.ref: Reporting an inability to obtain evidence about opening balances, distinguished from a misstatement

written.scenario: Nandkarni & Associates are the statutory auditors of Ashgrove Cements Ltd, a listed company. Four things happened during the year ended 31 March 2026. First, a firm in Singapore that belongs to Nandkarni's international network and uses the same brand name was engaged by Ashgrove's wholly owned subsidiary to design and implement its new financial reporting system, for a fee of ₹85 lakh. Second, the spouse of a partner of Nandkarni & Associates, a practising actuary in her own right, valued the parent company's gratuity liability for a fee of ₹6 lakh. Third, the firm itself was asked to certify Ashgrove's foreign remittances under the Income-tax Act for ₹2 lakh, and the audit committee approved the engagement before it began. Fourth, the company's turnover rose 14% over the previous year.
written.question: Examine each of the three engagements under the Companies Act 2013, and state the consequence for the auditor of having rendered a service the Act forbids.

points.text: Set out the prohibition in section 144: the auditor of a company may not render certain specified services, namely accounting and book keeping services, internal audit, design and implementation of any financial information system, actuarial services, investment advisory services, investment banking services, rendering of outsourced financial services, and management services.

citation.ref: Section 144 — services an auditor of a company shall not render

keywords: design and implementation of any financial information system

points.text: The prohibition is not confined to the audited company itself — it extends to services rendered to the company, to its holding company and to its subsidiary, so an engagement taken at the wholly owned subsidiary is squarely within reach.

citation.ref: Section 144 — prohibition extends to the company, its holding company and its subsidiary

points.text: Explain "directly or indirectly". For a firm of auditors it covers a service rendered by any partner of the firm, by any parent, subsidiary or associate entity of the firm, and by any entity whose name, trade mark or brand is used by the firm or any of its partners.

citation.ref: Section 144 — Explanation defining rendering of services directly or indirectly

points.text: The Singapore network firm's engagement is prohibited on both limbs — the service is design and implementation of a financial information system, and it is rendered by an entity using the firm's brand name, hence rendered indirectly by the auditor, to the audited company's subsidiary. The ₹85 lakh fee and the arm's-length appearance of a separate legal entity make no difference.

citation.ref: Section 144 — design and implementation of any financial information system, rendered indirectly through a brand-sharing entity

keywords: design and implementation of a financial information system

points.text: The gratuity valuation by the partner's spouse is prohibited. Actuarial services are a listed service, and the indirect limb reaches a relative of a partner, so her holding a separate practice does not take the engagement outside the section.

citation.ref: Section 144 — actuarial services, read with the Explanation covering a relative of a partner

points.text: The certification of foreign remittances is permissible. Certification work of that kind is not among the services the section lists, and other services may be rendered provided they are approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee — which was obtained here before the engagement began.

citation.ref: Section 144 — other services rendered only with the approval of the Board of Directors or the audit committee

keywords: approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee

points.text: State the consequence. An auditor who renders a prohibited service incurs the corresponding disqualification, and an auditor who incurs a disqualification after appointment is deemed to have vacated office, the resulting vacancy being treated as a casual vacancy to be filled by the company; contravention of section 144 also exposes the auditor personally to the penalty the Act prescribes for an auditor's contravention.

citation.ref: Section 141(4) — deemed vacation of office on incurring a disqualification, the vacancy being a casual vacancy

written.scenario: Prathamesh & Co are the statutory auditors of Konark Alloys Ltd, an unlisted public company with no government shareholding. On 14 August 2026, after the board refused to write off ₹9 crore of "business development expenses" for which no supporting records exist, the firm resigned with immediate effect by an email to the managing director. It filed nothing with the Registrar of Companies, taking the view that the resignation was a private matter between the firm and the company. The board appointed a new auditor by a board resolution passed on 2 September 2026 and did not put the appointment to the members, saying the next annual general meeting is eleven months away. The company's turnover grew 20% during the year.
written.question: State the resigning auditor's obligations on resignation and the consequence of not meeting them, and say whether the company has filled the resulting vacancy correctly.

points.text: On resigning, the auditor must file a statement in the prescribed form with the company and with the Registrar within thirty days of the resignation, indicating the reasons for resigning and any other facts relevant to it. An email to the managing director discharges neither limb.

citation.ref: Section 140(2) — statement to be filed by a resigning auditor with the company and the Registrar within thirty days

points.text: Where the company is a government company or one in which the Comptroller and Auditor-General appoints the auditor, the statement also goes to the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Konark Alloys has no government shareholding, so this limb does not apply on these facts.

citation.ref: Section 140(2) — additional filing with the Comptroller and Auditor-General for companies referred to in section 139(5)

points.text: State the consequence of failure. The default attracts a penalty on the auditor personally, not on the company — the obligation is the auditor's own and survives the ending of the engagement.

citation.ref: Section 140(3) — penalty on an auditor who fails to comply with section 140(2)

points.text: A resignation creates a casual vacancy in the office of auditor. A casual vacancy caused by resignation is filled by the Board of Directors within thirty days, but that appointment must also be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the Board's recommendation.

citation.ref: Section 139(8) — casual vacancy caused by resignation, filled by the Board and approved by the company in general meeting within three months

keywords: Board of Directors within thirty days
approved by the company at a general meeting

points.text: Apply it. The board resolution of 2 September falls within thirty days of the 14 August resignation and is in order, but the company is wrong to wait for the annual general meeting — a general meeting must be convened within three months to approve the appointment, and the auditor so appointed holds office only until the conclusion of the next annual general meeting.

citation.ref: Section 139(8) — tenure of an auditor appointed in a casual vacancy

keywords: holds office only until the conclusion of the next annual general meeting

written.scenario: Suvarna Capital Ltd is a non-banking financial company with an asset size of ₹4,200 crore as at 31 March 2026. It does not accept public deposits and is not named in the Reserve Bank's published list of upper layer NBFCs. Three matters arise on your audit. The board tells you the company must be in the base layer because it takes no deposits. A borrower's instalment and interest have been overdue for 105 days and the account is still carried as a standard asset with the interest recognised as income. You also find that the company's net owned fund has fallen below the minimum the Reserve Bank requires. The engagement partner on the audit was rotated during the year.
written.question: State the layer the company falls into and why, the correct classification of the overdue account, and your duty in respect of the net owned fund shortfall, including whom you must report it to.

points.text: Describe the framework: the Reserve Bank regulates NBFCs in four layers — base, middle, upper and a top layer that is ordinarily kept empty — set by size, activity and perceived riskiness, with regulatory intensity rising through the stack.

citation.source: RBI Scale Based Regulation — a revised regulatory framework for NBFCs
citation.ref: The four-layer regulatory structure for NBFCs

points.text: Correct the board. Not taking deposits does not put a company in the base layer. The base layer holds non-deposit-taking NBFCs below the prescribed asset-size threshold; a non-deposit-taking NBFC at or above that threshold sits in the middle layer along with every deposit-taking NBFC. At ₹4,200 crore of assets Suvarna Capital is a middle layer NBFC, and the middle layer's prudential requirements apply to it.

citation.source: RBI Scale Based Regulation — a revised regulatory framework for NBFCs
citation.ref: Composition of the base layer and the middle layer by asset size and acceptance of deposits

points.text: The account is misclassified. Under the harmonised norm an NBFC asset becomes non-performing when the instalment or interest is overdue beyond ninety days, so at 105 days the account is non-performing and must be classified as sub-standard.

citation.source: RBI Scale Based Regulation — a revised regulatory framework for NBFCs
citation.ref: Harmonised ninety-day overdue norm for classification of an NBFC asset as non-performing

points.text: Draw out the two consequences of that reclassification — the prescribed provision on a sub-standard asset must be created, and interest already recognised as income on the account must be reversed, income recognition on a non-performing asset being permitted only on realisation.

citation.source: RBI Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning applicable to NBFCs
citation.ref: Income recognition on a non-performing asset and provisioning on a sub-standard asset

points.text: On the net owned fund shortfall, the auditor's duty runs beyond the audit report on the financial statements. The auditor must include in a separate report to the Board of Directors a statement on the prescribed matters, of which whether the company holds the minimum net owned fund required is one, and must state the reasons where the answer is unfavourable or qualified.

citation.source: RBI Master Direction — Non-Banking Financial Companies Auditor's Report (Reserve Bank) Directions
citation.ref: Matters to be included in the auditor's separate report to the Board, including minimum net owned fund

keywords: separate report to the Board of Directors

points.text: State the consequence in full. Where such a statement is unfavourable or qualified, or where the auditor is of the opinion that the company has not complied with the Reserve Bank of India Act or these Directions, the auditor is under an obligation to report the matter directly to the Regional Office of the Department of Supervision of the Reserve Bank — a duty owed to the regulator, not discharged by telling the board alone.

citation.source: RBI Master Direction — Non-Banking Financial Companies Auditor's Report (Reserve Bank) Directions
citation.ref: Obligation of the auditor to report directly to the Regional Office of the Department of Supervision of the Reserve Bank

keywords: Regional Office of the Department of Supervision

written.scenario: The audit committee of Hansraj Infra Ltd suspects that about ₹1.4 crore has been siphoned out through twenty-three payments averaging ₹6 lakh each, made to a single vendor over eighteen months. Materiality for the statutory audit of the company is ₹3 crore. The committee asks your firm's forensic team to investigate and wants a report that will, in its words, "hold up if we go to the police". A partner replies that each payment is below audit materiality so the scope can be limited to the largest three, that the findings can be expressed as a qualified opinion in the usual audit format, and that the vendor's invoices and approvals can be examined from scanned copies emailed across by the accounts department that made the payments.
written.question: Explain how a forensic engagement differs from the statutory audit, and state what is wrong with each of the partner's three propositions.

points.text: Identify the framework and the objective. A forensic engagement is conducted under the Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards issued by the Institute, not under the Standards on Auditing, and its objective is to establish findings of fact about a suspected act — not to express assurance on financial statements.

citation.source: ICAI Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards
citation.ref: Basis, objective and scope of a forensic accounting and investigation engagement

points.text: The mindset differs at the root. The statutory auditor works with professional scepticism from a neutral starting position, neither assuming dishonesty nor unquestioned honesty; the investigator proceeds on the hypothesis that a fraud may have occurred and designs procedures to test that hypothesis to a conclusion.

citation.source: ICAI Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards
citation.ref: The investigation mindset distinguished from the audit mindset

keywords: neither assuming dishonesty nor unquestioned honesty

points.text: The materiality proposition is wrong. An audit materiality threshold does not scope anything out of a forensic engagement — the scope is fixed by the suspected act and the agreed terms of the engagement, and a series of small payments is precisely the pattern an investigation must follow through in full, so limiting work to the largest three would defeat the engagement.

citation.source: ICAI Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards
citation.ref: Scope of a forensic engagement is set by the suspected act, not by audit materiality

keywords: scope is fixed by the suspected act

points.text: The reporting proposition is wrong. A forensic report states findings of fact with the basis for each finding and the limitations on the work performed. It carries no audit opinion and no assurance conclusion, so there is nothing in it that can be "qualified".

citation.source: ICAI Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards
citation.ref: Reporting findings of fact rather than an opinion or an assurance conclusion

points.text: The evidence proposition is wrong, and it is the one that would destroy the committee's stated purpose. Evidence intended to stand in legal proceedings requires the integrity of the source to be preserved — originals or forensically sound images of digital records, an unbroken chain of custody, corroboration from sources independent of the suspected persons, and documentation to litigation grade. Scanned copies routed through the very department under suspicion satisfy none of that.

citation.source: ICAI Forensic Accounting and Investigation Standards
citation.ref: Evidence — chain of custody, corroboration and documentation to litigation standard

written.scenario: CA Devansh, a member in practice, made four payments during the year. He paid ₹1.5 lakh, being 20% of his fee for a valuation assignment, to Mr Rane, a business intermediary who is not a member of any professional body, for having referred the client. He paid ₹80,000 out of an audit fee to CA Bhoomi, a member of the Institute in practice, who worked on that engagement under a sub-contract. He paid ₹40,000 to the widow of his deceased partner, being her share under the partnership deed. He paid his office manager, not a member, a year-end bonus of ₹60,000 computed as 5% of the firm's gross professional fees. The firm's turnover grew 30% that year.
written.question: Examine each payment under the Chartered Accountants Act 1949, and state the consequence for CA Devansh of the payments that are not permitted.

points.text: State the clause. A member in practice is guilty of professional misconduct if he pays or allows, or agrees to pay or allow, directly or indirectly, any share, commission or brokerage in the fees or profits of his professional business to any person other than a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner, the legal representative of a deceased partner, or a member of such other professional body or with such other qualifications as may be prescribed.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause (2) — paying a share, commission or brokerage out of professional fees

keywords: legal representative of a deceased partner

points.text: The payment to Mr Rane is misconduct.
