points.text: Step one is objectives and scope: a vague instruction is not accepted as it stands, and Mehra obtains clearly written instructions covering the object, scope and purpose and the period to be covered, since results can be affected by changes since the loan was contemplated. Step two is the programme, drawn to the nature and structure of the business and the client's instructions, concentrating on relevant areas rather than a wide-ranging verification and narrowing progressively as work proceeds; the junior's verification of everything is the opposite of that. Steps three to five are collection of evidence, analysis, and reporting.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 — Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
citation.ref: Steps in investigation — determination of objectives and scope, formulation of the programme

points.text: For a lending bank Mehra collects the purpose of the loan and how it will be invested, the repayment schedule and the reasonableness of its assumptions about cash profits, the standing and integrity of the directors, whether the memorandum and articles authorise the borrowing for that purpose, the five-year history and performance, the likely effect of economic, political and social change over the loan period, and whether any other bank rejected an application and why. To test the repayment schedule he prepares a condensed statement of profit and loss for five years, adds the profit expected from the borrowed funds, and computes the ratios — sales to average inventory, sales to fixed assets, equity to fixed assets, current ratio, quick ratio, equity to long-term loans, sales to book debts and return on capital employed — with a product-wise break-up of sales.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 — Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
citation.ref: Investigation on behalf of a bank proposing to advance a loan — the information to collect, the five-year statement and the ratios

points.text: Receivables are scheduled by composition and segregated into debts whose credit period has not expired, debts due within six months, and debts due but unrecovered for over six months, with bad or doubtful debts and the provision, amounts due from directors, officers, employees, subsidiaries and affiliates, and recoveries after the balance sheet date. Inventory is scheduled by raw materials, work in progress and finished goods with the basis of valuation, slow-moving or obsolete items shown separately with any allowance, movements after the balance sheet date, and any pledge. The revalued factory is shown with the amount and date of revaluation and, if warranted, a comment on the basis; contingent liabilities not disclosed are ascertained by direct enquiry and scheduled.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 — Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
citation.ref: Verification of assets and liabilities for the bank — receivables ageing bands, inventory, fixed assets, contingent liabilities

points.text: The report contains nothing irrelevant, links every conclusion to evidence, states its bases and assumptions explicitly and makes assumptions only where unavoidable, spells out the nature, objective, scope and limitations of the assignment and any restrictions the client imposed with their impact, is written in paragraphs with headings with detailed figures in annexures, and carries Mehra's opinion in the final paragraph. A list of everything found is not a report.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 — Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting
citation.ref: Reporting of findings — the eight matters an investigator keeps in mind

written.scenario: Aravalli Cement Ltd, among the top 1000 listed companies, publishes an integrated report alongside its BRSR. This year it commissioned a new grinding unit, patented a low-clinker blend after three years of research, trained every plant operator in kiln safety, raised ₹400 crore of green bonds, restored the quarry it had exhausted, and renewed its community water-sharing agreement with the villages around the plant. The board asks under which capital each belongs, what GRI, CDP, TCFD and the ISSB each add that the others do not, and, separately, what the statutory auditors will do about climate risk in the audit of the financial statements, given the sector.
written.question: Map the six items to the six capitals, distinguish the four frameworks, and state the auditor's consideration of climate-related risk.

points.text: The grinding unit is manufactured capital, human-created production-oriented equipment and infrastructure; the patented blend is intellectual capital, the R&D and innovation that determine future earning potential; operator training is human capital, people's skills, capacity and motivation; the green bonds are financial capital, the pool of funds obtained through financing; quarry restoration is natural capital, the land, minerals and ecosystem health the activities affect; and the water-sharing agreement is social capital, the relationships and trust with the community that make up the social licence to operate.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 — Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
citation.ref: Integrated reporting — the six capitals

points.text: GRI is the most widely used framework, reporting economic, environmental and social impacts to all stakeholders; CDP captures environmental performance data on greenhouse gas emissions, water, forests and supply chain, addressed to investors and buyers; TCFD, created by the Financial Stability Board in 2015, targets consistent climate-related financial disclosures, particularly for banks and insurers; and the ISSB, created by the IFRS Foundation in November 2021, sets a global baseline of sustainability disclosure standards for investors assessing enterprise value, its IFRS S2 on climate building on the TCFD recommendations and SASB's industry-based requirements, alongside IFRS S1 on general sustainability disclosures.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 — Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
citation.ref: Global trends in sustainability reporting — GRI, CDP, TCFD, the ISSB and IFRS S1 and S2

points.text: The statutory auditors' role is unchanged, reasonable assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement, but in understanding the entity they consider climate-related risks and their relevance to the audit, and cement sits in the materials and buildings sectors where they are more relevant. They determine whether the company has appropriately disclosed relevant climate-related information under the applicable framework, may add an Emphasis of Matter paragraph to draw attention to a disclosure of fundamental importance, and read the other information, including the integrated report and press releases, for consistency with the financial statements under SA 720; the auditor's report itself follows the auditing standards, not investor pressure for climate commentary.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 — Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance
citation.ref: Role of auditor — consideration of climate-related risks in an audit of financial statements; SA 720

written.scenario: Meridian Tooling Ltd has current liabilities exceeding current assets by ₹42 crore at the year end. A ₹30 crore term loan falls due for repayment in four months and the lender has not yet agreed to renew it. Management has prepared the financial statements on a going concern basis and has included a note in the financial statements describing the loan, the pending renewal, and its plan to refinance through a second lender with whom talks are at an advanced stage. You are satisfied the note is a fair description of the position.
written.question: State how you would report, and explain how your report would differ if management had refused to include any note at all.

points.text: Identify that the conditions described are events or conditions casting significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern, and that a material uncertainty accordingly exists.

citation.ref: Going Concern — identifying material uncertainty

points.text: Where the disclosure is adequate, the opinion is NOT modified. Say this explicitly — a material uncertainty that is properly disclosed is not a qualification.

citation.ref: Use of going concern basis appropriate but a material uncertainty exists

points.text: The report carries a separate section headed "Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern", which draws attention to the note and states that the opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.

citation.ref: Reporting — separate section and its required wording

keywords: Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern

points.text: Had management given no note, the disclosure would be inadequate, the financial statements materially misstated, and the opinion modified — qualified or adverse according to how pervasive the effect is.

citation.ref: Inadequate disclosure of a material uncertainty

written.scenario: You signed your audit report on Harbourline Ltd on 20 May. On 3 June, before the financial statements were issued to members, you learn that a customer owing ₹6 crore — a balance you had accepted as fully recoverable — was admitted into insolvency on 12 May. Management agrees the amount is now doubtful and is willing to amend the financial statements.
written.question: Explain your responsibility, distinguishing it from your responsibility for facts arising before the date of your report, and state how the amended report would be dated.

points.text: Distinguish the two periods. Up to the date of the auditor's report the auditor has an active duty to perform procedures designed to identify subsequent events requiring adjustment or disclosure.

citation.ref: Events occurring between the date of the financial statements and the date of the auditor's report

points.text: After the date of the report the auditor has NO obligation to perform any audit procedures. The duty arises only on a fact becoming known that, had it been known at the report date, may have caused amendment to the report.

citation.ref: Facts which become known to the auditor after the date of the auditor's report

points.text: On such a fact becoming known: discuss with management, ask how they intend to address it in the financial statements, and determine whether amendment is needed.

citation.ref: Auditor's response to facts becoming known after the report date

points.text: Where management amends, carry out the procedures necessary on the amendment and either extend procedures to the new date and date the report anew, or dual-date the report — restricting the new date to the amendment alone.

citation.ref: Dating of the auditor's report on amended financial statements

points.text: Note the classification point that drives the amendment: the insolvency on 12 May confirms a condition existing at the balance sheet date, so it is an adjusting event, not merely a disclosure.

citation.ref: Adjusting events after the reporting period

keywords: condition existing at the balance sheet date

written.scenario: While auditing Castleford Industries Ltd you find that a purchase manager has, over two years, routed ₹1.8 crore to a supplier he controls through invoices for goods never received. Separately you find a second, unrelated matter: a store keeper has pilfered stock worth about ₹6 lakh.
written.question: State your reporting responsibilities for each, and what your audit report must say.

points.text: Separate the two by amount. The reporting route under section 143(12) turns on whether the fraud involves an amount of ₹1 crore or above.

citation.ref: Section 143(12) read with Rule 13, Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014

points.text: For the ₹1.8 crore fraud: report to the Board or Audit Committee seeking their reply within 45 days, then forward the report, their reply and your comments to the Central Government in Form ADT-4.

citation.ref: Rule 13 — manner of reporting fraud to the Central Government

points.text: For the ₹6 lakh fraud, being below the threshold: report to the Audit Committee or the Board. It does not go to the Central Government, and it is disclosed in the Board's report.

citation.ref: Rule 13 — frauds below the prescribed amount

points.text: Report under CARO 2020 clause 3(xi): whether any fraud by the company or on the company has been noticed or reported during the year, and whether a report under section 143(12) in Form ADT-4 has been filed.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xi)

points.text: Note that reporting a fraud to the Central Government under section 143(12) is not a breach of confidentiality — a disclosure required by law is outside the duty.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I Clause 1 — disclosure permitted by law

written.scenario: The engagement partner on Rowanbridge Ltd tells you that management integrity has never been in question across nine years of audit, that the control environment is strong, and that you may therefore treat the risk of management override as low and drop the procedures aimed at it.
written.question: State your view, and list the procedures required regardless of the assessment.

points.text: Disagree, with the reason: management override of controls is present in every entity because management is uniquely able to manipulate records and override controls that otherwise appear to operate effectively. The risk is not assessable down to nothing.

citation.ref: Risks of material misstatement due to management override of controls

points.text: Test the appropriateness of journal entries recorded in the general ledger and other adjustments made in preparing the financial statements.

citation.ref: Procedures to address management override — journal entries

points.text: Review accounting estimates for bias and evaluate whether the circumstances producing any bias represent a risk of material misstatement due to fraud, including a retrospective review of prior-year estimates.

citation.ref: Procedures to address management override — accounting estimates and retrospective review

keywords: risk of material misstatement due to fraud

points.text: For significant transactions outside the normal course of business, or otherwise appearing unusual, evaluate whether the business rationale suggests fraudulent financial reporting or concealment of misappropriation.

citation.ref: Procedures to address management override — significant unusual transactions

keywords: outside the normal course of business

written.scenario: CA Rhea is offered the statutory audit of Vellore Springs Ltd. The company tells her the previous auditor has already resigned and that there is therefore nobody to write to. Keen not to lose the engagement, she accepts the same day and begins work. Her fee is agreed at a percentage of the company's turnover.
written.question: Discuss her position under the Chartered Accountants Act 1949.

points.text: Communication with the previous auditor in writing is required under Clause 8 before accepting a position previously held by another chartered accountant. Resignation does not remove the requirement — the point is that the incoming auditor learns of any professional reason not to accept.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I Clause 8

points.text: The communication must be by a means that provides evidence of delivery — registered post with acknowledgement due, or hand delivery against a written acknowledgement. Accepting on the company's word that there is nobody to write to does not discharge it.

citation.ref: Guidance on Clause 8 — mode of communication

points.text: Charging fees as a percentage of turnover is separately professional misconduct under Clause 10, being a fee contingent on the results of the employment save as permitted by regulation.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I Clause 10

keywords: contingent on the results of the employment

points.text: Conclude: CA Rhea is guilty of professional misconduct on both counts — under Clause 8 and under Clause 10.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I

written.scenario: Mr. Rakesh, a resident individual, sold a plot of urban land on 10th August 2025 for ₹95,00,000. The stamp duty value on the date of registration was ₹1,10,00,000; there was no earlier agreement. He had bought the plot in F.Y. 2012-13 for ₹18,00,000 and spent ₹4,00,000 on levelling and boundary work in F.Y. 2013-14. Brokerage on the sale was ₹1,00,000. On 5th December 2025 he invested ₹50,00,000 in bonds of the National Highways Authority of India redeemable after five years. Cost Inflation Index — F.Y. 2012-13: 200; F.Y. 2013-14: 220; F.Y. 2025-26: 376. Ignore surcharge and cess.
written.question: Compute the long-term capital gains chargeable to tax for A.Y. 2026-27 and the tax on them, and advise Mr. Rakesh which basis of taxation he should choose.

points.text: Apply section 50C first. The stamp duty value of ₹1,10,00,000 exceeds 110% of the consideration received (110% of ₹95,00,000 is ₹1,04,50,000), so the stamp duty value is deemed to be the full value of consideration.

citation.ref: Section 50C(1) read with the proviso on the 110% tolerance

points.text: Compute the gain without indexation — ₹1,10,00,000 less brokerage of ₹1,00,000, less cost of acquisition ₹18,00,000 and cost of improvement ₹4,00,000 — giving ₹87,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 48 — mode of computation of capital gains

points.text: Allow exemption under section 54EC. The investment is in long-term specified assets within six months of the transfer and the asset transferred is land, but the maximum is ₹50 lakh, so ₹50,00,000 is exempt and ₹37,00,000 remains chargeable.

citation.ref: Section 54EC — investment in bonds of NHAI or RECL, ₹50 lakh ceiling

points.text: Because he is a resident individual and the land was acquired before 23.7.2024, he also has the option of indexation under section 112. Indexed cost of acquisition is ₹18,00,000 x 376/200 = ₹33,84,000 and indexed cost of improvement is ₹4,00,000 x 376/220 = ₹6,83,636, giving a gain of ₹68,32,364 and, after section 54EC, ₹18,32,364 chargeable.

citation.ref: Section 112 — proviso giving resident individuals and HUFs the indexation option for land or building acquired before 23.7.2024

written.scenario: Vantage Polymers Pvt Ltd follows the mercantile system. written.scenario: Mr. Kabir is resident in India. written.scenario: On 15th June 2026 the Assessing Officer of Cobalt Traders Pvt Ltd proposes to reopen the assessment for A.Y. 2021-22. points.text: Section 147 lets the Assessing Officer assess or reassess income that has escaped assessment for the relevant assessment year, subject to sections 148 to 153. points.text: Section 263(1) lets the Principal Commissioner revise an order of the Assessing Officer, or of the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA, which is erroneous in so far as it is prejudicial to the interests of the Revenue, after giving the assessee an opportunity of being heard and after making an enquiry.

written.scenario: Corvus Media Inc is incorporated in and resident of Country C. It also ran a free advertisement-funded platform on which it systematically and continuously interacted with 4,10,000 users in India, from whom no payment arose. written.question: Examine whether Corvus Media Inc has a business connection in India and what income is deemed to accrue or arise here. State how the position would differ if India had a tax treaty with Country C.

points.text: Significant economic presence of a non-resident constitutes a business connection in India. It arises on either of two limbs — aggregate payments from transactions in goods, services or property exceeding ₹2 crore in the previous year, or systematic and continuous soliciting of business or interaction with at least 3 lakh users in India.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A to section 9(1)(i)

points.text: The first limb is met. Transactions in respect of goods, services or property include the provision of download of data or software in India, and the aggregate of payments of ₹2,30,00,000 crosses ₹2 crore.

citation.ref: Explanation 2A(a) to section 9(1)(i)

points.text: The second limb is met independently. 4,10,000 users is at least 3 lakh, and the second limb turns on users, not on payments, so it applies even though the platform is free.

keywords: turns on users, not on payments

points.text: It makes no difference that the agreement was entered outside India, that the company has no residence or place of business in India, or that it renders no services in India. purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export
do not constitute significant economic presence

written.scenario: Aurora Components Ltd, an Indian company, exported 2,00,000 units of a component to Aurora GmbH, its associated enterprise, at ₹96 per unit in P.Y. 2025-26. The comparable uncontrolled price method is the most appropriate method, and the dataset constructed from comparable uncontrolled transactions has eight entries, in ascending order: ₹100, ₹104, ₹108, ₹112, ₹116, ₹120, ₹124 and ₹130 per unit.
written.question: Determine the arm's length price and the transfer pricing adjustment, and state the consequences of that adjustment.

points.text: The range applies here, because the most appropriate method is one of the four listed — comparable uncontrolled price, resale price, cost plus or transactional net margin — and the dataset consists of six or more entries. The arm's length range begins at the thirty-fifth percentile and ends at the sixty-fifth percentile of the dataset.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(4)

points.text: The thirty-fifth percentile is the lowest value such that at least 35% of the values are equal to or less than it. 35% of eight values is 2.8, which is not a whole number, so take the third value — ₹108.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(8)(a)

keywords: lowest value such that at least 35% of the values

points.text: The sixty-fifth percentile is the lowest value such that at least 65% of the values are equal to or less than it. 65% of eight values is 5.2, again not a whole number, so take the sixth value — ₹120. The arm's length range is therefore ₹108 to ₹120 per unit.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(8)(b)

points.text: The actual price of ₹96 falls outside the range, so the arm's length price is the median. 50% of eight values is four, which is a whole number, so the median is the arithmetic mean of the fourth value and the one immediately succeeding it — (₹112 + ₹116) / 2 = ₹114.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(6) read with Rule 10CA(8)(c)

keywords: arm's length price is the median

points.text: The transfer pricing adjustment is (₹114 minus ₹96) x 2,00,000 units = ₹36,00,000, which is added to the total income of Aurora Components Ltd.

citation.ref: Section 92C(3) and (4)

points.text: No deduction under section 10AA or Chapter VI-A is allowed on the income by which the total income is so enhanced. The tolerance band has no application where the range is used, and no secondary adjustment arises because the primary adjustment does not exceed ₹1 crore.

written.scenario: Solstice Systems Ltd, an Indian company, paid ₹80,00,000 in P.Y. 2025-26 to Nordlys AS, a company incorporated in and resident of Country N, as fees for technical services under an agreement with the Indian company. written.scenario: Mr. Girish, a resident individual aged 40, has exercised the option of shifting out of the default tax regime under section 115BAC(1A). His particulars for the previous year 2025-26 are: income from salary (computed) ₹6,00,000; loss from a let-out house property ₹3,20,000; loss from his non-speculation trading business ₹1,50,000; profit from a speculation business ₹60,000; short-term capital gain on sale of a plot ₹90,000; income from the activity of owning and maintaining race horses ₹30,000. He also has two brought-forward losses: long-term capital loss of ₹40,000 relating to A.Y. 2024-25 and a loss of ₹45,000 from the activity of owning and maintaining race horses relating to A.Y. 2022-23. All returns of loss were filed in time.
written.question: Compute the total income of Mr. Girish for A.Y. 2026-27, state the amount of each loss that can be carried forward, and state how the answer would change on the house property loss alone had he paid tax under the default tax regime.

points.text: Loss from house property of ₹3,20,000 can be set off against income under any other head only to the extent of ₹2,00,000 in the same year; the balance ₹1,20,000 is carried forward under section 71B for eight assessment years, to be set off only against income from house property.

points.text: The non-speculation business loss of ₹1,50,000 is first set off against the speculation profit of ₹60,000, because a loss from a non-speculation business can be adjusted against profits from speculation business even though the reverse is barred; ₹90,000 of business loss remains.

citation.ref: Section 70 read with section 73(1) — speculation loss is ring-fenced, a non-speculation loss is not

points.text: The remaining business loss of ₹90,000 cannot be set off against salary; it is set off against the short-term capital gain of ₹90,000 under section 71, which allows a business loss against any head other than salaries including capital gains. Setting it against the capital gain rather than the race-horse income leaves that income free for its own brought-forward loss.

citation.ref: Section 71(1) and 71(2A) — business loss against any other head except salaries

keywords: cannot be set off against salary

points.text: The brought-forward race-horse loss of A.Y. 2022-23 can be set off only against income from the activity of owning and maintaining race horses and can be carried forward for four assessment years, so A.Y. 2026-27 is its last year: ₹30,000 is set off against the race-horse income and the balance ₹15,000 lapses.

citation.ref: Section 74A(3) — set-off only against the same activity, carry forward for four assessment years

points.text: The brought-forward long-term capital loss of ₹40,000 can be set off only against long-term capital gain, of which there is none this year; it is carried forward, and may be set off up to A.Y. 2032-33, eight assessment years after A.Y. 2024-25.

citation.ref: Section 74(1) — long-term capital loss against long-term capital gain only, eight-year carry forward

points.text: Total income for A.Y. 2026-27 is ₹4,00,000: salary ₹6,00,000 less house property loss ₹2,00,000, with business income, capital gains and other sources each nil after set-off. Losses carried forward: house property ₹1,20,000 and long-term capital loss ₹40,000.

citation.ref: Sections 70, 71, 71B, 74 and 74A applied together

points.text: Had he paid tax under the default tax regime, the loss from house property could not be set off against income under any other head at all, and the unabsorbed loss could not be carried forward to the following year either.

citation.ref: Section 115BAC read with section 71B — no inter-head set-off and no carry forward of house property loss under the default regime

written.scenario: Zenith Traders Pvt Ltd is a company in which the public are not substantially interested and is not an eligible start-up under section 80-IAC. On 31 March 2024 its equity shares were held by Mr. Anil (35% of voting power), Mr. Bhavesh (25%) and Mr. Chandan (40%). The company had a business loss of ₹18,00,000 for A.Y. 2024-25, for which the return was filed within the time allowed under section 139(1). For A.Y. 2025-26 it had a business loss of ₹6,00,000 and unabsorbed depreciation of ₹4,00,000; the return for that year was filed on 12 January 2026, after the due date under section 139(1). During the previous year 2025-26, Mr. Chandan sold his entire 40% holding to Ms. Deepa, an unrelated investor, and Mr. Bhavesh gifted shares carrying 10% voting power to his son. On 31 March 2026 the holdings were: Anil 35%, Bhavesh 15%, Bhavesh's son 10%, Deepa 40%. The business income for the previous year 2025-26, after current-year depreciation, is ₹20,00,000.
written.question: Determine whether the brought-forward losses and unabsorbed depreciation can be set off against the income of A.Y. 2026-27, compute the total income, and state what is carried forward.

points.text: Under section 79, a closely held company that is not an eligible start-up may carry forward and set off a loss of an earlier year only if, on the last day of the previous year, shares carrying not less than 51% of the voting power are beneficially held by persons who held shares carrying not less than 51% of the voting power on the last day of the year in which the loss was incurred. Anil and Bhavesh, who held shares on 31 March 2024, hold 35% plus 15% on 31 March 2026, which alone is 50%.

citation.ref: Section 79(1) — the 51% continuity test for a company in which the public are not substantially interested

keywords: last day of the previous year

points.text: The restriction does not apply to a change in shareholding on account of a transfer of shares by way of gift to a relative of the shareholder. The 10% gifted by Bhavesh to his son is therefore not counted as a change, the continuing holders stand at 60%, and the test is met; the sale by Chandan to Deepa is what the section is aimed at, and it still leaves the continuing holding above 51%.

citation.ref: Section 79(2)(a) — change in voting power on death or on gift to a relative is disregarded

points.text: Section 80 permits a business loss to be carried forward only if it was determined in pursuance of a return of loss filed under section 139(3) within the time allowed under section 139(1). The A.Y. 2025-26 business loss of ₹6,00,000, whose return was filed after the due date, cannot be carried forward and lapses. The A.Y. 2024-25 loss of ₹18,00,000, whose return was in time, survives.

citation.ref: Section 80 read with section 139(3) — a loss not determined in a timely return of loss is not carried forward

points.text: The section 80 condition does not apply to unabsorbed depreciation carried forward under section 32(2), so the ₹4,00,000 is available despite the late return. By section 72(2) the brought-forward business loss is set off before unabsorbed depreciation: ₹20,00,000 less ₹18,00,000 leaves ₹2,00,000, against which ₹2,00,000 of unabsorbed depreciation is set off.

citation.ref: Section 80 (not applicable to section 32(2) depreciation) and section 72(2) — order of set-off

points.text: Total income for A.Y. 2026-27 is nil. Unabsorbed depreciation of ₹2,00,000 is carried forward without any time limit; no business loss remains to be carried forward.

citation.ref: Section 32(2) — unabsorbed depreciation carried forward indefinitely

written.scenario: Ms. Nandini, a resident individual, received the following during the previous year 2025-26. (i) Cash gifts of ₹30,000 from a college friend in June 2025 and ₹25,000 from a colleague in December 2025. (ii) A residential flat with a stamp duty value of ₹42,00,000, gifted by her father's brother. (iii) A plot of land bought from an unrelated seller for ₹20,00,000; the stamp duty value on the date of registration was ₹23,50,000 and no earlier agreement was made. (iv) Listed shares with a fair market value of ₹80,000, given by a friend on the occasion of her marriage. (v) A painting with a fair market value of ₹45,000 from a client and a gold chain with a fair market value of ₹20,000 from a neighbour, both without consideration. (vi) ₹2,00,000 received under the will of her grandmother. (vii) A motor car with a fair market value of ₹4,00,000, gifted by a family friend. None of the items is stock-in-trade of any business of hers.
written.question: Compute the amount chargeable to tax in the hands of Ms. Nandini under the head Income from Other Sources for A.Y. 2026-27, giving reasons for each item.

points.text: Cash gifts: where the aggregate sum of money received without consideration from all non-relatives in the year exceeds ₹50,000, the whole of the aggregate is chargeable. The two gifts total ₹55,000, so ₹55,000 is taxable, not merely the excess.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x)(a) — sum of money exceeding ₹50,000 in aggregate is taxable in full

points.text: The flat from her father's brother is not taxable: the brother or sister of either of the parents of the individual is a relative, and a receipt from any relative is outside section 56(2)(x) whatever its value.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 56(2)(x) and the definition of relative — brother or sister of either parent

points.text: The plot bought for inadequate consideration: the stamp duty value exceeds the consideration by ₹3,50,000, which is more than the higher of ₹50,000 and 10% of the consideration (₹2,00,000), so the difference of ₹3,50,000 is chargeable.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x)(b)(B) — immovable property for inadequate consideration, the ₹50,000 / 10% tolerance

points.text: The shares received on the occasion of her marriage are not taxable, since any sum or property received on the occasion of the marriage of the individual is excluded, and the ₹2,00,000 under her grandmother's will is not taxable, being received under a will or by way of inheritance.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 56(2)(x) — receipts on marriage and under a will or inheritance

points.text: Movable property without consideration is taxed on its aggregate fair market value if that exceeds ₹50,000. Paintings and jewellery are both property for this purpose, so the painting and the gold chain together, ₹65,000, are taxable in full.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x)(c) and the definition of property — paintings and jewellery included

points.text: The motor car is not taxable at all, because a motor car is not within the defined list of property — land or building, shares and securities, jewellery, archaeological collections, drawings, paintings, sculptures, any work of art, bullion and virtual digital assets. The total chargeable under Income from Other Sources is ₹4,70,000 (₹55,000 + ₹3,50,000 + ₹65,000).

citation.ref: Explanation to section 56(2)(x) — the closed list of property

written.scenario: Mr. Yash, who pays tax under the default tax regime under section 115BAC, holds equity shares carrying 25% of the voting power in Kalpa Designs Pvt Ltd. His wife, Mrs. Rhea, is employed there as human resources manager on a salary of ₹4,80,000 for the previous year 2025-26; she holds no qualification in human resources or management. On 1 April 2025 Yash gifted ₹10,00,000 to Rhea. She placed ₹6,00,000 of it in a bank fixed deposit at 8% per annum for the whole year, and put ₹4,00,000 into her existing boutique business as additional capital on the same day, when her own capital in the boutique stood at ₹12,00,000. The boutique earned a profit of ₹3,20,000 for the year. Of the fixed deposit interest received, she reinvested ₹24,000 in a recurring deposit that earned ₹1,200 during the year. Their son Kabir, aged 14, earned ₹60,000 acting in a television serial and ₹24,000 as interest on a fixed deposit gifted to him by his grandfather. Yash's total income, excluding all the items above, is higher than Rhea's.
written.question: Compute the amount to be included in the total income of Mr. Yash by way of clubbing for A.Y. 2026-27, with reasons for each inclusion and exclusion.

points.text: Rhea's salary from Kalpa Designs Pvt Ltd is clubbed with Yash's income under section 64(1)(ii): he has a substantial interest, since he beneficially owns equity shares carrying 20% or more of the voting power, and the exception for remuneration attributable solely to the spouse's technical or professional qualifications does not apply because she holds none. The amount included is ₹4,80,000 less the standard deduction of ₹75,000, ₹4,05,000.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(ii) and the Explanation defining substantial interest; standard deduction under section 16(ia) as it applies under section 115BAC

points.text: Interest on the fixed deposit made from the gifted sum, ₹48,000 (8% of ₹6,00,000), is income from an asset transferred to the spouse without adequate consideration and is clubbed under section 64(1)(iv); natural love and affection is not adequate consideration. The ₹1,200 earned on the recurring deposit is income from accretion, earned by investing the clubbed income, and is not clubbed.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(iv) — income from the transferred asset is clubbed, income on that income is not

points.text: Where the transferred asset is invested by the spouse in a business, the proportionate income is clubbed, taking the gifted investment against the total capital in the business on the first day of the previous year: ₹4,00,000 out of ₹16,00,000, so one-fourth of the profit of ₹3,20,000, ₹80,000, is included in Yash's income.

citation.ref: Section 64(1)(iv) read with Explanation 3 to section 64(1) — proportionate income where the transferred asset is invested in a business

keywords: first day of the previous year

points.text: Kabir's ₹60,000 from acting is not clubbed, being income from the exercise of his skill or talent. His fixed deposit interest of ₹24,000 is clubbed under section 64(1A) with the parent whose total income is greater, Yash. The exemption of ₹1,500 per child under section 10(32) is available only to a parent who has shifted out of the default tax regime, so the full ₹24,000 is included. Total clubbed in Yash's hands: ₹5,57,000.

citation.ref: Section 64(1A) with its proviso for skill, talent or specialised knowledge; section 10(32) unavailable under section 115BAC

written.scenario: Sarvodaya Charitable Trust is registered under section 12AB and runs schools. For the previous year 2025-26 it had income from property held under trust of ₹40,00,000 and voluntary contributions of ₹10,00,000 without any direction. It also received ₹8,00,000 as voluntary contributions with a specific direction that they form part of the corpus, and invested that sum in a scheduled bank deposit. During the year it spent ₹22,00,000 on running its schools, ₹5,00,000 on constructing a classroom block, ₹4,00,000 as a payment to a building contractor on which it deducted no tax at source, and gave ₹6,00,000 as an ordinary donation and ₹2,00,000 as a corpus donation to another trust registered under section 12AB. It set apart ₹6,00,000 for building a hostel within three years, filed Form 10 on 20 July 2026 and invested the sum in government securities. Its return for A.Y. 2026-27 is due on 31 October 2026 and was filed on 30 September 2026.
written.question: Compute the total income of the trust for A.Y. 2026-27, stating how each receipt and each outgoing is treated.

points.text: The corpus donations of ₹8,00,000 received with a specific direction and invested in a mode specified in section 11(5) are exempt under section 11(1)(d) and are not part of the income against which the 85% test is applied. Income for the test is ₹50,00,000: the property income of ₹40,00,000 and the ordinary voluntary contributions of ₹10,00,000, which section 12 deems income derived from property.

citation.ref: Section 11(1)(d) and section 12(1) — corpus contributions invested in section 11(5) modes; other voluntary contributions deemed income

points.text: At least 85% of the income, ₹42,50,000, must be applied to charitable purposes in India during the year; up to 15%, ₹7,50,000, may be accumulated without any condition other than being invested in the modes of section 11(5).

citation.ref: Section 11(1)(a) — application of 85% and free accumulation of 15%

points.text: The ₹22,00,000 spent on running the schools and the ₹5,00,000 spent on the classroom block are both application, whether revenue or capital in nature, making ₹27,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 11(1)(a) — application of income to the purposes of the trust

points.text: Of the ₹6,00,000 donated to another registered trust out of current-year income, only 85%, ₹5,10,000, is treated as application under Explanation 4(iii) to section 11(1); the ₹2,00,000 corpus donation to that trust is not application at all under Explanation 2.

citation.ref: Explanation 4(iii) and Explanation 2 to section 11(1), with CBDT Circular No. 3/2024

points.text: The ₹4,00,000 paid to the contractor without deducting tax at source is application only to the extent of 70%: by Explanation 3 to section 11(1), section 40(a)(ia) applies and 30%, ₹1,20,000, is not treated as application this year, though it will be in the year the tax is deducted and paid. Application from this payment is ₹2,80,000.

citation.ref: Explanation 3 to section 11(1) read with section 40(a)(ia)

points.text: The ₹6,00,000 set apart for the hostel is deemed applied under section 11(2): the purpose and period are stated in Form 10, the period does not exceed five years, the money is invested in a section 11(5) mode, and Form 10 was filed on 20 July 2026, more than two months before the return's due date of 31 October 2026, and the return itself was filed in time.

citation.ref: Section 11(2) and section 13(9) — accumulation on Form 10, five-year limit, investment in section 11(5) modes, filing before the due date

points.text: Application totals ₹40,90,000 (₹27,00,000 + ₹5,10,000 + ₹2,80,000 + ₹6,00,000 accumulated), against income of ₹50,00,000 less the free accumulation of ₹7,50,000, so ₹1,60,000 falls short of the 85% and is the total income chargeable to tax for A.Y. 2026-27.

citation.ref: Section 11(1)(a) applied with the Explanations to section 11(1) and section 11(2)

written.scenario: Jeevan Jyoti Foundation, a charitable trust registered under section 12AB that runs a hospital, received donations of ₹1,00,00,000 during the previous year 2025-26. For ₹12,00,000 of this it maintains no record of the name and address of the donors. It applied ₹78,00,000 of its total income of ₹1,00,00,000 to its objects during the year. A separate wholly religious trust in the same city received ₹4,00,000 of donations with no donor records and asks whether it faces the same treatment.
written.question: Compute the tax treatment of the anonymous donations in the hands of the Foundation, and answer the religious trust.

points.text: Anonymous donations, being those for which the trust keeps no record of the donor's identity, are taxed at 30% under section 115BBC to the extent they exceed the higher of 5% of the total donations received, ₹5,00,000, and ₹1,00,000. So ₹7,00,000 is charged at 30%, a tax of ₹2,10,000 before surcharge and cess.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC(1) — 30% on anonymous donations exceeding the higher of 5% of total donations and ₹1 lakh

points.text: The remaining ₹5,00,000 of anonymous donations is treated like any other donation and forms part of the income to which section 11 applies, so the 85% application test and the 15% accumulation are worked on the total income reduced by the ₹7,00,000 taxed at 30%.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC(1)(ii) — tax on the balance total income as reduced by the anonymous donations taxed at 30%

points.text: A trust established wholly for religious purposes is outside section 115BBC, so the religious trust's ₹4,00,000 is not charged at 30%; the charge reaches a partly religious and charitable trust only for anonymous donations made to a university, school, hospital or medical institution it runs.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC(2) — exclusion of wholly religious trusts, and of partly religious and charitable trusts except for donations to their educational or medical institutions

written.scenario: Nexa Retail Ltd, whose turnover in the previous year 2024-25 was ₹12 crore, made the following payments to residents during the previous year 2025-26, none of them holding a certificate for lower deduction: (i) three bills of ₹28,000, ₹25,000 and ₹52,000 to Mr. Pramod, an individual contractor, for shop fit-outs; (ii) commission of ₹18,000 to a selling agent; (iii) purchases of goods of ₹75,00,000 from Suvarna Traders, on which no tax was collectible at source; (iv) a foreign holiday package worth ₹1,50,000 given free to its best-performing dealer; (v) ₹48,00,000 paid to Mr. Dinesh for an office flat whose stamp duty value was ₹55,00,000; (vi) fees for technical services of ₹45,000 and royalty of ₹40,000 to the same consultant. Nexa Retail Ltd is also a partner in a partnership firm, which paid it remuneration of ₹6,00,000 and interest on capital of ₹1,80,000 during the year.
written.question: State, with reasons and amounts, the tax deductible at source in each case, and whether the partnership firm must deduct tax on what it paid to the company.

points.text: Contractor: the first two bills do not exceed ₹30,000 singly, but the third does, and the aggregate of ₹1,05,000 exceeds ₹1,00,000 for the year, so tax is deductible under section 194C on the whole ₹1,05,000 at 1%, the rate for an individual payee — ₹1,050.

citation.ref: Section 194C(5) — the ₹30,000 single and ₹1,00,000 aggregate limits — and section 194C(1), 1% for an individual or HUF contractor

points.text: Commission: no deduction under section 194H, because the aggregate of ₹18,000 does not exceed the ₹20,000 threshold for the year. Fees for technical services and royalty: the ₹50,000 limit under section 194J applies separately to each nature of payment, so neither ₹45,000 nor ₹40,000 crosses it and no tax is deductible on either.

citation.ref: Section 194H (threshold ₹20,000) and section 194J (₹50,000 for each nature of payment separately)

points.text: Purchase of goods: the company's turnover in the preceding year exceeded ₹10 crore and the purchases from one seller exceed ₹50 lakh, so under section 194Q tax at 0.1% is deductible on the amount exceeding ₹50 lakh — 0.1% of ₹25,00,000, that is ₹2,500.

citation.ref: Section 194Q(1) — a buyer with turnover above ₹10 crore, 0.1% on purchases from a seller exceeding ₹50 lakh in the year

points.text: Holiday package: a benefit or perquisite arising from business provided to a resident attracts section 194R at 10% of its value, ₹15,000, and since it is wholly in kind the company must ensure the tax is paid before releasing the benefit.

citation.ref: Section 194R(1) — 10% of the value of a benefit or perquisite arising from business or profession, ensured before it is provided

points.text: Office flat: section 194-IA applies because the stamp duty value is not less than ₹50 lakh even though the consideration is, and tax is deducted at 1% of the higher of the consideration and the stamp duty value — 1% of ₹55,00,000, that is ₹55,000.

citation.ref: Section 194-IA(1) and (2) — 1% of the higher of consideration and stamp duty value; no deduction only when both are below ₹50 lakh

points.text: The firm: under section 194T a firm paying salary, remuneration, commission, bonus or interest to a partner deducts tax at 10% where the aggregate exceeds ₹20,000 in the year, at credit (including credit to the capital account) or payment, whichever is earlier — 10% of ₹7,80,000, that is ₹78,000.

citation.ref: Section 194T — 10% on remuneration, commission, bonus or interest paid by a firm to a partner above ₹20,000 in a year

written.scenario: Vega Exports Ltd, a company paying tax under the normal provisions of the Act, has a unit in a Special Economic Zone that began manufacturing on 1 October 2019 under a letter of approval issued in 2019. For the previous year 2025-26 the unit's profits are ₹80,00,000. Its total turnover is ₹5,00,00,000, of which export turnover per the accounts is ₹3,20,00,000 and domestic sales ₹1,80,00,000. Of the export turnover, ₹3,00,00,000 was received in India in convertible foreign exchange by 30 September 2026 and ₹20,00,000 in November 2026, with no extension from the Reserve Bank of India. The export turnover includes ₹10,00,000 of freight and insurance attributable to delivery of the goods outside India. The company's total income before this deduction is ₹1,10,00,000. The chartered accountant's report was furnished on 25 September 2026 and the return on 31 October 2026.
written.question: Compute the deduction available under section 10AA for A.Y. 2026-27.

points.text: The unit began in the previous year 2019-20, so A.Y. 2020-21 is its first year: 100% of export profits for A.Y. 2020-21 to A.Y. 2024-25, and 50% for A.Y. 2025-26 to A.Y. 2029-30. A.Y. 2026-27 is in the 50% band and needs no reserve.

citation.ref: Section 10AA(1)(i) and (ii) — five years at 100% then five at 50%

points.text: Export turnover counts only consideration received in India in convertible foreign exchange within six months from the end of the previous year, so the ₹20,00,000 received in November 2026 without an extension is excluded, leaving ₹3,00,00,000.

citation.ref: Explanation 1(ia) to section 10AA — receipt in convertible foreign exchange within six months

points.text: Freight and insurance attributable to delivery outside India, ₹10,00,000, are excluded from export turnover, and by Circular 4/2018 the same sum is excluded from total turnover as well. Export turnover is ₹2,90,00,000 and total turnover ₹4,90,00,000.

citation.ref: Explanation 1(ia) to section 10AA and CBDT Circular No. 4/2018 dated 14 August 2018
Section 10AA(7) — profits of the unit in the proportion of export turnover to total turnover

points.text: The deduction is allowed from the total income computed before giving effect to section 10AA and cannot exceed it; ₹23,67,347 is within ₹1,10,00,000, so the full amount is allowed.

citation.ref: Explanation below section 10AA(1)

points.text: The conditions are met: the return was furnished by the due date under section 139(1), 31 October 2026, and the chartered accountant's report was furnished one month before that date, on 25 September 2026; had the return been late, no deduction at all would have been allowed.

citation.ref: Section 10AA read with section 44AB's specified date — report one month before the due date, return by the due date

written.scenario: Helios Holdings Ltd is a resident of Country X. Under the tax treaty between India and Country X, capital gains from the sale of shares of an Indian company are taxable only in Country X if the seller is a resident of Country X, except where the seller holds more than 10% of the capital of the Indian company. In May 2022 Helios formed three wholly owned subsidiaries in Country X, each with no staff, office or activity of its own, and in June 2022 each of them bought 8% of the equity of Indus Motors Ltd, an Indian company, together 24%. In the previous year 2025-26 all three subsidiaries sold their shares to a buyer at a gain, and each claims exemption under the treaty as a holder of less than 10%. The Indian tax that the arrangement saves, taken together for the three subsidiaries, is ₹5 crore.
written.question: Can the General Anti-Avoidance Rule be invoked, and with what consequences? State the procedure the Assessing Officer must follow before it applies.

points.text: An impermissible avoidance arrangement under section 96 needs two things together: the main purpose, or one of the main purposes, of the arrangement is to obtain a tax benefit, and at least one of four tainted elements is present — rights or obligations not ordinarily created at arm's length, misuse or abuse of the Act, lack of commercial substance under section 97, or a manner not ordinarily employed for bona fide purposes.

citation.ref: Section 96(1) — the purpose test and the four tainted elements, read with section 102(10) defining tax benefit

points.text: Splitting a 24% holding into three holdings of 8% through subsidiaries that exist for nothing else appears designed to bring each seller under the treaty's 10% line: the tax benefit is the main purpose. The subsidiaries change nothing about the investor's business risk or cash flow, so the arrangement lacks commercial substance, and it reveals an abuse of the treaty; two tainted elements are present.

citation.ref: Section 96(1)(b) and (c) with section 97, as applied in the module's own example of an investment split between two subsidiaries to stay under a treaty threshold

points.text: Nothing in Rule 10U excludes it. The tax benefit arising in aggregate to all parties in the year, ₹5 crore, exceeds ₹3 crore; the shares were acquired in June 2022, after 1 April 2017, so the grandfathering of investments made before that date does not apply; and none of the sellers is a foreign institutional investor of the kind the rule protects.

citation.ref: Rule 10U(1)(a) — ₹3 crore aggregate tax benefit — and Rule 10U(1)(d) — investments made before 1 April 2017

points.text: Consequence: under section 98 the tax authorities may disregard the two extra subsidiaries or treat all three as one and the same company, so that a single holder of 24% is above the treaty line and the gains are taxable in India; the treaty benefit is denied. Section 90(2A) makes Chapter X-A apply even where the treaty would otherwise be more beneficial to the assessee.

citation.ref: Section 98(1) — consequences of an impermissible avoidance arrangement — and section 90(2A) — GAAR applies notwithstanding a more beneficial treaty

points.text: Procedure: the Assessing Officer must first issue a written notice to the assessee seeking its objections to the applicability of GAAR under Rule 10UB(1), and only then make a reference to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner under section 144BA(1).

citation.ref: Rule 10UB(1) read with section 144BA(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

written.scenario: Mr. Rohan bought 10,000 units of an equity-oriented mutual fund on 1 May 2025 at ₹40 per unit. The fund announced a bonus of one unit for every unit held, with 20 June 2025 as the record date, and Rohan was allotted 10,000 bonus units without payment. On 10 December 2025 he sold the original 10,000 units at ₹22 per unit while continuing to hold all the bonus units, and wishes to set the resulting loss against his other capital gains.
written.question: Examine the treatment of the loss under the Income-tax Act, 1961, and state what changes if the original units are sold instead on 15 April 2026.

points.text: Section 94(8) applies when a person buys units within three months before the record date, is allotted additional units without payment on the basis of that holding, and sells all or any of the original units within nine months after the record date while continuing to hold all or any of the bonus units. Rohan bought on 1 May 2025, within three months before 20 June 2025, and sold on 10 December 2025, within nine months after it, still holding the bonus units — all three conditions are met.

citation.ref: Section 94(8) — the conditions for a bonus stripping transaction

points.text: The loss of ₹1,80,000 on the original units (₹4,00,000 cost less ₹2,20,000 sale proceeds) is ignored in computing his income chargeable to tax and cannot be set off against any capital gain.

citation.ref: Section 94(8)(i) — the loss on the original units sold within nine months is ignored

points.text: The loss so ignored, ₹1,80,000, is deemed to be the cost of acquisition of the 10,000 bonus units he continues to hold, so it is recovered when those units are sold rather than lost outright.

citation.ref: Section 94(8)(ii) — the ignored loss becomes the cost of the bonus units held

points.text: A sale of the original units on 15 April 2026 falls outside nine months from the record date of 20 June 2025 (which end on 20 March 2026), so section 94(8) does not apply and the loss is allowed in the ordinary way, with the bonus units keeping a nil cost.

citation.ref: Section 94(8)(c) — the nine-month window

written.scenario: Mr. Vikram, a cloth trader with income chargeable to tax, did the following during the previous year 2025-26, every payment in cash: (i) took a loan of ₹15,000 from Mr. Ajay on 1 June 2025 and, while it was still unpaid, another ₹8,000 from him on 10 July 2025; (ii) received ₹1,50,000 from Mr. Bimal on 5 August 2025 for the sale of his car and ₹80,000 from the same Mr. Bimal the same day for the sale of a motorcycle; (iii) received ₹2,50,000 from Mr. Chetan as advance against the sale of his shop, a sale that later fell through; (iv) repaid a deposit of ₹18,000 with interest of ₹3,000 to Mr. Dhruv; (v) received ₹1,90,000 each from two relatives, on different days, as gifts on his daughter's wedding; (vi) withdrew ₹3,00,000 from his own bank account.
written.question: Examine each transaction under sections 269SS, 269ST and 269T and state the penalty, if any, that can be imposed.

points.text: (i) Section 269SS bars taking a loan otherwise than by account payee cheque, draft or electronic mode where the loan, together with any earlier loan from the same person still unpaid, is ₹20,000 or more. The ₹8,000 taken on 10 July with ₹15,000 still unpaid makes ₹23,000, so that loan contravenes the section, and penalty under section 271D equal to the loan so taken, ₹8,000, can be imposed by the Assessing Officer.

citation.ref: Section 269SS(b) — aggregate with an earlier unpaid loan — and section 271D

points.text: (ii) Section 269ST bars receiving ₹2,00,000 or more in cash in aggregate from a person in a day. The ₹1,50,000 and ₹80,000 from Mr. Bimal on 5 August total ₹2,30,000, so penalty under section 271DA equal to the receipt, ₹2,30,000, is imposable unless he proves good and sufficient reasons for the contravention.

citation.ref: Section 269ST(a) and section 271DA

points.text: (iii) An advance received in relation to the transfer of immovable property, whether or not the transfer takes place, is a specified sum under section 269SS; ₹2,50,000 in cash contravenes it and attracts penalty under section 271D of ₹2,50,000. Section 269ST does not apply to a transaction of the nature referred to in section 269SS, so there is no second penalty.

citation.ref: Section 269SS with the definition of specified sum, section 271D, and the exclusion in section 269ST for transactions of the nature referred to in section 269SS

keywords: whether or not the transfer takes place

points.text: (iv) Section 269T bars repaying a deposit in cash where the deposit together with the interest payable on it is ₹20,000 or more; ₹18,000 with ₹3,000 interest is ₹21,000, so penalty under section 271E equal to the amount repaid, ₹21,000, is imposable.

citation.ref: Section 269T(a) and section 271E

points.text: (v) The wedding gifts are receipts relating to one occasion, but the limit in section 269ST(c) is tested per person, and each relative gave ₹1,90,000, below ₹2,00,000; no contravention. (vi) A cash withdrawal from his own bank account is excluded from section 269ST by notification, so no penalty arises on it.

citation.ref: Section 269ST(c) and Notification No. 28/2017 dated 5 April 2017 excluding withdrawals from a bank

written.scenario: Ms. Anvi, a resident individual aged 45 who has exercised the option of shifting out of the default tax regime, has income of ₹8,00,000 in India for the previous year 2025-26 after all deductions. She also earned professional fees of ₹2,00,000 from work performed in Country Z, with which India has no agreement for the avoidance of double taxation, and paid income-tax of ₹30,000 on it there. Ignore surcharge.
written.question: Compute the tax payable by Ms. Anvi in India for A.Y. 2026-27 after the relief available to her, stating the conditions for that relief.

points.text: Relief is available under section 91, not section 90, because there is no agreement with Country Z. Its conditions are met: she is resident in India in the year, the income accrued outside India and is not deemed to accrue in India, it was subjected to income-tax in Country Z in her hands, and she has paid that tax.

citation.ref: Section 91(1) — the six conditions for unilateral relief

points.text: The foreign income is included in her total income, ₹10,00,000, and Indian tax is computed on the whole: ₹12,500 on the slab up to ₹5,00,000 and ₹1,00,000 at 20% on the next ₹5,00,000, ₹1,12,500, plus health and education cess at 4%, ₹4,500 — ₹1,17,000.

citation.ref: Section 5(1)(c) — global income of a resident — and the rates for A.Y. 2026-27 under the normal provisions

points.text: The Indian rate of tax is the Indian income-tax after cess but before double taxation relief divided by total income, ₹1,17,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000, that is 11.7%. The rate of tax in Country Z is ₹30,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000, that is 15%.

citation.ref: Explanation to section 91 — Indian rate of tax and rate of tax of the said country

points.text: The deduction is the doubly taxed income at the lower of the two rates: ₹2,00,000 at 11.7%, that is ₹23,400. Tax payable in India is ₹1,17,000 less ₹23,400, ₹93,600.

citation.ref: Section 91(1) — deduction at the Indian rate or the foreign rate, whichever is lower

written.scenario: Zephyr GmbH, a company resident in Germany, proposes to license technology to Bharat Autoparts Ltd, an Indian company, for a consideration of ₹150 crore over three years, and wants certainty on whether the receipts are taxable in India before it signs. Zephyr's assessment for an earlier year, in which the very same question arose on a smaller licence, is pending in appeal before the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal. Bharat Autoparts Ltd separately proposes to route a part of the payment through a subsidiary in a third country and wants to know whether that arrangement would be an impermissible avoidance arrangement.
written.question: Advise both companies on applying to the Board for Advance Rulings: who may apply, the fee, whether the Board can take up each question, the time it takes, and the remedy against the ruling.

points.text: Zephyr, a non-resident, may apply for a ruling on a transaction undertaken or proposed to be undertaken by it under section 245N(a)(i); Bharat Autoparts Ltd, a resident, may itself apply under section 245N(a)(ii) for a determination of the non-resident's tax liability arising out of a transaction it proposes to undertake with that non-resident.

citation.ref: Section 245N(a)(i) and (ii) with section 245N(b)(A)(i) and (ii) — who is an applicant

points.text: The application is made in quadruplicate in the prescribed form with the fee under Rule 44E, which for a transaction exceeding ₹100 crore but not ₹300 crore is ₹5 lakh (₹2 lakh up to ₹100 crore, ₹10 lakh above ₹300 crore, and ₹10,000 for other applicants); it may be withdrawn within 30 days of being made.

citation.ref: Section 245Q(2) and (3) read with Rule 44E of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

points.text: The Board shall not allow Zephyr's application, because the question raised is already pending before the Appellate Tribunal in its own case; the exception for a pending question applies only to a resident of a class notified by the Central Government. Bharat Autoparts' question can be taken up: although the Board refuses a question on a transaction designed prima facie for avoidance, a resident or non-resident may specifically seek a ruling on whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement under section 245N(a)(iv).

citation.ref: Section 245R(2) — the bars on allowing an application — and section 245N(a)(iv)

points.text: No application is rejected without an opportunity of being heard and reasons in the order. Where allowed, the Board pronounces its ruling within 6 months from receipt of the application, after hearing the applicant if a request is made, and sends a signed copy to the applicant and the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner.

citation.ref: Section 245R(3), (4) and (6) — hearing, rejection with reasons, and the six-month time limit

points.text: An applicant aggrieved by the ruling may appeal to the High Court within sixty days of its communication, extendable by a further thirty days for sufficient cause, under section 245W; and a ruling obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts may be declared void ab initio under section 245T, after which the Act applies as if it had never been made.

citation.ref: Section 245W(1) — appeal to the High Court — and section 245T — ruling void for fraud or misrepresentation

written.scenario: Mr. Dev, an Indian citizen employed by a company in Country Y, spent 190 days in India during the previous year 2025-26 and is a resident of India under section 6. Country Y treats him as its resident under its own law because he is domiciled there. He owns a flat in Mumbai where his wife and children live and keeps an apartment in Country Y on a five-year lease. His salary comes from Country Y; his investments, bank accounts, social and family ties are in India. India and Country Y have a tax treaty whose Article 4 follows the OECD Model.
written.question: Determine Mr. Dev's residential status for the purposes of the treaty, showing each step of the tie-breaker in order, and state what the outcome does and does not decide.

points.text: Under paragraph 1 of Article 4 he is a resident of both States, each under its own law — India by his stay, Country Y by his domicile — so paragraph 2, the tie-breaker, applies to deem him a resident of one State only for the treaty.

citation.ref: Article 4(1) and 4(2) — dual residence of an individual and the tie-breaker

points.text: First test, permanent home: he has a permanent home available to him in both States, the owned flat in Mumbai and the leased apartment in Country Y, so the first limb does not settle it and the same clause moves to the centre of vital interests.

citation.ref: Article 4(2)(a) — permanent home, then centre of vital interests

points.text: Centre of vital interests: the State with which his personal and economic relations are closer. His family, investments, bank accounts and social ties are in India against a salary from Country Y, so his personal and economic relations are closer to India and he is deemed a resident only of India.

citation.ref: Article 4(2)(a) — centre of vital interests

points.text: Had that been indeterminable, the order continues: habitual abode, then nationality, then settlement by mutual agreement of the competent authorities. The outcome fixes which State is the residence State for applying the treaty's articles; it does not alter his status under section 6, under which he remains resident in India for the Income-tax Act.

citation.ref: Article 4(2)(b) to (d) — habitual abode, nationality, mutual agreement — read with section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 1961

written.scenario: Ms. Riya, a salaried resident with no business income, did the following in the previous year 2025-26. She sold on an Indian exchange a crypto-asset she had bought for ₹3,00,000, receiving ₹5,00,000 after the exchange charged brokerage of ₹8,000. She sold a non-fungible token bought for ₹1,00,000 for ₹60,000. She received crypto-assets with a fair market value of ₹70,000 as a gift from a friend. She also sold a crypto-asset for ₹45,000 to Mr. Karan, an individual with no business income, who paid her directly; that was his only payment to her in the year.
written.question: Compute the income chargeable in her hands from these transactions and the tax on it, and state the tax deductible at source on each sale.

points.text: Income from the transfer of a virtual digital asset is taxed at 30% under section 115BBH, and in computing it no deduction is allowed for any expenditure or allowance other than the cost of acquisition. The crypto gain is ₹5,00,000 less ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000, with the brokerage of ₹8,000 not deductible; tax on it is ₹60,000 plus cess.

citation.ref: Section 115BBH(1) and (2)(a) — 30% with no deduction except cost of acquisition

points.text: The loss of ₹40,000 on the non-fungible token, itself a virtual digital asset, cannot be set off against the crypto gain or any other income, and cannot be carried forward to a later year.

citation.ref: Section 115BBH(2)(b) — no set-off or carry forward of a loss from a virtual digital asset

points.text: A virtual digital asset is property for section 56(2)(x), so the gift from a friend, whose aggregate fair market value of ₹70,000 exceeds ₹50,000, is taxable in full as income from other sources at her normal rates; it would have been exempt only from a relative.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(x) read with the definition of property including a virtual digital asset

points.text: Under section 194S the person paying consideration for a transfer of a virtual digital asset deducts tax at 1%: the exchange deducts ₹5,000 on the ₹5,00,000 sale. Mr. Karan, a specified person with no business income, need not deduct because his aggregate consideration to her in the year, ₹45,000, does not exceed ₹50,000; for any other payer the threshold is ₹10,000.

citation.ref: Section 194S(1) and (3) — 1% on consideration, with thresholds of ₹50,000 for a specified person and ₹10,000 for others

written.scenario: A multinational group within the scope of the GloBE Rules has constituent entities in Country B whose Net GloBE Income for the fiscal year is €20,000,000 and whose adjusted covered taxes are €2,400,000. The Substance-based Income Exclusion for Country B, worked from payroll and tangible assets there, is €2,000,000. There is no Additional Current Top-up Tax and Country B has no qualified domestic minimum top-up tax.
written.question: Compute the Jurisdictional Top-up Tax for Country B and state how it is collected.

points.text: The Effective Tax Rate for the jurisdiction is adjusted covered taxes over Net GloBE Income, €2,400,000 ÷ €20,000,000, that is 12%, below the minimum rate of 15%.

citation.ref: Chapter 5 — jurisdictional Effective Tax Rate and the 15% minimum rate

points.text: The Top-up Tax Percentage is the minimum rate less the Effective Tax Rate, 15% − 12% = 3%, computed on the aggregate Net GloBE Income of the jurisdiction.

citation.ref: Article 5.2.1 — Top-up Tax Percentage

points.text: Excess Profit is Net GloBE Income less the Substance-based Income Exclusion, €20,000,000 − €2,000,000 = €18,000,000, so the Jurisdictional Top-up Tax is 3% of €18,000,000, €540,000, with nothing to add for Additional Current Top-up Tax and nothing to subtract for a domestic top-up tax.

citation.ref: Article 5.2 — Jurisdictional Top-up Tax = (Top-up Tax Percentage × Excess Profit) + Additional Current Top-up Tax − Domestic Top-up Tax

points.text: The top-up tax is collected under the Income Inclusion Rule at the level of the ultimate parent entity, or a lower parent where the parent's jurisdiction has not adopted it, with the Undertaxed Profits Rule as the backstop that denies deductions or makes an equivalent adjustment for any amount the Income Inclusion Rule leaves uncollected.

citation.ref: Chapter 2 — the Income Inclusion Rule and the Undertaxed Profits Rule

written.scenario: Mr Devraj, aged 45, is a resident individual paying tax under the default regime of section 115BAC for the previous year 2025-26. His income from a wholesale business, after every deduction, is ₹15,00,000. He also owns farmland in Punjab from which his net agricultural income for the year is ₹4,00,000. He has no capital gains and no dividend income, and no deduction under Chapter VI-A is available to him under the default regime. His accountant says the agricultural income is exempt under section 10(1) and can be ignored altogether.
written.question: Is the accountant right? State the conditions under which agricultural income is brought into the tax computation, and compute Mr Devraj's tax liability for the assessment year 2026-27 showing each step.

points.text: The accountant is wrong. Agricultural income is exempt under section 10(1), but for an individual, HUF, AOP, BOI or artificial juridical person it is partially integrated with non-agricultural income when two conditions hold: net agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000, and non-agricultural income exceeds the basic exemption limit, which under the default regime is ₹4,00,000 whatever the person's age. Both hold here. The aggregation does not apply to a company, LLP, firm, co-operative society or local authority.

citation.ref: Section 2(1A) with section 10(1) and the Finance Act's partial integration rule — the two conditions

points.text: Step 1: tax on the aggregate of non-agricultural and net agricultural income, ₹19,00,000, at the default-regime slabs — nil up to ₹4,00,000, 5% on the next ₹4,00,000 (₹20,000), 10% on the next ₹4,00,000 (₹40,000), 15% on the next ₹4,00,000 (₹60,000) and 20% on the remaining ₹3,00,000 (₹60,000) — is ₹1,80,000.

citation.ref: Section 115BAC(1A) slabs for the previous year 2025-26 — step 1 of partial integration

points.text: Step 2: tax on net agricultural income plus the basic exemption limit, ₹4,00,000 plus ₹4,00,000 = ₹8,00,000, is 5% of ₹4,00,000 = ₹20,000.

citation.ref: Partial integration — step 2, tax on agricultural income plus the exemption limit

points.text: Step 3: the tax on non-agricultural income is step 1 less step 2, ₹1,80,000 less ₹20,000 = ₹1,60,000. No surcharge applies because total income does not exceed ₹50 lakh.

citation.ref: Partial integration — step 3 and step 4, surcharge only above ₹50 lakh

points.text: Health and education cess at 4% on ₹1,60,000 is ₹6,400, so the tax liability is ₹1,66,400.

citation.ref: Health and education cess at 4% — step 5 of partial integration

points.text: The effect is that the agricultural income itself is never taxed: it only pushes the non-agricultural income into higher slabs. Had the ₹4,00,000 been ignored, tax before cess on ₹15,00,000 alone would have been ₹1,05,000, so integration costs Mr Devraj ₹55,000 more before cess.

citation.ref: Object of partial integration — non-agricultural income taxed at a higher rate, agricultural income itself untaxed

written.scenario: Four growers in Kerala and Assam ask how much of their profit for the previous year 2025-26 is agricultural income. Assam Leaf grows tea and manufactures it in India, with a profit of ₹20 lakh. Malabar Beans grows coffee, cures it, roasts and grinds it, mixing chicory, with a profit of ₹10 lakh. Wayanad Estates grows coffee and only cures it before sale, with a profit of ₹4 lakh. Kottayam Rubber grows rubber plants and sells centrifuged latex made from its own field latex, with a profit of ₹8 lakh. Each is an individual proprietor.
written.question: For each grower, state the rule that applies and split the profit between business income and agricultural income, and say what the agricultural part means for their tax.

points.text: Assam Leaf: Rule 8 applies where the assessee grows tea leaves and manufactures tea in India — 40% of the profit, ₹8 lakh, is business income and 60%, ₹12 lakh, is agricultural income.

citation.ref: Rule 8 — tea grown and manufactured, 40% business and 60% agricultural

points.text: Malabar Beans: under Rule 7B, coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground by the seller in India, with or without chicory or flavouring, is split 40% business, ₹4 lakh, and 60% agricultural, ₹6 lakh.

citation.ref: Rule 7B(1A) — coffee grown, cured, roasted and ground, 40% business and 60% agricultural

points.text: Wayanad Estates: coffee grown and only cured by the seller in India is split under Rule 7B as 25% business income, ₹1 lakh, and 75% agricultural income, ₹3 lakh — the less the grower does after the field, the larger the agricultural share.

citation.ref: Rule 7B(1) — coffee grown and cured, 25% business and 75% agricultural

points.text: Kottayam Rubber: Rule 7A covers centrifuged latex, cenex, crepes and block rubber made from field latex of rubber plants grown by the seller in India — 35% of the profit, ₹2.8 lakh, is business income and 65%, ₹5.2 lakh, is agricultural. For each grower the agricultural part is exempt under section 10(1) but, being an individual with net agricultural income above ₹5,000, it is counted for partial integration when the business income exceeds the basic exemption limit.

citation.ref: Rule 7A — rubber, 35% business and 65% agricultural; section 10(1) exemption with partial integration

written.scenario: A search under section 132 was carried out on Meridian Traders, whose Assessing Officer sits in Jaipur. The search was conducted by an authorised officer of the Delhi Investigation wing who has no jurisdiction over Meridian, and the last panchnama was drawn on 10 July 2026. The authorised officer wishes to keep the seized books, provisionally attach a warehouse belonging to Meridian, and have the seized jewellery valued. On 1 August 2026 a separate survey under section 133A was conducted at Meridian's branch; the survey officer impounded the branch's ledgers and, without anyone's approval, has held them for twenty-five working days, and also carried away ₹6 lakh in cash found there.
written.question: Examine each of the officers' actions against the time limits and the powers in sections 132 and 133A.

points.text: Since the authorised officer has no jurisdiction over Meridian, section 132(9A) requires the seized books, money, jewellery and other assets to be handed over to the Assessing Officer having jurisdiction within 60 days from the date on which the last of the authorisations for search was executed — here 10 July 2026, the date of the last panchnama — and thereafter the powers under sub-sections (8) and (9) are the Jaipur officer's.

citation.ref: Section 132(9A) and the Explanation on the last of the authorisations — sixty days to hand over

points.text: The warehouse can be provisionally attached under section 132(9B) during the search or within sixty days from the last authorisation, for reasons recorded in writing and with the prior approval of the Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director; under section 132(9C) the attachment ceases to have effect six months from the date of the order.

citation.ref: Sections 132(9B) and 132(9C) — provisional attachment, sixty days to order it and six months of life

points.text: The jewellery may be referred under section 132(9D) to a Valuation Officer under section 142A, or to an approved valuer, during the search or within 60 days of the last authorisation; the valuer must report the fair market value within 60 days of receiving the reference.

citation.ref: Section 132(9D) — reference for valuation within sixty days, report within sixty days

points.text: Seized books cannot be retained beyond 30 days after the assessment proceedings for the years to which they relate are completed unless reasons are recorded in writing and the approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, Principal Director General or Director General is obtained under section 132(8).

citation.ref: Section 132(8) — retention of seized books beyond thirty days after assessment needs approval

points.text: Under section 133A(3) the survey officer may impound the ledgers after recording reasons, but cannot retain them beyond 15 days, excluding holidays, without the approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director — so twenty-five working days without approval exceeds his power. Carrying away the ₹6 lakh is beyond section 133A altogether: section 133A(4) forbids the removal of any cash, stock or valuable article from the place surveyed.

citation.ref: Sections 133A(3) and 133A(4) — fifteen days without approval, and nothing removed from the premises

written.scenario: Four taxpayers received orders for the assessment year 2025-26 and ask whether they can go to the Dispute Resolution Committee instead of appealing. Ms Priya, who returned a total income of ₹42 lakh, received an intimation under section 143(1) adjusting her income by ₹7 lakh, which she disputes.
