Her brother Mr Arjun returned ₹65 lakh and received an assessment order adding ₹9 lakh. Verma & Co, a firm, returned ₹38 lakh and received an assessment order adding ₹12 lakh. Kriti Pvt Ltd returned ₹30 lakh and received an assessment order adding ₹6 lakh, framed on the basis of a survey under section 133A at its premises. None of them has been detained or prosecuted under any law.
written.question: Advise each taxpayer on eligibility, and describe for the eligible one the application, the Committee, what it may do and by when, and the relief on penalty and prosecution.

points.text: Section 245MA reaches a specified order — which includes an intimation under section 143(1) that the assessee objects to and an order of assessment or reassessment — where three conditions hold: the aggregate variation proposed or made does not exceed ₹10 lakh; a return was furnished and the returned total income does not exceed ₹50 lakh; and the order is not based on a search under section 132 or requisition under section 132A, a survey under section 133A, or information received under a section 90 or 90A agreement.

citation.ref: Explanation (b) to section 245MA with Rule 44DAD(ii) — specified order and its three conditions

points.text: Ms Priya is eligible: variation ₹7 lakh within ₹10 lakh, returned income ₹42 lakh within ₹50 lakh, and no search or survey. Mr Arjun fails on returned income of ₹65 lakh; Verma & Co fails on a variation of ₹12 lakh; Kriti Pvt Ltd fails because its order is based on a survey under section 133A, even though its figures are within both limits.

citation.ref: Section 245MA conditions applied — variation, returned income, and orders founded on search or survey

points.text: Ms Priya applies in the prescribed form under Rule 44DAB with a fee of ₹1,000. The Committee under Rule 44DAA has three members — two retired officers of the Indian Revenue Service who held the post of Commissioner or higher for five years or more, and one serving officer not below Principal Commissioner or Commissioner — appointed for three years, deciding by majority.

citation.ref: Rules 44DAA and 44DAB — composition of the Committee and the application with its fee

points.text: The Committee may modify the specified order, but only in a manner not prejudicial to the assessee, or dispose of the application without modification, and must do so within six months from the end of the month in which the application is admitted; its order must accord with the Act, and a copy goes to the Assessing Officer and the assessee.

citation.ref: Section 245MA(2) with the e-Dispute Resolution Scheme, 2022 — modification not prejudicial, six months from the end of the month of admission

points.text: Under Rule 44DAC, on confirmation that the demand is paid, the Committee grants waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution in respect of that order if Ms Priya has paid the tax on the returned income in full and co-operated in the proceedings, for reasons recorded in writing; no immunity is granted where prosecution was initiated before the application was received, and immunity is withdrawn if any condition attached to it is breached.

citation.ref: Rule 44DAC — conditions for waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution, and their withdrawal

written.scenario: For the previous year 2025-26, five clients ask whether their accounts must be audited under section 44AB. Vardhan Traders has a turnover of ₹8.5 crore, with cash receipts at 3% of total receipts and cash payments at 4% of total payments. Kamla Stores has a turnover of ₹9 crore, with cash receipts at 6% of total receipts and cash payments at 2% of total payments. Dr Rao, a physician, has gross professional receipts of ₹55 lakh. Nakul Ltd runs a textile business with a turnover of ₹7 crore and a retail business with a turnover of ₹4 crore, every transaction through account-payee banking. Mr Sen, who declared profits under section 44AD for the previous year 2024-25, now declares a profit lower than the presumptive rate for 2025-26, and his total income exceeds the basic exemption limit. Kamla Stores did not get its accounts audited and asks what the penalty could be.
written.question: Advise each client on whether a tax audit is required, which forms are furnished and by when, and quantify the penalty exposure of Kamla Stores.

points.text: Vardhan Traders is not required to be audited: the ₹1 crore business limit is lifted to ₹10 crore where aggregate cash receipts do not exceed 5% of total receipts and aggregate cash payments do not exceed 5% of total payments, and its 3% and 4% satisfy both.

citation.ref: Section 44AB(a) proviso — ten crore limit where cash receipts and cash payments are each within five per cent

points.text: Kamla Stores must be audited: the twin conditions must be satisfied together, and cash receipts at 6% breach the 5% test, so the ordinary ₹1 crore limit applies and ₹9 crore exceeds it. A cheque or draft that is not account payee counts as cash for this test.

citation.ref: Section 44AB(a) proviso — the two cash conditions apply together; non-account-payee instruments are cash

points.text: Dr Rao must be audited because gross receipts in profession exceed ₹50 lakh. Nakul Ltd must be audited because turnover from all businesses is aggregated — ₹11 crore exceeds ₹10 crore, and above ₹10 crore the audit is required even where every transaction is through banking channels.

citation.ref: Section 44AB(b) — profession above fifty lakh; section 44AB(a) — turnover of all businesses aggregated

points.text: Mr Sen must be audited under section 44AB(e): section 44AD(4) applies to a person who opted out of the presumptive scheme after declaring under it, and his income exceeds the basic exemption limit.

citation.ref: Section 44AB(e) — a person covered by section 44AD(4) whose income exceeds the exemption limit

points.text: The audit must be completed and the report furnished before one month prior to the due date under section 139(1). A person whose accounts are audited under another law furnishes that audit report with a further report in Form 3CA; anyone else furnishes Form 3CB; the particulars in either case go in Form 3CD under Rule 6G.

citation.ref: Rule 6G — Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD; section 44AB — specified date one month before the section 139(1) due date

points.text: Under section 271B the Assessing Officer may levy the lower of one-half per cent of turnover or ₹1,50,000: half a per cent of ₹9 crore is ₹4,50,000, so the exposure is capped at ₹1,50,000, and no penalty is imposable under section 273B if reasonable cause for the failure is proved.

citation.ref: Section 271B — half per cent or ₹1,50,000, whichever is less; section 273B reasonable cause

written.scenario: The treasury head of an Indian group that is setting up holding and financing companies abroad has read that India is a member of the Inclusive Framework on BEPS. She asks which of the fifteen BEPS Actions India is bound to implement, whether India must enact controlled foreign company rules, and what a treaty must now contain to stop a group routing income through a third country only for the treaty's sake.
written.question: Answer her three questions, distinguishing the kinds of commitment in the BEPS package.

points.text: The BEPS measures are of three kinds: new minimum standards, which every state implements because non-implementation spills over onto others; revisions of standards that already exist, such as treaty and transfer pricing guidance, which not every participant has endorsed; and best practices, which are optional recommendations.

citation.ref: The three tiers of BEPS commitment — minimum standard, revision of an existing standard, best practice

points.text: India, as an Inclusive Framework member, is bound to implement the four minimum standards — Action 5 on harmful tax practices, Action 6 on treaty abuse, Action 13 on country-by-country reporting and Action 14 on making dispute resolution more effective — and to take part in the peer review of each.

citation.ref: The four minimum standards, Actions 5, 6, 13 and 14, each subject to peer review

points.text: Controlled foreign company rules are not a minimum standard: the Action 3 report offers building blocks as a best practice, so India is free to enact them or not, and it has not.

citation.source: OECD/G20 BEPS Project — Action 3 Final Report
citation.ref: No minimum standard for controlled foreign company rules — recommendations only

points.text: Under the Action 6 minimum standard against treaty shopping, a treaty must carry an express statement that the parties intend to eliminate double taxation without creating opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through evasion or avoidance, and must adopt one of three: a combined Limitation of Benefits rule and Principal Purpose Test, the Principal Purpose Test alone, or a Limitation of Benefits rule supplemented by a mechanism against conduit financing arrangements.

citation.source: OECD/G20 BEPS Project — Action 6 Final Report
citation.ref: Treaty shopping minimum standard — express statement plus LOB and PPT, PPT alone, or LOB with an anti-conduit rule

written.scenario: Fjord Engineering AS, resident in State N, wins two contracts in India: an installation project at a refinery lasting eight months, and a consultancy engagement under which its engineers will be present in India for 200 days spread over a twelve-month period. It will also license a process patent to the refinery for a royalty. State N's treaty with India is being renegotiated, and the two drafts on the table follow the OECD Model and the UN Model respectively.
written.question: Explain how the answer on permanent establishment and on the taxation of the royalty differs between the two drafts.

points.text: Under Article 5(3)(a) of the OECD Model a building site or construction or installation project is a permanent establishment only if it lasts more than twelve months, so an eight-month installation is no PE; the UN Model is wider — it also covers assembly or installation projects and supervisory activities connected with them and needs the activity to continue for only six months, so the same project is a PE.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention, 2017 and UN Model Double Taxation Convention, 2021
citation.ref: Article 5(3)(a) — twelve months in the OECD Model against six months, with assembly and supervisory activities, in the UN Model

points.text: Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model creates a Service PE where an enterprise furnishes services, including consultancy, through employees or other personnel for a period or periods aggregating more than 183 days in any twelve-month period, so 200 days of engineers makes a PE; the OECD Model has no Service PE clause and the presence would have to be tested under the fixed-place basic rule of Article 5(1).

citation.source: UN Model Double Taxation Convention, 2021 and OECD Model Tax Convention, 2017
citation.ref: Article 5(3)(b) of the UN Model — Service PE at 183 days; absence of the clause in the OECD Model

points.text: Under Article 12 of the OECD Model, royalties arising in the source state and beneficially owned by a resident of the other state are taxable only in the residence state, so India could not tax the patent royalty; the UN Model lets the source state tax it too, at a rate not exceeding a percentage settled by bilateral negotiation, and its definition of royalties also takes in equipment rentals and film or tape rentals that the OECD definition leaves out.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention, 2017 and UN Model Double Taxation Convention, 2021
citation.ref: Article 12 — exclusive residence taxation in the OECD Model against shared source taxation and a wider definition in the UN Model

written.scenario: Mr. Kunal, who has opted out of the default regime, owns two houses. House one is let at ₹35,000 a month throughout 2025-26; its municipal value is ₹3,60,000, fair rent ₹4,20,000 and standard rent ₹3,90,000; he paid municipal tax of ₹40,000 and interest of ₹3,10,000 on the loan taken to buy it. House two is self-occupied; its construction loan was taken in May 2021, construction was completed in March 2024, the lender has certified interest of ₹2,60,000 for the year. In February 2026 he also recovered ₹90,000 of rent from a tenant who had vacated house one in 2023, which he had written off as unrealised in that year.
written.question: Compute Mr. Kunal's income under the head Income from house property for A.Y. 2026-27, explaining each step.

points.text: House one, gross annual value. Expected rent is the higher of fair rent ₹4,20,000 and municipal value ₹3,60,000, restricted to the standard rent of ₹3,90,000, so ₹3,90,000. Gross annual value is the higher of expected rent and actual rent received or receivable, ₹4,20,000, so the gross annual value is ₹4,20,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Basic Concepts, Income from house property
citation.ref: Determination of annual value — expected rent restricted to standard rent; GAV the higher of expected and actual rent

points.text: Net annual value is gross annual value less municipal tax paid by the owner during the year: ₹4,20,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹3,80,000. Deductions under section 24: standard deduction at 30 per cent of net annual value, ₹1,14,000, and interest on borrowed capital, fully allowed for a let-out property, ₹3,10,000. Income from house one is ₹3,80,000 − ₹1,14,000 − ₹3,10,000 = a loss of ₹44,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Basic Concepts, Income from house property
citation.ref: Deductions from net annual value — 30 per cent under section 24(a); interest fully allowed on let-out property

points.text: House two, self-occupied: annual value is nil and no municipal tax is deductible. Interest on a loan for acquisition or construction is allowed up to ₹2,00,000 in total for one or two self-occupied properties where the acquisition or construction is completed within five years from the end of the financial year in which the capital was borrowed and the lender certifies the interest; otherwise the cap is ₹30,000. The loan was taken in 2021-22, so completion by 31 March 2027 suffices and March 2024 is within time, and the certificate exists; of the ₹2,60,000, ₹2,00,000 is allowed, a loss of ₹2,00,000. The deduction is available only because he has opted out of the default regime.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Basic Concepts, Income from house property
citation.ref: Self-occupied property — nil annual value; interest capped at 2,00,000 with five-year completion and lender's certificate

points.text: The ₹90,000 of unrealised rent realised later is deemed income from house property in the year of receipt under section 25A, whether or not he still owns the property, and section 25A(2) allows a deduction of 30 per cent: ₹90,000 − ₹27,000 = ₹63,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Basic Concepts, Income from house property
citation.ref: Section 25A — unrealised rent realised subsequently taxed in the year of receipt with 30 per cent deduction

points.text: Income from house property for A.Y. 2026-27: (₹44,000) + (₹2,00,000) + ₹63,000 = a loss of ₹1,81,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Basic Concepts, Income from house property
citation.ref: Aggregation of income under the head

written.scenario: Four sums reached Ms. Ira in 2025-26. (a) ₹14,00,000 on maturity of a traditional policy issued on 1 July 2015 with an actual capital sum assured of ₹10,00,000 and an annual premium of ₹1,20,000. (b) ₹36,00,000 on maturity of a unit linked policy issued on 1 March 2022 with a sum assured of ₹30,00,000 and an annual premium of ₹2,80,000. (c) Two traditional policies issued on 1 May 2023, sums assured ₹40,00,000 and ₹30,00,000 with annual premiums of ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,40,000, both of which paid out on surrender. (d) ₹25,00,000 on the death of her husband under a policy whose premium was 15 per cent of the sum assured.
written.question: State, with reasons, whether each sum is exempt under section 10(10D).

points.text: (a) Not exempt. For a policy issued on or after 1 April 2013 the exemption is lost if the premium payable for any year during the term exceeds 10 per cent of the actual capital sum assured; ₹1,20,000 is 12 per cent of ₹10,00,000. The 15 per cent limit applies only where the insured is a person with disability under section 80U or a disease under section 80DDB.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Incomes which do not form part of total income
citation.ref: Section 10(10D) — 10 per cent of actual capital sum assured for policies issued on or after 1 April 2013; 15 per cent for disability or disease

points.text: (b) Not exempt. The premium of ₹2,80,000 is 9.33 per cent of the sum assured and passes the 10 per cent test, but for a unit linked policy issued on or after 1 February 2021 the exemption is also lost if the premium payable exceeds ₹2,50,000 for any previous year during the term. The ceiling does not apply to a policy issued by an IFSC insurance office.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Incomes which do not form part of total income
citation.ref: Section 10(10D) — ULIP issued on or after 1 February 2021, premium above 2,50,000

points.text: (c) For policies other than unit linked issued on or after 1 April 2023 the exemption is lost if the premium exceeds ₹5,00,000 for any year, and where premiums are payable on more than one such policy and the aggregate exceeds ₹5,00,000, exemption is available, at the assessee's option, for those policies whose aggregate premium does not exceed ₹5,00,000. Both policies pass the 10 per cent test (7.5 and 8 per cent), but the aggregate premium is ₹5,40,000, so Ira may choose either the ₹3,00,000-premium policy or the ₹2,40,000-premium policy as exempt, not both; she should choose the one with the larger receipt.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Incomes which do not form part of total income
citation.ref: Section 10(10D) — policies issued on or after 1 April 2023, premium above 5,00,000; option across several policies

points.text: (d) Exempt in full. Any sum received on the death of a person is exempt irrespective of the premium payable; none of the 10, 15 or 20 per cent tests or the ₹2,50,000 and ₹5,00,000 ceilings applies.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Incomes which do not form part of total income
citation.ref: Section 10(10D) — sum received on death exempt irrespective of premium

points.text: Two receipts are never exempt under section 10(10D): a sum received under a keyman insurance policy, and an amount received under section 80DD(3) where the disabled dependant for whom a deposit was made predeceases the depositor, which is deemed the depositor's income of the year of receipt.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Incomes which do not form part of total income
citation.ref: Section 10(10D) — keyman insurance policy and section 80DD(3) receipts excluded

written.scenario: Tejas Industries Ltd sold its packaging division, run since 2015, as a going concern on 1 October 2025 for a lump sum of ₹42 crore, without values being assigned to individual assets, though the conveyance deed states a value for the land for stamp duty. The division's books on that date showed: land ₹6 crore (stamp duty value ₹15 crore); plant and machinery ₹9 crore, equal to its written down value for tax; self-generated goodwill ₹3 crore; debtors and stock ₹7 crore; liabilities ₹10 crore, of which ₹1 crore is a provision for warranty claims not yet ascertained. The CFO proposes to compute the gain as ₹42 crore less the book net worth of ₹15 crore, with indexation from 2015, and to file the accountant's report with the return in November 2026.
written.question: State whether the transfer is a slump sale, compute the capital gain and the tax on it, and correct the CFO's three proposals.

points.text: It is a slump sale under section 2(42C): a transfer of an undertaking, by any means, for a lump sum consideration without values being assigned to the individual assets and liabilities. A value stated solely for stamp duty, registration fees or similar taxes is not regarded as an assignment of values, so the land figure in the deed does not defeat it. Having been held for more than 36 months, the gain is long-term under section 50B(1).

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Capital Gains
citation.ref: Section 2(42C) and 50B(1) — slump sale; stamp duty value not an assignment; 36-month test

points.text: Net worth is the deemed cost of acquisition and improvement, with no indexation benefit. It is the aggregate value of the total assets less the liabilities as they appear in the books, ignoring any revaluation, with depreciable assets taken at written down value, self-generated goodwill at nil and assets wholly deducted under section 35AD at nil, and all other assets at book value: plant ₹9 crore + land ₹6 crore + goodwill nil + current assets ₹7 crore − liabilities ₹10 crore = ₹12 crore. The CFO's ₹15 crore wrongly counts the goodwill, and indexation is not available.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Capital Gains
citation.ref: Section 50B(2)(i) and Explanations 1 and 2 — net worth as deemed cost; WDV, self-generated goodwill nil, no indexation

points.text: The full value of consideration is the fair market value of the capital assets on the date of transfer under Rule 11UAE, the higher of FMV1 and FMV2. FMV1 = A + B + C + D − L: A, the book value of assets other than jewellery, artistic work, shares, securities and immovable property, is ₹9 + ₹3 + ₹7 = ₹19 crore (the goodwill counts here at its book value); D, the stamp duty value of the immovable property, is ₹15 crore; L, the book liabilities excluding provisions for unascertained liabilities, is ₹9 crore. FMV1 = ₹25 crore.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Capital Gains
citation.ref: Rule 11UAE — FMV1 as A + B + C + D − L; stamp duty value of immovable property; unascertained provisions excluded from L

points.text: FMV2 is the fair market value of the consideration received: the monetary consideration of ₹42 crore. The full value of consideration is the higher, ₹42 crore. Long-term capital gain = ₹42 crore − ₹12 crore = ₹30 crore, taxable at 12.5 per cent under section 112 without indexation: ₹3.75 crore before surcharge and cess.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Capital Gains
citation.ref: Rule 11UAE — FMV2; higher of FMV1 and FMV2 as full value; LTCG on slump sale taxed at 12.5 per cent

points.text: The report of a chartered accountant in the prescribed form, indicating the computation of net worth and certifying it, must be furnished on or before the specified date under section 44AB, 30 September of the assessment year, one month before the due date for the return, not with the return in November.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Capital Gains
citation.ref: Section 50B(3) — chartered accountant's report by the specified date under section 44AB

written.scenario: Meher Textiles Pvt Ltd, a closely held company whose business is not money-lending, had accumulated profits of ₹18,00,000 on 1 April 2025. During 2025-26 it advanced ₹10,00,000 in April to Rohan, who holds 15 per cent of its equity; ₹6,00,000 in July to a partnership firm in which Rohan has a 25 per cent share of profits; ₹5,00,000 in September to Priya, who holds 8 per cent; and in December it paid ₹1,50,000 of Rohan's personal travel bills. Rohan repaid his loan with interest at the market rate in March 2026. The company declared no dividend.
written.question: Determine the amount deemed to be dividend under section 2(22)(e) in each case and in whose hands, and state the effect of the repayment with interest.

points.text: Any payment by a company in which the public are not substantially interested, by way of advance or loan to a shareholder who is the beneficial owner of 10 per cent or more of the voting power, is deemed dividend to the extent of the accumulated profits; a loan not covered by accumulated profits is not deemed dividend. Rohan holds 15 per cent, so the April loan of ₹10,00,000 is deemed dividend in his hands, leaving accumulated profits of ₹8,00,000 for later payments.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income from Other Sources
citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e) — loan to a shareholder with 10 per cent or more voting power, to the extent of accumulated profits

points.text: A payment to a concern, a firm, HUF, AOP, BOI or company, in which such a shareholder is a member or partner and has a substantial interest, at least 20 per cent of the income of the concern, is likewise deemed dividend. Rohan has 25 per cent in the firm, so the July loan of ₹6,00,000 is deemed dividend, leaving ₹2,00,000 of accumulated profits.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income from Other Sources
citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e) — loan to a concern in which the shareholder has a substantial interest of 20 per cent

points.text: Priya holds only 8 per cent, below the 10 per cent test, so the ₹5,00,000 loan to her is not deemed dividend.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income from Other Sources
citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e) — shareholder below 10 per cent voting power

points.text: Any payment by such a company on behalf of, or for the individual benefit of, such a shareholder is also deemed dividend, subject to the same ceiling of accumulated profits. The ₹1,50,000 of travel bills is deemed dividend in Rohan's hands, within the ₹2,00,000 remaining. Total deemed dividend for the year: ₹17,50,000, all taxable as income from other sources.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income from Other Sources
citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e) — payment on behalf of or for the benefit of the shareholder; ceiling of accumulated profits

points.text: Subsequent repayment of the loan, or the charging of interest at the market rate, does not take the payment out of section 2(22)(e). The exceptions are different: a loan in the ordinary course of business where money-lending is a substantial part of the company's business, which does not apply here; a loan between two group entities one of which is a finance company whose listed parent is outside India; and a dividend later declared and set off against the loan, which is not taxed twice.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income from Other Sources
citation.ref: Section 2(22)(e) — repayment and market interest irrelevant; exceptions for ordinary-course lending, group finance entities and set-off of dividend

written.scenario: Mr. Sen's total income before clubbing is ₹14,00,000 and Mrs. Sen's ₹9,00,000; both have opted out of the default regime. Their son Aarav, aged 14, earned ₹40,000 of interest on deposits gifted by his grandfather and ₹75,000 as prize money for winning a state chess championship. Their daughter Diya, aged 16 and married, receives rent of ₹2,40,000 from a flat her father gifted her last year. Their son Vihaan, aged 8, who has a disability specified in section 80U, earned ₹20,000 of interest on his own savings. Mr. Sen wants everything assessed in the children's hands "since the money is theirs".
written.question: State what is clubbed, with whom and how much, and what is assessed in each child's own hands.

points.text: All income of a minor child is included in the income of the parent whose total income is greater, here Mr. Sen; once clubbed with one parent it continues with that parent in later years unless the Assessing Officer, after hearing the other parent, is satisfied a change is necessary. Aarav's interest of ₹40,000 is clubbed with Mr. Sen.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income of other persons included in assessee's total income
citation.ref: Section 64(1A) — minor's income clubbed with the parent whose total income is greater

points.text: Income derived by a minor from manual work or from any activity involving skill, talent or specialised knowledge or experience is not clubbed. The chess prize of ₹75,000 is assessed in Aarav's own hands.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income of other persons included in assessee's total income
citation.ref: Section 64(1A) — exception for income from manual work or skill, talent or specialised knowledge

points.text: Clubbing applies to the income of a minor married daughter as well. Where a house property is transferred without consideration to a minor child other than a married daughter, the transferor is the deemed owner under section 27(i) and the rent is his own; that route does not apply to Diya because she is married, so her rent is taxed as her income and then clubbed with Mr. Sen under section 64(1A): ₹2,40,000 less the 30 per cent standard deduction, ₹1,68,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income of other persons included in assessee's total income
citation.ref: Section 64(1A) applies to a minor married daughter; section 27(i) deemed ownership excludes her

points.text: The income of a minor child suffering from a disability of the nature specified in section 80U is not clubbed and is assessed in the child's own hands; Vihaan's ₹20,000 stays with him.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income of other persons included in assessee's total income
citation.ref: Section 64(1A) — income of a minor with a section 80U disability assessed in the child's hands

points.text: Under section 10(32) the parent is exempt to the extent of ₹1,500 for each minor whose income is clubbed, or the whole income if it is less than ₹1,500, but only outside the default regime, which the Sens have left. Clubbed with Mr. Sen: Aarav ₹40,000 − ₹1,500 = ₹38,500 and Diya ₹1,68,000 − ₹1,500 = ₹1,66,500, a total of ₹2,05,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income of other persons included in assessee's total income
citation.ref: Section 10(32) — 1,500 per minor child, only outside the default regime under section 115BAC

written.scenario: Nirali Apparels Ltd, an existing garment manufacturer whose accounts are audited under section 44AB, had 300 employees on 31 March 2025. During 2025-26 it took on: 60 regular workers from 1 May 2025 at ₹22,000 a month; 30 supervisors from 1 June 2025 at ₹28,000 a month; 40 workers from 1 December 2025 at ₹20,000 a month; 25 casual workers at ₹18,000 a month who are not in the recognised provident fund; and 10 workers at ₹21,000 a month paid in cash. Twenty employees left during the year. All regular employees join the recognised provident fund. The company pays tax under section 115BAA and its accountant says that rules out section 80JJAA.
written.question: Compute the deduction under section 80JJAA for A.Y. 2026-27, state for how many years it runs, deal with the December joiners, and correct the accountant.

points.text: Where the gross total income of an assessee to whom section 44AB applies includes profits of business, a deduction of 30 per cent of the additional employee cost incurred in the year is allowed for three assessment years, including the one relevant to the year the employment is provided. The business must not be formed by splitting up or reconstruction of an existing business or acquired by transfer, and the accountant's report must be furnished before the specified date under section 44AB.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Deductions from Gross Total Income
citation.ref: Section 80JJAA — 30 per cent of additional employee cost for three assessment years; conditions

points.text: For an existing business the additional employee cost is nil unless the total number of employees has increased from the last day of the preceding year; here the net increase is 165 − 20 = 145, so the test is met. An additional employee excludes one whose total emoluments exceed ₹25,000 a month, one whose entire pension contribution is paid by the Government, one employed for fewer than 240 days in the year, or fewer than 150 days for a business of manufacturing apparel, footwear or leather products, and one who does not participate in the recognised provident fund. Emoluments paid otherwise than by account payee cheque, bank draft, electronic clearing or the prescribed electronic modes are also left out of the cost.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Deductions from Gross Total Income
citation.ref: Section 80JJAA — additional employee exclusions; 150 days for apparel; cash emoluments excluded

points.text: Applying the exclusions: the 30 supervisors at ₹28,000 exceed ₹25,000; the 25 casual workers are outside the provident fund; the 10 cash-paid workers fail the mode of payment; the 40 December joiners served 121 days, fewer than 150. Only the 60 May joiners count. Additional employee cost = 60 × ₹22,000 × 11 months = ₹1,45,20,000, and the deduction = 30 per cent = ₹43,56,000 for each of A.Y. 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Deductions from Gross Total Income
citation.ref: Section 80JJAA — computation of additional employee cost and deduction

points.text: The 40 December joiners are not lost: an employee employed for fewer than 150 days in the year but for 150 days or more in the immediately succeeding year is deemed to have been employed in the succeeding year, so 30 per cent of their cost is deductible for three years from A.Y. 2027-28 if they stay through 2026-27.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Deductions from Gross Total Income
citation.ref: Section 80JJAA — deeming of employment in the succeeding year

points.text: The accountant is wrong. The deduction under section 80JJAA is available irrespective of the regime under which the assessee pays tax; section 115BAA computes total income without the deductions of Chapter VI-A other than sections 80JJAA and 80M, so the ₹43,56,000 survives the option.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Deductions from Gross Total Income
citation.ref: Section 80JJAA available irrespective of regime; 115BAA preserves 80JJAA and 80M

written.scenario: Suvarna Tools Ltd, a domestic company, has a total income of ₹9 crore for 2025-26 under the normal provisions, after claiming a deduction of ₹1.2 crore under section 10AA for its SEZ unit, additional depreciation of ₹0.6 crore under section 32(1)(iia), a deduction of ₹0.4 crore under section 80JJAA, ₹0.3 crore under section 80M, and set-off of ₹0.5 crore of brought-forward unabsorbed additional depreciation. It carries forward MAT credit of ₹0.8 crore. Its minimum alternate tax for the year is lower than its normal tax. The CFO wants to opt for section 115BAA this year "because 22 per cent beats 30".
written.question: Explain how total income and tax are computed under section 115BAA, compute the tax under both routes, and advise whether and when the option should be exercised.

points.text: Under section 115BAA any domestic company may pay tax at 22 per cent, with surcharge at a flat 10 per cent with no threshold and therefore no marginal relief, and cess at 4 per cent, an effective 25.168 per cent; minimum alternate tax does not apply to a company that opts.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Section 115BAA — 22 per cent, 10 per cent surcharge, 4 per cent cess, 25.168 per cent effective; MAT not applicable

points.text: The price is that total income is computed without the deductions under sections 10AA, 32(1)(iia), 33AB, 33ABA, 35(1)(ii), (iia) and (iii), 35(2AA), 35(2AB), 35AD, 35CCC and 35CCD, and without Chapter VI-A other than sections 80JJAA and 80M; depreciation on any block entitled to more than 40 per cent is restricted to 40 per cent. Suvarna therefore adds back ₹1.2 crore and ₹0.6 crore while keeping the ₹0.4 crore and ₹0.3 crore.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Section 115BAA — deductions not available; Chapter VI-A other than 80JJAA and 80M; depreciation restricted to 40 per cent

points.text: Total income is also computed without set-off of any brought-forward loss or depreciation attributable to those deductions, and such loss or depreciation is deemed to have been given effect to, with no deduction in any later year. The ₹0.5 crore of unabsorbed additional depreciation is lost for good if the option is taken now. Total income under section 115BAA: ₹9 + ₹1.2 + ₹0.6 + ₹0.5 = ₹11.3 crore; tax at 25.168 per cent = ₹2,84,39,840.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Section 115BAA — loss and depreciation attributable to forgone deductions deemed given effect; computation

points.text: Under the normal provisions: tax at 30 per cent on ₹9 crore = ₹2,70,00,000, surcharge at 7 per cent because total income exceeds ₹1 crore but not ₹10 crore = ₹18,90,000, cess at 4 per cent on ₹2,88,90,000 = ₹11,55,600, total ₹3,00,45,600. Brought-forward MAT credit of ₹0.8 crore is set off against it, leaving ₹2,20,45,600 to pay. Under section 115BAA the MAT credit cannot be set off at all.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Normal rates for a domestic company; MAT credit not available against income under 115BAA

points.text: There is no time limit within which the option must be exercised, so a company with brought-forward losses or depreciation from the forgone deductions, or with MAT credit, may postpone the option to a later year after exhausting them. Suvarna should stay on the normal provisions for A.Y. 2026-27, use the ₹0.8 crore credit and the ₹0.5 crore depreciation, and opt for section 115BAA thereafter; once exercised the option cannot be withdrawn, and a failure of the conditions in any year makes it invalid for that year and all later years.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment of Various Entities
citation.ref: Section 115BAA — no timeline for the option; exhaust MAT credit and losses first; failure of conditions

written.scenario: Four payments for virtual digital assets were made in 2025-26. (a) Mr. Dev, a salaried employee with no business income, paid ₹80,000 in June to Ms. Rhea, a resident, for a cryptocurrency. (b) Zenith Ltd paid ₹9,000 in July and ₹4,000 in November to a resident trader for tokens. (c) Ms. Tara, a resident, exchanged one cryptocurrency worth ₹3,00,000 for another with a resident counterparty, no cash changing hands. (d) An exchange credited ₹2,00,000 of sale consideration to a "pending settlements" account in its books in March 2026 and paid the seller in April.
written.question: State in each case whether tax is deductible under section 194S, how much and when.

points.text: Any person responsible for paying a resident any sum by way of consideration for transfer of a virtual digital asset must deduct tax at 1 per cent, at the time of credit of the consideration to the account of the resident or of payment by any mode, whichever is earlier.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Taxation of Digital Transactions
citation.ref: Section 194S — 1 per cent on consideration for transfer of a virtual digital asset; time of deduction

points.text: (a) Mr. Dev is a specified person, an individual with no income under the head profits and gains of business or profession, for whom no tax is deductible where the aggregate consideration in the financial year does not exceed ₹50,000. His payment of ₹80,000 exceeds it, so he deducts ₹800 in June.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Taxation of Digital Transactions
citation.ref: Section 194S — specified person threshold of 50,000

points.text: (b) Zenith Ltd is not a specified person, so its threshold is ₹10,000 of aggregate consideration in the year. The July payment of ₹9,000 alone was within it, but the November payment takes the aggregate to ₹13,000, so tax at 1 per cent is deductible once the threshold is crossed.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Taxation of Digital Transactions
citation.ref: Section 194S — threshold of 10,000 for persons other than specified persons; aggregate in the financial year

points.text: (c) Where the consideration is wholly in kind, or in exchange of another virtual digital asset with no cash part, or partly in cash with the cash part insufficient to meet the deduction, the person responsible for paying must, before releasing the consideration, ensure that the tax required to be deducted has been paid in respect of the transfer. Ms. Tara must see that 1 per cent of ₹3,00,000 is paid before the swap is settled.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Taxation of Digital Transactions
citation.ref: Section 194S — consideration wholly or partly in kind; ensure tax paid before release

points.text: (d) Credit of the sum to any account in the books of the person liable to pay, by whatever name called, including a suspense account, is deemed to be credit to the payee's account; tax of ₹2,000 was deductible in March 2026 on the credit to the pending settlements account, not in April on payment.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Taxation of Digital Transactions
citation.ref: Section 194S — credit to a suspense account deemed credit to the payee

written.scenario: A survey team enters a restaurant, open from noon to midnight, at 11 p.m. and works until 3 a.m.; it impounds the day books and retains them for 25 working days on the Assessing Officer's own authority; it takes ₹8 lakh of cash counter takings to the office "for safe custody"; it records the manager's statement; and, on the owner saying that his stock register is kept at his flat, a second team enters the flat at 9 p.m. the same night. At the company's head office a separate team surveying for TDS compliance under section 133A(2A) makes an inventory of the cash in the safe. The owner refuses to give any information.
written.question: Examine each action against section 133A, and state what the authority may do about the owner's refusal.

points.text: Entry to a place of business or profession is permitted only during the hours at which it is open for the conduct of business; entering the restaurant at 11 p.m., within its noon-to-midnight hours, is valid, and once validly begun the survey may continue beyond closing time, so working until 3 a.m. is permitted.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income Tax Authorities
citation.ref: Section 133A(2) — entry during business hours; survey may continue after closing

points.text: The power extends to any place, whether or not business is carried on there, in which the person states that his books of account, documents, cash, stock or valuable articles are kept, so the flat may be surveyed on the owner's statement; but for any place other than a place of business, entry is permitted only after sunrise and before sunset, so entering the flat at 9 p.m. is not.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income Tax Authorities
citation.ref: Section 133A(1) and (2) — place where books are stated to be kept; other places only after sunrise and before sunset

points.text: The authority may impound and retain books of account or documents inspected after recording reasons, but may not retain them for more than 15 days, excluding holidays, without the approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director or Director; retention for 25 working days on the Assessing Officer's own authority is not permitted.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income Tax Authorities
citation.ref: Section 133A(3) — impounding after recording reasons; 15 days without higher approval

points.text: Recording the manager's statement is permitted, as is making an inventory of cash, stock or valuables and placing marks of identification and taking extracts and copies. But no income-tax authority may remove, or cause to be removed, any cash, stock or other valuable article from the place entered; taking the ₹8 lakh away is illegal whatever the stated reason.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income Tax Authorities
citation.ref: Section 133A(3) and (4) — statements and inventory permitted; removal of cash or stock prohibited

points.text: A survey for verification of tax deducted or collected at source under section 133A(2A) allows entry after sunrise and before sunset to inspect books and obtain information, but the authority acting under it shall not impound or retain books or make an inventory of cash, stock or valuables; the head-office inventory is beyond that power. Where a person refuses or evades affording the facility to inspect, verify, furnish information or have a statement recorded, the authority may use all the powers vested in it under section 131(1) to enforce compliance.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Income Tax Authorities
citation.ref: Section 133A(2A) — no impounding or inventory in a TDS survey; section 133A(6) — powers under 131(1) on refusal

written.scenario: During the scrutiny of Ratnadeep Gems Ltd, a diamond trader with several thousand consignment and job-work transactions a year, the Assessing Officer directs a special audit under section 142(2A) without hearing the company and without any approval, nominates the company's own statutory auditor to do it, fixes 60 days for the report and then extends the time twice to 200 days in all, tells the company to pay the auditor, and uses the report in the assessment without showing it to the company. The company argues that its accounts were already audited, so no special audit lies.
written.question: Examine each of the officer's steps and the company's argument against section 142, and state what follows if a company fails to comply with a valid direction.

points.text: The Assessing Officer may direct a special audit, or an inventory valuation by a cost accountant, at any stage of the proceedings if, having regard to the nature and complexity of the accounts, their volume, doubts about their correctness, the multiplicity of transactions or the specialised nature of the business, and the interests of the revenue, he considers it necessary; the diamond trade with thousands of consignment transactions fits. But the direction needs the previous approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and the assessee must be given an opportunity of being heard before it is issued. Both were skipped, so the direction is bad.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment Procedure
citation.ref: Section 142(2A) — grounds for special audit; previous approval; opportunity of being heard

points.text: The accountant is nominated by the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner specifically for the purpose, from the panel each Chief Commissioner maintains, not chosen by the Assessing Officer and not the assessee's own auditor. The company's argument fails: a special audit may be directed even if the accounts have already been audited under any other law or otherwise.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment Procedure
citation.ref: Section 142(2A) — accountant nominated by the Chief Commissioner or Commissioner; audit even where already audited

points.text: The report must be furnished within the period the officer specifies, which he may extend on his own motion or on the assessee's application for good and sufficient reason, but the original period and all extensions together cannot exceed 180 days from the date the assessee receives the direction; 200 days is beyond the ceiling.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment Procedure
citation.ref: Section 142(2C) — extension; aggregate period not to exceed 180 days from receipt of the direction

points.text: The expenses of and incidental to the special audit, including the accountant's remuneration, are determined by the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner or Commissioner under the prescribed guidelines, at not less than ₹3,750 and not more than ₹7,500 for every hour of the period specified, and are paid by the Central Government, not the company.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment Procedure
citation.ref: Section 142(2D) and Rule 14B — expenses determined by the Commissioner and paid by the Central Government; 3,750 to 7,500 an hour

points.text: The assessee must be given an opportunity of being heard on any material gathered in the audit that is proposed to be used in the assessment, except where the assessment is a best judgement under section 144. If a company fails to comply with a valid direction, the officer may make a best judgement assessment under section 144, besides penalty and other steps under the law.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Assessment Procedure
citation.ref: Section 142(3) — opportunity on audit material; failure to comply leads to section 144

written.scenario: The Commissioner (Appeals) communicated an order to Vardhan Ceramics Ltd on 12 June 2026, partly allowing its appeal; the assessed income is ₹3.2 crore and the demand still standing is ₹90 lakh. The company wants to take the disallowed grounds to the Tribunal, asks whether it can wait until 30 September, what fee it pays, and whether it can stop recovery meanwhile without paying anything. The Principal Commissioner, unhappy with the part allowed, wants to know what he can do and by when. In August the company learns that the department has already filed an appeal on the part it lost.
written.question: Advise on the time limits, fees, the cross-objection and the stay of demand.

points.text: An assessee aggrieved by an order of the Commissioner (Appeals) under section 250 may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal under section 253(1). The appeal must be filed within two months from the end of the month in which the order is communicated, so by 31 August 2026; 30 September is late. The Tribunal may admit an appeal after the time limit if satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay, but that is a discretion, not a right.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Appeals and Revision
citation.ref: Section 253(1) and (3) — appealable orders; two months from the end of the month of communication; condonation

points.text: The fee depends on the total income as computed by the Assessing Officer: ₹500 where it is ₹1,00,000 or less, ₹1,500 where it exceeds ₹1,00,000 but not ₹2,00,000, and 1 per cent of the assessed income subject to a maximum of ₹10,000 above ₹2,00,000. On ₹3.2 crore the fee is the maximum, ₹10,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Appeals and Revision
citation.ref: Section 253(6) — fees for appeal to the Tribunal

points.text: The Principal Commissioner may, if he objects to the order of the Commissioner (Appeals), direct the Assessing Officer to appeal to the Tribunal under section 253(2), within the same two months from the end of the month of communication; no fee is payable on a departmental appeal.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Appeals and Revision
citation.ref: Section 253(2) — Commissioner's direction to the Assessing Officer to appeal; no fee

points.text: On receiving notice of the department's appeal, Vardhan may file a memorandum of cross-objections within 30 days of receipt of the notice against any part of the order, and the Tribunal disposes of it as if it were an appeal filed in time; this route remains open even after the company's own two months have run, and the Tribunal may permit a late cross-objection for sufficient cause.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Appeals and Revision
citation.ref: Section 253(4) — memorandum of cross-objections within 30 days of notice

points.text: Under section 254(2A) the Tribunal may stay the demand for up to 180 days from the date of the stay, only if the assessee deposits not less than 20 per cent of the tax, interest, fee, penalty or other sum payable, or furnishes security of equal amount; a stay with nothing paid is not available. Extension needs an application, compliance with the 20 per cent condition and a finding that the delay is not attributable to the assessee, and the total stay cannot exceed 365 days, after which it stands vacated even if the delay was not the assessee's. On ₹90 lakh the deposit or security is ₹18 lakh.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Appeals and Revision
citation.ref: Section 254(2A) — stay up to 180 days on 20 per cent deposit or security; extension; 365-day ceiling

written.scenario: Four taxpayers ask whether they may apply to the Dispute Resolution Committee. (a) Mr. Anand, returned income ₹38 lakh, faces an assessment order adding ₹8 lakh. (b) Mrs. Bhavna, returned income ₹62 lakh, faces an addition of ₹6 lakh. (c) Chirag Traders, returned income ₹30 lakh, faces an addition of ₹9 lakh in an assessment that followed a survey of its shop under section 133A. (d) Dhruv Ltd, returned income ₹45 lakh, faces an order under section 201 treating it as an assessee in default for ₹7 lakh of payments on which it deducted no tax; its director was convicted last year under the Prevention of Corruption Act. Each received the order on 10 July 2026.
written.question: Advise each on eligibility, and state the fee, the time limit and what happens if the Committee rejects an application.

points.text: A person may opt for dispute resolution in respect of a dispute arising from a variation in a specified order in his case if he fulfils the specified conditions. A specified order includes a draft order under section 144C(1), an intimation under sections 143(1), 200A(1) or 206CB(1) where the adjustments are objected to, an order of assessment or reassessment other than one following Dispute Resolution Panel directions, a rectification order under section 154 enhancing the assessment or reducing the loss, and an order under section 201 or 206C(6A) deeming a person an assessee in default; and the aggregate variation must not exceed ₹10 lakh, the return must have been furnished with total income not exceeding ₹50 lakh, and the order must not be based on a search or requisition, a survey under section 133A, or information received under a section 90 or 90A agreement.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Dispute Resolution
citation.ref: Section 245MA and Rule 44DAD — specified order; 10 lakh variation; 50 lakh returned income; search, survey and treaty exclusions

points.text: (a) Mr. Anand is eligible: an assessment order, variation ₹8 lakh within ₹10 lakh, returned income ₹38 lakh within ₹50 lakh. (b) Mrs. Bhavna is not: her returned income of ₹62 lakh exceeds ₹50 lakh though the variation is small. (c) Chirag Traders is not: the order is based on a survey under section 133A, whatever the amounts.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Dispute Resolution
citation.ref: Application of the specified order tests

points.text: (d) An order under section 201 is a specified order and the variation of ₹7 lakh, the amount on which tax was not deducted, is within limits, but the specified conditions also exclude a person in respect of whom prosecution under the Prevention of Corruption Act, among other listed Acts, has been instituted and who has been convicted; if the conviction is of the company itself it is barred, and if only of the director in his personal capacity the company is not thereby excluded. The other exclusions are detention under the COFEPOSA Act not revoked or set aside, prosecution initiated by an income-tax authority, notification under the Special Court Act, and pending Black Money Act proceedings for the year.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Dispute Resolution
citation.ref: Section 245MA Explanation (a) and Rule 44DAD — specified conditions; convictions under listed Acts; Black Money Act

points.text: The application is made in the prescribed form with a fee of ₹1,000, within one month from receipt of the specified order, so by 10 August 2026, or within such time from the Committee's constitution as the Board specifies where an appeal is already pending before the Commissioner (Appeals). If the Committee proposes rejection it issues a show-cause notice, hears the applicant by video if requested, and communicates its decision by e-mail; on rejection the assessee may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals), with the time the Committee took on admission excluded from the appeal period, and on admission proof of withdrawal of any pending appeal must be filed within 30 days.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Dispute Resolution
citation.ref: Rule 44DAB — fee of 1,000; one month from receipt; screening, rejection and exclusion of time for appeal

written.scenario: During reassessment proceedings against Meru Exports Ltd for income that escaped assessment, the Assessing Officer, fearing the company will sell its warehouse, provisionally attaches it on 1 March 2026 by an order in writing without any approval, writing "valid until the assessment is completed". In May 2026 the company offers a guarantee from a scheduled bank for the warehouse's fair market value and asks how soon the attachment must be lifted; the officer refers the valuation to the Valuation Officer. In January 2027 the company lets the guarantee lapse without renewing it.
written.question: Examine the attachment order, state the validity and extension rules, and explain the bank guarantee route with its clocks.

points.text: Under section 281B the Assessing Officer may, by order in writing, provisionally attach any property of the assessee during the pendency of assessment or reassessment of escaped income, or of penalty proceedings under section 271AAD where the penalty likely exceeds ₹2 crore, if he is of opinion that it is necessary to protect the interests of the revenue, in the manner of the Second Schedule. It requires the prior approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner, Chief Commissioner, Principal Commissioner, Commissioner, Principal Director General, Director General, Principal Director or Director; an order without approval is bad.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Miscellaneous Provisions
citation.ref: Section 281B(1) — provisional attachment during pendency; prior approval; 271AAD above 2 crore

points.text: The attachment is valid for six months from the date of the order, not until the assessment ends. The approving authority may extend it for reasons recorded in writing, but the total period of extension cannot exceed two years, or sixty days after the date of the assessment or reassessment order, whichever is later.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Miscellaneous Provisions
citation.ref: Section 281B(2) — six months; extension not beyond two years or sixty days after assessment, whichever later

points.text: Where the assessee furnishes a guarantee from a scheduled bank for an amount not less than the fair market value of the attached property, or sufficient to protect the revenue, the officer shall by order in writing revoke the attachment. To fix the fair market value he may refer the property to the Valuation Officer, who reports within 30 days of the reference. The revocation order must be made within 45 days of receipt of the guarantee where a reference is made, and within 15 days in any other case.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Miscellaneous Provisions
citation.ref: Section 281B(3) to (5) — bank guarantee in lieu; Valuation Officer's 30 days; revocation within 45 or 15 days

points.text: The guarantee is not a formality. If a notice of demand is served and the sum is not paid within the time specified, the officer may invoke the guarantee wholly or partly to recover it; and if the assessee fails to renew the guarantee, or to furnish a new one from a scheduled bank for an equal amount, fifteen days before its expiry, the officer shall invoke it in the interests of the revenue. Letting it lapse in January 2027 triggers invocation.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Miscellaneous Provisions
citation.ref: Section 281B(6) and (7) — invocation on non-payment of demand or failure to renew fifteen days before expiry

written.scenario: Three persons did not file returns by the due date for A.Y. 2025-26. (a) Ms. Esha, a consultant, filed on 20 March 2026; the tax on her assessed income after TDS came to ₹6,000. (b) Mr. Farhan filed nothing; on regular assessment the tax payable after advance tax, self-assessment tax and TDS is ₹9,000. (c) Gagan Ltd filed nothing; the tax evaded is ₹40 lakh. After the assessments, Gagan Ltd asks whether it can buy peace by paying up.
written.question: State whether each is exposed to prosecution under section 276CC and the punishment, and explain the immunity route under section 270AA.

points.text: Section 276CC punishes wilful failure to furnish in due time a return required under section 139(1) or by notice under section 142(1)(i) or section 148. Where the tax sought to be evaded exceeds ₹25 lakh the punishment is rigorous imprisonment of six months to seven years with fine; in other cases three months to two years with fine.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
citation.ref: Section 276CC — wilful failure to furnish return; punishment bands at 25 lakh

points.text: No prosecution lies where the return is furnished before the expiry of the assessment year, or an updated return is furnished within the time under section 139(8A). Ms. Esha filed on 20 March 2026, within A.Y. 2025-26, so she is not liable under section 276CC whatever the tax involved; late-filing fee and interest still apply.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
citation.ref: Section 276CC proviso — return before the end of the assessment year or an updated return

points.text: No prosecution also lies where the tax payable by a person other than a company, on the income determined on regular assessment, reduced by advance tax and self-assessment tax paid before the end of the assessment year and any TDS or TCS, does not exceed ₹10,000. Mr. Farhan's ₹9,000 is within that, so he is not prosecuted. The exception is for persons other than companies, so it would not have saved Gagan Ltd even at a small figure.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
citation.ref: Section 276CC proviso — non-company with tax after credits not exceeding 10,000

points.text: Gagan Ltd is exposed: it filed nothing and the tax evaded is ₹40 lakh, above ₹25 lakh, so the band is six months to seven years with fine. Its way out is section 270AA: an assessee may apply to the Assessing Officer for immunity from penalty under section 270A and from prosecution under sections 276C and 276CC if it pays the tax and interest per the assessment order within the time in the notice of demand and does not appeal against the order, applying within one month from the end of the month in which the order is received.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
citation.ref: Section 270AA(1) and (2) — immunity on payment within the demand and no appeal; one month

points.text: The officer must grant immunity once the conditions are met and the appeal period has expired, unless the penalty proceedings were initiated for misreporting: misrepresentation or suppression of facts, unrecorded investments, unsubstantiated expenditure, false entries, unrecorded receipts bearing on income, or unreported international or specified domestic transactions. He decides within three months from the end of the month the application is received, cannot reject without hearing the assessee, and his order is final.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Provisions to Counteract Unethical Tax Practices
citation.ref: Section 270AA(3) to (5) — no immunity where penalty is for misreporting; three months; hearing; finality

written.scenario: Hemant, a chartered accountant, signed the tax audit report of Ketki Foods Ltd, whose accounts are audited under the Companies Act, on 25 September 2026, reporting ₹42 lakh of GST and bonus unpaid and disallowable under section 43B. On 20 October 2026, before filing its return, the company paid ₹30 lakh of it and asks Hemant to "just re-issue the report with the new figure". In the same season a sole-trader client with turnover of ₹4 crore, whose accountant fell seriously ill in August, furnished no report at all; the Assessing Officer proposes the full penalty. A third client discovers that a certificate Hemant issued carried an incorrect figure.
written.question: Advise on the form of report, whether and how the report may be revised, the penalty on the sole trader and its defence, and Hemant's own exposure.

points.text: A person required to be audited furnishes by the specified date, 30 September of the assessment year, one month before the return due date, a report in the forms prescribed under Rule 6G: Form 3CA where the accounts are audited under any other law, as Ketki Foods' are under the Companies Act, or Form 3CB otherwise, in each case with the particulars in Form 3CD. Where the other-law audit is done before the specified date, it suffices to furnish that audit with the prescribed report by the same date.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Tax Audit and Ethical Compliances
citation.ref: Section 44AB and Rule 6G — specified date; Forms 3CA, 3CB and 3CD; audit under another law

points.text: The report may be revised, by obtaining a revised report duly signed and verified by a chartered accountant, where there is a payment after the report is furnished which necessitates recalculation of a disallowance under section 40 or section 43B, and the revised report must be furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year. The ₹30 lakh paid before the return due date is such a payment, so revision is proper; it is not a mere re-issue.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Tax Audit and Ethical Compliances
citation.ref: Revision of the tax audit report — payment necessitating recalculation under sections 40 or 43B; before the end of the assessment year

keywords: end of the relevant assessment year

points.text: There is no limit on the number of revisions, but revision is only to meet technical requirements or amendments in law, and all revisions needed should be made at one time. The revised report must carry the reference of the earlier report, state that it is a revised report and the reason for revision, be signed on the current date with a new UDIN, and follow the Guidance Note, SA 560 and the CBDT's rules on revision.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Tax Audit and Ethical Compliances
citation.ref: Revision — reference to the earlier report, reason, current date, new UDIN, SA 560

points.text: Failure to get the accounts audited or to furnish the report by the specified date attracts a penalty under section 271B of the lower of one-half per cent of total sales, turnover or gross receipts and ₹1,50,000: on ₹4 crore, half a per cent is ₹2,00,000, so the penalty is ₹1,50,000. But no penalty is leviable under section 271B if the person proves reasonable cause for the failure under section 273B; the accountant's serious illness from August is a defence to be established on the facts.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Tax Audit and Ethical Compliances
citation.ref: Section 271B — half a per cent or 1,50,000, whichever lower; section 273B reasonable cause

points.text: For furnishing incorrect information in a report or certificate, section 271J makes the accountant, merchant banker or registered valuer liable to a penalty of ₹10,000 for each such report or certificate, leviable by the Assessing Officer, the Joint Commissioner (Appeals) or the Commissioner (Appeals) who finds it in the course of proceedings; Hemant faces ₹10,000 on the incorrect certificate, subject to reasonable cause.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Tax Audit and Ethical Compliances
citation.ref: Section 271J — 10,000 per incorrect report or certificate

written.scenario: Helvet AG, a Swiss company, receives ₹4 crore of royalty from an Indian licensee in 2025-26 and claims the treaty rate. It furnishes a letter from its own auditors confirming Swiss residence, and says a government certificate "takes months". The licensee's tax head also asks whether, since the treaty is silent on how the royalty is computed, the Act or the treaty governs the computation, and whether the treaty can be applied to some items and the Act to others.
written.question: Advise on the certificate and the particulars required for treaty relief, and answer the tax head's two questions.

points.text: Sections 90(4) and 90A(4) allow a non-resident to claim relief under an agreement only if it furnishes a tax residency certificate obtained from the Government of the other country or specified territory, declaring its residence there. The provision was enacted because third-country residents were claiming unintended treaty benefits. An auditor's letter is not a certificate from the Government and does not qualify.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Double Taxation Relief
citation.ref: Sections 90(4) and 90A(4) — tax residency certificate from the Government of the other country

points.text: A certificate issued by the foreign Government is proof of residence without any further condition as to its contents, but sections 90(5) and 90A(5) require the assessee to provide the prescribed documents and information as well: its status, its nationality or country of incorporation, its tax identification number in the country of residence or a unique identifying number, the period for which the residential status in the certificate applies, and its address there during that period. Any of these already in the certificate need not be repeated, and the assessee must keep documents substantiating them for production on demand.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Double Taxation Relief
citation.ref: Sections 90(5) and 90A(5) with Notification 57/2013 — prescribed particulars beyond the certificate

points.text: Under section 90(2) the provisions of the Act apply to the extent they are more beneficial to the taxpayer, and Circular 333 of 1982 says a specific provision of the agreement prevails over the general provisions of the Act, but where the agreement has no specific provision the Act applies. A treaty generally only distributes taxing rights between the residence and source states; the computation mechanism is usually not in it and is governed by the domestic law of each country, so the royalty is computed under the Act at the rate the treaty caps.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Double Taxation Relief
citation.ref: Section 90(2) and Circular 333 — treaty prevails where specific; computation under domestic law

points.text: The taxpayer may claim relief by applying the beneficial provisions of either the treaty or the domestic law; the choice is made item by item under section 90(2), which is why the answer on computation and on rate can come from different sources.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Double Taxation Relief
citation.ref: Section 90(2) — beneficial provisions of the treaty or the domestic law

written.scenario: Norvale Ltd, a non-resident, proposes a ₹250 crore transaction with an Indian company and applies to the Board for Advance Rulings with a fee of ₹10,000, a single copy of the application, and a question that is already pending in a section 143(3) proceeding of its Indian counterparty on the same facts. The Board rejects the application without hearing Norvale. Norvale asks whether it can withdraw and re-apply, how long a ruling takes, what happens if a ruling is later found to rest on facts it misstated, and where it can appeal.
written.question: Advise on each point under sections 245Q, 245R, 245T and 245W.

points.text: An application under section 245Q is made in the prescribed form stating the question, in quadruplicate, with a fee of ₹10,000 or the prescribed fee, whichever is higher. Under Rule 44E the fee for a non-resident or similar applicant is ₹2 lakh where the transactions do not exceed ₹100 crore, ₹5 lakh where they exceed ₹100 crore but not ₹300 crore, and ₹10 lakh above ₹300 crore; on ₹250 crore Norvale owes ₹5 lakh, and proof of payment accompanies the application. It may withdraw within 30 days of the application.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Advance Rulings
citation.ref: Section 245Q and Rule 44E — quadruplicate; fee tiers of 2, 5 and 10 lakh; withdrawal within 30 days

points.text: The Board shall not allow an application where the question is already pending before any income-tax authority, Tribunal or court, involves determination of the fair market value of any property, or relates to a transaction designed prima facie for avoidance of income-tax, with limited exceptions for notified residents and for a ruling on whether a proposed arrangement is an impermissible avoidance arrangement. The pending question is a bar. But no application may be rejected without an opportunity of being heard, the reasons must be given in the order and a copy sent to the applicant and the Commissioner, so the rejection without hearing is bad.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Advance Rulings
citation.ref: Section 245R(2) — bars on pending question, fair market value and avoidance; hearing before rejection

points.text: Where the application is allowed, the Board pronounces its ruling after examining further material, hears the applicant if requested, and must pronounce within six months of receiving the application; a signed certified copy goes to the applicant and the Commissioner.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Advance Rulings
citation.ref: Section 245R — pronouncement within six months

points.text: Under section 245T, where the Board finds, on a representation by the Commissioner or otherwise, that a ruling was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts, it may by order declare the ruling void ab initio, and the Act then applies to the applicant as if the ruling had never been made, excluding the period between the ruling and the order.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Advance Rulings
citation.ref: Section 245T — ruling void ab initio for fraud or misrepresentation

points.text: Under section 245W the applicant aggrieved by a ruling or order of the Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from communication, in the prescribed form; the High Court may allow a further thirty days where the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause. The Assessing Officer's appeal runs under a scheme the Central Government notifies.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Advance Rulings
citation.ref: Section 245W — appeal to the High Court within sixty days, extendable by thirty

written.scenario: Orion Components Pvt Ltd is the Indian subsidiary of a group whose parent in Country X had consolidated revenue of ₹7,100 crore in the accounting year ended 31 December 2024. Orion's own international transactions in the year ended 31 December 2025 were ₹62 crore, of which ₹8 crore was for use of the parent's brand. Country X requires country-by-country reports and exchanges them with India. A sister company, Orion Services Pvt Ltd, is also resident in India. The group's parent filed its report in Country X on time. Orion's CFO believes that, as a mere subsidiary, it has nothing to file in India.
written.question: State Orion's obligations under section 286 and the master file rules, with forms and dates, and the penalties for default.

points.text: Country-by-country reporting applies to an international group whose total consolidated revenue in the preceding accounting year exceeds ₹6,400 crore, converted at the telegraphic transfer buying rate on the last day of that year; ₹7,100 crore is above it. The parent entity or alternate reporting entity resident in India files Form 3CEAD within twelve months of the end of the reporting accounting year; here the parent is abroad.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Fundamentals of BEPS, Action 13 and section 286
citation.ref: Section 286(7) and Rule 10DB — 6,400 crore threshold; Form 3CEAD within twelve months

points.text: A constituent entity resident in India whose parent is not resident in India must notify the designated Joint Director, at least two months before the due date for the report, whether it is the alternate reporting entity or, if not, the details of the parent or alternate reporting entity and their country of residence, in Form 3CEAC. Orion must file that by 31 October 2026 for the year ended 31 December 2025.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Fundamentals of BEPS, Action 13 and section 286
citation.ref: Section 286(1) — Form 3CEAC at least two months before the due date for the report

points.text: Orion need not file the report itself: a resident constituent entity files it only where the parent's country does not require such a report, has no exchange arrangement with India, or has a systemic failure intimated to the entity; none applies to Country X. Where more than one Indian constituent entity would otherwise be liable, the group may nominate one of them by Form 3CEAE.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Fundamentals of BEPS, Action 13 and section 286
citation.ref: Section 286(4) and (5) — when a resident constituent entity files; nomination in Form 3CEAE

points.text: Master file: a constituent entity must keep and furnish the information under Rule 10DA where the group's consolidated revenue exceeds ₹500 crore and its international transactions in the year exceed ₹50 crore, or those relating to intangible property exceed ₹10 crore. Orion meets the revenue test and the ₹62 crore transactions test, so it furnishes Form 3CEAA in full by the due date for its return under section 139(1); Part A of Form 3CEAA is furnished by every constituent entity whether or not the tests are met. Where several Indian entities are liable, one may be designated to file for all by Form 3CEAB at least 30 days before the due date.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Fundamentals of BEPS, Action 13 and section 286
citation.ref: Rule 10DA — 500 crore and 50 or 10 crore tests; Form 3CEAA by the return due date; Part A for all; Form 3CEAB 30 days before

points.text: Section 271GB penalises a reporting entity that fails to furnish the report: ₹5,000 a day for a delay of up to a month, ₹15,000 a day for the period beyond a month, and ₹50,000 a day for default continuing after service of the penalty order. Failure to produce information called for under section 286(6) within the time allowed costs ₹5,000 a day, rising to ₹50,000 a day after the penalty order; and inaccurate information in the report, known and not disclosed, or discovered and not corrected within fifteen days, or furnished in response to a notice, attracts ₹5,00,000.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Fundamentals of BEPS, Action 13 and section 286
citation.ref: Section 271GB — 5,000, 15,000 and 50,000 a day; 5,00,000 for inaccurate information

written.scenario: Three foreign enterprises ask whether they have a permanent establishment in India under a treaty modelled on Article 5.
