(a) Gulf Remit LLC runs a liaison office in Mumbai which downloads beneficiary details from its servers abroad, prints drafts and couriers them; the Reserve Bank has not permitted it to do business. (b) Kore Shipbuilders has a two-person project office in Delhi set up solely to liaise between it and the Indian customer; no contract work is done or paid for there. (c) Vento GmbH has an Indian liaison office whose staff identify customers, negotiate prices and secure orders that the head office then signs. (d) Aster Inc has no office but an Indian agent who habitually concludes contracts in its name.
written.question: Explain the concept of permanent establishment and its relation to business connection, and advise each enterprise.

points.text: A permanent establishment under Article 5(1) is a fixed place of business through which the business of an enterprise is wholly or partly carried on, and section 92F(iiia) defines it the same way; Article 5(2) lists places included, a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory, a workshop, a warehouse, a sales outlet, and a mine, oil or gas well, quarry or other place of extraction. Under the Act a non-resident is taxed on business income through a business connection under section 9; under a treaty, business income is taxed in India only if there is a permanent establishment, and only so much of the profits as is attributable to it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties, Article 5
citation.ref: Article 5(1) and (2) — fixed place of business; inclusions; business connection against permanent establishment; attribution

points.text: (a) No permanent establishment. In Union of India v. UAE Exchange Centre the Supreme Court held that a liaison office engaged in remittance services, downloading beneficiary details, printing drafts and dispatching them, with no Reserve Bank permission to carry on primary business activity, would not constitute a permanent establishment; even if its activities were business activities they were of a preparatory or auxiliary character.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties, Article 5
citation.ref: Union of India v. UAE Exchange Centre (2020) — liaison office; preparatory or auxiliary

points.text: (b) No permanent establishment. In DIT v. Samsung Heavy Industries Ltd the Supreme Court held that a project office set up solely as an auxiliary office to liaise between the customer and the enterprise, incurring no expenditure on execution of the contract and staffed by two persons not qualified for any core activity, is not a fixed place of business through which the core business is carried on.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties, Article 5
citation.ref: DIT v. Samsung Heavy Industries Ltd (2020) — project office as auxiliary office

points.text: (c) Permanent establishment. A liaison office that identifies new customers, markets, negotiates prices, discusses commercial issues and secures and processes orders has gone beyond auxiliary work and forms a permanent establishment. (d) Permanent establishment too: a non-resident carrying on business through an agent, other than an independent agent, who habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts, regularly delivers goods or habitually secures orders on its behalf has a permanent establishment in India, and the profits attributable to the agent's activities are taxable here.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Application and Interpretation of Tax Treaties, Article 5
citation.ref: Liaison office securing orders forms a PE; dependent agent habitually concluding contracts

written.scenario: Indian payers make three payments to a company resident in Country D, whose treaty with India follows the UN Model including Articles 12A and 12B. (a) ₹3 crore to a bank for bespoke research and advice on restructuring a client's debt, and separately ₹40 lakh for card payment processing. (b) ₹5 crore for subscriptions to a music streaming platform that serves millions of users with the same software. (c) ₹2 crore for the right to use a patented process, which the payer's adviser says "is digital so falls under 12B". The Country D company argues that under the OECD Model none of this is taxable in India without a permanent establishment.
written.question: Explain Articles 12A and 12B, apply them to each payment, and comment on the OECD Model argument.

points.text: Article 12A of the UN Model, which has no counterpart in the OECD Model, allows fees for technical services to be taxed in the residence state without making that exclusive, and gives the state in which the fees arise the right to tax under its domestic law, capped at a maximum rate on the gross amount fixed by bilateral negotiation where the beneficial owner is a resident of the other state. India pioneered the concept, in the Act since 1976.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Overview of Model Tax Conventions, Article 12A
citation.ref: Article 12A — source state may tax fees for technical services at a negotiated ceiling; absent from the OECD Model

points.text: Fees for technical services are payments for managerial, technical or consultancy services, excluding payments to an employee, for teaching in or by an educational institution, and by an individual for personal use. Technical means the application of specialised knowledge, skill or expertise; consultancy means advice or services of a specialised nature. (a) The bank's research and advice for a specific client's circumstances is a technical service and taxable at source; the card processing is a non-specialised payment and transmission service involving no specialised knowledge on behalf of a particular client, and is not.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Overview of Model Tax Conventions, Article 12A
citation.ref: Definition of fees for technical services; financial institution example distinguishing advice from payment services

points.text: Article 12B, added to the UN Model in 2021 with no OECD counterpart, preserves the source state's right to tax income from automated digital services, again at a negotiated ceiling on the gross amount. An automated digital service is one provided on the internet or another electronic network requiring minimal human involvement from the provider, the indicator being the ability to scale to new users at the same basic processes; paragraph 6 lists online advertising, supply of user data, search engines, intermediation platforms, social media, digital content, online gaming, cloud computing and standardised online teaching. (b) The streaming subscriptions are digital content services delivered with minimal human involvement and fall within Article 12B.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Overview of Model Tax Conventions, Article 12B
citation.ref: Article 12B — automated digital services; minimal human involvement; the paragraph 6 list

points.text: (c) Wrong. Paragraph 7 provides that Article 12B does not apply where the payments qualify as royalty or fees for technical services under Article 12 or 12A; a payment for the use of a patented process is a royalty under Article 12 and is taxed there, not under 12B. The OECD Model argument fails because the treaty follows the UN Model, whose Articles 12A and 12B give India taxing rights on these payments without any permanent establishment.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Overview of Model Tax Conventions, Article 12B
citation.ref: Article 12B(7) — exclusion where Article 12 or 12A applies; UN against OECD Model

written.scenario: A company in a developing country whose per-capita income is well below the World Bank line pays ₹60 crore of interest and ₹25 crore of royalties to its parent in a jurisdiction that taxes such receipts at a nominal corporate rate of 6 per cent. The group has consolidated revenue above EUR 750 million. The parent's adviser says the group is already inside the global minimum tax, so the developing country "has nothing more to claim" and, in any case, the minimum-tax rules come first.
written.question: Explain the two components of Pillar Two, the subject-to-tax rule's conditions, and correct the adviser on both points.

points.text: Pillar Two consists of the Global Anti-Base Erosion rules, a coordinated system implemented in domestic law that imposes a 15 per cent global minimum tax on groups with consolidated revenue of at least EUR 750 million, measured jurisdiction by jurisdiction on the effective tax rate, with a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax available locally; and a treaty-based subject-to-tax rule. Adoption of the GloBE rules is a common approach, not mandatory, but those who adopt them must do so consistently.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Latest Developments in International Taxation, Pillar Two
citation.ref: GloBE rules — 15 per cent minimum tax; EUR 750 million; jurisdictional blending; common approach

points.text: The subject-to-tax rule allows a source jurisdiction to impose limited additional tax on certain cross-border payments between connected companies where the recipient is subject to a nominal corporate income tax rate below 9 per cent, recovering taxing rights ceded under a treaty. It applies to covered payments by an entity in a developing country, one with gross national income per capita of USD 12,535 or less on the World Bank Atlas method, to a group entity in another country; connected persons are those with more than 50 per cent direct or indirect ownership or de facto control; and it applies only if the covered income in the source country exceeds 250,000 or 1 million a year depending on whether its GDP is below or above 40 billion. Covered payments include interest, royalties, distribution rights, insurance premiums, guarantee or financing fees, equipment rentals and services.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Latest Developments in International Taxation, Pillar Two
citation.ref: Subject-to-tax rule — 9 per cent nominal rate; developing country at USD 12,535; connected persons; thresholds; covered payments

points.text: The adviser is wrong on both counts. The interest and royalties are covered payments to a connected person taxed at 6 per cent, below 9 per cent, so the developing country may tax back under the subject-to-tax rule regardless of the group's GloBE position; and the rule works in priority to the GloBE rules under the prescribed rule order, so the source country's claim comes first, not last. The rule is implemented by signing the multilateral instrument or by bilateral treaty amendment when a developing member requests it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 4 — Latest Developments in International Taxation, Pillar Two
citation.ref: STTR takes priority over the GloBE rules; implementation through the MLI or bilateral amendment

written.scenario: Kanha Traders, registered in Madhya Pradesh, sells two products in the festive season. The first is a gift hamper containing sweets, dry fruits, a decorative brass diya and a greeting card, packed together in a single box and sold for one price of ₹2,400. The items are not sold separately at that price and the customer cannot decline any of them. The four items would individually bear GST at 5%, 5%, 5% and 18%. The second is an annual maintenance contract for a water purifier at ₹4,000, under which Kanha Traders services the purifier four times a year and replaces the filter cartridges as and when needed. The service attracts 18% and the cartridges 5%; the customer buys the contract for the servicing and the cartridges follow from it.
written.question: Classify each of the two supplies under the CGST Act, 2017 and determine the rate of tax applicable to each, giving reasons.

points.text: State the test. A composite supply comprises two or more taxable supplies which are naturally bundled and supplied in conjunction with each other in the ordinary course of business, one of which is a principal supply. Anything bundled that is not naturally bundled is a mixed supply.

citation.ref: Sections 2(30) and 2(74)

keywords: in the ordinary course of business

points.text: The gift hamper is a mixed supply. Sweets, dry fruits, a diya and a card are each capable of being supplied separately and are put together only because it is a festive season, so they are not naturally bundled; they are supplied for a single price.

citation.ref: Section 2(74)

points.text: A mixed supply is treated as a supply of that particular supply which attracts the highest rate of tax, so the whole hamper of ₹2,400 bears GST at 18 per cent, the rate of the item taxed highest.

citation.ref: Section 8(b)

points.text: The maintenance contract is a composite supply. The servicing and the cartridges are naturally bundled, the customer contracts for the servicing, and the cartridges are ancillary to it, so the servicing is the principal supply and the whole ₹4,000 bears GST at 18 per cent.

citation.ref: Section 8(a) read with sections 2(30) and 2(90)

written.scenario: Vasudha Ltd. is registered in Maharashtra and has a second registration in Karnataka for its branch there. During the year the following happen. It transfers finished goods worth ₹8,00,000 from the Maharashtra unit to the Karnataka branch for onward sale, charging nothing. It scraps a machine on which input tax credit had been taken and gives it away free to a scrap dealer. It gives each of its 40 employees a watch costing ₹35,000 and, to one employee, a second gift later in the same financial year costing ₹22,000. It also receives management consultancy from its holding company in Singapore free of charge, for its business in India.
written.question: State, with reasons, which of these are supplies under the CGST Act, 2017 even though no consideration passes.

points.text: The stock transfer to the Karnataka branch is a supply. Establishments of the same person in two States are distinct persons, and a supply between distinct persons in the course or furtherance of business is a supply even without consideration.

citation.ref: Paragraph 2 of Schedule I read with section 25(4)

points.text: Giving away the scrapped machine is a supply, because it is a permanent transfer or disposal of business assets on which input tax credit has been availed.

citation.ref: Paragraph 1 of Schedule I

keywords: permanent transfer or disposal of business assets
input tax credit has been availed

points.text: An employer and employee are related persons, so gifts are caught, but the proviso exempts gifts not exceeding fifty thousand rupees in value in a financial year. The ₹35,000 watch alone is below the line; the same employee's further gift of ₹22,000 takes that employee past ₹50,000 in the year, so the excess is a supply for him.

citation.ref: Paragraph 2 of Schedule I and its proviso

keywords: fifty thousand rupees in value in a financial year

points.text: The free consultancy from the Singapore holding company is a supply. Import of services by a person from a related person outside India, in the course or furtherance of business, is a supply even without consideration.

citation.ref: Paragraph 4 of Schedule I

written.scenario: Reckon Advisors LLP, registered in Delhi, asks you about four items in its accounts. Salaries of ₹1,20,00,000 paid to its own employees. Wages of ₹6,00,000 paid to casual workers engaged directly by the firm and paid daily. Court fees of ₹80,000 paid to a District Court. Sitting fees of ₹4,00,000 paid to its non-executive directors.
written.question: Explain which of these are treated neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of services, and what follows for the ones that are not so treated.

points.text: Services by an employee to the employer in the course of or in relation to his employment are treated neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of services, so the salaries of ₹1,20,00,000 are outside GST altogether.

citation.ref: Paragraph 1 of Schedule III

keywords: in the course of or in relation to his employment
neither as a supply of goods nor a supply of services

points.text: The casual workers paid daily by the firm are also employees for this purpose. Services provided by a casual worker to an employer who pays wages on a daily basis are services in the course of employment, so the ₹6,00,000 is outside GST too.

citation.ref: Paragraph 1 of Schedule III, as explained in the ICAI Study Material

points.text: Services by any court or Tribunal established under any law for the time being in force are in Schedule III, so the court fees of ₹80,000 attract no GST.

citation.ref: Paragraph 2 of Schedule III

points.text: Sitting fees to non-executive directors are not employment. A director who is not an employee supplies services to the company, and the company pays the tax on them under reverse charge, so the ₹4,00,000 is taxable in the LLP's hands as recipient.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) read with the reverse charge notification for services by a director

written.scenario: Advise on four transactions of Nirmal Enterprises, registered in Gujarat. It sells goods for ₹5,00,000 in the ordinary way. It exchanges an old delivery van for a new one with a dealer, paying ₹3,00,000 and handing over the van. Its proprietor sells his personal furniture from his home for ₹40,000, having taken no credit on it and never used it in the business. It leases a godown it owns to another trader for ₹15,000 a month.
written.question: Determine whether each transaction falls within the scope of supply under section 7 of the CGST Act, 2017.

points.text: Set out the gate. Supply includes all forms of supply of goods or services or both, such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal, made or agreed to be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(a)

keywords: in the course or furtherance of business

points.text: The ordinary sale of ₹5,00,000 is a supply on every limb: it is a sale, for a consideration, in the course of business.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(a)

points.text: The van traded in is a supply. Exchange is named in section 7(1)(a), so a part-exchange is two supplies and not one net payment; the consideration for the old van is the reduction in the price of the new one.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(a)

points.text: The proprietor's personal furniture is not a supply. It is sold for a consideration but not in the course or furtherance of business, and both limbs must be satisfied.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(a)

keywords: not in the course or furtherance of business

points.text: The godown lease is a supply of services. Lease is named in section 7(1)(a), and Schedule II puts any lease or letting out of a building for business beyond doubt by treating it as a supply of services.

citation.ref: Section 7(1)(a) read with paragraph 2 of Schedule II

written.scenario: Two registered persons ask whether they may compound, and at what cost, for the current financial year. Aakar Steels manufactures steel furniture in Maharashtra and had an aggregate turnover of ₹1,35,00,000 in the preceding financial year; in the current year its turnover in the State is ₹90,00,000, of which ₹10,00,000 is exempt supplies. Meena Provisions is a trader in Meghalaya with an aggregate turnover of ₹68,00,000 in the preceding financial year; in the current year its turnover in the State is ₹52,00,000, of which ₹12,00,000 is exempt supplies of unbranded food grains. Neither makes inter-State outward supplies or supplies through an electronic commerce operator.
written.question: Advise each on eligibility for the composition scheme for goods and compute the tax payable for the current year on the figures given.

points.text: State the turnover gate. The limit in section 10(1) is fifty lakh rupees, raised by notification to ₹1.5 crore, and it is tested on aggregate turnover of the preceding financial year computed on an all India basis for the same Permanent Account Number.

citation.ref: Section 10(1) read with Notification No. 14/2019 CT dated 07.03.2019

points.text: Aakar Steels is eligible. ₹1,35,00,000 is within the ₹1.5 crore limit that applies in Maharashtra.

citation.ref: Section 10(1), first proviso

points.text: Meena Provisions is eligible, but on a lower limit. Meghalaya is one of the eight Special Category States for which the notification sets the limit at ₹75 lakh, and ₹68,00,000 is within it.

citation.ref: Notification No. 14/2019 CT dated 07.03.2019

points.text: Compute Aakar Steels. A manufacturer pays one per cent, half central tax and half State tax, of the turnover in State, and that base is the entire turnover including exempt supplies. One per cent of ₹90,00,000 is ₹90,000.

citation.ref: Rule 7 read with section 10(1)(a)

points.text: Compute Meena Provisions. A trader also pays one per cent, but of the turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in State, so the ₹12,00,000 of exempt supplies is left out. One per cent of ₹40,00,000 is ₹40,000.

citation.ref: Rule 7 read with section 10(1)(c)

keywords: turnover of taxable supplies of goods and services in State

points.text: Add the common conditions. Neither may collect the tax from customers and neither takes any input tax credit; the amount comes out of the supplier's own pocket.

citation.ref: Section 10(4)

keywords: may collect the tax from customers

written.scenario: Two people ask about compounding where services are involved. Prakash runs a small hardware shop in Rajasthan with an aggregate turnover of ₹42,00,000 in the preceding financial year, and alongside it earns ₹4,50,000 a year fitting and repairing what he sells. Sunita runs an interior design practice in Rajasthan, supplying no goods at all, with an aggregate turnover of ₹46,00,000 in the preceding financial year.
written.question: Advise each whether a composition scheme is open to them and at what rate.

points.text: Prakash may stay in the composition scheme for goods. A person paying tax under section 10(1) may also supply services of value not exceeding ten per cent of turnover in a State in the preceding financial year or five lakh rupees, whichever is higher.

citation.ref: Section 10(1), second proviso

keywords: five lakh rupees, whichever is higher

points.text: Apply it to his figures. Ten per cent of ₹42,00,000 is ₹4,20,000 and five lakh rupees is higher, so his ceiling for services is ₹5,00,000 and his ₹4,50,000 of fitting and repair is within it.

citation.ref: Section 10(1), second proviso

points.text: Sunita cannot use the scheme for goods, because a person engaged in the supply of services is barred from it except to the limited extent of that proviso.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)(a)

keywords: engaged in the supply of services

points.text: She may instead opt for the separate scheme for suppliers of services, which is open where aggregate turnover in the preceding financial year did not exceed fifty lakh rupees. ₹46,00,000 is within it, and the rate is six per cent of turnover in State.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A) read with rule 7 of the CGST Rules, 2017

written.scenario: Bharat Handlooms, a trader registered in Tamil Nadu, has been paying tax under the composition scheme for goods. In October it receives a large order from a buyer in Kerala and despatches goods worth ₹6,00,000 to him. In February its aggregate turnover for the year crosses ₹1.5 crore. Its accountant proposes to carry on under the scheme until the end of March and switch from 1st April.
written.question: Advise on the effect of the Kerala despatch and of crossing the turnover limit, and say whether the accountant's proposal is correct.

points.text: The Kerala despatch takes it out of the scheme. A person is eligible to opt only if he is not engaged in making any inter-State outward supplies of goods, and this is one.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)(c)

points.text: Note the asymmetry, because it is the point most often missed. The bar is on outward supplies; buying goods from another State does not disqualify a composition supplier.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)(c)

points.text: The accountant is wrong about the turnover as well. The option lapses with effect from the day on which aggregate turnover during a financial year exceeds the limit, not from the beginning of the next year.

citation.ref: Section 10(3)

keywords: lapses with effect from the day

written.scenario: Sunrise Mills Ltd., a registered company in Gujarat, pays the following in a month. Freight of ₹2,00,000 to a goods transport agency which has not exercised the option to pay tax itself and has taken no input tax credit on the goods and services used in supplying the service. Fees of ₹1,50,000 to an individual advocate for advice on a contract dispute. Fees of ₹90,000 to a firm of advocates for representation before a tribunal.
written.question: State who is liable to pay GST on each payment and at what rate, giving reasons.

points.text: State the mechanism. On categories of supply notified by the Government on the recommendations of the Council, the tax is paid by the recipient on reverse charge, and all the provisions of the Act apply to him as if he were the person liable to pay tax.

citation.ref: Section 9(3)

keywords: as if he were the person liable to pay tax

points.text: On the freight, Sunrise Mills pays. Where the goods transport agency has not exercised the option to pay tax itself, the recipient pays, and the rate is 5 per cent, being 2.5 per cent central tax and 2.5 per cent State tax, because the agency has taken no input tax credit.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) read with the reverse charge notification for goods transport agency services

points.text: On the advocate's fee, Sunrise Mills pays. Legal services supplied by an individual advocate to a business entity located in the taxable territory are covered, whether the advice is given directly or indirectly.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) read with the reverse charge notification for legal services

keywords: business entity located in the taxable territory

points.text: On the firm of advocates, Sunrise Mills also pays. The entry covers an individual advocate including a senior advocate or a firm of advocates alike, so the form of the supplier makes no difference.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) read with the reverse charge notification for legal services

points.text: Add the practical consequence. Tax under reverse charge must be paid in cash and cannot be set off against input tax credit at the time of payment; credit of it is taken afterwards, subject to the ordinary conditions.

citation.ref: Section 49(4) read with section 9(3)

keywords: credit of it is taken afterwards

written.scenario: Anand Constructions, registered in Karnataka, does three things in a quarter. It builds a warehouse for a client on the client's land, supplying both materials and labour under a single contract for ₹80,00,000. It runs a canteen on its own site, serving food to workmen for ₹6,00,000 and serving no alcohol. It transfers a used concrete mixer, on which it had taken input tax credit, to its proprietor for his personal use free of charge.
written.question: Classify each as a supply of goods or a supply of services under Schedule II to the CGST Act, 2017 and say why the classification matters.

points.text: The warehouse contract is a works contract, and Schedule II treats a works contract as a supply of services, so the whole ₹80,00,000 is a service even though materials dominate the cost.

citation.ref: Paragraph 6(a) of Schedule II

points.text: The canteen is a supply of services. Supply of food or any other article for human consumption, by way of or as part of any service, is treated as a supply of services, which is why a restaurant is never a supply of goods under GST.

citation.ref: Paragraph 6(b) of Schedule II

keywords: food or any other article for human consumption
treated as a supply of services

points.text: The mixer given to the proprietor is a supply of goods. Where goods forming part of the assets of a business are transferred so as no longer to form part of those assets, that transfer is a supply of goods, whether or not for a consideration.

citation.ref: Paragraph 4(a) of Schedule II

keywords: no longer to form part of those assets

points.text: Say why it matters. The classification decides the rate, the time of supply and the place of supply, and each of those runs on different rules for goods and for services.

citation.ref: Schedule II read with sections 12, 13 and the IGST Act, 2017

written.scenario: Meghdoot Builders, registered in Maharashtra, sells flats in a residential project. Flat A is booked in June and the buyer pays ₹40,00,000 in instalments while construction is running; the completion certificate is issued in the following March. Flat B is sold in April of the next year for ₹55,00,000, the entire consideration being received after the completion certificate was issued. Flat C is booked before completion, the buyer pays a deposit of ₹5,00,000, and he cancels in the month after the completion certificate is issued.
written.question: Determine the GST treatment of each flat, and explain the principle that separates them.

points.text: State the principle. Construction of a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer is a supply of services, except where the entire consideration has been received after the issue of the completion certificate or after first occupation, whichever is earlier.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II

keywords: intended for sale to a buyer

points.text: Flat A is taxable. Consideration was received while construction was running, so the exception does not apply and the ₹40,00,000 is a supply of services.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II

points.text: Flat B is not a supply at all. The entire consideration of ₹55,00,000 came after the completion certificate, so it is the sale of a completed building, which Schedule III treats as neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II read with paragraph 5 of Schedule III

keywords: neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services

points.text: Flat C was taxable when the deposit was received, because at that time part of the consideration had come before completion. Cancellation afterwards is dealt with by a credit note and not by treating the original receipt as never taxable.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II read with section 34

written.scenario: Prakash Foods, registered in Rajasthan, makes taxable packaged snacks and exempt puffed rice. For October 2026 the input tax on its inputs and input services comes to ₹3,00,000, made up as follows: ₹20,000 on goods used only at the proprietor's residence; ₹60,000 on inputs used only in making the exempt puffed rice; ₹15,000 on outdoor catering for a staff party; ₹1,25,000 on inputs used only in making the taxable snacks; and the balance on electricity, packaging film and factory rent used for both products. Turnover in Rajasthan for the month was ₹4 crore of taxable snacks and ₹1 crore of exempt puffed rice.
written.question: Compute the input tax credit Prakash Foods may take for October 2026 and the amount it must reverse under rule 42 of the CGST Rules, 2017, showing each step. State what happens to these figures at the end of the financial year.

points.text: Start from the total input tax T of ₹3,00,000 and take out what never enters the credit ledger: T1 ₹20,000 used exclusively for non-business purposes, T2 ₹60,000 used exclusively for exempt supplies, and T3 ₹15,000 on outdoor catering, which is a blocked credit under section 17(5). C1, the amount credited to the electronic credit ledger, is ₹3,00,000 less ₹95,000, that is ₹2,05,000.

citation.ref: Rule 42(1)(a) to (f) read with section 17(2) and 17(5) of the CGST Act, 2017

points.text: From C1 take out T4, the ₹1,25,000 on inputs used exclusively for taxable supplies, which is allowed in full. What is left is the common credit C2 of ₹80,000, on the electricity, packaging film and rent used for both products, and only C2 is apportioned.

citation.ref: Rule 42(1)(g) and (h)

points.text: Apportion the common credit. D1, the part attributable to exempt supplies, is E divided by F times C2: exempt turnover ₹1 crore over total turnover in the State ₹5 crore, so one-fifth of ₹80,000, which is ₹16,000. D2, the part deemed attributable to non-business use, is a flat 5 per cent of C2, that is ₹4,000. Both are computed on the month's own turnover.

citation.ref: Rule 42(1)(i) and (j)

points.text: Reverse D1 plus D2, ₹20,000, by adding it to the output tax for October. The eligible common credit C3 is ₹80,000 less ₹20,000, ₹60,000, so the month's credit is ₹1,25,000 plus ₹60,000, that is ₹1,85,000. D1 and D2 are recomputed for the whole financial year on the year's turnover before the due date of the return for September of the following year: any shortfall is reversed with interest at 18 per cent from 1 April, and any excess reversed during the year is claimed back as credit by that return.

citation.ref: Rule 42(1)(k) and (m), rule 42(2) read with section 50 of the CGST Act, 2017

written.scenario: Meera Realty, registered in Telangana, incurred four kinds of expenditure in 2026-27. First, it engaged a works contractor to build its own head-office block, which it capitalised. Second, on its own account it bought cement, steel and the services of an architect to put up a warehouse, which it lets out on rent to tenants; the rent is taxable, and the warehouse was built for no purpose other than that letting. Third, it paid a contractor to repair the roof of its existing factory and charged the whole cost to the profit and loss account. Fourth, it paid a works contractor to install a boiler, fixed to the earth by a concrete foundation, inside that factory.
written.question: Advise Meera Realty on the input tax credit available on each of the four, with reasons and with reference to the decision of the Supreme Court in Safari Retreats.

points.text: Set out the two clauses. Section 17(5)(c) blocks credit on works contract services supplied for construction of an immovable property other than plant and machinery, except where they are an input service for further supply of works contract service. Section 17(5)(d) blocks credit on goods or services received by a taxable person for construction of an immovable property other than plant or machinery on his own account, including when used in the course or furtherance of business.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(c) and (d)

points.text: The head-office block is squarely within clause (c): a works contract for an immovable property, capitalised, and an office is not plant and machinery. That credit is blocked. The boiler is the opposite case. Plant and machinery means apparatus, equipment and machinery fixed to earth by foundation or structural support and used for making outward supplies, excluding land, buildings and other civil structures, telecommunication towers and pipelines laid outside the factory. A boiler on a foundation is within that definition, so the works contract for installing it is outside the block and the credit is available.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(c) read with the Explanation to section 17

points.text: The roof repair is allowed. Construction, for both clauses, includes re-construction, renovation, additions, alterations and repairs only to the extent of capitalisation to the immovable property. A repair charged to the profit and loss account is not capitalised, so it is not construction at all and section 17(5) does not reach it.

citation.ref: Explanation to section 17(5)(c) and (d)

points.text: The warehouse turns on Safari Retreats. The Supreme Court held that plant or machinery in clause (d) is a different expression from the defined plant and machinery, chosen deliberately, and is not governed by that definition. Whether a building is a plant is a question of fact, answered by the functionality test: if the building is essential to the business of supplying the services of renting or leasing it, it can be a plant, and then it falls outside clause (d). A warehouse built only to be let out on taxable rent meets that test, so the credit on the cement, steel and architect is not blocked. The Court upheld the validity of clauses (c) and (d) and of section 16(4).

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(d) as read in Chief Commissioner of CGST v. Safari Retreats Pvt. Ltd. (2024) 23 Centax 62 (SC)

written.scenario: Arjun Tours, registered in Karnataka, runs taxi and coach services and also carries customers' luggage. During 2026-27 it bought a seven-seater car used to carry passengers for hire, a five-seater car for the managing director's own travel, a twenty-six-seater bus used to bring staff to the depot, and a truck used to carry luggage. It paid general insurance and repair bills on each of the two cars. It also paid for outdoor catering at its annual staff day, for a canteen it runs for depot workers because a labour law requires it, and for health insurance for its drivers, which no law requires it to provide.
written.question: State, with reasons, whether input tax credit is available to Arjun Tours on each of these inward supplies.

points.text: The block in section 17(5)(a) is on motor vehicles for transportation of persons with an approved seating capacity of not more than thirteen persons including the driver, and it lifts when such a vehicle is used for further supply of such vehicles, for transportation of passengers, or for imparting training on driving them. Vehicles above thirteen seats and vehicles for transporting goods were never inside the block.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a)

points.text: Apply it. The seven-seater carries passengers for hire, so its credit is available under the exception. The five-seater for the managing director is used for none of the three purposes and its credit is blocked. The twenty-six-seater bus is above thirteen seats and the truck carries goods, so neither is an ineligible vehicle and credit is available on both.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a)

points.text: Insurance, servicing, repair and maintenance follow the vehicle they relate to. Section 17(5)(ab) blocks them where they relate to a vehicle whose own credit is blocked, so the bills on the managing director's car are blocked, while the bills on the seven-seater are allowed because that vehicle is used for passenger transport.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(ab)

points.text: Food and beverages, outdoor catering and health insurance are blocked by section 17(5)(b) unless the same category is used to make an outward taxable supply of that category, or the employer is obliged by a law for the time being in force to provide it to its employees. The canteen is a statutory obligation, so its credit is allowed. The outdoor catering for the staff day and the drivers' health insurance are provided under no statutory obligation and their credit is blocked.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(b) with its proviso

written.scenario: Vidhi Ceramics, registered in Gujarat, supplies tiles to an unrelated buyer in July 2026. The list price is ₹1,00,000, on which a trade discount of 5 per cent is shown on the invoice. The invoice separately charges a municipal cess of ₹2,000 levied under a State law and ₹3,000 for special packing the buyer asked for. Under the contract Vidhi was liable to pay ₹4,000 to the transporter, but the buyer paid it directly and it is not in the price. An industry association pays Vidhi a subsidy of ₹10,000 on every such consignment, linked to the price, and the State Government pays it ₹8,000 under a promotion scheme. The buyer paid late and Vidhi collected ₹1,500 as interest in September 2026.
written.question: Determine the value of the supply under section 15 of the CGST Act, 2017, explaining the treatment of each item.

points.text: The starting point is the transaction value: the price actually paid or payable, since the parties are not related and price is the sole consideration. A discount given before or at the time of supply and duly recorded in the invoice is excluded, so the 5 per cent trade discount of ₹5,000 comes off and the price is ₹95,000.

citation.ref: Section 15(1) and 15(3)(a)

points.text: Three additions under section 15(2). The municipal cess is a tax levied under a law other than the GST laws and is charged separately, so ₹2,000 is included. The packing is an incidental expense charged by the supplier, so ₹3,000 is included. The ₹4,000 the buyer paid to the transporter is an amount the supplier was liable to pay in relation to the supply, incurred by the recipient and not in the price, so it is included too.

citation.ref: Section 15(2)(a), (b) and (c)

points.text: Subsidies directly linked to the price are included except those provided by the Central Government and State Governments. The association's ₹10,000 is included in the value of the supplier who receives it. The State Government's ₹8,000 is excluded.

citation.ref: Section 15(2)(e) with its Explanation

points.text: The value of the July supply is ₹95,000 plus ₹2,000 plus ₹3,000 plus ₹4,000 plus ₹10,000, that is ₹1,14,000. The ₹1,500 of interest for delayed payment is also part of the value under section 15(2)(d); it is brought to tax when it is received, in September, as an addition to the value of the same supply.

citation.ref: Section 15(2)(d) read with section 12(6)

written.scenario: Nirmal Distributors, registered in Punjab, sold goods to a retailer in April 2026 for ₹5,00,000 plus GST. In March 2026 the two had signed an agreement giving the retailer a turnover discount of 2 per cent at the year end, calculated on and named against the invoices of the year. In September 2026 Nirmal also allowed a goodwill discount of ₹10,000 on the April invoice, which nobody had agreed to beforehand. Nirmal wants both discounts to reduce its GST liability.
written.question: Explain which of the two discounts can reduce the value of the April supply, how Nirmal gives effect to it, and what happens if the retailer does not reverse the input tax credit.

points.text: A discount given after the supply is excluded from value only if two conditions are both met: it is established in terms of an agreement entered into at or before the time of such supply and specifically linked to the relevant invoices, and the input tax credit attributable to the discount has been reversed by the recipient on the strength of the document issued by the supplier.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)

keywords: at or before the time of such supply

points.text: The turnover discount qualifies: the agreement was signed in March, before the April supply, and it is linked to the invoices. Nirmal gives effect to it by issuing a credit note under section 34 for ₹10,000 and the tax on it, and declaring the note in the return for the month it is issued, but not later than 30 November following the end of the financial year or the date of the annual return, whichever is earlier; its output tax for that month reduces accordingly.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)(i) read with section 34(1) and 34(2)

points.text: The goodwill discount fails the first condition: there was no agreement at or before the supply. It cannot reduce the value. Nirmal may still give it, but only through a commercial credit note without any adjustment of tax, and the tax already paid on the full ₹5,00,000 stays paid.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)(i)

points.text: If the retailer does not reverse the credit attributable to the turnover discount, the second condition in section 15(3)(b)(ii) is not met and Nirmal cannot reduce its output tax liability by the credit note, even though the agreement was in place. The reduction depends on the recipient's reversal.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)(ii) read with section 34(2)

written.scenario: Sagar Pumps has its head office registered in Maharashtra and a branch registered in Karnataka under the same PAN. In June 2026 the head office sends 500 pumps to the branch and raises an invoice at ₹6,000 a pump. The head office sells the same pumps to unrelated dealers at ₹7,000. The branch sells them as such, without any change, to its own unrelated customers at ₹8,000. The branch is entitled to full input tax credit. In the same month the head office gives a corporate guarantee to a bank for a loan of ₹5 crore taken by its subsidiary company, and charges the subsidiary nothing for it.
written.question: Determine the value of the supply of the pumps to the branch and of the corporate guarantee under the CGST Rules, 2017, stating the options open to Sagar Pumps.

points.text: The head office and the branch hold separate registrations under one PAN, so they are distinct persons under section 25(4), and a supply between distinct persons in the course of business is a supply even without consideration under paragraph 2 of Schedule I. Section 15(1) cannot apply between them, and the value is found under rule 28.

citation.ref: Section 25(4), Schedule I paragraph 2 and section 15(4) read with rule 28 of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: Rule 28(1) runs in sequence: the open market value, here ₹7,000, the price at which the head office sells to unrelated dealers; failing that, the value of goods of like kind and quality; failing that, rule 30 or rule 31. The first proviso gives an option where the goods are intended for further supply as such by the recipient: ninety per cent of the price the branch charges its unrelated customers, ₹7,200. The option is the supplier's and is not compulsory.

citation.ref: Rule 28(1)(a) to (c) and its first proviso

points.text: The second proviso decides this case. Where the recipient is eligible for full input tax credit, the value declared in the invoice is deemed to be the open market value. The branch takes full credit, so the invoice value of ₹6,000 a pump is accepted as the value and neither the ₹7,000 nor the ₹7,200 has to be used. The tax is a wash between the two registrations, which is why the law lets the declared value stand.

citation.ref: Second proviso to rule 28(1)

points.text: The guarantee is a supply of service between related persons and is valued under rule 28(2): one per cent per annum of the amount guaranteed, or the actual consideration, whichever is higher. With no consideration charged, the value is one per cent of ₹5 crore, that is ₹5,00,000 per annum, and tax is payable on it by the head office.

citation.ref: Rule 28(2)

written.scenario: Zenith Events, registered in Delhi, organised three events in 2026: a dealer conference in Goa for Rathi Motors, registered in Rajasthan; a wedding in Jaipur for an individual living in Mumbai who is not registered; and a product launch in Dubai for a company registered in Gujarat. Swift Couriers, also registered in Delhi, carried three consignments: goods from Delhi to Chennai for a company registered in Haryana; a parcel from Delhi to Pune for a student who is not registered; and goods from Chennai to a buyer in London for a company registered in Tamil Nadu.
written.question: Determine the place of supply of each of the six services under the IGST Act, 2017, with reasons.

points.text: Organisation of an event, and services ancillary to it or the assignment of sponsorship, is a specific case under section 12(7). Supplied to a registered person, the place of supply is the location of the recipient. Supplied to an unregistered person, it is the place where the event is actually held; and if the event is held outside India, it is the location of the recipient.

citation.ref: Section 12(7)

keywords: where the event is actually held

points.text: Apply it. The dealer conference is for a registered person, so the place of supply is Rajasthan, not Goa where it was held. The wedding is for an unregistered person, so it is Jaipur, where the event was held, not Mumbai. The Dubai launch is for a registered person, so it is Gujarat; being registered, the recipient's location governs whether or not the event is in India.

citation.ref: Section 12(7)(a)

points.text: Transportation of goods, including by mail or courier, is a specific case under section 12(8). Supplied to a registered person, the place of supply is the location of that person. Supplied to an unregistered person, it is the location at which the goods are handed over for their transportation.

citation.ref: Section 12(8)

points.text: The Delhi to Chennai consignment is for a registered person, so the place of supply is Haryana, where the recipient is. The student's parcel is for an unregistered person, so it is Delhi, where it was handed over. The consignment to London is for a registered person, so it is Tamil Nadu: with the supplier and the recipient both in India, the fact that the destination is outside India changes nothing, the earlier proviso that made the destination the place of supply having been omitted.

citation.ref: Section 12(8), the proviso having been omitted by the Finance Act, 2023

written.scenario: Tejas Engineering, registered in Pune, did five things in 2026 with parties outside India. It repaired a turbine that a German company shipped to its Pune workshop, the turbine being temporarily imported for the repair and re-exported afterwards without any other use in India. It repaired a second machine that the same German company had sold years earlier to an Indian factory, the machine being brought to Pune for the work. Sitting in Pune, it diagnosed and corrected by remote electronic means a fault in a machine standing in a factory in Singapore. It arranged, for a commission from a seller in Vietnam, the sale of that seller's goods to an Indian buyer. And it hired a yacht from a company in Dubai for twenty days for a client event.
written.question: Determine the place of supply of each of the five services under section 13 of the IGST Act, 2017, with reasons.

points.text: Where the supplier or the recipient is outside India, section 13 applies. Services supplied in respect of goods that are required to be made physically available by the recipient to the supplier fall under section 13(3)(a): the place of supply is the location where the services are actually performed.

citation.ref: Section 13(3)(a)

points.text: Two provisos cut that back. Where the service is provided from a remote location by electronic means, the place of supply is the location where the goods are situated at the time of supply. And where goods are temporarily imported into India for repairs or any other treatment or process and are exported after it without being put to any other use in India, clause (a) does not apply at all and the general rule in section 13(2), the location of the recipient, takes over.

citation.ref: First and second provisos to section 13(3)(a), read with section 13(2)

points.text: Apply it. The turbine was temporarily imported for repair and re-exported, so the second proviso lifts it out of clause (a) and the place of supply is the recipient's location, Germany. The second machine belongs to an Indian factory and was made physically available in Pune, so the place of supply is Pune, where the work was performed. The Singapore machine was serviced remotely by electronic means, so the place of supply is Singapore, where the goods stood.

citation.ref: Section 13(3)(a) with its provisos

points.text: Section 13(8) fixes the place of supply at the location of the supplier of services for three cases: services by a bank or financial institution to account holders, intermediary services, and hiring of means of transport other than aircraft and vessels up to a period of one month. Tejas arranging the Vietnamese seller's sale for a commission is an intermediary, so the place of supply is Pune. The yacht hire for twenty days is hiring of a means of transport up to one month, so the place of supply is Dubai, where the supplier is, and it is therefore not an import of service.

citation.ref: Section 13(8)(b) and (c)

written.scenario: Ojas Instruments imports a testing machine by air from Japan. The exporter's ex-factory price is US $9,000. Transport from the factory to Osaka airport cost US $400 and handling at Osaka airport US $100, both paid by Ojas. Air freight from Osaka to Delhi was US $3,000. No insurance document is available. Ojas paid ₹5,000 for unloading at Delhi airport and ₹12,000 to truck the machine from the airport to its plant in Jaipur. On the date the bill of entry was presented the rate of exchange notified by the CBIC was ₹84 to the dollar and the RBI reference rate was ₹83.50.
written.question: Compute the assessable value of the machine under section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007, showing your treatment of each figure.

points.text: Build the FOB value first. The price at the exporter's factory is US $9,000, and the transport to the airport of loading and the handling there are costs of delivering the goods to the point of export, so they go in: US $9,000 plus $400 plus $100 gives an FOB value of US $9,500.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2)(a) read with section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962

points.text: The cost of transport to the place of importation is added, but for goods imported by air, where the cost is ascertainable, it cannot exceed 20 per cent of the FOB value. The actual freight of US $3,000 is therefore capped at 20 per cent of US $9,500, that is US $1,900.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Proviso to rule 10(2)

points.text: Insurance is added, and where its cost is not ascertainable it is taken at 1.125 per cent of the FOB value: 1.125 per cent of US $9,500 is US $106.875. Had the actual premium been known it would have been used as it stood.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2)(c) and its proviso

points.text: Nothing after arrival is added: the unloading and handling at Delhi airport, the place of importation, and the trucking to Jaipur are both excluded, the old one per cent landing charge having been removed in 2017. The value is US $9,500 plus $1,900 plus $106.875, that is US $11,506.875, converted at the CBIC rate of ₹84 and not the RBI rate, which gives an assessable value of ₹9,66,578 after rounding.

citation.ref: Section 14(1) with clause (a) of its Explanation, and rule 10(2) of the 2007 Rules as amended from 26 September 2017

written.scenario: Hira Textiles imports a printing machine from Italy at an FOB price of ₹50,00,000. Apart from the price it paid or bore the following: ₹1,00,000 as commission to its own agent in India who found the supplier; ₹80,000 as commission to the seller's agent in Italy; ₹2,00,000 for design work on the machine done in Italy and billed separately; ₹1,50,000 for design work done in India by an Indian consultant; ₹3,00,000 as royalty payable to the seller for the right to use its patented process on the machine, which the sale contract made a condition of the sale; ₹2,00,000 being the seller's share of the proceeds when Hira resells output, as the contract requires; and tooling worth ₹60,000 that Hira supplied free to the seller for use in making the machine. Sea freight to Mumbai was ₹2,50,000 and the insurance premium ₹40,000, both documented.
written.question: Compute the assessable value of the machine, stating for each item whether it is added under rule 10 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and why.

points.text: Rule 10(1)(a) adds commissions and brokerage except buying commission. The ₹1,00,000 paid to Hira's own agent for finding the supplier is buying commission and is not added. The ₹80,000 to the seller's agent is selling commission and is added.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(a)(i)

points.text: Rule 10(1)(b) adds the value, apportioned as appropriate, of goods and services supplied by the buyer free of charge or at reduced cost for use in producing the imported goods, including engineering and design work undertaken elsewhere than in India. The ₹2,00,000 of design work done in Italy is added, and so is the ₹60,000 of tooling supplied free of charge. The ₹1,50,000 of design work done in India is not added.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(b)(ii) and (iv)

points.text: Rule 10(1)(c) adds royalties and licence fees related to the imported goods that the buyer must pay as a condition of sale of the goods, so the ₹3,00,000 royalty is added. Rule 10(1)(d) adds the value of any part of the proceeds of any subsequent resale, disposal or use of the imported goods that accrues to the seller, so the ₹2,00,000 share of proceeds is added too.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(c) and (d)

points.text: The FOB value is ₹50,00,000 plus ₹80,000 plus ₹2,00,000 plus ₹60,000 plus ₹3,00,000 plus ₹2,00,000, that is ₹58,40,000. Under rule 10(2) the documented sea freight of ₹2,50,000 and insurance of ₹40,000 are added as they stand, the fallbacks of 20 per cent and 1.125 per cent applying only where the actual figures are not ascertainable. The assessable value is ₹61,30,000.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2)(a) and (c) read with section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962

written.scenario: Four people ask whether they must register in 2026-27, and none of them makes any inter-State supply. Mohan, in Uttar Pradesh, trades only in taxable goods within the State with a turnover of ₹35 lakh, and earns ₹2 lakh of interest on fixed deposits. Rekha, in Manipur, trades in taxable goods within the State with a turnover of ₹12 lakh. Vivek, in Telangana, trades in taxable goods within the State with a turnover of ₹30 lakh. Priya, in Maharashtra, trades in taxable goods within the State with a turnover of ₹30 lakh and also earns ₹2 lakh from taxable repair services.
written.question: State, with reasons, whether each of the four is liable to be registered under the CGST Act, 2017, identifying the threshold that applies to each.

points.text: Section 22(1) makes registration compulsory where aggregate turnover in a financial year exceeds ₹20 lakh, and ₹10 lakh for the special category States, which for registration means Mizoram, Tripura, Manipur and Nagaland only. Notification No. 10/2019-CT lifts the limit to ₹40 lakh for a person engaged exclusively in the supply of goods, with named exceptions. Aggregate turnover under section 2(6) counts taxable and exempt supplies together, on an all-India basis.

citation.ref: Section 22(1) with its provisos and Explanation (iii), section 2(6), and Notification No. 10/2019-Central Tax dated 7 March 2019

keywords: exclusively in the supply of goods

points.text: Mohan is not liable. The Explanation to section 22(1) says a person is still engaged exclusively in the supply of goods even if he also makes exempt supplies of extending deposits, loans or advances where the consideration is interest or discount, so the fixed-deposit interest does not cost him the higher limit. His aggregate turnover of ₹37 lakh, interest included, is within ₹40 lakh.

citation.ref: Explanation to section 22(1) read with Notification No. 10/2019-Central Tax

points.text: Rekha is liable. Manipur is a special category State for registration, so her limit is ₹10 lakh and ₹12 lakh exceeds it. Vivek is also liable, though his goods are within ₹40 lakh: Telangana is one of the States the notification carves out of the ₹40 lakh limit, along with Arunachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Puducherry and the four special category States, so his limit is ₹20 lakh and ₹30 lakh exceeds it.

citation.ref: First proviso to section 22(1); exception (c) in Notification No. 10/2019-Central Tax

points.text: Priya is liable. The ₹40 lakh limit is only for a person engaged exclusively in the supply of goods, and taxable repair services are neither goods nor the one exempt financial service the Explanation forgives. She is a supplier of goods and services, her limit is ₹20 lakh, and her aggregate turnover of ₹32 lakh exceeds it.

citation.ref: Section 22(1) read with Notification No. 10/2019-Central Tax

written.scenario: Six persons, each with aggregate turnover below every threshold, ask whether they must register in 2026-27. An artisan in Delhi supplies notified handicraft goods to buyers in other States for ₹15 lakh. A consultant in Pune supplies taxable services to clients in other States for ₹12 lakh. A trader in Kolkata sells goods to buyers in other States for ₹8 lakh. A firm in Jaipur supplies only security services to companies, tax on which is payable by the recipient under section 9(3). A retailer in Chennai with a turnover of ₹6 lakh engages an advocate whose fee is taxed under reverse charge. A seller in Indore sells goods within Madhya Pradesh through an electronic commerce operator that collects tax at source, for ₹9 lakh.
written.question: State, with reasons, which of the six must register compulsorily under section 24 of the CGST Act, 2017 regardless of turnover, and which may stay unregistered.

points.text: Section 24 lists persons who must register irrespective of the threshold, and the list starts with persons making any inter-State taxable supply. But the threshold of ₹20 lakh, ₹10 lakh in the four special category States, is restored by notification for inter-State supply of taxable services and of notified handicraft and hand-made goods. So the Delhi artisan and the Pune consultant may both stay unregistered, while the Kolkata trader, making inter-State supplies of ordinary goods, must register.

citation.ref: Section 24(i) read with Notification No. 10/2017-Integrated Tax and Notification No. 3/2018-Integrated Tax

points.text: Persons required to pay tax under reverse charge on their inward supplies must register under section 24(iii) whatever their turnover. The Chennai retailer receives an advocate's services on which he is the person liable to pay, so he must register even at ₹6 lakh.

citation.ref: Section 24(iii) read with section 9(3)

points.text: The Jaipur firm is the opposite case. It makes only outward supplies on which the whole tax is payable by the recipient under section 9(3), and such persons are exempted from registration by notification under section 23(2); the exemption does not extend to suppliers of metal scrap. The firm may stay unregistered.

citation.ref: Section 23(2) read with Notification No. 5/2017-Central Tax dated 19 June 2017

points.text: A person supplying through an electronic commerce operator that collects tax at source is on the section 24 list, but the threshold is made available by notification to a person making intra-State supplies of goods through such an operator, as it is for services supplied through one. The Indore seller supplies within the State and is under the limit, so he may stay unregistered.

citation.ref: Section 24(ix) read with Notification No. 34/2023-Central Tax dated 31 July 2023

written.scenario: Aarav Traders, a new firm in Gujarat, expects to sell almost entirely to registered dealers, with output tax on those sales of about ₹1.8 lakh a month. It wants registration quickly and without a site visit. Its adviser mentions a simplified route introduced on 1 November 2025. Six months later the firm's business grows and its monthly output tax on supplies to registered persons is set to cross ₹2.5 lakh.
written.question: Explain the simplified registration under rule 14A of the CGST Rules, 2017: who may opt for it, what it gives, what it restricts, and how Aarav Traders leaves it when it outgrows it.

points.text: Rule 14A, in force from 1 November 2025, is for a person applying under rule 8 whose total output tax liability on supplies to registered persons, counting CGST, SGST or UTGST, IGST and compensation cess together, does not exceed ₹2.5 lakh per month, and who opts for and successfully completes Aadhaar authentication. Aarav Traders qualifies at ₹1.8 lakh a month.

citation.ref: Rule 14A(1) and (2), inserted by Notification No. 18/2025-Central Tax dated 31 October 2025

points.text: Once the Aadhaar number is authenticated, registration is granted electronically by the common portal within three working days of the application, with no physical verification of the premises. The restriction is one registration per State or Union territory against the same PAN under this option, overriding the separate registrations for multiple places of business that rule 11 otherwise allows.

citation.ref: Rule 14A(3) and (4)

points.text: To leave the option Aarav Traders files an application for withdrawal, which is allowed only if it has furnished the return for at least one tax period and every return due from the effective date of registration to the date of the application, and no cancellation proceedings under section 29 have been initiated against it. Any change in its registered particulars must be amended before the application.

citation.ref: Rule 14A(5) and (6)

points.text: After the officer's order allowing withdrawal, the firm may declare output tax on supplies to registered persons above ₹2.5 lakh from the first day of the succeeding month after the order, and not for any earlier period. If cancellation proceedings are begun while the withdrawal is pending, the application is rejected and the deemed approval under rule 9(5) does not apply.

citation.ref: Rule 14A(7) to (9)

written.scenario: Nakul Consultants, registered in Delhi, supplied four services in 2026. First, an audit completed on 10 April, invoiced on 25 April, paid on 15 May. Second, a valuation completed on 10 April, invoiced on 20 May, paid on 30 May. Third, a retainer for which the client paid ₹50,000 in advance on 1 June against a service provided in July and invoiced on 31 July. Fourth, an invoice for ₹1,00,000 on 5 August against which the client paid ₹1,00,800 on 20 August, and ₹2,000 of interest for late payment received on 30 September.
written.question: Determine the time of supply of each service under section 13 of the CGST Act, 2017, with reasons.

points.text: Under section 13(2), where the invoice is issued within the period section 31 allows, thirty days from the supply of the service, the time of supply is the earlier of the date of invoice and the date of receipt of payment. The audit was invoiced on 25 April, within thirty days of 10 April, and paid later, so the time of supply is 25 April.

citation.ref: Section 13(2)(a) read with section 31(2) and rule 47 of the CGST Rules, 2017

points.text: Where the invoice is not issued within thirty days, the time of supply is the earlier of the date of provision of the service and the date of receipt of payment. The valuation was invoiced on 20 May, more than thirty days after 10 April, so the late invoice is ignored and the time of supply is 10 April, the date the service was provided; the tax fell due in April, not May.

citation.ref: Section 13(2)(b)

points.text: The retainer is an advance. Payment received before the invoice fixes the time of supply to the extent of the payment, so for ₹50,000 the time of supply is 1 June, the date the payment was entered in the books or credited to the bank, whichever is earlier. The option to defer tax on advances exists for goods by notification and not for services.

citation.ref: Section 13(2) with Explanation (i) and (ii)

points.text: The ₹800 received over the invoice is within the ₹1,000 that the proviso to section 13(2) allows, so at the supplier's option the time of supply for that excess is the date of the invoice issued for it, rather than 20 August. The ₹2,000 of interest for delayed payment is an addition to value under section 15(2)(d), and section 13(6) fixes its time of supply as the date the supplier receives it, 30 September.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 13(2) and section 13(6)

written.scenario: Rudra Metals, registered in Jharkhand, has three inward supplies on which it must pay tax under reverse charge in 2026. Metal scrap from an unregistered dealer: invoice dated 1 May, goods received 5 May, payment entered in the books on 20 June and debited from the bank on 22 June. Security services from a firm: invoice dated 1 May, payment on 10 August. A management fee from its associated enterprise in Singapore: entered in Rudra's books on 15 March 2026, invoice dated 1 April 2026, paid on 30 June 2026.
written.question: Determine the time of supply of each under sections 12(3) and 13(3) of the CGST Act, 2017, with reasons.

points.text: For goods under reverse charge, section 12(3) takes the earliest of the date of receipt of the goods, the date of payment as entered in the recipient's books or debited from his bank account whichever is earlier, and the day immediately following thirty days from the supplier's invoice. For the scrap those dates are 5 May, 20 June and 31 May, so the time of supply is 5 May.

citation.ref: Section 12(3)(a) to (c)

points.text: For services under reverse charge, section 13(3) drops the receipt limb and stretches the outer date: the earlier of the date of payment and the day immediately following sixty days from the invoice. For the security services those are 10 August and 1 July, so the time of supply is 1 July, and the tax fell due in July although nothing was paid until August.

citation.ref: Section 13(3)(a) and (b)

points.text: Where the supplier is an associated enterprise located outside India, the proviso to section 13(3) makes the time of supply the date of entry in the recipient's books of account or the date of payment, whichever is earlier. The fee was entered on 15 March 2026, before the invoice and the payment, so the time of supply is 15 March 2026 and the liability falls in 2025-26, not 2026-27.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 13(3)

written.scenario: The rate of tax on the service Chaitanya Wellness supplies fell from 18 per cent to 5 per cent with effect from 22 September 2025. Four transactions straddle that date. First, a service supplied on 10 September, invoiced on 25 September, paid on 30 September. Second, a service supplied on 10 September, invoiced on 15 September, paid on 30 September. Third, a service supplied on 10 October, invoiced on 15 September, paid on 30 September. Fourth, a service supplied on 10 October, invoiced on 15 September, with the payment entered in the books on 18 September but credited to the bank only on 29 September.
written.question: Determine the time of supply and the rate applicable to each transaction under section 14 of the CGST Act, 2017, with reasons.

points.text: Section 14 overrides sections 12 and 13 whenever the rate changes, and turns on where the supply, the invoice and the payment each fall against the date of change. Where the supply was before the change and both invoice and payment came after it, the time of supply is the earlier of the two. The first service was supplied on 10 September and invoiced and paid after 22 September, so the time of supply is 25 September and the new rate of 5 per cent applies.

citation.ref: Section 14(a)(i)

points.text: Where the supply was before the change and the invoice was also before it but the payment came after, the time of supply is the date of the invoice. The second service was supplied and invoiced before 22 September, so the time of supply is 15 September and the old rate of 18 per cent applies although the money arrived under the new rate.

citation.ref: Section 14(a)(ii)

points.text: Where the supply was after the change, the invoice before it and the payment after it, the time of supply is the date of receipt of payment. The third service was supplied on 10 October, so the time of supply is 30 September and the new rate of 5 per cent applies; the early invoice does not carry the old rate forward.

citation.ref: Section 14(b)(i)

points.text: The fourth looks like invoice and payment both before the change, which would make the time of supply the earlier of the two and keep 18 per cent. But the proviso to section 14 says the date of receipt of payment is the date of credit in the bank account where that credit comes more than four working days after the date of change. 29 September is more than four working days after 22 September, so the payment is treated as received on 29 September, after the change, and the case becomes supply after, invoice before, payment after: the time of supply is 29 September at 5 per cent.

citation.ref: Section 14(b)(i) read with the proviso and Explanation to section 14

written.scenario: Tanvi Agro, registered in Haryana, makes a product taxed at 5 per cent from inputs taxed at 18 per cent. For the quarter ended 31 December 2026 it bought inputs worth ₹20,00,000 and took credit of ₹3,60,000 on them; it took credit of ₹40,000 on input services and ₹90,000 on a machine. Its outward supply of the 5 per cent product was ₹30,00,000, on which tax of ₹1,50,000 was payable, and it also supplied other goods taxed at 18 per cent for ₹10,00,000. It has made no exempt or zero-rated supply.
written.question: Compute the maximum refund of unutilised input tax credit Tanvi Agro may claim for the quarter on account of the inverted duty structure under section 54(3) of the CGST Act, 2017 read with rule 89(5) of the CGST Rules, 2017, explaining each term.

points.text: Section 54(3)(ii) allows refund of unutilised credit accumulated because the rate of tax on inputs is higher than the rate on output supplies, other than nil-rated or exempt supplies and other than the goods and services the Government has notified as excluded. A 5 per cent product made from 18 per cent inputs is an inverted duty structure, and the claim is filed within two years of the relevant date.

citation.ref: Section 54(3) proviso (ii) and Explanation 2 to section 54

points.text: Net ITC for rule 89(5) means the credit availed on inputs during the relevant period, and inputs under section 2(59) are goods other than capital goods. So Net ITC is ₹3,60,000: the ₹40,000 on input services and the ₹90,000 on the machine are both left out, and neither is refundable under this head. The denominator in the second limb, the credit availed on inputs and input services, is ₹4,00,000.

citation.ref: Explanation (a) to rule 89(5) read with section 2(59) of the CGST Act, 2017

points.text: Turnover of inverted rated supply of goods is ₹30,00,000. Adjusted total turnover is the turnover in the State excluding exempt supplies other than zero-rated ones, here ₹30,00,000 plus ₹10,00,000, that is ₹40,00,000, because the 18 per cent goods are part of the turnover even though no refund arises on them.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) read with rule 89(4)(E)

points.text: The formula is the turnover of inverted rated supply times Net ITC divided by adjusted total turnover, less the tax payable on the inverted rated supply times Net ITC divided by the credit availed on inputs and input services. That is ₹30,00,000 times ₹3,60,000 over ₹40,00,000, which is ₹2,70,000, less ₹1,50,000 times ₹3,60,000 over ₹4,00,000, which is ₹1,35,000. The maximum refund is ₹1,35,000.

citation.ref: Rule 89(5) as substituted by Notification No. 14/2022-Central Tax dated 5 July 2022

written.scenario: Ishaan Exports, registered in Gujarat, exports under a letter of undertaking without payment of tax and claims refund of unutilised credit. One consignment was loaded on a vessel at Mundra on 10 March 2024 and the vessel left India on 14 March 2024. A second consignment went by road to Nepal and crossed the frontier on 20 March 2024. A software service was completed for a client in Ireland on 15 January 2024 and the payment arrived in convertible foreign exchange on 20 May 2024. On a fourth claim, filed on 1 February 2026, the officer issued a deficiency memo on 25 February 2026 asking for a fresh application.
written.question: State the relevant date and the last date for filing the refund claim in each of the first three cases, and explain how the deficiency memo affects the fourth.

points.text: A refund application is made before the expiry of two years from the relevant date, and Explanation 2 to section 54 fixes that date by the ground of the claim. For goods exported by sea or air it is the date on which the ship or aircraft in which the goods are loaded leaves India, so the first consignment's relevant date is 14 March 2024, not the loading date, and the claim may be filed up to 14 March 2026.

citation.ref: Section 54(1) and Explanation 2(a)(i) to section 54

points.text: For goods exported by land the relevant date is the date on which the goods pass the frontier, so for the Nepal consignment it is 20 March 2024 and the claim may be filed up to 20 March 2026.

citation.ref: Explanation 2(a)(ii) to section 54

points.text: For export of services where the supply was completed before the payment was received, the relevant date is the date of receipt of payment in convertible foreign exchange, or in Indian rupees where the Reserve Bank permits it. The Irish service's relevant date is therefore 20 May 2024, not the completion date, and the claim may be filed up to 20 May 2026.

citation.ref: Explanation 2(c)(i) to section 54

points.text: Where the officer issues a deficiency memo requiring a fresh claim, the period from the date the claim was filed to the date the deficiencies were communicated is excluded from the two years. For the fourth claim the days from 1 February 2026 to 25 February 2026 do not count against Ishaan Exports when it files the fresh application.

citation.ref: Proviso to rule 90(3)

written.scenario: Two exporters file refund claims for unutilised credit on zero-rated supplies made under a letter of undertaking in November 2026. Kavya Textiles has completed Aadhaar authentication and exports garments. Pankaj Agro has not undergone Aadhaar authentication and exports areca nuts. Separately, Kavya Textiles asks whether it must prove that it did not pass the tax on to anyone, and how long the department has to decide its claim.
written.question: Explain the provisional refund available to each exporter after the changes effective 1 October 2025, the time limit for the final order, and whether the doctrine of unjust enrichment applies to these claims.

points.text: Section 54(6) lets the proper officer refund on a provisional basis 90 per cent of the amount claimed on account of zero-rated supplies, ahead of final settlement under section 54(5), except for categories of registered persons the Government notifies. Rule 91(2), as substituted with effect from 1 October 2025, ties the provisional sanction to the identification and evaluation of risk by the system and requires the order within seven days of the acknowledgement of the claim.

citation.ref: Section 54(6) read with rule 91(2) of the CGST Rules, 2017 as substituted by Notification No. 13/2025-Central Tax dated 17 September 2025

points.text: The officer may, for reasons recorded in writing, decline the provisional route in a given case and proceed straight to the final order under rule 92; that order does not need revalidation. Kavya Textiles is otherwise inside the provisional route and can expect 90 per cent within seven days unless the officer records reasons not to.

citation.ref: Rule 91(2) as substituted with effect from 1 October 2025
