In 2025-26 it charged fees at all four, collected entrance examination fees for the college, and bought bus transport and catering for the school and the college, security for the college, online journal subscriptions for the school and the college, and admission-processing services from an agency for the college.
written.question: State which of the trust's supplies and purchases are exempt under Entry 66 of the exemption notification, with reasons.

points.text: The exemption turns on the definition of educational institution: an institution providing pre-school education and education up to higher secondary school or equivalent, education as part of a curriculum for obtaining a qualification recognised by any law for the time being in force, or education as part of an approved vocational education course. The school and the AICTE-recognised college qualify. The coaching centre does not, because its training leads to no qualification recognised by law. The private ITI qualifies only for the electrician course, a designated trade under the Apprentices Act run by an NCVET-affiliated ITI; the mobile-repair course is not an approved vocational course.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Exemptions from GST
citation.ref: Entry 66 — definition of educational institution; coaching institutes; private ITI and designated trades, Circular 55/29/2018

points.text: Output services: services provided by an educational institution to its students, faculty and staff are exempt, so the school fees, the college fees and the ITI fees for the electrician trade are exempt; the coaching fees and the mobile-repair fees are taxable. The college's entrance examination fees are exempt under item (aa), conduct of entrance examination against consideration in the form of entrance fee.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Exemptions from GST
citation.ref: Entry 66(a) and (aa) — services to students, faculty and staff; entrance examination fees

points.text: Input services: transportation of students, faculty and staff, catering including any government-sponsored mid-day meal scheme, and security, cleaning or housekeeping performed in the institution are exempt only when supplied to an institution providing pre-school education and education up to higher secondary school or equivalent. The school's bus transport and catering are exempt; the college's bus transport, catering and security are taxable.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Exemptions from GST
citation.ref: Entry 66(b)(i) to (iii) and the proviso — transport, catering, security only for schools up to higher secondary

points.text: Online educational journals or periodicals supplied to an educational institution are exempt, but not where the institution provides pre-school or school education up to higher secondary or an approved vocational course; the college's subscriptions are exempt and the school's are taxable, the mirror image of the transport rule.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Exemptions from GST
citation.ref: Entry 66(b)(v) and the second proviso — online journals not exempt for schools or vocational courses

points.text: Services relating to admission to, or conduct of examination by, an educational institution are exempt for every educational institution, so the agency's admission-processing services to the college are exempt. The same applies to a private ITI in respect of designated trades, where services relating to admission or examination supplied to it are exempt and its own entrance examination fees are too, while for other trades GST is payable on services by and to the ITI.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Exemptions from GST
citation.ref: Entry 66(b)(iv) — admission and examination services; private ITI in designated trades

written.scenario: RideOn, an electronic commerce operator located in India, lists six kinds of supply: (a) 20-seater bus rides by Sahil Travels Pvt Ltd; (b) 20-seater bus rides by Mr. Rakesh, an individual operator; (c) motorcab rides by drivers who are not registered; (d) plumbing services by a plumber registered under GST with a turnover of ₹35 lakh; (e) rooms in a guest house whose owner has a turnover of ₹12 lakh and is unregistered; and (f) meals from a restaurant inside a hotel whose declared tariff is ₹9,000 a room a day.
written.question: State for each supply who is liable to pay the tax under section 9(5), and explain what it means for an operator to be liable.

points.text: Under section 9(5) the tax on notified categories of services supplied through an electronic commerce operator is paid by the operator, and all the provisions of the Act apply to it as if it were the supplier liable for paying the tax, so the invoice for such services is issued by the operator and not the supplier. It applies only to services. Where the operator has no physical presence in the taxable territory its representative pays, and where it has neither presence nor representative, a person it appoints for the purpose.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Electronic Commerce Transactions
citation.ref: Section 9(5) — ECO liable as if it were the supplier; invoice by the ECO; representative or appointee

points.text: Transportation of passengers by an omnibus, a motor vehicle constructed or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, is a notified service except where the person supplying it through the operator is a company. (a) Sahil Travels Pvt Ltd is a company, so the tax on its bus rides is not payable by RideOn; the company pays it itself. (b) Mr. Rakesh is not a company, so RideOn pays the tax on his rides.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Electronic Commerce Transactions
citation.ref: Notification 17/2017 CT(R) entry for omnibus — company exclusion; definition of omnibus

points.text: (c) Transportation of passengers by a radio-taxi, motorcab, maxicab or motorcycle is notified without any exception, so RideOn pays the tax on the motorcab rides whether or not the drivers are registered or liable to registration.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Electronic Commerce Transactions
citation.ref: Notified passenger transport — ECO liable irrespective of the supplier's registration

points.text: Housekeeping services such as plumbing and carpentry, and accommodation in hotels, guest houses and similar places, are notified except where the supplier is liable to registration under section 22(1), that is, where its aggregate turnover exceeds the ₹20 lakh threshold, ₹10 lakh in a special category State. (d) The plumber at ₹35 lakh is liable to registration, so he pays the tax himself. (e) The guest house at ₹12 lakh is not, so RideOn pays.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Electronic Commerce Transactions
citation.ref: Housekeeping and accommodation entries — ECO liable only where the supplier is not liable to registration under section 22

points.text: (f) Restaurant service supplied through an operator is notified other than service supplied by a restaurant located at specified premises, meaning premises providing hotel accommodation with a declared tariff above ₹7,500 a unit a day. The hotel's tariff is ₹9,000, so its restaurant is at specified premises and pays the tax itself; RideOn is not liable.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Electronic Commerce Transactions
citation.ref: Restaurant service entry — exclusion for specified premises with declared tariff above 7,500

written.scenario: Five events in 2025-26. (a) Alpha Ltd and Beta Ltd were amalgamated by a Tribunal order dated 15 January 2026 taking effect from 1 April 2025; between those dates they supplied goods worth ₹3 crore to each other, and their accountant says those supplies "vanish" on amalgamation. (b) Mr. Deepak, a sole proprietor, died in July; his son continues the business; a demand of ₹4 lakh for 2024-25 was determined in December. (c) A Hindu undivided family partitioned its property in September; ₹2 lakh of tax up to that date was determined later. (d) A firm was dissolved in October owing ₹6 lakh. (e) A minor's business was run by his guardian until the guardianship ended in March.
written.question: State who is liable in each case, and to what extent, under sections 87, 91 and 93.

points.text: Section 87: where companies are amalgamated or merged under an order of a court or Tribunal or otherwise, the order takes effect from a date earlier than its date, and the companies supplied or received goods or services to or from each other in the period from the effective date to the date of the order, those transactions are included in the turnover of supply or receipt of the respective companies and they are liable to pay tax on them. The companies are treated as distinct companies up to the date of the order, and their registrations are cancelled with effect from that date. The ₹3 crore does not vanish; each company pays on its supplies to the other.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
citation.ref: Section 87 — supplies between amalgamating companies before the order; distinct companies until the order

points.text: Section 93(1): where a person liable to pay tax, interest or penalty dies and the business is continued by his legal representative or any other person, that person is liable for the dues; where the business is discontinued, the legal representative is liable out of the estate of the deceased, to the extent the estate can meet the charge, whether the dues were determined before death and unpaid or determined after death. Deepak's son, continuing the business, is liable for the ₹4 lakh; a successor is liable for the transferor's dues where the business passes on the death of a sole proprietor.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
citation.ref: Section 93(1) — death; business continued or discontinued; legal representative and the estate

points.text: Section 93(2) and (3): on partition of the property of a Hindu undivided family or an association of persons, each member or group of members is jointly and severally liable for the dues up to the time of partition; on dissolution of a firm, every person who was a partner is jointly and severally liable for the dues up to the time of dissolution, in each case whether determined before the event and unpaid or after it. The ₹2 lakh and ₹6 lakh may be recovered in full from any member or any former partner.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
citation.ref: Section 93(2) and (3) — partition of HUF or AOP; dissolution of a firm; joint and several liability

points.text: Section 91: where a business is carried on by a guardian, trustee or agent of a minor or other incapacitated person on his behalf and for his benefit, the tax, interest or penalty is levied on and recovered from the guardian, trustee or agent, in like manner and to the same extent as it would be from the minor as if he were a major conducting the business himself. Section 92 applies the same rule to a Court of Wards, Administrator General, Official Trustee, receiver or manager appointed by a court who controls the estate.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
citation.ref: Sections 91 and 92 — guardians, trustees and agents; Court of Wards and receivers

points.text: Section 93(4): where the taxable person is the guardian of a ward or a trustee for a beneficiary and the guardianship or trust is terminated, the ward or the beneficiary becomes liable for the tax, interest or penalty due from the taxable person; the minor, now of age, answers for the dues after March. Every provision of section 93 is subject to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Liability to Pay in Certain Cases
citation.ref: Section 93(4) — termination of guardianship or trust; subject to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code

written.scenario: The Authority for Advance Ruling pronounced a ruling in favour of Zeta Ltd on 10 February 2026. On 5 July 2026 the jurisdictional officer points out a mistake apparent from the record whose correction would increase Zeta's tax, and the Authority amends the ruling the same day without hearing Zeta. A competitor in the same State starts relying on the ruling. In October the officer shows that Zeta suppressed a material contract from its application; the Authority proposes to declare the ruling void, and to summon Zeta's accountant to produce records, which Zeta says it cannot do.
written.question: Examine each step under sections 102 to 106.

points.text: Under section 102 the Authority and the Appellate Authority may amend their order to rectify any mistake apparent from the record within six months from the date of the order, on their own motion or where the mistake is brought to their notice by the applicant or the concerned or jurisdictional officer. 5 July is within six months of 10 February, so the rectification is in time; but where a rectification has the effect of enhancing the tax liability or reducing input tax credit, the applicant must be heard before the order is passed, so amending without hearing Zeta is bad.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Advance Ruling
citation.ref: Section 102 — rectification within six months; hearing where tax is enhanced or credit reduced

points.text: Under section 103 the ruling binds only the applicant and the concerned or jurisdictional officer in respect of the applicant; it does not extend to similarly placed taxable persons in the State, so the competitor cannot rely on it. It binds for no fixed period but until the law, facts or circumstances supporting it change.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Advance Ruling
citation.ref: Section 103 — binding only on the applicant and its officer; until law, facts or circumstances change

points.text: Under section 104, where the Authority or Appellate Authority finds that a ruling was obtained by fraud, suppression of material facts or misrepresentation, it may by order declare the ruling void ab initio, after hearing the applicant, and all provisions of the Act then apply as if the ruling had never been made, excluding the period from the ruling to the order declaring it void; a copy goes to the applicant and the officers. The suppressed contract is such a fact.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Advance Ruling
citation.ref: Section 104 — void ab initio for fraud, suppression or misrepresentation; hearing; excluded period

points.text: Zeta is wrong. Under sections 105 and 106 both authorities have the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure for discovery and inspection, enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath, issuing commissions and compelling production of books of account and other records; they are deemed a civil court for section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, their proceedings are judicial proceedings under the Penal Code, and they regulate their own procedure. The accountant can be summoned and the records compelled.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Advance Ruling
citation.ref: Sections 105 and 106 — civil court powers; judicial proceeding; own procedure

written.scenario: An adjudication order dated 10 April 2026 against Vyom Traders totals the demand at ₹18,40,000 where the line items add to ₹14,80,000, and decides against Vyom a point on which two High Courts differ. Vyom writes to the officer on 20 August 2026 asking for both to be corrected. The officer replies that he can do nothing after three months, and in any event proposes on 20 November 2026 to correct the total upward for another slip he has found. Vyom also argues that the show cause notice quoted the wrong section, so the whole order is invalid, though it had replied to the notice on merits, and threatens a civil suit.
written.question: Advise on each point under sections 160, 161 and 162.

points.text: Section 161, which overrides the Act except section 160, lets any authority that has passed or issued a decision, order, notice, certificate or other document rectify an error apparent on the face of the record in it. The totalling error is such an error. The point on which High Courts differ is not: a decision on a debatable point of law is not a mistake apparent from the record, so it must go on appeal, not rectification.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Miscellaneous Provisions
citation.ref: Section 161 — error apparent on the face of the record; a debatable point of law is not one

points.text: The authority may rectify on its own motion, when a GST officer brings the error to its notice, or when the affected person does so within three months from the date of issue of the document. Vyom's letter of 20 August is more than three months after 10 April, so Vyom cannot compel a rectification on its own application; but the officer is wrong that he can do nothing, because he may rectify on his own motion within six months of the order, that is, by 10 October 2026, and a purely clerical or arithmetical error arising from an accidental slip may be corrected even after six months. The 20 November correction of the slip is therefore permitted.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Miscellaneous Provisions
citation.ref: Section 161 — three months for the affected person; six months overall; no limit for clerical or arithmetical errors

points.text: Principles of natural justice must be followed where the rectification adversely affects any person, so Vyom must be heard before the total is raised in November.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Miscellaneous Provisions
citation.ref: Section 161 — hearing where rectification adversely affects a person

points.text: Under section 160 an assessment, adjudication, notice or other proceeding is not invalid merely for a mistake, defect or omission if in substance and effect it conforms to the intents, purposes and requirements of the Act; and the service of a notice, order or communication cannot be questioned where the person has already acted on it or did not question it in the earliest proceedings, so a wrong section number in a notice Vyom answered on merits does not void the order. Section 162 bars civil courts from any suit, proceeding or question arising from any action taken under the Act; the civil suit will not lie.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Miscellaneous Provisions
citation.ref: Section 160 — proceedings not invalid for mistake; service not questionable once acted upon; section 162 bar on civil courts

written.scenario: Kaveri Imports faced four situations in 2026. (a) It presented a bill of entry for home consumption on 1 March for machinery arriving by a vessel that reached port on 3 March and was granted entry inwards on 5 March; the duty rate rose from 10 per cent to 15 per cent by a notification effective 4 March. (b) It warehoused a consignment of chemicals under an into-bond bill of entry on 10 March when the rate was 15 per cent; an exemption on 20 June cut the rate to 7.5 per cent, and it filed the ex-bond bill of entry for home consumption on 25 June. (c) Two of fifty cartons in a third consignment were found missing after unloading, before the clearance order, with the outer packing tampered. (d) It imported components at a concessional rate under an end-use notification. The department applied 10 per cent to (a), 15 per cent to (b), and full duty on all fifty cartons in (c).
written.question: Determine the correct treatment of (a), (b) and (c), and state what Kaveri must do under the rules governing (d).

points.text: Section 15 fixes the relevant date for the rate of duty and tariff valuation: for goods entered for home consumption, the date of presentation of the bill of entry or the date of entry inwards of the vessel or arrival of the aircraft or vehicle, whichever is later; for goods cleared from a warehouse, the date on which the bill of entry for home consumption is presented; for any other goods, the date of payment of duty. Section 15 governs only the rate and tariff valuation, not the valuation of the goods under section 14.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
citation.ref: Section 15 — relevant date for home consumption, warehouse clearance and other goods; distinct from section 14

keywords: bill of entry for home consumption

points.text: (a) The bill of entry was presented on 1 March but entry inwards was granted on 5 March, the later date, so the bill of entry is deemed presented on 5 March and the rate in force that day, 15 per cent, applies; the department is wrong to apply 10 per cent.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
citation.ref: Section 15(1)(a) — later of bill of entry and entry inwards

points.text: (b) For goods cleared from a warehouse the relevant date is the presentation of the bill of entry for home consumption, 25 June, when the exemption had reduced the rate to 7.5 per cent; the rate on the into-bond bill of entry is irrelevant, so the department is wrong to charge 15 per cent.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
citation.ref: Section 15(1)(b) — ex-bond bill of entry fixes the rate; module illustration on a later exemption

points.text: (c) Under section 13 an importer is not liable to duty on goods pilfered after unloading and before the proper officer's order for clearance for home consumption or deposit in a warehouse, unless the goods are restored to him; the custodian is liable for that duty under section 46. Pilfer means petty theft of unit articles, not loss of a whole package, and the claim needs evidence of tampering, blank space for the missing articles and missing unit articles. Two tampered cartons missing from fifty fit, so duty is payable on forty-eight cartons.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
citation.ref: Section 13 — pilferage after unloading and before clearance; custodian liable; conditions for the claim

points.text: (d) The Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022 apply where the benefit of a notification depends on the imported goods being used for manufacture, an output service or a specified end use. Kaveri gives one-time prior information on the common portal, covering its premises, job worker, the goods, the notification, the end-use recipient and the intended ports, on which an IGCR identification number is generated; and it furnishes a continuity bond with surety or security to the jurisdictional Deputy or Assistant Commissioner undertaking to pay the difference between the full duty and the duty paid, with interest from the date of import, if the goods are not so used. Goods sent for job work go under an invoice or e-way bill and are recorded in the monthly statement.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 5 — Levy of and Exemptions from Customs Duty
citation.ref: IGCR Rules 2022 — one-time prior information, identification number, continuity bond with interest, job work

written.scenario: Vasudha Polymers Limited, a listed company reporting under Ind AS, is acquiring Neelkanth Chemicals Limited under a scheme of arrangement. The scheme names an appointed date of 1st April 20X1. The shareholders' agreement is signed on 1st June 20X1. Vasudha obtains board representation, and with it control over Neelkanth's financial and operating policies, on 1st July 20X1. The consideration is paid on 15th July 20X1 and the shares are transferred on 1st August 20X1. At 1st July 20X1 both the value of the Vasudha shares issued and the fair value of Neelkanth's net assets are determined only provisionally, at ₹20 crore and ₹15 crore. On 30th November 20X1 they are finally determined at ₹22 crore and ₹16 crore. Vasudha's share price has since fallen and its directors wish to use the value at 1st February 20X2, which would put the consideration at ₹18 crore. The agreement also provides that a further ₹4 crore will be paid if Neelkanth's turnover reaches ₹160 crore within two years; the fair value of that promise on 1st July 20X1 was ₹3 crore, and by February 20X2 the target is unlikely to be met. The exchange ratio was fixed by an independent valuer engaged by Vasudha's management, using weights of 50 per cent to earnings per share, 25 per cent to market price and 25 per cent to book value. Vasudha's statutory auditor proposes to rely on that valuer's report for the fair values in the acquisition accounting.
written.question: Determine the acquisition date and the amounts at which the consideration transferred and the net assets acquired are to be measured. Explain the treatment of the contingent consideration on acquisition and when the turnover target is later missed. State what Vasudha must be able to show before it can say the deal creates value for its own shareholders, and what the statutory auditor must do before using the valuer's report as audit evidence.

points.text: The acquisition date is the date on which the acquirer obtains control of the acquiree, which here is 1st July 20X1, when board representation was obtained. The appointed date named in the scheme is not the acquisition date, because the acquirer did not have control on that date; neither is the date of payment nor the date the shares moved.

citation.ref: Determination of the acquisition date, as illustrated in the ICAI Study Material on Ind AS 103

points.text: Where the initial accounting is incomplete at the end of the reporting period the acquirer reports provisional amounts and retrospectively adjusts them during the measurement period to reflect new information about facts and circumstances that existed at the acquisition date; the measurement period shall not exceed one year from the acquisition date. So the amounts finally determined on 30th November 20X1 are used, ₹22 crore and ₹16 crore, and the directors cannot substitute the February 20X2 figure of ₹18 crore, which reflects a fall in price after the acquisition rather than a fact existing at it.

citation.ref: Paragraph 45

points.text: The acquirer recognises the acquisition-date fair value of contingent consideration of ₹3 crore as part of the consideration transferred, making the consideration ₹25 crore in all. A later change caused by an event after the acquisition date, such as failing to meet an earnings target, is not a measurement period adjustment; contingent consideration classified as a liability is remeasured at fair value at each reporting date and the change is recognised in profit or loss, while contingent consideration classified as equity is not remeasured at all.

citation.ref: Paragraphs 37, 39 and 58

keywords: acquisition-date fair value of contingent consideration

points.text: On the finance side the exchange ratio only settles how a gain is divided, not whether there is one. There are gains only if the combined value exceeds the sum of the two standalone values, and that excess is the synergy; the net gain to the acquirer is the value of synergy minus the premium paid over the target's market value. A ratio generous enough to hand the whole of the synergy to Neelkanth's shareholders leaves Vasudha nothing, however defensible the weights on earnings, market price and book value are.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 Advanced Financial Management
citation.ref: Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring — gains from mergers or synergy

points.text: The valuer is a management's expert, so the auditor cannot simply attach the report. Having regard to the significance of that expert's work for his purposes he must evaluate the competence, capabilities and objectivity of that expert, obtain an understanding of the work of that expert, and evaluate the appropriateness of that expert's work as audit evidence for the relevant assertion, including whether the assumptions and methods used are generally accepted in that field and appropriate for financial reporting purposes.

citation.ref: Requirement on information prepared using the work of a management's expert

written.scenario: Aarohan Robotics Private Limited manufactures robotic machinery. For the year ended 31st March 2025 its turnover is ₹120 crore, its borrowings from banks ₹35 crore, its paid-up share capital ₹20 crore and its profit before tax ₹15 crore. M/s Gaur and Associates are the statutory auditors and CA Gaurav is the engagement partner. Substantive procedures show a sharp rise in sales in the last quarter, of which ₹8 crore is a single new customer, TechSynergy Solutions Private Limited, incorporated on 1st October 2024. Payment for those sales was received on 5th April 2025, days before the audit began. An audit assistant finds that one of TechSynergy's directors is the husband of the daughter of Aarohan's Chief Financial Officer. The CFO calls it a coincidence, says the sales were at arm's length, points out that the money has been received, and refuses to disclose the relationship, saying it is not a related party transaction under the applicable financial reporting framework. No resolution was passed before the contract with TechSynergy was entered into. Separately, CA Gaurav learns that his father holds 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each in AutoBots Limited, a subsidiary of Aarohan whose paid-up capital is ₹5 crore. Management presses for an unmodified opinion, saying a modification would put a funding deal at risk.
written.question: Advise CA Gaurav on whether the framework makes TechSynergy a related party, on what the Standards on Auditing require of him once the relationship comes to light, on the consequences under the Companies Act, 2013 of the missing resolution and of his father's shareholding, and on the opinion he should express.

points.text: Close members of the family of a person are those family members who may be expected to influence, or be influenced by, that person in their dealings with the entity, and the list that follows — children, spouse, brother, sister, father and mother, the children of the spouse, and dependants — is inclusive and not a closed list. The Chief Financial Officer is a member of the key management personnel and so a related party himself, and the question on these facts is whether his daughter and her husband are people who may be expected to influence or be influenced by him. The relationship cannot be dismissed as coincidence merely because a son-in-law is not named in the list.

citation.ref: Definitions of close members of the family of a person and of key management personnel

points.text: A large sale in the last quarter to a company incorporated during the year, settled only after the year end, and connected to an officer of the entity, is a significant unusual transaction. The auditor must treat it as indicative of a significant risk of material misstatement and weigh the implications for the audit, including the reliability of management's representations. The money having been received removes the credit risk and not the risk of fraudulent financial reporting, which is the risk in question.

citation.source: SA 240, The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud in an Audit of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Professional scepticism and significant unusual transactions

points.text: On a previously unidentified related party the auditor must determine whether the underlying circumstances confirm the existence of the relationship, communicate the information within the engagement team, request management to identify all transactions with the newly identified related party, perform substantive procedures on those transactions, and reconsider the risk that other related parties remain undisclosed. Where the non-disclosure by management appears intentional he must evaluate the implications for the audit as a whole.

citation.ref: Requirements on identification of previously unidentified or undisclosed related party transactions

points.text: For a significant related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business the auditor must inspect the underlying contracts, evaluate the business rationale of the transaction and whether its terms are consistent with management's explanations, and obtain audit evidence that the transaction has been appropriately authorised and approved. Here no resolution was passed before the contract was made, so the approval the Companies Act, 2013 requires for a related party contract is simply absent.

citation.source: SA 550, Related Parties, read with the Companies Act, 2013
citation.ref: Significant related party transactions outside the entity's normal course of business, read with section 188

points.text: A father is a relative. An auditor is disqualified where he or his relative holds any security or interest in the company, its subsidiary, its holding company or its associate company, the proviso permitting a relative to hold securities of face value not exceeding ₹1,00,000. The father's holding in the subsidiary has a face value of ₹10,00,000, so CA Gaurav is disqualified from being the auditor of Aarohan, and continuing while disqualified is itself professional misconduct.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(d)(i) with its proviso, read with Clause (9) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

points.text: Taken together — an ₹8 crore revenue transaction whose disclosure management refuses, against a profit before tax of ₹15 crore, and the doubt this casts on management's integrity — the misstatements are both material and pervasive, because their effects are not confined to specific elements, accounts or items of the financial statements. That calls for an adverse opinion rather than a qualified one, and the funding deal is not a matter the auditor may weigh at all.

citation.source: SA 705 (Revised), Modifications to the Opinion in the Independent Auditor's Report
citation.ref: Qualified opinion, adverse opinion and the meaning of pervasive

written.scenario: Arvind Edibles Limited is a listed company manufacturing edible oils, with a net worth of ₹500 crore, turnover of ₹1,000 crore and net profit of ₹5 crore in the immediately preceding financial year. It has constituted a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board, which has recommended a policy and the amount of expenditure. For the year under audit ₹20 lakh remains unspent in respect of projects that are not ongoing projects, and a further ₹12 lakh remains unspent on one ongoing project. During the audit CA Harsh learns that the Enforcement Directorate has issued show-cause notices to the company for several non-compliances under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, and that regulatory action may follow. The Board has not mentioned the notices in its report because the outcome is uncertain, and nothing about them appears anywhere in the financial statements. CA Harsh considers the matter relevant to users' understanding, but does not consider that it requires him to modify his opinion, and the matter has not been determined to be a key audit matter.
written.question: State what CA Harsh must report on each of the two unspent amounts, how the show-cause notices should have been dealt with in the financial statements, and where and on what conditions he may bring the notices to the reader's attention in his report.

points.text: In respect of other than ongoing projects the auditor must state whether the company has transferred the unspent amount to a Fund specified in Schedule VII to the Companies Act within a period of six months of the expiry of the financial year, in compliance with the second proviso to sub-section (5) of section 135. The ₹20 lakh falls under this clause.

citation.ref: Paragraph 3(xx)(a), read with the second proviso to section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013

keywords: six months of the expiry of the financial year

points.text: The ₹12 lakh unspent on an ongoing project falls under a separate clause: the auditor states whether any amount remaining unspent under sub-section (5) of section 135 pursuant to any ongoing project has been transferred to a special account in compliance with sub-section (6) of section 135. The two amounts therefore travel to two different places and are reported separately, not netted.

citation.ref: Paragraph 3(xx)(b), read with section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013

points.text: The show-cause notices are a possible obligation arising from past events whose existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of uncertain future events not wholly within the control of the company. That is a contingent liability rather than a provision, and a contingent liability is disclosed unless the possibility of an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits is remote. Nothing on these facts makes an outflow remote, so the uncertainty of the outcome is the reason to disclose and not a reason to stay silent.

citation.source: Ind AS 37, Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
citation.ref: Definition of a contingent liability and the requirement to disclose one

points.text: Because the matter is nowhere in the financial statements it cannot go in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, which by definition refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements and is of such importance that it is fundamental to users' understanding of them. It belongs in an Other Matter paragraph, which refers to a matter other than those presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the auditor's report.

citation.source: SA 706 (Revised), Emphasis of Matter Paragraphs and Other Matter Paragraphs in the Independent Auditor's Report
citation.ref: Definitions of an Emphasis of Matter paragraph and an Other Matter paragraph

keywords: other than those presented or disclosed

points.text: The paragraph is available only on conditions, and both are met here: it must not be prohibited by law or regulation, and where SA 701 applies the matter must not have been determined to be a key audit matter. Had the auditor concluded that the omission required him to modify the opinion, no additional paragraph would have cured it.

citation.source: SA 706 (Revised), Emphasis of Matter Paragraphs and Other Matter Paragraphs in the Independent Auditor's Report
citation.ref: Conditions for including an Other Matter paragraph

points.text: A second reporting duty runs alongside. Under the rules prescribing other matters to be included in the auditor's report, the auditor gives his views and comments on whether the company has disclosed the impact, if any, of pending litigations on its financial position in its financial statements, so the regulatory proceedings reach the reader by that route as well.

citation.ref: Rule 11(1), read with section 143(3)(j) of the Companies Act, 2013

written.scenario: Purvai Castings Private Limited has been hit by an economic downturn and by operational inefficiencies. Its cash flow statements show recurring negative cash flows, its interim financial statements show a sharp decline in profitability, it has defaulted on loan covenants, and ongoing litigation could bring substantial liabilities. Management says it will restructure the debt, secure additional funding from related parties and cut operating costs, but has produced no formal documentation of any of this. The auditors have identified events and conditions casting significant doubt on the entity's ability to continue as a going concern. The engagement team proposes to proceed as follows. (i) As long as management provides a representation letter stating its plans to address the financing difficulties, the auditor is not bound by the terms of the breached loan agreements. (ii) Confirm the existence, legality and enforceability of arrangements to provide financial support, from related parties and third parties, but treat the assessment of the financial ability of those parties to provide the promised support as immaterial. (iii) Evaluate the assumptions underlying the cash flow, profit and other forecasts, considering historical accuracy and current market conditions. (iv) Consider whether facts and information have become available since the date of management's initial assessment that could affect the going concern conclusion. (v) Review the minutes of meetings of shareholders, of those charged with governance and of the relevant committees for references to financial difficulties and to plans for mitigating action. (vi) If management has not yet performed an assessment, treat the entity as not a going concern and issue a modified opinion without further evidence.
written.question: State the basis on which the financial statements are to be prepared and the period management's assessment must cover, identify which of the six proposed positions are wrong and say why in each case, and state what the auditor must report under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 about the company's ability to meet its liabilities.

points.text: Financial statements are prepared on a going concern basis unless management either intends to liquidate the entity or to cease trading, or has no realistic alternative but to do so. Management must assess the entity's ability to continue as a going concern when preparing the financial statements, and that assessment must cover at least twelve months from the end of the reporting period. Twelve months is a minimum and not a ceiling: an entity could not use the going concern basis while intending to cease operations eighteen months out.

citation.source: Ind AS 1, Presentation of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Going concern

keywords: at least twelve months from the end of the reporting period

points.text: Several of the listed indicators are present on these facts: negative operating cash flows indicated by historical or prospective financial statements, adverse key financial ratios, and inability to comply with the terms of loan agreements. The list is neither all-inclusive nor does the existence of one or more of the items always signify that a material uncertainty exists, so their presence begins the inquiry rather than settling it.

citation.source: Ind AS 1, Presentation of Financial Statements
citation.ref: Examples of events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the ability to continue as a going concern

keywords: inability to comply with the terms of loan agreements

points.text: Four of the six proposed positions are wrong. Position (i) is wrong because a representation letter does not release the auditor from the terms of the breached loan agreements. Position (ii) is wrong because the financial ability of the party promising support cannot be treated as immaterial; a promise from a party unable to keep it is worth nothing. Position (iv) is wrong as a proposal to treat the step as optional, since considering facts arising since management's initial assessment is required. Position (vi) is wrong because where management has not yet performed an assessment the auditor requests one, rather than concluding to a modified opinion without evidence.

citation.ref: Additional audit procedures when events or conditions casting significant doubt are identified

keywords: management has not yet performed an assessment

points.text: The two positions that stand are (iii) and (v): evaluating the assumptions underlying the cash flow, profit and other forecasts against their historical accuracy and current market conditions, and reviewing the minutes of meetings of shareholders, of those charged with governance and of the relevant committees for references to financial difficulties and to plans for mitigating action. Both go to evidence the auditor can test rather than to assurances he is asked to accept.

citation.ref: Evaluation of management's plans and of cash flow forecasts

points.text: Under the Order the auditor states, on the basis of the financial ratios, ageing and expected dates of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities, other information accompanying the financial statements, and his knowledge of the Board and of management plans, whether he is of the opinion that no material uncertainty exists as on the date of the audit report that the company is capable of meeting its liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet as and when they fall due within a period of one year from the balance sheet date.

citation.ref: Paragraph 3(xix)

keywords: ageing and expected dates of realisation
within a period of one year from the balance sheet date

written.scenario: Setu Infotech Limited, a public company reporting under Ind AS, acquired a business two years ago and allocated goodwill of ₹60 crore to its Analytics cash-generating unit. The company's stated practice is to test that unit for impairment only when its own managers raise a concern, and no test was carried out in 20X1-20X2 even though the unit's largest customer had left during that year. In 20X2-20X3 the unit is tested. Its carrying amount including goodwill is ₹180 crore, made up of goodwill ₹60 crore, a building ₹40 crore, plant ₹60 crore and an intangible ₹20 crore. Fair value less costs of disposal for the unit is ₹140 crore and value in use, on management's own forecast, is ₹150 crore. The building's own fair value less costs of disposal is ₹38 crore. One comparative year, 20X1-20X2, is presented. Management proposes to write the goodwill down this year and to write it back when the unit recovers. The company is not a small company and its turnover is well above ₹50 crore.
written.question: State whether the unit had to be tested in 20X1-20X2 and why, compute the impairment loss for 20X2-20X3 and allocate it, say whether the write-back management proposes is open to it, state how the omission in the earlier year is corrected, and state what the auditor must report on internal financial controls.

points.text: Goodwill acquired in a business combination must be tested for impairment at least annually, irrespective of whether there is any indication that it may be impaired, and again whenever there is an indication that the unit may be impaired. Testing only when a manager raises a concern is not a practice the standard permits, so the unit had to be tested in 20X1-20X2 as well, and the loss of its largest customer was in any case an indication in its own right.

citation.ref: Requirement for annual review and testing of a cash-generating unit to which goodwill has been allocated

keywords: irrespective of whether there is any indication

points.text: Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, so it is ₹150 crore and not ₹140 crore. A unit is impaired when its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount, and ₹180 crore exceeds ₹150 crore, so an impairment loss of ₹30 crore is recognised for the unit.

citation.ref: Definition of recoverable amount and recognition of an impairment loss for a cash-generating unit

keywords: higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use

points.text: The loss is allocated first to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill allocated to the unit, and then to the other assets of the unit pro rata on the basis of the carrying amount of each asset in the unit. Goodwill of ₹60 crore absorbs the whole ₹30 crore, so no other asset is touched. Had the loss been larger, no individual asset could have been reduced below the highest of its fair value less costs of disposal, its value in use and zero, which is why the building could not have gone below ₹38 crore, and the amount so restricted would have been reallocated pro rata to the rest.

citation.ref: Allocation of an impairment loss to the assets of a cash-generating unit

keywords: first to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill

points.text: An impairment loss recognised for goodwill shall not be reversed in a subsequent period. Management's plan to write the goodwill back when the Analytics unit recovers is therefore not open to it, whatever the unit later earns.

citation.ref: Prohibition on reversal of an impairment loss recognised for goodwill

keywords: shall not be reversed in a subsequent period

points.text: The failure to test in 20X1-20X2 is a prior period error, being an omission arising from a failure to use reliable information that was available when those financial statements were approved for issue and could reasonably have been expected to be taken into account. Unless impracticable, a material prior period error is corrected retrospectively in the first set of financial statements approved for issue after its discovery, by restating the comparative amounts for the prior period in which the error occurred.

citation.source: Ind AS 8, Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors
citation.ref: Definition of prior period errors and their correction

points.text: The auditor must state in his report whether the company has adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and the operating effectiveness of such controls. A control meant to run an annual impairment test which did not run for a whole year is a deficiency to be weighed under that clause, and the exemption from it is available only to certain private companies below the prescribed turnover and borrowing limits, which this company is not.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(i)

keywords: adequate internal financial controls with reference to financial statements

written.scenario: Dhruv Alloys Limited is a listed company with an Audit Committee constituted under section 177 of the Companies Act, 2013. During the audit for the year ended 31st March 2025 the engagement partner, CA Meera, establishes two things. First, on 5th June 2025 she has reason to believe that a purchase manager routed ₹1.8 crore of purchases during the year through a supplier he controls, at inflated rates. Second, on 8th June 2025 she has reason to believe that a storekeeper took ₹6 lakh of scrap sale proceeds in cash and kept them. Management asks her to hold both matters and set them out in a single letter when the audit is finished, arguing that the amounts are small against the company's size and that early reporting would be premature while its own inquiry is running.
written.question: For each of the two matters state to whom CA Meera must report, within what time, in what form, and what the company must then do. State what she must say in her report under the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020, and the consequence to her of not complying.

points.text: The ₹1.8 crore matter involves an amount of ₹1 crore or above and is a fraud against the company by its officers or employees, so it goes to the Central Government. The auditor reports the matter to the Board or the Audit Committee immediately but not later than 2 days of his knowledge of the fraud, seeking their reply or observations within 45 days; on receipt of the reply he forwards his report, the reply or observations, and his comments on them to the Central Government within 15 days from the date of receipt.

citation.source: Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014
citation.ref: Section 143(12) and Rule 13(1)

keywords: not later than 2 days of his knowledge

points.text: If no reply or observations reach her within the stipulated period of 45 days she does not wait. She forwards her report to the Central Government along with a note containing the details of the report earlier forwarded to the Board or the Audit Committee for which she has received no reply.

citation.ref: Rule 13(1), manner of reporting to the Central Government

points.text: The report is in the form of a statement in Form ADT-4, sent to the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs in a sealed cover by Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due or by Speed Post followed by an e-mail in confirmation, on the auditor's letterhead carrying her postal address, e-mail address and contact number, signed with her seal and indicating her membership number.

citation.ref: Rule 13, manner of reporting to the Central Government

points.text: The ₹6 lakh matter is below ₹1 crore, so it does not go to the Central Government at all. She reports it to the Audit Committee constituted under section 177 immediately but not later than 2 days of her knowledge of the fraud, specifying the nature of the fraud with a description, the approximate amount involved and the parties involved. The company must then disclose in the Board's Report the nature of the fraud with description, the approximate amount involved, the parties involved if remedial action has not been taken, and the remedial actions taken.

citation.source: Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014
citation.ref: Section 143(12) and Rules 13(3) and 13(4)

points.text: Neither route waits for the end of the audit, so management's request cannot be met. Separately, under the Order the auditor states whether any fraud by the company or any fraud on the company has been noticed or reported during the year and, if so, the nature and the amount involved.

citation.ref: Paragraph 3(xi)

keywords: any fraud by the company or any fraud on the company
the nature and the amount involved

points.text: Reporting done in good faith is protected: no duty to which the auditor is subject is regarded as having been contravened by reason of her so reporting. Failure to comply attracts a penalty of five lakh rupees in the case of a listed company and one lakh rupees in any other case, and the same obligation applies mutatis mutandis to the cost auditor and the secretarial auditor in the performance of their duties.

citation.ref: Section 143(13) and the penalty for non-compliance with section 143(12), read with sections 148 and 204

written.scenario: Parivar Holdings Limited has a wholly-owned subsidiary, a 60 per cent subsidiary audited by another firm, and a 30 per cent associate. During 20X1-20X2 it acquired 51 per cent of Kshitij Limited intending to sell it on, and in 20X2-20X3 it sold 20 per cent of that holding. It consolidated Kshitij in neither year, saying that its control was temporary throughout. Within the group there are management fees charged by the parent to the subsidiaries, unrealised profit on goods transferred between two subsidiaries, and intra-group loans. The 60 per cent subsidiary follows a depreciation policy different from the parent's, and its component auditor has expressed a qualified opinion on its standalone financial statements. The auditor of Parivar's consolidated financial statements is planning materiality and deciding what to obtain from the component auditors.
written.question: Advise on whether Kshitij had to be consolidated and for which periods, on the statutory obligation to consolidate and what is attached to the financial statements, on the classification of the group adjustments, on how materiality is set and what is obtained from the component auditor, and on what the Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 requires in the report on the consolidated financial statements.

points.text: Consolidation of an investee begins from the date the investor obtains control of the investee and ceases when the investor loses control of the investee. There is no exemption for temporary control, or for operation under severe long-term funds transfer restrictions, so an intention to sell the holding on is not a ground for leaving Kshitij out. It had to be consolidated from the date control was obtained in 20X1-20X2 and until control was lost.

citation.ref: Paragraph 20, as applied in the ICAI Study Material on Group Audits

keywords: begins from the date the investor obtains control
ceases when the investor loses control

points.text: Where a company has one or more subsidiaries, including an associate company and a joint venture, it shall, in addition to its own financial statements, prepare consolidated financial statements of the company and of all the subsidiaries in the same form and manner as that of its own. The provisions applicable to the preparation, adoption and audit of a holding company's financial statements apply mutatis mutandis to the consolidated financial statements, and a separate statement containing the salient features of each subsidiary's financial statement is attached in Form AOC-1.

citation.ref: Sections 129(3) and 129(4), read with the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014

keywords: including an associate company and a joint venture

points.text: Determination of goodwill or capital reserve, and determination of the amount of equity attributable to non-controlling interests, are permanent consolidation adjustments. They are made on the first occasion and again on any subsequent occasion on which the shareholding in a consolidated entity changes, which the sale of 20 per cent of Kshitij is, and the auditor must pay particular attention to the pre-acquisition reserves and to how they have been split between the parent and the non-controlling interests.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Group Audits — permanent consolidation adjustments

points.text: The management fees, the unrealised intra-group profit on assets transferred between the subsidiaries, the deferred tax to be recorded on that elimination in accordance with Ind AS 12, the intra-group indebtedness, the harmonising of the differing depreciation policies, and the adjustments for recognised subsequent events occurring between the balance sheet date and the date of the auditor's report on the consolidated financial statements are all current period consolidation adjustments.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Group Audits — current period consolidation adjustments

points.text: Materiality for the consolidated financial statements is computed for the group as a whole and used to assess the appropriateness of both the permanent and the current period consolidation adjustments, and to decide whether further components should be scoped in. The principal auditor also computes materiality for each component and communicates it to the component auditor where he believes that is needed for a true and fair view on the consolidated statements, and obtains confirmations from component auditors on matters such as independence and the code of ethics. In weighing the component auditor's qualified opinion he must comply with the requirements on using the work of another auditor.

citation.source: SA 600, Using the Work of Another Auditor
citation.ref: Materiality in the audit of consolidated financial statements, as set out in the ICAI Study Material on Group Audits

points.text: The Order does not apply to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements except clause (xxi) of paragraph 3, under which the auditor states whether there have been any qualifications or adverse remarks by the respective auditors in the CARO reports of the companies included in the consolidated financial statements and, if so, gives the details of those companies and the paragraph numbers concerned.

citation.ref: Applicability to consolidated financial statements and paragraph 3(xxi)

written.scenario: Shreyas Limited has agreed, subject to confirmation, to buy Tarang Foods Limited for ₹210 crore, a price arrived at from Tarang's net worth and the trend of its profitability. It engages M/s Nandita and Associates, Chartered Accountants, to carry out a financial due diligence review. Shreyas is not an audit client of the firm. The firm is offered a fee of one per cent of the price finally paid. The review finds the following. Tarang has received show-cause notices from the tax authorities which have not matured into demands and which are not shown as contingent liabilities. It has given letters of comfort to two banks. When it sold a division two years ago it agreed to take over and indemnify the liabilities and contingent liabilities of that division up to the date of transfer, and nothing about this appears in its books. Receivables of ₹9 crore are more than three years old. Investments are carried at cost although their realisable value is far lower, and an intangible is carried at ₹6 crore for a brand the company no longer uses.
written.question: Distinguish the exercise from an audit and state its objective, classify each of the findings, explain how the findings bear on the price Shreyas should pay, and advise the firm on whether the proposed fee arrangement is permissible.

points.text: Audit is an independent examination of financial information leading to an opinion on it, whereas due diligence is an examination of a potential investment to confirm all material facts before entering into the transaction. The objective of the exercise is to look specifically for any hidden liabilities or over-valued assets, and the net worth of the business has to be arrived at after taking into account the impact of the over-valuation and under-valuation of assets and liabilities.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — difference between due diligence and audit, and the objective of the review

points.text: The first three findings are hidden liabilities. A company may not show as contingent liabilities the show cause notices which have not matured into demands, and these may be material and important. Letters of comfort given to banks and financial institutions are not guarantees and so may not be disclosed in the balance sheet at all. Where a business has been sold with an agreement to take over and indemnify its liabilities and contingent liabilities prior to the date of transfer, that too may not be reflected in the books of account.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Due Diligence — hidden liabilities

points.text: The last three are over-valued assets. Uncollected or uncollectable receivables, investments carried at cost though realisable value is much lower, and intangible assets of no value are each named as such, and the accountant should pay particular attention to the valuation of intangible assets.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Due Diligence — over-valued assets

points.text: The price was set on net worth and the trend of profitability on the assumption that all contingent liabilities that may impact the future of the business have been recorded, and that assumption has failed on these facts. Restating net worth downwards lowers the standalone value of the target, which widens the premium implicit in the agreed ₹210 crore; since the net gain to the acquirer is the value of synergy minus the premium paid, the same synergy now buys Shreyas a smaller gain, and may buy it none.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 2 Advanced Financial Management and Paper 3 Advanced Auditing, Assurance and Professional Ethics
citation.ref: Gains from mergers or synergy, read with the objective of financial due diligence

points.text: A chartered accountant in practice is deemed guilty of professional misconduct if he charges or offers to charge, accepts or offers to accept, in respect of any professional employment, fees which are based on a percentage of profits or which are contingent upon the findings, or results, of such employment, except as permitted under regulations made under the Act. Regulation 192 sets out the permitted cases, and the Council has added non-assurance services to non-audit clients to that list. Since Shreyas is not an audit client of the firm, the answer turns on whether this engagement falls within that permitted class, and not on the bare fact that the fee is a percentage.

citation.ref: Clause (10) of Part I of the First Schedule, read with Regulation 192

written.scenario: M/s Vidhi and Company, a firm of twelve partners, audits Deep Limited for the year 2024-25, with CA Lata as engagement partner. Three misstatements are identified. A calculation error in the depreciation schedule of ₹1 lakh. Management's estimate of inventory valuation, which the auditor considers unreasonable and which overstates inventory by ₹5 lakh. An error of ₹60,000 found in a sample of sales invoices drawn from a population of ₹1 crore, from which the auditor's best estimate of the misstatement in the population is ₹6 lakh. CA Lata has set ₹75,000 as the amount below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial. She communicates the uncorrected misstatements to those charged with governance and asks for their correction; management corrects the inventory valuation only, saying the other two are immaterial. The same firm audits Crypto Limited, an unlisted public company which is neither covered under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018 nor referred to the Quality Review Board by NFRA, and Glitch Limited, a listed company, where a whistle-blower has complained that the firm failed to identify related parties and that 95 per cent of sales went to an unidentified related party.
written.question: Classify each of the three misstatements and say what follows for the ₹60,000 invoice error. State what the audit documentation must contain in respect of these misstatements and what it need not contain. State which body may review which of the two audits, and why.

points.text: A factual misstatement is one about which there is no doubt, so the ₹1 lakh depreciation calculation error is factual. A judgemental misstatement is a difference arising from the judgements of management concerning accounting estimates that the auditor considers unreasonable, or from the selection or application of accounting policies the auditor considers inappropriate, so the ₹5 lakh inventory overstatement is judgemental. A projected misstatement is the auditor's best estimate of misstatement in a population, involving the projection of misstatements identified in the audit sample to the whole population from which the sample was drawn, so the ₹6 lakh is projected.

citation.source: SA 450, Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
citation.ref: Factual, judgemental and projected misstatements

points.text: The ₹60,000 found in the sample is below the ₹75,000 the auditor fixed as clearly trivial, but that threshold is applied to a misstatement and not to the projection drawn from it. The ₹6 lakh projected to the population is far above the threshold, so the population error cannot be set aside on the ground that the individual invoice error was small.

citation.source: SA 450, Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
citation.ref: The amount below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial

points.text: The audit documentation shall include the amount below which misstatements would be regarded as clearly trivial, all misstatements accumulated during the audit and whether they have been corrected — which takes in the inventory misstatement even though management corrected it — and the auditor's conclusion as to whether uncorrected misstatements are material, individually or in aggregate, together with the basis for that conclusion.

citation.source: SA 450, Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
citation.ref: Documentation requirements

keywords: all misstatements accumulated during the audit

points.text: What the documentation need not contain is a justification for not communicating identified misstatements to those charged with governance. Communicating them and requesting their correction is itself a requirement, so there is no such decision to justify, and the auditor here did communicate them.

citation.source: SA 450, Evaluation of Misstatements Identified during the Audit
citation.ref: Communication with those charged with governance, and documentation

points.text: Overseeing the quality of audit services of listed companies falls within the purview of the National Financial Reporting Authority, so the Glitch Limited audit belongs to NFRA, which has begun its investigation under section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013. The Quality Review Board may review the quality of audit services provided by members of the Institute only in respect of entities other than those specified under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018 and those referred to it by NFRA. It may therefore review the Crypto Limited audit and not the Glitch Limited audit, and the two bodies do not have overlapping jurisdiction over a listed entity.

citation.ref: Section 132(4), read with Rule 3 of the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules, 2018

written.scenario: At the annual general meeting of Kalpavriksha Steels Limited held on 20th September 2025, CA Raja was appointed statutory auditor for the year 2025-26, but he declined the appointment. The Board of Directors then appointed CA Rani in his place, and she accepted. She did not write to the outgoing auditor before accepting, and did not ask the company whether the requirements governing her appointment had been complied with. The auditor who held office before all this had resigned in the previous year; he considered that there were professional reasons connected with the resignation that should be brought to the notice of the Board, wrote to the Board giving those reasons, and sent a copy of that communication to the Institute. The year 2024-25 was audited by him. On beginning work CA Rani finds that the closing inventory of 2024-25 was arrived at on a valuation policy different from the one the company now uses, and that the supporting records for part of it are missing.
written.question: Advise on the validity of CA Rani's appointment and on the position where no auditor is appointed at an annual general meeting, on whether she has committed professional misconduct, on what she was obliged to obtain before accepting, on what the Standards on Auditing require of her in respect of the opening balances, and on how she reports if the evidence is not available.

points.text: The Board may fill a casual vacancy in the office of auditor, but a person declining an appointment does not create a casual vacancy; it is deemed that no auditor was appointed at the annual general meeting. Where at any annual general meeting no auditor is appointed or re-appointed, the existing auditor shall continue to be the auditor of the company. The Board's appointment of CA Rani is therefore defective in law.

citation.ref: Sections 139(8) and 139(10)

keywords: no auditor is appointed or re-appointed

points.text: She is guilty on two counts. A member is deemed guilty of professional misconduct if he accepts a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him in writing. He is also deemed guilty if he accepts an appointment as auditor of a company without first ascertaining from it whether the requirements now contained in sections 139 and 140 of the Companies Act, 2013 in respect of such appointment have been duly complied with.

citation.ref: Clauses (8) and (9) of Part I of the First Schedule

keywords: previously held by another chartered accountant

points.text: The reason for the second obligation is practical and not formal. It is obligatory on the incoming auditor to satisfy himself that the appropriate procedure in the matter of his appointment has been duly complied with, so that no shareholder or retiring auditor may at a later date challenge the validity of that appointment — which is exactly the risk CA Rani has now taken on.

citation.ref: Clause (9) of Part I of the First Schedule, as explained in the ICAI Study Material on Professional Ethics

points.text: Where an auditor resigns and considers that there are professional reasons connected with the resignation which should be brought to the notice of the Board of Directors, he sends a written communication to the Board giving those reasons and a copy of it to the Institute. It is obligatory on the incoming auditor, before accepting appointment, to obtain a copy of such communication from the Board of Directors and to consider it. CA Rani did not, and the Ethical Standards Board reviews such cases and reports to the Council.

citation.source: Guidelines of the Ethical Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India on removal and resignation of auditors
citation.ref: Paragraph A of the guidelines, as set out in the ICAI Study Material on Professional Ethics

points.text: This is an initial audit engagement, because the financial statements for the prior period were audited by a predecessor auditor. She must read the most recent financial statements and the predecessor auditor's report, determine whether the prior period's closing balances have been correctly brought forward, determine whether the opening balances reflect appropriate accounting policies, obtain audit evidence as to whether the accounting policies are consistently applied and, where they have changed, whether the change is properly accounted for, presented and disclosed, and perform audit procedures on the opening balances themselves.

citation.source: SA 510, Initial Audit Engagements — Opening Balances
citation.ref: Audit procedures on opening balances and on the consistency of accounting policies

points.text: If she is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances, she expresses a qualified opinion or disclaims an opinion. If she concludes that the opening balances contain a misstatement which is not properly presented or disclosed, or that the accounting policies were not consistently applied in relation to the opening balances and the change was not properly accounted for, the opinion is qualified or adverse.

citation.source: SA 510, Initial Audit Engagements — Opening Balances
citation.ref: Audit conclusions and reporting on opening balances

keywords: qualified opinion or disclaims an opinion
